### Series Title Page

**The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age down to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, based on the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, and corrected with the utmost diligence; continuously illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the extensive editions published during the last three centuries, as well as by the works omitted from those editions; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or each author of some importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, and also with headings distinguishing the upper margins of the individual pages and indicating their subject matter; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by others possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: the first, of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the second, of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be ascertained which Fathers have commented on the individual texts of the several books of Scripture, and in what places of their works.**

**The most accurate edition, and easily to be preferred to all others, if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the extremely convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and above all this collection—single, methodical, and chronological—which brings together for the first time in our library six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, collected from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.**

**First Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

## The Complete Works of St. Eusebius Jerome, Presbyter of Stridon

After the revision of the monks of the Order of St. Benedict from the Congregation of St. Maur, and especially that of Jean Martianay of the same order, again corrected against Roman, Ambrosian, Veronese, and many other manuscripts, as well as against all French and foreign editions; enlarged by very many monuments previously altogether unpublished, and by other labors of the holy Doctor that had been published separately only; illustrated with innumerable notes, observations, and corrections through the study and labor of Vallarsi and Maffei, presbyters of Verona, assisted by other learned men in that same city.

The latest Paris edition, revised from the second edition by the Veronese editors themselves through their later labors, and so enriched by more recently discovered material that the present edition, by its greater extent alone, while leaving aside all other improvements, materially surpasses all preceding editions, even the Benedictine, by a third or one-third; prepared and finally revised by J. P. Migne, publisher of the Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

# The Complete Works of Jerome

## Preface

We have now reached that part of our edition in which the genre of Jerome’s writings is completed which, on account of the supreme dignity of the divine Scriptures that it treats, is certainly superior to all the others; but which, on account of the author’s extraordinary learning, excels to such a degree that, if—after nearly two years since I devoted myself entirely to his study—I may openly profess what I think, either the love of the task I undertook in adorning these Commentaries deceives me, or no one, since the human race began, has ever investigated more deeply the mysteries of sacred things, or explained them more brilliantly, drawing on the whole memory of antiquity and every kind of discipline.

If the interpretations of the Old Testament that we reviewed in the preceding volumes sustained such glory in that field, those that we now present from the New Testament, complete in every respect, possess, besides that distinction, this almost unique feature: each work was completed in a very short time—not, I mean, months, but days—and this entire volume, if one calculates everything together, was produced by scarcely four or five months of labor. Such was the abundance of learning that welled up from his mind—*a soul exalted above discourse* (*ψυχὴ ὑπερφρονέουσα λόγων*). In this regard it seems almost miraculous to me that, although he himself admits in the Prologue to another book on the Epistle to the Ephesians that he sometimes reached as many as a thousand verses in a single day, he could combine with such speed of dictation—one to which scarcely any secretaries could match one another in writing—such purity of expression and such abundance and judgment in his thoughts.

The works of the holy Father contained in this volume explain, although not all, the most distinguished portions of the New Testament: namely, Matthew’s Gospel; then selected chapters of Luke, rendered from Origen’s Greek into Latin in thirty-nine Homilies; and finally four of Paul’s Epistles, to the Galatians and Ephesians, to Titus and Philemon.

To explain what should be presented to the reader in advance about each work, especially the time of composition: the holy Father produced the four books of the Commentaries on Matthew, which occur first in the order of Scripture, in scarcely fifteen days, with Easter already approaching, when Eusebius of Cremona, about to sail suddenly from the East to Rome, had asked him to give him this work as a sort of traveling provision. Jerome had only just begun to recover from an illness of three months.

From these circumstances, which the author himself records in the Prologue to the first book, it can plainly be gathered to which year—or rather to which very brief portion of a year—the work belongs. That three-month illness, during which the days of Lent allowed him to breathe somewhat freely, is clearly the same one that he records in Letter 71 of our recension, to Lucinius: “I, held by a prolonged illness, scarcely began to breathe again during the days of Lent”; and much more fully in Letter 73, to Evangelus: “After a prolonged illness, I could scarcely be free from fever during the days of Lent, and, while preparing myself for another work, I spent the few remaining days in the exposition of Matthew.”

By definite arguments, drawn chiefly from the chronology of Jerome’s affairs, we have shown in the Chronological Notes to those letters that those three months must be reckoned from the beginning of the year 398, so to speak, or, if one prefers, from the preceding December. Thus the date of the work must be assigned to March of that year, when the holy Father had recovered somewhat from his illness and, with excessive eagerness, resumed the studies he had interrupted in order to dictate these Commentaries on Matthew. Easter, which he said was already approaching, fell that year on April 18.

This same conclusion may also be established from Eusebius’s arrival in Italy. Jerome testifies in Letter 74 of our recension, to Rufinus—not the Aquileian Rufinus, but the one commonly known as the Roman presbyter—that Eusebius was in Rome in the latter part of this very year. “I rejoice,” he says, “over the testimony of your holiness toward me and your love for the holy presbyter Eusebius; nor do I doubt that you publicly commend me.” The same fact is also clear from the Aquileian Rufinus’s journey to Rome. For in Book III of his Apology against the same man, section 24, Eusebius is said to have arrived a year after Rufinus had reached that place: “Paulinius and Eusebius departed a year after your voyage.”

There is no doubt that Rufinus had already been living in Rome under Siricius since the preceding year, 397, after returning from Palestine; the whole history of his actions confirms this. Therefore no one should be troubled by the passage in chapter 2 of Matthew, where the holy Father says that he had recently produced the prophet Hosea from the Hebrew, although it is established by our method of calculation that the work had been completed nearly six years earlier. For the word “recently,” both in Jerome and in other writers of his age, denotes an indefinite and vague period, so that it is entirely impossible to determine from it any fixed span of time or the reference that the author had in mind while writing.

I shall offer from these very Commentaries on Matthew an example of this ambiguous meaning that is certainly worthy of the reader’s attention. In commenting on chapter 12, verse 13, the holy Doctor says that he had “recently translated into Greek from the Hebrew language” the Gospel of the Nazarenes. At the very least, one would have to suppose that he was designating the sixth year before this one, since he mentions that same translation from the Hebrew in chapter 2 of the *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, which, by universal agreement, he composed in the year 392. But what shall we say when, in that very chapter of the *Catalogue*, he also uses the adverb “recently” to indicate the time of his translation? “The Gospel called according to the Hebrews,” he says, “was recently translated by me into Greek and Latin.” Here, too, if one wishes to designate years, one will calculate not six years but twelve at the earlier point. However one twists the matter, one will never arrive at a point where a certain reckoning of time can be established from that indication.

Having set aside these matters, which moved the distinguished Tillemont quite without justification, it is now useful to refute in passing the author of the *Dissertation on the Foundations of the Christian Religion*. He believed that Jerome held the view that Matthew 27:9, concerning the thirty pieces of silver, “the price of the one who was appraised,” cited from an apocryphal book of Jeremiah that a Hebrew of the Nazarene sect had offered him.

This was not Jerome’s intention. Jerome says that he had indeed seen a book falsely attributed to Jeremiah in which the words cited by Matthew were found literally; but, as far as his own view is concerned, he was so far from thinking that they had been taken from that apocryphal work that he rather maintained that they were drawn from the prophet Zechariah.

“I recently read,” he says, “in a certain Hebrew volume, which a Hebrew of the Nazarene sect offered me, an APOCRYPHAL BOOK OF JEREMIAH, in which I found written word for word the following: ‘And they took thirty pieces of silver, the price of the one who was appraised, whom they appraised among the children of Israel, etc.’ Nevertheless, it seems to me that the testimony was rather taken from Zechariah: in the customary manner of the Evangelists and Apostles, who, passing over the order of the words, bring forward only the sense from the Old Testament as an example.”

Origen held precisely the same view. I scarcely doubt that Jerome borrowed this, as he did much else in this Commentary, from Origen. Indeed, when we revised the work, we devoted no less effort to correcting and refining Jerome’s text than to distinguishing and presenting the Origenian fragments that he translated into his own work.

We append to the sequence of the Scriptures thirty-nine Homilies on Luke, which Jerome long ago translated from the Greek of the celebrated Origen into Latin, and which we now join for the first time to the fullest collection of his works. We have brought them here from Genebrard’s edition, making them more complete by restoring a considerable number of passages.

As for their Greek exemplar, it was long believed to have perished through the injustice of time; but we have recently heard from the latest editor of Origen’s works that it has been found, at least in considerable part. These Homilies, which are marked as having been delivered on Sundays and which our translator calls a youthful exercise, are indeed the work of one Adamantius, but they are not all of one and the same offspring. The final six, namely, do not continue the exposition of Luke that had been begun, nor do they follow directly upon the preceding thirty-three, which preserve the proper order; they seem to have been excerpted from another collection of Homilies.

The distinguished Huet likewise proves that a much larger collection of these Homilies once existed from the fact that, in volume 13, in his work on John, the author declares that he has explained in the Homilies on Luke *τὰ περὶ τῶν ἑκατὸν προβάτων*—“the matters concerning the hundred sheep.” Since nothing of this kind is found in the surviving thirty-nine, it is entirely reasonable to believe that other Homilies, which did not survive to our time and in which that Gospel passage was explained, were once composed by the author.

As for their Latin translator and the method of his translation, I do not know whether Rufinus maliciously or truthfully challenges the holy Doctor’s fidelity in rendering them and accuses him of having either added many things according to his own pleasure or subtracted them. His words are found in Book II of the *Invectives*, section 26:

“I followed what I had seen you do in the Homilies on the Gospel according to Luke: when you did not find correctly in the Greek what concerned the Son of God, you passed it over, as in the passage where it says, ‘My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior.’ You know that, whenever the subject was the soul, you did not pass over those things that are customarily said; rather, adding certain assertions from yourself, you wrote them even more clearly, as in the passage, ‘Behold, as the voice of your greeting came into my ears, the infant leaped in my womb.’ There, where you say that this was not the beginning of his substance, you added from your own words, ‘and of his nature.’”

And shortly afterward:

“But concerning the faith—that is, concerning the Trinity—when in certain places you found matters stated differently from what seemed right to you, you omitted them.”

Since the Greek archetype is lacking, it is not easy for us to investigate the matter more deeply and to judge it correctly and in due order, especially since the holy Father himself made no reply to his rival’s slander touching this specific charge.

Nevertheless, when Rufinus says that Jerome inserted certain things where the soul of John, leaping in his mother’s womb, was discussed—namely, “this was not the beginning of his substance,” and that he added from himself “and of his nature”—either this is the slander of a man pursuing hatred more than Vatinian, or, as I would rather suspect, those words, or rather the entire passage, were afterward removed from the Jerome manuscript. For there is no trace or vestige of the matter in all five Homilies from the seventh through the twelfth, although such a discussion could have occurred either from the stated Gospel text or as the occasion arose.

Yet the whole sequence of the discourse coheres so closely that even Origen himself, much less his translator, appears to have refrained from such a discussion. Nor can the statement be found in the other passages where the leaping of the Forerunner in the womb is praised in foreign contexts. Tillemont therefore finally began to doubt whether these were the very Homilies of Origen on Luke that Jerome translated and Rufinus attacked.

But there is no basis for that doubt. All the remaining evidence agrees in confirming both the authenticity of this translation and the circumstances of the work, as well as the monuments and testimonies of the ancients.

As for the time when the holy Father prepared this translation, I would assign it to the year 389 rather than, as is commonly held, to the preceding year. He himself seems to indicate this in the *Catalogue*, where, immediately after Didymus’s book *On the Holy Spirit*—which we likewise establish as having been translated into Latin in that year—he mentions this translation of the Homilies.

The sequence of the works immediately preceding it suggests the same conclusion, especially the books *On Places* and *On Hebrew Names*, which we have assigned to the preceding year, 388. Finally, there is the testimony that he himself gives in the Prologue to this translation: “I set aside for a little while the books of the Hebrew Questions, so that, at the request of Paula and Eustochium, I might dictate this work—whatever it may be—not my own, but another’s.”

In this passage Tillemont is conspicuously mistaken when, for this very reason, he accuses Jerome of negligence in arranging his writings according to age, because, after several intervening books following the *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, Jerome counts these Homilies only afterward and not in their proper place.

But when Jerome says that he interrupted the *Hebrew Questions* for a little while in order to devote himself to translating these works from Adamantius, he did not, as Tillemont falsely thinks, mean the *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, which he had published long before. Rather, he meant simply the books of the *Hebrew Questions*—that is, those concerning the rest of Scripture—a work that he kept before him for a long time and perhaps even rejected out of weariness at the delay.

Tillemont ought to have noticed this, lest, as he is fond of doing, he unjustly accuse the most diligent of writers of negligence.

From here we proceed to the Commentaries on the four Epistles of Paul that the holy Father alone wrote and that we have undertaken to revise. Those who, from the time of Cassiodorus onward, believed that the whole Apostle had been illustrated by Jerome’s Commentaries were very far from the truth; hence Cassiodorus labored long and hard, but fruitlessly, to discover the rest.

I think that passage in the Prologue to the second book on the Epistle to the Ephesians misled learned men. There the holy Doctor says without qualification, “We are attempting to expound Paul’s Epistles,” and they understood this as referring to all of them, whereas he spoke only of those that he then had in hand.

The deception was furthered by a Commentary on all Paul’s Epistles, except that to the Hebrews, which was falsely attributed to Jerome in ancient books. Yet this work is so far from being Jerome’s that it belongs to his bitterest enemy, the wicked heresiarch Pelagius. To avoid the odium attached to his name, scribes substituted Jerome’s name; they also had an interest in making the merchandise more marketable.

The fraud has long since been detected, and the work has been relegated to the final volume among the spurious writings. We shall review it there in its proper place.

Jerome therefore devoted his efforts solely to explaining these four Epistles. He began writing with the one addressed to Philemon, which was last in order, in order to accommodate Paula and Eustochium. As he himself reports in the first words of the Commentary, they had insisted that, although he was refusing to write on Paul’s Epistles, he should at least discuss the shortest one—the one that seemed last both in the number of its verses and in its sense and order.

He completed the brief little book in a single short sitting, as we may reasonably believe, and immediately proceeded to explain the Epistle addressed to the Galatians. “Only a very few days have passed,” he himself says in the Prologue, “since I interpreted Paul’s Epistle to Philemon and moved on to the Galatians.”

He contained this work in three books. Although everything the author explains in them is useful and particularly noteworthy, an important passage must especially be pointed out: in the commentary on chapter 1, verse 4, he discusses the variant meaning and wording of the text. By restoring this passage, which had hitherto been monstrously dislocated, we have finally brought to light the true and very elegant sense of the holy Doctor and established, against the calumnies of his adversaries, his profound mastery of the Hebrew letters—a mastery demonstrated in entire books.

Again, after a few days, he turned from that Commentary to expound the Epistle addressed to the Ephesians, as he testifies in the Preface. In this work he appears to have pleased himself so greatly that he wished his fidelity—which his adversaries accused of favoring Origen—to be judged at some later time by reference to it.

Finally, he explained the Epistle addressed to Titus in a short Commentary soon afterward. He himself indicates the time in the commentary on the eleventh verse of the first chapter, where he says: “A few months ago I dictated three volumes in the exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians.”

From the entire sequence of these Expositions we infer that they all belong to the same year, and we have discovered, by calculating the time required for each, that they occupied only a few months. Which year that was can easily be understood from the place they occupy in the *Catalogue*, where they immediately precede the *Questions on Genesis*.

The conclusion is confirmed still more strongly by the testimony found in chapter 5 of the Epistle to the Ephesians, where at that very time he declares that he was undertaking the work of the *Hebrew Questions*. If, therefore, we have assigned the *Hebrew Questions on Genesis* correctly to the year 388 and the preceding works to 387, there can be no doubt.

The volume is completed by an Appendix containing the *Brief Summary of the Psalter* and other Treatises on the Psalms falsely attributed to Jerome. [Note: In the appendix to our edition the Commentary on Job holds first place; we transferred it there for the reasons set out at the beginning of that commentary.] We have spoken of these sufficiently and at length in the special Admonition prefixed to them.

Only one matter remains: since it is no small honor for the name of Jerome to have pleased princes, you should know that our edition owes a great deal to the illustrious bishop of our Church, Jo. Bragadenus. He long ago received it with the greatest kindness and supported it by his humane patronage; finally, he also caused us to hope for a reward.

I say this not so much because I wish a public monument of his favor to stand, more enduring than bronze, as because I wish the learned world to offer every good wish for his most generous devotion to letters and to hope for ever greater growth in knowledge and piety.

# St. Eusebius Jerome, Presbyter of Stridon

## Four Books of Commentaries on the Gospel of Matthew, Addressed to Eusebius

[Note: Six manuscript codices assisted in the revision of this Commentary on Matthew. One, of very large format but of good quality, came from the Library of St. Cross in Jerusalem at Rome. Three were designated Vatican-Palatine, numbers 176, 177, and 181; the first two are notable for their antiquity and correction. There was also another Palatine manuscript, number 5, which we consulted only for passages that had been corrupted. Finally, there was one Vatican manuscript, formerly belonging to Queen Christina of Sweden, number 40, which we found especially rich in good readings.]

## Prologue

### 1–2

There were many who wrote Gospels, as the evangelist Luke also testifies when he says: “Since many have undertaken to arrange an account of the events that have been fulfilled among us, just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word delivered them to us.” [Note: The codex of St. Cross reads: “and were ministers of the word.”] And the writings that have survived down to the present likewise make this clear. These works, published by different authors, became the beginnings of different heresies.

[Note: This pseudo-Gospel was widely used by the Encratites, Julius Cassianus, the Valentinians, and the Sabellians. Clement of Alexandria cites and explains certain passages from it in *Stromata* III. Origen also mentions it in Homily 1 on Luke, and Epiphanius in *Heresies* 62, to omit more recent writers. St. Ambrose’s Prologue to Luke should nevertheless be compared, for he also mentions the Gospel according to Thomas. This appears to be the same work that others call the Gospel of the Infancy of the Savior—for example Irenaeus, Epiphanius, Athanasius, Eusebius, Chrysostom, Cyril, and many others—and it still exists in Arabic; in a Greek fragment, however, it is ascribed to the apostle Thomas. Ambrose, in the place cited, also knows another Gospel according to Matthias, although he may seem to have borrowed the testimony from Origen. The Gospel of Bartholomew is also mentioned by other Fathers: by Gelasius in his decree on apocryphal books and by Bede in his Commentary on Luke. Learned men, however, reasonably suspect that what was regarded as the Gospel of Bartholomew was the Hebrew Gospel of Matthew, which Bartholomew is said to have carried to India and Pantaenus to have found there, according to Eusebius, *History* V.10, and Nicephorus IV.32. Finally, Ambrose, Theophylact, and others knew the Gospel of the Twelve Apostles. When our Jerome mentions it again at the beginning of Dialogue 3 against the Pelagians, he calls “according to the Apostles” that very Gospel commonly called “according to the Hebrews,” which the Nazarenes then used. Recall what we formerly observed on this passage.]

Such is the work according to the Egyptians, and that according to Thomas, Matthias, and Bartholomew, and also that according to the Twelve Apostles, and those of Basilides and Apelles, together with the others whose enumeration would be excessively long.

[Note: Origen and Ambrose, in their works on Luke, mention the Gospel of Basilides. Eusebius, *History* IV.7, reports from St. Irenaeus that Basilides wrote twenty-four books on the Gospel, to which Irenaeus opposed a most vigorous refutation. Bede also knows the Gospel of Apelles at the beginning of his Commentary on Luke. Yet Apelles seems not to have been the author of a new Gospel, but rather a corrupter and interpolator of the old genuine ones; learned men infer this from Origen’s Letter to his dear friends at Alexandria.]

For the present it is necessary to say only this: there were certain people who, without the Spirit and grace of God, attempted to arrange a narrative rather than weave the truth of history. To them the prophetic saying may rightly be applied: “Woe to those who prophesy from their own heart, who walk after their own spirit, who say, ‘Thus says the Lord,’ when the Lord has not sent them” (Ezek. 13:3).

Concerning them the Savior also speaks in the Gospel of John: “All who came before me were thieves and robbers” (John 10:8)—those who came, not those who were sent. For he himself says: “They kept coming, although I had not sent them” (Jer. 14:14; 23:21). In those who come there is the presumption of rashness; in those who are sent, the obedience of service.

The Church, however, which was founded upon the Lord’s rock by his voice, which the king brought into his chamber (Song 1–2), and to which he stretched out his hand through the opening of a hidden descent (Song 5), resembling a doe and a young stag (Song 2:9), and pouring forth four rivers like Paradise (Gen. 2), possesses four corners and four rings. Through these it is carried like the Ark of the Covenant and the guardian of the Lord’s Law, upon immovable wooden poles (Exod. 25:10 ff.).

[Note: In the excellent codex of our monastery of St. Andrew near Avignon, the reading is “it is carried on movable wooden poles”; in another codex of our monastery, that of St. Remigius, we read, “it is carried on imperishable wooden poles.” This variant reading could have been correct on account of the poles of shittim wood, Exodus 25:13, if the following verse, 15, did not say, “They shall always remain in the rings; they shall never be removed from them.” Thus the error of the first manuscript is exposed. Jerome therefore called the poles immovable and the wood immovable. — Martianay.

Three of our manuscripts read “movable,” and two “imperishable,” with a second hand correcting the latter to “immovable.” Martianay rightly observed that “immovable” must be retained, on the basis of the verse in Exodus 25:15 to which the holy Doctor alludes, concerning the wood that would always remain in the rings and never be removed from them.]

First of all is Matthew, a publican surnamed Levi, who published the Gospel in Hebrew speech in Judaea, chiefly for the sake of those who had come to believe in Jesus from among the Jews and no longer observed the shadow of the Law, the truth of the Gospel having succeeded it.

[Col. 0018C] **Note.** The opinion of very learned men seems closer to the truth to us: namely, that the Gospel held to have been first written by Matthew was originally written by him in Greek. We have gathered arguments for this in chapter 3 of the *Catalogue*, which it is tedious to repeat here. Papias, according to Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* III.39, is regarded as the author of the contrary opinion, which Jerome also approves. Meanwhile, I would rather suppose that the holy Doctor drew this opinion, as he did many others in his Commentaries, from Origen. The words are almost identical with those in the Fragment of the first book of the *Commentary on Matthew*, which I am pleased to transcribe here:

[Col. 0018D] “First, the Gospel according to Matthew was written by the former publican and later apostle of Jesus Christ, who published it, composed in Hebrew characters, for those among the Jews who had believed. Second was the Gospel according to Mark, who recorded in writing what Peter had related to him, etc.”

The second was Mark, the interpreter of the apostle Peter and first bishop of the Alexandrian church. He himself did not see the Lord and Savior, but, according to the reliability of the events, related what he had heard his teacher proclaim rather than following their sequence.

The third was Luke, a physician, Syrian by birth and from Antioch—whose praise is contained in the Gospel—who was also a disciple of the apostle Paul and composed his volume in the regions of Achaia and Boeotia (II Cor. VIII), going back further for certain matters and, as he himself admits in his preface, describing what he had heard rather than what he had seen.

[Col. 0018B] **Note.** Most manuscripts prefer “Bithynia” to “Boeotia.” Many testimonies of the ancients, and above all the authority of the Syriac version, which reports that Luke’s Gospel was worked out in Egypt, or at Alexandria, oppose Jerome’s opinion concerning Achaia and Boeotia.

The last was John, the apostle and evangelist, whom Jesus loved most dearly. Reclining upon the Lord’s breast (John XIII and XXI), he drank from the purest streams of doctrine, and alone among them deserved to hear from the cross: “Behold your mother” (John XIX.27). When he was in Asia, and the seeds of the heretics Cerinthus, Ebion, and the others who deny that Christ came in the flesh were already sprouting—men whom he himself calls antichrists in his epistle (I John II.18), and whom the apostle Paul frequently attacks (Rom. III; II Cor. V)—he was compelled by nearly all the bishops of Asia at that time and by deputations from many churches to write more profoundly concerning the divinity of the Savior, and to burst forth, so to speak, toward the very Word of God, with a boldness not so much audacious as blessed in its success.

[Col. 0019C] **Note.** The printed editions read: “And Ecclesiastical history relates, etc.” In several manuscript codices, after the word “burst forth,” there follows: “as Ecclesiastical history relates, etc.” Others retain the reading that we have published. MART.

[Col. 0019D] In continuous sequence, two older Palatine manuscripts read: “burst forth, as Ecclesiastical history relates.” Others, as in the previously published books, read: “And Ecclesiastical, etc.”

And Ecclesiastical history relates that, when his brothers compelled him to write, he answered that he would do so if all of them, after a fast had been proclaimed, would pray to God together. When this had been completed, filled with revelation, he poured forth from heaven that preface: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; he was in the beginning with God” (John I).

These four Gospels, therefore, foretold long beforehand, are also demonstrated by the book of Ezekiel, in which the first vision is woven together as follows: “And in the midst was something resembling four living creatures; and their faces were the faces of a man, and the face of a lion, and the face of a calf, and the face of an eagle” (Ezek. I.5, 10).

The first face, that of a man, signifies Matthew, who began to write as though from a human being: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham” (Matt. I). The second signifies Mark, in whose Gospel the voice of the lion roaring in the wilderness is heard: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness [or: desert], prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight” (Mark I.3). The third is that of the calf, which foreshadows the evangelist Luke’s beginning with the priest Zechariah. The fourth is that of John the evangelist, who, taking up the eagle’s wings and hastening toward higher things, discusses the Word of God.

The rest of what follows advances in the same sense: “Their legs were straight, and their feet were winged; and wherever the spirit went, they went, and they did not turn back; and their backs were full of eyes, and sparks and lamps were darting about in their midst, and a wheel was within a wheel, and each of the four had four faces.”

Hence also John’s Apocalypse, after its exposition of the twenty-four elders who, holding harps and bowls, worshipped [or: worship] the Lamb of God, introduces lightning, thunder, and seven spirits moving about, and a sea of glass, and four living creatures full of eyes (Rev. IV and V), saying: “The first living creature was like a lion, the second like a calf, the third had the appearance of a man, and the fourth was like a flying eagle.” And shortly afterward: “They were full,” he says, “of eyes, and they had no rest day or night, saying: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, who was, and who is, and who is to come” (Rev. IV.7–8).

From all these things it is plainly shown that only four Gospels ought to be accepted, and that all the ravings of the apocrypha should be sung to the dead heretics rather than to the living churches.

[Col. 0019D] **Note.** One manuscript of Saint-Croix reads: “and all the poisons of the apocrypha to the dead, etc.” Eusebius, whom the holy Doctor addresses, is that celebrated Eusebius of Cremona, to whom he dedicated his Commentaries on Jeremiah and whom he praises frequently elsewhere.

I am sufficiently astonished, dearest Eusebius, that, since you are suddenly about to sail to Rome, you wished this little *sitarcia*, as it were, to be given to you by me, so that, while briefly explaining Matthew, I might compress the words and expand the meanings.

[Col. 0019D–0020C] **Note.** Our manuscripts have the less correct spelling *sistarchia* or *sistarcia*, which is nevertheless common in old books. In Greek it is called σιταρκία (*sitarkia*), and it means provisions; in Latin it is more often used for a basket in which foodstuffs are kept.

If you had remembered my reply, you would never have asked in a few days for a task requiring years. First, it is difficult to read all those who have written on the Gospels. Then it is much more difficult, after applying judgment, to select what is best.

[Col. 0020C] **Note.** Two manuscripts read, “I confess that I have read,” and shortly afterward prefer “the name of Adamantius” instead of “of Origen”; finally, they read *commaticum quoque* rather than *commaticumque*.

I confess that many years ago I read Origen’s twenty-five books on Matthew, as well as the same number of his Homilies, and his fragmentary method of interpretation; also the Commentaries of Theophilus, bishop of Antioch; and those of Hippolytus the martyr, Theodore of Heraclea, Apollinaris of Laodicea, and Didymus of Alexandria; and, among the Latins, those of Hilary, Victorinus, and Fortunatianus. Even if I were to glean only a little from them, something worthy of remembrance could be written.

[Col. 0020C–D] **Note.** In other manuscripts he is called Fortunatus; concerning him, see the *Book of Illustrious Men*, chapter 97. Shortly afterward, instead of *carperem*, which our manuscripts substitute, earlier copies read *caperem*.

But you compel me to dictate within two weeks, with Easter already approaching and the winds blowing: without considering when the shorthand writers will take things down, when the sheets will be written, when they will be corrected, and within what interval they will be arranged in a clean copy,

[Col. 0020D] **Note.** Two Palatine manuscripts add, “without paying the least attention.” The following words should also be referred here: what Jerome himself says at the end of Letter 73 to Evangelus concerning his poor health and this very Commentary on Matthew: “After a long illness,” he says, “I could scarcely go without fever for a few days during Lent; and, while I was preparing myself for another work, I spent the few days that remained on an exposition of Matthew. I returned to my interrupted studies with such eagerness that what benefited the exercise of my tongue harmed my bodily health.”

especially since you know that I have been so ill for three months that only now am I beginning to walk again, and that I cannot compensate for the magnitude of the labor with the shortness of the time.

Therefore, setting aside the authority of the ancients, whom I have been given neither the opportunity to read nor the ability to follow, I have briefly arranged the historical interpretation that you especially requested, and I have occasionally mingled with it flowers of spiritual understanding, reserving a complete work for the future.

[Col. 0020D–0021B] **Note.** Victorinus reads: “If life is granted me more generously,” that is, life which is not continually troubled by poor health; this reading is therefore preferable. Jerome survived this work by approximately twenty years, and Martianus was quite mistaken in noting that the holy Doctor did not live long enough to complete his Commentaries on Matthew, as he had hoped to do, nor wrote on the Song of Songs because prolonged illness and finally death excluded him from these works. For it is clear from the sequence of Jerome’s activities that he refrained from revising the former Commentary and beginning the latter for other reasons.

But if my life should be prolonged, or if, on your return, you fulfill your promises, I shall then strive to complete what remains. Indeed, having laid the foundations and partly built the walls, I shall place upon them a most beautiful roof, so that you may know the difference between the sudden boldness of dictation and the painstaking diligence of deliberate writing.

Certainly you know—and I would be ashamed to call you as a witness to my falsehood—that I dictated this little work with such speed that you might think I was more engaged in reading the works of others than in composing my own. Do not suppose that I say this from arrogance or confidence in my talent, but because I wish to show you how much influence you have over me: I have preferred to risk myself before learned men rather than refuse anything to you, who ask so earnestly.

Therefore I beg you: if my speech is less polished and the discourse does not proceed with its customary fluency, attribute this to haste, not to incompetence. And when you come to Rome, give copies to the virgin of Christ, Principia, who asked me to write on the Song of Songs. Excluded from that work by prolonged illness, I have deferred my hope to the future.

[Col. 0022A–B] **Note.** Refer here to the final words of Letter 65, addressed to the same Principia: “So that you who have understood part of the poem may, if life accompanies me, understand the whole Song of Songs.”

I bind you by this condition: if you withhold from her what has been written to you, she too must afterward lock away in her little cabinet what is later to be written for herself.

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 0021]

## Chapter I

### Verse 1

[Col. 0021B] “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ.”

In Isaiah we read: “Who shall recount his generation?” (Isa. LIII.8). Therefore, we must not think that the evangelist contradicts the prophet, so that what the prophet declared impossible to express the evangelist begins to narrate; for the former speaks of the generation of divinity, while the latter speaks of the incarnation. He began with what is human, so that through the human being we might begin to speak of God.

“The son of David, the son of Abraham.”

“Abraham begot Isaac. Isaac begot Jacob. Jacob begot Judah and his brothers.”

The order is reversed, but necessarily rearranged. For if he had placed Abraham first and David afterward, he would again have had to return to Abraham in order to weave together the sequence of the generation. He named only these men as fathers, omitting the others, because the promise concerning Christ was made only to them. To Abraham: “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII.18), and that seed is Christ. To David: “I shall set upon your throne one from the fruit of your womb” (Ps. CXXXI.11).

### Verse 3

“Judah begot Phares and Zarah by Tamar. Phares begot Esron. Esron begot Aram. Aram begot Aminadab. Aminadab begot Naasson.”

It should be noted that no holy women are included in the Savior’s genealogy, but rather women whom Scripture reproves, so that he who had come on account of sinners, being born from sinners, might wipe away the sins of all.

[Col. 0021D] **Note.** Rabbanus reads: “from sinful women.”

Hence Ruth the Moabite is also mentioned later, as is Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah.

### Verses 4 and following

[Col. 0022B] “Naasson begot Salmon.”

[Col. 0021D–0022D] **Note.** Here too our manuscripts omit the remainder of the scriptural text. They continue instead as follows: “This Salmon is the prince of the tribe,” etc. Formerly the printed editions incorrectly preferred “Salmon” in place of “Naasson.” In the same way, in the following passage they omit the remaining verses after the words “Joathan begot Achaz”; finally, they read “in the Fourth Book of Kings” instead of “of Kingdoms.”

“Salmon begot Booz by Rahab. Booz begot Obed by Ruth. Obed begot Jesse. Jesse begot David the king. David the king begot Solomon by her who had been the wife of Uriah. Solomon begot Roboam. Roboam begot Abia. Abia begot Asa. Asa begot Josaphat. Josaphat begot Joram.”

This is Naasson, prince of the tribe of Judah, as we read in Numbers (Num. I and II).

“Joram begot Ozias. Ozias begot Joathan. Joathan begot Achaz. Achaz begot Ezechias. Ezechias begot Manasses. Manasses begot Amon. Amon begot Josias. Josias begot Jechonias and his brothers at the time of the deportation to Babylon.”

In the Fourth Book of Kings (chapters III, VIII, and following) we read that Ochozias was begotten from Joram. After Ochozias died, Josabeth, daughter of King Joram and sister of Ochozias, took Joas, the son of her brother, and rescued him from the slaughter being carried out by Athalia.

[Col. 0022D] **Note.** Some manuscripts read Atholia.

Joas was succeeded in the kingdom by his son Amasias; after him reigned his son Azarias, who is also called Ozias.

[Col. 0022D] **Note.** Some manuscripts read Ochozias.

His son Joathan succeeded him.

You therefore see that, according to the historical account, three kings intervened whom the evangelist omitted. Joram did not beget Ozias but Ochozias, followed by the others whom we have listed. But because the evangelist’s purpose was to set out three groups of fourteen generations in the several periods of time, and because Joram had allied himself by marriage with the most impious Jezebel, his memory is removed up to the third generation, so that he might not be placed in the sequence of the holy birth.

[Col. 0022D–0023A] **Note.** Nearly all manuscripts have this reading, including those consulted by Martianus. The Greek reads τεσσαρεσκαιδέκαδες (*tessareskaidekades*, “fourteens”). Formerly the form was *tessaradecades*, which Rabbanus also prefers.

### Verses 12 and following

“After the deportation to Babylon, Jechonias begot Salathiel. Salathiel begot Zorobabel. Zorobabel begot Abiud. Abiud begot Eliacim. Eliacim begot Azor. Azor begot Sadoc. Sadoc begot Achim. Achim begot Eliud. Eliud begot Eleazar. Eleazar begot Matthan. Matthan begot Jacob.”

If we place Jechonias at the end of the first group of fourteen, the following group will contain not fourteen but thirteen. We should therefore understand that the first Jechonias is the same person as Joacim, whereas the second is his son, not his father. The former is written with *c* and *m*, the latter with *ch* and *n*. Through the error of scribes and the passage of time, the names became confused among both the Greeks and the Latins.

[Col. 0023C–D] **Note.** Two Palatine manuscripts read: “The second, however, is Joachin, the son, not the father,” etc. Recall that Jerome himself discusses this matter at greater length in his Commentary on Daniel, chapter I: “Let no one think that the Joacim at the beginning of Daniel is the same as the Joachin written at the beginning of Ezekiel. The latter has the final syllable *chin*, the former *cim*. For this reason one generation appears to be missing in the Gospel according to Matthew: the second group of fourteen ends with Joacim, son of Josias, and the third begins with Joachin, son of Joacim. Porphyry, ignorant of this, constructs a slander against the Church, displaying his own ignorance while attempting to accuse the evangelist Matthew of falsehood.” See also our observations on this passage. The same Palatine manuscripts shortly afterward read *prior* with K and M, and *sequens* with X and N, using Greek letters.

### Verse 16

“Jacob begot Joseph.”

On this passage Julian Augustus brought against us the alleged discrepancy among the evangelists: why Matthew called Joseph the son of Jacob, while Luke called him the son of Heli. He did not understand the custom of Scripture, namely, that one man may be his father according to nature and another according to the Law.

[Col. 0023D–0024C] **Note.** Rabbanus has the more correct text. Julian Augustus raised this passage against us in his *On the Disagreement of the Evangelists*. Rabbanus adds Africanus’s words from his Letter to Aristides on the disagreement of the Gospels: “It therefore remains for us … they transmitted their deeds according to the truth,” and so forth. These words differ considerably from Eusebius, who quotes this very testimony of Africanus in Book I, chapter 7, of his *History*. See also Nicephorus, Book I, chapter 11. MART.

For we know that Moses, by God’s command, prescribed that if a brother or relative died without children, another should take his wife in order to raise up offspring for his deceased brother or relative (Deut. II). Africanus, the historian of chronology, and Eusebius of Caesarea have discussed this matter more fully in their books *On the Disagreement of the Gospels* (*διαφωνία εὐαγγελίων*, “the disagreement of the Gospels”).

### Verse 17

“The husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ.”

When you hear “husband,” do not let suspicion of sexual union arise in you. Rather, remember the custom of Scripture, in which betrothed men are called husbands and betrothed women wives.

### Verse 18

“From the deportation to Babylon to Christ, there are fourteen generations.”

Count from Jechonias to Joseph, and you will find thirteen generations. The fourteenth generation, therefore, is reckoned in Christ himself.

The generation of Christ was as follows.

Let the attentive reader ask: Since Joseph was not the father of the Lord and Savior, what relevance does the sequence of the genealogy extending to Joseph have for the Lord? We answer first that it is not the custom of Scripture to weave the sequence of women into genealogies. Furthermore, Joseph and Mary were from one tribe. Therefore, by the Law he was compelled to take her as a relative, and they were registered together at Bethlehem because they were, evidently, descended from one lineage.

“His mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph.”

[Col. 0024C] **Note.** For the name Joseph, which all the manuscripts omit, one Cistercian manuscript substitutes: “It is asked why,” etc.

Why was she conceived not from a virgin simply, but from one who had been betrothed? First, so that through the genealogy of Joseph Mary’s origin might be shown. Second, so that she might not be stoned by the Jews as an adulteress. Third, so that, when she fled into Egypt, she might have the support of a husband.

[Col. 0024D] **Note.** Most printed books omit the word “husband.” One Sorbonne manuscript, as Martianus reports, has *maritale* (“marital”), which also seems superfluous. The pseudo-Theophilus of Antioch, in Book I of his Commentaries on the Gospels, copied this passage from Jerome word for word, but read “husband” instead of “marital.” Finally, the fourth reason, which is added from Saint Ignatius the martyr, is found to some extent at the end of his Letter to the Ephesians. An old manuscript of the Verona chapter, containing Alcuin’s minor works, cites this passage from Jerome; the name of Saint Ignatius the martyr is omitted, and it reads only: “Fourth, so that the child,” etc. Jerome, however, probably quoted it from Origen’s sixth Homily on Luke rather than from Ignatius himself.

“Before they came together, she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit.”

She was found so by no one other than Joseph, who, with almost marital authority, knew everything concerning his future wife. What is said, “Before they came together,” does not imply that afterward they came together; rather, Scripture indicates what did not happen.

### Verse 19

“Joseph her husband, being a just man and unwilling to expose her, wished to dismiss her secretly.”

If anyone joins himself to a prostitute, he becomes one body with her (I Cor. VI.16). The Law also commands that not only those who commit crimes but those who know of them are liable to sin (Lev. V). How, then, is Joseph called just when he conceals his wife’s crime? But this is testimony on Mary’s behalf: Joseph knew her chastity, marveled at what had happened, and, because he did not know its mystery, concealed it in silence.

### Verse 20

“Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary your wife. For what has been born in her is of the Holy Spirit. She will bear a son.”

We have already said above that betrothed women are called wives; this is taught more fully in the book against Helvidius. The angel speaks to Joseph in a dream with an affectionate tenderness, thereby approving the justice of his silence. It should also be noted that Joseph is said to be the son of David, so that Mary too might be shown to be from the stock of David.

[Col. 0024D–0025A] **Note.** Three Palatine manuscripts read “your wife,” a word which Jerome also approves in the exposition that follows.

### Verse 21

“You shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.”

*Jesus* means “Savior” in Hebrew. The evangelist therefore marked the etymology of his name by saying: “You shall call his name Jesus,” because he will save his people.

[Col. 0025C] **Note.** In several manuscript copies: “His name shall be called Savior,” or “You shall call his name Savior.” MART.—The same manuscripts, together with a Cistercian manuscript, add: “You shall call his name Savior, because he will save,” etc. Martianus found the same reading in other copies.

### Verses 22 and following

“All this happened so that what had been spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘Behold, a virgin shall have a child in her womb and shall bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel,’ which is translated, ‘God with us.’”

Joseph rose from sleep and did as the angel of the Lord had commanded him.

Where the evangelist Matthew says, “She shall have a child in her womb,” the prophet has written, “She shall receive a child in her womb.” But since the prophet foretells the future, he signifies what is going to happen and writes “shall receive”; the evangelist, however, because he narrates a past event rather than a future one, changed “shall receive” and wrote “shall have.” For one who has something is by no means going to receive it.

We read something similar in the Psalms: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he received gifts among men” (Ps. LXVII.19). When the apostle cites this testimony, he does not say “he received” but “he gave,” because there the future was signified—what he was going to receive—whereas here he narrates the history of one who had already given what he had received.

[Col. 0025C] **Note.** Other manuscripts read: “Here the history is narrated of one who had already given,” etc.

### Verse 25

“He took his wife, and did not know her until she had borne her firstborn son; and he called his name Jesus.”

From this passage certain people perversely suppose that Mary had other sons, arguing that one is not called “firstborn” unless he has brothers. But it is the custom of divine Scripture to call “firstborn” not one who is followed by brothers, but the one who is born first. Read the aforementioned little book against Helvidius.

## Chapter II

### Verses 2 and following

“We have seen his star in the East, and have come to worship him. When King Herod heard this, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. Gathering together all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he asked them where Christ was to be born.”

To the confusion of the Jews, so that they might learn Christ’s birth from the Gentiles, a star arose in the East. The Magi knew of it from the prophecy of Balaam, whose successors they were.

[Col. 0025D] **Note.** Two Palatine manuscripts insert the word “had foretold.”

Read the Book of Numbers (chapter XXIV). The Magi were brought to Judaea by the sign of the star so that, when questioned by the Magi about where Christ would be born, the priests might be rendered without excuse concerning his coming.

### Verse 5

“They said to him: ‘In Bethlehem of Judaea.’ For so it is written through the prophet: ‘And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah. For from you shall come forth a ruler who will govern my people Israel.’”

This is a scribal error. We think the evangelist originally published the text as we read it in the Hebrew copy: “Bethlehem of Judah,” not “of Judaea.”

[Col. 0025D–0026B] **Note.** It is easy to understand that Jerome here calls the Nazarene codex, which he often cites and himself translated from the Greek, “Hebrew.” Nor is it entirely convincing to attribute to scribal error the writing of “Judaea” for “Judah.” The Septuagint also calls the land of the tribe of Judah τὴν Ἰουδαίαν (*tēn Ioudaian*), and does not by that term designate the whole territory of the Hebrews, or Palestine, but a particular region subject to the kings of Judah descended from David. It was properly distinguished by that name not only from other peoples but also from the regions of the other tribes of Israel. Thus, what is Hebrew in Jeremiah XIV.2 and Joel III.20 is called Ἰουδαία (*Ioudaia*) in Greek; and in the Vulgate it is translated “of Judah” in I Kings XVII.1, although the Greek has Ἰουδαίας (*Ioudaias*).

For what other Bethlehem is there among the nations, so that “of Judaea” should be added here to distinguish it? “Of Judah” is written because there is another Bethlehem in Galilee. Read the Book of Joshua son of Nun (Josh. XIX). Finally, the testimony itself, taken from the prophecy of Micah, reads: “And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah” (Mic. V.2).

### Verse 11

“Opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.”

The sacramental meaning of the gifts was beautifully compressed by the presbyter Juvencus in one verse:

> They bring frankincense, gold, and myrrh  
> As gifts to the king, the man, and God.

“And having received an answer in a dream not to return to Herod, they went back to their country by another way,” and so forth.

Those who had offered gifts to the Lord consequently receive an answer. This answer—which in Greek is called χρηματισθέντες (*chrēmatistʰentes*, “having received an oracle” or “having been divinely instructed”)—does not come through an angel but through the Lord himself, so that Joseph’s privilege of merit might be demonstrated.

[Col. 0025D–0028C] **Note.** I was formerly almost persuaded that this passage contained a textual error, and that *ipsum Dominum* (“the Lord himself”) ought to be corrected by a single word to *insomnium* (“a dream”), so that the meaning would be that the Magi received a message through a dream, but Saint Joseph received one through an angel. This would make Saint Jerome consistent with himself, since he assigns Saint Joseph a privilege over the vision granted to the Magi and praises it precisely for this reason: to demonstrate Joseph’s superior merit. For the matter would be entirely different if he said that the Magi were warned by the Lord himself but Joseph by an angel, since the condition of the God who warns would then be inferior, contrary to the truth and to the explicit claim of the holy Father himself.

Accordingly, it may seem that the error arose among the ancient copyists from a similarity between the words *ipsum Dominum* and *insomnium*. A critic may easily have taken them as two separate words, as though divided into *in som* and *nium*, which have no meaning separately, and then thought that *insom* should be corrected to *ipsum* and *nium* to *Dominum*. The rest of the passage, however, as well as the sacred text, supports the reading *insomnium*; so does the truth of the matter and, finally, the very character and force of the Latin word *insomnium*, which means a vision foretelling what afterward takes place.

But if we properly grasp the holy Doctor’s meaning, it will become clear, after considering the matter somewhat more deeply, that there is nothing here to correct. He held that answers received in dreams, κατ’ ὄναρ (*kat’ onar*, “in a dream”), which the Greeks call χρησμούς (*chrēsmous*, “oracles”), come through God himself, and that a χρησμός (*chrēsmos*) is said to occur whenever God answers directly. His view can be recognized throughout his Commentaries on the Prophets and elsewhere. Indeed, the Greek lexicographers themselves refer the doctrine to the name of Jerome as a learned opinion concerning the more hidden teaching of the term χρησμός (*chrēsmos*).

Thus, in the sacred text, where the Magi are being discussed, the verb χρησμῳδέω (*chrēsmōdeō*), derived from the noun χρησμός, is used with precisely the same meaning. In accordance with this doctrine of the holy Father and of the Greeks, the answer is understood to have come through the Lord himself. If the same sacred text indicates that the answer given to Joseph came through an angel, while declaring that both events occurred κατ’ ὄναρ, that is, in a dream, it nevertheless testifies that both were divine, or brought about by the Lord himself. Joseph’s answer has the greater honor and praise in this respect: an angel was sent by the Lord himself to announce it, so that Joseph’s privilege of merit might be demonstrated.

The meaning and the fact therefore remain intact; nor should one rashly lay hands upon the text of the holy Father, which all books, manuscripts and printed editions alike, as many as exist and as many as have existed, unanimously preserve and approve.

They return by another way because they were not to be mixed with the unbelief of the Jews.

### Verses 13–14

“Behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph, saying: ‘Rise, take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt; and remain there until I tell you. For Herod is about to seek the child in order to destroy him.’”

He rose, took the child and his mother by night, and withdrew into Egypt; and he remained there until Herod’s death.

When he takes the child and his mother in order to go into Egypt, he takes them by night and in darkness. But when he returns to Judaea, neither night nor darkness is mentioned in the Gospel.

### Verses 15–16

“So that what had been spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘Out of Egypt I called my son.’”

Then Herod, seeing that he had been deceived by the Magi, became exceedingly angry. He sent and killed all the boys who were in Bethlehem and throughout all its borders, from two years old and under, according to the time that he had ascertained from the Magi.

Let those who deny the truth of the Hebrew books answer where this is read in the Greek translators of the Septuagint. When they do not find it, we shall tell them that it is written in the prophet Hosea (chapter XI), as the copies we recently published can also prove.

We can also reconcile this passage in another way for the sake of contentious people, whose practice the apostle Paul denies that he has, as does the Church of Christ (I Cor. XI). We produce a testimony from Numbers, where Balaam says: “God called him out of Egypt; his glory is like that of a unicorn” (Num. XXIII.22).

[Col. 0028D] **Note.** The printed books have here an extremely inept reading: “We can also console this passage in another way for contentious people.” It should read: “We can also reconcile this passage in another way,” or “confirm it in another way …”; and we produce a testimony from Numbers, etc. For everywhere we read in the singular, “I called my son,” or “I called him,” not, as the Septuagint has it in the plural, “I called my sons.” MART.

### Verses 17 and following

“Then what had been spoken through Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled: ‘A voice was heard in Rama, lamentation and great wailing; Rachel weeping for her children, and she refused to be comforted because they are not’” (Jer. XXXI.15).

When Herod had died, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, saying: “Rise, take the child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel.”

Benjamin was born from Rachel, and Bethlehem is not in his tribe (Gen. XXXV). How, then, is Rachel said to mourn the children of Judah—that is, of Bethlehem—as though they were her own?

We shall answer briefly that she was buried near Bethlehem in Ephrata and, from the maternal lodging of her little body, received the name of mother.

[Col. 0028D] **Note.** Our manuscripts, as well as two cited by Martianus, read: “from the inward lodging of her little body.”

Or it may be because Judah and Benjamin were two adjoining tribes, and Herod had ordered that the children be killed not only in Bethlehem but also throughout all its borders. Through the slaughter at Bethlehem we understand that many from Benjamin too were killed.

She mourns her children and does not accept consolation in accordance with a twofold interpretation: either because she considered them dead forever, or because she refused to be consoled for those whom she knew would live.

As for the statement “in Rama,” we should not think that this is the name of a place near Gabaa, but that *rama* means “high,” so that the sense is: “A voice was heard on high,” that is, spread far and wide.

[Col. 0028D] **Note.** The Palatine codices read: “not the name of a place that is near Gabaa.”

### Verse 20

“For those who sought the child’s life have died.”

From this passage we understand that not only Herod but also the priests and scribes were at that same time plotting the Lord’s death.

(Vers. 21.) “When he had risen, he took the child and his mother and came into the land of Israel.” [Note: [Col. 0028D] The same manuscripts, instead of the words “and came into the land of Israel,” add only “by night.”] He did not say, “He took his son and his wife,” but “the child and his mother,” as a guardian rather than a husband.

(Vers. 22.) “But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning in Judaea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there; and being warned in a dream, he withdrew into the regions of Galilee.” Many fall into error through ignorance of history, supposing that this was the same Herod by whom the Lord was mocked during his Passion, and who is now reported to have died. That Herod, therefore, who later became friends with Pilate, was the son of this Herod and the brother of Archelaus. Tiberius Caesar exiled him also to Lugdunum, a city of Gaul, and made his brother Herod successor to the kingdom. Read Josephus’s history.

[Note: [Col. 0028D] Yet Josephus himself, whose historical reliability he invokes, says in Book XVII, chapter 13, that, by order of Tiberius, Herod was deported not to Lugdunum but to Vienna: “giving him Vienna, a city of Gaul, as his place of residence” (δοὺς οἰκητήριον αὐτῷ Βίενναμ πόλιν τῆς Γαλατίας). Compare also Eusebius in the *Chronicle*.]

(Vers. 23.) “And coming, he lived in a city called Nazareth, so that what was spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled: ‘He shall be called a Nazaraean.’” If he had set down a fixed example from Scripture, he would never have said “what was spoken through the prophets,” but simply “what was spoken through the prophet.” By now calling the prophets collectively, he shows that he took not the words but the meaning from Scripture. *Nazaraean* is interpreted as “holy.” That the Lord would be holy is proclaimed throughout all Scripture. We can also say that, with the very same words, it is written in Isaiah according to the Hebrew truth: “A shoot shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a Nazaraean shall rise from his root” (Isa. XI, 1).

(Cap. III.—Vers. 1.) “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven will draw near.” John the Baptist is the first to preach the kingdom of heaven, so that, as the Lord’s forerunner, he may be honored with this privilege.

(Vers. 3.) “For this is he who was spoken of through Isaiah the prophet, saying: ‘The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.’” He was preparing the souls of believers, in whom the Lord was to walk, so that he might walk as one pure in utterly pure ways, saying: “I will dwell in them and walk among them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people” (Lev. XXVI, 12).

Porphyry compares this passage with the beginning of Mark the Evangelist, where it is written: “The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, as it is written in [Note: [Col. 0029D] Most Greek copies of this Gospel, however, read ἐν τοῖς Προφήταις (“in the Prophets”) here rather than ἐν τῷ Ἰσαΐᾳ (“in Isaiah”).] Isaiah the prophet: ‘Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way. The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight’” (Isa. XL, 3). Since the testimony from Malachi (chap. III) and Isaiah has been woven together, he asks how we can suppose that the example was taken as though from Isaiah alone. Ecclesiastical men have answered him fully.

But we think that the name Isaiah was added through a scribal error, as we can prove also in other passages; or certainly that a single composite testimony was formed from various testimonies of Scripture. Read the thirteenth Psalm, and you will find this same thing.

[Note: [Col. 0029D] Since this thirteenth Psalm does not at all appear to have been composed from several testimonies, Clericus conjectures that something has fallen out of Jerome’s text, and supplies the passage as follows: “Read the Epistle to the Romans and the thirteenth Psalm.” For in that Epistle, chapter III, this Psalm is quoted more than once.]

(Vers. 4.) “John himself had a garment of camel hair and a leather belt around his waist.” He says that John had one made of hair, not of wool. The one is a sign of austere clothing, the other of softer luxury. The leather belt with which Elijah too was girded is a sign [Al. symbol] of mortification (IV Kings I).

Moreover, what follows:

“And his food was locusts and wild honey.” It is fitting for one dwelling in the wilderness to satisfy not the refinements of food but the necessity of human flesh.

[Col. 0029D] (Vers. 9.) “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham.” He calls the Gentiles “stones,” on account of the hardness of their hearts. Read Ezekiel: “I will take away,” he says, “the stony heart from you, and I will give you a heart of flesh” (Ezek. XXXVI, 26). In stone, hardness is indicated; in flesh, softness [Al. tenderness]. Or he simply indicates the power of God: he who made all things from nothing can also bring forth a people from the hardest rocks.

[Col. 0030A] (Vers. 10, 11.) [Note: [Col. 0030D] All our manuscripts and four belonging to Martianaeus read: “Behold, the axe.”] “For now the axe has been laid at the root of the trees. Therefore every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire. I indeed baptize you in water for repentance; but the one who is coming after me is mightier than I.”

The preaching of the Gospel word, which is a sword sharpened on both sides, is called an axe, in accordance with the prophet Jeremiah, who compares the word of the Lord to an axe cutting stone (Jer. XLVI).

“Whose sandals I am not worthy to carry.” In another Gospel he says: “Whose sandal strap I am not worthy to loosen.” Here humility is shown; there, a mystery: Christ is the bridegroom, and John is not worthy to loosen the bridegroom’s sandal strap, lest his house be called, according to the law of Moses and the example of Ruth, “the house of the barefooted one” (Deut. XXV and Ruth IV).

(Vers. 12.) “He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire. His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor; he will gather his wheat into his barn, but he will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire.”

Either because the Holy Spirit is fire, as the Acts of the Apostles teaches: when he descended, something like fire sat upon each of the believers [Al. “tongues”] (Acts II); and the Lord’s saying was fulfilled: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I will? That it be kindled” (Luke XII, 49).

Or because in the present we are baptized in the Spirit, and in the future in fire, in accordance with the Apostle’s meaning: “The fire will test the quality of each one’s work” (I Cor. III, 13).

(Vers. 13, 14.) “Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan, to John, to be baptized by him. But John tried to prevent him, saying: ‘I ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me?’ But Jesus answered and said to him.”

The Savior received baptism from John for three reasons. First, because he had been born human, in order to fulfill all the righteousness and humility of the Law. Second, in order to confirm John’s baptism by his own baptism. Third, in order to sanctify the waters of the Jordan and, through the descent of the dove, to show the coming of the Holy Spirit into the bath of believers.

(Vers. 15.) “Let it be so for now.” He aptly said “for now,” to show that Christ was to be baptized in water, while John was to be baptized by Christ in the Spirit.

Or otherwise: “Let it be so for now,” so that I, who have assumed the form of a servant, may also fulfill the servant’s humility. Otherwise, know that on the day of judgment you must be baptized with my baptism.

The Lord Jesus says: “For now, I have another baptism with which I must be baptized. You baptize me in water, so that I may baptize you for my sake in your blood.”

(Vers. 16.) “For thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” Then he allowed him. “And when Jesus had been baptized, immediately he came up from the water.” He did not add “the righteousness of the Law” or “of nature,” so that we might understand both: if God received baptism from a human being, no one should disdain to receive it from a fellow servant.

(Vers. 17.) “And behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him. And behold, a voice from the heavens saying: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.’”

The mystery of the Trinity is demonstrated in the baptism: the Lord is baptized, the Spirit descends in the form [Al. appearance] of a dove, and the voice of the Father, bearing witness to the Son, is heard. The heavens are opened not by the elements being physically unfastened, but to spiritual eyes—the same eyes by which Ezekiel, at the beginning of his book, also records that they were opened.

A dove also settled upon Jesus’ head, lest anyone think that the Father’s voice had been directed to John rather than to the Lord.

[Col. 0031B] (Cap. IV.—Vers. 1.) “Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness.” There is no doubt that this means by the Holy Spirit. For what follows is:

“To be tempted by the devil.” He was led not unwillingly or as a captive, but by his will to do battle.

20 (Vers. 2.) “And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterward he was hungry. And the tempter approached and said to him: ‘If you are the Son of God.’”

In this number, forty, the mystery is shown to us: Moses fasted on Mount Sinai (Exod. XXIV), and Elijah near Mount Horeb (III Kings XIX). The body is allowed to become hungry so that the devil may be given an opportunity to tempt.

(Vers. 3.) “Say that these stones become loaves of bread.” It is fittingly said to one who is hungry: “Say that these stones become loaves of bread.” But, O devil, you are held by two contrary arguments. If, at his command, stones can become bread, then you tempt one whose power is so great for no reason. But if he cannot do this, then you suspect the Son of God for no reason.

[Note: [Col. 0031D] Victorius adds: “saying.”]

“If you are the Son of God, say that these stones become loaves of bread.”

(Vers. 4.) “He answered and said: ‘It is written: Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.’”

The testimony is taken from Deuteronomy (Deut. VIII, 3). The Lord answered in this way because he had resolved to conquer the devil by humility, not by power.

At the same time, it must be observed that, unless the Lord had begun to fast, the devil would have had no opportunity to tempt him, in accordance with the saying: “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. II, 1).

The Savior’s very response also indicates that it was a human being who was tempted: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.” Therefore, if someone does not feed upon the word of God, that person does not live.

(Vers. 5.) “Then the devil took him into the holy city.” This taking, as it is called, did not arise from any weakness in the Lord, but from the enemy’s pride, who supposes the Savior’s will to be necessity.

From this passage we understand what is meant by the statement written elsewhere: “They went into the holy city, and appeared to many” (Matt. XXVII, 53).

(Vers. 6.) “And he set him upon the pinnacle of the temple and said to him.” He who had tempted him with hunger now tempted him also with vainglory.

“If you are the Son of God.” In every temptation the devil tries to discover whether he is the Son of God; but the Lord so carefully shapes his answer that he leaves him uncertain.

“Throw yourself down.” “For it is written.” This is the devil’s voice, since he always desires everyone to fall downward. “Throw yourself down,” he says; he can persuade, but he cannot compel the fall.

21 “He has commanded his angels concerning you, and they will lift you up in their hands, lest perhaps you strike your foot against a stone.” We read this in the ninetieth Psalm; yet there the prophecy is not about Christ but about a holy man.

The devil therefore interprets the Scriptures badly. Certainly, if he truly knew that it had been written about the Savior, he ought also to have said what follows in that same Psalm against himself: “You will walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample the lion and the dragon.” He speaks of the angels’ assistance as though the Savior were weak; like one who evades the issue, he is silent about his own being trampled.

(Vers. 7.) “Jesus said to him again: ‘It is written: You shall not tempt the Lord your God.’” He breaks the devil’s false arrows drawn from Scripture with the true shields of Scripture. It should also be noted that he brought forth the necessary testimonies only from Deuteronomy, to reveal the mysteries of the second Law.

[Col. 0032C] (Vers. 8.) “Again the devil took him onto a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, [Note: [Col. 0031D] All our manuscripts omit the words “and said to him.” Some read *peritura* (“which will perish”) shortly afterward, instead of *praeteritura* (“which will pass away”).] and said to him.”

The glory of the world, which will pass away with the world, is displayed upon a mountain and a lofty height. The Lord, however, descended to low places and level ground, so that he might overcome the devil by humility. Moreover, the devil hastens to lead him to the mountains, so that, through the places by which he himself had fallen, the others might fall as well, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Lest, being puffed up, he fall into the judgment of the devil” (I Tim. III, 6).

(Vers. 9.) “I will give you all these things, if you will fall down and worship me.” Arrogant and proud, he says this also boastfully—not because the devil has power over the whole world or can give all the kingdoms, since we know that many holy men have been made kings by God.

[Note: [Col. 0031D] More correctly, in the Rabb. manuscript, “so that.”]

“If you will fall down,” he says, “and worship me.” Therefore, whoever is going to worship the devil has first fallen.

(Vers. 10.) “Then Jesus says to him: ‘Go, Satan. For it is written:’”

[Note: [Col. 0031D] The Cistercian manuscript inserts *retro* (“back”)—“Go back”—and consistently below has *audit*, “Go back, Satan.” As we have already pointed out more than once, manuscripts and printed books often connect the Scripture sections differently: they frequently omit certain verses, which the following exposition also does not address.]

It is not the case, as many suppose, that Satan and the Apostle Peter are condemned by the same sentence. To Peter it is said: “Go behind me, Satan” (Matt. XVI, 23), that is, “Follow me, since you oppose my will.” Here, however, he hears, “Go, Satan”; and it is not said to him, “behind me,” so that the implied meaning is: “Go into the eternal fire that has been prepared for you and your angels.”

22 “You shall worship the Lord your God, and you shall serve him alone.” When the devil said to the Savior, “If you will fall down and worship me,” he hears in return that he himself ought rather to worship him as his Lord and God.
