(Vers. 11.) “Then the devil left him; and behold, angels approached and ministered to him.” Temptation comes first, so that victory may follow. The angels minister in order to confirm the dignity of the victor.

(Vers. 15, 16.) “Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, the way of the sea beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles: the people who [Note: [Col. 0033D] Victorius restores *sedebat* (“was sitting”), from the Vulgate and the Greek καθήμενος. He says that the holy Doctor himself supports this reading in his *Commentaries on Isaiah*, chapter IX. Indeed, in Matthew too he reads *sedebat* (“was sitting”); in Isaiah he wishes to read *ambulabat* (“was walking”), based on Jerome’s text: “so that the people who either sat or walked in darkness might see the light.”] walked in darkness saw a great light, and for those sitting in the region and shadow of death, light has risen.”

These were the first to hear the Lord preaching, so that where Israel’s first captivity by the Assyrians had occurred, there the proclamation of the Redeemer might be born.

[Note: [Col. 0034D] One Cistercian manuscript and one Palatine manuscript read *nosceretur* (“might be recognized”).]

(Vers. 17, 18.) “From that time Jesus began to preach and to say: ‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven will draw near.’ As Jesus was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. And he said to them.”

After John had been handed over, Jesus rightly begins to preach himself: when the Law comes to an end, the Gospel consequently arises. If the Savior preaches the same things that John the Baptist had previously proclaimed, he shows that he is the Son of the same God whose prophet John was.

(Vers. 19, 20.) “Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of human beings.” “Immediately they left their nets and followed him.” These were the first to be called to follow the Lord. Fishermen and uneducated men are sent to preach, lest the faith of believers be thought to arise not through God’s power but through eloquence and learning.

(Vers. 24.) “And he healed the lunatics and the paralytics. And great crowds followed him from Galilee and the Decapolis, from Jerusalem and Judaea, and from beyond the Jordan.”

They were not truly lunatics, but were thought to be lunatics because of the deception of demons, who, observing the phases of the moon, desired to defame the creature so that the blasphemy might rebound upon the Creator.

(Cap. V.—Vers. 1, 2.) “When Jesus saw the crowds, he went up onto the mountain; and when he had sat down, his disciples approached him. And opening his mouth, he taught them, saying.”

The Lord ascends into the mountains so that he may draw the crowds upward with him. But the crowds are unable to ascend. The disciples follow, and to them he speaks not while standing but while sitting and stooping [Al. “he himself does not stand”]. They could not understand him shining in his majesty.

According to the literal interpretation, some of the simpler brethren think that he taught the Beatitudes and what follows on the Mount of Olives. This is by no means so: from what precedes and follows, the place is shown to be in Galilee. We think it was either Mount Tabor or some other high mountain.

Finally, after he had finished his discourses, the text immediately continues: “When he had entered Capernaum.”

(Vers. 3.) “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” This is what we read elsewhere: “And he will save the humble in spirit” (Ps. XXXIII, 16).

But lest anyone think that the poverty which is sometimes borne from necessity is being proclaimed by the Lord, he added “in spirit,” so that you might understand humility, not destitution.

“Blessed are the poor in spirit,” those who are poor by choice for the sake of the Holy Spirit. Accordingly, the Savior also speaks through Isaiah concerning such poor: “The Lord has anointed me; therefore he has sent me to evangelize the poor” (Isa. VI, 1).

(Vers. 4.) “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.” [Col. 0034B] Not the land of Judah [Al. Judaea], nor the earth of this world; not the cursed earth that brings forth thorns and thistles (Gen. V), which the most cruel and warlike person is more likely to possess; but the earth desired by the Psalmist, who says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. XXVI, 13).

Such a possessor, triumphant after victory, is also described in the forty-fourth Psalm: “And direct yourself, advance prosperously [Al. “and prosperously advance”], and reign, because of truth and meekness and righteousness.” No one possesses this earth through meekness, but through pride.

(Vers. 5.) “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.” This mourning is not mourning for the dead according to the common law of nature, but for the sins and vices of those who are dead in sin.

Thus Samuel also wept for Saul, because God regretted that he had made him king over Israel (I Kings XV). Likewise the Apostle Paul says that he weeps and mourns for those who, after fornication and impurity, have not repented (II Cor. XII).

24 (Vers. 6.) “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied.” It is not enough for us to desire righteousness unless we suffer hunger for righteousness, so that under this example we may understand ourselves never to be sufficiently righteous, but always to hunger for works of righteousness.

(Vers. 7.) “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.” Mercy is understood not only in almsgiving, but in every sin of a brother, if we bear one another’s burdens (Gal. VI).

(Vers. 8.) “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” Those whom no consciousness of sin accuses. A pure person is seen by a pure heart; the temple of God cannot be polluted.

(Vers. 9.) “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.” These first make peace in their own hearts, and then among brothers who are at odds. For what does it profit if others are reconciled through you, while wars of vices exist in your own soul?

(Vers. 10.) “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” He significantly added [Al. “says”], “for righteousness’ sake.” Many suffer persecution because of their sins and are not righteous. At the same time, consider that the eighth beatitude, that of true circumcision, ends in martyrdom.

(Vers. 11.) “Blessed are you when people curse you, persecute you, and speak every evil against you falsely because of me.” That curse is to be despised which creates blessedness and is uttered falsely by the mouth of the one who curses.

Accordingly, he specifically defined what kind of curse is blessed: “every curse,” he says, “against you, falsely, because of me.” Therefore, wherever Christ is the cause, there the curse is also to be desired.

(Vers. 12.) “Rejoice and exult, for your reward is great in heaven. For so they persecuted the prophets who were before you.”

I do not know who among us could fulfill this—to have our reputation torn by insults while we exult in the Lord. One who pursues empty glory cannot fulfill this. We must therefore rejoice and exult, so that a reward may be prepared for us in the heavens.

We read elegantly in a certain volume: “Do not seek glory, and you will not grieve when you are without glory.”

(Vers. 13.) “You are the salt of the earth.” The apostles are called salt because through them the entire human race is seasoned.

25 “But if the salt has become tasteless, with what will it be salted?” If a teacher has gone astray, by what other teacher will he be corrected?

“It is no longer useful for anything except to be thrown outside and trampled underfoot by people.” The example is taken from agriculture. Salt is necessary both as a seasoning for food and for drying meats; it has no other use.

Certainly we read in Scripture that certain cities were sown with salt by the anger [Al. “in this way”] of the victors, so that nothing would sprout in them (Judit. IX). Let teachers and bishops therefore beware and consider: “The mighty will suffer mighty torments” (Wis. VI, 7); there is no remedy, but the ruin of those above leads to Tartarus.

(Vers. 14 ff.) “You are the light of the world. A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden; nor do they light a lamp and put it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that it may shine for all who are in the house. Thus let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.”

[Col. 0036A] He teaches confidence in preaching, so that the apostles may not hide themselves through fear and become like a lamp beneath a bushel, but may reveal themselves with complete freedom, so that what they heard in private rooms they may preach from the rooftops (Matt. X, 27).

(Vers. 17.) “Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the prophets. I have not come to abolish, but to fulfill.” Either because he fulfilled what had been prophesied about himself through others, or because he completed through his preaching those things which, on account of the weakness of his hearers, had previously been rudimentary and imperfect (Matt. V)—removing anger, excluding retaliation, and condemning hidden desire in the mind [Note: [Col. 0035D] The older Palatine manuscript and Victorius’s edition add “condemning.”]

(Vers. 18.) “Until heaven and earth pass away.” New heavens and a new earth are promised to us, which the Lord God will make. If, therefore, new things are to be created, the old things will consequently pass away.

As for what follows:

“Not one iota or one stroke will pass from the Law until all things come to pass.” From the shape of a letter it is shown that even the things considered least important in the Law are full of spiritual mysteries, and that everything is recapitulated in the Gospel.

What learning, and what kind of teaching, is required to show that even the various sacrifices and the things that appear superstitious are fulfilled daily in the victims?

(Vers. 19 ff.) “Therefore whoever loosens one of these least commandments and teaches people to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven; but whoever does and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven. For I say to you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven. You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not kill; and whoever kills will be liable to judgment.’ But I say to you.”

This passage is joined to the preceding testimony, in which he had said: “Not one iota or one stroke will pass from the Law until all things come to pass.”

He therefore censures the Pharisees, who, having disregarded God’s commandments, established their own traditions: their teaching among the people will not benefit them if they destroy even the smallest commandment given in the Law.

We can also understand it in another way: the teacher’s learning, even if he is liable to a small sin, brings him down from the highest rank; it does not profit him to teach righteousness when the smallest fault destroys it. Perfect blessedness consists in fulfilling in deed what one has taught in word.

(Vers. 22.) “For everyone who is angry with his brother [Note: [Col. 0035D] More correctly, our manuscripts omit the words “will be liable to judgment.” What he says are added in some manuscripts without cause, we have explained elsewhere in the Notes on Epistle 13 and in Book II of the *Dialogue against the Pelagians*, no. 5. More will be said below at the beginning of Book III of the *Commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians*. Latin manuscripts too still prevail that retain this added clause. One such is the Veronese manuscript, easily the foremost of all; others are also among those to which Martianaeus assigned the Gospel of the Italian version. The older Latin Fathers likewise read it: Cyprian, *Testimonies*, Book III, no. 8; Hilary, *On Matthew*; and Augustine, *On the Sermon on the Mount*, Book I, chapter 9. Yet in *Retractions*, chapter 19, Augustine warns that these words are not found in the Greek manuscripts. Justin agrees with our Jerome in his *First Apology to Antoninus*, where he omits the word εἰκῇ (“without cause”).] will be liable to judgment.”

In certain manuscripts “without cause” is added. But in the genuine text the sentence is absolute, and anger is entirely removed, as Scripture says: “Whoever is angry with his brother.”

For if we are commanded to offer the other cheek to one who strikes us, to love our enemies, and to pray for those who persecute us (Luke VI), every occasion for anger is removed. Therefore “without cause” must be deleted, because “the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God” (James I).

[Col. 0037A] “But whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ [Note: [Col. 0037D] Here too our manuscripts more correctly omit the words “will be liable to the council.” Saint Gregory says in Book XXI, chapter 5, of the *Moralia*: “Raca, in Hebrew speech, is the word of one who is indignant; it reveals the spirit of the angry person, but does not yet express a complete word of anger.” Compare Saint Hilary on Matthew, chapter 4; Saint Basil’s *Rule*, chapter 145; and Avitus of Vienne, Letter 1.] will be liable to the council.”

This word is properly Hebrew. *Raca* is called κενός, that is, “empty” or “vacant”; we can render it by the common insult “brainless.”

If we are going to give an account for an idle word, how much more for an insult (Matt. XI)! It is also significantly added: “Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca.’” For no one is our brother except one who has the same Father as we do. When he likewise believes in God and knows Christ to be the wisdom of God (I Cor. I), by what right can he be branded with the epithet of foolishness?

“But whoever says, ‘Fool,’ will be liable to the fire of Gehenna.” By *apo koinou* [Greek: ἀπὸ κοινοῦ], that is, by understanding words in common from the preceding construction, the following is implied: “Whoever says to his brother, ‘Fool,’ will be liable to Gehenna.” For whoever says “Fool” to one who likewise believes in God is impious toward religion.

(Vers. 23, 24.) “Therefore, if you bring your gift to the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go first to be reconciled with your brother; and then come and offer your gift.”

He did not say, “If you have something against your brother,” but “If your brother has something against you,” so that a more demanding necessity of reconciliation might be imposed upon you. As long as we cannot appease him, I do not know whether we can fittingly offer our gifts to God.

(Vers. 25 ff.) “Be well disposed toward your adversary quickly, while you are with him on the way, lest perhaps your adversary hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the attendant, and you be thrown into prison. Amen I say to you, you will not come out from there until you have paid the last quadrans. You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I say to you, everyone…”

In place of what our Latin manuscripts have, *consentiens* (“agreeing”), the Greek has Εὐνοῶν, which means “well disposed” or “kind.”

From what precedes and follows, the meaning is clear: while we are running along the way of this world, the Lord and our Savior urges us toward peace and harmony, in accordance with the Apostle, who says: “If it is possible, insofar as it depends on you, live at peace with all people” (Rom. XII, 18).

For in the preceding passage he had said: “If you bring your gift to the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you”; and, having finished this, he immediately adds: “Be well disposed [Note: [Col. 0037D] In place of *consentiens*, three Palatine manuscripts have *benivolus* (“well-disposed”). [Col. 0038D] We correct less significant matters below.] or kind toward your adversary,” and what follows.

In what follows he commands: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you; and pray for those who persecute and slander you.”

Although this meaning is clear and consistent, many think that the passage concerns the flesh and the soul, [Note: [Col. 0038D] The same manuscripts have “or the spirit alone,” without “the soul.” A little later they read “if the soul should not have agreed,” instead of “if the soul,” etc., in the nominative.] or the soul and the spirit. This is utterly impossible.

For how could either the flesh be sent into prison if the soul had not consented—since both soul and flesh must be shut up together, and the flesh can do nothing except what the mind commands—or could the Holy Spirit dwelling in us hand over to the judge either flesh or soul when they resist, since he himself is the judge?

Others, following the Epistle of Peter, which says: “Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion” (I Pet. V, 8), and what follows, interpret the adversary as the devil. They want the Savior to command that, while it is in our power, we should be well disposed toward the devil, who is an enemy and avenger, and should not make him suffer punishments on our behalf.

Since he himself supplies the incentives to vice, and since we also sin by our own will, if we consent to him when he suggests vices, he too must be tormented on our account. They say that each of the saints is well disposed toward his adversary if he does not make him suffer torments on his behalf.

Some argue more forcibly that in baptism each person enters into a pact with the devil and says: “I renounce you, devil, and your pomp, your vices, and your world, which is placed in the evil one” (I John V, 19).

If, therefore, we keep the pact, we are well disposed and consenting toward our adversary, and we will by no means be shut up in prison. But if we transgress anything of what we had promised to the devil, we will be handed over to the judge and the attendant, thrown into prison, and will not come out until we have paid the last quadrans.

The quadrans is a kind of coin worth two small coins. Thus in another Gospel the poor widow is said to have put a quadrans into the treasury (Mark XII), while in another she is said to have put in two small coins (Luke XXI). The Gospels do not disagree: one quadrans consists of two small coins.

This, then, is what he says: “You will not leave the prison until you have paid even the smallest sins.”

[Note: [Col. 0038D] From this passage the inexperienced Joannes Clericus should be refuted, since he thought Jerome did not ordinarily use the word *recludere* in the sense of “to shut up.” Above too it is said that soul and flesh must be shut up together. See our *Defense of Jerome’s Learning*. MART.]

(Vers. 28.) “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”

The difference between πάθος and προπάθεια—that is, between *passion* and *propassion*—is this: passion is counted as a vice; propassion, although it has the fault of a beginning [Al. “of vice”], is nevertheless not held as a crime.

Therefore, whoever looks at a woman and whose soul is stirred by the impulse has been struck by propassion. But if he consents and turns the thought into an attachment, as it is written concerning David, “They passed over into the affection of the heart” (Ps. LXXII, 7), he has passed from propassion to passion. What is lacking in him is not the will to sin but the opportunity.

Therefore, whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her—that is, if he looks so that he may desire her, with the intention of acting—is rightly said to commit adultery with her in his heart.

(Verses 29–30.) “But if your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you. For it is better for you that one of your members perish than that your whole body be cast into Gehenna. And if your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you. For it is better for you that one of your members perish than that your whole body be cast into Gehenna.”

Since he had spoken above about desire for a woman, he now rightly calls the thought and sense wandering in different directions an “eye.” By the right hand and the other parts of the body, he indicates the beginnings of the will and the affections [Note: The Palatine manuscripts unanimously read “the beginnings of the affections,” instead of “and the affections,” etc.], so that what we conceive in the mind we may complete in deed. [Col. 0039B] We must therefore beware lest what is best in us quickly slide into vice. For if the right eye and the right hand cause stumbling, how much more those things in us that are left-handed! If the soul slips, how much more the body, which is more inclined toward sins!

Alternatively: In the right eye and the right hand is shown the affection for brothers, wives, children, relatives, and kinsmen. If we perceive that these impede us from contemplating the true light, we must cut off such portions, lest, while wishing to make others gain, we ourselves perish forever. Hence it is also said concerning the high priest, whose soul is dedicated to the worship of God: “He shall not be defiled for father or mother or children” (Lev. 21:11)—that is, he shall know no affection except for the one to whose worship he has been dedicated. [Col. 0039C]

(Verses 31ff.) “It was also said: Whoever divorces his wife, let him give her a bill of divorce. But I say to you that everyone who divorces his wife, except on account of fornication, makes her commit adultery; and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.”

Later, in the Gospel, the Savior explains this passage more fully: Moses commanded that a bill of divorce be given because of the hardness of husbands’ hearts—not granting separation, but preventing murder (Deut. 24). For it is much better, even though a painful discord may result, than that blood should be shed through hatred.

(Verses 34ff.) “But I say to you, do not swear at all: neither by heaven, because it is God’s throne; nor by the earth, because it is the footstool of his feet; nor by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great King. Nor shall you swear by your head, because you cannot make one hair white or black. Let your speech be, ‘Yes, yes,’ ‘No, no’; whatever is more than these is from evil.”

The Jews are known always to have had this very bad custom of swearing by the elements, as the prophetic word frequently reproves them (Isa. 65). Whoever swears either venerates or loves the one by whom he swears. In the Law it was commanded that we swear only by the Lord our God (Deut. 6 and 7). The Jews, swearing by angels, the city of Jerusalem, the Temple, and the elements, venerated created things and bodily realities [Note: “With the honor and service owed to God disregarded. Finally, etc.” —Rabanus] with the honor and service due to God [Note: Let the guarantor be St. Hilary, who says in this passage: “For by these names of the elements it was a religious practice among the Jews to swear—by heaven and earth, and Jerusalem, and also by their own head—by which things they offered the reverence of an oath in insult to God.”].

Consider, finally, that here the Savior did not forbid swearing by God, but by heaven, earth, Jerusalem, and one’s own head. This had been conceded to them as to little children: just as they sacrificed victims to God, lest they should sacrifice them to idols, so they were permitted to swear by God—not because they did this rightly, but because it was better to offer this to God than to demons. The truth of the Gospel, however, does not admit an oath, since every faithful word stands in place of an oath. [Col. 0040B]

(Verses 38.) “You have heard that it was said: An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth. But I say to you, do not resist evil.”

The one who says “an eye for an eye” does not wish to remove one eye from another, but to preserve both. Our Lord, abolishing retaliation, cuts off the beginnings of sins. In the Law there is retribution; in the Gospel, grace. There guilt is corrected; here the beginnings of sins are removed.

(Verses 39.) [31] “But if someone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also. And to one who wishes to contend with you in judgment and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well. And whoever presses you into service for one mile, go with him for two.”

The ecclesiastical person is depicted as an imitator of the one who says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (below, 11:29). Having been struck on the cheek, he confirms his promise: “If I have spoken wrongly, bear witness to the wrong; but if rightly, why do you strike me?” (John 18:23). David also says something similar in the Psalm: “If I have repaid those who repaid me with evil” (Ps. 7:5). And Jeremiah in the Lamentations: “It is good for a man when he has borne” [Al. “when he has sat under,” etc.] “the yoke from his youth. Let him give his cheek to the one who strikes him; let him be filled with reproaches” (Lam. 3:27, 30).

This is directed against those who think that the God of the Law is one and the God of the Gospel another: for both there and here gentleness is taught. [Note: One older Palatine manuscript reads, “another prophetic meaning, another meaning of the Gospel.” A later hand restored the printed reading in the margin. At the end of the section, corruptly—as again below—Martianaeus had read lacessat (“may provoke”) for lassescat (“grows weary”).] According to the mystical interpretations, when our right cheek has been struck, we are not commanded to offer the left, but the other—that is, the other right cheek. [Col. 0040D] For the righteous person has no left side. If a heretic strikes us in debate and wishes to wound the right doctrine, another testimony from the Scriptures should be set against him; and we should offer him successive right hands to strike until the enemy’s anger grows weary.

(Verses 42–43.) “Give to the one who asks you, and do not turn away from the one who wishes to borrow from you. You have heard that it was said: You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.”

If we understand this as referring only to almsgiving, it cannot hold in the case of most poor people. But even the rich, if they always give, will not be able to give forever. After the goodness of almsgiving, therefore, instructions are given to the apostles—that is, to teachers—that those who received freely should give freely (Matt. 10). This kind of money never runs out; rather, the more it is given, the more abundantly it is multiplied. And when it waters the fields subject to it, the fountain’s stream never dries up.

(Verses 44.) “But I say to you: Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you.”

Many judge God’s commands by their own weakness rather than by the strength of the saints. They think that what has been commanded is impossible, and say that it is enough for virtue not to hate one’s enemies; but that loving them is commanded beyond what human nature can bear. We must therefore understand that Christ commands not the impossible but the perfect—something David did with Saul and Absalom (1 Sam. 24 and 26; 2 Sam. 18). The martyr Stephen also prayed for those stoning him (Acts 7). And Paul desires to be accursed for his persecutors (Rom. 9). Jesus both taught and did these things, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

(Verses 45.) “So that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust. For if you love those who love you, what reward will you have? Do not even tax collectors do this? And if you greet only your brothers, what more are you doing? Do not even the Gentiles do this? Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your heavenly Father is perfect.”

If someone becomes a son of God by keeping God’s commands, then he is not a son by nature but by his own choice.

(Chapter 6.—Verse 1.) “Take care that you do not perform your righteousness before men, in order to be seen by them; otherwise you will have no reward with your Father who is in heaven.” [Note: Another verse—“Therefore, when you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before you as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, so that they may be honored by men”—is added unanimously by the Palatine codices, which otherwise are more sparing than the others in reproducing the words of Scripture. In fact, the entire exposition that follows refers to this verse.]

The one who sounds a trumpet while giving alms is a hypocrite. The one who, while fasting, disfigures his face in order to display the emptiness of his stomach in his appearance is also a hypocrite. The one who prays in synagogues and at street corners in order to be seen by men is a hypocrite. From all these examples it is gathered that hypocrites are those who do whatever they do in order to be glorified [Al. “honored”] by men.

It seems to me that the one who says to his brother, “Let me remove the speck from your eye” (Matt. 7:4), also does this for the sake of glory, so that he himself may appear righteous [Note: Formerly, “for he seems to do this for glory,” a reading whose meaning was not sufficiently clear. On the authority of the Palatine manuscripts, we have introduced the adverb “for” and the verb “seems,” restoring the sense to its original clarity in accordance with the manuscripts.]. Hence the Lord says to him: “Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your eye.” [Note: Two of our manuscripts and an equal number of those in Martianaeus insert here the following sentence: “Only then is the virtue of the observance acceptable to God, if it is done for God’s cause.”]

It is therefore not the virtue, but the cause of the virtue, that has a reward with God. Even if you turn aside a little from the straight road, it makes no difference whether you go to the right or to the left, since you have lost the true path. [Col. 0042A]

(Verses 3–4.) “But when you give alms, let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing, so that your alms may be in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you. And when you pray, you shall not be like the hypocrites, who love to pray standing in the synagogues and at the corners of the streets, so that they may be seen by men.”

Not only almsgiving, but whatever good work you do, should be unknown to the left hand. For if it knows, the works of the right hand are immediately defiled.

“Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward.” Not God’s reward, but their own. For they have been praised by men, for whose sake they practiced their virtues. [Col. 0042B]

(Verses 6.) “But when you pray, enter your room, and after shutting the door, pray to your Father in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.”

Taken simply, this instruction educates the hearer, so that he may avoid the empty glory of prayer. But it seems to me that it is more particularly commanded that we pray with the thought enclosed within the breast and the lips pressed together, as we also read that Hannah did in the Book of Kings: “Only her lips moved” [Note: The same Palatine manuscripts add: “and her voice was not heard.”] (1 Sam. 1:13).

(Verses 7.) “When you pray, do not speak at length, as the Gentiles do. For they think that they will be heard because of their many words. Do not therefore imitate them.”

If the Gentile speaks at length in prayer, then the Christian ought to speak little. For God is the hearer not of words but of the heart (Wis. 1:6). [Col. 0042C]

(Verses 8.) “For your Father knows what you need before you ask him. Therefore you shall pray in this way.”

At this point a certain heresy arises, along with the perverse doctrine of philosophers [Note: This was the argument—or rather the madness—of the Epicureans, concerning which Maximus of Tyre composed a very eloquent dissertation], who say: “If God knows what we are going to pray for, and knows what we need before we ask, we speak uselessly to one who already knows.” We should answer them briefly that we are not informers but petitioners. For it is one thing to tell something to one who does not know, and another to ask one who knows. In the former there is information; here there is service. There we faithfully make something known; here we implore in misery.

(Verses 9.) “Our Father, who are in heaven.”

By saying “Father,” they confess themselves to be sons.

[Col. 0042D] “Hallowed be your name.”

Not in you, but in us. For if God’s name is blasphemed among the Gentiles on account of sinners (Rom. 2:24), conversely it is sanctified on account of the righteous.

[Col. 0043A] (Verse 10.) “Your kingdom come.”

Either he asks generally for the kingdom of the whole world, so that the devil may cease to reign in the world, or that God may reign in each person and sin may not reign in the mortal body of human beings (Rom. 6). At the same time, we must note that it requires great boldness and a pure conscience to ask for God’s kingdom without fearing the judgment.

“Your will be done, as in heaven and on earth.”

May human beings serve you on earth just as the angels serve you blamelessly in heaven. Let those who daily claim that there are collapses in heaven be ashamed by this statement. For what benefit is the likeness of the heavens to us if there is sin even in heaven?

(Verses 11–13.) “Give us today our supersubstantial bread. And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. And do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil.”

What we have rendered “supersubstantial” is found in Greek as ἐπιούσιον; the translators of the Septuagint very frequently render this word as περιούσιον. We therefore examined the Hebrew, and wherever they rendered it περιούσιον, we found SGOLLA () [Note: The manuscripts read Sogolla, as we also noted at the end of the commentary on Malachi, chapter 3. Recall that passage, if you wish.], which Symmachus translated as ἐξαίρετον—that is, “special” or “excellent,” although in one passage he interpreted it as “peculiar.”

Therefore, when we ask God to grant us a peculiar or special bread, we ask for the bread of which he says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:51).

In the Gospel called “according to the Hebrews,” instead of “supersubstantial bread,” I found MAHAR () [Note: Two manuscripts read Moar, others Maar. Jerome, however, may have found Damhar or Damahar in that Gospel, if indeed he found the word meaning “tomorrow”; for Mahar in Hebrew means only “tomorrow,” whereas with the article it means “the morrow”—“our bread for the morrow.” Yet that article is characteristic not of Hebrew but of Chaldean and Syriac. From this one may again conclude that although Jerome says absolutely that that Gospel was written in Hebrew, it was written not in the Hebrew language but in Chaldean, Syriac, or Jerusalem Chaldean, and merely in Hebrew letters.], which is said to mean “for the morrow.” Thus the sense is: [Col. 0043C] “Give us today our bread for the morrow,” that is, our future bread.

We can also understand “supersubstantial bread” in another way: as bread that is above all substances and surpasses every creature. Others simply think, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement—“Having food and clothing, with these we shall be content” (1 Tim. 6:8)—that the saints are to concern themselves only with present food. Hence the later command: “Do not think about tomorrow.”

Amen. This is the seal of the Lord’s Prayer. Aquila interprets it as “faithfully”; we may say “truly.”

(Verses 14.) “For if you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your offenses.” [Note: One Palatine manuscript reads: “If this is what is written.”]

The statement, “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High’; but you shall die like human beings, and fall like one of the princes” (Ps. 82:6–7), is addressed to those who, because of their sins, deserved to become human beings from gods. Therefore those whose sins are forgiven are rightly also called human beings.

(Verses 16.) “For they disfigure their faces so that they may appear to men to be fasting. Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward.”

The word “disfigure,” which through the fault of translators has become common in ecclesiastical Scriptures, means something quite different from what is generally understood. Those who are expelled are “exterminated,” being sent outside the boundaries. In place of this expression, therefore, we should always understand “demolish,” which in Greek is ἀφανίζουσι. The hypocrite demolishes his face in order to feign sadness and, although his spirit may be rejoicing, to display mourning in his countenance.

(Verses 17ff.) “But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, so that you may not appear to men to be fasting, but to your Father who is in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.”

“Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where rust and moth destroy, and where thieves break in and steal.”

He speaks according to the custom of the province of Palestine, where on feast days people customarily anoint their heads. He therefore commanded that when we fast, we should show ourselves joyful and festive.

Many, reading the Psalmist’s words, “May the oil of the sinner not fatten my head” (Ps. 141:5), wish “good oil” to be intended in contrast, the oil of which it is said elsewhere: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 45:8) [Note: Three Palatine codices read: “with the oil of gladness.”]. They also hold that we are commanded, when practicing the virtues, to anoint the ruling faculty (ἡγεμονικὸν) of our heart with spiritual oil.

(Verses 21.) “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”

This should be understood not only of money, but of all passions [Al. “possessions”]. The glutton’s god is his belly; therefore he has his heart where he has his treasure [Al. “where his treasure is”]. The treasure of the luxurious person is banquets; of the wanton, amusements; of the lover, lust. “Everyone is enslaved by whatever overcomes him” (2 Pet. 2:19). [Col. 0044C]

(Verses 22–23.) “If your eye is simple, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark. Therefore, if the light that is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness be!”

Those suffering from eye disease [Al. “the eyes”] commonly see multiple lamps; the simple and pure eye looks upon simple and pure things. Transfer all this to the meaning. For just as the whole body is in darkness if the eye is not simple, so, if the soul has lost its ruling brightness, the whole understanding will remain in gloom. “Therefore, if the light that is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness be!” If the understanding, which is the light, is darkened by the soul’s fault, by what darkness, do you suppose, will that very gloom be enveloped?

(Verses 24.) “You cannot serve God and Mammon.”

Mammon is the Syriac word for “riches.” “You cannot serve God and Mammon.” Let the miser hear this; let the one who bears the Christian name hear that he cannot serve both riches and Christ. Yet he did not say “the one who has riches,” but “the one who serves riches.” For the slave of riches guards riches like a servant; but the one who has shaken off the yoke of servitude distributes them like a master.

(Verses 25.) “Therefore I say to you: Do not be anxious about your soul, what you shall eat, nor about your body, what you shall wear.”

In some codices “nor what you shall drink” has been added. Therefore, as for what nature grants to all and what is common to beasts, animals, and human beings, we are entirely freed from concern for it [Note: We have removed from this passage the negative particle that earlier editions inserted, contrary to all the manuscripts we use and to two others cited by Martianaeus. The printed books add the negative particle: “we are not entirely freed from concern for it.” The manuscript codices, however, retain the passage without the negation. Neither reading is contradictory if we take “concern” to mean anxiety. —Mart.].

But we are commanded not to be anxious about what we shall eat, because we prepare our bread in the sweat of our face. Work must be undertaken; anxiety must be removed. What is said—“Do not be anxious about your soul, what you shall eat, nor about your body, what you shall wear” (Gen. 3)—let us understand as referring to bodily food and clothing. As for spiritual foods and garments, we must always be concerned.

(Verses 26.) “Is not the soul more than food, and the body more than clothing?”

What he says is this: The one who provided greater things will certainly provide lesser things also.

“Look at the birds of heaven: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth much more than they?”

The Apostle commands us not to be wiser than we ought to be (Rom. 12:3). This testimony must also be preserved in the present chapter. There are some who, wishing to exceed the boundaries of the Fathers and fly to lofty heights, sink into the depths. They say that the “birds of heaven” are angels and the other powers engaged in God’s service, who are nourished by God’s providence without concern for themselves.

If this is how they wish the passage to be understood, how does the statement that follows, addressed to human beings, make sense: “Are you not worth much more than they?” [Note: Three Palatine manuscripts omit the word “more.”]

It should therefore be understood simply: If birds, which exist today and will not exist tomorrow, are fed by God’s providence without care or hardship, how much more are human beings, to whom eternity is promised, governed by God’s will! [Note: Here too the printed books and many manuscripts add: “whose soul is mortal, and when they cease to exist, they will never exist again.” This addition seems to have been inserted into Jerome’s text [Col. 0046D], which is complete without the sentence. We have therefore followed the manuscript of our monastery of St. Peter above the Diva. —Mart. The gloss, which the books printed before Martianaeus also contained, is as follows: “whose soul is mortal, and when they cease to exist, they will never exist again.” Two of our manuscripts, the Cistercian and the Palatine, as well as several examined by Martianaeus, retain it here.]

(Verses 27.) “Which of you, by thinking, can add one cubit to his stature? And why are you anxious about clothing?”

Just as he demonstrated by comparison with the birds that the soul is more than food, so he shows by what follows that the body is more than clothing, saying:

(Verses 28–30.) “Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow. They neither labor nor spin. But I say to you that not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these. If God so clothes the grass of the field, which exists today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, you of little faith!”

And truly, what silk, what royal purple, what work of the weavers can be compared with flowers? What is as red as the rose? What is as white as the lily? That violets possess purple, surpassed by no sea-purple dye, is a judgment for the eyes rather than for words.

(Verses 31ff.) “Do not be anxious, saying: What shall we eat? or What shall we drink? or With what shall we be clothed? For the Gentiles seek all these things. Your Father knows that you need all these things. Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow.” [Note: The Palatine manuscripts read “Do not be anxious about tomorrow,” omitting the remainder of the Scriptural text.]

“For tomorrow will be anxious for itself.” He has therefore granted that we should be concerned with present things, while forbidding us to think about the future. Hence the Apostle says: “Working night and day with our hands, so that we might not burden any of you” (1 Thess. 2:9).

In Scripture “tomorrow” signifies the future time, as Jacob says: “Tomorrow my righteousness will answer for me” (Gen. 30:33). And in the apparition of Samuel, the pythoness says to Saul: “Tomorrow you shall be with me” (1 Sam. 28:19).

(Verses 34.) “Sufficient for the day is its own trouble.”

Here he uses “trouble” not in opposition to virtue, but for labor, affliction, and the anxieties of the world—just as Sarah afflicted her maidservant Hagar (Gen. 16), which is expressed significantly in Greek as ἐκάκωσεν αὐτὴν. The concern of the present time is therefore sufficient for us; let us leave the care of the future, which is uncertain.

(Chapter 7.—Verses 1–2.) “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged. For with the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged; and with the measure with which you measure, it will be measured to you.”

If he forbids judging, how does Paul, in Corinth, judge the fornicator (1 Cor. 5), and Peter convict Ananias and Sapphira of lying (Acts 5)? But from what follows he shows what he forbade, saying: “For just as you have judged, so judgment will be made concerning you.” [Note: In place of the adverb “therefore,” which our manuscripts substitute, “here” was formerly read.] He therefore did not forbid judging, but taught how to judge.

(Verses 3–5.) “Why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye, but do not see the beam in your own eye? Or how do you say to your brother, ‘Brother, let me remove the speck from your eye,’ while behold, there is a beam in your eye? Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your eye, and then you will see how to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.”

He speaks of those who, although they themselves are guilty of a mortal crime, do not tolerate lesser sins in their brothers—“straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel” (Matt. 23:24). Therefore these people too, through a pretense of righteousness, as we said above, are rightly called hypocrites, because through the beam in their own eye they see the speck in their brother’s eye.

(Verses 6.) “Do not give what is holy to dogs.”

What is holy is the bread of the children. We must not therefore take the children’s bread and give it to dogs.

“Nor cast your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet and, turning, tear you apart.”

A pig, which wallows in mud, does not receive adornment. And according to Solomon’s Proverbs: “If it has a golden ring, it is found to be more disgusting” (Prov. 11:22).

Some wish dogs to be understood as those who, after the faith of Christ, return to the vomit of their sins; and swine as those who have not yet believed the Gospel and wallow in the mud of unbelief and vice. Such people ought not quickly to be entrusted with the Gospel pearl, lest they trample it and, turning, begin to destroy us.

(Verses 7ff.) “Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives; and the one who seeks finds; and to the one who knocks it will be opened.”

“Or what man is there among you who, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a serpent?”

Having previously forbidden the asking of bodily things, he shows what we ought to seek. If it is given to the one who asks, if the one who seeks finds, and if it is opened to the one who knocks, then it is clear that the one to whom it is not given, who does not find, and for whom it is not opened has not asked, sought, or knocked properly.

Let us therefore knock at Christ’s door, of which it is said: “This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it” (Ps. 118:20), so that when we have entered, the hidden and dark treasures in Christ Jesus may be opened to us, in whom all knowledge exists (Col. 2).

(Verses 11–12.) “If you, although you are evil, know how to give good things to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him! Therefore, whatever you wish people to do to you, do also to them. For this is the Law and the Prophets.”

It should be noted that he called the apostles evil—unless, under the person of the apostles, the whole human race is condemned, whose heart from infancy is inclined toward evil in comparison with divine mercy. Read Genesis (Gen. 8). Nor is it surprising that he calls the people of this world evil, since the Apostle Paul also says: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Eph. 5:16).

(Verses 13–14.) “Enter through the narrow gate, because the gate is wide and the way is broad that leads to destruction, and there are many who enter through it. How narrow the gate and constricted the way that leads to life! And there are few who find it.”

The broad way is the pleasure of the world, which people desire. The narrow way is opened through labors and fasts, and the Apostle also entered it (2 Cor. 6 and 11), exhorting Timothy to enter by it (1 Tim. 5).

At the same time, consider how precisely he spoke of the two ways. Many walk along the broad way; few find the narrow one. We do not seek the broad way, nor is finding it necessary: it offers itself spontaneously and is the way of those who wander. But not everyone finds the narrow way, nor do those who find it immediately enter by it. Indeed, many, after finding the way of truth, are captivated by the pleasures of the world and turn back from the middle of the journey.

(Verses 15ff.) “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves. You will know them by their fruits. Do people gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles? Thus every good tree bears good fruit, but the evil tree bears evil fruit.”

This can indeed be understood of all who promise one thing in appearance and speech but demonstrate another in their conduct. But it should be understood especially of heretics, who appear to clothe themselves in a garment of piety through continence, chastity, and fasting, while inwardly possessing a poisoned mind and deceiving the hearts of their simpler brothers. Thus, from the fruits of their souls by which they drag the innocent toward ruin, they are compared with ravenous wolves. [Col. 0048B] [Note: Our manuscripts supply the word “indeed.” They correct several other minor matters below.]

(Verses 18ff.) “A good tree cannot bear evil fruit, nor can an evil tree bear good fruit. Every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire. Therefore you will know them by their fruits.”

Let us ask the heretics, who say that there are two natures opposed to one another, whether, according to their understanding, a good tree can never bear evil fruit. How then did Moses, a good tree, sin at the waters of contradiction (Deut. 32)? How did David, after killing Uriah, lie with Bathsheba (2 Sam. 11)? How did Peter, in the Passion of the Lord, deny him, saying, “I do not know the man” (Matt. 26:72) [Note: Rabanus reads “the Lord”]? Or how, conversely, did Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law—a bad tree, since he did not believe in the God of Israel—give Moses good advice (Exod. 18)? How did Achior say something useful to Holofernes (Judit. 5)? And how did the Comic poet say what the Apostle confirmed as well said: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15:33)?

And when they find nothing to answer, we will bring forward Judas as well (John 13), once a good tree, who bore evil fruit after he betrayed [Al. “had betrayed”] the Savior; and Saul (Phil. 3), an evil tree while he was persecuting the Church of Christ, who afterward bore good fruit when he was transformed from a persecutor into a vessel of election (Acts 9).

A good tree therefore does not bear evil fruit only so long as it perseveres in the pursuit of goodness; and an evil tree remains in the fruits of sin only so long as it does not turn to repentance. For no one who remains what he was begins to be what he had not yet begun to be.

(Verses 21.) “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven will enter the kingdom of heaven.”

Just as he said above that those who possessed the clothing of a good life would not be accepted because of the wickedness of their doctrines, so now, conversely, he asserts that faith must not be granted even to those who, although strong in the integrity of faith, live shamefully and destroy the integrity of their doctrine by evil works. Both are necessary for God’s servants: that their works be confirmed by speech and their speech by works.

The following statement may seem contrary to this: “No one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:3). But it is customary in Scripture to take statements as referring to deeds, as is immediately demonstrated in what follows, where those who boast that they possess knowledge of the Lord without works are refuted and hear from the Savior: “Depart from me, workers of iniquity; I do not know you” (Luke 13:27). The Apostle speaks in the same sense: “They profess to know God, but they deny him by their deeds” (Titus 1:16).

(Verses 22.) “Many will say to me on that day: ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many mighty works?’”

To prophesy, perform mighty works, and cast out demons is sometimes not the merit of the one who performs them. Either the invocation of Christ’s name accomplishes this, or it is granted for the condemnation of those who invoke the name and for the benefit of those who see and hear, so that although people may despise those who perform signs, they may nevertheless honor God, at whose invocation such great miracles occur.

For Saul (1 Sam. 10), Balaam (Num. 23), and Caiaphas (John 11) prophesied without knowing what they were saying; and Pharaoh (Gen. 41) and Nebuchadnezzar (Dan. 2) learned future events through dreams. In the Acts of the Apostles, the sons of Sceva also appeared to cast out demons (Acts 19). Judas the apostle is likewise said to have performed many signs together with the other apostles, although he possessed the mind of a betrayer.

[42] (Verse 23.) “And then I will confess to them: ‘I never knew you.’”

He significantly said “I will confess,” because for a long time previously he had refrained from saying, “I do not know you.” The Lord does not know those who perish. But observe why he added, “I never knew you,” if, according to certain people, all human beings have always been among rational creatures.

(Vers. 24.) “Depart from me, you who work iniquity.” [Col. 0049D] Therefore everyone who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house upon rock. He did not say, “you who worked iniquity,” lest he seem to remove the possibility of repentance, but “you who work [iniquity]”—that is, who, up to the present hour, when the time of judgment has arrived, although you no longer have the ability to sin, nevertheless still retain the inclination.

(Vers. 25.) “And the rain fell, and the rivers came, and the winds blew; and they rushed upon that house, and it did not fall.” This rain, which tries to overturn the house, is the devil. The rivers are all the Antichrists who think contrary to Christ [Note: [Col. 0049] Earlier printed editions read “rivers, Antichrists,” without “all,” which word the manuscripts insert.]. The winds are “the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. VI).

[Col. 0050A] (Vers. 26.) “For it was founded upon rock. And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man.” Upon this rock the Lord founded the Church (Matt. XV); from this rock the apostle Peter received his name. Upon such a rock the serpent’s tracks are not found (Prov. XXX). Of this rock the prophet also speaks confidently: “He set my feet upon a rock” (Ps. XXXIX, 3). And elsewhere: “The rock is a refuge for the hares, or for the hyraxes” (Ps. CIII, 8). For a timid animal withdraws into the caverns of the rock; and, with its rough skin entirely armed with darts, it protects itself by such shelter. Hence Moses too is told, at the time when he had fled from Egypt and was the Lord’s little hare: “Stand in the cleft of the rock, and you shall see my back” (Exod. XXXIII, 21).

[Col. 0050B] (Vers. 27, 28.) “Who built his house upon sand; and the rain fell, and the rivers came, and the winds blew, and they rushed upon that house, and it fell; and its fall was great. And when Jesus had finished these words, the crowds were astonished at his teaching.” The foundation that the Apostle, the architect, laid (I Cor. III) is one: our Lord Jesus Christ. Upon this stable and firm foundation, itself founded upon a solid and powerful mass, the Church of Christ is built. But upon sand, which is fluid and cannot be joined together or brought into a single bond, every discourse of the heretics is built for the purpose of collapsing.

(Vers. 29.) “For he was teaching them as one having authority, and not as their scribes and Pharisees.” For they taught the peoples what had been written in Moses and the Prophets. But Jesus, as God and Lord of Moses himself, in accordance with the freedom of his will, either added to the law matters that seemed less important, or preached it among the peoples after changing it, as we have also read above: “It was said to the ancients: But I say to you.”

(Cap. VIII.—Vers. 1.) “When Jesus had come down from the mountain, great crowds followed him; and behold, a leper came and worshiped him, saying.” When the Lord descends from the mountain, the crowds meet him, because they were unable to ascend to higher things. And the leper is the first to meet him. For he was not yet able, with his leprosy, to hear such an extensive discourse from the Savior on the mountain. It should also be noted that he was the first to be healed individually; second, the centurion’s servant; third, Peter’s mother-in-law, feverish in Capernaum; fourth, those who were brought to him possessed by demons, whose spirits he expelled by a word, when he healed all who were ill. “And behold, a leper came and worshiped him, saying.” Properly after preaching and teaching, an occasion for a sign is offered, so that through the power of the miracle [Al. “the power of the miracle”], the discourse previously delivered may be confirmed for the hearers.

(Vers. 2.) “Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.” Whoever asks about his will does not doubt his power.

(Vers. 3.) “And Jesus stretched out his hand, touched him, and said: I will; be clean. And immediately his leprosy was cleansed.” When the Lord stretched out his hand, the leprosy immediately fled. At the same time, consider how humble and free from boastfulness the response is. He had said, “If you will”; the Lord answered, “I will.” He had first said, “You can make me clean”; the Lord joined this to his reply and said, “Be clean.” Therefore, contrary to what most Latins think, the words should not be joined and read, “I will make you clean,” but separated, so that he first says, “I will,” and then, commanding, says, “Be clean” [Al. “commands: ‘Be clean.’”].

(Vers. 4.) “And Jesus said to him: See that you tell no one.” And indeed, what need was there for him to boast in words of what he carried visibly in his body?

44 “But go, show yourself to the priests, and offer the gift that Moses commanded as a testimony to them.” He sends him to the priests for various reasons. First, on account of humility, so that he might seem to give honor to the priests [Note: [Col. 0051] The Palatine manuscripts read *deferre videatur*, “so that he may seem to render,” without *honorem*, “honor.”]. For the law had commanded that those who had been cleansed from leprosy should offer gifts to the priests. Then, so that when they saw the leper cleansed, they might either believe in the Savior or not believe. If they believed, they would be saved; if they did not believe, they would be without excuse. And at the same time, so that he would not seem to violate the law, as they very frequently accused him of doing.

(Vers. 5 ff.) “A centurion approached him, asking him and saying: Lord, my servant lies at home paralyzed and is grievously tormented. And Jesus said to him: I will come and heal him” [Note: [Col. 0051D] The same manuscripts add, “and heal him.”]. And the centurion answered and said: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof; but only say the word, and my servant will be healed.” We should not accuse the Lord of boastfulness because he immediately promises that he will go and heal him, since he saw the centurion’s faith, humility, and prudence. His faith: because, although he was a Gentile, he believed that a paralytic could be healed by the Savior. His humility: because he judged himself unworthy that the Lord should enter under his roof. His prudence: because beneath the covering of the body he perceived the hidden divinity, knowing that what was also visible to unbelievers would not benefit him, but rather what was hidden within. Concerning this prudence he also says:

(Vers. 9.) [Note: [Col. 0051D] Again, the same manuscripts read: “Behold, I too, although I am a man, say to this one,” etc.] “For I too am a man under authority” [Al. “established under authority”], “having soldiers under me; and I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.” He wished to show that the Lord also could accomplish whatever he wished, not merely through the coming of his body, but through the ministry of angels.

(Vers. 10.) “When Jesus heard this, he marveled, and said to those who followed him” [Note: [Col. 0051D] The words “he marveled,” which were absent from earlier printed editions, are supplied by our manuscripts, whose reading gives a complete sense.]. He marveled that he saw the centurion understand his majesty. For bodily infirmities, or hostile powers [Col. 0051D] by which a human being is often reduced to weakness, had to be driven away both by the word of the Lord and by the ministries of angels.

“Amen I say to you, I have not found such faith in Israel.” He is speaking of those present, not of all the patriarchs and prophets of earlier times; unless perhaps, in the centurion, the faith of the Gentiles is preferred to that of Israel.

(Vers. 11.) “But I say to you that many will come from the East and the West, and will recline with Abraham, [Col. 0052A] Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.” Since the God of Abraham, the Creator of heaven, is the Father of Christ, Abraham too is in the kingdom of heaven, and with him the nations who have believed in Christ, the Son of the Creator, will recline. The meaning we mentioned above is likewise fulfilled: in the centurion’s faith, the prerogative of the Gentiles is established, since peoples who will believe are recalled from the East and the West in response to his belief.

(Vers. 12.) “But the sons of the kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness.” He signifies the Jews as the sons of the kingdom, over whom God formerly reigned. “They will be cast into the outer darkness.” Darkness is always inward, not outward. But because the one who is expelled outside by the Lord leaves the light, it is for this reason called “outer darkness.”

[Col. 0052B] “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” If weeping belongs to the eyes and gnashing of teeth demonstrates the bones, then the resurrection of bodies and of those same members that had fallen is real.

(Vers. 14.) “And when Jesus had come into Peter’s house, he saw his mother-in-law lying sick with fever” [Al. “feverish”], “and he touched her hand, and the fever left her.” The woman’s hand is touched, and when her works have been healed, the infirmity of sins flees. Human nature is such that after a fever bodies become more exhausted [Note: [Col. 0052D] It was corruptly read as *lacessant*, “may they harass,” instead of *lassescant*, “may they grow weary”; we corrected the same error a little earlier in Martianus.]. At the beginning of recovery they feel the evils of their illness. But the health bestowed by the Lord restores everything at once [Note: [Col. 0052D] Two manuscripts read, “restores everything together,” and add that it is not enough merely to have been healed.]; it is not enough merely to be healed. Rather, to indicate an intensification (*epitasis*, ἐπίτασις) of strength, it is added:

(Vers. 15.) “And she arose, and ministered to them.” The hand that ministered was the hand that had been touched and healed.

(Vers. 16–18.) “When evening had come, they brought to him many who had demons; and he cast out the spirits with a word, and healed all who were ill” [Al. “healed”], “so that what had been spoken through the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: He himself took our infirmities and bore our diseases. When Jesus saw great crowds around him, he ordered the disciples to go across the lake.” All are healed not in the morning or at midday, but in the evening, when the sun is about to set; when the grain of wheat 46 dies in the earth, so that it may bear much fruit (John XII).

(Vers. 19, 20.) “And a certain scribe approached and said to him: Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go. And Jesus said to him: Foxes have dens and the birds of heaven nests, [Col. 0052D] but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.” This scribe of the law, who knew only the letter that kills, would not have been rejected by the Lord if he had said, “Lord, I will follow you wherever you go.” But because he considered him merely one teacher among many, and was a man of letters—which is expressed more significantly in Greek by *grammateus* (γραμματεύς)—and not a spiritual hearer, he therefore has no place in which Jesus can lay his head. [Col. 0053A] It is also shown to us, and for this reason the scribe was rejected, that although he had seen the greatness of the signs, he wished to follow the Savior in order to seek profits from the miracles of his works, desiring the same thing that Simon Magus had wished to buy from Peter (Acts VIII). Such faith is therefore justly condemned by the Lord’s sentence, and he is told: “Why do you wish to follow me for wealth and the profits of the world, when I am so poor that I do not even have a little lodging, and do not use a roof of my own?”

(Vers. 21.) “Another of his disciples said to him: Lord, permit me first to go and bury my father.” What similarity is there between the scribe and the disciple? The former calls him teacher; the latter confesses him to be Lord. The former desires to go and bury his father under the pretext of filial duty; the latter promises that he will follow him everywhere, seeking not the teacher but profit from the teacher.

(Vers. 22.) “But Jesus said to him: Follow me, and leave the dead to bury their own dead.” Whoever does not believe is dead. But if a dead man buries a dead man, we should not concern ourselves with the dead but with the living, lest, while we are anxious about the dead, we too should be called dead.

(Vers. 23.) “And when he had entered the boat, his disciples followed him; and behold, a great storm arose on the sea, so that the boat was covered by the waves.” He performed the fifth sign when, embarking from Capernaum, he commanded the winds and the sea. The sixth, when in the region of the Gerasenes he gave the demons power over the pigs. The seventh, when, entering his own city, he healed a second paralytic on a bed. For the first paralytic was the centurion’s servant.

(Vers. 24, 25.) “But he was sleeping. And they approached him and woke him, saying: Lord, save us; we are perishing. And Jesus said to them: Why are you afraid, you of little faith?” We read the type of this sign in Jonah (Jon. I), when, while the others are in danger, he himself is secure and sleeps, and is awakened; and by the command and sacrament of his passion he delivers those who awaken him.

(Vers. 26.) “Then he arose and commanded the winds and the sea, and a great calm arose.” From this passage we understand that all creatures perceive the Creator. For those whom he rebukes and those whom he commands perceive the one who commands—not according to the error of the heretics, who think that all things are animate [Note: [Col. 0053D] Some manuscripts add, “are sentient”; others, conversely, read, “are insentient.”], but by the majesty of the Creator, to whom what is insentient among us is sentient.

(Vers. 27–29.) “The men marveled, saying: What sort of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him? And when Jesus had come across the lake into the region of the Gerasenes, two men possessed by demons met him, coming out from the tombs, exceedingly savage, so that no one could pass along that road. And behold, they cried out, saying.” It was not the disciples but the sailors and the others who were in the boat who marveled. [Col. 0054A] But if someone stubbornly insists that those who marveled were the disciples, we will answer that they were rightly called “men,” since they did not yet know the Savior’s power.

(Vers. 30, 31.) “What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of God? Have you come here before the time to torment us?” A herd of many pigs was grazing not far from them. “The demons begged him, saying.” This is not a confession of the will, followed by a reward for the one who confesses, but an extortion imposed by necessity, which compels the unwilling—just as when runaway slaves, after a long time, see their master: they ask for nothing except to be spared the blows. So too, when the demons suddenly saw the Lord moving about on earth, they believed that he had come to judge them. The Savior’s presence is the demons’ torment. [Col. 0054B] Some people absurdly think that the demons knew that he was the Son of God, while the devil did not, on the grounds that these demons were less wicked than the one whose satellites they are. Since all the knowledge of disciples must be referred back to their teacher, both the demons and the devil should be understood to suspect rather than know that he is the Son of God [Al. “should be understood as suspecting”]. “No one knows the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Matt. XI, 27) [Note: [Col. 0054D] Two Palatine manuscripts insert the words of the sacred text: “nor does anyone know the Son except the Father.”].

(Vers. 32, 33.) “If you cast us out, send us into the herd of pigs. And he said to them: Go. And they went out and departed into the pigs. And behold, the whole herd rushed with great force down the precipice into the sea, and they died in the waters. The herdsmen fled, and when they came into the city, they reported everything, including what had happened to those who had been possessed by demons.” It was not because the Savior granted the demons what they requested that he said, “Go,” [Col. 0054C] but so that, through the destruction of the pigs, an opportunity for the salvation of human beings might be provided. For when the herdsmen saw this, they immediately reported it to the city. Let Manichaeus be ashamed: if the souls of human beings and beasts are of the same substance and from the same author, how are two thousand pigs drowned for the salvation of one human being?

(Vers. 34.) “And behold, the whole city came out to meet Jesus; and when they saw him, they begged him to depart from their territory.” Their request that he depart from their territory was not made out of pride, as some think, but out of humility, because they judged themselves unworthy of the Lord’s presence, just as Peter too, falling at the Savior’s knees after the catch of fish, said: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man” (Luke V, 8).

[Col. 0054D] (Cap. IX.—Vers. 1, 2.) “And Jesus entered the boat, crossed over, and came to his own city. And behold, they brought him a paralytic lying on a bed. When Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic: Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven.” We understand his city to be none other than Nazareth, from which he was also called a Nazarene. They brought him, as we said above, a second paralytic lying on a bed, because he was unable to enter by himself. When Jesus saw not the faith of the one being brought but of those who brought him, he said to the paralytic: “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven.” O marvelous humility! He calls “son” the one who was despised and weak, whose limbs were wholly disjointed, and whom the priests did not deign to touch. Or certainly he calls him “son” because his sins are forgiven. In the tropological sense, a soul sometimes lies in its body, with all the powers of its limbs dissolved; a perfect teacher brings it to the Lord to be healed. If it has been healed by his mercy, it receives such strength that it immediately carries its bed.

(Vers. 3, 4.) “And behold, certain scribes said within themselves: This man blasphemes. And when Jesus saw their thoughts, he said: Why are you thinking evil in your hearts?” We read in the Prophet that God says: “I am he who blots out your iniquities” (Isa. XLIII, 25). Consequently, because the scribes thought he was a human being and did not understand the words of God, they accuse him of blasphemy. But the Lord, seeing their thoughts, shows himself to be God, who can know the hidden things of the heart, and, as it were, speaks silently: “By the same majesty and power with which I behold your thoughts, I can also forgive the sins of human beings. Understand from yourselves what the paralytic receives.”

(Vers. 5, 6.) “Which is easier to say: ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say: ‘Rise and walk’? But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—then he said to the paralytic. There is a great difference between saying and doing. Whether the paralytic’s sins had been forgiven was known only by the one who forgave them. But “Rise and walk” could be confirmed both by the one who rose and by those who saw him rising. A bodily sign is therefore performed to prove a spiritual one, although forgiving the faults of body and soul belongs to the same power. We are also given the understanding that many bodily weaknesses occur on account of sins. And perhaps for this reason he first says, “Your sins are forgiven” [Al. “your” is omitted], so that when the causes of the weakness have been removed, health may be restored.

(Vers. 7, 8.) “Rise, take up your bed, and go to your house. And he rose and went to his house. When the crowds saw this, they were afraid and glorified God, who had given such authority to human beings.” Likewise, if the paralytic soul has risen and recovered its former strength, it carries the bed on which it had previously lain dissolved, and carries it into the house of its virtues.

[Col. 0055D] (Vers. 9.) “As Jesus passed on from there, he saw a man sitting at the tax booth, named Matthew. And he said to him: Follow me. And he rose and followed him.” The other evangelists, out of modesty and respect for Matthew, did not wish to call him by his familiar name, but called him Levi; for he had a double name. Matthew himself, however, in accordance with what is prescribed [Al. “said”] by Solomon—“The righteous man is his own first accuser” (Prov. XVIII, 17)—and elsewhere, “Declare your sins, so that you may be justified” (Isa. XLIII, 26), names himself Matthew and publican, in order to show readers that no one should despair of salvation if he has turned toward better things, since he himself was suddenly changed from a publican into an apostle.

Here Porphyry and Julian Augustus accuse either the ignorance of a historian who lies or the folly of those who immediately followed the Savior, as though they had irrationally followed just any man who called them, although such great virtues and such great signs had preceded him, which the Apostles unquestionably saw before they believed. Certainly the very radiance and majesty of the hidden divinity, which shone even in the human face, could draw people to itself at first sight. [Note: [Col. 0055D] Here are two passages parallel to those found below in chapter XXI. From them, however, one may infer that Jerome did not think this to have been a natural and inherent comeliness of Christ’s own body, but that he assumed the radiance of majesty for a time when he wished to draw people into admiration of himself and join them to himself, even against their will. See Epistle 65, to Principia, note 8.] For if a power of this kind is said to exist in the lodestone and in amber, so that they attract rings, straw, and bits of wood to themselves, how much more could the Lord of all creatures draw to himself those whom he wished?

(Vers. 10 ff.) “And it happened that, as he reclined at table in the house, behold, many publicans and sinners came and reclined with Jesus and his disciples. When the Pharisees saw this, they said to his disciples: Why does your teacher eat with publicans and sinners? But when Jesus heard this, he said: Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are ill. Go and learn what this means.” They saw that the publican had turned from sins to better things and had found a place for repentance; and therefore they too did not despair of salvation. Nor did they come to Jesus while remaining in their former vices, as the Pharisees and scribes murmured; rather, they came in repentance, as the Lord’s following discourse signifies when he says:

(Vers. 13.) “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice. For I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.” The Lord went to the banquets of sinners in order to have an opportunity to teach and to provide his hosts with spiritual food. In fact, although he is frequently described as going to banquets, nothing else is reported except what he did and taught there, so that both the Lord’s humility in going to sinners and the power of his teaching in the conversion of penitents might be demonstrated. In what follows—“I desire mercy, and not sacrifice” (Hos. VI, 6), and “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners”—by adducing testimony from the prophet, he rebukes the scribes and Pharisees, who, judging themselves righteous, avoided the company of sinners and publicans.

(Vers. 14.) “Then the disciples of John approached him, saying: Why do we and the Pharisees fast frequently, but your disciples do not fast?” A proud question, full of Pharisaic arrogance. At the very least, even if we say nothing else, the boasting of fasting must be condemned. Nor could the disciples of John be free from blame, since they slandered the one whom they knew had been proclaimed by their teacher’s words, and joined themselves to the Pharisees, whom they knew had been condemned by John, when he said (above, III, 7): “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” [Note: [Col. 0056D] Martianus restored the phrase “when he says.”]

(Vers. 15.) “And Jesus said to them: Can the sons of the bridegroom mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? But days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast.” Christ is the bridegroom; the Church is the bride. From this holy and spiritual marriage the Apostles were begotten.
