They cannot mourn as long as they see the bride in the bridal chamber and know that the bridegroom is with the bride [Note: [Col. 0057D] Rabanus adds, “and fast.”]. But when the wedding has passed and the time of the passion and resurrection has arrived, then the sons of the bridegroom will fast.

Some think that for this reason fasts should be undertaken after the forty days of the Passion, although the arrival of the day of Pentecost and of the Holy Spirit immediately afterward indicates to us that it is a festival [Note: [Col. 0057D] Earlier it was incorrectly read *indicent*, “they may accuse”; recall Epistle 41, in our recension, to Marcella, no. 3, and our observations there.]. Taking occasion from this testimony, Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla also observe a forty-day fast after Pentecost, because, when the bridegroom has been taken away, the sons of the bridegroom ought to fast. The custom of the Church, however, approaches the Lord’s passion and resurrection through humility of the flesh, so that by fasting we may prepare ourselves for spiritual nourishment.

According to the tropological sense, it should be understood that as long as the bridegroom is with us and we are in joy, we can neither fast nor mourn. But when he has withdrawn from us on account of sins [Note: [Col. 0057D] Three Palatine manuscripts add, “and flown away”], then a fast must be proclaimed, and then mourning must be taken up.

(Vers. 16, 17.) “No one puts a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment” [Al. “on an old garment”]. “For it takes away its fullness from the garment, and a worse tear is made. Nor do they put new wine into old wineskins; otherwise the wineskins burst, and the wine is spilled, and the wineskins perish. But they put new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved.” These things he was saying to them. His meaning is this: until a person has been reborn and, having laid aside the old man through my passion, has put on the new man, he cannot bear the stricter commands of fasting and continence, lest, through excessive austerity, he also lose the faith that he now appears to possess [Note: [Col. 0058D] Martianus read incorrectly *crudelitatem*, “cruelty.”].

He gives two examples, that of old and new wineskins and that of the garment. By the old wineskins we must understand the scribes and Pharisees. The patch of the new garment and the new wine signify the Gospel commandments, which the Jews cannot bear, lest a greater tear be made. The Galatians too wished to do something similar: to mix the commandments of the Law with the Gospel and put new wine into old wineskins. But the Apostle says to them: “O foolish [Al. “senseless”] Galatians! Who has bewitched you so that you should not obey the truth?” (Gal. III, 1). The Gospel discourse must therefore be poured into the Apostles rather than into the scribes and Pharisees, who, corrupted by the traditions of their ancestors, could not preserve the purity of Christ’s commandments.

For one thing is the purity of a virginal soul, unpolluted by any contagion of former vice, and another are the filthinesses of the soul that has been subjected to the lust of many [Note: [Col. 0058D] We have preferred this reading of all the manuscripts, both those used by us and those used by Martianus, to the other reading found in the printed editions: “and another is that of the soul which has been subject to the lust of many filthinesses.”].

(Vers. 18, 19.) “Behold, a certain ruler approached” [Note: [Col. 0058D] Our manuscripts add, “to Jesus”; this is also found in certain Greek copies: προσελθὼν τῷ Ἰησοῦ], “and worshiped him, saying: My daughter has just died; but come, lay your hand upon her” [Al. “your” is omitted], “and she will live. And Jesus rose and followed him, along with his disciples.”

This is the eighth sign, in which the ruler asks that his daughter be raised, unwilling to be excluded from the mystery of true circumcision. But a woman suffering from a flow of blood enters in, and is healed in the eighth place, so that the ruler’s daughter, excluded from this number, comes to the ninth, in accordance with what is said in the Psalms: “Ethiopia [Al. “from Ethiopia”] will hasten to stretch out her hands to God” (Ps. LXVII, 32). And: “When the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Rom. XI, 25–26).

[Col. 0058B] (Vers. 20.) “And behold, a woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years approached from behind and touched the fringe of his garment.” In the Gospel according to Luke it is written that the ruler’s daughter was twelve years old (Luke VIII). Note, therefore, that this woman—that is, the people of the Gentiles—began to suffer at the time when the Jewish nation believed [Al. “race”]. For vice is not revealed except by comparison with virtues.

This woman suffering from a flow of blood does not approach the Lord in a house or in a city, because according to the Law she was excluded from cities (Lev. XV; Num. V); she approaches him on the road, while the Lord is walking, so that as he goes to one person, another may be healed. Hence the Apostles also say: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first; but since you have judged yourselves unworthy of salvation, we are turning to the Gentiles” (Acts XIII, 46).

(Vers. 21.) “For she said within herself: If I only touch his garment, I shall be saved. But Jesus turned and, seeing her, said.” According to the Law, whoever touched a menstruating woman or one suffering from a flow of blood was unclean (Lev. XXV). She therefore touches the Lord so that she too may be healed of the affliction of blood.

(Vers. 22.) “Take courage, daughter; your faith has saved you. And the woman was saved from that hour.” He calls her “daughter” because her faith has saved her. He did not say, “Your faith will save you,” but, “It has saved you.” For in the very fact that you believed, you have already been saved.

(Vers. 23.) “And when Jesus had come into the ruler’s house and had seen the flute players and the crowd making a commotion, he said.” To this day the girl lies dead in the ruler’s house, and those who appear to be teachers are flute players singing a mournful song. The crowd of the Jews is not a crowd of believers but a crowd making a commotion.

(Vers. 24.) “Depart; for the girl is not dead, but sleeping.” And they mocked him. For all things live to God.

(Vers. 25.) “And when the crowd had been put outside, he entered.” For they were not worthy to see the mystery of the one rising, since they mocked the one who raised her with unworthy insults.

(Vers. 26.) “And he took her by the hand. And the girl arose. And this report went out into that entire land.” Unless the hands of the Jews, which are full of blood, are first cleansed, their synagogue, which is dead, will not rise again.

(Vers. 27.) “And as Jesus was passing on from there, two blind men followed him, crying out and saying” [Note: [Col. 0059D] Our manuscripts unanimously supply the rest of the verse: “Have mercy on us, Son of David. And when he had come into the house, the blind men approached him.”]. As the Lord Jesus passed through the ruler’s house and proceeded to his own house, as we read above—“He entered the boat, crossed over, and came to his own city”—two blind men cried out, saying: “Have mercy on us, Son of David.” Yet they are not healed on the road, or in passing, as they thought they would be; rather, after he came into his house, they approached him and entered, and their faith was first tested, so that they might then receive the light of true faith.

This is appropriately joined to the preceding sign, which we explained concerning the ruler’s daughter and the woman with the hemorrhage: there death and weakness were displayed, while here blindness is demonstrated. For both peoples were blind while the Lord was passing through this world and desiring to return to his house. Unless they confess and say, “Have mercy on us, Son of David,” and, when Jesus asks, “Do you believe that I can do this?” answer him, “Yes, Lord,” they will not receive their former light.

In another Gospel one blind man is recorded, sitting in Jericho with his garments torn, whom the Apostles forbid to cry out; but through his shameless persistence he receives healing (Mark X). That passage properly concerns the people of the Gentiles and must be expounded in its own volume.

(Vers. 28, 29.) “Have mercy on us, Son of David.” [Note: [Col. 0059D] Here the same manuscripts omit the entire scriptural passage that follows, beginning, “And when he had come…”] “And when he had come into the house, the blind men approached him, and Jesus said to them: Do you believe that I can do this for you? They said to him: Yes, Lord. Then he touched their eyes, saying: Let it be done for you according to your faith. And their eyes were opened.”

Let Marcion and Manichaeus and the other heretics who tear apart the Old Testament hear this, and let them learn that the Savior is called the Son of David. For if he was not born in the flesh, how is he called the Son of David?

(Vers. 30, 31.) “And Jesus sternly charged them, saying: See that no one knows. But when they went out, they spread his fame throughout that entire land.” Because of humility, the Lord, fleeing the glory of boastfulness, had given this command; but they, out of remembrance of the grace they had received, could not keep the benefit silent. Note, therefore, that there is something contradictory in the command given to them [Note: [Col. 0059D] Three manuscripts read *justum*, “right,” instead of *jussum*, “command,” as does Rabanus [Col. 0060D].]. These blind men are healed in the tenth place.

(Vers. 32.) “As they were going out, behold, they brought him a mute man possessed by a demon” [Note: [Col. 0060D] The oldest Gospel book of the Verona Library adds, “and deaf,” thus giving both interpretations of the word κωφοῦ], “and when the demon had been expelled, the mute man spoke.” The eleventh is the mute man, who receives his tongue for speaking. The Greek word *kōphon* (κωφόν), however, is more commonly used in ordinary speech to mean “deaf” rather than “mute.” But it is the custom of Scripture to use *kōphon* indifferently for either a mute or a deaf person. Spiritually, just as the blind receive light, so the tongue of the mute is loosened for speaking, so that he may confess the one whom he had previously denied.

(Vers. 33, 34.) “And the crowds marveled, saying: Nothing like this has ever appeared in Israel. But the Pharisees said: He casts out demons by the ruler of demons.” The crowd confesses God’s works and says: “Nothing like this has ever appeared in Israel.” In the crowd there is the confession of the nations. But the Pharisees, because they could not deny the power of God, slander his works and say: “He casts out demons by the ruler of demons,” thereby, through their slander, demonstrating the unbelief of the Jews down to the present day.

(Vers. 35.) And Jesus went around all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the Gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease and every infirmity. You see that he preached the Gospel equally in villages, cities, and towns—that is, among great and small—so that he might consider not the power of the nobility but the salvation of believers. He went around the cities, carrying out the work that the Father had commanded him, and possessing this hunger: to save unbelievers through his teaching. He taught the Gospel of the kingdom in synagogues and villages; and after preaching and teaching, he healed every disease and every infirmity, so that those whom speech had not persuaded might be persuaded by deeds. [Col. 0060C] Of the Lord it is properly said: “Healing every disease and every infirmity,” for nothing is impossible for him.

(Vers. 36.) But when he saw the crowds, he had compassion on them, because they were harassed and lying helpless, like sheep without a shepherd. Then he says to his disciples: The distress of the flock, the sheep, and the crowds is the fault of shepherds and the defect of teachers. Hence it follows:

(Vers. 37, 38.) “The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few. Therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest.” The plentiful harvest signifies the multitude of the peoples; the few laborers, the scarcity of teachers. And he commands them to ask the Lord of the harvest to [Note: [Col. 0060D] Two manuscripts have “drive out” (*ejiciat*) instead of “send” (*mittat*); and shortly afterward, “they will reap in exultation” (*in exsultatione metent*) instead of “in joy” (*in gaudio*). A little later they read “sowing seeds” (*mittentes semina*) instead of “carrying seeds” (*portantes*).] send laborers into his harvest. These are the laborers of whom the Psalmist speaks, saying: “Those who sow in tears will reap in joy. Going forth, they went and wept, carrying their seeds. But coming, they will come with exultation, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. CXXV, 7–8). And, to speak more plainly, the plentiful harvest is the whole crowd of believers; the few laborers are the apostles and their imitators, who are sent into the harvest.

(Cap. X.—Vers. 1.) And having summoned his twelve disciples, [Col. 0061A] he gave them power over unclean spirits, to cast them out and to heal every disease and every infirmity. The kind and merciful Lord and master does not begrudge his servants and disciples his powers. And just as he himself healed every disease and every infirmity, so he also grants his apostles power to heal every disease and every infirmity among the people. But there is a great difference between possessing and bestowing, giving and receiving. Whatever the one does, he does by the Lord’s power; if they do anything, they confess both their own weakness and the Lord’s power, saying: “In the name of Jesus, arise and walk” (Acts III, 6). It should be noted that in the twelfth place power to perform signs is granted to the apostles.

[Col. 0061B] (Vers. 2.) Now these are the names of the twelve apostles. The catalogue of the apostles is given so that all those who will be false apostles besides these may be excluded.

(Vers. 3.) First, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother; James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother; Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew the tax collector; and James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus. It belonged to him who searches the secrets of the heart to distribute the order of the apostles and the merit of each one. Simon, surnamed Peter, is written first, to distinguish him from the other Simon, who is called the Cananaean, from the village of Cana in Galilee, where the Lord turned water into wine (John II). He likewise calls James “the son of Zebedee,” because another James, the son of Alphaeus, follows. And he joins together the paired yokes of the apostles. [Note: [Col. 0061D] Earlier the text had *jugaque*; in one or two manuscripts, *juga quaeque*. Rhabb. reads: “he associates pairs in both cases.”] He joins Peter [Col. 0061C] and Andrew as brothers, not so much in flesh as in spirit; James and John, who, leaving their father’s bread, followed the true Father; Philip and Bartholomew; and likewise Thomas and Matthew the tax collector. The other evangelists, in joining the names, put Matthew first and Thomas afterward; nor do they add the name “tax collector,” lest they seem to insult the Evangelist by recalling his former way of life. But this man, as we said above, both places himself after Thomas and calls himself a tax collector, so that where iniquity abounded, grace might abound still more (Rom. V, 20).

(Vers. 4.) Simon the Cananaean. He is the one who in another Evangelist [variant: Gospel] is written “the Zealot” (Luke VI). For *Chana* is interpreted “zeal.” Ecclesiastical history relates that the apostle Thaddaeus was sent to Edessa [Col. 0061D] to Abgar, king of Osroene [Note: [Col. 0061D] In Erasmus’s edition we corruptly read, “to Abagar, king of Chosroene”; similarly in the Marian edition, “to Abagar, king of Chosidene.” Neither is true, nor do I know what kingdom Chosroene or Chosidene could have been. The true reading, retained by all the manuscript codices, is: “to Abgar, king of Osroene.” Osroene, or Osdroene, was a region of Syria on the Mesopotamian frontier [Col. 0062D], containing the cities of Edessa and Nicephorium beside the river Euphrates. Hence the Osroene people in Stephanus. MART.—Formerly, “Abagar, king of Chosidene.” See Eusebius, book I, chapter 15.], who is called Judas of James by the evangelist Luke and is elsewhere called Lebbaeus (Acts I), which means “little heart.” One must believe that he had three names, just as Simon was called Peter (Mark III), and the sons of Zebedee were named Boanerges [variant: Banerges], [Col. 0062A] because of the steadfastness and greatness of their faith.

And Judas Iscariot [Note: [Col. 0062D] Our manuscripts read more aptly: “But Judas Schariotes, either from the village in which he was born, or from the tribe,” etc.], who also betrayed him. He took his name either from the village or city in which he was born, or from the tribe of Issachar, so that he was born, as it were, by a prophecy for his own condemnation. For Issachar is interpreted “reward,” signifying the price of the traitor.

(Vers. 5, 6.) Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans; but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. This passage is not contrary to the command later given: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19). For this was commanded before the resurrection, that after the resurrection. [Note: [Col. 0062D] Victorius omits the word “command.”] Christ’s first coming had first to be announced to the Jews, [Col. 0062B] lest they have a just excuse in saying that they rejected the Lord because he had sent the apostles to the Gentiles and Samaritans. But tropologically we who are called by Christ’s name are commanded not to walk in the way of Gentiles and heretics by error, so that, where religion is divided, life too may be divided.

(Vers. 7, 8.) As you go, preach, saying: “The kingdom of heaven has drawn near. Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons.” Lest no one believe unlearned and illiterate men, rustic and without eloquence, when they promise the kingdom of heaven, he gives them power to heal the sick, cleanse lepers, and cast out demons, so that the greatness of the signs may prove the greatness of the promises. [Col. 0062C] And because spiritual gifts always become cheaper if payment intervenes, condemnation of greed is added.

“You received freely; give freely.” I, your master and Lord, bestowed this upon you without price; and you, give without price, lest the grace of the Gospel be corrupted.

(Vers. 9, 10.) Do not possess gold, silver, or money in your belts; no bag for the road, nor two tunics, nor shoes, nor a staff. [Note: [Col. 0062D] Some manuscripts add “in the hand.” They then read “hireling” instead of “laborer.”] For the laborer is worthy of his food. He appropriately gives these commands to proclaimers of truth, to whom he had previously said: “You received freely; give freely.” For if they preach in such a way as to receive no payment, possession of gold, silver, and coin is superfluous. For if they had gold and silver, [Col. 0062D] they would seem to preach not for the salvation of people but for gain. Nor bronze in pouches. Having cut off riches, he almost cuts off even life’s necessities, so that the apostles, teachers of true religion, who taught [variant: instructed] that all things are governed by God’s providence, might show themselves to give no thought [Col. 0063A] to tomorrow. No bag for the road. By this command he rebukes the philosophers commonly called [Note: [Col. 0063D] In Victorius, corruptly, *Bactroperatae*. They derived their name from staff and bag. Paschasius Rathertus, copying this passage almost from Jerome, says: “He restrains the belly and rebukes the philosophers called Bachnionites” [variant manuscript: Bactroperites], “who, regarding everything in the world as nothing, carried cellars with them.”] Bactroperites, because, though despising the world and treating all things as nothing, they carried a pantry with them. Nor two tunics. By the two tunics he seems to me to mean a double garment—not that in Scythia and places frozen by icy snow one ought to be content with a single tunic, but that by “tunic” we should understand clothing, lest, clad in one garment, we keep another out of fear of the future. Nor shoes. Plato too commanded that the two extremities of the body should not be covered and should not be habituated to the softness of head and feet. For when these have firmness, the other parts are more robust. Nor a staff: since we have the Lord’s help, why should we seek the protection of a stick? And because he had in a sense [Col. 0063B] sent the apostles out naked and unencumbered to preach, and the teachers’ condition seemed harsh, he tempered the severity of the command with the following sentence: “The laborer is worthy of his food.” “Receive only,” he says, “what is necessary for food and clothing.” Hence the Apostle also repeats: “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these” (I Tim. VI, 8). And elsewhere: “Let him who is instructed in the word share every good thing with him who instructs him” (Gal. VI, 6) [Note: [Col. 0063D] Martianus had omitted the word *verbo*, “in the word.”], so that those whose disciples reap spiritual things may make them partners in their material goods—not for greed, but for need. We have said this historically. But according to the anagogical sense, teachers may not possess gold, silver, and money in their belts. We often read gold for understanding, silver [Col. 0063C] for speech, bronze for voice; we may not receive these from others, but must possess them as given by the Lord. Nor may we accept the doctrines of heretics, philosophers, and perverse teaching; we must not be weighed down by worldly burden, be double-minded, or have our feet bound with deadly fetters; but, entering holy ground, must be barefoot; neither must we have a staff that turns into a serpent, nor rely upon any support of the flesh (Exod. IV, 7; IV Kings XVIII), because a staff and reed-like support of that sort is such that, if you press it a little, it breaks and pierces the hand of the one leaning upon it (Isa. XXXVI).

(Vers. 11.) Into whatever city or town you enter, inquire who in it is worthy, and remain there until you depart. Paul says concerning the ordination of [Col. 0063D] a bishop and deacon: “Moreover, they must have a good testimony from those outside” (I Tim. III, 7). When the apostles entered a new city, they could not know what sort of person each might be. Therefore the host is to be chosen by the people’s report and the neighbors’ judgment, lest the dignity of preaching be stained by the infamy of the host. Though they must preach to all, one host is chosen, not as conferring a benefit upon the one with whom he will stay, but as receiving one. For this is what is meant by “who in it is worthy” [variant: becomes]: that he may know he receives a favor rather than gives one.

(Vers. 12, 13.) On entering the house, greet it. And if that house is worthy, your peace will come upon it; but if it is not worthy, your peace will return to you. He covertly expresses the greeting of Hebrew and Syriac speech. For what is called *chaire* in Greek and *ave* in Latin is called in Hebrew and Syriac *shalom lakh* [SALOM LACH] or [Note: [Col. 0064D] I would not reject the reading preferred by our manuscripts, *Salamalach*, just as Cotelerius found it written in Latin letters in one Royal manuscript, no. 240.] *shalom immakh* [SALOM EMMACH], that is, “peace be with you.” What he commands means this: on entering a house, wish peace upon the host, and, as far as lies in you, calm the wars of discord. But if opposition arises, you will have the reward for the peace you offered; [Col. 0064B] they who wished to have war will possess it.

(Vers. 14.) Whoever does not receive you or hear your words, when you go out from that house or city, shake the dust from your feet. The dust is shaken from the feet as testimony to their labor: that they entered the city and apostolic preaching reached even to them. Or the dust is shaken off so that they receive nothing from them, not even what is necessary for food, since they despised the Gospel.

(Vers. 15.) Amen, I tell you: it will be more tolerable for the land of the Sodomites and Gomorrheans on the day of judgment than for that city. If it will be more tolerable for the land of the Sodomites and Gomorrheans [variant: the Gomorrheans] than for the city that did not receive the Gospel—and more tolerable because Sodom and Gomorrah were not preached to, whereas this city was preached to and yet did not receive the Gospel—then punishments among sinners are different.

(Vers. 16.) Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves. He calls the scribes and Pharisees wolves; they are the clergy of the Jews.

(Vers. 17, 18.) Therefore be prudent as serpents and simple as doves. But beware of people: for they will hand you over in councils, flog you in their synagogues, and bring you before governors and kings for my sake, as a testimony to them and the Gentiles. By prudence they are to avoid snares; by simplicity they are not to do [Note: [Col. 0064D] Rhabb. more correctly omits “evil” and refers this to snares.] evil. The serpent’s cunning is set forth as an example, because it hides its head with its whole body [Note: [Col. 0064D] Two Palatine manuscripts insert “when it is in danger.”] and protects [Col. 0064D] that in which its life is. So too, at the risk of our whole body, let us guard our head, which is Christ. The simplicity of doves is shown by the form of the Holy Spirit. Hence the Apostle also says: “Be infants in malice” (I Cor. XIV, 20).

(Vers. 19, 20.) But when they hand you over, do not be anxious how or what you are to say. For in that hour you will be given what to say. For it is not you [Col. 0065A] who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you. Above he had said: “They will hand you over in councils, flog you in their synagogues, and bring you before governors and kings for my sake.” Therefore, when we are brought before judges for Christ’s sake, we need only offer our will for Christ. Besides, Christ himself, who dwells in us, will speak for himself, and the grace of the Holy Spirit will be supplied in answering.

(Vers. 21.) Brother will hand brother over to death, and father son; children will rise against parents and put them to death. And you will be hated by all because of my name. We often see this happen in persecutions; and there is no faithful affection among those whose faith is different.

(Vers. 22.) But whoever perseveres to the end [Col. 0065B] will be saved. For it is not beginning, but finishing, that belongs to virtue.

(Vers. 23, 24.) When they persecute you in this city, flee to another. Amen, I tell you, you will not finish the cities of Israel before the Son of Man comes. A disciple is not above his master, nor a servant above his lord. It is enough for the disciple to be as his master, and the servant as his lord. This must be referred to the time when the apostles were sent to preach, to whom it is specifically said: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans” (above, same chapter); they should not fear persecution [variant: and should], but avoid it. We see [variant: saw] this done by believers at the beginning: when persecution arose in Jerusalem, [Col. 0065C] they were scattered throughout all Judea, so that the occasion of tribulation became the seedbed of the Gospel. Spiritually, however, we can say: when we have been persecuted in one city—that is, in one book or testimony of the Scriptures—we should flee to other cities, that is, to other volumes. Though the persecutor be contentious, the Savior’s help will arrive before victory is granted to the adversaries.

(Vers. 25.) If they called the master of the house Beelzebub, how much more his household! Therefore do not fear them. Beelzebub is the idol of Ekron, called in the book of Kings the idol of the fly (IV Kings I). Beel is Bel, or Baal; *zebub* means “fly.” Thus they called the prince of demons by the name of the filthiest idol, which is called a fly because of the uncleanness [Col. 0065D] that destroys the sweetness of oil (Eccl. X).

(Vers. 26.) For nothing is covered that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known. How, then, in the present age are the faults of many unknown? But this is written of the future time [variant: age], when God will judge the hidden [variant: concealed] things of people, illuminate the recesses of darkness, and make manifest the counsels of hearts. [Note: [Col. 0065D] So read many manuscript codices: one from the monastery of Bec, another of Sylva Major, one from the monastery of Blessed Mary above the Dives, and a fourth from the church of Narbonne. The printed editions read “of the future age,” and afterward retain “concealed things of people” for “hidden things,” [Col. 0066D] and “will make manifest” for “will make evident.” MART.] The meaning is: do not fear the cruelty of persecutors and the rage of blasphemers, [Col. 0066A] for the day of judgment will come, in which both your virtue and their wickedness will be displayed.

(Vers. 27.) What I tell you in darkness, say in the light; and what you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops. What you have heard in mystery, preach more openly; what you have learned secretly [variant: in secret], speak publicly; what I taught you in the small region of Judea, proclaim boldly [variant: say] in every city and throughout the whole world.

(Vers. 28.) And do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. If those who kill the body cannot kill the soul, then the soul is invisible and incorporeal, I mean in comparison with the more gross substance of our body. Or at least it will then be punished and feel torments when it receives its former [Col. 0066B] body again, so that it may be punished in the very body with which it sinned.

But rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna. The name Gehenna is not found in the old books, but is first introduced by the Savior. Let us therefore inquire into the occasion for this expression. More than once we read that an idol of Baal stood near Jerusalem at the foot of Mount Moriah, where Siloam flows (III Kings XI). This valley [Note: [Col. 0066D] Our manuscripts and some in Martianus, as well as the old printed books, read “and a small level plain”; then Victorius reads “numerous” for “wooded.”] and small level plain was watered and wooded, full of delights, and in it was a grove consecrated to the idol. The people of Israel had fallen into such madness that, abandoning the temple’s vicinity, they sacrificed there; delights overcame religious rigor, and they burned or initiated their sons to demons. That place was called *gehennom*, [Col. 0066C] that is, “the valley of the sons [variant: son] of Hennom.” The book of Kings (IV Kings XXIII), Chronicles (II Chron. XXVIII), and Jeremiah (Jer. VII, XIX, and XXXII) relate this most fully. God threatens to fill the place itself with corpses of the dead, so that it may no longer be called Tophet and Baal but Polyandrium, that is, “the tomb of the dead.” Thus future torments and everlasting punishments, by which sinners are to be tortured, are denoted by the name of this place. That Gehenna is twofold, of excessive fire and cold, we read most fully in Job (Job XXIV).

(Vers. 29 ff.) Are not two sparrows sold for an assarion? Yet not one of them falls to the ground without your Father. But even all the hairs of your head are numbered. Therefore do not fear; you are worth more than many sparrows. Everyone, then, who confesses me before people, I too will confess before my Father who is in heaven. But whoever denies me before people, I too will deny before my Father who is in heaven. The Lord’s discourse holds together, and what follows depends upon what precedes. Prudent reader, always beware a superstitious interpretation: do not make Scripture conform to your own meaning, but join your meaning to Scripture and understand what follows. Above he had said: [Col. 0067A] “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul”; now he continues: “Are not two sparrows sold for an assarion? Yet not one of them falls to the ground without your Father?” The meaning is: if small and cheap animals do not fall without God as author, if providence is in all things, and things that will perish in them do not perish without God’s will, then you, who are eternal, ought not to fear that you live apart from God’s providence. This meaning was also stated above: “Look at the birds of heaven: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth more than they?” [Note: [Col. 0067D] Two Palatine manuscripts read, “Are you not worth much more?”; and a little below, “of little faith” for “of scant faith,” etc.] And next: “Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow,” and the rest. “But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow cast into the oven, how much more you, [Col. 0067B] of scant faith!” Some force an interpretation of the two sparrows as soul and body. They similarly refer the five sparrows, according to Luke (Luke XII), sold for two assaria, to the senses. But how that interpretation can be fitted to the whole body of the Gospel discourse is no small difficulty. “But even all the hairs of your head are numbered. Therefore do not fear; you are worth more than many sparrows.” The meaning of our preceding exposition has been expressed more plainly: they ought not to fear those who can kill the body but cannot kill the soul, because if even small animals do not fall without God’s knowledge, how much more a person supported by apostolic rank! When he says, “But even all the hairs of your head are numbered,” he shows God’s immense providence toward people [Col. 0067C] and indicates his ineffable care: nothing of ours escapes God, and even small and idle things do not escape his knowledge. Those who deny the resurrection of the flesh mock the ecclesiastical interpretation at this point, as though we said that all hairs which have been numbered and cut off by the barber will rise again, whereas the Savior did not say, “All the hairs of your head are to be saved,” but “are numbered.” Where there is number, knowledge of the number is shown, not preservation of that same number.

(Vers. 34.) Do not think that I came to bring peace upon earth. I came not to bring peace, but a sword. Above he had said: “What I tell you in darkness, say in the light; and what you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops.” Now he adds what follows after preaching. At faith in Christ the whole world has been divided against itself: every household has had both unbelievers and believers, and therefore a good war has been sent, that a bad peace might be broken. Scripture records that God did something similar in Genesis against rebellious people who had moved from the East and were hastening to build a tower (Gen. XI) through which they might penetrate heaven’s heights: he divided their languages. Hence David also prays in the psalm: “Scatter, Lord, the nations that desire wars” (Ps. LXVII, 32).

(Vers. 35.) For I came to divide a man against [Col. 0068A] his father, a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a person’s enemies are those of his own household. This passage is written in almost the same words in the prophet Micah (Mic. VII). And it should be noted, wherever testimony from the Old Testament is adduced, whether only the sense or also the wording agrees. [Note: [Col. 0068D] Palatine codices: “whether also the words agree.”]

(Vers. 37.) Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me. And whoever loves son or daughter above me is not worthy of me. Since he had previously said: “I came not to bring peace, but a sword,” and to divide people against father, mother, and mother-in-law, lest anyone prefer family affection to religion, he added: “Whoever loves [Col. 0068B] father or mother more than me.” And in the Song of Songs we read: “Order love in me” (Song II, 4). This order is necessary in every affection. Love your father after God; love your mother; love your children. But if necessity comes, so that love for parents and children is compared with love for God and both cannot be preserved, let there be hatred toward one’s own and devotion toward God [variant: is]. He therefore did not forbid love for father or mother, but significantly added: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me.”

(Vers. 38, 39.) Whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me. Whoever finds [variant: has found] his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for my sake will find it. In another Gospel it is written: “Whoever does not take up his cross daily.” Let us not suppose that a single ardor of faith can suffice: the cross must always be carried, so that we may always learn to love Christ [Col. 0068C].

(Vers. 40.) Whoever receives you receives me; and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. A most beautiful order. He sends them to preach, teaches that dangers need not be feared, and makes affection subject to religion. Above he had taken away gold and shaken bronze from the belt. The Evangelists’ condition was harsh. Whence, then, expenses? Whence the necessities of life? He tempers the austerity of the commands by the hope of promises. “Whoever receives you,” he says, “receives me; and whoever receives me receives him who sent me,” so that in receiving apostles every believer may think that he has received Christ.

(Vers. 41.) Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward. And whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward. Whoever [Col. 0068D] receives a prophet as a prophet and understands him to speak of future things will receive a prophet’s reward. Therefore Jews, understanding the prophets carnally, will not receive the prophets’ reward. Alternatively: in every profession tares are mixed with wheat. He had said before: “Whoever receives you receives me; and whoever receives me receives him who sent me.” He had encouraged disciples to receive teachers. But believers might secretly reply: “Must we therefore receive false prophets and Judas the traitor also, and supply them with food?” Foreseeing this, the Lord says [Col. 0069A] that persons are not to be received, but titles; and that those who receive them do not lose their reward, even if the person received proves unworthy.

(Vers. 42.) Whoever gives one of these least ones only a cup of cold water to drink in the name of a disciple, amen, I tell you, will not lose his reward. We read in the prophet David: “To make excuses for excuses in sins” (Ps. CXL, 4): many allege seemingly just occasions for their sins, so that what they commit willingly may seem to be done from necessity. The Lord, searcher of hearts and reins, looks upon each person’s future thoughts. He had said: “Whoever receives you receives me.” But many false prophets and false preachers could impede this command; he also remedied this stumbling block, [Col. 0069B] saying: “Whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward.” Again, someone could make an excuse and say: “Poverty prevents me; my slender means hold me back, [Col. 0070A] so that I cannot be hospitable.” He dissolves this excuse by a very slight command: that we offer a cup of cold water with all our heart. “Cold water,” he says, not warm, lest in the warm water too an excuse be sought in poverty [Note: [Col. 0069B] Victorius reads “from lack of wood,” etc.] and lack of firewood. The Apostle also commanded something similar to the Galatians, as we have already said: “Let him who is instructed in the word share every good thing with him who instructs him” (Gal. VI, 6), and exhorts disciples to provide refreshment for their teachers. Because anyone could plead poverty and evade the command, before he proposes it, he resolves the impending question, saying: “Do not be deceived: God is not mocked. For whatever a person has sown, that also will he reap.” The meaning is: you vainly plead want, when your conscience has something else [Note: [Col. 0069B] The Cistercian and Palatine manuscripts do not have the word “your.”] [Note: [Col. 0069B] The printed editions retain another sense, namely, “lest you think you can deceive [Col. 0070B] the one exhorting.” In this manner I restore many things without notes, because it would be too long to enumerate each restoration of the text. MART.] You can deceive me [Col. 0070B] as I exhort you; but know that, however much you sow, so much you will reap.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0069]

67 (Cap. XI.—Vers. 1, 2.) [Note: [Col. 0069D] In place of the printed Gospel passage, our manuscripts prefer the following: “But when John had heard about the works of Christ, he sent two of his disciples and said to him: ‘Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?’” Some manuscripts also add, after “had heard,” “while in prison.”] And it happened that, when Jesus had finished instructing his twelve disciples, he departed from there to teach and preach in their cities. He does not ask as though he were ignorant; for he himself had shown him to the others, who were ignorant, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John I, 29). He had also heard the voice of the Father thundering: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III, 17). Rather, just as the Savior asks where Lazarus had been laid so that those who pointed out the place of the tomb might at least in this way be prepared for faith and see the dead man rising, so John, about to be killed by Herod, sends his disciples to Christ so that, by this opportunity, seeing the signs and mighty works, they might believe in him and learn for themselves through their master’s question. That John’s disciples, moreover, were becoming proud against the Lord and possessed some sharpness arising from jealousy and envy, the earlier question also demonstrated, as the Evangelist reports: “Then the disciples of John approached him, saying: ‘Why do we and the Pharisees fast frequently, but your disciples do not fast?’” (ibid., IX, 14). And elsewhere: “Teacher, the one to whom you bore witness at the Jordan—behold, his disciples are baptizing, and [Note: [Col. 0070D] In place of “all,” which is also reflected in the Greek *pantes*, the Palatine manuscripts, as also the edition of Victorius, have “many.”] everyone is coming to him” (John III, 26), as though they had said: “We are being deserted; there are few with us, while the crowd runs to him.”

(Vers. 3.) “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?” He does not say, “Are you the one who has come?” but, “Are you the one who is to come?” The meaning is: “Send me word, because I am about to descend to the underworld: should I announce to the dead that you are the one whom I announced to the living? Or is it unfitting for the Son of God to taste death, and are you going to send another for these mysteries?”

[Col. 0070C] (Vers. 4, 5.) And Jesus answered and said to them: “Go and report to John what you hear and see: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise.” John had asked through his disciples: “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?” Christ demonstrates signs, not answering what he had been asked, but addressing the scandal of the messengers: “Go,” he says, “and tell John the signs that you see: the blind seeing, the lame walking, and the rest.” And what is no less than these:

“The poor are evangelized.” Whether “the poor in spirit,” or certainly those poor in possessions [Note: [Col. 0070D] Some manuscripts read “works” (*operibus*) instead of “possessions” (*opibus*).], so that in preaching there may be no distinction between noble and ignoble, rich and needy. These things demonstrate the rigor of the teacher and confirm the truth of the instructor: that with him everyone who can be saved is equal. But when he says:

(Vers. 6.) “And blessed is the one who is not scandalized by me,” he strikes at the messengers, as will be shown in what follows.

(Vers. 7.) But as they were going away, Jesus began to say to the crowds concerning John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? But what did you go out [Col. 0071A] to see? A man dressed in soft garments? Behold, those who wear soft garments are in kings’ houses.”

If the preceding statement was spoken against John, as many think, in the words, “Blessed is he who is not offended by me,” how is John now praised with such great commendations? But since the surrounding crowd did not know the mystery of the question and thought that John was doubting about Christ—the one whom he himself had pointed out with his finger—so that they might understand that John had not asked for himself but for his disciples, he says: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? Surely not to see a man like a reed, who is carried about by every wind and, through fickleness of mind, doubts about the one whom he had previously preached? Or perhaps he is compelled by the goads of envy against me, and his preaching pursues empty [Col. 0071B] glory, so that he may seek profits from it? Why would he desire riches, so that he might abound in sumptuous food? He feeds on locusts and wild honey. Or in order to be dressed in soft garments? Camel hair is his covering. Such food and clothing are received in the lodging of a prison, and such is the dwelling place of the preaching of truth. But flatterers, those who pursue profits, seek riches, abound in luxuries, and wear soft garments—these are in kings’ houses.” From this it is shown that a strict life and austere preaching ought to avoid the courts of kings and withdraw from the palaces of soft-living men.

(Vers. 8.) “But what did you go out to see—a prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.” John is greater than the other prophets in this respect: the one whom they had preached as coming, he demonstrated with his finger to have come, [Col. 0071C] saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold, the one who takes away the sins of the world.”

And because, in addition to the prophetic privilege, a further distinction was granted to the Baptist, that he should baptize his Lord [Note: Rhabb.: “and to whom the Baptist also received, in addition to the height of prophecy, the privilege that his own, etc.”], he therefore adds [Al. “whence adds”] an αὔξησιν (increase, augmentation) of merits [Note: In manuscript codices: “making an αὔξησιν of merits,” that is, an augmentation. MART.], bearing testimony from Malachi, in whom the angel is also proclaimed (Malach. II). Let us not think that John is called an angel here by participation in nature, but by the dignity of his office—that is, “messenger”—because he announced the Lord who was to come.

(Vers. 11.) “Amen I say to you, there has not arisen among those born of women anyone greater than John the Baptist.” He says, “among those born of women.” He is therefore preferred to those human beings who are born of women and from the intercourse of man, but not to the one who was born of the Virgin and of the Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, in saying, “There has not arisen among those born of women anyone greater than John the Baptist,” he did not place John above the other prophets and patriarchs and all human beings, [Col. 0071D] but equated the others with John. [Note: This is how all the manuscripts read in the earlier editions; but they made John equal to the others. MART.] For it does not immediately follow that, if others are not greater than he, he is greater than the others; rather, it means that he has equality with the other saints.

But “the one who is lesser in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.” Many wish this to be understood of the Savior: that the one who is lesser in time is greater in dignity. But let us understand it simply: every saint who is already with God is greater than the one who is still standing in the battle. For it is one thing to possess the crown of victory, another still to fight in the line of battle. Some wish to understand this as referring to the last angel in heaven who ministers to the Lord, preferring him to any first-ranking human being who remains on earth.

(Vers. 12.) “But from the days of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it.” If John was the first—as we said above—to announce repentance to the peoples, saying, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is drawing near,” then consequently from his days the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it. For great is the violence involved in being born on earth and seeking a dwelling in heaven, possessing by virtue what we did not possess by nature.

(Vers. 13.) “For all the prophets and the Law prophesied until John.” This does not exclude the prophets after John. For we read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts XI, 21) that Agabus prophesied, as did the four virgin daughters of Philip. Rather, it means that the Law and the prophets whom we read as having been written—whatever they prophesied—prophesied concerning the Lord. Therefore, when it is said, “All the prophets and the Law prophesied until John,” the time of Christ is indicated, so that the one whom they said was to come, John might show to have come.

(Vers. 14, 15.) “And if you are willing to receive it, he is Elijah who is to come. Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.” That the statement, “If you are willing to receive it, he is Elijah,” is mystical and requires understanding, the Lord’s following words demonstrate when he says, “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.” For if the meaning were plain and the statement obvious, why would it have been necessary to prepare us for its understanding?

John is therefore called Elijah, not according to the foolish philosophers and certain heretics who introduce μετεμψύχωσιν (transmigration of souls), but because, according to another testimony of the Gospel, he came “in the spirit and power of Elijah,” possessing either the same grace of the Holy Spirit or the same measure of it. The austerity of life and strictness of mind in Elijah and John are also alike. The one was in the wilderness, and the other in the wilderness; the one was girded with a leather belt, and the other had a similar girdle. Because Elijah denounced King Ahab and Jezebel for their impiety, he was forced to flee (III Kings XIX); because John denounced the unlawful marriage of Herod and Herodias, he was beheaded. Some think that John is called Elijah for this reason: just as Elijah, according to Malachi, will precede the Savior’s second coming and announce the Judge who is to come, 71 so John did this at the first coming; and each is the messenger either of the Lord’s first coming or of his second.

(Vers. 16 ff.) “But to what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplace, who call to their companions and say: We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we mourned for you, and you did not lament [Note: Most codices omit “for you”; others read “we mourned” instead of “we lamented.”]. For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say: He has a demon. The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say: Behold, a glutton and a drinker of wine, a friend of tax collectors and sinners. And wisdom was justified by her children.”

The generation of the Jews is compared to children sitting and crying out in the marketplace and saying to their companions, “We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we mourned, and you did not lament,” as Scripture says: “To what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplace,” and so forth.

We are therefore not granted unrestricted interpretation or a free allegorical interpretation [Note: In manuscript copies, “with a positive allegorical interpretation.” MART. Two Palatine manuscripts read “interpretation.” Some prefer “and allegorical” in place of “for allegory.” The expression is evidently open to both senses: whether “allegory” or “interpretation of allegory,” Jerome calls it *passiva*. Thus Tertullian, *To His Wife*, book I, says *passivam licentiam*, “license exercised by all”; and in *Against the Valentinians*, chapter 5: *passivos discipulos*, that is, “dissolute disciples”; and in *Against Marcion*, book I, chapter 7: *passivum*, “that which is permitted also to others,” namely, promiscuous or common. Finally, in *On Monogamy* he likewise speaks of *passivum sensum*, which Rhenanus explains as unlimited, wandering, free, and licentious. Jerome uses the word again below in chapter 12, so that the context of the passage does not fluctuate in different directions as something passive and wandering. MART.]. Rather, whatever we shall say about the children is to be referred to the likeness of the generation.

These children who sit in the marketplace are those of whom Isaiah speaks: “Behold, I and my children, whom God has given me” (Isa. VIII, 18). And in the eighteenth psalm (verse 8): “The testimony of the Lord is faithful, giving wisdom to the little ones.” And elsewhere: “From the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have perfected praise” (Ps. VIII, 3).

These children therefore sat in the marketplace—or ἐν ἀγορᾷ, as it is more significantly said in Greek—the place where many things are offered for sale. And because the Jewish people did not wish to hear, they did not merely speak to them but cried out with full throats: “We played the flute for you, and you did not dance.” We urged you to perform good works in response to our song and to dance to our pipe, just as David also danced before the ark of the Lord (II Kings VI), but you were unwilling. “We mourned,” and we urged you to repentance, but you were unwilling even to do this, despising both kinds of preaching: the exhortation to virtues and repentance after sins.

Nor is it surprising that you have rejected the twofold way of salvation, since you have equally spurned both God’s [Al. the reading omits “God’s”] fasting and his abundance. 72 If fasting pleases you, why did John displease you? If abundance, why did the Son of Man displease you? You call one of them demon-possessed and the other a glutton and a drunkard [Al. “you called”]. Since you were unwilling to accept either discipline, “wisdom was justified by her children”—that is, God’s dispensation and teaching.

And I, who am the power of God and the wisdom of God (I Cor. I), have been rightly shown by my children, the apostles, to have acted justly; to them the Father revealed what he had hidden from the wise and prudent in their own eyes (John XVII). In some Gospels it is read: “Wisdom was justified by her works” (Luke VII, 35). For wisdom does not seek the testimony of words but of works.

(Vers. 20.) “Then he began to reproach the cities in which most of his mighty works had been performed, because they had not repented.” The reproach of the cities of Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum is disclosed by the heading of this section: he reproached them because, after so many mighty works and signs had been performed, they had not repented.

(Vers. 21, 22.) “Woe to you, Chorazin; woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works that were performed in you had been performed in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes. Nevertheless I say to you: It will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you.”

Chorazin and Bethsaida, cities of Galilee, are mourned by the Savior because, after such great signs and mighty works, they did not repent. Tyre and Sidon, cities devoted to idolatry and vices, are preferred to them. They are preferred because Tyre and Sidon trampled only upon the natural law, whereas these cities, after transgressing both the natural and the written Law, also regarded as insignificant the signs performed among them.

We ask where it is written that the Lord performed signs in Chorazin and Bethsaida. Above we read: “And he went around all the cities and villages, healing every illness,” and so forth (above IV, 23). Among the other cities and villages, therefore, it should be understood that the Lord also performed signs in Chorazin and Bethsaida.

(Vers. 23.) “And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You will descend to hell?” [Note: The reading of the most ancient Veronese manuscript should be noted: “Will you be exalted up to heaven, or down to hell?”]

In another copy we find: “And you, Capernaum, which have been exalted to heaven, will descend to the netherworld.” There is a twofold interpretation. Either you will descend to the netherworld because you resisted my preaching with extreme arrogance; or because, having been exalted to heaven through my lodging with you and through my signs and mighty works, and possessing such privilege, you will be punished with greater punishments because you were unwilling to believe even these things.

(Vers. 23, 24.) “For if the mighty works that were performed in you [Al. “in Sidon”] had been performed in Sodom, they might perhaps have remained until this day.” [Note: Two Palatine manuscripts omit the adverb “perhaps.”]

“Nevertheless I say to you: It will be more bearable for the land of Sodom than for you on the day of judgment.”

Let the prudent reader ask and say: If Tyre, Sidon, and Sodom could have repented at the preaching of the Savior and at the miracles of his signs, they are not at fault for having failed to believe; rather, the guilt of silence lies with the one who was unwilling to preach to those who would have repented.

The answer is easy and clear: We do not know God’s judgments, nor do we understand the mysteries of his individual dispensations. It had been the Lord’s purpose not to go beyond the boundaries of Judea, lest he give the Pharisees and priests a just occasion for persecution. Hence, before his passion, he also commanded the apostles: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans” (above X, 5).

Chorazin and Bethsaida are therefore condemned because they were unwilling to believe in the Lord who was present. Tyre and Sidon are justified because they believed in his apostles. Do not inquire into times when you see the salvation of believers.

But in Capernaum, whose name is interpreted as “most beautiful village,” unbelieving Jerusalem is condemned. To it Ezekiel says: “Sodom was justified in comparison with you” (Ezek. XVI, 52).

(Vers. 25.) “At that time Jesus answered and said: I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth.” Confession does not always signify repentance but also thanksgiving, as we read very often in the Psalms.

Let those who slander the Savior as created rather than born hear that he calls his Father the Lord of heaven and earth. For if he too is a creature, and a creature can call its Creator “father,” it was foolish for him not likewise to call the Lord of himself, heaven, and earth “Father.”

“For you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and have revealed them to little ones.” He gives thanks and rejoices in the Father because he has opened to the apostles the mysteries of his coming, which the scribes and Pharisees—who seem wise to themselves and prudent in their own eyes—did not know. “Wisdom was justified by her children.”

(Vers. 26.) “Yes, Father, because this was pleasing before you.” He speaks to the Father with the affection of one who seeks to please, so that the benefit begun in the apostles may be completed.

[Col. 0075C] (Vers. 27.) “All things have been handed over to me by my Father.” Understand mystically both the Father who hands over and the Son who receives. Otherwise, if we wish to understand it according to our weakness, when the one who receives begins to possess, the one who gave will begin not to possess.

The statement that all things have been handed over to him does not mean heaven and earth, the elements, and the other things that he himself made and created. Rather, it means those who, through the Son, have access to the Father—those who were formerly rebellious but afterward began to know God.

“And no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him.”

Let Eunomius be ashamed, since he claims for himself as much knowledge of the Father and the Son as they have of one another [Note: Victorinus has “boasting.”]. But if he argues from this and consoles his madness with the words that follow, “and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him,” he should understand that it is one thing to know what you know by equality of nature, and another to know by the graciousness of the one who reveals.

(Vers. 28, 29.) “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls.”

That sins are heavy burdens is also attested by the prophet Zechariah, who says that iniquity sits upon a talent of lead (Zech. V). And the Psalmist laments: “My iniquities have grown heavy over me” (Ps. XXXVII, 6).

Or certainly he invites those who were oppressed by the very heavy yoke of the Law to the grace of the Gospel.

[Col. 0076A] (Vers. 30.) “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” How is the Gospel lighter than the Law, when in the Law homicide is condemned, but in the Gospel anger is condemned? In what way is the grace of the Gospel easier, when in the Law adultery is punished, but in the Gospel desire is punished?

There are many commandments in the Law which the Apostle teaches cannot be fully carried out (Acts XV). In the Law, works are required, and whoever performs them will live by them. In the Gospel, the will is sought; even if it does not achieve its effect, it nevertheless does not lose its reward.

The Gospel commands what lies within our power—namely, that we should not desire; this is within our will. The Law, while it does not punish the will, punishes the act, so that you do not commit adultery.

Imagine that, during a persecution, some virgin is prostituted. Under the Gospel, because she does not sin by her will, she is received as a virgin; under the Law, she is rejected as corrupted.

(Cap. XII.—Vers. 1.) At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath; and his disciples, being hungry, began to pluck ears of grain and eat them.

In another Evangelist we also read that, because of the extreme pressure of the crowds, they did not even have an opportunity to eat, and therefore, as human beings, they were hungry (Mark II and Luke VI). The fact that they rub the ears of grain in their hands and relieve their hunger is an indication of a more austere life: they seek not prepared dishes but simple food.

(Vers. 2.) But when the Pharisees saw this, they said to him: “Behold, your disciples are doing what is not lawful for them to do on the Sabbaths.”

Observe that the first apostles of the Savior destroy the literal observance of the Sabbath, against the Ebionites, who, while accepting the other apostles, reject Paul as a transgressor of the Law.

(Vers. 3, 4.) But he said to them: “Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him: how he entered the house of God and ate the loaves of the Presence, which it was not lawful for him to eat, nor for those who were with him, but only for the priests?”

To refute the Pharisees’ slander, he recalls an event from ancient history: when David, fleeing from Saul, came to Nob and was received by the priest Ahimelech, he asked for food. Since he had no ordinary bread, Ahimelech gave him consecrated bread, which it was lawful for no one but the priests and Levites to eat.

Ahimelech asked only whether the young men were clean with respect to women; when David answered that they had been so from yesterday and the day before, he did not hesitate to give them the bread. He judged it better, as the prophet says, to free human beings from the danger of hunger than to offer sacrifice to God: “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice” (Hosea VI, 6). For the sacrifice pleasing to God is the salvation of human beings.

The Lord therefore argues: If David is holy and Ahimelech the high priest is not reproached by you, but both transgressed the commandment of the Law with a plausible excuse, and hunger was the cause, why do you not approve the same hunger in the apostles that you approve in others?

Although there is also a great difference in this matter: these men rub ears of grain with their hands on the Sabbath, while those men ate Levitical loaves; and the days of the Neomenia, on which he had been invited to a banquet, were approaching the Sabbath solemnity when he fled from the royal court.

Observe that neither David nor his young men received the loaves of the Presence before they had answered that they were clean with respect to women.

(Vers. 5.) “Or have you not read in the Law that on the Sabbaths the priests in the Temple violate the Sabbath and are without blame?”

“You slander my disciples,” he says, “because, as they pass through the grainfields, they have rubbed the ears of grain, doing so because hunger compelled them, although you yourselves violate the Sabbath in the Temple: you sacrifice victims, slaughter bulls, and burn holocausts in the fire upon a pile of wood; and, according to the testimony of another Gospel (John VI), you circumcise little children on the Sabbath, so that, while wishing to observe another commandment of the Law, you destroy the Sabbath.”

The Laws of God, however, are never opposed to one another. Prudently, where his disciples could be accused of transgression, he says that they followed the examples of David and Ahimelech. But the true violation of the Sabbath, without the excuse of necessity, he directs against those who had made the accusation.

(Vers. 6.) “But I say to you, something greater than the Temple is here.” [Note: All our manuscripts, and some manuscripts in Martianay, indicate that *hic* should be read not as a pronoun but as an adverb of place.]

“Here” is not a pronoun but an adverb of place: the place that contains the Lord of the Temple is greater than the Temple.

(Vers. 7.) “But if you had known what this means, ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice’ (Hosea VI, 6), you would never have condemned the innocent.”

What “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice” means, we explained above. What follows—“you would never have condemned the innocent”—is to be understood of the apostles.

The meaning is this: If you approved Ahimelech because he refreshed David and his young men when they were endangered by hunger, why do you condemn my disciples, who have done nothing of the kind?

(Vers. 8.) “And having departed from there, he came into their synagogue. And behold, there was a man who had a withered hand.”

This is the thirteenth man who is healed in a synagogue. And it should be noted that the withered hand was healed not on the road or outside, but in the assembly of the Jews.

(Vers. 9.) “And they questioned him, saying: Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbaths?”—so that they might accuse him.

Because the Pharisees had defended, by a plausible example, the destruction of the Sabbath of which they accused [Al. “by which they also accused the disciples”], they wish to slander him personally. They ask whether it is lawful to heal on the Sabbaths, so that if he does not heal they may accuse him of cruelty or weakness, and if he heals, of transgression [Al. “they may accuse”].

(Vers. 10 ff.) But he said to them: “What man will there be among you who has one sheep, and if it falls into a pit on the Sabbaths, will not take hold of it and lift it out [Al. “raise it up”]? How much more valuable is a human being than a sheep! Therefore it is lawful to do good on the Sabbaths.”

He resolves the proposed question in such a way as to condemn the questioners for avarice. “If,” he says, “on the Sabbath you hasten to rescue a sheep or any other animal that falls into a pit, caring not for the animal but for your own avarice, how much more should I rescue a human being, who is much more valuable than a sheep?”

(Vers. 13.) Then he said to the man: “Stretch out your hand.” And he stretched it out, and it was restored to health like the other.

In the Gospel used by the Nazarenes [Note: We have discussed this Gospel elsewhere, especially in the second chapter of the *Catalogue*. As for Jerome’s statement here that the Ebionites also used it, more recent critics deny this, since the Gospels of the Nazarenes and Ebionites did not differ from one another in merely one or two passages. In particular, the account of the Savior’s baptism, which the holy Father himself cites from the Nazarene text in his commentary on Isaiah XI, is presented differently and more briefly by Epiphanius, *Heresies* 30, § 13. But nothing further can be established from this than that certain passages were interpolated by the Nazarenes and others by the Ebionites—not, however, in such a way that their Gospels could be called different, since they agreed for the most part. Jerome therefore rightly treated them as one.], and by the Ebionites—a Gospel which we recently translated from Hebrew into Greek and which many call the authentic Gospel of Matthew—this man who had the withered hand is described as a mason. He begs for help in words of this kind: “I was a mason, earning my livelihood with my hands; I beg you, Jesus, to restore my health, so that I may not disgracefully beg for food.”

Until the coming of the Savior, the hand of the Jewish synagogue was withered, and God’s works were not performed in it. After he came into the world, the right hand was restored in the believing apostles and returned to its former work.

(Vers. 14.) But the Pharisees went out and took counsel against him, how they might destroy him.

The reason they plotted against the Lord was envy. [Note: Our manuscripts restore “his own”; we silently correct other minor matters of this sort throughout.] For what had he done to provoke the Pharisees to seek his death? Nothing except that a man had stretched out his hand.

Who among the Pharisees does not stretch out his hand on the Sabbath, carrying food, offering a cup, and performing the other things necessary for nourishment? If, therefore, stretching out the hand and lifting food or drink on the Sabbath is not a crime, why do they accuse another of what they themselves are shown to do—especially since this mason carried nothing of the kind but merely stretched out his hand at the Lord’s command?

(Vers. 15 ff.) But Jesus, knowing this, withdrew from there, and many followed him, and he healed them all. And he commanded them not to make him known, so that what had been spoken through the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled:

Knowing their plots and that they wished to destroy their Savior, he withdrew from there in order to remove from the Pharisees an occasion for impiety against him.

(Vers. 18.) “Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved, in whom my soul is well pleased. I will place my Spirit upon him, and he will announce judgment to the Gentiles. He will not contend, nor will he cry out.”

Through the prophet Isaiah this is spoken in the person of the Father: “I will place my Spirit upon him” (Isa. XLII, 1). The Spirit is placed not upon the Word of God and the Only-Begotten, who proceeded from the bosom of the Father, but upon the one of whom it was said: “Behold my servant” (ibid.).

(Vers. 19.) “Nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets.”

“For broad and spacious is the way that leads to destruction, and many enter through it” (above VIII). The many do not hear the voice of the Savior because they are not on the narrow way but on the spacious one.

(Vers. 20, 21.) “He will not break a bruised reed, and he will not extinguish smoking flax, until he sends forth judgment to victory; and in his name the Gentiles will hope.”

Whoever does not extend a hand to a sinner or bear his brother’s burden breaks the bruised reed. And whoever despises the small spark of faith in little ones extinguishes smoking flax. Christ did neither of these things; for he came to save what had perished.

(Vers. 22.) Then a demon-possessed man was brought to him, blind and mute, and he healed him, so that he spoke and saw. And all the crowds were astonished and said: “Can this be the son of David?”

But when the Pharisees heard this, they said: “This man does not cast out demons except by Beelzebub, the prince of demons.”

Three signs were performed together in one man: the blind sees, the mute speaks, and the demon-possessed is freed. This happened then in a bodily sense, but it is also fulfilled every day in the conversion of believers: when the demon has been expelled, they first behold the light of faith, and then mouths that were previously silent are opened in praise of God.

[Col. 0079C] (Vers. 25.) But Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said to them: “Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste, and every city or house divided against itself will not stand.” [Note: Two manuscripts read, “divided against itself will be laid waste”; others, “is laid waste.”]

The crowds were astonished and confessed that the one who performed such great signs was the son of David. But the Pharisees attributed God’s works to the prince of demons. The Lord responded not to their words but to their thoughts, so that in this way they might be compelled to believe in the power of the one who saw the hidden things of the heart.

(Vers. 26.) “And if Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself; how then will his kingdom stand?”

A kingdom and a city divided against themselves cannot endure. Just as small things grow through agreement, so great things collapse through discord.

If Satan fights against himself, and a demon is the enemy of a demon, the end of the world should already have come, so that the hostile powers would have no place in it—powers whose war among themselves is peace for human beings.

But if you think, O scribes and Pharisees, that the departure of demons is obedience to their prince, by which they deceive ignorant people through fraudulent pretense, what can you say about the healings of bodies that the Lord performed? Unless, perhaps, you also attribute the weakness of bodily members and the marks of spiritual powers to demons.

(Vers. 27.) “And if I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges.”

By “the sons” of the Jews he either customarily means the exorcists of that people or the apostles, born from their stock.

If he means the exorcists, who cast out demons by invoking God, he constrains them by a prudent question to confess that this is the work of the Holy Spirit. “If,” he says, “the expulsion of demons in your sons is attributed to God and not to demons, why should the same work in me not have the same cause?”

Therefore they will be your judges—not by authority but by comparison: they attribute the expulsion of demons to God, while you attribute it to Beelzebub, the prince of demons.

But if this is said of the apostles, as we ought rather to understand it, they will be their judges because they will sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Matt. XIX and Luke XXII).

(Vers. 28.) “But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God.” [Col. 0080B] In Luke we read this passage as follows: “But if I cast out demons by the finger of God” (Luke XI, 20).

This is the finger which even the magicians confess, when they performed signs against Moses and Aaron, saying: “This is the finger of God” (Exod. IV, 29); by it the stone tablets were written on Mount Sinai (Deut. IX).

If, therefore, the hand and arm of God is the Son, and his finger is the Holy Spirit, there is one substance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Let the inequality of the members not scandalize you, since the unity of the body edifies.

“Therefore the kingdom of God has come upon you.”

Either he signifies himself, concerning whom it is written elsewhere: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke XVII, 21), and: “He stands among you whom you do not know” (John XXVI); or certainly that kingdom which both John and the Lord himself preached: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is drawing near” (above III, 2).

There is also a third kingdom of Holy Scripture, which is taken away from the Jews and given to a nation producing its fruits (below XXI).

(Vers. 29.) “Or how can anyone enter the house of the strong man and seize his goods, unless he first binds the strong man, and then plunders his house?”

We must not be secure: that the Adversary is strong is also confirmed by the words of the victor. His house is the world, which lies in the evil one (I John V)—not by the dignity of the Creator but by the magnitude of the transgressor. We were once his goods.

The strong man has been bound and consigned to Tartarus, and crushed beneath the Lord’s foot; and when the tyrant’s dwelling was plundered, captivity was led captive.

[Col. 0080D] (Vers. 30, 31.) “He who is not with me is against me, and he who does not gather with me scatters. Therefore I say to you: Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven human beings, but blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven.”

No one should think that this is spoken about heretics and schismatics—although that too could be understood as an additional sense—but, from what follows and from the sequence of the discourse, it refers to the devil, because the works of the Savior cannot be compared with the works of Beelzebub.

The devil desires to hold human souls captive; the Lord desires to free them. The devil preaches idols; the Lord, knowledge of the one God. The devil leads people toward vices; the Lord calls them back to virtues. How, then, can those whose works are divided [Al. different] have harmony with one another?

[Col. 0081A] (Vers. 32.) “And whoever says a word against the Son of Man, it will be forgiven him; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, neither in this age nor in the age to come.”

How, then, do some of our people receive bishops and presbyters back into their rank after blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, when the Savior says that every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven human beings, but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in the present age or in the future?

Unless perhaps we take the example from Mark the Evangelist, who expressed the cause of such great anger more clearly when he said: “Because they were saying, ‘He has an unclean spirit.’” Therefore, whoever attributes the Savior’s works to Beelzebub, the prince of demons, and says that the Son of God has an unclean spirit, will never have his blasphemy forgiven (Mark III, 22).
