Or this passage should be understood in the following way: Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man, being offended by my flesh and thinking that I am merely a man—that I am the son of a carpenter and have brothers, James, Joseph, and Jude, and that I am a glutton and a drinker of wine—such an opinion and blasphemy [Note: It formerly read “opinion without blasphemy.” This reading was judged false, especially because our manuscripts contradict it; with their aid we have restored “and” in place of “without.”], although it is not free from the fault of error, nevertheless receives forgiveness because of the lowliness of the body (Mark VI, Luke III, Matt. XI).

But whoever clearly understands the works of God and, unable to deny their power, slanders them, driven by the same envy, saying that Christ, the Word of God, and the works of the Holy Spirit are Beelzebub—this person will not be forgiven, either in the present age or in the age to come.

[Col. 0081C] (Vers. 33.) “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad; for the tree is known by its fruit.”

He constrains them with a syllogism that the Greeks call ἄφυκτον (inescapable), which we may call “inevitable.” It encloses those questioned from both sides and presses them between its two horns.

“If,” he says, “the devil is evil, he cannot perform good works. But if the things you see being done are good, it follows that the one who does them is not the devil. For it cannot happen that good arises from evil or evil from good.”

But what follows:

### (Verse 34)

“Brood of vipers, how can you speak good things, since you are evil? For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.” He shows that they are a bad tree and that they produce such fruits of blasphemy as overflow from the devil’s seeds.

**[Variant:** *redundantis*, “overflowing,” instead of *redundantes*, “overflowing [fruits].”]

### (Verse 35)

“A good man brings forth good things from a good treasury, and an evil man brings forth evil things from an evil treasury.” Either he shows that the Jews themselves, blaspheming the Lord, bring forth blasphemies from a treasury of what sort; or the statement remains connected with the preceding question: just as a good man cannot bring forth evil things, nor an evil man good things, so Christ cannot perform evil works, nor the devil good works.

### (Verses 36–37)

“But I say to you that for every idle word which people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment. For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.” This too is connected with what precedes. The meaning is: If an idle word, which in no way edifies those who hear it, is not without danger to the one who speaks, and if each person will give an account on the day of judgment of his words, how much more will you, who slander the works of the Holy Spirit and say that I cast out demons by Beelzebub, have to give an account of your slander!

An idle word is one spoken without benefit either to the speaker or to the hearer: when, setting serious matters aside, we talk about frivolous things and tell old stories. But whoever repeats buffooneries, loosens people’s mouths into laughter, and utters something shameful will be held guilty not of an idle word but of a criminal one.

### (Verse 38)

“Then certain of the scribes and Pharisees answered him, saying: ‘Teacher, we wish to see a sign from you.’” They ask for a sign as though the signs they had seen were not signs. But another Evangelist explains more fully what they request: “We wish to see a sign from you from heaven” (Mark VIII, 11). Either they wanted fire to come down from above, after the manner of Elijah, or, in imitation of Samuel, thunder to roar, lightning to flash, and rains to pour during the summer, contrary to the nature of the place—as though they could not slander those phenomena as well and say that they had resulted from hidden and various disturbances of the air. For if you slander the things you see with your eyes, hold in your hands, and experience through their usefulness, what will you do with things that come from heaven? You will certainly answer that the magicians in Egypt also performed many signs from heaven (Exodus VII).

**[Note: [Col. 0082D]** The words are contrary to the nature of the locality; Rhabanus does not know them.]

### (Verse 39)

“He answered and said to them: ‘An evil and adulterous generation.’” He aptly said “adulterous,” because it had abandoned its husband and, according to Ezekiel, joined itself to many lovers (Ezekiel XVI).

### (Verse 40)

“It seeks a sign, and no sign will be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah” (Jonah II). “For just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea-monster three days and three nights, so will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights.”

We have discussed this passage more fully in the Commentary on the Prophet Jonah; we therefore refer the reader’s diligence to that work. For now, it is enough to say briefly that the whole is understood synecdochically, that is, from a part: not that the Lord remained in hell for all three days and three nights, but that the portion of Friday, the Lord’s Day, and the whole day of the Sabbath are understood as three days and as many nights.

### (Verse 41)

“The men of Nineveh will rise in the judgment with this generation and will condemn it, because they repented at the preaching of Jonah.” Not by the authority of pronouncing judgment, but by the example of comparison.

“And behold, something greater than Jonah is here.” Understand “here” as an adverb of place, not as a pronoun. According to the Septuagint translators, Jonah preached for three days; I, for so long a time. He preached to the unbelieving Assyrian nation; I, to the Jewish people, God’s people. He preached to foreigners; I, to citizens. He spoke with a simple voice, performing no signs; I, performing so many signs, endure the calumny concerning Beelzebub. Therefore something greater than Jonah is here—that is, presently among you.

**[Note: [Col. 0083D]** Rhabanus: “and, performing no sign, he was accepted; I, with so many [signs],” etc.]

### (Verse 42)

“The queen of the South will rise in the judgment with this generation and will condemn it, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon. And behold, something greater than Solomon is here.”

In the same way that the men of Nineveh will condemn unbelieving Israel, the queen of the South will condemn the Jewish people. This is the queen of Sheba, about whom we read in the Book of Kings and in Chronicles (1 Kings X; 2 Chronicles IX). Overcoming so many difficulties, abandoning her people and her kingdom, she came to Judea to hear Solomon’s wisdom and brought him many gifts. In Nineveh and in the queen of Sheba, the faith of the nations is secretly preferred to Israel.

**[Col. 0083B]** In Nineveh and in the queen of Sheba, the faith of the nations is secretly preferred to Israel.  
**[Variant:** *occulta*, “hidden,” instead of *occulte*, “secretly.”]

### (Verse 43)

“When the unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it passes through dry places, seeking rest, and does not find it. Then it says…”

Some think that this passage is spoken about heretics: that the unclean spirit which formerly dwelt in them, when they were pagans, is cast out when they profess the true faith; but afterward, when they have turned to heresy and adorned their house with feigned virtues, the devil returns to them, joined by seven other wicked spirits, and dwells in them, so that their last condition becomes worse than the first. Heretics are indeed in a much worse condition than pagans: in the latter there is hope of faith, whereas in the former there is the conflict of dissension.

Although this interpretation displays a certain attractiveness and the appearance of learning, I do not know whether it possesses the truth. For since, once either the parable or the example has been completed, the statement follows, “So will it be also with this most wicked generation,” we are compelled to refer the parable not to heretics and just anyone, but to the Jewish people, so that the context of the passage may not fluctuate passively and aimlessly in different directions, and be thrown into confusion after the manner of foolish people;

**[Note: [Col. 0083D]** The printed editions read, “so that the context of the passage may not fluctuate everywhere and aimlessly in different directions,” because the earlier editors did not know that Jerome calls a context “passive” when it suffers free, violent, and forced interpretations; above he likewise calls the interpretation of allegory “passive,” saying: “We are therefore not granted a free understanding, and the interpretation of allegory is passive.” **[Col. 0084D] MART.—** Victorius: *passim*. Recall what we observe a little above in chapter XI concerning this word.]

rather, it should remain connected with itself and answer either what comes before or what follows.

The unclean spirit went out from the Jews when they received the Law, and it passed through dry places, seeking rest for itself. Having been expelled, so to speak, from the Jews, it passed through the solitudes of the nations. When these nations afterward believed in the Lord, the spirit, finding no place among the nations, said:

### (Verse 44)

“I will return to my house from which I came.”

**[Note: [Col. 0084D]** The Palatine manuscripts add *pristinam*, “former.”]

**[Col. 0083D]** That is: “I will go back to the Jews, whom I had previously left.”

### (Verse 45)

“And when it comes, it finds the house vacant, swept clean, and put in order. Then it goes and takes with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and they enter and dwell there; and the last condition of that person becomes worse than the first. So will it be also with this most wicked generation.”

The temple of the Jews was vacant, for it did not have Christ as its guest, who said, “Rise; let us go from here” (John XIV, 31). And elsewhere: “Your house will be left to you desolate” (Luke XIII, 35). Since, therefore, they had neither the protection of God nor that of the angels, and since they were adorned with the superfluous observances of the Law and the traditions of the Pharisees, the devil returns to his former seat. After adding to himself a sevenfold number of demons, he inhabits his former house, and the last condition of that people becomes worse than the first.

They are now possessed by a much greater number of demons, blaspheming Jesus Christ in their synagogues, than they had been possessed in Egypt before they knew the Law. For it is one thing not to believe in someone who is to come, and another not to receive the one who has come.

Understand the sevenfold number added to the devil either with reference to the Sabbath, or with reference to the number of the Holy Spirit: just as in Isaiah seven spirits of virtues are said to have descended upon the branch from the root of Jesse and upon the flower that rises from the root (Isaiah XI), so, conversely, the number of vices may be consecrated in the devil.

### (Verses 46 and following)

“While he was still speaking to the crowds, behold, his mother and his brothers were standing outside, seeking to speak with him. Someone said to him: ‘Behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking you.’ But he answered the one who told him and said: ‘Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?’ And stretching out his hand toward his disciples, he said…”

The Lord was occupied with the work of speaking, teaching the peoples, and carrying out the ministry of preaching. His mother and brothers came, stood outside, and desired to speak with him. Then someone announced to the Savior that his mother and brothers were standing outside, seeking him.

It seems to me that the one who announced this did not announce it by chance and simply, but was laying a trap for the Savior, to see whether he would prefer flesh and blood to spiritual work. Therefore the Lord did not disdain to go out because he was denying his mother and brothers; rather, answering the one who was setting the trap, he stretched out his hand toward the disciples and said:

### (Verses 49–50)

“Behold, my mother and my brothers. For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother and sister and mother.”

These are my mother, who daily give birth to me in the minds of believers. These are my brothers, who do the works of my Father. Thus, contrary to Marcion and Manichaeus, he did not deny his mother so that he might be thought to have been born from a phantom; rather, he placed the apostles before his kinship, so that we too, in comparing loves, might prefer the spirit to the flesh.

“Behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking you.”

Some suppose that the brothers of the Lord were sons of Joseph by another wife, following the fantasies of the apocrypha and inventing a certain little woman named Melcha or Escha.

**[Note: [Col. 0084D]** I restore this reading from several manuscript codices. Marianus read *Moecham* in several copies, and not *Melcham*. The apocryphal books assigned to the other, invented wife of Joseph the name of one of the daughters of Aran; for the name of the first daughter of Aran, who married Nahor, was Melcha, while the other, Abraham’s wife, was called Jescha and Sarai.

**[Col. 0085C] MART.** Certain manuscripts have *Mecham*; two Palatine manuscripts mention only *Escham*, as do the editions published before Martianay; Victorius found *Moecham* in other copies. These are the names of Aran’s daughters, namely Melcha and Jescha, one of whom married Nahor and the other Abraham. They occur in chapter XVII and following of the *Protoevangelium of James* and in the *Gospel of the Infancy of the Lord*, the laughable fantasies of apocryphal books. Yet I do not deny that there is an ancient, though uncertain, tradition that Joseph was a widower and the father of six children by his former wife when Mary was betrothed to him. Epiphanius more or less followed this tradition (*Against Heresies* 51, § 10). Hippolytus of Thebes, as well as others among the ancients, report that Joseph had four sons and two daughters: James, Simon, Judas, and Joses; and that the daughters were named Esther and Thamar, whom others often call Martha, with the letters transposed. They themselves make his wife Escha or Salome, the daughter of Anchaeus, the brother of Zechariah, who was the father of John the Baptist. Sophronius, in a Fragment published by Lambecius, added a third daughter, Salome, bearing the same name as her mother, who later became the wife of Zebedee, by whom James and the Evangelist John were born. But it is tiresome to pursue these fantasies of the apocrypha. Rhabanus reads only *Escham*.]

But, as is contained in the book which we wrote against Helvidius, we understand the brothers of the Lord not as Joseph’s sons but as the Savior’s cousins, the children of Mary’s sister, who is said to have been the mother of James the Less, Joseph, and Judas—those whom we read called the Lord’s brothers elsewhere in the Gospel. That cousins are called brothers is demonstrated by all Scripture.

Let us give another interpretation. The Savior speaks to the crowds and inwardly teaches the nations. His mother and brothers—that is, the synagogue and the Jewish people—stand outside and desire to enter, but become unworthy of his speech. When they ask, seek, and send a messenger, they will receive the answer that they are free in their choice and can enter if they themselves also wish to believe; yet they will not be able to enter unless they ask others.

**[Variants:** *accipiunt*, “receive,” instead of *accipient*, “will receive”; *potuerunt*, “were able,” instead of *poterunt*, “will be able.”]

### Chapter XIII

### (Verse 1)

“On that day Jesus went out from the house and sat beside the sea. And great crowds gathered around him, so that he got into a boat and sat down, while all the crowd stood on the shore.”

The people could not enter Jesus’ house, nor be there where the apostles heard the mysteries. Therefore the compassionate and merciful Lord goes out from his house and sits beside the sea of this world, so that great crowds may gather around him

**[Variant:** *sedit*, “sat,” instead of *sedet*, “sits.”] and hear on the shore what they had not deserved to hear inside. He got into a boat and sat down, while all the crowd stood on the shore.

Jesus is amid the waves; the sea beats against him from one side and the other, yet in his majesty he is secure and brings his boat near the shore. The people, however, enduring no danger and surrounded by no temptations which they could not bear, stand on the fixed shore with firm footing, so that they may hear what is said.

**[Note: [Col. 0086D]** Two of our manuscripts insert the word *multae*, “great.”]

### (Verse 3)

“And he spoke many things to them in parables, saying…”

The crowd is not of one opinion but of various dispositions in each individual. Therefore he speaks to it in many parables, so that, according to their diverse inclinations, they may receive different teachings. It should be noted that he did not speak everything to them in parables, but many things. If he had said everything in parables, they would have departed without benefit. He mixes clear matters with obscure ones, so that through what they understand they may be drawn toward knowledge of what they do not understand.

### (Verse 4)

“Behold, the sower went out to sow. And while he was sowing…”

He was inside, staying at home and speaking the mysteries to the disciples. Therefore the sower who sows the word of God went out from his house to sow among the crowds. This sower is signified to be the Son of God, sowing the Father’s word among the peoples.

At the same time, observe that this is the first parable to be set down together with its interpretation. We must be cautious wherever the Lord explains his own words and, when asked by the disciples, discusses them inwardly: we should not presume to understand either something else, or more, or less, than what he himself has explained.

**[Note: [Col. 0086D]** The same manuscripts have: “either something else, or something more, or something less, than we should wish to understand,” etc. In Victorius’ edition *vel minus* is missing, apparently through an error arising from the similarity of the expressions *vel minus* and *velimus*.]

### (Verses 5 and following)

“Some fell beside the road, and the birds of the sky came and ate them. Others fell upon rocky ground **[Variant: *petrosis*, “rocky places,” instead of *petrosa*, “rocky ground.”]**, where they did not have much soil; and immediately they sprang up, because they had no depth of earth. When the sun rose, they were scorched; and because they had no root, they withered. Others fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked them. Others fell on good soil and gave fruit, one a hundredfold, another sixtyfold, another thirtyfold.”

Valentinus adopts this parable to support his heresy, introducing three natures: spiritual, natural or animal, and earthly. Yet here there are four: one beside the road, another rocky, a third full of thorns, and a fourth good soil. We shall postpone its interpretation for a little while, wishing to hear privately what is said with the disciples.

**[Note: [Col. 0086D]** The Palatine manuscripts and the old printed books have “spiritual, animal, and earthly,” with the word *natural* deleted, since it seems superfluous to the context. Rhabanus agrees with them.]

### (Verse 9)

“He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”

Whenever we are admonished by these words, we are summoned to understand what has been said.

**[Variant:** *commonemur*, “are admonished,” instead of *commovemur*, “are moved.”]

### (Verses 10–11)

“And the disciples came to him and said: ‘Why do you speak to them in parables?’ He answered and said to them: ‘Because it has been given to you to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given.’”

It must be asked how the disciples approach him when Jesus is sitting in the boat—unless, perhaps, we are to understand that they had boarded the boat with him earlier and, standing there, questioned him about the interpretation of the parable.

### (Verse 12)

“For whoever has, to him will be given, and he will abound; but whoever does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him.”

It is not that, according to an equal standard of judgment, something is added to those who have and that what those who do not have seem to possess is taken away. Rather, what is granted is given to the apostles, who possess faith in Christ, even if they have somewhat less in the way of virtues; but from the Jews, who did not believe in the Son of God, even whatever they possess through the good of nature is taken away. For those who do not possess the head of wisdom cannot understand anything wisely.

**[Note: [Col. 0087D]** Two of our manuscripts, and one belonging to Martianay, prefer *aequitate*, “equity,” to *aequalitate*, “equality.”]

### (Verses 13–14)

“Therefore I speak to them in parables: because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear, nor do they understand, so that in them the prophecy of Isaiah may be fulfilled, which says: ‘You will hear by hearing and will not understand; and seeing you will see and will not see.’”

This concerns those who stand on the shore and are separated from Jesus; while the sound of the waves roars around them, they do not hear clearly what is said. The prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled in them: “You will hear by hearing and will not understand; and seeing you will see and will not see” (Isaiah VI, 9).

These things were prophesied about the crowds who stand on the shore and are not worthy to hear the word of God. Let us therefore approach Jesus with the disciples and ask him to explain the parable, lest, together with the crowds, we appear uselessly to possess ears and eyes.

### (Verse 15)

“For the heart of this people has become dull, and they have heard heavily with their ears.”

He gives the reasons why, seeing, they do not see, and hearing, they do not hear: “The heart of this people,” he says, “has become dull, and they have heard heavily with their ears.”

And lest we perhaps think that the dullness of the heart and the heaviness of the ears belong to nature rather than to the will, he adds the fault of free choice and says:

“And they have closed their eyes, lest they should ever see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and turn, and I should heal them.”

Thus they hear in parables and in riddles because, with their eyes closed, they do not wish to perceive the truth.

### (Verse 16)

“But blessed are your eyes, because they see, and your ears, because they hear.”

If we had not read above that hearers were summoned to understanding, when the Savior said, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear,” we might now think that the eyes and ears receiving blessedness were understood as bodily ones.

But it seems to me that those blessed eyes are the ones able to recognize Christ’s mysteries, the eyes which Jesus commanded to be lifted on high so that they might behold the whitening harvests (John IV, 9). And those blessed ears are the ones of which Isaiah speaks: “The Lord opened my ear” (Isaiah L, 5).

**[Variant:** *corporales*, “bodily,” instead of *carni*, “of the flesh.”]

### (Verses 17–18)

“For truly I say to you, many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it. Therefore hear the parable of the sower.”

This passage appears contrary to what is said elsewhere: “Abraham desired to see my day; he saw it and rejoiced” (John VIII, 56). But he did not say, “All the prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see,” but “many.” Among many, it can happen that some saw and others did not, although even in this there is danger in interpreting the passage, lest we seem to make any distinction among the merits of the saints.

Therefore Abraham saw in a riddle; he did not see in the visible form. But you possess him in his presence, have your Lord, question him at will, and eat with him.

**[Note: [Col. 0087D]** The older printed books more correctly have the passage without the negative particle: “He saw in visible form.”]

### (Verse 19)

“Everyone who hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it…”

By saying this beforehand, he urges us to hear more attentively what is spoken.

### (Verses 20–21)

“The evil one comes and snatches away what was sown in his heart. This is the one who was sown beside the road. But the one sown upon rocky ground is the one who hears the word and immediately receives it with joy, yet has no root in himself and is temporary.”

The evil one snatches away the good seed. At the same time, understand that what is sown is in the heart, and that the different soils are the souls of believers.

“But when tribulation and persecution arise because of the word, he is immediately scandalized.”

Observe that it says “immediately scandalized.” There is therefore a difference between one who is compelled to deny Christ by many tribulations and punishments and one who is immediately scandalized and falls at the first persecution.

### (Verse 22)

“But the one who was sown among thorns is the one who hears the word, and the anxiety of this age and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and it becomes fruitless.”

It seems to me that what is said literally to Adam also signifies this mystically: “You shall eat your bread among thorns and thistles” (Genesis III, 18). Whoever gives himself over to the pleasures of the age and the cares of this world eats heavenly bread and true food among thorns.

And he aptly adds: “The deceitfulness of riches chokes the word.” Riches are flattering: they do one thing while promising another. Their possession is slippery; while they are carried here and there, with unstable footing they either abandon those who possess them or fill up those who do not possess them.

**[Note: [Col. 0088D]** Some manuscripts have *reficiunt*, “restore,” whereas formerly the reading was *resarciunt*, “patch up.” The printed reading is excellent.]

Therefore the Lord also asserts that the rich enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty, because riches choke the word of God and soften the strictness of the virtues.

### (Verse 23)

“But the one sown on good soil is the one who hears the word and understands it and bears fruit, one a hundredfold, another sixtyfold, and another thirtyfold.”

Just as in the bad soil there were three kinds—beside the road, rocky, and thorny places—so in the good soil there is a threefold difference: the fruit of a hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold.

In both the former and the latter, the substance does not change, but the will does. The hearts both of unbelievers and of believers are what receive the seed. “The evil one comes,” he says, “and snatches away what was sown in his heart.” And a second and third time he says, “This is the one who hears the word.”

**[Note: [Col. 0090D]** [This note is printed at the foot of column 90, but its callout letter, *d*, does not appear in the text.] Two Palatine manuscripts have *tantam*, “so great,” here and below, instead of *totam*, “the whole.” In Greek, however, the word is Πᾶσαν (*pasan*, “all”), and the Vulgate edition likewise reads *omnem*, “all.” Jerome, as Victorius also notes, adds: “Therefore what the Lord said could be accomplished by faith comparable to a mustard seed, the Apostle teaches can be accomplished by complete faith.”]

In the interpretation of the good soil as well, he says, “This is the one who hears the word.” First, therefore, we must hear; then understand; and after understanding, produce the fruit of teachings, bearing either a hundredfold fruit, or sixtyfold, or thirtyfold. We have discussed these matters more fully in the book against Jovinianus, and now touch on them briefly: assigning the hundredfold fruit to virgins, the sixtyfold to widows and the continent, and the thirtyfold to chaste marriage.

“For marriage is honorable, and the marriage bed undefiled” (Hebrews XIII, 4).

**[Note: [Col. 0089D]** The same Palatine manuscripts read *sancto*, “holy,” instead of *casto*, “chaste.” Compare the earlier book against Jovinianus.]

Some of our people refer the hundredfold fruit to martyrs. If that is so, the holy unions of marriage are excluded from good fruit.

### (Verses 24 and following)

“He set before them another parable, saying: ‘The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field. But while the people were sleeping, his enemy came and sowed weeds over the wheat and went away. When the plant had grown and produced fruit, then the weeds also appeared. The servants of the master of the household came and said to him: “Lord, did you not sow good seed in your field? From where, then, does it have weeds?” He said to them: “An enemy has done this.” The servants said to him: “Do you want us to go and gather them?” He said: “No, lest while gathering the weeds you uproot the wheat along with them. Let both grow until the harvest, and at harvest time I will say to the reapers: Gather the weeds first and bind them into bundles to burn them; but gather the wheat into my barn.”’”

This is the second parable whose interpretation is not immediately set down with it, but is explained after other parables have intervened. It is proposed here, and later, after the crowds have been dismissed, they come into the house and his disciples approach him, asking: “Explain to us the parable of the weeds of the field,” and so forth.

We should therefore not, through an overhasty desire to understand, seek its meaning before it has been explained by the Lord.

### (Verse 31)

“He set before them another parable, saying…”

The Lord was sitting in the boat, while the crowd stood on the shore. The crowd heard from a distance, while the disciples heard more closely. He sets before them another parable, as a rich master of a household might refresh invited guests with various foods, so that each might receive different nourishment according to the condition of his stomach.

Therefore in the earlier parable he did not say “another” in the sense of a different one, but “another” in the sense of an additional one. If he had introduced it as a different parable, we could not have expected a third; by saying “another,” he indicated that more would follow.

### (Verse 32)

“The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed, which a man took and sowed in his field. It is indeed the smallest of all seeds; but when it has grown, it is greater than all garden plants and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the sky come and dwell in its branches.”

Let it not trouble the reader if we set out the whole parables. Obscure matters must be discussed more fully, lest excessive brevity conceal rather than explain their meaning.

The kingdom of heaven is the preaching of the Gospel and the knowledge of the Scriptures which leads to life. Concerning it, he says to the Jews: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (below, XXI, 43).

Such a kingdom, therefore, is like a mustard seed, which a man took and sowed in his field. By the man who sows in his field, most understand the Savior, because he sows in the souls of believers. Others understand the man himself as the one sowing in his own field—that is, in himself and in his own heart.

Who is this sower except our understanding and mind, which, receiving the seed of preaching and nurturing the sowing with the moisture of faith, causes it to sprout in the field of its own breast?

The preaching of the Gospel is the smallest of all systems of teaching. At the first hearing it does not possess the appearance of truth, preaching God as man, God as dead, and the scandal of the cross. Compare such a teaching with the doctrines of the philosophers and their books, with the splendor of eloquence and the arrangement of their speeches, and you will see how much smaller the sowing of the Gospel is than the other seeds.

But when those other teachings have grown, they display nothing sharp, nothing vigorous, nothing alive; rather, everything flaccid, withered, and softened boils up into vegetables and herbs, which quickly dry up and fall.

**[Note: [Col. 0089D]** The words “and softened” are absent from our manuscripts.] This preaching, however, which seemed small at the beginning, when it has been sown either in the soul of a believer or throughout the whole world, does not rise into vegetables but grows into a tree, so that the birds of the sky—which we should understand either as the souls of believers or as powers devoted to God’s service—come and dwell in its branches.

I think that the branches of the evangelical tree which grew from the mustard seed are the diversities of doctrines, in each of which one of the birds mentioned above finds rest. Let us also take up the wings of a dove (Psalm LIV), so that, flying toward higher things, we may be able to dwell in the branches of this tree and make for ourselves little nests of teachings; fleeing earthly things, let us hasten toward heavenly ones.

Many people, reading that the mustard seed is the smallest of all seeds, and also reading what the disciples say in the Gospel, “Lord, increase our faith” (Luke XVII, 6), followed by the Savior’s answer, “Truly I say to you, if you have faith like a mustard seed and say to this mountain, ‘Move from this place,’ it will move,” think that the apostles either ask for a small faith or that the Lord doubts concerning a small faith.

But the Apostle Paul judges the faith compared with a mustard seed to be the greatest. For what does he say? “If I have all faith, so that I remove mountains, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians XIII, 2). Therefore what the Lord said could be accomplished by faith comparable to a mustard seed, the Apostle teaches can be accomplished by complete faith.

**[Note: [Col. 0089D]** Three Palatine codices have: “If you had faith like a mustard seed, you would say to this mountain, ‘Move from this place,’ and it would move.”]

### (Verse 33)

“He spoke another parable to them: ‘The kingdom of heaven is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour until the whole was leavened.’”

People’s tastes are different: some delight in bitter foods, others in sweet, others in harsher foods, and others in mild ones.

**[Variant:** *hi . . . illi*, “these . . . those,” instead of *alii . . . alii*, “some . . . others.”] Therefore, as we said above, the Lord sets forth different parables, so that there may also be different medicines according to the variety of wounds.

This woman who took the leaven and hid it in three measures of flour until the whole was leavened seems to me either to represent the apostolic preaching or the Church, which has been gathered from different nations. She takes the leaven—that is, the knowledge and understanding of the Scriptures—and hides it in three measures of flour, so that spirit, soul, and body, brought together into one, may not disagree among themselves; but when two or three have agreed, they may obtain from the Father whatever they ask (Matthew XVIII).

This passage is also interpreted in another way. We read in Plato, and the philosophical doctrine is widely known, that there are three passions in the human soul: τὸ λογικόν (*to logikon*), which we can interpret as “the rational faculty”; τὸ θυμικόν (*to thymikon*), which we may call “full of anger,” or “the irascible faculty”; and τὸ ἐπιθυμητικόν (*to epithymētikon*), which we call “the concupiscible faculty.”

That philosopher thinks that our rational faculty dwells in the brain, anger in the gall, and desire in the liver.

Therefore, if we too receive the evangelical leaven of the holy Scriptures mentioned above, the three passions of the human soul will be brought into unity, so that in reason we may possess prudence, in anger hatred of vices, and in desire longing for virtues. All this will be accomplished through the evangelical teaching which Mother Church has given us.

**[Note: [Col. 0091D]** In most manuscripts: τὸ λογιστικόν (*to logistikon*), “the rational faculty,” which… Rhabanus has “rational”; τὸ ὀργηστικόν (*to orgēstikon*), “that which we call full of anger,” or “the irascible faculty”; τὸ ἐπιθυμητικόν (*to epithymētikon*), “that which we call…”]

Let me also give a third interpretation, so that the curious reader may choose whichever he prefers from among several. They too interpret this woman as the Church, which has mixed the faith of human beings into three measures of flour: faith in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. When it has been leavened into one, it leads us not to knowledge of a threefold God but to knowledge of one divinity.

The three measures of flour likewise, since there is not a different nature in each, draw us toward the unity of substance.

**[Variant:** *quippe*, “indeed,” instead of *quoque*, “likewise.”]

This is indeed a pious interpretation, but the meaning of a parable or the uncertain understanding of riddles can never contribute authority to doctrines. A *satum* is a type of measure, according to the custom of the province of Palestine, containing one and a half *modii*. Other things are also said about this parable, but it is not part of the present subject to discuss everything concerning it.

### (Verse 34)

“All these things Jesus spoke to the crowds in parables, and without a parable he did not speak to them.”

He speaks in parables not to the disciples but to the crowds; and even to this day the crowds hear in parables, while the disciples question the Savior at home.

**[Note: [Col. 0091D]** Martianay had read *Domini*, “of the Lord,” but Jerome shows below from the Gospel itself that the disciples were accustomed to question Jesus at home.]

### (Verse 35)

So that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled:

> “I will open my mouth in parables;  
> I will utter things hidden from the foundation of the world.”

This testimony is taken from Psalm 77 (verse 2). I have read in some manuscripts—and the diligent reader may perhaps find the same—that in passage 95, where we have placed it, the Vulgate edition reads: “So that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled,” and there it is written, “through the prophet Isaiah, saying.”

[Note: We have noted the same matter elsewhere. And, so that here we may gather together other testimonies of the ancients, the author of Homily XVIII, under the name of Pope Clement, reads “through Isaiah.” The author of the *Breviary on the Psalter*, under the name of St. Jerome, p. 316, says: “Thus it is said in Matthew: ‘These things,’ he says, ‘were done so that what was written in Asaph the prophet might be fulfilled.’ Thus it is found in all the ancient manuscripts; but ignorant people removed it—that is, they took away ‘Asaph.’ Indeed, many Gospels still have it in this form: ‘so that what was written through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled: I will open in parables,’ etc. Isaiah does not say this, but Asaph. Finally, the impious Porphyry also brings this charge against us and says: ‘Your evangelist Matthew was so ignorant that he said, “what was written through Isaiah the prophet.”’ To these may be added the Anonymous author cited in the *Exposition of the Greek Fathers on the Psalms*, Psalm 77. Sabatier should have noticed this, although he presses upon us the Vulgate—and indeed that Italian recension—from some Colbertine manuscript or other, and idly discusses this passage of Jerome both in his preface and in his notes. It would have been better to observe that the holy Father calls it the Vulgate Edition, which, as the word itself indicates, held precedence over all the others. For when he was writing these Commentaries, he had already, about fifteen years earlier, revised the Gospels against the Greek manuscripts at the command of Damasus, and certainly had undertaken to revise no edition other than the Vulgate. Therefore the things he says about that Vulgate must be carefully noted: namely, that it was the oldest of all the translations, in which “through Asaph” was first written, then replaced by “through Isaiah,” and finally, afterward, this name too was removed by prudent men.]

Since this was not found in Isaiah, I think that it was afterward removed by prudent men. But it seems to me that it was originally published in this form: “What was written through Asaph the prophet, saying.” For Psalm 77, from which this testimony is taken, is inscribed with the title of the prophet Asaph. And the first copyist did not understand Asaph, but thought it was a scribal error, and corrected the name to Isaiah, whose designation was more familiar.

It must therefore be understood that in the psalms, hymns, and songs of God, not only David but also the others whose names are prefixed are to be called prophets: namely Asaph, Jeduthun, Heman the Ezrahite, Ethan, the sons of Korah, and the rest whom Scripture mentions.

And since it is said in the person of the Lord, “I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden from the foundation of the world,” we must consider more attentively and discover that Israel’s departure from Egypt is being described, and that all the signs contained in the history of Exodus are recounted. From this we understand that all those things that have been written are to be understood figuratively: that the letter does not merely resound openly, but also contains hidden mysteries. For this is what the Savior promises that he will declare, opening his mouth in parables and uttering things hidden from the foundation of the world.

### (Verse 36)

Then, having dismissed the crowds, he came into the house; and his disciples came to him, saying: “Explain to us the parable of the weeds of the field.”

Jesus dismisses the crowds and returns to the house so that the disciples may approach him and privately ask about those things which the people neither deserved to hear nor were able to understand.

“Explain to us the parable of the weeds of the field.”

### (Verses 37 and following)

In answer he said:

> “He who sows the good seed is the Son of Man. The field, however, is the world. The good seed—these are the children of the kingdom; but the weeds are wicked children. The enemy who sowed them is the devil. The harvest, however, is the consummation of the age; and the harvesters are angels. Therefore, just as the weeds are gathered and burned with fire, so will it be at the consummation of the age. The Son of Man will therefore send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all causes of stumbling and those who practice wickedness, and they will throw them into the furnace of fire; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

He plainly explained that the field is the world; the sower, the Son of Man; the good seed, the children of the kingdom; the weeds, wicked children; the sower of the weeds, the devil; the harvest, the consummation of the world; and the harvesters, the angels. All causes of stumbling are assigned to the weeds; the righteous are reckoned among the children of the kingdom.

Therefore, as I said above, we ought to give credence to those things that have been explained by the Lord. But the things that he left unspoken and entrusted to our understanding must be touched upon briefly.

By the men who sleep, understand the teachers of the churches. By the householders’ servants, understand none other than the angels, who daily see the face of the Father (Matthew 18). The devil is called “the enemy man” for this reason: because he ceased to be God. And in Psalm 9 it is written of him: “Arise, O Lord; let man not prevail” (Psalm 9:20).

For this reason, let the one who has been placed over the Church not sleep, lest through his negligence the enemy man sow weeds over the top—that is, the doctrines of heretics.

But when it is said, “Lest perhaps, while gathering the weeds, you uproot the wheat along with them,” room is granted for repentance, and we are warned not to cut off a brother too quickly. For it may happen that the person who today has been corrupted by a harmful doctrine may repent tomorrow and begin to defend the truth.

The statement that follows also seems to be contrary to that command:

> “Let both grow together until the harvest” (Deuteronomy 13:5),

as does:

> “Remove the evil from your midst” (Isaiah 1),

and the command that we should in no way associate with those who are called brothers but are adulterers and fornicators.

For if uprooting is forbidden and patience must be maintained until the harvest, how are certain people to be expelled from our midst?

Between wheat and weeds—the plant that we call *lolium*—as long as it is still grass and has not yet brought forth a stalk with an ear, there is a great similarity, and in distinguishing them there is either no difference at all or an extremely difficult one [variant: “substance”]. The Lord therefore warns us not to pronounce judgment quickly wherever something is ambiguous, but to reserve the end of judgment for God, so that when the day of judgment comes, he may cast the person out from the assembly of the saints not on suspicion of a crime but on the basis of manifest guilt.

But when he said that the bundles of weeds would be handed over to the fires and the wheat gathered into the barns, it is clear that all heretics and hypocrites will be burned in the fires of Gehenna, while the saints, who are called wheat, will be received into the barns—that is, the heavenly dwelling places.

### (Verse 43)

> “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father [variant: ‘their own Father’]. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”

In the present age the light of the saints shines before human beings; after the consummation of the world, however, the righteous themselves will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.

### (Verse 44)

> “The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field. When a man finds it, he hides it; and for joy over it he goes and sells everything that he has and buys that field.”

Delayed by the frequent obscurities of the parables, we are exceeding a clause-by-clause interpretation, so that we seem almost to have passed from one kind of interpretation to another.

This treasure, in which all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden, is either God the Word, who is seen hidden in the flesh of Christ (Colossians 2), or the holy Scriptures, in which knowledge of the Savior has been stored up. When someone finds him in them, he ought to despise all the profits of this world so that he may possess the one whom he has discovered.

But when it follows, “When a man finds it, he hides it,” this is said not because he does so out of envy, but because, fearing for what he possesses and unwilling to lose it, he hides in his heart the one whom he has preferred to his former possessions.

[Note: Two of our manuscripts read: “but because he preserves it according to custom.” Moreover, the entire preceding exposition is taken from Origen’s Commentary on this passage: “It seems to me, according to these things, that the field is Scripture, sown with those things that are clear in the words of the history of the Law and the prophets and in the remaining sayings. For the account of the words of the whole of Scripture is rich and varied. The treasure hidden in the field consists of the hidden and concealed meanings of the wisdom that lies beneath its clear words, hidden in the mystery and in Christ.”]

### (Verses 45–46)

> “Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking good pearls. When he has found one precious [variant: ‘most precious’] pearl, he went away and sold everything that he had and bought it.”

The same thing is said here in different words as above. The good pearls that the merchant seeks are the Law and the prophets.

Hear, Marcion; hear, Manichaeus: the good pearls are the Law and the prophets, and knowledge of the Old Testament. But there is one pearl of surpassing value: knowledge of the Savior, the mystery of his Passion, and the secret of his Resurrection.

[Note: Jerome also largely copied this from Origen. It is sufficient to quote his statement in Latin: “That precious pearl is Christ, the Word of God, surpassing the precious Scriptures and the meanings of the Law and the prophets. Once he has been found, all the remaining things are easily obtained,” together with the other matters that you may consult for yourself.]

When the merchant finds it—like the apostle Paul—he despises as refuse and rubbish all the mysteries of the Law and the prophets and his former observances, in which he had lived blamelessly, so that he may gain Christ (Philippians 3).

This does not mean that the discovery of the new pearl is a condemnation of the former pearls, but that, in comparison with it, every other gem is less valuable.

### (Verses 47 and following)

> “Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea and gathering fish of every kind. When it was full, they drew it out; and sitting beside the shore, they selected the good into vessels [Note: Three Palatine manuscripts add ‘their own,’ which is not reflected in the Greek]; but they threw the bad outside. So will it be at the consummation of the age: the angels will go out and separate the wicked from the midst of the righteous, and they will throw them into the furnace of fire; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

After the prophecy of Jeremiah had been fulfilled, when he says, “Behold, I will send many fishermen to you” (Jeremiah 16:16), and after Peter and Andrew, James and John, the sons of Zebedee, had heard, “Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matthew 4:19), they wove for themselves from the Old and New Testaments a net of evangelical doctrines and cast it into the sea of this age.

To this day it is stretched amid the waves, catching from the salty and bitter whirlpools whatever falls into it—that is, both good and bad people, and the best and worst fish.

When the consummation and end of the world comes, as he himself explains more clearly below, the net will then be drawn to shore. Then the true judgment of the fish that are to be separated will be revealed, and, as though in some very tranquil harbor, the good will be placed in vessels of the heavenly dwelling places. But the bad, to be burned and dried up, will be received by the flame of Gehenna.

[Note: Origen’s interpretation of this passage should be compared; Jerome’s is exceedingly similar to it. Theophylact also took this passage from Origen.]

### (Verse 51)

> “Have you understood all these things?”

They say to him: “Yes.”

He said to them:

The discourse is addressed specifically to the apostles. He asks them, “Have you understood all these things?” because he does not want them merely to hear as the people do, but to understand as future teachers.

### (Verse 52)

> “Therefore every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure things new and old.”

The apostles had been instructed: they were the scribes and secretaries of the Savior, who inscribed his words and commandments on tablets of fleshly hearts; they flourished in the mysteries of the kingdoms of heaven and abounded in the resources of the householder, bringing forth from the treasure of their teaching things new and old, so that whatever they preached in the Gospel they might confirm by the words of the Law and the prophets.

[Note: Rhabanus reads: “and they sprouted and flourished.”]

Hence the bride also says in the Song of Songs:

> “New things and old, my kinsman, I have kept for you” (Song of Songs 7:13).

[Note: In the manuscript copies of our monastery of St. Andrew near Avignon, and in one manuscript of St. Remigius, we read: “New things with old, my kinsman,” etc. —Martian. All our manuscripts, and those consulted by Martianaeus, read: “New things with old, my kinsman,” etc. Jerome, moreover, habitually expressed his interpretation of this passage from Adamantius. Chrysostom, Homily 47 on Matthew; Augustine, *Questions on the Gospel*; and Cyril, *On Worship in Spirit and in Truth*, should also be compared.]

### (Verses 53–54)

When Jesus had finished these parables, he departed from there. And coming into his own country [variant: “land,”] he taught them in their synagogue, so that they were astonished and said:

After the parables that he spoke to the people—and which only the apostles understood—he passes into his own country in order to teach there more openly.

> “Where did this man get this wisdom and these powers?”

What astonishing foolishness on the part of the Nazarenes! They wonder where wisdom has obtained wisdom and power has obtained powers. But the error is obvious: they suppose him to be the son of a carpenter.

### (Verses 55–56)

> “Is this not the carpenter’s son? Is not his mother called Mary, and his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas? And are not all his sisters with us? Where, then, did this man get all these things?”

And they were scandalized because of him.

The error of the Jews is our salvation, and the condemnation of heretics. For they saw Jesus Christ so entirely as a human being that they thought him the carpenter’s son: “Is this not the carpenter’s son?” Are you surprised that they were mistaken about his brothers, when they were mistaken about his father? This passage has been explained more fully in the book mentioned above against Helvidius.

### (Verse 57)

But Jesus said to them:

> “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country and in his own house.”

It is almost natural for citizens always to envy their fellow citizens. They do not consider a man’s present works, but remember his frail childhood, as though they themselves had not advanced through the same stages of life to mature age.

### (Verse 58)

> “And he did not perform many miracles there because of their unbelief.”

This does not mean that he could not have performed many miracles even for those unbelievers, but that, if he performed many miracles, he would condemn the unbelieving citizens.

It may also be understood in another way: Jesus is despised in his house and in his country—that is, among the Jewish people. Therefore he performed few signs there, lest they become completely without excuse. But among the nations he performs greater signs daily through the apostles, not so much in the healing of bodies as in the salvation of souls.

## Chapter 14

### (Verses 1–2)

At that time Herod the tetrarch heard the report about Jesus and said to his attendants:

> “This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead, and therefore powers are at work in him.”

One of the ecclesiastical interpreters seeks the reasons why Herod suspected this—why he thought that John had risen from the dead and that powers were therefore at work in him—as though we had to account for another person’s error, or as though the doctrine of *metempsychosis* (μετεμψύχωσις, the transmigration of souls) derived an opportunity from these words. Yet at the time when John was beheaded, the Lord was thirty years old, whereas *metempsychosis* teaches that after many cycles of years souls enter different bodies.

### (Verses 3–4)

For Herod had seized John, bound him, and put him in prison because of Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip.

For John had said to him:

> “It is not lawful for you to have her.”

[Note: Our manuscripts omit the name “Philip.”]

Ancient history relates that Philip, the son of Herod the Great—under whom the Lord fled into Egypt—and the brother of this Herod, under whom Christ suffered, married Herodias, the daughter of King Aretas. Later, after certain hostilities had arisen between her and her son-in-law, Aretas took his daughter away and, to avenge her former husband, joined her in marriage to Herod, his enemy.

[Note: Two Palatine manuscripts add “of the Arabs”; others read *Phethrai* instead of *Aretas*. Martianaeus also notes this reading from one manuscript of St. Remigius and adds that *Phetros* is the name of the region called Arabia Petraea. Origen, meanwhile, reports against those who wanted to say that Herod took his brother’s wife after Philip had died and left a daughter, that Herod’s crime was greater because he had taken his brother’s wife while the brother was still alive. Others agree with St. Jerome. Basil of Seleucia, in Oration 18, calls Herod’s marriage with Herodias adultery (μοιχεία) and says that he used the kingdom as an instrument of lust. Josephus, Book 18, chapter 5, and more recent interpreters should also be consulted.]

Which Philip this was, the evangelist Luke explains more fully:

> “In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, while Pontius Pilate was governing Judaea, and Herod was tetrarch of Galilee, while his brother Philip was tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis” (Luke 3:1).

Therefore John the Baptist, who had come in the spirit and power of Elijah, rebuked Herod and Herodias with the same authority by which Elijah had rebuked Ahab and Jezebel (1 Kings 21), because they had entered into an unlawful marriage, and because it was not lawful, while his brother was alive, to marry his wife.

He preferred to risk his life before the king rather than, for the sake of flattery, forget the commandments of God.

### (Verse 5)

And although he wanted to kill him, he feared the people, because they regarded him as a prophet.

He feared the uprising of the people on account of John, knowing that great crowds had been baptized by him in the Jordan. But he was overcome by love for his wife, because of whose passion he had also neglected the commandments of God (Genesis 40).

### (Verse 6)

But when Herod’s birthday was being celebrated, the daughter of Herodias danced in their midst, and she pleased Herod.

[Note: Jerome faithfully copied these words from Origen: “We have found nowhere in Scripture that a birthday was celebrated by a righteous person; for Herod was more wicked than that Pharaoh” (Genesis 40:20). And in Homily 8 on Leviticus: “Among all the saints, no one is found to have held a feast or great banquet on the day of his birth.” Yet histories report that King Agrippa, Antiochus, and many other men of good character celebrated their birthdays. See Fronto’s special dissertation on this subject.]

We find no one else observing his birthday except Herod and Pharaoh; and since their impiety was alike, their celebration was also the same.

### (Verse 7)

Therefore he promised her with an oath that he would give her whatever she asked of him.

But she, having been instructed by her mother.

[Verse 8]

> “Give me here on a platter the head of John the Baptist.”

I do not excuse Herod on the grounds that, unwillingly and against his will, he committed murder because of his oath. Perhaps he had sworn for the very purpose of preparing the machinery for the future killing.

Otherwise, if he claims that he did it because of his oath, suppose she had asked for the death of his father or his mother: would he have done it? Therefore what he would have rejected in his own case, he ought to have rejected in the case of the prophet as well.

[Note: Origen has the same meaning: “He ought rather to have broken his oath than kept it; for the rashness of an oath was not so serious a crime as putting a prophet to death because of that rash oath.”]

### (Verse 8)

> “Give me here,” she said, “on a platter the head of John the Baptist.”

Herodias feared that Herod might someday repent, or become reconciled to his brother Philip, and that the unlawful marriage might be dissolved by a repudiation. She therefore instructed her daughter to ask for John’s head at that very banquet: a fitting reward in blood for the work of her dancing.

And the king was grieved.

It is customary in Scripture for the historian to narrate the opinion of the multitude in the way in which it was believed by everyone at the time. Just as Joseph was called the father of Jesus even by Mary herself, so Herod is now said to have been grieved because the banqueters thought that he was grieved (Luke 2).

[Note: Victor reads: “The skillful murderer concealed the wickedness of his mind, presenting sadness on his face while having joy in his heart.”]

For he was a dissembler of his mind and a craftsman of murder, displaying sadness on his face while having joy in his heart.

### (Verses 9–10)

But because of the oath and because of those who were reclining with him, he ordered that it be given. He sent someone and beheaded John in prison.

He excuses his crime by an oath, so that under the pretext of piety he might become impious. When he added, “and because of those who were reclining with him,” he wanted all of them to be accomplices in his crime, so that bloody food might be served at a luxurious and impure banquet.

### (Verse 11)

His head was brought on a platter and given to the girl, and she brought it to her mother.

We read in Roman history that the Roman commander Flaminius, because a little prostitute reclining beside him said that she had never seen a man beheaded, consented to the execution of a person guilty of a capital crime during a banquet. The censors expelled him from the senate-house because he had mingled food with blood and had provided the death of a condemned man for another person’s pleasure, so that lust and murder might be mixed together.

How much more criminal were Herod, Herodias, and the girl who danced, who demanded the prophet’s head as the price of blood, so that she might have power over the tongue that had denounced the unlawful marriage.

Let this be understood according to the letter. But even to this day we see that in the head of John the prophet the Jews lost Christ, who is the head of the prophets.

[Note: Rhabanus reads: “because a little prostitute reclining beside him,” etc.]

And his disciples approached, took his body, and buried it.

Josephus reports that John was beheaded in a certain town of Arabia.

[Note: This was evidently the fortress of Machaerus. In *Antiquities*, Book 18, chapter 5, Josephus reports it.]

And in what follows—“His disciples approached, took the body”—we may understand both the disciples of John himself and those of the Savior.

### (Verse 13)

And they came and reported it to Jesus. When Jesus heard this, he withdrew from there in a boat to a deserted place by himself.

They announce the Baptist’s death to the Savior. When he heard it, he withdrew to a deserted place.

[Note: Victor adds “by himself.”]

He did not do this, as some think, out of fear of death, but sparing his enemies, lest they add one murder to another. Or he postponed his own death until the day of Passover, on which, for the sake of the mystery, the Lamb had to be sacrificed and the doorposts of believers sprinkled with blood (Exodus 12).

Or he withdrew in order to give us an example of avoiding the recklessness of those who voluntarily hand themselves over, since not everyone perseveres in torments with the same steadfastness with which they offer themselves to be tormented.

For this reason he also commands elsewhere:

> “When they persecute you in this city, flee into another” (Matthew 10:23).

The evangelist also says elegantly not that he “fled” into a deserted place, but that he “withdrew,” showing that he avoided his persecutors more than he feared them.

Alternatively: after the head of the prophet had been cut off by the Jews and by the king of the Jews, and prophecy had lost its tongue and voice among them, Jesus passes into the desert—the place of the Church, which previously had no husband.

And when the crowds heard this, they followed him on foot from the cities.

It may also be that he withdrew into a deserted place for another reason: having heard of John’s death, he wished to test the faith of those who believed. Accordingly, the crowds followed him on foot—not on animals or in various vehicles, but by the labor of their own feet, thereby showing the ardor of their minds.

If we wish to explain the reasons for each individual word, we shall exceed the brevity of the work proposed [variant: “will exceed”]. Nevertheless, it must be said in passing that, after the Lord came into the desert, very large crowds followed him. For before he came into the solitudes of the Gentiles, he was worshiped by one people alone.

### (Verse 14)

And when he went out, he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them and healed their sick.

In the Gospel discourses the spirit is always joined to the letter, and whatever at first sight seems cold becomes warm when you touch it.

[Note: Three Palatine manuscripts fittingly add “in meaning.” Thus Origen had earlier interpreted the passage: “The crowd followed him from their own cities because each person had left behind the ancestral customs of his native religion,” and so forth.]

The Lord was in a deserted place. The crowds followed him, leaving their cities—that is, their former ways of life and the diversity of their doctrines.

Jesus’ going out signifies that the crowds had the will to come, but did not have the strength to reach him. Therefore the Savior goes out from his own place and proceeds to meet them, just as in another parable he had gone out to meet the repentant son (Luke 15).

When he sees the crowd, he has compassion and heals their diseases, so that complete faith may immediately receive its reward.

### (Verse 15)

When evening came, his disciples approached him, saying:

> “The place is deserted, and the hour has already passed. Dismiss the crowds, so that they may go into the villages and buy food for themselves.”

Everything is full of mysteries. He departs from Judaea and comes into a deserted place; the crowds follow him, leaving their cities; Jesus goes out to meet them, has compassion on the crowds, and heals their sick. And he does this not in the morning, not as the day is growing, not at midday, but in the evening, when the sun of righteousness has set.

### (Verse 16)

But Jesus said to them:

> “They do not need to go away.”

They do not need to seek various foods or buy unfamiliar bread when they have the heavenly bread with them.

> “You yourselves give them something to eat.”

He challenges the apostles to break the bread, so that when they testify that they have nothing, the greatness of the sign may become more evident.

### (Verse 17)

They answered him:

> “We have nothing here except five loaves and two fish.”

In another Gospel we read: “There is a boy here who has five loaves” (John 6:9). He seems to me to signify Moses. By the two fish we may understand either both Testaments, or the fact that the even number refers to the Law.

[Note: It is not implausible that one Palatine manuscript adds “and the prophets,” since the context here seems to require it. A little later the same manuscript, together with other Palatine manuscripts, reads “in the bitter waters” instead of “in the waters of the sea.”]

Thus, before the Savior’s Passion and before the flash of the resplendent Gospel, the apostles had nothing but five loaves and two little fish, which moved in salty waters and in the waves of the sea.

### (Verse 18)

He said to them:

> “Bring them here to me.”

Hear, Marcion; hear, Manichaeus: Jesus commands that the five loaves and two little fish be brought to him, so that he may sanctify and multiply them.

### (Verse 19)

And when he had ordered the crowd to recline on the grass—

According to the letter, the meaning is clear; let us unfold the mysteries of the spiritual interpretation.

They are ordered to recline upon the grass and, according to another evangelist (Luke 9), upon the ground, in groups of fifty or one hundred. After they have trampled upon their flesh, all its flowers, and the pleasures of the world, and have laid them beneath themselves like withered grass, they then ascend through repentance, represented by the number fifty, to the perfect height of the number one hundred.

[Note: It would be useful to compare Origen in Latin: “Those who were going to rest in the nourishment of Jesus ought to be either in groups of one hundred, a sacred number consecrated to God because of unity, or in groups of fifty, a number that contains remission according to the mystery of the Jubilee, which occurs every fifty years,” and so forth. Huetius also explains this passage learnedly enough.]

He took the five loaves and the two fish, looked up to heaven, blessed them, broke them, and gave the loaves to the disciples.

He looks up to heaven in order to teach that eyes should be directed there. He took the five loaves and the two little fish in his hands, broke them, and handed them to the disciples.

As the Lord breaks them, a seedbed of food comes into being. For if they had remained whole and had not been broken into pieces and divided into a multitude of grains, they could not have fed such a crowd of men, children, and women.

Therefore the Law with the prophets is broken and torn into pieces, and its mysteries are brought into the midst, so that what, whole and remaining in its former condition, did not nourish, may, divided into parts, nourish the multitude of the Gentiles.

### (Verse 20)

But the disciples gave them to the crowds.

And they all ate and were satisfied.

The crowds receive food from the Lord through the apostles.

And they took up the leftover fragments, filling twelve baskets.

Each of the apostles fills his own basket from the Savior’s leftovers, either so that he may later have something with which to feed the Gentiles, or so that from the leftovers he may demonstrate that the loaves were real, since afterward they were multiplied.

At the same time, consider how in the wilderness and in so vast a solitude there were no loaves to be found except five, along with two little fish, while twelve baskets were so easily found.

[Note: Instead of “were found,” which is the only correct reading and is immediately clear from the context, the text has until now been read incorrectly as “were filled.” Jerome says that it is remarkable that only five loaves were found, etc., while twelve baskets were so easily found.]

### (Verse 21)

The number of those who ate was five thousand men, apart from women and little children.

The number of the five loaves corresponds to the multitude of five thousand men who ate. For they had not yet, according to the account of another passage, arrived at the number seven, those who ate being four thousand—a number close to that of the Gospels.

The five thousand men who had grown into the perfect man and followed him ate. Of him Zechariah says:

> “Behold, a man; his name is Rising” (Zechariah 6:12).

Women and little children, the weaker sex and the lesser age, are unworthy of being counted.

Hence in the Book of Numbers, whenever priests and Levites, armies, or crowds of combatants are described, servants, women, little children, and the ignoble common people are passed over without being counted.

[Note: Adamantius expressed the same point, though at greater length. We shall quote his view only in Latin: “Someone might say that, since many had eaten according to their merit and strength and had become participants in the loaves of blessing, those who were worthy of the number—as were those twenty years old who were counted in the Book of Numbers—were Israelite men; but those who were not worthy to be counted in such a ratio and number were children and women.”]

### (Verse 22)

And immediately Jesus compelled his disciples to get into the boat and go ahead of him across the strait until he had dismissed the crowds.

[Note: The word “immediately” is absent from our manuscripts. Here too the holy Doctor drew upon Adamantius for his interpretation of the sacred text.]

He commanded the disciples to cross over and compelled them to board the boat. By this wording it is shown that they withdrew from the Lord unwillingly, since in their love for their teacher they did not wish to be separated from him even for a moment.

### (Verse 23)

And after dismissing the crowd, he went up onto the mountain by himself to pray. When evening came, he was there alone.

If Peter, James, and John had been with him—the disciples who had seen him transfigured in glory—they might perhaps have gone up the mountain with him. But the crowd cannot follow into lofty places unless he has first taught it beside the sea, on the shore, and nourished it in the desert.

But when it says that he went up alone to pray, do not refer this to the one who fed five thousand men with five loaves, apart from the children and women. Refer it instead to the one who, having heard of John’s death, withdrew into solitude—not that we separate the person of the Lord, but that his works are divided between God and humanity.

### (Verse 24)

The boat was being tossed by the waves in the middle of the sea, for the wind was contrary.

The apostles had rightly withdrawn from the Lord as though unwilling and reluctant, lest, while he was absent, they should suffer shipwreck. Accordingly, while the Lord remained on the summit of the mountain, a contrary wind immediately arose, disturbed the sea, and placed the apostles in danger. The threatening shipwreck continued for as long as it took Jesus to come.

### (Verse 25)

But in the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking upon the sea.

Military stations and watches are divided into periods of three hours. Therefore, when he says that the Lord came to them in the fourth watch of the night, he shows that they had been in danger throughout the entire night, and that he would bring them help at the final part of the night and at the consummation of the world.

[Note: Victor reads: “and at the end of the night.”]

### (Verse 26)

And when they saw him walking upon the sea, they were troubled, saying:

> “It is a phantom.”

If, according to Marcion and Manichaeus, our Lord was not born of a Virgin but appeared as a phantom, how is it that the apostles now fear that they are seeing a phantom?

And because of fear they cried out.

A confused cry and an uncertain voice are signs of great fear.

(Vers. 27.) Immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying: “Take courage; it is I; do not be afraid.” He addresses what was foremost in the situation and takes care of it, commanding those who were afraid: “Take courage; do not be afraid.” And when he adds, “It is I,” without specifying who he is, either they could recognize him from his familiar voice, although he was speaking through the darkness of the obscure night, or they recalled that he himself was the one whom they knew to have spoken to Moses: “Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is’ has sent me to you” (Exod. 3:14).

[Note: One Palatine manuscript reads, “or they could know him himself, who had spoken,” etc. Again, where the old editions had *reputabant*, “they thought,” they read *repetebant*, “they recalled.” Rhabanus likewise has: “or they could know that it was he himself.”]

[Col. 0102D] (Vers. 28, 29.) But Peter answered and said: “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters.” And he said: “Come.” In every passage Peter is found to possess the most ardent faith. When the disciples are asked whom people say Jesus is, he confesses him to be the Son of God. When Jesus wishes to go to his passion, Peter forbids him; and although he is mistaken in his understanding, he is not mistaken in his devotion, since he does not wish him to die whom he had shortly before confessed to be the Son of God. He climbs the mountain with the Savior, first among the foremost; and in the passion he alone follows him. He immediately washes away, with bitter tears, the sin of denial that had arisen from sudden fear. [Note: The same manuscript places *Deinde*, “then,” before this sentence.]

After the passion, when they were at the lake of Gennesaret and were fishing, while the Lord stood on the shore and the others were slowly sailing, Peter does not tolerate delay. Girded with his *ependytes*—his outer garment—he immediately plunges into the waves. With the same ardor of faith that he always displayed, now too, while the others are silent, he believes that through the will of his Master he can do what the Master could do by nature. “Command me to come to you upon the waters.” You command, and at once the waves will become solid, and the body that is heavy by itself will become light.

And Peter, coming down from the boat, walked upon the water in order to come to Jesus. Let those who think that the Lord’s body was therefore not real because he walked upon soft, yielding, and airy waters answer how Peter walked—Peter whom they will certainly not deny to have been a real human being.

(Vers. 30.) But when he saw the strong wind, he was afraid. And when he began to sink, he cried out, saying: “Lord, save me.” The faith of his spirit was burning, but human frailty was dragging him down into the depths. Therefore he is left for a little while to temptation, so that his faith may be increased and he may understand that he was preserved not by the ease of his request, but by the power of the Lord.

(Vers. 31, 32.) And immediately Jesus stretched out his hand, [Col. 0104A] seized him, and said to him: “You of little faith, why did you doubt?” And when he had climbed into the boat, the wind ceased. If the apostle Peter, whose faith and ardor of mind we have described above, who had confidently asked the Savior, saying, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters,” is told, because he was afraid for a little while, “You of little faith, why did you doubt?” what should we say of ourselves, who possess not even the smallest portion of that little faith?

(Vers. 33.) But those who were in the boat came and worshiped him, saying: “Truly, you are the Son of God.” At a single sign, when calm had been restored to the sea—a thing that sometimes happens by chance even after violent storms—the sailors and passengers confess him truly to be the Son of God, while Arius proclaims in the Church that he is a creature.

[Col. 0104B] (Vers. 34.) And when they had crossed over, they came to the land of Gennesaret. If we knew what “Gennesaret” means in our language, we would understand how Jesus, through the figure of the apostles and the boat, brings the Church, delivered from the shipwreck of persecution, to the shore and makes her rest in the calmest harbor.

[Note: The editors Victor and Martianaeus uselessly suggest to Jerome an interpretation that he himself supposedly did not know. For the holy Father does not expressly profess his own ignorance, but that of the interpretation which Origen had applied to this passage. Jerome rendered it word for word into Latin. The Greek read:

“‘They came to the land of Gennesaret; if we knew its interpretation and derived some benefit from it, we would be helped by it to some extent in explaining the matters under discussion.’

“Jerome himself had written in the *Book of Names*—which was plainly composed in large part from Origen—that ‘Gennesar’ means ‘garden of princes.’ Thus I would prefer *ortus*, ‘garden,’ rather than *or­tus*, ‘rising,’ as we observed in the notes on this passage. But the editors, each according to his own ingenuity, have tried to devise one interpretation after another from this word.
