“Victor interprets Gennesaret from the Hebrew as ‘flowering valley,’ and says that this explanation fits Jerome’s meaning extremely well when he speaks of the shore and of the very peaceful harbor into which Christ conveyed the ship of the Church. Martianaeus himself adheres so closely to Victor that he differs from him not even by a word.

“On the contrary, the distinguished Huet thought that the origin of this expression should be referred to a difficult and obscure matter, since there is no mention of it at all in the Hebrew text of the Old Testament, while in the Syriac edition of the New Testament it is written [the source leaves the Syriac form blank]. It is pleasing, however, to reproduce the entire note of this most learned interpreter of Origen, to which we shall immediately append our own, which seems closer to the truth. He says:

“‘Some derive this name from [the source leaves the term blank], which they interpret as “flowering valley”; I would prefer “planted valley,” since the word signifies a shoot. Josephus, *Jewish War* 3.18, bears witness that this region is extraordinarily fertile, and so does his constant imitator Hegesippus, *Destruction of Jerusalem* 3.26. Some conjecture that [the source leaves the form blank] arose by the Chaldeans changing *kaph* into *gimel* and inserting *samekh*, which is true. Thus throughout the Old Testament you will find the region of Cinnereth called Gennesar and Gennesareth by the Chaldean paraphrasts.

“‘In that designation they took pleasure because, in their dialect, it supposedly meant “rising of princes”; and from the tribe of Naphtali, which was situated there, a thousand princes had set out to meet David (1 Chron. 12:34). Far more foolish is the etymology—or rather allusion—that Hegesippus gives in the passage cited: “Gennesar,” he says, “is called by a Greek word as though it meant producing for itself a breeze, water that is sweet and suitable for drinking.” From such obscure indications concerning this word, it is hardly surprising, he concludes, if Origen openly acknowledged his ignorance here, and Jerome after him.’

“Not to detain the reader any longer, I say that this word can suitably be derived from [the source leaves the form blank] as the complete expression [the source leaves the form blank], which means ‘ten gardens’—that is, the gardens of the Decapolis, or more precisely, the gardens of ten cities. The land of Gennesaret was so called because of the abundance of its gardens; it is the region beside the Lake of Galilee.

“The extraordinary fertility of this region is praised by the Hegesippus just cited by Huet, to say nothing meanwhile of the sacred authors Matthew, Luke, and Mark. Josephus likewise reports, *Jewish War*, chapter 35, that the land extends as far as the lake of the same name, Gennesar, which surpasses other regions both in its natural qualities and in the fertility of all its plants and trees.’”]

(Vers. 35.) And when the men of that place had recognized him, they sent word throughout that entire region. They recognized him by report, not by sight; or certainly, because of the magnitude of the signs he performed among the people, he was known to many even by his appearance. And observe how great was the faith of the people of the land of Gennesaret: they were not content with the healing of those who were present, but sent to the neighboring cities, so that all might run to the physician.

[Col. 0104C] (Vers. 36.) And they brought to him all who were ill, and begged him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment. [Col. 0105A] And all who touched it were made well. Those who are ill do not touch Jesus’ body, nor his entire garment, but only the outermost fringe; and all who touch it will be healed. Understand the fringe of his garment either as the smallest commandment—for whoever transgresses it will be called least in the kingdom of heaven (above, chapter 3)—or as the assumption of the body, through which we come to the Word of God and afterward enjoy his majesty.

(Cap. 15.—Vers. 1.) Then scribes and Pharisees came to him from Jerusalem, saying: “Why do your disciples transgress the traditions of the elders?” What astonishing folly on the part of the Pharisees and scribes: they accuse the Son of God because he does not observe the traditions and commandments of men!

[Col. 0105B] (Vers. 1, 2.) “For they do not wash their hands when they eat bread.” “Hands,” that is, works—not, of course, the hands of the body, [Note: Three of our manuscripts repeat the word “hands” here. This sentence itself is Origen’s, *κατὰ τὸ εὔλογον καθαίρειν πειρώμεθα ἑαυτῶν τὰς πράξεις, καὶ οὕτως τὰς τῶν ψυχῶν νίπτεσθαι χεῖρας*, “According to sound reason, let us try to purify our actions and thus wash the hands of our souls,” etc.] but those of the soul must be washed, so that the word of God may be in them.

(Vers. 3.) But he answered and said to them: “Why do you also transgress the commandment of God on account of your tradition?” He refutes a false accusation with a true answer. “When you,” he says, “neglect the Lord’s commandments because of human tradition, why do you think that my disciples should be accused because they disregard the commands of the elders in order to keep the decrees of God?”

(Vers. 4 ff.) “For God said: ‘Honor your father and your mother,’ and, ‘Whoever curses father or mother shall die the death.’ But you say: ‘Whoever says to his father or mother, “Whatever gift is from me will benefit you,” and does not honor his father or his mother,’—and you have made void the commandment of God because of your tradition. Hypocrites, Isaiah rightly prophesied about you, saying: ‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me’ (Exod. 20; Lev. 20). ‘In vain do they worship me, teaching doctrines and commandments of men.’”

And when he had called the crowds to himself, he said to them: “Hear and understand.” In the Scriptures, honor is understood not so much in greetings [Col. 0106A] and the performance of services as in almsgiving and the offering of gifts. [Note: Rhabanus confirms this reading.]

“Honor,” the Apostle says, “widows who are truly widows” (1 Tim. 5:3); here “honor” means a gift. And in another passage: “Let the presbyters be honored with double honor, especially those who labor in the word and teaching of God” (ibid., 17). Through this commandment we are also ordered not to muzzle the ox while it is threshing (Deut. 25), and that “the laborer is worthy of his wages” (Luke 10).

The Lord, considering either the weakness, the age, or the poverty of parents, had commanded that children honor their parents, even by supplying the necessities of life. The scribes and Pharisees wished to overturn this most provident law of God [Note: Jerome adheres closely here to Adamantius, whose learned exposition of this very obscure passage, variously understood by interpreters, is worth reproducing at least in Latin. He says:

“‘The Pharisees and scribes handed down a tradition contrary to the Law, expressed more obscurely in the Gospel, which we ourselves would not have understood had someone from among the Hebrews not handed down to us the matters relevant to this passage, as follows.

“‘It sometimes happens, he says, that moneylenders, when they encounter difficult debtors who can repay the debt but do not wish to do so, dedicate the debt to the account of the poor, into which money was deposited in the treasury according to the ability of each of those who wished to share their goods with them. They would sometimes say to their debtors in their own language: “It is *Corban*—that is, a gift—that which you owe me, for I have dedicated it to the poor as an act of piety toward God.”

“‘Then the debtor, as though he were no longer indebted to men but to God, and as though he were thereby bound by his piety toward God, was compelled, even unwillingly, to return the debt—not to the moneylender any longer, but now to God, for the account of the poor, in the moneylender’s name.

“‘What the moneylender did to the debtor, some sons occasionally did to their parents. They would say to them: “Whatever assistance you would have received from me, father or mother, know that you will receive it from *Corban*, from the account of the poor consecrated to God.” Then, when the parents heard that the *Corban* had been consecrated to God, they no longer wished to accept from their children what ought to have been given to them, even if they were in great need of life’s necessities.

“‘Thus the elders put forward such a tradition among the common people: whoever said to his father or mother that what should have been given to either of them was *Corban*, a gift, was no longer a debtor to his father or mother for supplying that person with the necessities of life. The Savior therefore reproved this tradition, not as sound, but as opposed to the commandment of God.

“‘For if God says, “Honor father and mother,” while the tradition said, “He who has consecrated to God as *Corban* what he was going to give to his parents need not honor father and mother by making a gift,” it is clear that the commandment of God concerning the honor of parents was annulled by the tradition of the Pharisees and scribes. Their tradition said that whoever had once consecrated to God what his parents would have received no longer had to honor father or mother.

“‘And the Pharisees, being greedy, taught these things so that under the pretext of the poor they might also receive what ought to have been given to someone’s parents.’”]

so that they might introduce impiety under the name of piety. They taught wicked children that if anyone wished to vow to God—who is the true Father—the things that ought to be offered to their parents, the Lord’s offering should be placed before gifts to parents. Or else the parents themselves, avoiding the sacrilege of accepting what they saw to have been consecrated to God, were worn down by poverty. Thus it happened that the offering of the children, under the pretext of the temple of God, accrued to the profit of the priests.

This evil tradition of the Pharisees arose from another circumstance. Many people who had debtors bound to them by money owed, and who did not wish to have what they had lent returned, assigned the debts to the priests, so that the money collected might serve the temple services and the priests’ own needs. [Note: Rhabanus has *tali*, “from such a circumstance.”]

The passage can also be understood briefly in this way: “Whatever is from me will benefit you.” “You compel,” he says, “children to say to their parents: ‘Whatever gift I was going to offer to God, I am using for your food, and it benefits you, father and mother.’” Thus the parents, fearing to accept what they saw to be dedicated to God, preferred to lead a life of poverty rather than eat what had been consecrated.

(Vers. 11.) “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth—that is what defiles a person.” The verb *communicat*—“makes common” or “defiles”—is properly scriptural and is not used in ordinary speech. [Col. 0107A] The Jewish people, boasting that they are God’s portion, call “common” the foods used by all human beings. For example, pork, [Note: Victor omits “oysters.”] oysters, hares, and animals of that kind, which do not divide the hoof and do not chew the cud, and fish that do not have scales. Hence it is also written in the Acts of the Apostles: “What God has cleansed, you must not call common” (Acts 10:15). “Common,” therefore, means what is open to other human beings and is, as it were, not part of God’s portion; it is called unclean.

“It is not what enters the mouth that makes a person common, but what comes out of the mouth—that defiles a person.” Let the prudent reader object and say: If what enters the mouth does not defile a person, why do we not eat food sacrificed to idols? And the Apostle writes: “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons” (1 Cor. 10:20). We must therefore understand that the foods themselves—and every creature of God—are clean in themselves, but that the invocation of idols and demons makes them unclean.

(Vers. 12.) Then his disciples approached and said to him: “Do you know that the Pharisees, when they heard this saying, were offended?” By one saying every superstitious observance of the Jews had been struck down; they thought their religion consisted in eating and rejecting particular foods.

And because the word “stumbling block” (*scandalum*) is frequently used in ecclesiastical writings, let us briefly explain what it means. [Note: All our manuscripts prefer *scolon* in Latin letters. On their authority, we have substituted *et*—“and”—for the verb *est*, “is,” in the phrase. The holy Father himself is a witness to this in Book 2 of his *Dialogue against the Pelagians*, no. 15: “Unless I am mistaken, *σκῶλον* and *σκάνδαλον* among the Greeks derive their names from offense and falling.” Martianaeus also incorrectly reads *σκολὸν* or *σκολίον* with the accent on the penultimate syllable. Marianus Victorius dared to alter this passage without the support of the manuscript witnesses, replacing *σκολὸν* or *σκολίον* with *πρόσκομμα* and *σκάνδαλον*. Below, too, he changes the Vulgate text in his edition, where Jerome says: “Although the thin liquid and fluid food, when it has entered the veins,” etc. As for *scolon*, which is read in the manuscript codices, or *σκολίον* with the accent on the penultimate syllable, we can understand it from the verb *σκολιόω*, which means “to twist,” or “to make crooked and perverse.” For things that are crooked and twisted provide an obstacle and a fall, or a striking of the foot, according to Jerome’s note. In Isaiah: “The crooked things shall become straight,” etc. MART.]

We can call *Σκῶλον* and *scandalum* an obstacle, or a fall and striking of the foot. Therefore, when we read, “Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble,” we understand it to mean one who gives anyone an occasion for falling by word or deed.

(Vers. 13.) But he answered and said: “Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted.” Even passages that appear straightforward in Scripture are full of questions. He says: “Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted.” Therefore that plant too will be uprooted of which the Apostle says: “I planted, Apollos watered” (1 Cor. 3:6).

But the question is resolved by what follows: “God, however, gave the growth” (ibid., 9). He also says: “You are God’s cultivated field, God’s building” (3 John 8). And elsewhere: “We are God’s fellow workers.” If we are fellow workers, then while Paul plants and Apollos waters, God plants and waters together with his fellow workers. [Note: Previously the text read, “The question is resolved by what is written,” and shortly afterward had *rigante Apolline*, “while Apollos waters,” instead of *Apollo*, the indeclinable name found in our manuscripts. Victor also read *pro alio*—“for another”—in the same passage, thinking that the two testimonies of 1 Cor. 3 had been joined together.]

Those who introduce different natures misuse this passage, saying: “If the plant that the Father did not plant will be uprooted, then the one that he planted cannot be uprooted.” But let them hear Jeremiah: “I planted you as a choice vine; how have you turned into the bitterness of a foreign vine?” (Jer. 2:21). God did plant it, and no one can uproot his planting. But since this planting exists within the will of free choice, no one else can uproot it unless it itself gives its consent.

(Vers. 14.) “Leave them; they are blind guides of the blind. But if the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit.” This is what the Apostle had commanded: “Avoid a heretical person after one or two admonitions, knowing that such a person is perverse and self-condemned” (Titus 3:10). In the same sense the Savior commanded that the worst teachers be left to their own devices, knowing that they could scarcely be drawn to the truth, that they were blind, and that they were leading a blind people into error.

(Vers. 15, 16.) [114] But Peter answered and said to him: “Explain this parable to us.” But he said: “Are you also still without understanding?” What had been said openly and was clear to the hearing, the apostle Peter thought had been spoken as a parable, and in a manifest matter he sought a mystical interpretation. The Lord rebukes him for thinking that something had been spoken figuratively when he had spoken plainly. From this we perceive that the hearer is defective who wishes either to understand obscure things plainly or plainly spoken things obscurely.

(Vers. 17, 18.) “Do you not understand that everything that enters the mouth goes into the stomach and is expelled into the privy? But the things that proceed from the mouth come out of the heart, and these defile a person.” Among heretics and perverse people, all the passages of the Gospels are full of stumbling blocks. From this little statement some slander the Lord, claiming that, ignorant of physical science, he thinks that all foods go into the stomach and are digested [another reading: “directed”] into the privy, although immediately after food has been taken in, it spreads through the limbs, veins, marrow, and nerves. Thus many who suffer continual vomiting because of a stomach disorder vomit immediately after dinner or a meal what they have consumed, and yet remain corpulent, because at the first contact liquid food and drink spread through the limbs.

But people of this kind, while they wish to criticize another’s ignorance, display their own. Although thin liquid and fluid food [Note: Victor supplies the words “is nevertheless poured into the body,” without which he thought the sense defective. But neither do the manuscripts support this, nor is there actually any loss of meaning.] when it has been concocted and digested in the veins and limbs, it descends through the body’s hidden passages—which the Greeks call *πόροι*, “pores”—to the lower parts and goes into the privy.

(Vers. 19, 20.) “For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, blasphemies. These are the things that defile a person. But to eat with unwashed hands does not defile a person.” He says: “Out of the heart come evil thoughts.” Therefore the ruling faculty of the soul is not, according to Plato, in the brain, but, according to Christ, in the heart. Those who think that thoughts are inserted by the devil and do not wish them to arise from their own will must be refuted on the basis of this statement.

The devil may be an assistant and kindler of evil thoughts, but he cannot be their author. If, however, he is always lying in wait and inflames the small spark of our thoughts with his fuel, we must not suppose that he also searches out the hidden things of the heart; rather, he estimates what we are turning over within from the posture and gestures of the body. For example, if he sees us repeatedly looking at a beautiful woman, he understands that the heart has been wounded by the dart of love. [Note: Two manuscript codices read: “the heart wounded by the eyes.” MART.]

[Note: At the beginning of the letter to Fabiola, Epistle 64, we discussed this matter; Jerome has an equivalent passage in Book 1 against Jovinianus, on the verse of the Song of Songs, “My beloved is mine, and I am his; he will dwell among my breasts”: “in the principal part,” he says, “of the heart, where the word of God has its lodging.” Most ecclesiastical authors agree. Origen, *Homily 9 on Exodus*: “That part within a person which is the most precious of all can exercise the priesthood within him. Some call it the principal part of the heart; others, the rational sense or intellectual substance; it may be called by whatever name one wishes—the portion of ourselves through which we are capable of God.” Tertullian repeatedly proves, especially in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 15, through many scriptural testimonies, that the *hegemonikon*—in Greek, *ἡγεμονικὸν*, “the ruling faculty”—of the soul is consecrated in the heart. Add Philo, *On What Is Worse Attacks What Is Better*; Gregory of Nyssa, *Oration 1 on the Resurrection of Christ*; Theodoret, *Sermon 3 on Providence*, and others. Lactantius, by contrast, in Book 1 of *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 16, left the matter undecided, whether it is situated in the heart or in the brain. Plato, whom Jerome refutes, placed it specifically in the head, or at the top of the body; hence he called the soul *ἐγκέφαλος*, “the brain.”]

(Vers. 21, 22.) And Jesus went out from there and withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon. And behold, a Canaanite woman came out from those borders and cried out, saying to him: Having left behind the calumniating scribes and Pharisees, he crosses into the region of Tyre and Sidon in order to heal the Tyrians and Sidonians. The Canaanite woman, however, comes out from her former borders so that, by crying out, she may obtain healing for her daughter. Observe that in the fifteenth passage the daughter of the Canaanite woman is healed.

[Col. 0109C] “Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David.” She knew to call him the Son of David because she had already gone out from her own borders and had abandoned the error of the Tyrians and Sidonians through a change of place and faith.

“My daughter is grievously tormented by a demon.” I think that the daughter of the Canaanite woman represents the souls of believers who were being grievously tormented by a demon because they did not know the Creator and worshiped a stone. [Note: Three Palatine codices read “of the Church” instead of “of the Canaanite woman.” This sentence too has been translated from Origen: “I think, in correspondence with the Jerusalem that is above, the free mother of Paul and those like her, that the Canaanite mother of the girl tormented by a demon should be understood as a symbol of such a soul.”]

(Vers. 23.) He did not answer her a word. This was not because of Pharisaic pride or the haughtiness of the scribes, but so that he would not appear to contradict his own command, by which he had ordered: “Do not go on the road of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans” (above, 10:5). He did not wish to give the calumniators an opportunity, and he reserved the complete salvation of the Gentiles for the time of his passion and resurrection.

And his disciples approached him and begged him, saying: “Send her away, because she is crying out after us.” At that time the disciples still did not know the Lord’s mysteries. They either, moved by compassion, interceded for the Canaanite woman—whom the other Evangelist calls a Syrophoenician (Mark 7)—or wished to be rid of her persistence, since she kept calling out to him not as a merciful but as a stern physician.

(Vers. 24.) But he answered and said: “I was not sent except to the sheep that have been lost [another reading: ‘that are lost’] of the house of Israel.” This does not mean that he was not also sent to the Gentiles, but that he was sent first to Israel, so that, when they did not receive the Gospel, the transfer to the Gentiles might be just. Significantly, he said “to the lost sheep of the house of Israel,” so that from this passage we may also understand the one wandering sheep in another parable.

(Vers. 25, 26.) But she came and worshiped him, saying: “Lord, help me.” He answered and said: “It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to dogs.” In the person of the Canaanite woman, the faith, patience, and humility of the Church are wonderfully proclaimed. Her faith is shown in believing that her daughter could be healed; her patience, in persevering in prayer after being so often rejected; her humility, in comparing herself not to dogs but to little dogs.

The Gentiles are called dogs because of idolatry; devoted to the eating of blood and the bodies of the dead, they are said to run mad. Observe that this Canaanite woman persistently calls him first “Son of David,” then “Lord,” and finally worships him as God.

(Vers. 27, 28.) But she said: “Yes, Lord; for even the little dogs eat from the crumbs that fall from the table of their masters.” Then Jesus answered and said to her: “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish.” And her daughter was healed from that hour.

“I know,” she says, “that I do not deserve the children’s bread, nor am I able to receive whole pieces of food, nor to sit at table with the father. But I am content with the scraps of the little dogs, so that through the humility of the crumbs I may come to the greatness of the whole loaf.”

O wondrous reversal of circumstances! Once Israel was the son, and we were dogs. According to the difference of faith, the order of names is changed. Of them it is later said: “Many dogs have surrounded me” (Ps. 21:17). And: “Beware of dogs, beware of evil workers, beware of the mutilation” (Phil. 3). We heard, together with the Syrophoenician woman and the woman who suffered from a flow of blood: “Great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish.” And: “Daughter, your faith has saved you.”

(Vers. 29, 30.) And when Jesus had crossed over from there, he came beside the Sea of Galilee. And he climbed the mountain and sat there. And great crowds came to him, bringing with them the mute, the blind, the lame, the disabled, and many others. And they cast them at his feet.

In the place where the Latin translator rendered the word *debiles*, “disabled,” the Greek has *κυλλούς*, which is not a general term for weakness but the name of a particular infirmity. Just as a person is called lame who limps on one foot, so *κυλλός* refers to someone who has one weak hand. We have no exact equivalent for this word. Therefore, in what follows, the Evangelist explains the healings of the other disabled people but says nothing about these. For what follows?

(Vers. 31.) And he healed them, so that the crowds marveled when they saw the mute speaking, the lame walking, and the blind seeing; and they glorified the God of Israel. He says nothing about the *κυλλοί*, because he had no corresponding description to give. This is about one word.

Let us also observe that after the daughter of the Canaanite woman has been healed, he returns to Judea and to the Sea of Galilee, and climbs the mountain. There, as though a bird were calling its tender young to fly, he sits, and the crowds gather around him, bringing or carrying with them people afflicted by various illnesses. After he heals them, he gives them food; and when this work is completed, he climbs into the boat and comes to the region of Magadan.

“He climbed the mountain and sat there, and the crowds came to him.” Observe that the mute, the lame, and the blind are brought to the mountain so that there they may be healed by the Lord.

(Vers. 32.) But Jesus called his disciples and said: “I have compassion on the crowd, because they have already remained with me for three days and have nothing to eat. And I do not wish to send them away fasting, lest they faint on the way.” He wishes to feed those whom he has healed. First he removes their weaknesses, so that afterward he may offer food to those who are well.

He also calls his disciples and tells them what he is about to do, either giving the teachers an example that plans should be shared with those who are lesser and with disciples, or so that from the conversation they may understand the greatness of the sign, replying that they do not have bread in the wilderness.

“I have compassion on the crowd, because they have already remained with me for three days.” He has compassion on the crowd because, in the number of three days, they believed in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

“And they have nothing to eat.” The crowd is always hungry and needs food unless it is filled by the Lord.

“And I do not wish to send them away fasting, lest they faint on the way.” They were hungry after great weaknesses and patiently awaited the food that was to come. [Col. 0112A] Jesus does not wish to send them away fasting, lest they faint on the way. Therefore the person who hastens to reach the desired dwelling without heavenly bread is in danger. Hence the angel also says to Elijah: “Arise and eat, because you have a great journey before you” (1 Kings 19:7).

(Vers. 33 ff.) And the disciples said to him: “Where then could we get so many loaves in the wilderness as to satisfy so great a crowd?” And Jesus said to them: “How many loaves do you have?” They said: “Seven, and a few little fish.” And he commanded the crowd to recline on the ground.

And taking the seven loaves and the fish, and giving thanks, he broke them and gave them to his disciples; and the disciples gave them to the people. And they all ate and were satisfied. And they took up what remained of the fragments, seven baskets full. Those who ate numbered four thousand men, besides children and women. And when he had dismissed the crowd, he climbed into the boat and came to the region of Magadan [Μαγδαλά].

We have already spoken above about this sign, and it would be tedious to repeat the same things. Let us dwell only on what differs. [Note: Adamantius himself made this comparison point by point; Jerome transferred a large part of it here into his own work.]

Above we read: “When evening came, his disciples approached him, saying: ‘The place is deserted’” (above, 14:15), and what follows. Here, after calling the disciples together, the Lord himself speaks: “I have compassion on the crowd, because they have already remained with me for three days.”

There, there were five loaves and two fish; here, seven loaves and a few little fish. There, they reclined on grass; here, on the ground. There, those who ate numbered five thousand, corresponding to the number of loaves they ate; here, four thousand. There, twelve baskets were filled with the remains of the fragments; here, seven baskets.

In the earlier sign, because they were close to and associated with the five senses, the Lord himself does not remember them, but the disciples do; they remember in the evening, when night was near and the sun was already declining.

Here, however, the Lord himself remembers; he says that he has compassion and explains the reason for his compassion: “because they have already remained with me for three days” [another reading: “with him,” or “with themselves”], and he does not wish to send them away fasting, lest they faint on the way.

Those who are nourished from the seven loaves—that is, from a sacred and perfect number—are not five thousand but four thousand. This number is always used in praise; the four-sided stone does not fluctuate and is not unstable. For this reason the Gospels too have been consecrated in that number.

## Chapter 16

### Verses 1 and following

The Pharisees and Sadducees came to him, testing him, and asked him to show them a sign from heaven. But he answered them:

“When evening comes, you say, ‘It will be fair weather, for the sky is red’; and in the morning, ‘Today there will be a storm, for the sky is red and gloomy.’ You know how to judge the appearance of the sky, but you cannot discern the signs of the times. An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah.”

**Note:** This is not the entire passage presented here. Jerome teaches that in most manuscripts the pericope is absent, except for the second and third verses, beginning with “When evening comes, you say” and ending with “but you cannot discern the signs of the times.” Indeed, three Palatine manuscripts omit the first verse, “The Pharisees and Sadducees came to him,” and the fourth, “An evil and adulterous generation,” neither of which Jerome included; these should altogether be excised from this sequence, lest Jerome himself appear to be in error. Moreover, the oldest of those same Palatine manuscripts does not state absolutely and indefinitely that this passage is absent, but adds “among the Greeks,” indicating that it is lacking in most Greek manuscripts. It may perhaps be easier to find Greek manuscripts of this kind—or at least manuscripts that omit a large part of these verses—than Latin ones. Certainly our very ancient Veronese manuscript, which we frequently cite, contains them, although its wording differs somewhat from the Vulgate.

This passage is absent from most manuscripts. Its meaning is clear: from the regularity and stability of the elements, both fair and rainy days can be predicted. But the scribes and Pharisees, who seemed to be teachers of the Law, were unable, from the prophets’ predictions, to understand the coming of the Savior.

**Note:** In one or another manuscript: “consonance”; shortly afterward, more elegantly, “rainy days” instead of “rain.” So also in Rabanus.

### Verse 5

And he left them and went away. When his disciples had come across the lake, they had forgotten to take bread.

He said to them: Having left the scribes and Pharisees, to whom he had said, “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah,” he rightly went across the lake and followed the peoples of the Gentiles. What the sign of Jonah means has already been explained above.

### Verses 6–7

“Pay attention, and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.”

But they were discussing among themselves, saying, “It is because we did not take bread.”

One who guards against the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees does not observe the precepts of the Law and the letter, but neglects human traditions in order to carry out God’s commandment.

### Verses 8 and following

But Jesus, knowing this, said to them:

“Why are you reasoning among yourselves, you of little faith, because you have no bread? Do you not yet understand, or remember the five loaves and the five thousand people, and how many baskets you took? Nor the seven loaves and the four thousand people, and how many baskets you took? Why do you not understand that I was not speaking to you about bread when I said, ‘Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees’?”

Then they understood that he had not said that they should beware of the leaven of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.

Through the occasion of the command that the Savior had given them—“Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees”—he teaches them what the five and the seven signify: the five thousand and the four thousand who were fed in the wilderness. Although the greatness of the signs is evident, another meaning is also demonstrated in spiritual understanding. For if the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees signifies not bodily bread but perverse traditions and heretical doctrines, why should the foods by which God’s people were nourished not also signify true and sound teaching?

Someone may ask: How did they not have bread, when, immediately after the seven baskets had been filled, they boarded the boat and came to the territory of Magedan, where, while sailing, they heard that they should beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees? But Scripture testifies that they had forgotten to take the bread with them.

This is the leaven of which the Apostle also speaks: “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (1 Cor. 5:6). Marcion, Valentinus, and all the heretics possessed this kind of leaven, which must be avoided by every means. Leaven has this power: when it is mixed with flour, what seemed small grows larger and draws the whole mixture—or, in the alternate reading, the whole conversion—toward its own flavor. So also heretical teaching, if it casts even a small spark into your breast, quickly grows into a great flame and draws the whole possession of a person toward itself.

Finally, it follows: “Then they understood that he had not said that they should beware of the leaven of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.”

## Book Three

### Verse 13

Now Jesus came into the region of Caesarea Philippi. This Philip was the brother of Herod, whom we mentioned above, tetrarch of Ituraea and Trachonitis.

**Note:** In the printed books, the plural is incorrectly read: “of the regions of Ituraea and Trachonitis,” whereas all our manuscripts retain the singular: “of the region of Trachonitis.” Then the printed editions and some manuscript copies add: “who, in honor of Tiberius Caesar, named Caesarea Philippi the city now called Paneas; and it is …” The reading of the manuscripts of the monastery of Saint Andrew near Avignon seemed preferable to us because it appeared clearer. —Martianay.

**Against this:** In his manuscripts Martianay found the plural, *regionum*, as in the older printed editions; then three Palatine manuscripts, together with the Cistercian manuscript, read: “he named Caesarea Philippi, which is now called Paneas, and it is in the province of Phoenicia,” and so forth. I do not know whether this may be the more genuine reading, since it is also shorter. With the Palatine and Cistercian manuscripts, Rabanus likewise omits those words. Shortly afterward he reads *Libiadem* instead of *Juliadem*.

He built Caesarea in honor of Tiberius Caesar, and in honor of Caesar as well as of himself he named it Caesarea Philippi. It is in the province of Phoenicia. He imitated his father Herod, who in honor of Augustus Caesar named Caesarea—the city formerly called Strato’s Tower—and, from the name of Augustus’s daughter, built Juliade beyond the Jordan.

**Note:** Some manuscripts retain *Libiadem* instead of *Juliadem*. Augustus Caesar’s daughter was not called Livia or Libia, but Julia. Hence I conjecture that the name *Libiadis* was introduced through scribal error, unless the error lies in the word “daughter,” for which the name of the wife, Livia, should be substituted. For Augustus’s wife, the mother of Tiberius Caesar, was called Livia or Libia. —Martianay.

I would rather believe that ancient copyists substituted “daughter” here for “wife,” thinking that the city could not have been called Juliade for any other reason than that it was named after Julia, Augustus’s daughter. For Jerome could not have been unaware that the city was dedicated to Augustus’s wife, not his daughter, since Josephus, in *The Jewish War*, book 2, chapter 13, states that it was built under Tiberius’s rule, long after Augustus’s daughter Julia had been exiled. As for the fact that the names Libia and Julia were used interchangeably, and that Josephus consistently calls it *Jouliada* while changing Livia’s name to Julia, this is thought to have happened because Livia, having been adopted into the Julian family, was likewise called Julia. Nevertheless, our manuscripts and those in Martianay’s possession read *Libiadem* here, as does Eusebius, who later says that Betharam was named Liviada by Herod. See Philo, *On the Embassy*, p. 729. See also the ancient inscription and the notable coin of Augustus reproduced by Patin in his notes on Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter 63. In the *Chronicle*, under the year 27 of Christ: “Philip the tetrarch called Paneas Caesarea Philippi, in which he had built many structures, and another city Juliade.” Shortly afterward, under the year 29: “Herod founded Tiberias and Libiade.” See Pontanus’s notes, p. 548.

This [or, in the alternate reading, That] is the site of Caesarea Philippi, where the Jordan rises at the foot of Lebanon. It has two springs, one called Jor and the other Dan; when they are joined together, they form the name Jordan.

And he was asking his disciples, saying:

“Who do people say that the Son of Man is?”

**Note:** The Veronese Gospel manuscript inserts “me,” thus: “Who do people say that I am,” and so forth; Jerome seems partly to reject this reading.

He did not say, “Who do people say that I am?” but “Who do they say the Son of Man is,” so that he would not seem to be asking about himself boastfully.

Note that wherever “son of man” is written in the Old Testament, the Hebrew has “son of Adam.” Thus [or, in the alternate reading, “thus also”] we read in the Psalm: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy-hearted?” (Ps. 4:3). In Hebrew this is said as “sons of Adam.”

**Note:** This is a notable passage for proving the corruption of the Hebrew source, if we were to believe Marianus, who thought that Jerome’s passage could prove that the Hebrew once read *bene Adam* (“sons of Adam”) rather than *bene isch* (“sons of man”). He says that the Jews corrupted the passage of the fourth Psalm is also evident from the fact that, instead of “heavy,” they made it read “my glory,” and so forth. But the editor of Jerome would have entirely abandoned this opinion if he had compared Jerome’s Hebrew Psalter with this passage in the *Commentary*. For from the Hebrew Jerome translates it: “Sons of men, how long will you, my illustrious ones, love vanity shamefully?” He would never have translated it in these words unless he had read in Hebrew *bene isch* (“sons of man”) and *kevodi* or, according to his customary form, *chebodai*, that is, “my illustrious ones.” I therefore acknowledge that Saint Jerome suffered a lapse of memory here and did not have the Hebrew Psalter before his eyes when he explained these words of Matthew in his *Commentary*. Moreover, the Greek scholiast tells us that all interpreters published *endoxoi mou*, that is, “my illustrious ones,” in accordance with Jerome’s version from the Hebrew. Thus the Hebrew source always read *kevodi* or *chebodai*, as the older interpreters read it—not *kebore* with a final resh, as Marianus thought, since he did not wish to examine the difficulty. —Martianay.

The Hebrew manuscripts that remain read “sons of Isch,” or “sons of man,” not “sons of Adam.” To speak briefly first about this difficulty, Martianay acknowledges that Saint Jerome suffered a lapse of memory here and did not have the Hebrew Psalter before his eyes when he explained these words of Matthew, since Jerome wrote that the Hebrew contained “sons of Adam” instead of “sons of Isch.”

Victorius, on the other hand, maintains that *Adam* once stood in the Hebrew text, and that this is evident not only from Jerome’s testimony here but also clearly from the Septuagint itself, which translated “sons of human beings” (*huioi anthrōpōn*). For whenever they translate the Hebrew word for “human being,” they use *anthrōpos*, whereas they render the word for “man” as *anēr*. Thus in the first Psalm, “blessed is the man” (*makarios anēr*); in Psalm 3, “blessed is the man”; in 1 Samuel 26, “he is not your man”; and likewise everywhere else. For just as the Hebrew word for “human being” is *anthrōpos* in Greek and *homo* in Latin, so the Hebrew word for “man” is *anēr* in Greek and *vir* in Latin.

I neither agree with the Benedictine editor, who says that Jerome rashly trusted a failing memory, nor with the bishop of Rieti, who prefers to believe that the Hebrew exemplar was altered by Jewish deceit. Rather, I think that both *Adam* and *Isch* were once read interchangeably, so that some manuscripts preferred “sons of man” and others “sons of Adam.” When Saint Jerome therefore wrote here that the Hebrew had “Adam,” he was using one such book, and perhaps another—although it is by no means necessary to suppose this—when, while translating the Psalter, he rendered it “sons of man,” not “sons of Adam.”

This is especially suggested by the Masoretic note, or circellus, which is placed above the reading in accurate editions of today and indicates that there was already at that time a variation in the method of writing. The versions of the ancient interpreters, Symmachus and Theodotion, also support this, for they have *huioi andros*, “sons of man.” Since—as Victorius concludes, and as is in fact found generally among all interpreters—the Hebrew word for “human being” is *anthrōpos* in Greek, while the Hebrew word for “man” is *anēr*, the cited interpreters, who used the latter word, show that they found it in the exemplar before them; whereas the Septuagint translated the Hebrew as “sons of human beings.”

I shall touch only briefly on the second difficulty that Victorius raises from this same verse, since it does not properly concern Jerome. He says that the passage also appears to have been corrupted by the Jews because they substituted one Hebrew reading for another, changing “heavy-hearted” into “my glory.” He wants the one reading to be true and most ancient: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy-hearted?” rather than “Sons of man, how long will my glory be?” But it is clear to everyone that this was the version of all the ancient interpreters, who therefore read “my glory,” not “heavy,” except for those interpreters cited only by Victorius—the Septuagint and the Vulgate—whose version the latter derived from them word for word.

He asks beautifully: “Who do people say the Son of Man is?” For those who speak about the Son of Man are human beings; but those who understand his divinity are called not human beings but gods.

### Verse 14

They said: “Some say John the Baptist, others Elijah, and others Jeremiah or one of the prophets.”

Jesus said to them:

I am surprised that certain interpreters investigate the causes of each person’s error and construct a very lengthy discussion about why some thought our Lord Jesus Christ was John, others Elijah, others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets. They could have gone astray about Elijah and Jeremiah in the same way that Herod went astray about John when he said: “John, whom I beheaded, has risen from the dead, and mighty works are at work in him” (Mark 6:16).

### Verses 15–16

“But you—who do you say that I am?”

Simon Peter answered: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

Prudent reader, observe that from what follows and from the tenor of the speech, the apostles are called not human beings but gods. For after saying, “Who do people say the Son of Man is?” he added: “But you—who do you say that I am?” Since those others, being human beings, form human opinions, you who are gods—whom do you consider me to be?

Peter, speaking for all the apostles, confesses: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” He calls him the living God in distinction from those gods who are thought to be gods but are dead: Saturn, Jupiter, Venus, Minerva—or Ceres—Liber, Hercules, and the other monstrous idols.

### Verse 17

Jesus answered and said to him:

“Blessed are you, Simon Barjona, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.”

By his testimony about himself, the Apostle receives a corresponding reward. Peter had said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God”; he received the reward of his true confession: “Blessed are you, Simon Barjona.” Why? Because flesh and blood did not reveal this to him, but the Father revealed it. What flesh and blood could not reveal was revealed by the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Thus, from his confession, he receives the name that indicates he has received revelation from the Holy Spirit and that he should be called the Spirit’s son. For *Barjona* means in our language “son of a dove.”

Others take the expression simply to mean that Simon—that is, Peter—is the son of John, in accordance with the question found in another passage: “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” (John 21:15). He replied, “Lord, you know.” They maintain that the text was corrupted through a scribal error, so that *Barjona* was written instead of *Bar Joanna*, that is, “son of John,” with one syllable removed. *Joanna* means “the grace of the Lord.”

Both names, however, can be understood mystically: the dove signifies the Holy Spirit, and the grace of God signifies a spiritual gift.

The statement “because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you” may also be compared with the Apostle’s account, where he says: “Immediately I did not consult flesh and blood” (Gal. 1:16), meaning the Jews by “flesh and blood.” Here too, in another sense, it is shown that Christ the Son of God was revealed to him not through the teaching of the Pharisees but through the grace of God.

### Verse 18

“And I say to you.”

What does he mean by “And I say to you”? You said to me, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” and I say to you—not with an empty word that accomplishes nothing, but I say to you because for me to say is to do.

“Because you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.”

Just as he gave light to the apostles so that they would be called the light of the world, and they received their other names from the Lord, so he gave the name Peter to Simon, who believed in Christ the rock.

According to the metaphor of the rock, therefore, he rightly says to him: “I will build my Church upon you.”

“And the gates of hell will not prevail against it.”

**Note:** He borrowed this allegory from Origen, and Saint Jerome repeats it in book 8 of his *Commentary on Isaiah*: “And just as I think the gates of death are sins, concerning which it is said to Peter, ‘The gates of hell will not prevail against you,’ so I think the gates of righteousness are all works of virtue,” and so forth.

I think the gates of hell are vices and sins, or certainly the doctrines of heretics, by which people who have been enticed are led to Tartarus. Let no one therefore think that this is said about death, as though the apostles were not subject to the condition of death; their martyrdoms shine forth as evidence.

### Verse 19

“And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.”

Bishops and presbyters, not understanding this passage, take upon themselves something of the Pharisees’ arrogance, so that they either condemn the innocent or imagine that they can absolve the guilty, whereas before God it is not the judgment of priests but the life of the accused that is examined.

**Note:** Origen, according to Huet’s Latin translation, says: “Since those who claim for themselves the office of bishop use this statement, just as Peter did, and, having received from the Savior the keys of the kingdom of heaven, teach that what they have bound—that is, condemned—has been bound also in heaven, it must be declared that they speak correctly if they also possess the deed on account of which it was said to Peter, ‘You are Peter’; and if they are such that the Church can be built upon them by Christ, and the statement can rightly be applied to them. The gates of hell ought not to prevail against one who wishes to bind and loose. But if he is bound by the cords of his own sins, he binds and looses in vain.”

Jerome has wisely and appropriately turned this dangerous and false opinion into a useful one. Origen wanted the authority of the Church’s ministers to depend upon their integrity; in this respect he is rightly criticized by learned men. Jerome, however, lest priests flatter themselves excessively about their authority and abuse it recklessly, says rather that before God the life of the guilty is examined, not the sentence of the priest.

We read in Leviticus 14 about lepers, where they are ordered to show themselves to the priests; and if they have leprosy, they are then declared unclean by the priest—not because priests make lepers unclean, but because they possess knowledge of the leprous and the non-leprous and can distinguish who is clean and who is unclean. Just as there, therefore, the priest makes the leper clean or unclean, so here the bishop and presbyter bind or loose—not those who are innocent or guilty in themselves, but, in accordance with their office, after hearing the various kinds of sins, they know who should be bound and who should be loosed.

### Verse 20

Then he commanded his disciples not to tell anyone that he was Jesus the Christ.

Earlier, when sending the disciples to preach, he had commanded them to announce his coming; here he ordered them not to say that he was Jesus Christ. It seems to me that preaching Christ is one thing, and preaching Jesus Christ another. “Christ” is a common title of dignity; “Jesus” is the proper name of the Savior.

It may be that before his passion and resurrection he did not wish to be preached as Jesus Christ for this reason: after the sacrament of his blood had been completed, he would more appropriately say to the apostles, “Go and teach all nations” (Matt. 28:19), and so forth. No one should think that this is merely our interpretation and not the meaning of the Gospel, since what follows explains the reasons why preaching was then forbidden.

### Verse 21

From that time Jesus began to show his disciples that he had to go to Jerusalem, suffer many things from the elders, scribes, and chief priests, be killed, and rise again on the third day.

The meaning is: Preach me when I have suffered these things. For it does not profit to preach Christ publicly and proclaim his majesty among the peoples when shortly afterward they will see him scourged and crucified, suffering many things from the elders, scribes, and chief priests.

Even now Jesus suffers many things from those who once again crucify the Son of God for themselves (Heb. 6:6). Although elders and chief priests are thought to be present in the Church, by following the simple letter they kill the Son of God, who is perceived wholly in the spirit.

### Verses 22–23

Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him, saying: “Far be it from you, Lord; this will never happen to you.”

But he turned and said to Peter: “Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling-block to me, because you do not think the things of God but those of human beings.”

We have often said that Peter possessed extraordinary fervor and the greatest love for the Lord and Savior. After his confession—“You are the Christ, the Son of the living God”—and after hearing the Savior’s reward, “Blessed are you, Simon Barjona, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven,” he suddenly hears from the Lord that he must go to Jerusalem, suffer many things from the elders, scribes, and chief priests, be killed, and rise on the third day.

He does not [Victorius omits “not”] want his confession destroyed, nor does he think it possible that the Son of God should be killed. He takes him into his own feelings, or leads him aside so that he will not seem to rebuke his teacher in the presence of his fellow disciples, and begins to rebuke him out of loving affection, wishing to say: “Far be it from you, Lord.” Or, as it is better expressed in Greek, *hileōs soi, Kyrie, ou mē estai soi touto*—that is, “May you be propitious to yourself, Lord; this will certainly not happen to you.”

**Note:** Once again, the reading of the Veronese Gospel manuscript deserves consideration: “Far be it from you; be propitious, Lord; this will not happen.”

He means: “Be favorable to yourself, Lord; this will not happen to you. It cannot happen; my ears cannot accept that the Son of God is to be killed.”

The Lord, turning, said to him: “Get back, Satan; you are a stumbling-block to me.” [Victorius adds “me”: “Get behind me, Satan.”]

Satan means “adversary” or “opponent.” Because you speak contrary to my will, he says, you must be called an adversary.

**Note:** Saint Hilary offers one interpretation for all: “Turning toward the one through whom this opinion was being suggested, he added, ‘Satan, you are a stumbling-block to me.’ For it is not fitting to think that the name Satan and the offense of a stumbling-block were assigned to Peter after such great proclamations of bestowed blessedness and so great a power. But because every unbelief is the work of the devil, the Lord, offended by Peter’s response, rejected the author of this unbelief with the reproach of the name.”

For this same reason Eusebius criticizes Marcellus in book 1 against him, chapter 2, because, failing to understand how the words “Satan, you are a stumbling-block to me” are spoken to the apostle and for what purpose, he asserts that they were spoken to the devil.

Many think that Peter was not rebuked, but that it was the opposing spirit that suggested these words to the Apostle—or, in the alternate reading, suggested the Apostle to say them.

To me, however, this apostolic error, arising from an affectionate concern, will never appear to be an incentive of the devil. “Get back, Satan,” is said to the devil; Peter hears, “Get behind me, Satan,” that is, “Follow my judgment.”

**Note:** Our editor prefers to accept Origen’s interpretation. He explains the words as though Jesus had said to Peter, “Go behind me,” since Peter had ceased to go behind him and follow him. Shortly afterward he says: “At the same time compare what he said to Peter, ‘Get behind me, Satan,’ with what he said to the devil when the devil told him, ‘All these things I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me’: ‘Go, Satan,’ without the addition ‘behind me.’ For to be behind Jesus is good,” and so forth. Eusebius, cited above in his work against Marcellus, and Ambrose in book 1 of *On Abraham*, section 55, agree with this.

“You do not think the things of God, but those of human beings.” It is my will, and that of the Father—whose will I came to do—that I should die for the salvation of human beings (John 6:38). But you, considering only your own will, do not want the grain of wheat to fall into the earth so that it may produce much fruit (John 12:24).

A prudent reader may ask how, after such great blessedness—“Blessed are you, Simon Barjona”; “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church”; “The gates of hell will not prevail against it”; “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven”; “Whatever you bind or loose on earth will be bound or loosed in heaven”—he now hears: “Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling-block to me.” What is this sudden change, that after such great rewards he should be called Satan?

**Note:** Perhaps our manuscripts read more correctly here: *si* (“if”) instead of *et* (“and”), and at the end of the sentence *intelliget* (“will understand”) instead of *nesciunt* (“they do not know”).

If the one who asks this considers the matter carefully, he will understand that Peter’s blessing, blessedness, power, and the building of the Church upon him were promised for the future, not given in the present. “I will build my Church upon you,” he says, “and the gates of hell will not prevail against it”; and, “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven.” Everything is in the future. If he had given these things to him immediately, there would never have been room in him for the error of a false opinion.

**Note:** Three Palatine manuscripts read “of his confession” instead of “of his opinion.”

### Verses 24 and following

Then Jesus said to his disciples:

“If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me. For whoever wishes to save his life will lose it; but whoever loses his life for my sake will find it. For what does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?”

**Note:** Jerome himself recites and explains the passage that follows in the beginning of Letter 121 to Algasia, question 3. He derived the exposition both of this verse and of the following verse almost entirely from Adamantius.

Whoever lays aside the old human being with his works (Col. 3) denies himself, saying: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20). He takes up his cross and is crucified to the world. Whoever has been crucified to the world follows the crucified Lord.

“Or what exchange will a person give for his soul?”

For Israel, Egypt, Ethiopia, and Syene are given as an exchange (Isa. 43:3–4). For the human soul there is only that recompense which the Psalmist sings: “What shall I repay the Lord for all that he has repaid me? I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 115:3).

**Note:** Almost all manuscripts read *Soene* or *Soeone*. The Hebrew has Cush and Seba. Jerome says concerning that passage in Isaiah: “Instead of Syene, the other interpreters placed Saba, from which came the Queen of the South, who came to hear Solomon’s wisdom.”

### Verse 27

“For the Son of Man is going to come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will repay each person according to his work.”

Peter had been scandalized at the preaching of the Lord’s death and had been rebuked by the Lord’s judgment. The disciples, having been provoked, were to deny themselves, take up their crosses, and follow their teacher with the disposition of those who are dying.

The terror of the hearers was great, and, since the chief of the apostles had been terrified, it could instill fear in the others as well. Therefore joyful things follow sorrowful ones, and he says: “The Son of Man is going to come in the glory of his Father with his angels.”

You fear death: hear of the glory of the triumphant one. You dread the cross: listen to the ministry of the angels. “And then,” he says, “he will repay each person according to his works” (Rom. 10:12). There is no distinction between Jew and Gentile, man and woman, poor and rich, where not persons but works are considered.

### Verse 28

“Amen, I say to you: there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.”

He wished to heal the apostles’ terror with the hope of his promises, saying: “The Son of Man is going to come in the glory of his Father with his angels.” He added the authority of the judge: “And he will repay each person according to his work.”

The apostles’ silent thought might have endured an objection of this kind: “You now say that execution and death are coming; but what you promise—that you will be present in the glory of your Father with the ministry of angels and the power of a judge—will occur only after many days and be deferred for a long time.”

Therefore, the knower of hidden things, foreseeing what they might object, balances present fear with a present reward. What does he say? “There are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.” Thus it may be shown in the present time, on account of your unbelief, what his later coming will be like.

## Chapter 17

### Verse 1

And after six days, Jesus took Peter, James, and his brother John.

We have often explained why Peter, James, and John are separated from the others in certain passages of the Gospels, and what privilege they possess beyond the other apostles. Now the question is how he took them after six days and led them privately onto a high mountain, since the evangelist Luke gives the number eight (Luke 9). The answer is easy: here the intervening days are counted, whereas there the first and last are added. For it does not say, “After eight days Jesus took Peter, James, and John,” but “on the eighth day.”

**Note:** The Palatine manuscripts read: “And it happened after six days,” and so forth.

He leads them privately onto a high mountain. To lead the disciples into the mountains is a part of the kingdom. They are led apart because “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20:16; 22:14).

### Verse 2

And he was transfigured before them.

As he will be at the time of judgment, so he appeared to the apostles. When it says, “He was transfigured before them,” no one should think that he lost or changed his former shape and appearance, or that he assumed either a spiritual or an ethereal body. The evangelist shows how he was transformed when he says:

“His face shone like the sun, and his garments became white like snow.”

When the radiance of his face is displayed and the whiteness of his garments described, his substance is not removed; only his glory is changed.

“His face shone like the sun.” Certainly the Lord was transformed into the glory in which he will later come in his kingdom. The transformation added radiance; it did not remove his face.

Even if his body had been spiritual, were his garments also changed? They became so white that another evangelist said: “Such as a fuller on earth cannot make them” (Mark 9:2). But what a fuller can make on earth is corporeal, subject to touch—not spiritual or ethereal, deceiving the eyes and appearing only as a phantom.

### Verse 3

And behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them, speaking with him.

**Note:** Here and below, wherever this passage occurs, our manuscripts prefer the singular *apparuit*, “appeared.” The interpretation that the Law and the Prophets are signified by Moses and Elijah is an obvious one, which Saint Jerome took from Origen.

When the scribes and Pharisees tested him and demanded signs from heaven, he did not grant their request but refuted their perverse petition with a prudent answer. Here, however, to increase the apostles’ faith, he gives a sign from heaven: Elijah descending from the place to which he had ascended, and Moses rising from the underworld. This also corresponds to what is commanded to Ahaz through Isaiah, that he ask for a sign either from above or from below (Isa. 7; 2 Kings 2).

For when it says, “Moses and Elijah appeared to them, speaking with him,” and another Gospel reports that they announced to him what he was about to suffer in Jerusalem (Luke 9:31), the Law and the Prophets are shown—those who repeatedly proclaimed both the Lord’s passion and his resurrection.

### Verse 4

Peter answered and said to Jesus: “Lord, it is good for us to be here.”

He who had climbed into the mountains does not wish to descend to earthly things, but to remain forever in the heights.

“If you wish, let us make three tabernacles here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.”

You are mistaken, Peter, as the other evangelist also testifies: “You do not know what you are saying” (Luke 9:33). Do not seek three tabernacles when there is one tabernacle of the Gospel, in which the Law and the Prophets must be recapitulated.

But if you seek three tabernacles, do not compare servants with the Lord. Rather, make three tabernacles—indeed, one for the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—so that, since they possess one divinity, there may also be one tabernacle in your breast.

(Vers. 5.) While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. And behold, a voice from the cloud, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him.” Because he had asked imprudently, he does not deserve the Lord’s answer; rather, the Father answers on behalf of the Son, so that the Lord’s word might be fulfilled: “I do not bear witness concerning myself, but the Father who sent me—he bears witness concerning me” (John 5:37; 8:18). The cloud appears bright and overshadows [Col. 0123A] them, so that those who were seeking a bodily tabernacle made of branches or tents might be covered by the shelter of a bright cloud. 131 A voice from heaven is also heard, of the Father speaking, both bearing witness to the Son and—Peter’s [Alternative: Peter’s] error having been removed—teaching the truth; indeed, through Peter, teaching the other apostles as well. “This,” he says, “is my beloved Son: for him the tabernacle must be established, and him you must obey. He is the Son; they are servants. Moses and Elijah also ought, together with you, to prepare a tabernacle for the Lord in the innermost chambers of their hearts.”

[Note: [Col. 0123D] Our manuscripts omit the causal clause “because.”]

(Vers. 6.) And when the disciples heard this, they fell on their faces and were greatly afraid. They are terrified with fear for three reasons: either because they realized that they had been mistaken, or because the bright cloud had covered them, or because they had heard the voice of God the Father speaking; [Note: [Col. 0123D] “Because” is the reading of the manuscripts.] for human [Col. 0123B] frailty cannot endure the sight of a greater glory, and, trembling in soul and body with its whole being, falls to the ground. The more greatly someone has sought, the more he collapses into lower things if he has failed to recognize his own measure.

(Vers. 7.) And Jesus approached and touched them. Because they were lying there and could not rise, he himself mercifully approaches and touches them, so that by his touch he might drive away their fear and strengthen their weakened limbs.

And he said to them: “Rise, and do not be afraid.” Those whom he had healed with his hand, he heals by his command. “Do not be afraid.” First fear is driven out, so that instruction may afterwards be given.

(Vers. 8.) And when they lifted up their eyes, they saw no one except Jesus alone. Reasonably, after they had risen, they saw no one except Jesus alone, lest, if Moses and Elijah had remained with the Lord, the Father’s voice should seem uncertain as to whom in particular it had borne witness. They therefore see Jesus standing, the cloud having been removed, and Moses and Elijah having vanished, because after [Col. 0123C] the shadow of the Law and the Prophets—which had covered the apostles with its veil—had departed, [Note: [Col. 0123D] The text previously made no sense: “whether light.” In several manuscripts the more correct reading is *verum* (“truly”); in most, however, both readings occur. This is the reading we have retained, although I would prefer that *unum* (“one”) be restored without the addition, namely *lumen* (“light”), rather than *vocem* (“voice”), which most manuscripts lack. That reading would be more consistent with Jerome’s meaning and with Origen’s interpretation, which says: “Moses, who is the Law, and Elijah, that is, the Prophets, became ONE and the same with Jesus, that is, the Gospel; and just as previously there were three, so they did not remain three, but the three became ONE.”] both lights are found in the Gospel.

(Vers. 9.) And as they were coming down from the mountain, Jesus commanded them, saying: “Tell no one about the vision until the Son of Man has risen from the dead.” The anticipation of the future kingdom and the glory of the triumphant one had been displayed on the mountain. He therefore does not wish this to be proclaimed among the people, lest it should both seem incredible because of the greatness of the matter and, after so great a glory, the succeeding cross should cause scandal in unformed minds. [Col. 0124A]

[Note: [Col. 0123D] This explanation was formerly Origen’s. For, he says, those who heard it—especially the crowds—would have been even more offended when they saw him affixed to the cross, whom they had received as one endowed with such glory. To pursue carefully, in annotation, each point that our author has taken from that writer would take too long.]

(Vers. 10.) And the disciples asked him, saying: “Why then do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?” Unless we know why the disciples asked about Elijah, their question seems foolish and out of the ordinary. For what connection does asking about Elijah’s coming have with what was written above? It is a tradition [Note: [Col. 0123D] Origen says: “The disciples remembered what is taught concerning Elijah by the scribes: namely, that before Christ’s coming Elijah would come and prepare the souls of those who would receive him. But that vision which occurred on the mountain, where Elijah appeared, seemed in no way to agree with what had been said, since Elijah appeared to have come not before Jesus but after him. Therefore, thinking that the scribes had lied, they say these things,” and so forth. Compare also Jerome’s commentaries on the cited passage in Malachi.] of the Pharisees, according to the prophet Malachi, who is the last among the Twelve, that Elijah will come before the coming of the Savior, turn the heart of the fathers to the children and the heart of the children to the fathers, and restore everything to its former condition (Malachi 4). The disciples therefore think that this transformation is the glory they are seeing on the mountain, and they say: [Col. 0124B] “If you have already come in glory, how is it that your forerunner does not appear—especially since they had seen Elijah depart?” When they add, “The scribes say that Elijah must come first,” by saying “first” they show that, unless Elijah has come, the Savior’s coming has not taken place according to the Scriptures.

(Vers. 11, 12.) But he answered them: “Elijah indeed will come, and he will restore everything. But I tell you that Elijah has already come.” He who is to come at the Savior’s second coming, according to the truth of the body, has now come through John in power and spirit. [Note: [Col. 0124D] The Palatine manuscripts add *Eliae* (“of Elijah”), and thus continue the text: “but they did not recognize him,” and so forth.]

“And they did not recognize him, but did to him whatever they wished”: that is, they despised him and beheaded him.

(Vers. 13.) “So also the Son of Man will suffer at their hands.” [Col. 0124C] Then the disciples understood that he had spoken to them about John the Baptist. But a question arises: since Herod and Herodias killed John, how can they also be said to have crucified Jesus, when we read that he was killed by the scribes and Pharisees? The brief answer is that the faction of the Pharisees also consented to John’s death, [Note: [Col. 0124D] Origen answers the very question proposed here: “They themselves”—the scribes and Pharisees—“provided the occasion for what Herod dared to perpetrate against him”—John. And immediately afterward: “As for what follows, expressed in these words, ‘So also the Son of Man will suffer at their hands,’ it can be referred to the scribes, if what precedes is also referred to the scribes,” and so forth.] and that, in the Lord’s killing, Herod joined his will to theirs: he sent Jesus, after mocking and despising him, back to Pilate so that they might crucify him.

(Vers. 14, 15.) “Lord, have mercy on my son, because he is epileptic and suffers terribly; for he often falls into [Col. 0125A] the fire and frequently into the water. And I brought him to your disciples, and they could not cure him.” We have explained above why the demon, observing the course of the moon, attacks human beings and seeks to bring the Creator into disrepute through his creatures. But in my view, according to the tropological interpretation, the lunatic (*lunaticus*) is one who changes from moment to moment toward vices, does not persist in what he has begun, but waxes and wanes; now he is carried into the fire in which the hearts of adulterers have been set ablaze (Hosea 7), now into the waters that cannot extinguish charity. But when he says, “I brought him to your disciples, and they could not cure him,” he covertly accuses the apostles, since the inability to cure sometimes refers not to the weakness of those who cure, but to the faith of those who are to be cured, as the Lord says: “Let it be done for you according to your faith” [Col. 0125B] (Mark 5:34; 10:52).

[Note: [Col. 0125C] Almost in the same words from Origen: “Perhaps, then, you would not be mistaken if you called such people—those who are cast down by spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places—‘lunatics,’ so to speak, in spirit, and said that they are frequently in a bad state, namely when disturbances and passions invade their souls, sometimes falling into the fire of inflamed passions, when they become, according to what is written in Hosea, ‘adulterers like an oven heated by flame for baking’; at other times into water, when the king of all the dragons that are in the waters casts them into the depths of the waves of human life, depriving them of the freedom of breathing which they seemed to enjoy.” Our author also took from the same Adamantius what he says here and above, at Matthew 4:24: that the unclean spirit observes the course of the moon, or certain phases of the moon, and operates in such a way that, when it has observed that people are afflicted under a particular lunar phase, the demon itself does not seem to be the cause of so great an evil, but the moon, which presides over the night and has no power of this evil over human beings; thus the demon strives to bring the Creator into disrepute through his creatures.]

(Vers. 16.) But Jesus answered: “O unbelieving and perverse generation, how long will I be with you? How long will I endure you? Bring him here to me.” This does not mean that he was overcome with weariness, he who was gentle and meek, who did not open his mouth like a lamb before its shearer (Isaiah 53), [Note: [Col. 0125D] The negative particle appears to require deletion; both the sense and Rabanus reject it.] nor that he burst into words of anger. Rather, it is as when a physician sees a sick person acting contrary to his instructions and says: “How long shall I come to your house? How long shall I waste the skill of my art, when I command one thing and you do another?” Yet he is not angry with the person but with the vice; and through one person he reproves the Jews for unbelief, so that he immediately adds: “Bring him here to me.”

(Vers. 17.) And Jesus rebuked him, and the demon came out of him, and the boy was cured from that hour. It was not the one who was suffering but the demon who ought to have been rebuked. Or else he rebuked the boy, and the demon came out of him, [Col. 0125C] because he had been oppressed by the demon on account of his sins.

[Note: [Col. 0126C] Adamantius had written that the lunatic had been handed over to the demon to be tormented for certain reasons, because he had not shown himself worthy to be entrusted to the guardianship of an angel.]

(Vers. 18.) And they said: “Why could we not cast it out?” Jesus said to them: “Because of your unbelief.” For “Amen” I say to you. This is what he says elsewhere: “Whatever you ask in my name, believing, you will receive” (John 15:2). Therefore, whenever we do not receive, the impossibility lies not with the one who grants, but with the fault of those who ask.

[Col. 0126A] (Vers. 19.) “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here,’ and it will move; and nothing will be impossible for you.” Some think that faith is called small because it is compared with a grain of mustard seed, just as the kingdom of heaven is compared with a grain of mustard seed. But the apostle says: “And if I have all faith, so that I move mountains” (1 Corinthians 15:2). [Note: In one or two manuscripts the reading is *si tantam* (“if so great”); in the Greek, however—as noted above—the reading is πᾶσαν, “all.”] Faith, therefore, is great when it is made equal to a grain of mustard seed. The moving of the mountain does not refer to the mountain that we behold with the eyes of the flesh, but to the one—the demon—that had been driven out of the lunatic by the Lord. For when he says, “You will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here,’ and it will move,” this is understood of the demon. [Note: [Col. 0126D] Three Palatine manuscripts do not contain the words “this is understood of the demon.” Yet this is the most widely accepted interpretation: the demon is to be understood, an interpretation which the holy Father drew from Origen. “By mountains,” he says, “I think are meant the opposing and hostile Powers, endowed with widely extended and immense wickedness, which are, as it were, founded and established in the souls of some people.” And shortly afterward: “Whoever is such will say to this mountain”—by which I mean the mute and deaf spirit understood to be in the one called a lunatic—“Move from there,” and so forth.]
