Hence those who contend that the apostles and all believers had not even a small amount of faith are to be convicted of folly, because none of them moved mountains. For the moving of a mountain from one place to another is not as beneficial—and the vain display of signs is not as worth seeking—as moving this mountain for the benefit of all, which the prophet says corrupts the whole earth (Zechariah 4). [Col. 0126B] 135

(Vers. 20.) “But this kind is not cast out except by prayer and fasting.” By teaching how the most wicked demon can be expelled, he instructs everyone in the way of life.

(Vers. 21 and following.) As they were moving about in Galilee, Jesus said to them: “The Son of Man will be handed over into the hands of men, and they will kill him; and on the third day he will rise again.” And they were exceedingly sorrowful. He always mixes sad things with prosperous ones, so that when they suddenly arrive they may not terrify the apostles, but may come upon minds prepared for them. For if they are saddened by the statement that he will be killed, they ought [Col. 0126C] to be gladdened by the statement that he will rise on the third day. Their sorrow—and their profound sorrow—does not arise from unbelief; otherwise, they would have known [Alternative: would know] that Peter had been rebuked because he did not understand the things of God but those of men. Rather, it arises because, out of love for their teacher, they cannot bear to hear anything sinister or humiliating about him.

(Vers. 24.) And when they had come to Capernaum, those who collected the didrachma approached Peter and said: “Does your teacher not pay the didrachma?” He said: “Yes.” [Note: [Col. 0126D] Scaliger rightly says in his *Animadversions on the Chronicle*: “If Judea became tributary only after Augustus Caesar, why does Jerome add that Joseph and Mary, of course under Augustus, registered themselves?” In fact, it became tributary much earlier, already from the time of Pompey. See the *Chronicle*.]

After Augustus Caesar, Judea became [Col. 0127A] tributary, and everyone was registered for the poll tax. Hence Joseph also registered in Bethlehem with Mary, his kinswoman. Again, because he had been raised in Nazareth—which is a town of Galilee subordinate to the city of Capernaum—they demand the tax according to custom. Yet, because of the greatness of his signs, those who collected it do not dare to approach him personally but confront his disciple. Or they ask maliciously whether he pays tribute or contradicts Caesar’s will, according to what we read elsewhere: “Is it lawful to pay Caesar’s tribute or not?” (Mark 12:14).

And when he had entered the house, Jesus anticipated him, saying—Those who collected the didrachma had approached Peter separately. When he entered the house, before Peter could tell him what had happened, the Lord questioned him, lest the disciples be scandalized by the demand for the tax when they saw that he knew what had been done in his absence. [Col. 0127B]

(Vers. 25.) “What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth receive tribute or census-tax—from their own sons or from strangers?” And he said: “From strangers.” Jesus said to him: “Then the sons are free.” Our Lord was the king’s son both according to the flesh and according to the spirit, whether as one born from David’s stock or as the Word of the almighty Father. Therefore, as the king’s son, he did not owe tribute; but because he had assumed the humility of the flesh, he ought to fulfill all righteousness. And we, wretched people who are registered under Christ’s name, do nothing worthy of so great a majesty: he endured the cross and paid the tax for us, while we do not pay taxes for his honor and, as though we were sons of the king, are exempt from fiscal burdens. [Col. 0127C]

(Vers. 26.) “But lest we scandalize them, go to the sea, cast in a hook, and take the first fish that comes up. When you open its mouth, you will find a stater; take it and give it to them for me and for you.” I do not know what I should admire first in this passage, whether the Savior’s foreknowledge or his greatness. His foreknowledge, because he knew that the fish had a stater in its mouth and that it would be the first one caught; his greatness and power, if the stater was immediately created in the fish’s mouth at his word, and if by speaking he himself brought about what was to happen.

According to mystical interpretation, it seems to me that this fish is the one that was caught first, which had been in the depths of the sea and dwelt in salty and bitter waters, so that the first [Col. 0127D] Adam might be freed through the second Adam. And what was found in its mouth—that is, in its confession—was to be paid for Peter and the Lord. It is fitting that the same price is given, but it is divided, because the price was paid for Peter as for a sinner; whereas our Lord had committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth (Isaiah 53). A stater is said to contain two didrachmas, so that the likeness of the flesh might be shown, since servant and Lord are both freed by the same price.

The literal interpretation also edifies the hearer: the Lord was so poor [Col. 0128A] [Note: [Col. 0127D] Three Palatine manuscripts read: “the Lord was, as we hear, so poor”] that he had nothing from which to pay the tax for himself and the apostle. If someone should object, “How then did Judas carry money in the purse?” we shall answer that he considered it unlawful to divert the property of the poor to his own uses, and by this he gave us an example as well.

(Cap. XVIII.—Vers. 1.) At that time the disciples approached Jesus, saying: “Who, do you think, is greater in the kingdom of heaven?” What I have often urged must also be observed now: the causes of each of the Lord’s sayings and actions must be sought. After the stater had been found and the tax paid, what does the apostles’ sudden question mean? “At that time the disciples approached Jesus, saying, ‘Who, do you think, is greater in the kingdom of heaven?’” Because they had seen the same tax paid for Peter and the Lord [Col. 0128B], they supposed, from the equality of the price, that Peter had been preferred to all the apostles, since he had been compared with the Lord in the payment of the tax. Therefore they ask who is greater in the kingdom of heaven. And Jesus, seeing their thoughts and understanding the reasons for their error, wishes to heal their desire for glory through the practice of humility.

(Vers. 2.) And Jesus called a little child, set him in their midst, and said—Either he simply set an ordinary little child there, in order to present the example of childhood and display its likeness to innocence. Or certainly he set himself, the little child, in their midst: he who had come not to be served but to serve, so as to give them an example of humility. Others interpret the little child as the Holy Spirit, whom he placed in the hearts of the disciples [Note: [Col. 0127D] The Cistercian manuscripts and others in Martianay read: “so that they might exchange pride for humility.” This interpretation also derives from Origen: “See whether you can say that the child summoned by Jesus is the Holy Spirit, who humbled himself, was increased by the Savior, and was established in the midst of the mind of Jesus’ disciples,” and so forth.] so that he might change pride into humility. [Col. 0128C]

(Vers. 3.) “Amen I say to you, unless you are converted and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.” The apostles are not commanded to possess the age of little children, but their innocence, and to possess by deliberate effort what children possess by their years: to be children in malice, not in wisdom.

(Vers. 4.) “Therefore, whoever humbles himself like this little child is greater in the kingdom of heaven.” Just as this little child, whose example I give you, does not persist in anger, does not remember having been hurt, is not delighted when he sees a beautiful woman, does not think one thing and say another, so you too, unless you possess such innocence and purity of heart, will not be able to enter the kingdom of heaven.

Or otherwise: “Whoever humbles himself like this little child is greater in the kingdom of heaven.” Whoever imitates me and humbles himself as my example—lowering himself as much as I lowered myself by taking the form of a servant—will enter the kingdom of heaven (Philippians 2). [Col. 0128D] 138 [Supplement: “myself.”]

(Vers. 5.) “And whoever receives one such little child in my name receives me.” When someone is such as to imitate Christ’s humility and innocence, Christ is received in that person. And prudently, lest the apostles, when this had been said to them, think that they were being honored, he added that they were to be received not on their own [Alternative: his own] merit but in honor of their teacher. [Col. 0129A]

(Vers. 6.) “But whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble”—note that the one who is scandalized is a little one; for the greater do not receive scandals.

“It would be better for him if a millstone turned by a donkey were hung around his neck and he were drowned in the depth of the sea.” Although this may be a general judgment against all who cause someone to stumble, nevertheless, according to the sequence of the discourse, it can also be understood as spoken against the apostles. By asking who was greater in the kingdom of heaven, they seemed to be contending among themselves over rank; and if they had persisted in this vice, they could have destroyed by their scandal those whom they were calling to the faith, when these people saw the apostles fighting among themselves for honor. [Col. 0129B]

When he said, “It would be better for him if a millstone turned by a donkey were hung around his neck,” he speaks according to the custom of the province, according to which, among the ancient Jews, this was the punishment for greater crimes: people were thrown into the depths with a stone tied to them. It is better for him because it is far better to receive a brief punishment for guilt than to be preserved for eternal torments. For the Lord will not exact vengeance twice for the same thing (Nahum 1) [Alternative: “will not judge”].

(Vers. 7.) “Woe to the world because of scandals! For scandals must come. Nevertheless, woe to the person through whom the scandal comes.”

This does not mean that scandals must necessarily come—for otherwise those who cause scandal would be without guilt—but, since scandals must occur in this world, each person exposes himself to scandals by his own fault. At the same time, Judas, who had prepared his heart for betrayal, is struck by this general judgment. [Col. 0129C]

[Note: [Col. 0129D] Origen writes: “And it is necessary that these things come, but it is not necessary that they arise through this particular person”—scandals must come, but not through just anyone—which he explains at greater length.]

(Vers. 8, 9.) “If your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you. It is better for you to enter life maimed or lame than, having two hands or two feet, to be cast into eternal fire. And if your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you. It is better for you to enter life with one eye than, having two eyes, to be cast into the fire of Gehenna.”

Scandals must indeed come; yet woe to the person who, by his own fault, causes what must occur in the world to occur through himself. Therefore every attachment must be cut off, and every relationship severed, lest, under the pretext of affection, any believer expose himself to scandals. “If,” he says, “someone is so closely connected with you as to be your hand, foot, or eye, and is useful, attentive, and sharp in perception, but causes you to stumble and, because of a discordance of character, drags you into Gehenna, it is better for you to be deprived both of his companionship and of carnal advantages, lest, while you wish to profit your relatives and friends, you have them become the cause of your ruin.” Therefore neither brother, nor wife, nor children, nor friends, nor any affection that can exclude us from the kingdom of heaven should be preferred to the love of the Lord. Each believer knows what harms him, or in what matter his mind is troubled and often tested. [Col. 0130A] [Note: [Col. 0129D] In Victor’s manuscript: “is often held fast.”] It is better to lead a solitary life than to lose eternal life on account of the necessities of the present life.

(Vers. 10, 11.) “See that you do not despise one of these little ones. For I tell you that their angels in heaven [Note: [Col. 0130D] In three Palatine manuscripts, the words “in heaven” are absent.] always see the face of my Father who is in heaven. For the Son of Man came to save what had perished.”

Above, he had said that all relationships and connections that could cause scandal—represented by the hand, foot, and eye—were to be cut off. He therefore softens the severity of the command by adding the following instruction: “See that you do not despise one of these little ones.” “I command severity,” he says, “in such a way that I teach mercy to be joined with it.” As far as lies within you, do not despise them, but, for the sake of your own salvation, seek their healing also. [Col. 0130B] But if you see that they persist in sins and serve their vices, it is better for you alone to be saved than to perish with many.

“For their angels in heaven always see the face of the Father.” Great is the dignity of souls, since each one has, from the beginning of its birth, an angel assigned to guard it. Hence we read in the Apocalypse of John: “To the angel of Ephesus, of Thyatira, and to the angel of Philadelphia, and to the angels of the four remaining churches, write this” (Revelation 1–3). The apostle also commands that women’s heads be veiled in churches because of the angels (1 Corinthians 11). 140

(Vers. 12, 13.) “What do you think? If someone has a hundred sheep and one of them goes astray, does he not leave the ninety-nine on the mountains and go to seek the one that went astray? And if it happens that he finds it, amen I say to you, he rejoices over it more than over the ninety-nine that did not go astray.”

Consistently, he calls them to mercy. He had first said: “See that you do not despise one of these little ones,” and then adds the parable of the ninety-nine sheep left on the mountains and the one that went astray, which the good shepherd, because it was unable to walk on account of its great weakness, carried back on his shoulders to the rest of the flock.

Some think that this shepherd is the one who, although he was in the form of God and did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, becoming obedient to the Father unto death—even death on a cross (Philippians 2:6 and following). For this reason he descended to earthly things, to save the one little sheep that had perished—that is, the human race.

Others think that the number ninety-nine in the sheep signifies the righteous, and that the one little sheep signifies the sinner, according to what he said elsewhere: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners; for the healthy do not need a physician, but those who are ill” (Luke 5:32). This parable is written in the Gospel according to Luke together with the other two parables of the ten drachmas and the two sons (Luke 15). [Col. 0130C]

(Vers. 14.) “So it is not the will of your Father who is in heaven that one of these little ones should perish.” This refers to the subject introduced above, where he had said: “See that you do not despise one of these little ones.” He teaches that the parable was set forth for this reason: so that the little ones would not be despised. In saying, “It is not the will of your Father that one of these little ones should perish,” he shows that whenever one of these little ones perishes, he has not perished by the Father’s will. [Col. 0131A]

(Vers. 15 and following.) “But if your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not listen to you, take with you one or two more, so that every word may stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses. But if he does not listen to them, tell it to the church. And if he does not listen to the church, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector.”

If our brother sins against us and injures us in any matter, [Col. 0131B] we have the power—or rather the obligation—to forgive, since we are commanded to forgive our debtors their debts. But if someone sins against God, that is not within our judgment. For divine Scripture says: “If a person sins against another person, the priest will pray for him. But if he sins against God, who will pray for him?”

We, on the contrary, are kind when God is insulted, but indulge our hatred when we ourselves are abused. A brother must be rebuked privately, lest, if he once loses his sense of shame and modesty, he remain in sin. If he listens, we gain his soul, and through another’s salvation our own salvation is also acquired. But if he refuses to listen, a brother is to be brought in. If he does not listen to that brother either, a third is to be brought in, either for the purpose of correction or so that he may be confronted in the presence of witnesses. [Col. 0131C] But if he refuses to listen even to them, then it must be told to many, so that they may hold him in contempt; and he who could not be saved by shame may be saved through disgrace.

When it says, “Let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector,” it shows that the one who acts under the name of a believer but performs the works of unbelievers is more detestable than those who are openly Gentiles. According to the tropological interpretation, tax collectors are those who pursue the profits of the world and exact revenues through commerce, fraud, theft, and criminal perjury.

(Vers. 18.) “Amen I say to you: whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven.” Because he had said, “If he does not listen to the church, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector,” the despised brother could respond secretly or think silently: “If you despise me, I despise you too; if you condemn me, you will be condemned by my judgment.” He therefore grants authority to the apostles, so that those who are condemned by such persons may know that a human judgment is confirmed by divine judgment, and that whatever has been bound on earth is likewise bound in heaven. [Col. 0131D]

(Vers. 19, 20.) “Again I say to you: if two of you agree on earth concerning any matter whatever that they ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven. For where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in their midst.”

[Col. 0132A] All the preceding discourse had called us to concord. Therefore he also promises a reward, so that we may hasten more diligently toward peace, since he says that he will be in the midst of two or three. This resembles the example of the tyrant who wished to test two friends whom he had captured: when one had returned to visit his mother and had given his friend as surety for himself, the tyrant released one while retaining the other. When the first returned on the appointed day, the tyrant, admiring the faithfulness of both, asked them to accept him as a third.

We can also understand this spiritually: when spirit, soul, and body agree and do not wage war against one another through conflicting desires [Alternative: pleasures], with the flesh desiring against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, they may obtain from the Father whatever they ask. There is no doubt that the request concerns good things when the body wishes to possess what the spirit desires. [Col. 0132B]

(Vers. 21, 22.) Then Peter approached him and said: “Lord, how often will my brother sin against me and I forgive him? Up to seven times?” Jesus said to him: “I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven.”

The Lord’s discourse coheres with itself and cannot be broken, like a threefold cord. Above, he had said: “See that you do not despise one of these little ones,” and had added: “If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between you and him alone.” He had promised a reward, saying: “If two of you agree on earth, they will obtain whatever they ask; and I will be in their midst.” Prompted by this, the apostle Peter asks how often he ought to forgive a brother who sins against him, and, together with his question, proposes the answer: “Up to seven times?” Jesus answered him: “Not up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven”—that is, 490 times—so that he should forgive a brother who sins as many times in a day as that brother could not possibly sin.

(Vers. 23.) “Therefore the kingdom of heaven has been compared to a king who wished to settle accounts with his servants.” It is familiar among the Syrians, and especially among the Palestinians, to attach parables to every discourse, so that what cannot be retained by hearers through a simple command may be retained through comparison and examples.

He therefore instructs Peter by the comparison of a king and lord and servant: a servant who owed ten thousand talents had obtained pardon from his lord by asking for it, so that he too might forgive his fellow servants who sinned in lesser matters. For if that king and lord so easily forgave a servant who owed ten thousand talents, how much more ought servants to forgive their fellow servants lesser debts?

To make this clearer, let us give an example: if one of us has committed adultery, murder, sacrilege, or other major crimes amounting to ten thousand talents, these are forgiven when we ask for forgiveness, provided that we also forgive those who sin in lesser matters. But if, on account of an insult, we are implacable and maintain perpetual hostilities because of a bitter word, do we not seem rightly to deserve being consigned to prison, and, according to the example of our own conduct, to have forgiveness for our greater offenses withheld from us? [Note: [Col. 0131D] *simul* was incorrectly printed for *simus* (“we are”).] [Col. 0132D]

[Col. 0133A] (Verses 24 and following.) And when he had begun to settle accounts, one was brought to him who owed ten thousand talents. Since he had nothing with which to repay, his master ordered that he, his wife, his children, and everything he possessed be sold, and payment made. Falling down, that servant begged him, saying: “Have patience with me, and I will repay you everything.” Moved with pity for that servant, the master released him and forgave him the debt. But when that servant had gone out, he found one of his fellow servants who owed him a hundred denarii; and seizing him, he choked him, saying: “Pay what you owe.” Falling down, his fellow servant begged him, saying: “Have patience with me, and I will repay you everything.” But he was unwilling; instead, he went away and had him thrown into prison until he should repay the debt. When his fellow servants saw what had happened, they were greatly distressed; and they came and reported to their master everything that had taken place. Then his master summoned him and said to him: “Wicked servant, I forgave you the entire debt because you begged me. Should you not therefore also have had pity on your fellow servant, just as I had pity on you?” And his master, angered, handed him over to the torturers until he should repay the entire debt.

[Note: [Col. 0133D] Certainly Origen did not stray much further, for he says that if one seeks among human beings the debtor of ten thousand talents, one will perhaps find him to be “the man of sin, the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God or worshiped”; but if one seeks outside the human race, who is he except the devil, who has destroyed so many human beings, by whom he himself has been accepted as the author of sin? Jerome does not adhere so strictly to Origen here as to follow him in a departure from ecclesiastical interpretation; indeed, he does not endorse it.]

I know that some interpret this man who owed ten thousand talents as the devil, and understand his wife and children, who are to be sold because he persists in wickedness, as folly and evil thoughts. For just as the wife of the righteous is called wisdom, so the wife of the unrighteous and sinner is called folly. But to say that the master forgives him ten thousand talents while he does not forgive us, his fellow servants, a hundred denarii, is neither an ecclesiastical interpretation nor one to be accepted by prudent men.

(Vers. 35.) “So also my heavenly Father will do to you, if each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts.” A fearful sentence, if God’s judgment is bent and altered according to our disposition. If we do not forgive our brothers their small offenses, God will not forgive us our great ones. And because someone may say, “I have nothing against him; he knows that. He has God as his judge. I am not concerned with what he chooses to do; I have forgiven him,” he confirms his sentence and overturns every pretense of feigned peace by saying: “If each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts.”

(Cap. XIX.—Verses 1 and following.) And it happened that when Jesus had finished these sayings, he departed from Galilee and came into the regions of Judea beyond the Jordan; and great crowds followed him, and he healed them there. And the Pharisees approached him, testing him and saying: “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any reason?”

He had come from Galilee into Judea. Therefore the faction of the Pharisees and scribes questions him whether it is lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any reason, so that they might hold him as though by a horned syllogism, and whatever answer he gave would expose him to a trap. If he said that wives could be divorced for any reason and others married, he would appear, as a preacher of chastity, to teach the opposite. But if he answered that a wife ought not to be divorced for every reason, he would be held guilty of sacrilege and judged to act against the teaching of Moses and, through Moses, of God. Therefore the Lord so moderates his answer that he passes beyond their snare, adducing Holy Scripture as a witness and setting the natural law and God’s first decision against the second one, which was granted not by God’s will but by the necessity of sinners.

(Vers. 4.) “He answered and said to them: Have you not read that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female?” This is written at the beginning of Genesis. By saying “male and female,” he shows that second marriages are to be avoided. For he did not say “male and females,” which would have been sought on the basis of repudiating the first wife, but “male and female,” so that they might be joined in the companionship of one spouse.

[Note: [Col. 0134D] The manuscript of Saint Remigius reads: “so that they might be joined in the companionship of one marriage.” MART.]

(Vers. 5, 6.) “And he said: For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh. Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh.” Likewise he says “he shall cling to his wife,” not “wives.” “And the two shall be one flesh”: the reward of marriage is that two become one flesh. Chastity joined to the spirit becomes one spirit.

Therefore, what God has joined together, let no human being separate. God joined them by making the flesh of man and woman one; no human being can separate this, unless perhaps God alone. A human being separates them when, because of the desire for a second wife, he dismisses the first. God separates them—he who had also joined them—when, by mutual consent for the sake of serving God, because “the time is short,” we have wives as though we had none (1 Cor. 7).

(Vers. 7.) They say to him: “Why then did Moses command that a bill of divorce be given and the wife dismissed?” They reveal the slander they had prepared. Certainly the Lord had not offered his own opinion, but had recalled the history of old and the commandments of God.

(Vers. 8.) He says to them: “Because Moses permitted you to dismiss your wives because of the hardness of your hearts; but from the beginning it was not so.” What he says amounts to this: Can God be self-contradictory, so that he first commanded one thing and then breaks his own decision by a new command? This must not be our understanding. Rather, when Moses saw that, because of the desire for second wives—whether richer, younger, or more beautiful—the first wives were being killed or forced to lead miserable lives, he preferred to permit discord rather than allow hatred and murder to continue (Deut. 24). At the same time, consider that he did not say, “Because of the hardness of your hearts God permitted you,” but “Moses,” so that, in accordance with the Apostle (1 Cor. 7), it is the counsel of a human being, not the command of God.

[Col. 0135A] (Vers. 9.) “But I say to you that whoever dismisses his wife, except on account of fornication, and marries another, commits adultery. And whoever marries a dismissed woman commits adultery.” Fornication alone overcomes the affection owed to a wife; indeed, once she has divided the one flesh into another and separated herself from her husband through fornication, she ought not to be retained, lest she also place her husband under a curse, as Scripture says: “He who keeps an adulteress is foolish and impious.” Wherever, therefore, there is fornication or suspicion of fornication, the wife may freely be dismissed. And because it could happen that someone might falsely accuse an innocent woman and, in order to contract a second marriage, bring a charge against the first, he is commanded to dismiss his former wife in such a way that he may not have a second wife while the first is alive. What he says amounts to this: If you dismiss your wife not because of lust but because of an injury, why, after experiencing the unhappiness of a first marriage, do you expose yourself to the danger of another? Moreover, because it could happen that, under the same law, a wife might also give her husband a divorce, the same precaution is prescribed: she must not take a second husband. And because a prostitute, and a woman who had once committed adultery, did not fear disgrace, it is prescribed to a second husband that, if he marries such a woman, he is liable to the charge of adultery.

[Note: [Col. 0135D] In one Palatine manuscript, “she is commanded not to marry a second husband” is corruptly written.]

(Vers. 10.) His disciples say to him: “If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is not expedient to marry.” Wives are a heavy burden if they may not be dismissed except on account of fornication. What if she is drunken, irascible, of bad character, extravagant, gluttonous, wandering, quarrelsome, or abusive? Must such a woman be retained? Whether we wish it or not, she must be endured. For while we were free, we voluntarily subjected ourselves to servitude. Seeing, therefore, the heavy yoke of wives, the apostles express the movement of their minds and say: “If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is not expedient to marry.”

(Vers. 11.) He said to them: “Not everyone receives this word, but those to whom it has been given.” Let no one think that this introduces either fate or fortune: that these are virgins to whom it has been given by God, or whom some chance has led to this state. Rather, it has been given to those who asked, who desired, and who labored in order to receive it. For everyone who asks will receive, the one who seeks will find, and to the one who knocks it will be opened (Matt. 7:8; Luke 11:10).

[Col. 0135D] (Vers. 12.) “For there are eunuchs who were born so from their mother’s womb; and there are eunuchs who were made so by human beings; and there are eunuchs who made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Let the one who can receive this receive it.” There are three kinds of eunuchs: two bodily kinds and a third spiritual kind. Some are born so from their mother’s womb. Others are made so either by captivity or by the pleasures of matrons. The third are those who made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, and who, although they could be men, become eunuchs for Christ’s sake. A reward is promised to these; but to the former, whose chastity is imposed by necessity rather than chosen by will, nothing at all is owed.

We can also explain it in another way. Eunuchs from their mother’s womb are those who are of a colder nature, who do not desire lust.

[Note: [Col. 0135D] This is Origen’s interpretation: “Eunuchs,” figuratively speaking, may be called those who are cold toward sexual desire and sluggish, and who do not pour themselves out into sexual lusts, obscenities, or similar things. And shortly afterward: “Others, however, led to this by exhortations and admonitions, abstain from sexual acts and from every form of wantonness concerning the female parts; yet the author of such a purpose, pursuit, and praiseworthy inclination, so to speak, was not the word of God, but human beings—whether those among the Gentiles who devoted themselves to philosophy, or the discourses of heretics who forbid marriage and enjoin abstinence from foods.”]

And there are others who are made so by human beings: whom philosophers make so, or who are softened into women because of the worship of idols; or who, through heretical persuasion, pretend to chastity in order to falsify the truth of religion. But none of them attains the kingdom of heaven except the one who has made himself a eunuch for Christ’s sake. Therefore he adds: “Let the one who can receive this receive it,” so that each person may consider his own strength, whether he can fulfill the commands of virginity and chastity. Chastity in itself is attractive and draws everyone to itself. But one’s strength must be considered, so that the one who can receive it may receive it. It is as though the voice of the Lord were encouraging and urging his soldiers toward the reward of chastity: “Let the one who can receive this receive it; let the one who can fight, fight, overcome, and triumph.”

(Vers. 13, 14.) Then little children were brought to him so that he might lay his hands on them and pray; but the disciples rebuked them. Jesus, however, said to them: “Let the little children come to me, and do not forbid them, for of such is the kingdom of heaven.” And when he had laid his hands on them, he departed from there. Significantly, he said “of such,” not “of these,” to show that it is not age but character that possesses the kingdom, and that a reward is promised to those who have a similar innocence and simplicity. The Apostle also agrees with this meaning: “Brothers, do not become children in understanding; but be little ones in wickedness, while in understanding be mature” (1 Cor. 14:20).

(Vers. 16.) And behold, one came up to him and said: “Good Teacher, what good thing shall I do to have eternal life?” He says to him: This man who asks how he may attain eternal life is both a young man and rich—and proud; and, according to another Evangelist, he asks not with the desire of a learner but as one testing him (Mark 10).

[Col. 0136D] (Vers. 17.) “Why do you ask me about the good? One is good, God.” Because he had called him “good teacher” and had not confessed him to be God or the Son of God, he learns that even a holy human being, in comparison with God, is not good, concerning whom it is said: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good” (Ps. 117:1). But lest anyone suppose that, when God is called good, the Son of God is excluded from goodness, we read elsewhere: “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (John 10). And in the Prophet, “the good Spirit” and “the good land.” Therefore the Savior does not reject the testimony of goodness; but he excludes the young man’s error in calling him a teacher apart from God.

(Vers. 18, 19.) “But if you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments.” He says to him: “Which ones?” Jesus said: “You shall not murder. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not bear false witness. Honor your father and mother, and you shall love your neighbor as yourself.” We can prove that this young man was a tester from the fact that, when the Lord said to him, “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments,” he deceitfully asks again which commandments they are—as though he had not himself read them, or as though the Lord could command things contrary to God.

(Vers. 20.) The young man says to him: “I have kept all these things from my youth; what do I still lack?”

[Note: [Col. 0137D] In the Palatine manuscripts, the words “from my youth” are absent.]

Jesus says to him: The young man is lying. For if he had fulfilled in practice what is included among the commandments—“You shall love your neighbor as yourself”—how, after hearing, “Go, sell what you possess and give to the poor,” would he have gone away sorrowful because he had many possessions?

(Vers. 21.) “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” It is within our power whether we wish to be perfect. Yet whoever wishes to be perfect must sell what he possesses—not sell only part, as Ananias and Sapphira did (Acts 5), but sell everything; and after selling it, give everything to the poor, and thus prepare treasure for himself in the kingdom of heaven.

[Note: [Col. 0137D] Two Palatine manuscripts read: “Nor is this sufficient for perfection”; shortly afterward, all read “will” rather than “pleasure.”]

Nor is this sufficient for perfection unless, after despising riches, he follows the Savior—that is, after abandoning evil, he does good. For a purse is more easily despised than pleasure. Many abandon riches but do not follow the Lord. The one who follows the Lord is the one who imitates him and walks in his footsteps. For whoever says that he believes in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked (1 John 2:6).

(Vers. 22.) He went away sorrowful, for he had many possessions. This is the sorrow that leads to death. The cause of the sorrow is given: he had many possessions—that is, thorns and thistles that choked the Lord’s seed.

(Vers. 23.) But Jesus said to his disciples: “Amen, I say to you, a rich man will enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty.”

[Col. 0137D] And how did Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who were rich, enter the kingdom of heaven (Gen. 13 and 36), and how are Matthew and Zacchaeus praised in the Gospel because, having abandoned their riches, they entered under the Lord’s testimony? We must consider that at the time when they entered, they ceased to be rich. Therefore they will not enter as long as they remain rich. Yet because riches are difficult to despise, he did not say, “It is impossible for the rich to enter the kingdom of heaven,” but “with difficulty.” Where “with difficulty” is stated, impossibility is not being asserted, but rarity is being shown.

(Vers. 24 and following.) “And again I say to you: It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven.” When they heard this, the disciples were exceedingly amazed, saying: “Who then can be saved?” But Jesus looked at them and said: “With human beings this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.”

[Note: [Col. 0137D] We came very close to preferring the reading of our manuscripts, which the following context also seems in some measure to support: “It is shown not to be impossible, but difficult.” It is well known that the camel which Jerome here, following the Fathers who preceded him, understands as an animal, most later interpreters understand as a thick nautical rope. Theophylact notes this in his commentary on Matthew: “Some say that the camel is not an animal but a thick rope used by sailors for casting anchors.” The Syriac word which Christ could easily have used signifies both a camel—the large humped animal—and a thicker rope. The scholiast on Aristophanes says that in Greek a thick rope is called κάμιλον τὸ παχὺ σχοινίον (“a thick rope”); and from the same, apparently, Syriac origin, it is called gomena in Italian. Moreover, the comparison itself seems to have been made with things sewn through a needle, such as thinner cords and threads, rather than with an enormous beast, which has scarcely any relation to a needle.]

By this statement it is shown not that it is impossible but that it is difficult. For if, just as a camel cannot enter through the eye of a needle, a rich man cannot enter the kingdom of heaven, no rich person will be saved. But if we read Isaiah, and see how the camels of Midian and Ephah come to Jerusalem with gifts and offerings (Isa. 60), and how those who were formerly bent and twisted by the crookedness of their vices enter the gates of Jerusalem, we shall understand how these camels also, to whom the rich are compared, can enter through the narrow gate and the constricted way that leads to life (above, 7), once they have laid down the heavy burden of sins and the crookedness of their entire body.

[Note: [Col. 0138] The older Palatine manuscript reads: “When they heard this, the disciples were exceedingly amazed, saying: ‘Who then can be saved?’ Mercy tempered the severity of the sentence,” and so forth. Two other manuscripts continue after “Who then will be saved?”: “But Jesus, looking at their thoughts, said: ‘With human beings this is impossible, but with God all things are possible. His mercy tempered the severity,’” and so forth. Both additions seem to have arisen from the ingenuity of a glossator.]

When the disciples asked and were astonished at the severity of the saying, “Who then will be saved?”, he tempered the severity of the sentence by his mercy, saying: “The things that are impossible with human beings are possible with God.”

(Vers. 27.) Then Peter answered and said to him: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you. What then will there be for us?” Great is his confidence. Peter was a fisherman; he had not been rich. He sought food by his own hands and skill, and yet he speaks confidently: “We have left everything.” And because merely leaving is not sufficient, he adds what makes the act perfect: “And we have followed you.” We have done what you commanded; what reward, then, will you give us?

(Vers. 28.) Jesus said to them: “Amen, I say to you, you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”

He did not say, “You who have left everything”—for the philosopher Crates did this, and many others despised riches—but “you who have followed me,” which properly belongs to the apostles and believers.

[Note: [Col. 0139C] Erasmus reads Socrates instead of Crates. I found the same error in all fourteen manuscript codices that I examined. Concerning this error of the ancient copyists, Mariano Victorio records the following: “We corrected Crates instead of Socrates at the prompting of the Brixian manuscripts.” For it was Crates, not Socrates—who is not recorded as having been rich—of whom this deed is reported. The error arose because Socrates was better known and more celebrated than Crates, and the names are nearly identical. Jerome makes this assertion about Crates in many places. In his letter to Paulinus, On the Institution of a Monk: “That Crates of Thebes, once an exceedingly wealthy man, when he was going to Athens to study philosophy, threw away a great weight of gold and did not think that he could possess both virtues and riches at once.” Likewise, in his letter to Pammachius, On the Death of Paula: “And yet, for a man who is not sufficiently perfect and complete, to despise wealth, scatter money, and throw away what can be lost and found again in a moment. Crates of Thebes did this; Antisthenes did it; many did it whom we read of as most vicious.” Likewise, to Lucinus: “To lay down gold is the act of fools, not of the perfect. Crates of Thebes did this; Antisthenes did it.” Likewise, in Book Two Against Jovinianus: “And that Crates of Thebes, after throwing a considerable weight of gold into the sea, said: ‘Away to destruction with evil desires! I will drown you, lest I myself be drowned by you.’” MART.]

[Note: [Col. 0139D] It is truly remarkable that in all our manuscripts and in fourteen others belonging to Martianay, this same corruption unanimously reads Socrates here instead of Crates. Victorius says that he corrected it at the prompting of the Brixian manuscripts, and he gathers here many testimonies from Jerome concerning Crates to establish the true reading. Such is the passage in Letter 58, to Paulinus: “That Crates of Thebes, once an exceedingly wealthy man, when he was going to Athens to study philosophy, threw away a great weight of gold.” He repeats this in Letters 66, to Pammachius, and 71, to Lucinus. Finally, also in Book Two Against Jovinianus: “That Crates of Thebes, after throwing a considerable weight of gold into the sea, said: ‘Away to destruction with evil desires! I will drown you, lest I myself be drowned by you.’” Yet in establishing this reading against the evidence of the manuscripts, nothing is more decisive than historical truth and Origen’s opinion, from whom Jerome copied the entire interpretation. Indeed, this story is told of Crates, not Socrates, by Philostratus in Book One, chapter 10, of The Life of Apollonius; by Diogenes Laertius in Book Six; by Plutarch in On Not Borrowing Money; and finally by Suidas, who reports that Crates adopted another way of despising wealth: “When he himself had abandoned uncultivated fields, he climbed to an elevated place and said: ‘Crates of Thebes makes Crates free.’” Origen’s opinion concerning this passage, to which, as we have said, Jerome adheres closely, is as follows, according to Huet’s interpretation: “They say that Crates of Thebes, when, in order to attain freedom, he had adopted a frugal and restrained way of life and wished to show himself blessed to the Greeks—and, as he imagined, lacking nothing—distributed to the people of Thebes all his possessions, which he had sold and converted into money, while declaring at the same time: ‘Today Crates makes Crates free.’” MART.]

“In the regeneration,” when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty—that is, when the dead rise incorruptible from corruption—you also will sit on judgment seats, condemning the twelve tribes of Israel, because they were unwilling to believe while you believed.

(Vers. 29, 30.) “And everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for my name’s sake will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life. But many who are first will be last, and the last first.”

This passage agrees with the saying in which the Savior declares: “I have not come to bring peace but a sword. For I have come to separate a man from his father, and a mother from her daughter, and a daughter-in-law from her mother-in-law; and a man’s enemies will be those of his household” (above, 10:34). Therefore, those who for the sake of faith in Christ and the preaching of the Gospel have despised every affection, as well as the riches and pleasures of the world, will receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life.

Taking this saying as an occasion, some introduce a thousand years after the resurrection, saying that then we shall receive a hundredfold of everything we have abandoned, together with eternal life. They do not understand that, if the promise is worthy of acceptance in the other respects, it would contain disgrace with regard to wives: that one who had abandoned one wife for the Lord would receive a hundred in the future.

The meaning, therefore, is this: Whoever has abandoned carnal things for the Savior will receive spiritual things, which, in comparison and according to their own worth, will be as though a hundredfold number were compared with a small number.

[Note: [Col. 0140D] Two Palatine manuscripts read “as though a small number,” with the word “if” deleted.]

Therefore the Apostle also says—he who had abandoned only one house and the small fields of a single province: “As having nothing, yet possessing everything” (2 Cor. 6:10).

(Cap. XX.—Verses 1 and following.) “The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard. And having agreed with the laborers for a denarius a day, he sent them into his vineyard. And going out about the third hour, he saw others standing idle in the marketplace and said to them: ‘Go, you also, into my vineyard, and whatever is just I will give you.’ And they went. Again he went out about the sixth and ninth hours and did likewise. But about the eleventh hour he went out and found others standing, and said to them: ‘Why do you stand here idle all day?’ They say to him: ‘Because no one has hired us.’ He says to them: ‘Go, you also, into my vineyard.’ When evening came, the lord of the vineyard said to his steward: ‘Call the laborers and pay them their wages, beginning with the last and proceeding to the first.’ Therefore, when those who had come at about the eleventh hour arrived, they received a denarius each. When the first also came, they thought that they would receive more; but they too received a denarius each. And receiving it, they murmured against the householder, saying: ‘These last have worked one hour, and you have made them equal to us, who have borne the burden of the day and the heat.’ But he answered one of them and said: ‘Friend, I do you no injury. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? Take what is yours and go. I wish to give this last one also as I give you. Or is it not lawful for me to do what I wish? Is your eye evil because I am good?’ So the last will be first, and the first last. For many are called, but few are chosen.”

This parable, or likeness of the kingdom of heaven, is understood from what has preceded. For it is written before it: “Many who are first will be last, and the last first.” Not with the Lord showing preference to time, but to faith.

[Note: [Col. 0140D] Victorius reads: “Not with the Lord showing preference to time, but to faith,” and so forth.]

He says that the householder went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard and fixed the price of the work at a denarius. Then, going out about the third hour, he saw others standing idle in the marketplace; to them he promised not a denarius but whatever was just. He did likewise at the sixth and ninth hours. At the eleventh hour he found others standing who had been idle all day and sent them into the vineyard. When evening came, he ordered his steward to begin paying from the last—that is, from the eleventh-hour laborers up to the first-hour laborers—and all, stirred up by envy against the last, accused the householder of injustice. Not because they received less than had been agreed, but because they wanted to receive more than those upon whom the employer’s kindness had been poured out.

It seems to me that the laborers of the first hour are Samuel, Jeremiah, and John the Baptist, who can say with the Psalmist: “From my mother’s womb you are my God” (Ps. 21:11). The laborers of the third hour are those who began to serve God from puberty. Those of the sixth hour are those who took up Christ’s yoke in mature age. Those of the ninth hour are those who did so when they were already declining toward old age. Those of the eleventh hour are those who did so in extreme old age. Yet all receive the same reward, although their labor is different.

There are some who explain this parable differently. They say that the first hour signifies Adam and the other patriarchs up to Noah, sent into the vineyard; the third, Noah himself up to Abraham and the circumcision given to him; the sixth, from Abraham up to Moses, when the Law was given; the ninth, Moses himself and the prophets; and the eleventh, the apostles and the people of the Gentiles, whom all envy.

[Note: [Col. 0141D] Origen above all gives this interpretation, from whom Hilary also borrowed it. “See,” he says, “whether you can call the first order the one that began with Adam together with the creation of the world. For the householder went out early in the morning and, so to speak, hired Adam and Eve to cultivate the vineyard of piety. The second order is that which is reckoned from Noah and the covenant made with him. The third belongs to Abraham, and should be understood to include also the things concerning the patriarchs up to Moses. The fourth likewise belongs to Moses and refers to all that was accomplished in Egypt and to the Laws established in the desert. Finally, the order of the eleventh hour signifies the coming of Christ Jesus.” Yet Adamantius does not omit the earlier interpretation approved by Jerome, according to which the whole of human life is represented by a day in the parable; many later interpreters have also embraced it.]

Understanding this, after the eleventh hour, when the sun was near setting and it was toward evening, John the Evangelist says: “Little children, it is the last hour” (1 John 2:13). At the same time, consider that all alike accuse the householder of injustice in the case of the eleventh-hour laborers, yet do not understand it in their own case. For if the householder is unjust, he is not unjust toward one alone but toward all, since the laborer of the third hour did not work as much as the one sent at the first hour. Similarly, the laborer of the sixth hour worked less than the laborer of the third hour, and the laborer of the ninth hour less than the laborer of the sixth. Every earlier calling, therefore, envies the Gentiles and is tormented by the grace of the Gospel. Thus the Savior concludes the parable: “The first will be last, and the last first.” The Jews are turned from the head into the tail, and we are changed from the tail into the head.

[Col. 0141D] (Vers. 13.) “Friend, I do you no injury.” I have read in someone’s book that this friend who is rebuked by the householder is understood as the laborer of the first hour, the first-formed human being, and those who believed at that time.

[Note: [Col. 0142D] He easily indicates Origen’s book without naming him, since Origen interprets it in this way: “But the householder said to one of them—perhaps to Adam himself: ‘Friend, I do you no injury,’” and so forth.]

[Col. 0142A] “Did you not agree with me for a denarius?” The denarius bears the image of a king. Therefore you received the wage that I had promised you—that is, my image and likeness. What more do you seek? And you desire not so much to receive more yourself as to prevent another from receiving anything, as though the merit of the reward were diminished by another’s participation?

(Vers. 14, 15.) “Take what is yours and go. I wish to give this last one also as I give you. Or is it not lawful for me to do what I wish?” The Jew is saved in the Law not by grace but by works: “Whoever does it shall live by it.” Therefore it is said to him:

(Vers. 16.) “Is your eye evil because I am good? So the last will be first, and the first last. For many are called, but few are chosen.” The same meaning is expressed in that parable of Luke, where the elder son envies the younger, does not wish to receive him when he repents, and accuses his father of injustice. And so that we may know that this is the meaning we have stated, the title and the conclusion of this parable agree. “So,” he says, “the last will be first, and the first last. For many are called, but few are chosen.”

(Vers. 17 and following.) And as Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, he took his twelve disciples aside privately and said to them: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over to the chief priests and scribes; they will condemn him to death and hand him over to the Gentiles to be mocked, scourged, and crucified, and on the third day he will rise.” He had often said this very thing to the disciples. But because, amid the many intervening discussions, what they had heard could slip from their memory, as he was going to Jerusalem and taking the apostles with him, he prepares them for the trial, so that when persecution and the disgrace of the cross come, they may not be scandalized.

(Vers. 20, 21.) Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee approached him with her sons, worshiping and asking something of him. He said to her: “What do you want?” She said to him: “Say that these two sons of mine may sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your kingdom.”

From where did the mother of the sons of Zebedee derive her expectation of the kingdom, when the Lord had said: “The Son of Man will be handed over to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn him to death and hand him over to the Gentiles to be mocked, scourged, and crucified,” and, while announcing the disgrace of the passion to the disciples who feared it, she asked for the glory of the triumphant one? I think it was for this reason: because afterward the Lord had said, “and on the third day he will rise,” the woman supposed that immediately after the resurrection he would begin to reign; and she thought that what is promised at the second coming was to be fulfilled at the first, and in feminine eagerness desired the present, forgetful of the future.

[Col. 0143A] But when the Lord asks, and in response to her request says, “What do you want?”, this does not arise from ignorance. Rather, it is said from the perspective of the one who was to be scourged and crucified, just as in the case of the woman with the hemorrhage: “Who touched me?” (Luke 8:15); and concerning Lazarus: “Where have you laid him?” (John 11:34). Likewise in the Old Testament: “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. 3:9); and: “Going down, I will see whether they have acted altogether according to the outcry that has come to me; but if not, I will know” (Gen. 18:21).

[Note: [Col. 0143D] Our manuscripts insert “their own,” and in the Greek text itself αὐτῶν (“their”) is added.]

The mother of the sons of Zebedee asks through a woman’s error and affection, not knowing what she was asking. Nor is it surprising that this ignorance is rebuked in her, when it is said of Peter, when he wished to make three tabernacles, that he did not know what he was saying (Mark 9).

(Vers. 22.) But Jesus answered and said: “You do not know [Col. 0143B] what you are asking.” The mother makes the request, but the Lord addresses the disciples, understanding that her petition proceeds from the sons’ desire.

“Can you drink the cup that I am going to drink?” They say to him: “We can.” In the divine Scriptures we understand the cup as the Passion, [Note: [Col. 0143D] Origen also cites just as many passages of Scripture in support of this interpretation, and speaks in nearly the same words: “To prove that martyrdom is signified twice, one may use not only that passage, ‘Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me’ . . . but also the passage found in Psalm 115: ‘What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I will take the cup of salvation, and I will call upon the name of the Lord.’” Immediately afterward: “Precious in the sight of the Lord,” and so forth. Saint Hilary adopted this same interpretation, as did many others after him.] according to the saying: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. XXVI, 39). And in the Psalm: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I will take the cup of salvation, and I will call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXV, 3 ff.); and immediately it explains what this cup is: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.”

(Vers. 23.) He says to them: “You will indeed drink my cup; but to sit at my right and left is not mine to give, but it belongs to those for whom it has been prepared by my Father.” [Col. 0143C] It is asked how the sons of Zebedee—namely, James and John—drank the cup of martyrdom, since Scripture reports that only the Apostle James was beheaded by Herod (Acts XII), while John ended his life by a natural death. But if we read the ecclesiastical histories, in which it is related that he too was sent, on account of his martyrdom, into a vessel of boiling oil, and that from it he came forth as Christ’s athlete to receive the crown, and was immediately banished to the island of Patmos, we shall see that he did not lack the resolve for martyrdom, and that John drank the cup of confession—the same cup that the three boys drank in the furnace of fire (Dan. III), even though the persecutor did not shed his blood.

But when he says, “To sit at my right and left is not mine to give, but to those for whom it has been prepared by my Father,” this is to be understood as follows: The kingdom of heaven belongs not to the one who gives, but to the one who receives. For “there is no partiality with God” (Acts X, 34); rather, whoever has so conducted himself as to become worthy of the kingdom of heaven will receive what has been prepared not for a person but for a way of life. If, then, you are such as to attain the kingdom of heaven, which my Father has prepared for those who triumph and conquer, you too will receive it.

Others wish this to have been said of Moses and Elijah, whom shortly before they had seen speaking with him on the mountain; but it does not seem so to me at all. For this reason the names of those who sit in the kingdom of heaven are not stated: lest, when a few were named, the others should be thought excluded.

(Vers. 24.) When the ten heard this, they were indignant at the two brothers. The ten apostles are not indignant at the mother of the sons of Zebedee, nor do they attribute the audacity of the request to the woman who made it; [Note: [Col. 0143D] Three Palatine manuscripts read, “nor do they refer the boldness of the request to the woman,” and so forth—perhaps more correctly. Rhabanus differs by a single word in the ablative of “request.”] rather, they are indignant at the sons, because, ignorant of their own measure, they burned with immoderate ambition. To them also the Lord had said: “You do not know what you are asking.” It is understood either from the Lord’s answer or from the apostles’ indignation that the sons had sent their mother to make these grand requests.

(Vers. 25 ff.) But Jesus called them to him and said: “You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who are great exercise authority over them. It shall not be so among you; but whoever wishes to become great among you shall be your minister. And whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your servant.”

The humble and gentle teacher neither rebukes the two [Al. “his own”] who make their immoderate request for their ambition, nor reproves the other ten for their indignation [Col. 0144C] and envy. Instead, he sets forth an example by which he teaches that the greater is the one who has been the lesser, and that the one who serves everyone becomes lord. It is therefore useless either for the former to have sought greatness without measure or for the latter to grieve over the desire of those who wanted to be greater, since one reaches the summit of virtue not through power but through humility.

Finally, he offers his own example, so that if they disregarded his words, they might blush at his deeds, and he says:

(Vers. 28.) “Just as the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve.” Observe that we have often said that the one who serves is called the Son of Man.

“And to give his life as a ransom for many.” He took the form of a servant in order to pour out his blood for the world (Philipp. II). He did not say that he would give his life as a ransom for [Note: [Col. 0143D] Do not imagine that this passage of Jerome can be enlisted in support of the heresy of the Predestinarians, who declare that Christ died only for certain human beings and not for every individual. Understand the Catholic position maintained by him as follows: Jerome says plainly that Christ gave his life as a ransom for all human beings; but he intended believers in particular to merit the benefit of that act, and, in a special manner, desired for the faithful the salvation which by his death he obtained for all others, and was concerned that it should be bestowed upon them.

And lest you think that, by a kindly interpretation, the words of the holy Father are here being rescued from a tendency toward error, know that he is speaking according to Scripture’s own usage. Such passages are to be explained in the same way as John III, 16: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.” So too this passage of Paul, I Tim. IV, 10: “We have hoped in the living God, who is the Savior of all, especially of believers.” The author of the book *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, chapter 31, and others in many places, explain these words most wisely in accordance with the Catholic faith.

Otherwise, you may see this passage of Jerome eagerly cited by other ecclesiastical writers as a defense of the Church’s faith, and thrown before heretics as a kind of bulwark. When Servatus Lupus had quoted these words of Jerome in his *Collection on Three Questions*, he adds: “The most celebrated Doctor very cautiously understood this to refer to believers of every sort, in view of the passage: ‘The brother for whom Christ died will perish through your knowledge.’” He also observes that Bede used these same words of Jerome in his *Exposition of Mark*, book IV, chapter 10.

But in his letter to King Charles the Bald he exaggerates the point, wishing to show that Jerome taught, by this interpretation and in accordance with the Catholic faith, that only the faithful are meant—whether those who would remain in grace or those who would withdraw from it through their own fault. Yet Jerome certainly does not think this way. In explicit words he professes that Christ took the form of a servant in order to pour out his blood for the world, absolutely speaking; and what the Evangelist says, “to give his life as a ransom for many,” he applies to a special kindness toward the faithful. Through this kindness, as Prosper says, Christ shows that there is a part of the human race which, by the merit of divinely inspired faith, is advanced through special benefits to the highest and eternal salvation.

Theophylact ingeniously explains “many” as “all.” “For,” he says, “οἱ πάντες, πολλοί”—“all are many.” And Euthymius says: “He now says ‘for many’ instead of ‘for all.’ For Scripture frequently says ‘many’ in place of ‘all.’” Thus he gave his life for all and redeemed all, although many of their own accord remained in slavery.] many—that is, for those who would wish to believe.

(Vers. 19 ff.) And as they were leaving Jericho, a great crowd followed him. And behold, two blind men sitting beside the road heard that Jesus was passing by, and they cried out, saying: “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David.” But the crowd rebuked them so that they would be silent. Yet they cried out even more, saying: “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David.”

There were many robbers in Jericho, who were accustomed to kill and wound those going out from Jerusalem and descending into Jericho. [Note: [Col. 0146C] Three Palatine manuscripts read: “those descending from Jerusalem into Jericho, to kill them,” and so forth.] For this reason the Lord came to Jericho with his disciples, to free the wounded and to draw a great crowd after him. Finally, when they wished to leave Jericho, a great crowd followed him. If he had remained in Jerusalem and had never descended to lowly things, the crowd would still to this day be sitting in darkness [Col. 0145B] and in the shadow of death.

There were also two blind men beside the road. He calls blind those who were not yet able to say: “In your light we shall see light” (Ps. XXXV, 10). They were beside the road because, although they seemed to possess knowledge of the Law, they did not know the way, which is Christ. Most understand them as Pharisees and Sadducees; others understand them as both peoples, that of the Old Testament and that of the New: the one following the written Law, the other the natural law, yet both blind without Christ.

Because they could not see by themselves, they heard the heralding of the Savior and confessed him to be the Son of David. But if the two blind men are understood as referring to the Jewish people, what follows—“the crowd rebuked them”—is to be understood of the Gentiles. The Apostle warns the Gentiles not to boast and grow proud against their root (Rom. XI); but since they themselves had been grafted from the wild olive into the good olive through the error of their predecessors, they must by no means envy the salvation of those who came before them. [Note: [Col. 0146C] So Origen understood it long ago: “We shall say that the two blind men are Israel and the Jews before Christ’s coming . . . sitting beside the road because they dwelt in the Law and the prophets; blind because before Christ’s coming into their souls they did not see the true and legitimate meanings contained in the Law and the prophets.”]

“Have mercy on us, Son of David.” They are rebuked by the crowds, yet they do not keep silent; rather, they repeat the same words more frequently, showing their intense desire for the true light.

(Vers. 32, 33.) And Jesus stood still and called them, and said: “What do you want me to do for you?” They say to him: “Lord, that our eyes may be opened.”

They were blind; they did not know where they were going and could not follow the Savior. There were many pits in Jericho, many cliffs and precipices sloping down into the depths. Therefore the Lord stands still so that they may be able to come, and he commands them to be called so that the crowd may not prevent them. He asks as though he did not know what they wanted, so that from the blind men’s answer their manifest weakness might be revealed and his power might be recognized from the remedy.

(Vers. 34.) Moved with pity for them, Jesus touched their eyes; and immediately they saw, and followed him.

He touches their eyes, and the Creator supplies what nature had not given—or, more precisely, mercy gives what weakness had taken away. Immediately they saw and followed him. Those who earlier sat helplessly in Jericho and knew only how to cry out afterward follow Jesus—not so much with their feet as with their virtues.

(Cap. XXI—Vers. 1 ff.) And when he had drawn near to Jerusalem and had come to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives, then Jesus sent two disciples, saying to them: “Go into the village that is opposite you, and immediately you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her; untie them and bring them to me. And if anyone says anything to you, say: ‘The Lord has need of them’; and immediately he will let them go.”

He leaves Jericho after leading out from it a very great number of crowds and restoring health to the blind, and he approaches Jerusalem enriched with great treasures: having restored salvation to believers, he wishes to enter the city of peace, the place of the vision of God, and the citadel [Note: [Col. 0146D] Several manuscripts read “the citadel of the watchman.” Jerome interprets Bethphage as “house of jaws,” drawing on Origen. In his book *On Hebrew Names* he says that Bethphage means “house of the mouth of the valleys” or “house of the cheek.” The word is Syriac, not Hebrew. Some think it means “house of jaws.” See the observations made on this word in that book, and also Letter 108 in our recension, where he calls Bethphage the village of priestly jaws. Rhabanus reads “of the watchman.”] of the watchtower.

When he approached Jerusalem and came to Bethphage, the house of jaws—a village of priests, symbolizing confession, situated on the Mount of Olives, where there is the light of knowledge and the rest from labors and sorrows—he sent two of his disciples, [Note: [Col. 0146D] Martianaeus says that Erasmus and Victorius fabricated the Greek words θεωρητικήν καὶ πρακτικήν; our manuscripts likewise prefer θεωρητικόν καὶ ἐργαστικόν, which I do not reject. One Palatine manuscript writes them in Latin letters, *Theoreticen et Practicen*.] θεωρητικόν καὶ ἐργαστικόν, that is, knowledge and action, so that they might enter the village.

And he said to them: “Go into the village that is opposite you.” It was opposite the apostles, for it did not wish to accept the yoke of doctrines. “And immediately,” he says, “you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her; untie them and bring them to me.”

The donkey was tied with many bonds of sins. The colt too was unruly and unable to endure the bridle; according to Luke’s Gospel (chapter XIX), [Note: [Col. 0147C] One Palatine manuscript transfers here the words “who claimed illicit authority for themselves,” which occur three verses later. Shortly afterward, instead of *subditus* (“subject”), *subditos* (“subjects”) was formerly read. But Victor says: “The colt of the donkey, by which the people of the Gentiles are signified, is said to have had many masters because it was not held subject to one error and one doctrine only, but was subject to many errors and doctrines,” calling the many errors “many masters.”] it had many masters, being subject not to one error and doctrine alone.

Yet the many masters who claimed illicit authority for themselves, seeing the true Lord and his servants who had come to untie them, did not dare resist. What the donkey and the donkey’s colt signify we shall explain below.

(Vers. 4, 5.) Now this took place so that what had been spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled, saying: “Tell the daughter of Zion: Behold, your king is coming to you, gentle, seated upon a donkey and a colt, the foal of a beast of burden.”

This is written in the prophet Zechariah. If time permits us to live, it will be discussed more fully in its proper place. For now, we must state briefly that, according to the literal sense, he could not have sat upon both animals during such a short stretch of road. Either he sat upon the donkey, while the colt remained without a rider, or, if he used the colt for riding, as is more fitting, the donkey was led along free.

Therefore, since the historical account involves either impossibility or impropriety, we pass on to higher meanings: the donkey, which was a beast of burden, tamed and broken in, and had borne the yoke of the Law, is to be understood as the Synagogue; the colt of the donkey, unruly and free, is the people of the Gentiles, upon whom Jesus sat, sending to them his two disciples, one to the Circumcision and the other to the Gentiles.

[Note: [Col. 0147D] Jerome learned this learnedly from Adamantius, whose words are these: “Consider whether these are not symbols of the Savior, who through his disciples sets free his own beasts from their bonds—namely, those who at that time, from this people as well as from the Gentiles, professed faith. For the ancient synagogue was bound and tied by sins; and with it the colt also was bound, namely the people newly formed from the Gentiles. When the Savior approached proud Jerusalem by the way where the ascent lies open, he commanded both to be loosed by the disciples conveying his instructions, giving them the Holy Spirit through these words: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit,’ and so forth.”]

(Vers. 6, 7.) The disciples went and did as Jesus had commanded them. They brought the donkey and the colt, placed their garments upon them, and made him sit on top of them.

This colt and donkey, upon which the apostles spread their garments so that Jesus might sit more comfortably, had been naked before the Savior’s coming. Since many claimed dominion over them, they shivered without covering. But after they received the apostles’ garments, they became more beautiful and had the Lord as their rider. [Note: [Col. 0148C] Origen should again be consulted here, together with Huet’s annotation on him.]

The apostolic garment may be understood either as instruction in virtues, or as exposition of the Scriptures, or as the variety of ecclesiastical doctrines. Unless the soul has been instructed and adorned with these, it does not deserve to have the Lord as its rider.

(Vers. 8.) But the very great crowd spread their garments on the road.

Observe the difference among the various persons. The apostles place their garments upon the donkey; the crowd, which is of lower rank, spreads its garments beneath the donkey’s feet, so that it may not strike against a stone, trample a thorn, or slip into a pit.

Others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road.

They cut branches from the fruit-bearing trees with which the Mount of Olives is planted, and spread them on the road, so that they might make crooked things straight and level uneven things, and so that Christ, conqueror of demons and vices, might advance more directly and safely in the hearts of believers.

[Col. 0148B] (Vers. 9.) The crowds that went before and those that followed cried out, saying: “Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!”

Since the historical account is clear, let us follow the spiritual order of exposition. The crowds that had come out of Jericho and followed the Savior and his disciples, after they saw the colt of the donkey released—though previously it had been bound—and adorned with the apostles’ garments, with the Lord Jesus seated upon it, placed their garments beneath it and spread branches of trees along the road.

When they had completed everything by their actions, they also offered testimony with their voices. Those going before and those following did not resound with a brief and silent confession, but with a full-throated cry: “Hosanna [Note: [Col. 0148D] In the manuscripts *Osianna* and *Osanna* are read indiscriminately. Three Palatine manuscripts prefer here and below, instead of “he who comes,” “he who is to come.”] to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name [Col. 0148C] of the Lord.”

When it says, “The crowds that went before and those that followed,” it shows that both peoples—the people who believed in the Lord before the Gospel and those who believed after the Gospel—praise Jesus with a harmonious voice of confession. In accordance with the example of the preceding parable, the laborers of different hours receive one reward of faith.

As for what follows, “Hosanna to the Son of David,” I remember having explained its meaning many years ago in a brief letter [Note: [Col. 0148D] The letter is number 20 in our recension, written at the beginning of the year 383; it is worthwhile to compare it here. See also Origen, from whom the holy Doctor drew a substantial part of the following discussion of *Hosanna*.] to Damasus, then bishop of the city of Rome. I shall now touch on it briefly.

In Psalm 117, which was plainly written concerning the Savior’s coming, we read, among other things: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. This is from the Lord [Al. “and”]; it is marvelous in our eyes.
