This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it.” Immediately afterward comes: “O Lord, save me; O Lord, prosper me. Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; we have blessed you from the house of the Lord,” and so forth (Ps. CXVII, 22 ff.).

Where the Septuagint has ὦ Κύριε, σῶσον δή, that is, “O Lord, save,” we read in Hebrew: **ANNA ADONAI OSIANNA** (). Symmachus translated this more clearly by saying: “I beseech you, Lord, save; I beseech you.” [Note: [Col. 0149C] Some manuscripts insert “me.” Shortly afterward, instead of *sermonem* (“expression”), *sermone* (“in the expression”) was formerly read. We silently correct minor matters of this kind from time to time.]

Therefore no one should think that the expression has been composed from two words, namely a Greek and a Hebrew one; it is entirely Hebrew, and signifies that Christ’s coming is the salvation of the world. Hence what follows: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” The Savior himself also confirms this in the Gospel: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me. Another will come in his own name, and you will receive him” (John V, 4).

Moreover, what is joined to it, “Hosanna,” that is, “salvation in the highest,” clearly shows that Christ’s coming is not merely the salvation of human beings but of the entire world, joining earthly things to heavenly things: “so that every knee should bow [Al. “bend”] to him, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Philipp. II, 10).

(Vers. 10.) And when he entered Jerusalem, the whole city was shaken, saying: “Who is this?” But the peoples [Al. “Many”] were saying:

When Jesus entered with the entire crowd, the city of Jerusalem was shaken, wondering at the multitude but not knowing the truth, and saying: “Who is this?” In another place, too, we read that the angels say: “Who is this King of glory?” (Ps. XXIII, 8).

While others either hesitate or ask questions, the lowly populace confesses him, beginning with lesser things in order to reach greater ones, and says:

This is Jesus the prophet from Nazareth of Galilee.

He is the prophet whom Moses had said would come, one like himself, and who among the Greeks is properly written with the article. [Note: [Col. 0149C] That is, with the article. Other codices read “with an asterisk”; others, “with the testimony,” a reading generally followed by Erasmus and Victorius, who read μετὰ τοῦ ἄρθρου μαρτυρίᾳ, that is, “with the testimony of the article.”] [Note: [Col. 0149D] The manuscript codices preserve no more. The books printed before ours read: “and who among the Greeks is written with τοῦ ἄρθρου μαρτυρίᾳ, that is, ‘with the testimony of the article,’” and so forth. These words seem to me to be an Erasmian composition and not part of Jerome’s text. MART.]

He is “from Nazareth of Galilee” because he had been brought up there, [Note: [Col. 0149D] Victorius omits this verse, “like the flower of the field,” and so forth.] so that he might be nourished like the flower of the field in the flower of virtues.

(Vers. 12, 13.) And Jesus entered the temple of God and drove out all who were selling and buying in the temple. He overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those selling doves. And he said to them: “It is written: ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer’; but you have made it a den of robbers.”

Accompanied by the crowd of believers—which had spread its garments so that the colt might proceed with unharmed feet—Jesus enters the temple and drives out all who were selling and buying in the temple. He overturns the tables of the money-changers and scatters the seats of those selling doves. Citing testimony from the Holy Scriptures (Isa. LVI), he tells them that his Father’s house ought to be a house of prayer [Col. 0150B] and not a den of robbers or a house of commerce (Jerem. VII), as it is written in another Gospel (John II).

First, we must understand that, in accordance with the commands of the Law, sacrifices without number were offered in the Lord’s temple, held in the highest reverence throughout the whole world. Since the Jewish people gathered there from nearly every region, innumerable victims were offered, especially on feast days: bulls, rams, and goats. The poor, lest they should be without a sacrifice, offered young pigeons and turtledoves.

It often happened that those who had come from far away did not have victims. The priests therefore devised a way to plunder the people: they sold all the animals needed for sacrifices, so that they could sell to those who had none and then themselves receive again what had been purchased. Their scheme was repeatedly frustrated by the poverty of those who came, since many needed financial means and not only lacked victims but had no resources even to buy birds and inexpensive offerings.

They therefore also appointed money-changers to lend money against security. But because the Law commanded (Lev. XXV; Deut. XXIII) that no one should accept interest, and money lent at interest could not be profitable if it yielded no gain and sometimes even involved loss of the principal, they devised another trick: instead of money-changers, they established Collybists, a term whose precise meaning the Latin language does not express. [Note: [Col. 0149D] We discussed the Collybists in the notes to the Origenian lexicon. Jerome is not contrary to those notes, since he is not speaking of the *collybus*, which was a type of coin and from which the Collybists received their name; rather, he is speaking of the small gifts that the Collybists accepted as interest when they had lent money—namely *collybi*. Money lent at interest was called *collybi*, and the gifts given for it were called *collyba*. Certainly *collibus* is what is given to a money-changer for changing money. See the Greek lexicons. MART.—Here Jerome defends a view different from the one commonly received among ancient writers, since he says that Collybists were those who, lending money at interest, demanded small gifts instead of the interest forbidden by the Law. So far as I know, Hesychius alone supports him, as cited by Huet, where he gives κόλλυβα, τρώγαλια: “collyba, delicacies, roasted chickpeas.” But Hesychius himself properly interprets κόλλυβος as “a type of coin, and the ox engraved on bronze”—a kind of coin whose bronze bore the image of an ox. Pollux, Suidas, and the glossators of the older writers agree especially in taking *collybus* as a kind of cheap little coin. Aristophanes says οὐδὲ κολλύβου, “not even for a collybus,” when speaking of buying a sickle; and Callimachus, exaggerating the cheapness of grain in the underworld, says βοῦν κολλύβῳ πιπρήσκουσι, “they sell an ox for a collybus.” From this came the Collybists, money-changers who exchanged valuable coins for cheaper ones—a craft Pollux calls ἀλλαγήν, which we call *cambium* in the same sense. Origen himself, from whom the holy Father borrowed much of his exposition, calls those Collybists who exchanged sound money for cheap and worthless little coins, thereby causing loss to those whose money they exchanged. I believe that this was due not only to the exchange for inferior bronze but also to their deducting a fixed fee from the principal for their own profit, which Jerome notes.] 

Among them, *collyba* are what we call *tragemata*, or inexpensive gifts—for example, roasted [Al. “fried”] chickpeas, dried grapes, and various kinds of fruit. Therefore, because the Collybists who had lent money could not accept interest, they accepted various goods in place of interest, exacting in those things purchased with money what they were not permitted to demand in money—as though Ezekiel had not proclaimed this very thing, saying: “You shall not take interest or increase” (Ezek. XXII, 12). [Note: [Col. 0151D] Read, with Rhabanus, “had forbidden this beforehand.”]

Seeing this sort of commerce or robbery in his Father’s house, the Lord, stirred by the heat of the spirit—as it is written in Psalm 68, verse 10, “Zeal for your house has consumed me”—made himself a whip of cords and drove such a great multitude of people from the temple, saying: “It is written: ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer’; but you have made it a den of robbers.”

A robber is one who pursues profits from religion and turns the temple of God into a robber’s cave, whose worship is not so much worship of God as an opportunity for commerce.

This is according to the historical sense. But according to the mystical meanings, Jesus enters the temple of his Father every day and drives out all [Note: [Col. 0151D] Jerome has, as usual, drawn much of the following interpretation from Origen.]—bishops, presbyters, and deacons, as well as laypeople and the whole crowd—from his Church, and regards sellers and buyers alike as guilty of one crime. For it is written: “You received freely; give freely.”

He also overturns the tables of the money-changers. Observe that, because of the avarice of the priests, God’s altars are called the tables of money-changers. He overturns the seats of those selling doves—those who sell the grace of the Holy Spirit and do everything they can to devour the peoples placed under them. Of such people it is said [Al. “it is written”]: “They devour my people as though they were eating bread” (Ps. XIII, 4).

According to the simple understanding, the doves were not in seats but in cages, unless perhaps the sellers of doves sat in seats. But that is entirely absurd, because in the seats the dignity of teachers is indicated, and that dignity is reduced to nothing when it has been mixed with profits.

What we have said about the Churches, let each person understand of himself. For the Apostle says: “You are the temple of God, and the Holy Spirit dwells in you” (I Cor. VI, 15; II Cor. III, 16). Let there be no commerce in the house of our heart, no exchange between buyers and sellers, no greed for gifts, lest Jesus enter in anger and severity and cleanse his temple in no other way than by applying the whip, so that from a den of robbers and a house of commerce he may make it a house of prayer.

(Vers. 14.) And the blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them.

Unless he had overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those selling doves, the blind and the lame would not have deserved to recover their former light and their vigorous step.

(Vers. 15.) But when the chief priests and the scribes saw the wonders he performed, and the children crying out in the temple and saying, “Hosanna to the Son of David,” they were indignant and said to him: “Do you hear what these are saying?”

Most people think that the greatest of the signs was the raising of Lazarus (John XI), the giving of sight to the man blind from birth (John IX), the voice of the Father heard at the Jordan (John III), or the transfiguration on the mountain, when he revealed the glory of the one who triumphs (Matt. XVII).

To me, among all the signs he performed, this seems the more marvelous: that one man, at that time despised and so insignificant that he was afterward crucified, was able, while the scribes and Pharisees raged against him and watched their profits being destroyed, to drive out so great a multitude with the blows of a single whip, overturn the tables, shatter the seats, and do other things that an entire army could not have done. [Note: [Col. 0151D] Origen thought the same. Elsewhere, in his *Commentary on John*, he says that he had proved by arguments that this was no minor one among Jesus’ astonishing works: “Although he was regarded as the son of a carpenter, he nevertheless acted with such confidence and authority that, in a public gathering, he drove from the temple those of whom it is written. Even the ruler of the nation, using such power, would not easily have accomplished what Jesus did.”]

For something fiery and star-like radiated from his eyes, and the majesty of divinity shone in his face. Although the priests did not dare to lay hands on him, they nevertheless slandered his works. They turned the testimony of the people and children who cried, “Hosanna to the Son of David,” into an accusation, since this was supposedly said only to the Son of God. Let bishops, then, and men however holy, consider with what danger they allow such words to be addressed to them, if what was truly said to the Lord—because the faith of believers was not yet solid—is charged as a crime. [Note: [Col. 0152D] Martianaeus elsewhere notes the practice of bishops and holy men being greeted with “Hosanna,” in his commentary on the book *On Hebrew Names*, drawing on the *Pilgrimage to Jerusalem* of the monk Antoninus, p. 30. “There,” he says, “women came to meet us with children, carrying palms in their hands and vessels of rose oil. Prostrate at our feet, they anointed the soles of our feet and sang in the Egyptian language, chanting the antiphon: ‘Blessed are you by the Lord, and blessed is your coming; Hosanna in the highest.’ Origen is also frequently engaged in this interpretation, comparing the faults of the temple priests with those of the bishops and ministers of the Church and cutting them back to the living root.”]

(Vers. 16.) But Jesus says to them: “Certainly. Have you never read: ‘From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise’?”

How moderate is the way he tempers his statement, and how balanced is the answer, open to neither side and giving no opportunity for accusation. He did not say what the scribes wanted to hear: “The children are right to bear witness to me”; nor did he say: “They are mistaken; they are children, and you ought to forgive their age.” Instead, he produces an example from the eighth Psalm, so that, while the Lord remained silent, the testimony of Scripture might confirm the children’s words.

(Vers. 17.) And leaving them, he went outside the city to Bethany, and remained there.

He left the unbelievers and, departing from the city of those who contradicted him, went to Bethany, which is interpreted as “house of obedience,” already then prefiguring the calling of the Gentiles. He remained there because he could not remain in Israel.

This too should be understood: he was so poor and had flattered no one to such an extent that in the great city he found no host and no lodging, but lived in a small country village with Lazarus and his sisters—for Bethany was their village.

[Col. 0153B] (Verses 18 and following.) But when he was returning to the city in the morning, he was hungry. And seeing one fig tree beside the road, he approached it and found nothing on it except leaves. And he said to it: “May no fruit ever again come from you,” and the fig tree immediately withered. And when the disciples saw it, they marveled, saying: “How did it wither immediately?”

When the darkness of night had been dispelled, the morning light was shining, and midday was approaching—the time at which the Lord was to illumine the world through his Passion—as he was returning to the city, he was hungry, either demonstrating the reality of his human flesh, or hungering for the salvation of believers and burning with zeal against Israel’s unbelief. And when he had seen one tree—which we understand as the Synagogue and the assembly of the Jews [Note: [Col. 0153D] Compare Adamantius, who expounds this figure at length as referring to the barren synagogue of the Jews.]—beside the road—for it possessed the Law, and therefore was beside the road, because it did not believe in the way—he approached it, standing, that is, and motionless, and having none of the feet of the Gospel. And he found nothing on it except leaves: the noise of promises, Pharisaic traditions, boasting in the Law, and verbal ornament without any fruits of truth.

For this reason another Evangelist also says: “For it was not yet the season” (Mark X, 13): either because the season of Israel’s salvation had not yet come, since the Gentile people had not yet entered in, or because the season of faith had passed, since, having first come to that people and been rejected, he had passed over to the nations. And he said to it: “May no fruit ever come from you,” either “forever” or “for an age”; for the Greek word αἰὼν [elsewhere αἰῶνα] signifies both. And the fig tree withered [Note: [Col. 0153D] Three Palatine manuscripts read *quia* (“because”) instead of *quae* (“which”).], which, while the Lord was hungry, did not possess the food he had desired.

The leaves, however, withered in such a way that the trunk itself remained, and though the branches had been broken, the root remained green [elsewhere, “alive”]. If at the end of time it should wish to believe, it may put forth shoots of faith, and the Scripture may be fulfilled which says: “There is hope for a tree” (Job XIV, 7).

According to the literal sense, however, since the Lord was to suffer among the peoples and bear the scandal of the cross, he ought to strengthen the disciples’ minds beforehand through the anticipation of this sign. Hence the disciples marvel, saying: “How did it wither immediately?” [Page 168] The Savior could therefore, by the same power, also have withered his enemies, had he not awaited their salvation through repentance.

(Verses 21, 22.) But Jesus answered and said to them: “Amen I say to you, if you have faith and do not hesitate, you will do not only what was done to the fig tree; but even if you say to this mountain, ‘Take yourself up and cast yourself into the sea,’ it will happen. [Note: [Col. 0153D] In some manuscripts: “Take yourself up,” etc.] And everything that you ask for in prayer, believing, you will receive.”

The dogs of the Gentiles bark at us in their writings, which they left behind as a memorial of their own impiety, asserting that the apostles did not possess faith because they were unable to move mountains. To them we shall reply that many signs were performed by the Lord, according to the testimony of John the Evangelist, which, if written down, the world could not contain (John XXI, 25). This does not mean that the world could not contain the volumes—which it could, even if they were numerous, in a single small cabinet or chest—but that it could not bear the greatness of the signs because of their miraculous character and its unbelief.

We therefore believe that the apostles also performed these things, but that they were not written down so that unbelievers might not be given a greater opportunity for contradiction. Otherwise, let us ask them whether they believe the signs that are reported in writing or not. And when we see them to be unbelievers, we shall consequently prove that they would not have believed greater signs, since they do not believe lesser ones.

So much against them. As for us, as we have already said, let us understand the mountain as the devil in his pride, boasting against his Creator, who is called by the prophet “a corrupted mountain” [Note: [Col. 0153D] Victorius notes that Jeremiah XLI has *ὄρος διεφθαρμένον* (“corrupted mountain”), whereas our text has *pestifer* (“pestilential”). [Col. 0154D]]. And when he has possessed a human soul and has become rooted in it, he can be transferred by the apostles and by those who are like the apostles into the sea—that is, into places that are salty, turbulent, and bitter, possessing no sweetness of God. [Note: [Col. 0154D] Older printed books added, “and in the mind of unbelievers, so that two thousand swine might be drowned,” which Martianay, before us, deleted at the prompting of the manuscripts.]

The same thing is also read in the Psalms: “We shall not fear when the earth is shaken and the mountains are transferred into the heart of the sea” (Psalm XLV, 2).

(Verses 23.) And when he had entered the temple, the chief priests and elders of the people approached him as he was teaching and said: “By what authority are you doing these things? And who gave you this authority?”

In different words they construct the same accusation as before, when they said: “By the prince of demons he casts out demons.” For when they say, “By what authority are you doing these things?” they doubt God’s authority and wish it to be understood that what he does belongs to the devil. By adding, “Who gave you this authority?” they most plainly deny that he is the Son of God, since they suppose that he performs signs not by his own powers but by those of another.

(Verses 24 and following.) But Jesus answered and said to them: “I also will ask you one question; if you answer me, I too will tell you by what authority I do these things. The baptism of John—where was it from, from heaven or from human beings?”

But they deliberated among themselves, saying: “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say to us, ‘Why, then, did you not believe him?’ But if we say, ‘From human beings,’ we fear the crowd.” For everyone regarded John as a prophet. And answering Jesus, they said: “We do not know.”

This is what is commonly expressed by the saying: “For a bad knot in a tree, a bad nail or wedge must be driven in.” [Note: [Col. 0155D] Rhabb. reads, more correctly, “but for this reason he asks.”]

The Lord could have refuted the slander of his tempters with an open answer, but he wisely questions them so that they themselves may be condemned either by their silence or by their opinion. If they had answered that John’s baptism was from heaven—as they had reasoned in their wicked wisdom—the obvious response would have been: “Why, then, were you not baptized by John?” If they wished to say that it had been contrived by human deception and possessed nothing divine, they feared the revolt of the people. For all the crowds had received John’s baptism in a body and regarded him as a prophet.

Thus the most impious faction answered, using the language of humility—by saying that they did not know—in order to arrange their ambush.

(Verses 27.) He himself also said to them: “Neither do I tell you by what authority I do these things.”

They lied when they answered that they did not know. Therefore, according to their answer, it would have followed that the Lord too should say, “Neither do I know.” But Truth cannot lie, and he says: “Neither do I tell you.” By this he shows both that they know but do not wish to answer, and that he knows but therefore does not speak, because they keep silent about what they know. Immediately he introduces a parable, which both accuses them of impiety and teaches that the kingdom of God is to be transferred to the Gentiles.

(Verses 28 and following.) [Page 170] “But what do you think? A certain man had two sons. And approaching the first, he said: ‘Son, go and work today in my vineyard.’ But he answered and said: ‘I do not want to.’ Afterwards, moved by repentance, he went. Approaching the other, he said the same. But he answered and said: ‘I am going, lord,’ and he did not go. Which of the two did the father’s will?” They say to him: “The first.” Jesus says to them (Luke XV):

These are the two sons who are also described in Luke’s parable, the frugal son and the profligate, and concerning whom the prophet Zechariah speaks: “I took for myself two staffs; the one I called Beauty, and the other I called Cord, and I pastured the flock” (Zechariah XI, 7).

[Note: [Col. 0155D] Refer these matters also to Adamantius, whom there is no leisure to expound here.]

To the first—the people of the Gentiles—he says through knowledge of the natural law: “Go and work in my vineyard”; that is, “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another” (Tobit IV). They proudly answered: “I do not want to.” But afterwards, at the Savior’s coming, having repented, they worked in God’s vineyard and corrected their insolence of speech through labor.

The second son is the Jewish people, who answered Moses: “Everything that the Lord has said we will do” (Exodus XXIV), but did not go into the vineyard, because, after killing the son of the householder, they thought themselves heirs.

Others, however, do not think that the parable concerns Gentiles and Jews, but simply sinners and righteous people, with the Lord himself later explaining his proposition.

“Amen I say to you, tax collectors and prostitutes will go before you into the kingdom of God.” For those who by evil works had denied that they served God later received John’s baptism of repentance. But the Pharisees, who displayed their righteousness and boasted that they fulfilled God’s Law, disregarded John’s baptism and fulfilled God’s commands. Hence he says:

(Verses 32.) “For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him; but the tax collectors and prostitutes believed him. But you, seeing this, did not even afterward repent so as to believe him.”

Regarding what is said—“Which of the two did the father’s will?”—and their answer, “The last one”: it should be known that in the true copies the last one is not found, [Page 171] but the first, so that they may be condemned by their own judgment. [Note: [Col. 0155D] Rhabb. reads “in the old copies.” Jerome is also persuaded that *veteribus* (“old”) was written instead of *veris* (“true”): for what if those copies that originally read *first* were then the true exemplars, and those that read *last* had been corrupted? Jerome himself has *last* in the passage under discussion; why does he prefer interpolated copies and set them before the true ones? But if he wrote *old*, the matter is in any case sound, and both readings deserve explanation. If one of them were produced by corrupt manuscripts, why should the holy Father have expanded his discussion to explain it? See Sabater.

Now we read that the Pharisees answered “the elder,” or “the first.” There are, however, ancient authorities who read that “the younger” was meant. Saint Hilary, on this passage, says: “They say that the younger obeyed the will.” Clearly, at that time the Vulgate reading was *novissimus* (“last”), and it remains in the extremely ancient Veronese Gospel manuscript that we subsequently cite. I do not know what passage agreeing with this is reported as if from Jerome in the *Catena Aurea*, which caused Erasmus once more to suspect that these Commentaries had been abridged long ago by some excessively fastidious person, since the passage is not found in these Commentaries. It would have been better to deny the authority of the *Catena*.]

If we wish to read “the last one,” the interpretation is clear: we should say that the Jews indeed understood the truth, but evaded it and did not wish to say what they thought, just as they knew that John’s baptism was from heaven but refused to say so.

(Verses 33.) “Hear another parable. There was a householder who planted a vineyard, surrounded it with a hedge, dug a winepress in it, built a tower, leased it to farmers, and went abroad.”

This is what the Lord signified by taking up the proverb: “It is hard to kick against the goad” (Acts IX, 5). The chief priests and elders of the people who had asked the Lord, “By what authority are you doing these things, and who gave you this authority?” and who had wished to ensnare Wisdom in his words, are overcome by their own craft. They hear in parables what they had not deserved to hear openly.

This householder is the same one who had two sons and who, in another parable, hired laborers for his vineyard. He planted the vineyard of which Isaiah speaks fully in his Song, concluding: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah V, 7). And in the Psalm: “You brought a vineyard out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it” (Psalm LXXIX, 9).

“And he surrounded it with a hedge”: either with the wall of the city or with the assistance of angels. “And he dug a winepress in it”: either an altar, or those winepresses whose titles appear at the head of three Psalms—the eighth, the eightieth, and the eighty-third. “And he built a tower”: clearly the temple, of which it is said through Micah: “And you, tower of the cloud, daughter of Zion” (Micah IV, 8).

“And he leased it to farmers,” whom elsewhere he called workers in the vineyard, who had been hired at the first, third, sixth, ninth, and eleventh hours (Matthew X). “And he went abroad”: not by a change of place—for where can God be absent, since all things are filled by him, and since he says through Jeremiah, “I am God who is near and not far away, says the Lord” (Jeremiah XXIII, 23)—but he appears to leave the vineyard so as to leave the vine-dressers free discretion in their work.

(Verses 34 and following.) “When the time of the fruits approached, he sent his servants to the farmers to receive its fruits. And the farmers seized his servants, struck one, killed another, and stoned another. Again he sent other servants, more than the first, and they treated them in the same way.” [Page 172]

[Note: [Col. 0157D] The author of this exposition is Adamantius; the brevity of the notes spares his more extended discussion.]

He had given them the Law and commanded them to work in this vineyard, so that they might display the fruit of the Law in their deeds. Afterwards he sent servants to them, whom they seized and either struck, as Jeremiah; killed, as Isaiah; or stoned, as Naboth (1 Kings XXI) and Zechariah, whom they killed between the temple and the altar (2 Chronicles XXIV). Let us read Paul’s Letter to the Hebrews (Hebrews XI); from it we shall learn in full what the servants of the Lord endured and how much they suffered. [Note: [Col. 0157D] One Palatine manuscript adds: “what the end of the Lord’s servants was.”]

(Verses 37, 38.) “Finally he sent his son to them, saying: ‘They will respect my son.’ But when the farmers saw the son, they said among themselves: ‘This is the heir; come, let us kill him and have his inheritance.’”

In what we read above—“Again he sent other servants, more than the first, and they treated them in the same way”—he shows the patience of the householder, who sent repeatedly in order to summon the wicked tenants to repentance. But they “stored up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath” (Romans II).

The statement that follows, “They will respect my son,” does not arise from ignorance. For what could the householder not know, when the householder understood here is God the Father? Yet God is always said to hesitate, so that human free will may be preserved.

Let us question Arius and Eunomius. Behold, the Father is said to be ignorant, and he moderates his statement; and, so far as you are concerned, he is proved to have lied. Whatever they answer on behalf of the Father, let them understand as applying to the Son, who says that he does not know the day of consummation. [Note: [Col. 0157D] Victor inserts: “perhaps here.”]

(Verses 39.) “And they seized him, cast him outside the vineyard, and killed him.”

The Apostle also says that Jesus was crucified outside the gate (Hebrews XIII). We can understand this in another way as well: he was cast outside the vineyard and killed there, so that, when the Gentiles received him, the vineyard might be leased to others.

(Verses 40, 41.) “Therefore, when the lord of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those farmers?” They say to him: “He will destroy those wicked men wickedly and lease his vineyard to other farmers who will give him the fruit in its seasons.”

The Lord asks them not because he is ignorant of what they will answer, but so that they may be condemned by their own answer. The vineyard has been leased to us, and leased on the condition that we return its fruit to the Lord in its seasons, and that at each season we know what we ought either to say or to do.

(Verses 42.) Jesus says to them: “Have you never read in the Scriptures: ‘The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the head of the corner. This was done by the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes’?” (Psalm CXVII, 22–23).

The same matters are woven together through various parables and different expressions. Those whom above he had called laborers, vine-dressers, and farmers, he now calls builders, that is, masons. Hence the Apostle says: “You are God’s cultivation, God’s building” (1 Corinthians III, 9).

Therefore, just as these masons received the vineyard as the vine-dressers did, so they received the stone, either to place it in the foundations, according to the architect Paul (ibid.), or in the corner, so that it might join together the two walls—that is, the two peoples (Ephesians II). Rejected by them, it became the head of the corner. This was done by the Lord, not by human strength but by God’s power.

Peter also speaks confidently about this stone of help: “This stone, which was rejected by you builders, has become the head of the corner” (1 Peter II, 7). And Isaiah says: “Behold, I will place in the foundations of Zion a chosen, precious, cornerstone; and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame” (Isaiah II, 16).

(Verses 43.) “Therefore I say to you: The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits.”

I have said several times that the kingdom of God is understood as the holy Scriptures, which the Lord took away from the Jews and handed over to us, so that we might produce their fruits. This is the vineyard that is handed over to farmers and vine-dressers; those who have not worked in it, possessing only the name of the Scriptures, will lose the fruits of the vineyard.

(Verses 44.) “And whoever falls upon this stone will be broken; but upon whomever it falls, it will crush him.”

It is one thing to stumble against Christ through evil works, another to deny him. Whoever is a sinner and yet believes in him falls upon the stone and is broken, but is not utterly crushed; through repentance he is preserved for salvation. But upon whomever it falls—that is, upon one whom the stone itself overwhelms, and who has utterly denied Christ—it will crush him, so that not even a potsherd remains from which a little water might be drawn.

(Verses 45, 46.) And when the chief priests and Pharisees had heard his parables, they understood that he was speaking about them. And while they sought to seize him, they feared the crowds, because they regarded him as a prophet.

Although they were hard-hearted and, because of their unbelief and impiety toward the Son of God, dull-minded [Note: [Col. 0157D] Martianaeus’s text corruptly read *habentes* (“having”), which he referred with useless meaning to the preceding propositions. With the help of the Palatine manuscripts, we have restored *hebetes* (“dull-minded”): namely, the Jews, who were obtuse and senseless because of their unbelief and impiety. In one manuscript we also find *responsiones* (“answers”) instead of *propositiones* (“propositions”). [Col. 0158D]], nevertheless they could not deny the statements that were plainly expressed, and they understood that all the Lord’s declarations were directed against them.

Therefore they wished to kill him, but feared the crowds, because they regarded him as a prophet. A crowd is always changeable and does not persist in a settled intention; like waves, it is driven here and there by the force of different winds [Note: [Col. 0159D] Our manuscripts supply *impetu* (“force”). Previously the reading was “by the force of different winds, here and there.”]. The one whom they now venerate and honor as a prophet, they later cry out against: “Crucify, crucify such a man!” (John XIX, 6).

(Cap. XXII—Verses 1, 2.) And Jesus answered and again spoke to them in parables, saying: “The kingdom of heaven has become like a king who made a wedding feast for his son.”

The Pharisees understood that the parables were spoken about them and sought to seize and kill him. Knowing this intention of theirs, the Lord nevertheless rebukes them in their fury, and is not overcome by fear so as to refrain from accusing sinners. [Note: [Col. 0159D] Origen says: “Clearly, figuratively, the king is said to be God and the Father of Christ; the wedding feast of the king’s son is the restoration of the Church of Christ, the bride, to her bridegroom Christ; and the servants sent to call those who had been invited to the wedding are the prophets, who by their prophecies timely turn those from the people toward joy,” and so forth.]

This king who made a wedding feast for his son is almighty God. He makes the wedding feast for our Lord Jesus Christ and the Church, which has been gathered both from the Jews and from the Gentiles.

(Verses 3.) “And he sent his servant to call those who had been invited to the wedding, and they did not want to come.”

There is no doubt that this means Moses, through whom he gave the Law to those who had been invited. But if we read “servants,” as most copies have it, the reference is to the prophets, through whom those who had been invited disdained to come. [Note: [Col. 0159D] The extremely ancient Veronese Gospel manuscript likewise prefers the plural “servants.”]

(Verses 4, 5.) “Again he sent other servants, saying: ‘Tell those who were invited: Behold, I have prepared my meal; my bulls and fattened animals have been slaughtered, and everything is ready. Come to the wedding.’ But they disregarded it.”

The servants sent the second time are better understood as prophets than as apostles, but only if “servant” was written above in the singular. If, however, you read “servants” there as well, the second servants here are to be understood as the apostles. [Note: [Col. 0159D] Origen held a different view: “The servants sent the second time are another group of prophets.”]

The prepared meal, the bulls, and the fattened animals that have been slaughtered either describe royal wealth metaphorically, so that spiritual things may be understood from carnal ones, or certainly signify the greatness of doctrines and the fullness of teaching according to God’s Law.

(Verses 6.) “But they went away, one to his farm, another to his business. The rest seized his servants, treated them shamefully, and killed them.”

Among those who do not receive the truth of the Gospel there is great diversity. Those who, occupied with other matters, did not wish to come are guilty of a lesser crime than those who, despising the affection of the one who invited them, turned kindness into cruelty and either treated the king’s servants shamefully after seizing them or killed them.

In this parable the bridegroom’s killing is not mentioned; through the deaths of the servants, contempt for the wedding is shown.

(Verses 7.) “But when the king heard, he was angry.”

Of the one who had earlier been called a man—when it was said, “The kingdom of heaven has become like a man who was a king” while he invited people to the wedding and performed works of mercy—the name “man” is used. But now, when he comes to punish, “man” is omitted and he is called only “king.”

“And sending his armies, he destroyed those murderers and burned their city.”

By the armies we may understand either avenging angels, concerning whom it is written in the Psalms: “He sent among them the sending of evil angels” [elsewhere, “wicked angels”] (Psalm LXXVII, 49), or the Romans under the leadership of Vespasian and Titus, who, after killing the peoples of Judea, burned the treacherous city. [Note: [Col. 0160D] Again from Origen: “The king’s anger is understood as that of which the Apostle speaks concerning the Jews: ‘Wrath has come upon them to the end.’ In addition, war was to be waged against the Jews, and the destruction of Jerusalem and of the people after Christ’s coming is foretold in these words.”]

(Col. 0160B) (Verses 8 and following.) “Then he said to his servants: ‘The wedding is indeed ready, but those who were invited were not worthy. Go therefore to the outlets of the roads, and invite to the wedding whomever you find.’ And his servants went out into the roads, gathered everyone whom they found, both bad and good, and the wedding was filled with those reclining at table.”

The people of the Gentiles were not on the roads but at the outlets of the roads. But the question arises: how were some good people found among those who were outside and bad? The Apostle treats this passage more fully in the Letter to the Romans [elsewhere “saying” is added] (Romans II, 14): the Gentiles who naturally do what belongs to the Law condemn the Jews, who did not fulfill the written Law. Among the Gentiles themselves there is also infinite diversity, since we know that some are inclined toward vices and rushing into evils, while others, because of the uprightness of their conduct, are devoted to virtues. [Page 176]

(Verses 11, 12.) “But the king entered to see those reclining at table, and he saw there a man not dressed in a wedding garment. And he said to him: ‘Friend, how did you enter here without having a wedding garment?’ But he was silent.”

Those who had been invited to the wedding had filled the king’s banquet from hedges and corners, streets, and various places. But afterwards, when the king had come to see those reclining at table in his banquet—that is, resting, as it were, in his faith, so that on the day of judgment he might visit the guests and distinguish the merits of each—he found one who was not dressed in a wedding garment.

This one man signifies all who have been joined to wickedness. [Note: [Col. 0160D] Origen says: “But he saw one not dressed in a wedding garment,” comprehending under one category or type the whole group who retained the wickedness that clung to them before faith and did not cast it off.]

The wedding garment consists of the Lord’s commandments and of the works fulfilled according to the Law and the Gospel, which constitute the clothing of the new person. Therefore, if at the time of judgment someone is found bearing the Christian name but not having a wedding garment—that is, the garment of the heavenly person [elsewhere, “celestial”]—but wearing a polluted garment, namely, the cast-off clothing of the old person, he is immediately rebuked and told: “Friend, how did you enter here?”

He calls him “friend” because he had been invited to the wedding; he accuses him of shamelessness because he polluted the cleanliness of the wedding feast with a filthy garment. “But he was silent.” For at that time there will be no place for repentance [Note: [Col. 0161B] Five manuscripts read *impudentiae* (“shamelessness”) instead of *poenitentiae* (“repentance”). Rhabb. likewise.], nor any opportunity for denial, since all the angels and the world itself will be witnesses of the sins.

(Verses 13.) “Then the king said to the attendants: ‘Bind his feet and hands and cast him into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.’”

Understand the hands bound, the feet bound, the weeping of the eyes, and the gnashing of the teeth either as confirming the truth of the resurrection. Or certainly the hands and feet are bound so that they may cease to do evil and to run in order to shed blood. [Note: [Col. 0161B] Adamantius says: “For he did not walk as he ought, nor did he do what he ought to have done.” Three manuscripts read “so that they may cease to run.”]

In the weeping of the eyes and the gnashing of the teeth, the greatness of the torments is shown metaphorically through the bodily members.

(Verses 14.) “For many are called, but few are chosen.”

He gathers all the parables into a brief statement: in the work of the vineyard, in the building of the house, and at the wedding banquet, it is not beginnings but the end that is sought.

(Verses 15.) Then the Pharisees went away and took counsel so that they might ensnare him in speech. And they sent their disciples to him with the Herodians, saying:

Recently, when Judea had been subjected to the Romans under Caesar Augustus, at the time when a census was proclaimed throughout the whole world, it had been made tributary, and there was great dissension among the people. Some said that taxes ought to be paid for the sake of safety and peace, since the Romans fought on behalf of all [Note: [Col. 0161C] Origen uses nearly the same words: “In the time of the Savior, when the Jews were ordered to pay tribute to the Romans, it was debated and deliberated among them whether it was fitting for a nation consecrated to God, and which was his portion, to pay tribute to rulers, or whether they should fight for freedom if they were not permitted to live according to their own will and not pay tribute at all. It is known that after the exile of Archelaus, one of the tetrarchs, Judea had been reduced to the form of a province and attached to Syria, and that thereafter the famous census was conducted by Quirinius, governor of Syria, who assessed the resources of the Jews. Josephus reports in *Antiquities* XVIII, chapter 1, that some then rebelled, especially a certain Judas the Gaulanite—Origen calls him a Galilean, whom Luke mentions in Acts—and incited many to revolt from the Romans.”], while the Pharisees, who applauded themselves for their righteousness, said on the contrary that the people of God—who paid tithes, gave first fruits, and performed the other things written in the Law—ought not to be subject to human laws. [Note: [Col. 0161C] Three Palatine manuscripts add *nitentibus* (“insisting”) after *econtrario* and read “insisting that they ought not,” omitting shortly afterward the word *faceret* (“did”). Rhabb. likewise.]

Caesar Augustus had appointed Herod, the son of Antipater, a foreigner and proselyte, king over the Jews, so that he might oversee the tribute and obey Roman rule. [Note: [Col. 0161D] Origen continues in the same order: “The tetrarch who then ruled—Herod Antipas, whom Jerome calls by the name Herod, the son of Antipater; in other books, Antipater—tried to persuade the people to adapt themselves to the present state of affairs, not to undertake a voluntary war against the more powerful, and to pay taxes.”]

The Pharisees therefore sent their disciples with the Herodians—that is, with Herod’s soldiers, or those whom the Pharisees mockingly called Herodians because they paid tribute to the Romans and were not devoted to divine worship. [Note: [Col. 0161D] Origen likewise concluded: “It is plausible that those who wished tribute to be paid to Caesar among the people were called Herodians by those who held that it ought not to be done. Those who were led by the appearance of freedom so as not to pay tribute to Caesar seem to have been the Pharisees,” and so forth. But Jerome’s earlier opinion is not far from the truth either: the Herodians were called Herod’s soldiers or his household tax collectors, men ready and equipped to demand the tax by force. Huet notes, however, that although soldiers who forcibly collected tribute existed in the time of Herod the Great, who first undertook the payment of tribute to Caesar, the same was not true under Herod Antipas, whose authority did not permit this, but only allowed him to pursue the matter through requests, influence, and advice.]

Some Latins absurdly think that the Herodians were those who believed Herod to be the Christ [Page 178], something we nowhere read. [Note: [Col. 0162C] Here Scaliger attacks Jerome in his notes on Eusebius. As he says, this was not reported by the Latins but by Epiphanius, who was himself Greek and a Greek writer. This is rashly stated, for the opinion belonged to Latin writers much older than Epiphanius, as Saint Jerome quite correctly observes. The Latin writer Tertullian—or the author of the other part of *On Prescription Against Heretics*—says in chapter 45: “I omit the Pharisees … and with them the Herodians, who said that Herod was the Christ.” Likewise the Latin Philaster of Brescia, who preceded Jerome by several years, says in *Heresy* 28, concerning the Herodians: “They expect Herod, king of the Jews, who was struck by an angel, believing him to be Christ.” From these statements—and, incidentally, to add this about the absurd opinion—you can see that the authors who wrote about it believed that different Herods had been regarded by the Herodians as the Messiah. For what Jerome notes concerning Herod Antipas, Philaster understands of Agrippa, son of Aristobulus, who is mentioned in Acts XII, 22. Epiphanius, whom Scaliger cites, and Nicetas in Book I of the *Treasury*, chapter 34, more correctly interpret it of Herod the Great, whom his followers regarded as Christ. Meanwhile, Huet thinks Jerome can be accused on another ground: although he says here that some Latins absurdly thought the Herodians were those who considered Herod Christ, he himself writes in the *Dialogue Against the Luciferians* that “the Herodians accepted Herod the king as Christ.” But he did not write this as an assertion, as Bishop Abricius reports; rather, passing over a poorly constructed story by a rhetorical figure, he says: “I say nothing of the fact that the Herodians accepted Herod the king as Christ.” Finally, in our manuscripts *crederent* (“believed”) is read instead of *credebant* (“believed” or “used to believe”).]

(Verses 16.) “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth, and that you do not care about anyone. For you do not regard the status of persons. Tell us, therefore, what you think: Is it lawful to pay the census to Caesar or not?”

The flattering and deceptive question provokes him to answer in such a way that he will fear God more than Caesar and say that taxes ought not to be paid, so that the Herodians, hearing this immediately, may seize him as the leader of a revolt against the Romans. [Note: [Col. 0162D] Origen again says: “By such praise they dissuade him from regarding the person of the Herodians or of the Caesareans, so that, if he affirmed according to the Pharisees’ opinion that tribute ought not to be paid to Caesar, he might be handed over to the Herodians by them. And slightly earlier: ‘Thus, by preventing the payment of the census to Caesar, they would have handed him over to the Romans as the author and instigator of revolt.’”] [Col. 0163A]

(Verses 18.) But Jesus, knowing their wickedness, said: “Why are you testing me, hypocrites?”

The first virtue of the one who answers is to understand the mind of those asking, and to call them not disciples but tempters. A hypocrite, therefore, is one who is one thing and pretends to be another—that is, who does one thing in action and presents another in speech.

(Verses 19.) “Show me the coin of the census.” And they offered him a denarius.

Wisdom always acts wisely, so that the tempters may be refuted especially by their own words. “Show me,” he says, “a denarius,” that is, the type of coin which was reckoned as ten coins and bore the image of Caesar.

(Col. 0163B) (Verses 20.) [Page 179] And Jesus said to them: “Whose image and inscription is this?”

Those who think that the Savior’s question expresses ignorance rather than providential economy should learn from the present passage that Jesus certainly could have known whose image was on the coin; but he asks so that he may respond appropriately to their words.

(Vers. 21.) They say to him: “Caesar’s.” Then he says to them: “Therefore give back to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” Let us not think that “Caesar” means Augustus, but rather Tiberius, his stepson, who succeeded him in the latter’s place [Note: Two of our manuscripts more correctly read, “in the place of his stepfather, under whom,” etc.], under whom the Lord suffered. All the Roman kings, beginning with Gaius Caesar, who had seized imperial power, were called “Caesars” [Alt. “are called”]. Moreover, by saying, “Give back to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s,” that is, the coin of the tribute and the money; and, “to God the things that are God’s,” let us understand the tithes, firstfruits, offerings, and sacrifices—as he himself also paid tribute for himself and Peter (Matt. XVII), and gave back to God the things that are God’s by doing the will of the Father (John VI).

(Vers. 22.) And when they heard this, they marveled. Those who ought to have believed because of such great wisdom marveled [Note: Origen says: “They marveled that no opportunity for plotting against him had been afforded them.”] that their cunning had found no opening for laying snares.

And they left him and went away. They carried away unbelief together with their amazement.

(Vers. 23.) On that day the Sadducees, who say that there is no resurrection, approached him. There were two sects among the Jews: one of the Pharisees, the other of the Sadducees. The Pharisees placed before the people the righteousness of traditions and observances, which they call δευτερώσεις (“second traditions”); hence they were also called “separated” from the people. The Sadducees, whose name is interpreted as “righteous,” also claimed for themselves what they were not. Whereas the former believed and confessed the resurrection of both body and soul, as well as angels and the Spirit, the Sadducees, following the Acts of the Apostles, denied everything (Acts IV). These are the two houses concerning which Isaiah teaches more explicitly that they would stumble against the stone of offense (Isa. VIII). [Note: Compare the holy Doctor in his Commentaries on this passage of Isaiah and in his Epistle to Titus; also the Epistle to Algasi[a], Question 10, and the Dialogue Against the Luciferians, no. 8.]

(Vers. 24 and following.) And they questioned him, saying: “Teacher, Moses said: If someone dies without having a son, his brother is to marry his wife and raise up offspring for his brother. Now there were seven brothers among us; and the first, after marrying, died, and, having no offspring, left his wife to his brother. Likewise the second and the third, down to the seventh. Last of all, the woman also died.” Those who did not believe in the resurrection of bodies and thought that the soul perished together with the bodies quite properly invent a story of this sort, which would expose as madness those who assert the resurrection of the dead. It is possible, however, that something of this kind really once happened among their people.

(Vers. 28.) “Therefore, in the resurrection, whose wife of the seven will she be? For they all had her.” They set forward the shamefulness of the story in order to deny the truth of the resurrection.

(Vers. 29.) But Jesus answered and said to them: “You are mistaken, because you do not know the Scriptures or the power of God.” They are mistaken because they do not know the Scriptures; and because they are ignorant of the Scriptures, consequently they do not know the power of God—that is, Christ, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God (I Cor. I).

(Vers. 30.) “For in the resurrection they neither marry [Note: Instead of *neque nubentur* (“nor are given in marriage”), the most ancient Veronese copy of the Gospels has *neque uxores ducent* (“nor will they take wives”), which is more appropriate to the propriety of Latin usage.] nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels of God in heaven.” Latin usage does not correspond to the Greek idiom. In strict usage, women are said to marry, while men take wives; but let us understand the statement simply, since Scripture speaks of men marrying and of wives being given in marriage. If in the resurrection they will neither marry nor be given in marriage, then the bodies that can marry and be given in marriage will rise [Note: Three Palatine manuscripts read: “bodies that, since they can marry,” etc.]. For no one says of a stone or a tree, or of things that do not possess sexual members, that they neither marry nor are given in marriage; rather, this is said of those who, although they can marry, nevertheless do not marry for another reason. But when it adds, “They are like the angels of God in heaven,” a spiritual manner of life is promised.

(Vers. 31 and following.) “But concerning the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was spoken by God when he said to you: I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob? He is not the God of the dead, but of the living.” And when the crowds heard this, they marveled at his teaching. To prove the truth of the resurrection, he could have used many other, clearer examples, among them: “The dead will be raised, and those who are in the tombs will rise” (Isa. XXVI, 19); and in another passage: “Many of those sleeping in the dust of the earth will rise, some to everlasting life and others to reproach and everlasting confusion” (Dan. XII, 2). It is therefore asked what the Lord intended by putting forward this testimony, which seems ambiguous or not sufficiently relevant to the truth of the resurrection: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob”; and, as though he had proved what he wished by producing this statement, immediately adding: “He is not the God of the dead, but of the living.” The surrounding crowd also, recognizing the mystery, marveled at his teaching [Note: The Palatine manuscripts read: “at the teaching of that answer”] and his responses.

We said above that the Sadducees confessed neither angel, nor spirit, nor the resurrection of bodies, and also proclaimed the destruction of souls. They accepted only the five books of Moses, rejecting the prophecies of the prophets. It would therefore have been foolish to produce testimonies from an authority whose teaching they did not follow. To prove the immortality of souls, he accordingly gives an example from Moses: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. III, 6). He immediately adds: “He is not the God of the dead, but of the living,” so that, once he had proved that souls continue to exist after death—for it could not be that he was the God of those who in no way continued to exist—the resurrection of bodies would consequently also be introduced, since bodies had done good or evil together with those souls. The apostle Paul treats this passage more fully in the final section of his First Epistle to the Corinthians (I Cor. XV).

[Note: Origen’s response is not only the same but expressed in nearly the same words: “To this we shall reply that, although the Savior could have proved by six hundred testimonies drawn from the Prophets that the life of man will continue in the future, he did not do so. The reason is that the Sadducees accepted only one Scripture of Moses, and he wished to refute them by reasoning drawn from it. The matter seems to stand as follows: God said to Moses, ‘I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,’ when he gave him the oracle from the bush. Therefore either God is the God of those who exist, or of those who do not exist. But it is absurd to say that God, who said, ‘I am the One who is; that is my name,’ is the God of those who in no way exist. If that is absurd, then he is certainly the God of those who exist, who live, who have being, and who acknowledge the benefit bestowed on them by God … Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob therefore live, continuing to acknowledge God’s benefit,” etc.]

[Col. 0166A] (Vers. 34 and following.) The Pharisees, hearing that he had silenced the Sadducees, gathered together; and one of them, a lawyer, questioned him, testing him: “Teacher, which is the great commandment in the law?” Jesus said to him: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind. This is the greatest and first commandment. The second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets.”

Just as we read that Herod and Pontius Pilate made peace with one another in the Lord’s death, so now we see this happening with the Pharisees and Sadducees. Although they are opposed to one another, they agree with a common purpose in testing Jesus. Those who had already been refuted above in the matter of displaying the denarius, and who had seen the faction of the opposing party overthrown, ought to have been warned by this example not to contrive further plots [Note: One Cistercian manuscript reads: “to be moved by the example, lest they,” etc.]; but malice and envy nourish shamelessness.

One of the lawyers asks—not wishing to learn, but testing whether the one questioned knew what he was being asked—what the greater commandment is. He is not asking about the commandments in general, but which commandment is the first and greatest. Since everything God has commanded is great, whatever answer he gives will provide an opportunity for accusation, as the questioner asserts that some other commandment among the many is great. Thus anyone who knows something and asks about it not from a desire to learn but from an eagerness to discover whether the one who will answer knows it, approaches in the likeness of the Pharisees—not as a disciple, but as a tester.

**BOOK FOUR**

[Col. 0165]

[Col. 0165D] (Vers. 41 and following.) When the Pharisees had gathered together, Jesus questioned them, saying: “What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?” They say to him: “David’s.” He says to them: “How then does David, in the Spirit, call him Lord, saying: ‘The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool beneath your feet’? If therefore David calls him Lord, how is he his son?”

Those who had gathered to test Jesus and were trying to seize the truth by a deceitful question supplied the occasion for their own refutation [Note: Victorinus has: “were trying to find fault with him,” etc.]. They are questioned about the Christ—whose son he is. Jesus’ question benefits us even today against the Jews. For those who confess that the Christ is to come assert that he is merely a human being and a holy man descended from David.

Let us therefore question them, taught by the Lord: If he is merely a human being and David’s son only, how does David call him his Lord—not through some uncertain error or by his own will, but in the Holy Spirit? The testimony he cites is taken from Psalm 109. The Lord is therefore called David’s Lord not according to the fact that he was born from David, but according to the fact that he was eternally born from the Father, preceding the very father of his flesh.

The Jews invent many frivolous explanations to evade the truth of the question, asserting that Melchizedek was Abraham’s household servant and that Eliezer of Damascus was his son, and that the psalm was written from Abraham’s perspective: after the slaughter of the five kings, the Lord God said to his own lord, Abraham, “Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool beneath your feet” (Gen. XIV). [Note: Rhabb.: “who was Melchizedek.”]

Let us ask them how God could have said to Abraham the words that follow: “With you is sovereignty on the day of your power, in the splendors of the holy ones; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you”; and: “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” And let us force them to answer how Abraham was begotten before the morning star and how he was a priest according to the order of Melchizedek—on whose behalf Melchizedek offered bread and wine, and from whom he received tithes of the spoils.

(Vers. 46.) And no one was able to answer him a word; nor did anyone dare, from that day onward, to question him any further. The Pharisees and Sadducees, seeking an opportunity for accusation and trying to find some word that would lie open to their plots [Col. 0167B], since they had been refuted in their arguments, no longer question him, but hand him over, already openly seized, to the Roman authority. From this we understand that the poisons of envy can indeed be overcome, but are difficult to quiet.

(Cap. XXIII—Vers. 1 and following.) Then Jesus spoke to the crowds and to his disciples, saying: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat. Therefore, whatever they tell you, observe and do; but do not act according to their works, for they say and do not do.”

What is more gentle, what is more kind than the Lord? He is tested by the Pharisees, their plots are broken, and, according to the Psalmist, “Their arrows have become their wounds” (Ps. LXIII, 8); nevertheless, because of the dignity of the priesthood and the name they bear, he urges the people to submit to them, considering not their works but their teaching.

When he says, “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat,” he indicates by the seat the teaching of the Law. Thus we should understand also what is said in the Psalm: “He did not sit in the seat of pestilence” (Ps. I, 1); and: “He overturned the seats of those selling doves” (above, XXI; Mark XI): these too should be understood as referring to teaching.

(Vers. 4.) “They bind heavy and unbearable burdens and place them on people’s shoulders, but they themselves do not wish to move them with their finger.” This is generally directed against all teachers who command difficult things [Note: Our manuscripts perhaps more correctly read: “who command great things”] but do not perform even lesser ones. It should also be noted that the shoulders, the finger, the burdens, and the cords by which the burdens are tied are to be understood spiritually.

(Vers. 5.) “They do all their works so that they may be seen by people.” Therefore, whoever does anything in such a way as to be seen by people is a scribe and a Pharisee.

(Vers. 6.) “For they enlarge their phylacteries and magnify their fringes. They love the first places at banquets, the first seats in the synagogues, greetings in the marketplace, and to be called Rabbi by people.”

Woe to us in our misery, for the vices of the Pharisees have passed over to us. After the Lord had given the commandments of the Law through Moses, he concluded: “You shall bind them on your hand, and they shall be immovable before your eyes” (Deut. VI, 8). [Note: The Hebrew has [uncertain OCR], “frontlets”; but the Septuagint, whose wording the holy Father follows here, has ἀσαλευτά, “immovable,” contrary to the Latin rendering, “and they were moved,” which Jerome himself translated according to the force of the Hebrew verb. It signifies shaking or moving the body, or something else, while walking; in this sense, in the following exposition, he describes the Pharisees’ frontlets. Compare, therefore, the following note.] The meaning is: Let my commandments be in your hand, so that they may be fulfilled in action; let them be before your eyes, so that you may meditate on them day and night.

The Pharisees, interpreting this wrongly, wrote the Decalogue of Moses—that is, the ten words of the Law—on little strips of parchment [Note: Formerly the reading was *membranis* (“on parchments”). The holy Father has a similar statement on Ezekiel XXIV: “The Hebrews say that, to this day, the Babylonian teachers of the Law, observing the commandments, write the Decalogue on little pieces of parchment, bind them around their heads, and understand these to be the things commanded to be before the eyes and hanging on the forehead, so that they may always see the commandments. But, as we observe concerning that passage, here too it must be admitted—if there is any credibility in the rabbis when they describe their own practices, and if anything in their present custom confirms it—that they were accustomed to write on little strips of parchment not the Mosaic Decalogue, as Jerome reports, but only certain passages of Scripture: two from Exodus and two from Deuteronomy. These they would bind to the forehead with bands hanging down on either side.”], folding them up, tying them to their foreheads, and making them, as it were, a crown around the head, so that they would always move before their eyes. The Indians, Persians [Note: Our manuscripts do not recognize the name “Persians.” So too Rhabb.], and Babylonians still do this today; whoever has such an object is judged religious among the people.

Moses had also commanded something else (Num. XV): they were to make hyacinth-colored fringes on the four corners of their cloaks, so that the people of Israel might be distinguished. Just as circumcision on the body gave a sign of the Jewish nation, so the garment was to have some distinguishing feature.

Superstitious teachers, seeking popular approval and pursuing profits from little women, made the fringes large and fastened extremely sharp thorns to them, so that when they walked or sat they would occasionally be pricked and, as though recalled by this reminder, be drawn back to the duties of the Lord and the service of his worship.

Since the Lord had said, “They do all their works so that they may be seen by people,” what he had accused them of generally he now divides into particulars. Those little tablets of the Decalogue they called phylacteries [Note: That is, little sheets; Victorinus also notes this, from the Greek πυκτάτιον, meaning a little book, small tablet, or similar object. A little later, instead of *monimentum* (“memorial”), it may perhaps be more correct to read *munimentum* (“protection”).], because whoever possessed them was thought to have them as a safeguard and memorial of himself. The Pharisees did not understand that these things were to be carried in the heart, not on the body. Otherwise cupboards and chests also have books, but do not possess knowledge of God.

Superstitious women among us still do this today with little Gospels, pieces of the wood of the cross, and things of this kind—things that indeed have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge (Rom. X)—“straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel” (below, in the same chapter). [Col. 0169A]

Such was the small and short fringe prescribed by the Law, which the woman suffering from a hemorrhage touched on the Lord’s cloak (above IX; Luke VIII). But she was not pricked by the superstitious thorns of the Pharisees; rather, she was healed by touching him. Although they needlessly enlarge their phylacteries and make their fringes large, seeking glory from people, they are nevertheless reproved in the remaining matters: why they seek the first places at banquets and the first seats in the synagogues, and why in public they pursue appetite and glory, and desire to be called Rabbi by people—“teacher” in Latin. Finally, it follows:

(Vers. 8 and following.) “But you must not be called Rabbi, for one is your teacher [Note: Our manuscripts lack the words “but you are all brothers.” They are also absent from the Greek itself, although in one or another ancient copy of the Greek they are added at the end of the following verse, after the words ‘who is in heaven.’]. But you are all brothers. And do not call anyone your father on earth, for one is your Father, who is in heaven. Nor be called teachers, for one is your teacher, Christ. The greater among you will be your servant. Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”

No one else is to be called teacher or father except God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ. He is Father because all things are from him; he is Teacher because all things are through him—or because, through the dispensation of his flesh, we have all been reconciled to God.

It is asked why, contrary to this commandment, the Apostle said that he was a teacher of the Gentiles (II Cor. V; Col. I), or how, in ordinary speech—especially in the monasteries of Palestine and Egypt—they call one another “Fathers.” The answer is this: being a father or teacher by nature is one thing; being called one through indulgence is another. When we call a human being “father,” we pay honor to his age; we do not present him as the author of our life. A person is also called “teacher” through association with the true Teacher.

Not to prolong the matter indefinitely: just as one God by nature and one Son do not prevent others from being called gods [Alt. “deities”] and sons by adoption, so the one Father and one Teacher do not prevent others from being called fathers and teachers in an extended sense.

(Vers. 13, 14.) “But woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you shut the kingdom of heaven before people. For you yourselves do not enter, nor do you allow those entering to enter. Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you devour widows’ houses, while praying long prayers; therefore you will receive the greater judgment.”

The scribes and Pharisees, possessing knowledge of the Law and the Prophets, know that Christ is the Son of God. They are not ignorant that he was born from a Virgin; but while they desire plunder from the people subjected to them, they neither enter the kingdoms of heaven themselves nor allow those who could enter to do so.

This is what the prophet Hosea rebukes: “The priests concealed the way; they murdered Shechem” (Hos. VI, 9). And again: “The priests did not say, ‘Where is the Lord?’” (Hos. IV). Or certainly, every teacher who scandalizes his disciples by evil works shuts the kingdom of heaven before them.

(Vers. 15.) “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you traverse sea and land to make one proselyte; and when he has been made, you make him twice as much a son of Gehenna as yourselves.”

We do not preserve what we have sought with the same zeal with which we seek it. The scribes and Pharisees, traversing the whole world, whether for commercial dealings or for various profits [Note: Victorinus says: “Three Florentine codices read: ‘or various profits to be obtained from disciples, as though through an appearance of holiness.’ We have changed nothing, since both readings are good.”], sought to make a proselyte from the Gentiles—that is, to bring in a foreigner and an uncircumcised person and join him to the people of God.

But the person who, while a pagan, had previously wandered in simplicity and was once a son of Gehenna, seeing the vices of his teachers and understanding that by their conduct they were destroying what they taught in words, returns to his vomit. Having become a Gentile in practice, as a transgressor he will be judged worthy of a greater punishment.

He is called a son of Gehenna in the same way as someone is called a son of destruction or a son of this age. Everyone is called the son of the one whose works he performs.

(Vers. 16 and following.) “Woe to you, blind guides, who say: Whoever swears by the temple, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gold of the temple is bound by his oath. Fools and blind! For which is greater, the gold, or the temple that sanctifies the gold? And whoever swears by the altar, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gift that is upon it is bound. Blind! For which is greater, the gift, or the altar that sanctifies the gift? Therefore, whoever swears by the altar swears by it and by everything that is upon it. And whoever swears by the temple swears by it and by him who dwells in it. And whoever swears by heaven swears by the throne of God and by him who sits upon it.”

Above, as it seemed to us, we explained what was signified by the Pharisaic tradition that said: “Whatever gift is from me will benefit you.” Now a twofold Pharisaic tradition, tending toward one occasion of avarice, is condemned, so that they may be shown to do everything for profit and not out of fear of God.

Just as, in enlarged phylacteries and fringes, the reputation of holiness sought glory and through the occasion of glory sought profits, so another fraudulent invention of tradition proves the teachers to be impious. If someone had sworn by the temple in a dispute, some quarrel, or an uncertain legal case, and afterward had been convicted of lying, he was not held guilty of the offense [Alt. “of it”]. But if he had sworn by the gold and money offered in the temple to the priests, he was immediately compelled to pay what he had sworn by.

Again, if someone had sworn by the altar, no one held him guilty of perjury [Alt. “retained him as guilty”]; but if he had perjured himself by the gift or offerings—that is, by sacrifices, victims, fine flour, and the other things offered to God upon the altar—these were demanded back with the greatest insistence.

The Lord therefore rebukes them for both folly and fraud: the temple is far greater than the gold, which is sanctified by the temple; and the altar is greater than the sacrifices, which are sanctified by the altar. They did everything, however, not out of fear of God but out of greed for wealth.

(Vers. 23.) “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have abandoned the weightier matters of the Law: judgment, mercy, and faith. These you ought to have done, without omitting the others.”

Many commandments are given in the Law that foreshadow future realities. Others are plain, according to the Psalmist who says: “The commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes” (Ps. XVIII, 9); these immediately demand action. For example: “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness,” and so forth.

The Pharisees, because the Lord had commanded that, for the support of the priests and Levites—whose portion was the Lord—tithes of all things should be offered in the temple, had only this one concern: that what had been commanded should be brought in. As for the other matters, which were greater, they cared little whether anyone did them or not.

In this passage, therefore, he also accuses them of avarice: they diligently demand tithes even of insignificant herbs, while neglecting judgment in the settlement of disputes, mercy toward the poor, orphans, and widows, and faith in God, which are the greater matters.

(Vers. 24.) “Blind guides, who strain out a gnat but swallow a camel.”

I think that, according to the meaning of the present passage, the camel signifies the magnitude of the commandments—judgment, mercy, and faith. The gnat signifies the tithes of mint, dill, cumin, and the remaining insignificant herbs. Against God’s commandment, we swallow and neglect the great matters, while in small things that yield profit we display carefulness in order to gain a reputation for religion.

(Vers. 25, 26.) “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you cleanse what is outside the cup and the dish, but inside you are full of plunder and uncleanness. Blind Pharisee, first cleanse what is inside the cup and the dish, so that what is outside may also become clean.”

In different words but with the same meaning as above, he rebukes the Pharisees for pretense and falsehood: outwardly they display one thing to people [Note: Previously the text read: “they show one thing”], while at home they do another. This does not mean that their superstition resided in cups and dishes, but that outwardly they displayed holiness to people—in clothing, speech, phylacteries, fringes, the length of their prayers, and other things of this kind—while inwardly they were full of the filth of vices.

(Vers. 27, 28.) “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you are like whitewashed tombs, which appear beautiful outwardly to people, but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead and of every impurity. So you also outwardly appear righteous to people, but inwardly you are full of hypocrisy and iniquity.”

What he had demonstrated by the cup and dish—that they were washed on the outside but filthy within—he now repeats by the example of tombs. Just as tombs are coated with plaster on the outside and decorated with marble, gold, and varied colors, but inside are full of the bones of the dead, so perverse teachers, who teach one thing and do another, display purity in their clothing and humility of speech, but inwardly are full of every impurity and lust.
