Finally, he expresses this very point more clearly when he adds: “So you also outwardly appear righteous to people, but inwardly you are full of hypocrisy and iniquity.”

(Vers. 29 and following.) “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you build the tombs of the prophets and adorn the monuments of the righteous, and say: If we had been in the days of our fathers, we would not have been their companions in the blood of the prophets. Thus you testify against yourselves that you are sons of those who killed the prophets.”

With a most skillful syllogism he proves them to be the sons of murderers. They themselves, in the eyes of the people and for the sake of glory, build tombs for the prophets whom their ancestors killed, and say: “If we had lived at that time, we would not have done what our fathers did.” Even if they do not say this in words, they proclaim it by their deeds, since they build ostentatious and magnificent memorials for those who were killed, while not denying that their fathers slaughtered them.

“And you—fill up the measure of your fathers.” Having proved by what preceded that they were the sons of murderers and of those who had killed the prophets, he now concludes what he intended and sets down, as it were, the final part of the syllogism: “And you—fill up the measure of your fathers.” Complete what was lacking in them. They killed the servants; you crucify the Lord. They killed the prophets; you kill the one whom the prophets foretold.

(Vers. 33.) “Serpents, offspring [Alt. the word ‘and’ is added] of vipers, how will you escape the judgment of Gehenna?” John the Baptist had also said this (Luke III). Therefore, just as vipers give birth to vipers, so, he says, you were born murderers from murderous fathers.

(Vers. 34.) “Therefore, behold, I send to you prophets, wise men, and scribes; and some of them you will kill and crucify, and some of them you will scourge in your synagogues and persecute from city to city.”

What we said earlier—“Fill up the measure of your fathers”—can refer to the person of the Lord, since he was to be killed by them; but it can also refer to his disciples, concerning whom he now says: “Behold, I send to you prophets, wise men, and scribes, and some of them you will kill and crucify, and you will scourge them in your synagogues and persecute them from city to city,” so that you may fill up the measure of your fathers.

At the same time, observe, in accordance with the Apostle writing to the Corinthians (I Cor. VII), that the gifts of Christ’s disciples are various: some are prophets, who proclaim what is to come; others are wise, who know when they ought to bring forth a word; others are scribes, most learned in the Law. Among them Stephen was stoned, Paul was killed, Peter was crucified, and the disciples were scourged in the Acts of the Apostles. They persecuted them from city to city, driving them out of Judea so that they might migrate to the people of the Gentiles.

### (Verses 35, 36)

“So that there may come upon you all the righteous blood that has been shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar. Truly I tell you, all these things will come upon this generation.”

There is no ambiguity concerning Abel: he is the one whom his brother Cain killed.

> **Note [Col. 0173C]:** The Rabbis [*Rhabb.*] have no doubt that he is the righteous man whom Cain, etc., killed. That he was righteous is confirmed not only by the Lord’s present judgment but also by the testimony of Genesis, where his offerings are said to have been accepted by God (Gen. 4).

We ask who this Zechariah son of Barachiah was, since we read of many Zechariahs. And so that no latitude for error might be granted us, it is added: “whom you killed between the temple and the altar.” I have read different opinions in different sources, and I ought to set down each of them.

Some say that Zechariah son of Barachiah was the eleventh of the Twelve Prophets, whose father’s name agrees with this one; but Scripture does not say where he was killed between the temple and the altar—especially since in his time scarcely even the ruins of the temple remained.

Others wish the father of John to be understood, approving this from certain dreams of the apocryphal writings: namely, that he was killed because he preached the Savior’s coming. Since this has no authority from Scripture, it is dismissed with the same ease with which it is approved.

Others want this to be the Zechariah who was killed by Joash, king of Judah, between the temple and the altar, as the history in Kings relates. But it must be observed that that Zechariah was not the son of Barachiah but the son of Jehoiada the priest.

> **Note [Cols. 0173C–0174A]:** This view, which Jerome also approves, seems nearer the truth: it identifies Zechariah son of Barachiah, of whom Matthew 23:35 speaks, with Zechariah son of Jehoiada, supported by the not inconsiderable authority of the Hebrew Gospel-book of the Nazarenes, in which the holy Father found the name Jehoiada in place of Barachiah. Distinguished interpreters had long ago adopted this view, though there is no time to name each of them. Those who defend another view object, besides the authority of the very ancient Fathers who commonly suppose that Matthew here means Zechariah, father of John the Baptist, that the Zechariah of whom Christ speaks is not said to have held the high priesthood, which the son of Jehoiada in fact held. They also object that Christ says he was put to death between the temple and the altar—that is, between the temple vestibule and the altar of burnt offerings, or west of that altar—whereas the son of Jehoiada was killed, according to the book of Chronicles, in the court of the house of the Lord, apparently the court of the people. Nevertheless, Jerome’s view greatly pleases me, and I adhere to it. Hence Scripture says: “Joash did not remember the kindness which Jehoiada his father had done for him” (2 Chron. 24:22).

> **Note [Col. 0173D]:** More correctly, in accordance with the Greek text, our manuscripts read “which he had done for him,” etc., in place of “because.”

Since, then, we have both the Zechariah and the location of the killing in agreement, we ask why he is called the son of Barachiah rather than of Jehoiada. Barachiah in our language means “blessed of the Lord,” and the righteousness of the priest Jehoiada is demonstrated in the Hebrew language.

> **Note:** Thus the Beccensis manuscript reads; others, with the printed editions, have: “is demonstrated by the Hebrew name.” Jehoiada therefore signifies “knowledge of the Lord,” not “righteousness,” as Jerome testifies in his book of Hebrew Names. But the righteousness of the priest Jehoiada is demonstrated in the Hebrew language, because among the Hebrews “knowledge of the Lord” is understood as righteousness and piety. Isaiah 11 says: “They shall not hurt, and they shall not kill, throughout all my holy mountain; for the earth is full of the knowledge of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea.” Here and elsewhere “knowledge” is understood as righteousness, the worship of God, and piety.  
> **MART.:** In the Cistercian manuscript: “by the name of the Hebrews”; the old printed editions: “by the Hebrew name.” I certainly know that *Joiadah* means “the Lord knows.” Hence Jerome also interprets it as “knowledge of the Lord.” But Victorius, before Martianay, attempted in some fashion to show how it could signify “righteousness,” on the ground that in Scripture “knowledge of the Lord” is understood as righteousness and truth. “For,” he says, “the word ‘righteousness’ has a broad range of meaning; hence Psalm 18: ‘The righteous ordinances of the Lord are right, rejoicing the heart; the commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes,’ has a similar meaning.” The Hebrew word there is not [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], but [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text]. Likewise Psalm 17: “I have not rejected his righteousness”; in Hebrew, instead of “his righteousness,” one reads [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text].

In the Gospel used by the Nazarenes, we find “son of Jehoiada” written instead of “son of Barachiah.”

The simpler brethren think that the rocks between the ruins of the temple and the altar—or at the exits of the gates leading toward Siloam—were stained by the blood of Zechariah. We do not condemn an error that proceeds from hatred of the Jews and devotion to the faith.

Let us briefly explain why the blood of righteous Abel, up to that of Zechariah son of Barachiah, is required of that generation, although it killed neither of them.

> **Note:** Three Palatine manuscripts read: “It is a rule of the Scriptures to recognize two generations of the good and the evil, that is, each having its own.”

It is a rule of Scripture to posit two generations, of the good and of the evil—that is, each class has its own generation.

Let us take examples from the good. “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord? Or who shall rest upon his holy mountain?” (Ps. 24:3). After describing the many who would ascend the mountain of the Lord, men of different ages, it adds: “This is the generation of those who seek him, who seek the face of the God of Jacob.” And elsewhere, concerning all the saints: “The generation of the righteous shall be blessed” (Ps. 112:2).

Concerning the wicked, however, as in the present passage: “Generation of vipers.” And: “All these things shall be required of this generation.” Likewise in Ezekiel, after describing the sins of the land, the prophetic word adds: “If Noah, Job, and Daniel were found there, I would not forgive the sins of that land” (Ezek. 14:14), wishing all the righteous who would be like them in virtue to be understood through Noah, Job, and Daniel.

Therefore those also who acted against the apostles in a manner like Cain and Joash are said to belong to one generation.

### (Verse 37)

“Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you! How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and you were unwilling!”

He calls Jerusalem not the stones and buildings of the city but its inhabitants, and he mourns for it with a father’s affection, just as we read elsewhere that he wept when he saw it (Luke 19).

When he says, “How often I wanted to gather your children,” he testifies that all the prophets previously sent were sent to it.

We also read in the song of Deuteronomy the comparison of a hen gathering her chicks beneath her wings: “As an eagle protects its nest and desires its young, spreading its wings, it received them and carried them upon its feathers” (Deut. 32:11).

> **Note:** The same manuscripts have *desiderat* (“desires”); but, in agreement with the Greek text and the old printed editions, they add *eos* (“them”) to *suscepit* (“received”): Greek, ἐδέξατο αὐτούς.

### (Verse 38)

“Behold, your house will be left to you desolate.”

He had already said this in the person of Jeremiah: “I have forsaken my house; I have abandoned my inheritance. My inheritance has become for me like a hyena’s den” (Jer. 12:7–8).

> **Note:** In the margin at the foot of the page in an older Palatine manuscript, the following words of a glossator are to be restored to the text: “It is an animal called in Greek *hyena*, in Latin *beast*, concerning which the Law says: ‘You shall not eat the hyena, nor anything like it, because it is an unclean animal.’ The *Physiologus* says of it that it has two natures, being at one time male and at another female. The children of Israel were considered like it, since at first they served the living God, but afterward, devoted to pleasures and luxury, they worshiped idols.”

We see with our own eyes the house of the Jews—that is, the temple, which had shone in such great magnificence—left desolate, because it lost Christ as its inhabitant and, eager to seize the inheritance, killed the heir.

> **Variant [Col. 0175D]:** The Palatine manuscripts read: “which had previously shone in majesty.”

### (Verse 39)

“For I tell you: from now on you will not see me until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.’”

> **Note:** Two manuscripts have: “who is to come.”

He speaks to Jerusalem and to the Jewish people. This verse, which even children and infants used at the entrance of the Lord and Savior into Jerusalem when they said, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; hosanna in the highest,” he took from Psalm 118, which was plainly written concerning the Lord’s coming.

What he says is to be understood as follows: Unless you repent (Luke 13) and confess that I am the one of whom the prophets sang, the Son of the almighty Father, you will not see my face.

The Jews have been given a time for repentance. Let them confess him who comes in the name of the Lord to be blessed, and they will behold the face of Christ.

## Chapter 24 — Verses 1–2

“And Jesus went out from the temple and was departing. His disciples came to him to show him the buildings of the temple. But he answered and said to them: ‘Do you see all these things? Truly I tell you: not one stone here will be left upon another that will not be destroyed.’”

The meaning according to the historical sense is clear. When the Lord departed from the temple, all the structures of the Law and the arrangement of its commandments were so destroyed that nothing could be fulfilled by the Jews; and when the head was removed, all the members clashed with one another.

### (Verses 3–4)

“While he was sitting on the Mount of Olives, the disciples came to him privately, saying: ‘Tell us when these things will happen, and what will be the sign of your coming and of the consummation of the age?’ And Jesus answered and said to them: ‘See that no one deceives you.’”

He sits on the Mount of Olives, where the true light of knowledge was arising. The disciples come to him privately because they wished to know the mysteries and the revelation of future events, and they ask about three things: when Jerusalem would be destroyed, when Christ would come, and when the consummation of the age would occur.

### (Verse 5)

“For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am the Christ,’ and they will lead many astray.”

One of these was Simon the Samaritan, whom we read about in the Acts of the Apostles. He claimed to be the great power of God (Acts 8), and, among other things, he left these statements written in his books: “I am the Word of God; I am the Beautiful One; I am the Paraclete; I am the Almighty; I am all things of God.”

> **Note:** The author of the *Apostolic Constitutions* says: “For we know that those who follow Simon and Cleobius, composing poisonous books under the name of Christ and his disciples, circulate them to deceive you.” The author also mentions, in *On the Divine Names*, chapter 6: “Simon’s refutational discourses.” In the Arabic preface to the Council of Nicaea: “These impious Simonites fabricated a Gospel for themselves, dividing it into four volumes, and called it the book of the four corners and hinges of the world.”

The apostle John also says in his letter: “You have heard that the Antichrist is coming; now there are many antichrists” (1 John 2:18).

I think that all the founders of heresies are antichrists, teaching under Christ’s name things contrary to Christ. It is no wonder that we see some people led astray by them, since the Lord said, “They will lead many astray.”

### (Verse 6)

“For you will hear of wars and reports of wars. See that you are not troubled. For these things must happen, but the end is not yet.”

When we see these things occurring, we should not think that the day of judgment is at hand, but that it is reserved for that time whose sign is clearly set forth in what follows.

### (Verses 7–8)

“For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom, and there will be plagues and famines and earthquakes in various places. But all these things are the beginning of sorrows.”

I do not doubt that these things too will occur according to the literal sense of what is written. But it seems to me that “kingdom against kingdom” and the plague of those whose word spreads like cancer (2 Tim. 2), the famine of hearing the word of God, the shaking of the whole earth, and separation from the true faith are more particularly to be understood of heretics, who fight against one another and thereby bring victory to the Church.

What he said—“But all these things are the beginning of sorrows”—is better translated as “of birth-pangs,” so that the coming of the Antichrist may be understood as a kind of conception, not yet a birth.

### (Verse 9)

“Then they will hand you over to tribulation and kill you, and you will be hated by all nations because of my name.”

Through the apostles the person of all believers is signified, not because the apostles themselves will then be found bodily present.

### (Verses 12–13)

“And because wickedness will abound, the love of many will grow cold. But the one who perseveres to the end will be saved.”

He did not deny the faith of everyone, but of many. “For many are called, but few are chosen.” Among the apostles and those like them, love will remain, concerning which it is written: “Many waters cannot extinguish love” (Song 8:7).

> **Note:** Most manuscripts have: “Many waters cannot extinguish.”

Paul himself says: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or famine?” (Rom. 8:35), and so forth.

### (Verse 14)

“And this Gospel of the kingdom will be preached throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come.”

A sign of the Lord’s coming is that the Gospel is preached throughout the whole world, so that no one may have an excuse. We see this either already completed or soon to be completed. For I do not think that any nation remains that is unaware of the name of Christ. Even if it has not had a preacher, it cannot be ignorant of the report of the faith among neighboring nations.

### (Verse 15)

“Therefore, when you see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet, standing in the holy place—let the reader understand.”

When we are summoned to understanding, what has been said is shown to be mystical.

We read in Daniel as follows: “And in the middle of the week the sacrifice and the offering will be taken away, and in the temple there will be the abomination of desolations until the consummation of time, and the consummation will be given over the desolation.”

Paul also speaks of this (2 Thess. 2): the man of iniquity and the adversary will be raised up against everything that is called God and worshiped, so that he dares to stand in the temple of God and show that he himself is God. His coming, according to the working of Satan, will destroy those who receive him and reduce them to the desolation of God.

> **Note:** One Palatine manuscript has “that he himself is Christ” instead of “that he himself is God.” Later it has “reduce it to desolation,” without the word “God.”

The passage may simply be understood either of the Antichrist, or of Caesar’s image, which Pilate placed in the temple, or of Hadrian’s equestrian statue, which stood in the very place of the Holy of Holies until the present day.

According to the ancient Scripture, an abomination is also called an idol. For this reason “of desolation” is added: an idol has been placed in a temple left desolate and destroyed.

### (Verses 16 and following)

“Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains; and let the one who is on the roof not come down to take anything from his house; and let the one who is in the field not return to take his tunic.”

The abomination of desolation may also be understood as every perverse doctrine. When we see it standing in the holy place—that is, in the Church—and showing itself to be God, we must flee from Judea to the mountains: that is, abandoning the letter that kills and Jewish perversity, we must draw near to the eternal mountains from which God wondrously gives light (Ps. 76).

We must be on the roof and the housetop, where the fiery darts of the devil cannot reach us, and must not descend to take anything from the house of our former way of life. We must not seek the things that are behind us, but rather sow in the field of the spiritual Scriptures, so that we may receive fruit from it. Nor should we take another tunic, which the apostles are forbidden to possess.

Porphyry blasphemed extensively against us concerning this passage—that is, concerning the abomination of desolation spoken of by Daniel the prophet, standing in the holy place—in the thirteenth book of his work. Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, answered him in three books: the eighteenth, nineteenth, and twentieth. Apollinaris also wrote very fully. He attempted unnecessarily to discuss in a single chapter a subject that has been treated in so many thousands of lines.

### (Verse 19)

“But woe to those who are pregnant and to those who nurse infants in those days.”

Woe to those souls that have not brought their offspring to the perfect man, but possess only the beginnings of faith and therefore need the nourishment of teachers.

This may also be said: during the persecution of the Antichrist, or the Roman captivity, pregnant women and nursing mothers, weighed down by the burden of wombs and children, will not be able to flee swiftly.

### (Verse 20)

“Pray that your flight may not take place in winter or on the Sabbath.”

If we wish to understand this of the captivity of Jerusalem, when it was captured by Titus and Vespasian, they should pray that their flight may not occur in winter or on the Sabbath. In the one case, the severity of the cold prevents them from going into the wilderness and hiding in the mountains and deserted places; in the other, either fleeing would be a transgression of the Law, or remaining would mean imminent death.

But if it is understood of the consummation of the world, he commands that our faith and love for Christ not grow cold, and that we not grow sluggish in God’s work, idle on the Sabbath of virtues.

### (Verse 22)

“And unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved; but for the sake of the elect those days will be shortened.”

We should understand the shortening of the days not according to the ravings of certain people, who think that the moments of time are altered and do not remember what is written: “By your ordinance the day endures” (Ps. 119:91), but according to the character of the times. That is, the days are shortened not in measure but in number.

Just as it is said in the blessing, “I will satisfy him with length of days” (Ps. 91:16), so now the days are to be understood as shortened, lest the duration of the times shake the faith of believers.

### (Verse 23)

“Then if anyone says to you, ‘Behold, here is the Christ,’ or ‘There,’ do not believe it.”

At the time of the Jewish captivity many leaders arose who claimed to be Christs, to such an extent that, while the Romans were besieging them, there were three factions within the city. But the passage is better understood of the consummation of the world.

### (Verse 24)

“For false Christs and false prophets will arise and give great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect. Behold, I have told you beforehand.”

As I have already said, this passage must be discussed in three ways: either of the time of the Roman siege, or of the consummation of the world, or of the struggle of heretics against the Church and of such antichrists, who fight against Christ under the appearance of false knowledge.

### (Verses 25–26)

“Therefore, if they say to you, ‘Behold, he is in the wilderness,’ do not go out; ‘Behold, he is in the inner rooms,’ do not believe it.”

If anyone promises you that Christ dwells in the wilderness of the Gentiles and in the doctrine of philosophers, or in the inner rooms of heretics who promise the secrets of God, do not go out; do not believe.

Or, since false prophets always find an opportunity for deception in times of persecution and distress, if anyone wishes to boast of himself under Christ’s name, do not immediately give him your faith.

### (Verse 27)

“For just as lightning comes out from the east and appears as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.”

Do not go out and do not believe that the Son of Man is either in the wilderness of the Gentiles or in the inner rooms of heretics. Rather, his faith shines from east to west in the catholic Churches.

It must also be said that the Savior’s second coming will be manifested not in humility, as before, but in glory. It is foolish to seek in a small or hidden place the one who is the light of the whole world.

### (Verse 28)

“Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered.”

We are instructed in the sacrament of Christ by an example from nature that we see every day. Eagles and vultures are said to sense corpses even across the seas and to gather for such food.

If irrational birds, separated by such great expanses of land and by the waves of the sea, perceive a small corpse wherever it lies, how much more should we, and the whole multitude of believers, hasten to him whose lightning comes out from the east and appears as far as the west!

We may understand the body—that is, *πτῶμα*, more significantly rendered in Latin as *cadaver*, “corpse,” from its falling through death—as the passion of Christ, to which we are summoned. Thus, wherever it is read in the Scriptures, let us gather to it, and through it may come to the Word of God, as in: “They pierced my hands and my feet” (Ps. 22:16), and in Isaiah: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter” (Isa. 53:7), and other passages of this kind.

> **Note:** Saint Hilary also says concerning this passage: “He called the saints eagles because of the flight of their spiritual body; with the angels gathering them, he shows that their assembly will take place at the place of the Passion.” But the word *πτῶμα* seems characteristic of Origen. See, and so forth.

The saints are called eagles because their youth is renewed like that of eagles, and because, according to Isaiah, they grow feathers and take up wings so as to come to Christ’s Passion (Isa. 40:31).

### (Verse 29)

“Immediately after the tribulation of those days, the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of heaven will be shaken.”

The sun and moon will be darkened and will not give their light; the other stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of heaven will be shaken—not through a diminution of light, since we read elsewhere that the sun will have sevenfold light (Isa. 30:26), but because, in comparison with the true light, everything will appear dark to the eye.

If, therefore, this sun that now glows throughout the whole world, the moon that is the second light, the stars that have been kindled for the consolation of night, and all the powers—which we understand as the multitudes of angels—will be counted as darkness at Christ’s coming, let the arrogance of those who consider themselves holy and do not fear the presence of the Judge be cast down.

### (Verse 30)

“And then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven.”

Here we may understand the sign either as the cross, so that the Jews may see the one whom they pierced, according to Zechariah (Zech. 12) and John (John 19), or as the standard of the triumphant victory.

“And then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty.”

Those will mourn who did not possess citizenship in heaven but are written on earth.

### (Verse 31)

“And he will send his angels with a trumpet and a great voice, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from the highest heavens to their boundaries.”

Paul also speaks of this trumpet (1 Cor. 15; 1 Thess. 4), and we read of it in the Apocalypse of John (Rev. 8). In the Old Testament it is commanded that trumpets be made of beaten gold, bronze, and silver (Num. 10), so that they may resound with the sublime mysteries of doctrine.

### (Verses 32–33)

“Learn a parable from the fig tree: when its branch has already become tender and its leaves have appeared, you know that summer is near. So also, when you see all these things, know that he is near, at the gates.”

Using the example of a tree, he taught about the coming of the consummation.

“When,” he says, “the tender shoots appear on the fig tree, the bud bursts into flower, and the bark brings forth leaves, you understand the coming of summer and the arrival of the west wind and spring. So when you see all these things that have been written, do not think that the consummation of the world has already arrived, but that certain preludes and forerunners are coming, showing that it is near and at the gates.”

> **Note:** Martianay incorrectly reads *caliculi* and criticizes Erasmus, who preferred *teneres … claviculi*. Our manuscripts, following Victorius, supply the correct reading; they also read: “and their bud burst forth,” and so forth.  
> **MART.:** Erasmus did not read correctly: “when tender shoots appear on the fig tree.” Marianus restored the true reading retained by our manuscripts.

> **Note:** One Palatine manuscript has “as preceding signs and forerunners,” and so forth. The excellent manuscript of the Church of Narbonne retains this reading: “as certain preceding signs and forerunners,” and so forth.  
> **MART.**

### (Verse 34)

“Truly I tell you: this generation will not pass away until all these things happen.”

We said above that there are distinct generations of the good and, conversely, of the evil. Therefore the phrase either signifies the whole human race or specifically the Jews.

### (Verse 35)

“Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.”

Heaven and earth will pass away by transformation, not by their abolition. Otherwise, how could the sun be darkened, the moon not give its light, and the stars fall, if heaven, in which these things are found, and earth did not remain?

### (Verse 36)

“But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven, but the Father alone.”

> **Note:** The words “and hour,” which are also absent from some Greek manuscripts, are not found here in two Palatine manuscripts.

Some Latin manuscripts add “nor the Son.”

> **Note:** The addition “nor the Son” is still found in the ancient Veronese copy of the Gospels. In the edition published by Martianay, it appears in what he calls the Italian version as “but not the Son.” In the Beccensis manuscript belonging to Martianay, this passage in Jerome’s Commentary has “nor the Son of Man.” If one consults the Greek copies, one Cambridge Greek-Latin manuscript has οὐδὲ ὁ υἱός, “nor the Son,” which Chrysostom himself also reads. Nevertheless, Saint Ambrose, in *On the Faith*, book 5, chapter 16, attributes this addition to the frauds of the Arians: “The ancient Greek manuscripts do not have ‘nor the Son,’ but it is not surprising if they falsified this too, since they interpolated the divine Scriptures.” The reason it appears to have been added is revealed by the fact that it was introduced into an interpretation of such great sacrilege.

Since this is not written in the Greek copies, especially those of Adamantius and Pierius, but is read in some, it seems necessary to discuss it.

Arius and Eunomius rejoice as though the teacher’s ignorance were the disciples’ glory, and say: “One who knows and one who is ignorant cannot be equal.”

Against them we must briefly say the following. Since Jesus—that is, the Word of God—made all times, for “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3), and the day of judgment is included among all times, how could he be ignorant of a part whose whole he knows?

This too must be said: Which is greater, knowledge of the Father or knowledge of the judgment? If he knows the greater, how can he be ignorant of the lesser?

We read: “All things that belong to the Father have been delivered to me” (Luke 10:22). If everything belonging to the Father belongs to the Son, why did he reserve the knowledge of one day for himself and refuse to share it with the Son?

We must add this also: If he is ignorant of the last day of the ages, he is ignorant of the nearly last day as well, and, going backward, of all the others. For it cannot happen that one who is ignorant of the first knows what the second is.

Since we have therefore shown that the Son is not ignorant of the day of the consummation, an explanation must be given for why he is said to be ignorant.

The apostle writes concerning the Savior: “In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. 2:3). All the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are therefore in Christ, but they are hidden.

Why are they hidden? After the resurrection, when the apostles asked him about the day, he answered more clearly: “It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has placed in his own authority” (Acts 1:7). When he says, “It is not for you to know,” he shows that he himself knows but that it is not useful for the apostles to know, so that, always uncertain about the Judge’s coming, they may live every day as though they were to be judged on that day.

Finally, the subsequent words of the Gospel compel us to understand the same thing when they say that the Father alone knows. In the Father, he includes the Son also, for every father is the name of a son.

### (Verses 37 and following)

“As it was in the days of Noah, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. For as they were in the days before the flood, eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day when Noah entered the ark, and they did not know until the flood came and took them all away, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.”

It is asked how it was written above, “Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom; and there will be plagues, famines, and earthquakes,” while now events that are signs of peace are said to be future.

We must suppose, in agreement with the apostle, that after wars, disagreements, plagues, famines, earthquakes, and the other things by which the human race is devastated, peace will soon follow, promising quiet to everything, so that the faith of believers may be tested: whether, after the evils have passed, they expect the Judge to come.

This is what we read in Paul: “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them, like labor pains upon a pregnant woman, and they will not escape” (1 Thess. 5:3).

### (Verses 40–41)

“Then two will be in the field: one will be taken and one will be left. Two women will be grinding at the mill: one will be taken and one will be left.”

“Then,” he says, “there will be two in the field,” namely at the time of the consummation and judgment, when two will be found together in the field, engaged in the same labor and apparently sowing equally, but not receiving the fruits of their labor equally.

Two women will likewise be grinding together: one will be taken and one will be left.

In the two who remain in the field and the two who grind together, understand either the Synagogue and the Church, which appear to grind together in the Law and to grind the flour of God’s commandments from the same Scriptures; or the other heresies, which seem to grind the flour of their doctrines from both Testaments or from one of them.

Although they have one common profession of the Christian name, they will not receive the same reward: some will be taken and others left behind.

### (Verses 42–43)

“Therefore keep watch, because you do not know at what hour your Lord will come. But know this: if the master of the house had known at what hour the thief would come, he would certainly have kept watch and would not have allowed his house to be broken into.”

He clearly shows why he said above: “Concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the Son of Man nor the angels, but the Father alone.”

> **Note:** Here too the Palatine manuscripts omit the words “and hour.” See the preceding note.

It is not useful for the apostles to know, so that, suspended in the uncertainty of expectation, they may always believe that the one whose time of coming they do not know will come.

He did not say, “Because we do not know at what hour the Lord will come,” but, “You do not know.” By introducing the example of the master of the house, he teaches more clearly why he conceals the day of the consummation, saying:

“Therefore you also must be ready, because you do not know at what hour the Son of Man will come. Who, then, do you think is the faithful and wise servant whom his master appointed over his household, to give them food at the proper time? Blessed is that servant whom his master, when he comes, finds doing so. Truly I tell you, he will appoint him over all his possessions.”

He emphasizes and repeats more fully why he said that neither the angels nor himself knew the day and hour of the consummation, but only the Father, because it is not useful for the apostles to know.

He inserts the example of the master of the household—that is, himself—and of the faithful servants—that is, the apostles—to encourage a vigilant mind, so that, in hope of rewards, they may provide their fellow servants with the food of doctrine at the proper time.

### (Verses 48–49)

“But if that wicked servant says in his heart, ‘My master is delaying his coming,’ and begins to beat his fellow servants, while he eats and drinks with drunkards—”

This follows from what came before. Just as the vigilant servant, always awaiting his master’s coming, gives his fellow servants their food at the proper time and is afterward appointed over all the master’s possessions, so, conversely, the one who says, according to Ezekiel, “This vision is for many days to come” (Ezek. 12:22), and does not think that his master will come soon, becomes secure and gives himself over to feasts and indulgence. He will find not a gentle master of the household but a most severe judge.

### (Verses 50–51)

“The master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and he will cut him in two and assign him his portion with the hypocrites. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

This teaches that the master will come precisely when he is not expected, and it admonishes stewards to remain watchful and diligent.

When it says that he will “cut him in two,” this does not mean that he will dissect him with a sword, but that he will separate him from the company of the saints and assign him his portion with the hypocrites—namely, with those who were in the field and those who were grinding, but who were nevertheless left behind.

We have often said that a hypocrite is one thing inwardly and displays another outwardly. So too in the field and at the mill he appeared to be doing the same thing as the ecclesiastical man, but the outcome revealed a different intention.

> **Additional textual apparatus:** At Matthew 23:35, some witnesses read “agrees” (*consentit*) rather than “may agree,” and “was preaching” (*praedicaret*) rather than “preached”; one reads “and” in place of “among.” In the rule concerning generations, three Palatine manuscripts read, “It is a rule of the Scriptures to recognize two generations of the good and the evil, that is, each having its own”; the Palatine manuscripts omit the word “through” in the phrase “through Noah, Job, and Daniel.” At Matthew 23:37, the manuscripts read *desiderat* (“hovers over” or “cherishes”), while the older editions, following Greek *ἐδέξατο αὐτούς*, add “them” to “received.” At Matthew 23:39, two manuscripts read “who is to come.” At Matthew 24:15, one Palatine manuscript reads “that he himself is Christ” rather than “God”; later it reads “reduce [them] to desolation,” omitting “God.” At 24:16, *Apollinarius* is a variant for *Apollinaris*. At 24:34, one Palatine manuscript reads “as preceding signs and forerunners”; the excellent manuscript of the Church of Narbonne reads “as certain preceding signs and forerunners.” At 24:36, the variant “God” is added after “Son” in some copies. At 24:37, “giving in marriage” has the variant *nuptum*. At 24:42–43, the Palatine manuscripts again omit “and hour,” and the Victorius text reads “nor the angels of heaven knew” in the preceding explanation. At 24:40–41, “or” is a variant before “the Church”; at 24:37, *brevis* is a variant for *brevi*.

> **Bibliographic/editorial note [Col. 0176D]:** The author of the *Apostolic Constitutions* writes: *Oidamen gar hoti hoi peri Simōna kai Kleobion iōdē syntaxantes biblia ep’ onomati Christou kai tōn mathētōn autou peripherousin eis apatēn*—“We know that those who follow Simon and Cleobius, composing poisonous books under the name of Christ and his disciples, circulate them to deceive you.” The author of *On the Divine Names*, chapter 6, also mentions *Simonōs antirrhētikous logous*, “Simon’s refutational discourses.” The Arabic preface to the Council of Nicaea says that the impious Simonites fabricated for themselves a Gospel, divided it into four volumes, and called it the book of the four corners and hinges of the world.

## Chapter XXV

### Verses 1ff.

“Then the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins who, taking their lamps, went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride. Five of them were foolish, and five prudent. But the five foolish, having taken their lamps, did not take oil with them. The prudent, however, took oil in their vessels along with their lamps.”

Some interpret this parable—that is, the comparison of the ten virgins, foolish and prudent—simply as referring to virgins: some, in accordance with the Apostle, are virgins both in body and in mind; others preserve only the virginity of their bodies, while either they do not possess other works resembling their profession, or, preserved by the guardianship of their parents, they have nevertheless married in their minds (1 Cor. VII).

But it seems to me that another meaning is indicated by what precedes, and that the comparison applies not to virgin bodies but to the whole human race. For just as the two in the field and the two women grinding signify two peoples, Christians and Jews, or the holy and the sinful—who, established in the Church, appear indeed themselves to plow and grind, but do everything in hypocrisy—so now the ten virgins embrace all human beings who seem to believe in God and boast in the Holy Scriptures, whether ecclesiastical persons, Jews, or heretics.

They are all called virgins for this reason: they glory in the knowledge of one God, and their mind is not defiled by the crowd [another reading: whirlwind] of idolatry. Those virgins have oil who are adorned both by faith and by works. Those do not have oil who seem indeed to confess the Lord with a similar faith, but neglect the works of virtue.

We can also interpret the five virgins, wise and foolish, as the five senses: some of them hasten toward heavenly things and desire what is above; others, gazing intently upon earthly filth, possess no fuel of truth with which to illuminate their hearts.

Of sight, hearing, and touch it is said spiritually: “What we have seen, what we have heard, what our eyes have looked upon, and what our hands have touched” (1 John I, 1). Of taste: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. XXXIII, 9). Of smell: “We run after the fragrance of your perfumes” (Song I, 3). And: “We are the good fragrance of Christ” (2 Cor. II, 15).

### Verse 5

“But while the bridegroom was delayed, they all became drowsy and fell asleep.”

For not a short time passes between the first and the second advent of the Lord. “They all became drowsy,” that is, they died, because the death of the saints is called sleep. Consequently it is also said, “they fell asleep,” because afterward they are to be raised.

### Verse 6

“But at midnight a cry was made: Behold, the bridegroom is coming; go out to meet him.”

For suddenly, as though in the dead of night, when all are secure and sleep is deepest, Christ’s advent will resound through the cry of the angels and the trumpets of the powers that precede him.

[Note: [Col. 0183D] Martianaeus has the corrupt reading “and crowds” (*et turbas*).]

Let us say something that may perhaps be useful to the reader. It is a Jewish tradition that Christ will come at midnight, in imitation of the time of Egypt, when the Passover was celebrated, the destroyer came, the Lord passed over the dwellings, and the doorposts of our foreheads were consecrated with the blood of the lamb (Exod. XII).

Hence I think that the apostolic tradition has also remained, so that on the day of the Paschal vigil it is not permitted to dismiss the people before midnight, while they await the advent of Christ.

[Note: Epiphanius also calls this an apostolic tradition, *Against Heresies* 70. Indeed, that apostolic ordinance was fashioned from it in the Clementine writings, book V, chapter 19: “Remaining until cockcrow on the Sabbath [before Paschal Sunday], and when the first day of the week dawns, which is the Lord’s Day, break your fast; keeping vigil from evening until cockcrow, and gathering together in the church, devote yourselves to vigils, prayers, and supplications to God.” More notable are the testimonies of others concerning the Paschal vigil—for example, Lactantius, book VII, chapter 19, which Isidore largely transcribed in *Etymologies* VI, 17: “This is the night that we celebrate as a vigil on account of the coming of our King and God, and this night has a twofold significance: on it he both regained life when he suffered, and afterward will regain the kingdom of the world.” Palladius, a near contemporary of Jerome, says in his *Life of Chrysostom*: “In our regions the people keep vigil until the first cockcrow,” and so forth. Among the Fathers generally, this night is known as the night of vigils.]

And after that time has passed, all, presuming themselves secure, celebrate the feast.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “so that after [that time] … they may observe the day”; others, with the editions long in print, “while all observe the feast day.” Victor preferred to emend it to “for all to observe the feast day.”]

Thus the Psalmist also said: “At midnight I arose to confess to you because of the judgments of your righteousness” (Ps. CXVIII, 62).

### Verse 7

“Then all those virgins arose and trimmed their lamps.”

All the virgins arose and each trimmed her own lamp—that is, her senses, in which they received the oil of knowledge—so that they might have works of virtue that would shine before the true Judge.

[Note: Victor, on the basis of three Florentine manuscripts, along with several Brixian manuscripts, rewrites the text as *ut alerent* (“so that they might nourish”), saying that this alludes more closely to the nature of oil, by which a flame is nourished.]

### Verse 8

“But the foolish said to the wise: Give us some of your oil, because our lamps are going out.”

By complaining that their lamps are going out, they show that their lamps shine in part; yet they do not possess unfailing light or enduring works.

Therefore, if anyone has a virginal soul and is a lover of chastity, he must not be content with mediocre things, which quickly grow stale and, when the heat arises, dry up. He should instead pursue perfect virtues, so that he may possess everlasting light.

### Verse 9

“But the wise answered, saying: Perhaps there will not be enough for us and for you.”

They answer this not from greed but from fear. For each person will receive a reward according to his works, and on the day of judgment the virtues of some cannot lift up the vices of others.

And just as, at the time of the Babylonian captivity, Jeremiah could not help sinners, and it was said to him, “Do not pray for this people” (Jerem. VII, 16), so that day will be full of dread, when each person will be concerned for himself.

“Go rather to those who sell, and buy some for yourselves.”

This oil is sold and bought at a very great price; it is acquired through difficult labor. By it we understand almsgiving, every virtue, and the teachings of the masters.

### Verse 10

“While they were going to buy, the bridegroom came.”

They give, as though prudent, advice that they ought not to meet the bridegroom without oil for their lamps. But because the time for buying had already passed, and when the day of judgment arrived there was no place for repentance—for the Psalmist says, “In hell, who will confess you?” (Ps. VI, 6)—they are compelled not to undertake new works but to render an account of those already past.

“And those who were ready went in with him to the wedding, and the door was closed.”

After the day of judgment, no opportunity for good works and righteousness is left [another reading: “will be left”].

### Verse 11

“Finally the remaining virgins also came, saying: Lord, Lord, open to us.”

This is indeed an excellent confession in their calling him Lord, and the repetition itself is an indication of faith. But what does it profit to invoke with the voice one whom you deny by your works?

### Verse 12

“But he answered and said: Truly I say to you, I do not know you.”

The Lord knows those who are his, and whoever does not know him will be unknown (2 Tim. II, 19). The Lord does not know workers of iniquity. And although they are virgins, and, according to the twofold interpretation, boast both of bodily purity and of confessing the true faith (1 Cor. XIV, 38), nevertheless, because they do not possess the oil of knowledge, it is punishment enough for them to be unknown by the bridegroom.

### Verse 13

“Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour.”

I always admonish the prudent reader not to yield to superstitious interpretations or to what is said fragmentarily at the whim of those who invent meanings, but to consider what comes before, what lies in the middle, and what follows, and to connect together everything that has been written.

From what follows, then—“Keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour”—we understand that all the things he has said, concerning the two who are in the field, the two women grinding, the master of the house who entrusts his property to his servant, and the ten virgins, have been set forth as parables for this reason: because we do not know the day of judgment, we should diligently prepare for ourselves the light of good works, lest, while we are unaware, the Judge should come.

[Note: Some manuscripts prefer “so that human beings” instead of “all”; others read simply “human beings.” Thus Rhobb.]

### Verses 14–15

“For it is like a man going on a journey, who called his servants and handed over his property to them. To one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one, to each according to his own ability; and immediately he departed.”

This man, the master of the household, is unquestionably Christ. After his resurrection he ascended victoriously to the Father, called the apostles, and entrusted to them the teaching of the Gospel—not giving more to one and less to another according to generosity or stinginess, but according to the capacities of those who received it. So too the Apostle says that he gave milk to those who could not take solid food (1 Cor. IV).

Finally, both the one who had made ten from five talents and the one who had made four from two received a similar joy; he did not consider the magnitude of the profit but the willingness of the effort.

In the five, two, and one talent, let us understand either the different graces entrusted to each person, or, in the first, all the senses examined; in the second, understanding and works; in the third, reason, by which we are separated from beasts.

### Verse 16

“Now the one who had received the five talents went away and worked with them, and gained five other talents.”

Having received earthly senses, he doubled for himself the knowledge of heavenly things: from created things understanding the Creator; from bodily things, incorporeal things; from visible things, invisible things; from temporal things, eternal things.

### Verse 17

“Similarly, the one who had received the two gained two others.”

This man, according to his ability, doubled in the Gospel whatever he had learned in the Law; or he understood knowledge and the works of the present life as figures of future blessedness.

### Verse 18

“But the one who had received the one went away, dug in the ground, and hid his master’s money.”

The wicked servant neglected and polluted God’s commandments through earthly works and the pleasures of the world. Yet another Evangelist says that he tied it up in a napkin (Luke XIX)—that is, by living softly and delicately, he weakened the master of the household’s teaching.

### Verses 19–20

“After a long time the lord of those servants came and settled accounts with them. And the one who had received the five talents came forward and brought five other talents, saying: Lord, you gave me five talents; behold, I have gained five others.”

A long period lies between the Savior’s ascension and his second advent. But if the apostles will have to render an account, and will rise again under fear of the Judge, what ought we to do?

[Note: In Victor’s text the words “and, under fear of the Judge, will rise again” are lacking.]

### Verses 21–23

“His lord said to him: Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.

“And the one who had received the two talents also came forward and said: Lord, you gave me two talents; behold, I have gained two others. His lord said to him: Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.”

To both servants, as I have already said—to the one who had made ten from five talents and to the one who had made four from two—the same language of the master of the household offers encouragement.

And it should be noted that everything we possess in the present, although it may seem great and abundant, is nevertheless small and little in comparison with future things. “Enter,” he says, “into the joy of your lord,” and receive what “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart” (1 Cor. II). What greater thing can be given to a faithful servant than to be with the Lord and to see the joy of his Lord?

### Verses 24–25

“Then the one who had received the one talent also came forward and said: Lord, I know that you are a hard man, reaping where you did not sow and gathering where you did not scatter. And, being afraid, I went away and hid your talent in the ground. Behold, you have what is yours.”

Truly what is written came to pass in this servant also: “For making excuses in sins” (Ps. CXL, 4). To laziness and negligence he added the crime of pride. For he ought simply to have confessed his inactivity and prayed to the master of the household; instead, he brings an accusation and says that he acted with prudent deliberation, lest, while seeking profit from the money, he should also endanger the principal.

### Verses 26–28

“His lord answered and said to him: Wicked and lazy servant, you knew that I reap where I do not sow and gather where I did not scatter. Therefore you ought to have entrusted my money to the money-changers, and when I came I would certainly have received what was mine with interest. Therefore take the talent away from him and give it to the one who has ten talents.”

What he thought he had said as an excuse is turned into his own condemnation. He is called a wicked servant because he brings an accusation against his lord; lazy because he did not wish to double the talent, so that in the one respect he might be condemned for pride, and in the other for negligence.

“If,” he says, “you knew me to be hard and cruel, and to pursue what belonged to others, reaping where I had not sown, why did such a thought not instill fear in you, so that you would know I would seek my own more diligently, and would give my money—or my silver—to the money-changers?”

For both words are expressed in Greek by **ἀργύριον** (*argyrion*). “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire, proved by the earth, purified sevenfold” (Ps. XI, 7).

Money and silver, therefore, signify the preaching of the Gospel and the divine word. These should have been given to the money-changers and bankers—that is, either to the other teachers, as the apostles did when they appointed presbyters and bishops in the individual provinces, or to all believers who can double the money and return it with interest, so that whatever they had learned in speech they might fulfill in action.

The talent is taken away and given to the one who made ten talents, so that we may understand that, although the lord’s joy is equal in the labor of both—the one who doubled five into ten and the one who doubled two into four—a greater reward is nevertheless owed to the one who has labored more with the lord’s money.

Hence the Apostle also says: “Honor presbyters who are truly presbyters, especially those who labor in the word of God” (1 Tim. V, 17).

From what the wicked servant dared to say—“You reap where you did not sow, and gather where you did not scatter”—we understand that the Lord also accepts the good life of Gentiles and philosophers, and distinguishes between those who act justly and those who act unjustly. Those who neglect the written law are condemned in comparison with one who obeys the natural law.

### Verse 29

“For to everyone who has, more will be given, and he will abound; but from the one who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away from him.”

Many people, although naturally wise and possessing intellectual sharpness, if they are negligent and corrupt the good of nature through idleness, lose that natural good when compared with someone who is somewhat slower but has compensated through labor and diligence for what he possessed to a lesser degree. They see the reward that had been promised to them pass over to others.

It can also be understood in this way: to the one who has faith and good will in the Lord, even if, as a human being, he possesses something less in works, it will be given by the good Judge. But whoever has not had faith will lose even the other virtues that he seemed naturally to possess.

And elegantly he says, “what he seems to have will be taken away from him.” For whatever exists without the faith of Christ ought not to be credited to the one who misused it, but to the one who bestowed the good of nature even upon a wicked servant.

### Verse 30

“And throw the useless servant into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

The Lord is light; whoever is cast out from him lacks true light. What the weeping and gnashing of teeth signify, we have explained above.

### Verses 31ff.

“But when the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then he will sit upon the throne of his majesty. And all the nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them from one another, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. And he will place the sheep at his right hand, but the goats at his left. Then the King will say to those who are at his right hand:”

Since he was going to celebrate the Passover after two days, be handed over to the cross, and be mocked by human beings, and given vinegar and gall to drink, he rightly sets forth beforehand the glory of the triumphant one, so that the scandals that would follow might be balanced by the reward of his promise.

It should also be noted that the one who will be seen in majesty is the Son of Man. And what follows—“He will place the sheep at his right hand, but the goats at his left”—should be understood in relation to what you read elsewhere: “The heart of the wise man is at his right hand, and the heart of the fool at his left” (Eccl. X, 2). And earlier in this same Gospel: “Let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing” (above VI, 3).

The sheep are commanded to stand at the right, among the righteous; the goats—that is, sinners—at the left, since goats are always offered for sin in the Law (Exod. XII). He did not say “she-goats,” which can bear young and, after being shorn, emerge from the washing, all with twin offspring and none barren among them (Song IV), but “kids”—a wanton and shameless animal, always inflamed with desire for intercourse.

### Verses 34ff.

“Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food. I was thirsty, and you gave me drink. I was a stranger, and you welcomed me. I was naked, and you clothed me. I was sick, and you visited me. I was in prison, and you came to me.

“Then the righteous will answer him, saying: Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, or thirsty and give you drink? And when did we see you a stranger and welcome you, or naked and clothe you? Or when did we see you sick or in prison and come to you?

“And the King will answer and say to them:”

This should be understood according to the foreknowledge of God, before whom future things are already accomplished.

### Verses 40–41

“Truly I say to you: Insofar as [another reading: “when”] you did it for one of the least of these my brothers, you did it for me.”

Then he will also say to those at his left: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry, and you did not give me food. I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink. I was a stranger, and you did not welcome me. I was naked, and you did not clothe me. I was sick and in prison, and you did not visit me.”

Then they too will answer him, saying: “Lord, when did we see you hungry, or thirsty, or a stranger, or naked, or sick, or in prison, and did not minister to you?”

Then he will answer them, saying: “Truly I say to you: Insofar as you did not do it for one of these least ones, you did not do it for me.”

It was readily open to our understanding that in every poor person Christ was hungry and fed, thirsty and given drink, a stranger and welcomed under a roof, naked and clothed, sick and visited, imprisoned and consoled by the company of one who spoke with him.

But from what follows—“Insofar as you did it for one of the least of these my brothers, you did it for me”—it does not seem to me that he spoke generally of the poor, but of those who are poor in spirit. To them he had extended his hand when he said: “These are my brothers and my mother, those who do the will of my Father” (Mark III, 34–35; Luke VIII, 21).

### Verse 46

“And these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.”

Prudent reader, pay attention: both punishment is eternal and life is everlasting, having no subsequent fear of collapse.

[Note: Those who malign Jerome and claim that, in the final chapter of his *Commentary on Isaiah* and in *Dialogue 1 Against the Pelagians*, no. 28, he supported the mad opinion of those who believed that punishments would have an end should at least recognize from this passage, which he deliberately places before the reader, that he understood in an entirely Catholic manner that punishments are eternal and life everlasting.]

## Chapter XXVI

### Verses 1ff.

“And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished all these words, that he said to his disciples: You know that after two days the Passover will take place, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified.”

Let those who think that the Savior feared death be ashamed, and that, from fear of his passion, he said, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Luke XXII, 42).

He knew that after two days he would celebrate the Passover and be handed over to be crucified, yet he neither avoided the ambush nor fled in terror. Indeed, while the others were unwilling to go, he proceeded fearlessly, when Thomas said: “Let us also go, that we may die with him” (John XI, 16).

And wishing to put an end to the bodily festival and, as the shadow passed away, to restore the truth of the Passover, he said: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” (Luke XXII, 15). For “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed,” provided that we eat it “with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Cor. V, 7).

As for what he says—“After two days the Passover will take place”—leaving aside the simple meaning, let us seek what is sacred [another reading: “the sacrament”].

After two days of the most brilliant light, that of the Old and New Testaments, the true Passover is celebrated for the world. Passover, which in Hebrew is called **PHASE** [the supplied text leaves a blank in the parentheses], is named not from *passion*, as many think, but from *passing over*, because, when the destroyer saw the blood, he passed over the doors of the Israelites and did not strike them.

Or the Lord himself, offering help to his people from above, passed over them. Read the Book of Exodus (chapters XI and XII); if life permits, we shall discuss it more fully elsewhere.

[Note: Nazianzenus explains this opinion more fully in Oration 2, *On Holy Pascha*, in Billius’s translation: “Some have thought that this name refers to the saving passion; then, by changing the letter Φ into Π and Κ into Χ, they adapted the word to the Greek language and called this day Pascha. But rightly, agreeing with Jerome, he himself says: ‘This great and venerable Pascha, Phaska, is called by the Hebrews according to their language; the word signifies passing over—historically, indeed, because of the flight and migration of the Israelites from Egypt into the region of Canaan,’ and so forth.”]

Our passing over—that is, **PHASE**—is celebrated in this way: we leave earthly things and Egypt behind and hasten toward heavenly things.

[Note: I believe he is alluding to the *Hebrew Questions on the Whole of Scripture*. Although only the portion on Genesis survives from that work, he had nevertheless prepared threads and woof for the remaining books of Scripture, which he either later abandoned after changing his mind or allowed to perish within the walls of his house. Certainly no exposition by Jerome on the Book of Exodus survives or has ever come to light.]

### Verses 3ff.

“Then the chief priests and the elders of the people gathered in the courtyard of the high priest, who was called Caiaphas, and they took counsel to seize Jesus by stealth and kill him. But they said: Not on the feast day, lest perhaps a disturbance arise among the people.”

They ought, with the Passover near, to have prepared the victims, smoothed the walls of the temple, swept the floors, cleansed the vessels, and purified themselves according to the rite of the Law, so that they might become worthy to eat the lamb. Instead, they gather and enter into counsel about how to kill the Lord.

The straightforward wording shows that they were not afraid of a disturbance, but were taking care lest he be taken from their hands with the help of the people.

### Verse 6

“Now when Jesus was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper.”

As he was about to suffer for the whole world and redeem all nations with his blood, he remains in Bethany, the house of obedience, which had once belonged to Simon the leper.

This does not mean that he remained a leper at that time, but that he had formerly been a leper and afterward had been cleansed by the Savior, while his former name remained, so that the power of the healer might be displayed.

For in the list of the apostles, Matthew is called a tax collector with reference to his former vice and occupation, although certainly he had ceased to be a tax collector.

Some wish Simon the leper’s house to be understood as that portion of the people which believed in the Lord and was healed by him. Simon himself is also called obedient; according to another interpretation, his name may be understood as “pure,” and in his house the Church was healed.

### Verse 7

“A woman came to him with an alabaster vessel of costly perfume and poured it over his head as he reclined.”

Let no one suppose that the woman who poured perfume over his head is the same as the woman who poured it over his feet. The latter washes his feet with tears, dries them with her hair, and is explicitly called a prostitute. Nothing of this sort is written about the former. Nor could a prostitute immediately become worthy of the Lord’s head.

[Note: Although Origen’s commentaries on this passage do not survive, I have no doubt that Jerome drew from Origen his opinion concerning the two women who anointed Christ. This was a distinctive opinion of his: the woman who washed Christ’s feet was a sinner, whereas the woman who anointed his head with perfume was holy; accordingly, one should be understood as appearing at the house of Simon the Pharisee and the other at the house of Simon the Leper.

In the *Homilies on the Song of Songs*, which Jerome rendered into Latin, he says in Homily 1: “Observe carefully what is said about the two who poured perfume over the Savior’s head. The sinful woman is shown to have poured it over his feet, whereas the woman who is not called sinful is shown to have poured it over his head.” And near the beginning of Homily 2: “The Gospel says that a woman came bearing an alabaster vessel of costly genuine nard—not that sinful woman, but the holy woman of whom I am now speaking. For I know that Luke spoke of a sinful woman, whereas Matthew and John did not speak of a sinful woman.” We have gathered further material concerning this opinion of his at the relevant passages.

Although there is no need here to revive a question debated by learned men in separate books, the very opinion Jerome approves nevertheless seems most probable: even if the same Simon is to be regarded as both Pharisee and Leper, the woman who anointed Christ’s head was not the same as the woman who washed his feet.]

Another Evangelist put “genuine nard” in place of “an alabaster vessel of costly perfume”—alabaster being a type of marble—namely, something true and without deceit, in order to signify the faith of the Church and of the nations (John XII).

### Verses 8–9

“When the disciples saw this, they were indignant, saying: Why this waste? For this could have been sold for much and given to the poor.”

I know that some malign this passage, asking why another Evangelist said that only Judas was grieved, because he kept the money box and had been a thief from the beginning, whereas Matthew writes that all the apostles were indignant. They do not know the rhetorical figure called **σύλληψις** (*sýllēpsis*), or synecdoche, by which all may be named for one and one for many.

For Paul also, in the Epistle written to the Hebrews—although many Latins doubt that it is his—after describing the sufferings and merits of the saints, added: “They were stoned, they were tested, they were sawn apart [another reading: “sawed”], they died by the edge of the sword” (Hebr. XI, 37), although the Jews maintain that only the prophet Isaiah was sawn apart.

We can also say otherwise: the apostles were truly indignant on account of the poor, whereas Judas was indignant on account of his own profits. Hence his murmuring is presented together with his crime: he did not care for the poor but wished to provide for his own theft.

[Note: Victor omits the words “or synecdoche.”]

### Verses 10–11

“But Jesus, knowing this, said to them: Why do you trouble this woman? For she has performed a good work toward me. For you will always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me.”

Another question arises: why did the Lord, after his resurrection, say to the disciples, “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age,” while here he says, “You will not always have me”?

It seems to me that in this passage he is speaking of bodily presence: after the resurrection he would not be with them in the manner in which he was then, in every shared meal and familiar association. Recalling this, the Apostle says: “Even if we had known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him in that way” (2 Cor. V, 16).

### Verse 12

“For by pouring this perfume on my body, she has done it for my burial.”

What you think is the waste of perfume is an act of burial. Nor is it surprising that she has given me the good fragrance of her faith, since I am about to pour out my blood for her.

### Verses 12–14

“Truly I say to you: Wherever this Gospel is preached in the whole world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her. Then one of the twelve, called Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests.”

It is not so much this woman as the Church that is preached throughout the whole world: the Church buried the Savior and anointed his head.

And observe his knowledge of future things: although he was going to suffer and die after two days, he knew that his Gospel would be celebrated throughout the whole world.

### Verse 15

“And he said to them: What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you?”

Unhappy Judas! The loss he thought he had suffered through the pouring out of the perfume, he wishes to compensate by the price of his master.

Yet he does not demand a fixed sum, so that the betrayal might at least appear profitable; rather, as though handing over a cheap slave, he left the amount to the will of the buyers.

[Note: Rhobbes reads “or at least the betrayal might be induced by profit.”]

### Verse 16

“And they fixed for him thirty pieces of silver. And from then on he sought an opportunity to hand him over.”

[Note: The reading of the Veronese Gospel manuscript should be noted: *stateres* in place of *argenteos*. For a *stater* is indeed a silver coin, the same as the Hebrew shekel, worth four Attic drachmas. Yet for this very reason the diligence of the earlier translation deserves praise, especially since the Greek has the word absolutely: **ἀργύρια**.]

[Note: Compare Saint Ambrose, *On Joseph*, chapter 3, who says that in some copies he found thirty gold or silver pieces, and in others fifteen or twenty-five. Saint Caesarius likewise, in the Appendix to volume V of Augustine’s works, Sermon LXXXI, *On Time*.]

Joseph was not sold for twenty pieces of gold, as many think, according to the Septuagint translators, but for twenty pieces of silver, according to the Hebrew Truth; for a servant could not be more valuable than the Lord.

### Verse 17

“On the first day of Unleavened Bread, the disciples came to Jesus, saying: Where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?”

The first day of Unleavened Bread is the fourteenth day of the first month, when the lamb is sacrificed, the moon is completely full, and leaven is cast away.

Among the disciples who came to Jesus asking, “Where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?” I think Judas the betrayer was also present.

### Verse 18

“But Jesus said: Go into the city to a certain man and say to him: The Teacher says: My time is near; I will celebrate the Passover with you and my disciples.”

The New Scripture preserves the custom of the Old Testament. We frequently read: “He said to that man,” or “in that place,” and so forth. In Hebrew this is expressed as **PHELONI ELMONI** [the supplied text includes a damaged or blank Hebrew/Greek form], although the name of the person or place is not given.

[Note: The name *Phelmoni* occurs in Daniel chapter VIII. Jerome says concerning it: “In place of another unknown person, which Symmachus translated as *τινὶ ποτε*, and which we also followed. Aquila, Theodotion, and the Septuagint placed the Hebrew word itself, *Φελμωνί*. Thus, while concealing the angel’s name, he indicated generally just any one of the angels. See this practice of Scripture in Ruth, chapter I, and 1 Kings 21, and consult volume II of our edition, column 242.

Erasmus and Marianus, for the single word *ELMONI*, inserted “and [damaged text]” against the testimony of the manuscripts. In the manuscripts of this Commentary on Matthew, however, only the Hebrew name *Elmoni* is found; it means “someone” or “a certain one,” whose proper name is not expressed. —MART.]

[Note: Concerning this matter, Martianaeus accuses the earlier editors Erasmus and Victor of having divided the single word *Elmoni* into two, *Phelmoni* and *Elmoni*, against the testimony of the manuscript copies. All our manuscripts, however, defend and approve the earlier reading; it has therefore been restored to us on their authority, and the sense also demands it, since the words are often used together in Scripture: in Greek, with one accent, *Φελωνιάλμωνι*; in the Septuagint, *Φελλανὶ μαεμωνὶ*, “Phellani Maemoni.” What these expressions signify Jerome himself clearly explains here. Nevertheless, recall his Commentary on Daniel, chapter VIII, verse 13.]

“And you will find there a certain man carrying a jar of water.”

The names are omitted for this reason: so that an unrestricted opportunity for the celebration might be opened to everyone who was going to celebrate the Passover.

(Vers. 19.) And the disciples did as Jesus had instructed them, and prepared the Passover. In another Evangelist it is written (Luke XXII) that they found a large upper room, furnished and cleansed, and there prepared it for him. It seems to me that the upper room signifies the spiritual law, which, emerging from the narrow confines of the letter, receives the Savior in a lofty place. Paul says the same thing (Philippians VIII), that the things he had previously regarded as gain he despised as refuse and rubbish, in order to prepare a lodging worthy of the Lord.

[Col. 0194A] (Vers. 20.) When evening had come, he was reclining at table with his twelve disciples. Judas does everything in such a way that suspicion of the betrayer may be removed.

(Vers. 21.) And while they were eating, he said: “Amen I say to you: one of you is going to betray me.” He who had foretold the Passion also foretells the betrayer, giving an opportunity for repentance, so that, when he understood that his thoughts and hidden plans were known, he might repent of his deed. Yet he does not identify him specifically, lest, being openly convicted, he should become more shameless. He casts the crime into the number, so that the guilty man may repent.

(Vers. 22.) And being greatly saddened, they began, each one, to say: “Surely I am the one, Lord?” And certainly the eleven apostles knew that they were contemplating nothing of this kind against the Lord; but they believed the Master more than themselves. Fearing their own weakness, they sorrowfully asked about a sin of which they had no consciousness.

(Vers. 23.) But he answered and said: “He who dips his hand with me into the dish is the one who will betray me.” O marvelous patience of the Lord! First he had said, “One of you is going to betray me.” The betrayer persists in evil; he is accused more plainly, and yet his name is not expressly identified.
