While the others were saddened, withdrawing their hands and restraining food from their mouths, Judas, with the recklessness and shamelessness with which he was about to betray him, also puts his hand into the dish with the Master, so that audacity might counterfeit a good conscience.

(Vers. 24.) [Note: [Col. 0194D] Our manuscripts, which, as we noted at the beginning, are generally more sparing than the others in quoting the verses of the sacred text, unanimously place here at the beginning: “The Son of Man indeed goes, as it is written of him. But woe,” etc.] “But woe to that man through whom the Son of Man will be betrayed.” Neither after the first nor after the second warning does he withdraw his foot from the betrayal; rather, the Lord’s patience nourishes his shamelessness, and he stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath (Rom. II). Punishment is foretold, so that the announced penalties may correct the man whom shame had not overcome. As for what follows:

“It would have been better for that man if he had not been born”: this does not mean that he existed before he was born—for no one can fare well except one who has existed—but is simply said to mean that it is much better not to exist than to exist badly.

(Vers. 25.) But Judas, who betrayed him, answering, said: Since the others, sorrowful and deeply sorrowful, had asked, “Surely I am the one, Lord?”—so that he might not seem to betray himself by remaining silent, he too asks in the same way, though his conscience was tormenting him, [Note: [Col. 0195D] All our manuscripts prefer *quia*, “because.”] he who had boldly put his hand into the dish:

“Surely I am the one, Rabbi?” He says to him: “You have said so.” And he joins to it either the manner of one who flatters or a sign of unbelief. For the others, who were not going to betray him, say: “Surely I am the one, Lord?” But this man, who was going to betray him, does not call him Lord but Master—as though he would have an excuse if, after denying the Lord, he had at least betrayed his master. And he says to him: “You have said so.” The betrayer was refuted by the same answer that he would later give to Pilate.

(Vers. 26 ff.) And while they were dining, Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: “Take and eat; this is my body.” And taking the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to them, saying: “Drink from it, all of you. For this is my blood of the new covenant, which will be poured out for many for the remission of sins.” After the typical Passover had been fulfilled, and he had eaten the flesh of the lamb with the apostles, he takes bread, which strengthens the human heart, and passes over to the sacrament of the true Passover. Thus, just as in its prefiguration Melchizedek, priest of the most high God, had offered bread and wine (Gen. XIV), so he himself also represented in the reality of his body and blood.

[Note: [Col. 0195D] From this passage refute the ignorance of a certain conceited scholar who does not wish the Savior to have eaten the flesh of the lamb with the apostles or to have celebrated the typical Passover. MART.]

[Note: [Col. 0195D] Three Palatine manuscripts have *ei*, “to him,” with a more explicit sense. One Bec manuscript, according to Martianay, has the reading *sacramenti*.]

[Note: [Col. 0195D] Formerly the text read *veritatem*, “the reality.” We have preferred to follow the reading of all our manuscripts, with the same meaning preserved: “in the reality”—not a figure, as the wretched modern heretics maliciously slander it—of his body and blood, which Christ represented in the bread and wine. This reading was also pleasing because it corresponds oppositely to the preceding phrase, “in its prefiguration.” In two manuscripts of the monastery of Bec and of Saint Peter upon the Dives the following is read: “He himself also represents in the reality of his body and blood.” You therefore have here the reality of Christ’s body and blood, not merely a figure and bare shadow, as the shameless doctrine of the Innovators teaches against the Church. I do not know whether the Catholic faith could be expounded today more clearly than it was here by Saint Jerome. I am therefore not surprised that heretics slander Jerome with such arrogance, especially ignorant clerics. MART.]

In Luke we read of two cups which he offered to the disciples (Luke XXII): one of the first month and the other of the second, so that whoever among the holy people could not eat the lamb in the first month might eat the kid in the second, among the penitents.

(Vers. 29.) “But I say to you, I shall not drink from this fruit of the vine from now on until that day when I shall drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father.” He passes from carnal things to spiritual ones. The vine transplanted from Egypt was the people of Israel, to whom the Lord speaks through Jeremiah: “I planted you as a true vine; how have you been changed into the bitterness of a foreign vine?” [or: “of a foreign vine-stock”] (Jer. II, 21). The prophet Isaiah says the same in the song he sings for his beloved, and all Scripture bears witness to it in various places. The Lord therefore says that he will by no means drink from this vine until he is in the kingdom of his Father. I think the kingdom of the Father is the faith of believers, as the Apostle also confirms: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke XVII, 21).

Therefore, when the Jews have received the kingdom of the Father—for notice that he says “of the Father,” not “of God”; every father is the name of a son—when, I say, they have believed in God the Father, and the Father has brought them to the Son, then the Lord will drink from their wine. And, in the likeness of Joseph reigning in Egypt, he will become intoxicated with his brothers (Gen. XLIII).

(Vers. 30.) And after singing a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives. This is what we read in a certain psalm: “All the rich of the earth have eaten and worshiped” (Ps. XXI, 30). Following this example, whoever has been filled with the Savior’s bread and made drunk with the cup can praise the Lord and climb the Mount of Olives, where there is refreshment from labor, consolation in sorrow, and knowledge of the true light.

(Vers. 31.) Then Jesus says to them: “You will all be scandalized because of me on this night.” He foretells what they are going to suffer, so that, when they have suffered it, they may not despair of salvation but, by doing penance, may be delivered. He significantly adds, “You will be scandalized on this night,” because just as those who become drunk become drunk at night, so those who are scandalized endure it at night and in darkness (I Thess. V). But let us say: “The night has passed, and the day has drawn near” (Rom. XIII, 12).

(Vers. 32.) “For it is written: ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.’ But after I have risen, I will go before you into Galilee.” This is written in other words in the prophet Zechariah; and, if I am not mistaken, it is spoken from the prophet’s perspective to God: “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (Zech. XIII, 7). The sixty-eighth psalm also agrees with this meaning; it is sung entirely by the Lord: “For they persecuted the one whom you struck.” The good shepherd is struck so that he may lay down his life for his sheep, and from the many flocks of errors there may become one flock and one shepherd (John X).

This testimony is explained more fully in the little work which we wrote on the best method of translating.

[Note: [Col. 0196D] Epistle 57 in our recension. It is worthwhile to transcribe the very words in which he explained that testimony: “In Matthew we read that the Lord foretold the Apostles’ flight and confirmed it with this testimony of Zechariah: ‘It is written,’ he says, ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.’ But in the Septuagint and in the Hebrew it is very different. For it is not spoken from God’s perspective, as the Evangelist would have it, but from the perspective of the prophet asking God the Father: ‘Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.’”]

(Vers. 33.) But Peter answered and said to him: “Even if all are scandalized because of you, I will never be scandalized.” This is neither recklessness nor a lie, but the faith of the apostle Peter and his ardent devotion toward the Lord and Savior, about which we spoke above.

(Vers. 34.) Jesus said to him: “Amen I say to you: on this night, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.” Peter was making his promise out of the ardor of faith, while the Savior, as God, knew the future. Notice also that Peter denies at night and denies three times. After the cock had crowed and, as the darkness diminished, the approaching light had been announced, he turned and wept bitterly, [Note: [Col. 0197C] In Victorius: “washing away with tears the stains of the threefold denial.”] washing away with the tears of repentance the filth of his denial.

(Vers. 36.) Then Jesus came with them to a country estate called Gethsemane and said to his disciples: “Sit here while I go over there and pray.” Gethsemane is interpreted as “a very fertile valley,” where he ordered the disciples to sit for a little while and await his return, until the Lord alone should pray for all.

[Note: [Col. 0197C] Other books have *pinguium*, “of the fertile ones”; others, as does the book of Names, *Vallis pinguedinum*, “valley of fatness.” Victorius writes in this passage: “To signify ‘valley of the fertile ones,’ it should be read *Gessemani*, which in Hebrew is … . But because the name is found written in Greek in Matthew as Γεθσεμανεί (*Gethsemanei*), some knowledgeable in Hebrew think that the names are rather Syriac than Hebrew: … and they assert that it means ‘cattle-fold of butter.’ For among the Syrians—whose language, brought from Babylon, the Jews then used—the term corresponding to the Hebrew … is …, and … is the same as …, that is, ‘butter.’ It may therefore have been a place named from the butter that was pressed there.” Jerome, always following Hebrew nomenclature, also in his book *On Hebrew Names*, persists in interpreting it as “valley of fatness,” taking … as equivalent to the word … . Since we said nothing in that book about the etymology of this name, let us offer something here. The opinion of the recent etymologists of Hebrew names is particularly pleasing: *Gethsemane*, in Greek Γεθσεμανή, may be interpreted as “press of signs,” with …, *simani*, feminine, derived from …, *siman*, “a sign.” It may be called “press of signs” because the first signal of the already established new moon was given there. This custom, or procedure, is carefully described in *Rosh Hashanah*, chapter 2, halakhot 2 and 3, and is said to have been carried out by raising flames. It could also have received the name “sign” for other reasons: either because Solomon placed there a sign made of stone or wood of Moloch, the idol of the Ammonites (I Kings XI, 7), or because the armies of the Assyrians once planted their standards there (Isa. XXXVI, 2), or finally because the people of Jerusalem inferred what was happening from the signs of that place.]

(Vers. 37.) And taking Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he began to be sorrowful and deeply distressed. What we said above about passion and pro-passion is also shown in the present chapter: the Lord, in order to prove the reality of the humanity he had assumed, was truly sorrowful, but, so that passion might not dominate his soul, he began to be sorrowful by means of pro-passion. For it is one thing to be sorrowful and another to begin to be sorrowful.

He was not sorrowful through fear of suffering—for he had come precisely in order to suffer, and had rebuked Peter for his fearfulness—but on account of the most wretched Judas, the scandal of all the apostles, the rejection of the Jewish people, and the destruction of miserable Jerusalem. Hence Jonah too was sorrowful over the withering of the gourd or ivy (Jonah IV), unwilling that his former shelter should perish.

But if heretics interpret the Savior’s sorrow not as the affection of his soul for those destined to perish, but as passion, let them explain how the following can be understood, which is spoken from God’s perspective through Ezekiel: “And in all these things you were causing me sorrow” (Ezek. XVI, according to the Septuagint).

[Note: [Col. 0198D] Our manuscripts read: “Peter had rebuked him for his recklessness.”]

(Vers. 38.) Then he says to them: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death. Remain here and keep watch with me.” It is the soul that is sorrowful; and it is sorrowful not because of death, but unto death, until by his Passion he sets the apostles free. When he commands, “Remain here and keep watch with me,” he is not forbidding sleep, whose time had not yet come in the face of the impending danger, but the sleep of unbelief and the torpor of the mind. Let those, therefore, who suppose that Jesus assumed an irrational soul say how it can be sorrowful and know the time of sorrow. For although brute animals also grieve, they nevertheless know neither the causes nor the time up to which they ought to grieve.

(Vers. 39.) And going forward a little, he fell upon his face, praying and saying: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me. Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.” Having given the apostles the command to remain and keep watch with the Lord, he went forward a little, fell upon his face, and displayed the humility of his mind through the posture of his flesh. He says affectionately, “My Father,” and asks that, if it is possible, the cup of suffering of which we spoke above might pass from him.

[Note: [Col. 0198D] I would prefer *procidens*, “falling down,” and would accordingly amend the punctuation as follows: “and keep watch with the Lord for a little while. Falling down, he rushed upon his face,” etc.]

He does not ask from fear of suffering, but out of mercy for the former people, lest he drink the cup offered by them. Hence he pointedly does not say, “Let the cup pass from me,” but “this cup”—that is, the cup of the Jewish people, who cannot claim the excuse of ignorance if they kill me, since they possess the Law and the prophets, who daily foretell me. Nevertheless, returning to himself, he confirms from the perspective of God and the Son what, from the perspective of humanity, he had hesitantly rejected: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.” He says: “Let not what I speak from human feeling be done, but let what I descended to earth by your will to accomplish be done.”

(Vers. 40.) And he came to his disciples [Note: [Col. 0198D] Our manuscripts and the Greek text itself lack the pronoun *suos*, “his,” which the Vulgate Translator has.] and found them sleeping, and said to Peter: “So you could not keep watch with me for one hour?” The man who had earlier said, “Even if all are scandalized because of you, I will never be scandalized,” now cannot overcome sleep because of the greatness of his sorrow.

(Vers. 41.) “Keep watch and pray, so that you may not enter into temptation.” It is impossible for the human soul not to be tempted. Hence in the Lord’s Prayer we say: “Do not lead us into temptation,” [Note: [Col. 0198D] Saint Jerome does not know the clause quoted here in this very Commentary on Matthew, chapter VI, verse 13, where he expounded the Lord’s Prayer most carefully. From this it is manifestly clear that it was appended not to Matthew’s Gospel but only to Luke’s. We have shown in the Notes to the Commentary on Ezekiel, chapter XLVIII, verse 16, with testimonies from other Fathers—especially Hilary, *On Psalm 118*, letter 1, and Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, book V—that it belonged to the text of the Prayer itself and was not, as some think, added by Jerome as an explanation.] “which we cannot bear” [or: “which we may not be able to bear”] (Matt. VI, 13; Luke XI, 4). We are not entirely rejecting temptation, but asking for the strength to endure temptations. Therefore here too he does not say, “Keep watch and pray, so that you may not be tempted,” but “so that you may not enter into temptation”—that is, so that temptation may not overcome and conquer you and hold you within its snares.

For example, the martyr who sheds his blood in confessing the Lord has indeed been tempted, but he is not bound in the nets of temptation. The one who denies, however, falls into the traps of temptation.

“The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” This is directed against the presumptuous, who think that whatever they believe they can accomplish. Therefore, as much as we trust in the ardor of the mind, let us fear the weakness of the flesh. Nevertheless, according to the Apostle, “in the spirit the deeds of the flesh are put to death” (I Peter III).

[Col. 0199B] (Vers. 42.) Again, a second time he went away and prayed, saying: “My Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, let your will be done.” He prays a second time that, if Nineveh cannot otherwise be saved unless the gourd withers, the will of the Father may be done. This will is not contrary to the will of the Son, who says through the prophet: “I desired to do your will, my God” (Ps. XXXIX, 9).

(Vers. 43, 44.) And he came again and found them sleeping, for their eyes were weighed down. And leaving them, he went away again and prayed a third time, saying the same words. He alone prays for all, just as he alone suffers for all. The apostles’ eyes were languishing and weighed down by the approaching denial.

(Vers. 45.) Then he came to his disciples and said to them: “Sleep now and rest. Behold, the hour has drawn near, and the Son of Man will be handed over into the hands of sinners” (Matt. XVIII and II Cor. XIII). After he had prayed three times, so that every word might stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses, and had obtained the correction of the apostles’ fear through the repentance that would follow, he proceeds confidently toward his persecutors, and willingly offers himself to be killed. He says to his disciples:

(Vers. 46, 47.) “Rise, let us go. Behold, the one who will betray me has drawn near.” While he was still speaking, behold, Judas, one of the twelve, came, and with him a great crowd with swords and clubs, sent by the chief priests and the elders of the people. Let us not allow them to find us as though we were afraid and drawing back; let us go willingly to our death, so that they may see the confidence and joy of the one who is about to suffer.

[Note: [Col. 0199D] Victorius, from three Florentine manuscripts, writes *retractantes*, “drawing back”; I would prefer *retrectantes*. So does Rhabanus.]

(Vers. 48.) Now the one who betrayed him gave them a sign, saying: “Whomever I kiss, he is the one; seize him.” Wretched Judas—and yet not deserving pity! With the same unbelief with which he betrayed his Master and Lord, he thought that the signs he had seen the Savior perform were done not by divine majesty but by magical arts. And because he had perhaps heard that he was transfigured on the mountain, he feared that by a similar transformation he might escape from the hands of the attendants. He therefore gives them a sign, so that they may know that this is the one whom he would indicate with a kiss.

[Col. 0200A] (Vers. 49.) And immediately approaching Jesus, he said: “Hail, Rabbi!” And he kissed him. It was certainly shameless and criminal confidence to call him “Master” and press a kiss upon the one whom he was betraying. Nevertheless, there is still something of a disciple’s modesty in that he does not openly hand him over to the persecutors but does so through the sign of a kiss. This is the sign that God placed upon Cain, so that whoever found him would not kill him (Gen. IV).

(Vers. 50.) And Jesus said to him: “Friend, what have you come for?” Then they approached, laid hands on Jesus, and seized him. The word “Friend” is to be understood either *κατὰ ἀντίφρασιν*—ironically—or certainly in accordance with what we read above: “Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?” (Matt. XXII, 12).

(Vers. 51.) And behold, one of those who were with Jesus, stretching out his hand, drew his sword, and striking the servant of the high priest, cut off his ear. In another Gospel [or: “in another Evangelist”] it is written that Peter did this, with the same ardor of mind as in the other matters. The servant of the high priest is also called Malchus [or: “was called Malchus”]; the ear that was cut off was the right one.

It should be said briefly that Malchus—that is, the people of the Jews, formerly a king—became a servant of the impiety and devouring greed of the priests. He lost his right ear so that he might hear the whole degradation of the letter on the left; but the Lord, among those Jews who wished to believe, restored the right ear and made the servant a royal and priestly race.

[Note: [Col. 0200D] The Palatine manuscripts read: “so that he may hear the lowliness of the letter.” Certainly this final word had to be restored in place of *utilitatem*, “usefulness,” which Martianay read.]

(Vers. 52.) Then Jesus said to him: “Return your sword to its place. For all who take up the sword will perish by the sword.” And although the one appointed as the avenger of the Lord’s anger against the one who does evil does not carry the sword without reason, nevertheless whoever takes up the sword will perish by the sword. By which sword? By the one that turns with fire before paradise (Gen. III), and by the sword of the Spirit, which is described as part of God’s armor (Eph. VI).

(Vers. 53, 54.) “Or do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he would presently provide me with more than twelve legions of angels? How then will the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must happen in this way?” I do not need the assistance of twelve apostles, even if all of them were to defend me, since I can have twelve legions of the angelic army. Among the ancients, one legion consisted of six thousand men.

[Note: [Col. 0200D] In one Palatine manuscript: “We did not have time to explain the forms of the numbers; it is enough merely to have stated,” etc.]

Because of the brevity of the time, we have not had occasion to explain the number; it is enough merely to have stated the figures: seventy-two thousand angels, corresponding to the number of nations into which the human language was divided, are represented by the twelve legions. The sentence that follows shows a spirit ready to suffer, since the prophets would have sung in vain unless the Lord had confirmed by his Passion that they truly spoke.

(Vers. 55.) At that hour Jesus said to the crowds: “As against a robber you have come out with swords and clubs to seize me. Every day I sat among you, teaching in the Temple, and you did not seize me.” It is foolish, he says, to seek with swords and clubs the one who willingly hands himself over to your hands, and to investigate through a betrayer, as though he were hiding at night and evading your eyes, the one who taught daily in the Temple. But for this reason you gather against me in darkness: your power belongs to darkness.

(Vers. 56.) But all this happened so that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled. Then all the disciples, abandoning him, fled. What are the Scriptures of the prophets? “They pierced my hands and my feet” (Ps. XXI, 17); and elsewhere: “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter” (Isa. LIII, 7). And in another passage: “Because of the iniquities of my people he was led to death” (ibid., according to the Septuagint).

(Vers. 57.) But those who had seized Jesus led him to Caiaphas the high priest, where the scribes and elders had assembled. Moses, at God’s command, had ordered that high priests should succeed their fathers and that a succession of generations should be maintained among the priests (Exod. XXIX). Josephus reports that this Caiaphas had purchased the high priesthood from Herod for only one year.

[Note: [Col. 0201D] Concerning Caiaphas, or Joseph, who was also called Caiaphas, Josephus does indeed speak twice in *Antiquities* XVIII, chapters 3 and 4; but I do not find in the historian the statement that he bought the high priesthood from Herod for a price.]

It is therefore no wonder if a wicked high priest judges unjustly.

(Vers. 58.) But Peter followed him from a distance, as far as the courtyard of the high priest. He followed from a distance who was going to deny the Lord.

(Vers. 59, 60.) And having entered inside, he sat with the attendants in order to see the outcome. But the chief priests and the whole council were seeking false testimony against Jesus, so that they might hand him over to death. And they did not find any, although many false witnesses came forward.

Whether out of love for his disciple or out of human curiosity, Peter wanted to know what judgment the high priest would pronounce concerning the Lord: whether he would condemn him to death or release him after having him scourged. Here too there is a difference between the ten apostles and Peter: they flee, while he, although at a distance, nevertheless follows the Savior.

(Vers. 61.) Finally two false witnesses came forward and said: “This man said: ‘I can destroy the Temple of God and rebuild it after three days.’” How are they false witnesses if they say what we read above that the Lord said? But a false witness is one who does not understand words in the same sense in which they are spoken. The Lord had spoken about the Temple of his body.

But they also slander him in the very words, adding or changing a few things as though they were making a legitimate accusation. The Savior had said: “Destroy this Temple.” They alter it and say: “I can destroy the Temple of God.” “You,” he said, “destroy it, not I,” because it is unlawful for us to lay hands upon ourselves. Then they change the words to: “and rebuild it after three days,” so that he might seem to have spoken specifically about the Jewish Temple. But the Lord, to show that the Temple was living and breathing, had said: “And I will raise it up in three days.” To build is one thing; to raise up is another.

(Vers. 62.) And the high priest rose and said to him: “Do you answer nothing to the things these men testify against you?” But Jesus remained silent. His sudden and impatient anger, finding no place for accusation, drives the high priest from his seat, so that he might demonstrate the madness of his mind through the movement of his body. The more Jesus remained silent before those unworthy of an answer—false witnesses and impious priests—the more the high priest, overcome by fury, provoked him to answer, in order to find some opportunity for accusation in whatever he said. Nevertheless, Jesus remained silent. For, as God, he knew that whatever he answered would be twisted into slander.

[Note: [Col. 0201D] Three manuscripts read *et impatientia*, “and impatience,” in place of *impatiens*, “impatient.”]

(Vers. 63.) And the high priest said to him: “I adjure you by the living God to tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of God.” Why do you adjure him, most impious of priests? Is it in order to accuse or in order to believe? If in order to accuse, the others are openly charging you: “Condemn the silent man.” [Note: [Col. 0201D] Victorius, whose copy previously had this passage mutilated and apparently meaningless, inserts here on his own: *voluntque, legens, voluntque condemnare tacentem*, “and they wish, reading it thus, to condemn the silent man.” But, apart from the fact that nothing should be permitted beyond the authority of the manuscript copies, the addition plainly seems superfluous to anyone who considers the context and the thought of the holy Doctor. He joins the accusers to the high priest in order to show that the question, for the purpose of accusation, was superfluous: while others were openly charging him, he at the same time says, “condemn the silent man.”]

If in order to believe, why did you refuse to believe the one who confessed?

(Vers. 64.) Jesus said to him: “You have said so. Nevertheless I say to you: from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the power of God and coming on the clouds of heaven.” His response to Pilate and to Caiaphas is similar, so that they may be condemned by their own sentence.

[Col. 0202C] (Vers. 65, 66.) Then the high priest tore his garments, saying: “He has blasphemed. What further need have we of witnesses? Behold, now you have heard the blasphemy. What do you think?” And they answered: “He is liable to death.”

The man whom fury had driven from the priestly seat is provoked by the same madness to tear his garments. He tore his garments to show that the Jews had lost the glory of the priesthood and that the high priests possessed an empty seat.

[Note: [Col. 0202D] One manuscript reads *Pontificis*, “of the high priest”; then all unanimously add: “something blasphemous, or something as if against God,” etc.]

It is also a custom of the Jews, whenever they hear something blasphemous or apparently directed against God, to tear their garments. We likewise read that Paul and Barnabas did this when they were being honored in Lycaonia with the worship of gods. Herod, however, because he did not give honor to God but yielded to the people’s excessive applause, was immediately struck by an angel.

(Vers. 67.) Then they spat in his face and struck him with blows. Thus was fulfilled what was said: “I gave my cheeks to blows, and I did not turn my face away from the shame of spitting” (Lam. III, 30).

[Col. 0203A] (Vers. 68.) But others struck him in the face with the palms of their hands, saying: “Prophesy to us, Christ! Who is the one who struck you?” It was foolish to answer those who were beating him and to prophesy concerning the one who was striking him, when the madness of the striker was plainly visible.

[Note: [Col. 0203D] Formerly the text read *caedentibus*, “those who were striking.” The reading we have restored is more correct and is found in all the manuscripts, in keeping with the thought of the holy Father.]

But just as he did not prophesy this to you, so he most clearly prophesied that Jerusalem would be surrounded by an army and that not one stone would be left upon another in the Temple.

(Vers. 69.) But Peter was sitting outside in the courtyard. He sat outside in order to see the outcome of the affair. And he did not approach Jesus, lest the attendants become suspicious of him.

(Vers. 72.) And again he denied with an oath: “I do not know the man.” And after a little while those who were standing there approached and said to Peter.

I know that some people, out of pious affection [or: “with pious affection”] toward the apostle Peter, interpreted this passage in such a way as to say that Peter did not deny God but the man, and that the meaning was: “I do not know the man, because I know God.”

[Note: [Col. 0203D] One of these appears to have been Saint Ambrose, whose statement is found in book X of his Commentary on Luke, section 82: “He rightly denied the man, because he knew God.” Perhaps Saint Hilary had earlier said the same thing, for in this passage he writes: “And truly, he was now denying the man without guilt, whom he had first recognized as the Son of God.” They may have spoken this out of a desire to excuse him, not to deny his guilt.]

A prudent reader understands how frivolous this is. In defending the Apostle in this way, they make God liable to a lie. For if Peter did not deny him, then the Lord lied when he said: “Amen I say to you: on this night, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.” Observe what he says: “You will deny me,” not “the man.”

(Vers. 73.) “Truly you too are one of them, for your speech also makes you manifest.” This does not mean that Peter spoke another language or belonged to a foreign nation. For all were Hebrews, both those who accused and the one who was accused [or: “those who were accused”]. Rather, each province and region has its own particularities and cannot avoid the sound of its native speech.

[Note: [Col. 0203D] The military watchword, commonly called among us *le mot du guet*—“the password”—was called *σύνθημα* or *σύμβολον*, a sign given to those going out to battle to prevent confusion. The Gileadites therefore had as their sign and password the word *shibboleth*, which the Ephraimites pronounced *sibboleth*. See the Book of Judges, chapter XII, verse 6. MART.—It might seem that the word *Shibboleth* itself, which the Ephraimites pronounced *Sibboleth*, is being proposed as the example. Nevertheless, the manuscripts have *σύνθημα*, or in Latin *synthema*, which here properly means a sign, mark, or indication by which the Gileadites were distinguished from the Ephraimites. We discussed this word elsewhere, at the beginning of Epistle 118 to Julian, although there it is understood with a somewhat different meaning.]

Hence the Ephraimites in the Book of Judges (chapter XII) cannot pronounce the *σύνθημα*.

(Vers. 74, 75.) Then he began to curse and swear that he did not know the man. And immediately the cock crowed. And Peter remembered Jesus’ word, which he had said: “Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.”

In another Gospel we read that, after Peter’s denial and the cockcrow, the Savior looked upon Peter, and by his gaze moved him to bitter tears. Nor could he remain in the darkness of denial whom the Light of the world had regarded.

And he went outside and wept bitterly. Sitting in the courtyard of Caiaphas, he could not do penance. He went outside, away from the council of the impious, so that he might wash away the filth of his fearful denial with bitter tears.

(Cap. XXVII.—Vers. 1 ff.) When morning came, all the chief priests and the elders of the people took counsel against Jesus in order to put him to death. And they bound him, led him away, and handed him over to Pontius Pilate the governor.

He was led not only to Pilate but also to Herod, so that both might mock the Lord. And observe the priests’ eagerness for evil. They kept watch throughout the whole night in order to commit murder. And they handed him over to Pilate bound. For they had this custom: whoever they had condemned to death they handed over to the judge in bonds.

Then Judas, who betrayed him, seeing that he had been condemned, moved by repentance, returned the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, saying: “I sinned by betraying innocent blood.” The magnitude of his avarice shut out the weight of his impiety. [Col. 0204B] When Judas saw that the Lord had been sentenced to death, he returned the price to the priests, as though it lay within his power to change the persecutors’ decision.

Thus, although he changed his own intention, he did not change the outcome of his original intention. But if the one who betrayed innocent blood sinned, how much more did the Jews sin, who purchased innocent blood and, by offering the price, provoked the disciple to betrayal?

Those who attempt to introduce different natures and say that Judas the betrayer was of an evil nature and could not have been saved through the choice of apostleship should answer how an evil nature could have repented.

### (Verse 5)

But they said: “What is that to us? You see to it.” And throwing the silver pieces into the temple, he withdrew; and he went away and hanged himself. It did him no good to have repented, since by that repentance he could not correct his crime. If at some time a brother sins against a brother in such a way that he is able to amend what he has done wrong, he can be forgiven. But if the deeds remain, repentance is assumed in vain by words. This is what is said in the Psalm about that most unfortunate Judas: “And let his prayer become sin” (Ps. 108:7), so that he was not only unable to amend the wickedness of his betrayal, but also added to his former crime the guilt of his own murder. The Apostle speaks similarly in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians: “Lest the brother be swallowed up by excessive sorrow” (2 Cor. 2:7).

[Note: Victor also has, “His late repentance did him no good, by which …,” etc.]

### (Verse 6)

But the chief priests, having received the silver pieces, said: “It is not lawful to put them into the *corban* [Al. *corbona*], because it is the price of blood.” Truly they strain out a gnat and swallow a camel. For if they do not put the money into the *corban*—that is, into the treasury and the gifts of God—because it is the price of blood, why is the blood itself poured out?

[Note: Victor again has: “Why do they themselves pour out the blood?”]

### (Verses 7, 8)

After taking counsel, they bought with them the potter’s field, for the burial of strangers. Therefore that field was called *Acheldemach*—that is, “Field of Blood”—to the present day. They certainly acted with another intention, so that through the purchase of the field they might leave an everlasting memorial of their impiety. But we, who were strangers to the Law and the prophets, have received their perverse efforts for our salvation, and we rest in the price of his blood. It is called the potter’s field because Christ is our potter.

### (Verses 9, 10)

Then was fulfilled what was spoken through the prophet Jeremiah, who said: “And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of the one whose price was set, whom they priced among the children of Israel, and they gave them for the potter’s field, just as the Lord appointed for me.”

[Note: We have restored *whom they priced* in accordance with all the manuscripts we use and, in addition, with the Greek text itself, ὃν ἐτιμήσαντο. Previously it read *which*.]

This testimony is not found in Jeremiah. In Zechariah, however, who is almost the last of the Twelve Prophets, a certain resemblance is found (Zech. 11); and although the meaning does not differ greatly, the order and the words are different. Recently I read in a certain Hebrew volume, which a Hebrew man of the Nazarene sect had presented to me, an apocryphal work of Jeremiah, in which I found these words written exactly. Nevertheless, it seems to me that the testimony was taken rather from Zechariah, in accordance with the customary practice of the Evangelists and Apostles, who, setting aside the order of the words, bring forward only the sense of the Old Testament as an example.

[Note: Eusebius, in Book X of the *Evangelical Demonstration*, believes that this testimony was once read in Jeremiah, but that it was subsequently erased there through the treachery of the Jews, or that the name Zechariah was substituted here through the carelessness of copyists for Jeremiah. Augustine, in Book III, chapter 7, of *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, appears to refer it to a lapse of memory in the sacred writer—a concession I would make only with difficulty. More recent writers generally blame the confusion on corrupted Greek manuscripts of Jeremiah’s prophecies. Others conjecture that the Greek autograph of Matthew once read Ζορίου, for which copyists, deceived by the similarity of the letters, wrote Ἰρίου, although abbreviations of such an ancient usage do not seem to have existed. Therefore the opinion closer to the truth is that the Evangelist wrote simply, ἐν τοῖς προφήταις, “in the prophets,” as some of the Greek Fathers, and especially Saint Epiphanius, seems to have read it. But some zealous person, wishing to name the prophet himself, may have written “Zechariah” in the margin of the manuscript; after the reading “in the prophets” had been erased, others may have imported that name into the text. Certainly the most ancient Veronese manuscript of the Latin version of the Gospels does not recognize the name Jeremiah, but reads simply: “It was spoken through the prophet.” The opinion of Theophylact is also worth noting: he reads, “through Jeremiah and the prophet.” “Observe,” he says, “the very conjunction *and*, and read: ‘through Jeremiah and the prophet,’ that is, Zechariah. For the things spoken by both have been confused. Zechariah speaks of what concerns the price, in chapter 11; Jeremiah of what concerns the field, in chapter 19.” 

### (Verse 11)

But Jesus stood before the governor, and the governor questioned him, saying: “Are you the king of the Jews?” Since Pilate asked no other question concerning the charge except whether he was the king of the Jews, the Jews are convicted of impiety, because they could not even falsely find anything to allege against the Savior.

Jesus said to him: “You say so.” He answered in such a way that he both spoke the truth and left no opening for his words to be made into a calumny. Observe that he gave some sort of answer to Pilate, who was unwillingly pronouncing the sentence, but refused to answer the priests and rulers, judging them unworthy of his words.

### (Verses 13 and following)

Then Pilate said to him: “Do you not hear how many testimonies they bring against you?” And he did not answer him a single word, so that the governor marveled greatly.

[Note: For the following passage of the sacred text, some of our manuscripts substitute these words: “But Jesus did not wish to answer anything. The Gentile …,” etc.]

On the solemn day the governor was accustomed to release to the people one prisoner whom they wished. It is indeed a Gentile who condemns Jesus, but he shifts the responsibility for the charge onto the Jewish people. “Do you not hear how many testimonies they bring against you?” But Jesus did not wish to answer anything, lest by dispelling the charge he should be released by the governor and the benefit of the cross be delayed.

### (Verses 16 and following)

At that time he had a notorious prisoner called Barabbas. Therefore, when they had gathered, Pilate said to them: “Whom do you wish me to release to you, Barabbas or Jesus who is called Christ?” For he knew that they had handed him over out of envy.

In the Gospel written according to the Hebrews, Barabbas is interpreted as the son of their master, who had been condemned on account of sedition and murder. Pilate offers them the choice of releasing whichever they wish, the robber or Jesus, having no doubt that Jesus ought rather to be chosen, since he knew that he had been handed over out of envy. Thus envy is plainly the cause of the cross.

### (Verses 19 and following)

While he was sitting on the tribunal, his wife sent to him, saying: “Have nothing to do with that just man, for I have suffered many things today in a dream because of him.”

[Note: Some manuscripts insert the word “is.”]

But the chief priests and elders persuaded the crowds to ask for Barabbas and to destroy Jesus. The governor answered and said to them: “Which of the two do you wish me to release to you?” They said: “Barabbas.”

Observe that God often reveals dreams to the Gentiles, and that, through Pilate and his wife confessing the Lord to be just, the testimony of a Gentile people is given.

### (Verses 22, 23)

Pilate said to them: “What then shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?” They all said: “Let him be crucified.” The governor said to them: “What evil has he done?” But they shouted all the more, saying: “Let him be crucified.”

Pilate offered many opportunities for freeing the Savior. First, by setting the robber beside the just man. Then by asking: “What then shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?”—that is, “who is your king.” When they answered, “Let him be crucified,” he did not immediately yield, but, following the prompting of his wife, who had sent word, “Have nothing to do with that just man,” he himself also replied: “What evil has he done?” By saying this, Pilate acquitted Jesus. But they shouted all the more, saying: “Let him be crucified.”

Thus was fulfilled what he had said in the twenty-first Psalm: “Many dogs have surrounded me, and the assembly of the wicked has besieged me” (Ps. 21:12). And the words of Jeremiah: “My inheritance has become to me like a lion in the forest; they raised their voice against me” (Jer. 12:8). Isaiah also agrees with this meaning: “I expected that they would execute judgment, but they committed iniquity; not justice, but a cry” (Isa. 5:7).

### (Verse 24)

But when Pilate saw that he was accomplishing nothing, and that rather a tumult was arising, he took water and washed his hands before the people, saying: “I am innocent of the blood of this just man; you will see to it.”

Pilate took water, in accordance with the prophetic saying: “I will wash my hands among the innocent” (Ps. 25:6), so that in the washing of his hands the works of the Gentiles might be cleansed, and so that he might make us, in a certain sense, strangers to the impiety of the Jews who cried, “Crucify him.” He was testifying to this and saying: “I wished to release an innocent man; but since a sedition is arising, and the charge of rebellion against Caesar is being brought against me: I am innocent of the blood of this just man.”

The judge who is compelled to pronounce sentence against Christ does not condemn the one brought before him; rather, he accuses those who brought him, declaring that the one who is to be crucified is just. “You,” he says, “will see to it. I am the servant of the laws; your voice pours out blood.”

### (Verse 25)

And all the people answered and said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”

This curse remains upon the Jews to the present day, and the blood of the Lord is not removed from them. Therefore he speaks through Isaiah: “When you stretch out your hands to me, I will not hear you; your hands are full of blood” (Isa. 1:15). The Jews leave their children an excellent inheritance, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”

### (Verse 26)

Then he released Barabbas to them, but after scourging Jesus he handed him over to them to be crucified.

Barabbas, the robber who caused seditions among the crowds and was responsible for murders, was released to the Jewish people—that is, the devil, who rules among them to this day; and for this reason they cannot have peace. But Jesus, handed over by the Jews, is acquitted by Pilate’s wife and is called just by the governor himself. The centurion confesses that he truly is the Son of God.

Let the learned reader ask how it is consistent for Pilate to have washed his hands and said, “I am innocent of the blood of this just man,” and afterward to have handed Jesus over, after scourging him, to be crucified. But it must be understood that he was administering Roman laws, by which it was decreed that one who was crucified should first be beaten with scourges. Thus Jesus was handed over to the soldiers to be flogged, and the scourges tore that most sacred body and that breast capable of bearing God.

This happened because it was written: “Many are the scourges of sinners” (Ps. 32:10), and so, when he was scourged, we might be freed from blows, as Scripture says to the just man: “The scourge will not approach your dwelling” (Ps. 91:10).

[Note: In place of these words—“with Scripture saying to the just man”—two Palatine manuscripts have only: “according to what is written.”]

### (Verses 27 and following)

Then the governor’s soldiers took Jesus into the praetorium, gathered the whole cohort around him, and stripped him and put a scarlet cloak around him.

[Note: Victor restores *praetorium* both in the text and in the Commentary, since this is the better reading, as it appears in the more carefully corrected printed editions. Nearly all the manuscripts of the Bible in his possession retain it, numbering about forty, among which he greatly values the book of the monastery of Saint Paul, which he often mentions. The very ancient manuscripts of Monte Cassino, written in Lombard characters and numbering seventeen, also agree with this reading, as do all the manuscripts of the Louvain theologians. The Greek manuscript, the source of the same reading, likewise has εἰς τὸ πραιτώριον.]

And plaiting a crown of thorns, they placed it on his head, and a reed in his right hand. Kneeling before him, they mocked him, saying: “Hail, king of the Jews!”

The soldiers acted this way because he had been called the king of the Jews, and because the scribes and priests had brought against him the charge that he was usurping authority over the people of Israel. They mocked him by stripping him of his former garments and clothing him in a scarlet cloak instead of the red border used by ancient kings; instead of a diadem they placed on him a crown of thorns; instead of a royal scepter they gave him a reed; and they worshiped him as though he were a king.

But let us understand all these things mystically. Just as Caiaphas said, “It is better that one man should die for the people” (John 11:50), without knowing what he was saying, so these men, whatever they did, though they did it with another intention, nevertheless bestowed sacraments upon us who believe. In the scarlet cloak he bears the bloodstained works of the nations; in the crown of thorns he removes the ancient curse; with the reed he kills poisonous creatures. Or perhaps he held the reed in his hand in order to write the sacrilege of the Jews.

[Note: The Palatine manuscripts perhaps more correctly have *russo*, “red.” Trebellius in his account of Claudius and Vopiscus in his account of Aurelian mention red garments of this kind worn by kings.]

### (Verse 30)

And spitting upon him, they took the reed and struck his head. At that time it was fulfilled: “I did not turn my face away from the shame of spitting” (Isa. 50:6). Yet when they strike his head with a reed, he patiently endures everything, so that he might show the truth of Isaiah’s prophecy: “He will not break a bruised reed” (Isa. 42:3).

### (Verse 31)

And after they had mocked him, they stripped him of the cloak and put his garments on him, and led him away to crucify him.

When Jesus is scourged, spat upon, and mocked, he does not wear his own garments, but those which he had taken on account of our sins. But when he is crucified, and the spectacle of mockery and derision has passed, then he receives his former garments and assumes his proper adornment. Immediately the elements are disturbed, and creation gives testimony to the Creator.

### (Verse 32)

As they went out, they found a Cyrenian man named Simon. They compelled him to carry his cross.

Let no one think that this passage contradicts the account of John the Evangelist. John says that, as the Lord was going out from the praetorium, he carried his own cross; Matthew reports that they found a Cyrenian man named Simon and, compelling him, placed Jesus’ cross upon him. This should be understood as follows: as he went out from the praetorium, Jesus himself carried his cross; afterward they encountered Simon, upon whom they imposed the task of carrying the cross.

According to the allegorical interpretation, the nations take up Jesus’ cross, and the stranger who obeys carries the Savior’s shame.

### (Verse 33)

And they came to a place called Golgotha, which is called the Place of the Skull.

I heard someone explain that Golgotha was the place where Adam was buried, and that it was therefore so called because the head of the ancient man had been buried there. He said that this was what the Apostle meant: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you.”

A favorable interpretation, pleasing to the ears of the people, but not true. Outside the city and beyond the gate there are places where the heads of condemned men are cut off, and these places received the name of Golgotha—that is, of the beheaded. The Lord was crucified there so that, where formerly there had been a place of execution, there the standards of martyrdom might be erected.

And just as for our sake he became the curse of the cross, was scourged, and was crucified, so for the salvation of all he was crucified as though he were a criminal among criminals. But if someone should insist that the Lord was crucified there so that his blood might drip upon Adam’s tomb, let us ask him why the other robbers were also crucified in the same place. From this it is clear that Golgotha signifies not the tomb of the first man but the place of the beheaded, so that where sin abounded, grace might abound all the more (Rom. 5).

We read in the book of Jesus son of Nave that Adam was buried near Hebron and Arbee (Josh. 14).

[Note: Consult the book *On Places* under the entry “Arboc.” Saint Epiphanius’ work against Tatian should also be consulted.]

[Note: Paula and Eustochium expressed this view in Letter 46 among the letters attributed to Jerome, addressed to Marcella; the common opinion is that Jerome supplied the interpretation for the letter. They say: “The place in which our Lord was crucified is called Calvary, because there the skull of the ancient man was buried, so that the second Adam—that is, the blood of Christ dripping from the cross—might wash away the sins of the first Adam, the prostrate first-created man.” But elsewhere Jerome himself blows away this story as though it were mere fantasy. The person whom he says here that he heard expounding the matter he describes more fully in his Commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians 5:14:

> “I know that I heard someone arguing about this place who, in a theatrical miracle, displayed to the people a form never before seen, so as to please them. He said: ‘This testimony refers to Adam, buried in the place of Calvary, where the Lord was crucified. It was called Calvary for this reason, that the head of the ancient man had been buried there. Therefore, at the time when the Lord was crucified and hung above his tomb, this prophecy was fulfilled: “Rise, Adam, you who sleep, and arise from the dead”; not as we read, ἐπιφαύσει σοι Χριστός, “Christ will shine upon you,” but ἐπιψαύσει, “Christ will touch you.” For by the touch of his blood and of his hanging body, Adam would be given life and rise; and then that type would also be fulfilled in reality, when Elisha raised a dead man.’”

Whether these things are true or not I leave to the judgment of the reader. Certainly at that time they pleased the people and were received with a kind of applause and rejoicing. We shall note certain matters at the relevant place in this same Epistle. Among other men of great name, Saint Ambrose supported this opinion in his Commentary on Luke 23; there he also says—something difficult to believe—that the opinion was handed down as having originated among the Hebrews.]

### (Verse 34)

And they gave him vinegar mixed with gall to drink, and when he had tasted it, he refused to drink.

[Note: Nearly all the manuscripts prefer *wine* here instead of *vinegar*. The Greek archetypes also differ: some prefer οἶνον, “wine,” and others ὄξος, “vinegar.”]

God says to Jerusalem: “I planted you as a true vine; how have you become a bitter vine of another kind?” (Jer. 2:21). A bitter vine produces bitter wine, which it offers to the Lord Jesus, so that what is written might be fulfilled: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. 69:22).

But the statement, “When he had tasted it, he refused to drink,” indicates that he indeed tasted the bitterness of death for us, but rose again on the third day.

### (Verse 35)

After they had crucified him, they divided his garments, casting lots, so that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled: “They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast a lot.”

This too had been prophesied in the same Psalm: “They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast a lot” (Ps. 22:19).

### (Verse 36)

And sitting down, they kept watch over him.

The vigilance of the soldiers and priests benefits us, so that the power of the one who rose again might appear greater and more evident.

### (Verse 37)

And they placed above his head the written charge against him: “This is Jesus, the king of the Jews.”

I cannot sufficiently marvel, considering the greatness of the matter, that after paying for false witnesses and stirring up the wretched people to sedition and shouting, they found no other charge for his execution than that he was the king of the Jews. Perhaps they did this while mocking and laughing at him. But Pilate, even against their wishes, answered: “What I have written, I have written.”

Whether you wish it or not, Jews, the whole multitude of the nations answers you: Jesus is the king of the Jews—that is, the ruler of those who believe and confess.

[Note: One Palatine manuscript reads: “who believed false witnesses”; others omit the word *for a price*.]

### (Verse 38)

Then two robbers were crucified with him, one on his right and one on his left.

If Golgotha is Adam’s tomb and not the place of condemned men, and if the Lord was therefore crucified there in order to raise Adam, why were the two robbers crucified in that same place?

### (Verses 39 and following)

But those passing by blasphemed him, shaking their heads and saying: “Ah! You who destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days, save yourself. If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross.”

In the same way the chief priests, mocking him with the scribes and elders, also said so.

They blasphemed because they were passing beyond the way and did not wish to walk on the true road of the Scriptures. They shook their heads because they had already moved their feet and were not standing upon the rock. The foolish people, mocking him, say the very thing that the false witnesses had fabricated.

### (Verse 42)

“He saved others; he cannot save himself.”

Even unwillingly, the scribes and Pharisees confess that he saved others. Thus your own sentence condemns you. For the one who saved others could certainly have saved himself, if he had wished.

### (Verse 43)

“If he is the king of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him. He trusted in God; let him deliver him now if he wishes. For he said, ‘I am the Son of God.’”

A deceitful promise. What is greater: for a living man still to come down from the cross, or for a dead man to rise from the grave? He rose, and you did not believe. Therefore, even if he had come down from the cross, you likewise would not have believed.

But it seems to me that the demons were prompting them to say this. As soon as the Lord was crucified, they perceived the power of the cross and understood that their own strength had been broken. They therefore acted to make him come down from the cross. But the Lord, knowing the ambushes of his adversaries, remained on the gallows in order to destroy the devil.

[Note: Some manuscripts insert the word *now*.]

### (Verse 44)

The robbers who were crucified with him also reproached him in the same way.

Here, by the figure called *σύλληψις*—“collective expression”—both robbers are introduced as having blasphemed, although the statement concerns only one of them. Luke, however, asserts that while one blasphemed, the other confessed and, in turn, rebuked the blasphemer (Luke 23).

The Gospels do not disagree. Rather, both first blasphemed; afterward, when the sun had withdrawn, the earth had been shaken, the rocks split, and darkness had come on, one believed in Jesus and corrected his former denial by his subsequent confession. In the two robbers, both peoples—the Gentiles and the Jews—initially blasphemed the Lord. Later, one of them, terrified by the greatness of the signs, repented and, even to the present day, rebukes the blaspheming Jews.

[Note: The copyists of the ancient manuscripts seem to have preferred to read σύμμειξις, meaning “mixture.” Nearly all of them have the erroneous form σύμΗΚτις or συμέωξις.]

### (Verse 45)

From the sixth hour darkness came over the whole earth until the ninth hour.

Those who wrote against the Gospels suppose that this was an eclipse of the sun, which ordinarily occurs at fixed and appointed times, and that Christ’s disciples, through ignorance, interpreted it as referring to the Lord’s resurrection. But an eclipse of the sun can never occur except when the moon is present. No one doubts that at the time of Passover the moon was completely full.

And lest it perhaps be thought that the shadow of the earth, or the disk of the moon passing in front of the sun, produced a brief and rusty darkness, a period of three hours is specified, so that every opportunity for such explanations might be removed. I think this happened so that the prophecy might be fulfilled: “The sun shall set at noon, and the day shall be darkened over the earth” (Amos 8:9); and elsewhere: “The sun set while it was still midday” (Jer. 15:9).

It seems to me that the brilliant light of the world—that is, the greater luminary—drew back its rays, lest it either look upon the Lord hanging there or allow the impious blasphemers to enjoy its light.

### (Verse 46)

And about the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying: “Eli, Eli, lammasabacthani”—that is, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”

[Note: Three manuscripts have *Lemasabacthani*, and immediately afterward: “Why have you forsaken,” etc.]

He made use of the beginning of the twenty-first Psalm, and the words read in the middle of the verse, “Look upon me,” are superfluous. For the Hebrew reads: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”

[Note: The same is found in the title of the Psalm itself. The Hebrews have this inscription differently: “For the hind of the morning.” Through a perverse interpretation they think that the entire twenty-first Psalm was composed concerning Esther. They say that through her danger and intercession with the king the Israelite people were delivered from danger.]

Therefore those are impious who think that this Psalm was spoken in the person of David, or of Esther and Mordecai, since even the Evangelists understand its testimonies, taken from it, as referring to the Savior. Such is the passage: “They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast a lot.” And also: “They pierced my hands and my feet.”

Do not be surprised by the lowliness of the words and by the complaints of one who has been abandoned. Since you know that he took the form of a servant, behold the scandal of the cross.

[Note: The Pseudo-Jerome’s *Breviary on the Psalms* says: “The Lord, hanging on the cross, used this verse; from this we understand that the entire Psalm was sung by the Lord while he was placed upon the cross. But the words it contains in the middle, ‘Attend to me,’ are not found in the Hebrew manuscripts, and the addition is revealed by the Lord’s voice, which also omitted it in the Gospel,” etc.]

### (Verse 47)

But some of those standing there and hearing him said: “This man is calling Elijah.”

Not all of them, but some—whom I think were Roman soldiers—did not understand the peculiar character of the Hebrew expression. Because he said, “Eli, Eli,” they thought that he was calling Elijah. But if we wish to understand that it was Jews who said this, they acted according to their customary practice, namely, to slander the Lord’s weakness by claiming that he was imploring Elijah’s help.

### (Verse 48)

And immediately one of them ran, took a sponge, filled it with vinegar, put it on a reed, and gave him drink.

This too happened so that the prophecy might be fulfilled: “In my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. 69:22).

To this day the Jews and all who do not believe in the Lord’s resurrection give Jesus vinegar and gall to drink, and they give him myrrh-flavored wine to lull him to sleep, so that he may not see their evils.

### (Verse 50)

But Jesus, again crying out with a loud voice, released his spirit.

To release his spirit is a sign of divine power, as he himself had also said: “No one can take my life from me, but I lay it down of my own accord, and I will take it up again” (John 10:18).

### (Verse 51)

And behold, the veil of the Temple was torn in two from top to bottom.

The veil of the Temple was torn, and all the mysteries of the Law that had previously been concealed were revealed and passed over to the people of the Gentiles.

In the Gospel which we often mention, we read that the lintel of the Temple, of immense size, was broken and divided.

[Note: Eusebius appears to have imposed this upon Jerome. Eusebius records this miracle from Josephus in his *Chronicle* under the year of Christ 33, to which he also assigns Christ’s death. Josephus, he says, a native Jewish writer, testifies that around this time, on the day of Pentecost, the priests first perceived movements of the place and certain noises. Then suddenly a voice burst forth from the inner sanctuary saying: “Let us depart from these dwellings.” Jerome, writing these Commentaries with a hurried pen, faithfully drew this from Eusebius and does not seem to have consulted the text of Josephus, just as he did not when he composed Letters 18 to Damasus and 120 to Hedibia, question 8, or elsewhere. But when he wrote his Commentary on Isaiah, he used better judgment and, following Josephus’ own historical testimony, correctly places this portent not in the year Christ died but nearly thirty-two years after his Passion, among the events preceding the destruction of the Temple and the calamity of Jerusalem. “At that time,” he says—that is, at the time of the destruction of Jerusalem—“the wailings of priests and Levites, of the common people, of women, and of children were heard both in the city and in the Temple, when the Lord repaid his enemies, fulfilling the threat in which he had said, ‘Your house will be left to you desolate,’ and the prophecy, ‘I have abandoned my house’; when the guardians of the Temple, with one angelic voice, said: ‘Let us leave these dwellings,’ of which Josephus, the writer of Jewish history, etc.” This is indeed how Josephus’ testimony reads in Book VI, chapter 5, where he recounts the signs that portended and immediately preceded the destruction of Jerusalem:

> Κατὰ δὲ τὴν ἑορτὴν ἣ Πεντηκοστὴ καλεῖται, νύκτωρ οἱ ἱερεῖς παρελθόντες εἰς τὸ ἔνδον ἱερὸν, ὥσπερ αὐτοῖς ἔθος ἦν πρὸς τὰς λειτουργίας, πρῶτον μὲν κινήσεως ἀντιλαβέσθαι φασὶ καὶ κτύπου, μετὰ δὲ ταῦτα καὶ φωνῆς ἀθρόας, Μεταβαίνωμεν ἐντεῦθεν.

> “On the festival called Pentecost, the priests, having entered the inner sanctuary at night to perform the customary services, said that at first they perceived a movement and a noise, and then a sudden voice, as of a multitude crying together: ‘Let us depart from here.’”

It is therefore very likely that Eusebius came upon corrupted and badly confused copies of Josephus, as learned men noted long ago.]

Josephus likewise reports that the angelic powers, formerly guardians of the Temple, cried out together at that time: “Let us depart from these dwellings.”

### (Verse 52)

And the earth was shaken, and the rocks were split, and the tombs were opened.

No one doubts that, according to the literal sense, the greatness of the signs signifies that heaven, earth, and all things were demonstrating their crucified Lord. But it seems to me that the earthquake and the other events symbolize believers: after abandoning their former errors and having the hardness of their hearts softened, those who had previously been like the tombs of the dead afterward recognized the Creator.

### (Verse 53)

And many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose. And coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, they came into the holy city and appeared to many.

Just as Lazarus, who had died, rose again, so many bodies of the saints rose, to reveal the Lord rising again (John 11). Yet although the tombs had been opened, they did not rise before the Lord rose, so that he might be the firstborn of the resurrection from the dead.

As for the holy city in which the risen appeared, let us understand either the heavenly Jerusalem or this earthly city, which had formerly been holy. Matthew too is called a publican—not because he still remained a publican even as an Apostle, but because he retained his former designation. Jerusalem was called holy because of the Temple and the Holy of Holies, and to distinguish it from the other cities in which idols were worshiped.

When it is said that they appeared to many, it is shown that this was not a general resurrection visible to everyone, but a particular one visible to many, so that those who deserved to see might see.

### (Verse 54)

But the centurion and those who were with him, guarding Jesus, when they saw the earthquake and the things that were happening, were greatly afraid, saying: “Truly this was the Son of God.”

In another Gospel the more immediate reason for the centurion’s astonishment after the earthquake is made clearer: when he saw that Jesus had released his spirit, he said, “Truly this was the Son of God.” For no one has the power to release his spirit except the one who is the Creator of souls.

Let us understand “spirit” in this passage as “soul,” either because he makes the body spiritual and alive, or because the substance of the soul is spirit, according to what is written: “You will take away their spirit, and they will fail” (Ps. 104:29).

We should also consider that the centurion confessed the Son of God truly before the cross, at the very scandal of the Passion, while Arius preaches a creature within the Church.

### (Verses 55, 56)

There were also many women there, watching from a distance, who had followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering to him. Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of the sons of Zebedee.

It was a custom of the Jews, and according to the ancient practice of the nation it was not considered blameworthy, for women to provide teachers with food and clothing from their own resources. Because this could cause scandal among the nations, Paul recalls that he had rejected the practice. For he himself says: “Do we not have the right to lead about believing women as sisters, as the other Apostles also do?” (1 Cor. 9:5).

They ministered to the Lord from their resources, so that he might reap their material things, just as they reaped spiritual things from him. It was not that the Lord, the Creator of all things, needed food, but that he might present the example of teachers: they ought to be content with food and clothing from their disciples.

But let us see what sort of companions he had: Mary Magdalene, from whom he had expelled seven demons; Mary the mother of James and Joseph, his maternal aunt, the sister of Mary, the mother of the Lord; and the mother of the sons of Zebedee, who shortly before had asked that the kingdom be granted to her sons; and the other women whom we read about in the remaining Gospels (Luke 8).

(Verses 57–58.) When evening had come, a certain rich man from Arimathea, named Joseph, arrived; he too was a disciple of Jesus. He approached Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Then Pilate ordered the body to be handed over.

He is called rich, not because the writer wished boastfully to portray Jesus as having had a noble and exceedingly wealthy man as a disciple, but to show why he was able to obtain Jesus’ body from Pilate. For it was not for a poor and unknown man to approach Pilate, the representative of Roman power, and obtain the body of a crucified man.

In another Gospel (Luke 23), this Joseph is called a *βουλευτής*—that is, a councillor—and some think that the first psalm was composed about him: “Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly,” and what follows.

[Note: The manuscripts uniformly read ΒΟΥΛΗΣ. Moreover, that this opinion concerning Joseph pleased not merely some but many is attested by the second Exposition of the Psalms, which we append, having itself been falsely attributed to Jerome from part of the Breviary on the Psalms: “Generally this is said of any righteous man, although many think it was said of Joseph from Arimathea, who did not go in the counsel of the Jews.”]

(Verses 59.) And having taken the body, Joseph wrapped it in a clean linen cloth.

[Note: In place of the name Joseph, three Palatine manuscripts have *Jesu*, that is, “the body of Jesus.”]

By the Lord’s simple burial, the ostentation of the rich is condemned, since they cannot be without riches even in their tombs. According to the spiritual understanding, we can also perceive this: the Lord’s body should be wrapped not in gold, gems, and silk, but in pure linen. Yet this too signifies that the one who received Jesus in a clean linen cloth received him with a pure mind.

(Verses 60.) And he placed it in his own new tomb, which he had cut out in the rock, and he rolled a great stone against the entrance of the tomb, and departed.

He is placed in a new tomb so that, after the resurrection, when the other bodies remained, no one might pretend that someone else had risen. The new tomb may also signify Mary’s virginal womb; and the stone placed at its entrance, together with the great size of the stone, may show that the tomb could not have been opened without the assistance of many people.

(Verses 61 and following.) Now Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there, sitting opposite the tomb. On the next day, which is after the Preparation, the chief priests and Pharisees assembled before Pilate, saying: “Lord, we remember that while that deceiver was still alive he said, ‘After three days I shall rise again.’”

When the others abandoned the Lord, the women persevered in their duty, awaiting what Jesus had promised. Therefore they deserved to be the first to see him rising, because “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10:22; 24:13).

(Verses 64 and following.) “Therefore command that the tomb be guarded until the third day, lest his disciples perhaps come and steal him and say to the people, ‘He has risen from the dead,’ and the last error be worse than the first.” Pilate said to them: “You have a guard. Go, guard it as you know how.” But they went and secured the tomb, sealing the stone together with the guards.

It had not been enough for the chief priests, scribes, and Pharisees to crucify the Lord and Savior, unless they also guarded the tomb, accepted a cohort, and sealed the stone—so far as lay in their power placing their hand against the one who was rising—so that their diligence might serve our faith. For the more carefully he is guarded, the more clearly the power of the resurrection is displayed.

Thus he was also laid in a new tomb that had been cut out in the rock, so that, if it had been built from many stones, people might say that, after the foundations of the tomb had been undermined, he had been secretly removed. That he was to be placed in a tomb is testified by the prophet, who says: “He will dwell in a cave cut out of the strongest rock” (Isaiah 33:16). Immediately, two verses later, it follows: “You shall see the King in his glory” (ibid., 17).

## Chapter 28

### Verse 1

Now late on the Sabbath, as the first day of the week was dawning, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb.

The fact that different times are assigned to these women in the Gospels is not, as the impious object, a sign of falsehood. Rather, it reflects their diligent visiting, as they repeatedly went and returned and did not permit themselves to remain long or far away from the Lord’s tomb.

### Verses 2–3

And behold, a great earthquake occurred. For an angel of the Lord descended from heaven and came and rolled away the stone, and sat upon it. His appearance was like lightning [Variant: *brightness*], and his clothing was like snow.

Our Lord, one and the same Son of God and Son of Man, displays, according to his two natures—divinity and flesh—sometimes the signs of his greatness and sometimes those of his humility. Thus, in the present passage, although it is a man who was crucified, buried, and shut within a tomb, whom the stone placed against it confines, nevertheless the events occurring outside reveal the Son of God: the sun fleeing, darkness advancing, the earth shaken, the veil torn, rocks split apart, the dead raised, and the ministries of angels—all of which proved him to be God from the beginning of his birth.

Gabriel comes to Mary; an angel speaks with Joseph; the same angel announces him to the shepherds; afterward a choir of angels is heard saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2). He is tempted in the wilderness, and immediately after the victory angels minister to him. Now also an angel comes as guardian of the Lord’s tomb, and by his white clothing signifies the glory of the triumphant one. Moreover, when the Lord ascends into heaven, two angels are seen on the Mount of Olives, promising the apostles the Savior’s second coming (Acts 1).

### Verses 4–5

Because of their fear of him, the guards were terrified and became like dead men. But the angel answered and said to the women: “Do not be afraid, you. For I know that you are seeking Jesus, who was crucified. He is not here, for he has risen, just as he said.”

The guards, terrified by fear, lie stunned like dead men; yet the angel consoles not them but the women: “Do not be afraid, you.” Let them, he says, be afraid; let terror remain in those in whom unbelief remains. But because you are seeking Jesus who was crucified, hear that he has risen and fulfilled his promises.

### Verses 6–7

“Come and see the place where the Lord was laid.”

[Note: The Palatine manuscripts omit the word “place.”]

“And go quickly and tell his disciples: If you do not believe my words, believe the empty tomb; go with rapid steps and announce it to his disciples.”

“For he has risen, and behold, he goes before you into Galilee. There you will see him. Behold, I have told you.”

This is into the rolling-place of the nations, where previously there was error and slipperiness, and no one set down a firm and stable footprint.

### Verse 8

And they went out quickly from the tomb with fear and great joy, running to announce it to his disciples.

A twofold feeling held the minds of the women: fear and joy—the one arising from the greatness of the miracle, the other from their desire for the risen one. Yet each feeling quickened their feminine steps. They proceeded to the apostles so that through them the seedbed of faith might be scattered.

### Verse 9

And behold, Jesus met them, saying: “Greetings.”

Those who sought him in this way and ran so eagerly deserved to have the risen Lord meet them and to hear “Greetings” first, so that the curse of the woman Eve might be overturned among women.

They approached and took hold of his feet and worshiped him. They approach and hold his feet because they worshiped him. But the woman who was seeking the living among the dead, and did not yet know that the Son of God had risen, deserved to hear: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20:17).

### Verse 10

Then Jesus said to them: “Do not be afraid.”

In both the Old and the New Testament, this should always be observed: whenever a more exalted vision appears, fear is first driven away, so that, with the mind thus calmed, what is said may be heard.

“Go, announce to my brothers that they should go into Galilee; there they will see me.”

When they had departed, behold, some of the guards came into the city and reported to the chief priests everything that had happened. These are the brothers of whom he said elsewhere: “I shall proclaim your name to my brothers” (Psalm 21:23). They do not see the Savior in Judea, but among the multitude of the nations.

### Verses 12 and following
