And when they had assembled with the elders and taken counsel, they gave the soldiers a large sum of money, saying: “Say that his disciples came by night and stole him while we were sleeping. And if this should come to the governor’s attention, we shall persuade him and make you secure.”

They, having received the money, did as they had been instructed. And this report has been spread among the Jews to the present day.

The guards confess the miracle; they hasten back to the city; they report to the chief priests what they had seen and what they had plainly witnessed. Those who ought to have been converted to repentance and to have sought Jesus risen persist in wickedness. They turn the money that had been given for the temple’s needs into the purchase of a lie, just as earlier they had given thirty pieces of silver to the betrayer Judas.

Therefore all who misuse temple offerings and the contributions made for the needs of the Church for other purposes, by which they may satisfy their own will, are like the scribes and priests who purchase a lie and the Savior’s blood.

### Verses 16–17

Now the eleven disciples went into Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them. And when they saw him, they worshiped him; but some doubted.

After the resurrection, Jesus is seen on a mountain in Galilee, and there he is worshiped—although some doubt, and their doubt increases our faith. Later he shows himself more plainly to Thomas, displaying both the side wounded by the spear and the hands fixed with nails.

### Verse 18

And Jesus approached and spoke to them, saying: “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth.”

Authority was given to the one who shortly before had been crucified, who had been buried in a tomb, who had lain dead, and who afterward rose again. Authority was given to him in heaven and on earth, so that the one who had previously reigned in heaven might, through the faith of believers, reign on earth.

### Verse 19

“Therefore go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.”

First they teach all nations; then, once taught, they immerse them in water. For the body cannot receive the sacrament of baptism unless the soul has first received the truth of faith. They are baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit so that, since their divinity is one, their gift also may be one; and the name of the Trinity is one God.

### Verse 20

“Teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you.”

The proper order is this: he commanded the apostles first to teach all nations, then to immerse them in the sacrament of faith, and after faith and baptism to instruct them in what was to be observed.

[Note: Some, with Garnerius, think that this passage of Jerome is one of the three passages which Saint Augustine notes and attacks in his book *On Faith and Works*, although he conceals the author’s name out of reverence, as he says, for so great a man. Augustine contends that this very opinion—that the sacrament of baptism ought to precede, and instruction in the conduct and morals of life should follow—is perverse and out of order. But just as the first of those passages, concerning the admission of everyone without distinction to baptism, so that even those guilty of the gravest crimes, including those who persist and refuse to amend their lives, should not be excluded, cannot in any way be attributed to Jerome, since nothing consistent with this error is found in him, so he is not to be blamed in this passage either, nor considered the one whom Augustine criticizes, although without naming him. Jerome does not actually hold what the bishop of Hippo condemns, as is clear from what precedes and from the full context, where he commands that the doctrine of faith be placed first without interruption: ‘For,’ he says, ‘the body cannot receive the sacrament of baptism unless the soul has first received the truth of faith.’ As for moral instruction, he is not very concerned whether it precedes baptism; he cares only that it not be omitted altogether. Certainly it is to be imparted after baptism as well. Further, we have shown in the first dialogue against the Pelagians and in the commentary on the final chapter of Isaiah that the third passage was also falsely reported by Augustine.]

“And behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age.”

By promising that he will be with the disciples until the consummation of the age, he shows both that they will always live and that he will never withdraw from believers. But the one who promises his presence until the consummation of his world is not ignorant of the day on which he knows he will be with the apostles.

# Translation of the Thirty-Nine Homilies of Origen on the Gospel of Luke by Saint Eusebius Jerome, Presbyter of Stridon, to Paula and Eustochium (C)

[Note: Rufinus, in Book II, no. 21 of his *Invectives*, recites this very preface in full, except that its final period is truncated, in order to create hostility toward Jerome by means of the name of Origen.]

## Prologue

A few days ago you said that you had read certain commentaries on Matthew and Luke, of which one was dull both in thought and in language, while the other played with words and slept through its arguments. Therefore you asked me, setting aside such trifles, at least to translate the thirty-nine homilies of our Adamantius on Luke, as they are found in Greek.

[Note: From Rufinus’s reading we have supplied the number thirty-nine, lacking in the previously published books, so that Jerome might appear to have translated into Latin all—and indeed many more than these—of Adamantius’s homilies on Luke. For we have shown elsewhere, and in the preface placed before this volume, that Origen composed many more.]

It is an irksome task, resembling torture, to write in another person’s stomach, as Tully says, and not one’s own; nevertheless I shall do it now because you do not ask for loftier works.

For that which holy Blaesilla once requested at Rome—that I translate into our language twenty-five volumes of his works on Matthew, five more on Luke, and thirty-two on John—is beyond my strength, leisure, and labor.

[Note: The published books formerly read “thirty-six” here, and Rufinus likewise had “twenty-six.” We did not hesitate to restore “twenty-five,” since Jerome himself numbers neither more nor fewer in the preceding prologue to his Commentary on Matthew. “I confess,” he says, “that many years ago I read Origen’s twenty-five volumes on Matthew”; Eusebius agrees with this number in Book VI, chapter 36, of his *Ecclesiastical History*. This was also the ancient and entirely correct reading in the formerly published manuscripts of Rufinus’s *Invectives*.]

[Note: Here too all the printed books incorrectly gave “thirty-nine” or “thirty-four” instead of “thirty-two.” We restored the reading from Rufinus’s testimony. Eusebius, in the history just cited, knows only twenty-two volumes from this entire collection of commentaries; but perhaps “thirty-two” should also be read there. At present scarcely nine survive.]

You perceive how much your authority and desire have power with me. I have set aside for a little while the books of the Hebrew Questions, so that, according to your wishes, I might dictate these works—whatever they are—not my own but another’s—as a remunerative undertaking.

Especially since I hear an ill-omened raven croaking from the left and, though himself wholly dark, laughing strangely at the colors of all birds.

[Note: Rufinus falsely alleges that Jerome here marks Saint Ambrose under the name of the raven: first because among the Latins a commentary on Luke was attributed only to Ambrose and to no one else; and second because Jerome possessed a letter of his own in which, while excusing himself concerning other men, he turned suspicion against Ambrose. Yet no one, even on oath, should believe Rufinus capable of thinking that the holy Father could have meant Ambrose, whom he always held in the highest esteem and often praised in his books as occasion required.]

I confess, therefore, before he objects, that in these treatises Origen plays with dice like a child; he has other works that are manly and others that are serious and worthy of old age.

[Note: We restore “a child” in place of the corrupt reading “again.” Shortly afterward we also emend “to play” in place of the corrupt “I might play.” These readings are confirmed by the truth of the subject and its meaning, as well as by Rufinus’s additional testimony. In place of “dice,” other books have “tablets.”]

If I wish, if I am able, and if the Lord grants me the opportunity to turn them into Latin, and if I first complete the work I have set aside, then you will be able to see—or rather, through you the Roman language will learn—how much good it previously did not know and has now begun to know.

Moreover, I have decided to send you in a few days the commentaries of the most eloquent man Hilary and of the blessed martyr Victorinus, which they published on Matthew in different styles but with one grace of the Spirit, so that you may not be unaware that our own people too once devoted themselves to the sacred Scriptures.

# The Thirty-Nine Homilies on Luke Delivered on Sundays Begin

## Homily I

### On the Prologue of Luke up to the Passage Where He Says, “To Write to You, Most Excellent Theophilus”

Just as formerly, among the Jewish people, many claimed to prophesy and some were false prophets—one of whom was Hananiah, son of Agot—while others were prophets, and there was among the people a grace for discerning spirits, by which some were admitted among the prophets and others rejected as though by highly trained money-changers, so now also in the New Testament many have attempted to write Gospels, but not all have been accepted.

And so that you may know that not only four Gospels but many were written, from which the ones we possess were selected and handed on to the churches, let us understand this from Luke’s own prologue, which is composed as follows: “Since many have attempted to arrange a narrative” (Luke 1).

The phrase “have attempted” contains a hidden accusation against those who rushed to write Gospels without the grace of the Holy Spirit. Matthew, Mark, John, and Luke did not attempt to write; filled with the Holy Spirit, they wrote the Gospels.

Many, therefore, have attempted to arrange a narrative concerning the matters that have been most fully known among us. The Church has four Gospels; heresies have many.

[Note: The earlier printed books incorrectly read “very many,” that is, “heresies,” although the entire discussion here concerns pseudo-Gospels. Jerome transferred almost the whole passage word for word into his own work, as noted above in the preface to the Commentary on Matthew.]

One is written according to the Egyptians, another according to the Twelve Apostles. Basilides also dared to write a Gospel and to title it with his own name.

Many have attempted to write, and many have attempted to arrange. Only four Gospels have been approved, from which doctrines are to be brought forth under the person of our Lord and Savior.

I know of a certain Gospel called “According to Thomas,” and one “According to Matthias,” and many others that we have read, so that we might not appear ignorant of anything, for the sake of those who think they know something if they have learned these things. Yet among all these we approve nothing except what the Church approves—that is, that only four Gospels are to be received.

This is why it was read at the beginning: “Many have attempted to arrange a narrative concerning the matters that have been confirmed among us.” They tried and attempted to write about matters that have been most fully established among us.

Luke indicates the result in the wording he uses: “Among us they have been most fully demonstrated,” that is, *πεπληροφορημένων*.

[Note: Everyone recognizes that this is an addition from the translator’s pen, enclosed in parentheses, not from the author. Similar additions occur below. They misled the more audacious critics, Daille in *On the Writings of Ignatius*, pages 439 and following, and Matthew Larroquan in his *Annotations on Pearson’s Vindication of Ignatius*, pages 94 and following, into wrongly denying these homilies to Adamantius and claiming that they were the work of a Latin author. In its proper place we shall refute the objection to the genuineness of the work.]

The Latin language does not explain this in a single word. For Luke had known it with certain faith and understanding, and was not wavering in any way as to whether it was so or otherwise.

This happens to those who have believed most faithfully, who have attained what the prophet implores, and who say: “Establish me in your words” (Psalm 118). Hence the Apostle says of those who were firm and strong: “That you may be rooted and grounded in faith” (Ephesians 3).

For if anyone is rooted and grounded in faith, even if a storm arises, even if winds blow, even if rain pours down, he will not be uprooted or fall, because the building is founded with solid mass upon the rock (Matthew 7).

Let us not suppose that the firmness of faith is bestowed by these bodily eyes, which the mind and reason provide. Let all unbelievers believe in signs and wonders that human vision beholds. But let the faithful, more prudent and strong, follow reason and the word, and thus judge what is true and what is false.

“As those who from the beginning themselves saw and were ministers of the word handed them on to us.”

It is written in Exodus: “The people saw the voice of God” (Exodus 19). Certainly a voice is heard before it is seen; but it was written thus so that it might be shown to us that we see the voice of God with other eyes—with those by which the people who deserve it behold it.

In the Gospel, however, it is not a voice that is seen but the word, which is superior to a voice. Hence it now says: “As those who from the beginning themselves saw and were ministers of the word handed them on to us.”

Therefore the apostles themselves saw the Word—not because they had looked upon the body of the Lord and Savior, but because they saw the Word.

For if they had seen Jesus according to the body, that is, if they had seen the Word of God, then Pilate, who condemned him, also saw the Word, as did Judas the betrayer and all those who cried, “Crucify him, crucify him” (Matthew 26), “Take such a one from the earth”; they would have seen the Word of God. But far be it from us that any unbeliever should have seen the Word of God.

To see the Word of God is like what the Savior says: “Whoever sees me sees also the Father who sent me.”

“As those who from the beginning themselves saw and were ministers of the word handed them on to us” (John 14).

From Luke’s words we are secretly taught that the end of one kind of teaching is teaching itself, while the end of another kind of teaching is reckoned in action.

For example, the science of geometry has as its end only knowledge and instruction. But there is another science whose end requires action. In medicine, for instance, I must know the reasoning and principles of medicine, not merely so that I may know what I ought to do, but so that I may do it: so that I may cut wounds, prescribe a moderate and disciplined diet, feel the heat of fevers in the pulse of the veins, and through periodic treatments dry, temper, and restrain an excess of bodily fluids.

If someone has only known these things and has not followed them with action, his knowledge will be empty.

Something analogous to medical knowledge and practice is found in knowledge of and service to the word: “As those who from the beginning themselves saw and were ministers of the word handed them on to us.”

By the words “themselves saw,” doctrine and knowledge are signified; and by the words “were ministers of the word,” we understand that actions are demonstrated.

“Having attained from the beginning”: “It seemed good to me also, having attained from the beginning”—he repeats and reinforces that what he is about to write he did not learn by hearsay, but had himself attained from the beginning.

Hence he is rightly praised by the Apostle, who says: “His praise is in the Gospel throughout all the churches” (2 Corinthians 8). This is said of no one else, and it is handed down as having been said of Luke:

“It seemed good to me also, having attained from the beginning, to write everything carefully and in order for you, most excellent Theophilus.”

Someone may think that he wrote the Gospel to some particular Theophilus. All of you who hear us speaking, if you are such as to be loved by God, are also Theophili, and the Gospel is written to you.

If someone is a Theophilus, he is most excellent and most strong; for this is expressed more significantly in Greek by *κράτιστος* (*kratistos*).

[Note: This comma too is from the translator, not the author. The Greek word *κράτιστος* properly means “most strong,” whereas the manuscripts of the Latin translation render it “most excellent.”]

No Theophilus is weak. And just as it is written concerning the people of Israel when they departed from Egypt (Exodus 14), that there was not one weak person among their tribes, so, if I may speak boldly, I shall say that everyone who is a Theophilus is strong, possessing robust strength from God, as from his word, so that he may be able to know the truth of the words by which he was formed, understanding the word of the Gospel in Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

## Homily II

### On the Passage That Says, “Now Both Were Righteous before God, Walking in All the Commandments and Ordinances of the Lord Blamelessly”

### Chapter 1

Those who wish to place some excuse over their sins think that no one is without sin, and they use the testimony written in Job: “No one is clean from defilement, not even if his life upon the earth has been but a single day. His months are countable” (Job 14). They merely produce the sound of the words, while wholly ignoring their interpretation.

Against them we shall answer briefly that being without sin is understood in Scripture in two ways: one, as never having sinned at all; the other, as having ceased to sin.

If they say that the one who never sinned is called without sin, we agree that no one is without sin, because we have all sinned at some time, even if afterward we followed virtue.

[Note: The reader should be warned that the Virgin Mary is considered exempt from this judgment by a special privilege of God; this should be noted because Origen, as must be said below concerning Homily 14, impiously includes her too under this infirmity common to all human beings.]

But if they understand that a person is not without sin in such a way as to deny that anyone can turn from vices to virtues and thereafter never sin at all, their opinion is false.

For someone who sinned previously and has ceased to sin can be called without sin. Thus our Lord Jesus Christ presented to himself a glorious Church, “not having spot” (Ephesians 5)—not because the ecclesiastical person had never had a spot, but because he is no longer stained by it; “not having wrinkle,” not because the wrinkle of the old person had never previously been in him, but because he has ceased to have it.

In the same way, what follows is to be understood: that she is holy and unblemished—not because she was unblemished from the beginning, for it cannot even be imagined concerning a human being that his soul was never stained, but because the soul that has ceased to be stained thereafter is reckoned pure and sincere.

We have said this in order to teach that a person can be called without sin and unblemished because he has ceased to sin.

Thus it is written most plainly concerning Zechariah and Elizabeth: “Both were righteous before God, walking” in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord without blame.

Let us examine more carefully the praises of Zechariah and Elizabeth that holy Luke records in his history—not merely so that we may know that they were praiseworthy, but so that, taking up a holy zeal, we too may become worthy of praise.

He could have written simply: “Both were righteous, walking in all the commandments.” But now he necessarily adds: “Both were righteous before God.”

For it can happen that someone is righteous in the sight of human beings but not in the sight of God.

For example, when no one has anything bad to say about me, and, examining everything about me, finds nothing to criticize, I am righteous in the sight of human beings. Suppose that everyone holds the same opinion of me and seeks something to criticize but cannot find it, instead praising me with a unanimous voice: I am righteous in the sight of many people.

Yet human judgment is not certain. People do not know whether I have ever sinned secretly in my heart, whether I have looked at a woman in order to desire her (Matthew 5), and whether adultery has arisen in my heart.

People do not know, when they see me giving alms according to my means, whether I did so because of God’s command or whether I sought human praise and favor.

It is difficult to be righteous in the sight of God: to do good for no other reason than the good itself, and to seek God alone as the rewarder of a good work.

The Apostle says something similar: “Their praise is not from human beings but from God” (Romans 2).

Blessed is the one who is righteous and praiseworthy in the sight of God. For although human beings may appear to possess certain judgment, they cannot pronounce a fully certain verdict.

It sometimes happens that they praise one who is not praiseworthy and criticize one who is in no way worthy of criticism. God alone is a just judge both in praise and in blame.

Therefore, appropriately, this is now added to the praise of the righteous: “Both were righteous before God.”

Solomon also exhorts to something similar in Proverbs, saying: “My son, provide what is good in the sight of God and human beings” (Proverbs 3).

Another praise of Zechariah and Elizabeth follows: “Walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord.”

When we judge well and rightly concerning certain people, we walk in the ordinances of the Lord. When we do this or that, we walk in his commandments.

Therefore I think that holy Luke, wishing to praise them with complete praise, said: “Both were righteous, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord.”

Someone might say to me: If this praise is complete, what does the phrase “without blame” mean? It would have been sufficient to say, “walking in all the ways and ordinances of the Lord,” unless it could happen that someone walks in all God’s commandments and yet does not walk without blame.

How can it happen that someone walking in all God’s commandments and ordinances is nevertheless under blame?

I shall answer briefly: If this were not so, we would never find it written elsewhere: “Pursue justly what is just” (Deuteronomy 16). For unless there were something just that we might not pursue justly, we would never be commanded to pursue justly what is just.

When we carry out God’s command but sprinkle the conscience with the filth of vainglory in order to please human beings, or when some other motive displeasing to God precedes the good work, although we are carrying out God’s command, we do not do it without blame; and we pursue unjustly what is just.

It is difficult, therefore, to walk in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord without blame, according to the testimony and praise of God in Christ Jesus.

This praise will be rendered on the day of judgment by him before whose tribunal we must all be revealed, so that each may receive what he has done through the body, whether good or bad (2 Corinthians 5). For we shall all stand before the tribunal of God, to receive what we deserve in Christ Jesus.

To him belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## Homily III

### On the Passage That Says, “The Angel of the Lord Appeared to Him, Standing at the Right Side of the Altar of Incense”

[Variant: “of the kindled offering.”]

### Chapter 1
Things that are corporeal and devoid of sense, in order to be seen by someone else, accomplish nothing by themselves; rather, the eye of another, fixed upon them—whether they wish it or not—sees them when it directs its contemplation toward them. For what can a human being, or any other thing enclosed in a dense body, do, when present, to prevent itself from being seen? Conversely, things that are heavenly and divine, when present, are not seen unless they themselves wish it; and it lies within their will whether they are seen or not seen.

It was by the grace of God that He appeared to Abraham, or to the other prophets—not that Abraham’s heart alone was responsible for his seeing God, but that God’s grace spontaneously offered itself to the righteous man to be seen. This, however, you should understand not only of God the Father, but also [255–256] of the Lord and Savior, and of the Holy Spirit, and, to come to lesser beings, of the Cherubim and Seraphim.

[Note: [Col. 0225D] Many ecclesiastical writers, both before and after Origen, were persuaded that, whenever God is said in the history of the Old Testament to have appeared to the patriarchs or prophets and the Son is said to have been present among them, one should understand that the Son, following the custom of the Father, presented Himself to them in visible form and acquired the names of God, angel, or Lord according to the various persona He assumed. They also held that He was substantially joined to them, though not by a ὑποστατική—“hypostatic”—union, but by a σχετική—“relative”—union. Others rightly criticized this opinion; yet we do not seize upon it as an occasion for indicting Origen. But since here he assigns the same role both to God the Father and to the Holy Spirit, his paradoxical and distinctive doctrine cannot be allowed to pass without criticism. For the reasoning by which the Adamantine was led to this position deprives him of the very basis that seems to have led the others to it: namely, the words of Exodus XXXIII, “No one shall ever see God the Father and live,” and, conversely, Christ’s words in John VIII, “Abraham rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad,” and similar passages.]

For it may happen that even now, while we are speaking, an angel is present with us, and yet, because we are not worthy, we cannot see him. For even if the eye of our body or of our soul is intent upon contemplation, unless the angel appears of his own accord and offers himself to be seen, even the one who truly desires to see him will not see him. Therefore, wherever it is written, “God appeared to this person or that,” or, as here, “An angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing at the right side of the altar of incense,” understand it in the way I have explained. Whether it is God or an angel who appears to Abraham or Zechariah, whether he wishes or does not wish to be seen, he will either not be seen or will be seen.

And we say this not only of the present age, but also of the future, when we have departed from the world: neither God nor the angels appear to everyone. That is, not everyone who has departed from the body immediately deserves to see the angels, the Holy Spirit, the Lord and Savior, and God the Father Himself. Only the one who has a pure heart will see Him (Matt. V), the one who has made himself worthy of the sight of God.

And although the one with a pure heart and the one who is still stained by some impurity may be in the same place, that one place can neither harm nor help either of them. For the one who has a pure heart will see God, whereas the other, being as he is, will not see what the former sees.

I understand something similar concerning Christ, who was once visible in the body, though not everyone who saw Him was able to see Him. They saw only His body; but, insofar as He was Christ, they could not see Him. The disciples, however, saw Him and contemplated the greatness of His divinity. For this reason, I think that when Philip entreated Him and said, “Show us the Father, and it is enough for us,” the Savior replied: “I have been with you for so long, and you have not known me? Philip, the one who sees me sees the Father also” (John XIV).

For Pilate, who saw Jesus, did not behold the Father, nor did the traitor Judas. Neither Pilate nor Judas saw Christ insofar as He was Christ, nor did the crowd that pressed around Him. Those alone saw Jesus whom He knew to be worthy of His sight.

Let us therefore labor so that God may appear to us even in the present. For the holy word of Scripture has promised that He will be found by those who do not tempt Him; and He appears to those who are not unbelieving toward Him. In the future, may He not be hidden from us, but may we see Him face to face, possess the confidence that comes from a good life, and enjoy the sight of almighty God in Christ Jesus and in the Holy Spirit, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY IV

Concerning the passage that is written: “Do not be afraid, Zechariah,” up to the place where it says concerning John: “He will go before Him in the spirit and power of Elijah.” Chapter I.

[Col. 0227B]

When Zechariah saw the angel, he was terrified. For a new form presenting itself to human eyes disturbs the mind and throws the soul into confusion. Therefore the angel, knowing this to be human nature, first remedies his agitation by saying: “Do not be afraid, Zechariah”; and he refreshes the trembling man and gladdens him with a new announcement, adding: “Your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear a son, and you will call his name John, and he will be your joy and exultation.”

When a righteous person is born into the world and enters the arena of this life, the ministers of his birth rejoice and raise themselves up on high. But when one is born who has been prepared for an evil life and, as though condemned to punishments, has been banished into a prison,

[Note: [Col. 0227D] There is no reason for us to criticize at length this opinion of Origen’s, according to which he maintains that souls drawn from heaven are bound to bodies by angels and are either sent down into bodies as into a prison because of sins committed above, or, on account of deeds rightly performed before this life, are assigned to various kinds of bodies in order to carry out God’s decrees. This is almost a characteristic mark of Origenism, which countless ancient and more recent writers have attacked. We too have discussed certain aspects of it elsewhere, especially in the synodical letter numbered 92 among the letters attributed to Jerome, which we first published and in which almost all the doctrines of the Origenian heresy are condemned.]

the minister is dismayed and collapses.

Do you want an example of a holy man whose entire fruit consists in praise? Consider Jacob, who is recorded as having fathered twelve males, all of whom became the peoples of God and the patriarchs and leaders of His portion. In all these sons Jacob, their father, rejoiced, just as now joy is announced to everyone at John’s birth. Whoever once descends, for the benefit of others, to the work of begetting children and wishes to devote himself to this ministry should entreat God that such a son may enter the world for him, one over whose birth he may rejoice more greatly.

It is therefore written concerning John: “He will be great in the sight of the Lord” (Luke I). This shows the greatness of John’s soul, which lies open to the eyes of God, and also something lesser, which is properly perceived in the virtue of the soul.

I understand in the same way the saying found in the Gospel: “Do not despise one of these least ones who are in the Church.” There “least” is understood in contrast with “greater.” I am not commanded to despise the one who is great, since the one who is great cannot be despised; rather, I am told not to despise one of the least. And so that you may know that “least” and “small” are not said by chance, Scripture says, according to the reasoning we have established: “Whoever causes one of these least ones to stumble” (Matt. XVIII). The least one can be caused to stumble; the great one cannot endure stumbling.

The passage concerning John continues: “And he will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb.” John’s birth too is full of wonder. For just as an archangel announced the coming of our Lord and Savior, so an archangel announces John’s birth: “He will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb.”

The Jewish people did not see our Lord performing signs and wonders and healing their illnesses. John, however, while still in his mother’s womb, rejoices; for he cannot bear it, and at the coming of Jesus’ mother he longs to leap forth from the womb. For, as Elizabeth says, “Behold, when the sound of your greeting came to my ears, the infant in my womb leaped for joy.” John was still in his mother’s womb, and already he had received the Holy Spirit.

That was not the beginning of his substance and nature of which Scripture says that he “will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God” (Matt. IV). John turned many, whereas the Lord turned not merely more, but all. His work is to turn everyone to God the Father.

“And he will go before Him in the spirit and power of Elijah.” It does not say “in the soul of Elijah,” but “in the spirit and power of Elijah.” There was power in Elijah, and spirit, as in all the prophets, and, according to the dispensation of the body, also in the Lord and Savior Himself. Concerning Him, shortly afterward, it is said to Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.”

Therefore the spirit that had been in John and the power that had been in him appeared also in this one. Elijah was transferred; John, however, was the Lord’s Forerunner, and he died before Him so that, when the Lord descended to the underworld, John might preach His coming there.

I think that the mystery of John is being fulfilled in the world even today. Whoever is going to believe in Christ Jesus has the spirit and power of John go before him into his soul, preparing for the Lord a perfect people, making straight paths amid the roughness of the heart, and directing the roads, “to prepare for the Lord a perfect people” (Matt. I).

The roads were not prepared and the paths made straight only at that time; even today the spirit and power of John precede the coming of the Lord and Savior.

[Col. 0228D]

O great mysteries of the Lord and of His dispensation! Angels go before Jesus; every day angels either ascend or descend over the salvation of human beings, in Christ Jesus (John I), to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY V

Concerning the fact that Zechariah became mute. Chapter I.

Zechariah the priest, while offering incense in the temple,

[Col. 0229A]

is condemned to silence and restrained; indeed, he speaks only by signs and remains mute until the birth of his son John. What is the purpose of this story?

Zechariah’s silence is the silence of the prophets among the people of Israel. God does not speak to them at all, and the Word who in the beginning was God with the Father has passed over to us, and Christ does not remain silent to us. Among them He is silent to this day; for this reason Zechariah the prophet too was silent.

It is proved most clearly from his own words that he was both prophet and priest. What does the following mean: “He was making signs to them,” compensating for the loss of his voice by gestures? I think that such deeds are without speech, deeds that differ in no respect from signs when considered according to reason. But when reason and speech have gone before and the deed has followed accordingly, the gestures should not be regarded as mere signs, since they are adorned with speech or reason.

If, then, you see the conduct of the Jews without reason or speech, so that they cannot give an account of what they do, understand that what previously took place in Zechariah is still being fulfilled in his image. Their circumcision resembles gestures. For unless an account is given of circumcision, circumcision is merely a sign and a mute deed. The Passover and the other solemnities are signs more than reality.

To this day the people of Israel are deaf and mute. It could not happen otherwise: the people who had rejected the Word from themselves had to be deaf and mute.

In former times Moses did speak: “But I am alogos” (Exod. V, 12).

[Note: [Col. 0229D] These too are the words of the holy interpreter. Since the Greek text of Exodus V has Ἐγὼ δὲ ἄλογός εἰμι—“But I am without a word”—while the Latin manuscripts do not reproduce the wording literally but only according to its sense, “since I have uncircumcised lips,” or, “since I am slow of speech,” Jerome was right to admonish the reader concerning this point.]

Although a Latin translator expressed this differently, it can properly be translated “without speech,” or “without reason.” After he said this, he received the reason and speech which he had confessed that he previously lacked.

Before receiving the Law, the people of Israel were, in a certain sense, mute, without reason and speech. Then they received the Word, whose image was Moses. This people, therefore, does not merely confess what Moses then confessed—that it is mute and alogos—but indicates by signs and silence that it has neither speech nor reason.

Does it not seem to you to be a confession of folly when none of them can give an account of the legal commandments and prophetic prophecy? Christ ceased to be among them; the Word left them. That saying written in Isaiah was fulfilled: “The daughter of Zion will be left like a shelter in a vineyard and like a watchman’s hut in a cucumber field, like a besieged city” (Isa. I).

After they were abandoned, salvation was transferred to the nations, so that they might be stirred to jealousy. Therefore, as we observe God’s dispensation and mystery, how Israel was rejected for the sake of our salvation, we must take care lest they too were cast out because of us and we prove worthy of greater punishment, since others were abandoned for our sake and we have done nothing worthy of God’s adoption and mercy, by which He adopted us and counted us among His children, in Christ Jesus (Rom. XI), to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY VI

Concerning the passage that is written: “When Elizabeth had conceived, she kept herself hidden,” up to the place where it says: “He will be great.” Chapter I.

When Elizabeth conceived, she kept herself hidden for five months, saying: “Thus the Lord has dealt with me in the days when He looked upon me, to take away my reproach among men.”

I ask for what reason, after realizing that she was pregnant, she avoided appearing in public. If I am not mistaken, the same point is made by the fact that those joined in marriage do not have every time available for intercourse between them, but there is a time when they withdraw from the work of marriage.

For if the man is elderly and the woman an old woman, it is most shameful for them to serve lust and to serve marriage—things which seem, by God’s will, to have been removed even from the care of the body and from old age. But Elizabeth, who had again been joined to a husband in accordance with the angel’s word and God’s dispensation, would be ashamed that, being old and almost decrepit, she had returned to the activity of the young.

Therefore she kept herself hidden for five months—not until the ninth month, when childbirth was imminent, but until Mary conceived. For when Mary conceived and came to her, and her greeting reached Elizabeth’s ears, the infant in Elizabeth’s womb leaped for joy; and she, filled with the Holy Spirit, prophesied and spoke the words recorded in the Gospel. “And these words were spread throughout all the hill country.”

When a report arose among the people that she was carrying a prophet in her womb and that the one carried by the Virgin was something greater than a human being, she no longer hid herself, but openly revealed herself and rejoiced that she had the Forerunner in her womb.

Then Scripture records that, in the sixth month of Elizabeth’s conception, the angel Gabriel was sent by God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin’s name was Mary.

Again turning the question over in my mind, I ask why God, when He had decided that the Savior should be born of a virgin, did not choose a girl without a fiancé, but chose precisely one who had already been betrothed. If I am not mistaken, the reason is this: He had to be born of a virgin who not only had a fiancé,

[Col. 0230D]

but, as Matthew writes, had already been given to a husband, although the husband had not yet known her (Matt. I), lest the very appearance of virginity expose her to disgrace if she were seen to have a swollen womb.

Therefore I have found the following elegantly written in a letter of a certain martyr—I mean Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, second after Peter,

[Note: [Col. 0229D] We also discussed this in the commentary of Jerome on Matthew, chapter II, where the holy Father praises the martyr Ignatius [Col. 0230D], who added a fourth reason why Christ was conceived by a betrothed woman: namely, so that His birth might be concealed from the devil, who would think that He was born not of a virgin but of a wife. It seems that Jerome did not quote the passage from Ignatius himself, but from this homily of Origen; for the holy Martyr did not state this precisely, though it can be gathered to some extent from his Letter to the Ephesians near the end.]

who fought the beasts at Rome during the persecution:

“The virginity of Mary was hidden from the ruler of this age. It was hidden because of Joseph; it was hidden because of the marriage; it was hidden because she was thought to have a husband. For if she had not had a fiancé and, as was thought, a husband, it could not have been hidden from the ruler of this age. Immediately the devil’s silent thought would have crept in: How is this woman, who has not had intercourse with a man, pregnant? This conception must be divine; it must be something higher than human nature.”

Conversely, the Savior had arranged that the devil should not know His dispensation and assumption of a body. Therefore He concealed it in His birth, and afterward commanded His disciples not to make Him known.

And when He was tempted by the devil himself, He nowhere confessed that He was the Son of God, but merely replied: “It is not right for me to worship you, nor to turn these stones into bread, nor to throw myself down from the height” (Matt. IV). In saying these things, He always kept silent about being the Son of God.

Search also in another Scripture, and you will find that it was Christ’s will that the devil should not know of the coming of the Son of God. For the Apostle, asserting that the hostile powers did not know His passion, says: “We speak wisdom among the mature—not the wisdom of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are being destroyed; but we speak God’s wisdom, hidden in a mystery, which none of the rulers of this age understood. For if they had understood it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Cor. II).

The Savior’s mystery, therefore, was hidden from the rulers of this age.

But an objection may be raised, and I think it should be answered before someone else puts it forward: How could what was hidden from the rulers of this age have been hidden from the devil, especially from the one who said in the Gospel, “You have come before the time to torment us; we know who you are, the Son of God” (Matt. IX)?

Consider, however, that the one lesser in wickedness recognized the Savior, whereas the one greater in crime, crafty and evil, is prevented from knowing the Son of God precisely because he is greater in evil.

We too, if we have less evil within us, can more easily advance toward virtue. But if there is more evil in us, we must sweat and labor greatly to be freed from our greater wickedness.

This concerns the fact that Mary had a fiancé.

Since the angel greeted Mary with a new expression, one that I have not been able to find anywhere in all Scripture, a few things must be said about it. The expression he used was, “Hail, full of grace,” which in Greek is κεχαριτωμένη. I do not remember having read it elsewhere in Scripture. Nor is such a greeting addressed to a man: “Hail, full of grace.” This greeting is reserved for Mary alone.

For if Mary had known that the same expression had been used of anyone else—and she possessed knowledge of the Law, was holy, and had learned the prophecies by daily meditation—the greeting would never have terrified her as something unfamiliar.

Therefore the angel says to her: “Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor before the Lord. Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you will call his name Jesus. He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High.”

John too is said to be great, and the angel Gabriel himself bears witness to this. But when Jesus, truly great and truly exalted, came, the one who had previously been great became lesser. For, it says, “He was the burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light” (John V).

The greatness of our Savior did not appear at the time when He was born; rather, it has now shone forth, after He seemed to have been oppressed by His adversaries.

See the greatness of the Lord: “His teaching’s sound has gone out through the whole earth, and His words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII).

Our Lord Jesus,

[Note: [Col. 0231D] I would prefer to read “which is the power,” so that it might more clearly be opposed to the opinion for which Genebrard and others accuse Origen on the basis of Treatise 34 on Matthew: namely, that they claim he thought Christ, insofar as He is Christ, or insofar as He offers His humanity to corporeal eyes, exists everywhere. Here, however, the Adamantine attributes this quality solely to His divine presence, and teaches most truthfully that Christ, insofar as He is the power of God, has been diffused throughout the whole world and pervades everything—heavenly, earthly, and infernal.]

who is the power of God (Rom. I and I Cor. I), has been diffused throughout the whole world and is even now with us, according to what is written in the Apostle: “When you are gathered together, and my spirit is present with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ” (I Cor. V).

The power of the Lord and Savior is with those who are separated from our world in Britain, and with those who are in Mauritania, and with all who under the sun have believed in His name.

See, therefore, the greatness of the Savior, how it has been diffused throughout the whole world. And certainly I have not yet explained His true greatness.

Ascend into the heavens and see how He has filled the heavenly realms. For He appeared to the angels. Descend in thought into the depths, and you will see that He descended there also. For the one who descended is the same one who ascended, “in order to fill all things,” so that “at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Eph. IV).

Consider the power of the Lord: He has filled the world—that is, the heavenly, earthly, and infernal realms. He has also penetrated heaven itself and ascended into the heights. For we read that “the Son of God has passed through the heavens” (Heb. IV).

If you see these things, you will likewise understand that “He will be great” was not spoken casually, but has been fulfilled in deed. Great is our Lord Jesus, both present and absent; and He grants this assembly and gathering of ours a share in His strength.

May we each deserve to receive this as well. Let us entreat the Lord God, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY VII

Concerning the passage that is written: “Mary arose and went with haste into the hill country,” up to the place where it says: “There will be a fulfillment of the things that have been spoken.” Chapter I.

The better come to the worse in order to confer some benefit upon them by their arrival. Thus the Savior also came to John in order to sanctify his baptism.

[Col. 0233A]

And Mary, as soon as she heard the angel announce that she had conceived the Savior and that her kinswoman Elizabeth had a child in her womb, arose and went with haste into the hill country and entered Elizabeth’s house.

[265–266] Jesus, who was in Mary’s womb, was already hastening to sanctify John, who was in his mother’s womb. Indeed, before Mary came and greeted Elizabeth, the infant in the womb did not leap for joy. But as soon as Mary spoke the word that the Son of God had suggested while in His mother’s womb, the infant leaped for joy, and then for the first time Jesus made His Forerunner a prophet.

It was also fitting that Mary, who was worthy to bear God’s offspring, should, after speaking with God, ascend into the hill country and dwell in higher places. Therefore it is written: “Mary arose in those days and went into the hill country.”

Since she was anxious but not sluggish, she ought to hasten in her concern, and, full of the Holy Spirit, be led to higher places and protected by the power of God, by which she had been overshadowed.

She therefore came to a city of Judah and to the house of Zechariah, and greeted Elizabeth. When Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the infant in her womb leaped, and she was filled with the Holy Spirit.

There is no doubt, then, that the woman who was filled with the Holy Spirit at that time was filled because of her son. For the mother did not first merit the Holy Spirit. Rather, when John, still enclosed in the womb, had received the Holy Spirit, she too was filled with the Holy Spirit after the sanctification of her son.

You can believe this if you also know something similar concerning the Savior. Blessed Mary is found prophesying, as we have discovered in some

[Note: [Col. 0233D] I believe he is referring to the words of the following verse, 45: “And blessed is she who believed, for there will be a fulfillment…” In some manuscripts of his age, these words—“And blessed is she who believed, for the things spoken to you by the Lord will be fulfilled”—were attributed to the Virgin Mary rather than to Elizabeth. No trace or remnant of that reading now survives.]

copies. For we are not unaware that, according to other manuscripts, Elizabeth is the one who prophesies these words.

Mary, therefore, was filled with the Holy Spirit when she began to have the Savior in her womb. As soon as she received the Holy Spirit, and the Creator of the Lord’s body and the Son of God began to be in her womb, she too was filled with the Holy Spirit.

The infant in Elizabeth’s womb leaped, and she was filled with the Holy Spirit, and she cried out with a loud voice and said:

“Blessed are you among women.”

At this point, lest simple people be deceived, we must refute the objections that heretics are accustomed to raise. Someone, I do not know who, has burst into such madness as to assert that Mary was rejected by the Savior because, after His birth,

[Col. 0233D]

she was joined to Joseph; and he who spoke such words himself knows with what frame of mind he spoke them.

[Note: [Col. 0234D] Helvidius later revived this heresy and made it the principal pretext for his claim that the brothers of the Lord are named in the Gospel. It is worthwhile to recall the truly golden little book of Saint Jerome against this heretic. We have now restored the confused context, since previously it read: “With what frame of mind he said it, he himself knows, who spoke.”]

Whenever heretics put such a thing before you, answer them and say: Certainly Elizabeth, full of the Holy Spirit, said, “Blessed are you among women.” If Mary is proclaimed blessed by the Holy Spirit, how did the Savior disown her?

Moreover, they have no proof for their assertion that she married after giving birth. For these sons who were called Joseph’s were not born of Mary, nor is there any Scripture that mentions such a thing.

“Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb. And how has this happened to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?”

When she says, “How has this happened to me?” she does not speak out of ignorance—especially since she is full of the Holy Spirit, as though she did not know that, according to God’s will, the mother of the Lord had come to her. Rather, she speaks in this sense: “What good have I done? What are my works, that the mother of the Lord should come to me? By what righteousness, from what good deeds, from what faithfulness of mind have I deserved that the mother of my Lord should come to me?”

“For behold, when the sound of your greeting came to my ears, the infant in my womb leaped for joy.”

The soul of blessed John was holy. While still enclosed in his mother’s womb and about to come into the world, he knew, as though through the sense of experience, what Israel did not know. Therefore he leaped. And he did not leap simply, but with joy. He had perceived that his Lord had come to sanctify His servant before the servant came forth from his mother’s womb.

May it happen to me that I am called foolish by unbelievers because I have believed such things. The deed itself and the truth show that I have believed not folly but wisdom, and that what is considered foolish by them is for me an occasion of salvation.

For if the Savior’s birth had not been heavenly and blessed, if it had contained nothing divine and had not surpassed human nature, His teaching would never have penetrated the whole world.

If He had been merely in Mary’s womb and had not been the Son of God, how could it have happened that, both then and now, not only illnesses of bodies but also the many diseases of souls were healed?

Which of us was not foolish, when now, through God’s mercy, we possess understanding and thirst for God? Which of us was not unbelieving with respect to righteousness, when now, through Christ, we possess righteousness and follow righteousness? Which of us was not wandering and astray, when now, through the Savior’s coming, we do not fluctuate and are not thrown into confusion, but are on the way—in Him who says, “I am the way” (John X)?

We can also gather the remaining passages and see that everything written about Him is recounted as worthy of divine wonder: His birth, His upbringing, His power, His passion, and His resurrection are at work not only at that time but also now in us.

Who gathered you, O catechumens, in the Church? What impulse moved you, after leaving your homes, to assemble in this gathering? We did not go around your homes one by one. Rather, the almighty Father, by an invisible power, places in the hearts of those whom He knows to be worthy this ardor, so that, as though unwilling and reluctant, you come to faith—especially at the beginning of your religion, when, trembling and fearful, you receive the faith of salvation with apprehension.

I beg you, O catechumens, do not be reluctant. Let none of you be afraid or tremble, but follow Jesus who goes before you. He draws you toward salvation and gathers you into the Church—now, indeed, upon earth; but if you produce worthy fruits, into the Church of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven.

“Blessed is she who believed, because there will be a fulfillment of the things that have been spoken to her by the Lord.”

Concerning these things blessed Mary also magnifies the Lord Jesus. The soul magnifies the Lord, while the spirit magnifies God. What interpretation these words have, if the Lord grants that we gather again in the Church, so that you may come joyfully to the house of God and lend your ears to divine reading, we shall seek, sift, and discuss in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

# HOMILY VIII

Concerning the passage that is written: “My soul magnifies the Lord,” up to the place where it says: “He brings about strength for those who fear Him.” Chapter I.

[Col. 0235B]

Before John, Elizabeth prophesies; before the birth of the Lord and Savior, Mary prophesies. And just as sin began with a woman and thereafter reached the man, so the beginning of salvation had its origin with women, so that other women also, laying aside the weakness of their sex, might imitate the life and conduct of those holy women who are now described especially in the Gospel.

Let us therefore examine the virginal prophecy. “My soul,” she says, “magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior” [Col. 0235C]. Two things—soul, namely, and spirit—perform a double act of praise. The soul proclaims the Lord; the spirit, God. Not that the praise of the Lord is one thing and that of God another, but because he who is God is also Lord, and he who is Lord is likewise God.

It is asked how she magnifies the Lord. For if the Lord can receive neither increase nor diminution, and what he is, he is, why does Mary now say, “My soul magnifies the Lord”? If I consider that the Lord the Savior is “the image of the invisible God” (Col. I), and see that my soul was made according to the image of the Creator, so that it might be the image of an image—for my soul is not itself specially the image of God, but was formed in the likeness of the prior image—then I shall understand that, just as those who ordinarily paint images take, for example, one countenance of a king and commend their artistic skill in reproducing the original likeness, so each one of us, forming his soul according to the image of Christ, gives it either a greater or a smaller image: either faded or dirty, or clear, shining, and radiant according to the likeness of the original image.

Therefore, when I have made the image of the image—namely, my soul—large, and have magnified it by work, 269–270 thought, and speech, then the image of God becomes great, and the Lord himself, whose image is in our soul, is magnified. And just as the Lord grows in our image [Col. 0236A], so, if we are sinners, he is diminished and grows smaller.

But in place of the Savior’s image we put on other images for ourselves. In place of the image of the Word, wisdom, justice, and the other virtues, we assume the form of the devil, so that it may be said of us: “Serpents, brood of vipers” (Matt. XXIII). We also put on the person of a lion, a dragon, and foxes when we are poisonous, cruel, and cunning; likewise that of a goat or a pig when we are more ready for lust.

I remember that once, while expounding Deuteronomy at the passage where it is written, “You shall not make any likeness of any animal” (Deut. IV), I said that spiritually one person makes the image of a male in some people, and another makes that of a female; one person gives someone the likeness of birds, another that of creeping things and serpents, and another makes the likeness of God. How these things are to be understood will be known by whoever reads them [Col. 0236B].

[Note: No work of Origen’s studies on Deuteronomy now survives. Cassiodorus mentions eight homilies in chapter I of the *Divine Institutions*.]

The soul of Mary, then, first magnifies the Lord, and afterward rejoices in God. Unless we had first believed, we could not rejoice. “Because he has regarded,” she says, “the lowliness of his handmaid.” At what lowliness of Mary did the Lord look? What humble and degraded thing did the Mother of the Savior possess, when she carried the Son of God in her womb?

What she says, therefore—“He has regarded the lowliness of his handmaid”—amounts to saying: He has regarded the justice of his handmaid; he has regarded her temperance; he has regarded her fortitude and wisdom. For it is fitting that he should regard virtues.

Someone may reply: “I understand how God regards the justice and wisdom of his handmaid; but how he regards lowliness is not sufficiently clear.” Let the person who asks such questions consider that in Scripture lowliness is properly proclaimed as one of the virtues. For the Savior says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. XI).

And if you wish to hear the name by which this virtue is also called by philosophers, listen: the lowliness that God regards is the same quality which they call ἀτυφία (*atyphia*), or μετριότης (*metriotēs*). We too can call it by a kind of circumlocution, when someone is not puffed up but humbles himself. For the one who is puffed up, according to the Apostle, falls into the judgment of the devil, since the devil also began from inflation and pride: “lest, being puffed up, he fall into the judgment of the devil” (I Tim. III).

“He has regarded the lowliness of his handmaid.” “He has regarded me,” she says, “as lowly and as pursuing the virtue of gentleness and self-abasement” [Col. 0236D]. “For behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed.”

If I understand “all generations” simply, I interpret it as referring to believers. But if I investigate something deeper, I shall observe how great a progress it is to say: “Because he who is mighty has done great things for me,” since “everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XVIII).

God, then, regarded the lowliness of blessed Mary; therefore he who is mighty did great things for her, and holy is his name. “And his mercy is from generation to generation.” The mercy of God extends not through one generation, nor two, nor three, nor even five, but into eternity, “from generation to generation,” toward those who fear his power.

“He has shown strength with his arm.” Although you have approached the Lord weak, if you fear him, you will be able to hear the promise that the Lord makes to you because of your fear. What is this promise? “Toward those who fear him,” he says, “he has shown strength.” Strength, or dominion, is royal power. For κράτος (*kratos*), which we can call “dominion” [Note: This clause too seems to have been added by Jerome: “which we can call dominion.”], is so called from the fact that it rules, or holds everything beneath itself.

Therefore, if you fear the Lord, he gives you strength, or dominion; he gives you a kingdom, so that, having become subject to the King of kings, you may possess the kingdom of heaven, in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

*271–272 HOMILY IX.* On the passage that is written, “She remained with her for three months,” up to the place where it says, “And he spoke, blessing the Lord.” Chapter I.

[Col. 0237B]

The things that are said, as well as the things that are reported as having happened, ought to have an explanation worthy of the Holy Spirit and of the faith of Christ, to which we who believe are called. Hence we must now seek the reason why Mary, after conceiving, went to Elizabeth and remained with her for three months; or what the reason was that Luke, who wrote the history of the Gospel, should also write that she remained with her for three months and afterward returned to her own house.

There must certainly be some explanation, which the following discourse will reveal if the Lord opens our heart. For if, merely because Mary came to Elizabeth and greeted her, the infant leaped for joy, and Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, prophesied the things written in the Gospel, and achieved so much progress in a single hour, then it is left to our conjecture what progress John made during the three months while Mary was with Elizabeth.

For it is very unfitting that the infant should leap and, in a manner, exult in joy at a moment and instant of time, and that Elizabeth should be filled with the Holy Spirit, while during three months neither John nor Elizabeth should have advanced through the presence of the Lord’s Mother and of the Savior himself.

John was therefore exercised, and, as it were, pressed in a sacred athletic training by his holy mother for three months; he was prepared in his mother’s womb so that, having been born wonderfully, he might be nourished even more wonderfully. For Scripture does not report how he was nourished contrary to ordinary practice—how he was suckled at his mother’s breasts or carried in the arms of a nurse—but immediately continues: “And he was in the deserts until the day of his manifestation to Israel.”

Then we read: “Now the time was fulfilled for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son.” Many think it superfluous to say, “Now the time was fulfilled for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son” (Mark I). For what woman can give birth unless the time for giving birth has first been completed?

But whoever examines the Scriptures most carefully and listens to the people speaking should attend to the reading, observing whether anywhere in either the Old or the New Testament he finds it written, concerning the birth of a sinner, “The time was fulfilled for her to give birth.” He will never find it at all. But wherever a righteous person is born, there the days are fulfilled; there his coming into the world is completed.

The birth of the righteous possesses fullness; the birth of the sinner, so to speak, emptiness and futility. These things concern the passage that is written: “The time was fulfilled for her to give birth.”

Her neighbors and relatives congratulated her mother and wished, in honor of the father, to give the child the name Zacharias. But Elizabeth, with the Holy Spirit suggesting it, said: “John is his name.”

Then, when they sought just reasons why he should be called John in particular, since no one in his family bore that name, they asked the father, who, unable to answer, spoke by hand and writing. For he wrote on a writing tablet: “John is his name.” And as soon as the stylus was pressed into the wax, the tongue that had previously been bound was released.

He regained speech—not human speech, since his tongue had been bound; yet it was not human speech. Unbelief had bound it. As soon as it was released, it ceased to be human, and he spoke, blessing God, and prophesied the things written in the Gospel. With the Lord Jesus Christ granting it, we shall discuss these things when the time comes; to him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

*273–274 HOMILY X.* On the passage that is written, “Filled with the Holy Spirit, he prophesied,” up to the place where it says, “For he will go before the Lord to prepare his ways.” Chapter I.

Filled with the Holy Spirit, Zacharias announces two prophecies in general: the first concerning Christ, the second concerning John. This is plainly confirmed by his own words, in which he speaks as though the Savior were present and moving about in the world, and afterward speaks of John:

“Being filled with the Holy Spirit, he prophesied, saying: Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, because he has visited and accomplished redemption for his people.”

When God visited and willed to redeem his people, Mary remained with Elizabeth for three months after the angel had spoken to her, so that, through an ineffable power, the present Savior might instruct not only John, as we said earlier, but also Zacharias, as the Gospel discourse now declares.

For he too gradually received increases of the Holy Spirit during those three months; he was taught without knowing it, and he prophesied about Christ, saying: “Who granted redemption to his people and raised up for us a horn of salvation in the house of David,” in which Christ was born according to the flesh.

And truly, because he was a horn of salvation, this prophecy is sung in the house of David. “A vineyard was made in a horn” (Isa. V). In what horn? In Christ Jesus, in him of whom it is now written: “He raised up for us a horn of salvation in the house of David his servant, as he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets: salvation from our enemies.”

Let us not think that this now refers to bodily enemies, but to spiritual ones. For the Lord Jesus came, mighty in battle, to destroy all our enemies, so that he might free us from their ambushes [Col. 0239A].

“And from the hand of our enemies and from the hand of those who hate us.” “To show mercy to our fathers.” I think that, at the coming of the Lord and Savior, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob also enjoyed the mercy of God. For it is not credible that those who formerly saw his day and rejoiced should afterward, at his coming and birth from the Virgin, have received no benefit.

And why should I speak of the patriarchs? Following the authority of Scripture, I shall boldly ascend to higher matters, since the presence of the Lord Jesus and his dispensation benefited not only earthly things but also heavenly things [Note: Huet suspects that by “heavenly beings,” whom the Lord’s dispensation benefited, Origen means not only the orders of angels but also the stars themselves, since he judged them to possess not merely soul but reason as well. And he believed that beings endowed with reason could be subject to sin and require purification—an office which he believed Christ performed for them by his death. Compare Homily 23 somewhat below, and what we say there, in accordance with Origen’s view, concerning the progress of the heavenly powers through Christ’s death and the preaching of the Church.].

Hence the Apostle also says: “Making peace through the blood of his cross, whether on earth or in the heavens” (Eph. II). But if the presence of the Lord benefited both heaven and earth, why should you hesitate to say that his coming also benefited the forefathers, so that what is said might be fulfilled: “To show mercy to our fathers, and to remember his holy covenant, the oath which he swore to Abraham our father, to grant us that, delivered from the hand of our enemies, we might serve him without fear”?

Some are often delivered from the hand of their enemies, but not without fear. For when danger has been preceded by fear, and someone has thus been snatched from the hand of enemies, he is indeed delivered, but not without fear.

The coming of the Lord Jesus, however, snatches us from the hand of our enemies without fear. We did not sense our enemies, nor did we see them resisting; but somehow, suddenly, in an instant and a moment, we were snatched from their jaws and ambushes, and he transferred us into the inheritance and portion of the righteous [Col. 0239C].

And we were delivered from the hand of our enemies without fear, so that we might serve God in holiness and righteousness before him all our days.

“And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High.”

As I seek within myself the reason why he does not speak as though about John, but addresses John himself, saying [variant: “and says”], “And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High,” and what follows—for it would have been superfluous to speak to one who could not hear and to address an infant still at the breast—I think I can find the explanation in this: just as John was wondrously born, came into the world with the angel announcing him, and was brought forth into the world while Mary remained beside Elizabeth for three months, so everything written about him is also reported as having happened wondrously.

But if you doubt that one brought forth immediately from his mother’s womb could hear the words of his father [Col. 0239D] and know what was being said to him—“And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High”—consider that what preceded was much more wondrous: “Behold, when the voice of your greeting came into my ears, the infant leaped for joy in my womb.”

If, while still enclosed in his mother’s womb, he heard Jesus, and, hearing him, leaped and rejoiced, why should you not believe that, once born, he could hear and understand his father’s prophecy, which said to him: “And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High, for you will go before the Lord to prepare his ways”?

For this reason, I think, Zacharias hastened to speak to the infant: he knew that John would shortly remain in the wilderness and that he himself would not be able to enjoy his presence. “For the child was in the deserts until the day of his manifestation to Israel” (Exod. III).

Moses also remained in the wilderness, but afterward, when he had completed the years of his life, he fled from Egypt and tended flocks for other years. John, however, immediately after he was born, went into the deserts; and he who was greater among those born of women appeared worthy of greater nourishment.

Of him the prophet speaks: “Behold, I send my angel before your face” (Mal. III). He is rightly called an angel who had been sent before the Lord, who could hear and understand his prophesying father immediately after he was born [Col. 0240B].

Therefore, let us who believe in such great wonders believe likewise in the resurrection; let us believe also in the promises that are to come, and in the kingdom of heaven which the Spirit promises us daily. Let us receive all these things, as they have been written, wondrously beyond what we can comprehend, in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

*HOMILY XI.* On the passage that is written, “The child grew and was strengthened in spirit,” up to the place where it says, “This was the first census that took place under the governor of Syria, Quirinius.” Chapters I and II.

There are two ways in which “growing” is spoken of in the Holy Scriptures: one bodily, where human will contributes nothing; the other spiritually, where the cause of growth consists in human diligence.

It is concerning the second—that is, spiritual growth—that the Evangelist now speaks: “The child grew and was strengthened in spirit.” What he says means this: he grew in spirit and did not remain at the same measure with which he had begun; rather, the spirit continually increased in him, and as the spirit grew from hour to hour and moment to moment, his soul also received its increases. Not only his soul, but also his senses and mind followed the growth of the spirit.

As for the command God gave, “Grow and multiply” (Gen. I), I do not know how those who take it simply and according to the letter can explain it. Let “multiply” refer to number: when people become more numerous than before, multiplication has a place. But what follows—“Grow”—does not lie within our power. For what person would not wish to add to his stature, so as to become taller (Matt. VI)?

If the command is given for this reason, it is foolish to command what the person commanded cannot do. We are commanded to grow; therefore we are commanded to do what we cannot do.

Do you wish to know how “Grow” is understood? Listen to what Isaac did, concerning whom it is said: “Isaac progressed and became greater, until he became great, or exceedingly great” (Gen. XXI). For his will, always stretching toward better things, continually made progress; his mind contemplated something more divine, and he exercised his memory so as to store more in its treasury and retain it more firmly.

In this way it happened that the person who cultivated all his virtues in the field of his soul fulfilled the command, “Grow.”

Therefore John, while still a little child, grew and multiplied. It is exceedingly difficult for a child to grow in spirit and among mortals of stone [reading uncertain: “and among mortals of stone”]. “The child grew and was strengthened in spirit” (Matt. XXIX).

“Grew” is one thing; “was strengthened” is another. Human nature is weak, and in order to become stronger it needs divine assistance. We read: “The flesh is weak.” By what assistance, then, must it be strengthened? Certainly by the spirit. “The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak.”

The person who wishes to become stronger must be strengthened in nothing except the Spirit. Many are strengthened in flesh and made robust in body; but God’s athlete must be strengthened in spirit. When he has been strengthened in this way, he will destroy the wisdom of the flesh, and, having become spiritual, will subject the body to the rule of the soul.

Let us not therefore think that a simple history concerning John has been written, one that has no relevance to us, in the statement that he “grew and was strengthened in spirit.” Rather, it is for our imitation, so that, having been spiritually multiplied according to the sense we have described, we too may receive increase.

“And he was in the deserts until the day of his manifestation to Israel.”

[Note: I would prefer *Dixi* in the direct first-person form. We silently correct a few other minor matters.]

He said recently that John’s conception also possessed something astonishing, when the infant leaped in the womb and recognized his Lord, though he had not yet been born; and that his birth was no less a miracle, when Zacharias’s prophetic speech was directed toward him as though he were listening: “And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High.”

Accordingly, he who had been conceived and born in this manner did not wait to be nourished by his father until the day of his manifestation to Israel. Instead, he withdrew, fleeing the tumult of cities, the crowds of the people, and the proximity of towns, and went into the deserts, where the air was purer, the sky more open, and God more accessible.

Since the sacrament of baptism and the time of preaching had not yet arrived, he devoted himself to prayers and conversed with the angels; he called upon the Lord and heard him answer and say: “Behold, here I am” (Matt. XI).

For just as Moses spoke and God answered him, so I think John spoke in the desert and the Lord answered him. I believe this, moved by a firm argument from Scripture. For if no one born of women was greater than John the Baptist, and God answered Moses, then he accordingly answered John, who was greater than Moses; John was nourished in the wilderness, and the same archangel who announced the Lord announced his birth, while his father, who did not believe that he would be born, became mute.

John was therefore in the desert and was nourished in a new manner, beyond human nature, as Matthew himself records: “His food was locusts and wild honey” (Matt. III).

Because he was the minister of the Savior’s first coming and spoke only about the dispensation of the Lord’s flesh, and because his prophecy foretold the one who had been born of the Virgin, he did not have domestic honey, strained through human diligence, but wild honey; nor did he have a large bird, one rising into the heights, but a small bird, scarcely rising from the ground, jumping rather than flying.

What more is there to say? It is stated most clearly that locusts were his food, a small and clean animal.

Consider, therefore, dearest brothers, that he who had been born in a new manner was nourished in a new manner.

After these things Scripture adds: “Now it happened in those days that an edict went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be enrolled” [Col. 0242A]. “This was the first census under the governor of Syria, Quirinius” (Luke II).

Someone may say: O Gospel narrative!
