Since the first census of the whole world took place under Caesar Augustus, and among all the others Joseph also registered himself with Mary, who was betrothed to him and pregnant, and since Jesus was born before the census was completed, closer examination seems to reveal a certain mystery: Christ too had to be registered in the enrollment of the whole world, so that, being enrolled with all, he might sanctify all; and, being registered with the world, he might grant the world a share in himself.

After this enrollment, he would enroll in the book of the living with himself all those from the world, so that whoever had believed in him might afterward be written with his saints in heaven—to him be glory and dominion forever and ever [Col. 0242C]. Amen.

*279–280 HOMILY XII.* On the passage that is written, that an angel came from heaven and announced the Lord’s birth to the shepherds. Chapter II.

My Lord Jesus was born, and an angel descended from heaven announcing his birth. Let us therefore see whom he sought in order to announce his coming. He did not come to Jerusalem; he did not seek the scribes and Pharisees; he did not enter the synagogue of the Jews. Rather, he found shepherds keeping watch over their flocks, and he spoke to them: “Today a Savior has been born, who is Christ the Lord.”

Do you think that the divine discourse of Scripture signifies nothing else, but only that the angel came to shepherds and spoke to them? Hear, shepherds of the churches, shepherds of God, that his angel always descends from heaven and announces to you that today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord.

For the shepherds of the churches will not be able to guard the flock well by themselves unless that shepherd comes; their guardianship is weak unless Christ feeds and guards it with them.

Earlier we read in the Apostle: “We are God’s fellow workers” (I Cor. III). The good shepherd, who imitates the good shepherd (John X), is a fellow worker of God and Christ. Therefore the good shepherd is the one who has with him the best shepherd, sharing the task of feeding him.

“For God has placed in the Church apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds, teachers, all for the perfection of the saints” (Eph. IV). These things have been stated in the simpler manner.

But if it is necessary to ascend to a more sacred understanding, I shall say that there were certain shepherds who were angels and governed human affairs. While each of them preserved his own charge, keeping watch by day and night, and could no longer bear the labor, yet diligently carrying out the task of governing the nations entrusted to him, the angel came at the Lord’s birth and announced to the shepherds that the true shepherd had arisen.

To give an example: there was a certain shepherd of Macedonia who needed the Lord’s assistance. Therefore a Macedonian man appeared to Paul in a dream, saying: “Cross over into Macedonia and help us” (Acts XVI).

Why should I speak of Paul, when it was not Paul but Jesus, who was in Paul, who spoke these words? The shepherds therefore need the presence of Christ.

For this reason the angel descended from heaven and said: “Do not be afraid. For behold, I announce to you great joy.” Truly it was great joy for those to whom the care of peoples and provinces had been entrusted that Christ had come into the world.

The angel who administered the affairs of the Egyptians received great benefit after the Lord descended from heaven so that the Egyptians might become Christians. It also benefited all those who governed different provinces—for example, the governor of Macedonia, the governor of Achaea, and the governors of the other regions.

For it is not right to believe that evil angels governed their provinces while good angels were not permitted to have those same provinces [Col. 0243C] entrusted to them.

What he says about individual provinces, I think we should also believe generally about all human beings. Two angels attend each person [Note: Concerning the angels appointed over the guardianship of human beings and provinces, according to Origen’s opinion—though he was not entirely consistent with himself—we shall speak somewhat further below, at Homilies 23 and 35]: one of justice, the other of iniquity.

If good thoughts are in our heart and justice has begun to flourish in our mind, there is no doubt that the angel of the Lord is speaking to us. But if evil thoughts are active in our heart, the angel of the devil speaks to us.

Therefore, just as there are two angels assigned to each person, so I think that different angels exist in each province: good ones and evil ones.

For example, in Ephesus, because there were sinners in that city, exceedingly wicked angels presided. Again, because many believers were there, there was also the angel of the Ephesian church, certainly a good one.

What we have said about Ephesus should be understood concerning all the provinces.

Before the coming of the Lord and Savior, these angels could bring little benefit to those entrusted to them, and their efforts could not produce corresponding results. This shows how little they could profit their subjects.

Listen to what we are saying. When the angel of the Egyptians was helping the Egyptians, scarcely one proselyte believed in God—and this occurred while the angel was administering the Egyptians.

Finally, because many of the Egyptians and Idumeans received the faith of Christ as proselytes, Scripture says: “You shall not abhor an Egyptian, because you were strangers in the land of Egypt, nor an Idumean, because he is your brother. If children are born to them, in the third generation they shall enter the assembly of God” (Deut. XXIII).

Thus it happened that from all the nations some became proselytes, with the assistance of the angels who had the nations subject to them.

Now, however, peoples of believers approach the faith of Jesus, and the angels to whom the churches have been entrusted, strengthened by the presence of the Savior, bring many proselytes, so that Christian assemblies may be gathered throughout the whole world.

Therefore, let us rise and praise the Lord, and let us become, in place of carnal Israel, spiritual Israel. Let us bless almighty God in deed, thought, and speech, in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

*HOMILY XIII.* On the passage that is written, “And a multitude of the heavenly army appeared,” up to the place where it says, “They found Mary and Jesus lying in a manger.” Chapter II.

[Col. 0244B]

Our Lord and Savior is in Bethlehem, and the multitude of the heavenly host praises God and says: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among people of good will.” The multitude of the heavenly host says this because it had already ceased to be able to offer human beings assistance, and saw that it could not fulfill the work entrusted to it without the one who could truly save, and also help the rulers themselves so that human beings might be saved.

How, then, is it written [Col. 0244C] in the Gospel that certain men, rowing across the sea against contrary winds, had already grown weary and, laboring for twenty-five or thirty stadia, could not reach the harbor; afterward the Lord came upon them, made the swelling waves rest, and rescued the boat, whose sides were being battered on either hand, from its impending danger (John 6)? Understand in the same way that the angels also wished to offer human beings assistance and grant them healing from their illnesses, since “all are ministering spirits sent out for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation” (Heb. 1). To the extent of their powers, they helped human beings.

But they saw that their own medicine was far inferior to what the care of those people required. To understand what we are saying by an example, [Col. 0244D] imagine for me a city in which very many people are sick and the hands of physicians are frequently employed. Let there be various wounds, and let corruption creeping daily into dead flesh penetrate further; yet let the physicians summoned to treat them be unable to discover any further remedies or, by their knowledge of the art, overcome the magnitude of the evil. When they find themselves in such circumstances, suppose that a chief physician arrives who possesses the highest knowledge of the art. When those who previously had been unable to heal see the putrefaction of the wounds cease at the master’s hand, let them not envy him or be tormented by jealousy, but break out in praise of the chief physician [Col. 0245A] and proclaim God, who has sent them and the sick people a man of such great skill.

In this same likeness, then, the multitude of the angelic host was heard saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among people of good will.” For after the Lord came to earth, he made peace through the blood of his cross, both for the things on earth and for the things in heaven (Eph. 1). Since the angels wished human beings to remember their Creator, and had done all that lay within their powers so that they might be healed, but human beings had been unwilling to look toward healing, they behold the one who was able to heal and, glorifying him, say: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace.”

Let the diligent reader of Scripture inquire how the Savior says: “I have not come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword” [Col. 0245B] (Matt. 10), 283–284, while now, at his birth, the angels sing, “On earth peace.” For elsewhere, too, he is represented as saying in his own person: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you. I do not give you peace as this world gives it; I give you peace” (John 14).

Let him therefore consider whether what we propose can resolve the question. If it had been written simply, “On earth peace,” and the sentence had ended there, the question would rightly arise. But what has been added—namely, the words that follow “peace,” “among people of good will”—resolves the question.

For the peace that the Lord does not give upon the earth is not the peace of good will. He does not simply say, “I have not come to bring peace,” but adds, “upon the earth”; nor, conversely, does he say, “I have not come to bring peace upon the earth among people of good will.”

This is what the angels said to the shepherds. They were not speaking only at that time; even today, unless they speak to shepherds and join their own work to theirs, the saying is addressed to them: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it labors in vain” (Ps. 127).

If one may boldly speak while following the meaning of Scripture, there are two bishops in each church: one visible, the other invisible—the former accessible to bodily sight, the latter to spiritual perception.

Just as a human being is praised by the Lord if he administers well the stewardship entrusted to him, but if badly, is subject to blame and fault, so also is an angel. For it is written in the Apocalypse of John: “But you have there a few names who have defiled this or that.” And again: “You have there those who teach the doctrine of the Nicolaitans” (Rev. 2). Then there are those committing this or that sin, and the angels to whom the churches have been entrusted are accused.

**Note:** Let us attribute this to the ingenuity of Adamantius: that he interprets the passage in Apocalypse 11 in this way and assigns two bishops to each church, one visible and the other by no means falling under the eyes—a point he repeats below in Homily 23. But that which he adds shortly afterward, namely, that the good guardian angels often fail to perform their office while we are laboring and are themselves at fault, must be rejected by every pious person as wholly contrary to the faith. See what we have remarked below, at Homily 23, against this solemn opinion of Origen concerning the fall of angels.

If the angels are concerned with how the churches are governed, what need is there to speak of human beings, and how great their fear must be if, laboring together with the angels who labor, they are to attain salvation? I think that both an angel and a human being can at the same time be good bishops of a church and, in a certain way, share in one work.

Since this is so, let us ask almighty God that the angels and human beings who are bishops of the churches may be our helpers, and let us know that both will be judged by the Lord on our behalf. But if they are judged and the fault and sin are found not in their negligence but in ours, we shall be accused and punished. Even though they do everything and strive for our salvation, we nevertheless remain free from sins. Yet it often happens that, while we are laboring, they do not fulfill their office and are at fault.

“And it happened,” he says, “when the angels had gone away from them into heaven, the shepherds said to one another” [Col. 0246B]: “Let us go as far as Bethlehem and see this word that has come to pass, which the Lord has shown us.” They came in haste and found Mary and Joseph and the child.

Because they had come in haste, and not slowly or with a weary step, they found Joseph, the steward of the Lord’s birth, and Mary, who had brought Jesus forth in childbirth, and the Savior himself lying in a manger.

This was the event concerning which the prophet had foretold, saying: “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger.” The ox is a clean animal, the donkey an unclean animal. “The donkey knows its master’s manger.” It was not the people of Israel who knew their Lord’s manger, but the unclean animal from the nations. “Israel did not know me, and my people did not understand” (Isa. 1).

Understanding this manger, [Col. 0246C] let us strive to know the Lord and to become worthy of knowledge of him, and also to embrace the birth and resurrection of his flesh, as well as his glorious and majestic second coming. To him belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## 285–286. HOMILY XIV

On the passage that is written: “When the days of his circumcision had been fulfilled,” up to the place where it says: “A pair of turtledoves and two young pigeons.” Chapter 2.

Since Christ died, he died for sin—not because he himself had sinned, for he committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth—but he died so that we, who were dead, might not live in sin and vices when he died to sins (Rom. 6).

Hence it is written: Just as we died together with him when he died and rose together with him when he arose, so we were circumcised with him and, after circumcision, cleansed by solemn purification. Therefore we no longer need bodily circumcision.

And so that you may know that he was circumcised for our sake, hear Paul proclaiming it most plainly: “In him,” he says, “the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him, who is the head of every principality and power. In him you were also circumcised with a circumcision not performed by hands, in the stripping away of the body of flesh, in the circumcision of Christ, having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised through faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead” (Col. 1).

His death, then, and resurrection and circumcision were all accomplished for us.

“When the days for circumcising the child had been fulfilled, his name was called Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived.” The name of Jesus is glorious and is to be uttered with every act of worship and reverence; it was not brought into the world by them, but by some higher and greater nature. Therefore the evangelist expressly added: “And his name was called Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb.”

Then it follows: “When the days of their purification had been fulfilled according to the law of Moses, they brought him to Jerusalem.” He says, “for their purification.” Whose purification? If it had been written, “for his purification,” that is, Mary’s, who had given birth, no question would arise, and we would confidently say that Mary, who was human, had needed purification after childbirth.

**Note:** Jerome judged kindly concerning Adamantius when, in the preface to this very translation, he said that he played like a child in such matters. For although he pronounced many things elsewhere in the Homilies on Luke to be absurd, there is no possible excuse for what he uttered in working out this fourteenth homily. Here he most boldly babbles that Mary, since she was human, needed purification and was therefore subject to sin. I know that Sixtus of Siena, in book 6 of his *Bibliotheca*, annotation 136, attempts to excuse him in this way: “Perhaps Origen understands not purification from the uncleanness and pollution of childbirth, to which no one doubts that Mary was not subject, but the rites and ceremonies by which Moses commanded women after childbirth to be purified. These had to be observed by the mother of the one who came to fulfill the law, not destroy it.” The distinguished Huet also supports this, confirming it from what Origen writes in Homily 8 on Leviticus: that only those women are unclean in childbirth who conceive and give birth after receiving semen, whereas she who gave birth without receiving semen is not unclean. There he also cites a notable passage of Origen from Homily 12 on Leviticus, in which the purity of Christ’s generation and of Mary’s virginal body is most explicitly proclaimed. Yet although it may be inferred that this man of immoderate and uncertain judgment thought correctly elsewhere, this does not at all remove the manifest offense. Since elsewhere also—in Homily 20 on this same Evangelist—he is insulting toward the Virgin Mary, whom he accuses of doubtful and uncertain faith, it was necessary to warn the pious reader to guard against scandal and to hold, against the blasphemies of heretics, the faith of the orthodox Church, which teaches that the Blessed Virgin, by a special privilege of God, never admitted any sin into herself.

But now, in that he says “the days of their purification,” the phrase does not seem to signify one person, but another or several. Therefore Jesus needed purification and was unclean, or polluted by some uncleanness.

**Note:** The Greek reading αὐτῶν (*autōn*, “their”), which is still found today, instead of αὐτῆς (*autēs*, “her”), led Adamantius into error. Huet also noted this and calls the reading corrupt, wishing the other reading, αὐτῆς—namely, “her”—to be substituted for it entirely, in accordance with the Vulgate and the Arabic translation of Erpenius’s edition, to which I add the Coptic. Indeed, Origen himself could have been warned against his error by the passage in Leviticus 12, which commands purification for the woman who has given birth, not for the infant as well. Now, although he declares that Jesus needed purification not because of sin—for the mind recoils from imagining this concerning Christ—he nevertheless says that he needed it because of pollution, and pronounces him unclean or defiled by some uncleanness. He also wrongly twists the passage from Job to his own meaning: “No one is clean from uncleanness,” and so forth. Most wickedly he inserts here his customary delirium: that the soul becomes defiled when it assumes a mortal body, and that Jesus likewise must be regarded as defiled according to the disgrace of the cross, since his soul joined itself to a body in a woman’s womb. Hence below he also abuses the twenty-first Psalm, making the Savior say: “I am a worm and not a man,” and so forth. He says that he saw the uncleanness of bodies in his mother’s womb, enclosed on every side by her viscera and suffering the constraints of earthly filth.

I may perhaps seem rash to say this, but I am moved by the authority of Scripture. Consider what is written in Job: “No one is clean from uncleanness, not even if his life is but a single day” (Job 15). It does not say, “No one is clean from sin,” but “No one is clean from uncleanness.” For uncleanness and sins do not mean the same thing. And so that you may know that uncleanness means one thing and sin another, Isaiah teaches this plainly, saying: “The Lord will wash away the uncleanness of the sons and daughters of Zion, and he will cleanse the blood from their midst, by the spirit of judgment the uncleanness, and by the spirit of burning the blood” (Isa. 4).

Every soul clothed in a human body has its own uncleanness. But so that you may know that Jesus too must be understood as defiled according to the disgrace of the cross, not according to the holy flesh that he assumed, concerning which the Apostle says that he was made “in the likeness of sinful flesh” by his own will, because he assumed a human body for our salvation, hear the prophet Zechariah saying: “Jesus was clothed in filthy garments” (Zech. 3).

This passage also works against those who deny that our Lord had a human body, claiming that it was woven from heavenly and spiritual elements.

**Note:** These were Marcionites and Ebionites, whom Gennadius reports in his *Book on Dogmas*, chapter 2, to have claimed that the Son of God brought flesh with him from heaven. It is therefore all the more surprising that he says Origen agreed with them, since Origen taught that Christ bore an imaginary body which merely appeared in outward form. I do not know, although elsewhere Adamantius rightly speaks of Christ’s true body, especially below in Homily 17, whether Origen’s faith can be defended by a clearer testimony than this very exposition concerning Christ’s filthy garments. Formerly Pamphilus removed this very charge from Adamantius’s writings.

If his body was heavenly—or, as they falsely assert, from the stars and from some other, higher and spiritual nature—let them answer why a spiritual body could be filthy, or how they interpret what we have cited: “Jesus was clothed in filthy garments.”

But if they are compelled by necessity to understand the filthy garment as a spiritual body, they must consequently say that what is set forth in the promises has been fulfilled, namely: “The natural body is sown; the spiritual body is raised” (1 Cor. 15), and that we rise polluted and filthy—which is itself a sacrilege even to think, especially for one who knows that it is written: “It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption. It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power. It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body.”

Therefore, on behalf of our Lord and Savior, who had been clothed in filthy garments and had assumed an earthly body, those things had to be offered which the Law ordinarily used to cleanse uncleanness.

I return to a question frequently raised among the brethren, occasioned by this passage. Infants are baptized for the forgiveness of sins. Whose sins are they, and when did they sin? Or how can any reason for washing exist in infants, unless it is according to the meaning about which we said shortly before: “No one is clean from uncleanness, not even if his life is but a single day upon the earth”?

**Note:** Either he said this with the meaning that those uncleannesses were uncleannesses of the soul, that is, sin—and thus he was blasphemous toward Christ—or, as is closer to his intention, he considered them bodily uncleannesses without guilt, and thereby removes original sin while comparing infant baptism to a legal ceremony. Indeed, there are other passages in Adamantius’s writings that bear the gravest suspicion of this error.

And because the uncleanness of birth is removed through the sacrament of baptism, infants too are baptized. “Unless someone is born again of water and Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3).

“When the days of their purification had been fulfilled.” The days of righteousness are fulfilled as well. For the soul is not purified immediately upon being born, nor can it attain perfect purity at the very moment of birth. Rather, as it is written in the Law: “If she gives birth to a male, the mother shall sit for seven days in the blood of her uncleanness, and then for thirty-three days in clean blood, and finally the infant himself shall sit in the purest blood” (Luke 2). Thus, because the law is spiritual and possesses “a shadow of the good things to come” (Rom. 7; Heb. 10), we can understand that true purification comes to us only after a period of time.

I think that even after the resurrection from the dead we shall need a sacrament that washes and purifies us, for no one can rise without uncleanness, nor can any soul be found that is immediately free of every vice.

**Note:** Similar statements occur below in Homily 24, where he declares that only those baptized by Christ in a river of fire will be purified who have been baptized with water and Spirit and require purification; the faults and vices of the wicked, however, will be utterly burned away by the flames. Genebrardus warns that this doctrine must be avoided. Sixtus of Siena explains it more leniently and refers it to the fire of the final conflagration, which will cleanse some of the elect who have not yet been sufficiently purified, while it will seize all the reprobate. Huet objects, arguing that Origen’s words cannot be understood in this sense, since he does not consider even the holiest men—Peter or Paul, for example—to be exempt from this fire. Suarez, in turn, answers him; in volume 4 of his commentary on the third part of Thomas Aquinas, question 46, section 4, he claims that these words are faulty and corrupted through the error of scribes, proving this chiefly from Origen’s statement shortly above that it is a sacrilege even to think that we rise polluted and filthy. “Indeed,” says Huet, “we find such great hesitation in Origen on many points that it is no novelty to me that, in the same homily, he should disclose diverse and contradictory views.” What could be clearer than this very statement: “For he cannot rise without uncleanness”? I therefore believe that those who strive to rescue this passage from the charge of error rely on a futile argument.

Thus, in the regeneration of baptism, the sacrament is assumed so that, just as Jesus was purified according to the dispensation of the flesh by an offering, so we too may be purified through spiritual regeneration.

According to the law of Moses, they brought him to Jerusalem to present him before the Lord. 289–290 Where are those who deny the God of the Law, who say that not this God but another was proclaimed in the Gospel? “God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the Law.” Is it therefore to be thought that the good God made his Son subject to the Law of the Creator and to the authority of an enemy whom he himself had appointed? Rather, he was made subject to the Law in order to redeem those who were under the Law (Gal. 4) and subject them to another law, of which we read earlier: “Attend, my people, to my law,” and what follows.

They brought him, therefore, and set him before the presence of the Lord. Whose scriptural precepts were they fulfilling? Clearly, those of that same Lord. “As it is written,” he says, “in the Law of Moses: Every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord, and every male shall appear three times a year before the Lord God.”

Male children who were holy because they had opened their mother’s womb were offered before the altar of the Lord. “Every male,” he says, “that opens the womb.” The phrase suggests something sacred. For although any male born from the womb may be called a male, no other opens his mother’s womb as the Lord Jesus did, because in the case of all other women it is not the child’s birth but intercourse with a man that opens the womb (Num. 8).

At the time of the Lord’s birth, his mother’s womb was opened, and the child was brought forth, because no male had touched that holy womb, worthy of every honor and veneration, before Christ’s birth.

**Note:** This is likewise an error of certain ancient writers, especially Tertullian in *On the Flesh of Christ*, chapter 23, and those whom Genebrardus and Huet cite—namely Ambrose, Athanasius, and Basil—who discuss the opening of the virginal enclosure in childbirth. Huet rightly observes that all of them must be given the exception that Thomas used to resolve Ambrose’s passage, in part 3, question 28, article 2. He speaks in this way: when those Fathers interpreted the Evangelist’s words, “Every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord,” the phrase was used according to the common manner of speaking, not to signify the breaking of the virgin’s seal in childbirth, but merely the child’s exit from the womb. Furthermore, as Huet notes, this is the teaching of the best part of the Fathers, both Greek and Latin, as well as the decree of the Council of Ephesus, confirmed by the perpetual consensus of the Church and strengthened by the oracle of Ezekiel: “This gate shall remain closed; it shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it, because the Lord, the God of Israel, has entered through it; and it shall remain closed to the prince.” This teaches that Mary’s virginity remained inviolate both in conception and in childbirth, and that Christ’s body came forth in the same way that he entered to the disciples through closed doors.

I dare to say this because, in the passage where it is written, “The Spirit of God will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1), there was both the beginning of the seed and conception, and a new fetus grew in the womb without the opening of the womb.

Hence the Savior also says: “I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people” (Ps. 21). He saw in his mother’s womb the uncleanness of bodies, was enclosed on every side by her viscera, and suffered the constraints of earthly filth; therefore he compares himself to a worm and says: “I am a worm and not a man.”

A human being ordinarily comes into existence from male and female, but I was not born from male and female according to human custom and nature; rather, I was born like a worm, whose seed does not come from elsewhere, but whose origin arises within and from the very bodies in which it comes together.

Therefore, because “every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord,” he was brought to Jerusalem to appear before God. This was also because of what follows: “To offer a sacrifice for him,” as it is written in the Law of the Lord: “A pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons” (Luke 2:24).

A pair of turtledoves and two young pigeons were offered on behalf of the Savior. I also think these blessed birds fortunate, since they were offered for the Lord’s birth. Just as I admire Balaam’s she-donkey and heap praise upon her good fortune because she was worthy not only to see the angel of God but also, with her mouth opened, to break forth into human speech, so I praise and exalt these birds even more because they were offered for our Lord and Savior.

“To offer on his behalf a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.” I may perhaps seem to be introducing something novel, but it is scarcely worthy of his majesty. Just as the Savior’s generation was new—not from man and woman, but from the Virgin alone—so the pair of turtledoves and the two young pigeons were not such as we behold with bodily eyes, but such as the Holy Spirit is, who descended and came upon the Savior in the form of a dove when he was baptized in the Jordan (Matt. 3).

Such also was the pair of turtledoves. They were not birds such as these, which fly through the air, but something divine and more august than human contemplation appeared under the form of a dove and a turtledove. Thus the one who was born for the whole world and destined to suffer was not cleansed before the Lord by sacrifices of the kind offered by all human beings, but, just as his dispensation was new in every respect, so it had new sacrifices as well, according to the will of almighty God in Christ Jesus.

**Note:** Origen rightly earned continual censure among the Fathers because, in expounding the Scriptures, he frequently ruined the historical sense and forestalled the truth of the matter by allegorical expositions. I certainly do not know with what excuse this interpretation can be covered, since he denies that the turtledoves offered for Christ were birds such as fly through the air, maintaining instead that something divine and more august than human contemplation appeared under the form of a dove and a turtledove.

To him belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XV

On Simeon, that he came to the temple in the Spirit, up to the place where it says: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, in peace.” Chapter 2.

A reason worthy of God’s gift must be sought. Simeon was a holy man and pleasing to the Lord. As it is written in the Gospel, he was awaiting the consolation of Israel and had received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ.

What benefit did it bring him to see Christ? Was this the whole content of the promise—that he would see him but gain no useful benefit from seeing him? Or is there some gift worthy of God hidden here, which blessed Simeon both deserved and received?

A woman touched the fringe of Jesus’ garment and was healed (Matt. 9). If she gained such benefit merely from touching the edge of his garment, what should we think of Simeon, who received the infant into his arms, held him against his breast, and rejoiced and exulted at seeing himself carry the child who had come to release those in bonds and to free Simeon himself from the bonds of the body? He knew that no one could release anyone from the prison of the body with hope of future life except the one whom he held in his arms.

Therefore he says to him: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, in peace.” As long as I did not hold Christ, as long as I did not clasp him in my arms, I was imprisoned and unable to leave my bonds. This must be understood not only of Simeon but of the whole human race.

If anyone departs from the world, if anyone is released from the prison and dwelling of captives in order to go and reign, let him take Jesus in his hands, encircle him with his arms, and hold him entirely in his bosom. Then, rejoicing, he will be able to go wherever he desires.

Consider how much providence preceded this, so that Simeon might be worthy to hold the Son of God. First he had received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ. Then he did not enter the temple by chance or casually, but came into the temple in the Spirit of God. “All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Rom. 8; Eph. 2).

The Holy Spirit therefore led him into the temple. You too, if you wish to hold Jesus, embrace him in your hands, and become worthy to leave prison, strive with every effort to have the Spirit as your guide and to come to the temple of God.

Behold, now you stand in the temple of the Lord Jesus, that is, in his church; this is the temple built from living stones. You stand in the temple of the Lord when your life and conduct are worthy to be called the church.

If you come in the Spirit to the temple, you will find the infant Jesus, lift him in your arms, and say: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, in peace, according to your word.”

At the same time, observe that peace has been added to release and dismissal. He does not say simply, “I wish to be dismissed,” but adds, “to be dismissed in peace.” The same thing was promised to blessed Abraham: “But you shall go to your fathers in peace, nourished in a good old age.”

Who dies in peace except one who possesses the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding and guards the heart of its possessor? Who departs from this world in peace except one who understands that “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself,” who has nothing hostile or opposed to God, but has taken on every peace and harmony through good works in himself, and is thus dismissed in peace to go to the holy Fathers, to whom holy Abraham also departed (Phil. 1)?

Why speak of the Fathers? We should go also to Jesus himself, who is the chief and Lord of the patriarchs, concerning whom it is said: “It is better to depart and be with Christ.”

He possesses Jesus who dares to say: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20).

Therefore, so that we too, standing in the temple, holding and embracing the Son of God, may be worthy of release [293–294] and departure to better things, let us pray to almighty God. Let us also pray to the little Jesus himself, whom we desire to address and hold in our arms.

**Note:** From this one may infer, as also from the conclusions of Homilies 18 and 36 and from many other passages noted in our comments on the Homilies on Jeremiah and Ezekiel, that Origen held that the Son should indeed be prayed to with the Father, but with a different kind of prayer. This teaching brought him much hostility, as though he had held: “The Son must not be prayed to, nor the Father together with the Son.” This is precisely the charge brought by Theophilus in the synodal letter first published by us among Jerome’s Epistles, 92, no. 2, col. 541; it is worth recalling.

To him belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XVI

On the passage that is written: “His father and mother were marveling at what was said about him,” up to the place where it says: “Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel.” Chapter 2.

And, he says, “his father and mother were marveling at the things that were being said about him.” Let us gather together what was said and written about Jesus at his birth, and now we shall be able to understand that each detail is worthy of wonder. Thus his father too—Joseph was called this because he had been his foster-father—marveled, and his mother marveled, at everything that was being said about him. What, then, were the reports that had spread abroad concerning the infant Jesus?

There were shepherds in that region, keeping watch and guarding the watches of the night over their flock. An angel came at the very hour of Jesus’ birth and said to them: “I announce to you great joy. Go, and you will find an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes and lying in a manger.” The angel had not yet finished speaking, and behold, a multitude of the heavenly army began to praise and bless God. When the shepherds had anxiously witnessed this and the angel had withdrawn from them, they said to one another: “Let us go to Bethlehem and see the event that the Lord has shown us.” They came and found the infant. Both they and his parents, seeing what had happened, marveled at it.

And concerning Simeon it is written that he increased the report of the miracle, or that he played a major part in it: he took the child in his arms and said: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, in peace, according to your word, because my eyes have seen your salvation.” Simeon’s words were the climax and, so to speak, the summit of all that was being proclaimed about Jesus, at which both his father and his mother marveled. For Simeon was not content merely to hold the infant and proclaim what had been written about himself; he also blessed his father and mother, and prophesied concerning the infant himself, saying: “Behold, this one is appointed for the downfall and resurrection of many in Israel, and for a sign that will be opposed. And a sword will pass through your own soul also, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.”

What does he mean by saying, “Behold, this one is appointed for the downfall and resurrection of many in Israel”? Something similar to this is found written in the Gospel according to John: “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9). Just as, then, he came for judgment so that those who did not see among the nations might see, while those who previously saw among Israel might become blind, so he came for the downfall and resurrection of many. For at the coming of the Lord and Savior, those who had previously stood fell, and those who had fallen rose. This is one interpretation of the saying: “Behold, this one is appointed for the downfall and resurrection of many in Israel.”

There is also a deeper meaning to be understood, directed especially against those who bark against the Creator and, gathering testimonies here and there from the Old Testament that they do not understand, deceive the hearts of the simple. They say: “Behold the God of the Law and the prophets; see what he is like: ‘I kill and I make alive; I strike, and I heal; and there is no one who can deliver from my hands’” (Deuteronomy 32). They hear “I kill,” but do not hear “I make alive”; they hear “I strike,” and refuse to hear “and I heal.” On such pretexts they slander the Creator.

Before, then, interpreting what is meant by “I kill and I make alive; I strike and I heal,” I shall set before them a testimony from the Gospel and speak against the heretics. Innumerable heresies accept the Gospel according to Luke. If the Creator is therefore bloody, so savage and cruel, because he says, “I kill and I make alive; I strike and I heal,” then it is most clearly established that Jesus is also his Son, since the same things have been written about him: “Behold, this one is appointed for the downfall and resurrection of many in Israel.” He is appointed not only for resurrection but also for downfall. If killing is evil, then coming for downfall must also be evil. What will they answer? Will they withdraw from his worship, or will they seek some interpretation and flee to allegorical explanations, so that the fact that he came for downfall may signify kindness rather than severity? And how will it be just, when something of this kind is found in the Gospel, to flee to allegories and novel interpretations, while, whenever it occurs in the Old Testament, they immediately accuse and accept no explanation, however plausible it may be?

The same applies to what follows: “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.” Even if they seek to explain this, they will not be able to fulfill their purpose. But because I desire to be called a member of the Church, not of some heresiarch, and to bear the name that is blessed on earth, and because I desire both in conduct and in understanding to be and to be called a Christian, I seek an equal interpretation in both the Old and the New Law.

[Note: Let us grant Origen this praise: that he waged unceasing war to the death against heretics and continually commanded that those things which the Church set forth be held firmly and believed. Pamphilus, in the *Apology*, says: “How, while destroying all the doctrines of the heretics, he himself, Origen, always confirmed the Apostolic faith—if we wished to gather all his opinions—would be a sufficiently lengthy task, burdensome both to us who write and tedious to those who read.”]

God says: “I kill.” I gladly accept that God should kill me. For when the old human being is in me and I am still living as a human being, I desire God to kill the old human being in me and to bring me to life from the dead. “The first human being,” it says, “was from the earth, earthly; the second human being is from heaven, heavenly. Just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly” (1 Corinthians 15).

In accordance with this meaning, the following also is understood: “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.” We all possess within us both sight and blindness. Adam both saw and did not see. Eve too is described as having seen before her eyes were opened. “The woman saw,” it says, “that the tree was good for food and excellent to the eyes for seeing; and she took of the fruit of the tree, ate, and gave it to her husband, and they ate” (Genesis 3). Thus they were not blind, but they saw. Then what follows says: “And their eyes were opened.” Therefore they had been blind and had not seen, since afterward their eyes were opened. But those who had previously seen well, after transgressing the Lord’s command, began to see badly; and when sin had stolen away the sight of obedience, they afterward lost it.

I understand in the same way what God says: “Who made the mute and the deaf, the seeing and the blind? Is it not I, the Lord God?” (Exodus 4). There is the bodily eye with which we behold earthly things—the eye according to the sense of the flesh, concerning which Scripture says: “You walk about vainly inflated by the sense of the flesh” (Colossians 2). We have another eye opposed to this one, a better and divinely wise eye. Because it was blind in us, Jesus came to make it see, so that those who did not see might see, and those who saw might become blind.

According to this meaning, what we now have before us is also to be understood: “Behold, this one is appointed for the downfall and resurrection of many in Israel.” There is something in me that stands badly, and the pride of sin raises itself up: let this fall, let this be overthrown. And if it falls—what had previously fallen—then, rising, it will stand. My inner human being once lay crushed, while the outer human being stood upright. Before I believed in Jesus, what was good in me lay prostrate, while what was evil stood. After he came, what was evil in me collapsed, and the saying was fulfilled: “Always carrying in the body the death of Jesus.” And also: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, idolatry, sorcery” (Colossians 3), and the rest. The downfall of all these things was beneficial.

Of this downfall it is said: “Wherever the corpse is, there the eagles will gather” (Matthew 24). The word “corpse” derives its name from falling.

[Note: It is by no means necessary to suppose that these words were supplied by the Latin translator: “corpse” derives its name from falling. Origen does not play upon this etymology only once, as Saint Epiphanius testifies in his letter to John of Jerusalem, among Jerome’s letters 51.4: “This body is called, according to the Greeks, δέμας, that is, ‘bond,’ or, according to another derivation, πτῶμα, that is, ‘corpse,’ because souls have fallen from heaven.” Indeed, the Greeks call an inanimate body πτῶμα. Adamantius, having found a convenient etymology for his exposition—an etymology which elsewhere he twisted in support of his opinion—here wrote: πτῶμα γοῦν ἀπὸ πτώσεως λέγεται, “A corpse, then, derives its name from falling.”]

This is the one downfall for which Jesus first came; and he cannot bring about resurrection unless downfall has preceded it. He came first to destroy what was evil in me, so that, after it has been destroyed and put to death, what is good may rise up and be brought to life in me, and so that through our Lord Jesus Christ we may attain the kingdom of heaven. To him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XVII

On the passage written: “His father and mother were marveling at the things that were being said about him,” continuing to the place where Anna is mentioned. Chapter 2.

Luke, who wrote: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who is born will be called the Son of God,” and who plainly handed down to us that Jesus is the son of a Virgin and was not conceived from human seed—this same Luke attested that Joseph was his father, saying: “His father and mother were marveling at the things that were being said about him.”

What reason, then, was there for him to call one who was not the father “father”? Whoever is content with a simple explanation says: “The Holy Spirit honored him with the title ‘father,’ because he had raised the Savior.” But whoever seeks something deeper can say: “Because the genealogical succession is traced from David to Joseph” (Matthew 1), and so that Joseph might not seem to be named without reason, since the genealogical succession had to have its place, he was called the Lord’s father (Luke 3).

His father and mother, therefore, marveled at the things that were being said about him, both by the angel and by the multitude of the heavenly army and by the shepherds. For when they heard all these things, they marveled exceedingly.

Then Scripture says: “Simeon blessed him and said to Mary his mother: ‘Behold, this one is appointed for the downfall and resurrection of many in Israel, and for a sign that will be opposed. And a sword will pass through your own soul, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.’” We must contemplate how the Savior came for the downfall and resurrection of many.

Whoever [Alternatively: What] explains the matter simply may say that he came for the downfall of unbelievers and the resurrection of believers. But the inquisitive interpreter says that no one can fall who has not previously stood. Tell me, then, who it was that stood and for whose downfall the Savior came, and also who it is that rises. For surely the one rises who previously fell.

We must consider whether perhaps the Savior came not for downfall and resurrection among different people, but among the same people, for both downfall and resurrection. “For judgment,” he says, “I came, so that those who did not see might see, and those who saw might become blind” (John 9). There is in us something that previously saw and afterward ceased to see, and something else that did not see and afterward began to see. For example: I want to see with those eyes with which previously I did not see, and which afterward were opened to me, since after the disobedience the eyes both of Adam and of Eve were opened, as we discussed in the preceding discourse.

Now we must interpret what is meant by the saying: “Behold, this one is appointed for the downfall and resurrection of many in Israel.” I must first fall, and when I have fallen, afterward rise well, lest the Savior be the cause of an evil downfall. Rather, he caused me to fall for the purpose of my rising, so that my downfall might prove far more beneficial to me than the time when I seemed to stand. I stood in sin at the time when I was living for sin; and because I stood in sin, my first benefit was to fall and die to sin.

Finally, the holy prophets too, whenever they contemplated something loftier, fell upon their faces. They fell for this reason: so that their sins might be more completely cleansed through their downfall. The Savior first grants you this very thing: that you should fall. You were a pagan: let the pagan in you fall. You loved a prostitute: first let the prostitute in you die. You were a sinner: let the sinner in you fall, so that afterward you may rise and say: “If we have died with him, we shall also live with him; and if we have been conformed to his death, we shall likewise be conformed to his resurrection” (Romans 6).

This one, then, is appointed for the downfall and resurrection of many in Israel—that is, among those who are able to behold with a full and clear gaze, and with reason. And he is “a sign that will be opposed.” Everything that history recounts about the Savior is opposed. The Virgin is his mother: this is a sign that is opposed. The Marcionites oppose this sign and say that he was not generated from a woman at all. The Ebionites oppose the sign, saying that he was born from man and woman in the same way that we are born.

He had a human body, and this is a sign that is opposed. Some say that he came from heaven; others say that he had a body like ours, so that through the likeness of his body he might redeem our bodies from sins and give us hope of resurrection.

[Note: Above, in Homily 14, it was most correctly observed that Origen believed and maintained that Christ truly bore a human body and did not merely pretend to do so. Now, therefore, when he denounces as heretics those who think that he had a body like ours, he seems at first sight to contradict himself and to depart further from the truth. The matter, however, must be understood differently. He is attacking the Ebionites, who impiously defined that Christ assumed a body generated from man and woman according to the common law of nature. He should therefore be understood as speaking of the difference which he himself establishes in the preface to the books *On First Principles* between our body and Christ’s body: “He was incarnate,” he says, “although he was God, and he remained what he was, God; he assumed a body like our body, differing in this one respect, that it was born of a Virgin through the Holy Spirit. And because this Jesus Christ was born and suffered in truth, and not in appearance, he truly died this common death, for he truly rose from the dead.”]

He rose from the dead, and this too is a sign that is opposed: how he rose, and whether it was he himself, and whether he rose with the same kind of body as that in which he died, or whether he rose in a body of a better substance. There is endless controversy: some say that he showed Thomas the imprint of the nails in his hands (John 20); others, arguing on the contrary, ask: if he had the same body, how did he enter when the doors were shut, and how did he stand there?

You see, then, how by various arguments even his resurrection is made a subject of dispute, and becomes a sign that is opposed. I also think that what was foretold by the mouths of the prophets is a sign that is opposed. For there are many heretics who assert that he was not foretold by the prophets at all.

And why must I pursue many examples? Everything that history recounts about him is a sign that is opposed. This does not mean that those who believe in him oppose it: we know that everything written is true. Rather, among unbelievers everything written about him is a sign that is opposed.

Then Simeon says: “And a sword will pass through your own soul.” What is this sword, which passes not only through the hearts of others but also through Mary’s heart? It is plainly written that at the time of the Passion all the apostles were scandalized, since the Lord himself said: “You will all be scandalized on this night” (Matthew 26). Therefore they were all scandalized, to such an extent that Peter, the chief of the apostles, denied him three times.

What then? Shall we suppose that, when the apostles were scandalized, the Mother of the Lord was free from scandal? If she did not suffer scandal in the Lord’s Passion, Jesus did not die for her sins. But if all have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified by his grace and redeemed, then Mary too was scandalized at that time.

This is what Simeon now prophesies, saying:

“And a sword will pass through your own soul”—you who know that you gave birth as a Virgin without a man, you who heard Gabriel say, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.” The sword of unbelief will pass through you; you will be struck by the blade of doubt; your thoughts will tear you apart in different directions when you see him whom you had heard called the Son of God, and whom you knew to have been born without the seed of a man, crucified and dying, subjected to human sufferings, and finally lamenting with tears and saying: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26).

“And a sword will pass through your own soul, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.” There were evil thoughts in human beings, and they were revealed for this reason: so that, brought into the open, they might be destroyed, put to death, and cease to exist; and so that the one who died for us might kill them. For as long as the thoughts were hidden and had not been brought into the open, it was impossible for them to be completely destroyed.

Therefore, if we have sinned, we too ought to say: “I made my sin known to you, and I did not hide my iniquity. I said, ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord’” (Psalm 32). For if we do this, and reveal our sins not only to God but also to those who can heal our wounds and sins, our sins will be wiped away by him who says: “Behold, I will wipe away your iniquities like a cloud, and your sins like mist” (Isaiah 44).

After Simeon’s prophecy, because women too had to be saved, a woman-prophet came, concerning whom it is written: “And there was Anna the prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher.”

What a beautiful order! The woman did not come before the man; first came Simeon, who took up the infant and held him in his arms; then came the woman, whose words are not set out in detail, but it is said generally that she confessed to the Lord and spoke about him to all who were awaiting the redemption of Israel.

And rightly did the holy woman deserve to receive the spirit of prophecy, because through prolonged chastity and prolonged fasts she had climbed to this summit. Look, women, at Anna’s testimony and imitate it, if it should ever happen to you that you lose your husbands. Consider what is written about her: “She lived seven years with her husband from her virginity,” and so forth; for this reason she was a prophetess. The Holy Spirit did not dwell in her casually or by chance.

It is good, and the first choice, if a woman can possess the grace of virginity. But if she cannot do this, and it happens that she loses her husband, let her remain a widow. Indeed, she ought to hold this intention not only after her husband’s death but even while he is alive, so that, even if his desire and purpose do not come to pass, she may be crowned by the Lord and say: “This I vow and promise: if something human happens to me that I do not wish for, I will do nothing else than remain undefiled and a widow.”

But now second, third, and fourth marriages are found, to say nothing of more. And we do not fail to recognize that such a marriage will cast us out of the kingdom of God.

[Note: This too is an absurd opinion concerning the doctrine of the Church, namely, that repeated marriages exclude one from the kingdom of God. Although shortly afterward Adamantius moderates his extreme severity and speaks more as one who fears than as one who asserts, nevertheless, since he condemns such marriages as unworthy of a pious and Christian person and is unwilling to regard a twice-married man as belonging to the Church or to the number of those who have neither wrinkle nor stain, he rightly receives censure from ecclesiastical writers, especially Theophilus, and seems to have understood the notion of the Church very poorly. Such opinions of the Montanists and Novatians were condemned by the anathema of the orthodox; nevertheless, it must be admitted that in Origen’s time second marriages were permitted, although they displayed a certain appearance of incontinence and were marked by the imposition of penance.]

For just as not only fornication but also marriage excludes one from ecclesiastical offices—neither a bishop, nor a presbyter, nor a deacon, nor a widow may be twice-married—so perhaps a twice-married person will also be expelled from the assembly of the first and undefiled Church, which has neither wrinkle nor stain. This does not mean that such a person will be cast into eternal fire, but that he will have no share in the kingdom of God.

I remember that, when I was interpreting what is written to the Corinthians—“the Church of God that is in Corinth, together with all who call upon him”—I said that there is a distinction between the Church and those who call upon the name of the Lord. For I think that the monogamous person, the virgin, and the one who perseveres in chastity belong to the Church of God; but the person who has married twice, even if he has a good way of life and excels in other virtues, nevertheless does not belong to the Church or to the number of those who have neither wrinkle nor stain or anything of that kind. Rather, he belongs to a second rank, to those who call upon the name of the Lord and who are indeed saved in the name of Jesus Christ, but are not crowned by him. To him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XVIII

On the passage written: “The child was growing and becoming strong,” continuing to the place where he says: “Did you not know that I must be in the things that belong to my Father?” Chapter 2.

My Lord Jesus was born, and his parents went up to Jerusalem to fulfill what had been commanded in the Law and to offer for him a pair of turtledoves and two young pigeons. Simeon held him in his arms, as was read earlier, and prophesied about him what the narrative recounts. After everything had been completed according to custom, his parents returned to where Jesus was living; and nevertheless he was growing and becoming strong in wisdom and grace.

He had not yet completed the forty days of purification, nor had he yet come to Nazareth, and already he was displaying complete wisdom. Scripture could have said, “He was growing and becoming strong, and he was receiving the spirit.” But he who had emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2), as soon as the sacrifice for his purification had been offered, filled again what he had emptied—not in the sense that his body immediately became larger, but in the sense that something more sacred was being shown, as Scripture reports: “The child was growing and becoming strong, and he was being filled with wisdom.”

[Note: Recall what we said above, in Homily 14, concerning this purification according to Origen’s understanding. To remove any suspicion of blasphemy, add the striking statement from his following Homily: “The soul of Jesus was never stained by the pollution of sin.”]

Let us inquire whether it is written elsewhere concerning a child that he was growing and becoming strong, so that by comparing several passages we may understand what more is said about our Lord. Concerning John: “The child was growing and becoming strong”; yet it is not added, “and he was being filled with wisdom,” but rather, “he was becoming strong in spirit.”

Here, however, concerning the Lord: “He was growing,” it says, “and becoming strong, and he was being filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was upon him” (Luke 2). All these things were said concerning the child who had not yet completed twelve years.

When he was twelve years old, he remained in Jerusalem. His parents, unaware of this, searched for him anxiously and did not find him. They sought him among their relatives, they sought him in the traveling party, they sought him among their acquaintances, and in all these places they did not find him.

Jesus was therefore sought by his parents, together with Joseph, who had been his foster-father and companion when he went down into Egypt; yet he was not found immediately when he was sought. For Jesus is not found among relatives and fleshly kin, nor among those who are physically joined to him. My Jesus cannot be found in the company of the multitude.

Learn where those who seek him find him, so that you too, seeking with Joseph and Mary, may find him. “And while they were seeking,” it says, “they found him in the temple.” Not just anywhere else, but in the temple. Nor simply in the temple, but in the midst of the teachers, listening to them and questioning them.

You too, then, seek Jesus in the temple of God; seek him in the Church. Seek him with the teachers who are in the temple and do not leave it. For if you seek in this way, you will find him.

But if someone says that he is a teacher and does not have Jesus, he is a teacher in name only; and therefore Jesus, the Word of God and Wisdom, cannot be found with him. “He was found,” it says, “in the midst of the teachers.” Understand this now as you understand what is written elsewhere concerning the prophets: “If something is revealed to another who is sitting, let the first be silent” (1 Corinthians 14).

They find him sitting in the midst of the teachers—and not only sitting, but also questioning and listening to them. Even now Jesus is present: he questions us and listens to us as we speak.

“And they were marveling,” it says, all of them. What were they marveling at? Not at his questions, although these too were marvelous, but at his answers. For one thing is to ask questions, another to answer. He questioned the teachers, and because they could not answer, he himself answered those whom he had questioned.

That the word “answer” signifies not an exchange of conversation but instruction in the holy Scriptures, let the divine Law teach you. Moses was speaking, but God answered him with a voice. That answer concerned the matters about which the Lord was instructing Moses in his ignorance.

Sometimes Jesus questions, sometimes he answers, as we have said above. Although his question is marvelous, his answer is much more marvelous. Therefore, so that we too may hear him and so that he may set before us questions that he himself will resolve, let us entreat him and seek him with great labor and pain. Then we shall be able to find the one whom we seek.

For it was not written without reason: “I and your father were seeking you in sorrow.” The person who seeks Jesus must seek him neither negligently, nor carelessly, nor superficially, as some seek him and therefore cannot find him. Let us instead say: “We are seeking you in sorrow.”

And when we have said this, he will answer our laboring soul, which seeks him with grief, and will say: “Did you not know that I must be in the things that belong to my Father?”

Where are the impious and senseless heretics who assert that the Law and the prophets do not belong to the Father of Jesus Christ? Certainly Jesus was in the temple that had been constructed by Solomon, and he confessed that temple to be the temple of his Father, whom he revealed to us and whose Son he declared himself to be.

Let them answer how one can be the good God and the other the just God. Since, therefore, the Savior is the Son of the Creator, let us praise the Father and the Son together, whose Law it is and whose temple it is. To him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XIX

On the passage written: “The child was growing and becoming strong,” continuing to the place where he questions the elders in the temple. Chapter 2.

[Col. 0262B]

Because some who seem to believe in Holy Scripture deny the divinity of the Savior, supposedly in order to glorify almighty God, it seems right to me that they should be instructed by the authority of those very Scriptures that something divine came into a human body—and not only into a human body, but also into a human soul. Indeed, if we attend carefully to the meaning of the Scriptures, that soul possessed something more than the other human souls. For every human soul, before it attains to the virtues, is stained by vices. But Jesus’ soul was never sullied by the stain of sin. For before he had reached his twelfth year, the Holy Spirit writes concerning him in Luke’s Gospel: “But the child was growing and becoming strong, and was being filled with wisdom” [Col. 0262C]. Human nature does not allow wisdom to be completed before the age of twelve. It is one thing to possess a share of wisdom, another to be filled with wisdom.

We do not doubt, therefore, that something divine appeared in Jesus’ flesh—and not only above a human being, but also above every rational creature. “And he was growing,” it says. For he had humbled himself, taking the form of a servant, and by the same power by which he had humbled himself, he grows. He had appeared weak, because he had assumed a weak body, and for that reason he is again strengthened. The Son of God had emptied himself (Phil. II), and therefore he is once more filled with wisdom; and the grace of God was upon him. Not when he came to adolescence, nor when he was teaching openly, but while he was still a little child he possessed the grace of God. And just as everything in him had been marvelous, so too his childhood was marvelous, so that he might be filled with the wisdom of God.

His parents therefore went, according to custom, to Jerusalem for the solemn day of Passover. And when he had become twelve years old—observe carefully that before he was twelve years old the wisdom of God, along with the other things written about him, was being fulfilled—when, as I have said, he was twelve years old, and the days of the festival had been completed according to custom, and his parents were returning with the child Jesus, the boy remained in Jerusalem, and his parents did not know it.

Here understand something higher than human nature permits. For he did not simply remain while his parents were ignorant of where he was; rather, just as it is written in John’s Gospel that the Jews were plotting against him, and he escaped from their midst and did not appear, so now also, I think, the boy remained in Jerusalem, while his parents did not know where he had remained [307–308]. Nor should we be surprised that they are called “parents,” since the one by reason of the birth and the other by reason of his service deserved the names of father and mother.

It follows: “We were seeking you in sorrow,” he says. I do not think that they were sorrowful because they supposed the boy had gone astray or perished. Nor could it have happened that Mary, who knew that she had conceived from the Holy Spirit, who had heard both the angel speaking, the shepherds hastening, and Simeon prophesying, feared that the child had been lost while wandering. Remove this supposition especially from Joseph, who had been commanded by an angel to take the child and go into Egypt, and who had heard: “Do not be afraid to take Mary your wife, for that which has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matt. I and II) [Col. 0263A]. He could never have feared for a lost infant whom he knew to be divine.

The sorrow and searching of the parents signify something other than what the simple reader understands. For just as you, whenever you read the Scriptures, seek in them their meaning with a certain sorrow and anguish—not because you think that the Scriptures have erred or contain anything improper, but because they contain inwardly a discourse and reasoning of truth, and you are unable to find what is true—so they too were seeking, lest perhaps he had withdrawn from them, lest, having left them, he had gone elsewhere; and, what I think even more likely [Note: [Col. 0263D] This, however, is more absurd than all the rest.], lest he had returned to the heavens, intending to descend again when it pleased him.

In sorrow, therefore, they were seeking the Son of God [Col. 0263C]. And when they sought him, they did not find him among their relatives. For human kinship could not contain the Son of God. They did not find him among his relatives because divine matters were greater than mortal knowledge and understanding.

Where, then, do they find him? In the temple. For there the Son of God is found. If you too ever seek the Son of God, seek him first in the temple; hasten there, and there you will find Christ, the Word and Wisdom—that is, the Son of God.

But because he was a child, he is found in the midst of the teachers, sanctifying and instructing them. Because he was a child, he is found in the midst of them, not teaching them but questioning them. He did this in accordance with the duty of his age, to teach us what is fitting for children, even when they are wise and educated: that they should listen to teachers rather than desire to teach, and should not boast of themselves in empty display [Col. 0263D].

He was questioning the teachers, I say, not in order to learn something, but so that by questioning he might instruct them. For from one and the same source of learning flow both the wise asking of questions and the wise giving of answers; and it belongs to the same knowledge to know what one should ask and what one should answer. It was fitting first for the Savior to become a teacher of learned questioning, so that afterward he might answer questions according to the reason and Word of God [Col. 0264A]. To him belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XX

On what is written: “Why were you seeking me?” up to the place where it says: “But Mary kept all these words in her heart.” Chapter II.

Mary and Joseph sought Jesus among their relatives, but they did not find him; they sought him among the company of travelers, and they could not find him. They sought him in the temple; but among the teachers, and in the midst of the instructors, they found him.

Wherever there are teachers, Jesus is found in the midst of the teachers—provided that the teacher sits in the temple and never goes out from it. Jesus benefited his teachers, and those whom he seemed to question he taught while speaking in their midst. In a certain sense he stirred them up to seek those things which, up to that point, they had been unable to know whether they understood or did not understand [Col. 0264B].

Jesus is found in the midst of the teachers, and when he is found he says to those who sought him: “Why is it that you were seeking me? Did you not know that I must be in the things that belong to my Father?”

First, understanding the passage simply, let us arm ourselves against the impious heretics who say that the creator is the father of Christ Jesus, but that he is not the God of the Law, nor of the prophets. Behold, the father is asserted to be the God of the temple. Let the Valentinians be ashamed when they hear Jesus saying: “I must be in the things that belong to my Father.” Let all the heretics be ashamed who receive the Gospel according to Luke and despise what is written in it.

Let these matters, as I have said, be understood in the simpler sense. But since it follows, “They themselves did not understand the word” [Col. 0264C], let us examine the meaning of Scripture more carefully: were they foolish and senseless, so that they did not know what he was saying, because the words “I must be in the things that belong to my Father” signified that he was in the temple, or did they signify something higher and more edifying for those who hear?

Each one of us, if he is good and perfect, is the possession of God the Father, and has Jesus in his midst. Let us believe the one who says: “I must be in the things that belong to my Father.” I suspect that this is a more reasonable, living, and true temple of God than that temple which was constructed in earthly work as a type. Hence, just as he was present in that temple typologically, so also he departed from it typologically. For he went out from the earthly temple, saying: “Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. XXIII), and leaving that house he came to the possession of God the Father, to the Churches dispersed throughout the whole world, and he says: “I must be in those who belong to my Father.”

Then they did not understand the word that he had spoken to them. At the same time, observe this also: as long as he was in the possession of his Father, he was above, because Joseph and [Note: [Col. 0263D] It is indeed true that Adamantius is highly disrespectful toward the Holy Virgin. Above, in Homily 14, he had said that she required purification; later, in Homily 17, that she had suffered scandal and doubt concerning her Son; now he accuses her, much more boldly, of unbelief or of insufficient faith. Recall what we said in the passages cited, to blunt the accusation and to vindicate the Mother of God from every stain of sin. [Col. 0264D] Now, if it is worthwhile to excuse Origen, let us append Sixtus of Siena’s annotation 140 in book V of the *Bibliotheca*. “I think,” he says, “that by the expression ‘full faith’ Origen understood the full knowledge of all the mysteries of Christ’s divinity and humanity, which the Virgin Mary did not yet possess at that time, although she held with the most certain and unwavering faith all that she then knew about Christ.”] Mary did not yet have full faith; for that reason they could not remain above with him. But it is said that he descended with them.

Jesus frequently descends with his disciples; he is not always on the mountain, nor does he hold the heights without end. On the mountain he is with Peter, with James, and with John, and again elsewhere with the other disciples (Matt. XVII). But because those who suffered from various illnesses were unable to climb the mountain, for that reason he descended and came to those who were below.

Now also it is written: “He descended with them and came to Nazareth, and was subject to them.” Let us learn, children, to be subject to our parents: the greater is made subject to the lesser. Since he saw that Joseph was older in age, for that reason he honored him with the respect due to a parent, giving all children an example, that they should be subject to their parents. And if they have no fathers, let them be subject to those who are of their fathers’ age [Col. 0265A].

Why do I speak of parents and children? If Jesus, the Son of God, is subject to Joseph and Mary, shall I not be subject to the bishop, who has been ordained for me by God as a father? Shall I not be subject to the presbyter, who by the Lord’s favor has been placed over me?

I think that Joseph understood that Jesus was greater than he, and that because Jesus was subject to him, Joseph exercised his authority with trembling restraint. Let each person therefore see that often an inferior is placed over better people, and that sometimes it happens that the one who is subject is better than the one who seems to have been placed over him. When the one superior in rank understands this, he will not be lifted up in pride because he is greater, but will know that a better person is subject to him in the same way that Jesus was subject to Joseph.

Then it follows: “But Mary kept all these words in her heart.” She suspected something more than a human being, and therefore kept all his words, not as those of a boy who was twelve years old, but as those of one who had been conceived from the Holy Spirit, whom she saw advancing in wisdom and grace with God and human beings.

Jesus was advancing in wisdom; he appeared wiser with each successive age. Was he not wise, so that he might become wiser? Or, because he had emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, was he recovering what he had lost and being filled with the virtues which, shortly before, when he had assumed a body, he had seemed to lay aside?

He was therefore advancing not only in wisdom but also in age. There is an advancement belonging to age. Two ages are spoken of in Scripture: one of the body, which is not within our power but is governed by the law of nature [Col. 0265D]; the other of the soul, which properly lies within us, according to which, if we wish, we grow daily and attain to the summit, so that we are no longer little children tossed about and carried around by every wind of doctrine, but, ceasing to be children, begin to be men and say: “When I became a man, I destroyed the things that belonged to a child” (I Cor. XV).

The advancement of this age, as I have said, which involves the growth of the soul, lies within our power. But if this testimony is not sufficient, let us also take an example from Paul: “Until we all attain,” he says, “to a perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ’s body” (Eph. IV).
