It is therefore within us to attain to the measure of the age of Christ’s body [Col. 0266A]. And if it lies within us, let us strive with every effort to put away the child, destroy it, and attain to the remaining ages, so that we too may be able to hear: “You shall go to your fathers in peace, nourished [Al. “nourished”] in a good old age”—that is, in a spiritual old age, which is truly a good old age, growing gray and reaching its end in Christ Jesus. To him belong glory, honor, and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXI

On what is written: “In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar,” up to the place where it says: “Make his paths straight.” Chapter III.

When the prophetic word was sent only to the Jews, the Jewish kings were placed in the title. For example: “The vision which Isaiah son of Amoz saw against Judah and Jerusalem in the reign of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah” (Isa. I). In Isaiah’s time I see no other ruler designated except the kings of Judah. In some prophets we also read of the kings of Israel, as there: “And in the days,” it says, “of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel” (Amos I).

But when the mystery of the Gospel was to be preached, and the Gospel was to be disseminated throughout the whole world—when John was its leader in the wilderness, and the Roman world was governed by the empire of Tiberius—then it is recorded that the word of the Lord came to John in the fifteenth year.

If salvation had been announced only to those from the nations who were going to believe, and Israel were to be entirely excluded, it would have been enough to say: “In the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governor of Judea.” But because many from Judea and Galilee were also going to believe, these kingdoms too are placed in the title, and it is said: “Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, Philip his brother tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, under the high priests Annas and Caiaphas, the word of the Lord came to John son of Zechariah in the wilderness” [Col. 0266B–C].

Formerly the word of God came to Jeremiah son of Hilkiah at Anathoth, in the days of Josiah king of Judah (Jer. I). Now the word of God comes to John son of Zechariah, whereas it had never come to the prophets in the wilderness. But because more children of the deserted woman than of her who has a husband were going to believe (Gal. IV; Isa. LIV), for that reason the word of God came to John son of Zechariah in the wilderness [Col. 0266D].

At the same time, consider that it makes more sense if “wilderness” is understood mystically and not according to the simple letter. For one who preaches in a wilderness acts uselessly by shouting there, where no one hears him speak. Therefore the forerunner of Christ, “the voice of one crying in the wilderness,” preaches in the wilderness of the soul, which did not have peace (John I).

Not only then, but also at the present time, first the burning and shining lamp comes and preaches a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins (Mark I); afterward the true light follows, when the lamp itself says: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John III).

The word came in the wilderness [Col. 0267A] and came to the entire region around the Jordan. What other places should the Baptist have traversed except those near the Jordan, so that all who wished to repent might be at hand for the washing of water?

Moreover, “Jordan” is interpreted as “descending” [Note: [Col. 0267] And indeed, in the Origenian Lexicon, κατάβασις (*katabasis*) is interpreted as “descent,” an etymology that also pleased Philo.]. The river of God, our Savior and Lord, is descending and running with a powerful current; in him we are baptized.

He preaches this true, saving water, also for the forgiveness of sins in baptism: “Come, catechumens; repent, so that you may receive baptism for the forgiveness of sins.” The one who receives baptism for the forgiveness of sins is the one who ceases to sin. For if someone comes to the washing while sinning, forgiveness of sins does not take place [Al. “for him”] [Col. 0267B].

Therefore I beg you: do not come to baptism without caution and careful examination. First show fruits worthy of repentance. Spend some time in a good way of life; keep yourselves pure from every defilement and vice. Then the forgiveness of sins will be granted to you, when you yourselves have begun to despise your own sins. “Forgive your offenses, and they will be forgiven you.”

This very passage, which is now taken from the Old Testament, we read written in the prophet Isaiah, where it says: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight” (Isa. XL).

The Lord wishes to find a way in you, so that he may enter your souls and make his journey. Prepare for him the path of which it is said: “Make his paths straight.”

“The voice of one crying in the wilderness”: the voice cries, “Prepare the way.” First the voice reaches the ears; then, after the voice—or rather, together with the voice—the word penetrates the hearing.

According to this meaning, Christ was announced by John. Let us therefore see what the voice announces concerning the Word. “Prepare,” he says, “the way for the Lord.”

What way should we prepare for the Lord? A bodily one? Or can the Word of God travel by such a road? Rather, must a straight way be prepared inwardly for the Lord, and an even path be laid out in our heart?

This is the way by which the Word of God entered, the Word who dwells within the capacity of the human body. Great is the human heart, spacious and capable, provided that it is pure. Do you wish to know its greatness and breadth? See how much it can contain of the greatness of divine understanding.

“He himself,” it says, “gave me knowledge of what exists: to understand the structure of the world, the activity of the elements, the beginning, end, and middle of ages, the alternations of seasons, the cycles of months, the circuits of years, the positions of stars, the natures of animals, the dispositions of wild beasts, the forces of spirits, the thoughts of human beings, the varieties of trees, and the powers of roots” (Wis. VII, 17).

You see that the human heart is not small, since it can contain so much. Understand that it is not in the size of the body but in its strength that it can contain such knowledge of the truth.

And to lead even the simple to belief by everyday examples that the human heart is great, let us consider the matter. Whatever cities we have passed through, we have them in our mind; their qualities and the arrangements of their streets, walls, and buildings revolve in our heart. The road on which we have entered we retain in the picture and description of our memory; the sea on which we have sailed we embrace in silent thought.

It is not small, as I have said, the human heart that can contain so much. If it is not small because it contains so much, consequently the way of the Lord is prepared in it, and a straight path is made, so that the Word of God and Wisdom may walk upon it.

Prepare the way for the Lord through a good way of life, and keep to the path through excellent works. Let the Word of God walk in you without any offense, and let it grant you knowledge of his mysteries and coming [Col. 0268B]. To him belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXII

On what is written: “Every valley shall be filled,” up to the place where it says: “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham.” Chapter III.

Let us see what is proclaimed at Christ’s coming. Among these things, the first written concerning John is: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.” What follows, however, belongs properly to the Lord and Savior. For every valley was not filled by John, but by the Lord and Savior.

Let each person consider who he was before he believed. Then he will recognize that he was a lowly valley, a precipitous valley sunk down into the depths. When the Lord Jesus came and sent the Holy Spirit, his representative, every valley was filled. It was filled with good works and the fruits of the Holy Spirit [315–316].

Love does not allow you to remain a valley. If you possess peace, wisdom, and goodness, you will not only cease to be a valley, but will also begin to be a mountain of God.

Yet we see this increasingly happening and being fulfilled every day among the nations: “Every valley shall be filled.” Concerning the people of Israel, who was cast down from a height, it says: “Every mountain and hill shall be humbled.” That people was once a mountain and a hill; it has been cast down and destroyed. Through their offense salvation was given to the nations in order to provoke them to emulation (Rom. XI).

And if you say that the opposing powers, which were rising up against mortals, are the mountains and hills that have been cast down, you will not be wrong. For in order that valleys of this sort may be filled, they must be humbled.

But let us also consider whether this, which was prophesied at Christ’s coming, has been fulfilled. It follows: “And all crooked things shall become straight.” Each one of us was crooked—unless he still remains so to this day—and through the coming of Christ, who has come to our soul, everything crooked has been made straight.

For what benefit is it to you if Christ once came in the flesh, unless he has also come to your soul? Let us pray that his coming may take place in us every day, and that we may be able to say: “But I live, now not I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. III).

For if Christ lives in Paul but does not live in me, what benefit will he be to me? But when he has also come to me, and I have enjoyed him as Paul enjoyed him, then I too will speak like Paul: “I live now not I, but Christ lives in me.”

Let us therefore consider the remaining things that are proclaimed at Christ’s coming. Nothing was rougher than you. Look at your former impulses; look at anger and the other vices—provided that they have ceased to be what they were—and you will understand that nothing was rougher than you and, to speak more significantly, that nothing was more uneven.

Your way of life was uneven, and so were your speech and works. Then my Lord Jesus came and made your rough places even; he turned everything disordered into level roads, so that a way without offense might be made in you, smooth [Forte *laeve*, “level”] and most pure. Thus God the Father might walk in you, and Christ the Lord might make his dwelling with you and say: “I and my Father will come, and we will make our dwelling with him” (John XIV) [Col. 0269B].

It follows: “And all flesh shall see the salvation of God.”

Once you were flesh; indeed, to speak more wonderfully, although you are still in the flesh, you see the salvation of God. But what is meant by the phrase “all flesh,” since no flesh is excluded that will not see the salvation of God, I leave for those who know the mysteries of the Scriptures to understand.

We must attend to what John says to the crowds going out to baptism. If anyone wishes to be baptized, let him go out. For one who remains in his former state, and does not leave behind his habits and way of life, does not come rightly to baptism.

But so that you may understand what it means to go out to baptism, receive this testimony and listen to the words with which God speaks to Abraham: “Go out from your land” (Gen. XII), and what follows.

As the crowds were going out to the washing—not having gone out already, but merely going out—John speaks the words that follow to them. For if they had already gone out, he would never have said to them, “Brood of vipers.”

Whatever, therefore, he says to them, he says to you, catechumens and catechumenae. You who are preparing to come to baptism, consider whether it may perhaps be said to you, “Brood of vipers.” And what follows will also be said to you unless you drive the wickedness and poisons of serpents from your heart: “Who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?”

Great wrath hangs over this world. The whole world will suffer the wrath of God. The vastness of the heavens, the breadth of the earth, the choirs of the stars, the splendor of the sun, and the nocturnal consolation of the moon—God’s wrath will overturn all these things [Col. 0269D]. For all these things will pass away on account of human sins.

Formerly, wrath came upon the earth alone, because all flesh had abandoned its way upon the earth (Gen. VI). But now the wrath of God will come upon heaven as well as earth. “The heavens will pass away, but you will remain” (this is said to God), “and they will all grow old like a garment” (Ps. CII).

See what kind and how great the wrath is that will consume the whole world, punish those who deserve punishment, and find material in which to exercise itself. Each one of us has prepared material for wrath from what he has done. “According to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of the just judgment of God,” it is said to the Romans (Rom. II).

Then it follows: “Who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” Therefore, “produce fruits worthy of repentance.”

To you also who are coming to baptism it is said: “Produce fruits worthy of repentance.” Do you wish to know what the fruits of repentance are? Love is a fruit of the Spirit, joy is a fruit of the Spirit, as are peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control, and the rest of this kind (Gal. V). If we possess all these things, we have produced fruits worthy of repentance [317–318].

Again, it is said to those who were coming to John’s baptism: “And do not begin to say among yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I say to you that God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham.”

John, the last of the prophets, prophesies the expulsion of the former people and the calling of the nations. To those who gloried in Abraham he says: “And do not begin to say among yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’” And concerning the nations he says again: “For I say to you that God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham.”

From what stones? Certainly he was not pointing to irrational, physical stones, but to senseless and formerly hard-hearted human beings. Because they worshiped stones and pieces of wood, the saying sung in the Psalm was fulfilled: “May those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” [Al. “become”] (Ps. CXV).

Truly, those who make idols and trust in them are like their gods: without sense, without reason, transformed into stones and pieces of wood. For although they see so much order, beauty, and function in created things, so much beauty in the world, they do not wish to understand the Creator from created things. Nor do they consider that there is some providence behind so great an arrangement, some ruler; rather, they are blind, seeing the world only with those eyes with which irrational beasts and animals see.

They do not perceive that the things they see are governed by reason or that reason exists within them.

This is why John had said: “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham.” Let us therefore also entreat God that, if we were once stones, we may be turned into children of Abraham in place of those children who have been cast out and through their own fault have lost the promise and adoption.

I will offer one more testimony concerning stones. In the Song of Exodus it is written: “Let them be turned into stones until your people pass over, Lord, until this people of yours whom you have acquired passes over” (Exod. XV).

God is therefore asked that they be turned into stones for a short time. For this is expressed more significantly by the Greek expression: ἀναλιθούσθωσαν (*analithousthōsan*), “let them be turned into stones,” until the Jewish people passes over [Note: [Col. 0269] This too, as everyone recognizes, is Jerome’s observation as translator.].

There is no doubt that after they have passed over, the stony nations will cease to be stony and, in place of a hard heart, will receive a human and rational nature in Christ.

To him belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXIII

On what is written: “Behold, the axe has been laid at the roots of the trees,” up to the place where it says: “But tax collectors also came to be baptized by him.” Chapter III.

[Col. 0271A]

John was speaking at that time: “Behold, the axe has already been laid at the roots of the trees.” If the consummation were already imminent and the end of the ages were at hand, I would have no difficulty. For I would say that what he says—“Behold, the axe has been laid at the roots of the tree”—and this—“For every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire”—was prophesied for this reason: because it was being fulfilled at that time. But since so many centuries have passed, and countless years have elapsed from that time until the present day [Col. 0271B], we must inquire how the Holy Spirit could say through the prophet: “Behold, the axe has been laid at the roots of the trees.”

I think that this is being prophesied concerning the Israelite people: that its cutting down is near. For to those who were going out to him to be baptized, among other things he said: “Produce fruits worthy of repentance”; and, as though speaking to the Jews, he said: “Do not begin to say among yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you that God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham.” Thus, when he says, “Behold, the axe has been laid at the roots of the trees,” he is speaking to the Jews.

The apostolic statement also agrees with this interpretation: that branches were broken off and cut away by the axe of unbelief, so that he might cut from the tree not the root, but what had sprouted from the root, in order that branches of the wild olive might be grafted onto the root of the former tree [Col. 0271C] (Rom. XI).

Every tree, therefore, that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire; for this is the end assigned to it, that it be consumed by burning.

Next, three groups are introduced as questioning John about their salvation: one whom Scripture calls the crowds going out to baptism, another whom it names the tax collectors, and a third designated by the term soldiers.

The crowds were asking him, saying: “What shall we do?” He answered them: “Let the one who has two tunics give to the one who has none; and let the one who has food do likewise.” I do not know whether this command properly applies to the crowds. It is more appropriate to the apostles than to the populace that whoever has two tunics should give one to the person who has none. And so that you may know that this applies more to the apostles than to the people, hear what the Savior says to them: [Col. 0271D] “Do not take two tunics on the road” (Matt. XX).

The double garment, therefore, with which each person is clothed, together with the command to give one to the person who has none, conveys another meaning. The Savior wants us, just as we are not to serve two masters, neither to have two tunics nor to be wrapped in a double garment, lest one garment be that of the old person and the other that of the new. On the contrary, he desires that we strip off the old person and put on the new.

Up to this point the interpretation is easy. But the question arises: in accordance with this interpretation, how are we commanded to give a garment to the person who has none [Col. 0272A]? Who is there who does not have even a single garment upon his flesh, who is naked, who is entirely covered by no clothing at all?

I do not say this in such a way as to deny that generosity and mercy toward the poor are commanded. There is a hyperbolic clemency here: that we should cover even naked people with a second tunic. But I maintain that this passage also looks toward a deeper understanding, and that we ought to give a tunic to the person who has none at all. Who, then, is the one who has no tunic? Surely the one who has no God whatsoever.

We must therefore strip ourselves and give to the one who is naked. One person has God; another has him not at all—an opposite condition, evidently. And just as it is written that we should cast our sins into the depths of the sea (Mic. VII), so our vices and sins must be thrown away from us and [Col. 0272B] cast upon the one who became their cause for us.

“And let the one who has food,” he says, “do likewise.” Let the one who has food give to the one who has none, so that he may bestow upon him not only clothing but also something that he can eat.

Then tax collectors also came to be baptized by him. According to the literal understanding, this teaches tax collectors to demand nothing beyond what has been prescribed in the Law. For those who exact more transgress not John’s command, but that of the Holy Spirit who spoke through John.

I do not know, however, whether, according to *anagogy* (ἀναγωγή), the passage may signify something more exalted, or whether we ought to disclose such mystical matters in an audience of this kind, especially among those who do not penetrate the marrow of the Scriptures but take pleasure only in their surface. It is dangerous, yet it must nevertheless be touched upon briefly and concisely [Col. 0272C].

When we have departed from the world and this life of ours has been changed, there will be certain beings seated at the boundaries of the world, as though performing the office of tax collectors, examining everything with the greatest care to see whether they can find anything belonging to them in us. It seems to me that the ruler of this world is like a tax collector; hence it is written of him: “The ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John XIV).

The statement that we read in the Apostle also has to be understood in a sacred sense: “Pay everyone what is owed: taxes to whom taxes are due, revenue to whom revenue, honor to whom honor; owe no one anything except to love one another” (Rom. XIII). Let us therefore consider whether, when we have nothing that we can pay as revenue, we may perhaps be dragged away on account of the debt, as happens even among the tax-paying subjects of this world when someone is confined so that he may serve the state itself in payment of a debt [Col. 0272D].

Many of us are to be held by tax collectors of this kind. That holy man Jacob was not greatly afraid of them, nor did he fear that anything belonging to the tax collectors would be found in him. Hence he boldly said to that tax collector Laban: “Search and see whether you have any of your possessions with me” (Gen. XXXI). Scripture bears witness to this, saying: “Laban found nothing belonging to Jacob.”

Our Savior and the Holy Spirit, therefore, who spoke through the prophets, teach that not only human beings, [Note: [Col. 0271D] Throughout this entire peroration he understands that the angels were taught by the Savior, by the prophets, and finally by the Church what they had not previously known, and that through their instruction they advanced toward salvation. Had he said that the angels did not possess a fully complete knowledge of the Lord’s incarnation and its mysteries, but had nevertheless asserted that these things were revealed and disclosed to them before they were revealed to human beings, and had thus believed that angels were instructed by the Church as witnesses and participants in these matters, his view would not have been inconsistent with the opinions of other Fathers. For Jerome himself, in the Commentary on Ephesians III, verse 10, which he discusses shortly afterward, teaches that the manifold wisdom of which the Apostle speaks, contained in the mysteries of Christ’s life, was unknown to the angels. But Adamantius, as is clearer from the context below, maintains that angels needed salvation through Christ’s death no less than human beings did, and that they were, as it were, disciples instructed by the teachings of the prophets and apostles and stirred to virtue. This opinion is manifestly opposed to the countless testimonies of Holy Scripture and to the decrees of orthodox faith. It is also the solemn corollary of that ridiculous doctrine by which he asserts that angels can sin and that their office depends solely upon merit. Hence he holds that the hostile powers, because of the offenses they have committed against human beings, take on a human body and suffer punishments in it; and, conversely, that souls are selected from the human race which, after rightly and piously completing the course of life on earth, are admitted into the order of angels. Our Jerome—to pass over others for the moment—frequently attacks this aberrant opinion in the preface to his Commentary on Malachi and elsewhere. See what we observed on nearly the same opinion in our note to Origen’s fourth Homily on Ezekiel.] but also angels and invisible powers [319–320; 321–322; Col. 0273A] are taught.

What shall I say of the Savior? The prophets and apostles themselves proclaim everything they utter not only to human beings but also to angels. To know that this is true, consider: “Give ear, O heaven, and I will speak”; “In the presence of the angels I will sing to you”; and, “Praise the Lord, heavens of heavens, and let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXLVIII, 4); and, “Let the angels praise him”; and, “Bless the Lord, my soul, in every place of his dominion.”

In many passages, and especially in the Psalms, you will find speech addressed to angels, with human beings being granted the power to address them—provided, however, that the person possesses the Holy Spirit. I will give one example, so that we may know that angels too are instructed by human speech. It is written in the Apocalypse of John: “Write to the angel of the church of the Ephesians [Col. 0273B]: I have this against you” (Apoc. II); and again: “Write to the angel of the church of Pergamum: I have something against you.” Certainly it is a human being who writes to angels and gives them a command.

I have no doubt that angels are present in our assembly—not only generally in the whole Church but also individually. Concerning them the Savior says: “Their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVIII). There is a twofold Church here: one of human beings and another of angels.

If we say anything in accordance with reason and in accordance with the intention of the Scriptures, the angels rejoice and pray with us. And because angels are present in the Church—at least in the Church that is worthy and belongs to Christ—women are commanded when they pray to have a veil over their head because of the angels, [Note: [Col. 0274D] Here, as in the aforementioned passage of the Apocalypse, nearly all the commentators very rightly teach that the term “angels” designates bishops and ministers of the sacraments; accordingly, Origen argues ineptly. Moreover, he does not seem to have held with certainty whether a guardian angel is assigned to each individual human being, or only to those who profess faith in Christ and are holy. For although he had earlier declared in Homily 12 that two beings are placed over every human being—one good and the other wicked—and now repeats that angels are present not only generally in the whole Church but also individually, he nevertheless adds that they are present only in the Church that is worthy and belongs to Christ. Elsewhere he more readily accepts this latter view. See what we note below on Homily 35.] namely, those who attend upon the saints and rejoice in the Church [Col. 0273C] (I Cor. XI).

We do not see them because our eyes have been blinded by the filth of our sins, but the apostles of Jesus see them, to whom he says: “Truly, truly, I tell you, you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man” (John I).

If I possessed the grace by which I could see as the apostles saw, and behold as Paul looked, I would now perceive the multitude of angels that Elisha saw, though Gehazi, who stood with him, did not see it. Gehazi was afraid that he would be captured by the enemy [Col. 0274A]; only Elisha could see. But Elisha, as the Lord’s prophet, prayed and said: “O Lord, open the eyes of this boy, and let him see that those who are with us are far more numerous than those who are with them” (IV Kings VI). Immediately, in response to the holy man’s prayers, Gehazi saw the angels whom he had not previously been able to see.

We have said these things to show that John taught tax collectors—not only those who serve in the revenues of the state, but also those who were coming to repentance. There were also tax collectors of a spiritual kind, just as there were other soldiers who were going out to the baptism of repentance.

For not John the prophet alone, but the Savior himself also, came to proclaim saving repentance to human beings, and [Note: [Col. 0274D] Recall the note on the immediately preceding page. The distinguished Huet attacks this paradox of Origen in a separate discussion.] to angels and the other powers, so that “at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. II) [Col. 0274B]. To him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXIV

On the passage that says, “I indeed baptize you with water,” up to the place where it says, “He himself will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.” Chapter III.

John, who is lesser than Christ, was received by the people, who supposed and considered that perhaps he himself was the Christ; but they did not receive the one who had come greater than he. Do you wish to know the reason? Understand it: John’s baptism was visible, whereas Christ’s baptism was invisible.

“For I,” he says [Col. 0274C], “baptize you with water; but the one who comes after me is greater than I: he himself will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.”

When does Jesus baptize with the Holy Spirit, and when again with fire? Does he baptize with Spirit and fire at one and the same time, or at different and separate times?

“You will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.” The apostles were baptized with the Holy Spirit after his ascension into heaven (Acts II); but Scripture does not record that they were baptized with fire.

Yet just as John waited beside the Jordan River [Col. 0275A] for those coming to baptism, driving some away by saying, “Brood of vipers,” and the rest, while receiving those who confessed their vices and sins, so the Lord Jesus will stand in the fiery river beside the flaming sword (Gen. III), so that, after this life has ended, he may baptize in this river anyone who desires to pass into paradise and requires purification, and send that person on to what he desires; but he will not baptize in the fiery washing anyone who does not bear the sign of the earlier baptisms.

For one must first be baptized with water and Spirit, so that, when one comes to the fiery river, one may show that one has preserved both the washing of water and that of the Spirit, and then may be deemed worthy also to receive the baptism of fire in Christ Jesus [Col. 0275A]. To him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0275C] Genebrard and other learned men have noted that Adamantius clearly professes purgatorial fire after death in this testimony. I could add six hundred other passages in which he declares the same thing most openly. For Origen was never accused of denying the existence of purgatory; rather, he was accused of establishing it in his own manner, namely, by teaching that no other fire and no other punishments await any sins than those of purgatory, and that souls are tortured by no punishments other than temporary ones. I would not dare affirm that he offers that impious doctrine in this passage as well. For although he says that anyone who desires to pass over after the end of this life is to be baptized in this river, and does not expressly exempt anyone—not even the holiest men, who are purified either by no punishment or certainly by temporary punishment, as we noted above in Homily 14, where he discusses this fiery baptism—nevertheless, by adding, as though moderating his position, “who requires purification,” he removes suspicion of error and indicates that he is speaking of those whose lesser faults must be expiated. Indeed, I do not know whether there is another passage in Origen’s writings that can be given so convenient an interpretation.]

## HOMILY XXV

On the suspicion the people had concerning John, that perhaps he himself was the Christ. Chapter III.

[Col. 0275B]

Love too has its danger if it exceeds its proper measure. For whoever loves someone ought to consider the nature and causes of the beloved, and should not love that person more than he deserves. If love exceeds its measure and proper limit, both the one who loves and the one who is loved will be in sin.

To make this clearer, let us offer an example. The people admired John and loved him; and he truly deserved their admiration, so that he should be accorded greater honor than other human beings, because he had lived differently from all mortals.

We are not all content with simple food, but delight in a variety of dishes. One wine would be enough for us to drink, yet we purchase wines of many flavors [Col. 0275C]. John, however, always fed on locusts and always on wild honey. He was content with simple and meager food, so that his body would not grow fat on richer dishes or be weighed down by elaborate meals [325–326]. For our bodies are of such a nature that they are burdened by excessive food; and when the body has been weighed down, the soul too is burdened, since it is diffused throughout the body and subject to its passions [Col. 0276A].

Therefore the command is rightly given to those who are able to observe it: “It is good not to eat meat, nor to drink wine, nor to do anything by which your brother is offended” (Rom. XIV).

John’s life, then, was extraordinary and very different from that of other human beings. He had no worldly possessions, no servant, not even a humble hut. He lived in the desert—not only until the day of his manifestation to Israel, but also during the time when he preached repentance to the people. He was nourished by simple water, so that even in his drink he differed from the rest.

We who live in cities, who are among the crowds, who seek finer clothing and foods and [Note: [Col. 0275D] Perhaps *altilia* (“fattened birds,” “fattening foods”) should be read.] delicacies, should observe what sort of garment [Col. 0276B] the man who lived in the wilderness wore. He had made himself a tunic of camel’s hair and was girded with a leather belt.

Everyone knew all these things about him, and because of the difference in his life all who saw him admired him; and in their admiration they honored him with the greatest devotion, above all because he baptized repentant people for the remission of sins.

For these reasons they loved him with complete justice, but they did not preserve moderation in their love. They were thinking that perhaps he himself was the Christ.

The Apostle Paul, guarding against such disordered and irrational love, spoke concerning himself: “I fear, however, lest anyone should think of me beyond what he sees in me or hears from me, and lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me” (I Cor. XII), and so forth.

Fearing that he too might fall into this, Paul did not wish to judge concerning himself all that he knew, lest anyone suppose him to be more than what could be seen, and, exceeding the measure of honor, say of him what had been said of John: that he himself was the Christ.

Some also said this concerning Dositheus [Note: [Col. 0276C] This passage should certainly be connected with the notable passage of the same Origen, *Against Celsus*, book I, no. 57, which reads thus in Latin: “At the time of the census, when Jesus is known to have been born, a certain Judas, a Galilean, breaking away from the Jewish people, drew many after him, both by the wisdom he pretended to possess and by the revolutionary measures he was undertaking. But after he paid the penalty for his crime, his teaching was immediately extinguished and retained standing only among a very few persons of no account. After Jesus’ time, a certain Dositheus the Samaritan also wished to persuade his followers that he was that Christ whom Moses had foretold, and he seemed to win some over to his teaching.” Others relate various things about Dositheus, whom even the Jewish writers themselves do not know sufficiently. Jerome too seems mistaken when, in *Dialogue against the Luciferians*, no. 23, he makes Dositheus the leader of the Samaritans, who rejected the prophets, and says that the Sadducees derived their origin from his root; for the Samaritans had rejected the Scriptures long before, and Dositheus was later than Zadok, founder of the Sadducees. Others invent several Dositheuses in order to reconcile the differing ancient testimonies about him. To all of these I prefer Origen, with whom agree Hegesippus in Eusebius, book IV, chapter 22; Theodoret, *Haeretical Fables*, book I, chapter 1; the *Recognitions* attributed to Clement, book II; and others.] the heresiarch of the Samaritans; others said it concerning Judas the Galilean.

Finally, certain people rushed into such reckless love that they invented new and unheard-of monstrosities about Paul. Some say that the statement about sitting at the right and left hand of the Savior [Col. 0277A] is spoken concerning Paul and Marcion: Paul sits at the right, while Marcion sits at the left.

Others, reading, “I will send you the Advocate, the Spirit of truth” (John XIV), refuse to understand a third [Note: [Col. 0277D] If anyone thinks that the term “Person” in reference to the divine beings is more recent than Origen’s time, let him consider that the holy translator used it for what the author wrote as ὑπόστασις (*hypostasis*). Moreover, in the second volume on John, Adamantius says very clearly: “We, at any rate, believing that there are three hypostases, the Father—and the Son, which is improperly missing in the printed books—and the Holy Spirit.” In Latin, from Ferrari’s version: “We, however, who believe that there are three Persons, the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.”] Person from the Father and the Son, and a divine and exalted nature, but instead understand the Apostle Paul.

Do they not all seem to you to have loved beyond what is proper? While admiring the virtue of each person, have they not lost the measure of love?

We suffer this in the Church. Many, while loving us more than we deserve, proclaim and say things in praise of our speech and teaching that our conscience does not accept. Others, slandering our treatises, accuse us of holding opinions that we know we have never held [Col. 0277B]. Neither those who love too much nor those who hate hold to the rule of truth. Some lie through love, others through hatred.

Therefore we must put reins upon love and allow it only as much freedom to roam as will keep it from falling over precipices.

It is written in Ecclesiastes: “Do not be excessively righteous, and do not think more than is fitting, lest you become bewildered.”

Following this example, I can say something similar [327–328]: Do not love a human being with your whole soul and your whole strength, nor love an angel with your whole heart, your whole soul, and your whole strength; reserve that command, according to the Savior’s word, for God alone.

“For you shall love,” he says, “the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength” (Matt. XXII).

Someone may answer me and say [Col. 0277C]: The Savior commands, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength, and your neighbor as yourself.” I want to love Christ; teach me, then, how I should love him.

For if I love him with all my heart, with all my soul, and with all my strength, I violate the command by loving another—apart from the one God—in this way. But if I love him less than I love the omnipotent Father, I fear that I may be found impious and profane toward the Firstborn of all creation. Teach me and show me how I ought to walk between the two, loving Christ.

Do you wish to know with what love Christ should be loved? Listen briefly: “You shall love the Lord your God in Christ.”

Do you think it is possible to have a different love for the Father and the Son? Love the Lord Christ together with the Father. Love the Father in the Son, and the Son in the Father, with all your heart, all your soul, and all your strength.

If someone asks and says, “Prove from the Scriptures what you assert,” let him hear the Apostle Paul, who possessed rational love, speaking: “For I am certain that neither death nor life, nor angels nor powers, nor things present nor things to come, nor strength nor height nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord and Savior” (Rom. VIII) [Col. 0278A]. To him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXVI

On the passage that says, “His winnowing fan is in his hand, and he will cleanse his threshing floor,” up to the place where it says, “And he will gather the wheat into the granary.” Chapter III.

Christ is God; and whoever worships him must worship in spirit and truth (John IV). Our God also [Col. 0278B] is “a consuming fire” (Deut. IV).

God is called both spirit and fire in two ways: spirit for the righteous, fire for sinners. But since angels too are called spirit and fire—“He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire” (Heb. I)—angels are spirits to the saints, but to those who deserve it they assign fire and supply ardor.

In accordance with this meaning, our God and Savior, being spirit, came to cast fire upon the earth. He is spirit according to what is written: “When you turn to the Lord, the veil will be removed; and the Lord is spirit” (II Cor. III). But he came to cast fire not upon heaven but upon earth, as he himself shows by saying: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it already be kindled?” (Luke XI) [Col. 0278C].

For if you turn to the Lord, who is spirit, Christ will be spirit to you, and he will not come to cast fire upon the earth. But if you do not turn to God, and possess the earth and its fruit, he comes to cast fire upon your earth.

Something similar is also written concerning God: “A fire has been kindled by his anger,” not up to heaven above but down to hell below; and it will devour not heaven but the earth and its growth.

Why have I recalled these things? Because the baptism with which Jesus baptizes is both in the Holy Spirit and in fire.

I remember what I said recently, and the earlier explanation has not escaped me; but I want to introduce something new as well. If you are holy, you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit; if you are a sinner, you will be plunged into fire. One and the same baptism will be turned into fire and condemnation for the unworthy and sinners [Col. 0278D]; but for those who are holy and turn to the Lord with complete faith, the grace and salvation of the Holy Spirit are to be bestowed.

The one, therefore, who is said to baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire has his winnowing fan in his hand. He will cleanse his threshing floor, gather his wheat into his granary, and burn the chaff with unquenchable fire [Col. 0279A].

I want to discover the reason why our Lord has a winnowing fan, and why, when a gentle wind blows, the light chaff is carried here and there, while the heavy wheat is brought together into one place. For wheat and chaff cannot be separated without wind. I think that temptations are to be understood as the wind: when the confused heap of believers is winnowed, they show some to be chaff and others wheat.

When your soul has been overcome by some temptation, the temptation does not turn you into chaff; rather, when you were chaff—light, that is, and unbelieving—the temptation revealed you to be what you had been hiding. Conversely, when you endure temptations with courage, temptation does not make you faithful and patient; rather, it brings into the open the virtue of patience and courage that was already in you but hidden [Col. 0279B].

“Do you think,” says the Lord, “that I spoke to you in any other way than so that you might prove righteous?” And elsewhere: “I afflicted you and subjected you to want, so that what was in your heart might become manifest.”

In the same way, a storm does not cause a building founded upon rock to stand, but one founded upon earth. When the storm arises, it will not overthrow what has been founded upon earth; but what wavers upon sand immediately proves that it was not well founded.

Therefore, before the storm arises, before the blasts of the winds rise, before the rivers swell—while everything is still quiet—let us direct all our concern toward the foundations of our buildings. Let us build our house with the varied and firm stones of God’s commandments, so that, when persecution rages against Christians and a harsh [Col. 0279C] whirlwind arises, we may show that we have a building founded upon Christ Jesus, the rock (Matt. VII).

But if anyone—which God forbid of us—denies him, let that person know that he did not deny Christ at the moment when he appeared to deny him. Rather, he already possessed ancient seeds and roots of denial; at that time what he possessed was recognized and brought into the open.

Let us therefore pray to the Lord that we may be a building that no storm can overthrow, founded upon the rock, through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXVII

On the passage that says, “And exhorting many other things, he announced the good news,” up to the place where it says, “The Holy Spirit descended upon him.” Chapter III.

[Col. 0279D] Whoever teaches the word of the Gospel does not announce one thing but many. Scripture indicates this when it says: “Exhorting many other things, he announced the good news.”

Thus John also preached other things to the people that have not been written down. But consider how many of the things that have been written announce Christ. He displayed the baptism of the Holy Spirit, proclaimed salvation to the tax collectors, taught discipline to the soldiers, and spoke of the threshing floor being cleansed, the trees being cut down, and the other matters narrated in the history of the Gospel.

Apart, therefore, from the things that have been written, he is shown to have announced also those that have not been written, in the statement: “Exhorting many other things, he announced the good news to the people.”

And just as in the Gospel according to John [Col. 0280A] it is related concerning Christ: “He spoke many other things that are not written in this book; and if they were written down, I do not think that the world itself could contain the books that would have to be written” (John XXI), so understand the present passage in this way. Perhaps Luke, because John was announcing certain things too great to be entrusted to writing, wished to specify them, but merely indicated that they had been spoken. For this reason he said: “Exhorting many other things, he announced the good news to the people.”

We should indeed marvel at John on account of what follows, and especially because “among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist” (Matt. XI), and because through the merit of his virtue he rose to such a high reputation that many thought he was the Christ.

But there is something much more marvelous. Herod the tetrarch possessed royal power and could have killed John whenever he wished [Col. 0280B] (Mark VI). Yet when Herod had committed an unjust act contrary to the Law of Moses by taking his brother’s wife—who had a daughter by her former husband—John did not fear him, did not show partiality, did not consider, as I have said, his royal power, and did not fear death. For he knew that even if he were not a prophet, Herod could kill him if provoked.

Knowing all these things, John nevertheless rebuked Herod with prophetic freedom. He condemned the incestuous marriage; and for this reason, after being shut up in prison, he was not concerned about his death or the uncertainty of judgment, but, even in chains, he was thinking about Christ, whom he had announced.

Since he could not go to Christ himself, he sent his disciples to ask: “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?”

Do you observe [Col. 0280C] that he taught even in prison? He saw that he had disciples in that place, and for this reason he instructed them there himself. When a question about Jesus also arose among them, he sent some of his disciples and asked: “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?”

The disciples returned and reported to their teacher what the Savior had commanded them to report. Armed with the Savior’s words for battle, John died confidently and willingly accepted beheading, strengthened by the Lord’s own voice and convinced that the one he believed in was truly the Son of God.

These things concern John and his freedom, and the madness of Herod, who, in addition to his many crimes, added this: first to shut John up in prison and then to behead him.

But since the Lord was baptized, the heavens were opened, and the Holy Spirit descended upon him, while a voice thundered from heaven [Col. 0280D], saying, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. XVII), we must say that at Jesus’ baptism heaven was opened for the dispensation and remission of sins—not his, since he had committed no sin and no deceit was found in his mouth (Eph. IV), but the heavens were opened for the whole world, and the Holy Spirit descended.

After the Lord had ascended on high and led captivity captive, he gave us the Spirit who had come to him. He had also given the Spirit at the time of the resurrection, saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive anyone’s sins, they will be forgiven; if you retain them, they will be retained” (John XX).

The Holy Spirit descended upon the Savior in the form of a dove, a gentle, innocent, and simple bird [Col. 0281A]. Hence we too are commanded to imitate the innocence of doves.

Such is the Holy Spirit: pure, winged, and rising to the heights. Therefore, when we pray, we say: “Who will give me wings like a dove, and I will rest?” (Ps. LV)—that is, who will give me the wings of the Holy Spirit?

And in another passage the prophetic word promises: “If you sleep among the midst of the allotted portions, you will have the wings of a dove covered with silver, and the back parts of it with the green sheen of gold” (Ps. LXVIII).

For if we rest among the allotted portions of the Old and New Testaments, wings of a dove covered with silver will be given to us—that is, the words of God—and its back parts will shine with the splendor and green sheen of gold, so that our understanding may be filled with the perceptions of the Holy Spirit; that is, so that our discourse and mind may be filled by his coming, and so that we may neither say nor understand anything except what he has suggested [Col. 0281B]. Rather, let all sanctification, both in heart and in words and deeds, come from the Holy Spirit in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXVIII

On the genealogy of the Savior, concerning the fact that different ancestors of his are recorded in Matthew and Luke. Chapter III.

Our Lord and Savior, the Savior of many, is now described as having been born according to the order of his ancestors—though Scripture has not taught which genealogy was the better. Although his divinity is not subject to a beginning, for your sake—since you were born in the flesh—he wished to be born; yet his birth is not narrated in the same order by the Evangelists. This matter greatly perplexed some people.

For Matthew, beginning to weave together the sequence of his birth, proceeds from Abraham until he says: “Now the generation of Christ Jesus was as follows”; and he describes not the one who was baptized, but the one who came into the world. Luke, however, in explaining his birth, does not descend from the higher to the lower; rather, having first spoken of him as baptized, he proceeds upward until he reaches God himself. Nor are the persons the same in his genealogy when he is said to descend and when he is said to ascend [333–334]. For the one who made him descend from heaven for you introduces women—not just any women, but sinners whom Scripture had reproved; whereas the one who narrates his baptism makes no mention of any woman.

In Matthew [Col. 0281D] (chapter I), as we have said, Tamar is named, who through deception lay with her father-in-law; and Ruth the Moabite, who was not of the race of Israel; and Rahab, of whom I cannot discover where she was taken from; and the wife of Uriah, who violated her husband’s marriage-bed. Since our Lord and Savior had come for this purpose: to take upon himself the sins of human beings (I Cor. V), and God made him who had not committed sin to be sin for us, therefore, descending into the world, he assumed the person of sinful and vicious human beings. He wished to be born from the line of Solomon, whose sins are recorded, and of Rehoboam, whose offenses are reported, and of the others, many of whom did evil in the sight of God.

But when he ascended from the baptismal washing, and the second order [Col. 0282A] is described, he was born not through Solomon but through Nathan, who reproved his father concerning Uriah’s death and the birth of Solomon. In Matthew the word “generation” is always added; here, however, it is entirely absent. For there it is written: “Abraham begot Isaac, Isaac begot Jacob, Jacob begot Judah and his brothers, Judah begot Perez and Zerah from Tamar,” and so on to the end: “begot” is always added. In Luke, however, when Jesus ascended from the baptismal washing, he is called “son”: “As was supposed, the son of Joseph.” And throughout that very long sequence of names, except for the statement that he was supposed to be the son of Joseph, the word “generation” is not written.

In Matthew it is not written that he “began”; here, however, because he was about to ascend from baptism, we read that he began, as Scripture reports: “And he himself was Jesus, beginning.” When he was baptized and assumed the mystery of a second generation, so that you too might destroy your former birth and be born in a second regeneration, then he is said to have begun.

And just as the Jewish people, when they were in Egypt, had no beginning of months, but when they had come out of Egypt it was then [variant: “now”] said to them, “This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first among the months of the year” (Exod. XII), so the one who has not yet been baptized is not said to have begun. Let us not suppose that the word “beginning” was added to the statement “He himself was Jesus” without reason.

Moreover, the phrase “about thirty years old” must be considered. Joseph was thirty years old when, released from his chains and having interpreted Pharaoh’s dream, he became [Col. 0282C] ruler of Egypt and gathered grain during the time of abundance, so that he would have something to distribute during the time of famine. I think that Joseph’s thirty years preceded the Savior’s thirty years.

This Joseph did not gather such grain as that Joseph in Egypt gathered, but true and heavenly grain, so that, having gathered grain during the time of abundance, he would have something to distribute when famine had been sent upon Egypt—not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of God. He gathers words of abundance from the prophets, from the Law, and from the apostles. Hence, when books are no longer being written, no new instrument is being produced, and the things that had been carried by Jesus into the apostles’ storehouses—that is, into their souls and those of all the saints—are no longer being sent by the apostles, he distributes and nourishes Egypt, which is endangered by famine, especially the brothers of whom it is written: “I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the Church I will sing to you” (Ps. XXI).

Other people also possess words of patience, words of judgment, and words concerning the other virtues. This is the grain that Joseph distributed to the Egyptians. But there is another grain that he distributed to the brothers—that is, to his disciples—from the land of Jesse, from the land that faces east: evangelical grain, apostolic grain.

From this grain we ought to make bread, but in such a way that it is not mixed with old leaven. Let us have new bread made from the grain of the Scriptures, flour ground together in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

**335–336 HOMILY XXIX. On the passage that is written: “But Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned”; and on his first temptation. Chapter IV.**

[Col. 0283A]

When you read in the Gospel, “But Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned,” and in the Acts of the Apostles that they were “filled with the Holy Spirit” (Acts II), take care not to think that the apostles were equal to the Savior. Rather, understand that Jesus, the apostles, and any other saint were filled with the Holy Spirit according to the measure of their vessel.

For example, if you wished to say, “These vessels are full of wine or oil,” you would not immediately judge that they were filled in equal measure, since one can hold a sextarius, another a jar, and another an amphora. In the same way, Jesus and Paul were full of the Holy Spirit, but Paul’s vessel was much smaller than Jesus’ vessel; nevertheless, each was filled according to its own measure.

After receiving baptism, the Savior, full of the Holy Spirit who had come upon him from heaven in the form of a dove, was led by the Spirit. For since “all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Rom. VIII), and he, uniquely beyond all others, was the Son of God, it was therefore necessary that he too be led by the Holy Spirit. For it is written: “He was led by the Spirit into the wilderness” (Matt. IV).

Jesus was tempted for forty days, but we do not know what his temptations were. Perhaps they were omitted because they were too great to be committed to writing. Or, to put it this way: just as the world could not contain all the books if everything Jesus did and taught had been written, so the world could not have borne the temptations of the forty days during which the Lord was tempted by the devil, if Scripture had related them.

It is enough for us to know only this: that he was in the wilderness for forty days, was tempted by the devil, and ate nothing during those days. By continual and unbroken fasting he mortified the sense of the flesh; and when the days had been completed, he was hungry.

The devil said to him: “If you are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread.” He says, “this stone.” Which stone? Clearly, the devil was pointing out the one he wanted to become bread.

What sort of temptation is this: that, when the Son asks the Father for bread, he should receive a stone instead of bread—the very thing that even the adversary himself did not want? For this is what the devil wanted: that the stone should become bread. Why did he not rather want—not to turn the stone into bread, but to turn into a stone the human being [Col. 0283D] whom the devil had pointed out as bread?

I think that even to this day the devil points out a stone and urges each person to speak: “Say that this stone should become bread.” In every temptation by which human beings were to be tempted, the Lord was first tempted according to the assumption of the flesh. He was tempted so that, when he conquered, we too might conquer.

What I am saying may perhaps seem obscure unless it is made clearer by an example. If you see heretics eating the falsehood of their doctrines instead of bread, know that their word is the stone which the devil points out. Nor should you think that he has only one stone. He has many stones, concerning which Matthew introduces him as saying: “Say that these stones should become loaves.”

Marcion spoke, and the devil’s stone became bread for him. Valentinus spoke, and another stone was turned into bread for him. Basilides had one of this kind, as did the other heretics. Therefore, we must carefully take precautions, lest, while eating the devil’s stone, we suppose that we are feeding on the bread of God.

Otherwise, what temptation would there have been in a stone becoming bread and being eaten by the Savior? Let us imagine that, at the devil’s proposal, the Lord had turned a stone into bread [variant: “turned it”], eaten what he himself had made by his power, and satisfied his hunger. What sort of temptation would that be, and what victory would there be, if the matter were written in such a simple way?

But, as we have said, when the meaning is examined, the account shows both that there would have been a temptation if the change had occurred, and that there was a victory because the proposed change was rejected. At the same time it is shown that this bread made from a stone is not the word of God, which nourishes the human being. Concerning that bread it is written: “Human beings shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.”

I will answer you, deceitful and wicked one, who do not hesitate to tempt me: there is another bread—the word of God, which gives life to the human being.

At the same time, let us observe that it is not the Son of God who speaks these words, but the human being whom the Son of God deigned to assume. For he answers as though speaking from the human being and says: “It is written, ‘Human beings shall not live by bread alone’” (Matt. IV). From this it is clear that it was not God but a human being who was tempted.

Carefully examining the meaning of Scripture, I think I can discover the reason why John did not describe the Lord’s temptation, but only Matthew, Luke, and Mark did. John, who had begun from God, saying, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I), could not weave together the order of the divine generation; he had expressed only that the Word was from God and with God, and added: “And the Word became flesh.”

Since God cannot be tempted, and since this was the subject of John’s discourse, he therefore does not introduce him as being tempted by the devil. But because the book of the generation of Jesus Christ is narrated in Matthew’s Gospel, and his generation is described in Luke, and in Mark it is a human being who is tempted, for this reason the same answer is attributed to him: “Human beings shall not live by bread alone.”

If, then, the Son of God, who is God, became a human being for your sake and was tempted, you, who are human by nature, ought not to be indignant if you are sometimes tempted. If, when tempted, you imitate the one who was tempted for you and conquer every temptation, you will have hope with him who was then a human being but now—

**[Note: [Col. 0283D]** Origen was indeed charged with this, as Pamphilus testifies in his *Apology*: that he believed the Savior did not remain in the flesh at the right hand of the Father, but stripped off the flesh and placed it in the sun. The charge was evidently drawn from that verse of the eighteenth Psalm: “He placed his tabernacle in the sun.” A similar madness is also attributed to Marcellus of Ancyra, namely, that the flesh would be rejected by Christ after the resurrection, with the result that he would cease to be a human being and a king.

But Origen’s reasoning here is different. When he says that Christ ceased to be a human being, he is not denying that he remained human, but that he remained mortal; nor does he mean that the Savior was stripped of flesh, but that the condition of humanity—death—had been overcome. Thus he concludes: “He who in no way dies is no longer a human being, but God.” But Christ is no longer subject to death; therefore Christ ceased to be a human being. His entire question concerns the name: he by no means wishes to count as a human being one who is not subject to death. Since he thinks correctly about the matter itself, perhaps only his affected subtlety should be censured.]**

a human being ceased to be. For if one who was once a human being, after being tempted and after the devil departed from him until the time of death, rises from the dead and will no longer die—and every human being is subject to death—then this one, who in no way dies, is no longer a human being, but is God.

If, then, he who was once a human being is God, and you ought to become like him, when we become like him and see him as he is, you too must become God, in Christ Jesus. To him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

**HOMILY XXX. The Savior’s second temptation. Chapter IV.**

Both the Son of God and the Antichrist desire to reign. But the Antichrist desires to reign in order to kill those whom he has subjected to himself; Christ reigns in order to save. [Col. 0285B] And each one of us, if he is blessed, is ruled by Christ—by the word, wisdom, justice, and truth. But if we are lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, we are ruled by sin, concerning which the Apostle says: “Therefore let not sin reign in your mortal body” (Rom. VI).

Thus two kings hasten to reign, striving against one another: the devil, king of sin, over sinners; and Christ, king of justice, over the just. Knowing that Christ had come to remove his kingdom, so that those who were under him might begin to be under Christ, the devil showed him all the kingdoms of the world and the people of this age: how some are ruled by fornication, others by greed; some are carried away by popular concern [variant: “breeze”], while others are captured by the allurements of beauty.

Nor should we suppose that, when he showed him the kingdoms of the world, he showed him, for example, the kingdom of the Persians or that of the Indians. Rather, he showed him all the kingdoms of the world—that is, his own kingdom, how he reigned in the world—in order that, urging Christ to do what he wanted, he might begin to have Christ himself subjected to him.

“Do you wish,” he said, “to reign over these human beings?” He showed him countless multitudes of people held under his power. And truly, if we wish simply to confess our misery and unhappiness, the devil is almost the king of the whole world. Hence he is also called by the Savior “the ruler of this age.”

Therefore, when he says, “You see these people who are under my kingdom,” he shows him, in a moment of time—that is, in the present course of time, which in comparison with eternity occupies the space of a moment. The Savior had no need for the dignities and affairs of this age to be shown to him. As soon as he turned the sight of his eyes toward contemplation, he saw both the sins that were reigning and those who were ruled by vices; and he saw the devil himself, the ruler of the age, approaching and rejoicing in his own destruction because he held so many under his power.

The devil therefore says to the Lord: “You have come for this purpose—to fight against me and remove from my power those whom I now hold subject? I do not want you to contend; I do not want you to struggle, lest you suffer any trouble in the contest. There is only one thing I ask: fall down and worship me, and receive the whole kingdom that I possess.”

But our Lord and Savior certainly wishes to reign, and for all nations to be subjected so that they may serve justice, truth, and the other virtues. Yet he wishes to reign as justice itself, so that he may reign without labor, doing nothing dishonorable. He does not wish to be crowned without labor by being subjected to the devil, nor to reign over others in such a way that he himself is ruled by the devil.

Therefore Jesus says to him: “It is written: You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Matt. IV). “I want all these people to be subject to me,” he says, “so that they may worship the Lord God and serve him alone. This is the desire of my kingdom. But you want me to receive from you the sins that I came to destroy and that I desire to take away from others as well.

“Know and understand that I remain in what I have said: the Lord God alone is to be worshiped. I will bring all these people under my power and subject them to my kingdom. Let us rejoice that we too are subject to him, and let us beseech the Lord that, while sin reigns in our body, he may mortify it, and that Christ Jesus alone may reign over us, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.”

**HOMILY XXXI. On the Savior’s third temptation. Chapter IV.**

“Search the Scriptures,” so that even in what appear to be simple matters you may discover no small mysteries. Let us search the beginning of the Gospel reading that we have all heard today, and what was hidden will come into the open.

“The devil led Jesus to Jerusalem.” It is incredible that the devil should lead the Son [Col. 0286C] of God and that he should follow. He followed plainly like an athlete going to the contest, proceeding of his own will. He did not fear the tempter, nor dread the ambushes of his most cunning enemy; in a certain sense he was saying: “Lead me wherever you wish; tempt me as you please. I offer myself willingly for temptation; I endure whatever you suggest. I present myself to whatever you may try against me; you will find me stronger in everything.”

He therefore led him to Jerusalem and set him on the pinnacle of the temple and said: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down.” He led him to the summit, to the highest point of the temple, and urged him to hurl himself from there.

When he deceitfully proposed this and strove under the pretext of glory, the Savior said: “It is written: You shall not tempt the Lord your God.”

At the same time, consider how the devil tempts. He dares to tempt from nowhere else except the divine books and the Psalms. He takes his testimony from them and says: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down; for it is written: ‘He has commanded his angels concerning you, and they will lift you up in their hands, lest you perhaps strike your foot against a stone.’”

How do you know this, devil—that these things are written? Have you read the prophets, or have you come to know the divine utterances? Though you remain silent, I will answer for you. You read them not so that you yourself might become better through reading the saints, but so that through their simplicity you might kill those who are friends of the letter.

You know that if you wish to speak to him from other volumes, you will not deceive him, nor will your assertions be able to command authority. Marcion reads the Scriptures like the devil; Basilides does so; Valentinus does so, so that together with the devil they might say to the Savior: “It is written: ‘He has commanded his angels concerning you, and they will lift you up in their hands, lest you strike your foot against a stone’” (Matt. IV).

Whenever you hear a testimony from Scripture, take care not immediately to assent to the speaker. Consider who he is, what his interpretation is, and what his intention is, lest he pretend to be holy when he is not, and lest, infected with the poisons of heresy, a wolf lurk beneath a sheep’s skin; lest the devil be speaking in him from the Scriptures.

But just as the devil speaks from the Scriptures by taking advantage of circumstances, so, conversely, Paul, for the benefit of those who hear, draws testimony not only from the Scriptures but also from [Note: [Col. 0287D] Read Jerome’s very illuminating discussion of this subject in *Letter 70 to Magnus*, section 2.] secular books, and says: “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies” (Titus I.12). And again, concerning another matter: “For we are indeed his offspring” (Acts XVII.28). Likewise, from the comic poet: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (I Cor. XV).

But neither can the devil deceive me on this account if he speaks from the Scriptures, nor can Paul in any way frighten me in his speech if he takes an example from pagan literature. Paul also took words from those outside the faith in order to sanctify them.

Let us see, then, how the devil speaks to the Lord from the Scriptures. “For it is written: ‘He has commanded his angels concerning you, and they will lift you up in their hands, lest you strike your foot against a stone.’”

See how he is deceitful even in these testimonies. He wants to diminish the Savior’s glory, as though he needed the angels’ help and would strike his foot unless their hands supported him. He takes a testimony and interprets it concerning Christ, although it was not written about Christ but about the saints generally.

I openly and with complete confidence contradict the devil: this cannot be understood of Christ. For he does not need the assistance of angels, being greater than the angels and having obtained a better inheritance and name than they. God never said to any angel: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Heb. I). He never spoke to any of them as to a son: “He makes his angels spirits and his ministers a burning fire” (Ps. II); rather, he spoke these words specifically to his own Son, concerning whom he says innumerable things through the prophets.

The Son of God does not need the assistance of angels. Rather, learn, devil, that unless Jesus helps the angels, they will strike their foot. [Note: Recall what we said above on this opinion of Origen in connection with Homilies 10 and 23.] And if any of the angels appeared to have stumbled—concerning whom it was formerly read that “we shall judge angels”—he stumbled because he did not stretch out his hand toward Jesus, so that, being grasped by him, he would not fall. Since you, trusting in your own strength, do not invoke Jesus’ protection, you stumble, and you have refused to believe in Jesus Christ, the Son of God.

But so that you may know that you have interpreted the passage wrongly, and that what follows is to be understood not of Christ but of the saints, listen. It is not Jesus Christ whom God delivers from the ruin and the noonday demon, but the saints. Read the ninetieth Psalm, whose beginning is: “He who dwells in the help of the Most High will abide under the protection of the God of heaven.” You will find that the following words fit a righteous man more than the Son of God: “A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand; but it shall not come near you. Nevertheless, with your eyes you shall see, and you shall behold the repayment of sinners,” and the rest, as you interpret it concerning the person of the righteous.

But even so, when the devil perversely brings forward testimonies to assert that they are understood of the Savior, he is silent and passes over the verses that were written against himself. For after he had said, “He has commanded his angels concerning you, and they will lift you up in their hands, lest you strike your foot against a stone,” he was silent about what follows: “You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample upon the lion and the dragon.”

Why are you silent, devil, unless it is because you are the basilisk, the king of all serpents, possessing more dangerous poisons than the others? As soon as you see someone, you kill him. And you take as your companion another opposing power, called the asp, which is subject to the righteous man; therefore you are silent about everything.

You are the dragon; you are the lion, concerning whom it is written: “You shall tread upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample upon the lion and the dragon.” But although you are silent, we [Note: Earlier, *vos* (“you”) was falsely read. Manifest errors of this sort are corrected more than once below without notifying the reader.] who read the Scriptures more correctly know that we have power to trample you, and that this authority has been given to us—not only in the Old Testament, as is now sung in the Psalm, but also in the New, when the Savior says: “Behold, I give you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall harm you” (Luke X).

Let us take up weapons, strengthened by such power, and do everything in such a way that through our way of life we may trample the lion and the dragon. To know how the lion is trampled and the dragon crushed, read Paul’s Epistle, in which he asserts that sinners are trampled by the Son of God.

Therefore, just as the sinner is trampled by the Son of God, so conversely the righteous person tramples the lion and the dragon, and tramples every power of the enemy in the name of Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

**HOMILY XXXII. On the passage that is written: “Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit,” up to the place where it says: “And the eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed upon him.” Chapter IV.**

[Col. 0288D]

At first, Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit in the wilderness for forty days. While he was being tempted by the devil and was still to contend against him by force, both the first and second time he is spoken of simply as being “in the Spirit,” without any added qualification. But when he had overcome in combat the three temptations that Scripture records, notice what is added concerning the Spirit with particular care: “And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit.”

“Power” is added because he had trampled the dragon and defeated the tempter face to face. Jesus therefore returned in the power of the Spirit to the land of Galilee, and his fame spread throughout the whole region. He was teaching in their synagogues, and was glorified by all.

Take care not to judge only those people blessed and to think that you are first in learning. If what is written is true, the Lord speaks not only then in the assemblies of the Jews but also today in this assembly. And not only in this one, but in another gathering as well, and throughout the whole world, Jesus teaches, seeking instruments through which he may teach.

Pray that he may find me also composed and fit for singing. For just as almighty God seeks prophets at a time when mortals need prophecy, and finds, for example, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel, so God seeks instruments through which he may teach his word or instruct peoples in their synagogues, and be glorified by all.

Now Jesus is glorified by all more than at that time when he was known only in one province.

Then he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up, and, entering the synagogue according to his custom on the Sabbath day, he stood up to read. The book of the prophet Isaiah was given to him. Unrolling the book, he found the place where it was written: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me” (Matt. X).
