He did not unroll the book by chance and happen upon the readings while prophesying within himself; this too was the providence of God. For just as it is written, “A sparrow does not fall into a snare without the will of the Father,” and since all the hairs of the apostles’ heads have been numbered, so perhaps this too—that the book of Isaiah in particular was found, and not another reading but this one, which spoke of the mystery of Christ, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me” (Isa. XV)—was not a matter of chance.

For it is Christ who speaks these words. We must not suppose that he came there casually or by accident, but through the providence and dispensation of God. Let us therefore consider what the prophet was saying and how he afterward speaks in the synagogue concerning himself.

“He sent me,” he says, “to evangelize the poor.” The poor signify the nations. They were poor, possessing nothing at all—not God, not the Law, not the Prophets, not righteousness, nor the other virtues. For this reason God sent him to announce good news to the poor: “to proclaim release to captives.”

We were captives, bound for so many years by Satan, who held us captive and subjected us to himself. Jesus came to proclaim release to captives, and sight to the blind. Through his word and the preaching of his teaching, the blind see. Therefore, the proclamation of release is to be understood as applying not only to captives but also to the blind.

**345–346** “To send the broken into freedom.” What was so broken and crushed as the human being who was released and healed by Jesus?

“To proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord.” According to the simple understanding, some say that the Savior preached the Gospel in Judea for one year, and that this is what is meant by “to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord,” and the day of retribution. Unless perhaps the divine word signifies some mystery in the proclamation of the Lord’s year.

There will be other days, not like those that we now see in the world; other months, and a different order of the kalends. Just as these things will be different, so the future year of the Lord will be a pleasing year.

All these things were foretold so that, after sight following blindness, after freedom following chains, and after healing from various wounds, we might come to the acceptable year of the Lord.

When Jesus had read these things, he rolled up the book, returned it to the attendant, and sat down; and the eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed upon him.

And now, if you wish, in this synagogue and assembly your eyes too can be fixed upon the Savior. When you direct the principal gaze of your heart toward contemplating wisdom, truth, and God’s Only-Begotten, your eyes look upon Jesus.

Blessed is the assembly of which Scripture bears witness that all eyes were fixed upon him. How I wish that this gathering might have a similar testimony, so that the eyes of all—the catechumens and the faithful, women and men, children—not the eyes of the body but of the soul—might look upon Jesus.

For when you have looked toward him, your faces will become brighter from his light and his gaze, and you will be able to say: “The light of your face has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Ps. IV). To him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

**HOMILY XXXIII. On the passage that is written: “Surely you will say to me this proverb,” and the rest, up to the place where he says: “But none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian.”**

In Capernaum, as far as the light of the historical account is concerned, Jesus had not yet stayed, nor is he described as having performed any sign there, since he had not been there. But before he came to Capernaum, he is shown to have been in his homeland, that is, in Nazareth.

“Surely you will say to me this proverb: ‘Physician, heal yourself.’ Whatever we have heard was done in Capernaum, do here also in your homeland.”

Therefore, I think that some mystery lies hidden in the present discourse, and that Nazareth has been presented as a type of the Jews and Capernaum as a type of the Gentiles (Rom. XI).

Knowing, then, that he would have no honor in his homeland—neither he, nor the prophet, nor the apostles—Jesus did not wish to preach there, but preached among the Gentiles, lest the people of his homeland say to him: “Surely you will say to me this proverb: ‘Physician, heal yourself.’”

For there will be a time when the Jewish people will say: “Whatever signs and wonders I have heard were done in Capernaum among the Gentiles, do here also in your homeland. What you have shown to the whole world, show also to us. Preach your word to the people of Israel, so that at least when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel may be saved” (Rom. XI).

For this reason it seems to me that the Savior answered the people of Nazareth who questioned him in the following order: “No prophet is acceptable in his homeland.” And I think that what is said is truer according to the mystery than according to the letter, although Jeremiah was not accepted in his homeland, Anathoth (Jer. I), nor Isaiah, whatever his homeland was, nor the other prophets.

Rather, it seems to me that it should be understood in this way: the homeland of all the prophets was the circumcised people, and this people did not receive the prophets or their prophecies; whereas the nations, who had been far from the prophets and had no knowledge of them, received the prophecy of Jesus Christ.

Therefore, no prophet is acceptable in his homeland—that is, among the Jewish people. But we, who were “alienated from the covenant and strangers to the promises” (Eph. II), received the prophets with our whole heart. We possess Moses and the prophets who preach Christ more fully than those who, because they did not receive Jesus, also failed to receive those who announced him.

Therefore, to the statement he had made, “No prophet is acceptable in his homeland,” he adds another: “In truth I tell you, there were many widows in the days of Elijah in Israel, when the sky was shut up for three years and six months.”

His meaning is this: Elijah was a prophet, but he was among the Jewish people. Yet when he was about to perform a wonderful deed, although there were many widows in Israel, he left them and went to a widow in Zarephath of Sidon, to a Gentile woman, explaining a figure of what was to come. For when famine prevailed—not famine of bread or thirst for water, but famine of hearing the word of God—he came to the widow, concerning whom the prophet also bears witness, saying: “The children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isa. LIV).

When he came, he multiplied her bread and provisions. You were the widow in Zarephath of Sidon, from whose borders the Canaanite woman came out, desiring that her daughter be healed; and because of her faith she deserved to receive what she asked.

There were therefore many widows among the people of Israel, but Elijah was sent to none of them except to the widow in Zarephath.

He also speaks another word relating to the same meaning: “There were many lepers in Israel in the days of Elisha the prophet, and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian,” who certainly was not from Israel.

Consider that even to the present day there are many lepers in Israel according to the flesh. Observe, conversely, [them] covered with the foulness of leprosy, while you are cleansed through the spiritual Elisha, our Lord and Savior. [Note: Either *absque* must be read in place of *atque*, with a sense not altogether unsuitable, or the text here is mutilated, miserably truncated through the loss of several words.] And it is said to you: “Arise and go to the Jordan, and wash, and your flesh shall be restored to you” (II Kings V).

Naaman arose and went, and by speaking he fulfilled the mystery of baptism. His flesh became like the flesh of a child who has been born in Christ Jesus in the washing of regeneration. To him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

**HOMILY XXXIV** [Note: [Col. 0291D] These final six homilies, since they do not preserve the continuous order found in the preceding material, clearly reveal themselves to have been extracted from the larger number of homilies that Adamantius composed. The author himself—as the distinguished Huetius also observed—declares in volume XIII on John that he had prepared more homilies than these thirty-nine that survive, translated into Latin by Jerome, when he says: “As for what concerns the hundred sheep, you have it in the homilies that we composed on Luke.” For you find nothing of this kind in the surviving *Homilies on Luke*.] On the passage that is written: “Teacher, what good thing must I do to possess eternal life?” up to the place where he says: “Go and do likewise.”

[Col. 0291D]

Although there are many commandments in the Law, the Savior set forth in the Gospel only those which, in a certain concise form, would lead the obedient to eternal things. For this is what the lawyer’s question concerns, when he asked Him, saying: “Teacher, what must I do to possess eternal life?” This passage, according to Luke, was read to you today. He replied: “What is written in the Law? How do you read it?” “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your strength, and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself.” And then He said: “You have answered well; do this, and you will live.” There is no doubt that by doing this you will receive eternal life, about which the lawyer had also asked.

At the same time, we are clearly taught in the commandment of the Law that we are to love God. It is written in Deuteronomy: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God. And you shall love the Lord your God with all your mind,” and so forth, “and your neighbor as yourself” (Deut. VI). Concerning these things the Savior also testified, saying: “On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matt. XXII).

But when the lawyer wished to justify himself and to show that no one was his neighbor, saying, “Who is my neighbor?” the Lord introduced a parable whose beginning is: “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho” (Luke X), and so forth. He teaches that no one was the descending man’s neighbor except the one who wished to keep the commandments and prepare himself to be the neighbor of every person who needs assistance. For this is what is placed at the end of the parable: “Which of these three, do you think, was the neighbor of the man who fell among robbers?” Neither the priest nor the Levite was his neighbor; but, as the lawyer himself also answered, the one who showed mercy was his neighbor. Hence the Savior also says: “Go, and you do likewise.”

One of the presbyters, wishing to interpret the parable, used to say that the man who went down was Adam; Jerusalem, paradise; Jericho, the world; the robbers, the opposing Powers; the priest, the Law; the Levite, the prophets; the Samaritan, Christ; the wounds, disobedience; the animal, the Lord’s body; and the inn—*pandochium*, that is, a lodging-house, which receives everyone who wishes to enter—as the Church.

[Editorial note: This too is a product of Jerome’s pen: *stabulum* is the Latin equivalent of the Greek πανδοχεῖον (*pandochium*).] He understood the two denarii to mean the Father and the Son, and the innkeeper to mean the overseer of the Church, to whom its administration has been entrusted. As for the Samaritan’s promise that he would return, he held that this signified the Savior’s second coming.

Although these things are said reasonably and beautifully, it must not nevertheless be thought that they apply to every person. For not every person went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, nor do all people therefore dwell in the present age—although the one who was sent came on account of the lost sheep of the house of Israel.

Therefore, the man who went down from Jerusalem to Jericho fell among robbers because he himself wished to go down. The robbers are no others than those of whom the Savior says: “All who came before me were thieves and robbers” (John X). Yet he did not fall among thieves, but among robbers far worse than thieves. When he had fallen among them while descending from Jerusalem, they stripped him and inflicted wounds upon him.

What are these wounds? What are the injuries with which the man was wounded? Vices and sins. Then, because the robbers who had stripped and wounded him did not remain beside the naked man but, after again laying wounds upon him, left him, it is for this reason that it is written: “Stripping him and inflicting wounds, they departed,” leaving him not dead but half-dead.

It happened that on the same road a priest first, and then a Levite, came down—perhaps they had done some good to other people, but not to this man who had gone down from Jerusalem to Jericho. The priest saw him—I think the Law saw him; the Levite, as I understand it, was the prophetic word. When they saw him, they left him and passed by.

Providence was preserving the half-dead man for the one who was stronger than the Law and the Prophets, namely the Samaritan, whose name means “guardian.” He is the one who neither slumbers nor sleeps while guarding Israel. For the sake of the half-dead man this Samaritan came—not by descending from Jerusalem to Jericho, as the priest and Levite did; or, if he did descend, he descended for this reason: to save and guard the man who was about to die.

To him the Jews said: “You are a Samaritan and have a demon” (John VIII). Although he denied having a demon, he did not wish to deny that he was a Samaritan. For he knew that he was a guardian.

And so, when he came to the half-dead man and saw him rolling in his own blood, he had compassion on him and approached him in order to become his neighbor. He bound his wounds and poured in oil mixed with wine; nor did he say what is read in the prophet: “It is not possible to apply a poultice, or oil, or bandages” (Isa. I).

This is the Samaritan whose care and assistance all who are ill require. Above all, the man who had gone down from Jerusalem, fallen among robbers, and been wounded by them and left half-alive required the help of this Samaritan.

Now, so that you may know that, according to God’s providence, this Samaritan descended to heal the man who had fallen among robbers, you will be clearly taught by the fact that he had bandages with him, oil with him, and wine with him. I think, however, that the Samaritan carried these things with him not only for this one half-dead man, but also for others who had been wounded for various reasons and needed bandages, oil, and wine.

He had oil of which it is written: “That he may gladden his face with oil” (Ps. II)—plainly so that by the oil the swellings of the wounds of the man who had been healed might also then be soothed. But with wine he cleanses the wounds, adding something of severity. And he placed the wounded man upon his animal, that is, upon his own body, in accordance with the fact that he deigned to assume humanity.

This Samaritan bears our sins (Isa. LIII), and suffers for us. He carries the half-dead man, brings him into the inn, that is, into the Church, which receives everyone and denies its assistance to no one. To it Jesus summons all, saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI).

After he had brought him in, he did not immediately depart. Rather, he remained with the half-dead man for one day in the lodging-house and treated his wounds not only by day but also by night, devoting to him the rest of his care and diligence.

When he wished to depart in the morning, he took two denarii from his tested silver, from his tested money, and entrusted them to the innkeeper—plainly the angel of the Church. He commanded him to care for the man diligently and bring him to complete health, the man whom, because of the shortness of time, he himself had also treated.

The two denarii seem to me to signify knowledge of the Father and the Son, and knowledge of the mystery: how the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father.

[Editorial note: In order to make the sense clear, I would prefer to insert the words “who wishes.” Read *donentur* with De La Rue, Origen’s editor, instead of *donantur*, and the matter will be settled.]

The wages are given to the angel who wishes to care more diligently for the man entrusted to him, and he is promised that whatever he spends from his own resources for the treatment of the half-dead man will immediately be repaid.

Truly this is the guardian of the Law and the prophets, the nearer guardian of souls, who showed mercy to the man who had fallen among robbers and proved to be his neighbor not so much in word as in deed.

Therefore, since it is possible, according to what follows, for us to imitate Christ and to have mercy on those who have fallen among robbers—to approach them, bind their wounds, pour in oil and wine, place them upon our own animal, and carry their burdens—the Son of God, exhorting us to such things, speaks not only to the lawyer but also to all of us: “Go, and you do likewise.”

If we do these things likewise, we shall obtain eternal life in Christ Jesus, to whom belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXV

On the passage: “When you go with your adversary,” and so forth, up to the place where he says: “You will pay the very last mite.”

If it were not implanted in our nature to judge what is just, the Savior would never say: “Why do you not judge for yourselves what is just?” (Luke XII). But, so that we may not go too far in proving this statement—especially since many more difficult matters are connected with this chapter—it will suffice for the moment to say that it signifies the proud.

Rather, let us spread the sails of our souls toward God and pray for the arrival of His word, so that He may interpret the parable of which it is written:

“When you go with your adversary to the magistrate, on the way make every effort to be released from him, lest perhaps he hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and you be thrown into prison. Truly I say to you, you will not come out from there until you have paid the very last mite” (Luke XII).

I see four persons being mentioned: the adversary, the magistrate, the judge, and the officer. Since the evangelist Matthew seems to have said something similar when he says, “Be well disposed toward your adversary while you are on the way with him,” I ask whether the meaning is identical or whether there is some proximity between them, since in Matthew one person has been omitted and another changed.

The magistrate has been omitted, and an officer has been inserted in place of the exactor; but the adversary and the judge are similarly mentioned by both. Thus we go with our adversary to the magistrate, and, while we are still on the way, we must labor earnestly to be released from him.

[Editorial note: The Greek verb in the sacred text is ambiguous; *κατασύρᾳ* (“he may drag”) seems here to be preferable to the Latin.]

For the verb is ambiguous and can refer either to the magistrate or to the adversary: “lest he”—whether the adversary or the magistrate—“hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer,” and you will not come out from there until you pay the last thing, in the neuter.

[Editorial note: He seems deliberately to prefer the reading of the Greek archetype, which has the neuter *τὸ ἔσχατον* (“the last thing”), over the other reading found in some copies, *τὸν ἔσχατον* (“the last one”).]

For this Matthew says: “Until you pay the last quadrans” (Matt. V). Both writers use the word “last,” but they seem to differ in that one has “quadrans,” while the other has “mite.”

Some more secret matters must be touched upon, so that we may understand that the adversary is one person, while the other three persons are the magistrate, the judge, and the officer.

We read—if anyone wishes to accept this kind of Scripture—that the angels of righteousness and iniquity dispute over Abraham’s salvation and destruction, while both companies wish to claim him for their own assembly. If anyone dislikes this, let him pass to the book written under the title *The Shepherd*, and he will find that two angels attend every human being: an evil one, who urges him toward perverse things, and a good one, who persuades him toward all that is best.

It is written elsewhere that double angels attend a person, whether for good or for evil. The Savior also mentions the good angels, saying: “Their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVIII).

At the same time, ask whether the angels of the little ones in the Church always see the face of the Father, while the angels of others do not have the freedom to look upon the Father’s face. For it is not to be hoped that everyone’s angels see the face of the Father who is in heaven.

If I belong to the Church, even though I am the least, my angel has the freedom and confidence always to see the face of my Father who is in heaven. But if I am outside, and do not belong to that Church which has neither spot nor wrinkle (Eph. V), or anything of this kind, and by the fact itself I am shown to be alien to such a congregation, my angel does not have the confidence to look upon the face of my Father who is in heaven.

For this reason the angels are concerned for the good, knowing that, if they govern us well and bring us to salvation, they too will have the confidence to see the face of the Father. For just as, when salvation is obtained for human beings through their care and diligence, they always look upon the Father’s face, so, if a human being falls through their negligence, they know that the matter also concerns their own danger.

And just as a good bishop and an excellent administrator of the Church knows that it is a matter of his merit and virtue if the sheep entrusted to him are kept safe, so understand the matter also concerning the angels.

It is a disgrace to an angel if a righteous person has been entrusted to him and sins; conversely, it is glory to an angel if even the least person in the Church has been entrusted to him. For they will see—not merely at some time but always—the face of the Father who is in heaven, while others will not always see it.

According to the merit of those whose angels they are, the angels will contemplate the face of God either always or never, either little or more. God knows the matter fully, and so does anyone—although such a person is rarely found—whom Christ has enlightened.

Let us therefore consider first who the adversary is with whom we travel. The adversary is always with us. Unhappy and wretched are we! Whenever we sin, our adversary rejoices, knowing that he has power with the ruler of this age, who has reason to rejoice and boast because the adversary has made this or that person subject to the ruler of this age through such and so many sins, through this offense or that.

Sometimes, however, if someone is prepared with the armor of God and has protected himself on every side, the adversary may attempt to inflict a wound but has no power to strike.

The adversary always walks with us; he never abandons us. He seeks an opportunity for ambush, to see whether he can overthrow us, so that he may place an evil thought in the ruling faculty [*ἡγεμονικῷ*] of our heart.

“When you go to the magistrate”—who is this magistrate? When the Most High divided the nations, when He scattered the sons of Adam, He established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God, and the Lord’s portion became His people Jacob, Israel the cord of His inheritance (Deut. X).

Thus, from the beginning, the earth was divided among rulers, that is, angels. Daniel more clearly testifies that those whom Moses called angels were rulers, saying: “The prince of the kingdom of the Persians,” “the prince of the kingdom of the Greeks,” and “Michael, the prince of the nations.”

Each of us has with him an attached adversary whose task is to lead us to his ruler and say: “O ruler—for example, of the kingdom of the Persians—this man who was formerly subject to you I guarded for you as was required. For none of the other rulers was able to transfer him to himself—not even the one who claimed that he had come for the purpose of snatching people from all the inheritances of the Persians, Greeks, and every nation, and making them subject as God’s inheritance.”

Christ our Lord conquered all the rulers. Passing beyond their boundaries, He transferred captive peoples to Himself for salvation. You too belonged to the portion of some ruler; Jesus came, snatched you from the power of evil, and offered you to God the Father.

Our adversary therefore walks along, leading us to his ruler. Since I believe that all the words of Scripture have a reason, I do not think that the judge is needlessly written in Greek with the article, which signifies individuality, while “ruler” is written without the article in a simple sense.

[Editorial note: Hieronymus added two little words from his own hand, both here and a little later, which are more clearly understood in Greek. The Greek reads *ἐπ’ ἄρχοντα* (“to a ruler”), without the article, and *πρὸς τὴν κριτὴν καὶ ὁ κριτὴς* (“to the judge, and the judge”), with the article.]

“When you go with your adversary.” He significantly says “your.” For not everyone’s adversaries are the same; individuals have individual adversaries who follow them everywhere and accompany them.

“When you go with your adversary to the ruler.” He did not place the article before “ruler,” so that he might not seem to indicate a definite one, but wrote it without the article in order to show that he is one among many. This is more clearly understood in Greek.

For each of us does not have his own particular ruler. The Syrian is under the ruler of the Syrians, and each person is under the ruler of his own nation—if it is enough for me to have proceeded this far and to pass from this discussion to another, greater one, in order to mention the other nations also. Hence it is said: “Look at Israel according to the flesh” (Num. XI).

To have begun wisely is to have spoken well, although here too the word may have begun among the people.

He who wishes to lead you to his ruler and to lead you away from another ruler says: “When you go with your adversary to the ruler, on the way make every effort to be released from him.”

Unless you labor with all diligence while you are still traveling the road, before you enter before the ruler, before the ruler hands you over to the judge, after the adversary has prepared you for this, you will strive in vain.

Therefore make every effort to be released from him—or from the ruler to whom the adversary is dragging you. Make every effort to possess wisdom, justice, courage, and temperance; then this will be fulfilled: “Behold, the man and his works are before his face.”

Unless you make the effort, you will not be able to break the adversary’s agreement, whose friendship is against God.

“When you go with your adversary to the ruler, on the way make every effort.” Something, I do not know what, lies hidden in this passage; there is a secret in the words “on the way make every effort.”

The Savior says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). If you make the effort to be released from the adversary, be in the way. And when you have stood in Him who says, “I am the way,” it is not enough merely to have stood there; make every effort to be released from the adversary.

Unless you make the effort to be released from the adversary, listen to what will follow. The adversary drags you to the judge; or, when the ruler has received you from the adversary, the ruler drags you to the judge.

What an elegant word, “drags,” showing in a certain way that those who resist and are unwilling are dragged and compelled to go to condemnation. For what murderer proceeds at a quick pace to the judge? Who hastens joyfully to his own condemnation, rather than being dragged there unwillingly and in resistance? He knows that he is going there to receive a sentence of death.

“Lest he drag you to the judge.” Who do you think this judge is? I know no other judge except my Lord Jesus Christ, of whom it is said elsewhere: “He will place the sheep at his right hand, but the goats at his left.” And again: “Whoever confesses me, I too will confess him before my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XXV). “But whoever denies me before human beings, I will deny him before my Father who is in heaven.”

“Let him drag you to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer.”

Each of us suffers loss through individual sins, and according to the character and proportion of the offense, the magnitude of the loss is reckoned.

I ought to bring forward some testimony from Scripture concerning loss and the penalty of money. One person suffers a loss of five hundred denarii and owes them; another is condemned for fifty denarii. The same total is remitted to both by the creditor.

Another, as Scripture says, “was brought to him who owed ten thousand talents” (Matt. XVIII), and is condemned in the amount of ten thousand talents. And why do I need to pursue more examples? Each person, according to the character and extent of his sin, pays a different sentence of punishment.

If what you sin is little, you will be struck with the loss of a mite, as Luke wrote; according to Matthew, with that of a quadrans. Nevertheless, the person who became a debtor must also pay this very thing. For you will not come out from there unless you have paid even the smallest debts.

But the faithful person is struck by no loss; rather, he grows richer every day.

[Editorial note: The sentence is taken from the Book of Proverbs, chapter XVII, after verse 6, according to the Septuagint: *τοῦ πιστοῦ ὅλος ὁ κόσμος τῶν χρημάτων, τοῦ δὲ ἀπίστου οὐδὲ ὀβολός* (“For the faithful, the whole world is wealth; but for the faithless, not even an obol”). Jerome interprets it in Letter 53 to Paulinus, §10: “For the believer, the whole world is wealth; but the unbeliever needs even an obol.” See our observations on this passage.]

“For the whole world of riches is his. But the unbeliever does not even possess an obol.”

One person is condemned to a denarius, another to a mina, another to a talent. There is an examiner of this matter who knows the measures of all sins: this offense is condemned to a talent; that sin deserves a punishment of this kind.

For it is written: “When he began to settle the account.” An account must be reckoned with all of us. There is no other time for settling the account than the time of judgment, when it will clearly be known what was entrusted to us, what profit or loss we produced, who among us received a mina, who one talent, who two, and who five (Matt. XXV).

There is no need to indicate more, since it is enough to have said this generally: that we shall render an account; and, if we are found to be debtors, we shall be dragged to the judge and handed over by the judge to the officer.

Each of us has our own officer. But the whole multitude is handed over to many, according to what is written in Isaiah: “My people, your officers strip you, and those who are powerful rule over you” (Isa. III).

The officers rule if we owe something. But if we have confidence and live with an unburdened face, I shall gladly keep the commandment: “Repay to all what is owed: tribute to whom tribute is due, fear to whom fear is due, tax to whom tax is due, honor to whom honor is due” (Rom. XIII).

If I have repaid everything to everyone, I come to the officer and answer with an undaunted mind: “I owe you nothing.” The officer comes to demand payment, but I resist him. For I know that, if I owe nothing, he has no power over me.

But if I am a debtor, my officer will send me to prison, according to the order described above. For the adversary leads me to the ruler, the ruler to the judge, the judge hands me over to the officer, and the officer sends me to prison.

[Editorial note: From this passage too the distinguished Huet infers that Origen believed a limit would be set to the punishments of the damned and that all things would at last somehow become one in God; he therefore admits no punishments except purgatorial ones. We, although above, at Homily 24, and in many other passages, have recognized Origen’s manifest error on the question of eternal punishments, nevertheless do not think that this passage is subject to the same fault. Rather, it seems to be one that may be adduced in his defense. Certainly, though Adamantius could conveniently have distorted the proposed parable perversely to his own view, he expounded it in an almost Catholic sense. Moreover, he very clearly decided that those guilty of graver crimes are to be consigned to eternal punishments, when he says: “If we owe a large sum, like the one who is written to have owed ten thousand talents, I cannot clearly state how long we shall be shut up in prison until we repay the debt. … Surely the one bound by so great a debt will be assigned INFINITE ages for repaying the debt.”]

What is the law of this prison? I do not leave it, nor does the officer allow me to leave, until I have paid the entire debt.

The officer has no power to remit even a quadrans or the smallest portion to me. There is one who can grant remission to debtors who have nothing with which to pay.

“It happened,” he says, “that one who owed five hundred denarii came to him, and another who owed fifty. And when they had nothing with which to repay, he forgave both” (Luke VII).

The one who forgave is the Lord. The one who is an officer, however, is not the lord, but has been appointed by the lord to demand debts.

You were not worthy to have five hundred or fifty denarii forgiven you, nor did you deserve to hear: “Your sins are forgiven.” Rather, you are sent to prison, and there you are required to pay through labor and works, or through penalties and punishments. You will not leave from there unless you have paid the quadrans or the last mite, which in Greek can be called “the small thing.”

[Editorial note: This clause too was added by Jerome, so that the Latin reader might understand the play made by Origen on the various meanings of the word *λεπτόν* (“mite,” literally “thin” or “small”).]

But our sins are fat. For it is written: “The heart of this people has become fat” (Matt. XIII; Acts XXVIII). Or, by comparison with something greater, they are thin and subtle.

Blessed, therefore, is the one who first does not sin; and second, the one who, by comparison, has at least a small sin. Even among small and subtle sins there is a difference.

If money were not something small, it would never be said: “You will not come out from there until you have paid the last quadrans.” How could he have said “the last mite,” which is a denarius, or a coin, or an obol, or a stater, without reference to money?

If we owe a large sum, like the one who is said to have owed ten thousand talents (Matt. XVIII), I cannot clearly state how long we will be shut up in prison until we repay the debt. For if the one who owes little will not leave until he has paid the mite or quadrans, surely the one who has been bound by so great a debt will be assigned infinite ages for repaying the debt.

[Editorial note: Previously *debemus* (“we owe”) was read incorrectly in place of *demus* (“let us give”).]

Therefore, let us make every effort to be released from the adversary while we are on the way, and let us be joined to the Lord Jesus, to whom belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXVI

On the passage: “Whoever wishes to save his soul will lose it,” up to the place where he says: “The kingdom of God is within you.”

“He who seeks,” he says, “to save his soul will lose it; and he who loses it will save it.”

The martyrs seek to save their souls; therefore they lose them in order to save them. But those who wish to save their souls so as not to lose them—these lose both body and soul together in Gehenna.

Therefore, “do not fear those who can kill the body,” he says, “but fear rather him who can destroy soul and body in Gehenna” (Luke XVII).

Concerning the present subject, we shall say this briefly, according to the capacity of our understanding. “The animal person does not receive the things of the Spirit” (1 Cor. II), and for this reason cannot be saved. “The animal body is sown; the spiritual body rises” (1 Cor. XV).

But whoever clings to the Lord becomes one spirit. Therefore, if the one who is joined to the Lord, having been animal, is thereby transformed into the spiritual and becomes one spirit, then let us also lose our souls, so that, by clinging to the Lord, we may be transformed into one spirit.

When He was also asked about the kingdom of God, the Savior answered the Pharisees: “When it comes, the kingdom of God does not come with observation, nor will they say, ‘Look here,’ or, ‘Look there.’ For behold, the kingdom of God is within you” (Luke XVII).

The Savior does not say to everyone, “The kingdom of God is within you.” For in sinners the kingdom of sin is present; and without any ambiguity, either the kingdom of sin or the kingdom of God rules in our heart.

Therefore, whether we consider what we do, what we say, or what we think, let us examine these things more attentively. Then we shall see whether the rule of God reigns in us, or the rule of sins.

Knowing this distinction, the Apostle admonishes certain people, saying: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body” (Rom. VI).

If one of us desires the kingdom of God, he is ruled by it. If someone is tormented by the passion of greed, he is ruled by greed. If someone has injustice as his queen, he is ruled by it. If someone is lifted up by ambition for empty glory, the breath of popular approval rules him.

The person who mourns, the person who fears something, the person who loves, and the person who desires—each of these passions rules him, according as he is possessed by various disturbances.

Recognizing all these things, and how many kinds of kingdoms there are, let us rise and pray to God that He may take away from us the kingdom of the enemy, and that we may be under the kingdom of God Almighty—that is, under the kingdom of wisdom, peace, justice, and truth. All these are understood in the only-begotten Son of God, to whom belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXVII

On the passage concerning the foal of the donkey being untied by the disciples.

It was read in the Gospel according to Luke how, when the Savior had come to Bethphage and Bethany near the Mount of Olives, He sent two of His disciples to untie a foal of a donkey that was bound and on which no human being had ever sat (Luke XIX).

This seems to me to pertain more to a higher understanding than to a simple historical account.

The donkey was bound. Where? Opposite Bethphage and Bethany. Bethany is interpreted as “house of obedience,” while Bethphage means “house of jaws”—a certain priestly place. For jaws were given to priests, as the Law prescribes.

[Editorial note: Compare the books of *Names* and our observations on the etymologies of these words. Jerome repeatedly interprets Bethphage as “the village of priestly jaws.”]

Therefore, to the place where there is obedience, where there is a place dedicated to priests, the Savior sends His disciples to untie the foal of a donkey on which no human being had ever sat.

What else can sit upon a donkey apart from a human being? I wish to take an example for a little while, so that what I am about to say may be understood.

It is written in Isaiah: “The vision of the four-footed creatures in distress and anguish” (Isa. XXX), and so forth, up to the place where he says: “The riches of the asps will not profit them.”

Let each of us consider how great a wealth of asps he previously carried, how great a wealth of beasts, and how no rational human being had ever sat upon our donkey—not the word of Moses, not of Isaiah, not of Jeremiah, nor of any of the other prophets.

Then he will see that the word and reason of God sat upon us when the Lord Jesus came and commanded His disciples, as they went, to untie the foal of the donkey, which had previously been bound, so that it might walk free.

The foal of the donkey, once untied, is brought to Jesus. When sending the disciples to untie it, He had said: “If anyone asks you why you are untying the foal, say to him: ‘Because the Lord has need of it.’”

Many were the lords of this foal before the Savior had need of it.

[Editorial note: Jerome’s exposition of this passage in his *Commentary on Matthew* should be recalled; it is constructed throughout from precisely the same meanings.]

But after He began to be its lord, the many lords ceased to be lords. For no one can serve God and Mammon.

When we have served wickedness, we are subject to many passions and vices. The foal is therefore untied because the Lord has need of it.

You are the foal of the donkey. What does the Son of God need from you? What does He seek from you? He needs your salvation; He desires you to be released from the bonds of sins.

Then the disciples place their garments upon the donkey and make the Savior sit upon it. They take the word of God and place it upon the souls of their hearers.

They remove their garments and spread them beneath Him on the road. The garments of the apostles are upon us: their good works are our adornments. The apostles wish their garments to be trampled by us.

And indeed, the donkey, released by the disciples and carrying Jesus, falls upon the garments of the apostles when it imitates their teaching and life.

Who among us is so blessed that Jesus might sit upon him?

As long as He was on the mountain, He remained with His apostles. But when He began to draw near to the descent, then a crowd of peoples met Him. If He had not come to the descent, the multitude could not have met Him.

He descended and sat upon the foal of the donkey, and the whole people with one voice praised God.

When the Pharisees saw this, they said to the Lord: “Rebuke them.” He answered them: “If these are silent, the stones will cry out” (Matt. III).

When we speak, the stones are silent; when we are silent, the stones cry out. For the Lord can raise up children for Abraham from these stones.

When will we be silent? When the love of many has grown cold, when what was proclaimed by the Savior has been fulfilled: “Do you suppose that when the Son of Man comes, he will find faith on the earth?”

Therefore, let us implore the Lord’s mercy, so that when we are silent the stones may not cry out, but so that we may speak and praise God in the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, to whom belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY XXXVIII

On the passage: “When he drew near, he saw the city and wept over it,” up to the place where he says: “He drove out all those who were selling doves.” Chapter XIX.

[Col. 0302B]

[363–364] As our Lord was drawing near to Jerusalem, he saw it and wept, saying: “If you had known, even you, on this day, the things that make for your peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes, because days will come upon you when your enemies will surround you with a rampart.” These are mysteries, and we hope, with God opening them, to be able to disclose what lies hidden. First, therefore, we must consider his weeping.

Jesus confirms by his own example all the beatitudes that he proclaimed in the Gospel, and proves what he taught by his own testimony. “Blessed,” he says, “are the meek.” This has a similar counterpart in what he says of himself: “Learn from me, for I am meek” (Matt. XI). “Blessed are the peacemakers.” And who was so much a peacemaker as my Lord Jesus, who is our peace, who dissolved hostility and destroyed it in his own flesh? “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake.” No one suffered persecution for righteousness’ sake as did the Lord Jesus, who was crucified for our sins.

Thus the Lord displayed all the beatitudes in himself. Accordingly, he also fulfilled by weeping what he had said, “Blessed are those who weep,” so that he might lay the foundation of this beatitude as well. He wept over Jerusalem, saying: “If you had known, even you, on this day, the things that make for your peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes,” and so forth, up to the place where he says: “Because you did not recognize the time of your visitation.”

One of the listeners may say: “What is being said is clear, and was fulfilled in reality with respect to Jerusalem. For the Roman army surrounded it and ravaged it to the point of complete destruction, and the time will come when no stone will be left upon stone in it.” I do not deny that that Jerusalem was indeed destroyed because of the crimes of its inhabitants, but I ask whether this weeping also applies to our Jerusalem. For we are the Jerusalem over which he weeps—we who seem to ourselves to possess the greater understanding. If, after the mysteries of truth, after the word of the Gospel, after the teaching of the Church, after seeing its mysteries, one of us sins, he is mourned and wept over.

No pagan is mourned, but the one who was of Jerusalem: for after his sins, enemies—namely, hostile powers and evil spirits—surround him, cast up a rampart around him, besiege him, and leave no stone upon stone, especially if, after much continence and several years of chastity, someone is overcome and, enticed by the allurements of the flesh, loses his patience and purity. If you commit fornication, they will leave no stone upon stone over you. For elsewhere he says: “I will not remember his former righteousnesses; in the sin in which he is found, in that I will judge him” (Ezek. XXVIII).

This, then, is the Jerusalem that is mourned. After this it is said: “He entered the temple.” When he had entered, he drove out those who were selling doves. He did not drive out the buyers, for those who buy possess what they have bought. Jesus expelled from his Father’s temple those who sell and throw away what they had possessed, in imitation of that prodigal son who received his substance from his father and squandered everything by excessive drinking (Luke XV).

Therefore, if anyone sells, he is expelled—especially if he was selling doves. Why did he mention no other birds but doves? This animal is simple and beautiful. I fear that a vice of this kind may also be found in us. For if I sell for a price what has been revealed and entrusted to me by the Holy Spirit so that I might make it known to the people, and if I do not teach without payment, what else am I doing but selling doves—that is, the Holy Spirit? When I have sold him, I am expelled from the temple of God.

Let us therefore beseech the Lord that we may all buy rather than sell. For if we do not sell, we recognize and understand our salvation; otherwise, enemies will surround our city. And if the hostile army once encircles us, we shall not be worthy of God’s tears.

Let us therefore rise at dawn and entreat the Lord that at least we may be able to eat the crumbs that fall from his table. Scripture marvels that the queen of Sheba came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom. When she saw his meal, his furnishings, and the services of his household, she was astonished and entirely filled with wonder (III Kings X). If we do not gladly embrace the riches of our Lord, the abundance of his discourse, and the wealth of his teachings; if we do not eat the bread of life; if we do not feed on Christ’s flesh and drink his blood; if we despise the banquets of our Savior, we must know that God possesses both kindness and severity. Of these, we ought rather to implore his kindness, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

[365–366]

### HOMILY XXXIX

On the question of the Sadducees, which they put to the Lord, concerning their woman who had seven husbands; and again concerning the denarius that the Savior commanded to be shown to him. Chapter XX.

There is a heresy among the Jews called that of the Sadducees. It denies the resurrection of the dead and thinks that the soul perishes with the body and does not breathe again after death. Accordingly, when they put their question to the Lord, they constructed the story of a woman with seven husbands: after her first husband, she married another in order to raise up offspring for the first; when he died, she married a third, and then a fourth; and in this way she reached the seventh. The question, therefore, is: at the resurrection of the dead, which of the seven brothers will claim her as his wife?

They proposed this problem while lying in wait for the Savior’s words, at the time when they had seen him teaching his disciples about the resurrection. The Savior answered them: “You are mistaken, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. For in the resurrection of the dead they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but they will be like angels in heaven.”

Those who will be like angels will certainly be angels. At the same time, we must learn that angels do not have marriages. Here, however, where there is death, marriage, and the necessity of children, these things exist; where there are immortals, neither marriage nor children is needed.

I shall propose to myself a very troublesome question, one not easily resolved, on behalf of those who are most devoted to the Scriptures and meditate day and night on the Law of the Lord (Ps. I). They say: “Where is it written, ‘They neither marry nor are given in marriage’? As I search through both the Old and the New Testament in memory and thought, I do not remember such a statement anywhere. If I am perhaps mistaken, let the one who knows more teach me. I gladly learn what I do not know.” But, as far as I judge, nothing of this kind will be found either in the Old or in the New Instrument.

Their whole error, therefore, arose from a prophetic passage that they do not understand. Among these is the statement in Isaiah: “My chosen ones shall not have children for a curse” (Isa. LXV). And in Deuteronomy, among the blessings: “Blessed shall be the offspring of your womb” (Deut. XXVIII). They think that these things will occur in the resurrection, not understanding that spiritual blessings were foretold.

For Paul, the vessel of election, interpreting spiritually all these blessings that are set forth in the Law, and knowing that they are not carnal, says to the Ephesians: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing,” when, rising from the dead, we were to attain eternal blessedness (Eph. I).

But when they find something similar in the Psalms, they fall into the same error. “Your wife,” it says, “shall be like a fruitful vine within the sides of your house; your children like olive shoots around your table” (Ps. CXXVII), up to the place where it says: “May the Lord bless you from Zion, and may you see the good things of Jerusalem.”

Therefore, when Jerusalem has been furnished and restored to its former condition, then he will see the good things that Scripture mentions. Those who understand Jerusalem spiritually, and know that the things said of it concern the heavenly Jerusalem, which is above and is our mother (Gal. IV), will see its good things, about which we have often spoken, including what we have now quoted from the Psalm: “Your wife shall be like a fruitful vine within the sides of your house; your children like olive shoots around your table.”

The Sadducees, who were a portion of the Jewish people, understood all these things bodily. To them the Savior says: “You do not know the Scriptures, nor the power of God.”

Let this suffice as a brief treatment of the question that the Sadducees put to the Lord.

As for what has been added concerning the image of Caesar, we must also touch briefly upon it. Some think that the Savior simply said: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s”—that is, “Pay the tribute that you owe.” For who among us contradicts the payment of tribute to Caesar? This passage, however, contains something mystical and secret.

There are two images of a human being. One is the image received from God when humanity was created in the beginning, as it is written in Genesis: “According to the image and likeness of God” (Gen. I). The other is the earthly image, the image of one made from dust, which humanity assumed after being expelled from paradise because of disobedience and sin, persuaded by the allurements of the ruler of this age.

Just as a coin and denarius bear the image of the rulers of the world, so the one who performs the works of the rulers of this darkness bears the image of the one whose works he possesses. Jesus commanded that this image be given back and cast away from our face, and that we assume the image according to which we were created from the beginning in the likeness of God. Thus it comes about that we render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.

“Show me a coin,” he says. In Matthew, a denarius is written instead (Matt. XXII, 19). When he had received it, he said: “Whose inscription does it bear?” They answered him: “Caesar’s.” Then he said to them again: “Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”

Paul also spoke of the consequence of this, saying: “Just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly” (I Cor. XV). Therefore, when he says, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s,” he means: “Lay aside the person of the earthly one; cast off the earthly image, so that, putting on the person of the heavenly one, you may render to God the things that are God’s.”

God asks us for ourselves again. What does he ask back? Read Moses: “And now, what does the Lord your God require of you?” and the rest that follows. God therefore asks and entreats something from us—not because he needs anything that we should give him. Yet after we have given it to him, he gives that same thing back to us for our salvation.

To make this clearer, I shall set forth the parable of the minas. The one who had received one mina and made ten from it offered it to the Lord, from whom the mina had been entrusted to him, and received another that he had not possessed before. The Lord commands that the mina of the one who had not multiplied what he received be taken away and given to the one who has the others: “Take the mina,” he says, “and give it to the one who has ten minas.”

In this way, whatever we give to God he returns to us, together with things we did not previously possess. God demands and asks something from us so that he may have the opportunity to give, so that he may bestow it upon the one who has distributed it. For it is by his grace that the mina was doubled, and to each person worthy of it more was given than he had hoped.

Let us therefore rise and pray to God that we may be worthy to offer him gifts which he will return to us, and that, in place of earthly things, he may bestow heavenly things, through Christ Jesus, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

### The Three Books of the Commentaries of Saint Eusebius Hieronymus, Presbyter of Stridon, on the Epistle to the Galatians (C)

#### Prologue

[367–368] There are only a few days since, after interpreting Paul’s Epistle to Philemon, I passed on to the Epistle to the Galatians, leaving many intervening matters untouched. And behold, suddenly letters were brought to me from Rome, announcing both that the venerable old woman Albina had been restored to the Lord’s presence and that the holy Marcella had been deprived of the companionship of her mother and now, Paula and Eustochium, was asking more urgently for your consolation.

Since this cannot be done for the time being because of the great stretches of sea and land between us, I wished at least to treat the wound suddenly inflicted with the medicine of Scripture. I know her fervor; I know the faith that she always carries as a flame in her breast—how it surpasses her sex, forgets human concerns, and, while the drum of the divine books resounds, crosses the Red Sea of this world.

Certainly, when I was in Rome, she never saw me in such haste that she did not ask me something about the Scriptures. Nor did she, in Pythagorean fashion, regard as correct whatever I had answered; nor did a preconceived authority carry weight with her without reason. She examined everything and weighed it all with an acute mind, so that I felt I had not so much a disciple as a judge.

Therefore, since I think this work will be very pleasing to her in her absence and useful to you who are present here, I shall undertake a task not previously attempted by writers in our language, and scarcely undertaken even by a few Greeks, although the dignity of the subject demanded it.

I do not mean that I am unaware that Gaius Marius Victorinus, who taught rhetoric at Rome when I was a boy, published commentaries on the Apostle. But he was occupied with the learning of secular literature and was wholly ignorant of the Holy Scriptures; and no one, however eloquent, can discuss well what he does not know.

What, then? Am I foolish or reckless to promise what he could not accomplish? Not at all. Rather, as it seems to me, I am more cautious and timid in this matter, for, aware of the weakness of my powers, I have followed Origen’s Commentaries.

That man wrote five books specifically on Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians and filled the tenth book of his *Stromata* with a concise discussion of its interpretation. He also composed various treatises and excerpts which, even by themselves, could suffice. I pass over Didymus, my sighted teacher; Apollinaris of Laodicea, who has recently departed from the Church; the ancient heretic Alexander; Eusebius of Emesa; and Theodore of Heraclea, who likewise left behind some brief commentaries—or commentaries—on this subject. If I were to select even a few passages from these authors, something would result that could not be wholly despised.

To confess the matter plainly, I read all these works, accumulated many things in my mind, and, calling in a secretary, dictated what was either my own or another’s, retaining at times neither the order, nor the wording, nor even the meaning. It now depends entirely upon the Lord’s mercy that what others have said well may not perish through our inexperience, and that what pleases among our own people may not displease among strangers.

Therefore, briefly gathering the subject of this Epistle, I call it to your attention in this preface, so that you may know that the subject of Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians is the same as that of the Epistle written to the Romans. The difference between them is that in the latter he used a higher sense and deeper arguments, whereas here, writing as though to people concerning whom he later says, “O foolish Galatians,” and, “Are you so foolish?”, he moderated his speech accordingly. He rebuked rather than taught, clothing common ideas in common language so that the foolish might understand and so that those whom reason could not persuade might be recalled by authority.

There is no speech of the Apostle, whether in an Epistle or in his present writing, in which he does not labor to teach that the burdens of the ancient Law have been laid aside, and that all those things which came before in types and images—that is, Sabbath rest, the injury of circumcision, the recurrence of the Kalends and of the three annual festivals, scrupulousness concerning foods, and daily washings that had to be dirtied again—ceased when the grace of the Gospel entered, a grace fulfilled not by the blood of victims but by the faith of the believing soul.

Elsewhere this matter was discussed in part, as it arose incidentally while he was treating another subject, and was touched upon almost in passing. In these two Epistles, however, as I have said, the cessation of the ancient Law and the introduction of the new are set forth specifically.

The Epistle to the Galatians has this particular feature: Paul is not writing to those who had believed in Christ from among the Jews and thought that the ceremonies of their ancestors had to be observed, but to those who had received the faith of the Gospel from among the Gentiles and, having fallen back again, had been deterred by the authority of certain people who asserted that Peter, James, and all the churches of Judea had mixed the Gospel of Christ with the old Law.

They claimed also that Paul himself did one thing in Judea and preached another thing to the nations, and that it was useless for them to believe in the Crucified One if they thought that what the leaders of the Apostles observed could be neglected.

For this reason Paul proceeds so cautiously and maintains such a middle position between the two sides that he neither betrays the grace of the Gospel, pressed by the weight and authority of his elders, nor does injury to his predecessors while asserting grace. Indirectly, and as though advancing secretly through hidden passages, he teaches that Peter acted in accordance with the people of the circumcision entrusted to him, lest, suddenly abandoning their ancient way of life, they should be scandalized by the cross and refuse to believe.

Since the preaching of the Gentiles had been entrusted to him, Paul teaches that it was right for him to defend as truth what another feigned for the sake of administrative accommodation.

Porphyry, that Bataneote and wicked man, not understanding this, objected in the first book of his work against us that Peter had been rebuked by Paul because he was not walking with a straight foot in evangelizing. He wished both to brand Peter with the stain of error and Paul with insolence, and to accuse them jointly of the falsehood of an invented doctrine, on the grounds that the leaders of the churches disagreed among themselves.

At your prayers, we have now touched lightly upon the sense in which these things were said, and we shall explain them more fully in their proper places. But it is now time, after setting down the Apostle’s own words, to unfold each point.

### Editorial Note

The reason why Porphyry is called a Bataneote by Jerome has long been disputed among scholars. Most have adopted the view that the word itself lies in an error and have attempted to emend it according to their individual judgment. Sirmond, in a letter to Holstenius, conjectured that it should be restored as *βαλανεώτης*, whose meaning—“busybody,” “perverse,” “affected,” and similar terms—is not inconsistent with the character of that philosopher.

Holstenius himself, however, was by no means pleased with this conjecture. He preferred *βιοθάνατος*, because he had found it written in ancient books as *Biothaniotes* or *Bethaniotes*. This word also suits Porphyry, an impious man who deserved to have life taken from him by a violent death.

Others think that his native place is being indicated: Batanea, a town in Syria, of which Stephanus of Byzantium speaks as easily having been a colony of the Tyrians. Thus Porphyry may also have received citizenship from the Tyrians, since Eunapius and the *Life of Plotinus*, chapter 7, commonly report that he was a Tyrian.

Finally, others have thought that “Bataneote” was used as an insult because, like bulls, he had attacked Christ and his faith with the reckless boldness of *βατανεῶται*. For my part, to speak carefully, I would more willingly combine these two conjectures, since they support one another.

I cannot be persuaded that some defect had grown into the word and that the name had been corrupted through the fault of copyists. For Porphyry is called a *βατανεώτης* both by Chrysostom, in Homily 6 on the First Epistle to the Corinthians, and by Anastasius Sinaita in the *Hodegos*, where he attacks Severian as a new Porphyry. If one wishes to attribute the word in Jerome to Latin scribes falsely representing a foreign term, one would likewise have to suppose the same thing of the native Greek writers—Chrysostom and the Sinaita—which is utterly contrary to every appearance of truth.

I therefore think that, since it was readily possible to turn the name of his homeland into an insult through the meaning of the word itself, Porphyry was called a Bataneote by Jerome and by other writers in order to reproach the more fully the impious and unrestrained character of the man. Something nearly similar occurs when our Evagrius Ponticus is called an “Hyperborean” in the *Epistle to Ctesiphon* (133), meaning one who is “beyond the Iberians,” a bad man among his own countrymen.

### Book One

#### Chapter I — Verse 1

“Paul, an apostle, not from human beings, nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead.”

Paul does not present himself as an Apostle “not from human beings, nor through a human being” arrogantly, as some think, but necessarily. He does so through Jesus Christ and God the Father in order to confound by this authority those who paraded Paul as someone outside the twelve Apostles, claiming that he had suddenly appeared from who knows where or had been appointed by his elders.

The statement may also be understood as indirectly directed against Peter and the others: Paul’s Gospel was not handed on to him by the Apostles but by Jesus Christ himself, who had also chosen those Apostles.

All this is prepared so that no one who argues for the grace of the Gospel against the burdens of the Law may be answered: “But Peter said this”; “The Apostles established this”; “Your predecessors decreed something else.” In what follows Paul makes this clearer, though for the moment he anticipates it in veiled language, when he says that nothing was conferred upon him by those who seemed to be something, and writes that he withstood Peter to his face, saying that he was compelled by no necessity to yield to the hypocrisy of the Jews.

If it seems rash to some that he spoke, even covertly, against the Apostles—he who went to Jerusalem for the purpose of comparing the Gospel with them, lest he should be running or should have run in vain—we may apply this understanding: even to the present day, apostles are sent by the patriarchs of the Jews. I think that the Galatians were then corrupted by these patriarchs and began to observe the Law, or at least that others from among the Jews who believed in Christ went to Galatia and asserted that Peter, the leader of the Apostles, and James, the brother of the Lord, observed the ceremonies of the Law.

To distinguish those who are sent by human beings from himself, who was sent by Christ, Paul took this beginning: “Paul, an apostle, not from human beings, nor through a human being.”

“Apostle,” that is, “one who is sent,” is properly a Hebrew word. It also corresponds to *Silas*—or *Silai*—whose name was given from the act of sending. The Hebrews say that even among the prophets and holy men there are some who are both prophets and apostles, while others are only prophets.

Thus Moses, to whom it is said, “I will send you to Pharaoh” (Exod. III, 10–11), and who replies, “Provide another whom you may send”; and Isaiah, to whom God says, “Whom shall I send, and who will go to this people?” (Isa. VI, 8), are both apostles and prophets.

From this we may also understand that John the Baptist should be called both prophet and apostle, since Scripture says: “There was a man sent from God, whose name was John” (John I, 6).

For this reason, in the Epistle to the Hebrews (Hebr. III), Paul did not place either his own name or the title “apostle” at the beginning according to customary practice: he was going to speak of Christ, saying, “Therefore, having Jesus the high priest and apostle of our confession.” It would not have been fitting for Paul also to be called an apostle where Christ was to be named an apostle.

There are four kinds of apostles. The first is not from human beings and not through a human being, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father. The second is from God, but through a human being. The third is from a human being and not from God. The fourth is neither from God, nor through a human being, nor from a human being, but from oneself.

Isaiah, the other prophets, and the Apostle Paul himself may belong to the first kind: they were sent neither from human beings nor through a human being, but by God the Father and Christ.

The second kind is Joshua, son of Nun, who was indeed appointed an apostle by God, but through Moses.

The third kind occurs when someone is appointed through human favor and zeal. Thus nowadays we see very many people assigned to the priesthood not by God’s judgment but by purchased popular favor.

The fourth kind belongs to false prophets and false apostles, concerning whom the Apostle says: “Such are false apostles, workers of iniquity, transforming themselves into apostles of Christ,” who say, “Thus says the Lord,” although the Lord did not send them (II Cor. X, 13).

Paul, however, is not such an apostle. He was sent neither from human beings nor through a human being, but by God the Father through Jesus Christ.

From this it is demonstrated that the heresy of Ebion and Photinus must also be refuted here: our Lord Jesus Christ is God, since the Apostle, being sent by Christ to preach the Gospel, denies that he was sent by a human being.

At this point the other heresies also intrude—those that claim that Christ’s flesh was merely apparent and say that Christ is God but not human. There is also the new heresy that asserts that Christ’s dispensation was only partial.

Thus, amid the shipwreck of so many false doctrines, the faith of the Church stands firm. If it confesses Christ to be human, Ebion and Photinus creep in; if it insists that he is God, Manichaeus and Marcion, authors of a new doctrine, burst forth.

Let them all therefore hear that Christ is both God and human. It is not that one is God and another is human, but that the one who was always God graciously became human for our salvation.

We should also note that Marcion’s *Apostolicus* did not contain the words “and God the Father.” He wished to explain that Christ was raised not by God the Father but by himself, as in the statement: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it” (John II, 19). And elsewhere: “No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it up again” (ibid., X, 18).

#### Verse 2

“And all the brothers who are with me, to the churches of Galatia.”

In the other Epistles, Sosthenes and Silvanus, and at times Timothy, are placed at the beginning. In this one alone, because the authority of many was necessary, the name of all the brothers is assumed. They themselves were perhaps from the circumcision and were not held in contempt by the Galatians.

For the agreement and consensus of many concerning one matter contributes greatly to correcting a people.

When he says “to the churches of Galatia,” this too must be noted: here alone he writes generally, not to the church of a single city but to the churches of the entire province, and calls “churches” those whom he later accuses of having been corrupted by error.

From this we should recognize that “church” can be understood in two ways: the Church that has neither spot nor wrinkle and is truly the body of Christ (Eph. V), and the assembly that gathers in Christ’s name without possessing complete and perfect virtues.

The wise likewise receive the name in two ways: those who possess full and perfect virtue, and those who are beginning and are situated in progress. Of the perfect it is said: “I will send wise men among you” (Luke XI, 49). Of the foolish it is said: “Reprove a wise man, and he will love you” (Prov. VIII, 9).

One who possesses complete and consummated virtue does not need correction. The same should be understood of the other virtues: “strong,” “prudent,” “pious,” “chaste,” “just,” and “temperate” are sometimes used in their full sense and sometimes in an extended or figurative sense.

#### Verse 3

“Grace to you and peace from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Unlike the other Epistles, he does not place the grace and peace of God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ in the usual way, by which our former sins were granted to us without merit of works and peace was bestowed after pardon. Rather, he now wisely argues against those who had been forestalled by the Law and thought that they could be justified by works, so that they might know that they were saved by grace and ought to persevere in what they had begun.

### Editorial and Textual Notes

- [Col. 0303D] On the contrary, as Jerome very learnedly observes in Epistle 75 to Theodora, no. 2: “When he says, ‘They neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven,’ the nature and substance of bodies are not abolished, but the greatness of glory is shown. For it is not written, ‘They will be angels,’ but ‘like angels’: likeness is promised, reality denied. ‘They will be like angels,’ he says, that is, similar to angels; therefore they will not cease to be human beings.” The holy doctor refutes this notion of Origen’s in many places.

- [Col. 0305C] After Dallaeus, some have thought that Origen here supposed the Sadducees—who, as is certain and as he himself by no means denies, admitted only the books of Moses into the canon of sacred Scripture—to have attributed the same authority also to the prophets and the Psalms. For he says that they understood bodily the testimonies from Isaiah 65 and Psalm 127 which he cites, and for ignorance of which the Savior accuses them. But even if we grant that the preceding context hangs together in such a way that Origen says the Sadducees wrongly accepted the words of the prophet and David which he quotes, one nevertheless cannot infer that he thought those books had been included by the Sadducees in the canon of Scripture. He may have had in view only the testimony of Deuteronomy 28, which the Sadducees certainly did receive.

- [Col. 0306C] Earlier editions read *quae* (“the things which”) here, by a manifest error, in place of *quod* (“that”) or *quia* (“because”).

- [Col. 0307B] These commentaries on the Epistle to the Galatians, and the following commentaries on the remaining three epistles—to the Ephesians, Titus, and Philemon—have been edited against three manuscript copies: one, Palatine no. 340, of proven antiquity and character; and two others from the Cistercian library at Rome, formerly of the monastery of Nonantola, one catalogued as no. 61 and the other unnumbered, both distinguished for their correction and antiquity. Nor have we passed over Rabanus, who, as usual, copied Jerome word for word and incorporated him into his own commentaries, since, amid the innumerable errors with which he abounds, he quite often supplies a better reading from the very ancient copies that he used. Finally, we also collated, not without benefit, the rarer printed books, including the Cologne edition of John Gymnich of 1531.

- [Col. 0307C] Our manuscripts, and those cited by Martianus, read “that [I had interpreted] the Epistle,” etc.

- [Col. 0307C] Earlier the text was read, either falsely or with an unsuitable sense, as “who taught boys rhetoric at Rome,” or, as some manuscripts have it, “who taught me, when I was a boy, rhetoric at Rome,” or finally, “who at Rome [taught] me from boyhood,” etc. We have restored the true reading, assisted by one Cistercian manuscript and another Cluniac manuscript cited by the Benedictine editor himself in the Addenda. Jerome did not hear Victorinus; perhaps he could not have done so in his still infant age. He himself vouches for this fact in the *Chronicle* under the year 358, where he says: “Victorinus the rhetorician and Donatus the grammarian, my teacher”—not “my teachers,” in the plural—“are distinguished at Rome.” See also *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 101, and our notes there.

- [Col. 0308B] The Palatine manuscript does not have the word “holy.”

- [Col. 0308C] In the following passage of nearly twenty lines, the holy doctor offers an apology for himself; he also inserts it in his Epistle 112 to Augustine, no. 4, in our recension: “First,” he says, “I reply that your prudence ought to have remembered the little preface to my Commentaries, speaking in my person: ‘What then, am I foolish?’” etc.

- [Col. 0308C] The Palatine manuscript reads: “Rather, as it seems to me, more cautious and timid, since I am aware of the weakness,” etc.

- [Col. 0308C] Earlier editions had *propria* (“his own”), less correctly.

- [Col. 0309A] Alternative reading: “could suffice” (*possent*) instead of “could suffice” (*possint*).

- [Col. 0309A] Alternative reading: “commentaries” (*Commentarios*) instead of “brief commentaries” (*Commentariolos*).

- [Col. 0309C] In the Epistle to Augustine just cited, the text is shorter: “nor even the meaning. It now depends upon the Lord’s mercy,” etc.

- [Col. 0309C] The Palatine manuscript reads: “I give this warning in the preface”; shortly afterward, “the subject of the Epistle,” without the conjunction “and.”

- [Col. 0309C] The same Palatine codex reads: “There is no discourse, or epistle, of the Apostle in which he does not labor,” etc., deleting the intervening words “whether in an epistle or in the present [discourse].”

- [Col. 0309C] In Rabanus, the reading is singular: “the leader observes,” rather than plural “the leaders observe.”

- [Col. 0309C] The Palatine manuscript reads: “it was right to defend for truth,” etc.

- [Col. 0311D] The words “they maintained,” and, a little below, “he writes,” are absent from the Palatine codex.

- [Col. 0311D] On the Jewish patriarchs and apostles in these times, Father Bacchini discusses the matter clearly in his book *On Ecclesiastical Metropolises*.

- [Col. 0312D] Two manuscripts have the plural “authors.”

- [Col. 0313D] Other books read “in Marcion’s *Apostolicus*.” Marcion, having rejected all the other books of Scripture, had recommended only two: one was the Gospel of Luke; the other was the *Apostolicus*, or *Apostle*, containing ten epistles of Paul disfigured by his various interpolations. See Tertullian, Book I against this heresiarch, chapter 1, and Book IV, chapter 4, as well as Saint Epiphanius, *Heresy* 42.

- Textual alternatives not otherwise represented above: “he had gone” (*perrexerat*) for “he went”; “and” (*et*) for “as though”; “they disagreed” (*discreparent*) for “they disagreed among themselves”; “Silai” for “Silas”; “to the church” (*Ecclesiae*) for “to the churches” (*Ecclesiis*); and “if it confessed” (*fateretur*) for “if it confesses.”

### (Verse 4)

Who gave himself for our sins, so that he might rescue us from the present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father, to whom be glory unto ages of ages. Amen.

Neither did the Son give himself for our sins without the Father’s will, nor did the Father hand over the Son without the Son’s will. Rather, this is the Son’s will: to fulfill the Father’s will, as he himself says in the Psalm: “I desired to do your will, O my God” (Ps. 39:9).
