The Son gave himself so that he might himself overthrow the injustice that was in us by means of justice. Wisdom handed itself over so that it might conquer folly. Holiness and strength offered themselves so that they might destroy filth and weakness.

[Note: We have removed from this place the superfluous word “ignorance” (*inscitiam*), which our manuscripts and Rabbanus himself formerly did not contain. Immediately after, one Palatine manuscript reads: “according to the promised hope which we believe.”]

And thus he freed us not only in the future age, according to the promised hope in which we believe, but also here from the present age: for, having died with Christ, we are transformed into a newness of understanding, and we are not of this world, by which we are rightly not loved.

The question arises how the present age came to be called evil. Heretics commonly seize upon this as an opportunity to assert that one creator made the age of light and the future age, and another the age of darkness and the present age.

We, however, say that it is not so much the age itself—which proceeds through days and nights, years and months—that is called evil, but rather, by homonymy (ὁμωνύμως), the things that take place in the age. Thus “the day’s own trouble” is said to be sufficient (Matt. 6:34), and Jacob’s days are described as few and evil (Gen. 47:9). This does not mean that the period of time in which Jacob lived was evil, but that the things he endured exercised him through various trials.

Indeed, while he was serving for his wives and was beset by many hardships (Gen. 29), Esau was at rest; and thus the same period of time was good for one and evil for another. Nor would it have been written in Ecclesiastes, “Do not say, ‘Why were the former days better than these?’” (Eccl. 7:10), except by way of comparison with evils.

Hence John says: “The whole world lies in the evil one” (1 John 5:19). This does not mean that the world itself is evil, but that evil things are done in the world by people who say, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (Isa. 22:13).

And the Apostle himself says: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Eph. 5:16).

Forests too are disgraced when they are full of robberies—not because the earth or the woods sin, but because the places themselves have acquired the infamy of murder. We detest the sword by which human blood has been poured out, and the cup in which poison has been mixed—not because of any sin of the sword or cup, but because those who have misused them deserve hatred.

So too the age, which is a span of time, is neither good nor evil in itself; it is called good or evil because of those who are in it.

Therefore the ravings and fables of Valentinus must be despised. From the fact that Scripture speaks of “ages,” he fabricated his thirty αἰῶνες, claiming that they were living beings and that, through groups of four, eight, ten, and twelve, they produced as many series of ages as the sow of Aeneas produced piglets.

[Note: Two manuscripts read “thirty aeons” in accordance with their own interpretation, since Scripture speaks of “ages,” and so forth.]

The reference is to the well-known prophecy of Helenus in Virgil, *Aeneid* 3:

> A huge sow, beneath the ilex trees along the shore,  
> will be found lying, having brought forth thirty young;  
> white, reclining upon the ground, with white offspring around her teats, etc.

Virgil repeats these verses near the beginning of Book 8.

We must also inquire what distinction there is between “age,” “age of the age,” and “ages of ages,” and where the expression denotes a short period of time and where eternity. For in Hebrew, *age*—that is, עוֹלָם (*olam*)—when it contains the letter ו (*vav*), signifies eternity; but when it is written without the *vav*, it signifies the fiftieth year, which they call the Jubilee.

[Note: Martianaeus had written the word incorrectly, with an aleph in place of the *vav*.]

For this reason, the Hebrew slave who, because of his love for his wife and children, loves his master and is subjected to servitude with his ear pierced is commanded to serve “forever” (*in saeculum*) (Exod. 21)—that is, until the fiftieth year.

[Note: This observation of Jerome concerning the differing spelling, and therefore the differing meaning, of the word *olam* did not escape the severe criticisms of recent scholars, especially John Clericus, who took it as the occasion for composing his famous book of *Jerome’s Questions*. They loudly declare, along with the example from Deuteronomy cited by Jerome, that the interpretation is false, since the word is written fully there; and they appeal to a considerable number of other passages in which the word occurs in full, that is, with the *vav*, although eternity in the proper sense is not being discussed. They also accuse Jerome of rabbinic subtlety and carelessness, claiming that he allowed himself to be deceived by a Jewish teacher and had not himself consulted the sacred text with his own eyes.

Nor are we unaware of what has hitherto been offered in Jerome’s defense: namely, that he did not intend the distinction of meanings to apply to every passage of Scripture in which the word occurs either fully or defectively, but only to the two passages—Exodus and Deuteronomy—which he adduces as examples.

Indeed, the first of these passages is still written without the *vav* in Hebrew books. As for the second, although it is now written fully, it is reasonable to suppose, from Jerome’s own testimony, that the *vav* was absent in the manuscript he used.

I venture to declare with complete confidence that no one has yet understood Jerome’s intention, or examined his actual words—something all the more astonishing after this passage has been so thoroughly harassed by the ingenuity of learned men. All of them, with equal agreement, understand the two examples as serving the same purpose: namely, to indicate a short period of time by the defective spelling of the word. Consequently, since Jerome plainly teaches the opposite, some have accused him falsely and rashly, while those who tried to defend him have applied a wretched exception to an error that they themselves had assumed.

Jerome wishes, in the second testimony, from Deuteronomy, to present an example of perpetual duration, indicated by the fully written word, and to set it in contrast with the first example from Exodus, where the defective spelling of the word indicates a short period, namely the fiftieth year.

This becomes perfectly clear if one observes only that the holy Doctor explicitly proposed to demonstrate two points from scriptural evidence concerning the word *olam* and its meaning: first, where it denotes a short period of time; second, where it denotes eternity. Since he demonstrated the first point—the short or determinate period—from the testimony of Exodus, he necessarily took the second example from Deuteronomy as a sign of eternal duration. This is what he actually means, and the whole sequence of his argument required him to say it in order to complete the second part of his proposal.

The matter itself makes clear that he was right to say this and could not have meant otherwise. The Ammonites and Moabites were excluded forever from public offices among the people of God; their example could not be understood in any other way than as signifying perpetual duration. The very wording of the sacred text, which the holy Father almost quotes verbatim, immediately comes to mind: “The Ammonite and the Moabite shall not enter the assembly of the Lord, even to the tenth generation; they shall not enter the assembly of the Lord forever. You shall not seek their peace or their prosperity all your days, forever.”

The phrase itself, which Jerome presses throughout his argument, and the spelling to which he appeals, also testify to this: the word is written fully, both here and elsewhere in all the books. It is plainly useless, and rests on no probability, to suppose that the *vav* was absent in the manuscript used by the holy Doctor.

Moreover, Jerome seems to intensify the very meaning of the scriptural statement. Moses says “not even after the tenth generation”; Jerome extends it to the fifteenth generation. Nor does his use of the adverb “until” imply that he thought the peoples would afterward be admitted. In keeping with the idiom of Scripture, he shows that this would never happen and had not happened.

Add to this that fifteen generations, each of which, according to scriptural usage and Jerome’s own calculation in his commentary on Ezekiel 26, extends to seventy years or more, together exceed a thousand years. Who, I ask, could regard this as a short interval of time—not merely short in itself, but short in comparison with fifty years, so as to be comparable and equivalent to the period of the Jubilee?

Indeed, however one examines this passage, one cannot cease wondering how a preconceived human opinion could have twisted it into a meaning entirely opposite to the one the author most truly intended.

But what value would it have if I were to point out the causes of the error and restore the holy Father’s meaning from the monstrous dislocation under which it suffers? To put the matter very briefly: the clause appended to this second example—“because every harsh condition was released at the arrival of the Jubilee”—which seemed capable of being referred to the sense of that example, provided the whole occasion for the error.

It is plainly misplaced through a scribal transposition. It must be moved and attached to the preceding example, nearly three lines earlier, after the words “that is, until the fiftieth year.”

No handwritten or printed book supports this restoration, but we shall establish it so decisively by argument that no doubt will remain and Jerome’s text will no longer be exposed to this slander or require any further defense.

This is one of those kinds of scribal error that frequently occur in ancient manuscripts: words written in the margin by the author—as Jerome says—or omitted by copyists and noted at the edge of the book were later inserted into the text by another copyist, who carelessly placed them in the wrong location.

The arguments, however, are readily apparent.

First, the Jubilee had no relation whatsoever to the Moabites and Ammonites, who were not of the Jewish people, nor could it ever have had any relation to them. It would therefore be absurd to apply that passage to peoples whose circumstances differed so radically from the relevant customs. On the contrary, it concerns a Hebrew slave, specifically one who, after deliberately renouncing his freedom out of love for his wife and children, as stated in Exodus 21:5–6, is ordered to serve “forever”—that is, until the Jubilee—whether that year was near or far away.

Second, the Jubilee recurred every fiftieth year, and it is appropriately said to release Hebrew slaves from their harsh condition at its arrival, since by law their longest servitude could not extend beyond the fiftieth year. The Moabites and Ammonites, however, were rejected both “after the tenth generation” and forever.

Third, however one understands Jerome’s exposition—even if, against Scripture and the truth of the matter, one wishes this second example also to indicate a determinate period, one must nevertheless admit that it is a very long period, which cannot in any way be reconciled with the Jubilee—the entire purpose of the passage is destroyed by the concluding clause. That clause forces Jerome to contradict himself if he is made to say that the Moabites and Ammonites were excluded from the Church of God until the fifteenth generation, yet admitted every fifty years.

I think you understand that the holy Doctor could not have written this unless those words had originally followed the first example, to which they fit perfectly.

Read, then—at my own risk—the complete text in this form:

> For this reason the Hebrew who, because of his wife and children, loves his master and is subjected to servitude with his ear pierced, is commanded to serve forever, that is, until the fiftieth year, because every harsh condition was released at the arrival of the Jubilee. But the Moabites and Ammonites shall not enter the assembly of the Lord until the fifteenth generation and forever. Some say that the meaning is the same, etc.

We have refrained from altering the text itself, because no authority of an ancient book or reliable writer supports such a change. Once the reading has been restored in this way, however, the holy Doctor is entirely vindicated from every accusation.

It is no longer necessary to ask whether the same rule concerning the full or defective spelling of *olam* and its varying meaning applies in all the other passages of Scripture. It is sufficient for the proposed defense to demonstrate that the two examples Jerome cites for his purpose have precisely the meaning he assigns to them.]

“And the Moabites and Ammonites” (Deut. 23) “shall not enter the assembly of the Lord until the fifteenth generation and forever: because every harsh condition was released at the arrival of the Jubilee.”

Some say that the meaning of “ages of ages” is the same as that of “holy of holies,” “heaven of heavens,” “work of works,” and “Song of songs.” Just as heaven is distinguished from the things that belong to the heavens, holy things from those that are holier by comparison with other holy things, works from works that are better by the superiority of their works, and songs from those that surpass all other songs, so too “age” has the same relation to “ages”: the ages are those that are distinguished by comparison with the age.

They accordingly explain the present age by saying that it is to be reckoned from the time when heaven and earth were created and continues until the consummation of the world, when Christ will judge all things.

They extend the inquiry still further and advance into earlier periods, discussing past and future ages, whether they were or will be good or evil. They fall into such profound questions that they have composed books and innumerable volumes on the subject.

As for the fact that Paul’s prologue concludes with “Amen,” *Amen* (אָמֵן) in Hebrew, the Seventy translated it as γένοιτο, “let it be”; Aquila as πεπιστωμένος, “truly” or “faithfully.” The Savior also constantly uses it in the Gospel, confirming his words with his “Amen.”

### (Verse 6)

I am astonished that you are so quickly transferring yourselves from him who called you into the grace of Christ Jesus to another gospel—which is not another gospel—except that there are some who trouble you and want to distort the gospel of Christ.

[Note: Two manuscripts and the old edition read, “that you are thus so quickly transferring yourselves,” here and below, wherever this passage recurs.]

We first read the verb “transfer” in Genesis 5, where God transferred Enoch, and he was no longer found. Later we read it in the Books of Kings (1 Kings 21), when Jezebel transferred Ahab from the worship of God to the veneration of idols, so that he might do everything that the Amorite had done, whom the Lord destroyed from before the children of Israel.

Although both are transfers, the one is God’s and the other the devil’s. Whoever is transferred by God is not found by his enemies, and the ambusher cannot creep upon him. I believe this is what is signified by “and he was not found.”

Whoever is transferred by the devil, however, is transferred into what appears to be but is not.

The philosophers of this age likewise call those who are transferred from one doctrine to another *transferred*, as was the case with that Dionysius—whose original opinion was that pain is not evil, but who, after being overwhelmed by calamities and tormented by pain, began to affirm that pain was the greatest of all evils. He was consequently called *Transposed* or *Transferred*, because, abandoning his former judgment, he had fallen into its opposite.

[Note: The earlier text read “to doctrines,” less correctly. The Greeks call those who revise their former opinion μετατιθεμένους. Dionysius himself—whom Jerome mocks because, after first being a student of Zeno of Citium, he later defected from the Stoics to the Cyrenaics—was known by the surname *Metathemenus*, “the one who changed sides.” See Athenaeus, Book 10, where the translator poorly renders μεταθέμενον as “transposer” instead of “transferred,” or “changed,” as Jerome translates it. Diogenes Laërtius gives much information about this philosopher.]

Paul is therefore astonished, first, that they have been transferred from the freedom of the Gospel into the slavery of legal works. Then he is astonished that they were transferred so quickly, because the guilt is not the same when someone is transferred with difficulty and when he is transferred quickly. Thus in martyrdom the one who sprang immediately to denial without struggle or torture does not suffer the same punishment as the one who, twisted on the rack, under cords and fire, was compelled to deny what he believed.

The preaching of the Gospel was still recent; not much time had elapsed since the Apostle had brought the Galatians from idols to Christ. He is therefore astonished that they have so quickly withdrawn from the one whose name had only recently made them Christians.

The passage itself also contains a hyperbaton (ὑπέρβατον), and may be read in its proper order as follows:

> I am astonished that you are so quickly transferring yourselves from Christ Jesus, who called you into grace, saying: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Mark 2:17). For by grace we have been saved, and not through the law (Eph. 2:8).

“But you have been transferred,” he says, “to another gospel, which is not another,” because everything false does not subsist, and what is contrary to the truth does not exist. Thus it is said: “Do not hand over, O Lord, your scepter to those who are not” (Esth. 14:11).

And God called into being the things that were not, in order to make what was not exist.

[Note: A Palatine manuscript reads, “in order to make the things that were not exist.”]

If this is said of people who believed in the same God and possessed the same Scriptures, that they have been transferred to another gospel—which is not a gospel—what should we think of Marcion and the other heretics, who reject the Creator and pretend that Christ belongs to another God?

They do not merely wander and fall through an interpretation of the law and the letter, or through a conflict between flesh and spirit; they disagree concerning the entire right of the Church.

[Note: Victorinus has “in the interpretation of the law”; elsewhere the words “the conflict of the letter” or “of the spirit” are variously transmitted.]

He says beautifully: “Except that there are some who trouble you and want to distort the gospel of Christ.” They want, he says, to change, distort, and trouble the gospel of Christ, but they cannot. For its nature is such that it cannot be anything other than what is true.

[Note: The reading “than what is true” is perhaps more correct; a Rabban manuscript has “than that which is true.”]

Everyone who interprets the Gospel with a spirit and mind different from that in which it was written troubles believers and distorts the gospel of Christ, making what is before the face lie behind the back and turning what is behind the back toward the face.

If someone follows only the letter, he places what is later before the face. If someone submits to Jewish interpretations, he casts behind the back those things that by their nature have been placed before the face.

The use of the word “transfer” in relation to the Galatians is also appropriate:

“For Galatia,” he says, “means ‘transfer’ in our language.”

[Note: This follows the etymologies of the Book of Names commonly accepted at that time, allegedly based on 1 Corinthians. Everyone recognizes, however, that *Galatia* is a Greek word, not a Hebrew one, and means nothing other than the region of the Galatians. Its etymology is derived from γάλα, “milk.” Among the Greeks, the most widely accepted view is that the Gauls—or, as Livy calls them, the Gallo-Greeks—who crossed Greece under King Seleucus Nicator and invaded Asia, received this name from the milky color of their bodies. Compare shortly afterward the other preface, or the preface to the second book, by the holy Father.]

### (Verse 8)

But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you something contrary to what we preached to you, let him be accursed. As we said before, and now I say again: if anyone preaches to you something contrary to what you received, let him be accursed.

This may also be understood as spoken hypothetically—not because either an apostle or an angel could preach differently from what they had once proclaimed, but because, even if it could happen that apostles and angels were changed, one must nevertheless not depart from what had once been received.

This is especially so since the Apostle himself elsewhere demonstrates the steadfastness of his faith, saying: “I am certain that neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. 8:38–39). “I speak the truth in Christ; I do not lie, my conscience bearing witness with me” (Rom. 9:1).

These are not the words of one who could ever depart from the faith and love of Christ.

[Note: In place of the words καθ’ ὑπόθεσιν, “hypothetically,” which I now restore from a Cistercian manuscript, the reading ὑπερβολικῶς, “hyperbolically,” had until now been accepted. The antiquarians were misled by the fact that Jerome had used this word a few lines earlier: “This may also be understood as spoken hyperbolically.” They could therefore easily substitute it from their own ingenuity, with scarcely any loss of apparent sense.

But the reading we restore is both much more elegant and more consonant with the holy Father’s meaning, and it alone is genuine: καθ’ ὑπόθεσιν. It is also much more difficult to recognize in the manuscript, since it is written continuously as ΚαΘΥΝΟΘΕϹ. Everyone knows that καθ’ ὑπόθεσιν means “by supposition,” that is, to assert something not as established or true.]

Those who refuse to understand this statement hypothetically but take it as a literal assertion—that apostles and angels could indeed be turned toward worse things—object that Paul himself knew that he could fall if he acted negligently, saying: “I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be found disqualified” (1 Cor. 9:27).

They also say that angels are changeable: those who did not preserve their own position but abandoned their proper dwelling are kept in eternal chains under darkness for the judgment of the great day (Jude 6).

Only God’s nature is immutable, as it is written: “But you are the same” (Ps. 101:28). And he says of himself: “I am your God, and I do not change” (Mal. 3:6).

Lucifer fell, although he was rising in the morning; and the one who had once sent him to all the nations has been crushed upon the earth.

[Note: A Palatine manuscript reads: “the one who once sent him to be a stumbling block to all the nations is upon the earth,” and so forth.]

The most learned Tertullian, in his work against Apelles and his virgin Philumene—whom a certain angel of a diabolical and perverse spirit had filled—aptly writes in this passage that this is the angel against whom, long before Apelles was born, the Apostle prophetically pronounced an anathema through the prophecy of the Holy Spirit.

The word ἀνάθεμα is properly a Jewish term. It is used both in Joshua (Josh. 6:17) and in Numbers (Num. 21), when the Lord commanded that everything in Jericho and among the Midianites should be regarded as detestable and devoted to destruction.

Let us ask those who assert that Christ and the Apostle Paul are either the son or servant of the good God, previously unknown until that time—those who say that he does not know how to curse or condemn anyone—how the Apostle now uses a Jewish word, that is, a word belonging to the Creator, and wishes either an angel or an apostle to perish, when that good God himself is supposedly not accustomed to exact vengeance.

The addition, “as we said before, and now I say again,” shows that at the beginning he had warned them of this very matter and pronounced an anathema on those who were going to preach otherwise; and that now, after the contrary preaching has occurred, he decrees the anathema which he had foretold.

For this reason he pronounced an anathema both upon himself—although in Judea they accused him of doing one thing and teaching another—and upon the angel, who was plainly considered greater even than the apostles who preceded him. Thus Peter and John’s authority would not appear great, since neither Paul, who had previously taught them, nor an angel was permitted to preach differently from what they had once learned.

He therefore explicitly names himself and the angel, but leaves the others unnamed. “If anyone,” he says, “preaches to you,” using a general expression so as not to insult his predecessors, while nevertheless covertly indicating their names.

### (Verse 10)

For now am I persuading people, or God? Or am I seeking to please people? If I were still pleasing people, I would not be Christ’s servant.

We must not suppose that the Apostle teaches us by his example to disregard human judgments, since elsewhere he says: “Knowing therefore the fear of the Lord, we persuade people; but we are manifest to God” (2 Cor. 5:11). And again: “Be without offense to Jews, Greeks, and the Church of God, just as I also please everyone in everything, not seeking my own advantage but that of many, so that they may be saved” (1 Cor. 10:32–33).

But if it is possible for us to please both God and people at the same time, then we should please people as well. If, however, we cannot please people except by displeasing God, then we must please God rather than people.

Otherwise Paul himself explains why he pleases everyone in everything: “Not seeking,” he says, “what is advantageous for me, but what is advantageous for many, so that they may be saved.”

Whoever, through that love which does not seek its own things but those of others, pleases everyone so that they may be saved, certainly pleases God first, for the salvation of human beings is his concern.

The word “now,” which is specifically added here, also indicates that one may either please people or displease them according to the circumstances: someone who now does not please because of the truth of the Gospel may once have pleased for the sake of the salvation of many.

Paul once pleased the Jews, when, as a zealot for the traditions of his ancestors, he lived blamelessly under the law. He possessed such ardor and faith in the ceremonies of his forefathers that he became a participant in the death of Stephen and went to Damascus to bind those who had departed from the law (Acts 9).

But after he was transferred from being a persecutor into a chosen vessel and began to preach the faith that he had once attacked, he began equally to displease the Jews whom he had previously pleased.

This, then, is what he says: “Am I seeking to please the Jews, whom, by displeasing, I have pleased God? For if I were pleasing them, I would not be Christ’s servant.” I would be upholding the law and destroying the grace of the Gospel.

But now, for this reason, I am not even induced to observe the law by way of pretense: because I cannot please God and the Jews at the same time.

The word “persuade,” taken from ordinary human usage, is used when someone tries to implant in others what he himself possesses and has once absorbed. It is found in many passages of Scripture, including this one: “Persuasion is not from him who called you” (Gal. 5:8).

Likewise in the Acts of the Apostles: “Many Jews came to him at his lodging. He explained matters to them, testifying to the kingdom of God and persuading them concerning Jesus from the Law of Moses and the Prophets, from morning until evening.”

All this occurred because a report had been spread about him—or, according to another reading, because he had been accused—that he secretly observed the Law and had joined himself in Jerusalem to those who practiced Judaism.

[Col. 0322A] (Verses 11–12.) For I make known to you, brothers, the Gospel that was preached by me: that it is not according to man. For neither did I receive it from man, nor did I learn it, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ.

By this passage the doctrine of Ebion and Photinus is overthrown: Christ is God, and not merely man. For if Paul’s Gospel is not according to man, and he neither received it from man nor learned it, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ, then Jesus Christ, who revealed the Gospel to Paul, is certainly not man. And if he is not man, he is consequently God. This does not mean that we deny that he assumed humanity, but that we reject the notion that he is merely human.

It is asked whether all the churches of God throughout the world received the Gospel from God or from man: for how many of us learned through the revelation of Christ and did not come to know it through a human preacher? To this we shall reply by referring to those who can say: “Do you seek proof of the Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. 13:3); and: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20). Such people do not so much teach themselves as have God teaching in them—the God who speaks to the saints: “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81:6). Immediately afterward he speaks of sinners: “But you shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes.” Since, then, Paul speaks, and Peter speaks—men who do not die like men or fall like one of the princes—it is clear that they are gods. And those who are gods hand on the Gospel of God, not of man.

Marcion, Basilides, and the other plagues of the heretics do not possess the Gospel of God, because they do not possess the Holy Spirit, without whom the Gospel that is taught becomes human. Nor should we think that the Gospel consists in the words of Scripture, but in its meaning; not on the surface, but in the marrow; not in the leaves of its expressions, but in the root of its reasoning.

The prophet says of God: “His words are good with him” (Mic. 2:7). Scripture is useful to its hearers when it is not spoken apart from Christ, when it is not brought forth apart from the Father, and when the preacher does not impart it without the Spirit [Note: [Col. 0321D] Perhaps *discitur*, “is learned,” should be restored. Shortly afterward one Cistercian manuscript has *non prophetatur*, “is not prophesied,” instead of *non profertur*, “is not brought forth.” And a little later: “Otherwise the devil too speaks from the Scriptures,” and so forth.]. Otherwise the devil also, who speaks from the Scriptures, and all the heresies, following Ezekiel (chapter 13), sew pillows for themselves from them, to place beneath the elbow of every age.

I myself also, who am speaking, if I have Christ in me, do not possess the gospel of man. But if I am a sinner, it is said to me: “God said to the sinner: Why do you recite my statutes and take my covenant upon your lips? You hate discipline and cast my words behind you” (Ps. 49:16–17), together with what follows.

There is great danger in speaking in the Church, lest through a perverse interpretation the Gospel of Christ become the gospel of man—or, what is worse, the gospel of the devil.

The difference between receiving and learning is this: the person who first has the Gospel imparted to him and is brought to faith receives it, so that he may believe that what is written belongs to you [Col. 0323A]. But the person who learns it comes to understand those things which are represented in it through riddles and parables, once they have been explained and expounded; and he recognizes them, not because a human being has revealed them, but because Christ has revealed them to Paul [Note: [Col. 0323D] Two of our manuscripts omit the words *et cognoscit*, “and he recognizes.”], or through Paul, in whom Christ speaks [Note: [Col. 0323D] The Cistercian manuscript does not have the words *aut per Paulum*, “or through Paul.” Moreover, what the holy Father says here—that the word *ἀποκαλύψεως* properly belongs to Scripture and was used by none of the Greek sages of the world—corresponds very well to what we noted in chapter 9 of the *Catalogue*, where Jerome relates that John, exiled to the island of Patmos, wrote the Apocalypse, which Justin Martyr and Irenaeus interpret. These revered Fathers called that revelation, or writing, of John by the name *Apocalypse*. Recall what we noted there.].

The very word *ἀποκαλύψεως*, that is, “revelation,” properly belongs to Scripture and was used by none of the wise men of the world among the Greeks. Hence it seems to me that, just as in other words which the translators of the Septuagint rendered from Hebrew into Greek, so also in this case they took great pains to express the proper force of a foreign language, fashioning new words for new realities. The word suggests that when something hidden and covered is shown and brought into the light after its covering has been removed, it is “revealed” (*revelatur*).

To make this clearer, consider an example. When Moses spoke with God with his face revealed and uncovered (Exod. 33–34), that is, without a veil, he placed a veil over his face when speaking to the people, because they could not look upon his face (Num. 4). A veil was also spread before the Ark of the Covenant. When it had been drawn back, the things that had previously been hidden were disclosed; and, to use the very word, they were “revealed.”

If, then, those accustomed to reading the eloquent writers of the world begin to mock us for the novelty and lowliness of our language, let us send them to Cicero’s books which are prefaced by discussions of philosophical questions. Let them see how great a necessity compelled him there to produce such monstrous words as no Roman ear had ever heard—and this while translating from Greek, a language close to our own, into Latin [Col. 0323C]. What must those endure who attempt, amid Hebrew difficulties, to express the proper meanings of its terms? And yet, in the vast volumes of Scripture, there are far fewer expressions that sound novel than those which Cicero assembled in a small work.

It is possible, as we said at the beginning when explaining the words “the apostle Paul, not from men nor through man,” that the present passage may likewise be understood indirectly of Peter and of Paul’s other predecessors: that the person who has Christ alone as teacher of the Gospel is swayed by no one’s law or authority [Note: [Col. 0324D] One Palatine manuscript has *habeat praecessorem*, “has Christ as predecessor.”]. The revelation means, moreover, that when Paul was going to Damascus, he was granted to hear Christ’s voice on the road; and, once his eyes had been blinded, he looked upon the true light of the world.

(Verses 13.) For you have heard of my former manner of life in Judaism: how excessively I persecuted the Church of God and devastated it; and how I advanced in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries in my race [Note: [Col. 0324D] We have removed the word *meos*, “my,” which the printed books inserted here and below, on the authority of our manuscripts, since it is absent from the Greek exemplar.], being more abundantly zealous for the traditions of my fathers.

This account is extremely useful to the Galatians: it shows how Paul, once the devastator of the Church and the fiercest defender of Judaism, suddenly turned to faith in Christ. This occurred at the very time when the Crucified One was first being proclaimed throughout the world, when the new doctrine was being driven out to the borders of the whole world by both Gentiles and Jews.

They could say: “If the man who from childhood was trained in the disciplines of the Pharisees, who surpassed all his contemporaries in Jewish tradition, now defends the Church which he once persecuted with the greatest violence, and prefers to possess the grace and novelty of Christ amid universal hatred rather than the antiquity of the Law amid the praise of many, what ought we to do, who have begun to become Christians from paganism?”

He rightly added: “I persecuted the Church of God excessively,” so that from this too admiration might arise: it was not just anyone among those who lightly persecuted the Church, but the man who surpassed the others in persecution, who had turned to the faith [Note: [Col. 0324D] Two manuscripts read: “not just anyone among those who persecuted the Church,” and so forth.].

And wisely, while recounting one matter, he inserts that he served not so much the Law of God as the traditions of his fathers—that is, of the Pharisees—who teach “the doctrines and commandments of men” (Matt. 15; Mark 7) and reject the Law of God in order to establish their own traditions.

How beautiful is the precision and weight of the words: “You have heard,” he says, “of my former manner of life in Judaism”—manner of life, not grace; formerly, not now; in Judaism, not in the Law of God. “For I persecuted the Church of God excessively and devastated it.” He did not persecute it like the others, but excessively. Nor was a merely vehement persecution enough for him; like some brigand and plunderer, he devastated the Church. He does not say “the Church of Christ,” as he then thought—Christ whom he regarded with contempt and persecuted [Al. “was regarded with contempt”]—but, as he now believes, “the Church of God,” either signifying that Christ himself is God, or that the Church belongs to the same God who formerly gave the Law.

“And I advanced,” he says, “in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries in my race, being more abundantly zealous for the traditions of my fathers.” Again, he calls his progress an advance in Judaism, not in the Law of God. Nor does he say “beyond all,” but “beyond many”; nor “beyond the old,” but “beyond my contemporaries,” so that he might indicate his zeal for the Law while avoiding boastfulness.

By recalling the traditions of his fathers, rather than the commandments of the Lord, he showed himself to be a Pharisee of Pharisees and to have possessed zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.

To this day, those who understand the Scriptures in a Jewish manner persecute the Church of Christ and devastate it—not from zeal for the Law of God, but corrupted by human traditions.

(Verses 15.) But when it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace, to reveal his Son in me, so that I might preach him among the Gentiles.

Not only here, but also in the Letter to the Romans, Paul writes that he was set apart for the Gospel of God. Jeremiah too, before he was formed in the womb and conceived in his mother’s belly, is said to have been known and sanctified by God (Jer. 1). And of the righteous man—or, as some think, in the person of the Savior—it is said: “Upon you I was cast from the womb; from my mother’s womb you are my God” (Ps. 21:11).

By contrast, David sings of sinners: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Ps. 50:7). And elsewhere: “Sinners have been estranged from the womb” (Ps. 57:4). Before the little ones were born, in either direction, it is said: “God loved Jacob, but hated Esau” (Mal. 1:1–2).

Heretics who assert that there are different natures—spiritual, animal, and *χοϊκή* (“earthly”)—and that one is saved, another perishes, and another stands between the two, find an opening here. For they say that no righteous person would ever have been chosen before doing anything good, nor would a wicked person have done something good, nor would a sinner have been hated before sin, unless there were a different nature belonging to those who perish and those who are saved [Note: [Col. 0325C] Up to this point the reading *justus intelligeretur antequam*, “a righteous person would be understood before,” was corrupt. With the support of Rabanus we have restored *eligeretur*, “would be chosen.” Yet I would prefer the still more harmonious reading *diligeretur*, “would be loved.” This word corresponds more appropriately to the following *odiretur*, “would be hated,” and seems closer to Jerome’s intention, since he repeats it throughout the passage. One Palatine manuscript differs considerably: “that no righteous person would ever be chosen, nor would any wicked person do something good, nor would a sinner be hated before sin,” and so forth.].

A simple response can be made: this happens through God’s foreknowledge, so that he loves the person whom he knows will become righteous before that person is born from the womb, and hates the person whom he knows will be a sinner before he sins [Note: [Col. 0325D] The theological school teaches what qualification should be applied to this opinion.]. This does not mean that God is unjust in love or hatred, but that he must regard people according to what he knows they will become—sinners or righteous persons—whereas we, as human beings, judge only by present circumstances. God, for whom future things are already accomplished, judges the end of matters, not their beginnings.

These things have been stated rather simply and, without deeper discussion, may in some measure satisfy the reader. [Note: [Col. 0325D] These remarks, as also the whole following context, very truly target Origen and his followers. He incurred this blasphemy both elsewhere and in Homily 20 on Joshua, where he posits within us many divine powers caring for souls or bodies, and likewise many harmful powers besieging and plotting against us. Hence also in Book VIII *Against Celsus*: “Let the wise men of the Greeks say that the human soul has been allotted demons from birth.” We have touched above on nearly identical material from Homily 12 on Luke.] But those who strive to assert that God is unjust, after the passage we cited earlier—“Sinners have been estranged from the womb”—also bring forward the words that follow: “They have gone astray from the womb; they have spoken falsehood.” And they say: How did sinners go astray from the womb and speak falsehood immediately, when they could neither speak nor possess understanding? Or what sort of justice is there in God’s foreknowledge, for him to love and protect one person before he is born and detest another?

They refer the causes of this matter to a previous life, saying that each person, according to his merit, is assigned from his very first birth to good or evil angels. And they so dispute the entire passage about Jacob and Esau, which we have now mentioned, as it is written in the Letter to the Romans (Rom. 9), that it would require, not without effort, Chrysippus’ hellebore to answer them [Note: [Col. 0326C] I do not find Chrysippus’ hellebore, but Carneades the Academic’s, who, when about to write against the books of the Stoic Zeno, is said to have been accustomed to purge the upper part of his body with white hellebore, lest humors corrupted in the stomach overflow as far as the seat of the mind and weaken the mind’s concentration and vigor. Jerome teaches here that questions with heretics are difficult, so that we need Chrysippus’ dialectic in order to avoid the subtleties of heretics who misuse Scripture. MART.—Although I know that there are other sound authorities, cited by Menage in the *Life of Carneades*, who report that Chrysippus used hellebore before undertaking to write, I do not object if someone wishes to suspect that the very word *hellebore* lies in an error. Certainly Chrysippus possessed a distinctive and peculiar subtlety in argument; but the ancient writers unanimously ascribe the purging of the brain with hellebore to Carneades when about to dispute against Zeno.].

Nor is the statement itself, “to reveal his Son in me,” equivalent to “to reveal his Son to me,” as though that were what he said. For what is revealed to someone is something that was previously not in him. But in the person in whom something is revealed, what is revealed is something that was previously in him and was afterward disclosed.

The same is true of the Gospel saying: “There stands among you one whom you do not know” (John 1:26). And elsewhere: “He was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into the world” (ibid., 9). From this it is evident that knowledge of God is naturally present in everyone; no one is born without Christ or without possessing within himself the seeds of wisdom, justice, and the remaining virtues.

Hence many people, without faith or the Gospel of Christ, act either wisely or virtuously: they obey their parents, extend a hand to the needy, do not oppress their neighbors, and do not seize what belongs to others. They thereby become all the more liable to God’s judgment because, possessing within themselves the principles of virtue and the seeds of God, they do not believe in him without whom they cannot exist [Al. “do not believe,” rather than “they do not believe”].

The Son of God may also be understood as having been revealed in Paul in another way: through Paul’s preaching, the Gentiles came to recognize the one whom previously they did not know.

[Col. 0326C] (Verse 16.) Immediately I did not submit to flesh and blood.

Or, as the Greek has it more accurately [Note: [Col. 0326D] Cistercian manuscripts read more accurately: “I did not confer with flesh and blood.”]: “I did not confer with flesh and blood.”

I know that most people think this was said about the apostles. Porphyry too objects that, after the revelation of Christ, Paul did not deign to go to human beings and confer with them, lest, after God’s teaching, he should be instructed by flesh and blood.

But far be it from me to think that Peter, John, and James were flesh and blood, which cannot possess the kingdom of God (1 Cor. 15). If the spiritual apostles are flesh and blood, what are we to think of the *χοϊκοί* (“earthly” or “material” people) [Note: [Col. 0326D] The Palatine manuscript reads: “If the spiritual apostles are human beings,” and so forth.]?

Clearly Paul did not confer with flesh and blood after the revelation of Christ, because he did not wish to cast pearls before swine or give what is holy to dogs (Matt. 7). See what is written about sinners: “My spirit shall not remain in these people, because they are flesh” [Al. “flesh,” plural] (Gen. 6:3).

With such people—who were flesh and blood, and who had not revealed the Son of God even to Peter (Matt. 16)—the Apostle did not confer the Gospel that had been revealed to him. Rather, he gradually turned them from flesh and blood into spirit, and only then entrusted to them the hidden mysteries of the Gospel.

Someone may say: If he did not immediately confer the Gospel with flesh and blood, nevertheless it is implied that afterward he did confer with flesh and blood; and this interpretation, by which the apostles are excused from being flesh and blood, cannot stand, since the person who at first did not confer with flesh and blood nevertheless afterward, as I have said, conferred with flesh and blood.

The preposition therefore constrains us to distinguish the passage in such a way that we do not immediately join “with flesh and blood” to what follows, but attach it to the preceding words, reading:

“But when it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb, to reveal his Son in me, and finally to preach him among the Gentiles, immediately: I did not confer with flesh and blood.”

Thus the statement should be understood to begin from its own proper point: the person who was immediately sent, after Christ’s revelation, to preach the Gospel to the Gentiles did not remain behind, nor did he prolong the time by going to the apostles and conferring the Lord’s revelation with human beings. Rather, he went away to Arabia, returned again to Damascus, preached the Gospel, and then, after three years, came to Jerusalem and saw Peter, John, and James.

(Verses 17.) Nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me.

If he had said of the apostles, “I did not confer with flesh and blood,” why was it necessary to repeat the same thing by saying, “Nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me”? We must therefore retain the interpretation that we set forth above.

But I went away to Arabia and returned again to Damascus.

The order of the history does not seem to agree with Luke’s account in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 9). Luke relates that, after Paul had confidently preached the Gospel in Damascus for many days following his faith in Christ, plots were made against him; that he was lowered by night through the wall in a basket; and that he came to Jerusalem, attempting to join himself to the disciples. When they avoided him and were afraid to approach him, Barnabas led him to the apostles. There he related how he had seen the Lord on the road and had acted boldly in Damascus in the name of the Lord [Al. adds “Jesus”].

“He was with them,” Luke says, “going in and going out in Jerusalem, acting boldly in the name of the Lord” [Al. “they were acting boldly”]. “He also spoke and disputed with the Greeks; but they sought to kill him. When the brothers learned this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus” (Acts 9:28–30).

Here, however, Paul says that he first went to Arabia, returned again to Damascus, and after three years came to Jerusalem, saw Peter, remained with him fifteen days, and met no other of the apostles except James, the Lord’s brother.

To make these statements believable—for they could seem doubtful to those who were absent—he confirms them by solemn testimony, saying: “As for what I am writing to you, behold, before God I do not lie.”

We may therefore suppose that, according to Luke’s history, Paul did indeed come to Jerusalem, but not as though he were going to the apostles who preceded him in order to learn something from them. Rather, he went there to avoid the force of the persecution that had been stirred up against him in Damascus because of the Gospel of Christ, and he came to Jerusalem as one might come to any other city.

From there, because of the plots, he immediately withdrew and went to Arabia—or to Damascus—and afterward, after three years, returned to Jerusalem to see Peter.

Or certainly the sequence may be understood in this way: Immediately after he had been baptized and strengthened by receiving food, he remained for several days with the disciples who were in Damascus. While everyone in the synagogues of the Jews was astonished, he immediately preached that Jesus was the Son of God. Then he went to Arabia, returned from Arabia to Damascus, and remained there for three years.

Scripture testifies to these many days when it says: “When many days had passed, the Jews took counsel to kill him” (Acts 9:23). Their plots against Saul became known, and they guarded the gates day and night in order to kill him. His disciples therefore took him by night and lowered him through the wall in a basket. When he came to Jerusalem, he attempted to join himself to the disciples.

Luke omitted Arabia because perhaps Paul had done nothing there worthy of the apostolate, and therefore he mentioned, in a concise account, those things that seemed worthy of the Gospel of Christ. Nor should it be attributed to the Apostle’s negligence if he had remained in Arabia without result [Al. “if he had stayed there without result”], but rather to some dispensation or command of God that he should remain silent. For later too we read that Paul, after setting out with Silas, was forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia (Acts 16).

Alternatively:

“But I went away to Arabia and returned again to Damascus.”

What benefit is there in this account if I read that Paul, immediately after the revelation of Christ, went to Arabia and immediately returned from Arabia to Damascus, without knowing what he did there or what benefit his journey and return produced?

The Apostle himself gives me an opportunity for a deeper understanding in this same Letter, when, discussing Abraham, Hagar, and Sarah, he says: “These things have been spoken allegorically. For these are the two covenants: one indeed from Mount Sinai, generating slavery, which is Hagar. For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia, joined to the Jerusalem that now exists” (Gal. 4:24–25).

He teaches that the Old Testament—that is, the son of the slave woman—was established in Arabia, which is interpreted as “humble” and “western.” Immediately, then, after Paul believed, he turned toward the Law, the Prophets, and the mysteries of the Old Testament, already situated in the west. In them he sought Christ, whom he had been commanded to preach among the Gentiles. Having found him, he did not remain there longer, but returned to Damascus—that is, to the blood and passion of Christ. From there, strengthened by prophetic reading, he proceeded to Jerusalem, the place of vision and peace—not so much to learn anything from the apostles as to confer with them the Gospel that he had taught.

(Verses 18.) Then, after three years, I went up to Jerusalem to see Peter.

He did not go to look at his eyes, cheeks, and face—to see whether he was thin or fat, whether he had a hooked nose or a straight one, or whether hair covered his forehead, or whether—as Clement reports in his *Periods*—he had baldness on his head. Nor do I think it consistent with apostolic dignity that, after so lengthy a preparation of three years, he should have wished to observe something merely human in Peter [Note: [Col. 0329D] Nothing of this kind can be found today in the books of the *Recognitions* wrongly attributed to Clement. Shortly afterward one Cistercian manuscript reads “three years of preaching.”].

Rather, he looked upon him with those eyes with which Peter also now appears to us in his Letters. Paul saw Cephas with those eyes with which Paul himself is now perceived by all prudent people.

If this interpretation does not satisfy anyone, let him join these words to the preceding sense: the apostles had contributed nothing to him. And even if he was ordered to go to Jerusalem, he went there in order to see the apostle [Note: [Col. 0329D] Two manuscripts read: “not from a desire to see him, because he too,” and so forth. Previously the text had *qui*, “who,” instead of *quia*, “because.”], not with the desire to learn, since he too had the same source of preaching, but to pay honor to the apostle who preceded him.

[Col. 0329C] And I remained with him fifteen days.

A person who had prepared himself for so long to see Peter did not require a lengthy period of instruction. Although it may seem superfluous to some to observe even the numbers found in Scripture, I nevertheless think that the fifteen days Paul spent in Peter’s company signify full knowledge and completed doctrine.

There are fifteen songs in the Psalter, and fifteen steps by which people ascend to sing to God; the righteous person ascends to stand in his courts. Hezekiah too, when fifteen years were granted to him for life, deserved to receive a sign in the steps (Isa. 38); and the solemnities of God begin on the fifteenth day (Exod. 12).

Moreover, since we are following a twofold interpretation, he specifies fifteen days in order to show that the time in which he could have learned something from Peter was not long, so that everything may be referred back to the sense with which he began: that he was taught not by man, but by God.

(Verses 19.) But I saw none of the other apostles except James, the Lord’s brother.

I remember that, while I was in Rome, at the urging of the brothers, I published a book on the perpetual virginity of holy Mary. In it I had to discuss at length those who are called the Lord’s brothers. Whatever the merits of what we wrote there, we must now be content with it.

For the present let this suffice: because of his outstanding character and incomparable faith and wisdom—wisdom not middling, but of the highest degree, full and complete—he was called the Lord’s brother [Note: [Col. 0329D] Marianus Victorius did not understand this word and therefore inserted *modicam*, “moderate,” on his own authority, contrary to the agreement of all our manuscript codices, which retain *sapientiamque non mediam*, that is, “not middling,” but of the highest degree, complete and consummate. MART. — Victorius preferred *non modicam*, “not moderate.” See also what we observed in the cited book against Helvidius concerning Jerome’s opinion of the Lord’s brothers, to which the entire theological school subscribes. The statement must be explained at greater length: James is called the Lord’s brother according to the relationship commonly recognized among the Jews, since he was born of Mary, the sister of the Mother of God. This Mary was the wife of Cleophas, and bore him James, Joses, Simon, and Judas; and all of them are called the Lord’s brothers by the Jews in Matthew. The Hebrews customarily called such relatives or cousins “brothers,” just as we sometimes call them blood relatives or “full brothers.” The entire difficulty lies in the fact that this James, like the others, is called the son of Alphaeus, not of Cleophas. We resolve this by showing that the name was familiar among the Jews and could be read both as *Chalphai* and as *Cleophai*, and was therefore rendered by the Latin or Greek translator in one place as *Halphai* and in another as *Cleophai*. See the commentary above on Matthew 12.], and because he was the first to preside over the Church which, being the first to believe in Christ, had been gathered from the Jews.

The other apostles too are called the Lord’s brothers, as in the Gospel: “Go, tell my brothers: I am going to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God” (John 20:17). And in the Psalm: “I shall declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the Church I shall sing to you” (Ps. 21:22).

But this man is called the brother in a special sense, because, when the Lord was going to the Father, he entrusted to him the sons of his mother. Just as Job and the other patriarchs were indeed called servants of God, but Moses possessed something exceptional, so that it could be written of him, “Not as Moses, my servant” (Heb. 3:5), so blessed James was likewise specially called the Lord’s brother, as we said earlier.

As for the fact that certain people, apart from the Twelve, are called apostles, the reason is that all who had seen the Lord and afterward preached him were called apostles. Thus it is written to the Corinthians: “He appeared to Cephas, then to the Eleven; afterward he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once, of whom many remain to the present, but some have fallen asleep; afterward he appeared to James, then to all the apostles” (1 Cor. 15:5–7).

As time gradually proceeded, others were appointed apostles by those whom the Lord had chosen, as the statement addressed to the Philippians makes clear: “I considered it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus, my brother, fellow worker, and fellow soldier, but your apostle and minister of my need” (Phil. 2:25). And concerning such persons it is written to the Corinthians: “Whether apostles of the churches, the glory of God” (2 Cor. 8:23) [Al. “in the glory of God”].

Silas and Judas too were called apostles by the apostles. Hence the person who thought that this James was the apostle, the brother of John, greatly erred [Note: [Col. 0331D] One author seems to have held this view, the author of the *Questions on Sacred Scripture* among the works of St. Athanasius, question 132, since he interprets the Apostle’s words in Hebrews 11:35—“others were tortured on the rack”—of James, the Lord’s brother.]. That James, it is clear from the testimony of the Acts of the Apostles, shed his blood for Christ after Stephen (Acts 12).

This James, however, was the first bishop of Jerusalem, surnamed “the Just.” He was a man of such holiness and such reputation among the people that they eagerly competed to touch the fringe of his garment. He too was later thrown from the temple by the Jews and was succeeded by Simon, whom they likewise report to have been crucified for the Lord.

Paul therefore denies that he met any other of the apostles besides these, lest a hidden contradiction arise: even if you were not taught by Peter, you had other apostles as teachers. He did not see the others, not because he held them in contempt, but because they had been scattered throughout the whole world to preach the Gospel.

(Verses 20.) As for what I am writing to you, behold, before God I do not lie.

This may be understood simply, so that the meaning is: “What I am writing to you is true, and I confirm it with God as my witness; it is embellished by neither verbal trickery nor any fabricated lie.”

Or it may be understood more deeply, so that it reads: “What I am writing to you is before God,” that is, worthy of God’s sight. Why is it worthy of God’s sight? Because I do not lie. Just as the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous (Ps. 33), while he turns his face away from the sight of the impious, so the things now being written are before the Lord, because I, who write them, do not lie. They would not be before the Lord if I were lying.

This can be understood not only of what he is now writing to the Galatians, but also generally of all his Letters: what he writes is not false, and his heart and words do not disagree.

(Verses 21.) Then I came into the regions of Syria and Cilicia.

After seeing Jerusalem, he came to Syria, whose name among us means “lofty” and “sublime.” From there he went into Cilicia, which he desired to bring into the faith of Christ, preaching to it the call to repentance. Cilicia is interpreted as “the received” or “a lamentable calling.”

(Verses 22–24.) But I was unknown by face to the churches of Judaea that are in Christ Jesus. They had only heard that the one who formerly persecuted us now preaches the faith that he once devastated; and they glorified God in me.

The churches that were in Judaea knew Paul only by report. Most of them had seen him more as a persecutor than as an apostle. Syria, however, and the regions of Cilicia, Arabia, and Damascus perhaps knew him by sight as well, because the teacher of the Gentiles preached the Gospel of Christ not to Jews but to Gentiles.

The whole point of what he is doing is to show that he could never have become renowned among those very people whom he had previously persecuted unless his preaching had also been confirmed by the judgment of those who had known his former wickedness [Note: [Col. 0331D] Previously the reading was *quod ait, contradicentibus*, “what he says, with the manuscripts contradicting”; the manuscripts support *quod agit*, “what he is doing.” [Col. 0332D] Two manuscripts, Rabanus, and Victorius read *eum male noverant*, “had known him badly.”].

He also returns covertly to his purpose, affirming that he spent so short a time in Judaea that he was unknown even by face to believers. From this he shows that Peter, James, and John were not his teachers, but Christ, who had revealed the Gospel to him.

At the same time, we should note that above he is said to have persecuted the Church, whereas here he persecuted the faith: there, persons; here, the cause itself. Thus it could now [Al. “then”] more appropriately be stated: “He preaches the faith that he once persecuted.” For the same expression could not have been used of the Church.

## Chapter II

### Verses 1–2

“Then, after fourteen years, I again went up to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus also. I went up, however, according to revelation; and I laid before them the Gospel that I preach among the Gentiles, but privately before those who seemed to be something, lest perhaps I should be running, or should have run, in vain.”

What the earlier Latin translator rendered here as *acquievi*—“I submitted”—in the passage where it is written, “Immediately I did not submit to flesh and blood,” he has rendered in the present passage by *contuli*, “I conferred,” rather than by *acquievi*. And, to speak more accurately, the Greek expression ἀνεθέμην means something different from what it conveys among us: namely, when we discuss what we know with a friend and, as it were, place it in his bosom and confidence, so that by common counsel what we know may either be approved or rejected.

[Note: Let those unlearned clerics hear this, who refuse to allow Jerome any knowledge of Greek except the slightest and almost none. — Martianaeus.]

Thus, after fourteen years he went up to Jerusalem. Whereas previously he had gone only to see Peter and had stayed with him fifteen days, now he says that he went in order to confer the Gospel with the apostles. He took with him the circumcised Barnabas and Titus, who was from the Gentiles and still had his foreskin, so that “at the mouth of two or three witnesses every word might stand” (Deut. 19:15).

To confer is one thing; to learn is another. Among those who confer there is equality; between a teacher and a learner, the one who learns is inferior. At the beginning of his faith, Paul saw the apostles in passing. After seventeen years, as he himself says, he speaks with them fully and humbles himself, investigating lest perhaps he should be running, or should have run, in vain.

This has a twofold purpose: first, to display the humility of Paul, who, already a teacher throughout the whole Gentile world, ran to the apostles who had preceded him; and second, so that the Galatians might learn that his Gospel had not been rejected even by those who presided over the churches in Judaea.

At the same time he teaches that, for the sake of the faith of Christ and the freedom of the Gospel, he dared to bring Titus, an uncircumcised man, before those very men who had learned many things about him: that he violated the Law, destroyed Moses, and entirely abolished circumcision. Even amid so great a multitude of Jews and his enemies—men who, supposedly out of zeal for the Law, desired to drink his blood—neither he nor Titus was overcome by terror so as to yield to necessity. Such a concession might have been excused by the place, by the authority of their elders, by the number of the churches of Jews who believed in Christ, or by the circumstances of the time, so that they might not at once endure so much hostility.

Some say that Paul went up to Jerusalem after fourteen years on the occasion when a dispute arose among the believers at Antioch concerning which observances of the Law should be maintained or set aside. It was then decided to go to Jerusalem and await the judgment of the elders, and Paul and Barnabas themselves were sent. They identify this event with what is read in the Latin manuscripts: “To whom we yielded in submission for an hour, so that the truth of the Gospel might remain among you.”

That is, Paul and Barnabas allowed themselves to be sent to Jerusalem concerning an evident matter as though it were doubtful, so that, once the grace of the Gospel had also been confirmed by the judgment of the elders, it might be approved by the believers, and no further doubt might remain concerning the omission of circumcision—since the apostles had commanded by letter that the yoke of the Law be removed from those who, from the Gentiles, had believed in Christ.

[Note: Our manuscripts do not contain the words “from the Gentiles.”]

What he says—“I laid before them the Gospel that I preach among the Gentiles, but privately before those who seemed to be something, lest perhaps I should be running, or should have run, in vain”—may also be understood in this way: he privately conferred with the apostles about the grace of evangelical freedom and the antiquity of the abolished Law, because of the multitude of Jewish believers who could not yet hear that Christ was the fulfillment and end of the Law. Even in Paul’s absence, these people had proclaimed at Jerusalem that he was running, or had run, in vain, because he thought that the old Law should not be followed.

Paul did not fear that, over seventeen years, he had preached a false Gospel among the Gentiles. Rather, he wished to show his predecessors that he was not running, or had not run, in vain, as those who were ignorant supposed.

### Verses 3–5

“But not even Titus, who was with me, although he was a Gentile, was compelled to be circumcised. But because of the false brothers who had slipped in, who had entered secretly to spy out our freedom, which we have in Christ Jesus, so that they might bring us into slavery—to whom we did not yield in submission even for an hour, so that the truth of the Gospel might remain among you.”

If Titus, though a Gentile, could not be compelled by any terror to be circumcised at Jerusalem, the capital city of the Jews, where such violent hatred against Paul was burning because of his supposed blasphemy against Moses that he was later almost killed by the Jews, when he was rescued by the tribune and sent in chains to Rome to Caesar—how can some think

[Note: I think the authors of the old Latin translation, called the Italic, are being criticized. That it had this reading without the negative particle may be inferred both from the very ancient Latin manuscripts of Paul’s Epistles and from several Latin Fathers who cite the passage in this way. Tertullian, in Book V, chapter 5 of *Against Marcion*, not only rejects the negative particle himself, but further maintains against the heretic who read it with the particle that it is a manifest corruption of Scripture. Present Latin and Greek copies, however, support Jerome’s reading, “to whom we did not yield even for an hour.” What the holy Father says a little below concerning variation among Greek manuscripts of his time is also observed by Ambrosiaster.] how can some think that the passage should be read, “To whom we yielded in submission for an hour, so that the truth of the Gospel might remain among you,” and understand that Titus himself, who previously could not be compelled to circumcision, was again circumcised and subjected?

Or what kind of Gospel truth would it be to yield to the hypocrisy of the Jews, to observe and regard as something the things that one had previously considered refuse and despised as losses, when they are nothing? This also greatly contradicts the sense of the Epistle itself, for it would recall the Galatians to circumcision.

Throughout this entire discourse Paul is doing this: teaching that, although he was a Hebrew from Hebrews, once observing all the works of the Law, circumcised on the eighth day according to the Law of the Pharisees, he nevertheless despises everything for the sake of Christ. When he went to Jerusalem and the false brothers who had believed from circumcision wanted to compel him to circumcise Titus, neither Titus nor Paul yielded to violence, so that they might preserve the truth of the Gospel.

But if he says that he was overcome by necessity and circumcised Titus, how can he recall the Galatians from circumcision, when at Jerusalem he could not excuse Titus, who had been a Gentile companion of his, from circumcision?

Therefore, either the passage must be read according to the Greek manuscripts: “To whom we did not yield in submission even for an hour,” so that what follows may naturally be understood: “so that the truth of the Gospel might remain among you.” Or, if one prefers the reading of some Latin exemplar, we must understand it according to the preceding interpretation: the yielding for an hour concerned not the circumcision of Titus but the journey to Jerusalem.

Paul and Barnabas yielded to the submission involved in going to Jerusalem because a disturbance concerning the Law had arisen at Antioch, so that their judgment might be confirmed by the letter of the apostles, and the truth of the Gospel might remain among the Galatians. That truth was not in the letter but in the spirit, not in carnal understanding but in spiritual insight, neither in open Judaism but in what was hidden.

It should be recognized that the conjunction *autem*—“but”—in the present passage, “But because of the false brothers who had slipped in,” is superfluous. If it is read, it has nothing corresponding to it or completing it. The order of the reading and meaning is rather this:

“But not even Titus, who was with me, although he was a Gentile, was compelled to be circumcised.” Immediately he adds the reason why Titus was being unwillingly driven toward circumcision: “Because of the false brothers,” he says, “who had slipped in to spy out our freedom, which we have in Christ Jesus, so that they might bring us into slavery.”

When these men were terrifying us with threats and, by their numbers, wanted to transfer us from the freedom of Christ into slavery to the Law, we did not yield to them even for a time by circumcising Titus. This was especially so since some necessity arising from ecclesiastical peace might have excused us. We did the whole thing so that no occasion would be given you to depart from the grace of the Gospel.

If, then, at Jerusalem, amid so many Jews, with false brothers threatening us from every side and with those who were elders restraining us to some extent, we could not be compelled by any force or argument to observe circumcision, which we knew had come to an end, how could you Gentiles, you who are in Galatia and against whom no force can be brought to bear, voluntarily withdraw from grace and cross over again to the antiquity of the now-abolished Law?

[Note: One Palatine manuscript reads: “When they wanted to terrify the multitude with threats and to lead us from freedom,” etc.]

### Verse 6

“But from those who seemed to be something—what they once were makes no difference to me; God does not accept a person’s status.”

Even if, he says, the Lord had Peter and John as his apostles with him, and they saw him transfigured on the mountain (Matt. 12; Mark 9), and the foundation of the Church was placed upon them, it makes no difference to me. I am not speaking against those who followed the Lord at that time; I am speaking against those who now place the Law before grace. I do not disparage my predecessors, nor do I accuse the elders in any respect. I say only this: “God does not accept a person’s status.”

For he did not accept Moses, nor David, nor others; therefore he will not accept those who seem for a time to yield to certain people, although they themselves agree with me. Peter also says: “In truth I understand that God is not a respecter of persons, but in every place whoever fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts 10:34–35).

The holy apostle Peter uses this very argument against those who took offense at Cornelius, a Gentile who had been baptized without circumcision, and he calms them by saying that he could not deny water to those who had received the Holy Spirit. In the same way the holy apostle Paul now argues against Peter himself: God is not a respecter of persons, but judges each person according to the truth.

Thus he proceeds carefully and step by step between Peter’s praise and rebuke. He shows deference to the apostle who preceded him, yet nevertheless boldly resists him to his face, compelled by the truth.

“But from those who seemed to be something, I received nothing.”

Above he conferred with them and reported many things that he was accomplishing among the Gentiles. They contributed nothing to him; they merely approved what he said, gave him and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, and confirmed that his Gospel and theirs were one.

It should again be noted that the verb “contributed” is the very Greek verb discussed earlier.

[Note: Older printed editions insert the Greek verb itself: προσανέθεντο, “they contributed,” etc.]

### Verses 7–8

“On the contrary, when they saw that I had been entrusted with the Gospel of the uncircumcision, just as Peter had been entrusted with that of the circumcision—for he who worked in Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision also worked in me among the Gentiles—and when they recognized the grace that had been given to me, Peter and James and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave the right hand of fellowship to me and Barnabas, so that we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcision.”

[Note: One Palatine manuscript omits the word *societatis*, “fellowship.”]

This is a case of *hyperbaton*. If the intervening material is removed, it can be read briefly as follows:

“For those who seemed to be something contributed nothing to me; but, on the contrary, they gave the right hand of fellowship to me and Barnabas.”

Or perhaps the hidden meaning, without any boasting on his part, is this:

“Those who seemed to be something contributed nothing to me; but, on the contrary, something was contributed by me to them, as they were made stronger in the grace of the Gospel.”

The whole meaning is this: the same Gospel of the uncircumcision was entrusted to me, and that of the circumcision to Peter. He sent me to the Gentiles; he placed Peter in Judaea.

The Gentiles, already grown to maturity, could not be afflicted by the pain of circumcision, which would no longer benefit them, nor could they abstain from foods to which they had always been accustomed and which God had created for use. Nor could those who had believed from the Jews and had been circumcised—who, through custom as though through a second nature, thought they possessed more than the other nations—easily despise the things in which they gloried.

Therefore, by God’s providence, one apostle was given to the circumcised, appearing to acquiesce in the shadows of the Law; another was given to those in the uncircumcision, so that he might regard the grace of the Gospel not as slavery but as free faith. This was so that, under no pretext, an obstacle to faith might arise and people might fail to believe in Christ because of circumcision or uncircumcision.

We do not say that Peter—who in the Acts of the Apostles himself testified that no human being was common or unclean (Acts 10), and who, in the vessel sent down from heaven by its four corners, was taught that it makes no difference whether someone is a Jew or a Gentile—forgot his earlier teaching and thought that the Law should be observed in addition to the grace of the Gospel.

Rather, while pretending that he too observed the Law, he gradually led the Jews away from their ancient manner of life. They could not suddenly despise so great a burden of observance and such a carefully guarded ancient way of life as though it were mere refuse and loss.

From this we understand why Peter, James, and John gave Paul and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship: so that, because of differing practices, the Gospel of Christ would not be thought to be different, but so that there might be one communion both of the circumcised and of those who possessed the foreskin.

He wisely prepared the way by saying, “He who worked in Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision.” He did this so that no one would think that he was disparaging Peter.
