Rather, after the praises already given him, it should be understood that Peter accepted circumcision to some extent in order to win those who among the Jews had been entrusted to him and preserve them in the faith and Gospel of Christ.

[Note: The same manuscript implies also: “that if he did this without fault, and by observing for a time what is not lawful so as not to lose those entrusted to him, I ought all the more to do what has been entrusted to me in the uncircumcision for the truth of the Gospel.”]

It is also implied that, if Peter did this without fault—observing for a time what is not lawful so as not to lose those entrusted to him—then Paul ought all the more to do what had been entrusted to him among the uncircumcised, lest the Gentiles, deterred by the burden and difficulty of the Law, depart from the faith and belief of Christ.

[Note: Earlier editions, through a gross error, read “cruelty” (*crudelitate*) for “belief” (*credulitate*).]

Here a hidden question arises: What, then? If Peter encountered Gentiles, did he not lead them to the faith? Or if Paul encountered some from the circumcision, did he not invite them to Christ’s baptism?

The answer is that each had received his principal commission with respect to Jews or Gentiles, so that those who defended the Law might have someone to follow, while those who preferred grace to the Law would not lack a teacher and guide. Their common purpose, however, was to gather a Church for Christ from all the nations.

For we read that the Gentile Cornelius was baptized by the holy Peter, and that Christ was very often preached by Paul in the synagogues of the Jews.

### “Peter, James, and John, who seemed to be pillars”

Three times we read above of the apostles: “privately before those who seemed to be something”; “from those who seemed to be something”; and “from those who seemed to be something, I received nothing.”

I had carefully asked what he meant by “those who seemed,” but now he has freed me from every doubt by adding, “who seemed to be pillars.”

The apostles, then—and especially Peter, James, and John—are pillars of the Church. Two of them were worthy to ascend the mountain with the Lord. One of them, in the Apocalypse, introduces the Savior as saying: “Whoever conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God” (Rev. 3:12). This teaches that all believers who conquer the adversary can become pillars of the Church.

Writing to Timothy, Paul says: “So that you may know how one ought to conduct oneself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth” (1 Tim. 2:15).

From this and other passages we learn that, in Scripture, the apostles and all believers, as well as the Church herself, are called a pillar. It makes no difference whether the statement concerns the body or its members, since the body is divided into members and the members belong to the body.

Peter, James, and John, who seemed to be pillars, therefore gave Paul and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship. They did not give them to Titus, who was with them. He had not yet reached that measure at which the commerce of Christ could be entrusted to him on equal terms with his elders, nor could he hold the same place in this business which Barnabas and Paul held.

[Note: Understand “he could be entrusted,” a verb which the holy Father, following the genius of the Latin language, does not repeat. Victorius unnecessarily restored the verb *teneret*, since the Latin expression otherwise seemed to him defective.]

### Verse 10

“They asked only that we should remember the poor, which was the very thing I was eager to do.”

The holy poor, whose care was especially entrusted by the apostles to Paul and Barnabas, are those believers from the Jews who brought the prices of their possessions to the apostles’ feet, to be distributed to the needy. Alternatively, they may be those who, because they were regarded as deserters of the Law and believers in a crucified man, were hated and considered accursed by their fellow tribesmen, relatives, and parents.

The Epistles of the holy apostle Paul testify how much labor he expended in serving these people. He wrote to the Corinthians, the Thessalonians, and all the churches of the Gentiles, asking them to prepare this gift for conveyance to Jerusalem, either by themselves or through others whom they approved.

Therefore he now says confidently: “This was the very thing I was eager to do.”

The poor may also be understood in another sense, namely those of whom the Gospel says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). Such people deserve to remain in the apostles’ remembrance.

There are also those poor of whom it is written in Solomon: “A man’s redemption is his own wealth” (Prov. 13:8). But the poor man does not endure a threat. He cannot hear the terror of future punishments: poor in faith, poor in grace, possessing neither spiritual riches nor knowledge of the Scriptures, which are compared with gold, silver, and precious stones.

Since the healthy do not need a physician, but those who are ill do, it was therefore also fitting, in the apostles’ fellowship of the right hands, that they should not despise the poor or look down upon sinners, but always remember them. Paul remembered the Corinthian man whom, in his first Epistle, he had grieved for a time so that, while his body suffered through repentance, his spirit might be saved (1 Cor. 5). In the second Epistle he restored him to the Church lest he be swallowed up by excessive grief. He asks everyone to confirm their love toward him and to forgive their brother, just as he himself had forgiven each of them in the presence of Christ, fulfilling the agreement he had made at Jerusalem always to remember the poor.

### Verses 11ff.

“But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he was blameworthy. For before certain men came from James, he ate with the Gentiles. But when they came, he withdrew and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision. And the rest of the Jews joined him in his hypocrisy, so that even Barnabas was led along by them into that hypocrisy.”

From the fact that Peter ate with the Gentiles before certain men came from Jerusalem to Antioch, it is shown that he had not forgotten the commandment not to call any human being common or unclean. But because of those who still thought that the Law should be observed, he withdrew for a time from the table of the Gentiles. The others who were from the Jews did the same, and even Barnabas, who preached the Gospel among the Gentiles with Paul, was compelled to do so.

Consequently, those who had believed in Antioch from the Gentiles and had not been circumcised were driven to take upon themselves the burdens of the Law. They did not understand Peter’s dispensation, by which he desired the Jews to be saved; rather, they thought that this was the proper manner of observing the Gospel.

When the apostle Paul saw that the grace of Christ was endangered, as a new fighter he employed the old art of warfare. In order to correct Peter’s dispensation—by which Peter desired the Jews to be saved—through a new dispensation of contradiction, Paul opposed him to his face. He was not attacking Peter’s intention, but contradicted him publicly, so that, through Paul’s resistance in rebuking him, those who had believed from the Gentiles might be saved.

[Note: We restore *vetus*, “old,” with Victorius, instead of *nova*, which Martianaeus retained less appropriately.]

If someone thinks that Paul truly resisted the apostle Peter and, for the truth of the Gospel, fearlessly insulted his predecessor, the following consideration will not support that view: Paul himself became a Jew to the Jews in order to win the Jews, and would likewise be guilty of the same hypocrisy when he shaved his head at Cenchrea and, after cutting off his hair, presented an offering in Jerusalem (Acts 18), circumcised Timothy (Acts 16), and practiced going barefoot—practices which are unmistakably part of the ceremonies of the Jews.

If Paul himself, who had been sent to preach to the Gentiles, did not consider it inappropriate to say, “Be without offense to Jews and to the Church of God” (1 Cor. 10:32), and, “I please all people in all things, not seeking my own advantage but that of many, so that they may be saved,” and if he did things contrary to evangelical freedom so as not to scandalize the Jews, by what authority or with what confidence would he dare to rebuke Peter for doing what the apostle of the Gentiles himself is accused of having done, when Peter was the apostle of the circumcision?

But, as we have already said, Paul resisted Peter and the others publicly, so that the hypocrisy of observing the Law—which harmed those who had believed from the Gentiles—might be corrected by the hypocrisy of the rebuke, and both peoples might be saved. Those who praised circumcision could follow Peter, while those who did not wish to be circumcised could proclaim Paul’s freedom.

When Paul says that Peter “was blameworthy,” he moderated the severity of his language. We are to understand that Peter was not so much blameworthy in Paul’s eyes as he was blameworthy in the eyes of those brothers with whom he had previously eaten but from whom he afterward separated himself.

That useful hypocrisy, and one to be adopted at the proper time, is taught by the example of Jehu, king of Israel. He could not have killed the priests of Baal unless he had pretended that he wanted to worship the idol, saying: “Gather all the priests of Baal for me. If Ahab served Baal a little, I will serve him much” (2 Kings 10:18).

The same is shown by David when he changed his appearance before Abimelech, who dismissed him and allowed him to depart (1 Sam. 21).

Nor is it surprising that righteous men should sometimes pretend to something for a time, for the sake of their own salvation and that of others, since our Lord himself, although he had no sin and no sinful flesh, assumed the appearance of sinful flesh, so that, by condemning sin in the flesh, he might make us the righteousness of God in himself.

Paul had certainly read in the Gospel that the Lord commanded: “If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother” (Luke 17:3).

Since the Lord had commanded that this should be done even in the case of lesser brothers, how did Paul dare to rebuke the greatest of the apostles so openly and so firmly before the public, unless Peter himself had been willing to be rebuked in this way, and unless Paul was not insulting the man of whom he had previously said: “I went up to Jerusalem to see Peter, and I remained with him fifteen days; but I saw none of the other apostles”?

And again: “He who worked in Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision.” And below: “Peter, James, and John, who seemed to be pillars,” along with the other passages in which he elaborates Peter’s praises.

When I was a young man declaiming controversial cases at Rome and exercising myself in fictitious disputes, I used to run to the tribunals of the judges.

[Note: The Royal manuscript no. 3758 retains this true reading. The Erasmian edition and some manuscripts corruptly read *fictis militibus exercerem*, “I was exercised by imaginary soldiers.” Victorius altered the former reading *fictis militibus* to *me litibus*, “in lawsuits,” on the authority of manuscripts agreeing with ours, except for one which has *factis* for *fictis*. — Martianaeus.] There I saw the most eloquent orators contending with such bitterness that, often setting aside the cases themselves, they turned to personal insults and bit one another with a playful tooth.

If those men did this so as to avoid any suspicion of collusion before the defendants and to deceive the surrounding crowd, what should we think that the great pillars of the Church, Peter and Paul, those great vessels of wisdom, ought to have done amid Jews and Gentiles who were in disagreement? Surely it was so that their feigned contention might become the peace of believers, and that the faith of the Church might be established through their holy quarrel in concord.

There are some who do not think that Cephas—the man whom Paul writes that he opposed to his face here—was the apostle Peter, but another of the seventy disciples who bore this name.

[Note: It is not my task here to revive an ancient question, one which has drawn highly esteemed authorities into opposing camps. It will be sufficient to refer to the Fathers whom Jerome mentions, as well as those whom later ages produced, who adopted the view that the Cephas rebuked by Paul was someone other than Peter.

Among the earliest, Saint Clement of Alexandria deserves praise, in the fifth book of the *Hypotyposeis*, as does Eusebius Pamphilus, who cites his testimony in Book I, chapter 12, of his *Ecclesiastical History*. In the fourth century this view was supported by Dorotheus of Tyre, who counted the Cephas rebuked by Paul not among the apostles but among the seventy disciples, and by Chrysostom, volume V, homily 64. Jerome’s testimony, as well as another from Gregory the Great in *Homilies on Ezekiel*, homily 18, supports the same position, since both testify that in their own age there were some who distinguished Cephas from Peter.

I pass over the author of the Alexandrian Chronicle at the year 30 of Christ and, much later, Oecumenius; likewise the author of the commentary on Paul’s Epistles improperly attributed to Saint Anselm, and other more recent men of great name who approved either their own or another’s opinion that Cephas, one of the seventy disciples, was a different person from Peter, the chief of the apostles.

There are also many considerations arising from the sequence of the sacred text and from the history of Paul’s affairs which draw me toward the same conclusion. To state the principal point once and for all: the strongest argument is that Peter was not in Antioch at the time when Paul rebuked Cephas. I could readily demonstrate this with new and very strong arguments, but doing so would take us farther than the purpose of the Notes allows.

In the meantime, it is certain that almost all Latin writers—Cyprian, Tertullian, Hilary the Deacon, Gregory the Great, Thomas, and a great many later interpreters, not excepting Augustine himself, who nevertheless opposed Jerome’s approved interpretation—regarded Peter and Cephas as one and the same person. Our Jerome also maintained this opinion much later, almost at the end of his life, when writing against the Pelagians: that Peter had truly erred at that time and that Paul had rightly and deservedly been angry with him. “Who,” he says, “will be indignant that something is denied to him which the chief of the apostles himself did not have?”]

They say that Peter could not possibly have withdrawn from fellowship with the Gentiles, since he had baptized the centurion Cornelius. And when he had gone up to Jerusalem, those who were from the circumcision disputed with him, saying: “Why did you enter men who had the foreskin and eat with them?” (Acts 11:3). After recounting the vision, he concluded his answer with these words:

“If, therefore, God gave them the same grace as he gave us who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could hinder God?”

When they heard these things, they were silent and glorified God, saying: “Then God has also granted repentance unto life to the Gentiles.”

Moreover, Luke, the writer of the history, makes no mention of this disagreement. He never says that Peter was at Antioch with Paul. Otherwise, Porphyry would have an opportunity to blaspheme if Peter were thought to have erred or Paul to have insolently refuted the chief of the apostles.

First, then, we must answer that we know the name of no other Cephas except the one who is written both in the Gospel, in Paul’s other Epistles, and in this very passage, now as Cephas and now as Peter.

This does not mean that Peter signifies one thing and Cephas another. Rather, what we call *petra* in Latin and Greek, the Hebrews and Syrians, because of the affinity of their languages, call *Cephas*.

[Note: The Palatine manuscript reads: “Whom we call Peter in Latin and Greek, the Hebrews call Cephas,” etc. Cephas comes from the root from which rocks are called *petrae* in the plural in Jeremiah 4:29 and Job 30:6. Erasmus is foolish when he says that Jerome denies Cephas to be a Hebrew name, claiming instead that it is Syriac and means “solid.”]

Furthermore, the entire argument of the Epistle, which speaks indirectly of Peter, James, and John, opposes this interpretation. It is not surprising that Luke was silent about the matter, since, through the historian’s freedom, he omitted many other things that Paul recalls having endured. It is not immediately contradictory if one writer thought something worthy of mention while another left it among other matters.

Finally, we have received the tradition that Peter was the first bishop of the church of Antioch and was afterward transferred to Rome, a fact which Luke entirely omitted.

In conclusion, if, because of Porphyry’s blasphemy, another Cephas must be invented for us so that Peter will not appear to have erred, then countless passages from the divine Scriptures will have to be erased—passages which Porphyry condemns because he does not understand them.

We shall also fight against Porphyry on another occasion, if Christ commands it. For now, let us continue with the remaining material.

### Verse 14

“But when I saw that they were not walking uprightly according to the truth of the Gospel, I said to Peter before them all…”

[Note: Victorius restores *incederent*, “were walking,” as in the Vulgate, and maintains that the Greek incorrectly has ὀρθοποδοῦσι instead of ὀρθοποδῶσι; he further claims that the printed reading follows neither the sense nor the rules of grammar.]

Just as those who pretend to limp with healthy feet do not have a defect in their feet, but some reason for which they limp, so Peter, knowing that circumcision and uncircumcision are nothing but that the observance of God’s commandments is what matters, had previously eaten with the Gentiles. For a time, however, he withdrew from them so as not to cause the Jews to lose the faith of Christ.

Paul therefore opposed Peter to his face by the same strategy by which Peter had pretended. He spoke before everyone, not so much to rebuke Peter as to correct those for whose sake Peter had pretended, and also to remove arrogance from the Jews and despair from the Gentiles.

[Note: I do not know whether the reading in one Palatine manuscript is more correct: “not so much so that Peter might be corrected as so that those for whose sake Peter had pretended might be corrected.” The remaining words that follow here—“or so that arrogance might also be removed from the Jews and despair from the Gentiles”—are omitted by Victorius and by the older edition.]

If someone does not accept this interpretation—according to which neither Peter is shown to have sinned nor Paul to have insolently rebuked his superior—he must explain by what sequence of reasoning Paul rebukes in another person what he himself committed.

[Note: The reference is especially to Saint Augustine, who, in his letters to Jerome, numbered 56 and 57 in our recension, argues against this interpretation.]

[Textual variants: “sees” for “saw” in the reference to Paul’s first sight of the apostles; “might say” for “might learn” concerning the Galatians; “are” for “were allowed” concerning Paul and Barnabas being sent to Jerusalem; “kept asserting” for “had proclaimed” concerning the claims at Jerusalem; the singular imperative “gather” for “gather together” in Jehu’s command; “may be able” for “could” concerning Titus’s fitness; “themselves” for “among them” concerning the Church’s concord; and “future” for “of future punishments” in the reference to the poor man unable to endure threats.]

If you, although you are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you compel the Gentiles to Judaize? With an indissoluble argument he binds Peter—or rather, through Peter, those who were forcing him to do contradictory things among themselves: “If, Peter, you are by nature a Jew, circumcised from infancy and observing all the precepts of the Law, yet now, because of Christ’s grace, you know that these things have no usefulness in themselves but are models and images of things to come, and you eat with those who are from the Gentiles—not at all as before, superstitiously, but living freely and without distinction—how can you now, withdrawing from those who have believed from the Gentiles and separating and distinguishing yourself from them as though from the polluted, compel them to Judaize? For if those from whom you withdraw are unclean, and you withdraw for that reason, because they do not have circumcision, you compel them to be circumcised and to become Jews, although you yourself, born a Jew, have lived like a Gentile.” And he gladly demonstrates why he had argued against him: namely, because by his pretense he was compelling the Gentiles to Judaize, while they desired to imitate him.

> **Note [Col. 0342D].** The text was corruptly printed as *dum enim*. We silently correct such obvious errors of this kind more than once.

### (Verse 15)

“We are Jews by nature, and not sinners from the Gentiles.”

At this point the heretics intrude, inventing ridiculous and foolish notions. They say that a spiritual nature cannot sin, nor can an earthly nature do anything justly. Let us ask them why branches were broken off from the good olive tree, and why a branch from the wild olive was grafted into the root of the good olive, if nothing can fall from what is good and nothing can rise from what is evil. Or how could Paul have previously persecuted the Church, if he belonged to a spiritual nature? Or how could he afterward have become an apostle, if he had been generated from earthly dregs? But if they maintain that he was not earthly, let us set forth his own words: “We were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. II, 3).

A Jew by nature is one who is descended from Abraham and was circumcised by his parents on the eighth day.

> **Note [Col. 0343D].** Martianay’s text again had the opposite meaning through corruption: *Nam natura*, instead of *Non natura*, and so forth.

He is not a Jew by nature who was afterward made one from the Gentiles.

To gather the whole argument into a brief statement, its meaning is this: “We”—that is, I and you, Peter—for he combines his own person with Peter’s so that he might not appear to wrong him—“when we were Jews by nature, doing the things prescribed by the Law, and not sinners from the Gentiles,” who are sinners either generally because they serve idols, or those whom we now regard as unclean—“knowing that we cannot be saved by works of the Law but by faith in Christ, believed in Christ, so that what the Law had not given us, faith might grant, the faith that we had” [variant: *have*] “in Christ.

“But if, withdrawing from the Law, in which we could not be saved, we passed over to faith, in which circumcision of the flesh is not sought but devotion of a pure heart; and if now, by withdrawing from the Gentiles, we act so that everyone who is uncircumcised is unclean, then faith in Christ, in which we previously thought we were saved, is more a minister of sin than of righteousness, since it removes circumcision, without which a person is unclean.

“But far be it from me to reassert what I once destroyed and knew to have been of no benefit to me. Once having departed from the Law, I died to the Law, so that I might live to Christ; and, fastened to his cross and reborn as a new person, I might subsist by faith rather than by the flesh, and depart from the world with Christ. What I once undertook, I hold fast. Christ did not die for me in vain: I believed in him in vain” [note: our manuscripts and those consulted by Victorius preferred this reading to *if I thought*], “if I could be saved without his faith under the former Law.”

### (Verse 16)

“Knowing that a person is not justified by works of the Law except through faith in Jesus Christ: we too have believed in Christ Jesus, so that we might be justified by faith in Christ, and not by works of the Law.”

Some say: If what Paul asserts is true—that no one is justified by works of the Law but by faith in Jesus Christ—then the patriarchs, prophets, and saints who lived before Christ’s coming were imperfect. We must remind them that those are said not to have attained righteousness who believe that they can be justified solely by works. The saints of ancient times, however, were justified by faith in Christ. Abraham saw Christ’s day and rejoiced. Moses considered the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt, “for he was looking to the reward.” Isaiah saw Christ’s glory (Isa. VI), as the evangelist John recalls; and Jude speaks generally of all things: “I wish to remind you, though you know all things once for all, that Jesus, having saved the people from the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe” (Jude 5).

Therefore it is not so much the works of the Law that are condemned as those who trust that they can be justified solely by works. The Savior likewise says to his disciples: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V, 20).

Here we must gather together how many commandments there are in the Law, which no one can fulfill. Conversely, we must say that some of the Law’s commandments are also performed by those who do not know the Law. Yet those who perform them are not justified because they perform them without the faith of Christ: for example, not sleeping with a man in the manner of a woman’s intercourse, not committing adultery, not stealing, but rather honoring father and mother and doing the other things that were commanded.

If they produce examples from holy men, saying that those men, having been occupied with the Law, performed the things belonging to the Law, we shall reply: “The Law is not laid down for the righteous but for the lawless and disobedient, the ungodly and sinners, the defiled and unclean” (I Tim. I). But one who has been taught by God does not need to be taught even charity, as Paul says: “Concerning mutual love, I have no need to write to you, for you yourselves have been taught by God to love one another” (I Thess. IV, 9).

> **Note [Col. 0343D].** Two of our manuscripts and Rabanus read: “so that he may at least be taught about charity.”

### (Verses 17–18)

“For this reason, by works of the Law no flesh will be justified.” [The manuscripts in our possession omit the passage of the sacred text that follows here.]

“But if, while seeking to be justified in Christ, we ourselves have also been found to be sinners, is Christ therefore a minister of sin? Certainly not. For if I rebuild the things that I destroyed, I show myself to be a transgressor.”

That flesh will not be justified [variant: *is not justified*] by works of the Law of which it is written: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field” (Isa. XL, 6).

> **Note [Col. 0344D].** Victorius restores *of grass*, from the Greek *chórtou* (χόρτου), with the support of the manuscripts. He thinks that the unlearned substituted *of the field*, because they were unaware of Jerome’s practice—namely, that the Septuagint, rather than his own edition, is being quoted. The authority of the manuscripts does not permit us to accept this conjecture.

That flesh, however, is justified by faith in Jesus Christ of which it is said in the mystery of the resurrection: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke III, 6).

But, according to the more modest interpretation, formerly not all flesh was justified by the Law, but only those people who were in Palestine. Now, however, all flesh is justified by faith in Jesus Christ, while his Church is founded throughout the whole world.

### (Verse 19)

“For through the Law I died to the Law, so that I might live to God.”

> **Note [Col. 0344D].** One Palatine manuscript reads: “It is one thing to die to the Law through the Law, and another thing…”

It is one thing to die through the Law, and another to die to the Law. Whoever dies to the Law was previously living for it, observing sabbaths, new moons, and feast days, the ritual exactness of sacrifices, Jewish fables, and genealogies.

But after Christ came, and after the Law of which it is written, “We know that the Law is spiritual” (Rom. VII, 14), he died to the former Law through the evangelical Law. The soul which, according to what is written to the Romans, “while her husband lives, would be called an adulteress if she married another, but when her husband dies”—that is, the old Law—“she is free to marry” the spiritual Law, so that she might bear fruit for God. Hence in Hosea it is said to her: “From me your fruit has been found” (Hos. XIV, 9).

To this is beautifully added that mystical saying: “Who is wise and will understand these things? Intelligent, and will know them?” [variant: *or, understanding*]. Whoever, therefore, through the spiritual Law, dies to the Law of the letter, lives to God, since he is not without the Law of God but is within the Law of Christ.

Whoever, however, dies to the law because of sins is indeed dead, but it cannot be said of him that which follows, namely, that he lives to God.

That there is another spiritual Law apart from the Law of the letter is also taught elsewhere by the Apostle, who says: “Thus the Law is indeed holy, and the commandment holy and just and good” (Rom. VII, 12). Ezekiel likewise speaks in God’s person: “I brought them,” that is, the Jewish people, “out of the land of Egypt, and I led them into the wilderness, and I gave them my commandments and showed them my judgments, which a person shall do and live in them” (Ezek. XX, 10).

Of that Law which produces wrath, and to which the Apostle also died, he later adds: “And I gave them commandments that were not good, and judgments in which they would not live” (ibid., 25). The same is signified in the Psalter: “Because I did not know letters, I shall enter into the strength of the Lord” (Ps. LXX, 51).

### “I have been crucified with Christ”

Because he had said that he had died to the Law through the Law, he shows how he died: “I have been crucified with Christ,” taking up his cross and following Christ, and in that very passion praying: “Remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke XXIII, 42–43).

> **Note [Col. 0345D].** Other books read: “and observing in that very passion,” and so forth. Immediately he heard: “Today you will be with me in paradise.”

If anyone, having put his members to death upon the earth and died to the world, has been conformed to the death of Jesus Christ, he is crucified with Jesus and fastens the trophy of his mortification to the wood of the Lord’s passion.

### (Verse 20)

“But I live, now not I; Christ, however, lives in me.”

The one who formerly lived in the Law does not live, since he persecuted the Church. Christ lives in him: wisdom, strength, the Word, peace, joy, and the other virtues. Whoever does not possess these cannot say: “Christ lives in me.” Throughout this entire passage he discusses Peter, against Peter, while speaking in his own person.

### “But what I now live in the flesh”

It is one thing to be in the flesh and another to live in the flesh. For those who are in the flesh cannot please God (Rom. VIII, 8–9). Hence it is said to those who live well: “But you are not in the flesh.”

### “I live in faith in the Son of God”

> **Note [Col. 0345D].** Two manuscripts and Rabbanus insert *and of Christ*, but the Greek text itself rejects these words.

“He who loved me and gave himself for me.”

In the Epistle to the Romans he speaks of God, saying that he did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us. Here, however, he speaks of Christ, saying that he himself gave himself up: “He loved me,” he says, “and gave himself for me.”

In the Gospel, where the apostles are listed, it is added: “And Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed him” [variant: *Scarioth*] (Luke VI, 16). Again, in the same Gospel: “Behold, the one who will betray me has drawn near” (Matt. XXVI, 46).

Concerning the chief priests and the elders of the people, Scripture recalls that they condemned Jesus to death and, after binding him, led him away and handed him over to Pilate the governor (ibid., XXVII; Mark XV). Then concerning Pilate: “He released Barabbas to them, but Jesus, after scourging him, he handed over to them to be crucified” (John XIX).

Thus the Father handed over the Son; the Son himself handed himself over; Judas and the priests handed him over to the rulers; and finally Pilate, after he had been handed over to him, handed him over himself.

But the Father handed him over in order to save the lost world; Jesus handed himself over in order to accomplish the will of the Father and his own; Judas, the priests, the elders of the people, and Pilate, without understanding, handed life over to death.

Since life itself also handed itself over for our salvation, blessed and exceedingly happy is the person who, with Christ living in him, can say through each thought and deed: “I live in faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.”

### (Verse 21)

“I do not reject the grace of God; for if righteousness comes through the Law, then Christ died for nothing” [variants: *that*; *let Christ have died for nothing*].

He rejects the grace of God both whoever, after the Gospel, lives according to the Law and whoever, after baptism, soils himself with sins.

Whoever can say with the Apostle, “His grace toward me was not empty” (I Cor. XV, 10), can also confidently say this: “I do not reject the grace of God.”

What follows is especially necessary against those who think that, after faith in Christ, the precepts of the Law must be observed. We must say to them: “If righteousness comes through the Law, then Christ died for nothing” [variants: *therefore*; *let Christ have died for nothing*]. Or let them teach how Christ did not die for nothing if works justify [variant: *should justify*].

Although they are dull-witted, they will not dare to say that Christ died without cause. Therefore, concerning the part of the syllogism proposed here—“For if righteousness comes through the Law, then Christ died for nothing”—we must assume what follows consequently and cannot be denied: Christ did not die for nothing. We must conclude: Therefore righteousness does not come through the Law.

Thus far he has been speaking against Peter; now he returns to the Galatians.

## Chapter III

### (Verse 1)

“O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you?”

> **Note [Col. 0345D].** In the earlier printed books the words “not to obey the truth” were falsely added. Jerome himself shows that these words were not found in the copies of Adamantius, which the saintly writer followed. Martianay.
>
> The words “not to obey the truth,” formerly added here from the Vulgate translator, were rightly removed by Victorius long ago. Jerome’s exposition itself, which follows, makes clear that he omitted them because they were not found in Origen’s copies. The same is confirmed most clearly below, when the words of chapter five are explained: “You were running well; who hindered you from obeying the truth?” Moreover, they are not found in the manuscripts we use.

This passage can be understood in two ways. Either the Galatians are called foolish because, coming from greater things to lesser, they began with the spirit but are being brought to completion by the flesh; or because each province has its own characteristics.

The Apostle confirms that the Cretans were rightly called “always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies,” words truly spoken by the poet Epimenides. The Latin historian attacks the vain Moors and savage Dalmatians. All poets tear apart the timid Phrygians. Philosophers boast that more accomplished minds are born at Athens. Cicero mocks the fickle Greeks in the speech of Gaius Caesar, saying: “Either of fickle Greeks or savage barbarians.” In *For Flaccus* he says: “Inborn fickleness and learned vanity.”

All the Scriptures accuse Israel itself of being heavy-hearted and stiff-necked. In this way, therefore, I think that the Apostle also attacked the Galatians on account of the character of their region.

Some, however, plunging into profound questions, supposedly to avoid the heresy that introduces different natures, say that Tyrians and Sidonians, Moabites and Ammonites, Idumeans, Babylonians and Egyptians, and all the nations named in Scripture possess certain peculiar characteristics arising from preceding causes and from the merit of their former deeds, lest God’s justice be called into question—for each nation is said to possess either some good or some evil that another does not possess.

Avoiding these lofty questions, we shall follow what was said above: either that they are accused of folly because they cannot distinguish the spirit of the Law from its letter, or that they are reproved for the fault of their nation, because they are uninstructed and senseless and slower to attain wisdom.

As for what follows, “Who has bewitched you?” (I Cor. XI), we ought to explain it in a manner worthy of Paul, who, although unskilled in speech, was not unskilled in knowledge. He does not mean that he knew there was a spell of the sort commonly thought to cause harm; rather, he used an ordinary expression, taking up here, as elsewhere, a word from everyday speech.

We read in Proverbs: “The gift of the envious tortures the eyes.” What we call an envious person is expressed more significantly in Greek by *fascinator*, “one who bewitches.” And in the book called the Wisdom of Solomon: “The bewitchment of wickedness obscures good things” (Wis. IV, 22).

These examples teach us either that an envious person is tormented by another’s happiness, or that someone in whom there are certain good qualities is harmed by another who bewitches him—that is, envies him.

A spell is said properly to harm infants, the tenderest age, and those who have not yet planted a firm step. Hence one of the Gentiles says:

> “Some unknown eye bewitches my tender lambs.”  
> *(Virgil, Eclogue 3)*

Whether this is true or not, God will judge. For it may be that demons also serve this sin, and that, whenever they recognize people to have begun or progressed in God’s work, they turn them away from good deeds.

For the present, what matters is that we think the example was taken from popular belief: just as tender age is said to be harmed by a spell, so the Galatians, newly born in faith in Christ and nourished with milk rather than solid food (I Cor. III), may have been harmed, as it were, by someone’s bewitchment. Their stomach, nauseated by faith, vomited up the food of the Holy Spirit [variant: *they, nauseated*].

If anyone objects, let him explain how the following examples were taken from common opinion: the Valley of the Titans in the Books of Kings (IV Kings XXIII), Sirens and Onocentaurs in Isaiah (ch. XXXIV), Arcturus, Orion, and the Pleiades in Job (ch. IX), and other similar expressions, whose names certainly possess their causes and origins in Gentile myths.

Let us therefore ask Marcion at this point, since he rejects the prophets, how he will interpret what follows.

### “Before whose eyes Jesus Christ…”

“Before whose eyes Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed [variant: *was proclaimed*], crucified among you.”

> **Note [Col. 0347D].** The printed books likewise read *proscribed*, but the manuscript copies consistently retain *prescribed*. Jerome’s explanations sufficiently show that this is how it should be read: he says that Christ was prescribed for us, that is, foretold, in all the prophets. Martianay.
>
> Martianay prefers *prescribed*, as Jerome also favors it in the exposition that follows and says he found it in his own manuscripts. Our copies, on the contrary, support the printed reading, which in reality does not differ from Jerome’s interpretation and agrees with the Greek text, *proegráphē* (προεγράφη). Victorius reads *proscribed* throughout.

Christ was rightly prescribed for us, since the entire chorus of the prophets foretold his cross and passion, his blows and scourging. Thus we know his cross not only from the Gospel, where he is reported as crucified, but from long before he deigned to descend to earth and assume the human being who was to be crucified.

Nor is the Galatians’ praise small: they believed in the crucified one in such a way that he had been prescribed to them beforehand. Thus, reading the prophets and learning all the mysteries of the Old Law, they came to faith by a proper path and order.

Some copies read: “Who has bewitched you, not to obey the truth?” But because this is not found in the copies of Adamantius, we have omitted it.

### (Verse 2)

“This alone I wish to learn from you: Did you receive the Spirit from works of the Law, or from hearing with faith?”

“There are,” he says, “many things that could compel you by questioning to prefer the Gospel to the Law. But since you are foolish and cannot hear such arguments, I speak with you in a simple manner and ask about what is obvious: Did the Holy Spirit whom you received come to you through the works of the Law—the observance of the sabbath, circumcision, and the superstition of new moons—or through the hearing of faith, by which you believed as Gentiles?”

If it cannot be denied that the Holy Spirit and the gifts of power that accompanied the Spirit received at the beginning of faith were given not through works of the Law but through faith in Christ, it is clear that, having begun with better things, you have fallen into worse ones [variant: *having hated better things*].

Let us carefully consider that he did not say, “I wish to learn from you whether you received the Spirit from works,” but added, “from works of the Law.” For he knew that the centurion Cornelius had also received the Spirit through works (Acts X), but not through works of the Law, which he did not know.

If someone argues conversely, “Then the Spirit can be received even without hearing with faith,” we shall reply that Cornelius did indeed receive the Spirit, but from hearing with faith and from the natural law, which speaks in our hearts of the good that must be done and the evil that must be avoided.

> **Note [Col. 0349D].** Here Jerome may seem to attribute too much to the Law of Nature. Nevertheless, he must be understood in the same sense in which, in his commentary on Isaiah XXIV, 5, he writes that those who have kept the natural Law will obtain rewards; and in Ezekiel XX, 17, that we are condemned by comparison with the Gentiles if they act according to the natural Law while we neglect the written Law. Augustine should be consulted, whose authority on this question is especially weighty, *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chs. XXVII and following, as well as Fulgentius, *On the Incarnation and the Grace of Christ*, ch. XXVI.

Through this natural law, as we have already related, Abraham, Moses, and the other saints were justified. The observance of works and the righteousness of the Law can afterward increase it, but not the righteousness of the carnal Law that has passed away; rather, that of the spiritual Law, because the Law is spiritual.

Nor, because we give faith precedence, do we destroy the works of the Law (Rom. III), nor do we say, as certain people do, “Let us do evil until good comes”—their condemnation is just. Rather, we place grace before servitude.

We say that what the Jews do because of fear, we do because of love; that they are slaves, whereas we are sons; that they are compelled to do good, whereas we accept the good willingly.

Faith in Christ, therefore, does not give rise to permission to sin. Rather, from love of faith the will to do good is increased, since we do good not because we fear the judge but because we know that these things please the one in whom we believe.

Someone may ask: If faith comes only from hearing, how can those born deaf become Christians? One can understand God the Father from the greatness and beauty of created things, and the Creator is consequently recognized from his creatures. But Christ’s birth, cross, death, and resurrection cannot be known except through hearing.

Therefore either deaf people are not Christians, or, if deaf people are Christians, the Apostle’s statement elsewhere is false: “Thus faith is from hearing, and hearing through the word of God.”

Whoever is content with a simple answer to this says that the Apostle did not speak generally, as though everyone’s faith came from hearing. Rather, “faith is from hearing” can be understood both partially and wholly: the faith, namely, of those who hear and believe.

But whoever tries to satisfy this difficulty will first attempt to assert that deaf people can learn the Gospel through signs, daily conversation, and, so to speak, the speech of the whole body through gesture.

> **Note [Col. 0350D].** One Palatine manuscript reads: “to raise difficulties.” Then he will also say that God’s word, to which nothing is deaf, speaks especially to those ears of which he himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke VIII, 8). And in the Apocalypse: “Whoever has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches” (Apoc. II, 11). Isaiah likewise says: “The Lord added an ear to me” (Isa. VI, 33 and 35).

This is another person, one to whom God speaks secretly, who cries out in the heart of the believer: “Abba, Father” (Rom. VIII, 15). As we have often explained, just as the body has all its members and senses, so the soul also has all its senses and members, including ears.

> **Note [Col. 0350D].** Victorius reads: “we read, and among the other things, etc.” Whoever possesses these will have little need of bodily ears in order to know the Gospel of Christ.

At the same time, observe also that here “Spirit,” without any added qualification, is understood to mean the Holy Spirit, whom we receive as a gift from God and not from man. Of him it is written elsewhere: “The incorruptible Spirit is in all things” (Wis. XII, 1). And: “The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit” [variant: *will bear witness*] (Rom. VIII, 16). And elsewhere: “No one knows the things that are in a person except the spirit of the person that is in him” (I Cor. II, 11). And in Daniel: “Bless the Lord, spirits and souls of the righteous” (Dan. III, 86).

### (Verse 3)

“Are you so foolish that, having begun with the Spirit, you are now being brought to completion by the flesh?”

If the Galatians had received the Holy Spirit, how were they foolish? The matter is immediately resolved: they had indeed begun with the Spirit, but because they were being brought to completion by the flesh, the Spirit had been taken away from them. Hence they suffered so many things without cause.

To prevent this from happening to him after sin, David prays: “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Ps. L, 13).

Pay close attention: whoever follows the Scriptures according to the letter is said to be brought to completion by the flesh. Therefore the statement written to the Corinthians—“Although we live in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh” (II Cor. X, 3)—can better be understood in this way: those who explain the Old Testament in a humble manner are said to wage war in the flesh.

Those who follow the spiritual understanding are indeed in the flesh, because they have the same letter that the Jews have, but they do not wage war according to the flesh, passing over from flesh to spirit.

When you see someone who first believes from among the Gentiles and puts his hand to Christ’s plow, proceeding through the path of the Law toward the Gospel under the guidance of some prudent teacher, so that he understands worthily before God all those things written there concerning the sabbath, unleavened bread, circumcision, and sacrifices, and then, after reading the Gospel, is persuaded by some Jew or companion of Jews to abandon the shadows and clouds of allegory and interpret the Scriptures exactly as they are written, you may say of him: “Are you so foolish that, having begun with the spirit, you are now being brought to completion by the flesh?”

### (Verse 4)

“Have you suffered so many things without cause—if indeed without cause?”

Let us consider the unfortunate Jews, how they live among the other nations with immense superstition and laborious observance, saying: “Do not touch; do not taste; do not handle.” We shall prove that the statement is true: “You have suffered so many things without cause.”

But the verdict is not immediately directed against them, and it becomes doubtful through the words “if indeed without cause,” because this is said of those who can return from the Law to the Gospel.

It may better be understood in this way: The Galatians, who first believed in the Crucified One, endured many reproaches from both Jews and Gentiles and suffered no small persecutions. They are accused of having suffered these things in vain if they withdraw from Christ’s grace, for which they suffered so much.

There is also this hope: Whoever labors for the faith of Christ and afterward falls into sin is said to have suffered his earlier hardships in vain while he sins; yet he will not lose them if he returns to his former faith and ancient devotion.

> **Note [Col. 0350D].** In Victorius: “and here too it should be noted that….”

Another interpretation: “If you think,” he says, “that circumcision must be followed after grace, then, since you have lived without circumcision up to the present, everything you have suffered has been rendered void. Yet it seems to me that you did not suffer these things in vain, since I know that the Law has no validity after the Gospel.”

Or certainly it may be understood as follows: “The loss would not have been slight if, by following circumcision, you had lost only the labor of your former faith. But now, in addition to this loss, the punishment of transgression is joined to it, so that you have both suffered the past without cause and will be tormented in the future.”

Some understand the passage more forcibly in this way: “Consider the former freedom of grace and the present burdens of observance under the Law, and you will see how many things you have done with futile zeal. Yet the fruit of this error must not be regarded as entirely hopeless, since zeal for God led you to this very point.”

For forgiveness can be granted to those who were ignorant, if, having turned to better things, they show that knowledge had wavered within them, not devotion.

### (Verse 5)

“Therefore, does the one who supplies the Spirit to you and works powers among you do so through works of the Law or through hearing with faith?”

“Supplies”—that is, “administers”—must be read as a present-tense expression, so that it may be shown that the Holy Spirit is continually supplied, hour by hour and moment by moment, to those who are worthy. The more someone advances in God’s work and love, the more he possesses within himself the powers of the Holy Spirit, which are brought to completion by hearing with faith and not by works of the Law.

This does not mean that the works of the Law should be despised and that simple faith should be sought without them. Rather, the works themselves are adorned by faith in Christ.

The wise man’s saying is well known: “It is not the faithful who live from righteousness, but the righteous who live from faith.”

At the same time, it is shown that after receiving the Holy Spirit through faith, the Galatians possessed gifts of power: prophecy, varieties of tongues, healings of diseases, and the other gifts enumerated in the discussion of spiritual gifts addressed to the Corinthians (I Cor. VII). Yet after such great things—perhaps because they did not possess the grace of discerning spirits—they were ensnared by false teachers.

We must also observe that people are said to work powers even when they do not hold the truth of the Gospel. Thus those who did not follow the Lord were casting out demons in his name, as John especially complains: “Teacher, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we forbade him because he does not follow us” (Mark IX, 37).

This is directed against heretics who think that they prove their faith by performing some sign. Even if they eat and drink in the Lord’s name—for they too have a sacrilegious altar—and boast that they have performed many signs by invoking the Savior, on the day of judgment they will deserve to hear: “I do not know you; depart from me, you workers of iniquity” (Matt. VII, 23).

### (Verse 6)

“Just as Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.”

From this point up to the place where it is written, “Those who are from faith will be blessed with faithful Abraham,” Marcion erased the passage from his Apostle. But what did it profit him to remove this, when the other things he left behind are opposed to his madness?

Abraham believed God, leaving his homeland for a land he did not know (Gen. XII and following); trusting that Sarah, ninety years old and barren, would give birth; and, after hearing God’s promise that his offspring would be called in Isaac, offering Isaac himself as a sacrifice without doubting the Lord’s promise.

> **Note [Col. 0351D].** Two manuscripts read: “bringing the sacrifice upon Isaac himself.”

Faith is rightly reckoned as righteousness to such a man, who surpassed the works of the Law and pleased God not through fear but through love [variant: *pleased*].

### (Verse 7)

“Know, therefore, that those who are from faith—these are the sons of Abraham.”

He discusses this more fully in the Epistle to the Romans: that faith was reckoned to Abraham as righteousness not in circumcision but in uncircumcision (Rom. IV).

Carefully observing this, he teaches that all who believe with the same disposition with which Abraham believed while uncircumcised are sons of Abraham. Abraham “rejoiced that he might see the Lord’s day; he saw it and rejoiced” (John VIII).

Hence it is also said to the unbelieving Jews: “If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of Abraham” (ibid., 39). What other work was the Lord seeking from them at that time, when these things were said, except belief in the Son of God whom the Father had sent to speak: “Whoever believes in me does not believe in me but in him who sent me” (John XII, 44)?

Elsewhere, too, those who boast of the antiquity and nobility of their lineage are answered: “Do not say, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matt. III, 9).

No one doubts that the hard hearts of the Gentiles are signified there by the stones; afterward they were softened and received the seal of faith.

Let the diligent reader enumerate Abraham’s virtues, by which he pleased God before circumcision, and whenever he finds people engaged in similar conduct, let him say that they are sons of Abraham—justified in uncircumcision. Abraham received circumcision not as a reward for works but as a sign of his prior faith.

Because Christ was to arise from his seed—in whom the blessing of all the nations had been promised, and many ages were to pass from Abraham to Christ—God, foreseeing that the offspring of his beloved Abraham might become mixed with the other nations and that his family might gradually become uncertain, marked the Israelite flock with the cautery of circumcision, so that, living among Egyptians, Assyrians, Babylonians, and Chaldeans, they might be distinguished by this sign.

Finally, for forty years in the wilderness no one was circumcised, since they alone lived without admixture with another nation. As soon as the people crossed the banks of the Jordan and the Jewish multitude poured into the land of Palestine, circumcision—foreseeing the future danger of mixture with the Gentiles—became necessary.

> **Note [Col. 0351D].** It is established that many other peoples who did not belong to God’s people also received circumcision from the East. Jerome himself does not deny this elsewhere, especially below, Book II, chapter 4: “The priests of Egypt, the Ishmaelites, and the Midianites did not have a foreskin.”

When it is written that the people were circumcised a second time under Joshua the leader (Josh. V), this signifies both that circumcision, which was reasonably practiced in Egypt, had ceased in the wilderness, and that believers are to be cleansed by the spiritual circumcision of the Lord Jesus Christ.

## (Verses 8, 9)

But Scripture, foreseeing that God justifies the Gentiles by faith, announced beforehand to Abraham: “In you all the nations shall be blessed.” Therefore those who are of faith shall be blessed with faithful Abraham.

This does not mean that Scripture itself—namely, ink and parchment, which are insensible—could foresee the future; rather, it means that the Holy Spirit, and the meaning hidden in the letter, foretold events that would occur many centuries later.

[**Note:** Two manuscripts read “which are invisible”; accordingly, below we restore *is hidden* in place of *being hidden*.]

Moreover, the example taken from Genesis is contained in its own book as follows: “And all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in your seed” (Gen. 26:4). The apostle, interpreting this with reference to Christ, says: “It does not say, ‘in seeds,’ as though referring to many, but as though referring to one: ‘and in your seed,’ who is Christ.”

We should observe this in nearly all [another reading: “new”] testimonies that have been taken from the ancient books and incorporated into the New Testament: the evangelists or apostles trusted their memory, and, once the sense had been explained, often changed the order, and sometimes either removed or added words.

No one, however, doubts that all the nations were not blessed in Isaac and Jacob, or in the twelve patriarchs and the others descended from Abraham’s stock, but in Christ Jesus, through whom all the nations praise God and a new name is blessed upon the earth.

[**Note:** Victorius is silent concerning the word “may be understood.”]

The apostle may also be understood to have taken his example concerning the seed from another passage in Genesis, where it is written: “And God brought him”—there is no doubt that this was Abraham—“outside and said to him: ‘Look up at the heavens and count the stars, if you are able to count them.’ And he said to him: ‘So shall your seed be’; and Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. 15:5–6).

Therefore, all who believe shall be blessed with faithful Abraham, who, on account of his outstanding faith in God, is said to have believed in him first. Similarly, because of his pre-eminent and surpassing hope in God, Enos is said to have hoped to call upon the Lord God (Gen. 4:26). This does not mean that Abel—of whom the Lord says, “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me” (ibid. 4:10)—and the others thereafter did not hope to call upon God; rather, each person is designated according to the quality that is most characteristic of him.

# BOOK TWO

[Column 0353]

**425–426.** What I had left untouched in the first book of the Commentary on Galatians, when I was discussing the distinct characteristics of the nations, now seems to require treatment in the second: who the Galatians were, and by what route and from where they migrated; whether the land they now inhabit gave birth to them as indigenous inhabitants, or received them as immigrants; and whether they lost their language through intermarriage, or learned a new one without losing their own.

Marcus Varro, the most diligent investigator of all antiquities, and the others who followed him, transmitted much about this people, much that is worthy of remembrance. But since it is our purpose not to introduce uncircumcised men into the temple of God—and, to speak plainly, it is many years since we ceased reading these matters—we shall quote what our Lactantius thought about this people in the third book of his work addressed to Probus:

> “The Gauls,” he says, “were anciently called Galatae because of the whiteness of their bodies; and the Sibyl calls them by this name. The poet intended to signify this when he says:
>
> “ ‘Then milk-white necks—  
> “ ‘Are encircled with gold’  
>
> (Virgil, Book VIII of the *Aeneid*), although he could have said ‘white.’ Hence, certainly, the province of Galatia, into which the Gauls came at some time and mingled with the Greeks. For this reason that region was first called Gallograecia, and afterward Galatia.”

It is not surprising that he said this about the Galatians and recorded that Western peoples, leaving such vast intervening distances, settled in the region of the East, since it is also established that, conversely, swarms of peoples from the East and from Greece reached the farthest regions of the West.

The Phocaeans founded Massilia; Varro says that its people are trilingual, because they speak Greek, Latin, and Gaulish. The town of Rhoda was settled by colonists from Rhodes; from this, he says, the river Rhodanus received its name.

[**Note:** Learned men before us have observed that Saint Jerome borrowed this statement about Rhoda, namely, that it gave its name to the Rhodanus, from Pliny, Book III, chapter 4: “And where Rhoda, a colony of the Rhodians, once stood, from which the river Rhodanus, by far the most fertile of the rivers of Gaul, was named.” But since this is still farther from the appearance of truth, pardon must be granted to Jerome, who allowed himself to be deceived by a highly learned author. We readily acknowledge that Rhoda was a colony of the Rhodians—not a town of Gaul, but of Spain—situated at a vast distance from the Rhodanus. It could neither have given the river its name because of the distance between the places, nor because of chronology, since the Rhodanus had existed and borne its name for a long time before Rhoda. Today the Spanish town is called Roses, while the place near the Rhodanus is called Rhodanusia. It is clear that Pliny was deceived by the similarity of the names: just as he made no mention of Rhoda in Spain, so he made no mention of Rhodanusia near the Rhodanus. Moreover, everyone can understand that Rhodanusia did not give its name to the Rhodanus, but received its own name from it.]

I pass over the Tyrians who founded Carthage, and the city of Agenor; I pass over the Thebes of Liber, which he founded in Africa and which is now called Thebestis. I leave aside that part of Libya which is filled with Greek cities.

I proceed to Spain. Did not Greeks who had come from the island of Zacynthus found Saguntum? And is it not reported that Greek Ionians settled the town of Tartesson, which is now called Carteia?

[**Note:** The Palatine manuscript reads *Carceia*. Moreover, in conjunction with the Cistercian manuscripts, it reads *Hydria* instead of *Idrus*, and *Gymnasiae* instead of *Gymnesiae*. Consult Pliny.]

The mountains of Spain also—Calpe, [**Note:** The manuscripts read not *Idrus* but *Hydria*: “Calpe, Hydria, Pyrene.” MART.] Idrus, and Pyrene—as well as the islands Aphrodisiades and Gymnesiae, which are called the Balearic Islands—do they not display indications of the Greek language?

Italy itself, occupied by Greek peoples, was once called Greater Greece. Certainly, what cannot be denied is that the Romans were descended from the stock of Aeneas, an Asian man.

From this it has resulted that Greek intellects are often found in the West, while in the East they may bear the stamp of barbarian dullness [another reading: “the dullness of barbarians”].

We do not say this because different qualities do not arise in both regions; rather, we say that, for the most part, even other things that are not alike are given their names from these general characteristics.

Thus it is not surprising that the Galatians were called foolish and slow to understand, since Hilary too, the Rhodanus of Latin eloquence—a Gaul himself, born at Pictavis—calls the Gauls unlearned in his hymn-poem.

[**Note:** Hilary himself teaches in his exposition of Psalm 54 that *hymn* and *song* mean the same thing. None of his hymns survive, and it is merely plausible that some of them were adopted into ecclesiastical psalmody.]

And the fact that they are now fertile in orators has less to do with the careful cultivation of the region than with rhetorical [another reading: “rhetoricians’”] bombast, especially since Aquitania [another reading: “Aquitanian Gaul”] boasts of Greek origins, whereas the Galatians came not from that part of the world but from the more ferocious Gauls.

Would you like to know, Paula and Eustochium, how the apostle marked each province according to its particular characteristics? To this day the same traces either of virtues or of errors remain.

The faith of the Roman people is praised (Rom. 1). Where else do people gather to the churches and the tombs of the martyrs with such zeal and in such numbers? Where else does “Amen” echo like a heavenly thunderclap, and the empty temples of idols tremble?

This is not because the Romans have a different faith from that possessed by all the churches of Christ, but because their devotion is greater and their simplicity in believing more pronounced.

Again, they are accused of frivolity and pride. Of frivolity, in the passage:

> “I urge you, brothers, to watch out for those who create dissensions and obstacles contrary to the teaching that you have learned, and avoid them. For such people do not serve Christ the Lord [another reading adds: ‘our Lord’], but their own belly, and through sweet words and blessings they deceive the hearts of the innocent. For your obedience has become known everywhere. Therefore I rejoice in you, and I want you to be wise in what is good and simple in what is evil” (Rom. 16:17–19).

Of pride:

> “Do not be high-minded, but fear” (Rom. 2:20, 25).

And:

> “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of this mystery, lest you be wise in your own estimation.”

And later:

> “For by the grace given to me I say to everyone among you: do not think more highly of yourselves than you ought to think, but think with sober judgment” (Rom. 12:3).

And more plainly:

> “Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep. Have the same mind toward one another. Do not be high-minded, but associate with the lowly. Do not be wise in your own estimation” (ibid. 12:15–16).

He also marks the Corinthians because their women go about with uncovered heads and their men grow their hair long (1 Cor. 11), and because they eat indiscriminately in temples [another reading: “at times”] (2 Cor. 10:20); and because, puffed up with worldly wisdom, they deny the resurrection of the flesh. Anyone who has seen Achaia cannot doubt that these traits continue there, at least in part (1 Cor. 4).

The Macedonians are praised for their love and for their hospitality and reception of the brethren. Hence he writes to them:

> “Concerning brotherly love, we have no need to write to you. For you yourselves have been taught by God to love one another. Indeed, you do this toward all the brothers throughout Macedonia” (1 Thess. 4:9–10).

But they are reproved because, being idle, they go around from house to house; while waiting for someone else’s food, they seek to please each individual, run here and there, and report what is happening in each household.

For he continues:

> “But we urge you, brothers, to abound more and more, and to make it your aim to live quietly, to attend to your own business, and to work with your hands, as we instructed you, so that you may walk honorably before those who are outside and desire nothing from anyone” (ibid. 4:10–12).

[**Note:** Our manuscripts likewise prefer this reading, as does the Greek text: *καὶ πράσσειν τὰ ἴδια*, “and to attend to your own business.” Previously the words “and your own” were missing.]

Lest anyone think that this admonition was given more in the capacity of a teacher than because of a fault characteristic of the nation, he repeats and reinforces it in his second letter to the same people, saying:

> “For even when we were with you, we commanded you this: if anyone is unwilling to work, neither should he eat. For we hear that some among you are living disorderly lives, doing no work but meddling. Now such persons we command and exhort in the Lord Jesus Christ to work quietly and eat their own bread” (2 Thess. 3:10–12).

It would take too long, if I wished to observe in the apostle and in all the Scriptures the virtues and vices of each nation, since we have been led to these matters precisely because the Galatians have been pronounced foolish and senseless.

Anyone who, like me, has seen Ancyra [another reading: Anchira], the metropolis and city of Galatia, knows how many schisms tear it apart to this day and how many varieties of doctrine have defiled it.

I pass over the Cataphrygians, Ophites, Borborites, and Manichaeans, for these names of human misery are already well known. Who has ever heard in any part of the Roman world of the Passaloryncitae, the Ascodrobi, the Artotyrites, and the other monstrosities that are more like portents than names [another reading: “deities”]?

[**Note:** I would prefer to read *Ascodrogi* or *Tascodrogi*, both on the basis of the testimonies of other ancient writers and because of the derivation and meaning of the monstrous name itself. Saint Epiphanius calls them by this name in the *Panarion*. Elsewhere Quintilian also reports that they bore this name: they were heretics who derived their name from Quintilla, a woman of flagrant wickedness against whom Tertullian wrote *On Baptism*. Theodoret likewise calls them Tascodrogi, or Tascodrugetae, and joins them with the Marcosians; he does not fail to mention that their deceptions and criminal doctrines imitated Quintilla. Timothy of Constantinople and Antiochus the Monk, also so called, who was a Galatian by nationality, from the village of Medosaga, twenty miles from Ancyra, likewise mention the *Ἀσκοδρουγηταί*, the Ascodrugitae. Finally, in the Code of Theodosius the Elder, Book 5, *Concerning Heretics*, they are called Tascodrocitae—Gothofredus emends this in his commentaries to Tascodrogitae—and in Law 63 they are called Ascodrogitae; in the *Novellae* of Theodosius the Younger, 3, at the end, Ascodrogi. The word is derived from the Phrygian or Galatian idiom and is composed of two words, one of which, *τάσκος*, means “finger” in Latin; the other, *δροῦγγος*, means “nostril.” For, while praying, these utterly deranged people inserted a finger into their nostrils. The Greeks call them by another name, with the same meaning, Passaloryncitae or Paxillonassones. Since Jerome also mentions this name here, you should not suppose that he is inventing a different heresy; he is giving two names for one and the same group, a group whose equally bizarre name is frightening.]

The traces of ancient foolishness remain to this day.

There is one point that we shall add, thereby fulfilling the promise made at the beginning: apart from the Greek language, which is spoken throughout the entire East, the Galatians have their own language, almost the same as that of the Treveri. It makes no difference if they have corrupted some elements of it, since the Africans too have changed the Phoenician language to some extent.

[**Note:** From this Saint Augustine appears to have been misled in his *Preliminary Exposition of the Epistle to the Romans*, where he says that those who are questioned near Carthage or Hippo about the origin of their people answer in Punic, “Canaanites”—that is, with a corrupted pronunciation, as commonly happens in such cases—and that they therefore answer nothing other than “Canaanites.” Yet the word is not corrupted; it is entirely Punic.]

Latin itself also changes daily, both according to region and according to time. But let us now return to the subject at hand.

For all who are of the works of the Law are under a curse. For it is written:

> “Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all the things written in the book of the Law, to do them.”

I make it my practice, whenever anything is taken from the Old Testament by the apostles, to return to the original books and examine carefully how it is written in its own context.

I therefore found that in Deuteronomy the passage is given as follows by the Septuagint translators:

> “Cursed is every person who does not continue in all the words of this Law, to do them”; and all the people shall say [another reading: “says”], “Let it be so” (Deut. 27:26).

Aquila has it as follows:

> “Cursed is he who does not establish the words of this Law, to do them”; and all the people shall say, “Truly.”

Symmachus:

> “Cursed is he who does not confirm the words [one manuscript adds: ‘these’] of this Law, to do them”; and all the people shall say, “Amen.”

Theodotion translated it as follows:

> “Cursed is he who does not raise up the words of this Law, to do them”; and all the people shall say, “Amen.”

From this we understand that, as elsewhere, the apostle has set down the meaning of the testimony rather than its exact words. We are uncertain whether the Septuagint translators added “every person” and “in all,” or whether these words stood in the ancient Hebrew and were later deleted by the Jews.

This suspicion is strengthened in me by the fact that the apostle—who was skilled in Hebrew and exceedingly learned in the Law—would never have introduced the words “everyone” and “in all,” as though they were necessary to the meaning, in order to prove that all who are of the works of the Law are under a curse, unless those words were found in the Hebrew books.

For this reason, when rereading the Hebrew books of the Samaritans, I found the word **CHOL**, which means “every” or “all,” written there, and agreeing with the Septuagint translators.

[**Note:** In the Samaritan characters [the word is written thus], although this word is placed only in the other passage, and not, as in the Septuagint, in the first as well. Jerome’s observation here is exceedingly learned; from it we are persuaded that he was also acquainted with Samaritan letters.]

The Jews therefore removed it in vain, lest they should appear to be under a curse if they could not fulfill everything that was written, since the more ancient writings of another people also testify that it was placed there.

Since no one can fulfill the Law and do everything that has been commanded, the apostle also testifies elsewhere, saying:

> “For what was impossible for the Law, in that it was weakened by the flesh, God, by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and on account of sin, condemned sin in the flesh” (Rom. 8:3).

If this is true, someone may object to us: “Then are Moses, Isaiah, and the other prophets, who were under the works of the Law, also under a curse?”

He will not hesitate to agree who has read the apostle saying:

> “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us.”

And he will answer that each of the saints, in his own time, became a curse for the people.

Yet when he attributes this even to righteous men, he will not thereby seem to detract from the Savior, as though, by becoming a curse for us, he possessed nothing exceptional or pre-eminent, since others too became a curse for others.

For none of them, although he himself became a curse, freed anyone from the curse, except the Lord Jesus Christ, who by his precious blood redeemed us all—and them as well, by “them” I mean Moses and Aaron, all the prophets, and the patriarchs—from the curse of the Law.

Do not think that this is merely my own opinion. Scripture itself bears witness:

> “Christ died for all by the grace of God,” or, as it is read in certain manuscripts, “apart from God” (2 Cor. 5).

But if he died for all, then he died also for Moses and for all the prophets, none of whom was able to erase the ancient bond that stood written against us and nail it to the cross (Col. 2:14):

> “All have sinned and lack the glory”—that is, the grace—“of God” (Rom. 3:23).

The Preacher also confirms this judgment:

> “There is no righteous person on earth who does good and does not sin” (Eccl. 7:20).

Finally, the apostle’s statement farther below clearly teaches that neither Moses nor any illustrious man of ancient times could be justified before God through the Law. For he continues:

## (Verses 11, 12)

Since no one is justified before God by the Law, it is evident that “the righteous person lives by faith.” But the Law is not based on faith; rather, “the one who does these things shall live by them.”

He took the example by which it is proved that the righteous person lives by faith and not by works from Habakkuk, whose words the Septuagint translators rendered as follows:

> “But the righteous person shall live by my faith” (Hab. 2:4).

[**Note:** This passage is omitted from the recent collection of the *Hexapla*. It should, however, be compared with the testimony found in the holy Father’s own commentary on this verse of Habakkuk:

> “Where the Septuagint has, ‘But the righteous person shall live by my faith,’ all the others have translated alike, ‘He shall live by his faith.’ Finally, Symmachus, translating more precisely, says, ‘But the righteous person shall live through his own faith,’ which in Greek is …”

Here you see that Aquila and Theodotion translated “by his faith,” that is, by God’s faith, whereas in that passage he teaches that all, except Symmachus, translated alike “by his faith.” Moreover, “shall live” should be restored here instead of “lives,” as Victorius immediately does, following the Greek of the Septuagint, **ζήσεται**.]

Aquila and Theodotion have:

> “But the righteous person shall live by his faith,” that is, by God’s faith.

It must therefore be considered that he did not say, “A human being” or “a man lives by faith,” lest he provide an occasion for despising works of virtue. Rather, he said, “The righteous person lives by faith,” so that whoever is faithful and is to live by faith could not come to faith or live in it in any other way than by first becoming righteous and ascending to faith, as though by certain steps formed from purity of life.

It can therefore happen that someone is righteous and yet does not live without the faith of Christ.

[**Note:** The negative particle appears to be expunged here; Victorius also rejects it. Yet one should not infer from this that Jerome thought anyone could attain the righteousness necessary for salvation without faith in Christ. Compare Saint Augustine, *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 44; *On the Forgiveness of Sins*, Book II, chapter 9; *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 33; and finally Letters 157 and 190.]

If this troubles the reader, let him accept Paul’s words, in which he says of himself:

> “According to the righteousness that is in the Law, blameless” (Phil. 3:6).

Paul was therefore righteous at that time according to the Law, but he could not yet live, because Christ did not yet speak within him, saying, “I am the life” (John 11:25). Afterward, when he believed in Christ, he also began to live.
