Let us too construct something similar to what is said, “The righteous person lives by faith,” and say: “The chaste person lives by faith; the wise person lives by faith; the courageous person lives by faith.” Let us produce a similar statement from the other parts of virtue against those who, while not believing in Christ, think themselves courageous, wise, temperate, or righteous, so that they may know that no one lives without Christ, without whom every virtue is a vice.

The present testimony can also be read in this way: “Because the righteous person lives by faith,” so that what follows may be supplied, “he lives” or “shall live.”

But when he says, “The Law is not based on faith, but the one who does these things shall live by them,” it is shown most clearly that he is not speaking of life in a simple sense, but of life that is referred to something.

The righteous person lives by faith, and the words “in these things” or “in those things” are not added. But the person living in the Law who does these things lives in them—that is, in the things he has done and has considered good. His reward for his labor consists only in the works he has performed, whether in the length of life, as the Jews think, or in avoiding the punishment by which the transgressor of the Law is put to death.

Let us not think, however, that the words “to live in them” belong to the apostle, but to the prophet Ezekiel, who says:

> “I brought them out into the wilderness, and I gave them my commandments and showed them my ordinances, which a person shall do and shall live in them” (Ezek. 20:10–11).

After saying that those who walked in the commandments and ordinances would live, he added:

> “And I gave them commandments that were not good, and ordinances in which they will not live” (ibid. 20:25).

[**Note:** Here and below, wherever this passage recurs, our manuscripts read “they will live” instead of “they would live.” The Greek text likewise has **ζήσονται**, “they shall live.”]

How carefully the words are considered! Where he said, “I gave them commandments and ordinances in which they would live,” he did not add “good.” But where he said, “in which they would not live,” he added:

> “And I gave them commandments that were not good, and ordinances in which they will not live.”

But these matters are treated more fully in Ezekiel. Let us now return to the order of the Epistle.

## (Verse 13)

> “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us.”

At this point Marcion intrudes concerning the power of the Creator, whom he brands as bloodthirsty, cruel, and vengeful [another reading: “judging,”] asserting that we were redeemed by Christ, who is the Son of another, good God.

If he understood the difference between *buying* and *redeeming*—because the one who buys purchases what belongs to someone else, whereas the one who redeems purchases specifically what was his own and ceased to be his—he would never twist the straightforward words of Scripture into a charge against his own doctrine.

Christ therefore redeemed us from the curse of the Law, which was established for sinners. He himself rebukes them through the prophet, saying:

> “Behold, you were sold because of your sins, and in your iniquities I sent away your mother” (Isa. 50:1).

The apostle repeats this same point, saying:

> “But I am carnal, sold under sin” (Rom. 7:14).

The curses of the Law that are written in Leviticus and Deuteronomy are not fulfilled because God is their author; rather, through the prophetic Spirit, those who were going to sin are told what would happen to them.

But if someone wishes to press us with the apostle’s testimony:

> “All who are of the works of the Law are under a curse; for it is written, ‘Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all the things written in the book of the Law, to do them’” (Deut. 27:26),

and to assert that all who were under the Law were accursed, let us ask him whether those who are under the Gospel of Christ and do not carry out his commandments are accursed or not.

If he says that they are accursed, then the Gospel contains what we have in the Law. If he denies that they are accursed, then the commandments of the Gospel have been set down to no purpose, and those who fulfill them will receive no reward.

Both points are therefore resolved in this way: just as Christ Jesus freed us from the curse of the Law by becoming a curse for us, so too he rescues us from the curse of the Gospel that has been established against those who do not fulfill its commandments, himself becoming a curse for us. He knows that he does not overlook even the smallest portion of the talent and that he demands the final quadrans as well (Matt. 5; Mark 12).

### (Verse 14.) [Cols. 0360D–0364A]

For it is written: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree,” so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus, so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.

[Note: Two manuscripts read “so that we may receive the promises”; the Greek has **ἐπαγγελίαι**, “promises.”]

Before we discuss the Apostle’s meaning and wording, it seems right briefly to repeat the testimony from Deuteronomy, from which the Apostle also took these words (Deut. 21:22–23), and to compare it with the other editions.

The translators of the Septuagint therefore rendered this passage as follows:

> “But if there should be sin in anyone and a judgment of death, and he should be put to death, and you hang him on a tree, his body shall not remain upon the tree, but burying you shall bury him on that day; because everyone who hangs upon a tree is accursed by God; and you shall not defile your land, which the Lord your God will give you as an inheritance.”

[Note: The wording is almost identical to that of the Greek Oxford manuscript, where **ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν δώσει ὑμῖν** means “our God will give you.” Two of our manuscripts read “your God will give you.” A little later, both Aquila’s and Symmachus’s versions read “you shall hang him” in the plural rather than “you shall hang him” in the singular; the Greek text of these translators is lacking.]

Aquila:

> “And when there is in a man a sin [alternative: and] deserving the judgment of death, and he has been killed, and you hang him upon a tree, his corpse shall not remain upon the tree, but burying you shall bury him on that day, because the one who has been hanged is the curse of God; and you shall not defile your land, which the Lord your God will give you as an inheritance.”

[Note: A Cistercian manuscript reads, incorrectly, “because he who is hanged is accursed,” although Aquila and Theodotion likewise translated, “because the one who is hanged is the curse of God”; Jerome himself is the authority for this reading.]

Symmachus:

> “But if there is in a man a sin deserving the judgment of death, and he has been killed, and you hang him upon a tree, his corpse shall not spend the night upon the tree, but you shall bury him [alternative: it] with burial on that very day, because he has been hanged on account of blasphemy against God; and you shall not defile your land, which the Lord your God will give you as an inheritance.”

Theodotion:

> “And because there is in a man a sin [alternative: omits ‘in’] deserving the judgment of death, and he dies, and you hang him on a tree, his corpse shall not sleep upon the tree, because you shall bury him with burial on that day, because the one who has been hanged is the curse of God; and you shall not defile your *adama* [alternative spelling: *adamam*], which the Lord your God has given you as an inheritance.”

Now **ADAMA** (אֲדָמָה), “earth” or “soil,” is the Hebrew word. In that place where Aquila and Theodotion translated alike, saying, “because the one who has been hanged is the curse of God,” the Hebrew reads:

> **CHI CALALATH ELOIM THALUI.**

[Note: The source identifies these as Hebrew words; the Hebrew characters themselves are not legible in the supplied text.]

That heresiarch Ebion, who was half-Christian and half-Jewish, interpreted these words as follows:

> **ὅτι ὕβρις Θεοῦ ὁ κρεμάμενος**, that is, “because the one who has been hanged is an insult to God.”

[Note: Jerome also cites this disputation at the beginning of his *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, without identifying its subject or naming its author. Since the work was long ago lost, scholars debate its authorship. In the sixth book of the *Hypotyposes*, Clement of Alexandria says that it was written by Saint Luke as handed down; Maximus, who cites this testimony in his scholia on Dionysius’s *Mystical Theology*, ch. 1, attributes it to Aristo of Pella. Among the works of Saint Cyprian there survives a preface by a certain Celsus to this disputation; Celsus testifies that he himself translated it into Latin and dedicates his work to some bishop Vigilius. From various passages of this preface it may be gathered that Celsus wrote while the Church was still suffering persecutions and the minds of the Roman emperors had not yet been imbued with the religion of Christ.]

I remember finding the following in the *Disputation of Jason and Papiscus*, which was written in Greek:

> **λοιδορία Θεοῦ ὁ κρεμάμενος**, that is, “the curse of God is the one who has been hanged.”

A Hebrew who instructed me to some extent in the Scriptures told me that the passage could also be read in this way: “because God has been hanged insultingly.”

[Note: From this Morinus—and Martianay after him—inferred that Jerome’s teacher was a Hebrew Christian; for, they say, a Jew who adhered to the Law would not have spoken thus. Yet Jerome, who simply calls him “a Hebrew,” would, I think, not have passed over that distinction in silence. Indeed, the testimony has greater weight precisely because it comes from a man of the Hebrew religion and is cited by Jerome for that reason. Moreover, he seems to be the same man whom Jerome named Barhamnas shortly before in the preface to Ephesians, and there is no doubt that he was a Jew.]

Jerome continues:

We have assembled these materials because this is a very famous question, and the Jews regularly bring it against us as a reproach: that our Savior and Lord was under the curse of God.

First, then, we must observe that not everyone who has hung upon a tree is accursed before God, but only one who has sinned, has been condemned to death because of his crime, and has been lifted up upon a cross. He is not accursed because he was crucified, but because he fell into such guilt that he deserved crucifixion.

Next, we must bring forward the point that the reason for the punishment of the gallows is more fully explained below, with Scripture reporting that he was crucified on account of a curse and blasphemy against God. Symmachus translated this more clearly, saying: “because he has been hanged on account of blasphemy against God.”

Finally, let us ask them whether, if Ananias, Azariah, and Mishael, who refused to worship Nebuchadnezzar’s idol, had been hanged upon a tree (Dan. 3), and Eleazar, a man of ninety years, under Antiochus, king of Syria, together with the glorious mother and her seven sons, had been hanged, they would judge them accursed (2 Macc. 7), or rather most worthy of every blessing.

Certainly, if Haman had not himself, according to his deserts, mounted the cross that he had prepared for Mordecai (Esth. 7), I think Mordecai would have ascended it [alternative reading: “had ascended it”]—not as an accursed man, but as a holy one.

These and other similar examples prove that the accursed person is the one who has committed a crime worthy of the gallows—not the one who has been crucified through the injustice of judges, the power of enemies, the shouting of the crowd, envy of his virtues, or the anger of a king.

And once Naboth [alternative: Nabuth] was condemned to death by the whole city of Jezreel, by Jezebel’s letters (3 Kings 21); but his blood, as a type of Christ, was avenged many ages later, when the Lord said to Hosea: “Call his name Jezreel, because in a little while I will avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu” (Hos. 1:4).

This is what may be said against the Jews.

But, to return to our argument, I cannot understand why the Apostle either removed something from or added something to what is written: “Everyone who hangs upon a tree is accursed by God” (Deut. 21:2). For if he was following the authority of the translators of the Septuagint, he ought to have added the name of God, just as they published it.

But if, as a Hebrew of Hebrews, he thought that what he had read in his own language was the most accurate, he ought not to have taken up either “everyone” or “on a tree,” since neither expression is found in the Hebrew [alternative reading: “ought not to take them up”].

From this I think either that the ancient Hebrew books had a different wording from that which they now have; or that the Apostle, as I have already said, set down the meaning of the Scriptures rather than their words; or—and this is the explanation that deserves the greatest consideration—that after Christ’s passion someone added the name of God both in the Hebrew books and in ours, in order to brand us with disgrace because we believe in Christ, who was accursed by God.

Accordingly, I advance boldly into this contest, appealing to the books: nowhere is it written that anyone is accursed by God, and wherever a curse is mentioned, the name of God is never added.

To the serpent it is said: “Cursed are you above all beasts” (Gen. 3:14). And to Adam: “Cursed is the earth in your works” (ibid., 17). And to Cain: “Cursed are you upon the earth” (Gen. 4:11). Elsewhere: “Cursed be Canaan; he shall be a servant to his brothers” (Gen. 9:25). And in another place: “Cursed be their anger, because it was bold, and their wrath, because it was harsh” (Gen. 49:7).

It would take too long to enumerate all the curses written in Leviticus, Deuteronomy, and Joshua. Yet in none of them is the name of God added. Indeed, even Satan himself, when he promised concerning Job that, if he were pressed by great distresses, he would blaspheme, expressed this from the more favorable side, saying: “Unless he bless you to your face” (Job 1:11).

And in the Books of Kings, Naboth [alternative: Nabuth] is said to have been stoned for this reason: because he had “blessed”—that is, cursed—God and the king (3 Kings 21).

No one should be troubled, however, by the fact that Christ became a curse for us. For God, who is said to have made him a curse, likewise made him sin for us, although Christ knew no sin. And the Savior, from the fullness of the Father, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2): life died [alternative reading: “he died”], and the wisdom of God was called foolishness, so that what was foolish in God might become wiser than human beings (1 Cor. 1).

And in the sixty-eighth Psalm he speaks concerning himself:

> “O God, you know my foolishness, and my offenses are not hidden from you” (Ps. 68:7).

The Lord’s dishonor, therefore, is our glory. He died so that we might live. He descended to the underworld so that we might ascend to heaven. He became foolishness so that we might become wisdom. He emptied himself of the fullness and form of God, taking the form of a servant, so that the fullness of divinity might dwell in us and we might become lords from being servants.

He hung upon a tree so that, by being hanged upon the tree, he might erase the sin we had committed upon the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

His cross changed bitter waters into sweet taste, and raised up the lost axe, sunk into the depths, when it was thrown into the waters of the Jordan (4 Kings 6).

Finally, he became a curse—became one, I say, not was born one—so that the blessings promised to Abraham might, through him as author and guide, be transferred to the Gentiles, and so that the promise of the Spirit might be fulfilled in us through his faith. This promise must be understood in two ways: either as the spiritual gifts of virtues, or as the spiritual understanding of the Scriptures (1 Cor. 9).

### (Verses 15ff.) [Cols. 0364B–0365C]

Brothers, I speak in human terms: even a human testament, once confirmed, no one rejects or adds a supplementary provision to it. The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his offspring. He does not say, “and to offspring,” as though referring to many, but as though referring to one: “and to your offspring,” who is Christ. Now I say this: a testament confirmed by God is not annulled by the Law, which came four hundred and thirty years later, so as to abolish the promise. For if the inheritance comes from the Law, it no longer comes from the promise. But God granted it to Abraham through the promise.

The Apostle, who became all things to all people in order to win them all, debtor to Greeks and barbarians, to the wise and the foolish, also became foolish to the Galatians, whom shortly before he had called foolish.

He did not use with them the arguments he used with the Romans, but simpler arguments—arguments that fools could understand, and almost arguments from the street. Yet, lest this appear to have been done through incompetence rather than skill, he first conciliates the prudent reader and moderates what he is about to say by the preface: “Brothers, I speak in human terms.” [Note: Victor’s text reads, “lest he seem to have acted prudently, he first conciliates,” and so forth.]

What I am about to say, he means, I do not say according to God; I do not speak according to hidden wisdom, or to those who can eat solid food, but according to those who, because of the tenderness of their stomach, are nourished with the dew of milk and are not yet able to hear things that are weighty (1 Cor. 5).

Thus also, to the Corinthians, among whom fornication was being heard of—a fornication such as did not exist even among the Gentiles—he says: “I speak, and not the Lord” (1 Cor. 7:12). And to the same people in the second letter: “What I am saying, I am not saying according to the Lord, but as though in foolishness” (2 Cor. 11:17).

Some think that, because he was about to discuss a human testament, the death of the testator, and other examples drawn from human analogy, he said: “Brothers, I speak in human terms.” [Note: The words “death and the rest” are absent from the Palatine manuscript.]

But it seems to me that this preface was given not only for the reason they suppose, but especially because of what follows: “He does not say, ‘and to offspring,’ as though referring to many, but as though referring to one, ‘and to your offspring,’ who is Christ.”

As I have traversed all the Scriptures in meaning and memory, I have never found “offspring” written in the plural, whether in a good or a bad sense; it is always in the singular.

Likewise, when he adds: “Now I say this: a testament confirmed by God,” anyone who carefully compares the Hebrew volumes and the other editions with the translation of the Septuagint will find that where “testament” is written, the word does not signify a testament but a covenant, which in Hebrew is called **BERITH** (בְּרִית).

It is therefore clear that the Apostle did what he promised: he did not use hidden meanings with the Galatians, but everyday, lowly arguments—arguments that might have displeased the prudent, had he not prefaced them with “I speak in human terms.”

At this point there is a question concerning the reckoning of the years from the time when the Lord spoke to Abraham, saying, “In your offspring all the nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18), up to Moses the lawgiver: whether there were four hundred and thirty years, or how, in Genesis, the Lord promises Abraham himself that after four hundred years his descendants would come out from the land of slavery.

This is not a minor matter, and it has been investigated by many; I do not know whether anyone has discovered the answer.

There is also a passage in the same book concerning Tamar and her two little sons (Gen. 38). The first, called Zerah, put out his hand; the midwife tied a scarlet thread around it; then, when he drew his hand back inside, the other, called Perez, thrust out his hand.

This is appropriate to the present passage because it shows Israel extending its hand in the work of the Law, and contracting it, stained with the blood of the prophets and of the Savior himself.

[Note: The same manuscript also omits the repeated word “hand.” At the end of the sentence Victorius reads “you withdrew” instead of “you drew back,” in accordance with the preceding wording.]

Afterward the people of the Gentiles burst forth; for their sake the hedge is said to have been destroyed, and the dividing wall that had stood between Jews and Gentiles was broken down, so that there might be one flock and one shepherd, and so that there might be glory, honor, and peace for everyone who works good, for the Jew first and also for the Greek.

The simple sense woven through this passage is that the Apostle teaches that the promises previously made to Abraham cannot be destroyed by the Law given later, and that what came afterward cannot prejudice what came before. The promises had been given to Abraham four hundred and thirty years earlier: all nations would be blessed in him.

The observance of the Law—namely, that the one who did it would live by it—was given to Moses on Mount Sinai after four hundred and thirty years.

Conversely, one might ask: Why was it necessary for the Law to be given after so long a period following the promise? Once the Law had been given, suspicion could arise [alternative: might be thought to arise] that the promise had been destroyed, and since the Law, while the promise remained, seemed to have been given without benefit, why was it given?

The Apostle, foreseeing this question, proposes and explains it himself in what follows, saying:

### (Verses 19–20.) [Cols. 0366A–0367B]

Why, then, was the Law given? It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made; it was ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator. Now a mediator does not belong to one party alone, but God is one.

[Note: We have corrected the reading “one” after Victorius, supported not only by the Vulgate edition and the Greek manuscript but also by two Hieronymian manuscripts, one Palatine and the other Cistercian.]

Since the promise made to Abraham remained, and the Law was afterward given through Moses, it seemed pointless for the Law to have been introduced. The Apostle explains why it was given: “because of transgressions,” he says.

After the people’s offense in the wilderness, after they worshiped the calf and murmured against the Lord, the Law came in order to prohibit transgressions. For the Law is not established for the just, but for the unrighteous and disobedient, for the ungodly and sinners (1 Tim. 1:9).

To go back still further: after the idolatry to which they had been enslaved in Egypt, so that they forgot the God of their fathers and afterward said, “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt,” the rites for worshiping God and the punishment of those who transgress were established by the hand of the mediator, Christ Jesus.

For all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made—not only heaven, earth, the sea, and all that we see, but also those things that were imposed upon the hard-hearted people through Moses as a kind of yoke of the Law (John 1).

It is also written to Timothy: “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2:5).

After he deigned to be born for our salvation from the Virgin’s womb, the mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, was called an intermediary.

[Note: This passage is copied almost word for word from Origen. A notable passage is preserved in Pamphilus’s *Apology*: “The Law of Moses was given through angels into the hand and power of the mediator Christ, who, being in the beginning the Word, with God, and God the Word, ministered to the Father in all things. All things were made through him: not only created things, but also the Law and the Prophets; and he himself is mediator of God and human beings. Although at the end of the ages the Word became the human being Jesus Christ, before this manifest coming in the flesh he was mediator of human beings, though not yet human. Yet even then he was mediator of God and human beings; hence the Law, given through angels, is said to have been given into the hands of that mediator, so that the Law might be holy, and the commandment holy, just, and good, and all these things sanctified by Christ.” Jerome distinguishes this earlier mediation, called without the addition “human being,” more expressly from the later one: before taking a human body, Christ conveyed the commands of God the Father to patriarchs and prophets, especially the Law to Moses; afterward, through the union of both natures, being both God and human, he reconciled humanity to God.]

Before he assumed a human body, when he was God the Word in the beginning and was with the Father, he was called merely the mediator—without the addition of “human being”—to all the saints to whom the word of God came: Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and afterward Moses and all the prophets whom Scripture mentions.

As for the statement, “The Law was ordained through angels,” this is to be understood as referring to every place in the Old Testament where an angel is first said to have appeared and afterward is introduced as speaking in the manner of God.

The one who appeared was truly an angel, whoever he may have been among the many ministers [one Palatine manuscript omits these words]; but the mediator was speaking in him, saying: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. 3:6).

Nor is it surprising that God speaks in angels, since God also speaks through angels who are in human beings—that is, through the prophets—as Zechariah says: “And the angel who spoke in me said” (Zech. 2:3).

[Note: The reading “Zechariah” is restored on the authority of our manuscripts and Rabanus; Victor had already corrected the erroneous “Haggai” from ancient manuscripts. This testimony occurs in Zechariah 2 in the Septuagint, but nowhere in Haggai.]

He then continues: “Thus says the Lord Almighty.”

For the angel who was said to be in the prophet would not dare to speak in his own person: “Thus says the Lord Almighty.”

[Note: Among the ancients it was a very widespread opinion that the Son had made himself visible to human beings from the beginning of the world under the form of an angel. Athanasius, *Oration 4 against the Arians*, says: “The one perceived by the eyes was indeed an angel, but God spoke in the angel.” Hilary, *On the Trinity* 12: “Certainly he who was formerly angel is now also human, lest the diversity of this assumed creature lead one to suppose that this is the natural form of God.” See also Augustine, Epistle 147 and *Against Maximinus* 2, Gregory the Great’s preface to Job, and many others.]

By “the hand of the mediator” we must understand his power and might. Although, according to his divinity, he is one with the Father, according to the office of mediator he is understood to be distinct from him.

Because the order of the reading is confused and disrupted by hyperbaton, it seems that it should be restored for us in this way:

> “The Law was given through angels by the hand of the mediator; it was ordained through angels because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made.”

There can be no doubt that the offspring signifies Christ, as is also proved at the beginning of Matthew, where he is shown to be the son of Abraham. Scripture says:

> “The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.”

### (Verses 21ff.) [Cols. 0367C–0368A]

Is the Law, then, contrary to the promises of God? Certainly not. For if a Law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would truly be from the Law. But Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, so that the promise might be given to those who believe through the faith of Jesus Christ.

Before faith came, we were guarded under the Law, imprisoned for that faith which was to be revealed.

Just as the mediator between God and human beings stood between the one who gives and the one who receives the Law, so the Law itself, which was given after the promise, inserted itself between the promise and its fulfillment.

It must not therefore be considered to exclude the promise merely because, having followed it, it seems to abolish what came first. Rather, because it could not give life or bestow what the first promise had pledged, it is evident that it was given to guard the promise, not to overthrow it.

If a Law had been given that could provide life and display what the promise had pledged, the promise would rightly be thought to have been excluded by the Law.

But since the Law was established because of transgressions, as we said above, it more clearly charges those people with sin. After the promise, it was given to them for protection and, so to speak, as a prison, so that, because they had refused through the freedom of their will to await the promised gift innocently, they might be guarded by being obstructed by legal bonds and reduced to the servitude of commandments until the coming of the future faith in Christ, which would bring the promise to its conclusion.

[Note: Compare Chrysostom, *Homilies on Romans* 10, where he maintains that the Law was given in order to rebuke much more sharply the Jews, now voluntarily unfree and dissolute. Augustine, *Against Julian* 2, should also be consulted.]

Nor should Scripture be considered the author of sin because it is said to have imprisoned everything under sin. A commandment imposed by law exposes and accuses sin; it is not the cause of sin.

In the same way, a judge is not the author of crime when he binds wicked people. Rather, he confines them and, by the authority of his sentence, declares them guilty, so that afterward, if he wishes, the ruler may release those who are liable to punishment through an act of mercy.

### (Verses 24ff.) [Cols. 0368B–0368C]

Thus the Law was our pedagogue in Christ, so that we might be justified by faith.

[Note: The Palatine manuscript adds the name “Jesus.” It reads “we may be justified” instead of “we might be justified.”]

But when faith came, we are no longer under a pedagogue. For you are all sons of God through faith, which is in Christ Jesus.

A pedagogue is assigned to children so that an unruly age may be restrained and hearts inclined toward vices may be held in check, while tender childhood is trained in studies and prepared, through fear of punishment, for the higher disciplines of philosophy and the governance of the state.

Yet a pedagogue is not a teacher and father, nor does the one being educated expect either the pedagogue’s inheritance or his learning. The pedagogue guards another man’s son, and after the child has reached the lawful age for receiving his inheritance, the pedagogue withdraws from him.

Indeed, the very name *pedagogue* says this: it is compounded from the idea of leading boys, that is, guiding them.

Thus the Law of Moses was also imposed upon the unruly people like a stricter pedagogue, so that it might guard them and prepare them for the future faith. After that faith came and we believed in Christ, we are no longer under a pedagogue; the tutor and guardian withdraw from us, and when we enter the lawful age, we are called true sons of the true God.

It is not the abolished Law that gives birth to us, but Mother Faith, which is in Christ Jesus.

If someone, after completing the period of his youth—when he is already called heir, free person, and son—wishes to remain under a pedagogue, he should know that he cannot live by the laws of a child.

For where can this now be fulfilled?

> “Three times every male of yours shall appear in the presence of the Lord your God” (Exod. 23:17),

with Jerusalem overthrown and the temple destroyed down to its ashes?

Where are the saving sacrifices and the sacrifices for sin? Where is the perpetual fire of holocausts for the image of the heavenly stars, when the altar has been wholly destroyed?

What punishment can now be imposed upon the guilty, when Scripture says: “Remove the evil from your midst” (Deut. 13:5), while the Jews are serving and the Romans ruling?

Thus it comes about that they live neither under a father nor under a pedagogue: the Law cannot be fulfilled after the succession of faith, and faith is not held when the pedagogical Law is sought.

### (Verses 27–28.) [Cols. 0368D–0369C]

For all of you who were baptized in Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek; there is neither slave nor free; there is neither male nor female. For you are all one in Christ Jesus.

He shows how we are born as sons of God through faith, which is in Christ Jesus, when he says: “For all of you who were baptized in Christ have put on Christ.”

That Christ is clothing is proved not only by the present passage but also by another, where Paul himself exhorts us:

> “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. 13:14).

If, therefore, those who have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ, it is clear that those who have not put on Christ were not baptized in Christ.

The command, “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ,” was addressed to those who were considered believers and had received Christ’s baptism.

If someone receives only the bodily washing of water, which is seen with the eyes of the flesh, he has not put on the Lord Jesus Christ.

For Simon, too, in the Acts of the Apostles, had received the washing of water; but because he did not have the Holy Spirit, he had not put on Christ (Acts 8).

Heretics, hypocrites, and those who live shamefully appear indeed to receive baptism, but I do not know whether they possess the clothing of Christ.

Let us therefore consider whether someone may perhaps be found among us who, because he does not possess Christ’s clothing, is shown not to have been baptized in Christ.

When someone has once put on Christ and, cast into the flames, has shone white with the heat of the Holy Spirit, it cannot be discerned whether he is gold or silver. As long as the heat possesses the whole mass in this way, there is one fiery color, and every distinction of origin, status, and bodily condition is removed by such clothing.

For there is neither Jew nor Greek.

By “Greek” we must understand a Gentile, because **Ἕλλην** signifies both “Greek” and “pagan.” [Note: This is how the Fathers commonly understand the term. For example, the Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon write: **μήτε συνάπτειν πρὸς γάμον αἱρετικῷ, ἢ Ἰουδαίῳ, ἢ Ἕλληνι**, “not to enter into marriage with a heretic, a Jew, or a Greek,” and so forth.]

A Jew is not better because he is circumcised, nor is a Gentile worse because he has a foreskin. Rather, according to the quality of faith, a Jew or a Greek may be better or worse.

Slave and free person are likewise not separated by social condition but by faith. A slave may be better than a free person, and a free person may surpass a slave in the quality of faith.

Male and female are similarly distinguished by the strength and weakness of their bodies. Faith, however, is judged according to the devotion of the mind. It often happens that a woman becomes the cause of a man’s salvation, and that a man surpasses a woman in religious devotion.

Since this is so, and since every distinction of origin, status, and bodily condition is removed by Christ’s baptism and by putting on Christ, we are all one in Christ Jesus. Just as the Father and the Son are one in themselves, so we too may be one in them.

### (Verse 29.) [Cols. 0369D–0370A]

But if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to the promise.

Because the promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring, who is Christ Jesus, it follows that those who are Christ’s sons—that is, his offspring—are also called Abraham’s offspring, since they are his offspring from the offspring.

Whenever our Lord Jesus is called the offspring of Abraham, this must be understood bodily: he was born from Abraham’s stock.

Whenever we, having received the Savior’s word and believed in him, have received the nobility of the race of Abraham, to whom the promise was made, then we must understand ourselves spiritually as the offspring of faith and preaching.

This too must be considered: when he speaks of the Lord—“The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his offspring,” that is, to Christ Jesus—he uses “promises” in the plural.

But when he speaks of those who through Christ are Abraham’s offspring, he calls the promise singular, as in the present passage: “Then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to the promise.”

It was fitting that what was spoken of Christ, the one, in the plural, should be expressed of many human beings in the singular.

The text continues:

### (Chapter 4, verses 1–2.) [Cols. 0370B–0371A]

Now I say that, as long as the heir is a child, he differs in nothing from a slave, although he is lord of all; but he is under tutors and guardians until the time appointed by his father.

This child who is heir, who differs in nothing from a slave although he is lord of all, but is under tutors and guardians until the time appointed by his father, signifies the entire human race up to the coming of Christ and, to say more, up to the consummation of the world.

For just as all die in the first-created man, Adam, although they have not yet been born, so all those who were born before Christ’s coming are made alive in the second Adam.

Thus it comes about that we served the Law in our fathers, while they are saved by grace in their children.

This interpretation agrees with the Catholic Church, which asserts one providence of both the Old and the New Testament and does not distinguish in time those whom it has joined together by condition.

We have all been built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Jesus Christ our Lord as the cornerstone. He made both one, destroying in his flesh the dividing wall and abolishing the hostility between the two peoples, and he changed the difficulty of the ancient Law through the integrity of the doctrines of the Gospel (Eph. 2:20).

Truly, in Christ we are all one bread, and the two of us have agreed upon earth.

And just as we are founded upon the prophets, so the patriarchs stood upon the foundation of the apostles.

The tutors and guardians may also be understood as the prophets, whose words instructed us daily until the coming of the Savior, just as the Law of Moses was discussed above as a pedagogue.

They may also be understood as the angels of the little ones, who daily see the face of the Father and intercede for them. Of these it is said:

> “He will send his angels around those who fear him, and he will deliver them” (Ps. 33:8).

They may also be understood as priests and rulers, who at that time exercised authority over the people and are now considered to provide a model.

And rightly they are said to be under tutors and guardians: they possess the spirit of fear but have not yet deserved to receive the spirit of freedom and adoption.

The age of infancy fears sins, fears the pedagogue, and does not dare to regard itself as free, although by nature it is lord.

According to either interpretation—whether we understand the tutors and guardians as prophets or as angels—this child remains under guardians and tutors until he reaches the lawful age of the perfect man.

Just as, according to Roman laws, the lawful age is completed over a period of twenty-five years, so, for the perfection of the human race, the coming of Christ is reckoned as the appointed time.

As soon as he comes and we have all grown into a perfect man, the pedagogue and tutor withdraw from us.

Then we shall enjoy the Lord’s authority and possession of the inheritance, in which, although born earlier, we were in a certain sense considered strangers.

### (Verse 3)

So also we, when we were children, were enslaved under the elements of this world. By “elements of the world” he calls the same persons whom above he had called guardians and stewards: for, having first been placed under these rulers, we were instructed in the meantime, since we were not yet able to receive the coming of the Son of God to us.

Some think that these are angels who preside over the four elements of the world—namely, earth, water, fire, and air—and that before anyone believes in Christ, it is necessary for him to be governed by these overseers. Most consider “the elements of the world” to mean heaven and earth and the things contained within them: namely, the sun, moon, seas, and gods of the forests and mountains, as well as the wise men of Greece, the barbarian nations, and the Romans, the cesspool of every superstition. When Christ came, we were freed from these, understanding that they are creatures, not deities.

Others interpret “the elements of the world” as the Law of Moses and the utterances of the prophets, because through these, as through the beginnings and rudiments of letters, we receive the fear of God, which is the beginning of wisdom. Accordingly, to those who ought already to have been perfect, but who, neglecting the truth, still clung to the rudiments of instruction, the Apostle writes in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “For although you ought to be teachers by this time, you again need someone to teach you what are the elements of the beginning of the words of God” (Hebrews 5:12).

Conversely, it may be objected to us that, writing to the Colossians, the Apostle Paul called other things “the elements of the world”: “See to it,” he says, “that no one plunders you through philosophy and empty deception, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ” (Colossians 2:8). But by adding “according to human tradition” and “empty deception,” he shows that different elements are being named to the Colossians and to the Galatians. From the former elements, after the fullness of time had come, we are redeemed, and, advancing toward greater things, receive the adoption of sons. Of the latter, however, nothing of this sort is said to follow; the elements are simply understood as letters.

Thus, as we have said, the Law of Moses and the prophets may be understood as the elements of letters, because through them syllables and words are joined together, and they are learned not so much for their own sake as for the usefulness of another thing.

> **Note:** The Palatine manuscript reads: “and are learned not so much for the usefulness of another thing than that we might be able,” etc.

This enables us to read a connected sentence, in which the meaning and order of the words are considered more than the beginnings of the letters.

Since we have interpreted the Law and the prophets as “the elements of the world,” it is customary for “the world” to be understood as meaning those who are in the world, as the same Paul says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5:19). And in the Gospel: “The world was made through him, and the world did not receive him” (John 1:10).

Some venture even more freely into that interpretation: since the Law possesses “a shadow of the good things to come,” they ask whether, in another world—of which the Savior says, “I am not of this world” (John 8:23)—we are first children and are placed under the elements of beginnings, proceeding gradually toward the highest things and receiving the place of adoption that we once lost.

### (Verse 4)

But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the Law, so that he might redeem those who were under the Law, so that we might receive the adoption of sons.

Pay close attention to the fact that he did not say “made through a woman,” as Marcion and the other heresies wish, who pretend that Christ’s flesh was merely apparent, but “from a woman,” so that he might be believed to have been born not through her but from her.

As for his calling the holy and blessed Mother of the Lord “woman,” and not “Virgin,” the same expression is also written in the Gospel according to Matthew, when she is called Joseph’s wife (Luke 2), and when she is reproved by the Lord himself as “woman” (John 2:4). It was not necessary always to call her “Virgin,” as though cautiously and timidly, since “woman” signifies her sex more than intercourse with a man. Moreover, according to the usage of Greek, γυνή (*gynē*) can be interpreted as either “wife” or “woman.”

But to pass over everything else: just as he was made under the Law in order to redeem those who were under the Law, so, for the sake of those who had been born from a woman, he wished to be born from a woman.

For this reason also, although he was free from sins, he received baptism in the waters of the Jordan as though he were repentant: to teach the others that they must be cleansed through baptism and begotten as sons through the new adoption of the Spirit. John the Baptist, not understanding this, forbade him to approach the washing, saying: “I have need to be baptized by you” (Matthew 3:14). Immediately the mystery is taught:

> “Let it be so for now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.”

He did this lest the one who had come for the salvation of human beings should omit anything belonging to human conduct.

> **Note:** One Palatine manuscript perhaps more correctly reads “conversion” (*conversio*) rather than “conduct” (*conversatio*).

Someone may ask and say: If he was made under the Law in order to redeem those who were under the Law—because, evidently, it was impossible for those who were under the Law to be redeemed unless he himself had been made under the Law—then either he was made without the Law in order to redeem those who were not under the Law, or, if he was not made without the Law, he does not redeem those who had not been under the Law. But if it was possible for those who were without the Law to be redeemed without his himself being made without the Law, then he was made under the Law unnecessarily, in order to redeem those who were under the Law.

Anyone who uses the following example will briefly resolve this question: he was reckoned among those who were without the Law. For although, because of the translators’ simplicity, the Latin manuscripts have been incorrectly printed, “He was reckoned among the wicked” (Luke 22:37), it must nevertheless be understood that the Greek word ἄνομος (*anomos*), which is written here, means one thing, while the word ἄδικος (*adikos*), found in the Latin volumes, means another.

Ἄνομος means one who is without law and bound by no legal right. Ἄδικος means wicked or unjust. Hence the Apostle himself says elsewhere: “When I was not without the Law of God, but was in the Law of Christ” (1 Corinthians 9:21). Certainly in this testimony also the Greek reads ἄνομος; and the one who translated the word correctly here could have translated the same word similarly there, unless ambiguity had misled him.

Another person will examine the word “redeem” more sharply and will say that those are called “redeemed” who first belonged to God and afterward ceased to do so; those who had not been under the Law, however, were not so much redeemed as purchased. Accordingly, to the Corinthians, among whom fornication was being heard of—and such fornication as did not even occur among the Gentiles (1 Corinthians 5:1)—it is written: “You were bought with a price,” not “redeemed,” since they had not been under the Law.

We therefore receive the adoption of the sons of God; and, redeemed by Christ, we cease to be under the slavery of the elements of the world and the authority of guardians and stewards. But since we have shown what difference there is between “redeeming” and “buying,” let us consider what difference there is between “receiving” and “recovering” the adoption of sons.

### (Verse 6)

And because you are sons of God, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba, Father.”

The Apostle Paul plainly names three spirits: the Spirit of the Son of God, as in the present passage, “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts” (Romans 8:14); the Spirit of God, as in the statement, “As many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God”; and the Holy Spirit, as in the words, “Your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit, who is in you” (1 Corinthians 6:19).

That the Holy Spirit is other than the Son of God is clearly proved also in the Gospel: “Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man, it will be forgiven him; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, neither in this age nor in the age to come” (Luke 12:10).

This is because many, through ignorance of the Scriptures—as Firmianus also does in the eighth book of his *Epistles to Demetrianus*—assert that the Holy Spirit is sometimes called the Father and sometimes the Son. And although we clearly believe in the Trinity, by removing the third person they wish it to be not his substance but merely his name.

> **Note:** I suspect that the numeral contains an error. Jerome himself lists only two books of Lactantius’ letters to his pupil Demetrianus, in chapter 80 of *On Illustrious Men*. I would therefore prefer, by conjecture, to read “the second” here instead of “the eighth,” although, since the manuscripts are silent, I change nothing. In addition, consult Saint Hilary, *On the Trinity*.

To avoid making this lengthy—for it is a commentary, not a dialogue—I will briefly show that three spirits are named in Psalm 50, where the prophet says:

> “Create in me a clean heart, O God,  
> and renew a right spirit within my inward parts.  
> Do not cast me away from your presence,  
> and do not take your Holy Spirit from me.  
> Restore to me the joy of your salvation,  
> and strengthen me with a principal spirit.”

He calls the principal spirit the Father, because the Son is from the Father, and the Father is not from the Son. By the “right spirit,” the spirit of truth and righteousness, he signifies Christ the Lord, because “the Father has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22), as David says:

> “Give your judgment to the king, O God,  
> and your power to the king’s son” (Psalm 71:1).

> **Note:** The Palatine manuscript reads “and your righteousness,” as Victorius had previously emended, with the support, as he says, of manuscripts and editions.

Finally, he calls the Holy Spirit by its explicit name.

Although these names and persons differ, they are joined in substance and nature; and, because of their shared nature, the same Spirit is indifferently said now to belong to the Father and now to the Son.

The argument by which the Apostle seeks to assert that we are no longer under the Law but under the grace of the Lord Jesus concludes in this way. Above he had said, “so that we might receive the adoption of sons”; now he proves from the Spirit whom we possess within us that we are sons of God.

For, he says, we would never dare to say, “Our Father who are in heaven, hallowed be your name,” unless, from the consciousness of the Spirit dwelling in us, a great voice of understanding and doctrine were crying, “Abba, Father” (Romans 8:15).

“Abba” is Hebrew and signifies the same thing as “Father.” Scripture preserves this custom in many places, placing the Hebrew word together with its interpretation: Bartimaeus, “son of Timaeus”; Aser, “riches”; Tabitha, “Dorcas” (Acts 9:36); and in Genesis, Mesech, “vernacular,” and other similar examples.

Since “Abba Father” is said in Hebrew and Syriac, and since our Lord commands in the Gospel that no one be called father except God (Matthew 23:9), I do not know with what license in monasteries we either call others by this name or consent to be called by it ourselves.

Certainly the one who gave this command was the same one who had said that we must not swear (Matthew 5:34). If we do not swear, let us not call anyone “father” either. If we interpret the matter of “father” one way and the matter of swearing another way, we will be forced to think differently about the two commands.

It should also be noted that in Scripture “crying out” does not mean the emission of a loud voice, but the greatness of knowledge and doctrine. For in Exodus the Lord also replied to Moses, “Why are you crying out to me?” (Exodus 14:15), although no actual voice had preceded from Moses. Rather, Scripture called the pierced heart and the tearful groaning on behalf of the people a cry.

Therefore, just as the one who has the Spirit of the Son of God is a son of God, so conversely the one who does not have the Spirit of the Son of God cannot be called a son of God.

### (Verse 7)

Therefore he is no longer a slave but a son. And if a son, also an heir through Christ.

> **Note:** Two manuscripts read “through God” (*per Deum*) for “through Christ”; the Greek has both, *κληρονόμος Θεοῦ διὰ Χριστοῦ*, to which it would be preferable to restore the reading: “an heir of God through Christ.”

“Having,” he says, “the Spirit of the Son of God crying within you, ‘Abba, Father,’ you have begun to be not slaves but sons.” Previously you differed in no respect from a slave, although by nature you were indeed of God; but you lived as children under guardians and stewards.

If you are sons, inheritance consequently belongs to you, so that, just as by receiving the Spirit of the Son of God you have become sons of God, so, changed from slavery into freedom, you may be heirs with Christ Jesus, the Father’s heir. Speaking in the person of the assumed human nature, he says in the Psalm:

> “The Lord said to me, ‘You are my Son;  
> today I have begotten you.  
> Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance,  
> and your possession to the ends of the earth’” (Psalm 2:7–8).

What we say in this passage we must also observe elsewhere: the whole human race is discussed in the singular number. For all believers are one in Christ Jesus, members of his body, and, having been brought into the form of the perfect man, we have him as our head, because “Christ is the head of the man” (1 Corinthians 11:3).

### (Verses 8–9)

But at that time, when you did not know God, you served those who by nature were not gods. But now that you know God—or rather, are known by God—how can you turn back again to the weak and impoverished elements, to which you wish to be enslaved once more?

He reproves the Galatians because they had been transferred from the worship of idols to faith in the true God, and yet, having abandoned the idols that by nature were not gods, and having come to know God—or rather, having been known by him and having received the Spirit of adoption—they now wish, like children again under guardians and a tutor, to return to the weak and impoverished elements that were given in the wilderness to a people weak and poor in understanding, because they could neither receive nor sustain greater things.

> **Note:** The same manuscripts read “return to the weak and impoverished elements.”

The same elements that he has now called weak and impoverished he earlier called simply “the elements of the world.” Where they were called “the elements of the world,” “weak and impoverished” was not added; and where they are again called “weak,” the word “world,” as we said above, is omitted.

I therefore think that as long as someone is a child and has not fulfilled the time appointed by the father, so that he can be called a son and heir, he is under the elements of the world—that is, under the Law of Moses. But when, after the freedom owed to a son, he returns again to the Law, wishing to be circumcised and to follow the whole letter of Jewish superstition, then the elements that had previously been merely the elements of the world are also called weak and impoverished beginnings.

They are so utterly useless to their worshipers that they cannot even provide them with what they had formerly provided, since Jerusalem, the Temple, and the altar have been destroyed.

Someone may answer and say: If the Law and the commandments written in the Law are weak and impoverished elements, and if those who know God—or rather, are known by him—ought not to observe the Law, lest they begin not so much to worship the God by whom they have been known as to return to those who by nature are not gods, then either Moses and the prophets observed the Law and did not know God, nor were they known by him; or, if they knew God, they did not fulfill the commandments of the Law at all.

To say either of these things is dangerous: either that they did not do what belongs to the Law and thus knew God, or that they did not know God while they kept the weak and impoverished elements of the Law.

This may be resolved by saying that they acted as Paul did when he became a Jew to the Jews in order to win the Jews (1 Corinthians 9:20), and when, in accordance with his vow, he cut his hair at Cenchreae (Acts 18:18), and practiced going barefoot and shaving the head in the Temple at Jerusalem, in order to calm the jealousy of those who had been catechized against him because they had heard that he acted against the Law of Moses and the God of the prophets.

> **Note:** Victorius restores, on the authority of his manuscripts, “who had complained about him,” etc.; our manuscripts agree with the printed reading.

In the same way, the holy men did what belonged to the Law, but followed the meaning of the Law more than its letter. No less than Abraham, after the veil had been removed from their faces, they desired to see the day of Christ, and they saw it and rejoiced. They became weak to the weak people in order to win the weak (1 Corinthians 9:22), and became as though under the Law to those who were under the Law, so that they might separate them from the idols to which they had become accustomed in Egypt.

For it is absurd to suppose that Moses and the other friends of God were in such a condition that we should not believe them, that the time appointed by the Father had come, that they had been redeemed from legal slavery, that they had obtained the adoption of sons, and that they had received an inheritance with Christ.

> **Note:** The Palatine manuscripts omit the negative particle: “that we should believe them.”

Whatever the wisdom of God granted to the whole human race as though to one Son, he has always granted to each of the saints in its proper order and dispensation.

> **Note:** Other printed books read: “as though in the Son he granted,” etc.

When we say that the Law of Moses is weak and impoverished elements, heretics find an opportunity to disparage the Creator, because he created the world and established the Law. We will answer them with what we said above: the elements are weak and impoverished for those who return to them after the grace of the Gospel.

Before the time appointed by the Father had come, the elements were not so much called weak and impoverished as “of the world.” Accordingly, before the Gospel of Christ shone throughout the whole world, the legal commandments possessed their own splendor. But after the greater light of evangelical grace shone forth, and the sun of righteousness revealed itself to the whole world, the light of the stars was concealed and their rays grew dark, so that the Apostle said elsewhere:

> “For what had been glorified was not glorified in this respect, because of the surpassing glory” (2 Corinthians 3:10).

He now says the same thing in other words: the Law of Moses, which before the Gospel was rich, abundant, and splendid, after Christ’s coming was, by comparison with him, weakened and impoverished, diminished and destroyed by the one who was greater than Solomon, the Temple, and Jonah.

What is written—“He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30)—I think was said not so much in the person of John as in the person of the Law, because lesser things always yield to greater things, and perfection is placed before beginnings.

In another sense, we may affirm that the weak and impoverished elements are the traditions of the Jews and the worthless understanding according to the letter—things that are “ordinances that are not good” and “commandments that are not good.”

The spiritual understanding of the Law is strong and rich (Ezekiel 20:25), so that it ought either not to be called an element at all, or should be called an element only in comparison with the age to come and the life in Christ Jesus, in which the angels and the heavenly powers now live. But when compared with the Jewish understanding, it should be called not so much an element—that is, a beginning—as a perfection.

When he says, “But now that you know God, or rather, are known by God,” he shows that after the worship of idols the Galatians understood God—or rather, were judged worthy of being known by him. This does not mean that the Creator of all things is ignorant of anything, but that those alone are said to know whom he recognizes as having changed error into devotion.

“The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2:19). And the Savior says in the Gospel: “I am the good shepherd, and I know my own, and my own know me” (John 10:14). Conversely, to the impious he says: “I do not know you; depart from me, workers of iniquity” (Luke 13:27). And to the foolish virgins: “I do not know you” (Matthew 25:12).

### (Verses 10–11)

You observe days, months, seasons, and years. I fear for you, lest perhaps I have labored among you without purpose.

Whoever does not worship the Father in spirit and truth does not know the Sabbath-rest prepared for the saints, concerning which God says: “If they shall enter into my rest” (Psalm 94:11). Nor does he remember those times of which it is written: “Remember the days of the age” (Isaiah 46:9); and elsewhere: “I remembered the ancient days, and I kept the eternal years in mind” (Psalm 76:6).

He observes Jewish days, months, seasons, and years.

He observes days such as the Sabbaths and new moons, and the period from the tenth day of the first month to the fourteenth, when the bodily lamb is reserved for sacrifice; and from the fourteenth to the twenty-first day of the same month, when unleavened bread is eaten—not in sincerity and truth, but with the old leaven of the Pharisees’ malice and wickedness.

He also celebrates the seven weeks which, according to Jewish custom, he counts after the unleavened bread, observing the day of Israelite Pentecost. Likewise he observes the blowing of trumpets on the first day of the seventh month. On the tenth day of the same month, by fixing the customary expiation, fast, and Feast of Tabernacles, he observes Jewish days.

He keeps months who observes the first and seventh month without understanding the mystery of truth.

He also worships seasons who, coming to Jerusalem three times each year, thinks that he fulfills the Lord’s command:

> “Three times in the year you shall celebrate a feast for me: the feast of unleavened bread, the feast of the harvest of the firstfruits, and the feast of ingathering at the end of the year” (Exodus 23:14–16).

And elsewhere:

> “Three times in the year every male of yours shall appear before the Lord your God” (Exodus 23:17).

When he says “and years,” I think he refers to the seventh year of remission and to the fiftieth, which they call the Jubilee.

The Apostle explains this passage more fully to the Colossians, saying:

> “Therefore let no one judge you in food or drink, or in respect of a feast, or of a new moon, or of Sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come” (Colossians 2:16–17).

Here he uses “a part of a feast” to distinguish it from perpetual festivity, so that we may possess not a brief portion—or, so to speak, a mere fragment of the whole body—but the entire span of our life as a perpetual celebration in Christ.

And, to connect what came earlier with what follows, in this same Epistle he immediately adds what he thinks about the Law of Moses and excessive concern over foods:

> “If you have died with Christ to the elements of this world, why, as though you were living in the world, do you make decisions? Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle—things that all perish in their very use, according to human commandments and teachings” (Colossians 2:20–22).

Someone may say: If it is not permitted to observe days, months, seasons, and years, then we too incur a similar charge when we observe the fourth day of the week, the Preparation, the Lord’s Day, the fast of Lent, the feast of Easter, the joy of Pentecost, and, according to the variety of regions, the different seasons established in honor of the martyrs.

One who answers simply will say that the days of Jewish observance are not the same as ours. We do not celebrate a Passover of unleavened bread, but one of the resurrection and the cross. Nor do we count seven weeks according to Israelite custom for Pentecost; we venerate the coming of the Holy Spirit.

And so that an undisciplined gathering of the people might not diminish faith in Christ, certain days were appointed, so that we might all come together in unity.

> **Note:** One Palatine manuscript reads: “lest the faith of a disorderly assembled people,” etc. This does not mean that the day on which we gather is more sacred, but that, on whatever day we should gather, greater joy may arise from seeing one another.

One who attempts to answer the opposing question more incisively asserts that all days are equal: Christ is not crucified only on the Preparation, nor does he rise only on the Lord’s Day; rather, every day is holy because of the resurrection, and every day he feeds us with the Lord’s flesh. Fasts and gatherings between the days were established by prudent men for the sake of those who devote themselves more to the world than to God, and who cannot—or rather, do not wish to—gather in the Church throughout the whole course of their lives and offer the sacrifice of their prayers to God before their human affairs.

> **Note:** Dallaeus draws encouragement from this passage in attempting to prove that fasts were instituted not by the apostles but later by prudent men. Yet this context makes wholly clear that Jerome means no others than the apostles by “prudent men,” since he considers the Lord’s Day, the gatherings held on its days, and the fasts to have the same institution. No one, I think, will deny that the Lord’s Day was already established by the apostles for sacred observance. Elsewhere, moreover, the holy Father expressly declares in Letter 41 to Marcella, entitled *Against Montanus*, that Lent is fasted according to apostolic tradition; he teaches that it must be observed annually from necessity, not choice, because it originated with the apostles. Add that in several manuscripts and in Rabanus “believing men” is read here for “prudent men.”

For how many people are there who consistently observe even these few prescribed practices—times of prayer or fasting? Thus, just as we are permitted either always to fast or always to pray, and, rejoicing, to celebrate the Lord’s Day continually by receiving the Lord’s body, so it is not permitted to the Jews at all times to sacrifice a lamb, celebrate Pentecost, erect tabernacles, or fast every day.

He moderated his words very carefully between the Apostle’s authority and the holy man’s gentleness when he added: “I fear for you, lest perhaps I have labored among you without purpose.” If he had wished to condemn them abruptly, he would certainly have said: “I fear you, for I have labored among you without purpose.” But now, seeing that they possessed zeal for God, though not according to knowledge, he did not utterly despair of the salvation of those who had been deceived by a pious error; nor, on the other hand, did he leave them without correction, lest he give them an opportunity to persist in error and others an opportunity to err in the same way.

“I fear for you” means “I fear on your account.” A teacher labors in vain when he himself urges his disciples toward greater things, while they fall backward and return to lesser and lower things.

### (Verse 12)

Become as I am, because I also became as you are.

His meaning is this: Just as I became weak for you who were weak, and could not speak as to spiritual people but only as to carnal people and children in Christ; and because you were not yet able to eat solid food, I fed you only with evangelical milk, not wishing you to remain forever in the age of infancy, but gradually to lead you onward to adolescence and youth, so that you might be able to receive solid food—in the same way you ought to become as I am: namely, you should think of more perfect things, leave milk behind, and pass on to stronger foods and greater nourishment.

He says this as an imitator of the Savior, who did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and was found in appearance as a human being, so that we might become gods from human beings and no longer die, but, rising together with Christ, be called his friends and brothers;

> **Note:** The Palatine manuscripts again read “but rising” (*sed resurgentes*); a little above they read “rising together” (*conresurgentes*) for the simple *consurgentes*. so that the disciple might be like his teacher and the servant like his lord.

The passage may also be understood in this way: “I beseech you, brothers,” he says, “that, having rejected the Jewish observance of days, months, seasons, and years—which are shadows of things to come—you imitate me. I lived in the Law without complaint, but regarded everything as refuse and rubbish in order to gain Christ. For I too was once as you now are, held fast by the same observances, and persecuted and ravaged the Church of Christ because it did not practice them.”

### (Verse 13)

Brothers, I beseech you: you have done me no wrong. You know that because of an infirmity of the flesh I preached the Gospel to you long ago.

Join this to the preceding sentence. To make the arrangement clearer, let it be the order that we propose:

> “I beseech you, brothers, become as I am, because I also became as you are.”

The same expression occurs here:

> “We entreat you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5:20).

And elsewhere:

> “I urge first of all that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made” (1 Timothy 2:1).

Peter also says:

> “I appeal to the elders among you, as a fellow elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ” (1 Peter 5:1).

These words call us to humility and strike down the arrogance of bishops who, as though placed upon some lofty watchtower, scarcely deign to see mortal people or address their fellow servants. Let them learn from the Apostle to call the erring and foolish Galatians brothers. Let them learn, after rebuke, the gentle words with which he says, “I beseech you.”

What he beseeches them to do is to be his imitators, just as he is Christ’s; or rather, to follow the present passage, he asks nothing difficult: just as he made himself lower for their sake from a higher position, so they should climb from lesser things to greater.

“You have done me no wrong,” he says. A disciple wrongs his teacher if, through his negligence, he destroys his teaching and labor. The Galatians had not wronged the Apostle up to that present time, because they were preserving his Gospel and commandments.

Or the meaning may be this: When I first announced the Gospel to you, and because of the weakness of your flesh—since you could not receive greater mysteries—I preached to you as to children and pretended to be weak myself in order to win you who were weak, did you not receive me as an angel, as Christ Jesus?

Since at that time you had done me no wrong in any respect, and had regarded me—because of you—as humble, cast down, and like the Son of God, how is it that, when I urge you toward greater things, I am now wronged by you, my labor being lost and that dispensation by which I had pretended to be a child being made void—and do you now grieve?

> **Note:** One Palatine manuscript perhaps more correctly reads *lugens*, “grieving,” which should be referred to Paul himself.

By “the weakness of the flesh,” Paul means not his own flesh but that of his hearers. He announces the Gospel to the Galatians, who could not subject the flesh to the word of God, but, being as it were fleshly, received nothing of spiritual understanding.

To make this clearer, let us give an example. He teaches according to the weakness of the flesh when he says:

> “If they cannot contain themselves, let them marry.”

And:

> “If a woman’s husband has died, she is free to marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:9, 39).

But he does not teach according to the weakness of the flesh when he says:

> “Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife.”

And:

> “The time is short, so let those who have wives live as though they had none” (1 Corinthians 7:27, 29).

Some commandments are given to spiritual people and others to fleshly people. It is one thing to command according to authority and another to command according to concession.

### (Verse 14)

And you did not despise or reject your trial, which was in my flesh; rather, you received me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus.

This is an obscure passage and requires particularly careful attention.

“I,” he says, “preached the Gospel to you long ago, as to children and infants, because of the weakness of your flesh. I began with lesser things and, so to speak, almost babbled among you. This accommodation and pretence of weak preaching was my administration; but it was your trial, testing whether you would be pleased by and consider great those things which, according to their own nature, were lesser and which I brought forth as humble things.

You received these things not as small but as great, and admired them so greatly that you received me, who spoke them, as an angel—or, to say even more, as the Son of God.

Thus this trial of yours, by which I tested you through the proclamation of my carnal speech, was neither despised nor considered worthless; rather, it possessed more dignity than I had estimated.”

The passage may also be explained in this way: When I came to you, I did not come with a message of wisdom, but as a humble and despised man, bringing nothing great except the crucified one.

> **Note:** Marianus Victorius adds on his own the particle “except,” making the sense: “bringing nothing great except the crucified one.” The manuscripts read what we have printed. The meaning appears to be either “bringing nothing great apart from the crucified one” or “bringing nothing great, bringing only the crucified one.”  
> **MART.:** Our manuscripts likewise prefer the reading, which gives a sufficiently good sense. Victorius has added *nisi* on his own: “bringing nothing great except the Crucified.”

When you saw me, therefore, established in a body subject to infirmities and promising the heavenly kingdoms, you did not mock me or consider me worthy of contempt. You understood that the humility of my flesh and the poverty of my appearance were brought about for your testing: namely, whether you would despise the one who was considered pitiable by unbelievers. Instead, you received that humble, poor, and despised man as an angel, and more than an angel.

Or we may conjecture that when the Apostle first came to the Galatians he was ill, and, although afflicted by some bodily weakness, nevertheless did not cease or silence his voice so as not to preach the Gospel he had begun. For they report that he often suffered an extremely severe headache, and that this was the angel of Satan assigned to him to buffet him in the flesh, lest he become exalted.

This weakness and bodily illness was a trial among those to whom the Gospel was announced: whether they would despise the one who promised sublime things while they saw him subjected to bodily ailments.

It may also be said that at the beginning of his arrival among the Galatians he endured insults, persecutions, and bodily wounds from those who opposed the Gospel, and that this was the greatest trial for the Galatians, who saw the Apostle of Christ being beaten.

When he says, “You received me as an angel, as Christ Jesus,” he shows that Christ is greater than an angel. According to the dispensation of his body, the Psalmist had sung that Christ was made lower, saying:

> “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Psalm 8:6).

He also demonstrates that his words had such force at the beginning that they were thought to be angels and Christs.

(Vers. 15, 16.) Where, then, is your blessedness? For I bear you witness that, if it had been possible, you would have torn out your eyes and given them to me. Have I therefore become your enemy by telling you the truth?

Blessed is the person who walks in the way of the virtues—but only if he reaches the virtues themselves. It does no good to have withdrawn from vices unless you grasp what is best. For it is not so much the beginnings of good studies that deserve praise as their end. [Note: One Palatine manuscript reads, not wrongly, “it is not so much the beginnings of our endeavor that deserve praise,” and so forth.]

For just as in a vineyard there are many stages up to the pressing of the grapes, and it is first necessary for the vine to bud into shoots and promise fruit in its blossoms, then, when the blossom has fallen, for the appearance of the future cluster to take shape, and for the grape gradually swelling to come to birth, so that, pressed in the winepresses, it may exude sweet must—so also in instruction each stage [Al.: “advance”] has its own blessedness: that someone should hear the word of God, conceive it, that it should grow in the womb of his soul and reach birth; that, when he has given birth to it, he should nourish it with milk, and through infancy, boyhood, adolescence, and youth bring it to mature manhood.

Since, then, as we have said, each stage has its own blessedness according to its progress, if the end—or, so to speak, the final touch—is lacking, the whole labor will be fruitless, and it will be said: “Where, then, is your blessedness?”

“Although,” he says, “at the time when you received the Gospel according to the flesh I called you blessed, because you were fervent at the beginning, now, because I do not see the summit set upon the building and the foundations laid almost not at all [Note: Victorinus reads, “the foundations laid almost in vain.”], I am compelled to say: Where, then, is your blessedness, by which I formerly praised you, thinking you blessed?”

Indeed, I myself confess that at the beginning you loved me, as I preached humble things to you and was afflicted by persecutions, so greatly that, if it had been possible—these words must be understood hyperbolically—you would have torn out your own eyes and given them to me, so that I might see more clearly than all your eyes. You wished to be blind because of your ineffable love for me, so that the light of the Gospel might rise more abundantly in my heart; you wanted my gain to grow through your losses. And this was at the time when, as though you were little children and infants, I announced small and humble things to you, either because of the weakness of your flesh or because, on account of the injuries suffered by my own flesh, I seemed unworthy of faith.
