But now, because I have begun with elements, syllables, and childish reading to summon you to greater studies, so that you may hold books in your hands and learn words full of instruction and meaning, you kick against me and grow angry; the perfection of doctrine seems burdensome to you. You have been changed so completely in your affections that you now regard as an enemy the one whom you received as an angel and as Christ, to whom you wished to give your eyes—because I announce the full truth to you.

He ended the thought elegantly when he said: “Have I therefore become your enemy by telling you the truth?” He thereby showed that the beginnings of his preaching had been not so much the truth as a shadow and image of the truth.

A similar and famous saying occurs among the Roman poets (Terence, *Andria* I.1):

> Compliance produces friends; truth produces hatred.

But observe how much better the Apostle is here than that poet. The Apostle tempered this saying for those whom he had called foolish and little children, and made it specific, directing it particularly to the persons of the Galatians. The other poet, declaring that this was his relation toward everyone, made the saying general and was gravely mistaken. For the compliance by which he thought friends were made, when truth is removed, is not so much compliance as flattery and sycophancy; and it is clear that these should be called secret enmities rather than friendships.

At the same time, we must consider that even today, as long as we explain the Scriptures according to the letter to little children and infants, and to those in whose hearts Christ has never grown up or advanced in age, wisdom, and grace before God and human beings, we are praised, admired, and held in esteem. [Note: Victorinus, with two manuscripts, reads, “Christ has never risen or advanced.”] But as soon as we begin to urge them to pass on to greater things, they become enemies of those who proclaim the Gospel, and prefer to follow Jews rather than the apostles, who, abandoning the teaching and traditions of the Pharisees, entered into Christ himself as the propitiatory sacrifice and into the perfection of the Law. [Note: Victorinus reads, “and when, departing from the teaching and traditions of the Pharisees, ...”]

Nor do they deign to accept the divine word, which commands teachers of the Church to ascend to loftier doctrines, to raise their voice with all their strength, and not to fear the clamor of barking children. It says [Al.: “saying”]:

> Ascend upon a high mountain, you who proclaim good news to Zion.  
> Raise your voice with strength, you who proclaim good news to Jerusalem.  
> Raise it; do not fear.  
> (Isa. 40:9)

(Vers. 17, 18.) They court you—not well; but they want to shut you out, so that you may court them. But court what is good in what is good always, and not only when I am present among you. [Note: The Palatine manuscript reads, “They court you—not well.”]

Those court well who, when they see that certain people possess graces, gifts, and virtues, desire to become like them and strive to imitate the faith, life, and diligence by which those people earned such things, so that they too may attain what is worthy of good imitation.

The Apostle says of these things: “Court spiritual gifts, but especially that you may prophesy.” And again: “Since you are zealous for spiritual gifts, seek to abound in them for the edification of the Church.” And again: “Therefore, brothers, be zealous to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues.”

But those court wrongly who do not themselves desire to become better, imitating those worthy of imitation, so much as they wish to make those very people worse and drag them backward through perverse rivalry.

Let the following serve as an example. Suppose someone is a Christian who reads Moses and the prophets and understands that everything happened beforehand to that people in shadow and image, but was written for us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come. He understands circumcision to concern not the foreskin so much as the ears and the heart. He has risen with Christ and seeks the things that are above. He has been freed from the burden and slavery of the Law that commands, “Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle.” If someone tries to persuade him, using the words of Scripture, to accept what is written not through allegorical interpretation but according to the letter that kills, so that he may become a Jew openly rather than secretly, that person courts him wrongly. He hastens to drag him back as he advances swiftly toward greater things, so that he may instead imitate the one who is going backward—or at least so that he may not advance much farther. [Note: Victorinus likewise reads, “or certainly so that he may not advance much farther.”]

The Apostle is therefore speaking to the Galatians, who had been persuaded by defenders of the Law to imitate them, although those defenders ought rather to have imitated the Galatians. For it is natural that the greater should be made from the lesser, not the lesser from the greater. He says: “Court what is good in what is good”—that is, do not imitate defenders of Jewish observance, but imitate the things that are good.

For just as someone who imitates another’s wealth, power, or rank courts not so much what is good as what ought to be avoided, so you, on the contrary, should court what is good in what is good, seeking spiritual things rather than carnal ones, so that you may teach them that you are Christians, not that they are Jews.

Do this always, so that by a persevering step you may reach the end of a good work. You did indeed court what was good in what was good when I was with you; but after I departed from you, you lost everything I had taught. From a secure station and a safe harbor you were once again carried out to sea as the wave receded.

Nor is it surprising that, when the Apostle—the vessel of election, in whom Christ the Lord was speaking—departed, the Galatians were changed, since even now we see the same thing happening in the churches. Whenever a teacher happens to arise in a church who is eloquent in speech and exemplary in life, and who urges his hearers toward virtue as though with goads, we see the whole people hastening, burning with zeal, and running about to give alms, fast, practice chastity, receive the poor, bury the dead, and perform other similar acts. But when he has departed, they gradually wither; deprived of food, they become thin, pale, and weak, and everything that previously flourished moves toward destruction.

Therefore, since “the harvest is plentiful but the laborers are few” (Matt. 9:37), let us pray to the Lord of the harvest to send laborers to reap: men who will harvest the ears of the Christian people standing in the Church, prepared for the wheat of the future, gather them, carry them into the barns, and allow none of them to perish.

This concerns the zeal and perverse rivalry of which it is also said elsewhere: “Do not be envious of evildoers” (Ps. 36:1), and here: “They court you—not well.”

We also find another kind of zeal, by which the sons of Jacob were jealous of their brother Joseph (Gen. 37 ff.), and Miriam and Aaron of Moses, the Lord’s friend (Num. 12). Neither they nor the others were stirred to jealousy because they wanted to be better than Joseph and Moses, but because they grieved that those men were better. This zeal is close to envy.

It would take too long if I wished to bring forward from the treasury of Scripture all the kinds of zeal, good and bad. We read of good zeal in Phinehas (Num. 25), Elijah (1 Kings 19), Mattathias (1 Macc. 2), and the apostle Jude—not the betrayer—who, because of the distinguished virtue of his zeal, received the name “Zealot” as well (Acts 1). Of evil zeal we read in Cain toward Abel (Gen. 4), and in others toward other people. There is also the “jealousy of a husband,” about which it is written: “And the spirit of jealousy comes upon him” (Num. 5).

Unless perhaps this is a middle kind of zeal, which cannot be understood in either a good or a bad sense; rather, between the two it is called jealousy.

Alternatively: Those who were from the circumcision, seeing that the Galatians from the nations abounded in the virtues of the Holy Spirit, while they themselves did not speak in tongues, possess gifts of healing, or have the grace of prophecy, desired, stirred by the goads of jealousy, to lead the Galatians over to the burdens of the Law, so that they too might begin to resemble them.

(Vers. 19.) My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.

With how many difficulties and pains children are brought forth from the womb, the first curse declares when it says: “In sorrow you shall bear children” (Gen. 3:16). Wishing, therefore, to show the teacher’s concern for his disciples and what feelings teachers endure lest their followers fall away from salvation, Paul says: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor.”

Elsewhere he had spoken almost as a father: “Though you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, you do not have many fathers” (1 Cor. 4:15). Here he speaks not as a father but as a mother in Christ, so that they may recognize in him the anxiety and devotion of both parents.

Moses also spoke in a similar way concerning the people: “Did I conceive this entire people in my womb?” (Num. 11:12). Who among us, do you think, is so anxious for the salvation of his disciples that he is tormented not for a few hours, or at most for two or three days, but throughout his entire life, until Christ is formed in them?

We must carefully retain the example of the pregnant woman that he adopted, who conceives and forms seeds within herself, so that we may understand what is being said. Nature is not to be shamed but revered. [Note: Jerome was indeed blamed for using indecent and shameful examples in his discussion. St. Augustine aptly says (*City of God* XIV.23): “Whoever approaches these writings with an impure mind should blame his own fault, not nature; let him condemn the deeds of his own shamefulness, not the words of our necessity. In these matters a chaste reader or hearer will readily pardon me.”] For just as a shapeless seed is first cast into a woman’s womb, so that it may adhere to its furrows and base as though to a kind of glue—and the prophet, recalling his own beginning, says: “Your eyes saw my unformed substance” (Ps. 139:16)—then, over nine months, with the blood held back, the future human being is coagulated, embodied, nourished, and given its distinct form, so that after it has stirred in the womb it may, at the appointed time, be brought forth into the light, and is born amid as many difficulties as those by which it is later nourished lest it perish—so also the seed of Christ’s word, once it has fallen into a soul that hears, grows through its successive stages.

To pass over much—for we can readily transfer the bodily description to spiritual understanding—it remains in uncertainty as long as the one who conceived it has not given birth. Giving birth is not immediately the end of the labor; rather, it is the beginning of another labor, so that through persistent nourishment and instruction he may bring infancy to the full stature of Christ.

And just as in marriage a man’s seed is often prevented from producing children, sometimes a barren wife does not retain the seed, frequently neither partner is capable of generation, and conversely both are fertile, so among those who sow the word of God this fourfold division is maintained. A teacher may fulfill his own duty while the hearer is barren; or the hearer may be of good disposition, but through the teacher’s lack of skill the seed of the word may perish; or the one being taught may be as foolish as the one who teaches; and it rarely happens that teacher and disciple agree with one another—namely, that the teacher teaches only as much as the disciple can absorb, or that the learned person receives only as much as the teacher can impart.

Yet now we are all judges. We do not know which psalm it is, what part of prophecy, or which chapter of the Law, and with facility of speech we boldly interpret what we do not understand at all. It is not our concern that Christ be formed in the people, so that each person, returning home, may possess the seed of God’s word and, having conceived it, be able to say with the prophet: “Because of your fear, O Lord, we conceived and gave birth [Note: For “and gave birth,” Victorinus has the fuller reading, “we were in labor and gave birth to the spirit”; the Vulgate reads, “and, as it were, we were in labor and gave birth to the spirit”; the Greek likewise adds καὶ ὠδινήσαμεν καὶ ἐτέκομεν πνεῦμα, “and we were in labor and gave birth to the spirit.”]; we have made the children of your salvation upon the earth” (Isa. 26:17–18).

Such people pass over into the ranks of the apostles and deserve to hear from the Savior: “Whoever does the will of my Father, that person is my brother, sister, and mother” (Matt. 12:50), with the diversity of progress displayed through the different names. [Al.: “with the diversity of progress displaying itself.”]

Christ is also formed in the hearts of believers when all the mysteries are disclosed to them and what had seemed obscure becomes clear.

We must also observe that the person who, through sin, had in a certain sense ceased to be human is conceived again by the teacher through repentance, and Christ’s formation is once more promised in him. [Note: The Palatine manuscript reads, “the person who had in some sense ceased to be a sinner”; Rabanus merely omits the word “human.”] This is directed against the Novatians, who do not wish those whom sins have once crushed to be reformed.

(Vers. 20.) I would like to be with you now and change my voice, because I am at a loss among you. [Al.: “I am perplexed.”]

Divine Scripture builds us up even when it is read, but it is much more beneficial if it is changed from writing into speech, so that the one who taught through a letter may instruct his hearers while present.

A living voice has great force: a voice resounding from the mouth of its author, pronounced and articulated with the very intonation in which it was generated in the human heart. Since the Apostle knew that speech addressed to those present had greater force, he desired to change the epistolary voice—the voice contained in writing—into personal presence, and, because this was more useful for those who had been corrupted by error, to draw them back to the truth through living speech. [Note: This passage is corrupt in earlier editions, which read approximately as follows: “He wishes to change his apostolic voice, contained in writing, into presence.” The Regius manuscript reads coherently: “He would endeavor, while alive, to draw them back to the truth by speech.” MART. The Cistercian manuscript agrees almost entirely with the older editions: “He wishes to change the apostolic voice, the voice contained in writing, into presence.” A little later it reads: “living speeches draw them back to the truth.”]

He says this because he is perplexed about them. The Greek expression is more precise. Ἀποροῦμαι (*aporoumai*) signifies not so much confusion—which among the Greeks is called αἰσχύνη (*aischynē*), “shame,” or σύγχυσις (*synchysis*), “confusion”—as need and poverty.

The sense, then, is: “I wish to be present with you now and utter in person the voice of my letter, because I am in need among you.” I do not possess the fruits that teachers usually receive from their disciples, and the seed of instruction has been sown without purpose, since I suffer complete poverty among you, so that I can burst forth with Jeremiah’s words: “I have not profited, nor has anyone profited me” (Jer. 23:23).

This passage can also be interpreted in another way. The Apostle Paul became a Jew to the Jews in order to win Jews (1 Cor. 9), and to those under the Law he became as one under the Law, and to the weak he became weak in order to win the weak. According to the character of those whom he wished to save, he changed his voice. Like an actor—indeed, he became a theater to the world, to angels, and to human beings (1 Cor. 4)—he assumed various appearances and voices. This does not mean that he was what he pretended to be, but that he appeared to be only what was beneficial to others.

He sees that the Galatians need a different teaching and must be saved by a different path, not by the one through which they had first been brought from paganism to faith in Christ. He is therefore compelled to say: “I would like to be with you now and change my voice, because I am perplexed about you.” “I do not see,” he says, “that I am benefiting you if I say the things I said before. Therefore, not knowing what to do, pulled in different directions, I am torn, perplexed, and mangled.” [Note: Victorinus omits the two words “because I am perplexed.”]

Just as physicians, when they see that the power of their art is not effective with the first medicine, turn to another and test various remedies until they reach a cure—so that what could not be healed by the gentleness of a particular poultice may be cured by a more biting powder and a harsher treatment—so I, because I am perplexed about you and am distracted by uncertainty this way and that, wish, while present, to utter the voice of my letter from my own mouth, so that I might correct you myself with greater severity than usual. A letter cannot express the voice of one who rebukes; it cannot reproduce the cry of one who is angry or set forth in written characters the pain of the heart.

The passage may also be understood more simply. Until now I have used gentle words with you, saying: “Brothers, I beg you,” and: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.” But I, who have spoken to you gently and softly, as a father, because of the love by which I cannot endure my children to perish or to continue in error [Note: Victorinus reads, “by which I cannot endure you to perish,” and so forth.], would now wish to be present—if the bonds of my confinement did not restrain me—and change my gentle voice into words of rebuke. Nor is it fickleness if I am now gentle and now angry; love urges me, and pain urges me, to speak with different emotions.

For I do not know what words I should utter first, or with what medicine I ought to heal you, because I am perplexed about you.

(Vers. 21.) Tell me, you who wish to be under the Law: have you not heard the Law?

It must be noted that the Law here means the history of Genesis, not—as people commonly suppose—what ought to be done or avoided, but the entire account woven concerning Abraham, his wives, and his children, which is called “the Law” (John 15).

We also read elsewhere that the Prophets are called the Law. Therefore, the person who hears the Law is the one who, according to Paul, looks into its marrow rather than its surface. The person who does not hear the Law is like the Galatians, following only its outer shell.

[Col. 0388A] (Vers. 22, 23.) For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and one by the free woman. But the one by the slave woman was born according to the flesh, while the one by the free woman was born through promise.

It is extremely difficult to demonstrate that only Isaac, who was born of Sarah, was generated through promise, and not also Ishmael, who was born of Hagar, the Egyptian slave woman. Scripture relates that when Hagar, pregnant and fleeing from Sarah’s persecution, came into the desert, an angel came to her and urged her to submit to her mistress’s authority. That same angel also said: “I will multiply your seed exceedingly, and it shall not be numbered because of its multitude” (Gen. 16:10).

Later, concerning Ishmael—words which no one would doubt to be words of promise—it says: “He shall be a wild man; his hand shall be against everyone, and everyone’s hand against him, and he shall dwell opposite all his brothers.”

One may answer that the promise of an angel has less authority than the promise of God himself. For just as a star does not shine when the sun has risen, so the angel’s words, in comparison with God’s promise, seem to be darkened, to vanish, and to be reckoned as nothing.

This answer does seem to have some force, but it is immediately crushed by the authority of the following Scripture. For it is written: “Abraham said to God: ‘May this Ishmael live before you’” (Gen. 17:18 ff.). And God answered him as follows: “Behold, Sarah your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac. I will establish my covenant with him as an everlasting covenant, and with his seed after him.”

But concerning Ishmael: “Behold, I have heard you, and behold, I have blessed him, and I will increase him and multiply him exceedingly. He shall beget twelve nations, and I will make him into a great nation. But I will establish my covenant with Isaac, whom Sarah shall bear to you at this time in the coming year.”

From this it is evident that Ishmael too was generated, according to the very words of God, through promise.

This difficulty is resolved as follows: the promise is properly fulfilled in the granting of the covenant. To bless, increase, and multiply greatly—as is written concerning Ishmael—is one thing; to make someone an heir through a covenant—as is said concerning Isaac—is another: “I will establish my covenant with him as an everlasting covenant, and with his seed after him.” And later: “I will establish my covenant with Isaac, whom Sarah shall bear to you” (Gen. 17:19).

Just as gifts are one thing and substance another, bequests one thing and inheritance another—for we read that gifts were given to Abraham’s sons by his concubines, while the entire inheritance of his substance was left to the son of Sarah—so, as we have said, blessing and bequests are one thing, and the covenant another.

It may also be said that, in the case of Ishmael, either the angel or God spoke after his conception; but in the case of Isaac, God made the promise before he was conceived in Sarah’s womb.

For the present, let these remarks suffice, insofar as the limitations of our modest ability permit. But if someone can discover a more substantial explanation of how Ishmael, who was born of the slave woman, is not the son of promise, while Isaac, who was born of the free woman, is, that person should be heard. And if you think differently, says the Apostle, God will reveal this also to you.

We must now briefly proceed toward higher things, and say that each of us is first born not according to promise, as long as he is instructed in the simple words of Scripture and still delights in Jewish interpretations. But when he has passed on to loftier matters and understood the spiritual Law, then he is born through promise.

To speak more plainly: every day those who perform the works of Abraham are born from Abraham. But those who possess again the spirit of slavery in fear are born from the Egyptian slave woman; those who have received the spirit of adoption are born from Sarah the free woman, by the freedom with which we have been endowed by Christ.

The Lord speaks to the Jews, who still preferred to be sons of the slave woman: “If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will make you free” (John 8:31–32). Since they did not understand that what was being said was mystical, they replied: “We are Abraham’s seed and have never been enslaved to anyone. How can you say, ‘You will be free’?”

Jesus answered them: “Amen, amen, I say to you, everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin. A slave does not remain in the house forever, but a son remains forever.” If we are slaves of sin, the Egyptian Hagar has given birth to us; but if sin does not reign in our mortal body, we are truly sons of God.

(Vers. 24.) These things are spoken allegorically. [Note: The Palatine manuscript and Victorinus read, “These things, indeed, are allegorical.”]

Allegory properly belongs to the art of grammar, and we learn in school as children how it differs from metaphor and the other figures of speech. It presents one thing in its words but signifies another in its meaning. The books of orators and poets are full of allegories. Divine Scripture too is composed in no small part through this method.

The Apostle Paul understood this—for he had also touched, to some extent, upon secular literature—and used the very term for a figure, calling it allegory, as it is called among his people. In this way he showed that the Greek expression in this passage is being used in a broader or improper sense.

That Paul knew secular literature, though not perfectly, is proved by his own words: “One of them, their own prophet, said: ‘Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies’” (Titus 1:12). This heroic verse belongs to the poet Epimenides, whom Plato and the other ancient writers also mention.

Likewise, when he was defending himself at Athens in the Areopagus, he added: “As some of your poets have also said: ‘For we are indeed his offspring’” (Acts 17:28). This half-line is found, they say, in Aratus, who wrote about the heavens and the stars.

There is also the saying: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15:33), an iambic trimeter taken from Menander’s comedy.

From these and other examples it is evident that Paul was not ignorant of secular literature, and that what he calls allegory here he calls spiritual understanding elsewhere. Thus: “We know that the Law is spiritual” (Rom. 7:14), meaning allegorical or figuratively spiritual.

And elsewhere: “They all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:3–4). No one doubts that the manna, the sudden outpouring of the spring, and the rock itself which followed are to be understood allegorically.

I know what may be opposed to this from the other side: “Brothers, if someone is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual should restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness” (Gal. 6:1). And in another place: “The spiritual person judges all things, but is judged by no one” (1 Cor. 2:15). Clearly, the expression “spiritual” there conveys something other than what we have said above.

But because the spiritual person judges all things and is judged by no one, we call him the person who, knowing all the mysteries of Scripture, understands them sublimely, sees Christ in the divine books, and admits nothing of Jewish tradition into them.

(Vers. 25, 26.) For these are two covenants: one indeed from Mount Sinai, generating slavery, which is Hagar. For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia, adjoining the Jerusalem that now exists, and it is in slavery with its children. But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is the mother of us all.

Almost everyone’s explanation of this passage is that Hagar, the slave woman, is interpreted as the Law and the Jewish people, while Sarah, the free woman, is interpreted as the Church gathered from the nations, which is the mother of the saints, as Paul says: “She is the mother of us all.”

For a long time this woman did not give birth, before Christ was born from the Virgin, and she was barren. Isaac, the laughter of the world, had not yet rung out from the chosen father with the voice of sublime doctrines. Indeed, Abraham is rendered in our language as “chosen father with sound.” [Note: This is how Philo interpreted the name, as Martianus notes: Ἀβραὰμ, πατὴρ ἐκλεκτὸς ἠχοῦς, “Abraham, chosen father of sound”—rather forcibly, as though these three words consisted of “father,” “chosen,” and “sound.” Nor is Jerome’s approval of this interpretation evident, since, when he explained the name according to his own judgment, he interpreted it better than anyone from the evidence of the sacred text itself, Genesis 17:5: “father of a multitude of nations,” from the Hebrew words for “father,” “multitude,” and [a further term expressing] crowds, peoples, nations, and that kind of immense number.]

But Hagar, whose name is interpreted as παροικία (*paroikia*), that is, dwelling among foreigners, pilgrimage, or sojourn, gives birth to Ishmael, who merely hears God’s commands and does not fulfill them—a rustic, bloodthirsty man who pursues deserts, hostile to all his brothers born from the free woman and resisting them with an opposing face.

Nor is it surprising that the Old Testament, which was established and written on Mount Sinai in Arabia, adjoining the Jerusalem that now exists, is not perpetual, since a sojourn differs from permanent possession; since the name “Sinai” signifies temptation; and since “Arabia” signifies setting or decline.

Conversely, the Jerusalem above, which is free and the mother of the saints, demonstrates that this Jerusalem, which exists in the present, is below, and has been cast down into a low and humble place. [Note: Earlier editions read less coherently, “weak and low,” in place of “low and deepest.” The manuscripts prefer the latter. In one Palatine manuscript, the words are separated as “in the dung,” which also yields a satisfactory sense.]

Some understand the two covenants in another way: they interpret divine Scripture, both Old and New, according to the diversity of meaning and the judgment of those who read it, as either slave or free. They hold that those who are still slaves to the letter and possess the spirit of fear for slavery are born from Hagar the Egyptian, while those who climb to higher things and wish to understand what is written allegorically are sons of Sarah, who in our language is interpreted as ἄρχουσα (*archousa*), that is, “ruler” or “princess,” in the feminine gender.

They assert [Al.: “asserts”] that they adopt this interpretation out of necessity, because it would be unjust to understand Moses and all the prophets as begotten from the slave woman, while understanding any Gentiles whatsoever as begotten from the free woman. Therefore, it is better to judge not only those who are in the Church, according to the diversity of their interpretations—as we said above—as some slaves and others free, but also one and the same person: as long as he follows the historical account, he is a son of the slave woman; but when Jesus opens the Scriptures, his heart burns within him, and in the breaking of bread he recognizes the one whom he had not previously seen (Luke 24), then he too may be called a son of Sarah.

Marcion and Manichaeus did not wish to remove from their copy this passage in which the Apostle said, “These things are allegorical,” nor the other words that follow, thinking that it had been left there against us—namely, that the Law ought to be understood otherwise than it was written. Yet even if it is to be received allegorically—as we also admit, and as Paul teaches—it was not composed according to the reader’s will or the writer’s authority.

They are therefore crushed by the very thing which they appeared to preserve against us: Moses, the servant of the Creator God, wrote spiritual things, and their own apostle teaches the same, although they assert that he was the preacher of another Christ and a better God. [Note: This refers to the book entitled *The Apostle* according to Marcion’s recension. See above, chapter 1, column 375, note b [in our edition, column 313, note a].]

(Vers. 27.) For it is written:

> Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear;  
> break forth and cry aloud, you who are not in labor;  
> for the children of the deserted woman are more numerous  
> than those of her who has a husband.  
> (Isa. 54:1)

The synagogue had the Law as its husband and, according to the prophecy concerning Hannah as well, was once fertile in children (1 Sam. 1). But the barren Church, without the husband Christ and without any address from the Bridegroom’s word, lay for a long time in the desert.

But after that woman received the bill of repudiation into her hands and turned all her husband’s ornaments into the adornment of an idol, then the husband, when the former belt had rotted, wove another belt around his loins from the nations, another girdle. As soon as she was joined to her husband, she conceived and gave birth.

And in Isaiah the Lord cries out through the prophet: “Can a nation be born all at once?” (Isa. 66:8), when in a single day three thousand and five thousand people believed in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 2–4 ff.).

Nor do I think it necessary to speak of the multitude of Christians and the small number of Jews, since throughout the whole world the banners of the cross shine brightly, while scarcely any Jew who is rare and conspicuous appears in the cities.

### (Verse 28)

But we, brothers, are children of the promise according to Isaac. There is no difficulty in understanding that the Apostle and those like him are children of the promise according to Isaac. But because Origen, explaining this passage, presented the Apostle’s wording as follows—“But you, brothers, are children of the promise according to Isaac”—the question arises how he can now call Galatians, whom he had called foolish and had said began in the spirit but were bringing their course to completion in the flesh, children of the promise according to Isaac. We therefore say that the Apostle calls them children of the promise according to Isaac because he does not despair entirely of their salvation and believes that they will return again to the spirit with which they had begun, and become children of the free woman. But if they are brought to completion in the flesh, they are children of the slave woman.

### (Verses 29–31)

But just as at that time the one born according to the flesh persecuted the one born according to the spirit, so it is now. But what does Scripture say? “Cast out the slave woman and her son; for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac.” Therefore, brothers, we are not children of the slave woman but of the free woman—the freedom with which Christ set us free.

I do not think it impossible to find where Ishmael persecuted Isaac; but Scripture records only that, when the son of the Egyptian woman, who was older, was playing with Isaac, Sarah was indignant and said to Abraham: “Cast out the slave woman and her son; for the son of the slave woman shall not inherit with my son Isaac” (Genesis 21:10). Yet an ordinary game between children is surely unworthy of expulsion and disinheritance.

But the Apostle, a Hebrew of Hebrews and instructed at the feet of the teacher Gamaliel, who once restrained the Pharisees when they were raging against the Lord [Alternative: him] in the council, understood from Sarah’s words—“the son of the slave woman shall not inherit with my son Isaac”—that the game had not been an ordinary one. Perhaps Ishmael, being older and circumcised at an age when he could already understand and feel what he had suffered, was claiming the privileges of the firstborn for himself; therefore Scripture called the quarrel of the children a “game.” Hence Sarah, unable to tolerate these things and unwilling from the children’s earliest age to endure the son of the slave woman’s habitual claim to the privileges of the firstborn, burst out: “Cast out the slave woman with her son; for the son of the slave woman shall not inherit with my son Isaac.”

When this seemed harsh to Abraham—for greater privileges are always owed to firstborn sons—not only that Ishmael should cease to be the elder, but that he should not even receive an equal portion with his younger brother, God, who wished the free woman to be within and the slave woman to be cast outside, confirmed Sarah’s words and said to Abraham: “Let it not be harsh in your sight concerning the boy and the slave woman. In everything that Sarah says to you, listen to her voice, for in Isaac your offspring shall be called.”

Thus, just as at that time the elder brother Ishmael persecuted Isaac, who was still nursing and a little child, claiming for himself the privilege of circumcision and the rights of the firstborn, so now Israel according to the flesh [Alternative: Ishmael] rises up, puffs itself up, and exalts itself against its younger brother, the people from the nations who are Christian.

Let us consider the madness of the Jews, who both killed the Lord, persecuted the prophets and apostles, and oppose the will of God; and we shall see that the persecutions stirred up by the Jews against Christians, as history also teaches us, have been far greater than those stirred up by the nations.

Are we surprised at the Jews?

[Note: One Palatine manuscript, under the mark of an assertor, reads: “Are we surprised at the Jews today, because those who are in Christ,” and so forth.]

Even today those who are little ones in Christ and live carnally persecute those who have been born of water and the Spirit; and, rising with Christ, they seek the things that are above, not those below. Let them do what they wish: let them persecute Isaac with Ishmael. They will be cast out with the slave woman, their Egyptian mother, and they will not receive the inheritance, which only the one born from the promise will obtain.

Elegant, too, is the point that the one born according to the flesh persecutes the spiritual person. For the spiritual person never persecutes the carnal person; rather, he forgives him as a rustic brother and knows that he can make progress with time. And whenever he sees the son of the Egyptian woman becoming angry, he remembers the one Father who created light, oxen, and a gnat—

[Note: The same manuscripts read, “who created oxen from light,” and so forth. In the word *light* the printed edition and the manuscripts alike are entirely at fault.]

—and that in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also wooden and earthen vessels.

Therefore, with the Apostle Paul let us say: “We are not children of the slave woman but of the free woman” (2 Timothy 2); and, renewed in Christ, let us hear the words of the Lord speaking to the Jews: “If you remain in my word, you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free” (John 8:31–32). The Apostle, too, set free by this freedom, said: “For although I am free from all” (1 Corinthians 9:19). He knew himself to be free from every vice and alien to every desire and error, and rightly rejoiced in the freedom of Christ, saying: “We are not children of the slave woman but of the free woman, with the freedom with which Christ set us free” (John 8:34).

## Chapter V

### Verse 1

“Stand firm, and do not submit again to the yoke of slavery.”

From this it is also shown that the person who clings to the yoke of slavery has not stood firm. The one who has been granted freedom by Christ remains under the yoke only so long as he possesses the spirit of slavery in fear and follows the beginnings of the Law.

When he says, “Stand firm,” he exhorts them to firm and stable faith in Christ, so that the Galatian churches may remain with a fixed foot in the Savior. Concerning this the righteous man also speaks elsewhere: “He established my feet upon the rock” (Psalm 39:3), meaning, upon Christ, so that they may not be carried about by every wind of doctrine and swept in different directions (Ephesians 4). Hence it is also said to those who stand: “Let the one who stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Corinthians 10:12). And elsewhere: “Stand firm, act manfully, be strengthened” (ibid. 16:13), so that they may stand with him whom Stephen, persevering in martyrdom, saw standing at the right hand of the Father (Acts 7), and who said to Moses: “But stand with me” (Exodus 34:2).

The yoke of slavery he calls the Law: harsh, difficult, burdensome, and such that day and night it exhausts its worshipers with oppressive labor. Thus Peter also says in the Acts of the Apostles: “Why are you testing God by placing upon the neck of the brothers a heavy yoke which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear?” (Acts 15:10).

His addition of the word “again” does not mean that the Galatians had previously kept the Law; rather, the yoke of idolatry is also heavy. Under it the people of Egypt were oppressed and, like lead, submerged in the Red Sea (Exodus 15). In keeping with this meaning he had said above: “How are you turning again to the weak and beggarly elements, to which you wish to be enslaved again, observing days, months, seasons, and years?”

The Galatians, who at the preaching of the apostle Paul had abandoned their idols and immediately risen to the grace of the Gospel, were not returning to the slavery of the Jewish Law, which they had never previously known. Rather, by wishing to observe seasons, to be circumcised in the flesh, and to offer bodily sacrifices, they were in a certain sense returning to the same rites in which they had formerly served through idolatry.

For they say that the priests of the Egyptians, the Ishmaelites, and the Midianites do not have a foreskin. As for the nations’ observance of days, months, and years, would that we did not know of it, lest our festivity ever be mixed with theirs.

### Verse 2

“Behold, I, Paul, say to you that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing.”

[Note: Victorius says: “The Vulgate edition consistently reads *will profit nothing* in all copies, both printed and manuscript; likewise the Greek codex reads οὐκ ὠφελήσει (*will not profit*). Jerome in his commentary reads *profits nothing* five times—that is, wherever he cites the passage. Lacking the support of Jerome’s manuscripts, we have not dared to alter the reading. This, perhaps, is how he read it.”]

In the Gospel the Savior says to the disciples: “The one who hears you hears me; and the one who receives you receives me” (Luke 10:16). The Apostle also testifies, saying: “I live, yet no longer I; but Christ lives in me” (above, 2:20); and elsewhere: “Do you seek proof of the Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Corinthians 13:3). From this it is plainly established that what he now says—“Behold, I, Paul, say to you”—is not to be received as Paul’s words alone, but as the Lord’s.

For when he had prefaced his first letter to the Corinthians with: “To those who are married I give this command—not I, but the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:10), and immediately added: “To the rest I give this command—I, not the Lord” (ibid. 12), lest his authority should be considered worthless, he says: “I think that I too have the Spirit of God.” Thus, with the Spirit and Christ speaking in him, he would not be despised when, imitating the prophets, he said: “Thus says the Lord Almighty.”

What has been said becomes even more forceful if the statement “Behold, I, Paul, say to you: if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” is joined to the opening in which he says: “Paul, an apostle, not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ,” and what follows. Thus those who hear will be moved not so much by the authority of the one sent as by the authority of the one who sends.

Someone may say that this passage is contradicted by what is written to the Romans: “Circumcision indeed profits, if you keep the Law” (Romans 2:25); and below: “What then is the advantage of the Jew, or what is the benefit of circumcision? Much in every way. First, indeed, because the oracles of God were entrusted to them” (ibid. 3:1–2). If Christ profits nothing those who have been circumcised, how does circumcision profit those who keep the Law?

This will be resolved by the following answer: the letter written to the Romans was composed for those who had believed from both Jews and nations. Paul acted so that neither people would be offended, and so that each community might retain its privilege: the gentiles were not to be circumcised, and those who had been circumcised were not to adopt the foreskin.

But in writing to the Galatians he used a different argument. They were not from the circumcision but from the nations who had believed. Circumcision could not benefit those who, after the grace of the Gospel, were returning again to the legal elements.

The history in the Acts of the Apostles also relates that when certain men arose from the circumcision and asserted that those who had believed from the nations ought to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses, the elders and apostles gathered together at Jerusalem decided by letter that no yoke of the Law should be placed upon them and that they should observe nothing further except to keep themselves from offerings made to idols, from blood, and from sexual immorality—or, as it is written in some copies, from what has been strangled.

[Note: Most of the Fathers know and praise this clause as having been handed down from the apostles, while only a few among the ancients pass over it in silence. Among these are Saint Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book 3, chapter 12; Saint Cyprian, book 3 of the *Testimonies*; and certain others. Therefore the Pseudo-Ambrose should not be heeded in his commentary on this letter of Paul, chapter 2, where he claims that this sacred text was inserted by Greek sophists.]

And so that no doubt may remain that circumcision is of no benefit, while Paul moderated his statement about circumcision in the letter to the Romans because of those who had believed from the Jews, he gradually proceeded toward the later portions of that same letter and showed that neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any value, saying: “Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of God’s commandments” (1 Corinthians 7:19).

Circumcision is so entirely nothing that it benefited even the Israelite people, which boasted of its circumcision, nothing at all, as the prophet declares: “All the nations are uncircumcised in flesh, but the house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart” (Ezekiel 44:9). And Melchizedek, though uncircumcised, blessed Abraham, who was circumcised.

When he says, “If you are circumcised” (Genesis 44), the meaning is as though he had wished to say, “if you are circumcised in the flesh.”

[Note: In other books the wording is: “as though he wished to say,” and so forth.]

Elsewhere he calls this not circumcision but mutilation, saying: “Watch out for the mutilation. For we are the circumcision, who serve God in the Spirit and glory in Christ and do not put confidence in the flesh” (Philippians 3:2–3). He does not put confidence in the flesh who expects every benefit from Christ and does not sow in the flesh so as to reap corruption from the flesh, but in the Spirit, from whom eternal life is generated.

The statement must be examined more subtly: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing.” This means not only that circumcision itself is of no benefit if they are circumcised, but also that even if they appear to possess the other virtues in Christ apart from circumcision, all of them perish when they have been circumcised after faith in Christ.

What, then? Did circumcision benefit Timothy nothing? It benefited him greatly in every way. He was not circumcised so much because he thought he could obtain some advantage from circumcision itself, but so that he might win others (1 Corinthians 9:20)—becoming a Jew to Jews, in order to lead Jews to faith in Christ through his circumcision. Circumcision therefore does not profit when it is thought to bring benefit by itself.

### Verse 3

“I testify again to every person who circumcises himself that he is obligated to perform the whole Law.”

God, who first commanded circumcision to Abraham and then through Moses in the Law, established that not circumcision alone but also many other things were to be observed: the festivals to be attended at Jerusalem; burnt offerings of sacrifices, always morning and evening; the sacrifice of a lamb in one place only; a festival for the land in the seventh year; the fiftieth year of remission; and the other requirements that each reader can easily extract from the Scriptures.

We shall therefore press Ebion and his followers, who, believing in Christ after the Gospel, think that people ought to be circumcised: either let them perform circumcision and the other things prescribed in the Law, or, if it is impossible for everything to be done, let circumcision also cease, since it has been omitted along with the other requirements as though it were mutilated.

If they answer that they ought to do only what is possible—for God does not demand from us what we cannot do, but what we can fulfill—we shall say to them that it is not the work of the same God both to wish the Law to be kept and to abandon those who keep the Law. Or how can he make them guilty on account of neglecting the Law when, even if they wished to, they could not fulfill everything?

We, however, follow the spiritual law, which says: “You shall not muzzle the ox while it is treading out the grain” (Deuteronomy 25:4), and with the Apostle understand: “Is God concerned about oxen?” (1 Timothy 10:18; 1 Corinthians 9:9). Rather, he says this for our sake. We observe delicate Sabbaths (Isaiah 58:13), not so that our ox and donkey and worthless animals may rejoice on the Sabbath, but those human beings and animals of whom it is written: “You will save human beings and beasts, Lord” (Psalm 35:7).

The human beings are all rational and spiritual men; the animals are those of slower understanding, who are instructed by spiritual persons to perform the Lord’s Sabbaths.

[Note: Two of our manuscripts read “is built up from faith in Christ”; on their authority we have shortly corrected the text to “rests,” whereas it formerly read “does not rest,” with precisely the opposite sense. Victorius had already restored this reading from Brescian codices, observing that *conquiescit* here means “ceases.” Jerome immediately explains it in this sense, adding: for κατηργήθητε ἀπὸ τοῦ Χριστοῦ means not, as it has been badly translated into Latin, “you have been emptied of Christ,” but “you have ceased in Christ’s work,” and so forth.]

Nor is this contrary to what was said above: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing,” and what follows: “I testify to every person who circumcises himself that he is obligated to perform the whole Law.” It corresponds to what we add: “For not the hearers of the Law are righteous before God, but the doers of the Law will be justified.”

The person who is a doer of the Law is the one who can say: “We are the circumcision,” and, “A Jew inwardly,” and, “We know that the Law is spiritual.” But the one who follows the mutilation and the letter that kills is not a doer of the Law; he is truly an enemy of the Law, especially after the coming of the Savior, who removes the veil from the heart of those who turn to him, so that all, beholding the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, may be transformed from the oldness of the letter into the newness of the Spirit.

### Verse 4

“You have been severed from Christ, you who are justified in the Law; you have fallen away from grace.”

Just as no one can serve two masters (Matthew 6), so it is difficult to fulfill both the shadow and the truth of the Law at the same time. There is shadow in the Old Law until the day dawns and the shadows are removed; there is truth in the Gospel of Christ: “For grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17).

Therefore the person who thinks he is justified by some observance of the Law loses the grace of Christ and forfeits the Gospel that he had held. Once he has lost grace, he is deprived of faith in Christ and rests in his work. For κατηργήθητε ἀπὸ τοῦ Χριστοῦ (*you have been rendered ineffective from Christ*) is better understood not as it has been wrongly translated into Latin, “You have been emptied of Christ,” but, “you have ceased in the work of Christ” [Alternative: “in Christ’s work”].

[Note: In Victorius the negative particle is present: “not from the whole,” and so forth.]

Thus what he had specifically commanded above concerning circumcision—“If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing”—he now embraces generally concerning the whole Law: those who believe they are to be justified by any observance of the Law make no progress in Christ’s work.

### Verse 5

“For through the Spirit, by faith, we await the hope of righteousness.”

He placed “Spirit” in contrast with the letter. The hope of righteousness is to be understood as Christ, because he himself is truth, patience, hope, righteousness, and every virtue. We await his second coming, when he will judge all things and will come no longer in patience but in righteousness, to repay each person according to his works.

Those who await the presence of this God, the Apostle and those like him, say: “Let your kingdom come” (Matthew 6:10), so that when the Son has handed the kingdom over to God the Father and he himself has become subject along with all things that have been subjected, then the head may be subjected in the body and God may be all in all (1 Corinthians 15). For what now exists partially, in individuals, will then begin to exist wholly in everyone.

[Note: The Palatine manuscript, together with Victorius, reads: “the presence of whose day,” and shortly afterward, more correctly, “when the Son has handed the kingdom over to God the Father.”]

### Verse 6

“For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any value, but faith working through love.”

Those who wish to live in Christ Jesus ought to pursue virtues and flee vices. The things that lie between virtues and vices are neither to be fled nor pursued, such as circumcision and uncircumcision and other things of this kind.

Circumcision indeed profits if you keep the Law. It was useful to those who lived under the Law, not because they were circumcised, but because the oracles of God were entrusted to them. By turning those oracles into practice, they were not excluded from salvation.

Nor should we be troubled by the fact that Zipporah, taking a flint, circumcised her son and kept the angel who was strangling him away from her husband (Exodus 4); or, as it is reported differently in the Hebrew, because the present statement testifies not so much that circumcision is entirely of no benefit as that it has no force in Christ Jesus. From the time when the Gospel shone throughout the whole world, the injury of circumcision has been superfluous.

At that time, like the other requirements of the Law, it had value, when bodily blessings were also promised to those who kept the Law: namely, that if they fulfilled it, they would be blessed in the city and blessed in the field, would have full granaries, and would receive many other things contained in the promises (Deuteronomy 28).

But we wish to have strength and firmness in Christ Jesus—in true circumcision, not in Jewish mutilation. For it is not the one who is a Jew outwardly, nor circumcision that is manifest in the flesh, but the Jew inwardly and circumcision of the heart in the Spirit, not in the letter (Romans 2:28–29).

Thus bodily circumcision profits nothing in Christ, but circumcision of the heart and ears does, removing the reproach of the Jews: “Behold, your ears are uncircumcised, and you cannot hear” (Exodus 6:12).

Circumcision of the lips also profits—the circumcision which Moses, in humility, claimed that he did not yet possess, as it is written in Hebrew: “But I am one who has a foreskin on my lips.”

Circumcision also provides great benefit in sexual matters, when chastity cuts away unchastity.

Therefore, in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor bodily uncircumcision has value, because these are placed in the middle—that is, between vices and virtues—but faith, which works through love. Thus the faith that was counted to Abraham as righteousness is also proved genuine, and every work of faith is placed in love, since the whole Law and the Prophets depend upon love.

The Savior affirmed that the Law and the Prophets stand upon these two commandments: “You shall love the Lord your God,” and, “You shall love your neighbor.” Paul likewise says elsewhere: “You shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not covet; and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying: You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Romans 13:9).

If every commandment is summed up in the statement “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” and faith working through love is of the greatest value, it is clear that the working of faith through love contains the fullness of all commandments.

Just as, according to the Apostle James, faith without works is dead (James 3), so without faith, even good works are counted as dead. Those who do not believe in Christ but have upright conduct—what more do they possess than works of virtue?

Let that prostitute in the Gospel provide an example of faith working through love. When, while the Lord was reclining in the house of the Pharisee, she washed his feet with her tears, wiped them with her hair, and anointed them with ointment, and when the Pharisee murmured, the Lord proposed the parable of the debtor who owed fifty and five hundred denarii, and added: “For this reason I say to you: her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke 7:47, 50). Turning to the woman herself, he said: “Your faith has saved you; go in peace.”

For this passage plainly demonstrates that this woman possessed faith working through love, which had great power in Christ.

Suppose someone says: He has properly shown that circumcision has no value in Christ, although he knew that it once had value. But was anyone uncertain about uncircumcision, so that he should say, “Neither uncircumcision”? If we consider the many Christians—that is, people from among us—who have been grafted from a wild olive into the root of the good olive tree (Romans 11), exulting against the broken branches of the Jewish people and saying that uncircumcision, in which Abraham pleased God and his faith was counted to him as righteousness, is more valuable than circumcision, which was given as a sign of faith and did not benefit the Israelite who possessed it, we shall see that this presumption of certain people has now also been most carefully excluded.

# Book Three

[Column 399]

### 483–484

We are composing this third volume on the Epistle to the Galatians, O Paula and Eustochium, not unaware of our weakness and of the slender stream of our talent, which we scarcely perceive murmuring softly.

[Note: Other books read “we compose”; shortly afterward, “with a resounding murmur”; and finally, “the simplicity of the Apostles.”]

For now these things are also sought in the churches. The simplicity and purity of the apostles’ words have been abandoned, and people gather as though at the Athenaeum

[Note: The Athenaeum was a place dedicated to Minerva where professors displayed their studies and where they delivered rhetorical declamations, and so forth. —Martianus.]

and lecture halls, so that the applause of those standing around may be aroused; so that a speech disguised by the falsehoods of rhetorical art may come forth into public like a little prostitute, seeking not so much to educate the crowds as to win the crowd’s favor, and, like a psaltery or flute singing sweetly, caress the understanding of its hearers.

Thus the saying of the prophet Ezekiel can truly be applied to our times, when the Lord says to him: “And you became to them like the sound of a harp singing sweetly and well composed; they hear your words but do not do them” (Ezekiel 33:32).

But what shall I do? Shall I remain silent? Yet it is written: “You shall not appear empty before the presence of your Lord.” And Isaiah—as it is nevertheless found in the Hebrew volumes—groans: “Woe to me, miserable man, because I was silent.”

Shall I speak? But every elegance of speech and beauty of Latin expression has been soiled by the harshness of reading Hebrew.

You yourselves know that for more than fifteen years

[Note: Compare Letter 22, to Eustochium, section 30.]

no Cicero, no Virgil, and no other author of pagan literature has come into my hands; and if something from that literature should perhaps slip in while we are speaking, we remember it as though something ancient remembered through the haze of a dream.

I leave to the judgment of others what I have gained from the tireless study of that language; I know what I have lost in my own.

Added to this is the fact that, because of the weakness of my eyes and of my entire little body, I do not write with my own hand. Nor can I compensate for the slowness of my speech by labor and diligence. They say that Virgil too shaped his books by licking them into form like a bear’s offspring—

[Alternative: offspring, plural.]

but when I summon a secretary, I either dictate immediately whatever comes to my mouth, or, if I wish to think for a little while in order to produce something better, that silent man then reproves me, contracts his hand, wrinkles his forehead, and by the whole gesture of his body makes clear that he is present in vain.

Speech, even when it has proceeded from a naturally gifted mind, distinguished by inventions and adorned with a flower of words, nevertheless, unless it has been smoothed and polished by the hand of its author, is not bright and does not possess dignity blended with beauty. Rather, like the possessions of wealthy peasants, it is more exposed than adorned by its riches.

Why am I saying this? Clearly, so that both you and the others who may perhaps wish to read may have an answer: I am not writing a panegyric or a rhetorical controversy, but a commentary. That is, my purpose is not that my words should be praised, but that what another has said well should be understood just as it was said.

It is my duty to explain obscure matters, touch briefly upon what is clear, and linger over what is doubtful. Hence the work of many commentators is called an exposition.

If someone seeks eloquence or delights in declamations, he has Demosthenes and Cicero, Polemon and Quintilian, in the two languages. The Church of Christ has been gathered not from the Academy and the Lyceum but from the lowly common people.

Hence the Apostle says: “Consider your calling, brothers: not many are wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble. But God chose the foolish things of this world to confound the wise; God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong; and God chose the ignoble things of this world and the despised, and things that are not, to destroy the things that are” (1 Corinthians 1:26–28).

Because the world had not known God through wisdom from the order, variety, and stability of created things,

[Note: Two manuscripts read: “with varying consistency.”]

it pleased God, through the foolishness of preaching, to save those who believe—not through the wisdom of speech, lest the cross of Christ be emptied.

Where is the wise person? Where is the grammarian? Where are the investigators of natural causes? Not in persuasive words of wisdom, but in the demonstration of power and Spirit, so that the faith of believers might not rest in human wisdom but in the power of God.

For this reason the Apostle himself also said to the same Corinthians: “When I came to you, brothers, I did not come with superiority of speech or wisdom, proclaiming to you the testimony of the Lord. For I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2:1–2).

### 487–488

And lest he perhaps be thought, by saying this, to be a preacher of foolishness, with prophetic foreknowledge he overturned what might be brought against him.

“But,” he says, “we speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, the wisdom that has been hidden.” No one among the rulers of this age knew it.

How many people read Aristotle now? How many know even the books or the name of Plato? Scarcely do those old men recall them in idle corners. But the whole world speaks of our rustic people and fishermen; the entire world resounds with them.

Therefore their simple words must be unfolded in simple speech. I say, their words, not their meanings.

But if, in response to your prayers, I could have in explaining their letters the spirit that they possessed when dictating them, then you would see that there was in them as much true wisdom, majesty, and breadth as there was arrogance and vanity in the learned men of the world.

I briefly confess to you the secret of my mind: whoever is going to understand the Apostle through me, I do not want him to understand my writings with difficulty and then seek another interpreter in order to understand the interpreter.

But it is now time for us to pursue what remains.

### Verse 7

“You were running well. Who hindered you from obeying the truth?”

What the Latin translator has now placed—“from obeying the truth”—is written in Greek as τῇ ἀληθείᾳ μὴ πείθεσθαι (*not to obey the truth*). In the earlier passage he translated it as “not to believe the truth.” We noted in its proper place that this reading is not found in the ancient manuscripts, although the Greek copies too have been confused by this error.

The meaning is as follows: You worshiped the Father in spirit and truth, and, receiving from the fullness of Christ, you knew that the Law was given through Moses only to that people and was not also accomplished. But grace and truth were not only given but also brought into being through Jesus Christ.

Since you were running so well, serving the truth rather than images, by what perverse teacher have you been hindered, so that you follow the shadow of the Law and abandon the truth of the Gospel?

It follows:

“You should agree with no one.”

But because we have found this written neither in the Greek books nor in those who have commented on the Apostle, it seems that it should be passed over.

### Verse 8

“Your persuasion is not from the one who called you.”

In the Latin manuscripts I found the following written: “Your persuasion is from God, who called you.” I think that the reading originally had *from him*, but, because it was not understood, *from God* gradually became common through similarity, replacing *from him*.

But even in this form the meaning cannot stand: those whom he had just accused of not obeying the truth, showing that it lay within their own choice either to obey or not to obey, he now, on the contrary, seems to assert that their persuasion and obedience come not so much from those who are called as from the one who calls.

It is therefore better and more correctly read: “Your persuasion is not from the one who called you.”

The work of God is one thing, and the work of human beings another. God’s work is to call; the human being’s work is either to believe or not to believe.

[Note: The printed books insert the word “elsewhere,” which all our manuscripts lack.]

And wherever human free choice is affirmed in the Scriptures, as in the passage: “If you are willing and hear me” (Exodus 19:5), and again: “And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God require of you?” (Deuteronomy 10:12), this passage above all confirms it.

But the simpler people, thinking that they were honoring God by placing even our persuasion within his power, removed the word “not” and gave the Apostle an opposite meaning.

Whether, therefore, for good or for evil, neither God nor the devil is responsible, because our persuasion is not from the one who called us, but from us, who either consent or do not consent to the one who calls.

Alternatively: “This persuasion which you are now following is not from God, who called you in the beginning, but from those who later disturbed you.”

### (Verse 9.) “A little leaven leavens the whole lump” [Col. 0402C]

In our manuscripts it is wrongly written, “A little leaven corrupts the whole mass”; the translator has rendered his own meaning rather than the Apostle’s words. Paul uses this very same statement in his Letter to the Corinthians, where he commanded that the man who had his father’s wife should be removed from their midst and handed over to repentance, for the destruction and affliction of the flesh through fasts and illnesses, so that his spirit might be saved on the day of the Lord Jesus Christ. For he says: “Your glorying is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven corrupts the whole mass?” (1 Cor. 5:5–6 and following)—or, as we have now corrected it, “leavens the whole lump”? [Some copies add “our” after “the Lord.”] Immediately he adds: “Purge out the old leaven, so that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened; for Christ our Passover has been sacrificed. Therefore let us feast, not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.”

Now, through this same statement, he teaches that the spiritual bread of the Church, which descended from heaven, must not be violated by a Judaic interpretation. The Lord likewise instructed his disciples to beware of the leaven of the Pharisees (John 6). The evangelist, making the point clearer, added: “He had spoken to them of the doctrine of the Pharisees” (Matt. 16:12). What other doctrine of the Pharisees is there, then, except observance of the Law according to the flesh?

The meaning, therefore, is this: Do not suppose that the plots of a few men who come from Judea and teach something else are to be disregarded. A spark is a small thing and, while it can scarcely be discerned, is almost invisible; but if it catches hold of tinder and finds fuel for itself, even though the fire is small, it consumes walls, cities, vast forests, and entire regions. Leaven also, whose parable in the Gospel is applied to another subject (Luke 13), appears to be a small and worthless thing; but when it has been mixed into flour and corrupted the whole mass by its force, everything mixed with it passes into its power. So too perverse doctrine, beginning with one foolish person, scarcely finds two or three hearers at first; but gradually it spreads through the body like a cancer, and, as the common proverb says, the mange of one sheep stains the entire flock.

Therefore the spark must be extinguished as soon as it appears; the leaven must be removed from the neighborhood of the mass; rotten flesh must be cut away; and the mangy animal must be driven from the sheepfold, lest the whole household, mass, body, and flock burn, be corrupted, rot, and perish.

Arius was a single spark in Alexandria; but because it was not immediately suppressed, his flame devastated the whole world. [490] [Al. *oppressed*: *oppressed* is masculine in one copy.]

### (Verse 9.) “I have confidence in you in the Lord, that you will think nothing else.”

Paul does not declare this conjecturally, as some wish, but by the prophetic Spirit: he announces that the Galatians will return to the way of truth, which they had lost (1 Cor. 12). For he himself, who urged others to desire spiritual gifts, and especially to prophesy, spoke while filled with the same grace: “We know in part, and we prophesy in part” (ibid., 13:9). Foreseeing in the Spirit, therefore, that they would believe nothing other than what they were being taught through the Letter, he says: “I have confidence in you in the Lord, that you will think nothing else.”

The addition of the Lord’s name also signifies this very point. If he had judged the matter conjecturally, he could have said, “I have confidence in you.” But now, by adding “in the Lord,” he prophesied, trusting through a certain divine Spirit that he knew what would happen.

### (Verse 10.) “But the one who troubles you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be.”

“Secretly,” they say, “he is attacking Peter, of whom he writes above that he resisted him to his face because Peter had not walked with a straight step toward the truth of the Gospel.” But Paul would not speak with such insolent abuse of the head of the Church (Gal. 2), nor would Peter deserve to become liable for a troubled Church. We must therefore suppose that this is said of someone else—someone who had either been with the Apostles, or had come from Judea, or had believed while belonging to the Pharisees, or certainly was held in great esteem among the Galatians—so that “whoever he may be” will bear the judgment of the troubled Church.

“To bear the judgment” means what he expressed in other words below: “Each one will bear his own burden.” I think that in Scripture “burden” may be understood both in a good and in a bad sense: both of those who are weighed down by serious sins and of those who sustain the light burdens of virtues.

Regarding sins, the penitent speaks in the psalm: “My iniquities have risen above my head; like a heavy burden they have weighed heavily upon me” (Ps. 37:5). Regarding virtues and the teaching of virtues, the Savior says: “For my yoke is gentle, and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:30).

That doctrine too may be understood as a burden is made clear in the Gospel. The Pharisees “tie up heavy burdens, impossible to bear, and lay them on people’s shoulders, while they themselves are unwilling to touch them with one finger” (ibid., 23). How grievous it is to disturb someone from tranquility and to stir the peaceful hearts of human beings as though with waves is testified by the Savior’s words to the Apostles: “Let not your heart be troubled, nor let it be afraid” (John 14).

It is beneficial for the one who troubles and scandalizes someone in the Church that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be thrown into the sea, rather than that he should scandalize one of these little ones whom the Savior points out (Luke 17).

The Galatians, then, had been troubled between spirit and letter, circumcision and mutilation, hidden and manifest Judaism, not knowing what they should do. The passage may also be understood more briefly in this way: Whoever he may be who draws you back to the doctrine of the Pharisees and desires to have you circumcised in the flesh, however eloquent he may be and however much he may boast of his knowledge of the Law—I say nothing more than this, which you yourselves cannot deny: he will bear judgment for this deed and receive the reward of his labor.

### (Verse 11.) “But I, brothers, if I preach circumcision, why am I still persecuted? Therefore the offense of the cross has been abolished”—or, as the Greek more correctly has it, “has ceased.”

We read in the Acts of the Apostles, and the Apostle Paul himself often recalls in his Letters, that he endured very frequent persecutions from the Jews because he taught that those from the Gentiles who had believed in Christ ought not to be circumcised.

Therefore, in order to deceive the Galatians, those of whom he said above, “But the one who troubles you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be,” added this as well: “Not only Peter, James, John, and the other Apostles in Judea observe circumcision and the other precepts of the Law, but Paul himself, who taught you otherwise, has circumcised Timothy and has frequently become a Jew to the Jews, compelled by the truth of the matter.”

Now wishing to remove this opinion from the minds of the Galatians, Paul says: “But I, brothers, if I preach circumcision, why am I still persecuted?” All the hatred of the Jews against me, he says, and all the madness with which they rage against me, arises from nothing else than that I teach the Gentiles that they ought not to be circumcised or to observe the burdens of the Law, which are superfluous and have already been abolished.

Since I am persecuted, it is evident that I do not preach circumcision, which I destroy. For I do not suffer persecution from the Jews so much because I preach the Crucified One and say that Jesus is the Christ whom the Law and the Prophets foretold, as because I teach that the Law has been fulfilled.

That the cross is an offense to the Jews and folly to the Gentiles, our Lord himself demonstrated when he is called “a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense” (Matt. 21; Luke 20). I think this is for no other reason than that, when preaching has advanced toward its hearers with full sails, as soon as it comes to the cross it strikes against it and can by no means proceed farther on its free course.

[Note: [Col. 0405D] The Palatine Codex has: “to proceed farther. But [uncertain: *haeres*, ‘heir’], and the cross is an offense among the Jews.”]

Yet this cross, which is an offense among the Jews and folly among the Gentiles, is power and wisdom to us who believe. For “Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24), so that, because of what was called folly, “the foolishness of God” became wiser than human beings; and because of what was called weakness and offense, “the weakness of God” became stronger than human beings.

“When,” he says, “the offense of Christ’s cross remains, and I suffer persecution—a persecution I would not suffer if the offense did not remain—it is useless for some to boast that I preach circumcision, since by opposing it I endure persecution.”

### (Verse 12.) “I wish that those who trouble you would also mutilate themselves.”

The question is how Paul, the disciple of the one who said, “Bless those who curse you,” and who himself said, “Bless and do not curse” (Rom. 12:14), and elsewhere, “Nor will those who curse inherit the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 15), can now have cursed those who trouble the Churches of Galatia, and can have cursed them with the language of a wish: “I wish that those who trouble you would also mutilate themselves.”

The mutilation is so detestable that both the one who inflicts it on an unwilling person is punished by public laws and the one who castrates himself is held infamous. For, they say, even if this statement is true: “Christ lives in me” (2 Cor. 13:3), and this one as well: “Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?”—certainly a voice of cursing cannot belong to the one who says: “Learn from me, because I am humble, gentle, and meek in heart” (Matt. 11:29).

It is rather thought that, overcome by Jewish fury and a kind of unrestrained madness, he was unable to restrain himself, than that he imitated the one who, “like a lamb before its shearer, did not open his mouth,” and who did not return a curse to those who cursed him (Isa. 53). He surrendered himself to death after being condemned.

The one who responds on Paul’s behalf will say this: His words arose not so much from fury against his opponents as from love for the Churches of God. He saw that the whole province, which he himself had brought from idolatry to faith in Christ through his own blood and dangers, had been thrown into confusion by a sudden persuasion; and, overcome by apostolic grief, the grief of a father, he could not contain himself. He changed his tone and became angry with those whom he had previously soothed, so that he might retain by reproach those whom he had been unable to retain by gentleness.

Nor is it surprising that the Apostle, as a human being and still enclosed in a weak vessel, seeing another law in his body taking him captive and leading him into the law of sin, should once have spoken in this way—a lapse into which we clearly see holy men frequently fall.

It may also be said—although some may consider it superfluous—that Paul did not so much curse them as pray for them, wishing that they might lose those parts of the body through which they were compelled to sin.
