Just as it is said in the Gospel that it is better for someone to enter the kingdom of heaven without an eye, without a hand, without a foot, or without any other bodily member than to go whole into Gehenna (Matt. 18), so here he wishes that they would rather lose one bodily part than be condemned to everlasting fire through the occasion of an intact body.

When this passage is sometimes criticized by pagans, we have shown how one might answer them. Now let us bring it forward against heretics—namely Marcion, Valentinus, and all who bark against the Old Testament—to ask how those who accuse the Creator of being bloodthirsty, severe, warlike, and a great judge can excuse this passage in the Apostle of the good God.

[Note: [Col. 0405D] Two of our manuscripts insert “the Manichaeans” here.]

Certainly, I do not think that anywhere in the Old Law there is a sentence so savage and bloody as this: “I wish that those who trouble you would also mutilate themselves.”

They cannot say that the Apostle prayed for the enemies of Christ who were troubling his Churches, nor that the words arose from love, since their very weight demonstrates that they are filled with swelling indignation. Whatever defense they may offer on behalf of the Apostle, we shall not defend this passage on behalf of the Old Law.

[Note: [Col. 0405D] The same manuscripts and Victor read: “I think that no law is found, in any respect, [to contain] so savage and bloody a sentence.”]

### (Verse 13.) “For you were called to freedom, brothers; only do not give freedom as an opportunity to the flesh”—with “give” understood.

Because this word is not found in the Greek, the Latin translator supplied it.

Since this passage is very obscure, I have thought it appropriate to transfer it word for word from the tenth book of the *Stromata*. [Col. 0405D]

[Note: [Col. 0405D] Jerome praises this same tenth book in his earlier preface, saying that Origen completed it in a brief, sentence-by-sentence treatment of the explanation of Paul’s Letter to the Galatians. The book had already been lost for a long time; I think that this is the largest surviving fragment (*ἀποσπασμάτιον*, “excerpt”) of that work, which Jerome presents here in Latin.]

This is not because the individual points cannot be explained in their proper places and according to their meanings, but because, separated from the preceding discussion, they form one difficult body; and if they are understood merely as they sound, they seem to oppose one another incoherently and abruptly and to overflow with contradictions.

These, then, are Origen’s words:

> “This is a difficult passage, and it seems to me that it must be discussed as follows. The one who is free, and who follows the Spirit and the truth with a higher understanding, disregards what came before, the types, and the letter. Yet for that reason he must not despise those who are lesser or give occasion to those who cannot perceive higher things to despair completely of themselves.
>
> “Although they are weak and are called flesh in comparison with the Spirit, they are nevertheless Christ’s flesh. If he understands the mystery of love that serves the weaker, let him do something for the sake of the weak, lest his brother perish through his knowledge, the brother for whom Christ died.
>
> [Note: [Col. 0406D] The Palatine manuscript reads: “serving the weaker, let him do something,” etc.]
>
> “Pay close attention, therefore, to whether this meaning can be constructed from what follows. ‘You,’ he says, ‘brothers, were called to freedom,’ perhaps because not everyone was able to receive the call to freedom. For this reason you now hear: ‘Only do not give freedom as an opportunity to the flesh.’
>
> “The greater must serve the lesser through love, because ‘the one who wishes to be greater will be the servant of all’ (Matt. 20; Mark 10). Therefore let the spiritual person not tear Christ’s flesh, nor give them an opportunity to bite one another and consume one another by provoking them.
>
> “The one who walks by the Spirit and follows the words of Scripture according to the Spirit must not fulfill the desire of their flesh. But if we understand simply what is said, ‘Walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desire of the flesh,’ as most people think, Paul will suddenly break into this statement contrary to the argument and hypothesis of the entire Letter. For immediately he continues: ‘But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the Law.’
>
> “Although up to this point the discourse coheres with itself to some degree, if we again follow the simple interpretation, he suddenly transfers us to disordered commands by discussing flesh and spirit: ‘Now the works of the flesh are manifest—this and that.’ And conversely: ‘But the fruit of the Spirit is love,’ and what follows.
>
> “Yet even here we must not despair of finding coherence. The history contained in the divine books includes the works of the flesh, but it does not greatly benefit those who understand it only as it is written. Who would not be taught to serve luxury and to regard fornication as nothing, when he reads of Judah entering in to a prostitute (Gen. 38), and of the patriarchs having many wives at the same time?
>
> “How could someone not be provoked to idolatry who thinks that the blood of bulls and the other sacrifices of Leviticus signify no more than what the letter says? That the plain wording of Scripture teaches hostility is also proved by this passage: ‘Daughter of Babylon, miserable one, blessed is he who will repay you with the repayment with which you repaid us. Blessed is he who will seize and dash your little ones against the rock’ (Ps. 136:8–9). And by that other passage: ‘In the morning I killed all the sinners of the land’ (Ps. 100:8), and other similar passages—namely, passages about contentions, rivalry, anger, quarrels, and dissensions.
>
> “If we do not perceive something deeper, the examples of the histories provoke us more than they prohibit us.
>
> [Note: [Col. 0407D] In the contrary sense, one Palatine manuscript, without the negative particle, reads: “if we perceive something deeper.”]
>
> Heresies too, as many judge, have arisen more from a carnal understanding of Scripture than from the work of the flesh in our own lives.
>
> “We also learn envy and drunkenness from the letter of the Law. Noah becomes drunk after the Flood, and the patriarchs become drunk before their brother Joseph in Egypt (Gen. 9 and 43). Banquets too are recorded in the Book of Kings, when David danced and beat the tambourines before the Ark of the covenant of God (1 Kings 6), along with similar examples.
>
> “It may be asked how the plain discourse of divine Scripture, which is called ‘flesh,’ can provoke us to magic and sorcery, unless we rise up to the Spirit of that same Scripture.
>
> [Note: [Col. 0407D] The same manuscript reads: “how its flesh can provoke us.”] I think this is signified by the fact that Daniel and the three youths were found ten times wiser than the magicians, Gazarenes, and Chaldeans, and that Moses was trained in all the wisdom and instruction of the Egyptians.
>
> “There is therefore an occasion for many evils if someone remains in the flesh of Scripture. Those who do such things will not consequently inherit the kingdom of God. Let us therefore seek the Spirit and the fruits of Scripture, which are not said to be manifest. For the fruit of the Spirit is found in Scripture only through much labor and sweat and worthy cultivation.
>
> “Hence I think Paul spoke carefully and cautiously about the carnal meanings of Scripture: ‘The works of the flesh are manifest’ (Gal. 5:19). Regarding spiritual things, however, he did not write there, ‘The fruit of the Spirit is manifest,’ but rather: ‘The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace,’ and what follows (ibid., 22).
>
> “If, leaving the types behind, we pass over to the truth and Spirit of Scripture, the first thing immediately revealed to us is love; proceeding from there to joy, we arrive at peace, through which we obtain patience.
>
> “Who would not be instructed in compassion and goodness if he understood that even those things that some consider grievous—the punishments and battles in the Law, the overthrow of nations, and the threats made through the prophets against peoples—are remedies rather than punishments? For ‘the Lord will not be angry forever’ (Isa. 57).
>
> “When these things have been opened to us, we shall have a more reasonable faith; self-control will accompany corrected conduct, and continence and chastity will follow it. After all this, the Law will begin to exist for our benefit.”
>
> [Note: [Col. 0408D] Earlier editions read “continence”; our manuscripts correctly read “self-control.”]

Thus far Origen.

We may add to this by saying that those who have been called from legal servitude to the freedom of the Gospel—of whom it was said above, “Stand firm, and do not again be held by the yoke of slavery”—are now also warned, as they follow Christ’s easy yoke and the delightful commands of the Gospel, not to think that they may use this very freedom as an opportunity for the flesh: that is, to live according to the flesh and to be circumcised according to the flesh. Rather, they should stand by the Spirit, circumcise the foreskin of the flesh by the Spirit, and, striving toward the higher things of the Spirit, leave behind the lowliness of the letter.

The passage may also be understood in another way. Someone might say: “If I have ceased to be under the Law, O Paul, and have been called from servitude to freedom, then I ought to live in a manner appropriate to freedom, bound by no commands, but doing, fulfilling, and pursuing whatever pleases me and whatever my will suggests.”

To this the Apostle replies: We have indeed been called to the freedom of the Spirit, but in such a way that freedom itself does not serve the flesh. We must not think that because everything is permitted to us, everything is beneficial. Rather, because we have ceased to be slaves of the Law and have been made free, let us serve one another more through love, so that the Law’s long and elaborate commandments may be brought to completion in the one commandment of love.

### (Verse 14.) “But through love serve one another, for the whole Law is fulfilled in one saying: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’”

Although he was free from all things, he made himself the servant of all for the sake of love, so that he might win the greater number (1 Cor. 13). He rightly urges the others also to serve one another through love, which does not seek what is its own but what belongs to the neighbor.

“For the one who wishes to become first will be the servant of all” (Mark 10:44). Thus, just as the Savior, existing in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and, found in appearance as a human being, humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross (Phil. 2)—so we too must now understand that whatever we previously seemed to do under the necessity of the Law, we who are free must do rather through love.

Love is such a great good that the whole Law is recapitulated in it. In another place the Apostle enumerates love’s virtues, saying: “It is not jealous; it does not act perversely” (1 Cor. 13:7–8). After repeating many things in between, he concludes: “It hopes all things, endures all things; love never fails.”

The Savior likewise says in the Gospel that this is the mark of his disciple: that he love his neighbor (Matt. 22). I think this applies not only to human beings but also to angels.

The same thing is expressed in other words: “Do not do to others what you do not wish to be done to you, and whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them” (ibid., 7:12).

I do not want my wife to be adulterated; I do not want my property to be seized; I do not want to be oppressed by false testimony; and, to include everything in a brief statement, I resent anything unjust being done to me. If, through love working in me, I neither do nor wish such things to another, the whole Law has been fulfilled.

It is not difficult to show how all the commandments—“You shall not kill,” “You shall not commit adultery,” “You shall not steal,” “You shall not bear false witness,” and other similar commands—are maintained by the single observance of love.

It is difficult, however, to show how the sacrifices commanded in Leviticus, and the abstinence from or permission to eat various foods, since some are called clean and others unclean, as well as the continual annual recurrence of the festivals, are recapitulated in the one commandment of love.

Unless someone perhaps adopts the following position: The Law is spiritual, and before the true High Priest arrived we served images and representations of heavenly things; but after he offered himself once as a sacrifice and redeemed us with his blood, all the variety and difficulty of the ancient Law was fulfilled in his love for human beings. For “God so loved the world that he gave his most beloved and only-begotten Son for us.”

But for the person who, once living by the Spirit, has put the works of the flesh to death, and who, loved by the Savior, is called not a slave but a friend, there is no longer any Law imposed—the Law that was established for the impious and sinners, for the disobedient and profane.

Yet now, although we perform at least some part of all the more difficult things, we do not do the one thing that is both easier to do and without which everything we do is empty.

The body feels the hardship of fasting; vigils torment the flesh; alms are obtained through labor; in martyrdom, although faith burns, blood is not poured out without pain and fear. There are people who do all these things. Love alone is without labor.

And because love alone makes the heart pure, it is attacked in us by the devil, so that we may not see God with a pure mind. For when I sit and speak against my brother and place a scandal before the son of my mother (Ps. 49:20), when I am tortured by another’s happiness and turn another’s good into my own evil, is not this saying fulfilled in me: “If you bite and devour one another, see that you are not consumed by one another”?

[Note: [Col. 0409D] Martianus had read “my brother’s,” instead of “the son of my mother”; the manuscripts and the sacred text to which Jerome alludes disagree with him.]

Love is a rare possession.

[Note: [Col. 0409D] The Palatine Codex, under the notation of an asserter, has: “Love is a rare possession for the one who wishes to become anathema for his brothers,” and so forth.]

Who wishes, following the Apostle, to become anathema from Christ for the sake of his brothers? Who, mourning with those who mourn and rejoicing with those who rejoice, is wounded by another’s wound? Who is destroyed by his brother’s death?

We are all more lovers of ourselves than lovers of God.

See how great a good love is. If we perform martyrdom in such a way that we want our relics to be honored by human beings; if, pursuing popular opinion, we shed our blood fearlessly and give away our possessions until we reduce ourselves to beggary, this work deserves not so much a reward as a punishment; it is more a torment of faithlessness than a crown of victory.

### (Verse 15.) “But if you bite and devour one another, see that you are not consumed by one another.”

This may be understood simply: Let us not slander one another; let us not think that we avenge ourselves by cursing; let us not desire to grieve others because we have been grieved; and let us not, like beasts, bite and be bitten in turn, so that destruction and consumption follow the bites.

It is better, however, lest Paul suddenly break into extraordinary commands contrary to the reasoning and whole sequence of the Letter, to understand everything as referring to circumcision and observance of the Law.

“If others,” he says, “trouble you, you are troubled. If, when reading the entire Old Scripture, you understand it as it is written—‘An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth’ (Deut. 19:21)—and anger desires vengeance, while vengeance inflicts pain; and if the Law not only does not prohibit this but even commands it, restoring justice through retaliation, then it follows that the stripped person strips another, the wounded person wounds another in return, the one who has been eaten bites back, and what appears to be justice becomes consumption—not avenging one person alone, but consuming both.”

[Note: [Col. 0409D] The Palatine manuscript more correctly has “and the one who has been gnawed bites back.” Earlier, three lines above, the corrupt reading was “establishing justice in such a burden,” instead of “restoring justice through retaliation.”]

### (Verse 16.) “But I say: Walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desire of the flesh.”

This too must be understood in two ways, in accordance with what precedes. We may say that those who have put the works of the flesh to death by the Spirit and have sown in the Spirit, so that they may reap eternal life from the Spirit, whenever they feel the flesh’s pleasure titillating them, must not fulfill its desire—which, if fulfilled, seems to flatter them for a time—but must restrain it by the Spirit and, according to the judgment of the historian Sallust, “live more by the rule of the mind than by the service of the body.”

[Note: [Col. 0410D] The same manuscript, with the negative particle, reads “does not seem to flatter.” Sallust’s statement quoted here is: “One should live more by the command of the mind than by the service of the body.”]

We may also say that, because “the Law is spiritual” (Rom. 7), and the true Jew is not the one who is a Jew outwardly but the one who is one inwardly, with circumcision of the heart in the Spirit and not in the letter, those walk by the Spirit and do not fulfill the desire of the flesh who spiritually go out from Egypt and draw spiritual food and drink from the spiritual rock; who are not judged concerning food, drink, a festival, a new moon, or a sabbath, but walk spiritually in all things, not fulfilling the desire of the fleshly Law or of the letter, but reaping the fruits of spiritual understanding.

[Note: [Col. 0410D–0411D] Two manuscripts read: “not because one is a Jew outwardly, but because one is inwardly, and [there is] circumcision of the heart in the Spirit, not in the letter.” They therefore take Paul to command those who interpret Scripture spiritually to walk by the Spirit and not fulfill the desire of the flesh.]

A third interpretation has also been offered by some for this passage, though it does not differ greatly from the second. They assert that “the desire of the flesh” belongs to those who are children in Christ, while the path of the Spirit belongs to mature men; and that the meaning is: “Walk in the gravity of the Spirit, that is, on the path of the mature man, and you will not carry out the desires of children.”

### (Verse 17)

For the flesh desires against the spirit, but the spirit against the flesh. For these are opposed to one another, so that you do not do whatever you wish. The flesh delights in present and fleeting things; the spirit, in everlasting and future things.

Between these conflicts stands the soul, having good and evil, willing and unwilling, in its own power, but not having that very willing and unwilling as permanent; for it may happen that, after it has consented to the flesh and done its works, it is again stung by repentance, joins itself to the spirit, and performs its works. [501]

> **Note:** [Col. 0411D] This is Origen’s position: the soul is, in a certain sense, intermediate between spirit and flesh. “When he says,” Origen writes in Book I of his commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, “that the flesh desires against the spirit, but the spirit against the flesh, the soul is doubtless placed in the middle; it may either yield to the desires of the spirit or incline toward the desires of the flesh.” Similar statements are found in many of his books; indeed, there is no doubt that Jerome drew this doctrine from him, whose imitation he does not deny having undertaken. Yet it is also certain that the expression may be understood positively, and that what these authors call “spirit” should, in their own sense, be understood as the soul’s **ἡγεμονικόν**—that is, its ruling or principal faculty. Many other Fathers are likewise found who, in this sense, give the higher part of the soul almost the name “spirit” as its father. Augustine alone may be cited for all the rest: [Col. 0412D] in Book II, chapter 12, of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, he writes that the soul, placed as it were in the middle, is sometimes dragged down by the flesh toward vice and sometimes raised by the spirit toward virtue. There are many other passages in his works—more than can be listed—in which he understands the spirit opposed to the flesh as the soul’s ruling faculty, plainly in accordance with Origen. It is therefore all the more surprising that Jansenius accuses this view of Pelagianism and calls it the distinctive teaching of all the Pelagians whose writings he was able to see, when it is so clearly approved not only by Jerome but also by Augustine, whose judgment and authority against those heretics were supreme.

This is what the Apostle means when he says: “For these are opposed to one another”—that is, flesh and spirit—“so that you do not do whatever you wish.” He does not thereby take away our free choice, by which we may assent either to the flesh or to the spirit; rather, what we do is not properly our own, but the action itself is assigned either to the flesh or to the spirit [*Al.* “may be assigned”].

It requires great labor and very extensive discussion, after the works of the flesh and of the spirit have been displayed, to discover certain intermediate works that seem to belong neither to the flesh nor to the spirit. We are called carnal when we give ourselves wholly to pleasures. We are spiritual when we follow the Holy Spirit as our guide—that is, when we think with him as our instructor and are taught under his authority. I believe philosophers are “soulish” or “natural” people, who think their own thoughts are wisdom; of them it is rightly said: “The natural person does not receive [*Al.* “perceive”] the things that are of the spirit.” For such things are foolishness to him. [Col. 0411C]

To make this clearer, let us take an example. Let the flesh be called earth, the soul gold, and the spirit fire. As long as gold remains in the earth, it loses its own name and is called by the name of the earth with which it has been mixed. When separated from the soil, it receives both the appearance and the name of gold, but it has not yet been tested. If it is then refined and purified by fire, it receives the splendor of gold and the dignity of its beauty. [Col. 0412A]

So also the soul, standing between earth and fire—that is, between flesh and spirit—when it gives itself to the flesh is called flesh; when it gives itself to the spirit, it is called spirit.

> **Note:** [Col. 0412D] Two manuscripts read: “When it has given itself to its own thought,” and so forth.

But if it trusts its own thought and supposes that it can discover the truth without the grace of the Holy Spirit, it is marked, like sullied gold, with the designation “natural person” [*Al.* “will be marked”]. [Col. 0412B]

This passage can be explained better in the following way, as though it formed one connected and coherent whole, with each part linked to the others and without contradiction:

Brothers, you have been called from the slavery of the Law into the freedom of the Gospel. But I beg you, do not misuse freedom as a license, and do not suppose that everything is permissible for you merely because it is allowed; do not give an opportunity to the flesh and to wantonness. Rather, learn that this freedom is a greater form of service, so that whereas the Law formerly extorted obedience from the unwilling, you may now serve one another through love.

For the whole burden of the Law and its many commandments have not so much been abolished through the grace of the Gospel as shortened into the single saying of love: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” For whoever loves his neighbor fulfills the whole Law (Matt. XXII), [Col. 0412C] giving him good and doing him no harm.

> **Note:** [Col. 0412D] In the Palatine manuscripts: “As though love should cease”; a second hand reads: “As though love were thus.”

But if love ceases and charity is absent, through which the whole Law is fulfilled, there will be a kind of public robbery among human beings, so that, stealing from one another and biting one another, they will be consumed by one another.

But you, brothers, must live according to the spiritual Law for this reason: that you may not fulfill the desires of the flesh. For the flesh fears cold, rejects hunger, is weakened by vigils, burns with lust, and desires everything soft and pleasant. The spirit, by contrast, seeks those things that are opposed to the flesh and that can weaken it.

And so it happens that you must not suppose yourselves free merely because you have ceased to be under the slavery of the Law. Rather, know that you remain held by the law of nature. For it does not immediately follow that, if the Law no longer commands, nature too has ceased, so that your will is not followed by actions; rather, often you are compelled to do what you do not wish, because the flesh resists the spirit. [Col. 0413A]

Therefore, brothers, I beg you not to give your freedom as an opportunity to the flesh, but rather to serve the spirit, so that you may begin to do what you wish and owe nothing to the Law—that is, so that you may not be under the flesh. For you will truly be able to possess in the Gospel the freedom of the abolished Law when the flesh no longer compels you to do what you do not wish, but, serving the spirit, you show that you are not under the Law.

> **Note:** [Col. 0413D] The same manuscripts read “the freedom of the abolished flesh.”

And since above we had begun to explain this passage according to a twofold interpretation, what we omitted must now be supplied. “The flesh desires against the spirit”: that is, the historical and carnal understanding of Scripture struggles against allegory and spiritual teaching. “But the spirit against the flesh”: that is, higher things resist lower things, eternal things resist fleeting things, and truth resists shadow. [Col. 0413B]

And the carnal sense of Scripture, which cannot be fulfilled [*Al.* “because it cannot be fulfilled”—the manuscripts differ], shows that we are not placed in control of fulfilling the Law, since even if we wished to follow the letter, impossibility does not permit it.

### (Verse 18)

But if you are led by the spirit, you are not under the Law.

By “spirit” he does not mean the spirit of which the Apostle speaks elsewhere: “The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God” (Rom. VIII, 16)—that is, he does not mean the human spirit that is within a person, but the Holy Spirit. By following him, we become spiritual and cease to be under the Law. [Col. 0413C]

It must therefore be noted that here “Spirit” does not occur with the **ἄρθρῳ** (*article*) or with any qualifying addition, as in the other passages where we read “the spirit of gentleness” and “the spirit of faith,” but is simply called “Spirit.” These small distinctions, which are observed more carefully in Greek than in our language—for we have no articles at all—seem nevertheless to have some significance.

A question arises here. If everyone who is led by the spirit is not under the Law, were Moses and the prophets led by the spirit and yet lived under the Law, which the Apostle denies? Or, possessing the spirit, were they not under the Law, which the Apostle asserts here? Or is there a third possibility: that, while living under the Law, they did not possess the spirit—which it would be impious to believe of such men? [Col. 0413D]

We shall answer briefly: being under the Law is not the same as being as though under the Law, just as “in the likeness of sinful flesh” is not the same as being in sinful flesh. Nor does the true serpent mean the same thing as the likeness of a serpent made of bronze, which Moses suspended in the wilderness (Num. XXI).

Thus the holy prophets and Moses, walking in the spirit and living by the spirit, lived not under the Law but as though under the Law. They appeared indeed to be under the Law, but they did so in order to win those who were under the Law and call them from the lowliness of the letter to the height of the spirit. [Col. 0414A]

For Paul too, who became a Jew to the Jews and all things to all people in order to win all (I Cor. IX), did not say that he became “under the Law,” but “as though under the Law,” to show that he had observed not the reality of the Law but its likeness. We seem to have resolved the question proposed.

But what shall we do with that passage of Paul in which he says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the Law, in order to redeem those who were under the Law” (above)? [Col. 0414B] For if Christ was under the Law and not merely as though under the Law, the whole preceding argument will be rendered void.

Yet this objection too will be resolved in its proper place. The one who was made under the Law in order to redeem those who were under the Law was certainly free from the Law and submitted himself to the Law by his own will. He was much freer than Paul, who testified that he had been not under the Law but as though under the Law.

And just as, for our sake, he descended into the filth and abyss of death while we cried out, saying, “Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. VII, 14), so he also willed to be born of a woman and to be under the Law, in order to save those who had been born of a woman and were under the Law. [Col. 0414C]

Certainly, however, he was not born of a woman—that is, of a married woman—but of a virgin. Yet, by an improper usage, the virgin was called “woman,” because of those who did not know that she had been a virgin.

> **Note:** [Col. 0413D] Two manuscripts have *nesciunt* (“do not know”) for *habere* (“to have”), and read *maritatam* (“married”) in place of *maritum* (“a husband”); *maritam* (“a married woman”) should perhaps be read, as it is more harmonious.

Thus, just as “woman” was used for “virgin” on account of those who thought that holy Mary had a husband, so, on account of those who thought that Christ was under the Law and did not know that he had become for those under the Law as though under the Law, he is also said to have become under the Law.

### (Verses 19–21)

Now the works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, impurity, wantonness, idolatrous service, sorceries, enmities, contentions, rivalries, angers, quarrels, dissensions, heresies, envies, drunkennesses, carousings, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God.

> **Note:** [Col. 0413D] Two manuscripts insert *impudicitia* (“immodesty” or “unchastity”), a word that Jerome himself testifies, at the end of the following exposition, is found written in the Latin manuscripts in this catalogue of vices. [Col. 0414D]

Earlier, when we were explaining the flesh and the spirit, we said that there were three interpretations. Either those are “fleshly” who are children and bodily persons, unable to receive solid food in Christ and the nourishment of mature age; or those are “carnal” who, in the Jewish manner, follow only the historical account and the letter; or, according to the simple meaning, flesh and spirit coexist in the human person, and according to the difference of their substance there are either works of the flesh or works of the spirit.

Now, therefore, the works of the flesh named here—namely, fornication, impurity, wantonness, and the rest that follow—seem to me to refer more to the simple understanding of flesh and spirit than to the flesh of the Law and children in Christ, although in that passage where we previously translated word for word something from the tenth book of Origen’s *Stromata*, what may also be thought about these matters has been set out. [Col. 0414D]

> **Note:** Instead of *expressum sit* (“has been set out”), our manuscripts read *exemplo praesumpsi* (“I presumed by way of example”); I do not know whether this is more correct.

When he says, “The works of the flesh are manifest,” he either shows that they are known to everyone, because they are plainly evil and to be avoided by their very nature, to such an extent that even those who do them wish to conceal what they are doing; or else he means that they are manifest only to those who have believed in Christ. Many pagans glory in their disgraceful acts and think that, if they have satisfied their pleasure, they have achieved a kind of victory over shame. [Col. 0415A]

It is also elegantly said that he placed “works” in the flesh and “fruit” in the spirit, because vices end and perish in themselves, whereas virtues sprout and overflow with fruits.

Nor should we think that the soul has no activity when vices are assigned to the flesh and virtues to the spirit. For, as we said above, the soul, placed in a kind of middle position, either joins itself to the flesh, and it is said of it: “My spirit shall not remain in these human beings, because they are flesh” (Gen. VI, 3); or it is joined to the spirit and passes into the designation “spirit.” “Whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (I Cor. VI, 17). [Col. 0415B]

The first work of the flesh, therefore, is fornication. He placed it at the beginning as something obvious, so that we might not be uncertain about the middle terms. Everything else that a person does is outside the body; but whoever commits fornication sins against his own body. And we are not our own, for we were bought at a price. Let us glorify and bear God in our body.

The fornicator is guilty of a greater crime in this respect: he takes the members of Christ and makes them members of a prostitute. “The two shall be one flesh.” The unbeliever who does not believe in Christ makes his own members members of a prostitute; the believer who commits fornication makes Christ’s members members of a prostitute.

As for the unbeliever in his fornication, I do not know whether he violates or builds an idol’s temple. For demons are worshiped especially through vices. But this one thing I know: whoever commits fornication after believing in Christ violates the temple of God. [Col. 0415C]

The second work of the flesh is called impurity, and wantonness follows it. Just as in the Old Law Scripture generally gathered together the unspeakable crimes committed in secret—crimes whose very naming is most shameful, lest both the mouth of the speaker and the ears of the hearers be polluted—when it said, “Make the children of Israel reverent, or respectful, toward every impurity” (Lev. XV, 31), so here it has called the other extraordinary pleasures, including the acts of marriage themselves if they are carried out without modesty and decency, as though under the eyes of God and with service rendered only to children, “impurity” and “wantonness.” [Col. 0415D]

In the catalogue of the works of the flesh, idolatry holds the fourth place. Whoever once gives himself over to wantonness and pleasure no longer looks toward the Creator. Otherwise, all idolatry delights in festivals, gluttony, the belly, and the things below the belly.

And lest perhaps sorceries and magical arts should seem not to be forbidden in the New Testament, they too are named among the works of the flesh. For it often happens through magical arts both that the wretched love and that they are loved.

Enmity, which is placed after sorceries, is shown to be a manifest crime by its being subjected to condemnation.

> **Note:** [Col. 0415D] In Victorius, the phrase *manifesti criminis subjectio* (“its subjection to a manifest crime”) makes this clear.

As far as depends on us, we ought to be the enemy of no one, but to have peace with everyone. If, however, by speaking the truth we incur some people’s enmity, we are not so much their enemies as they are enemies of the truth. [Col. 0416A]

For when it is said to Abraham in Genesis, “I will be an enemy to your enemies and will oppose those who oppose you,” this should be understood, as above, not as meaning that Abraham was their enemy so much as that they were enemies of Abraham’s virtues and religion, through which, after trampling down idols, he reverently recognized the known God.

Likewise, when the people of Israel are commanded to be enemies of the Midianites with everlasting hatred and hostility handed down to their descendants (Num. XXXI), this is said as to those who were under a pedagogue and who elsewhere deserved to hear: “You shall hate your enemy” (Matt. V, 43).

Or else the disagreement concerned not so much persons as ways of life. Just as God beneficially placed enmity between the serpent and the woman, lest their friendship be harmful to humanity, through which humanity was cast out of paradise, so among the Israelites and the Midianites it was a difference of life, rather than a single condemned nation, that was at issue. [Col. 0416B]

Contention holds the seventh place among the works of the flesh, placed among the vices in a kind of sacred and prominent rank. “The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward everyone, a teacher, patient, instructing with gentleness even those who argue against him” (II Tim. II, 24–25).

After contention comes rivalry in the eighth place. In Greek it is more significantly and more familiarly called **ζῆλος** (*zēlos*, zeal or jealousy). I do not know which of us is free from this evil. The patriarchs were jealous of their brother Joseph; and Mary the prophetess and Aaron, God’s priest, were led astray by this passion against Moses (Gen. XXXVII; Num. XII). [Col. 0416C]

Indeed, she of whom Scripture had reported, saying, “And Mary the prophetess took a tambourine” (Exod. XV, 20), and so forth, was afterward cast outside the camp, polluted by the affliction of leprosy, and marked her repentance by seven days of separation (Num. XII).

> **Note:** [Col. 0416D] One Palatine manuscript has “and a lyre” instead of “and so forth.” Shortly afterward it fails to recognize the word through a division of the text.

Then comes anger, which does not produce the righteousness of God (James I) and is a form of fury. The difference between irascibility and anger is this: an irascible person is always angry, whereas an angry person is stirred up for a time. And I do not know who could possess the kingdom of God when the person who becomes angry is separated from the kingdom (Matt. V).

Quarrels too, which the Greeks call **ἐριθεῖαι** (*eritheiai*, contentious disputes), using another significant term—for a quarrel is called **μάχη** (*machē*)—exclude people from the kingdom of God.

**Eritheia** is present when someone is always ready to contradict, takes pleasure in another’s irritation, contends with a woman’s quarrelsomeness, and provokes the person who is contending. Among the Greeks this is also called **φιλονεικία** (*philoneikia*, contentiousness or love of strife).

Dissensions too are works of the flesh, when someone who is by no means perfect does not speak with the same understanding and the same judgment, saying: “I am of Paul,” “I of Apollos,” “I of Cephas,” and “I of Christ” (I Cor. I, 12). [Col. 0417A]

The same dissension is also found among households: husbands against wives, fathers against sons, brothers against brothers, fellow servants against fellow servants, soldiers against their comrades, craftsmen against craftsmen of the same trade.

Sometimes dissension even arises in expositions of Scripture, from which the heresies now placed among the works of the flesh also boil up. For if the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God (Rom. VIII)—and all doctrines of falsehood that oppose God are hostile to him—then heresies too are consequently hostile to God and are referred to the works of the flesh.

In Greek, **αἵρεσις** (*hairesis*, heresy) is derived from “choice,” because each person chooses for himself the discipline that he thinks is better. Therefore anyone who understands Scripture differently from what the sense of the Holy Spirit requires—the Spirit by whom it was written—may be called a heretic, even if he has not withdrawn from the Church. Such a person belongs among the works of the flesh, choosing what is worse. [Col. 0417B]

Heresies are followed by envy. We should not think that envy is the same as zeal, because zeal can be understood positively when someone strives to imitate what is better.

Envy, however, is tormented by another person’s happiness, and it is divided into two forms of passion: either a person wants to be something himself that he does not want another to be, or, seeing another to be better, he is grieved that he is not like that person.

A certain writer among the moderns, elegantly translating a Greek verse and playing with envy in elegiac meter, wrote:

> Nothing is more just than envy: it immediately  
> Gnaws at its author and torments his spirit.

The blessed Cyprian also wrote a very fine book *On Jealousy and Envy*. Whoever reads it will not hesitate to count envy among the works of the flesh. [Col. 0417C]

The difference between an envious person and one who is envied is this: the envious person envies someone more fortunate.

> **Note:** [Col. 0417D] The same manuscript reads “he envies happier things” instead of “he envies someone more fortunate.”

The person who is envied, however, is one who suffers envy from another.

Drunkenness holds the fourteenth place among the works of the flesh. For drunkards will not possess the kingdom of God. The Lord also says to his disciples: “Take care lest your hearts perhaps be weighed down by wine and drunkenness” (Luke XXI, 34).

Wine overturns a person’s senses; the feet collapse; the mind reels; lust is kindled. Hence the Apostle cries out: “And wine, in which is wantonness” (Eph. V, 18).

Everyone has authority over his own judgment. I follow the Apostle: wantonness is in wine, and drunkenness is in wine. No one who is overcome by these passions can deny that drunkenness and wantonness are numbered among the works of the flesh.

And although some think I should be criticized for saying in the book I wrote *On Preserving Virginity* that young women ought to flee wine as they would poison, I shall not repent of my judgment. For there we condemned the effect of wine rather than God’s creature, and took away permission from a virgin burning with the heat of youth, lest, under the pretext of drinking little, she drink too much and perish. [Col. 0417D]

Otherwise, we knew that wine is consecrated into the blood of Christ and that Timothy was commanded to drink wine.

Drunkenness can arise not only from wine but also from the other kinds of drink that are prepared in various ways. Hence it is also said of the holy one: “He shall drink neither wine nor strong drink” (Luke I, 15). *Sicera* is interpreted as “drunkenness.” [Col. 0418A]

And lest anyone think that, by not drinking wine, he was permitted to drink something else, every excuse is removed when everything that can intoxicate is taken away along with wine.

> **Note:** [Col. 0417D] The Palatine manuscript reads *exclusa cautio est* (“the precaution is excluded”) instead of *exclusa causatio est* (“every excuse is removed”).

The fifteenth and final work among the works of the flesh is carousing. “The people ate and drank, and rose up to play” (Exod. XXXII, 6). Wantonness is always joined to drunkenness.

A certain not insignificant orator, beautifully describing a drunken man awakened from sleep, said: “Once awakened, he could neither sleep; drunk, he could not remain awake.” By this saying he expressed, in a certain manner, that the man was neither dead nor alive.

It would be a lengthy task to go through all the works of the flesh and make a catalogue of vices. He therefore concluded them all in one phrase, saying: “And things like these.” [Col. 0418B]

Would that we could avoid them as easily as we understand them. “I warn you,” he says, “as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God.”

Earlier he had said: “Let sin not reign in your mortal body, so as to obey its desires” (Rom. VI, 12). Sin has all these forms, in distinguishing which we have perhaps lingered longer than was necessary.

Therefore, in the soul in which sin has reigned, the kingdom of God cannot reign. For what partnership is there between righteousness and iniquity? What fellowship does light have with darkness? What agreement does Christ have with Belial? (II Cor. VI, 14–15).

Do we suppose that we shall attain the kingdom of God if we are free from fornication, idolatry, and sorceries? Behold, enmities, contention, anger, quarrel, dissension, drunkenness, and the other things we consider small exclude us from the kingdom of God. [Col. 0418C]

It makes no difference whether someone is excluded from blessedness because of one vice or because of several, since all exclude in the same way.

> **Note:** [Col. 0418D] The same manuscript reads: “Nor does it matter if one person is excluded.”

In the Latin manuscripts, adultery, immodesty, and murder are also reported as written in this catalogue of vices.

> **Note:** [Col. 0418D] Two manuscripts omit “and murders.”

It must be understood, however, that no more than fifteen works of the flesh have been named, and these are the ones we have discussed. [Col. 0419A]

### (Verse 22)

But the fruit of the spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control. Against such things there is no Law.

What other fruit among the fruits of the spirit ought to hold the first place except love, without which the other virtues are not reckoned as virtues and from which everything good arises?

For in both the Law and the Gospel it holds the chief place: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength; and you shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Deut. VI, 5; Matt. XXII, 37). [Col. 0418D]

We have already touched briefly above on how many blessings love contains, and for now it is enough to say little more: love does not seek what is its own, but what belongs to another (I Cor. XIII).

Even if someone, through his own fault, is hostile to the person who loves him and tries to stir his peace into waves of hatred, the loving person is nevertheless never disturbed and never considers God’s creature worthy of hatred. “Love covers a multitude of sins” (I Pet. IV, 8). [Col. 0419A]

The saying of the Savior—“A good tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor can a bad tree bear good fruit” (Matt. VII, 18)—was, I think, pronounced not so much about human beings as about the fruits of the flesh and of the spirit. For the spirit can never commit those vices that have been numbered among the works of the flesh, nor can the flesh overflow with those fruits that arise from the spirit.

It can happen through the negligence of the person who possesses it that the spirit dwelling in a human being does not bear its own fruits; conversely, when the works of the flesh have been put to death, the flesh may cease to sin.

They do not, however, go so far that a neglected tree of the spirit should bear the works of the flesh, or that a cultivated tree of the flesh should produce spiritual fruits. [Col. 0419B]

Joy is placed in the second place among the spiritual fruits. The Stoics too, who distinguish more subtly between terms, think that it is something different from gladness.

They say that joy is the elevation of the spirit exulting over things that deserve exultation; gladness, however, is an unrestrained elevation of the spirit that knows no limit and rejoices even in things mixed with vice.

> **Note:** [Col. 0419D] Cicero should be consulted here, speaking in the voice of the Stoics in Book IV of the *Tusculan Disputations*, where he likewise distinguishes between joy and gladness. Lactantius too, in Book VI, chapter 11, of the *Divine Institutes*, says: “Gladness is nothing other than overflowing joy.” If desired, see Caelius Rhodiginus, Book V, chapter 33. Cicero’s passage says that when the mind is moved calmly and steadily by reason, this is called joy; but when the mind exults vainly and extravagantly, that may be called gladness—exultant or excessive.

Others, on the contrary, place pleasure in opposition to joy—not that pleasure which excites the body toward lust, tickles the senses, and caresses them with a sweet feeling, but another pleasure homonymous with it, which, without moderation or any dignity of gladness, raises its voice in laughter.

If this is true, and if their distinction between the terms neither deceives nor is itself deceived, let us consider whether this may be why it is said: “There is no joy for the wicked, says the Lord” (Isa. LVII, 21).

At the same time, we should note that joy follows love. Whoever loves someone always rejoices in that person’s happiness. If he sees the beloved deceived by some error and having fallen into the slippery path of sins, he will indeed grieve and hasten to rescue him; but he will not be able to change his joy into sorrow, knowing that none of God’s rational creatures perishes forever.

The third fruit of the spirit is peace. Solomon, who preceded us as a type of Christ, also received his name from it. And the Psalmist sings of the Church: “His place was made in peace” (Ps. LXXV, 2).

> **Note:** [Col. 0419D] Our manuscripts, the exemplar of Rabanus, and the older printed books all have “among the eight blessings of the Gospel.” Victorius, followed by Martianaeus, emends it to “the Beatitudes.” The Erasmian edition retains the reading of certain older manuscripts, namely, “among the eight benedictions of the Gospel.” This reading may rightly be called excellent, since the Gospel’s beatitudes are blessings pronounced by Christ the Lord upon peacemakers, mourners, and the others arranged in a group of eight. —MART.

Among the eight blessings of the Gospel it is written: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. V, 9).

In the first of the psalms of ascent it is also sung: “With those who hated peace, I was peaceful” (Ps. CXIX, 6).

Nor should we think that peace is to be sought only in this, that we do not quarrel with another. The peace of Christ—that is, our inheritance—is with us when a tranquil mind is disturbed by no passions.

After peace comes patience, or long-suffering, since we can translate **μακροθυμία** (*makrothymia*) in either way. [Col. 0420A]

Its opposite is faintheartedness, of which it is written: “The fainthearted person is exceedingly foolish.”

> **Note:** [Col. 0420D] Our manuscripts have the plural: “The fainthearted are exceedingly foolish.”

But the patient person who sustains everything is wise (Ecclus. VII).

And with an **ἐπίτασις** (*epitasis*, an intensifying expression), he is called “very wise,” as it is also written in Proverbs: “The long-suffering person is abundant in prudence” (Prov. XIV, 29).

Kindness, or gentleness—for among the Greeks **χρηστότης** (*chrēstotēs*) signifies both—is a mild, gracious, tranquil virtue, suited to the fellowship of all good people, inviting others to intimacy with itself, sweet in speech, and tempered in conduct.

The Stoics accordingly define it in this way: “Kindness is a virtue willingly disposed toward doing good.” [Col. 0420B]

Goodness does not differ greatly from kindness, since it too appears disposed toward doing good. But it differs in this respect: goodness may be more severe, with a stern expression and wrinkled brow, doing good and supplying what is requested, yet not being pleasant in companionship or inviting everyone by its sweetness.

The followers of Zeno likewise define it as follows: “Goodness is a virtue that benefits”; or, “a virtue from which usefulness arises”; or, “a virtue for its own sake”; or, “an affection that is the source of benefits.”

Among the fruits of the spirit, faith holds the seventh and more sacred place. Elsewhere it is also placed among three things: hope, faith, and love.

It is not surprising that hope is not listed in this catalogue, since what is hoped for is contained in faith. Thus the Apostle defines it when writing to the Hebrews: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not yet seen” (Heb. XI, 1). [Col. 0420C]

For what we hope will come and is not yet present, we possess through faith, hoping that we hold what we believe.

The question also arises how faith is placed in love. Whoever loves never thinks that he is being harmed; he suspects nothing except what he loves and what is loved.

> **Note:** [Col. 0420D] Perhaps the words “and is loved” are more correct; our manuscripts do not contain them.

But when love is far away, faith likewise departs.

After faith, gentleness is numbered. It is opposed to anger, quarrels, and dissensions, and it is never provoked toward what contradicts itself. Truly, producing good fruits from the good tree of the spirit, it bears fruit that is good.

Through this virtue God’s servant Moses deserved to receive the testimony of Scripture: “Moses was gentle, more than all human beings upon the earth” (Num. XII, 3).

It says, “upon the earth.” For he could not be gentle above those who saw God face to face, since we are often compelled by the weakness of the flesh to do many things. [Col. 0420D]

Concerning David also—although many think that the prophecy refers to our Lord, which we too do not deny—the Holy Spirit sings in a type of the one who was to come: “Remember, Lord, David and all his gentleness” (Ps. CV, 1). [Col. 0421A]

His gentleness was especially evident toward Saul, Absalom, and Shimei (I Sam. XXIV; II Sam. XV): one of whom wanted to kill him; another, plotting revolution, sought to deprive him of his rule; another threw stones at him, scattering dust, and shouted: “Go out, go out, you wicked man” (ibid., XVI, 7).

Self-control is placed last among the fruits of the spirit. We must understand it not only in chastity, but also in food and drink, in anger and agitation of mind, and in the desire to slander. [Col. 0421B]

The difference between modesty and self-control is this: modesty belongs to perfect men of consummate virtue, of whom the Savior says: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. V, 4); and of himself: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble, and gentle in heart” (Matt. XI, 29).

Self-control, however, is on the way toward virtue but has not yet reached its completion. Desires still arise in the thoughts of the person who exercises self-control and pollute the ruling faculty of the mind, although they do not overcome him or drag him into action.

Self-control is necessary not only in desires and covetousness but also in the three remaining disturbances: grief, joy, and fear.

Against such fruits of the spirit there is no Law. For “the Law is not laid down for the just, but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and sinners” (I Tim. I, 9).

The Law says to me: “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not kill; you shall not bear false witness; you shall not defraud; you shall not desire what belongs to another; you shall not swear falsely; you shall not steal” (Exod. XX, 12 and following). [Col. 0421C]

If, while the fruit of the spirit—love—reigns in me, I do none of these things, the commandments of the Law are superfluous for me.

Finally, the wise men of the world also held this opinion about philosophy: what public laws compel people to do by necessity, philosophy persuades them to do willingly.

**(Verse 24.)** But those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its vices and desires.

Origen, connecting this passage with what precedes, reads it as follows: “Against such things there is no Law—those who have crucified Christ’s flesh with its vices and desires.” [Note: One Palatine manuscript omits the name “Christ” here.] Thus the meaning is not, as the Latin sounds, that those who belong to Christ have crucified their own flesh with its vices and desires, but that Christ’s flesh has been crucified by these people together with its vices and desires.

He asks how, among those who possess the fruits of the Spirit and against whom the Law has ceased to exist, the crucifixion of the Lord’s flesh can be presented as praise, when in the Epistle to the Hebrews it is stated as a reproach: “Crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and exposing him to public disgrace” (Heb. 6:6). [514] In place of “crucifying again,” the Greek has the better single compound word ἀνασταυροῦντες (*anastaurountes*), which we may translate as “recrucifying.” First, therefore, we must note that crucifying and recrucifying are different things. Next, recrucifying the Son of God is not the same as crucifying Christ’s flesh with its vices and desires. [Col. 0421D]

Christ’s flesh is not, in the primary and proper sense, the Son of God; rather, Jesus Christ—who in the beginning was with the Father, the Word and God—became flesh and emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, in order to crucify the flesh and strip the principalities and powers, triumphing over them on the tree (Phil. 2), so that the Apostle’s saying might be fulfilled: “For in that he died, he died to sin once” (Rom. 6:10). [Col. 0422A]

Therefore, if our bodies are members of Christ, consequently our flesh also is Christ’s flesh. We crucify it when through it we put to death on earth fornication, uncleanness, passion, evil desire, and greed. And this is now stated in our praise: that they “have crucified the flesh of Christ Jesus with its vices and desires,” and that we always carry in our body the death of Jesus, so that his life may also be manifested in our flesh. It is no small labor to live in the present age in such a way that the life of Jesus may already now be manifested in our flesh. For in this way our mortal bodies too will be made alive through the Spirit dwelling in us. [Col. 0422B]

Where the Latin translator has rendered *vices*, the Greek reads παθήματα (*pathēmata*), that is, “passions.” And because “passion” can signify pain as well as the other necessities of the little body, the Apostle carefully added “desires,” so that he would not appear, in spiritual people, to deny the nature of the body but only its vices.

This should be understood in this way if we follow the Vulgate edition, reading: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its vices and desires.” [Note: Other Vulgate manuscripts read, “have crucified their own flesh,” and so forth.] On that reading, we say that they crucified not Christ’s flesh but their own. [Col. 0422C]

I had almost forgotten the second interpretation. I had said that everything that follows should be referred to the Law and to circumcision. The meaning, then, is this: Those in whom there are the fruits of the Spirit—love, joy, and the rest—have crucified the bodily understanding of Scripture, which is now called “Christ’s flesh,” together with its passions and desires, which produce the fuel of vices for little ones and infants. [515]

[Note: Two manuscripts and Rabbanus read, “He crucified such flesh of Christ.”]

He has crucified Christ’s flesh who does not serve the history according to the flesh but follows the guiding Spirit of allegory.

**(Verse 25.)** If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit. [Note: A Palatine manuscript, together with Victorius, reads: “If we live by the Spirit, let us obey the Spirit.” “Let us use,” and so forth. The interpretation appended to these readings agrees more closely with them.] [Col. 0422D]

Let us use this testimony against those who do not wish to understand the Scriptures spiritually. Who is it who lives by the Spirit, except our hidden person, who sometimes also habitually lives according to the flesh? But when he has lived by the Spirit, he walks by the Spirit. When he wishes to walk in the flesh, he is dead while living.

The perfect man in Christ always lives by the Spirit; he obeys the Spirit and never lives in the flesh. Conversely, the one who has given himself wholly to the flesh and assigned himself to the passions never lives by the Spirit. Between these are those whom we can call neither spiritual nor fleshly: wavering between virtues and vices, they are now drawn back toward better things and are spiritual; now they are overthrown by the slippery path of the flesh and are fleshly.

**(Verse 26.)** Let us not become desirous of empty glory, provoking one another and envying one another. [Col. 0423A]

The Greeks have one word, κενόδοξοι (*kenodoxoi*), which the Latin translator expressed through a circumlocution of three words. How many definitions and meanings the word “glory” has is shown by the innumerable books of the philosophers and by Cicero’s two volumes written on glory.

But since we are attempting to explain not the etymologies of words but the meaning of Scripture, we shall connect this passage with what precedes as follows: “If we live by the Spirit, let us obey the Spirit,” serving one another not through the Law but through love. [Note: Victorius reads, “If we live by the Spirit.”] We must not quarrel over the interpretation of the Scriptures and say, “Circumcision is better”; “No, the foreskin is better.” One party says that history must be despised and allegory followed; [Col. 0423B] the other says that allegory is empty and shadowy, fixed upon no foundations of truth. Hence it happens that envies arise among them. For, he says, “They wish to exclude you so that you may imitate them”—not so much wishing to teach the truth of the Law as to prevail.

But lest we entirely pass over the word “glory” without examining it, leaving the philosophers their foolishness, let us reconsider some matters from the Scriptures. [516]

The opinion of the common people and the praise sought through human favor are signified by the name “glory” where it is said: “They do everything so that they may be glorified by human beings” (Matt. 23:5). And elsewhere: “How can you believe, when you seek glory from one another?” (John 5:44). Yet in the same passage the word is used in a good sense: “And you do not seek the glory that comes from the only God.” From this we understand that the same word now signifies virtue and now vice. If I seek glory from human beings, it is vice; if from God, it is virtue. God also urges us toward true glory, saying: “Those who glorify me, I will glorify.” [Col. 0423C]

In the divine Scriptures “glory” has another meaning as well, when something more exalted and more divine presents itself to human sight. The glory of the Lord was seen in the tabernacle, and there was glory in the temple constructed by Solomon (1 Kings 8). It was also seen in the face of Moses, when he did not know that his face had been glorified (Exod. 40). I think the Apostle speaks of this glory of the face as well: “But we all, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of God” (2 Cor. 3:18). The Savior himself is called “the radiance of glory and the form of God’s substance” (Heb. 1). Stephen also saw “the glory of God, and Jesus standing at his right hand” (Acts 7). [Col. 0423D]

To presume that we too may invent names—since, as someone says, new names must be coined for new things, [Note: This is evidently Cicero, whom he praises shortly above, *Academica* 1, in the person of Atticus addressing Varro: “For either new names must be made for new things, or they must be transferred from other things,” and so forth.] because it has here been said, “Let us not become desirous of empty or vacant glory”—let us assert that those are desirous of full glory who desire the glory of God, praise proportionate to virtue, and the sight of something displaying greater divinity. Hence in many passages our translators have rendered *glory* by *majesty*. [Col. 0424A]

For a long time I have wanted to burst into words, but I am held back by fear of speaking. Yet I shall speak, and I shall not conceal my distress—a distress almost universal: not concerning riches, power, beauty, or bodily attractiveness, for these are plainly named among the works of the flesh. [Note: Two manuscripts read differently: “are enumerated.”] [Col. 0424B]

If almsgiving is done for the sake of praise, it is empty glory; so too long prayer and the pallor resulting from fasting. These are not my words, but the Savior’s, thundering in the Gospel (Matt. 6).

Even chastity in marriage, widowhood, and virginity often seeks human applause. And what I have long feared to say, but must say: martyrdom itself, if it is undertaken so that we may be admired and praised by our brothers, has had its blood shed in vain. Let the Apostle speak, let the chosen vessel speak: “If I give my body so that I may glory, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3). [517]

The man who had said, “I know a man in Christ, fourteen years ago—whether in the body I do not know, or outside the body I do not know; God knows—caught up to the third heaven” (2 Cor. 12:2), and shortly afterward, “Caught up into paradise, he heard secret words that it is not permitted for a human being to speak”—that man, I say, who labored more than all the others, was given a thorn in his flesh, an angel of Satan to strike him with blows, so that he would not be exalted by the greatness of the revelations. Certainly he asked the Lord three times that it might depart from him, but he was told: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness.” [Col. 0424C]

What is so much the work of God as reading the Scriptures, preaching in the Church, desiring the priesthood, and ministering before the altar of the Lord? Yet even these things, unless someone guards his heart with every care, arise from a desire for praise.

You may see many people—just as Tully also says—entitle their books “On Despising Glory,” and, for the sake of glory, place the titles of their own names at the front. [Note: In a Palatine manuscript: “and for the sake of the glory of his name, preface the titles.”]

We interpret the Scriptures; we often turn the stylus; we write what is worthy of reading. Yet unless these things are done for Christ’s sake, but for remembrance among posterity and fame among the peoples, all our labor will prove futile, and we shall be like “a sounding drum and a clanging cymbal” (1 Cor. 13). [Col. 0424D]

You may see many people arguing with one another about the Scriptures, making God’s word an athletic boundary. [Note: Up to this point it was incorrectly read *scomma*; on the authority of the manuscripts, and compelled by the correct sense, we have restored *scamma*. The *athleticum scamma* was a place, trench, or line marked out, beyond which the athletes competing there could not pass. The name comes from the Greek verb σκάπτω (*skapto*), meaning “I dig.” Jerome himself explains it very clearly elsewhere, in the book *Against John of Jerusalem*: “Why, leaving aside the matters over which the contest is being waged, do you go beyond the *scamma* and the place of combat?” More broadly, it is often used for the contest itself, as here by our author and by Tertullian in *To the Martyrs*: “Your trainer is Christ Jesus, who anointed you with the Spirit and led you to this *scamma*.” Saint Ambrose likewise says in *On Duties* 1.16: “Why do you eagerly feast before the contest has ended? The people are still watching; the athletes are still in the *scamma*.” In *On Elijah and Fasting* 3: “If someone lifts you by the hand in the *scamma*.” And in chapter 21: “Having advanced into the *scamma*, you must necessarily receive the dust.” Again: “A wrestler in the *scamma*,” to pass over other ecclesiastical writers.] [Col. 0425D]

They provoke one another, and if they are defeated, they envy one another; for they are desirous of empty glory. [Col. 0425A]

I know that in the Latin manuscripts, in the testimony quoted above—“If I give my body so that I may glory”—some have *ardeam* (“that I may burn”) instead of *glorier* (“that I may glory”). [518] [Note: This reading, *glorier*, which Jerome approves, is scarcely found in more than one or two manuscripts in place of *ardeam*—perhaps in the Greek of Vechelius’s edition and in the Coptic. It is scarcely approved by any ancient or modern interpreter; the Greek καυθήσομαι (*kauthēsomai*) and the Latin *ardeam* are read with virtually unanimous agreement by the Fathers and by the Pauline manuscripts.] But because of the similarity of the words—among the Greeks “that I may burn” and “that I may glory,” καυθήσομαι (*kauthēsomai*) and καυχήσομαι (*kauchēsomai*), being distinguished by only one letter—an error became established among our people. There are also diverse manuscripts among the Greeks themselves. [Col. 0425D]

**(Chapter 6—Verse 1.)** Brothers, if someone is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual should restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you too be tempted. [Col. 0425B]

Paul knew that he was a worshiper of that God who does not desire the death of a sinner but repentance (Ezek. 18; 33), and that, apart from the Trinity, every creature, although it does not sin, is nevertheless able to sin. He therefore exhorts even the spiritual person, through fear for himself, to stretch out a hand to the fallen.

And appropriately he calls the one overtaken in an offense a “human being,” one who can die, displaying through the very name the fragility of his condition. Such a person is worthy of pardon because, deceived by error like a human being and sunk into an abyss, he cannot raise himself up without help and assistance.

The word “human” is not added to “spiritual”; rather, it is as though God himself were commanded to restore the person overtaken in an offense. Or, as the Greek more correctly has it, “perfect him in a spirit of gentleness.” One who is perfected does not lack everything, but only certain things. [Note: From the previously published text we have supplied the word *si* (“if”), omitted by Martianay, and joined what follows as a single sentence.] [Col. 0425C]

Finally, if someone has not been overtaken by many sins but has erred through some particular fault, the spiritual person should apply a spirit of gentleness and meekness in correcting the sinner. He should not wish to correct the one who has gone astray harshly, angrily, or sorrowfully; rather, he should encourage him by promising salvation and assuring him of pardon. He should bring forward Christ’s testimony: that Christ invites those weighed down by the heavy burden of the Law and sins to his easy yoke and light burden, so that they may learn that he is humble, gentle, and meek in heart (Matt. 11), and may find rest for their souls.

Let us use this testimony against heretics who invent various fables about different natures and say that the spiritual person is a good tree and never produces bad fruits. Behold, the Apostle—whose authority they themselves follow—says that those who are spiritual can sin if they are puffed up by the loftiness of their hearts and fall. We too acknowledge this, and we acknowledge that the χοϊκοί (*choikoi*, “earthly people”) become spiritual if they return to better things. [519]

Someone may object to us with what is written to the Corinthians: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness?” (1 Cor. 4:21). If there he says that he will come to sinners not in a spirit of gentleness but with a rod, how is it that here, for those overtaken in some sin, he applies not the rod but a spirit of gentleness? [Col. 0425D]

The answer is that there he is speaking to people who, after their sin, did not recognize their error and did not wish to submit to their superiors or to be corrected through repentance. But where the sinner understands his wound and hands himself over to the physician to be healed, there a rod is not necessary but a spirit of gentleness. [Col. 0426A]

It may also be asked whether, if someone must therefore restore the sinner in a spirit of gentleness because he considers himself, lest he too be tempted, a righteous person who is certain of his own mind and knows that he cannot fall ought not to restore the sinner in a spirit of gentleness. [Note: A Palatine manuscript reads, “who knows that he cannot fall will not restore the sinner.”] [Col. 0426B]

To this we shall reply that even if the righteous person has conquered, knowing how great a labor was required for his victory, he will all the more generously grant pardon to the sinner. The Savior too was tempted “in every respect as we are, yet without sin,” so that he might be able to sympathize with and feel compassion for our weaknesses, having learned by his own example how difficult victory is in the flesh. [Note: The same manuscript, together with another Cistercian manuscript, reads, “teaching by his own example.”]

If someone has remained a virgin into old age, let him forgive the person deceived at some time by the heat of adolescence, knowing through how many difficulties he himself passed through that age. [Note: Previously the reading was *quondam* (“formerly”); we judged this manuscript reading to be better.] [Col. 0426D]

If someone has been tortured for confessing Christ’s name and sees another deny him under torment, let him have compassion on the denier’s wounds, and let him not so much marvel at that person’s defeat as at his own victory.

Observe also the caution of the writer: he did not say, “Considering yourself, lest you fall,” but “lest you too be tempted.” To be conquered or to conquer is sometimes in our own power; [520] but to be tempted is in the power of the tempter. If the Savior himself was tempted, who can be secure that he will cross the seas of this life without being tempted? [Col. 0426C]

Those who think that Paul spoke according to humility and not truthfully when he said, “Though unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge,” should defend the sequence of this passage. For he ought, according to the order, to have said: “You who are spiritual, restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourselves, lest you too be tempted,” rather than introduce a singular number after using the plural.

A Hebrew of Hebrews, and one who was most learned in his native language, could not express profound meanings in another language; nor did he greatly concern himself with words, since he had secured the meaning. This is according to the simple understanding.

But, to pursue the order of the second exposition as well, this passage must be explained from the conclusion of the Epistle to the Romans. There, when he was similarly writing about the foods and observances of the Jews, and describing as strong and perfect those who despised the precepts of the Law according to the letter, but as weak and childish those who were still guided by ancient custom, he saw that there was a quarrel between the spiritual and the fleshly. He admonished the spiritual not to despise the fleshly and said: [Col. 0426D]

“Welcome the one who is weak in faith, not for disputes over thoughts. One person believes that he may eat everything; but the one who is weak eats vegetables. [Note: Victorius restores, from the reading of the Vulgate translator, “eats.”] Let the one who eats not despise the one who does not eat, and let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats, for God has accepted him. Who are you to judge another person’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master. And he will stand, for God is able to make him stand” (Rom. 14:1–4). [Col. 0427A]

After discussing the meaning at length in the intervening passage, he added at the end: “Do not destroy the work of God for the sake of food.” And again: “We who are stronger ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak and not to please ourselves. Let each of you please his neighbor for his good, for edification” (Rom. 15:1–2).

**(Verse 2.)** Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ. [Col. 0427B]

That sin is a burden is also testified by the Psalmist, who says: “My iniquities have risen above my head; like a heavy burden they have weighed heavily upon me” (Ps. 37:5). And Zechariah, in the form of a woman, saw iniquity sitting upon a talent of lead (Zech. 5). [521]

The Savior bore this burden for us, teaching us by his own example what we ought to do. He bears our iniquities and suffers for us (Isa. 53), and he invites those weighed down by the burden of sins and the Law to the light burden of virtue, saying: “My yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:30).

Therefore, whoever does not despair of his brother’s salvation but stretches out a hand to the one who pleads, and, as far as he is able, weeps with the one who weeps and is weak with the weak, judging another’s sins as his own, fulfills the law of Christ through love. [Col. 0427C]

What is Christ’s law? “This is my commandment: that you love one another” (John 13:34). What is the law of the Son of God? “Love one another, just as I have loved you.” How did the Son of God love us? “Greater love than this no one has, that someone should lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13).

Whoever lacks compassion and is not clothed with the inner organs of mercy and tears, even if he is spiritual, will not fulfill Christ’s law.

But let us also connect this passage with what precedes. For we follow a twofold understanding. If someone is weak in faith, still nourished with the milk of infancy, and unable to pass so quickly from legal observance to spiritual mysteries, you who are stronger should bear his burdens, lest your knowledge cause the brother for whom Christ died to perish. [Col. 0427D]

The one who helps a poor person burdened by the weight of need also bears his brother’s necessity, and makes friends for himself from unrighteous mammon (Luke 16). After his resurrection Christ addresses such a person: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink” (Matt. 25:34–35).

In accordance with this meaning, in another Epistle Paul also instructed Timothy and added: “Command the rich in the present age not to be high-minded” (that is, not to be proud), “nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in God, who richly supplies all things for enjoyment; to do good, to be rich in good works, to give readily, to share, storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of the true life” (1 Tim. 6:17–19). [Col. 0428A]

Whoever takes hold of the true life—namely, the one who says, “I am the life” (John 14:6)—has fulfilled Christ’s law, which tends toward life. [Note: Two of our manuscripts insert *apprehendit* (“takes hold of”) here.]

**(Verse 3.)** For if anyone thinks that he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself. [522]
