If someone does not wish to bear another’s burdens, is without compassion, and is content only with his own work and virtue, not seeking what belongs to another but only what is his own—that is, if he loves only himself and not also God—he deceives himself.

The passage can be read and punctuated in two ways: either, “If anyone thinks that he is something when he is nothing”; or, “If anyone thinks that he is something, so that we may then add, ‘when he is nothing, he deceives himself.’” This distinction is more evident in Greek than in Latin. [Col. 0428B]

The sense of the first punctuation is: Whoever thinks himself to be something when he is nothing deceives himself.

The second sense is deeper and is the one we prefer: If anyone thinks that he is something in the very fact that he considers himself something—not through kindness toward his neighbor, but judging himself by his own work and labor and being content with his own virtue—that person, through this very arrogance, becomes nothing, and deceives himself. This is expressed better in Greek by φρεναπατᾷ (*phrenapata*), that is, “he deceives his own mind,” for which the Latin translator wrote, “he deceives himself.” [Col. 0428C]

He deceives his own mind who thinks himself wise and, according to Isaiah, is wise in himself and intelligent in his own sight (Isa. 5).

With reference to circumcision and the Law, the meaning of this passage is connected in the following way: The spiritual person who has no mercy toward his neighbor and despises the humble because he himself is higher deceives himself, not knowing that this is the law of the Spirit: that we should love one another.

**(Verse 4.)** Let each person test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself alone and not in another.

The meaning is this: You who consider yourself spiritual and stronger because of another’s weakness must consider not the weakness of the one who lies fallen but your own strength. For if someone else cannot pass perfectly from Judaism to Christianity, that does not make you a perfect Christian. Rather, if your own conscience does not reproach you, you have glory in yourself and not in another. [Note: One Palatine manuscript, with the opposite meaning, reads: “because of another’s strength.”] [Col. 0428D]

An athlete is not strong merely because he has defeated a weak opponent and overcome the feeble limbs of his adversary. He is strong if he is robust and glories in his own strength, not in another’s weakness. [523]

The passage can also be understood differently. Whoever has a good conscience and, examining himself, does not condemn his own work should not glory in this before another, pour his praise outward, share it with everyone, and seek vainglory from human approval. Rather, he should have glory in himself and say: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me and I to the world.” Whoever seeks glory from another has neither had the world crucified to him nor been crucified with Christ. He has received what he sought from human beings—his reward. [Col. 0429A]

**(Verse 5.)** For each person will bear his own burden.

This appears to contradict what was said above: “Bear one another’s burdens.” For if each person will bear his own burden, one person will not be able to bear another’s burden.

But we must observe that there he commanded us to support one another in this life when we sin, and to be mutual assistance to one another in the present age. Here, however, he is speaking [variant: “was speaking”] of the Lord’s judgment upon us: we shall be judged as sinners or as saints not according to another person’s sin and in comparison with someone worse, but according to our own work, each receiving according to his work. [Note: Following the manuscripts, we restore *opus* (“work”) in place of the previously printed *onus* (“burden”), producing the more coherent sense.] [Col. 0429B]

Although obscurely, we are taught through this brief statement a new doctrine that lies concealed: while we are in the present age, we can help one another either by prayers or by counsels. But when we come before the tribunal of Christ, neither Job, nor Daniel, nor Noah will be able to plead for anyone; each person will bear his own work (Ezek. 14). [Col. 0429D]

**(Verse 6.)** Let the one who is being instructed in the word share all good things with the one who instructs him.

Marcion interpreted this passage as meaning that believers and catechumens ought to pray together, and that the teacher should share in prayer with his disciples. He was especially encouraged by what follows: “in all good things.” [Col. 0429C]

Yet if the subject had been prayer, the command should not have been given to the one being instructed, but to the one who instructs him—that is, not to the disciple but to the teacher. [Note: The Palatine and Cistercian manuscripts omit the word *se* (“himself”) here, perhaps more correctly.] [Col. 0429D]

Moreover, the rest of what follows does not agree with Marcion’s interpretation: “Whatever a person sows, that he will also reap,” and, “In doing good, let us not grow weary, for in due season we shall reap, if we do not grow weary.” [524]

The meaning, then, is this: Since above he had commanded the spiritual to instruct those who had been overtaken in some offense in a spirit of gentleness and to bear one another’s burdens, fulfilling Christ’s law, he now commands, conversely, those who were still weaker, disciples, and fleshly, to provide carnal things to their teachers just as they themselves reap spiritual things from spiritual teachers.

Those teachers, devoting themselves wholly to divine instruction and study, may need the necessities of this life; and the saying written about the manna may be fulfilled: “The one who gathered much did not have too much, and the one who gathered little did not have too little” (2 Cor. 8:15). [Col. 0429D]

In the present passage he has called “good things,” according to common popular usage, food, clothing, and the other things that human beings count as goods: “Having food and clothing, with these we shall be content” (1 Tim. 6:8). [Col. 0430A]

Nor is it surprising that Paul designated things necessary for the body by the term “good,” since our Savior also said to those who had not yet climbed to the summit of the virtues but were still walking on a lower level and asking that faith be added to them: “If you, though evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give good things to those who ask him?” (Matt. 7:11).

I think Job too, when he spoke to his wife as though to one of the foolish women, used the language of bodily riches with regard to her opinion: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord” (Job 2:10). And again, concerning hardships, pressures, and temptation that bring victory: “Why should we not endure evil?” In reality, evils and goods are not located in riches and pressures but in virtues and vices, as the righteous person says in the psalm: “Who is the person who desires life and wishes to see good days? Keep your tongue from evil and your lips from speaking deceit. Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 33:13–15; 36:27). [Note: The same manuscripts read: “and your mouth from speaking deceit.”] [Col. 0430B]

Properly speaking, “evil” is what we must avoid; “good” is what we must do.

That rich man in the Gospel, who did not possess knowledge of good and evil, rightly considered the abundance of his fields good, saying: “Soul, you have good things stored up for many years; rest, eat, drink, and rejoice” (Luke 12:19). And another man who lay clothed in purple and lived in luxury heard Abraham say to him in the underworld: “You received good things during your life” (Luke 16:25).

We should also consider whether this may perhaps be understood as a command given to disciples: that they should share the word with those who instruct them, obey them, and show themselves teachable and accommodating. This applies, however, to those things that are good and spiritual, not those perverted by heretical or Jewish corruption.

**(Verse 7.)** Do not be deceived: God is not mocked. For whatever a person sows, that he will also reap. [Col. 0430C]

Foreseeing by the Spirit that those who were being taught, and who ought to provide their teachers with expenses and the necessities of life, might plead poverty and say, “My field has dried up this year from drought; hail has destroyed my vineyard; the revenues that might have existed [variant: “will exist”] have been seized by taxes; I have nothing from which to provide what is commanded,” he added: “Do not be deceived: God is not mocked.” [Col. 0430D]

He knows, he says, your hearts; he is not ignorant of your resources. A plausible excuse may in some measure satisfy a human being, but it cannot deceive God.

At the same time, he encourages them to provide what has been commanded, calling it “seed,” so that they will not think lost what they are going to receive back with multiplied interest.

To the Corinthians also he taught the reckoning of what is given and received through a similar example: “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows with blessings will also reap from blessings. Let each person give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:6–7).

### (Verse 8)

For whoever sows in his own flesh will reap corruption from the flesh; but whoever sows in the spirit will reap eternal life from the spirit. Everything that we speak, do, or think is sown in one of two fields: flesh or spirit. If the things that proceed from hand, mouth, and heart are good, having been sown in the spirit, they will overflow with the fruits of eternal life. If they are evil, having been received from the field of the flesh, they will cause a harvest of corruption to sprout for us. [Col. 0431A]

Alternatively: Whoever understands the Law carnally also expects carnal promises and things that are corrupted in the present age. But whoever is a spiritual hearer sows in the spirit and will reap everlasting life from the spirit. [526]

[Note: Palatine manuscripts read, perhaps more correctly: “At the same time, the order of the discourse should be noted and joined with what precedes: the man is called one who sows in the spirit because, when he begins to reap eternal life, he perhaps ceases to be a man.”] [Col. 0431D]

Let us also note the continuity of the discourse and connect it with what precedes: a person is called one who sows in the spirit because, when he begins to reap eternal life, he perhaps ceases to be a human being.

[Note: Up to this point the printed books commonly substitute Tatian for Cassianus. Martianaeus did not hesitate to oppose the authority of his own copies, deceived by the presumption of the printed reading, even though the Cluniac and Royal manuscripts praised by him preferred Cassianus. “This,” he says, “is an error of ancient copyists, to whom Cassianus was better known than Tatianus.” On the contrary, the conclusion should have been drawn entirely in the opposite direction. Julius Cassianus, from the impious swarm of the Valentinians, was almost less well known than Tatianus; and since Jerome here plainly attacks the Encratites, the very well-known name of Tatianus, the leader of that sect, would readily have led inexperienced copyists to substitute it for the very similar name Cassianus. And indeed, as we have done, Cassianus should be restored: the agreement of all the manuscript copies we have seen in this reading compels it. The context itself also proves this, as does the history of the heresy that Jerome attacks. For it was not Tatianus but Julius Cassianus who introduced the notion that Christ’s flesh was only apparent, or who first attributed to the Lord an unreal body. He is even said by Saint Clement of Alexandria, in Book III of the *Stromata*, to have been “the founder of docetism” (*τῆς δοκήσεως ἐξάρχων*), that is, the leader of the Docetae. Indeed, I readily believe that the book whose arguments Jerome refutes below is the very work that the aforementioned Clement of Alexandria says was composed by Cassianus and entitled *On Continence or On Castration* (*περὶ ἐγκρατείας ἢ περὶ εὐνουχίας*).] [Col. 0431D; Col. 0432D]

Cassianus, who, introducing the notion that Christ’s flesh was only apparent, considered every union of male with female unclean, was among the fiercest heresiarchs of the Encratites. On the basis of the present passage he employed the following argument against us: [Col. 0431B]

“If someone sows in the flesh, he will reap corruption from the flesh. But the one who joins himself to a woman sows in the flesh. Therefore, the man who uses a wife and sows in her flesh will reap corruption from the flesh.”

He will be answered, first, that Paul did not say, “the one who sows in the flesh,” but “the one who sows in his own flesh.” No one has intercourse with himself and sows in his own flesh. Then, even if we grant him, for the sake of completeness, the observation we have noted—that the text says “in his own flesh”—we must add that those who eat, drink, sleep, or do anything for the refreshment of the body likewise sow in the flesh and reap corruption from it.

If he takes refuge in saying that those who drink, eat, or sleep nevertheless do everything rationally in the name of the Lord do not sow in the flesh but in the spirit, we will answer him in the same way: those who rationally follow God’s first sentence, “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. I, 22), sow not in the flesh but in the spirit. [Col. 0431C]

His syllogism, therefore, is futile and unstable; by a sophism it first deceives the listener. But when carefully examined, it is easily refuted. For we cannot say that Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and the other holy men who were born from the promise, or even the Lord’s forerunner, because he was born in the flesh, sprang from a seed of corruption. [527]

It should likewise be observed that the phrase “the one who sows in the flesh” is accompanied by the addition “his own flesh”; whereas the one who sows in the spirit is not said to sow “in his own spirit,” but simply “in the spirit.” [Col. 0431D]

[Note: One Palatine manuscript reads not “he is not said to sow in the spirit,” but simply “in spirit”; this is not as good. Shortly afterward it reads *non in suo quopiam* (“not in anything belonging to himself”) instead of *non in suo quippiam*.] [Col. 0432D]

For whoever sows good things sows them not in anything belonging to himself, but in the Spirit of God, from which he will also reap eternal life. [Col. 0432A]

### (Verse 9)

But let us not grow weary in doing good, for at the proper time we shall reap, if we do not give up. He exhorts to the practice of perseverance those who await the reward of good work in this life, unaware that, just as in sowing there is one season for planting and another for harvest, so in the present life our works are the sowing—which are reaped either in the spirit or in the flesh—and the future judgment is the harvest. According to the quality and variety of the sowing, we produce different harvests: a hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold. No one can reap such a crop if he gives up. “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X, 22). [Col. 0432B]

As it is also commanded elsewhere: “Be unfailing” (Isa. V). But how can it be right that, while sinners increase daily in evil works, we grow weary in doing good?

### (Verse 10)

Therefore, while we have time, let us do good to all, but especially to those who belong to the household of faith. The time of sowing, as we have said, is the present time and the life through which we are passing. In this life we are permitted to sow whatever we wish; when this life has passed, the time for working is taken away. Hence the Savior also says: “Work while it is day; night is coming, when no one can work any longer” (John IX, 4). [Col. 0432C]

The word of God, the true sun, has risen for us, and the beasts that withdraw to their dens have gathered together. Let us go forth like human beings to our work and labor until evening, as it is mystically sung in the psalm:

“You set darkness, and it became night. In it all the beasts of the forest pass through, the young lions roaring, seeking to seize prey and asking food from God. The sun has risen, and they have gathered together and lain down in their dens. Man goes out to his work and to his labor until evening” (Ps. CIII, 20 ff.).

Whether we are sick or healthy, humble or powerful, poor or rich, obscure or honored, hungry or eating, let us do everything in the name of the Lord with patience and equanimity. Then what is written will be fulfilled in us: “For those who love the Lord, all things work together for good.” [528]

Anger itself, lust, and the injury that desires revenge—if I restrain myself; if for God’s sake I remain silent; if, amid each thorn of agitation and each incitement to vice, I remember God watching me from above—become for me occasions of triumph. [Col. 0432D; Col. 0433A]

Let us not say when giving: “He is my friend; I do not know this man. This one ought to receive; that one ought to be despised.” Let us imitate our Father, who makes his sun rise over the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the unjust (Matt. V). The fountain of goodness is open to all. Slave and free, commoner and king, rich and poor drink from it alike. When a lamp has been lit in a house, it shines equally for everyone.

If the reins of generosity are loosened indiscriminately toward all, how much more should they be loosened toward those who belong to the household of faith and toward Christians, who have the same Father and are recognized by the title of his disciples! It seems to me that this passage can also be connected with what precedes, so that he calls “those who belong to the household of faith” the teachers whom above he had commanded their hearers to support with everything considered good. [Col. 0433B]

This life’s course is brief. This very thing that I say, speak, write, correct, and reread either adds to or diminishes my time.

[Note: The same manuscript reads: “that is written, that I correct, that I read again.”] [Col. 0433D]

Titus, the son of Vespasian, who entered Rome in triumph after the destruction of Jerusalem in vengeance for the Lord’s blood, is said to have been so good that, when he remembered one evening at dinner that he had done nothing good that day, he said to his friends: “Today I have lost a day.”

[Note: Our manuscripts do not recognize the word *sero* (“late”). Shortly afterward they read: “Friends, today I have lost a day.”] [Col. 0433D]

Do we suppose that an hour, a day, moments, time, or years do not perish for us when we speak an idle word, for which we shall have to render an account on the day of judgment (Matt. XII)? If that man, without the Law, without the Gospel, without the teaching of the Savior and the apostles, both said and did this naturally, what ought we to do, when, to our condemnation, even Juno has her women of one husband, Vesta her virgins, and other idols their self-restrained adherents? [Col. 0433C]

[Note: That is, he was in his ninety-fourth year, according to Epiphanius’s calculations, Book I, chapter 12. Compare Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 9. A little later, the manuscripts support restoring “to join his voice into several words,” in place of “words of speech,” etc.] [Col. 0433D; Col. 0434D]

When the blessed evangelist John lived at Ephesus into extreme old age, and could scarcely be carried to church in the hands of his disciples, unable to join his voice into several words, he used to say nothing at each gathering except this: “Little children, love one another.” [529]

At last the disciples and brothers who were present, wearied because they always heard the same thing, said: “Teacher, why do you always say this?” He replied with a statement worthy of John: “Because it is the Lord’s command, and if it is done alone, it is sufficient.”

This is relevant to the apostle’s present command: “Let us do good to all, but especially to those who belong to the household of faith.”

[Col. 0433D]

### (Verse 11)

See with what large letters I have written to you with my own hand.

Those who wanted to circumcise the Galatians had spread the claim that Paul did one thing and preached another, destroying by his actions what he taught—[Note: Victorius reads: “and to destroy his discourse by his action,” etc.]—since the man who asserted that the Law had been abolished was himself found to be living under the Law. Because Paul could not personally overturn this opinion before everyone—for he was prevented by the chains he endured on account of Christ’s martyrdom—he presents himself through a letter. [Col. 0434A]

And lest any suspicion arise that the letter had been forged, from this point to the end he wrote it out himself, showing that the preceding portion had been written by someone else. That letters were also sent under his name by false teachers, he demonstrates to the Thessalonians when he writes:

“We ask you, brothers, concerning the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our gathering together to him, that you not be quickly shaken in mind or alarmed, either by a spirit or by a word or by a letter supposedly sent by us, as though the day of the Lord were at hand, lest anyone deceive you in any way” (II Thess. II, 1 ff.).

And in order to free the entire letter he was sending from suspicion of forgery, he added his signature in his own hand at the end, saying: “The greeting is by my hand—Paul’s—which is the sign in every letter; this is how I write: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all” (II Thess. III, 17–18). [Col. 0434B]

[Note: The Palatine manuscript reads: “this is how I subscribe.”] [Col. 0434D]

Likewise, he personally appended a note to the letter to the Colossians, which he had dictated: “The greeting is by my hand—Paul’s. Remember my chains.” Wherever he knew that false teachers were present who might use the apostle’s authority to sow new doctrines, he subscribed the letter in his own hand.

Finally, writing to the Corinthians, among whom there were schisms and heresies, with each one saying, “I belong to Paul,” “I to Apollos,” and “I to Cephas” (I Cor. I, 12), he marked his letter with this note: “The greeting is by my hand—Paul’s. If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be accursed: Maranatha,” and so forth. [530]

For this reason, wishing to remove every opportunity from the false teachers who had corrupted the Galatians from the truth of the Gospel, he completed the end of the letter with a note in his own hand, saying: “See with what large letters I have written to you.” This does not mean that the letters themselves were large—for that is what the Greek *πηλίκοις* signifies—but that the traces of his own hand were recognizable to them, so that, when they recognized the strokes of the letters, they might think they were seeing the very man who had written them. [Col. 0434C]

At this point I am astonished that a man highly learned in our own times should have said something so ridiculous.

[Note: Although Chrysostomus seems almost to hold this view, which Jerome attacks, I do not think that he is being indicated here.] [Col. 0434D]

“Paul,” he says, “was a Hebrew and did not know Greek letters. Since necessity required him to sign the letter in his own hand, contrary to his custom he scarcely formed the curved lines of the letters, expressing them in large strokes; even in this he showed signs of his affection for the Galatians, because for their sake he attempted to do even what he could not do.”

Paul therefore wrote the letter in large letters because its meaning was great in its letters, and it had been written by the Spirit of the living God, not with ink or a pen. When he added “with my own hand,” let us understand this as referring to works done by the hand. For this reason it is frequently written in the prophets: “The word of God that came by the hand of Jeremiah,” or “of Haggai,” so that by this likeness too we may know that the word of God was accomplished through Paul’s hand. [Col. 0434D; Col. 0435A]

Paul writes large letters not only then to the Galatians but also today to all people. Although the strokes with which his letters are written are small, the letters are nevertheless large, because their meaning is great.

### (Verse 12)

All those who wish to make a good showing in the flesh compel you to be circumcised, merely so that they may not suffer persecution for the cross of Christ.

[Note: Our manuscripts omit the negative particle, although the Greek text also supports it.] [Col. 0435D]

Above he showed the point at which he had subscribed the letter with his own hand; now he repeats what he had written.

Gaius Caesar, Octavian Augustus, and Tiberius, the successor of Augustus, had promulgated laws allowing the Jews dispersed throughout the entire Roman Empire to live according to their own rite and to practice the ceremonies of their ancestors. Therefore, whoever was circumcised, even if he believed in Christ, was regarded by the Gentiles as a Jew. [531] [Col. 0435B]

But whoever, without circumcision, displayed his foreskin as proof that he was not a Jew became subject to persecution from both Gentiles and Jews. Those who had corrupted the Galatians therefore wished to avoid these persecutions and persuaded the disciples to accept circumcision as a defense. The apostle now calls this confidence “in the flesh,” because they proposed circumcision in persecution both to the Gentiles whom they feared and to the Jews whom they wished to please.

For neither Jews nor Gentiles could persecute them: the Jews could not do so because they saw them circumcising even proselytes, while the Gentiles could not because they saw them observing the precepts of the Law.

For neither do those who are circumcised keep the Law themselves, but they wish you to be circumcised so that they may boast in your flesh.

[Note: Our manuscripts read *qui circumciduntur* (“those who are circumcised”); the Greek copies also vary, some preferring *περιτεμνόμενοι* (“those being circumcised”), others *περιτετμημένοι* (“those who have been circumcised”).] [Col. 0435D; Col. 0436D]

“Because of the weakness of the flesh,” he says, “the Law cannot be fulfilled.” Hence the Jews keep human precepts and teachings rather than the commands of God. They fulfill neither the Law bodily—for that is impossible—nor spiritually, because they do not understand it. [Col. 0435C]

Thus everything they study, do, and strive for has this purpose: that among the Jews they may boast about the injury done to your flesh and vaunt that Gentiles have been circumcised through their instruction. They do all this so as to please the Jews and quiet the resentment aroused by the Law’s defeat.

### (Verse 14)

But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.

Only the person who takes up the cross of Christ and follows the Savior can boast in Christ’s cross—the person who has crucified his flesh with its vices and desires, who has died to the world and does not contemplate the things that are seen but those that are unseen, seeing the world crucified and its form passing away. [Col. 0435D]

The world is crucified to the righteous—the world of which the Savior says: “I have overcome the world” (John XVI, 33), and: “Do not love the world,” and: “You did not receive the spirit from the world.”

For the one to whom the world has been crucified, the world is also dead. The consummation of the world has already come for him; he has become worthy of a new heaven, a new earth, and a new covenant. He sings a new song and receives a new name written on a stone, which no one knows except the one who receives it. [532] [Col. 0436A]

It is asked how Paul can now say, “Far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ,” when elsewhere he boasts about other things, as when he says: “By your glory, which I have in Christ Jesus” (I Cor. XV, 31); and again: “I will gladly boast in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me” (II Cor. XII, 9); and elsewhere: “It would be better for me to die than for anyone to deprive me of my glory” (I Cor. IX, 15), along with the other passages written in this vein.

[Note: In place of *ait* (“he says”), which all our manuscripts prefer, the phrase had previously been read as though it were a particle from the sacred text.] [Col. 0436D]

But we should understand that all such boasting, when referred to the cross, is glory in the cross; and whatever worthy deed is accomplished through virtue is done because of the Lord’s passion. [Col. 0436B]

### (Verse 15)

For neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation.

Just as the faithful and the unfaithful, although one in substance, are divided into two according to their differing understanding, as the apostle says, “Stripping off the old man with his works and putting on the new, which is renewed in knowledge according to the image of its Creator” (Col. III, 9–10), so also the world, although one according to its substance, becomes one thing or another according to one’s perception. [Col. 0436B]

For the sinner, the world is old; for the holy person, it is new. When the world has been crucified to the holy person, there is no longer circumcision or uncircumcision for him, neither Jew nor Gentile, but a new creation, into which the body of our humility is transformed, conformed to the body of Christ’s glory: “The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new” (II Cor. V). [Col. 0436C]

And just as the glory of the sun is one, that of the moon another, and that of the stars another—for star differs from star in glory—so also is the resurrection of the dead (I Cor. XV, 41–42).

Daniel agrees with this in the same words, saying: “Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will rise, some to eternal life and some to eternal disgrace and confusion” (Dan. XII, 2); and: “Those who understand will shine like the brightness of the firmament.” Concerning the righteous he also says: “Many, like the stars, forever.”

For in the sun, moon, firmament, and stars neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any value; rather, there is a new condition without those bodily parts that can be cut away.

Thus we too, who love God, for whom things have been prepared that “no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart” (I Cor. II), when we have been transformed from a body of humility into the glorious body of the Lord Jesus Christ, will possess a body that neither the Jew can mutilate nor the Gentile preserve with its foreskin. [533] [Col. 0436D]

This does not mean that it is different in substance, but that it is different in glory. For “this mortal must put on immortality, and this corruptible must be clothed with incorruption” (I Cor. XV, 53).

The blessed evangelist John, perceiving something similar, spoke as follows: “Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet been revealed what we shall be. We know that when it is revealed, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (I John III, 2). [Col. 0437A]

Since, therefore, that glorious body of Jesus Christ has not yet been revealed—the body that after the resurrection still bore the marks of the nails and entered through closed doors—we who have already risen with Christ in baptism and have been reborn into the new man should serve neither circumcision nor uncircumcision. Rather, let us believe that we already are what we shall be.

### (Verse 16)

And upon all who follow this rule be peace and mercy, and upon the Israel of God.

Everything is directed according to a standard; and when the rule has been applied, it reveals whether things are crooked or straight. So too the teaching of God is a kind of standard of speech, judging between what is just and what is unjust. Whoever follows it will have within himself the peace that surpasses all understanding; and, after peace, mercy, which is especially found in the Israel of God. [Col. 0437B]

He says “the Israel of God” to distinguish it from the one who has ceased to be the Israel of God. They say that they are Jews, but they are not; they lie, since they belong to the synagogue of Satan.

Nor should you be surprised that, in imitation of spiritual Israel, there is a carnal Israel that possesses neither peace nor mercy. Concerning it, Scripture also says to the Corinthians: “Consider Israel according to the flesh” (I Cor. X, 18). In imitation of God and the Lord there are likewise many gods and many lords, whether in heaven or on earth.

Beautifully, in a single expression, as he brings the letter to an end according to its intended argument, he calls it “the Israel of God,” showing that everything said above was discussed not outside the case but because of it. [Col. 0437C]

### (Verse 17)

From now on let no one cause me trouble.

This does not mean that he had grown weary of teaching, but that the farmer has this grief when the plants he has planted dry up, and the shepherd has this anxiety when the sheep he has gathered are scattered and torn apart. [534]

[Note: Two manuscripts read: “that he should have this grief.”] [Col. 0437D]

The Greek is therefore better read as: “From now on let no one give me labors”—that is, so that I may not again have to labor among you.

The teacher is given labor by the disciple who lives and thinks differently from what the teacher has taught and done. Paul may also be anticipating their future disputes, should any of them wish to contradict him, as he did in the passage to the Corinthians concerning the veiling of a woman’s head and the non-veiling of a man’s head, where after much discussion he says: “But if anyone seems to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor the churches of God” (I Cor. XI, 16). [Col. 0437D]

That is: We have said what seemed honorable and just to us. But if someone, unwilling to assent to the truth, seeks what he may answer and what arguments he may rely upon against it, let him know that he is not worthy of an answer, since he is more prepared to argue than to be taught. [Col. 0438A]

But I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus.

After Christ’s coming in the flesh, the person who is circumcised does not bear the marks of the Lord Jesus; rather, he has glory in his shame. But the person who has been beaten beyond measure, frequently imprisoned, flogged three times, stoned once, and endured the other sufferings listed in the catalogue of things in which he boasts—he bears the marks of the Lord Jesus in his body.

Perhaps the person who disciplines his body and brings it into subjection, lest, after preaching to others, he himself should be found disqualified, also bears the marks of the Lord Jesus in his body (I Cor. IX).

The apostles also rejoiced that they had been found worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus (Acts V). [Col. 0438B]

### (Verse 18)

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen.

Let there be not dissension, not bondage to the Law, not quarrelling, not strife, but the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ with your spirit.

Not with the flesh, not with the soul—either because, having become spiritual, you have ceased to be flesh and soul, or because, even in the principal element, lesser things are also included. For soul and flesh are subject to the spirit.

Concerning this Ecclesiastes also says: “The spirit will return to him who gave it” (Eccl. XII, 7). And Paul says elsewhere: “The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit” (Rom. VIII, 16).

This grace of the Lord Jesus is not with everyone, but with those who deserve to be called brothers by the apostle: faithful brothers and true brothers. This is what the word *Amen* signifies, for it is Hebrew. [535] [Col. 0438C]

The Septuagint translators rendered *Amen* as “May it be”; Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion rendered it “faithfully” or “truly.”

Just as in the Old Testament God confirms his words by a kind of oath-taking formula, saying, “As I live, says the Lord” (Num. XIV, 28), and oaths are also made by the saints—“As your soul lives”—so our Savior in the Gospel, through the word *Amen*, shows that what he says is true.

That *Amen* signifies the assent of the hearer and serves as a seal of truth is also taught by the First Letter to the Corinthians, in which Paul says: “Otherwise, if you bless in the spirit, how will the one who occupies the place of the unlearned say ‘Amen’ at your blessing, since he does not know what you are saying?” (I Cor. XIV, 16). [536] [Col. 0438D]

From this he shows that the unlearned person cannot answer that what is said is true unless he has understood what is being taught.

[Note: The same manuscripts read “what is said” instead of “what is taught.”] [Col. 0438D]

[Col. 0439]

## Saint Eusebius Jerome, presbyter of Stridon, Three Books of Commentaries on the Epistle to the Ephesians. (C)

### Prologue
[Col. 0439A] 537–538 If there is anything, Paula and Eustochium, that can hold a wise man in this life and persuade him to remain calm amid the pressures and storms of the world, I consider that it is, first and foremost, meditation on and knowledge of the Scriptures. For since we differ above all from the other living creatures in being rational animals and able to speak—and since all reason and speech are contained in the divine books, through which we learn both about God and why we were created—I am amazed that some have existed who either give themselves over to idleness and sleep and do not wish to learn what is excellent, or think that those who pursue such study ought to be reproached. To them I could respond more sternly and dismiss them either offended or appeased by briefly saying that it is much better to read the Scriptures than to long for the increase and accumulation of riches. I shall say what I could obtain even from the most unjust judge: that I find my leisure pleasing, and solitude more delightful than every public gathering. And just as I do not reproach or condemn what they do, so they ought to grant me my foolish pursuits. I am not eloquent—what is that to you? Read someone more eloquent. I do not adequately translate Greek into Latin—either read the Greeks, if you possess knowledge of that language, or, if you are only a Latin-speaker, do not judge a free gift; and, as the common proverb has it, “Look at the teeth of a gift horse.” Am I dragging you into court with joined hands because you do not write our works [perhaps: “because you do not read ours”]? Anyone less learned than I will read me; perhaps Cicero will admire your words, if you write them. Did Tertullian deter the blessed martyr Cyprian, or Cyprian Lactantius, or Lactantius Hilary, from writing? I say nothing of the other little writers who chatter with me in their books. Unless small things exist, great things cannot stand out. The first is not spoken of unless the second and third follow. We do not climb to the heights unless we walk through the depths.

Therefore I beg both you who are present here and the holy Marcella, the unique model of widowhood, not readily to hand over my little works to slanderers and envious people; nor to give what is holy to dogs and cast pearls before swine (Matt. 7). Since they cannot imitate good things, they envy the only thing they can do; and they consider themselves learned and educated if they disparage others. I beg you to answer them that they themselves should set pen to paper, join together three words, as the saying goes, sweat a little, test themselves, and learn from their own labor to pardon those who labor. You yourselves know that you compelled me to this work of explanations against my will and after much resistance. This is not because, from my youth, I have ever ceased either to read or to question learned men about what I did not know, or because I have considered only myself, as most people do, my teacher. Indeed, I recently went to Alexandria for this very reason above all: to see Didymus and ask him about all the difficulties I had in the Scriptures.

But composing one’s own books is one thing—for example, on avarice, faith, virginity, or widows—joining secular eloquence to testimonies of Scripture gathered here and there on each subject, and displaying an ornate speech on almost commonplace themes; entering into the meaning of a prophet or apostle is another thing: understanding why they wrote, by what reasoning they established their position, and what particular significance the Idumaeans, Moabites, Ammonites, Tyrians, Philistines, Egyptians, and Assyrians have in the Old Law; and, again, what significance the Romans, Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, Thessalonians, Hebrews, and Colossians have in the New Testament—and what significance the Epistle to the Ephesians, which we now have in our hands, has. For according to the differences of the places, times, and people to whom they were written, they must have different causes, arguments, and origins. And just as blessed John, when writing in his Apocalypse to seven Churches, either reproves particular faults or approves particular virtues in each of them, so the holy apostle Paul treats the wounds inflicted upon each Church, and does not wish, like an inexperienced physician, to cure everyone’s eyes with one and the same eye-salve.

And since, at your request, we expressed a few days ago what seemed to us appropriate concerning the Epistle to the Galatians, we must now proceed to the Ephesians—the middle Epistle of the Apostle, both in order and in meaning. I call it “middle” not because the one following the first is greater than those at the end, but as the heart is in the middle of an animal, so that from this you may understand with what difficulties and how profound questions it is entangled.

He was writing to the Ephesians, who worshipped Diana—not this huntress who holds a bow and is girded up, but that many-breasted image which the Greeks call πολύμαστον (*polýmaston*), “many-breasted,” so that from the very figure of the statue they might falsely claim that she was the nurse of all beasts and living creatures.

[Note: [Col. 0441D] Those who have read the writings of the ancient pagans, or have seen on ancient coins and statues that many-breasted image of Diana of Ephesus, which took its name from the city and was held in veneration, certainly know this. Nevertheless, Petrus Faber attempted to overturn this universally known account in an acute disputation, attacking this testimony of Jerome and flatly denying that a many-breasted Diana, distinguished from the huntress by her high-girded dress, ever existed. Instead, he claimed that the ancients called a many-breasted figure Ceres. To prove this, he manipulates—or rather quite openly corrupts—a passage of Minucius Felix. For when Minucius had written, “Diana meanwhile is a huntress, high-girded, and the Ephesian one is many-breasted and furnished with spits,” Faber wishes it to be read: “The Ephesian huntress, and Ceres furnished with many breasts.” Although many very certain testimonies of the ancients occur to us in defense of our author, it will be sufficient to set against him that very clear passage from Apuleius, *The Milesian Tales*, book II: “The sister of Phoebus” (surely not Ceres but Diana), “after being restored by soothing remedies for the delivery of women in labor, nourishes peoples and is worshipped in splendid shrines at Ephesus.”]

He was writing to the metropolis of Asia, a city in which idolatry—and what always follows idolatry, the magical deceptions of the arts—had flourished so greatly that Demetrius said: “The temple of the great goddess Diana will be counted as nothing, and her majesty also will be destroyed, whom all Asia and the whole world worship” (Acts 19:27).

[Note: [Col. 0442D] A notable example is recorded in Acts 19:19: the magical books that Paul had consigned to the flames at Ephesus in a single day were calculated to have been worth fifty thousand denarii.]

Finally, the Apostle remained there for three years, preaching the Gospel of God night and day, so that, once the stronghold of idolatry had been destroyed, the temples of the smaller cities might easily be captured. Scripture itself reports how Paul spoke to the Ephesians, saying: “Therefore keep watch, remembering that for three years, night and day, I did not cease admonishing each one of you with tears. And now I commend you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build up and give you an inheritance among all the sanctified” (Acts 20:31–32). For those whom the error of demons had held for so long needed the Apostle’s commendation to God; they knew that there were certain spiritual powers and had recognized some likeness of divinity in entrails, auguries, and divinations. Therefore he speaks to them again:

“Wherefore I testify to you this day that I am clean from the blood of all. For I have not held back from announcing to you the whole will of God.” And in another [or: the same] passage: “How I held back nothing that was profitable to you, so as to announce and teach it publicly and from house to house” (ibid. 20).

He had read in Ezekiel (ibid. 26–27) that if a watchman did not announce the enemy’s approach to the people, the blood of the citizens would be required from his hands; therefore he recalled that he had announced the whole will of God and everything that would be useful to them, so that he might be free from their blood.

But so that you may know that those who had believed at Ephesus had been bound by demonic deceptions and magical arts, the same Acts of the Apostles repeats the matter and says: “Many also of those who had practiced curious arts, bringing their books together, burned them before everyone; and when they had calculated their value, they found it to be fifty thousand pieces of silver. Thus the word of the Lord grew powerfully and was strengthened” (Acts 19:19).

We have recalled all these things for this reason: to show why the Apostle, in this Epistle above all, gathered obscure meanings and mysteries unknown to the ages, and taught about the power of holy and hostile virtues—who the demons are, what they can do, what they formerly were, and how, after Christ’s coming, they were overthrown and destroyed. Concerning them he says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of this darkness, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6:12). And elsewhere: “I will remain at Ephesus until Pentecost. For a great and effective door has been opened to me, and there are many adversaries” (1 Cor. 16:8–9).

He remained at Ephesus until Pentecost, the season of joy and victory, when we do not bend our knees or bow toward the earth, but, rising with the Lord, are lifted up to the heights of heaven. And he remained because a door was open to him—not a small door but a great one—so that, after binding and overcoming the strong man, he might invade his house, plunder it, overthrow it, and lead captivity captive (Matt. 12). He had gathered the ranks of his followers and fought against the Apostle with his entire battle line, but was defeated.

Who the Ephesians are is also shown most clearly by this: just as John, when he was about to relate the mystery of the Lord’s ancient birth, reclined upon his breast and drew a stream of teachings from the purest fountain (John 13 and 21), so these men, rushing upon Paul’s neck as he departed (Acts 20), showed by their kisses and embraces that they possessed with him one and the same treasure of knowledge, and testified with tears to their longing for their teacher.

I also remind you in this preface that Origen wrote three volumes on this Epistle, whom we have followed in part.

[Note: [Col. 0442D] The commentaries of these three men—Origen, Apollinarius, and Didymus—on this Epistle had long since perished.]

Apollinarius and Didymus likewise published certain brief commentaries, from which we have selected a few passages and to which we have added or from which we have removed some things that seemed appropriate to us, so that the attentive reader may recognize at once, at the beginning, whether this work is another’s or our own.

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 0443]

[Col. 0443A] (Chapter I—Verse 1.) “Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God.”

If the preposition *through* indicates the ministry of the one through whom an action is carried out, this meaning seems to me to correspond to the statement: “No one comes to me unless my Father has drawn him to me” (John 6:44). Thus what is read in John’s Gospel—“All things were made through him” (John 1:3), unquestionably through the Son—will not prejudice our Lord Jesus Christ, as though he were inferior because he obeys the Father’s will. In the same way, it does not now prejudice the Father that Paul is an apostle of Jesus Christ through his will.

Others understand the passage in this way: that Paul is shown to be an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, who is Christ. Thus, just as Christ is called the Wisdom, Word, and Power of God, and also Truth, Resurrection, and Way, so he is likewise called the Will.

Some consider it irrelevant whether he said “through the will of God” or “from the will of God,” because the Apostle uses these prepositions indiscriminately, and “through the will of God” means the same as if he had said “from the will of God.”

“To all the saints who are [at Ephesus].”

[Note: [Col. 0443C] It is clear from the entire context below that, when Jerome proposed to explain this heading of Paul’s Epistle, he omitted the name “at Ephesus.” I say this not merely because it is commonly known that certain ancient copies, both Greek and Latin, did not include the name of the city—just as other copies read not “at Ephesus” but “at Laodicea.” I am moved above all by the fact that immediately after the attached exposition the holy Father notes that some, on the basis of the absence of any name of a Church or city, more inquisitively supposed that those who are saints and faithful were designated by the term “being.” Others, however, simply think that it was written not “to those who are,” but “to those who are saints and faithful at Ephesus.” For if “at Ephesus” had been added in the heading, there would have been no reason to recite these interpretations, not even on account of the variation or omission of a word among the copies; yet both are reported, since each contributes more than the others to explaining the passage, and each indicates by its own argument that the word “at Ephesus” was absent from the archetype.

I should also not omit, concerning the first opinion, that Jerome reports Basil, who in book II *Against Eunomius* praises very ancient books that, without the addition ἐν Ἐφέσῳ (*en Ephésō*, “at Ephesus”), read τοῖς ἁγίοις τοῖς οὖσι καὶ πιστοῖς (“to the saints who are and the faithful”), and thus understood the recipients as being called by the Apostle “saints” in a distinctive sense, or by their own dignity, and in a certain way by nature—after the pattern of the saying in Exodus 3:14: “I am who I am.” This, however, seems to have been said more playfully than seriously.

But since we are engaged in this discussion, I will also mention in passing Tertullian’s testimony: he contends that Marcion interpolated the title of the Epistle and substituted “to the Laodiceans” for “to the Ephesians.” “The Church,” he says in book V, chapter 17 of *Against Marcion*, “in truth holds this Epistle as having been sent to the Ephesians, not to the Laodiceans; but Marcion was eager at one time to tamper with its title, as though he were in this respect also a most diligent investigator.” Finally, the conjectures of more recent interpreters seem closer to the truth: they think that this Epistle was sent, in the manner of an encyclical, to several Churches of Asia Minor, and that the Apostle omitted the name of the particular Church to which it was sent, in something like this form: “To the saints who are … and faithful in Christ,” and so forth.]

[Col. 0443D] 545 Some think, more inquisitively than necessary, that because it was said to Moses, “Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me’” (Exod. 3:14), those who are saints and faithful at Ephesus were also called by the term “being.” Just as saints derive their name from the Holy One, righteous people from the Just One, and wise people from the Wise One:

[Note: [Col. 0444D] We restore “from the wise one,” according to the testimony of the ancient manuscripts and early editors, as well as the sequence of the context; previously it read “from wisdom.”]

so, from “the One who is,” those who are may be called “those who are.” And, according to the same Apostle, God chose the things that were not in order to destroy the things that were. They also explain the very Scripture brought forward as testimony in this way, understanding the destruction of the things that were from what follows: “so that no flesh,” he says, “might boast in the presence of God” (1 Cor. 1:29). For if, they say, someone progresses from what he was not into what he is [or: was] by God’s making, but does not give thanks to the giver and considers his existence the result of his own merit and virtue, then what he is is immediately destroyed, and he begins not to be what he had been.

Others, however, simply think that it was written not to those who are, but to those who are saints and faithful at Ephesus.

“And to the faithful in Christ Jesus.”

“For the unbelieving wife is sanctified in the faithful brother, and the unbelieving husband is sanctified in the faithful wife” (1 Cor. 7:14). There are also holy vessels and mute animals that are sacrificed to God in the temple (Num. 4 and 31). Therefore those whom he had called holy he also called faithful, because faith proceeds from the decision of one’s own mind, whereas sanctification is sometimes received from the generosity of the one who sanctifies, even without our will.

But when he says “the faithful in Christ Jesus,” this too has been carefully placed for the sake of distinction. For there are many faithful people, but not in Christ Jesus. If someone returns a deposit; if someone does not deny what has been entrusted to him, shows himself to be a faithful friend, and is prepared to betray his soul rather than his trust—as we read of certain philosophers (and, lest they boast too much, an Athenian prostitute did the same)—that person is indeed faithful, but he is not faithful in Christ Jesus.

(Verse 2.) “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.”

Either both expressions refer to both persons—that is, both grace and peace refer both to God the Father and to our Lord Jesus Christ—or the expressions are to be distributed individually, so that grace refers to God the Father, while peace refers to Christ. For the text immediately continues: “To the praise of the glory of his grace, in which he glorified us in the Beloved,” so that the Father’s grace consists in his deigning to send the Son for our salvation, while the Son’s peace consists in our being reconciled through him to the Father, and in his making the two one by destroying the dividing wall and abolishing hostility in his flesh.

(Verse 3.) “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places, in Christ.”

Just as God, good according to his substance and nature, makes us good through participation in himself and says to Israel, “Be holy, because I am holy” (Lev. 20:7), so may he himself, being blessed, grant that we be blessed. The lawgiver gives blessings, and “the blessing of the Lord is upon the head of the righteous” (Prov. 10); from this blessing Baruch takes his name, which in our language means “blessed.”

He blessed us not with one blessing but with all of them—not in the sense that we all attain everything, but that, while individuals possess one or several of all the blessings, we all possess them through one another.

[Note: [Col. 0445D] The Cistercian manuscript reads: “we possess all or individual blessings.”]

And he blessed us not with earthly blessings but with spiritual ones. Earthly blessings include having children, abounding in wealth, and enjoying honor and health; such earthly blessing extends even to irrational beasts. For it is said of them: “The Lord blessed them and said: ‘Increase and multiply’” (Gen. 1:22).

Spiritual blessings, however, are in the heavenly places, because the earth cannot contain spiritual blessing. Indeed, those blessings that are promised in Leviticus to those who obey God’s commandments—for example, lending at interest to foreign nations, having storehouses full of grain, and being blessed in the cities (Deut. 28), blessed in the fields, and other things of this kind—we shall not see [or: do not see] fulfilled in the prophets, who “wandered in sheepskins and goatskins,” in poverty, distress, deserts, mountains, caves, and clefts of rocks, avoiding the assaults of their persecutors (Heb. 11).

Therefore everything must be understood spiritually, and spiritual blessings must be awaited not in earthly places but in heavenly ones. But when he says, “He has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places,” as though this had already happened in the past and had not been promised for the future—that is, “he has blessed,” not “he will bless”—the question arises how, while we are still placed on earth, he has blessed us with a heavenly blessing.

Either, then, because our citizenship is in heaven and we are not of this world; because, having laid aside the image of the earthly creature, we bear the image of the heavenly one; because we do not live in the flesh but in the spirit; and because we store up treasures for ourselves in heaven, where our heart also is—we are said now to have been blessed with a heavenly blessing; or certainly because every spiritual blessing, although it is on earth, is nevertheless reckoned as coming from the heavenly places.

“He has blessed us,” he says, “with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ”: in the word of God, wisdom, truth, and the other virtues.

The sentence may also be read in two ways: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,” so that “blessed be God,” who is the creator of all things, concludes the first unit, and the next clause follows: “who is also the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ”; or in this way, so that “God and Father” is referred jointly to “our Lord.”

Blessed is the God of the assumed man, and the Father of him who in the beginning was God the Word with God. This does not mean that one is the assumed man and another the Word who assumed him, but that one and the same person is proclaimed now in exalted terms and now in humble terms, according to the variety of circumstances.

(Verse 4.) “Just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him.”

[Note: [Col. 0445D] Jerome, wishing to clear himself of the suspicion of favoring Origen, set these Commentaries on Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians in particular against Rufinus’s slanders, since they could demonstrate his own faith. Rufinus eagerly seized the opportunity, looking for a knot in a rush, and examined these very books with the most hostile diligence, perversely twisting them toward the discredit of Origen’s teaching and beginning his accusations with these words. We shall occasionally make observations in defense of the holy Doctor against the Aquileian presbyter; but since the force of the arguments cannot be set before the eyes within the narrow limits of notes, we advise readers to consult Rufinus’s books of invective, from section twenty-three of the first book to the end of the second, and judge for themselves.]

For “before the foundation of the world,” the Greek has written πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου (*pro katabolēs kosmou*). But *katabolē* does not mean exactly what *constitutio*—“foundation” or “establishment”—means. Therefore, because of the poverty of our language and the novelty of the subject, and as someone has said, because Greek speech is broader and the language more fortunate, we shall attempt not so much to translate word for word, which is impossible, as to explain the force of the word through a certain circumlocution.

Καταβολή (*katabolē*) properly refers to the act of throwing something downward, sending it from a height to a lower place, or to the beginning taken by something. Thus those who lay the first foundations of future buildings are said to have καταβεβληκέναι (*katabeblēkenai*), that is, to have cast down the beginnings of the foundations.

Paul therefore wished to show that God fashioned all things out of nothing. He did not refer to a condition, creature, or created thing, but to a καταβολή—that is, the beginning of a foundation—so that, contrary to Manichaeus and the other heresies that posit a maker and matter, nothing from which creatures were made preceded creatures, but all things came into existence from nothing.

When he testifies that God chose us to be holy and blameless before him—that is, before God—before the world’s creation, this pertains to God’s foreknowledge, for whom all future things are already accomplished, and everything is known before it comes to be. Thus Paul himself was predestined in his mother’s womb, and Jeremiah was sanctified in the womb (Jer. 1), chosen, strengthened, and sent as a prophet to the nations as a type of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0446D] In his *Apology against Rufinus*, the holy Father does not deny that this other person is Origen; he explains why he suppressed his name: “For it is the commentator’s task to present the opinions of many, and I had promised in the preface that I would do this. I also included Origen’s exposition without the odium of his name, saying: ‘Another, however, who attempts to demonstrate that God is just,’ and so forth.”]

Another, however, who attempts to demonstrate that God chooses each person not through the prejudice of his foreknowledge but according to the merit of the chosen, says that, before the visible creatures—heaven, earth, seas, and everything contained in them—there were other invisible creatures, among which were souls. For certain reasons known only to God, these souls had been cast downward into this valley of tears, into the place of our affliction and exile, in which the saint prayed to be restored to his former position, saying: “Woe is me, that my sojourning has been prolonged! I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Cedar; my soul has been much in exile” (Ps. 119:5). And elsewhere: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” And: “It is better to return and be with Christ.” And elsewhere: “Before I was humbled, I sinned” (Ps. 118:67), and other things like these.

Therefore, they say, before the souls were hurled into the world, and the world was made from souls [or: animals] together with its inhabitants, God chose Paul and those like him—he himself having been cast down into the lowest place—to be holy and blameless before him. No one is chosen except from among many, and where there are some who are inferior, election takes place.

Just as, during the Babylonian captivity, when the people were led away by Nebuchadnezzar into Chaldea, the prophets Ezekiel, Daniel, the three youths, Haggai, and Zechariah were sent—not because they themselves deserved captivity, but to be a consolation to the captives—so, in that casting down of the world, those whom God had chosen before the world was made were sent to instruct and teach sinful souls, so that at their preaching they might return to the place from which they had fallen.

This, they say, is what Moses means in Psalm 89: “Lord, you have become our refuge from generation to generation: before the mountains were established, and before the earth and the world were made” (Ps. 89:1). That is, before the world was made and the whole human generation took its beginning, God was a refuge for his saints.

When he says, “that we should be holy and blameless before him,” there is this difference between “holy” and “blameless”: someone who is blameless may also be understood as holy, but someone who is blameless is not thereby immediately holy. Little children are blameless, because, with their bodies still undefiled, they have committed no sin; yet they are not holy, because holiness is acquired through the will and through effort.

And one who has not committed sins can be called blameless, whereas one who is full of virtues is holy, according to what is written in a certain psalm: “He who walks without blemish and practices righteousness” (Ps. 14:2). And in the Song of Songs: “You are altogether beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (Song 4:7).

The question arises how anyone can be holy and blameless before God, when the prophet testifies: “No living person shall be justified in your sight.” For either the Ephesians are holy and blameless before God, and the statement “No living person shall be justified in your sight” is false; or, if no one is justified in God’s sight, the preceding statement that they are holy and blameless before God is false.

The answer is twofold. Paul does not say: “He chose us before the foundation of the world when we were holy and blameless,” but: “He chose us so that we should be holy and blameless”—that is, we were not previously holy and blameless, but were to become so afterward. This can also be said of sinners who have turned to better things, and the statement will stand: “No living person shall be justified in your sight”—that is, throughout his life, during all the time he lived in this world.

Indeed, understood in this way, it also contradicts the one who says that souls were chosen before the world was made because of their holiness and freedom from every sinful fault. For, as we have already said, Paul and those like him are not chosen because they were holy and blameless; they are chosen and predestined so that in the subsequent life they may become holy and blameless through works and virtues.

Moreover, this too must be understood: he did not say, “No individual living person shall be justified in your sight,” but “Every living person”—that is, not everyone will be justified, but some will be justified.

(Verse 5.) “Predestining us in love for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ to himself.”

This may be read in two ways, so that “in love” is connected either with what precedes or with what follows. With what precedes: “that we should be holy and blameless before him in love,” followed by “predestining us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ to himself” [or: in him]. With what follows: “in love predestining us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ to himself.”

The Latin language does not express the distinction between the Greek forms προορίσας (*proorisas*, “having predestined”) and ὁρισθέντος (*horisthentos*, “having been appointed or defined”).

The former statement refers to those who previously did not exist: they were thought of before they came to be, and afterward came into existence. The latter refers to one whom no prior thought or will preceded, but who always existed and never received a beginning in order to exist. Therefore, concerning those who previously did not exist but later came into being, προορισθέντες (*prooristhentes*, “predestined”) is correctly used.

But concerning the Son—that is, our Lord Jesus Christ—it is written elsewhere, ὁρισθέντος (*horisthentos*, “appointed” or “defined”), because he was always with the Father, and the Father’s will never preceded him in order that he might exist. From this it follows that the Father has always existed and the Son has always existed, and that where eternity is coequal, the nature is the same.

It must also be added that although God predestines or predefines us [or: defines us] for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, we cannot become sons beforehand unless we receive faith in and understanding of his Son Jesus Christ. He is Son by nature; we are sons by adoption. He was never not the Son; we were predestined before we existed, and then received the spirit of adoption when we believed in the Son of God.

“According to the good pleasure of his will.”

The word εὐδοκία (*eudokia*), which the Latin language translated as *placitum*, “pleasure” or “decision,” is formed in Greek from two complete words, ἀπὸ τοῦ Εὖ καὶ τοῦ Δοκεῖν (*apo tou Eu kai tou Dokein*), “from well” and “from seeming” or “from approval.” We can call it *beneplacitum*, “good pleasure,” because not everything that pleases is immediately also rightly pleasing; rather, εὐδοκία—that is, “good pleasure”—is used only where what has pleased is shown to have pleased rightly.

The Septuagint interpreters translated this expression from the Hebrew RESON [reading uncertain], fashioning new words for new things.

Here, therefore, those who think that before the creation of the world souls lived with angels and the other orders of powers in the heavenly Jerusalem seize an opportunity. For they cannot understand it as either the good pleasure of God or the praise of his glory if some are born naked, barbarous, enslaved, and weak, while others are born wealthy, Roman, free, and healthy; some obscure and others noble, in different regions of the world—unless causes preceded these circumstances, by whose merits each soul received its particular lot.

They apply to the same meaning the passage in Romans that some think they know but do not know: “Does the potter not have power over the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Rom. 9:21). They argue that, just as life in this world is lived in goodness or evil, hardship or ease, without purpose unless we believe that God’s judgment is to come, so the diversity of those born into this world proves God’s justice unless the merits of souls preceded it.

For, they say, if we do not understand these things in this way, it will neither be according to the good pleasure of God’s will nor to the praise of his glory and grace that he chose some before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless and to receive adoption through Jesus Christ, while he destined others for the lowest condition and everlasting punishments.

[Note: [Col. 0449D] Rufinus adds here the word “will be referred.”]

(Vers. 6.) “To the praise of the glory of his grace, with which he has graced us in the Beloved.” What, they ask, is this praise of the glory of God’s grace: to grace some in Christ, but prepare others for eternal punishments; to love Jacob before he was born from the womb, and hate Esau before he had committed anything worthy of hatred—unless causes preceded them that demonstrate the justice of God? Therefore every grace that we receive is completed in the glory and praise of him who justified [another reading: graced] us in the Beloved—that is, in our Lord and Savior—because apart from wisdom, truth, justice, peace, redemption, and the other virtues, no good can be understood.

Nor should we suppose that the Latin manuscripts have written “in his beloved Son,” but simply “in the Beloved.” If “beloved of God” or “beloved of the Father” had been added, the meaning would have been straightforward and universally familiar: that our Lord Jesus Christ was loved by the Father. But we would not thereby grant anything remarkable to the Son’s uniqueness, since the Son would be loved in the same way as everything else. For it is said to God [another reading: “to him”]: “You love all things, and reject none of the things that you have made; for you would not have made anything if you hated it” (Wis. 11:23).

Or if the phrase had read, “with which he graced us in the Beloved above all,” every difficulty would have been removed, since we know that the patriarchs, prophets, and all holy men were loved by God. But now, because he spoke absolutely, saying “in the Beloved,” it seems to me that the phrase “by all” is to be understood. For if Christ, as we have often said, is wisdom, justice, peace, joy, self-control, and the other virtues, even those who cannot follow these virtues love the names of them; and no one is so openly criminal that he does not claim to love wisdom and justice.

Just as there is universal agreement among all human beings concerning the substance of God—that it is divine and cannot easily be comprehended by anyone’s understanding—although each person goes astray in imagining it to be of one kind or another, so too everyone loves Christ insofar as he signifies the various virtues, even though many cannot prove by their deeds that they love what they profess to love. This is the Beloved whom I think is also signified in Isaiah: “I will sing for my beloved the song of my beloved concerning my vineyard” (Isa. 5:1); and, “A vineyard was made for my beloved”; and in the twenty-eighth Psalm: “The Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon and crush them, like the calf of Lebanon, and the Beloved like the son of unicorns” (Ps. 28:6).

(Vers. 7.) “In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins.” The person who is redeemed is one who is captive and, having fallen into the power of enemies, has ceased to be free. Thus, some say that we too are captives in this world, held under rulers and powers by the yoke of servitude, unable to unbind hands fettered with chains or raise our eyes upward until the Redeemer comes.

“But who,” they ask, “is so great and powerful that he can redeem the whole world by his price?” Jesus Christ, the Son of God, gave his own blood and, rescuing us from slavery, granted us freedom. Indeed, if we believe the histories of the pagans—that Codrus, Curtius, and the Decii Mures checked the calamities of cities, pestilence, famine, and wars by their deaths—how much more should this be judged possible in the Son of God, who by his blood cleansed not one city but the whole world!

**Editorial note on Codrus, Curtius, and the Decii.** Ancient copyists did not know that the Decii were surnamed Mures (as in P. Decius Mus in Valerius Maximus, book I, *On Dreams*, chapter 7). Therefore they read *Mures* separately among the disasters that Decii and others had restrained by their deaths. Neither Erasmus nor Marianus Victorius corrected this error in his edition; both wrote uncorrected material from uncorrected copies, although otherwise they were learned men.

Codrus, king of the Athenians, exposed himself to certain death for the safety of his country. The Peloponnesians had received an oracle that they would rule only if they killed the enemy king. He therefore deceived them by disguising himself as a beggar and, provoking them to kill him by picking quarrels, fulfilled the oracle without being recognized. Hence Virgil has the following in his fifth Eclogue:

> Whether you have the fires of Phyllis,  
> or praise for Alcon, or the quarrels of Codrus.

Curtius—whose praenomen was Marcus—was a young and noble Roman who devoted himself to the *Di Manes* for the safety of his country. When the earth had sunk open in the middle of the forum with an enormous chasm, and it had been foretold that the fissure would not close unless one of the finest young men threw himself into it, Curtius did not hesitate to expend upon his country the life he had received from it. Mounting his horse, he immediately cast himself headlong into the chasm. Livy, book VI, says that three Curtii devoted themselves for the safety of the state. Valerius mentions only two, in book V, *On Piety toward the Fatherland*, chapter 4: namely, the man who first brought the consulship into his family, and his son, who followed his father’s example. Concerning both, Valerius Maximus says at the cited passage: “Thus it is difficult to determine whether the Roman state benefited more from the Decii as leaders or suffered more by losing them. Their life prevented them from being conquered; their death made it conquer.”

There were, however, three Decii: father, son, and grandson. Cicero says in the first *Tusculan Disputation*: “For when the father Decius was fighting against the Latins, the son against the Etruscans, and the grandson even against Pyrrhus, they exposed themselves to the weapons of the enemy,” and so forth.

**MART.**—Martianay also noted that *Mures* was the surname of the Decii, and that the older editions were therefore in error when they read *Mures* separately and counted it among the disasters that one of the Decii had checked by his death. To establish the truly correct reading, we shall cite several testimonies of the ancients. Cicero, *Philippic* XIII, no. 13: “There is also Decius, by those—if I am not mistaken—called the Decii Mures,” and so forth. Livy, book VIII: “They elected as consuls T. Manlius Torquatus for the third time and P. Decius Mus.” Then, in book X: “The new consuls were Q. Fabius Maximus for the third time and P. Decius Mus.” Finally, Frontinus, *On Aqueducts*: “The Appia was brought in under Appius Claudius, when M. Valerius Maximus and P. Decius Mus were consuls, in the twenty-first year after the beginning of the Samnite war,” and so forth.

Moreover, without the surname *Mus*, three Decii are very well known in Roman history—father, son, and grandson—who hastened toward certain death, as Cicero says in the first *Tusculan Disputation*, no. 37: “The father Decius while fighting against the Latins, the son against the Etruscans, and the grandson against Pyrrhus.” No histories of Codrus, king of the Athenians, and Curtius, the Roman knight, are concealed here.

Blood and flesh of Christ are understood in two ways: either as that spiritual and divine flesh of which he himself said, “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John 6:56), and, “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have eternal life” (ibid., 6:54); or as the flesh that was crucified and the blood that was poured out by the soldier’s lance.

**Note.** One Cistercian manuscript reads equally well: “and which was drawn out by the soldier’s lance.”

**Note.** Jerome calls Christ’s flesh divine and spiritual here because it is consecrated by divine power in the sacrament of the Eucharist; it exists spiritually and invisibly in that sacrament and, finally, is received and eaten invisibly and spiritually under a visible form. Although in all these respects it is divine and spiritual flesh, it is nevertheless true and substantial, according to the comparison that Jerome subsequently makes concerning the difference between blood and flesh in the Christian person.

**MART.**—Martianay also noted before us that Jerome calls it spiritual flesh because in the sacrament of the Eucharist it is spiritual and invisible, yet divine and true flesh, as is clear from the context itself.

According to this division, a diversity of blood and flesh is also understood among his saints, so that one kind of flesh is that which will see the salvation of God, while another flesh and blood is that which cannot possess the kingdom of God.

Consequently, after the redemption through Christ’s blood, we are said to have received forgiveness of sins, because unless we have been redeemed, our sins are forgiven us in vain.
