Nor can we receive forgiveness for our offenses and cease to be slaves until the once-bloodstained Victor has received the price on our behalf.

(Vers. 8.) “According to the riches of his grace, which has abounded in us” [another reading: “with which he has abounded in us”]. Whoever understands the statement, “You have been saved by grace, and not from works” (Eph. 2), and the debtor of fifty and five hundred denarii in the Gospel (Luke 7)—the one to whom more is forgiven loving more—can understand that, according to his riches, God’s grace has abounded in us. This is especially true in the Church gathered from the Gentiles, which had been alien to the covenant and the promises of Israel, through whose offense we obtained salvation.

Is there not an abundance of grace in Paul and in the other saints, of whom it is said, “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” (1 Cor. 5:3), and elsewhere, “Into which things angels long to look” (1 Pet. 1:12), and again, “Father, grant that just as I and you are one, so they too may be one in us” (John 17:21)? Whoever strives, labors, and contends to the utmost of human weakness, and says with the Apostle, “His grace toward me was not empty” (1 Cor. 15:10), does not render these riches of grace empty in himself. But whoever, forgetting the greatness of the benefit, slips into worse things—though rich in the grace of God and in his abundant generosity—is impoverished by poverty.

**Note.** The reading of the Cistercian manuscript is noteworthy: *parva* (“small”) instead of *vacua* (“empty”). We know that older copies of the Latin translation once preferred *parca* (“scant”), from which Ambrosiaster is said to have read *paupera* (“poor”); and the Greek text likewise varies in some books, where it has πτωχή (*ptōchē*, “poor”) instead of κενή (*kenē*, “empty”).

(Vers. 9.) “Making known to us, in all wisdom and prudence, the mystery of his will.” The Stoics too hold that wisdom and prudence are different, saying: “Wisdom is knowledge of divine and human things; prudence, however, concerns only mortal things.” According to this distinction, we may take wisdom as pertaining to invisible things and visible things, but prudence as pertaining only to visible things.

It is therefore asked how God has made known to us, in all wisdom and prudence, the mystery of his will. First, the statement should be understood simply: the mystery of his will is our redemption through the blood of his Son and the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace with which he has abounded in us. Thus, by believing in the Lord’s Passion—which is foolishness to those who do not believe—we possess wisdom and prudence.

Next, he made all the mysteries known to us through his Scriptures: how he first constructed heaven and earth, and made, ordered, and distinguished everything within them; how the created human being came into existence and the world was filled up to the Passion of Christ; and how invisible things are known from visible things.

Finally, even earthly things require wisdom and prudence. For how many of us know what it is that suspends birds in the air, fish in the waves, advances human footsteps, and rouses the fury of beasts?

**Note.** This reading, especially that of the Cistercian manuscripts, is very pleasing: *necnon* (“and also”), rather than the nonsensical *non necet* formerly printed in the editions.

But a careful reader will immediately object: If Paul knows in part, prophesies in part, and now sees through a mirror in an enigma (1 Cor. 13), how was the mystery of God revealed either to him or to the Ephesians in all wisdom and prudence?

We are therefore compelled by this difficulty to change the order of reading and arrange the passage as follows: “According to the good pleasure of his will, to the praise of the glory of your grace, with which he graced us in the Beloved; in whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace with which he has abounded in us in all wisdom and prudence.” Once we have thus distinguished the phrase “in all wisdom and prudence,” joining it to what precedes, we may then continue: “Making known to us the mystery of his will according to his good pleasure.”

The sentence may also retain its existing form: although they see in part and prophesy in part, the mystery may now be said to have been revealed to them in all wisdom and prudence. This does not mean that they learned the mystery in all wisdom and prudence, but that God, in all his wisdom and prudence, revealed the mystery to them according to what they were able to attain.

(Vers. 10.) “According to his good pleasure, which he purposed in him for the dispensation of the fullness of times.” Above he had said, “according to the good pleasure of his will”; here, “according to his good pleasure,” with “will” omitted.

**Note.** In one Cistercian manuscript, *voluntate* (“will”) has been deleted.

There he used προορισμός (*proorismos*), that is, “predestination,” for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ; here, however, he uses πρόθεσις (*prothesis*), that is, “purpose” or “proposal.” Those who habitually distinguish words argue that predestination and purpose differ in this respect: predestination prefigures, long beforehand in the mind of the one who predestines, what is going to happen; purpose, however, occurs when the execution is already near and the effect almost follows upon the thought.

What he says, “which he purposed in him,” refers to the mystery. For above he had said that he made known to us the mystery of his will; and this mystery is the dispensation of the fullness of times, so that everything might be completed at the appointed time. Just as an heir, while he is a child, although the property is his, does not yet possess the inheritance because it is not yet due to him (Gal. 4), so the mystery that had been predestined by God for the adoption of his sons could not previously be dispensed until its proper time arrived.

Concerning this Paul also says elsewhere, using the singular number: “But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son” (ibid., 4:4). He could not come earlier unless the mystery of the time had been fulfilled.

(Vers. 10.) “To recapitulate all things in Christ, those in heaven and those on earth” [another reading adds: “which are”], “in him.” In the Latin manuscripts, instead of *recapitulare* (“to recapitulate”), *instaurare* [another reading: *restaurare*] (“to restore” or “renew”) is written. I am surprised that the translators did not use the very Greek word, since they adopted from Greek such expressions as dialectic and philosophy.

Orators too, in epilogues or before epilogues, at the end of their cases, for the sake of reminding judges and those who had heard the proceedings, customarily make a recapitulation—that is, ἀνακεφαλαίωσις (*anakephalaiōsis*)—so that what they had previously discussed at greater length might later be gathered into a brief speech, and each person might begin to remember what he had heard.

**Note.** I would prefer to write *recapitulationem* (“recapitulation”), both because of the argument and because of the meaning of the Greek word. In any case, several Latin Fathers are known to have read *recapitulare* here, which Jerome prefers in accordance with the Greek text: Tertullian, *Against Marcion* V.17, and the translator of St. Irenaeus I.1.

The meaning of the present passage is therefore this: the entire dispensation that began both before the world and afterward in the world, concerning invisible as well as visible creatures, promised the coming of the Son of God. Adam, who was expelled from paradise, was to be recalled through the Savior (Gen. 3). The division of languages at the construction of the tower (Gen. 11) foretold the gift of tongues in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 2). Isaac, as a type of the Lord, himself carried his cross (Gen. 3). Samson, nourishing his sacred hair, loved the embraces of the poor woman Delilah and confessed all the secrets of his heart to her (Judg. 16); this signified the mystery of the Savior and of the Church from the Gentiles, truly poor and needy (John 19).

In the Lord’s cross and Passion, therefore, everything was recapitulated—that is, everything was reckoned together in this ἀνακεφαλαίωσις (*anakephalaiōsis*). To make this clearer, let us give an example from daily life. Suppose that I spent twenty denarii, then five more, and another fifteen; at different times I also gave thirty and three times ten. If I wish to add these together, the sum of one hundred appears to me, and in this single number I possess everything that I previously set out.

Thus all the mysteries and the entire dispensation of antiquity—not only what took place on earth, but also what took place in heaven—are completed in Christ’s Passion. Once Christ has suffered, been buried, risen, and ascended victoriously to the Father, I no longer need the earlier reckoning, because I hold everything in one. Pay close attention: not only all the histories of Scripture that the Holy Spirit recounts as having taken place on earth, but also those heavenly things hidden from us, are held as recapitulated in Christ’s Passion.

(Vers. 11.) “In whom we have also been called by lot, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who accomplishes everything according to the counsel of his will.” The language of inheritance and lot, through which we come to have a share in Christ, shows that we have migrated from one power to another. According to what is written in Deuteronomy, “When the Most High divided the nations, when he scattered the sons of Adam” (Deut. 32:8), we have been transferred from the dominion of angels to the portion of the Lord.

Those powers retained what belonged to another, whether it had been entrusted to them or usurped by them. But this one received what was his. “And ascending on high, he led captivity captive” (Ps. 68:18): that is, those who had previously been taken captive into destruction, he himself captured for life, in order to lead them back on high. In a certain sense, captivity itself was captured, since through a second captivity those who had previously been captured were liberated.

It should be considered that here too προορισμός (*proorismos*) and πρόθεσις (*prothesis*), that is, predestination and purpose, are placed together, according to which God accomplishes all things according to the counsel of his will. This does not mean that everything that happens in the world is carried out by God’s will and counsel; otherwise evils too could be attributed to God. Rather, it means that everything he does, he does with counsel and will, so that it is full of reason and of the power of the one who acts.

We human beings often wish to do things with deliberation, but the result by no means follows our will. No one, however, can resist God so that he does not do everything he wills. He wills whatever is full of reason and counsel; he wills that all be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. 2). But because no one is saved without his own will—for we possess free choice—he wills that we will the good, so that, when we have willed it, he too may fulfill his own counsel in us.

(Vers. 12.) “So that we may be to the praise of his glory, who have previously hoped in Christ.” If he had said only “we have hoped in Christ,” and had not prefixed “previously”—which in Greek is προηλπικότες (*proēlpikotes*)—the meaning would have been clearer: that those who hoped in Christ were called by lot and predestined according to the purpose of him who accomplishes everything according to the counsel of his will.

But now the addition of the preposition leads us to the interpretation about which we discussed above, explaining the statement:

**Note.** Rufinus, whom one may consult at I.29–30 and following, inserts here “that is, before.” A little later he also reads “he blessed” and “he chose” instead of “he has blessed” and “he has chosen,” and similarly elsewhere. “He blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, so that we should be holy and blameless before him.” Thus, just as we are said to have been blessed with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places and chosen before the foundation of the world, so now we are also said to have previously hoped in Christ, from the time when we were chosen, predestined, and blessed in the heavenly places.

Another interpreter, unwilling to accept the doctrine that we existed and hoped in Christ before we lived in this body, will transfer the meaning and say that, at the coming of the Lord Savior—when every knee of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth will bow in his name, and every tongue will confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. 2)—when everything has been subjected to him, some willingly and others by necessity, those who previously hoped in him before his majestic presence will be for the praise of his glory and will be called ἀπηλπικότες (*apēlpikotes*, “those who have despaired”) [the manuscript has προηλπικότας]. Those, however, who are found to believe by necessity, at the time when neither the devil nor his angels will be able to deny that he reigns, will be hoping—but not to the praise of his glory.

We now see this being fulfilled in part, since the reward of the one who follows God willingly is different from that of the one who follows by necessity. Nevertheless, whether through opportunity or through truth, let Christ be proclaimed—provided that the one who hopes, and the one who has previously hoped, understands that they will receive different rewards according to the diversity of their hope.

(Vers. 13.) “In whom you also, having heard the word of truth, the Gospel of your salvation—in whom also, having believed, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise.” “In whom”: plainly, in Christ. Among the others who heard, you too, Ephesians, heard the word of truth, the Gospel of your salvation; believing in it, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise.

According to the order of reading, however, the sentence does not seem to stand, nor is anything supplied to follow what was first stated—“in whom you also, having heard the word of truth, the Gospel of your salvation”—because “in whom” is immediately repeated a second time. Since this is superfluous, removing it from the middle can restore the text to a proper reading.

Paul endured this because of his excessive love for Christ: he always named the one whom he loved, even unnecessarily and beyond ordinary usage. A diligent reader can find this throughout all his Epistles. Thus the second occurrence of “in whom” appears to have disturbed the order of the sentence and left the preceding proposition unfinished.

Nor is it a small praise of the Ephesians that they heard not merely preaching but the word of truth. For we read in another Epistle that there is a great difference between preaching and the word of truth: “My word and my preaching,” he says, “were not in persuasive words of wisdom, but in a demonstration of the Spirit and of power” (1 Cor. 2:4).

Let us investigate more carefully where else it is written that someone heard the word of truth, so that Paul’s meaning may be made clear by comparison. Let us also see where the Gospel is named, either with an accompanying qualification or absolutely. With a qualification: “my Gospel” (Rom. 16:25), “the Gospel of Jesus Christ” (2 Cor. 2:12), “the eternal Gospel” (Rev. 14:6), or what is now said to the Ephesians, “the Gospel of your salvation.” Absolutely, as when he speaks of Luke: “Whose praise in the Gospel is throughout all the churches” (2 Cor. 8:18).

The person who has heard the word of truth and believed in it is sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise. For there are many who have heard but, remaining unbelieving, have by no means obtained the seal of the Holy Spirit.

It is also said to the prince of Tyre, “You are the seal of the likeness of God” (Ezek. 28:12). The seal of God is this: just as the first human being was created in the image and likeness of God, so in the second regeneration whoever has obtained the Holy Spirit is sealed by him and receives the form of the Creator.

It should also be sought where else “the Holy Spirit of promise” is written, and what it signifies. For I think that just as the Holy Spirit makes holy the person into whom he has been infused; the spirit of wisdom makes wise; the spirit of understanding makes understanding; the spirit of counsel makes cautious and deliberate; the spirit of fortitude makes strong; the spirit of knowledge makes knowledgeable; the spirit of piety makes pious; and the spirit of fear makes fearful and trembling with the fear of God—so also the spirit of promise, or the Spirit of God, makes a person in whom he dwells a guarantor and a god.

Conversely, the unclean spirit makes a person unclean and, as an unclean inhabitant, prepares for himself a polluted house. The spirit of fornication makes fornicators, of whom the prophet also says, “They were led astray by the spirit of fornication” (Hos. 4:12). The evil spirit makes people evil and perverse; and the demonic spirit makes demons.

**Note.** The Royal manuscript reads, “and the demonic spirit makes the possessed,” a reading that cannot be wholly rejected. MART.

Whatever the liquid may have been that was poured into new clay, the vessel retains its odor and [probably, “flavor”] for a long time.

(Vers. 14.) “Who is the pledge of our inheritance, for the redemption of the possession, to the praise of his glory.” The Latin translator used *pignus* (“pledge”) for *arrhabo* (“guarantee” or “earnest”). But *arrhabo* does not mean the same thing as *pignus*. An *arrhabo* is given as a kind of testimony and bond for a future purchase. A *pignus*, however—that is, ἐνέχυρον (*enechuron*)—is pledged against a mutual loan, so that when the debt has been repaid, the creditor returns the pledge to the one who repaid it.

Again, where he says “for the redemption of the adoption,” the Greek does not have υἱοθεσία (*huiothesia*, “adoption”), but περιποίησις

**Note.** Several manuscripts and authors still attest that the Old Latin translation read *adoptionis*: the Codex Claromontanus, the Codex Sangermanensis, Ambrosiaster, Hieronymiaster, and others.

(*peripoiēsis*), (*peripoiēsis*), which we may call “acquisition” or “possession”; yet even this does not express the full force of the wording.

There are many words that cannot be transferred from Greek into Latin, nor from Hebrew into Greek, and conversely neither from Latin into Greek nor from Greek into Hebrew. Therefore, whoever has received not merely the Holy Spirit but the Holy Spirit of promise will at the same time receive the guarantee of the inheritance—and that inheritance is everlasting life.

Just as the future purchase and possession are estimated from the guarantee—for example, from ten solidi one may infer a property worth one hundred solidi, and from one hundred solidi a possession worth one thousand—so from the quality of the guarantee the greatness of the inheritance that will afterward follow may be recognized.

Although someone may be holy and perfect and, in everyone’s judgment, considered worthy of blessedness, he has nevertheless received the Spirit as a guarantee of the future inheritance. If the guarantee is so great, how great will the possession itself be?

And just as the guarantee given to us is not outside us but within us, so the inheritance itself—the kingdom of God, which is within us—is located inwardly in us. For what greater inheritance could there be than to contemplate and see, by perception, the beauty of Wisdom, the Word, Truth, and Light, and to behold the ineffable and magnificent nature of God himself, as well as the substance of all things created in the likeness of God?

This Holy Spirit of promise, therefore, who is the guarantee of our inheritance, is now given to the saints so that they may be redeemed and joined to God, to the praise of his glory. This does not mean that God needs anyone’s praise, but that the praise of God benefits those who praise him; and, as they recognize his majesty and greatness through each of his works, they burst forth in wonder and astonishment to praise him.

(Vers. 15 ff.) “Therefore I too, having heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus and toward all the saints, do not cease giving thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers: that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, with the eyes of your heart enlightened.”

Although a word-for-word translation might excuse the Apostle to a careful reader—since the entire construction of the sentence appears to overflow and become solecistic—the same defect is also heard in the Greek. Therefore, responding especially to our Greek critics, we shall attempt to arrange the order of reading according to the sense, so that we say:

“Having heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus and toward all his saints, and seeing the difference between your faith in the Lord and in all his saints, I do not cease giving thanks and remembering you in my prayers, so that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, but the Father of glory, may give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation.”

What follows—“with the eyes of your heart enlightened”—may be rendered by hyperbaton as follows:

“Therefore I too, having heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus in the knowledge of him, with the eyes of your heart enlightened, and toward all the saints, do not cease giving thanks for you and remembering you in my prayers, so that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge, so that you may know what is the hope of your calling,” and so forth.

Two Cistercian manuscripts prefer *gratiae* (“of grace”) instead of *gloriae* (“of glory”).

The phrase “the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, but the Father of glory” should be understood as follows. Just as our Lord Jesus Christ himself is the Word, Wisdom, Truth, Peace, Justice, and Fortitude, so he is also Glory, according to what is said elsewhere: “The glory of God will appear” (Lev. 9:23). In nearly the whole of the Old Law it is written that the glory of God was seen above the tabernacle of testimony (Num. 9). The Psalmist also sings: “Arise, my glory; arise” (Ps. 108:2).

This Glory, illuminating the world with its radiance, fashioned for itself a temple from the Virgin’s womb. God becomes the Father of this temple’s glory. Wherever Christ is Glory, there alone the Father is named; wherever Jesus is named, his God is mentioned without any additional designation.

This God, therefore, is the God of the assumed human being, while the Father of glory, wisdom, and truth gives believers in his Son the spirit of wisdom and revelation, so that they may become wise and, with unveiled face, contemplate the glory of the Lord.

When this wisdom and revelation have made them wise and opened hidden mysteries to them, it immediately follows that they have the eyes of their heart enlightened. The present words establish that, corresponding to the external members of the human being, the members of the inner human being are also spoken of. For he plainly called them the eyes of the heart, although we cannot understand this without perception and mind.

The following statement of the Psalmist also agrees with this: “Illuminate my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death” (Ps. 13:4). And elsewhere: “The eyes of the wise are in his head” (Eccl. 2:14). If we understand “eyes” simply as the eyes of the flesh, then the eyes of the wise person, no less than those of the foolish, are in his head. The head of the wise person therefore signifies understanding, because it is also called by other words: mind, spirit, and the governing principle of the heart.

As for the phrase “in the knowledge of him”—that is, ἐπιγνώσει αὐτοῦ (*epignōsei autou*)—some understand it

**Note.** The same manuscripts read εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν (“for knowledge”) without the added αὐτοῦ (“of him”). Compare Rufinus, I.38.

by distinguishing between γνῶσις (*gnōsis*) and ἐπίγνωσις (*epignōsis*), that is, between “notion” and “knowledge.” by distinguishing between γνῶσις (*gnōsis*) and ἐπίγνωσις (*epignōsis*), that is, between “notion” and “knowledge.” They say that *notion* concerns things that we previously did not know but afterward began to know, whereas *knowledge* concerns things that we once knew but later ceased to know and afterward remembered. From this they conjecture that we had an earlier life in the heavenly places, after which we were cast into these bodies and forgot God the Father; now, through revelation, we have come to know him again, according to the statement: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord” (Ps. 22:27), and other similar passages that they repeat.

(Vers. 18 ff.) “So that you may know what is the hope of his calling, what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance among the saints, and what is the surpassing greatness of his power toward us who believe [Al. “believed”], according to the working of the might of his power [Col. 0459C], which he exercised in Christ, raising him from the dead.”

To whoever, according to Paul’s prayer, the spirit of wisdom and revelation has once been given, so that, with the eyes of his heart opened, he may behold these things, it will become known what has been stored up for those who are called, what is to be hoped for by God’s saints, and what he will abundantly and generously give to those who possess his inheritance.

For this knowledge, the greatness of God’s power is necessary in those who, like Paul, are called as believers. Through this power God worked in Christ Jesus, whom he raised from the dead.

“[Inheritance]” is to be understood in two ways: either that the soul of our Lord Jesus Christ—the one assumed from the body and soul of a human being—is the inheritance of the firstborn of every creature, and that we, together with the inheritance of that soul, may inherit God the Word;

[Note: [Col. 0460D] The Cistercian manuscripts once again read more fully, “and of the one who,” etc.]

or that, in Christ, our inheritance is the one divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: just as the inheritance of houses and estates is called that very property which is possessed by the heirs, so God himself is the inheritance of believers and saints.

It is also written in the Old Testament: “But you shall not give an inheritance to the sons of Levi among their brothers, because I am their portion” (Num. XVIII, 20); and elsewhere: “The Lord is their inheritance” (Deut. XVIII, 2). And the saint who knows that he possesses nothing apart from God speaks boldly: “The Lord is my portion” (Ps. LXXII, 26); and: “You are the portion of my inheritance and of my cup” (Ps. XV, 5).

[Col. 0460A] It is therefore no small matter of concern that we should know the hope of our calling and the riches of God’s glorious inheritance among the saints. For we need, in order to know these things, the same power by which God also acted in raising his Son—whom he raised not once only, but continually, from the dead, and made him free among the dead, unstained by any contagion of death.

Christ rises daily from the dead; he is raised daily in penitents. This is not to say that, according to the flesh, he did not also possess the power to lay down his soul and take it up again—for no one takes it from him unless he lays it down of his own accord—but rather that, according to the dispensation of the flesh and of the Son, the man and the Son are said to have been raised by God the Father.

[Col. 0460B] (Vers. 21.) “And making him sit at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality and power and virtue and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come.”

By means of a human likeness he demonstrated God’s power—not that a throne is set up, with God the Father sitting upon it and having the Son seated beside him, but because we cannot understand him as judging and reigning in any other way than through our own words.

To this also belongs what is written in the one-hundred-ninth Psalm: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet” (Ps. CIX, 1). For if the Son sits at the Father’s right hand in accordance with the appearance of a reigning sovereign, it is necessary that, by the same likeness, he should be greater than the one who sits on the left.

[Col. 0460C] But that we may know that this is to be understood otherwise than the letter sounds, the same psalm teaches in what follows, saying: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek: the Lord is at your right hand.” For how, if the Son sits at the Father’s right hand, is the Father again said to be at his right hand? Or how is the earth the footstool of his feet and heaven his throne, when he is also said, according to Isaiah, to hold the earth in his fist and to measure heaven with the span of his hand (Isa. XL)?

For that which is contained by someone cannot be within that same person; nor can he hold enclosed in his hand that by which he himself, according to the appearance of one seated, is surrounded.

Therefore, just as being near to God or withdrawing far from him is to be understood not according to distances of place but according to merits—for the saints are near him, while sinners, of whom the prophet says, “Behold, those who distance themselves from you shall perish” (Ps. LXXII, 27), are removed from all proximity to him—so also being at God’s right or left hand is to be understood in this sense: the saints are at his right hand, while sinners are at his left, as the Savior himself confirms in the Gospel when he speaks of the sheep as being at the right hand and the goats at the left (Matt. XXV).

The very word “to sit,” moreover, signifies the authority of a kingdom, by which God grants a benefit to those over whom he deigns to sit: namely, that he rules them, has them in his chariot, and turns their previously wandering and free necks according to his own command.

After this, the question arises how what follows can be understood: “above every principality and power and virtue and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come.” Something has already been said about the right and left hands and about sitting. Now we must ask where the Apostle found these four names—principality, power, virtue, and dominion—and from where he brought them forth.

For it is not permissible to think that a man instructed in divine reading spoke of something that is not found in the sacred books. I therefore suppose either that he brought forth from the traditions of the Hebrews those matters that are secret,

[Col. 0461B] or certainly that, understanding the Law to be spiritual, he understood more sublimely that what is written in a quasi-historical manner—what is related in Numbers and in the Books of Kings about kings, princes, commanders, tribunes, and centurions—is an image of other princes and kingdoms: namely, that in the heavenly places there are principalities, powers, dominions, and virtues, along with the other designations of ministries, which neither can we name nor, I think, could Paul himself enumerate, being confined within a small and weighty body.

[Note: [Col. 0461C] This conjecture of Jerome’s preceded Grotius’s, who very learnedly demonstrated that these names of dignities had been devised after the model of those who held the highest offices at the Persian court. Indeed, the number of seven angels who stand before God with the highest dignity corresponds excellently with the seven ministers who stood before the king of Persia and could see him, address him, and consult him whenever they wished. Nor is there doubt that Scripture frequently conforms itself to those matters that were closer to the Hebrews’ conception and way of thinking.]

But if there are principalities, powers, virtues, and dominions, they must also have subjects—those who fear them, serve them, and are strengthened by their might.

[Note: [Col. 0461D] Rufinus has, “those who are strengthened by their own strength,” etc. See Book II of the Invectives, no. 37.]

These distributions of offices will exist not only in the present age but also in the age to come, so that, through successive advances, honors, and ascents,

[Note: [Col. 0461D] Our manuscripts and those of Rufinus supply the word “also,” which adds, I do not know how much significance.]

and also descents, one may either increase or decrease and become subject to one or another power, virtue, principality, and dominion.

[Note: [Col. 0461D] This sentence might seem to smell of Origen’s doctrine. Thus Saint Jerome, inflamed by the accusations of the Aquileian presbyter, defends himself in Book I of the Apology, no. 23: “But if he thinks that I follow Origen for this reason—that I have introduced advances, honors, ascents, descents, increases, and diminutions in my exposition—let him know that there is a great difference between saying that angels, seraphim, and cherubim become demons and men, which Origen asserts, and saying that the angels themselves have been assigned different kinds of offices, which is not contrary to the Church. Accordingly, Huet may not have properly understood the mind of the holy Father when he thinks that Jerome does not deny that even now angels aspire to higher things, descend to lower things by doing evil, that some become subject to one power or principality and others to another, and that such changes will continue eternally, though only within the limits of angelic nature—and that the sole difference between Origen’s doctrine and Jerome’s is that Origen thought angels could descend also into the nature of men and demons. On the contrary, Jerome posits no change of rank among the angels themselves, as will be clear to anyone who attends to the context of the cited Apology, where he explains his opinion more fully. He merely holds that the various ranks—archangels, principalities, powers, and so forth—are assigned to angels according to their merits and virtues, or that the angels themselves can still receive different names according to the office to which they are appointed.”]

We little human beings, soon to be dissolved into ashes and dust, if by the agreement of men we are raised to be kings, have so many differences and multitudes of ministers that we can more easily perceive them than describe them. For example:

[Note: [Col. 0462D] One Cistercian manuscript reads: “that the prefect in the civil administration has judges in the provinces,” etc.]

a prefect in the civil administration has judges, provinces, and his own order; again, the army is divided into so many counts, commanders, tribunes, and various forces. Do we suppose that God, Lord of lords and King of kings, is content with a single ministry?

(Vers. 22, 23.) “And he subjected all things under his feet, and gave him as head over all things to the Church, which is his body, the fullness of him who is fulfilled in all things.”

[Note: [Col. 0462D] The same manuscripts adhere more closely to the Greek: “he subjected [them] under his feet,” ὑπέταξεν ὑπὸ τοὺς πόδας. Shortly afterward, the Vulgate translator prefers “over the whole Church” to “over all things of the Church.” This is less satisfactory; and when we reach that passage in Jerome’s version, we shall say that this phrase does not seem to have been revised according to the judgment of the holy Doctor, although we know that one or another Greek manuscript reads πᾶσαν τὴν Ἐκκλησίαν, “the whole Church.”]

This appears to contradict what is written elsewhere: “For we do not yet see all things subjected to him.” And also: “For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet” (I Cor. XV, 25). If all things have not yet been subjected to him, and he must reign until all things are subjected to him, how has God now subjected everything under his feet? Especially since Paul himself testifies elsewhere: “But when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all” (I Cor. XV, 28).

Either, therefore, he speaks according to foreknowledge [Al. “presence”], mentioning as already accomplished what is still future, in accordance with the sense we explained above, where he says: “He blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ.”

Or, if this is to be understood of the past, we should take it in this way: even those things that are not subjected to him willingly serve him by the condition of their nature—for example, demons, Jews, and Gentiles. They do not serve Christ, nor are they subjected to his feet; nevertheless, because they were created by him for a good purpose, they are subject against their will to his power, even though by the freedom of their will they resist him.

In this sense what follows also fits: “And he gave him as head over all things to the Church, which [568] is his body.” For just as a head has many members subjected to it, among which some are diseased and weak, so also our Lord Jesus Christ, being the head of the Church, has as members all who are gathered into the Church, both saints and sinners: the saints subjected to him by their will, but sinners subjected to him by necessity. Thus even his enemies are subjected to his feet.

Therefore, in saying “all things,” he seems to raise a difficulty. For the statement, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool” (Ps. CIX, 1), and elsewhere, “He must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet” (I Cor. XV, 25), requires no particularly elaborate interpreter: those things that are hostile, once they have been overcome, are subjected to his feet and pass into the power of the victor.

[Note: [Col. 0463D] Two Cistercian manuscripts read, “under his feet.”]

But why all things—that is, angels, thrones, dominions, powers, and the other virtues—which have never been hostile to God, should be subjected to his feet seems obscure.

It may therefore be answered that no one is without sin, and that the stars themselves are not clean before God, and that all creation trembles at the coming of the Creator (Job XV). Hence the cross of the Savior is said to have purified not only the things on earth but also those in heaven.

[Note: [Col. 0463D] He repeats similar arguments below, in Book II, chapter II, verse 24, and in Book II, chapter III, verse 10, and finally in chapter IV. Everywhere he adopts the view that Christ’s cross benefited not only us but also the higher angels and the other celestial powers. We have touched on some of these matters in connection with Origen’s Homily 23, where he rather absurdly declares that angels, no less than human beings, needed Christ’s death for salvation. Jerome does not exaggerate the matter to quite that extent, and his meaning can be explained in a sufficiently acceptable sense, whatever Rufinus may mutter against it in Book I, no. 38. We shall discuss these matters more fully shortly, in connection with chapter I, verse 10, where the holy Father explains himself more clearly.]

Another interprets “all things” not as referring to the totality but only to those matters under discussion:

[Note: [Col. 0464D] Our manuscripts read, “as in this way.”]

for example, “the whole city shouted,” not because no one in the city remained silent, but because even the lesser elements are called “the whole” in the sense of the greater part.

The Apostle Paul likewise says: “All seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Phil. II, 21); and: “All abandoned me.” He does not mean that Timothy and the other disciples who were with him at the time when the Epistles were written had abandoned him; rather, because he had been deserted by many, he complains that he had been deserted by all—that is, by the greater part.

Something similar is heard in the Psalm: “All have turned aside; together they have become useless. There is no one who does good, not even one” (Ps. XIII, 3). For if all have turned aside, then the one who speaks has also turned aside.

And elsewhere: “I said in the excess of my mind, Every man is a liar” (Ps. CXV, 2). For either what he said is true or it is false. If every man is a liar, then the one who speaks is also a liar. But if the one who speaks is also a liar, then even what he says—that every man is a liar—is not true. If, however, the statement is true, “all” must be understood in the sense stated above: that the greater part of humanity lies.

The Apostle also writes elsewhere: “Teaching every man” (Col. III, 16). And again: “Admonishing every man.” He does not mean that he taught every human being—for how many there are even today who have heard neither the Apostle’s teaching nor his name! Rather, he teaches and admonishes all who are in the Church and desire to know the things of God.

It follows: “The fullness of him who is fulfilled in all things.” This must be understood in the same manner as the statement: “Then he himself will be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all” (I Cor. XV, 28).

At present God is in each person only partially: in one there is justice, in another chastity, in another temperance, in another wisdom, in another courage. It is difficult even for holy and perfect men to possess all the virtues simultaneously.

But when, at the end of all things and the consummation of the world, everything has been subjected to him, he will be fulfilled in all things: so that, just as God is full of every virtue, he may be fulfilled in all things, and all may possess everything that previously each possessed individually.

This statement also—“And he gave him as head over all things to the Church, which is his body, the fullness of him who is fulfilled in all things”—can be understood of the Church not only of human beings but also of angels, all the powers, and rational creatures.

[Note: [Col. 0464D] From this passage Rufinus again accuses Jerome of Origenism in Book II, no. 34.]

Nor should the words “who is fulfilled in all things” be understood simply as they sound. For he does not say, “who fulfills all things in all,” but “who is fulfilled in all things.”

[570] To fulfill and to be fulfilled are different: in the one case the verb concerns the agent, in the other the recipient.

Therefore, just as an emperor is fulfilled when his army increases daily, new provinces are added, and the multitude of peoples grows, so our Lord Jesus Christ, in that all things believe in him and come daily to his faith, is himself fulfilled in all things. This happens in such a way, however, that all things are fulfilled in all: that is, those who believe in him are full of every virtue and, according to the Gospel, cause him to advance in age, wisdom, and grace, not only before God but also before men (Luke II).

(Cap. II—Vers. 1 ff.) “And you, when you were dead in your trespasses and sins, in which you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit who now works in the sons of unbelief, in which we all once lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the wills of the flesh and of our thoughts, and we were by nature children of wrath, even as the others. But God, who is rich in mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, made us alive together with Christ.”

[Note: [Col. 0464D] Victorius substitutes “of minds” (*mentium*) for “of thoughts” (*cogitationum*), because he inferred that Jerome had read it from the explanation which follows, although both the Vulgate edition and the Greek word διανοιῶν oppose this. The Interpreter’s words that especially moved him are these: “He says, ‘doing,’ not one will of the flesh but many; and not only the wills of the flesh but also of minds, for which Latin codices have ‘of thoughts.’ I think that the difference between sin of the flesh and of minds is this: sin of the flesh is unchastity and lust, and those things which are fulfilled in sensual indulgences through its ministry; but the trespass of minds concerns doctrines contrary to truth and heretical perversity.” We judged that we ought not to alter anything without the support of manuscripts, especially since the sole variant reading in Greek, cited from a manuscript by John Gregory—namely, ἐπιθυμιῶν—is much farther removed. A little later the Cistercian manuscripts prefer “exceeding love” (*nimiam charitatem*) instead of “great love,” etc.]

[Col. 0465A] Before we discuss the meaning of each individual word, it seems to us that the order of the reading should be restored as follows:

“And you, when you were dead in trespasses and sins, God made you alive together with Christ—he who is rich in mercy because of his great love with which he loved us”—and:

“When we were dead in trespasses, in which we once walked according to the age of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit who now works in the sons of unbelief, in which we all once lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the wills of the flesh and of our thoughts, and we were by nature children of wrath, he made us alive together with Christ.”

[Note: [Col. 0465D] The Cistercian manuscripts insert here the words “he had mercy on us.”]

Thus the phrase “he made us alive together with Christ” is to be understood ἀπὸ κοινοῦ (*apo koinou*, “in common”), as though it had been said twice.

[Note: [Col. 0465D] The same manuscripts, omitting the little word “so that,” read: “it is understood”—and shortly afterward omit two other little words, “and us.”]

The causal conjunction in the passage, “But God, who is rich in mercy,” we think was either added by unlearned copyists, with the error gradually becoming established, or was used superfluously by Paul himself, who was unskilled in speech though not in knowledge (II Cor. XI).

[571] Sin is plainly said to be the death of the soul, in accordance with what is written in Ezekiel: “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. XVIII, 4).

And since the trespasses called παραπτώματα (paraptōmata) in Greek, according to the etymology of that language, are properly a Scriptural term—although trespasses are more correctly translated πλημμέλειαι (plēmmeleiai)—we ask what they signify and how they differ from sins: that is, what difference there is between παραπτώματα and ἁμαρτίαι (hamartiai).

They say that παραπτώματα are, as it were, the beginnings of sins, when a silent thought creeps in and, with us assenting to some extent [Al. “restraining”], though it has not yet driven us to ruin. Hence it is written in the eighteenth Psalm: “Who understands trespasses?” (Ps. XVIII, 13)—because it is difficult to perceive the roots and beginnings of sins.

Sin, however, occurs when something has been completed in deed and has reached its end.

We also ask what is meant by “in which you once walked according to the age of this world”: whether there is another age that does not belong to this world but to other worlds, about which Clement also writes in his Epistle: “The Ocean, boundless for human beings, and the worlds that are beyond it.”

[Note: [Col. 0465D] The Greek text of Saint Clement’s First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 20, has the fuller reading: Ὠκεανὸς ἀνθρώποις ἀπέραντος καὶ οἱ μετ’ αὐτὸν κόσμοι, “The Ocean is impassable for human beings, and the worlds that are beyond it.” Jerome seems to have taken this from Origen, for the same sentence is twice recited in full in Book II of On First Principles, chapter 3: “The Ocean is impassable for human beings, and these worlds that are beyond it.” Origen is said to have wished to infer from this the existence of what the Greeks call ἀντίχθονες and the Latins antichthones, commonly called antipodes. For this reason Photius criticizes him in codex 126. Most of the ancients, as is well known from Lactantius, Augustine, and others, denied that antipodes existed. Saint Clement, however, may have intended not several worlds but distant and previously unknown regions of the world beyond the Ocean.]

or whether this is the one world that, from the beginning of the age in which Adam was created until its end, revolves and passes away;

or whether, certainly, the prince of this air, who now works in the sons of unbelief, is called “the world” by another name.

It is also written to the Galatians: “That he might rescue us from the present evil age” (Gal. I, 4). And in this same Epistle: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (below, V, 16). Jacob’s days are also called few and evil (Gen. XLVII), either because the time of this life, during which we are confined in the age, is grievous and laborious, or because Satan himself, as we said above, is designated by the terms “this world” and “this age.”

[Note: [Col. 0466D] Other books read: “of this world,” etc.]

Of him it immediately says in what follows: “According to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit who now works in the sons of unbelief.”

The prince of the air and the spirit of the power that is in this air is understood to be the devil, who now works in the sons of unbelief. He cannot work in those who believe in the Lord.

Of him he says below as well: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.”

This does not mean that the devil and his satellites, who wander through this world and instill sins in human beings, can be in heaven, from which they fell because of their merits. Rather, “heaven” is called this air that is above us, in accordance with the Savior’s words: “Consider the birds of heaven” (Matt. VI, 26), and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0466D] In a Cistercian manuscript: “the airy region which is above,” etc.]

For it is clear that birds do not fly through heaven but through the air.

It follows: “Among whom we all once lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the wills of the flesh and of our thoughts.”

[Col. 0466C] The phrase “in which” refers to the trespasses. Above, he had placed the two together: “And you, when you were dead in trespasses and sins,” and he had referred to the sins when he said, “in which you once walked.” But with regard to the trespasses, nothing similar seemed to follow that could complete the sense. Now he says, “in which trespasses we all also lived.” And lest, in saying “your sins in which you once walked,” he should seem through pride to exclude himself from sin, he adds, “among whom we all lived.”

Whoever says that he has lived among them speaks of past trespasses, not present ones. “We once lived,” he says, not in a single desire but in the desires of our flesh. For the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh (Gal. V, 17).

We did not perform one will of the flesh but many; and not only the wills of the flesh but also of our thoughts, for which the Latin manuscripts have “cogitations,” thoughts.

I think the difference between the sin of the flesh and that of the thoughts is this: the sin of the flesh is impurity and wantonness, and those acts that are fulfilled through its service in lusts. The trespass of the thoughts, however, concerns dogmas contrary to the truth and heretical perversity.

Thus we may say that most heretics—although this is rare—perform the wills of their thoughts and not the wills of the flesh; while, conversely, many members of the Church perform the wills of the flesh and not of the thoughts; and that there are many who perform equally the wills both of the flesh and of the thoughts.

We have said this not because heretics do not perform the wills of the flesh—for there are more bodily vices among them than among our people—but so that, by giving an example, what we intended might be understood more easily.

“And we were,” he says, “by nature children of wrath, as also the others.”

Let the heretics who maintain that there are different natures answer how Paul—whose spiritual nature is beyond doubt—could have been by nature a child of wrath, like the others who are still placed in error.

[Note: [Col. 0467D] See Rufinus, Book I of the *Invectives*, no. 38.]

We, however, say first that all human beings are by nature children of wrath, either because of the body of our lowliness and the body of death, and because from youth the human mind is inclined toward evil (Gen. VIII); hence Solomon says: “There is no just person on earth who does good and does not sin” (Eccl. VII, 21);

or because, from the time when we are able to have knowledge of God and reach puberty, we all sin either in deed, or in word, or in thought.

[Col. 0467C] We were therefore by nature children of wrath, as also the others, and all the saints who have been redeemed from wrath by the blood of Christ.

For if Paul, who conducted himself blamelessly according to the righteousness that was in the Law, says that he was by nature a child of wrath, why should we hesitate to testify that the holy men of former times were also children of wrath?

Of all these it can truly be said: “When the commandment came, sin revived, but they themselves died.”

“Child of wrath” is to be understood in the same way as “child of perdition,” “child of iniquity,” and “child of death.” It does not mean that some wrath, death, iniquity, or perdition exists in its own nature and has children; rather, people are called children of that thing which works in each person. Thus those who are to be consumed by the fires of Gehenna are called children of Gehenna.

Another person thinks that those called children of wrath are called so as children of the devil. For the devil is perdition, wrath, and death. “Death, growing strong, devoured” (Isa. LII, according to the Septuagint); and: “The last enemy, death, will be destroyed” (I Cor. XV, 26); and to the devil: “You have become perdition” (Ezek. XXVIII, according to the Septuagint).

“You have become,” he says, by your own will, not because you were created so from the beginning.

How, then, is he called death, since through the devil’s envy death entered the world (Wis. II), and through him those who previously lived died; and how is he called perdition, since he destroys whoever he deceives?

In the same way he is called wrath because of the fierceness that he exercises against human beings.

There are those who think that the wrath in the Books of Kings, when David numbered the people of Israel and provoked God’s wrath against himself, refers to the devil. Scripture says: “And the wrath of God continued to burn against Israel, and he stirred up David, saying …” (II Reg. XXIV, 1).

For, according to the characteristic usage of the Greek language, it does not say “the wrath of God,” using the feminine participle λέγουσα (legousa), that is, “which said,” but λέγων (legōn), “who said,” using the masculine gender. For the Lord sends his wrath and fury through evil angels.

God, therefore, who is rich in mercy, and rich because of his love with which he loved the human race—not with a simple love but with a great one—when we were dead because of our trespasses, made us alive; and he did not merely make us alive, for this would have been too little for his goodness and greatness, but made us alive together with Christ Jesus, granting us one and the same life with Christ.

Some, instead of “we were by nature children of wrath,” have translated “by nature”—because the word φύσει (physei) is ambiguous—as “entirely” or “altogether.” Even if the sentence sounds this way, it must be explained according to what we have said.

“You have been saved by grace.” If the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us (Rom. VIII), then we have been saved by grace rather than by works. For we can repay the Lord nothing for all that he has repaid us.

(Vers. 6.) “And he raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus.”

Above he had said that God raised Christ from the dead and made him sit at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality and power and virtue and dominion and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come.

[Col. 0468C] Now he adds that he has also raised us together with him and made us sit in the heavenly places at his right hand.

The question therefore arises how God, who saved us and raised us up, made us sit together with Christ.

The person who gives the simpler answer asserts that, according to God’s foreknowledge, he has spoken of what is still future as though it had already happened. It is the custom of Scripture sometimes to express future events in the past tense.

For example, concerning the Lord’s cross: “They pierced my hands and feet” (Ps. XXI, 17). And elsewhere concerning his passion: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter” (Isa. LIII, 7). And again concerning the injuries caused by the scourging: “By his bruising we were healed” (ibid., 5). And elsewhere [Al. “in the same place”]: “Because of the sins of my people he was led to death” (ibid., 8, according to the Septuagint).

[Col. 0468D] This is so that, because future things are always uncertain, human hope may not fluctuate and waver. Things that God knows will happen—for nothing is uncertain with him—are remembered as though they had already happened, so that, since even according to the philosophers what is past cannot become undone, those who hear may regard future things as already accomplished.

Another person, who understands the resurrection and kingdom of Christ spiritually, does not hesitate to say that the saints already sit and reign with Christ.

For just as a saint is not in the flesh at all, although he lives in the flesh, and has his way of life in the heavenly places, although he walks on earth, and, ceasing to be flesh, is wholly transformed into spirit, so he sits in the heavenly places with Christ.

For “the kingdom of God is within us” (Luke XVII, 21), and “where our treasure is, there will our heart be also” (Matt. VI, 21). Firm and steadfast, we sit with Christ—with wisdom, the Word, justice, and truth.

It may also be said that, just as we have received the pledge of the Holy Spirit without yet having obtained his entire fullness, so too we sit and reign with Christ without yet possessing a perfect session in the heavenly places.

(Vers. 7.) To show in the ages to come the abundant riches of his grace in goodness toward us in Christ Jesus. The greatness of the benefit, and the manifold grace by which the Lord, having freed us from the disturbances of this age, has made us sit and reign with Christ, is demonstrated above all by this: that, not in one but in all future ages, he will show all rational creatures his glory concerning us and display his riches. We who were once held under the law of hell, and who, because of our vices and sins, were destined for punishments just as we were for the works of the flesh, now reign and sit with Christ.

We sit, moreover, not in some lowly place, but above every principality, authority, power, and dominion, and above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come. For if Christ, raised from the dead, sits at the right hand of God in the heavenly places, above every principality, authority, power, [Note: Rufinus reads more fully: “and above every name that has been named, not only in this age but also in the age to come; and we shall sit and reign with Christ,” etc. Compare Book II, nos. 35 ff.] and so forth, and we sit and reign with Christ, then necessarily we sit above those things above which he sits. [Note: Rufinus again reads somewhat differently: “above these, and above those things upon which he sits,” etc. Moreover, the person whom the holy Doctor here calls “the attentive reader,” he does not deny to be Origen; likewise, he reveals that the one of whom he adds below, “But another interpreter,” was Apollinarius. “In Book I Against Rufinus,” he says, “we set forth a threefold exposition: in the first, what seemed to us; in the second, what Origen objected; in the third, what Apollinarius explained straightforwardly”; there he also defends at greater length his calling Origen “the attentive reader.”] But the attentive reader immediately asks and says: “What, then? Is a human being greater than the angels and all the heavenly powers?” Since it is dangerous to answer this, he will refer the principalities, authorities, powers, dominions, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come—especially since all things have been subjected beneath Christ’s feet—not to the good side but to the opposing one. Thus he will say that they are fallen angels, the prince of this world, and Lucifer who rose in the morning; over these the saints will sit with Christ at the end, granting them also [Note: The presbyter of Aquileia reads: “will sit at the end of the age, granting them also the benefit”—that is, Christ granting it—“who now wander without restraint, abusing their liberty badly,” etc. For *infreni*, although it is preferable to Rufinus’s reading, I would rather read *infrenes* in the nominative.] the benefit—those who now wander about without restraint [Al. “may wander”], abusing their liberty badly, and fall headlong [Al. “may fall”] into sins.

When such beings have them as their occupants, they will begin to be governed according to the will of those who sit upon them. But another interpreter will transfer the words “to show in the ages to come the abundant riches of his grace in goodness toward us in Christ Jesus” to the following meaning: that we were saved not by our merit but by his grace, and that it is a greater sign of goodness to die for sinners than for the righteous. “For a good person,” perhaps, “someone might dare to die”; and he will give us what “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. II). He has already given us some share in all these things in Christ Jesus, because nothing apart from Christ can be called good.

(Vers. 8, 9.) For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves: for it is God’s gift, not from works, lest anyone should boast. Therefore, he says, he will display the abundant riches of his grace in goodness in the ages to come, because you have been saved by grace through faith, not through works. And this faith itself is not from you, but from him who called you. This is said lest a secret thought perhaps creep into our minds: “If we were not saved through our works, then surely we were saved through faith; and what saves us is ours in another way.” Therefore he added and said that faith itself is not a matter of our will but a gift of God. This does not remove free choice from human beings, nor does it mean, according to the Apostle’s statement to the Romans, that it depends “not on the one who wills or runs, but on God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX); rather, it means that freedom of choice itself has God as its author, and that everything must be referred to his benefit, since he himself has allowed us even to will what is good. All this is said lest anyone boast of being saved from himself rather than from God.

(Vers. 10.) For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared so that we might walk in them. He has supplied the reasons why we have been saved by grace through faith, and why this itself is not from us but from God’s gift, saying: “For we are his workmanship”—that is, the fact that we live, breathe, understand, and are able to believe belongs to him, because he is our creator.

Observe carefully that he did not say, “We are his figure and molding,” but “We are his workmanship.” Molding derives its origin from the clay of the earth; workmanship, however, takes its beginning according to the likeness and image of God. This is also placed together with a different meaning in the hundred and eighteenth Psalm: “Your hands made me and fashioned me” (Ps. CXVIII, 73). Workmanship holds the first place; molding follows.

And because the words “creation” and “making” are always customarily joined to great works—for example, “that city was founded,” and “the world was created in the beginning”—and each of the saints, through various doctrines and virtues, is wholly a world within himself, therefore we are now said to have been created in Christ and created for good works, whether the works we ourselves have done or will do, or works in other creatures toward which our way of life is to be transferred, so that we may walk in those things which God has prepared. Great hope has already been given to us, since we are going to walk in those things which God has prepared with the greatest care.

And since we have once come to the word “creation,” and Wisdom says in the Proverbs of Solomon that she was created as the beginning of God’s ways (Prov. VIII), many, fearing that they may be compelled to call Christ a creature, deny the whole mystery of Christ and say that by this Wisdom the wisdom of the world is meant, not Christ. We, however, freely proclaim that there is no danger in calling him a creature whom, with the full confidence of all our hope, we confess to be a worm, a human being, crucified, and a curse—especially since, in the two preceding verses, Wisdom herself promises that she will declare what will be after the ages (Prov. XXII).

Since Christ made the ages, and since the things he goes on to speak of are those which he promised he would declare after the ages, what follows must be referred to the mystery of the incarnation, not to the nature of God. In the Hebrew manuscripts, however, the text does not read, “The Lord created me, the beginning of his ways,” [Note: In the *Commentaries on Isaiah* XXVI, 13: “And concerning Wisdom we read, according to the Hebrew, who speaks in Proverbs: ‘God possessed me, the beginning of his ways,’ although some copies improperly have ‘creation’ instead of ‘possession.’” He has similar statements in the *Commentary on Micah*, chapter IV, and in Letter 140 to Cyprian, no. 6. See what we have observed concerning these passages.] but “The Lord possessed me.”

There is a great difference between possession and creation: for what is possessed exists and subsists, and belongs to the one who possesses it. A creator, however, creates what did not exist before it was made—or, at least, transfers something that existed into another state, just as we too are now said to have been created in Christ Jesus. We were created not because we previously did not exist, but because we were created for good works.

David also prays for this in the fiftieth Psalm, saying: “Create a clean heart in me, O God” (Ps. L, 11). Certainly he had possessed a clean heart before his sin, when the Lord spoke of him: “I have found David, son of Jesse, a man according to my heart” (Acts XIII, 22). But just as creation there signifies restoration, so in us and in Christ, through individual works and stages of progress, the terms “creation” and “making” can be understood: so that each day, in believers—for people are variously called mountains, valleys, hills, and plains according to their different merits—Christ is created, born, and formed.

(Vers. 12.) Therefore remember that formerly you Gentiles in the flesh, who were called uncircumcision by what is called circumcision in the flesh, made by hand, were at that time without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers to the covenants of the promise [Al. *repromissionis*], having no hope and without God in the world.

By calling the Ephesians Gentiles in the flesh, he shows that in the spirit they are not Gentiles; conversely, the Jews are Gentiles in the spirit and Israelites in the flesh. The Jews and Gentiles are therefore divided in four ways.

Some are circumcised in the flesh and in the spirit, as were Moses and Aaron, the Apostles, and Nathanael, whose hidden Judaism the Lord perceived when he said: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (John I, 47).

Others are circumcised neither in flesh nor in spirit, as were Nebuchadnezzar and Pharaoh, and as is the multitude today of barbarian and Roman peoples who do not believe in God.

A third group is circumcised only in the flesh and has an uncircumcised spirit. To them the prophet says: “Circumcise yourselves to your God, and do not circumcise the flesh of your foreskin” (Jer. IV, 4). And elsewhere: “All the nations are uncircumcised [Al. *incircumcisa*] in the flesh, but the house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart” (Jer. IX, 26).

The last group is the one now described: “You Gentiles in the flesh, who were called uncircumcision by what is called circumcision in the flesh, made by hand.” Such is the entire multitude of believers today, and the whole world is filled with people from the Gentiles.

To distinguish them from the spiritual Gentiles and Jews, the Ephesians are called Gentiles in the flesh, because according to the spirit they are Israelites. Scripture also mentions an Israel according to the flesh when it says: “See Israel according to the flesh” (1 Cor. X), because Israel was not present in the spirit.

He has also chosen his words carefully: “who were called uncircumcision.” “You were called,” he says, “uncircumcision,” and you were not so in reality, by what is called circumcision in the flesh, made by hand. This is not because there is no circumcision, but because that circumcision assumes the name for itself and is truly circumcision made by hand, not by the spirit. [Note: Two Cistercian manuscripts read, “and you were from that which is called circumcision,” that is, “you were absent from it.”]

At the same time, we must observe that although he formerly described us as being without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the promises and covenant of God, now that we have believed in Christ, just as we have received his promises and covenants, so too we are said to possess the commonwealth of Israel. The entire legal way of life is fulfilled in us because the law is spiritual; we are more truly circumcised, and we keep the Sabbath [Note: The same manuscripts read: “we keep the Sabbath in the spirit, abandoning sacrifices.”] in the spirit, offering spiritual sacrifices. Their temple and altar having been destroyed, we offer to God the tithes of our fruits; we sacrifice the spotless lamb; and, with our loins girded and unencumbered, we eat the Passover.

Just as circumcision is called circumcision in the flesh, made by hand, so, by way of distinction, another circumcision is understood to exist which is not [Al. *sicut*], as we have said, made by hand but by the spirit.

When he says, “having no hope and without God in the world,” he does not mean that the Ephesians had not possessed and worshiped many gods before believing in Christ; rather, whoever is without the true God has no god. The words “without God in the world” have been added significantly. They did have God, whom God foreknew they would possess; and in God’s foreknowledge they were not without God, but they were in the world without God.

(Vers. 13, 14.) But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far away have been brought near by the blood of Christ; for he himself is our peace.

God is everywhere, and wholly everywhere. From him, how can anyone be separated, since everything is in him? He himself also speaks through the prophet: “I am God who is near, and not far away” (Jer. XXIII, 23). And the Psalmist testifies: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 8). [Note: The Cistercian manuscripts again read: “If I ascend into heaven, and if I descend into hell, you are there.”] Since everything is in him, nevertheless he is said to be far from the wicked, according to the saying: “The Lord is far from the wicked” (Prov. XV, 29). The one from whom the wicked are far is near to the saints.

Thus, although he was far from the Ephesians, he was brought near to them in the blood of Jesus. We must observe carefully that without the blood of the Lord Jesus no one approaches God, for he is our peace, saying: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John XIV, 27). For just as wisdom makes people wise, righteousness makes them righteous, sanctification makes them holy, and life makes them alive, so he himself makes us peaceful, so that we may say: “With those who hated peace I was peaceful” (Ps. CXIX, 7). If Christ is the peace of believers, then whoever is without peace consequently does not have Christ.

(Vers. 15 ff.) Who made both one, and, by breaking down the middle wall of the partition, the hostility in his flesh, abolishing the law of commandments in ordinances, so that he might create the two in himself as one new man, making peace, and reconcile both in one body to God, killing the hostility in it through the cross; and coming, he preached peace to you who were far away and peace to those who were near, for through him we both have access in one spirit to the Father.

This is the middle wall and partition that divided the two peoples from one another. Concerning it, in Genesis, the midwife says at the birth of the twins: “Why has the fence been broken down because of you?” (Gen. XXXVIII, 29).

After the Savior destroyed in his own flesh the wisdom of the flesh, which is hostile to God (Rom. VIII), and exchanged the legal precepts for the teachings of the Gospel, so that he might make one Christian people from Jew and Gentile, preaching peace to us who were far away—that is, to the Gentiles—and to the remnants of the Jews who believed from Israel through the Apostles, then through him we approached God and came to recognize that we have one Father in the spirit.

Thus was fulfilled what the Lord said in the Gospel: “There will be one shepherd and one flock” (John X, 16). Again he said: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold,” signifying us, who were to be gathered from the Gentiles.

The hostility destroyed in the Savior’s flesh was also killed through the cross. For it is written: “To reconcile both in one body to God, killing the hostility in it through the cross.” The Latin manuscripts do not read “in himself,” [Note: If one aspirates the Greek pronoun αὐτῷ, it is equivalent to ἑμαυτῷ, σεαυτῷ, or ἑαυτῷ, meaning “in himself.” Conversely, as Jerome prefers, if αὐτῷ is written with the smooth breathing, it refers to the word σταυρῷ and sounds as “in it,” that is, “in the cross.” The entire ambiguity of the pronoun has therefore arisen from neglect of the grammarians’ rule. Many Greek Fathers support Jerome’s view, among them Chrysostom, Theodoret, Theophylact, and others, who explain a very similar passage in the Epistle to the Colossians II, 15—“openly triumphing over them in himself”—with ἐν ξύλῳ, “on the wood,” that is, “on the cross.” Origen, Primasius, and others prefer the opposite interpretation.] because of the ambiguity of the Greek pronoun. For ἐν αὐτῷ (*en autō*) can mean both “in himself” and “in it,” that is, in the cross, since the cross—σταυρός (*stauros*) in Greek—is masculine in gender.

The law of commandments was also overthrown in ordinances. Circumcision, Sabbath observance, the Passover, Pentecost, and the command not to appear before God empty-handed were understood in a deeper sense than their literal wording suggests. Having departed from the letter that kills, we began to follow the life-giving spirit.

When he says, “Coming, he preached peace to you who were far away,” that is, to the Gentiles, “and peace to those who were near,” that is, to the Jews, it seems to me that he has offered testimony from Isaiah in different words [Al. “these words”], and has used the sense of Scripture as though it were his own. For it is written there: “I have seen his ways and healed him, and consoled him, and given him true consolation: peace upon peace to those who were far away and to those who were near” (Isa. LVII, 18). [Note: Rufinus maliciously misrepresents almost the entire exposition that follows this verse; see Book I, no. 38.]

These remarks have been made according to the Vulgate interpretation. But whoever reads the Apostle’s statement concerning Christ—“making peace through the blood of his cross for the things that are on earth and the things that are in heaven,” and the other words spoken in that passage—will not think that we, who are called Israel according to the spirit, were far away, while the Jews, who are called Israel only according to the flesh, were near.

He will instead adapt this entire interpretation to the angels, the heavenly powers, and human souls: Christ joined together in his blood the earthly and heavenly things that had previously been at variance. The good shepherd carried the sick sheep back to the mountains so that it might be with the others; he joined the drachma that had been lost to the drachmas that had remained safe (Luke XV); and he drew the legal commandments back to those teachings according to whose type and image Moses saw the things that were to be made in the tabernacle (Exod. XX).

Thus the Lord’s cross benefited not only the earth but also heaven [Note: Recall what we said on this subject above, Book I, chapter I, verse 33]; not only human beings but also angels; and every creature was cleansed by the blood of its Lord.

When he says, “So that he might create the two in himself as one new man”—a statement that seems more suited to the earlier interpretation concerning Jews and Gentiles—he adapts it to his own understanding by saying that the human being, made according to the image and likeness of God, will receive after reconciliation the same form that the angels now possess, and that he himself had lost.

He says that the new man is the one who is renewed each day and will dwell in the new world, when there will be a new heaven and a new earth (Isa. LXV), and he will drink the new cup of Jesus in the kingdom of God (Mark XIV), sing a new song (Ps. XXXII, 5; XCVII), and rejoice in the reading of the Old and New Testaments.

He will also understand the statement written elsewhere, “Behold, I make new things, which now shall arise” (Isa. XLIII, 19), as meaning that the beginning of renewal takes place in the present age. He will not think, however, that perfect and complete newness can yet be fulfilled in this age.

Just as now “we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Cor. XIII), so the renewal of the new man will then be fully and perfectly completed, when heavenly and earthly things have been joined together and we approach the Father in one spirit, with one understanding and one judgment.

Paul seems to hint at something similar in another Epistle—if one accepts it—when he says to prudent readers: “All these, having received testimony through faith, did not obtain the promise, God having provided something better for us, so that they might not be perfected without us” (Heb. XI, 39–40).

Therefore all creation groans together with us, who groan in this tabernacle, and suffers with us; we, who conceived and suffer through the fear of God, await [Al. “awaits”] the revelation of the sons of God, so that creation may be freed from the vanity of the slavery to which it is now subjected, and so that there may be one shepherd and one flock.
