Then the Lord’s Prayer will be fulfilled: “Your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth” (Matt. VI, 10).

(Vers. 19 ff.) Therefore you are no longer strangers and sojourners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the Apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone. In him the whole building, joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord. In him you also are built together into a dwelling place of God in the spirit.

To what he had said above—“strangers to the covenants and promise”—he now responds: “Therefore you are no longer strangers and sojourners.” And to what he had previously said—“alienated from the commonwealth of Israel”—he now returns: “You are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household.”

This passage applies especially against those who attempt to introduce different natures. For how did they become fellow citizens with the saints, and how were they once members of God’s household while alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, if nature cannot be changed either for the better or for the worse?

What follows—“built upon the foundation of the Apostles and prophets”—agrees more with the first interpretation than with the second, in which we said above that before Christ’s passion Israel was near and the Gentiles were far away.

We can also use this testimony against Marcion and the other ancient heretics who preach that the God of the Law is different from the God of the Gospel. For if they are no longer strangers and sojourners but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the Apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone, and if in him the whole building, joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord, and in him the Ephesians too are built together into a tabernacle of God in the spirit, then there is one God, one building, and one temple, built upon the foundation of the Apostles and prophets.

If the whole building, joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord, we must strive with every effort to become those stones of which it is written: “Holy stones are rolled upon the earth” (Zech. IX, 16). When we have become living stones, hewn smooth on every side, polished, and without any roughness, let us be built into a temple and become a dwelling place for God.

Let the ark of the covenant, guardian of the law of the Lord, be established in us; let there be the Cherubim, a multitude of knowledge; and let the innermost parts of our hearts pass into a new name. Let us be called *DABIR* (), which we may render “oracle” or “answer,” or, if we express the word more exactly word for word, λαλητήριον (*lalētērion*), that is, “the place of speech,” so that with the Apostle we may burst forth in the words: “Do you seek proof of the Christ who speaks in me?” (1 Cor. XIII, 3).

The whole building constructed upon the foundation of the Apostles and prophets may also signify not only us but the heavenly powers, [Note: Two Cistercian manuscripts read: “the heavenly powers magnify.”] so that all together may become a dwelling place of God in the spirit. For they say that it is incongruous for a building compacted and harmoniously joined from human beings to grow into a holy temple in the Lord and become a dwelling place of God in the spirit, while angels and all the blessed powers who serve God in heaven are thought to be excluded from this blessedness.

The chief cornerstone, which contains both peoples—or, according to the second interpretation, joins heavenly and earthly things—is Christ our Lord, the stone cut from the mountain without hands. Concerning him the Psalmist also testifies, saying: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner. This is the Lord’s doing” (Ps. CXVII, 22).

He was rejected by the Pharisees, who seemed to possess knowledge of the Law and to build God’s temple with legal commandments; but he was taken up by God as the cornerstone, so that he himself might hold together the two walls and through him both peoples might have access to God.

For those who do not believe, this cornerstone is a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense. Whoever falls upon it will be broken, but upon whomever it falls, it will crush him (Luke XX).

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0475]

In accordance with your prayers, O Paula and Eustochium, I now undertake the Book on the Epistle to the Ephesians, intending also to send new little gifts to Rome. Not because the senate of the learned will deign to read them and enter them in the libraries of the ancients, but because holy Marcella insistently requests through her letters that this be done.

Whenever I recall her studies, talent, and labor, I condemn my own idleness, since, established in the solitude of the monastery and looking toward that manger in which the hastening shepherds worshiped the crying infant (Luke II), I cannot do what a noble woman accomplishes amid the bustle of her household and the administration of her home, in the spare moments of her work.

Therefore I jointly beg her, and you, and anyone who may perhaps read these words, to understand that I am not presenting a discourse long contemplated and polished, but that, in order to disclose the mysteries of the Scriptures, I use almost common, everyday words and sometimes reach, day by day, the number of a thousand lines, so that the exposition begun on the Apostle may be completed through the prayers of Paul himself, whose Epistles we are attempting to explain.

(Cap. III.—Vers. 1 ff.) For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ for you Gentiles—if indeed you have heard of the stewardship of God’s grace that was given to me for you. For by revelation the mystery was made known to me, as I wrote briefly before; so that, when you read, you may be able to understand my insight into the mystery of Christ.

As far as the sequence and literal wording of the discourse are concerned, when we diligently investigate what he connected with what he had said before—“For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ for you Gentiles”—we can find nothing that supplies the connection. For he did not say, “For this reason I, Paul, did this or that, or taught this or that,” but, while leaving the sentence suspended, he passed on to other matters.

Unless, perhaps, we pardon him because he himself confessed, saying: “And if I am unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge” (2 Cor. XI, 6), and seek in him an order of meanings rather than of words. It can be restored in this way: “For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and a prisoner for you who are from the Gentiles, came to know the mystery, so that I might also transmit it to you,” as I spoke shortly before in this same Epistle.

You ought to hear of the stewardship of God’s grace that was given to me for you who are from the Gentiles, for whom I am also a prisoner of Jesus Christ.

That Paul was a prisoner of Jesus Christ for the Gentiles may also be understood of martyrdom: thrown into chains at Rome, he sent this Epistle at the time when, as we have shown elsewhere, he wrote the Epistles to Philemon, the Colossians, and the Philippians.

Or perhaps, because it is read in several places that the body is called the bond of the soul, by which it is held enclosed as in a prison, we say that Paul was restrained by the bonds of the body and did not return to be with Christ, so that the preaching entrusted to him might be completed among the Gentiles. [Note: Rufinus exults here, openly treating the holy Doctor as guilty of holding Origen’s opinion; see Book I, no. 40. But what the holy Father replies to him in Book I of the *Apology* completely turns aside his opponent’s attack. There he assigns each doctrine to its author: “And in this matter,” he says, “as above, I have set forth a threefold exposition: first, what seemed to me; second, what Origen asserted; third, what Apollinarius, proceeding against that doctrine, held. Read the Greek Commentaries, and if you do not find it so, I shall confess the charge.”]

Although some introduce another meaning here [Note: Rufinus reads, “introduces it in this passage”]: that Paul, predestined and sanctified from his mother’s womb for the preaching of the Gentiles before he was born, later received the bonds of the flesh.

I think, however, that the expression in this passage is also defective. Instead of saying what he ought to have said—“For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ for you Gentiles, came to know the mystery, as I wrote briefly before, so that, when you read, you may be able to understand”—he says: “For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner, according to revelation the mystery was made known to me,” and so forth.

If anyone can nevertheless demonstrate, according to the continuity of the speech and its wording, that the Apostle was perfect and did not fall into grammatical faults, that person should rather be heard. Whenever we have noted solecisms [Note: Compare Letter 120 to Hedibia, question 11; the following letter to Algasia, question 10; and, above, the *Commentary on Galatians* IV, 24. Chrysostom, *Homily* 3 on 1 Corinthians; Theodoret, *On the Cure of Greek Affections*, discourse 8; and others should also be consulted.] or anything of that kind, we are not attacking the Apostle, as malicious people accuse us, but are rather defending the Apostle: for, being a Hebrew of Hebrews, he could never have led the whole world to the faith of Christ without rhetorical polish of speech, arrangement of words, and elegance of expression, unless he preached the Gospel not in the wisdom of speech but in the power of God.

For he himself says to the Corinthians: “And I, when I came to you, brothers, came not with superiority of speech or wisdom, proclaiming to you the testimony of God” (1 Cor. II, 1). And again: “My word and my preaching were not in persuasive words of wisdom, but in a demonstration of spirit and power, so that your faith might not be in the wisdom of human beings but in the power of God” (ibid., 4–5).

This man, then, who commits solecisms in his words, who cannot resolve a hyperbaton or bring a sentence to completion, boldly claims wisdom for himself and says: “For by revelation the mystery was made known to me, as I wrote briefly before.”

Indeed, if anyone examines the preceding sections of this Epistle, he will see that mysteries were revealed to him, of which he touched upon a certain small part in his own words—not bringing forth all that he knew, but showing through a little of it what he had left unsaid.

“So that you may be able,” he says, “when you read, to understand my insight,” or wisdom, “in the mystery of Christ.” This is what we said in the preface: none of Paul’s Epistles contains such great mysteries, or is wrapped in meanings so deeply hidden—meanings of which the Apostle boasts that he knows and briefly indicates to us—so that we may read again more attentively what has been written.

[Col. 0478D] (Verses 5 and following.) And [another reading: “which”] in other generations was not made known to the sons of men, as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets in the Spirit: that the Gentiles are co-heirs, members of the same body, and fellow-partakers of the promise in Christ through the Gospel, of which I became a minister according to the gift of God’s grace, which was given to me in accordance with the operation of his power. [Col. 0479A]

The mystery of Christ, which the Apostle has explained above in part—how it was unknown to other generations—seems to require fuller reconsideration: whether Abraham, Jacob, and Moses, Isaiah and the other prophets were ignorant of it or not. Scripture records that they foretold the coming of Christ and the calling of the Gentiles. Abraham indeed saw his day and rejoiced (John VIII, 56), and it was said to him: “All nations shall be blessed in your seed” (Gen. XXII, 18). Jacob too speaks prophetically of him who would arise from Judah: “And he himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (ibid. XLIX, 10).

Moses also considered “the reproach of Christ” greater riches than the treasures of Egypt. And Isaiah says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son” (Isa. VII, 14). And elsewhere: “There shall be a rod of Jesse, and he who shall arise to rule the nations; in him the nations shall hope” (ibid. XI, 10).

And, to avoid prolonging the discussion, it is enough to mention a few passages from the Psalms: “And all the families of the nations shall worship before him” (Ps. XXI, 28). And again: “All nations shall serve him” (Ps. XVII, 11). And still more explicitly concerning the people of Israel and the Lord the Savior: “Visit this vine and perfect it, which your right hand planted, and upon the son whom you established for yourself” (Ps. LXXIX, 15–16). The dispensation of his body is also indicated in what follows: “Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand, and upon the son of man whom you established for yourself” (ibid., 18).

Either, then, we must accept, with Montanus, that the patriarchs and prophets spoke in ecstasy and did not know what they said; or, if this is impious—for “the spirit of the prophets is subject to the prophets”—they certainly understood what they spoke. And if they understood, the question arises how Paul can now say that what was not known to other generations was revealed to Christ’s apostles.

Either, then, this must be the answer: that Paul carefully and expressly testified that the mystery was unknown to the sons of men, not to the sons of God, to whom he speaks: “I said: You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Ps. LXXXI, 6). That is, those who received the spirit of adoption—and among whom were the patriarchs and prophets—knew the mystery of God.

Or, if this is not accepted and seems too forced and contrived, the argument will proceed as follows: Paul did not say definitively and generally that the Lord’s mystery was altogether unknown to other generations, but that the ancient patriarchs and prophets did not know it in the manner in which it has now been revealed to his saints and apostles. For it is one thing to know future events in the spirit, and another to behold them accomplished in reality.

Thus John is called greater than all the prophets (Luke VII), because he saw the one whom the others had prophesied and pointed him out with his finger, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John I, 29). In accordance with this interpretation, the following passage too can be explained: “Many prophets and righteous men desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it” (Luke X, 24). They certainly desired to see and hear what they knew would come. For if they did not know what was to come, how could they desire what they entirely ignored?

We read in the Books of Kings that the Lord promised and said to Solomon in a dream: “Because you asked this thing of me, and did not ask for yourself long life, nor request riches, nor the lives of your enemies, but asked that you might understand and hear judgment: behold, I have done according to your word, and I have given you a wise and understanding heart, such as none had before you, and such as shall not arise after you” (II Kings III, 11–12). [589]

[Note: In Victorius, “according to your word.” For the rest, see what we observe a little below at verse 10.]

How, then, do some people think that the mystery was revealed to Christ’s apostles although it was unknown to Solomon, when Solomon was wiser than all the apostles, and when the divine voice had made promises to the patriarchs of old? He himself also speaks confidently concerning himself: “God taught me wisdom, and I know the understanding of the holy ones” (Wis. VII, 21). David too boasts of his knowledge of the hidden mystery, saying: “You have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom” (Ps. L, 8). And to the one who vaunted himself over his wisdom, God says through the prophet: “Are you wiser than Daniel?” (Ezek. XXVIII, 3).

Either, then, the interpretation we discussed above must be retained: that the patriarchs and prophets did not know Christ’s mystery as it has now been revealed to the apostles, because it is one thing to hold something in one’s hands and another to foresee the future in the spirit.

Or it must be said that, just as faces are not alike, so hearts are not alike; and, according to the Apostle, gifts are diverse: one has prophecy, another kinds of tongues, another gifts of healing, another helps and administrations; one is wise, another faithful, one excels in knowledge of secrets, while another is content with simple faith (I Cor. XII).

For not everyone, following Solomon’s example, spoke similarly about the natures of beasts, birds, and plants, so as to discuss everything from the cedar of Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall. Conversely, perhaps Solomon did not see matters in the way Moses did—the various kinds of sacrifices and the worship of God; nor did the Lord speak to him face to face; nor did he possess or understand such an extensive array of vessels as the Lord showed Moses on the mountain (III Kings IV; Exod. XXXIII, XXV).

And just as it must be believed that the patriarchs and prophets possessed certain things which the apostles did not possess, so conversely, according to the needs of the time and the preaching of the Gospel, the apostles had a fuller knowledge of the mystery of Christ. The holy men of ancient times certainly knew it, but not in the same way as the apostles, who were charged with the necessity of preaching.

[Col. 0479B] What, then, is this mystery which, as it is now, was not revealed to other generations? Clearly it is what follows: that the Gentiles are co-heirs, members of the same body, and fellow-partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the Gospel, of which Paul became a minister according to the gift of God’s grace, which was given to him in accordance with the operation of God’s power.

I know that the addition of the conjunction by which the text says “co-heirs, members of the same body, and fellow-partakers” makes the sentence inelegant in Latin. But because this is how it stands in Greek, and because each word, syllable, letter, and point in the divine Scriptures is full of meaning, we prefer to risk something in the arrangement and structure of the words rather than in the understanding.

The Gentiles, then, are co-heirs with Israel—or, as we think better, co-heirs with Christ—so that God may be our inheritance and we may be co-heirs with Christ. This too is written elsewhere: “Heirs of God, and co-heirs with Christ” (Rom. VIII, 17). This does not mean that some possession is divided among us, but that the Lord himself is our inheritance and possession. For the Lord says: “The Lord himself is your inheritance” (Deut. XVIII, 2); and elsewhere: “The Lord is my portion and my inheritance” (Ps. XV, 5).

“Members of the same body” signifies that, just as in one body there are many members—for example, eyes, hands, ears, feet, the belly, and knees—and although they belong to one body they have their own distinctions and rejoice and suffer for one another, so those who have believed in Christ, although they possess diverse gifts, are nevertheless gathered together in the one body of the Church.

In the two preceding words—namely, when he says “co-heirs” and “members of the same body”—one might have suspected that something different was intended within the one body. But when he added “and fellow-partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus,” every distinction was entirely removed. Where there is one common participation, everything is shared.

He also beautifully added “through the Gospel,” of which I became a minister according to the gift of grace that was given to me in accordance with the operation of God’s power, so that he might demonstrate God’s grace, not his own merit. For he knew that he had been a persecutor and had devastated Christ’s Church; by this humility, every charge of arrogance is completely excluded.

Some think that he should be criticized on this point, because he said that the mystery was revealed to him although it had been unknown to the patriarchs and prophets. For a disciple of humility would never swell with words of arrogance, saying that the Gospel of which he is a minister was the result not of his own merit but of God’s grace.

Those who wish the prophets not to have understood what they said, and to have spoken as though in ecstasy, draw also upon the passage found in many copies of the Epistle to the Romans in support of their doctrine. They read: “To him who is able to strengthen you according to my Gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery kept silent through eternal times, but now manifested through the prophetic Scriptures and the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ,” and what follows.

They must be answered briefly that Christ’s mystery was kept silent in past times, not among those who promised that it would come, but among all the nations to whom it was afterward manifested. It must likewise be noted that the sacrament of our faith cannot be revealed except through the prophetic Scriptures and the coming of Christ.

Let those, therefore, who do not understand the prophets, nor wish to understand them, and who assert that they are content only with the Gospel, know that they do not know Christ’s mystery, which through eternal times was unknown to all the nations.

(Verses 8, 9.) To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given: to preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, and to enlighten all [Note: Other books omit the word “all,” which is absent from several Greek manuscripts.] concerning the administration of the mystery hidden from the ages in God, who created all things.

I do not think that the Apostle Paul was so at variance with the secret judgment of his mind that he truly said he was the least of all the saints—for example, of those who were in Ephesus, Corinth, or Thessalonica, or of those who had believed throughout the whole world. Although it is an indication of humility to call oneself the least of all the saints, it is nevertheless a charge of falsehood to have one thing locked in the heart and another brought forth by the tongue.

We must therefore find an interpretation by which Paul was truly the least of all the saints and yet did not fall from apostolic dignity. The Lord says in the Gospel to his disciples: “Whoever wishes to be greater among you, let him become the least of all; and whoever wishes to be first, let him be the last of all” (Matt. XX, 26–27). Paul fulfilled this in deed when he said: “For I think that God has displayed us apostles as the last, as men condemned to death” (I Cor. IV, 9).

Paul, therefore, was weaker than all who desired to be weak for Christ’s sake, and for that very reason he was greater. “For I labored more than all of them,” he says, “yet not I, but the grace of God which is with me.”

Because of this humility, while he is the least of all the saints, this grace was given to him among the Gentiles, so that he might preach the unsearchable riches of Christ and teach the administration of the mystery hidden from the ages in God, who created all things.

If the riches of Christ are unsearchable, how are they preached among the people? If the mystery has been hidden from the ages in God, how is it proclaimed through Paul among the Gentiles?

But “unsearchable” and “hidden” must be understood in two ways. Either the riches were formerly unsearchable and have now been opened after the Lord’s Passion. Or, alternatively, those things which by their nature were unsearchable to human beings have become known through God’s revelation.

For it is one thing to reach a secret through one’s own curiosity; once it has been discovered, it ceases to be unsearchable. It is another thing to be entirely unable to comprehend it through one’s own diligence, but to know it by God’s grace; when you have learned it and shown it to others, it nevertheless remains unsearchable, since, insofar as it depended on you, it was hidden until it was revealed.

The Psalmist also bears witness to the unsearchable riches of Christ, speaking of Christ himself: “How great is the multitude of your goodness, which you have hidden for those who fear you” (Ps. XXX, 20). These riches of his goodness were hidden from all past ages in God, who is the creator of all.

Where are Marcion and Valentinus, and all the heretics who assert that there is one creator of the world—that is, of visible things—and another creator of invisible things? They call the former just, and the latter some unknown being, supremely good, who is the Father of Christ.

Behold: the God in whom Christ’s mystery was hidden from all past ages is proclaimed to be the creator of all things. From this it is shown that the God of the New and Old Testament is the same.

The mystery hidden from the ages can also be understood in another way: that the ages themselves were ignorant of it—that is, all the spiritual and rational creatures that existed in the ages. For “age” is often understood to mean those things that exist in the age. Thus Paul says to the Galatians: “That he might rescue us from the present evil age” (Gal. I, 4). And elsewhere: “That he might show in the ages to come” (Eph. II, 7), meaning those things that were to occur in all the succeeding ages.

(Verses 10, 11.) So that now the manifold wisdom of God might be made known through the Church to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places, according to the purpose of the ages, which he accomplished in Christ Jesus our Lord.

According to the gift of God’s grace that was given to the Apostle, so that he might preach the unsearchable riches of Christ and teach among the Gentiles the mystery which had been unknown from the ages, that same mystery was revealed to him so that it might become manifest not only to the Gentiles, but [Note: He is evidently speaking according to the view of certain ancient Fathers of the Church. As Huetius observed long ago, this passage of the Apostle was the reason why they believed that many of God’s mysteries had been learned by the angels through the Church—not those which necessarily belong to the divine nature, for they learned those when the ability to behold God was once granted to them, but those which God freely performs externally. Nyssenus, in Homily 8 on the Song of Songs, teaches that through the Church the angels learned the mysteries of the Incarnation, redemption, cross, and death of Christ. Chrysostom likewise clearly declares that the angels acquired knowledge from the very mouth of the apostles concerning matters previously hidden and unknown to them, especially the conversion of the Gentiles to faith in Christ, of which they had previously been ignorant. These words may, however, be taken in a more acceptable sense according to Jerome, if he seems to assert that the angels were instructed through the Church as witnesses and participants in these events, not as disciples. In this he rightly and deservedly differs from Origen’s opinion, which we criticized in his twenty-third homily. For it conflicts with the testimonies of sacred Scripture to suppose that the mystery of the Incarnation was revealed to human beings before it was revealed to the angels, although one may reasonably suppose that they had scarcely any knowledge of the benefits that would follow from it, such as the conversion of the Gentiles to faith; and that these were among the things in which they advanced through Christ’s death.]

and so that the manifold wisdom of God might be made manifest through the Church to the principalities and powers. According to the purpose of the ancient ages, it had long ago been destined and is now seen to have been brought to completion in Christ.

But if the principalities and powers in the heavens—whom we must understand as holy ministers of God, although some interpret them as the prince of this air and his angels—were ignorant of the manifold wisdom of God, which has now been revealed to them through the Church, how much more was it unknown to the patriarchs and prophets, whom we have shown above not to have been ignorant of Christ’s mystery, but not to have known it in the manner of the apostles?

The manifold wisdom of God, called in Greek πολυποίκιλος (*polypoikilos*), that is, so to speak, “many-sided” or “manifold,” has now been revealed through God’s Church both to the principalities and to the powers. God had long ago determined it in his mind as something that would come to be, and we recognize that it has now been perfected from what we see.

The cross of Christ, therefore, benefited not only us but also the angels and all the powers in heaven, and it opened a mystery that they had previously not known. Finally, when they marvel at God returning to heaven with his body, they say: “Who is this who comes up from Edom, with his garments shining from Bosor, so beautiful in his white robe?” [another reading: “here”] (Isa. LXIII, 1). And elsewhere: “Who is this King of glory? The Lord of hosts—he is the King of glory” (Ps. XXIII, 10).

Let us not therefore think that there is a simple faith in the Church, but that its wisdom is manifold and many-sided, so that it is not merely varied but distinguished by great variety.

You see Christ’s cradle: look also at heaven. You behold the infant crying in the manger: but listen at the same time to the angels praising him. Herod persecutes him, but the Magi worship him (Matt. II). The Pharisees are ignorant, but the star reveals him. He is baptized by a servant, but the voice of God thundered from above (Matt. III). He is plunged into the waters, but a dove descends—or rather, the Spirit in the form of a dove (ibid., 16).

He comes to his Passion and fears to suffer; he wishes the cup to pass from him, and he rebukes Peter because Peter feared the cup. What is wiser than this foolishness, what more richly distinguished by variety, what more obscure than the wisdom which God made in Christ Jesus our Lord?

Although many, following the order and connection of the words, may understand the phrase as referring both to the Church and to the *prothesis*, that is, the “purpose” or “intention,” which we have rendered in Latin by the neuter noun *propositum*, nevertheless “wisdom made in Christ” may resonate more strongly than the other possibilities. For “the foolishness of God is wiser than human beings” (I Cor. I, 25).

And if, according to mystical interpretations, wisdom is said to have been made in Christ (Ecclus. XXIV), let the Arians understand that they boast in vain concerning that passage in which Wisdom says that she was created, born, and founded at the beginning of God’s ways. According to them, she was created and could not have been born. But if she was born, how is she also said to have been founded and created?

(Vers. 12.) In whom we have boldness and access with confidence through faith in him.

Nothing can provide us with such boldness before God, and such purity of conscience—of which it is said, “If our conscience does not condemn us, we have confidence toward God” (I John III, 21)—as the Word, truth, wisdom, and righteousness, all of which are understood in Christ.

Just as these grant us boldness before God, so they also grant access, so that our understanding may approach him, contemplate him more carefully, and take and claim something of his majesty for itself; and, as though borrowing from the sun’s rays, may borrow a certain warmth and brilliance of light and say: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Ps. IV, 7).

It is a great thing, therefore, not only to have boldness, but also to have it with confidence. Nor is it enough merely to have access; for that access to be firmer, one must have it with confidence. The beginning and origin of this confidence and access is faith in Christ.

Whoever, then, does everything rationally and in due order believes in Christ as Word and Reason. Whoever is able to comprehend wisdom believes in Christ as Wisdom. Whoever understands truth believes in Christ as Truth. Whoever lives justly believes in him as Righteousness. There is no need to say more, since I have often been compelled to discuss Christ in the same way.

(Vers. 13.) Therefore I ask that you not grow faint in my tribulations for you, which is your glory.

What the Latin translator has rendered “that you not grow faint” can, because of the ambiguity of the Greek, also be read as “that I not grow faint.” The sense would then be: “Therefore I ask that I not grow faint in my tribulations for you,” and so forth.

This, then, is what the Apostle asks and earnestly entreats from the Lord: that he may not grow faint in his hardships. He saw that he had preached the Gospel from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum, had gone to Rome, and had either reached Spain or intended to proceed there (Rom. XV). The whole world was being wrested from the power of its ruler by his teaching: idols were abandoned, and the temples, deserted by their worshipers, were filled with squalor and filth.

For this reason the entire army of demons and the whole host of hostile powers fought against him after forming ranks, so that through tribulations and distress he might cease preaching the Gospel of Christ and finally, wearied, take rest.

This, therefore, is what he says: “I ask that I not grow faint in my tribulations for you.” Everything that I suffer, everything that troubles and constrains me, is for the sake of your salvation, while I desire to announce the Gospel to you; and these tribulations of mine are your glory.

Moreover, he spoke as though unskilled in expression when he joined a singular “glory” to the plural “tribulations,” saying: “In my tribulations for you, which is your glory,” instead of saying, “which tribulations are your glory.” Unless, perhaps, someone thinks that the phrase must be referred more profoundly, through hyperbaton, either to “boldness,” “access,” or “faith,” and says: “In whom we have boldness, access, and faith. This boldness, access, and faith is your glory.” But the earlier interpretation is preferable.

According to what the Latin expresses—“Therefore I ask that you not grow faint in my tribulations for you, which is your glory”—the passage can also be explained as Paul’s asking on behalf of the Ephesians that they not become weary and faint under the apostle’s hardships.

The words that follow agree more closely with this interpretation: “For this reason I bend my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, that he may grant you to be strengthened with power according to the riches of his glory.” They certainly needed strength so that they would not be overcome by tribulations.

Someone might say: If the Ephesians had been placed in distress, Paul could rightly have prayed for them, that they might not grow faint and weary. But now it is ridiculous for Paul, who is suffering tribulations, to ask that the Ephesians not grow faint in his labor.

To resolve this little question, we may take the following example: “You did not despise or reject your temptation in my flesh.” This saying shows that temptation arose for others in Paul’s flesh.

Let us consider the people of the whole world—and instead of speaking generally about everyone, let us examine those who are thought to believe in Christ—and we shall see that they are especially tempted by this question: why do many adversities befall holy men who serve God, while the wicked, impious, and murderous flourish, prosper, and become rich and powerful.

David expresses their words in his own person when he says: “How good God is to Israel, to those who are upright in heart. But my feet were almost moved; my steps were nearly poured out. For I was jealous of the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners” (Ps. LXXII, 1 and following), and what follows.

He then adds: “But I said: Therefore I have justified my heart without cause, and washed my hands among the innocent, and I have been scourged all day long.”

It is therefore not surprising that, while Paul was pressed by many hardships in Ephesus and Asia, the Ephesians were themselves tempted and needed the assistance of his prayers, so that they would not grow faint in his distress.

That the Apostle suffered many things in Ephesus and Asia is recorded in the Acts of the Apostles; but we learn it more clearly from Paul’s own Epistles, in which he says: “If, as a man, I fought with beasts at Ephesus, what does it benefit me if the dead are not raised?” (I Cor. XV, 32).

And in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning our tribulation which occurred in Asia, because we were weighed down beyond measure, beyond our strength, so that we even despaired of life. But we ourselves had within ourselves the sentence of death, so that we would not trust in ourselves but in God, who raises the dead; he delivered us from such great deaths, and he delivers us; and we hope that he will also deliver us” (II Cor. I, 8 and following).

How great do you think the burden of tribulations pressed upon him, when he said: “He who delivered us from such great and terrible deaths”?

He therefore rightly asks that the faith of the Ephesians not grow faint under his distresses and hardships, which he suffers precisely because he was preaching the Gospel to the Ephesians. These hardships are punishments among unbelievers, but glory and victory among the faithful, because to conquer is not to yield to one’s adversaries in times of distress.

(Vers. 14.) For this reason I bend my knees to the Father [Note: Victorius removes the words “of our Lord Jesus Christ,” because in the exposition that follows Jerome does not appear to have known them. “Moreover,” he says, “what follows—‘to the Father, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named’—should be read not as it has been added in the Latin books, ‘to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,’ but simply ‘to the Father,’ so that the name of God the Father may be applied not to our Lord Jesus Christ but to all rational creatures. Indeed, ancient Greek manuscripts are now available which do not recognize the words τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησού Χριστοῦ, ‘of our Lord Jesus Christ’; and two ancient versions, the Ethiopic and the Coptic, likewise omit them.] of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named.

Just as it was shown above that spiritual eyes correspond to the forms of bodily lights, so now we must understand that there are knees of the outward human being and knees of the inward human being.

For the saying in Isaiah, “Strengthen the weak hands and make firm the feeble knees” (Isa. XXXV, 3), and the Apostle’s statement elsewhere, “That at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. II, 10), refer not to the knees of the body but to the submission of the mind, the inclination of the soul, and the obedience of the heart, which makes itself level with the earth, as the Psalmist also sings: “My soul has clung to the pavement” (Ps. CXVIII, 25).

How could a spiritual and incorporeal soul cling to a bodily pavement? Suppose that earthly beings bend the knee at the name of Jesus. Can we affirm that angels and the other powers who remain in the heavens have bodily forms, so that they bend the knee at his name? Or can we say that souls in the underworld, freed from the bonds of the body, bend a knee which they do not possess?

How, then, everyone who is subject to the Savior is said to bend the knee before him, so the one who is a slave of sin and has again received a spirit of slavery in fear is written to have bent the knee before sin.

“The Lord has left me,” he says, “seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal” (III Kings XIX, 18)—that is, before the idol and sin.

The fornicator, who runs through brothels and after prostitutes, bends his knee to lust. The furious person worships anger on bended knee. The one who looks to Mammon, whose god is his belly, bends his knees to greed and luxury. Why need I go through each case? We bend the knee to the devil as often as we sin.

But although we explain these things spiritually, we do not immediately abolish the literal practice of prayer by which we worship God suppliantly on bended knee and, with the knee fixed to the ground, obtain more readily what we ask of him. For we read that Paul also prayed in this way on the shore, and that kneeling was commanded in prayer (Acts XXVII).

Yet just as this practice edifies the simple, so we teach that true kneeling takes place in the mind, because many who bend the bodily knee have by no means bent the knee of the soul. Conversely, others who pray to God with the body erect have bent themselves more deeply in spirit.

As for what follows—“to the Father, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named”—it should be read not as it has been added in the Latin books, “to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,” but simply “to the Father,” so that the name of God the Father may be applied not to our Lord Jesus Christ but to all rational creatures.

We must therefore ask how every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named from God the Father. Before anything is discussed, we must note that he did not say “from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth was born” or “was created,” but “from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named.”

For it is one thing to merit the designation of fatherhood and another to share in its nature. The fatherhood which in Greek is called πατριὰ (*patria*) and in Hebrew MESPHATH (), that is, “kinship” or “family,” is also found in Numbers: “Take the census of the whole assembly of Israel according to their kinships and peoples, according to the houses of their fatherhoods, according to the number of their names” (Num. I, 2).

And shortly afterward (verse 16): “These are the chosen leaders of the assembly, the princes of their tribes, the chiefs of Israel according to their fatherhoods.”

And again concerning the tribe of Levi: “The Lord spoke to Moses in the desert of Sinai, saying: Number the sons of Levi according to the houses of their fatherhoods, according to their peoples, according to their kinships; count every male from one month old and above” (Num. III, 15).

These passages concern the people of Israel and the priestly and Levitical tribe. But as I consider the matter within myself, where the Gentiles are concerned [Note: Jerome himself wrote very learnedly in Book 14 of his work Against Helvidius: “By kinship they are called brothers who belong to one family, that is, one *patria*, which the Latins interpret as ‘fatherhoods,’ when a multitude of descendants spreads from one root.” In connection with this passage we cited Tertullian, who preserved the word *patria* in the fourth poem Against Marcion:

“To whom, it is plainly acknowledged, every knee bends,”]

From which every paternity in heaven and on earth is named.

Although I have read the term “paternities,” for the present I find no other testimony than that of Psalm 21, in which it is written: “And all the families [*patriae*] of the nations shall worship before him” (Ps. XXI, 30); and Psalm 28: “Bring to the Lord, families of the nations; bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Ps. XXVIII, 1).

[Note: I find this passage corrupted in different ways in Erasmus and Marianus. Erasmus added the words “and in Psalm 95” on his own authority; he also altered the text to read “and in Psalm 28.” Marianus retained Erasmus’s addition but deleted “and in Psalm 28.” We have restored the text in accordance with all the manuscript copies: “and in Psalm 28,” etc., although from the context Jerome is thereby clearly shown to be mistaken, since he has indiscriminately accepted and recited Psalm 28 together with Psalm 95. MART.

The Cistercian manuscripts have “Psalm 27,” but that too is incorrect. For neither in Psalm 27 nor in Psalm 28, which the printed text prefers, is there any mention of a *patria*. It is plainly evident that the verse “Bring to the Lord, families of the nations,” etc., belongs to Psalm 95, just as Erasmus did not hesitate to rewrite it when compelled by the facts. Victorius, on the contrary, preferred to delete the words “and in Psalm 28,” together with that verse of the psalm, since he thought they had been inserted by some ignorant person. We do not dislike Erasmus’s restoration, and we consider it clear that the error was not Jerome’s but that of scribes who frequently made mistakes in numerical designations. Nevertheless, we alter nothing against the testimony of the manuscripts.]

How, then, does God also grant to the other elements the name of his essence and substance, so that they too are said to “be”—not because they exist according to their nature (for there was a time when none of the universe existed, and again, if he wills, they will return to nothing), but because they are said to exist by a gift bestowed through God’s goodness? In the same way he has bestowed upon all things from himself the name of paternity.

To make this clearer, I shall produce the testimony of Scripture [another reading: “they shall produce”]. The Lord speaks in Exodus: “I am who I am” (Exod. III, 14); and: “Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you.’” Was God alone, then, and did the rest not exist? Certainly the angels, heaven, earth, and seas existed; Moses himself, to whom the Lord was speaking, existed; and Israel and the Egyptians existed—the people to whom and against whom the ruler and adversary was being sent. How, then, does God claim for himself the common name of substance?

The reason is, as we said, that the other things received their existence as a benefit from God. But God, who always is, who has no beginning from elsewhere, who is himself the origin and cause of his own substance, cannot be understood to have received from elsewhere that by which he exists. For in fire, too, the thing that is hot is one thing, and the thing made hot another. Fire cannot be understood without heat. Other things, which are warmed by fire, borrow its heat; and little by little, when the fire has withdrawn and the heat has weakened, they return to their own nature and are no longer called hot.

In accordance with this sense, the Gospel also says to the man who regarded the Savior not as the Son of God but as a good teacher: “Why do you call me good? No one is good except one, God” (Luke XVIII, 19). Certainly we read of good soil (Luke VIII), a good man (Matt. XII), and a good shepherd (John X); but no one is good according to nature except God alone. Other things, in order to be called good, derive this from his goodness.

Therefore, just as the one who alone is good makes others good, and the one who alone is immortal grants immortality, and the one who alone is true bestows the name of truth, so the Father alone—because he is the Creator of all things and the cause of the substance of the universe—enables the others to be called fathers.

Let us contemplate heavenly things through earthly ones. Adam, whom God first fashioned, had God as both his Creator and his Father; certainly he knows that he owes to God the Father the fact that he exists. Again, those who were begotten from Adam recognize him as their father, from whom they originated. Hence, in the Gospel according to Luke, when the genealogy had been reckoned backward step by step from Christ through David and Abraham, Scripture finally says: “The son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God” (Luke III, 38), showing that the name of paternity on earth first arose from God.

The question, however, is why every paternity in heaven is also named from him. Just as we, who are not descended from Abraham, are called Abraham’s sons if we have his faith; and just as we call the patriarchs and prophets our fathers, provided that sins do not separate us from them; so, I think, the angels and the other powers have the leaders of their respective kinds in heaven, whom they rejoice to call fathers.

For an archangel cannot be called such unless he is the archangel of angels; nor can dominion, principality, or power be so called unless they have inferiors subject to them. It may therefore also be said that, because God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ is Father according to substance, and because the Only-Begotten is Son not by adoption but by nature, the other creatures have earned the name of paternity by adoption.

Whatever we say about the Father and the Son, let us understand that the same is said about the Holy Spirit. Our Savior too knows himself to be a father, saying: “Son, your sins are forgiven you” (Mark II, 5); and: “Daughter, your faith has saved you” (Matt. IX, 22); and: “My little children, I am with you only a little longer” (John XIII, 13). Through the Holy Spirit, moreover, all the righteous are adopted as sons.

Valentinus thinks that the *probolai* [προβολαί, “emanations” or “productions”] and marriages of his ages are confirmed especially by this passage, entirely failing to understand, as we said above, that in the likeness of God the Father, paternities in heaven and on earth are not made but named.

[Note: Up to this point the reading “the emanations of his ages” (*saeculorum suorum parabolas*) had prevailed through a supine error. We have restored *probolas*, even without manuscript support, compelled by the truth of the matter. Indeed, the Valentinian *probolē* [προβολή] meant “production,” namely, that once the Pleroma had been constituted, each of the Aeons contributed, according to its own will, whatever seemed most excellent to it toward the production of a new offspring. We have collected much material on this word in Book II of the *Apology against Rufinus*, no. 19, where Saint Jerome says: “Candidus, a defender of the Valentinian heresy, says that the Son is from the Father’s substance, erring in asserting a *probolē*, that is, a bringing forth.” See what we note there, so that it would be tedious to repeat the same material here.]

### (Verses 16ff.)

“May he grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner man; may Christ dwell through faith in your hearts; rooted and founded in love, so that you may be able, with all the saints, to comprehend what is the breadth and length and depth and height; and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, so that you may be filled with all the fullness [another reading: “the whole fullness”] of God.”

“For this reason,” he says, “I bend my knees to the Father, after whose likeness every paternity in heaven and on earth is named,” beseeching and entreating him to grant you the power of his glory—that is, to share in his majesty—and to strengthen and confirm you through the Holy Spirit, since no strength exists without the Holy Spirit.

He is to strengthen and confirm you in the inner man. For we do not seek bodily strength but strength of soul; nor do we desire the outer man but the inner man to be strengthened, so that after Christ has dwelt in the inner man, he may dwell in the ruling faculty of that inner man, that is, in our hearts—not running through all its members, but dwelling in its rational faculty and establishing his dwelling and seat there.

This will all take place through faith, if we believe in him. Therefore he says: “That Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts.” This dwelling, which is constructed through the beginning of faith, has its roots and foundation in love, so that, since we are God’s cultivation and God’s building (I Cor. III), everything may grow and be built up in love.

When we know that Christ dwells in the inner man, rooted and founded in love (Eph. III), with complete confidence of mind, then we shall begin, together with the other saints, to reach toward those things also, so that with a discerning mind we may comprehend what is breadth and length, depth and height. And not only this: we shall also desire to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, so that, after all these things have been completed in us in due order and reason, we may then be filled with the fullness of God.

[Note: Victorius preferred “into the whole fullness,” as in the Vulgate and the Greek, or “in all fullness,” as below.]

Let us first learn breadth and length, depth and height from bodily things, so that through them we may be able to pass to spiritual things. For example, let the breadth of this heaven and earth—that is, of the whole world—be from east to west; its length, from south to north; its depth, in the abysses and in hell; and its height, that which is raised above the heavenly realms.

But since many, in accordance with Ecclesiastes (chapter I), assert that heaven is round and turns in the form of a sphere, and since no round body has breadth and length, height and depth, but is equal on every side, we are compelled to understand the height as the angels and the higher powers, and the depth as the lower regions and what lies beneath them. Length and breadth, then, are the intermediate regions situated between those above and those below.

Since it follows that something is either near the higher regions or near the lower, whatever begins to progress toward better things, toward heavenly and lofty things, may be called length. Whatever is closer to the lower region and falls into vices may be given the name of breadth. For broad and spacious is the way that leads to death (Matt. VII, 13).

All these things can also be understood in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ. For “ascending on high, he led captivity captive” (Ps. LXVII, 19), and he descended into the lower parts of the earth. After height and depth, the preaching of the cross went forth into the whole earth. Thus it possesses height, depth, length, and breadth.

Nor is it surprising that the cross of Christ possesses all things, since even anyone who has been crucified with Christ possesses the same power. Such a person will first know breadth, beginning from the lower things and recognizing what is lesser. Next, length: those who, placed on earth, hasten toward sublime and lofty things. After this, depth: the opposing and hostile powers that wage war against us in this world. Finally, height: after gaining knowledge of them and making them subject beneath our feet, we shall then deserve to climb to the lofty and exalted realms.

Nor should we think that the end of our labor consists in this—that, rooted and founded in love, we can comprehend with all the saints what is breadth, length, depth, and height—unless we also desire with every effort to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge. It must be known to us not as ordinary love but as love surpassing knowledge.

Nor is possessing knowledge of Christ’s surpassing love the limit, unless we add something further: that we may attain the surpassing love of knowledge. From this we must observe that Christ has a great and immeasurable love of knowledge—that is, love for those who desire to know him, who meditate on his law day and night, who turn words into deeds and complete by their hands what they meditate upon with their mouths.

Whoever is such that, through his knowledge, he is worthy to possess Christ’s surpassing love ought to think of nothing else besides knowledge. Thus he will be filled with all the fullness of God—not only in the present age but also in the future—so that the one who has now begun to be filled through devotion to reading may afterward be filled more perfectly by God, who is the fullness of all things, as he completes him.

### (Verses 20–21)

“To him who is able to do exceedingly abundantly beyond all that we ask or understand, according to the power that works in us, to him be glory in the Church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations of the age of ages. Amen.”

To what he had said above—“For this reason I bend my knees to the Father, from whom every paternity in heaven and on earth is named, so that he may grant you, according to his riches, to be strengthened with power,” and the rest—he now adds: “To him who is able to do exceedingly abundantly beyond all that we ask or understand.”

By this he shows that, in accordance with human weakness, he asked for what seemed beneficial to them; but, as regards the truth of the matter itself, God is able to grant more than is requested, and his gifts surpass our hopes. For we do not know how we ought to pray, and often we ask for things against ourselves, judging them to be advantageous to us. How much better it would have been for the fornicator to be sick and afflicted with weakness than to make the members of a prostitute into Christ’s temple!

God is therefore able to grant not only beyond what we ask but also beyond what we understand. Sometimes we do not express our meaning in speech, and words do not explain the mind; in silent thought, with inexpressible groans, as the Apostle says, we entreat for something that we cannot utter.

He will therefore provide beyond what we ask or understand, according to the power that works in us. Just as now, not according to our merit but beyond our desires, he gives us certain things that we did not dare to ask for and that, even if we had asked for them, we would not have thought ourselves worthy to receive, so may he grant the other things that the mind cannot conceive and the tongue cannot express.

To God himself, then, be glory: first, in the Church, which is pure, without spot or wrinkle, and which can therefore receive the glory of God because it is Christ’s body. Then in Christ Jesus, because in the body of the man he assumed—the body whose members are all believers—the whole divinity dwells bodily.

This glory does not extend only through the present time and end with future ages; rather, it remains, grows, and increases throughout all generations and through the age of ages, in ineffable eternity.

### (Chapter IV—Verse 1)

“Therefore I beseech you, I who am bound in the Lord, to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called.”

He may have written this while bound in Christ’s chains and imprisoned for martyrdom; but it is better to understand “the Lord’s prisoner” [another reading adds “our”] as meaning one bound in Christ’s love.

Clement also bears witness to this when writing to the Corinthians: “Who can explain the bond of God’s love?” (I Cor. XIII).

[Note: Clearly, this is the First Epistle, no. 49: “Who can explain the bond of God’s love?” (*τὸν δεσμὸν τῆς ἀγάπης τοῦ Θεοῦ τίς δύναται ἐξηγήσασθαι*).]

In the First Book of Kings we also read: “After these things, Jonathan’s soul was bound to David’s soul” (I Reg. XVIII, 1). And the prophet says of the apostles: “After you they shall follow, carrying bonds in their hands” (Ps. CVI). For those who love Christ follow him, bound together by the chains of love.

There is another interpretation, whether it should be accepted or not being left to the reader: this body may be called the bond of the soul, and because Paul received this body for the ministry of the Gospel, he is consequently called Christ’s prisoner.

That the body is called a bond, and that those who are bound in the body are called prisoners of the earth, Jeremiah also testifies in the second alphabet, saying: “To crush beneath his feet all the prisoners of the earth” (Lam. III, 34).

[Note: Marianus placed “third” instead of “second,” because he did not at all understand Saint Jerome’s intention. In the *Lamentations of Jeremiah*, this holy Doctor recognizes only two alphabets, on account of the twofold kind of meter and the different arrangement of the letters. In the first, second, and fourth chapters of the *Lamentations*, there is one simple alphabet of twenty-two letters, composed in a meter almost like the Sapphic; but in the third chapter there is another alphabet, written in a kind of trimeter, with three verses joined together under each Hebrew letter, which is repeated three times. See our annotations on the *Lamentations of Jeremiah*.

Our manuscripts likewise read “second,” following Martianaeus, and this is entirely correct. Jerome calls it the second alphabet because he means the one different from the other. Of the four alphabets that make up Jeremiah’s *Lamentations*, Jerome himself testifies that the first two are written almost in Sapphic meter, because the three connected verses that begin with one letter only are concluded by a heroic colon. He says also: “The fourth alphabet is similar to the first and second”; hence here he counts those three as one. But the third, written in trimeter and beginning three verses under each of the same letters repeated three times, he correctly takes here as the second alphabet, or as the one different from the others. This begins with the third chapter of the *Lamentations*. That fact misled Victorius, so that he thought the third alphabet was being cited here and rashly rewrote the text accordingly.]

Elsewhere we read this very thing from the person of Christ, who says: “Say to those who were in chains, ‘Come out,’ and to those who are in darkness, ‘Be revealed’” (Isa. XLIX, 9).

The prophet may indeed be showing that the bond of sin and the darkness of ignorance were dissolved by Christ’s coming and preaching. But the earlier interpretation also has a place: the bond is the body, and the darkness is this earthly dwelling, where the rulers of darkness and the dark mountains are found—mountains against which we are forbidden to strike our feet.

As for what he says—“to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called”—the person who enters through him who says, “I am the way” (John XIV, 6; and Isa. XXX), and who does not turn aside, neither to the right nor to the left, but turns his foot away from every evil way (Prov. IV), should be considered to walk worthily of his calling. In him is fulfilled the saying: “The steps of a man are directed by the Lord” (Ps. XXXVI, 22).

### (Verse 2)

“With all humility and gentleness, with patience.”

Whoever knows that he is earth and ashes and will shortly dissolve into dust will never be lifted up by pride. Whoever, having contemplated God’s eternity, considers the brief span of human life—scarcely longer than a moment—will always have death before his eyes and will be humble and cast down.

“For the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and this earthly dwelling burdens the mind that is concerned with many things” (Wis. IX, 15). Therefore, with all humility, let us say: “Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up” (Ps. CXXX, 1).

All humility exists not so much in speech as in the mind, so that our conscience may know us to be humble and we may never consider ourselves to know, understand, or be anything. Gentleness is likewise that which is disturbed by no passion and is not broken, especially by anger and rage.

Whoever possesses this will attain the blessedness promised by the Lord’s word: he will possess the earth—that is, he will rule his body and exercise dominion over what is subject to him. This will be his first inheritance: to live in the flesh without living according to the flesh.

Some people, with wrinkled brows, lowered eyebrows, and carefully weighed words, claim for themselves the authority of teachers and judges—not because they themselves know anything worthy of such arrogance, but because, by comparison with themselves, they see simple members of the brotherhood as knowing nothing.

“Bearing with one another in love.”

If anyone understands what “bearing with one another in love” means, he will not think that this command applies to holy men but rather to those who are still at the beginnings of the virtues. The saints will have nothing to bear with in one another; those who still, like human beings, are overcome by some passion will.

Nor is it surprising that the Ephesians hear this, since among the multitude of believers there are some who must still bear with one another. The same thing seems to be signified by what is written to the Galatians: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Gal. VI, 2).

We can therefore interpret both testimonies in another way, saying that those fulfill the command to bear one another’s burdens or to bear with one another in love who are rich and relieve the poverty of the poor.

If someone offers service to a sick brother, he bears with him in love. If someone who passes his life in blessed celibacy helps another who has a wife and children and can scarcely provide food for himself, and consoles him as far as he can, he will be praised for having carried another’s burden.

There is someone who sees his widowed mother or sister wasting away in poverty but cannot help her. If another extends a hand to her, he has sustained her in love.

Whether we follow the first interpretation or the second, the person who lacks love and despises the Apostle’s admonition neither consoles a sinful brother nor helps one in need: “But we who are stronger ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak and not to please ourselves” (Rom. XV, 1).

### (Verses 3–4)

“Eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace: one body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling.”

To the Ephesians, who had already attained the unity of the Holy Spirit, it is rightly said: “Eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.” For the one who possesses something is commanded to take care to preserve it; the one who does not possess it is commanded to strive to obtain it.

This passage is especially directed against heretics, who, after disrupting and corrupting the bond of peace, think that they possess the unity of the Spirit, although the unity of the Spirit is preserved in the bond of peace. For when we do not all speak the same thing and one says, “I am of Paul,” another, “I am of Apollos,” and another, “I am of Cephas” (I Cor. I, 12), we divide the unity of the Spirit and tear it into parts and members.

Let no one immediately object: How, then, are there different graces and various spiritual gifts if the unity of the Spirit must be guarded? There are indeed various gifts, but in the same Spirit; different ministries, but the same Lord; and many kinds of activity, but it is the same God who works all things in all (I Cor. XII, 4ff.).

When he says “one body and one Spirit,” this may simply be understood as one body of Christ, which is the Church. Or it may refer to the body that he deigned to assume from the Virgin; let no one suppose that he took on a body as many times as he appeared in the Old Testament.

And “one Holy Spirit”: for he is the one giver and sanctifier of all.

Alternatively, “one body” refers to life and works, which in Greek are called *praktikos bios* [πρακτικὸς βίος], “the practical life,” and “one Spirit” refers to knowledge and contemplation, which properly takes place in the heart and is called by them *theōria* [θεωρία].

When someone is a member of the Church and is not separated from its one Spirit, he will consequently be in the one hope of his calling.

The question arises how there can be one hope of calling when there are different dwelling places with the Father. To this we shall answer that the one hope of calling is the kingdom of heaven, as it were one house of God the Father, with different dwelling places in the one house.

“For one glory is that of the sun, another that of the moon, and another that of the stars” (I Cor. XV, 41).

Or perhaps something more subtle is indicated: at the end and consummation of things, all things will be restored to their original state, when we shall all become one body and be re-formed into a perfect man, and the Savior’s prayer for us will be fulfilled: “Father, grant that just as I and you are one, so they too may be one in us” (John XVII, 21).

[Note: Here too we have followed Rufinus’s reading, formerly reading less correctly: “in the present, we are made . . . we are re-formed . . . it is filled.” See Book I of the *Invectives*, no. 41.]

I am not unaware that in what I have just explained—“eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace”—many understand “Spirit” not as the Holy Spirit but as the disposition and judgment of the mind, according to which all believers had one soul and one heart (Acts IV). The Apostle also commands the virgin to be holy both in body and in spirit (I Cor. VII, 34), meaning in the work of the flesh and in the disposition of the mind.

But the general explanation can also be applied to the particular interpretation: the person preserves the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace who is not carried about by every wind of doctrine and does not, like a fool, change like the moon (Ecclus. XXVII), now serving the devil and now God.

Let him have one body of good works and always present his flesh to God as a temple. And let him have one spirit, always thinking the same things, in the one hope of his calling, so that, never doubting the promises, he may trust with steadfast mind in the resurrection and restoration of all things.

### (Verses 5–6)

“One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all, through all, and in all.”

Just as faith is distinct from baptism, God, and Lord, so baptism, Lord, and God are distinct from the three individual realities named together. I say this on account of Sabellius, who considers the same one to be God the Father and the Son and confuses the persons because he finds the same divinity in both.

Behold: most clearly, the one Lord is called the Son, and the one God is called the Father. The same is written more fully to the Corinthians: “But for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him” (I Cor. VIII, 6).

For just as the Son does not deprive God the Father of being Lord, although the Son alone is called Lord, so the Father does not deprive the Son of being God, although only the Father is called God.

We read in another place: “Know that the Lord himself is God” (Ps. XCIX, 2); and elsewhere: “The Lord your God is one God” (Deut. VI, 4). For if, as the Arians suppose, God the Father alone is God, then by the same logic Jesus Christ alone will be Lord, and neither the Father will be Lord nor the Son God.

But far be it from us to say that there is no divinity in lordship or lordship in divinity. There is one Lord and one God because the lordship of the Father and the Son is one divinity.

Therefore faith is also called one, because we believe in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit alike. And baptism is one, for we are baptized in the same way into the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. We are immersed three times so that the one sacrament of the Trinity may be manifested.

We are not baptized into the names of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit but into one name, which is understood to be “God.”

I marvel at how Arius, Macedonius, and Eunomius, divided by their disagreement but united in impiety, could suspect diversity of nature in one word, one action, and one sacrament, and, while holding a polluted fountain of the Son and the Holy Spirit as creatures, draw different streams of heresy from it.

“One baptism” is also directed against Valentinus, who insists that there are two baptisms, and against all heretics, so that they may know that they do not possess baptisms but that there is one life-giving font in the one Church of Christ.

“One baptism” may also be understood in this way: although we are baptized three times because of the mystery of the Trinity, it is nevertheless counted as one baptism. There is also one baptism in water, in the Spirit, and in fire. It is of this that the Lord says: “I have a baptism with which I must be baptized” (Luke XII, 50); and elsewhere: “You shall be baptized with my baptism” (Mark X, 39).

The difference among the prepositions in the phrase “one God and Father of all, who is above all, through all, and in all” suggests different interpretations.

God the Father is above all because he is the source of all things. The Son is through all because he passes through and proceeds through everything. The Holy Spirit is in all because nothing exists without him.

Nor should we think that “one God and Father of all” is meant universally, so that the name “Father” could be applied even to irrational animals. If there were ten men, five sons and five slaves, and we said of them all, “Of these ten there is one lord and one father,” we would not thereby call him the father or lord of all alike. So here too, when he says “one God and Father of all,” he must be understood as the Father of some and the God of others.

Zeno and his fellow Stoics have a similar notion concerning creatures and God. Following him, Virgil says (*Aeneid* VI):

> For God moves through all things,
>
> through the lands and the expanses of the sea,

and:

> In the beginning, heaven and earth and the watery fields,
>
> the shining sphere of the moon and the Titanian stars,
>
> a spirit within nourishes,
>
> and Mind, infused through the limbs, moves the whole mass
>
> and mingles with the great body.

Some think that the words “above all, through all, and in all” should be referred in this way to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: the Father is above all because he is the source of all; the Son is through all because all things were created through the Son; and the Holy Spirit is in all, for he is given to believers, and we are the temple of the Holy Spirit. The Father and the Son also dwell in us.

### (Verse 7)

“But grace was given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift.”

Although God the Father is above all, through all, and in all, grace is nevertheless given to believers according to a measure.

This does not mean that God grants the Spirit and grace by measure—for his magnificence has no end—but that, according to the measure of the vessels, he pours in the liquid, bestowing as much of the gift as the recipient is able to receive.

For God does not give the Spirit by measure; nor can that which is equally diffused everywhere have a measure. To make this clearer, let us take an example, although it is imperfect and does not fully correspond to the matter under discussion.

The sea is certainly immense, and its capacity is known to God alone. If someone wished to distribute from it to many people according to what each was able to carry, it would be necessary to give to each according to measure; and their portions would receive a measure, although the whole mass of the sea is immeasurable.

So too the Holy Spirit is indeed immeasurable and confined by no limit; nevertheless, he is given to each according to what is expedient.

It should also be noted that this same grace, which is said to have now been bestowed, has been given to us according to the measure of Christ’s gift.

[Note: This is how the manuscript reads. The Royal manuscript likewise reads this way, as did the first hand of a very ancient copy from Cluny; but a later hand changed *solidum* to *solum*. The printed editions retain neither *solidum* nor *solum* but read *solium*. Let Erasmus and Marianus, the editors, see what sense they make of it. MART.

The Cistercian manuscripts likewise have *solium*, following the old printed editions. Martianaeus found *solum* in other books.]

### (Verse 8)

“For this reason he says: ‘Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to human beings.’” Since he had said above, “But grace was given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift,” in order to confirm that these very gifts—which shortly afterward he also enumerates, saying, “And he himself gave some as apostles, some as prophets, others as evangelists, others as pastors and teachers,” and so forth—were given by the Savior, he took his testimony from the sixty-seventh Psalm, so that we might know that these are the spoils distributed among human beings, which Christ won as victor.

For “ascending on high, he led captivity captive.” We who now believe in Christ, gathered from the nations, although we were God’s creation, had been taken captive by the devil and distributed among his minions. Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ came, bringing with him, according to Ezekiel (chapters 9 and 12), the vessels of captivity. With his head covered, so that he would not be recognized by his adversaries, he proclaimed release to those who were captive and liberation to those who were held in bonds; and he freed us from the chains and fetters of the enemy, just as he did the woman in the Gospel about whom he himself says: “And ought not this daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has bound for eighteen years already, to be released from this bond on the Sabbath day?” (Luke 13:16).

After freeing us, and rescuing us from our former captivity through a new captivity, he led us with him into heaven; and to those very people whom he had victoriously snatched from the hand of the enemies, he generously bestowed diverse gifts of grace.

Elegantly, here he says, “he gave gifts among human beings,” whereas in the Psalter it is written, “he received gifts among human beings” (Psalm 67:19). There, since the event had not yet occurred but was being promised as future, it is therefore said that he received them. Here, however, when the Apostle writes, because he had already given them and Churches had been established throughout the world, it is accordingly written not that he received them but that he gave them.

Others explain this passage in the following way: Our Lord Jesus Christ ascended victoriously into heaven for the purpose of sending from there angels and the other powers to guard his Churches. Since this earthly place is unworthy to have the presence of the higher powers, they had, in a certain sense, endured captivity. “For this reason,” they say, “he ascended on high, so that, taking captivity captive, he might bestow gifts upon human beings.”

The Apostle repeats all this so that, having said earlier, “bearing with one another in love, eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace,” he might teach that the Church is harmonious amid diverse charisms, and that the occasion for schisms and dissensions is not immediately to be created merely because each of us has received gifts according to the measure of Christ’s gift. We have not all been called to one body and one Spirit in order to possess identical gifts, but in order to be one: just as there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and one God and Father, so we too should be one in love, preserving the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

### (Verse 9)

“But that he ascended—what does it mean except that he also descended into the lower regions of the earth?” The one who is now said to have ascended ascended for this reason: because he had previously descended. For this is what the words mean: “But that he ascended—what does it mean except that he also descended?”

We must therefore inquire concerning what is written elsewhere: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man” (John 3:13): how did he ascend, having first descended? When he was saying these things, after his descent from heaven, he was showing that he had once ascended to heaven.
