We must likewise reconsider how that descent and ascent should be understood: whether according to the body, locally; or spiritually, above the body; or, certainly, in both ways. “The lower regions of the earth” is understood as the underworld, to which our Lord and Savior descended in order to lead victoriously with him to heaven the souls of the saints who were held confined there. Hence, after his resurrection, many bodies of the righteous were seen in the holy city (Matthew 27).

The Psalmist also testifies that the underworld is in the lower part of the earth, saying: “The earth opened and swallowed Dathan, and covered over the assembly of Abiron” (Psalm 105:17). This is explained more fully in the Book of Numbers (chapter 16). We also read elsewhere: “Let death come upon them, and let them descend alive into the underworld” (Psalm 54:16).

### (Verse 10)

“The one who descended is himself the one who ascended above all the heavens, in order to fill all things.” Did he pass bodily through and transcend all the heavens, all the heights, and the circles of heaven—which philosophers call spheres—and stand at the summit of the vault of heaven, or, to use the very word, at the *apsis*? Or should we rather believe that, scorning and despising all bodily things and contemplating eternal realities, he stood above the heavens—that is, above invisible things? I consider the latter interpretation better.

Therefore the Son of God descended into the lower regions of the earth and ascended above all the heavens, so that he might fulfill not only the Law and the Prophets but also certain other hidden dispensations, which he alone knows together with the Father. For we cannot know how Christ’s blood benefited both the angels and those who were in the underworld; yet we cannot fail to know that it did benefit them.

He also descended to the underworld and ascended to the heavens in order to fill those who were in those regions, according to what they were able to receive. From this we should understand that before Christ descended and ascended, all things were empty and needed his fullness.

This passage is especially directed against Ebion and Photinus. For if the one who ascended into heaven is the one who had previously descended from heaven, how can our Lord Jesus Christ not have existed before Mary, but only after Mary? It also bears against those who, in their insane error, invent two sons: namely, the Son of God and the son of man. Here it is stated most plainly that he himself is the one who ascends and descends.

By saying these things, however, we do not immediately grant a place to another heresy, which asserts a divided dispensation of Christ. Rather, we confess one Son, both of God and of man, lest, believing only in part the dispensation of the man who was assumed—through which we were saved—we mutilate it by accepting only a portion.

### (Verses 11–12)

“And he himself gave some as apostles, some as prophets, others as evangelists, and others as pastors and teachers, for the instruction of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ.”

From this passage it is demonstrated most clearly that the Father and the Son have one divinity. For what Christ is here described as having bestowed, God the Father is said to have given in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “For God has appointed some in the Church: first apostles, second prophets, third teachers; then miracles, gifts of healings, helps, administrations, kinds of tongues” (1 Corinthians 12:28).

Sabellius, failing to understand this, confuses the Father and the Son, since he does not think that the same activity can belong to different persons. At the same time, we should note that here Christ is said to have given apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers, whereas there the same persons are remembered as having been appointed by the Father. Thus the Father and the Son both appointed or gave, first, apostles and, second, prophets—not those who prophesy future events, such as we read of in the Old Testament, but those who rebuke and judge unbelievers and the uninstructed. In another Epistle he defines such persons as prophets of the New Testament (2 Corinthians 11).

Third come evangelists, “whose feet are beautiful for announcing peace” (Romans 10). We should not think, however, that just as he said above that some are apostles, others prophets, and others evangelists, so he also distinguished different offices between pastors and teachers. For he does not say, “others as pastors, and others as teachers,” but “others as pastors and teachers,” so that the one who is a pastor must also be a teacher. No one should assume the name of pastor in the Churches, however holy he may be, unless he can teach those whom he feeds.

Or it may be understood in another way: one and the same head of a Church is both pastor and teacher—pastor of sheep, teacher of human beings: “You will save both humans and animals, Lord” (Psalm 35:7).

I believe that today too, just as a prophet and an evangelist are found in the Churches, so a pastor and teacher may be found; likewise an apostle may be found in one who fulfills the signs and marks of apostleship. Conversely, there are very many, both outside and inside, both in the Church and among the heresies, who are false apostles, false prophets, false evangelists, false pastors, and false teachers.

With regard to the heresies, there is no doubt that, according to their false faith, they possess everything in false form. But in the Churches, do not those pastors seem false to you who do not feed the sheep with discipline, but, like mercenaries, give no thought whatever to the flock’s salvation? They do not bring back what has gone astray or seek what has perished; they merely seek milk and wool from the sheep—that is, food and clothing.

Nor should we think that the Apostle suddenly entered upon these matters without order. Rather, because he had first said that God is above all, through all, and in all, and that grace had been given to each of the saints according to the measure of Christ’s gift, he now adds that some apostles, some prophets, some evangelists, and some pastors and teachers have been distributed throughout the Church. They are necessary for the perfection and instruction of the saints, for the work of ministry, and for the building up of Christ’s body.

Since the Church is the Lord’s body, and the Church is built from living stones, those whom we have mentioned as appointed in the Church have this task: according to the dispensation and offices entrusted to them, they are to build up the Church of Christ—that is, his body. Therefore, if someone does not build up the Church of Christ and does not instruct the people subject to him, so that the Church of Christ may be constructed from that subject people, he should not be called an apostle, prophet, evangelist, pastor, or teacher.

### (Verses 13 and following)

“Until we all come to the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, so that we may no longer be children, tossed about and carried around by every wind of doctrine, by the deceit of human beings and by craftiness directed toward the trickery of error. But practicing the truth in love, let us grow in all things into him who is the head, Christ.”

We must ask whom he means by “all” when he says that they should come to the unity of faith: all human beings, all the saints, or certainly all who are capable of reason? It seems to me that he is speaking of all human beings, because there are many winds of doctrines; when their blasts stir up the waves, human beings are carried here and there on an uncertain course and in varied error.

Therefore we must labor with every effort, first to arrive at the unity of faith, and then, in that same unity, to possess the knowledge of the Son of God. When we have acquired secure possession of these things, we shall cease to be children and receive the measure of the inner person—which is the measure of fullness, the measure of Christ—and shall acquire the designation “perfect men.”

This is nevertheless to be understood in such a way that [alternative reading: *ut* omitted] the whole company of believers reaches the complete stature of the fullness of Christ, and does not fluctuate in doctrines, carried about like children on the whirlpool of unbelief, uncertainly borne along while winds blow from every direction—namely, the diverse and conflicting arguments of heretics or of the sages of this age. These either bring shipwreck upon their hearers or threaten to do so. Some preach things that are false, though without deliberately intending deception; others, constructing snares with every kind of deceitfulness, hasten to deceive and overcome us.

When the saints have come together and reached the stature of the man mentioned above, then, understanding Christ’s love, they will increase in him all the seeds of truth that they had received, having the Lord Jesus as the head of the body, the Church.

But since he says, “so that we may no longer be children, tossed about,” and the rest, thereby also confessing that he himself is tossed about and a child, it seems necessary to reconsider whether he spoke these words according to humility, or whether, seeing in part and knowing in part, he understood how far he was from perfect knowledge and spoke in accordance with the true state of his conscience.

If someone wishes to say that he spoke these words according to humility, he may use this example: “When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I thought as a child, I reasoned as a child. When I became a man, I abolished the things of the child” (1 Corinthians 13:11).

Another may respond that, in comparison with many, the Apostle had reached the stature of a perfect man, but that, with respect to the things stored up for the saints, he was still called a child. For the prophet refers to all the apostles who believe in Christ as children, saying: “Behold, I and the children whom God has given me” (Isaiah 8:18).

After this, the matter must be discussed more attentively, lest perhaps the Apostle truly said, according to humility, not only that he was a child but also that he was tossed about and carried in different directions by every wind of doctrine, by the deceit of human beings and by wickedness, toward the trickery of error.

But the person who wishes to say that he spoke these words not out of humility but from consciousness of his condition says: Paul the Apostle was a man of sharp and penetrating intelligence, and whenever disputants first began their arguments, his discerning mind anticipated what would have to be answered. He therefore often saw both sides arguing in such a way, and such plausible claims being made concerning opposing matters, that they could cause the hearer to doubt.

For this reason, as a human being still dwelling in a fragile body, he was indeed carried around by every wind of doctrine, but he was not dashed against the rocks, nor was his ship filled by the whirlpools. He stood at the stern, holding the rudder, and by the security of faith broke the foaming waves of heresy.

Yet he did not look upon the winds blowing from every direction fearlessly and securely, calmly and peacefully; rather, he listened attentively and overcame opposing arguments, but his victory was not effortless. Because he saw that the words and arguments of his adversaries, by which they attempted to overthrow the truth, could not easily be defeated, and that they were full of every kind of cunning, woven together by dialectical skill—or rather, by the devil’s art—he hoped for God’s assistance. He hoped that God would drive every doubt from his mind, enabling him to believe the truth with certainty and steadfastness, without disturbance, and to increase it in the love of Christ, whom he knew to be the head both of himself and of the whole body of the Church.

We should know that this passage is clearer in Greek. When it is transferred word for word from Greek into Latin, however, the sense, entangled in the wording, has made what is being said obscure. [Alternative reading: *facere* (“to make”) for *fecere* (“they made”).]

### (Verse 16)

“From him the whole body, joined and knit together through every supporting joint, according to the working in the measure of each individual member, produces the body’s growth for the building up of itself in love.”

At the end of all things, when we have begun to see God face to face and have reached the measure of the fullness of Christ’s stature—“from whose fullness we have all now received” (John 1)—so that Christ is not only partly in us but wholly in us; when, leaving behind the beginnings of childhood, we have grown into that man of whom the Prophet says, “Behold the man: ‘The East’ is his name” (Zechariah 6:12); and John the Baptist also recalls, “After me comes [alternative reading: “will come”] a man who has been made before me, because he was before me” (John 1:30)—then, at the coming together into one faith and one knowledge of the Son of God, whom now, because of the variety of our minds, we do not recognize with one single and identical faith and knowledge, the whole body, which had previously been scattered and torn apart in different directions, will be restored to its own structure and articulation.

Then one ministry, one and the same working, and the completed perfection of one stature will cause the whole body to grow equally, and all the members will receive the increase of stature according to their own measure. This entire building, through which the Church’s body grows in its several parts, will be completed through mutual love.

Let us understand all rational creatures by the example of one rational animal. Whatever we say about its members and parts, we should know that it is to be referred to each rational creature.

Let us imagine this animal so torn apart through its limbs, veins, and flesh that bone is not attached to bone, nor sinew joined to sinew; that the eyes lie separately, the nostrils apart, the hands occupy one place, the feet have been thrown into another, and the remaining members are scattered and divided among themselves in the same fashion.

Imagine someone coming who is such a skilled physician that, following the stories of the pagans, he could imitate Asclepius and raise up Virbius in a new form and with a new name. He would necessarily have to restore each member to its proper place, join structure to structure, and, restoring the parts by a kind of adhesive, make one body.

Thus far the illustration has proceeded as a single comparison. Now let another example be drawn from the same comparison to explain what we wish to understand.

Let a child grow and, through the hidden passage of time, mature into full adulthood. The hands will have their own increase; the feet will feel their own growth; the belly will be filled while we are unaware; the shoulders will broaden while the eyes are deceived. All the members will grow in their several parts, each according to its own measure, yet they will seem to increase not for themselves but for the body.

So also, at the restoration of all things, when Christ Jesus, the true physician, comes to heal the body of the entire Church, now scattered and torn apart, each person will receive his own place according to the measure of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God—who is said to be recognized because he was known previously and later ceased to be known—and will begin to be what he had been.

This is to be understood, however, in such a way that, contrary to another heresy, all are not placed in one single stature—that is, that all are transformed into angels. Rather, each member will be perfect according to its own measure and function. For example, a fallen angel will begin to be what he was created to be, and a human being who had been expelled from paradise will be restored once more to the cultivation of paradise.

All these things will happen in such a way that they are joined to one another in love. While one member rejoices with another and delights in the advancement of the other, the body of Christ—the Church of the firstborn—will dwell in the heavenly Jerusalem, which the Apostle in another passage calls the mother of the saints (Galatians 4).

For this reason, as we said above, these matters are more obscure to us, because in Greek they are expressed metaphorically. Every metaphor, when transferred word for word from one language into another, chokes the sense and shoots of the discourse with what are, as it were, thorns.

[Note: More truly, “we all,” as Rufinus read it, where he also very maliciously attacks the entire following exposition in Book 1, section 41. See that passage.]

[Note: Jerome indicates in Book 1, section 26 of his *Apology* that here he is not speaking in his own voice but from the person of Adamantius. Concerning this Pauline passage he says: “We have compressed Origen’s very extensive exposition, which turns the same meanings over in various words, into a brief discourse, taking nothing away from his examples and assertions. When we had reached the end, we added the following: ‘Therefore also in the restoration of all things,’ and so forth.”]

[Note: This was more than sufficient to clear Jerome of suspicion of Origenism, since he declares that all these ideas originated in the ingenuity of heretics. Rufinus himself replies: “When I say, ‘so that, contrary to another heresy, all are placed in one stature,’ I show that the matters I am discussing are heretical and differ from another heresy. What, then, are the two heresies? One says that all rational creatures are transformed into angels; the other asserts that, in the restoration of the world, each thing will become what it was created to be.” It will be useful to consult this passage.]

### (Verses 17 and following)

“Therefore I say this and testify in the Lord: you must no longer walk as the Gentiles walk, in the vanity of their mind, darkened in understanding, alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart. Having despaired of themselves, they have given themselves over to licentiousness, for the working of every impurity in greed.”

“This,” he says, “I say to you, O Ephesians, and I testify to you: since you are going to come to the measure of the fullness of Christ’s stature, do not walk as the Gentiles walk. They serve idols and abuse both understanding and mind for wicked purposes. Although they received soul and intellect for the purpose of knowing God, they have become alienated from his way—which we know to be no other way than Christ—and walk in the blindness of their own heart.

Would that it were enough merely to have sinned, and that they should, even late, repent and condemn the vices in which they have continually indulged. There would then be a remedy in recovering their senses after error. But instead, having become without hope, they have surrendered themselves, plunging into the mud and abyss like irrational beasts, to licentiousness and lust. They do whatever the body wants, the mind desires, and passion suggests.

And since they have omitted nothing at all that is impure, they have done all this in greed, since they are never satisfied by their lustful indulgence and their pleasure has no limit. Or perhaps, going beyond the permitted union of man and woman, they ascend to greater excesses, committing shameful acts with males, and receiving within themselves the due reward of their error.

The vanity of the mind and the darkness of understanding are divided in two ways: into the affairs of this age and into worldly wisdom. We are involved either in the things of this world, which quickly pass away, or in the knowledge of things that will not profit us.

Does not the person seem to you to walk in vanity of mind and darkness of understanding who is tormented day and night in the art of dialectic; who, as a natural philosopher, raises his eyes beyond the heavens and plunges beyond the depths of the earth into a kind of emptiness of the abyss [alternative reading: “is plunged”]; who constructs an iamb; who diligently distinguishes and heaps up in his mind such a vast forest of meters—and, to pass over the other side, who seeks riches by right and wrong; flatters kings; seizes other people’s inheritances; and gathers wealth without knowing for whom he will leave it in a moment?”

When he says, “having become without feeling, they gave themselves over”—that is, *apēlgēkotes heautous*—the Greek signifies something quite different from the Latin. Those called *apēlgēkotes* are people who, after they have sinned, do not grieve; who, not at all perceiving their own ruin, rush headlong and, like beasts that see a sword, plunge toward death.

Place before me two people caught in the same vice: one who understands and grieves over what he has done, and another who delights in the crime, not only failing to grieve but even boasting and thinking that he has achieved some prize and victory in shameful acts. Does not the former seem to you to grieve, and the latter to feel no grief at all?

Let us express the word from word to word, if we can, and render *apēlgēkotes* as “without pain,” or “insensible to pain.” For one of the philosophers also proclaimed *analgēsia*, that is, insensibility to pain.

Those who introduce diverse natures should understand why the Gentiles walk in the vanity of their mind, with their understanding darkened: because they have surrendered themselves to ignorance and blindness. No one is called uninstructed and blind except one who is capable of knowing and seeing. We do not call a stone blind, nor say that a brute animal is ignorant, because nothing is demanded from it and it is not of such a nature as to know and see.

But if it was part of the nature of the Gentiles to understand and see the life of God, then the difference lies not in a variety of natures—of earthly and spiritual beings—but in the will.

Above we said that “the working of every impurity in greed” does not refer to greed in the ordinary sense, as the words seem simply to indicate, but to lust and sexual excess. We ought to confirm this interpretation by the testimony of another passage.

In the First Epistle to the Thessalonians it is written: “For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from fornication; that each of you know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor, not in the passion of desire, like the Gentiles who do not know God; and that no one transgress and defraud his brother in the matter, because the Lord is an avenger concerning all these things, just as we told you before and testified. For God did not call us to impurity but to sanctification” (1 Thessalonians 4:3 and following).

Observe carefully that, urging us to chastity and wishing us to be content with our wives alone, he says, “that no one transgress and defraud his brother in the matter”—that is, that no one, abandoning his own wife, seek to pollute another man’s wife.

Where we have, “and defraud his brother in the matter,” the Greek reads: *kai pleonektein en tō pragmati ton adelphon autou*—“and to be greedy against his brother in the matter.” *Pleonexia* is called greed, which we can express here, transferring the force of the word, as follows: “that no one transgress and, in his greed, defraud his brother in the matter.”

For what connection is there, either in the passage we have now summoned as an example or in this passage that we are principally attempting to explain to the Ephesians, between licentiousness and impurity, or between chastity and marital affection, and the sudden, extraordinary mention of greed?

Do not be displeased if we linger for a long time over obscure matters. At the beginning we complained that, among all Paul’s Epistles, this one in particular is deeply entangled both in words and in meanings.

[Note: Dionysius, surnamed Metathemenus, had previously held the opinion that pain is not an evil. See Jerome above, in the first chapter of the Epistle to the Galatians.]

### (Verse 20)

“But you did not learn Christ in this way, if indeed you heard him and were taught in him.”

If all those who appear to hear Christ truly heard him, the Apostle would never have said to the Ephesians—and certainly to those to whom he had revealed the mysteries of Christ—“if indeed you heard him.”

To learn Christ is the same as to know virtue. And “hear him” differs in no way from saying “hear wisdom, justice, fortitude, temperance,” and the other things by which Christ is called.

Therefore, if someone has heard Christ and learned him, he will not walk in the vanity of his mind; he will not walk with his understanding darkened; he will not be alienated from the life of God. He will also possess knowledge once ignorance has been dispelled, and when light has been introduced into the darkness, every blindness will be removed from the eyes of his heart.

When he possesses this, he will not give himself over to licentiousness, nor will he work every impurity in greed, transgressing the permitted boundaries of marriage. If it should sometimes happen that he is overcome by some passion, he will grieve over his wound and suffer the torments of conscience, because he has lost the freedom of an open countenance and the purity of an undefiled mind.

Let us therefore learn Christ and hear him. Let anyone who is able say: “Are you seeking proof of the Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Corinthians 13:3). Let us run to him day and night and hang upon his mouth and speech. Christ speaks to us; the words he promises are of the Holy Spirit. For God established in the Church first apostles, second prophets, and third teachers.

Nor should we despair of this: sometimes Christ himself may speak in our minds, teach us directly, and have no need of another’s mouth as his instrument. Let us only not be subject to sin; let our bodies not be possessed by offenses, and wisdom will enter into them.

### (Verse 21)

“As there is truth in Jesus.”

The name “Jesus” sometimes signifies the human being who was assumed from the Virgin by God the Word, according to the saying: “You shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins” (Luke 1:31). Elsewhere: “Jesus, therefore, wearied from the journey” (John 4:6), and so forth.

At other times it signifies God the Word: “For us there is one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things.”

Therefore, whenever Jesus says, “I am the way and the truth” (John 14:6), he speaks according to the fact that he is the Son of God. But when Paul writes, “as there is truth in Jesus,” he is speaking of the temple of the body in which the Word, God, dwells. “For the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

Unless perhaps both expressions are to be understood of God the Word: just as life dwells in him and he himself is life—“For just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5:26)—so the Son may also be called truth, and truth may be shown to dwell in him.

We say these things without separating Jesus from Christ, and without again saying that God the Word is a different human being from the one whom he assumed. Rather, according to the meanings of his acts or circumstances, we call the one whom we believe to be one Son, both Son of Man and Son of God, one thing before the Virgin and another after the Virgin.

The words may also be understood in another way: “as there is truth in Jesus.” In none of the patriarchs, in none of the prophets, in none of the apostles was truth present except in Jesus alone. The others knew in part, prophesied in part, and saw through a mirror in an enigma (1 Corinthians 13).

In Jesus alone the truth of God appeared, which confidently says, “I am the truth” (John 14:6), and which grants freedom to those who believe in it according to the rule of faith. For whoever knows the truth is given freedom by the truth.

That truth therefore assumed the form of a servant and humbled itself, becoming obedient to the Father even unto death (Philippians 2), in order to make the servant free. “Where the Spirit of God is, there is freedom.”

If we wish to recognize the form of the free person in Jesus and to behold the face of truth, let us ascend with him onto the mountain and see him transfigured. There his garments—that is, the Scriptures that announce him—are changed; and Moses and Elijah, that is, the Law and the Prophets, are seen in glory (Matthew 17).

As long as the Lord does not change the form of the servant and does not ascend the mountain, the Law remains in squalor and the Prophets in foulness. When he has ascended to higher things and wishes to change his garments, and when the understanding of the servant has become clear and free, then the faces and garments of Moses and Elijah are also changed.

### (Verse 22)

“To put off, according to your former way of life, the old man, who is being corrupted according to the desires of error.”

Because the sentence appears, according to the order and wording of the passage, to overflow its proper bounds, it should be read in this way:

“But you did not learn Christ in this manner—if indeed you heard him and were taught in him—to put off, according to your former way of life, the old man, who is being corrupted according to the desires of error, as there is truth in Jesus.”

The sense is this: just as there is truth in Jesus, so there will be truth in you who have learned Christ, heard him, and been taught to put off, according to your former way of life, the old man, who is being corrupted according to the desires of error.

I think that the old man whom he commands us to put off is called “old” because he has become aged through wickedness. For, according to his former way of life and the desires of error, he is always wandering, wallowing in the work of corruption; he is corrupted and defiled.

And because he continually remains in the desires of error and never ceases from vice, he is not said to have been corrupted, but to be being corrupted: for day by day, hour by hour, point by point, and moment by moment he is corrupted, destroyed, and defiled.

The word of God, however, which kills in order to give life to the dead, and which, when the dead have been given life, causes them to seek the Lord whom they did not know before, has not corrupted the old man but kills him: “I kill and I make alive,” it says (Deuteronomy 32:39); and, “When he killed them, then they sought him” (Psalm 77:34).

Nor should we think that what he now says—“who is being corrupted according to the desires of error”—contradicts what is written elsewhere: “Even if our outward person is being corrupted, the inner person is being renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16). For the corruption of the outward person is the renewal of the inner person; and conversely, the corruption of the inner person is the restoration of the outward person.

Someone may think that Paul is speaking simply when he says: “If anyone corrupts God’s temple, God will corrupt him. For God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Corinthians 3:17). But perhaps something is also concealed there that appears hidden from us.

If we are God’s temple, according to what is written, “God’s temple is holy, and that is what you are,” and if there is one who corrupts God’s temple and another thing that is corrupted, we must ask who it is that corrupts God’s temple.

If you discover the enemies of Jerusalem corrupting and defiling the temple constructed from stones, you will likewise see the one who corrupts and defiles God’s temple—the one whom God will corrupt and defile as he avenges the corruption of his temple.

Nevertheless, the temple itself, which offered itself to the plots of the corrupter—although it is living and possesses sensation—will also pay the penalty, precisely because, having been corrupted and defiled, it has lost the spirit of incorruption.

(Verse 23, 24.) But be renewed in the spirit of your understanding, and put on the new man, who has been created according to God in the justice and holiness of truth. We are not renewed in the understanding without the spirit, nor in the spirit without the understanding; rather, we are renewed together in the spirit of our understanding. Thus, just as we sing with the spirit and also sing with the understanding, and pray with the spirit and also pray with the understanding, so let us be renewed in the spirit of our understanding. When the understanding has become pure and cleansed, and is free from every stain of filthy coagulation, then let the spirit also be joined to it, and let them be bound together by a kind of bond of unity, so that it is no longer called simply “spirit,” but “the spirit of the understanding.”

When we have been renewed in the spirit—which is the spirit of our understanding—then we shall put on the new man, who has been created according to God. I think this is the same thing expressed in other words in another passage: “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. XIII, 14). For he is the new man, with whom all believers ought to be clothed and dressed. What was not new in the man assumed by our Savior? His conception, birth, delivery, infancy, instruction, life, and virtues—and finally, the cross and passion, in which he stripped the principalities and powers and displayed them openly; likewise his resurrection and ascension into heaven. He, therefore, was truly created in the justice and holiness of truth, because he was true God, the Son of the true God, and in him all the religion and justice of God was completed in truth.

Whoever, then, can imitate his manner of life, express all his virtues in himself, and be gentle as he was gentle and humble of heart; whoever lays down his life for his friends, as he laid it down for his sheep; whoever, when beaten, does not retaliate, and when cursed, does not curse in return, but conquers pride through humility—this person has put on the new man and can say with the Apostle: “But I live—now not I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. II, 10). And: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (I Cor. XI, 1). He can also take up John’s words: “Whoever says that he believes in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked” (I John II, 6).

But when he says, “who has been created according to God,” he does not mean the same thing in Latin speech as in Greek. [Note: Here Saint Augustine, *Against the Adversaries of the Law and the Prophets*, book I, chapter 23, should be consulted. He nevertheless asserts that in Scripture “made” and “created” are equally used of things indiscriminately, whether they arise from some material or from none. Among the pagans, very many examples would have to be praised. Virgil, *Aeneid* X:

> The woodland Faunus, whom the nymph Dryope had created.

And Claudian, *On the Rape of Proserpina*, book I:

> Whatever matter  
> Begets anywhere, is created by you granting it.

] For among us “creation” is called generation or birth, whereas among the Greeks, under the name of creation, the word of making and forming is understood. What among us is called “formation,” therefore, among the Greeks sounds as “creation.” Hence also the heresy that slanders Christ’s birth appropriates Solomon’s example: “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways” (Prov. VIII, 22).

We must therefore consider that “creation” and “formation” are never named except in connection with great works. For example, the world was created; a city was founded. A house, however great it may be, is said rather to have been built than founded or created. In great works and acts of making, the word “creation” is employed. From this we should understand that this new man, who has been created according to God in Christ, is a great work of God and surpasses the other creatures, since he is said to have been formed as the world was, and to have been created as the beginning of God’s ways and at the origin of all the elements.

(Verse 25.) Therefore, putting away falsehood, speak the truth, each one with his neighbor, because we are members of one another. The Apostle did not command this simply, as some think [Note: Here and a little farther below, Rufinus’s book II, no. 2, should be consulted. In accordance with its reading, we occasionally make slight corrections in Jerome’s text.], nor merely in a moral sense: having abandoned falsehood, we are to speak the truth with our neighbors. Otherwise, if we speak the truth only with our neighbors, anyone who is not our neighbor ought to hear a lie. The Law itself, moreover, commands: “You shall not commit adultery with your neighbor’s wife” [Col. 0509C] (Exod. XX, 17). If “neighbor” means only a relative or friend, it would rightly permit adultery with strangers. But it calls every human being a neighbor, since everyone has been born from the same parent as we have.

The parable also signifies this: the man descending from Jerusalem to Jericho who fell among thieves, and, while the priest and Levite passed by, was cared for by a Samaritan and carried back to an inn (Luke X). Afterward the Lord declares that the one who showed him mercy was his neighbor, wishing to show that all human beings are neighbors to all others. Understood in this way, the passage edifies its hearers.

Yet what follows—“because we are members of one another”—seems to me rather to signify a mystery, and to speak of those who are our neighbors in faith and virtue. For members of one another are only the faithful of the faithful, Christians of Christians, and the perfect of those who possess complete and consummate virtue. Therefore Paul himself, being perfect, said in another Epistle: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (I Cor. II, 6).

Accordingly, he commands that each one speak with his neighbor of the mystical and secret things, and of those things that are full of God’s truth; that “day utter speech unto day, and night show knowledge unto night” (Ps. XVIII)—that is, that he disclose things clear and luminous to those who deserve to hear: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. V, 14). But let him report things dark and obscure, veiled in every night of the mysteries, to those who themselves are night, darkness, or gloom, of whom it is said: “And darkness was under his feet” (Ps. XVII, 10)—without doubt, God’s feet. For on Mount Sinai Moses enters into the whirlwind and darkness where God was (Exod. XIX), and it is written of God himself: “He made darkness his hiding place” (Ps. XVII, 12).

Let each one therefore speak truth and mystery with his neighbor, and not give what is holy to dogs or cast his pearls before swine (Matt. VII); but whoever possesses the oil of truth, let him bring such people into the bridegroom’s chamber and the king’s inner room. As for the words, “Speak the truth, each one with his neighbor,” let us know that they are taken from the prophet Zechariah (Zech. VIII, 16).

(Verse 26.) “Be angry, and do not sin.” No one doubts that this has been taken from the fourth Psalm, and it seems contrary to what is said elsewhere: “But now put away from you all anger, indignation, malice, blasphemy, and filthy speech from your mouth” (Coloss. III, 8). Understood simply, however, it is harmful, since it may be thought to loosen the reins of anger.

The word “anger” has a twofold meaning, not only among us but also among philosophers. It may refer to the state in which, provoked by an injury, we are stirred by natural impulses; or to the state in which, after the surge has subsided and the fury has been extinguished, the mind is capable of judgment but nevertheless desires vengeance against the one whom it believes to have caused the injury.

I therefore think that anger is spoken of here in the former sense. We are permitted, as human beings, to be moved at the sight of something unworthy, and for the tranquility of our mind to be disturbed as by a gentle breeze; yet we must not be lifted up by the force of fury into swelling whirlpools. Our Firmianus composed a book *On the Anger of God* in learned and eloquent language. Whoever reads it, I think, will find it more than sufficient for understanding anger.

“Let not the sun go down upon your anger.” If we understand this simply of the sun that is seen by the eyes of the flesh, we sin whenever we become angry and our anger persists after sunset. But we do not sin when, for example, becoming angry from the first hour until the eleventh, we do whatever indignation, fury, or anger has suggested. By that interpretation nothing seems more absurd: as though someone could not rage from sunrise to sunset in such great crimes that he could not expiate them with tears throughout his entire life. Or as though anger were not more likely to find a place during the day, since night is certainly a rest from fury, and when sleep follows, even if we are angry, we postpone our anger until the day.

Because the true sun, just as it set upon the wicked prophets, according to what is written, “The sun shall set upon your prophets at noon” (Amos VIII, 9) [Note: Victorius preferred *occidet* (“shall set”), on the basis of the text of Amos itself.], likewise sets upon all sinners, granting them none of the light of its rising, the Apostle now commands that we not do such things, overcome by fury, through which the sun may set for us and the governing principle of the heart be wrapped in darkness.

Some think this should be understood simply in the same way as that verse of the fourth Psalm, from which it seems to have been taken: “What you say in your hearts, and be pricked in your beds” (Ps. IV, 5)—that is, whatever you sin in the day, whether in deed, word, or thought, cleanse through the night by the repentance that follows; let anger be brief and not be postponed until the following day.

(Verse 27.) “Nor give place to the devil.” “Devil” is a Greek word, which in Latin is called *accuser*; in the Hebrew language he is called Satan, that is, “adversary” or “opponent”; and by the Apostle he is called Belial (II Cor. VI) [Note: Some, rather contentiously, prefer to interpret the word as *without ascent*, that is, of the lowest condition, worthless, and wicked. Jerome more appropriately derived *Belial* from [the Hebrew terms], one of which signifies “yoke” and the other is a particle of negation. This etymology is in fact also current among the Hebrews: Rabbi Solomon explains “son of Belial” as one who has cast off the yoke of heaven. Aquila’s translation, *apostate* (ἀποστάτης), which the holy Father praises, agrees with this; and Suidas says: “Belial, in the language of the Hebrews, signifies the apostate.”]—that is, one who has cast off the yoke and rejected God’s service from his neck. Aquila translated it as “apostate.”

It should be known that wherever the sons of pestilence are written of in the Old Law, as in the passage, “The sons of Eli were sons of pestilence” (I Sam. II), the Hebrew books have *Belial*—that is, they name the devil instead of pestilence [Col. 0511C], although many corruptly read *Beliar* for *Belial* in the Apostle [Note: Here we corrected *Beliar* in place of the corrupt reading *Belian*. *Beliar* is found everywhere among ancient writers, especially the Greeks; *Belian* nowhere and never. We may take Jerome himself as witness in the *Book of Names*, from II Corinthians: “Beliar: blind distress, or blind light, or son of transgression”; but more correctly it is called *Belial*.].

“Therefore,” he says, “do not give place to the devil,” who, like a roaring lion, seeks an entrance through which he may burst in. For just as the Father and the Son stand before the door and knock, so that they may enter and dine with the one who receives them (Rev. III), so the adversary is always ready to burst in upon us; and when we give him an opening, he enters.

Before he comes, however, he usually sends certain darts ahead and makes a thought the herald of his arrival. If we receive and nourish this thought within our heart, and cause it to grow, then, when he sees that his offspring has grown within us, he too will dare to enter.

Thus, into the heart of Judas Iscariot he first cast the arrow that he should betray the Savior. If that wretched man had not cherished the arrow after receiving it, Satan would never, after the morsel had been dipped in the dish, have entered into him. Observe carefully also that the devil found no place to enter Judas, whose breast he had already struck, except at the Savior’s meal (John XIII). For it is then above all that we are handed over to his power, when we are conquered neither by the humanity, clemency, nor gentleness of the one whom we unjustly hate.

To this command that is now given—“Nor give place to the devil”—the statement in Ecclesiasticus may be compared: “If the spirit of one who has power rises up against you, do not give up your place to him” (Ecclus. X, 4). That proud and reckless spirit wishes to climb up and enter; but even if he thinks that he has overwhelmed you and raises himself up, do not give him your place. For the devil’s power lies not in his boldness and boastfulness, but in your will.

(Verse 28.) “Let the one who stole steal no longer, but rather let him labor, working with his hands what is good, so that he may have something to share with the one who is in need.” Those who live amid the occupations of this life are compelled, for the sake of food and necessary uses, either to buy or sell something and to pursue profits from trade. It is difficult even for those who have been freed from other passions—namely, fornication, idolatry, adultery, and murder—not to be held by this vice.

For this reason he now warns the Ephesians not to incur the crime of theft under the pretext of profit. He calls theft everything that is acquired to another’s detriment. It is just, however, that each person, working with his hands and obtaining his livelihood by labor, should distribute to those who have nothing.

He does not say, “Let him labor, working with his hands what is good, so that he may not be in need, have food, and trouble no one”; rather, he says, “Let him labor with his hands at what is good, so that he may have something with which to share with the needy.” Whoever therefore labors only so that he himself may not be in need, and withdraws his hand from others, has not fulfilled the Apostle’s command, even though he applauds himself.

The passage may also be understood in a deeper sense: “Let the one who stole steal no longer,” and so forth, in light of what is written about the false prophets: “They steal each one the words of his neighbor” (Jerem. XXIII, 30). And in the Gospel: “All who came before me were thieves and robbers” (John X, 8). And to the Romans: “You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal?” (Rom. II, 21). Thus we are forbidden to commit spiritual theft.

For what follows—“but rather let him labor, working with his hands what is good”—cannot rightly be referred to the necessities of this life, so that whatever is perishable and belongs to the mammon of iniquity may be called good. Although just labor may produce wealth honestly acquired, it will be enough if such wealth is not called evil; strictly speaking, it cannot be called good.

He therefore performs what is good who turns away from evil, does good, and works in the field of his soul so that he may be filled with spiritual bread and may be able to lend to the hungry and to sustain the one in need, “giving food to his fellow servants at the proper time.” If such a person is one who does good, then the one who steals consequently steals words and doctrines as well, living by theft, sewing himself cushions out of stolen material, and gathering scraps of Scripture here and there so that he may make a torn tunic, one that is below rather than above.

For the tunic of the Church—that is, the body of Christ—is woven from above, without seams, and cannot be torn apart in any part, not even by enemies.

(Verse 29.) “Let no evil word proceed from your mouth, but only such as is good for the edification of the need, so that it may give grace to those who hear.” A good word is one that is useful for edification and gives grace to those who hear it, teaching virtues to be pursued and vices to be avoided. An evil word is one that incites to sins and drives those already inclined toward ruin even more readily to destruction.

In place of what we have rendered “for the edification of the need,” the Greek text has τῆς χρείας, “of the need.” The translator changed this in the Latin manuscripts for the sake of euphony and wrote “for the edification of faith.” Whenever someone makes progress through our speech, and, in accordance with the suitability of the place, time, and person, edifies those who hear, a good word has proceeded from our mouth. But whenever we speak either at the wrong time, in an unsuitable place, or in a manner inappropriate to the hearers, an evil word proceeds from our mouth, to the destruction of those who hear.

Let us therefore consider what we say, because we shall give an account for every idle word on the day of judgment (Matt. XII). Even if we do no harm, yet if we do not edify, we shall have to pay the penalty for an evil word.

(Verse 30.) “And do not grieve the holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.” The grief of the Holy Spirit must be understood in the same way as the anger of God, his sleep, and the other passions attributed to him in human likeness. It is not that the Spirit is grieved or that the divinity experiences any disturbance; rather, through these words we learn God’s feelings, namely, that he grieves whenever we sin and mourns over sinners.

The Savior too, while present in the body, wept over Jerusalem (Luke XIX), and in the prophet he laments the whole human race, saying: “Alas for me, my soul, for the one who returns [or: reveres] has perished from the earth. There is no one among human beings who corrects; all are judged in blood” (Micah VII). And in Ezekiel, while enumerating the works of the holy city, he says: “In all these things you were grieving me” (Ezek. XX).

We have been sealed with the Spirit of God so that both our spirit and our soul may be impressed with God’s seal and that we may receive that image and likeness [Note: It seems that he held the very Spirit of God to be the breath of life that God breathed into the first-formed man. Georgius Bullus praises several Fathers who held this view in his *Defense of the Nicene Faith*, §21; he also takes Rufinus’s side.] according to which we were formed in the beginning. This seal of the Holy Spirit is stamped by God’s impress, in accordance with the Savior’s declaration: “For him the Father, God, has sealed” (John VI, 27).

Everyone who, because he has believed in God, has sealed himself—for God is true—is therefore sealed by the Father through the Holy Spirit. He is sealed so that he may preserve the seal and display it on the day of redemption, pure, sincere, and in no part mutilated, and so that he may thereby be counted among those who have been redeemed.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0513]

I have discussed sufficiently and abundantly, O Paula and Eustochium, the subject of Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians in the preface to the first book. Wherever an occasion arose, I also showed, though briefly, that the blessed Apostle wrote no Epistle to any of the churches in such a mystical manner or revealed mysteries hidden for ages so fully.

Now, therefore, since I am supported by the help of your prayers and of holy Marcella, and am dictating a third—that is, final—book on the same Epistle, it seems right that I should also demonstrate that the etymology of its name agrees with the meaning I explained above. [Note: Jerome borrowed such etymologies of Greek names from Origen, who composed a lexicon of Hebrew names from the New Testament and, rather absurdly, wished to interpret Greek and Latin names as though they were Hebrew. Consult the *Book of Hebrew Names*, volume III, of Martianay. —In that *Book of Names*, which was commonly available and which Jerome himself explained in Latin. Nevertheless, as we have often said, no one should rightly infer from this that Jerome himself approved these etymologies, since he explicitly rejects some of them. [Col. 0514D] This is one of that class: he interprets Ephesus as “will” or “my counsel in her.” It has also been noted by us, in the aforementioned *Book of Names*, that this word can more conveniently be derived from Greek, and that, as Heraclides reports, it may have been so named because Hercules permitted that land to the Amazons. Everyone knows that ἔφεσις in Greek means “permission.” Pausanias, book VII, says that it received its name from Ephesius, whom they mythically say was the son of the river Cayster.]

“Ephesus” is interpreted into Latin as “will,” or “my counsel in her,” or certainly “my soul in her.” The will, counsel, and soul of God are in the one who can say: “For he himself gave me knowledge of all things” (Eccl. I, and I John V). When the uncertain and hidden things of God’s wisdom have been revealed to him, he will receive the testimony of the speaker: “I have found David of Bethlehem, son of Jesse, a man according to my heart, who will do all my wills” (Acts XIII, 22).

The prophet Hosea also signifies such a man when he says: “Who is wise and will understand these things? Who is prudent and will know them?” (Hos. XIV, 10) [Al. “understands and recognizes them”]. But so that you may know how great is the difference between a simple just man and a wise just man, consider what glory each will receive in the resurrection of the dead:

“Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall arise: some to everlasting life, and some to everlasting reproach and confusion. And those who understand shall shine like the splendor of the firmament, and many of the just like the stars forever” (Dan. XII, 2).

“The just,” he says, “shall shine like the stars forever”; but those who understand—that is, those who possess knowledge of the Scriptures—shall shine like the splendor of heaven. This does not mean that a learned man ought not also to be just; rather, an uneducated just man is as far from a wise just man as the radiance of the stars is from the light of the firmament.

If someone is instructed only through meditation on the Law but neglects his life and does not dare to say, “Through your commandments I have gained understanding; therefore I directed myself according to all your commandments” (Ps. CXVIII, 10), he is like sounding bronze, a clanging cymbal, and salt that has lost its savor, to be trampled in the dung (I Cor. XIII; Mark IX; Luke XIV).

If, however, a choice were offered among individuals—setting aside the one who possesses both wisdom and justice—I would rather choose a just rustic than a learned wicked man. In the former, though the glory may be lesser, there is nevertheless the glory of being equal to the light of the stars; in the latter, the greater his progress in knowledge, the greater his punishments. “The powerful shall suffer powerful torments” (Wis. VI, 7); and, “The servant who knew his master’s will and did not do it shall be beaten with many stripes” (Luke XII, 47).

I have said this to show why the name of the Ephesians signifies the soul, counsel, and will of God: for they abandoned the deceits of magical arts and transferred their zeal from error to the pursuit of truth. For their salvation Paul struggled with such great labor that he wrote to the Corinthians: “If, in human terms, I fought with beasts at Ephesus, what does it profit me if the dead are not raised?” (I Cor. XV, 32).

What are these beasts? Surely those of whom the Psalmist prays: “Do not deliver the soul confessing to you to the beasts” (Ps. LXXIII, 13). And elsewhere: “Rebuke the beasts of the reed” (Ps. LXVII, 31). For our adversary the devil “walks about like a roaring lion” (I Pet. V, 8).

When he saw the chief city of Asia being snatched from his jaws by Paul’s teaching, he gathered all the battalions of his satellites and tried to crush him. Insolently exalting himself, he wished, like an eagle, to place his nest over him (Isa. XIV; Prov. IV). The Apostle perceived this and guarded his heart with every care—for he was not ignorant of the devil’s schemes—and after victory, though not an unbloody victory, he said:

“We do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of our tribulation which happened to us in Asia; for we were burdened beyond measure, beyond our strength, so that we were even weary of living” (II Cor. I, 8).

The fact that the Epistle was sent through Tychicus is highly appropriate to the mysteries of that same Epistle (I Thess. IV). The title of the ninth Psalm also announces these mysteries: “For the hidden things of the Son.” For Tychicus is interpreted as “silent” [Note: Again this comes from the *Book of Names* that was commonly available, where Τυχικός is interpreted as σιγῶν, which the holy Father himself also rendered as “Tychicus, silent.” In my opinion, no one is unaware that this is a Greek rather than a Hebrew name, meaning “fortunate” in Latin. Victorius is therefore mistaken when, supposing that Jerome himself approved a Hebrew etymology, he tries to derive it from a Hebrew word meaning “hidden” or “uncertain,” as in Psalm L, and “inner parts” in Job XXXVIII; he also relates it to a word meaning “to cover with crusts” in Leviticus XIV and I Chronicles XXIX, and to one meaning “to plaster” in Ezekiel XIII.], not casting pearls before swine, nor giving what is holy to dogs, but speaking freely to God:

“I have hidden your words in my heart, that I might not sin against you” (Ps. CXVIII, 11).

(Verse 31.) “Let all bitterness, fury, anger, clamor, and blasphemy be taken away from you, together with all malice.” Bitterness is contrary to sweetness; hence people are commonly called bitter and sweet. Jeremiah also speaks of it, saying: “And your bitterness rose up against me” (Jerem. XV, 17).

Fury is anger beginning and indignation growing hot in the mind. Anger, however—of which bitterness and fury are forms—is what, after fury has been extinguished, desires vengeance and wishes to harm the one whom it thinks has caused injury. Although these things are often spoken of with reference to God, according to the statement, “O Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger” (Ps. VI, 1), they must not be counted as disturbances of mind in him as they are in us. For in him all things are measured and ordered, and the punishment by which sinners are corrected is named in our language.

But when we become angry, we are disturbed and, carried away by fury, cease to belong to ourselves. Therefore all bitterness, fury, and anger must be completely removed from us.

As for the Gospel saying, “Whoever is angry with his brother without cause shall be liable to judgment” (Matt. V, 12), the addition “without cause” has been made in vain [Note: There is no need to repeat what we discussed concerning this addition both in Epistle 13, to Castorina, and shortly above in chapter V of Matthew. To the witnesses cited there may nevertheless be added Chrysostom, *Homily* 16 on Matthew and *Homily* 6 *On the Praises of Paul*, the author of the *Incomplete Work*, *Homily* 2, and the *Sayings of the Fathers* in Cotelerius, volume I, among others. Cassian, book VIII, chapter 20, argues quite clearly that the addition is superfluous in certain copies. He holds that it was added by those who thought that anger should never be imputed when there were just causes, since no one who is moved without reason would say that he is angry without cause. If one considers only the meaning, however, it agrees with Jewish opinions, according to which the pagan Canons preserved by Maimonides permit anger “on account of a great or important matter.”], because we are not permitted to become angry even with cause, as the Apostle now says most plainly: “Let bitterness, fury, and anger be taken away from you.” And the thirty-sixth Psalm removes all disturbance of mind in general: “Cease from anger, and abandon fury.”

If anger desires vengeance, and every vengeance seeks to repay evil to the one from whom it thinks it has suffered injury, while a Christian must not return evil for evil but must conquer evil with good (I Pet. III; Rom. XII, 19), and if the Lord says, “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Deut. XXXII, 35), then everyone who becomes angry sins: “For the anger of man does not accomplish the justice of God” (James I, 20).

After bitterness, fury, and anger, clamor and blasphemy are rightly forbidden among us as well. For whoever has once been overcome by fury must burst into shouting, and, raging turbulently, be tossed here and there like a leaf in the wind, saying: “O injustice of the world! O unjust judgments of God!”—and the other things commonly spoken by those who, through the fury of indignation, have lost the judgment of their mind.

Blasphemy, however, is not only open and born of anger; it can also be uttered without anger, with a calm mind. This happens when someone complains about the government of this world and says, “That ought not to be so, but this ought to be so”; or when someone established in the Church and believing in God falls into doctrines that one is not permitted to ignore, thinking differently about the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit from the truth of the matter; not believing in the resurrection of the dead as the Scriptures teach; or envying another’s wisdom and declaring that a person of Catholic faith thinks wrongly, while, out of flattery toward a heretic who serves him, affirming that the heretic is Catholic—calling sweet bitter and bitter sweet.

Therefore we must read the Scriptures with every diligence and meditate day and night on the Law of the Lord, so that, like tested money-changers, we may know which coin is genuine and which is counterfeit.

Let us remove bitterness, fury, anger, clamor, and blasphemy from ourselves in such a way that they are removed together with every kind of malice. Malice may be understood either as the opposite of virtue, which we call vice by another name, or as malignity and wickedness, which are recognized in evasion and deceitfulness.

(Chapter V—Verse 1.) “But be kind to one another, compassionate, forgiving one another, just as God in Christ forgave you.” Above we said that sweetness is contrary to bitterness. The Apostle now calls it by another word, χρηστότητα, that is, “kindness” or rather “pleasantness,” rather than benevolence. He commands that, once we have condemned all bitterness, fury, anger, clamor, blasphemy, turbulent disturbance, and a certain harshness of countenance, we should be merciful and gracious, and voluntarily invite people into our friendship, so that no one is afraid to approach us. This friendship is acquired above all through mercy.

Nor, when we provide something for others, do we immediately cease to possess what we have given. For it follows: “Forgiving one another,” because what is done well for another is stored up more for the one who provides it than for the one to whom it is given. “He who has mercy on the poor shall himself be satisfied”; and “he who gives to him lends to God.”

Alternatively, the words may be understood in this way: when we are pleasant and compassionate, and, abandoning the disturbances that troubled us, pass over to gentleness and self-control, the gift is given and granted to us ourselves, as we turn from evil to good. We give ourselves these very things that God the Father gave us in Christ.

For if, leaving aside vices, we pursue virtues—and all virtues, wisdom, truth, justice, gentleness, and the rest, are understood with reference to Christ—then, when we possess these virtues, we also acquire them for ourselves through our own effort and cause ourselves to have what God gave us in Christ.

Another person will understand the words “forgiving one another” simply, as though, just as it was said above, “Be pleasant toward one another,” so it is now said, “Forgive one another,” in place of “forgive each other.” Just as God in Christ forgave us our sins, so we too should forgive those who have sinned against us.

To demonstrate that the forgiveness of sins is called a gift in Scripture, he may take the example recorded in Luke, where one debtor owed five hundred denarii to a certain creditor and another fifty (Luke VII); the creditor forgave both, and, when the Savior asked, the one questioned replied that the greater gratitude belonged to the one to whom more had been forgiven. It is also said in the Lord’s Prayer: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI, 12).

God forgave us in Christ, not as someone situated outside him, but as one dwelling in him, because the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father. Nor is the one in whom forgiveness is given immediately inferior to the one who gives it in himself, since the Apostle also says: “If I have forgiven anything, I have forgiven it in the presence of Christ and God” (II Cor. II, 10).

“Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children.” Whoever understands how it was said, “Be perfect, just as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matt. V, 48), will know how it is now also said, “Be imitators of God” (I Cor. IV, 16).

Writing to the Corinthians, Paul says: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (I Cor. XI, 1). For they could not immediately become imitators of Christ; it was a great thing for them if they could become imitators of Christ’s imitator.

But to the Ephesians, as people whom he had already taught such great mysteries, he does not say, “Be my imitators,” nor “Be imitators of Christ,” but “Be imitators of God.” This is not because being an imitator of Christ is less than being an imitator of God—for Christ is God—but because one thing is to imitate according to the human nature and another according to the divine.

Although we once knew Christ according to the flesh, now we know him no longer according to the flesh. The Savior himself speaks, displaying the humility of his dispensation: “Whatever he sees the Father doing, the Son does likewise” (John V, 19). This does not mean that the Father made one heaven and one earth, and that Christ, in their likeness, made another heaven, another earth, and the other elements. Rather, whatever the Father does, the Son does the same.

In what way we can become like God, he has already testified above, saying: “Forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you.” I do not think that in all the other things God has done a human being can imitate God. Rather, for example, just as he is merciful and sends rain upon the good and the evil, so let us pour out our goodness upon all human beings. When we have done this, we shall be beloved children—either of Paul himself or, as I think better, of God.

## (Verse 2)

And walk in love, just as Christ also loved us and handed himself over for us as an offering and sacrifice to God, for a pleasing fragrance. Whoever fights against sin for the salvation of others even to the shedding of his blood, so that he gives up his own life for them—such a person walks in love, imitating Christ, who loved us so greatly that he endured the cross for the salvation of all. For just as he gave himself up for us, so this person, willingly dying for those whom he can help, will imitate him who handed himself over to the Father as an offering and sacrifice for a pleasing fragrance; he too will become an offering and sacrifice of God for a pleasing fragrance.

## (Verses 3, 4)

But fornication and every kind of impurity or greed must not even be named among you, as is fitting for holy people; nor obscenity, foolish talk, or vulgarity, which have nothing to do with the matter, but rather thanksgiving.

If a certain Cynic philosopher had not arisen who taught that every bodily titillation and emission of semen arising from any sort of friction or touch need not be avoided at the proper time, and if some wise men of this age had not consented to this disgraceful and shameful heresy, the holy Apostle, writing to the Ephesians, would never have joined every kind of impurity to fornication, nor greed to impurity—not the greed by which we desire to accumulate money, but that of which we spoke above: “Let no one transgress and defraud his brother in business.” Such a person, insatiable and never satisfied, runs through every kind of shamefulness and wantonness.

“As is fitting,” he says, “for holy people.” From this it follows that no one can be called holy who, apart from fornication, is found in any impurity or greed for pleasures that have delighted him.

If anyone thinks that greed should not be understood in the sense we have described, let him explain why, among fornication, impurity, obscenity, foolish talk, and vulgarity, he placed greed in the middle in an exceptional position.

Moreover, I think that foolish talk belongs not only to those who tell shameful stories in order to provoke laughter and, by feigned stupidity, mock all the more those whose approval they desire, but also to those who are regarded as the wise men of this age and, discussing physical matters, say that they have clearly comprehended the sands of the shores, the drops of the Ocean, the extent of the heavens, and the point of the earth.

There is also foolish talk in the Church. If someone, deceived by the words of Isaiah, whom he does not understand, thinks that heaven is curved like a vault; and that a throne has been placed in the heavens, with God seated upon it; and that, after the manner of an emperor and judge, angels stand around him, obeying the words of the one who commands and being sent to various duties (Isaiah 6)—this too is foolish talk.

But since “vulgarity” follows “foolish talk,” foolish talk should rather be referred to foolish and pointless stories. The difference between foolish talk and vulgarity is this: foolish talk contains nothing wise or worthy of the human heart. Vulgarity, however, proceeds from a prudent mind and deliberately seeks certain refined, rustic, shameful, or witty expressions—what we may call “joking” by another word—in order to provoke laughter in those who hear it.

Yet even this must be entirely driven away from holy men, for whom it is more fitting to weep and mourn, as we also read in the Hebrew Gospel, where the Lord speaks to the disciples: “Never,” he says, “be joyful unless you have seen your brother in love.”

Up to this point, he seems to have introduced nothing foreign to the subject or to the sequence and order of the text. But someone may ask what the concluding phrase means: “But rather thanksgiving.” Why, after forbidding fornication, impurity, wantonness, obscenity, foolish talk, and vulgarity, does he place thanksgiving?

For if he was free to introduce any virtue he wished, he could have said, “but rather justice, truth, or love.” Yet just as this would be incongruous, so those alternatives would also have been incongruous, and under the same freedom there would have been no order.

Perhaps, therefore, “thanksgiving” is not named here in the sense in which we give thanks to God, but in the sense in which we are called “gracious” or “pleasing,” and witty, by human beings. It is not fitting for a Christian to be a foolish speaker or a vulgar person. It is fitting, however, that his speech be seasoned with salt, so that he may have favor with those who hear him.

And because it is not customary among the Greeks, except among the learned, to use εὐχαριστίαν (*eucharistian*)—“thanksgiving”—in distinction from the Eucharist, that is, to mean “to be gracious” or “to give thanks,” I think that the Apostle, as a Hebrew of Hebrews, used a familiar word and wished to explain his meaning by means of another sense of the word. This is especially so because among the Hebrews [Note: [Col. 0519D] *hhonen* or *hhannun* means “gracious” in Hebrew, and also signified “giving thanks,” as they themselves testified in Jerome’s time, saying that both meanings were expressed, as they say, in a single word. MART.] “gracious” and “giving thanks” are said, as they claim, with one and the same word.

Hence I think that Proverbs is written in the following way: “A woman [Note: [Col. 0519D] Martianaeus, relying—as he says—on a Cluniac manuscript, rewrites the word as εὐχαριπὸς, a word unknown to the whole of Greece. He was mistaken in thinking that Jerome had read the Greek of Proverbs differently from the common text, or had established that it should be read differently. On the contrary, while leaving the genuine reading εὐχάριστος entirely unchanged, the holy Father insists only that it must be given a special meaning: namely, that it does not mean “thankful” or “giving thanks,” but properly “gracious,” a meaning confirmed by the sequence of the sacred text and by the authority of the ancient translators Aquila, Theodotion, and Symmachus. We have restored the ancient reading. —MART.

Thus the Cluniac manuscript reads it; the entire context of Jerome likewise shows that it should be read this way. Jerome thought that Proverbs should be read differently from the common text: not γυνὴ εὐχάριστος, “a woman giving thanks,” but γυνὴ εὐχαριπὸς, “a gracious woman,” graceful in appearance and beautiful. MART.] εὐχάριστος ἐγείρει ἀνδρὶ δόξαν”—“a gracious woman raises glory for her husband” (Proverbs 11:16)—where the meaning is “gracious.” We might seem to do violence to Scripture by boldly taking “a woman giving thanks” in place of “a gracious woman,” unless the other editions also agreed with our opinion.

For Aquila, Theodotion, and Symmachus likewise rendered it γυνὴ χάριτος, that is, “a gracious woman,” and not εὐχάριστος, which refers to the act of giving thanks.

[Note: [Col. 0520D] Erasmus and Marianus corrupted this reading. Instead of the words of the Greek translators, γυνὴ χάριτος, “a woman of grace,” or “of beauty,” they inserted words of their own invention, γυνὴ χαροπός. We have often observed the same thing elsewhere. MART.

Drusius, however, and the Roman edition of the Septuagint, which preceded him, report that the text is read in the scholia of Symmachus as γυνὴ ἀγαθή, “a good woman.” This may derive from another edition of Symmachus, as Montfaucon also observes. Victorius, on the other hand, reads γυνὴ χαροπός.]”

## (Verse 5)

But know this: no fornicator, impure person, or greedy person—which is the same as an idolater—has an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God.

It should be noted that, although six vices were forbidden above— fornication, impurity, greed, obscenity, foolish talk, and vulgarity—he now mentions only three: fornication, impurity, and greed. Whoever is subject to these cannot possess an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God.

For if foolish speakers and vulgar people were likewise excluded from the kingdom of God, how would it not seem cruel, when he has specifically separated these three, not to pardon human weakness and frailty, since he would then condemn even words spoken in jest? “Whoever does not stumble in speech is perfect” (James 3:2).

Nor, by saying this, do we give license to foolish talk and vulgarity simply because they do not exclude a person from the kingdom. Rather, just as there are different dwelling places with the Father, and one star differs from another in glory (John 14; 1 Corinthians 15), so too there is a difference in the resurrection of the dead. Even if someone is free from fornication, impurity, and wantonness, yet if he is foolish in speech and vulgar, he will not occupy the place he would have possessed had he not had these vices.

Someone may reply: “Granted that foolish talk and vulgarity do not incur the same guilt as fornication, impurity, and greed; should he not nevertheless have named obscenity together with the three preceding vices?”

The answer is that obscenity here signifies a hidden thought, when our senses are inflamed with lust, and the soul is kindled by the titillations of the flesh, yet is restrained by the fear of God and the judgment of the mind.

Indeed, above he named three together without obscenity, saying: “But fornication and every impurity and greed must not even be named among you”; and afterward obscenity was counted together with foolish talk and vulgarity. Just as foolish talk and vulgarity do not destroy a person or exclude him forever from the kingdom, so this obscenity likewise does not do so.

Since above, on the basis of what we had read elsewhere—“Let no one transgress and defraud his brother in business” (1 Thessalonians 4:6)—we said that “greed” had been put in the place of adultery, we now ask whether the phrase “or greedy, which is idolatry,” agrees with that interpretation or with the commonly accepted interpretation.

In many passages of the prophets we find idolatry called fornication: “They fornicated after their idols” (Hosea 4:12); and, “They were led astray by the spirit of fornication.” Thus fornication can also be understood as referring to idolatry.

But if the greedy person is understood as one who acquires money by whatever means and desires to possess coins by right or wrong, taking delight in the full abundance of this age, he is an idolater in this respect: he worships the image of the coin itself and venerates the idols engraved upon it. Just as the belly is the god of the gluttonous, so money can rightly be called the god of the covetous—especially since elsewhere the Apostle calls covetousness idolatry.

We must also examine what he wished to convey when he said, “in the kingdom of Christ and God” (1 Corinthians 10). Is the kingdom of Christ one thing and the kingdom of God another, or is the kingdom of the Father and the Son one and the same?

If he had said, “in the kingdom of the Son and the Father,” we would come through the Son to the Father; and although there would be a distinction of persons, the majesty of those who reign would nevertheless be one. But since he says, “in the kingdom of Christ and God,” we should understand God himself and Christ, because even when he hands over the kingdom to God and the Father, the Father will not be “all in all,” but God will be “all in all.” Wherever God is, the Father as well as the Son can be understood.

Moreover, what we say concerning the Father and the Son, we should understand in the same way concerning the Holy Spirit.

## (Verse 6)

Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the children of distrust.

Words that deceive and overthrow are empty and void. But words that build up their hearers are full, rich, and abundant.

Since, therefore, there are many who say that there will be no punishments for sins, nor tortures inflicted from outside, but that sin itself and the consciousness of guilt constitute the punishment—since the worm does not die in the heart and fire is kindled in the soul, like a fever that does not torture a sick person externally but, seizing the body itself, punishes it without the imposition of external torments—he called these beliefs and fraudulent snares “empty and void words.” They seem to have a certain rhetorical bloom and to flatter sinners, but while they give them confidence, they carry them all the more toward eternal punishments.

For God is not angry over anything as he is when a sinner becomes proud, standing erect and stiff-necked, refusing to bend toward weeping or to ask mercy for his offense.
