“Because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the children of distrust,” or “of unpersuadableness.” For ἀπείθεια (*apeitheia*) can be understood as deriving more from “persuasion” than, conversely, from “trust.” The children of unpersuadableness, or distrust, are named in the same way as the children of destruction, the children of fornication, the children of death, the children of Gehenna, and other similar expressions, which are very easy to find in various passages of Scripture.

[Note: [Col. 0522D] He is easily attacking the Origenists, who may have learned this delirium from Origen himself, *On First Principles*, Book II, chapter 2. Orosius also reports it in his commentary on Saint Augustine, where, among other things, he says that the Origenists were accustomed to proclaim publicly that the eternal fire by which sinners are punished is not real fire, asserting that the phrase referred to the punishment of conscience itself—as though, after the purification of conscience, the souls of sinners would return to unity with the body of Christ.]

## (Verse 7)

Therefore do not become fellow-participants with them.

A person becomes a participant or fellow-participant with the children of distrust when he is found in fornication, impurity, and greed, because of which the wrath of God comes upon the children of distrust.

A participant is so called from the thing in which he participates and with which he shares the communion of evil works. A fellow-participant, however, is one who is a participant together with others; and in “fellow-participant,” “participant” is also understood. But in “participant,” “fellow-participant” is not necessarily implied.

Observe carefully the words “fellow-participant” and “participant.” For I think that in Scripture “participant” is always taken in a good sense, and “fellow-participant” in a bad one. For example: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your participants” (Psalm 44:8); and elsewhere: “For we have become participants in Christ, if indeed we hold the beginning of our substance firm to the end” (Hebrews 3:14).

I do not remember reading “fellow-participant” elsewhere except in the present passage; nevertheless, it is clear that here it is used not in a good sense but in the opposite one.

## (Verse 8)

For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.

If it is possible for darkness to be changed into light, then, contrary to the claims of certain heretics, nature is not something doomed to perish and incapable of receiving salvation. Let us therefore ask those who invent such ideas whether all the ungodly are darkness or not. Some who were called darkness because of their wickedness, after turning to better things, are now called light in the Lord.

Just as the righteous are the light of the world, so the wicked will consequently be called darkness. The righteous, being light, will see light in light; but the unrighteous, being darkness, are the people sitting in darkness and seeing nothing.

We understand the difference and separation between them from their fruits. Everyone who does evil hates the light, and, refusing to come to the light, is darkness and a child of night and darkness. But whoever does the truth comes to the light; he is light and a child of light and of day (John 3:20–21).

Those who shine, or those who are dark, are recognized by the light or darkness of their hearts. In addition, you may ask whether, to distinguish those who are light but are not light “in the Lord,” the phrase “now you are light in the Lord” is spoken of the righteous. It is fittingly written to the Ephesians, who had risen to the summit of knowledge, that they are light in the Lord.

Nor is darkness itself changed into light, or light into darkness. Rather, those who have acquired the name either of virtue or of vice from what they are, if they are converted from one condition to another, will receive, by a common name, the designation of the darkness or light by which they are possessed.

Walk as children of light.

If God is light, and there is no darkness in him, the children of God are children of light. Likewise, if Christ is the true light, his children too—to whom he says, “Little children, I am with you only a little longer” (John 13:33)—are children of the true light. From this it follows that those who are children of Christ Jesus are also children of God the Father.

## (Verse 9)

For the fruit of light consists in all goodness, justice, and truth.

Against Marcion—who separates the just God from the good God and thinks that the Creator is just, while some other unknown God, whose son is this Christ who has come, is good—we should bring forward this testimony. The fruit of light consists not only in goodness but also in justice and truth. Therefore, wherever goodness is, there is also justice; and wherever justice is, there consequently is truth.

Thus, according to the good Father of Christ—as they themselves also acknowledge—there are truth and goodness. But wherever goodness and truth are found with him, and not with another, there is also justice, as the Apostle now teaches.

Marcion should also understand that Christ himself is called goodness, truth, and justice. He is called goodness because he gives grace to those who believe in him, not according to their works but according to his mercy. He is called justice because he repays each person according to what he deserves. He is called truth because he alone knows the causes of all creatures and of all things.

## (Verse 10)

Testing what is pleasing to God.

Everything must be done with deliberation, so that, being cautious and attentive, we do only what we know to be pleasing to God—like a very prudent money-changer who tests a stamped coin not only with his eye but also by its weight and its ring.

Since the sequence of the discourse seems disturbed at this point and the whole sentence appears disordered, the passage should be restored to this order:

“Therefore do not become fellow-participants with them, testing what is pleasing to God. For although you were once darkness, now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light, displaying the fruit of light in all goodness, justice, and truth.”

## (Verse 11)

And do not participate in the unfruitful works of darkness.

In the Epistle to the Galatians he used the word “fruit” with reference to the Spirit, but “works” with reference to the flesh, saying: “The works of the flesh are manifest, which are fornication” (Galatians 5:19), and the rest. But “the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace” (ibid., 5:22), and the others.

Here, however, he called the works of darkness “unfruitful.” Those who perform them become participants in them.

But rather, reprove them.

Among the other commandments, the ability to reprove sinners is a mark of the greatest freedom. Yet only someone who does not deserve to hear, “Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your own eye, and then you will be able to remove the splinter from your brother’s eye” (Luke 6:42), can do this.

For this reason the prophets, who themselves were stained by no defilement of sin and whose consciences were not seared, could reprove others who were sinning. From this we must understand that the person able to reprove is one who is not himself reproved in his own conscience.

## (Verse 12)

For the things they do in secret, it is shameful even to speak of.

The sequence of the discourse does not seem to stand, if what is now said—“For the things they do in secret”—is made to depend on what precedes, since it cannot be known to whom the phrase should chiefly refer. Unless we place the hyperbaton farther back and connect it with the children of disobedience, so that the meaning is:

“For the things done secretly by the children of distrust—it is shameful even to speak of them”—namely, fornication, impurity, and every kind of greed.

## (Verse 13)

But everything reproved is manifested by the light; for everything that is manifested is light.

There is no doubt that “everything” refers to the things secretly done by the children of disobedience. These are manifested when reproved by the light.

The light reproves what was previously darkness and afterward became light in the Lord, so that, by being corrected, such things may be changed for the better; and, once changed, may be manifested publicly and, having been made public, may become light, because everything that is manifested is light.

## (Verse 14)

Therefore he says:

“Awake, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ will shine upon you” (or, “Christ will rise upon you”).

Since the works of darkness are reproved by the light and, once reproved, are changed into light, these words are spoken to those who sleep and to the dead, because they have performed the works of darkness: “Awake, you who sleep, and rise from the dead.”

Someone may ask who it is who says, “Awake, you who sleep, and rise from the dead,” or from whose testimony the Apostle borrowed these words.

A person satisfied with a simple answer will say that the Apostle brought forward words read in the hidden prophets and in writings called apocryphal—just as it is clear that he did in other passages—not because he approved the apocrypha, but because he also used verses of Aratus, Epimenides, and Menander to establish in due time what he wished to prove.

Yet not everything written by Aratus, Epimenides, and Menander is holy merely because he testified that they had said something true.

Another person may say that the Apostle formed a προσωποποιΐα (*prosopopoiia*), a personification of the Holy Spirit, and that these words were spoken as an exhortation to repentance.

For my part, according to my limited ability, I have carefully examined all the editions of the ancient Scriptures and the Hebrew volumes themselves, and I have never found this written anywhere.

Unless we say the following: just as formerly the prophets spoke in the assembly of the people, “Thus says the Lord,” and, “Because the Lord has spoken,” so the Apostle, filled with the Holy Spirit, suddenly burst into words that Christ was speaking through him and said, “Thus says the Lord.”

We must also discuss how one and the same person can be addressed as though living with the words, “Awake, you who sleep,” and as though dead with the words, “Rise from the dead.”

Since there is the human spirit, which we always remember being written of in a good sense, and the soul, whose weaknesses and deaths as a result of sins we read about, what is now said—“Awake, you who sleep”—should be referred to the spirit, while what follows—“Rise from the dead”—should be applied to the soul. For “the soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezekiel 18:4). But we never read that the spirit dies at all.

Thus Christ, the true light, will rise upon the person who has arisen from sleep and has been raised from the dead.

I know that I once heard someone discussing this passage in the Church who, in order to present the people with a theatrical marvel never previously seen, introduced the following attractive claim:

“This testimony,” he said, “is addressed to Adam, who was buried at the place of Calvary, where the Lord was crucified. It is called Calvary because there the head of the ancient man was buried. Therefore, at the time when the Lord was crucified and hung above Adam’s tomb, this prophecy was fulfilled:

‘Awake, Adam, you who sleep, and rise from the dead.’”

[Note: [Col. 0525D] We have also seen above that Jerome refers to this unknown person in his commentary on Matthew 27:33. Since the notion invented to produce a popular miracle—that Adam was buried at the place of Calvary, where Christ was crucified—is itself widespread, it is certainly paradoxical that this person applied these words, “Awake, you who sleep,” to Adam. Saint Ambrose, in his commentary on this Epistle, and Augustine, in his commentary on Psalm 3, likewise read “and they will touch you,” a reading Jerome approves. Erasmus, followed by Victorius, conjecturally introduced the Greek ἐφάψεται in place of ἐπιψαύσει. Chrysostom, Homily 18 on this passage, writes: “Some say, ‘And you will touch Christ’; others say, ‘Christ will shine upon you’; and the latter is more correct.”]

“And not as we read, ἐπιφαύσει σοι Χριστός, that is, ‘Christ will rise upon you,’ but ἐπιψαύσει, that is, ‘Christ will touch you.’”

For, by the touch of his blood and of his hanging body, Adam would be brought to life and rise. Then that type too would be fulfilled in reality, when Elisha raised a dead man by means of a dead man (2 Kings 13).

Whether these things are true or not I leave to the judgment of the reader. Certainly, at that time they pleased the people and were received with a kind of applause and rejoicing. I will say only what I know: this interpretation does not agree with the meaning and sequence of the passage.

[Note: [Col. 0525D] Saint Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 42, p. 372, apparently thought that this testimony was cited from the apocryphal *Book of Elijah*. George Syncellus, in his *Chronography*, p. 121, says that it comes “from the apocryphal writings attributed to Jeremiah.” Others, by contrast, think that it can be found in the canonical books. Saint Thomas derives it from Isaiah 60: “Arise, shine, Jerusalem, for your light has come.” Others prefer Isaiah 26:19: “Your dead shall live; my slain shall rise ... for the dew of light is your dew”; or, finally, Isaiah 9:2: “The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; light has risen upon those dwelling in the land and shadow of death.” Consult the commentators on these passages.]

[Note: [Col. 0526D] Who would have believed that scarcely any Greek word quoted by Jerome has not been corrupted by Erasmus and, after him, Marianus? In place of ἐπιψαύσει, those editors inserted ἐφάψεται, contrary to the evidence of the manuscript codices. Jerome spoke of the same interpretation above in his commentary on Matthew 27. MART.]

## (Verse 15)

Therefore see carefully how you walk, not as unwise people but as wise.

It is rightly said to the Ephesians that they should walk carefully, since they had trained faculties for discerning good and evil; and, testing everything, they retained what they had determined to be good.

Whoever sees how he walks and how carefully he places his step, lest he perhaps strike his foot against a stone, and says, “Your word, Lord, is a lamp for my feet” (Psalm 118:105), is certainly wise.

For I do not think that an ordinary person, even if he wishes to walk carefully, can fulfill this command, since it is given to the wise and not to the unwise.

From this we understand that even the moral commandments—which many consider obvious because of what is said in Psalm 18:9, “The commandment of the Lord is lucid, enlightening the eyes”—require a prudent and careful interpretation. That lucid commandment enlightens the eyes of those who, having abandoned folly, have devoted themselves to the study of wisdom.

## (Verse 16)

Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.

Whoever is wise, and therefore walks carefully, redeems the time. He redeems the time because the days are evil.

When we spend time in a good work, we purchase it and make our own what had been sold by the wickedness of human beings. But no one who seeks the necessities of this life and thinks about riches and anxieties—which the Gospel calls “thorns” (Mark 4; Luke 8)—can redeem time for himself.

By redeeming time that exists amid evil days, we in a certain sense change it. We turn evil days into good days, and make them belong not to the present age but to the future one.

This passage may also be explained in another way:

“O Ephesians, for whom Christ, the sun of righteousness, has risen as you arose from the sleep of this age, walk carefully and prudently. Cast away folly and hold fast to wisdom, so that you may not be changed with the changing times, but may make the diversity of times into one time for yourselves.

“Since there are many persecutions—for at the beginning of the faith the Churches were harassed almost every day—maintain one course, and know that this must be preserved: do not be changed like a foolish person, as the moon changes, but hold firmly with a steadfast mind to what you once began. Otherwise, if you see a persecuting judge, you may change together with the judge’s will.

“Again, if someone who praises your doctrine appears, acknowledge that you are Christians; but preserve what you are at all times.”

Let us give an example from Scripture, so that what we are saying may become clearer.

Joseph had one purpose: to please God. This was not changed by any variation of time—not by his brothers’ envy, nor by his condition of slavery, nor by the allurements of youth, nor by his mistress’s promises, nor by the squalor of prison, nor afterward by the pride of Egyptian power. He was always one and the same; and, as we have said, by redeeming for himself the changing times, he turned evil days into good ones.

The same must be understood of Job. Although he was afflicted by various trials, he was changed neither by riches, nor by losses, nor by bereavement, nor by wounds, nor by the reproaches of his friends, nor by solitude, nor afterward by the restoration of all his goods. He had redeemed time for himself and had made evil days good.

## (Verse 17)

Therefore do not become foolish, but understand what the will of God is.

Since the time is evil and, as we said above, must be redeemed, wisdom should first be sought, so that through it we may be able to understand what the will of God is.

For we cannot walk carefully unless we first understand the will of God. Thus, in every action, we must first consider what God wills; and, after forming our judgment, do what has been shown to be pleasing to him.

## (Verse 18)

And do not become drunk with wine, in which is wantonness, but be filled with the Spirit.

Just as we cannot serve two masters, God and Mammon (Matthew 6), so we cannot be filled both with the Spirit and with wine.

The person filled with the Spirit possesses prudence, gentleness, modesty, and chastity. The person filled with wine possesses folly, rage, shamelessness, and lust. I think that “wantonness” signifies all this in a single word.

If certain people understood this, they would never have accused me of rashness and heresy because, in my discussion of preserving virginity, I said that young people should avoid wine, that oil should not be poured upon a flame, and that the natural heat of the flesh should not be increased by the fuel of pleasure.

The wine “in which is wantonness” may also be understood as the wine mentioned in the Song of Moses: “The fury of dragons is their wine, and the incurable fury of serpents” (Deuteronomy 32:33). All who are drunk with the concerns of this age drink this wine, become insane, vomit, and fall headlong. In accordance with the story of the Lapiths and Centaurs, they are driven toward mutual destruction.

Opposed to this wine is the wine that the Lord promises to drink with us in his kingdom (Mark 14).

We have frequently observed that the word “spirit,” when used without qualification, is placed in a good sense. This too seems to be observed here.

[Note: [Col. 0527D] He is referring to his treatise, or letter, 22, *On Preserving Virginity*, addressed to Eustochium, section 8: “This I first advise and this I solemnly urge: let the bride of Christ avoid wine as poison. These are the first weapons of the demons against youth,” and so forth.]

## (Verse 19)

Speaking to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord.

Whoever abstains from drunkenness with wine, in which is wantonness, and is instead filled with the Spirit, can understand all these things spiritually: psalms, hymns, and songs.

We learn in the Psalter most fully what difference there is between a psalm, a hymn, and a song. For the present, however, we should briefly say that hymns are those that proclaim the strength and majesty of God and continually marvel at either his benefits or his deeds. All the psalms contain this, when “Alleluia” is placed either before or after them.

Psalms, properly speaking, concern the ethical sphere, so that through the organ of the body we may know what must be done and what must be avoided.

But whoever discusses higher matters and, as a subtle reasoner, explains the harmony of the world and the order and concord of all creatures sings a spiritual song.

Or, to express what we mean more clearly for simpler people: the psalm refers to the body, while the song refers to the mind.

We should therefore sing, make melody, and praise the Lord more with the mind than with the voice. This is what is meant by: “Singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord.”

Let young men hear this; let those hear it whose duty is to sing psalms in church: God must be sung to not with the voice but with the heart. The throat and jaws should not be smeared with sweet medicines in the manner of tragic actors, so that theatrical melodies and songs may be heard in church, but rather there should be fear, works, and knowledge of the Scriptures.

Even if someone is, as they commonly call it, κακόφωνος (*kakophonos*, “harsh-voiced”), if he has good works he is a sweet singer before God.

Let the servant of Christ sing in such a way that it is not the singer’s voice but the words being read that please. Thus the evil spirit that was in Saul (1 Samuel 16) may be driven out from those who are similarly possessed by it, and may not be introduced into those who have made the house of God into a theater for the crowds.

[Note: [Col. 0529D] This ancient custom, although condemned by the Fathers, still flourishes today in our churches, where theatrical melodies and sweet songs are heard—songs that turn the house of God into a stage for crowds who gather to soothe their ears with the voices and melodies of tragic actors, whom the common people call “the opera.”]

### (Verse 20)

“Giving thanks always for all things, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to God and the Father.” Something similar is written in the First Epistle to the Thessalonians: “Always rejoice, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all things” (I Thess. 5:16, 17). Only the person who knows by God’s providence that even the five sparrows sold for two asses are governed by it can keep this commandment—for not one of them falls into the snare without the Father’s will (Luke 12).

When he says “giving thanks,” and adds “always” and “for all things,” this must be understood in two ways: we are to give thanks to God both at every time and for everything that happens to us. Thus, not only for what we consider good, but also when things constrain us and come against our will, the joyful mind should break forth in praise of God, and we should say: “Naked I came out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return; as it pleased the Lord, so it happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21).

This thanksgiving is observed by prudent men both generally and particularly. Generally, we give thanks to God because the sun rises for us, the day runs its course, night changes into rest, darkness is tempered by the moon’s brightness, and the seasons change and return with the rising and setting of the stars; because the rains serve us, the earth gives birth, and the elements minister to us; because such great varieties of animals have been given to us for carrying, working, eating, clothing, example, or wonder; and finally, because we have been born, because we continue to exist, because in the world—as in a certain house of a most powerful master—we carry out our stewardship, and understand that everything in the world has been created for our sake.

Particularly, we give thanks when we rejoice in the benefits of God that come to us. But the Gentile does this, and the Jew, and the tax collector, and the pagan. The distinctive virtue of Christians is to give thanks to the Creator even in what are thought to be adverse circumstances. If the house has collapsed; if a most loving wife and children have been taken away by captivity, poison, or shipwreck; if we have lost our wealth through confiscation; if innumerable diseases and the weakness of gout, which the afflicted must always expect, have broken our health—those who consider themselves more holy commonly give thanks to God because they have been freed from dangers or miseries. But according to the Apostle, the greatest virtue is to give thanks to God amid the very dangers and miseries themselves, and always to say: “Blessed be God; I know that I suffer less than I deserve. These things are small in comparison with my sins; nothing worthy of me is being inflicted.”

This is the Christian mind; this is the mind that takes up its cross and follows the Savior, whom neither bereavement nor losses weaken. Of him Horace says in a lyric poem:

> If the broken universe should fall upon him,  
> its ruins would strike him undismayed.

But whoever, as we have said, gives thanks to God and the Father should offer that thanksgiving through the mediator between God and human beings, Jesus Christ, because we cannot approach the Father except through him.

### (Verse 21)

“Submitting to one another in the fear of Christ.”

Let bishops hear this, let presbyters hear it, let every order of teachers hear it: they are subject to their subjects. Let them imitate the Apostle who says: “Although I was free from all, I made myself the servant of all, that I might win the more” (I Cor. 9:19). And elsewhere: “Through love serve one another” (Gal. 5:13). Therefore, by this same love, he himself served all the Churches of the Gentiles.

The Savior also took the form of a servant in order to serve his disciples, and washed their feet (John 13). This is the difference between the rulers of the Gentiles and Christians: they dominate their subjects, whereas we serve; and we are greater precisely if we become the least of all.

The phrase “in the fear of Christ” should also be understood in this way: this submission is to be made not for human glory, but because of the fear of Christ, as we fear offending him.

Another person may interpret the passage, “submitting to one another in the fear of Christ,” by saying that this general statement is divided and distributed in what follows: “Wives, be subject to your husbands”; “Children, obey your parents”; and “Slaves, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling.” Thus not only wife to husband, children to parents, and slaves to masters, but also husbands to wives, according to the duty that has been commanded; fathers to children, so that they do not provoke them to anger; and masters to slaves, by abandoning threats and supplying them with what they need—all are to be subject to one another. They are to do this out of the fear of Christ, so that just as he was subject to his servants, those who seem to be greater may also be subject to their inferiors by performing the duties that are commanded.

Here we can understand “fear” as *eulabeia* (εὐλάβεια), that is, reverence, which is closer to love. It is certainly not fitting for the Ephesians to do anything from fear rather than from love of Christ.

### (Verses 22–23)

“Wives, be subject to your husbands as to the Lord, because the husband is the head of the wife, just as Christ is the head of the Church.”

The words “be subject,” which have been added in the Latin copies, are not found in the Greek manuscripts. The phrase refers back to what precedes, and is to be understood as: “Submitting to one another in the fear of Christ,” so that the expression *apo koinou* (ἀπὸ κοινοῦ) supplies “be subject”: “and wives to their husbands as to the Lord.” This is more readily understood in Greek than in Latin.

Therefore, just as the Church is subject to Christ, so let the wife be subject to her husband. The husband and wife are bound to the same order as that which exists between Christ and the Church, in which Christ exercises authority and the Church submits. Yet we must see to it that, just as there is a holy union in Christ and the holy Church, so there may be a holy union between husband and wife.

Just as not every gathering of heretics can be called the Church of Christ, nor is Christ their head, so not every marriage in which a woman is not joined to her husband in accordance with Christ’s commandments can rightly be called marriage; it is rather adultery.

In another sense, the wife is subject to her husband as to her lord, because her turning is toward him, and he shall rule over her (Gen. 3). Sarah also called Abraham “lord” (Gen. 18). This voluntary servitude, the more it is submitted to willingly, the more it begins to be equal; indeed, by her services she brings the ruler into servitude.

Some interpret this passage allegorically, saying that the wife is understood as the body and the husband as the mind. Just as the Church is subject to Christ, so the body ought to be subject to the mind and brought into one spirit, if it has been joined to the Lord. “Whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (I Cor. 6:17).

“He himself is the Savior of the body.”

Because the nature of the Church is closer and lower in relation to the substance of Christ, I think that it has been called the body of Christ; Christ Jesus is the Savior of this body—that is, the Word, wisdom, and the other virtues in which the Son of God is understood.

Search more carefully to see whether you can find anywhere in the divine books the word “flesh” used of the Church. For now the Church is called not flesh, but the body of Christ. It is clear, moreover, that whatever is flesh is consequently also body; but not everything that is body is consequently flesh.

### (Verse 24)

“But just as the Church is subject to Christ, so also wives to their husbands in everything” [Another reading: “as”].

The Church of Christ is glorious, having no stain or wrinkle or anything of that kind. Therefore, whoever is a sinner and stained by some filth cannot be called part of the Church of Christ, nor said to be subject to Christ.

It is possible, however, that just as the Church, which formerly had wrinkle and stain, was later restored to youth and purity, so the sinner may run to the physician—for “those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Luke 5)—and have his wounds healed, becoming part of the Church, which is the body of Christ.

Speaking to the Ephesians with great elegance and caution, he says: “Just as the Church is subject to Christ, so also wives to their husbands.” If a wife is to be subject to her husband as the Church is to Christ, there will be a holy union between husband and wife, and they will never serve the passions of the body.

If someone should oppose us with what is written to the Corinthians—that “the husband should give the wife her due, and likewise the wife to the husband” (I Cor. 7)—let him observe that there is a great difference between the Corinthians and the Ephesians. The Corinthians are addressed as little children and infants, among whom there were dissensions and schisms, and fornication of such a kind as was not even heard of among the Gentiles. Therefore they are permitted, after prayer, to return to the same union, lest they be tempted by Satan; although even there, in what follows, the Apostle says that he forgives them not according to their will but according to *synkatabasis* (συγκατάβασις), condescension.

The Ephesians, among whom he spent three years and opened all the mysteries of Christ, are instructed differently. Each person has the free power of choice either to follow the Corinthians or the Ephesians, and to be saved either by the Corinthians’ servitude or by the Ephesians’ freedom.

“Woe,” says the Savior, “to those who are pregnant and nursing in that day” (Luke 21:23)—that is, the day of judgment—for these things properly concern the works of marriage. Therefore we must strive with every effort to imitate the Ephesians rather than the Corinthians, and not be found, as though in the flood, buying and selling, marrying and being given in marriage; but, with our loins girded, let us hold lamps in our hands (Matt. 24).

### (Verse 25 and following)

“Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the Church and gave himself for her, to sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word, so that he might present the glorious Church to himself, having no stain or wrinkle or anything of that kind, but holy and immaculate.”

Although husband and wife are held together by mutual love—such as that of the wife of Hasdrubal, who, when her husband was captured, threw herself into the flames of her country, and of the other women who refused to outlive their dead husbands—a wise man will never compare that love with the love of Christ and the Church.

This, then, is to be understood as a holy love: the love with which Isaac loved his wife Rebekah (Gen. 24), whose name is interpreted as “patience,” and brought her from the land of Mesopotamia, which is surrounded on every side by the waves of this world, into the promised land, so that he might be comforted after the death of his mother. He tempered the destruction of the Synagogue by the union of the Church.

By saying these things we give an opportunity to heretics who think that all marriages must be rejected, and they make especially much use of this testimony. They must be answered briefly: the Apostle forbids passions, impurity, and lust between husband and wife here, not the holy union. Otherwise, if he were prohibiting marriage altogether, why was it necessary for him to say “your wives,” when he could have said, “Husbands, love women,” or simply “wives”? The expression “your wives” specifically signifies marriage.

Again, in what follows: “Husbands ought to love their wives as their own bodies”; and still more clearly: “He who loves his wife loves himself. For no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it.” For according to the decree of the ancient Law and the restoration brought by the Gospel, husband and wife become one flesh.

Thus the procreation of children, as we have said, is permitted within marriage. Pleasures obtained from the embraces of prostitutes, however, are condemned in a wife. Let every husband and wife who read this understand that after conception they ought to devote themselves more to prayer than to marital intercourse.

And what is prescribed by the very law of nature among animals and beasts—that pregnant females do not mate until giving birth—let human beings know has been left to their own choice, so that abstinence from pleasures might be rewarded.

Since, according to the allegorical interpretation, we have said that husbands signify souls and wives bodies, the soul should love the flesh [another reading: “body”] as Christ loved the Church, so that it may give itself for the flesh’s salvation and sanctify it by the word of teaching, presenting it to itself without any stain or wrinkle of old age—especially since it knows that the flesh will be saved in the resurrection and will see the salvation of God.

Such a husband has Christ as his head. When, for the salvation of the flesh, he humbles himself and becomes one flesh with his wife, he draws her back to the spirit; and, joined to the Lord, he ceases to be flesh.

He also beautifully derives “stain” and “wrinkle,” since he was speaking of marriage, from the example of women and applies them to the beauty of the Church. Just as women’s bodies may be soiled by moles, marked by wrinkles, or disfigured by freckles, and all women’s care is to wipe away whatever seems to deform them and present bodily beauty to their husbands, so souls must be cleansed from every stain of sin, so that the wrinkle of the old person may be stretched out in youth and be renewed into the new person from day to day.

**Note:** Thus reads the manuscript of the King’s Library, which we have followed. The very ancient Cluniac manuscript retains this reading: “so that the wrinkle of the old person may be extended in beauty.” I cannot conjecture how the reading found in the editions of Erasmus and Marianus—“may be extended in youth”—arose. MART. [Martianaeus], having found it in a certain Royal manuscript, restored it and insists that it must be retained, rejecting the old editions, which had “in youth.” We have written “youth,” as the context requires; nor, I think, will anyone fail immediately to understand that Martianaeus rashly corrupted this passage.

### (Verse 28)

“So husbands ought to love their wives as their own bodies.”

In Genesis, Adam is written as saying: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Gen. 2:23). The same point is confirmed in the Gospel when the Lord later says: “He who created them from the beginning made them male and female, and said: For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Mark 10:6–8).

Since husband and wife are one flesh, wives must be cared for as our own bodies. No one loves his body shamefully, nor does he love himself for the sake of sexual intercourse; rather, he cherishes and nourishes his body as a vessel of his soul, lest, when the vessel is broken, what it contained should flow out and escape.

Even according to the literal sense, as long as a woman is devoted to childbirth and children, she has this difference from her husband that the body has from the soul. But if she wishes to serve Christ more than the world, she will cease to be a woman and will be called a man, because we all desire to attain to the perfect man.

If we refer this also to the allegorical interpretation, we shall love our body and the senses of the body. They are indeed of a lower condition than the mind, but through them the disciplines of good arts and virtues pass into the mind.

### (Verse 29)

“He who loves his wife loves himself; for no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ also does the Church.”

As far as the simple meaning is concerned, after commanding holy love between husband and wife, we are now ordered to nourish and cherish our spouses—that is, to provide them with food, clothing, and whatever is necessary.

**Note:** Jerome admits that Origen raises this question in Book I of his *Apology*, section 30, and that he says the following in Origen’s person without naming him.

But someone may object that the Apostle’s statement—“No one ever hated his own flesh”—is not true, since those suffering from jaundice, consumption, cancer, and catarrh prefer death to life and hate their own bodies.

**Note:** He prefers to prove the point in this way: “Immediately,” he says, “because I myself felt this, I added: ‘Let the statement therefore be referred rather to the allegorical interpretation.’ When I say ‘allegorical,’ I show that what is said is not literally true, but is veiled in an allegorical mist. Nevertheless, let us set down the very words contained in the third book of Origen, through the end of the section: ‘Let us say that he loves that flesh which will see,’ and so forth.”

The passage should therefore be referred rather to the allegorical interpretation, and we should say that the soul loves, nourishes, and cherishes that flesh which will see the salvation of God, educating it through disciplines, fattening it with heavenly bread, and irrigating it with the blood of Christ, so that, restored and cleansed, it may follow the man freely and not be weighed down by any weakness or burden of infirmity [another reading: “by no burden of weakness”].

It is also beautifully compared with Christ nourishing and cherishing the Church and saying to Jerusalem: “How often I wanted to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling.” In the same way souls cherish their bodies, so that this corruptible may put on incorruption and, suspended by the lightness of wings, rise more easily into the air.

Let us therefore husbands cherish our wives, and souls our bodies, so that wives may be brought into husbands and bodies into souls. Let there be no difference of sex at all; but just as among the angels there is neither male nor female, so let us, who will be like the angels, already begin to be what has been promised to us in heaven.

### (Verse 30)

“For we are members of his body, of his flesh, and of his bones.”

Because we are members of Christ’s body, and Christ nourishes and cherishes the Church, we too nourish and cherish our flesh, which no one has ever hated.

We are members of Christ’s body not according to the nature of the eternal divinity, but according to what he deigned to assume: humanity. Although the human nature that was assumed has the nature of our bodies, it does not have our origin. We are formed from human seed; he was born from the Holy Spirit.

It can also be said differently: since the body of Christ is the Church, and the Church is gathered from all believers, Paul and the Ephesians are members of the body—that is, of the Church of Christ.

### (Verse 31)

“For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother, and the two shall be one flesh.”

We have often noted that the apostles and evangelists did not use the same words as the examples of the Old Testament contained in their original books. We prove the same thing here. The testimony is written in Genesis as follows: “For this reason a man shall leave his father and his mother, and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2:24).

But here the Apostle has placed, instead of the phrase found there, *heneken toutou* (ἕνεκεν τούτου), that is, “for this reason,” *anti toutou* (ἀντὶ τούτου), which cannot be expressed in Latin by other words. Then, instead of “his father and his mother,” he removed the pronouns and wrote only “father and mother.” He entirely omitted the intervening phrase, “and he shall cling to his wife,” and joined to what precedes only the final statement, writing: “and the two shall be one flesh.”

We have noted all this now so that, in other places also, whenever testimonies seem to have been taken by the apostles from the prophets and the Old Testament but are not found in our copies, we may not immediately run to the absurdities and ravings of apocryphal books. Rather, we should know that such passages are indeed written in the Old Testament, but were not issued by the apostles in precisely the same form; the sense was appropriated, and it is not easy for anyone except the diligent to discover where they are written.

Accordingly, for the exhortation to mutual affection between wife and husband, he took the example of Adam and Eve. Just as a rib is taken from Adam and built into a wife, and the wife is again reduced into one flesh with the man—because he who loves his wife loves himself—so we too should love our wives.

The same point is interpreted allegorically with reference to Christ and the Church: Adam prefigured Christ, and Eve the Church. “The last Adam became a life-giving spirit” (I Cor. 15:45). Just as the whole human race is born from Adam and his wife, so the whole multitude of believers has been generated from Christ and the Church.

Having become one body of the Church, it is again placed in Christ’s side, fills the place of the rib, and becomes one body with the man, while the Lord himself asks this in the Gospel: “Father, grant that just as you and I are one, so they too may be one in us” (John 17:21).

Let us ask Marcion by what logic he can interpret this passage, which has been taken from the Old Testament, with reference to Christ and the Church, since according to him the Old Scripture has no connection with Christ at all.

### (Verse 32)

“This mystery is great; but I speak with reference to Christ and the Church.”

Not everything in the history written about Adam and Eve in Genesis can easily be referred to Christ and the Church, as most people think. Only what is placed in the present passage can be so referred: “For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother, and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.”

For the first human being and first prophet, Adam, prophesied this concerning Christ and the Church: that our Lord and Savior would leave his Father, God, and his mother, the heavenly Jerusalem, and come to the earth for the sake of his body, the Church; that he would fashion the Church from his side; and that for her sake the Word would become flesh.

Since mysteries are not all equal, but one mystery is greater and another lesser, he now says: “This mystery is great.” At the same time, he indicates his humility when he adds: “But I speak with reference to Christ and the Church.”

Gregory of Nazianzus, a very eloquent man and thoroughly learned in the Scriptures, used to say to me, when he was discussing this passage with me: “See how great the mystery of this chapter is. The Apostle, interpreting it with reference to Christ and the Church, does not claim to have expressed it in a manner equal to the dignity of the testimony; rather, he seems in some way to have said:

> I know that this passage is full of ineffable mysteries, and that it seeks a divine heart as its interpreter. But, in view of the weakness of my understanding, for the moment I think it should be understood with reference to Christ and the Church—not because anything is greater than Christ and the Church, but because it is difficult to interpret everything said about Adam and Eve with reference to Christ and the Church.”

### (Verse 33)

“Nevertheless, let each one of you love his own wife as himself.”

Someone might think that the Apostle commands the same love between husband and wife as that commanded toward one’s neighbor. Thus it is written: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Lev. 19:18), and here: “Let each one love his own wife as himself.” Therefore, the same love would exist toward one’s neighbor and toward one’s wife.

But if, according to the Savior’s interpretation, every human being is a neighbor to every other human being, there would then be no difference in love between a wife and any other person—a very absurd conclusion.

In the case of one’s neighbor, the comparison is made so that you love him as yourself and desire that he be saved. In the case of one’s wife, however, the comparative adverb “as” does not express likeness, but approval and confirmation, with a certain force. We say of a man, “He acted as a man,” and it is written of the Savior: “We saw his glory, as the glory of the only-begotten” (John 1:14). This does not mean that the Savior possessed glory by comparison with another only-begotten one; he himself is the only-begotten. And if there were another only-begotten one, he could not be called the only-begotten.

Therefore, he did not need the example of another only-begotten; rather, he possessed glory as the only-begotten—that is, glory appropriate to himself.

The same is expressed at the beginning of Psalm 72, according to the Greek: “How good is God to Israel, to those who are upright in heart” (ὡς ἀγαθὸς ὁ Θεὸς τῷ Ἰσραὴλ τοῖς εὐθέσι τῇ καρδίᾳ), which our translators rendered: “How good God is to Israel, to those who are upright in heart” (Ps. 72:1). Otherwise, according to the Greek, *hōs* (ὡς), that is, “as,” seems to signify likeness more than the firmness of the statements, if one hears it not as confirmation but as an example [another reading omits “as”].

At the same time, we must note that the man is commanded to love his wife, but the woman to fear her husband. Love suits the man, fear the woman; to a slave are added not only fear but trembling. Hence he says in what follows: “Slaves, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling.”

“But let the woman fear her husband.”

If fear of God, because of fear of punishment, does not allow the person who fears to be perfect, how much more imperfect will the woman be if she fears not only God but also her husband? We must therefore inquire whether the wife and her fear are to be understood carnally, since wives are often found to be much better than their husbands: they command them, manage the household, raise the children, and maintain discipline in the family, while their husbands indulge themselves and run after prostitutes. Whether such women ought to rule their husbands or fear them, I leave to the reader’s judgment.

But if, according to the allegory, as we said above, the wife is understood as the body and the husband as the mind, there is nothing incongruous in the wife’s fearing her husband as a maidservant does, since she is established in a secondary and lower substance. For, as Crispus says, we use the authority of the mind more, and the service of the body.

But the person who follows the simple interpretation of woman and husband will show that the word “fear” has two meanings. One is the meaning of which John says: “He who fears has punishment, and he who fears is not perfect” (I John 4:18). In accordance with this meaning, slaves have a spirit of servitude in fear, which is demanded of them by the Lord when he says: “If I am a father, where is my glory? And if I am a lord, where is my fear?” (Mal. 1:6).

The other meaning is what philosophers call *eulabeia* (εὐλάβεια), which may be rendered in our language, though not with complete exactness, as reverence.

The prophet also knows the fear of the perfect, by which the one who fears is perfect, when he says in Psalm 33: “There is no want for those who fear him” (Ps. 34:9). Thus this fear may simply be commanded to the wife, so that she may fear—that is, revere—her husband.

### (Chapter 6, Verse 1)

“Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is just. Honor your father and your mother”—which is the first commandment with a promise—“so that it may be well with you and you may live long upon the earth.”

It is ambiguous whether children ought to obey their parents in the Lord, or whether children ought to obey their parents who are in the Lord. Both must be done: we must obey those parents who begot us in the Lord, as Paul and the apostles did, and do whatever they command; and we must obey our parents according to the flesh in the Lord, fulfilling what is not contrary to the Lord’s will.

At the same time, we will constrain the heretics who refuse to believe that the Old Testament belongs to the good God, whose Son is Christ. How can Christ, the Son of the good God, use the Scripture of the Creator, and derive the obedience of children from the ancient Law?

This testimony is taken from Exodus, where it is joined together as follows: “Honor your father and your mother, so that it may be well with you and you may live long upon the earth which the Lord your God will give you” (Exod. 20:12). Here the Apostle removed the final words. This commandment is fifth in the Decalogue.

We must therefore ask why he now says, “which is the first commandment,” when the first commandment is: “You shall have no other gods besides me.” For this reason some read the passage as: “which is the first commandment with a promise,” as though the other four commandments stated earlier had no promises, and the promise were attached only to this one: “so that it may be well with you and you may live long upon the earth which the Lord your God will give you.”

But they seem not to have observed carefully enough that a promise is also joined to the second commandment. It says: “You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor any likeness of those things that are in heaven above, or on the earth below, or in the waters under the earth. You shall not worship them or sacrifice to them. For I am the Lord your God, a jealous God, visiting the sins of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, and showing mercy to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments” (Exod. 20:4–6).

Observe that these are words of promise: “showing mercy to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.”

Perhaps, then, because the Decalogue was the first Law given to the people departing from Egypt, each commandment of the Decalogue should be called the first commandment in comparison with the precepts that were later written in the Law.

But the person who tries to retain the earlier interpretation—that is, “which is the first commandment with a promise”—will say that “Honor your father and your mother” is a commandment in itself, and that afterward the promise is placed in its proper position: “so that you may live long upon the earth which the Lord your God will give you.”

In this commandment, “You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor any likeness,” the promise is not separate, but, within one continuous text and statement, it is not so much a promise that is given as a sentence concluding with praise of God, who shows mercy to thousands of those who love him and keep his commandments.

Again, the person who maintains that all the commandments of the Decalogue are the first commandment will show that the promise—“so that you may live long upon the earth which the Lord your God will give you”—applies not only to those who obey their parents, but also to countless other commandments. He will have to review all the commandments in which this reward and prize is promised: that they may live long upon the earth which the Lord their God will give them.

That interpreter, in turn, must require him to demonstrate that the commandments he has produced were written before this commandment. If he cannot prove this, he will mention in vain that this promise is attached to the other commandments as well.

After this, we must reconsider whether the promise made for honoring father and mother is Jewish and carnal: that children should live long upon the earth which the Lord their God will give them. For we must believe that many people have obeyed their parents and died young, while others who were impious toward their parents lived to extreme old age.

Let the Jews and those like the Jews answer: if length of this life is among the promises, and remaining long in the body is happiness, what does the statement in the Psalms mean: “Woe is me, for my sojourning has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar” (Ps. 120:5)?

And what does Solomon say in Ecclesiastes: “I praised all the dead who had already died more than the living who are still alive; and better than both is the one who has not yet been born and has not seen all the evil work that is done under the sun” (Eccles. 4:2–3)?

A little later he says: “If a man begets a hundred children, lives many years, and the days of his years are many, and his soul is filled with good things, but he has no burial, I said that an untimely birth is better than he, for it comes in vanity and its name will be covered in darkness; indeed, it has not seen the sun” (Eccles. 6:3–5), and so forth.

If the dead are praised above the living—and according to some, who think that souls exist in heaven before descending into these bodies, the one who has not yet been born is said to be better than both, and this whole life is a trial; and according to Job, “Death is rest for a man” (Job 3:13); and according to him and Jeremiah, “Cursed is the day on which we were born” (Jer. 20:14)—how is it that those who honor father and mother are now promised that they will live long upon the earth which the Lord their God will give them?

We must therefore seek the earth that the Lord promises and grants to those who have left the spiritual Egypt, crossed with all patience the great and terrible deserts of this life, conquered the great kings whom the Lord strikes down, and entered Judea, which flows with milk and honey; who, under the leadership of Jesus, with Jericho fallen and Ai—which is interpreted as “ruin”—destroyed, have come to Jerusalem; for whom the temple is built under Solomon, the peaceful king (Josh. 6–8); and who possess the land prepared for the meek: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. 5:5). This is truly the land of the living, as the Psalmist also says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 27:13).

Wisdom also holds the length of this life in her right hand, while in her left she holds riches and glory.

**Note:** Jerome himself does not know the word “all” in his *Commentaries on this Book*, although there he adapted himself more closely to the usage of the translators of the Septuagint. It also seems to have arisen through scribal error that it appears in the Vatican copy of his version. The translation of Aquila may have been responsible: when, with excessive zeal, he translated the Hebrew article with the Greek *syn* (σύν), and consequently rendered “with the dead” as *syn tous tethnekotas* (σὺν τοὺς τεθνηκότας), as it appears in the Alexandrian manuscript, the Vatican copyist, thinking that the words *syn tous* meant nothing, made them *sympantas* (σύμπαντας), “all.” From this the Latin translations were derived. The Hebrew text and the Vulgate translator, however, do not have “all.”

**Note:** Victorius supplies “sons.”

[Col. 0539C] **(Verse 4.)** And fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord. The sin of children is not to obey their parents; and because parents might command something perverse, he added, “in the Lord.” The sin of parents, however, is to provoke little children and infants to anger, or else to impose upon those already adolescents and of more mature age burdensome commands. Therefore, just as obedience and the reward of submission were demonstrated in the case of children, so parents are commanded to exercise measured authority, so that they may know that they rule not as over slaves but as over sons.

Nor was he content with this limit to the command, but added this also: “Bring them up in the discipline and correction of the Lord.” What we read as “correction” is better expressed in Greek by *νουθεσία* (*nouthesia*), which signifies admonition and instruction more than austerity. Let bishops and presbyters read this—those who educate their sons in secular literature and make them read comedies [Note: [Col. 0539C] Abelard formerly read differently in the books of *Christian Theology*: “and the shameful writings of love,” etc., instead of “and the shameful writings of mimes,” etc.], and sing the shameful writings of mimes, perhaps having educated them at the expense of the Church: [Col. 0540B] whatever a virgin, widow, or any poor person, pouring out his entire substance, had offered in the *corbona* for sin, this the grammarian and orator converts into a New Year’s gift, a Saturnalian allowance, and a Minervalian present, either into household expenses, or into offerings for temples, or into filthy prostitutes.

[Note: [Col. 0539C]

Not sufficiently understanding this passage, Erasmus and Marianus corrupt it in different ways: Erasmus by adding the preposition *in* before *kalendariam strenam*, and Marianus by changing it to “or into the temple’s collections.” For he reads: “or into household expenses, the temple’s collections.” The manuscript codices retain the pure reading that we have published, whose meaning is this: Let bishops and presbyters read these things—those who perhaps hand over their sons, educated at the expense of the Church, to pagan grammarians—and let them see to it that what a virgin, widow, or poor person has offered is not turned by the grammarian and orator who receives it, as a New Year’s gift, Saturnalian allowance, and so forth, either into household expenses, or into offerings for the temples of their gods, and finally into filthy prostitutes.

Now, a New Year’s gift (*kalendaria strena*), or a Saturnalian allowance, as well as a Minervalian present, were formerly gifts given to teachers on the Kalends of January and on the festivals of Saturn and Minerva. The emperor Tiberius prohibited by edict the exchange of New Year’s gifts, so that they would no longer be practiced beyond the Kalends of January. See Suetonius, *Life of Tiberius*. MART.]

It is well known that *kalendaria strena* was the gift given at the beginning of the year as a good omen. Suetonius, in *Caligula*, chapter 42: “He announced that he would receive New Year’s gifts at the beginning of the year, and stood in the vestibule of his house on the Kalends of January to collect contributions.” A Saturnalian allowance was of this kind, although it belonged to the month of December; the Minervalian gift, however, was specifically the present that pupils paid to their teachers.

For the words that follow shortly, “or into offerings for temples,” and because Martianaeus explains them as referring to the temples of idols, Victorius, thinking that Christian temples were intended, removed the words “or into” and more conveniently restored the passage—if only the manuscripts supported him—so that the meaning would be that presbyters give the collections of the temple to pagan grammarians, who would convert them either into household expenses or into filthy prostitutes.] 

The grammarian and orator converts the New Year’s gift, the Saturnalian allowance, and the Minervalian present either into household expenses, or into offerings for temples, or into filthy prostitutes.

Eli himself was a holy priest, but because he did not educate his sons in every discipline and correction, he fell backward and died (1 Sam. 2). For he could not extend himself toward what lay before him, but fell backward; and [Note: [Col. 0540D] In *Epistle 147 to Sabinianus*, where we first restored this word, we read: “Eli, while he is too lenient with his sons, offended God; and so far is it from being possible for the justice of your bishop to free you, that it must be feared that, falling from his throne because of you, he may perish by an incurable *opisthotonus* [*ὀπισθότονος*]. See what we noted there.] falling backward in an incurable *opisthotonus*—that is, with his body bent backward—he looked back toward Sodom with Lot’s wife.

And certainly he had rebuked his sons, saying: “Why do you do these things, the evil things that I hear from all the people about you? No, my sons; for the report that I hear about you is not good” (1 Sam. 2:23–24). Concerning fathers of this kind Isaiah also complains in a mournful voice, saying: “And the sons of foreigners have been born to them” (Isa. 2).

But if he gave this command to the laymen of Ephesus, and to the many who, as commonly happens among the people, are occupied with the affairs of this life—that they should educate their sons in every discipline and admonition of the Lord—what must be thought concerning priests, of whose order he writes to Timothy, saying: “Having children who are obedient, with all dignity” (1 Tim. 3:4)? And he impresses and repeats the same point to Titus: “Having faithful children, not accused of debauchery or disobedient” (Tit. 1:6–7). Then, as though the vices of children were imputed to their parents, inserting a causal conjunction, he says: “For a bishop must be blameless, as God’s steward” (Tit. 1:7). A bishop, therefore, is not blameless if his son is disobedient and accused of debauchery.

**(Verse 5 and following.)** “Slaves, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling, in the simplicity of your hearts, as you would Christ; not serving merely for appearances, as those who please everyone, but as servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart; serving with good will, as to the Lord and not to human beings; knowing that whatever good each person does, he will receive this back from the Lord, whether slave or free.”

When the prophet says to Jerusalem: “Whom did you fear, a mortal man and a son of man?” (Isa. 51); and Peter in his Epistle: “Do not fear their fear, but sanctify the Lord Jesus Christ in your hearts” (1 Pet. 3:14–15); and the Savior likewise declares: “Do not fear those who can kill the body and after that have nothing more that they can do to you; but fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matt. 10:28); and Solomon likewise bears witness: “My son, honor the Lord, and you will be strengthened; besides him, do not fear another” (Prov. 7)—the Apostle appears to command different things: that slaves should obey earthly masters with fear and trembling, and that a wife should fear her husband.

The person who answers more simply will say that these commands were not given to perfect slaves, or to those who have come to know the secrets of wisdom, but to those who possessed only the beginnings of faith and needed more elementary instruction. Another, however, will maintain that someone who does not have the spirit of slavery again unto fear is in no way subject to this sentence, so as to obey earthly masters with fear and trembling; and he will say the same concerning a wife, who is commanded to fear her husband.

A third person, moreover, will think that here too, as in the case of the woman, “fear” is used for reverence. But he will be constrained by the fact that trembling has been added to fear. Reverence can suit a wife, so that in reverence she fears her husband. But where there is trembling, the word does not signify reverence but fear.

Therefore it was necessarily added in the case of slaves that, after the fear of the Lord, they should also have trembling; and, to distinguish the spiritual Lord, the other is now called an earthly master. Thus, for a slave who has believed in God but has not yet reached the fullness of knowledge, it is not improper to serve an earthly master with fear and trembling, in the simplicity of his heart, and to serve him faithfully as he would Christ.

He is not to serve merely for appearances, as those do who desire to please human beings, but to turn necessity into willingness and to make a reward out of slavery—especially since the master of the flesh commands nothing different from the Lord of the spirit. For this is what he says: “Not serving merely for appearances, as those who please human beings, but as servants of Christ, doing the will of God.” The slave should also possess this very faithfulness not under compulsion but voluntarily and from the heart, serving his master as Christ, from whom he will receive the reward of faithful service, no less than if he had served as a free person by his own will.

At the same time, we should note that he attached different forms of obedience to sons and slaves. To sons he says: “Obey your parents in the Lord”; but to slaves: “Obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling.” Thus, just as fear differs between a slave and a wife, so obedience would also differ between sons and slaves.

And beautifully, when commanding slaves to obey their masters, he added “as Christ,” and again, “as servants of Christ, doing the will of God,” so that a slave should not obey an earthly master if he wishes to command what is contrary to God’s precepts.

Just as he had earlier written to the Corinthians, in view of the circumstances of the time (1 Cor. 7), that divorces should not occur between husbands and wives on the pretext of faith in Christ, if one of the two wished to believe, so to the Ephesians and Colossians—because at the beginnings of faith many thought that Gentile masters should be despised—he now establishes moderate precepts concerning social conditions. Thus he neither appears to incite slaves against their masters, nor, conversely, does he teach that masters should be obeyed if they give vicious and impious commands.

**(Verse 9.)** “And masters, do the same things toward them, giving up threats, knowing that both their Master and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with him.”

What are these things that he earlier commanded slaves, so that he would say that masters should do the same things toward slaves? I think they are the things he had said: “in the simplicity of the heart,” and “doing the will of God,” and “from the heart,” and with faithfulness or goodwill toward slaves, since *εὔνοια* (*eunoia*) can signify both.

“For whatever good each person does, he will receive this back from the Lord,” whether a servant has served, as was said, or a free person has exercised authority as he ought: so that he may not be terrifying or ready [Note: [Col. 0541D] Martianaeus has the faulty reading “ready for words.”] to use blows, knowing that he too has a Master in heaven, with whom there is no partiality, and who alone judges intentions and, according to them, prefers the better to the worse, choosing deeds rather than persons.

[Col. 0542D] **(Verse 10.)** “Finally, be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might.”

I know that in Greek, in place of “virtue,” “strength” is used—that is, *ἰσχύς* (*ischys*), since among them “virtue” is called *ἀρετή* (*aretē*). But among us it is the custom of the Scriptures to call both *ischys* and *aretē* indiscriminately “virtue,” especially since bodily strength is regarded as a virtue of the soul. Among philosophers also, strength is placed among the four virtues; and it is clearly a quality of the soul, not of the body.

Therefore, when he says, “Be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might,” the whole meaning is understood in Christ, so that those who believe may be strengthened in all the virtues that are understood to reside in him. And wisely, after the specific commands concerning what husbands and wives, fathers and sons, masters and slaves must observe, he now gives a general command to all together: strengthened in the Lord and in his power, they are to prepare themselves against the devil, about whom he writes in what follows.

**(Verse 11.)** “Put on the whole armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil.”

From what we read below, and from what is said throughout the Scriptures about the Lord Savior, it is most clearly established that the whole armor of God with which we are now commanded to be clothed [or: which he is now commanded to put on] is to be understood as the Savior himself. Thus it is one and the same thing to say, “Put on the whole armor of God,” as if he had said, “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ.”

For if the belt is truth and the breastplate is righteousness, while the Savior is called both Truth and Righteousness, there is no doubt that he himself is both the belt and the breastplate. Accordingly, in keeping with this, he will also be the preparation of the gospel of peace, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God—a living and effective utterance, sharper than every two-edged sword.

What other armor of God, then, can we suppose that the person who must be clothed in order to fight against the devil’s schemes can have, apart from the virtue that is Christ? [Note: [Col. 0543D] Martianaeus again has the corrupt reading “For here,” instead of “For this person,” that is, Christ.]

For the person who has been clothed with him, according to all that is understood about him, will be able to resist all the devil’s snares. Insofar as he is girded with truth, he will not easily be led into doctrines of falsehood. Insofar as he is clothed with the breastplate of righteousness, he will not be pierced by the arrows of wickedness.

And when he has put on the most beautiful footwear in the preparation of the gospel of peace—like one who prepared his works at the end and therefore became a man of peace—he will neither undertake anything warlike or tumultuous, nor will he be condemned along with those who are unprepared.

Unfaithfulness also, which is the enemy of faith, will have no power wherever the shield of faith is present. The head, and the ruling part of the heart and soul in which all the senses are situated, will not be shaken when surrounded by the helmet of salvation.

Finally, like a strong and warlike man, holding in his hand the sword of the Spirit—that is, the word of God—he will cut down, kill, and slaughter every sect opposed to the truth.

Because the Apostle wished to display the devil’s manifold designs, by which he attempts to seize us through the places in which we do not guard our heart with complete vigilance, he called them his *μεθοδεῖαι* (*methodeiai*), that is, his contrivances or schemes. If we abstain from bodily pleasure, he captures us when we are insufficiently cautious through greed. If we also despise greed along with pleasure, he creeps in through luxury, makes our belly into a god, and through this conquers even those things that seemed strong.

Just as wise commanders of armies usually attack above all those parts of cities that are poorly fortified, so that, having entered through them, they may easily capture the fortified places, so the devil seeks to burst in through the places he sees lying open, or at least not firmly closed, and to reach the very citadel of the heart and soul.

Why do I need to speak of his many other snares, when his remaining kinds of schemes can be recognized from these?

“Devil” is a Greek name, which is interpreted as “accuser.” According to the character of the Hebrew language, however, since the tribe of Zebulun also has a certain resemblance to this word, he may be called *καταρύων* (*kataryōn*), that is, “flowing downward,” because he gradually flowed from virtue into vice and fell from heavenly things to earthly ones.

For our struggle is not against blood and flesh, but against principalities, against powers, against the world-rulers of these darknesses, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.

I do not think that Paul, writing to the Corinthians, could have said: “Your struggle is not against flesh and blood,” when he says to them: “No temptation has overtaken you except what is human. But God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you are able to bear” (1 Cor. 10:13).

For I think that the contests against flesh and blood are those which are there called human temptations: when the flesh desires against the spirit and urges us to do its works—sexual immorality, uncleanness, debauchery, idolatry, hostilities, strife, jealousy, anger, quarrels, dissensions, factions, intrigues, drunkenness, revelries (Gal. 5), and the rest of the things like these.

But the temptation is not human, nor is the struggle against flesh and blood, when Satan himself, transformed into an angel of light, attempts to persuade us to think that he is an angel of light, or when he does something similar, with all power, false signs and wonders, and every deception of wickedness.

For when the enemy has ensnared someone so that he receives him and speaks in him, the Lord says that this does not happen as though flesh and blood deceived him, or as though it were a human temptation, but as though it were a principality and power, a ruler of darkness and a spiritual wickedness (Eph. 4).

Therefore let us not give place to the devil; and even if a spirit possessing authority rises up against us, let us, in accordance with what is written, give him no place.

Someone may say that the statement, “Our struggle is not against blood and flesh, but against principalities and powers” (Eccl. 10:4), and the other things that follow, is said in order to teach us that even the vices which we think are supplied to us by the flesh do not belong to flesh or blood, but are suggested by certain spiritual wickednesses.

For there are certain demons devoted to amorous affairs and love songs, as the prophet also recalls, saying: “They were seduced by a spirit of fornication” (Hos. 4:12). It is also said that they have certain barbarous names, as those whom the common people truly call sorcerers have often confessed; and that incantations, prayers, various colors, and different kinds either of metals or of foods are associated with them, so that demons, summoned by these means, are said to attend and seize wretched souls.

Others produce anger, fury, and wars; others preside over hostilities and stir up hatred among human beings.

Because, therefore, the Apostle is said to wish to teach us that these kinds of vice are not produced by the nature of the body or from the substance of flesh and blood, but by the prompting of demons, he says for that reason: “Our struggle is not against blood and flesh, but against principalities and powers,” and the rest.

We have brought forward examples of those who serve these unhappy magical arts and are said to perform such things in order to blunt the opinion of those who think that all vices belong to flesh and blood and that demons have no power to incite us to sin.

I think that Jacob’s struggle was a struggle of this kind [Note: [Col. 0545C] Beware of asserting from this passage, with a recent and ignorant writer, that Jerome thought Jacob wrestled with a demon. See the *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, where that holy Doctor discussed the struggle more fully. MART.—Procopius states, concerning this passage in Genesis, that some of the ancients believed a demon existed who wrestled with Jacob under the appearance and spoils of Esau. Since some recent writer, whoever he was, thought that this opinion could be proved from Jerome here, Martianaeus accuses him of ignorance and chastises him severely. Yet if Jerome’s meaning is properly weighed, the whole context represents the other one, struggling with excessive sweat, as a demon, while the man who assists and strengthens him is understood, from the whole sense of the discourse, to be an angel who came to Jacob’s aid in his struggle. Moreover, even if the matter is to be judged from the opinions of others, most come close to this interpretation—especially the Rabbis, who say that Esau’s own angel wrestled with Jacob; and Origen, who in Book III of *On First Principles* thinks that Jacob wrestled with an angel, whom he did not experience as an adversary but, on the contrary, as an ally against the demon by whom he was being attacked. The holy Father adheres more closely to this opinion.]

We suppose that Jacob’s struggle was such that he did not contend against flesh and blood, when he remained alone and wrestled with a man who assisted and strengthened him against another, who was fighting with excessive sweat.

At the same time, consider whether those who think that Jacob wrestled the whole night in the manner of ordinary wrestlers are not perhaps ridiculous. What would be remarkable if, as they say, while wrestling he either conquered or was defeated? But according to the rational and appropriate struggle of the patriarch, we must believe that his struggle was of the kind possessed by those who could say: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood.”

It is not necessary now to examine the whole mystery of that passage, since, if I live, it will be discussed more fully in its proper place.

We ask, however (see the *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*), where Paul read these things in the Old Testament, or by what authority he published things that are nowhere written.
