We infer from the accounts written in the Law, Joshua, the Book of Judges, the Books of Kings, and Chronicles concerning battles and single combats—for example, David against Goliath, the children of Israel against foreigners, and other nations—that the Apostle understood these things more deeply and perceived a spiritual war through a bodily one, in which the combatants were defeated or prevailed, while the officials of each place signified the heavenly powers, and the kings of the individual nations represented those now called the world-rulers and rulers of darkness; the evil spiritual forces in the heavenly places were represented by wicked human beings. [Col. 0546A]

The Apostle seems to say these things in other words: “O Ephesians, the battles you read about between Israel and the nations seem indeed to speak of flesh or blood—for example, of Egyptians, Idumeans, Ammonites, Moabites, and the other nations—but if you truly wish to know, recognize that all those things were happening to them figuratively” (1 Cor. 10).

They were written for our sake, upon whom the ends of the ages have come, so that from them we might understand that our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against certain spiritual and invisible powers, against the rulers of the darkness that hangs over this world and inflicts the error of unbelief upon human beings, and against spiritual wickednesses that dwell in the heavenly places.

This does not mean that demons dwell in the heavenly places, but that the air above us has received this name. Hence birds that fly through the air are called “the birds of heaven.”

In another passage, too, the Apostle says of demons that they roam in this air: “In which you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now works in the sons of disobedience” (Eph. 2:2).

It is the opinion of all the learned that this air, which divides and separates heaven and earth and is called the void, is full of hostile powers. [Col. 0547D]

After this it must be reconsidered from whom principalities, powers, rulers of the darkness of this world, and spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places received the power to be what they are.

Another person may say that the apostate devil assigned various offices to his followers, and that God was not the author of these distributions. An attentive reader may object to him: “How, then, is it written, ‘There is no authority except from God’ (Rom. 13:1)?” If this is said of human beings, how much more does it apply to those who are of a subtler and better nature?

Nor does the person who thinks this immediately incur the charge of blasphemy, since each one received different ministries according to his own will.

For just as in cities we see those who have committed some crime assigned either to feed wild beasts, to cut marble, to clean the filth of sewers, or to preside over gladiators and be appointed to shed the blood of condemned persons, so demons, by the freedom of their own judgment, have chosen the province of ambushes, frauds, crimes, perjury, and the remaining vices, so that they are rulers of darkness because they did not wish to be rulers of light.

When these rulers of the world and of darkness have defeated someone in their struggle against him and made him fall, they immediately attach him to their world and to the darkness over which they rule.

For this reason we must labor more earnestly, so that we who have once heard, “I chose you out of this world; you are no longer of this world. If you were of the world, the world would love what was its own” (John 15:19), may not return to the world or become subject to it.

Rather, let the world be crucified to us, and we to it, so that Jesus, the ruler of light, may join us to his own world and place us under the dominion of the Father, having rescued us from the power of spiritual wickedness and from their heaven, which will pass away and cannot be called the dwelling place of God.

For it is impious to believe that spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places possess the heaven of which God says: “Heaven is my throne” (Isa. 66:1).

Therefore, whoever understands how many things are done in this world to us, both to those present and to those absent, while we cannot see them—either because of this fragile and earthly body of our humiliation, in which the soul is wrapped, or because the more subtle nature is not revealed to bodily eyes—will see what the darkness is that the Apostle now mentions.

He will understand either that this entire earthly life is called darkness—“the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:5)—or that the soul’s light and understanding are overshadowed, covered, and blinded by the earthly body, the body of death and humiliation.

Let us also know that, apart from the present passage, we have never read *κοσμοκράτορες* (*kosmokratores*), that is, “world-rulers,” either in the Old or the New Testament. The Apostle Paul coined this name because, arguing with the Ephesians about new and invisible realities, he needed to fit new names to them.

Furthermore, because he says “in the heavenly places,” which seems ambiguous, it must be said that the phrase “in the heavenly places” may be understood as applying to all the preceding terms, so that the meaning is: “Our struggle is not against powers in the heavenly places, nor against the rulers of these darknesses in the heavenly places, nor against spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places”; and not merely against spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places. [Note: [Col. 0548D] The words that follow—“and not merely against spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places”—are absent from Victorius’s edition.]

This is especially so if we understand, as has already been explained above, how things are called heavenly because of the birds of heaven, and because ordinary speech says that rain comes from heaven, although rain does not come from heaven.

Philosophers say that the clouds from which rains are poured and showers fall are no more than two thousand paces distant from the earth. In this sense, too, the floodgates of heaven are said to have been opened during the Flood.

Nevertheless, the worse a person is, the closer he will be to the places near the earth and to denser substance. For both the earth and the air surrounding us possess their own density.

Some say that souls freed from bodies, if they have been attenuated in the present life and worn down, as it were, by the file of *ἀσκησις* (*askesis*, discipline) and virtues into a subtle body, will not dwell in denser places but will be near God, who is incorporeal.

But if they are such as those of whom it can be said, “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy, or thick of heart?” (Ps. 4:3), then, according to the weight of their density, they are dragged down to the lowest places and burdened by their heaviness.

After this, the further question must likewise be discussed: whether in this earth and air there is some denser place called by many “hell,” in which those who are called the dead below (*inferi*) dwell. Who these are, and what relationship or difference they have to those called spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places, is not a matter for discussion at present.

It remains that we should learn more clearly, from two passages in the Apostle, the difference between the struggle against flesh and blood and the rulers of these darknesses and spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places.

When he wishes to indicate human temptations—that is, the struggle against flesh and blood—he speaks of them dismissively and contemptuously: “Who will separate us from the love of God? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? As it is written: ‘For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter.’ But in all these things we overcome, because of him who loved us” (Rom. 8:35–36).

But when he wishes to teach us about opposing powers, the rulers of darkness, and spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places, he begins from another point, as from a different head, and says: “For I am convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither things present nor things future, neither strength nor height nor depth nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

Perhaps I have discussed this chapter at greater length than the reader would wish. But I ask him to forgive the difficulty of the passage itself and of the Ephesians, who, after their magical practices, needed to know by whom they had once been deceived.

[Col. 0549B] (Verse 13.) Therefore take up the whole armor of God, so that you may be able to resist on the evil day and, having accomplished everything, to stand. The evil day either indicates the present time, of which he had said above, “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Eph. V, 16), on account of the distress and labors of this life—for we do not reach the palm of victory without sweat and struggle—or certainly the day of consummation and judgment, when the devil, our enemy and avenger, will wish to retain us on his side. From that side the one who understands the poor and needy will be delivered: “For on the evil day the Lord will deliver him” (Ps. XL, 1). This is the day of which it is also written elsewhere: “Behold, the day of the Lord’s wrath is coming” (Isa. XIII, 9); and elsewhere: “For the day of the Lord, an incurable day, will come, a day of fury and wrath” (Isa. XXII, 6); and again: “Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord! Why do you want the day of the Lord? It is darkness and not light.” Just as if a man flees from the face of a lion and encounters a bear, enters his house, leans his hands against the wall, and a serpent bites him: “Is not the day of the Lord darkness and not light, gloom without brightness?” (Amos V, 18). For how is this day not evil, when it is wrapped in darkness and gloom? The prophet Joel also recalls it, saying: “Blow the trumpet in Zion; proclaim on my holy mountain; and let all who inhabit the earth be confounded, because the day of the Lord is present, because the day of darkness and storm is near, the day of cloud and gloom” (Joel II, 1). Zephaniah likewise speaks of the same day, saying: “The great day of the Lord is near, near and exceedingly swift. The voice of the day of the Lord is bitter, harsh, and mighty: that day is a day of wrath, a day of distress and necessity” (Zeph. I, 14 ff.), and the rest. After this he adds: “And I will afflict the people, and they will walk like blind men, because they have sinned against the Lord” (Apoc. XII).

Therefore, so that someone may be able to resist the devil on that day—for he is the accuser of our brothers—let him take up the whole armor of God (for this is what πανοπλία means, not simply “arms,” as it has been translated in Latin). Girded with every weapon and defense, which are explained in what follows, he should know that he can stand then if he has accomplished everything, so that, filled with every virtue, he may plant his foot firmly and not be moved from the battle line. Let him be among those of whom the Lord says: “There are some standing here” (Matt. XVI, 28); and elsewhere: “For you stand by faith” (II Cor. I, 22); and the Psalmist says: “He has set my feet upon a rock” (Ps. XXXIX, 5).

A third interpretation is also introduced by some, who say that not every battle against the devil ends in death; rather, when we have departed from this world, a stronger and more open conflict will then take place for us, present beings against present beings. In this way they explain what we quoted a little earlier: “Neither things present nor things to come” (Rom. VIII, 38), taking “things to come” to mean the conflicts that must be entered upon after this life. They likewise interpret: “Therefore we strive, whether present or future, to please him” (II Cor. V, 9), supposing that the present signifies this life and the future the time after death. They refer this same statement—“and, having accomplished everything, to stand”—to the same meaning, as though no one could accomplish everything in the present life, but could do something only in part, just as he sees in part and prophesies in part; and as though he could stand perfectly only when he had accomplished everything.

Another explains these words more simply, saying that Paul exhorted and warned the Ephesians concerning the future temptations and persecutions that, through prophetic insight, he saw would befall them after this letter, so that they might do everything by which they could stand firm in the faith of the Gospel and not fall during persecution. We think that the evil day is here specifically taken from the forty-eighth Psalm.

(Verses 14.) “Stand therefore, with your loins girded in truth.” No one doubts that in Scripture all the members of the soul are called by the names of the members of the flesh and body. I think that one of these members is here understood to be the loins, which we are commanded to gird with truth. It is also written in the Gospel according to Luke: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands” (Luke XII, 35).

Since the loins are always understood in relation to generation and seed, according to the saying, “From the fruit of your loins I will set upon your throne” (Ps. CXXXI, 11), and elsewhere, “Levi was still in the loins of his father Abraham when Melchizedek met him” (Hebr. VII, 10), it seems to us that the man has girded his loins who in no way renders the debt owed to a wife, nor serves lust, but imitates the unbegotten God, not serving the business of generation.

I think that the same thing is signified by the fact that John had a leather belt around his loins (Matt. III), and was not among the unclean, who, because of the discharge of semen, were cast outside the camp and could not dwell with the ark of the Lord (Lev. XIII); nor was he among those of whom it is written in Numbers: “Let his garments be torn” (Num. VIII). But whoever is girded with truth for Christ gathers these garments upward and draws them above; he covers, tightens, and encloses the shamefulness of his naked sides with a spiritual belt. He is ready for battle and possesses works that shine, which are called burning lamps.

“679 And having put on the breastplate of righteousness.” Just as the man who has put on a breastplate of virtue, densely woven with hooks and interlocking iron rings, is wounded only with difficulty, especially in those places that preserve life, so the man surrounded by the many-layered garment of righteousness will neither, like a stag, receive an arrow in the liver, nor fall into desires and passions. He will be pure in heart, having God as the craftsman of this breastplate—the God who fashions all weapons for each of the saints and does not allow him to be struck and burned alike by the flying dart of the day or by the flaming arrows.

(Verses 15.) “And having shod your feet with the preparation of the Gospel of peace.” Observe carefully that he has called a certain virtue of the soul “feet,” by which we enter into him who says, “I am the way” (John XIV, 6), and which we ought to shoe with the preparation of the Gospel of peace.

As a figure of these shoes, those shoes in Exodus came beforehand, which those eating the Passover and those prepared to make a journey are commanded to have. For he says: “You shall eat it thus: with your loins girded, your sandals on your feet, and your staffs in your hands; and you shall eat it in haste, for it is the Lord’s Passover” (Exod. XII, 11). Eating in haste and with shod feet is plainly a sign of preparation, so that, strengthened by the paschal food, they may be able to cross the broad and dreadful wilderness.

Therefore, let the one who is still walking put on shoes; but let the one who has already crossed the Jordan and entered the promised land uncover his foot. “Take off your shoe,” he says, “from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy ground” (Exod. III, 5). If someone is not Jesus son of Nun (Cap. V), nor an apostle, let him shoe his feet with the preparation of the Gospel of peace. But if someone is an apostle and can be numbered among the Twelve, let him by no means put on footwear for the road, nor cover his heel in order to avoid scorpions and serpents; rather, already perfected and complete, let him stand on holy ground, live in Christ, and follow the Lamb wherever he goes.

It is asked whether he has now said “the Gospel of peace” to distinguish it from another Gospel, or whether it is proper to this Gospel that it should be called the Gospel of peace. Whoever therefore has peace is shod with the Gospel of Christ; and when he has been shod, he is prepared. But once prepared, he should not think himself perfect; rather, he should prepare himself for this: to proceed, and by proceeding to arrive at the end.

“680 (Verse 16.) Above all, taking up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one.” It is as though he had said: In every work carry the shield of faith, so that, covered and protected, you may receive the arrows that come against you and skillfully turn them aside here and there by the art of war.

This is the faith by which Abraham, after many works and virtues, could scarcely obtain such merit that Scripture would say of him: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. XV, 6). The darts of the evil one are clear enough: he wishes to shoot them into our hearts through the worst thoughts. One of these he cast into the heart of Judas, so that he might betray the Savior.

Therefore, the enemy will not even be able to begin wounding the soul if we hold the shield of faith. On it, not only are the weapons that come against us broken, but the very fire of the weapons is extinguished. Concerning this the prophet also laments, saying: “All of them are adulterers; their hearts are like an oven” (Hos. VII, 4).

Whoever holds this boss of faith with a strong hand and, trusting in the Lord, knows that he is secure from the darts that come against him, will speak fearlessly: “I trust in the Lord; how do you say to my soul, ‘Flee to the mountain like a sparrow’? For behold, sinners have bent the bow, they have prepared their arrows in the quivers, to shoot in darkness at the upright in heart” (Ps. X, 1–2). Since, he says, I trust in the Lord, on what grounds do you advise me not to stand against the assaults of the enemies and against the arrows that they have prepared in their quivers against me, wishing to strike not only me but all who are upright in heart? Behold, I stand upon the rock and do not flee to the dark mountains; and all the weapons of the enemies, repelled, are turned back upon those who direct them.

(Verses 17.) “And receive the helmet of salvation.” Because of this helmet of salvation, all the faculties of our head remain whole, and especially the eyes, concerning which Solomon says in Ecclesiastes: “The eyes of the wise man are in his head” (Eccles. II, 14). For he knew what the head of a man was and which eyes were placed in a man’s head.

If the head of a man is Christ, and the eyes of the wise man are in his head, it follows that all our faculties—mind, thought, speech, and counsel, if indeed we are wise—are in Christ: in Christ the Word, the light, righteousness, truth, and every virtue.

(Verses 18, 19.) “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God; with all prayer and supplication, praying at all times in the Spirit; and in this keeping watch with all perseverance and supplication for all the saints and for me. 681” The word of God flows from the Holy Spirit; but the contrary word speaks from the earth and takes its beginning from there. “He who is from the earth speaks from the earth. He who comes from heaven is above all; and what he has seen and heard, that he testifies” (John III, 31–32).

Moreover, the word of God is the sword of the Spirit, concerning which Paul now says: “The sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Hebr. IV). For the word of God is living and effective, sharper than every two-edged sword, penetrating even to the joints of the soul, the bones, and the marrow. The Spirit cuts and divides this word, greatly advancing through the prayer and supplication of those who at all times beseech the Lord in the Spirit, according to the saying: “I will pray with the spirit; I will pray also with the mind” (I Cor. XIV, 15).

Advancing in this way through vigils and persistent prayer, the apostle is enriched in God’s word and teaching. And all this abundance should contribute to the salvation of others, so that it may also benefit those who make supplication for him.

At the same time, the apostle’s humility is admirable: he asks the Ephesians to make supplications for him. For he says: “With all perseverance and supplication for all the saints and for me,” mentioning the saints separately and himself separately.

(Verses 20.) “So that speech may be given to me in the opening of my mouth, to make known with confidence the mystery of the Gospel, for which I am an ambassador in chains, so that in it I may dare to speak as I ought.” What he now says, “in the opening of my mouth,” and elsewhere, “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians” (II Cor. VI, 11); and, “Opening his mouth, he taught his disciples, saying” (Matt. V, 2); and, “I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit” (Ps. CXVIII, 131); and, “I will open my mouth in parables” (Ps. LXXVII, 2), and other similar passages, should be understood as though he had said: Let the treasures be opened, and let the mysteries hidden from the ages be disclosed, so that the Holy Spirit may enter to bring forth the things that lie concealed.

For that this is the meaning of this testimony—“that speech may be given to me in the opening of my mouth”—the following words prove. “With confidence,” he says, “to make known the mystery of the Gospel,” not in parables and proverbs, as both the prophets and the Lord himself, while still dwelling in the body, spoke when he said: “The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in proverbs, but I will announce the Father to you openly” (John XVI, 25).

Only the one who has no self-accusing heart will be able to obtain this speech of confidence: “If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence toward God, and whatever we ask, we receive from him” (I John III). Therefore, one who makes the mystery of the Gospel known with confidence is rare, because one who has confidence toward God is rare. For “who will boast that he has a pure heart? Or who will stand and say that he is clean from sins?” (Prov. XX, 9).

After this, what he says—“for which I am an ambassador in chains,” namely, that he might make the mystery of the Gospel known—must be touched upon briefly. One who understands it simply will say that, for the testimony of Christ, he wrote these things from prison and from chains while he was at Rome.

[Note: [Col. 0553D] Anyone who has spent even a little time in his writings will understand that this is Origen. Therefore Rufinus is wrong when, in Book I of his Invectives, no. 40, he slanders these words as though they were Jerome’s own.]

But another will contend that he said these things because of “the body of our humiliation,” and because of this chain by which we are surrounded and in which we do not yet know according to what we ought to know, and because “we see through a mirror in an enigma.” He will say that he could then truly open the mysteries of the Gospel with confidence when he had laid aside the chain and gone free from prison—unless perhaps the one whose manner of life is in heaven, and of whom it can be said, “You are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you” (Rom. VIII, 9), is to be counted as being in bonds without bonds.

(Verses 21, 22.) “But so that you also may know what concerns me and what I am doing, Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord, will make everything known to you. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, so that you may know what concerns us and that he may comfort your hearts.” Understand this in two ways.

Either Tychicus was sent to Ephesus so that he might report to them that the bonds of the apostle Paul had become known throughout the whole praetorium, and that his chains had advanced the faith of the Gospel. This was at the time when he also wrote to the Colossians, saying: “Everything that concerns me Tychicus, the beloved brother, minister, and fellow servant in the Lord, will make known to you. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, so that you may know what concerns us and that he may comfort your hearts, together with Onesimus, the beloved and faithful brother, who is one of you, who will make known to you everything that is being done here” (Col. IV, 7 ff.).

For it was a great consolation to hear that Paul was triumphing over prison and chains in Rome, the mistress of cities and the citadel of the Roman empire.

Or certainly Tychicus was sent for this reason: that he might announce to them the life and conduct of Paul, which they did not know, and give those learning the deeds and virtues of the apostle a kind of model for living, so that they might wish to imitate him. The consolation of those desiring to emulate him could not have been small when they learned what the apostle had done.

(Verses 23.) “Peace to the brothers, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.”

[Note: [Col. 0554D] Martianus retained the reading, “If there are any foreign gifts,” and so forth. We correct the lighter matters below.]

If there are any other gifts that are bestowed by God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, peace holds no small place among them. It surpasses all understanding and guards the hearts and understanding of the saints; it is a certain serenity and tranquility of the resting soul, driving away every storm and whirlwind of disturbances.

Love with faith is similar to this peace. God the Father and the Son together bestow this love also, so that we may love God with our whole heart, our neighbors as ourselves, and pray for our enemies. This peace and love, which the apostle invokes upon believers, belong only to those who deserve to be called brothers. For he says, “Peace to the brothers, and love with faith and peace.” Therefore the Father grants both love and faith in the same way as the Son; and the heresy that refuses to allow the Son to do what the Father does is silenced.

(Verses 24.) “Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ in incorruption. Amen.”

Some have interpreted this in such a way that they thought the one who loves our Lord Jesus Christ is the person who is removed from works of corruption, understanding “works of corruption” as sexual intercourse. Hence ordinary usage and popular speech call virgins “incorrupt,” and those who have not known intercourse with women; but they call “corrupted” those who have tasted such pleasure. They also adapt the testimony: “If anyone corrupts the temple of God, God will corrupt him” (I Cor. III, 17).

But I do not know whether they can explain by this what is written: “Each person has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that” (ibid. VII, 7). Let us therefore see whether it may be better to understand every sin as the corruption of the soul and to call those who are free from sin incorrupt, so that those who love the Lord Jesus Christ are in incorruption because they are not held by the bonds of sin, and the grace of God is with them.

At the same time, I think that, to distinguish those who love the Lord Jesus Christ but are not said here to love him in incorruption, the apostle says that those who love him in incorruption have the grace of Christ. For how many love the Lord, ready for exile, ready for martyrdom, ready for poverty, ready to endure every kind of insult for his sake, and nevertheless are overcome by the passion of the flesh! But the apostle does not invoke grace upon these, because the Lord’s grace is with all who love him in incorruption.

[Col. 0555]

SAINT EUSEBIUS HIERONYMUS, PRESBYTER OF STRIDON, ONE BOOK OF COMMENTARIES ON THE EPISTLE TO TITUS. (C)

Prologue.

[Col. 0555A] 685–686 Although they are not worthy of trust—those who have made their original faith void, I mean Marcion and Basilides and all the heretics who tear apart the Old Testament—we would nevertheless tolerate them to some extent if at least they kept their hands off the New Testament and did not dare to violate either Christ, whom they themselves boast to be the Son of the good God, or the evangelists or the apostles. But now, since they have also scattered his Gospels and made the apostles’ letters not the letters of Christ’s apostles but their own, I am amazed at how they dare to claim for themselves the name of Christians.

To say nothing of the other Epistles, from which they erased whatever they saw to be contrary to their doctrine, they judged certain ones unworthy of acceptance in their entirety: namely, both letters to Timothy, the Epistle to the Hebrews, and the Epistle to Titus, which we are now attempting to explain. If they gave reasons why they did not think these were by the apostle, we would try to answer something and perhaps satisfy the reader. But now, since they pronounce with heretical authority and say, “That letter is Paul’s; this one is not,” let them understand that they are refuted for the truth by the same authority with which they themselves do not blush to fabricate falsehoods.

[Note: [Col. 0555B] Recall what we said a little earlier about Tatian in chapter 6 of the commentary on Galatians.]

But Tatian, the patriarch of the Encratites, who himself rejected certain of Paul’s letters, judged this one above all—that is, the letter to Titus—to be declared apostolic, disregarding the assertion of Marcion and of the others who agree with him on this point.

The apostle therefore writes, O Paula and Eustochium, from Nicopolis, which is situated on the Actian coast and is now for the most part your estate; and he writes to Titus, his disciple and son in Christ, whom he had left in Crete to instruct the churches. He ordered him, when either Artemas or Tychicus should arrive in Crete, to come to Nicopolis himself.

[Note: [Col. 0555B] I am readily persuaded that the Nicopolis intended here is not Nicopolis of Thrace, within the borders of Macedonia, as most Greek writers assert, but the city of Epirus beside the Gulf of Ambracia, as learned writers generally think after Jerome. I do not know, however, by what other testimonies of the ancients I could confirm that this city was a very substantial part of Paula and Eustochium’s estate.]

For it was right that the man who had said, “My concern is for all the churches,” and who, setting out from Jerusalem, had founded the Gospel of Christ as far as Illyricum, should not allow the Cretans to be abandoned through the absence both of himself and of Titus. It was among them that the seeds of idolatry first began to sprout. Rather, he should send Artemas or Tychicus in his place and that of Titus, so that they might be strengthened by their teaching and consolation.

BEGINNING OF THE BOOK.

[Col. 0555]

[Col. 0555C] (Chapter I.—Verse 1.) “Paul, servant of God, but apostle of Jesus Christ.” In the Epistle to the Romans he began as follows: “Paul, servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle.” Here, however, he calls himself the servant of God but the apostle of Jesus Christ. If the Father and the Son are one, and whoever believes in the Son also believes in the Father, then the servitude of the apostle Paul may indifferently be referred either to the Father or to the Son.

This servitude is not the one of which the apostle himself says: “You did not receive the spirit of servitude again in fear [variant: ‘to fear’], but you received the spirit of adoption [variant: adds ‘of sons’], in which we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. VIII, 15). Rather, it is a noble servitude, of which David also says to God: “I am your servant, the son of your handmaid” (Ps. CXV, 16). And blessed Mary says to the angel: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word [variant: ‘according to’]” (Luke I, 38).

Moses also possessed this servitude, concerning whom the Lord says to Jesus son of Nun: “Moses, my servant, is dead” (Josh. I, 2). And elsewhere: “Moses, the servant of the Lord, died in the land of Moab by the word of the Lord” (Deut. XXXIV, 5). Far be it from us to believe that Moses and Mary possessed the spirit of servitude in fear and not in love of God.

Nor is it surprising that holy people are nobly called servants of God, since through the prophet Isaiah the Father speaks to the Son: “It is a great thing for you to be called my servant” (Isa. XLIX, 6), which is said in Greek:

[Note: [Col. 0557D] All the manuscript codices—the Cluniac manuscripts, those of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, and those of the Augustinian Fathers at Toulouse—read this way. Therefore the Greek context should be restored in the Bibles, where τὸ is missing, and in the editions of Erasmus and Marianus, in which τοῦ is absent. MART. The earlier editors, Erasmus and Victorius, had read μέγα σοί ἐστι τὸ κληθῆναι, “it is a great thing for you to be called,” whereas in the Greek archetype there is τοῦ κληθῆναι, a reading sound in both form and sense. Martianus, deceived by the error of some of his manuscripts, inserted both little words, τοῦ and τὸ, here at the same time, and argued that the Greek text itself should be restored according to the reading he had supplied, both in the Bibles, he says, where τὸ is missing, and in the editions of Erasmus and Marianus, in which τοῦ is absent. [Col. 0558D] But, I think, no one fails to see—and the matter itself cries out—that he has strayed very far from every appearance of truth. He should have said that τοῦτο, “this,” was to be read as one word: the manuscripts’ own reading conveniently suggested this obvious conjecture. Otherwise, it is clear that either τοῦ or τὸ is redundant. It was easy for some learned person to annotate in the margin that τό should be read there in place of τοῦ; afterward an unskilled scribe imported that word into the text as well, after τό.]

μέγα σοί ἐστι τοῦ κληθῆναί σε παῖδά μου.

“It is a great thing for you to be called my servant.”

But “servant”—that is, παῖς—for according to the Greeks it can signify both “servant” and “son”—we investigated in the Hebrew and found that it is not written “my son” but “my servant,” namely, ABDI. Hence also the prophet Obadiah, whose name is interpreted as “servant of the Lord,” received his name from the service of God.

If it troubles anyone that the Lord and Savior, who is the creator of the universe, is called the servant of God, he will not be troubled when he hears him speaking to the apostles: “Whoever wishes to be greater among you, let him be the servant of all”; and, “The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve” (Matt. XX, 27–28). To prevent the appearance that he was teaching only in words, he demonstrated it by his example. For, taking a linen cloth, he girded himself, filled a basin with water, and washed the disciples’ feet (John XIII).

It is therefore not impious to believe that he who assumed the form of a servant did those things that belong to servants, so that he may be said to have served the Father’s will, since he himself served his servants. This servitude is the servitude of love, through which we are commanded to serve one another. The apostle himself, although free from all, made himself the servant of all (I Cor. IX, 19). And elsewhere: “I am your servant,” he says, “for Christ’s sake.” He is the servant of God who is not the servant of sin. For “everyone who commits sin is the servant of sin” (John VIII, 34).

Therefore the apostle, who was not the servant of sin, is rightly called the servant both of God the Father and of Christ.

Moreover, when he says, “but apostle of Jesus Christ,” it seems to me equivalent to saying “praetorian prefect of Augustus Caesar” or “commander of the army of the emperor Tiberius.” For just as the judges of this world, in order to appear more noble, take their titles from the kings whom they serve and from the rank with which they swell with pride, so the apostle, claiming for himself a great dignity among Christians, prefixed to himself the title “apostle of Christ,” so that, from the authority of the name itself, he might terrify those who were going to read him, indicating that all who believed in Christ ought to be subject to him.

Moreover, the expression that we quoted shortly before from Romans, “servant of Jesus Christ,” is no different from saying “servant of wisdom, servant of righteousness, servant of sanctification, servant of redemption.” For Christ was made for us by God the Father “wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption” [Note: [Col. 0558D] The Cistercian manuscripts add: “And the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve.”] (I Cor. I, 30).

(Verses 2 ff.) “According to the faith of God’s elect and the knowledge of the truth that is according to godliness, in hope of eternal life, which God, who does not lie, promised before eternal ages, but manifested in its proper times his word in the proclamation entrusted to me according to the command of God our Savior—to Titus, my most beloved son according to the common faith: grace and peace from God the Father and Jesus Christ our Savior.”

He had not spoken according to humility, as most people think, but had truly said: “Though unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge; a Hebrew of Hebrews, according to the law a Pharisee.” He does not explain profound meanings in Greek speech and scarcely brings what he thinks into words. Therefore let us discuss each point as it has been written, following the order of the meanings and the substance of the matter rather than the words.

“According to the faith,” he says, “of God’s elect.” Refer this to what he introduced above: “Paul, servant of God, but apostle of Jesus Christ according to the faith of God’s elect”—that is, of those who have not merely been called but also chosen.

There is also great diversity among the elect themselves, according to the variety of their works, thoughts, and words. Nor is everyone immediately who is God’s elect in possession of faith according to his election, or in possession of knowledge according to his faith. Hence the Savior also spoke to the Jews who had believed in him: “If you remain in my word, you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free” (John VIII, 31–32).

The evangelist testifies that he said this to believers, but to believers who did not know the truth, which they could attain if they remained in his word and, having been made free, ceased to be servants.

It is asked why, to the phrase “according to the faith of God’s elect and the knowledge of the truth,” he added “which is according to godliness.” Is there perhaps some truth that is not situated in godliness, so that he now introduces, by way of distinction from it, the knowledge of truth that is according to godliness?

There plainly is a truth that does not possess godliness. If someone knows the art of grammar or dialectic, so that he has a method of speaking correctly and can distinguish between false and true, geometry, arithmetic, and music also possess truth within their own knowledge; but that knowledge is not the knowledge of godliness.

The knowledge of godliness is to know the Law, understand the prophets, believe the Gospel, and not be ignorant of the apostles. Conversely, there are many who possess true knowledge of godliness but do not immediately possess the truth of the other arts, including those we mentioned above.

This truth, therefore, whose knowledge is according to godliness, is situated in the hope of eternal life, because it immediately grants the reward of immortality to the one who has come to know it. Without godliness, knowledge of the truth delights for the present, but it does not possess an eternity of rewards, which God, who does not lie, promised before the eternal ages and manifested in its proper times in Christ Jesus.

To whom did he make the promise beforehand, and afterward make it clear, except to his Wisdom, which was always with the Father, when she rejoiced over the completed world and delighted in the sons of men, promising that all who would believe in her would possess eternal life?

Before the world laid its foundations, before he spread out the seas, fixed the mountains, suspended the sky, and solidified the earth by casting down its mass, God made this promise—God in whom there is no falsehood. This is not because he could lie but did not wish to break out into words of falsehood; rather, because, being the Father of truth, he contains no falsehood in himself, according to the saying: “Let God be true, and every man a liar” (Rom. III, 4).

For this reason God is called “not lying”: indeed, when he makes certain promises under oath in the prophets, it is so that, made more secure, we may hope more confidently that what has been foretold will come to pass, and, believing with our whole mind, may prepare ourselves to attain what is to come.

It seems not out of place to touch briefly upon why, in the Apostle’s words, God alone is called truthful, and every human being a liar. Unless I am mistaken, this is like saying that he alone possesses immortality, although he made angels and many rational creatures to whom he gave immortality. He is likewise said to be alone truthful—not because the others are neither immortal nor lovers of truth, but because he alone is by nature both immortal and truthful. The others obtain immortality and truth from his generosity. It is one thing to be true, [Note: Cistercian manuscripts read: “and it is another thing to be true that you may possess,”] another to possess truth through oneself, and another to have what one has in the power of the giver.

Nor, I think, should we pass over in silence how God, who is not a liar, promised eternal life before the eternal ages. According to the historical account in Genesis, the world came into being, and through the succession of nights and days, months likewise and years, periods of time were established. Within this cycle and wheel of the world, times pass away and come on, and things are either going to be or have been. Hence certain philosophers do not think that the present exists as time, but only either the past or the future, because everything that we speak, do, or think either passes away while it is happening or, if it has not yet happened, is awaited.

Before these times of the world, therefore, we must believe that there existed a certain eternity of ages, in which the Father was always with the Son and the Holy Spirit. And, so to speak, the one time of God is the whole of eternity; indeed, there are innumerable times, since he himself is infinite and, existing before times, surpasses every time.

[Note: Saint Jerome presents similar views, whether from his own opinion or that of others, in Letter 18 to Damasus, no. 7: namely, that angels existed before this world was created, and even that some had fallen before then; and that human beings were subsequently created so that they might complete the number of the blessed assembly. Tertullian and several other early writers also approved this view. Nevertheless, through the authority of far more numerous Fathers of the Church, the opposite doctrine prevailed and rests on stronger arguments: that the angels were created with heaven, earth, and light on the first day of the world.]

Not even a thousand years of our world have yet been completed; how many earlier eternities, how many periods of time, and how many beginnings of ages must we suppose there were in which angels, thrones, dominions, and the other powers served God and, at his command, continued to exist without the succession and measurement of times!

Before all these times—which neither speech can express, nor the mind comprehend, nor silent thought dare approach—God the Father promised that the Word of his wisdom, his very Wisdom, and the life of those who were to believe would come into the world. Pay close attention to the text and order of the reading, since the eternal life that God, who does not lie, promised before the eternal ages is not something other than the Word of God. “He manifested,” it says, “his word in its proper times.” Therefore the eternal life that he had promised is itself his Word, which “in the beginning was with the Father,” and “the Word was God,” and “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1).

That the Word of God—that is, Christ himself—is life, he testifies elsewhere when he says: “I am the life” (John 14:6). This life is not brief, nor confined within certain periods, but perpetual and eternal. It was manifested in the last ages through the preaching entrusted to Paul, the teacher and instructor of the Gentiles, so that it might be announced throughout the world and become known to human beings, according to the command of God our Savior, who desired that we should be saved by fulfilling what he had promised.

The Apostle writes to Titus, his dearest son, using the expression that in Greek is called γνησίῳ τέκνῳ, which cannot be fully expressed in Latin. For γνήσιος more properly conveys the sense of someone called faithful and one’s own—and, so to speak, legitimate or genuine—without comparison with another. From this we understand that there was also great distinction among Paul’s sons: some were γνησίοι, that is, most genuinely his, closely united to him, born of a true marriage and of a free woman; others were like those born of the slave woman and of Hagar, who cannot receive an inheritance together with Isaac, the son of the free woman.

For the speech, wisdom, and teaching with which Titus instructed the Churches of Christ made him the Apostle’s own son and separated him from association with all the others.

Let us examine what follows: “According to the common faith.” Did he call the faith common to all who believed in Christ, or common only to himself and Titus? It seems better to me that the faith of the Apostle Paul and Titus was called common than that of all believers. Among them, because of the diversity of their minds, their faith could not be common but was diverse.

Finally, the preface and greeting of the Apostle’s letter to Titus conclude with these words: “Grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior.” This may mean either that both grace and peace are from God the Father as well as from Christ Jesus, so that each may be understood as given by both; or that grace refers to the Father and peace to the Son.

We should not pass without reflection over the fact that the Apostle prayed for some people that grace and peace might be multiplied for them, whereas now, in addressing Titus, peace and grace are stated without multiplication. Noah, a righteous man who alone was preserved when the world was shipwrecked, is not said to have found many graces but one grace in the sight of God. Moses likewise says to the Lord: “If I have found grace in your sight” (Exodus 33:13). Wherever else grace is mentioned in the person of the saints, investigate and you will find that they are not said to have found graces, but grace.

That merchant in the Gospel who possessed many pearls finally found one precious pearl, which alone among the many pearls he purchased (Matthew 13). It belongs to the perfect to buy one pearl and one treasure by an exchange for all their pearls and their entire substance; beginners, however, and those still on the journey have not merely one and only one pearl, but several.

### (Verse 5)

“For this reason I left you in Crete, so that you might correct what was lacking.”

It belongs to apostolic dignity to lay the foundation of a Church, which no one can lay unless he is an architect. “No other foundation can be laid besides Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:11). Those who are subordinate craftsmen can build structures upon the foundations.

Paul, therefore, as a wise architect—and striving with all his labor not to glory in what had already been prepared—after softening the hard hearts of the Cretans toward faith in Christ, subduing and instructing them both by his word and by signs, and teaching them to believe not in their native Jupiter but in God the Father and in Christ, left his disciple Titus in Crete to strengthen the beginnings of the newly born Church and to correct whatever seemed to be lacking. He himself proceeded to other nations, in order once again to lay Christ’s foundation among them.

When he says, “so that you might correct what was lacking,” he shows that they had not yet come to a complete knowledge of the truth. Although they had been corrected by the Apostle, they still required correction. Everything that is corrected is imperfect. In Greek, moreover, the addition of the preposition in the word ἐπιδιορθώσῃ does not convey precisely the same meaning as διορθώσῃ, that is, “you might correct,” but, so to speak, “you might correct further”: namely, that what had been corrected by me, but had not yet been restored [or: revised] to the full line of truth, might be corrected by you and receive the standard of equality.

“And appoint presbyters in every city, as I directed you.” [Alternative reading (Al.): “So that you might appoint presbyters in every city.”]

Let bishops who possess the authority to appoint presbyters in each city hear under what law the order of ecclesiastical constitution is to be maintained. Let them not suppose that these are the Apostle’s words merely, but Christ’s, who says to the disciples: “He who rejects you rejects me; and he who rejects me rejects him who sent me” (Luke 10:16). Likewise: “He who hears you hears me; and he who hears me hears him who sent me.”

From this it is clear that those who, disregarding the Apostle’s law, wish to confer an ecclesiastical rank on someone not because of merit but through favor, act against Christ, who through his Apostle has explained in what manner a presbyter ought to be appointed in the Church.

Moses, the friend of God, to whom God spoke face to face (Deuteronomy 5 and 31), could certainly have made his sons successors to his leadership and left his particular dignity to his descendants. Yet Jesus, a stranger from another tribe, is chosen, so that we might know that leadership over peoples is to be conferred not upon blood but upon life.

But now we see many making this a matter of patronage, so that they do not seek to raise as pillars in the Church those who can benefit the Church most, but rather those whom they themselves love, or by whose services they have been won over, or for whom some person of influence has interceded—and, to say nothing worse, those who have obtained clerical status through gifts.

[Note: We have followed the manuscript of Saint-Martin-des-Champs and others. In Erasmus we read corruptly: “who can benefit the Church more and raise up pillars in the Church.” Marianus introduced an even worse reading from Gratian’s Decree into Jerome, saying: “But now we see many making this a matter of patronage: so that they do not seek to raise as pillars in the Church those whom they know to be more useful to the Church, but those whom,” and so forth. Clearly he did not compare the editions with the manuscript copies, but here treated Gratian as Jerome. Therefore, those who can benefit the Church most are the pillars of that same Church, as Saint Jerome observes here. In the manuscript copy of the Augustinians of Toulouse we read: “many making honor a matter of patronage,” and so forth. MART.—Victorius, whom Martianay corrects, altered this passage from Gratian as follows: “Let them not seek to raise as pillars of the Church those whom they know to be more useful to the Church,” and so forth. Shortly afterward, our manuscripts read “the Apostle’s command” instead of “the Apostle’s words.”]

Let us attend carefully to the Apostle’s words: “That you might appoint presbyters in every city, as I directed you.” Explaining what sort of presbyter ought to be ordained, he says later: “If anyone is without reproach, the husband of one wife,” and so forth. He then adds: “For a bishop must be without reproach, as God’s steward.”

A presbyter, therefore, is the same as a bishop. Before divisions arose in religion through the devil’s instigation, and before people began saying among themselves, “I belong to Paul,” “I to Apollos,” and “I to Cephas” (1 Corinthians 1:12), the Churches were governed by the common counsel of the presbyters. But after each person began to regard as his own, and not Christ’s, those whom he had baptized, it was decreed throughout the whole world that one of the presbyters should be chosen and placed over the others, so that the entire care of the Church might belong to him and the seeds of schisms might be removed.

[Note: Cistercian manuscripts read: “so that then one of the presbyters might be chosen and set over the rest.” See Letter 146 to Evangelus and our remarks there on Jerome’s view of the dignity of bishops above presbyters.]

Someone may suppose [Alternative reading (Al.): “Someone supposes.”] that the claim that a bishop and a presbyter are one and the same is not scriptural but our own opinion, and that the difference is one of age while the name of the office is the same. Let him reread the Apostle’s words to the Philippians: “Paul and Timothy, servants of Jesus Christ, to all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi, with the bishops and deacons: grace to you and peace” (Philippians 1:1–2), and what follows. [Note: Our manuscripts omit the words “to all the saints in Christ Jesus.” Again, we remind the reader to refer here to what has been noted on the Letter to Evangelus. Alternative reading (Al.): “and with the bishops and deacons.”]

Philippi is one city of Macedonia, and certainly several bishops, as they are now called, could not have existed in one city. [Note: Two manuscripts read more correctly: “as bishops are now supposed to be.”] But because at that time the same people were also called presbyters, he spoke indifferently of bishops as though of presbyters.

Even now this may seem ambiguous to someone unless it is confirmed by another testimony. In the Acts of the Apostles it is written that, when the Apostle had come to Miletus, he sent to Ephesus and summoned the presbyters of that Church. Among other things he afterward said to them: “Pay attention to yourselves and to the whole flock in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops, to shepherd the Church of the Lord, which he acquired with his blood” (Acts 20:28).

Here too observe carefully how, after summoning the presbyters of the one city of Ephesus, he later called those same men bishops.

If anyone wishes to accept the letter written under Paul’s name to the Hebrews, there too the care of the Church is divided equally among several persons. For he writes to the people: “Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they are keeping watch over your souls as those who will give an account, so that they may do this without groaning, since that would be of no advantage to you” (Hebrews 13:17).

Peter too, who received his name from the firmness of his faith, speaks in his letter, saying: “Therefore I appeal to the presbyters among you, as a fellow presbyter and a witness of Christ’s sufferings, as well as a sharer in the glory that is to be revealed: shepherd the flock of the Lord that is among you, not under compulsion but willingly” (1 Peter 5:1–2).

I have said this to show that among the ancients the same people were presbyters as were bishops; gradually, however, so that the shoots of dissension might be uprooted, all responsibility was transferred to one person.

Just as presbyters know that by ecclesiastical custom they are subject to the one placed over them, so bishops should know that they are greater than presbyters more by custom than by the truth of the Lord’s arrangement, and that they ought to govern the Church together with them, imitating Moses. Although he had the authority to preside alone over the people of Israel, he chose seventy with whom he might judge the people (Numbers 11).

Let us therefore examine what sort of presbyter, or bishop, ought to be ordained.

### (Verse 6)

“If anyone is without reproach, the husband of one wife, having faithful children, not accused of debauchery or being insubordinate.”

First, then, he must be without reproach. I think this is what is called “irreproachable” in another passage addressed to Timothy (1 Timothy 3). This does not mean [Alternative reading (Al.): “not for the reason that.”] that he must be without any fault only at the time when he is to be ordained, having washed away former stains through a new way of life. Rather, from the time when he was reborn in Christ, no consciousness of sin should gnaw at him.

For how can the ruler of a Church remove evil from its midst if he himself has fallen into a similar offense? Or with what freedom can he rebuke someone who sins, when he silently answers himself that he has committed the same acts for which he reproves another?

Therefore, whoever desires the office of bishop desires a good work. He says “work,” not honor or glory. He must also have a good testimony from those outside, so that he may not fall into disgrace and the devil’s snare.

When he says “the husband of one wife,” we should understand this not as though we considered every monogamous man better than a man married twice, but so that someone might exhort others to monogamy and continence while presenting his own example in his teaching.

Suppose that one man lost his wife in youth and, overcome by the necessity of the flesh, took a second wife, whom he also soon lost, and afterward lived continently; while another remained married and continued marital relations into old age, never ceasing from the work of the flesh, which most people regard as happiness. Which of the two seems to you the better, more chaste, and more continent? Surely the one who was unfortunate even in his second marriage and afterward lived chastely and holily, not the one who was not separated from his wife’s embraces even by old age. [Note: The same manuscripts falsely read: “who was also fortunate,” etc.]

Therefore let no one congratulate himself, when chosen as though monogamous, that he is better than every man married twice, since in him happiness has been chosen more than will.

Some understand this passage as follows: “It was the custom of the Jews either to have two wives or more, as we also read in the Old Law concerning Abraham and Jacob. What is commanded here,” they say, “is that the man to be chosen as bishop must not at one time have two wives simultaneously.”

Many, with more superstition than truth, also think that men who were Gentiles and had one wife, but after losing her took another after the baptism of Christ, should not be chosen for the priesthood. [Note: The whole Letter to Oceanus, no. 69 in our recension, is relevant here, where the holy Father sets out the arguments for his opinion. See also our observations in the earlier note on that letter.] Yet if this is to be observed, those ought rather to be excluded from the episcopate who previously practiced wandering lust among prostitutes and, after being regenerated, took one wife. It is far more detestable to have fornicated with many than to be found married twice, because in one case there is the misfortune of marriage, while in the other there is a lustfulness inclined toward sin.

Montanus and those who follow the schism of Novatus arrogated to themselves the name of purity, and think that second marriages should be excluded from communion with the Church. Yet when the Apostle gives this command concerning bishops and presbyters, he plainly grants relaxation in other cases—not because he encourages second marriages, but because he makes allowance for the necessity of the flesh.

Tertullian also wrote a heretical book entitled *On Monogamy*. No one who has read the Apostle will be unaware that it contradicts him.

Certainly, it lies within our power for a bishop or presbyter to be without reproach and to have one wife. But what follows—“having faithful children, not accused of debauchery or being insubordinate”—lies outside our control.

Suppose that parents have properly instructed their children and from early childhood have continually taught them the Lord’s commandments. If those children later give themselves over to debauchery, and, overcome by their vices, yield the reins to lust, will the fault not rebound upon the parents, and will the children’s sins stain the father’s holiness?

If anyone properly instructed his children, I think Isaac was among such men. Surely we must believe that he properly educated his son Esau. Yet Esau, a fornicator and profane man, sold his birthright for one meal (Genesis 25).

Samuel, too, was such a man that he called upon the Lord, and the Lord heard him, and in the season of harvest he obtained rain during winter. Yet he had sons who turned toward greed, accepted bribes, and became such unjust judges that the people, unable to endure them, demanded a king for themselves like those of the other nations (1 Samuel 12). [Alternative reading (Al.): “the Lord had heard him.”]

Therefore, if priests were being chosen, would Isaac be considered unworthy of the priesthood because of Esau, and Samuel because of his sons? Although the sins of parents are not charged against their children, so that the saying “the parents have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge” is no longer in force (Ezekiel 18:2), will the vices of children prejudice their parents?

First, then, it must be said that the name of the priesthood is so holy that even what lies outside us is counted against us—not so that we may fail to become bishops because of our own vices, but so that we may be barred from this rank because of the lack of continence in our children.

For with what freedom can we rebuke the children of others and teach what is right, when the person rebuked can immediately retort: “First teach your own children”? Or with what face can I rebuke another fornicating man when my own conscience answers me: “Then disinherit your fornicating son; cast out your children who serve their vices”?

When a wicked son lives with you in the same house, do you dare to remove the speck from another’s eye while failing to see the beam in your own (Matthew 7; Luke 6)? [Note: Erasmus reads “shares [with you].” Mariano prefers “lives with [you].” In some manuscripts we read “lives with you in the same house.” MART.—This too, which Victorius preferred, our manuscripts prefer as “lives with [you]”; formerly the reading was “shares [with you].”]

A righteous man is not therefore polluted by the vices of his children. But the Apostle reserves for the head of the Church the freedom to become such a person that he does not fear rebuking outsiders because of the vices of his children. [Alternative reading (Al.): “so that he may become such a person.”]

Furthermore, this must also be brought against those who grow arrogant over the episcopate and think that they have obtained not Christ’s stewardship but dominion: those who imagine that, simply because they have not been ordained bishops, everyone else is immediately inferior to them, and who, because they have been chosen, consider themselves more approved than others.

Let them understand instead that some have been removed from the priesthood because the vices of their children hindered them. If the sins of children prevent a righteous man from becoming a bishop, how much more will each person, considering himself and knowing that “the powerful will suffer powerful torments” (Wisdom 6), withdraw from this position, which is less an honor than a burden, and refrain from seeking to occupy the place of others who are more worthy! [Alternative reading (Al.): “withdraws.”]

Finally, it must be said that in Scripture sons are understood as λογισμοὺς, that is, thoughts, while daughters are understood as πράξεις, that is, deeds. The command, then, is that a person should become a bishop who has both his thoughts and his deeds under his control, who truly believes in Christ, and who is not stained by any contamination of creeping vices.

### (Verse 7)

“For a bishop must be without reproach, as God’s steward: not arrogant, not irritable, not addicted to wine, not violent, not greedy for dishonest gain.”

Among stewards, therefore, the question is that someone be found faithful, not one who, eating and drinking with the drunken, beats male and female servants, but one who awaits God’s uncertain coming and gives his fellow servants their food at the proper time.

The only difference between a steward and the household is that a fellow servant is placed over his fellow servants. Therefore, let the bishop and presbyter know that the people are their fellow servants, not their slaves.

The remaining qualifications lie within our control:

“Not arrogant,” that is, not puffed up and pleased with himself because he is a bishop, but, like a good steward, seeking what will benefit the greatest number.

“Not irritable.” An irritable man is one who is always angry and is shaken by the slightest breath of an answer or an offense, like a leaf by the wind.

Indeed, nothing is uglier than a furious teacher. He ought to be gentle—and, according to what is written, “The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward all, an able teacher, patient, instructing opponents with gentleness” (1 Timothy 2). Yet, on the contrary, with a grim face, trembling lips, furrowed brow, uncontrolled insults, and a countenance shifting between pallor and redness, he may resound with shouting. By his savagery he does not so much bring the erring back to the good as drive them headlong into evil.

Hence Solomon also says: “Anger destroys even the wise” (Proverbs 21), and: “The anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God” (James 1:20).

Nor is everyone who becomes angry on some occasion an irritable person. That name belongs to one who is frequently overcome by this passion.

He also forbids a bishop to be addicted to wine, as it is written to Timothy: “Not devoted to much wine” (1 Timothy 3:8).

What is it like to see a bishop addicted to wine, so that, with his judgment occupied, he either, contrary to the dignity of seriousness, heightens his laughter and guffaws with loosened lips, or, if he happens to remember some slightly sad matter, bursts into sobs and tears amid his cups?

It would take too long to go through each instance and explain the insanities suggested by drunkenness. You see some turning drinking cups into weapons and hurling a goblet into a fellow guest’s face; others, with their garments torn, rushing upon another’s wounds; others shouting; others sleeping. Whoever has drunk more is considered stronger. It becomes an occasion for accusation if someone, having been adjured by the king, drinks less frequently.

They vomit so that they may drink, and drink so that they may vomit. The digestion of the belly and the throat are occupied with one and the same duty.

For now it is enough to say that, according to the Apostle, “luxury is in wine.” Wherever there is gluttony and drunkenness, there let lust rule.

[Note: Saint Jerome has taken this from the beginning of Tertullian’s *On Fasting Against the Psychics*: “Observe the body, and it is one region; finally, according to the arrangement of the limbs, there is an order of vices. First comes the belly, and immediately afterward comes the wantonness built upon the rest of the stuffing; through overeating deceit passes.”]

Look at the belly and the genitals, and at the order of the limbs according to the quality of the vices. I will never consider a drunkard chaste. Even if he sleeps after being overcome by wine, he could nevertheless have sinned through wine.

We are surprised that the Apostle condemned drunkenness in bishops and presbyters, since in the Old Law too it was commanded that priests, when entering the temple to minister to God, should not drink wine at all (Leviticus 10). A Nazirite, as long as he allowed his sacred hair to grow, saw nothing defiled and nothing mortal, and was to abstain from wine, raisins, and the weaker drink usually made from grape marc, [Note: In attempting an emendation, Victorius corrupts this passage by reading “and from a more delicate [drink],” etc.] as well as from every strong drink that turns the mind away from sound health (Numbers 6).

Let each person say what he wishes; I speak from my conscience. I know that abstinence has both harmed me when interrupted and benefited me when resumed.

After drunkenness he commands that a man not be violent. Taken simply, this instruction edifies the hearer, warning him not readily to stretch out his hand to strike, or, in madness, to break out into blows against another’s face.

It is better, however, to say that he is not violent who, gentle and patient, knows what ought to be said at the proper time and what ought to be left unsaid, and does not wound the conscience of the weak with useless speech.

For in forming the head of the Church, the Apostle does not forbid him to be a boxer or a pancratiast—παγκρατιαστὴν, that is, an athlete—which would be condemned even in a commoner or in any Gentile. Rather, as I have said, he forbids him to be insulting and talkative, lest he destroy someone whom he could have corrected through moderation and gentleness.

The desire for dishonest gain must likewise be alien to anyone who is to become a bishop. There are many who teach what ought not to be taught for the sake of dishonest gain; they overturn entire households and think that godliness is a means of profit.

According to Solomon, a small gain with righteousness is better than many fruits with injustice (Proverbs 16:8); [Alternative reading (Al.): “many products.”] and a good name in poverty is more desirable than an evil name amid riches.

A bishop who wishes to imitate the Apostle, having food and clothing, ought to be content with these alone (1 Timothy 6). “Those who serve at the altar should live from the altar” (1 Corinthians 9). He says “live,” not “become rich.”

Hence money is shaken out of our belts, and we wear only one tunic (Matthew 10; Mark 6), nor do we think about tomorrow. The desire for dishonest gain consists in thinking about more than what is present.

Up to this point the Apostle has taught in his words what a bishop or presbyter ought not to have. Now, conversely, what he ought to have is explained.

### (Verses 8–9)

“But hospitable, a lover of good things, [Col. 0568A] chaste, just, holy, self-controlled—or abstinent—holding firmly to the faithful word that accords with the teaching, so that he may be able to exhort in sound doctrine and refute those who contradict.”

Above all, hospitality is enjoined upon the future bishop. For if everyone desires to hear that saying from the Gospel, “I was a stranger, and you welcomed me” (Matt. 25:35), how much more so the bishop, whose house ought to be a common lodging for all! A layman who receives one or two, or a few, will fulfill [Al. “fulfilled”] the duty of hospitality. Unless the bishop receives everyone, he is inhuman.

But I fear that, just as the queen of the South, coming from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom (Matt. 12), will judge the people of her own time, and the men of Nineveh, having repented at Jonah’s preaching, [Col. 0568B] will condemn those who refused to hear the Savior, who is greater than Jonah, so many among the people may judge bishops who withdraw from the ecclesiastical rank and practice what is not fitting for a bishop [Note: In one or another Cistercian manuscript, the negative particle is absent.]. I think that John wrote about such men to Gaius:

“My dearest Gaius, you act faithfully in whatever you do for the brothers, and especially for strangers, who have testified to your love before the Church. You will do well to send them on their journey in a manner worthy of God; for they have gone out for the sake of the Name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles” (3 John 5–8).

And truly, with the Holy Spirit speaking within him, he already reproved what was going to happen in the Churches, saying:

“I wrote something to the Church; but Diotrephes [Al. Dioprepes], who desires to hold the first place among them, does not receive us. Therefore, when I come, I will call attention to his works, which he does by speaking evil against us. And not content with refusing to receive the brothers himself, he also prevents those who wish to do so and expels them from the Church” (3 John 9–10).

Indeed, now one can see what was foretold occurring in many cities: bishops or presbyters, when they see laymen who are hospitable and lovers of good things, envy them, rage against them, excommunicate them, and expel them from the Church, as though it were impermissible to do what the bishop himself does not do, and as though the existence of such laymen might be a condemnation of the priests [Al. “is”]. They regard them as burdensome and, as if placed upon their own necks, harass them with various persecutions in order to draw them away from good works.

The bishop should also be chaste—what the Greeks call σώφρων (*sōphrōn*). The Latin translator, deceived by the ambiguity of the word, rendered it “prudent” instead of “chaste.” If laymen are commanded, for the sake of prayer, to abstain from intercourse with their wives, what should be thought of the bishop, who must daily offer to God undefiled sacrifices for his own sins and those of the people?

Let us read the Books of Kings [Al. Kingdoms], and we shall find that the priest Abimelech first refused to give David and his young men the bread of the Presence unless he asked whether the young men were clean from a woman—not from another woman, certainly, but from their wives (1 Sam. 21). Unless he had heard from them that they had abstained from marital intercourse since the previous day and the day before, he would certainly not have granted them the bread he had initially refused.

[Note: A more ancient Cistercian manuscript perhaps reads more correctly: “How great is the difference between the bread of the Presence and the body of Christ? What difference is there between the shadow…” The passage is marked as a question.]

There is as much difference between the bread of the Presence and the body of Christ as there is between a shadow and bodies, between an image and reality, between copies of things to come and the very things prefigured by those copies.

Therefore, just as gentleness, patience, sobriety, moderation, freedom from greed, hospitality, and kindness ought especially to be found in a bishop and ought to make him distinguished among all laymen, so also his own chastity—and, so to speak, priestly purity—must be such that he not only abstains from unclean acts but is also free from the casting of the eye and the wandering of thought, so that the mind which is to prepare Christ’s body may remain pure.

The bishop must also be just and holy, so that he may practice justice among the people over whom he presides, rendering to each what he deserves [Col. 0569B] and showing no partiality in judgment. The justice of a layman differs from that of a bishop in this respect: a layman may appear just among a few, whereas a bishop can practice justice among as many as he has subjects. [Note: Two manuscripts read “must” for “can,” and shortly afterward ἅγιος for ὅσιος.]

“Holy,” which in Greek is ὅσιος (*hosios*), signifies more particularly holiness mingled with piety and directed toward God. The one whom we call “holy,” the Greeks call ἅγιος (*hagios*); but the one whom they call ὅσιος, we may call “pious toward God.”

The bishop should also be abstinent—not merely, as some think, from lust and the embrace of his wife, but from every disturbance of the soul: so that he is not provoked to anger, cast down by sadness, agitated by fear, or lifted up by excessive joy. Abstinence is also numbered by the Apostle among the fruits of the Spirit.

If abstinence is required of everyone, how much more of the bishop, who ought patiently and gently to bear the faults of sinners, console the fainthearted, support the weak, and return evil to no one for evil, but overcome evil with good.

Finally, he should hold firmly to the faithful word that accords with the teaching, so that, just as the word of God is faithful and worthy of complete acceptance, he too may show himself faithful, so that everything he says may be regarded as worthy of belief and his words may be a rule of truth.

He should also be able to console those who are harassed by the storms of this age and, through sound doctrine, destroy unsound and feeble teachings. Doctrine is called “sound” in contrast to doctrine that is sick and weak.

He should likewise be such as to refute those who contradict him—heretics, Jews, and the wise men of this age. The qualities he listed above among the virtues of a bishop pertain to life. But what he says here—“so that he may be able to console in sound doctrine and refute those who contradict”—pertains to knowledge.

For if the bishop has only a holy life, such a life can benefit himself. But if he has been educated in doctrine and speech, he can instruct himself and others [Note: Two manuscripts add “others also”], and not merely instruct and teach his own people, but also strike back at opponents. Unless these opponents are refuted and convicted, they can easily corrupt the hearts of the simple.

This passage is directed against those who give themselves to idleness, leisure, and sleep, and think it sinful to read the Scriptures, while they despise those who meditate on the law of the Lord day and night as chatterers and useless men. They fail to notice that, after listing the conduct of a bishop, the Apostle likewise commanded doctrinal instruction.

### (Verses 10–11)

“For there are many who are disobedient, empty talkers, and deceivers of minds, especially those of the circumcision, whose mouths must be silenced. They overturn whole households, teaching things that ought not to be taught for the sake of shameful gain.”

He who is to become the leader of the Church should unite eloquence with integrity of life, so that his works may not be speechless and his words may not be put to shame by the failure of his deeds. There are especially not a few, but many who are not submissive but insolent, who do not care to say with the Psalmist, “Is not my soul subject to God?” (Ps. 62:1).

Instead, they corrupt by empty persuasion the good seed of minds [Al. “of good minds”], which naturally possess knowledge of God. This is what Paul seems to have meant when he says φρεναπάται (*phrenapat​ai*): not simply, as the Latin translator rendered it, “deceivers,” but “deceivers of minds.”

Indeed, without the authority of the Scriptures their chatter would have no credibility, unless they appeared to support their perverse doctrine with divine testimonies. These are Jews of the circumcision, who at that time were trying to subvert the emerging Church of Christ and introduce legal precepts. Paul discusses them more fully both in Romans and in Galatians.
