A few months ago we also dictated three volumes in explanation of the Epistle to the Galatians.

Such men the Doctor of the Church, to whom the souls of the people have been entrusted, ought to overcome by the reasoning of the Scriptures and impose silence upon them by the weight of testimony. They overturn not one household or a few, but whole households, together with their masters and families, teaching about distinctions among foods, about the injury of circumcision, long since abolished—and would that they did this out of zeal for the faith! To some extent they could be pardoned, since the Apostle says: “I testify that they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom. 10:2).

But because their god is their belly, they wish to make disciples for themselves for the sake of shameful gain, so that, like teachers, they may be nourished by their followers.

We can also interpret in another way the phrase “for the sake of shameful gain”: we may suppose that the Apostle used a common expression by which all heretics, when they teach perversely, are accustomed to claim that they are gaining people, although it is not gain but destruction to kill the souls of those they deceive.

By contrast, whoever rebukes his erring brother according to the Gospel, and the brother is converted, has gained him. What greater gain could there be, or what could be more precious, than for someone to gain a human soul? Therefore every teacher of the Church who persuades someone to the faith of Christ by right reasoning is an honorable gainer. And every heretic who deceives and is himself deceived by various tricks, speaking things that ought not to be spoken, does so for the sake of shameful gain.

### (Verses 12 and following)

“One of them, their own prophet, said: ‘Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies.’ This testimony is true. For this reason rebuke them sharply [Note: Cistercian manuscripts read “severely” instead of “sharply,” farther from the Greek ἀποτόμως], so that they may be sound in the faith and not attend to Jewish myths and commandments of people who turn away from the truth.”

As regards the wording and the context of the passage, the statement “one of them, their own prophet, said” appears to refer to those of whom he spoke above—especially those of the circumcision—who must be restrained, since they overturn whole households, teaching things that ought not to be taught for the sake of shameful gain. The sequence would then be: “One of them, their own prophet, said.”

Because this hexameter verse is found in none of the prophets who prophesied in Judaea, it seems to me that the passage should be read in two ways. The words “one of them, their own prophet, said” may be joined to what precedes, so that the meaning is: “For this reason I left you in Crete, so that you might correct what was lacking,” followed by: “One of them, their own prophet, said”—that is, the prophet of the Cretans.

But because much intervenes between these statements, and this interpretation seems awkward and perhaps no one will accept it, it must instead be fitted to the nearer preceding words. We should read it as follows:

“There are many who are disobedient, empty talkers, and deceivers of minds, especially those of the circumcision. These many who are disobedient, empty talkers, and deceivers of minds, together with those of the circumcision, must be restrained. They overturn whole households, teaching things that ought not to be taught for the sake of shameful gain. One of them, their own prophet, said…”

Thus “their own prophet” does not refer specifically to the Jews, and especially to those of the circumcision, but to the many who are disobedient, empty talkers, and deceivers of minds. Since they were in Crete, they must certainly be believed to have been Cretans.

This verse is said to be found in the oracles of the Cretan poet Epimenides [Note: There is no doubt that the Apostle used Epimenides’ statement. But the account handed down by the holy Father—that Epimenides was perhaps called a prophet because he wrote about oracles, and that the verse was taken from the book entitled *Oracles*—is supported by Socrates, book 3, chapter 16, and Nicephorus, book 10, chapter 26. Perhaps it is also supported at the beginning of the first volume of Lucian’s Scholia: “Epimenides was a Cretan, an interpreter of oracles, and his is also the saying, ‘Cretans are always liars.’” Many ancient authors attributed prophetic powers to Epimenides: Plato, *Laws*, book 2; Aristotle, *Rhetoric*, book 6, chapter 17; Plutarch, *Solon*; Laertius, book 1; and others. Apuleius, *Florida*, book 2, calls Epimenides a famous epic poet, a Cretan by nationality. His fellow citizens reported many marvelous things about him, though mixed with fables, as Laertius and Cicero, *On Divination*, book 1, attest; thus he was regarded as a prophet, foreknowing future events.]

Whether in the present passage he called him a prophet mockingly or allusively [Al. “alluding”]—namely, because such Christians deserved to have such prophets, just as there were prophets of Baal, prophets of confusion, and others associated with offenses, as well as all the vicious prophets mentioned by Scripture—or truly, because he wrote about oracles and responses that themselves foretold the future and announced beforehand things that were to come.

In any event, the book itself bears the title *Oracles*. Because it appeared to promise something divine, I think that the Apostle examined it in order to see what the divination of the Gentiles promised, and then made use of the verse at the appropriate time when writing to Titus, who was in Crete, so that he might convict the false teachers of the Cretans by their own island’s teacher. [Note: Two Cistercian manuscripts read, “it mattered by the author of his own island.”]

Paul is found to have done this not only here but also elsewhere. In the Acts of the Apostles, when he was addressing the people and disputing in the Areopagus, which is the court of the Athenians, he said among other things: “As some of your own poets have said: ‘For we are indeed his offspring’” (Acts 17:28). This half-line is found in Aratus’ *Phenomena*, which Cicero translated into Latin, as did Caesar Germanicus, the more recent Avienus, and many others whose names it would take too long to list.

To the Corinthians also (1 Cor. 15:33), who themselves had been polished by Attic eloquence and, because of the nearness of their region, had been imbued with Athenian refinement, he took an iambic verse from Menander’s comedy:

“Bad conversations corrupt good morals.”

Nor is it surprising that he used the verses of Gentile poets as the occasion required, since, changing something in the inscription of an altar, he also spoke to the Athenians:

“As I passed through your city and observed the objects of your worship, I found also an altar on which was inscribed: ‘To an unknown god.’ What you worship without knowing, this I proclaim to you.”

The inscription on the altar was not, however, exactly as Paul asserted—“To an unknown god”—but rather:

“To the gods of Asia, Europe, and Africa; to unknown and foreign gods.”

[Note: Recent critics have discussed this question concerning the true Athenian inscription in very substantial dissertations, which the reader would do well to consult. Nevertheless, so that no one may regret the omission of what Victorius noted here, I shall append it. “Clement of Alexandria,” he says, “in the first book of the *Stromata*, writes that Paul used a tragic iamb when he said, Φθείρουσιν ἤθη χρηστὰ ὁμιλίαι κακαί—‘Bad company corrupts good morals.’ Jerome likewise writes that the iamb was taken from Menander’s comedy. It is similarly established that the statement Paul uses in Acts 17 was taken from Aratus’ *Phenomena*: ‘As some of your poets have said: For we are indeed his offspring’—τοῦ γὰρ καὶ γένος ἐσμέν, says Aratus. The words Κρῆτες ἀεὶ ψεῦσται, κακὰ θηρία, γαστέρες ἀργαί—‘Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies’—belong to the poet Epimenides, as Jerome learnedly writes, and were also used by Callimachus. As for the altar ἀγνώστῳ Θεῷ, ‘To an unknown god,’ it is clear not only from the Acts of the Apostles but also from Diogenes Laertius’ life of Epimenides that one was erected by the Athenians. Diogenes’ words are these:

‘Therefore, when the Athenians were once suffering from a plague, and received an oracle from the Pythia that the city ought to be purified, they sent Nicias, son of Niceratus, by ship and summoned Epimenides from Crete. He set out in the twenty-seventh Olympiad, purified the city, and checked the plague in this way: he took sheep with black and white fleeces, led them to the Areopagus, and then allowed them to go wherever they wished, instructing those who followed them to sacrifice each sheep, wherever it lay down, to some particular god. In this way the plague ceased. From that time to the present, it is certain that altars without names can be found throughout the Athenian districts, as a memorial of that purification.’

This does not mean that what Jerome reports should be called false—namely, that an altar had been erected with this inscription: ‘To the gods of Asia, Europe, and Africa; to unknown and foreign gods.’ It is clear that altars were established to unknown and foreign gods, and that the second inscription explains rather than destroys the first, especially since, among the many altars—which Diogenes makes clear were numerous—one could have borne the first inscription and another the second.”]

But because Paul did not need several unknown gods, but only one unknown God, he used the singular, so that he might teach that the God who was designated in the title of the altar by the Athenians was his own God, and that they ought rightly to worship knowingly the one whom they had worshiped unknowingly, whom they could not fail to know.

Paul did this rarely, and only when the appropriateness of the place, rather than display, required it, following the example of bees, which are accustomed to compose honey from various flowers and fit together the cells of their combs.

Some think that this verse was taken from Callimachus, the poet of Cyrene, and in part they are not mistaken. For when Callimachus was writing in praise of Jupiter against the Cretans, who boasted that they could show his tomb, he said:

“Cretans are always liars,”

for they had also fashioned his tomb with sacrilegious intent.

But, as we said above, the Apostle took the complete verse from the poet Epimenides, and Callimachus used it as the beginning of his own poem.

Alternatively, the Apostle may have rendered in meter a common proverb by which the Cretans were called deceitful, without stealing another’s work.

Some think that the Apostle should be criticized because he slipped through ignorance and, while reproving false teachers, approved that verse. They say [Al. “are said”] that the Cretans are called deceitful because they built an empty tomb for Jupiter.

For if, they argue, Epimenides or Callimachus called the Cretans deceitful, evil beasts, and lazy bellies because they had no perception of divine things and imagined that Jupiter, who reigns in heaven, had been buried on their island, and if the Apostle’s judgment confirms what they said, then it follows that Jupiter was not dead but alive.

Thus, through lack of skill, Paul—the destroyer of idolatry—while opposing perverse teachers, would have asserted the gods whom he was attacking.

They should be answered briefly in the same way as in the statements “Evil conversations [Al. ‘bad’] corrupt good morals” and “For we are indeed his offspring”: [Al. ‘and so’] Paul did not thereby approve the whole comedy of Menander or the entire book of Aratus, but made use of a verse when the occasion required. Likewise, in the present passage, he did not confirm the entire work of Callimachus or Epimenides—one of whom sings Jupiter’s praises and the other writes extensively about oracles—through a single verse. Rather, he rebuked the Cretans only for being liars as a national vice, not because of the opinion for which the poets criticized them, but because of their innate readiness to lie; and he refuted them by the testimony of their own national author.

Those who think that one must follow an entire book whenever one uses a part of it seem to me also to admit the apocryphal book of Enoch [Al. the apocryphal books of Enoch]—to which the Apostle Jude bears witness in his Epistle—among the Scriptures of the Church, as well as many other writings about which the Apostle Paul spoke from hidden sources.

By the same argument we could say that, since Paul declared that the Athenians worshiped an unknown god whom they had inscribed on an altar, he ought also to follow everything else written on the altar and do what the Athenians did, because he had agreed with them in part concerning the worship of an unknown god.

Far be it from me to turn an argument and scholastic elegance into a slander. No one is so murderous, so murderous toward his parents, or so poisonous that he has not at some time done something good. Therefore, if I see one good thing in someone and approve it, am I consequently obliged to approve whatever else in him is evil?

If an enemy brings charges against us and cries out, will he not say something true amid the words of hostility and quarrel—something that we too do not altogether reject, even though he is speaking against us?

Thus Callimachus and Epimenides did not thereby speak the truth about Jupiter’s being a god, or about the other matters contained in their poems, simply because the Cretans are deceitful. Rather, they spoke the truth only in expressing the Cretans’ innate vice of lying. Because the Cretans are deceitful, it does not follow that they never speak the truth.

Jupiter would not cease to be a god if the Cretans spoke the truth. Nevertheless, if they had remained silent about him, though he was dead, he would not have possessed the title of god.

Finally, so that we may know that the Apostle did not speak against the Cretans casually or in passing, as some suppose, but deliberately and carefully, protecting himself on every side, he says: “This testimony is true.” He does not mean the entire poem from which the testimony was taken, nor the whole work, but only this testimony, this verse in which they are called liars.

And certainly, whoever agreed with only one part of a poem must be understood to have rejected the rest.

We discussed in the Epistle of Paul to the Galatians how the Cretans are marked by their own vice as liars, the Galatians as foolish, Israel as stiff-necked, and each province by its particular fault.

Since we can add nothing further here, we are content with that discussion.

For this reason, he says, rebuke them sharply: for they are liars, evil beasts, and lazy bellies. They persuade others of falsehood; like wild animals, they thirst for the blood of those they deceive; and, rather than working quietly, they eat their own bread. Their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame. Rebuke them so that they may be sound in the faith.

He speaks of this soundness of faith in what follows:

“Older men are to be sober, honorable, chaste, sound in faith, love, and endurance.”

Doctrine is likewise called sound by analogy with sound faith.

“There will be a time,” he says [Al. “for”], “when they will not endure sound doctrine.”

There are also “words of health,” about which he speaks to Timothy in the First Epistle:

“If anyone teaches otherwise and does not assent to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and to the teaching that accords with piety” (1 Tim. 6:3).

And in the Second:

“Having the pattern of sound words that you have heard from me” (2 Tim. 1:13).

Those who possess this soundness of faith, doctrine, and words do not attend to Jewish myths and the commandments of people who turn away from the truth. [Note: In Martianay’s Hiulcus [reading uncertain], the sense is “not attending.” Immediately afterward, Cistercian manuscripts read “and the lies of men,” etc., for “commandments,” incorrectly.]

Let us for a little while listen patiently to the Jews and to the absurdities of those who are called wise among them. Then we shall understand what Jewish myths are [Al. “may be”]: inventions concerning certain animals and fables without the authority of Scripture or any assertion of reason.

Isaiah prophesied about them, saying:

“This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. In vain do they worship me, teaching doctrines and commandments of men” (Isa. 29:13).

The Savior confirms this testimony in the Gospel and accuses them of placing human commandments above the law of God. God says:

“Honor your father and your mother.”

But they have handed down this teaching:

“Whoever says to his father and mother, ‘Whatever gift is from me will benefit you,’ does not honor his father and mother” (Matt. 15:3–6).

If, after Christ’s coming, someone is mutilated rather than circumcised, he serves Jewish myths and the commandments of people who turn away from the truth [Al. “from truth”].

“For it is not the one who is a Jew outwardly, but the one who is a Jew inwardly; and circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter.”

If someone celebrates Passover not in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, so as to remove from his soul all the old leaven of malice and wickedness, he attends to myths and follows shadows while neglecting the truth.

If someone has not risen with Christ and does not seek the things above, but the things below, and says, “Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle” things that perish through use, he follows, according to the commandments and doctrines of men, regulations that are not good and commandments that are not good.

But where truth and the spiritual law are found, there are good ordinances and excellent commandments; whoever does them will live by them.

### (Verse 15)

“To the pure all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure; rather, both their mind and their conscience are defiled.”

Because he had said above:

“There are many who are disobedient, empty talkers, and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision,”

and, concerning those who had been deceived by them, had consequently added:

“Rebuke them sharply, so that they may be sound in the faith and not attend to Jewish myths and the commandments of people who turn away from the truth,”

and because, as is discussed most fully in Galatians and Romans, they thought there was a distinction among foods, with some appearing clean and others unclean, he now adds:

“All things are pure to the pure”—namely, to those who believe in Christ and know that every creature is good and that nothing is to be rejected when it is received with thanksgiving.

“But to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure,” because both their mind and their conscience are defiled. Therefore even things that are pure by nature become unclean for them.

This does not mean that something is intrinsically either clean or unclean. Rather, according to the quality of those who eat, what is clean becomes clean to the pure, and what is unclean becomes contaminated to the defiled.

Otherwise, even the bread of blessing and the Lord’s cup do not benefit unbelievers and defiled persons, because whoever eats that bread and drinks from the cup unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself (1 Cor. 11:29).

At Christ’s coming everything was purified. We cannot call common what he has cleansed.

But when discussing these matters, we must take care not to give an occasion to that heresy which, according to the Apocalypse and the Apostle Paul’s letter to the Corinthians, thinks that one ought to eat food sacrificed to idols, because “all things are pure to the pure” (1 Cor. 8).

The Apostle’s purpose here was not to discuss things sacrificed to demons, but to oppose Jews who, according to the discipline of the abolished Law, considered some things clean and others unclean.

“For,” he says, “we cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons, nor can we drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons” (1 Cor. 10:20–21).

It therefore depends on us whether we eat what is clean or what is unclean. If we are pure, creation is pure for us. But if we are unclean and unbelieving, everything becomes common to us [Col. 0576C], either because of the heresy dwelling in our hearts or because of the consciousness of our sins.

But if our conscience does not condemn us and we possess confidence in piety toward the Lord, we shall pray with the spirit and pray also with the mind; we shall sing psalms with the spirit and sing psalms also with the mind (1 Cor. 14:15). We shall be far from those of whom it is now written:

“Both their mind and their conscience are defiled.”

### (Verse 16)

“They profess to know God, but they deny him by their deeds; they are detestable, disobedient, and unfit for every good work.”

Those whose mind and conscience are defiled profess to know God, but deny him by their deeds, according to what is said in Isaiah:

“This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29:13).

Therefore, just as someone honors with his lips but withdraws far away in his heart, so someone who confesses God in speech denies him by his works.

Whoever denies God by his deeds is rightly detestable and profane through his false confession. Since he is persuaded by no principle of truth, he is called disobedient and unbelieving.

Consequently, he is unfit for every good work. Even if, perhaps overcome by natural goodness, he performs things that are good, they are not good, since they are rejected by the perversity of his mind.

Some think that God is denied only if someone, seized by the Gentiles during persecution, refuses to acknowledge himself a Christian [Al. one manuscript adds “to be”]. But the Apostle declares that God is denied by every perverse deed.

Christ is wisdom, justice, truth, holiness, and strength. Wisdom is denied through folly, justice through iniquity, truth through falsehood, holiness through disgrace, and strength through weakness of spirit. Whenever we are overcome by vices and sins, we deny God.

Conversely [Al. “And conversely”], whenever we do something good, we confess God.

Nor should we think that on the day of judgment the Son of God will deny only those who denied Christ in martyrdom. Through every work, word, and thought, Christ either denies those who deny him or confesses those who confess him.

I think that it is concerning this confession that he also commanded the disciples, saying:

“You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth” (Acts 1:8),

so that in every good work and word the mind devoted to Christ might confess him.

There is also a praiseworthy denial, about which the Apostle himself says:

“Denying ungodliness and worldly desires, let us live soberly, justly, and piously in the present age, awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of our great God and Savior” (Titus 2:12–13).

Whoever undertakes this denial and wishes to follow the Savior, who says, “Whoever will wish [Al. ‘wishes’] to come after me, let him deny himself” (Luke 9:23), stripping off the old person with his works and putting on the new, will follow his God.

How one should deny oneself must be considered. The chaste denies the fornicator he formerly was; the wise denies the foolish; the just, the unjust; the strong, the weak.

To speak generally of all things, we deny ourselves whenever, trampling upon our former vices, we cease to be what we were and begin to be what we previously were not.

### Chapter 2, Verse 1

“But you must speak what accords with sound doctrine.”

It is one thing to speak sound doctrine and another to teach what accords with sound doctrine. In the first case there is only simple instruction; in the second, together with teaching, there is also correction of life.

“For whoever loosens one of these least commandments and teaches people to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:19).

The Lord commands the disciples not merely to labor in meditation upon the Scriptures, repeating what has been written and storing it in the treasury of memory, but first to do what has been commanded.

“Whoever does and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.”

Unless our righteousness surpasses the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, we cannot enter the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 5).

They sit upon Moses’ seat, say things but do not do them, and tie up burdens that cannot be carried, placing them on people’s shoulders, while they themselves do not wish to touch them even with a finger.

The Apostle now teaches Titus, his son in Christ and his disciple, to speak what accords with sound doctrine, because doctrine is sound when the teacher’s doctrine and life agree with one another.

### (Verse 2.) 

“Older men are to be sober, dignified, temperate, sound in faith, love, and endurance.”

Having first generally instructed Titus concerning what he himself ought to say to everyone, when he says, “But you, speak what accords with sound doctrine,” he now explains, according to each category, what is fitting for every age. [Note: MSS.: “what is fitting for each age,” etc.] 714 First, what is suitable for elderly men; then, what is fitting for old women; third, what is appropriate for young women and young men alike. Although, in the command concerning old women, he has inserted instructions about young women, he did so not so much to teach the young women himself as to explain what they should be taught by the old women. Finally, concerning slaves, and concerning each age and social condition, he establishes his commands so appropriately that his discourse becomes a rule for life and conduct.

The older men, then, are to be sober [Note: Victorius adds, “he commands.”], or watchful, because among the Greeks νηφάλιοι (*nēphalioi*) has both meanings: dignified, so that the gravity of their age may be adorned by gravity of character; temperate, lest they indulge in the pleasures of another age, and, though their blood is already cold for lust, become an example leading young men to ruin.

“Sound in faith”—concerning the soundness of faith we have spoken above. But they are to be sound not only in faith, but also in love and endurance, so that, once they have possessed the first soundness of faith, they may hear from the Savior: “Your faith has saved you” (Mark 10:52). And elsewhere: “I have not found such faith even in Israel” (Matthew 8:10). Because of this same soundness of faith, let them become sons of Abraham, of whom it is written: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:8). And Habakkuk, speaking of this soundness of faith, says: “But the righteous lives [Al.: will live] by my faith” (Habakkuk 2:3).

Read again the Epistle of the Apostle Paul to the Hebrews—or, if you think it belongs to some other author, since it has already been received among the ecclesiastical writings [Note: He seems to have held a different view in the *Catalogue*, at chapter 5: “The Epistle that is called ‘to the Hebrews’ is not believed to be his [Paul’s], because of the difference in style and language; rather, according to Tertullian, it is by Barnabas; according to some, by Luke the Evangelist; or by Clement, later bishop of the Roman Church, whom they say, as Paul’s associate, arranged and adorned Paul’s thoughts in his own language. Or certainly, because Paul was writing to the Hebrews and, on account of the hostility toward his name among them, omitted the title at the beginning of the greeting. Compare what we have noted concerning that passage, along with many others that we now omit.”]—and enumerate that entire catalogue of faith, in which it is written: “By faith Abel offered God a greater sacrifice than Cain” (Hebrews 11:4 and following). Also: “Enoch was taken away, so that he would not see death”; and Noah, believing God concerning things he did not yet see, built an ark; and Abraham departed for a land he did not know.

And lest Scripture seem to provide no example of faith among women, the same Epistle says that Sarah also received strength to conceive offspring when she was already beyond the proper time of life, because she considered him faithful who had promised. The faith of Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, Rahab, and the others is also praised there; these are better known to one who reads the Epistle itself.

Just as soundness is found in faith, so the same soundness is found in love. Who possesses soundness of love except the one who first loves God with all his soul, with all his heart, and with all his strength? Then, hearing Christ’s command concerning his neighbor—“You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 5)—he divides his love accordingly, because “on these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets.”

Whoever possesses soundness of love is not jealous, is not arrogant, does not act wrongly or dishonorably, is not provoked to anger, does not devise evil, does not rejoice [Al.: rejoice together] over iniquity, but rejoices with the truth; he bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things (1 Corinthians 13). And because love never fails, whoever is sound in love never himself falls.

Indeed, neither tribulation, nor distress, nor famine, nor persecution, nor nakedness, nor danger, nor the sword can separate him from the soundness of love that he possesses in Christ Jesus. Why speak of the sword and the lesser things, which cannot divide the one who possesses the soundness of love, when neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature can separate the one who possesses the soundness of love in Christ Jesus?

If we have understood the soundness of love, let us take from the Scriptures an example of those who are weak in love. The Savior says concerning the last times: “Because lawlessness will have increased, the love of many will grow cold” (Matthew 24:12). Love is warm in those who burn in spirit; but it is cold, icy, and frozen in those who have received the harshest blasts of the north wind. “From the north evil will blaze forth upon all who dwell in the land” (Jeremiah 1:14). Because of this coldness of love, Amnon also grew cold toward his sister Tamar (2 Samuel 13).

We must therefore fear lest we too should at some time be overcome by this weakness of love. For it sometimes happens that at first our affection for a virgin, or for any woman, is holy; but when the mind has been softened into emotional attachment, the soundness of love gradually grows pale through sickness, begins to weaken, and brings the one who loves to final death.

Therefore the Apostle carefully and prudently commands Timothy to exhort young women “in all purity” (1 Timothy 5:2). All purity is purity of flesh, spirit, and soul: lest the eye be scandalized; lest, clinging to the beauty of a woman’s face, we remain fascinated [Al.: lavish attention]; lest it please us to hear flattering words; lest the mind, previously firm, should first wither under simulated speech. Let young men and old men alike, young women and old women alike, beware, as we have said, and guard their hearts with every diligence, lest through the soundness of affection the disease of love enter, and through holy love an unholy affection arise that drags them to Gehenna.

Whoever is sound in faith, and sound in love, must also be sound in endurance—and endurance is especially proved in temptations. For it is of no benefit to have possessed all the things listed above unless all the wealth and merchandise with which the ship is laden are preserved in the storm, and, while winds blow from every direction, what has been rightly acquired is brought safely through without shipwreck. “The one who endures to the end will be saved” (Matthew 24:13).

### (Verses 3 and following.)

“Old women likewise are to be reverent in demeanor, not slanderers, not enslaved to much wine; they are to teach what is good, so that they may train the young women to love their husbands, to love their children, to be temperate, chaste, managing their households well, kind, submissive to their husbands, so that the word of God may not be blasphemed.”

Although the Apostle Peter commanded that husbands should give honor to their wives as to a weaker vessel, it must not therefore be supposed that a wife, who possesses a weaker bodily vessel, is immediately weaker in soul as well. Hence they are now commanded that in them too the Apostle’s statement should be fulfilled: “Power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). They are told also to possess everything commanded generally to older men, in the words, “Old women likewise”—that is, just as older men are to be honorable, sober, temperate, sound in faith, love, and endurance in all things—and, according to their sex, to possess this distinctive quality: that they be reverent in demeanor, or, as it is better read in Greek, ἐν καταστήματι ἱεροπρεπεῖς (*en katastēmati hieroprepeis*), “reverent in sacred deportment,” so that their very bearing and movements, their face, speech, and silence, may display a certain dignity of sacred propriety.

And because this class of little women is usually talkative, in accordance with the saying: “At the same time they learn to go about from house to house—not only idle, but also talkative and inquisitive, saying things they ought not” (1 Timothy 5:13), he therefore wishes them not to be slanderers—that is, not accusers, not women who, in order to please others, speak evil of others.

Or perhaps, since they themselves have already passed beyond youth, they may discuss the ages of young women and say: “That one dresses herself in this way; that one adorns herself in that way; this is how she goes out; she loves that man, and is loved by him.” Yet even if these things are true, they ought not so much to accuse the young women before others as to correct them privately in the love of Christ, and to teach them not to do such things rather than publicly accuse them of having done them.

[Note: Earlier printed books make no sense of this passage; they read: “These ages are accustomed, because they have cooled the lust of the body (although very many are not ashamed even of their gray hairs and, before a flock of grandchildren, arrange themselves as trembling little girls), to give themselves over to wine,” etc. We have taken care, on the authority of manuscript exemplars, to restore the sense and wording. MART.] These ages are accustomed, because they have worn away the lust of the body [Al.: lust]—although very many are not ashamed even of their gray hairs and, before a flock of grandchildren, arrange themselves as trembling little girls [Note: Martianus inserts the little word “thus” here; once introduced, it entirely destroys the charm and force of Jerome’s thought. The holy Father, jokingly and ironically, calls “trembling little girls” those old women who polish their aged wrinkles and, while making themselves up like young women, tremble from age. He ridicules such women in exactly the same words in Letter 38, *On the Illness of Blesilla*, to Marcella, no. 3: “who, finally, before a flock of grandchildren, arrange themselves as trembling little girls,” etc.]—to give themselves over to wine for lust. And when, amid their cups, they have seemed wise and eloquent to themselves, they assume a kind of austerity of character, saying what they themselves imagine themselves to be, and not remembering what they once were.

Let old women therefore be prohibited from excessive drinking of wine, since what lust is in the young, drunkenness is in the old. Or how can an old woman teach young women chastity if, should a young woman imitate the drunkenness of an old woman, she cannot remain temperate?

He expressly [Note: Two manuscripts read: “He expressly and explicitly says: ‘Not enslaved to much wine.’”] emphasized: “Not enslaved to much wine.” For it is a kind of slavery, indeed the lowest condition, for a person’s senses to be occupied by wine, so that he belongs not to himself but to wine.

Since, therefore, he first taught what kind of women the old women ought to be, and then explained what they have in common with older men, he also set out their particular qualities: that they should be filled with honorable and holy conduct and every propriety, neither slanderers nor detractors, and not have their senses occupied by wine. Now, consistently with his teaching, he gives them permission to teach, so that, when they are such women, they may have the freedom to teach—namely, to teach what is good.

Although he said elsewhere, “I do not permit women to teach” (1 Timothy 2:12), this must be understood as meaning that teaching men is withheld from them. Otherwise, they should teach young women as their own daughters. First, chastity, because the enemy fights against it most fiercely in the flowering period of life, and all his power against women is directed toward the navel of the belly; then, that they should love their husbands and love their children.

What kind of instruction is it to love husbands, when this is established not in the speech of the teacher but in the heart of the one who loves? He wishes them to love their husbands chastely; he wishes there to be a modest affection between husband and wife, so that, with modesty, shame, and as though compelled by the necessity of sex, she may render the debt to her husband rather than demand it from him, and may believe that she is carrying out the work of producing children before the eyes of God and the angels; [Note: In Erasmus’s edition we read: “so that she too may be ashamed,” etc.; Marianus corrects this by changing *erubescet* to *erubescat*: “so that she may be ashamed.” “Thus,” he says, “she should devote herself honorably and chastely to the begetting of children, so that she may do nothing disgraceful even in the marriage chamber, and for that reason be ashamed of it.” Some, however, think that it should rather be read affirmatively, in this form: “Thus she too will be ashamed even of the secret marriage chamber.” That is, if she always has God before her eyes, she will be ashamed to do anything dishonorable or immodest even in the privacy of the marriage chamber.] so that she will not be ashamed even of the secret marriage chamber, the darkness of night, and her closed room, when she considers that everything lies open to the eyes of God.

They love their children, moreover, if they educate them in the discipline of God. But to refuse to distress them by teaching what is good, and to grant them freedom to sin, is not to love their children but to hate them.

The young women are also to be trained to manage their households well. And because it could happen that household management would be conducted harshly, and that through this command of the Apostle the matron might become more severe toward her servants, he therefore added “kind,” so that she would consider herself to be governing her husband’s household well only if she commanded her servants with kindness, not with terror. [Note: Perhaps one Cistercian manuscript reads more truly: “if she obtained this from her servants by kindness, not by terror.”]

And also “submissive to their husbands,” lest, puffed up by wealth and nobility, they forget God’s sentence by which they are subject to their husbands. For he says to the woman: “Your turning shall be toward your husband [Note: Two of our manuscripts omit the word “your,” although it belongs to the sacred text.], and he shall rule over you” (Genesis 3:16).

Here the wisdom of Holy Scripture must be considered: the Lord did not say this to the man, saying, “You shall rule over your wife,” but to the woman herself, leaving her the reward of obedience. For it lies within her power, if she wishes to obey God’s commands, to serve her husband and be subject to him, so that in a certain sense her servitude may be free and full of love. Thus she serves her husband while fearing to offend him.

For the man was not created because of the woman, but the woman because of the man. And since the man is the head of the woman, while Christ is the head of the man, any wife who is not subject to her husband—that is, to her head—is guilty of the same offense as a man who is not subject to Christ, his head.

But the word of the Lord is blasphemed either when God’s original sentence is despised and treated as nothing, or [Note: Victorinus supplies, “or when Christ is defamed,” etc.] when the Gospel of Christ is brought into disrepute, while she who is a Christian and, according to God’s law, subject to her husband, desires to rule over him contrary to the law and faith of nature—although even pagan women serve their husbands according to the common law of nature.

### (Verses 6 and following.)

“Likewise exhort young men to be temperate in all things, presenting yourself as an example of good works, in doctrine, in integrity and chastity, in sound and irreproachable speech, so that the one who is opposed may be put to shame, having nothing evil to say about us.”

Just as, in what he commanded above—saying, “Old women likewise in reverent demeanor”—we said that the likeness of the old women was to be referred to the older men, so now, in what he adds, “Exhort young men likewise to be temperate,” we think that the likeness of the young men is to be applied to the old women and, through the old women, to the older men. Thus they are to possess the sobriety of the old men, and to be honorable, temperate, sound in faith, love, and endurance.

As for the old women, they are to possess holiness of demeanor [Al.: holiness in demeanor], so that they are not accusers, are not enslaved to much wine, teach what is good, and so forth.

He made this the particular quality of young men: that they should be temperate in all things—that is, in mind as well as body, in deed as well as thought—so that there be no suspicion of disgrace in a young man.

Although some [Note: Here too two of our manuscripts omit the words “among the Latins”; nevertheless, the distinction of sense rejected by the holy Father still prevails today.] Latin writers think it should be read as follows: “Likewise exhort young men to be temperate,” and then continue, “in all things presenting yourself as a model of good works,” we should know that “in all things” is to be referred to what comes before: that is, “exhort them to be temperate in all things.”

It should also be understood that self-restraint is necessary not only in the activity of the flesh and the desires of the mind, but in all matters: that we should not seek undeserved honors, should not be inflamed by greed, and should not be overcome by any passion.

“Presenting yourself,” he says, “as a model of good works.” It is of no benefit for someone to be practiced in speaking and to have worn out his tongue through talking, unless he teaches more by example than by word.

Accordingly, an immodest man, however eloquent he may be, if he exhorts his hearers to chastity, has a weak speech and possesses no authority to exhort. Conversely, however uncultivated and slow in speech he may be, if he is chaste, he can by his example urge people toward a likeness of his life.

What he says, “in incorruption,” is to be understood as meaning that *incorruption* properly signifies virginity. Thus those who are virgins are commonly called “uncorrupted,” while those who have ceased to be virgins are called “corrupted”; and we say of a woman who was formerly a virgin, “She has been corrupted.”

For this reason I think that Titus, before he was occupied with the work of the flesh, received baptism as a believer in the Gospel, remained a virgin, and is now admonished by the Apostle to present himself as a model in incorruption. Yet [Note: The interpolated Epistle of St. Ignatius to the Philadelphians, and the monk Antiochus in Homily 112, nevertheless reckon Timothy himself among virgins—not to mention that Theophylact, Oecumenius, and others interpret ἐν ἁγνείᾳ, “in chastity” (1 Timothy 4:12), as referring to virginity.] we do not find this same incorruption in Timothy. For when he said to him, “Let no one despise your youth, but be an example of the believers [Al.: sons] in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in chastity” (1 Timothy 4:12), he said nothing about incorruption and mentioned only chastity.

Chastity, however, can be understood even in celibacy without virginity. Unless perhaps we take chastity to refer to the mind and incorruption to the body, in accordance with what is written elsewhere in the definition of a virgin: “that she may be holy in body and spirit” (1 Corinthians 7:34).

And now he likewise adds: “in doctrine, in incorruption, in chastity.” We could [Al.: We can] also interpret “chastity” [Note: Victorinus rewrites the passage: “and the incorruption of chastity even in the integrity of doctrine,” etc.] and “incorruption” as referring to integrity in doctrine, except that what follows—“in sound and irreproachable speech”—has a specific command concerning the instruction of doctrine.

When he says “irreproachable speech,” he does not mean that anyone possesses such eloquence and wisdom that no one finds fault with him—for even the apostles and evangelists are criticized by heretics and pagans—but that he should say or do nothing deserving of criticism, even though adversaries are ready to criticize.

And because there are many who are insubordinate, empty talkers, and deceivers of minds, who hate the one who reproves at the gate and abominate holy speech, let us therefore present ourselves as an example in all things: in doctrine, in integrity, 721 in chastity, and in sound and irreproachable speech. Thus, terrified by the soundness of our life and teaching, our adversaries will not dare to accuse us—that is, to fabricate anything plausible in their accusation.

And indeed, even to this day we see certain people in the churches—although such a rare bird is seldom found—possessing such gravity and self-restraint that they even receive testimony from their adversaries, who say: “That man is great, and of holy conduct and honorable character—if only he were not a heretic.”

For no one is so immoderately shameless that he can accuse the rays of the sun of darkness or cast the obscurity of night over bright light. Hence the Apostle, taking precautions against these things, says: “So that I may remove the opportunity from those who desire an opportunity” (2 Corinthians 11:12). [Note: Martianus reads this with the opposite and false meaning: “so that I may offer an opportunity,” and also incorrectly cites 1 Corinthians 7:11.]

But “the one who is opposed” may also be understood as the devil, who is the accuser of our brothers, as the Evangelist John proclaims. When he has nothing evil to bring against us, he is put to shame, and the accuser cannot accuse. The devil, moreover, in the Latin language means “accuser.”

### (Verses 9–10.)

“Slaves are to be submissive to their masters in everything; they are to be pleasing, not argumentative, not stealing, but showing complete and genuine fidelity, so that in everything they may adorn the doctrine of God our Savior.”

Since our Lord and Savior, who says in the Gospel, “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28), considers no social condition, age, or sex to be excluded from blessedness, the Apostle therefore now establishes commands for slaves as well, since they are part of the Church and members of Christ’s body.

And just as above he taught what Titus ought to teach older men, old women, young women, and young men, so now he establishes commands appropriate to slaves.

First, that they should be submissive to their masters in everything. This means in all things that are not contrary to God: if a master commands things that are not opposed to the Holy Scriptures, the slave should submit to his master. But if he commands things contrary to them, the spirit should obey rather than the master of the body.

Pay close attention to how he assigns commands suited to the persons concerned. “Slaves,” he says, “are to be submissive to their masters in everything” (Ephesians 6:5). Elsewhere, discussing children, he says: “Children, obey your parents” (Colossians 3:20). It is fitting for children to obey their parents; but slaves are to be subject to the master who commands them.

Nor should we think it contradictory that in another Epistle he says, “Women are to be subject to their husbands” (Ephesians 5:22; Colossians 3:18), and in this one he likewise asserts that wives are subject to their husbands, as though he had used the same word concerning slaves and wives. In a certain sense, a husband is the lord of his wife. “He himself,” it says, “shall rule over you” (Genesis 3:16).

The Savior too was subject to his parents (Luke 2), but he was still twelve years old [Note: Two of our manuscripts prefer “eleven”], and, being not yet different from a slave, he was nevertheless Lord of all; for he had not yet reached the full age of manhood at which he could receive the inheritance.

But elsewhere it is also written concerning him: “When all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:28). All things will be subjected to him when he says: “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet” (Psalm 109:1).

Among subjected slaves, the Lord is subjected. And just as he is said to have become a curse for us, although he is not a curse but a true blessing, so for us he is written either as subject or as not subject, according as we are subject or not subject to God.

Some read this passage as follows: “Slaves are to be submissive to their masters,” stopping there, and then continue: “in everything let them be pleasing.” But in Greek the order of reading is different: “Slaves are to be submissive to their masters in everything,” followed by εὐαρέστους εἶναι (*euarestous einai*), which we can translate, though not fully, at least in part as “to be pleasing to themselves”—namely, so that they may not appear to regard God’s judgment concerning their condition as unjust.

But just as a poor person can be saved according to his measure, and a woman is not excluded from the kingdom of God because of the weakness of her sex, and every condition can attain blessedness according to its proper order, so slaves too should be pleased that they are slaves. They should not think that they cannot serve God because they are subject to human beings; rather, they should wish to please God’s will all the more by being submissive to their masters in everything and by being content with their condition.

They should then carry out what the Apostle commands next: that they are not to be argumentative or stealing. One of the greatest vices of slaves is to contradict their masters and, when they have been ordered to do something, to mutter among themselves. Titus therefore warns that through sound teaching he should remove this passion from Christian slaves.

If a slave necessarily has to carry out what his master commands, why should he not do that same thing willingly, rather than offend his master and nevertheless do what he is ordered to do—especially since God was offended even by the water of contradiction? Elsewhere, speaking of the murmuring people, he says: “Let their murmuring cease from me, and they shall not die” (Numbers 14:27).

After contradiction, let the teaching of Christ correct another vice of slaves, so that they do not steal. A thief is judged not only in great matters but also in small ones. For it is not merely what has been taken by theft that is considered, but the mind of the thief.

Just as in fornication and adultery the offense is not different because the woman is beautiful or wealthy, ugly or poor, a prostitute or an adulteress, but, whatever she may be, it is one fornication or one adultery, so also in theft: however much a slave may have taken, he incurs the crime of theft.

Hence, under the law of Moses, thieves are sometimes compelled to repay sevenfold, sometimes fourfold; at times the thief himself is put to death, and at times he is sold because of the theft. I remember recently explaining these matters to you in Leviticus.

But if this is prohibited in a slave, how much more in a free person, lest a judge rob or a soldier, not content with his pay, devastate what belongs to others?

A certain exceptionally grave man made a fine reply when someone praised the integrity of a particular judge and said of him, “He is not a thief.” He answered, “He would make an excellent slave if he were not also a runaway.” So far should suspicion of theft be removed from every free person.

Let slaves, then, be submissive to their masters in everything; let them be content with their condition, so that they do not bear slavery bitterly, do not contradict their masters, and do not steal; and after this, let them show genuine fidelity in everything, so that they may adorn the doctrine of God our Savior in everything.

For if they are faithful in small matters before earthly masters, greater things will begin to be entrusted to them by God. The person who does what is suited to his condition adorns the Lord’s doctrine. Conversely, the one who is not submissive in everything, whose condition displeases him, and who in nothing shows genuine fidelity by contradiction and fraud, brings that doctrine into disgrace.

For how can one be faithful in the things belonging to God who has not been able to show fidelity to an earthly master?

### 724 (Verses 12ff.)

“For the grace of God our Savior has appeared to all people, instructing us to renounce ungodliness and worldly desires, and to live temperately, justly, and devoutly in this present age, awaiting the blessed hope and the manifestation of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us in order to redeem us from all iniquity and to cleanse for himself a special people, zealous for good works.”

After the catalogue of instruction that he ought to give Titus concerning old men, old women, young women and young men, and finally slaves, he has now rightly added: “For the grace of God our Savior has appeared to all people.” There is no distinction between free and slave, Greek and barbarian, circumcised and uncircumcised, woman and man; rather, we are all one in Christ, we are all called to the kingdom of God, and after our offense we are all to be reconciled to our Father—not through our merits, but through the grace of the Savior. [Note: One Cistercian manuscript reads, “we have been reconciled.”]

Alternatively, this may mean that Christ himself is the living and subsisting grace of God the Father; or that this grace belongs to Christ, God and Savior, and that we have been saved not through our own merit, in accordance with what is said elsewhere: “You will save them for nothing” (Psalm 55:8 [56:8]). This grace therefore appeared to all people in order to instruct us to renounce ungodliness and worldly desires and to live temperately, justly, and devoutly in this present age.

What it means to renounce ungodliness and worldly desires, I am confident can be understood from what we explained above: “They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him”; and the contrary may be argued from the contrary. Worldly desires, then, are those suggested by the ruler of this world; and since they belong to the age, they pass away together with the cloud of this age.

But when we have lived in Christ temperately and justly, sinning neither in body nor in mind, we shall also live devoutly in this age. This devotion awaits the blessed hope and the manifestation of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ. For just as ungodliness dreads the coming of the great God, so devotion, secure in its conduct and faith, awaits him expectantly.

Where is the serpent Arius? Where is the snake Eunomius? Jesus Christ, the great God, is called Savior—not “the firstborn of all creation,” not “the Word of God and Wisdom,” but Jesus Christ. These titles belong to the man assumed by him. Nor do we say that Jesus Christ and the Word are two different beings, as the new heresy slanderously claims. Rather, we call the same one who existed before the ages and after the ages, before the world and after Mary—indeed, from Mary—the great God, our Savior Jesus Christ. He gave himself for us so that by his precious blood he might redeem us from all iniquity and cleanse for himself a people **περιούσιον** (*periousion*, “special,” “peculiar”—so it is found in Greek), making them zealous for good works.

Often considering with myself what the word **περιούσιον** might mean, and asking the learned men of this age whether they had perhaps read it anywhere, I could never find anyone who would explain to me what it signified. Therefore I was compelled to turn to the Old Testament, from which I supposed that the Apostle had also taken what he said. For, being a Hebrew of Hebrews and a Pharisee according to the Law, he would certainly have placed in his Epistle what he had read in the Old Testament.

In Deuteronomy, then, I found: “For you are a holy people to the Lord your God, and the Lord your God was pleased with you, so that you might be for him a people **περιούσιον**, from all the peoples who are upon the face of the earth” (Deuteronomy 7:6). And in Psalm 134, where we have: “Sing to his name, for it is good; for the Lord chose Jacob for himself, Israel as his possession” (Psalm 134:3–4), in place of “as his possession” the Greek reads **εἰς περιουσιασμόν** (“for possession”). Aquila and the Fifth Edition rendered this **εἰς περιούσιον**. The Septuagint and Theodotion, however, translating it as **περιουσιασμόν**, changed the syllable but not the meaning.

Symmachus therefore rendered the Hebrew word corresponding to the Greek **περιούσιον** as **SGOLLA** [Hebrew *segullah*], expressing it with **ἐξαίρετον**, that is, “special” or “excellent.” In another Latin volume he interpreted the word as *peculiarem* (“peculiar” or “special”).

[**Note:** In several manuscripts we read here *sogola* or *sogolla*; but in one particularly fine and ancient manuscript I found *regula* written instead of *segula*. The ancients, moreover, used *o* and *ou* interchangeably, or *u* and *ou*; hence *sogola* for *segula*, and *segolla* for *segulla*. Similarly, *Sodoma* occurs for *Sedoma*, as we have said elsewhere. **MART.**—The manuscripts have *sogolla*, just as, toward the end, we said it is found in Matthew 6 and Malachi 3. Martianay, however, who had read *sgolla* in the passages cited, here preferred *segula* on the basis of a single manuscript, in which it was nevertheless written incorrectly as *regula*. From this testimony of Jerome, the renderings of the Fifth Edition, Theodotion, and Symmachus must be supplied in the Hexapla; these had escaped the notice of the distinguished Montfaucon, their recent editor.]

[**Note:** The reading that has hitherto prevailed in all books, *peculiarem*, has plainly caused the most learned interpreters no small difficulty. Some—including especially Hody, who deserves particular praise in his *History of the Ancient Interpretations of Scripture*, p. 587—conclude from it that some work, or some book of Scripture, had been explained in Latin by Symmachus. Others, on the contrary, understand what the holy Father says, using the Latin language, as though he had said “the Latin translator,” and had meant the ancient Vulgate translator. Fabricius, to mention here also a recent writer, prefers this view in volume 2 of his *Bibliotheca Graeca*, p. 339.

It should not, I think, require much demonstration to show how far both interpretations are from the truth and from every appearance of probability. Who could persuade himself that a man entirely ignorant of Latin, a Samaritan by birth and religion, later a Jew and finally an Ebionite, had composed something in Latin? Or what empty verbosity and impropriety of language would it be to call someone using the Latin tongue the author of the Vulgate translation? Yet if the received reading is retained, one can scarcely find a satisfactory sense in which to explain it.

I shall therefore say by what method I would cleanse the passage of its corruption. If three little letters, which the ignorance of Latin scribes added, are removed, the meaning of the holy Doctor can be restored clearly and correctly. It has long been settled in my mind that this passage concerns no other language than that of the ancient Greek translator Symmachus, as the entire context makes clear.

What, then, was that “other volume” in which he had used, as Jerome says, a Latin expression in translating? Since, apart from the examples already cited, the word *SGOLLA* occurs nowhere else except Ecclesiastes 2:8, we were certain that this was the very book whose name the holy Doctor suppresses.

When we learned—and the Scholia of the Roman edition of the Septuagint, or the fragments of ancient versions annotated by Flaminius, taught us this—that in that passage Symmachus rendered the word as **πεκούλια**, *peculia*, the corrupted reading that had been suspected in Jerome’s text, together with the genuine sense that ought to be restored, immediately came to mind.

That is, if instead of *peculiarem*—a word that no one could persuade himself had been used by any Greek writer—you write **πεκουλία**, or, if you prefer, *peculia* in Latin letters, everything becomes clear. *Peculium* is a Latin word whose meaning is so broad that it denotes any possessions whatsoever: patrimony, wealth, income, resources, fortunes, household goods, estates, and more besides.

I do not know whether there is any Greek word that corresponds to it equally well, except perhaps **τὰ χρήματα** or **τὰ ὑπάρχοντα** (“possessions” or “things belonging to someone”). It could easily have passed from Latium into Greece, been adopted by Greek writers, and been inflected according to the vernacular ending, just as the lexicons compiled by more recent grammarians represent it: **πεκούλιον, οὐσία**.

The word also suited Symmachus when translating the passage in Ecclesiastes where the speaker says that, after silver and gold, he gathered for himself the possessions of kings. Where the Septuagint had rendered this **περιουσιασμοὺς βασιλέων** (“possessions of kings”), Symmachus, attending more closely to the subject matter and to the Hebrew sense, translated it **πεκούλια βασιλέων** (“the peculia of kings”).

This is precisely what Jerome notes here about Symmachus, and the sole reason he says that Symmachus used the Latin language: he employed a word of Latin origin. If this reading is restored, both the truth of the matter and the clarity of the sense will stand perfectly.]

Christ Jesus, therefore, rightly—our great God and Savior—redeemed us by his blood in order to make us his special people, who could be special only if they became zealous for good works.

Hence also the statement written in the Gospel, according to the Latin interpreters: “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matthew 6:11). In Greek it is better expressed as “our **ἐπιούσιον** bread,” that is, “special,” “excellent,” or “peculiar”—namely, the bread that descended from heaven and said: “I am the bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:5). Surely it would be absurd for us, who are forbidden to think about tomorrow, to be commanded in the Lord’s Prayer to ask for bread that shortly must be digested and cast out into the latrine.

There is not much difference between **ἐπιούσιον** and **περιούσιον**: only the preposition has been changed, not the word.

Some think that **ἐπιούσιον** is used of the bread in the Lord’s Prayer because it is above all **οὐσίαι** (“substances”), that is, above every substance. If this is accepted, it does not differ greatly from the sense we have explained. For whatever is excellent and special stands outside and above everything.

### Verse 15

“Speak these things, exhort, and rebuke with all authority.”

He uses three terms: “speak,” “exhort,” and “rebuke.” The word “speak” seems to refer to teaching. What he adds, “exhort”—that is, **παρακάλεε**—means something different in Greek from what it does in Latin. **Παράκλησις** signifies consolation more than exhortation.

He used this word earlier concerning young men: “Likewise, console the young men, so that they may be temperate in all things.” We explained that passage in its proper place as though the Latin text had *exhortare*, “exhort.”

The one who says, “We beseech you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5:20), consoles his hearer; he also humbles and subordinates himself in order to win the one whom he consoles.

The third term, “rebuke,” seems contrary to consolation: whoever has despised consolation is worthy of rebuke and deserves to hear: “You have forgotten the consolation that speaks to you as to children.” We also read in the Letter to Timothy of one consolation and another rebuke, when the Apostle says: “Be urgent in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, console” (2 Timothy 4:2). There rebuke is taken up first, and afterward severity is tempered with consolation.

Here, however, he wishes the disciples first to be consoled; if they make no progress through consolation, then they are to be corrected—and corrected “with all authority.” Thus I understand the statement “rebuke with all authority” as referring specifically to rebuke and not collectively to the two preceding commands. For it would not be fitting to say “console with all authority” or “speak with all authority,” but only “rebuke with all authority.”

“No one should despise you.”

Someone might think that this is now being written to Titus in the same sense as what was said to Timothy: “Let no one despise your youth” (1 Timothy 4:14). We, however, in accordance with the distinction in the Greek, think that **περιφρονείτω**, written here, signifies one thing, and **καταφρονείτω**, said to Timothy, another; the prepositions **περί** and **κατά** produce a difference in meaning.

That Paul the Apostle does not use different nouns and verbs casually or arbitrarily, but also uses different prepositions according to the variety of circumstances, can be made clear by what he says: “For woman is from man, but man through woman” (2 Corinthians 11:12). Elsewhere: “Because from him and through him and in him are all things” (Romans 11:36). And again: “Paul, an apostle not from human beings nor through a human being” (Galatians 1:1).

We therefore think that **καταφρόνησις** properly refers to contempt—for example, when someone stretched upon the torture-horse and between metal plates despises pain, fearing neither the judge’s threats nor the roar of the surrounding crowd, but, for the confession of martyrdom, scorns and disregards every punishment.

There is also a bad contempt of the opposite kind, concerning which Habakkuk testifies with the Holy Spirit speaking through him: “Look at the despisers; behold and wonder at wonders, and perish” (Habakkuk 1:5).

Accordingly, we also said that what is written to Timothy, “Let no one despise your youth” (1 Timothy 4:12), means: “I do not want you to conduct yourself in such a way that anyone could rightly despise you.”

**Περιφρόνησις**, on the other hand, has the meaning asserted by the Stoics, who carefully distinguish between words: it describes someone who, confident in himself and considering himself better than another, despises the person whom he thinks inferior, and, being “above”—that is, wiser—judges the humbler person worthy of contempt.

Inflated by such empty arrogance, and scorning even heaven and the sun, someone among the Greeks is mockingly represented as having said:

**Ἀεροβατῶ καὶ περιφρονῶ τὸν ἥλιον**

—which we can render in Latin: “I walk through the air, and I know myself to be more important than the sun.”

The **περιφρόνησις** now used in the passage addressed to Titus therefore has this meaning: “Let none of those who are in the churches live in such a way, while you act sluggishly, that he thinks himself better than you.” For what kind of edification would a disciple provide if he understood himself to be greater than his teacher?

Hence not only bishops, presbyters, and deacons must take great care to surpass in conduct and speech the entire people over whom they preside, but so must those of the lower ranks—exorcists, readers, doorkeepers—and absolutely all who serve in the house of God. For it profoundly destroys the Church of Christ when laypeople are better than clergy.

[**Note:** Strepsiades in Aristophanes’ *Clouds*, final scene.]

[**Note:** Martianay’s text lacked the words “and wonder,” which occur in other books and especially in the edition of the Septuagint used by Jerome: **καὶ θαυμάσατε θαυμάσια**, “and wonder at wonders,” etc.]

[**Note:** Victorius restored *conversatione, sermone ac scientia* (“in conduct, speech, and knowledge”) in accordance with the reading of Gratian, *Decretum* VIII, question 1, chapter “Qualis.” There he adds that, beyond the doorkeepers—whom Gratian calls guardians of the buildings—mention is also made of acolytes. This was more than sufficient for him to understand the passage of the holy Father as Gratian had adapted it.]

### Chapter 3, verses 1–2

“Remind them to be subject to rulers and authorities, to obey, to be ready for every good work, to speak evil of no one, not to be quarrelsome, to be gentle, showing every meekness toward all people.”

Something similar is written to the Romans: “Let every soul be subject to the higher authorities. For there is no authority except from God” (Romans 13:1).

I think this command was given both here and there because at that time the doctrine of Judas the Galilean was still flourishing and had many followers. It is also mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles, where Scripture reports: “Before these days Theudas arose, saying that he was someone great; and about three thousand men joined him” (Acts 5:36). “After him Judas the Galilean arose in the days of the census.” Among other things, he put forward from the Law this apparently plausible argument: that no one should be called Lord except God alone, and that those who brought tithes to the Temple should not pay tribute to Caesar.

This heresy had grown so far that it even disturbed the Pharisees and a large part of the people, so that the question was also brought to our Lord: “Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar or not?” (Matthew 22:17). The Lord answered them prudently and cautiously: “Give to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God” (ibid., 21).

The Apostle Paul, agreeing with this response, teaches that believers ought to be subject to rulers and authorities. The Greek **ἀρχαί**, which is read in the text, signifies “rulerships” or “authorities” more than “rulers,” and denotes the authority itself rather than the human beings who possess authority.

But since he had said, “Remind them to be subject to rulers and authorities,” an opportunity could be given to those who fear torture to deny the faith. They might claim, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement, that they were subject to rulers and authorities and would do whatever they commanded. Therefore he added: “To obey for every good work.” If what the emperor or governor commands is good, obey the will of the one giving the command. But if it is evil and opposed to God, answer with the words from the Acts of the Apostles: “We must obey God rather than human beings” (Acts 5:29).

We should understand the same principle concerning slaves in relation to their masters, wives in relation to their husbands, and children in relation to their parents: they are to be subject to their masters, husbands, and parents only in matters that do not conflict with God’s commands.

What follows, “to be ready,” can be read in two ways. Either “to be ready for every good work” is to be understood; or the phrase may be joined to what precedes, so that “to obey for every good work” ends there, and “to be ready” constitutes another distinct and specific command, in accordance with what is written in Leviticus: “The goat that is sent away, bearing the curse of the people, is to be handed over to a ready man” (Leviticus 16:21).

If, then, someone is ready to take the scapegoat, lead him—or, alternatively, escort him—into the wilderness, destroy him there, and, as far as he is able, remove him by the lot of the curse, then, when he has obeyed, he will also be ready for every good work.

“Be ready” can also be understood in another way: they should anticipate inwardly everything that may happen to them, so that when events occur they do not endure them as something new, but have everything prepared in advance. [Note: Other printed editions read *in animo praefigerent* (“they should prefigure in their mind”).]

Nor is “to speak evil of no one” to be understood in a simple sense. He does not say “to speak evil of no human being,” but absolutely “no one”—neither an angel nor any creature of God. For everything made by God is very good.

When the archangel Michael disputed with the devil over the body of Moses, he did not dare to bring a blasphemous judgment against him, but said: “May God rebuke you” (Jude 9). If Michael did not dare to pronounce a blasphemous judgment against the devil, who was certainly worthy of a curse, how much more ought we to be pure from every curse!

The devil deserved a curse, but blasphemy ought not to issue from the mouth of an archangel.

Read the ancient books again and see which three tribes were established on Mount Gerizim to bless the people, and which on the other mountain to curse them. Reuben, who had defiled his father’s bed, Zebulun, Leah’s youngest son, and the sons of the slave women were placed on Mount Ebal [alternatively, “Eliel”] to curse those who were worthy of cursing (Deuteronomy 27).

It would take too long to enumerate now how Jacob, who had called his sons to blessing (Genesis 49:1), saying, “that I may bless you,” later included, as though within a blessing, the words: “Cursed be their anger, for it was insolent.” The Lord himself also speaks in Genesis: “Cursed is the earth in your labors” (Genesis 3:17).

For now, it is enough to say this: the disciples of Christ ought not to speak evil, nor should they be quarrelsome.

[**Note:** In the manuscripts of Cistercian provenance: *non fuerant* (“had not been”), and shortly afterward *dupliciter intelligendum* (“to be understood in two ways”), in place of *legendum* (“to be read”).]

For if we are children of peace, and wish peace to rest upon us, and have approached the heavenly Jerusalem, which received its name from peace, then with those who hate peace we should still maintain peace. As far as it lies within us, we should be at peace with all people—not only with the gentle but also with the quarrelsome, because there is no virtue in bearing with the gentle.

Let us give place to anger, showing every meekness toward all people—not because, from a desire for empty glory, we ought to display our meekness to everyone, but because, while we endure everyone and do not repay injury with injury, our deeds themselves may become known to all.

Someone may, for the sake of boasting, public opinion, and popular favor, pretend to be meek toward certain people and feign goodness. But where meekness is not true, genuine, and solid, I do not know whether he can persuade everyone that he is meek.

### Verses 3ff.

“For we too were once foolish, disobedient, deceived, slaves to various desires and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful and hating one another. But when the goodness and humanity of God our Savior appeared, not because of works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that, having been justified by his grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life.”

Someone may ask how Paul could have been foolish, unbelieving, and deceived, serving various desires and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful and hating others, before the goodness and kindness of our Savior saved him through the washing of the second regeneration—not because of works of righteousness that he had done, but through his mercy, when the Holy Spirit was poured out abundantly and generously upon the apostles and believers through Jesus Christ, so that, having obtained the inheritance of grace, they might possess the hope of life forever.

Yet we certainly read that he was circumcised on the eighth day, according to the righteousness that is in the Law, blameless (Philippians 3:5): a Hebrew of Hebrews, according to the Law a Pharisee, from the tribe of Benjamin, educated at the feet of Gamaliel, and instructed from infancy in the sacred Scriptures (Acts 22).

The answer is that the Jews who, before the Savior’s coming, passion, and resurrection, lived according to the Law possessed a certain righteousness, though not a complete one, at least to some degree. Simeon and Anna the prophetess, who served in the Temple of God, were likewise found righteous.

But after the people cried out, “Crucify him, crucify him! We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15), and, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 25:27), and the kingdom of God was taken away from them and given to a nation producing its fruits, from that time whoever did not believe in Christ became foolish, wandering, unbelieving, and enslaved to various pleasures.

Does Paul not seem to us—or, according to another reading, to you—to have been foolish when he had zeal for God, but not according to knowledge; when he persecuted the Church and guarded the clothing of those stoning Stephen? He was inflamed by such hatred against the Savior that he received letters from the priests and went to Damascus to bind those who believed in Christ.

Could he have possessed any virtues without the virtue of God in Christ Jesus? Could he extinguish the burning flame of pleasures when he was not a temple of God?

What greater malice and envy could there be than to obtain letters against people who were absent, ravage the disciples of Christ everywhere, refuse to let him be saved, envy others who might have been saved, hate Christians, and consequently deserve hatred from everyone?

What greater error, disobedience, and folly could there be than, after the day had dawned and the shadows had passed away, to wish to observe the abolished Law and say: “Do not handle, do not touch, do not taste,” while solid and manly food had appeared, and to desire to be carried along on the milk of infancy?

[**Note:** Martianay’s text incorrectly read *portari* (“to be carried”).]

[**Note:** Earlier editions read *vivificavit* (“made alive”); the manuscripts oppose this reading.]

Let us pay closer attention, and we shall find the Trinity most clearly expressed in the present chapter.
