The goodness and kindness of our Savior God—no other than God the Father—through the washing of regeneration and the renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out abundantly upon us through Jesus Christ our Savior, justified us for eternal life.

The salvation of believers is the mystery of the Trinity.

Some understand this passage differently, thinking that it does not concern Paul and the apostles but, under the person of the apostles, concerns others. Just as Paul, speaking in his own person and in that of Apollo and Cephas, addressed the dissension and schism that he was correcting among the Corinthians, so here too, naming himself and the apostles, he showed what all who believed in Christ had been like before the regeneration of the life-giving washing.

At the same time, his humility is admirable: he who regarded all the humility and righteousness of the Law as refuse and rubbish nevertheless rightly confessed that, without Christ, he had served every vice. [Alternative reading: *utilitatem* (“usefulness”) for *humilitatem* (“humility”).]

### Verse 8

“This saying is trustworthy, and I want you to affirm these things confidently, so that those who believe in God may be careful to devote themselves to good works. These things are good and useful for people.” [Alternative reading: *affirmare* (“affirm”) for *confirmare* (“confirm”).]

The statement “This saying is trustworthy” must be joined to what precedes, where he had said that, having been justified by his grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life. The saying concerning the inheritance of God and the hope of eternal life is worthy of belief.

Therefore one must believe these things without doubt or fear, and affirm them so that others may believe them as well. Not only this, but he must also affirm these matters to all the others who wish to believe; hence he says: “And I want you to affirm these things confidently.”

Those who truly believe that these things are so must necessarily take care to perform good works, through which the inheritance of God and the hope of eternal life are prepared.

He expressed this beautifully in order to produce greater faith: he did not say “those who believe in human beings,” but “those who believe in God.” They must necessarily take care for good works, which, when fulfilled and carried out with every diligence, are good and useful to believers.

(Vers. 9.) “But avoid foolish questions, genealogies, contentions, and quarrels that arise from the Law. For they are useless and vain.” Since questions are numerous and varied, Solomon spoke concerning those who seek God, saying: “But those who seek him rightly have found peace” (Prov. 8:35). Those, therefore, who do not seek God rightly cannot find peace.

There are many examples of people who do not seek God rightly. The Jews seek God perversely, hoping that they can find him without Christ. Heretics, clamoring with the empty din of their words, seek one whom they cannot find. Philosophers also, and barbarians who hold various opinions about God, sought God. But because they did not seek him rightly, their questions were foolish: they thought that God could be grasped by human understanding. Paul therefore recalls us from such questions.

On the other hand, he urges and encourages us more strongly toward questions that are wise and supported by the authority of Scripture, being mindful of the Savior’s commandments, in which he says: “Seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you; ask, and it will be given to you. For everyone who seeks finds [Al. will find], and whoever asks receives [Al. will receive], and to whoever knocks it will be opened” (Luke 11:9–10)—provided only that our body is not subjected to sins; then wisdom will enter into us. Let the understanding be exercised; let the mind be fed daily by divine reading; and our questions will not be foolish questions.

But when he says, “Avoid genealogies, contentions, and quarrels that arise from the Law,” he is specifically striking at the Jews, who boast in this and think that they possess knowledge of the Law if they know the names of each individual. Since these names are barbarous, and we do not know their etymologies, they are often pronounced incorrectly by us. And if we happen to err [Al. have erred] in the accent, in the length or shortness of a syllable—either lengthening short syllables or shortening long ones—they customarily ridicule our ignorance, especially in the aspirates and in pronouncing certain letters with a scraping of the throat.

This happens because the Seventy translators, through whom the divine Law was translated into the Greek language, represented specifically the letter HETH and AIN, and the other letters of this kind, by adding other letters, since they could not transfer them into Greek with their double aspiration. For example, they rendered רחל as Rachel rather than Rahel; יריחו as Jericho rather than Jeriho; חברון as Chebron rather than Hebron; and צער as Segor rather than Seor. In other cases this effort failed them [Al. failed].

For we and the Greeks have only one letter *s*, whereas they have three: SAMECH, SADE, and SIN, which possess different sounds. Isaac and Sion are written with SADE; Israel with SIN, and yet it does not sound as it is written. Seon, king of the Amorites, is both pronounced and written with the letter SAMECH.

If, therefore, the names and idioms of the language are not expressed by us—because they are barbarous—as they are pronounced by the Hebrews, they customarily raise a loud laugh and swear that they have no idea what we are saying. Hence we took care, from copies made in the Caesarean library, to correct against the very originals all the books of the Old Law that the learned Adamantius had arranged in the *Hexapla*. In these books the Hebrew words themselves are written in their proper characters, and beside them are expressed in a closely corresponding path by Greek letters. Aquila and Symmachus, as well as the Septuagint and Theodotion, each retain their own order.

Some books—and especially those composed in verse among the Hebrews—also contain three additional editions. These they call the fifth, sixth, and seventh translations, though they acquired authority without the names of their translators.

[Note: It is preferable, for the reader’s benefit, to insert here an actual specimen of the *Hexapla*, from the margin of the Barberini manuscript at Hosea 11:1:

**Hebrew, represented in Greek letters:**  
Χι νερ Ισραηλ ουεαβηου μεμμεσραιμ καραθι βανι.  
“For Israel was a child, and I loved him; and from Egypt I called my son.”

**Aquila:**  
Ὅτι παῖς Ἰσραὴλ καὶ ἠγάπησα αὐτὸν καὶ ἀπὸ Αἰγύπτου ἐκάλεσα τὸν υἱόν μου.  
“For Israel was a child, and I loved him, and from Egypt I called my son.”

**Symmachus:**  
Ὅτι παῖς Ἰσραὴλ καὶ ἠγαπημένος, ἐξ Αἰγύπτου κέκληται υἱός μου.  
“For Israel was a child and beloved; from Egypt my son has been called.”

**The Septuagint:**  
Ὅτι νήπιος Ἰσραὴλ καὶ ἐγὼ ἠγάπησα αὐτὸν, καὶ ἐξ Αἰγύπτου κέκληται υἱός μου.  
“For Israel was an infant, and I loved him, and from Egypt my son has been called.”

**Theodotion:**  
Ὅτι νήπιος Ἰσραὴλ καὶ ἠγάπησα αὐτὸν, ἐκάλεσα υἱόν μου ἐξ Αἰγύπτου.  
“For Israel was an infant, and I loved him; I called my son from Egypt.”

Furthermore, wherever in some books he added a fifth, sixth, and finally a seventh edition, each followed Theodotion in its own order.]

That immortal genius, through his labor, bestowed these materials upon us, so that we need not greatly fear the haughtiness of the Jews, who delight in lips loosened, tongue twisted, saliva hissing, and throat scraped raw. They have another occasion for pride as well. Just as we who are Latins more easily commit to memory Latin names and origins derived [Al. drawn] from our own language, so they, from early childhood, have absorbed the words of their native speech into the deepest faculties of their minds.

[Al. “have imbibed them [and from the beginning of Adam to the last of Zerubbabel they run through all the generations so rapidly and accurately from memory that you would think they were reciting their own name.” We, who have either learned other letters, or at least believed in Christ late, or even, though infants, have been dedicated to the Church, follow the meaning of Scripture more than its words. If we perhaps do not know them so well [Al. *ita* is omitted], they think themselves more learned in reciting names, reckoning years, and listing grandchildren, great-grandchildren, grandparents, great-grandparents, and ancestors.]

I myself heard a certain Jew who pretended to have believed in Christ at Rome raise a question concerning the genealogies of our Lord Jesus Christ written in Matthew and Luke: namely, that from Solomon to Joseph they agree neither in their number nor in the equality of their names. After he had perverted the hearts of simple people, he produced, as though from secret shrines and an oracle, certain solutions that seemed satisfactory to him, when he ought rather to have sought justice, mercy, and the love of God, and only afterward, if the matter arose, to have disputed about names and numbers.

Perhaps we have said enough—and more than necessary—about Jewish haughtiness. But we have been given an occasion to discuss genealogies, contention, and quarrels that arise from the Law.

Dialecticians, whose leader is Aristotle, customarily spread the nets of argument and confine the free-ranging liberty of rhetoric within the thorny thickets of syllogisms. These men, who wear away whole days and nights in this pursuit—whether asking or answering, proposing or accepting, assuming, confirming, and concluding—call certain people contentious, people who argue as they please, not by reason but by the temper of litigants.

If those men do this, whose proper art is contention, what should a Christian do except flee contention altogether? Legal quarrels too must be entirely rejected and left to the foolishness of the Jews. They are useless and vain; they possess only the appearance of knowledge, and in fact benefit neither those who speak nor those who listen.

For what benefit is it to me to know how many years Methuselah lived, or in what year of his life Solomon took a wife, lest perhaps Rehoboam be thought to have been born in the eleventh year of Solomon’s life? And what benefit is there in many similar matters, which are either difficult to discover because of the variety of books and the errors that have become entrenched—since uncorrected texts are gradually copied from uncorrected texts—or which, even if we should discover them through great diligence and labor, we know would profit us nothing?

It frequently happens that we engage in disputes about the Law, not from a desire for truth but from a desire for the display of our glory, wishing to be considered learned by those who hear us; or at least, from this little bit of publicity, we pursue shameful profits.

For what benefit is there in chattering with foaming lips and the barking of dogs, when a simple and moderate answer can either calm you, if it is true, or, if it is false, correct you gently and peaceably?

[Col. 0594D]

[Col. 0598A]

(Vers. 10, 11.) “Avoid a heretical person after one and a second correction, knowing that such a person is perverted and sins, being condemned by himself.”

The name “heresy” also occurs in the Epistle to the Corinthians: “For there must also be heresies among you, so that those who are approved may become manifest” (1 Cor. 11:19). And in the Epistle to the Galatians it is counted among the works of the flesh: “Now the works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, uncleanness, wantonness, idolatry, sorcery, enmities, contentions, jealousies, angers, quarrels, dissensions, heresies, envies, drunkennesses, revelries, and things similar to these, which I foretell to you, as I have foretold: those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God” (Gal. 5:19 ff.).

In this passage we must carefully observe that, just as the other vices enumerated among the works of the flesh exclude us [Al. are excluded] from the kingdom of God, so heresies also take the kingdom of God away from us; and it makes no difference in what manner someone is excluded, so long as he is excluded from the kingdom.

What is more remarkable is that the matter in the Acts of the Apostles also appears to require rereading: our faith in Christ and the discipline of the Church were already then called “heresy” by wicked men. For the Jews say to the apostle Paul:

“We have neither received letters from Judea concerning you [Al. ‘from you … from Judea’], nor has anyone of the brothers come and reported or spoken anything evil about you. But we ask to hear from you what you think; for concerning this heresy it is known to us that it is opposed everywhere” (Acts 28:21–22).

And although the name “heresy” is not spoken at Miletus, Paul nevertheless names its works when speaking to the presbyters of the Church:

“I know that after my departure grievous wolves will come among you, not sparing the flock; and from among your own selves men will arise speaking perverse things, to draw the disciples after them” (Acts 20:29–30).

Let this have been said in passing, wherever else heresy may be called by that name. Now the term itself must be examined fully.

“Heresy” in Greek is named from “choice” (*hairesis*), since each person chooses for himself what seems better to him. The philosophers too—Stoics, Peripatetics, Academics, Epicureans—are called followers of this or that heresy. It would be superfluous to go through them individually and enumerate Marcion, Valentinus, Apelles, Ebion, Montanus, and Manichaeus with their doctrines, since it is very easy for anyone to recognize by what errors each is led.

If only Arius and Eunomius, and the originator of the new heresy, were not so well known! Perhaps they would have deceived far fewer people.

“Avoid a heretical person after one admonition,” or, as it is better expressed in Greek, after one **νουθεσία** (*nouthesia*). *Nouthesia* signifies rather a warning and instruction without rebuke.

The Latin manuscripts read—and Pope Athanasius also approved this as the true reading—“after one and a second admonition.” This means that it is not enough merely to rebuke or admonish once someone who has been corrupted by some error; a second instruction must also be given him, so that “every word may stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses.”

[Note: This reading is now found alone in nearly all copies and among ancient writers.]

Why, then, is he to be avoided after the first and second correction? He gives the reasons, saying: “because such a person is perverted and sins, being condemned by himself.”

For someone who, after being admonished once and twice and having heard his error, does not wish to be corrected, considers the one correcting him to be in error. Conversely, by preparing himself for verbal disputes and quarrels, he wishes to win over the very person by whom he is being instructed.

He is therefore said to be condemned “by himself,” because a fornicator, adulterer, murderer, and those guilty of other vices are expelled from the Church by priests. Heretics, however, pronounce sentence upon themselves by withdrawing from the Church according to their own judgment; this withdrawal appears to be a condemnation imposed by their own conscience.

[Note: Victorius, in his reading of Gratian, chapter *Inter*, 24, question 3, and also on the basis of manuscripts, restores here *arbitramur* (“we judge”) and shortly afterward *separet* (“separates”) in place of *separetur* (“is separated”); finally, he adds the word *diversum* (“different”) where “different” may be understood. Rabbanus, who, as we have said, copied this passage with the greatest care, has: “Schism, because of episcopal disagreement, separates from the Church.” This can indeed be understood as partly true at the beginning.]

They think that this is the distinction between heresy and schism: heresy possesses a perverse doctrine, whereas schism separates from the Church because of episcopal disagreement. This can indeed be understood as partly true at the beginning. In fact, no schism fails to invent some heresy for itself, so that it may appear to have withdrawn from the Church rightly.

(Vers. 12.) “When I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, hasten to come to me at Nicopolis, for I have decided to winter there.”

We read at the beginning of this Epistle: “For this reason I left you in Crete, so that you might correct what was lacking and appoint presbyters in every city, as I arranged for you.” Since the Cretans had only recently believed, Paul did not want them, after his departure and passage to other Churches, to be left orphaned; rather, they were to have an apostolic man who would correct what appeared to be lacking.

Therefore, because Titus was necessary after the foundations of the other Churches had been laid, so that he might build the structure upon them, Paul writes to him that, once he had sent Artemas or Tychicus—one of the two who had been with him—to Crete to fill his place [Al. “who would fill his place,”] Titus himself should come to Nicopolis, declaring that he intended to winter there.

From this we perceive Paul’s fatherly affection for the Cretans [Al. “we may perceive it”]. He needs Titus for the ministry of the Gospel, yet he does not want him to come to him before Artemas or Tychicus, his successor, has arrived in his place.

Nicopolis is the city that received its name because of Augustus’s victory, since he defeated Antony and Cleopatra there.

(Vers. 13.) “Diligently send on their way Zenas the lawyer and Apollo, so that nothing may be lacking for them” [739].

This is the Apollo of whom it is also written to the Corinthians: “Each of you says: ‘I am of Paul,’ ‘but I am of Apollo,’ ‘but I am of Cephas’” (1 Cor. 1:12). He was an Alexandrian man of Jewish origin, very eloquent and accomplished in the Law, and bishop of the Corinthians. Because of the dissensions that existed in Corinth, he should be thought to have crossed over with Zenas the lawyer to the neighboring island of Crete. When Paul’s Epistle had calmed the dissensions that had arisen at Corinth, he returned to Corinth [Col. 0598D].

As for Zenas the lawyer, we cannot say from another passage of Scripture who he was, except that he too was an apostolic man and had undertaken the work that Apollo performed: building up the Churches of Christ.

[Note: Our manuscripts read: “to instruct the Churches of Christ.”]

He therefore instructs Titus that, since they were going to sail from Crete to Greece, he should not allow them to be in need of provisions, but should ensure that they had what was necessary for the journey.

[Col. 0599A]

(Vers. 14.) “And let our people also learn to take the lead in good works for necessary uses, so that they may not be unfruitful.”

Above he had said: “Diligently send on their way Zenas the lawyer and Apollo, so that nothing may be lacking for them.” Since an unspoken objection could therefore arise—so that Titus, or anyone reading the Epistle, might say, “Where was Titus to obtain the means to provide a journey for those who had none?”—he resolves this question and, as though no objection had been made, disposes of it by saying: “Let our people also learn to take the lead in good works for necessary uses, so that they may not be unfruitful.”

He calls “our people” his own people, those who had believed in Christ. Since they belonged to Christ, they rightly deserved to be called both Paul’s and Titus’s people.

“You have authority,” he says, “over the disciples; teach them not to be unfruitful, but to minister to evangelists and apostolic men who serve in good works.” And they are to minister not in just any matters, but “for necessary uses”: “Having food and clothing [Al. ‘covering’], with these let us be content” (1 Tim. 6:8); “those who serve at the altar should live from the altar”; and those who have become participants in our spiritual blessings ought to share their material blessings with us.

And lest they perhaps too easily disregard either Paul’s Epistle or Titus’s command, he calls unfruitful all who have not ministered to evangelists.

Solomon also says in Proverbs: “The fruit is almsgiving” (Prov. 3:12). Paul himself calls love the first fruit of the Spirit (Gal. 5). Love, however, is demonstrated above all in sharing and service.

“So that they may not be unfruitful.” For every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and cast into the fire (Matt. 5:10).

I say this because “whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly.” To be unwilling to provide for apostolic men and the evangelizers of Christ in necessary matters is to condemn oneself to barrenness.

[Col. 0599B]

(Vers. 15.) “All who are with me greet you.”

Either he used his customary manner of speaking, saying that Titus was greeted by all who were with him; or else he meant this specifically of Titus, because he was such a man that he deserved the love of everyone who was with Paul. It is a great praise of Titus that Paul says he is greeted by all.

[Col. 0600A]

“Greet those who love us in the faith.”

If everyone who loves did so in the faith, and there were no others who loved without faith, Paul would never have added faith to love by saying: “Greet those who love us in the faith.”

Mothers love their children, so that they are prepared to die for them; but they do not love in the faith. Wives love their husbands, with whom they very often die; but that love is not the love of faith. Only the love of the saints loves in the faith, so much so that even if the one who is loved is an unbeliever, the saint nevertheless loves him in the faith, according to the saying:

[Note: Victor adds: “Stand in the faith,” and then, following the sense as he understands Jerome, who is speaking about love, and also following the wording of both the Greek and Latin Vulgate editions, he writes: “Let all your things be done in love,” instead of “in the faith.” But all our manuscripts support the printed reading.]

“Let all your things be done in the faith” (1 Cor. 16:14).

And elsewhere: “Love your enemies” (Luke 6:35). The saint loves his enemies, and therefore loves them in the faith, because he believes in the one who promised that he would reward the fulfillment of the commandment.

[Col. 0600B]

“The grace of our Lord be with all of you.”

It should be known that the Greek manuscripts read as follows: “Grace be with all of you,” so that neither “of the Lord” nor “our” appears in the authentic books.

Thus he invokes grace collectively upon the saints and believers, Titus and the others who were with him. Just as the patriarch Isaac blessed his son Jacob (Gen. 27), and Jacob himself blessed the twelve patriarchs (ibid., verse 29), so the Apostles, when entering a house, used to say: “Peace to this house” (Matt. 10:12). If the house was worthy, their peace rested upon it; but if it showed itself unworthy, the peace returned to those who had invoked it.

So now, at the end of his Epistle, the Apostle invokes grace upon the believers. With the blessing, it had its effect as a prayer, and it was within the power of the believers to make themselves such as the one blessed wished them to be when he gave the blessing.

[Col. 0599]

# ONE BOOK OF THE COMMENTARIES OF SAINT EUSEBIUS HIERONYMUS, PRESBYTER OF STRIDON, ON THE EPISTLE TO PHILEMON. (C)

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0599D] 741–742

Those who do not wish to receive the Epistle written to Philemon among Paul’s Epistles say that the Apostle did not always speak all things with Christ speaking in him. For human weakness could not have endured the uninterrupted tenor of the Holy Spirit, nor could the necessities of this little body always have been fulfilled in the presence of the Lord—such matters as arranging lunch, taking food, being hungry, being satisfied, digesting what has been eaten, and replenishing what has been exhausted. I say nothing of the other matters that they repeat with great precision and insistence [Al. “forcefully”], in order to assert that there was some time when Paul would not have dared to say: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20); or: “Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?” (2 Cor. 13:3).

“What sort of proof of Christ,” they ask, “is it to hear: ‘Bring the cloak that I left at Troas with Carpus when you come’ (2 Tim. 4:13)? Or this statement to the Galatians: ‘Would that those who trouble you would even cut themselves off’ (Gal. 5:12)? Or in this very Epistle: ‘At the same time, prepare a lodging for me’?”

They say that the same thing happened not only to the Apostles but also to the prophets. Hence it is often written: “The word of the Lord came to Ezekiel” (Ezek. 22), or to some other prophet, because, after completing the prophecy, the prophet returned again into himself and became an ordinary man rather than a prophet. They say that, except for our Lord Jesus Christ, the Holy Spirit remained in no one [Al. “remained”].

John the Baptist too received this sign, so that he might recognize the one upon whom he saw the Holy Spirit descending and remaining as the one who was the Messiah (John 1). From this it is shown [Al. “it is shown”] that the Holy Spirit indeed descends upon many, but that this is uniquely the Savior’s distinction: that the Spirit remains in him.

From these and similar arguments they wish to conclude either that the Epistle written to Philemon is not Paul’s, or that, even if it is Paul’s, it contains nothing capable of building us up. They say that it was rejected by many of the ancients because it was written merely for the purpose of recommending someone, not for teaching.

On the contrary, those who defend its genuine authority say that it was never received throughout the whole world by all the Churches unless it was believed to be the Epistle of the apostle Paul. On this principle, they say, they ought not to receive even the Second Epistle to Timothy or the Epistle to the Galatians, concerning which Paul himself supplied examples of human weakness:

“Bring the cloak that I left at Troas with Carpus when you come”; and: “Would that those who trouble you would even cut themselves off.”

[Note: Martianaeus, following Erasmus, and they themselves, supplied examples of human weakness.]

Many passages can also be found in Romans and in the other Epistles to the Churches, especially to the Corinthians, written in a more relaxed and almost conversational manner, in which the Apostle says: “To the rest I say, not the Lord.” Since these passages too contain something of this kind, either they should not be considered Paul’s Epistles, or, if those are received, the Epistle to Philemon must also be received by the precedent of similar accepted writings.

They are greatly and plainly mistaken if they think that buying food, preparing lodging, procuring clothing, and attending to the needs of the body are sins, and assert that the Holy Spirit is driven away if we devote even a little attention to the necessities of the body.

The Apostle says: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (Eph. 4:30). The prophet recalls by what actions the Holy Spirit is grieved, arranging many vices and sins in sequence and finally concluding: “In all these things you were grieving me.”

Otherwise, it would be a sin to offer a cup of cold water, wash feet, sacrifice a calf, or prepare a meal, although we know that through such things certain people are adopted as sons of God.

It is not the time now to answer everything, since we have not introduced all the arguments that they customarily raise. But if they do not think that the small things belong to the one to whom the great things belong, then, following Valentinus, Marcion, and Apelles, they ought to introduce one creator of ants, worms, gnats, and locusts, and another creator of heaven, earth, the sea, and angels.

Or rather, does it not belong to the same power to refuse to deny, in lesser things as well, the skill that it has exercised in greater things?

And since we have mentioned Marcion, let them at least learn from Marcion himself that the Epistle to Philemon is Paul’s.

[Note: Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book 5, final chapter: “Its brevity alone benefited this Epistle, so that it escaped the falsifying hands of Marcion.” Yet Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*, book 1, chapter 41, section 9, complains that even among the Marcionites this Epistle itself was thoroughly corrupted.]

Although Marcion either did not receive Paul’s other Epistles or altered and mutilated certain passages in them, he did not dare to lay hands upon this one alone, because its brevity defended it.

But it seems to me that, while they accuse the Epistle of simplicity, they reveal their own ignorance, not understanding what power and wisdom lie hidden in each of its statements. With your prayers, and with the Holy Spirit himself suggesting to us—by whom these things were written—we shall try to explain them in their proper places.

But if brevity is held in contempt, let them also despise Obadiah, Nahum, Zephaniah, and the other twelve prophets [Al. “the prophets”], in whom such extraordinary and sublime things are proclaimed that you cannot tell whether you ought to admire in them the brevity of their words or the greatness of their meanings.

If those who reject the Epistle to Philemon understood this, they would never despise brevity, which, in place of the sprawling burdens of the Law, has been composed with evangelical elegance, since the Lord makes a brief and completed word upon the earth.

But now the Apostle’s own words must be set forth, which begin as follows.

## THE BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0603]

[Col. 0603A]

(Vers. 1 ff.) “Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ, and Timothy, a brother, to Philemon, our beloved and fellow worker, and to Apphia the sister, and to Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the Church that is in your house: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord [Note: “our” has been added; neither the Greek archetype nor our manuscripts acknowledge it.] our Jesus Christ.”

In an inverted and irregular order, I have undertaken to dictate to you my commentary on Paul’s Epistles. For although you repeatedly asked me to do this, Paula and Eustochium, and I firmly refused, you compelled me at least to discuss the shortest Epistle, which seemed to you to be last not only in the number of its verses but also in its meaning and arrangement.

I shall therefore attempt the matter of the beginning at the end. What another person would immediately ask at the opening of the Apostle’s Epistle—why, at what time, or through whose naming, he received the name Paul from Saul—I am now compelled to address, so that I may not ever—

[Note: In the manuscripts the syllable *mu* is written in the phrase: “not even *mu*”; some read “not even something mute” or “not even something moved.” One manuscript of Saint-Martin-des-Champs retains *ut tum*. Marianus reads *muth*, but the better reading is the syllable *mu* alone, without added letters. Jerome says here: “I did not even dare to make a *mu* about Paul from Saul before this day,” that is, “I did not dare to murmur or mutter why Paul was called what he was, when previously he had been called Saul.”

Now *mussare*—“to mutter”—is so called because mute people say no more than *mu*, μῦ. I think Jerome took this from Varro, who says: “What is least, he does not dare even to make, as they say, a μῦ.” See book 6 of *On the Latin Language*. Martianaeus—who examined some manuscripts with us—reports “not even something mute.” It is certainly corrupt, as I have no doubt. We have spoken about *mu*. See also the Greek μῦ, an interjection, in the Epistle 12 to the monk Antony, where Jerome says: “You do not deign even to make a *mu*.” Lucilius:]

Nor ever to praise a man, nor ever to utter *mu*.” I indeed have never before this day dared to utter even *mu* against him, as the saying goes. Nor should we suppose, as simpler Latin readers do, that he was previously called *Saulus* rather than *Saul*: for he was from the tribe of Benjamin, among whom this name was more familiar. That Saul too, the king of Judaea and persecutor of David, was from the tribe of Benjamin.

That we call him *Saulus* is not surprising. Hebrew names are declined in imitation of Greek and Roman case forms, so that, just as Joseph becomes *Josephus* and Jacob becomes *Jacobus*, so Saul too is rendered *Saulus* in our language and speech.

The question, therefore, is why, at whose command, or for what reason he either lost his former name or assumed a new one. That Abram should be called Abraham was accomplished by God’s command (Gen. XVII and following); likewise, that Sarai should receive the name Sarah was God’s decree. And, to come to the New Testament, that Simon should receive the name Peter (Mark III), and that the sons of Zebedee should be called *BANE REEM* (), that is, “sons of thunder,” was commanded by the voice of our Lord Jesus Christ (ibid.).

[Note: Several manuscripts read this way; one retains the name *Boarnerges*, which is closer to the Greek βοανεργὲς and the Syriac *benaireghese* than to the Hebrew *bene reem*, or *bane reem*. Nevertheless, this reading should be retained, because Jerome is speaking Hebrew here. MART. — One manuscript, as also Rabbanus, reads *Boanerges*, and Victor accordingly writes it thus. In Hebrew letters, , which is the Greek βοανεργὲς; and he wishes the name here to be pronounced in Syriac, not Hebrew. Elsewhere we have often discussed, following Jerome’s judgment, the correct pronunciation of this name. See the Book of Names, under John, where he says: “*Banereem*, sons of thunder; the form *Boanerges*, which usage has established corruptly.” And in the Commentary on Daniel I, 7: “The sons of Zebedee were called sons of thunder, which is read more correctly not, as most think, *Boanerges*, but *Beneraham*.” We do not deny, however, that the Syrians at that time used this word to signify thunder; the Arabic root still confirms this.]

But Scripture nowhere records why he was called Paul instead of Saul. I shall therefore speak boldly, though perhaps truly, in affirming my conjecture from the Acts of the Apostles.

[Col. 0604A] We read there that the Holy Spirit said at Antioch: “Separate Barnabas and Saul for me, for the work to which I have called them.” Then, after fasting and praying and laying hands upon them, they sent them away (Acts XIII, 3 and following). When they had gone down to Seleucia in Syria and, sailing to Salamis in Cyprus—which is now called Constantia—had arrived there, they had John with them in their ministry—the cause of the ecclesiastical quarrel that later arose—and, after traversing the whole island, had come as far as Paphos. There they found a certain magician [or: “a great man”], a false prophet named Bar-Jesus, with the proconsul Sergius Paulus, an intelligent man. After summoning Barnabas and Saul [or: Paul], he desired to hear the word of God from them.

But when the magician [or: “great man”] resisted and was corrupting Sergius, turning him away from the true faith, Saul—Scripture says—“who is also Paul,” filled with the Holy Spirit and gazing at him, said: “O man full of every deceit and every fraud, son of the devil, enemy of all righteousness, will you not cease perverting the straight ways of the Lord? And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you, and you will be blind, not seeing the sun for a time.” Immediately mist and darkness fell upon him, and he went around seeking someone to lead him by the hand. Then the proconsul, when he had seen what happened, believed, marveling at the teaching of the Lord.

When Paul and those who were with him had sailed from Paphos, they came to Perga in Pamphylia. Pay close attention: here he first received the name Paul. Just as Scipio, after Africa had been subjected, assumed the name Africanus; and Metellus, after the island of Crete had been conquered, brought back the distinction of Creticus for his family; and Roman emperors even to the present day are called Adiabenici, Parthici, and Sarmatici from the peoples they have subdued—so Saul, sent to preach to the nations, carried back the trophies of his victory from the proconsul Sergius Paulus, the Church’s first spoil, and raised his standard, so that he was called Paul instead of Saul.

If an interpretation of the name is also sought, *Paulus* in Hebrew signifies “wonderful.” Truly it is wonderful that, after Saul—whose name means “desired,” because he had been requested by the devil for the harassment of the Church—he should become, from a persecutor, a vessel of election.

[Note: In place of *expetitus* (“desired”), our manuscripts and Rabbanus substitute a reading that Martianaeus had less correctly printed as *repetitus* (“recalled”). Take Jerome himself as your authority in the Book of Names on the Acts of the Apostles: “Saul, desired, or petition.” The Hebrew agrees, , about which we have spoken there.]

[Col. 0605A] More has perhaps been argued than was necessary, but it was necessary. As for what follows, “a prisoner of Jesus Christ,” he does not use this title in any Epistle, although in the body of the Epistles—to the Ephesians, Philippians, and Colossians—he testifies that he is in chains for his confession.

To me, however, it seems a mark of greater boldness to call himself “a prisoner of Jesus Christ” than “an apostle.” The apostles gloried in having been found worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus Christ (Acts V, 41); but the authority of chains was necessary. Since he was going to plead for Onesimus, the person making the plea had to be one who could obtain what he requested.

Happy indeed is the one who glories not in wisdom, riches, eloquence, or worldly power, but in the sufferings of Christ. With such a statement he also concludes the Epistle to the Galatians: “From now on let no one trouble me; for I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus Christ in my body” (Gal. VI). Not everyone who is imprisoned is a prisoner of Christ; rather, whoever is imprisoned for Christ’s name and confession is truly called a prisoner of Jesus Christ. And shed blood makes a martyr only when it is shed for Christ’s name.

He therefore writes to Philemon from Rome, imprisoned in the jail. It seems to me that this was at the time when the Epistles to the Philippians, Colossians, and Ephesians were composed. The Epistle to the Philippians belongs to this period for the following reasons: first, he writes it with Timothy alone, as he does this Epistle; and, further, he says that his chains have become known as being for Christ “throughout the whole praetorium.”

What the praetorium is, he indicates at the end of that Epistle: “All the saints greet you, especially those who are of Caesar’s household.” Sent by Caesar into prison, he became better known to Caesar’s household and made the persecutor’s house into a Church of Christ. Then he says: “Some indeed preach Christ out of rivalry, not sincerely, supposing that they are stirring up affliction for my chains” (Phil. I, 17).

[Note: He also argues a little later from the fact that Onesimus was the bearer of letters to both recipients. Yet, after Theodoret, nearly all interpreters judge that the Epistle to the Colossians was sent somewhat later, when Onesimus had returned to Rome a second time.]

The beginning of the Epistle to the Colossians is similar: “Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, and Timothy, a brother.” And later: “I, Paul, have become his minister, and now rejoice in sufferings for you, and complete in my flesh what is lacking of Christ’s sufferings for his body, which is the Church” (Col. I, 2, 23–24). And at the end: “The greeting of Paul with my own hand. Remember my chains” (Col. IV, 18).

This is so that we may know that these Epistles too were composed in prison and in chains. The Epistle to the Colossians has this distinctive feature: the same Onesimus who is now commended to Philemon was also the bearer of this message. For he says: “Tychicus, the beloved brother, faithful minister, and fellow servant in the Lord, will make known to you all that concerns me. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that he may learn what concerns you and comfort your hearts, together with Onesimus, the beloved and faithful brother, who is one of you” (ibid., 7–8).

If Philemon, to whom this Epistle is written, is Onesimus’s master—indeed, if he has begun to be his brother in the Lord—and if it is reported to the Colossians that Onesimus is one of them, reason and the order of events themselves lead us to conclude that Philemon too was a Colossian, and that Onesimus carried this common Epistle to the whole Church at the same time as he received the private letter commending him to his master.

There is another indication: Archippus is also named in this same Epistle. To him Paul writes here together with Philemon: “Say to Archippus: Take heed to the ministry which you have received in the Lord, so that you may fulfill it.” What ministry did Archippus receive from the Lord? In the Epistle to Philemon we read: “And to Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the Church that is in your house.”

[Note: In nearly the same words Pseudo-Ambrose argues that Archippus was a bishop, though some were persuaded that he was not bishop of Colossae but of Laodicea in Phrygia, which is less plausible. The author of the Commentary on Paul’s Epistles under Jerome’s name, which the final volume will present, says: “He was a deacon. Concerning him he says to the Colossians: ‘Say to Archippus: Take heed to the ministry which you have received, so that you may fulfill it.’” It is closer to the truth that he exercised the office of bishop at Colossae in place of Epaphras, while the latter was with Saint Paul at Rome.]

From this I think either that he was bishop of the Church at Colossae, and is urged to preside over it earnestly and diligently as a preacher of the Gospel—or, if that is not so, this is sufficient for me for the present: Philemon, Archippus, and Onesimus himself, who carried the letter, were Colossians, and four Epistles were written at the same time, as we said earlier.

The Epistle to the Ephesians belongs to this period because here too he says that he is imprisoned for Christ, and at the end of this Epistle he gives the same commands that he had given to the Colossians: that wives should be subject to their husbands, husbands should love their wives, children should obey their parents, fathers should not provoke their children to anger, slaves should obey their masters according to the flesh, and masters, abandoning threats, should provide their slaves with what is just. Finally, he concludes his Epistle with these words: “Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord, will make known to you everything that concerns me. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know what concerns me and that he may comfort your hearts.” Tychicus is the one who is sent to the Colossians with Onesimus, and he had Onesimus as his companion at the time when Onesimus was carrying the letter to Philemon.

### “And Timothy, a brother”

In other Epistles Sosthenes and Silvanus, and sometimes Timothy, are included as brothers [one manuscript omits “brother”]. Timothy is included in only four Epistles, either because they were composed at the same time or because Timothy and the others were present. I think this was done for two reasons: so that the Epistle might possess greater authority, since it was not written by one person alone; and because there was no rivalry among the apostles. If, while Paul was dictating, the Spirit suggested something to someone else, Paul added it to the letter he was dictating without any resentment.

He himself instructed the Corinthians that if something is revealed to another while one is prophesying, the one who was previously prophesying should keep silent (1 Cor. XIV). Thus he too fulfilled his own instruction in practice; and because, at another’s suggestion, he had added a few points, he prefaced the other’s Epistle as he did his own.

“Philemon,” he says, “the beloved.” The Greek does not have ἠγαπημένῳ, which means “beloved,” but ἀγαπητῷ, that is, “worthy of love” or “lovable.” The difference between one who is beloved and one who is worthy of love is that a person may be called beloved even if he does not deserve love. One who is worthy of love, however, is only the person who is loved deservedly. Thus we are commanded to love even our enemies, who are beloved but not lovable. We love them not because they deserve to be loved, but because we are commanded not to hate them.

Likewise, what is written in the title of the forty-fourth Psalm—“for the beloved”—is better rendered in Greek as “for the one worthy of love.” That passage is most clearly understood of Christ. Although the Jews think that Solomon is called *IDIDIA* (), that is, “beloved of God,” because God gave him this name on account of his wisdom (2 Kings XII), who can more truly be called God’s beloved than the one of whom the Father speaks in the Gospel: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him” (Luke IX, 36)?

Thus Isaiah also has it written: “I will sing for my beloved a song of my beloved’s vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard” (Isa. V, 1). Thinking that this referred to the circumcision of the Jewish people, he stumbled against the stone of offense and the rock of stumbling, failing to recognize that the vineyard brought out of Egypt is the house of Israel, and that Christ is here called either the one worthy of love or the beloved—since he deserves to be loved by the saints, and the saints love him, offering him love rather than seeking any rewards of love in return.

Paul and Timothy therefore write to Philemon, “most beloved” and “fellow worker,” who is called most beloved because he is engaged in the same work of Christ; to Apphia [or: Appia], a sister, who has nothing false or feigned in her relationship; and to Archippus, their fellow soldier. I think that he fought together with Paul and Timothy against their adversaries for Christ’s name, emerged victorious, and is therefore now called a fellow soldier because he prevailed in the same struggle and battle.

The letter is also written to the Church that is in his house. This is ambiguous: does it mean the Church that is in Archippus’s house, or the Church that is in Philemon’s house? It seems to me that it should refer not to Archippus but to Philemon, to whom the Epistle itself is also addressed. Although Paul and Timothy jointly write to Philemon, Apphia, Archippus, and the Church, what follows shows that Paul writes only to Philemon and converses with one person alone.

“I give thanks to my God always” [our manuscripts add “for you,” words unknown to the Greek text and likewise to the Latin translator] “making mention of you.” You will find this manner of writing in several of his Epistles: although several people, and several recipients, are named in the preface, afterward throughout the whole body of the Epistle one person is introduced as speaking.

What the Apostle says when writing to the Galatians—that in the faith of Christ it makes no difference whether someone is Gentile or Jew, male or female, slave or free (Gal. III, 28)—is also made evident here. Between two men and apostles, between Paul’s fellow worker and his fellow soldier, the name of Apphia is inserted in the middle, so that, supported by such company on either side, she may not appear to have rank according to sex, but according to merit.

When he says, “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ,” he is still writing from two persons to several, and the beginning is almost the same in all the Epistles: he invokes grace and peace upon them from God the Father and Christ the Lord.

[Note: Martianay wrongly has *quale*; other slight errors of this kind are corrected here and there.]

From this it is shown that the Son and the Father have one nature, since the Son can grant what the Father grants, and the Father is said to grant what the Son grants.

Grace is that by which we are saved without any merit or work of our own. Peace is that by which we have been reconciled to God through Christ, as in the words: “We beseech you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God” (2 Cor. V, 20).

### (Verses 4 and following)

“I give thanks to my God always, making mention of you in my prayers, hearing of your love and of the faith which you have in the Lord Jesus and toward all his saints, so that the fellowship of your faith may become evident in the knowledge of every good thing that is in you [or: in us] in Christ.”

[Note: The Cistercian manuscripts read “in us”; the Greek text also varies between ὑμῖν (“you”) and ἡμῖν (“us”).]

This is no longer Paul and Timothy speaking to Philemon and the others, but Paul alone speaking to Philemon alone: “I give thanks,” he says, “to my God always [one manuscript adds ‘and’], making mention of you in my prayers.” It is ambiguous whether he means that he always gives thanks to his God, or that he always makes mention of him in his prayers. Both meanings can be understood.

For the one who instructs others to give thanks to God in all things could not be so constrained by any troubles that he himself would fail always to give thanks to God. If Paul always prayed for the saints and for all who were superior in virtue—and Philemon too is a saint, possessing such faith and love that it was known not merely by report but also by his actions—it is credible that Paul always prayed for Philemon. In this way, the faith and love that he had in Christ and toward all his saints might, through the fellowship of faith and the practice that comes from knowledge of every good thing, be preserved by Christ’s mercy.

There is no difficulty in interpreting the love that he had in Christ Jesus and toward all his saints: it is the love by which, after God, we are commanded to love our neighbors. The question now is how someone can have the same faith in Christ Jesus and in his saints. For the phrase ἀπὸ κοινοῦ—“by common construction”—extends to both clauses: “the love which you have in the Lord Jesus and toward all his saints,” and “the faith which you have in the Lord Jesus and toward all his saints.”

[Note: Here we have followed the authority of the older Cistercian manuscript for the two following lines: “and the faith which you have in the Lord Jesus and toward all his saints.” These words are necessary to the completeness of the sentence, but, because the same words recur and conclude the immediately preceding sense, they are thought to have escaped the copyist’s eyes through a very common lapse. Rabbanus too once read them in his copy.]

For an explanation of this passage, let us take an example from Exodus: “The people believed God and Moses his servant” (Exod. XIX). One and the same act of belief is referred to Moses and to God, so that the people who believed in the Lord are likewise said to have believed in his servant.

This applies not only to Moses but to all his saints: whoever believes in God cannot receive faith in him in any other way than by believing also in his saints. Love and faith in God are not perfect if they are weakened by hatred and unbelief toward his ministers.

What I mean is this: someone believes in God the Creator. He cannot believe unless he has first believed that the things written about his saints are true: that Adam was fashioned by God; that Eve was formed from his rib and side; that Enoch was translated; that Noah alone was preserved from the shipwreck of the world; that Abraham was the first to be commanded to leave his land and his kin, and left to his descendants the circumcision he had received as a sign of the offspring to come; that Isaac was offered as a sacrifice, and that the ram slaughtered in his place and crowned with thorns prefigured the Lord’s Passion; that Moses and Aaron afflicted Egypt with ten plagues; and that, at the voice and prayers of Jesus son of Nun, the sun stood still at Gibeon and the moon in the valley of Aijalon.

It would be lengthy to review all the deeds of the Judges and to draw the entire story of Samson into the mystery of the true sun—for that is what his name signifies. Let me come to the Books of the Kings: when, at Samuel’s prayer, rain fell from heaven in the season of harvest and suddenly streams flowed; when David was anointed king; when Nathan and Gad prophesied mysteries; when Elijah was carried away in a fiery chariot; and when Elisha, possessing a double spirit, raised the dead.

These and the other things written about the saints must all be believed. Unless someone believes them all, he will not be able to believe in the God of the saints. Nor can anyone be brought to faith in the Old Testament unless he acknowledges as true everything that history recounts about the patriarchs, prophets, and other distinguished men.

[Note: Victor has “has confirmed as true” instead.]

Thus, from faith in the Law he comes to faith in the Gospel, and the righteousness of God is revealed in him “from faith to faith,” as it is written: “But the righteous shall live by faith” (Hab. II).

Elsewhere too we are commanded: “Be holy, for I am holy, says the Lord your God” (Lev. XIX, 2). The same holiness is owed to servants and to the Lord, for “the sanctifying one and those who are sanctified are all from one.”

Let us not regard Philemon’s profession of faith as insignificant if he has the same faith in the saints as he has in God. Whoever believes that God is holy certainly does not err. But if someone believes that a human being who is not holy is holy, and joins him to the fellowship of God, he violates Christ, whose body we all are.

“He who says,” Scripture says, “that the just is unjust and the unjust just, is abominable before God” (Prov. XVII, 15). Likewise, whoever says that one who is not holy is holy, or again asserts that one who is holy is not holy, is abominable before God.

According to the Apostle, all believers become—or, in another reading, “we become”—the body of Christ (1 Cor. VI). Whoever errs and stumbles in regard to Christ’s body by asserting that one of his members is holy when it is not, or is not holy when it is holy, should consider what crime he incurs: “Woe,” says Isaiah, “to those who call evil good and good evil, who put darkness for light and light for darkness” (Isa. V, 20).

I think that holiness is “sweet,” while what is opposed to holiness is “bitter”; likewise, holiness can be understood as light and what is opposed to holiness as darkness. What money-changer among us, skilled in testing coins, do you think would not err in discerning the saints?

When someone has equal love and faith toward God and toward his saints, he ought to have an equal fellowship in that faith, so that, just as he believes and loves, he may complete his love and faith through his actions. Hence he says: “That it may become evident in the knowledge of every good thing,” or, as the Greek more correctly has it, “effective.” For ἐνεργής can properly be translated “effective” or “operative.” We should not believe that faith and love toward God and his saints are sufficient in themselves; what we believe must be completed through action.

It can happen that someone has faith and completes it through action, but does so simply and without possessing knowledge or understanding of it, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement: “I testify that they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom. X, 2). Today there are many simple people who perform works of righteousness but do not possess knowledge of the things they themselves do.

Therefore he adds: “So that the fellowship of your faith may become operative in the knowledge of every good thing.”

[Note: The Cistercian manuscripts read: “and with how many advances the discourse extends itself toward higher things,” and so forth.]

With how many stages and leaps the apostolic discourse stretches toward higher things! Someone has love and faith in God and in his saints, but perhaps he does not distribute that love equally among all. Perhaps he distributes it among all, but does not complete it through action. Perhaps he fulfills it both in intention and in action, but cannot possess perfect knowledge of his deeds.

[Note: Two manuscripts read: “someone may fulfill the intention, etc.”]

There may also be someone who possesses both action and knowledge, but does not possess knowledge of every good thing; for, while performing many deeds justly, gently, and diligently, he remains in some respect unequal to his own virtues.

Was Philemon not such a person? He possesses the fellowship of operative faith and love in the knowledge of every good thing. Since this is found in the apostles, let us not suppose that it is perfect merely because it is in them. Rather, it is wholly present because it belongs to Christ, so that whatever good is praised in Philemon and taken from the example of the apostles is good because it is drawn from Christ’s fountain.

[Note: The same manuscripts read: “that it is secure in him,” etc.]

### (Verse 7)

“For we had great joy and consolation in your love, because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you, brother.”

He more fully repeats and explains why he said: “I give thanks to my God, always making mention of you in my prayers.” It was indeed worthy to give thanks to God for Philemon’s love, since, by receiving and refreshing the saints’ inward affection of heart and the deep recesses of their souls, he had restored them.

This too is an idiom of the Apostle: he always uses the word “hearts” when he wishes to display complete love of mind. Thus, rejoicing with those who rejoice and believing himself refreshed with those who had been refreshed, he possesses not a passing and slight joy, such as may occur by chance, but a great joy, corresponding to and surpassing the love that was in Philemon. This joy was increased by the consolation flowing from Philemon’s love, full of the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation.

### (Verses 8–9)

“Therefore, although I have great confidence in Christ Jesus to command you what is fitting, for love’s sake I rather entreat you—being such a person as Paul, an old man, and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ.”

After first setting forth many praises of Philemon, and since the matter for which he was making a request was beneficial both to the one who was to grant it and to the one who asked it, Paul could have commanded rather than requested. This confidence arose from the fact that one who had accomplished such great works for Christ could not be unequal to himself in other matters.

But he prefers to ask rather than command, placing before him the great authority of the one who asks: the Apostle, an old man, and a prisoner of Jesus Christ.

Everything for which he asks is this: Onesimus, Philemon’s slave, having compounded his flight with theft, had plundered certain household property; then, going toward Italy so that he might be less easily apprehended nearby, he had squandered his master’s money in dissipation.

[Note: The manuscripts formerly read here *emendant* (“they correct”); Petrus Petitus in his book *Miscellaneous Questions* had likewise conjectured that this should be restored.]

Let no one think that we have invented this rashly and arbitrarily; he may learn it from what follows. Paul would never have said: “If he has wronged you or owes you anything, charge it to my account. I, Paul, have written this with my own hand; I will repay it,” nor would he have become surety for property that had been taken unless what had been taken had been dissipated.

While Paul was therefore imprisoned at Rome for confessing Christ, Onesimus believed in Christ and was baptized by him. Through worthy repentance he wiped away the stains of his former life, to such an extent that the apostle who became the witness of his conversion was the same man who had once rebuked Peter for not walking with the right step in the truth of the Gospel (Gal. II).

So far as the sin and crime by which he had injured his master are concerned, he does not deserve pardon. But so far as the testimony of the Apostle is concerned—who knows that he has been thoroughly converted—the one who is asked to pardon him is weighed down by a great obligation: the man who had been a fugitive slave and a robber has become the Apostle’s minister.

(What other ministry does the Apostle have except that of the Gospel of Christ Jesus?) He should now be pardoned not as a master’s slave, but as a fellow servant and fellow evangelist, since he is likewise a slave and minister of Christ.

### (Verses 10 and following)

“I entreat you concerning my son, whom I have begotten in my chains, Onesimus, who was once useless to you, but now is useful both to you and to me. I have sent him back to you. You, then, receive him—that is, my own heart—whom I wished to keep with me, so that he might minister to me in my chains for the Gospel.”

Wishing to obtain what he requests, Paul now says that he is pleading not for Philemon’s slave but for his own son—and for a son whom he has begotten in the chains of the Gospel, that is, in the sufferings he endured for Christ’s Gospel.

Previously Onesimus had been useless only to his master—for a slave who is a thief and fugitive harms no one except his master. Now, by contrast, through the compensation of usefulness—since he is useful to that same master, to Paul, and through Paul to others—he deserves more love than he had previously deserved hatred.

Hence he says: “Who was once useless to you.” “To you alone,” he says, “not to others; but now he is useful both to me and to you.” He is useful to his master because he could serve Paul in place of his master; he is useful to Paul because, while Paul is detained in prison and confined in chains, Onesimus can minister to him in the Gospel.

At the same time, we should admire the Apostle’s greatness of spirit and his mind burning with love for Christ. He is held in prison, bound with chains, constrained by the filth of his body, separation from his loved ones, and the darkness of punishment; yet he feels no injury, is not tortured by grief, and knows nothing else except thinking about the Gospel of Christ.

He knew that Onesimus was a slave; he knew that he was a fugitive; he knew that he had once been a robber, but had been converted to the faith of Christ. It requires great labor for such a man to persevere in what he has begun.

For this reason Paul repeatedly emphasizes that Onesimus is his son, the son of his chains, and the minister of the Gospel in which he is imprisoned. He does so so that Philemon, who had been praised so prudently and deliberately in the preface, would not dare to refuse, lest he appear unworthy of his own praises.

When he says, “You, then, receive him—that is, my own heart,” this means what I said shortly before: “heart” signifies inward affection and the full willingness of the soul, when everything that is within us is received by the person being asked. In another sense, all free persons are the hearts of their parents.

### (Verse 14)

“But I wished to do nothing without your counsel, so that your good deed might not be as though compelled, but voluntary.”

This passage can resolve the question that many raise and revisit repeatedly: why, when God created humanity, did he not make human beings good and upright from the beginning?

If God is good voluntarily and not by necessity, then, when making humanity in his own image and likeness, he ought to have made human beings in such a way that they too would be good voluntarily and not by necessity.

Those who assert that humanity ought to have been made so that it could not receive evil are saying that it ought to have been made good by necessity, not by will. But if humanity had been made in such a way as to accomplish good not voluntarily but necessarily, it would not have been like God, who is good because he wills to be good, not because he is compelled.

It is therefore clear that they demand contradictory things of one another. When they say, “Humanity ought to have been made like God,” they ask that humanity be created with free choice, as God himself is. But when they add that humanity ought to have been made unable to receive evil, thereby imposing the necessity of goodness upon it, they want humanity not to be like God.

The Apostle Paul could therefore have retained Onesimus in his ministry without Philemon’s consent. But if he had done this without Philemon’s will, it would indeed have been good, but not voluntary. What is not voluntary is shown, in another respect, not to be good. Nothing can be called good unless it is freely chosen.

Here we should consider the Apostle’s prudence: for this reason he sends the fugitive slave back to his master, so that he may benefit his master; he could not benefit him if he were kept while his master was absent.

The earlier question is therefore resolved in this way: God could have made humanity good without humanity’s will. But if he had done so, the goodness would not have been voluntary but necessary. What is good by necessity is not good, and in another respect is shown to be evil.

Therefore, by leaving us to our own judgment, he made us more in his own image and likeness. To be like God is unconditionally good.

(Verses 15–16.) For perhaps this reason he departed from you for an hour, so that you might receive him back forever. Now no longer as a slave, but as more than a slave, a most beloved brother—especially to me, but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.

Sometimes evil becomes an occasion of good, and God turns the wicked plans of human beings toward what is right. What I mean will become clearer by an example. Joseph’s brothers, driven on by the goads of jealousy, sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty [Note: At this place, according to the interpreters of the Septuagint, who put twenty gold pieces where there were twenty pieces of silver. On this, see Jerome himself in his commentary on Matthew, chapter 26. MART. — It was also noted by the same holy Doctor above, in his Commentary on Matthew, chapter 26, that Joseph was not sold, as many think, for twenty gold pieces according to the Septuagint interpreters (though Jerome agrees with them here), but, according to the Hebrew truth, for twenty pieces of silver.] gold pieces (Genesis 37). This became the beginning of every good thing both for his father, his brothers, and all Egypt. Finally, he later said to his brothers: “You intended evil against me, but God intended good” (Genesis 45:8).

We can understand something similar in Onesimus: that evil beginnings became occasions for a good outcome. For if he had not fled from his master, he would never have come to Rome, where Paul was bound in prison. If he had not seen Paul in chains, he would not have received faith in Christ. If he had not received faith in Christ, he would never, having become Paul’s son, have been sent out for the work of the Gospel. Thus, by gradual stages and through the reversal of the argument, Onesimus became a minister of the Gospel because he had fled from his master.

By beautifully adding the word “perhaps,” however, Paul moderated his statement. For God’s judgments are hidden, and it is rash to pronounce as certain what is doubtful. “Perhaps,” he says, “he departed for this reason”: cautiously, hesitantly, tremblingly, and without setting his foot down with complete firmness. For if he had not added “perhaps,” all slaves would have had to flee in order to become apostolic men.

When he joined the words “for an hour,” we should understand “hour” as “a period of time.” In comparison with eternity, all time is brief. “So that you might receive him forever.” No master of a slave is eternal: his power and the condition of both parties end in death. But Onesimus, who through faith in Christ has become eternal, began to be an eternal brother to the eternal Philemon, since Philemon too had believed in Christ and had received the spirit of freedom. He became not merely a slave, but a most beloved brother, an eternal brother—also to the eternal Apostle, his master, to whom Onesimus is joined in spirit just as he had previously been joined according to the condition of his flesh.

At that time, when he was subject to Philemon in the flesh, he was not joined to him in the Lord; but now he is joined to him both in the flesh and in the Lord. From this we understand that a slave who believes in Christ is bound to his twofold master by a twofold law: for a time he is joined to him by the necessity of the flesh, and forever he is united to him in spirit.

(Vers. 17.) “If, therefore, you regard me as a partner, receive him as you would receive me.” [Note: In Martianay’s text, incorrectly: “Philemon.”]

Philemon desired to have Paul as a partner; and, believing in Christ, he wished to have such attainments that he might become like Paul and share with him in his chains. Let us therefore consider how greatly Onesimus is praised here, and how much progress he is said to have made, since he is to be received as the Apostle himself, and since his master ought to desire Paul’s companionship in the same way.

Briefly, what Paul says is this: “If you wish to have me as a partner, then have Onesimus also, whom I regard as my partner, my son, and my own heart. If you do not receive him, and do not wish to have him, you yourself understand that you cannot have me either.”

(Vers. 18.) “But if he has wronged you in anything, or owes you anything, charge it to me.”

As an imitator of his Lord and as one who has Christ speaking in him, Paul ought, according to his strength, to do what Christ did. For if Christ bore our weaknesses and grieved over our wounds, the Apostle rightly takes his stand on behalf of Onesimus and pledges what Onesimus owed.

As we said above, the whole matter was this: what had been taken by theft and squandered through extravagance could not otherwise be discharged. Philemon reckoned it at a great price [Al. “compensated for it”], since in place of a runaway slave and lost money he received both a most beloved brother and an eternal brother, and through him made the Apostle his debtor.

(Vers. 19.) “I, Paul, have written this with my own hand. I will repay it—not to mention that you owe me even your own self.”

What he says amounts to this: “What Onesimus took by theft, I pledge that I will repay. This letter and my own hand are witnesses to my pledge, for I did not dictate it in the usual manner, but wrote it myself with my own hand. Believe me, then, when I make this promise on behalf of Onesimus.

“But I say this as though I were speaking to someone unrelated to me. However, if I return to my rightful claim, on account of the message of Christ that I preached to you, through which you became a Christian, you owe me your very self. And if you are mine, and all that is yours is mine, then Onesimus too, since he is yours, is mine. I could therefore use him as my own; but I leave him to your will, so that by forgiving him you may have the reward.”

(Vers. 20.) “Yes, brother, may I enjoy you in the Lord.”

The Latin expression does not convey the distinctive force of the Greek. [Note: The old manuscripts and early printed books suffice to restore the negative particle which Martianay rashly omitted.] For when he says, ναὶ, ἀδελφέ—“yes, brother”—the ναί is a kind of adverb expressing affectionate entreaty. But when we translate it as “yes, brother,” we sound something more commonplace and diluted than what is written.

For just as the Hebrew word אָֽנָּא (anna), for which the Septuagint interpreters often used ὦ δή, expresses in its own language the feeling of one who entreats—and therefore Symmachus sometimes translated anna as δέομαι, that is, “I beseech”—so we too experience in the Greek language the same force that the Greeks encounter in the Hebrew.

But when Paul says, “May I enjoy you in the Lord,” the meaning is very different from what is generally supposed. The Apostle enjoys only one who possesses many virtues harmoniously joined together, and everything that is called “Christ” according to the variety of circumstances: wisdom, justice, continence, gentleness, self-control, and chastity. He invokes these virtues upon Philemon, so that when Philemon abounds in them, Paul himself may be filled by enjoying him.

And so that you may not think that he is speaking of the kind of enjoyment by which we often delight in one another’s presence, he adds, “in the Lord.” By attaching the Lord’s name, he indicates that there is another kind of enjoyment by which someone may enjoy a person apart from the Lord.

“Refresh my heart in Christ.” Just as Paul wishes to enjoy Philemon in the Lord, so he wishes his own heart—namely, Onesimus, whom he also called by this name above—to be refreshed through Philemon. The expression is deliberately ambiguous: is Onesimus Paul’s heart in Christ, or is Onesimus Paul’s heart to be refreshed through Philemon in Christ?

If you choose the first interpretation, Onesimus is rightly called Paul’s heart in Christ, since Paul begot him for Christ while in chains. If the second, Onesimus is to be refreshed in Christ by Philemon, as he is instructed by Philemon’s words concerning Christ.

(Vers. 21.) “Confident of your obedience, I have written to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say.”

Whoever presumes upon the obedience of the person whom he is about to ask thereby, in a certain sense, prejudges the matter, so that the person asked cannot refuse what is requested. Moreover, if the one who asks knows that the person asked will do more than he has requested, he asks for less so that the person asked may have a willing response and a greater reward through his performance.

But if Philemon does these things at a human command, how much more will he do them out of love for God? Thus he is rightly praised by the Apostle’s voice, because he anticipates Paul’s commands in his action and can say: “May the free offerings of my mouth please you, O Lord” (Psalm 118:108). By doing more than was commanded, he surpasses those who merely did what was ordered and who are commanded to say: “We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we were obliged to do” (Luke 17:10).

Virginity too is crowned with a greater reward for this reason: because it has no commandment from the Lord and extends itself beyond what is commanded.

(Vers. 22.) “At the same time, prepare a lodging for me.”

I do not think that the Apostle was so wealthy, or so occupied with such great burdens, that he required a lodging to be prepared for him, and that, not content with a single room, he considered a dwelling of limited space sufficient for his body to be a spacious house. [Note: Formerly the text read: “so that he might concern himself with preparing a lodging,” and, “not content with a single room, he considered a dwelling of limited space for his body sufficient.” Victorius long ago restored the printed reading and explains it in this way: the Apostle regarded even very small and narrow dwellings as extremely spacious in proportion to the space occupied by his body.]

Rather, while Philemon is expecting him to come to him, Paul wants Philemon to do more fully what he has been asked. But if anyone thinks that Paul’s instruction to prepare lodging was not a matter of administrative prudence but was literally intended, then lodging must be prepared for the Apostle more than for Paul.

He was going to come to a new city to preach the Crucified One and bring unheard-of doctrines. He knew that very many people would flock to him. It was therefore necessary, first, that the house should be in a prominent part of the city, where people could easily gather. Second, it should be free from every kind of disturbance; it should be large enough to hold many hearers; it should not be near places of public spectacles; it should not be made detestable by a shameful neighborhood; and, finally, it should be situated on level ground rather than in an upper room.

For this reason I think that even at Rome he remained for two years in a rented dwelling [Al. “for two years”]. Nor, I think, was it a small lodging to which crowds of Jews came together every day.

“For I hope that through your prayers I shall be granted to you.” God, when entreated, grants the Son to the Father, and a brother is often saved through the prayer of his brother. The Apostle is granted through the prayers of the whole Church, for the benefit of those who will hear him.

This gift is said to be bestowed less upon the one who is being transferred from martyrdom to martyrdom, already prepared for it, than upon those to whom the Apostle is sent. Paul himself says elsewhere that he was frequently in prison and was released from his chains: “In prisons frequently” (2 Corinthians 11). Sometimes, by the Lord’s help, he was released because the persecutors themselves found nothing in him worthy of death.

For senatorial decrees against the Christian name had not yet been issued, nor had Nero’s sword consecrated Christian blood. But because the preaching was new, whether by envious Jews or by those who saw their idols being destroyed, Paul and the others were sent to prison when the crowds had been stirred to fury; then, when the violence and rage had subsided, they were released.

The Acts of the Apostles testify that this is so. There Felix says to Agrippa that Paul could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar (Acts 25). Felix had found no charge against him except certain questions concerning their own religion and concerning a certain Jesus whom Paul declared to be alive.

From this we observe that Paul could similarly have been released by the other judges, the Lord arranging matters so that the new preaching might be spread throughout the whole world.

(Verses 23–24.) “Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, greets you, as do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers.”

This confirms what we said at the beginning: that the Epistle to the Colossians was written at the same time and carried by the same bearer of the letters as the Epistle to Philemon. The names of those introduced as sending greetings also demonstrate this.

For in the Epistle to the Colossians it is written: “Aristarchus, my fellow prisoner, greets you, and Mark, the cousin of Barnabas, and Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ” (Colossians 4:10, 12). A little farther on: “Luke, the most beloved physician, greets you, and Demas; and say to Archippus: ‘See to the ministry that you have received in the Lord, so that you may fulfill it’” (ibid., 14, 17). And: “Remember my chains” (ibid., 18).

If anyone does not think that the two letters were written at the same time because only a few of the names listed here appear in the Epistle to the Colossians, let him know that not everyone is a friend or acquaintance of everyone else, and that a private letter to one person is one thing, while a public letter addressed to the whole Church is another.

“Epaphras,” he says, “my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, greets you.” We have received the following account of who Epaphras, Paul’s fellow prisoner, was.
