They say that the parents of the Apostle Paul came from the region of Gyscalis in Judea, and that, when the whole province was devastated by Roman force and the Jews were scattered throughout the world, they were transferred to Tarsus, a city of Cilicia. The young Paul followed the condition of his parents.

Thus the statements that he himself makes can stand: “Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they the seed of Abraham? So am I” (2 Corinthians 11:22); and again elsewhere: “A Hebrew of Hebrews” (Philippians 3:5), together with the other statements that indicate him to have been more a Jew than a native of Tarsus.

If this is so, we may also suppose that Epaphras was captured at the time when Paul was captured, and that, having been settled with his parents in Colossae, a city of Asia, he later received the message of Christ. Thus, as we said above, the Epistle to the Colossians says: “Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ, always striving for you in his prayers” (Colossians 4:12).

If this is the case, Aristarchus too, who in the same Epistle is called his fellow prisoner, will be brought under the same interpretation—unless perhaps the word “captivity” points, as some think, to something hidden and sacred: that those who were captured and bound together were brought into this valley of tears.

If neither interpretation is accepted, then from the addition “in Christ Jesus” we may suppose that Aristarchus endured at Rome the same chains for Christ that Paul did; and just as he was called Christ’s prisoner, so he could also be called Christ’s captive.

Or it may mean that Aristarchus too was noble among the apostles, like Andronicus and Junia, concerning whom Paul writes to the Romans: “Greet Andronicus and Junia, my relatives and fellow prisoners, who are notable among the apostles and who were in Christ before me” (Romans 16:7).

This concerns Epaphras. As for the fellow workers in the Gospel and in his chains, when Paul wrote to Philemon he lists Mark, whom I think to have been the author of the Gospel; Aristarchus, whom we mentioned above; and Demas, concerning whom he complains elsewhere: “Demas has deserted me, loving the present age, and has gone to Thessalonica.”

He also lists Luke the physician, who, leaving the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles to the Churches, was transformed from a physician of bodies into a physician of souls—just as the Apostles, from fishermen of fish, became fishers of human beings (Matthew 4). Concerning Luke Paul says elsewhere: “I sent with him the brother whose praise in the Gospel is throughout all the Churches” (2 Corinthians 8:18). Whenever his book is read in the Churches, his healing work does not cease.

(Vers. 25.) “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.”

Just as the people of Israel are counted from the better part of the human being, the head, when Scripture says, “according to their heads” (Numbers 1:2), so in the whole human being and in every part of the saints there is the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ.

But from the greater and better part—that is, from the spirit—what is said by synecdoche concerning the whole human being is: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.” When grace is in the spirit, it makes the whole person spiritual, so that the flesh serves the spirit, and the soul is not conquered by the flesh. Thus, being drawn together into a spiritual substance, it clings to the Lord, because “whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit” (2 Corinthians 6).

According to the Jews [Al. “Hebrews”], Paul is interpreted as “admirable”; Timothy, “beneficent”; Philemon, “wonderfully gifted,” or “mouth of bread,” from mouth, not from bone; Apphia, “self-controlled” or “freedom”; Archippus, “length of work”; Onesimus, “answering”; Epaphras, “fruitful,” and “seeing,” or “growing up”; Mark, “lofty in command”; Aristarchus, “a mountain of greater work”; Demas, “silent”; Luke, “himself rising.”

If you wish to understand these names according to their interpretations, it is not difficult to see that the admirable and beneficent one writes especially to him to whom it has been granted to conquer every vice [Note: Two Cistercian manuscripts read: “to whom it has been granted to conquer vices”], and whose mouth is open toward heavenly bread.

Then he writes to one who is self-controlled and free, and to one marked by length of labor, who never ceases from holy toil. He writes on behalf of one who answers to his testimony, and also to the one to whom the Epistle is specially dedicated, greeting him from the abundance that continues to grow.

He writes also to the one who has been made loftier through commandments, and to the one who has grown upward through greater works even to the mountain; and to the one who has set a guard over his mouth and a fortified door upon his lips—who perhaps was silent for this reason, because he had abandoned the Apostle for a short time.

Finally, he writes to the one who rises by his own strength each day, increasing and making progress, while the world is filled with his Gospel and he grows each time that his message is heard and read and builds people up.

---

# APPENDIX TO VOLUME SEVEN OF THE WORKS OF ST. EUSEBIUS HIERONYMUS, CONTAINING THE COMMENTARIES ON JOB AND THE BRIEF COMMENTARY ON THE PSALMS

[Col. 0619]

## COMMENTARIES ON THE BOOK OF JOB (C, G, S)*

The Commentaries on Job, which the editor of Verona had appended to the commentaries on the Major Prophets in order to enlarge the fifth volume, we have transferred here, following the biblical order from another source, so that our volume might not exceed its proper size.

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0619A] Job, whose name is interpreted as “sorrowing” or [Note: Read “great” without qualification; see the Book of Names, col. 121, and elsewhere], “great,” bore the figure of Christ. His friends, however, represent heretics, who, under the name of Christ, blaspheme and oppose Christ. Elihu and Baldad [Al. “Bildad”] present the type of philosophers, because, standing outside—that is, outside the faith—they lie in wait for the Church of God.

These men impose precious names upon themselves, as though they were themselves the gold of God or his foremost watchers. For Eliphaz in Latin sounds like “the gold of my God.” Baldad means “foremost,” “ancient secrets.” Sophar means “the dispersal of the watchtowers,” or “one who disperses the watcher,” or “I shall see the watcher.” [Note: In the same Book of Names: Eliphaz, “contempt of God”; Baldad, “mere antiquity”; Sophar, “the dispersal of the watchtowers,” or “one who disperses the watcher,” or “I shall see the watcher.”]

These men, puffed up because through the natural good of their minds they preached certain things wisely, boast among themselves of severity, though they are advocates of falsehood. For they speak about Christ not in a manner fitting his divinity, but in a manner suited to their own impiety.

## THE CHAPTERS BEGIN TO BE EXPOUNDED

[Col. 0619]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0619B]

“There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job. That man was simple and upright, fearing God and turning away from evil. Seven sons and three daughters were born to him. His possessions were seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen, and five hundred she-donkeys, together with a very large household. That man was greater than all the men of the East.

“His sons went and held banquets in their houses, each on his appointed day. They sent and summoned their three sisters to eat and drink with them. When the days of the banquets had gone round, Job sent for them and sanctified them; rising early at dawn, and so forth.”

Uz and Buz were sons of Nahor, Abraham’s brother, and of Milcah, Sarah’s sister; Job descended from their line. He was not, as some falsely suppose, of the race of Esau (Jerome, Questions on Genesis). For Eliphaz was born of Adah, Esau’s wife, and ruled in Teman; hence he was also called a Temanite. Teman, Idumaea, Seir, Daroma, and Zebora were regions of Esau.

Job, a great man, lived in the land of Uz, which is interpreted as “counseling.” Likewise Elkanah, whose name is interpreted as “possession of God,” the father of the most holy prophet Samuel, is called one man. He was not carried about unstable and changeable in different directions; rather, standing firm and unshaken, he was one man. Therefore he lived on Mount Ephraim, a fruitful mountain: in the high contemplation of virtues, so that the sublimity of his mind would not be cast down or divided by any movements of vices lying beneath and barking around him.

Accordingly, this great and distinguished man Job is said to have lived in the land of Uz, which is interpreted as “counseling.” The land of his flesh did not rule over his soul; rather, he did everything according to the counsel of his commanding mind. Hence he himself says: “I made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not even think upon a virgin.”

Thus his inner and outer human being once made this counsel and covenant with one another: that his earth—that is, his flesh—by obeying should become a counselor to the spirit, so that in it iniquity might not rule.

And because, according to the divine testimony, the man was simple, dwelling in his house, he possessed four virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance.

“He offered burnt offerings for each one. For he said: ‘Perhaps my sons have sinned and cursed God in their hearts.’ Thus Job did all his days.

“Now one day, when the sons of God had come to stand before the Lord, Satan was also present among them. The Lord said to him: ‘Where have you come from?’ He answered: ‘I have gone around the earth and traversed it.’ The Lord said to him: ‘Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth: a simple and upright man, fearing God and turning away from evil?’

“Satan answered the Lord: ‘Does Job fear God for no reason? Have you not fenced him in, together with his house and all his possessions, on every side? You have blessed the works of his hands, and his possessions have increased in the land. But stretch out your hand a little and touch everything he possesses; surely he will bless you to your face.’

“Then the Lord said to Satan: ‘Behold, everything he has is in your hand; only do not stretch out your hand against him.’ And Satan went out from the presence of the Lord.

“Now one day, when his sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their firstborn brother, a messenger came to Job and said: ‘The oxen were plowing and the she-donkeys were grazing beside them, when the Sabaeans fell upon them, took everything, and struck the servants with the sword. I alone escaped to tell you.’

“While he was still speaking, another came and said: ‘The fire of God fell from heaven and consumed the sheep and the servants. I alone escaped to tell you.’

“While he was still speaking, another came and said: ‘The Chaldaeans formed three companies, attacked the camels, and took them. They also struck the servants with the sword. I alone escaped to tell you.’

“While he was still speaking, behold, another entered and said: ‘While your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their firstborn brother, suddenly a violent wind rushed in from the desert region and shook the four corners of the house. As it collapsed, it crushed your children, and they died. I alone escaped to tell you.’”

Job governed his sons in such a way that through continual sacrifices he sought divine mercy not merely for their manifest sins, but also for the hidden sins of their hearts, which can escape even human knowledge.

The privilege of offering sacrifices for firstborn sons belonged especially to kings, on account either of the excellence of their wisdom or the nobility of their lineage.

And since we have said that Job bore the figure of Christ, let us now see what the land of Uz signifies in Christ. By this land we understand the true human being assumed from Mary. It is called “counseling” because, when the Son of God assumed it, the treasures of divine wisdom and knowledge came to dwell hidden within it through the divinity of the one who assumed it. He joined it to himself in such an inseparable union that he himself is one Son of God in the Trinity.

The seven sons seem to signify the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, and the three daughters the Law, the Prophecy, and the Gospel.

He calls the sheep the people of Christ because of their innocence: in baptism they have laid aside the filth of their sins. In the camels he displays the wickedness of the nations, coming to Christ under the burden of their crimes and with twisted understandings.

In the oxen, which are clean animals, he indicates the people of the Jews. In the donkeys, an unclean herd, he indicates the people of the nations. Hence Isaiah says: “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger.” This means that both Jews in part and the nations have recognized Christ’s birth in the flesh, and that they have approached the manger of the Lord’s altar as clean animals through Baptism.

Perhaps the saying in the Gospel also refers to this: “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” In the yoke he signified the Jews; in the donkey, to which the burden is more properly assigned, he signified the nations, as we said above.

Christ is called great among all the men of the East, according to the saying: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.”

The number of the animals—seven, three thousand, and five hundred—is sacred. For seven, according to the authority of Scripture, signifies a certain fullness of the sacred mystery, as in the seven spirits, the seven lampstands, and the seven Churches.

In the three thousand, the soul, body, and spirit may be understood; or the knowledge of the threefold teaching in the holy Scriptures; or the sacrament of the blessed Trinity. This is because the whole multitude of believers, walking a journey of three days, desires to reach the perfection of eternity.

The five hundred, which arise from five and, multiplied fivefold, make fifty-five [the numerical wording is uncertain], signify that after passing through the instabilities of an unsteady age, the human being has crossed over into a mature and perfect person. Through ten times five they reach fifty, and through ten times fifty they rise to five hundred.

Similarly, the entire Church is signified, the pillar and foundation of Christ’s truth, in which our senses receive either purification or forgiveness of sins. For in this number not only the forgiveness of sins but also the coming of the Holy Spirit is declared.

The sons of God are to be understood either as angels or as saints, who by the gift of the grace of the Holy Spirit are called sons of God. Among these, therefore, the devil is said to stand, because by God’s permission he often dares to tempt the saints.

How remarkable was the brotherly harmony of Job’s sons! But because we have shown that Job bears the figure of Christ, we say that these sons signify figuratively the seven graces of the Church. They take part in the spiritual sacramental banquet and, having with them the three sisters—Law, Prophecy, and the Gospels—are filled with the nourishment of the understanding of the divine utterances.

In the collapse of the house that crushed Job’s sons, he shows the persecution of the ancient rulers and kingdoms, and their savagery against the Church. The one who alone remained in order to report it indicates the scarcity of the persecutors themselves.

“Sabaeans” is interpreted as “captives,” and “Chaldaeans” as “demons.” These captives of demons attack the Church. Not only do they drive away the Lord’s flocks wherever they can, but they also consume them with their own fire—which they falsely claim to be heavenly—through heresies or the perversity of superstition.

The violent winds, like the presence of fiercely hostile kings, shake the house of Christ, which is confirmed by the four Gospels as though by four corners, so that the seven sons and three daughters perish together with the house itself.

[Col. 0623A] “Then Job arose, tore his garments, and, having shaved his head, fell upon the ground and worshiped. And he said: ‘Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall return there. The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord.’”

He arose for the endurance of patience. For Job—that is, Christ—also arose to give peace to the Church, so that the event might signify vengeance.

He tore his garments: he separated the faithful from the unfaithful. He fell upon the ground when he emptied himself from the form of God into the form of a servant. He came naked from his mother’s womb, not sprinkled with any stain of original sin.

Speaking in the person of humanity, he says: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away.” The Father gave good people as an inheritance and excluded evil people from the kingdom of his Son.

[Col. 0623B] “In all these things Job did not sin with his lips, nor did he speak anything foolish against God.”

This is said because the Wisdom of the Father could not speak foolishly, nor could the immaculate Lamb commit sin.

## CHAPTER II

“Now it happened that one day, when the sons of God had come and stood before the Lord, Satan also came among them and stood in his presence. The Lord said to Satan: ‘Where have you come from?’ He answered: ‘I have gone around the earth and traversed it.’

“And the Lord said to Satan: ‘Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth: a simple and upright man, fearing God, turning away from evil, and still holding fast to his innocence? But you have stirred me up against him, so that I might afflict him without cause.’

“Satan answered him: ‘Skin for skin, and everything a man has he will give for his life. But now stretch out your hand, touch his mouth and his flesh, and then you will see whether he will bless you to your face.’

“Then the Lord said to Satan: ‘Behold, he is in your hand; nevertheless, preserve his life.’

“So Satan went out from the presence of the Lord and struck Job with a most grievous ulcer, from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head. He scraped the discharge with a potsherd and sat in the place of refuse.

“His wife said to him: ‘Are you still persisting in your simplicity? Bless God and die.’

“He answered her: ‘You have spoken as one of the foolish women speaks. If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things?’ In all these things Job did not sin with his lips.

“Then the three friends of Job, hearing of all the evil that had happened to him, came, each from his own place: Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite. For they had agreed to come together to visit him and console him.

“When they had lifted their eyes from afar, they did not recognize him.”

This was not because God is ignorant, but to teach us what Satan, whose name means “adversary,” would answer.

[Col. 0623D] “They cried out and wept, and, tearing their garments, they scattered dust upon their heads toward heaven. They sat with him on the ground for seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his pain was very great.”

All heretics also claim to be friends of Christ, boasting that they have been redeemed by his blood. Later they become his enemies by attacking his Church.

The fact that, when they saw his wound, they tore their garments and threw dust upon their heads signifies those heretics who believe Christ to be God in heavenly glory but do not believe in his incarnation and passion. Offended by his reproaches and humiliation, they burst into blasphemy, tear the faith apart, and depart from the unity of the body.

By throwing dust upon their heads, they cover and bury their hearts under an earthly and dead understanding. Throughout the entire period of their life, which is contained in the seven days and nights, they condemn their unworthy mouths by the mute wickedness of unbelief, and “the mouth of those who speak iniquity” is stopped.

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0624B]

“After this Job opened his mouth and cursed his day. He spoke: ‘Let the day perish in which I was born, and the night in which it was said: A man has been conceived. Let that day be turned into darkness.’”

After this, as the writer of this history says—tradition holds that it was Moses—Job opened his mouth and cursed his day, saying: “Let the day perish in which I was born, and the night in which it was said: A man has been conceived.”

Job, who bore in himself the figure of the Savior, mourned the mortality of the human race, which was inflicted upon humanity because of sin by the just sentence of God.

“Let the day perish in which I was born”: let immortality return through Christ, which Adam lost through the guilt of transgression, and let death depart from me, which I contracted through the sin of another.

Jeremiah likewise says: “Cursed be the day on which I was born.” Hence no one doubts that all these men detest Adam’s transgression.

Spiritually, therefore, the day together with its night may be understood as the devil and mortality—not because the devil is a day, but because he was one when he remained with God, and, departing from him, became night; or because he appears to be a day to the wicked and sinners who rejoice in their prosperity and happiness.

Hence it is said:

“His light shall be taken away from the wicked. Let God not seek him from above.”

That is: let his memory not be made known before God for good.

“And let him not be enlightened by light.”

That is, by the light of the knowledge of God or of repentance.

“Let darkness and the shadow of death obscure him.”

Darkness means sins and envy.

“Let gloom seize him and let him be wrapped in bitterness.”

That is, blindness of heart.

“Let a dark whirlwind possess that night.”

Because he provokes God to bitterness, as do his other attendants; seized by the fury of God’s anger, let him be surrounded by every evil and wrapped in it.

“Let a dark whirlwind possess that night”: that is, the devil, who took away from humanity the day of happiness and turbulently brought in the night of an unsettled life.

“Let it not be counted among the days of the year.”

The year is understood as Christ, who turns all things within himself and contains them. Therefore let the devil not be counted among the days of this year; that is, let him not be joined to the number of the saints.

[Col. 0625A] “Nor let it be numbered among the months.”

Here we rightly understand the months as the holy Apostles, who, like the trees of paradise, bring forth spiritual fruits for the Church.

Let that night be solitary and unworthy of praise—namely, without the preaching of the apostles, through which the day of salvation is recognized, the day that Abraham saw and rejoiced.

Let those who curse the day curse it—those who are ready to rouse Leviathan. The saints, certainly, curse the day of their transgression and death with abhorrence; for, by refusing to serve vices, they rouse against themselves the dragon, that exceedingly powerful enemy.

Let the stars be darkened by its gloom. That is, let sinners—who, in the night of the world, think that they shine through its riches and honors—be darkened by the gloom of blindness and, as they deserve, fail to see the light of the Gospel.

[Col. 0625B] Let it await the light and not see it. Neither can the night of transgression and death, in which the devil holds his kingdom, recognize the light of Christ the Redeemer; nor can those who are born in it, unless they destroy it by being reborn through baptism.

Nor the rising of the dawn. He signified the resurrection of Christ; hence, in the psalm, it is called the morning watch.

For he did not close the doors of the womb that carried me, nor remove evils from my eyes. Why did I not die in the womb? Why, having come forth from the womb, did I not immediately perish? Why was I received upon knees? Why was I suckled at breasts? In his own person he laments the miseries of the human race: why should one who is destined to die again endure the evils of this life? Why should death itself not have extinguished a mortal in the womb?

Now, sleeping, I would be silent and rest in my sleep with the kings and consuls of the earth, who build themselves solitudes; or with princes who possess gold and fill their houses with silver. Princes, kings, and consuls—even if they suffer the squalors of Tartarus in hell—do not now feel torments in their bodies. I would have wished death to come to me under this condition.

Or, like a hidden abortion, I would not have endured; or like those conceived who did not see the light. In various ways and by various examples he says that he ought not to have suffered the punishments in which he found himself. Why did I not die in the womb? And afterward he says: Now, sleeping, I would be silent and rest in my sleep with kings and consuls. Perhaps this is an argument against those who say that only those who have been born in due order will rise again. For if those conceived die in the womb, it is necessary that they once lived; and whatever dies will undoubtedly rise again. Thus, whatever existed and lived in the limbs, even if nature gave it less, will be restored whole in the resurrection. For the restoration of the human race will return in its entirety for the better whatever nature had withheld.

He also says that abortions, which have degenerated within human nature, are free from punishments, as are those who build solitudes rather than houses for themselves. For the devil dwells in desolate cities and deserted houses. They have no guest in God, and they possess gold—as do philosophers and the other wise men of this world—the brilliance of a good intellect and the splendor of eloquence.

There the impious cease from turmoil. Without doubt, in hell. And as the Septuagint translated it, “There the impious laid down their fury”; that is, the arrogance and pride, together with the savagery of those who glory in this age, have been humbled in hell.

And there those weary in strength rested. As another translation has it: “There those fatigued in body rested”—freed, certainly, from oppression and misery, and also from the labor of this world.

And formerly the bound dwell together without distress. He says that those who bind and those who were formerly bound dwell together in hell, yet without injury or distress to the ones who were bound—not as here, where, besides punishments, people are held by captivity or harsh servitude and by various other calamities, under the domination and injustice of the wicked.

They did not hear the voice of the exactor. They do not fear the commands of rulers or of those who demand unjustly.

The small and the great are there, and the servant is free from his master. Why, then, is light given to the miserable, and life to those whose souls are in bitterness? They await death, and it does not come, as though they were digging for a treasure; and they rejoice exceedingly when they find a tomb. Since, as I see, there is equality of persons in hell, and no one fears another’s domination, why has this light and life been given to me, miserable as I am, like those whose souls are in bitterness, when the prison-houses of hell are better than the miserable life of this world, full of torments? Here, because of their anguish, people seek death and await it with great desire, longing for it to come. He supplied an excellent example when he said: “As though digging for a treasure,” since they certainly rejoice when they find the burial they have desired.

To the man whose life is hidden, and whom God has surrounded with darkness. He speaks of himself: Thus I walked in God’s commandments, believing that the fruit of my righteousness would answer for me; but the merit of my life has been hidden, and for this I have been surrounded by the darkness of punishments, so that the good has been taken away from me and this evil added. But that he called the punishments “darkness,” hear what follows:

Before I eat, I sigh, and my roaring is like overflowing waters. Among his other torments, the devil had also inflicted on him this illness, which physicians call *bolimiodes*. This illness is said to have such a punishment that the sick man is tormented before eating and suffers unceasing pains after eating. Hence he says: “My roaring is like overflowing waters.”

For the fear that I feared has come upon me. I feared, by sinning, to offend God, and that, once offended, he would exercise the anger of his justice against me. But what did it profit me to avoid sins, when I am tortured as though guilty of all sins? It follows:

And what I feared has happened. In other words, he repeats what he had said above. In Scripture such things are commonly repeated to confirm what has been said. He does not say this arrogantly, as though to do God an injury, but speaks freely in accordance with the testimony of his conscience.

Did I not dissemble? By not repaying those who repaid me with evil.

Did I not keep silent? “To avoid sinning with my tongue, I set a guard over my mouth.”

Did I not remain quiet? Knowing that, when God arose for judgment, he would save all the meek of the earth.

And indignation came upon me. Here he calls the mass of blows “indignation,” saying that it fell upon him, under whose weight and pains he laments that he was overwhelmed. Yet, as he said above, he himself was afflicted with diseases; in what follows he calls these punishments “arrows,” as when he says: “The arrows of the Lord are in me; their indignation has drunk up my spirit,” or, as another translation has it, “has drunk up my blood.” More properly, the arrows may be understood as worms, since he was pierced by their unceasing stings, as Job himself says: “Those who devoured me do not sleep.” The devil made them more eager to consume him, and they, as though indignant and angry, dug into his flesh with their bites, so that, like arrows, they penetrated into his inner organs.

Here ends the passage in which Job cursed the day of his birth.

## CHAPTER IV

Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said: If we begin to speak to you, perhaps you will take it badly. But who can restrain the word he has conceived? Thus he brings forth the words he has conceived as an injury to the hearer, and says:

Behold, you have instructed many. That is, by your skill and goodness you have recalled very many from error.

And you have strengthened weary hands. Your words have confirmed those who were wavering, and you have strengthened trembling knees. But now the blow has come upon you, and you have failed; it has touched you, and you are troubled. Where is your fear, your strength, your patience, and the perfection of your ways? These things are said to holy Job with mockery, and their meaning is this: If you had done what I have said, you would never have fallen into such great evils as an example to mortals, because we know God, the creator of all things, to be good and just.

Remember, I beg you: Has an innocent person ever perished, or when have the upright been destroyed? Rather, I have seen those who work iniquity and sow pains reap them, perish at God’s breath, and be consumed by the spirit of his anger. Do you therefore not know that Abel, innocent at the beginning, was killed, and that Abraham the patriarch was placed in danger because of his wife? Without distinguishing such cases, you pronounce a general judgment: when some people are chastised by the Lord so that they may be corrected, and others so that they may be tested—as is the case with this man—why do you reproach him as though he were guilty? Rather, those who worked iniquity perished at God’s breath; that is, they were lifted up by the sentence of the judge like a most violent wind and carried away from the hope of eternal life.

The roar of the lion, the voice of the lioness, and the teeth of the lion’s cubs are broken. By the roar and voice of the lioness he wished to signify the savagery of one who plunders.

The tiger perished because it had no prey, and the lion’s cubs were scattered. Moreover, a hidden word was spoken to me. In the tiger he describes its speed in stripping people and seizing prey from them; its cubs, likewise resembling it, were scattered and killed. In another edition, instead of “tiger” there is *myrmicoleon*—that is, “ant-lion,” an ant and a lion—which we may more truly call the devil. When he pursues prey and takes from the saints as though from greater things, he is to be regarded as a lion; but when he seeks to carry off the smallest things, he is to be called an ant. And just as an ant carries grains away from the threshing floor, so he carries good thoughts away from human hearts.

And my ear received, as though furtively, the veins of his whisper. In the horror of a nocturnal vision, when sleep usually overtakes people, fear and trembling seized me, and all my bones were terrified. When a spirit passed before me, the hairs of my flesh bristled. Something stood there whose face I did not recognize, an image before my eyes, and I heard a voice like a gentle breeze. Can a human being be justified in comparison with God, or can a man be purer than his maker? That is, the force of the judgment secretly penetrated to the ear of my heart like a certain breath.

Behold, those who serve him are not steadfast, and he finds perversity in his angels. How much more in those who dwell in houses of clay. This is indeed said of the devil, who was once a holy angel, because he did not remain in the truth and by his own will fell from that angelic sublimity. Yet it is not immediately a universal statement, as though perversity—which is sin—were found in all angels just as in him. For every created nature is undoubtedly capable of sin, as appeared in the angel of whom I have spoken, because he did not remain in the truth. Nevertheless, through the gift and grace of their creator they have passed into such love of charity that they now neither wish to sin nor are able to do so.

Those whose foundation is earthly will be consumed like a moth. If our bodies are houses of clay, the foundation of our houses must be understood as this temporary life; once it is taken away, our houses of clay collapse into death.

From morning until evening they will be cut down, and because no one understands, they will perish forever. Those who remain will be taken away from them; they will die, and not in wisdom. In one day he displayed the whole life of human beings, which flourishes in this world. It blooms in infancy, grows strong in youth, and is strengthened in mature age; in old age, as in fruits, it reaches completion, and finally it is finished in decrepit age, which he here called evening. Hence the psalm says: “In the morning may he pass away like grass,” and so forth: it falls in death and becomes hardened in a corpse.

## CHAPTER V

Call, then, if there is anyone who will answer you, and turn to one of the saints. Anger kills the foolish man, and envy slays the simple. I saw a fool firmly rooted, and immediately I cursed his beauty. His children will be far from salvation; they will be crushed at the gate, and there will be no one to rescue them. He calls “foolish” the one who boasts of his merits. Here, however, he calls “beauty” what is really false happiness; it must be cursed and execrated, because everlasting destruction follows it.

The hungry will eat his harvest, the armed man will carry him away, and the thirsty will drink his riches. Let nothing exist on earth without cause, and let no pain come forth from the ground. The thirsty, hungry, and armed may be understood as the devil and his followers, who receive power from God to lay waste to the wicked. Or they may be those who thirst for human death, so that every good of nature—what is called “riches”—is swallowed by them as though they had drained a cup. Or they may be wicked people who oppress their subjects.

A human being is born for labor, and a bird for flight. Therefore I will entreat the Lord and address my words to God. That is, labor warns [another reading: “awaits”] a person to proceed chastened from all vices.

[Col. 0629B] He does great and unsearchable things, and wonders without number. He gives rain upon the face of the earth and waters everything. He places the humble on high and raises the sorrowful to safety. Thus, in the Son of God, Christ the man is God, and through him the Church is raised.

He frustrates the thoughts of the wicked, so that their hands cannot accomplish what they had begun. This refers to the Jews, who thought they would extinguish Christ and erase his name from the earth. Or, in the martyrs, he frustrated the thoughts of those persecutors who opposed the Church, as he did Herod’s designs in Peter’s case. Alternatively: They do not fill their hands with what they desire, because some of their victims are delivered for a time, while others are brought through the gate of death into life; God will save both groups—some by openly delivering them, others by secretly crowning them.

He catches the wise in their craftiness and frustrates the counsel of the perverse. This refers to philosophers, or to the Jews, whom he convicts through apostolic teaching and reduces their errors to nothing.

By day they will encounter darkness. There was a “day” among the Jews, who gloried in kingdom, priesthood, law, and the religion of the one God; but because they did not believe in Christ, they fell into the darkness of faithlessness.

And at noon they will grope as in the night. That is, in the very prosperity that, with the customary splendor surrounding the fortunate of this age, had been increased by empty glory. They thought that, secured by a long period of safety, they would possess it until the evening of their life. But in the sudden tribulation called “night,” hemmed in by extreme confusion and struck by fear of death, they are said to grope about, having lost counsel and not knowing what to do.

But he will save the needy from the sword of their mouth, and the poor from the hand of the violent. Christ is saved from the blasphemies of the Jews, because their tongue was a sharp sword when they said, “Crucify him.”

And the needy will have hope, but iniquity will contract its mouth. Blessed is the person who is corrected by the Lord. Therefore do not reject the Lord’s rebuke, because he wounds and heals; he strikes, and his hands will heal. In six tribulations he will deliver you, and in the seventh evil will not touch you. In famine he will rescue you from death. He displayed the power of Christ’s resurrection.

And in war, from the hand of the sword. But let us see whether perhaps he calls sin a sword, fighting against the human soul in order to overthrow it when it yields to him. Sin is called “sword” by the prophet, as he says: “If the watchman sees the sword coming.”

You will be hidden from the scourge of the tongue, and you will not fear calamity when it comes. If you turn to God, the swords of words hurled through the tongue will not penetrate your inner being, and you will not fear the calamities—or evils—that God inflicts upon sinners.

In devastation and famine you will laugh. He said “you will laugh” instead of “you will rejoice,” and you will be glad and cheerful when you see others afflicted by famine, whether present famine or intellectual famine.

You will not fear the beasts of the earth. This is the seventh and final tribulation. The beasts of the earth may be understood as those animals without reason that are given power to devour human beings; and wicked people are also called beasts because they have habits resembling those of animals. Against such beasts the Apostle says that he fought at Ephesus. Therefore, he says, you will not fear this evil when, corrected by the Lord, you have entered upon the way of amendment.

But with the stones of the region you will have a covenant. By a metaphor he called stable and peaceful people “stones”; these are the just and holy. For they are firm in God like stones, established throughout various regions. With these, therefore, you will have a covenant of solid charity, so that tribulation can never tear you away from them.

And the beasts of the earth will be at peace with you. That is, people formerly savage and wicked, transformed in innocence as though into sheep, while retaining their former name, as when the evangelist Matthew is called “Matthew the tax collector.”

And you will know that your tabernacle is at peace. Your tabernacle—or dwelling, or bodily house—will be safe from all those who attack it as though they were enemies.

And when you visit your appearance, you will not sin. He says this: I ask, O Job, that you present your human appearance as worthy of divine visitation. By the terms “dwelling” and “inhabitant” he signified the whole human being as intact.

And you will know that your seed will be numerous, and your offspring like the grass of the earth. We can understand this spiritually as spoken of all the saints, who have children in good works. Such children, conceived from the seed of thoughts, are brought forth in action, and the saints glory in the multitude of this generation, because they wished to please God more through such children than through bodily offspring. Eliphaz, therefore, could have said to Job, as though offering counsel: If you turn to God so that you repent of your former works, you will abound in the virtues of your heart as in seeds. From these you will be able to bring forth good works as children of holiness, so that the offspring of your works may be compared with the multitude of green grasses. If you hold their roots fixed within your heart through hope, your earth will bring forth flowers together with fruits.

You will enter the tomb in abundance, as a heap of grain is brought in at its proper time. When the years of advanced age have been completed, and you are full of days, you will be placed in the tomb and rest, so that at the time of God’s just judgment you may be found cleansed of the smallest and lightest stains of sins, like grain gathered into a threshing floor.

Behold, as we have investigated it, so it is; consider in your mind what you have heard. He says that you should know as true, after careful investigation, everything I have told you, and that you ought to receive it in your heart for your correction.

## CHAPTER VI

Job answered and said: Would that my sins, by which I deserved anger, and the calamity that I suffer were weighed in the balance; it would appear heavier than the sand of the sea. Therefore my words are full of grief. You say that I suffer these things because of my sins; for this reason I would wish my sins to be weighed against this calamity that I suffer, and then you would immediately see that this very calamity outweighs the merits of those sins like the sand of the sea.

For the arrows of the Lord are in me; their indignation has drunk up my spirit, and the terrors of the Lord wage war against me. Here it may be understood that above he called worms “arrows.” He was continually pierced by them and was not permitted to speak—not because the worms possessed such understanding that they did this by judgment, but because, by God’s permission, they were moved by the opposing power to be more severe, just as the locusts, flies, and frogs were in Egypt. When he says, “The terrors of the Lord wage war against me,” the devil himself and his followers may be understood. Having inflicted torments in order to strike Job and make him lose his innocence and holiness, they also threatened him with terrors. Many persecutors, ministers of the devil, likewise wished to do this to the holy martyrs.

They surrounded my tabernacle in a circle. Here he clearly shows that the devil and his followers were waging fierce war like enemies and adversaries. For these evil spirits receive power in different ways: for the condemnation of some, the correction of others, and the testing of still others. According to their conduct or ministry, they are called evils, terrors, or even robbers. “He gave everything into their hands”—that is, into the hands of the plunderers. Everything he possessed, certainly, whether my children or my substance; and just as God gave me myself into the hands of the devil or his followers.

[Col. 0631D] Does the wild ass bray when it has grass, or does the ox low when it stands before a full manger? Just as those animals, when they have abundant fodder, utter no complaint to protest a lack of food, so, he says, I too would utter no bitter or harsh speech if I had peace and rest rather than war in my limbs and in my soul.

Or can what is tasteless be eaten, without being seasoned with salt? Just as natural reason does not permit anything tasteless to be eaten, so I have done nothing tasteless, nothing foolish against God, nothing not seasoned with the salt of faith.

Or can anyone taste what, once tasted, brings death? For to a hungry soul even bitter things seem sweet. Just as no one eats something deadly and thereby acts as an enemy of his own life, so I was afraid even to touch sin.

What my soul formerly refused to touch, these are now my foods because of anguish. That is, harsh and bitter words are now forced from me by the immensity of my punishment. I was afraid to bring these words forth from my mouth when I lived peacefully and quietly in holiness and righteousness. Yet it must not be passed over that Job also suffered this among his other punishments: even his food seemed foul to him, like the smell of a lion—bestial and exceedingly horrible. When this odor burst from his entrails, his food tasted to him of what the inward parts of his fevers exhaled. He showed this himself when he said: “My inward parts boil without any rest”; that is, they have already been cooked and putrefied.

Who will grant that my request may come, and that God may grant me what I await? Let this be my consolation: that I may obtain the remedies of death as the end of my punishment or torments.

And that he who began may himself crush me. May he release his hand and cut me down; and let this be my consolation, that, afflicting me with pain, he does not spare me. Nor will I contradict the holy words. For what is my strength, that I should endure? Or what is my end, that I should act patiently? Job therefore desires this death to be handed over to divine power, so that, falling away from it, he may fall into this temporal death and thereby escape his present punishments, as a tree is cut down from this life.

My strength is not the strength of stones, nor is my flesh bronze. My flesh is corrupted by the pus and decay of wounds, because I do not possess such strength as stones have, so that I would not feel pain.

Behold, I have no help in myself, and even my necessary companions have withdrawn from me. The prophet says this both in his own person and in the person of Christ.

Whoever takes mercy away from his enemy abandons the fear of the Lord. My brothers have passed me by like a torrent that swiftly runs through the valleys. Mercy consists in turning toward the miseries of those who suffer, through compassion and sorrow of heart. While you refuse to show this to a friend, you abandon the fear of the Lord.

Those who fear frost will have snow fall upon them. When they have been scattered, they will perish. I was afraid to commit even the smallest sins, lest God’s vengeance rage against me on their account; and behold, I am now punished as though I had committed monstrous crimes.

And when they have grown hot, they will melt from their place. When his name had begun to boil among the peoples, he did not appear in the place of his glory, just as snow dissolves in the heat.

The paths of their steps are wrapped up; they will walk in vain and perish. He called the paths the virtues of the soul, in which he diligently walked in order to please God. He says that these paths have been wrapped up and entangled by the evils he suffered, since the evils of punishments were mingled with the good works of his life.

Consider the paths of Teman, the roads of Sheba, and wait a little. They were confounded because I hoped. They also came as far as me, and they were covered with shame. That is: Look at these places I have mentioned, and through their very silence you will recognize that what I said is true. Look at the roads of the various kingdoms, along which the crowds of all nations once flocked to me, and you will see them deserted by the scarcity—or rather, the solitude—of their people.

Now you have come, and, seeing my wound, you are afraid. Did I ever say: “Bring me something, and give me a gift from your substance”? Or: “Deliver me from the hand of the enemy, and rescue me from the hand of the strong”? Teach me, and I will be silent; and if perhaps I have been ignorant of anything, instruct me. Why have you detracted from words of truth, when there is no one among you who can rebuke me? You compose speeches only for reproach and pour out words into the wind. He says that his friends, following his example, also feared a ruin like his own. Did I not remain quiet? Did I not dissemble—namely, patience or vengeance regarding evils? Did I not keep silent, restraining my tongue so that I would not answer those reproaching me with evils, or so that iniquity might not be named against me altogether? Therefore you have detracted from these words of truth, since you judged me not merely deceitful in these matters but also guilty in other things, although none of you is so free from sin that he could rebuke anyone with a clear conscience.

You rush upon the orphan, and seek to overthrow your friend. Nevertheless, complete what you have begun. Lend your ear and see whether I am lying. He means one left desolate by parents and friends.

Answer, I beg you, without contention, and, speaking what is just, judge. You will not find in my tongue iniquity, nor will folly resound in my lips. Let there be no zeal for contradiction, which generates the disease of contention. Then, not disturbed by the darkness of hostility, you will be able to judge what is just both in me and in yourselves.

## CHAPTER VII

Human life is a campaign upon the earth, and his days are like the days of a hired laborer. He fights against invisible adversaries.

As the stag longs for shade, and as the hired laborer awaits the end of his work, so I too have had empty months and have counted out laborious nights for myself. If I lie down to sleep, I say, “When shall I arise?” And again I await evening, and I am filled with pains until darkness. My flesh is clothed with decay. Likewise, I thought I would attain this, but instead of the shade of refreshment I fell into the heat of punishments, and instead of the reward for my work I was sent away empty.

My skin has dried and contracted from the filth of dust, and my days have passed more swiftly than a web is cut from the weaver; they have been consumed without any hope. Remember that my life is wind, and my eye will not return to see good things. This too contributed to the pain of his torments: the pus flowing from the decay of his inflamed wounds, mixed with the filth of dust, dried and contracted his skin.

Nor will the sight of a human being look upon me. In that peace, glory, wealth, and honor in which I formerly lived, I am no longer to be seen by human beings.

Your eyes are upon me, and I will not remain. As a cloud is consumed and passes away, so one who descends to the underworld will not ascend; he will not return again to his house. Since your eyes, as though filled with anger, are fixed upon me, my enemies therefore accumulate heavier blows.

Nor will its place know it any longer. Therefore I too will not spare my mouth; I will speak in the tribulation of my spirit, and converse in the bitterness of my soul. Am I the sea, or a sea monster, that you have enclosed me in a prison? If I say, “My bed will console me, and I will be relieved as I speak with myself”—that is, the former way of life of this world will not exist in the transformed human being.

You will terrify me on my bed through dreams and shake me with horror through visions. Job said that he suffered this from God, although he suffered it from demons. They had received power from God to do such things, and undoubtedly appeared to him in dreams with grim and threatening faces, gnashing their teeth and opening their mouths as though to devour him. Thus he was shaken from his bed by the horror of an unfamiliar vision; awakened, he fled from sleep, in which excessive pains are usually softened, and continual wakefulness followed, so that he was tortured by unceasing torments. Or the wounds he saw daily with his waking eyes—the putrid pus and the multitude of worms running through the hollows of his wounds—were shown to him in dreams by demons.

Therefore my soul chose hanging, and my bones chose death. It is better, he says, and much more tolerable than sin, if, overcome by torments, I think about my death rather than inflict blasphemy upon your majesty.

I have despaired; I will no longer live. I have despaired by saying these things, which I ought not to have said. Therefore, for this word by which he laments that he fell into sin, he immediately professes repentance, saying:

Spare me, Lord, for my days are nothing. What is a human being, that you magnify him, or why do you set your heart upon him? You visit him at dawn and suddenly test him. As though he were saying: Receive me as one who repents at this time, and be gracious to me as I plead for this offense.

How long will you not spare me? That is, you do not desist from the punishments pressing upon me.

Nor do you let me go so that I may swallow my saliva? Among his other evils of pain and torment, he says that he had *synanche*, an illness in which a swollen throat blocks a person’s breath and he is often extinguished as though strangled by a noose.

I have sinned. What shall I do to you, O guardian of humankind? I sinned in the things I said above, which it was not fitting for me to say. What can I do to you, who are just?

Why have you made me opposed to you? You gave me the opportunity to answer, so that I might say to you: Punishments do not suit a righteous person; they are rather inflicted upon sinners. Thus a human being speaks these things to God—a creature to the creator, a molded form to the potter.

And I have become burdensome to myself. For I ought not, as a servant to my Lord, to have answered in so complaining a voice.

Why do you not take away my sin, and why do you not remove my iniquity? Behold, now I shall sleep in the dust. That is: Will you take away my pains, through which I, who until now had been righteous, am now compelled to sin?

And if you seek me in the morning, I will not remain. After the night of this age, at the beginning of that future age, when the blessed resurrection of the saints will take place, when I am sought I will not be found, because I will not be worthy to stand before your face by the merit of holiness. If I depart from here as a sinner, one to whom you had not previously been reconciled, afterward I will no longer be before your sight, where the other saints are.

## CHAPTER VIII

Baldad the Shuhite answered and said: How long will you speak such things, and how long will the spirit of your mouth’s many words continue? Baldad was offended by the words of holy Job: first, because he had spoken rashly to God; then, because he said that he had been more powerful than the other kings in the kingdom and that he was suffering this blow while innocent. Baldad therefore reproves him, as though he were speaking not with a free and sober mind but rather as though he were driven by some unknown spirit.

Does God pervert judgment, or does the Almighty subvert what is just? He says this because you are suffering God’s justice, receiving what you deserve.

Even if your children sinned against him and he handed them over to the power of their iniquity, nevertheless, if you rise at dawn to God and entreat the Almighty; if you walk pure and upright, he will immediately awaken for you and make the dwelling of your righteousness peaceful, so that, if your former state was small, your latter state may be greatly multiplied. If your children, he says, doing evil, were handed over by God so that the power given against them on account of their iniquity might accomplish their destruction, this can harm you in no way, provided that you, still lying in the blindness of folly, rise at dawn to the knowledge of divine justice and entreat God, who can grant all things, for your errors and offenses. He, who seemed to be sleeping because he neither heard nor saw you, will immediately awaken for you and hasten to prepare your happiness. Thus, if your former state was small, your latter state will be greatly multiplied.

If, therefore, you turn to God, he says, away from the iniquities on account of which you now suffer punishments, and if, through satisfaction, you wish to reconcile to yourself the one greatly angered against you according to your merits, you will immediately possess so great a measure of his grace that, in comparison with your latter blessings—which he will suddenly be able to bestow in compensation—your former blessings will be counted as very small and insignificant.

The younger son in the Gospel portrayed such sinners. After he had prodigally squandered the good of nature, as though it were riches, by living with prostitutes—that is, with pleasures—the calf, Christ, was slaughtered for him when he repented. The ring of faith, by which all promises are sealed with a certain impression, was also given to his hand; he received safeguards for his steps, so that he could walk securely over serpents and scorpions; and he was also given the eternal robe of immortality.

For ask the former generation and diligently investigate the memory of the fathers. We are of yesterday and know nothing, because our days upon the earth are like a shadow. They will teach you. They will speak to you and bring forth words from their heart. This is what he means: Since we are of yesterday, ask the ancients, and you will find that some received their judgments for their sins in the Flood, others in Sodom, and others in various places.

Can the rush become green without moisture, or can the sedge grow without water? This means: Just as a rush or sedge cannot live without water, so you could not remain in your former happiness without the nourishment and moisture of righteousness.

While it is still in flower and has not been plucked by hand, it withers before all other plants: so are the ways of all who forget God. He says that holy Job flourished like a plant, yet before he reached the maturity of his established glory he was plunged into such great evils that he might not be taken from the world in his own time—as though, at the fullness of his days, when his most flourishing kingdom had been brought to completion, by the hand of God’s power, in which all kingdoms subsist. Therefore, because you did not act in such a way that, in peace, at the completion of your time, you might be brought to your tomb [Col. 0636C], for this reason you have been dried up by the heat of the sun before all other plants—that is, before all sinners, who are often called “plants”—and have yielded in your heart to tribulations together with unbelievers. But when he says, “It withers before all other plants,” whoever among human beings is burdened with many sins, as you are, begins to pay the penalties before the other sinners, under the weight of his crimes.

“And the hope of the hypocrite will perish.” A hypocrite is one who pretends to holiness of life. Yet, according to God’s testimony, as he himself says, Job was simple, upright, and innocent: “If I have walked in vanity.”

“He will not be pleased with his folly, and his confidence is like a spider’s web.” Truly, it is great folly and madness to act before God fictitiously and deceitfully; this will not prosper for them, since he is the searcher of heart and kidneys. Such people are rebuked in the Gospels: they are adorned outwardly with the appearance of holiness, but inwardly are full of the rottenness of sin, like the tombs of the dead.

“He will lean upon his house, and it will not stand.” By trusting in himself and strengthening the flesh of his arm, he will not be able to stand; rather, his pride will fall. For “all flesh is grass.”

“He will support it, and it will not rise.” He tries to raise himself by his own strength, but he will by no means rise, because the Lord is not his strength—the one upon whom those who lean are held most firmly.

“He appears moist before the sun comes.” He speaks of the prosperity of a flourishing man [Col. 0637A]: when he is struck by the heat of tribulation, he is broken by adversities, and all the former greenness of his joy, consumed by grief, dries up.

“And at its rising its shoot will come forth.” At the beginning, he says, of his prosperity, the sinner appears to prosper, but he will not remain so, like a green plant. This is sudden joy, as in the Psalm: “When sinners have sprung up like grass and appeared”—that is, when they have emerged like plants into the greenness of present joy—“as soon as the heat arrives, they will perish.” But the righteous will not flourish like grass, to which, as I have said, the glory of sinners is compared; rather, “he will flourish like the palm,” says the prophet. Its roots are established so deeply that it fears neither storm nor [Col. 0637B] the heat of the sun. And when, under the sacred number, it has reached as many as one hundred knots, by which its height is solidly held together, then it will bear the sweetest fruits of charity, at the very summit of perfection, to which it boasts of having ascended through increases of virtue, as though through the many successive ages of years.

“His roots will be thickened upon a heap of rocks, and he will dwell among stones.” Since his roots, established in good soil so that they might bear the fruit of patience, will not be fixed there, but will instead be compressed upon a heap of rocks, without having there the moisture of life, he will certainly die, dried first by aridity.

“And he will dwell among stones.” Metaphorically, “stones” here may be understood as unbelievers and hard-hearted people [Col. 0637C]. Among them every sinner will dwell, equal to them in the likeness of his life; they do not perceive God, like senseless metals. Or certainly he called sins “stones.” Hence the prophet says: “Take the stones out of the way”—that is, remove sins from the way of holy conduct.

“If it is swallowed up from its place, it will deny him and say: ‘I do not know you.’” When he has been swallowed up and transferred from this life to the squalid places of the underworld, he will certainly be denied as unworthy of the sight of God. A person’s “place” may be called the quality of his conduct, in which he stands either by his manner of life or by his mind—that is, the discipline or grace that he has received or chosen to pursue.

“For this is the joy of his way.” This is said ironically: “This is the joy of his way,” as though he were saying: “He walked in good works pleasing to God while he lived, so that he might arrive at everlasting sorrows.”

“So that others may again spring up from the earth.” God acts as a just judge when he excludes unbelieving Jews from the promises that are in Christ because of their faithlessness and admits the Gentiles because of their obedience. Or, by appointing Matthias in Judas’s place, he declared his just judgments.

“God will not cast away the simple, nor will he extend his hand to the wicked.” He means that it is not fitting to favor those who practice iniquity, yet he will extend the hand of his mercy so that he may convert sinners to repentance.

“Until your mouth is filled with laughter, and your lips with rejoicing.” By “laughter,” understand joy of heart; by “rejoicing,” perceive the voice of one exulting.

[Col. 0638A] “Those who hate you will be clothed with shame.” Since you will have been such as I described above, those who hate you will rightly be put to shame.

“And the tent of the impious will not endure.” Some say this about Job, but they are mistaken. For it is clear that the tent of the impious will perish forever—that is, the devil and his ministers, or even the present age.

## CHAPTER IX

And Job answered and said: “Truly I know that this is so, and that a human being cannot be justified in comparison with God. If he wishes to contend with him, he will not be able to answer him one thing out of a thousand. He is wise in heart and strong in power.” Therefore do not think of me in such a way that I would even dare to imagine this, since I know that a creature cannot in any respect be compared with its Creator [Col. 0638B].

“Who has resisted him and had peace?” Who, acting against God, has not stirred up against himself the warfare of his wrath, as did Dathan and the others?

“He removes mountains, and they do not know it, those whom he overturns in his anger.” “He moves the earth from its place.” Metaphorically, “mountains” are to be understood as human beings or angels, whose exaltation of mind swelled to such an extent that they are compared with lofty mountains.

“And its pillars are shaken.” Here let us understand “pillars” as referring to the stability of the earth, which God founded upon itself with an utterly immovable mass.

“He commands the sun, and it does not rise, and he seals up the stars as under a seal. He alone stretches out the heavens and walks upon the waves of the sea.” Through the alternation of day and [Col. 0638C] night, we see that these things are accomplished daily by the arrangement of God, who governs all things.

“He makes Arcturus, Orion, and the Hyades, and the inner regions of the south.” In these constellations, which in the firmament of heaven are known to nearly everyone better than the other stars, he says that the whole army of the stars belongs to God’s governance, though human beings do not know its great and marvelous workings.

Hence the Lord himself says: “Do you know the order of heaven, and can you establish its account?”

Morally, also: “He moves the earth from its place.” God moved a human being from the place of his former life and shook and weakened the pleasurable but harmful thoughts upon which he had leaned and rested, as upon pillars, and by which he was sustained, so that he might change him into holiness of life.

“He commands the sun, and it does not rise.” For sinners struck by blindness of heart, Christ, the sun of justice, does not rise; nor do the stars rise—that is, the merits of the saints, by which some differ from others in glory—who, while they are hidden here, are shut up as under a seal.

“He stretches out his heavens.” He spreads the Apostles and the other saints, made into heavens, everywhere through preaching; or, by revealing the Scriptures to their hearts—Scriptures that are often signified by the name “heavens”—he opens them to their understanding, as it says: “For I shall see the heavens, the works of your fingers.”

“He goes forth upon the waves of the sea.” Upon the restless, proud, and turbulent people of this age, so that, after their swelling has been laid aside, they may be subdued into gentleness and peacefulness.

“He makes Arcturus,” that is, those who are first in the resurrection of the Church, so that they may be glorious and shining [Col. 0639A] like midday, kindled by the heat of God’s charity and illumined by the light of faith.

“He does great things, and incomprehensible and wonderful things, whose number is beyond counting.” It is a great thing that God does when he establishes fragile human beings, subject to death, through Christ in the hope of blessed resurrection.

“And the inner regions of the south.” There the candlestick is placed, with its lamps shining—the sevenfold spirit, namely, of grace and understanding.

“If he comes to me, I shall not see him; if he departs, I shall not understand. If he suddenly questions me, who will answer him? Or who can say to him, ‘Why do you act in this way?’ God, whose anger no one can resist.” He says more: the presence of God who comes is made known when it becomes manifest to a human being, while, when it is hidden, the absence of one who has departed is indicated, as it were.

[Col. 0639B] “And beneath him those who bear the world are bent.” How great, then, am I, that I should answer him and speak with him in my own words? Even if I had something just to say, I would not answer, but would entreat my judge.

Those who bear the world are rightly understood as the saints, who are great and powerful before God through the glory of their merits. They are therefore bent down before him in humility of heart to intervene for sinners. Thus the saints bear the world while they sustain it by the strength of their prayers, lest it fall and perish.

“The pillars of heaven tremble and quake at his nod.” The Apostles, the prophets, all apostolic men, the saints also, and the other faithful are to be understood here. Among them are Peter, James, and John, who appeared to be pillars. Or the saints, bent and falling prostrate before God, adore him; they bear the world—that is, their whole human nature—which the learned call the lesser world. They place it upon the perfection of the Cross, and, lest it be loosened or deflected within its thoughts through the vanities of the world, they govern and restrain it within themselves through God’s grace.

“And when he hears me calling, I do not believe that he has heard my voice.” He permits those who assail me to inflict injury upon me, even though I strive to live blamelessly. He has been heard in this: that he may merit God’s blessings. Yet he does not believe himself heard because he suffers evils.

“For he will crush me in a whirlwind and multiply my wounds even without cause.” The devil may be understood as the whirlwind, since, like a whirlwind, he descended upon Job to devastate him.

[Col. 0639D] “He does not grant my spirit rest.” He said that he had become asthmatic; for this is a disease that develops in the lungs. Certain passages of the lungs become obstructed—passages that the Greeks call πόροι, “pores”—and, as the physicians say, they are so constricted and closed within the lungs that, because the lungs have been narrowed, they cannot adequately give out or take in breath. With excessive pain, breath is repeatedly drawn in through hurried sighing, and a broken exhalation is emitted.

“And he fills me with bitterness.” If strength is sought, he is exceedingly strong. If equity of judgment is in question, no one dares to bear witness on my behalf. If I wish to justify myself, my mouth will condemn me. If I show myself innocent, it will prove me perverse. Even if I am simple, my soul will not recognize this [Col. 0640A] itself, and I shall be weary of my life. There is one thing I have said: he himself consumes both the innocent and the impious. My soul, surrounded and besieged by every kind of blow and infirmity, is filled with gall, blasphemy, and bitterness. Thus my hard and harsh mouth is compelled to speak, and I shall be weary of my life. Yet this alone I know: that I am punished by the evils of the present life.

“If he scourges, let him kill at once, and let him not laugh at the punishments of the innocent.” Here he has spoken harshly enough against God. In the whole book there is no passage harsher than this, except the other one cited above, where he says: “Therefore my soul chose hanging, and my bones chose death.” At the end of the book he answered God concerning these words: “I have spoken once; would that I had not said it,” and the other words, “I will add nothing further.” Job’s entire dispute with his friends consists in this: he declared himself righteous, while they pronounced him impious.

“The earth has been given into the hand of the impious.” The flesh of Christ was placed under the power of Herod or Pilate; or Job himself was placed under the power of the devil.

“He covers the face of its judgment.” But if it is not he, who is it, then?

“My days were swifter than a runner; they fled and did not see good. They passed like ships carrying apples, like an eagle flying toward prey.” Here he calls the judgment of the mind “the face,” because it has been covered by God’s just judgment. The hearts of the attendants of the impious devil were to be blinded; he called them judges here so that they might torture holy Job more cruelly.

[Col. 0640C] “When I say, ‘I will not speak in this way.’” He says, “I will certainly not speak in this way”—that is, when, compelled by torment, I speak harsh and hard words against God, at that same moment, coming to my senses, I determine that I ought not to speak to God in such a manner.

“I change my face, and I am tormented by grief.” I feared all my works, knowing that you would not spare the transgressor. But if I am impious even in this, why have I labored in vain? That is, because of the excess of grief I contract and become sorrowful; and at the very moment of my resolve, I am so suddenly and unexpectedly troubled and tortured by the goads of pain that I again bring forth words of bitterness and gall.

“If I wash myself as with waters of snow, and my hands shine as though most clean, you will nevertheless stain me with filth.” In the washing of snow-water, therefore, the whiteness of the mind is shown; and in the hand, the purity of the fruits of holy works is demonstrated. Baptism can rightly be compared with snow. By rain and abundant showers, therefore, the legislator wished to indicate the word of teaching. By dew and snow, however, he indicated a meaning that, together with its illumination, penetrates the inner recesses of the heart.

“And my garments would abominate me.” For I would not answer a human being who is like me, nor one who could be heard on equal terms with me in judgment. Such great evils have been inflicted upon me that, because of the squalor of my wound and, if one may say so, of my rottenness, even things without sensation would recoil from me.

“There is no one who can accuse both.” That is, who is there who can accuse God of injustice, as though he were unrighteous, except someone reckless and blasphemous? Who can, as though against a defendant of iniquity, pronounce sentence with an extended hand? But Job, in accordance with God’s testimony, by which he had been praised because he was innocent, truly said of himself that there was none among those with whom he was disputing who could rightly accuse him. For the one who dares most justly to judge another is the one whose conscience is not held guilty by those things that he judges in the other.

“And place his hand upon both.” “Let him remove his rod from me, and let not his dread terrify me. I shall speak and not fear him, for in fear I cannot answer.” I shall then be able to answer securely and confidently if he removes these two things from me: the greatness of his power [Col. 0641B] and the punishments of these torments.

## CHAPTER X

“My soul is weary of my life; I will give free course to my complaint.” I shall speak in the bitterness of my soul; I shall say to God: “Do not condemn me. Tell me why you judge me in this way. Does it seem good to you if you slander me and oppress the work of your hands, and assist the counsel of the impious? Do you have eyes of flesh? Or will you see as a human being sees? Are your days like the days of a human being, and your years like human times, so that you seek out my iniquity and examine my sin? And do you know that I have done nothing impious, since no one can snatch anything from your hand? Your hands, Lord, made me and fashioned me altogether round about, and do you suddenly cast me down?” [Col. 0641C] “Remember, I beg you, that you made me like clay and will reduce me to dust. Did you not milk me like milk and curdle me like cheese? You clothed me with skin and flesh; you joined me together with bones and sinews.”

When he says that he was made altogether round about, he spoke against the heretics who say that the soul was made by one God and the body fashioned by another.

“You granted me life and mercy, and your visitation guarded my spirit.” Although you conceal these things in your heart, I nevertheless know that you remember all things. If I have sinned and you have spared me for a time, why do you not permit me to be clean from my iniquity? And if I am impious, woe is me; and if I am righteous …”

Here “life” refers to the soul itself, not to the life of the soul, because the acts of the soul can also be called its life.

“I shall not lift up my head, filled with affliction and misery.” And because of pride. That is, contracted by pain and the torments of my inner organs, I cannot raise my head, which has been lowered to the ground; or, filled with shame and grief, I cannot raise it.

“You will seize me like a lioness.” Thus, says Job, you liken me—a humble and rejected human being—to this beast.

“And returning, you torment me wondrously.” He said that God returned to him when, together with the former punishments, he felt newer and more recent pains in his body, wondrously.

“You renew your witnesses against me.” He means that our chastisements and punishments are witnesses to divine justice. Or I think that the torments are called “witnesses” for this reason: while he wailed and roared, his sufferings returned testimony to God, as it were.

“And you have multiplied your anger against me, and punishments wage war against me. Why did you bring me forth from the womb? Would that I had been consumed, so that no eye might see me. I would have been as though I had not been, carried from the womb to the tomb. Will not the small number of my days soon come to an end?”

The devil may be understood as the anger of God, through whose agency Job suffered bitter pains. The punishments are said to wage war against him because, succeeding one another according to a certain order of evils, they carry out the duty of cruelty assigned to them.

“Leave me, therefore, so that I may mourn my pain for a little while.” That is, grant me some rest from these torments, so that I may mourn somewhat the pain of my punishments [Col. 0642B] which I endure in my body, or the punishment that I dread will come upon me in hell.

“Before I go—and do not return—to the land of darkness and covered with the shadow of death; to a land of misery and darkness, where the shadow of death dwells, and there is no order, but everlasting horror.” No one doubts that he has described the land of the underworld. There is no order of life there; it is dark, as I said, unquestionably like a prison, into which sinners and the impious who hated the light, as sons of darkness, will be confined. That land is covered with the darkness of death, so that, shut up in eternal night, they may never behold any light of repentance.

“There is the shadow of death for the wretched.” These are to be understood here as punishments. For just as the shadows of bodies are not far from the bodies that produce them, so punishments are not far from death, since they bring about death.

“I shall not return to this mortality, where I suffer such great evils.”
