“The divine Spirit, which is in my nostrils.” Because it pressed upon him, gasping under the constraints of his pains, with the strength of consolations.

“Who will grant me that you may protect me in hell and hide me until your anger passes, and appoint a time for me at which you will remember me?” The fury of God’s anger passed—the anger that Adam earned by sinning—when Christ’s coming erased the document written against the death of his children. Therefore, let no one among the saints be surprised that, at the Lord’s coming, they were freed from the underworld and, by the example of Christ’s resurrection, established in the hope of their own blessed resurrection.

## CHAPTER XI

[Col. 0642D] Now Sophar the Naamathite answered and said: “Will one who speaks much not be heard? Or will a talkative man be justified?” As though he had said: “Can a verbose man be regarded with admiration or exalted with praise, when he is hateful because of his display of excessive talkativeness? Rather, he ought to hear what he deserves, lest, lifted up by vanity, he should think himself the only wise man.”

“Will people be silent to you alone? And when you have mocked the others, will no one refute you?” These are not consolations of friends but weapons of enemies. Thus we may now say of you: “The teeth of men are their weapons and arrows.”

[Col. 0643A] For he said: “‘My speech is pure, and I am clean in your sight.’” He did not say this as though he were pure and clean—that is, as though he were spotless before God in his thoughts and words—but he said: “I have done nothing impious.”

“And would that God himself might speak with you and open his lips to you.” He indicated by what judgment Job ought to be condemned. In speaking, he wished, as I think, to indicate the voice of God, whose sound the ears receive. In the opening of his lips, however, he demonstrated the meaning of the voice.

“That he might show you the hidden things of wisdom, and that his law is manifold.” You would know the hidden and remote things of his heart, in which he is manifold and unfathomable in judgment.

[Col. 0643B] “And you would understand that far less is demanded of you by him than your iniquity deserves.” That is, you ought to suffer more torments than you claim to endure.

“Perhaps you will grasp the footsteps of God and discover the Almighty to perfection.” The footsteps of God are revealed when, by his condescension, he makes himself known to human beings. Therefore we track him when he deigns to manifest himself to us to some extent. These, then, are God’s footsteps: when you understand and believe that he is incomprehensible.

“He is higher than heaven—what can you do? Deeper than hell—how can you know? His measure is longer than the earth and broader than the sea. If he overturns all things or confines them into one, who will oppose him? Or who can say to him, ‘Why do you act in this way?’” We believe that God is everywhere, and that within him all things created by him are contained.

“For he knows the vanity of human beings; and when he sees iniquity, does he not consider it?” He knows the works of the wicked, and when he sees unjust deeds, he does not neglect them, because he punishes the iniquitous and impious.

“A vain man is lifted up in pride and thinks himself born free like a young wild donkey.” He says that Job is like a young wild donkey, an unbridled and wandering animal, because he thinks so of himself—that he ought to belong to no one.

“But you have made your heart firm and spread out your hands toward him.” “You have made your heart firm,” he says—not so that you might satisfy God through repentance and remove this most grievous plague raging in your flesh. “You have spread out your hands toward him”: that is, you have magnified the false merits of your works with an empty mouth, since works are often designated by the name “hands.”

“If you remove from yourself the iniquity that is in your hand, and injustice does not remain in your tent.” He accuses Job reproachfully, saying: “If the iniquity that is in the hand of your work and the injustice in the tent of your heart do not remain.”

“Then you will be able to lift up your face without stain, and you will be stable and will not fear.” Possessing a holy conscience, you will raise your face freely to entreat God. For Cain, the fratricide, lived in the land of Nod, that is, he became unstable. Therefore, lest Job also incur such a punishment and perpetual fear concerning his death [Col. 0644A], Sophar urges him, saying: “If you do the things we have said above, you will be stable.”

This must certainly be understood: there is a “shaking” in which the sinner, remaining in his crimes, does not stand before the face. “Your face will be like pure water; you will be stripped of filth and will not fear.” Whoever has a sincere and purified mind, clean from every stain, dreads vices; stripped of them as of cast-off garments and brought forth, as it were, from darkness, he will shine.

A person who presents the face of his mind radiant with the purity of whiteness signifies the people of the Jews, who in a certain sense killed Christ, their father.

“You will also forget misery, and you will not remember it like waters that have passed away.” By the passage of waters, Sophar wishes to indicate that pains can depart from him just as quickly, provided that Job is willing to amend himself—just as waters flow away in an instant to other places—and that the misery of this plague can be completely wiped away from him, so that he remembers it only faintly, as though it had never existed.

“And like the brightness of midday, it will rise for you toward evening.” “And when you think yourself consumed, you will rise like Lucifer.” Spiritually, this may be understood as follows: “It will rise for you toward evening,” that is, at the completion of the labors of your evils, Christ, the sun of justice, will come to you as consolation; or, rising after death, you will rise into glory.

Alternatively, it may refer to this destruction of yours, in which you waste away and decline daily in such great corruption that you already think yourself utterly consumed. If you do what I have now said [Col. 0644C], then, from having been completely and utterly reduced to nothing, you will suddenly rise like Lucifer, who, circling the sky through the hidden stages of his course, is said to appear again after two years in the radiance of the dawn itself. So also it may happen to you after the night and the denser darkness of this prolonged temptation, if you recognize your faults.

“And you will have confidence in the hope set before you, and, buried, you will sleep securely. You will rest, and there will be no one to terrify you. And many will entreat your face.” You will have this confidence: buried in death and made certain of the resurrection, you will sleep securely and rest in the underworld, established in the hope of a sure expectation. There will be no hostile torturer or enemy there to terrify you and inflict infernal punishments upon you; rather, whoever they are [Col. 0644D], they will pour out suppliant prayers for you, so that their Tartarean torments may be tempered by your prayers.

“But the eyes of the impious will fail, and escape will perish from them, and their hope will be an abomination to their soul.” That is, the expectation of impious people will end in this way: at the time of another’s glory, they themselves will be found worthy not of absolution but of abomination.

## CHAPTER XII

Now Job answered and said: “So you alone are human beings, and wisdom will die with you? I too have a heart, as you do, and I am not inferior to you. For who does not know the things that you know? One who is mocked by his friend, as I am, will call upon God, and he will hear him.” The simplicity of the righteous is mocked.

This means: “Why do you alone speak as wise men and suppose that after you there will be no wise person?”

“A lamp despised in the thoughts of the rich, prepared for the appointed time. The tents of robbers abound, and they boldly provoke God, although he has placed everything in their hands.” He calls himself a lamp despised by the rich, clearly indicating that they were proud because they scorned him, afflicted by torments and by the contempt of his relatives, although inwardly he shone with great faith and the oil of good works.

Or, the lamp despised by the rich is Christ, despised by the Jews, who, rising from the dead, illuminated the whole world with the splendor of his grace. The Jews are called “rich,” however, because they received the utterances of God.

[Col. 0645B] “Indeed, ask the beasts, and they will teach you; and the birds of heaven, and they will tell you. Speak to the earth, and it will answer you; and the fish of the sea will recount it to you. Who does not know that the hand of the Lord made all these things? In whose hand is the soul of every living thing and the spirit of all human flesh. Does not the ear distinguish words, and the palate of the eater taste? In the ancient there is wisdom, and in length of time there is understanding. With him are wisdom and strength; he possesses counsel and understanding.”

That all things pertain to God’s providence and governance, including irrational and insensible things, is shown by the fact that, questioned in a certain rational manner concerning the truth, they answer.

According to mystical interpretation, uncultivated people, irrational in their conduct, may be understood as beasts. The birds, however, signify demons [Col. 0645C], or light-minded, exalted, and proud people; or certainly astrologers. The earth signifies pleasure-loving and carnal people who have earthly tastes. The fish signify philosophers and those like them, who are excessively occupied with investigating the affairs of the world and its qualities.

Alternatively: the beasts are good horses, animals that will dwell in the inheritance of the Lord, for whom the voluntary rain of the Gospel has been separated from the unbelievers. The birds are those who have their hearts above and desire heavenly things, or those who will go to meet Christ in the air after rising from the dead. The flesh of the saints is most rightly understood as the earth, and, when the Lord reigns, it will exult.

The fish are those who, swimming amid the waves and storms of this world, look forward to secure and peaceful places in eternity. Or those fish are to be understood as receiving life through water; they immediately migrate from the baptismal font to Christ, or to God, as some say.

“If he destroys, there is no one who can build.” It is clear that whatever he wishes to disperse and destroy by the judgment of his wisdom, no one can resist his strength as though he were powerful.

Thus he destroyed the tower and the kingdoms of many nations, and also Jerusalem, where the legal precepts themselves, like written stones, were foretold as destined to be dissolved in the presence of his grace.

Thus also, according to Job’s prophecy, the wall of hostility—namely, the law of commandments—was destroyed through Christ, so that he might create the two in himself as one new man, making peace.

Christ God destroyed and unlocked the prison-bars of hell, and deposed from the kingdom of dominion the devil who held the power of death. Therefore Christ God destroyed death: he accepted it so that he might deign to die in it, and on the cross he destroyed the body of sin, killing there our old man who was being put to death, so that he might restore for us the way into eternity.

Thus he destroyed death and illuminated life. He destroyed the counsels of those persecuting the Church, who were striving to eradicate his name from beneath heaven—namely, the Jews and the Gentiles.

He destroyed the doctrines and various errors of the heretics from the Church by the indissoluble edifice of right faith. Concerning these Solomon says: “The wise man ascends the cities of the strong and destroys their fortifications.” He also destroyed every worship of idols.

“If he shuts a person in, there is no one who can open.” [Col. 0646B] God shut Noah in during the Flood; Lot in Segor; Jonah in the belly of the whale; Jeremiah and Baruch, so that they might not be found. He also shuts in those of whom it is said: “He will send his angel around those who fear him, and he will deliver them.”

Or, if a person has been placed under the sentence of death by God’s judgment, who can call him back? Pharaoh was shut in amid the waters; Dathan and Abiram were shut in alive in hell; the people of Israel were shut in in the wilderness for forty years.

God encloses a person in tribulations so that he may be refined, or else surrounds the sinner with corrections and scourges so that he may amend. Who is there who can open some means of avoiding it, as though an entrance by which he might escape, as Job himself says: “God has enclosed me with the unjust and delivered me into the hands of the impious”?

The devil may be understood by “the man” here: once shut up in hell, he could not free himself, though he abominably imagines himself strong against God, who is most strong.

“If he restrains the waters, everything will dry up; and if he releases them, they will overturn the earth.” We have no doubt that this happened in Noah’s time, according to the testimony of Scripture.

Now, spiritually, the waters of teachings are withheld among the Jewish peoples, so that the streams of the Law may be a wilderness for them and the outflows of waters thirst. Having earthly desires and luxuries like those waters, they may be scattered and overthrown; but in the land of the Church, after leaving behind the rational image of the earthly human being, they may advance by turning toward spiritual life.

“With him are strength and wisdom.” That is, the Son with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0646D] He himself knows both the deceiver and the one who is deceived. He knew that Balaam, Ahab, and Aena would arise as false prophets; he knew Aena, but through these examples he revealed the merit of the sinful people, so that he might announce their destruction through false prophecies, and so that those who refuse to hear God and the prophets speaking truth might be deceived by the false predictions of false prophets. The children of Israel also, as we read in the Book of Judges, were deceived by God’s most just judgment. When they had gathered together against the Benjaminites on account of the Levite’s wife, so that the crime of adultery might be punished, the crime of sacrilege was first avenged among themselves, because they themselves ought first to have been corrected—or certainly because they had to destroy those who worshiped idols in contempt of God. Their brother’s injury had mattered more to them than God’s, and for that reason it was first avenged in them. But the Lord knows both the deceiver and the deceived through his foreknowledge. This may also be understood of Abel and Cain, and of Delilah and Samson, who mystically possessed the grace of the Holy Spirit in his seven locks.

God certainly knew all these things before they happened, as one who foreknew the future; but he permitted a human being, who exercised free choice, to disobey God’s command and, moreover, to believe that he could become like God, so that by God’s justice he might most deservedly suffer the punishment of disobedience. All of them bore a type of Christ. In Samson, however, who seized and killed the lion and found a honeycomb in the mouth of the dead lion, it was signified that afterward there would be the sweetness of praise and God’s grace in the proud, in whose mouths there had been the stench of blasphemy. And just as that thirsty Samson drew water from the molar tooth of a donkey, after calling upon God, so Christ was refreshed by the believing people from the unclean and hardened Gentile people, as though by a people providing relief. The jawbone of that same donkey, from whose molar abundant water had flowed, killed a thousand men. In the jaws and teeth, the eloquence of the mouth is understood. Thus the teaching of those from the Gentiles who believed is brought to completion by a certain perfect number.

Samson killed and destroyed his enemies and adversaries in three ways: some perish by refusing to believe; others, by believing, die to sin. This deed is called “the raising up of the jawbone.” For the teaching and preaching of the Gospel was exalted over the whole earth, so that all nations everywhere marvel at it when it is raised up. In those foxes, therefore, it was figuratively shown that through deceitful men hostile to sound faith—whose rule is in their tails—the part left behind and the part around the fruits of those who oppose Christ would be laid waste.

He brings counselors to a foolish end and judges to bewilderment. Thus he acted against the magicians of the Egyptians, who told Pharaoh that the king of the Chaldeans would not come to devastate Egypt; or, alternatively, he turned Nebuchadnezzar himself into madness, or struck Belshazzar with terror.

He loosens the belt of kings and girds their loins with a rope. In the belt, the glory of the reigning king is understood; in the rope, the disgrace of one deposed from royal power—as happened to Zedekiah and Manasseh, at God’s command. Or it may refer to the Jewish people, who through their unbelief were separated from Christ’s kingdom. But even now all those reborn in Christ are kings, called to adoption as sons of the eternal King. Those who have committed deeds deserving the limits of repentance are rightly separated from that lofty honor. As the prophet says: “You will be girded with a rope instead of a belt.”

He leads priests away inglorious. Thus he did with the sons of Eli, and with many others of the same nation.

And he supplants nobles. God does not supplant by deceit, for there is no iniquity in him. He is said to supplant in this manner: when he removes the unjust and the wicked, and substitutes a good and just man in the place that someone unworthy seems to occupy, as he substituted David in Saul’s place.

[Col. 0648A] Changing the truthful speech and removing the teaching of the elders. He pours contempt upon princes and raises up those who had been oppressed. When, because of sins and after the promises have been withdrawn, he is compelled to give the flames of eternal Gehenna to those adopted as sons.

He reveals deep things from darkness and brings the shadow of death into the light. He multiplies nations and destroys them, and restores those that have been overthrown to wholeness. He changes the heart of the rulers of the people of the earth and deceives them, so that they walk in vain along an impassable path. They will grope as in darkness and not in light, and he will make them wander like drunken men. The shadow of death is the devil himself: he does not protect human beings but presses them toward death. He is brought into the light when he is separated from a faithful soul.

## CHAPTER XIII

[Col. 0648B] “Behold, my eye has seen all these things, and my ear has heard them, and I have understood each one. According to your knowledge, I too know; I am not inferior to you. Yet I will speak to the Almighty, and I desire to argue with God, first showing you to be fabricators of lies and worshipers of perverse doctrines. Would that you were silent, so that you might be thought wise! Hear, then, my corrections, and attend to the judgment of my lips. Does God need your lie, so that you may speak deceitfully on his behalf? Do you show partiality to his person and attempt to judge on behalf of God? Or will he be pleased with one whom nothing can conceal? Or will he be deceived, like a human being, by your frauds?” There was deceit in them, because under words of consolation they were striking him with an inimical heart.

[Col. 0648C] He himself will rebuke you, because in secret you accept his face. As soon as he stirs himself, he will trouble you, and his terror will rush upon you. Your memory will be compared with ashes, and your necks will be reduced to clay. Be silent for a little while, so that I may speak whatever my mind suggests. You are worthy to be rebuked by God: secretly—that is, as though he were unaware—you assume his person in yourselves in order to condemn me, as though anything could remain hidden from him, so that you might thus try to elude him.

Why do I tear my flesh with my teeth? As he was tormented by excessive sufferings, he tore his hands or lips with his teeth.

And I carry my soul in my hands. Even if he kills me, I will hope in him. Nevertheless, I will bring my ways to judgment in his sight, and he will be my savior. [Col. 0648D] For no hypocrite will come into his presence. Hear my speech and perceive the riddles with your ears. If I am judged, I know that I will be found just. Who is there who will be judged with me? Let him come. Why am I consumed in silence? Do only two things not to me, and then I will not hide from your face. Remove your hand far from me, and let your dread not terrify me. Call me, and I will answer you; or else I will speak, and you answer me. How many iniquities and sins I have!

He says that he carries in his hands his very life, which is customarily called the soul: that is, with his soul already failing and departing amid his torments, he carries it as though it were to be borne out in his hands.

Show me my crimes and my transgressions, so that I may know for what reason you torment me in this way.

[Col. 0649A] Why do you hide your face and regard me as your enemy? Against a leaf carried away by the wind you display your power, and you pursue a dry straw. For you write bitter things against me and wish to consume me for the sins of my youth. You have put my foot in fetters, and you have watched all my paths and considered the tracks of my feet. I am like something to be consumed by decay, and like a garment eaten by moths.

While you permit me to be punished in this way, regarding me as an enemy, it pains me that you, who know everything most perfectly, know that the one who has resisted you is rather harmed.

## CHAPTER XIV

A human being, born of woman, lives for a short time and is filled with many miseries. He comes forth like a flower, is crushed, flees like a shadow, and never remains in the same condition. By “flower” here we should understand the frailty of the human race, not the fragrant beauty and loveliness of scent.

And do you consider it worthy to open your eyes over such a one and bring him with you into judgment? Who can make clean what was conceived from unclean seed? Is it not you alone? The days of a human being are short; the number of his months is with you. You have set his boundaries, which cannot be passed.

This means: you consider it worthy, for the sake of the human race, to wish your Only-Begotten to be born a human being. Or otherwise: you also permit me to speak with you and unfold my miseries.

Withdraw, therefore, from him for a little while, so that he may rest until his desired time comes, and until his days are like those of a hired laborer. That is, [Col. 0649C] remove your scourge from me, and do not permit me to be tested in this manner any longer.

A tree has hope. If it is cut down, it sprouts again, and its branches put forth shoots. If its root grows old in the earth and its trunk has died in the dust, at the smell of water it will bud and produce foliage as when it was first planted.

We should understand this to be a rational tree, of which it is said: “For there is hope for a tree.” This tree was cut down through disobedience, when it dwelt among the trees of paradise, before it died by God’s sentence. In baptism, its old condition is cut away, so that it may live again through the resurrection of faith in the life of the new human being, Jesus Christ, and its branches may put forth shoots of virtues—that is, its works may advance through holy living.

[Col. 0649D] But when a human being has died, and has been stripped bare and consumed, where, I ask, is he? A human being without hope in Christ, like the Gentiles who do not know God, when he has died—having not been reborn through baptism, deprived also of life and stripped of present enjoyment—will without doubt receive the sentence of eternal damnation.

As when the waters withdraw from the sea and a river, emptied of its waters, dries up, so a human being, when he has fallen asleep, will not rise again. Until the heavens are worn away, he will not awaken, nor rise from his sleep. Who will grant me this: that you may protect me in hell and hide me until your fury has passed, and appoint me a time in which you will remember me? Do you suppose that a dead human being will live again? [Col. 0650A] All the days in which I now serve as a soldier, I wait until my transformation comes.

He says: If it can happen that the waters of God’s saving commandments withdraw from the sea of the Holy Scriptures, whose perpetual abundance never fails; and if it can happen that the river of holy baptism dries up through some lack of divine mercy, is no longer full of grace, and no longer overflows with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, then it will also be possible for a human being, when he has died, not to rise again.

You will call me, and I will answer you. You will extend your right hand to the work of your hands. All the dead will be called at the end of the ages, and they will be raised from their tombs at the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God. All will answer in this way: when, at the word of his majesty and power, the ashes and dust [Col. 0650B] of human bodies are brought to life, they will rise from the dead incorruptible.

You have indeed counted my steps, but spare my sins: the thoughts and works of my youth.

You have sealed up my transgressions as in a sack, but you have healed my iniquity. The sack, by its significant name, may be understood as the entire sinful mass of Adam’s generation. In it, as though under the seal of his image, Adam begot the whole of his offspring in his own image and likeness, the whole having been made transgressive in him. God kept it closed under sin for many ages, yet in the last times of the ages he healed the wounds of its transgressions through his redemption.

But if Job seems to have said this about himself, as I think, the meaning is this: “If,” he says, “throughout the whole span of my life I have committed sins against God, you have gathered them all together into one, through the various intervals of time, so that according to the rigor of your justice you might repay me for all of them at once.”

A mountain falling flows away, and a rock is moved from its place. Waters hollow out stones; through their flooding, the earth is gradually consumed, and so you destroy human beings as well.

We should understand this mountain to be the devil, or the proud human being, who swells up against God like a mountain through the elevation of his mind. Thus, by raising himself up, he falls headlong, flows away, and, dissolved into dust, is reduced to nothing.

I think the rock is likened to those who, since they ought to have remained in the goodness of their nature like stones, with a similar firmness, have by their own will been changed into a kind of stupidity and hardness of heart. Therefore, from the dwelling place of their detestation—which they presumed to possess as though it were based on their own merits—they will be cast down to places worthy of them.

These waters, however, which always seek the lower regions, through which destruction once came as well, signify hostile powers and the storms and whirlwinds of the world. These waters, I say, wear away in an unceasing fall those human beings who presume upon themselves, thinking themselves very strong and solid and trusting in their own strength; hence they are compared with stones.

I consider the earth to signify those who, unable to remove temptations and dangers, allow themselves to be shaken. “So you destroy human beings as well”—that is, your saints, who preserve your image within themselves.

[Col. 0651A] You strengthened him for a little while, so that he might pass away forever. That is, in this life you did not permit your saints to be overcome by temptations.

You will change his face and send him away. That is, when this mortal being has put on immortality and incorruption. Or otherwise, we understand “face” as the soul, which, when it has recovered its natural serenity, contemplates the glory of the divine majesty and, when it has rejoiced together with its body, will not be wounded by any disturbance of vice.

Whether his sons are noble or ignoble, he will not know. This means: not sons of the flesh, but sons of the mind—that is, works of virtue. The saints, therefore, do not know in this life, before the day of judgment, what sort of sons they certainly have, whether pleasing to God or displeasing.

[Col. 0651B] You strengthened him for a little while, so that he might pass away forever, according to the form of a servant that he assumed. I do not think this can be applied to Christ God. For when, in the part by which he is human, he was weakened as his passion approached, the Evangelist says: “An angel of the Lord appeared from heaven, strengthening him.” Thus, having accomplished our redemption for a short time, he passed into that eternal age, penetrating the heavens. “You will change his face”: that is, when the whole human being passed into God, while the distinct property of each substance was preserved in the unity of the person.

Nevertheless, while his flesh lives, it will suffer, and his soul will mourn over itself. Our Savior assumed true flesh in such a way that he was able to feel pain. Or his soul grieved when he said: “My soul is sorrowful [Col. 0651C] even unto death.” Or it may refer to the Church, which is his flesh: it grieves when it is pressed by the trials of the world, because the Church itself is a daughter in the one who is initiated into Christ through faith in baptism. And again she is a mother when the one incorporated into the members of Christ undertakes the ministry of baptizing.

## CHAPTER XV

Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said: “Will a wise man answer as though speaking into the wind?” His meaning seems to have been: Would any wise man, devoted to philosophical discipline, be so carried away by fury and possessed by madness that, without any regard for the fear of God or religion, he would speak in such a way that his words resembled a breath of air and melted away like something scattered by the wind? For this reason Eliphaz dared to rebuke holy Job as fearful before the spirit of pride and the wind.

And he will fill his stomach with heat. By “heat” he wished to indicate Job’s panting spirit, inflamed with the gall of anger, which had presumed to rage against God as though he were his equal.

Another interpretation reads: “And he will fill his belly with pain.” Let us understand “belly,” a capacious receptacle, as a certain recess of the soul. Just as the body has a receptacle in which the vital organs of the viscera are contained, and we call this by the name “belly,” so by a change of name he has designated a certain capacity of the soul, capable of exercises, which is filled with thoughts in the same way that a person’s belly is filled with food.

Eliphaz therefore rebukes Job [Col. 0652A] for having filled such a belly with pain—that is, for thinking those things that torment his soul, or on account of which he deservedly suffers bodily pains.

You rebuke one who is not your equal with words, and speak what is not fitting for you. By saying this, he marks him as rebellious and opposed to God. Perhaps this is because in the preceding speech Job had said among other things to God: “And you regard me as your enemy.”

As far as you are concerned, you have emptied yourself of fear and removed prayers from before God. “You have become so exalted,” he says, “that you are entirely empty of divine fear and no longer deem it worthwhile to entreat God.” Hence he says: “You have removed prayers from before God”—that is, as though they were unnecessary for you, you have taken them away from yourself.

[Col. 0652B] For your iniquity has taught your mouth, and you imitate the tongue of blasphemers. The evil of your mind has taught your mouth to speak, and therefore you are an imitator and disciple of those who always have their tongues ready to blaspheme God.

Your mouth will condemn you, and not I; your lips will answer you. That is, you will receive the due reward of your words.

Were you born as the first human being, and were you formed before all the hills? Then you began to exist before the human race came into being, attributing much to yourself by claiming that you are wiser than other human beings. Here, in a mocking speech, he could have meant the first Adam, whom we know to have been made exceedingly wise by God. Thus he attacks holy Job, saying: “Did you begin to exist before the father of the human race and before the creation of the angels?”

Have you heard God’s counsel, and is his wisdom inferior to you? Next he accuses him of excessive pride and boasting against the true God who is pleasing to him, and sharply rebukes him, saying that he not only thinks he knows God’s counsel but that God’s wisdom is even inferior to him. It is evident that a mind full of envy is directing the darts of reproach without cause against a just man, so as to overwhelm the innocent with insults.

What do you know that we do not know? What do you understand that we do not understand? Very much indeed: plainly, first he knew God himself more fully; then he discerned in spirit the mysteries that were to be revealed in Christ.

The elders and the ancient ones among us are much older than your fathers. The elders and ancient men among us, who through their great age have acquired a great deal of learning and knowledge, have not dared to say anything rash against God, as you do.

Is it a great thing that God should console you? But your wicked words prevent this. It is plainly neither great nor difficult for the Almighty, in his mercy, to console a human being—to hear one who calls upon him and rescue him from the oppression of tribulation. But by belching out blasphemies you aggravate God still further toward your punishment, when you could have appeased him through humility and satisfaction.

Why does your heart lift you up, and why, as though you were thinking great thoughts, do you keep your eyes staring? Why does your spirit swell against God, so that you utter such words from your mouth? [Col. 0653A] What is a human being, that he should be clean, or one born of woman, that he should appear just? Behold, among his saints no one is unchangeable, and the heavens are not clean in his sight. How much more abominable and worthless is a human being who drinks iniquity like water?

The heart, eyes, and spirit signify the whole soul of a human being, but in the heart we should recognize human wisdom; in the eyes, clarity of understanding; and in the spirit, the movement of the soul, by which it is ceaselessly driven by thoughts toward whatever it is to do.

Thus, by the elevation of the heart, the staring of the eyes, and the swelling of the spirit, Eliphaz, Job’s friend, reproaches holy Job as exceedingly proud and greatly puffed up against God. For he had been offended by those words which blessed Job had previously spoken to God: “If I am judged, I know [Col. 0653B] that I will be found just.” Against this statement he speaks here: “What is a human being, that he should appear clean?”

I will show you; listen to me. I will recount what I have seen. I am speaking of something tested by experience, which you should know that I have learned and seen.

The wise confess, and do not conceal their fathers. In various ways and through various examples he wishes to force and constrain him toward repentance, so that he may confess that he endured that blow of punishments on account of his merits. Or alternatively: they do not defend themselves or their fathers who are like them, or those whom they have begun to regard as parents because they imitate them; they neither cover up their own sins nor those of their parents, nor conceal them. Or they do not hide their fathers—that is, their elders or priests, to whom it is salutary to confess sins.

[Col. 0653C] To them alone the earth was given, and no stranger will pass through them. Frequently, on account of sins, God hands over the land of the wicked to other nations. Thus he speaks of the conduct and approach of Sophar as he addresses Job: “In their bitterness they will go and come upon him, terrifying men”—that is, as though stirred by the anger of gall and turned by the poison of envy toward bitterness and fury—“they will remain continually around you.”

Or, morally: those wise men are wise in Christ and foolish in the world. Through the satisfaction of repentance, by turning to God in faith, they confess their sins or the errors of heresy and reveal the authors either of their crimes or of their doctrines, so that they may possess the earth of their body for themselves alone—that is, so that vices or hostile wickedness may not rule over it. And no stranger will pass through him—that is, the devil will have no power over him. He is truly called a stranger because he made himself a stranger from God and from the fellowship of the angels.

The wicked man is proud throughout all his days, and the number of his years is uncertain. Eliphaz seems to direct these words against Job, carrying them through to the end of this speech. I, however, think that, inspired by the spirit of prophecy, he spoke all these things about any wicked person, or about the devil himself or his companions.

The sound of terror is always in his ears, as happened to the Egyptians.

And when there is peace, he always suspects ambushes. The wicked man persists continually in crime because of the evil of his conscience; for he knows, according to God’s just judgment, what recompense has been set apart for the wicked.

He does not believe that he can return from darkness to light. He is deceived by a vain error, thinking that he must be redeemed at some price. This wicked man, descending into the depths of sins, has despaired of being able to obtain life. Therefore he does not believe that he can return from the darkness of sins to the light of repentance. He explains the cause of this distrust as follows:

Looking around everywhere for a sword. That is, on every side—or awaiting death. We have said that the devil was given as food to unclean spirits, because they live by his wickedness. The vultures are understood to be sinful and unclean human beings. When these have been converted, then, in a reversal, they will have the enemy who was devouring them as food, [Col. 0654B] because he is the dragon whom God gave as food to the peoples of Ethiopia. These peoples were once Ethiopians because of the blackness of their sins, but now, through faith, they have become light in the Lord.

They consume and devour this wicked one, or dragon, when through faith they admit his entire body—which certainly consists of sinners—into the body, that is, into the Church, in accordance with what was said to Peter: “Arise, kill, and eat.” For this reason Moses also compelled the children of Israel to drink the calf after it had been ground up, so that just as they had been swallowed up by it in error, they might pass into the body of God’s people, leaving error behind.

When he moves to seek bread, he knows that a day of darkness has been prepared in his hand. The movement of the mind is the beginning of thought. When this man, always guilty and conscious of evil, remembers how he might live, nothing else occurs to him but that terrible time of God’s judgment, when he fears the eternal punishments that will be inflicted.

Tribulation will terrify him, and anguish will surround him like a king preparing for battle. Before the foretold day arrives, he will be tormented by the evil of fear; hemmed in on every side by pressures and anguish, he will be confined like a king setting out for battle. Under the name “king,” I think the wicked human being, or the devil, is signified: one who daily prepares wars against God—blasphemies, conflicts, and battles of vice.

For he has stretched out his hand against God and strengthened himself against the Almighty. By the elevation or extension of the hand, he shows one resisting God, whom he calls strong through the defiance of an inflated mind.

He ran against him with his neck erect. He indicates the abrupt and headlong mind of the proud person: possessed by madness, he resisted God with audacity and did not advance with slow steps.

And he armed himself with a fat neck. By mentioning the fatness of the neck, he indicated overflowing and excessive pride. As the prophet says when speaking of the same human pride: “Their iniquities have come forth as if from fatness.” A newer edition expresses this testimony more clearly: “Their eyes have protruded from fatness”—that is, the perceptions or [Col. 0655A] thoughts of the exceedingly proud have burst forth into blasphemy.

Fatness covered his face. The face often signifies the mind of the soul, as the Apostle says: “But we, with unveiled face, behold the glory of the Lord.” The devil, or the wicked person, does not possess this face—serene or clear—through holiness or humility; rather, it is covered by the thick substance of pride, so that the heart is blind and dull.

Another edition reads: “He covered his face as with his fat.” As though it said: he did not clothe himself with the precious covering of the virtue of humility, which is fine and translucent, but with black pride, the author of all vices. Instead, he made pride itself into a kind of mockery and dark garment for him, by which he obscured it through the thick blindness of the heart.

[Col. 0655B] And fat hangs down from his sides. His sides may be understood as his ministers or companions, who became like him. It is also not unreasonable to understand them as the ears, which are certainly made fat in hearing; hence excessive deafness is produced in the obstinate, according to the saying: “The heart of this people has grown fat.”

Another edition reads: “He made a halter over his thighs.” It seems to me that this verse contains the following meaning: the wicked man is rebuked because he did not wish to have the bridle of discipline by which he could have been restrained toward virtue. Instead, having laid aside the firmness of his spirit, he cast himself into a kind of dissolution, so that, as though the rein had been loosened, he might be led toward pleasure and luxury.

He dwelt in desolate cities and in deserted houses that had been reduced to burial mounds. Thus he calls unclean spirits the dwelling places of beasts and unclean birds: they dwell in human beings whom God has abandoned. For this one dwells in human beings abandoned by God, and for that reason they have become tombs of the dead. And if sins are sometimes called “the dead” in Scripture, sinners and the wicked must necessarily be tombs of the dead. Thus “cities” may be a general name for all sinners, while “houses” may refer specifically to each individual sinner and wicked person.

He will not become rich, nor will his substance endure. Here “substance” should not be understood as riches of possessions but as sins, concerning which the Holy Spirit says in the Apocalypse of John: “Babylon the great city has fallen, has fallen, and has become a dwelling place of demons and a prison of every unclean spirit.” When he says, “He will not become rich,” [Col. 0655D] he seems to mean that the time will not be long in which his life will grow fat on the riches of crimes, since even the substance of his collected vices will not endure.

Nor will he send his root into the earth. That is, because he will die like a tree torn out by the roots, he will not have eternal stability in the land of the living or fellowship with them, because he did not first send forth here the hope or root of faith. He will not have even a breath of salvation, so as to live under the shade of refreshment.

He will not depart from darkness. Others have said, “He will not escape darkness”: that is, he has undergone eternal punishments and will not escape darkness. By “he will not depart from darkness,” however, we understand the darkness of unbelief. This wicked man refuses to come to the light of repentance.

His branches will be dried up by flame. In the branches we should understand the fruits of evil works, as Solomon says: “The fruits of the wicked are sins.” Gehenna’s fire will consume them like wood, hay, and straw.

And he will be taken away from him by the breath of his mouth. Since his spirit is anger against God, and he does not cease to breathe blasphemies against him, the text says that he is condemned by the judgment of his own mouth.

According to the ancient edition, therefore, I think that the origin of the wicked man’s life is signified in the trunk or foliage, which the Spirit of God strikes with the sentence of judgment, as a wind beats against a tree. Thus, like a dried-up tree, the wicked man dies immediately, and all the flower of his honor and glory falls away.

[Col. 0656B] He will not depart, deceived by a vain error, thinking that he must be redeemed at some price. This, then, is what he means: perhaps the devil, or the wicked man persisting in impiety through hardness of heart, thinks that God will not repay him according to his merits. Yet God by no means spares him; and even if he pleads with powerful and carefully arranged words in order to obtain mercy, he has already, according to God’s just judgment, been assigned to eternal torments.

Before his days are fulfilled, he will perish. The days of each person are said to be fulfilled when the recompense of good and evil people has come. Here, therefore, this human being, or the devil, will perish before the day of the manifest sentence that the Lord will pronounce upon them in judgment; he will perish by foreknowledge in predestination [Alt.: “foreknown, he will perish,” and so forth].

And his hands will wither. He has no fruit of any good work within himself.

His cluster will be harmed like a vine in its first flowering, and like an olive tree shedding its blossom. There is no doubt that the fruit of the work mentioned above is understood in the cluster. Thus he will not be able to bring the flower of temporal joy to the ripeness of everlasting fruit, because in the very hope of false glory he will be scattered by the hot wind of pride. Or he will be harmed by the frost of God’s love, as by hoarfrost, as I think is said with the same meaning in what follows.

“And like an olive tree shedding its blossom.” In the divine Scriptures, the olive tree and the vine sometimes signify a human being alone, and sometimes a people, whether good or bad. What he says—“he will be devastated,” or “overthrown”—should be understood as it is written in the Apocalypse: “Whoever keeps the Lord’s commandments will not be harmed by the second death.”

The vine and the olive tree may therefore be understood as the Jewish people. This vine will lose or forfeit the fruit of holiness and righteousness, because it did not wish to have Christ, the first and finest blossom of all the saints, in the field of the Law. For he himself says: “I am the flower of the field.” But, being faithless and unbelieving, so that the faith of Christ might not burn for it, it cast him away from itself. And while it casts him outside the vineyard and shakes him off from itself like a blossom, it itself is torn away from the root of the patriarchs and stripped of Christ, the fruit of our salvation.

For the assembly of the hypocrite is barren. In these words he marks holy Job as a plunderer, a violent man, and a pretender, and says that riches gathered through iniquity will not benefit him. For he spoke against Job in this way in his first speech as well, where he compared him with a lion, a lioness, a lion’s cub, and a tiger. But we should believe God more, for when praising Job he did not call him a pretender but proclaimed him innocent and upright.

But as for what Eliphaz says:

And fire will devour the tents of those who willingly accept gifts. This cannot apply to holy Job. For, as I have already said, according to God’s testimony he spoke about himself in this way when speaking of gifts: “If a stain has clung to my hands.” By mentioning fire, I think he signified Gehenna, because the tents—that is, the bodies—of the wicked are to be consumed. Concerning this fire Sophar also says later: “Fire that is not kindled will devour him,” that is, the wicked man.

[Col. 0657B] He conceived pain and gave birth to iniquity, and his womb prepares deceits. David later spoke of this kind of thing as follows: “Behold, he travailed with injustice, conceived pain, and gave birth to iniquity.” Pain, therefore, is injustice and iniquity. The wicked man gave birth to what he had conceived, yet the womb of his heart does not cease preparing deceits. It produces them when works proceed into action. In conception, therefore, an unjust thought is understood; in birth, the effect of the evil thought is recognized.

Eliphaz spoke all these things against Job. But we have already said above that, through the ministry of prophecy, these words may appear to have been spoken through Job’s person about the devil or any wicked person, just as may also be the case with the other things spoken by his friends.

## CHAPTER XVI

[Col. 0657C]

Job answered and said: “I have often heard such things. You are all troublesome comforters. Will windy words never end, or is something burdensome to you if you speak? I too could speak things like yours. Would that your soul were in place of my soul!”

“If you,” he says, “were suffering what I suffer, I would not treat you as you never cease treating me.”

I too would comfort you with words and shake my head over you. I would strengthen you with my mouth and move my lips as though sparing you. Rather, by the soothing of my words I would encourage you; and I would support your minds, worn down by bitter tribulations, so that they would not fall into the danger of blasphemy, with gentle and peaceful speech.

But what can I do? If I speak, my pain will not be quiet, and if I am silent, it will not depart from me. That is, whether I speak these things to you now or remain silent, I confess that I know only this: I am tormented by unceasing pain.

But now my pain has crushed me, and all my limbs have been reduced to nothing. This too is to be understood of Christ.

My wrinkles testify against me. The contraction of my skin, which I suffer as that same discharge dries it up, in a certain way gives testimony against me by making itself manifest; it seems almost to speak of how many pains or torments I endure.

[Col. 0658A] And a liar rises up against my face, contradicting me. He has gathered his fury against me. Here he calls Eliphaz himself a liar, because he reproaches holy Job for enduring these things on account of the merits of his sins; or the devil, who had called him a sinner. Alternatively, “the liar” is to be understood as Judas or the Jewish people, who gave false testimony against Christ.

And threatening me, he growled against me with his teeth. Through the mouths of his friends disputing against holy Job, the devil threatened; or the Jews growled against the Savior. Another edition reads: “The arrows of pirates fell upon me.” These pirates are the devil’s ministers, whether human beings or demons; in Scripture they are called pirates when this present age is called the sea. The arrows are to be understood as the pains or torments that he endured, so that, pierced through by them, he might die in blasphemy. Thus at last they would take from him the gold and silver of his wisdom and knowledge, as well as the precious garments of his virtues, hope, and faith in God, and the jewels acquired at great cost.

My enemy looked at me with terrifying eyes. In “terrifying eyes” he describes the invisible enemy who wounded the soul within him and threatened him with menace, whether through nocturnal visions or through the terrifying appearance of his friends. Thus, while Job’s friends answered the saint with unspeakable words and frightened him even with gestures of mockery, this is to be understood of Christ.

They opened their mouths against me, and reproaching me, struck my cheek; they were satisfied with my sufferings. [Col. 0658C] Thus “cheek” signifies nobility of birth, or some evident honor. As others have said, he was struck severely on the cheeks, so that he became alienated from honor, nobility, and riches, when he firmly offered the cheek of his faith to be struck by the devil, while the devil tried to disturb it by his blows, as though breaking down a certain door of divine confession—whether when they gave false testimony against Christ, or when they said, “Crucify him.”

God has shut me up with the wicked, and delivered me into the hands of the impious. That is, to the devil and his angels. Or this is to be understood of Christ, when he was delivered into the hands of the Jews.

I, once prosperous, was suddenly crushed. He seized my neck, broke me, and set me up for himself [Col. 0658D] as though for a target. That is, from rich he became poor; or Christ, born from God as man.

He surrounded me with his spears; he pierced my loins with wounds. He did not spare me, but poured out my entrails upon the earth. The spears mentioned here are appropriately understood as the stings of pain that Job suffered; or, concerning Christ, they are to be understood as the blasphemies he endured from the Jews. Job had not only putrefied outwardly in his whole body, but was also liquefying with the foul discharge of his corruption, so that Job himself said, “My wife abhorred my breath.” Everything around his loins had putrefied. Or this is to be understood of Christ: “He pierced my loins with wounds.” For the Jews persecuted the apostles even to this point, those who had been born, as it were, from the loins of his teaching, so that by denying Christ they might wound them with the injury of unbelief, while Peter says, “I do not know the man.” And “he seized my neck,” or, as others have said, “holding my hair, he tore it away.” Accordingly, let us now understand with what fury and power the devil moved and shook this man, or broke him, so that he even tried to tear away the hair of his head, which he had seized all at once. Or this is to be understood of Christ in this way: At the time of the Passion, the adversary, by his own permission, seized him and bent him down even to the sleep of death; he had already broken him with scourges and the fastening of nails, and they set up the sign of salvation in the opposite direction.

He tears me apart with wound upon wound; he rushes upon me like a giant. While innumerable blows are added to my sicknesses and wounds, I am divided, wholly undone and shattered, so that no part of my body remains in me that can stand with any solidity. This is also to be understood of Christ: When Judas was slain by the wound of deadly apostasy, he did not spare him. For he raged with such savagery that he even proclaimed with his mouth the crime he had conceived in his mind; or they added the wounds of the nails to the wounds of the cross.

I have sewn sackcloth upon my skin and covered my flesh with ashes. This likewise seems to me to refer to the humiliation of his kingdom. In Scripture, “horn” is called a kingdom, according to the saying, “He will exalt the horn of his Christ.” Christ called the very nation from which he had sprung “sackcloth.” With ashes he covered the rulers of the Jews when, because of the sacrilege of their denial, he transferred the kingdom from them [Col. 0659C] to the nations.

My face is swollen with weeping, and my eyelids have grown dim. In a human being, weeping or tears arise either from pains or from sadness. Yet tears sometimes flow silently down the cheeks, whereas weeping, though it includes tears, is accompanied by voice and bodily agitation. Job testifies that he had such weeping, which arose in him from the distress of his soul and the torments of his punishments. Alternatively: The prophets are understood as the face of God because they know future things. When they contemplated the destruction of the impious in the spirit, we should understand that they wept for them with continual groans. The eyes of Christ also grew dim when martyrs or saints, wavering amid temptations, were thrown into confusion; [Col. 0659D] but, liberated by God’s grace, they remained in the light.

I have suffered these things without wrongdoing by my hands, while my prayers to God were pure. No saint has prayers to God so pure and undefiled, without even the smallest stain of thought, as the mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, who committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth. Such prayers and supplications must indeed be understood as offered to God according to the human nature that he assumed; according to his divinity, he himself, together with the Father, hears them. Or this is to be understood of the saints who suffered for his name: they were killed by their persecutors without the guilt of rebellion or any crime; as far as those persecutors were concerned, they were delivered to death without cause.

[Col. 0660A] Earth, do not cover my blood, and let my cry find no place of concealment in you. The whole meaning of this is that the merit of an innocent person, conscious of his own righteousness, should not remain hidden—especially since he declares that he, an innocent man, has suffered such great evils. By the name of “blood” he wished to signify the condition of this present life. In this passage “cry” denotes his holiness itself, crying out against the punishments inflicted upon him—punishments that are rightly imposed upon the wicked for vengeance, but upon the righteous for testing. At times in Scripture, “cry” also indicates an intense movement of the soul directed toward God, or even the cry of the people’s wickedness, who were expected to produce grapes but produced thorns. Nor is every wickedness called a cry, but only that which is committed publicly.

For behold, my witness is in heaven, and the one who knows me is on high. [Col. 0660B] For God has borne witness concerning him.

My friends are wordy. One who speaks words unrelated to God is called “wordy”; but one who speaks the words of God cannot be judged wordy.

My eye drips toward God. With tears he appeals to God.

Would that a man might be judged with God, as a son of man is judged with his companion. This is what he says: Would that I had the opportunity to dispute with a human being, so that I could prove myself innocent. But I do not want my God to enter into judgment with me, for he is God, examining hearts and kidneys; his judgment cannot possibly be deceived, nor is he accustomed to be examined by anyone.

For behold, my brief years are passing, and I walk along a path by which I shall not return. He believed that he would not again return either to his mortal body or to the torments of his body.

## CHAPTER XVII

My spirit will be weakened, and my days will be shortened. He says that, in the brevity of his life, his spirit has gradually been weakened and has failed.

And the grave alone remains for me. For death is the end of all torments.

I have not sinned, and my eye remains amid bitterness. It is true that, as one pleasing to God, I have not sinned. Yet this passage can also be understood to mean that he did not sin against God, and nevertheless, as though he had sinned in God, he suffers the punishments of those who blaspheme. And perhaps, since he is praised by God in the present, he had not sinned; [Col. 0660D] but he does not deny that he sinned in the earlier times of his youth.

Release me and set me beside you, and let anyone’s hand fight against me. Thus he desires to hide beneath the shield of God’s protection, so that, fortified and defended by it, he may not fear the raging enemy.

You have put their heart far from discipline; therefore they will not be exalted. Since Job speaks these words to God, the sins of the devil and his satellites had gone before them; for these they received the punishment of hardening. The reason, then, for the subject of which we speak is that they were distanced and did not apprehend discipline: by their own will they lost the exaltation owed to their good nature.

[Col. 0661A] He promises prey to his companions, and the eyes of his sons will fail. He has made me as a proverb of the common people, and I am an example before them. The companions or sons of the devil are his ministers; they are called companions because of their fellowship in conspiracy against God, and sons because they imitate the devil himself. Thus their father, the devil, the head of rebellion, was promising that blessed Job would be given as prey to these demons, believing that through such great pains he would be driven to blasphemy and consequently abandoned by God; or this is to be understood of the time when he stripped him of all the glory of his household and children.

My eye has grown dim with indignation, and my limbs have been reduced almost to nothing. According to the saying of the Gospel, “The lamp of your body is your eye.” [Col. 0661B] Job therefore complains that this eye of his had grown dim through that indignation by which the merits of his holiness were preserved, because in good conscience he was suffering undeserved punishments.

The righteous will be astonished at this. They will marvel at God’s righteous judgments: how a righteous and blameless man is afflicted with punishments.

And the innocent will rise up against the hypocrite. The hypocrite is the devil himself. Although he is of darkness—that is, the inventor of sin—he became dark by withdrawing from the true light. As though he were Lucifer, he set his throne in heaven and transformed himself into an angel of light. Or certainly Job called each of his friends a hypocrite, because under consoling words they deceitfully spoke treacherously to him.

[Col. 0661C] And the righteous will hold to his way, and he whose hands are clean will add strength. In these virtues, certainly, he declares that he is growing stronger.

Therefore, all of you, turn and come, and I shall find no wise man among you. “Turn,” he says, “from the perversity of your judgment, by which you do not cease with the greatest zeal to condemn me. ‘Come’ is the speech of one inviting others to advance toward a better life. It means: O hypocrites, and not true or faithful friends, approach the recognition of the truth, which you plainly do not know how to possess.”

My days have passed. These days can be understood as the days of his former happiness, in which blessed Job lived, strong in virtues. He speaks of these days as having passed from him, not without a groan, when he was surrounded by many miseries [Col. 0661D] and suffered pain from an intolerable wound.

My thoughts have been scattered, tormenting my heart. They have turned night into day, and again after darkness I hope for light. When I had been devoted to the contemplation of a single object and had always kept my thoughts directed toward God, I now see that the misery of this affliction that has come upon me has scattered those same thoughts from their former unity and solidity within me. For this reason my heart is tormented, because it is tortured by their tearing apart, seeing me endure evils incompatible with my simplicity.

If I endure, the underworld is my house, and in darkness I have spread my bed. He was being driven, as he says, by bodily punishments and the goads of his thoughts through unceasing time, and therefore he cried out that he was already suffering the punishments of the underworld. Or perhaps that separation by which he was made alien from human beings outside the city, sitting on the dunghill, was called “darkness,” because he had no light of human consolation.

I said to corruption, “You are my father”; to my mother and sister, “You are worms.” “For so long,” he says, “I have been rotting that I call corruption itself, and the worms born in its discharge, my parents. Thus, just as no mortal can exist without parents, so I too have become as though I could not exist without corruption and worms. They are in my flesh as though in their own nature, as though I myself subsisted from them, although they are rather generated in me from the discharge of my flesh, and I am not generated from them.” Here he more clearly signified mortality brought about by sin, in which there is corruption, and in corruption, decay. He called the origin of the human race itself in Adam “father,” since through corruption it was made subject to decay. He called human nature, corrupted by decay, “mother.” He called all Adam’s posterity “sister,” since it is born from the corruption of mortality as from the foul discharge of decay. Bildad also said this: “Man is corruption, and the son of man is a worm.”

Where, then, is my expectation now, and who considers my patience? In saying, “Who considers my patience?” he openly shows himself to be strong amid those torments; he complains, as it were, that he has been unable to attain the reward for so great a labor.

[Col. 0662C] All that is mine will descend into the deepest underworld. Others have said, “All my goods.” He says that his goods will descend to the underworld, namely, his soul; or that he himself will descend there on their behalf. We truly do not believe, concerning justice, that so great and noble a man could have been frustrated of the reward for his holy works. But when he says:

Do you think that at least there I shall have rest? This is the meaning: If I suffer the punishments of the underworld in this life, do you think that there will be any rest for me in the places of punishment? He speaks this while weighed down by miseries, rather than overcome by despair, since elsewhere he says to the Lord: “I know that in the underworld you will protect me, until your anger has passed away.”

## CHAPTER XVIII

[Col. 0662D] Then Bildad the Shuhite answered and said: How long will you keep throwing out words? Understand first, and then let us speak. That is: What will be the end of this wordiness, as though it were not sincere? Or Bildad accuses Job alone of being wordy; or he suggests that, as though stirred up by some unknown spirit, Job does not cease speaking.

Why are we counted as beasts and considered filthy in your sight? He says that holy Job has despised them as though they were brute animals and has regarded them as utterly base and unworthy of conversation; and that they are so possessed by anger that they seem to be suffering madness.

Why do you destroy my soul in your fury? By speaking against divine justice, stirred up by the madness of fury, you must bring death upon your own soul.

[Col. 0663A] Will the earth be abandoned because of you, and will the rocks be moved from their place? As though he were saying: Will the world, because of you, no longer belong to its ruler, so that, if he finds sinners—as he has found you himself—he will not punish them? By “earth” and “rocks,” metaphorically, the whole multitude of peoples and all the lofty, worldly, proud, and powerful can be understood. Rocks can also be understood as human souls, just as earth can signify human flesh. Angels too, because of the height of their nature and their eminent honor, can be called rocks.

Will not the light of the impious be extinguished, and will the flame of his fire not shine? By “light” he signified the present happiness in which holy Job had lived gloriously, just as Solomon also says: “The light of the impious will be extinguished.” [Col. 0663B] He therefore said that this light was extinguished when Job was deprived of all present happiness. But when he says, “Nor will the flame of his fire shine,” he means that he will not return to his former happiness.

The light will grow dark in his tent, and the lamp above him will be extinguished. “Not only,” he says, “will he lose present happiness, but also the light of the remembrance of God, which was in the tent of his heart, will grow dark, so that God will not rise into his memory; and, in accordance with his deserts, the lamp of divine protection that had been above him will be extinguished.”

The steps of his strength will be hemmed in, and his own counsel will cast him down. As a proud man, trusting in his strength, believes that he walks uprightly, so he will be enclosed by the narrowness and pressures of tribulations, so that he cannot escape from them at all.

For he has thrust his feet into a net, and he walks in its meshes. By the net and its meshes an unavoidable evil is signified: whenever anyone wishes to cast it off, the very effort by which he tries to do so hinders and entangles him, so that he falls.

His heel will be caught in a snare, and thirst will burn against him. Here the snare can suitably be understood as the devil himself, who watches for the opportunity to trip sinners by the heel; and he is likewise called “thirst,” because, as though burning with desire for some good, he thirsts for the death of human beings.

His snare lies hidden in the earth, and his trap is on the path. The ruined man does not know what ambushes await him; or he has the snare by which his feet are hindered hidden within himself [Col. 0663D]—that is, the bondage of sin. In the savagery of his conduct, by which he thinks that he is walking rightly, the trap of this error lies concealed.

Terrifying things will frighten him on every side and entangle his feet. Or, “pains” will do so. The proud man will always be terrified by fear of the coming calamity. “Terrifying things” can also be understood here not as feelings of the heart, but rather as the devil’s ministers themselves. These, then, tried in many ways to frighten holy Job, so that he would yield to them.

Let his strength be weakened by hunger, and let deprivation invade his ribs. Hunger itself can be understood as the devil, who suffers this kind of hunger, by which he is never satisfied with the slaughter of human beings. Or he himself suffers hunger because he is not worthy to receive the word that proceeds from the mouth of God. Therefore, under the name of “ribs,” the defenses of the chest are signified, with which he has fortified himself, as though with a certain hardening, so that the nourishment of divine speech cannot reach him. Or he is also describing the wound of the impious.

Let the firstborn of death devour the beauty of his skin and consume his arms. The devil destroyed the beauty of his skin—that is, the adornments of his virtues—and his arms, the strength of his kingdom. He is called “the firstborn of death” because through him death first entered the world, and he is the inventor of his own death.

Let his confidence be torn from his tent, and let the king of destruction trample upon him. He called this destruction the devil, who is king over all the sons of pride; but he could not trample upon holy Job in order to overthrow him.

Let his companions dwell in his tent, the one who is not. His companions, associates, or sons, as stated above, are the devil’s ministers. Here he is said “not to be”; although he subsists according to the property of his nature, nevertheless he is not, as I have said, because through transgression he became alienated from God.

Let sulfur be scattered over his tent. Let him experience here the smoke of Gehenna.

Let his roots below be dried up, and above let his harvest be crushed. “Harvest” can be understood as his works, which burst forth outwardly and publicly from within and arise from the root of faith. Alternatively: “Let his roots below be dried up”—that is, let the works he committed in this age be found dead and dry, like dead things. “Above let his harvest be crushed”—that is, in the future he will by no means obtain the reward of his labor.

Let his memory perish from the earth. That is, let him do nothing worthy of remembrance; or let his memory perish from the land of the living.

And let his name not be celebrated in the streets. Kings sat in the street, among whom he wishes that the man should not merit a reputation for justice. The streets are understood as virtues, in which wisdom acts confidently and moves about the city of God, Jerusalem, in which the broad commandment of the Scriptures is contained in divine sacraments and mysteries. Therefore, the old men, old women, and children will play vehemently in these streets.

It will drive him from light into darkness, and remove him from the inhabited city. From this temporary light he will be sent into the eternal darkness of the underworld; or he will be thrust from the portion of the lot of the saints into the darkness of punishments.

He will have neither seed nor offspring among his people. He says that he will leave descendants unworthy of the memory of their nation or homeland, according to the psalmist’s saying: “The generation of the upright will be blessed.” He did not wish to beget such a generation among his people, one in which he could glory spiritually and in his homeland.

Nor will there be any remnant in his regions. It is evident [Col. 0665A] that nothing remained for holy Job. Spiritually, however, this is to be understood as meaning that the impious will have no remnant of his generation in the future.

In his day the last will be astonished. That is, at the time of his condemnation.

And terror will seize the first. That is, the lowly and the great will be terrified; in other words, powerful and mighty kings. Or “the last” and “the first” can reasonably be understood as human beings and angels, as well as saints and sinners.

These, then, are the tents of the wicked, and this is the place of the one who does not know God. He seems to deliver the sentence of the curse he has pronounced and to say where such a proud and impious man will dwell. But Job is not wicked, for God calls him upright and innocent.

## CHAPTER XIX

[Col. 0665B] Then Job answered and said: How long will you afflict my soul and wear me down with words? It is clear that he has been worn down, afflicted, fatigued, and crushed by the replies of his friends.

Behold, you have confounded me ten times, and you are not ashamed to oppress me. He named ten days for the whole period. But just as in the Apocalypse a greater number of time is understood by a small number, so here too, by this same total, a lesser quantity is signified, so that we may recognize that, while this number remains whole and complete, different places in the divine Scriptures signify sometimes a greater number and sometimes a smaller one.

Indeed, even if I have been ignorant, my ignorance will remain with me. But you rise up against me and reproach me with my own disgrace. [Col. 0665C] “You think,” he says, “that I do not know God, just as you say. Is it fitting for friends to insult the oppressed, from whom they ought rather to expect the offering of consolation in their affliction? This is not the work of faithful friends, but rather the mockery of those who ridicule.”

At least now understand that God has not afflicted me with an impartial judgment and has surrounded me with his scourges. Behold, I will cry out, suffering violence, and no one will hear. I will shout, and there is no one to judge. He said that he was unjustly suffering the troubles of punishments, whereas they spoke as though he were suffering deservedly as a wicked man. They think that he was mistaken in this aspect of his understanding, and therefore later he says to God: “I have spoken foolishly, and of things that exceeded my knowledge beyond measure.”

He has fenced in my path, and I cannot pass through. [Col. 0665D] Along it I was proceeding uprightly and blamelessly toward the glory of my merits. He has therefore fenced off and blocked this path with the disgrace of such suffering, so that I cannot reach that glory.

And he has put darkness on my road. That is, on my track, the path of my disciplined life, along which, as though through a narrow and confined way, I was proceeding with certain hope toward a just rewarder. On it I found the darkness of this misery and calamity.

He has stripped me of my glory and taken the crown from my head. He deprived me of the glory of my kingdom; he also took away the confidence of my faith, which he drew down from the very summit of my mind—the head of rational nature—as though it were a crown of honor.

[Col. 0666A] He has destroyed me on every side, and I perish; like a tree torn up, he has taken away my hope. I have been deprived of my house, kingdom, family, children, friends, and bodily health. With all these things removed, I see myself perishing, and even the hope of my life has been taken away like a tree.

His fury has become angry against me, and he has treated me as his enemy. Here “the fury of God” can be understood as the devil himself, who attacked blessed Job in various ways—that is, with blasphemies and torments of his flesh.

His robbers came together and made a way through me. The fury of God is the devil, while the robbers are his ministers. This is what he means by “they made a way through me”: when they stripped him either of the world’s possessions or of bodily health. Hence it is beautifully said:

And they surrounded my tent in a circle. He has put my brothers far from me, and my acquaintances have withdrawn from me as though from a stranger. My relatives have abandoned me, and those who knew me have forgotten me. The inhabitants of my house and my maidservants have treated me as a stranger, and I was like a foreigner in their eyes. I called my servant, and he did not answer; with my own mouth I pleaded with him. That is, they lay in wait outside. Or they surrounded his tent in a circle; that is, they placed torments upon his body. But they could not bend his soul toward sin.

My wife abhorred my breath. “I have rotted entirely within,” he says, “so that even my wife could not endure the stench of my breath.” It could have happened that he had an abscess in his entrails, occupying the whole cavity of his belly, and that, speaking from it, he exhaled a foul odor from the purulence of a deep wound.

And I pleaded with the sons of my womb. Even fools despised me. In the divine Scriptures, “sons” also refers to grandsons and to those born in a more distant succession. Therefore, when he said “the sons of my womb,” he looked back upon himself as the fountain and origin of his posterity, from whom the families of his relations flowed like streams. He could also have called “sons of his womb” those whom he had formed through the teaching of his wisdom, as though by seed from the womb of his heart, possessing within himself, through God’s grace, the form of grace and the discipline of the natural law in truth.

And when I had withdrawn from them, they slandered me. My former counselors abhorred me, and the one whom I loved most has turned away from me. This may perhaps mean that he had passed into their forgetfulness and withdrawn from their affections and hearts.

My bone has clung to my skin and flesh, which has been consumed. His flesh had become so dry that no moisture remained in him, and therefore his skin had in a certain way been glued to his bones. Physicians call this illness marasmus.
