Only my lips remain around my teeth. The devil consumed the flesh of holy Job but deliberately left his lips intact so that, placed amid torments, he would have something with which he could easily blaspheme—as though the blasphemy of the heart did not count, for which Job himself, as for his other sins, used to offer holocausts to God on behalf of his children on the seventh day. But the devil preserved his tongue so that he might discover whether Job, because of the simplicity of his heart, would bring forth blasphemy upon his lips.

Have pity on me, have pity on me, at least you, my friends, because the hand of the Lord has touched me. He therefore called the wound that he was suffering “the hand of the Lord,” because it had been inflicted by the Lord’s power. “Touched” is to be understood as “afflicted.”

Why do you persecute me like God and glut yourselves on my flesh? God acted toward me in judgment, and he alone is permitted to do everything in his work. Why do you presume to act like God and afflict an innocent man? That belongs to God alone according to his dispensation; or does God need your dispensation?

Who will grant me that my words be written? Who will give me that they be inscribed in a book with an iron stylus and a plate of lead, or carved with a chisel in rock? Since he could find consolation from no human being, he turned to God and prophesied in the spirit the future resurrection, in which he would receive a reward for these evils. He desires that these words be inscribed in hard stones, so that the words of his prophecy might endure through the long ages of the world.

For I know that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth. And again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God. With this shield the Church, which confesses the true Incarnation of the Only-Begotten Son of God and most truly believes that the resurrection of the dead will come, arms and protects itself and refutes and conquers its enemies. Where are those [Col. 0667C] who say that in the resurrection we shall have different bodies? Let them hear this man, praised by the mouth of God, saying:

Whom I myself shall see. I myself, Job, who lie in the dung, wholly rotting in the discharge of my wounds—I, Job, I say, now corrupted and dissolved by wounds, glorified in this mortal flesh through the incorruptible resurrection that is to come, shall see God. And to express the restoration of his very own body, he therefore says:

And my eyes shall see, and not another. This hope of mine is laid up in my bosom. All these things have been completed in my bosom.

Why, then, do you now say, “Let us persecute him”? Why do you act now as though I were worthless and believed nothing, so that I should not fear God; or because I am alien from divine religion, you wish to persecute me, piercing me with your pointed words?

Let us find the root of the word against him. You see, therefore, that you do not act toward me faithfully as true friends, but as deceitful men you prepare snares for me from my own words, since you wish to find in those very words an occasion—like a certain root—for accusation against me.

Flee, then, from the face of the sword, for the sword is the avenger of iniquities. This is what he says: If you withdraw from attacking me, you will be able to escape the sword of God’s just sentence. For the sword is the tongue of a king, and not a material sword, as Solomon says.

[Col. 0668A] And know that there is a judgment. By that judgment of the righteous Judge, God, I may be judged concerning those who mock me.

## CHAPTER XX

Then Zophar the Naamathite answered and said: Therefore my varied thoughts succeed one another, and my mind is carried in different directions. “Therefore,” he says, “I am agitated and troubled in thought, because you say that you suffer these evils without cause from God the judge, whereas nothing unfavorable ought to be suspected of God.

I will hear the instruction by which you reproach me, and the spirit of my understanding will answer me. I will indeed hear you rebuking and reproving me, because perhaps I ought not to scold one who is in pain; but it is fitting for me to give the most righteous answer concerning God: you could not be punished by him in this way unless you were conscious of evil and guilty of many crimes.

[Col. 0668B] I have known this from the beginning, from the time when man was placed upon the earth: that the praise of the impious is brief, and the joy of the hypocrite is like a point. Now he has begun to assail holy Job with curses, openly asserting that he is impious and a hypocrite, because he pretended to be righteous and has now proved rebellious against God.

Though his pride should ascend even to heaven, and his head touch the clouds. This is a clear and certain hyperbole: he describes a person as excessively exalted and puffed up.

Like a dunghill, he will perish at the end, and those who had seen him will say, “Where is he?” You have in every respect been compared to a dunghill, and now you see yourself rotted away. Those who once saw you reigning in glory now say in a voice of mockery: “Where is that wisest of men and mightiest of kings?”

[Col. 0668C] Like a dream flying away, he will not be found; he will pass away like a vision of the night. This is clear, as it says: “He vanished like the dream of one awakening.”

The eye that saw him will not see him, nor will his place behold him any longer. That is, the honor of the impious cannot be restored.

His children will be crushed by poverty. Whether, then, his bodily children, or works that are sometimes called children, or those who imitated him as a father, they will by God’s judgment be reduced to nothing—which you already see partly fulfilled in your children and also in your carnal works.

And his hands will repay him his pain. For he did that by which he deserved to receive the evil of vengeance through the working of God’s justice.

[Col. 0668D] His bones will be filled with the vices of his youth. He means that from his youth, when he began to commit more serious sins, he remained in those same sins even into old age, for which he was never willing to repent. Therefore it follows:

And they will sleep with him in the dust. That is, after the death of the vices that is in the soul; or until death, which comes by the dissolution of this body. Here it is not unreasonable to understand “bones” as old age itself, by which the weariness of years and the now premature hardness of senility are signified. Or: “His bones will be filled with the vices of his youth,” and so forth. If there are any natural virtues of the soul in an impious person, from his youth they grow old, are dissolved, or flow away through his vices, so that nothing solid and strong remains in them. For they are covered and overlaid by those same vices as by fluid flesh—that is, by unstable things—whereas the virtues ought rather, like solid and very firm bones, to restrain, contain, and govern vices, like fluid and loosened flesh. Thus they sleep in the dust of his flesh because, with vices resisting and prevailing, they lose the firmness of their good nature.

[Col. 0669A] For when evil is sweet in his mouth, he hides it beneath his tongue. Sweet evils are impiety, blasphemy, and the other sins of the mouth. He hides it beneath his tongue, saying, “Where is there labor and pain for him?” and he will defend and conceal it, as Scripture says: “He who covers his iniquity will not prosper.”

[Col. 0669B]

He will spare it and not abandon it. That is, he strokes, cherishes, and nourishes his evil, and, taking delight in it, never repents so as to depart from it.

And he will conceal it in his throat. He seems to me to mean that he is always prepared to blaspheme and does not first pause even briefly to consider what he is going to say, because he already has blasphemy prepared, which he pours forth together with the curse of his heart.

His bread will be changed in his belly into the gall of asps within. The bread, that is, the whole life of such a man, is the delight of sins, the sweetness of enticements, and the pleasure that will afterward become bitter and deadly for him. By saying “in his belly,” he means that even in his heart, on account of his iniquities, he suffers bitter, harsh, and excessive pains while conscience torments him. [Col. 0669C]

He will vomit up the riches that he swallowed, and God will draw them out of his belly. The head of the asp will rise up, and the tongue of the viper will kill him. What he seized and appropriated unjustly and violently, God rightly repaid him as punishment for the crimes he had committed; thus what he had unjustly taken will be wrested from the wicked man. That angel who killed one hundred and eighty-five thousand seems to have been a good angel, because angels are reapers: the tares destined to be burned in eternal fires.

He will not see the streams of the river, the torrent of honey, and of butter. Let us understand that the pleasantness, or delights, of paradise, as well as its abundance, are signified by these names. And that these kings who were not adversaries of the truth are themselves those rushings of the river that gladden the city [Col. 0669D] is not absurdly understood—namely, as flowing from the fountain, or from the river, of the Scriptures. Or we may rightly understand these same apostles as those rushings, going out from the fountain of the Gospel to irrigate the barren lands of the peoples. We should also understand them as torrents, because their teaching was poured swiftly over all; and this divine teaching is most truly compared with honey because of the sweetness of the utterances of God, and with butter because of the same teaching’s simple and innocent nourishment. In the psalm also he says that the wicked man will not possess this sweetness.

He will pay for everything he has done, yet he will not be consumed. That is, Gehenna is a kind of perpetual incorruption and an eternal continuance of torments. [Col. 0670A]

According to the multitude of his devices, so will he suffer, because, while crushing, he stripped the poor man’s house; he seized it and did not build it. This accords with what the prophet says to God: “For you will repay each one according to his works.”

His belly was not satisfied. I think that “belly” here denotes a certain receptacle of the soul, in which his thoughts are stored like morsels of food; he calls it inexplicable.

And when he has obtained what he desired, he will not be able to possess it. Just as you yourself, who by God’s just judgment have lost your entire patrimony.

Nothing remained of his food, and therefore nothing will remain of his goods. He brands him with inhumanity, because from the abundance of his table he provided refreshment to no stranger or guest. But Zophar is mistaken, because holy Job says: “If I have eaten my morsel alone.” Nothing will remain of his foods because his goods will not flourish. [Col. 0670B]

When he is satisfied, he will be constricted; he will burn with heat, and every pain will rush upon him. When, that is, he has been filled with riches and abundance of every kind, sudden destruction will come upon him. Constricted and confined by the calamity that rushes upon him, he will burn amid the disasters of his misfortunes.

May his belly be filled, so that He may send against him the anger of His wrath. Above we understood the belly of the soul as a certain capacity or spacious bosom. He therefore says that he is already full of the most wicked thoughts, until blasphemy is heaped up to the very limit of his mouth. Or we may not absurdly understand this as the anger of the devil’s fury directed against the soul, through which the saints are tested. [Col. 0670C]

And may he rain his battle upon him. Because of its multitude, “battle” can be understood as the hostile powers. These therefore wage war against God when they attack his saints. But when he says, “May he rain it abundantly upon him,” he prays that the misery of calamity be poured out upon him. Or the impious man who wages the war of blasphemy against God will receive his own work.

He will flee iron weapons and rush upon a bronze bow. It is as though he said: When he thinks that he can flee from lighter calamities, he will fall into more severe ones. Or otherwise: If he flees the devil’s companions and ministers, he will run into the prince of darkness himself. Although those companions are rebellious in wickedness, strong and hard-hearted like iron weapons, he will nevertheless strike against the worse author of all evil, as against a bronze bow. I think that the bow is named here for this reason: he never ceases to kill unsuspecting people by ambush and deceit. For arrows are usually shot from a bow at those who do not expect them. And he will not be delivered from the hand of the sword. This means that he will not escape the devil’s everlasting death.

A sword drawn and coming out of its sheath, flashing in its bitterness. Since we said that the devil may be understood under the transferred name of “bow,” he, by transgressing the boundaries through disobedience and, lifted up in pride, surpassing the limits of holy humility, was, as it were, drawn out of the sheath of blessed habitation and expelled by God’s just judgment. Or let us understand that, drawn from its sheath, he is signified as always ready to kill the one fleeing from him. [Col. 0671A]

A bronze arrow will wound him. Bronze is enduring; the devil is compared with this metal because he never fails in killing and is not consumed by any old age. He also flashes—that is, he transforms himself into an angel of light.

They will go and come upon him in terror. That is, his companions.

All darknesses are hidden in his eyes. In this passage, “darknesses” should be understood as sins, whether those committed by the impious man or those that are to be committed, which lie hidden in his heart, affection, and thoughts. They are said to be hidden in the secrets of his mind because he favors them and takes the greatest delight in them.

[Col. 0671B] Fire that is not kindled will devour him. We may not absurdly understand this fire as Gehenna. It does not live by certain materials or fuel in order to burn, but, alive through itself as it was created, it consumes everything cast into it. Therefore this fire will devour the impious man, swallowing and absorbing him as though he were rational, so that he may be tormented in it by eternal punishments.

He will be afflicted, abandoned in his tent. Because of his impiety, the wicked man will be abandoned by God, so that he may be tortured by perpetual punishments in the tent of his body.

The heavens will reveal his iniquity, and the earth will rise up against him. The angels and holy human beings will certainly serve as witnesses, so that they may know that he is suffering punishments most justly. [Col. 0671C]

The offspring of his house will be exposed. At God’s judgment, when the impious man is to be condemned, not only all the thoughts of his heart but also the beginnings of his destroyed thoughts must be disclosed to God and made manifest in a clearer light.

He will be dragged away on the day of God’s wrath. On the day of judgment he will be sent into the outer darkness. The “day” may also have been Job’s impious day, when he was struck by the plague and concluded his speech by saying:

“This is the portion of the impious man from God?” Here, as though abruptly, he shows that he had said all these things about holy Job. What follows is:

“And the inheritance of his words is from the Lord.” That is, the repayment of his deeds. Others translated it, “And the inheritance of his words is from the bishop,” because just as the Lord is known from his dominion over all things, so the bishop is most truly called such because he oversees every creature. For God will not punish sinners as one disturbed and agitated in mind, since he is immutable, as he said to Moses: “I am who I am”—not only everlasting, but eternally gentle. Furthermore, let us understand that such things are said of God anthropopathically, not properly according to his unchangeable substance, but by transferring names expressive of a passible creature to the uncreated and unmade creature who is rather the creator of all.

## CHAPTER XXI

Then Job answered and said: “Hear, I beg you, my words, and repent. Bear with me, so that I too may speak; and afterward, if it seems good, laugh at my words.” After such great insults he was not provoked to answer bitterly. Rather, he addresses them with a plea and asks them to give attention to his words, so that, after hearing and understanding them, they may know that they ought to repent of such bitterness of speech.

“Is my dispute against a human being, so that I should not rightly be sorrowful?” First of all, this is a burden and a very grievous and terrible thing for me: that I have to plead not with a human being but with God, to whom I was presenting a purified righteousness so that he might repay the reward of this work. Behold, now, as though guilty of crimes, I am afflicted by every misery. Here he says that he is sorrowful because he knows that God does nothing unjustly.

[Col. 0672B] “Attend to me, be astonished, and put your finger upon your mouth.” The secret is this: how can the good and just God act toward me in such a way, especially when I have his favorable testimony concerning me?

“And when I remember, I am afraid, and trembling shakes my flesh.” When I consider this plague, which I endure though living justly, and remember God’s judgment—for he afflicts no innocent person—I am exceedingly afraid. I know very well that no one suffers any evil unless he himself has permitted it; he inflicts evil on no one unless he has judged it most just to inflict it. But these things happened to Job so that what was inwardly before God might become outwardly evident to human beings.

“Why then do the impious live, are raised up, and strengthened by riches? Their offspring endure before them, a multitude of relatives and descendants in their sight. Their houses are secure and peaceful, and God’s rod is not upon them. Their ox conceives and does not miscarry; their cow gives birth and is not deprived of her young. Their little ones go out like flocks, and their children exult in play. They hold the tambourine and the lyre, and rejoice at the sound of the organ. They spend their days in prosperity, and in a moment they descend to the underworld. They said to God, ‘Depart from us; we do not want the knowledge of your ways. Who is the Almighty, that we should serve him? And what profit is there for us if we pray to him?’ Another said: ‘Why does the life of the impious prosper?’ And another said: ‘Why do you not look upon those who practice iniquity?’ Answer me, I beg you: If I am impious and forgetful of good works according to righteousness, as you assert, and suffer these things, why do the impious live, and why are they raised up and strengthened by riches?” Thus, I say, I beg you, answer this: Do you, who in this passage defend God’s justice against me, thereby mark him as unjust, so that he is an unjust avenger toward me and merciful toward those like me? The end and destruction of those of whom he now speaks will therefore be eternal death and the perdition of hell.

“Nevertheless, since their goods are not in their own hand, may the counsel of the impious be far from me.” Because, in exchange for this glory and temporary bloom, they will be clothed with everlasting disgrace before the angels.

“How often will the lamp of the impious be extinguished, and an inundation come upon them, and pains divide the fury of his wrath? They will be like straw before the face of the wind, and like chaff which the whirlwind scatters.” The light of the righteous, however, is everlasting: in this night of the age, the lamp of faith is not extinguished by any wind of temptation, and there it is prepared for the glory of eternal light. But the sinner’s light is extinguished within the brief span of life, because he will pass away like a shadow. “It will not be,” and an inundation will come upon the impious, as Job says—that is, an abundance of torments. “And pains divide his fury.” Without doubt, by saying that God divides the pains, he means that he will repay each person punishments according to his deserts. [Col. 0673A]

“God will store up the pain of the father for his children, and when he repays it, then he will know.” He stores up the punishments of Gehenna for the devil, so that those whom he has made his children by the example of his wickedness may be punished together with him. When God repays this, their father the devil will then know—that is, then he will feel it—when he suffers eternal punishments together with his children.

“His eyes will see his slaughter,” or, as others have said, “his death.” For it is a double torment to see the punishments that one suffers.

“And he will drink from the fury of the Almighty.” He himself is the Lord’s golden cup in the hand of Babylon.

“For what does his house after him concern him, even if the number of his months is cut in half?” He speaks of the same devil, about whom Solomon says: “When the impious comes into the depths of his evils and crimes, he despises them in despair.” For he already knows that he and those who are his house and kingdom are to be condemned forever, because he has no will to repent.

“Will anyone teach God knowledge, who judges those on high?” Since he has a just judgment concerning the lofty and exalted angelic powers, how could anyone teach him, so that his judgment might be criticized in the matters mentioned above?

“This one dies strong and healthy, rich and happy; his inward parts are full of fat, and his bones are watered with marrow. Another dies in the bitterness of his soul, without any possessions, and yet they sleep together in the dust, and worms cover them.” He says that the fortunate in this world and the unfortunate in this life share a common condition: “His inward parts,” or “intestines,” as others have said, are full of fat, and his bones are watered with marrow. Another dies in the bitterness of his soul without any possessions, and yet they sleep together in the dust, and worms cover them. The meaning of this entire passage is therefore that in this world the righteous and sinners live without distinction, but that this difference will be changed in the future, as happened with the rich man and poor Lazarus. [Col. 0673D]

“Certainly I know your thoughts and your unjust opinions against me.” “Therefore,” he says, “I rightly conclude what you see: that in this age the condition of dying is one and the same for the sinner and the saint. Yet afterward they will be separated, so that the righteous may be changed for reward, while sinners are carried away for punishment. But you pass an unjust sentence upon an innocent man.”

“And you say.” They insult and mock me.

“Where is the house of the prince, and where are the tents of the impious?” Ask any traveler, and you will recognize that he understands these same things. Since you therefore think this about me—that the time of my condemnation has now arrived—it is not as you suppose you have determined. This chastisement of God is temporary, not eternal condemnation.

“For the wicked man is kept for the day of destruction, and he will be led to the day of wrath.” He is to be led to the day of God’s wrath, so that he may receive the sentence of eternal death. All the saints are rightly called travelers, because, unencumbered and joyful as they pass through the age, they tread the earth with manly courage and, hastening toward their blessed homeland, complete the laborious journey of this world. Thus those who ascend to the foreign—or girded—people gird the loins of their mind against the dissolution of vices with the belt of faith. [Col. 0674B]

“Who will rebuke him to his face concerning his way, and who will repay him for what he has done?” It seems to me that Job spoke specifically about the devil, although it can also be understood generally of all sinners. What human being can rebuke him because of his most polluted way, by which he brought the whole world into sin? Or what creature could repay him what he deserves, except that one Lamb of God who committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth?

“He will be led to the graves.” To the death of torments, namely, which he inflicted upon human beings in Adam; and he himself will be led to the underworld, so that he may be punished there forever.

“And he will keep watch in the heap of the dead.” Although he is to be condemned and led away to punishments, nevertheless, rejoicing in the death of human beings, he will watch over the heap of those same dead with every eager effort, so as to gaze upon their destruction; or certainly he will live forever in death.

“Sweet was the gravel of Cocytus.” They say that Cocytus is a river of the underworld. In the divine Scriptures, however, we read of this same river as a torrent, a well, a furnace, eternal fire, a lake, a pool, and Gehenna. By the name “gravel” I think are signified the very offices of Tartarus and the ministers of infernal punishments, bound in places of torment. The phrase is spoken as if ironically, because the inhabitants of the underworld desire and long for him to punish and to be satiated by his destruction. Or certainly he was sweet to death because he acquired for it so many countless peoples. [Col. 0674D]

“And after him he will drag every human being.” Those who follow his example by imitation; or, according to the transgression of the human race in Adam, he drags every human being after him.

“And innumerable before him.” Those whom he deceived, and whom he sends ahead to punishments so that he himself may follow them.

“How then do you comfort me in vain, when your answer has been shown to contradict the truth?” In this verse he concluded the whole dispute of his argument. He proves his friends wrong for contending against him without cause on the basis they had stated: while they distrust that the impious and sinners are punished in this world, and condemn him among them, he proves that those who are most glorified in this age are the ones being led to the judgment of condemnation. [Col. 0675A]

## CHAPTER XXII

Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said: “Can a human being be compared with God, even when he has perfect knowledge?” These words are spoken as a reproach to Job, who arrogates entirely to himself the claim that he speaks from the wisdom proper to his own heart.

“What profit is it to God if you are righteous, or what do you confer upon him if your life is blameless?” No one has made God better by his righteousness and holiness, because the source and origin of every good has no need of anyone’s goodness, according to the prophet who says: “You have no need of my goods.”

[Col. 0675B] “Will he rebuke you because he fears you, and will he come with you into judgment?” Is the reason for God’s fear that God should fear you? Perhaps you might at some point become powerful and, made his equal, resist him? These words are spoken rather in mockery and derision.

“And not because of your very great wickedness and your infinite iniquities?” “He does not rebuke you because he fears you,” he says, “by the corrections of this severe plague, but because of all your evils, to which you devoted yourself.” Since, therefore, the principal evil—that is, Job’s wickedness—is very great, from which the other evils hang as though from a cluster of grapes, he adds and recounts them individually, saying:

“For you took your brothers’ pledge without cause.” He means that he violently and in a hostile manner seized what belonged to others, or unjustly extorted pledges; or that under the appearance of justice he despoiled them through false accusation. The crime is aggravated when he says that he spared not even his own blood. [Col. 0675C]

“And you stripped the naked of their clothing.” Here it becomes clear what you did to the clothed, since in your presence not even the naked were found immune from your plunder.

“You gave no water to the weary.” This is clear.

“And you withheld bread from the hungry.” Not to give is serious; to withhold is more serious. It is therefore a great sin not to provide hospitality to those placed in need. Yet we know that Eliphaz plainly lied, since below we read how many good works Job performed.

“By the strength of your arm you possessed the land, and as the most powerful you held it.” He nevertheless accuses him as a proud man and tyrant, who did not govern the peoples of his kingdom with justice and equity, but subjected them by harsh behavior, as though by the strength of his arm, to a hard burden of servitude. No one, on account of his exceedingly harsh rule, lived except as subject to his condition. [Col. 0675D]

“You sent widows away empty.” You were unwilling to listen to them, abandoned, afflicted by troubles, and humbled, in order to help them. You sent each one away empty when she could not obtain from you what she requested.

“And you crushed the arms of orphans.” If they had any strength by which they could be sustained, you took it away and broke their spirits through despair of life; or, by failing to defend them from evil people, you crushed the strength of their hope, by which they looked to you, while you allowed them to be oppressed. [Col. 0676A]

“Therefore you are surrounded by snares, and sudden terror troubles you.” Eliphaz said that blessed Job was disturbed by the fear of a bad conscience and that, when the same fear suddenly came upon him, he was utterly dismayed and lost the resolve to endure adversity.

“But you thought you would not see darkness and would not be overwhelmed by the rush of overflowing waters.” You acted with such security and power amid iniquities that you did not believe these evils would come upon you as a reciprocal consequence of your merits. By these darknesses of misery and calamity, as though by the rush of overflowing waters, you have suddenly been submerged, so that with your heart darkened you do not see what patience teaches to be right. In many ways the divine Scriptures call sins “darkness”; the term may also denote ignorance, tribulation, or even the obscurity of the divine books.

“Or do you think that God is higher than heaven and is exalted above the summit of the stars? And you say, ‘What does God know?’ and, as though through mist, he judges.” First, therefore, Eliphaz accuses holy Job of asserting that ignorance can befall God, and that there are many things in his creatures that he does not know. Then he accuses him of affirming that God’s judgment is uncertain and doubtful, and therefore that he judges through mist—that is, as though judging something merely probable. [Col. 0676B]

“Clouds are his hiding place; he does not consider our affairs, and he walks around the hinges of heaven.” He fabricates all these things as though they came from the thoughts of blessed Job, so that he may call him not only a blasphemer but also one who says that God is ignorant and confined to places. To think this about God is certainly a great sacrilege.

“Do you wish to keep the path of the ages, which wicked men have trodden?” He said “do you wish to keep” instead of “observe.” That is: do you desire to follow the conduct and ruined life of those who perished in the Flood, in Sodom, and in the wilderness, or of those who do not believe that God cares for human affairs?

“They were taken away before their time.” Such as Dathan and Abiram, or those who perished by sudden death.

“And a river overturned their foundation.” When God’s wrath threatened them, the stability of their present life was overturned like the force of a river; or, as though a river of pressure had come upon them, the foundation of their bodies was demolished, so that the walls of their lives collapsed.

“They said to God, ‘Depart from us.’” They were condemned because of their apostasy. But Job is not like them, for he says: “Even if he kills me, I will hope in him.”

“And they thought that the Almighty could do nothing, although he had filled their houses with good things.” The impious therefore did not fear that, because of sin and offense against God, they might incur punishment in return for the good things he had provided.

“Let their counsel be far from me.” And he places the holy man among the number of blasphemers, though Job detests them as he detests those same men.

“The righteous will see and rejoice.” Or, as others have said, “will laugh.” He speaks of the downfall of the unbelieving people.

“And the innocent will mock them.” How can this not also be said of his saints, when they see sinners condemned by God’s just judgment? “They will see and rejoice.” They delight in God’s justice, just as God himself does. But although Eliphaz may perhaps have spoken rightly here, he judged wrongly in comparing blessed Job with the impious and sinners.

“Has not their exaltation been cut down?” Their pride and stubbornness were indeed cut down by the examples of punishment mentioned above and handed over to everlasting destruction.

[Col. 0677B] “And fire devoured their remnant?” He also called “remnant” the final residue of sins, to be punished on the day of judgment, because in this age no punishment condemns the gravest sinners as they deserve. Or we may understand by “remnant” the descendants of wicked people, who, by imitating them as their fathers, may be called their remnants. Or the word may be taken in a good sense, according to this: “For the thought of a human being will confess to you, and the remnant of thought will keep a feast for you.” The thought of a human being thus pertains to the confession of sins, while the remnant is the eternal reward of that confession, by which, once his sins have been forgiven, he rejoices in spiritual gladness as though at a festival. “Remnant” may also be understood as “the last things,” according to: “The remnants of the impious will perish.” [Col. 0677C]

“Therefore submit to him, and have peace; and through these things you will have excellent fruits.” He urges holy Job now to think of correcting himself and gives advice to one who had not asked for it, that through patience he should turn to God. Thus, after the battle of the horrible plague pressing upon him, he could have the peace of safety.

“Receive the law from his mouth, and place his words in your heart.” Or this was said to mean: hear what he has commanded and preserve it.

“If you return to the Almighty, you will be built up.” If you repent of your deeds, you will be built up—that is, day by day you will be fortified and protected by divine guardianship. This outstanding example should be set before those who delay acting in repentance, for this exhortation is necessary: through it sinners can restore their lost glory. [Col. 0677D]

“And you will put iniquity far from your tent.” If you wish to amend and correct yourself, God will ascribe to you the act of putting your iniquity far from you, although he himself rather removes it from you. Or the devil himself is called “iniquity”; that is, the one who takes you into his power will be driven away.

“He will give flint instead of earth, and golden torrents instead of flint.” He means that if God’s favor establishes him upon his most firm commandments, he will not devote himself to earthly things and bodily pleasures, but will rather advance toward the strength of virtues, through which he may reach the flowing riches of heaven. For Eliphaz says this metaphorically to holy Job: if you are placed upon the rock of the strength of your good conscience, the perception of divine wisdom will overflow for you like a golden torrent. [Col. 0678A]

“And the Almighty will be against your enemies.” “When you do his will,” he says, “you will have him as your defender.”

“And silver will be heaped up for you.” We said that gold is understood as perception, and silver as the utterance of justification. The commandments and judgments of God are therefore themselves divine utterances. When you have turned and remained in these through constant meditation, a varied and abundant utterance, explaining the understanding of diverse meanings, will be heaped up for you.

“Then you will abound in delights in the Almighty.” You will be filled with the spiritual delights mentioned above when you see the petitions of your heart fulfilled through the grace of the Holy Spirit and perceive them accomplished in the joy of your mind. [Col. 0678B]

“And you will lift your face to God.” You will raise a free brow to entreat God; or, no longer guilty or bent downward by a bad conscience, you will lift your soul to God.

“You will entreat him, and he will hear you, and you will fulfill your vows.” He cannot hear you as a sinner unless you first entreat him for your sins.

“You will decide a matter, and it will come to you.” You will obtain from God only a matter that is just, holy, and honorable, which you have requested.

“And light will shine upon your ways.” Your ways will be your good deeds, and your light will be knowledge of God, God’s visitation and protection, by which the deeds of your ways will be corrected and illuminated, lest perhaps through the error of ignorance you stumble upon dark mountains. [Col. 0678C]

“For whoever has been humbled will be in glory, and whoever has lowered his eyes will himself be saved.” And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”

“The innocent will be saved, and he will be saved by the purity of his hands.” That is, by the grace of good works, or by their brightness. The ancients translated it this way: “Rescue the innocent, and you will be saved by the purity of your hands.” Here the phrase seems to express repayment: “Rescue the innocent,” so that you may be saved by the innocence of your hands.

## CHAPTER XXIII

[Col. 0678D] Then Job answered and said: “Even now my speech is in bitterness, and the hand of my plague is heavier than my groaning.” Having left behind his faithless friends, who declare that he is justly suffering the misery of this calamity and add to his bitterness, I will turn wholly to God and say to him, with confidence in my conscience, what follows:

“Who will grant me that I may know and find him, and come even to his throne?” He said that he knows God through understanding; he also said that he finds him through good works, and that he comes even to his throne through progress in knowledge of the future and reflection upon judgment, advancing to the very contemplation of divine power, which the pure in heart will behold. Holy Job says that he possessed such a heart, purified by many cleansings of conduct. [Col. 0679A]

“I will set judgment before him.” “I will set,” he says, “the judgment of your righteousness before the sight of my God,” according to: “From him I will seek the equity of his judgment.” Yet before his final sentence concerning me, I will bring many accusations against him, because, since I know his unique justice, why do I, a just man, suffer torments that rather belong to the wicked and impious? He says this in what follows:

“And I will fill my mouth with rebukes, so that I may know the words with which he will answer me, and understand what he will say to me.” That is, with complaints of justified sorrow.

“I do not wish him to contend with me with great strength, nor to press me with the weight of his greatness. Let him set equity before me, and my judgment will reach victory.” By the weight of his majesty, let us understand a shudder, not something corporeal, because God is spirit. “I am certain,” he says, “that when he himself judges, it will become clear that I am enduring these miseries of affliction without any desert of sins.” Hence he says: “My judgment will reach victory.” [Col. 0679B]

“If I go to the east, he does not appear; if to the west, I will not understand him; if to the left, what shall I do? I will not apprehend him. If I turn to the right, I will not see him. But he knows my way, and he will test me like gold that passes through fire.” While he enumerates the regions of the world, he says that God dwells wholly everywhere; yet he confesses that God is entirely invisible to him, because his divinity is not subject to the sight of a creature. He says that God knows his entire way of life, because he knew it perfectly.

“My foot followed his footsteps; I guarded his way and did not turn aside from it. I did not depart from the commandments of his lips, and I did not hide the words of his mouth in my bosom.” This means that what he wished to be guarded I guarded.

“For he alone exists, and no one can turn aside his thought; and his soul does whatever he wishes.” This means that his judgments are unsearchable and his ways untraceable.

“And when he has fulfilled his will in me, many other similar things are also ready for him.” When he has already afflicted me with whatever torments he wished, he can still inflict upon me as many others as he wishes; even insensible things tremble before him as do things endowed with sensation. [Col. 0679D]

“And therefore I am troubled before his face.” That is, I feel it in my mind and understand it in part.

“And while considering him, I am disturbed by fear.” That is, I dread the shuddering majesty of his presence.

“God has softened my heart, and the Almighty has troubled me.” Here we should understand “softened heart” as one dissolved by excessive fear and dread, not as one softened from the hardness of unbelief in order to receive faith, since Job himself remained strong in God through faith. Hence what follows: “The Almighty has troubled me”—this means the same as what was said above.

“For I have not perished because of the darknesses that threaten, nor has gloom covered my face.” He called the miseries of his calamity “darknesses,” wishing to say that they were like sudden ruins threatening him. Yet, although they pressed upon him, he says that he did not perish through despair, nor did unbelief or denial of God blind the face of his mind. [Col. 0680A]

## CHAPTER XXIV

“Times are not hidden from the Almighty, but those who know him do not know his days.” Those who perceive and understand God do not know the days of his eternity. In that eternity neither times nor days, which belong to times, are found; there is one eternal day. Or otherwise: he knows everything that I now say or suffer.

“Others moved boundaries, plundered flocks, and pastured them.” That is, they moved the flocks and ate them. This is clear according to the literal sense. Let us now see what it signifies according to the mystical understanding. By those who move boundaries he signified heretics, namely, those who tear down the established limits of the Church. Through the novelty of perverse doctrine they overstep the boundaries fixed by the evangelical law and the apostles, and thus by deceptive persuasion they seize the Lord’s flocks—that is, the peoples who believe in Christ.

They drove away the ass of the orphans and took the widow’s ox as a pledge. They overturned the way of the poor and alike oppressed the meek of the earth.

Orphans are indeed the tender ones: either infants in faith, or those who do not have God as Father, so that they may be defended by him against their adversaries. The heretics drive away their understanding, as though it were a strong and necessary beast for carrying them by faith within themselves to God, in the manner of robbers, while through their deceits they strip them of the strength of their spirit. Or else they take away from them the gentile understanding, designated by the name of an unclean animal, while under the pretext of true religion they lead them into faithlessness.

Widows, too, are those souls that have lost their husband, their God and Lord. From them the heretics attempt to take away, as a pledge of their faithlessness—that is, of the confession by which they are initiated into their false inventions and become their debtors—the purity of holy virtues and useful works of the spirit.

The poor in this passage are also to be understood as those who lack the testimony of faith. Others are rich in faith. The heretics have overturned the way of these people’s religion, by which they could have returned to God, through their own errors.

But let us understand the meek here as those who do not possess the steadfastness to resist their enemies and who, because of the cowardice of their spirit, are easily led astray. These, therefore, are oppressed by many doctrines of error and by various superstitions of error.

In a favorable sense, however, widows are those who mortify themselves together with their vices; the poor are the apostles. From this number the heretics attempt to take some of the poor away, when they persuade certain holy people or circumvent the meek, who are unable to resist them but patiently listen because of their simplicity. The heretics, however, strive to destroy them.

Others, like wild asses, go out into the desert to their work; and, keeping watch, they prepare bread for their children as prey. They are violent men, who rob openly. They are plunderers and bandits who come out from hiding for their activities—activities certainly not of God.

They reap a field that is not their own and harvest the vineyard of the one whom they have violently oppressed. A field or vineyard is each person’s particular way of life, which each cultivates when the filth and certain growths of vices are cleansed or even uprooted. Since the diligence of this cultivation is of no benefit when the whole goodness of nature is not referred to faith—for “the righteous person lives by faith”—the aforementioned worshipers of idols, while oppressing the hearts of the faithful, even of those who live honorably, lead them into error by a kind of seductive reasoning, violently carrying them off as though they were destroying their field or vineyard and scattering its produce.

They also leave people naked, taking away their clothing, while stripping them of good works.

For whom there is no covering in the cold. They strip those who do not possess the garment of God’s charity and therefore grow cold in unbelief, because they are not deemed worthy to be clothed in the tunic of the fervent spirit.

Whom the rains of the mountains water. Thus he says that these people, deprived of their homes through misery, are covered by caves and shelters in the mountains, and he describes how great is their need to dwell in those mountains. “Whom the rains of the mountains water,” that is, they are cleansed by waters flowing abundantly from those very mountains.

“Whom the rains of the mountains water.” They are not watered by the rains of heaven, but by the mountains that exalt themselves against the knowledge of God, which is from heaven.

And, having no covering, they embrace stones. Others expressed it more clearly: “When they have no covering, they are sheltered by a rock.” “And, having no covering, they embrace stones”: that is, without the garment of virtues, they delight in their sins and errors.

They used violence, plundering the orphans. From this it is understood what they did to those who possessed something, since they showed no mercy to those of the most meager means.

“They used violence, plundering the orphans”: they also plundered those who possessed some knowledge according to the goodness of nature but could not defend it, living with a fragile and childish spirit, by inflicting violence through perverse persuasions.

And they stripped the poor common people. They also stripped the mass of the people, poor in deeds and ignorance, of whatever justice or even natural innocence it perhaps possessed, while dragging it into the greater evil of its error.

They took away ears of grain from the naked who went about without clothing and from the hungry. From those naked in faith and deprived of God’s protection, who possess neither the garments of hope and divine charity nor the safeguards of the other virtues with which souls are adorned, they also took away the ears of grain in which they had a hidden knowledge of God, lest, hungering for the knowledge of God, they should one day uncover the veil and receive the very naked truth as bread of vital nourishment.

Among their heaps they took their midday rest—those who thirst though they have trodden the winepresses. This is a great and most unjust evil: that some should rest beneath the labor and amid the fruit of others, and be intoxicated with the wine of those who, after gathering their harvests, thirst.

“Among their heaps they took their midday rest—those who thirst though they have trodden the winepresses.” After the ears of grain had been removed—ears that figuratively contained within themselves the knowledge of the divine name, from which those who possessed them would have prepared solid food through full reflection—the violent deceivers rest among the good works of others, as among heaps, boasting and claiming them for themselves.

If one of the gentiles has followed natural virtues and from them, as from seeds, has built up in himself heaps of works, yet the deceived, having trampled the vintage of those virtues and pressed it out, remain thirsty, because they did not find the cup of truth among those by whom they had been drawn away into error.

From the cities they made men groan. “Not only,” he says, “do they strip those who live without protection and afflict them under the rule of harsh superstition; they also attack those who inhabit cities of the mind fortified by good morals, overthrowing them by fighting with the battering rams of errors.”

This is clearly what happened to many philosophers: although they had been great and renowned for their self-restraint regarding their bodies, nevertheless, amid groaning and immense labor, they were unable to attain knowledge of the truth.

And the soul of the wounded cried out, and God does not permit it to go unavenged. God does not permit the voice of those who implore him to go unavenged, but grants vengeance against errors, so that when those wounded by the injuries of sins turn toward the truth, falsehood may be convicted and punished. For he punishes when he abandons the conversion of those who had been led astray.

When he says, “the soul of the wounded,” let us understand this as referring to those who cry out to God in agreement. The distress of the devastated, however, reached the point of groaning among the inhabitants of the city. The wounded are not to be understood only as those whose bodies are pierced by others, but also as those whose souls are struck as though by a sword through excessive fear of their enemies.

They were rebels against the light; they did not know its ways, nor did they return by its paths. These are to be understood as demons, heretics, philosophers, and indeed all the impious, who attempt to oppose the teaching of God. For the commandment of life is light; and in nature there is a light that exists in itself. Darkness, however, is blindness of heart.

Therefore, if blindness of heart is darkness, the “outer darkness” is rightly understood as punishment. Thus the wicked are cast from the darkness of their sins into the darkness of torments. Inside and outside alike, God’s sentence is completed before the angels of God, and they are clothed, as it were in a double garment, with the disgrace of their shame.

As for the wild asses who dwell in the desert, we may understand them as all the pagans who, through the error of their gentile religion, are in the desert of true religion, since they are not held by the yoke of a definite religion. These, then, go out to their work. They are said to go out when they reveal their desires through corrupt teachings to those whom they lead astray.

Thus, with every resource of skill, they plunder souls wandering in error, so that they leave to the multitude of their lost posterity, as food, the obstinacy of a deadly doctrine.

In the early morning the murderer rises; he kills the needy and the poor. “Morning” is again mentioned because the evil is committed publicly and in broad daylight, as though the crime were a glory to its perpetrators. Following the example of the Sodomites, they did not conceal their sin but proclaimed it.

He may also have been speaking of unjust judges, who rise earlier for this purpose: to betray the case of the needy and poor after being corrupted by gifts.

Or otherwise: this murderer may rightly be understood as any heretic, one of those who kill human souls with harmful and deadly opinions. When he says that he rises in the early morning, the meaning is this: when those who have recently been initiated into the faith possess their morning—that is, the beginning of holy religion—or when they themselves have become morning, having been made, from darkness and sons of night, sons of God in the Lord, these men hasten to administer the poison of their faithlessness in order to deceive them.

Or otherwise: “morning” is to be understood as Christ, at whose resurrection heresies began to arise in the Church.

By night he is like a thief. All the opinions of heretics are to be compared with night and darkness, because they do not possess the light of truth. They are also adulterers, because they corrupt the chaste utterances of God through adulterous interpretation.

I think “night” is used because dishonest agents seek a certain secret time, as though it were nighttime, when they receive gifts for betraying cases.

The adulterer’s eye watches for darkness, saying, “No eye will see me,” and he covers his face. Or, as others have said: “He placed a hiding-place over his face.” That is, the eye of his heart has been blinded by forgetfulness, so that it would not rise into his memory that God is the inspector and knower of all human thoughts and evil deeds.

He breaks into houses in the darkness, as they had arranged with one another by day, and they did not know the light. It is clear that by day they plan this robbery in their thoughts, before they come into the darkness of the crimes themselves.

“He breaks into houses in the darkness, as they had arranged with one another by day.” Every heretic, established in the perversity of his doctrine, does not penetrate the houses of souls with the sweet and gentle speech of the Gospel, descending upon the souls of the faithful like calm rain and silent dew; rather, he breaks into them with something harsh and exceedingly sharp for wounding.

For this is what the heretics had arranged with one another, as it were by day: to pierce all mortals with the darts of harmful doctrine, when they had already arranged to create heresies in the Church, that is, while they were still situated in the day of truth.

If the dawn should suddenly appear, they think it the shadow of death, and so they walk in darkness as though in light. As soon as the light of justice and uprightness begins to appear from elsewhere and to be brought upon their conscience, they already think that they are suffering the punishments of death, because justice and holiness, as divine Scripture says, are hateful to the wicked.

“If the dawn should suddenly appear, they think it the shadow of death, and so they walk in darkness as though in light.” If some disputant should arise to expound the light of manifest truth against them, they, being convicted, think that they have encountered the shadow of death; nevertheless, in the darkness of their folly they glory as though in the light of wisdom.

The devil, too, may be understood as murderer, thief, and adulterer. He was made a murderer for the deception of humanity, as the Lord says: “He was a murderer from the beginning.” By arrogating divinity to himself through pride, which he attempted to seize through the presumption of his spirit, he was found to be like a thief, endeavoring to take what belonged to another.

He also lost that virginal and chaste love of God when, by forming adulterous designs against the love of his God and Lord, he sought his own will.

Thus this one rose in the early morning—that is, around the very birth of the first-formed human being—to deceive him through his woman. He killed him through the deception of a treacherous persuasion, as one needy of counsel and poor, who, being less cautious through lack of experience, was easily deceived.

He himself brought about the night of sin when, like a thief, he attempted to steal his way into divinity, saying: “Above the stars of heaven I will set my throne, and I will be like the Most High.” From then on, together with those whom he called the stars of heaven, he was named night and darkness, and the prince of darkness. And rightly so, because he had lost the light of the Lord.

Now established in the darkness of his sins, he covered the face of his evil conscience through hardening, unwilling to repent. Therefore, deprived of the divine light, he strives and watches so that he may commit deeds worthy of darkness and gloom.

Hence, living in these works, he will dig for himself houses of habitation in the lower world, together with those ministers of his with whom he attempted to raise himself against God and the Creator.

These ministers of his, while they were still blessed in that eternal happiness, in that day which is entirely everlasting and has neither beginning nor end, conferred with their prince about this sacrilegious tyranny. They thought that God, who is true, wise, and intelligible light, would leave their evil of disobedience unpunished and would not cast them down from that blessed and glorious seat.

And I think this is what he meant by “they did not know the light”: they supposed that God would not do this to them. Therefore, with their minds blinded, they became eternal darkness, and they were also called the powers of darkness—that is, of sinful human beings.

This is why, whenever they hear the name of God, they tremble; and we think that this is signified by the word “dawn.”

His thought—that is, the devil’s—could reach only speech, not accomplishment. He did not reign there; he was immediately cast down when he uttered aloud what he had conceived, and he was driven headlong downward.

Consequently, it appears that he spoke of the devices of his heart, by which he was plotting against God, in order to persuade the other angels. When many consented, a kind of single conspiracy was formed against God, if such a thing may be imagined.

Nevertheless, this must be held immovably: the duties of the heavenly host were in no way carried out in silence. We read that the angelic powers resound with unwearied voices in praise of his glory before the seat of the Lord. Nor would the Apostle have said, “If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels,” unless there were such tongues, and unless the angels had tongues as human beings do, although angelic tongues differ from human ones.

There is therefore some very great distinction concerning the diversity of tongues between earthly beings and the heavenly ministries. On this matter the canonical book of the New Testament, which contains the apostolic deeds, has instructed us sufficiently.

He is light upon the face of the water. Because they are not of the great Church—that is, of the weighty and holy people who are compared with grains of the best and most fertile wheat and who are to be stored in the granary of eternal dwellings—they will float upon the element of water like light straw without any weight, which contributes nothing toward weighing down the fruits of virtue, so that they may be carried away by the faintest breath of air.

Or otherwise: these waters represent human beings who love the present age, because they are always inclined toward lower things and carry much mud with them, which is deposited with murky weight into the chaos of the lower world.

Let his portion be cursed upon the earth. For whoever is not upon the earth of the saints, which is the land of the living, will be accursed. Or, “let his portion be cursed upon the earth,” that is, in the mass of the human race.

And let him not walk by the way of the vineyards. That is, let his conduct on this earth be so accursed that he neither imitates nor walks among the peoples of God, or the holy souls, who are fruitful like vineyards full of produce.

Teachers cultivate these vineyards as farmers, working them with doctrines as with hoes, so that they may harvest the wine of good works. This wine, pressed out in faith—that is, in the winepress of the Church—under the weight of tribulation, burns through the grace of Christ with a most fragrant odor, together with the power of merits, and is stored in the chambers of the heavenly dwellings.

Let him pass from the waters of snow to excessive heat. Holy Job seems to me to be speaking of two forms of Gehenna, fire and cold, through which the devil, the heretic, and the impious person will be transferred.

Perhaps those who are tormented in Gehenna will experience such a torment of the senses that at one moment they feel a burning fire and at another an excessive blaze of cold. This penal change will make them feel cold at one moment and heat at another, so that they think they are passing from one place to another.

Perhaps for this reason the Lord says in the Gospel: “Send him into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth,” so that the gnashing of teeth may arise from the severity of the cold.

Here we can find a certain likeness in our own bodies. In them, an abundance of red [humour; reading uncertain], which is extremely hot, is preceded in bodily symptoms by an unbearable chill, followed by the most burning fever. Physicians say that these two things, which are recognized as opposites, are produced in a human being from the same humor of the bile.

And his sin reaches to the lower world. The sin of the impious and wicked person is so great and so heavy that it sinks him into hell like lead in exceedingly deep water.

May mercy forget him. That is, may the one who is called not only merciful but also Mercy itself forget him, because “merciful” derives from “mercy,” and therefore, as a name formed from another, it is greater than the derivative designation.

Thus, although any of the saints may be called merciful, truthful, or just, none of them can rightly be called Mercy, Truth, or Justice.

His sweetness shall be worms. This is said by antiphrasis, meaning, “let him die swarming with worms.” And in the Gospel: “Their worm will not die.” Such, therefore, will be the sweetness of the wicked and of those who hate God.

Let him not be remembered. That is, let him not attain the forgiveness of mercy. We have learned from the holy Scriptures that this will be the fate of the devil, his heretics, and the impious.

But let him be crushed like an unfruitful tree. In accordance with this: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.”

Or let us understand the tree as the sin that occurred through the tree. Through that tree the devil added to the accumulation of his crimes by rebelling against God and also driving the human being into death. Hence he has already been condemned to eternal destruction.

For this reason the devil himself can be called an incurable and fruitless tree, because he will never be healed by the medicine of repentance.

But concerning the tree of life—that is, the cross—or concerning Christ, it is said: “According to the days of the tree, the days of my people shall be.”

For he fed the barren one. That is, he nourished and cherished souls barren and fruitless in virtues.

And the one who does not bear. He also fed those souls with the pleasures of their assent which, although they could bring forth good things from the womb of the heart, were unwilling to do so, as David says concerning such people: “He was unwilling to understand, so as to do good.”

And he did not do well for the widow. He was unwilling to console the widow—the soul deprived of the strength of holiness, which had had God as its husband—with exhortation, so that she might act in such a way as to be able to return to her former husband.

He struck down the strong in his strength. Others said: “In anger he overthrows the weak.” That is, he cast down and dragged away the strong, those endowed with virtues.

And when he stands, he will not trust in his life. God gave him an opportunity for repentance, and he abuses it in pride. Yet his eyes are upon his ways. Even when he is prosperous, he still does not think, with conscience biting him, that he will enjoy that same happiness perpetually, since he possesses such a stubborn and hardened spirit and believes that he can remain in that life of his, so utterly ruined.

They are exalted for a little while, but will not endure; they will be humbled like all things and will be taken away. “For a little while” refers to the brevity of the present life, in which the wicked are exalted for a time.

“They will be taken away like all things,” that is, like all things belonging to the opposing party, or when all temporal things have been taken away at the end of the age.

And like the tops of ears of grain they will be crushed. Just as the tops of ears of grain, things exceedingly fragile, are broken apart with such ease that they are reduced to nothing, so those of whom I have spoken will be like the finest dust or like downy ash before the face of God when they have been crushed by the insult of shame.

But if this is not so, who can convict me of having lied and set my words before God? For who among you will be able to convict me that what I have said will not happen, and to prove me false, since you assert that God gives sinners in this present time everything they deserve, thereby casting such claims at me more as a reproach born of contentious zeal?

## CHAPTER XXV

Then Bildad the Shuhite answered and said: “Power and terror are with him, who makes concord in his high places. Is there any number of his hosts?” Refuted by blessed Job’s assertion that God’s judgment belongs rather to the future, Bildad turns to say that power and terror are with God; that is, he does not now exercise judgment, but holds it stored up and reserved for the future. Yet he makes the concord of perpetual peace among those in the heights—that is, among his angels or holy people—by preserving them so that through any fall into sin they do not incur the enmity of heavenly offence.

“And over whom will not his light arise?” For he enlightens every person coming into this world.

“Can a human being be justified in comparison with God, or can one born of a woman appear clean?” It is clear that, for want of an answer, they repeat more frequently what they had said.

“Behold, even the moon does not shine, and the stars are not clean in his sight.” Under the name of the moon or stars we may understand the angels and heavenly powers, who in comparison with divine majesty can appear unclean and dark, since the nature of created being, although they do not sin, is nevertheless capable of sin—as was apparent in other angels of the same nature who sinned. But we should believe that after them no angel sinned, because they turned their entire free will toward the love of God alone; thus they became immovable, remaining in the truth in which the aforesaid angel and his companions refused to stand. Therefore the will of the angels was made unchangeable through the love of God, which is in God by nature. Hence honour and glory belong to him alone who is incorruptible. He may also speak of these elements, which are called unclean because they do not always shine, or because they illuminate bodies only and not minds, as God habitually does both.

“How much more is man corruption, and the son of man a worm?” For if, he says, angels and even the bodies of heaven are called unclean in comparison with God, what do you suppose a human being is, when he himself is corruption and the son of man a worm, arising from the same corruption as the worm?

## CHAPTER XXVI

Then Job answered and said: “Whose helper are you? Do you assist one who is weak, and support the arm of one who is not strong? To whom have you given counsel? Perhaps to one who has no wisdom, and have you displayed your abundant prudence? Whom did you intend to teach? Was it not him who made the breath of life?” Seeing that an injury was being done to God, Job, moved by righteous indignation, rebukes Bildad the Shuhite more harshly at the very beginning of his speech, because he spoke as though God were weak and had no strength of arm and needed his help. Job observes that a drop is a lesser share compared with the whole: a droplet compared with an unfailing spring; a spark hidden in ashes compared with the divine fire by which all things are warmed; the body’s lamp compared with the Sun of righteousness; a potsherd compared with its potter; the soul compared with God. Therefore Job marvels that he dared to seek to teach him from whom he himself has being.

“Behold, the giants groan beneath the waters, and those who dwell with them.” Divine Scripture calls proud, rebellious, and obstinate human beings giants. The devil too, and his followers, are called giants by a transferred name because of their pride. When it says that giants groan beneath the waters, it means, as if it had said, beneath the earth—that is, in the lower regions of the earth, where hell is said to be, and from which the infernal regions take their name. For water is of such a nature that it cannot exist without earth. “Behold, the giants groan beneath the waters”: their groaning arose from the pains and squalor of their tartarean dwelling.

“Hell is naked before him, and there is no covering for destruction.” This means that nothing can be hidden from God’s knowledge, and that Destruction, whom we not unreasonably understand as the devil, cannot hide himself from God’s omnipotence.

“He stretches out the north over the void, and hangs the earth upon nothing.” This should be understood either as meaning that the earth was made from nothing, or that there is nothing beneath the earth by which it is supported, though it itself supports all things and is held in balance throughout by the power of God, because all things are in him and all are sustained by him. Of him the Apostle says: “Upholding all things by the word of his power.” And because in Scripture the north wind is sometimes figuratively understood as the devil—for Solomon calls the north a harsh wind, while he is called ‘right-hand’ by name: he is indeed called right-hand by his own people, but is wholly the author of a left-hand work—he is spread out over the void, that is, over those cold in faith and unbelieving, over those empty and void of true religion, in order to rule them as a king. Again, those same unbelievers, whom holy Job called earth, are hung upon the devil, who has been made nothing by God, so that they may always be uncertain and the members may imitate their head: that, like their head who is said to be nothing, they may be suspended over void and nothing.

“He binds the waters in his clouds, so that they do not burst forth all at once below.” In the heights of the wide expanse of air, waters are gathered in these clouds, as elsewhere we read of God: “Sifting waters from his clouds.” They are said to be bound because they are not poured out upon the earth all at once, as we read happened in the Flood. The spiritual interpretation is that the clouds are the holy teachers of the Church, who carry the waters of the Gospel to be poured out upon peoples and bring them, governed by the Holy Spirit, so that the lands of the peoples may be watered and fruits of virtue may be multiplied through spiritual activity by this heavenly rain. God binds in his clouds these waters flowing down from heavenly abundance, so that he may pour out upon each person, according to the capacity of that person’s heart, as much teaching as the recipient can receive, lest they perhaps harm hearts less able to receive fuller teaching if they are poured out all at once.

“He holds the face of his throne.” He reserves the sentence of his judgment for the future. God is said to hold the seat of his justice and mercy, gleaming in every creature with the glory of truth; that is, to fence about and hide the disclosure of his secret judgments, so that the Gospel of Christ is concealed in those who perish.

“And he spreads his cloud over it.” As the Lord says to his disciples in the Gospel: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of heaven.” He also spreads over the Gospel itself the covering of his divine protection, as a cloud of his defence, so that no adversary, however fierce, can prevail against it; concerning this cloud the Apostle says: “Our fathers were all under the cloud.”

“He set a boundary around the waters, until light and darkness are ended.” Under the name of waters, by synecdoche—that is, a part for the whole—he seems to me to have spoken of the end of the world, because the alternation of night and day will pass away. Or he speaks of the peoples of the ungodly, or of the tribulations of the saints, which are often called waters in Scripture. These waters received a limit from God, either so that the wicked and sinners should remain so, or so that the faithful God should not permit his saints to suffer tribulations beyond what they can bear. These things will occur until the prosperity and wickedness of the ungodly pass away, signified here by the names of light and darkness.

“The pillars of heaven tremble and are afraid at his nod.” By the name of pillars let us understand the enduring stability found in the nature of angels, because they not only persevere immovably in holiness, but are also splendid with the glory of eternal blessedness. For concerning the future immovability of human beings the Son of God says: “The one who conquers, I will make a pillar in the temple of my God.” The Church itself, the congregation of all saints, is called the pillar and foundation of truth because of its eternal stability in the Lord. This may also be understood of holy angels: they are called pillars on account of the regard of their charity and love, because they care for the salvation of human beings, for whom they are solicitous with pious affection; this seems to add, as it were, weight to their thoughts. In the figurative sense, heaven signifies the Church, in which the mysteries of heaven are celebrated. The pillars of this heaven, that is, of the Church, are the apostles and others endowed with like grace, who bear and endure the dangers of diverse persecutions that come upon them. Human souls too are sometimes understood as heavens. The pillars of these souls, which we have metaphorically called heavens, are their thoughts: by these the soul is supported and guided, and is strengthened by the stability of counsel lest it waver and stagger through the rust of sin. Human frailty often experiences this: where those who look on are less watchful, the pillars—that is, good thoughts—are driven aside by the impulse of sin. Therefore they tremble and fear at the nod of God who threatens and foretells his dreadful judgment. For these thoughts of the soul are not its own as though they belonged to it by nature; they are indeed in a nature that exists and are a function of that existing nature, without which rational nature does not exist. For, as I said, they do not exist independently but are invisible movements of a subsisting nature.

“In his strength the seas were suddenly gathered together.” We read that this happened in the beginning of Genesis.

“And by his wisdom he struck the proud one.” Who can doubt that the proud one here is principally the devil? He was first struck by God when God cast him down from that blessed and lofty seat of heaven, of which the prophet says: “You humbled the proud one as one wounded.” Spiritually, we rightly understand these seas as the peoples of the Jews and the nations. The prophet David declares that the true Solomon would rule them, saying: “He shall rule from sea to sea.” For the Gospel of Christ began from the sea—that is, from the Jewish people—because the law went forth from Zion and reached the sea of the nations. Thus these seas of peoples were suddenly gathered by the strength and power of Christ’s resurrection, through the ministry of the apostles and evangelists and of the others mentioned above, into one body of the Church and joined in one bond of faith by Christ’s love.

“His spirit adorned the heavens.” We read in the beginning of Genesis that on the fourth day God placed the stars in heaven, or in the firmament. He also adorned rational heavens by the Holy Spirit; by these we understand the apostles and apostolic men, who in many places of Scripture receive the designation of heavens, according to the prophet’s words: “His power covered the heavens.” “And by his wisdom he struck the proud one”: Christ, the power of God and wisdom of God, struck the proud devil. These saints, therefore, are distinguished by the gifts of grace from the Holy Spirit as by starry lights.

“And by his midwifing hand the twisting serpent was brought forth.” The saints, adorned by the word of God, scatter seed among the peoples. Hence, through the fear of the Lord, they conceived in the womb the spirit of salvation. Thus the hand and wisdom of the Father, Jesus Christ, is said by holy Job in his condescension to stand beside souls fruitful with manifold virtue, that he may render a kind of service of his mercy to those giving birth to children of the age to come, console them when they are in the pains of persecution, and invisibly aid those giving birth by his inward operation. For without him no result of good works—works which above we called children—will follow them. Therefore, as he watches over this ministry by the charity of his mercy with which he greatly loved us, and as his mercy acts as midwife so that holy souls may bring forth such offspring, the twisting serpent, in whom there is nothing straight, is brought forth from them and expelled from their hearts.

“Behold, these things have been spoken in part concerning his ways.” These are the ways of the Lord, of which the Savior himself says through Solomon when he foretells his own birth: “The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways for his works.” Therefore the Lord Jesus Christ was created by God the Father from the Virgin Mary to show and make known the paths of the commandments, from which the work of God—that is, the human being—had strayed.

“And when we have scarcely heard a small drop of his speech.” Let us understand the small drop as the assumed human being, who in the psalm is called the little mountain Hermon, and in Daniel the stone cut out, and in the Song of Songs a bundle of myrrh.

Who can behold the thunder of his greatness?
