He means this: if the assumption of the form of a servant contains mysteries almost beyond expression, and if, in comparison with the God who assumes it, it is an exceedingly small drop, how much more will no one be able to behold the thunder of his greatness—that is, the divinity itself, which is called “thunder” for this reason: when the report of his name, from on high, resounded throughout the earth in Christ Jesus his Son, and became known to human beings with this terrible crash, nevertheless none of them could contemplate with understanding the whole greatness of his divinity—that is, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” [Col. 0691C].

## CHAPTER XXVII

Job also continued, taking up his parable, and said:

“God lives, who has taken away my judgment, and the Almighty, who has brought bitterness upon my soul.”

By allowing him, though innocent, to suffer the punishments of the wicked, he also filled his soul with the bitterness of present misery. “God lives, who has taken away my judgment.” According to the form of the servant that he assumed, this means the judgment of the human will; and it was spoken from the person of the assumed man, when he prayed to the Father: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” He therefore said, “my judgment,” because in himself he demonstrated the weakness of the human race, having truly assumed a human being [Col. 0691D].

“And the Almighty, who has brought bitterness upon my soul.” The cup of death, which our Savior had come to drink, was bitter. It was from the bitterness of that cup that he said to his disciples: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death.” The word “brought,” however, is to be understood according to the Apostle, who says of God the Father: “He did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all.” He was not delivered to death unwillingly. Elsewhere the same Apostle says of the Savior: “He delivered himself for our sins.”

“For as long as breath remains in me, and the spirit of God is in my nostrils, my lips shall not speak iniquity, nor shall my tongue meditate deceit. Far be it from me to judge you righteous.”

This also belongs with what is written concerning the Lord in Isaiah: “Cease from man, whose breath is in his nostrils, for he is accounted exalted.” We should not understand the adverb “until,” according to the interpretation by which we have woven this exposition concerning our Savior, as though it were said in its ordinary sense, as if he had said, “As long as the breath of this life is in me”—that is, “before I die.” Rather, we should recognize that “until” is used here to mean “always and forever.”

Thus the Lord himself says to the people through the prophet: “I am, says the Lord, and until you grow old, I am.” God will not cease to exist after human beings grow old; rather, he remains with them forever even as they grow old.

But what shall we say about what the Psalmist says: “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet’”? Are we to say that, after the enemies have been subjected, Christ will no longer sit at the right hand of God the Father? And where then will be the saying of the angel: “His kingdom shall have no end”? For this reason, in such passages, as I have said, “until” is to be understood as “forever.”

The same applies to what the Evangelist says concerning Joseph and blessed Mary: “He did not know her until she had borne a son.” Who could be so blasphemous concerning the virginity of the venerable blessed Mary as even to dare think that, after she had borne God the Savior, her son, she subsequently knew a man? Therefore, according to the truth of the Catholic faith, here too let us understand “until” in the sense stated above, as “forever.”

The Lord Jesus therefore says: “The breath of divinity is always in me,” because, inasmuch as I am human, I have been formed and created in God; I possess within me the spirit of my Father, and it is substantially my own. He continues as follows:

“Until I perish, I shall not depart from my innocence.”

For I did not acquire innocence through moral effort; rather, just as I was born in it, so I am just and innocent.

“Until I perish, I shall not depart from my innocence.”

Even if I die amid these torments, I shall not depart from my innocence, which you assert that I have lost in them, as though I were a blasphemer.

“I shall not abandon my justification, which I began to hold.”

The Savior could have said this as a human being assumed into God, whose beginning according to the flesh is from the virgin Mary. He neither possessed human sin by being born nor contracted it by his actions; and therefore he alone says truthfully:

“For indeed my heart does not reproach me throughout my whole life. May my enemy be as the wicked man, and my adversary as the unrighteous.”

Here “my whole life” is to be understood as the present life, the time when he was saying these things—as though he were saying: “All my present conduct is beyond reproach.” “My heart does not reproach me throughout my whole life”: that is, I did not consent to those who offered evil counsel and urged me toward blasphemy, as you do; even my wife urged me to do this.

“For indeed my heart does not reproach me throughout my whole life. May my enemy be as the wicked man, and my adversary as the unrighteous.”

He does not curse by wishing evil, but foretells prophetically, speaking according to the deserts of sinful human beings and predicting what each person who persists in sins will receive from him. Let us now return to the passage:

“For what hope does the hypocrite have, if he greedily plunders and God does not deliver his soul?”

A hypocrite is understood as one who is false in friendship or deceitful. “How much desire,” he says, “and, as it were, thirst for greed you suffer at my destruction, so that you may already drag me by your wishes into Tartarus! What hope of pardon will you have before God for this impious desire, if you will not obey God and strive to amend yourselves in this life?”

“Will God hear his cry when distress comes upon him?”

At the time of recompense, therefore, when distress comes upon the wicked, there will be no remedy for sinners, because the Lord will not receive their prayers on the day of vengeance [Col. 0693B].

“Or can he delight in the Almighty and call upon God at every time?”

He will be able to delight in God and call upon him who is rightly confident because his conscience is good, and who has shown himself such that he deserves to be heard at any time.

“I shall teach you by the hand of God what the Almighty possesses, and I shall not conceal it.”

Behold, you all know it; why then do you speak vainly without cause? This is the portion of the wicked man with God, and the inheritance that the violent will receive from the Almighty. He speaks of what God has in his hand and power, and in his secret judgments.

“If his sons are multiplied, they shall be for the sword, and his descendants shall not be satisfied with bread.”

By “sons” and “descendants” he signified all the remaining offspring of an evil generation. In Scripture, people are sometimes called “sons” not only because of bodily descent, but also because of similarity in conduct.

“Those who remain of him shall be buried in destruction, and his widows shall not weep.”

This seems to me to signify that, as time passes, the offspring or generation of the wicked man will be reduced to the greatest poverty or misery, and that their widows, because of the excessive evil pressing upon them, will be unable to weep.

“If he gathers silver as though it were earth, and prepares garments as though they were clay.”

He speaks of the insatiable desire and a kind of abyss of this wicked man’s inexhaustible greed.

“He has indeed prepared them, but the righteous shall wear them, and the innocent shall divide the silver.”

Solomon also says: “He who increases his riches through usury gathers them for one who pities the poor.”

“He built his house like a moth, and like a watchman he made a shelter.”

By these words he says that the wicked man labored in vain, since the condition of his house is compared either with things that quickly pass away or with moths that destroy them.

Alternatively:

“If he gathers silver as though it were earth, and prepares a garment as though it were clay, he will indeed prepare it, but the righteous shall wear it, and the innocent shall divide the silver. He built his house like a moth, and like a watchman he made a shelter.”

Here, then, is the wicked man whom we said above is the devil. In Adam’s transgression he made all precious and illustrious human beings worthless, like dust and clay; from them he also stripped their virtues and natural goods as though they were garments, together with their gold, by which the riches of the mind are signified. They had been made beautiful and well ordered by the riches of the image and likeness of their Creator; but by taking these riches away from them, he reduced them to the greatest poverty and degradation.

Human beings deceived by the devil in Adam are compared with these things, which appear to be the least valuable in the creation of the world. But the righteous Lord and our God, taking away from the devil the spoils of the captives mentioned above and freeing the captives themselves whom the enemy had prepared for destruction, formed from them a holy Church for himself. He cleansed her with the washing of water in the word and made her without spot or wrinkle—that is, pure from sin and simple in the confession of faith—and clothed her in a precious garment [Col. 0694B].

The innocent and spotless Lamb of God also divides the silver, by which, as I have already said, those who are transparent and illustrious in this world are understood, when he sends believers into blessed life and eternal glory, and sends unbelievers into destruction.

Alternatively, “silver” may mean the clear and shining eloquence of secular learning, which is taken from the world through Christ so that the Gospel may be clothed in the eloquence of believers, in radiant and pure speech. For just as human souls are clothed in garments of virtue, so thoughts, when expressed through the preaching of evangelists, are in a certain way clothed in words.

“He built his house like a moth, and like a watchman he made a shelter.”

As a moth consumes and destroys its dwelling, so the devil builds the house of his ruined people for their destruction. He prepared for himself a temporary dwelling, gradually liable to collapse, while he himself is destined to possess eternal punishments.

This, then, is the wicked hypocrite who greedily plunders. In the one who does not turn back there will be no hope of pardon, since, in addition to these things, he rages with a kind of greed, dragging human beings to destruction. He is called a hypocrite because he transforms himself into an angel of light. The Lord will not hear even his late cry of supplication when he has been confined within the straits of punishment.

Nor will he have any confidence of delight in God arising from a good conscience; nor will he be able to move him to praise and confession who, like countless sons of his, will be struck by the divine sentence with the sword of God.

“His descendants” also refers to those who are deceived by people whom the devil himself had previously deceived. His descendants, I say, shall not be satisfied with the bread of the vision of God, but will suffer hunger and want. For all the saints who contemplate God will be refreshed and nourished by him, by whom the angels are now satisfied.

We can also understand “the remnants of the devil” as his final generation, which, like the devil himself and his sons and descendants, will be buried in destruction together with the whole body of his people.

Those widows—that is, the souls whom the devil had weakened through their vices and the allurements of pleasures and had made soft, so that they lost all strength and manliness—will not weep with any correction or satisfaction, so as at least eventually to return to repentance toward God, whom they had lost as a husband by clinging to vices as to adulterers [Col. 0695A].

“When the rich man sleeps, he will take nothing with him; he will open his eyes, and find nothing.”

The rich man is understood in many ways in the divine Scriptures. One is rich in earthly possessions; but if he trusts in those riches, he will fall. When this rich man is in the sleep of death, he will carry none of his possessions with him, because he came naked when he was born and returns naked to the earth when he dies. At the resurrection he will open his eyes and find no merit from a good work.

The Jewish people, because of the innumerable divine benefits, the oracles of the prophets, the many promises, and God’s frequent address to them, are also called rich. Therefore the Lord says to the same Jews in the Gospel: “Woe to you who are rich” [Col. 0695B].

The proud, who do not possess poverty of spirit, are also called rich. Philosophers, too, who possess eloquence and worldly knowledge, are called rich. When these are raised on the day of resurrection, they will find no remedy by which they may be saved.

Every heretic may also be called rich, because he presumes to possess much—indeed, everything—from the rewards of the holy Church: the forgiveness of sins, the interpretation of the Spirit, even the pledge of the Lord’s body, and an inheritance with the holy angels in the heavenly kingdom.

All these people, whether because they suffer the scandal of the cross or because, through the presumption of their hearts, they have abandoned the path of truth in order to walk in error, or because, having an understanding darkened and the freedom of their will obscured, they persist in unbelief, or because they have become detestable by exalting their hearts, will open their eyes after the sleep of death, at the resurrection, and find nothing [Col. 0695C].

“Scarcity of water shall seize him; at night a storm shall overwhelm him.”

He signifies that sudden poverty will come upon the rich men mentioned above like an oncoming flood. They will be overwhelmed by misery and unexpected distress, called “a storm,” at night—that is, suddenly, while they are unaware—according to the Apostle’s saying: “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them.”

“An oppressive wind shall carry him away and remove him, and like a whirlwind it shall snatch him from his place.”

By the name “wind” he speaks of the sentence by which each of them will be cast away like dust from the face of the earth. This wind is called the burning wind of the divine sentence because it leads or drives them to the burning of Gehenna.

“He will send it upon him, and will not spare him.”

The wind of God’s sentence, or God himself through the sentence of his justice, will send punishments upon him; that is, he will receive the due of his crimes. He will not spare him when he repays him according to his works.

“Fleeing from his hand, he shall flee.”

“He will not be held,” he says, “by the hand of God so as to be saved”; rather, as though in flight, he will fall into ruin through swift collapse. What he says—“fleeing he shall flee,” or, as others have rendered it, “he shall flee in flight”—signifies the sinner perishing forever, because he will never be recalled to life, and there will be no place for repentance there [Col. 0696A].

“He will clap his hands over him and hiss at him, looking upon his place.”

Others have said: “He will beat his hands over him and drag him from his place.” In this passage he describes, through certain gestures of the human body, the severity of God when he is indignant and angry against the sinful rich man. He also indicates, as though hissing, how terrible a place of punishment has been reserved for him.

Judas Iscariot also went to such a place.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

“Silver has the sources of its veins, and there is a place where gold is refined. Iron is taken from the earth, and stone, released by heat, is turned into bronze.”

It seems to me that, through an enigma and a parable, he describes under the names of these metals the conduct of human beings and the virtues of souls, while, in the manner of the prophets, by no means observing an orderly sequence.

By the terms “silver” and “gold,” according to the authority of Scripture, he wished to indicate the expression of the word and the thoughts of the mind. Explaining these matters, let us speak as follows:

“Silver has the sources of its veins, and there is a place where gold is refined.”

The veins of silver—that is, the beginning of eloquence—arise from the mind’s thoughts. But the golden sense is fashioned by the judgment of reason and wisdom, and, in order to be excellent, is refined by testing in the fire of divine examination.

Strength, which is called by the name of iron, is that by which we remove from ourselves the evil of the earth—that is, of our flesh. Against it, warring against us and acting contrary to the law of the spirit, we resist with firmness of mind and strength.

By the name “stone” the hardness of the heart is signified. Melted and softened through the heat and fervor of faith, it first becomes able to receive within itself the words of the writer. Then, like bronze, which is resonant, it will advance through the merit of holiness and reach, through the solidity of faith, the offering of praises and thanks to God.

“He appointed a time for darkness, and he himself considers the end of all things.”

In the divine Scriptures sinful human beings, demons, ignorance, tribulations, and sins are called “darkness,” according to circumstance and context.

“And the stone of darkness, and the shadow of death.”

Here we may metaphorically understand the devil as the stone of darkness. Because of the errors with which he had enveloped the whole world, he was called the stone of darkness. Although he is strong and powerful by the nature with which he was created by God, he trusted through pride in his own power and not in the Lord and God his Creator. Thus he lost the light of wisdom, being turned into folly and darkness; and for this reason he could be called the stone of darkness, according to the saying: “A fool walks in darkness.”

Therefore, just as the devil is called the stone of darkness, so he is also called the shadow of death, because those who think that they are defended and protected by him will, like the devil himself, be handed over to the eternal fires of Gehenna [Col. 0696D].

“A torrent separates from the wandering people those whom the foot of the needy man has forgotten, and those without a path.”

He means this: the torrent will separate the “pathless”—that is, the wandering—and those whom the foot of the needy man has forgotten, from the wandering people, because his step has forgotten them.

Alternatively, the present conduct of the needy man is signified by the name “foot.” He said “has forgotten” to mean that the needy man who was sent beforehand did not pray to God for such people, although almsgiving does pray to God—that is, the good work that a person has done speaks to God through a kind of manifestation of itself.

Saint Job therefore says that the torrent of fire will separate those who live without the path of true religion and who did not show mercy to the poor, that is, to the brothers of Christ; it will also separate them from the fellowship of the saints.

Alternatively, this needy man may properly be understood as our Savior, who, although he was rich, became needy and poor for our sake. In his foot, observe the dispensation of either the man whom he assumed or his entering the world. Hence the prophet says: “You went forth for the salvation of your people.”

Those, therefore, who did not receive the dispensation of their salvation in the Gospel have been given over to forgetfulness, because they refused to believe through the hardness of their own will. For this reason they are called “pathless,” because they did not receive Christ, who is the way [Col. 0697B].

“The earth from which bread arose was overturned by fire in its place.”

He connects various and obscure things, so that the lower statements do not cohere with those above. It seems to me, therefore, that here he describes the land of Sodom, whose abundance and beauty he praises with admiration.

“The earth from which bread arose was overturned by fire in its place.”

This earth may also be understood as Judaea, in which the bread of God’s law was produced for the peoples through the teaching of the prophets. Through the love of God and faith in Christ, the understanding of the carnal law was overturned and established in straight paths and spiritual meanings, so that it no longer follows the letter that kills [Col. 0697C].

“The place of sapphire—its stones—and its clods are gold.”

He says metaphorically that in Sodom everything was exceedingly abundant and excellent, comparable even with gold and precious stones.

“The place of sapphire—its stones.”

Thus the Lord says to it through the prophet: “Behold, I shall lay your stones in order, and establish you upon sapphires,” and what follows. Judaea was adorned with this beauty of precious stones—that is, with all those who believed in Christ through God the Father—when the people of the nations were joined to it through faith in Christ [Col. 0697D].

“The place of sapphire—its stones—and its clods are gold.”

Precious stones and gold are said to be found not in the best land but in remote and barren places. Thus, according to this interpretation, Judaea, barren in faith and unproductive in virtues, possessed within itself these precious stones—that is, the patriarchs and prophets and the whole multitude of the saints.

“The place of sapphire—its stones—and its clods are gold.”

He called the holy clods of the earth of the Church “saints,” because of their fruitfulness in good works. The Holy Spirit also wished them to be called clods because of the distributions of graces, so that they might be reckoned as gold. In their hidden veins, like seeds of souls, great and precious thoughts are born [Col. 0698A].

“The bird did not know the path.”

The multitude of inhabitants had made many exits in the same region, and therefore perhaps he said that, because of the great number of people, birds had neither the opportunity to observe paths there nor the ability to respond or walk along them.

“Nor did the eye of the vulture behold it.”

Because it was planted with such dense thickets and closely packed trees that birds flying above could not forage upon it.

“The bird did not know the path, nor did the eye of the vulture behold it.”

We may say that by “the bird” and “the vulture” the devil himself and his followers are meant. They were entirely unable to know the path of spiritual understanding in the Law and the prophets—that is, the things secretly foretold concerning Judaea. Nor were they able to discern by any trace of knowledge the mysteries of the dispensation that had been hidden from the ages.

Concerning these things the Apostle says: “We speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, which has been hidden, which none of the rulers of this age has known.”

“The bird did not know the path, nor did the eye of the vulture behold it.”

Here two peoples may reasonably be understood: the Jews and the nations.

Carnal Judaea, not possessing faith in Christ but living rather by the works of the law, did not know Christ, who was made for us the path or way by which one returns to the homeland, because of its pride, by which it thought it could be justified through works of the law. It is called a bird because it was light and wandering, and unstable in those very works of the law.

The people of the nations, however, seem to be compared to a vulture because it wandered among the errors of dead human beings and fed upon dead things. Thus they could not altogether perceive Christ, who was covered by the letter of the law, or the land of promise that was to come through Christ, because of the shadowy coverings of symbolic obscurities [Col. 0698C].

“The bird did not know the path, nor did the eye of the vulture behold it.”

Under these names—“bird” (or, according to another reading, “gold”) and “vulture”—let us understand the enemies of the Church, whose understanding was darkened by darkness and who did not know the path of her calling, by which she walks toward God and returns through faith. Carried away by various errors concerning dead human beings, they are to be regarded as though they were flying.

“The sons of the merchants did not tread it.”

He says that the land of Sodom was so filled with every good thing that it had no need of the commerce of any country [Col. 0698D].

“The sons of the merchants did not tread it.”

“Merchants,” or traders, are understood here as mentioned above. For merchants are evil and proud; this also pertains to the devil himself, who devised pride as the greatest sin. He was called a merchant because of the multitude of sins that he sought either for himself or for the destruction of human beings.

These people will not be able to tread the land of promise, which is reserved for the gentle and humble in heart so that they may dwell in it, because they will not even have permission to pass through it as inhabitants.

Alternatively:

This Judaea, to which the bread of teaching was supplied in its place by the prophets and priests—that is, in its own place and not in God’s place, namely, in the place of its delight, where it burned with pleasures and allurements—was overturned and consumed by the fire of its vices, as the prophet says: “All of them are adulterers; their hearts are like an oven.” And in the Psalm it is said of it: “Consumed by fire and uprooted and dug up by the work of its own hands, it has been utterly destroyed.”

This fire may also be understood as the vengeance for sins, as the Apostle says: “The earth that produces thorns and thistles is rejected and near to a curse; its end is for burning.” David speaks of this fire of wrath: “Fire consumed their young men.”

“The sons of the merchants did not tread it.”

The sons of the merchants are to be understood as the disciples of the apostles and apostolic men who preached the Gospel to the nations. These people did not tread upon Judaea, the land of unbelievers, in order to announce the Gospel to it. Concerning them it is said in the Acts of the Apostles: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first; but since you judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the nations.”

Thus, through these evangelists preaching the word, it came about that Christ the mountain was transplanted into the sea of the nations. Hence the Psalm says: “The mountains shall be transferred into the heart of the sea”—that is, the oracles either of the prophets or of the evangelists shall be transferred to the peoples of the nations who will believe.

“The sons of the merchants did not tread it.”

These merchants or traders are reprobate and unworthy of praise, gathering sins upon sins for themselves as though they were riches. Concerning them Revelation says: “All that was bright and luxurious has perished from you.”

These merchants, therefore, concerned with the riches of sins, will not tread upon the Church—that is, they will not dwell in her—because the Lord will possess her as holy and undefiled [Col. 0699C].

“Nor did the lioness pass through it.”

Because of the innumerable peoples living in Sodom, wild beasts could not pass through the middle of that region.

“Nor did the lioness pass through it.”

The lioness may be understood as the dominion of the devil, or as the pride of the Jews. When he says, “it did not pass through,” he means that it did not depart from Judaea, but that unbelieving pride remained there.

Alternatively, this may be understood of the Church. In that place necessary for her redemption, where she stands through faith, the glory of her virtues was overturned by fire. It was that fire of which the Lord himself says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth.”

By this fire the Church—that is, the land of the saints—burns and is overturned through the desire for the love of God, so that carnal desire may not possess her. She is overturned in this way so that, while living in the land of her flesh, the vices of the flesh may die within her, as the Apostle says: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires.”

“Nor did the lioness pass through it.”

Or, as others have said, “the lion.” Here the lion may reasonably be understood as the devil, who was unable to pass through the land of the holy Church, since he could not conquer her through severe persecutions [Col. 0699D].

“He stretched out his hand toward the flint.”

It seems to me that holy Job has offered another enigma. Because of its solidity and strength, the flint may signify Christ according to the human being whom he assumed; he is also called rock and stone by the prophets and apostles.

God the Father therefore stretched out his hand toward the flint, that is, toward his Son, through whom he created all things. He also calls him his right hand and arm and sent him to receive the human being, as the Apostle said: “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh.”

Therefore let us recognize that the extension of the hand of God the Father and of his Son signifies his coming to us; and through him, as follows:

“He overturned the mountains from their roots.”

By metaphor we rightly understand these as demons or proud human beings, because “he openly triumphed over principalities and powers in himself” [Col. 0700A].

“He cut channels through the rocks.”

That is, in the hard hearts of the nations, bound by excessive unbelief, he bestowed the abundance of his graces and, like flowing channels of water, granted a rich supply of teachings.

He is understood to have distributed the very thing that he is said to have cut, as the Apostle says: “To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge.”

Others have said: “He broke through the banks of the rivers,” so that the spiritual teaching of the Law and the prophets—which Isaiah refers to when he says, “You who thirst, go to the water”—which had flowed within one nation as though confined by certain narrow limits and had been enclosed by the precepts of the Mosaic law like barriers along riverbanks, might, after those obstacles were broken, flow abundantly from the channel of the law over the whole earth through the Gospel.

Alternatively, we can call this land the Church. Hence the prophet says: “The land shall be split by rivers.” We should understand that it is split and broken open when it makes itself receptive to receive the word of God. The force of those same rivers brings about this kind of opening of receptivity, which occurs through the obedience of the earth endowed with reason [Col. 0700C].

“And his eye saw every precious thing.”

When the channels of God’s graces had been brought forth, God saw how immense and innumerable were the benefits of his mercy. He said “saw” because the fulfillment or effect of his will came to exist before his sight in his Church.

“He also searched out the depths of the rivers and brought hidden things into the light.”

We may reasonably understand these rivers individually as the books of the Old Testament. In their great depths lay the mysteries of the Church, which God the Father searched out for the time of the Savior, revealing, for their fulfillment, all the things that had been foretold.

Alternatively, since the name “rivers” sometimes signifies multitudes of peoples, as the prophet Nahum says, “The gates of the rivers have been opened,” let us understand here by “the depths of the rivers” the secrets of human consciences. God is their searcher and knower; on the day of judgment, by bringing forth all the secrets of hearts, he will repay each person according to his works [Col. 0700D].

“But where is wisdom found, and what is the place of understanding?”

By asking this question, he wished to indicate a difficult matter, scarcely found—or rather, one that could neither be found nor possessed by human beings unless God revealed it. Job himself made this clear in what follows, saying:

“And he said to the human being”—that is, God said: “Behold, the fear of the Lord—that is wisdom, and to depart from evil—that is understanding” [Col. 0701A].

“Humanity does not know its price.”

By saying this he signified that the wisdom of the fear of God is beyond valuation.

“Nor is it found in the land of those who live pleasantly.”

No one possesses this wisdom of the fear of God unless he has crucified his flesh with its vices and desires, unless he has lived as the Apostle Paul and all the saints lived—in tribulations, persecutions, distress, and oppression.

Therefore those are said to live pleasantly who are held by no yoke of discipline and, unrestrained and headlong, rush into the mire of vices [Col. 0701B].

“The abyss says, ‘It is not in me,’ and the sea says, ‘It is not with me.’”

Here we should understand the abyss as hell, as the Apostle says: “Or who has descended into the abyss?” And the sea is this world, as we learn from the Psalmist’s song: “This great and spacious sea.”

Hell, therefore, and this world testify that they do not possess the wisdom of the fear of God. He says that places speak, meaning those who are in the places, whether of the world or of hell.

Here he speaks of those who are possessed by the allurements of the world through carnal conduct. This figure of speech is called prosopopoeia, in which a speaking person is assumed where speech is impossible, and what contains something is used in place of what is contained. The world or hell contains; the human being is contained.

This sea of the present world does not possess this wisdom, except for the Church alone. Because of the waves of enemies raging against her, she is called an island in Scripture, just as she is also represented figuratively as a little boat in the Gospel [Col. 0701C].

“Refined gold shall not be given for it, nor shall silver be weighed out in exchange for it.”

He says that no thing, however precious, can be compared with this wisdom. Alternatively, since in Scripture gold or silver may signify figuratively a meaning or discourse, he says that no one could perceive this wisdom according to its worth or express it in words.

“It shall not be compared with the colors of dyed India, nor with the most precious sardonyx stone or sapphire.”

This divine wisdom is preferred to various precious things. Nevertheless, it should be known that these precious metals and stones are found especially in the southern climate [Col. 0701D].

Since all worshipers of idols are signified by India, where, as I have said, precious colors either arise or are produced, I think this may be understood as follows: among the nations where the fear of the true God is absent, religion is artificial and, in a certain sense, earthly. Under the pretext of God’s name, it is composed in the falsehood of errors with the diverse and varied colors of speech, like a painting; and, like a precious stone, it shines through eloquence or glitters under the name of divinity.

India, and also Ethiopia, signify the blackness or darkness of sins, which are found especially in the worship of idols.

“Gold or glass shall not be made equal to it, nor shall vessels of gold be exchanged for it.”

Gold or glass, and also vessels of gold, signify all those who are precious and illustrious, who shine in this world through the name of dignity and the glory of riches. Since they do not possess the fear of true religion, they will be regarded as nothing, because they cannot, as though according to the merit of their glory, approach the exchange for this singular wisdom [Col. 0702A].

“Things lofty and exalted shall not be mentioned in comparison with it.”

Even if all the things among creatures are lofty and exceedingly exalted—including the angelic powers—all will be considered insignificant, indeed unworthy of mention, in comparison with that wisdom which caused every rational creature to please God and to be joined to him in holy love.

For this reason this kind of wisdom—the wisdom of fear—is preferred to those exalted and lofty things: without it they are nothing before God, just as the devil himself, having lost the fear of divine reverence, lost himself [Col. 0702B].

“Wisdom, however, is drawn from hidden places.”

This wisdom, therefore, cannot be taken from anywhere except from above; or it is drawn from the innermost affections of the heart through the gift of the Holy Spirit, as the prophet says: “I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit,” so that a human being may know God and fear him, and understand that he must depart from evil.

[Cols. 0702C–0703C]

The topaz of Ethiopia cannot be compared with it, nor can the purest dye be matched to it. By various expressions and under various names for gold and precious furnishings, holy Job says that the fear of the Lord cannot in any way be compared with them.

From where, then, does wisdom come, and where is the place of understanding? He asks and seeks to know, and says that every creature, or at least the whole of creation, is ignorant of this wisdom.

It is hidden from the eyes of all the living; it is also concealed from the birds of heaven. “The living” is to be understood of those who live in the world, concerning whom he said above, when speaking of this wisdom: “It is not found in the land of those who live pleasantly.” But when he said that this wisdom was hidden from the birds of heaven, the proud and frivolous are to be understood—those who have lofty thoughts, which pertains to the swelling of arrogance—or else the evil spirits, who, according to the Gospel parable, eat the Lord’s seed sown beside the road. He therefore says that the good of the fear of God is hidden from them.

“Destruction and death said, ‘With our ears we have heard its fame.’” The devil may be called by both these names, or he may be called “death,” while his satellites are called “destruction.” They therefore said that they had heard the fame of the fear of God. They cannot deny that they heard it, since they received it implanted in the good of their nature; but through the evil of disobedience they did not wish to retain it.

“God understands its way, and he himself knows its place.” God certainly knows that this wisdom hastens toward its place—namely, the place of rest and everlasting peace—where, through this same wisdom of his fear, he delights to rest his words upon the quiet, humble, and trembling person. Or else: “God understands its way,” the way that has been proclaimed throughout all lands by the preaching of the Gospel. Hence what follows also speaks of God:

“For he looks to the ends of the world, and he sees everything that is under heaven.” Who can doubt that God knows even things that are still to come? But here God, the knower of future things, rather looked upon what his Apostle later said: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son.” In this way, then, by visiting us through his coming, he looked upon the ends of the world—in these times of ours, into which the ends of the ages have arrived.

“He who made a weight for the winds and weighed the waters by measure, when he gave a law to the rains and a way to the resounding storms.” It is clear that every creature is held in the hand and by the power of his might. Alternatively: the Church received the very graces of the Holy Spirit, as it were at the beginning, through the apostles, when there came from heaven a sound like that of a violently rushing wind. Scripture mentions winds, or spirits, which God is to bring forth for human beings by distributing them from the hidden treasuries of heavenly secrets, according to the prophet who says: “He brings forth the winds from his treasuries.”

At times these varieties of graces are designated by the name of the Holy Spirit, who gives these graces, according to the Apostle’s statement: “The spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets.” They are also said to have a “weight” on account of the working and effect of their divine sanctification, so that, according to the strength of each person, preachers of the word of God might give milk to some and offer solid food to others, wherever and to whomever they might speak. Hence the prophet says: “I will give you the early and the late rain”—that is, the New and the Old Testament.

“Then he saw it, declared it, prepared it, investigated it, and said it to humankind.” That is, in his Church God foresaw this future wisdom, namely, that the whole world would possess his fear.

“Behold, the fear of the Lord is wisdom itself, and to turn away from evil is understanding.” One fear is that a person should not offend God; the other is felt after one has offended him. The former is holy and praiseworthy; the latter does not possess love, but punishment. Accordingly, the Psalmist speaks of this praiseworthy fear: “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring forever and ever.” The evangelist John speaks of the other fear in his Epistle, saying: “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear.” That fear indeed has punishment, because it lacks the merit of love.

[Cols. 0703D–0706A]

## CHAPTER XXIX

Job also added, taking up his parable, and said. According to the rule stated above, here too we draw the line of interpretation in such a way that, whenever what follows cannot suitably be referred to the Savior, we try to bend the meaning of the exposition toward the structure of his members. This can rightly be done, so that what the Lord himself, the head of his Church, cannot receive into himself may be understood of his body, which is the Church.

“Who will grant me that I may be as in former months, according to the days when God guarded me?” Holy Job longs and desires that he may now be freed from that squalor and those torments and return to the glory of his former happiness, in which he had once lived while the Lord prospered him.

“When his lamp shone over my head.” In the divine Scriptures, “lamp” is called by many names. Here Job may have used it for the glory of this temporal life, which he had received from God and possessed in honor, power, and riches.

“And by its light I walked through darkness.” Among sins, and among the things I did not know, as though among the rough and obscure conditions of this life, I proceeded by the light of virtue or of that consolation.

“As I was in the days of my youth, and when God was secretly in my tabernacle.” He wished to call his mind his “secret place,” because there the tumultuous crowds of vices made no noise at all.

“When the Almighty was with me, and my servants were all around me.” When he had God in his tabernacle, virtues are said to stand before him like servants. They are called masculine on account of the vigor with which they resist vices. Blessed Job was surrounded by such attendants.

“When I washed my feet with butter.” In the divine Scriptures, the word “feet” generally signifies a certain manner of human conduct. “I washed,” he says, “my actions from every stain of sin, and I lived with innocence and simplicity.”

“And the rock poured out streams of oil for me.” In keeping with this meaning Moses says: “They sucked honey from the rock, and oil from the hardest rock.” According to the delight of those who desired it, it tasted sweet in the mouth. Although, according to the Apostle, that rock prefigured Christ, holy Job nevertheless wished to show that he had received this oil—the gifts of the Holy Spirit—in abundant outpouring. This, then, is the living and true oil: the Holy Spirit, consubstantial with the Father and the Son. Holy Job therefore abounded in this oil, by which he was also filled with the richness of love.

“When I went out to the gate of the city and prepared my seat for myself in the square.” It is clear that the judges of the Jews sat at the gates in order to administer justice to the people.

“The young men saw me and hid themselves, and the old men rose and stood. The princes stopped speaking and placed their finger over their mouth. The leaders restrained their voice, and their tongue clung to their throat.” In these verses he demonstrated the reverence and devout fear that not only every age but also every authority rightly offered him.

“The ear that heard blessed me, and the eye that saw bore witness to me, because I delivered the poor man who cried out, and the orphan who had no helper.” His conduct, he says, was so holy in the present life that its reputation bore witness to it.

“The blessing of the perishing came upon me, and I comforted the heart of the widow.” The orphan, the poor person, and the widow signify every kind of humble and afflicted person, none of whom holy Job passed by or despised.

“I clothed myself with justice, and it clothed me as with a garment and as a diadem with my judgment.” Justice, righteous judgment, and mercy were the garments of his soul.

“I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame.” These words demonstrate the feeling of his piety and mercy. Alternatively, he gave the light of truth to those walking in the darkness of ignorance, and showed the right paths to one who limped along the ways of the Lord.

“I was a father to the poor, and I investigated most diligently the case I did not know.” By taking up the affairs and cases of the poor against the powerful, he became their defender and judge. Therefore, so that they might not be oppressed by either side of the dispute, he said that he investigated their cases after exposing their frauds.

“I crushed the jaws of the wicked, and took the prey from his teeth.” Here he describes an unjust man as a rapacious and violent beast, from whose mouth he had forcibly taken away the substance of the poor.

“And I said: ‘In my little nest I shall die, and like the palm tree I shall multiply my days.’” His nest is to be understood as his external person, which had been made and enclosed by God from the hay of his flesh. For “all flesh is grass.” In this nest, therefore, he said under oath that he would always die, since he did not live according to the vices and desires of the world. For this reason, in the resurrection he will have many and eternal days, like the palm tree.

“My root is open beside the waters, and the dew will remain in my harvest.” My hope and faith, which arise from this expectation of mine, are open toward the divine words. By their consolation, my mind is watered, lest its greenness wither in unbelief.

“My glory will always be renewed, and my bow will be restored in my hand.” Those who heard me waited for my judgment and remained attentive and silent for my counsel. “My glory,” and the rest, can be understood as the fruit of a good conscience growing in virtue and as ever-new progress. In the bow, I believe, the vigor of one who resists and fights is signified—a vigor prepared in the hands of holy works against every adversary and every hostile assault of the vices. As David says in the Psalm: “You have made my arms like a bronze bow”; that is, you have made the intention of my good works tireless.

“They did not dare to add anything to my words, and my eloquence dripped upon them.” Since the authority of his wisdom had already been spread everywhere, no one, as though criticizing him, dared to add anything to his words. Rather, his eloquence dripped upon them—that is, its inner meaning penetrated their inmost being, so that, infused into their hearts, they might be made perfect and excellent disciples by such a teacher.

“They waited for me as for rain, and they opened their mouths as for the late rain.” By the name of rain he demonstrates the great abundance of the instruction of his knowledge, and he praises his hearers because, while he was discoursing, they awaited him with intense desire.

“If I ever laughed at them, they did not believe it.” He says that he was held in such reverence and honor by those mentioned above that his wisdom and gravity could not accommodate any indulgence or relaxation, which would have belonged more properly to the moderation of ordinary conduct. Therefore he did this as an act of kindness, so that their feelings of love and affection might grow through their admiration of him.

“And the light of my face did not fall to the ground.” The grace of reverence that they saw shining in his face was not considered worthless by those mentioned above. They did not think that anything was done for no reason at his nod; therefore they received as something great and exceptional whatever they observed in the serenity of his face.

“If I wished to go to them, I sat first. And when I sat, like a king with an army surrounding him, I was nevertheless a comforter of the sorrowful.” In these words he reveals his condescension and holy humility, by which he went to his inferiors as to friends and equals, and presented himself in the power of a king to the wretched and sorrowful.

[Cols. 0706B–0708D]

## CHAPTER XXX

“But now those younger in age mock me.” This is clear.

“Whose fathers I did not consider worthy to place with the dogs of my flock.” He had not done this through arrogant pride or boastfulness about his wealth, but because of the worthlessness of the ungodly men who mocked him, whose fathers had once not been worthy to be compared even with his dogs.

“Whose strength of hands was considered nothing by me, and they were thought unworthy of life itself, barren through poverty and hunger.” That is, they were despised as worthless through the disgrace of their low condition.

“They gnawed in the wilderness, squalid through calamity and misery. They ate herbs and the bark of trees, and the root of the juniper was their food. From the valleys they snatched these things, and whenever they found any of them, they ran toward them with a shout.” Through misery and greed they attacked even things that were outside human or animal food as though they were banquets and delicacies, sucking up the damp valleys because of their extreme poverty.

“They lived in the deserts of the torrents and in the caves of the earth, or upon the gravel. They rejoiced among such things.” As he says, they lived in sterile and waterless places, or among thorns, creeping upon the earth like reptiles, in holes watered by the mountain rains.

“And they considered it a delight to be under the thorns.” That is, if, in their heat, they covered themselves with the leaves of the most worthless plants.

“Sons of fools and of ignoble people, and utterly without name upon the earth. Now I have become their song, and I have become a proverb to them. They abhor me, flee far from me, and are not afraid to spit in my face.” They were obscure and utterly unworthy of remembrance.

“For he opened his quiver, afflicted me, and placed a bridle in my mouth.” I think that the quiver here should be understood as the multitude of blows, or the devil himself, or his power. As Job says, God opened it when the devil exercised his power against him; thus he afflicted him with the arrows of torments. Moreover, he placed a bridle of silence in his mouth so that he would not speak.

“At the right hand of the rising one my calamities suddenly arose.” That is, they arose in the very time of his prosperity, which proves most grievous; or they were imposed by permission of divine power. For he himself is the one who rises from on high; he himself is the right hand and power of the Most High.

“They overturned my feet and crushed me along their paths as though by waves.” That is, my calamities, afflicting me through repeated assaults, overturned all the straight paths of my conduct like waves.

“They destroyed my ways, lay in wait for me, prevailed, and there was no one to bring help.” That is, my enemies disturbed the paths by which I had proceeded daily through the way of justice and progress. Bursting unexpectedly upon me as though from an ambush, they left my closest companions unwilling to offer me the help of consolation.

“Like a breached wall and an opened gate, they rushed upon me and rolled down upon my miseries.” The evils mentioned above, he says, rushed upon me with such swift force that, with no obstacle resisting, they rolled down upon me from above.

“I have been reduced to nothing. He took away my desire like the wind, and my salvation passed like a cloud.” The rewards that I awaited from you for keeping your commandments, together with salvation, you snatched away with the force of the wind and the speed of a flying cloud—[alternative reading: “for us”]—because you permitted them to be taken away.

“Then my soul withers within me, and days of affliction possess me.” It withers—that is, it is dissolved from the vigor of its purpose.

“At night my bones are pierced by pains, and those who consume me do not sleep.” It is clear that the worms that were eating his flesh kept watch through the nights.

“By their multitude my garment is consumed, and they girded me like the collar of my tunic.” The multitude of swarming worms, continually moving and running through the various openings of my wounds, wore away my garment as it ceaselessly crawled over me. This swarm surrounds me entirely on every side and, as though I had been reduced to a single wound, tortures me with unceasing eating and devouring.

“I have been compared to mud and made like dust and ashes.” He says that he has been brought to the lowest degradation: because of his wounds and pus he rotted and stank like mud, while the dirt of dust dried out the putrefaction of his flesh.

“I cry out to you, and you do not hear me; I stand, and you do not look upon me.” In crying out, the earnestness of one praying to God is expressed. In saying that he stands, he declares that he possesses unwavering perseverance toward God. Holy Job speaks freely because of his confidence in his own righteousness before God.

“You have changed toward me into cruelty, and in the hardness of your hand you oppose me. You lifted me up and, setting me upon the wind, dashed me down violently.” He says that the pious and merciful God, who had been so in his prosperity, became hard and cruel when he endured the hardness of his hand and grievous and dreadful punishments.

“I know that you will hand me over to death, where the house appointed for every living being is.” After the transgression of the parent, he says, the house of the lower regions was established—that is, death itself—not created according to the original condition of humanity. You therefore wished me also, as a son of sinful Adam, to go there according to a just sentence.

“Yet not for their destruction.” He prophesies the reconciliation of the world that was to come in Christ, saying that human beings would not be reduced to everlasting destruction but would someday be recalled from the lower regions.

“You will stretch out your hand; and if they fall, you yourself will save them.” If, after the redemption by which we are saved through faith in Christ, human beings should fall again through sin, he himself will save them by the hand of mercy lifting them up through repentance.

“I once wept over the afflicted, and my soul had compassion on the poor. I expected good things, and evils came upon me; I awaited light, and darkness burst upon me.” It happened that, in place of the expectation of good things with which I used to console the wretched, I now endured every evil; and in place of the light of prosperity I encountered the darkness of torments.

“My inward parts boiled without any rest; days of affliction came before me.” When he says that the days of affliction came before him, I think he wished to indicate the time of judgment. He seems to say that he was anticipated by it because he had thought it would not yet come upon him. Here too he signifies the great pain of hell, by comparing his punishments with those days.

“Mourning, I walked about; I rose without fury; in the assembly I cried out.” Sad and afflicted with sorrow because I did not know the reason for my punishment, and without the anger of rage, I rose in hope through the strength of my soul, because God had taught me patience, so that I might bear it with equanimity, crying out and pleading publicly.

“I was a brother to dragons and a companion to ostriches.” Afflicted by the torment of punishments, I tempered my pain with hisses, as dragons are said to do when they are captured by elephants. As the prophet says: “I will make mourning like dragons”—which they do, as I have said, when they are killed by elephants. “And a companion to ostriches”: I became foolish and senseless like an ostrich, the most foolish of birds, so that they might think that I had labored in vain because of my grief.

“My skin has become black upon me, and my bones have dried up from the heat.” This too belonged to the accumulation of his punishments: stationed in dung, he endured for a long time the sun’s most burning rays, penetrating even to his bones.

“My lyre has been turned into mourning, and my pipe into the voice of those who weep.” By these things he says that the joy and delight of his fortunate days and prosperity had been turned into mourning.

[Cols. 0709A–0713C]

### ITEM. The exposition is turned to the person of Christ.

“Who will grant me that I may be as in former months,” and so forth. In the man assumed by Jesus Christ—that is, in the second or last Adam—the voice is that of Adam the first-created, remembering what he lost and to what good he wishes to return. Through the evil of disobedience he had lost the good of immortality and the delights of paradise; he desires these to be restored to him through Jesus Christ our Lord. For by taking the son of man into himself, the Son of God also took up in him the prayers of the human race.

“When his lamp shone over my head, and by its light I walked through darkness.” He signified the glory of divine grace by the name of the lamp with which he had flourished in paradise.

“As I was in the days of my youth, when God was secretly in my tabernacle.” By “youth” the beginnings of Adam may be understood, or happiness itself: before sin, he is said to have been ever fresh with youthful vigor, without any decline of age, as though in the days of youth.

“When the Almighty was with me, and my servants were around me.” Adam’s servants are to be understood as the powers of the soul. We may also reasonably understand Christ’s servants as the angels who ministered to him in the days of his flesh, or the apostles, or all the saints.

“When I washed my feet with butter, and the rock poured out streams of oil for me.” The feet of the Savior are therefore to be understood as the preachers of truth, who proclaim the Gospel throughout the whole world. Jesus Christ, our Job, washed and cleansed these feet of his with milk or butter when he made them pure and spotless from the pressures of tribulations, teaching them through his Spirit a life of simple innocence. In this way, the feet of the one announcing the peace of the Gospel are cleansed, so that they may not be defiled by the mud of carnal wisdom.

“The rock,” he says, “poured out streams of oil for me.” Therefore the rock—the Church, founded upon Christ, the firmest rock—pours forth from itself the grace of the Holy Spirit like streams. This was made evident at Pentecost, in the house of Cornelius, among the twelve, and throughout the whole Church; and it continues to be made evident to this day.

“When I went out to the gate of the city, and they placed my seat for me in the square.” Therefore, like a king and first Lord of the city of his Church, Christ goes out to its gate—that is, at the time of its beginnings, when, preparing its entrance, he said to everyone: “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened.” The elevated seat is to be understood as the knowledge of Christ. The square of the city is to be understood either as his public preaching or according to the Psalmist’s meaning: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad.” It extends not only into a threefold exposition but also into disputation.

“The young men saw me and hid themselves, and the old men rose and stood.” John writes of these, saying: “I write to you, young men, because you are strong and have conquered the evil one.” Through faith in the Lord they see the Savior in the spirit, while they hide themselves in the earthly body: restraining vices within themselves and fighting against them, putting themselves to death with respect to sins and the desires of the world. Hence the prophet says: “Ascend, you, into the land.”

But the old men are mature and perfect sons, who are daily lifted up in mind toward heaven and stand in the Lord, firm in the faith of an unshaken life.

“The princes ceased speaking and placed their finger over their mouth; the leaders restrained their voice, and their tongue clung to their throat.” At my coming, he says, the prophecy of all my saints was concluded and sealed, as was prefigured in Zechariah’s silence. The prophecy was indeed closed in the mystery of what had been announced, but it was opened in the mysteries of the sacraments. The princes and leaders of that Jewish people were kings, priests, and prophets. Alternatively, princes and leaders may be understood as all the powerful and eloquent people of this world who, because of the lies of their deception, held authority over the peoples. These fell silent at Christ’s coming.

“The ear that heard blessed me.” This is the people of the Gentiles, to whom my Gospel came through the proclamation of preaching. Offering praise for its redemption, it blessed me by giving thanks.

“And the eye that saw bore witness to me.” This is the people of the Jews, to whom I had been foretold through my prophets; at the presence of my coming it bore witness to me.

“Because I delivered the poor man who cried out, and the orphan who had no helper.” This poor man and orphan are to be understood as the people of the saints, who were called poor because of the humility of their contrite spirit. They were called orphans because their father is temporarily absent, as he says: “I will not leave you orphans.”

“The blessing of the child”—or, as others have said, “of the perishing”—“came upon me, and I comforted the heart of the widow.” The faithful and holy person is called an orphan; he is called a child because of his restored innocence. He is also called “lost,” because he was acquired by the blood of the Lord.

“I clothed myself with justice, and it clothed me as with a diadem, with my judgment.” “This justice,” the Lord says, “the justice of my piety, clothed me as with a garment.” “And as a diadem, with my judgment.” By this garment, in which the Father’s justice is revealed through the Gospel, he says that he is surrounded in the Church. His garment on the mountain of his transfiguration bore its figure.

“I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame.” “I am light,” he says, “to the sinner walking in the darkness of his vices, and I have become a step for the one who limps along the paths of my commandments.” Hence he himself says: “I am the way.”

“I was a father to the poor”—that is, to the humble in heart.

“And when I did not know the case, I investigated it diligently.” This case of sins, which through the mercy of my compassion I was about to pardon, I searched out most diligently, seeking the root of the wounds in order to cure it, so that I might free from every sinful offense the sinner who, when examined by me, confessed his sins. Or alternatively: Our Lord Jesus Christ did not know the causes of sin—the causes that the Jews were seeking from him.

“I crushed the jaws of the wicked, and took the prey from his teeth.” We rightly understand this wicked one to be the devil, whose teeth and molars are savage and fierce spiritual impulses bent on destruction. From such teeth, he says, he snatched the human race as captive prey, freeing it from the destruction of death. All the ungodly are the devil’s teeth. Any heretic may also be understood, in whose teeth a plainly expressed doctrine may be perceived, while in the molars hidden, remote, secret, and abominable mysteries may lie concealed.

“And I said: ‘In my little nest I shall die, and like the palm tree I shall multiply its days.’” The Lord and Savior’s nest may be understood as his Church. In this nest of his, which he gathered for himself from the hay of human flesh, and in which he brings forth and nurtures children, the Lord is said to die, since his members, of whom he is the head, die to the vices and desires of this world.

It follows: “And like the palm tree I shall multiply its days.” After the humility of the Church, which the Lord indicated above by the nest, he wished to show its glory and exaltation in the palm tree. Its root appears rough in the earth, which is why it is also called a nest; but its crown is beautiful beneath the heavens. When it has been glorified through the resurrection, it will attain the height of the palm tree—that is, it will attain the merits of its virtues, which are signified by the palm.

Alternatively, this nest may be understood as the people of the Jews. In this nest he wished to suffer and die for us, as he says to the Jews: “I shall die, and I shall be crucified in their minds.” There, according to his humanity, he lived and was born; and among the Gentiles, where the palm of his victory and the banner of the cross were raised, he will multiply his days, saying to them: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age.”

“My root is open beside the waters, and the dew will remain in my harvest.” Thus there will be a root among the nations—that is, faith, by which I wished to please God, as all the saints pleased him in former times. It will be open to the waters of the nations—that is, to the people—so that they may believe in me. For them, in the eternal reward, there will be a dew of grace and gift, flowing abundantly because I bestow it.

Or else it is the root of my charity and love, which is fixed in the hearts of those who love me; it is open within them to the waters of my words.

“My glory will always be renewed.” Here we may understand the Church as glory. The Son is indeed the glory of the Father, to whom the Father says: “Arise, my glory; arise.” But in another sense the Church is glory, having been justified by grace.

“And my bow will be restored in my hand.” We may understand this bow as the virtue by which he does not cease to fight for his Church until the end of the age.

“Those who heard me waited for my judgment, and they remained attentive and silent for my counsel.” Every day Christ cries out through the stewards of his word, and those who obey him await the sentence of his judgment. “And they remained attentive and silent for my counsel.” By this word of silence the obedience of the saints is signified: they are slow to speak but quick to act. Or else, because in the very investigation of the law the saints are said to remain attentive.

“They did not dare to add anything to my words.” They do not overthrow the statutes and decrees of the Church, in which they establish the foundation of truth. But heretics and schismatics, through the presumptuous pride by which they set themselves above others, attempt to impose upon the words of the Lord doctrines discovered in their own hearts and superfluous dogmas of fullness.

“And my eloquence dripped upon them.” Gradually, the word of my teaching and my diligence penetrated the inmost parts of those who diligently loved me. In this, the daily progress of souls in virtue is to be understood. As from a small drop of beginnings, one reaches the full life of perfection, like rain saturating the soil of the heart with abundance.

“They waited for me as for rain, and they opened their mouths as for the late rain.” All the ancient saints awaited the coming of the Savior in the flesh, and all now await without doubt his coming for judgment. For his late rain—that is, the Gospel—they now open the mouths of their hearts in thirst, because, as Ecclesiastes says, “the latter words are better than their beginning.”

“If I ever laughed at them, they did not believe it.” That is, the Jews will not believe me when, in joyful compassion, I promise the happiness of the future and the joys of eternity. Sinners, because of the guilt of their conscience, will scarcely believe in my mercy and will despair that salvation can be granted to them because of the greatness of their crimes, although I will bestow upon those who turn to me things greater than they can contain in hope.

“And the light of my face did not fall to the ground.” The grace, he says, of my presence, by which I became known to the whole world, illuminates the hearts of the faithful, because I am the light of the world. Whatever I promise to those who keep my covenant will not be void; everything will be fulfilled at the time of the reward.

“If I wished to go to them, I sat first. And when I sat, like a king with an army surrounding him, I was nevertheless a comforter of the sorrowful.” This is to be understood as referring to the one who, although he dwells in greatness and on high among his saints—who are often called angels, and of whom, according to another edition, he says, “I was like a king surrounded by mighty ones”—nevertheless did not despise the contrite and brokenhearted.

## CHAPTER XXX

“But now those younger in age mock me.” We read in the Gospel how he was mocked and derided.

“Whose fathers I did not deem worthy to place with the dogs of my flock.” I think that “dogs” is used in a favorable sense: they vigilantly defend the Lord’s flock from spiritual beasts. Of them the prophet says: “Dumb dogs, unable to bark.” The fathers of the Jews, who were certainly priests, were not placed, he says, with the holy guardians of the flock of his sheep, because the pastoral dignity had been taken away from them on account of the wickedness of their unbelief. “I rejected them,” he says, “so that they might not exercise the priesthood for me.” This too is said in the Gospel: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you,” and so forth. There he begins to take the bread of the children and give it to the dogs, as it is said to him in the Gospel under the figure of the Church: “For even the little dogs eat from the crumbs that fall from the table of their masters.”

“Whose strength of hands was nothing to me.” The strength of the hands of the Jews consisted in their serving the commandments of the elders and their observances. Or this passage may be understood as referring to the time of the Lord’s Passion, so that the strength of their works extended even to the Savior’s death. Or it may be understood this way: when they mourned that his life had been ended by the cross, the power of their evil efforts was reduced to nothing by the triumph of the one rising from the dead.

“And they were thought unworthy even of life itself, barren through poverty and hunger.” Made poor through the shameful poverty of their vices and crimes, and made barren and beggarly through hunger for the words of God, they were considered unworthy even of the present life, as the prophet says to God: “Scatter them by your power.” Hence now they are in the midst of the nations like captives, living a degraded life.

“They gnawed in the wilderness, squalid through calamity and misery; they ate herbs and the bark of trees, and the root of the juniper was their food. From the valleys they snatched these things, and whenever they found any of them, they ran toward them with a shout.” Wherever God does not dwell—that is, where he is not worshiped—is often called a wilderness or desert. According to the Apocalypse, the woman—that is, corruption—is said to sit there.

To eat or gnaw is the work of the teeth, since articulate speech is produced by the teeth and the plectrum of the tongue. Therefore, by these words the doctrine of those people is signified: by chewing and gnawing peoples, as though they were herbs and the roots of fruitless trees, they draw them into their manifold errors as into their own body.

They think they are feeding themselves if they strip away whatever is vital from human beings, whom Scripture commonly calls trees. They are likewise nourished by the roots of junipers—trees, that is, that live for a long time, and in whose wood fire lasts much longer than in other woods. These are the woods called *arceuthina*. Under the name of these trees we may understand the great men among the Jewish people, whose innermost parts the teachers mentioned above consume, stealing from them, through their preaching of the former law, the good of Christ’s grace.

Those who, having snatched these things from the valleys, whenever they found each one, ran toward them with a shout. From the valleys, then, they seize the herbs, like thieves, as other translators have rendered it, [Col. 0713D] and the bark of trees. For they could not find in high places, or in places of a similar kind, those whom we have understood allegorically as herbs, bark, and the roots of trees; rather, they found them in valleys—in low places, that is, depressed toward the depths—where the carnal people of the Jews are signified. Their understanding remains in the sense of the letter that kills, as though dwelling in lower regions. Hence their leaders plunder them, while the blind provide guidance to the blind.

They dwelt in desert places, in the torrents’ ravines, and in caves of the earth; or upon gravel—people who rejoiced amid such things and counted it a delight to be beneath thorns. They did not dwell only in the deserts of those mentioned above, where the worship of God [Col. 0714A] was absent, but also in caves of the earth and upon gravel. By this gravel, I think, the law is to be understood carnally, where nothing rich is mingled with spiritual understanding by which, through the fertility of abundance, it might bring forth children of holiness, with grace as their mother, through faith. For this reason they are said to be in caves of the earth, clinging, that is, to earthly understandings. Concerning such people the Apostle says with tears that they are enemies of the cross of Christ.

Alternatively: torrents are sinners who flow through the deserts of knowledge into this sea of the world. These people therefore dwell in the caves of the senses and take delight in their functions for the purpose of sinning; they are the windows of the house through which death enters. Or the cave of the serpent is our breast when we conceal within it poisonous counsels and death-dealing deeds. Such people likewise dwell upon gravel, [Col. 0714B] cultivating their soil without any diligent care for God’s words, so that, having received the richness of fertility, they may be able to produce fruits of holiness.

“Who rejoiced amid such things and counted it a delight to be beneath thorns.” Amid the evils mentioned above, they live in such exultant joy as though they were seeking virtues.

“Children of fools and of ignoble people, and not appearing at all upon the earth.” Thus the prophet had already foretold concerning their fathers: “A crooked and perverse generation, a foolish people and without understanding, alienated from the land of the living.”

“Now I have become their song, and I have become their byword.” That is, in their first speech and in their mouths I am; and they take me up as an object of pleasurable abuse. [Col. 0714C]

“They abhor me and flee from me, and are not afraid to spit in my face.” The face of the Lord and Savior being spat upon is plainly shown to us in the Gospel by his very Passion.

“For he opened his quiver and afflicted me.” Here the devil may be understood as the quiver. And since we believe that the Savior assumed true humanity, it is not unreasonable to believe that he also willed to feel bodily pains in his Passion, according to the prophet’s statement: “He himself took our infirmities and suffers for us.”

“And he put a bridle in my mouth.” His patience demonstrated the insults inflicted upon him, just as the Son himself says to the Father in the psalm: “For you are my patience, O Lord.” [Col. 0714D] And in the Gospel, when Jesus was questioned, he did not answer.

“At the right hand of the east, my calamities immediately rose up.” That is, by the will of the Father, at whose right hand the Son sits. Or he means that even to the Son of God, including that aspect by which he is impassible, the insult suffered by the assumed man reached, according to the Apostle who says: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.” For he is the Father’s right hand, hand and arm, through whom all things were made and are governed; and the disciples were more truly at his right hand, yet they abandoned him at the time of his Passion. Concerning them he says: “I looked to the right, and there was no one who recognized me.”

[Col. 0715A] “They overturned my feet and crushed them. They scattered my paths like waves along their ways. They lay in wait for me and prevailed, and there was no one to bring help, as though a wall had been broken and a door opened, and they had poured down upon my miseries.” The feet may be understood as the human substance that they crucified, or certainly as the office of evangelizing. By the waves he shows the Jews to be bitter and restless toward the preachers of the Gospel.

“They also scattered my paths.” Through the prophecies of my prophets I promised them the presence of my coming in the flesh, and in visions of revelations I often came to them. These, then, were the paths of my coming, and they scattered them through their unbelief and the crime of their impiety. His feet may also be understood as his preachers or apostles. [Col. 0715B] “And there was no one to bring help,” because the disciples too, having abandoned him, fled for refuge. “As though a wall had been broken and a door opened, they rushed upon me and poured down upon my miseries”—that is, through my death they fell into their own ruin, so that, like most savage and fierce enemies, having broken through the fortifications of cities and battered down their houses, they might all alike spring forward to kill me. The miseries are the sufferings: scourging, mockery, insults, blows, spitting, strikes, thorns, and the disgrace of the cross.

“I have been reduced to nothing.” The Jews, despising him, regarded him as nothing.

“You have taken away my desire like the wind, and my salvation has passed like a cloud.” The present life may be understood as the wind, since it is often called by the name of wind, or spirit. Therefore, from the person of the old man assumed by God, the man Jesus Christ speaks these words. The desire of the old man was that he might not lose this temporal life, as the Lord himself demonstrates when near his Passion, saying to the Father: “Let this cup pass from me.” Yet, he says, “not what I will, but what you will.”

“Now my soul withers within me, and days of affliction possess me.” His days of affliction are the days of his Passion. Hence the Savior says in the Gospel: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death.”

“At night my bone is pierced with pains, and those who consume me do not sleep.” At night, because he was seized in the evening and was heard throughout the night by the scribes and rulers under interrogation. Or he speaks of the night of sadness [Col. 0715D] and Passion.
