He calls the apostles “bones” on account of the strength of his love and charity; pierced by the goads of pain and fear, they were pierced even to the guilt of denial—that is, the wavering of faith penetrated the strength of their spirit, so that at the hour of temptation they faltered in the firmness of charity. But those who appear to consume me by persecuting me unto death do not sleep: that is, they apply themselves with complete vigilance of mind so as to reach me and devour me.

“In the multitude of them my garment is consumed.” When the Jews gathered together as one, my flesh was exhausted by insults, nails, the cross, and death.

“And like the collar of a tunic they girded me.” To kill me, they surrounded me on every side, as though strangling me; and to suffocate me in death, like a collar about a head, they girded me with strong nooses—namely, false testimonies—and enclosed me within my Passion and cross as though within a tunic. [Col. 0716A]

“I have been compared to mud and made like dust and ashes.” Through the death that I willingly accepted, I have been compared to things that are vile, subject to sin, and condemned in Adam by God’s sentence, although I myself am not a sinner and was not born as all sinners were.

“I cry to you, and you do not hear me; I stand, and you do not look upon me.” Thus also, in the twenty-first psalm, he cried to the Father on the cross: “My God,” and the rest: “I will cry by day, and you will not hear,” and so forth. These words, then, are spoken from the person of the Crucified, as are the others that I have already discussed above. “I will cry to you by day,” he says—that is, in the prosperous circumstances of this life, asking that they not be changed, and you do not hear me in the words of sins. “I will cry also at night,” that is, I will cry amid the adversities of this life, asking that they prosper, and likewise you will not hear me. Nor is this sufficient for my folly; rather, it is so that I may understand what you wish me to cry: not words of sin arising from desire for temporal life, but words of conversion to you for eternal life. [Col. 0716B]

“You have changed for me into a cruel one, and in the harshness of your hand you oppose me.” When the Father did not spare his only Son but handed him over for us all, it seemed an act of cruelty, although it was an expression of loving providence.

[Col. 0716C] “You have lifted me up, and, placing me as though upon the wind, you have violently dashed me down.” This means: you lifted me up upon the cross and, because the Jews did not believe, you dashed me down.

“I know that you will hand me over to death, where a house is established for every living thing.” For before the Lord’s resurrection even the righteous are believed to have been in the regions of hell.

“Yet you do not stretch out your hand for their destruction, and if they fall, you yourself will save them.” You hand me over to death for this purpose: that those who by divine judgment have been assigned to eternal death may not be destroyed by the penalty they deserve, but rather may be saved by my death. When he says, “If they fall, you yourself will save them,” he promises, after the grace of baptism, a remedy of salvation to sinners through repentance.

“I once wept over one who was afflicted.” The Savior wept over Jerusalem for two reasons. One was that, weeping for those who were converted, he prayed to the Father. The other was that he sorrowed and wept for those who did not believe, foreseeing as God their destruction on account of the hardness of their unbelief. [Col. 0716D]

“And my soul had compassion on the poor man.” In Scripture, holy souls are called poor because they do not possess the spirit of pride or sins as the riches of this world. Conversely, all sinners are called poor because they swell with the spirit of pride and are destitute of holiness. Concerning them the psalm sings: “Sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, bound in chains, in poverty and iron.” To weep for such poor people, God, who is rich in mercies, endured sadness out of an impulse of compassion. [Col. 0717A]

“I expected good things, and evils came upon me.” I therefore waited patiently, hoping that I might joyfully receive the good of their conversion once they had been corrected. But they contemptuously rejected the riches of my goodness and patience, and stored up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath and of the revelation of my righteous judgment. These evils of theirs, then, will come into my sight, so that I may repay each one according to his works.

“I waited for light, and darkness broke forth.” I waited for the light of faith and holy works in them, but the darkness of their unbelief and vices prevailed.

“My inward parts seethed without any rest.” Either because, touched by sorrow, his inner spirit seethed with concern and anxiety over their destruction; [Col. 0717B] or because, with the Word made flesh and dwelling in the name of Jesus our Savior, his inward parts—that is, the movements of his soul—burned without cessation with divine fire.

“The days of affliction came before me.” The days of affliction will be the days of judgment, when I shall judge the people mentioned above. Yet even now, in this present time, they have preceded me by their enormous crimes, so that according to my righteous judgment I may repay them. This later happened in the Passion, when Jerusalem and the Temple were overthrown by the Romans.

“Mourning, I went about; rising without anger, I cried out in the darkness.” He was without any fury of anger, since he had come to pardon and forgive their sins, not to punish them. The Evangelist also says: “Jesus stood and cried out: ‘Whoever thirsts, let him come to me and drink.’” [Col. 0717C]

“I was a brother to dragons and a companion of ostriches.” In the Gospel the Lord frequently calls the Jews serpents and vipers, saying: “Serpents, offspring of vipers.” And the prophet says: “They broke open the eggs of asps,” when he saw the generation of evildoers multiplying. Again: “The fury of dragons is their wine, and the fury of asps is incurable.” He therefore called himself their brother because, according to the flesh, he was born from their race. Concerning them he says in the psalm: “I have become a stranger to my brothers and a guest to the sons of my mother.” And because, according to the present life, during which he was mortal here, he lived among them, he called himself their companion, that is, he dwelt in the same nation with fools and senseless people, as the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Fools and blind.”

“My skin has become black upon me.” By “skin” we are to understand that he refers to his flesh—that is, to the Jewish people, his own nation, from which the Savior assumed flesh—using a part for the whole. When he says, “upon me my skin has become black,” it is as though he were saying: because of me, that is, in my person, through the hatred of persecution, the crime of blasphemy, and the guilt of unspeakable sins, the flesh of my race has become foul and black. Like an Ethiopian woman, it does not lose its dark color; and it is all the more wretched because it has acquired this blackness of night and darkness not on the surface of the body but in the heart. [Col. 0718A] Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “I have made your mother like the night.”

“And my bones have dried up from the heat.” The bones of the body of the Church, whose head is Christ, are to be understood as all the saints, but especially the apostles; through the strength and virtue of their holiness all the Church’s weaker members are sustained. The richest fat of these bones—their charity—therefore boiled away in the excessive heat of persecution during the Savior’s Passion. Concerning them the Lord himself says in the psalm: “And my bones have dried up like kindling.” Again, in another psalm: “I have been poured out like water, and all my bones have been scattered,” as the Evangelist says: “And the disciples left Jesus and fled.” But afterward, through confessing his name and being richly nourished by his charity, they were made fat again, so that thereafter, amid no matter how fierce a heat of persecutions, neither the faith of Christ nor the good of charity in them would wither. [Col. 0718B]

“My harp has turned into mourning, and my organ into the voice of weepers.” In the harp and organ, joy and exultation are understood. Christ demonstrates that he possesses these when he rejoices over the salvation of believers, as he himself says in the Gospel, where he gives the parable of the hundred sheep, saying that one of them had perished; when it was found, he said: “Amen I say to you, he will rejoice over it more than over the ninety-nine others.” Likewise, when the apostles reported to the Lord that many healings had been performed through them in his name, the Evangelist says: “In that hour Jesus rejoiced in spirit.” These musical names therefore signify the joy of the heart, which was turned into sadness over the hardening of unbelievers, as the Evangelist says of the same Lord: “And he was saddened over the hardness of their hearts.” As for what follows up to the end of the parable, which we explained above according to the virtue of holy Job, we have already acknowledged that we cannot discuss it according to its mystical meanings. If anyone can reasonably adapt those passages to an allegorical interpretation, I shall confess that I agree.

## CHAPTER XXXI

“I made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not even think about a virgin. For what portion would God have in me from above, and what inheritance would the Almighty have from on high? Is not destruction for the unjust, and alienation for those who work iniquity? Does he not himself consider my ways and number all my steps?” From this point to the end, he recounts his acts of righteousness, and especially his mercies and virtues, arranging them into as many as fifteen items, like a perfect man who, setting ascents in his heart, reaches the house of God by ascending through certain stages of progress. “I determined and resolved,” he says, “in my mind and together with these eyes of my flesh, that they should report to me nothing shameful or obscene within, which I might turn over within myself through the pleasure of desire and wicked thoughts.” I believe that he had perhaps at some time felt his flesh being titillated by pleasure and the allurements of desire, and therefore girded himself with the virtue of continence, fearing the eye of God, since he is the searcher of the heart and knows [Col. 0719A] all the ways of human conduct and every step of mortal actions.

“If I have walked in vanity, and my foot has hastened in deceit, let him weigh me in a just balance, and let God know my simplicity.” Holy Job, confident in the equity of God’s justice, wishes to be revealed to human beings. For God does not lack knowledge, so that he may learn by examining; but “let God know,” blessed Job said, so that he may make others know, according to the statement: “The Lord your God tests you, to know whether you love him”—that is, to make the others know.

“If I have turned my steps from the way, and if my eye has followed my heart, and if a stain has clung to my hands, then let me sow and another eat, and let my offspring be uprooted.” I have passed over none of God’s commandments, he says, because my heart did not consent and follow my eyes when they offered it images of desire, before I made a covenant with them that they should convey nothing shameful inwardly. Therefore no stain of sin could cling to the works of my hands; and he confirms this with a kind of oath involving a curse.

“If my heart has been deceived concerning a woman, and if I have lain in wait at the door of my friend, let my wife be another man’s prostitute, and let others bow over her.” This is a wickedness and a very great iniquity: it is a fire devouring unto destruction and eradicating every offspring. He speaks according to the good of nature, as it is written in Tobit: “What you do not want done to you, do not do to another.” Therefore he says that it is a vile deed and a very great iniquity: to think or do such deadly and detestable things [Col. 0719C] is the fire of inflamed lust, devouring every good of the virtues and consuming in a person every growth of holy things.

“If I have refused to enter into judgment with my servant and my maidservant when they disputed against me”—or, as others have said, “before me.”

“For what shall I do when God rises to judge, and when he asks, ‘What shall I answer him?’ Did not the one who made him in the womb also make me, and did not the same one form us in the womb?” Great is the humility of this holy man, and great his thought concerning the judgment to come.

“If I denied the poor what they wanted, and made the eyes of the widow wait.” This is clear.

“If I ate my morsel alone, and the orphan did not eat from it, because compassion grew with me from my childhood and came forth with me from my mother’s womb.” This is clear.

“If I looked down upon a passerby who had no clothing, and upon the poor man without covering; if his sides did not bless me, and he was warmed by the fleeces of my sheep.” By this statement he shows how an act of mercy ought to be performed: one must not take away from some what one thinks one is rightly giving to others. Hence Solomon says: “Honor God from your just labors.” And Isaiah: “I am the Lord; I love judgment and hate robbery for burnt offering.”

“If I raised my hand against the orphan, even when I saw myself superior in the gate, may my shoulder fall from its joint, and may my arm be broken together with its bones.” For I always feared God as though waves were swelling against me, and I could not bear his weight. The shoulder may be taken as works; the arm, as perseverance and persistence in good works. “Otherwise,” he says, “let all my labors be found worthless before God.” [Col. 0720A]

“If I thought gold was my strength, and said to fine gold, ‘My confidence’; if I rejoiced over my many riches because my hand had found very much.” A man of true philosophy was held by no vice. As a most steadfast despiser of greed and pride in the present passage, he testifies that he regarded even gold as nothing.

“If I looked upon the sun when it shone, and the moon moving brightly, and my heart secretly rejoiced, and I kissed my hand with my mouth, which is a very great iniquity and denial against the Most High God.” Such great virtues are of no benefit, however wise, great, and renowned someone may be in practicing them, if he is held by the folly of errors. “I was not delighted,” he says, “with the worship of any idols whatsoever; nor, as though worshiping them, did I kiss my hand amid their veneration on account of the beauty and appearance of these great lights; nor did I revere the creature in place of the Creator”—something which the holy Apostle condemns in the Epistle to the Romans. [Col. 0720B]

“If I rejoiced at the ruin of one who hated me, and exulted because evil had found him.” For I did not give my tongue to sin, so as to seek his soul while cursing him. If it is a great thing for someone not to strive to avenge himself upon his enemies when he can, how much more diligently should one refrain before God from rejoicing over their ruin, even in one’s heart!

“If the men of my tent did not say, ‘Who will give us some of his flesh, that we may be filled?’ No stranger remained outside; my door was open to the traveler.” Because of his hospitality, and the virtue by which the other saints also pleased God, he had incurred the hatred of his servants.

“If, like a man, I concealed my sin and hid my iniquity in my bosom.” It seems to me that here he speaks only of sins committed in thought, since he was unwilling to conceal even these, seeing that he had revealed the innermost secrets of his soul to human beings and shown that he had not shared in the sinful consent of any iniquity. [Col. 0720D]

“If I was terrified by the excessive multitude, and the contempt of my relatives frightened me, and I was not rather silent and did not go out the door.” This passage concerns the persons of his relatives who despised him and continually inflicted insults upon him while he lay amid the miseries of his calamities. Against them, when they quarreled with him, he placed a guard over his mouth.

“Who will grant me a hearer, that the Almighty may hear my desire, and that he who judges may himself write a book, so that I may carry it on my shoulder and surround myself with it as with a crown? At each of my steps I shall proclaim it, and present it as to a prince.” Holy Job presents this book to others upon his shoulder, in a place plainly visible to all; for, crowned by the book as by a crown of glory in return for his labors, he proclaims before God, by recounting each step of his virtues or the increase of his progress, what he has achieved. [Col. 0721A]

“If my land cries out against me, and its furrows weep with it; if I have eaten its fruits without payment and afflicted the souls of its farmers, may the thistle spring up for me instead of wheat, and the thorn instead of barley.” The land is rightly understood as human flesh. Blessed Job says that it was not adversarial toward him, necessarily because he had made it obedient to him in the matter of the adornment of virtues. He also metaphorically calls its furrows those which he made, either for cultivating good morals or for containing the water of God’s word divinely poured into his soil, according to the Psalmist’s statement: “Watering its furrows, multiply its generations.” The farmers of this land, as I think, blessed Job called his holy thoughts, by which the living field of his mind was diligently cultivated. He refers to the soul of these farmers as one soul so that we may understand that their agreement was one. It is not remarkable or blameworthy in the conduct of the saints when they praise themselves. They are not held by the vice of boasting, as though they sought human glory in their praises; rather, they do this with the intention of truth, by which they live simply and sincerely before God.

## CHAPTER XXXII

“These three men ceased to answer Job, because he seemed righteous to himself.” When his adversaries yielded, Job himself also ended his speech, after the many mysteries of his prophecy. But the statement, “These three men ceased to answer Job, because he seemed righteous to himself,” was spoken by the writer of this history from the perspective of those answering—that he seemed righteous to himself—not according to the writer’s own judgment. In reporting or writing what he commended in his style to the memory of posterity as the praise of so great a man, he spoke in that manner.

“And Elihu, son of Barachel the Buzite, of the kindred of Ram, was angry and indignant.” Job and Elihu were born from the lineage and generation of Huz and Buz, the sons of Nahor and Milcah, sister of Sarah, Abraham’s wife. Job was born from Huz, and this Elihu from Buz; hence he is called a Buzite, and, as it is written here, he was the son of Barachel. The most learned students of Scripture say that this Elihu was Balaam the diviner, whom Balak, king of the Moabites, hired to curse Israel, as related in the Book of Numbers. This Scripture states that Elihu was of the kindred of Ram; and we are to understand this Ram as Abraham, from whose kindred and family Elihu was born. Thus the descendants of his brother Nahor were unquestionably Abraham’s relatives. Here the writer of this book—whom the Hebrews assert was Moses—wished, through the names in Elihu’s genealogy, to display the nobility of his birth. [Col. 0721D]

As for the fact that in this book Abram is called Ram, as though the name had been divided or shortened, so too in various places the Scripture of God names the holy man according to the increases of divine grace in him. Thus, when he is called Ram, let him be understood as “exalted”; when Abram, as “an exalted father progressing in virtues.” Again, when his faith is set before the nations for their rule, let him be called Abraham, that is, “father of many nations.” This Elihu, then, as it appears, was a righteous man according to the good of nature, and he possessed the spirit of prophecy; but I think not in the same manner or with the same grace as the holy prophets. Hence the Lord himself said of him to holy Job: “Who is this who wraps up judgments in unskilled words?” That is, the prophetic sense is narrated in words of reproach and disordered speech. The Lord does not reject what Elihu says, but he censures the fact that it is spoken by him prematurely. [Col. 0722B]

Concerning this Elihu and those like him, we said at the beginning of this book that even those who had strayed from the true religion made use of the mystery of prophecy, because God also gave them his word so that they might announce future mysteries to human beings. This was especially so that the faith and wonder of the Gentiles might be sustained: those who would not believe our prophets might at least believe their own divine men and seers. We therefore said that this Elihu, who is Balaam, represents the Gentiles opposing Christ, just as the friends of blessed Job represent the heretics. When it says, “The words of Job are ended,” we may understand it as though it said: the divine words have been firmly established and cannot be annulled; they lead those who faithfully believe to the eternal promise. But these people, who dare to examine the righteous and everlasting man through the presumption of invented doctrines, will eventually fall silent in eternal silence. That Elihu is called by two names is not surprising. It is familiar in the divine Scripture: Solomon was called Jedidiah; Moses’ relative was called Jethro and Reuel; and Peter was called Simon. Hence this variety of names often presents no small obscurity to readers. [Col. 0722C]

“But he was angry against Job because he said that he was righteous before God. He was also indignant against his friends because they had not found a reasonable answer but had merely condemned Job.” Elihu therefore waited for Job to speak because the speakers were older. But when he saw that the three could not answer, he became exceedingly angry. “And Elihu, son of Barachel the Buzite, answered and said.” It seems to me that the events we read here took place before those reported in Numbers concerning this same Elihu, or Balaam. This Elihu, then, who says that he waited for Job and his friends to speak, shows that he did what he did out of honor and reverence, yielding to his elders. The words spoken here are now Elihu’s own:

“I am younger in time, but you are older; therefore, with bowed head, I was afraid to declare my opinion to you. For I hoped that greater age would speak, and that a multitude of years would teach wisdom. But, as I see, it is the spirit in human beings, and the inspiration of the Almighty gives understanding. The long-lived are not necessarily wise, nor do the elders understand judgment.” He says that it seems to him rather that human beings are moved by the spirit to whom Almighty God has granted the inspiration of his wisdom. He says this indirectly as a reproach to those mentioned above, as though this good of wisdom had been granted to him alone. It should be noted that here Elihu follows himself through four speeches, as the text of the reading shows. In each of them he attempts either to revise the earlier replies as though with greater learning or to destroy before holy Job the several passages that Job had spoken too harshly. For after an extensive preface, in his first speech he set down these words from holy Job, saying:

“I am pure and immaculate, without sin, and there is no iniquity in me. Because he found complaints against me, he therefore considered me his enemy. He put my feet in fetters and watched all my paths.” [Col. 0723B]

In his second speech he presented Job’s words as follows: “I am righteous, and God has overturned my judgment. In judging me there is falsehood; my arrow is violent, without any sin.” His third speech is as follows, with the same Elihu saying to Job: “He said, ‘You are not pleased with what is right’; that is, he said to God, ‘What does it profit you if I sin?’” The fourth speech of Elihu contains his intention to speak on God’s behalf and to establish God’s righteousness by his works. This he pursues with great sharpness and utmost persistence amid the mysteries of his prophecy, all the way to the end of this fourth speech, and he does not desist.

“Therefore I shall speak; listen to me, and I too shall show you my wisdom. For I waited for your speeches; I heard your prudence until you had disputed with your words. For what is yours has now become manifest to me.” There is no doubt that he says this ironically. Since above he had mockingly called Job’s friends prudent, he follows by making this explicit.

“And while I thought that you were saying something, I paid attention. But, as I see, there is no one among you who can refute Job and answer his words. Do not perhaps say, ‘We have found wisdom; God has cast him down, not man.’ He has said nothing to me, and I shall not answer him according to your words.” They were afraid and did not answer further; they withdrew speech from themselves. “Job,” he says, “had no dispute with me, nor do I attack him, as you do, with the curses of victors and insults.” [Col. 0723D]

“Since I waited and they did not speak, they stood and did not answer further, I too shall answer my part and show my knowledge.” Therefore Elihu says: “I too shall attempt to answer according to my ability, and I shall show you my knowledge, and Job as well.” It is sufficiently apparent that he says this out of boastful vanity, when he adds:

“For I am full of words, and the spirit of my belly constrains me. Behold, my belly is like wine without a vent, which bursts new wineskins. I shall speak and breathe for a little while; I shall open my lips and answer.” In the anagogical, catachrestic sense (καταχριστῷ), he called his belly, or womb, his very memory, because he had gathered within the capacity of his memory almost all the words of Job and his friends, who had been disputing for some time, as though they were food. [Col. 0724A]

“I shall not accept the person of a man, nor equate God with man. For I do not know how long I shall remain, and presently my Maker may take me away.” “This,” he says, “is the judgment of my just judgment: neither to spare man by withholding the truth nor to wrong God by claiming that he has done something unjustly.”

## CHAPTER XXXIII

“Therefore, Job, hear my speeches, and listen to all my words. Behold, I have opened my mouth; let my tongue speak in my throat. My words shall speak from the simplicity of my heart, and my lips shall utter a pure judgment.” The Lord therefore looks down upon Elihu when he says of him, “Who is this?” For it was unworthy and out of order that a great man, pleasing to God—even if, as a human being, he had sinned in some respect—should be rebuked by one who was far from the true religion. But if anyone is perhaps troubled because this Elihu foretold many things that were to occur in the times of the Savior, so that we may receive them as prophecy, let whoever is troubled by this know that those things which were foretold by the Spirit of God are to be accepted and believed by us. But those things drawn from the arrogance of his heart are to be rejected, because he spoke from his own concerns, like the devil, not from God.

“The Spirit of God made me, and the breath of the Almighty gave me life.” To give authority to his being heard, he spoke in this way, as though one who had been made by the Spirit of God and animated by the breath of the Almighty could not fail to speak what was right and true. Here we must understand the Trinity in God: in “God,” the Father; in “the Almighty,” the Son; and in “the Spirit,” the Holy Spirit. For the triune God created all things. But when he made the human being, he wished to manifest himself through a particular and special signification of names, by naming the diversity of his works, as the Lawgiver says: “And God created the human being; in the image of God he created him; male and female he made them.” Likewise: “And God made the human being from the clay of the earth. And he breathed into his face the breath of life, and the human being became a living soul.” In the one who creates, breathes, and also blesses, we must perceive the Trinity at work, without any distinction or discord of will. For the words “created,” “breathed,” and “blessed” do not signify anything different or lead us to understand anything divergent; according to the unity of nature, there is one will and one common work.

If you can, answer me, and stand before my face: behold, God made me just as he made you, and I too was formed from the same clay. Nevertheless, let my wonder not terrify you, and let my eloquence not weigh heavily upon you. About to bring forth his words, he demands a response, so that, under a kind of flattery and feigned consolation, he might also instill the terror of threats, whereby Job, thrown into confusion, might easily yield to his loquacity.

You have spoken in my ears, and I have heard the voice of your words: “I am clean, and without guilt, blameless, and there is no iniquity in me.” Therefore, when Elihu [Col. 0725A] says to Job, “This, then, is the matter in which you have not been justified,” that is, you ought to have accused yourself, not praised yourself. You ought not to have said, “I am clean, without sin and blameless; there is no iniquity in me.” This, I say, is the matter in which you have not been justified, because justification is acquired through humility. Praise, however, born of exaltation, deserves condemnation. As a just man, and one with a good conscience regarding his holy deeds, Job could indeed have said some things that were true to God with confidence; yet he could not, like a sacrilegious man, have spoken the things Elihu falsely attributes to him. Finally, the words which Elihu says Job spoke are these:

“Because he found complaints against me, he therefore considered me his enemy. He put my feet in the stocks; he guarded all my paths. This, then, is the matter in which you have not been justified.” [Col. 0725B] We do not read that Job said these things. Elihu composed them here in his own words, as though they had been spoken from Job’s mind and uttered by holy Job. Therefore, let us recognize that Elihu himself is not speaking correctly, rather than believe that holy Job said these things.

I will answer you, because God is greater than man. You contend against him because he has not answered you concerning every word. God speaks once, and does not repeat the same thing a second time. In a dream, in a nocturnal vision, when sleep falls upon men and they sleep in their beds, then he opens the ears of men and, instructing them, teaches them discipline, so that he may turn a man away from the things he has done and deliver him from pride, rescuing his soul from corruption and his life from passing into the sword. From the very beginning of the world and ever afterward, God has always spoken to human beings [Col. 0725C], and nevertheless he speaks once; but when God is said to speak frequently, either the multiplicity of his law or the diversity of his prophets and commandments is indicated. When, however, he is said to speak once, his settled and definitive judgment is shown. For God’s speaking is understood as the effect of his action. “God speaks once, and does not repeat the same thing a second time”—that is, God does not change it, unless a change in our life should demand this very thing. In this passage Elihu carefully describes two degrees of correction and says that divine instruction, or chastisement, occurs in relation to a human being both in visions of the night and likewise in bed. Hence he says: “Let him cause the man to waste away until he reaches the extremities of this life.” And when some holy person has intervened on his behalf, as Isaiah did for King Hezekiah [Col. 0725D], let him be restored to his former health. In what follows, Elihu says that this operates upon a human being three times—that is, evidently, plausibly, and in a confirmatory manner—or because of the perfection of the number three, or because of the truth of the three witnesses. In this way also he signifies God’s patience and clemency, since he chastises and reproves the sinner not immediately but gradually and in stages; and in this God is charged neither with a judgment that disregards the commands of truth, nor with an unprofitable leniency, nor with the iniquity of injustice.

He also reproves him through pain in bed, and makes all his bones waste away. Bread becomes abhorrent to him in his life, and food that was formerly desirable to his soul. His flesh wastes away, and the bones that had been covered are laid bare. [Col. 0726A] His soul will draw near to corruption, and his life to things that bring death. If there should be for him an angel, one among the similar ones, speaking to announce the man’s uprightness, he will have mercy on him and say: “Deliver him, so that he may not descend into corruption. I have found a means by which I may be merciful to him.” Or, as others have said: “His soul has drawn near to death, and he makes all his limbs waste away.” Therefore, when a man, corrected and consumed by these things, has drawn near to death and to the ministers of hell, if there is some one of the saints who deserves to bear the name of a holy angel, he may intercede for one who is being chastised by God in this way for his sins—provided that, among the many good works which he ought to have performed, he has been able to find at least one good work of his which he may offer to God on his behalf as an acceptable sacrifice. [Col. 0726B] “He will hear,” he says, “and will command that the person mentioned above not descend into the correction of infernal torments,” because he was a certain great man whose prayers God could not fail to hear. And any angel from heaven standing before the face of God can intercede for any sinner placed under the scourges of chastisement. For God has especially entrusted them with the care of bringing the help of their protection or guardianship to different people or nations. Concerning them the Apostle says: “Are they not all ministering spirits sent out for service, for the sake of those who are to receive the inheritance of salvation?”

We retain in the divine Scriptures examples of the present matters about which we are now speaking. There we read that human beings were chastised in dreams: Nebuchadnezzar, the exceedingly proud king [Col. 0726C]; Laban, who was planning the destruction of his kinsman Jacob; King Abimelech, who attempted to defile the house of holy Abraham; and Pilate’s wife, who said to him concerning our Lord Jesus Christ: “Have nothing to do with that just man, for I have suffered many things in a dream because of him.” The Magi in the Gospel, too, warned in a dream, departed by another way. Faithful men are also instructed by God in dreams, as was the patriarch Jacob. We read as well that others were made ill on account of their sins; among them was the paralytic, of whom we learn that he had been so afflicted and to whom the Lord said: “Your sins are forgiven you.” We also read that holy men were sick, such as Trophimus and Epaphroditus. We should certainly believe that they were examined by such chastisement as just men, not scourged by the blow of infirmity as sinners. [Col. 0726D] It follows:

“His flesh has been consumed by punishments; let him return to the days of his youth.” He has received, he says, evils according to his merits, and the measure of punishments and penalties. Let these scourges of chastisement, by which he has been recalled to correction, be sufficient for him. Now, through the indulgence of divine mercy, let him return to the days of his youth—that is, let him again be healthy and unharmed.

“He will entreat God, and he will be favorable to him; he will see his face with rejoicing, and he will restore his righteousness to man.” This occurs meanwhile in the heart, when a good conscience is possessed through God. He will see God’s face, perceiving that his countenance is favorable toward him, and he will restore righteousness to him by an appropriate satisfaction.

[Col. 0727A] “He will look upon men and say: ‘I have sinned, and truly I have transgressed, and I have not received what I deserved.’” It is a great thing, and exceedingly acceptable to God, when a person is not ashamed to confess his errors—especially if he understands that he is being chastised for them and humbles himself in such a way that, whatever chastisement he has endured, he declares that he has suffered little in comparison with his merits.

“He delivered his soul, so that it would not go into destruction, but, living, would see the light.” Behold, God does all these things three times for each person, to recall their souls from corruption and illuminate them with the light of the living. That is, having been enlightened, the person would recognize the light of the knowledge of God and his immeasurable benefits.

“Pay attention, Job, and listen to me, and be silent while I speak. But if you have something to say, answer me. Speak, [Col. 0727B] for I wish you to appear just. But if you do not, listen to me: be silent, and I will teach you wisdom.” As though by this reasoning Elihu had convicted holy Job, he says to him: “Listen to me”—that is, be obedient to your teacher and give your assent. When he orders him to be silent, he commands a man who is eloquent yet, as it were, less instructed or impatient, to keep quiet.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

Thus Elihu, declaring his judgment, spoke these things also. Elihu is said, as it were, to pronounce a judgment, and he encourages the friends present with holy Job to listen to him.

“Hear my words, you wise men, and listen to me, you learned. For the ear tests words, and the throat distinguishes foods by taste.” Therefore, he says, just as flavor is discerned by the throat from foods [Col. 0727C], and for this reason Elihu says:

“Let us choose judgment for ourselves, and among ourselves let us see what is better.” That is, let us first examine the matter before we condemn the man.

“Because Job said: ‘I am just.’” Job did not speak this sentence; but when he made known the virtues of his righteousness, he undoubtedly showed himself to be just—he whom the Lord had already called just. What is said here is:

“And God has perverted my judgment. In judging me there is falsehood, and my arrow is violent, without any sin.” We likewise do not read this very wording, but we have it written: “As God lives, who has taken away my judgment.” To pervert judgment refers to the injustice of the judge; but to take away judgment—that is, to defer it for a time—belongs to the dispensation of a just judge. “And he has multiplied my wounds even without cause.” Therefore, since Elihu asserts this here, the sense appears to be that when Job said, “He has deceived my judgment; he has not judged rightly and truly,” he was saying, “Therefore I am being treated deceitfully.” Yet Job’s words should be understood as having been spoken rather incautiously and presumptuously, relying upon God’s justice. Accordingly, God justly and deservedly says to him: “Indeed, the one who argues with God must answer him”—words in which God reproves him. This is consistent with the fact that blessed Job did not speak certain things correctly; but God, who knew very well that Job possessed many good qualities, and who had therefore been pleased with him, allows what pain in his extreme distress compelled him to say immoderately.

[Col. 0728A] “What man is like Job, who drinks mockery as water, who walks with those who work iniquity and goes about with wicked men?” His inward parts are filled, as with an abundance of water, with the poison of this suffering.

For he said: “A man will not please God, even if he runs with him.” Elihu falsely claims that Job spoke of him out of envy, for we do not believe that blessed Job held such an unhappy opinion, nor do we remember that he said this anywhere.

“Therefore, men of understanding, hear me: far be impiety from God, and iniquity from the Almighty. For he will repay a man according to his work, and according to the ways of each he will restore to them. Truly God will not condemn without cause, nor will the Almighty pervert judgment.” It is as though he had exposed the impiety of holy Job and, in the midst of his hearers, brought it forward to make Job odious, as though he had spoken impiously. [Col. 0728B]

“Whom has he appointed as another over the earth? Or whom has he placed over the world that he fashioned?” That is, has he perhaps appointed another ruler who would diverge from the Creator’s justice? Therefore, as he is a powerful Creator, so he is a loving governor, because he recognizes and loves his work.

“If he should set his heart upon him, he will draw his spirit and breath to himself. All flesh will fail together, and man will return to ashes.” That is, he speaks of the world. For if God wished to regard all the things that take place in it each day according to the rule of his justice, it would fail and perish; but he governs and sustains it rather with compassion. For if he were to observe iniquity, who could endure it? By “spirit” [Col. 0728C] he means the soul, which gives life to man; and by “breath,” the present life itself, which is supplied to our bodies through breathing from this air. Thus Elihu says that God draws these to himself when he takes away from human beings the life he had given them by creating them.

Through the spirit of prophecy these passages can also be understood as figurative, so that they are now fulfilled in Christ. When, through the dispensation of the flesh he assumed, the Father directed his very Son—through whom he made all things—from his own heart, as though cast forth into this world, so that he might draw his spirit and breath back to himself; that is, so that through the humility of the cross he might take away from him the spirit, namely, the pride of the worldly spirit, and also the breath of swelling eloquence, by which he exulted while breathing out his boasts in his speeches. In this way, too, man would fail once his swelling had been restrained; and, returning [Col. 0728D] to himself, he would recognize that he is earth and ashes. Here, according to the moral interpretation, we understand that verse from the Psalm: “You take away their spirit, and they fail, and they return to their earth.”

After Elihu had spoken about God’s power and justice in the foregoing passage, he turns again to Job and says:

“If you have understanding, then hear what is said, and listen to the voice of my eloquence. Can one who does not love judgment be healed? And do you so greatly condemn the one who is just, who says to a king, ‘Apostate,’ and calls rulers impious?” It is clear, he says, that one who does not love judging justly and rightly can neither heal a soul from its vices nor correct anyone. How, then, are you a healer of our illnesses, when you presume to point out iniquities? [Col. 0729A]

“He does not accept the persons of princes, nor does he recognize the tyrant when he argues against the poor. For all of them are the work of his hands.” According to the mystical interpretation, these princes can be understood as the Jews, the scribes, the Pharisees, and the priests whom he rebukes in the Gospel. We should understand the tyrant, not inappropriately, as that same Jewish people, which today argues against the assembly of the saints of the Church—the poor, humble in spirit, contrite in heart—by rejecting them. Nor did it cease doing this in the time of the apostles, when it stirred up battles and seditions against them throughout all the cities. The Lord will not recognize these people as unbelieving and impious; to them he will also plainly say: “I do not know you; depart from me, all you who work iniquity.” Elihu continues, speaking about those of whom he said above:

“They will die suddenly, and in the middle of the night.” According to the Apostle’s meaning, this is said of the sons of darkness. For when they say, “Peace and security,” sudden destruction will come upon them. I think “the middle of the night” is mentioned because, placed in the deep blindness of their hearts, they die spiritually.

“The peoples will be shaken and will pass away, and he will remove the violent man without a hand. For his eyes are upon the ways of men, and he considers all their steps.” According to the Psalmist: “When the righteous man sees the vengeance upon the wicked,” that is, fearing the example of sinful men, “he will wash his hands in the blood of the sinner.” In this way, then, the peoples will be shaken—by that disturbance through which we read that the sensible earth was shaken, as the prophet says to God: “You have moved the earth and troubled it; heal its fractures, for it has been shaken.” Thus, like good travelers, they will pass through to the world to come, where there will be no place for the impious. Otherwise, the violent man will have no help by which he may be defended or rescued from those dragging him away to the punishment of death.

“There are no darknesses, and there is no shadow of death, in which those who work iniquity may be hidden.” Or, as others have said at the end of this verse: “So that those who commit iniquity may lie concealed.” Both readings accord with the sense of the Psalmist, who says: “Where shall I go from your spirit, and where shall I flee from your face?”

[Col. 0729D] “For it is no longer in a man’s power to come to God for judgment.” That is, if it is in his power to come, it can also be in his power not to come.

“He will crush many, both innumerable ones, and he will make others stand in their place.” For example, Eli the priest and Samuel; Saul and David; the people of the Jews and the nations.

“For he knows their works, and therefore he will bring night, and they will be crushed.” It is as though he struck the impious in the place of those who see. Under these words Elihu could also have signified that, on account of their merits, the Jews would be blinded by the night of unbelief, so that they might be crushed and humbled, as the prophet and the Apostle say: “God gave them a spirit of compunction.”

“They have withdrawn from him as though deliberately, and they have not wished to understand all his ways, so that they might cause the cry of the needy to reach him [Col. 0730A], and that he might hear the voice of the poor.” All sinners and impious people act against the good of nature implanted in them, as the Apostle says: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God.” But where did they know God, except through the inspiration and judgment of the mind? Where, then, did they hold his glory in contempt? Where did they withdraw from it against their conscience, and refuse to know and understand all the ways of God’s commandments, which they possess as innate in their hearts, when they also acted so impiously and unjustly toward human beings that the cry of the oppressed poor ascended to God?

Or, God struck the impious and unbelieving Jews in the place of those who see—that is, in the Mosaic Law—where the prophets, who are called “those who see,” dwell. In that very hope of the Law and arrangement of the promises, as in a certain place of those who see, they were justly struck by God, to such an extent that the prayer of the one who, although rich, became poor for our sake ascended to God: “Scatter them by your power.”

Or, all those who live by faith in Christ are “the living.” For, placed in this hope, they contemplate future blessedness with the mind. In this place, then, where they stand, as it were, by faith, certain people under the name of faith possess the appearance of piety but deny its power. These very people, who are understood as heretics, standing wrongly in the place of God, are struck by God, while the apostles and teachers of the Churches—that is, the poor of Christ—resist them and cry out to God on their behalf.

“For when he grants peace, who is there that can condemn?” [Col. 0730C] The prophet says to the people: “Pray for the life of Nebuchadnezzar, so that there may be peace for you through his peace.” Or, he himself grants peace and tranquility to the Church when the struggles of persecutions do not rise up against it, or when the disputes and scandals of heretics come to rest. Against the battles of vices also, he himself grants the silence of rest and peace, when, after they have been conquered and vanquished like fierce enemies, the highest peace of virtues is established in a person.

But when he says:

“Since he has hidden his face, who is there that can behold him? Both over nations and over all human beings,” this is the meaning: unless he himself deigns to reveal himself to a human being, who is there who can, by his own strength, behold him or approach his majesty by searching it out?

[Col. 0730D] “Who makes a hypocritical man reign on account of the sins of the people.” This plainly appeared in King Saul, and as the Lord says: “I will remove from Jerusalem judge and prophet and wise man and counselor; and I will make their children rulers, and the effeminate will dominate them.” Nebuchadnezzar, too, by the just judgment of God, received many kingdoms and very numerous nations.

This man can also be understood as the devil, who, having lost his angelic dignity, acquired the name of “man.” Concerning him the Lord says in the Gospel: “An enemy has done this.” He is called a hypocrite and pretender because he transforms himself into an angel of light, although he himself is rather the author of darkness—that is, the inventor of every crime and sin.

[Col. 0731A] “Because I have spoken to God, I will not restrain you either.” As though Job had been placed in a court of judgment, Elihu permits him to speak in turn, so that, if he has something to say, he may not remain silent.

“If I have erred, teach me. If I have spoken iniquity, I will not add any more.” That is, I will not speak further.

“Does God demand this from you because it displeased you? For you began to speak, and not I. But if you know anything better, speak.” You said that God was unjust, because he demanded from you, through an unjust correction, the iniquity and injustice of your life; and because, being unjustly afflicted, you were compelled to speak unjustly against him. Therefore, he says, God displeased you, since you do not wish the justice by which he punishes you, though innocent, to be true justice.

“Let men of understanding speak to me, and let a wise man hear me.” [Col. 0731B] Elihu, despising holy Job, turns to those who were standing nearby and, pronouncing this judgment about blessed Job, says to them:

“Job has spoken foolishly, and his words do not sound like discipline.” This is clear.

“My father.” Because man was created and fashioned by him. “Let Job be tested,” Elihu says; “let him not be examined”—which is ordinarily said with reference to testing one’s learning.

“Let Job be tested.” That is, let him be revealed; let it be proved to all, and let it be clear to everyone, what sort of man Job is. Let Job, I say, be tested before you.

“To the end. Do not cease from the man of iniquity.” That is, let the wound of this scourge continually remain in him; do not cease to inflict punishments upon those who work iniquity.

[Col. 0731C] “Who has added blasphemy to his sins.” That is, in addition to being a sinner, he adds to the heap of his sins, so that he breaks out into the crime of blasphemy, on account of which he endures these evils and torments.

“Meanwhile, let him be confined among us, and then let him challenge God to judgment with his words.” Let him meanwhile be condemned among us, so that this may not also be reckoned to us as injustice. We shall be free from guilt if afterward he attempts to challenge God.

## CHAPTER XXXV

Thus Elihu spoke again:

“Does your thought seem right to you, when you say: ‘I am more righteous than God’? For you have said: ‘What is right does not please you; or what will it profit you if I sin?’” It is possible that, from the words in which Job spoke somewhat harshly to God, more harshly perhaps than he ought to have done, Elihu has recorded something here [Col. 0731D], and, out of envy, wished to present the sense of his own words as though it were Job’s.

“Therefore I will answer your words, and your friends along with you.” This is because they were unable to answer him rationally.

“Look toward heaven, and behold, and contemplate the sky, which is higher than you.” That is, whom do you presume to make yourself equal to? Elihu says this because he thought that God was physically contained in places, and that the Lord God dwelt only in lofty and exalted regions.

“Therefore, if you sin, what harm will you do him? And if your iniquities are multiplied, what will you do against him?” It seems to me that he said this in the following sense: when you sin, no loss is inflicted upon God; or, if he wishes to punish you for the multitude [Col. 0732A] of your sins, will you be able to oppose him?

“But if you act justly, what will you give him, or what will he receive from your hand?” From this David says that God has no need of my good things.

“Your impiety will harm a man who is like you, and your righteousness will help a son of man.” That is, your impiety can harm a man if he imitates you while you act wickedly, just as your righteousness will help a son of man if he imitates your ways when you walk rightly.

“Because of the multitude of oppressors they will cry out, and because of the violence of tyrants they will lament.” In this form of argument, Elihu associates holy Job with such people and judges him to be like them, when he calls the oppressors [Col. 0732B] and tyrants wicked men, by whose slanders and power man and the son of man, being oppressed, groan. In a spiritual sense, we may not improperly understand this man and son of man as the holy people, who, because of the unity of the entire body of the Church, are called one man, as the Apostle says, and, according to the Psalmist, are called the son of man, who says: “Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand, and upon the son of man whom you strengthened for yourself.” This can also be said of invisible enemies, who rule over minds through the hidden assault of vices. For this reason the faithful, lamenting in prayer to God, say: “Deliver me from my enemies, my God.”

“And he did not say.” When the aforementioned wicked people were afflicting those whom, with God’s permission, [Col. 0732C] they had subjected to themselves through unjust domination, so that these people, placed under such great pressure and distress, lamented and cried out to God, the wicked did not pay attention, nor did they direct their minds toward heaven, so as to understand that all these things displeased God their Creator. This multitude of the wicked—or of demons—did not, I say, say such things to itself.

“Where is God who made me, who gives songs in the night?” Elihu says this. Therefore, although God permits the just and those who live rightly to be afflicted by the people mentioned above, he nevertheless grants them consolation during the night of their tribulations. For the night itself is understood as tribulation, according to the Psalmist: “You tested my heart and visited me in the night.” Prosperity, likewise, is sometimes called day, because the one who is prosperous is illuminated, as it were, by a certain happiness. Hence he says in the Psalm: “The sun [Col. 0732D] will not burn you by day, nor the moon by night.”

Elihu says: Just men receive such great endurance from God that even in the night of tribulation they delight in the songs of spiritual hymns. A song, therefore, belongs above all to the exultation of the heart. This exultation is born in the hearts of those who sing from the hope of future joy, and they act like travelers, because they pass through this world as travelers and pilgrims. In order to reach the place appointed for them without weariness, they console and lighten the fatigue of their journey with song.

According to the mystical interpretations, let us understand “night” as a certain secret and remote silence of divine discourse, which, as the Apostle says, “was not revealed to the sons of men” in other ages. This night is divided into four watches. [Col. 0733A] Thus, from the beginning of the world to Christ our Lord, we may call this period a night. Its first watch is Adam himself, the first man and father of humanity; through his creation the human mind awakens to believe that God is the Creator of all things. The second watch belongs to the time of Noah, when the shipwreck of the world took place, so that human beings might awaken and not perish themselves. The third watch is assigned to the times of holy Abraham, through whom the world learns how one must live by faith and please God. The fourth watch is around the time of the prophets, who were nearer to the dawn and the approaching light of day, and who, with the eyes of faith, looked toward Christ himself, the day almost already present to them.

In this night, therefore, throughout the successive [Col. 0733B] ages of the persons mentioned above, whether through prophecies or through signs, things concerning Christ—joyful and filled with gladness—were foretold. Likewise, in comparison with the future revelation of the sons of God, when they will receive the glory of that eternal day and possess blessedness in reality, the present life is night. Its fruits are hidden for the future, and it is still night because you do not yet see what you hope for. Therefore, in this night of expectation, the hymns and songs of the Scriptures have been spoken for us, until, when the night of faith has been dispelled, we reach the day of our eternal dwelling.

“Who teaches us more than the beasts of the earth, and instructs us beyond the birds of heaven.” He teaches the learned in ordinary matters through subtler things; he teaches not only through the gifts of nature but also through the gifts of grace. According to the figurative interpretation [Col. 0733C], beasts generally signify carnal people, who are devoted to gluttony, the belly, and luxury. Others are compared to flying creatures, either because of the lightness of their morals or because of the pride by which, swollen with arrogance, they are lifted up as though into the heights. Hence the Apostle says: “Do not set your mind on high things.” And the Lord says in the Gospel: “What is exalted among human beings is an abomination before God.” In Greek, a proud person is called ὑπερήφανος (*hyperēphanos*), which means “appearing above,” signifying a human mind that is exalted and swollen.

“There they will cry out, and he will not hear, because of the pride of the wicked.” By saying “there they will cry out,” he may perhaps have intended to signify the place of punishments, where sinners will not be heard because of the pride of the wicked. Or, as others have said, “because of the injuries of the wicked,” since the wicked do not cease inflicting the injuries of persecution upon the good and the just.

[Col. 0733D] “Therefore God will not hear in vain, and the Almighty will regard the causes of each.” He says that God does not hear sinners who persist in their evils, because they cry out to him without cause, since they do not deserve to be heard.

“Even when you say, ‘He does not consider it,’ judge before him and wait for him.” When you see, Job, that God does not immediately repay sinners what they deserve, do not be broken by faintheartedness so that you burst into blasphemy and call God unjust or iniquitous. Rather, you must judge together with him—that is, consent to his judgments—and not rush against him with your presumptuous judgment, to his injury.

[Col. 0734A] “For now he does not bring on his fury, nor does he take vengeance very severely.” Since he has appointed a day on which he will judge the inhabited world, therefore at the present time he does not exercise the vengeance of his justice universally. He says all this as a reproach to holy Job, whom, as though guilty of crimes, God’s judgment condemns in part to this evil of punishments. Hence he writes that much remains for him, which he will afterward receive.

“Therefore Job opens his mouth in vain and multiplies words without knowledge.” In accordance with these statements, Elihu considers holy Job convicted and, by a certain reasoning of words, trapped.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

Elihu added and spoke these things:

“Wait for me [Col. 0734B] a little, and I will show you. For I still have something to say on behalf of God.” That is, on behalf of God’s justice and cause.

“I will repeat my knowledge from the beginning, and I will prove my Maker just. For my speech is truly without falsehood, and perfect knowledge will be made manifest to you.” In this fourth speech of his, he pursues at great length, and with abundant discourse, the singular justice of the Lord. Here he seems to speak of many hidden matters stored away in the obscurity of mysteries, and of mysteries far removed from ordinary understanding.

“God does not reject the powerful, since he himself is powerful; but he does not save the impious.” This is the immensity of his justice and the goodwill of his good nature: he envies no one, because no one, however powerful he may be, can be equal to him.

“And he grants judgment to the poor,” according to the tenor of his just equity [Col. 0734C]. Divine Scripture customarily calls holy and innocent men “the poor.”

“He does not take his eyes away from the just.” Blessed David says the same: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the just,” and so forth.

“And he places kings upon the throne forever, and they are raised up there.” Here “kings” can signify not only the kings of this world but also the kings and superiors of the Church. According to the figurative interpretations, kings are the human minds that rightly rule their bodies. To them it is said in the Psalm: “And now, O kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth.” Thus these kings are raised up by God, so that they may sit with princes.

“And if they are in chains and are bound with ropes of poverty, he will declare to them their works and their crimes, because they were violent.” These people, therefore, are bound with strong chains—namely, the chains of God’s judgment—and with ropes of poverty; that is, lacking the help of divine assistance, they will be fastened by temporal punishments as by bonds, having been made poor in every good thing according to the quality of their merits.

[Col. 0734D] “He will also open their ear, to correct them, and he will speak so that they may turn back from iniquity.” God, he says, will open the ear of their heart for obedience to him through chastisements and secret inspirations.

“If they hear and observe, they will complete their days in goodness and their years in glory.” This is what Solomon says: “The memory of the just is with praises.”

“But if they do not hear, they will pass through the sword and be consumed in folly.” That is, if they despise listening when God, [Col. 0735A] who teaches man knowledge, instructs them, they will pass from this world through the sword—that is, through this mortality—so that in folly, namely, in those places where fools will be counted, who say in their hearts, “There is no God,” they may be consumed by eternal torments.

“Hypocrites and crafty men provoke the wrath of God, and they will not cry out when they have been bound.” Here Elihu seems to strike holy Job more openly, as though indirectly, alleging that he himself acted craftily and wickedly and pretended to be an excellent man. Even when he was bound by the fetters of this scourge, he would not trouble himself to cry out to God and invoke him, so that he might be released from the punitive snares with which he was bound. He would do this, certainly, either from despair or from contempt.

[Col. 0735B] This may similarly be understood of other sinners, who, when they have entered the depths of evils, will despise correction; and of the Jews and heretics, who, covering fabricated doctrines with a veil of truth, persist with stubborn and hardened hearts in the faithlessness of night.

“Their soul will die in the storm, and their life among the effeminate.” We should understand these as vices and vicious people. Just as the passions possess nothing quiet, manly, or disciplined from the virtues of the soul, but everything turbulent, lax, and fragile, so they must always disturb the soul with their allurements like a storm. They do not allow a person to reach the harbor of the virtues, and what Solomon says occurs amid such waves: the soul lies as though in the heart of the sea, like a helmsman in a great storm.

Or, alternatively, the storm is the coming and judgment of God, of which he says: “Around him there is a mighty storm.”

[Col. 0735C] “He will rescue the poor man from his distress.” By “the poor man” we understand our Savior, who became poor for our sake and who, in the days of his flesh, offered prayers and supplications to the Father, so that he might save the poor man from death: the holy people of God, humble in spirit. Or he will rescue any just poor man from the distress of afflictions, just as we also read in various ways in the divine Scriptures that people have been delivered.

“And he will reveal his ear to him in tribulation.” That is, let each of them be strong in tribulation. When a human being is permitted by God to be afflicted, and divine visitation gives him strength, he will receive consolation by hearing the Lord in the ear of his heart there.

[Col. 0735D] “Therefore he will save you from the narrow mouth, beneath which there is no foundation.” In this passage Heliu describes the dwellings of hell, which, because of their immeasurable vastness, have no foundation. Yet concerning their foundations we read in the prophets that Lucifer, who rose at dawn, was cast down there, together with multitudes of kings and innumerable peoples of the nations. Hell is called “narrow-mouthed” because it is wide for receiving but narrow for releasing, since it holds the dead within itself and does not permit them to emerge into life. Holy David likewise says to God: “Deliver me from those who hate me, and from the depths of the waters. Let not the storm of water overwhelm me, nor let the deep swallow me; let not the pit close its mouth over me.” Therefore we should understand that, according to the testimony of Scripture, the places of the infernal prisons are established amid the immeasurable waters of the abyss. From those seats of hell no human being has been freed by his own merit, except by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. And, says Heliu, you will not merely be freed from the narrow places of Tartarus; you will also walk freely, as though through spacious fields, in the broadest grove of refreshment.

“But the rest of your table will be full of fatness.” By calling it “rest,” he signifies the pleasantness of paradise and its delight. He wished to demonstrate the immense abundance of the blessed life, which would be full of the richness of fertility and filled with the delights of that happy place, whose holy land the meek will possess according to the Lord’s promise.

“Your cause was judged as that of an impious man; you will receive cause and judgment.” By God’s judgment you were found impious, guilty, and liable to punishment; therefore, according to the merit of your case, you received a most severe judgment. Where it says, “You will receive judgment and sentence,” some have said that this refers to the impiety of the gifts they were accepting; by the plural form of the expression, Heliu appears here to be attacking holy Job in his speech.

“Therefore, do not let anger overcome you, so that you oppress anyone; nor let the multitude of gifts incline you.” Heliu teaches that the man of patience and integrity is exceedingly strong in virtue. The best judge is one who is not held by those two most evil vices, anger and greed; it is for these that Heliu accuses and rebukes the holy man in this passage.

[Col. 0736C] “Lay aside your greatness without tribulation, and all those strong in strength.” That is: do not oppress either the small or the great by your unjust domination; or, lay aside all impulses, strengthened as you are by the strength of pride.

“Do not prolong the night, so that peoples may rise up against them.” It is already enough to have lived until now in this blindness. Strive now to come to the light of prudence and justice. Or understand the night as that which you have woven for yourself from various sins, so that you might walk in it as in continuous, unbroken, and perpetual darkness. “I beg you,” he says, “do not prolong it any further; do not, as though making a rope by adding sins to sins, take pleasure in extending it at length. By the light of this correction, then, put an end to such sins, for by this prolongation your life will become incorrigible, so that, on account of all your evil deeds, the prayers of the peoples may rise up [Col. 0736D] to God”—the peoples whom you were oppressing with the greatest injustice, and who, appealing against you, would lay before the seat of divine justice the miseries inflicted upon them by you.

“Beware lest you turn aside to iniquity; for after misery you have begun to follow this.” “I ask,” says Heliu, “that you not turn toward despair, and that you now beware of the iniquity of blasphemy, but hasten to return to God. For I see that, after the dreadful misery of this affliction of yours, you wish to follow this ruin of impiety to your destruction, and, cast down by faintheartedness, to direct your will and thought toward the adversary.”

“Behold, God is exalted in his strength, and there is none like him among legislators.” If anyone could be like him in power and strength, he could also be found like him in justice and wisdom, in the multiplication of law, and in his judgments. “Therefore,” he says, “recognize that no one can be unjustly condemned by God, who alone is strong and wise.”

“Who can search out his ways?” Who, indeed, unless he is impious, proud, or sacrilegious, would presume to search out the ways of God’s works? This is not permitted; and even if someone investigates them with every possible exertion of mind, he will not be able to discover them.

“Or who dares say to him: You have acted unjustly?” Who, then, is so rash, wicked, and unjust as to dare say this? All these things are said as an insult against Job.

“Remember that you do not know his work, of which men have sung.” Either this means his whole work in general, or certainly his particular work. Above all his great and wondrous works stands the mystery of Christ’s dispensation, which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man.” Others have said: “Remember that his works are great, which men have praised.” He speaks of all God’s works, which holy men rightly praised in honor of divine worship.

“All human beings see him; each one beholds him from afar.” Through the goodness of nature, knowledge of the Creator is present in human hearts. Although someone may be so insignificant and cold that he strives to be alienated from his Creator, God, nevertheless no one hides from his warmth. Therefore each mortal, even from afar, senses and understands him—though in an altogether different way. For one does not sense or understand that God exists as a body, or like any created spirit, but in another, far different, and ineffable manner, by which God is to be contemplated with the mind’s eye. In that very act of the heart’s contemplation, by understanding, a person sees that the divine name he strives to contemplate is above him.

“Behold, God is great, surpassing our knowledge. The number of his years is beyond calculation.” He surpasses our knowledge by the greatness of his knowledge and the height of his judgments.

“He takes away the drops of rain and pours out showers like torrents.” Let us understand this rain as the Law of Moses, which came from heaven like rain upon the Jewish people. It is called rain because of the multitude of its commandments, just as Moses himself says concerning that same Jewish people: “Let my speech be awaited like rain.” From this rain, then, God took away its drops from that people—whether concerning the incarnation, passion, or resurrection of Christ, which the Jews, blinded in heart, refused to believe. These are the small legal commandments, which he transferred to faith in the Gospel, as the Apostle says: “For the word, consummating and shortening in iniquity,” and so forth. From these drops and small droplets, while the Gospel thundered, the showers of Christ’s preaching were poured over the earth. These showers are said to be like torrents because, when they descend abundantly upon the earth, they contain within themselves the depth and obscurity of the mysteries that were expressed or enacted in the Law and the prophets through figures and likenesses. At the revelation of the Lord’s coming, they were found to be like closed signs, obscure in themselves and profound in their mysteries. By the name “showers,” we should understand the grace of the Holy Spirit poured out abundantly, as the Apostle says: “Through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ.”

“They flow from the clouds, which cover everything above.” We know that in Scripture the saints are often called clouds, as is clear in the passage where the Lord says: “I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon her”—that is, upon the vineyard, which means upon the sinful Jewish people—so that they would not pour out upon it the rain of salvation through their words. From such clouds, namely the apostles and apostolic men, preachers of the truth, those showers rain down a rain that contains the likeness of torrents because of the obscurity of heavenly secrets. Hence the saying of David applies aptly: “Dark water is in the clouds of the air.” These clouds, then, through which showers like torrents flow upon the earth, “cover everything above.” Since they contain within themselves the waters of the Gospel, so that living waters may flow from their bellies, they create an obstacle for the carnal and earthly through the higher mysteries, as though by a covering and obscurity of waters.

“If he wishes to spread out the clouds as his tent, and flash with his light, he will also cover the hinges of the sea from above.” He spread out the aforementioned clouds in such a way that through them their sound went out into all the earth and their words to the ends of the inhabited world, just as he later said to his disciples—that is, to his clouds: “You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in Judea and Samaria, and to the very ends of the earth.” Through these clouds, certainly, the flashes of his preaching shone forth, and the fame of Christ’s name flashed from heaven like light. He also occupied the hinges of the sea—that is, of this world. Or we may understand the hinges of the world as the rulers and leaders of the various nations, through whose errors and evil persuasions the world was turning, like a hinge, in the place of superstition and demonic worship.

“Through these he judges the peoples and gives food to many mortals.” Through these foretold sacramental realities, God, by the judgment of his mercy, determined to show pity to all peoples and to give the food of his word’s teaching—or of his mysteries—to all mortals, according to what he himself says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven.”

“In his hands he hides the light and commands it to return.” By the power of his just judgment, he hides the light of knowledge of himself from sinners who do evil, and commands it to come again for the illumination of the mind, if anyone faithfully seeks God as his helper.

“He announces concerning it to his friend that it is his possession, and that he can ascend to it.” By the light of his manifestation, God teaches and instructs his faithful friend in the heart. As he trains him, he also announces that the light—whether that grace of illumination or the love of divine promises—is his possession, and that, if he establishes ascents in his heart, he will reach it by advancing day after day.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

“Therefore my heart trembled.” Or, as others have said, “My heart was stunned.”

“And it was moved from its place.” When the divine mysteries spoken above had been revealed, together with the light of the knowledge of God—which is shown only to God’s friends and faithful ones—“my heart,” says Heliu, “was terrified and, through zeal arising from ignorance, was transferred to the knowledge of the mysteries.”

“Hear the sound in the terror of his voice, and the noise proceeding from his mouth.” In whatever manner God wishes what he says to be heard, hear it thus, because his voice is terrifying, exceedingly powerful through such great mysteries; and hear in the same way the sound of his mouth—or, as others have said, the roar. This, then, is the sound of God’s jaws. Perhaps it is called a “sound,” not simply speech, so that a louder voice might strike the disobedient deaf and those unbelieving in hardened hearts, and move them wholly to fear the Lord.

“He himself regards what is beneath all the heavens, and his light is over the boundaries of the earth.” What is surprising about this concerning the omnipotence of God, who is everywhere—in heaven, on earth, in the sea, and in the abysses? But let us see, according to allegorical understanding, what Heliu means when he says of God: “He regards what is beneath all the heavens.” Divine Scripture is accustomed to call holy men “heavens,” because of their heavenly way of life; to them it is said: “Your citizenship is in heaven.” The Lord, then, regards what is beneath these heavens, either when, as the searcher of secrets, he looks into what is within them, or when he governs and sustains the weakness of their bodies, which they have subjected to the rule of the mind through the power of the cross, and strengthens them against the battles of carnal passions. According to this sense, the prophet, shaken by fear, says: “And beneath me my condition was troubled.”

The boundaries, or ends, of the earth are likewise the saints themselves, because they impose an end upon earthly passions and desires. They are not in the midst of Babylon, nor are they surrounded by the vices of this age, according to what the apostle Peter says: “Christ, therefore, having suffered in the flesh, left us an example, because he who has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sins, so that henceforth, for the remaining time in the flesh, he should live not for human desires but for the will of God.” That is, while living for the appointed time, with sins in the flesh brought to an end, he dwells as though within the boundaries of the flesh. Within these boundaries the queen of Sheba, who prefigured the Church, was placed and deserved to hear the wisdom of the true Solomon. God therefore illuminates such boundaries with the light of his grace and knowledge.
