“After him the sound will roar.” Or, as others have said, “The voice will roar.”

“God will thunder with the voice of his greatness, and his voice will not be investigated when it has been heard.” When God is remembered by people placed at the end of the earth, immediately, groaning over the weakness of their mortality, they will roar toward him, as the prophet says: “I roared from the groaning of my heart.” Then this roaring will make a sound in the affection of prayer, of those crying out to God, which will reach [Col. 0740A] heaven. Hence the Lord will thunder for them with the voice of his commandments, so that they may fear before him. By this crash of thunder, understand at the same time that, before their desire, God is unsearchable and immeasurable.

“God will thunder wondrously with his voice; he who does great and unsearchable things.” Others have said: “God will thunder.” God works wondrously when he causes this thunder of his name—by which knowledge of his fame grows throughout the whole world—to resound in the ears of the soul.

“He commands the snow to descend upon the earth, and the rains of winter, and the shower of his strength.” Above we said that snow could signify the whiteness of grace, through which the gifts of the Holy Spirit are bestowed upon the faithful by baptism, and there we produced many scriptural testimonies as examples. Among them is the saying of David in the psalm: “They will be whitened with snow in Salmon,” which means “in the shadow.” Here, then, he says that the heavenly one—that is, God coming from heaven—will also distinguish and separate kings. Or they are to be whitened in the shadow; and this seems to me to signify that the regeneration of the most ancient peoples would be accomplished in Christ, with the Holy Spirit casting its shadow over them.

This grace, therefore, signified by the name of snow, descends upon the earth at the command of the Godhead—that is, it comes to human beings through Jesus Christ—and through it our old condition is restored to something better. In contrast to Christ’s grace, he wished to indicate the future tribulations of persecutions by the winter rains; and he called them winter rains because of their severe pressures. Yet the shower of the Spirit’s strength would overcome them, because it was said to them: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.”

“He marks in the hand of every human being, so that each may know his own works.” In the hand—that is, in the power of free choice, according to the image and likeness of God in which the human being was formed and created by God—he possesses this wisdom, impressed as though by a sign of divine activity, so that, according to the judgment of free choice, every person may know his own works. Or, as others have said, so that he may know his weakness: that is, so that he may know himself to be a fragile vessel, liable to be shattered by sudden death.

“The beast will enter its hiding place and will remain in its den.” We may reasonably understand this beast as the devil, the inventor of evils. He is called a solitary wild creature because his malice precedes, or surpasses, the malice of all who practice iniquity. This rational beast therefore enters its hiding place, namely the human breast, when, by permission of God’s judgment, it receives power to dominate human beings and establishes for itself a dwelling in the den that it has made its own. Or by the devil’s den, or hiding place, we should understand all sinners: hard, indeed stony, through unbelief, whom he possesses by their vices and enticements, and in whose hearts and crimes he rests.

“From the inner places the storm will go forth, and from Arcturus the cold.” It does not seem to me that he was speaking here about the regions, qualities, or even hidden movements of this world. Rather, just as we said that the den or hiding place of demons is the human heart, so by these inner places we should understand, once they have entered them, their secret and hidden counsels. From there the storms of persecutions are believed to come into this world, so that they may crush sinners, as happened to the Egyptians, upon whom an attack was sent through evil angels. The saints too are greatly disturbed by the same storm of tribulations, as one of them says: “We were burdened beyond our strength, so that we were even weary of living.” Its cold is likewise sent forth—the cold of unbelief—so that, withdrawing from the love of God and the warmth of faith, they fall into the chill of denial. All these things the demons send through the agency of rulers, the decrees of princes, and unbelieving powers. Arcturus, because it is situated on the left side of the world, signifies the opposing party; from that region the cold north wind blows against the south.

“When God blows, the frost thickens, and again the waters are poured out very widely.” What he says here—that when God blows the waters thicken, that is, freeze and become solid—he expresses in the opposite way in the psalm: “He will blow,” he says, “and the waters will flow,” that is, they will be loosened and stream away. But whether here “God blows,” or in the psalm “his Spirit will blow,” we can understand either that God commands or that the Spirit commands. And what he says here, “the frost thickens,” he expresses in the preceding verse of the psalm: “He sends his crystal like pieces of bread.” We know that this happens in winter, when, as God blows—that is, commands—waters become dense or even freeze because of the extreme cold, and are again loosened when the weather changes.

According to mystical understanding, however, in former generations, when God abandoned the human race on account of its merit, and the sentence of his justice flowed from the breath of his mouth, every creature, as it was removed from the divine fire, became solid like frost and was constricted by the immensity of its cold, away from the true knowledge of God. But now, through the grace of our Lord and Savior, as the apostle Peter says, God “overlooking the times of ignorance,” the waters of the peoples are once again released from that chill of forgetfulness and hardness—which had become hardened like the frost of a long age—by the fire of God’s love, so that they may flow and return to God.

“The grain desires the clouds.” This is the grain of which the Lord says in the Gospel by way of a parable: “Gather the weeds into bundles to burn them, but gather the wheat into my barn.” Therefore this living grain desires to hear the teachers of the Church, who, like clouds, carry the waters of the Gospel. So also those who belonged to this grain of the Lord, living in Antioch of Pisidia, asked Paul and Barnabas to speak the word of God to them; and the apostles did so, urging them to remain in the grace of God. Cornelius also said to Peter: “Now therefore we are all present before you, to hear everything that has been commanded you by the Lord.” And Moses says: “Let my speech be received like rain, and let my words descend like dew.” Hence the Apostle says: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.”

This cloud may also be understood as the Lord himself, that is, the assumed human being united to God, as the prophet foretold, saying: “Behold, the Lord descends upon a light cloud into Egypt.” Through him divine grace and heavenly teaching were foretold as being poured out upon the world. And beautifully he is called a “light cloud,” either because the Savior himself, the Lamb of God, committed no sin, or because the virgin Mary, the mother of the Lord, not made heavy by human seed, is called a light cloud.

“And the clouds scatter their light.” They illuminate everything around, wherever the will of the one who governs them leads them, for everything he has commanded them upon the face of the inhabited world. They send forth the light, certainly, through the flashing of Gospel preaching; they scatter the light of the Gospel over the hearts of believers. Other interpreters have said: “And it itself turns around through the steering mechanisms, to perform everything he had commanded them.”

These, then, are the things he commanded and ordered his other clouds, saying: “Go into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every creature.” Therefore, as though driven by the wind of God’s Spirit, by which they were moved like clouds, they were prevented from going to Bithynia, while they were commanded to pass from Judea to Rome; and thus, as the edition states, they traveled around illuminating the whole world.

“Whether in one tribe, or in their own land, or in whatever place he has commanded them to be found by his mercy.” This is what the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in Samaria, and to the very ends of the earth.” Here we must especially note what he says: “In whatever place he has commanded them to be found by his mercy.” By this he signified that, through the grace of Christ and the mercy of his goodness, they were to be recalled to the faith.

“Listen to these things, Job; stand and consider the wonders of God.” Heliu admonishes Job to attend carefully with the ear of his heart to the mysteries destined to be fulfilled in Christ and the Church, and, established in the mirror of his mind—where he is also taught the vigilance of standing and observing—to consider the future mysteries of God’s miracles, which he would accomplish through rational clouds.

“Do you know when God commanded the rains to show the light of his clouds?” In the manner of the prophets, he speaks of future things as though they had already happened. God therefore commands the evangelical rains so that the teachers, his clouds, may demonstrate their light—that is, their holy works—through the infusion of faith; and heavenly mercy accomplishes these things for the illumination of human beings.

[Col. 0742D] “Do you know the great paths of the clouds and their perfect knowledge?” By saying “perfect sciences,” he clearly shows that he is speaking of rational clouds, of the ways of preachers, and of the paths of subtle meanings. Tell me, please: were you able to know which paths in the clouds are great and perfect sciences?

By saying this, he was depicting the apostolic clouds. One of them, a very swift cloud, says to the Savior: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Because it was suspended from the earth and near to heaven, the Lord answers him: “Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father.” Another apostle, like a cloud full of the waters of perfect knowledge, pours out a plentiful rain from the thunder of the Gospel, saying: “In the beginning was the Word,” and so forth. When this most powerful thunder resounded everywhere, so that it might shake the whole earth with trembling toward the faith of religion, another, arising in Judea through a repeated birth, grew like a small cloud and, expanded by the breath of the Spirit, scattered the rains of mysteries hidden from the ages, of perfect knowledge, as far as Illyricum, and watered other regions of the whole world with abundant outpourings. Hence some of them were called “sons of thunder,” while another was called “the son of him who suspends the waters.”

“Are your garments not warm when the earth has been blown through by the south wind?” Others have said: “Is your robe warm?” It is certainly true that the southern wind is warm, and when it blows, even human garments become hot—or the bodies that are the garments of souls. But because the truth of prophecy compels us to understand the clouds as holy human beings, let us understand the warm wind blowing from the south as fervent faith or the burning grace of the Holy Spirit, which illuminates more clearly—or as our Lord himself, of whom we read: “God will come from the south.” When he blows through the rational earth, the powers of the soul, which are the garments of the inner human being, blaze up. They are therefore called garments because those who use them make the soul beautiful and honorable.

For this reason the Apostle exhorts us, saying: “Brothers, clothe yourselves as God’s chosen and beloved ones with compassion, kindness, humility, modesty, patience,” and so forth. These things, then, as well as the others, are spoken by Heliu in the spirit of prophecy.

[Col. 0743C] “Perhaps you fashioned the heavens with him, which are as solid as though cast from bronze.” Literally, these words are spoken by Heliu ironically as an insult against Job. Let this be the initial, surface understanding of what has been said. Now, according to the spirit of prophecy, let us pursue the mystical meaning, so that we may understand the heavens as the holy Scriptures, which were given to human beings from heaven, and whose perpetuity he wished to demonstrate by the solidity of bronze.

But someone may say: How will the divine Scriptures be eternal if the world, as God declares, is to be brought to an end at a fixed time? For he says in the Gospel: “Heaven and earth will pass away.” It is indeed true that the skins of the books, together with the written letters, are to be destroyed. But because the Lord adds, “My words, however, will not pass away,” there can be no doubt that what he promises in those same letters will be eternal.

These heavens, then, says Heliu, in which the secret ordering of divinity is found, you perhaps fashioned with God, as though endowed with a similar wisdom. God, who is eternal, determined these before the foundation of the world to burst forth at some time into the bodies of written letters. They existed eternally in him—not already existing in their own right, but visible only to him in the light of his foreknowledge.

We may also reasonably understand the heavens as the holy angels, who, because of their habitation in heaven, are rightly called heavens and are solidified like bronze by eternity. Concerning them the Psalmist says in the singular: “The heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord.” According to the figurative understanding, all the saints are called heavens because of their heavenly way of life and because of their preaching of heavenly commandments.

If Heliu possessed the spirit of prophecy, he could, according to the understanding we have described, have recognized through contemplation of his mind these things destined to be revealed in Christ, as well as other meanings by which he appears to have understood the designation “heavens,” although this very statement ought not to have been spoken in mockery of holy Job.

“Show us what we should say to him. For we are enveloped in darkness.” The words “show us” are those of one insulting and reproaching. Although he says this, he remains in the darkness of ignorance in comparison with knowledge. For how can he inquire about learning from holy Job, whom he censures and rejects in his words? “Show us,” he says, “O Job, if you think that you know anything more or better, since we are held in the darkness of great ignorance and lack of understanding.” It is therefore certain that Heliu says these things while mocking and deriding Job.

“Who will recount to him what I say? Even if a human being speaks, he will be swallowed up.” “I did tell you, O Job, to show me what I might say; but who has dared to speak to God about these very things that I say concerning him? Certainly, if anyone speaks what is wholly unfitting for him to say, he will be swallowed up for that very sin of rashness and irreverence,” as Heliu says here.

Thus we read in the psalms: “Their judges were swallowed up beside the rock.” This is understood of the judges of the people of Israel in the wilderness, who were swallowed up and absorbed by the sin of unbelief because they did not believe that rivers of water could be brought forth from the rock by the power of the divine promise.

“But now they do not see the light. Suddenly the air will be condensed into clouds, and a passing wind will drive them away.” They have been blinded by such misfortune that they become like the air when it thickens into clouds; and thus, in the just judgment of God, they will be carried away like winds in a gust, like the impious whom the wind casts down from the face of the earth.

Others have said: “But the light that shines in the clouds is not visible to all, and the spirit passes through and drives them away.” Here he has spoken something mystical: the illumination of the Gospel no longer shines for everyone. It does not shine for those whose understanding God has blinded, so that they do not see the light of the Gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of the invisible Father. This spirit of God’s just sentence will drive them away from the assembly of the blessed, so that they will not see the light of the Gospel of Christ’s glory.

“From the north gold will come, and from God a fearful praise.” I have heard someone say that in summer, when the sun rises in the north, the dawn glows more intensely, so that the sun itself displays a golden color. Hence Heliu seems to say that gold comes forth: that is, that the sun’s fiery disk rises over the world, and that, before this brilliant star, there is a praise offered to God by human beings in fear.

We, however, understand the gold as the saints, who, according to the spiritual sense, are redeemed from the north—from the devil—by the blood of the Lord. In this way the assembly of the saints comes to God, praising him with trembling and considering it an incredible thing, with a certain fear, that they were able to be freed from so powerful an enemy. Every day they are also brought out from the furnace of this world through trials, like gold refined by the flames of temptation.

Others have said: “From the north comes a cloud of golden color; in it there is great glory and honor of the Almighty; we find no likeness of his power.” The cold of the north therefore tests the holy people, who are God’s clouds, so that it may make them precious and radiant with the fire of love. For this reason there is great glory of the Lord and honor of the Almighty. No one else of comparable power is found who would hope for such good things from opposing circumstances.

“We cannot find him worthily.” He is great in strength, judgment, and justice, and he cannot be narrated. “Therefore men will fear him, and all who seem wise to themselves will not dare to contemplate him.” For, he says, just as God is great and powerful in strength, so he is true in judgment and justice, and cannot be narrated. Therefore, as he truly is, he cannot be found by his creature, which is so weak and feeble. For this reason great and courageous men will not presume to search out the incomprehensible, nor will they attempt to contemplate the invisible.

All this, however, is said as a reproach against holy Job, who had said that he was scourged by God without any merit of iniquity.

Others have said: “He who judges justly—do you not think he hears him? Therefore people will fear him, and the wise will also fear him.” They say this because God judges justly, and with him there is no acceptance of persons. All—the wise and the unlearned—will fear him when they consider themselves, knowing that he is the avenger of iniquities according to the measure of his justice; for he will hear those who suffer unjustly.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

[Col. 0745C]

“Then the Lord answered Job from the whirlwind and said.” Job, who was to be rebuked with a terrifying and corrective speech, received an answer from the Lord. The fact that it is said to come from the whirlwind pertains to the terror of the rebuke: as I have said, Job was to be reproved by the Lord. For Job had said that, though just, he was unjustly scourged by the Lord. Therefore the Lord spoke from the whirlwind:

“Who is this who wraps up his arguments in words without understanding?” By these words Heliu is removed, together with his confused and intermixed disputations against Job; here the words of God appear to be understood. And if you, O Job, have committed some offenses by speaking such things against me, who is this who dares rebuke you—especially since he is not fit to rebuke, being the one who, as though better, ought to reproach you? Thus, once Heliu and his ignorant arguments have been removed from the scene, the Lord turns to Job and tells him to prepare himself to hear his rebuke, saying as follows:

“Gird your loins like a man; I will question you, and you will answer me.” Everyone who is going to speak with God is first commanded to gird his loins with chastity. The people, too, when they were going to hear the Law and celebrate the Passover in the wilderness, were commanded to gird the loins of their minds, lest the fluctuating folds of carnal thoughts impede the progress of their holy way of life. Or we gird our bodily garments around our physical loins.

Therefore, by saying:

“Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Tell me, if you have understanding.” Job could not answer God. God speaks to him as though in this manner: “You, Job, who accuse me of acting unjustly concerning one little human being—where were you when I governed the world that I had made from nothing? And when I ruled every creature by the moderation of justice, was I in you to do something unjust?”

Here, under the names of animals and birds, God weaves together great and exceedingly obscure mysteries of the Church. According to mystical understanding, God established the chief apostles, the holy foundations of the Church, in his predestination, as the Apostle says: “Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets.” Or, as others have said: “Where were you when I founded the earth?”—that is, when I gathered the Church from the human race taken from the earth and established it by the power of faith.

Who set its measurements, if you know, or who stretched the measuring line over it? God describes his own power, authority, and measurements, and the ordering of the world, over which he stretched the line of his good and upright work.

Alternatively: The measurements of the Church extend from the rising of the sun to its setting. In them we may also understand the equality and fullness of the Trinity, to which the Church is addressed through the prophet:

“Enlarge the place of your tent toward the sunrise, and stretch out the skins of your tents; do not spare. Lengthen your cords and strengthen your stakes. You shall penetrate to the right and to the left; for your seed shall inherit the nations and inhabit deserted cities.”

Over these measurements of all places, therefore, he stretched the whole world of right faith, [Col. 0746C] so that all who believe in Christ might have one lip. These mysteries, then, were established before the ages—mysteries which Job, since he did not yet exist, could not have known.

Or we may rightly understand the measurements of the Church as the diversities of grace, which the Apostle called “distributions of the Spirit.” Speaking of different graces, he says: “But all these things are effected by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills.” Again he says: “To each of us grace has been given according to the measure of Christ’s gift.” Through these graces, therefore, there is the intention of contemplation, like a straight line of those who rightly believe in God, as it is said in the Acts of the Apostles: “They had one heart and one soul directed toward God.”

Upon what were its bases made firm? How could a rational and wise creature have known the work of the Creator before [Col. 0746D] it existed, when even now the mind can scarcely grasp any of his works?

Alternatively: Upon what are the bases of the earth—that is, of the Church—firmly established, unless upon Christ the rock, who is the beginning of its foundations? The bases of the Church are all the holy, powerful, and strong persons by whom it is sustained and governed.

Others have said: “Upon what are its circles fixed?” Thus we may understand the weight of the world’s stability according to the sense in which the Psalmist speaks of it, saying: “For he has established the world, and it shall not be moved.” A circle, indeed, is a round figure, more beautiful than the other figures. For a circle is harmonious and equal to itself on every side; wholly solid in itself, it proceeds between the range of the eyes through [Col. 0747A] its infinite form, since, without any end, it always returns into itself and is drawn onward in an incomprehensible manner.

This, therefore, seems to signify to me a person who is nowhere at odds with himself and does not oppose himself in any part—such as they will be in the blessed age to come. Then the flesh will not desire against the spirit, nor the spirit against the flesh. Although some saints have even in this age partially anticipated the blessedness of this peace—not by feeling no disagreement at all within themselves between the interior and exterior person, but by overcoming the hostile army of vices with virtues stronger than the resistance they offered, as it is said of Elkanah, the father of the holy Samuel, that he was “one man.”

Thus he will be wholly self-consistent, harmonious with himself, and established immovably in that glory without end. These circles, therefore, figured by the bond of love, [Col. 0747B] have been fastened to the wood of the cross, and each of them says: “For I am confident that neither death nor life,” and so forth.

Or who cast down its cornerstone? This cornerstone is Christ, who was placed by God the Father in the foundation of the Lord’s earth. He is not only foundational but also angular, in whom the two peoples—the Jews, namely, and the Gentiles—are contained. Of him the Psalmist says: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.” And the Apostle says: “With Christ Jesus himself as the chief cornerstone, in whom the whole structure, joined together, grows into a holy temple.” The Father therefore cast him down upon the earth so that he might be placed as its foundation.

When the morning stars praised me together and all the sons of God shouted for joy, [Col. 0747C] then, after the precious stone had been cast into the foundations of Zion—the second man from heaven, the heavenly one—“the morning stars praised me together,” he says, “and all the sons of God shouted for joy.”

The stars and the sons of God are understood as angels, who rejoiced at the Savior’s birth. As the angel said to the shepherds: “Behold, I announce to you great joy, because a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David.” Likewise the Evangelist says: “And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude,” and so forth.

The angels are called morning stars because, among rational creatures, they were made first, on the day which is Christ, and because they are sons of God. They are not sons of darkness, like those who fell from their number and became not only sons of darkness but also rulers of darkness—that is, of sinful human beings. [Col. 0747D] Then, as was said above, all my angels praised me with a loud voice, rejoicing as they praised God for the salvation of that little sheep, the human race.

Likewise, we may not improperly understand the morning stars as all the children of the Church, who are reborn to Christ through baptism, as the Apostle writes to the Church: “You are all sons through faith in Christ Jesus.” They are called morning stars because of the morning watch in which the Lord rose, or because a new light of grace was beginning for them; hence they are also called neophytes.

Who enclosed the sea with doors when it burst forth, proceeding as though from the womb? When, at the creation of the world, the waters covered the whole earth and darkness was over [Col. 0748A] the face of the abyss, then, according to the faith of the Book of Genesis, God commanded on the third day that all the waters should be gathered into one place. He also imposed a limit and boundary upon them, so that they would not again pour beyond their borders and cover the earth.

The womb from which the sea had proceeded we may, improperly (*καταχρηστικῶς*), understand as the underlying earth, so that we may believe that the water was created by God from it and within it. For God made two great divisions of the world—the heaven and the earth—from nothing. He made their lowest parts from unformed matter, but established the other creatures as distinct and formed. Among their creation we believe that the waters too were made, although we do not read of their creation at the beginning of Genesis; the creation of nearly all the others, however, is recounted in the divine books.

Yet [Col. 0748B] holy David also spoke of the sea itself when he was speaking of the blessed man: “His hope is in the Lord his God, who made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them.” I therefore think that this coming forth of the sea means the pouring out of the waters which issued from the hidden boundaries of the earth’s veins and covered the whole face of the earth. We read that this happened more clearly in the Flood, where it is said: “And all the fountains of the great abyss burst forth.”

Accordingly, I think that the womb of the sea was called the earth’s bosom, so that we may know that the sea was brought forth from it. But someone may say: “I say that the mass of the waters was created together with heaven and earth, and came into being at the same time. For God made, or produced, the other creatures from the waters just as he did from the earth.”

If this confirms that view, so that the waters too are said to have been created from nothing [Col. 0748C] because many creatures proceeded from them and from within them at God’s command, what shall we say of heaven, which is the more excellent part of the world? We do not read that anything was produced from it as though from unformed matter. In it, moreover, for the greater beauty of its adornment, God made, ordered, and arranged the stars and the various spheres of the stars.

According to this argument, then, the elements of the sea and earth would be better than heaven, whose most beautiful adornment we admire as we look upward, since it surpasses the other creatures to the greatest degree.

When I made the cloud its garment and wrapped it in darkness as though in the swaddling clothes of infancy: “Although the sea,” he says, “is great in breadth, length, and depth, [Col. 0748D] yet by the strength of my power I covered it as though it were a small element, with a cloud as with a garment, and with darkness; that is, I covered it with small and humble things resembling the swaddling clothes of infancy.”

And because above we said that the sea proceeded as though from a womb, preserving the metaphor of the name and treating the sea itself as something newly born, he says that it was wrapped in darkness as in swaddling clothes—or, as others have said, that it was also wrapped in mist.

I surrounded it with my boundaries, and set a bar and doors, and said: “You shall come this far and go no farther, and here your swelling waves shall be broken.”

These boundaries are the divine words, understood as boundaries fixed by an immovable sentence. [Col. 0749A] The same applies to what follows, where God says: “I set a bar and doors.” Alternatively: Who enclosed the sea with doors?

Scripture frequently calls this age “the sea,” as holy David also says: “This sea is great and broad in its expanses.” Again: “Those who go down to the sea in ships.” And Habakkuk: “You sent your horses into the sea.” And Isaiah: “He slew the whale that is in the sea.”

This sea, therefore, is enclosed by divine commands, as by certain boundaries of sacred utterances, so that it might no longer burst forth from the womb of its heart—where, as though from seed, it conceived worldly cares and the allurements of pleasures through its thoughts—and pour itself out into the commission of various crimes.

Therefore, when the prophet saw the world believing in God and possessing within itself this good of self-restraint, [Col. 0749B] he rejoicingly said to God: “You established the sea by your power.” By the world I mean the faithful people of the holy Church, who are specially called “the sea” and dwell in this world.

This is that world of believers of which the Lord says: “For God so loved this world that he gave his only-begotten Son for it.” There is also the world of unbelievers, of which the Lord likewise says to his disciples: “If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you,” and so forth.

Thus we say that two worlds of peoples dwell in this bodily and animal world. They may also be called two seas, according to the example given above, receiving metaphorical names from this sea of waters: just as there is a good house or a bad one, and a best or worst city. [Col. 0749C] The peoples who fluctuate and are tossed about in this life by restless and uncertain motion are metaphorically called “the sea.”

When I made the cloud its garment and wrapped it in darkness as in the swaddling clothes of infancy: Let us understand the cloud that covers all things as the Holy Spirit, infused and spread over all creatures, of whom it says: “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters.” Darkness, however, may be understood as whatever is empty beyond the world, where there is lightness—that is, a falling backward or decline.

Morally, according to the authority of Scripture, clouds are each announcer of truth. Through the consoling words and teaching of these men, therefore, sprinkling from above, the Lord says that he protected the world of believers from the heat of temptations and gave it shade under the promise of eternal blessedness. This is the garment which, through his holy [Col. 0749D] ministers of the Gospel, he spread over the sea of peoples, so that it would not be scorched by the heat of unbelief. That sea of peoples, placed within the perfect preaching of the Gospel, is also covered, because of the childishness of the morals of some, with a milky teaching as with humbler garments, since they are unable to contemplate the more sacred mysteries, which are wrapped in the darkness of understanding.

I surrounded it with my boundaries, and set a bar and doors. “You shall come this far and go no farther, and here your swelling waves shall be broken.”

“With the boundaries,” God says, “of my commandments, I gathered and enclosed that sea within the confession of one faith. To condense and restrain itself, I set against it the strongest bar of love, and I also [Col. 0750A] closed the doors of unbelief, so that, however great the violence of storms and persecutions, it might not be compelled to go beyond the fixed boundaries of obedience. Let it never leap over the enclosure of my love, to which I said: ‘You shall come this far and go no farther, and here your swelling waves shall be broken.’”

That is: If perhaps some waves of evil thoughts are raging within the sea of your heart, and a strong wind of afflictions attempts to shake you utterly and drive you from your position onto dry barrenness, as though onto sterile sand, take care not to cross these fortifications of my faith and love. Then it will happen that the threatening winds, rising and dashed against the strongest rock, will be shattered.

Have you, after your birth, commanded the dawn and shown the morning its place? The Lord says this to [Col. 0750B] Job: He himself arranges that the things he created and concealed should return daily, through their recurring cycles, to their ordered places. Job is therefore reproved because he said that God, the maker and governor of all things, acted without any regulation of justice.

It is as though he said to him: “You who consider yourself very wise, and think that you were fashioned almost as the equal of my light, and believe that you can dispute my judgments—if the elements of the stars fulfill the Creator’s command, perhaps they pursue the course of their mystery under your arrangement, although these things were created before you existed through me in Adam.”

Alternatively: This dawn is our Savior, who is also called the Sun of righteousness. By the warmth of faith and the splendor of his grace he illumines the Church, that is, the rational world. Therefore, [Col. 0750C] Job, did you command this dawn to rise from heaven, shining upon those who sat in darkness and the shadow of death?

Just as, Job, after your beginning you could not command the eternal things that there should be dawn for a world established in the darkness of errors, so after his setting in death you could not show the place of his resurrection and his glory at the right hand of his Father. After the death which he willingly accepted, I recalled him again to myself. As the Lord Jesus himself says in the Gospel: “If, therefore, you see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before.”

And did you take hold of the trembling extremities of the earth and shake the wicked out of it? This earth may be understood as the Church. Concerning its foundations the Lord spoke above; from it, at the ends of the earth—that is, at the end of the age [Col. 0750D]—sinners will be shaken out. Thus the Lord himself says: “Behold, I will command, and I will shake the house of Israel among all the nations, as grain is shaken in a sieve.”

The God who, according to the prophet, measured the waters in his fist, weighed the heavens with a span, and hung the earth upon three fingers—he, holding the edges of the earth with both hands according to his greatness, shakes it back and forth like a sieve, or shakes it as one shakes a garment, so that he may shake the wicked—like chaff and weeds—from the grain of the righteous.

All these things therefore demonstrate not only the strength but also the justice of the one who performs them. Hence the Lord speaks to holy Job with a rebuke, because he had said that the punishment of an extremely severe temptation had been inflicted upon an innocent man.

According to the moral [Col. 0751A] sense of this passage, however, as I think, there is an easier interpretation if we understand the earth as human nature, since “human” (*homo*) is named from “earth” (*humus*), and the extremities are the life of the saints, because, although placed in the flesh, they live without carnal enticements.

For this reason they are said to be at the extremities of the earth: they go forth from earthly actions and do not remain in the middle, as though living entirely in the flesh. These extremities, or ends of the earth, are in the Lord’s hand, as the prophet says: “For in his hand are all the ends of the earth.” Here the Lord says that he holds and shakes them, so that they tremble before his face, as the prophet says of him: “He looks upon the earth and makes it tremble.”

Thus the Lord shakes the wicked out of their earth—that is, the wickedness of their vices—from the saints. He shakes the wicked of this world away from his holy ones when he establishes them as innocent [Col. 0751B] after purifying them from those people.

Concerning such wicked and sinful persons the prophet said: “In the morning”—that is, when the knowledge of God rises as the lamp of faith in me—“I was destroying all the sinners of the earth, so that I might eliminate from the city of the Lord” every soul that works iniquity.

Or, at the end of time, God will hold the world as guilty before his judgment. At that time even the extremities of the earth will be shaken by the trembling of conscience. There we may understand as the extremities of the earth those who are least, who themselves also, by God’s just judgment, are to be shaken as proud and wicked people from the earth of the meek. For “blessed are the meek, because they shall possess the earth.”

It will be restored like clay to a seal, and will stand like a garment. This seal is understood as the human soul, [Col. 0751C] which was made in the image of God. The likeness of God’s goodness and the beauty of all the virtues were impressed upon it.

This seal of God’s image and likeness had been worn away and obliterated through Adam’s sin, but it will be restored through Christ by a renewed impression. Even now that seal is renewed through faith and the grace of baptism, and is engraved upon the mind by a better life. But at the resurrection it will be restored completely in every respect: just as the clay of the human body will be repaired in incorruption, so the soul, together with it, will be clothed in the garment of immortality as in a robe of glory.

Thus, just as glory and the incorruption of immortality—that is, Christ—remain forever, so the one who has been clothed in them will remain glorious without end. Concerning this [Col. 0751D] garment, looking toward the clay of his flesh, the Apostle says: “This corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.”

This point, however, must be examined more carefully, because in Scripture “garments” are used with different meanings. Sometimes our very body is called a garment, with which the soul is surrounded as by a covering, as the prophet says to the sinful soul: “Your iniquity will cover your garment.”

Again, the virtues of the soul are garments, by which that same soul is arranged and adorned. Concerning these he says to the righteous person who practices mercy: “Then your morning light will break forth, and your garments will quickly arise.” Since these garments are living and rational, they will not be made for you from outside, but [Col. 0752A] will arise within you.

Sometimes sins are also called garments, as the prophet Zechariah says: “And Jesus was clothed in filthy garments.” He said to those standing before him: “Take the filthy garments away from him.” Then he said to him: “Behold, I have taken your iniquity away.”

Above we said that the garment is the glory of immortality, in whose never-failing light a person is to be clothed eternally.

Other interpreters have said: “And you, taking the clay of the earth, fashioned man and set him as a famous one upon the earth”—that is, preeminent over all creatures.

While the Lord says these things to Job, he is sharply reproving him. According to the mystical interpretations, however, with the Holy Spirit overshadowing him, the man Jesus Christ was fashioned from the earth of the Virgin Mary. This man was taken from the clay of human flesh. [Col. 0752B] Let us understand that “clay” is used here not because of the lowliness of the word, but because of the material from which Christ was taken, like Adam at the beginning, who was formed from the mud of the earth.

And just as that one came into being from the bosom of the earth through the One who made him, so this one was formed in his mother’s womb through the One who created him. Thus he is famous over the whole earth, and hence the name of the Lord is now praised from the rising of the sun to its setting.

The light of the wicked will be taken away, and the uplifted arm will be broken. The light of the wicked is the glory and prosperity of this world, which will pass away as the world itself passes, just as Solomon also says: “The light of the wicked will be extinguished.” Their strength and power, called by the name “arm,” will likewise immediately be crushed.

[Col. 0752C] Have you entered into the depths of the sea, and walked about in the farthest parts of the abyss? God signifies in these passages, in a very full and abundant discourse, his providence by which he disposes and governs all things.

Thus he says to Job: “If you can be everywhere and know all the things that have been created; if you have been able to penetrate the hidden recesses of the earth, and if you have traversed the depths of the sea and its farthest and most remote abyss.”

These words are therefore spoken as a rebuke to Job. Others have said: “Have you entered the spring of the sea?” He seems to mean the beginning and source from which the sea itself, as from a womb, flows from the Ocean. We know that this occurs through the Ocean’s perpetual flow and return, and they report and affirm that the immense outpouring of the Ocean sea, passing through the rivers of all regions and provinces, [Col. 0752D] takes place at a single moment in time.

Yet we know that through the alternating succession of all days and nights it arrives over twenty-four hours. After three quarters of an equinoctial hour have passed, it flows back more slowly but without interruption, whether by day or by night, and after five equinoctial hours it rises again by a violent tide and forceful surge—whether only in hidden places or also against the checked courses of great rivers—ascending toward the higher regions. Then, over seven hours of the same measure, it flows away with a somewhat gentler current and empties only those places which had been filled during the five hours.

It may therefore seem incredible that in that same sea a kind of spring of such vast waters should boil up, from whose deep and sufficient abyss those waters, at a time fixed [Col. 0753A] for themselves, spread over the surface and then, returning, fall back into the same deepest recesses. They rush away and, by the perpetual law established for them by God, continually boil up from below and again flow down into the depths.

Perhaps therefore God said to holy Job: “Have you entered the spring of the sea?” For only God knows the things he has created.

According to the mystical interpretations, however, I think that God said this because, near the end of the age, he was to descend into the underworld for the redemption of humanity. There, by the authority of the one descending, he is said to have walked about, because it was impossible for him, as though guilty of sin, to be held by infernal chains. For he alone became like a human being. For the present, indeed, without assistance, yet nevertheless free among the dead. [Col. 0753B]

That the underworld is in the depths of the earth is clearly demonstrated by the prophet Jonah, who specifically bore the figure of the Savior, in the prayer he poured out from the belly of the fish. The waters of the abyss also surrounded him in the underworld, and many other passages of Scripture speak about the nature of the realms below.

We may also understand this passage morally in the following way: Since we know that this age is figuratively called “the sea,” its depths are all the wicked and sinners who, however much they love it, sink into its most obscure depths, so that they do not see at all the light of the Gospel and the glory of Christ.

The farthest parts of the abyss, however, are all the wicked and sacrilegious, who descend into the deeper darkness of sins and are overwhelmed, as by a mass of waters, through the excessive flood of their lusts. [Col. 0753C] Our Lord deigned to come to these people, despising no one and desiring to save all, so that he might illumine by his grace their hearts blinded by unbelief. Having been made light in the Lord, they might become his temple, so that he might walk in them and dwell in them and be their God.

Have the gates of death been opened to you, and have you seen the dark doors? No creature, however powerful and strong, can resist the majesty of God. Because creatures perceive their Creator by nature, they yield to the divine power, which they are wholly unable to oppose.

Hence the ancient interpreters said: “Have the gates of death been opened to you?” They understood that such gates, which are certainly feared, are not insensible and lifeless things, but rather those [Col. 0753D] unclean spirits, our enemies—adversarial powers through which access to death was found for the human race.

They are also the dark doors, whose malicious minds, filled with the darkness of envy, God alone sees through. Since those of whom we speak became darkness by withdrawing from the true light and were called the powers of darkness—that is, rulers of sinful human beings—they are also called dark doors because, through their deception, an entrance into death was made available to humanity through the darkness of sins.

Where it is said, then, “Have you seen the dark doors?” other interpreters translated the passage more plainly, saying: “Or did the gatekeepers of hell see [Col. 0754A] you and fear?” This passage requires no explanation; rather, it makes entirely clear what had previously been said obscurely.

Or certainly these words are brighter than light in the passion and death of the Lord. He opened the bars of the underworld and freed the souls of the saints from there; emerging from the lower realms, he loosed the laws of Tartarus; rising again, he annulled the sentence of death; and he led forth, confidently or openly triumphing in himself, the trembling principalities and powers who were the gatekeepers and the doors.

According to the tropological interpretation, however, the gates of death are our senses. Those gates are then closed to virtues because they are held by vices, and through them the death of sin enters the citadel of the mind. They are called dark doors because they open an entrance into the darkness of sins and also of punishments. [Col. 0754B]

These gates, therefore, or these doors, are opened to human beings for salvation when, after their vices have been defeated like enemies, conquered, and put to flight, they open them with the virtues of holiness. Then they hear the prophet’s exhorting words: “Open to me the gates of righteousness; entering through them, I will confess to the Lord.”

The holy person enters in order to possess the testimony of holiness and the jewels of the virtues, preserving and rejoicing in them, because through participation in the common treasure they become “one heart and one soul directed toward God.” Thus, placed together in this world as though in a furnace of testing, they bless God as if with one mouth at all times, and his praise is always in their mouths.

Have you considered the breadth of the earth? Tell [Col. 0754C] me, if you know everything. What human being could know how greatly it extends, except the one who alone established all things? Of him the prophet says: “He measured the waters with his hand, and the heavens with a span, and enclosed the whole earth in his fist.”

Alternatively: “Have you, Job, foreseen the breadth of the earth”—that is, the future Church—which I have expanded throughout the whole world as the Gospel increased everywhere? Tell me, then, whether you were able to understand or ever perceive this.

Or: Have you been able to foresee the breadth of my wisdom, which I bestowed upon the earth, my house—that is, upon the Church? Could you, anticipating what was to come, inspect it by yourself with the eye of your mind kindled?

This is the wisdom that enlarged Solomon’s heart like the sand on the seashore and gave him exceedingly great prudence. It is sung in the Exodus, and confidently acts in the breadth [Col. 0754D] of its ways. That same wisdom commands its manifold meanings, rich in the breadth of its discussions, to be inscribed three times in the human heart.

These words, therefore, may be understood as spoken by the Father concerning Wisdom, which is the Son.

In what way does the light dwell, and where is the place of darkness, so that you may lead each one to his boundaries and understand the paths of his house? In the way of a person’s holy conduct, the light of virtues dwells. The place of darkness—that is, of vices—is the sinful person, or that place of which he says: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.”

Do you therefore know, Job, how to distinguish each person’s merit and, according to justice, lead each one of them to the predetermined boundaries [Col. 0755A] of retribution? Were you able to understand the thoughts of their hearts as the paths of their houses?

Alternatively, “in what way,” or, as others have said, “upon what earth, does the light dwell?” The light of faith and knowledge dwells in the heart of the believer; or, the light upon the earth is Christ in the Church. The place of darkness—that is, of ignorance and unbelief—is the heart of the foolish and unbelieving.

Therefore, by whatever paths the good and the wicked proceed, they reach, according to their merit, the house of eternal existence, with the just and good Lord leading them.

Did you know then that you would be born, and did you know the number of your days? What human being knows, before he exists, that he is going to be, and knows the days or years of his life?

Alternatively: In Adam, the sinner who became a son [Col. 0755B] of death, when could you know or understand that you would be born through the Spirit and the grace of baptism from the womb of Mother Church, that you would be restored forever according to the final resurrection, and that you would have a number of days without end? How could you know this by yourself?

Have you entered the treasuries of snow, or have you looked upon the treasuries of hail, which I have prepared for the time of the enemy and for the day of battle and war? God wished through these words to demonstrate the power which he possesses even in the secret and invisible things of his creation, saying to Job: “Have you entered the treasuries of snow, or have you looked upon the treasuries of hail?”

These are not certain places, spacious through their immense capacity in some part of the world, containing within themselves masses and heaps [Col. 0755C] of infinite snow, so that they might rightly be called treasure-houses from which these forms, once gathered there, could later be brought forth whenever God wished.

Rather, the matter is as the Lord himself says elsewhere: “The beauty of the field is with me.” Whatever he wishes to do, his will immediately proceeds into action. Therefore they are called treasuries not because they have been established in some immense and capacious place, but in his will and arrangement.

As he says elsewhere: “The beauty of the field is with me.” Nothing is imperfect with him, because his thinking is not one thing and his doing another; rather, whatever he wills is immediately done.

Job is therefore asked whether he can enter into this secret disposition of the divine heart, in which these treasuries of such things existed while they did not yet exist bodily in themselves. [Col. 0755D] No one can approach or know that secret of the divine majesty except the Son, who is in the bosom of the Father and is of one nature and substance with him.

These things are therefore said to have been prepared by God for the time of the enemy, for battle and war. In many different ways, and through countless other judgments, God scourges and corrects the human race, as he also devastated the Egyptians with thunderbolts and hail.

In general, he repeatedly chastises human beings through other means: he humbles them by hostile invasion, devastates them through earthquakes and chasms, destroys them in whirlwinds, crushes them under ruins, drowns them in shipwrecks, and strikes them with countless other blows—whether slow illnesses, acute diseases, or corrupted air.

Thus in Deuteronomy [Col. 0756A] we read what he prepares for enemies who resist and rebel against him, so that according to his justice he may inflict upon them the punishments of tribulation that they deserve.

Alternatively: We understand snow sometimes in a good sense and sometimes in an adverse one. For this reason, under the name of snow, they gather here a prefiguration of the body of the opposing powers, which has departed far from the love of God—that is, has abandoned God dwelling in heaven—so that by God’s just judgment it might be cast upon the earth.

God wished to call the treasuries of this snow and hail, which had passed into a kind of hardness, as though forgetful of its nature, the secret machinations of their thoughts. Thus the prophet Ezekiel says concerning their prince: “Through the abundance of your commerce your inner parts have been filled with iniquity.”

The Lord [Col. 0756B] alone is the knower and examiner of all such thoughts. These treasuries, then, which through enigmas are called snow and hail, God says that he prepared for the time of the enemy, for the day of battle and war.

And because they would never turn to God with an understanding heart, by divine dispensation they were made ministers of punishment: so that, by God’s judgment, they might chastise some with corrective scourges for their amendment; punish others according to the just sentence of God; and make still others, afflicted by harsh tribulations, more renowned.

This was clearly manifested in the case of holy Job, and was similarly demonstrated in the Egyptians, upon whom dreadful plagues were inflicted through evil angels, although they did not fight against God willingly.

Again: “Have you entered the treasuries of snow,” and so forth? [Col. 0756C] The Lord could have said this concerning his coming in the flesh. As the eternal fire, the fire of heaven, and the divine fire by which all rational creatures grow warm, he deigned to descend to earth. Coming, as it were, to a snowy and cold region—to this world, hardened like hail by the excessive cold of unbelief—he cried out and said: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth.”

He therefore professes that he has entered such treasuries of human hearts, made exceedingly cold by forgetfulness of their God, so that, after the cold of faithlessness had been expelled, they might burn with love of him and say: “My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation the fire was kindled.”

Coming from the cold of folly to the fire of understanding through the progress of faith, they might say: “Was not our heart burning within us when Jesus, with our heart illumined and the fountain [Col. 0756D] of love kindled, opened the Scriptures to us?”

Thus, entering the world and visiting it, he observes the hearts of mortals, which are also called treasures by the Lord himself in the Gospel, where he says: “The good man brings forth good things from the good treasure of his heart.”

God therefore prepared to do the things we have mentioned for the time of the enemy, battle, and war—namely, when he died for our sake. He triumphed in the underworld over the grave and most troublesome enemy, the devil, and, rising from the dead, overcame in Judea the adversaries of his faith.

By what way is light distributed, and heat divided over the earth? Who could properly know, among mortals, what the sun’s path is, by which it proceeds in an ordered course in the right region of the sky [Col. 0757A], scattering light over the lands, or how heat is divided in turn according to the seasons or across all regions, so that at the same time it burns more intensely in one place while elsewhere it is felt with moderated warmth?

Again: “By what way is light distributed, and heat divided over the earth?” The way is the preaching of the Gospel, through which the light of faith is scattered over the hearts of believers. And fittingly it is said to be “scattered,” because minds dried up by unbelief are sprinkled with the abundance of divine grace; and thus the heat of the Holy Spirit is divided over the earth of the faithful. It is divided, I say, when grace is given to each according to the measure of the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ. Or it is divided in this way: to some the proclamation of Christ is an aroma of life leading to life, but to others an aroma of death leading to death. Thus the very good of the [Col. 0757B] Gospel is divided, so that it grants life to some and brings about death for others through the crime of unbelief.

Likewise, the way of a person’s holy conduct, and the light of the fear of God, is scattered over the whole earth of the body, so that the darkness of sins may flee from it and the heat of temptations may be moderated for it by the help of God’s grace, lest, when the sun’s heat has risen over it, it boil over. Thus, too, heat is divided when the entire burden of tribulations is not imposed upon them all at once, as the Apostle says: “For God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted,” and so forth. And Solomon: “A prudent son will escape the heat, but an evil son is corrupted by the wind at harvest.”

Who gave the fiercest rain its course, and a path to the resounding thunder, so that it might rain upon the earth without a human being in the desert, where no mortal dwells, [Col. 0757C] to fill the trackless and desolate place and bring forth green grasses?

This fiercest rain is the Gospel of the Savior, who sent forth his utterance upon the earth so that his word might run swiftly. This rain, I say, rose up on the mountains of Jerusalem from the depths of the earth to the heights. “For the law will go forth from Zion,” says the prophet, “and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.” Raised up by the holy apostolic clouds, like flowing water it runs abundantly; with the breeze of the Holy Spirit blowing upon it, it made for itself a path of faith among the nations, with the terror of God’s name and the thunder of miracles going before it.

Others have translated: “He prepared a river for all peoples.” And, I say, he prepared the river of the Church, so that it might be flooded with the copious and powerful rain of the Holy Spirit, as was shown at the very beginning of the Church’s birth [Col. 0757D] among the holy apostles and the others.

As for the fact that, in praise of the evangelical rain, it is said to have rained upon an uninhabited earth that had no human being: it would not be remarkable if this were understood merely as the words sound. But “in the desert,” that is, among the nations, he poured out abundantly the teaching of the Lord’s preaching. In the desert, I say, where no human being had dwelt: that is, because no prophet had been sent by God to the Gentiles, in order to fill the trackless and desolate places and bring forth the green grasses of the Gospel.

The rain of the earth of the Church, which had been desolated by God, filled it with the fatness of God’s charity, and, in its richness, caused it to bring forth and produce green grasses of cultivated [Col. 0758A] seed according to their kind, as it says in the psalm: “And he will flourish from the city like the grass of the earth.” By multiplying its fruits, it produced, according to the Lord’s parable, some thirtyfold, some sixtyfold, and some a hundredfold; and it heard itself consoled by the exhortation: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, because the children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband.”

Who is the father of the rain, or who begot the drops of dew?

Who is the author and creator of this rain and of this rain-shower of the Lord, except God? This is the voluntary rain that he set apart for his inheritance, as the Father says to the Son: “Son, ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession.” The same God also begot the drops of dew. Hence the prophet [Col. 0758B] says to God: “For the dew that is from you is healing for them.”

Accordingly, in the river he demonstrated the exceedingly abundant flow and generosity of divine grace; but in the dew, that same grace gradually becoming familiar to the inward parts and penetrating the marrow of the soul. Others have translated: “Or who begot the clods of dew?” It will not be absurd, therefore, to understand these clods as each of the saints who are in the field of the Church, to whom the Apostle says: “You are God’s cultivated field.” There, then, these clods have been begotten through baptism in Christ, as the Apostle says: “Created in Christ Jesus for good works.” Thus, drenched with this heavenly dew, they became rich and abundant in holy fruits.

From whose womb did the ice come forth?

By the name “womb,” it seems to me, he signified the secret place of the heart. For we ought not plausibly to understand ice as having come forth from the mouth of God, but rather as a just and strict judgment having flowed from the secret and inscrutable decision of his mind. Therefore he said “ice comes forth” instead of “judgment comes forth,” by which, according to their deserts, certain human beings are struck with the blow of hardening, and their hearts are constricted by a very hard, unbreakable, and intensely cold frost, so that they do not feel the warmth of fervent divine charity.

This can most truly be said of the apostate angels, and it is to be understood especially of the Jews, for whom the waters of the heavenly utterances have been frozen, so that they might flow forth, through the abundance of grace, in the fruits of the nations. Concerning their calling it was said in the preceding verse, and concerning them: “He made the desert into pools of water, and dry lands into outlets of water, and caused the hungry to dwell there”—that is, those who hunger for righteousness. “And they sowed fields, and planted vineyards, and produced the fruit of birth; and he blessed them, and they multiplied greatly.”

Whoever, therefore, now observes spiritually, with the mind, the Church established everywhere sees that its earth, which once was desolate before God, now abounds in all the spiritual resources mentioned above. Thus the Church received the aforementioned drops of dew flowing down from heaven; and, according to the Book of Judges, in the event that we read took place in the time of Gideon the leader, the dew of one little sheep and of a small nation—Christ, who is that dew—poured the grace of blessing over the whole earth that believes in Christ. And that mystery was fulfilled which the Psalmist had foretold when he said: “Like the dew of Hermon.”

Hermon [Col. 0759A] is a mountain whose name is interpreted as “anathema,” or “devoted thing,” and by its height signifies the Jewish people. Its dew, therefore—that is, the dew of grace and blessing—descended upon Mount Zion. For Mount Zion, exalted in virtues and sublime, is the Church. Upon it is established the watchtower of contemplation for believers in what is to come. Hence the very form of the virtues is interpreted by the name Zion.

And so that we might know the proper name of this dew, the Psalmist says: “For there the Lord commanded blessing, namely on Mount Zion, and life forevermore.” And the Lord continues, saying:

And who begot the frost from heaven?

In this way, then, the impious are struck from heaven with the sentence of hardening. This evil is rightly said to be begotten for them by God, as in the case of Pharaoh and the Jews, whom we read were hardened because of their unbelief [Col. 0759B] and the excessive obstinacy of their hearts. Concerning such people the Lord continues, saying:

The waters are hardened into the likeness of a stone.

By the name “waters,” according to the authority of Scripture, peoples are understood, as the apostle John says: “The waters are peoples.” And David says to the Lord: “Deliver me from many waters, from the hand of foreign sons.” He seems, therefore, to be speaking of those who have grown numb through the excessive cold of forgetfulness of God and have become solid and exceedingly hard, like stones.

Then he says:

And the surface of the abyss is congealed.

By “the abyss,” I think we should understand the deepest darkness of the mind, which is so covered over by the dullness of excessive unbelief and congealed by a certain frost of impiety that it becomes like stone. Thus, in such a mind, there is no passage by which it may draw breath toward God, according to what the Apostle said when he took up a prophetic testimony concerning the Jews: “God gave them a spirit of compunction, eyes so that they would not see, and ears so that they would not hear, to this very day.”

In the one hundred and forty-seventh psalm also, it is clear that the prophet spoke mystically of frost, ice, and crystal according to this meaning in which we read here that the Lord spoke. We can also understand these passages in a simple, literal way: “Who begot the frost from heaven?”—calling the icy mountains and the summits of lofty peaks “heaven,” as well as the places throughout the immense air that are nearer or more closely adjacent to the heavens. According to this scriptural usage, the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “The birds of heaven.” Setting aside these matters according to the letter, we ought rather to understand and believe those things that have been proclaimed in a sacred sense by God.

Will you join together the shining Pleiades, or can you disperse the circuit of Arcturus?

Now he speaks to Job about the order of the heavens and the revolution of the stars. He calls “Pleiades” the stars that are shown joined together, as though they were seven. Since the Greeks observed that these were many together, they gave them their name from their multitude: for πληθύς or πλῆθος means “multitude,” and from this the name “Pleiades” was derived.

The Lord therefore says to Job: “Were you able, by your power, to make these stars joined together and united?” Likewise, can you disperse the circuit of the constellation of the North, or Arcturus, which I have made return upon itself in an unceasing circuit through the left-hand region of the world, so that it continually goes forth and returns upon itself?

Concerning the stars of heaven, or the constellations, we read in other places of Scripture also, as in Joshua and Judges: “The boundary of the Amorite,” it says, “was from the ascent of the Scorpion Rock, and the upper regions.”

To express the Lord’s words according to mystical interpretations, let us interpret “heaven” as the Church, which above the Lord called by the name “earth,” although there it was called earth because of its origin. Here, however, since it has been exalted through Christ into glory, it is rightly understood as heaven.

In this heaven, then, the stars—the Pleiades and those of the North—contain within themselves a single form of sacred interpretation. For the number seven itself demonstrates within it the graces of the sevenfold Spirit [Col. 0760B], which shine in this number; and the very spirits of these graces shine in the same firmament of heaven.

These stars are therefore called by the prophet “the seven eyes of the Lord.” The graces and virtues of these eyes the prophet Isaiah enumerates when he prophesies concerning the Savior’s birth, saying: “And the Spirit of God will rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and piety; the spirit of the fear of God has filled him.”

Just as no one can join together the spiritual stars of indivisible light, so it is altogether impossible for these stars of grace, illuminating my Church all around, to be separated from their unbreakable unity.

But what others have translated as “or have you understood the bonds of the Pleiades?” raises the mind of the observer toward spiritual understanding, so that he may labor to seek some allegorical meaning.

Will you bring forth Lucifer in his season, and cause Vesper to rise over the children of the earth?

There is a star that we call Lucifer, brighter than the other stars. The teachers of the Church also say that it is one of the five stars that they call planets, because they have a course unlike that of the other stars and a much swifter one. Hence they are called planets—that is, “wandering” or “errant”—because their course is not fixed but changeable.

They maintain, therefore, that this Lucifer, which will appear to the lands, is born in the East after two years. But another star, which he called Vesper because it appears to the world at its appointed time around evening, God says to Job: “Do you cause this star to rise over the children of the earth?”

You who understand the power of the one who governs all things, recognize the justice that operates in you. Many think that this star is called Hesperus. Hence Italy was also called Hesperia, because it first appears there at its appointed time.

Spiritually, however, these are the words of the Father concerning his Son, our Savior, who says: “Will you bring forth Lucifer in his season, and cause Vesper to rise over the children of the earth?” Here the advent of the Lord who was to come in the flesh is signified, and his resurrection from the dead is prefigured, when the fullness of time had come.

He says: “God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the law.” In this appointed time, therefore, he was brought forth by God the Father to visit the earth [Col. 0761A]. He was called Lucifer because, coming from the heights, he arose—as though after two years, after the Law and the Prophets—and displayed to us, who were placed in darkness and the shadow of death, the light of faith and timely knowledge.

Vesper, on the other hand, is called the same Son of Man, who set on the cross at the time of his passion. Concerning him the prophet says to the peoples who would believe: “He will make a way for him who ascends over the setting sun; the Lord is his name.” At the time of sunset, when he said to the Father, “Into your hands I commend my spirit,” he placed darkness, and darkness came to be in the hearts of the unbelieving Jews.

This one, therefore, God the Father raised up as the great shepherd of the sheep. This Vesper, I say, because he offered the evening sacrifice at the evening of the ages, he caused to rise as the Son of Man over the children of the earth. Would that they not be flesh and earth, food for the serpent, nor children of night and darkness, but children of Lucifer, children of God.

Do you know the order of heaven, and can you establish its plan upon the earth?

If some mortal can know the number of all the stars, he can also investigate the order of their host. No one, therefore, truly knows these things except the one who created them.

In the spiritual sense it may be understood as follows: “Do you, Job, as though you were a knower of the future, already know in what order, in the heaven of the Church, the various and manifold spirits of my graces shine like stars? Or with what glory, or in what order of merits, will the saints shine in the resurrection like the globes of radiant stars?”

Others translate this passage as: “So that all things beneath heaven may be made together.” Here they seem to say that through the revolving movement either of the seasons or of the stars, it returns and comes back through successive intervals.

Spiritually, however, it should be understood to mean that the dispensation of human reconciliation through Christ increases until the end of the age, unto the knowledge of all nations; or because the saints, in order to reach the goal of virtue, progress daily in holiness of conduct, and therefore are established beneath heaven—that is, beneath obedience to ecclesiastical discipline.

Will you raise your voice in the cloud, and will the rush of waters cover you?

At first hearing this should be understood in the following way: Do you have such power that, at your command and nod, rains pouring down and covering everything immediately descend from heaven?

According to a higher understanding, however, he says: “I raise my voice,” says the Lord, “when I cry out to human beings: ‘Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened,’ and when, in an attitude of compassion, I strike the hidden places of their minds. There is there, as it were, a cloud—the darkness of sin—and a very obscure forgetfulness of my name, so that, surrounded by countless peoples obedient to my voice, I may be covered, as it were, by waters flowing in a rush, and may be clothed with them as with a garment, so that I may dwell in them, as the prophet says: ‘As a bridegroom clothes me with a garment.’”

Others have translated: “You will call the cloud with your voice, and in the trembling of mighty water it will obey you.” Mighty water is the terrifying command of the divine will, which God orders each saint to observe by his voice—that is, by the impulse of a cry, and by the prompting of inward instruction—so that, by obeying, he may be saved.

Could you, Job, do anything like this?

Will you send forth lightning, and will it go, and, returning, say to you, “Here we are”?

In these words of God, we must believe that whatever he wills is present to his power, for whom even all insensible things are as though they were sensible. Thus the prophet says: “The earth was moved at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of Jacob.”

The lightning is called “returning” because these are sent by God to illuminate the world through the preaching of the Gospel. To them the Lord says: “You are the light of the world.” And again: “I have appointed you as a light to the nations, so that you may be salvation to the ends of the earth.”

At the end of the age, returning with the fruits of their sheaves, they will come with rejoicing, and [Col. 0762B] say: “You gave me five talents; behold, I have gained five others.”

Or the lightning consists of divine inspirations by which the hearts of the saints are illuminated, so that, once kindled by them, they may burn with the love of Christ’s charity. These lightning flashes of God’s illumination return to God, who had sent them forth to awaken desire for himself, when through that same divine visitation they accomplished the work of his illumination with ardent and fervent hearts.

Who placed wisdom in the inward parts of a human being, or who gave the rooster understanding?

It is clear that when the human being was made in the image and likeness of God, he received the wisdom of reason, so that he might surpass the other living creatures, which lack reason and prudence. As for the good gifts with which God endowed the human being, I refer the reader to those who have written extensively about the good of nature and its virtues.

God also gave the domestic rooster this kind of perception: when the time of night has passed, as though remembering the approaching light, it announces its return to the world by singing.

According to spiritual understanding, however, it should be understood as follows: Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. The Father placed him in the inward parts of the human being. For the Wisdom of God, who is his Son, said this when Peter had confessed him as the Son of God: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” “Flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.” And the Apostle says: “When it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me by his grace, to reveal his Son in me.”

I think, however, that the rooster is each of the saints who, in the night and darkness of this world, receive faith, understanding, and steadfastness of virtue to cry out to God, asking him to breathe upon them the day that endures forever and to remove the shadows of the present life. With urgent and repeated cries of their prayers they say: “Send forth your light and your truth.”

We can understand this also of the prophets, who vied with one another in announcing the coming of the day and of the sun.

In this passage, however, the interpretation of others is quite different. They have said: “Who gave women wisdom in weaving, and knowledge of various designs?” If knowledge of variety and wisdom in the work of weaving were given by God only to women, concerning whom it is said, “But the skilled women made what they knew for the work of the tabernacle,” then the Lord in this passage seems to say specifically: “Who gave women wisdom in weaving, and knowledge of various designs?”
