Thus in Exodus, Bezalel and Oholiab wove the garments of the priests and of the tabernacle with varied and embroidered work. Let us therefore understand that there are holy souls who, even now, have received the ability to perform this work in the historical sense through the understanding of the Spirit. To them, as it is written, “God gave wisdom and understanding”; whatever can be devised through craftsmanship, he placed in their hearts.

Thus they were filled with the spirit of wisdom and understanding, with wisdom or knowledge, and with every kind of learning, so as to conceive and make every work, because that tabernacle of the Law bore the image [Col. 0763B] of the holy Church.

Let us speak of this variety of conduct or merits as a garment truly serving Solomon, which the queen of Sheba figuratively described when, praising his wisdom, she marveled at his house, food, dwelling places, the order of his servants, their garments and attendants, and the holocausts that they continually offered in the house of the Lord.

This variety of offices is woven throughout the different Churches in the whole world: in one place the married, in another the continent, in another virgins; some adorn the body of Christ through almsgiving, others through the renunciation of all their possessions, others through the cross and the mortification of earthly desires, others through knowledge of the Scriptures, with the manifold graces of the Holy Spirit serving as various colors. Thus they prepare for themselves garments of eternal glory and immortality.

With perfect understanding they also weave together faith in the Trinity, like a threefold cord that is not quickly broken. Such garments are fashioned by these spiritual women—that is, whether by holy souls or by the Churches established throughout the various regions of the world.

Who can recount the order of the heavens, and who will make the harmony of heaven sleep?

It is certain that no one will be able either to recount in words or to conceive in the mind the order of the heavens or the course of the stars. But when he says, “Who will make the harmony of heaven sleep?” the elements are said in many places of Scripture to praise God, because through their arrangement and beauty God is proclaimed either by human beings or by angels.

That is: Who will cause human beings, while exercising themselves in his praises, to sleep—that is, to rest—from those praises? In return for this honor, which is rendered by the assembly of the Church, who other than he himself will give rest and refreshment forever?

“Sleep” is sometimes understood as “rest” in Scripture, as the prophet Isaiah says: “Righteousness slept in her”—that is, in Jerusalem the equity of righteousness rested, but now there are murderers. And a certain holy person, upon whom the light of the Lord’s countenance had been marked, says in the psalm: “In peace, in the same place, I will sleep and rest.” Again, in another passage he says: “If you sleep among the middle portions,” that is, “if you rest among the lots of the two Testaments.”

“And who will make the harmony of heaven sleep?” Let us understand the holy angels, who, because of the dwelling of heaven itself, are called “heaven” by the prophet in this way: “Heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord.” [Col. 0764A]

Of this heaven’s harmony, therefore, the Lord says: Who will make it sleep—that is, who will be able to restrain them so that they cease from the perpetual praises with which they bless me, endlessly singing, “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord,” and, as it were, fall asleep?

Who will recount the order of the heavens? The saints are also frequently called “heavens.” Concerning them the prophet prophesies according to mystical interpretations, saying: “The heavens declare the glory of God.” Who, then, will be able to recount the order of their gifts, which they possess in different ways according to God’s grace, or even the order of their faith?

When was the dust poured into the earth, and the clods fastened together?

The dust of which the Lord speaks signifies the unbelief of the nations. This dry and loose dust is mixed with the apostolic foundation in the Church, so that, through faith and the bonds or joints of charity, the cementing together in Christ by the covenant of union and peace may grow and advance, like solid earth, toward the increase of God.

Thus the clods of the Lord’s field, made fruitful, are fastened together into one body of the Church by the bond of charity.

The holy Scriptures are also rightly called “heavens,” because they have been given to human beings from above, or because they contain heavenly mysteries within themselves. Who, then, will be able to search out in his mind the order of these heavens—that is, of the Scriptures—which are shadowed and deep because of the obscurities of their mysteries; or bring it forth in speech? Who will command their prophecies to cease?

The ancient interpreters said: “Who bent the instruments of heaven down to earth?” That is: Who is the one who brought the songs of the heavens praising God down to human knowledge, so that, by imitating that praise, they might deserve to become companions of the angels?

Will you seize prey for the lioness, and fill the souls of her cubs?

Of the creatures he enumerates throughout the whole text of this speech, there are six quadrupeds and four flying creatures. In this perfect number of ten it may be seen that God intended every creature to be understood, since it is governed by him as its author. The number ten is perfect because, by repetition through it, every number is multiplied infinitely.

According to the surface of the letter, therefore, he says this: I, who provide for everything through a just dispensation, seem to be unjust only toward you, Job.

According to the spiritual understanding, the lioness, or also the lion, is to be understood as the devil, who is so named in many places of Scripture because of his ferocity and strength. Concerning him the Lord says that he can harm no one unless he has received power from God. They are therefore handed over to him by God’s just judgment, because he has no power at all to rule unless God himself permits it.

“Will you seize prey for the lioness?”—that is, just as I permit her to seize it.

I think that the cubs are called cubs here because he had named the lioness; she had nourished them with the poison of her malice or wickedness, as though with milk, to destroy human beings. From the deaths of these people the souls of the most wicked spirits are refreshed. Concerning them the psalm says: “The young lions roar, so that they may seize and seek their food from God.”

God is therefore said to give food to these lions and dragons [Col. 0765A] when he places in their power those whom they desire.

When do they lie in their dens? Others have translated, “in the forests.” And do they lie in wait in their caves?

The dens or caves are the hearts of impious human beings. In these hiding places they sit or lie in ambush in order to kill the innocent.

Who prepares food for the raven when its young cry out to God, wandering because they have no food?

I think that here too the raven signifies the opposing party, as do its young. Thus, just as above we understood the lioness and her cubs as the devil and the crowd of his lost ones, so here we should understand the raven together with its young as the same devil and his followers.

What is indicated by the word “wandering” is that they suffer something like the madness of hunger against the human race, so that they may consume the destruction of its portion as food. For this reason they seem to strive with every effort until they achieve the object of their desires, as we have heard the Holy Spirit saying through Solomon: “The eye that mocks its father and dishonors the old age of its mother—may the ravens of the valleys dig it out, and the young of the eagles devour it.”

We can also understand it in this way: We once had the raven—that is, the devil—and all his companions as fathers, when we resembled their errors and vices; and for this reason we were also called by the name of their young.

But when we left them—which the bride is also taught to do, and we are that bride, to whom it is said: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house”—and now invoke the Lord, it may be that we are still called by our former name. Thus the prophet says, speaking of God: “Who gives their food to the beasts, and to the young ravens that call upon him.”

I think that we are designated by our former name so that we may know what we were and what we now are through the grace of Christ. Recognizing this great good, we may give thanks to God all the more, saying with the Apostle: “Thanks be to God the Father, who rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his glory.”

It is the custom of holy Scripture frequently to recall former names of faults in the saints, as the blessed prophet Isaiah says concerning God: “The beasts of the field will bless me”; and the apostle Matthew is called a publican.

Let us see whether we can also expound this passage in a favorable sense, so that we may interpret this raven as Christ. For according to the usage of Scripture we call our Lord a mountain, and we likewise call the devil a mountain; we also speak of a rock and a stone, and of a tree and a sword. Perhaps, then, we may also speak of a raven.

For the bride, the Church, among the other praises with which she praises Christ, says in the Song of Songs: “His locks are like fir branches, black as a raven.” When, therefore, we apply the name raven to the devil, we say that he is black with crimes and foul, dwelling in the darkness of wickedness. But when we say that the Savior is signified by that name, we understand him in his Scriptures to be most obscure in the secrets of the mysteries.

And although we know that the devil is called a serpent in Scripture, who would dare to believe this of the Lord unless he himself had expressed the likeness of the serpent in his own words, saying: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so the Son of Man must be lifted up”? And he instructed his disciples to be like this, saying: “Be wise as serpents.”

The serpent—that is, the devil—was cursed by God because he deceived Eve through cunning. Christ is also called accursed, because “cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.” By taking upon himself the curse of humanity—that is, the death which had come from God’s sentence—he hung the curse upon the tree. Hence it is that Christ became a curse for us.

We have offered these examples to confirm the sense stated above. Let us examine what follows.

Now, with Christ figuratively called a raven, the Father prepares food for him when he summons believers from the nations, as the prophet says concerning the same Father: “He raised up the righteous man from the East; he called him to follow. He will give nations into his presence, and he will rule over kings.”

When these people have been called to faith, the Lord Christ is refreshed by them as by food, with the joy of exultation. This people—that is, the disciples and all believers—cry out to God in prayer, asking daily for their substantial bread. They do this while wandering because they are pilgrims and strangers upon the earth and have not established for themselves a firm and stable dwelling. Rather, they say with the Apostle: “We are unsettled.”

They do indeed have the food of the Scriptures, by whose consolation they are nourished; but it is the food of hope and faith, not the nourishment of a permanently existing reality. For this reason they are said to wander in this world until they reach a certain immovability in the age to come.

This spiritual interpretation also pertains to the claim that these ravens are said to be nourished by dew, as philologists report having investigated.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

Do you know the time when the wild goats give birth upon the rocks, or have you watched the does in labor?

These ibices are the animals that the Greeks call τραγέλαφοι (*tragelaphos*), a name compounded from “goat” and “deer,” because these animals must possess something resembling one another. I think that one of them is called a “little doe” in the Song of Songs, and that at certain times it was also called a “wild goat” and was slaughtered according to the Law.

In the Song of Songs they are frequently placed together, and they are called clean because they have horns, chew the cud, and divide the hoof. There are also other animals of the ibex’s kind, such as the birds of the raven species, concerning which the Law says: “You shall not eat any birds of the raven kind.”

These animals are especially nourished among rocks and in the hollows of cliffs. “Do you know the time when the ibices give birth?” the Lord says to Job. “Or have you watched when the does give birth?”

How many other things there are in Scripture that are even more obscure and far removed from human knowledge than those about which the Lord himself seems to have spoken in this book, compared with what he is now saying to Job! For what difficulty is there in knowing the time when does and ibices give birth? Or why should it be so hidden from human knowledge that one could be entirely ignorant of the time when these animals give birth, especially since these very animals live almost [Col. 0767A] in the midst of human beings?

Therefore, lest the Lord’s speech seem trivial to some people, or be judged by them to be superfluous, we must look more deeply into what he said. We should say that, in the mysteries, the apostles, apostolic men, and all preachers of the truth were prefigured under the names of these animals.

Through the strength of faith and patience, as though upon rocks, by the Spirit who imbues them, they give birth within themselves to the perfectly formed word of the Gospel; or they give birth amid the pains of persecutions.

The one who said, “For in Christ I gave you birth through the Gospel,” was also giving birth upon a rock.

I have established this future time, and perhaps you, with the souls of those mentioned above likened to does—which conceive through fear of me so as to give birth to the spirit of salvation upon the earth—have watched it with the utmost diligence, as though performing the office of a midwife, giving them a mouth and wisdom from the womb of their mind, so that they might bring forth into this light the word of preaching, perhaps less solid or complete, like a fetus.

Have you counted the months of their conception, and have you known the time of their giving birth? The living and powerful word of God, penetrating to the division of soul and spirit, and also of joints and marrow, works in this spiritual conception certain stages of growth, as though through the months of time in the recesses of hearts. This first appeared in the apostles, who at the beginning of their preaching seemed small and insignificant; but gradually, as the Spirit strengthened them, the word was shown to have reached its full measure of grace. Giving birth to it, as it were, they brought it forth whole, perfect, and complete in the divine promises, writing it down and publishing it for the various Churches. Therefore, from where could you, Job, have known the times of such conception and birth—births that take place in this spiritual womb of the heart—and whose times have been established in the Gospel according to the plan of my foreknowledge? When it is said, “and have you known the time of their giving birth?” others have rendered it, “and have you relieved their pains?” The pains are the persecutions and tribulations inflicted upon preachers; they are released from these pains when, invited to rest, they are released from the body. Or they are released from the pains of persecution when, set in hope, they look beyond present evils toward the promise of eternal reward.

They bend down toward the offspring and give birth, and they send forth cries. By offering milk-like teaching to unbelievers and the weak, as the Apostle says, “I gave you milk to drink, not food,” preachers are in a certain sense humbled and descend from the height of wisdom to lower things, so that the mature man may become a little one, and that he may be to those without the law as though he himself were without the law. While they strive to form and give birth to them in Christ, they send forth cries, being burdened by Christ’s enemies beyond measure and beyond their strength, so that they become weary even of living. Of such people the Apostle also says, “And now, weeping, I say that they are enemies of the cross of Christ.” Or they send forth such cries out of the affection of charity, as the same Apostle says: “I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart.” Again he says: “Because of great tribulation and anguish of heart I wrote to you with many tears.” [Col. 0768A] In grief, from the depths of charity, he says to such people: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.” Again, in the Acts of the Apostles, when he addresses the whole assembled brotherhood, he says: “Keep watch, remembering that for three years, night and day, I did not cease to admonish each one of you with tears.” And again he says: “You yourselves know how I was with you throughout the whole time, serving the Lord with all humility and tears.” These things have been said so that we may know that tribulation, anguish, tears, and continual pain of heart belong to the groans and cries of the saints.

Alternatively, they bend down toward the offspring, give birth, and send forth cries when preachers of the truth have begun to preach the word of faith by the publication of their teaching. At once they are bent down by their adversaries—that is, humbled by prison custody and beatings. But because the word of God is not bound even in chains, there also they nevertheless bring forth for the peoples that by which they too are born in Christ. As the holy Apostle said, as we have mentioned, to those regenerated: “In Christ Jesus, through the Gospel, I begot you.” Then they send forth cries of prayer to God, either entreating God for their persecutors or humbly imploring the perseverance of the faithful and the assistance of divine grace. Alternatively, they send forth cries because “whoever increases knowledge increases sorrow”: the saints groan as they consider how great are the dangers of this life and how far they are from the virtues they seek.

Their young separate themselves and go out to pasture; they go forth and do not return to them. By apostolic childbirth, the children whom the saints have begotten in Christ are separated either from their former errors or even from carnal works—things of which they are now ashamed, so that they may no longer live for themselves but for Christ, who died and rose again for them. They go out to pasture—that is, daily awakened through knowledge of deeper understanding, they advance by their way of life, saying, like the holy creatures of the true shepherd: “The Lord rules me, and I shall lack nothing,” and the other words that follow in the same psalm. Thus, I say, the holy children of those who proclaim peace go out to pasture, as I have already said: they grow and advance. They go out to the Lord’s pasture, to this nourishment of holy souls and these spiritual delights, daily progressing beyond the infancy of their conduct, advancing in the merit of virtue toward a perfect man. And they do not return to them. They do not return, so that they need to be taught again what are the elementary beginnings of the words of God. They do not return to what lies behind, but stretch themselves toward what lies ahead. They do not return like certain people to whom the Apostle says: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.” Rather, they ascend the stages of ascent and walk from virtue to virtue. Such children therefore cannot hear, as the Galatians did, the voice of the rebuking Apostle: “I wish I were present with you and could change my tone.” Thus this word of God, under the figure of does and ibexes, describes the apostles, as I have already said, and apostolic men, as well as all the teachers of the Church, [Col. 0769A] through whose teaching the Church begets spiritual children for herself. Every soul that conceives from the word of God gives birth to children of good works; yet it must be like a doe and an ibex, so that it may dwell upon the mountains and nourish its young among the rocks, and be swift and eager to run the Lord’s way. It also brings serpents out of its land and lives for a long time, hearing the prophet: “The years of your life shall be increased.” For such does there are lofty mountains, which the Lord’s voice perfects and whose feet he will bring to completion.

Who set the wild ass free, and who loosed its bonds? Above we showed that in the doe and the ibex the figure of the Church is represented. Now, however, by the name of the wild ass we believe that the Jewish people can be understood: God abandoned them because of their unbelief, as he says: “And he gave them over to the desires of their heart.” God testifies in many other passages of Scripture that this would happen. We do not absurdly understand its bonds to be the legal commandments. For the prophet rebukes and reproves this same stubborn and rebellious people, saying: “Israel is a wanton heifer; you have broken the yoke and burst the bonds.” Thus the Lord left this people like a wild ass—an unclean and unbridled animal—so that, because it had always resisted obedience, it might be released from the yoke of his rule and from the bonds of the commandments of the devil, and, according to the Apostle, being a slave of sin, might be free in relation to righteousness. For the Lord himself says of the Jews in the psalm: “Let us break their bonds and cast their yoke from us”—where the Trinity of God itself seems to have spoken. Just as in Genesis, when the human being was made, God spoke in the plural: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness,” so here too he said: “Let us break their bonds and cast their yoke from us.” The Acts of the Apostles clearly explain this passage in the same way. There the apostles raised their voice to God and said: “Lord, you who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, who through the Holy Spirit, by the mouth of our father David, your servant, said: ‘Why did the nations rage, and the peoples devise futile things? The kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ.’” Therefore, because of the great crime committed against Christ, the Son of God, the Father—who had foretold through his Spirit that this would happen—said: “Let us break their bonds [Col. 0769D] and cast their yoke from us.” A great and abominable sin was committed when they crucified the Savior, so that rightly the bonds of God’s commandments were broken by them and the yoke of the law was cast off.

But since the yoke and bonds are said to be theirs, although they belonged rather to God than to the Jews, to whom he had given the law and the commandments, this must especially be investigated: why is it said in this way? The reason is that the Jews, understanding the law carnally and supposing that they fulfilled it through works, had made it as though their own, as the Apostle says: “Israel, pursuing the law of righteousness, did not attain the law of righteousness.” Why? “Because it was not from faith, but from works.” And therefore he continues concerning them: “For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to the righteousness of God.” [Col. 0770A] When he says that they wished to establish their own righteousness, he does not mean that the law had been established by them. Rather, in the law that comes from God they had established their own righteousness when they believed that they could fulfill that same law by their own strength. For this reason, in accordance with this interpretation, the bonds of the Jews are said to be broken by God and their yoke cast off.

To whom he gave a house in the wilderness. I made the just, who were abandoned in the wilderness, dwell there, bereft of the protection of my defense, as I later also spoke through the prophetic mouth, saying: “Let their dwelling be desolate, and let there be no one inhabiting their tents.” That people therefore became a wilderness and a desert, because they were deprived and bereft of the law, prophecy, the priesthood, sacrifice, [Col. 0770B] divine benefits, and even the protection of grace.

And its tents in a land of salt. So that it might live without any hope of God’s promise, sterile and fruitless, it is said to have received a land of salt, where, apart from the bitterness by which it would provoke God to anger, it would have nothing. Thus elsewhere the prophet says to God: “You have made rivers into a desert and the outlets of waters into thirst; a fruitful land into salt because of the wickedness of those who dwell in it.”

It despises the multitude of the city and does not hear the cry of the taskmaster. This city is the Church, which consists of an innumerable multitude of peoples, of which the Lord says: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden.” Therefore every Jew who despises this city and rejects it [Col. 0770C] disdains it; he also does not hear the cry of anyone preaching the word of God and demanding the obedience of faith—that is, he refuses to obey. For this reason their heart has become fat, and they have closed their eyes, lest they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, and understand with their heart.

It surveys the mountains of its pasture and searches out every green thing. The mountains are the proud teachers—namely, the scribes and Pharisees of their law. As though looking up to them and paying them honor, it circles around them with the pursuit of flattery. It certainly does not withdraw from those in whom there is human teaching; in those mountains, where they boast that they possess the pasture of the carnal law, it searches out every green thing belonging to the delights of the flesh and delicate Sabbaths—things which, like the surface of a greening law in its histories, possess no fruit of the figures they contain.

Will the rhinoceros wish to serve you, or will it remain at your manger? Or, as others have said: “Will the monoceros wish to serve you?” From the different editions of the translators we understand that the rhinoceros and the monoceros are the same animal, and that in Latin it is understood as unicornis, “unicorn,” or as having a horn above its nose. Such wild beasts are found in the wilderness of the East, and are sometimes seen or captured by human beings. This monoceros, therefore, prefigures the image of the gentile people; its pride is also signified by the horn. Thus the prophet says to certain sinners and proud people on God’s behalf: “I said to the wicked, ‘Do not act wickedly,’ and to the sinners, ‘Do not raise your horn.’ Do not lift your horn on high,” because in those whom God rebukes there is a long-standing and ancient pride. In another edition, at this same place in the psalm, we read: “Do not raise your horn on high, speaking with an ancient neck.” In many other passages of Scripture, too, we read that pride is designated by the word “horn,” although “horn” can also be spoken in a good sense, as in: “He will exalt the horn of his Christ.” The Lord Christ himself, because of his unique sovereignty, is sometimes also called a unicorn. We also read that horns signify kingdoms, as is contained in Daniel and the Apocalypse.

This monoceros, which through worldly wisdom had been stretched upward by the swelling of pride, will it be subjected to you, the Lord says to Job, so that through faith, serving in holiness and righteousness, it may submit the neck of its obedience and, becoming gentle and humble, return to the Lord’s manger and be filled with the sacred nourishment of the words of God and of the assumed humanity. Or will it be subjected so that it may dwell within the enclosure of my Church, which will be a stable for travelers and a saving refuge for those who renounce this world? There it may grow fat on the nourishment of spiritual foods, teachings, and heavenly words, and what was later to be proclaimed through the prophet may be fulfilled in it: “The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master’s manger.” In the monoceros mentioned here, just as in the prophet by the ass, the unclean and uncircumcised people of all nations is signified.

Will you bind the rhinoceroses to the plow with your cord, or will it break up the clods of the valleys behind you? In this passage we must understand the cord as the very charity of Christ, which is foremost among all virtues. Of it the Apostle says to those who love and cherish God: “Bound together in charity.” The prophet had formerly foretold that they would be bound by its bonds, saying to God: “The labor of Egypt, the commerce of Ethiopia, and the men of Saba, tall men, shall pass over to you and shall be yours; they shall walk behind you, bound with bracelets.” David also speaks of how believers would be bound by the bonds of God’s charity through the ministers of the word, saying: “To bind their kings with fetters.” By these names for bonds he wished to demonstrate the strength of Christ’s charity, which, strong and powerful even in iron bracelets, constrains people to the love of the Lord.

This rhinoceros, therefore—that is, the once-uncircumcised people, unclean through the foreskin of carnal pleasures and through unbelief—bound by this exceedingly strong cord of Christ’s charity, so that no creature can separate it from Christ, breaks up in the body the clods of the valleys, that is, the hardness of sins, and cultivates in its body the Lord’s land, according to the Apostle, who says: “You are not your own.” Therefore this land is especially the Lord’s, in which first there takes place a cleansing of all sins, as though of thorns and briars. Then, by the plow of the cross and the iron of the Lord’s Passion, hardness of heart is worn down and the clods of the valleys are broken. By the name of valleys I think people humbled by sins and cast down into the depths are signified, as we have in the psalm: “He has arranged ascents in his heart, in the valley of weeping.” Hence Isaiah, when prophesying with rebuke against sinful Jerusalem, placed this title at the head of his prophecy: “The burden of the valley of vision.”

The monoceros therefore crushes the clods of such valleys when it subdues the earth of the humbled body and prepares it to receive the seeds of heavenly commandments and to produce fruits; when, with the Apostle, it chastises its body and brings it into subjection; when it strives to remove from itself all dullness and the hard stupidity of an obstinate heart. Yet, the Lord says, it will be able to accomplish this only if it obediently follows me as its ruler and guide. Hence the Lord says to Job: “Or will it break up the clods of the valleys behind you?”—as we have in the psalm: “My soul has clung to you.” And the prophet says concerning such people: “They shall walk behind you, bound in fetters.” Here I see feet worthy of wonder: the more tightly they are fettered, the more swiftly they go forth without stumbling.

Will you have confidence in its great strength, and will you leave your labors to it? Will you believe it, that it will return seed to you and gather your threshing floor? I, the Lord, know the strength of its charity, its patience, and its long-suffering. Therefore I left to it, for imitation of me, all the labors of my dispensation. By believing in me it will understand what I endured for its sake: I bore slaps, blows, and spitting, and labored for it. Flying back to the heavens, I left it examples of labor and virtue. What I entrusted and committed to it, with my grace helping it, may it return as multiplied seed; may it make the thirtieth, sixtieth, and hundredfold fruit grow in the threshing floor of my Church, and gather your threshing floor—as the apostles did, and many teachers after the apostles.

The wing of the ostrich is like the wings of the heron and the hawk. Three kinds of herons are said to exist. Some report that one of them is white in color; another, somewhat like a crane, is varied with different colors; and they assert that the third kind is black, not only swift and savage in pursuing prey but also exceedingly uncontrolled in mating, so much so that at the time of mating blood boils from its eyes. The heron is named in the one hundred and third psalm: “The house of the heron is their leader,” where the prophet speaks figuratively of the trees of the Lord. It is also mentioned in Deuteronomy and Leviticus, where Moses prohibits unclean birds from being taken as food, and it is placed there in the same way. There are also several forms or kinds of hawks. The ostrich is therefore compared in its wings to these exceedingly rapacious birds, which live by hunting and prey, as others have said: “The ostrich mixed with the wings of the heron and the hawk.”

Accordingly, in accordance with spiritual understanding and divine meanings, we do not unreasonably understand the ostrich as the Church. Through the bath of regeneration and the word she has been made clean in Christ, and indeed has a wing like the wings of birds that feed on flesh and blood. But those birds use the rowing of their wings in this air, as though upon a sea, to seize prey from other birds. Under this figure, therefore, our spiritual enemies are understood. The ostrich, however, uses its wings in a very different way: it stretches them as though living by faith and by the governance of the two Testaments, which dwell within it. This bird, the Lord says to Job:

When it leaves its eggs upon the earth, will you perhaps warm them in the dust? We must understand the eggs—or the children, as is said later—as the new creation generated in Christ and the white offspring of the holy Church. Let us know that those who are nourished by daily instruction, like offspring of the mother Church, are in the eggs. At length, proceeding from the frugality and imperfection of their beginnings, they emerge from the shell of virtues, as though with the joints of their limbs distinguished and formed, when in this way they have been made light in the Lord from the darkness of vices, daily progressing toward solidity of age and conduct. Let them hear the prophet speaking of them: “Days will be formed, and no one will be in them”—that is, no vice will dominate in them, by which they might be attacked and overcome.

By the children, let us understand those who are already stronger than usual, composed and formed in faith and virtues through the growth of virtues, as through a succession of years, possessing nothing of the disorder of an infirm life. These, as the Lord says, are left upon the earth by the Church when they suffer persecution from the ungodly and from those who think according to earthly things. The Church is said to leave them when she does not resist those who oppose them. The Lord makes them hard through the fervor of faith and patience and exceedingly strong in that fire which he sent upon the earth and in the dust of their fragile flesh.

It forgets that the foot may trample them or that the wild beast of the field may crush them. The Church forgets her children when she does not prevent the adversaries from bringing upon them the troubles of oppression. I think there is a distinction here among tribulations, because it says “the foot may trample” and then says “the beasts of the field may crush.” The crushing by beasts occurs when openly fierce, savage people, resembling beasts in the brutality and cruelty of their character, afflict those who confess Christ even to the atrocity of death. The trampling of the foot, however, is a tribulation of this kind: when, through the insults and excessive contempt of the wicked, the saints are humbled everywhere, crushed as though by trampling.

She is hardened toward her children, as though they were not hers; she has labored in vain, with no fear compelling her. In the tribulations of her children, the Church appears hard and impious because she does not groan or lament the anguish and destruction of her offspring. In her figure, the holy mother of the Maccabees rejoiced over the tortures of her children. In spirit she saw—as the holy mother Church also daily contemplates through faith—how great a glory the present sufferings, endured in confession of the accepted truth, would bring forth eternally. Therefore what follows, “she has labored in vain, with no fear compelling her,” signifies the Church, which prepares her children for temptation and the troubles of this world, hoping from God, in exchange for these temporal evils, for the glory of her children and the everlasting blessedness of incorruption. Alternatively, even if she had grieved for her consecrated children, she would have grieved in vain, because she had no reason for fear: she had not lost them but gained them.

For God deprived her of wisdom and did not give her understanding. The Church has been deprived by God of the wisdom and understanding of this world. The Apostle also commands that this be done, saying: “Whoever wishes to be wise, let him become foolish, so that he may be wise,” because “the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God.”

When the time comes, she raises her wings on high and mocks the horse and its rider. When, he says, the more burdensome and exceedingly bitter affliction of the persecutor breaks in, then the greater is the devotion of the one who entreats God concerning his affliction. He is in a certain sense awakened and, though humbled, is raised by the most watchful concentration of his prayer. With eager effort he lifts his faith and hope on high, like wings supported by the help of God’s grace. When his steps have been sustained by the assistance of such wings, they become swifter and more rapid, so that he mocks his pursuing enemies—that is, the horse and its rider, meaning the devil and the human minister of the enemy, who, in carrying out persecutions against the Church, sits upon any horse of his own, namely, in the heart of the persecuting human being.

Will you give the horse strength, or will you clothe its neck with a neigh? I think this horse can be understood as the hostile power, which is pale, as it is written in the Apocalypse, and is followed by death and [Col. 0774C] Hades. In the prophet Zechariah it is said to be red, sprinkled with the deaths and blood of human beings. Therefore, when God permits strength to be given to it, it is said to be equipped with strength, and its neck with a neigh, so that through the patience and goodness of God it may store up wrath for itself on the day of wrath and the revelation of the righteous judgment of God. For this reason the neigh of pride is signified in its neck, by which it swells up against God and speaks blasphemy.

Will you rouse it like locusts? Our adversary is said to be roused in the manner of locusts when he is said to leap from his places in order to divide regions and lay them waste, as the psalmist says of God: “He spoke, and the locust came.” But I think this rousing signifies eagerness to accomplish a work. Hence it is said to Pharaoh: “For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth.”

The glory of its nostrils is terror. Or, as others have said: “The glory of its breast is boldness.” To put his adversary, namely Christ’s soldier, to flight, the enemy terrifies him even by his breathing. This is the odor of death; this is the furious spirit breathing out slaughter against a human being. He looks backward who turns again to sins or yields to tribulations, as the Lord explains by a parable in the Gospel.

It digs the earth with its hoof. Or, as others have said: “Digging in the field, it exults”—that is, it tramples and crushes carnal people and those who think according to earthly things. When it has humbled and subjected them to itself, it makes them crushed with the kind of contrition that is the contrition and misery found in the ways of ungodly people. In the breadth of such vices, therefore, exulting as though in a field, it digs in order to withdraw from human beings the foundations of virtues, so that, their solidity undermined, they may fall into ruin.

It exults boldly. The proud one rejoices in the audacity of presumption as long as it fights wickedly against human beings.

It advances to meet the armed. The Apostle carefully recounts what the weapons of the saints are against spiritual wickedness. Clothed with such weapons, the enemy is said to advance to meet them when, attempting to storm the citadel of the mind, he throws the battering rams of vices against the wall of virtues. He dared to come out to meet the Lord in the wilderness in order to tempt him, and he also came out to meet the apostles in every city while they were preaching Christ, when he stirred up the people to riots against them, as we also read in the Acts of the Apostles. Hence Paul says in one place: “A great and evident door has been opened to me, but there are many adversaries.” In many other places he does not remain silent about this attack by opponents, which the devil instigated.

It despises fear and does not yield to the sword. It is clear that the devil is driven away by God’s command and invocation. But if we consider his obstinacy and his exceedingly wicked and shameless will, he is not frightened by fear, does not blush, even when terrified and put to flight by the iron sword of God; he returns again and does not depart when refuted.

[Col. 0775C] Above it the quiver will sound; the spear will flash, and the shield. Why does the enemy have a quiver? So that Jews, gentiles, and heretics sitting in it—people in whom there are arrows of death, namely deadly doctrines of error—may shoot those who are upright in heart in the darkness. He has a spear with which to stab sinners with accusations and other vices; arrows signify subtler deceits, while the spear signifies beam-like and deadly offenses. He has a shield with which, through the fullness of malice, he occupies the entire breast of his soldiers. So that they may not be pierced by the darts of the words of God, he knocks them aside, renders them ineffective, and parries them. From this horse, transformed into an angel of light, the spear and shield flash with a certain terrifying brilliance, and through the speech of falsehood the abrupt perversities of the heretics resound. On account of the unceasing intensity and practice of flattering, they are said to flash.

Boiling and snorting, it swallows the earth. The devil, the enemy of the saints, is boiling with vices, burning with the fire of every crime, and snorting in the fury of envy against the human being, so that he may now swallow the sinner with enticements and transfer him, once devoured, into the body of his ruined assembly. The prophet said that he might perhaps be swallowed up in this body unless the Lord were within him, saying: “If the Lord had not been with us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive.” This, therefore, is our adversary, to whom God said: “You shall eat the earth all the days of your life.” For this reason he and his companions, as the Lord’s enemies, will lick the earth.

Nor does it consider the sound of the trumpet’s blast. That is, it refuses to hear the rebuke of the prophets and apostles, to whom it is said: “Raise your voice like a trumpet.” Instead it rages more fiercely, as the true Pharaoh says: “Pursuing, I will seize; I will divide the spoils,” and so forth. In the passages we have mentioned, others have translated: “Above it the bow rejoices, and the sword, the lance, and the spear; by trembling and anger it overturns the earth; nor does it believe until the trumpet has sounded.” I think the same meaning is contained there as in our interpretation. In the bow, sword, and other weapons of the enemy, all his devices are to be understood—devices that rejoice in him and that, by these means as by weapons, kill the human being.

When it hears the trumpet, it says, “Ha!” From afar it smells the battle, the exhortation of the commanders, and the howl of the army. When, he says, our adversary hears the trumpet of God—that is, each teacher of the Church exhorting his fellow soldiers, according to the imperial and divine command, to stand firm in battle against their adversary—he says “Ha!” with a bewildered and scrutinizing mind and astonished ears, as though he were saying: “What am I hearing? Does anyone presume to have such boldness as even to think of preparing battles against me?”

When it says “Ha!” others have rendered it “Bravo!” (“Euge”), which, according to the context, may be understood either favorably or unfavorably, as in the Psalter: “Let them be confounded and ashamed who say to me, ‘Bravo, bravo!’” Therefore in this passage “bravo” is spoken with a mocking mind and a derisive expression. For the subtle, watchful, and exceedingly cunning enemy, who is concerned to destroy the whole earth, when he senses in a human being some beginnings or signs of how he should be resisted, strives to anticipate those who oppose him, as though fattening them for slaughter, lest the weapons of holiness taken up against the devil defend them, and lest they become worthy of veneration when the eternal King arrives.

The howl—or sound, as others have said—of the army of the true commander occurs when the members encourage one another with one spirit, one charity, and one faith, joining together the forces of the fear of the Lord, and address one another so that they may persevere in battle until iniquity passes away. For, because the charity of their King has been poured into them through the Holy Spirit who has been given to them, they are concerned for one another as members of one body.

Will you rouse it like locusts? I caused it to leap from place to place and inflamed it from the present delight of the world toward desire for the future age. Thus it was roused from the body of unbelief, like the sun when warmth arrives. Let us understand that these changes do not concern bodily places, for they are movements of the soul’s affections.

The glory of its nostrils is terror. It terrifies sinners, hating what they are and saying to them concerning God: “Unless you are converted, he will brandish his sword,” and so forth. The glory of its nostrils is this, for the Spirit of God is in its nostrils, as holy Job also said: “The Spirit of God is in my nostrils.” The Church has been drenched with this ointment, namely the Spirit of God, as the Apostle John writes: “And you have an anointing from the Holy One.” [Col. 0777A] Therefore the one of whom we are speaking was fragrant in this passage with what is good in the inner sense of his human being. In that sense, according to the choice of the will, he is for some “the odor of death unto death,” and for others “the odor of life unto life,” because, when the world was filled with the myrrh of faith poured out upon Christ—that is, [Note: [Col. 0777D] Up to this point, “mirae fidei” (“of wondrous faith”) had been printed erroneously; we had no doubt that it should be corrected to “myro,” that is, “ointment.” See Jerome’s Prologue to the books of Samuel and Malachi, [Col. 0778D] at the end, where he calls it “the most precious myrrh of faith,” and the observations we make there.] with the myrrh of faith—the peoples of all believers have been anointed with that same sacred chrism. For this reason the ointment itself, which before the Savior’s coming to be known was kept within the narrow confines of an alabaster vessel, was given the name *pisticum*, so that we might understand that the peoples of believers, as he said, have been consecrated with chrism. By the glory of this fragrance, therefore, the inner sense is filled with something like the terror of birth.

It digs the earth with its hoof. It exults boldly and advances to meet the armed. Whatever it possesses in itself that is most important for perseverance of substance, by that good of virtue it cleaves and stirs the earth. It does not permit the ground to remain uncultivated merely for walking upon, but strives to make the field fruitful and rich. Hence it exults boldly before God, so that it may hear said of itself, as of others: “Coming, they shall come with exultation, carrying their sheaves.” And likewise may it hear: “Good servant, because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much.”

It advances to meet the armed before it is overwhelmed by the darts of vices or persecutions from spiritual enemies. Standing in the battle line of virtues, it forestalls the enemies rushing upon it, lest it be wounded by any blow of desire or even of distrust. Thus it advances to meet the enemies armed with vices and prepared for attack. In accordance with this meaning, holy David says: “I will pursue my enemies and overtake them,” and so forth.

It despises fear and does not yield to the sword. However many threats are made, with great terror, so that when enemies seek to inspire fear it may say: “The Lord is my illumination and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the defender of my life; I shall fear none of my adversaries when evildoers draw near against me to eat my flesh.” Therefore, because I hope in this salvation of God’s light: “Though armies encamp against me, my heart will not fear. And though battle rise against me, I will not yield to the sword,” for I eagerly desire to undergo death for Christ.

Over him the quiver will resound; the spear and shield will flash. Above the outer and bodily man—of whom the prophet says, “And beneath me my dullness was troubled”—we understand the soul to be like a citadel, in which each of the saints, in his inner man, has the arrows of God’s words as though within a quiver. When he brings them forth for caution, or draws them into the midst through frequent correction like piercing darts, he intends to strike with their blows those who ought rightly to be wounded for salvation.

Over him, I say, the quiver of God’s words resounds, though he walks in agitation. From this it is understood that the one rightly sings psalms and corrects delinquents whose holiness advances daily toward what lies ahead. Thus the great apostle, the powerful horse of the Lord, says: “But forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead.” Or, to put it more briefly and plainly: this quiver is the place of the heart, in which the arrows of God’s words are stored and kept. And the Lord significantly says that this quiver resounds over him—that is, over the horse—because over his exterior man the quiver of his heart, filled with divine words, reigns while he evangelizes the word with great power as the Lord’s warrior and a strong man in battle.

Over this horse likewise the spear and shield are brandished. The spear is the vigilant strength or steadfastness of the mind, which rebukes sinners or mortifies the vices within itself that must be pierced. The shield, however, is the shield of faith, by which it can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one. Because of their unceasing use in warfare, these weapons are said to be brandished; they are always prepared for battle. For of such shining weapons it is said: “Your darts will go forth into the light, into the splendor of the flashing of your years.”

**“Fervent and roaring, he swallows the earth.”**

Fervent in faith through the Spirit, and roaring like the Savior, who, when he spiritually raises one dead in vices, groans in the spirit. So this one, I say, will roar against his enemies, whether vices or even open persecutors; and thus he swallows his earth when he converts it from a carnal way of life to a spiritual one. Roaring in this manner, and greatly angry with himself in indignation, he swallows it, as I have said, so that he may transfer it into the affection of his spirit, where there is “the hidden man of the heart in incorruptibility, with a quiet and modest spirit,” who is wealthy in the sight of God.

**“He does not reckon the sound of the trumpet’s blast.”**

He is clothed with such strength of mind that he fears no terror from his adversaries, since he is prepared at every sound of enemies challenging him.

**“When he hears the trumpet, he says, ‘Well done!’”**

From afar he scents war, the exhortation of commanders, and the howling of the army. When he hears the Gospel preached in a loud voice, he rejoices and exults, which is what “Well done!” signifies. When he hears the examples of all the strongest men among the leaders who proclaim the divine Scriptures, and also the congregation of the whole Church, which is called the army of God, sounding with unanimity and a single faith, he says, “Well done!” He hears both the joyful exhortation of the commanders and the army’s howl.

Here “howl” signifies what occurs when warriors standing in battle formation and preparing to fight encourage one another. But someone may say: How can it happen that one and the same thing is understood figuratively sometimes in a good sense and sometimes in a bad one, as we have done here, saying that this horse can be understood allegorically in both a bad and a good sense?

I answer that whenever a noun occurs in Scripture without qualification—for example, simply “mountain,” without the addition “Mount Zion” or “corrupt mountain”—I think it is not unreasonable that an exposition of the same thing may freely be taken in either direction. But where there is a qualification, such as “the lion from the tribe of Judah,” or “he sits in ambush like a lion,” there Christ is understood without hesitation, or else the devil, our adversary.

If it pleases us, let us give an example concerning the tree. In the Gospel the Lord says to his disciples: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this tree, ‘Be uprooted and transplanted into the sea,’ and it will obey you.” Some have understood this to mean that the faith of believers uproots the enemy and tears him from the earth of the Church—that is, from the land of Judea and confession—and transfers him into the sea of the peoples, namely, of impious men. The evil spirits in the Gospel can also signify this very thing: together with the unclean and sinful men indicated by the name of swine, they were cast into the sea.

Others, however, have wished the same tree to signify the Lord, and have interpreted it in this way: through the preaching of the apostles, who received the grace of Christ and the power of faith, Christ the Lord is in a certain sense uprooted from that nation of the Jews, in which he was held as though by the stock of his lineage, and transplanted into the sea of the nations, just as the Lord himself said to those same Jews: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits.”

**“Does the hawk grow feathers through your wisdom, spreading its wings toward the south?”**

It follows that we should understand this hawk in a good sense: namely, as the holy person who, through conversion, has received wisdom, so that he has ceased to plunder and seize, and has stopped living on the flesh of worldly perceptions. He has laid aside the garments of the old man in baptism, and, growing feathers, has in a certain sense been renewed, so that his youth is like the eagle’s—especially since, possessing the promise of the present life and of the future life, which is signified by the wings, he has turned toward the south, from which comes the warmth of faith, and from which he has learned that Christ came.

The prophet had also foretold that this should be done, saying: “God will come from the south, and the Holy One from the shadowed and dark mountain.” Those looking toward Bethlehem, the city of the Lord, know that Jerusalem lies to the south, that is, in the South. According to the tropological interpretation, the Bridegroom invites this warm wind, so that the spices of grace may grow fervent, saying: “Rise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow upon my garden, and blow upon my spices.”

Where, then, it says, “spreading its wings toward the South,” some have said: “With wings spread out, motionless, and looking toward the South.” Thus it speaks of the perseverance of one who, living by the governance of the two Testaments through the warmth of faith, contemplates the splendor of eternal blessedness.

**“Will the eagle be lifted up at your command?”**

Sometimes “eagle” is understood in a good sense and refers to God himself, as Moses says: “As an eagle protects its nest and hovers over its young,” as we said above. Here, however, an adversarial power is called an eagle by God. Raised up by God’s permission into pride, it can accomplish much, as the prophet says: “And he will be like an eagle over the house of God.” The prophets also mark him in many places in their writings as exceedingly proud—that is, the devil. Hence he is also called great, because he rises in swelling pride above the mountains of the north and sets his throne above the stars of heaven, desiring to make himself equal to the Most High.

**“And he will place his nest in lofty places.”**

In the great and elevated things of this world, and among evil men, he establishes his seat, so that he may dwell among them like a harsh lord and a fierce and very powerful king.

**“He dwells among the rocks.”**

That is, he dwells and lives among lofty, hard things, strong in wickedness.

**“And he remains among precipitous cliffs.”**

The precipitous cliffs are understood as blasphemers, whose hearts are exceedingly hard and untamed and who, weighed down by the burden of their sins, hang inclined toward their own ruin.

**“And among inaccessible crags.”**

The inaccessible crags are people stretched upward through excessive pride of heart. No one approaches their arrogance, which, as though unique and belonging to them alone, serves their own evil.

**“From there he surveys his prey.”**

Through those whom we have said are excessively lifted up by pride—whom we understand as heresiarchs, Jews, or the wise men of the world, that is, philosophers—he captures all the lost in his snares as his prey through their errors, in accordance with the prophet, who says the same thing about the devil: “His prey is choice.”

**“And his eyes look out from afar.”**

By the name “eyes,” God has designated the mind of our very shrewd and watchful adversary, as he searches out the strength of the saints who are fighting. When he says “from afar,” he means that the gaze of his mind looks ahead with subtle attention, because through the shrewd suspicion of practiced wickedness he foresees even what is to come. The reference is not to distances between places but to the beginnings of the human disposition toward right living.

This, I say, he sees from afar: his subtle spirit and gaze, exceedingly ready for every evil, acts from the very beginnings, suppressing and extinguishing the good things that are beginning to sprout before the human endeavor is strengthened in any way, and making the slain man stink with sin.

**“His young ones lick blood, and wherever there is a carcass, he is immediately present.”**

His young ones are his sons or his companions, who, in a conspiracy of tyranny, plotted iniquity with him against God. These, thirsting for human blood through the lividness of envy, lick it. When he says, “wherever there is a carcass, he is immediately present,” some have said, “wherever there is a carcass, they are immediately found.” Whether this is said of the author of evil or of his satellites, wherever there is a carcass, sin is immediately generated there, and it stinks in the soul as a wound does in the body.

And the Lord added and spoke to Job:

**“Will the one who contends with God so easily be silent? Surely the one who reproves God must answer him.”**

The whole dispute woven through the earlier parts of this book is explained by the Lord at this point, when he says: “Will the one who contends with God?” Hence it becomes clear that Job spoke against God with a certain presumptuous boldness, relying on the confidence of a good conscience; yet he did not blaspheme God, as some think.

If he said anything harsher, he said it with reference to the same matter to which God referred—namely, that God is just. He spoke with regard to the tenor of God’s justice, not in order to blaspheme God. Thus, by seeking him according to his just judgment, he almost constrains him and says that he should either spare him or declare him unjust. For how could he think that God judged him unjustly when he knew him to be perfectly just?

Having therefore received from God the reason for the things he had spoken—namely, that God himself governed and ruled everything he had created, and that nothing unjust could possibly come from him—Job was convicted, as is clearly shown here, and remained silent. But the Lord admonishes and compels him: since he had contended with God and attempted to reprove him, he himself must answer the questions put to him.

And the writer of this book says:

**“But Job answered the Lord and said: Since I have spoken lightly, what can I answer?”**

Blessed Job, acknowledging that he had spoken lightly and not with complete understanding, says that he is altogether unable to answer God. For this reason he desires to restrain himself in silence, as he says:

**“I will place my hand over my mouth. I have spoken once; would that I had not spoken, and a second time, but I will add no more.”**

Because he had spoken one word and another by which he might have caused offense, I think these are the words I identified above:

“I choose hanging for my soul, and death for my bones; and if he scourges, let him kill at once, and let him not laugh at the punishments of the innocent.”

## CHAPTER XL

[Col. 0781C]

**“And the Lord answered Job and spoke from the whirlwind.”**

That is, either from the force of rebuke or from the darkened air and clouds of the disturbed atmosphere.

**“Gird your loins like a man; I will question you, and you will answer me.”**

Or, as others have said: “No; rather, gird your loins like a man,” and so forth. The meaning is: “I do not want you to remain silent,” God says, “as you yourself intend; rather, speak, and answer me concerning what I ask you.”

The letters of Scripture indicate in many ways how God speaks to human beings, although he himself is spirit: thus the Father speaks to the Son from a cloud, to Moses in a flame of fire, and the word of the Lord comes to Ezekiel as he sits with the elders of Israel, while he alone hears what is spoken by the Lord.

[Col. 0781D]

**“Will you annul my judgment and condemn me, so that you may be justified?”**

In this passage the Lord makes clear the sense in which holy Job spoke the words written above. He rebukes him for this very reason: Job wished to justify himself by insulting and disparaging God, calling justice injustice on account of the very sufferings he asserted had been unjustly inflicted upon him.

**“And if you have an arm like God, and thunder with a voice like his, surround yourself with majesty, raise yourself on high, and be glorious; clothe yourself in splendid garments. Scatter the proud in your fury, confound them, and humble every arrogant person when you look upon him. Look upon all the proud, confound them, and crush the wicked in their place. Hide them together in the dust, and plunge their faces into the pit; then I too will confess that your right hand can save you. Behold Behemoth, whom I made with you; he will eat grass like an ox.”**

This is what he means: Can you overcome and scatter those very demons by whose tribulations you are attacked and crushed? Even if you were to contend against God, if you possessed strength like God’s and the voice of your command thundered fearfully throughout the world, could you surround yourself with the majesty of eternity, be exalted in the glory of honor and sublimity, and fortify yourself with all the virtues of holiness as with splendid garments? Could you nevertheless scatter all the proud by the just judgment of your indignation and anger, drive them into their place—that is, into the prison of hell—and crush them? Could you even hide them together in the dust, separated from the light of the saints, or, as others have said, shut them beneath the earth? Could you plunge their faces—that is, their souls together with their intellectual faculties, like the lights of their eyes—into the pit of hell?

Since it is impossible for a human being to possess these things, it is equally foolish for him to speak against God as though he were his equal. Rather, he ought humbly to hope for mercy from him, so that by his right hand—that is, by his power—he may be saved from the proud, the arrogant, and the wicked whom I have mentioned.

Know this very thing: the strong devil, your most powerful enemy, whom, because of the savage fury of his monstrous spirit, I have called Behemoth, after a ferocious beast—I will make him eat grass in your presence as an ox, a tame animal, not flesh as a lion does. For when flesh is eaten, it cannot happen without the death of a living creature.

But with respect to you it is not so, as I have already said, for by the command of my authority I ordered this concerning him: “Behold, he is in your hand; preserve his life.”

The teachers of the Church who knew Hebrew writings have generally rendered *Behemoth* in Latin as though it meant “many.” Therefore, in this passage the enemy devil is described together with the whole body of his satellites. Because of the plurality expressed by his name, the ancients interpreted it in this way: “Behold the beasts that I made with you; they eat grass like oxen.” That is, it was also accomplished by the power of my right hand that they should receive your substance and possessions to devour—things which, because of the riches of your precious mind, are compared to grass.

Thus he took away from you only lowly and temporal things, signified by the name “grass,” not great and lofty things—that is, the ornaments of the soul—which, if you were stripped of them, the ruin of blasphemy would overwhelm you. By such a sin the whole human being is devoured by the devil.

Thus God speaks of him:

**“His strength is in his loins, and his power in the navel of his belly.”**

In the loins and the navels of the belly, the pleasure of the belly or the luxury of the flesh is understood. This was inserted into the genital members after the fall of the first man, so that, beyond the measure of natural law, those members might be tickled by the incentives of lust even when a person does not wish it.

Thus the followers of pleasure, supplying strength to the devil through their own vices, become his portion and his associates, so that they are his members, while he himself is their head, as though of his own body.

[Col. 0783A]

**“He tightens his tail like a cedar.”**

This seems to me to mean that he will not return to God even in his final members, which are signified by the tail. That is, he will never repent of his proud and wicked tyranny. Rather, exalted like a cedar, he will be broken and shattered by the voice of the Lord who judges justly.

He is tightened because he is compared with very hard wood—namely, the hardness of heart—so that he may not understand, becoming foolish, and, blinded, may not see to the end.

Or “he tightens his tail” may be understood as follows: the prophet speaks falsely; according to the authority of the holy prophets, the tail is falsehood. Thus Behemoth binds these beings to himself as enemies, associates, and ministers, joining them in the bond of a united conspiracy. Of them the ancient interpreters said: “He raised his tail like a cypress,” signifying the lifting of their minds on high by naming a tree that rises upward from a single trunk to a lofty summit.

[Col. 0783B]

**“The sinews of his testicles are intertwined.”**

By “sinews,” he seems to me to refer to certain exceedingly strong and alluring bonds of pleasure by which he entangles carnal men. Concerning such vices the prophet also blames human beings, saying among other things: “But those who turn aside toward bonds.” I think the prophet is speaking simply of an almost inextinguishable pleasure in human members, to which our flesh would surrender as a captive unless God’s grace came to its aid, in accordance with the Apostle.

**“His bones are like tubes of bronze; his cartilage is like plates of iron.”**

By these names for the members it is indicated that the devil and his companions are hard, rigid, stubborn, and inflexible. In the bones and cartilage, within and without—that is, in thought and deed—the perfection of his wickedness is demonstrated.

As for the statement “his cartilage is like plates of iron,” others have said, “His spine is molten iron,” so that it may be understood that the devil will never humble himself before God through repentance.

**“He is the beginning of the ways of God. The one who made him will apply his sword to him.”**

The sense here seems to me to be that, for walking in the ways of God and observing the Lord’s commandments through obedience, he was created by God first among the other creatures; hence it is said, “He is the beginning of the ways of the Lord.”

For in the prophet Ezekiel, at the head of the fiery stones, he is reported to have been first of all the angels, and to have been a crown in the hand of the Lord.

Or the statement may be understood in this way: God, always remaining in his eternity, appears, as it were, to go forth into the making of creatures, and these are his ways, so that invisible things might appear through visible ones. Or each creature is a way of God, by which one goes toward knowledge of God, since what is known by him comes to be known. Or the ways of God are those occasions when God, as though coming to a rational creature, makes himself known to it.

Thus Behemoth is called the beginning of the ways of God because, being created first, he received knowledge of his God, by whom he was created.

The Lord Christ, however, is reported as created at the beginning of God’s ways, so that, by reconciling the world through his blood, he might walk the way of the Father’s commandments as his works. He demonstrated this at the beginning of his Gospel preaching.

When the Lord says, “The one who made him will apply his sword to him,” the meaning is: the one who made Behemoth will apply his own sword to him; that is, he will be punished by the evil with which he killed others. The Holy Spirit also spoke of his kind in the psalm: “Sinners have drawn the sword,” and, “Let their sword enter their own heart.”

We must nevertheless note here a change of persons. Earlier the Lord said that he himself had made Behemoth the beast, but now he says that another created him, saying: “He is the beginning of the ways of God, who made all things.” This may be explained by saying that the Father made all things in the Son, as the prophet says to God: “You made all things in wisdom.”

Others have said: “He is the beginning of the Lord’s creation, to be mocked by his angels,” that is, by the saints.

He is mocked by them when, through the grace of the Holy Spirit and the merit of holiness, he is subjected to them and is driven from possessed bodies by the invocation of Christ’s name. This is done by those who, putting away all malice, deceit, and hypocrisy, are, according to Isaiah, newborn infants in Christ. Concerning them he prophesied, through the power of Christ’s grace, against their adversary, the devil, in the spirit of foresight, saying: “The infant will delight over the hole of the asp, and into the den of the basilisk the weaned child will put his hand.”

And the Lord, speaking of his entire body, said to those whom he had made innocent and little ones: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and they will harm you not at all.”

**“The mountains bear herbs for him; all the beasts of the field play there.”**

These mountains are situated in the northern region, where the proud devil says that he will sit, declaring: “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High.” We may reasonably understand these mountains as proud and excessively exalted men who imitate the swelling of his heart.

Dwelling among them, he feeds upon the temporary pleasure called by the name “herbs,” and delights in the evil, flourishing, and vigorous harmful pleasure that grows among them. On these mountains all the beasts of the field also play.

These beasts are the devil’s companions and ministers. Concerning them the prophet prays to God: “Do not hand over to beasts the soul that confesses you.” The field, according to the Lord’s authority, is this world, as he says in the Gospel: “The field is this world.”

On such mountains, which bear the herbs of luxury and not fruit-bearing trees, these beasts—namely, the adversarial powers, lacking the firmness of virtues—play amid the flow and wantonness of vices. On all their mountains, that is, in their crimes and unspeakable offenses, they glory.

Others have said concerning this passage: “They ascended a precipitous mountain; he made joy for the four-footed creatures in Tartarus.” I think the precipitous mountain signifies the summit of the devil’s pride, to which he raised himself exceedingly, so that from it they might fall all the way into the depths of hell.

Thus he made joy—that is, he gave consolation—either to those who, agreeing with his pride, were cast from heaven and destined for Tartarus, or to those sinners who through him fell into the depths of hell. In their person the prophetic word speaks to the prince of the demons himself:

“You too are wounded as we are, and have become like us. Your pride has been brought down to the underworld; your corpse has fallen. He made joy for the four-footed creatures,” as it was said—that is, for sinners who, bent toward the earth or sinking into Tartarus, cannot look up to heaven.

**“Under the shadow he sleeps in the secret place of the reed, in moist places.”**

No one doubts that bodily shadows are meant by the word “shadow.” But in the divine Scriptures, “shadow” sometimes signifies rest and refreshment, and sometimes punishment. Hence it is said, “the shadow of death.” At times shadows are said to be sins, which are as close to death as a shadow is to a body.

Therefore the devil dwells in sins and rests in the secret place of thoughts, or even of the loins; hence these places are called moist. Or he dwells in secret places—that is, in the hidden things of God, which God does not seek out and does not visit, as though they were unworthy of him. Concerning these hidden things the prophet says to God: “Their belly has been filled from your hidden things.”

Thus sins are hidden like darkness from the light of truth. Or, as we have already said, the devil dwells in a remote place of the heart: the heart that is empty of the fear of God lies open to vanity, luxury, and every enticement of vice. This signifies the shadow that does not know the sun and the secret places of the reed.

Others have said: “He sleeps under every kind of tree, beside the rush, the reed, and the sedge.” He means every kind of tree, although all of them are fruitless, possessing neither the marrow of the love of God nor the fruits of good works.

**“The shades protect his shade.”**

His sins rise above the sins and impieties of all the wicked; by a certain protection of his wickedness he defends and conceals them.

Others have said: “Great trees are overshadowed in him.” By this, it seems to me, they meant that although the evil spirits—or the human ministers of the devil—are exalted in pride, the devil surpasses them in the magnitude of his offenses, because he is the inventor of a more wicked crime than the imitator of sin.

**“The willows of the torrent will surround him.”**

Or, as others have said, “the shoots and thickets.” This mortal world is called by the name of a torrent because of its swift and unstable movement, just as the prophet says when prophesying about the Lord’s Passion: “He will drink from the torrent on the way.”

In that dispensation by which he deigned to come to us, he drank on the cross the cup of death, concerning which he said to the Father: “If it is possible, let this cup pass from me.”

The devil is surrounded by the people of this world, who are exceedingly bitter, like leaves, in the perceptions of sin and the faithlessness of unbelief, while pretending to bear the fruit of good works. These people are also joined with him as his associates and companions.

**“Behold, he will swallow the river and will not be amazed; he trusts that the Jordan will flow into his mouth.”**

In many places in Scripture we know that the human race is signified by the name “river.” The adversarial power itself says concerning this: “The river is mine, and I made myself.”

To this river—that is, to the human race—he insinuates desires for lust, pleasure, and love of the present world as it flows downward into the lowest and inferior regions, in the manner of a descending river, so that he can swallow it and, like the underworld, gulp it down. For the human race will rush headlong into the vices mentioned above, so that it can easily be devoured by the enemy.

When he says, “He trusts that the Jordan will flow into his mouth,” the river Jordan contains the sacrament of baptism. When Christ the Lord was baptized in it, our baptism was consecrated.

According to mystical interpretations, its mountains and hills, rams and lambs of sheep, rejoice before the God of Jacob, who, by believing, the younger brother, supplanted the unbelieving elder brother. Concerning the land of this Jordan—that is, the Church—the prophet says in the person of the believer that he remembers the Lord.

Beginning, as it were, from Christ, the modest mountain, who was made modest through his Passion and was made lower than the angels by obeying the Father unto death, this Behemoth, lifted up by excessive presumption, trusts that he can drain into his mouth the Jordan mentioned above, which signifies the sacraments of the Church, and, eager to devour it, enclose it within his belly.

That is, he seeks to make his own again even those whom the blood of Christ has redeemed through the water of regeneration, which the Jordan prefigures, and through the washing of the Holy Spirit—whether by hidden persuasion or open attack—so that they may return to his power and harsh dominion.

**“With a hook in his eyes he will capture him.”**

These words concern the Father’s relation to the Son, according to the address mentioned above, where the Father speaks about him when the subject was the devil: “He is the beginning of the ways of God.”

The Father says concerning the Son that the man of divine majesty, clothed in the assumed flesh of man, will capture this Behemoth—that is, the devil—in his eyes.

“In his eyes,” he says, that is, in the very light of understanding, where the vision of wisdom and of rational nature is found.
