There, I say, divine wisdom was captured while the devil, through his own cunning and craftiness, failed to see whose flesh death had seized to devour. In this way, therefore, the devil was captured.

**“And with stakes he will pierce his nostrils.”**

That is, Christ our Lord will crush and drive back his raging fury, which pants for the destruction of the saints. I think that the saints may rightly be understood here because of the wood of the cross. Thus the Lord humbles and breaks the enemy, and every attack of raging envy, when through those same saints he blunts it against the wood of his cross.

**“Can you draw out Leviathan with a hook?”**

He has changed the figure of the riddle, so that the devil whom above he called Behemoth by a transferred name he now calls Leviathan. There he describes him as a beast inhabiting the earth; here he names him as one who seems to dwell in the waters of the sea.

Hence others have rendered *Leviathan* as “dragon.” It may therefore appear to be some dreadful kind of dragon called Leviathan, whose wickedness and power the devil fittingly represents.

Behemoth is so called because many are with him. For *Behemoth* is said to sound in Latin as though it meant “many.” Thus he may be understood together with his associates and ministers, and rightly as one who is, so to speak, “not of God.”

Some say that *Leviathan* means “addition.” Because he did not stand in the truth, and by exceeding the measure of presumption added pride to himself, he went beyond the good of nature into the swelling and sickness of arrogance. Therefore he was called “addition”: a name formed from crime covered over the condition of the good nature that the good God had created.

The prophet Isaiah prophesies concerning him, saying: “On that day”—whether at the time of Christ’s Passion or at the time of his judgment—“on that day the Lord will visit with his hard, great, and strong sword Leviathan the barred serpent, and Leviathan the twisting serpent, and he will kill the whale that is in the sea.”

This agrees with what another prophet similarly says to God: “You broke the sea by your strength; you broke the heads of the dragons upon the waters.” Here the same devil is described as the head together with his members, and his body and scales are said to be joined by an indissoluble bond.

Thus, the Lord says to Job concerning this typical dragon, Leviathan: Can you perhaps draw him out of the sea of the peoples, so that he will not dominate the waters of the nations? I have resolved, as was said above, to draw him out by the hook of my power through the faith of believers and to dry him up.

In this sense we should understand what the Lord also says in the Gospel: “When a strong man, armed, guards his courtyard, the things he possesses are at peace,” and so forth.

At Christ’s first coming, this was accomplished through the grace of his redemption: people were rescued from the devil’s association and the domination of his people. At his second coming, however, all the devil’s power will be taken away, since the sea—that is, the world—will no longer exist, and the race of his associates will perish from the earth.

Then his sin will also be sought and will not be found, while the Lord reigns forever and ever, death and the inventors of death having been swallowed up in the victory of the resurrection.

When God says in this book that Leviathan will be drawn out with a hook, he speaks of it through another prophet, saying: “I will spread my net over you among a multitude of peoples, and I will draw you out in my dragnet.”

I think the difference between a hook and a dragnet is this: by the hook itself we should understand the Savior, the Son of God clothed in flesh; by the dragnet may be understood the preaching of the Gospel, cast out over an immense expanse from the rising of the sun to its setting, just as the prophet says: “Great is the Lord,” and so forth. He then adds, “extending rejoicing over the whole earth.”

This dragnet of Christ’s preaching is solidly strengthened by the figures of the Old Testament, by images of its meanings, and by many such testimonies of Scripture, tied together as though by knots. Many whales and exceedingly savage dragons of this impious and powerful world have attempted to tear and break it, but have not been able to do so, because God has made its foundation firm, and it cannot be shaken.

For if God is for us, who can be against us?

According to this interpretation, therefore, the same meaning is discerned in the hook and in the dragnet. When the Lord had said to Job, “Can you draw out Leviathan with a hook?” he said to him:

**“And will you bind his tongue with a cord?”**

Just as a cord is woven from many small strands of material to make a bond by which things can be tied together, so the devil, from the multitude of his sins—as though from the strands of small cords—binds for himself the bonds of sacrilegious people. Like a cord made of blasphemies, he binds their tongue, so that the mouth of one speaking iniquity is stopped and closed.

In the Proverbs of Solomon it is written concerning those like him: “Each person is bound by the bonds of his sins.” For this reason the Lord says that the lazy and useless servant, with his hands and feet bound, is to be sent into the outer darkness—that is, bound by the bonds of his sins, which he committed, and sent to punishment according to divine judgment.

The Lord himself also demonstrated this most clearly in a certain passage when he made a whip from the cords of the Jews and drove them from the temple while scourging them with it.

**“Will you put a ring in his nostrils, or pierce his jaw with a bracelet?”**

Or, as others have said, “with a hook.” And “will you pierce with a bracelet,” or, as others have said, “will you pierce his lip with tongs.”

By the names ring, hook, tongs, and bracelet are understood the words of divine power, by which the proud and blasphemous one has been humbled and crushed by God.

**“Will he multiply supplications to you, or speak gentle words to you?”**

Or, as others have said: “Will he speak flatteringly to you?”

He is subject only to God, whom he recognizes as his creator; and his proud mind submits only to the one whom his very conscience fears.

“Will you strike a covenant with him, and will you take him as an everlasting servant?” Although he is rebellious and exceedingly swollen with pride, he is nevertheless compelled and forced, by that good of his very nature which has not entirely perished in him as a testimony to his just condemnation, to confess his Lord and Creator, at least as a wicked servant. This is the covenant, or testament, which he has been commanded to enter into with God. Hence the Lord himself also says: “And you will take him as an everlasting servant.” For he does this by no inclination of his mind, but by the command of divine power. He is therefore called by God an everlasting servant because he will never receive the adoption of the sons of God, or that primacy of angelic dignity. [Col. 0788D]

“Will you mock him as a bird, or bind him for your maidservants?” “To such an extent,” says the Lord, “will the strength of this dragon be humbled and utterly reduced to nothing that he will be regarded as an object of mockery, and will be assigned to be mocked by the holy angels,” as has already been said above. But in saying that he is mocked as though he were a bird, He wished to show by the name “bird” that he is regarded as a small and insignificant thing in comparison with God’s power. And when he is said to be bound for maidservants, this means what the Lord himself says in the Gospel to his disciples: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall harm you.” Thus he is bound and mocked by God’s holy souls, who are Christ’s maidservants, while they command him and his associates, and force him to depart from bodies possessed by him. Every day, throughout the whole world, captivity is taken captive from him; and so, according to the Apocalypse, he is said to be bound for a thousand years. This is understood from the part as referring to the whole, in accordance with the apostle who says: “Little children, it is the last hour”—that is, from the time of the Lord’s coming in our flesh. Thus he is bound so that he may not deceive those who are to be saved by Christ’s grace and redemption.

Others have translated: “Will you bind him like a sparrow for a child?” This means that he is held by a child at the command of my authority and, as though bound, is delivered into his power. This is the child of whom Isaiah says: “The child shall put his hand into the hole of the asp.” Although this prophetic child is a boy of a hundred years, he will die through Christ’s grace—that is, the holy and innocent person will depart from this world to God. We must therefore understand this child as each of the saints who has been reborn to God from the font—that is, from the womb of Mother Church—as a child, and who sucks the Lord’s commandments from her breasts as though they were milk-like nourishment.

“His friends will cut him to pieces; merchants will divide him.” These friends and merchants are to be understood as the saints, and also as all preachers of the truth, to whom Christ the Son of God says: “You are my friends.” Likewise, concerning these same people, he says in a parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking a good pearl,” and so forth. They have set before the world the kingdom of God and the reward of eternal life as a most precious pearl, so that each of the faithful may sell whatever he possesses—namely, the delight of the present life—and exchange it in these transactions and purchase the pearl.

Therefore, the body of this dragon is cut to pieces and divided by the friends and merchants mentioned above, as through them a very great multitude of those who had been lost is separated from his fellowship and brought to the faith of Christ. For many of his powerful ones, strong in wickedness, are separated from his company like his limbs, just as the prophet Habakkuk says to the Lord: “You cut off, in the astonishment of the mind, the heads of the mighty.” And again he says to the Lord: “You have sent death upon the heads of the enemies”—the death, certainly, of vices, so that they may no longer live for themselves but for him who died and rose again for them.

These heads of God’s enemies—that is, the rulers of ungodly peoples—are the kings and nobles of this spiritual dragon. According to the interpretation of the names and another figurative expression, they are said to be bound by the friends and merchants mentioned above, just as the prophet David says: “To bind their kings with fetters and their nobles with iron chains.” These kings and nobles are themselves both dragons and members of that dragon, concerning whom the prophet says to God: “You have broken the heads of the dragons upon the waters.”

“Will you fill nets with the skin of him, and a fish-basket with his head?” All who cling to the devil by agreement in wickedness and imitation are rightly called his skins. I think they are called “skin” because they are joined to him by an inseparable connection and can never, or scarcely ever, be separated from him. Concerning these, therefore, the Lord says that the nets are to be filled.

“Place your hand upon him. Remember the battle; do not speak any further.” This is how He seems to have spoken to me: Having conquered your adversary through me, place your hand upon him, so that you too may mock him. Or, “Place your hand upon him,” as though He had said: If you think that you possess his power and strength, place your hand upon him—that is, if you can, accomplish by the power of your strength that this dragon should tremble and fear you, as he fears me, to whom alone he owes this. But because you can in no way make this great and powerful dragon in wickedness subject to you, remember, amid this tribulation of your punishments, what a fierce and savage enemy you had to fight. Let it be enough for you that you spoke harsh words against me, where I wished you to know that you could not overcome and conquer this strongest of your enemies unless, by the command of my authority, he had been delivered into your power, while your soul was nevertheless guarded by me. Thus you were given into his dominion in such a way that he could afflict you no further than your strength allowed. [Col. 0790B]

“Behold, his hope will deceive him, and before all who see him he will be cast down.” When he has been cast into gehenna and eternal fire in the sight of the holy angels and the innumerable multitude of blessed human beings, his hope—that by which he thinks himself strong enough to escape—will be frustrated by the dreadful and just judgment, and his empty and futile thoughts will be brought to nothing.

## CHAPTER XLI

[Col. 0790C]

“Not as though he were cruel will He raise him up. For who can resist my face, and who has given to me beforehand that I should repay him? All that is under heaven is mine.”

God does not raise up this enemy as a cruel being who desires to punish him or to destroy any of the saints by placing him among them; rather, eternal goodness belongs especially to the excellence of His nature. God is said now to raise up Leviathan in this manner so that He may reveal to others what he is, allowing him, like Pharaoh, to insult them for a longer time through prolonged impunity. God permits this to happen by His most just judgment, either for the exercise and testing of the saints or for the punishment of the wicked.

“For who can resist my face?” Here He seems to have said that every creature yields and trembles at the mere sight of God’s majesty. “Who has given to me beforehand that I should repay him? All that is under heaven is mine.” He did not receive power from anyone, He says, which He might perhaps not previously have possessed, so that He should thank that person for the benefit or offer him some repayment. The apostle speaks according to this meaning as well: “Or who,” he says, “has given to him, and it shall be repaid to him?” In these words God is shown to have always existed.

“I will not spare him with powerful words composed for entreaty.” Perhaps we can understand this as referring to the devil, whose words He is discussing here. Although he is rebellious against God and defiant, he nevertheless feels his trembling Creator; and although forgetful of his condition, he at least, compelled like a wicked servant, pretends to entreat his Lord. [Col. 0791A]

“Who will uncover the face of his garment?” Job says that the devil’s face is veiled by this garment because he transforms himself into an angel of light. His face is uncovered by the Lord when the devices of his wickedness are exposed.

“And who will enter into the midst of his mouth?” Here the devil’s mouth may be understood as his unceasing blasphemy, which must be stopped and closed when it has been penetrated by the word of the Lord. Or, “Who will enter into the midst of his mouth?” may be understood in this way: the devil’s mouth may signify hell, into which the Savior descended to free the human beings who had been devoured by the devil. Therefore He spoke of what was still to occur: “Who will enter into the midst of his mouth?” [Col. 0791B]

“Who will open the doors of his face?” The Lord says that He will disclose the hidden strength of the devil’s hypocrisy, concealed in profound secrecy. He openly manifested it in His passion and cross, when, having exposed him with his rulers and powers, the Son of God triumphed over him, though he displayed little confidence.

“Fear is round about his teeth.” He calls this enemy a devourer and insatiable, who, like a most savage beast, consumes everything with his teeth. Therefore fear and terror are around his teeth, because they are prepared for devouring.

“His body is like cast shields, joined together with scales pressing upon one another. One is joined to another, and not even a breath passes between them. One clings to another, and they hold one another and can in no way be separated.”

These three continuous verses, through the repetition of different expressions, speak of one and the same thing. The devil’s body, therefore, is to be understood as all his associates and the unclean spirits, whom God says are joined to him with such agreement and conspiracy that they are connected to him by an inseparable bond. He also called them “scales” in allegorical language: they are so densely packed and tightly joined to one another that they have no opening through which to breathe toward God, since through that mutual connection they are in no way loosened for the healing of repentance.

The demons, however, as the devil’s wicked ministers, are compared to cast shields. By this name the Lord signifies that their resistance against God is exceedingly persistent and obstinate, solid and enduring in its strength. The old edition compared the devil to an emerald, a stone naturally rough, which smooths other things by friction while itself does not cease to be rough; it reduces everything to fragments without experiencing any diminution of itself.

“His sneezing is like the brightness of fire, and his eyes like the eyelids of dawn.” Others have translated: “In his sneezing the sun shines, and his eyes are like the appearance of Lucifer.”

Sneezing expels the impurities of the brain and cleanses away vices conceived within. The devil, therefore, who is wholly filthy and foul, seems to reveal himself in this brightness when, transforming himself into an angel of light, he works and pours forth the filth of his wickedness with delight for the destruction of human beings; and from envy—that is, from the source of all evils—he stirs up and produces his poisons. [Col. 0792A]

The devil’s eyes are to be understood as false prophets, of whom holy Isaiah speaks when addressing the sinful people and saying concerning God: “He will close your eyes.” Inspired by him, they speak things that seem close to the light of truth, just as the eyelids of dawn are—although they possess none of God’s light. For even if they appear to show in themselves the beginning of light, which arises in them from the leaven of hypocrisy, they nevertheless cover the darkness of lies with the appearance of truth.

“From his mouth proceed lamps, like torches of blazing fire.” Just as the mouth of the Lord has spoken, so all the impious, sacrilegious, and blasphemous are rightly called the devil’s mouth. From it proceed blazing firebrands—or, as others have translated, burning torches—that is, fire and the cause of punishments are suggested. In the Apocalypse, where these ministers of the devil are described under the likeness of horses, it is said of them: “Fire and smoke and sulphur came out of their mouths.” They do not visibly come out of their mouths in this way; rather, the words of blasphemers are fire, smoke, and sulphur, just as the Lord says to him through the prophet: “I will bring fire out from your midst, and it shall devour you.”

“Smoke proceeds from his nostrils”—that is, pride.

“Like a pot burning and boiling.” For his vapor produces the causes of eternal fire, either for himself or for those who obey him. The spirit of pride is shown in the breathing of the nostrils, by which he gladly exhales the swelling of his mind. Yet above he is said to be humbled and restrained by the Lord: “Will you place a ring in his nostrils and pierce his jaw with a bracelet?” [Col. 0792C]

“His breath makes coals burn.” This is his smoke, arising from his companions and from his breath, by which he supplies for himself an eternal fire and its smoke. Thus the Lord also says to those like him: “Walk in the light of your fire and in the flames that you have kindled for yourselves.”

“And flame will go out from his mouth.” Others have translated: “But flame is rolled together from his mouth.” The meaning is the same: the punishments of blasphemies, rolled together, go out from the devil’s mouth.

“Strength will dwell in his neck, and want will go before his face.” By “neck,” that is, the nape, He signifies the swelling of the devil’s arrogance. The prophet says to him: “Your neck is an iron sinew,” in which the principal evil of sin dwells. In this strength of pride, the prophet also speaks words concerning him, saying: “I will make strength,” and for this reason the Lord rebukes him, saying: “In your wisdom you made strength for yourself.” Again He says to him: “In your business dealings you multiplied strength for yourself.” And likewise: “Your heart was lifted up in your strength.”

But when He says, “Want will go before his face,” this means that wherever the devil approaches, all the powers of life and soul are immediately drained away, and one’s substance is consumed.

“The members of his flesh cling to one another.” The devil’s members are those whom above He called scales and cast shields. They are called “members of his flesh” because, devoted to carnal and shameful acts, they cling to him as the author of evils.

[Col. 0793A]

“He will send lightning bolts against him, and they will not be carried elsewhere.” The order of God’s speech seems obscure here. While speaking about the devil, He suddenly changes persons and says: “He will send lightning bolts against him, and they will not be carried elsewhere.” We must believe that these lightning bolts are sent by God against the devil, according to the passage where it is said: “The Lord rained from the Lord.” We think this has been said here in the sense: God did what God spoke.

The dragon, the devil, is struck by lightning from God when he is rebuked by God’s fiery words from the holy clouds. These lightning bolts, sent and directed to their appointed place, will not be cast in vain; they will not be carried elsewhere, nor will the devil boast that he has escaped them with impunity.

“His heart will be hardened like a stone, and it will be compressed like the anvil of a smith.” Others have translated more plainly: “And he stands like an unwearied anvil.”

The devil’s heart is hard and inflexible, dull as stone and rigid. It is compressed—or stands like an anvil, which is not extended. An anvil is struck but is not stretched out; it subdues what is placed upon it, while it itself remains immovable. Such is the devil. He is beaten by the rebukes of the faithful, struck by the words of the prophets, and crushed by the victory of the martyrs; yet, remaining rigid, hard, and untamed, he is assigned to eternal punishments.

“When he is lifted up, the angels will fear, and, terrified, they will be purified.” This may be understood as referring to the times of the first age. The holy angels could already know how great an evil pride is when the presumptuous tyrant was cast down from the citadel of heaven. They could also know it from the merit by which they stood in the truth, in which he had not stood. In this way they are believed to have been made blessed, so that they might become entirely certain that no fall into sin would ever need to be feared for them.

Therefore, when it is said that, once the devil has been lifted up, the angels will fear and, terrified, will be purified, this must not be understood to mean that they will become more correct by taking greater care to avoid the sin of pride, terrified by the example of so great a condemnation. It is entirely clear that they would not be blessed if they had to devote more anxious care to avoiding sin. To avoid sin or resist sin belongs to the punitive miseries of this world, not to the glory of the age to come.

I think, however, that “these” refers to human beings who will attain fellowship with the angels, as though they were new angels. When the devil has been condemned, they will be purified through terror, seeing what sort of and how great an enemy they have escaped, together with the dreadful punishment of such condemnation. They will be purified—that is, they will be rendered purer to God—when they perceive so great a divine benefit bestowed upon them.

Nor is the meaning inconsistent with the words “terrified” or “they will fear,” since a rational creature may marvel at every benefit and every judgment of its Creator—not with punitive but with reverent fear. Indeed, what greater purification or cleansing could there be before God for an angelic human being than always to refer every good thing, with exultation—for the one to whom it is offered is loving—and with trembling—for the one to whom it is offered is God—to the praise of the Creator, in the glory of their most certain security and everlasting glory? [Col. 0794A]

“When the sword takes hold of him, he will not stand, nor the spear, nor the breastplate.” Others have translated more clearly: “If spears encounter him, they will do nothing to him.” That is, he cannot be corrected by any weapons of metal, by terrors, or by rebukes.

In the spear and breastplate may be understood those who, clothed in the breastplate of righteousness and armed on the right hand with holy works, strive to resist him. They will not be able to punish or conquer him, because he is so strong and evil that he despises what opposes him and is entirely unwilling to be converted.

Accordingly, whatever strength of spirit exists in the saints is called by the name of iron. Whatever virtue there is is also reckoned by the brilliance or endurance of bronze.

“For he will regard iron as straw and bronze as rotten wood.” He has clothed himself in such great strength of pride that he counts all these weapons taken up against him as nothing. Rather, he himself performs works like heaps of straw and fruitless wood, old and collapsing with decay, which must be burned in unquenchable fire.

“No archer will make him flee.” Even if any of the saints should have the quiver of his heart full of rebuking words, like piercing arrows, this hard and exceedingly iron-like being cannot be penetrated by them. Therefore, because he does not feel the wounds of compunction, he is not driven away by such an archer.

Others have translated: “An arrow of bronze does not wound him.” The incorruptible and enduring word of God is compared to a bronze arrow, by which the devil could never be wounded unto repentance. According to the hardness of his heart, he stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s just judgment. [Col. 0794C]

“Stones of the sling are counted by him as straw.” The sling may be understood as any of the saints who are held in the Lord’s hand. Through these saints, therefore, He hurls hard words—strong and harsh like stones—against this impious being, so that, struck by them, he may give honor to God. But because he possesses singular wickedness, he turns those same words into straw for himself; while he counts them as nothing, they become for him like straw that kindles the smoking balls of Tartarean fire.

Others expressed the same meaning: “Regard the stones hurled from the sling as hay.”

[Col. 0794D]

“He will regard the hammer as straw.” The divine word, nevertheless—heavy and strong, crushing him and wearing down the vast hardness of his impiety—will be regarded by him as straw when he is assailed by the saints. Overwhelmed by wickedness, he will not feel the weight of what strikes him from above, because his heart has become like a stone and like an untamed anvil, which, though beaten beyond measure, is never extended.

“And he will mock the brandished spear.” Others have translated: “the trembling word.” He will not merely fail to fear the powerful word of any saint, sent against him with the strength and virtue of the spirit; he will even mock either the word itself or the one hurling it.

God says all this about the devil in various ways and through various comparisons in order to show human beings how great an evil he is, how powerful, and how wholly beyond reversal.

“Under him will be the rays of the sun, and he will spread gold beneath him like mud.” Christ God is the Sun of righteousness, in whose wings there is healing. These rays—that is, the saints who are His children of light—are held subject to this prince of darkness through Adam’s transgression and his sin. Even those already redeemed through Christ, when they commit capital crimes, he makes his own, subjects them to himself as captives and slaves, and subjugates them.

Those angels whom the devil dragged down with him may also be understood as these rays. Concerning them it is said in the Apocalypse: “And he dragged with him a third of the stars to the earth.” These are the rays of the sun which, having departed from God, the true light, became darkness and princes of darkness. They are under him, for the devil is their king and lord. [Col. 0795B]

“Gold,” according to the meaning we have given, is likewise the rays of the sun, because under the name of gold all that is precious—and all that is evil—is understood. He spreads these beneath him like mud when he makes them subject to himself through sins, filthy and vile.

Dragons are said to dwell in secret places and hidden recesses of the earth, especially where gold-bearing metal is found. For this reason, I think this metaphor has been preserved in a spiritual interpretation: this red dragon spreads beneath himself a couch made from the gold of the good whom he has cast down. That is, he will have beneath him, like gold, all the spiritual riches of this world—the holiness, righteousness, and other virtues of good people—when he has reduced them, asleep in the faith, to the immense mud of sins.

[Col. 0795C]

“He will make the deep boil like a pot, and he will make the sea like those who boil ointments.” We have learned, according to allegorical interpretations, that this sea is the world, which is darkened by its obscurity and the excessive blindness of its foolishness. The devil kindles it with carnal desire so that it boils with love of earthly things.

If, however, we understand “ointments” in a good sense, interpreting them here as the fervent thanksgiving of the saints, then, by contrast, the devil, inhabitant of this sea, acts so that just as people boil with love for spiritual graces in the Holy Spirit, so they may burn with love for this world through the desire of the present life, as though by certain fiery kindlings.

Others have translated: “He makes the abyss boil; he regards the bronze vessel as guilt, and the abyss of Tartarus as a captive.” In this passage I think God spoke about the devil in the following sense: because the devil is said to be of this world, under the name “abyss,” he has judged within himself that what has been erased from the divine memory will not be remembered at all. The prophet recalls his most impious thought in the ninth Psalm, saying: “For he has said in his heart, ‘He will not require it.’” Likewise: “For he has said in his heart, ‘God has forgotten; he has turned away his face, so that he may never see.’”

He also held Tartarus, the abyss—that is, hell, in which the sinners of this world will be confined—as a captive, thrust down under the harshest domination and held in infernal chains. Thus the devil, exulting and rejoicing, imagined that he would possess all God’s creation—that is, the entire world—as king and lord forever, not knowing that it is ruled by the Lord God forever and unto ages of ages; that the impious nations, having been destroyed from His land, would be judged; and that the orphans and humble would be defended, so that a human being—that is, the devil—would no longer continue to exalt himself over the earth. [Col. 0796A]

“After him the path will shine.” He will seek to return to God only when the time for repentance will no longer benefit him. I think this is the path of his conversion: it will shine upon him, hardened in heart and blind, through a late repentance, when, after he has received it, it will be of no benefit to him.

“He will regard the abyss as growing old.” Others have translated: “as a walkway.” Above we said that the abyss signifies this world. The devil regards it as growing old and aging, remaining in sins, not knowing that at the Lord’s coming it will be freed from its ancient sins.

“There is no power upon earth comparable to him.” No creature possesses such power, nor does any sinful creature possess such wickedness. Therefore, in either respect, no one can be compared with him.

“He was made so that he would fear no one.” By the free choice of his own will, he was lifted up into pride and made what he became; that is, he was so corrupted by his own wickedness that he feared no one, not even the Lord God, his Creator. He does fear Him as a wicked and transgressing servant, but he does not possess within himself the fear of love for God.

“He sees every lofty thing.” “He is raised up,” He says, “to what is lofty and exalted”; that is, he is elevated to the summit of his own immeasurable pride, so that, as a blasphemer, he may place his mouth in heaven, saying: “I will set my throne in heaven, and I will be like the Most High.”

“He is king over all the sons of pride.” That is, he is the head and prince of all the proud. Imitating him, angels, impious human beings, and transgressors have become sons of his pride.

## CHAPTER XLII

Job answered the Lord and said:

“I know that you can do all things”—that is, you humble the devil as you will and when you will.

“And no thought is hidden from you.” Who can be hidden from the One who searches the heart and the kidneys? Here it becomes evident that holy Job, in these words by which he penitently confesses to God, is accusing his own thoughts. He remembers that through them he had attributed very much to himself on account of the merits of his righteousness and had attempted to charge God, as though He were an uncultivated man, with injustice.

“Who is this who conceals counsel without knowledge?” That is, no one can hide counsel from your consciousness. In what follows he most plainly demonstrates his error and confesses his ignorance, by which, not knowing, he had exceeded the proper manner of speaking to God, saying:

“Therefore I have spoken foolishly, and about things that exceed my knowledge beyond measure. Hear, and I will speak; I will question you, and you will answer me.”

Having now laid aside his ignorance and rejected the presumption of foolishness, corrected through knowledge of the divine rebuke and purified by the testing of his present chastisement, he nevertheless dares to question God, saying: “Hear.” He shows the mercy of the divine indignation. He seems to say that God had brought that affliction upon him in a very different way from the way he had previously judged, and for this reason he wishes to be taught by God and asks that this very matter be shown to him.

After Job had received, as we must believe from his words, the oracle of the divine visitation, he said to God:

“With the hearing of the ear I heard you, but now my eye sees you.” Having drawn nearer to the knowledge of God after the testing of temptation, he says that he now sees God, whom previously, while he was being examined, he had said that he heard.

To hear or see God, who is invisible and incomprehensible, is not the function of these eyes or these ears, but rather of the mind and heart. Hence blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.

“Therefore I condemn myself and repent in dust and ashes.”

After the Lord had spoken these words to Job, He said to Eliphaz the Temanite: “My wrath is kindled against you and against your two friends, because you have not spoken rightly before me, as my servant Job has. Therefore take for yourselves seven bulls and seven rams, and go to my servant Job and offer a burnt offering for yourselves. My servant Job shall pray for you. I will accept his face, so that your folly may not be imputed to you. For you have not spoken rightly before me, as my servant Job has.”

So Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite went and did as the Lord had spoken to them.

Others have translated this passage: “Therefore I despised myself, and wasted away, and regarded myself as earth and ashes.” The fact that Job’s friends did not speak rightly, to the injury of holy Job, is openly shown here, when the Lord imputes it to them. Hence He says to them that their sin of reproach cannot be forgiven unless blessed Job prays for them and offers a propitiatory burnt offering.

Here we observe that blessed Job performed the office of a priest. Let it be understood in this passage that no one should, with exultation and reproach, condemn a person who is established under God’s chastisement and amid the labors of tribulations. For He says that, even before Job offered sacrifice for them, He willingly accepted his face in order to hear him.

And the Lord adds double portions. In what follows the meaning of this is sought, and the writer of this book carefully explains how the doubling took place. The brothers and sisters who came to blessed Job after the blow of his chastisement are to be understood as all the thoughts and the household of his lineage. All his acquaintances and friends, who had previously known his royal power and singular wisdom, came to him and ate with him at the banquet of his honor. In this it is signified that all the filth and squalor had been wiped away from him.

In the movement of the head, we should understand that the joy of those who came to him was indicated. Each of them, as a gift, gave him, as though he were needy and possessed absolutely nothing, one sheep and one gold earring.

In this consolation, although it was small and a doubling of his former goods only in its beginning, it may be observed that a great multitude came to him: although he received little from each person, he suddenly became the owner of such great riches.

The writer of this book may also have spoken by anticipation, so that after that temptation, for the hundred and forty years of his life, he would possess, with the Lord’s blessing, riches accumulated twofold. We do not read that the number of his children was doubled. Therefore I think that when those things which had entirely perished were restored to him twofold, his twenty children were also restored to him in place of the ten.

Those first ten, whom the collapse of the falling house had crushed, are not considered destroyed before God. For the building up of our faith, therefore, we must understand that as many children were given back to him by God as he had lost, so that, with all his possessions restored to him twofold by the Lord, he might also believe that he possessed children twofold. As a most faithful servant of God, he should by no means doubt that those whom he had sent ahead to God had not perished.

Thus, having perceived throughout this entire book that holy Job bore the figure of the Savior, we have expounded it insofar as His grace has granted and deemed worthy to bestow this understanding upon us. In certain passages we have understood his friends to signify heretics, and we have likewise explained that Elihu bore the image of the Gentile world.

But because through Christ there is reconciliation for the impious and the erring—“For there is no other name under heaven by which it is necessary for us to be saved”—therefore, now that the Gentile religion has been extinguished and abolished, heretics are sent by God the Father to Christ, so that through the One by whom they were formerly saved, having fallen away, they may again be reconciled to God through the same Mediator.

In the burnt offering of seven bulls and seven rams are signified the satisfaction of prayers and almsgiving, the complete and perfect cleansing of pride and anger, and repentance made perfect through labor and innocence.

But when it says:

“And the Lord accepted Job’s face,” the Lord also turned toward Job’s repentance when he prayed for his friends. This is what the apostle says: “Christ Jesus, who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us.” According to the apostle John, He is our advocate and propitiation with the Father. Thus the Savior’s face is accepted by the Father, while He both hears and is heard.

“And the Lord added to all that had belonged to Job, double portions.” Those things, therefore, were added to Christ the Lord and our God when, through faith, the multitude of the Gentiles was added to the people of Israel, and will be added in the kingdom.

All his brothers came to him, and all his sisters, and all who had known him before, and they ate bread with him in his house. And they shook their heads over him. By saying “they came,” Scripture means that they were incorporated into him through faith, so that all believers in him, gathered within the Church in one Spirit, might be his members. His brothers and sisters signify that whole kinship of the Jewish people from whose family Christ was born. Or, more generally, we may understand by “brothers and sisters” the multitudes of all nations, since he assumed flesh from the mass of the human race, through which he deigned [Col. 0799A] to make the rest his brothers. Of them he says to the Father: “I shall declare your name to my brothers, and in the midst of the Church I shall praise you.” And in the Gospel he says: “Whoever does the will of God is my brother, and sister, and mother.”

“And all who had known him before came to him”: this too must be understood of them, because all the saints and prophets knew him beforehand; they certainly saw him in the Spirit, and announced that he would also come in the flesh, just as the Lord himself says: “Many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it.” They saw him in the Spirit, but desired to see the presence of his coming in the flesh, as did the holy Abraham, of whom the Lord says: “Abraham desired to see my day; he saw it and rejoiced.”

Thus [Col. 0799B] the saints mentioned above came, because, possessing the same spirit of faith, they prophesied as righteous people living by faith and, foreseeing in the Spirit the future mystery of Christ’s incarnation, came through that same repentance to the faith of Christ—that is, “from faith to faith”—so that they might be one under Christ the Head and themselves be constituted in the body of the Church. There, now that Christ has been glorified by the resurrection and restored from the dishonor of his Passion to his former honor, all who come to him through faith eat the bread of his sacraments in his house, the Church.

They are said to eat bread with him because he said: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age.” Or because he himself is the consecrator of those same mysteries, in which we receive him as the one who blesses and [Col. 0799C] consecrates them; for he himself said: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven.” The word of the Scriptures is Christ’s bread, by which they are nourished in the house of the Savior, the Church, and by whose exhortation they are refreshed—those who once were poor in faith and, while they were strangers to God in this world, suffered hunger for the divine word.

“And all who had known him before came to him”: that is, those who had known him on earth were deemed worthy to come to him in heaven. “And they shook,” says Scripture, “their heads over him,” namely, rejoicing that they had been made participants in Christ’s spiritual and sacred banquets, as the Lord says in the psalm: “I shall fulfill my vows before those who fear him; the poor shall eat and be satisfied, and they shall praise the Lord who seek him.”

[Col. 0799D] And they consoled him concerning all the evil that the Lord had inflicted upon him. Our Savior is consoled in no small measure by one who believes with joy in his Passion, which he accepted for the redemption of the world, and faithfully contemplates it with the eyes of faith. He himself was filled with such consolation when, seeing the crowd of believers, he rejoiced in the Spirit, as we have learned from the writing of the holy Evangelist.

That God the Father inflicted upon his Son the evil of Passion and death, we say in accordance with the Apostle: “He did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all.” From this we derive great consolation: the one who accepted our evils will give us his good things.

And each of them gave him one sheep and one golden [Col. 0800A] earring. Each of those who come to Christ through faith offers him his innocence and the obedience of his mind. For the Apostle teaches those who have been made holy from sinners to live in this way, saying: “I beseech you, brothers, to present your bodies as a living, holy sacrifice, pleasing to God.”

Thus those who come to Christ become the Lord’s sheep, holy sheep, those rational sheep ascending from the washing and bearing twin offspring, when, reborn in Christ through obedience to God’s commandments, they become innocent and simple workers and faithful people.

But the Lord blessed Job’s latter days more than his beginning. And he had fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, a thousand yoke of oxen, and a thousand she-asses. The beginnings of Christ God and our Lord [Col. 0800B] are signified by the beginnings of Moses’ Law. His latter days, however, are shown to be the Gospel. Hence Ecclesiastes says: “The latter things of a speech are better than its beginning.”

Therefore the mysteries of the Gospel, revealed in Christ, are better than the Law’s signs and figures; the sacrifices of contrite hearts are better than the holocausts of animals; and the manifestation of truth in the Gospel is better than the shadow of allegories in the Old Testament.

Thus the Lord blessed Job’s latter days more than his beginning, so that grace might abound among both peoples, Jews and Gentiles. Scripture wished to designate these peoples according to the qualities of their character, as though under the names of different animals. What meaning, however, these same names of the animals contain in themselves [Col. 0800C], I remember having explained at the beginning of this work.

I think that the doubled number of these animals refers to the two peoples, or to the more abundant grace of the Gospel, as we have already said. Of this the Apostle says: “Our sufficiency is from God, who also made us capable ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.”

And he had seven sons and three daughters. The statement that he had seven sons and three daughters indicates the sevenfold number of graces: of the Law, Prophecy, and Grace, as I said at the beginning of this work. Their father, as he was dying, made these daughters coheirs with their brothers—that is, the souls whom he incorporates through the Spirit of graces into the covenant of the divine Scriptures, he makes participants in his promises. The names of those daughters, which are also significantly given, contain within them a great mystery.

[Col. 0800D] And he called the name of one Day, and the name of the second Cassia, and the name of the third Horn of Stibium. But women more beautiful than the daughters of Job were not found in all the land. And their father gave them an inheritance among their brothers.

Job lived after these scourges for one hundred and forty years, and he saw his sons and his sons’ sons, to the fourth generation; and he died old and full of days.

Day, therefore, is the law of God, which illumines the night of human ignorance for the knowledge of truth. Cassia is the gift of holy anointing. The Horn of Stibium is most appropriately suited to the Gospel riches [Col. 0801A] and the wealth of the Church, which is the treasury of spiritual things. The horn pertains to royal distinction and the dignity of the Church, as the prophet says: “He has exalted the horn of his Christ.”

Holy Job therefore clearly possessed the figure of the Savior. This is also shown in the fact that, from being exceedingly rich, he became needy and poor, so that we might be enriched. The devil exercised all his power against his body, but achieved nothing, as the Lord himself says: “The prince of this world will come, and he will find nothing in me.”

Just as blessed Job, after the loss of his unbelieving sons, was enriched in his children, so the Savior, after the loss of his unbelieving sons, was enriched in the Gentiles. In many respects, therefore, holy Job also prefigured the Passion and endurance of our Lord. In the number of his sons and in the names of his daughters, he foretold the sevenfold [Col. 0801B] grace of the Holy Spirit—of the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel—and the future fullness in our Savior:

[Col. 0802A]

> In him rested the spirit of wisdom and understanding,  
> the spirit of counsel and strength,  
> the spirit of knowledge and piety;  
> the spirit of the fear of God filled him.

This is to be understood as “full of days.”

At last, relieved of the burden of this lengthy exposition, breathing as though I had set down a heavy load, I direct the conclusion of my discourse to you, most blessed Father Vecterius. I ask that, if you have perceived anything in this work worthy of approval as true, you should marvel also at the most generous gifts of our Lord even in regard to my smallness. I beseech you not to caress me with friendly favor or defend me with benevolent excuse. For I do not wish you to lower the eminence of your judgment from the height of its dignity. Rather, make my little work praiseworthy in this way: by revising it as you correct what is disordered, and by chastising it through thorough [Col. 0802B] emendation.

## [BREVIARY ON THE PSALMS]

[Col. 0801]

## [ADMONITION TO THE FOLLOWING BREVIARY ON THE PSALMS, AND COMMENTARIES ON PSALMS I, III, AND IV]

## [ADMONITION]

[Col. 0801] After at last reviewing all the genuine commentaries of the great Jerome on the whole of Scripture, we deliberately reserved this place for the *Breviary on the Psalms*. For although this book is wrongly ascribed to the holy Father, it is nevertheless superior to all the other works among the spurious productions and, by its own dignity, does not permit itself to be relegated to the final volume, nor has it been assigned that position in the editions published up to now.

This was not merely the policy of all the editors who preceded us; it was also sanctioned by the authority of the supreme pontiff, the most holy Pius V himself. According to Victorius, he ordered that, immediately after Jerome’s genuine writings and before the works of others were reached, this volume on the Psalms should be placed as doubtful.

Although we attach much greater weight to the arguments that separate it from Jerome, we nevertheless perceive that fragments of Jerome’s labor are scattered here and there within it, and that these fragments almost reveal themselves by their own light. The opinion generally held, and the one nearer the truth, is that the author of this *Breviary* was a compiler of earlier Fathers. He drew much from Origen, Hilary, Eusebius, and from Eucherius of Lyons, considerably later than these men, whom he cites on Psalm XVI. Yet for the greater part he transcribed from Jerome’s commentaries—either those on the Psalms from Psalm X through Psalm XVI, which have perished, or those on other portions of Scripture, where many passages of the Psalms are occasionally explained in contexts far removed from them—and adapted the material to his own work and intellect.

To prevent you from denying this, at least the stronger arguments must be set forth: those formerly advanced by Erasmus, then by Sixtus of Siena in Book IV of the *Bibliotheca Sancta*, likewise by Victorius, Martianaeus, Du Pin, and Tillemont, not to mention others. They can be reduced to the following principal points.

First, the kind of diction and style—which in distinguishing authors is like a Lydian touchstone—as well as the flavor and savor of the author’s learning, differ so greatly from Jerome’s that it is more than enough merely to have glanced through this *Breviary*, or to have compared it for a short time with Jerome’s genuine commentaries, to understand immediately that it falls far below the ability of the holy Father.

Indeed, anyone who is even a visitor to Jerome’s writings must fail to notice that, contrary to the holy Doctor’s consistently maintained practice, this work here habitually places the exposition of the historical sense and of the literal text below everything else, while devoting the whole of its effort to allegories and tropological interpretations concerning Christ and the Church. Its treatment of Hebrew and Greek learning is also so superficial that, whenever it introduces such material, it seems to have borrowed it from others word for word rather than derived it from itself or from the source.

Martianaeus has further observed that whenever this author appeals to the Hebrew text, he means nothing by that designation except either Aquila’s Greek version or Jerome’s Latin translation from the Hebrew. Thus, on Psalm V, he says that the Hebrew has *epiboulon* (ἐπίβουλον), “plotting” or “treacherous,” in place of [lacuna]; and on Psalm CXIX, *arkeuthinois* or *arkeuthinais* (ἀρκευθίνοις or ἀρκευθίναις), in place of [lacuna]. Both interpretations belong to Aquila. Likewise, when he says that *sela* is rendered as “forever,” he took this from Jerome’s version, not from the original text.

Finally, this author differs from Jerome’s taste in so many ways that the fact that he sometimes differs even from himself indicates that the work had not one but several patchwork compilers. Some psalms he explains in the manner of a commentator, drawing with reasonable learning on the sound opinions of other Fathers. Others he treats like a preacher, in a homiletic style addressed to the people or to an assembly of brothers. And—something especially alien to the genius and manner of life of the holy Doctor—he frequently breaks into formulas of address, either interrupting his listeners or concluding his exposition with some prayer poured out to God.

[Col. 0803] He explains the somewhat longer Psalm CXVIII in three homilies. As for Psalm CXI, which he cannot pursue at greater length in exposition, he excuses himself by saying that the hour does not permit it. You will find similar features throughout almost the entire book, features that in no way resemble Jerome’s manner of explaining Scripture, though it would be tedious now to repeat each one individually.

Second, the author defends not only many views that are foreign to Jerome but even views wholly contrary to Jerome’s. A prime example is his interpretation of the *cynomyia* in Psalm CIV as “dog-fly.” Jerome, by contrast, in Letter 104 to Sunnias and Fretela, wishes *koinomyia* (κοινομυῖα) to be read and renders it “every kind of fly,” or, in accordance with Aquila’s sense, who translated *pammikton* (πάμμικτον), “every sort of fly.”

In the following Psalm, Psalm CV, this author takes the land of Ham, which Jerome had most learnedly asserted in the *Hebrew Questions on Genesis* to be Egypt, as Palestine itself—namely, the land into which the Hebrews succeeded after the nations had been destroyed. And what the holy Doctor states in the same *Questions on Genesis* IV, namely, that Naid or Nod should not at all be considered, in accordance with Greek and Latin opinion, the land inhabited by Cain, this author treats as a proper name.

The true Jerome, in Letter 140 to Cyprian, attributes Psalm LXXXIX to Moses as its author. Indeed, in Book I *Against Rufinus*, he argues that the following eleven psalms, which have no titles, likewise belong to Moses. He proves this opinion—which he himself had received from Origen, while this author received it from Huillus—again in other places, and especially in the preface to Malachi.

By contrast, in his lengthy exposition of the titles, the author of the *Breviary* prefers to attribute those psalms also to David, and in that whole confused dispute, whose meaning is sufficiently uncertain, he quite clearly shows that he was entirely ignorant of the doctrine.

You yourself, reader, can find other examples like these if you compare this Treatise with the letters to Sunnias and Fretela and to Cyprian, and with the two other letters in which the holy Father explained several psalms: Letter 34 to Marcella and Letter 65 to Principia. We have occasionally noted some matters in the annotations as well, lest we should draw you farther away here when we ought to be contending with the sheer number of examples.

Yet while we do not conceal the faults of the pseudonymous author, we are also distressed that he is sometimes burdened with unjust accusations. Martianaeus, for example, charges him with ignorance because, speaking of the name “Iscariot,” he said it was uncertain whether it meant “his father” or “his village,” as though he had thought the expressions “his father” or “his village” themselves to be the etymology.

But this was not his meaning or intention. While accepting the commonly received view that the name is composed of two words and signifies “a man from Charioth,” he said that it was uncertain whether the second element referred to a father or to a village—that is, to the name of the land in which he was born.

Nor is the other accusation any fairer, concerning the passage of Psalm CXV, “Every human being is a liar,” where the author notes that the Hebrew has “Every human being, falsehood,” which is said to be *chazab*. Martianaeus found *zecam* instead of *chazab* in the manuscripts he used, and argues that the author himself wrote this, so as to accuse him of such great ignorance that he confused the final letter of *chazab* with the first letter of the following Hebrew word, *ma*, and furthermore mistook *kaph* for *beth*, thereby combining letters into a word with no meaning.

In truth, it is more likely that the manuscripts are at fault and that the blame should not be placed on the Treatise’s author, who originally wrote the passage correctly, but on the copyists, who later badly corrupted a reading unfamiliar to them. I believe this will be clear from Martianaeus’s own argument. For if the author knew Hebrew well enough to consult the original and derive his reading from it, however much he might have erred, he could not possibly have committed so many errors in a single little word.

Let us grant that, through a hurried glance, he took *kaph* for *beth*. But he also omitted the first *kaph*, the formative letter of the word; finally, he rashly supplied a third letter, *mem*, from another word. Yet if one assumes that the man whom one accuses of this lapse was certainly capable of handling and reading a Hebrew codex, it is hardly credible that he should have gone astray through three errors in three letters.

Therefore, since the books previously published have *chazab* correctly, that reading must be retained without question. We should judge that the author himself wrote it thus, rather than dragging him into this slander because of the carelessness of copyists. Those who have devoted themselves to the study of manuscript codices know how often, and into what monstrous forms, Latin scribes deform foreign words, so that if their testimony were always followed, even Jerome would seem not to have known Hebrew or Greek.

Third, arguments intended to prove the fraudulence of the writing are drawn from the author’s own testimony about himself and from the genuine Jerome’s testimony about himself. Yet, to state plainly what I think, the arguments commonly produced seem to me weaker.

Victorius was moved above all by the fact that, near the beginning of Psalm CXXXII, the author says that he has a secular brother, whereas tradition reports that Jerome had only one brother, Paulinianus, whom Saint Epiphanius ordered to become a priest while still quite young.

Victorius attempts to remove the difficulty by saying either that Paulinianus was not yet a priest when Jerome wrote this, or that Jerome had another brother in the world whom we do not know. But the passage in question is plainly allegorical, and there the author calls the world itself, which he had renounced, his secular brother. This is clear from the very words:

> “We dismissed one brother,” he says, “and behold how many we have found! My secular brother”—by which, since I am speaking of my own, I speak of each individual—“not only loves me but also my substance.”

Martianaeus had promised to produce other testimonies by which he would establish from the Treatise’s own words that its author lived in Egypt and there expounded the Psalms as they were read or sung in an assembly of monks. But when he came to that point, I was content to send the reader to Psalm CXLIII. Its exposition does indeed contain some things that indicate a man of a later age than Jerome’s, but nothing that indicates an inhabitant of Egypt or Palestine.

From this we arrive at a conjecture that seems more credible than the others: it is drawn from Psalm CXXXV, where the author almost openly [Col. 0805] reveals that he lived as a monk in Britain. For he names Britain immediately when he takes an example from some region to show that stars appear everywhere with an equal brilliance of rays. “The star,” he says, “which is seen in Britain is itself seen everywhere.” Yet do not, at the first thought that occurs to you, suppose that this was Bede. Rather, it was another abbot of the Scots in that period, namely the seventh or eighth century, when many Scots flourished with great distinction for their learning.

I say, in that period, because both the character of his commentary and his mention of Eucherius of Lyons, who flourished in the middle of the fifth century, clearly point to a later age. I could even name one of these men, especially Saint Columbanus, abbot of Luxeuil, born in Ireland, the island of the Scots. Sigebert, the Anonymous of Melk, Trithemius, and others celebrate his commentaries on the entire Psalter, composed when he was still young and therefore before he departed from Britain.

But there will be an opportunity to speak of him shortly, when we also present a sample of an unpublished commentary that we obtained from his monastery at Bobbio. For now, the testimonies of Jerome himself concerning himself, which separate this work from him, deserve precedence.

The clearest of these occurs in the sixty-third chapter of Isaiah, a book that he composed around the year 410, almost at the end of his life. When the discussion turned to Psalms VIII and LXXXIII, he openly confessed that he had not yet explained them:

> “Psalms concerning the winepresses, the eighth and the eighty-third, are written in a favorable sense. Concerning them, in their proper places, if life accompanies me, by the Lord’s provision, I shall speak.”

The remaining time of his life amounted to roughly a decade. Thus he could scarcely have put the finishing hand to his prophetic work; he left his commentaries on Jeremiah, which alone remained, unfinished because death intervened.

Even more decisive is the fact that, while explaining Jeremiah himself, he promises something similar in the second chapter: namely, that he would discuss more fully, in their proper place, the Gates mentioned in Psalm XXIII. From this it is perfectly clear that Jerome did not compose that work. He himself states, near the end of his life, that he intended to work out certain parts of it—parts neither previously omitted for definite reasons nor joined together in any order—and therefore could not already have completed it.

Nevertheless, other arguments of no less strength persuade us of what we proposed at the beginning: that this entire work is often composed from fragments of the genuine Jerome. Anyone can know this for himself by comparing the scattered passages of the Psalms interpreted by the holy Father—most of which are collected in the index of each volume—with the passages in the *Breviary*, and by noting the long paraphrases and the frequent recurrence not only of the same ideas but even of the same words.

It is likewise reasonable to suppose that the seven treatises on Psalms X through XVI, which Jerome himself includes in the catalogue of his works but which are thought to have perished long ago because they are not preserved separately with a definite mark of authenticity, were inserted here. This very circumstance may have provided an industrious compiler with the opportunity to embellish commentaries on the remaining psalms.

Moreover, when ancient authors praise or transcribe passages from Jerome on one psalm or another, and those passages are expressed in precisely the same words in this *Breviary*, it is scarcely possible to explain the matter otherwise than by assuming that a pseudepigraphic book was interpolated with additions that genuinely came from the pen of the holy Doctor.

The most reliable of all witnesses, Saint Augustine, Jerome’s contemporary, quotes a passage from the exposition of Psalm XCIII in his *Commonitory to Fortunatianus*, or Letter 148. He was so certain that the writing was genuinely Jerome’s that he particularly pressed this authority of so great a name against his opponents:

> “To avoid making further delays by recalling many things, I shall introduce this one testimony of Saint Jerome.”

And shortly afterward:

> “When that man, most learned in the Scriptures, was explaining the psalm where it is said, ‘Understand, then, you who are foolish among the people, and you fools, become wise at last: he who planted the ear, will he not hear? Or he who formed the eye, does he not observe?’—among other things he said:
>
> ‘This passage is directed especially against those who are Anthropomorphites, who say that God has the members which we also have. For example, God is said to have eyes: “The eyes of the Lord look upon all things”; hands, because he made all things. And Adam, it says, heard the sound of the feet of the Lord walking in paradise.
>
> ‘They hear these things in a simple-minded way and refer human weaknesses to the majesty of God. But I say that God is wholly eye, wholly hand, wholly foot. He is wholly eye because he sees everything; wholly hand because he works everything; wholly foot because he is everywhere.
>
> ‘“He who planted the ear, will he not hear? And he who formed the eyes, does he not observe?” He did not say, “He who planted the ear therefore does not himself have an ear.” He did not say, “Therefore he himself does not have eyes.” Rather, he said: “He who planted the ear, will he not hear? And he who formed the eyes, does he not observe?” He used the terms for members, but assigned them their functions.’”

Indeed, you find this nowhere else in Jerome than in this very *Breviary*, wrongly ascribed to him. There the passage from Psalm XCIII is transcribed in exactly the same words, so that it appears to have been taken almost from that original source.

Although in our general preface this seemed to us to have been drawn not from a commentary on the Psalms but from one of the holy Doctor’s letters that have perished, we nevertheless did not doubt that it was Jerome’s, with Augustine guaranteeing its authenticity.

There are also other passages that Servatus Lupus cites from this *Breviary* as Jerome’s in his *Collection on Three Questions*, such as the passage in the explanation of Psalm I, which we shall examine in its proper place. Other passages are quoted by Saint Gregory VII—who, according to the more credible opinion, is the true author of the commentary on the penitential psalms, not Saint Gregory the Great, to whom it is commonly attributed—from the exposition of verse 17 of Psalm L. He attributes them to Jerome.

These passages, if they do not establish the authenticity of the entire work, at least contribute greatly to establishing the γνησιότης (*gnēsiotēs*), the genuineness, of the sentences they quote; they also show how many centuries ago those passages were already regarded as Jerome’s.

[Col. 0807] Finally, although I believe that many of Jerome’s doctrines and even words are present in this *Breviary*, the principal reason is the testimony that the holy Father gives concerning himself: he says that he expounded the Psalter in daily informal commentaries in an assembly of brothers.

His words in Book I *Against Rufinus*, section 19, are most explicit:

> “Rufinus is said to criticize the fact that, while interpreting the second psalm, in place of what we read in Latin, ‘Embrace discipline,’ and what is written in the Hebrew volume, *nescubar*, I said in my informal commentaries, ‘Worship the Son.’”

And again, while translating the entire Psalter into the Roman idiom, he says that, as though forgetful of his earlier exposition, he set down, “Worship purely,” which everyone sees to be contrary to the former rendering.

After he had dissolved this objection with great learning in what follows, he adds:

> “What, then, have I done wrong if I translated an ambiguous word in different ways? In the informal commentaries, where there is freedom of discussion, I had said, ‘Worship the Son’; but in the body of the text, so as not to appear a violent interpreter and to leave room for Jewish slander, I said, ‘Worship purely,’ or ‘with choice,’ and so forth.”

Therefore there is no doubt that the holy Father produced certain shorter commentaries on the Psalms. The reason why he does not list them in his catalogue of works was explained in our general preface: above all, they were delivered orally and were not written down by him, and therefore could not properly be counted among his writings.

That they were nevertheless captured on paper, in some fashion, by one of his hearers and then circulated publicly is proved by Rufinus’s mockery and by the very context of Jerome’s reply. It is evident in many places that the hurried shorthand writers were concerned more with the ideas, which they would rework in private cells, than with the words.

As a result, that still-rough work came into the hands of others bearing Jerome’s name, but so gaping, inept, and shapeless that it seemed more like threads for constructing a work than a work itself. Every industrious person therefore thought he might combine it with other additions and patch that quilt together according to his own understanding.

I am persuaded of this, and by this one explanation I think the various opinions of learned men can be reconciled, as can the varied character of the exposition—what teaches Jerome in some passages and disgraces him in others. This is the one explanation, and the one especially worthy of consideration by the editors of this book, for the existence of so many copies of his *Breviary* under Jerome’s name, so different from one another.

The first thing, then, was the holy Father’s αὐτοσχεδίασμα (*autoschediasma*), an extemporaneous composition, hastily taken down from the mouth of one speaking. Interpolators subsequently recast it in different ways according to their own skill and convenience, and it emerged into public circulation at different times, as though under different midwives.

To understand the matter properly, it will now be worthwhile to bring forward some of the materials hidden in libraries, which we have inspected with our own eyes and, when they seemed important enough, copied in part. For when these witnesses differ among themselves, they simultaneously provide the surest evidence and accuse the work of νόθεία (*notheia*), spuriousness.

Two works have recently become known in print, at least in part, so that the question of the author might be tested. The first is entitled *Exposition of the Psalms*. From it Martianaeus appended at the end of the *Breviary* what seemed to him to have been omitted by its compiler.

He took the text from two manuscript codices. One was carefully collated and transcribed by his associate, D. Francis Levacher, from a manuscript of the monastery of Saint Peter of Pratellis; the other was handled by Martianaeus himself, a Corbie codex.

We encountered another, most elegant copy in the Ambrosian Library at Milan, bound in small folio format and numbered 120. Insofar as comparison allowed us to determine the portion published by Martianaeus, it presents the same exposition in exactly the same words, ascribing it to our Jerome.

Before us, a highly learned man had examined that codex and judged that the work should be attributed to Florus, the deacon of Lyons. His chief reason for asserting this was that, at the end of the codex, after all the expositions, forty-two verses on David were written. In them Florus, humbly, dedicates the Book of Psalms to Floradus the abbot.

They begin:

> This boy minstrel, in lyrical harmonies,  
> brought forth these hymns in praise of you,  
> good Christ.

And they end with these lines:

> And now farewell, and remember your Florus without end,  
> so that he himself may be able to remain free from his sins.

We do not deny that these verses belong to Florus of Lyons. We know that he took extraordinary pleasure in composing poems of this kind on the books of Holy Scripture, and we regard the ancient inscription of his name as a very certain argument for their authenticity.

But we maintain that the exposition or commentary itself cannot be attributed to him, either for this reason or in any other way. The very context of the verses openly reveals that they were composed in praise and for the revision of the Psalter itself, not for its exposition.

It will not be troublesome to learn the whole matter from the verses that the author adds after he had digressed into praise of the royal Prophet:

> Therefore, with unceasing prayers and everlasting song,  
> may this lyre, Father, resound from your mouth—  
> the lyre with which the ancient elders sang,  
> whom the mighty mouths of the Nile  
> and the waves of the thunderous sea  
> feared.
>
> And the sacred Jerome restored it  
> from the corruption of a long age  
> to its ancient splendor.
>
> By his genius, it is equipped with beautiful arrows  
> and glitters throughout with the radiant brilliance of stars  
> [that is, obeli and asterisks].
>
> A diligent hand, with the sweat of much labor,  
> restored these marks to their ancient places  
> at your request.

[Col. 0809]

> For while the slippery lyre wandered through uncultivated hands,  
> sweet and dyed with ambrosial liquid,  
> it had lost the shining marks of the yellow metal  
> and covered its melodious strings  
> with dark and filthy neglect.
>
> Yet once more [MS: *versus*] polished according to Hebrew method,  
> and at the same time newly adorned  
> by an Argolic hand,
>
> it scatters honeyed voices of heaven  
> across the stars  
> and resounds with sacred songs  
> in angelic harmony.
>
> Receive this corrected volume  
> with a grateful heart,  
> and, Father, I beg you, take care  
> that it remain so.
>
> For no fruit will attend our efforts—  
> we who, having erased its faults,  
> have supplied what was good—
>
> unless the scribe, watchful and discerning  
> through your zeal, most excellent Father,  
> preserves what now remains correct.

Here you see no mention of Florus’s having prepared an exposition of his own; rather, the whole point is to commend the diligence devoted to a recently corrected manuscript. Yet, I think, no one could persuade himself that this was possible if Florus had also elucidated the Psalms in that commentary, while failing at least to mention the matter to his abbot Flordaus. Indeed, he would have commended the importance and care of so great a work to many people, since he magnifies the praises of the new recension—and perhaps of one fashioned by another diligent hand. Moreover, it is entirely clear from other arguments that Florus never applied himself to composing commentaries on the Psalms, nor did later writers anywhere remember such a work, although they compiled catalogues of distinguished living teachers and of Florus’s own writings.

Finally, as with many other matters because of the closeness of the subject, we know that the verses of that deacon were brought in from elsewhere and joined to the commentary by the person who assembled the manuscript. For we have seen them, more appropriately, prefixed to the Psalter itself in one or another Vatican manuscript of the Psalter, in what is called the Gallican version. Florus, therefore, is not the author of the commentary. Rather, it was some later person—whoever he may have been—the interpolator of the *Breviary on the Psalms*, who ordered not only those expositions which Martianay edited but almost all the rest, which he took from there, to migrate into one form and then another; and, so as to impose more securely upon the faith of his readers, he assumed the person of Jerome.

The pieces which he prefixed in place of prefaces are not merely false but wholly unworthy of Jerome’s name. The first is that celebrated letter to Damasus, “I have read the letter of your apostleship, asking me to hasten to translate the Psalmist, who is to be sung according to the simplicity of the Seventy interpreters” [the manuscript reads, “singing the Psalmody”], and so forth. Martianay published it long ago; it is so full of monstrous statements and expressions that I shall never cease to wonder how Henschen, otherwise a learned man, could have regarded it as genuine. The remaining pieces are of much the same kind:

“Form of the Psalter. The Psalter is the sonorous hollow of wood fashioned in the shape of the letter delta,” and so forth.

Then follows this passage:

“Because the spirit is not always present to the minds of the prophets, so that, when they do not possess it, they may then recognize that they possess it from the Lord, when they possessed it.”

After these comes the genuine preface of the holy Doctor to the Psalms, which he corrected again according to the Greek exemplar and which begins: “While I was long ago staying at Rome, I corrected the Psalter,” and so forth.

The lengthy exposition of the Psalms itself follows, for whose sake we have discussed these matters:

“I. A Psalm of David concerning Christ. Some think that the key to this psalm must be referred to the person of Christ our Lord, so that this blessed man is Christ according to his humanity,” and so forth.

Martianay found this text in his manuscript, and after him we shall print it at the end of the *Breviary*. After the Psalms, the Canticles are also expounded; then the Lord’s Prayer is interpreted, where the expositor reads “supersubstantial bread” instead of “daily bread.” The Apostles’ Creed and the Catholic Faith of Saint Athanasius are also briefly explained. In the latter, the article concerning the remission of sins is omitted, which would seem to indicate that the Creed is of very great antiquity—for it does not appear in the forms recited by Tertullian, Irenaeus, or Origen—unless it is more truly to be thought that the scribes, through negligence, omitted it in this exposition.

After this comes:

“Here ends Jerome on the Psalter.”

Two verses are added:

> Let those who read these writings remember Francis,  
> And often pour forth prayers to him to whom all things are subject.

There is no point in pursuing the rest, since we have now spoken of Florus’s little poem.

Let us return to Martianay. To the matters we have discussed he added a long preface concerning the Book of Psalms, which he found in three manuscript copies of the canon of Hebrew truth.
