The distinguished Cotelerius had already most accurately declared in his notes on volume III of the *Monuments of the Greek Church* that it belonged neither to Jerome nor to the compiler who assumed Jerome’s name. There is no doubt that the whole thing was copied from the arguments of Eusebius of Caesarea on the Psalms, which he calls Ὑποθίσεις (*Hypotheses*), although the Latin translator—whoever he may have been—seems to have had a competent knowledge of neither language.

We too found a much more carefully corrected copy of this Prologue in the Ambrosian Library, manuscript I, 6, formerly belonging to Saint Columbanus of Bobbio. From it we present the text, in its proper place, in a more corrected form, so that nothing may be lacking.

The collectors of the recent *Anecdota*, the distinguished Edmund Martene and Ursinus Durand, produce another interpretation of the Psalms from a manuscript at Anchin. That book, however, names not Jerome but Hilary of Poitiers as its author. The editors just mentioned also attribute to Hilary a certain portion of the work—namely, four treatises on Psalms XV, XXXI, XLI, and CXLIX—which they are publishing for the first time. Of the rest they do not deny that it belongs to an excerptor who assumed Jerome’s name. For, they say, when they took up the *Breviary on the Psalms*, which Erasmus and Marianus Victorius attribute to the holy Doctor, they found that complete expositions attributed to him were reproduced there.

I shall say nothing about their falsely praising Erasmus here as an advocate of the *Breviary*. I shall, however, maintain that these four treatises do not have Hilary as their author, just as we know with certainty that all the rest falsely claim Jerome. Anyone may see the arguments for this conclusion by examining the treatises themselves and comparing them with Hilary’s sermons.

It will be enough for my purpose to consider briefly the reasons they advance and to show that the Anchin manuscript is nothing other than a somewhat different copy of the compiler’s *Breviary*. They say that these four expositions, which they found still unpublished in that manuscript, are absent from Hilary’s edited works. They further observe in them Hilary’s method of writing, his style, and the most ancient version of Scripture. They therefore saw no serious obstacle to attributing them to Hilary.

This argument was not properly constructed. They would have reasoned badly if only those four pieces had fallen away from Hilary’s commentary. For just as one adds as much cloth as is needed to mend a garment, so what is added does not thereby have the same weave and wool as the rest of the garment. But many more expositions of Hilary on another fifteen Psalms are missing, while they are all present in that manuscript. This very fact shows that the manuscript is excessively fluid and arbitrary, and that the editors act according to their own judgment rather than on the authority of the manuscript when, after rejecting all the others, they admit these four.

The entire collection belongs to a pseudonymous author. The genuine treatises that survive in the Hilary edition differ enormously from those in this collection. The pieces they reject are plainly the work of the compiler who assumed Jerome’s name, taken from the *Breviary*, where they are transcribed word for word. Some of them even contain matters incompatible with Hilary’s age and character. On the other hand, the four pieces they accept are entirely different from those found in the commonly circulated *Breviary*, and they do not conflict with the style and character of the bishop of Poitiers.

Indeed, this is precisely what moves us to think that the opposite conclusion must be drawn from their own arguments. If the pseudonymous author patched together the whole remaining work, why not these four treatises as well, which constitute a very small part of such a long work? Who could persuade himself that, after collecting everything else from fragments of various Fathers, he transcribed these passages *autolexei*—word for word—from Hilary and attached them to his cento without changing either their ideas or their language?

The conclusion ought rather to have been formulated as follows: if some parts of the commentary plainly diverge from Hilary’s age and therefore cannot at all be attributed to him, then none of the pieces can justly be counted among his writings. Otherwise, not only these four homilies but any others that do not differ from Hilary’s age would immediately have to be regarded as Hilary’s. In that way, even writings whose authorship by the bishop of Poitiers is doubtful would suffice to fill out a body of alien work under his name.

The fact that those four pieces are completely different from the ones presented in the compiler’s *Breviary* does nothing to support Hilary. As we have said, copies of that book differ widely from one another. This is customary with such collections: when each person, according to his own inclination, either prepares a discourse for delivery to the people or constructs for himself a manuscript of commentaries on the Psalms, he extracts some treatises from other authors and interpolates them with other testimonies.

The other argument, drawn from style, is equally weak and superficial. Even if we were to grant that these passages differ only slightly from Hilary’s style, the compiler who assumed Jerome’s name contains many other treatises which no one would attribute to Hilary; yet they do not depart even by a finger’s breadth from the character and method of these four. Each compiler plundered fragments from other Fathers, as well as from Hilary. One of them transferred Origen into his own work, and it is therefore no wonder if some passages bear the scent of one or the other.

But let us now pursue our purpose and review the various manuscripts of the *Breviary* that exist.

In Florence, in the Medicean Laurentian Library, shelf XVIII, there is a parchment manuscript numbered 20. It begins with Psalm 119 and reaches Psalm 145. It is written in a sufficiently ancient hand, although at the end a modern hand supplies some leaves worn away by age. An old librarian notes that it contains Jerome’s *Exposition on the Psalms*. The person who first copied the manuscript, however, gave it only this title: *Commentary on the Psalms of David*.

In the same city, in the library of the Fathers of Saint Mark, two very ancient copies bear the name of the holy Doctor. One is entitled *Commentaries of the Lord Jerome on the Psalms*; the other, *The Breviary of the Lord Jerome*.

It is often called *Exposition of the Psalter*, and manuscripts of later times frequently appear under this title. Among them we may mention one marked with the letter R and number 42 in the Ambrosian Library at Milan. Some are found with the single inscription *Jerome on the Psalms*. We likewise observe one there marked with the letter C and numbered slightly above 300.

We have also seen several in Rome. Among them, because of its greater antiquity, a catalogue preserved in a Palatine-Vatican manuscript numbered 27 deserves mention. On its first two pages it contains a catalogue of the books of some ancient library, I know not whose. Among these are listed:

“Saint Jerome’s work on the Psalter, from the first Psalm through Psalm LXXVI, taken from Origen, in one manuscript; and another twenty-six [perhaps read LXXIV] of the same work through the end. Also, an *Exposition of the Penitential Psalms* in one manuscript.”

We also transcribed many passages from the latter work from a square-format manuscript of good age and character, formerly belonging to Saint Columbanus of Bobbio and now in the Ambrosian Library under the letter R and number 42. Its title reads:

> Here begin the Psalms which blessed Jerome arranged to be sung for penitence.

But the various glosses which we then excerpted from printed and unprinted books, though they differed from one another, do not now seem important enough to offer to a reader interested in Jerome’s name.

For, in general, even if I wished carefully to set forth the innumerable disagreements among the manuscripts, I should neither perform work worth the effort nor be able adequately to accomplish the task itself. It is certain that ecclesiastical writers formerly showed great eagerness to cut up and combine homilies of this kind in large numbers. Anyone who hopes to determine what each person contributed is attempting something like draining the sea.

Nevertheless, the matter seemed worthy of attention, especially in view of the scholarly spirit of the present age. We found one manuscript far superior to all the others and wholly different from the commonly circulated copies, and we judged it deserving of more careful examination, as well as of being represented to readers by some specimen, since it was not possible to reproduce the entire work here.

In the Ambrosian Library at Milan, so often praised, there is therefore an extremely ancient book written with a pen. It contains, under Jerome’s name, an *Exposition on the Psalms* entirely different from those that have hitherto become known—and, indeed, a more elegant one. If any such work seemed not unworthy of a place among the writings of the holy Father, this one could stand honorably above the others.

The manuscript is marked with the letter C and a number slightly above 300. It is in the form called oblong, in folio. It formerly belonged to the monastery of Saint Columbanus of Bobbio, from which the most precious monuments of antiquity were brought here.

It is written in what antiquaries like to call an older form of cursive script, one that approaches most closely the shape of the characters that we still see today in Egyptian papyri. Consequently, it is often extremely difficult to read, and much practice is needed to distinguish the characters. At times, because the letters have been worn away by age, the writing escapes the sharpness of the eye. Thus, in more than one place, we thought it better to tolerate a few lacunae than to supply the text by conjecture when this could not be done safely.

The first leaf, which the scribe used as a wrapper for the codex, is written entirely in Latin letters, and these are more or less similar to the character of the rest of the codex. The distinguished man to whom I attribute the highest authority said that the language they represented was unknown to him, or perhaps ancient Illyrian.

I would say—if it matters to the reader to know—that they are Hebrew. The evidence for this is that, although most of the rest has been obliterated, a few Hebrew endings and words indicating the sound can still be read. Above all, there is the interpretation written beside the word *hiruzech* at the edge of the book: “the city of our strength.”

Thus the words that compose that expression are *hir*, Hebrew [Hebrew term], meaning “city”; *uz*, Hebrew [Hebrew term], meaning “strength”; and finally the suffix *ch*, Hebrew [Hebrew term], which is the pronoun “your.” You will therefore say that it ought to be rewritten in Latin as “the city of your strength,” not “of our strength,” so as to correspond to the Hebrew. I do not deny this. Yet I think that the note was added by some learned person not to explain that word in Latin, but to indicate that the Latin reading differed slightly from it.

Whoever he was, he imitated Origen’s diligence. Origen transcribed the Hebrew text for himself in Greek letters in the *Hexapla*; this writer substituted Latin letters. Each, in his own way, used the vernacular script. Perhaps he also represented in Latin a copy of Origen’s transcription rather than the Hebrew archetype. That may be why he often fails to reproduce the peculiar sounds of the original language, its abundant forms of aspiration, and other features of that kind, which he forcibly twists into Latin letters that are even less suitable for the purpose; as a result, the writing often seems to give the sound without understanding it.

But these matters are incidental. Let us now continue with the transcription of the commentary itself.

We have said that it is attributed to Jerome, for the inscription of the codex says so, and its first leaves contain genuinely Hieronymian prefaces to the Psalter. The book begins:

> Here begins the Preface of Jerome on the Psalms in Christ.

At the end it reads:

> Here ends the Prologue of Saint Jerome.

These prefaces are the very ones which the holy Doctor either gave to Paula in the form of letters or prefixed to the Psalter itself, first corrected by him and then translated from Hebrew into Latin.

Nevertheless, so that we conceal nothing, in both places Jerome’s name was added not by the original hand that wrote the codex but by another hand, although that hand too is ancient and approximately contemporary, and appears to have used a different ink.

The commentary follows. From it we have transcribed the expositions of the first and third Psalms and most of the fourth, and we present them here as a test of the authorship. We lost the complete exposition of the second Psalm, I think through the negligence of the person to whom we entrusted our sheets for copying. But since we are offering only a specimen of his work, that loss will scarcely hinder either our purpose or the reader’s interest.

This specimen, I think, will be sufficient for learned men to identify the author. For, if it were to be attributed to Jerome, nothing in what we have so far discussed permits such a suspicion in any way. For my part, unless the conjecture is too bold to be supported by sufficiently good arguments, I should be inclined to attribute it to Saint Columbanus, whom we praised above: first abbot of Luxeuil in Burgundy, then of Bobbio in Italy, from whose monastery this book itself was brought into the Milanese Library.

The few monuments of his genius that have been made public—for most are said to lie in libraries, especially that of Fleury—seem to have the same flavor and character as this commentary. The expression of Scripture is also the same, as far as it has been possible to understand from comparison of several passages.

It is established from other authors, and especially from Sigebert, chapter 60, that Saint Columbanus was endowed with so great a treasure of wisdom that, while still a young man, he wrote a book of Psalms in polished language. From this Trithemius, chapter 223, says:

> While he was still young, he devoted himself greatly to the sacred writings, so that he wrote, in an elegant style, a single book of commentaries on the entire Psalter.

In addition, the chronology of his life—namely, the sixth century, through the end of which the holy abbot lived—agrees quite well with the other circumstances of his Scripture. This is attested by Fredegar in his *Chronicle* and by Aimo in Book III of *The Deeds of the Franks*. Finally, the place from which the work emerged—that very monastery which Saint Columbanus founded and governed for a long time—adds considerable weight to the conjecture.

Nevertheless, we do not wish these matters to be regarded as certain. We leave the identification of the true author to the judgment of learned men who will read this material.

## Psalm One (C, S)

### [Col. 0815A]

Some have wished to say that the first Psalm was spoken concerning King Joash, who was raised by Jehoiada the chief priest and, after Athaliah had been killed, was placed upon the throne. Their reason is that throughout the whole period during which he was instructed in the law of God by the priest, he meditated upon it night and day.

But we must not listen to those who, in order to exclude the true exposition of the Psalms, attempt to introduce false analogies drawn from history. For how could David have designated this man as blessed, free from every error and devoted to the love of virtue, when the Books of Kings offer him no testimony of goodness or anything similar? [At this point the editor has supplied conjecturally the name “David,” and shortly afterward, in this same sentence, the word “Kings,” where the manuscript writing disappears; both are enclosed in brackets so as not to mislead the reader.] In those books it is said:

> And Joash did what was right before the Lord all the days during which Jehoiada the priest instructed him; nevertheless, he did not remove the high places: the people were still sacrificing on the high places.

By saying, “all the days during which Jehoiada the chief priest instructed him, he did what was right before the Lord,” the text indicates that during the remaining days, when Jehoiada’s instruction had ceased, he departed from the right path—that is, that his later conduct did not agree with his early formation.

It is also related in the same Books of Kings that Joash removed Hazael, king of Syria, from his attack on Jerusalem by means of an offering [namely, of consecrated silver and gold; see the note below]. He sent these gifts, which had been taken from the Temple, to Hazael. Yet Joash himself, as well as the kings of Judah—his ancestors—had previously offered them to God, before this deed was committed. The text reads as follows; for it is good for us to approach the knowledge of the event through the testimony of the reading:

> And Joash king of Judah took all the consecrated things which Jehoshaphat, Joram, and Ahaziah, his fathers and kings of Judah, had consecrated, and his own consecrated things, and all the gold that was found in the treasuries of the house of the Lord and in the king’s house, and sent it to Hazael king of Syria.

How, then, could the crown of blessedness have been bestowed upon this man, who despoiled the Temple of the Lord, gathered together all the gifts placed within it, and sent them to a foreign, impious, and sacrilegious man? [The abbreviated and obsolete manuscript signs seemed to offer the reading “which David proclaims,” but this produces an inept sense.]

Therefore, this inappropriate use of history [the manuscript’s whole sentence is badly confused and gaping; see the note below] cannot be fitted to the proof offered by the present Psalm, in which David is pronounced blessed—the man of whom we are speaking, conspicuous for the perfection of every virtue.

At the end of the Psalm it is said:

> Therefore the impious shall not rise in judgment, nor sinners … he shall perish.

This statement applies to those who can even die perfected and possess no small confidence before the Lord because of the goodness of their way of life.

Joash, however, is not shown by the reading of the historical books to have been such a person that he could be proved worthy of blessedness. The Psalm is therefore moral in character, as appears from what follows, where it discusses the desire for vices and abstention from error—matters which cannot properly apply to Joash.

For, during the time when he was brought up by Jehoiada the priest, the child could never have rejected evils by his own judgment, nor could he have devoted diligent care to meditation on the Law, since he was led in every pursuit according to the will of his guardian. [The manuscript corruptly reads *ducebat*; “for, as he was completing his seventh year of life,” or something similar, seems preferable. The conjunction has also been supplied here to complete the sense.] For he was completing his seventh year when the honor and insignia of royal dignity were placed upon him.

There are therefore two things which make a person attain blessedness: right teachings and right judgment—that is, that he think piously about God and [a lacuna]—and an amended formation, before he lives honorably and devoutly. Neither of these two kinds is sufficient for perfection by itself; each supplies the other as a companion, but faith holds the first place.

Just as, in an honorable body, the head and the remaining limbs are considered in relation to perfection, yet the human being also requires the addition and joining together of the other limbs, so, for the completion of life, both things must come together: faith and life. Faith, because it involves attaining perfect understanding, is difficult and arduous [some words may have fallen out here, since the sense is defective]; the discipline of conduct, however, is easy.

The ordering of life is readily understood and seems equally accessible to everyone, both in the desire for good things and in the avoidance of evil. Its practical performance, however, requires no small work and labor. Nevertheless, the merit of one’s life sometimes opens an entrance to faith, while, conversely, sins bar the way to perfect knowledge. For, like certain darknesses of one’s conduct, they block the sure path and make it especially difficult to cultivate this one part of divine Scripture concerning Moses. [“Path” is to be supplied; elsewhere, to make the sense at all coherent, we have supplied “more purely” for the manuscript’s *puritas*, “one” for *unum*, and made one word, *excolere*, out of the two-word manuscript reading *ex colore*. I do not know whether it would have been easier to clean out the Augean stable.]

And so, in the present Psalm also, moral instruction is prescribed before the lessons of discipline. Let us learn, on the testimony of the Apostle, that moral vices are absent from perfect faith. He says to the Corinthians:

> I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as infants in Christ.

And he adds:

> Since there is jealousy among you … are you not carnal and walking according to human standards?

Whereas Cornelius, by contrast, was [a lacuna] toward faith.

### [Col. 0817B]

The subject, then, of the present Psalm is a person beseeching the Lord to unlock understanding and to grant access to it. If, for the sake of our discussion, it should be necessary to explain at greater length some of the matters that arise, we shall not forget the brevity which we promised in the preface.

We shall observe this principle especially in the present Psalm, and in all the others: reducing the whole meaning to a summary, we shall explain briefly what must be said. For it is not our purpose to pursue everything at length, but to touch upon the sense of all that has been stated in outline, so that the first surface of the exposition may shine before those who read it. We leave them opportunities for deeper understanding, should they wish to add something, provided that their additions do not depart from the interpretation already given.

For this is the true apprehension of meaning: to adapt the course of the exposition to the testimony of the history and to present continuously and coherently what must be said. [The reading may perhaps be *continenter*, “continuously.”]

Editorial notes: The manuscript reads *referente*, corruptly, and *Acraelem* for *Azaelem* (Hazael). The omitted offering is evidently that of consecrated silver and gold; the sacred text to be cited below is IV Kings XII.18, and the reader may supply the lacuna with that expression. The preceding biblical testimony should be compared with the Vulgate translation: “King Joash took all the consecrated things which Jehoshaphat, Joram, and Ahaziah, his fathers, kings of Judah, had consecrated, and what he himself had offered, and all the silver that could be found in the treasuries of the house of the Lord and in the king’s palace, and sent it to Hazael king of Syria.” Our text adheres more closely to the Greek.

The abbreviated, obsolete manuscript signs seemed to yield “which David proclaims,” but that gives an inept sense. The manuscript period concerning the inappropriate historical application is exceedingly tangled and defective; the editor merely applied a healing hand so that the sense might stand, proposing *approbat* (“proves”) as a possible reading. If this conjecture seems too bold, the reader may exercise his own skill; shortly afterward the manuscript has *profectum*, where “perfected” has been restored.

Words now obliterated by age have been supplied conjecturally in the moral explanation; *de vitiorum appetitu et de erroris abstinentia* replaces the corrupt *devitiarum appetitum et de errore abstinentia*. The editor supplied “are” after “two”; the third following verse begins with a one-word lacuna, readily supplied from the sequence of the sentence, while the remaining context was gravely corrupt. Nothing was changed in *priusquam*, although “of life” or “of morals,” with an added *ut*, might seem preferable; *sancteque* replaces manuscript *saneque*, and *Neutrum* replaces a nonsensical two-word reading *nec non*. Some words have fallen out after the discussion of faith and perfect understanding. For the manifestly corrupt *et quam*, one may read *aequa* or *aeque*. The sequence is again somewhat obstructed where the merit of a good life is said to open the way to faith; it would be still more defective if the author were thought to maintain that faith can be gained through the merit of a good life. *Obstruit* has been confidently restored for the corrupt *obstinuit*.

The text also contains a supplied second negative particle after *propositum est*; it reads *facie* corruptly for “surface,” and *relinquentibus* for “leaving.”

Blessed is the man who has not gone in counsel …, has sat. Sometimes divine Scripture distinguishes between the ungodly and the sinner: it calls one ungodly who has no knowledge of the true God, but a sinner who does not keep to the path of what is honorable and right. Yet where it signifies both by a common term, here it nevertheless seems to make a distinction, since it wishes to express who is the follower of perfection, to whom blessedness is rightly believed to belong, either because of perfect knowledge of the Godhead or because of his pursuit of a better life.

But when it says, “he has not gone,” “he has not stood,” “he has not sat,” it indicates the movements of the soul by bodily signs. For when we undertake to accomplish something, first we are moved to seize the task [Col. 0818A] … [lacuna]; then we come to a halt when the matter has begun to be in our hands; but we turn to sitting when the business has already been completed.

[Note: [Col. 0818D] I suspect that *peracto* (“completed”) should be restored.]

This is what holy David says: that the man is truly blessed who did not even approach or enter the thought of ungodliness at its first traces, who did not find … [lacuna] the inclination toward an evil deed, and who is not entangled by any snare of the allurements of evil affection. This is shown by the terms “seat” and “sitting,” so that he might join himself to their company, [Note: [Col. 0818D] I would prefer *qui* (“who”) to be restored in place of *sed* (“but”).] but rather those who infect the simplicity of others with the poison of their depravity.

For these he calls “pestilent,” whose association is plainly diseased. It is characteristic of a pestilence, after all, to pass from one person to another, infecting and corrupting the bodies of many. Thus, by saying “he has not gone,” he marked the assent of the thoughts by which we are hurried toward evil suggestions and in which we take pleasure in fulfilling [Col. 0818B] what is proper to us. But when he says, “he has not stood,” he indicates that he has never gone out into the deed toward which thought had suggested that the mind proceed; yet we fulfill it when we take pleasure in fixing our step in other actions … [lacuna] and repeatedly lingering.

By sitting in the seat he signifies the man who takes such pleasure in, and rests in, an evil habit that he mingles without any shameful consent with the other people devoted to the same pursuit. By saying “the counsels of the ungodly” and “the works of sinners,” he has sufficiently considered both. Ungodliness pertains to the agitation of the mind and to the movement of a soul that does not think rightly; sin, however, is action already carried into effect.

The third element he added to both [Note: [Col. 0818D] The manuscript seemed to prefer *utriusque* (“of both”); shortly afterward, I would prefer *quod* (“which”) or *quoniam* (“since”) in place of *quam* (“whom”); and finally, *vocarentur* (“might be called”) in place of *vocaretur* (“might be called,” singular).] is that not only those are called pestilent who, by thinking wrongly, corrupt the rest and destroy them through their association [Col. 0818C], but also those who weaken the goodness of their upright conduct through the contagion of their fellowship. Not to mingle with them at all is to be … [Note: [Col. 0818D] Supply in the blank *hominis* (“of a man”), or *animi* (“of the mind”), or something similar.] … one who provides for himself most wisely.

And therefore the reading of the present psalm defines as blessed the man who in every respect avoids such people: one who watches over his actions so carefully that he also withdraws from the evil solicitation of others [Note: [Col. 0818D] The preposition *ab* (“from”) was missing in the manuscript.] and fears that his own brightness and purity may be darkened by the stains of others. [Note: [Col. 0818D] We restored this passage conjecturally as *Quoniam* (“Since”), and at the end of the verse *tantum* (“only”), in place of the corrupt *quam* and *tamen* found in the copy.]

Since, in striving toward blessedness, it is not enough merely to withdraw from evil, it is also necessary to do good. Below he says: “But his will was in the law of the Lord,” and so forth, “by day and by night.” He says: “He not only strives to avoid the company of the wicked, but by constant and continual meditation on the law learns how he ought to shape himself.”

And, in order to set forth the fruitfulness of the pursuit which he is trying to commend [Col. 0819A], he introduces a comparison by which the good and blessed man of whom he speaks may be made manifest to people. “And he shall be like a tree planted beside streams,” and so forth, “and all that he does shall prosper.” He says: “Like a tree whose nature is to flourish … [lacuna], it is also given life by the benefit of the place in which it has been planted, so that it is protected from dryness by flowing waters and, through them, is full of abundant fruits. It feels neither the injuries of air, nor of place, nor of season.”

This is indicated by what follows: “And everything that he does shall prosper,” conspicuous alike for perpetual greenness and for the abundance of its fruits. Thus, too, the man who has abstained from evil and bound himself to the love of good pursuits will be illustrious. No work of sin will deceive him, and continual meditation on the law will adorn him. [Note: [Col. 0819C] In this middle verse the manuscript was written in abbreviated characters [Col. 0819D] as *ss. aeternae* (“of eternal …”), perhaps a gloss imported rashly from the margin into the text.]

… eternal … [lacuna]

“Not so the ungodly, not so, but like,” and so forth, “from the face of the earth.” In the preceding statements he summoned everyone to the pursuit of virtue; in the present ones he frightens them away from vices. By comparing them with dust he shows how great is the worthlessness of the ungodly, [Note: [Col. 0819D] I would readily agree with the corrector who restores *numquam* (“never”) in place of the manuscript’s awkward reading, and *aestimentur* (“may be judged”) in place of *aestimantur* (“are judged”).] and how little they are ever deemed worthy of any approval; and he shows that when evils overtake them they are easily driven along and cannot stand, like dust which, because of its extreme thinness and lightness, is scattered here and there by blasts of wind … [lacuna]

Therefore the ungodly do not rise, and so forth, “of the righteous.” In saying this he does not deny a resurrection to the ungodly. Indeed, if they were not to rise, they would escape the future punishments which they will certainly suffer only after being restored to the body. [Note: [Col. 0819D] Several ancient copies, both versions and commentators, are known to have read *resurgant* (“let them rise”) here. Nevertheless, our author is not so consistent that shortly afterward he does not prefer *resurgent* (“they will rise”) in the future tense.]

Thus the punishment of soul and body will be common, just as participation in sin was common [Col. 0819C] … [lacuna]. It is just as if, when we have a judge dealing with manifest crimes, we were to apply no delay to the investigation but immediately pronounce the sentence of condemnation. Likewise, the ungodly, rising for punishment, will not have that delay [Note: [Col. 0820D] The manuscript plainly has *dilectionem* (“affection”) instead of *dilationem* (“delay”); shortly afterward, *vis* (“force”) should be read in place of *vi* (“by force”).] which the force of judgment usually applies during interrogations. The psalm indicates that a heavier punishment awaits them [Note: [Col. 0820D] It seems necessary to supply: “but immediately the sentence of the criminals,” and so forth.] … [lacuna] they will be thrust into the place due to their merits and into final destruction.

Therefore he did not say simply, “they will not rise,” but added, “in judgment.” They will not rise for examination, but they will rise in order immediately to receive the sentence [Col. 0820A] of condemnation. And lest, from the common designation of resurrection, we should suppose that the expulsion of all will likewise be common [Note: [Col. 0820D] The manuscript had the obscure reading *aestimantes* (“thinking”), and in the following verse *cum* (“when”) in place of *quod* (“that”). A little later, we printed *differentia* (“difference”) rather than what the erased letters in the manuscript seemed to indicate, based on the context and sequence of the argument.], he shows that at the very moment of resurrection there will be a great difference: one will be led through it to honor, another sent into punishment. For to some it will be precious and rewarding, while to others it will be grievous and terrifying. [Note: [Col. 0820D] In the manuscript *enim* (“for”) was corruptly written in place of *inter* (“between”).]

Or he made a distinction between the ungodly and the sinner: he says that the ungodly do not rise for judgment—that is, as we said above, they do not come into [Note: [Col. 0820D] It is scarcely possible to say by what errors this verse had been defaced and had to be corrected conjecturally. The manuscripts had *excommunicationem* (“excommunication”) in place of *communicationem* (“participation”); *peccatoris* (“of the sinner”) in place of *peccatores* (“sinners”); and, what made the matter still more difficult, *hi* (“these”) without any mark of distinction in place of *hos* (“them”).] participation with the sinner—but that the sinners do not share in the assembly of the righteous, that is, that they have no communion in the reward of the righteous. Therefore they too will be handed over to punishments, not because through their sins they are excluded from the former; they will undoubtedly receive penalties belonging to those who do things different from the former [the text is difficult] [Col. 0820B].

The difference will be this: the ungodly will rise not to be examined but to be assigned immediately to their places [Note: [Col. 0820D] We conjecturally printed *suis* (“their own”), supplied from letters that had faded in the manuscript]; whereas the sinners will be joined to the righteous by no communion. This is shown more clearly by what follows: “For the Lord knows the way of the righteous”—that is, he will fully demonstrate by the testimony of reward that it is pleasing and acceptable to him—“but the path of the ungodly will perish.” For the ungodly do not rise for examination precisely because the perfect knowledge of God contains the paths of all; and without any delay their condition and their deserving lot will receive their resurrection.

# THE THIRD PSALM (C, S)*

A psalm of David, when he fled from the face of Absalom his son. Absalom, whose name is interpreted as “peace of the father,” signifies Judas the traitor. David—that is, Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God—fled from his face when, after the devil had entered his heart, he abandoned him by a hidden judgment.

## “Lord, how they have multiplied.”

This is the voice of Christ to the Father concerning his persecutors, that is, the Jews; and the Church addresses the Lord concerning all its enemies. Here the Lord Christ is speaking against the people who had risen up against him, although he had come to them for the sake of salvation. By saying, “They trouble me,” he shows that he deeply grieved over their blindness, because with obstinate minds they rejected him.

## “Many say.”

They were so numerous that even the traitor Judas, one of the number of the Jews, was added to them. “Many say”: for when “many” is repeated so often, the savage multitude of the ungodly is displayed.

## “There is no salvation.”

This refers to those words of the Jews: “He saved others; he cannot save himself.”

## “But you, Lord.”

The Word made flesh is the assumption of humanity, and of the Church. Therefore the flesh speaks of its own glory and of the exaltation of the head which the almighty Word assumed.

## “With my voice.”

The Gospel words make this clear, where the Son says: “Father, glorify your Son,” and so forth.

## “And he heard me from his holy mountain.”

That is, from the exceedingly high summit of his divinity, when he said: “I have glorified, and I will glorify again.”

## “I slept.”

He comes to the second part, in which he expresses Christ’s sleeping and slumbering in the Passion, and his resurrection. Concerning this he himself said: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it again.” Therefore he rose, because divine power assumed his human nature.

Alternatively: The Church slept through unbelief but rose through the illumination of faith. Christ slept in death through the Passion and rose through the glory of the resurrection.

## “I will not fear thousands.”

In the Passion of the Savior a great multitude of people surrounded him, but he did not fear it in the least, because he knew that he would rise again after three days.

## “And my flesh was saved.”

The Church speaks concerning Christ its Lord—that is, the body speaks to its head. When he rose, it too was saved.

## “For you have struck.”

Not only Christ’s adversaries—that is, the Savior’s persecutors—but also heretics are struck with blindness of mind, for they gnaw at the words of truth with the teeth of slander. So too, when the Jews were saying, “If he is the king of Israel, let him come down from the cross, and we will believe him,” the enemies of Christ’s name were struck down by confusion. Therefore they were crushed, because they immediately recognized that he had risen in glory.

## “Salvation belongs to the Lord.”

Eternal life cannot be destroyed, nor can the Savior’s salvation in any way be cut off. Therefore everlasting blessing follows those who believe in him.

# THE FOURTH PSALM (C, S)*

A psalm of David, “for the end,” with songs. Here “end” signifies perfection, not completion. The psalm refers to action, while the song refers to knowledge or joy.

## “When I called.”

The mother Church rejoices that she has been heard by the God of her righteousness, from whom she possesses everything that is just and right—her righteousness—for she confesses the unity and omnipotence of the holy Trinity. She says that she has been enlarged when confessors are made and martyrs are crowned.

Alternatively: “From the narrow places of sorrow you led me into the breadth of joys.”

## “Have mercy on me.”

The devout mother said that mercy ought to be shown her if her prayer were heard on behalf of her children.

## “Sons of men, how long,” etc.

The holy Church rightly confesses that those who, after the preaching of truth, chose instead to worship the idols of falsehood had long been heavy of heart. These idols are vanity and a lie. They rightly received such a name because they were raised up against the dignity of truth.

## “And know.”

That is, believe that Christ, whom the Jews crucified, was glorified by God the Father in the resurrection and ascension. The Son himself also heard his Church whenever they cried out to him, and rightly so, because she herself preached him to the peoples for glorification.

## “Be angry.”

You ought to be angry at your past sins, so that you may be able to escape present wickedness; and do not do evil again.

## “Be pierced.”

Bring forward your evil thoughts before you commit the crimes which you always turn over in your hearts. “Be pierced,” that is, for repentance. What he named “heart” above, here he has called “bed.”

## “Sacrifice.”

Here he begins another matter. The most merciful mother teaches and says: “Sacrifice the sacrifice of righteousness,” that is, live rightly, and always offer your hearts, cleansed, to the divinity.

“And hope in the Lord,” so that a more fortunate hope may follow a good life.

“Many,” and so forth.

[NOTA.]

These passages will have been more than sufficient as a specimen for grasping the work, unless they should perhaps seem to have been transcribed more extensively than was appropriate for careless readers. But, to return to my purpose, I shall conclude this admonition, as a kind of coda, with one further example, from which you may understand how little trustworthy the author of the *Breviarium* is—he who at one time passed himself off as Augustine and who also invaded Augustine’s own exposition of the Psalms.

This was long ago noted by the Benedictine editors in three manuscripts—namely, the Vatican, the Royal, and the Clermont manuscript of the Dominican Fathers—which contain Augustine’s treatises on the Psalms. They observed that the exposition of Psalm XIV taken from the author of the *Breviarium*, with scarcely more than a few words changed, is found there and placed immediately before the other exposition, which truly belongs to Augustine.

It is copied there, as it is at the beginning under the false name of Jerome:

“Appropriately the fourteenth psalm has been read, and according to the order it has turned out so,” and so forth, through to the end. It is further secured by this subscription:

“Here ends the treatise of Aurelius Augustine, bishop, on Psalm XIV.”

If we had at hand the handwritten codices of the other ancient authors who wrote on the Psalms, I have no doubt that comparable examples would be found among them. For either this pseudonymous author of the *Breviarium* compiled the writings of all the commentators who preceded him, or certainly assumed their identities.

[Col. 0821]

# BREVIARIUM ON THE PSALMS (C, G, S)

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0821C]

Recently, when we were reading together Origen’s *Psalter*, which he called the *Enchiridion*, annotated with brief and necessary interpretations, we both discovered that he had either touched upon some matters only lightly or left them wholly untouched. He discussed these matters at length in another work, because he did not think it a small undertaking to conclude them in a brief discourse.

Therefore, in view of the intimacy between us, you earnestly and diligently requested that I should mark whatever seemed worthy of remembrance to me, using certain signs rather than interpretations. Just as those who draw the locations of lands and cities on a small tablet, and attempt to display very extensive regions within a limited space, do this, so in the vast work of the Psalter I might touch upon certain matters in passing, so that from the few things I had treated, the force and rationale of the others that had been omitted might also be understood.

This is not because I think I can say what he passed over, but because I shall bring into this narrow little commentary what he himself discussed in his volumes or homilies, or what I consider worthy of reading. The *Psalter* is Greek, and in Latin it is called an *organum*; the Hebrews call it *NEBEL*. A psalm is so called because it takes its name from the *psalterium*, or because it is sung (*psallendo*).

Although David sang all the psalms, nevertheless all the psalms refer to the person of Christ. And those which do not appear to bear headings among the Hebrews are counted as one psalm. For through the heading the meaning of each psalm is understood.

What is a heading except a key? Just as, so to speak, no one enters a house except through a key, so the meaning of each psalm is understood through its key, that is, through its heading: in whose person it is sung, whether in the person of Christ, or in the person of the Church, or in the person of the prophet.

[Note: [Col. 0823A] This comparison is taken from Origen, who himself professes that he learned it from a certain Hebrew. Saint Hilary also approved it. We shall discuss it later in the preface to the other exposition of the Psalms, which we shall likewise append as falsely attributed to Jerome.]

# THE PSALMS BEGIN TO BE EXPOUNDED

[Col. 0823]

# THE FIRST PSALM

[Col. 0823B]

## “Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly.”

Some say that this psalm is like a preface of the Holy Spirit, and therefore has no heading. Others say that, because it is the first, it has the beginning of its own order, and that it is an error of *pleonasm*—πλεονασμός—to call it “first,” since there is none before it.

Alternatively: Among the Hebrews the first and second psalms are one psalm, as is also confirmed in the Acts of the Apostles. Finally, because it began with blessedness, it ends in blessedness, saying: “Blessed are all who trust in him.”

Alternatively: Blessed is the man who has not thought, done, or taught evil.

Alternatively: Blessed is the man who is neither Jew, gentile, nor heretic.

Alternatively: Tertullian, in his book *On Spectacles*, maintains that this psalm can be understood both of Joseph, who buried the Lord’s body, and of those who do not gather for the spectacles of the nations.

## “And has not stood in the way of sinners.”

He did not say, “and has not walked in the way of sinners.” For this is impossible, since no one is without sin, even if his life should last only a single hour. He does not say that anyone is without sin, but “has not stood in the way of sinners”: that is, he has not persevered in wrongdoing, but has turned toward better things through repentance.

## “And has not sat in the seat of pestilence.”

In Hebrew, instead of “the pestilent,” it has “scoffers,” meaning that every perverse teacher mocks all his disciples. Hence Jeremiah says: “I did not sit,” he says, “in the assembly of those who jest” (Jeremiah XV).

## “But his will was in the law of the Lord.”

He has referred to two of the three elements, so that the man may have the will and join effort to the will.

## “And in his law he will meditate day and night.”

[Col. 0823D]

Meditation on the law consists not only in reading the Scriptures but also in doing what is written. Therefore the righteous man, whether he eats, drinks, or sleeps, does everything in the name of the Lord and meditates on his law day and night.

## “And he shall be like a tree that has been planted,” etc.

For “planted,” Aquila translated “transplanted.” I think that the tree to which the blessed man is compared is wisdom, concerning which Solomon also speaks: “She is a tree of life to those who follow her” (Proverbs III). Through the Apostle, wisdom is declared to be Christ, the Son of God: “Christ,” he says, “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (I Corinthians I). That is, having certainly been conformed to Christ, the Son of God, in the body of his glory.

## “Which shall give its fruit in its season.”

For he will give fruit not at just any time, but at the appointed time—namely, when, after conquering the powers and principalities, he will hand over the kingdom to God the Father, conformed to the glory of his body.

As for the fact that the Lord wished to be called a tree, he says: “Either make the tree good and its fruit good” (Matthew XII). And concerning the wood he said: “If they do this in the green wood, what will happen in the dry?” (Luke XXIII).

[Col. 0824C]

## “And its leaf shall not fall.”

These are the words of teaching which benefit the nations for salvation, in accordance with the statement in the Apocalypse: “And the leaves of this tree are for the healing of the nations. And everything that he does shall prosper” (Revelation XXII).

The Jews think that this psalm was spoken concerning Josiah, because he alone among profane kings did not go in the counsel of the ungodly but followed the law of God. Yet what has just been read—“and everything that he does shall prosper”—cannot be understood of Josiah, nor indeed of any of the saints, except perhaps in the future age.

We therefore understand it better of that man who was assumed and saved by our Savior—not in the sense that we testify that one person assumed another person, or that one was the assumer and another the one assumed, but in the sense that the one and the same Son of God and son of man, who before the ages was always the Word, afterward deigned to assume flesh.

[Col. 0824D]

## “Not so the ungodly, not so.”

The second “not so” does not occur in the Hebrew books, nor even among the translators of the Septuagint. For when I was reading Origen’s copies in the Caesarean library, I found it written only once.

There is this difference between the ungodly and the sinner: the ungodly denies God; the sinner confesses him and sins.

Just as the righteous man is compared with a tree, so the ungodly is compared with dust. The righteous man is compared with the tree of paradise; the ungodly, however, is compared with dust.

## “But like dust which the wind drives away from the face of the earth.”

Although dust comes from the earth, it nevertheless ceases to be earth. So wretched will the ungodly man be that he will not even be earthly dust. He seems to possess the substance of earth, but he possesses his own substance: he has nothing solid, but whatever he has, he has for punishment.

He is scattered here and there; he is never in one place. Wherever the wind has drawn him, there its force directs him. So too the ungodly man, who once has denied God, is led by error wherever the breath of the devil has drawn him.

## “Therefore the ungodly do not rise in judgment.”

Not because they do not rise, but because they do not rise in judgment: for judgment concerning them has already been made. [Note: [Col. 0825D] Servatus Lupus is known to cite this passage of Jerome in his *Collection on Three Questions* in these words: “The same Doctor [Jerome] expressed the meaning of predestination in another formulation in his exposition of the first psalm: ‘He who does not believe,’ he says, ‘has already been judged; for he has already been forejudged to punishment.’ Compare now the genuine Jerome, *Dialogue against the Pelagians*, no. 28: ‘In the first psalm,’ he says, ‘it is sung that the ungodly do not rise in judgment. For they have already been forejudged to destruction. Nor do sinners rise in the assembly of the righteous; for it is one thing to await the glory of rising, another to perish forever.’]

## “Nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous.”

If sinners do not rise in the assembly of the righteous, the resurrection of sinners and of the righteous is different.

## “For the Lord knows the way of the righteous.”

The Lord knows nothing except what is worthy of his knowledge. For the Lord knows those who are his; and if anyone does not know, he will not be known (II Timothy). And to sinners it is said: “Depart from me, workers of iniquity; I do not know you” (Luke XIII).

As for “the way of the righteous,” I think it refers to him who says: “I am the way” (John XIV). Concerning him the prophet also says: “See what is the good way.” “And the way of the ungodly will perish” (Jeremiah VI). How mercifully expressed: not that the ungodly will perish, but that ungodliness will perish.

# THE SECOND PSALM

## “Why did the nations rage, and the peoples meditate on vain things?”

It is presumptuous to wish to interpret this psalm after Peter—or rather to understand it in a way different from what Peter said in the Acts of the Apostles.

## “The kings of the earth stood, and the princes gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ.”

It was not only King Herod but also those kings whose kingdoms the devil showed him in a moment of time who stood against the Lord.

## “Let us break their bonds and cast them away,” etc.

The four preceding verses were spoken either by angels or by prophets, who marvel that human recklessness rose up against the Son of God. From the fifth verse onward the Lord himself answered, exhorting the gentile people and all those among the Jews who would believe in him to dissolve the legal bonds and cast off the heavy burden of the Law, which their fathers had been unable to bear, and to follow him whose yoke is easy and whose burden is light.

## “He who dwells in the heavens will mock them.”

Through examples drawn from human speech we learn about God’s affections—not because he mocks anyone, but because we do things worthy of mockery.

## “And the Lord will deride them.”

Derision is properly expressed with a wrinkled brow and a contracted nose. Therefore let us not imagine that this applies bodily to God, something which some people even consider worthy of criticism in serious men.

## “Then he will speak to them in his anger.”

Lactantius wrote a very fine book on the anger of God, and Origen himself discusses it frequently. Their point is that it is not so much anger as necessary correction, like that of a father toward a son, a physician toward a sick person, or a teacher toward a pupil.

Anger may seem to belong to those who endure it, not because God corrects while angry.

## “And in his fury he will trouble them.”

As in the Epistle to the Romans: “The wrath of God is revealed” (Romans I), so that those who understand it is to come may strive to avoid it. Thus in the present passage he speaks kindly: he does not say “he will punish,” but “he will trouble,” so that the troubled person may be corrected without punishments.

## “But I have been appointed king.”

This is the voice of Christ. “I have been appointed king” is said with reference to the flesh.

## “By him, God the Father.”

## “Upon Zion.”

That is, upon the Church. Zion is interpreted as “watchtower of life.”

## “Upon his holy mountain.”

The mountain is the Church, or Christ himself, as in the statement: “And it shall come to pass in the last days that the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains, preaching the commandment of the Lord” (Isaiah II). This means the teaching of the Gospel.

## “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you.”

Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever. Rightly, then, to him who was born in time it is said:

[Col. 0826C]

## “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance.”

As if he were saying: “While the Jews were unwilling to receive you, all the nations will come to you as your inheritance.”

## “You shall rule them with an iron rod.”

With the harsh discipline of the Romans. Or, by “an iron rod,” an intolerable discipline, because their hearts were crooked.

## “You shall break them like a potter’s vessel.”

Before a potter’s vessel has hardened into earthenware, if it is broken, it can be reshaped. Read Jeremiah (Jeremiah XIX). But once earthenware has been broken, it cannot be fitted together again intact. Yet what is impossible among human beings is possible with God.

The potter is Christ; the vessel is the human being, as in the statement: “As a vessel is in the hand of the potter, so are you in my hand, says the Lord” (ibid., XVIII).

Alternatively: It is broken either into repentance or, on the day of judgment, into fire.

## “Now understand, you kings.”

All the kings of the age, or the holy kings, the apostles: understand these things stated above.

## “Be instructed.”

That is, instruct yourselves or others—those who judge the earth, the holy Church.

## “Serve the Lord in fear.”

He said “in fear” to remove arrogance from them, because he had called them kings.

## “And rejoice in him.”

He said this to encourage them again, as in: “Rejoice and exult, with trembling” [Col. 0827A]—so that they might be with trembling, that is, with trembling of body and fear of soul.

## “Embrace discipline, lest the Lord become angry.”

For the Greek phrase δράξασθε παιδίας (*draxasthe paideias*, “grasp instruction”) corresponds to the Hebrew *NESCU BAR*, which can be interpreted as “worship the Son.”

This is therefore a most explicit prophecy concerning Christ, and the order of the command is: “Worship the Son, lest the Lord”—that is, the Father—“become angry.”

## “And you perish from the righteous way.”

The Lord was angry with the Jews who refused to worship the Son, and they perished from the straight way. The righteous or straight way is Christ. We are in the way when we fulfill God’s commandments. We perish from the way when we turn aside from them.

## “When his anger is brief.”

That is, at the departure of each person. Or “brief anger” means on the day of judgment, as in: “When people say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them” (I Thessalonians V).

## “Blessed are all who trust in him.”

Not in human beings, nor in themselves, but in God. As we said earlier, this psalm ends in blessedness, from which the preceding psalm begins; therefore among the Hebrews they are counted as one.

# THE THIRD PSALM

A psalm of David, when he fled from the face of Absalom his son. This psalm comes later than many of those which seem to belong to the history of Saul. David suffered Saul’s ambushes before Absalom took up arms against him.

But since David’s purpose was not merely to recount what he had suffered but to instruct all human beings through his example, he placed the second events before the first, in order to teach the sequence of temptations. For first we are reproved on account of sins, and afterward tested on account of virtue.

In David, however, the order of temptations was reversed. Under Saul he was innocent during the persecution; under Absalom he is held manifestly guilty of a crime, since he had killed Uriah. Read the heading of the fiftieth psalm, and you will understand that, according to the earlier order, this is the third.

## “Lord, why have those who trouble me multiplied? Many rise up against me.”

This psalm can apply to David, to Christ, and through him to all the saints.

## “He heard me from his holy mountain.”

I think the holy mountain is the only-begotten Son of God, toward whom the peoples will flow in the last days, as Isaiah and Micah prophesy.

But it can also be understood of the Church, because “a city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden.”

[Col. 0827D]

## “I slept, and was overcome with sleep, and rose again, because the Lord received me.”

“It was like sleep,” he says, “and its place was persecution.”

## “I will not fear thousands of people surrounding me.”

David can say this concerning Absalom and his army; and the Lord can say it concerning the Jews raging against him and crying: “Take him away, take him away, crucify him” (John XXIX).

## “For you have struck all those who oppose me without cause.”

The Lord strikes the vineyards of foreigners with hail; and the Savior, who became all things for us, is written to have been struck by the Father: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered” (Zechariah XIII).

Instead of “without cause,” the Hebrew reads *maxilla*, that is, *LECHI*. Since he had mentioned the cheek, what follows is introduced accordingly:

## “You have crushed the teeth of sinners.”

Let the friends of history alone answer how God strikes the cheek and breaks the teeth of sinners, as boxers fighting against him would do.

“You have crushed the teeth of sinners”: the princes of the Jews; or the teeth are the heretical teachers, or their words.

## “Salvation belongs to the Lord.”

That is, it comes not from a human being but from God. He alone can bring a person from death into life, and through him this is possible.

## “And upon your people.”

That is, upon the Christian people.

## “Your blessing.”

He pours blessing upon the believing people, transmitting the Holy Spirit to them; or in the future, when he will say: “Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew XXV).

# THE FOURTH PSALM

[Col. 0828B]

A psalm of David, “for the end,” with songs. “For the end,” that is, in Christ. For Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes. “With songs,” that is, with praises. “A psalm of David,” that is, the praise of Christ.

## “When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me.”

It is incongruous to understand this of David: he who in the preceding psalm was almost killed by his son because of Uriah’s murder would now dare to say, “The God of my righteousness heard me.”

Therefore the entire psalm must be referred to Christ, and through Christ to the righteous. Jacob also spoke something similar when he said: “My righteousness will hear me tomorrow” (Genesis XXX).

## “In my tribulation you enlarged me.”

“Have mercy on me and hear my prayer.” Although you have brought me help and enlarged me in my tribulation, nevertheless I always need your mercy.

## “Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?”

### “Diapsalma.”

The word *SELA* was translated as *diapsalma* by the Septuagint translators, Symmachus, and Theodotion. Aquila translated it as “always.” I think it is either a sign of some musical sound or an indication of the permanence of what has been foretold. Thus wherever *SELA*, that is, *diapsalma*, or “always,” is added, we should understand that what follows or what precedes belongs not merely to the present time but also to eternity.

## “What you say in your hearts, and be pierced in your beds.”

What you sinfully ponder during the day, expiate at night through tears.

## “Sacrifice the sacrifice of righteousness, and hope in the Lord.”

Offer righteousness as a sacrifice to God, and consequently you will hope in the Lord.

The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord. He upon whose face the light of the Lord has been marked contemplates the glory of the Lord with unveiled face. The Lord commanded that a similar sign be marked on the foreheads of those who groan in the book of the prophet Ezekiel (Ezek. IX).

They have been filled with the fruit of their grain and wine. The reading found in several manuscripts, “and their oil,” I did not find when I consulted Origen’s old copy of the Psalter, which had been corrected by his own hand—neither in the Hebrew, nor in the other editions, nor among the Septuagint interpreters themselves.

## PSALM V

**For the end, concerning her who receives the inheritance; a psalm of David.** This psalm is composed concerning the Church, which at the end and consummation of the world will receive the inheritance among all nations that believe in Christ. Accordingly, its prayer is addressed to the Lord in her person.

Attend to my words with your ears, O Lord. No one possesses this confidence except the Church. The sinner does not dare to say, “Attend to my words with your ears, O Lord”; the one who is angry and curses does not dare to say, “Attend to my words with your ears, O Lord,” but wishes God to close his ears. Understand my cry, etc. In Scripture, a cry is not of the voice but of the heart. Thus it is said to Moses: “Why do you cry out to me?” (Exod. XIV), although Moses had not previously cried out. “Understand my cry.” And the Apostle says: “Crying out in our hearts, Abba, Father” (Gal. IV). Certainly, one who cries out does not cry out in his heart but with his tongue. How, then, does the Apostle say, “crying out in our hearts”? Whenever our groaning and our conscience make supplication, God understands this cry. Hence Jeremiah also says: “Let the pupil of my eye not be silent” (Lam. II). See what he says: “Let the pupil of my eye not be silent”; and at times the pupil of the eye cries out to God. Certainly, if it cries out, it cries out with the tongue, not with the pupil of the eye. But just as we cry out in our hearts when we beseech the Lord with groaning, so, when we pour out tears before God, at that time the pupil of our eye cries out to the Lord.

My king and my God. He has truly dared to say, “My king and my God,” for whom sin does not reign in his mortal body. “My king and my God,” because you reign in me and sin does not reign; therefore you are my God. You are my God, because the belly is not my god; gold is not my god; lust is not my god. Since you are power, and I desire to possess virtues, therefore you are my God—that is, my virtue.

In the morning you will hear my voice. Some interpret this more simply: “I rise at dawn to pray and beseech you.” But what sort of interpretation is it to say that he hears us in the morning, but does not hear us in the evening or at midnight? Rather, see what he says: “As long as I am in the darkness of error, he does not hear me. But when the sun of righteousness comes into my heart, then he hears me: in the morning you will hear my voice.” He did not say, “at the third hour”; he did not say, “at the sixth hour”; he did not say, “in full daylight.” Instead, see what he says: “In the morning”—as soon as the darkness has begun to flee, you hear me; at the very beginning of the good work you hear me; you do not wait for its completion. It is mine to will; yours to accomplish.

In the morning I will stand before you. Observe the order: in the morning, not in the evening, not in darkness, but in the morning. “In the morning I will stand before you”: I will stand steadfastly and imitate Moses. “In the morning I will stand before you”: I will stand before you, not before others. When morning has come, and I have stood, and have stood before you, then I shall be worthy to see you.

And I will see. “You” is understood. Many read this incorrectly and say *καὶ ἐπόψειμε*; but we should know that this is an error. It is written *καὶ ἐπόψομαι*, that is, “and I will see.” Thus the order we have described is maintained: when the light of virtues begins in my soul, when I begin to stand before you—not sit, not lie down, but stand—and you set my feet upon the rock, then, by these steps, [Col. 0830A] I shall be worthy to see you.

For you are God who does not desire iniquity. Therefore you do not hear me in full daylight, but in the morning, because you, God, do not desire iniquity. When I begin to withdraw from iniquity, I shall immediately become worthy of your hearing.

Nor will the wicked dwell near you. When someone who is evil withdraws from us, let us rejoice: what happened in the Lord is taking place in us also. For see what the Holy Spirit says: “Nor will the wicked dwell near you.” What fellowship is there between light and darkness? What agreement is there between Christ and Belial? Therefore, when some depart from among us, let us also say: “They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John XII). It is said to God: “The wicked will not dwell near you.” For if God is fire, and a consuming fire, whoever is straw and whoever is wood flees from the fire, lest he be consumed by the fire.

The unjust will not remain before your eyes. When it says, “they will not remain,” it shows that they once remained. The unjust did once remain before the eyes of God: they remained while God awaited their repentance. But because they continued to be unjust, therefore they did not remain before the eyes of God.

You hate all who work iniquity. Unfortunate is the one whom God hates. Who is the one whom God hates? The one who works iniquity. For if we all sin, and everyone who sins is hated by God, then we are hated by the Lord. But if we are hated by the Lord, how have we been saved by grace?

“You hate all who work iniquity.” He did not say, “who have worked iniquity,” but “who work iniquity.” Those who persist in sin are hated by the Lord; those who have abandoned it are loved by the Lord.

You will destroy all who speak falsehood. I see something remarkable. The one who does evil is hated; the one who lies perishes. Let us consider which is worse: to be hated by the Lord or to perish. Unfortunate indeed is the one who is hated by the Lord, but he still lives. The one who speaks falsehood and perishes ceases already to exist. Therefore the one who speaks falsehood is more unfortunate than the one who works iniquity: the one who works iniquity is hated; the one who speaks falsehood perishes. “For the mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. I). And how is it written: “That God may be true, and every human being a liar” (Rom. III)? But if everyone who speaks falsehood already perishes and kills his own soul, and we all lie, will we all perish?

This statement, “You will destroy all who speak falsehood,” can be understood from what follows in the psalm and from its very order as referring to heretics. The one who works iniquity kills only his own soul; but the one who is a heretic and speaks falsehood kills as many people as he has led astray.

The Lord will abominate the man of bloodshed and deceit. The man of bloodshed is every heretic: daily he pours out the blood of souls. He rightly called him deceitful: he is both a murderer and deceitful.

[Col. 0831A] But I, in the abundance of your mercy, will enter your house. They go out of your house in their iniquity; I will enter your house by your mercy. “I will enter your house,” which is the Church.

I will worship toward your temple, etc. It is the same house that is also the temple.

O Lord, lead me in your righteousness. I desire to enter your house and wish to enter by your straight way; but because my enemies place obstacles along the paths, and set snares on the road for me as I desire to go into your house, I therefore ask you to direct my feet to the end. It is mine to place my feet on your way; it is yours to correct my steps.

Because of my enemies, make my way straight before your eyes. That is: make your straight way straight for me because of my enemies who lie in wait for me. What is this way? Reading the Scriptures—that is, may I not fall in your Scriptures, through which I desire to enter your Church. For everyone who understands the Scriptures wrongly falls on the way of God.

For there is no truth in their mouth. The heretics are being described; the man of bloodshed and deceit whom the Lord will abominate is being described. “There is no truth in their mouth.” They do not have Christ, who is the truth, in their mouth, because they do not have him in their heart either. Their heart is empty. In Hebrew, *ἐπίβουλον*—“treacherous”—is found more appropriately. For truly the heart of heretics plots against all whom it deceives.

Their throat is an open tomb. Unfortunate are the heretics, who are whitewashed tombs filled with the bones of the dead. “Their throat is an open tomb.” Arius, Eunomius, and the other heretics have tongues like arrows; they have made their throats a tomb. “Their throat is an open tomb.” He rightly said “open,” for whenever someone deceived wishes to enter, the heretic is ready and receives him. Heretics never close their mouths but always open them.

They dealt deceitfully with their tongues. They held one thing in their heart and promised another in their speech. They spoke of piety and concealed impiety. They speak of Christ and conceal Antichrist. They know that no one could be led astray if they brought forth Antichrist openly. They present light in order to conceal darkness, so that by means of the light they may lead people into darkness.

Judge them, O God. They know that you are judge; they know that you regard human affairs. You who will judge at the end, judge even now. You who will judge universally, judge partially now. Let those who do not wish to acknowledge the Father experience the Judge.

Judge them, O God. Why? For what reason? It follows:

Let them fall from their own counsels. For if in the present you repay them what they deserve, they begin to withdraw from their evil counsels. As long as they do not perceive you as judge, they do not fear. “Let them fall from their own counsels.” He said this excellently: “from their own counsels.” For every day heretics change their doctrines. Thus, if an ecclesiastical man learned in the Scriptures contends against them and refutes them with the holy Scriptures, they immediately seek how they may discover some other new doctrine. They do not seek how to be saved but how to prevail. Therefore he now says: “Let them fall from their own counsels,” and let them have one counsel—that is, let them have one thought.

According to the multitude of their impieties, drive them out. He did not say from where he should drive them out—from heaven, from earth. Scripture does not say from where he should drive them out; rather, the expression is *ὑπερβατόν* and *ὕστερον πρότερον*—a transposed and inverted construction. We must therefore read: “According to the multitude of their impieties, drive them out.” What does this mean? By your mercy drive them out from their many impieties—that is, let them no longer remain in their many impieties.

It can also be interpreted otherwise: Because they have been exceedingly impious and have not wished to fall away from their own counsels, and because they increase impieties by impieties, gathering more of them every day, therefore drive them out. From where? From her who receives the inheritance. Drive them out from there, so that, since they do not have faith in the Church, they may not move about within her.

For they have provoked you, O Lord. You, Lord, are by nature sweet; but sinners and heretics turn the nature of your sweetness into bitterness by their own fault.

And let all who hope in you rejoice. Let them perish, and let the members of the Church rejoice.

They will exult forever. Here “forever” should not be understood of the present age but of the future. He did not say, “They exult in the age,” but “they will exult”; it is spoken of the future. Here there is sorrow, but there there is joy. Heretics laugh in the present, but in the future they will mourn. We mourn in the present so that we may laugh in the future.

They will exult forever. What will be the exultation of holy men?

And you will dwell in them. Blessed will be those who are found worthy to have Christ as their guest; [Col. 0832C] blessed those who will be Christ’s tabernacle.

And all who love your name will glory in you. Whoever loves God will glory in the Lord. “Those who love.” He did not say, “those who fear,” but “those who love.” Wherever there is fear, there is no love. For perfect love casts out fear. Whoever loves the name of the Lord will glory.

They will glory. Our blessedness is future; everything that is promised concerns the future. Let others reign; let others possess; let others glory. We are wretched here so that afterward we may be happy. Let us follow Christ our Lord.

Whoever says that he believes in Christ ought to walk as he walked. Christ the Son of God did not come to be served but to serve. He did not come to command but to serve. He did not come to have his feet washed but to wash the feet of his disciples. He did not come to strike but to be struck. He did not strike another’s cheek but received a blow. He did not crucify but was crucified. He did not kill others but himself suffered. He was poor so that he might make us rich. He received a wound for us so that, when we were beaten, we would not feel pain.

Whenever we are struck, let us offer our cheek, let us present our back, let us imitate Christ. The one who is struck imitates Christ; the one who strikes, Antichrist.

Why do I say all this? So that in the present age, which we endure, we may glorify the name of the Lord for Christ’s sake. While we speak, while we walk, we are suddenly taken away. I myself, who speak to you today, do not know what will happen to me tomorrow. If a slight fever comes, where is that voice? Where is the pride? Suddenly it is turned to ashes. What does earth and ashes boast of? According to the nature of the body, we are earth and ashes. You are earth, and to earth you will go; yet earth boasts against its maker. It follows:

For you will bless the righteous. Blessedness, therefore, is deferred to the future.

O Lord, as with the shield of your good will, etc. In the world, a shield is one thing and a crown another; with God, however, he himself is both shield and crown. As a shield he protects; as God he crowns. He himself is our shield, and he himself is our crown. Therefore he says: “O Lord, as with the shield of your good will you have crowned us.” You protected us with your shield, and your protection became our crown; that is, our crown was your shield—that is, our victory. For “crown” is interpreted as “victory.”

Let us give thanks to God and beseech him to be himself our shield and crown in his good will, so that we may never withdraw from him, but follow him and say with Jeremiah: “And following after you, I have not grown weary, O Lord, as with the shield of your good will you have crowned us” (Lam. I). We are protected by the shield, and when we have been perfected, we are crowned.

## PSALM VI

**For the end, with stringed instruments, concerning the eighth; a psalm of David.** This psalm and the eleventh have the superscription “concerning the eighth,” containing the mystery of our resurrection, repentance, and therefore salvation. In it the human race asks that we indeed be corrected and judged by God, but not in his anger and fury.

It would take too long to recall many examples concerning the mystery of this number. Eight souls entered Noah’s ark and were saved in the flood. David was the eighth son of Jesse; he was disregarded by his father but chosen by God alone. On the eighth day the firstborn are circumcised and cease to be unclean. Zechariah, the father of John, also speaks on the eighth day of his son’s circumcision. And after eight days—or six, for both are read in different Evangelists—the Lord is transformed on the mountain, so that the number eight is contained in the number six, just as in the sixth psalm the superscription of the octave is placed.

O Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, etc. This is a psalm of repentance. It does not refuse to be corrected and rebuked, but asks not to be corrected in fury and anger, because it is weak and its bones are troubled. Sometimes fury comes first and anger afterward, although essentially they are one. Yet fury belongs to the present, anger to the future.

[Col. 0833D] Have mercy on me, O Lord. The voice of the Church. “Have mercy on me, because I am wretched.” He finds the mercy of God who confesses himself wretched.

For I am weak; heal me, O Lord. As if he were saying: “I am weak because of sin; heal me, because you are the physician. I am sick; you are the physician. I have sickness; you have health. I am weak through sin; heal me through mercy.”

For all my bones are troubled. As if he were saying: “All the virtues—which he has called bones—were transgressed or destroyed in the first man. From that time my soul has been troubled.” This occurs so that we may be corrected through repentance.

And you, O Lord, how long? “How long,” that is, until you rescue, correct, and amend my soul, which is greatly troubled?
