Turn, O Lord, and rescue my soul. Unless he first turns our soul, he cannot rescue it from danger. Or else: “Lord, who have turned your face away from us, turn and deign to look upon us, and rescue our soul.”

For there is no one in death who remembers you. The dead will not praise you, O Lord, but we who are alive, because God is not the God of the dead but of the living. In hell, however, who will confess you? He did not say this as impossible, but as rare. For the holy man delights in all the judgments of God and praises his judgments.

I have labored in my groaning. Have mercy on me, because I have done these things and the things that follow.

Every night I will wash my bed. Whoever waters his bed daily with tears cannot allow the pageant of lusts to creep into his thoughts.

I will water my bed with my tears. What an abundance of tears, that his bed should be watered with tears!

My eye is troubled by fury. Where are the friends of the text? Certainly that bodily eye is not troubled there by anger—unless perhaps we are raised to such madness that even the appearance and features of our face are changed. It is therefore that eye which is troubled; if it is scandalized, it will be plucked out.

He does not say, “My eye is troubled by my anger,” but “by your anger.” O God, through whom I fear the punishments prepared for me: my mind is troubled, and the ruling principle of my entire heart trembles.

I have grown old among all my enemies. My enemies are not waging new wars against me; my enemy is ancient.

Alternatively: I cannot attain the maturity of the person who is renewed day by day, because I carry the old person with his vices and desires, my enemies, fighting against me.

Depart from me, all you who work iniquity. After he himself has obtained mercy, he teaches or exhorts the others to depart from him. He does not wish to have the company of the wicked.

At the same time, this too should be noted, as we said above: he commands not those who have worked iniquity, but those who work iniquity, to depart from him.

Let them turn and be greatly ashamed very quickly. He does not pray against his enemies but for his enemies: that they may turn and be ashamed of their sins—not lightly, but vehemently; not after a delayed period, but quickly.

## PSALM VII

**A psalm of David, which he sang to the Lord concerning the words of Chusi, son of Jemini.** Most people, especially those who do not possess knowledge of the Hebrew language, suppose that this psalm was sung at the time when Chusi the son of Arachi, David’s friend, overturned the counsel of Achitophel and sent messengers to him, telling him not to remain any longer in the wilderness but to flee far away, lest he be overcome by his son.

But it must be understood that they are greatly mistaken. First, because the name Chusi is written with the letter *samekh*, whereas here it is written with *sin*. Further, David—who had commanded Joab and the other commanders of his army, saying, “Spare the boy Absalom” (2 Sam. XVIII)—would never have spoken about the death of his son in the words: “He conceived pain and gave birth to iniquity; he opened a pit and dug it, and he fell into the pit which he made”; especially since, upon hearing of his death, he covered his head and cried aloud: “My son Absalom, my son Absalom.”

Finally, there Chusi, David’s friend, is written as the son of Arachi; here, however, as the son of Jemini. Therefore it must be known that Chusi is interpreted as “Ethiopian,” and that the entire psalm was written against Saul, who was persecuting David and who fell into the pit he had dug himself. He calls him an Ethiopian because of his bloodthirsty, savage, and cruel character.

“Jemini” means “of the family,” referring to the tribe of Benjamin, from which Saul arose, as the Books of Kings testify. Scripture says: “There was a man from the sons of Benjamin, and his name was Kish, son of Abiel, son of Seror, son of Bechor, son of Aphiah, son of a man of Jemini, a mighty man; and he had a son, whose name was Saul” (1 Sam. IX).

That Shimei who threw stones and dust at David was also of Saul’s family—that is, a Jeminite—as is written in the same books: “A man went out from the kindred of the house of Saul, and his name was Shimei, the son of Gera” (2 Sam. XVII). David is later represented as speaking of him: “Behold, my son, who came out from my body, seeks my life; how much more now this son of Jemini?”

Aquila translated this passage as follows: “For the ignorance of David, who sang to the Lord concerning the words of the Ethiopian.” Symmachus rendered it in this way: “For the ignorance of David, who sang to the Lord concerning the words of Chusi, son of Jemini.”

I have discussed all this at greater length because highly learned men thought that this psalm had been composed not against Saul but against Absalom; I have shown that this is partly incorrect.

O Lord my God, in you I have hoped, etc. I have not hoped in my sword; I have not hoped in my strength; I have hoped in your help.

Lest he seize my soul like a lion, etc. This suits Saul; it does not suit Absalom. For how could David call Absalom a lion, when he says of him, “Spare my boy Absalom”? If he calls him a boy there, as though he were a child and ignorant, how does he call him a lion here?

This is according to the historical sense for the moment; many things could be said, and the entire psalm can be interpreted as referring to Saul. But since we are concerned to interpret it not only according to history but also according to spiritual understanding, we interpret this Ethiopian Chusi as no one other than the devil.

It is asked how this Chusi can be the son of Jemini, and how the devil, an Ethiopian, can be the son of the right hand. He is an Ethiopian through his own vice; he is the son of the right hand because he was created by God. It is rightly said of him: “Lest he seize my soul like a lion.” Our adversary, the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may seize.

O Lord my God, if I have done this. Behold the prince of this world, and he found nothing in me.

If there is iniquity in my hands. For he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.

If I have repaid evil to those who repaid me evil. Saul was twice delivered into his hands, but David did not wish to kill him, saying: “I will not touch the Lord’s anointed” (1 Sam. XXIV). Thus he did not repay evil for evil to the one who repaid him evil for good.

“If,” he says, “I repaid evil to my enemies for evil, I shall not rise; and if I sought evil for evil, they will repay evil for good.”

[Col. 0836A] Let me rightly fall empty before my enemies. In Hebrew, instead of “empty,” *reḳam* is written. Hence we understand what is contained in the Gospel: “Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca’ and ‘Fool’” (Matt. V), and what interpretation it has.

Let the enemy pursue my soul, etc. Death is the final enemy of the soul, and it has been destroyed. Let him trample my life upon the earth. It cannot be trampled, because he did not do the things mentioned above.

And let him bring my glory down into the dust. “If,” he says, “I repaid evil to my enemies for evil, I will not rise again.”

Arise, O Lord, in your anger. Since they did not perceive you through your benefits, let them perceive you through anger.

And be exalted in the regions of my enemies. He prays for his enemies, so that you may be exalted in the regions of his enemies. When they cease to be enemies, then you, O Lord, will be exalted in them.

And arise, O Lord my God, according to the commandment which you gave, etc. This is what we say; believing this, we speak. For the persons in the Psalms are constantly changing. It would take too long now to say how many and how various the persons are who change.

“Arise, O Lord my God, according to the commandment which you gave”: this is what we say—you suffered for us, you were crucified; arise and save us. Therefore arise, so that a very great multitude may believe in you. When you have arisen, what else do we ask except that you return to the Father?

And for its sake return on high. For what? For the synagogue of the peoples. The fact that you died, you died for us; the fact that you rose, you rose for us; the fact that you ascended to the Father, you ascended for us. “And for its sake return on high.” No one ascends into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.

Judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness, etc. David cannot say this; it properly belongs to the Savior, who did not sin.

Let the wickedness of sinners be brought to an end, and you will direct the righteous. My righteousness cannot be directed unless their iniquity has been fulfilled—that is, the iniquity of the Jews.

Unless you are converted, he will brandish his sword. This passage admits of a twofold interpretation. Many think it is spoken of God, so that it may be addressed to sinners. What does it say? “Unless you are converted, he will brandish his sword”: that is, unless you repent, the Lord will strike you with his sword.

But let us see whether what follows can be fitted to the person of the Lord: “He has bent his bow,” etc. This can be said of God. “And he prepared vessels of death against him.” This is difficult, for the Lord does not have vessels of death but vessels of life. Yet this too can be understood of the person of the Savior.

But what follows is:

Behold, he conceived iniquity, etc. This means that the heretics were stirred up to contempt of God.

He opened a pit, etc., by which he would destroy them. And he fell into the pit which he made. For in the pit of death which he had opened, he himself first perished, as it is written concerning Arius.

That is: unless you are converted, unless you repent, the devil always has his bow prepared; he sends arrows with which to strike us. Those whose hearts burn with lust, vices, and passions have been conquered by the devil.

He made his arrows for the burning ones. He rightly said “for the burning ones”; he did not say “for those about to burn”—that is, those who will be burned by his arrows—but those whose hearts he sees burning, he strikes. The Apostle says that the devil has burning arrows (Eph. VI).

Behold, he conceived iniquity, conceived pain, and gave birth to wickedness. This is how the devil conceives, gives birth, nourishes, and exalts.

He opened a pit and dug it, and he fell into the pit which he made. The devil himself is the pit; he himself is the ditch. “He opened a pit.” But because, according to Jeremiah, it cannot hold water, his pit has therefore been turned into a ditch. All the gatherings of heretics are the devil’s ditches.

But what we passed over above is this: “God searches hearts and kidneys; my just help is from God.” In Hebrew it is written in this way: “God, the just one, searches hearts and kidneys,” followed by: “My help is from God, who saves the upright in heart.”

Will he be angry every day? More accurately, the Hebrew has: “He threatens every day,” which Aquila also translated. He says beautifully: “Threatening and grinding his teeth every day.” For because, in his patience, he does not punish sins in this way, he waits, as though angry and threatening, for the day of vengeance, so that he may correct the delinquent through fear. Let us follow the order.

His pain will return upon his head, etc. Just as, if someone throws a stone upward without taking care, and the stone comes down upon his head, he is wounded by his own wound, so the devil is killed by his own pride: he is exalted and falls.

Now he wishes to raise his head, but cannot, because his pain will return upon his head and crush him. According to the rule of Scripture, the devil is read in Genesis: he is the serpent, the snake that spoke to Eve, because he clings entirely to the earth.

Although the other animals walk upon the earth (Gen. III), they do not have their whole bodies lying upon the earth. Though they have their feet on the earth, another part of their bodies is raised above it. But the devil—that is, the ancient serpent and snake—is, according to Isaiah, entirely in the earth (Isa. XIV); he has his head and the rest of his body on the same level.

His pain will return upon his head, and his iniquity will descend upon the crown of his head. See what he says: upon his head and upon the crown of his head. When iniquity presses upon his head and presses upon his crown, where is the devil’s power? This is the devil’s end: his pain will return upon his head, and his iniquity will descend upon the crown of his head.

I will confess to the Lord according to his righteousness. He did not permit those who fear him to be destroyed.

And I will sing psalms to the name of the Most High. He led us from laments of sorrow into everlasting joys.

## PSALM VIII

**For the end, concerning the winepresses; a psalm of David.** Three psalms of different authors are prescribed as being “concerning the winepresses”: those of David, Asaph, and the sons of Korah. They pertain to the mystery of the Church; therefore they bear the numbers eight and eighty. Since the eighty-third is the final psalm marked “concerning the winepresses,” this shows that the mystery of the Church’s resurrection is contained in the Trinity.

O Lord our Lord. The first name “Lord” among the Hebrews consists of four letters: *yod, he, vau, he*. It properly denotes the name of God and can be read ΙΑΗΟ; the Hebrews regard it as *ἄρρητον*, that is, ineffable. The second, *Adonai*, is common to all and is often used even of human beings.

How wonderful is your name throughout the whole earth. The fact that you became human for us, that you died, and that you rose again has been proclaimed among all nations.

For your majesty has been exalted above the heavens. This refers to your ascending into heaven after the resurrection with the triumph of glory.

[Col. 0838B] From the mouth of infants and sucklings you have perfected praise. Although much that contains the praise of the Lord is found in the teaching of the elder prophets, the Lord himself declares in the Gospel that this verse was fulfilled when the children cried out: “Hosanna to the Son of David” (Matt. XXI).

Because of your enemies. For the confusion of the Jews.

That you may destroy the enemy and the avenger. The heretic, who attacks the Church with his wickedness while pretending to defend her.

For I will see the heavens, the works of your fingers. We understand the heavens as the holy Scriptures, which were brought forth by God’s finger—that is, by the Holy Spirit.

“For I will see the heavens, the works of your fingers.” The one who promises that he will see does not yet see what is present. “I will see,” he says. Then I will also understand the rationale and course of his work. A helmsman sees a ship in one way, a physician sees a sick person in another, and a painter sees a painting in another way than the untrained eyes of the inexperienced.

The moon and the stars which you established. The Church, or her teachers.

What is man, that you remember him? What merit belongs to man, that, remembering him, you should take flesh for his redemption?

Or the son of man, that you visit him? The Son of God became the Son of Man—that is, the Son of the Virgin Mary—who visited the body of our lowliness, which he deigned to assume.

You made him a little less than the angels. In Hebrew, where it has “than the angels,” who are called *malakhim*, it has “than God,” that is, *Elohim*. The Apostle interprets this passage concerning Christ in the Epistle to the Hebrews (Heb. II).

You crowned him with glory and honor. With glory, when at his descent the underworld shone forth; with honor, when he conquered death; with a crown, when, surrounded by the choir of the saints, he returned triumphantly from the underworld.

And you appointed him over the works, etc. So that all things might be subject to him, except the one who subjected them to him.

You subjected all things beneath his feet. When he ascended into heaven.

All sheep and oxen. Holy souls producing the fruit of innocence.

Moreover, also the beasts of the field. People of lesser merit.

The birds of heaven. Those who speak iniquity on high through pride.

And the fish of the sea, which travel the paths of the sea. Those who, through excessive curiosity, do not contemplate heavenly things and, amid the waves of this age, suppose that eternal life is found.

O Lord our Lord, how wonderful is your name, etc. It begins with blessedness, or with praise, and ends in praise. The Church marvels at how holy people willingly suffer for the name of Christ, or at how we have all been redeemed by the Creator of the world.

## PSALM IX
# For the End, Concerning the Hidden Things of the Son, a Psalm of David

Although Aquila rendered *pro absconditis filii*—“concerning the hidden things of the son”—as “the youth of the son,” it must nevertheless be understood that the Hebrew has “concerning the death of the son.” Symmachus, moreover, translated it in this way: “for victory over the death of the son.” Thus the entire psalm, by way of typological interpretation, pertains to the mystery of Christ. Hence the Seventy translators wished to conceal Christ’s passion and resurrection—previously unknown to the world—through the word “concealment” [Col. 0839B], so that they might not easily be recognized by the Gentiles at that time.

Here he speaks of the son mentioned above, not of that son according to the historical sense, namely Absalom, whose deeds were not hidden but manifest and evil against his father; rather, this is understood of the Only-Begotten Son of God the Father.

We know of two advents, the first and the second. In the first advent he came both manifestly and secretly: manifest in the flesh, secret in his divinity. In the second advent he will come both secretly and manifestly: secretly, because we do not know the day or the hour; manifestly, because every eye will see him. He is secret in another way as well, because we do not know God’s hidden judgment—that is, why the Jews have been rejected and the Gentiles chosen.

Alternatively: We see the saints afflicted, but we do not know whether this is for testing or for correction, so that their glory may increase toward what is better. We see others afflicted, whose punishment begins here and remains with them in the future. We see still others who are neither afflicted nor suffer injury, but are healthy in body and abound in every temporal joy. Such people are dangerous, because we believe that God does not visit them, since they are not worthy to be visited, so that afterward they may be punished without end.

This entire psalm is sung by the prophet in the person of the Church concerning Antichrist.

## “I will confess to you, O Lord,” etc.

The voice of the Church. A threefold confession resounds here: that of sinners, martyrs, and confessors; thanksgiving, or praise, as in the Gospel: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth” (Matthew 11). Here, too, a threefold love is understood: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength” (Matthew 22).

## “I will recount all your wonders.”

How does he say that he recounts all God’s wonders, since no human being can either see or comprehend God? For if we wished to recount all God’s wonders, it would be impossible. Why can we not? Because elsewhere he says: “I will declare all your judgments” (Psalm 18). A human being cannot do this either. Why can he not? Because the Lord says: “Everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15).

But why did he not recount the day of judgment, instead saying: “It is not for you to know the times or seasons which the Father has placed in his own authority” (Acts 1)? This question is resolved when he adds, “all your judgments”; afterward he says, “of your mouth,” as though the prophet—or any saint—were saying: “As much as you have taught me, so much will I recount.” For if you recount as much as you understand, you recount all God’s wonders [Col. 0839D], although they are more numerous in themselves.

Or: “I will recount all your wonders”—not only those in which the dead are raised, the blind illuminated, and the like, but also the fact that through you lost souls are restored to an unexpected salvation.

## “I will rejoice and exult in you.”

“I will rejoice” in hope, and “I will exult” in reality, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (2 Corinthians 10).

## “And I will sing to your name, O Most High.”

“I will sing”—I will fulfill in works—“to your name.” The Son is the name of the Father; the Most High himself is God. Or: “I will sing to your name”—here praise is joined with works.

## “When my enemy is turned back.”

What enemy? The devil, because the Lord said: “Get behind me, Satan” (Mark 8). Before Christ’s coming, the devil was the leader on the road to death; afterward, following behind the Church, he is like a dog. Hence elsewhere he says: “You shall crush his head, and he shall watch your heel” (Genesis 3)—that is, the end of each person’s life. The woman is the Church; the serpent is the devil.

## “They will be weakened and perish before your face.”

The impious will perish from their impiety. Or, just as he spoke above in the singular, so here he speaks in the plural, including all his minions together, who will perish on the day of judgment.

Why will they be weakened? Because previously they were strong on account of our sins; but now God’s weakness has made us strong and them weak, as the Apostle says: “What is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (1 Corinthians 1).

## “For you have carried out my judgment.”

The voice of the Church, as though it were saying: “You openly chose the Gentiles and rejected the Jews.” When it says “my judgment,” it becomes evident [Col. 0840C] that the Church came from the Gentiles.

## “And my cause.”

As though the Church were saying: “You acted on my behalf against my adversaries, vindicated me, and made my cause just.”

## “You sat upon the throne.”

“Throne” is Greek; in Latin it means “seat.” Each saint is the seat of God, as he himself says: “Heaven is my throne” (Isaiah 66). And elsewhere: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom” (Wisdom 7).

One of these thrones speaks—namely Paul: “Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?” (2 Corinthians 13).

## “You who judge equity.”

That is, justice. “You, Father, judged my cause justly, so that you might raise me up, because they handed me over to death unjustly.”

## “You rebuked the nations.”

Through preachers, who rebuked those who worshiped idols—wood and stones.

## “And the impious perished.”

The devil, who is worshiped in those woods and stones. Or: through apostolic preaching the nations were rebuked, and the one who had previously made them impious was destroyed.

## “You blotted out their name forever.”

That is, their memory. The name of impiety will no longer be remembered among them, because those who believed in you received your new name, which will be blessed throughout the earth.

## “The enemies’ swords have failed utterly.”

As though he were saying: The devil’s weapons, which were his members—the sinners through whom the devil persecuted others—have failed.

Or otherwise: “The enemies have failed from the sword,” as though he were saying that through the sword, which is the word of God, they will fail in the future judgment, when they will be judged by that very word.

## “And you have destroyed their cities.”

That is, sinners. As many as are the vices of sinners, so many are their cities—that is, their strongholds—in which the devil reigned. As though he were saying: They have failed through your preachers [Col. 0841A].

## “Their memory perished with a tumult.”

The sound of their teaching—or the evils of the heretics—perished with them. Or “with a tumult,” that is, through the preaching of the Gospel.

## “And the Lord remains forever.”

He and those devoted to him will perish amid their tumult, while the Lord, as we have said, remains forever together with his saints.

## “He prepared his throne for judgment,” etc.

“For the Father has given all judgment to the Son.” He prepared his throne for judgment—that is, the Church—from which he will judge the world, namely all the nations.

## “He will judge the peoples in equity.”

What is equity is also justice—that is, Christ. Or, at his second coming, he will give rewards to the righteous and hell and punishment to the unjust [Col. 0841B].

## “And the Lord became a refuge for the poor.”

Between the poor person and his adversary—that is, the devil—Christ will be judge. He will judge between the Church and its adversary, namely the devil. Hence he is also called in the Apocalypse “the accuser of our brothers.”

Or these poor are those who became poor for his sake and distributed their possessions as food for the poor.

## “A helper in times of trouble.”

He is the helper of his Church in tribulation, whenever it is opportune, as the Apostle says: “God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure, lest we be condemned with sinners in eternal punishment” (1 Corinthians 10).

## “Let them hope in you.”

That is, not in themselves but in you, and not in the desires of the world.

## “Those who know your name.”

Whether your power or your magnificence. Or “your name,” that is, your Son.

Why? Because of what follows:

## “For you have not abandoned those who seek you, O Lord.”

Therefore they hope in you, according to the saying: “If they kill the body, but cannot kill the soul.” Nevertheless, he permits them to be tested, but not beyond all measure.

## “Sing to the Lord.”

That is, sing to the Lord, preach, and fulfill in works.

## “Who dwells in Zion.”

Zion means “watchtower,” that is, Jerusalem, “vision of peace.” At present the Church is a watchtower, because it watches for God’s future judgment. But when it comes to the heavenly Jerusalem, it will no longer be a watchtower but a vision. Hence Paul says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13).

## “Declare among the nations his purposes.”

The prophet’s voice admonishes preachers to preach. “Declare his purposes”—that is, preach his commandments.

Perhaps they will say: “We will die if we go to the Gentiles.” But the prophet adds:

## “For, when he seeks their blood…”

And the Lord says: “Do not fear those who kill the body, but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10).

## “The Lord remembered, and did not forget the prayer of the poor.”

As though the prophet were saying: “He has not forgotten to avenge your blood.” Hence the Lord himself said: “Will God not avenge his elect who cry to him day and night?” (Luke 18).

## “Have mercy on me, O Lord.”

The voice of the Church: “See my humility before my enemies; you who lift me up from the gates of death,” etc.

The gates of death are the practices of the ancestors who worshiped various gods of demons. They were the gates of death, whose teaching led to death.

Alternatively: The gates of death are the teaching of the heretics. From these gates the Church has been lifted up and sent into the gates of the daughter of Zion, which are the gates of life. Just as by bad teaching we understand gates of death, which lead us to destruction, so we understand gates of life to be good preachers, who through their teaching lead us to eternal life [Col. 0842A].

## “I will rejoice in your salvation.”

“I will rejoice,” that is, I will be glad, “in your salvation,” in your Christ.

## “The nations are caught in the destruction which they made.”

That is, they are trapped in the evil works they committed; there they are fixed, and from them they will be judged.

## “In the snare which they hid,” etc.

Because each person first falls into the snare he prepares for another’s downfall.

## “The Lord will be known when he executes judgments.”

He will be known—that is, at the judgment.

## “The sinner has been caught in the works of his hands.”

Each sinner carries with him his own ropes, bonds, and torments by which he will suffer evils. It is not necessary for others to prepare what will torture him, since he himself prepares what belongs to his punishment.

## “Let sinners be turned into hell.”

That is, because they wish to live beyond the end of the world, let them be turned into hell.

## “All the nations that forget God.”

That is, those who say that God forgets and has no care for his affairs: let them be forgotten by the Lord. For they do not speak truth when they say that God forgets his creatures, because he says:

## “For forgetfulness will not be unto the end,” etc.

Even if he delays, he does not withdraw his help from his saints.

## “Arise, O Lord; let man not prevail.”

The voice of the Church sounds against Antichrist: “Arise”—for judgment. “Let man not prevail”—that is, sinful man, Antichrist.

## “Let the nations be judged in your sight.”

In the first of two ways, they have already been judged in God’s foreknowledge. Why? Because they do not belong to the Church but to Antichrist, since it is said: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3).

## “Appoint, O Lord, a lawgiver over them.”

That is, Antichrist, who brings an evil law of teaching, as Paul says: “They refused to receive the truth, but consented to iniquity” (2 Thessalonians 2) [Col. 0842D].

## “Let the nations know that they are human beings.”

When they have been condemned, they will then know that they placed their hope in a human being and not in God, who alone can save.

## “Why, O Lord, have you withdrawn far away?”

Why do you prolong your salvation when we are inflamed by expectation of your coming? Hence the Lord said in the Gospel: “Unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved” (Matthew 24).

## “You disregard in times of trouble,” etc.

They seem to disregard us when the Church’s opportune time has come for him to help, but he does not immediately come to her aid in tribulation.

Why? So that he may exercise her according to his will. For the more he delays, the more the Church expands in her desire [Col. 0843A].

## “While the impious man is proud,” etc.

While the impious man—Antichrist—is proud, the poor person, the Church in tribulation, is inflamed by Antichrist’s pride.

## “They are caught in their counsels,” etc.

For those who are opposed to God are bound by their own thoughts.

## “For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul,” etc.

The sinner is praised by flatterers, not by the righteous. When one sinner praises another, they praise one another while destroying one another.

## “The sinner has provoked the Lord.”

Antichrist himself.

## “According to the abundance of his wrath.”

Because he has not received the scourges of correction.

## “He will not seek.”

That they may worship him as though he were God. That is, he is not worthy to be sought, but to be punished.

## “God is not before his eyes.”

Because he does nothing worthy of God.

## “His ways are defiled,” etc.

For he does not walk along the straight way, which is Christ.

## “Your judgments have been removed,” etc.

Because he does not believe that judgment will come upon him.

“All his enemies”—and certainly Christians as well—are mentioned, in order to test those who refuse to follow him.

## “For he has said in his heart,” etc.

“I will always seduce human beings, so that by persevering in evil they may resist God’s will.”

He has said—that is, Antichrist. What has he said?

## “I shall not be moved from generation to generation without evil.”

That is: “I will do such great evils among one nation that, before I come to another nation, they will already have heard of me and fear me.”

Alternatively: “I shall not be moved from a carnal generation to a spiritual generation”—that is, “I will ascend from the earth with my body into heaven”—“without evil,” as though he were saying, “without suffering any injury.”

When he wishes to ascend the Mount of Olives, the Lord will kill him with the spirit of his mouth. One of his members, Simon Magus, wished to ascend into heaven, but perished.

## “His mouth is full of cursing and bitterness.”

As though he were saying: Whoever boasts of his own righteousness in order to be God is accursed before God.

## “Under his tongue.”

Under his heart.

## “Labor and sorrow.”

Sorrow is for himself, while he apportions labor and sorrow to others.

## “He sits in ambush with the rich.”

That is, the devil lies in ambush through his members, over whom he presides, and harms others.

## “To kill the innocent.”

That is, to make the innocent guilty—and to harm himself first.

## “His eyes…”

That is, the eyes of Antichrist.

## “Look toward the poor.”

That is, toward the Church, which is the body of Christ. He looks toward it to harm, not to help.

## “He lies in ambush secretly, like a lion in his den.”

The devil can be called a lion and a dragon. He is a dragon when he harms secretly, and a lion when he openly persecutes.

## “To seize the poor.”

That is, the Christian.

## “To seize the poor as he draws him away.”

## “He will humble him in his snare; he will bend down and fall,” etc.

He seems to bend down as though toward humility, so that he may appear gentle and holy; but when he has bent down, he is then about to fall [Col. 0844A]. For while he expects to be far from death, sudden destruction will overtake him.

## “For he has said in his heart, ‘God has forgotten; he has turned his face away so as not to see unto the end.’”

“He has forgotten,” as though he were saying: “Everything is mine as long as the world endures, and God has handed it over to forgetfulness; he has never used these things. But they are mine, because I am God.”

## “Arise, O Lord.”

That is, for judgment. The Church speaks against Antichrist.

## “And let your hand be exalted.”

That is, your power, while Antichrist boasts that he possesses everything without end.

## “Do not forget the poor unto the end.”

While he claims that he will reign unto the end. For this reason he says above:

## “The impious man has provoked God.”

That is, Antichrist.

## “For he has said in his heart, ‘God will not require it.’”

Antichrist says: “God does not care about this present world” [Col. 0844B].

## “For you see labor and sorrow.”

The prophet speaks to God: Because Antichrist meditates on how to do harm, you see it.

## “To deliver them into your hands.”

Those who carry out God’s just vengeance upon sinners are called the hands of God. For this reason they are called “hands,” because through them God is avenged.

Alternatively: “To deliver them into your hands”—that is, into their own works, so that those who have done unworthy things may be worthy to be handed over to them. For they have handed themselves over to their own miseries, and he has abandoned them to all their desires.

## “For the poor person has been left to you.”

That is, the Church.

As though he were saying: “She is yours to save.”

## “You will be the helper of the orphan.”

An *pupillus* is one who has no father; an orphan (*orphanus*) is one who has neither father nor mother.

A *pupillus* is one who does not have the devil as father, as in the Gospel: “Do not call anyone your father on earth” (Matthew 23). And he who has no mother—that is, no pagan identity.

As though he were saying: “You will be a helper to this one” [Col. 0844C].

## “Breaking the arm of the sinner.”

These things pertain to Antichrist, because the Lord will break his strength.

## “And of the wicked.”

He himself is the wicked one.

## “His sin will be sought, and it will not be found.”

That is, he is not worthy to come to correction.

Or otherwise: It will not be found that he has sin, so that in his own estimation he may be like God, who has no sin.

## “The Lord will reign forever, without end.”

For then the kingdom will be in tranquility, as Paul says: “When he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father, when God will be all in all” (1 Corinthians 15).

## “You will perish, nations, from his land.”

Those who received Antichrist will perish from the Church—that is, out of the Church. While Christ reigns, nations of crimes will waste away from the human body [Col. 0844D].

## “The Lord has heard the desire of the poor.”

That is, the Lord has heard his Church, so that she may be vindicated.

He has heard in order to grant them the kingdoms of heaven.

## “Your ear has heard the preparation of their heart.”

That is, your mercy. The Lord’s ears are said to hear when he deigns to hear—that is, when he grants the eternal life which the Church desires. When he has given it to her, she will finally enjoy in reality what she once desired.

## “To judge the orphan and the humble.”

Here he speaks in the dative case, not the accusative. That is, not “so that he may judge the orphan,” but “so that the orphan and humble person may be judged”—that is, so that they may receive eternal life [Col. 0845A].

## “So that a human being may no longer continue to exalt himself upon the earth.”

So that from this point Antichrist may not rise up against God’s elect or test them. Overcome by the reign of the Son of God, he will exist no longer.

Let us also pray to the Lord that he may deign to preserve us unharmed from Antichrist’s works, so that, having become orphans from him and recognizing Christ the Lord as our Father, we may follow him in faith, hold him in our hearts, and glorify him in our works. For to him, together with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, belong honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# PSALM X

## “For the End, a Psalm of David”

The tenth psalm is sung against heretics and those who believe wrongly.

## “In the Lord I trust.”

The voice of the Church against the heretics, or of Christ against the demons.

## “Move to the mountain like a sparrow.”

He wishes the righteous man to flee into deserts, so that he may more easily destroy him there.

Or, because the heretics are deceitful, concerning whom the prophet says: “Woe to those who call sweet bitter and bitter sweet” (Isaiah 5), they wish to seduce the righteous to themselves, saying: “Move over to us.”

He replies to them: “My hope is in the Lord.” How, he says, “shall I move to your mountains”—that is, to your pride?

As for the phrase “like a sparrow,” we often read that a sparrow is used to signify prudence. Therefore they say: “Come over to us like a prudent person,” although their prudence is foolish.

## “For, behold, sinners have bent the bow.”

That is, the heretics have bent their mouths like a bow against the Church—the power of their verbosity [Col. 0845C].

## “They have prepared their arrows.”

That is, their words.

## “In the quiver, in themselves.”

For they themselves are the quivers, where they secretly retain empty words and poisonous opinions that they compose from the holy Scriptures.

## “To shoot in darkness at the upright in heart.”

For they never fight in the light but always in darkness. Therefore the righteous man said: “Your word, O Lord, is a lamp to my feet” (Psalm 118).

They shoot in darkness at the upright in heart when they see inexperienced or simple people in the Church, ensnaring them with deceitful and hidden snares.

## “For they have destroyed what you perfected.”

What did you make? Your Church in unity. Hence it says: “From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise” (Psalm 8).

The heretics wish to destroy this both in themselves and in others, because they tear unity apart.

Alternatively: Whom did you perfect? Christ, conceived from the Holy Spirit, whom the Jews killed.

But what did the righteous man do? When the heretics slander and disagree among themselves, the Church replies in the person of the Church: “You disagree among yourselves, but Christ does not remain silent concerning you,” because he said: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14).

And alternatively: What did the righteous man do? He redeemed the world and gave himself for the world [Col. 0845D].

## “The Lord is in his holy temple.”

As though the prophet were saying: “Although you heretics reject the Church, nevertheless the Lord will be in the temple”—that is, in the Church.

The Apostle says: “You are the temple of the living God” (2 Corinthians 6).

“The Lord is in his holy temple”—in the Church which he presented to himself as holy [Col. 0846A].

## “The Lord’s throne is in heaven.”

“In heaven,” that is, in the holy preacher. Hence he said: “Heaven is my throne” (Isaiah 66).

And the soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom—the soul of the righteous person who meditates on heavenly things.

## “His eyes look upon the poor.”

The eyes of Christ, through the sight of his divinity, look toward the Christian people.

For what purpose do they look? To help.

## “His eyelids question the children of human beings.”

The subtlety of divinity—that is, God’s hidden judgments—in which he questions us. Through this he knows what each person possesses, because God’s judgments are hidden.

As Scripture is sometimes obscured so that we may recognize our weakness, and then opened again so that we may not despair, so in another way he questions us through prosperity and adversity, because through these God tests what each person is like.

In another way: We see one nation being scourged and know the reason for its scourging; these are manifest judgments.

In another way: We see people being scourged but do not know for what reason; these are hidden judgments, included in what was said above.

## “The Lord questions the righteous and the impious.”

That is, he tests them.

## “But whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul.”

That is, he destroys it.

## “He will rain snares upon sinners: fire,” etc.

Historically, this happened when the Lord rained sulfur and fire upon Sodom. As the Apostle Jude says, it was made an example of eternal fire.

“He will rain upon sinners.” In two ways the heretics also rain down evil teaching.

Just as one rain irrigates both fertile and barren earth, so there is one preaching from God that pours itself into good earth—that is, the saints—and into bad earth, the sinners to whom what follows pertains:

Fire: desire.

Sulfur: the corruption of sinners.

The spirit of storms: the spirit of tempest.

The spirit of storms indicates the punishment of eternal judgment and the scourges of sinners, whom fire consumes and the storm deprives of life.

The prophet says: “Around him is a powerful storm” (Psalm 49).

## “The portion of their cup.”

Why did he say “portion”? Because each person will receive his just vengeance according to his portion, as though from a cup, receiving according to what he has done in his misery. As the prophet says: “God will repay each person according to his works” (Psalm 61; Jeremiah 25) [Col. 0846D].

## “For the Lord is righteous, and he has loved righteousness; his face has seen equity.”

For, as though in a mirror, when each person comes into his presence, he will see his own iniquity; and he himself foresees their iniquity.

Or: God’s presence saw the saints in order to govern them. For he loves righteousness, because he judges each person according to his own work.

“His face has seen equity,” so that he may grant rewards to the saints and punishment to sinners.

May he deign to make us worthy by his calling, and not impose punishments upon us according to our sins, but grant us forgiveness according to his great mercy. For to him, together with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, belong honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# PSALM XI

## “For the End, for the Eighth, a Psalm of David”

This psalm is sung concerning the passion of Christ. “For the eighth,” as we said above.

## “Save me, O Lord.”

The voice of Christ to the Father, with reference to the flesh, in the passion.

## “For the holy one has failed.”

Apart from you, no one remains who can save.

## “For truths have been diminished among the children of human beings.”

Why did he say “truths,” when we do not know who the Truth is, as he says: “I am the way and the truth” (John 14)?

Just as there are many churches and one Church, so there are many truths: the works of many righteous people, and many who do good.

But why have they been diminished? Because before Christ’s advent, whether prophets or patriarchs—whether those of good nature or those who, having fallen in part, saw that they served—were diminished in many ways, because the head, that is, the Truth who is Christ, had not yet come. The members were diminished until their head, which is Christ, arrived [Col. 0847B].

## “They have spoken vain things,” etc.

First, Peter, when he said: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you.” Likewise all the disciples said this (Matthew 26). But all of them spoke vainly, since they were unable to fulfill what they had proposed.

The heretics and evil teachers, who teach perverse doctrine, have also spoken vainly, each one to his neighbor.

Christ the Lord, who speaks these things, is everyone’s neighbor. He showed mercy by binding our wounds through his death. Against him the Jews exercised themselves in empty speech.

## “With a deceitful lip and a divided heart they have spoken.”

Symmachus translated it this way: “Slippery lips, with one thing in the heart and another on the tongue.”

Deceitful lips are called double-tongued, because they speak with two tongues: they say one thing and retain another.

Thus deceitful lips have spoken evil from heart to heart: contrary to what they conceived in their hearts, they brought forth with their mouths in their works [Col. 0847C].

## “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips.”

Does he say this as a curse? No. It is not the custom of the saints to curse; rather, he declared what would happen, not wishing it, but prophesying it (John 8).

Who are the deceitful lips? Heretics and evil preachers.

## “And the tongue that speaks great things.”

That is, those who speak arrogantly.

## “Those who said, ‘We will magnify our tongue.’”

That is, those who praise themselves among themselves and magnify their works.

## “Our lips are from ourselves.”

As though they were saying: “We have our teachers from ourselves, not from elsewhere.”

For they applaud themselves in empty verbosity, saying: “We are children of Abraham, and we have never been enslaved to anyone. Who is our lord?” As though they were saying: “We have no lord, because we know everything” [Col. 0847D].

## “Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor.”

This is the voice of the Father.

Who was miserable except the human race in the world, which entered into the misery in which it groaned in sins? There was also groaning in hell, among those who dwelt in punishments.

## “Now I will arise, says the Lord.”

That is: “I will send my Son, who will redeem them”—both those who are in misery in the world and those who dwell in hell.

This came to pass: God the Father sent his Son to us who were miserable, so that he might free us and so that through his poverty we might become rich [Col. 0848A].

## “I will place him in my salvation.”

He said “in salvation” but did not say what he would place. The implied sense is: “the salvation of the nations.”

And what else will I place? Joy in place of groaning, and spiritual riches in place of poverty.

## “I will act confidently in him.”

The voice of the Father concerning the Son, as though he were saying: “With confidence I do everything through him,” because divinity strengthened humanity. As it is written, “he acted freely.”

## “The words of the Lord are pure words.”

He includes together the teaching of both Testaments.

They are pure when they are preached incorruptibly and without corruption by good preachers.

This will be so if, when they preach, they are moved neither by love of their ancestors nor by fear of the powerful, neither by present gifts nor by empty honor.

Alternatively: They are pure when the preachers neither dare to add anything beyond what is written nor to diminish anything, whether in the Old or the New Testament, but preach faithfully [Col. 0848B].

## “Silver tested by fire.”

That is, tested by the Holy Spirit.

It is not they who test the divine words; rather, the Holy Spirit enlightens those who preach them. Thus in Isaiah the angel took a coal from the altar and touched his lips, saying: “Behold, I have touched your lips, and your iniquity will be taken away, and your sin will be cleansed.”

By silver, the Old Testament is understood; by gold, the New. Thus the literal and spiritual senses are as though gold were produced from silver.

## “Tested on the earth.”

That is, the Church. Those divine words have been tested through the Holy Spirit, whom the Church received.

Alternatively: “Tested on the earth,” that is, Christ the Lord, who came in humanity through that part of the flesh which he received from Mary, just as the Lord assumed the earth [Col. 0848C].

## “Purified sevenfold.”

The seven gifts that were in Christ—not so that he himself might be purified, but so that those who were to receive these gifts might be purified.

## “You, O Lord, will preserve us.”

That is, in faith; the Church prays.

## “And you will guard us from this generation.”

He includes together the whole crowd of evils: heretics, dialecticians, and the rest. From the generation of these people the Lord separated his Church.

Hence in the Gospel: “All these things will come upon that generation, from the blood of Abel that was shed to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom they killed between the temple and the altar” (Matthew 23).

## “The impious walk around.”

When they have transferred us from the present age into the future, then the impious will walk outside; they will not be able to enter with the saints whom you, according to your greatness, preserved through your care.

The impious walk around because they will not attain eternal life.

Alternatively: When the elect have been received, those outside the door will cry: “Lord, Lord, open to us.”

Alternatively: They will walk around them, and it will be said to them: “I do not know you.”

## “You have multiplied the children of human beings according to your sublimity.”

That is, the children of God.

According to the multitude and abundance of your mercy, because the Church is multiplied through his compassion and mercy. In the future repayment of blessedness, when they receive your promises and become conformed to the body of your glory, honor and glory will belong to you, together with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

# PSALM XII

## “For the End, a Psalm of David”

The twelfth psalm contains the voice of the faithful soul seeking God [Col. 0849A].

## “How long, O Lord, will you forget me forever?”

The voice of the Church, as though she were saying: “How long?”

Why does he say “forever”? A human being consists of four elements: fire, air, water, and earth. Earth is lower than the other created things, because earth is the end of creatures. Therefore the Church says:

“Even if I am lower—utterly low, like earth—how long will you forget me? Do not forget me forever because I am lowly, and because I am the end of the other creatures. Do not forget me on that account.”

## “How long will you turn your face away from me?”

So that I may have neither knowledge nor illumination of your thought before the end of this life [Col. 0849B].

## “How long shall I place counsels in my soul?”

“I suffer these things,” he says, “until I seek you through spiritual counsel.”

## “Sorrow in my heart by day.”

Through that light of your knowledge which I had long lost, I will set sorrow upon the darkness of my sins—that is, I will do penance.

## “How long will my enemy be exalted over me?”

As long as I have not turned back to you, the devil, who is the enemy of the human race, rises up against me.

“How long will my enemy be exalted over me?” As though he were saying: “How long does the adversary have dominion over the Church?”

Forever.

## “Look and hear me, O Lord my God.”

This is the prayer of the Church, and it can be understood of three persons.

“Look” upon me in tribulation—or in help—“and hear” me in what I implore.

## “Illuminate my eyes.”

That is, the eyes of my heart.

## “Lest I ever sleep in death.”

We know that a person in torment cannot sleep, but he uses “sleep” for that night.

Hence above he says: “Death without death, and failure without failure.”

The Lord slept in the boat when he was awakened by the disciples. It must be noted that the Lord slept when the faith of the apostles faltered. The Lord keeps watch over each person according to his faith, and through faith he is awakened. When faith is absent, he seems to sleep.

Hence it is said: “Awaken your faith, and then you awaken Christ.”

## “Look and hear me, O Lord my God.”

## “Illuminate my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death.”

For you are the true light that illuminates every person coming into this world [Col. 0849D]. You illuminate the eyes of our hearts, lest the sleep of eternal death overtake us.

## “Lest at any time my enemy say,” etc.

“Lest at any time”—that is, at the future judgment—“my enemy say, ‘I have prevailed against him,’” that is, “I seduced him so that I might deceive him.”

As though he were saying: “If the adversary can find us asleep in unbelief, then he prevails over us.”

## “They will rejoice if I am moved.”

Those whose feet have been moved because they did not stand in the truth of God will rejoice if they can move my feet—that is, my understanding—from the Catholic faith.

Then they will rejoice, that is, be glad, as the prophet says: “My feet were almost moved.” But I hope in your mercy, so that I may be established in faith.

My heart shall rejoice in your salvation: in the Lord Jesus Christ. I shall sing to the Lord—that is, I shall praise and proclaim him—who grants me good things, namely, the supports of this present life by which we subsist, so that, scorning the spectacles of the world, I might behold spiritual things with the mind. Alternatively: “He grants good things”: the virtues of the Church, namely faith, hope, and charity, and in the future eternal life. “I shall sing praise to your name, O Most High”: that is, what I sing and proclaim, I shall fulfill in action. Rightly, therefore, Lord Jesus Christ, praise is sung to your name, because you are rich in mercy, grant victory to the righteous, and invite sinners to turn to you. To you be glory and honor, with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM XIII

The thirteenth psalm has no inscription, but declares that our redemption will proceed from Zion. First, indeed, it speaks against the impious, who, trusting in the riches of the world, are ignorant of God, who bestows them.

“The fool said in his heart.” In Hebrew, instead of *insipiens* (“fool”), the word *Nabal* is used. Hence Abigail also says of her husband Nabal on Mount Carmel: “He is truly foolish, according to his name” (1 Samuel 25). “There is none who does good, not even one.” They refer this psalm to Christ’s passion, when everyone abandoned the Lord—to such an extent that Peter also, who was the foremost of the apostles, denied him. “They said in their heart, ‘There is no God.’” They said it in their heart, not with their mouth. Why? Because they did not dare to do so, lest they violate the divinity of their gods. “The fool said”: the Jewish people, who say in their heart, “There is no God; there is no Christ, the Son of God.” One of them not only did not regard him as God, but did not even believe him to be a prophet, when he said: “If this man were a prophet, he would certainly know what sort of woman this is who touches him, for she is a sinner” (Luke 7). And another said: “If he is the Son of God, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him” (Mark 15).

“They are corrupt.” They have degenerated from the integrity of good nature. “They have become abominable”: that is, hateful. “In their desires”: that is, in their deeds. “They are corrupt and have become abominable in their desires.” For if they had possessed knowledge of God, they would not have been corrupt and abominable. “There is none who does good, not even one.” Unless someone acknowledges Christ, who is the only-begotten of the Father, he cannot possibly be good. “There is none who does good, not even one.” Here it becomes clear that this psalm concerns the passion, because none of the disciples—not even Peter, who is the head of the Church, since he too denied him—nor any human being, because the whole world had turned toward the lower region, was righteous, except the one man who is Christ.

“The Lord looked down from heaven”: to give salvation to the human race. Or, “from heaven,” that is, from the saints, “upon the sons of men,” whom he makes his saints. Or, “from his holy place, upon the sons of men,” that is, upon the human race: “to see”—that is, to cause him to see his saints—through whom and in whom he looks upon them and dwells. “The Lord looked down from heaven upon the sons of men, to see whether there is one who understands or seeks God.” He looks through holy souls, which we have often called heaven, to see whether there is anyone wise who seeks God with the mind; for nothing is hidden from divine power.

“They have all turned aside.” The whole human race had turned toward the lower region. “Together they have become useless,” both to themselves and to others. “They have all turned aside; together they have become useless. There is none who does good, not even one.” He says this concerning the nations. But because he inserts “all,” he adds the Jews as included, since they often mingled with the nations in their filth and idolatries.

“Their throat is an open tomb.” From this [Note: [Col. 0851D] It is fitting now to hear the genuine Jerome in the Preface to Book XVI of his Commentaries on Isaiah: “Just as,” he says, “almost the entire Epistle to the Romans is constructed from the Old Testament, so this testimony too is woven together from the Psalms and Isaiah. For the first two verses, ‘Their throat is an open tomb; they acted deceitfully with their tongues,’ belong to the fifth psalm. What follows, ‘The poison of asps is under their lips,’ belongs to the one hundred and thirty-ninth psalm. Again, the words, ‘Whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness,’ are taken from the ninth psalm. But the three verses that follow, from ‘Their feet are swift’ up to ‘they have not known the way of peace,’ I found in the prophet Isaiah, etc. Moreover, the reason why they were all brought together in Psalm 13 in the Old Latin translation, and still more in the Greek text of the Alexandrian exemplar, was that very testimony of Paul, taken contrary to the Apostle’s intention, so that the individual verses were thought to have been drawn from the same psalm. The final three are also found in Proverbs 1:16, which Jerome suppresses; but nothing at all similar is to be found in Deuteronomy, as this Pseudo-Jerome relates.] verse up to the place where he says, “There is no fear of God before their eyes,” it is not found in the Hebrew manuscripts. The question therefore arises how the Apostle used this testimony in the Epistle he wrote to the Romans (Romans 3). We answer that the Apostle wove this testimony together from Deuteronomy, the Psalter, and the other places of Scripture.

“There they trembled with fear”—the phrase that follows, “where there was no fear,” is not found in the Hebrew books.

“Their throat is an open tomb.” Through their deceits they have piled human beings into their mouths as into tombs. For a similar expression occurs elsewhere: “Unless the Lord had been with us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive” (Psalm 123). “They acted deceitfully with their tongues,” corrupting good morals through evil conversations. “The poison of asps is under their lips,” because, like asps, they block their ears so that they do not hear the commands of the divine Law. The poison is understood as the deceit of wicked conversations.

“Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness.” The blessing of flattery brings a curse. “Bitterness” refers to this: because, by thinking wrongly, they have made the sweet words of God bitter to their own destruction. “Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness,” because their teaching harms both themselves and others, and condemns them in the future. “Their feet are swift to shed blood.” They kill both bodily and spiritually, while they desire to drive Christ, who is the life of the soul, out of the soul itself.

“Destruction and unhappiness are in their ways”: destruction of the body, unhappiness of the soul. “In their ways”: in their deeds. Sinners are always unhappily crushed in their way. “For they have not known the way of peace,” which is Christ the Lord—neither through faith nor through conduct. Why have they not known it? Because of what follows: “For there is no fear of God before their eyes.” They have not set God before their understanding, in memory and holy fear. “There is no fear of God before their eyes.” They do not fear the future judgment, and therefore do not observe his commandments.

“Will not all who work iniquity know that vengeance is coming?” It is as though he said: If they do not know now, they will know at the judgment, when he comes. “They devour my people as though eating bread”: the heretics devour the Christian people. Just as bread enters into all foods, and no one can be satisfied without it, but it is eaten with every kind of food, so heretics are never satisfied with their iniquities; they are satisfied only with the people of God, or with the Church, wherever they are able to seize them. “They devour their own people,” the ecclesiastical people, “as though eating bread,” because there is no living bread except the one who came down from heaven. “They did not call upon the Lord.” For if they had called upon him, they would certainly have been saved. Alternatively: “They did not call upon God.” Why? Because many call upon someone, but not upon God; instead, they make some other thing that they desire to possess into their god, rather than God himself.

“There they trembled with fear, where there was no fear.” The nations fear their own gods, and the Jews fear the powerful themselves, when they said concerning Christ: “If we let him live, the Romans will come and take away both our kingdom and our nation.” They trembled with fear where there was no fear: certainly in idols and the empty rites of images.

“For the Lord is in the generation of the righteous”: in the Christian people. He was also among the Jews, because he took flesh from them. “You have confounded the plan of the poor.” The Jews refused to believe in Christ; that is, they refused to believe the mystery of his incarnation at his coming. Christ is called “poor,” as Paul says: “Although he was rich, he became poor, so that by his poverty he might make us rich” (2 Corinthians 8). “You have confounded the plan of the poor,” that is, of Christ, not understanding that he had proceeded from God while offering counsel and saying: “Repent.” “For the Lord is his hope”: the Father, certainly, because of the flesh he assumed, since his humanity was strengthened by divinity.

“Who will give salvation to Israel from Zion?” Who but God, who is in Zion? He gave salvation—Christ himself—in the holy Church. Alternatively: “Who will give salvation to Israel from Zion?” Christ the Lord, whom the inhabitants of that earthly Zion did not believe. “When the Lord turns away the captivity of his people.” We have already been redeemed from the captivity of transgression, but we are still in the captivity of this life. And alternatively: concerning the Jewish people—that they themselves will be turned away from captivity in the time of Elijah and Enoch, as Paul said: “When the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel will be saved.” Alternatively: “When the Lord turns away the captivity of his people,” through his own passion. “Let Jacob rejoice, and Israel exult.” He is the same person, Jacob and Israel; but here he is Jacob, and there Israel. Here he is the supplanter of vices; there he is the one who sees God face to face, when God will be all in all—he who, having abandoned worldly things, beholds the Lord with the mind. May he deign to grant us that, having become Jacob in deed by supplanting our vices and truly becoming Israelites, we may deserve to see him with the mind and hold him in our hearts—to whom, with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, belong honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM XIV

A psalm of David.

The fourteenth psalm has been read appropriately. According to the order, it has turned out as though it had been read almost deliberately; it has been read in its proper sequence. I think this happened by God’s providence, so that what was beneficial to you might be recited today in the order of exposition. The fourteenth psalm has been read, and it bears the title “A psalm of David.” Our David is Christ, as we have often said. Then we read in Exodus that the lamb is sacrificed on the fourteenth day (Exodus 12). It is sacrificed on the fourteenth day, when the moon is full, when none of its light is lacking. See, therefore, that Christ is sacrificed only in perfect and full light. Since, then, the lamb must be sacrificed for you on the fourteenth day, the prophet now marvels and asks:

“Lord, who will dwell in your tabernacle?” You who wish to dwell in the Lord’s tabernacle, hear what the Lord says: “Lord, who will dwell in your tabernacle?” Here we understand “tabernacle” as eternity, although in other places it signifies works. For in this present tabernacle, which is the Church, many dwell bodily but not by faith. Since here we are still inferior, we remain as though in a tabernacle until, after victory, we reach the house. Alternatively: “Lord, who will dwell in your tabernacle?” Who, he says, can become an earthly temple of God and dwell in the city of the living God? The Apostle speaks much about it. “Or who will rest upon your holy mountain?” Who, he says, will be worthy to be conformed to the image of the Son of God (Hebrews 12; Romans 9), who is often called a mountain? Here is the stone cut from the mountain without hands; here it became a great mountain; here it filled the breadth of the earth (Daniel 2); in it the souls of the saints rest. In it, therefore, no one receives rest except the one who enters without blemish and practices righteousness: the one who is free from every stain of sin and keeps God’s commandments inviolably.

Alternatively: “Or who will rest upon your holy mountain?” Not first on the mountain and afterward in the tabernacle, but first in the tabernacle and then on the mountain. A tabernacle is not a permanent house; a tabernacle has no foundation, but is moved here and there and moves with the one who migrates, because a tabernacle has no foundation and is an uncertain dwelling. A permanent house, however, has foundations. “Mountain” signifies eternal life.

“He who enters without blemish.” That is, without mortal sins, since we cannot be without lesser sins. Hence it is said: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” Or alternatively: “He who enters without blemish.” Consider what is commanded. He did not say, “the one who reaches the end without blemish,” but “the one who is still on the journey and has no blemish.” Someone may say: “I have no blemish; I have done no evil.” It is not enough for us not to do evil unless we also do good. Accordingly, it follows: “And practices righteousness.”

He did not say, “practices chastity,” “practices wisdom,” or “practices courage.” These virtues, indeed, are excellent. Wisdom benefits us; courage benefits us, so that we may resist persecutions. Temperance and chastity are also necessary for us, lest we lose our souls. Righteousness alone is a great virtue and the mother of all virtues.

Someone may ask: How is righteousness greater than the other virtues? The other virtues delight the person who possesses them; righteousness does not delight the one who possesses it, but others. If I am wise, my wisdom delights me; if I am courageous, my courage delights me; if I am chaste, my chastity is my joy. Righteousness, however, benefits not those who possess it, but the other wretched people who do not possess it. Alternatively: “And practices righteousness,” that is, keeps the commandments, as in the saying: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matthew 19).

“He who speaks truth in his heart.” Many speak truth with their lips, but not in their heart; they appear to speak truly, but their heart does not agree with their lips. Alternatively: “He who speaks truth in his heart,” so that he thinks true things about the Truth, who is Christ, and does not mingle himself with heretical assertions, which are always found to be false and empty. Hence Paul said: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10).

“He who has not acted deceitfully with his tongue.” He did not deceitfully put forward Catholic doctrine in order to deceive, but fulfilled in action what he spoke with his mouth. He acts deceitfully who thinks one thing and says another, as the prophet says: “Keep your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit” (Psalm 33).

“He has not done evil to his neighbor.” The one who shows mercy is the neighbor. Christ the Lord showed mercy, so that he might redeem us through his passion; let no one turn his teaching toward evil, as the heretics do. Every Christian person is our neighbor. “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another.” Elsewhere he says: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” And again he says: “Turn away from evil and do good.”

Some think that a neighbor is a brother, or a person who lives nearby, or a relative, or a kinsman. But our Lord teaches in the Gospel, in the parable where someone went down from Jerusalem to Jericho: a priest passed by, a Levite passed by, and neither showed mercy; a Samaritan passed by and showed mercy. Afterwards the Lord asks and says: “Which of these was the neighbor?” Immediately the answer is given: “The one who did good.” And the Lord concludes: “Go, and you also do likewise” (Luke 10). Therefore all human beings are our neighbors, and we ought to do evil to none.

“And he has not accepted reproach,” and so forth. He is never accused by his neighbors as though he were guilty. “But he glorifies those who fear the Lord.” He does not glorify the rich or the powerful, but only those who fear the Lord. “And he has not accepted reproach against his neighbors.” He does not accept the reproach of slander against a brother if he does not first believe it before testing it. It is as though he says: Whoever keeps these things that he has stated above is without blemish and practices righteousness. Such a person dwells in the tabernacle and will rest upon your holy mountain—that is, in eternal life.

“The wicked is brought to nothing in his sight.” In the sight of that righteous person, the devil is brought to nothing. For in the Church, whoever is wicked is counted as nothing in the sight of the holy person. “He is brought to nothing,” because in the sight of such a saint he is regarded as nothing: although he was an angel, he became a renegade; and just as he was made from nothing, after losing the good things he had, he was reduced to nothing. And since he is nothing, the strongest saints do not fear him.

“He magnifies those who fear the Lord.” The voice of the Church: The Lord magnifies those who fear him with holy fear. Alternatively, in the moral sense: “He magnifies those who fear the Lord.” For he knows that God dwells in them, as the Lord says: “Whoever loves you loves me” (John 14).

“He who swears to his neighbor and does not deceive him.” This person is already below perfection. Even if he does good, because he does not deceive in keeping his oath, nevertheless such people are censured by the commandment that says: “Do not swear at all, neither by heaven nor by earth; let your speech be, ‘Yes, yes; no, no.’” This saying concerns the perfect: not to swear (Matthew 5). For when the soul promises to keep God’s commandments, if the neighbor is understood as the body, then it deceives him if it does not observe what it promises.

“He has not given his money at interest.” Even if someone does not sin by receiving exactly as much as he gives, this is nevertheless not perfection, because it is said: “Break your bread for the hungry” (Isaiah 58). And “it is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20). Until he reaches these things, he is below perfection.

Alternatively: “He has not given his money at interest.” The Lord’s money is preaching. Many do not wish to give it unless they receive payment from it. Nevertheless, it is permitted to receive food and clothing from that preaching, as Saint Paul says: “Those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel” (1 Corinthians 9). And the Lord says: “The laborer is worthy of his food” (Matthew 10). But whoever wishes to demand more is considered to be charging interest.

Hence Paul says: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your material things?” (1 Corinthians 9). It is as though he says: “It is not a great matter” in exchange for the spiritual things that we announce to you. “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these things” (1 Timothy 6).

Just as visible money is forbidden to be lent at interest, lest the lender exploit the borrower even more, so also the word of God, which is a great treasure, ought to be freely imparted not only to the rich, who feed and reward the preacher, but also to the needy and poor, with the Lord saying: “You received freely; give freely” (Matthew 10).

“And he has not accepted gifts against the innocent,” so that those offering gifts may not disturb the judgment of truth. Alternatively: So that he may not become like Judas, who, after receiving a weight of silver, sold the innocent man. As the prophet says: “He who shakes his hands free from every gift will dwell in the heights” (Isaiah 33).

“He who does these things will not be shaken forever.” All these things, just as they should be retained allegorically, must also be observed according to the literal sense in one’s conduct. If anyone keeps them irreproachably, he will not only be secure from the agitation of the eternal Judge, but will also deserve to possess the very mountain and heavenly tabernacle, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom, with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, belong honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM XV

An inscription of a title belonging to David.

An inscription of a title is placed on monuments and tombs, which contain the bodies of the dead. Instead of this, Aquila and Symmachus rendered it “humble,” “simple,” and “undefiled,” signifying that the psalm properly concerns Christ, who says: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart, and meek” (Matthew 11).

As we have said, the psalm preserves without diminution the voice of our King, which he utters in the assumed man, while retaining the divinity sent from the Father. David—that is, Christ himself. This psalm concerns the passion.

There are three kinds of titles that are written: one upon the tombs of the dead; another on the thresholds of cities or houses; and a third in the king’s victory. Here, therefore, he speaks of the title of the king’s victory, just as this king was Christ, and it was written above his head at Passover after the victory—that is, after the devil had been conquered and the human race redeemed—in three languages: Greek, Hebrew, and Latin. Hence Pilate also said: “What I have written, I have written.” And he placed above his head the charge against Christ: “This is the King of the Jews” (Matthew 27).

“Preserve me, Lord, for I have hoped in you.” The voice of Christ to the Father in the passion, in the person of the assumed man. It is as though he says: May I be guarded in the passion by the Father from whom I came, because you are my hope.

“I said to the Lord, ‘You are my God.’” He shows himself to be man in the humility of the flesh, although he is equal in the omnipotence of majesty. For if he had said, “You are my Lord,” he would have indicated a lesser Son and a greater Father. Therefore he said: “I said to the Lord, ‘You are my God,’” because in divinity he is equal to the Father.

“For you have no need of my good things.” We read the same line in Job: “What does it profit if you make your way pure?” All the good things, therefore, that the Lord displayed in the flesh according to the form of a servant benefit not the Father, but the human race.

“For you do not need my good things.” The voice of Christ. What are Christ’s good things? His incarnation, passion, resurrection, and our redemption. Or alternatively: The good things are the heavens and what is in them, and the good earth and what is in it, which God created. The Father had no need of these things after they were made, nor before. They are not useful or necessary to the Father. But to whom are they necessary?

“To his saints who are on earth.” All these things are necessary to them. “They are his on earth,” that is, in the Church. “He has made all his desires wonderful among them.” Through his saints Christ has made his mysteries wonderful—that is, he has magnified them.

“Their infirmities have been multiplied; afterward they hastened.” The nations from whom I now gather the Church knew God naturally before their idols were multiplied. But after the idols were multiplied—which the Septuagint interpreted as “infirmities”—they abandoned them and returned to me with the greatest haste.

“I will not gather their assemblies from blood.” For the religion of the New Testament is spiritual. “Nor will I remember their names with my lips.” We are changed in the washing, and from sons of men we are called sons of God.

“Nor will I remember their names with my lips.” The voice of Christ: I will not remember the names of those apostles as they possessed them before faith, when they had unbelief. I will not remember those former names, because as their merits increased, new names were added, such as Abraham and Sarah, and Peter and the others. Previously they were slaves of sin, but afterward they became friends, as the Lord said: “I shall no longer call you servants, but friends” (John 15). And Saint Paul also belonged to this company when he said: “We too were once foolish and unbelieving, like the rest; but we obtained the mercy of God” (Titus 3). And again: “But you were washed; but you were sanctified” (1 Corinthians 6).

“The Lord is the portion of my inheritance.” The voice of Christ to the Father. Christ’s inheritance is the Church, and the Lord is the portion of his body. He speaks concerning the portion of the assumed man, because he received humanity from us, and we receive immortality from him.

“And of my cup.” Why did he say “cup”? Because through the cup each person receives according to his measure, but Christ receives more than his members, as Paul says: “He is the firstborn among many brothers” (Romans 8).
