“You are the one who will restore my inheritance to me.” This is what is said in the Gospel: “No one comes to me unless my Father draws him to himself” (John 6). According to the historical sense, Christ’s inheritance was the Jews, to whom Christ came. But it was then scattered when they crucified him. It will be restored in the future, when the fullness of the nations has entered.

Alternatively: God the Father will restore Christ’s inheritance when he has drawn his elect, the body of the holy Church, to that integrity in which, after receiving their bodies at the resurrection, they will live incorruptible and immortal, because they lost that immortality in Adam.

“The measuring lines have fallen for me in excellent places”: in the best places. In place of one Israel, he has received the inheritance of the whole world.

Measuring lines are assigned in an inheritance. Therefore what he said, “They have fallen for me in excellent places,” means the same as if he said: among the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles; or, whoever the Father calls, Christ receives with himself. For this reason he said “in excellent places”: among the saints or apostles.

“I will bless the Lord, who has given me understanding.” The voice of the head together with the members. He has given understanding to distinguish between good and evil, between sense and letter, between God and neighbor, between light and darkness.

“I will bless the Lord, who has given me understanding.” He who is the wisdom of God does not need wisdom itself. But this should be understood according to what is said in the Gospel: “Jesus advanced in age, wisdom, and grace before God and men” (Luke 2).

“Moreover, even until night my kidneys reproved me.” “Night” signifies the time of the passion, in which human weakness was inwardly instructed by divinity.

“Moreover, even until night my kidneys reproved me.” Carnal pleasures reprove me when they suggest that I sin, when the flesh takes pleasure. But unless you had been at my right hand, I might have grown weak.

“I set the Lord before me always.” The Son sets the Father before him; the Church sets Christ before her.

“For he is at my right hand, so that I may not be shaken.” It is as though he says: If you had not been at my right hand, I might have been shaken from faith into unbelief, from good into evil.

“Therefore my heart rejoiced,” and so forth. I rejoiced because of the resurrection, because through it the world was liberated.

Alternatively: “Therefore my heart rejoiced, and my tongue exulted.” Because you help me, my heart rejoices and my tongue proclaims.

“Moreover, my flesh shall rest in hope.” The voice of Christ. He rests in hope on behalf of the body. It is as though he says: The Church, which is my flesh, now rests in hope—that is, in the hope of the resurrection—so that where the head has gone before, the members may follow.

“For you will not abandon my soul in the underworld.” You will not abandon it, because he descended there for the purpose of bringing out his elect and binding the devil. Previously the devil boasted that he possessed all the kingdoms of the world; but now he was not only unable to hold him, but is rather said to have been bound by Christ.

“Nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption.” How does he say, “You will not allow him to see corruption,” when elsewhere he says: “What benefit is there in my blood, when I descend into corruption?” (Psalm 29). He is not speaking of the corruption of Christ’s body in the tomb, but of the other saints.

“You have made known to me the paths of life.” The voice of the head on behalf of the body. The paths of life are Christ’s commandments, as it is written: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matthew 19).

“You will fill me with joy in your presence.” Then joy will be full, when the body of the Church has been gathered together into the kingdom of God—that is, when he has handed the kingdom over to God his Father. Then God will be all in all.

“Pleasures are at your right hand forever.” The Father’s right hand is the Son. The pleasure of eternal life is at the right hand—that is, in the prosperity granted to the Son—“forever,” as though he said, without end. For Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes, because the fullness of the Law is charity, and the end of the commandment is charity.

Alternatively: “Pleasures are at your right hand forever”: in that delightful power of yours in which the saints will reign with you, a power enclosed by no end. Hence we beseech them that, never separated from these things, if we do not deserve to be clothed in glory, we may not be excluded from forgiveness. For to you, with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, belong honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM XVI

The sixteenth psalm contains the prayer of the Lord’s person together with the body joined to him, which is the Church.

A prayer of David.

This is understood of three persons. This prayer is found in four psalms. This psalm is sung from the person of Christ against the Jews, and from the person of the Church against the heretics. The Hebrews explain that when David sang the psalm and said, “Hear, Lord, my righteousness,” he fell into guilt because of the presumption with which he boasted that he was heard on account of his righteousness.

“Hear, Lord, my righteousness.” According to the Septuagint: “O God of righteousness,” or “O God righteous by nature.” For, “Hear, God, my righteousness”—here the person of Christ is understood.

> **Note:** The Septuagint certainly does not add *meam* (“my”), since they have only **εἰσάκουσον, Κύριε, τῆς δικαιοσύνης** (“Hear, Lord, of righteousness”); indeed, as the ancient scholiast notes, the earlier translators themselves did not add **τὸ μοῦ** (“my”).

“Hear, God, my righteousness”: the voice of Christ in the passion, and the voice of the Church in tribulation. Or the Church calls righteousness hers and not hers. Why hers? Because she fulfills God’s commandments in action. Not hers? Because it is given by God, not produced by herself.

“Hear, God, my righteousness,” because I was obedient to you unto death.

“Give heed to my prayer.” There is a difference between *oratio* (“prayer”) and *deprecatio* (“supplication”). The prayer of the saints is for the devout, that they may persevere in the good. Supplication is for their own sins or those of others. This is the supplication of all.

“Give ear to my prayer.” That is: in what I ask, give ear to my prayer. He prays not because of any diminution of divinity, but because of the weakness of the flesh.

“Not with deceitful lips,” but through the purity that is pleasing to you.

“Let my judgment come forth from your face.” “Not with deceitful lips.” It is as though he says: Hear my prayer, because I pray with my whole heart, not like those with deceitful lips, who say one thing but have another in their heart—whether heretics or Jews.

“Let my judgment come forth from your face, not with deceitful lips.” The voice of Christ to the Father. Those who have deceitful lips judge me, but judge them in the future. The prophet speaks not by wishing, but by declaring. He shows what the Lord will do in judgment.

“Let my eyes see equity.” The eyes of Christ are the holy preachers. Let them see—that is, understand—equity, that is, equality, so that they may fulfill in action the righteousness they preach.

“You have tested my heart, O God, and visited me by night.” You tested me even in hardships, because I am sorrowful and, as it were, under the pressure of a dark night.

“You have tested my heart, O God.” The voice of Christ to the Father. You tested Christ in the passion, and the Church in tribulation.

“You examined me with fire.” That is, through the tribulation itself you put my sins to shame.

“And in me no iniquity was found.” So that my mouth may not speak the works of men.

What are the works of men? The vanities that they themselves love, or various worldly occupations: these are the works of men, as the Lord says in the Gospel (Matthew 21). If an account is required even for an idle word, how much more for the works of men, which they deliberately express from their own understanding.

“Because of the words of your lips, I have kept difficult ways.” Because of your preaching and because of the things promised in heaven, I have kept difficult ways.

How does he call them “difficult” here, when it is said in the Gospel: “My yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11)? It is easy for those who are willing; it is difficult for those who are unwilling. Although it may seem difficult to the saints because of bodily tribulation, it is nevertheless easy because they have hope of eternal life.

Alternatively: “Because of the words of your lips, I have kept difficult ways.” It is as though he says: Fearing the future punishments with which you have threatened transgressors of the Law, I exercised myself through difficult labors and subjected the body to the power of the soul.

“Perfect my steps in your paths.” Perfect my understanding in your commandments. The voice of the Church. To begin is from God, and to finish is from God.

“Steps”: understanding.

“So that my footsteps may not be moved.” Away from those whose feet have been moved—that is, whoever has acted wickedly.

“I cried out,” and so forth. Why did he say, “I cried out”? Because he believed through faith; therefore he said, “I cried out.”

“Incline your ear to me,” and so forth. Christ inclines his ear when he deigns to hear. By analogy with a sick person who is lying in bed and asks the physician to come and heal his illnesses, the human race was likewise sick when it lay in bed—that is, in sin. It asked that the true physician, who is Christ in the flesh, might come and heal its sicknesses.

“Make your mercies wonderful, Lord,” and so forth. Were they not wonderful before? He made his mercies wonderful at that time when, through the holy apostles and his saints, he healed illnesses.

“From those who resist your right hand.” You save in three ways from those who resist your right hand: demons resist God; the Jews resist Christ; heretics resist the Church.

“Guard me, Lord, as the apple of the eye.” The voice of the Church. The eye signifies the body of the Church, and the pupil signifies the humility of Christ, by whose example we live and see. The Church asks that she may be able to preserve the humility that Christ taught. For if the eye is not guarded through the pupil, it cannot see at all.

The eyes signify the preachers, and through the pupil the spiritual understanding is signified. The body of Christ, which is the Church, asks that the understanding of the preachers, which is the eye, may be guarded, lest it be carried away into the unbelief of the heretics.

Under the shadow of your wings protect me. Shadow consists of two things: light and body. By light, divinity is understood; by body, humanity. Hence it is also said to Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1). Under this shadow protect me, so that the kite may not snatch me away. And under the two wings of the Testaments—that is, their teachings by which one lives, is guarded, and is covered like a hen—for by the hen the wisdom of God the Father is understood. For just as a hen hides its young under its wings because of kites, so divine wisdom, and the two wings that are the two Testaments, protect the Church from the kite—that is, from the devil. From the face of the ungodly who afflicted me: the Jews afflicted Christ in his Passion, and heretics the Church.

My enemies have surrounded my soul. The Jews surrounded Christ in his Passion. I said “soul” [the manuscript reads: “said,” *dixit*], not “body,” because the devil does not know inwardly what a person is thinking unless he recognizes it through outward movements, and, observing in what each person takes pleasure, introduces various suggestions. This pertains to the Church. They have enclosed their own fat. What is signified by “fat” except the malice of the Jews? In the Old Testament, eating fat is forbidden because their heart had grown fat. Hence he said in the Song of Deuteronomy: “The beloved grew fat and kicked” (Deut. 32). Why? Because he had grown fat with malice and kicked, since he did not wish to observe God’s commandments. The Jewish people were beloved by God because he rained down divine manna upon them—which pertains to us, because we eat Christ. But the Jews despised themselves; that is, they bound themselves in malice. Their mouth spoke arrogance. The mouth of the ungodly, because they act against Christ and against the Church.

As they cast me out, they now surrounded me; they fixed their eyes on turning toward the earth. When Christ suffered, the whole earth trembled, the stars were darkened, and the rocks were split. But the Jews fixed their eyes on the earth because they regarded him as merely human and did not understand his divinity. Or they fixed their eyes on the earth because they were thinking about earthly deeds but were not meditating on heavenly things.

They received me like a lion ready for prey, and so forth. Just as a lion is ready for prey, so the Jews received Christ in his Passion. And like a lion’s cub. The lion is the devil; the cub is his son, the Antichrist. Or otherwise: the lion is the devil, and his sons are the Jews. “In hidden places”: in their hearts, as though in darkness. The devil—or his members, in whom the devil dwells—are called hidden places.

Arise, Lord; go before them, and so forth. The voice of Christ speaks to the divinity, asking that it go before his soul, lest it be snatched away by the devilish prince—which is precisely what happened. He went before him, bound him, and led him down to hell. The devil came to claim something of his own in Christ, but found nothing in him, as he said in the Gospel: “The prince of this world is coming, and he found nothing in me” (John 14). The holy Church also asks, before it is overthrown by the devil and by his snares, which are heretics, that our Catholic one, who is Christ, may come and overturn the enemy’s schemes—that is, overthrow them.

Deliver my soul from the ungodly, your sword from the enemies of your hand. I pray: deliver the sword of your hand from your enemies, for the enemy has received power to punish us on account of our sins. “Those whom I handed over to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme,” the Apostle says (1 Tim. 1). Deliver my soul from the ungodly. The voice of Christ speaks to God the Father; that is, deliver my soul from the devil. And the voice of the Church asks Christ for this: that it may be freed from the devil, or from heretics and from every evil person. Your sword from the enemies of your hand. “Sword” is understood of Christ and of the Church. The sword of God the Father is Christ’s soul, by which he exacts just vengeance. The devil is his sword, and with that sword he exacts vengeance in the world.

[Col. 0862A] Lord, separate them from the few, from the earth, and so forth. The voice of the Church. “From the few, from the earth.” The Church wishes to be separated from the carnal, from the weeds, and from the chaff before the day of judgment, but without cause, because it received an answer from God, as the Lord said in the Gospel: “Let both grow until the harvest” (Matt. 13)—that is, until the day of judgment. For here the Church is mixed with sinners. It prays for those who are predestined, that they may come and be separated from those who are not predestined, as it is said: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 22). Overthrow those who are in ungodliness, so that they may either be corrected here or be overthrown in the future through vengeance.

Their belly has been filled from your hidden treasures. “Belly” is understood here in three ways. “Belly” signifies chastity, as Eucherius says.

[Note: [Col. 0861D] Eucherius, whom he praises, flourished almost a century after Jerome.]

The belly of the angels was filled with the mysteries of God before they fell; the belly of the Jews, with the mysteries of the Law; and the belly of heretics, with the mysteries of the Church.

They were satisfied with sons. The Jews were satisfied because they multiplied through the begetting of children and through the things of the world. When he says,

[Note: [Col. 0861D] Thus indeed, “they were satisfied with pork,” or “with swine’s flesh”; certain old Latin manuscripts read from the Greek, where, instead of υἱῶν, “sons,” they read ὑῶν, “swine,” or ὑείων, as the present Greek text also has, meaning “swine’s flesh” or “pork.” Consult Saint Paulinus’s Letter 50 to Augustine, and Augustine’s Letter 149 to the same, no. 4 and following. As regards Symmachus’s translation, most manuscript copies read υἱοὶ, in the nominative case, “the sons will be satisfied,” as Agellius in his work against Symmachus, as well as Eusebius, Theodoret, and others, likewise attest.]

“they were satisfied with pork,” this signifies the uncleanness of the Jews. They left their remnants to their little ones. That is, they left behind the just vengeance owed to them. They left their remnants to their little ones; that is, when they said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27). The sons of heretics will likewise have condemnation. Who are their remnants? Their disciples, who were regenerated from that evil teaching of theirs.

“They were satisfied with sons, and they left the remainder to their little ones.” Because of the ambiguity of the word, some think that “pork” was written instead of “sons.” Symmachus, expressing the Hebrew truth, translated: “They will be satisfied with sons, and they will leave the remainder to their little ones.” They were satisfied with sons, and they left their remnants—their uncleanness and iniquity—trampling upon the pearls of your words. And they left their remnants to their little ones, crying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”

[Col. 0862D] But I shall appear with righteousness before you. The voice of the Church. “With righteousness”: that is, fulfilling your commandments. “I shall appear before you”: that is, in your presence in the future. I shall be satisfied—with heavenly nourishment. When your glory appears: your Son, who is salvation, life, and the glory of all the saints, because Christ is called both salvation and glory.

But I shall appear in righteousness, death having been conquered. Before you I shall be satisfied, ascending into heaven. When your glory appears to your saints and elect who believed through me, because what has been granted to them belongs to me. For I am in them, and they are in me with you.

But we, redeemed by you, Lord Jesus, beholding such power and mercy, humbly implore you: once tested by the divine fire, may we not be detractors of human works, but, steadfast and fixed in you, may we continually exalt your glory in our deeds, proclaim it in faith, and praise it with our voice. Amen.

## PSALM XVII

For the end; for the servant of the Lord, David; the words of this song that he spoke to the Lord on the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul. This entire psalm, under the person of David, pertains to Christ. David bears the type of Christ, who is “strong of hand,” from whose seed comes our David, who is Christ.

“For the servant of the Lord”—that is, of God the Father—as the prophet says: “It is a great thing for you to be called my son.” For, “Behold, I and the children whom God has given me.” And the prophet Isaiah: “A child is given to us; a son is born to us.”

“The words of this song that he spoke to the Lord.” David, according to the historical account, sang this song when he was being persecuted by his enemies; and Christ, who is our head, sang it to the Father in his Passion; the Church sings it in persecution.

“The Lord delivered him”: that is, David from Saul’s persecution, and God the Father delivered Christ in his Passion from the hand of his enemies—that is, from the hand of the Jews—and from the hand of Saul. Saul is interpreted as “desire,” because they sought him as king against the will of God. This Saul bore the type of the devil. These enemies are members of the devil: that is, the Jews who persecuted Christ, and the demons—or their members—who persecute the Church.

[Col. 0863C] “I will love you, O Lord, my strength.” Others say, “my fortitude,” but strength and fortitude are one. This whole psalm, under the person of David, pertains to Christ, who is true strength. “I will love you, my strength.” This is the voice of Christ. “My strength,” that is, his divinity, the strength of the assumed man. The Church too is Christ’s strength, who says: “I will love you, O Lord.” If this is Christ’s voice, since they are one, and the substance of divinity is one—for it has been said, “One power, one will, one majesty of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit”—how does he say, “I will love you, O Lord”? The Father is called so because he has a Son, and the Son because he has a Father. The Holy Spirit is neither Father nor Son, but the love which the Father has in the Son and the Son in the Father. Hence the Apostle Paul said: “Because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us” (Rom. 5).

[Col. 0863D] “The Lord is my support.” This is the voice of Christ and the voice of the Church. A support, as the prophet says: “a tower of strength from the face of the enemy” (Ps. 60). “And my refuge.” The voice of Christ and the voice of the Church. Christ’s refuge is in the Father, and the Church’s refuge is in Christ. “And my deliverer,” in tribulation.

“My God, who created me. My helper,” in necessities. “I shall hope in him”: in him I shall place all my hope.

“My protector,” who protects or defends me. “And the horn of my salvation.” The horn of salvation, because he strengthened our weakness. For before Christ’s coming [Col. 0864A] the Church was weakened by sin, but afterwards was strengthened by Christ, as the prophet says: “He raised up for us the horn of our salvation” (Luke 1). As though he said: He gave us a strong kingdom, as in: “And he made us a kingdom to God his Father” (1 Thess. 2). Therefore I trust that I have help, not in that horn of pride, but in the horn of your salvation. “My receiver.” Christ was received by the Father in his humanity, and the Church is received in faith.

“Praising, I shall call upon the Lord.” The righteous praise him because he delivered them from all evils, as follows: “And I shall be saved from my enemies.” “I called upon the Lord.” Christ called upon God the Father, and the Church upon Christ. “And I shall be saved from my enemies”: Christ from the Jews and the Church from heretics.

[Col. 0864B] “The groanings of death surrounded me.” This is the voice of Christ and of the Church. Those who groaned in hell, who were in hell, surrounded Christ, and likewise the Church. “And the torrents of iniquity troubled me.” By torrents he means waters that pass away. A torrent is called that which descends from rains or from mountains into valleys and goes into the sea, not from a spring or living water. What do torrents signify except all nations, which descend by the mountain of flesh into this sea? Hence it is written: “A generation goes and a generation comes” (Eccles. 1). And otherwise: “The torrents of iniquity troubled me”: crowds of the wicked, which, like torrents, swell in winter and immediately flow away.

“The pains of hell surrounded me.” On the day of those who slander, [Col. 0864C] who work hellish death. “The snares of death came before me.” In the Passion the enemies came before Christ, before the vengeance of the cross, with snares of death which adversaries laid for him.

“And in my tribulation I called upon the Lord.” Humanity called upon divinity, and the Church upon Christ, not with the voice of the mouth but of the heart. “And I cried to my God, and he heard my voice from his holy temple.” The temple is the Lord’s body, in which humanity was heard by divinity, and likewise the Church by Christ. The temple is the holy Church. And otherwise: it is my heart, which he sanctified, in which holy temple he dwells. “And my cry entered before him into his ears.” His ears, that is, the power of hearing. Power is strength, by which the saints pray strongly, because it is said: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it.”

[Col. 0864D] “The earth was shaken and trembled.” According to history, this occurred when Moses received the Law on Mount Sinai. The earth trembled; this prefigured Christ’s Passion, because in Christ’s Passion the whole earth trembled, when the new Law was given to the Christian people. Otherwise, the earth was shaken when they came from unbelief to faith, and earthly believers became heaven. “The foundations of the mountains were troubled and shaken.” Here mountains mean the proud. Their foundations are demons, just as the foundations of the saints are prophets and apostles. Hence Saint Paul says: “Built [Col. 0865A] upon the foundations of prophets and apostles” (Eph. 2). “The foundations of the mountains were troubled and shaken”: the pride of those who trust in this world, because God was angry with them—that is, with those mountains or persecutors—scattering their hope in worldly pleasures.

“Smoke ascended in his anger,” and so forth. Smoke is made from two things, fire and water. By smoke tears are stirred; by fire, compunction of heart is understood; and by tears, water. “Coals were kindled by him.” What do coals signify except the human race, good by nature, extinguished through Adam and illumined at Christ’s coming through baptism or penitence? Coals are extinguished by water, which is desire, and illumined by grace, [Col. 0865B] which is the Holy Spirit.

“He bowed the heavens and came down.” This is what he says in another psalm: “He came down like rain upon fleece” (Ps. 71), because he showed himself to us humble, hidden and concealed in the form of a servant. Or otherwise, the heavens are angels: they bowed when Gabriel came to Mary, and Christ came down and entered flesh. Or again, the heavens are the holy apostles or their imitators. They bowed down from height—that is, from contemplation—to teach the unlearned and weak in the Church, through compassion for their neighbours. Or they do so for married persons, as Saint Paul says: “Let the husband render the debt to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband” (1 Cor. 7). “And darkness was under his feet.” It signifies the invisible substance of God and the hidden things of his judgments. Or otherwise, darkness means the depth of the Scriptures, which God gave to his feet, who are his saints, that is, his Church; for in the understanding of the saints is the depth of the Scriptures, and Christ presides over them.

“And he ascended above the Cherubim.” That is, Christ ascended with his body above all angels and archangels, above the fullness of knowledge. Cherubim is interpreted “fullness of knowledge,” which is love, because the fullness of the Law is love, that is, charity. Christ ascended above this, as the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “No one has greater love than that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15). Christ did this, giving his life for his friends. “And he flew,” and so forth. [Col. 0865D] According to the historical sense, he flew above the wings of the winds, because wind is swifter than all creatures, and the Lord is swifter than wind, because he penetrates to the ends of the earth and orders all things sweetly. Since he is beyond wind, he is swifter. In the moral sense he intended wind to signify the soul. As this wind is invisible, so is the soul. Wind moves the body, and the soul likewise moves the body. But why did he call the soul wind? Because God breathed into Adam—not that God the Father is bodily, but because he then breathed when he gave the soul, as the prophet says: “You, Lord, create every breath” (Isa. 57). From this we understand that all souls are [Col. 0866A] created by God. “And he flew”: he flew above the wings of the winds, that is, above the virtues of holy souls, because Christ is swifter than wind, lighter than the soul, and higher than angels and saints.

“He made darkness his hiding-place,” and so forth. In the Scriptures he called himself his hiding-place. “Round about him was his tabernacle.” Christ was in Mary as a bridegroom in a bridal chamber, and Mary’s body was like a tabernacle. He calls it darkness because his Incarnation or Nativity is obscure to us. “Dark water in the clouds of the air.” The clouds are prophets, and the water their teaching, because the Scriptures of the prophets are obscure. For as clouds bear rain and water dry ground, so prophets water dry hearts through their teaching.

“Before the brightness in his presence the clouds passed.” [Col. 0866B] Lightnings are the illumination of the Holy Spirit. The clouds, namely the prophets, passed from the Jews to the Gentiles, guided by the Holy Spirit. By fiery lightnings compunction of heart is understood. “Hail and coals of fire.” In hail, blows; in fire, the kindling of charity is shown, by which the hearts of believers are moved to know God.

“And the Lord thundered from heaven.” Through his saints he thundered: as from heaven he evangelized through the hearts of the righteous. “And the Most High gave his voice.” Through the evangelists he scattered human wickedness. The Most High gave his voice, that is, preaching, as the prophet says: “The voice of your thunder in the wheel” (Ps. 76), that is, their preaching throughout the whole world.

“And he sent his arrows and scattered them.” He sent [Col. 0866C] his holy words like arrows, which are fully preached both to the evil and to the good. God rewards the good if they do them, and crushes the evil if they hear and do not do them. Hence the holy Apostle says: “To some indeed we are an odour of life unto life, and to others an odour of death unto death” (2 Cor. 2). They are an odour of life to those who hear and do, and an odour of death to those who hear and do not do. Since preachers do not know who are predestined, nevertheless they preach with confidence. “And he multiplied lightnings and troubled them.” Lightnings are miracles and the brightness of his power. He troubled them. Through those miracles of the apostles, those who said to Peter were pricked: “What shall we do, brethren?” And he said: “Do penance, and let every one of you be baptized” (Acts 2).

[Col. 0866D] “And the fountains of waters appeared.” The fountains are the apostles, as though watered from one fountain. The apostles were satisfied from the one fountain which is Christ, as he said in the Gospel: “Whoever drinks the water which I shall give him shall never thirst” (John 4). Otherwise, the fountains of waters are those who, through the sacrament of baptism, became for sinners a fountain of living water springing up into eternal life. “And the foundations of the world were revealed”: the prophets and apostles upon whom the foundations of all the Churches are laid. The foundations of the world were revealed, according to history, when in the Passion the veil of the temple was torn from top to bottom and the things which were in the temple appeared. In the spiritual sense derived from the letter, what had lain hidden there in figure became open to all through the mysteries.

[Col. 0867A] “At your rebuke, O Lord, at the breathing of the spirit of your anger.” At your rebuke, O Lord, when you said: “Unless the Son sets you free, you shall die in your sins” (John 8). At the breathing of the spirit of your anger, promising in these things that the kingdom of God was drawing near.

“He sent from on high and received me,” calling me. “And he took me up from the multitude of waters,” from opposing peoples. Or otherwise: “He sent from on high and received me and took me up from the multitude of waters.” God the Father sent his Son, as it is said: “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1). He sent the bridegroom to the bride; he joined the true bridegroom to the bride, that is, flesh in the womb of the Virgin Mary. “He took me up from the multitude of waters”: that is, the Church was gathered from a multitude of people. Many waters are many peoples.

[Col. 0867B] “He delivered me from my very strong enemies.” God the Father delivered Christ from the Jews and the Church from heretics. “And from those who hated me, because they were strengthened above me.” The Jews hated the Lord and heretics the Church, because they were strengthened above me, as though they could conquer.

“They came before me,” as we said above, before the vengeance of the cross. “And the Lord became my protector.” God the Father protected his Son, and the Son his Church.

“He led me out into breadth.” He led the Church out of tribulation, as from narrowness, into breadth, which is hope of the future or the reward of eternal life. “He saved me because he willed me.” This is the Church’s voice: he willed me, that he might present the Church to himself. “Because he willed me”: by his own will, and not from my merit, he called me, as the Apostle says: “You are saved by grace through faith, and this is not from yourselves” (Eph. 2).

[Col. 0867C] “And the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness, and according to the innocence of my hands will repay me.” What his righteousness and innocence of hands are, hear what follows: “For,” he says, “I have kept [them], so that the ways of God may be kept and nothing concerning him may be thought wickedly with heretics.”

“For I have kept the ways of the Lord,” that is, his commandments. “And I have not acted wickedly away from my God,” so as to turn praise toward an idol.

[Col. 0867D] “For all his judgments are always before my eyes.” There are four judgments of God: two in the present and two in the future. In the present, the prosperity of the wicked and the tribulation of the saints; in the future, the reward of saints and the condemnation of sinners. The Church cleaves to Christ, because Christ did not commit sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth. And the Church cleaves to Christ, because all his judgments are always before my eyes. “And I did not reject his righteousnesses from me,” but embraced them.

“And I shall be spotless with him, and shall keep myself from my iniquity.” I shall persevere in that innocence in which I was called. “And I shall keep myself from my iniquity,” that is, I shall not return to that iniquity in which I was formerly in unbelief.

[Col. 0868A] “And the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness, and according to the purity of my hands in the sight of his eyes.” By eyes is understood the gaze of divinity, because he sees whatever a person does in God’s commandments. In the recompense of the blessed, I consider it through the height of hope.

“With the holy man you will be holy,” with him who is sanctified by you. “And with the innocent man you will be innocent,” with him who has not corrupted his life by vices.

“And with the chosen you will be chosen,” with him whom you know to be foreknown. “And with the perverse you will be overturned,” with the heretic who, by understanding badly, perverts the divine utterances; as elsewhere the Lord himself says to the Jews: “If you walk [Col. 0868B] perversely before me, I too will walk perversely toward you.”

“With the holy man you will be holy.” You, Christ, are holy by nature; he whom you sanctify will know from you that you are holy. The prophet’s voice to Christ: he whom you make innocent will know from you that you are innocent, because you harm no one and therefore are innocent. He whom you choose, that he may be chosen, will know from you that you are chosen, as Paul says: “I shall apprehend that for which I was apprehended” (Phil. 3). The perverse are those who turn away from rectitude to perversity, as the devil, Judas, heretics, and all the proud. Whenever God carries out just vengeance, they reproach him: when he chooses the poor and rejects the powerful, when he chose fishermen such as Peter and left nobles. This seems perverse to the perverse, as the prophet says: “The ways of the Lord are straight” (Hos. 14), but your ways are perverse.

“For you will save the humble people,” as we said above, “and humble the eyes of the proud.” For you will save the humble people who do penance and humble the eyes of the proud, because, lifted up by pride, they disdain to do penance.

“For you light my lamp.” What is a lamp except the understanding of the soul? As the eyes of the body do not see in darkness if they have no light from an outward lamp, so the understanding of the soul does not see unless it is enlightened by another, that is, by Christ. As he says in the Gospel: “He was the true light, which [Col. 0868D] enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1). “Lord my God, enlighten my darkness,” that is, the ignorance of my heart. Hence it is written: “If the light which is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness itself be!” (Matt. 6). And the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (Eph. 5).

“For in you I shall be delivered from temptation.” This is the Church’s voice. Unless I am delivered by God, I can in no way do so by myself. “And in God I shall pass over the wall.” The Church calls the wall our sins, which we build by increasing sins with sins. Unless those sins are destroyed by God, we cannot pass through them to God by ourselves.

“My God, his way is spotless.” A spotless way [Col. 0869A] is his Incarnation, because he was conceived not from male seed but from the Holy Spirit. And otherwise, the perfect faith of the Church is called his spotless way, by which God comes to us. “The words of the Lord tried by fire.” The words of the Lord are his commandments; they are pleasing in God—not because they themselves have been tested by fire or had been defiled, but because whoever receives them, they make him like pure gold purified by fire. “He is protector of all who hope in him”: God protects those who believe in him and fear him with holy fear.

“For who is God besides the Lord, or who is God besides our God?” The Trinity is understood here. By “besides the Lord” God the Father is understood; by “besides our God,” the Son; and the third person is the Holy Spirit, because God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit are one God.

[Col. 0869B] “God who girded me with strength.” By a comparison: a person girds his garments so that they do not harm his feet, which are the senses, and his hands, which are works. “He girded,” that is, so that he may restrain the folds of desire, as I said above, lest they be impeded by desire. Or otherwise: “God who girded me with strength” is the Holy Spirit, who arms us against wicked powers, according to the Apostle: “Put on the armour of God and the sword of the Holy Spirit, that you may be able to resist the devil” (Eph. 6). Let heretics now be silent, seeing the Trinity expressly set forth here, and let them recognize that the Son, whom they call less than the Father, was first foretold by the prophet, not as earlier but as in no way inferior. “And he made my way spotless,” that is, my faith, lest I should be violated away from it.

“He made my feet perfect like those of stags.” As stags tread thorns underfoot and leap over woods, so the saints tread thorns, that is, sins; leap over woods, that is, unbelief; and rise up to God, that is, to the height of charity. “He made my feet perfect like those of stags,” for leaping over the impediments of this world. “And he set me upon high places.” The high places are the holy Church; Christ is upon high places, and high places upon high places, that is, upon the height of the Church. “He set me upon high places”: he placed my hope in heavenly things.

“He teaches my hands for battle”: my works against [Col. 0869D] the devil, the destroyer. “He teaches my hands for battle,” for overcoming wicked deeds. “And he made my arms like a bronze bow.” The bronze bow is intention, the arms are strength: that is, so that they may not fail in doing good.

“You gave me the protection of your salvation.” This is the Church’s voice to Christ. “Of your salvation,” because he himself is our salvation, as it says: “Salvation belongs to the Lord.” “You gave me the protection of your salvation,” lest I be oppressed by evils. “And your right hand received me.” Christ is the right hand of the Father. He received me, the Church, through the Incarnation. “Your discipline corrected me to the end.” “For whom the Lord loves he corrects.” Therefore we who had previously fallen are raised up when we have been chastised by the Lord. “And your teaching itself [Col. 0870A] will teach me.” While we are here, it is necessary to be under teaching. Hence Paul says: “All discipline at present does not seem to be of joy but of sorrow, but afterwards in the future it yields a very great fruit” (Heb. 12).

“You enlarged my steps beneath me.” This is the Church’s meaning: beneath me, beneath the Church’s authority. “You enlarged my steps beneath me,” in the breadth of your charity. “And my footprints have not been weakened.” The Church’s footprints, by example, have not been weakened by successors, because they were impressed upon those who follow me. Hence the voice of Christ after the resurrection.

“I shall pursue my enemies and overtake them,” namely the Jews, who became enemies to him unjustly. Or otherwise: “I shall pursue my enemies,” the carnal affections, [Col. 0870B] “and overtake them before I am overtaken by them. And I shall not turn back until they fail,” and so forth. I shall not turn back from fighting against them, or from this purpose, until they fail either from malice or from evil thoughts. I shall afflict them with many evils, as we read has already occurred in the time of Titus. “And they shall not be able to stand,” because they were wicked and had risen in pride. “They shall fall beneath my feet,” either to worship or to be trampled.

“You girded me with strength for battle,” against death or its ministers. “You girded me with strength,” that is, with fortitude against the devil or against the aforesaid vices. “You overthrew beneath me those rising against me,” those who raised themselves above my head.

“And you gave me the backs of my enemies.” For they were unwilling to turn their face toward me. “And you gave me the back of my enemies.” My enemies give their back when they flee and when they go behind me. “And you destroyed those who hate me.” God destroyed all enemies of the Church, or the vices and sins themselves. “And you destroyed those who hate me”: for each one is scattered in his own malice.

“They cried out, and there was none to save them: to the Lord, and he did not hear them,” because they were unworthy of being heard by him. “They will cry out.” Who will cry out? Wicked demons, Jews, and heretics will cry out at the future judgment, and there will be none to save them. Because when God cried to them through the prophets or the other Scriptures, they refused to hear, therefore they will cry out and there will be none to hear them, as [Col. 0870D] Solomon says: “I called and you refused; I stretched out my hand and there was none who looked. You despised all my counsel and neglected my rebukes. Therefore I too will laugh at your destruction, when what you feared comes upon you. I will mock when sudden calamity rushes upon you. Then you will call upon me, and I will not hear.”

“And I shall grind them as dust before the face of the wind.” I shall reduce the aforesaid carnal affections to nothing. “And I shall grind them as dust before the face of the wind,” because, dry and without the rain of mercy, they were cast down and ground in their pride and scattered like the dust of the field. “I shall wipe them away like the mud of streets,” in the manner of muddy mire.

[Col. 0871A] “Deliver me from the contradictions of the people; you will set me as head of the nations.” This is Christ’s voice to the Father: You will deliver me from the contradictions of the Jewish people, certainly, because when some said, “He is truthful,” they said the contrary: “No, but he deceives the crowd.” Deliver me from those unbelieving peoples who contradict me. Deliver me from the unbelieving Jews and set me as their head, that is, as head of the nations.

“A people whom I did not know served me,” that is, Gentiles who did not know me either through faith or through the Law will serve me. “A people whom I did not know will serve me.” For I did not know it when it served idols; now, believing, it has become known and made a servant to me. “At the hearing of the ear it obeyed me.” They obeyed me by their ears because they did not see miracles [Col. 0871B] or my bodily presence. Afterwards they heard and believed. The Church, instructed by preachers, received the spiritual ear, by which, understanding, it may keep the divine precepts.

“Foreign children.” Isaiah says the same: “Woe to the sinful nation, foreign children, a people full of sins” (Isa. 1). By the ancient designation, the Jews were called children of God, but they became alienated because they became children of the devil. And the same Jews, whose father is the devil, “lied to me, because they did not stand in truth, as did their father. Foreign children grew old,” that is, because they did not receive the coming of the new man, they remained in the old man. “And they limped from their paths.” They limp because they believe the Father and do not believe the Son. They have one foot and lack the other; hence [Col. 0871C] they limp in the letter of the Law. The voice of the Church.

The Lord lives—the one whom they had shut in the tomb under the placement of seals. And my God is blessed by God the Father. “The Lord lives, and blessed is the Lord my God.” Did he not live before? But he says this with reference to the Incarnation, just as Saint Paul says: “He who died for a time through the weakness of the flesh, but lives by the power of God. For he no longer dies; death will no longer rule over him” (Rom. VI). And let the God of my salvation be exalted. The voice of the Church addressed to Christ: Christ was exalted in the Ascension. Or otherwise: “Let the God of my salvation be exalted”: let him always be exalted in me, whose calling is my salvation, so that I may think nothing base of him.

God, who give me vengeance, by overthrowing the Jews [Col. 0871D]—or Judas the betrayer himself. Or otherwise: “God, who give me vengeance.” The voice of the Church addressed to Christ. God gave the Church the authority to bind and loose, and to exercise discipline, just as Peter and Paul received authority through the Spirit of the Lord, as he said: “Behold, I have given you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and upon every power of the enemy” (Luke X). And you subjected peoples beneath me, beneath the authority of the Church, for governing unbelieving nations. The Lord is my deliverer from wrathful nations: Christ in his Passion, from the Jews who cried, “Crucify him, crucify him,” and the Church from heretics, and the soul from all the vices which he called nations.

And from those rising up against me you will exalt me—that is, from [Col. 0872A] persecutors. From the unjust man you will rescue me—that is, from the devil, as it is said: “An enemy has done this.”

Therefore I will confess to you among the peoples, O Lord. The Church says: I will praise you among believers. I will sing a psalm to you among the nations—that is, I will praise and act: “Therefore I will confess to you among the peoples, O Lord. I will sing a psalm to your name.” Because I am in them, I will confess to you, Father; and I will sing psalms—the prophet’s voice.

Magnifying the salvation of his king, Christ the Lord, because he rose again. Or otherwise: the prophet speaks to God the Father, because he brings healing and salvation to each person, drawing souls through preaching, so that there may be salvation for believers who believe in the salvation of that king. And showing mercy to his Christ, David [Col. 0872B]—that is, to his only-begotten Son. “David” is interpreted as “strong of hand,” which is Christ. And to his offspring unto the end. His offspring are his saints. The Lord always shows mercy to his saints without end. And showing mercy to his Christ, David, and to his offspring forever: to Jesus the Lord himself, the mediator, and to the ecclesiastical people who believed through his word. May he himself, our most powerful deliverer, deign to rescue us from this world and establish us in faith through the Gospel, because to him belong glory and dominion with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM XVIII

For the end; a psalm of David. The psalm contains the voice of the prophet speaking about Christ. This psalm is sung by the prophet in the person of Christ and in [Col. 0872C] the person of the Church.

The heavens declare the glory of God, etc. From created things the Creator is consequently recognized. Alternatively: “The heavens declare the glory of God”; the earth cannot declare it. According to the historical sense, heaven and earth, together with the rest of their created things, proclaim the glory of God, as Paul says: “Through the things that have been made, the things understood are seen” (Rom. I)—that is, they are seen by those who understand. This heaven is the firmament. Hence he said: “And God placed the firmament in the midst of the waters,” that is, heaven (Gen. I). Alternatively, according to the spiritual sense: the heavens are the apostles; “glory” means work; and “declare” means announce, because they preach the glory of God. And so that we may know that this is the firmament which Genesis also calls heaven: “And God called the firmament heaven.” They announce. Hence also the Lord said to the disciples: “All things that I have heard from my Father I have announced to you” (John XV).

Day pours forth the word to day, and night shows knowledge to night. He related like things to like, so that through the order of times we may arrive more fully at knowledge of God. “Day pours forth the word to day, and night shows knowledge to night.” Yesterday’s day announced today’s day, and today’s day tomorrow’s day. According to the spiritual sense, “day” is Christ. Alternatively, “day” means the apostles. Just as Christ is day, as he says, “I am the light of the world” (John VIII), so the apostles are also day, as he says, “You are the light of the world” (Matt. V). And one day has twelve hours. Hence the Lord himself said in the Gospel: “Are there not twelve hours of the day?” (John XI). These are understood as the twelve apostles. “Night to night”: night is Judas, and to the night—that is, to the Jews—he shows knowledge, namely when he said, “Whomever I kiss, he is the one; seize him” (Matt. XXVI). Alternatively, “night,” the depth of the Scriptures in the prophets, announces the depth of the Old Testament.

There are no languages or speeches whose words are not heard. “There are no languages,” as if he said, tongues; nor “speeches,” since there are many speeches among languages. Or by “speeches” varieties of words are understood, as if he said: There were no utterances which the apostles did not receive in the diversity of languages, and therefore there were no languages which did not hear the apostles’ speeches, since he says: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” [Col. 0873B]—that is, to all the islands and boundaries of the world.

Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world—namely, the sound and words of the apostles and of the Gospels.

He set his tabernacle in the sun. In Hebrew it reads: “He set the tabernacle for the sun in them,” that is, in the heavens. God set his tabernacle in the sun, and he himself is like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber. “In the sun”: in the womb of the holy Virgin Mary. Mary is interpreted as “star of the sea.” The light of the sun shines more brightly than that of the stars. The Lord is the sun of righteousness, as the prophet says: “The sun of righteousness will rise for you” (Mal. IV)—that is, Christ. This sun illuminated the star, that is, Mary, so that she might be like the sun. Therefore he set his tabernacle [Col. 0873C] in the sun when he assumed a body from her womb. And he himself is like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber. The bridegroom is the Father’s Word; the bride is human flesh, with which he came forth from the bridal chamber—that is, from the Virgin’s womb.

He rejoiced like a giant to run his course. Through the sun, Christ is mystically understood. “He rejoiced like a giant to run his course.” Here “giant” is used for Christ’s strength, because he himself bound the strong man, the devil, and plundered his vessels, which we had been. “To run his course,” because he had no delays here. How so? Once born here, he came to his Passion, rose again, and ascended. His going forth is from the summit of heaven, and his course reaches to its summit. “From the summit of heaven”—that is, from the Father, which is the principal name—not because he is greater than the Son according to divinity, but on account of the name “Father.” From the summit—that is, from eternity—comes his going forth. And his course reaches to its summit: his course is in the equality of eternity. For he ascended to heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father, where he was before and where he has always been with him. And there is no one who can hide himself from his heat. For there is no one who does not possess seeds of the knowledge of God. Nor is there anyone who can hide himself from his heat. There is no one who does not have from his heat something which he received through the many divisions of the gifts of grace, as Paul said: “To one is given the word of wisdom; to another, the word of knowledge” (1 Cor. XII).

The law of the Lord is blameless. The law itself is Christ, who did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it (Matt. V). Blameless, because he had no sin. The law [Col. 0874A] of the Lord is immaculate. He who had previously praised God through created things now begins to proclaim him through the giving of the law. Converting souls from captivity into freedom. The testimony of the Lord is faithful. What testimony? Surely this: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. XI). Faithful, because it does not lie. Giving wisdom to the little ones—not little in understanding, but in humility. Hence it is written: “For you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. X).

The judgments of the Lord are right, making hearts glad. “Judgments,” that is, decisions; “right,” because God judges rightly, and the right possess right judgments. Making hearts glad: the souls of the saints. The commandment of the Lord is radiant: the New Testament. [Col. 0874B] Enlightening the eyes—that is, the eyes of the heart.

The fear of the Lord is holy and endures forever and ever. Fear together with charity. Hence he said: “Perfect charity casts out fear” (1 John IV). Let one fear—not with the fear of Gehenna or the fear of punishment, but with holy fear; let him fear in such a way that through negligence he does not lose the one whom he loves. The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves—not by another, but by themselves. For God deceives no one.

They are more desirable than gold and much precious stone, more beloved than all worldly treasures. And sweeter than honey and the honeycomb, because no precious metal can be compared with the judgments or wisdom of God—neither gold nor precious stone, nor anything pertaining to adornment and clothing, nor honey, by which one is nourished. By these two things a person is clothed and nourished, as Paul says: “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these” (1 Tim. III). If you are a precious stone, tested like gold, you will deserve to understand the judgments and wisdom of God.

Indeed, your servant keeps them; in keeping them there is great reward. Why does he keep them, except because in keeping them there is great reward? “If you keep my commandments,” says the Lord, “you will remain in my love” (John XV). What greater reward is there than for someone to be loved by God?

Who understands transgressions? Whoever is in transgressions—that is, in sins—does not understand the judgments of God, nor his own sins, as long as he remains in transgressions. “Who understands transgressions?” This is the third division of praise, by which he teaches that what was impossible under the law, through the transgression of the law, when sin had become more apparent in the world, was completed by the grace of the Gospel; and that no one can be freed from the filth of his thoughts except through the coming of the Holy Spirit. “Who understands transgressions,” except God, the searcher of hearts, who is also able to forgive them? Cleanse me from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from the alien ones. “From the hidden”: that is, from past sins; and “from the alien ones”: that is, from those which are still to come and have not yet reached me. Or otherwise: “From the hidden,” that is, from all that is within me; and “from the alien sins,” because the devil secretly possessed pride and was cast down. Afterwards he was alien from Adam, before Adam himself had sinned. But after Adam consented to him, they were joined in pride and will, and from one sin the devil made two judgments for himself, so that he might be judged doubly, because he killed both himself and another.

If they do not rule over me, then I shall be blameless. If these sins do not rule over me, then I shall be blameless. And I shall be cleansed from the greatest transgression—that is, from pride, because pride is the beginning of every sin.

And the words of my mouth will be pleasing. Then my words will please you. And the meditation of my heart will always be in your sight—that is, arising from the remembrance of humility.

O Lord, my helper and my redeemer. Helper in tribulation and in necessities. And my redeemer, because you redeemed me with your precious blood. You are the helper of the human race when you make us draw near to you. You are the redeemer, because through your Passion and resurrection you redeemed us from destruction. May you deign continually to guard us as we walk in your law, because to you, with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, belong honor and glory throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM XIX

For the end; a psalm of David. The prophet sings this psalm in the person of the Church concerning Christ. The prophet foresaw Christ coming in the flesh for our redemption and praying for his enemies. Hence he said: “May he hear.”

May the Lord hear you in the day of tribulation. He said “in the day of tribulation” with reference to the flesh. Some think that this psalm was spoken by the voice of the people addressing Christ, both king and priest.

[Col. 0875C] May he send you help from the holy place. Since he had taken the form of a servant, it is rightly as though help is invoked for him as a man. “May he send you help from the holy place”—that is, from himself, because that divinity was in the body itself. And from Zion may he receive you: that is, from Zion itself, which is the Church, and he himself is in the Church.

May the Lord remember all your sacrifice. That is, so that he may redeem through his Passion. For Christ himself is king, priest, and victim, because he offered himself in the Passion, since he gave his blood for us. May your whole burnt offering become fat—that is, may it be acceptable to God. A whole burnt offering is something completely consumed by fire, because Christ ascended the cross with body and soul. All your victims: Christ’s sacrifice, whether what we all offer him in supplication, or what he himself poured out as his blood for [Col. 0875D] all. The meaning is: Do not allow anyone to perish, since you died for all, and may the Father fulfill your entire will. Hence he says: “I will that, just as you and I are one, they also may be one in us” (John XVII).

May the Lord grant you according to your heart—that is, whether the request is made for the humanity of Christ’s flesh or for his body, which is the Church, so that it may be heard. And may he confirm all your counsel—that is, the counsel of the Trinity.

We shall rejoice in your salvation. The voice of the Church: in the salvation which you gave by suffering. And in the name of the Lord our God we shall be magnified—not in ourselves but in him, because in the Church we have been gathered in your name.

May the Lord fulfill all your petitions. Up to this point he spoke about the Passion; now he speaks about the resurrection, ascension, and reward. There are two petitions of Christ when he says, “May the Lord hear you,” and “May he fulfill all your petitions.” When Christ said to the Father: “Glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had before the world existed” (John XVII). And elsewhere: “Holy Father, preserve them in your name, whom you have given me, so that just as we are one, they also may be one” (ibid.). Now I know that the Lord has saved his Christ. The prophet now speaks of the time when he received the Holy Spirit. Then he knew that God the Father would save his Son.

And he will hear him from his holy heaven—that is, from himself and from the holy Church. In powers is the salvation of his right hand. In the powers of the holy Church, through which salvation has been made by Christ, who is his right hand—that is, the right hand of God the Father—because the Church possesses the authority to bind and loose and to exercise discipline. And the Lord says: “Behold, I have given you authority to tread upon serpents and all the powers of the enemy” (Luke X). Hence Paul says: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love?” (1 Cor. IV). “In powers is the salvation of his right hand”: in that power by which he rose victorious from the dead.

Some trust in chariots, and some in horses. Chariots and horses are always reproved in the Egyptians. Let others trust in idols and demons; let us trust in Christ. Or otherwise: “Some in chariots, and some in horses.” By chariots, the pleasure of the world, or the desire for all worldly things, is signified, because just as wheels are unstable, so they themselves run here and there in their minds. By horses, the proud are signified, and they too are desirous. But we will call upon the name of the Lord our God—not upon those things mentioned above, but upon the name of the Lord.

They are bound and have fallen: those who are tied by the cords of vices and cannot ascend to higher things, but fall, as it says: “They went backward and fell” (John XVIII). But we have risen again and have been raised upright. We rose from unbelief; we were raised upright through faith, because we had been twisted in sins.

O Lord, save the king, and hear us on the day when we call upon you. “Save the king”—that is, Christ, with reference to the flesh. “And hear us”: the Church asks to be heard at the proper time. “O Lord, save the king, and hear us on the day when we call upon you.” [Col. 0876D] In Hebrew it is written: “O Lord, save the king who will hear us on whatever day we call upon you.”

## PSALM XX

O Lord, the king will rejoice in your strength. This is the king for whose salvation, according to the form of a servant, prayer was offered in the preceding psalm. Christ is King of kings and Lord of lords. And he will rejoice exceedingly in your salvation—that is, in the fact that you saved human beings: your Son, who is the Savior, will rejoice.

You gave him the desire of his heart, and you did not deny him the will of his lips. For now we are no longer servants but friends. What he asked has been fulfilled. Just as he and the Father are one, so we also are one in him. Or otherwise: You granted him the desire of his soul. The Son of God desired to come and redeem the human race. Hence he said: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” (Luke XXII). And you did not deny him the will of his lips. This also refers to when the Lord said: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John XIV).

For you went before him with blessings of sweetness. This was from afar, when Melchizedek blessed Abraham (Gen. XIV). And thereafter, whatever blessings there were among the patriarchs up to the coming of Christ, Christ was blessed in them. “For you went before him”: that is, you went before him with blessings of sweetness before he had tasted the gall offered by the Jews, because these blessings came to him beforehand. [Col. 0877B] He tasted it and did not wish to drink (Matt. XXVII). He tasted it because he took upon himself our death. He did not wish to drink because he rose again on the third day. He did not wish to drink—that is, he did not remain in death. You placed upon his head a crown of precious stone. God’s crown is the Church, a congregation gathered from various nations. Concerning it Paul says in the person of believers: “My joy and crown” (Phil. IV).

He asked for life, and you gave it to him. As a man he died; as a man he rose again, since God could not ask for life. Length of days forever and ever. Let the impious synagogue be silent. What human being lives forever and ever? David and Solomon reigned no more than forty years each.

Great is his glory in your salvation. What he himself requested in the Gospel has been fulfilled: “Father, glorify me [Col. 0877C] with yourself” (John XIII, XVII). “Great is his glory in your salvation,” as if he said: Great is his glory; it is a great thing that a human being has been taken up to the right hand of God the Father. You will place glory and great beauty upon him: the glory of the resurrection; beauty when his face shone like the sun on the mountain and his garments became white like snow (Matt. XVII).

For you will give him blessing forever and ever, because every creature blesses him. You will make him glad with joy in your presence—that is, he will always be with you in heaven. “You will make him glad with joy in your presence.” Then you will make the Son rejoice with joy, when that multitude of saints has been united and the number restored to him. Christ will rejoice over those whom he acquired, for whom he suffered.

For the king hopes in the Lord, according to the dispensation of the body, or as the human being assumed into divinity. And he will not be shaken in the mercy of the Most High. Neither the humanity of the Son nor the primitive Church will be shaken at the end. Up to this point, the prophet spoke in the person of the Church to God the Father concerning the humanity of Christ; now he speaks to the divinity. Hence he said:

Let your hand be found by all your enemies. Let your enemies encounter your power, so that they may turn toward what is good. Let the power of God find those who refused to believe in Christ in his humility; let it find them in vengeance. Let your right hand find all those who hate you. God’s great clemency wishes to convert those who hate him, since he even desires to find his enemies.

You will set them like a fiery oven at the time of your presence [Col. 0878A]—in the good sense, so that their sins may be burned up. Just as an oven burns within, so their conscience will burn within, because they did not do good things. O Lord, in your anger you will trouble them. Here too God’s clemency does not punish but troubles, so that they may be converted to repentance. Fire will devour them: the Holy Spirit will consume their sins. Fire will devour them at the time of God’s presence, when he comes to judge the world.

You will destroy their fruit from the earth—that is, you will destroy them, or their works from the holy Church. And fire will consume them. This is the fire of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke XII). Concerning this fire also, the two to whom the Savior opened the Scriptures on the road said: “Was not our heart burning within us on the way, when he opened the Scriptures to us?” (ibid. XXIV). And their offspring from among the children of men. “Offspring,” that is, the children who were begotten in evil doctrine. “From among the children of men”: that is, you will remove them from the fellowship of the good.

For they turned evil upon you. The Jews turned upon Christ what they ought to have received upon themselves through just vengeance, when they said that he was worthy of death and that it was better for one man to die than for the whole nation to perish (John XI). They devised a plan which they could not establish, when they said to Pilate: “Lord, we remember that that deceiver said while he was still alive, ‘After three days I will rise again.’ Therefore command the tomb to be guarded until the third day.” But he said to them: “You have a guard; go, guard it as you know.” Afterwards they placed seals, but the dead could not hold the living [Col. 0878C] (Matt. XXVII). He rose again, which they neither wished for nor believed. Then they could not establish the plan they had devised.

For you will set them as a back. In two ways. “Back,” because they always desire earthly things; alternatively, “back,” so that they may fall backward, or when they look backward. In your remnants you will prepare their face. Instead of “remnants,” the Hebrew has “in good things.” The meaning therefore runs as follows: In the likeness of the saints whom you have preserved for yourself from the whole world, make even those who have been purified by torments become such, so that, in accordance with the face of the saints, the faces of sinners also may begin to be such—that is, so that those who were sinners may become like those who are saints. Or otherwise: “In your remnants you will prepare their face” [Col. 0878D]—that is, the prophets whom their fathers killed. Their remnants are the sons of the Jews who killed the head of the prophets, so that the vengeance which began with the prophets may come upon those who killed the Lord. Alternatively: “In your remnants you will prepare their face”—that is, at the end they will believe through Elijah and Enoch. You will prepare their face: the face of those who believe in you, so that it may be fulfilled: “To turn the hearts of the fathers toward the children” (Luke I).

Be exalted, O Lord, in your strength. The voice of the Church. “Be exalted in your strength”: that is, display your power and majesty, because you first came in humility, but now come in majesty. We shall sing and chant your mighty deeds, O Lord. We shall sing in the heart; we shall chant in our works; we announce your mighty deeds.

## PSALM XXI

For the end; concerning the morning taking-up; a psalm of David. The morning taking-up signifies the mystery of the Lord’s resurrection and ascension to the Father. The Hebrews have this inscription differently: “For the morning stag,” and, through a perverse interpretation, they think that the entire twenty-first psalm was composed concerning Esther, because through her danger and intercession with the king the Israelite people were delivered from danger.

[Note: [Col. 0879D] The true Jerome, in his Commentary on Matthew, chapter XXVII: “They are impious who think that this psalm was spoken in the person of David, or of Esther and Mordecai, since the evangelist too understands the testimonies taken from it as referring to the Savior.”]

But we understand the stag that kills serpents and consumes poisons to be no one other than Christ, as the whole context of the psalm shows.

My God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me? The Lord used this verse while hanging on the cross. From this we observe that the entire psalm was sung by the Lord while placed upon the cross. As for the phrase “Give heed to me,” which occurs in the middle, it is not found in the Hebrew codices, and its insertion is shown by the voice of the Lord, who also omitted it in the Gospel, as if he said: “Why have you forsaken me?” Here humanity speaks of how it was forsaken in Adam, when he transgressed the commandment. Or Christ was forsaken in the Passion with reference to the flesh. The words of my sins are far from my salvation. “Far”: here divinity speaks. “The words of my sins”: because he reckons our sins as his own. For there is no sin in his salvation; rather, salvation is far from the sinner. Or otherwise: “The words of my sins are far from my salvation.” Aquila interpreted this passage as follows: “The words [Note: [Col. 0880D] Aquila has βρυχήματός μου, properly ‘my roar,’ not ‘my groan’; but I fear that here he confuses the sixth edition with that of Theodotion, who in fact translated βοήσεώς μου, ‘my cry,’ as did the fifth; for the sixth has δεήσεών μου, namely, ‘my supplications.’] of my groaning.” Symmachus: “The words of my groanings.” The fifth and sixth editions: “The words of my cry.” According to the other interpreters, the meaning is this: My groanings and efforts, by which I continually sought to save the people of Israel, have been far from my salvation, which I wished to grant the people, because they themselves did not wish to receive healing. According to the Seventy interpreters, however, the meaning is: In saying that I plead for salvation and complain that I have been forsaken, I do not speak in my own person but in that of the people, whose sins I myself took upon my body. Hence I say: These words which I pour forth are far from my salvation. For I do not ask for salvation so much for myself, who am God, as for the people who need salvation.

I shall cry by day, and you will not hear; and by night, and it will not be folly for me. While hanging in the daytime, he is not heard by the Father; at night he rises victorious from the dead. Alternatively: Whoever is not heard in joy is heard in tears. Hence he says: “Not as folly for me,” that is, I did not cry out in vain. And Aquila translated from the Hebrew, saying: “And by night, and you will not be silent”—that is, you will hear me; you will answer me; you will do what I prayed.

My God, I shall cry by day, and you will not hear, and by night. Christ cried out on the cross and prayed for his own; he was heard and not heard. He was heard on behalf of the predestined—for example, on behalf of the eight thousand, or of those one hundred and twenty and five hundred [Col. 0880A] brothers. And he was not heard on behalf of those who were not predestined. Hence the evangelist said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII). Therefore “day” is understood here for the good, and “night” for the evil. Or day and night signify prosperity and adversity in the Church. The Church is not heard in prosperity, so that it may not exalt itself, and is not heard in adversity, so that it may be more thoroughly cleansed. And “not as folly for me”: that is, the Son, coeternal with the Father, knows why he was not heard on the day of the Passion—that is, on behalf of the children of death—and why he was not heard in the prosperity and tribulation of his Church.

But you dwell in the holy place: the praise of Israel. The voice of the prophet. “You dwell in the holy place”—that is, in his own body, or in heaven, or in the Church.

[Col. 0880B] In you our fathers hoped, O Lord; they hoped, and you delivered them. The patriarchs and prophets, or the others, hoped; and you delivered them—that is, from Egypt or from Babylon. They were not confounded, because you fulfilled what you promised: namely, the promised land and long life. Alternatively: “In you our fathers hoped”—the teachers of the Church. They were not confounded, because you are always their hope.

But I am a worm and not a man. He says this on account of the humility of the assumed body, while Isaiah also sings the same thing: “Do not fear, worm of Jacob” (Isa. XLI). The reproach of men and the rejection of the people. What greater reproach is there than the cross? And the rejection of the people—that is, the mockery of the Jewish people. Why “worm and not man,” when he says in the Gospel: “The Son of Man has come to redeem what had perished” (Luke XIX)? Christ is called both worm and man. He is a worm, as the prophet says: “Do not fear, worm of Jacob”; and a man, because he was born from Mary. His birth is likened to that of a worm, because a worm born in wood has no father, but only a mother. So Christ was born from Mary without intercourse with a man.

God made two dwelling places: heaven and earth. Heaven is the dwelling place of angels, and earth the dwelling place of worms. God made the worm ascend to heaven and the angel descend to earth. Through humility Christ ascended above all the angels, and through pride the devil was cast down to earth. The reproach of men and the rejection of the people: reproach when the Jews said, “You are his disciple” (John IX); rejection when they expelled him outside the city and crucified [Col. 0880D] him.

All who saw me mocked me. This is said with reference to the wicked, just as the Jews themselves said: “If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross,” or, “Hail, King of the Jews” (Matt. XXVII). They spoke with their lips and shook their heads. They spoke with their lips because they uttered in words what they had in their hearts. They shook their heads: that is, they abandoned the one head, who is Christ, and made many heads for themselves—demons.

He hoped in the Lord; let him deliver him; let him save him, because he desires him. The voice of the prophet speaking of humanity. “He hoped in the Lord”: humanity in divinity. “Let him deliver him”: that is, from the Jews. “Because he desires him”: God the Father wished to have such a Son, without sin, through whom he might take away the sins of the world, as the prophet says: “He himself took our infirmities and bore our sicknesses” (Isa. LII).

For you are the one who brought me forth from the womb. The voice of humanity. “You brought me forth from the womb”: that is, from the womb of the holy Mary, or from the synagogue, because through the prophecy of the prophets he was conceived and, in the spiritual sense, was brought forth as though from a womb. “My hope from my mother’s breasts,” etc.: Christ did not disdain to suck the breasts of his mother—that is, the breasts of Mary. Or “the breasts of his mother” means the law of the synagogue. It is said to have two breasts because it possesses the letter and the meaning. But they—that is, the Jews—received only one breast: that is, they observe only the letter of the law. You are my God; do not depart from me on the day of the Passion.

For tribulation is near. As he himself said: “Rise, let us go; behold, the one who will betray me has drawn near” (John XIV). There is no one to help, neither angel nor man, except you, Father.

Many calves surrounded me: wanton calves—that is, the Jews, who were wanton and uncontrolled. Fat bulls surrounded me. Instead of “fat,” Symmachus translated “fattened.” In Hebrew the word *Bashan* is used, which can also be translated as “ignominy,” because they surrounded me. They are called bulls on account of their pride—that is, their leaders, Annas and Caiaphas, or the others. “Fat,” on account of the grossness of their malice.
