They opened their mouths against me. When they said, “Let him be crucified.” Like a lion seizing and roaring—that is, when they were considering how to kill him. “Seizing,” when they apprehended him with swords and clubs.

I have been poured out like water, and all my bones have been scattered. Thus the Jews wished to extinguish Christ like water, which is drawn up, scattered, and does not return. “All my bones have been scattered.” The bones of Christ are called the apostles, because just as flesh is strengthened by bones, so the body of Christ, which is the Church, is strengthened by the apostles or teachers.

My heart has become. The heart of Christ is understood as the Church [Col. 0881D], before Christ ascended the cross. It seemed hard because few were suffering for his name. Hence it is said: “Who dies for a just man?” Like melting wax. For after Christ ascended the cross, all the saints began to endure tribulation for him, because of the hope of the reward to come (Rom. V). In the midst of my belly—that is, in the midst of the Church. “My heart has become like melting wax in the midst of my belly.” My wisdom, which previously was not understood, grew hot when kindled by the fire of the Passion and was received by the Church.

My strength has dried up like a potsherd. Before a potsherd is placed in the fire, it is weak; after it is placed in the fire, it is strengthened. And after Christ ascended the gallows of the cross, he strengthened his Church. Therefore it did not dry up like grass, so that it might fall, but like a potsherd, so that it might be made firm. And my tongue has cleaved to my jaws. That is, the tongues of the apostles fell silent at the time of the Passion. Although one spoke, he did so by denying rather than confessing—namely, Peter. For the disciples, keeping my commandments, will speak about me afterward. And they led me down into the mire of death. That is, into the Incarnation, or into the underworld, when he led the souls of the saints out from there with him. And they led me down into the mire of death. Just as the impious are cast down by the wind, so they supposed that I would fall into death, as though I would not be able to rise again.

For many dogs have surrounded me. It is characteristic of dogs to rejoice with their master and bark at the thief. Here the Jews are understood as dogs, because they barked at Christ and rejoiced with the thief—namely, Barabbas—when they asked for him and killed Christ (John XVIII). For many dogs have surrounded me: they did not speak what was right, but barked wicked things. The assembly of the wicked has besieged me. The congregation of the Jews. Many dogs. In Hebrew, *chelabim* is found instead of “dogs,” which Aquila and Theodotion interpreted as “hunters.” The assembly of the wicked has besieged me. The Jews besieged him—that is, they surrounded Christ.

They pierced my hands and my feet. The past tense is used for the future. “They pierced”: they fastened nails, and found great fruit—that is, the salvation of the nations. And they counted all my bones. They saw his limbs stretched out upon the cross.

But they themselves looked on, and so forth. Saying: “He saved others; he cannot save himself” (Matthew XXVII).

They divided my garments among themselves. Giving each soldier his portion. And over my clothing they cast lots. They discussed the tunic: “Let us not tear it, but let us cast lots to determine whose it shall be.” Or otherwise: They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast lots. The fact that four soldiers made four portions but did not divide the tunic signified the unity of the Church, which was not to be torn apart. Heretics wish to tear it apart, but they cannot.

But you, Lord, do not keep your help far from me. [Col. 0882D] Humanity speaks to divinity, asking that it assist him in the time of the Passion. But you, Lord, do not keep your help far from me; instead, raise me up immediately. Look upon my defense. May that voracious region of hell not prevail against me.

Deliver my soul from the sword. Deliver it from the sword or malice of the Jews. Or, deliver my soul from that power which slays by seducing. And from the hand of the dog my only one. “Dogs”: the Jews. “My only one”: that is, the soul of Christ. It is called “only one” because that soul has no sin, and other souls are cleansed by it. Or “my only one” means the Church; and “from the hand of the dog” means from the mouth of hell, which greedily devours in the manner of a dog.

Save me from the mouth of the lion. The mouth of the lion is the Jewish people, because of the strength of their wickedness. And from the horns of the unicorns my lowliness. The unicorn is understood as that same Jewish people, because it has one horn—that is, one law—from which it used to toss all the nations before their transgression. And from the horns of the unicorns my lowliness: from the servants of Satan, through whom human beings are individually exalted in pride. Up to this point he has spoken of the Passion; now he speaks of the resurrection when he says:

I shall proclaim your name to my brothers. The voice of Christ. “Brothers” means the apostles, after he rose again, as he himself says: “Go, announce to my brothers that they should go to Galilee; there they will see me” (Matthew X). In the midst of the Church I shall praise you. That is, in the unity of the Church, in the midst of believing peoples. I shall praise you; I shall preach you. [Col. 0883B]

You who fear the Lord, praise him. All the saints who fear him with holy fear praise him. All the seed of Jacob, glorify him. That is, the lesser people—the supplanters of vices—glorify him: namely, the seed of Christians, to whom the greater shall serve (Genesis XXV).

Let all the seed of Israel fear him. That is, all who see God, who, reborn through baptism, see God with the mind. For he did not despise or disdain the prayer of the poor: my prayer, since I became poor for you. Or, God did not despise Christian peoples, but heard them.

Nor did he turn his face away from me. Instead, he raised me from the dead. And when I cried to him, he heard me. Responding: “I have glorified, and I will glorify again” (John XII). Christ was heard in the Passion, and the Church in tribulation.

With you is my praise in the great Church. That is, with the Father, as he said: “I and the Father are one” (John X). With you is my praise in the great Church, which has spread throughout the whole world through faith. I shall fulfill my vows to the Lord in the presence of those who fear him. The vows of Christ are his birth or Passion; the vows of the Church are good works. Or, may they offer the mystery of my body and blood together with those who celebrate these things in his fear.

The poor shall eat and be satisfied. The poor—the apostles—shall eat the body of Christ. They shall praise the Lord who seek him. Through the consummation and through their works they recognize that he is the living bread which came down from heaven (John VI). [Col. 0883D]

Their hearts shall live for ever and ever. “Heart” means their souls. Without end, because whoever eats of this bread shall live in it through spiritual understanding forever.

All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord. That is, the Lord God made the Christian people so that they might remember him and turn back from their crooked ways. The whole multitude of the nations recognizes that it is wrapped in darkness; therefore they draw near in order to be enlightened.

All the families of the nations shall worship in his presence. They worship here and also in the future, because, according to the Apostle, “every knee shall bend” (Philippians II).

For the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he himself shall rule the nations. The kingdom of the devil has fallen, and the kingdom of Christ has come. When he ascended into heaven, all things were subjected to him. [Col. 0884A]

All the rich of the earth have eaten and worshiped. That is, the apostles and the other saints have eaten the body of Christ, as was said above. “The rich of the earth”: rich in faith, works, or virtues, recognizing that the Lord is good. In his presence all who descend into the earth shall fall. They shall prostrate themselves—that is, sinners shall be in the presence of God on the day of judgment. They descend from the pride of the world so that they may worship with a sense of pure humility.

My soul shall live for him, and my seed shall serve him. The Church, which no longer lives for itself, but Christ lives in it. Or otherwise: My soul shall live for him, and my seed shall serve him. The soul of Christ lives for God the Father, and death shall no longer rule over him (Romans VIII). Or, the Church shall live for Christ. “My seed,” the children of the Church, shall serve him—the people of believers.

A coming generation shall be announced to the Lord. The prophet says: “A coming generation,” that is, the people of the nations who were to come to believe in him before Christ came into the world. Or, “a coming generation” means the complete splendor on the day of judgment. The heavens shall announce his righteousness. That is, the apostles or teachers. “His righteousness”: that is, his commandments. To a people that shall be born. That is, through the word of preaching. Whom the Lord has made. That is, whom he predestined before the ages. A people that shall be born, whom the Lord has made: those who approach through faith and are reborn in Christ through baptism.

May he deign to grant us to have his wounds before our eyes and, with Thomas, to touch the imprint of his nails (John XX). Or, while preserving constant remembrance of the humility of his Passion, and recalling with a sigh that he also penetrated the underworld for our sins, may we always act in this earthly body so that we may deserve to be joined to him in the kingdom. Amen.

## PSALM XXII

A psalm of David. This psalm contains the voice of the Church praising Christ together with others.

The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing. Ezekiel also speaks of this shepherd: “I will raise up a shepherd, and my servant David shall feed them” (Ezekiel XXXIV). Or otherwise: He is the good shepherd who laid down his life for me (John X); he rules me with equitable guidance, and therefore I lack nothing. Or otherwise: He rules me. The Church speaks confidently through faith, because before the coming of Christ the devil ruled the world, but now Christ rules his Church. What we say is, “The Lord rules me.” The Hebrews say, as was written above: “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing.” Whoever has God, and whoever clings to God, lacks no good thing, as the prophet says: “Nothing is lacking to those who fear him” (Psalm XXIII).

He has placed me there in a place of pasture. As though he were saying: In the unity of faith, in the unity of the Church. He has placed me there in a place of pasture: he has established my hope in future blessedness. For “pasture” is understood as future blessedness.

He has led me beside the water of refreshment. By cleansing me through baptism he nourished me; or through the teaching of the patriarchs, prophets, or apostles. He restored my soul. So that it might know him; that is, the soul of the Church. Formerly it had descended into hell through the guilt of the first man, Adam; but now it has been turned toward Christ through faith.

He led me along the path of righteousness—that is, along the path of the commandments, by the narrow way. For his name’s sake, not for the sake of my merit.

For even if I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, through the darkness of this age, I shall fear no evil, for you are with me. Lord, I hold you in my heart. Or otherwise: “Shadow” is made in two ways, namely, by a body and by light. Through the body, death is understood; through the shadow, sins and ignorance. Nevertheless, although the Church walks amid the things mentioned above, she does not fear, because she has the Lord with her, as he himself said: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew, last chapter). Therefore the Church does not fear.

Your rod and your staff—they have comforted me. “The Lord chastises the one whom he loves” (Proverbs III). By the rod is understood tribulation, or the discipline of the Father, or the persecution of the Church. And your staff, with which you chastise spiritual children. Or, by the staff are understood future support and consolation. “They have comforted me”: they instructed me by consoling me; they did not afflict me by putting me to death.

You have prepared a table before me, and so forth. So that I may no longer be nourished with milk like a little child, but with solid food—that is, so that, chewing the holy Scriptures with spiritual teeth, I may be able to resist the perverse. You have prepared a table before me against those who trouble me. The table is the divine Scripture. Just as consolation and refreshment are found on a table after labor, so the saints have consolation and refreshment through the table—that is, through divine Scripture—namely, hope, faith, and charity. Against those who trouble me: the persecutors of the Church, who are demons, Jews, and heretics. Against all these we find consolation in the holy Scriptures.

You have made my head rich with oil. By “head”—that is, the governing faculty of the mind—the Church is understood. For the mind is called the head, because just as the members are governed from the head, so thoughts are arranged by the mind. By oil consolation is understood, because just as the body is comforted by oil, so the mind of the Church is comforted through the consolation of the Scriptures. You have anointed my head with oil: you have gladdened my mind with spiritual joy, for it is the head of the whole body. And how splendid is my inebriating cup! The cup is understood as the word of God. “Inebriating,” because through preaching a person is pierced in mind when it separates one person—that is, a father from his son, a son from his father, a mother from her daughter, and a daughter from her mother, and a daughter-in-law from her mother-in-law. It inebriates us when it does these things. By the cup, measure is understood, because God distributes—that is, gives—to each person according to what he deserves or is able to receive. Or, you have inebriated me with the mystical cup, so that I might consign the pleasures of my former life to oblivion.

And your mercy, Lord, shall follow me. The voice of the Church to Christ. The mercy of God both precedes and follows. It precedes through faith; it follows in the keeping of God’s commandments. All the days of my life, as long as I dwell in this body.

And that I may dwell in the house of the Lord. Here the Church remains as though in a tabernacle. For just as a tabernacle is moved from place to place, so the Church is transferred from this tabernacle into a house—that is, into eternal or everlasting life, where the saints shall dwell without end. Through length of days: through days without end. That I may dwell in the house of the Lord through length of days: that is, may I dwell in the heavenly Jerusalem together with all the saints gathered in me through faith.

## PSALM XXIII

A psalm of David, for the first day of the week. This psalm sometimes contains the voice of the prophet speaking about the Church.

The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness. When those who think earthly thoughts have been converted. The earth is the Lord’s—that is, the whole world—and its fullness—that is, the inhabitants of this world. Or, the earth is the Lord’s—that is, the Church—and its fullness—that is, all the saints. The world and all who dwell in it. When Jesus was glorified, the faith of all nations became one Church.

He founded it upon the seas. By “seas” are meant the disturbances of this world, because from the beginning the waves of the age have trampled upon and overcome the Church. But “he founded” means that he strengthened his Church in faith. He established it upon the waves of this age so that it would not be swept away by them. And upon the rivers he prepared it. By “rivers” are understood the powerful or greedy of this age, as Solomon says: “All the rivers enter the sea.” So these powerful people, although they possess great wealth, are never satisfied. The Church is above these rivers so that she may preach to them, and those who possess power may be converted. If they refuse to listen, he prepared her above the rivers. He established her above the desires of this age so that she might be superior to them, clean and without stain or wrinkle.

Who shall ascend the mountain of David? The voice of the prophet asking: that is, who shall ascend into the heavenly Jerusalem? “Who” is used in place of “for charity.” Or this mountain signifies lofty righteousness, as in: “Go, sell everything you possess and give to the poor, and you shall have treasure in heaven” (Luke XVIII). Or who shall stand in his holy place? Upon his highest righteousness—as though he were saying: Who shall persevere? For many ascend, but do not persevere.

Innocent in hands and pure in heart. Pure in deed, because by “hands” works are understood; and pure in heart—that is, with pure speech. Or “pure in heart” means holy in thought. He who has not received his soul in vain: he who has not stained it with any filth of sins after baptism. He has not received his soul in vain who performs good works. Nor has he sworn deceitfully to his neighbor. He does not swear deceitfully to his neighbor who proclaims what he thinks and fulfills it in deed. For there are many who swear deceitfully in order to deceive their neighbor, which God, the Father of lights, abhors, as Peter says: “You have not lied to human beings, but to God” (Acts V). Therefore, whoever has guarded himself from these stains—

He shall receive a blessing from the Lord and mercy from God his Savior. From Christ, equal to the Father, by whose death he has been saved. Or otherwise: He shall receive a blessing from the Lord. Concerning the person mentioned above—the one who does not swear deceitfully to his neighbor—he says: He shall receive a blessing from the Lord when he is told: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew XXV). And mercy from God his Savior. He obtains mercy from God who considers himself wretched.

This is the generation of those who seek the Lord. Above he spoke in the singular: “He shall receive a blessing”; now he speaks in the plural, because the Church is gathered from many persons, yet she is called one because of the unity of faith. This generation—that is, the Christian people—which, lying in darkness, sought the true Lord and Savior.

Of those who seek the face of the God of Jacob. That is, the Christian people seek the face of the God of Jacob. Hence it was said: “The greater shall serve the lesser” (Genesis XXV), because he gave primacy to the one born later. A *diapsalma* intervenes in order to change the speaker. For now the Lord himself is announced as returning to the heavenly kingdoms. Therefore, as he ascended with the angels, those who went before or accompanied him cried out to the other angelic leaders:

Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates. That is, open the heavenly entrances; let the entrance into eternity be opened. Or, “Lift up your gates, O princes”: the voice of the good angels [Note: Genebrardus suspects from this commentary on the psalm that Jerome adhered to Origen’s error concerning holy men who were angels by true nature. Yet how far the holy doctor was from this error is demonstrated by the letter to Evangelus on Melchizedek in our edition, 73, and Letter 121 to Algasius, Question 1, and so forth. Indeed, from this one may conversely derive a new argument against the authenticity of this work. See what we noted on chapter I of Haggai.] to the evil angels, whose prince is the devil. “Your gates, O princes”: that is, desire and fear. He rightly joined desire and fear, because whoever gathers through desire guards what he has gathered through fear and malice, so as not to lose it; and whoever possesses fear, desire, and malice does not cast the evil spirit out from himself. And be lifted up, eternal gates: that is, faith and charity. They are called eternal because they lay below from Adam until Christ; and therefore they are said to be lifted up. And the King of glory shall enter: that is, Christ, because through faith and charity Christ entered the Church. And the King of glory shall enter: Christ the Lord, retaining the kingdom of immense splendor. Then, astonished and struck with amazement of mind, they say:

Who is this King of glory? The voice of the greater demons. As though they were saying: We have our own king, the devil; who is this King of glory? “Who,” he says, “is this King of glory?” He who speaks answers: The Lord, strong and mighty. The voice of the good angels. He is strong who bound your strong prince (Mark III). Strong when he accepted death; mighty when he conquered hell. In battle, after plundering Tartarus, he led back with him a multitude of captives. He cries out again and says:

Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates. Let the heavenly doors be lifted up; let the gates of the eternal dwellings be opened. And the King of glory shall enter. For after the resurrection he not only possessed immense glory, but also that glory which he had possessed equally with the Father before the world was made. Therefore, worshiping the unique and singular power of such great glory, they say:

Who is this King of glory? They are answered: The Lord of hosts—he himself is the King of glory. Here “hosts” is understood of Christ in the plural, because he sits above the nine heavenly powers. Or he is called “of hosts” because the Lord is above all the powers of the devil. Or he is called “of hosts” because the devil held the nine orders of angels under his dominion, whether good or evil.

Lift up the gates. The voice of the good angels. Or the voice of the Lord to the good angels. Lift up the gates, because when Adam sinned, the gates of paradise were closed, and a fiery sword was given to the angel Seraphim so that he might guard it. But after Christ came into the world and struggled with the devil, he opened hell and led the souls of the saints out with him; and with the good angels he returned to the heavenly places. Then the gates of paradise, which had previously been closed, were opened. Or the eternal gates are called angels, through whose guardianship we ascend to the heavenly places. They are said to be lifted up because previously all the souls of the saints descended into hell. But after Christ ascended with his body above all the heavenly powers, the angels rejoiced, because he had led the souls of the saints there to be with him.

Who is this King of glory? The voice of the angels who had always been with the Father, as though they were saying: We see the Father and the Son always together; who is this King of glory? They spoke with reference to the flesh: “Lift up the gates.” The voice of the prophet concerning the Jews: “Lift up the gates”—that is, pride, desire, and avarice—because through these three every human being was descending into hell. Or, “Lift up your gates, O princes,” for which the Hebrew has: “Lift up your heads, O gates; let them be carried along the straight path.” He says that a person cannot come to perfect purity, nor can anyone attain perfect purity. The eternal gates that he says are to be lifted up are faith, charity, and chastity, because through these three Christ enters the Church.

Who is this King of glory? Human frailty answers: Who is this? As though they were saying: This is the one whom we crucified, insulted, and regarded as nothing. They answer: The Lord of hosts—that is, the one who died for a time through the weakness of the flesh but now lives through the power of God. Or he was “power” when he said to Thomas: “Put your finger into the place of the nails, and place your hand in my side, and do not be unbelieving but believing” (John [XX, not XXVI]). The Lord of hosts is named, as Paul says: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?” (Romans VIII)—“tribulation, or distress, or persecution,” and so forth.

Again: Lift up your gates, O princes. The voice of the angels who descended with Christ into hell, speaking to those subject to the devil. They show that they are leading their prince away bound: “Lift up the gates,” because the gates have been broken—that is, their power was then taken away. And be lifted up, eternal gates. Then the eternal ones were lifted up—that is, the souls of the saints from hell. They are called eternal because they will reign with God forever without end.

The Lord of hosts—he himself is the King of glory. Instead of “Lord of hosts,” Hebrew reads *Dominus Sabaoth*, which the Septuagint translators rendered elsewhere as “Almighty.” Rightly is he called Lord of hosts, who for our sake became human; was handed over to death and consigned to the darkness of the underworld; mercifully accepted this, patiently endured it, powerfully conquered it, and wondrously completed it. With his own power he trampled hell; returning to the heights in triumph; ascending to heaven in glory; he now sits at the right hand of God the almighty Father, continually interceding for our sins. Amen.

## PSALM XXIV

A psalm of David. The twenty-fourth psalm contains the voice of our mediator, sent to the Father; at times it contains the cry of the Church making supplication.

To you, Lord, I have lifted up my soul. Here the voice of the Church to Christ is understood. “I have lifted” means “I have raised,” because previously the Church lay in the valley of tears or in the depths, before Christ came into the world. To what has she lifted it? That is, into hope, faith, and charity, through sanctification. For if wheat lies below, it rots; if it is lifted upward, it is preserved. So too, if the soul lies in the rottenness of sins—that is, if it lies below—it rots and perishes. But if it is lifted upward into the things mentioned above—hope, faith, and charity—it is preserved by God. Or: To you, Lord, I have lifted my soul through the cross.

My God, in you I trust. This is the confession of the Church: “I trust in you,” not in myself, but in you. I shall not be put to shame, because I do not trust in a human being, concerning whom it is said: “Cursed is the man who places his hope in man” (Jeremiah XVII); and: “Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord” (Psalm XXXV). Let there be no delay in the resurrection, which would produce reproach among believers.

Nor may my enemies mock me. They had mocked me earlier when I said: “I can destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days” (Matthew XXVI). Nor may my enemies mock me: that is, those who trust only in a human being, because after he has failed, their enemies mock him. The enemies of the Church are demons, heretics, vices, and sins. For all who await you—all who rely upon you—shall not be confounded, neither here nor in the future: the apostles, or those who will come to believe in you through their word.

Let those who act wickedly in vain be confounded. The prophet says this not by wishing but by prophesying: Let those who persevere in their wickedness to the end be confounded on the day of judgment—those who added to the crime committed against me by securing the tomb with seals. Up to this point the Lord has spoken about his Passion; from here the voice of the Church follows, which after the Lord’s resurrection asks to be instructed.

Make your ways known to me, Lord, and teach me your paths. Those by which one comes into your kingdom; or your ways—that is, your commandments—make them known, that is, show them to me. Teach me your paths. A path is smaller than a road; by “path” is understood the narrow and confined way that leads to life.

Guide me in your truth. The voice of the Church. Guide me, because I am crooked. In your truth—that is, in your Christ—teach me, so that I may do nothing perversely. For you are my God and Savior. Through your resurrection my salvation has been bestowed upon me. And I have waited for you all day long. That is, throughout the whole period. They saw me endure on your behalf through the entire time of this life. For I had heard through the voices of the prophets that you would come into the world. I waited through the light of faith until you called me.

Remember your mercies, Lord, and so forth. Through them you became human in order to redeem us. Or the Christian people speak, asking that he make them upright through his mercy, as in: “Your mercies are many, Lord”; “Your mercies are from of old” (Psalm CXVIII); and: “You promised us your mercies from the beginning of the age” (ibid.).

Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorances, Lord. Those things I did in adolescence, before I came forth from the house of the unrighteous father. Or, “the sins of my youth” means those committed before baptism, and “my ignorances” means those committed after baptism.

According to your great mercy, remember me, God. That is, not according to my merits but according to your mercy. For your mercy is immense, since you call things that are not as though they were. For your goodness, Lord. Because you summon sinners to repentance.

The Lord is sweet and upright. Sweet because he is the bread of life. Sweet because he promises future rewards. Upright because he repays each person according to his works. Therefore he shall give a law to those who sin on the way: the law of charity, through which, when we forgive offenses, we are reconciled to God. “To those who sin on the way”: to sinners in this life.

He shall guide the meek in judgment. He shall guide the meek and humble of heart in judgment—that is, here in the present he makes a distinction between body and soul, so that they may correct one another in the ways of God’s commandments. Or, it refers to what was written above: “Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorances.” Age excuses this person, and ignorance excuses him. From this we understand that the one who sins in adolescence but is not ignorant has no pardon. For the servant who knows the will of his lord and does not do it shall be beaten severely (Luke XII).

All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth, because mercy itself has also been balanced on just scales. He shall teach the meek his ways: mercy and truth, and that they should love him with their whole heart, which is the true way. For it follows:

All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth. Mercy, because he redeemed us; and truth, because he will judge the wicked. The Lord is sweet and upright, because God has mercy on the one who confesses himself wretched. To those who seek his covenant. He shows mercy to those who seek the New Testament, through which he reconciled us to God the Father by his blood. And his testimonies: the prophets and apostles, through whose testimonies the Church has been gathered.

For your name’s sake, Lord, you will be gracious toward my sin. Not for the sake of my merits, but for the sake of your mercy. For it is great. My sin is great. “Great,” he says, “is the universal sin”; unless God deigns to erase it through baptism, it cannot be washed away in any other manner.

Who is the person who fears the Lord? He establishes a law for him on the way he has chosen. So that he may be directed toward the things he has chosen. The Lord declares something similar through Moses to the people, saying: “Behold, today I have set before your eyes fire and water, good and evil, life and death; choose life, and you shall live” (Deuteronomy XXX).

His soul shall dwell among good things, if he has chosen life. And his seed shall inherit the earth. Through works of righteousness he shall receive an inheritance in the land of the living. Or, his soul shall dwell among good things: that is, he shall hope in future rewards; and his seed shall possess the earth as an inheritance. His seed—his works—shall possess the earth, that is, eternal life.

The Lord is the strength of those who fear him. We are weak and feeble, but through him we are urged not to be shaken by the waves of this age. And his covenant shall be made manifest to them. This is the New Testament. The law that announced him, veiled in the letter, is made manifest in Christ.

My eyes are always toward the Lord (Ecclesiasticus II). The eyes of the heart, with the mind intent upon God, concerning which it is said: “The eyes of the wise are in his head.” For he himself will draw my feet out of the snare—that is, my understanding out of the snare of the devil, by whom I was previously captured through the pleasures of the world.

Look upon me and have mercy on me. “Look upon me” means “look upon me for aid”; “have mercy” because I am wretched. For I am the only one and poor. This pertains to Christ, because Christ is the only one without sin, as the prophet says: “He committed no sin” (Isaiah LIII). He became poor for us, as Paul says: “Although he was rich, he became poor, so that through his poverty we might become rich” (II Corinthians VIII). Or “solitary” means the Christian people. Yet he rightly calls himself solitary, because he is the only-begotten of the Father. Poor, born in the flesh, he became the sole price of the world.

For I am the only one and poor. So too Elijah remained alone (III Kings XVIII); and Jeremiah sat and wept alone, separated from evil people (Jeremiah XV). Hence David also says elsewhere: “He makes those of one manner dwell in a house” (Psalm LXVII).

The tribulations of my heart have multiplied. Through the Passion. Deliver me from my necessities. My necessities are that, as a human being, I should die for human beings, and therefore be rescued by you so that I may rise again.

See my lowliness, through which I assumed flesh, and my labor, by which I am subjected to death. Or otherwise: See my lowliness and my labor. The Church speaks to Christ. “Lowliness,” because sinners humble her; “labor,” in tribulation. And forgive all my sins: the sins of the people, which I took upon myself.

Look upon my enemies—the Jews, certainly—so that they may be confounded. Look upon my enemies, for they have multiplied. The voice of the Church concerning her persecutors. With wicked hatred they hated me. “Wicked hatred” is said in contrast to the just. For if they had not hated me, they certainly would not have condemned me to death.

Guard my soul and deliver me. The Church asks to be guarded and delivered from every evil. Let me not be confounded, because I have called upon you. “Into your hands I commend my spirit.” Let me not be confounded, neither here nor in the future, because I have called upon you.

The innocent and upright have clung to me. The innocent are those who have preserved purity of life from the beginning of their birth. Just as the head clings to the neck and the limbs are contained in the same body, so the Church has clung to Christ through righteousness, and her members are contained in the same body. “The innocent”: the successors of the apostles, or the other saints and upright people whose hearts did not become perverse after foreign gods. They have clung to me as I returned from the underworld. For I have waited for you, Lord. I have fulfilled your will, Father.

Deliver me, God of Israel, from all my tribulations. So that death may no longer rule me, as the Apostle says: “Know that Christ, rising from the dead, no longer dies; death shall no longer rule over him” (Romans VI). It must nevertheless be understood that the humility of the prayer refers not to divinity but to the humility of the assumed flesh. Let us, however, beseech the Lord that, while living without stain, we may deserve to be delivered from the anguish of the underworld. For I have waited for you, Lord. Deliver me, God of Israel. “Israel,” that is, of souls who see God. From all distresses, from all my tribulations.

## PSALM XXV

For the end, a psalm of David. This psalm bears witness concerning the human being and Christ, and contains the voice of the whole Church perfected in Christ.

Judge me, Lord, for I have entered in my innocence. So that your judgment may be mercy for me, because I walk along the way of innocence. Above it was said: “Judge me, Lord.” This is the voice of the Church to Christ. “Judge me,” not because she asks God for the future judgment, but for discernment, concerning which we read in another psalm: “Judge me, God, and discern my cause” (Psalm XLII). That is, may you not judge me in the future as the other sinners will be judged.

For I have entered in my innocence. The Church speaks on her own behalf. As though she were saying: I am ready to live innocently, because the Church has harmed no one and does not desire to harm anyone. “I have entered”: that is, among sinners, where she dwells until the end. And, hoping in the Lord, I shall not grow weak. Rather, I am strengthened in faith. “I shall not grow weak”: that is, among these sinners, because I hope in you, not in myself.

Test me, Lord, and try me. The Church asks to be tested so that she may know herself and be recognized by others as tested. Job was tested in this way, so that he might know himself and others might know him, as those kings did who visited him. Test me, Lord, in temptations; and try me, so that no sin may remain in me. Burn my kidneys and my heart. What “kidneys” signify is shown by “heart,” because your mercy is before my eyes. Thus he asks for judgment so that he may remember mercy. Burn my kidneys and my heart. Apply the Holy Spirit to my desires and thoughts, so that, burning away both, he may make me worthy. “Burn,” that is, with the fire of the Holy Spirit, concerning which he says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke XII).

For your mercy is before my eyes, so that I may be tested by this fire and not consumed. And I have pleased in your truth. In your Christ, so that I might please not in my falsehood but in your truth.

I did not sit in the council of vanity. I was not joined to those who, against you, my Christ, were engaged in a vain council. I did not sit in the council of vanity—that is, the Church did not sit in the council of those who are always thinking about earthly things. And with those who commit iniquity I will not enter. I did not place my hidden conscience among them.

I hated the assembly of the wicked: whether Jews or heretics. And with the impious I will not sit: I will not make a pact with them. And with the impious I will not sit—that is, they not only conceived their plans in words, but carried them out in deeds.

I will wash my hands among the innocent. In good works I will wash my hands, which were previously soiled by sins. “Hands” means works. He washes through tears, through baptism, and through repentance. And I will surround your altar, O Lord. I will embrace your sublime things, so that I may learn to praise you. “Altar” means faith. “I will surround” means with good works. Every saint has the Lord’s altar within himself: it is faith.

So that I may hear the voice of your praise and recount all your wonders. Once I have learned it, I will explain that miracle to others: how you either suffered or rose again for us. And I will recount all your wonders, your praise—that is, whatever good we do is reckoned as coming from God, while whatever evil we do comes from ourselves. God’s praise is perfect, whereas human praise is imperfect.

Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells. I have made my mind beautiful, so that it might be a dwelling worthy of you, in which, dwelling, you might glorify me with your glory. The Lord’s house is the Church. The priests and the dwelling of your glory are those in whom God dwells.

Do not destroy my soul with the impious—with those who through impiety betrayed the meek one—nor my life with men of blood. With those who, plotting deceitfully, shed your blood.

In whose hands are iniquities. That is, in their deeds. Their right hand is filled with gifts. He teaches that gifts must be rejected, condemning those who accept them—those who commit iniquity and regard the profit of this impiety as some sort of gain, as the traitor Judas himself did.

Their right hand is filled with gifts. They made a right hand for themselves out of the left, because the future life is called the right hand, and the present life the left. They preferred the left to the right. Thus it is said: “There is a gift from the tongue, and there is a gift from the hand, and there is a gift from service.” From the tongue: praise, that is, human favor. From the hand: earthly possessions. From service: service improperly rendered. But better is what the prophet says: “He who shakes his hands free from every gift dwells on high” (Isaiah 33).

But I have entered in my innocence. The Church speaks on behalf of the good, through the practice of a holy life, after former sins. “I have entered”: among sinners. Free me from tribulation. And have mercy on me, because I am miserable.

For my foot has stood on the straight path. My understanding is in Christ, because he himself is the way. “My foot has stood on the straight path,” so that they might not prevail against me: namely, in him through whom I began to approach you by the way of righteousness. In the churches I will bless the Lord. He speaks of the unity of the assembly. In the Church—not in hiding, but in the gatherings of the peoples—I bless you. I will proclaim that love by which you redeemed me with your blood, washed me in baptism, and, filling me with heavenly bread and sacred food, restored me to innocence and a better life.

# PSALM XXVI

For the end; a psalm of David, before he was anointed. David was anointed three times: once by his father Jesse in Bethlehem (1 Kings 16); a second time in Hebron (2 Kings 2); and a third time when he reigned over all Israel in Jerusalem (2 Kings 5). Consider, therefore, to which anointing this psalm most properly belongs. It should be known, however, that the words “before he was anointed” are not found in the Hebrew volumes. Of these three anointings, the middle one belongs to this psalm. David bears the figure of Christ, because Christ too was anointed at baptism, when the Holy Spirit came upon him in the form of a dove. David did not receive the kingdom at his first anointing; likewise Christ, according to the flesh, did not receive the kingdom at the time of his Passion, but only after he ascended.

The Lord is my illumination and my salvation; whom shall I fear? He whom the Lord always illuminates and saves does not fear being covered by any darkness. “The Lord is my illumination and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” The voice of the Church addressing Christ. In all the psalms the words are those of the Holy Spirit. Just as the eyes of the body are illuminated by another light, so the eyes of our heart are illuminated by the power of faith—that is, by Christ. Hence it is said: “He who illuminates every human being coming into this world” (John 10).

The Lord is the defender of my life; from whom shall I tremble? He is the faithful protection of the soul itself; therefore he does not fear the enemy. He is both defender and salvation, but “defender” is also called “helper.” “From whom shall I tremble?” The Church says: From no one—not from the devil, nor from a heretic, nor from a persecutor—so long as I have him as my defender.

When evildoers draw near against me, to eat my flesh. They approach in order to awaken my former sins and tear my body apart with ravenous teeth. Or: “When evildoers draw near against me, to eat my flesh,” that is, demons or persecutors. “Flesh” means the impulses of the flesh, because this is their food. Yet they are given flesh to eat—that is, the bodies of the saints for persecution. But the saints have consolation from the Lord, as he says in the Gospel: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10).

My enemies who trouble me—they themselves were weakened and fell. Because the Lord is my illumination, my enemies who trouble me—demons or persecutors—were themselves weakened and fell. They were weakened when Christ assumed our humanity.

If armies encamp against me, my heart will not fear. The Lord is a mighty warrior; he himself will fight for me. “If armies encamp against me”: that is, the strength of demons or persecutors. He says “armies” in accordance with the passage: “They encamped” (Numbers 33). “My heart will not fear.” The Church says this because of what the Lord said: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28).

If battle rises against me, in this I will hope. Even if battles are stirred up against me, I remain confident in these things, because God, who is my hope, can turn the unjust weapons of the enemies back upon their own mouths. “If battle rises against me”: these are the battles mentioned above, the warfare of demons. “I will hope,” says the Church, “in your help and your defense.”

One thing I asked of the Lord; this I will seek. Some think that “one” refers to charity or grace, or certainly to a single petition, since *ahath*, the Hebrew word, means simply “one” in the neuter gender and should be read: “One thing I asked of the Lord”—that is, the Lord himself. “Him I will seek,” that is, the Lord himself.

That I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life. “In the house of the Lord”: in perpetual life. Although the Church is called a house here, it is not properly but only conventionally so called. Hence it says: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord” (Psalm 83).

That I may see the will of the Lord—that is, the love of God—as in the passage: “We shall see him as he is” (John 3), though here it is through a mirror.

“One thing I asked of the Lord; this I will seek.” Let us see what the one petition is: “That I may dwell,” he says, “in the house of the Lord all the days of my life”—so that in this mortal life I may be made a holy temple in which God may deign to dwell. And that I may visit his temple. May I become a participant with those who, placed on earth, live a heavenly life. And may I be protected in his holy temple—that is, may I have protection from the one mentioned above.

For he hid me in his tabernacle. In it he dwells with me through faith, so that the storms of temptations may not confront me. The tabernacle of divinity is Christ’s humanity. He hid the Church in his tabernacle, because Christ is our head and we are his members. Therefore he hid the Church with himself, as it is said: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3).

In the day of evils. Are the days themselves evil? No, but they are called evil because of our deeds, as Paul says: “Because the days are evil” (Ephesians 5). He speaks of these present days. Although the head is above, the members are still below until the end. I also think this is signified when he alone was on the mountain while the boat was tossed by waves on the sea, and therefore they needed his protection (Matthew 8).

“In the day of evils”: in the prosperity of those who lie in wait. He protected me in the hidden place of his tabernacle: in the heart that believes unto righteousness.

On a rock he exalted me. In Christ he exalted me through faith. The rock is Christ, as Paul says: “The rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10). “On a rock he exalted me”: in himself, who is the firm rock and truest foundation.

And now he has exalted my head above my enemies. “Now,” in the present time. “Above my enemies”—that is, above those mentioned earlier—our head, which is Christ, has been exalted above all the enemies of the Church. Or: “He has exalted my head above my enemies,” above the carnal movements that often humbled me, preventing me from contemplating heavenly things.

I will go around and sacrifice in his tabernacle a sacrifice of jubilation. “I will go around”: I will exercise myself in God’s creatures, contemplating the world that believes in Christ. When someone observes God’s creatures—heaven and earth, or the sea with its adornments—he finds what he may offer to God, namely, praise. “I will go around”: throughout the four regions of the world I will seek examples of the saints, and there God’s praise is found.

And I will sacrifice in his tabernacle a sacrifice of acclamation. I will joyfully proclaim that he endured humiliation for us for a time, because he delights in such sacrifices. A sacrifice of jubilation—that is, of proclamation. “Jubilus” is what cannot express the greatness of God’s praise through letters, syllables, or words.

A “hostia,” or sacrificial victim, is divided into parts; its blood is poured around the altar, and the victim itself is burned outside. “Sacrifice” refers to wine and oil, and to the middle portion of an animal; “holocaust” is what is wholly burned; and “victim” refers to the animal before it is killed. Hence Paul says: “A living sacrifice” (Romans 12).

I will sing and make a psalm to the Lord. “I will sing”: I will proclaim. “I will make a psalm”: I will fulfill it in action; or I will sing spiritual praises with an expanded mind.

Hear, O Lord, my voice, with which I cried to you; have mercy on me and hear me. Through the cry of the inner person I beseech you to hear me.

My heart said to you, “My face has sought you”; your face, O Lord, I will seek. Rightly does the heart of the just seek the face of the living God, because it trusts that it can see him. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5). “My face has sought your face”: that is, my Church has sought your face—that is, your presence.

Do not turn your face away from me. Elsewhere he says: “Turn your face away from my sins” (Psalm 50). This too must be prayed. But here he says: “Do not turn your face away”—that is, do not leave me to my own will, as it is said: “God handed them over to a reprobate mind” (Romans 1), that is, he permitted it.

Do not turn away in anger from your servant. If a servant offends an earthly master, he is filled with trembling and fear; how much more so a human being who offends the heavenly God? Therefore the Church asks that he correct her here and look upon her; that he not depart from her in anger, but that she may do those things from which he does not turn away, and that he may look upon her with a propitious face.

Be my helper, O Lord; do not abandon me, nor despise me, my God and savior. “Helper” concerns the present. “Be” pertains both to the present and to the future. “Do not abandon me”: neither here nor in the future. “Nor despise me, my God and savior.” Christ is our savior, and the Church asks not to be despised by him—that is, not to commit the sin through which she would be despised by God.

“Do not abandon me”: while I crucify my flesh with its vices and desires. “Nor despise me, my God and savior”: for although I am mortal, I seek heavenly things.

For my father and my mother abandoned me. The father is the devil; the mother is Babylon, or paganism. Before Christ came into the world, they were our parents. Now our father is God, and our mother is the heavenly Jerusalem, as Paul says: “Jerusalem is our mother” (Galatians 4).

“For my father and my mother abandoned me, but the Lord took me up.” I left the kingdom of the world and the cities of this age that gave me birth and promised transient things; taken up by you, I have been abandoned by them.

“For my father and my mother abandoned me.” This may also be understood simply of David, who, the youngest among his brothers and despised by his parents, was chosen by God through Samuel. More generally, the love of parents for their children ends with death; the love of God grows with time.

Establish a law for me, O Lord. The law is yourself, because he himself is the law. “In your way”: that is, in your commandments. What are those commandments? Not to turn aside to the right or to the left, and not to look back, as in the passage: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of heaven” (Luke 9, 6). And again: “Remember Lot’s wife” (Luke 17). And: “Seek the things that are above, not the things that are on earth.”

“Establish a law for me, O Lord, in your way, and guide me on a straight path.” May I not turn aside to the right or the left, but, following your commandments and walking the royal road, may I enter the promised land. “Because of my enemies”: carnal impulses, demons, heretics, and persecutors.

Do not hand me over to the souls of those who persecute me, so that their soul may not be satisfied with the adversities that befall me.

For unjust witnesses have risen against me, and iniquity has lied to itself. They rose against me, speaking falsehood; but because I trusted in you, they were destroyed in their own lie.

“For unjust witnesses have risen against me.” Unjust witnesses rose against Christ when the Jews said: “He said, ‘Destroy this temple, and in three days I will rebuild it’” (Matthew 26). Or the adversaries speak thus against the Church.

“And iniquity has lied to itself”: they lied to themselves, not to me, because each person’s vice returns upon its own author. “And iniquity has lied to itself.” Wicked witnesses, in lying against others, lie to themselves while preparing punishments for themselves, thinking that God will not avenge lies.

I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living. The voice of the Church. “In the land of the living,” because we have our pledge above, and that pledge is Christ. He received from our earth a mortal body, and from him we received hope and faith. Believing through hope and faith, we shall arrive in the land of the living, where the saints will receive the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven.

Wait for the Lord. That is, until the end of the age patiently endure for Christ whatever may come upon you. [The reading *accesserit* is uncertain; perhaps *acciderit*, “may befall you.”]

Act manfully. That is, act courageously, as the Angel said to Joshua: “Be strong and courageous” (Joshua 1). And let your heart be strengthened—that is, your soul. And wait for the Lord—that is, endure for the Lord.

Here the prophet exhorts the faithful person who has spoken up to this point, saying: First wait, so that you may be strengthened by God against the struggles of the world. Then wait, so that, victorious, you may be crowned by the same Lord, because no one will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully. Let us, however, beseech the Lord that, while he strengthens us, we may manfully endure the storms of the world’s waves and wait in faith until he comes to grant what he has deigned to promise.

# PSALM XXVII

A psalm of David. The psalm bears the voice of the mediator himself, speaking to the Father amid the conflict of the Passion. The things wished against the enemies are not expressions of malice, but the prophetic declaration of what is impending for them because of their evils. Or it is the voice of the assumed human being in the divinity: Jesus cried out on the cross and said, “Eli, Eli.”

To you, O Lord, I cried; my God. So that you may glorify me with that glory which I had with you before the world existed, because now I have assumed humanity. Do not be silent toward me, but speak, because I share eternity with you. “Do not be silent toward me”: that is, do not abandon me.

And I will be like those who descend into the pit. That is, into the misery of this life. For if divinity had departed from him, he would have been like us in misery. “If you are silent, I will be like those who perish”; nevertheless, if you remain silent, you will not be known.

Hear the voice of my supplication when I pray to you. Christ prayed on the cross for the whole world, for the Jews, and for the apostles.

When I lift up my hands toward your holy temple. “I lift up my hands”: I stretched them out on the cross. “Toward the holy temple”: I stretched them out for this purpose, so that I might prepare a temple for you—that is, the body of the Church.

And I will be like those who descend into the pit. The pit signifies hell, namely, the place of those who are held in custody. Elsewhere too it is written: “As far as the captive woman who was in the pit” (Exodus 12).

Hear the voice of my supplication when I pray to you, when I lift up my hands toward your holy temple—that is, on the cross, for those who believe, who are to become your temple.

Do not hand me over together with sinners. Sinners: the thieves among whom he was hanging, as the prophet says: “He was reckoned among the wicked” (Isaiah 53). Do not destroy me with those who work iniquity. That is, on the day of judgment, with these thieves or other evil persons. This applies both to Christ and to the Church, so that I may not perish in this way, receiving death as the workers of iniquity do.

With those who speak peace with their neighbor, but evil is in their hearts, and so forth. The Jews spoke peace with Christ, saying: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and that you have come from God as a teacher, and teach the way of God in truth” (Matthew 22). But evil was in their hearts when they asked him: “Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar or not?” (Mark 12).

Give them according to their works. Let those who do not understand you through benefits understand through punishments, so that, doing evil, they may be unable to find your good things. The prophet does not say this as a wish, but as a prediction, as though he had said: You are going to give them vengeance on the day of judgment.

And according to the wickedness of their devices, and so forth. Their aims are directed toward harming me and laying traps of temptation; therefore it is just that they should fail through these same things. Repay them their recompense. For they rendered evil for good, because they did not understand you.

For they did not understand the works of the Lord, and so forth. May the engines of war that are raised against my Church prevail nothing.

Blessed is the Lord, the Father, because he has heard the voice of my supplication. He answers before the Passion: “I have glorified, and I will glorify again” (John 12).

The Lord is my helper: in the Passion. And my protector: in death. And in him my heart hoped: humanity in divinity. And I was helped: in tribulation, so that I might rise again.

And my flesh blossomed anew. Christ’s flesh blossomed anew in the resurrection. Or: “My flesh blossomed anew”—the apostles blossomed anew, because after their denial they came to faith. “My flesh blossomed anew,” emerging incorrupt from the tomb.

“My flesh blossomed anew.” In place of “flesh,” Theodotion interpreted “heart.” Alternatively: We have risen together with Christ. Concerning the resurrection it is said: “Your bones shall spring up like grass” (Isaiah 66).

And by my will I will confess to him. To the Father, as in the passage: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to infants” (Matthew 11). And the Church confesses to Christ, as in the passage: “Shepherding the flock, not under compulsion but willingly” (1 Peter 5); and again: “Willingly I will sacrifice to you, and I will confess to your name” (Psalm 53). “By my will I will confess to him,” not out of necessity. I will confess to you through baptism.

The Lord is the strength of his people: of the Christian people. And he is the protector of the salvations of his Christ. Whoever has been baptized in Christ is himself also called Christ.

It should be known that this psalm too, except for one letter, is written in the Hebrew volumes according to the order of the letters.

“Protector”: that is, defender. “Of the salvations of his Christ”: he speaks in the plural, because the divinity of Christ guards all his virtues.

Save your people, O Lord—that is, the Christian people. Or: Save your people, O Lord, whom I redeemed by my death. And bless your inheritance, which you gathered in the Church through the mystery of my body and blood. Christ’s inheritance is his Church, of which he said: “I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Isaiah 2).

And rule them and lift them up forever. “Rule them,” as though he said: You rule them, not the devil or sin. “And lift them up forever”: that is, defend them forever, in eternal life.

You, O Lord, rule us and raise us up, because we are your people, so that in this life you may lift us, who do what pleases you, from mortality into immortality—that is, raise us up in the heavenly places, where we shall reign with your saints.

# PSALM XXVIII

For the end; a psalm of David, at the completion of the tabernacle. When the ark was brought back from captivity among the Philistines—after they had suffered many evils because of it—it was set down at Shiloh, and David built a tabernacle for it, in which he exhorted the people to offer sacrifices to God (1 Kings 4, 5, and following).

David most clearly bears the figure of Christ, and the ark the figure of the Church. Just as David brought the ark back from captivity, so Christ brought back the ark—that is, the holy Church—from captivity, that is, from the power of the devil. The psalm therefore contains the voice of the prophet speaking about the perfection of the Church gathered in this age.

Bring to the Lord, sons of God, you who by grace have been called to adoption as sons. The voice of Christ admonishes the preachers: Bring preaching and example, or faith and works.

Bring to the Lord the sons of rams, whom the apostles, leaders of the flocks, begot through the Gospel. The apostles are called rams. Rams have two horns on their heads, and the holy apostles had two horns—that is, they preached the two Testaments. The sons of rams are the successors of the apostles, whom they begot through the word of preaching.

The completion of the tabernacle, according to its meaning, is the perfection of the Church joined together from Jews and Gentiles here in the present age.

Bring glory and honor to the Lord, so that through your works the eternal God may be glorified through word and example. Hence it says: “They honored and glorified.” They beget sons, as we said, through preaching, as Paul said: “Through the Gospel I begot you” (1 Corinthians 4). This is the glory and honor of God.

Bring glory to the Lord’s name. Through you may his glorious name become known everywhere. The Father’s name is the Son; the glory of Christ is the Church. Adore the Lord in his holy court. Expand your heart in perfect holiness, in which God may dwell—that is, in the Church or in the conscience, where each person ought to adore him.

The voice of the Lord: the Lord’s preaching. Upon the waters: upon the peoples, as in the passage: “Many waters, many peoples” (Revelation 17). Or: “The voice of the Lord upon the waters,” that is, in baptism, upon Christ, as he says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3). “Upon the waters”: because the people who were present there heard the voice. Or “upon the waters,” as he said to the apostles: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28).

The God of majesty: the God of power. The Lord thundered over the many waters. From the tabernacle of the assumed body he proclaimed conversion terrifyingly to the peoples, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matthew 3). Just as thunder proceeds from a cloud, so Christ thundered from a cloud—that is, from his body—when he said: “Repent.”

The voice of the Lord in power. It became powerful among believers when he said: “Lazarus, come out” (John 11). Or “in power”: by the power through which he speaks in each saint.

The voice of the Lord in magnificence. When he is magnified through the works of the saints. Magnificence is spread throughout the churches.

The voice of the Lord breaking cedars. Cedars are called all those who are lofty and exalted, or proud. He will break them either through repentance or by vengeance on the day of judgment. “Cedars”: all the proud. “Behold, the axe is laid at the roots of the trees.” “Breaking cedars”: humbling the proud.

It should be known that “cedar,” like “unicorn,” has two interpretations: in the good sense it signifies the righteous; in the bad sense, sinners and the proud. And the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon. Through repentance he will crush their arrogance and shatter it, choosing things that are lowly in order to crush and confound the strong.

And he will break them like the calves of Lebanon, striking their branches and shoots with his hooves. For this the Hebrew has: “and the calf of Lebanon.” Once their pride and insolence have been cut down, he brings them to imitate his humanity, because he was sacrificed like a calf. This is the fattened calf that was killed: Christ, for the salvation of the world.

Just as a calf breaks tender branches with its horns, so Christ broke the Jews. Hence he said: “Now the axe is laid at the roots of the trees” (Matthew 3).

And the beloved one, like the son of unicorns. The beloved Son of God became, through the assumption of the body, the son of the Jews, and he crushed those who, through singular pride, attempted to raise up their own righteousness. Christ is the son of the Jews because according to the flesh he was from their stock. The Jews are called unicorns because of the one law they possessed, through which they lifted themselves up in pride.

The voice of the Lord cutting through the flame of fire. John, preaching repentance in the desert, extinguished the whole burning of Gehenna. “Cutting through,” that is, dividing the raging anger of the persecutors: while some said, “This is the Christ,” and others said, “No, but he misleads the crowd” (John 7). Cutting off this fury, he drew believers into his love but left unbelievers behind.

After the flame came a sound; so too after preaching came persecution. “The voice of the Lord cutting through”: that is, his help among the persecutors, because he assists his saints.

“Cutting through the flame”: the flame of the idol, where the three boys were. Or daily in each one of us he cuts through the flame of lust by confession and the grace of the Holy Spirit—that is, through the priest’s prayer he causes it to cease, just as we read that God did through Aaron in the desert (Numbers 16).

The voice of the Lord shaking the desert. The soul that had been deserted, occupied by the vices that previously possessed it, will be moved by the words of repentance, so that, when the vices depart from it, it may become habitable for God.

“The voice of the Lord shaking the desert”: moving deserted nations to faith, nations in which no furrow of preaching had been laid for receiving the word of God. Or the nations that had been deserted were converted from unbelief to faith through the word of preaching.

And the Lord will shake the desert of Kadesh. Then the holy words of the Law will be celebrated in this wilderness of the world, though previously they were not understood by the Jews, because Kadesh is interpreted as “Holy.”

Or otherwise: “The shaking of the moth.” He rightly compared them to a moth, because just as a moth eats clothing, so their conscience was eating them. It is called “the shaking of the moth” because he moved them from their wicked conscience to the faith of the Church.

The voice of the Lord preparing the stags. Some wish the stags to be understood as conquerors of poisonous tongues in the Church. The stags are preachers. He prepared them when he sent them to preach. Stags cross over and trample thorns or serpents; likewise the preachers pass through the poisons of the devil and the thorns of sins and flee to higher things—that is, to the contemplative life.

And he will reveal the dense places. Through the Holy Spirit he disclosed the obscure things of the divine Scriptures and the heavenly mysteries. Hence those two to whom he appeared in the Gospel said: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24).

And in his temple—that is, in the Church. All will say, “Glory.” They praise the splendor of God. Or: “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.”

The Lord makes the flood dwell. God does not possess dry land. At the same time, attend to the force of the word: he did not say “waters,” but “flood,” in order to show the abundance of spiritual grace, protecting the saints from the waves of this age as Noah’s ark did. Now too the flood dwells in the conscience through the abundance of the Holy Spirit, through whom sins are wiped away.

And the Lord will sit as king forever. In the churches or in the saints, who have become his seats; or the humanity of Christ at the right hand of God the Father. The saints are called kings because they rule themselves.

The Lord will give strength to his people: the strength of faith. To his people, the Christian people, fighting against the storms and tempests of this world. And he will bless his people with peace. He will bless the Christian people both here and in the future, when he will say: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matthew 25).

“With peace”: in himself, because he himself is our peace, who made both one (Ephesians 2). The true peace, Christ the Lord, blesses us in himself; we are the ecclesiastical people.

# PSALM XXIX

A psalm of song at the dedication of David’s house. “A psalm of song”: praise accompanied by works. “The dedication of David’s house” signifies the resurrection of the Savior, in which all the bodies of life are dedicated.

David bears the figure of Christ. David’s house is Christ’s house—that is, humanity, the house of divinity. He built the house when he assumed the humanity of flesh. He dedicated it when he caused him to rise from the dead. Even now David’s house, that is, Christ’s house, is being built: the Church is being built until the end, but it will be dedicated at the resurrection, when it is to receive immortality.

It contains the voice of our Redeemer, who, through the resurrection of his body, dedicated to his name the Church—which is the mother of all—that he had acquired.

I will exalt you, O Lord, because you have taken me up. I will glorify you on high, Father, because you have taken me up from death. “I will exalt you, O Lord”: the voice of Christ to the Father, and the voice of the Church to Christ. “I will exalt you”: I will praise you. “Because you have taken me up”: Christ to the right hand of the Father. And Christ took up the Church when he assumed the humanity of flesh.

And you did not delight my enemies over me, so that they might rejoice in my destruction. How does he say, “You did not delight my enemies,” when the Jews crucified Christ, spat upon him, and scourged him, and persecutors rejoice over the Church when they persecute it?

But the Jews did not rejoice over Christ, because they could not extinguish him as they wished. Here, however, this should not be understood of human beings but of demons, because they began to rejoice when they thought that he would be led with the thieves into hell, just as he allowed himself to be led by the same tempter onto the mountain (Luke 4). But the demons did not rejoice, because then he bound both their prince and his subjects.

Nor will they rejoice over the Church on the day of judgment, when the saints will say: “Where, O death, is your sting? Where, O death, is your victory? Death has been swallowed up in victory” (1 Corinthians 15)—that is, death has been destroyed in the victory of the saints.

Lord my God, I cried to you, and you healed me. “Lord my God”: the prayer of Christ or of the Church. “You healed me”: you caused me to rise again, so that the body subject to mortality would not be corrupted by death.

You brought my soul back from the underworld: God brought Christ’s soul, together with the souls of the other saints, back from hell. He declares himself to have been raised by the Father, as the Apostle says: “Whoever believes that God raised him from the dead will be saved” (Romans 4).

You saved me from those who descend into the pit. That is, from the misery of this present life. Or from the pit of hell, where the souls of sinners are, so that I would not, like them, fall headlong into death. Seeing this immeasurable miracle, the prophet rejoices and says:

Sing psalms to the Lord, his saints, and so forth. He sanctified you by remembering you, calling you to knowledge of his name. “Sing psalms to the Lord, his saints.” The prophet exhorts the saints to praise the one by whom they were saved.

And confess to the memory of his holiness. “Memory”: so that you may remember his benefits, how he came to redeem you from sin.

For there is anger in his indignation, and life in his will. This does not mean that anger or indignation exists in God, but that there is just vengeance. God’s indignation occurred when Adam sinned. “Anger” means just vengeance, when he cast him from paradise.

“And life is in his will”: just as just vengeance came upon Adam through God, so through him—that is, through God—life was restored when he assumed the humanity of flesh.

“For there is anger in his indignation,” when he avenges himself upon the impious. “And life is in his will”: so that whoever does his will may remain forever.

At evening weeping will linger. When everything was covered in darkness during his Passion, the apostles remained in weeping and lamentation. And in the morning, joy. He prefigured the future glory of the Lord, which dawned beforehand in his morning resurrection. At evening weeping will linger, and in the morning, joy. “Evening” is said of the time after midday: after midday Adam heard the voice of the Lord walking in the paradise, and, trembling because he had transgressed the covenant, hid himself beneath the leaves of a tree. “Evening” is understood as this entire present life, because, on account of Adam’s sin, everyone groans until the end of the age. Weeping, because a person weeps when he remembers the good things of paradise that he lost in Adam. And in the morning, joy—that is, in the resurrection, when you will restore all together to freedom. Or, “evening,” when Mary and the apostles were weeping during the Lord’s Passion; and “morning, joy,” when he rose again, as it was said to the women: “Go and tell my brothers to go to Galilee; there they will see me” (Matt. 28). And the women said to the apostles: “We have seen the Lord, and this is what he said to us” (John 20). At evening weeping will linger, and in the morning joy. This may be understood both of the time of the Passion, as above, and of the resurrection and the consummation of the age.

But I said in my abundance: I shall not be moved forever. The redeemed people say this: “Now, satisfied by you, I suffer no lack; nor, fixed upon you, am I shaken.” But I said in my abundance: I shall not be moved forever. This is Adam’s voice in paradise, because he thought that he would remain there without end. And while he was thinking in this way, although God had given him such great blessings, he began to consider why God had commanded him not to touch the forbidden fruit. “But this,” he said, “I wish to test.” And he [Al. “to him”] touched it and tested it—and was cast out.

Lord, in your favor you granted strength to my beauty. [Col. 0904D] This too is Adam’s voice after he had been cast out of paradise because of his fault. Then he understood that the wisdom of light had departed from him, and that he had been placed by God in paradise, the place of abundance, not by himself. You turned your face away from me, and I became troubled. God then turned his face away from Adam, when he sinned. And he became troubled when he was cast out of paradise under the curse. So too every person is troubled when he is distressed by his own sins.

Or otherwise: Lord, in your favor, and not through my own doing, you granted strength to my beauty, to the body you assumed, so that I might know you. You turned your face away from me when I sinned, and I became troubled. For I did not yet know the light of your truth.

[Col. 0905A] To you, Lord, I shall cry out, and to my God I shall plead. Christ the Lord says this, interceding with the Father on behalf of the redeemed people. Christ cried out on the cross, and the Church in persecution.

What profit is there in my blood, when I descend into corruption? If I do not rise again: for, since my blood has been poured out, I shall rise, and there will be profit, so that by my resurrection I may acquire all the nations. Christ’s humanity speaks to the Father, as though it had said: “There is no profit in my having shed my blood unless I rise from the dead.”

Or, what profit is there in my blood—that is, in my people? There is no profit in the Jews, because they do not believe, except merely in the human being. They not only failed to believe, but also opened his side.

[Col. 0905B] Will dust confess to you? [Al. “is silent to you.”] The crowd of impious people, which still, like dust, is moved by every wind of doctrine, will not be justified if I do not rise again. If I do not rise again, dust will not confess to you. “Dust,” that is, the impious or the unfruitful. Or will it proclaim your truth? That is, your Christ—as though he said: “If I do not rise again, they will not proclaim him.”

The Lord heard, and had mercy on me. The Lord, God the Father, heard and had mercy on me. This is Christ’s voice, because he caused me to rise from the dead. The Lord became my helper. My defender, who made me the firstborn from the dead.

You turned my mourning into joy. When I said: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death.” Into joy for me. When, rising again, I said: “Go, tell my brothers to go to Galilee; there they will see me.” But these words are spoken both by Christ and by the Church: her mourning, when the Lord rose again, was turned into joy, and thereafter, cleansed by the blood of the Lamb, she says with the Lord and to the Lord:

You tore apart my sackcloth. The covering of my sins, because sackcloth and haircloth belong to sinners. Thus, when he says: “You tore apart my sackcloth,” and elsewhere says: “I put on sackcloth and humbled my soul with fasting” (Ps. 4), Christ indeed did not use that garment. What is Christ’s sackcloth except the mortality he assumed from us? This sackcloth was torn apart when he rose again and became immortal. And although he had sackcloth, he did not have the function of sackcloth—that is, sin—of which it is written: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (Isa. 53). We, therefore, must put on sackcloth and haircloth, because we have had the function of sackcloth—that is, sin. You girded me with joy. That is, with the joy of the resurrection, whether referring to Christ or to the Church in the future: clothing me with the first robe of immortality through your resurrection.

So that my glory may sing to you. [Al. “may sing.”] In those who have believed in the glory of the resurrection. And I may not be pierced. By the goads of sins. Nor Christ, because he had no sin.

Lord my God, forever I shall confess to you. [Col. 0906A] That is, I shall praise you without end. In these people, as I have already said, I shall sing to you and confess you—those who were gathered into me through my resurrection.
