For everything that is said humbly of Christ in this psalm should be referred more to the assumption of the body than to the power of the Godhead.

We too humbly beseech you: may the Lord turn our mourning into joy, the burden of our crimes having been removed, and, gladdened by the mystery of his resurrection, may he graciously lift us into heaven—for our sake he graciously descended into hell.

## PSALM XXX

For the end; a psalm of David, etc. This psalm initially contains the voice of the Mediator himself; then, in the person of the prophet, the voice of the people redeemed by his blood, giving thanks, is introduced. Thus the Redeemer says [Col. 0906B] to the Father:

In you, Lord, I have hoped; I shall not be confounded forever. In you, Father, is the strengthening of my hope, while adversaries insult or mock me as though I were like other human beings. Or the prophet, speaking in the person of the Church, says: “I shall not be confounded,” because I rightly confess the end of the Trinity. In you, Lord, I have hoped. In you, not in myself. I shall not be confounded forever, because those who confess him fully will not be confounded, either here or in the future.

And in your justice deliver me and rescue me. From the pit that they prepared for my soul. For unless we are justified by God, we cannot be justified by ourselves. Hence it is written: “Whoever justifies himself condemns himself” (Job 9). Hence Paul also says of certain people: “Seeking to establish their own justice, they have not submitted to the justice of God” (Rom. 10).

Incline your ear to me. The Church’s voice to Christ. God’s kindness is understood by “ear.” Christ inclines his ear when he graciously consents to hear. Or God inclined his ear when he sent his Word and heard us in the world; and he inclined it so far that he wrote our sins with his finger on the ground. Hasten to rescue me. “Hasten,” that is, make haste, to rescue me. Holy Church desires to be freed from the body, as Paul says: “I desire to depart and be with Christ” (Phil. 1).

Be my protecting God. The Church’s voice. A protecting God, a defending God, because there are many harmful gods who do no good. Hence Paul says: “Indeed, there are many gods and many lords; yet for us there is one God, one faith, one baptism” (1 Cor. 8). Be my protecting God, as one who is near. And be a house of refuge for me, so that you may save me. For in the storm of persecution the Church has refuge in God. Save me from sinners. The house of refuge is he himself, in whom the Father dwells. Many wish to flee from God’s presence, but they cannot escape, as the prophet says: “And from your face, where shall I flee?” (Ps. 138). But we, the Church says, have refuge together in the house—that is, in him who is God.

For you are my strength and my refuge. To sustain those who rage against me. Or, the strength of faith; and you are my refuge. He says “my refuge,” because the Church has refuge in Christ, as the prophet says: “Lord, you have become our refuge” (Ps. 89). For your name’s sake you will lead me out. So that I may make this known to the nations who will believe. For your name’s sake you will be my leader. When I do anything good, the Lord’s name is glorified through it.

And you will nourish me. Gathering the saints little by little, you lead out your Church, which is founded in me. And you will nourish me. He nourished the Church when he assumed our flesh. Hence Paul also says: “No one ever hates his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it” (Eph. 5). And he nourished us so that we might be strong.

And you will lead me out of the snare that they hid for me. A snare is called a capture, because as long as you are on the way—that is, in Christ—you do not fear falling into a snare; snares are set beside the road. The way is Christ, as he himself says: “I am the way” (John 14). And if you are on the way—that is, in Christ—you do not fear falling into the devil’s snare, because every snare comes from him.

For you are my protector: into your hands I commend my spirit. Christ’s voice to the Father in the Passion, when he commended his soul and said: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46). What is commended is received safely. And he himself said: “I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10).

You are my protector. The Church’s voice. Into your hands I commend my spirit—that is, I commend my soul into your power. The Church received this example from Christ. [Col. 0907C] Saint Stephen did this too; and the saints pray in this way when they depart from the body, as in: “They commend their souls to a faithful Creator in good works.” This the Lord said while hanging on the cross: that he had commended his spirit into the Father’s hands, soon to receive it again when the Father raised him.

Now let the people redeemed by the blood of the Lamb say: You redeemed me, Lord, God of truth. You who are truth and life, because God does not lie about what he promised. Just as he promised through his servants the prophets, so he also came and redeemed us by his blood. Hence Paul says: “You were bought with a great price” (1 Cor. 6).

You have hated all who observe vanity, to no purpose. He says “to no purpose,” not because God hates anyone. Far be it from us to think this. But those who love only this present life and despise heavenly things, vainly hoping in the blessedness of the deceptive world—God is said to hate them. This does not mean that hatred, as I said, exists in God; rather, God is said to hate those who act in this way, that is, to reject them, because God rejects them.

But I have hoped in you, Lord. The Church’s voice: “Not in myself, but in you I have hoped and hope, awaiting your resurrection.” I shall exult and rejoice in your mercy. For what shall I exult, and for what shall I rejoice? For what follows.

For you looked upon my humility. I shall exult in body; I shall rejoice in mind. He looked upon it when he assumed flesh, because the Church was contemptible, captive, and despised. I shall exult and rejoice in your mercy [Col. 0908A] because of the benefit of such great compassion, by which you redeemed me through your death: for you looked upon my humility, placed in that hope through which invisible things are desired.

You saved my soul from necessities. The body has many necessities: eating, drinking, sleeping, and whatever else must necessarily be done. But the soul has one necessity alone: eternal life. God saved the soul from its necessity because he gave it eternal life, which is its necessity. Therefore you saved from the necessities of perpetual death my soul, which was bound to you by love.

And you did not shut me into the hands of the enemy. Those are shut into the enemy’s hands who persevere in their sins. But I, the Church says, shall not be shut in, because I do not wish to persevere in evil. You set my feet in a spacious place. You enlarged the unity of the Church throughout the whole world. How does he say “in a place”? Is God perhaps local? He is both local and nonlocal. He is local for those who come to him, and nonlocal because he is everywhere; yet he is found in a place by those who seek him purely. As in: “And the place where they were sitting was shaken” (Acts 4). In a spacious place: my feet—that is, the holy preachers who carry the word of preaching throughout the whole world; or, into the Church, which through your resurrection you enlarged into the breadth of freedom.

Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am afflicted. Have mercy on me—as though he said: “Show mercy toward me, for I am afflicted.” This is the voice of those who are afflicted by any tribulation. Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am afflicted. [Col. 0908C] No longer fearing death, but fearing the persecution of vices. My eye was troubled in anger. The Church is troubled by vices and sins, both her own and those of others. But we must pray that anger not be turned into hatred, and that a beam not be made from a splinter. Or the eye is troubled by the future judgment. My eye was troubled in anger—the eye with which I perceived you in my mind. My soul, with which I loved you. And my belly, with which I remembered you. All these were troubled because of former offenses.

For my life has failed in sorrow. It is in sorrow because the Church cannot correct the wicked or separate the wicked from the saints until the end. Hence the Lord said: “Let both grow until the harvest, and at harvest time I shall say to the reapers: Gather first the weeds and bind them into bundles to burn” (Matt. 13). My life and my years are in groaning. As long as each person is here in the present life, he has groaning and weeping: For my life has failed in sorrow, and my years in groaning, while I suffer persecution for your name. The present life fails because my times are limited, whereas I confess eternity.

My strength has grown weak in poverty. The Church’s voice. The Church has grown weak among wicked people, among whom she dwells in the present life, because sinners are many and saints are few. Or otherwise: My strength has grown weak in poverty—the health of this body amid the torments of sufferings.

And my bones have been troubled. Certainly, my strength. The bones are the strong saints; or the bones are the virtues of the Church or of the saints. They have been troubled by that one. Hence above he says, in accordance with the Apostle: “We know that the whole creation groans together; and not only it, but we ourselves groan within ourselves” (Rom. 8).

I have become a reproach to all my enemies. To those who persecute me on account of your name. I have become a reproach to my neighbors. The voice both of Christ and of the Church. The Jews spoke many reproaches against the Lord; heretics and persecutors speak them against the Church. And to my neighbors exceedingly. To those who draw near in order to believe. And a terror to my acquaintances. Because my friends, out of fear of the enemies, withdrew far from me. The whole psalm may be understood both of David according to the historical account and of the Lord according to prophecy. Exceedingly, and a terror to my acquaintances—that is, to the apostles, who were afraid during the Passion. Or “acquaintances” means wicked Christians, who say that they believe in God but deny him by their works and despise the life of the saints. They are called “neighbors” on account of faith, and “acquaintances” on account of their Christianity.

Those who saw me fled outside from me. That is, the apostles, who saw Christ seized during the Passion and, leaving him, fled. Or the Jews flee from the sacraments of the Church’s mystery, that is, from Christ’s body and blood. All who saw me fled outside from me: not understanding my inner hope, for which I suffer, they fled toward outward, visible things.

I was forgotten, like a dead man, from their hearts. They forgot me in their hearts, as though I had already died. I was forgotten, like a dead man, from their hearts. That is, the Jews regarded Christ as a dead man, as nothing.

And I have become like a lost vessel. The Jews regarded Christ as a lost vessel—that is, a dead man in his sin. So the saints are regarded among heretics, like a lost man. For I heard the reproach of many. That is, Christ’s reproach from the Jews, and the Church’s from the heretics. Of those dwelling around. That is, around Christ and around the Church, whom those mentioned above surrounded. For I heard the reproach of many dwelling around. They were reproaching me, placed in the pilgrimage of this earth, following the circuit of the ages and unwilling to return to the eternal homeland.

[Col. 0909D] While they gathered together against me, they conspired to take my soul. The persecutors gathered and formed a plan to seize my soul, in order to compel me to agree with them in the crimes of death. To take my soul—that is, the Jews sought Christ’s soul, and the heretics the Church’s. They devised evil plans, not good ones. They conspired to seek and take Christ’s soul, the Jews, and the Church’s soul, the heretics.

But I have hoped in you, Lord; I said: You are my God. You alone are strong enough to deliver. Or the Church’s voice: I have hoped in you. In you, not in myself. Sinners too say: “I have hoped in you.” But the saints possess both faith and works. Sinners hope in God and do not fear him.

Into your hands are my lots. That is, the grace of the Holy Spirit. The conduct of this life, which is lived in this world, comes not from myself but from you.

Deliver me from the hand of my enemies and from those who persecute me. May they not prevail against me.

Make your face shine upon your servant. “Make it shine,” that is, look upon and discern whoever among your saints is better. And save me in your mercy; Lord, let me not be confounded, because I have called upon you. May the illumination of your regard shine upon me, so that I may not be confounded but be saved from these persecutors.

Let the impious be put to shame and be led down into hell. Let the impious—demons, heretics, or those who do not believe in the resurrection—be put to shame. Let them be put to shame when they see those saints whom they held in contempt crowned, and themselves condemned. Or those who, abandoning the true God, worship wood and venerate stones. Let deceitful lips be silenced, which speak iniquity against the just in pride and abuse: mocking the Crucified One and ignorant of the risen One. Seeing this, the prophet cries out in exultation and says:

How great is the abundance of your sweetness, Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you! For your sweetness is abundantly manifold, and you have reserved it for those who fear your name. You did not display it amid these temptations, lest, having received security, we should depart from the way of justice. Or, how great is the abundance of your sweetness, Lord! That is, how great a glory and how great rewards you have prepared for your Church, so that she may remain forever with the angels without end. Which you have hidden for those who fear you: that is, you have hidden the blessings of the saints in yourself.

You perfected it for those who hope in you. “You perfected it,” as though he said: “You will perfect it.” In the presence of the children of men, who were not ashamed to confess what they believe before kings and powers, as the prophet says: “And I spoke of your testimonies in the presence of kings, and was not confounded” (Ps. 118). Which you have hidden for those who fear you: because here they do not fully receive their reward through tribulation, but await it in the future. And you perfected it for those who hope in you. When hope had been fulfilled, you repaid what was awaited in its visible reality. In the presence of the children of men who sought human things and not heavenly things. Or, when they go into eternal punishment; but the righteous into eternal life.

[Col. 0910D] You will hide them in the hiding place of your face, from the disturbance of men. The illumination of your countenance will cover them, so that they may not be troubled by human wickedness. In the hiding place of your face—that is, hidden within your justice; this means in your secret place, just as Job, himself and all that he possessed, were hidden in God. From the disturbance of men, from the persecution of sinners.

You will protect them in your tabernacle from the contradiction of tongues. In the tabernacle of faith, those who say, “Who knows these things?” or, “Who has returned from the underworld?” are sheltered from the uproar of evil tongues.

Blessed is the Lord. Every creature blesses him. How does he say, “Blessed is the Lord”? Does he perhaps need our blessing? No, but so that we may deserve to receive blessing from him. For he has made his mercy wondrous in a fortified city. In the city of Jerusalem, in the middle of the world. It is called a fortified city because it is strengthened and made robust, and all the nations surround it in a circle. Throughout the Church spread everywhere, the Lord made his mercy wondrous there, because there he was born, there he suffered, there he rose again, and from there he ascended into the heavens, as the prophet says: “He worked salvation in the midst of the earth” (Ps. 73). Or otherwise: the heavenly Jerusalem, fortified by the gathering of angels and human beings.

But I said in the excess of my mind. The Church, when she remembers paradise—how she could have been immortal and how she could have remained there—and recalls what she is and how God spoke to Adam through an angel (Gen. 3), and how she saw God with her inner eyes: when the Church considers these things, she is in an excess of mind. But I said in the excess of my mind: I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes. The people converted to Christ say this: “I thought,” they say, “that I had been cast away from contemplation of your lights, and I was terrified when you permitted me to suffer so much on account of your name.” Or, I have been cast away from the face of your eyes. When Adam transgressed God’s commandment, he was cast away from God’s face (ibid.), both he himself and we and all his posterity after him.

Therefore you heard the voice of my supplication when I cried out to you. Therefore, the Church says, you heard the voice of my prayer, because I understood where I could be, and I recognize where I am now. You heard the voice of the inner person, praying to you in the splendor of the mind, and you removed the dreadful tribulations.

Love the Lord, all his saints, because the Lord seeks truth and abundantly repays those who act proudly. Having humbled the proud, he will establish his saints in great steadfastness. Love the Lord, all his saints. “Love,” that is, cherish him. Because the Lord seeks truth in those who persevere in goodness to the end, as it was said: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 24).

Act courageously. That is, immovably. And let your heart be strengthened, all you who hope in the Lord. Your heart—that is, your soul, always in the Lord. Act courageously, and let your heart be strengthened, all you who hope in the Lord. Guard your purpose firmly and steadfastly, so that you may reap fruit in Christ. We humbly beseech him to impress upon our minds the care of loving him, and to enable us continually to confess that he suffered for us, so that we may deserve to fight courageously against wicked pride with the weapons of humility.

## PSALM XXXI

The understanding of David. The understanding of Christ. There is a twofold understanding in this title, especially concerning the Publican and the Pharisee who were praying in the temple (Luke 18): one justified himself, while the other condemned himself—that is, accused himself. The psalm contains the prophet’s voice, showing that a person can be saved not by his own merits but by God’s grace, if he confesses his offenses.

[Col. 0912A] Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered. “Blessed” means immortal, praiseworthy, or glorious. Yet no one can be blessed in himself unless he receives it from the one who justifies the impious, namely, God. Hence Paul also says: “To the one who believes in him who justifies the impious, his faith is reckoned as righteousness” (Rom. 4). Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven: those whose sins are washed away by the Lord through confession.

In what ways are sins forgiven? In three ways. They are forgiven through baptism; covered through love; and not counted through martyrdom. And whose sins have been covered through love, according to the saying: “Love covers a multitude of sins” (Jas. 5). Or, whose sins have been covered: that is, so that they are veiled here through repentance and not revealed in the judgment.

[Col. 0912B] Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin. He is the one who has been able to cleanse himself diligently in this world, or through martyrdom. What is covered is not seen; what is not seen is not counted; what is not counted will not be punished. And there is no deceit in his mouth. This refers to the mouth of the one who confesses himself to be a sinner, like Nathanael. Hence the Lord said: “Behold, truly an Israelite in whom there is no deceit” (John 1). And it refers to that Publican of whom we spoke above, who confessed himself to be a sinner, saying: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18). There is no deceit in his mouth; believing God in truth, he held in his heart what he confessed with his mouth.

For when I was silent, all my bones grew old within me. I did not bring forth confession for salvation; therefore all my strength grew old in the weakness of the flesh. For when I was silent, all my bones grew old within me, while I cried out all day. “I was silent” is the voice of the wicked. “I was silent”: that is, they keep their sins silent and do not wish to confess them. The bones grew old—that is, the virtues they ought to have had grew old through sin. While I cried out—that is, they cry out. If they have anything good, they display it through vanity, as that impious Pharisee did when he said: “God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of humanity—robbers, adulterers.” While I cried out all day: during the brief moment of this life.

For day and night your hand was heavy upon me. Your power. When I was impious and blasphemous, your hand was heavy upon me—that is, your power—because upon those who do not reform here, the hand of God, that is, the power of vengeance, will weigh heavily on the day of judgment. I was turned into misery. Into continual tribulation under your scourges. While a thorn was fixed in me. The goad of a sinful conscience. I was turned into misery while a thorn was fixed in me: misery, that is, wretchedness. While a thorn was fixed in me: that is, while consciousness of sin pricks me.

I made my sin known to you, and I did not hide my iniquities. Rather, I confessed and disclosed everything. For I know that you quickly forgive offenses when they have been fully laid open to you, and therefore I said:

I shall confess my iniquities against myself to the Lord. I did not pronounce them against the Lord, but against myself, so that I might be justified. I said, I proclaimed my iniquities against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the wickedness of my sin. The prophet speaks in the person of those who are converted, like that son who went off to a distant country and said: “I shall go to my father” (Luke 15). He said this in his heart, where God is seen. And you forgave the impiety of my sin: the things I had previously done, you mercifully pardoned.

For this impiety every saint shall pray to you at an opportune time. The opportune time for pleading concerning sins is this life, in which the saints pray for this very reason: because no one is free from sins. For this iniquity—or for this forgiveness, which he mentioned above: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered.” Every saint—that is, through baptism; and whoever sins after baptism is later forgiven through repentance or martyrdom.

Nevertheless, in the flood of many waters they will not approach him. Many waves of the floodwaters will surround the impious at the judgment, but they will not harm the saints. Nevertheless, in the flood of many waters they will not approach him. The saints, he says, will not be able to approach God without the afflictions that are compared to overflowing waters, because “the one who endures to the end will be saved.” Or, in the flood of waters—that is, in the variety of heretical teachings: through this they will not approach God.

You are my refuge from the tribulation that surrounded me. The Church’s voice to Christ. She says this concerning the pressures of this world. My exultation. Because I rejoice in you. Deliver me from those surrounding me. Either from public enemies or from sins.

When he said, “My exultation, deliver me from those surrounding me,” how can he say “Deliver me,” when the one who is redeemed is in captivity, whereas those who exult do not need redemption? This concerns the meaning: it is the voice of those who are with God and who pray for those who are afflicted in this captivity.

I shall give you understanding and instruct you in this way in which you will walk. What sort of understanding God gives to his Church: so that she may understand why the saint is anxious while sinners prosper. I shall give you understanding and instruct you in this way in which you will walk. In the way, namely, of this confession, I shall teach you wisdom, so that you do not depart from it. I shall make you understand and teach you in this way in which you will walk. The voice of the Lord is introduced, speaking [Col. 0913D] and teaching how a person may deserve his help, namely, if he keeps God’s commandments and proceeds along the right path. Thus he says that a person cannot arrive at perfect purity. And although he cannot arrive at perfect purity, nevertheless he should not be carried headlong into vices like an animal.

I shall establish my eyes upon you. Christ’s voice to the Church. I shall establish my eyes upon you—that is, the gaze of divinity. I shall establish my eyes upon you so that you may remain in love of my light.

Do not become like a horse, etc. Those who wish to govern themselves not by God’s will but by their own impulse, and who fall, unbridled, into lust—against such people the prophet speaks with terrifying words:

[Col. 0914A] Restrain their jaws with bit and bridle. By the bridle and bit of his discipline, God restrains the useless blasphemies of the impious. The horse is untamed; the mule is sluggish. The Church asks God the Father to make the Gentile people, whom he called horses, draw near to him by means of the bridle—that is, preaching—from the broad and spacious way of this world; and to make the Jewish people, whom he called mules, and who are sluggish in believing in God, come to him by means of the bit—that is, compunction of heart. They do not draw near to you, but through pride they withdraw.

Many are the scourges of sinners. For there are certain sinners whose scourges begin in this life and who will suffer them without end in the future: many are the scourges of sinners who were unwilling to do penance. But mercy will surround those who hope in the Lord. That mercy by which they may deserve eternal life. Those who have right hope and faith in God will be surrounded by God’s mercy, as in: “The Lord sent an angel around those who fear him” (Ps. 32); and elsewhere: “The Lord guards all who love him” (Ps. 144).

Rejoice in the Lord and exult, righteous ones. The prophet urges the Church to rejoice in the hope of eternal life and regeneration; nevertheless, here too the Church rejoices amid tribulation. And glory, all you upright of heart. As Paul says: “Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1). Those are called upright of heart to whom all God’s judgments are pleasing, who accuse themselves of their sins, and who praise God always, whether in prosperity or adversity.

Rejoice in the Lord and exult, righteous ones; and glory, all you upright of heart. Let your glory be referred to him, as the Apostle says: “Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord.” We humbly beseech him that, our sins being covered through forgiveness and our offenses no longer counted, we may deserve to share in the saints’ perpetual exultation.

## PSALM XXXII

For the end; a psalm of David. This psalm contains the prophet’s voice exhorting the peoples to God and admonishing the righteous in whom they ought to exult.

Exult, righteous ones, in the Lord. The prophet urges the saints to praise God. Exult, righteous ones. Elsewhere he says, “Rejoice,” but the meaning is one. Some exult in the things of this world, some in the circus, others in the theater. But you, the prophet says to each saint, exult in the Lord and not in the world’s prosperity. Praise belongs to the upright. He calls upright those who direct their hearts according to the rule of truth, not the wicked, as the prophet says: “Woe to those who call sweet bitter and bitter sweet” (Isa. 5).

Confess to the Lord on the lyre. The lyre has a hollow space below and six strings. The works of the saints are understood by the lyre, and these are the six works of mercy. Some of those strings sing well; others murmur. So too among the saints: some are one way, others another. Confess to the Lord on the lyre: in the flesh mortified through the Lord’s cross to vices and desires.

Sing to him on the ten-stringed psaltery. In the Decalogue of the commandments. The psaltery has a hollow space above; preaching or commandments are understood in the saints, which come from above. Hence he said: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change or shadow of alteration” (Jas. 1).

The ten strings are the ten words of the law. Three commandments are on one tablet, pertaining to the end of the Trinity. These are: first, “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God”; second, “You shall not take the name of your God in vain”; third, “Observe the Sabbath day” (Deut. 6). The seven on the other tablet pertain to love of neighbor.

Sing to him a new song. That is, sing to him a new song: that is, a new life, because the new man has come into the world; he has established for us a new law and a new Church through baptism. Sing to him a new song, because he has risen, because he sits at the right hand of the Father. Sing well to him. He sings well who fulfills in action what he sings—that is, what he preaches. In jubilation. Jubilation (*iubilus*) is so called because how greatly a person ought to praise God can neither break forth nor be comprehended in words, syllables, letters, or voice. Sing well to him with a shout. Once, through the jubilation of the priests, Jericho—which retained the figure of the world—fell (Josh. VI); now, through our prayer, its desires are struck down.

For the word of the Lord is upright. It is not bent in any respect, but prospers in those things toward which he directs it. And all his works are in faith. As he says in the Gospel: “If you have complete faith and say to this mountain, ‘Move yourself and cast yourself into the sea,’ it will happen” (Matt. XVII). “And whatever things you ask for faithfully, believe that you will receive them, and they will come to you.” For the word of the Lord is upright, and all his works are in faith. He is upright among the upright. His works are in faith, in the faith of the saints, because what God promises his saints, he does not lie about.

The Lord loves mercy and judgment. How does he say that he loves mercy, when in another place he says, “You shall not show mercy to the poor in judgment” (Exod. XXII)? That is: neither on account of the poor nor on account of the rich, neither on account of a near person nor a distant one, neither on account of someone known nor someone unknown, should you turn aside from upright judgment. Rather, first judge with upright judgment, and afterward let mercy come to the aid. He loves mercy because, having assumed flesh, he redeemed us; and judgment, because he distinguishes between the impious and the righteous. The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord. The whole world. Or, the earth—that is, the holy Church—is full of the mercy of God, because just as he is everywhere, so his mercy is with him and inseparable from him. For he did not descend merely to preserve the righteous, but to redeem sinners and make them safe.

[Col. 0916A]

By the word of the Lord the heavens were established. The Word of the Father is the Son. The heavens were established: the holy apostles, through him, in faith. By the word of the Lord the heavens were established. In that Word which was in the beginning with God, both the visible heavens and the apostles were created. By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host. The majesty of the Trinity is most clearly declared: the Lord, the Word, and the Spirit of the Lord. And by the breath of his mouth all their host. That is, with the Paraclete cooperating, the virtues of these heavens were created. For in “Lord” the Father is declared, in “Word” the Son, and in “the breath of his mouth” the Holy Spirit. And because he says “of his mouth,” let no one suppose that the Spirit proceeds as though he were inferior. For just as the Son is from the Father and equal to the Father, so also the Holy Spirit is regarded as equal to the Father and the Son. Or, “by the breath of his mouth all their host”—that is, their virtues are through the Holy Spirit. For through the Holy Spirit they received various gifts—that is, virtues. For we have possessed nothing good through ourselves except through him.

Gathering the waters of the sea as in a wineskin. He shows the sea enclosed by its shores. Gathering the waters of the sea as in a wineskin. By the waters he signifies the tribulations of the world and the persecutions of the saints, because just as a person compresses water in a wineskin and scatters it when he wishes, so the Lord [restrains] the tribulations of the Church, as Paul says: “God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but will also provide an outcome, so that you may be able to endure” (I Cor. X). Gathering as in a wineskin, in the new man of the Church, the waters of the sea—that is, the peoples of the world—so that they may be new wine, as the Lord says, “into new wineskins” (Matt. IX): that is, the evangelical commandment stored in the hearts of believers.

Putting the abysses into storehouses. O great power of the Creator, storing the abysses in storehouses and bringing forth winds from the storehouses! Yet here we understand “abysses” as the height of the heavenly mysteries, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Rom. XI). Or, “in storehouses,” that is, in the hidden things of God. A storehouse—that is, generosity—means the depth of the Scriptures. Hence he says elsewhere: “He brings forth the wind from his storehouses” (Ps. CXXXIV). For as much as he wished to show us through his servants, so much were we able to understand through ourselves; but we are altogether unable to reach the very depth of the Scriptures.

Let all the earth fear the Lord. Let those who think earthly thoughts worship him rather than the creature. And let all who inhabit the world be moved by him. Some regard this as referring to the future judgment, but it looks more closely to the exposition that follows. Let all be moved by him, all who inhabit the world. Let all be moved by God himself—that is, from unbelief to faith. Or, “all”: all creatures come from him, and not, as sinners say, that time brings them into existence and not God; for God established times, days, years, and even moments.

For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created. Therefore let all things fear him, because they were either made or created by him. “He spoke”: that is, he spoke through the Son, who is the Word. “He commanded”: through authority—that is, ineffably.

The Lord brings to nothing the counsels of the nations. In accordance with this: “There is no counsel, no prudence, no wisdom, and no strength against God” (Prov. XII). The Lord brings to nothing the counsels of the nations: namely, of the Jews, who, as unbelievers, murmur against Christ God. Or he brings to nothing the counsels of those who wished to build a tower; he destroyed it, in accordance with this: “Come, let us confuse their languages there” (Gen. XI). But he rejects the thoughts of the peoples. That is, the counsels of the Jews, because they could not carry them out except to the extent predetermined by God. But he rejects the thoughts of the peoples: of the Pharisees, Sadducees, and the remaining classes of authorities. And he rejects the counsels of princes. That is, of Annas and Caiaphas, because they were the rulers of those priests who held the primacy in this crime. By rising again, the Lord destroyed all these together with their counsels.

But the counsel of the Lord remains forever. The counsel of the Lord was that he should rise from the dead, as he also did. The Jews and their rulers could not destroy this counsel. The thoughts of his heart are from generation to generation. Nothing will be diminished from them, in accordance with this: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matt. XXIV).

Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord. That is, those who believe that the Lord created those creatures of which he spoke above, and not that time brings them into existence. Or, blessed is the nation of Christians, whose God is the Lord. It chose to have the Lord as its God, having abandoned idols. The people whom the Lord chose for himself as an inheritance. He chose the Christian people as an inheritance for himself, as he said in another psalm: “I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession the ends of the earth” (Ps. II); and elsewhere: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Ps. XV); and again: “The Lord is my portion” (Ps. CXVIII). For himself as an inheritance. With the Jews rejected, we have been adopted as an inheritance.

From heaven the Lord looked down; he saw all the children of men. So that he might have mercy on all, because his regard was never without mercy. Or, the Lord looked down from heaven—that is, he had mercy on us. Upon the children of men. “Children of men”: the children of Adam. Or “children of men”: the successors of the apostles.

From his prepared dwelling-place he looked upon all who inhabit the earth. He who formed their hearts individually. So that to one may be given the word of wisdom, to another the interpretation of utterances, to another varieties of tongues, and so forth—things which one and the same Spirit accomplishes. Or, “who formed their hearts individually”: he formed the hearts of each one. Some deceitfully refer this passage to the idea that the soul is generated from the soul and that all souls are contained in Adam, because the Greek expression *καταμόνας* signifies not “one,” but “each one among many.”

He who formed their hearts individually. “Who formed”: that is, made. “Individually”: he understands all individually and knows all together. “Their hearts”: their works. He understands all their works. For he is the watcher who looks upon human acts from day to day. He understands all their works: that is, he himself dispenses how each soul possesses the gift of God.

[Col. 0918A]

A king is not saved by great strength, nor is a giant saved by the abundance of his strength. Rather, by righteousness and the help of God. For God also confounded the strength of Goliath through the hand of David, his servant. A king is not made safe by the multitude of his strength. Why? Because elsewhere he says: “The Lord is salvation” (Ps. III). Nor will a giant be saved by the abundance of his strength. “Giant” is said on account of his strength. Nor can he himself be saved through his strength, as was explained above concerning Goliath and David.

A horse is deceptive for salvation; in the abundance of its strength it will not be saved. Unless God is its rider. A horse is deceptive for salvation. The horse is the human body, the soul’s beast of burden, and therefore deceptive. But in the abundance of its strength it will not be saved—that is, neither the giant nor the king.

Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him. The eyes of God are the regard of his divinity. Upon those who fear him—those who fear him with holy fear. For God protects and defends those who hope in him with heavenly inspection. And upon those who hope in his mercy. To rescue their souls from death. That is, they hope in his mercy—in the mercy of God—for him to rescue their souls from everlasting death. Or, “from death”: that is, from the devil.

To rescue their souls from death and feed them in famine. While others suffer the scarcity of the word of God, these are brought to life by him.

But our soul waits for the Lord. That is, it is patient in the Lord. Whatever comes upon it, whether good or evil, it endures for God’s sake, as Paul says: “All things are pleasing to me” (I Cor. X). Or, “he feeds them in famine”: that is, he nourishes them. Hence he said: “He fed them for forty years in the desert” (Exod. XVI). For whenever human beings suffer hunger, God feeds his servants—not, indeed, only with earthly food, but with something greater, by which he feeds them with spiritual food: that is, with his teaching and his word. But our soul waits for the Lord, because he is our helper and protector. And our heart will rejoice in him, and we have hoped in his holy name. For we know that no one has hoped in him and departed confounded. Because he is our helper and protector. That is, because he is both the helper and defender of the Church. And our heart will rejoice in him. That is, our soul will rejoice in the hope of future recompense, and the Church will rejoice in tribulation. And we have hoped in his holy name. The name of the Father is the Son.

Let your mercy, Lord, be upon us, as we have hoped in you. It is the prayer of the Church. Nevertheless, each person ought to consider this verse before it is read, so that he may say faithfully, “as we have hoped in you,” lest his mind be elsewhere empty. Let your mercy, Lord, be upon us, as we have hoped in you. You who washed us through baptism, confirm us through the infusion of the Holy Spirit, as we see this done in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts II). May he now deign to come upon us, so that through his light we may be made worthy to become heirs of everlasting glory. Amen.

## PSALM XXXIII

[Col. 0919A]

A psalm of David, when he changed his countenance before Abimelech, and he dismissed him, and he departed. The changing of his countenance is shown in the changing of his words, when he pretended that he had been sent away by Saul. Or, if we wish to understand a real change of appearance, we should know that Abimelech was said [Note: [Col. 0919D]—namely, the name Abimelech, which means “father-king,” was common to the kings of Palestine, just as “Pharaoh” was the name of the kings of Egypt. This is evident from the very title of the psalm, where Achish is called Abimelech. Saint Basil [Col. 0920D] says concerning this passage: “The kings of the foreigners had the common name Abimelech.” The kings of the foreigners—of Palestine, or of the Philistines—were called Abimelech by a common name.] in place of Achish. Nor is there an error in the name, since he could also in some respect have been called Abimelech [the wording is uncertain]. For Abimelech is interpreted as “my father is king.”

How does he say, “He changed his countenance before Abimelech”? For in the Book of Kings we read that he fled to Gath, a city, to King Achish among the Philistines (I Reg. VIII). Or how did he dare to walk there, since he was their enemy and had previously killed Goliath, their champion? For this reason he went there, because the women had said: “Saul has struck down his thousand, and David his ten thousand.” Afterward the devil entered Saul through envy, and he said: “What remains for him except that he should also have the kingdom?” And David came to King Achish.

But afterward Achish sent his servants to bring David to him in order to kill him. When he found him at the gate of the city, David realized that they wanted to kill him and, compelled by necessity, turned aside to the citadel. Through God’s merciful providence, the Holy Spirit fell upon him, and he began to act irrationally, sending saliva over his beard. When they had brought him to the king, the king said to them: “Why have you brought this man, seized and raving, against me?” David was a handsome man, and when they seized him, he beat a tambourine at the city gate and was carried in their hands. When they had dismissed him and he had fled, he sang this psalm, which is wholly concerned with piety, wholly concerned with divine inspection, and wholly concerned with restraining the tribulations of the saints.

David bears the figure of Christ; Saul bears the figure of the devil. Abimelech is interpreted as “the kingdom of my father.” Achish is interpreted as “how is it?” or “ignorance,” or “black.” David came to Gath, to King Achish, and the Lord came into the kingdom of his Father—that is, into the kingdom of the Jews. He changed his countenance before Abimelech—that is, before the kingdom of his Father. Hence Saint Paul said: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but took the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man; he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death” (Phil. XVI).

Or otherwise: He changed his countenance—that is, into the priesthood. He changed it when Melchizedek offered bread and wine (Gen. XIV). He changed his countenance because, as the coming of Christ drew near, those figures were being opened up; for previously he offered sacrifices, but afterward they were fulfilled spiritually in the New Testament according to the order of Melchizedek. It does not say “according to the order of Aaron,” but “according to the order of Melchizedek.”

He beat a tambourine at the city gate. [Col. 0919D] A tambourine is stretched over leather. And the Lord stretched out his hands on the cross. The gates of the city signify the beginning of our faith, when we believe in the incarnation of Christ. By saliva, the weakness of the flesh which he deigned to assume is signified. That beard signifies the strength of divinity. He dismissed him and departed. Christ dismissed the Jews and came among the Gentiles. Hence it was said: “Because you judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts XIII).

I will bless the Lord at all times, etc. When he says “at all times” and “always,” he teaches us that we ought neither to collapse in adversity nor to become exalted in prosperity, but to endure both favorable and adverse circumstances with equanimity, setting the blessed person before our eyes and blessing the name of God in everything that happens. I will bless the Lord at all times. “I will bless”: that is, I will praise the Lord. At all times: in prosperity and adversity. David did this, and now the Church does so. His praise is always in my mouth. With mouth and heart, with an attentive mind, to praise God always.

In the Lord my soul shall be praised. That is, my life. When the soul, devoted to this pursuit, has endured the hardships of the world with an even mind, it is praised together with those who belong to the Lord. Let the meek hear. That is, the saints. And let them rejoice—not in earthly things, but in heavenly things: those who have no conflict of vices within themselves, those who restrain the clod of their body by such a testament. For blessed are the meek, because they shall possess the earth.

Magnify the Lord with me. Praise the Father, the Lord. And let us exalt his name together. As though the prophet said: As I love, so do you also. Or, “let us exalt his name together”: the Son, to whom the Father gave the name which is above every name.

I sought the Lord—the Holy Spirit—and he heard me and delivered me from all my tribulations, consuming the corruption of the flesh, which brought upon me the tribulations of sins, lest I should pray to him more attentively.

Draw near to the Lord. Believe in him. Draw near to the Lord not by place, but by faith and works. And be enlightened. That is, understand in your mind; for unless you believe, you will not understand. And your faces shall not be confounded—in the judgment in which the impious shall be confounded unto condemnation, on the day of judgment.

This poor man cried out. Christ the Lord, who became poor for us, cried to the Father in his passion. Or, this poor man—that is, David—cried out when he said: “Lord God, make the counsel of Ahithophel vain” (II Reg. XXVI). And the Church now cries out. And the Lord heard him and delivered him from all his tribulations, raising him from the dead.

The Lord sends forth his angel around those who fear him, and he will deliver them. That is, he gave them the angel of great counsel. There is no doubt that those who fear the Lord are guarded by angels, as the Lord himself teaches through the Gospel: “Amen, amen, I say to you, because their angels daily see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVIII). Therefore those who fear God from purity of heart are surrounded by angelic protection.

Taste, etc. Taste is apprehended through the throat; sight through the eyes, because one sees through the eyes. The prophet says, “I have tasted.” And how have I tasted? Thus I have found through faith, hope, and good works. Blessed is the man who hopes in him. Why blessed? Because he possesses him who possesses all things—that is, God. Therefore taste is spoken of here so that, when someone has known God, he may fear him; for, as though concerning taste, he says elsewhere: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. CX). But when he has begun to fear, then he keeps the commandments, and then he will know that the Lord is sweet, because he is the living bread who gives satisfaction to this world. Blessed is the man who hopes in him, and not in the uncertainty of riches.

Fear the Lord, all his saints. You who stand firm in his promises, fear lest, having received security, you be deceived. For nothing is lacking to those who fear him. To those whose God is Christ, nothing is lacking—that is, no good thing is lacking to them. Seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and the rest shall be added to you. For the righteousness of God supplies all things.

The rich have lacked and suffered hunger; but those who seek the Lord shall not be deprived of any good thing. There are many wealthy people in the world who lack the glory of God; among them was also that rich man at whose gate Lazarus lay. Thirsting in torments because he had not shown mercy, he did not deserve to receive a drop. But Lazarus, seeking not purple garments but heavenly kingdoms, deserved to be filled with every good thing in Abraham’s bosom (Luke XVI).

Come, children, hear me: I will teach you the fear of the Lord. It is prophetic usage to call disciples children, as Paul does: “My little children, for whom I am again in travail until Christ be formed in you” (Gal. IV). He teaches them that they should first of all be imbued with wisdom—that is, with the fear of the Lord. Come, children, hear me. Christ calls the Church to come to him—that is, by faith. The holy are called children of God, according to what was said in the Gospel: “But as many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God” (John I). And John says in his Epistle: “Now we are children of God” (I John III). I will teach you the fear of the Lord. As in: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclus. I). And elsewhere he says: “From fear is born the compunction of salvation.” To this each person ought to come: that he ought to have the fear of the Lord.

Who is the man who desires life? Eternal life, certainly. And desires to see good days, in which he may rejoice with the saints in the kingdom of God. Or it is the voice of the prophet asking, and another says, “I desire it”; and he says, “If you desire it, then do what follows, and you shall see life”—that is, you shall have eternal life and good days—that is, eternal days.

Keep your tongue from evil, and let not your lips speak deceit. Keep your tongue from detraction or bitterness, because it is said: “Death and life are in the hands of the tongue” (Prov. XVIII). For whoever guards his tongue guards his soul. And elsewhere he says: “The guardian of righteousness: silence and peace” (Isa. XXIII). If anyone thinks himself religious while not restraining his tongue, that person’s religion will be vain (Jas. I). And let not your lips speak deceit, lest you present one thing with your mouth and retain another in your heart.

Turn away from evil and do good. That is, destroy vices and build virtues. It is of no benefit if you destroy and do not build. That is, if you destroy vices and do not build virtues. As though he said: Who is the man who would desire life without these things? No one. For no good was in one who destroys no evil. Turn away from evil and do good. All evils proceed from the devil’s prompting, just as good things proceed from God’s. Therefore leave what the devil prompts and do what Christ commands.

Seek peace and pursue it. According to the Apostle, pursue peace and holiness, without which no one sees the kingdom of God (Heb. XII). Or the Jews sought peace—that is, Christ—to kill him, not to imitate him, because “to follow” is called “to imitate.” Seek peace and follow it—that is, Christ, because he is our peace. Or, follow: imitate. Hence it is said in the Gospel: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke IX). Seek peace and follow it. It is not enough to flee evil unless you also do good.

The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous. For by the regard of his mercy he continually beholds them. And his ears are open to their prayers, because they ask for what is just. The eyes of the Lord—that is, the gaze of divinity—are upon the righteous. And his ears are directed to their prayers. Whatever good thing the saints ask, he hears them, because God both hears and sees us; therefore let us do his will.

But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil. This psalm proceeds in the person of the good and in the person of the evil. Why is God’s face against those who do evil? To destroy their remembrance from the earth—that is, from the land of the living, as the prophet says: “Let them be blotted out from the book of the living” (Ps. LXXXVI). Here we understand “face” as wrath, which, threatening anger, destroys the remembrance of sin from the earth, so that it may plant the roots of its kindness from which it had cut it off. What is said of ears, eyes, and face is to be referred not to the bodily form of the Deity, but to the power of majesty.

The righteous cried out, and the Lord heard them, etc., because they cried out wholly from purity of heart. Or the three youths cried out amid the flames, and the Lord heard them (Dan. III). The sons of the Maccabees, or now each individual saint: he delivers both them and now each one from all tribulations.

The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart. He is never far from those who endure for his sake. He is with them in tribulation, not by place but by help, because God is not local. And he will save the humble in spirit, that he may grant them heavenly kingdoms. The humble in spirit are the meek, as in: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart” (Matt. XI). Or: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

Many are the tribulations of the righteous. Therefore one who suffers no tribulation is not righteous. The death of sinners is most evil. The tribulation of the righteous ends in death, but the punishments of sinners begin after death. Or, many are the tribulations of the righteous, and from all these the Lord delivered them. For they are tested so that, having been proved, they may become manifest. But there will be regard for them in due time, when they have judged nations and ruled peoples.

The Lord guards all their bones. That is, their virtues. Not one of them shall be broken. Concerning his saints in the future judgment, how does he say, “Not one of them shall be broken,” since many have broken bones, as we read of the holy martyrs? But here “bones” means the support or virtues of the soul. The Lord guards all their bones; not one of them shall be broken. He speaks of the eternity of everlasting life, which they bear through the hope of faith, or of the strength which they have in God himself to guard, lest amid these tribulations they grow lukewarm or be broken in any respect.

The death of sinners is most evil, because they are punished both here and without end in the future. And those who hate the righteous shall sin. The Jews hated Christ or his testament. They hated the righteous one—that is, Christ—and without cause. They shall sin—that is, they shall commit sin. Or whoever now hates the righteous—that is, any holy person—sins.

[Col. 0923B]

The Lord has redeemed the souls of his servants. Christ redeemed us with his precious blood, and now redeems us day by day. Or, the Lord has redeemed the souls of his servants from the power of the second death. And he will not forsake all who hope in him.

Those who hope in God he will not forsake, neither here nor in the future; but he is with them, according to his promise, until the consummation of the age. May he grant this to us, that his praise may always be in our mouth, and that, making moderate use of his teaching, neither prosperity may puff us up nor adversities be able to cast us down.

## PSALM XXXIV

Unto the end, a psalm of David himself. “Unto the end,” that is, unto Christ, as in: “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. X). Or, the end is the perfection of Christ. Hence the apostles also said: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John XIV). And the Lord: “He who sees me sees my Father, because I am in the Father and the Father is in me.” In this is the perfection of Christ. David is interpreted “strong in hand,” or “beloved.” And the Lord is strong in hand because he touched the bier and the widow’s young son arose. Or, strong, through whom all things were made. Beloved, because the saints so desire to see Christ that they even give up their bodies for him in martyrdom. Or, the psalm contains the mystery of the Lord’s passion. In it it should be noted that what is said in humility, weeping, and lamentation pertains not to the divinity but to the assumed flesh. Therefore he prays to the Lord Father, saying:

Judge, Lord, those who harm me; vanquish those who attack me. The Jews and the chief priests, who often attacked the Lord while he was in the flesh and wished to harm him. Judge, Lord, those who harm me. It is the voice of Christ in his passion and the voice of the Church in tribulation. “Judge”: that is, by a judgment of discernment. Or, judge—that is, distinguish between me and the Jews, between the Church and her persecutors. Vanquish those who attack me. As though he said: Take vengeance for me, as is said through Saint Paul: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Rom. XII). And again: “If God is for us, who is against us?” (Rom. VIII).

Take hold of weapons and shield, and rise up to help me. By the weapons he signifies heavenly aids; by the shield, divine protection, which according to the weakness of the flesh he asks to be supplied to him. But he also defends and fortifies us with spiritual weapons, according to the Apostle: “Put on the weapons of God” (Eph. VI). The weapons of the Lord are the protection of divinity. What is stronger, what is more beautiful, than Christ standing armed for his saints? As Saint Stephen saw when he said: “Behold, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God the Father” (Acts VII). Standing is the posture of one fighting or resisting. You cannot change your weapons; the Lord, approaching with weapons, makes a shield. And we ought to take up weapons, so that we may be able to resist in the evil day and stand perfect in all things.

Pour out the sword and bar the way against those who persecute me. Let the sword of your wrath, poured out, fall upon them and shut them in, lest they be able to range abroad to harm. By the sword is understood the Lord’s soul, through which God the Father executes just vengeance. Or, the sword is understood as the soul of each saint, because God accomplishes vengeance through holy souls, as he did through Peter against Ananias and Sapphira (Acts V), and through Elijah against the fifty men (IV Kings I). Lord, say to my soul: “I am your salvation.” It is the voice of the Church. Say to my soul, so that it may understand you: that you are my God; you are the salvation of my soul. Say to my soul: “I am your salvation.” “Through me,” he says, “it shall be made alive after death.”

Let those who seek my soul in order to take it away be confounded and ashamed. When you have raised me, then let them be confounded. Let those who wish me evil be turned backward and blush. Let them not advance forward, but turn backward so that they may perish; that is, let demons, Jews, or persecutors of the Church be turned backward in the future judgment. Let the Gentiles be confounded concerning idols; let them be confounded from unbelief unto faith in Christ. Hence Paul says: “What fruit, then, did you have at that time in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. VI). Or, let them turn backward—that is, those who have followed an evil course—as the Lord said to Peter: “Get behind me, Satan” (Matt. XVI).

Let them be as dust before the face of the wind, with the angel of the Lord pursuing them. That is, as the angel pursues them, let them be scattered, so that absolutely nothing, however small, may remain of them. Dust denotes light and unfruitful people, because as dust before the wind, so are sinners before the divine sentence on the day of judgment. And the angel of the Lord pursuing them. The angel of the Lord means an evil spirit. If evil, why of the Lord? If of the Lord, why evil? He is of the Lord because the Lord created him and holds him in his power. He is malign not by nature, but by his own devising. The devil has the will to harm, but not the power to do so, as the prophet says: “Incursions by evil angels” (Ps. LXXVII); that is, he has only as much power as the Lord permits him.

Let their ways be darkness and slipperiness. Darkness means ignorance; slipperiness, that is, lust. Because the devil pursues one whose mind is devoted to these things. Or otherwise: let them not know the light of truth, nor stand in a firm position, but let the steps of those who rage in this passion become slippery, and let them be afflicted by the angel of the Lord’s brightness.

Because without cause they hid from me the destruction of their snare. Rightly, “their,” because the destruction which they thought was the Lord’s became their snare. Because without cause they hid destruction from me. “Without cause,” that is, the Jews against Christ and persecutors against the Church. They ensnared themselves for vengeance. They reproached my soul to no purpose; for their reproach had no benefit.

Let the snare which they do not know come upon them. He threatens that destruction which came upon them in the time of Vespasian. Or each sinner is bound by the cords of his own vices on the day of judgment. And let the trap which he hid seize them; let them fall into the snare itself—namely, into the sudden death which they themselves secretly plotted against our Lord, as in: “They dug a pit before my face, and they themselves fell into it” (Ps. LVI). And again he says: “Into the pit which you prepared for your brother, you shall fall” (Prov. XXVI).

But my soul shall exult in the Lord: Christ in the Father, and the Church in Christ. It shall delight in his salvation, when it has been raised by him. Or, “it shall delight,” that is, it shall rejoice in his salvation. Our salvation is Christ, because the Church delights in him, as Solomon says: “Who is this who comes up whitewashed and leaning upon her little brother?” (Cant. III).

All my bones shall say: “Lord, who is like you?” By bones is understood eternity or strength, which is referred to the apostles: those to whom the words of the resurrection at first seemed like delirium now praise together and say, “Who is like you?” That is, who, as you, was able to call back from death? Or, bones means the stronger saints, or the virtues of the saints. Who is like you? As though he said: No one. Elsewhere he says: “God, who is like you?” (Ps. LXX). That is, no one.

Rescuing the needy from the hand of those stronger than he. Christ was needy for us, so that by his need he might make us rich. “From the hand of those stronger”: that is, God the Father delivered him from the hand of the Jews. Needy Christ speaks in the person of his members. The destitute and poor man from those who plunder him—from the powers of darkness, whose greatest strength is that they can plunder your poor people.

[Col. 0925D]

False witnesses rising up questioned me about things they did not know. The Gospel calls them false witnesses; the prophet, wicked ones. And those whom the Gospel calls false are questioned; but those of whom the prophet speaks question. Hence it should be understood that the chief priests are the wicked witnesses who questioned things they did not know, saying: “We adjure you by God to tell us whether you are the Son of God” (Matt. XXVI). But when he said, “I am,” they tore their garments and, as though giving testimony, cried out: “You yourselves have heard the blasphemy; why do we still seek witnesses?” For it was false testimony to say that he had blasphemed when he had spoken the truth.

And they repaid me evil for good: barrenness [Col. 0926A] of my soul. While I was offering them life, they condemned me to death; and while I promised the fruitfulness of heavenly goods, they inflicted the poverty of life upon me. Thus the Jews acted toward Christ: they repaid good with evil. “The barrenness of my soul”—that is, just as their souls were barren of goodness and full of sin, so they wished Christ’s soul to be.

But I, when they troubled me, clothed myself in sackcloth. These are the weapons of the saints. The whole psalm, however, is spoken in the person of Christ, and through Christ it can be referred to all the saints. “I clothed myself in sackcloth. And I humbled my soul with fasting.” We read of his fasting, but we do not read of his wearing sackcloth. Yet “sackcloth” signifies sinners, since it is the garment of repentance. “I clothed myself in sackcloth”—as if he were saying: The divinity clothed itself in flesh, and condemned sin because of sin. [Col. 0926B] “But I, when they troubled me, clothed myself in sackcloth, and humbled my soul with fasting, and my prayer shall return into my bosom.” For the Lord assumed the harshness of suffering and mourning over the hardness of the unbelieving people. He observed a fast until evening, when, at the evening of the world, he was offered for the salvation of the world. His prayer returned into the bosom of the Father when he was in no way frustrated by the Father; and the Father did not grant this to him as to one inferior, but in order to reveal the humanity he had assumed. Christ fasted not carnally but spiritually. Hungry, he came to the fig tree; thirsty, he came to the well. He hungered for the salvation of the human race; he thirsted for faith in the Church. He hungered in his passion, when everyone—and especially the apostles—denied him, except only the thief who confessed him on the cross. And [Col. 0926C] “my prayer shall return into my bosom.” That is, he was acting in the secret place of God the Father. The saints also pray in secret—that is, in the heart, where God is seen, as in the Gospel: “When you pray, enter into your room and pray to your Father in secret” (Matt. VI). Hannah also prayed in the temple (I Reg. I).

“As though for a neighbor, as though for our brother.” If we understand the psalm as spoken in David’s person, we take “neighbor” to mean Saul. If it is spoken in Christ’s person, he calls Judas the betrayer his neighbor. Or Christ was a neighbor and brother to the Jews, because he took his humanity from them. “Thus I was pleasing”—that is, to God the Father. He was brother and neighbor because of his bodily generation. “As one mourning and sorrowful, so I humbled myself.” For he mourned when, as the angel strengthened him, drops of his sweat fell to the ground like blood [Col. 0926D]. And he was sorrowful when he said: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. XXVI). “As one mourning and sorrowful.” Christ mourned on our behalf, as in the passage: “Seeing the city,” he says, “he wept over it” (Luke XIX). “So I humbled myself,” because Christ was humbled in his passion. Or, “thus I was pleasing,” because he was pleasing to the Father through faith and hope.

And they rejoiced against me. The Jews rejoiced when they seized Christ in order to crucify him. And they gathered together. They gathered for this purpose: to crucify Christ, not to believe. Or they assembled against me and gathered together when they had obtained a promise of my betrayal. [Col. 0927A] Scourges were gathered against me. They scourged Christ, as he said: “You have come out with swords and clubs against me” (Matt. XXVI). And Pilate said: “I will release him after correction”—that is, I will release him after he has been scourged. And I did not know. What he did not know is questioned. Some think that this means the pain of the wounds he suffered on the cross. But it is better referred to sins: he had no awareness of sins as the reason why he was crucified. And “I was ignorant,” not because Christ is ignorant of anything, but because I was ignorant in the sense that I had not committed the deed on account of which this happened to me. Or they were ignorant that God lay hidden under the covering of flesh.

They were scattered [Col. 0927B]—from the bond of charity. And they were not pierced—so that they might do penance. They tempted me. The Jews tempted Christ in many ways, as one of them said: “Teacher, which is the first commandment?” (Matt. XXII). They mocked me with mockery, deriding me and saying: “Hail, King of the Jews” (John XIX). They gnashed their teeth against me, crying: “Crucify him.” Through bodily movements the movement of the soul is displayed. By the teeth is understood malice, because through malice they crucified him and gnashed their teeth against him.

Lord, when will you look upon this? The prophet speaks in the person of the Church. It is as though he were saying: Look upon the wickedness of the evil and distinguish my righteousness from theirs. And restore my soul from their malignity, my only one from the lions. He calls the persecutors lions, for they tried to swallow his soul with their mouths; but they were confounded by his resurrection. Behold, his prayer returned [Col. 0927C] into his bosom when the only one—that is, the soul itself—was restored intact to the body. And who, you ask, restored it? He himself, together with the Father’s will, who said: “I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up again” (John X). And “from the lions, my only one.” The lion is the Jewish people itself, because of the strength of its malice. “My only one,” because Christ’s soul alone was without sin, according to the prophet: “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (Isa. LIII).

I will confess to you, Lord, in the great assembly—that is, spread throughout the whole world. “Among a weighty people I will praise you”—that is, among the Christian people I will praise you there. It is called “weighty” because it is not light-minded toward sin: not like something light which the wind casts like dust from the face of the earth [Col. 0927D], but weighty, founded upon a rock, and firmly observing the commandments. Here again he recalls his passion, by which he rather announces the judgment of death to them, saying:

Let not those who oppose me unjustly rejoice over me. The Jews rejoiced over Christ, and the persecutors of the Church. Those who hate me without cause and wink with their eyes. He says this so that the passion may not be repeated, since redemption too will not come again. “And they winked with their eyes,” because they displayed nothing good in their deeds.

For indeed they spoke peaceably to me. Such was their saying: “Teacher, is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar or not?” (Matt. XXII). Or when they said: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth” [Col. 0928A] (ibid.). But these peaceful words were full of deceit and anger. And in anger they devised deceits. They spoke in this way, but they intended to seize and bind him, as they later did. They did this in anger, as James says: “The anger of man does not work the righteousness of God” (James I). And as he says elsewhere: “Be angry and do not sin” (Ps. IV); “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. IV).

They opened their mouths wide against me. They opened them when they accused him of blasphemies. And “they opened their mouths wide against me” because they not only sinned against me but also insulted me, saying: “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross, and we will believe him” (Matt. XXVII). They said: “Good, good.” As the Gospel says: “Well done, good and faithful servant” (Luke XIX). Or this is the voice of the Jews [Col. 0928B], as if they were saying: Good—we see clearly that what we awaited, those powers you performed, were nothing. Or they said “good” deceitfully. “Our eyes have seen,” because you do not show partiality to any person and you have no concern for anyone.

You have seen, Lord—their mockeries, Father. It is as though he were saying: You have seen them, in order to judge them. Do not be silent, Lord; do not remain mute. He is silent now and is not silent: that is, he does not silence the commandment, but he is silent in judgment. I call you as witness when I judge the world. Do not depart from me, because the Father did not depart from the Son in his passion. Rather, may I cling to your right hand until they are punished with fitting vengeance.

Rise up, Lord, rise up. That is, come to my aid. Attend to my judgment—that is, distinguish between me and the [Col. 0928C] Jews. Attend to my judgment, because the punishment is equal but the guilt is different. That is, when he hung with those thieves, he himself hung innocent. Rise up and attend to my judgment: how those who judged condemned me to death. My God and my Lord, take up my cause. This is the voice of humanity speaking to divinity; it speaks on behalf of the flesh. Judge me according to your great mercy. Hence he said, “Attend to my judgment”—that is, make a distinction between me and them.

Judge me according to your righteousness, Lord my God. I judged the adulterous woman so that she would not be condemned; these men judged me, an innocent man, worthy of death. Therefore let each person receive the judgment deserved according to his own work. Let not my enemies rejoice over me; lest they say in their hearts, “Good, good for our soul”; [Col. 0928D] nor let them say, “We shall devour him.” Let their mouths not be opened further to devour me, lest they say, “We shall devour him.” A person devours what he puts into his mouth. But here he says “devour” because sinners wish to devour the saints—that is, to make them into one body.

Let those who rejoice at my misfortunes be ashamed and confounded together. That is, the demons, the Jews, the heretics, and the persecutors—those who rejoice at my misfortunes, meaning not only those who commit them but also those who consent to their perpetrators. Let those who speak evil against me be clothed with confusion and reverence. These aforementioned people will be clothed with eternal confusion. Hence he says: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire” (Matt. XXV), so that those who judged me as though I were a man [Col. 0929A] may see God judging. Here the prophet speaks to the Father.

Let those who desire my righteousness exult and rejoice. Those awaiting Christ, who is the Father’s righteousness. Or, “Let those who desire my righteousness exult and rejoice”: that is, let the saints who desire to fulfill God’s righteousness exult and rejoice in the reward of eternal life. And let them say: “The Lord be magnified forever,” those who desire the peace of his servant. He himself is our peace, according to the Apostle (Eph. II). “His servant”—that is, Christ, who is the servant of God the Father. Hence he says: “It is a great thing for you to be called my servant” (Isa. XLIX), speaking on behalf of the flesh.

But my tongue shall meditate on your righteousness. “My tongue” means the saints, who meditate upon Christ’s commandments. [Col. 0929B] “All the day long, your praise.” “All the day long” means praising God at all times. But “my tongue shall meditate on your righteousness” because, having died for the life of the people, you were not abandoned in the underworld. “All the day long, your praise,” because, having conquered death and triumphed, you were received into heaven by the Father, with whom, and with the Holy Spirit, you possess honor and glory. Amen.

## PSALM XXXV

A psalm of David, for the end, concerning the servant of the Lord. This psalm portrays the person of the sinner, marks out pride, reveals the fountain of eternal light.

The unjust man said within himself, so as to sin. That is, against himself: the unjust man, namely, the devil with his satellites—that is, the Jewish people—or he sinned against himself through his remaining members. No one else speaks through injustice in such a way as to sin, like the one who said: [Col. 0929C] “I will place my throne above the stars, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV). For iniquity always pierces itself with its own dart, according to the saying: “My son, if you become evil, you alone will suffer evil” (Prov. XII). Or otherwise: “The wicked man said that he would sin against himself”—that is, he resolved that he ought to sin. There is no fear of God before his eyes. For if he had the fear of God before his eyes, he would never commit detestable and abominable deeds. “There is no fear of God before his eyes”—that is, before the Jewish people, because if they had possessed the fear of the Lord before the eyes of their hearts, they would never have done such great evils.

For he acted deceitfully in his presence—the devil and the Jews before the sight of God. Or, “he acted deceitfully in his presence,” driven on by the flame of wicked desire, so that his iniquity and hatred might be discovered. While [Col. 0929D] he desired iniquity against righteousness, and was unable to take it away, he acquired hatred. But the following words also show that this concerns Judas the betrayer.

The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit. He said: “Hail, Rabbi,” and with a kiss he handed the teacher over to his enemies. Behold, the words of his mouth, full of deceit and iniquity. “The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit,” both in the devil and in the Jewish people. He refused to understand so as to act well. That is, the devil and his satellites, because not being able is one thing, and not wishing is another. Judas saw Christ every day with the apostles performing many wonders, but he did not understand. For wisdom does not enter into a malicious soul.

He devised iniquity in his bedchamber. In the secret place of the heart [Col. 0930A], where he ought to have been pierced with remorse, he devised iniquity, as we have already mentioned above. “In his bedchamber”—that is, in their heart. He stood upon every evil way. Because he stood there, he could attain no fruit of righteousness.
