But he did not hate wickedness; rather, he loved it, because they not only did not hate it but embraced it.

Lord, your mercy is in heaven. That is, in the holy angels who were established there and did not fall. Or, “your mercy is in heaven”—that is, in the holy Church. Lord, your mercy is in heaven: Christ the Lord, who, having compassion on human labors, descended from heaven to bind up our wounds. And your truth reaches to the clouds. “Truth” is Christ, as in the saying: “I am the way and the truth” (John XIV). “Clouds” are the holy preachers. [Col. 0930B] Hence it is said: “I will command my clouds not to rain rain upon it” (Isa. I). For just as clouds carry rain and water the earth, so the holy preachers carry the rain—that is, the teaching of the Gospel—and water hearts that are parched. “And your truth reaches to the clouds.” Those who refuse to understand the Scriptures spiritually should be asked how God’s truth reaches to the clouds.

Your righteousness [Col. 0930C] is like the mountains of God. The mountain of God is wisdom; the mountain of God is judgment; the mountain of God is sanctification. There are also many mountains of this kind, in which the secrets of God are stored—secrets that human nature can scarcely investigate—according to the Apostle: “How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” (Rom. XI). Or otherwise: “Your righteousness is like the mountains of God.” Your righteousness means your commandments. “The mountains of God” are the saints of greater merit, such as Saint John and the other apostles. Mountains are first illuminated by the sun, and afterward the valleys. But the mountains—that is, the saints—are illuminated not by themselves but by the sun, that is, by Christ. Hence he said: “The sun of righteousness shall rise for you” (Mal. IV). And your judgments are like the great abyss. “The great abyss” signifies the hidden judgments of God, because he rejects one and takes up another, as he said: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. I). Or the judgments are those by which blessedness is bestowed on the righteous and punishment on the wicked. They are compared with the abyss because they are contemplated in the depths of the New and Old Testament.

You will save human beings and beasts, Lord. Rational and irrational persons, according to the Apostle’s saying: “I am debtor both to the wise and to the foolish” [Col. 0930D] (Rom. I). How you have multiplied your mercy, O God. From the beginning your mercy was abundant; but it was multiplied when you redeemed us with your own blood.

But the sons of men will hope under the shelter of your wings. Not the brood of vipers, but those who are perfected in mind according to the image of God hope to be protected beneath the defense of your cross. Or, “the sons of men” means the sons of Christ, because he himself is the Son of Man, and the saints are sons of men. “In the protection of your wings,” or “under their shelter.” The two wings are the two Testaments, because through them the saints are protected by Christ. And they will be intoxicated—that is, these sons will be intoxicated by the abundance of your house, by the richness of the grace of the Holy Spirit. “Your house” means the holy Church [Col. 0931A]. Or, “they will be intoxicated” so that, having forgotten their sins, they may be joined to virtues. “From the abundance of your house”—from the understanding of ecclesiastical doctrines. And you will give them drink from the torrent of your delight. God’s torrent of delight is the Holy Spirit, who irrigates every soul with spiritual streams so that it may produce the fruit of holiness.

For with you, Lord, is the fountain of life. You are it, and with you is the source of all good things; and you grant baptism, through which, when crimes have been washed away, you bestow the way to eternity. Or, “the fountain of life,” because the teaching of God is life for the soul. In your light we shall see light. The light of the Father is Christ. In Christ, the Father’s light, we shall see the light of the Holy Spirit. Your light is the Father; doing his will, you came to illuminate the hidden things of darkness [Col. 0931B], so that in you, who are the light of the world, we might deserve to behold that light through the grace of a pure mind. For he says to Philip: “Whoever sees me sees my Father also” (John XIV). “In his light”—that is, in Christ—we shall see light: that is, the Holy Spirit, who appeared over the apostles in the form of illuminating fire (Acts II). And “in your light we shall see light” means that we shall be illuminated by Christ, as the Gospel says: “He was the true light which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John VIII).

Extend your mercy over those who know you—those who knew that you were to come into the world. Of them you later say in the Gospel: “Many righteous people and prophets desired to see what you see, and did not see it” (Matt. XI). Not over the proud and deceitful, but over the pure in heart. [Col. 0931C] Or, “Show your mercy to those who know you”—that is, show your mercy, Lord, to those who know and understand you. And your righteousness to those who are upright in heart: your righteousness, that is, your commandments. Those who are upright in heart are those who have no duplicity of heart.

Let not the foot of pride come against me. Lest, lifted up by vanity, I fall into the devil’s snare and be unable to escape. And let not the hand of sinners move me—that is, let not the works of evil people move me from good to evil. Let it not move me so that I am torn away from you.

There all who work iniquity have fallen. In this pride and vanity, against which they ought to have stood, they fell. They have been cast out—from the kingdom of God. Nor could they stand. The demons were cast out of heaven [Col. 0931D] and could not stand. Heaven could not contain them, because they had already fallen through the feet of pride. But let us pray to the Lord that he may instill in us the fear of his name, that he may customarily bestow mercy upon us from heaven, remove from us pride, which is hostile to his good gifts, and turn away every deceit; and that, having been illuminated by knowledge of his most holy light, he may make us worthy of his kingdom. Amen.

## PSALM XXXVI

A psalm of David. The thirty-sixth psalm glorifies the person of the righteous, marks the unjust, instructs conduct, teaches the goodness of God, and uproots perversity.

Do not emulate those who act maliciously. “Emulation” has many interpretations, which must be understood or explained according to their place [Col. 0932A]. Here he says: Do not become a participant with the wicked—not through zeal and not through envy, because zeal is anger, according to what the Lord says through the prophet: “With great indignation I have been zealous for Zion” (Zech. VIII). Envy, however, is resentment, according to the saying: “I killed the young man in my envy” (Gen. IV). Nor should you be zealous for those who commit iniquity. Do not imitate those who gather riches through wicked frauds and seek honor; but attend to God and seek apostolic goodness.

For they will quickly wither like grass, and like the green plants of herbs they will soon fall. Properly, this carnal glory and worldly power are compared with hay, according to Isaiah: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isa. XL). For the grass withered [Col. 0932B] and its flower fell. The Apostle James added to this judgment: “So also the rich man will wither in his ways” (James I). The same must be understood about green plants, since not all vegetables are suitable for the sick.

Hope in the Lord and do good. The divine word speaks to you as to a sick person, so that among the other graces that are the fruit of the Spirit, you may display goodness. “Hope in the Lord”: always have hope in the Lord. “And do good”: that is, fulfill the commandments. Inhabit the earth—the holy Church, or your body. Rule your flesh; let the flesh not rule you. And you will feed on its riches—in the sacred books. If this earth produces the fruit of holiness, then you too will rejoice in the riches of God.

[Col. 0932C] Delight in the Lord, and he will give you the requests of your heart. The heart always asks for wisdom. Therefore, if, after admitting these delights, you delight in the Lord, he will give you the treasures of his wisdom, or whatever you ask for through faith. Hence he said: “If two of you agree on earth concerning anything that they ask from my Father, it will be done for them” (Matt. XV).

Reveal your way to the Lord. Why does he say “reveal”? Does God not know something? No; rather, you must disclose to God in speech what you have in your heart through confession. Confess your actions to him, and always hope in him, and he himself will forgive your sins. And hope in him—that he is able to forgive the sinner. And he will act. And what, you ask, will he do?

And he will bring forth your righteousness like light. To the brightness [Col. 0932D] in which you believed him. “Your righteousness”—that is, your works in brightness. And your judgment—the judgment by which you chose what is good. Like midday, in the full splendor of his grace, which he reveals before his angels. Or “midday” signifies the works of the saints.

Submit yourself to the Lord. Not to sin, but be humble before the Lord. And pray to him for present and former offenses. Hence Paul said: “First of all, let prayers, supplications, petitions, and thanksgiving be made for kings and all who are in high positions” (I Tim. II).

Do not emulate him. Do not envy him, as above. And your judgment will be like midday. For then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father, and [Col. 0933A] everything that is now hidden will be clear. Or, “Do not emulate him who prospers in his way.” Do not let the brief prosperity of the wicked terrify you. Cease from anger and forsake wrath. Do not emulate him so as to do evil. Lay aside anger, lest, suffering injustice, you be compelled to repay in kind.

He who prospers in his way—that is, he who acts successfully in this age—acts unjustly. For by sinning he casts himself headlong [Col. 0933B]; do not desire to be with one who commits iniquity.

Cease from anger, which does not accomplish the righteousness of God (James I). Forsake wrath, which, according to Solomon, destroys even the wise (Prov. XIX). Or, “cease” means: desist from anger of soul and fury of body. Do not emulate him so as to act maliciously, lest, provoking others to wickedness, you yourself become wicked.

For those who act maliciously will be exterminated, because they have no root of piety. Or, they will be exterminated from the land of the living. But those who await the Lord will inherit the land—that is, the land of promise, which flows with milk and honey.

Yet a little while, and the sinner will not be. Wait a little, and the sinner will not be; he will be taken away from here because divine vengeance will crush him. And you will seek his place, and will not find it. In the future he will not exist, nor will he receive a place of rest; you will seek his place, and will not find it. If the devil’s place is sin, there will be a time when sin will not exist. This will happen when we exult in the abundance of peace.

But the meek will inherit the land. Those whom no storm of anger agitates [Col. 0933C] and no fire of desire inflames. They will inherit that land of the living, because the gentle and humble will possess the land—that is, eternal life. And they will delight in the abundance of peace. They will delight—that is, they will rejoice in the abundance of peace, namely, in Christ, when those who are united in Christ’s kingdom are joined together; he is our peace.

The sinner watches the righteous, seeking an opportunity to harm him, because through the works of the saints they themselves are tormented and tortured in the present life—that is, inwardly in the mind, by the malice and envy they possess. And he will gnash his teeth against him, with the teeth of wickedness and malice by which he tries to devour him. Through bodily movement, as we have said, he displays the movement of the soul.

But the Lord will mock him, because he sees that his day is coming [Col. 0933D]—the day of the vengeance of God’s anger. Does the Lord mock anyone? No; rather, they are worthy to be mocked in the hour of retribution. “Because he sees that his day is coming”: that is, the Lord knows when his destruction will come.

Sinners have drawn the sword, and so forth. The sword, or the arrows, of sinners are words of seduction. The bow or the sheath is their mind, from which those words are brought forth. Or, “sinners have drawn the sword”—that is, the sword of persecutors in persecution. They have bent the bow—that is, their snare against the saints—to deceive the poor and needy. Not the rich person of the world, but the poor person of Christ. To slaughter the upright in heart: to destroy by seduction those who believe rightly. For the soul’s blood is poured out when someone is gently seduced and falls into sin. But this must be referred to the heretics, against whom we must stand firmly, so that what the prophet adds may come upon them.

Let their sword enter into their own hearts, and so forth. For everyone who speaks against God, or whose mind overflows with the foolish vanity of arrogance and, failing to attend to the Scriptures spiritually, corrupts them through a vicious interpretation, kills himself with his own dagger. And just as the apostles’ peace, if a house is unworthy, returns to them (Matt. X), so the sword in the hearts of these people, if it is drawn against the innocent, is driven into them. Or, “Let their sword enter their own hearts”: that is, let vengeance fall upon their souls. And let their bow be broken—let their snare be broken.

Better is the little that the righteous person has than the many riches of sinners. For he fears what the Lord says in the Gospel: “What does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Matt. XVI). “The little” he mentioned is faith. Although it is compared with a grain of mustard seed, it nevertheless possesses great power. Better is the little that the righteous has than the many riches of sinners. Although they are small, they are better, because Solomon said: “Better is a small portion with rest than hands full with iniquity” (Eccles. IV).

For the arms of sinners will be broken. Their arms—that is, their strength—will be broken in vengeance, so that they cannot harm the innocent. But the Lord strengthens the righteous. He strengthens the weak among those who live in faith.

The Lord knows the ways of the blameless—that is, their manner of life. The Lord knows those who are his; but the unclean and those who do not know him he does not know. For everyone who is ignorant will be ignored. And their inheritance will be forever—in Christ, who is perpetual and eternal. Or, “it will be forever”: that is, in eternal life.

They will not be confounded in the evil time, and so forth. “The evil time” indicates the time of judgment. At that time, while the righteous suffer no hunger, it is said concerning sinners: “Woe to you who are full, for you shall hunger” (Luke VI). They will not be confounded in the evil time—in the time of examination, which will be evil for the wicked. And in the days of famine they will be satisfied; and even if they cease to be ministers of the word of God, they will be refreshed in Christ, who is the living bread. [Col. 0934D] Or, “in the days of famine they will be satisfied”: that is, when those sinners are empty, then the saints will be filled with the grace of God. For sinners will perish, because they do not keep God’s commandments, unless they reform.

But the enemies of the Lord, as soon as they have been honored—in earthly power—and exalted—in empty glory—they will fail; like smoke they will fail. When death arrives, all their glory will dissolve like smoke or mist, because everything passes quickly.

The sinner will borrow and will not repay, because he will not return the Lord’s money with interest. He borrowed from the Lord—that is, the five bodily senses, or riches—and he does not give thanks to God. But the righteous shows mercy and lends [Col. 0935A]. That is, he practices mercy both toward himself and toward others; this means that he disciplines the five bodily senses. Or, “the righteous shows mercy and lends”: he has received the word and supplies spiritual things to spiritual people, so that he may gain not only himself but others as well. In this verse the showing of mercy to the poor must also be understood.

For those who bless him will inherit the land, in which God’s good things have been stored. Those who always praise God will themselves possess the land: that is, they ordinarily possess this land, and afterward they will possess the land of the living. But those who curse him will perish, as the Lord promises: “I will be an enemy to your enemies, and I will afflict those who afflict you” (Exod. XXIII).

By the Lord a person’s steps will be directed—the steps by which he tries to cross over to him. Thus Rebecca went to inquire, not from place to place but from life to life (Gen. XXIV); and Moses, having loosened the bonds of his feet, crossed over to see the bush (Exod. III). And if you set your mind on passing from death to life, your steps will be directed by the Lord not through the steps of your feet but through the power of your mind. “By the Lord the steps of human beings will be directed”: the understanding of each person, as Solomon says: “A person prepares his way, but the Lord directs his steps” (Prov. XVI). And he will desire his way, so that he may come to him who is the way, the truth, and the life. Or he desires his commandments.

When he falls, he will not be shattered. Why? Because the Lord supports his hand—that is, his works. “When he falls,” because of the weakness of the flesh: “the righteous falls seven times [Col. 0935C] and rises again”; he will not be shattered because the Lord places his hand beneath him. He immediately shows mercy to the one who repents. Thus David and Peter, once they recognized their sin, cleansed it with tears and were strengthened by the Lord.

I was young, and now I am old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken. The Apostle says: “Do not become children in your understanding, but be infants in malice” (II Cor. XIV). Therefore this person was, from the beginning of his life, a child in malice but an old man in divine virtue. He understood that the righteous could never be forsaken by the Lord, nor his offspring seeking the bread of heavenly teaching—for he provided the word to the foolish. “Nor his offspring seeking bread”: his offspring means his works; “seeking bread” means the word of God.

All day long he shows mercy and lends. “Day” means the time when each person [Col. 0935D] practices goodness. Therefore this person, throughout all the days of his life, lends out the money of his Lord—not to acquire worldly profit but to obtain heavenly gain. “All day long” means at all times. “He shows mercy,” from God: that is, he ministers God’s teaching to others. And his offspring will be in blessing. The works he performed, or the teaching he taught, will be blessed by the Lord. “Offspring” may also refer to the Christian people, who are enriched in the Church by continual blessing. And his offspring will be in blessing—in abundance and glory.

Turn away from evil—in deed—and do good, what God has commanded. “Turn away from evil and do good”: turn away from evil, from the devil or from sin, and do good—that is, fulfill the commandments. And dwell forever and ever [Col. 0936A] in the Church, in the unity of faith; remain with him perpetually.

For the Lord loves judgment—righteous judgment, by which he distinguishes the righteous from the wicked.

And he will not forsake his saints, who have placed all their hope in him. They will be preserved forever. That is, perpetually, because they desired eternal things.

The unjust will be punished—in vengeance. And the offspring of the wicked will perish. “The offspring of the wicked” means their works: they will be punished with them in torments, and all their work will be destroyed because it is unjust.

But the righteous will possess the land as an inheritance—the land of the living. And they will dwell upon it forever and ever, upon that land which is without end, from which pain and groaning have fled.

The mouth of the righteous will meditate upon wisdom—that is, upon Christ [Col. 0936B]. Hence he says: “And he will meditate upon his law day and night” (Ps. I). When he says “he will meditate,” he signifies a future time, understood as the time of action in God’s kingdom, in which the mouths of the righteous will be filled not with the wine of indulgence or luxurious foods but with the wisdom of God. And his tongue will speak judgment. When he weighs everything carefully, he recounts what he thinks about God neither deceitfully nor in anger, but with just judgment. For in the one in whom spiritual grace abounds, everything is examined, even the deep things of God.

The law of his God is in his heart—that is, in the mind of the righteous person. Not only in his mouth and tongue, but also in the depth of his heart, works of holiness will bear fruit through the law of God. And his steps will not be tripped by the adversary—the steps by which he strives to reach God. Or, “his steps will not be tripped” [Col. 0936C]: his understanding will not be tripped by the devil or by sin.

The sinner watches the righteous, and so forth. For the Jewish people watched the righteous Son of God and gnashed their teeth against him, because he was burdensome even to see. So now also the enemy watches each one of us in order to destroy us. But if a person resists vigilantly, what follows will happen.

But the Lord will not abandon him into his hands—that is, into the other’s power. Nor will he condemn him when judgment is passed against him. The wicked passes judgment so that the righteous may perish, but the Lord does not condemn him because he has kept his law. Rather, he does not condemn that righteous person on the day of judgment, when he judges the wicked.

Wait for the Lord and keep his ways. God is awaited through firm hope [Col. 0936D] and unfailing observance of the commandments; therefore we must not be confounded amid the world’s various temptations. Wait for the Lord: whatever happens to you, in prosperity or adversity, wait patiently—that is, endure. He will exalt you so that you may inherit the land. That land, certainly, of eternal blessedness, in which the righteous will be exalted after their labors have ended. When sinners have perished, you will see. Then the righteous will see sinners perish when, with the Lord granting it, they receive the fruit of their reward.

I saw the wicked man exalted and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon, and I passed by, and behold, he was no more. When we have crossed the sea of this world, then we shall see that the devil is no more, and that his place—and sin—will by no means appear.

“Cedar” has two interpretations, but in this passage its explanation is as follows: just as a cedar appears exalted above the lofty mountains, yet often falls under the force of the winds, so the wicked man who, having abandoned God, trusts in the riches of the world—however much he may flourish, however much he may raise and exalt himself—will not be found when he has departed from this world. These words also refer to Judas the betrayer. Or, “the cedar of Lebanon” may signify the saints, because of the height of their merits, and priests, because of the fragrance of good works. The wicked are above them because they trample and oppress them.

“I passed by, and behold, he was no more.” Let the apostolic company say this, because I passed through the storm of Jesus’ passion, and when he had risen, “he was no more,” because he departed and hanged himself by a noose. “I sought him, and his place was not found.” That his place was not found and that his dwelling remained desolate, Peter revealed in the Acts of the Apostles when he appointed Matthias to his office (Acts I). Or, “I passed by, and behold, he was no more; I sought him, and his place was not found”—that is, the place of the wicked man himself. “His place was not found,” because of the great speed with which the wicked perish.

Guard innocence and observe equity. If you harm no one and are quarrelsome with no one, you will see Christ, because just as he is the way, the truth, and the life, so he is also understood as equity. For there is a future for the peaceful man. Whoever lives peacefully here, so as to be called a son of God: his future—that is, his mortal body—is reserved for the glory of the resurrection, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “This mortal body must put on immortality” (1 Cor. XV). The future of the wicked will perish. In place of “future,” the Hebrew has “last things.”

“But the unjust,” and so forth: “the future of the wicked will perish.” Their future is not preserved because of their pride, so that they may live forever; rather, they will perish in punishment by the fire of Gehenna.

But the salvation of the righteous is from the Lord. Through him they receive the present life and await the attainment of eternal life. “But the salvation of the righteous is from the Lord.” He himself is our salvation. “And he is their protector in time of tribulation.” “He will help them,” and so forth. Therefore he will save them, and he is their protector in time of tribulation, when they walk along the narrow way that leads to life, a way full of pains and hardships. And the Lord will help them and deliver them from sinners; he will save those who have hoped in him when he leads them to the perfection of a pure mind. They have deserved to come to him because they have hoped in him. For in all their troubles they placed their hope in him who said: “I am God, and there is no other besides me. I kill, and I make alive; I strike, and I heal” (Deut. XXXII). May he heal all the sicknesses of our minds and grant us to raise our hope with our whole heart, and give us to place it in him, so that, freed from sins, we may deserve, by his distribution, to obtain also the reward of eternity.

## PSALM XXXVII

[Col. 0938A]

To the end: a psalm of David, for the remembrance of the Sabbath day. “Sabbath” is interpreted as “rest”; that is, when the saints rest—when that Church rests in the paradise-rest which it lost in Adam. This psalm shows that if weakness befalls bodily frailty, it should not cease to seek heavenly medicine.

Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger. The whole psalm is spoken in the person of the penitent, but it can be referred to Christ, as can Psalm Sixty-Eight. “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger.” Anger, as we have often said, is a disturbance of the mind. Fury, however, is irrational vengeance, accompanied by the bitterness of gall. Therefore this man, who knows himself to be a sinner, asks to be rebuked not in anger but through mercy, and not in fury but through patience.

For your arrows are fixed in me. These are the words of instruction which, like a javelin, pierced my heart, so that I might do penance. And you have strengthened your hand upon me, so that, like a good teacher, you might make me, afflicted by the blows of correction, improved.

There is no health in my flesh because of the face of your anger. I saw the face of your anger, but not the anger itself; that is, through the holy Scriptures I understood how greatly you threaten sinners, and I trembled, asking that this anger itself might not descend upon me. There is no peace in my bones because of the face of my sins. I granted no rest either to my bones or to my limbs until I had cleansed them through repentance.

For my iniquities have risen above my head. They have prevailed against me, as follows: “They have been laid upon me like a heavy burden.” My sin is not light to me; I acknowledge that it has imposed upon me the heavy weight of judgment and has grown above the crown of my head. As a great weight, so are my sins upon me.

My wounds have become foul and corrupt. It is the custom of pigs to use mud or dung in place of good odors; nor do they understand that they are wallowing in these things most filthily. But my sins’ wounds stink and putrefy for me, and I eagerly seek a physician. And why, you ask, have they putrefied? “Because of the face of my foolishness.” Because I was unwilling to do penance. “Because of the face of my foolishness”: through this they putrefied, namely, through my foolishness, as Paul says: “What is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (1 Cor. II).

I have become wretched and bowed down to the end. Until I was cleansed by confessing, because sins are not forgiven without shame and grief. All day long I walked in sorrow, judging myself unworthy even to dare to lift my eyes to heaven; but, beating my breast, I said: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.”

For my loins are filled with mockeries. He confesses that he has been weakened and filled with those mockeries by which the devil entices the human race to sin. “God, you have known my foolishness, for my loins are filled with mockeries.” Let each person examine himself and recognize the body’s enticing pleasure; then he can say with the Apostle Paul: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. VII). And this: “For indeed I do not do what I want, but what I do not want.”

[Col. 0939A]

I am bowed down and humbled exceedingly. For repentance. I roared because of the groaning of my heart, asking with mourning for forgiveness. One thing is the groaning of the body, and another the groaning of the heart. The groaning of the body is groaning on account of earthly things or on account of death. The groaning of the heart is on account of one’s own sins or those of others. But Christ had nothing over which to groan, because he committed no sin. And my groaning was not hidden from you. That is, God knows whatever a person has. Whatever I have done wrong, whatever evil I have committed, I have disclosed everything to you with groaning, knowing that hidden things are not concealed from you.

My heart was troubled within me; my strength abandoned me. Because I dread incurring the anger I mentioned above. And the light of my eyes is not with me. Because, having set aside the light of truth, I had fallen into the darkness of sins. Thus, our predecessors taught that the prophet followed the whole sequence of this psalm in the person of the sinner. Let them think what they please. But I, from the place where he says, “My friends and my neighbors,” to the end of the psalm, see my Lord Jesus Christ surrounded by the Jews, hung upon the cross, and rising from the underworld. Therefore the Lord himself says concerning his passion:

My friends and my neighbors approached and stood against me. The Jews are called “friends” because of Abraham. “Neighbors,” because he assumed flesh from their lineage; they approached him in order to seize him. My friends and my acquaintances stood against me. This can also be understood of the disciples, who, terrified by fear during the passion, withdrew from the Lord, to such an extent that even Peter denied him. Or, they stood there accusing him.

And those who were near me stood far away. The apostles or the remaining disciples, of whom the evangelist says: “When they had seized him, all his acquaintances stood at a distance” (Luke XXIII). And those who sought my life used force. It was not the acquaintances but the Jews who used force—or against Peter, when they said: “You too are one of them” (Luke XXII); or against James, who, when he was being dragged away, left his linen garment and fled from them naked (Mark XIV). “And those who sought my life used force,” as though their strength belonged to them and they had not received that power from God.

[Col. 0939D]

And those who sought evil against me spoke vanities and meditated on deceit all day long. They meditated many deceits when they asked whether they ought to pay tribute to Caesar or not (Matt. XXII), or whether the woman caught in adultery should be stoned (John VIII). But they openly introduce deceit when they bring false witnesses. Or, “those who sought evil against me spoke vanity” when they said: “He casts out demons by Beelzebul” (Luke XI).

But I, like a deaf man, did not hear, and like a mute man who does not open his mouth. I always endured what they reproached me with and continually remained silent. Pilate also makes this clear when he says: “You do not answer me? Do you not know that I have authority to release you?” (John XIX). “But I, like a mute man who does not open his mouth.” The Lord did not speak before Pilate. Isaiah speaks of the same one: “Like a lamb led to the sacrifice, he did not open his mouth” (Isa. LII).

And I became like a man who does not hear and has no reproofs in his mouth. For when they smeared me with spittle, beat me with a reed, and mocked me on bended knee, I answered them nothing, moved by none of it. “And has no reproofs in his mouth.” Thus I remained silent when accused, as though I had nothing that I ought to say in my defense. In all things Christ gave an example, so that a person ought patiently to endure blows and correction.

For in you, Lord, I have hoped; you will hear me, Lord my God. So that you may raise me up. Or, “you will hear me”: that is, see their pride and my humility.

For I said, lest my enemies ever rejoice over me; and when my feet are shaken. Christ’s feet during the passion—or the holy apostles, who ought to have been Christ’s feet—were shaken from faith to unbelief. “My feet” can be shaken from their steadfastness, and the enemies can insult me, if, having been humbled in this death on the cross, I do not rise again. “They spoke great things against me,” saying: “If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross” (Matt. XXVII).

But I am ready for scourging. I prepare myself to endure the cross, the lance, gall, and vinegar, so that through this death I may redeem with my blood the perishing people, because Christ came for this purpose: to endure suffering. And my pain is always before me, until I bring forth victory in judgment.

For I shall declare my iniquity and consider my sin. Just as he became subject to the curse in order to free us from the curse of the Law, so also he professes himself a sinner, who bore our sins, in order that by devoted thought and a plan of mercy he might free us from those same sins. And I shall be anxious over my sin. Christ’s sin is the offenses of the human race; because of these he is now said to be subject to the Father.

But my enemies live. For they were not immediately punished by divine vengeance. And they were strengthened against me. They were strengthened in the letter of the Law, in which they did not understand what had been announced spiritually. And those who hate me unjustly have multiplied. Certainly, unjustly and without reason, because in this letter they thought that their offspring would multiply like the stars of heaven.

Those who repaid me evil for good. They gave him to drink vinegar and gall, though he brought the sweetness of eternal life. They slandered me, saying: “He saved others; he cannot save himself” (Luke XXIII). For I pursued goodness, so that, fulfilling the Father’s will, I might accept death for the life of the people.

Do not abandon me, Lord my God; do not depart from me. When I have penetrated the depths of the underworld.

Attend to my help, Lord, God of my salvation. It is clear, Lord Jesus, that the Father attended to you, raising you from the dead on the third day and placing you at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality and power, giving you the name that is above every name. Therefore, since the struggles of the flesh are severe, attend to our help, Lord, and be our salvation in time of tribulation.

## PSALM XXXVIII

To the end: a song of David, for Jeduthun. “Jeduthun” is interpreted as “leaping over them.” This psalm teaches patience, so that, restraining his mouth, a person may take care not to fall into sin through foolish words, because the prophet knows that an account must even be given for idle words. It also teaches us to store up in this age those things that contribute to the advancement of souls.

I said: I shall guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue. I know no other way to guard the paths of my life than not to speak foolish, inappropriate, or idle words. “From your words,” says the Lord, “you will be justified, and from your words you will be condemned.” “I said: I shall guard my ways”—that is, I resolved to guard my works, namely, the five bodily senses. “So that I may not sin with my tongue.” “I shall not sin”: I shall not commit sin, because “whoever guards his tongue guards his soul” (Prov. XVIII), and “death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Isa. XXXII). And again: “The worship of justice is silence and peace” (Ecclus. XXVIII).

I placed a guard over my mouth. In accordance with this: “Bind your money and gold securely, and make a door and bolt for your mouth.” For guarding the mouth makes a person blessed, when he does not utter empty things but things worthy of God. When the sinner stood against me. That is, the devil, who curses and slanders the righteous and is the instigator of those who lie in wait for the saints.

I was silent, lest I answer back to those rebuking me. I was silent and did not open my mouth, because you did it. Therefore I endure patiently, because I know that you have left me to temptations for testing. And I was humbled, to endure their reproaches. And I was silent from good things. Security proceeded from a good conscience; therefore I did not justify myself before human beings, nor did I publicize the good things that were in me, because I know that the Father, who sees in secret, will repay me. And my pain was renewed. For I had not yet come to the perfect man. For although I endured reproaches with pain, I did not yet know how to bless those who cursed me. Or, “my pain was renewed.” This is said of Christ’s pain, because they were not worthy to hear the words of the mystery, as the prophet says: “Woe is me, because I was silent” (Isa. VI). Or this: “I will make your tongue cling to the roof of your mouth, because the Lord is provoking” (Ezek. III).

My heart grew hot within me. The Church speaks. By the remembrance of former offenses. And in my meditation the fire will blaze. “What,” you ask, “were you meditating on?” This, certainly: how I might find that fire which would consume sins and illuminate the mind—which is the Holy Spirit. Concerning him Cleopas and those who were with him said: “Was not our heart burning within us when he spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke XXIV).

I spoke with my tongue. That is, I preached to all people, in accordance with this: “If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked man, I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezek. III). Make my end known to me, Lord, and what is the number of my days? The prophet does not ask to have the end of this life made known to him, but the end in which, after the powers have been emptied and death destroyed, he will be joined to Christ, who is the end of the Law. Nor does he wish to know the number of these days, but of those concerning which the Lord says: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John XIV). “And what is the number of my days?” That is: number without number, day without day, times without time. “What is it?” That which always is.

So that I may know what I lack. That is, so that you may make me understand all good things, so that, when I have come to know them, I may understand what is still lacking for me, while dwelling in this age, in order to attain the palm of blessedness. Paul was perfect, for he said: “I have fought the good fight; I have completed the course. Now the crown of righteousness is lacking for me, which the Lord will repay me” (2 Tim. IV). That he is not speaking these things about his own days is shown by what follows.

Behold, you have made my days measurable. Until now they belonged to the old man; now I desire the new—the one whom Abraham saw and rejoiced to see (John VIII). Elsewhere we are urged to rejoice in him, in whom the Lord God has shone upon us. He will not be illumined by the sun or the moon, but shines with perpetual light from the Lord himself. And my substance is as nothing before you. Receiving your brightness with a higher mind, I judged my substance as nothing.

Nevertheless, all is vanity; every living person. If he is a sinner and has flowed along in pleasures, he rests upon vanity. If he is righteous and desires to be dissolved and to be with Christ, his present life is nevertheless vanity for him.

Nevertheless, a person passes by as an image of God, but is troubled in vain.

[Note: The words “of God” are found neither in the Hebrew text nor in the Greek, nor finally in the Latin text as read by Saint Augustine; they seem to have entered the Roman Psalter, as it is called, from these commentaries or from Augustine’s own interpretation.]

Every person was made in the image of God. If, therefore, he appears to walk in that image while engaging in acts of robbery and desires, he is troubled in his conduct.

He treasures up, and does not know for whom he will gather them. Often many people treasure up and accumulate much, which either the laziness of their children overturns, or the treasury seizes, or strangers plunder. But blessed is the one who treasures up where thieves do not dig through or steal (Matt. VI), where he may deserve to hear: “As long as you did it for one of these least ones, you did it for me” (Matt. XXV).

And now what is my expectation? Is it not the Lord? And my substance is with you. Having abandoned everything, I shall await you, Lord, because the substance of this life cannot be compared with that eternal blessedness.

[Col. 0943A]

Deliver me from all my iniquities, past, present, and future. You have made me a reproach to the fool. While I was a sinner, I became a reproach to the foolish devil, who is both the originator and the accuser of all crimes. Therefore I desire to be cleansed in this age, lest he accuse me in your judgment.

I was silent and did not open my mouth, because you did it. When he attacked me with insults, anger, and various reproaches, I considered that I had been made by you and answered nothing to what was brought against me: “Remove your scourges from me.” For I know myself to have been corrected.

By the strength of your hand I have failed. As the hand of vengeance pressed upon me, the strength of sin failed, as the Apostle Paul says: “When I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Cor. XII). Because of iniquity you corrected a person with rebukes. Every person is rebuked because of iniquity, whom the divine majesty does not wish to destroy. “He scourges every son whom he accepts.”

You made his soul waste away like a spider’s web. The soul wastes away when the flesh is restrained from luxuries and desires. This is what it means to waste away: to be stunned by former offenses. But the one who does those things that belong to worldly vanity weaves spiderwebs, according to the prophet Isaiah (Isa. LIX); that is, day and night he is occupied with futile work and does not produce useful things, but things subject to dissolution rather than incorruptibility. But because the prophet says that the soul wastes away like a spider’s web, this must be understood as meaning that through abstinence it is refined to such subtlety that it is drawn out like those threads, so that it contains nothing coarse or hard belonging to sin. Nevertheless, every living person is troubled in vain, living amid the vanities of this age. But even for one who lives in God, this useless worldly disturbance is vain.

Hear my prayer, Lord, and my supplication; perceive my tears with your ears. Because I am a stranger from you, and I desire to be dissolved and to pass over to you.

Do not be silent, because I am a sojourner with you and a pilgrim, like all my fathers. He calls himself both a resident and a pilgrim, like all the saints, because, while they were in the body, they too were pilgrims away from the Lord.

Forgive me, so that I may be refreshed before I depart and exist no longer. Here forgive me, Lord, if I have done anything wrong, because in the underworld there is no forgiveness, since confession is of no avail there either. May you deem us worthy, rescued from the pilgrimage of this age, to become fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God the Father, so that, built upon the firmest foundation as a holy temple, we may deserve to be conformed to the body of your glory. Amen.

## PSALM XXXIX

To the end: a psalm of David. At its beginning this psalm contains the voice of the people called from the nations to the inheritance, and thereafter the voice of the Mediator himself speaking to the Father.

I waited patiently for the Lord. In the promises of the prophets, in which he illumined me, because the prophet foresaw through the Holy Spirit that Christ would come in the flesh. And he inclined toward me, through the splendor of the Gospels in which he illumined me.

And he heard my prayers. For he had hidden himself from the prophets and patriarchs, as he later said himself: “Many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see, and did not see it” (Luke X). He shines upon me in the New Testament. And he led me out of the pit of misery and the mire of filth, in which I was immersed when I worshiped mute images. Or, “the mire of filth,” because I had clung to earthly desires.

He established my feet upon a rock. “Upon a rock”—that is, upon Christ. “My feet”—my senses, in accordance with this: “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. X). In himself, who is the steadfast rock, he strengthened me, so that I would not waver under the assaults of this age. And he directed my steps, so that, coming to him, I would not look back. “And he directed my steps”—that is, the perceptions of good works. He directs the Church, because each person is crooked in himself.

And he put a new song into my mouth, namely, his praise, because a new man came into the world and gave the world a new law. “A song to our God”: praise to our God, so that I may no longer sing shameful and theatrical sounds, but may delight in the hymns of the living God through the harmony of the New Testament.

Many will see. They will see that he has been announced as having come. And they will fear, those who understand themselves to be sinners. And they will hope in the Lord, so that their former offenses may be forgiven them.

Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord. In this hope he is filled with every good thing. Happy is that soul which has firm faith and directed hope in Christ. And it did not turn toward vanities and false insanities. Everything that is in the world is vanity, according to Solomon (Eccles. I). False insanities are anger, quarrels, plunder, and the rest—in which people rage in order to sin—which the Apostle calls works of the flesh (Gal. I).

You have done many wonders, Lord my God, and no one is like you in your thoughts. You showed our fathers many wonders, which they did not believe. You revealed to them in the Law that you would come, and they did not understand; but we believed. Up to this point the believing people speak; from here the Lord himself begins to speak to the Father:

I announced and spoke. Saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. III). They have multiplied beyond number. The Jews in their wickedness. Or, “beyond number”—that is, sinners are beyond and outside the number, because they are not worthy to be counted among the number of the righteous.

Sacrifice and offerings you did not desire, but you prepared ears for me. You did not ask for burnt offerings or offerings for sin. The Apostle openly explains this: that when the Lord came, the sacrifices of the Jews ceased. “It is impossible,” he says, “for the blood of goats or bulls to take away sins” (Heb. X). Therefore, entering the world, he says: “You did not desire sacrifice and offering, but you prepared a body for me. You were not pleased with a burnt offering or an offering for sin unless I presented myself to you as a sacrifice for the sin of the whole world.”

Then I said: Behold, I come. In the heading of the book it is written concerning me. Because you changed the sacrifices and ceremonies of the Jews, the Sabbaths, and the superstitions of the old Law through the religion of the spiritual Gospel, therefore I come joyfully into the world, and it is written concerning me: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I). “Then I said: Behold, I come,” so that I might assume flesh in which to suffer. “In the heading of the book it is written concerning me.” The heading of the book of the Old Testament begins in this way: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. I)—that is, in Christ the Lord. John also perceived this mystery and began his Gospel in this way: “In the beginning,” he says, “was the Word, and the Word was God.” When the Jews asked him who he was, he himself replied: “The Beginning” (John VIII). Therefore understand “the heading of the book” as the beginning, which is Christ Jesus, who was announced in this heading of the book.

To do your will, my God, I desired. For I descended from heaven, not to do my own will but yours, Father. It is not the will of the flesh but of the Father, that I should die for the life of human beings. And your law is in the midst of my heart, the law which I did not come to abolish but to fulfill.

I announced your righteousness in the great Church. I give you thanks, Savior of the world, because you made your Church great, called from the four quarters of the world through evangelical preaching, gathered through your passion, and cleansed through your resurrection. In the great Church spread throughout the whole world.

Behold, I will not restrain my lips, Lord; you know, and so forth. I was not silent, nor did I speak anything secretly, but I preached incessantly all your power—that you are righteous, truthful, merciful, and the salvation of all—not only in the churches of the peoples but also in the synagogues of the Jews. “Behold, I will not restrain my lips.” Christ’s lips are holy. He does not restrain them from preaching, as Saint Paul says: “The word of God is not bound” (2 Tim. II). “You know”: you know that I did not do this—that is, I did not restrain them. “I did not hide your righteousness in my heart”—that is, your commandments. “I proclaimed your truth and your salvation.” Truth and salvation are Christ; the saints preach this. “I did not conceal your mercy and your truth from the great synagogue”—that is, I announced them to the entire people.

But you, Lord, do not keep your mercies far from me; your mercy and your truth have always received me. For evils beyond number have surrounded me. That he asks for the Father’s mercy, says that he is surrounded by the Jews and that iniquities have multiplied against him, says that he has been abandoned by his heart and again implores the Father’s protection—all this must be referred to the weakness of the flesh, so that he may be believed to be true God and true man. “But you, Lord, do not keep your mercies far from me.” Not far, but near. “Your mercy and your truth have always received me.” Mercy causes sins to be forgiven. Truth repays each person according to what he has done. My iniquities have seized me, and I could not see. That is, the human race is surrounded by original sins, and I could not see because that light of truth had been withdrawn. Hence it was said: “From the earth you will be blinded, and from the earth you will be illumined.”

They have multiplied beyond the hairs of my head. That is, these iniquities have multiplied against the human race. My heart has abandoned me. When a person sins, he does not have his heart. Hence David said: “Your servant found his heart” (2 Sam. VII). Therefore, before that, when he sinned, he did not possess it.

May it please you, Lord, to deliver me. The Church asks Christ: “May this please you, that you deliver me.” Look upon my help. Weakness has the desire to obtain, but not the power.

Let them be confounded. In their perverse thoughts, so that they may perceive what is right—either correct themselves here or be ashamed in the future. That is, so that they may have reverence.

Let them be turned backward, those who have followed an evil course.

Let them immediately bear their confusion, those who say to me, “Well done, well done.” In mercy he asks that they be confounded, so that they may immediately recognize justice. Let those who will not correct themselves carry their confusion. “Those who say to me, ‘Well done, well done.’” The Church has two enemies: flatteries and blasphemies.

Let those who desire my righteousness rejoice and be glad—that is, faith and works—and let them always say: “May the Lord be magnified.” May the people of the saints be magnified. Hence he said: “Let them see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V). Those who love your salvation—that is, your Christ. The prophet says this concerning those to whom the Lord himself says through the Gospel: “If you love me and my words remain in you, whatever you ask will be done for you” (John XV).

But I am needy and poor. God, help me. Christ was needy and poor: although he was rich, he became needy. The needy person is one who has something but lacks something else. The poor person is one who has nothing. “Helpless,” that is, without assistance.

Be my helper and deliverer, Lord; my God, do not delay. These words also must be referred to bodily fear. For the divinity that was in the assumed human being is subject to no suffering, but in the same power in which it was, it remains and will remain, now and then, forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM XL

To the end: a psalm of David. The prophet sang this psalm through the Holy Spirit in the person of Christ. At the beginning the psalm contains the voice of the prophet announcing Christ; thereafter, the voice of the Mediator himself speaking to the Father. These things were fulfilled most fully in the Gospels.

Blessed is the one who understands concerning the needy and the poor. Whoever recognizes that Christ came in the flesh he assumed, in which he became poor and needy for our sake, receives the riches of heavenly blessedness. The Lord himself became poor, since he had nowhere to lay his head (Luke IX). He became needy when he showed that he was refreshed in the needy. “Blessed is the one who understands.” Blessed and happy is the one who understands concerning the needy and the poor. Christ became needy and poor for our sake, so that his poverty might make us rich. “Who understands”: that is, who understands that he is true God and true man. On the evil day the Lord delivered him. On the day of judgment, on which Christ will condemn the Jews who do not understand us [variant: “do not understand”]. An evil day will come upon you if you do not understand concerning the needy and the poor.

May the Lord preserve him, so that he may not depart from this understanding in the present. And give him life, transferring him, while he perseveres in this wisdom, from death to life. And make him blessed with his saints in the kingdom of heaven. On earth, in the holy Church, or on the day of eternity. And do not hand him over to his enemies, that is, into the power of the devil, who always remains an enemy of our faith.

May the Lord assist him upon his bed of pain. “May he assist him”—that is, may he grant him help. “Upon the bed of pain,” in the weakness of the flesh. Or this can be understood of the paralytic, when the Lord said: “Rise, take up your bed” (Matt. IX), because “the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. IX). In the sickness of this body, in which the soul rests as in a little bed, may it be comforted by the help of the Lord’s protection. You have disturbed his entire bed in his sickness. The body, as we have said, is understood as the bed; you disturbed it through various tribulations, so that, tested and cleansed from enticements, you might take it up. Here the prophet changes the order and brings forth the voice of the Lord’s human nature speaking:

I said: Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you. His soul was sorrowful even to death—not because of an original crime, but because he was sorrowful for the sins of the people. Or the Church says: “Have mercy on me,” because there are many who commit sins but put forward words of excuse. Hence the Church says: “I accuse myself for my sins, because I have sinned.”

My enemies spoke evil against me: When will he die and his name perish? When they saw the blind being illumined, lepers cleansed, Sabbaths dissolved, and Lazarus raised from the dead; when they said: “Behold, the whole world has gone after him” (John XIV)—what else could they think except that his power should be taken from him by death? For one of them, named Caiaphas, although he did not know what he was saying, declared: “It is better that one man should die for the people, so that the whole nation may not perish.” “When will he die?” This is what is written in the Gospel parable, when the tenants said: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours, and his name will no longer be remembered” (Mark XII).

And if they entered to see, their hearts spoke vanity. Entering the praetorium, they spoke from an evil heart, saying: “Everyone who makes himself king opposes Caesar” (John XIX). Or they entered for this purpose: to extinguish the Church and to investigate, as Paul says: “False brothers who slipped in to spy out our freedom” (Gal. II). Their heart spoke vanity with a tongue feigning affection, in accordance with this: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth” (Matt. XXII). This is vanity. They gathered iniquity for themselves, crying: “What is that to us? You see to it. His blood be upon us and upon our children.”

They went out. Out, with Pilate. And they spoke among themselves. “All my enemies whispered against me; against me they devised evil.” Bringing forward unjust witnesses and seeking to kill me. “Against me they whispered”—that is, they murmured. “All my enemies devised evil against me”: the Jews mentioned above, or the heretics who now oppose the Church.

They contrived an unjust charge against me. Saying: “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone, but you take him and crucify him” (John XVIII). Or when they said: “He casts out demons by Beelzebul” (Luke XI); and they sent false witnesses not only against the living but also against the dead.

Does one who sleeps not add to this, that he should rise again? They hastened to kill me as though, after death, I would not rise again. This is to say: Will one who has been unjustly oppressed by the wicked in the sleep of death not rise? As another prophet said: “Will one who falls not rise?” (Jeremiah VIII). For the grain of wheat fell, and a plentiful harvest rose.

[Col. 0948C] Indeed, the man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, magnified his treachery against me. Here he most clearly denounces Judas as the betrayer, just as the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “The one to whom I shall give the morsel after dipping it is he” (John XIII); and elsewhere: “He has lifted his heel against me.” As for what he says, “who ate”: this means that he who, as an apostle, received and distributed to others the heavenly food that gives life to this world, himself handed this life over to death for the price of his greed.

But you, O Lord, have mercy on me, and raise me up, and I will repay them. Our Lord was raised by the Father’s power, and sits at his right hand. Before he rose again, vengeance overtook Judas, when the death he deserved rebuked him. By saying, “I will repay him,” he threatens him with future judgment.

[Col. 0948D] By this I know that you desired me. Raising me up. For my enemy will not rejoice over me. The devil, at whose prompting the Jews carried out these deeds, did not rejoice by retaining him in the underworld.

But you received me because of my innocence, and established me in your presence forever. Great indeed is this innocence, when the just man dies for the unjust—the one who bore not his own sins but ours. Because of this innocence, and because death had been conquered by the Father, he was received in heaven with the flesh he had assumed.

Blessed is the Lord God of Israel from age to age; and unto age, let it be, let it be. In place of “let it be, let it be,” the Hebrew has *amen, amen*, which Aquila translated as πεπιστομένως (*pepistomenōs*), that is, “truly” or “faithfully.” And it should be understood that here the first book of the Psalter ends. The second extends from Psalm XLI through Psalm LXXI; the third from Psalm LXXII through Psalm LXXXVIII; the fourth from Psalm LXXXIX through Psalm CV; and the fifth from Psalm CVI through the end.

## PSALM XLI

**For the end; an instruction for the sons of Korah. A psalm.** “For the end,” in Christ; “an instruction,” that is, spiritual understanding; “for the sons of Korah,” that is, for the sons of Christ, who are believers. The psalm contains the voice of the Church, or of the faithful person who longs for God.

As the deer longs for springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God. First, it must be understood why, or in what manner, the deer longs for springs of water. [Note: What is compared here to deer by nature, many of the ancient Fathers twist toward a moral interpretation, especially Epiphanius in the *Physiologus*, where he says that a deer, after drawing out serpents by its breath and devouring them, is destined to die unless it forestalls the poison within the space of three hours. Our author here seems to have taken this from Epiphanius’s testimony.]

For this is its habit: when it finds a serpent, it draws it in through its nostrils, and afterward, burning with heat, extinguishes its thirst. Thus the man of the Church, who had long lived in a poisonous practice, when he sees himself filled with the filth of fornication and the stench of idolatry, desires to come to Christ, in whom is the fountain of light, so that, washed in baptism, he may receive the gift of forgiveness. For he knows that unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not have eternal life (John III). But if any one of us today, with his vices extinguished, burns with desire for contemplation of the Lord, he too can say: “My soul longs for you, O God”; that is, having abandoned the world, I desire to pass over to you.

[Col. 0949C] My soul thirsted for the strong and living God. Not for dead images, but for him who said: “As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me” (Numbers XIV). He is living because he himself says: “As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so the one who believes in me will also live because of me” (John VI). When shall I come and appear before the face of my God? As though he were saying: When will the time come when, in that glory by which the saints are made conformed to your glory, I shall appear with them in splendor? Or, “when shall I come”—that is, when will the time arrive when the Church desires to be released from the body and to be with Christ? “And appear before the face of my God”—that is, before the sight of his divinity; and then we shall see him as he is.

My tears have been my bread by day and by night. [Col. 0949D] How can bread be made from tears? It can, because just as the body is satisfied with bread, so the soul is satisfied with tears, since by them it hopes to obtain forgiveness of sins. Weeping, groaning, and lamentation were mine because of my longing for you. While it is said to me every day: “Where is your God?” For the pagans point out their gods with a finger and therefore heap reproaches upon me. Let them know, then, that I keep my God hidden within my mind and dwell with him through the inner person.

[Col. 0950A] I remembered these things, and poured out my soul within me. While remembering this reproach, which I endured every day, my soul melted within me, and I wasted away in reflection: since I could not see my God visibly either in heaven or on earth, but found him in my mind, governing and directing me in that everlasting tabernacle of which I speak: “For I shall pass into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God.” The tabernacle of God is the Church, which is still a pilgrim, away from the Lord; through it one comes to the eternal tabernacles, that is, to the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the mother of us all. In it are many wondrous people, endowed with sacred virtues; because, built upon the foundation of the apostles, they are regarded as one house. Into this house, entering in his mind, the man who had abandoned idolatry and had already come to know the mysteries of baptism, marveling at the harmony of the spiritual song, approached the house of God—which is the Holy of Holies—through the sweetness of eternal delight. And as though someone were saying to him, “Who brought you here? Or how did you come here? Or what delighted you so that you approached this place?” he replied:

Amid the voice of exultation and confession, the sound of one feasting. This exultation, confession, and feasting are not fulfilled through musical arts, nor do they begin and pass away; rather, they are continually celebrated by angelic voices and the harmonies of the saints. While he, still placed in this world, contemplated this in his mind, groaning because this dwelling was being delayed for him, he says to his sorrowful soul:

Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you disturb me? [Col. 0950C] Because, he says, I have not yet received this present sweetness, and my adversary still watches against me and still lays snares for me. And the other replies: Hope in the Lord. Endure patiently. Or, “hope in God.” The soul encourages itself; or the inner person encourages the outer. For I shall still confess him, the salvation of my countenance and my God. I have already confessed my sins; afterward I shall confess his praise, through which he saved me from death destined to perish, or summoned me to eternal life.

My soul is troubled within me. Because of the remembrance of former sins. Therefore I shall remember you from the land of Jordan and Hermoniim, from the little mountain. Jordan is understood as baptism; Hermon is interpreted as “anathema.” Thus this man, who was a sinner and who, like a deer, desired springs of water, was mindful in the humility of repentance and, by the washing of baptism, washed away his former sins; he anathematized his sins and did not exalt himself by boasting, but made himself little through repentance.

Abyss calls to abyss. There are many opinions concerning the abyss, which will be explained in their proper places. Here, however, “abyss calls to abyss” when either the Old Testament announces the New, or the New calls the Old to bear witness. The Old announces the New when Moses says: “God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers” (Deuteronomy XVIII). The New calls the Old to bear witness when Paul says: “They drank from the rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians X). Because of the depth of their meaning, they are called abysses. At the sound of your waterfalls. At the voice of the prophets, which announced the coming of the Lord. They are called waterfalls because the Lord’s coming was obscure in their prophecy and was not understood by the Jews. For this voice announces the coming judgment, whether concerning the merits of the blessed or the punishments of the impious.

All your lofty things and your waves have passed over me. Lofty and powerful are these threats by which you threatened the judgment of death; they do not fall immediately because of your immense patience. The waves are the events that arrive after the threats have been uttered. Therefore he says that they have entered upon him: while living amid mortal desires, he was beaten with blows and instructed so that he might desire the living Lord.

By day the Lord commanded his mercy. Because through the light of the holy Scriptures he promised it. And by night, his song. When he was placed in tribulations, he showed it to him.

With me is my prayer. And not outside me. To the God of my life. So that at some time I may deserve to be joined to him, freed from this world. I shall say to God, “You are my protector.” Although I am exercised by tribulations, I nevertheless always ask you to protect and defend me.

Why have you forgotten me? And why have you rejected me? Why do you delay so long, and not bring me into that place of the wondrous tabernacle? Why do I go about sorrowful while the enemy afflicts me? The devil, who has laid many snares for me; or the persecutors of the Church.

While my bones are being crushed. While I see the stronger members of the Church yielding to scandals and various quarrels. Or the bones, the virtues of the Church, are as though crushed by those tribulations that the saints endure. My enemies reproached me. Whether in the martyrs or in other confessors.

While it is said to me every day: “Where is your God?” While I desired to please you through repentance and affliction of body and soul, my enemies, as though I were doing these things in vain, said: “Where is your God?” Not knowing the hidden things that God has prepared for those who love him. Why are you sad, my soul, and [Col. 0951D] why do you disturb me? Because my desire is prolonged.

Hope in God, for I shall still confess him, the salvation of my countenance and my God. In him let our hope always be attentive. May he himself calm all the waves; may he himself preserve us in temptations; may he satisfy our thirst through his contemplation and give us life through the salvation of his countenance.

## PSALM XLII

**A psalm of David.** Although this psalm signifies the Lord’s Passion in certain verses, it nevertheless has the voice of the faithful soul desiring the light of this world, that is, Christ.

Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation. I seek your judgment because you are merciful. But distinguish me from the chaff among which I groan in this world, desiring to be clothed upon, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life. It is also the voice of the Lord, addressed to those to whom he had earlier said, “Be holy, because I am holy” (Leviticus XX), but who did not fulfill this: “Deliver me from an unjust and deceitful man.” No one is more unjust and deceitful than the one who is the inventor of iniquity and the imitator of holiness: that is, the devil, who entered Judas’s heart so that he might betray Christ. But the faithful man whom we mentioned earlier also says:

For you are God, my strength. I know that I am weak and fragile, and I do not feel that I possess any strength by which I can be delivered unless you save me. Why have you rejected me? Our strength is Christ, who rejects us when we have sinned. Why do I go about sorrowful while the enemy afflicts me? I am sorrowful because of my sins, and therefore I am afflicted in various temptations by that same enemy, who above was called the unjust man. Since the darkness of sins troubles me, I flee suppliantly to you, who are the light of the world.

Send forth your light and your truth. You are the light, who said: “I am the light of the world” (John VIII). You are the truth, who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life”; may you deign to enlighten us, so that, abandoning the devil’s falsehood, we may follow your truth. They themselves shall lead me. Away from the error of sin. And they shall bring me to your holy mountain. Into your Church. Into your tabernacle. Into that heavenly Jerusalem, of which another psalm says (Psalm LXXXIII): “How beloved are your tabernacles, O Lord!”

I shall enter unto the altar of God, my God, where I shall no longer present calves and rams, but myself as a living sacrifice pleasing to him. To God, who gives joy to my youth. When the old leaven has been purged, he consoles me in the new man as a young bull.

I shall confess to you on the lyre, O God, my God. Through the mortification of the flesh, because the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world. Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you disturb me? Because I desire to see the one in whom I have placed my hope.

Hope in God, for I shall still confess him, and so forth. He confesses him; from him he asks that his sins be forgiven. He calls him the salvation of his countenance; he invokes and adores him. We too, confessing him, ask him to grant that we may be enlightened by his light, directed by his way, corrected by his truth, and enriched by his life. Or: “The salvation of my countenance is my God.” My God is the salvation of my soul, and my countenance—that is, the vision of my soul—is my God.

## PSALM XLIII

**For the end; for the sons of Korah; an instruction.** Korah is interpreted as “Calvary,” and the Lord was crucified on Mount Calvary. The sons of Korah are the sons of Christ: they are the holy apostles or martyrs. Hence it is said: “The sons of the bridegroom cannot mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them” (Matthew IX). “An instruction”: that is, so that we may understand him who, according to the flesh, took his beginning in time, yet was begotten before the ages. Or “an instruction” means that we should understand the present prosperity of sinners and the present tribulation of the saints. The psalm does not recount events of the past, but declares that the Church is reborn in Christ and urges the faithful within it to the contest, showing that no one can be crowned unless he has competed lawfully. In it, moreover, the voices of martyrs are often expressed.

O God, we have heard with our ears. Through spiritual understanding we have come to know, according to the Lord’s saying: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke VIII). And our fathers. The apostles and prophets, through whose preaching we were reborn to life. They announced to us the work that you performed in their days and in ancient days. The prophets announced what was accomplished in their own time; the apostles announced what they saw you doing.

[Col. 0953B] Your hand scattered the nations, and you planted them. You scattered from the Church the burdens of vices and planted the adornments of virtues—that is, righteous people who would produce the fruit of holiness. You afflicted peoples and drove them out: those who, having abandoned you, were turning toward idolatry.

For they did not possess the land by their own sword, but by gentleness of mind, because “blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the land of the living” (Matthew V). And their arm did not save them, but your right hand, your arm, and the light of your countenance. The right hand of the Father is Christ, as in the saying: “By his right hand he exalted us”—that is, the arm—as elsewhere: “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isaiah LIII). He is also the light, as in the words: “In your light we shall see light” (Psalm LIII). He, then, was sent by the Father to free his own. And he added why he freed them: “Because you were pleased with them.” For God wills that, just as he is well pleased in the Son, so we too should be pleasing in him, if we wish to be delivered.

You are he himself, my king. You who reign in me, and not sin. And my God. By whom I have been acquired. Who commands salvation for Jacob. That is, for the Christian people, which, after supplanting the elder, received the commandment of salvation through prophetic and apostolic teaching.

In you we shall winnow our enemies with the horn, and in your name we shall despise those who rise up against us. Something is winnowed by horns, as in the case of Zedekiah, who, having made two iron horns, said: “With these you shall winnow all Syria” (1 Kings XXI). Our horn, however, is Christ. He is likewise the name of the Father, in whom our adversaries are either winnowed or despised.

For I shall not hope in my bow, and my sword shall not save me, but your power.

For you saved us from those who afflicted us. Since I should not trust in my weapons, the reason is that you have always saved us from our persecutors and guarded us without our strength or our sword. You saved us from those who oppressed us, and you put to shame those who hated us. The powers turned away, and once they had been put to shame, we were freed by Christ the Lord.

[Col. 0954A] In God we shall praise all day long, because he is our praise and glory. And in your name we shall confess you forever, because we are called Christians from you, O Christ.

But now you have rejected and put us to shame. When he says “now,” he indicates the present time. Therefore, in the present time we are rejected for training, so that we may be glorified forever. For often even martyrs say in the present age: “And you will not go forth, O God, in our strength.” This is so that you may strengthen us afterward with everlasting power.

You turned us back before our enemies. Thus the Lord also turned Peter back, so that he might restore him to what was better. Therefore we too must turn back, lest our journey continue along crooked paths. We must also keep our enemies before us, so that we may know what we ought to avoid. And if we turn back after Christ, like Peter, keeping him before us, we shall fear nothing further. And those who hated us seized us for themselves. Because of your name they seized us, harassing us in prisons, with blows, and with other torments. But that tribulation did not separate us from your love.

You gave us like sheep for food. For just as the Lord, like a sheep led to slaughter, was given as food to the peoples when he said, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man, you will not have life in yourselves” (John VI), so the saints, as we said above, when given over to many tribulations, became food for the nations—either when they ministered the nourishment of eternal life, or when they satisfied the nations’ rapacity with their own sufferings. [Col. 0954C] And you scattered us among the nations, so that they might rule over us for a time.

You sold your people without price. [Note: Servatus Lupus, in the *Collectaneum on Three Questions*, near the end, quotes this passage in exactly the same words as though from Jerome’s Commentary; just as above, when describing another passage of this *Breviary* in the first psalm, he attributes it to Jerome.] Up to this point the martyrs have been speaking about themselves; now it is said concerning the people of the Jews, to whom it was said: “You were sold because of your sins” (Isaiah L). And therefore “without price,” because the blood of the Lamb was not poured out for them. And there was no abundance in our exchanges. The merchandise that was sold was of little value; therefore no exchange was made.
