For the Lord purchased the people whom he bought not with gold or silver, but with his own precious blood, as the apostle Peter says (1 Peter I).

You made us a reproach to our neighbors, a mockery and derision to those who are around us. “Neighbors” refers to the persecutors, because of their worldly dwelling alongside us. They often reproach us with ridicule, saying: “Let your God come and rescue you from our hands” (2 Chronicles XXXII).

You made us a likeness among the nations. Certainly, a likeness to you: just as the world first hated you, so afterward it would hate us. A shaking of the head among the peoples. For just as passersby shook their heads during your Passion, so they do among your martyrs. And if anyone now wishes to live devoutly in you, the wicked immediately blaspheme him with mockery or a shaking of the head.

[Col. 0955A] All day long my shame is before me, and the confusion of my face has covered me. The Lord speaks these words in the flesh he assumed; for our sake he suffers shame, is cursed, and is put to confusion, even to the very cross of the gibbet.

At the voice of the one reproaching and reviling. When it was said to him: “If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross” (Matthew XXVII). From the face of the enemy: Judas. And of the one persecuting: the Jewish people.

All these things came upon us, yet we did not forget you. The martyrs say this, because everything that you, Lord Jesus, endured, we too endured, but we always confessed you. Nor did we act wickedly in your covenant, but we proclaimed you truthfully. And our heart did not turn back, so that we might follow the fanatical errors from which we had departed. And you turned our paths away from your way. Our conduct has not been separated from your justifications.

For you humbled us in the place of affliction, in this body in which we exist and are afflicted for your sake. And the shadow of death covered us. It is rightly called the shadow of death that oppresses us in this world, and not death itself, because the martyrs and the other saints, even when they are afflicted and destined for death, nevertheless live to God. This death is a shadow to them, not the reality of death.

If we have forgotten the name of our God—that is, Christ—and if we have stretched out our hands toward a foreign god: toward an idol.

Will not God search this out? For he himself knows the secrets of the heart. That God knows human thoughts, he himself reveals in the Gospel when he says to the Pharisees: “Why are you thinking evil in your hearts?” (Luke V). Thus the martyrs also say: If anywhere we have departed from the ways of God, let him who knows the secrets of the heart inquire into it.

For because of you we are put to death all day long. We are oppressed by various tribulations for your sake, but willingly offer our necks to those who strike us. We are regarded as sheep for slaughter (Matthew X). For you had said that you would send us as sheep among wolves (Matthew VIII). But now, since you have withdrawn from these temptations and, as though sleeping in a boat, do not defend us from the storm, we awaken you, Lord, beseeching you with humble confession.

Rise up; why do you sleep, O Lord? Rise up, and do not reject us forever. You who died for us and rose again, may you be awakened in the hearts of those who confess that you died but do not believe that you rose again, so that at last they may cease persecuting us and not perish in eternal death forever.

Why do you turn your face away? God turns his face away for a time in order to test his elect. You forget our poverty and our tribulation. We suffer poverty, considering the riches of this world worthless; we desire the heavenly kingdom. For we are afflicted when our desire is delayed.

For our soul has been humbled in the dust, so that we might be bent down by those whom the wind casts like dust from the face of the earth. Our belly has clung to the earth. As though he were saying: The flesh is weakened, but the mind is attentive to heavenly things.

[Col. 0956A] Rise up, O Lord, help us, and redeem us for the sake of your name. May we now deserve your help in tribulations, so that we may be freed from these pressures—not because of our merit, but because of your name.

## PSALM XLIV

**For the end; for those who shall be changed; for the sons of Korah; for instruction; a song for the beloved.** In Hebrew it is written thus: *Lamanasse, al sosannim labne Core mescil sir Jedidoth*, which we translate as: “For the victor; concerning lilies; for the sons of Korah; a most beloved song of instruction.” By “for the beloved,” the whole psalm refers to Christ, concerning whom the Father speaks in the Gospel: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew XVII). Or the psalm contains the mystery of spiritual marriage, that is, the union of Christ with the Church. It therefore begins with the Father’s voice.

[Col. 0956B] My heart has uttered a good word. He did not produce, from a bodily union, but from his heart he brought forth the Word equal to himself, through whom all things were made. For this Word is good, because “what was made in him is life” (John I). I speak my works to the King. I speak to the Word himself, the kingly Son, and all things are brought to completion.

My tongue is the pen of a swiftly writing scribe. For just as what is written is neither trivial nor easy, but useful and health-giving, so the word of God, as though it were being written, is brought to fulfillment. As for swiftness, it means that the things he has spoken are not delayed but are quickly fulfilled; therefore he calls it a pen. And what does the pen signify? Or how is a pen compared with Christ? Just as a rock, a lion, the right hand, a mountain, and other such things pertain to Christ, so too does the pen—namely, because he measures and writes. Hence the prophet said: “Rise and take a pen, and measure the temple and the city” (Ezekiel XL). The pen of a scribe: the scribe himself is Christ. Hence he said in the Gospel: “Every learned scribe in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder” (Matthew XIII). Swiftly writing: because no one writes so quickly as the Lord himself writes in the hearts of the saints. What does he write, except his faith, hope, and charity, while granting the word of preaching?

You are beautiful beyond the sons of men. So that he may not be understood as equal to another human being, but as the Son of God with humanity; therefore he is called more beautiful than the other sons of men. The beauty of which he speaks, however, is not to be assigned to stature but to loveliness. Or how is he beautiful, when Isaiah says: “We saw him without appearance or beauty, but as one despised, humbled, struck, and scourged by God” (Isaiah LIII)? The prophet Isaiah says this in the person of the Jews, because they believed his human nature to be that of a mere man. But this prophet speaks according to his divinity. Moreover, the prophet Isaiah knew through the Holy Spirit that the Jews would see that humanity outwardly, but that they could not understand the divinity within.

Grace has been poured upon your lips. When you cure diseases by your word; when you make the sea grow quiet; when you command the winds to be still; when you order the fever to depart; when you call Lazarus and he comes; when you appeal to the Father and he hears—and not only hears but also answers—all that you say is accomplished through the grace of your lips. The pouring out of grace in the holy Scriptures is the grace of the Holy Spirit, or of Christ. The grace of the Holy Spirit was poured out at baptism in the form of a dove: when it descended upon the head, it came to the beard, and then to the edge of his garment. Our head is Christ; the beard, the holy apostles; the edge of his garment, the holy preachers, as the prophet says: “Like ointment upon the head, which runs down upon the beard of Aaron and down to the edge of his garment” (Psalm CXXXII). “Grace upon your lips,” because “the law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John I). Therefore God blessed you forever, because of this grace. For although Christ the Lord was always blessed in the Father, he is blessed in the flesh he assumed, when the Holy Spirit descended upon him at baptism and the Father said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew III). Or God the Father blessed his Son, and Christ blessed his Church.

Gird yourself with your sword upon your thigh, O most powerful one. A sword around the thigh. By the sword, the word; by the thigh, the incarnation. A man girds a sword for battle. But, “gird yourself with your sword, O most powerful one.” As though the prophet were saying: You, Christ, put on flesh; fight against the devil and free the human race from hell. Gird yourself with the sword of the word of preaching, which divided son from father, daughter from mother, daughter-in-law from mother-in-law; around your thigh, upon the flesh you assumed. “Most powerfully”: not sluggishly or lightly, but manfully.

[Col. 0957C] In your form and your beauty. In holiness and righteousness; or this pertains to divinity. Advance prosperously, go forth, and reign. If you direct yourself toward this, all things will always prosper for you. “Go forth,” that is, come from heaven. “And reign,” because previously the kingdom belonged to the devil. Hence we say in the Lord’s Prayer: “May your kingdom come among us, and may the devil’s kingdom depart” (Luke XI). “Advance prosperously”: see favorably. “Go forth,” from the bridal chamber of the virgin womb; “and reign,” having overthrown the dominion of death.

Because of truth, gentleness, and righteousness. Truth is Christ himself, because he is the truth. Thus, concerning that woman, he said to the Jews: “Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her” (John VIII). Gentleness: when he said, “Neither will I condemn you.” Righteousness: when he said, “Go, woman, and sin no more.” Because of truth, by which you fulfilled the things you had promised through the prophets. And gentleness, because like a sheep you were sacrificed for the life of the people. And righteousness, when you rescued the human being not by power but by humility. And your right hand shall lead you wondrously. Power, or strength. Or power shall lead you—that is, lead you into heaven.

Your arrows are sharp. Your preachings, piercing the hearts of human beings. Sharp, because they penetrate to the innermost heart. Peoples shall fall beneath you into the hearts of the king’s enemies. Through the compunction caused by preaching, they fall into their hearts so that they may not grow proud but believe humbly. Those who had been enemies of the king through unbelief become friends through belief. For those who were enemies of Christ afterward became his friends.

Your throne, O God, is forever and ever. Not temporal but eternal. Or the throne of God is the holy Church, or the soul, because the soul of the righteous person is the seat of wisdom. The rod of direction is the rod of your kingdom. By the rod, correction through discipline; for by that rule of truth the hearts that were crooked are directed.

You loved righteousness and hated iniquity. That is, you fulfilled the commandments of God the Father. And you hated iniquity—not that hatred falls upon God, but God is said to hate, that is, to reject. Iniquity is understood as the devil himself. [Col. 0958B] Or the rod is understood as heavenly discipline, by which he directed our crooked iniquity, which he hated, toward his own righteousness.

Therefore God, your God, anointed you. The Apostle says: “God, even your God, and Christ: God made him” (Hebrews I). With the oil of gladness beyond your companions. Other kings who foreshadowed him and were called his companions because they reigned were anointed with corruptible oil. But this one, the Son of God, was anointed by God the Father with the oil of exultation—that is, of resurrection, ascension, and dominion—because Christ was anointed by nature, while we are anointed by grace. For divinity was fully present in him, whereas in the saints it is given in portions.

Myrrh and drops and cassia flow from your garments. Myrrh is assigned to burial; the drop is understood against poisons. In cassia, the human being is signified, since cassia is often called a tree. [Col. 0958C] Therefore these things flowed from his garments—that is, from the flesh he assumed, with which divinity surrounded itself as with a garment. The fragrance of myrrh dripped when he was handed over to burial. The drop flowed when, having subdued the serpent’s poison, he extinguished the fires of Tartarus. Cassia also came forth when, in that human being through whom he overcame hell, he ascended into heaven.

From ivory houses, from which the daughters of kings delighted you in your honor. By ivory houses, because of the size of elephants, we understand spacious houses; for broad is the way that leads to destruction (Matthew VII). But ivory, unless it is scraped with files, divided by saws, and pierced with awls, is dark and dreadful. So too the apostles were before they were called and inhabited. But after they were called—cut with saws, scraped with claws, carved with chisels, kindled by flames, and polished by various sufferings—they became houses of God, in which Christ himself deigned to dwell. Following their examples, the martyrs became kings of their own bodies. The daughters of these kings are holy souls, who delighted in Christ by honoring his majestic name and proclaiming his mercy.

From ivory houses—from which they made you glad. Many, through error, say “from heavy things” instead of “from houses.” [Note: Although it would have been worthwhile to compare the whole of Jerome’s genuine Letter to Principia, no. 65 in our recension, which is entirely devoted to explaining Psalm XLIV, with this pseudo-Jeronymian exposition, it is nevertheless preferable here to transcribe the holy Father’s own words concerning this passage. There he says that, instead of what we translated as “from ivory houses,” because the Greek reads ἀπὸ βάρεων ἐλεφαντίνων (*apo bareōn elephantinōn*), certain Latins, because of the ambiguity of the word, translated “from heavy things,” since *baris*—βάρις—is a local Palestinian word, and even to this day enclosed buildings constructed like towers and public fortifications are called βάρεις (*bareis*). See also what we observe there.] For among the Greeks, the word βάρεων signifies both meanings.

[Col. 0959A] The queen stood at your right hand. For there is nothing left-handed in your kingdom. In a garment of gold. With the adornment of spiritual belief. Surrounded by variety. Of nations and peoples. Now the prophet speaks to the Church herself. The queen is the Church. Hence he says in the Song of Songs: “Who is this that ascends, made white, leaning upon her beloved?” She is called queen because she rules her own vices and sins. At your right hand. As in the passage: “He will indeed set the sheep at his right hand,” when he will say: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV). In a garment—that is, not naked, but clothed with spiritual understanding. Surrounded with variety. With the seventy-two languages—that is, with the diversity of nations, or with thanksgiving.

[Col. 0959B] Hear, daughter, and see. Believe, so that you may be cleansed. Daughter, because you have been reborn from him. Bride, because you have been joined to him. Or Christ calls his Church his daughter through faith. He calls her daughter so that she may be chaste in mind and body. And incline your ear. Listen or desire humbly and wisely. And hear with the ear of the heart, as in: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke VIII). And see—that is, with the eyes of the heart, by which God is seen, as he says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Mark V). And forget your people, etc. The fellowship of demons, or vices and sins, and the house of your father, the devil, who had previously begotten you, because “the whole world lay in the evil one” (I John V); therefore, incline your ear.

[Col. 0959C] Because the king desired your beauty. Christ Jesus, by whom you are ruled: because you were black in your father’s house, but now, after baptism, you hide yourself, cleansed of vices or made white by the grace of faith. For he himself is the Lord. By whom you have been redeemed. Your God. Whom now, having abandoned idols, you cultivate and adore. How does he speak of your appearance and beauty, when the Church was not beautiful or lovely, but previously foul and deformed? But afterward she became beautiful and lovely through the washing of baptism, because the just man died for the ungodly—that is, Christ—cleansing her through the washing of his blood, as the Apostle says: “Not having spot or wrinkle” (Eph. V).

And the daughters of Tyre shall adore him. Tyre is interpreted as “distress.” The daughters of Tyre are the daughters of distress. They adore Christ who are in distress. Or, they are believing souls from the Gentiles. In gifts they shall entreat your face; the wealthy of the people. These, storing up their treasures, seek you with a pure heart, because “where their treasures are, there will their heart also be” (Matt. VI). The Magi did this: they came with frankincense, myrrh, and gold, because they adored Christ not only with words but also with gifts.

[Col. 0959D] All the glory of the king’s daughter, the faithful soul, is within, clothed round about with golden fringes and varied adornments. Above we spoke of the variety of nations; here, of graces. All the glory of the king’s daughter is within—that is, the elders of the Church, or kings and powerful men, who now possess hope, faith, and charity: they offered themselves within—that is, in the conscience of the Church. Clothed round about with varied adornments in golden fringes. Those who enter offered themselves not only according to the letter but also according to spiritual understanding, or they have been filled with a variety of virtues.

[Col. 0960A] Virgins shall be brought to the king after her, her companions. Through the one Church, founded upon apostolic instruction, many are converted to Christ. They shall be brought to you in joy and exultation. Not in the sorrow of sin, nor in the tears of repentance, but in the joy of virtues and the exultation of thanksgivings. They shall be brought into the king’s temple. For John saw the holy city, Jerusalem, descending from heaven and possessing the glory of God, but he did not see a temple in it (Rev. XXI): “The Lord,” he says, “is its temple.” These virgins, therefore, shall be led into this temple—that is, the souls of the saints—so that they may be conformed to his glorious body.

In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you. Your fathers, O Church, were the apostles, because they themselves begot you. But now, because they have departed from the world, you have bishops as sons in their place, who have been created by you. For these too are your fathers, because you are ruled by them. You will appoint them princes over all the earth. Christ appointed his saints over all peoples. For the Gospel has been extended in the name of God to all the ends of the world, in which the princes of the Church—that is, the bishops—have been appointed.

[Col. 0960B] They shall remember your name throughout every generation and generation. Therefore they shall remember, because they never forget, but will always proclaim you, or build in the generations of the saints.

Therefore the peoples shall confess to you forever and unto ages of ages. Because of their preaching, the peoples will always confess their sins to you; they will recount your glory and announce your praise.

## PSALM XLV

To the end; for the sons of Korah; concerning hidden things. A psalm. Concerning hidden things—that is, concerning the hidden matters of the calling of the Gentiles and the rejection of the Jews. The psalm teaches us that we ought to place our hope in him who alone can deliver us from tribulation.

Our God is refuge and strength, a helper in tribulations that have found us exceedingly. For the world is full of troubles and pressures; and because there are other aids belonging to kings, strengths belonging to the powerful, and refuges belonging to cities, our protection is Christ, who can powerfully rescue us from these things.

Therefore we shall not fear, because we have faith in him [Mart. incorrectly: “cruelty”]. Though the earth be troubled. The generation of the Jews, who set their minds on earthly things. And the mountains be moved into the heart of the sea. The apostolic preachings [moved] into the hearts of the Gentiles of this world, as in the Gospel: “If you have faith,” he says, “like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here,’ and it will move” (Matt. XVII). Into the heart of the sea—that is, into the Gentile world.

Their waters roared and were troubled. The waters signify peoples; the movements signify demons. Now, being troubled, they gave forth a sound: together with the destroyers of idols, they either restored them or sought to prepare death. The mountains were troubled by his strength. The higher powers of the world.

The rush of the river makes glad the city of God. After the worship of demons had been overthrown, the washing of baptism, or the irrigation of the Holy Spirit, makes glad the soul, the city of God—or the Church, which is the city of God and, set upon a mountain, is not hidden (Matt. V). The Most High sanctified his tabernacle. The congregation of the faithful, in which he dwells through faith.

God is in its midst; it shall not be moved. Rather, it is strengthened, as he says: “Do not fear, Mary” (Luke I); or, the Church in tribulation. God will help her at the break of dawn. Through a holy visitation, by which a pure heart will merit [his help]. For “blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V).

[Col. 0961B] The nations were troubled. By vices and crimes. And kingdoms were brought low. The powers of demons, under the power of Christ. They gave their voice. In preachings. The earth was moved. The nations were astonished in their unbelief—that is, the Gentile world was moved from unbelief to faith in Christ.

The Lord of hosts is with us. Through the assumption of flesh, he became a participant for our sake. Therefore he is also Emmanuel, that is, “God with us.” The Lord of hosts, of angels and human beings. Our protector is the God of Jacob. He is the Lord of hosts who conquered the devil. He is our protector, so that he may preserve us forever. Our helper, the God of Jacob. Through Jacob, the overthrowing of vices.

Come and see the works of the Lord. Christ calls his Church to faith, or to belief. See—that is, understand—the works of the Lord, the powers of the Lord. Or, the works of the Lord: for, according to Daniel, the stone cut from the mountain without hands, having shattered the kingdoms of the world, occupied the breadth of the whole earth (Dan. II). He has placed wonders upon the earth. For he displayed many signs among the peoples, either before his bodily coming or after it. He removes wars to the ends of the earth. Many histories relate that all wars ceased at the Lord’s coming. But even now, in his Church, he daily restrains wars so that neither heretics nor Jews may rage. Or, “removing,” “taking away,” wars: that is, the battle, because there is always a battle of vices and sins. To the ends of the earth, to the end of the ages. The Lord removes this battle from us, for by ourselves we cannot.

He will break the bow. The hidden snares of evil people. And he will shatter the weapons. Present battles. And he will burn the shields with fire. The mad fantasies of diabolical protection, which he consumes entirely with that spiritual fire of which he says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth”—that is, into the Church (Luke XII).

Be still and see that I am the Lord. “I made, and I will not bear; I created, and I will sustain; I will redeem you and forgive your sins,” says the Lord (Isa. XLVI). Be still, therefore, so that you may know me and not be troubled by something else. I will be exalted among the nations. [Col. 0962A] Which have been converted to belief. I will be exalted in the earth. If some from the Jewish nation have returned to me, it is clear that they do not set their minds on earthly things.

The Lord of hosts is with us; our protector is the God of Jacob. For he graciously dwells always with believers, as he deigned to promise the apostles after the resurrection, saying: “Behold, I am with you all the days, unto the consummation of the age” (Matt., last chapter).

## PSALM XLVI

To the end; for the sons of Korah; a psalm. The sons of Korah, the sons of the bald man. It is the voice of one mocking. He says this concerning the forty-two boys who mocked Elisha and said: “Go up, bald man; go up, bald man,” and he cursed them in the name of the Lord (IV Kings II). And two bears came out and devoured them. Elisha represents Christ; those boys represent the Jews, who said: “Hail, King of the Jews.” Hence Paul says: “Do not become children in understanding, but be infants in malice” (I Cor. XIV). The physician came to heal the sick, but the sick killed the physician. The bears properly signify demons, because they devoured their hearts. The psalm contains the apostolic voice, admonishing us to rejoice in him alone, by whose blood we have been liberated.

All nations, clap your hands. Through the prophet, the Holy Spirit calls all nations to come to faith. All nations—that is, the whole world together—clap your hands. To clap means to praise. For applause is called praise. Rejoice in good works. Shout to God with a voice of exultation. With a sublime voice, confess the Lord in your very heart, and exult with the service of every limb. He says this because of the greatness of joy. The voice of exultation is something that a human being cannot comprehend in words, letters, or syllables—how greatly God ought to be praised.

For God is most high and terrible. He who was once provoked by the Jews, but, having obtained the Gentiles, ascended above the heavens and became terrible, sitting at the right hand of the Father. And a great king over all the earth. Not only over the Jewish nation, but over all the nations of the earth. Or, “over all the earth,” that is, over the whole Church, because the Church is called earth: Christ is over it, because authority has been given to him in heaven and on earth. Or concerning him the apostles now say:

He subjected peoples to us and nations beneath our feet. He chose his inheritance for us. They say that the Gentiles and peoples subjected to Christ have been placed beneath them; their wickedness has been trampled down, and they have been made worthy of Christ’s inheritance. Or, Christ’s inheritance is the holy Church. Hence he said elsewhere: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Ps. XV). Both we are his and he is ours, according to the saying: “The Lord is my portion” (Ps. CXVIII). The beauty of Jacob whom he loved. For, because of Jacob’s beauty, he chose the apostles who descended from his lineage, and they say these things. But hear the prophet concerning his love for him: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. I).

God ascended with jubilation. For his ascension was glorious, in which the multitude of angels said with great jubilation: “Lift up your gates, O princes” (Ps. XXIII); now the victor returns from battle. And the Lord with the sound of a trumpet. In this, when he was ascending, two angels, like a trumpet, cried out to the apostles: “This Jesus, who has been taken up from you, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts I). Or, after the victory by which he conquered the devil, he ascended in this manner. Hence he says in another psalm: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter” (Ps. XXIII). Or, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, when he ascended from the Mount of Olives: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts I).

Sing psalms to our God, sing psalms; sing psalms to our king, sing psalms. Having subdued the dominion of death, he lifted up to heaven the flesh with which he had lain in the tomb.

For God is king of all the earth. For now he is known not only in Judea and Jerusalem, but has been made manifest throughout the whole earth by the light of faith. Sing psalms wisely, so that you may understand spiritually what you sing according to the letter.

God will reign over all the nations. Which he received as an inheritance from the Father. Hence he says in another psalm: “I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. II). Or, “The Lord is exalted over all nations, and his glory is above the heavens” (Ps. CXII). God sits upon his holy throne. At the right hand of the Father. Or angels are called thrones because of their innocence, since they have not sinned. Hence he said: “Heaven is my throne” (Isa. LXVI). God sits upon his holy throne—that is, in the Church. Hence it has been said: “The soul of the just is the seat of wisdom” (Wis. VII).

Princes of the peoples. The apostles. They have assembled. For judgment. Or, “princes of the peoples,” that is, the elders of Christians, whose figure was represented by the centurion; or those who now hold the very faith that Abraham possessed. Hence it has been said: “Many will come from the east and the west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. II). With the God of Abraham. The God of Abraham is the true God, who is the God of the living, with whom the righteous will carry out judgment. For the Lord also says in the Gospel: “When the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” For the strong gods of the earth have been greatly exalted. The gods are the saints, as the prophet says: “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Ps. XXI). They have been greatly exalted. They have been exalted through faith and preaching. Or, those who have been lifted up in pride and, abandoning heavenly things, desired earthly things; to them it is said: “You shall die like human beings.” These will be judged by the God of Abraham or by his apostles. But let us pray to the Lord that, laying aside every swelling of pride, we may be so joined to him in this age that, separated from the left side at the judgment, nothing may be found in us that condemns us to punishment, but rather that which, through abundant mercy, advances us to the crown.

## PSALM XLVII

A psalm of song, for the sons of Korah, on the second day of the week. Through the psalm, a work or preaching is understood. Through the song, knowledge and praise. The sons of Korah are the holy apostles or martyrs. On the first day of the week, he made light; on the second day of the week, he made the firmament. Light signifies angels; the firmament, human beings. From this it has something in the New Testament. On the first day of the week, Christ the light rose again. Hence he says in the Gospel: “He was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John I). On the second day of the week, the Church was established in faith, when the Lord said: “And upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. XVI). The whole psalm dwells entirely upon the holy people and entirely upon the mysteries of the Church.

Great is the Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise. The voice of the Church. He is called great not by comparison, but because of the greatness of his glory. As though someone asked, “Where is he great? Where is he worthy of praise?” it answers: In the city of our God. The holy soul, whose citizens and household members are understood to be good works. On his holy mountain. In the assumed body of the Lord’s humanity.

Founded in the exultation of the whole earth. By his ascension he occupied the earth that had previously been subject to sins and curses, and spread throughout it the exultation and joy of faith. Or, the Church was and is founded in faith throughout the whole world. Mount Zion, the sides of the north, the city of the great King. To this mountain—that is, to Christ the Lord—two peoples came from Zion: one from the sides of the north, which is from the uncircumcision; the other from the circumcision. Therefore Christ the Lord, who is our peace, removed the dividing wall of enmity from the midst, made both one, and placed these peoples by faith in his Church, which is the city of the great King. Or, Mount Zion—that is, the holy Church. From the side of the north, because it was gathered from the wicked. Hence it has been said: “From the north evils shall arise that are upon the earth.” Here the north signifies the devil, to whom it is said: “Come, O north wind, blow through my garden” (Song IV)—that is, through the Church by temptations. Hence the Apostle says: “There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (I Cor. XI). Or, “the city of the great King”—that is, the holy Church.

God will be known in her houses when he receives her. He received her through grace. He is known in her ranks—that is, in the apostles or the other preachers—through whom the faith of the Church was proclaimed. For “by grace we have been saved through faith, and this is not from ourselves. It is the gift of God, so that no one may boast of himself.” Or, “in her houses,” that is, in the holy Church. “When he receives her,” in faith, because previously she was among the wicked.

For behold, the kings of the earth were gathered together. The rulers of the world, whose kingdom was in the worship of idols and demons. Coming from the sides of the north—that is, from the devil. Or, they were gathered and came together into one—that is, into the unity of the Church. They came together into one: upon the chief cornerstone founded in the foundation.

They saw and were thus astonished. At the glory and power of the Redeemer. Or, they were astonished at the powers of the apostles and were moved from unbelief to faith. They were troubled and shaken; trembling seized them. Because of the awareness of their sins, for it has been said: “Because of your fear we conceived and gave birth to the spirit of salvation” (Isa. XXVI).

There were pains there as of a woman in labor, in a violent spirit. When they have begun to discipline their bodies through abstinence: in a most powerful spirit—that is, the Holy Spirit. He shatters the ships of Tarshish. He humbles the pride of the nations, because Tarshish, in its origin, became proud and eminent through the navigation of merchants. Therefore they are compared here to this ship, those who are carried about amid the waves of this age by every wind of luxury and vanity. Now those who believe in it say:

As we have heard. Through the prophets. So we have seen in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God: God founded it forever. We saw in the Gospel what is the city of the powers. We saw in the Church what is the city of God, founded in that great kingdom.

We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your temple. In your Church we received the Holy Spirit, as did those earlier upon whom he was poured out in the Acts of the Apostles.

According to your name, O God, so also is your praise to the ends of the earth. When, having received the Holy Spirit, they spoke in the languages of all the nations. But your praise also always dwells in the breadth of the faithful people. Your right hand is full of justice. In those who are to be placed on the right side at the judgment.

Let Mount Zion rejoice. The Church in Christ. And let the daughters of Judah exult. The souls of confessors, because Judah is interpreted as “confession.” Because of your judgments, O Lord. [Col. 0965C] Because they guarded them in order to do penance. Or, “your judgments,” the hidden judgments of God: because the Jews were rejected and the Gentiles were chosen in faith.

Surround Zion. That is, defend the Church in your belief. And embrace her. In charity. Proclaim in her towers the praise and glory of Christ. “Proclaim,” that is, preach. The towers are the princes of your Church, because a tower is strong and watches in every direction. Thus the saints ought also to be strong and watchful, as sentinels among humankind.

Set your hearts upon her strength. Do not separate yourselves from the charity that he taught. “Set,” that is, understand. In her strength, in her charity, because they ought not only to teach but also to fulfill in deed what they preach. And distribute her houses. O teachers of the Churches, distribute the ranks of ordinations canonically and holily—not corrupted by rewards, nor deceived by flattery through favoritism. So that you may recount it to the next generation. Not only to those who believe, but also to those who will believe. But what, you ask, shall we recount?

For this is our God forever and unto ages of ages, and he himself will rule us forever. He is God because through him we were made. He is King because by him we are ruled. For he directed our slippery and crooked steps toward himself, who is the way of peace and the peace of our salvation.

## PSALM XLVIII

To the end; for the sons of Korah; a psalm. The sons of Korah are the holy apostles or martyrs. The Holy Spirit sang this psalm through the prophet in the person of preachers. Or this psalm is so called because it teaches that the riches of the world, together with its empty honors, are to be despised, that the cunning of the serpent is to be avoided, and it earnestly admonishes the whole world to hear the word of God, saying:

Hear these things, all nations; perceive them with your ears, all you who inhabit the world. Understand wisely with spiritual ears, which the Lord chose for hearing. In the Gospel he seeks the ear of the heart, through which God is heard. You who inhabit the world—that is, your bodies.

You who are earthborn and sons of human beings, together, rich and poor. It must be understood that he calls all the inhabitants of the earth to hear the word of God, so that neither the divine judgments nor the commandments may be hidden from any human being. Or, together, rich and poor in one—that is, slave and free. Or, poor, concerning whom he said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V).

My mouth shall speak wisdom. It will speak the wisdom that is hidden from the wise of this age and revealed to little ones—that is, so that the little ones of the Church may know that Christ is the wisdom of the Father, concerning whom all the prophets speak. Or, “my mouth shall speak wisdom,” that is, Christ, whom the Church preaches. And the meditation of my heart shall be understanding. I was always meditating in my heart so that, abandoning the foolish vanity of human beings, they might follow the prudence of Christ.

I will incline my ear to a parable. Because the prophet knows that Christ the Lord will come into the world and speak in likeness, he therefore prepares himself to hear—that is, to understand spiritually. Or, I will incline the ear of my heart toward humility. In a parable—that is, I will understand in a likeness. I will open my proposition on the psaltery. This is what I propose: that if what the Decalogue foretold is observed, the heavenly kingdoms will be bestowed. Or, what I proposed in my heart I will preach in speech and understand.

Why should I fear on the evil day? On the day of judgment. The iniquity of my heel will surround me. Because whoever sins in the heel slips. But “the iniquity of the heel” is also understood as original sin from Adam, as it was said to the woman: “I will put enmity between you and the serpent, and between your seed and his seed” (Gen. V). “You will watch”—that is, you will crush—his head, and he himself your heel.

Those who trust in their strength and glory in the abundance of their riches. These slip at the heel, because they do not walk through him who is the way, the truth, and the life; or, those who trust in their strength and glory in the abundance of their riches.

A brother does not redeem; a human being will redeem. If Christ did not redeem—the one who called himself the apostles’ brother and, rising again, became the firstborn of those who rise—Adam will not redeem, because the first human being died and did not rise again. For our brother is Christ, God and human being, who redeemed us. Or, what Moses did not redeem, Christ redeemed. He will not give God his propitiation. One who does not do penance, through which God is appeased.

[Col. 0967A] Nor the price of the redemption of his soul. He did not give alms, through which sins are erased. He labored forever. Placed in everlasting torments. And he will live to the end. Because he is not killed, but is continually restored for punishment.

He will not see destruction. He does not understand that death threatens him. When you see the wise dying. If he sees a wise person in God depart from this world, he says: “What did his fasts accomplish? What did his chastity accomplish? What did his almsgiving accomplish? Is he not dead as well?” The Jews, insulting our Redeemer in a similar way, said: “Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died, and the prophets died?” (John VIII). Together the foolish and the stupid will perish, and they will leave their riches to strangers. The foolish person is one who scorns possessing knowledge of God; concerning him the Apostle says: “Everyone who is ignorant will be ignored.” But the stupid person is one who hopes in riches and not in God. Both therefore lose their riches, because they gather them where thieves break in and steal (I Cor. XIV).

Their graves are their houses forever. Their dwellings from generation to generation. This will be their perpetual habitation, because they will not rise again to possess eternal life, but to be condemned to punishment.

They called their lands by their own names. For often the pagans, feasting beside the tombs of the dead and drinking in the name of those who have died, sing empty things with a kind of melody; but this benefits nothing those condemned in hell.

When a human being was in honor, he did not understand. That he had been formed in the image of God. He was compared with foolish beasts and became like them. Having laid aside the heavenly form, he became like foolish animals.

This way of theirs is a stumbling block to them. Because it leads them from judgment to punishment. And afterward they will take pleasure in their own mouth. But confession in hell accomplishes nothing.

Like sheep they have been placed in hell; death will feed upon them. Rightly are they fed upon by death, who refused to have Christ as their shepherd.

And the righteous will rule over them in the morning. At the resurrection. And their help will grow old in hell. They had riches, but when they descended into hell, they vanished. From their glory. Because they did not seek the glory of Christ, who now speaks about himself.

But truly God will redeem my soul from the hand of hell when he receives me. The God-human did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. Having also accepted death and been raised again by the Father’s power, he restored the human being who had fallen.

Do not fear when a human being becomes rich and when the glory of his house is multiplied, etc. The traitor Judas became rich by selling the Master, but he carried away with him nothing of the price he had accepted when he died. Thus now each person becomes rich and increases by oppressing the poor. Do not fear; it passes quickly and takes nothing of what he had seized with it, as the Lord says in the Gospels: “Fool, this night they will demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke XIII).

Because his soul will be blessed in his life. He is blessed by fools because of his power; but the abundance of food and drink produces a judgment not about one who lives well, but about one who feeds well. Yet these things do not excuse him from punishment. He will confess to you when you have done good to him. He gives thanks when he acquires some profit.

And he will enter unto the generations of his fathers; he will never see light forever. He hoped more in riches than in God, as did his parents; therefore it is said of him: “Cast him into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. XVI).

[Col. 0968B] When a human being was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared with foolish beasts and became like them. He did not know that all these things had been granted to him by God; therefore his foolishness is compared with senseless animals. But let us pray to the Lord that he himself may grant us understanding, so that, while we reject the things that are seen, we may be deemed worthy to attain those that are not seen.

## PSALM XLIX

A psalm of Asaph. Asaph is interpreted as “assembly.” The psalm distinguishes the righteous from the impious, the heavenly from the earthly, and the holy from sinners. In it he declares that it is not the prophet who speaks, but the Lord himself, saying:

The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken. God in the Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—one God; the God of gods, because he wished believers to be called gods. For he gave them power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name (John I). He is also Lord, because he rules over all who rule. And indeed he himself, who once spoke in the patriarchs and prophets, now speaks. And what, you ask, does he say? And he called the earth. Not some part of it; but hear what he added:

From the rising of the sun to its setting. He left nothing that he did not make worthy through his calling. From Zion, the appearance of his beauty. This is the faith and belief that begins from Zion. Hence the Lord says in the Gospels: “For it was necessary that Christ should suffer these things and rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem,” which is Zion (Luke XXIV).

God will come manifestly. Not secretly. Or, “God will come manifestly,” that is, on the day of judgment, because every human being will see him, as he says in the Apocalypse: “Every eye will see him” (Rev. I). Our God, and he will not be silent. Because he will come to judge, according to the saying: “I was silent; shall I always be silent?” (Isa. XLII). Now he is silent, yet even if he is silent in judgment, he is not silent in commandment. At his first coming he was silent because he appeared in humility.

Fire will burn before his presence. Here fire is understood to possess a twofold power. For it illuminates and consumes. Let the righteous rejoice, because they are illuminated by it. Let sinners fear, because they will be consumed by it. And around him there is a violent storm. It scourges and corrects sinners and separates wheat from chaff. Those whom the fire consumes, the storm envelops. And in another place he says: “He will cleanse his threshing floor and gather the wheat into his barn, but he will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire” (Luke V).

And he called heaven from above. The apostles or the other saints, who, despising earthly things, set their minds on things above. And the earth, to distinguish his people. He also distinguishes the earthly, so that when the heavenly are placed on the right, these may be placed on the left. Or, he will distinguish his people in the future judgment, when he will say: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire.” And to the saints: “Go into eternal life” (Matt. XXV).

Gather his saints to him. How wonderfully these things correspond to the holy Gospel! For after the dispensation of the end, hear what he says: “The Son of Man will send his angels with a trumpet and great power, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from the summit of the heavens” (Matt. XXIV). And here he says: “Gather all his saints to him.” Understand from this, therefore, that the arranger of the Old and New Testaments is one.

Those who establish his covenant above sacrifices. In whose mercies God delights above all sacrifices. Or, “establish,” meaning they preach and fulfill the New Testament above the old, because the old things pass away, and behold, all things have become new (II Cor. V).

And the heavens will proclaim his justice. The evangelists, or the law of Moses. Because God is judge. He causes the good to be separated from the evil. Or, the heavens are the saints; they will announce, they will preach, as in: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. XVIII). His justice, his commandments. Because God is judge: for he himself is the judge of the living and the dead. He is also our advocate, and he is judge, and he is our God.

Hear, my people, and I will speak to you, Israel. The voice of God the Father speaks to the Jewish people. Hear, my people. He seeks the ear of the heart, as the prophet says: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me” (Ps. LXXXIV). And elsewhere: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. VI). Or, receive ears for hearing, so that you may understand, Israel. And I will testify to you. If you have perceived with a spiritual mind. Or, “I will testify to you,” that is, through the patriarchs and prophets, as he said: “I am who I am” (Exod. V). For I am God, your God. I am God in omnipotence; but I am your God by grace, not the mute and deaf idols that you have until now worshiped. Or, “I am,” who always am the same.

I will not accuse you because of your sacrifices. Because I delight in a contrite heart. Your burnt offerings, however, are always before me. If you have directed to me the fragrance of right prayer, like an incense of sweetness.

I will not accept calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks. For I have rejected these things, because the blood of the true Lamb has been poured out for the sins of my people. Or, “I will not accept calves from your house,” that is, the incontinent and the proud. Nor goats from your flocks: goats, which are foul in sin.

For all the beasts of the forests are mine, the animals on the mountains and the oxen. Irrational people occupied with various mountains [Col. 0970A], whom it is necessary to save through the calling of the Son of God.

I have known all the birds of heaven. Either heretics or the rich of this world, who are exalted through worldly pride and irrational knowledge. And the beauty of the field is with me. For whenever I wish, the abundance of all things is either spread abroad or withheld. Or, “the beauty of the field is with me”: the power of the holy Church. The birds of heaven that you offer me—turtledoves and pigeons—I gave to you; and all things live before God before they come to be. Their place, the time at which they came, their weight and measure—all things are before God, as he says in the Gospel: “Even the hairs of your head are all numbered” (Luke XII). Or, “the birds of heaven”: the holy angels.

If I should be hungry, I will not tell you. God’s hunger is not for corruptible foods, but that someone should do his will, as he himself says in the Gospel: “My food is to do the will of my Father” (John IV). Therefore Christ keeps silent about his hunger, because he awaits sinners for repentance. For mine is the world and its fullness: the whole world. Or, “the world”: the holy Church. It is as though he said that it had been redeemed by his blood.

Will I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats? Here he declares that the ancient sacrifices must be abolished, and therefore seeks sacrifice in good conduct, saying:

Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High. This is the acceptable sacrifice; this is the rich burnt offering: that God should be praised by the human being whom he created and redeemed, and to whom he promises the heavenly kingdom. Or, the prophet’s voice admonishes the saints to offer sacrifice spiritually and to pay their vows, as he says: “Your vows are upon me, O God; I will render praises to you.”

Call upon me in the day of your tribulation, etc. We are tested so that we may be proved. Let us persevere in faith and call upon him in tribulation; when we have been delivered from dangers, let us magnify him.

But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my righteous deeds and take up my covenant upon your lips? Let the teachers, or the bishops of the churches, hear this—those who cut away the sins of the peoples by preaching. Hence Saint Paul says: “Those who have not upheld the commandment of Christ are manifest” (I Timothy V), that is, they do not fulfill in their conduct what they preach. Hence the Lord said to the apostles: “Do and observe whatever they tell you; but do not act according to their works” (Matthew XXIII).

But you hate discipline and have cast my words behind you. What you preached in the Church, you did not preserve in your life.

If you saw a thief, you ran with him, and with adulterers you placed your portion. You ran with the thief and became a partner with the adulterer when you joined yourself to them either in flattering praises or in pleasures shared with them. What he said above, “you placed your portion,” means: the portion that you ought to have had with God and the angels—you place that in hell.

Your mouth abounded in wickedness, and your tongue fashioned deceit. While he was acting wickedly, you wickedly and deceitfully praised his good conduct. Or, “your tongue fashioned deceit,” that is, Judas against Christ. His mouth abounded in wickedness when he made an agreement with the Jews to crucify him.

Sitting, you spoke against your brother, and against the son of your mother you set a stumbling-block. Christ is called “son,” because he proceeded from the synagogue. Or Judas is called the Lord’s brother, as the prophet says: “I will declare your name to my brothers” (Psalm XXI). Or otherwise: “brothers” means the stronger saints, and “sons” the simpler. Hence Saint Paul said: “We who are stronger ought to bear with the weaknesses of the weak” (Romans XV). “Sitting, you spoke against your brother”: the one who was reborn with you in baptism. “And against the son of your mother you set a stumbling-block”: the one whom the Church of God, like yourself, presented to Christ through faith. You have done these things, and I was silent. For I reserved them for examination at the future judgment. “And I was silent”: I did not immediately exact vengeance, but endured.

You thought, wicked one, that I would be like you. Because I do not take vengeance in the present, you supposed that I approved of those things, just as you approve of your own evils and those of others. I will rebuke you when you have been placed on the left side at the future judgment, and I will set those things before your face, so that, confounded by them, you may be condemned to everlasting death—that is, by those commandments that you did not keep; or by your own sins and those of others whom you left behind, as it is written: “If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked man, I will require his blood at your hand” (Ezekiel III). Would that in this world we placed our sins before ourselves, so that God would not set them before our face in judgment, where punishment no longer follows, but the judgment of death.

Understand these things now, you who forget God. The prophet’s voice admonishes each person not to put the Lord out of mind, nor his commandments (Job II). Lest he suddenly seize you, and there be no one to deliver you. “Lest he suddenly seize you”: either unto death or unto the day of judgment. Hence he says: “And there is no one who can rescue from your hand.” Or, “he seizes”: that is, he casts those who forget him headlong into death, and no one can deliver them.

A sacrifice of praise will honor me. For God is honored by every good work that the saints perform. Hence Paul said: “Whatever you do in word or deed, do everything in the glory of God” (I Corinthians X), and likewise in the Gospel: “That they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew V). For this reason he honors me before the angels, because I honored him before human beings with sacrifices of praise; and he fulfilled what he spoke in the Gospels: “Whoever confesses me before human beings, I will confess him before my Father and his angels” (Luke XII). And there is a way there. Christ’s way is through the works of the saints. Along it I will show him the salvation of God. The salvation of God the Father is the Son. In this sacrifice he points out the way that leads to life, that is, to Christ. May he deign to grant us that, separated from the chaff and filled with the fruit of sanctification, we may offer him a sacrifice of praise, so that, with him giving light, we may deserve to understand the way of our salvation. Amen.

## PSALM L

**For the end; a psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet came to him, when he had gone in to Bathsheba.**

This fiftieth psalm contains the voice of a repentant person, showing that whoever has fallen into sin may return to salvation by confessing his sins.

Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy. I confess immeasurable misery; therefore I ask for great mercy. For when someone considers himself miserable because of his sins, God shows great mercy toward him. There is a lesser mercy here in the present: namely, that when the human being did not exist, God created him from nothing so that he might exist, and rules and governs him. A greater mercy is spoken of when, in the future, he rewards the very human being whom he created. And according to the multitude of your mercies, etc. I flee to your mercies, so that you may pour the antidote of forgiveness into grievous wounds. He says “mercies,” because my sins are many and your mercies are many (Psalm LXVIII). Hence the prophet says elsewhere: “Your mercies are many, O Lord.”

Wash me yet more from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin. I ask you to wash me in the fountain of mercy, because you do not wish to preserve the wounds of sin forever—as though he said: You can forgive me more than I know how to ask.

For I know my iniquity. I place it before my face. If you declare your sins in confession, God will forgive you. And my sin is always against me, because my sins separate me from the riches of your goodness. Since I do not consign it to oblivion, I set it always before my eyes. For if you place it before yourself, God does not place it before himself.

Against you alone have I sinned, and I have done evil before you. Everyone sins against you when he sins, because you alone are without sin, as the Apostle says: “God is truthful, and every human being is a liar” (Romans III). Or David says: “I have sinned, and you alone are without sin,” as Isaiah says: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (Isaiah LIII). Or again: “Who will convict me of sin?” (John VIII). And again he says: “The ruler of this world is coming, and he found nothing in me” (John XIV).

So that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged. For you judge with a just judgment. On account of us transgressors and sinners, he was judged and condemned. Hence it was said: “The just man was judged by the wicked.” But in the future judgment he will judge and condemn others. You were justified, Lord Jesus, in your words when, led to death for the sins of the people, no deceit was found in your mouth. You prevailed when judged, since the prince of darkness found in you nothing deserving death. It is the prophet’s custom to speak of things done as though they were yet to be done.

For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother conceived me in sins. This verse explains the fall of the entire human race, as in Job: “Even if he were but one day old upon the earth, he cannot be clean from the stain of sin” (Job XV and XXV). A person is conceived and born in original sin, which is drawn from Adam, but is purified in baptism through the grace of Christ.

Or, “so that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged.” Paul explains this passage more carefully in the Epistle to the Romans: although God could distinguish our case with the authority of a judge, he does not do so, but wishes to be judged together with us, so that the justice of the judge may appear more clearly (Romans III). “In sins my mother conceived me”: an obscure passage requiring deeper reconsideration.

Behold, you have loved truth. When through the prophet you rebuked your sinful servant, you loved truth. Truth is Christ, because the Father loves his Son; or, he loves confession from the mouth of the sinner. You have revealed to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom. This is what he says elsewhere: “Open my eyes, and I will consider the wonders of your law” (Psalm CXVIII). It would be uncertain and hidden to me if you were to forgive such a crime. But it becomes manifest when you deign to pardon the offender. For it belongs to your wisdom first to rebuke and then to forgive. It was likewise hidden wisdom concerning your mercy for the Ninevites when they said: “Who knows whether God may turn from his anger, and we may not perish?” (Jonah III).

Or, God revealed the uncertain and hidden things through the prophet Nathan: that is, he told David, when he said, “Your sin has been forgiven,” just as the Ninevites turned from evil to good through Jonah’s preaching.

You will sprinkle me with hyssop, Lord, and I shall be clean. Just as earthly hyssop is suitable for treating the lungs, so that it removes swelling, so whoever is sprinkled with heavenly hyssop—that is, with humility of heart—is cleansed from every evil of pride. You will wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow. Since my sins are like scarlet, let them become white as snow. You, I say, Lord, are powerful enough to change pitch-black sin into milk-white brightness and to turn sooty ebony into the radiance of crystal. Or, “you will wash me”: that is, through repentance and baptism. “And I shall be whiter than snow,” as Isaiah said: “Though your sins be like scarlet, they shall become white as snow” (Isaiah I).

You will give joy and gladness to my hearing. When, lying in the sickness of sin, I deserve to hear, “Human being, your sins are forgiven you.” Or he says “to my hearing” when Nathan said: “Your sin has been forgiven.” And the humbled bones will rejoice—that is, the powers that had previously been humbled by sins. Or, it is the eternity of my hope, which had been humbled when I sinned, but which rejoices when you grant forgiveness.

Turn your face from my sins, and do not look upon them in such a way that they return to your remembrance. “Turn your face”: as though he said, Do not see them, and do not remember them. And blot out all my iniquities: past, present, and future.

Create a clean heart in me, O God, so that I may see you. As David prayed, so each person ought to do. “Create a clean heart in me, O God”: for this reason he prayed, that he might become clean from sin. And renew a right spirit within me, so that I may confess you rightly. Or, “a right spirit,” for seeing and discerning, as it was formerly right within me.

Do not cast me away from your face, as Cain, so that I may become an exile from you. “From your face”: that is, from your presence. And do not take your Holy Spirit from me, but, once my sins have been consumed by him, establish me before your sight. “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me”: that is, the spirit of prophecy.

Restore to me the joy of your salvation: the exultation of your Christ, which I had in him before I sinned. Christ is the salvation of God the Father. It is as though he said: Just as previously, through the Spirit, I foresaw Christ coming in the flesh, so now also make me do so. And establish me with your princely Spirit, so that he, and not vices, may rule within me.

But you who read Holy Scripture, understand here the holy Trinity. Or, “establish me”: in the kingdom. “The right spirit”: that is, renewing the Holy Spirit, namely the spirit of prophecy. “The princely Spirit”: the Father. “The right Spirit”: the Son. “The Holy Spirit”: the Holy Spirit.

I will teach the wicked your ways, and the ungodly will turn back to you. Thus, turning aside from crooked ways and practicing repentance, they may obtain mercy, just as I too have obtained mercy from you. “I will teach the wicked your ways, and the ungodly will turn back to you”: that is, I will present myself so that others may imitate my example.

Deliver me from bloodguilt, O God. From many sins, concerning which Paul also says: “Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God” (I Corinthians XV). O God of my salvation, from whom I am brought to life after sin. For no one else can do this. And my tongue will exult in your righteousnesses, through which, by punishing sin in me, you have shown mercy. Or, my tongue will proclaim your commandments.

Lord, open my lips, and my mouth will proclaim your praise. If you open my mouth as you once did for Moses, I will proclaim that you are holy, devout, and merciful. Or, my lips had been closed by sin: they could provide neither the place, nor the time, nor the person, nor the example, because praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner.

For if you had desired sacrifice, I would certainly have given it; you will not delight in burnt offerings. Let the Jews hear that their sacrifices have ceased. Let them also understand God speaking through another prophet: “My soul has hated your Sabbaths, burnt offerings, and new moons” (Isaiah I). What, then, will you offer, human being? Hear what he adds:

A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise. Rightly, among the other evangelical beatitudes, this beatitude holds the primacy. “Blessed,” he says, “are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew V). They are not puffed up by the vanities of the world, but receive from God the breath of life and pour the contrition of an anxious heart back into him who became humble for us.

Or, many have a contrite heart but do not have a humbled heart: they grieve over what they have done, yet afterward desire to return to the very things they had previously done and do not wish to repent of the past.

Do good, Lord. That is, make our hope pleasing. In your good will, O Zion, where we contemplate you. And let the walls of Jerusalem be built: the fortifications of that faith and charity which, placed in the Church, we have established in you.

Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness, offerings, and burnt offerings, when either you offer yourself for us to the Father or receive praises and acts of thanksgiving from us. Or, “the walls of Jerusalem” are the virtues of the soul or of the Church. “Then you will accept the sacrifice”: that is, confession from the mouth of the sinner; “the offering”: that is, praise; “and burnt offerings.” Then they will place calves upon your altar.

The altar is faith, because whatever you offer, you must offer through faith. The calf signifies praises, thoughts, or victims—namely, that I may offer myself as a living, holy, and pleasing sacrifice to you.

We too, your servants, suppliantly beseech you, Lord Jesus Christ, that, in accordance with the counsel of your mercy, you may bestow immense mercy upon our great crimes; and that, through the contrition of our humbled heart, by putting vices to death and cutting the throats of our sins, you may prepare us as a worthy and acceptable burnt offering for yourself. Amen.

## PSALM LI

**For the end; an instruction of David, when Doeg the Edomite came to him and reported to Saul, saying: “David has come to the house of Ahimelech.”**

In the Book of Kingdoms and in the Hebrew Psalter itself, it is written “Abimelech”; but since among the Hebrews the letters beth and kaph are distinguished by only a slight mark, the error more easily crept in. Abimelech is interpreted as “the kingdom of my father.” David is interpreted as “strong of hand.” David came into the house of Abimelech, and Christ came into the kingdom of the Jews. Saul signifies death; David, life. What does it mean that death persecutes life, except that from the beginning of the world death has always persecuted our life? For those who love present things persecute the holy Church, that is, those who love heavenly things.

The psalm contains the voice of the prophet reproaching the sins of the Jewish people. He speaks these words to that people itself, saying:

Why do you glory in wickedness? Why, opposing the divine admonitions, do you kill the prophets? You are powerful in iniquity. For, growing through God’s aid, you kill his prophets; and you increased your wickedness to its height by handing over the Lord himself to death.

Or, “Why do you glory in wickedness?” That is, Adam and the devil: what God built, they destroyed in themselves—the image of God and of the angels. “You are powerful in iniquity”: not in goodness, but in iniquity.

All day long: the whole time of your life, during which this wickedness was extended even to the shedding of the Lord’s blood. Your tongue devised injustice. The thought of the wise is conceived in the heart and brought forth by the mouth. But in the mouth of fools is their heart. It is as though he said: He did not deliberate in his heart what he vomits from his mouth; therefore he attributes this to the tongue’s thought.

Or, here “tongue” is used for “heart,” according to the passage: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will set my throne; on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north, I will ascend above the height of the clouds; I will be like the Most High’” (Isaiah XLI).

Like a sharp razor, you have practiced deceit. Deceit occurs when one thing is done while another is pretended. If a razor appears to be making the face smooth but wounds the cheeks with its cut, it practices deceit. Since he says “sharp,” he indicates that it is cunning in deceit. So too the Jews, although they ought to have worshiped the Lord, not only did not worship him, but, striving to overcome him by various deceits, killed him.

Or otherwise: by “razor,” persecutors are understood, because a razor cuts hair; and by hair is understood the excess of riches. “Like a sharp razor, you have practiced deceit.” Whoever circumvents his brother in business practices deceit. Hence Paul says: “Let no one defraud or overreach his brother in business, because the Lord is the avenger of all these things” (I Thessalonians IV).

You loved wickedness more than kindness, iniquity rather than speaking righteousness. That people loved wickedness when they killed him who had come in his own kindness to deliver them. But even now the Jews themselves speak falsely about him in whom they did not believe.

You loved all words of destruction, O deceitful tongue. Speaking in lofty terms of iniquity, they cast themselves headlong into the snare of condemnation. He says “words of destruction” because they cast themselves down, like the devil from heaven and Adam from paradise. “O deceitful tongue,” because they had one thing in their speech and another in their heart.

Therefore God will destroy you forever; he will uproot you and remove you from your tent, and your root from the land of the living. All these things were fulfilled in the Jewish people: they were destroyed from the letter of the law, uprooted from the city, and removed from the tabernacle of God.

But these words are also understood of those who do not believe in the tabernacle of the Lord’s body, for they will be excluded from fellowship with his glory and from the dwelling of the blessed seat, or from the land of the living that the saints will inherit. Or, “God will destroy you forever”: that is, the memory of the devil, as elsewhere: “So that man may no longer continue to exalt himself upon the earth” (Psalm XLIX). Hence the holy Apostle Paul said: “At the end of the ages the enemy, death, will be destroyed” (I Corinthians XV)—that is, the devil.

“He will uproot you and remove you from your tent, and your root from the land of the living.” Just as death was given dominion in Adam, so it rules over all his children. Hence it was said: “You are earth, and to earth you will go” (Genesis III). The devil and Adam uprooted themselves, and each person does likewise when he sins.

The just will see and fear, lest they desire such things. And they will laugh over him, because of the vengeance of his calamity. “They will see”: that is, they will understand their punishment; “and fear,” as Saint Paul says: “See that you too are not tempted” (Galatians VI). Or, “they will fear”: that is, they will not know their end. Hence it was said: “A human being does not know his end” (Ecclesiastes IX).

Again: “And they will laugh over him.” There are two times: a time for weeping and a time for laughing. Here the saints have a time for weeping, and in the future a time for laughing. And they will say: Behold the man who did not set God as his helper, but trusted in the multitude of his riches and prevailed in his vanity. Therefore this vengeance came down upon him.

Or he speaks of the rich man who was tormented in hell because he had received his good things during his life (Luke XVI), and of the other man to whom he says: “Fool, this night they demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke XI). So is the one who stores up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.

Is it therefore evil to have riches, provided they are obtained justly and thanks are returned to God who gave them? No. But it is evil to place one’s hope in riches, since another psalm says: “If riches abound, do not set your heart upon them” (Psalm LXI). It is permissible to have riches for necessity, but it is not permissible to possess them out of love. Abraham and the other good men also had riches, but they did not place their hope in riches.

But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house. The prophet compares himself to a fruitful olive tree because of the richness of wisdom, so that, placed in the Church of God and living within the allegory of the law, he may bring forth evangelical fruits. For the proclaimer of the Old and the New Testament is one God.

The fruitful olive tree is the holy Church, as in the passage: “Their storehouses are full, overflowing” (Psalm CXLIII). Here the image is taken in a good sense. There is also the unfruitful olive tree, as the prophet says: “The Lord called your name, ‘A beautiful olive tree, fruitful and fair’; but a fire was kindled in it at the sound of a great utterance, and its branches were burned” (Jeremiah XI). And again: “A luxuriant, beautiful, fruitful olive tree” (ibid.); but you were changed into a wild olive.

Again, he speaks in a good sense: “Although you were a wild olive, you were grafted into the good olive” (Romans XI), that is, into the faith of the patriarchs.

I have hoped in the mercy of God forever and for ages of ages. For human weakness has no power to save itself by its own strength, but is saved through the mercy of God.

I will confess to you forever, because you have done this. I ask that in this world, which you created by your word, I may deserve to offer confession, and that he may grant it through his accustomed clemency. And I will await your name, for it is good in the presence of your saints: that name blessed before all ages, which renders the saints their due reward. The prophet, thirsting for it, asks that in its presence he may receive a share in eternal blessedness.

May he deign to grant us that, free from every deceit and cleansed from all iniquity, confessing the Son of God as equal to the Father and to the Holy Spirit, we may deserve to be planted like a fruitful olive tree in the heavenly Jerusalem.

## PSALM LII

**For the end; concerning Amalech; an instruction for David.**

Machalath is interpreted as “sorrowful” or “in labor”; the body of Christ is understood. The Lord also sorrowed for our sins, because he possessed a true body, and he brought forth children. The Church, too, is Christ’s body: it grieves for its own sins and those of others, and gives birth to children through the word of preaching, as in the passage: “Through the Gospel I begot you” (I Corinthians IV). And again: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians IV).

[Note: The name “Amalech” occurs neither in the Hebrew nor in the Greek or Latin text. The name’s interpretation itself immediately rejects the written form, for Jerome does not interpret Amalech as “the woman in labor,” but as “the people who lick,” and so forth. It is commonly thought that it should be corrected to Machalath, in Hebrew [term not legible in the supplied text], or Maeleth, as some Latin codices have it. But Saint Jerome does not explain this name as “the woman in labor”; rather, he explains it as “choir” or “symphony,” as in Letter 21 to Damasus concerning the prodigal son. Indeed, it is established that [term not legible in the supplied text] denotes a choir in Psalm CXLIX:3 and elsewhere, from the root [term not legible in the supplied text], “to dance.” If it is necessary to interpret it as “the woman in labor,” the etymology of the name must be derived from *Chul*.]

This psalm contains the voice of the prophet rebuking sinners and the ungodly.

The fool said in his heart: There is no God. “The fool said”: the Jewish people, or the devil, said, “There is no God.” It is as though he said: “Christ the Son of God does not exist.”

They are corrupt. They have departed from the law of good nature. They have become abominable: that is, hateful. In their iniquities: that is, in their desires. Although fools did not dare to deny God with their mouths, in their hearts they say that he does not exist; by this evil they become horrible and abominable to God.

There is no one who does good; there is not even one. The prophet does not speak of everyone, but only of all those who deny God. For they sometimes speak good things, but never do them.

The Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of human beings, to see whether there was anyone with understanding or seeking God. That is, to find those whom he might choose, as he once did among the prophets and patriarchs, and, having found them, make them his own servants and foster children. To look forth and to see belong to one who is ignorant and seeking.

Does God know anything unknowingly? No. Rather, the heavens are the saints, as the prophet says: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Psalm XVIII). And elsewhere, according to the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians III). For the Holy Spirit causes the saints to love and cherish God, and the Holy Spirit himself is God. God looks forth through his saints, because he preaches and speaks through them, as the Lord says: “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew X).
