All have turned aside; together they have become useless. These fools, because they did not seek God, have all turned aside into passions; together they have become useless. One is called useless who does not perform anything good. Hence he says in the Gospel: “Take the talent away from him and cast the useless servant into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew XXV). Those who do not wish to fulfill God’s commandments are useless to themselves.

There is no one who does good; there is not even one. None of these fulfills the will of the heavenly Father.

Will all those who practice iniquity not understand—those who devour my people as though they were morsels of bread? They have not called upon God. They know that they are acting impiously, and not only do they fail to amend their ways, but they also devour God’s people with the teeth of their wickedness and disdain calling upon God.

There they trembled with fear where there was no fear. They feared idols and lifeless images, although they ought to have feared God.

For God scattered the bones of those who please human beings. God will shatter the hope of their eternity—of those who, to his dishonor, pleased themselves more than they pleased him. Those who please themselves have been confounded, that is, those who please human beings and not God. They have been confounded because God rejected them. Rightly is one rejected by God who has abandoned God; and whoever abandons him is justly confounded by him as one unknown, as the Apostle says: “Everyone who is ignorant will be ignored” (II Corinthians XIV).

Who will give salvation to Israel from Zion? From Zion, as the prophet says, “the law will go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isaiah II). Who will give it? God the Father gave his Son in Zion, that is, in the holy Church. “Salvation to Israel”: our salvation is Christ. Who will give it except the Lord at his coming, through whom we contemplate the glory of eternity?

When the Lord turns back the captivity of his people, he too, having turned away the captivity of vices, raises us into the freedom of virtues. Concerning this captivity he says: They have already been redeemed from Adam’s sin, yet they are still held in captivity, because their freedom is not complete; while we are in the body, we are exiles from the Lord.

And again he says: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (II Corinthians II). “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans VII). But on the day of judgment, when hostile death is destroyed, then true redemption will come.

Jacob will exult, and Israel will rejoice. The Christian people hear both names: it is Jacob when it supplants the Jewish people and receives its blessing, and Israel when it looks upon God with the eyes of faith.

Therefore we too suppliantly beseech God that, turning away from superfluous talk, and with him instructing us, we may understand that all things stand under his dominion. May he deign, once the captivity of vices has been removed, to raise us into the freedom of virtues.

## PSALM LIII

**For the end; an instruction in songs, of David, when the Ziphites came and said to Saul: “David is hidden among us in the cave of Ziph.”**

Ziph is a village, and from it the Ziphites take their name. The Ziphites are interpreted as “flourishing,” that is, sinners who appear to flourish and be green in the present life, as the prophet says: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field” (Isaiah XL), because what is dry is reserved for the fire. These are assigned to punishment; the saints to the kingdom.

Just as grass appears green today until the heat comes, so sinners, because they seem to flourish, will wither on the day of judgment. The saints, who here appear as though dry and withered, will then be flourishing and green. Hence it was said: “The just will flourish like a palm tree” (Psalm XCI).

David was hidden in the lower part of the earth; the Lord was hidden in the womb of holy Mary and among one people, the Jews; and divinity was hidden in Christ’s flesh. This psalm is recognized as containing the prayer of the Lord as man: of him who received the form of a servant and approached his passion in the form of a servant.

Save me, O God, by your name. He asks this of the Father in order to show the weakness of the flesh. “By your name”: that is, by the name of humility, which is salvation. And judge me by your strength. He wishes to be judged, so that through divinity he may ascend to that honorable name of majesty.

Humility was shown when he came from heaven into the womb, from the womb into the manger, and endured many things—slaps, spittle, and the rest. Strength was shown when he rose and ascended into heaven on the fortieth day, and on the fiftieth day the Holy Spirit came upon the apostles, who preached the teaching of the Gospel throughout the world.

Hence it was said: “He gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth; and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians II). And because he died for a time through the weakness of the flesh, he lives through the power of God. And again the Apostle says: “I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (II Corinthians II).

Or, “judge me”: the voice of the Church asks for discernment.

O God, hear my prayer. He also asks this, that he may deserve to be heard by God. For he alone knew how to pray steadfastly and not, as a human being, to be ignorant of what he should ask, according to the Apostle’s statement: “For we do not know what we ought to pray for” (Romans VIII). Give heed with your ears to the words of my mouth. This is the voice of the Church. The Lord is said to have ears when he deigns to hear.

For strangers have risen against me. These are the Jews, who, although they had belonged especially to God, made themselves strangers to him through transgression—not in knowledge, but in life and works. Hence he says: “The sons of strangers have lied to me” (Psalm XVII). And if they are sons, how are they strangers? They were from one tribe, but they were strangers because they wished to take the life of the one who had come to give them life.

And the powerful have sought my soul. Herod and the chief priests possessed worldly power. The Lord says: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above” (John XIX). The same applies to heretical persecutors against the holy Church. They have not set God before their eyes. They did not understand that divinity lay hidden beneath the bodily appearance.

The *diapsalma* inserted here changes the prayer, so that the one who had previously been praying as a human being may be shown to have obtained the effect of his prayer. Therefore he adds:

Behold, God helps me, because the Lord descended into death. And the Lord is the protector of my soul, for he will soon restore it. Or, God the Father received his Son, and Christ received his Church in faith.

Turn the evils upon my enemies, and scatter them in your truth. Those who did not understand me because of their wickedness, let them be scattered in your truth, as we now see has happened. For they were scattered among the nations. He says “truth” because it is true: that is, he will render to each according to his works. “Scatter them” on the day of judgment and in your just vengeance—that is, the devil and his members.

I will sacrifice to you willingly. Rightly, “willingly,” because by his own will the priest and victim himself offered himself to the Father for the sins of the people, so that this sacrifice might grant life to the world. “I will sacrifice to you willingly”: the voice of the Church. He says “willingly,” that is, not out of necessity or compulsion, but willingly, in accordance with the words: “Shepherding the flock not under compulsion, but freely” (1 Peter 5). “And I will give thanks to your name, for it is good.” I have confessed in the world, because I descended from heaven “not to do my own will, but yours, because it is good” (John 6). “I will give thanks”: that is, I will praise your name; this is good.

For you have delivered me from every tribulation, and my eye has looked down upon my enemies. Because he poured out a pure prayer at the beginning of the psalm, therefore, as God who foresees all things, he declares that he has been delivered from tribulations and that his enemies have been looked upon with paternal scrutiny: namely, so that you may understand that he reigns by that power by which, after the resurrection, he returned victorious to the stars. We humbly beseech him that, saved from enemies by his help and delivered from the tribulations of the world, we may follow in mind and deed our very Head, the Lord Jesus Christ, whom we behold in heaven.

## PSALM 54

For the end; in songs of understanding; of David. “For the end,” in Christ, as in the words: “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10). “For the end” is always understood of Christ. Hence the holy apostles also said: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John 14). You cannot fulfill the law unless it is fulfilled by him. All Holy Scripture concerns him. “In songs,” that is, in praises. Just as there are songs of the world, so there are songs of the Church; hence God’s praise is sung, and it is the consolation of the saints, because it is said: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father,” equal to the angels (Matthew 19). The psalm contains the voice of the Mediator, who, although he was God, assumed the form of a servant for our freedom.

Hear, O God, my prayer, and do not despise my supplication; attend to me and hear me. This threefold supplication is shown for the following reason: the first, while God as man remains in the condition of a servant, he sends forth from the consciousness of his holiness. The second, because he knows himself to be righteous, he asks that obedience not be despised. The third, because of the weakness of the flesh, he begs that attention be given to him. Understand, therefore, O human being, for this reason: unless you supplicate with a pure conscience, you will in no way be heard by God.

I was saddened in my exercise. The exercise that I undertook for the life of the world, since exercise is always directed toward useful and necessary things. I was troubled by the voice of the enemy. They rebuked me, calling me a Samaritan and one who had a demon, although I was God before the ages. Or, the voice of the Church. The Church has two enemies: one openly and one secretly. It ought to love one and hate the other: to love its neighbor, as in the words, “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Luke 6); and to despise and hate the other, namely the devil, who comes secretly through suggestions [Col. 0981D] and pleasures. And by the tribulation of the sinner. He who was always directing against me the snares of tribulation. For this reason God troubles sinners, either so that they may be corrected, or so that through them he may correct the good.

For they turned iniquities toward me. The people certainly turn toward iniquity when they bring forth a lie against their neighbor. Or, the Jews against the Lord, as they said: “By Beelzebul, the prince of demons, he casts out demons” (Matthew 12). And in anger they were troublesome to me, persecuting me in their envy. “And in anger they were troublesome.” “Troublesome” means savage. “In anger”: the straw, the beam, hatred. Anger causes disturbance; the beam causes blindness, as in the words: “My eye has been troubled because of anger” (Psalm 6).

My heart was troubled. According to his humanity, [Col. 0982A] but it was strengthened by divine power. For the Evangelist also says: “And an angel came and strengthened him” (Luke 22). And the fear of death fell upon me. The fear of the soul and the trembling of the body. Fear and trembling came upon me. Indeed, he himself said: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Mark 26). Darkness covered me. Evil people who persecute the Church are called darkness; they cover it in hatred, because “whoever hates his brother is in darkness.” “And darkness covered me”; but because I was light, they did not apprehend me.

And I said: Who will give me wings like a dove’s? And I will fly away and rest. No one other than myself can provide the supreme escape by which death is avoided. “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again,” so that I may return from darkness to heavenly things. In the dove he signifies a spiritual nature, as was shown at the baptism. The dove is a simple animal, without gall and foreign to the malice of gall, because the kiss signifies the soul’s charity. The Church has two wings, that is, the two commandments of charity: love of God, namely, and of neighbor.

Behold, I have fled far away. From the Jews. For salvation is far from sinners. And I remained in solitude. Among unbelieving Gentiles, whom I caused to flourish by my coming. Of them another prophet says: “Let the desert rejoice and blossom” (Isaiah 35). “Behold, I have fled far away, and I remained in solitude.” The dove flees human society, and the saints flee the company of human beings—not bodily, but spiritually, that is, in conscience, because they consider how they ought to defend themselves against the suggestions of the devil or of heretics.

I awaited him who saved me from faintheartedness of spirit and storm. While placed in the body, he awaits not only the Father’s salvation, so that he may be rescued from various storms, but also that he may receive vengeance upon his enemies. It continues:

Hurl them down, O Lord, and divide their tongues. Someone is often hurled down in water. Therefore let these men be submerged as in the Flood, and let them be scattered with divided tongues, as happened at the building of the tower. But he added why these things should happen: For I saw iniquity and contradiction in the city. “Iniquity,” when they did not believe. “Contradiction,” when they reproached him by contradicting him: “Is this not the son of Joseph the carpenter?” (Mark 6), and many other things.

By day and by night. That is, at all times. By day, when he was teaching the crowds and they did not believe. By night, when he suffered and they blasphemed. Thus their city, that is, Jerusalem, was surrounded and filled with these things, so that its iniquity overflowed above the walls.

And usury and deceit did not cease from its streets. For everything prohibited in the law increased, adding to the accumulation of sin. In the law, indeed, the taking of interest is forbidden (Deuteronomy 23). Usury is taking more than one gives. Hence the prophet says: “I have not lent at interest, nor has anyone lent to me at interest” (Jeremiah 15). And: “If you want what is forgiven you, forgive” (Matthew 6).

[Col. 0983A] For if my enemy had cursed me, I would surely have endured it; and if the one who hated me had spoken great things against me, perhaps I would have hidden myself from him. Here the Lord complains not only about the Passion, but also about the betraying disciple. For we read in the Gospels that he hid himself from the Jews (John 8). But he did not hide himself from Judas; rather, he even invited him to the holy meal, as follows:

But you, a man of one mind. You who were joined with the other apostles. My guide. Sent with the others to preach. And my acquaintance. Because through the mystery of the law you had known that I was to come. “My guide and my acquaintance”: the voice of Christ concerning Judas. He says “of one mind” because he appeared to the others to be good. He says “guide” because, by betraying Christ, he became a guide to death. “Acquaintance,” when he sent them two by two before his face to preach (Luke 10).

You who together with me used to take sweet foods. You were often refreshed by the commandments of life and the Father’s will. For sweet food is doing the Father’s will, as in the words: “The one who dips his hand with me in the dish will lift his heel against me” (Matthew 26). Or “sweet food,” that is, the body and blood of Christ, which he received unworthily. We walked in the house of God with harmony. For he often went with the Lord himself into Solomon’s temple, in agreement concerning the preaching.

Let death come upon them, and let them descend alive into hell. In order to show, according to his humanity, the greater sorrow of his heart, he therefore foretold, as though in a curse, what was to come upon them. “Let death come upon them, and let them descend alive into hell.” This happened to Dathan, Korah, and Abiron: fire came at the same time, they died, and the earth swallowed them alive (Numbers 16).

For wickedness is in their dwellings, in their midst. For they are full of wickedness both in deed and in thought.

But I cried to the Lord, and the Lord will save me. In the evening, in the morning, and at midday. In the evening, when he undertook the Passion; in the morning, when he rose; at midday, when, having been filled with the full splendor of his power, he ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father.

I will tell and proclaim, and he will hear my voice. He will redeem my soul in peace from those who draw near to me. He tells, namely, that the Father heard him quickly; that he rescued him from the tribulations of death; and that in peace he freed his soul from the enemies who had drawn near him to inflict death. Or, “I will tell” as of lesser things, and “I will proclaim” as of greater ones. “He freed my soul in peace.” “In peace,” that is, in himself, as Paul said: “He himself is our peace, who made both one” (Ephesians 1). “From those who draw near to me”: they draw near in body, not in life or merit. For they were with me among many. “Among many,” but not “among the few.” They were among the many, that is, in baptism and in faith that was not feigned. They were not among the few, that is, in firm faith, hope, and charity. Among the many who believed, they were with me, and yet they did not believe.

[Col. 0984A] God will hear. Me, who blesses, not them, who curse. “God will hear”: his saints. And he will humble them. That is, the proud. The one who is before the ages. Certainly the Father, whom they did not recognize as remaining in me, because he is before the ages and remains forever. The one who took his beginning from Mary was begotten before the ages.

For there is no change in them. From evil to good: they are not changed or transferred, according to the Gospel, from death to life. And they did not fear God. Therefore he proceeds to vengeance, as follows: He stretched out his hand in repayment. For when it had been extended to them in aid, they did not receive it. “They did not fear God”; therefore they did not turn from evil to good, because they did not recognize him. And he stretched out his hand in repayment to them. [Col. 0984B] He stretched out his hand, as the prophet says: “All day long I spread out my hands toward a people who did not believe and contradicted me” (Isaiah 65), because they did not believe my works and my power. “In repayment to them,” that is, in vengeance on the day of judgment, especially since I said to Abraham: “In your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 25), that is, in Christ; and in another place: “I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Psalm 2). Through the New Testament Christ acquired his inheritance.

They profaned his covenant. Because they did not understand the Lord Jesus, promised through the proclamation of holy men. And they were separated from the anger of his countenance. Their contemplation was separated from spiritual providence; [Col. 0984C] therefore their portion was placed with the unbelievers. After their reproach, the discourse returns to Judas, saying: And his heart drew near, so that, having been filled by the devil, he might betray Christ. “They profaned his covenant, and they were separated from the anger of his countenance,” that is, the heretics who wished to profane God’s covenant will be separated on the day of judgment, when they will receive the sentence of condemnation: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire” (Matthew 25). “And his heart drew near”: his will, because what they understand from the Scriptures they turn to evil, since they do not rightly believe concerning the faith of the Trinity. Hence it is said: “There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (1 Corinthians 11).

His words have been softened more than oil, yet they are arrows. When he says “they have been softened,” he speaks of several, although previously he had spoken of one. Therefore understand the devil and Judas as being named: he made his words gentler than oil when he said, “Hail, Rabbi,” and kissed him (Matthew 16). Rejecting such oil, while placed in tribulations, let us seek God’s help. God himself taught us this by his example, saying:

Cast your care upon the Lord, and he himself will nourish you. So that, brought up by him, you may resist your enemies with strength. You will not grant eternal wavering to the righteous. For if you are righteous, he does not allow you to be wearied by wicked waves. Whoever wavers is at sea. By the sea this world is understood, in which the saints waver.

But you, O God, will lead them down into the pit of destruction. So that those who did not wish to drink from the fountain of living water may be plunged into the pit of destruction. “Into the pit of destruction”: that is, into hell, by just vengeance upon them.

Men of blood and deceit. Those who shed the blood of our Redeemer. They will not complete half their days. Not only did they fail to fill the days of eternity, but they did not even deserve to reach half the span of his time. In a brief space they were slaughtered by their enemies in vengeance for the Lord.

But I will hope in you, O Lord. So that my days may be found complete. We also humbly beseech you, Lord, that, heard by you, neither smeared with the oil of sin, nourished by you, nor freed by you from the waves of this age, we may deserve to obtain length of days through good works. Amen.

## PSALM 55

[Col. 0985B]

For the end; for the people who have been made far from the saints; of David, for the inscription of the title, when the foreigners seized him in Gath. In Hebrew it reads: “For the mute dove of the distant ones, of David, humble and perfect, when the Philistines seized him in Gath.” The mute dove, and David humble and perfect, signify Christ in the Passion.

Have mercy on me, O God, for man has trampled me down; all day long, attacking, he has troubled me. By “man” and “warrior” he shows the assault of the devil or of the remaining spiritual wickednesses, at whose instigation the Lord suffered. “Day,” however, signifies bodily age. “Have mercy on me, O Lord,” as though he were saying: Show mercy in me. “For man has trampled me down,” that is, Christ was trampled by the Jews in the Passion, [Col. 0985C] and the Church by persecutors. One man is spoken of for many, and many are spoken of for one. “One” means the unity of wickedness. There are two cities in the world: Babylon and Jerusalem. By Babylon are understood the wicked, who persecute the saints; likewise Jerusalem, that is, the chosen soul, does not cease to pray for its enemies. “All day long, attacking, he troubled me”: “all day long,” throughout the entire time of the struggle.

My enemies have trampled me down. The Jews, certainly. “All day long,” from the time when he assumed flesh. I will fear from the height of day. This has two meanings. One, as though the Church were saying in prayer: I will not fear the height of the proud. The other, as an assertion: I will fear the height, that is, the height of divinity, because whoever does not fear acts presumptuously. For many are warring against me. They will fear from the height of day, because they placed their hopes not in God but in transitory things.

But I will hope in you; in God I will praise my words. Because I trust in his help and protection, as the Lord said: “My teaching is not mine, but that of the Father who sent me” (John 7). How much more ought we, who have received everything from him and have received him himself, always to praise him!

In God I will hope; I will not fear what man can do to me. Strengthened in him, I will not fear the wars that my adversary wages against me, because it is said: “If they kill the body, they cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10).

All day long they cursed my words against me. When they said: “This man is not the prophet, but he leads the crowd astray” (John 7). All their plans are for evil. For their plans were turned to evil when divine vengeance scourged them after the crimes of the Lord’s Passion. “All their plans are for evil”: the Jews against Christ, and sinners against the saints.

They will inhabit. With one mind. And they will hide. The snares of their wickedness. They will watch my heel. So that they may be able to trip me up, as they wished: either concerning the tribute coin (Luke 20), or concerning the woman caught in adultery (John 8). “They will watch my heel”: the Jews the end of Christ, and sinners the end of the Church, because “the righteous falls seven times and rises” (Proverbs 24). Or, “they will watch my heel,” as was said concerning that woman and the serpent (Genesis 3). By the head is understood the beginning of an evil suggestion, and by the heel the end [Col. 0986B] of life. Or the heretics seek to watch for the end in any statement.

As they waited for my soul. So that, having caught me in my words, they might accuse me before the rulers. You will save them for nothing. They are saved for nothing when they are not changed into glory but transferred to punishments. “You will save them for nothing,” because Christ did nothing for which he suffered, but the Jews sought to kill him. In anger you will crush the peoples. Because they have struck against the stone of stumbling and the rock of offense. After this vengeance, the prophet, rejoicing and foreseeing the future, sings:

O God, I have proclaimed my life to you. For you are my life and the life of the entire people who are to come for the redemption of the world. Each person ought to announce this through confession, as Paul did when he said: “I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man; but I received mercy, because I acted ignorantly in unbelief” (1 Timothy 1). And again he said: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2). You have placed my tears in your sight, as also in your promise. Then my enemies will turn back. Your promises were that you would turn former tears into new joys, with the enemies turned behind them, and would reward me with your glory together with the other saints. “You have placed my tears in your sight”: that is, you have heard and seen them. “As also in your promise.” God promised good things to his saints, but he nevertheless says: First confess your iniquities, so that you may be justified. “Then my enemies will turn back.” [Col. 0986D] The Church says this in desire, so that those who are running toward hell may turn back to God (Isaiah 43, according to the Septuagint).

On whatever day I call upon you, behold, I have known that you are my God. For in every necessity you, God, stand by, granting mercy to your own. “On whatever day I call upon you,” that is, whether in prosperity or adversity; “and I have known that you are my God.” The voice of the Church. Some come to know through the creation of heaven and earth, as Saint Paul says: “Through the things that have been made, understanding is conceived” (Romans 1). Others come to know through God, who inspires their souls, as he said to Thomas: “Put your finger here, and place your hand in my side, and recognize the places of the nails; and do not be unbelieving, but faithful” (John 20). And he himself, remembering this, says: “My Lord and my God.”

In God I will praise the Word, and in the Lord I will praise the utterance; in God I will hope, I will not fear what man can do to me. Again the prophet praises that Word, or utterance, which was in the beginning with the Father, because, hoping in him, he does not fear the threats of the adversary, saying:

In me are your vows, O God, which I will repay to you as praises. These are the prophet’s vows: that he may celebrate the Lord’s praise, as he says elsewhere: “Sacrifice a sacrifice of praise to God” (Psalm 40). And he added why he does these things:

For you have delivered my soul from death. The second death, certainly. My eyes from tears. So that it would no longer be necessary to mourn sins, as in the words: “God will wipe away every tear from their eyes on the day of judgment” (Revelation 7), because it is said: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted” (Matthew 5). My feet from falling. So that they might no longer fall into sins. “My feet,” that is, my faculties, from falling, because then there will be neither evil suggestion nor tribulation. So that I may please God in the light of the living. Christ is the light of the living, according to the words: “I am the light of the world” (John 8). And again: “He was the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world” (ibid. 1). Likewise, in the Apocalypse, concerning that holy city: “There was no lamp there, because the Lord God Almighty illumined it, and its lamp is the Lamb”; by him the saints, rescued from the darkness of this world, are made radiant (Revelation 21). The prophet prays these things not only for himself but also for us. Therefore let us beseech him that, with bodily wars suppressed and the temptations of the world overcome, we may deserve to please Jesus Christ in that very light. Amen.

## PSALM 56

For the end; “Do not destroy”; for David, in the inscription of the title, when he fled from the face of Saul, king of Israel, into the cave. “For David, in the inscription of the title, ‘Do not destroy’”: that is, do not corrupt the inscription of the title, when Pilate wrote above the Lord’s cross in three languages: “Jesus, King of the Jews.” And they said to him: “Do not write ‘King of the Jews,’ but that he said, ‘I am King of the Jews.’” And Pilate said: “What I have written, I have written” (John 19). David hidden in the cave, that is, in the lower part of the earth, prefigured the human body, in which that majesty was hidden in Christ’s body, as in the words: “I was handed over, and I did not go out” (Psalm 87). And Paul says: “For if they had understood, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2).

Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me, for my soul trusts in you. By doubling his plea for mercy, he adds the confidence that he has in the Father, so that he may more easily be heard. “For my soul trusts in you.” One person seems to speak, but one speaks for many, because it is said: “From the ends of the earth I have cried to you, O Lord” (Psalm 6). And elsewhere: “They had one soul and one heart” (Acts 2). And in the shadow of your wings I will hope. That is, in paternal protection. A shadow is sought from heat; but by heat persecution or tribulation is understood, and by shadow the protection of divinity, to which we ought always to flee. But the two wings are the two Testaments, or the two commandments of charity. Until iniquity passes away. The insult of the wicked. Through these words he teaches us to hope in the protection of spiritual wings. Hence the prophet speaks:

I will cry to God Most High, to God who has done good to me. These are the things that follow after the good things enumerated. “Until iniquity passes away,” that is, the devil with his members or his attendants. “I will cry to God Most High.” Christ cried to God the Father and prayed for false brothers. The Church also prays for its enemies. And “to God who has done good to me,” that is, who made me from nothing in his image, gave me all the good things of the present life, and afterward promised me eternal life in the future.

He sent from heaven and delivered me. He sent his Son from heaven [Col. 0988B] to rescue the human being from sin, or the human race from the power of the devil, or from hell. He gave over to disgrace those who trample me down: the wicked and those subject to sin, who neglected the prophetic word. Or, as elsewhere: “He gave the apostles power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy” (Luke 10).

God sent his mercy and his truth. Mercy and truth are Christ. In one they are contained; neither exists without the other. If there had been mercy alone, there would have been license to sin; and if truth alone, the human being could not have endured it. He rescued my soul from among lion cubs. The lions are the rulers of the Jews; the cubs are the subject populace, who cried, “Crucify him.” The lion is the devil, according to the Epistle of Peter: “Your adversary the devil prowls around like a lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter). Therefore the Lord himself is understood as mercy and truth: sent by the Father, he rescued our souls from the power of demons, who strove to devour us as the lions of the world. He also now speaks, saying: I slept while troubled. For he slept in the sleep of the Passion when he said: “Now my soul is troubled” (Psalm 6), because it is said: “I slept, and I was overcome with sleep, and I rose, because the Lord raised me,” according to the words: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10).

The sons of men—their teeth are weapons, and so forth. He says that the teeth of the enemies are like weapons of attack, which the Lord shattered by his resurrection.

[Col. 0988D] Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and so forth. There is no limit to divine exaltation. We know nothing of heaven except what we have seen. For when he says “above the heavens,” this exceeds human knowledge. Concerning the glory that is above the earth, this is understood from what the Lord himself says elsewhere: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew, final chapter). Hence again the Lord says:

They set a snare for my feet. When they brought deceitful questions against me. And they bent down my soul. In death, but it was not subjected to death forever. Thus the Jews wished to bend Christ down, so that his name might not be mentioned.

They dug a pit before my face, and they themselves fell into it. When, after the resurrection, they were handed over to their enemies, captured, killed, and scattered.

My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make melody to the Lord. Freed from that death, he exults and sings of its triumph. “I will sing”: I will preach. “I will make melody”: I will fulfill it in deed.

Awake, my glory; awake, psalter and lyre; I will awake at dawn. For he rose at dawn, in the morning, while darkness still lay over the earth. Thus the psalter and the lyre: the Davidic utterance had sung, “Awake, psalter and lyre.” What do these instruments signify? One is from above, the other from earthly things. What is understood by the psalter? Christ is understood, as in the words: “Go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind return to the light, the dead rise, the poor are evangelized, and blessed is the one who is not scandalized in me”—that is, divinity working through the flesh (Matthew 11). The lyre signifies earthly things: becoming weary, sleeping, lacking, hungering, thirsting, and the rest. Alternatively: the psalter pertains to us—hope, faith, charity, patience, goodness, and other things like them. By the lyre are understood the six works of mercy that we ought to fulfill: “I was hungry, I was thirsty, I was a stranger, naked, sick, in prison.” Again, the psalter means giving thanks to God in tribulation; it comes from above, through him by whom you endure. The lyre is the persecution and tribulation that you endure in the body. “I will awake at dawn.” Christ answered the Father. Hence above he said: “Awake, my glory.”

I will give thanks to you among the peoples, O Lord, and I will make melody to you among the nations. The nations whom I called through the prophets or apostles. “I will give thanks to you among the peoples, O Lord,” that is, after I have risen. “I will make melody to you among the nations,” that is, I will preach and fulfill it in deed.

For your mercy has been magnified even to the heavens. For by my resurrection all things in heaven and on earth have been reconciled to you. And your truth reaches to the clouds. Fulfilling through the prophets what you had foretold to us. The heavens are the saints when they contemplate things above; the clouds are the saints when they water human hearts through preaching.

Be exalted above the heavens, O God. The prophet says this concerning Christ’s glorious ascension. And your glory above all the earth. When you pour out the gift of the Holy Spirit upon all flesh. May you also now deign to grant this to us, [Col. 0989D] so that amid every pressure and all tribulations you may send your Holy Spirit: by whose help, protection, and defense we may deserve to be prepared for eternal joys and transferred to heavenly rewards. Amen.

## PSALM 57

For the end; “Do not destroy”; of David, in the inscription of the title. You suggest falsehood; I will not corrupt the truth: “What I have written, I have written” (John 19). The psalm contains the voice of the prophet admonishing concerning judgments and justice.

If indeed you speak righteousness, judge rightly, sons of men. He teaches that whoever among mortals has used public judgment, if he speaks truth, should also judge truly; he should not place in the flattering words of speech a trap of deception by which he secretly destroys the innocent. “If indeed you speak righteousness, judge rightly, sons of men.” The Jews spoke justly to Christ when they said: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful, and that you teach the way of God in truth” (Matthew 22). They did not judge justly when they asked for Barabbas, a son of death, and killed Christ, the Son of life (John 18). Or otherwise: “Judge rightly,” that is, you who judge justice to be good, judge rightly; that is, do not do to another what you do not want done to you.

Indeed, in your heart you work iniquities on earth. In this earth where you dwell, you do so through evil thought, while you appear to speak good things. Let your hands devise iniquity. [Col. 0990B] For your works, which are understood allegorically as hands, are filled with iniquity.

Sinners are alienated from the womb. Some understand this concerning the soul’s descent into the body; others understand it of the Jews, in that they were alienated from God from the time when Mary gave birth to the Savior. They went astray from the womb; they spoke falsehoods. God, who foreknows the future, destroys iniquity itself before it is born. Therefore he says that sinners speak falsely, and prophesies that they go astray and are alienated, just as once Esau, before he was born, was rejected from God’s inheritance (Malachi 1 and Romans 9).

Their fury is like that of a serpent. He speaks of those who, passing by in anger, wish to devour God’s servants with poisonous bites and neglect repentance. Like the deaf asp that stops up its ears, and so forth: he speaks of the devil or his attendants, who, although they harm daily, and certainly harm those to whom we make known the song through invocation of the Lord’s name, nevertheless, with the entrance of their ears stopped, do not cease to rage. The asp is a kind of serpent. The man who charms it is called a Marsian [Note: [Col. 0989] This well-known passage from Ovid, *De Medicamine Faciei*: “By means of the Marsian songs the snakes are split asunder.”], and he draws them from darkness into the light.

God will crush their teeth in their mouth; the Lord will break the molars of lions. In the teeth open persecution is signified; in the molars, hidden persecution. “God will crush their teeth in their mouth,” so that they may not be able to tear his servants with wicked bites. “The Lord will break the molars of lions”: the ambushes of wickedness, which are regarded as having molars like the teeth of lions for a stronger bite.

[Col. 0990D] They will come to nothing like water running away. For just as running water is either absorbed by the earth or disappears into the sea, so these people are brought to destruction. As water that has gone around since the beginning of the world, so is their doctrine. “Running water,” which is a torrent, that is, water that runs down from the mountains into the valleys. Or, like the winter waters, which dry up as soon as they come, so these people quickly pass away. Hence it is said: “From the torrent on the way he will drink” (Psalm 10). The Lord drank from the torrent on the way because he received from what is ours. He bends his bow until they are weakened. By the bow are understood God’s anger and threats. Hence he said: “Unless you are converted,” that is, from pride to humility, [Col. 0991A] he shot his bow, just as Paul heard: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9). “He bends his bow”: the future judgment; “until they are weakened”: that is, until their ambushes vanish.

Like wax that melts, they will be taken away. For just as wax is dissolved by fire, so these people will be destroyed by the fire of the future judgment. Fire fell upon them—the judgment upon the dead—and they did not see the sun. They did not understand Christ the Lord, who is the sun of righteousness; concerning him the wicked will say in judgment: “The sun of righteousness did not shine for us” (Wisdom 5). “Fire fell, and they did not see the sun.” Sinners see Christ as fire; the righteous see him as the sun of righteousness. Alternatively: whoever, terrified by the threats of Scripture, undertakes repentance, to him the true sun is shown through the fire of punishments.

Before your thorns understand the thornbush. As though alive, as though in anger, he will swallow them up. Before your sins reach their completion and the thorns of your thoughts boil up into the tree of sins, God will correct you—not in anger, but as though angry. For there is no anger in God, but correction; and he will correct you not as living beings, but as though living. Those who have the thorns of offenses do not deserve to be called living. “Before your thorns understood the thornbush”: he speaks these words to the sinful people. The thornbush is a kind of extremely prickly thorn, yet with a very pleasing flower. Hence it is understood to have a double power: of vengeance and of the recompense of good things. That is, it flowers for the adornment of the righteous, while it offers sinners thorns for [Note: [Col. 0991D] I would prefer *ad confingendum* (“for piercing” / “for breaking”), in place of the transmitted reading.] breaking.

[Col. 0991C] Like living beings, as though in anger he will swallow them. Punishment quickly swallows them, because “whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3). “Living beings,” that is, the worldly wise, who through their wisdom suppose themselves to be, as it were, living. But the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. The anger of God that he mentions is just vengeance.

The righteous man will rejoice when he sees vengeance. [That is, the vengeance] upon the wicked: for when they are condemned to punishments, these rejoice in rewards. He will wash his hands in the blood of sinners. Because this verse is difficult to understand, I shall set out the very words that earlier interpreters treated. Blessed Bishop Hilary, that great sustainer of the Church amid the storms of the world, so speaks about it: “The righteous man does not wash his hands in the blood of sinners; rather, while sinners are in blood, because they are guilty of bloodshed, he will keep his hands washed and free from every liability for blood.” The righteous man washes his hands in the blood of sinners when he sees vengeance inflicted upon them without the saints procuring it; and then he will rejoice when, after their departure, his works shine forth gloriously.

And a man will say, “Surely there is a reward for the righteous.” For then his reward will exist, when Christ the Lord has granted him a share in the kingdoms of heaven. “Surely there is a God judging them on earth.” Before the judgment of the end, they are judged on this earth, of whom we spoke above: “Whoever has not believed has already been judged.” And if we do not close our ears to God’s commandments; if with innocence we carry out the admonitions of the saints; if we are not afflicted by the thorns of our crimes; if, with the innocent, we wash hands kept free from every bloodguilt—Jesus the Lord will honor us with worthy rewards, with which the saints rejoice eternally together with him. Amen.

## PSALM LVIII

For the end; “Do not destroy”; of David, in the inscription of the title, when Saul sent men to guard his house in order to kill him. Because this psalm teaches through its title about David’s guarding, it declares the mystery of the Lord’s Passion, saying:

“Deliver me from my enemies, my God,” etc. Through these successive stages of hostility one ascends even to the shedding of blood. For the Jews were enemies of Jesus Christ our Lord when they secretly envied him. They rose up against him when they opposed his commandments. They became workers of iniquity when they armed their hands for his killing. They became men of bloodshed when they said that the blood of the righteous man would be upon themselves and their children (Matthew 27).

“For behold, they have seized my soul; the mighty have rushed upon me”—in order to hand me over to death.

“Neither my iniquity nor my sin, Lord; without iniquity I ran and directed my course.” David could not say this about himself, since in another psalm he acknowledged that he was full of sins; rather, it concerns the one who, bearing our sins, ran to the end of bodily death without any burden of iniquity. “Without iniquity I ran, and I directed my course.” This psalm can also be understood as spoken in the person of the Lord. For he says: “The prince of this world is coming, and he found nothing in me” (John 16). Or certainly, “he ran”—that is, he came from heaven into the womb, from the womb into the manger, from the manger to the cross, from the cross into the tomb, from the tomb to the underworld, and from the underworld he returned victoriously to the heavens. And he directed not his own senses but ours, because they were crooked and twisted. Hence the prophet said: “And crooked things shall become straight, and rough places into level roads” (Isaiah 14).

“Rise to meet me.” He speaks this to the Father, from whom he asks in the Gospels to be glorified. And the Father, as though meeting him and extending his hand, answered: “I have glorified, and I will glorify again” (John 12). He asks that this meeting be extended even to the visitation of the nations, saying: “But rise to meet me”—that is, make them understand concerning the course I have run, that I am equal to you. Hence he says: “His going forth is from the end of heaven, and his meeting-place reaches to its end” (Psalm 18)—that is, God the Father is above all spiritual creatures. “And see”—as though he were saying, “so that you may make them see”; that is, so that they may believe me to be equal to you.

“And you, Lord God of hosts, God of Israel, attend to visit all the nations; do not have mercy on all who work iniquity.” Thus, when divine visitation regards the righteous, let the punishment of sin bind those others. “And you, Lord God of hosts”—that is, of angels and human beings. “God of Israel”—that is, God of the souls that see God. Christ speaks to the Father: “Attend to visit all the nations,” not only in Judea but also among the nations.

“They will return toward evening and suffer hunger like dogs.” Until the end of their life they will suffer hunger for the word of God, and they will not be reproved amid their various evils so that they might do penance. “And they will go around the city.” Yet they find in it none of the joyful solemnities or sacrifices. Or he speaks about those among the Jews who will believe at the end. “For when the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11).

“Behold, they will speak with their mouth, and a sword is on their lips.” Their blasphemies and unbelief are compared to a sword. “For who has heard?” No human being hears when these men are mocked by the Lord, as follows:

“And you, Lord, will laugh at them”—those who hold you in derision and contempt. “You will reduce all the nations to nothing”—those who do not believe that you have risen. For among them there are many believers, who are not mocked by God. Or, “all the nations”: those who worshiped wood and stones, God brings to the knowledge of the truth without any preceding merits.

“I will keep my strength for you.” That is, I will keep all my virtues for you, not for myself but for you, because I always offer you praise in them, not relying on my own strength. Hence Paul says: “If you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4). “I will keep my strength for you, because you, God, are my protector.” He says that he keeps that strength because no one could take away his soul, as he himself says: “No one will take it from me, but I have power to lay it down and power to take it up again” (John 10). “My God, his mercy will go before me.” The Father’s mercy went before him when the centurion confessed him to be God before he had seen him rise from the dead. Many also, striking their breasts, returned, saying: “Truly this man was the Son of God” (Mark 15).

“God showed me over my enemies: do not kill them, lest my people at some time forget.” Even if they do not believe, let them nevertheless understand that he is God, in accordance with the saying: “And all flesh shall see the salvation of our God” (Luke 3). “And do not kill them, lest perhaps they forget your name.”

Disperse them by your strength. Do not utterly destroy the Jews, because they have always been called your people; but disperse them throughout the whole world, so that, corrected at least in this way, they may cease from pride and, in this dispersion, lament their crime in repentance. “And bring them down, my protector, Lord.” “The sin of their mouth, the words of their lips.” Let them be destroyed in their wickedness because of the words by which they denied your Christ, while nevertheless boasting that they are children of Abraham. “Let them be caught in their pride”—that is, let them become humble.

“And they will be proclaimed because of their cursing and lying at the consummation.” For they cursed the Lord when they called him the son of Joseph the carpenter (Matthew 13). They wove lies when they said that he had a demon (Matthew 9). “In the wrath of consummation, and they will not be.” Let them be unable to persist in their wickedness, but let them be brought to an end in it.

“And they will know that God will rule Jacob and the ends of the earth.” For there are some who boast that they descend by lineage from Jacob. “And the ends of the earth”—that is, all the nations.

“They will return toward evening and suffer hunger like dogs, and they will go around the city.” They will scatter in order to eat; but if they are not satisfied, they will murmur. After the *diapsalma*, he repeats the statement that the enemies will suffer hunger like dogs while they pursue the letter of the Law together with bodily circumcision and sacrifices involving the slaughter of animals. But because they celebrate these things in exile and are not spiritually refreshed by them, they murmur against God. Therefore, seeing the mystery of the Lord’s resurrection, the prophet rejoices and says:

“But I will sing of your strength, Lord,” because you have conquered death. Or I will proclaim the strength of your divinity—how you conquered the devil. “And I will rejoice in your mercy,” because you rose at dawn. “In the morning”—that is, when he turned in his youth. Or “in the morning,” the beginning of the Catholic faith; or “in the morning,” as I have said, the resurrection.

“For you became my protector and my refuge on the day of my tribulation.” You received me under the protection of your defense, so that my conscience would not be joined with theirs.

“My helper, I will sing psalms to you; for you, God, are my protector, my God, my mercy.” The prophet promises that he will sing continually to the Lord, by whose help he has been assisted and received. May he also deign to grant us that, fortified by his help, aided by mercy, and glorified by the resurrection, we may deserve to exalt his praises in the holy Church with undefiled understanding. Amen.

## PSALM LIX

For the end; for those who will be changed; in the inscription of the title; of David, for instruction, when he burned Mesopotamia of Syria and Syria of Zobah, and Joab returned and struck Edom in the Valley of Salt, twelve thousand men.

It is asked where this history is written. It is read most clearly in the books of the Kingdoms (2 Samuel 8). But there, instead of “Valley of Salt,” the Seventy Translators placed the Hebrew words themselves, *GEMELAII*. But because it has not been translated, its meaning is unknown to those who lack knowledge of the Hebrew language.

“God, you have rejected us and destroyed us.” This pertains to the Jewish people. When God permitted it to be afflicted, he seemed then to be rejecting it. And now he seems to reject the Church when he permits it to be tested through tribulation. For otherwise he does not reject it, since the holy Paul said: “God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew” (Romans 11). Hence the voice says to Jeremiah the prophet: “Go, and destroy, and overthrow, and tear out, and build” (Jeremiah 1). It is as though he had said: “Destroy vices and sins, and build virtues.” He rejects and destroys us when we sin; he has mercy and builds when we return to him in repentance. “You were angry, and you had mercy on us.” God’s anger is called just vengeance.

“You shook the earth”—namely, our body—“and you troubled it” when it produced thistles and thorns. “Heal its fractures, for it has been shaken.” For it has been shaken away from wickedness so that it may produce the fruit of holiness.

“You showed your people hard things,” so that it might seek you more attentively. For “you chastise every son whom you receive” (Hebrews 12). “You showed your people hard things”—that is, tribulation. Hence the holy Paul says: “All who desire to live piously in Christ suffer persecution” (2 Timothy 3). “You gave us to drink the wine of compunction,” so that, confounded by our crimes, compunction might lead us to return to you. By “wine,” the Law of God’s people is understood, and this compunction itself is the grace of God.

“You gave a sign to those who fear you, so that they might flee from the face of the bow, that your beloved might be delivered.” You provided baptism, by which, cleansed, we might flee from the coming wrath; through it not only sinners but also your beloved are delivered. “Save with your right hand”—your Christ, who is our salvation—“and hear me” when I call upon you. The right hand of the Father is the Son. “Save”: he speaks of those who will be saved when your Son sends me to your right hand on the day of judgment. Hence elsewhere he says: “The right hand of the Lord has shown strength” (Psalm 117).

“God spoke in his holy one.” The Father spoke in the God-man, concerning whom Gabriel said to Mary: “The holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1). Or, as the holy Paul says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5). “I will rejoice and divide Shechem, and I will measure the Valley of Tabernacles.” Some think Shechem means Samaria; they understand the Valley of Tabernacles as this earthly dwelling. Therefore, when the Lord comes in the joy of eternal splendor to judge the world, he will divide Samaria and measure the Valley of Tabernacles. Then he will transfer one part to blessedness, while he will punish the other, which he finds unjust, together with the unbelievers.

“Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine, and Ephraim is the strength of my head.” In Gilead and Manasseh he indicates that the whole world is subject to him. In Ephraim, however, he signifies the figure of the future people—that is, of the Church to be gathered—because of the blessing of Jacob that he poured out upon him. He calls the Church itself “strength,” since he has been made its head. “Gilead is mine; Manasseh is mine.” All these things are spoken concerning the calling of the nations, whose various virtues will be related under the interpretation of their individual names.

“Judah is my king.” Because Christ arose from the tribe of Judah: “A ruler will not fail from his stock until the Lord comes,” as Jacob said: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hand shall be on the necks of your enemies; you shall rule over your brothers” (Genesis 49). Christ is understood through Judah, as in the saying: “The lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Revelation 5:5).

“Moab is the pot of my hope.” In Genesis, Moab received the reproach of a curse (Genesis 19); after ten generations, however, he is received into the Church of God (Deuteronomy 23). Therefore he is also the “pot of hope,” as though burning away the cruelty of sin after his conversion. For God’s hope concerning sinners is that, once their sins have been boiled away, they may be converted and live. Hence the prophet Jeremiah says: “I saw a boiling pot, and its face was from the face of the north” (Jeremiah 1). And elsewhere he says: “From the north evils will burn forth that are upon the earth” (ibid.)—that is, tribulations come from the devil upon the earth, which is the Church, as Paul says: “Tribulation produces endurance; endurance, testing; testing, hope; and hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5).

“Into Idumea I will extend my sandal.” He declares that the feet of the apostles are to be directed as far as the region of Esau, because in sandals feet are understood, and in feet the apostolic steps, in accordance with the saying: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things” (Nahum 1 and Romans 10)! Idumea is interpreted as “bloody” or “earthly.” It is as though he said: “Upon such people I will display my sandal”—that is, my examples.

“To me the foreigners are subject.” “Foreigners”—that is, the nations—are subject to the Church. In the Philistines he points to the perversities of foreign nations, which until Christ’s coming dwelt in the darkness of ignorance. But now they are subject—that is, they listen humbly to the prophecy that announces Christ; through their faith they see the great light.

“Who will lead me into the fortified city?” Christ the Lord, who turns impiety away from Jacob—he will lead us into the city of Jerusalem, in which the saints surround the divine majesty. Or “into the fortified city”—that is, into the Church, which is fortified by faith. “Or who will lead me as far as Idumea?” The one who earlier promised to extend his sandal is also the one who commands the prophecy—that is, prophetic preaching—to be directed toward it.

“Are you not the God who rejected us?”—so that you might recognize us as tested. You rejected us because of our transgression, or Adam’s sin; that is, he destroyed idolatry, or our vices and sins. “And you will not go forth, O God, in our strengths,” because we are weakened by sins.

“Give us help from tribulation, for human salvation is vain.” Let those hear this who place their hopes in the power of human beings or in the splendor of earthly riches: human salvation is vain, and God alone provides timely help in our tribulations.

“In God we will do valiantly, and he himself will bring to nothing those who trouble us.” Let our strength be in him; in him let all our glory be. He himself will reduce to nothing both the vices that trouble us and the enemies who attack us and try to turn us back from the hope of eternity.

## PSALM LX

For the end; with hymns; a psalm of David. It contains the voice of the prophet giving thanks for the blessedness of eternity.

“Hear, O God, my supplication.” He confidently asks to be heard because he knows himself to be holy. “Attend to my prayer.” It is as though he said: “See whether it is just or pure,” where you alone hear and see in the heart, as was said to Moses: “Why are you crying out to me?” (Exodus 14). Does he mean that he cries out with an audible voice? No; he cries out with the voice of the heart.

“From the ends of the earth I cried to you, when my heart was anxious.” Not from the farthest boundaries of the earth, but from the dwelling of this body with which he longs to be clothed, he cried out from the pain of his inmost heart, so that what is mortal might be swallowed up by life. “From the ends”—that is, from the four parts of the world, as though one man were crying out. Or the one man is the one Church; it is called one because of its unity. Hence in the Song of Songs it is said: “My dove is one” (Song of Songs 6)—that is, the Church spread throughout the whole world. “When it was anxious”—that is, because of the transgression of others. Or, “at my end,” while a human being does not know his own end.

“On the rock you exalted me; you led me, because you became my hope.” He says that he was exalted in Christ, who according to the Apostle is called both the steadfast rock and the hope of believers. “On the rock you exalted me”—that is, in yourself, as in the saying: “The rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10). Peter is named from the rock. Hence the Lord said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16); and elsewhere: “The rivers came, the winds blew, and they rushed upon that house, and it did not fall, for it had been founded upon the firm rock” (Matthew 7), which is Christ. “You led me”—that is, in yourself, because you are my leader, you are my wayfarer. “Because you became my hope.” This is the voice of the Church to Christ. It is as though it said: “Just as you rose immortal, so we believe that we shall rise.” “A tower of strength against the face of the enemy.” This hope, Christ the Lord, has become a tower of strength for us against the face of the devil or his wickedness, so that he may fortify and defend us from his snares. God the Father also became a tower of strength for us, exalting us upon the rock—that is, in his Christ. You, Christ, are the tower of strength who conquered the devil and deigned to suffer for us.

There are therefore also towers of weakness—that is, those who trust in their own strength, as it is said in the Gospel: “If someone wishes to build a tower and does not calculate its cost,” and so forth; afterward, those who see him will mock him, saying: “This man began to build and was unable to finish.”

“I will dwell in your tabernacle forever”—in that place, certainly, where we shall remain without end and continually contemplate God. “I will be protected under the shelter of your wings,” etc. While I still dwell in this body, may I be fortified by your protection. “I will be protected”—that is, defended—“under the shelter of your wings.” Your wings are the two Testaments, by which the Church is protected. Or, under the protection of divinity.

“You gave an inheritance to those who fear your name”—that is, you granted them an inheritance in the kingdom of heaven, so that they might inherit eternal life.

“Days upon days of the king.” For the eternal King—that is, Christ the Lord—there are eternal days, which increase day by day, since no night interrupts his brightness. “You will add years to his years, unto the day of generation and generation.” The first generation of this king is that in which he is ineffably born from God the Father. The second is that in which he became the firstborn from the dead; it extends to the generation of the future judgment, concerning which the Lord says: “You who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19). Therefore days and years will be added between these generations of this king, when, after the elect have been gathered and the enemies placed beneath his feet, he will hand over the kingdom to God the Father, with the saints gathered together at the same time, as follows:

“He remains forever in the sight of God.” For he will remain eternal in those whom he has handed over to God the Father in the kingdom of heaven, making them co-heirs, conformed to him, and sharers with him, with the dominion of death no longer ruling over them. “In the sight of God”—that is, where there will be no mutability.

“Who will seek his mercy and truth?” Mercy is shown because he forgives our sins. Truth is shown so that we may sin no more, so that we may not add sin upon sin. Why does he say “who”? Because few possess anything good and seek God; rather, they attribute more to their own virtue or strength than to God’s gift. “Who will seek his mercy and truth?” His mercy and truth are not sought by those who stand in the fullness of God. Yet nothing is lacking even to them, in accordance with the Savior’s oracle: “On that day you will ask the Father nothing” (John 16). Placing his hope in this fullness, the prophet added:

“Thus I will sing psalms to your name, O God, forever and ever.” This is the voice of the Church. “I will sing psalms”: I will proclaim and fulfill it in my works. “That I may pay my vows from day to day.” “That I may pay my vows”—that is, whatever we have promised God to keep. “From day to day”—that is, both to praise you always here and without end in the future. He will sing continually and pay his vows unceasingly when this corruptible body has put on incorruption, this mortal body has put on immortality, and it has shone forth (1 Corinthians 15). May he also deign to grant us that, having been conformed to his glory and rescued from the corruption of the second death, we may deserve to sing to his name in the spiritual offering of vows.

## PSALM LXI

For the end; for Idithun; a psalm of David. This psalm teaches the prophet’s complete devotion to God, saying:

“Will not my soul be subject to God?” For from him comes my salvation. This may also be said by that man who, abandoning the ravings of vain philosophy and the mire of idolatrous error, subjected himself to the Lord with a pure heart.

“For he is also my God and my salvation.” He knows that the salvation of the world, Jesus Christ, assumed human form and transferred himself from death to life. “For from God himself comes my salvation,” as Simeon said: “My eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2). And elsewhere he says: “The salvation of my countenance, my God” (Psalm 41). “My helper, I will not be moved any longer.” For he confidently believes that he will stand firmly in him. He is a helper in the present and a protector in eternity. Afterward he does not fear falling. He has nowhere farther to run except toward God. The apostles said to Christ: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John 14).

“How long will you rush upon a man, killing all of you yourselves, like a leaning wall and a tottering fence?” He refuses to yield to the wicked, who compel the weak and corrupt minds of human beings to incline toward new crimes. “You will kill all of yourselves.” Whoever has the will to kill kills, even if he does not strike. “Like a leaning wall and a tottering fence.” When I have come to suffer the Passion, you compel me, as though unwilling, to die. Alternatively, according to Symmachus’s interpretation: “The natural sense in you has been overturned, so that although you were created upright, you are driven headlong toward ruin.”

“Nevertheless, they planned to drive away my price; I ran in thirst.” He withdraws from such people—those who not only attack sinners but also strive to take honor away from the righteous. Therefore he runs in holy thirst, because blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness (Matthew 5). “I ran in thirst.” Christ ran from heaven, came into the womb, from the womb into the manger, and so forth. Thirsting, he came to the fountain; hungering, he came to the tree. Or he thirsted—that is, on the cross he thirsted for the salvation of the human race. Hence it is said: “He drank from the torrent on the way” (Psalm 109). The saints also run and thirst. They run, as Paul says: “I have finished the course; I have kept the faith” (2 Timothy 4). They thirst, as it is said: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied.” “With their mouth they blessed, but with their heart they cursed.” With a poisonous mouth they uttered good things in order to seduce, while retaining evil in their hearts.

“Nevertheless, my soul will be subject to God; for from him comes my salvation. For he is also my God and my salvation; my helper, I will not depart.” “In God is my salvation and my glory; the God of my help, and my hope is in God.” After the interruption of the *diapsalma*, he professes that he has from him both help and glory—he who left us examples of all these things in the humiliation of his Passion.

“Hope in him, every assembly of the people.” He is both help and hope, in whom every ecclesiastical assembly ought to hope and pray, as follows: “Pour out your hearts before him; God is our helper forever.” If with tears we disclose to him the secrets of our hearts, as all the saints do, we shall obtain his help. But because sinners neglect these things, he added:

“Nevertheless, the sons of men are vain; the sons of men are liars in the balances, so that they may deceive; they are altogether vanity in themselves.” They deceive the innocent under the pretense of weighing out justice and through the vanity of eloquence. “Sons of man”—sons of Adam, sons of the transgressor. Hence he says: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” (Psalm 4). “Lying sons of men in the balances.” Solomon says: “A weight and a weight, a measure and a measure: both are abominable before God” (Proverbs 20). And elsewhere he says: “A deceitful balance is abominable to the Lord, but an accurate weight is his will” (Proverbs 11).

“Do not hope in iniquity, and do not desire plunder; if riches abound, do not set your heart upon them.” For whoever hopes in these things cannot obtain the heavenly kingdom. Hence the Apostle says to Timothy: “Command the rich of this age not to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who gives us all things abundantly for enjoyment” (1 Timothy 6).

“God spoke once; I heard two things.” The word “once” shows the firmness of his statements; “two” demonstrates that the New and Old Testaments have one author. “God spoke once; I heard two things.” “Once” does not refer to number but to the firmness of the sentence. What are the two things that he heard together? That God is able to do all things, and that in the truth of his judgment he has mercy. Some explain it this way: God spoke once in the Law, and again he commands the same things in the Gospel. “These things I heard: power belongs to God.” Through these two Testaments he recognized God’s power, mercy, and justice, as follows: “And to you, Lord, belongs mercy, for you will repay each one according to his works.” For he received all judgment from the Father (John 5), so that he might prepare condemnation for the negligent, mercy for the repentant, and rewards for the righteous; that he might rescue us from the judgment of death, make us his own foster children, and graciously admit us, conformed to his body, to everlasting eternity.

“For power belongs to God.” Power belonged to him because he created all creatures from nothing. Mercy consists in ruling and governing. Power was shown in the flood; mercy delivered Noah (Genesis 7–8). “For you will repay each one according to his works”: good things to the good, evil things to the evil. You condemn sinners and reward the righteous.

## PSALM LXII

A psalm of David when he was in the desert of Idumea. David bears the figure of Christ. David is interpreted as “strong of hand” or “desirable.” Idumea is interpreted as “bloody” or “earthly.” “Desert,” that is, abandoned, signifies the Jewish people—or the gentile people—who seem to dwell in blood or earthly things. The psalm declares the mystery of the Lord’s coming. Seeing himself as though enlightened by it, the prophet rejoices and says:

“O God, my God, to you I keep vigil from the light.” Although all the saints keep vigil before God day and night, here he nevertheless shines in his prayer with the full splendor of divine light.

“My soul thirsted for you; how greatly my flesh thirsted for you! In a desert, impassable, and waterless land.” He thirsts for God with the affection of both soul and heart, retaining nothing doubtful or hostile within himself; amid the aridity and solitude of this age, he desires him with his whole mind, possessing that ardor with which God’s righteousness is thirsted for. “My soul thirsted for you; how greatly my flesh thirsted for you!” The soul indeed desires God, but the desired end is reached through the labors of the flesh. Therefore the flesh seeks God greatly, because it is afflicted by many injuries. He describes the poverty, torments, vigils, and sickness of the righteous man. The Lord thirsted for the faith of the Church and hungered for the salvation of the human race. So also the Church thirsts for Christ daily. Hence it is said: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matthew 5). “How greatly my flesh thirsted”: because the flesh suffers more than the soul. Although the soul is tormented through thought within the body, the body nevertheless endures tribulation from without. It desires to be freed—that is, to lay down mortality.

“In a desert, impassable, and waterless land.” By the desert, where there is neither a road nor water, the world is understood. It is called a desert because of sinners. “Thus I appeared to you in the holy place.” Living in this thirst, I will appear holy to you. Here the prophet, because of his hope, puts the future for the past. “So that I might see your strength and your glory.” Certainly Christ, who according to the Apostle is both the Father’s strength and his brightness. “Strength,” because he conquered the devil and liberated the human race. He calls it strength because “what is weak of God is stronger than human beings” (1 Corinthians 1). “Thus I appeared to you in the holy place”—that is, in holy desire. “And your glory”—that is, the glory of the one rising from the dead and sitting at the right hand of the Father.

“For your mercy is better than lives.” Your mercy grants eternal life. The present life often produces death. Your mercy is that by which you freed us from the power of the devil. “My lips will praise you, Lord.” “Thus I will bless you in my life.” He rightly praises God with his lips in his life, whoever lives in him, because he knows that it is said elsewhere: “The dead will not praise you, Lord” (Psalm 113). After mercy comes praise: here through prayer, there through praise.

“And in your name I will lift up my hands.” By the good of perfect work I will be exalted by you. Christ stretched out his hands on the cross all day toward the people who did not believe and contradicted him. Or, like Paul, lifting up pure hands without anger and disputation in the person of the saints (Isaiah 65 and 1 Timothy 2). By hands, works are understood.

“May my soul be filled as with fat and richness, and my mouth will praise you with lips of jubilation.” Not with the fat and richness of goats or lambs, as was customary in the holocausts of ancient times, but with a pure heart and clean mouth I will sing to your name. Just as that holocaust was formerly acceptable to you, so may my soul be filled with the richness of the grace of the Holy Spirit. “My mouth will praise you with lips of jubilation.” Here there are prayers; there, praises and everlasting joy.

“Thus I remembered you upon my bed.” In the little bed of chastity and holiness I remember you, because I have forgotten worldly pleasure. “Thus I remembered you.” The Church says this: both in rest and in tribulation, I have not forgotten you. “In the mornings I will meditate on you, because you have been my helper.” They rightly confess him as helper, because through the integrity of faith he delights in his morning resurrection. Would that we too might deserve to delight in him with spiritual joy through the splendor of a pure heart.

“And under the shelter of your wings I will rejoice.” He considers himself protected by the defense of heavenly help; therefore he rejoices in it. “My soul clung to you; your right hand received me.” Having abandoned the world, he testifies that he has been received by God’s right hand—that is, by his saving power.

“But they”—that is, the enemies—“sought my soul in vain,” because they wished to harm him unsuccessfully. “They will enter into the lower parts of the earth.” They will be condemned in hell. “They will be handed over to the hands of the sword,” to everlasting torments, by which they will be cut down. “They will be the portion of foxes,” destined to receive the lot of Herod, who was called a fox by the Lord (Luke 13).

“But the king will rejoice in God.” Christ rejoices in the Father after the resurrection. “And all who hope in him will be praised”—those who have inviolably kept his sacraments after receiving them. “For the mouth of those who speak iniquity has been stopped.” The mouth of the Jews and the chief priests was closed when the Lord rose, as the testimony of truth increased.

And let us beseech the Lord that, keeping vigil in his light and continually thirsting for him, we may deserve, by his generosity, to be filled with good works.

## PSALM LXIII

For the end; a psalm of David. This psalm contains the voice of the prophet continually beseeching God that, with God protecting him, he may escape not only his own sins but also the other poisons of evil. We too must understand that what is sung in it can be fulfilled in believers.

“Hear, O God, my prayer when I beseech you; from the fear of the enemy deliver my soul.” For one who believes in God there are many temptations, according to the Apostle: “All who desire to live piously in Christ Jesus suffer persecution” (2 Timothy 3). Therefore we ought to keep vigilant watch in our prayers, so that we may be able to resist vices. “From the fear of the enemy”—that is, of the persecuting devil—in accordance with the saying: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can destroy both body and soul in Gehenna” (Matthew 10).
