“You protected me from the assembly of the wicked, from the multitude of those who work iniquity, because they sharpened their tongues like a sword.” The wicked act maliciously and sharpen their tongues in order to blaspheme; but the saint is not disturbed, because he is protected by God. “From the assembly of the wicked”—that is, of the Jews or persecutors. “They sharpened their tongues like a sword.” Elsewhere he says: “Their tongue is a sharp sword” (Psalm 56).

“They bent their bow”—their teaching—“at a bitter matter,” so that by deceitful teachings they might deceive the little ones of Christ, whether the newly baptized or one who still lacks knowledge of the mystery of heavenly doctrine.

Suddenly they will shoot at him, and will not be afraid. When poisonous men shoot him deceitfully. Suddenly, as though unexpectedly—that is, in a sudden onset. And they will not be afraid: that is, of God and his judgment. They have strengthened themselves in an evil argument. They have spoken in order to conceal snares; they said, “Who will see them?” When they fortify themselves in this wickedness, so as to set these snares of deception for the inexperienced, they do not think that God can know this—[Col. 1002D] he from whom nothing hidden remains, who is also powerful enough to defend our souls from their arrows by the abundant weapons of his mercy.

They searched out iniquities; those searching with scrutiny grew exhausted. Heretics too scrutinize the Holy Scriptures; and, since they do not treat them spiritually, they bring forth from them empty questions by which they desire to entrap us through iniquity and deceit. But, accomplishing nothing, they themselves, rather, having been searched out and emptied by God, have been left void.

A man will approach the deep heart, and God will be exalted. If someone approaches the understanding of the deep heart with the wisdom of God and distinguishes these things—that is, discerns truth from falsehood—then God will be exalted. Although he is [Col. 1003A] the Most High, whenever we think rightly about him, he is exalted within us.

The arrows of the little ones have become their wounds. For the discerning righteous, when they see this little one whom we explained above infected by the poison of persuasion, and when they raise their voice to correct him, will immediately become, to the wicked, as though their words were wounds. And their tongue was weakened against them. Their speech possesses no stability; rather, their deceit will render them weak.

All who saw them were troubled. Those who recognize that they themselves are entangled in a similar error were confounded and troubled. And every man was afraid: afraid that divine judgment was impending over him.

And they proclaimed the works of God, and understood his deeds. [Col. 1003B] For, pierced in heart, they understand and proclaim the wonders of God.

The righteous man will rejoice in the Lord and will hope in him. Just as the ungodly fears on account of his unbelief, so the righteous exults in the Lord through hope in his eternity. And all the upright in heart will be praised. Because they will see God. For, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V). May he deign to grant us that, freed from the arrows of our enemies and rescued from the bow of falsehood, we may deserve to be protected by him who grants all the saints, in hope of salvation, the glory of immortality.

## PSALM LXIV

[Col. 1003C]

For the end; a psalm of David; a song of Jeremiah and Ezekiel, and of the people concerning captivity. This psalm is sung in the person of Christ, and concerns the return from Babylon to Jerusalem, and our return to the heavenly Jerusalem.

Praise is fitting for you, O God, in Zion, and the vow will be paid to you in Jerusalem. Not in theaters or temples of idols, but to you, Almighty, praise and a vow must continually be rendered in Zion—that is, in the Church, which contemplates your glory—or in the heavenly Jerusalem, where you are worthily remembered as an inhabitant. Praise will therefore be rendered to you because you are God; a vow, because you are the Redeemer.

Hear my prayer. Through the Holy Spirit, who intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings. All flesh will come to you. It is as though he said: Every human being will turn to you.

The words of the wicked. The doctrines of the philosophers and the follies of the Gentiles. They have prevailed against us. When [Col. 1003D] we did not know you—just as Jeremiah said, “Truly our fathers spoke falsehood and vanity, and it did not profit them” (Jer. XVI). And you will be merciful toward our iniquities. We would have remained in error to the end unless you had been merciful to us—you who purchased us with your own blood. Thus the Apostle Paul also says: “He reconciled us to God the Father through the cross” (I Cor. V).

Blessed is the one whom you have chosen and taken to yourself; he will dwell in your courts. God calls everyone and rejects no one, but few follow. Therefore whoever presents himself as worthy of God’s choice dwells with him and with the holy apostles in everlasting tabernacles.

We shall be filled with the good things of your house. That is, of the Church, which abounds in the good things of various spiritual gifts. [Col. 1004A] Holy is your temple. That man in whom the fullness of divinity dwells, concerning whom it is said to Mary, “And the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke II), when the Lord would dwell in her to assume flesh. Wonderful in equity. For he himself wondrously revealed the truth to the unbelieving Jews.

Hear us, O God our salvation, hope of all the ends of the earth and of the distant sea. The prophet, foreseeing that Christ is the hope of the earth, the sea, and all the ends of the earth, proclaimed this. But when he asks to be heard by him, it is understood as though he said: Come now, so that through you I may deserve to be saved.

Preparing the mountains by your strength, girded with power. The Lord himself, the Word made flesh in the man he assumed. [Col. 1004B] Girded with power, he crushed the height of the mountains of the devil’s dominion and prepared them for everlasting fires. “Girded” contracts the garment of God. For we cannot comprehend the extended garment of his strength. You who disturb the depths of the sea. Stirring up, through apostolic preaching, the deep boastfulness of this age. Who will endure the sound of its waves? For, when idols are overthrown, the demons make a sound, enticing the pagans to kill the saints of God. But this sound is stopped by God’s power.

The nations will be troubled. When they have been unable to prevail against the saints. And the ends of the earth will fear your signs. They will fear the power of the cross, which had previously seemed foolishness to them; or they are pierced by these wonders. You will delight in the morning and [Col. 1004C] evening departures. God is delighted by the Church’s morning and evening hymns, through the faithful soul that, having abandoned the rite of empty superstitions, praises him devoutly. By morning: joy; by evening: sorrow.

You visited the earth. Certainly he visited the earth of our body by assuming the material of flesh. And you intoxicated it. Not with the wine of lust, but with the infusion of the Holy Spirit. You multiplied its wealth. With the riches of various graces.

The river of God has been filled with waters. Indeed, the Lord says in the Gospel, “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John VII). Attend to the evangelist: for he was speaking this about the Holy Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive. Therefore we who have believed are already the river of God. We are filled [Col. 1004D] with water when we are cleansed in baptism, and if we are worthy to be filled with the Holy Spirit. We are enriched by the rain of the same spiritual infusion when, filled from the fountain of eternal life, we are watered with spiritual gifts. You prepared their food, for such is its preparation. You prepared, I say, Lord, our food in the communion of your blessed body and blood; if we receive it worthily, we escape the judgment of death. For you are the bread of life that came down from heaven and gives life to the world.

Making its streams drunk, multiplying its offspring, in its showers. For streams flow within us from that river—that is, from the Holy Spirit—and intoxicate us with various gifts of grace, so that one receives the word of wisdom, [Col. 1005A] another prophecy, another healing, another interpretation, or the remaining gifts: “which one and the same Spirit works, distributing to each as he wills” (I Cor. XII). Through these kinds of gifts the Churches are multiplied. At first these gifts flow down upon us like showers; afterward they become streams. Then they are multiplied in generations, so that they may produce fruit—one a hundredfold, another sixtyfold, another thirtyfold (Matt. XIII). The one that germinates will rejoice. The earth, certainly, will rejoice (Isa. LVIII), when this spiritual fruit springs forth in it.

You will bless the crown of the year of your goodness. With it you will crown the saints with rewards, and yourself with their ranks. Another prophet declares that the acceptable year itself is the Lord: “You will bless the crown [Col. 1005B] of his year.” He called the circle and the seasons of the year, which continually run their course within it, a crown. Or certainly because, in the Lord’s passion, victory was received over the whole world. And your fields will be filled with abundance. The fields of the Law, which produced no fruit of joy in the letter, are now, understood spiritually, filled with the abundance of evangelical teaching.

The beautiful places of the desert will grow rich. The Church, certainly, which flows with the divine grace of God. And the hills will gird themselves with exultation. The martyrs, or the remaining saints, who, honored by God with immense rewards, will gird themselves with perpetual joys.

The rams of the sheep are clothed. The patriarchs, prophets, or apostles, who were leaders of the sheep of the ecclesiastical flock, transferred from death to life, are clothed with perpetual immortality. [Col. 1005C] And the valleys will abound in grain. The saints of lesser merit will cry out, and will not receive a crown; nevertheless, they will be nourished by the fruits of eternal life. They will cry out, for they will sing a hymn. All the elect together, according to the gifts of their various offices, sing perpetual praises to God. Praying that by their merits we may be gathered and joined to their rewards, we ask; and if we do not deserve to be honored with rewards or adorned with crowns, at least, having obtained pardon, may we escape the punishment of eternal judgment. Amen.

## PSALM LXV

For the end; a song, a psalm of the resurrection. Through “song,” spiritual understanding is signified; through “psalm,” the work of resurrection, because this psalm pertains to Christ’s resurrection.

[Col. 1005D]

Shout joyfully to God, all the earth; sing a psalm to his name. By saying “all the earth,” he shows that the whole human race is earthly. It ought continually to send forth joyful praise to God, so that it may be rescued from spiritual wickedness. Sing a psalm to his name. Many praise him but do not fulfill this in their works. Give glory to his praise. Just as you shout joyfully to him with your voices, so also glorify him through good deeds, so that, when people see your good works, they may glorify your Father who is in heaven. Or this: “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory” (Ps. CXIII).

Say to God, “How awesome are your works, O Lord!” So that they may not worship the creature, but may understand the power of the Creator in what they contemplate. How [Col. 1006A] awesome are your works! That is awesome which you are able to marvel at but unable to comprehend: namely, that the Jewish people were chosen and afterward rejected, while the nations, at first condemned, were afterward chosen. Or it concerns those who appear to be saints and are rejected, and sinners who appear to be rejected and are chosen. The judgments of God are hidden—awesome, that is, to be feared. In the multitude of your power your enemies will lie to you. When they saw the mighty deeds and signs in Egypt and at the Red Sea, they lied when they said, “Whatever the Lord has commanded us, we will do” (Exod. XXIV). Hence he says, “Iniquity has lied, and the enemies of the Lord have lied to him” (Ps. XXVI).

Let all the earth worship you, O God, and sing praise to you; let it sing a psalm to your name. Let it worship you and reverence you; let it sing to you, not to the creature whom you subjected to his [Col. 1006B] uses. Here he inserts a *diapsalma*, turning the words toward us, and says:

Come and see the works of the Lord, awesome in his counsels concerning the children of men. He invites the nations, which lived for a long time in fanatical error, as our fathers once did, to know God. He who, through awesome counsels, cared for the human race so that, recognizing the works of the Creator, they might know the maker of those works. Come and see the works of the Lord. Come, believe, see, understand. This is the voice of the preachers. How awesome he is in his counsels concerning the children of men! Awesome—that is, how one is rejected and another chosen. The Jews are rejected and the nations chosen, as he said in the Gospel: “Two will be in the field: one will be taken and one will be left. Two women will be grinding: one will be taken and the other will be left” (Matt. XXIV). [Col. 1006C] Two will be in bed: one will be taken and one will be left. It is awesome that, although all were created from one mass, some are chosen and others rejected.

He turned the sea into dry land; they will pass through the river on foot. He teaches the worship of the one who, at Israel’s crossing, dried up the sea and held back the waves of the Jordan (Exod. XIV). But the Lord himself, as leader, also passed through these waters, so to speak, on foot, with the people following. Therefore, just as those waters, under his leadership, were then divided and opened a way for the people into the promised land (Josh. III), so now, if we do not defile baptism, having been cleansed through him and with him going before us—the one in whom we were reborn—we enter the land of the living. Or “they will pass through on [Col. 1006D] foot”: the holy preachers walked steadfastly in preaching, because God prepares a way for them. Hence it is said, “Put shoes on your feet in preparation for the Gospel of peace” (Eph. VI). There we will rejoice in the same one, who rules in his power forever. “In the same one,” that is, in Christ: because he who was humbled here is the one who rules in eternity. For just as the dominion of his power is confined by no end, so our joy, by which we will be made like him, will remain forever.

His eyes look upon the nations. So that the Jews may be rejected and the Gentiles chosen; as in the saying, “Does he who formed the eye not see?” (Ps. XCIII). In holy contemplation he looks upon the peoples who will believe, for he is not distinguished [Col. 1007A] by bodily members. Those who provoke him must not exalt themselves. The Jews, certainly, who, through the bitterness of gall, place God’s glory in Abraham’s carnal descent, are continually humbled. The insertion of the *diapsalma* changes the order of what is said, so that he passes from prophetic prediction to apostolic exhortation.

Bless the Lord our God, O nations, and make the voice of his praise heard. The apostles proclaim these things so that the nations may bless God himself—the one whom the same apostles call their own—and may obey him, the one into whom they were reborn through baptism. Here the prophet speaks again:

He set my soul toward life, so that perpetual death would not consume it. Mors occidit mortem: [Col. 1007B] death killed death—that is, Christ’s death killed our death. And he did not allow my feet to be shaken. Rather, he established me in the preaching that I brought to the nations. Here the voice of the martyrs follows:

For you rejected us, O God; you examined us by fire, as silver is examined, and you led us into a snare; you placed tribulations on our back; you set men upon our heads. That is, the devil, so that he might be raised up against us for the purpose of testing us. Or otherwise: he did not speak of angels or saints, but of sinners; that is, you made sinners be over us, so that we might bear them with patience. As it is written, “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts XIV).

We passed through fire and water, and you brought us out into [Col. 1007C] refreshment. Here he displays the victories of the martyrs, which they merited through various sufferings, and leads them to one refreshment—that is, Christ the Lord. Through snares, crosses, scourges, fires, heat, and other diverse punishments, by which they also became an accepted whole offering, they reached him. Fire devours; water absorbs. Fire is temptation; water is prosperity. Or fire is the Holy Spirit. You brought us into refreshment—that is, into eternal blessedness.

I will enter your house with whole burnt offerings. Here the prophet does not speak only of himself, but also of those whom he mentioned above, who entered God’s house, so that they might present not only themselves to God as a living sacrifice, but also those who, following their example, suffered for the Lord’s name. I will pay you my vows, which my [Col. 1007D] lips have distinguished. What vows did my lips distinguish, except that they should join others to themselves in martyrdom? Or it is a promise that we should praise God and confess him as Creator. My mouth spoke in my tribulation. For they spoke so that no persecution would ever separate them from the love of Christ.

I will offer you whole burnt offerings rich in marrow. The faith of the soul, or the devotion of the body, or the body of Christ. The bones are lower than the flesh, and the marrow is lower than the bones. “Rich in marrow” means filled with the inward substance of body and soul. With incense. With the acceptable fragrance of prayer. And rams. The apostles, or teachers of the Churches.

I will offer you bulls. Those who, rejecting the stubbornness of the Law, submitted their necks to the Lord’s yoke, which is gentle. [Col. 1008A] [Col. 1008A] With goats. Those who, after sin, were converted and steadfastly persevered in martyrdom. Here all are offered to the Lord as a peaceful whole burnt offering. To them the prophet now, after the *diapsalma*, turns his speech, saying:

Come, hear, and I will tell all you who fear God what he has done for my soul. I cried out to him with my mouth, and exulted beneath my tongue. You who fear the Lord, draw near and consider how he established my soul in everlasting blessedness, because I not only ask with my mouth but also cried out to the Lord in the hidden places of a pure heart. “I cried out to him with my mouth”: this passage most clearly shows that, in Scripture, “crying out” is not to be understood as a matter of the voice, but of the heart.

[Col. 1008B]

[Col. 1008B] If I had seen iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have heard me. Therefore my God heard me and attended to the voice of my prayer. For I saw the purity of my mind, and therefore I presumed to ask.

Blessed is the Lord, who did not remove my prayer from him, nor his mercy from me. Full of mercy, he did not turn my supplication away from himself, because I was asking for what was just. For his merciful ears are always open to the prayers of the righteous. But let us humbly beseech the Lord to open his ears to our prayers, and may he himself, granting us forgiveness of sins, rescue us from our present hardships; and, when we have been made a pure whole burnt offering for him by slaughtering our vices, may he join us to the ranks of the saints. Amen.

## PSALM LXVI

[Col. 1008C]

For the end; with hymns; a psalm of the song of David. Although this psalm is short, it nevertheless contains the voice of the apostles and prophets, who proclaimed to the nations either that the Lord had come or that he would come.

May God have mercy on us and bless us. The first petition is that God may show mercy; afterward, that he may give blessing. Therefore the blessing that follows mercy should be such that, when carnal domination has been restrained, it makes the spirit triumph. Let him be not our judge but merciful. “May God have mercy on us”: this is the voice of the apostles speaking to the people gathered from the nations. You have indeed believed at our voice. Behold, this Church has been gathered in the Lord’s name; therefore we say, “May God have mercy on us and bless us.” May he dissolve the first curse in man [Col. 1008D] through his blessing.

May he make his face shine upon us. May we not see him sorrowful because of our sins, but rejoicing in our virtues. May we not experience him as judge, but as Father. May he make his face shine upon us. What is the face of God? Surely, his image. For the Apostle also says that the Son is the image of the Father (Rom. II). Therefore may he enlighten us with his image—that is, with his image, the Son—may he shine upon us so that he himself may enlighten us. The light of the Father is the light of the Son. Whoever sees the Father also sees the Son. Where there is no distinction between one glory and another, both are glory. The apostles and prophets pray these things: that, enlightened by God’s face, their preaching may become the light of all the nations.

[Col. 1009A]

So that we may know your way on earth, and your salvation among all the nations. May our preaching thus prevail that your way, or your salvation—that is, Christ the Lord—may be seen among those who now think earthly thoughts and are involved in the error of paganism. So that we may know your way on earth. We ask this so that you may make your face shine—that is, your image—upon us, an image that was always hidden with you and was, as it were, in the secrecy and darkness of your mysteries, according to what is written: “He made darkness his hiding place” (Ps. XVII). We ask that you shine upon us, so that the mystery hidden from generations may, according to the Apostle, be revealed in us (I Cor. II). But why do we ask and desire all this? Unless you enlighten [Col. 1009B] your image upon us, we cannot know your way and your knowledge, so that we may know on earth the majesty of your presence, which is known in heaven. So that we may know your way on earth. “I am,” he says, “the way, the life, and the truth” (John XIV). So that we may know your way on earth. Let us know it on earth: “Your will be done, as in heaven and on earth” (Matt. VI), so that the one whom the angels worship in heaven may also be worshiped by human beings on earth.

But someone may say: God’s way was known. “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel.” God was known, but God’s way was not known in Judea. Since, therefore, the way of God the Father was not known among the Jews, he now says: Your salvation among all the nations. Not among one people, but among all nations. Your salvation among all [Col. 1009C] the nations. Where we have *salutare* in Latin, the Hebrew has *Jesus*. Finally, the angel also says this: “And you shall call his name Jesus” (Luke II). For he will save his people. Your salvation among all the nations. Behold, what the apostles asked has been fulfilled: his salvation is known among all the nations. Wherever human speech can exist, there Jesus resounds.

May the peoples praise you, O God; may all the peoples praise you. The peoples of the Jews? No, but may all the peoples praise you. Just as all nations, so also all peoples. May the peoples praise you, O God. What should they confess? Surely their sins; or certainly, let them confess that your image is in you. Let them confess you in the Son, see you in him, and worship you in him.

[Col. 1009D]

Let the nations rejoice and exult. Because they have been freed from the captivity of the devil; because those who previously bowed down to worship idols, wood, and stones now lift their faces and look toward heaven. Because you judge the peoples with equity. Wherever there is equity and judgment, there is fear rather than joy for sinners. How, then, did he say, “May God have mercy on us and bless us,” and now say, “Let the nations rejoice and exult, because you judge the peoples with equity”? He seems to contradict himself. For if they need mercy, how do they rejoice and exult because you judge the peoples with equity? Wherever there is mercy, there is no judgment; but where there is judgment and equity of judgment, mercy is far away.

But the [Col. 1010A] meaning is this: Let the nations rejoice and exult. Why should they rejoice? Because you judge the peoples with equity, because you do not accept the person of one nation, but are God of all. The Jews alone do not please you; your whole world belongs to you.

Someone may say: “You are doing violence to Scripture; it did not say this in that sense.” Scripture, which speaks, interprets itself: “Because you judge the peoples with equity.” Which peoples? “And you guide the nations on earth.” You made the nations, which formerly did not walk with a straight foot, walk in your way. So that we might know your way on earth, so that we might walk in the way and not in trackless places, and come to you by one way—from whom the way proceeds. For we do not go to the Father except through the Son.

Someone may say: This is the doctrine of the Arians. Therefore the Father is approached through the Son. I say this [Col. 1010B] because through the image we go to the face, and in the light we see light; in the Son we see the Father. It is the mystery and dispensation that speaks. But if someone thinks it blasphemous that we have said the Son is the way and that through the way we go, as it were, to God, let us see what this same way says: “No one comes to me unless my Father draws him to me” (John VI). Therefore, just as the Son leads to the Father, so the Father leads to the Son. These are human words. In reality, the Son leads to the Father, and the Father leads to the Son; and there is one nature and one substance.

May the peoples praise you, O God; may all the peoples praise you. [Col. 1010C] He had already said this above, and in this short psalm he repeats these two verses. For above he had said, “May the peoples praise you, O God; may all the peoples praise you. Let the nations rejoice and exult,” and the rest. Now he repeats these verses again, as though the apostles were leading all the nations in song.

“Many times they have fought against me from my youth,” let Israel now say (Ps. CXXVIII). “Many times they have fought against me from my youth.” See how they lead the song and the multitude of all the nations responds. So now, when they say at the beginning, “May all the peoples praise you,” and the apostles command and say, “May the peoples praise you, O God; may all the peoples praise you,” because they see them falling silent, they repeat the same thing and say, “May the peoples praise you, O God; may all the peoples praise you.” We said it once, and you did not listen; we say it again, so that you may sing.

But why did we say all this once and twice, so that the peoples might praise God? Why do we say it? Why do we command it? [Col. 1010D] Because you judge the peoples with equity: the Jews, who, because of their excessive wickedness, are called “peoples,” according to the saying, “The peoples plotted empty things” (Ps. II). And you guide the nations on earth. He will guide them in the way of life, granting forgiveness of sins. When “all” is said, he prays not only for the people of the nations but also for the Jews, so that they too, once converted, may confess Christ the Son of God.

The earth has given its fruit. The earth is holy Mary, from our earth, from our seed, from this clay, from this mud, from Adam. “You are earth, and to earth you will go” (Gen. III). This earth has given its fruit. What it lost in paradise, it found in the Son. The earth has given its fruit. First it gave a flower. It also says in the [Col. 1011A] Song of Songs, “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song II). This flower, therefore, became fruit, so that we might eat it, so that we might consume his flesh. Do you wish to know who this fruit is? A virgin from a virgin; the Lord from a handmaid; God from a human being; a son from a mother; fruit from the earth.

See what the fruit itself says: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it cannot produce much fruit” (John XII). The earth has given its fruit; it gave a grain of wheat. That grain of wheat fell into the earth and died, and therefore bears much fruit. It was multiplied in the ear: what had fallen as one rose again as many. For a grain of wheat fell into the earth, and a plentiful crop arose. The earth has given its fruit. Therefore, may the peoples praise you, O God; may all the peoples [Col. 1011B] praise you. The earth has given its fruit. What is this fruit?

May God, our God, bless us; may God bless us. God the Father; our God, the Son. For he is our God. “And you shall call his name Emmanuel,” he says, that is, “God with us.” May our God bless us. God the Holy Spirit. Behold the mystery of the Trinity contained in a single verse. The earth has given its fruit. In this fruit the mystery of the Trinity is contained. May God, our God, bless us. He who by nature is God of all has become specifically our God. May God bless us. May he drive away the ancient curse. The curse cast us out of paradise; may blessing lead us back.

And may all the ends of the earth fear him. He did not say, “May all the ends of the earth love him.” [Col. 1011C] For perfect love casts out fear. To fear belongs to beginners; to love, to the perfect. Whoever still fears is placed at the beginning and does not possess perfect and complete faith. But whoever loves God will have everything work together for his good.

The statement appears brief and simple. But let us sift it, and in these simple words we will discover immense mysteries. We will find within what lies hidden outwardly. “For those who love the Lord, all things work together for good.” The holy man Job was tested. He lost his sons and daughters; his house collapsed; he lost everything; he suddenly lost all things. He was no longer father or master, for nothing remained to him in the health of his body except his tongue alone, with which he could blaspheme.

See the tempter, the devil. “From the sole of his foot,” it says, “to the crown [Col. 1011D] of his head he struck him with a terrible wound”—that is, elephantiasis (Job I). From there worms and putrefaction flowed over his whole body. He preserved only his tongue intact, so that he might be able to blaspheme his Lord. “In all these things Job did not sin with his lips.” See the greatness of the temptation; see the greatness of his virtue. See and consider that the Apostle’s saying was fulfilled: “For those who love the Lord, all things work together for good” (Rom. VIII).

At the time when he was losing his possessions and his children, the things that happened seemed contrary to him; but because he loved the Lord, those evils that he inflicted upon him worked together for his good. The worms of his body were preparing for him a crown in heaven. Before he was tested, [Col. 1012A] God had never spoken to him; but after he was tested, God came to him and spoke familiarly, as a friend with his friend. Let blows come, every kind of punishment, provided that after the blows Christ may come.

We have departed from the psalm, but not without purpose, because we had said, “And may all the ends of the earth fear him,” and we had said that fearing belongs to the little ones, whereas loving belongs to the perfect; and to establish this we had cited the Apostle: “For those who love the Lord, all things work together for good.”

And may all the ends of the earth fear him. Not Judea alone, but all the ends of the earth. According to the *tropology*, however, “all the ends of the earth” does not mean the middle of the earth—not those who are in the middle of the earth, but those who are at the earth’s end, who leave the earth and hasten to go to [Col. 1012B] heaven.

Therefore, what the apostles said at the beginning, let us say at the end: May God have mercy on us and bless us; may he make his face shine upon us and have mercy on us; and may he make his way known on earth. When Christ comes manifest in glory, then he will make known to all why he descended in such great humility of flesh.

The earth has given its fruit. Mary gave birth to the Savior.

## PSALM LXVII

For the end; a psalm of the song of David. The psalm signifies works; the song, the spiritual understanding of the mind. If the sixty-seventh psalm is understood spiritually, it is found to be filled with the mysteries of the Law and the Gospels, and it begins in the prophetic voice as follows:

Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered. This psalm is understood both specifically and generally. Specifically, [Col. 1012C] it concerns the Lord himself, that he may rise from the dead and destroy his enemies—that is, the devil and his army, or the Jews. Generally, it applies whenever we are in tribulation and distress and say, “Arise; why do you sleep, O Lord? Arise and help us” (Ps. 43). Likewise, the apostles awaken the sleeping Lord in the boat, saying, “Master, save us; we are perishing” (Matt. VIII). And let those who hate him flee from his face. He did not say, “Let them perish,” but “Let them flee,” because sinners cannot stand in the sight of God. The prophet foreseeing this prays that, when he rises, the dominions of the devil may flee, for even now it must be believed without doubt that they cannot stand at the invocation of his name.

As smoke fails, so may they fail. Not so that they may be reduced to [Col. 1012D] nothing, but so that they may cease from their sins. As wax melts before the face of fire. As wax is dissolved and does not lose its nature but becomes soft, so let these not perish, but let them lay aside their wickedness, turn to repentance, and be saved. So may sinners perish from the face of God, because sinners are not worthy to see God.

And let the righteous feast. Let those who remain in their righteousness, who have no vices, delight in the Lord. Or otherwise: let the punishment of judgment pursue them, so that they may fail like the thinness of smoke and dissolve like wax before the face of fire, while the saints feast upon heavenly goods. Let them exult in the sight of God and delight in gladness. [Col. 1013A] Great is the confidence of exulting in the sight of the Lord. Just as a steward who has handled badly and squandered the substance entrusted to him by the Lord fears the Lord’s presence, so one who has administered it well exults in the Lord’s presence. Let them exult in the sight of God and delight in gladness—not only because of vengeance, but also because of eternal blessedness.

Sing to God; sing a psalm to his name. In Scripture, “sing” in the *theorica* always signifies contemplation—that is, considering the mysteries and meaning of divine Scripture. To play the psalm, however, signifies good works in Scripture; for example, that hearing should perform its work. Likewise the mouth, eyes, hands, and all the limbs, if they agree, together strike the psaltery in virtues. Sing to the giver of everlasting joy and honor him with your voices.

Make a way for him who ascends above [Col. 1013B] the setting sun; the Lord is his name. He teaches that, when the swellings of sin have been restrained, we should prepare for him a level way in our hearts through righteousness. He ascended above the setting of death and returned victorious from the underworld. If the sun of iniquity does not set for us, the sun of righteousness cannot rise for us, whose healing is in the heavens.

Exult in his sight. For we ought to rejoice in his sight and not take delight in the enticements of this age. The fathers of orphans and judges of widows will be troubled before his face. Those who now call themselves protectors and judges, and on this pretext defraud the possessions of the needy, will be confounded when the Most High begins to look upon them.

God in his holy place. In the faithful soul. God always dwells in his saints. Wherever holiness is, there is God’s dwelling place. [Col. 1013C] God who makes those of one mind dwell in a house. In the Church, in which he pours the spirit of charity into those who remain faithfully united—those who are of one mind and do not change. For the righteous person does not change, because he has once decided to remain in righteousness. But the sinner changes. For “the foolish person changes like the moon” (Eccli. XXVII). In Hebrew, however, it reads: “The Lord makes monks dwell in a house”—that is, those with whom sin does not dwell.

He brings out the prisoners in strength. God himself, by his power, brings out those who are bound by the devil in sins, like the woman in the Gospel who had been bound by the devil for eighteen years (Luke XIII). Likewise, those who provoke him, who dwell in tombs. God is sweet by nature. Those who turn him toward bitterness, however, are sinners, and make God bitter for themselves. [Col. 1013D] They do not change his nature; rather, sinners themselves make God bitter for themselves. Those who dwell in tombs. He released those who had been bound within the house of the strong one—that is, the devil—and held captive by sins; and he freed those who, devoted to idols, had provoked God and lay dead as though in tombs, as in the Gospel passage: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, because you are like whitewashed tombs” (Matt. XXIII). Just as the saint is a temple of God, so the sinner makes himself a tomb.

God, when you went forth before your people. This is understood historically, when God went before his people as they departed from Egypt (Exod. XIV). [Col. 1014A] When you passed through the desert. God does not linger in the desert, but passes through it. The earth was shaken, and the heavens dripped before the face of God of Sinai, before the face of God of Israel. The heavens dripped—that is, manna (Exod. XVI). Sinai is interpreted as “temptation.” Therefore God dwells in those who are tempted and overcome. But he does not dwell in those who live in pleasures. For “the heavens dripped before the face of God of Sinai, before the face of God of Israel.” Here he indicates one author of the Old and New Testaments. For the one who went before the Israelite people in the desert himself visited the deserts of the nations in the Gospels. And the one through whom manna once flowed down on Sinai for that generation supplies the Christian people in the Church with the manna of his body and blood.

You will set apart, O God, a willing rain for your inheritance. [Col. 1014B] The holy preaching that descends through the apostles into human hearts in abundant irrigation. Or he speaks of the law, which was given through Moses. For it was weakened. Either when Paul had within himself the judgment of death, or when Peter denied the Lord three times, or when the other apostles, leaving the Lord during his Passion, fled (Matt. V). The law was weakened because no one could fulfill it except the Lord, who said: “I have not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it.” And according to the Apostle: “For what was impossible for the law, weakened as it was,” God sent his Son, “born of a woman, born under the law, in order to redeem those who were under the law” (Gal. IV). But you perfected it: your living creatures will dwell in it. For your resurrection, turning away what was wavering, brought this preaching [Col. 1014C] to perfection, so that in it the nations—who had previously been regarded as irrational animals—might dwell. “Your living creatures will dwell in it,” that is, in the inheritance. He called those who live in God “living creatures,” that is, the saints. Or otherwise: “You will set apart a willing rain.” We should understand “willing rain” either as the commandments or as manna. “And it was weakened; but you perfected it.” The law, which had been weakened through the transgression of the Jews, was completed when the grace of the Gospel came.

You prepared in your sweetness for the poor, O God. “The Lord will give the word to those who evangelize with great power.” In Hebrew it reads: “Women who evangelize”—that is, women who evangelized to the apostles, where it says: “Go and tell my brothers,” and so forth (Matt. XXVIII). [Col. 1014D] Or it signifies the souls that believed in Christ. According to the Septuagint interpreters, however, it is said to the apostles, because the Lord gave them power to preach the Gospel. This sweetness of rain, which surpasses the taste of honey and the honeycomb, flowed down upon the poor—that is, upon the saints of God—and proceeded from the mouths of the apostles at God’s command, with great power.

The King of the beloved’s forces, of the beloved’s. The beloved of God’s forces—that is, Christ’s—are the apostles. Therefore the Lord, who is the King of the beloved’s forces, will give great power in preaching to those who evangelize, so that, after the enemies—the Jews or demons—have been conquered, the spoils may be distributed among the churches. The beauty of the house is the Church, whose divided spoils are reported; that is, when those who believe, separated from [Col. 1015A] idols, have received different ranks of ministries within it, with the Father’s beloved himself distributing them and the Paraclete cooperating. “The King of the beloved’s forces.” The King is the Father; “of forces,” that is, of the saints; “of the beloved,” of the Son: “This is my beloved Son; listen to him” (Matt. XVII). “Beloved.” If someone loves another, he always has him on his lips. Thus the Holy Spirit, because of the love he has for the Son, frequently remembers him. “And of the beauty of the house, to divide the spoils.” The apostles themselves divide in the churches the spoils that they received from idols.

If you sleep among the midst of the lots, the wings of a silvered dove, and the hind parts of its back in the pallor of gold. When you believe in both Testaments, you will find the Holy Spirit in each. And although it is beautiful, even according to the letter, to know what you read, nevertheless the whole force of its beauty lies in its meaning. Thus the external ornament of the words is indicated [Col. 1015B] by the name of silver; but the more hidden mysteries are contained in the concealed gifts of gold. “If you sleep among the midst of the lots,” that is, if you rest between the New and Old Testaments, you will find in the two Testaments the grace of the Holy Spirit. The individual books are called “lots,” that is, Genesis, Exodus, Judges, the Gospels, and the Apostle. “The wings of a silvered dove.” “Silvered” signifies the clear word of divine Scripture [Note: [Col. 1015D] See Jerome, on chapter III of Isaiah and in Sermons 4 and 10.]. “And the hind parts of its back in the pallor of gold”: that is, in the interior parts, the mysteries are understood spiritually. If, until the completion of the present life—which is often understood as sleep—you rest between the two Testaments, that is, between the New and Old Testaments, you will find in them the Holy Spirit [Col. 1015C], whose wings in the preachers correspond in silver because of the beauty of their eloquence. In the hind parts, which are called the shoulders because they cover the breast, the fruit of a good conscience is displayed; after the Gospel has been completed, this is changed into the appearance of gold—that is, into royal honor.

While the heavenly one distinguishes, kings over her will be whitened with snow in Salmon. He calls “kings” the saints who resist their passions. These saints, therefore, are divided among the churches, as Paul among the Gentiles and Peter among the circumcision. The heavenly Lord established these, whom we mentioned above as separated from idolatries, as kings in the beauty of that house. But first they will be whitened with snow in Salmon. This is what he says: although they are saints, they are nevertheless in this age like a shadow, knowing only in part. Salmon is interpreted as “shadow.” [Col. 1015D] Therefore, when the heavenly King Christ begins to appoint and divide apostles and rulers in his Church, they will not possess complete light, but only a portion of knowledge, because “now we see in part, and we prophesy in part” (I Cor. XIII).

A mountain of God, a fruitful mountain; a mountain of curds, a fruitful mountain. This is the mountain to which, in Isaiah and Micah, they urge one another to go as they ascend (Isa. II and Mic. IV). As for what he says, “a mountain of curds,” it agrees with the words of the Apostle, who says: “I gave you milk to drink, not [Col. 1016A] food” (I Cor. III). Or it is the mountain that in Ezekiel wounds the prince of Tyre (Ezek. XXVI). By “mountain,” however, he means the Lord himself. Why do you suspect mountains of curds? He says this to the Jews, who think that Moses and the prophets are like the Savior.

The mountain in which it pleased God to dwell. The meaning is this: You must not think that there are many churches that possess breasts of doctrine and can nourish believers with the milk of knowledge. There is one Church, and one Christ, the bridegroom of the Church. For the Holy Spirit will dwell continually in no one other than the Savior, as John says: “The one on whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him” (John I). He is the one who, cut out without hands, filled the breadth of the whole earth—that is, the Lord’s human being [Note: [Col. 1016D] See what we observe in the volume [On the Spirit], vol. 2, col. 157.]. [Col. 1016B] For the Lord will dwell to the end. He will dwell in the body that he received from holy Mary, because he was carried up with it into heaven.

God’s chariot is multiplied ten thousandfold. Hyperbolically he speaks of ministering powers and saints, because they are innumerable, as he said in Daniel: “A thousand thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. VII). In Ezekiel also, the four Cherubim are described as having four faces in the four corners, with God as their charioteer (Ezek. I and X). “Cherubim” is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge.” The face of the lion signifies the royal, that is, reigning over the passions; the face of the human being, the rational; the face of the calf, work; the face of the eagle, [Col. 1016C] contemplation, that is, theory, which raises us up in the virtues. To state it all together: God’s throne is in the saints. “Multiplied ten thousandfold.” For many thousands of worldly chariots have been conquered by those evangelizing Christ throughout the world. “Thousands rejoicing—the Lord is among them.” He indicates that divine ministries are present here. “In Sinai, in the holy place.” That is, God is in the saints when they are tempted, and holiness follows temptation. It is impossible for anyone, even if he is holy, to pass through this world without temptation, according to Job: “Temptation is the life of a human being upon the earth” (Job VII).

You ascended on high; you took captivity captive. You ascended into the heavens; you took captive us who were held captive by the devil. The one who once descended on Sinai and gave the law to the people now ascended the heights of heaven in the holy one—that is, in the human being assumed [Col. 1016D] (of whom the angel said to Mary: “The holy one who will be born from you shall be called…” [Luke I]). He released those who were held in the devil’s captivity and, leading them away after himself as captives, restored them to eternal life. Thus he also raised the assumed flesh, as though captive, to the stars. You received gifts among human beings. He rightly said “you received.” He received from the Father; he received as a human being, but gives as God. And what he received, he received for human beings, in order to give it. For he himself is full and needs nothing. He gave gifts of spiritual graces to human beings [Col. 1017A] who afterward approached him through faith.

Even the unbelievers, that the Lord God might dwell [among them]. To these people also—that is, to the people from the nations—Christ granted this gift. They did not believe that God could dwell among mortals; these you saved, who did not believe that it was possible for God to dwell in human beings—that is, to receive the Savior in the flesh. Or he also ministered good things to those who had no hope that they could dwell in his Church.

Blessed be the Lord day by day. Whoever makes progress can bless God each day. For what does it profit me if I blessed him yesterday but cannot bless him today? Both for his former benefits and because he now prepares a level path for us to come to him, he must be blessed continually. [Col. 1017B] God, the God of our salvations, will make our journey prosperous. For we are saved by him. “God, the God of our salvations, will make our journey prosperous.” Be confident, sinner; do not doubt that you can bless God each day. For he says: “God will make our journey prosperous.” Therefore God helps us and cooperates with us. “He is our salvation.” He rightly spoke in the plural, “salvations,” because however many sins we have committed, we have just as many salvations. The diapsalma in Hebrew has *SELA*: that is, “always” and “continually.” Therefore God always helps us.

Our God. Because we know no other besides him. God of salvation, and the Lord, the Lord has the ways out from death. He is present to save those who are perishing, because he was born for our redemption. [Col. 1017C] And “the Lord, the Lord has the ways out from death,” because he first opened the way out of death, as the Apostle says: “He became,” he says, “the firstborn of the dead,” because he himself rose from the dead and made us rise together with him (Col. I; Rev. I). Alternatively: The devil is the entrance into death; the Lord, however, brings one out.

Yet God will crush the heads of his enemies. Having come forth from the ways out of death, he crushes the heads of the devil and all his powers. You crushed the heads of the dragon in the water. As many sins as there are, so many heads does the devil have: principalities and powers that, like a head, stood out above all—the diabolical dominations. The crown of the hair of those who walk in their offenses. The summit of the arrogance of those who neglect repentance and persist in sins. [Col. 1017D] His head is crushed so completely that no power remains in him with which to goad sinners. The summit of the head is the hair, and the hair is the crown. Therefore he says that not even the smallest thing remains in the devil that is not broken.

The Lord said: From Bashan I will turn back; I will turn back into the depth of the sea. So that your foot may be dipped in blood, the tongue of your dogs from the enemies, from him. Bashan is interpreted as “confusion.” Therefore God turns us back from confusion. This is because he endured the cross and his foot was drenched in his own blood, while the Jews cried out against him, saying: “Crucify him, crucify him” (John XIX). These Jews were goaded by Christ’s enemies—that is, by demons. But for all this to happen was the will of the Savior himself, who allowed these things to be done to him. [Col. 1018A] Or: “From the confusion of this age I will bring back the human race,” that is, through my Passion and cross, which these people consider foolishness and confusion. “I will bring back Bashan, my people. I will bring back from the depth of the sea”: that is, from the depths of the vices and sins of this age, from its agitation and waves, I will turn back my people. “So that your foot may be dipped in blood.” For his foot was dipped in his own blood: “I alone have trodden the winepress, and from the nations no man was with me” (Isa. LXIII). And again: “Who is this who comes from Edom, his garments bright red from Bozrah?” (Ibid.). Edom is interpreted as “blood”; Bozrah as “flesh.” This signifies our Lord crucified. [Col. 1018B] “The tongue of your dogs from the enemies, from him.” He calls the Jews themselves “dogs,” as above: those who cried, “Crucify him, crucify such a one; we have no king but Caesar” (John XIX). “From the enemies” means that, having been subjugated by demons, they denied the Savior and blasphemed him. Alternatively: Since you came and suffered by your own will, and by your own will were crucified by the Jews, the Lord’s foot was dipped in blood when the flesh he had assumed, in which divinity lay hidden, was pierced by the spear. From that blood, therefore, the tongue of those who said, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII) was also stained. But after the glorious triumph of the Lord’s ascension, by the Lord’s vengeance the foot of the enemies was dipped in their blood, and the canine rage of the enemies was thereby sated.

[Col. 1018C] They saw your entrances, O God, the entrances of my God, my King who is in the holy place. How wonderfully the Old Testament in this psalm agrees with the sayings of the Gospels! For the ways of Christ were seen in the crossing of the Red Sea (Exod. XIV), and they were seen in the Gospels in the case of our King himself, when, raised up in the holy human being, he was carried into heaven (John XX; Acts I).

The princes went ahead, joined to those singing psalms, in the midst of young women playing tambourines. Indeed, in that crossing of the sea the princes went ahead: that is, Moses and the other elders went out first and were joined to the young women on the heavenly journey. “The princes went ahead”: the souls of the holy angels, who sang the Lord’s praises with their bodies mortified, saying: “Lift up your gates, O princes, your gates, for the triumphant one of hell has already returned” (Ps. XXIII). They are called players of tambourines because their bodies had died to sin. And in Exodus Miriam, the sister of Moses and Aaron, holding a tambourine, went before those singing and said: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously exalted” (Exod. XV). Alternatively: “The princes went ahead, joined to those singing, in the midst of young women playing tambourines.” The apostles, together with the churches, went ahead with united step. He rightly testifies that they went ahead, because the princes of the faith are from the Jews.

In the churches bless the Lord. He has spoken more clearly about the women with tambourines whom he mentioned above. The Lord from the springs of Israel. Because salvation is from the Jews, and the first Church arose from there. For the Church’s doctrine proceeded from the shadow of the Law [Col. 1019A], and in it the Lord—who took flesh from the descent of the Israelite race—is now blessed.

There is Benjamin. The Apostle Paul, who descended from the tribe of Benjamin. “There,” in the Church. A young man. The last of all the apostles. In an ecstasy. The ecstasy that seized him when he was going to Damascus.

The princes of Judah are their leaders. The apostles are the princes of Judah—that is, of the Lord—as Jacob says: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you” (Gen. XLIX). Zebulun and the princes of Naphtali. Zebulun is interpreted as “flowing of night”; Naphtali as “breadth.” When we have been freed from the passion of lust—that is, from that flowing—then we begin the expanses of the virtues. Or otherwise: “The princes of Zebulun and the princes of Naphtali.” [Col. 1019B] He shows Peter and Andrew as princes of the apostles. In the thick darkness, announcing that great light, they were appointed teachers of the Gospel, according to the passage: “Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations: the people sitting in darkness saw a great light” (Isa. XLIX).

Command, O God, your power. Your Christ. Strengthen this, O God, which you have worked in us. May he strengthen through the infusion of the Holy Spirit the gift of baptism that he bestowed. “Strengthen this, O God, which you have worked in us”—that is, strengthen the salvation you granted us through your Passion, and give help, because we are human beings and cannot walk in the virtues unless we obtain your help.

From your temple, which is in Jerusalem, kings will offer gifts to you. He calls “kings” those who reign over themselves, according to what is written: “The heart of a king is in the hand of God” (Prov. XII). They will offer gifts to God. The virtues of the saints are God’s gifts. Or he means that bodily temple which they made holy by living well. The kings in whom sin no longer reigns will offer gifts to the eternal King in the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the Church of the firstborn—namely, offering themselves as a living sacrifice, pleasing to God in the sight of all the angels.

Rebuke the beasts of the reed. The beasts of the reed are demons, of fragile and feeble power. Or they are heretics who discuss and write against you in order to deceive us. For heresies must also exist among us. They are called wild beasts because they seize souls and kill them. [Col. 1019D] Or: “Rebuke the beasts of the reed”—the beastlike pride of the Jews. The congregation of bulls among the calves of the peoples. This signifies the heretics themselves, because they can deceive no one except the simpler and smaller ones—that is, the lesser calves. They cannot deceive bulls, that is, the great. “To exclude those who have been tested by silver.” And for this reason they deceive the simpler ones—that is, the multitude—so that they may reach the saints and exclude them from the kingdom of heaven. Or by the bulls he indicates the leaders of the Jews, who brought persecution against the Lord and his saints, as in the passage: “Fat bulls surrounded me” (Ps. XXI). By the calves he demonstrates the foolish souls of the people who follow them. This is shown when Samaria worshiped golden calves under Jeroboam (III Kings XII). Therefore, may the counsel they have—to draw the saints back from the way of righteousness—rest upon their own souls, according to the passage: “Let their sword enter their own heart,” so that those who, through many tribulations, have been tested like silver and found righteous may not be excluded from the kingdom of God. Jacob foresaw such counsel when he said: “May my soul not enter their counsel” (Gen. XLIX).

Scatter the nations that desire wars. The heretics or the Jews, who often prepare struggles against the Church. Envoys will come from Egypt; Ethiopia will hasten to stretch out its hands to God. Those who are placed amid the tribulations and errors of idolatry, or who are black and darkened by sins, believing that Christ the Lord is himself God the Son of God, offer him gifts—that is [Col. 1020B], minds purer and brighter than gold and silver, because “where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. V).

Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God; sing psalms to the Lord. [Col. 1020A] You, indeed, who formerly loved an earthly kingdom and did not know God, now, having overcome carnal envy, enter the heavenly kingdoms.

Sing psalms to God, who has ascended above the heaven of heaven toward the east. He indeed who once, at the setting of death, had ascended the cross, has now been carried above the stars and, victorious over death, sits gloriously. “Toward the east” either because he himself is called the East, or because through him all arise to life.

Behold, he will give his voice the voice of his power. The Lord’s voice will then be given the voice of power, when what he commands is accomplished; when the dead hear it, they will rise. Give [Col. 1020C] glory to God over Israel. Honor God rather than carnal Israel. Alternatively: Honor God not with the lips, like Israel, but with the heart.

His magnificence and his power are in the clouds. In the apostles and prophets. Hence he says: “I commanded my clouds to rain rain upon Israel” (Isa. V).

God is wonderful in his saints. God is wonderful in this respect: he loved the human race so greatly that he performs signs in his saints. God is more wonderful in these than in the other creatures, because after many tribulations he raised them to the heights of heaven. The God of Israel himself will give power and strength to his people, to endure worldly passions or spiritual wickednesses. Blessed be God, who may deign to transform us from death into life and from corruption into incorruption [Col. 1020D], so that, made participants in his saints, we may rejoice in everlasting joys in him. Amen.

## PSALM LXVIII

For the end, for those who will be changed; a psalm, for David himself. This psalm speaks of Christ’s Passion and from the person of his members, although some think that the phrase “for those who will be changed” does not suit him at all. Christ changed himself when, being equal to the Father, he took the form of a servant. Or we are changed from unbelief to faith, because, as we have said, this psalm contains the voice of the Lord’s human being coming to the Passion.

Save me, O God, because the waters have entered even to my soul. According to the condition of weakness, he asks the Father [Col. 1021A] to save him, because the assaults of the raging crowd rushed upon him.

I am fixed in the mire of the deep. In the ancient sins of this people. And there is no substance. By which I might escape from there, unless you save me.

I have come into the height of the sea. Into the depth of this age. And the tempest submerged me: the storm of the Jews.

I have labored, crying out; my throat has become hoarse. Although he is pressed by sinners, he does not cease to cry out the commandments that bring salvation. My eyes have failed while I hope in my God. According to the weakness of the flesh, he hoped that this cup might pass from him; but according to his divinity, he fulfilled the Father’s will.

Those who hate me without cause have multiplied beyond the hairs of my head. [Col. 1021B] They have grown strong, and so forth. For this reason they multiply and grow strong beyond the hairs of my head, because the number of the wicked is always greater than that of the righteous. What I did not steal, I then repaid. For he was not a debtor to death or sin, but in his Passion he fulfilled both sacrifices.

O God, you know my foolishness, and my offenses are not hidden from you. The Father knows that he did not bring these things from heaven but assumed them for our sake, as the prophet says: “He himself took our iniquities and bore our sicknesses” (Isa. LIII). And Paul says: “What is foolish in God is wiser than human beings, and what is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (I Cor. I). “My offenses are not hidden from you,” as in the passage: “I made my offense known to you” (Ps. XXXI).

Let those who hope in you, Lord, not be put to shame because of me [Col. 1021C], and so forth. May the hope of believers not be emptied because of my Passion; rather, let them know that I came to do your will, as follows.

Because for your sake I endured reproach; shame covered me, and so forth. For the Father’s will he endured the reproaches of evil people, and was covered with shame when he was struck in the flesh he had assumed, because the Father and the Son had one will concerning the Passion he endured. Or: “Confusion covered him” when the apostles denied him.

I have become a stranger to my brothers, and so forth. For he was a son of the Synagogue, as they were, according to the order of earthly incorporation; yet he was regarded by them as an outsider and a stranger because they were full of crimes, whereas he was without sin. “I have become a stranger to my brothers.” The Lord’s brothers are the apostles. Hence he said: “I will announce your name to my brothers” (Ps. XXI). A stranger to the sons of my mother. Christ was a stranger, as Cleopas says: “Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem?” (Luke XXIV). “The only one,” because he alone and first rose immortal. [Col. 1021D] And the mother is the Synagogue.

Because zeal for your house has consumed me. Because they made it a den of thieves. And the reproaches of those reproaching you have fallen upon me. They cast upon him the quarrel of their reproaches when they called him both a Samaritan and one who had a demon. Hence the Jews said against Christ: “If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross, and we will believe you. He saved others; he cannot save himself” (Matt. XXVII). Those who reproach the Son also reproach the Father, because whoever does not believe in the Son does not have the Father.

I covered my soul in fasting, and it became a reproach to me. Satan tried to bring reproach upon him when, tempting him, he said: “Say that these stones should become bread” (Matt. IV). Or when the disciples said: “Rabbi, eat.” He said: “I have food to eat of which you do not know” (John IV). And elsewhere: “Work for food not that which perishes, but that which remains unto eternal life” (John VI). But Christ hungered for the salvation of the human race. Or he hungered for the faith of the Church, because he found no food among the Jews.

I put on sackcloth as my garment, and I became a parable to them. Sackcloth displays mourning or weeping, which he used at Lazarus’s death; he became a parable to the Jews when, as he wept, they said: “See how he loved him” (John XI). Others said: “Could not this man, who opened the eyes of the man born blind, have made it so that this man also would not die?”

Those who sat at the gate exercised themselves against me. [Col. 1022B] Those, namely, who possessed the key of knowledge but neither entered nor allowed others to enter: the scribes and Pharisees, who judged cases while sitting in public judgment. And those who drank wine sang against me. Filled with the wine of iniquity, they sang together about how they would kill him. For a person who plots treachery against God sings foolishly. Since the prophet knew that singing can be foolish in certain cases, listen to how he teaches some people: “Sing,” he says, “wisely.” Or they were drunk with wine when they covered his head [Col. 1022C] and said: “Prophesy to us, Christ: who is the one who struck you?” (Luke XXII).

But I directed my prayer to you, Lord. I am not overcome by these passions, because I am with you in prayer. But I directed my prayer to you, O God. While the Jews cursed me and said, “Crucify him, crucify him,” I spoke while praying for them: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII). A time of favor, O God. The time of favor is the time of the Passion, when the Father said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III). A time of good pleasure, O God, in the abundance of your mercy. All your times are times of good pleasure, but especially this time, in which through my Passion you redeem the human race and, in a certain sense, make it more pleasing. [Col. 1022D] Hear me, Lord, in the truth of your salvation. So that after true death, the truth of the resurrection may be confirmed.

Deliver me from the mire, so that I may not be fixed in it. Ask, according to some interpreters, whether perhaps the mire signifies the lowliness of the flesh that he assumed. He prays not to be dissolved and corrupted in mire and dust, as the whole human race is. Free me from those who hate me. He clearly says this about the Jews, who never loved him. And from the depths of the waters. May the tempest of the water not submerge me. May this tempest of the Passion not hold him in the depth of the infernal abyss. Nor may the deep swallow me, into which, when he descended through death, he might not be devoured by it. Nor may its rotten mouth press upon me. The entrance of hell, or the devil.

[Col. 1023A] Hear me, Lord, because your mercy is kind; according to the multitude of your compassions, look upon me. According to the weakness of the human being, he asks this, saying: You who redeem others through my Passion, look upon me, with mercy going before.

Do not turn your face away from your servant. The voice of Christ to the Father, who took the form of a servant, as the prophet says: “It is a great thing for you to be called my servant” (Isa. XLIX). Because I am afflicted, hear me quickly. So that I may take back the spirit that I entrusted into your hands.

Attend to my soul and deliver it; because of my enemies rescue me. So that when I rise from the dead, they may be put to shame. Hence Christ said: “I have power to lay down my soul” (John X).

[Col. 1023B] You know my reproach and my confusion, and so forth. Which I endure in the flesh I have assumed.

In your sight are all those who trouble me. You see what sort of tribulations they inflict upon me and what mockeries they display. My heart expected reproach and misery. Reproach of the Passion and misery—that is, the insult of the cross.

I waited for one who would grieve with me, and so forth. From so great a multitude of wicked people, no one either shared my pain or proved a comforter.

They gave gall as my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink. We read in the Gospels that this was already fulfilled when, as the Lord thirsted on the cross, they offered him vinegar mixed with gall to drink (John XIX). From this testimony and from another it is understood [Col. 1023C] that the psalm should be referred to Christ.

Let their table become a snare before them. The words of the Law and the prophets, to which they often gathered and were refreshed. Into a snare, and into retributions, and into an occasion of stumbling. So that they would not understand that the Lord was announced there. For the Lord also said in the Gospels: “Moses accuses you, in whom you hope” (John V). For he wrote about me.

Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see. The divinity hidden beneath weakness. “So that they may not see.” This was what he prayed for when he asked that their table become a snare: namely, that they should not recognize the mysteries of the Law. And make their back always bent. So that they may always serve the Romans. Or under the burden of the Law, which no one could bear according to the letter.

[Col. 1023D] Pour out your wrath upon them, and let the fury of your anger seize them. Let their dwelling become desolate, and so forth. [Col. 1023D] All these things were fulfilled in the overthrow of Jerusalem under Titus and Vespasian. Or this is what he says: “Your house will be left to you desolate” (Matt. III). When Christ withdrew from Judea, all the powers likewise withdrew with him.

Because they persecuted the one whom you struck. Christ speaks these things about himself to the Father, just as elsewhere we read that the Father says through the prophet: “Because of the sins of the people I struck him” (Isa. LIII). And again: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (Zech. XIII). He was struck so that we might rise again; he was wounded so that he might heal us. [Col. 1024A] But the blood and water that came forth from the wound in his side (John XIX) also prefigured martyrdom and baptism, through which one goes to heaven. And upon the pain of my wounds they added more. When they persecuted either the Church or the apostles.

Add iniquity upon their iniquity. For just as their failure to believe in me was reckoned to them as iniquity, so let the fact that they persecuted me be added to this iniquity. And may they not enter into your righteousness. May they not receive the kingdoms of heaven with the righteous.

Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and let them not be written with the righteous. Here he indicates two books that have been written: that of the living and that of the righteous. Therefore it must be observed that the book of the living is the one in which the prophets and patriarchs were written before the coming of God. Concerning it Moses said, when the people had sinned: “If you do not forgive them their offense, blot me out of the book [Col. 1024B] that you have written” (Exod. XXXII). By the book of the righteous he means the one concerning which the Lord says to those who followed him through faith: “Rejoice and exult, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke X). Therefore these persecutors were both blotted out of the first book and not written in the second.

I am poor and sorrowful. In the Passion. And your salvation, O God, has received me. As one rising again. From this point the prophet speaks: “I am poor and sorrowful.” For although he was rich, he became poor for our sake, and he did not despise his fettered ones. We may use this verse whenever we deliver praises of the martyrs. Some also think that this should be understood of souls: although enclosed in bodies, they are not despised by God.

[Col. 1024C] I will praise the name of my God with a song; I will magnify him with praise. Whether because he triumphed over the devil or conquered the world.

It will please God. That is, the Father. More than a young bull. Who offered himself to the Father. Producing horns. Giving strength to the Church. And hoofs. With which it may trample underfoot and tear apart the sacrileges of the nations.

Let the poor see and rejoice. Because, with the superstition of the gentiles humbled, the kingdom of the Lord’s Church is exalted. Seek the Lord, and your soul shall live. Which now is dead through sins.

For the Lord has heard the poor. In order to raise them from the dead. And he did not despise his own prisoners. Because, having broken the bonds of the devil, he admitted them into his kingdom.

Let the heavens and the earth praise him, the sea and all the creatures that creep in it [Col. 1024D]. Let all these bow the knee before him—those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth.

For God will save Zion. The heavenly Jerusalem, in which he will unite his elect according to their merits in the one body of that heavenly mother. And the cities of Judah shall be built. The souls of the saints, who through confession are brought into the holy temple as living stones.

And they shall dwell there, and acquire it as an inheritance, and the offspring of his servants shall possess it, etc. The saints, certainly, who are transferred into it. Or their offspring, that is, those who have been converted through them. But because the title of the psalm is inscribed concerning those who will be changed, let us beseech the Lord that, having been converted from paganism, he may build us into the cities of Judah [Col. 1025A], and, having freed us from the yoke of the devil, may love us as his own offspring. Those whom he redeemed through the bitterness of gall, the harshness of vinegar, the sufferings of the cross, the wounds of the nails, the disgrace of death, and the glory of the resurrection—may he deign to preserve in this world in such a way that he makes them sharers with his saints in the kingdom. Amen.

## PSALM LXIX

To the end; a psalm of David, for remembrance, because the Lord saved him. This psalm is sung in the person of the Lord incorporated [in human form], as he implores the Father’s protection.

God, attend to my help; Lord, etc. Christ is our help, and now asks the Father’s assistance to refute those who oppose him.

[Col. 1025B] Let those who seek my soul to take it be put to shame and confounded. For they are confounded when they learn that the one whose soul they wished to take has risen again.

Let those who desire evil for me turn back and be put to shame. Let them not be changed in the resurrection together with the saints, but, turned backward, let them blush with shame, because they see the one whom they judged as a man judging as God.

Let those who say to me, “Good, good,” turn back at once in shame. This is the voice of mockers, referring to those who said: “If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross”; and again: “He trusted in God; let him deliver him, if he wants him” (Matt. XXVII). After the punishment of the wicked, it is turned toward the glory of the blessed.

Let all who seek you exult and rejoice in you [Col. 1025C]. Those who seek you, merciful as you are, through tears of repentance. And let those who love your salvation say always, “The Lord is magnified.” Having received forgiveness of sins. Those who love you because you are the life of all.

But I am needy and poor; the Lord, etc. Christ the Lord often calls himself needy and poor; his concern consists in the love of the Father’s compassion.

You are my helper and my protector, my God; do not delay. For at the time of his Passion he said to the disciple: “What you are going to do, do quickly” (John XIII), namely, so that the swift help of the resurrection might precede the suffering of the body. May he who was wounded for our sins and rose again for our justification now grant us help in the time of tribulation according to his customary mercy, so that, exulting with his saints [Col. 1025D], we may be able to magnify and extol him. Amen.

## PSALM LXX

A psalm of David, of the sons of Jonadab and of the first captives. This psalm contains the prophet’s voice: lamenting the bodily humility of the Redeemer and singing of his glorious resurrection.

In you, Lord, I have hoped; let me never be confounded. Our Mediator therefore prays that this confusion of death may not be lasting, as it is for all the others. And in your justice deliver me and rescue me. Incline, etc. For your justice is that whoever does your will should pass from death to life; and I now pray to be rescued through it. Or otherwise: Incline your ear to me and save me [Col. 1026A]. The Lord’s ears are mentioned when he deigns to hear, because, taking the form of a servant, he became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name.

Be for me a protecting God and a fortified place, so that you may save me. For apart from you, neither refuge nor fortification nor protection can be provided by anyone. Is God local, then? Although he is “local” to those who come to him, he is not local, because he is everywhere.

For you are my strength and my refuge. Strength, since the substance in him is equal; refuge, in accordance with bodily weakness.

My God, rescue me from the hand of the sinner and from the hand, etc. From the power of the Jewish people, who did not understand in the Law that I was to come. And from the unjust. The one who is always malicious. Not all sinners are also unjust. Sinners are transgressors—that is, Jews and wicked Christians—who transgress the Old and the New Testament. The unjust are those who do not believe, as Paul says: “Those who sinned without the law will also perish without the law.”

For you are my patience, Lord. Because I suffer for the sake of your will. My hope from my youth. From the beginning of bodily life. Therefore hope is not put to shame, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. II).

Upon you I have been strengthened from the womb. That is, from the time when I began to believe in the Law. From my mother’s womb. From the Synagogue, from which I came forth.
