You are my protector, Lord [Col. 1026C]. In you is my song always. May I be protected by you in the Passion, and may I sing your name among the nations.

I have become like a portent to many. For they said to him: “You are a Samaritan and have a demon” (John VIII; Matt. XVII). And you, Lord, are a strong helper. You said to me: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him.”

Let my mouth be filled with your praise, that I may sing your glory, your greatness all day long. There is one day for your saints in this world, which no night darkens; in it and with them I sing your praise, glory, and majesty, because I am among them. I sing to you. But even now the Lord himself opens our mouth, so that we may proclaim his glory and expound his praise.

[Col. 1026D] Do not cast me away in the time of old age, when my strength fails, etc. At the completion, certainly, of this age.

For my enemies have spoken against me. Saying: “He is not of God, because he does not keep the Sabbath” (John IX). And those who watched over my soul took counsel together, saying: “God has abandoned him,” etc. The wicked said these things and went astray, for their hearts were blinded by malice. But even during the Passion, as though God had abandoned him, they said: “Let him be; let Elijah come and save him” (Matt. XXVII).

God, do not be far from me; my God, etc. So that, having bound the strong man, I may return victorious from hell.

Let those who slander my soul be confounded and fail; let them be covered, etc. When I have been raised again.

[Col. 1027A] But I will always hope in you, Lord, etc. So that what the Law commanded you to be offered in its visible sacrifices, the redeemed people may carry out in their conduct.

My mouth will proclaim your justice, your salvation all day long. For, rising again, I will gather the Church in which I shall sing your praises.

For I have not known business dealings; I will enter into the powers of the Lord. He knew business dealings who sold the teacher. “I glorified you on earth; I completed the work that you gave me to do” (John XVII). Lord, I will remember your justice alone. The prophet says that he remembers the Father’s justice, just as he himself says in the Gospel: “I speak the things that I have heard from my Father” (John VIII).

God, you have taught me from my youth, and until now I shall proclaim your wonders, and even into old age and advanced years: God, do not abandon me [Col. 1027B]. Was he, then, abandoned by the Father? Rather, he always bore witness that he is truthful.

Until I proclaim your arm to every generation, etc. He proclaimed all these things to the Christian generation, which he acquired with his own blood and for which he suffered, as follows. What great things you have done, O God! Who is like you? You who sent me, according to your merciful plan, for the redemption of humanity.

How many and great tribulations you have shown me, and evil ones; and, turning back, you have given me life. Many tribulations were indeed shown to him in the weakness of the flesh for the salvation of the human race, but he endured them all vigorously. And from the abysses of the earth you brought me back again. This means, from the depth of hell [Col. 1027C]. Let the Jews now speak, who want this psalm to be sung of David alone: when was he brought out from the depth of the abyss?

You have multiplied your magnificence, O God, etc. When those who were held in hell returned with me.

For I too will give thanks to you with the vessels of the psalm. Those who, filled with that new wine of evangelical and apostolic preaching, understand me to have been proclaimed in the psalms: “I will sing your truth to you on the lyre, O holy God of Israel.” In those who retain you in their minds.

My lips will exult, etc. The prophet says these things at the conclusion of the psalm. And my soul, which you have redeemed. So that the second death might not rule over it.

But my tongue also shall meditate on your justice, when those who seek evil for me have been confounded and put to shame [Col. 1027D]. Whether vices or aerial powers, which inflict unjust attacks upon me. But let us beseech the Lord that, with the human mouth filled with his praises, we may always meditate in our hearts on the things we utter with voices pleasing to him.

## PSALM LXXI

For Solomon. This psalm too properly refers to Christ. For Solomon means “peaceful,” and Christ is peaceful; and he remains with the sun, and before the moon, throughout generations of generations. If this psalm is understood of Solomon, this cannot possibly stand. For Solomon did not remain either with the sun or with the moon. But if we wish to understand it of Christ, we must ask how Christ has no end, since the sun, the moon, heaven, and all things are said to grow old and pass away. But this seventy-first psalm, which the prophet sang, shows the Son of God coming into the world and, after the injuries of the assumed flesh and the liberation of the poor from the hand of the powerful, returned to heaven, having received all judgment from the Father. It therefore begins as follows:

Give the king your judgments, O God. The prophet therefore speaks, as we said, to the Father, asking him to give judgment to the Son—not because he does not possess it as one subsisting in the one Godhead, but to show that he would come in the body. And your justice to the king’s son. To the people who, taken into adoption as sons, were reborn in him through baptism. For it is fitting that the people should live by justice, while the king exercises the judgment that he received from the Father; the following verse confirms this.

To judge your people in justice. Whom you acquired through his Passion [Col. 1028B] and resurrection. And your poor in judgment. So that, after their present hardships, they may receive everlasting consolation.

Let the mountains receive peace for the people, and the hills your justice. We have often warned that mountains and hills have a twofold meaning: namely, the divine party and the opposing one. Therefore let those who, seduced by the adversary and supported by riches, have been raised up like hills and mountains now subjected to God receive that peace and justice which the people whom we previously called adopted possess—that is, Christ, who is our peace and our justice.

He will judge the poor of the people. So that, having become poor for their sake, they may be enriched with the heavenly kingdoms. And he will save the children of the poor. Those who have been converted through them. And he will humble the slanderer [Col. 1028C]. Having granted a reward to the just, he humbles the devil, who now acts as their accuser.

And he will remain with the sun. With the Father’s glory. For these things cannot be applied to this sun, because it will be dissolved with this world. And before the moon, throughout generations of generations. For he will stand before every congregation of the Church and will remain forever.

And he will descend like rain upon fleece. For just as rain descended upon Gideon’s fleece (Judg. VI) while the dry earth remained barren, so he too entered the virginal womb through the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. And like drops falling upon the earth. For the earth of the human body was dry when he came and could produce no fruit of holiness; but he filled it with eternal fruits after making it fertile through the drops of his preaching [Col. 1028D].

Justice shall arise in his days, and abundance of peace. This was fulfilled in the days of Augustus Caesar, when the Lord proceeded from the virginal bridal chamber. For in those days all wars were so quiet that even what another prophet sang was fulfilled: “They turned their swords into ploughshares and their spears into sickles” (Isa. II). His days are when he is conceived, when he is born, when he is nourished. His days are when he performs the Father’s works, when he suffers, when he descends to the lower regions, when he rises again, when he presents himself to the disciples, and when he ascends into heaven. Until the moon is taken away. Until the Church is raised up.

And he will rule from sea to sea, etc. The prophet testifies that this whole world, acquired and subjected through his Passion, belongs to Christ the Lord [Col. 1029A].

Before him the Ethiopians will fall. Those darkened by sins. And his enemies will lick the earth. According to the saying: “They shall adore you, and they shall lick the dust of your feet” (Isa. XLIX).

The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of Arabia and Sheba shall bring presents, etc. Here the prophet declares that every worldly power, its honors and ranks, will approach Christ the Lord, submit their necks to him, and bring gifts of good conduct. We understand this to have begun with the gifts of the Magi. For they are shown to have represented the nations and kings.

For he has delivered the poor from the powerful. The faithful people from the power of the devil. And the poor person who had no helper [Col. 1029B]. He will spare the poor and needy, etc. Those who, having cast aside the riches of the world, have done penance: they are spared and will be saved.

He will redeem their souls from usury and iniquities. So that they may not store up treasures on earth from perishable interest, but place in heaven purses that do not grow old. But usuries are also sins, when malice received from Satan is multiplied. And their name will be honorable before him. Before God the Father.

And he will live. In his saints, just as Paul also said: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. II). And he will be given gold from Arabia. They will offer him purity of mind, like Arabian gold glowing with very beautiful brilliance. And they will adore him continually. Because they have been freed from iniquities [Col. 1029C]. All day long they will bless him. Gathered into the one body of the Church.

And there will be strength upon the earth. For his advent, Passion, and resurrection brought great strength to the earth as it was collapsing. His fruit will be exalted above the summits of the mountains, above Lebanon. For the grace of baptism has been raised above all the heights of the age; through it sins are removed. And they will flower from the city. That is, from the heavenly Jerusalem. Like the grass of the earth. “Grass” has a twofold meaning. There is grass that withers and falls, and there is flowering grass that endures with a green crown, from which the crowns of the saints are adorned. Therefore the saints, reborn through baptism, will flower from the heavenly Jerusalem, splendid with the adornment of good works. Like the grass of the earth. Not of that earth subject to the curse [Col. 1029D], but of that which flows with honey and milk.

And his name will be blessed forever. He will be blessed perpetually by those whom he has transferred there. His name remains before the sun. Namely, the power of his name, according to the saying: “Before the morning star I begot you” (Ps. CIX).

And all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed in him; all nations shall magnify him. For the Evangelist recalls that the Lord said: “This Gospel will be preached throughout the whole world” (Matt. XXIV). And all nations shall come and adore before you, Lord.

Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, who alone does wonders. For he did them in the Old Testament, and he does them in the New, when he graciously calls those things that are not as though they were.

And blessed is the name of his majesty forever. According to the saying: “For those who believe in me there will be a new name, which will be blessed on earth,” that is, “Christian.” And all the earth will be filled with his majesty—let it be, let it be. When he pours out his Holy Spirit upon all flesh; we already read that this was fulfilled in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts II). May he now also deign to pour the Paraclete—that is, the Comforter—into us, so that we may understand that for our redemption he assumed an earthly body, underwent death, penetrated hell, and returned victorious to the heavens.

## PSALM LXXII

[Col. 1030B]

The hymns of David, son of Jesse, have ended. A psalm of Asaph. It must be known that the seventy-first psalm is the end of the second book; therefore it ends with “Let it be, let it be,” for which, as we demonstrated above, the Hebrew has “Amen, amen.” It must also be observed more carefully that “The hymns of David, son of Jesse, have ended” belongs to the end of the seventy-first psalm; what follows, “A psalm of Asaph,” is the beginning of the next.

How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart. For he is good to those who will see him, as the Lord says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V).

But my feet were almost moved; my steps were almost poured out. Because, etc. His steadfastness in holiness and his progress toward God were slipping, since he had been jealous of the peace and prosperity of the wicked.

[Col. 1030C] For there is no regard for their death, and there is strength in their affliction. And in the labor of human beings, etc. They quickly recover from weakness and wounds, nor are they shaken by the lashes of tribulations as righteous people are.

Therefore pride seized them; they were covered with iniquity and with their impiety. For through the arrogance of their prosperity they are weighed down by multiplied iniquity.

Their iniquity came forth as though from fatness. In the abundance of riches also, their forgotten iniquity came forth from them. For Moses too speaks of this fatness: “Jacob grew fat and kicked” (Deut. XXXII).

They passed over into the desire of the heart. So that they might do their own will and not God’s.

They thought and spoke wickedness, etc. Either the Jews, who blaspheming God placed in the flesh were laying snares of wickedness through perverse thoughts [Col. 1030D]; or heretics, who disparage God through unjust interpretations.

They set their mouth against heaven, and their tongue passed over the earth. Through the pride of knowledge they spoke against the inhabitant of heaven, but their wicked speech was humbled down to the earth and passed away, because it had no firm standing. Therefore the Lord speaks through these prophecies concerning his own, saying:

Therefore my people here shall turn back, and full days shall be found in them. The righteous who had previously been jealous of sinners, seeing these things and observing their peace, return to God so that they may receive the fullness of eternal days [Col. 1031A], knowing that the unjust do not even approach halfway.

And they said: How does God know, and is there knowledge in the Most High? For sinners are ignorant that God is able to know all things. Wretchedly unaware that nothing is hidden from his eyes.

Behold, these are sinners, and, abounding in the world, they have acquired riches. Abounding in the riches of the age, they have lost the gifts of paradise.

And I said: Then in vain I justified my heart and washed my hands among the innocent? Does the righteous person, seeing these things, then justify himself in vain, or has the innocent done the opposite? But the Lord himself says these things in the person of the righteous, as the following words teach.

And I was scourged all day long. For the Lord was often scourged by their deceits [Col. 1031B], but on the day of the Passion he was beaten with definite insults and actual blows. And my chastisement was in the morning. Judas indeed said: “What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you so that he may be seized?” (Matt. XXVI). But he himself was scourged in the morning, when on the following day after the Lord’s betrayal he went away and hanged himself with a noose.

If I said: I will speak thus—behold, I would betray the generation of your children. The order and meaning of the reading is this: While I accuse myself in my morning prayers, I found this, to say: If I speak in this way, if I wish to investigate the hidden things of God, I begin to become alienated from your children, as though no one were justified and no one were doing a just deed. Those who proclaim me and through me have become your children rise up against me. From here the prophet speaks [Col. 1031C]:

I considered how I might understand this; it was labor before me. I examined everything, even if laboriously. Yet I considered with the Apostle that “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in the saints” (Rom. VIII).

Until I enter the sanctuary of God and understand their end. I also understood this concerning those saints, entering mentally into their company: although they were afflicted in few things in their first life, in the last they will be well ordered in many things. From here the words turn toward those who trusted in the deceitfulness of riches.

Nevertheless, because of their deceits you set them. Because they troubled the righteous with wicked frauds. You cast them down when they were lifted up. Having been raised up by you through riches, they were cast down.

[Col. 1031D] How they have become desolation! This is the form of an interrogative utterance, followed by the respondent’s answer. Suddenly they failed; they perished because of their iniquity. For he explained the order of what happened, according to the Apostle’s saying: “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them” (1 Thess. V).

Like the dream of those who awake. Just as someone sleeping sees in a vision great treasures of gold and silver, and on rising loses everything, so they too will lose their riches after the life of this age, in which they have lived as though in a dream. Lord, in the city. In the heavenly Jerusalem, certainly. You will reduce their image to nothing. When they knock at the heavenly palace, you will say: “Depart from me, workers of iniquity, because I do not know you” (Luke XIII).

For my heart was inflamed. So that I might do the Father’s will. Christ the Lord speaks these things. And my kidneys were changed. So that the lust of human thought might not prevail over me. And I was reduced to nothing and did not know. He says that he was humbled and ignorant, to show the true human being. For God is deceived by no ignorance, but knows no sinners.

I became like a beast before you. Carrying in the flesh the sins of your people. And I am always with you. I in you, and you in me.

You held my right hand. As I descended into hell, because the devil’s left hand opposed me. And in your will you led me. Rising again. And with glory you received me [Col. 1032B]. Returning to the heavens.

For what is there for me in heaven, and what did I desire from you upon earth? This must be read emphatically: Such great things you prepared for me in heaven, and I, wretched as I am, was seeking small things from you on earth? Or otherwise: I sought no one besides you, either in heaven or on earth. For my will has been fulfilled by you, so that every knee may bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth. The voice of the Church follows, saying:

My heart and my flesh have failed; God of my heart and God my portion forever. After the God of her heart—that is, Christ the Lord, whose portion she has become—she desires him with all her heart and body. For the failing that she says she has must be understood not as diminution but as desire.

[Col. 1032C] For behold, those who distance themselves from you will perish; you have destroyed all who fornicate away from you. All who fornicate sin without God. But whoever sins is far from God and therefore near to destruction.

But for me it is good to cling to God. By whose blood I have been redeemed. To place my hope in the Lord God. For it is vain to trust in the goods of the age.

So that I may proclaim all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion. Through contemplation of the hope he has in God, he hopes to be led into the gates of the heavenly Jerusalem, to receive future blessedness with his elect. May Christ the Lord admit us into their fellowship—not as one who examines merits, but as the giver of pardon. Amen.

## PSALM LXXIII

[Col. 1032D] An instruction of Asaph. Therefore “instruction” is written beforehand in the title, because a twofold captivity follows: namely, carnal and spiritual.

Why, O God, have you rejected us forever? Is your anger furious against the sheep of your pasture? It is an immense gift of the Lord’s compassion that he rejects in such a way as to recall, and becomes angry in order to correct.

Remember your congregation, which you acquired from the beginning. The ecclesiastical congregation, certainly, which you prefigured through the patriarchs and prophets, either by their callings or by their sacrifices.

You redeemed the rod of your inheritance. The rod of God’s inheritance is Christ, as it is said to Jeremiah, who saw the watchful rod: “You have seen well, for I am watching over my people” (Jer. I); and again: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root, and the nations shall entreat him” (Isa. XI). This rod, therefore, was delivered from its pursuing enemies. Mount Zion, in which you dwelt. Either in the assumed body or in the Church. For both belong to the holy mountain.

Lift your hands against their pride forever. Against those who attempt to attack your Church. How greatly the enemy has acted wickedly in the holy place! So that he might make human persecutors of those whom he had ensnared with evil counsels.

And those who hated you gloried, etc. For they glory at the devil’s prompting when, out of hatred for God, they afflict the holy martyrs with punishments.

They set your sanctuary on fire in the land; they polluted the tabernacle of your name, etc. These things indeed happened according to history, either when Nebuchadnezzar led them away to Babylon (2 Kings XXV), or when Titus and Vespasian, after burning the city together with the temple and slaughtering the multitude with the sword, led the remaining populace away captive. But even now we must beware lest what then happened to Jerusalem now happen to the Christian people. As he said above in the verse we passed over: “They set up their signs, and they did not recognize the signs, as at the exit above.” Thus the Babylonians, lifted up by the swelling of arrogant victory, set up their signs in your temple, as trophies from enemies are customarily placed above the arches of gates. Symmachus interpreted this more clearly, saying: “They set up their signs openly on high, at the entrance of the gates” [Col. 1033C].

Therefore let each one of us have the banner of the cross in his heart—not the sign of the adversary, lest he be cut down from grace by his axe, but cleansed for glory by the evangelical sickle. Let him not be burned up in desires, but kindled by spiritual mysteries. Let him not be polluted by vices, but filled with virtues. Let him not suppose that God is unable to know anything, but confess that nothing is hidden from his eyes. Finally, let him not give consent to the devil’s insults, but glorify the name of his God.

Why do you turn your hand away, and your right hand from the midst of your bosom, forever? His bosom is his sanctuary, as another prophet says. For just as a shepherd warms his flock and carries the young in his bosom, so the Lord nourishes his people (Isa. XL). He turns away his observation or his power from this bosom when we sin against him.

But God our king is before the ages. As he says through Solomon, from Wisdom, which is Christ: “He created me at the beginning of his ways; before the ages he founded me” (Eccl. XXIV). He worked salvation in the midst of the earth. Either in Judea, which is called the center of the earth, or in the virginal womb.

You established the sea by your strength. The age, or the things in it. You crushed the heads of the dragon in the waters. In baptism you subjected the power of demons. You crushed the heads of the dragon in the waters—that is, of the devil. And you gave him as food to the peoples of Ethiopia. So that, in turn, he might be devoured or crushed by those whom he had previously devoured through false persuasions, by the sign of the cross [Col. 1034A].

You split open the springs, etc. The Apostles or the other preachers.

The day is yours, and the night is yours. The brightness of the Gospel or the obscurity of the Law, because both proclaim you. You made the sun. That man through whom those sitting in darkness saw a great light. And the moon. The Church, which shines amid the darkness of the age.

You made all the boundaries of the earth. For all things were created at your command. You formed summer and spring. Although God also made the seasons of the year and all the elements of the world, according to allegory we call it spring when the righteous flower in this age through good works, and summer when they receive the fruit of their labor.

[Col. 1034B] Remember this: the enemy has reproached the Lord, and a foolish people has provoked your name. Your martyrs stand in the contest; the devil reproaches, and the gentile people exasperates. You, Lord, remember those who suffer such things for love of your name.

Do not hand over to beasts the souls confessing you. O devil, O ministers of the devil, who do not wish to devour bodies but souls. For the soul is devoured by the mouth of the beast when it shows compliance with the devil’s will. Do not forget forever the souls of your poor. Even if they are subjected to tribulations for a time, let them not perish, but, having been tested, let them be revealed as genuine.

Look upon your covenant, because those who have been darkened by the thorns of the earth have been filled with them. “Thorns” are interpreted as briars [Col. 1034C]. Therefore those who have darkened your earth with their persecutions have been filled with the thorns of iniquity. But you, Lord, who through your covenant—whether the Old or the New, since both proceed from you and are regarded as one—promised to protect your own, now cut down the thorns and rescue us.

Let the humble one who has been made confounded not turn away. Let him not be forgotten by you who is worn down by many tribulations. The poor and needy will praise your name. When they have received what you promised.

Arise, O God; judge your cause. Because of these insults, which either you endured for us or which the Church now endures. Remember your insults, those uttered all day long by the fool. So that they may be confounded in judgment.

[Col. 1034D] Do not forget the voices of your enemies. Those who invoke you amid present pressures—let them be consoled by you. The pride of those who hate you always rises. For unless their pride rises, they are not humbled. Thus the Lord also says in the Apocalypse: “Let the unjust act unjustly still, and let the wicked do wickedness still” (Rev. XXII). “Behold, I come quickly, and my reward is with me.” We too, Lord, humbly beseech you: after the contempt of the world, deign to raise us, rescued from the thorns of iniquities and from the boot of ruinous pride, into heaven.

## PSALM LXXIV

[Col. 1035A]

To the end, “Do not destroy”; a psalm, a song of Asaph. It is interpreted as “synagogue.” In Hebrew it does not have “to the end,” but “victory.” And the Seventy Translators were not greatly mistaken, since victory is complete. He rightly said, “To the end, do not destroy.” This expression is interpreted in many ways. David also says to one of his friends: “Do not destroy him”—that is, Saul. See what he says. And elsewhere we read that David blessed the Lord because his hands had been kept safe—that is, so that he would not kill Saul. Therefore, whenever we do not kill someone, our hands too are kept safe. Others say that this psalm was composed by David and sung by Asaph. Others, however, say that Asaph himself both composed and sang it. Therefore, according to the Seventy, it says this: O Lord, who kept me from laying my hand upon Saul, your Christ, keep me safe to the end.

We will give thanks to you, God. Here “we will give thanks” does not signify repentance but glory. And we will call upon your name. The name of God is the Father, for previously he was unknown. The Lord says: “Father, I have revealed your name to human beings” (John XXVII). For every Son is the name of the Father.

We will proclaim your wonders. The Church says this; the multitude of believers says this. “We will proclaim your wonders.” This verse is joined to the preceding ones; the verse that follows, however, is spoken in the person of the Lord. For the ancient interpreters interpreted it in this way.

When I receive the appointed time, I will judge just judgments. For now he is not judge, but he will be. If he were judge now, sinners would not rise up and would not possess riches in the age. This scandalizes you: that the righteous flee while sinners pursue them? This scandalizes you: that iniquity reigns in the world? Hear the Lord saying: “When I receive the appointed time, I will judge just judgments.” The time of judgment has been reserved. At present there is not judgment but contest. For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son. Hearing this, do not be scandalized and say: “This one is lesser, since he receives from the one who gives.” But see what he says in the Gospel: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, because he is the Son of Man” (John III). He gives the reason why he received judgment: because he is the Son of Man. You hear “Son of Man” and doubt why he received it?

## PSALM LXXV

To the end, in hymns; a psalm of Asaph, a song concerning the Assyrians.

[Col. 1035D] God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel. Before the cross illumined the world, and before the Lord was seen on earth, God was known in Judah, but in Israel his name was great. When the Savior came, his sound went out into all the earth, and his words to the ends of the world (Ps. XVIII).

And his dwelling-place was established in peace. In Hebrew this is said to be in *Salem*. According to the letter, therefore, he seems to be speaking of Jerusalem, which was formerly called Salem, afterward Jebus, and later Jerusalem; there King Melchizedek lived. We read: “You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX). He did not say, “according to the order of Aaron,” but “of Melchizedek.” [Col. 1036A] What did he mean by saying, “You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek”? It is clear that this passage refers to Christ. But what does “according to the order of Melchizedek” mean? Aaron offered sacrifices; Aaron poured out the blood of victims. Melchizedek did none of these things, but offered only bread and wine (Gen. XIV). This, therefore, is what Melchizedek did, and for this reason it is said, “according to the order of Melchizedek.”

In Hebrew it reads: “And his shelter was established in Salem.” See what he says according to the tropological sense: the Lord has no shelter except where there is peace. Where there is jealousy and discord, God is not the protector. Let us also speak according to the Septuagint. God’s dwelling-place exists only in a soul that possesses peace. Therefore, let the soul that does not possess peace know that it is not God’s dwelling-place. “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John XIV). This is the Savior’s inheritance.

And his dwelling-place is in Zion. According to the letter, we can speak of Jerusalem and Zion, because the temple was there. According to the tropological and anagogical senses, however, we say that God’s dwelling-place is in Zion. Zion is interpreted as “watchtower.” Wherever, therefore, there is knowledge and teaching of the Scriptures in a soul, there God dwells.

There he broke the strength of bows. Where? In Jerusalem and Zion. Jerusalem is interpreted as “peace,” and Zion as “watchtower.” Let us therefore see what peace is and what the watchtower is. We may interpret this in two ways: either as the human soul in which there are God’s peace and contemplation, or as the Church, or indeed as Holy Scripture. For there are peace, dwelling-place, and God’s watchtower.

There he broke the strength of bows: those burning arrows that the devil used to shoot; shield, sword, and war. This is the war of which it is said elsewhere: “Scatter the nations that desire wars” (Ps. LXVII). And what follows? *Selah*, which the Septuagint interprets as *diapsalma*, while in Hebrew it is said to mean “always.” See, then, that the Lord always breaks the shield, the sword, and the war.

You illumine wondrously from the everlasting mountains. We interpret “mountains” in two ways: in the Old Testament, as the prophets; in the New Testament, as the apostles. Of these mountains he says: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains: from where will my help come?” (Ps. CXX). Upon these mountains the city of God has also been set. “A city cannot be hidden when it is set upon a mountain.” We were all sitting [Col. 1036D] in darkness and in the shadow of death, and the Lord illumined us from the everlasting mountains (Matt. V)—that is, from the prophets and apostles.

All the foolish in heart were troubled. We may apply this verse to unbelievers.

They slept their sleep and found nothing, and so forth. Truly this life, and riches, are a sleep. For when we seem to possess them, we immediately lose them. It is as it is written in the prophet: “As when someone who is thirsty sleeps, and, if he finds water, drinks; afterward, when he awakes, the thirst itself remains” (Isa. XXIX). Such are riches in this world: while we hold them, we lose them.

Those who mounted horses fell asleep. Let us speak according to the tropological sense. Pharaoh, for example, mounted horses, fell asleep, and perished. The Egyptians had horses, but they perished. For this reason it was also commanded in the Law that a Hebrew should not have horses. Solomon, accordingly, did not have a horse from Jerusalem or from Judea, but bought them for himself from Egypt (Deut. XVII; 3 Kings X). Horses are always sold in Egypt.

“Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we will call upon the name of the Lord our God” (Ps. XIX). Those, therefore, who mounted horses fell asleep and perished, along with their riders.

Our Lord, too, has horses; he also has shining mountains. Conversely, the devil has dark mountains. Just as there are shining mountains and dark mountains, so there are good horses and evil horses. We have spoken of the evil horses; let us also speak of the good horses.

At the time when they came to seize Elisha, the boy went out and saw an army surrounding the Assyrians, and Elisha said: “Do not be afraid, for there are more with us than with them” (4 Kings VI). It is also written there: “Lord, open the eyes of your servant, that he may see.” When his eyes had been opened, the boy saw chariots and horses. These were their helpers.

See, then, what he says: “chariots and horses.” No human being was upon them; there were only chariots and horses. This is what he means: they were a multitude of angels, themselves the chariots and themselves the horses; the rider, however, was the Lord. Therefore he says in the Song of Habakkuk: “Your riding is salvation” (Hab. III). This is said of God. If only we were God’s horses, and God would deem it worthy to mount us!

Those contrary horses, therefore, fell asleep, [Col. 1037C] along with their riders.

From that time your anger. From what time did God’s anger begin? When the people cried out to Aaron in the wilderness, saying: “Make gods for us to follow” (Exod. XXXII). “For this Moses, who brought us out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has happened to him.” You brought them out of the land of Egypt, and immediately they denied you.

You caused judgment to be heard from heaven. You spoke from heaven; the whole people heard and trembled, and yet they did not believe in you. The earth trembled and became still, but Israel neither feared nor became still.

For the thought of man will confess to you. This is what is said elsewhere: “Cleanse me from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those belonging to others” (Ps. XVIII)—those who are estranged from you, whom the devil brings under his power. And what follows? “If they do not dominate me, then I shall be blameless.” If evil thoughts do not overcome me, then I shall be clean in your sight.

And what follows immediately? “Then I shall be cleansed from the greatest sin.” See what he says. If a thought does not overcome me and bring me to action, I have been freed from a great sin. “For the thought of man will confess to you.” No one is clean in God’s sight—not even if his life were only one day long. “The stars are not clean in God’s sight, and he found perversity even among his angels” (Job XV, XXV). Why all this? Because if the stars are not clean, and perversity is found among angels, how much more is it found in the thought of human beings!

Where are those who say, “Depart from me, for I am clean”? Every day we suffer something; we know what is in our thoughts, and we are ashamed to say it. There are many who have not committed evil deeds; there are others who have not even spoken evil. But no human being is found who has not sinned in thought. Therefore he now says: “For the thought of man will confess to you.”

Terrible. To whom? To God. And to him who takes away the spirit of princes. When we see certain powerful people—for example, emperors, governors, and those who are exceedingly powerful in this world—let us also say to God: “You who take away the spirit of princes.”

We can understand “spirit” as referring to the soul; we can also understand it as referring to pride. Let us understand it in another way as well: “he who takes away the spirit of princes.” Here we understand “princes” to mean saints. It is as though he said: Solomon was a prince; the other saints were princes; the Apostle Judas was also a prince; and because they sinned, God took the Holy Spirit away from them.

Let no one therefore say, “I am a bishop,” or “a deacon,” or “a monk”; “I am a prince in this world.” God is powerful enough to take away the spirit of princes. To make you understand that God takes away the spirit, the good Spirit of God departed from Saul, and an evil spirit suffocated him. It follows: “And the evil spirit of God suffocated him” (1 Kings XVI). Does God, then, have an evil spirit? Certainly not. Rather, the Spirit of God had departed so that afterward the evil spirit might suffocate him; for this reason the Spirit of God is called evil.

Accordingly, holy David, knowing that the Spirit could be taken away from princes, begs God and says: “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Ps. L).

Terrible before the kings of the earth. This may be understood according to the letter. But may God grant that we be kings of the earth—kings so that we may rule our flesh. Hence the Apostle also says: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body” (Rom. VI). And elsewhere it is written: “The heart of the king is in the hand of God” (Prov. XXI).

The heart of the persecutor Julian was in God’s hand. Saul’s heart was in God’s hand. Manasseh’s heart was in God’s hand, and the hearts of all the impious kings of Judah were in the Lord’s hand. You see that this cannot stand according to the letter. The kings, therefore, are saints, and their hearts are in the Lord’s hand.

Let us, then, also ask God to make us kings, so that we may rule our flesh and make it subject to us. Hence the Apostle also says: “I chastise my body and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified” (1 Cor. IX).

Let our soul rule and the body serve, and Christ will immediately come and dwell in us. What, therefore, does he himself say in the Gospel? “I will come,” he says, “and stand at the door and knock; and if anyone opens to me, I will enter and dine with him” (Rev. III). Every day Christ stands at the door of our heart; he desires to enter. Let us open to him: he will enter into us and be our guest and our table-companion—that is, he will eat with us. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

PSALM LXXVI

For the end; for Jeduthun; a psalm of Asaph. In Hebrew, “through Jeduthun,” so that it signifies that the psalm was sung not “for” him but “through” him. The words that follow, “a psalm of Asaph,” are not found in the ancient copies.

With my voice I cried to the Lord; with my voice to God, and he attended to me. On the day of my tribulation I sought God. See how he is in tribulation: he entreats both the Lord and God, and yet there is one God.

With my voice I cried to the Lord. It is necessary to cry out at a time when the one who cries is far away. Therefore what this man says means: “Because of my sins I am far from you; therefore I cry out so that you may hear me.” “With my voice to the Lord, and he attended to me.” This is what he says elsewhere as well: “To the Lord I cried when I was in distress, and he heard me” (Ps. CXIX).

On the day of my tribulation I sought God. He speaks of a difficult matter. When we are afflicted, we are cast down to the earth; we think of nothing except our affliction. But this man, in the midst of affliction, is stirred up to entreat God. It is as though he were saying plainly: “I have lost my son; my house has been burned; I have been reduced to poverty. I do not seek what I have lost; I seek the Lord. For if I find him, I find everything in him. ‘Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you’” (Matt. VI).

With my hands by night toward him, and I was not deceived. In Hebrew it reads differently: “My hand is stretched out by night, and it does not rest.”

“With my hands by night toward him”—the omitted sense is, “I cried out.” See, therefore, that our works cry out to the Lord even when we are silent. Hence it is said: “The word of the Lord came to the hand of Haggai the prophet” (Haggai I). It did not come to his mouth—that is, in speech—but to his hand—that is, in deed.

“With my hands by night”—that is, “I cried out; I cried out with my hands.” For this reason it is also said to Moses: “Why do you cry out to me?” Yet it is not written there that Moses cried out to God, but that his heart cried: “Abba, Father” (Exod. XIV). Hence what is said in Jeremiah: “The pupil of my eye has not ceased” (Lam. II).

See, therefore, that even the pupil of our eye is not silent. Whenever we shed tears, we cry out to God. “With my hands by night toward God”—that is what is said: “By night lift up your hands toward the holy places and bless the Lord” (Ps. CXXXIII).

In the night of this age, and amid darkness, while others were hastening toward vices, I lifted my works to you alone. And I was not deceived, because I cried out in this way and cried out through my works.

“I was not deceived” can be understood in two ways: either I obtained what I wanted, or I was not deceived by the devil’s ambushes, by which he desired to entrap me. In Hebrew, however, it is written: “My hand is stretched out by night, and it does not rest.” The hand is always stretched out toward virtues; sometimes it is contracted by sins.

My soul refused consolation. As far as my sins were concerned, I could find no consolation in hope. I remembered God, and I rejoiced. As far as my sins were concerned, I could find no consolation. Then I thought again of God, and I rejoiced in his mercy.

In Hebrew it reads differently: “I remembered God, and I was troubled.” I considered his gentleness; I considered his compassion; I considered his purity; and, seeing myself to be impure, I was deeply troubled.

I was exercised, and my spirit failed. In Hebrew it reads better: “I spoke within myself, and my spirit failed”—whether through despair or through longing for God.

My eyes anticipated the watches. In Hebrew it reads differently: “I restrained the object of suspicion from my eyes; I was astonished and did not speak.” What he means is this: considering my sins, I did not dare lift my eyes toward heaven. For to the sinner God says: “Why do you recite my righteousness?” (Ps. XLIX). Therefore I was astonished, I was afraid, and I could not speak. This is according to the Hebrews.

“My eyes anticipated the watches”: before anyone else kept vigil, I was keeping vigil. We also read this in Daniel (chap. X): “And behold, a man”—that is, a watcher. “He neither slumbers nor sleeps who keeps Israel.” Therefore a monk who does not keep vigil cannot say this verse.

I was troubled, and I did not speak. This is what the Apostle says: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. IV). I was troubled as a human being; I did not speak as a Christian. Anger began in my heart, but I did not express my anger in words.

I considered the days of old, and I kept the eternal years in mind. As far as my sins were concerned, I despaired, and my soul had refused consolation. I began to think from the beginning of the world, when God made the human being, up to my own time—from Adam to my own age.

[Col. 1040C] I meditated by night with my heart, and I swept through my spirit. I was not thinking about anger; I was not thinking about my enemy. My entire thought was about God. The night, which is usually given either to rest or to lust, was for me a time of meditation on virtues.

“I meditated by night with my heart, and I swept through my spirit”: that is, I dug as though in a field, so that I might plant there the seed of the Lord’s teachings.

Will God cast off forever? This was my entire thought: God made the human being from the earth and promised him eternal life. How, then, was he cast out of paradise? Will he no longer continue to show favor?

Or will he cut off his mercy forever, from generation to generation? That is, will he cast off both generations—the former people and the later one? And if he cast off the people of the Jews, will he also cast off the Gentiles?

Or will he restrain his mercies in anger? He could not have expressed it more beautifully: even though he restrains himself so as not to show mercy, his mercy nevertheless conquers him.

And I said, “Now I have begun.” In Hebrew it reads differently: “And I said, ‘This is my weakness’”—that is, what I am suffering does not arise from God’s cruelty, but from my sins.

“This is the change of the right hand of the Most High”: so that the Lord may show mercy; so that he may grant his grace to the whole world; so that he may not restrain his mercies in anger.

“This is the change of the right hand of the Most High”: unless his right hand—that is, his Son—had been changed and taken on a human body, we could not receive mercy.

“And I said, ‘Now I have begun’: this is the change of the right hand of the Most High.” Though he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God to be robbery, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. II).

I remembered the works of the Lord—what he had done for Moses and what he had done for the saints. For I will remember your wonders from the beginning, and I will meditate on all your works, and so forth. My entire thought is of your virtues. I consider how you showed mercy to them, and I do not despair of myself.

God, your way is in holiness. Whoever, therefore, is not holy does not have God’s way within him. What is God’s way? “I am the way and the truth” (John XIV). The Savior says this. The Son, therefore, is God’s way, and God’s way exists only in the holy person. We want Christ to dwell in us; let us be holy. For God’s way is in the holy.

Who is a great God like our God? For just as there are many gods, so there are many lords. The Apostle says this: “God stood in the assembly of gods” (1 Cor. VIII). “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High’” (Ps. LXXXI). And to Moses: “I have appointed you as God to Pharaoh” (Exod. VII).

The saints are called gods. They are gods by grace; you, however, are God by nature. You are the God who works wonders. He did not say, “who worked wonders,” but “who works wonders.” Every day God works wonders, and the Son and the Holy Spirit work them as well.

You are the God who works wonders. Yesterday a thief, today a Christian. Yesterday a fornicator, today continent. Yesterday you were stealing what belonged to others; now you extend what belongs to you.

You have made your power known among the peoples. Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God, the mystery that had been hidden from the ages and has now been made known among the peoples.

You redeemed your people by your arm. “Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” You redeemed your people by your arm—that is, in Christ.

The sons of Jacob and Joseph. Both peoples: Jews and Christians. Jacob represents the Jewish people, and Joseph the people of the Gentiles. Joseph, moreover, is interpreted in Hebrew as “increase.” They went before us, and we were joined to them; therefore he says, “the sons of Jacob and Joseph.”

The waters saw you, O God; the waters saw you, and they were afraid. For the present, let us speak according to the letter; let us remain on the ground for the sake of the simpler hearers. When the people passed through the Red Sea and the Jordan, the waters recognized their Creator, but the people did not understand. And the abysses were troubled. “The sea saw and fled; the Jordan turned back” (Ps. XIII).

The multitude of the sound of the waters scattered the clouds. In place of “clouds,” the Hebrew has “waters.” When he says, “The clouds gave forth a voice,” they interpret this as referring to the time when God appeared on Mount Sinai.

For your arrows were passing through; the sound of your thunder was in the wheel. They also interpret this as referring to flashes of lightning, and they say that when God thunders, he produces a sound like that of a wheel. You see how I am still clinging to the earth and speaking according to the letter, which kills.

[Col. 1042A] Your flashes illumined the world. What will you do here, Jew? “Your way is in the sea, and your paths are in many waters.” This too may be understood either of the sea or of the Jordan. “And your footprints will not be known.” How do you understand this according to the letter?

For the sake of the simpler hearers, we have spoken according to the letter. Let us therefore return to the spiritual understanding.

The waters saw you, O God. Let us speak of the revelation of John. “The many waters,” he says, “are many peoples” (Rev. XVII). The waters saw you, O God. Which waters? “And the waters that are above the heavens, let them praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXLVIII). The waters saw you, O God: pure minds and souls. The waters saw you, and they were afraid. Their fear did not arise from hatred but from faith.

And the abysses were troubled. Let us say something according to the spiritual understanding. At the beginning of Genesis it is written: “And the Spirit,” he says, “was carried over the waters.” Then it is written: “Darkness,” he says, “was carried over the abysses.”

See, therefore, what is said at the beginning of Genesis—that is, according to the spiritual understanding: “The Spirit was carried over the waters.” Even then baptism was being signified. For baptism could not exist without the Spirit.

But over the abysses there was darkness. This is the abyss into which the demons begged not to be sent by Jesus. Over the abysses, therefore, there was darkness. In the waters there was purity; in the abysses, darkness. You understand what the abysses are without my saying it, since the demons are afraid to go into the abyss.

The clouds gave forth a voice. The clouds are the prophets. What they kept silent from the Jews, they spoke to us. The clouds gave forth a voice, for your arrows passed through. The preaching of Christ’s word ran throughout the whole world.

The sound of your thunder was in the wheel. Thunder is, properly speaking, a great voice. Accordingly, when God said, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased,” a sound like the thunder of a wheel was produced (Matt. III).

For this reason it is written: “Abyss calls to abyss in the voice of your cataracts” (Ps. XLI)—that is, the two Testaments, the New and the Old. “The sound of your thunder was in the wheel”: the sound of your preaching was in the wheel.

It is called a great voice because the preaching is great. “The sound of your thunder was in the wheel”: throughout the whole world, in its circuit. What you say is heard not only in Judea, but throughout the world.

This is what we have said in general. Let us speak specifically about the inner person.

A wheel rests upon the earth by a small part of itself. It not only stands there but seems to run: it does not stand still, but touches and passes on. When it turns, it rises to higher places.

So also the holy man, because he is in the body, must think about certain earthly things. When it comes to food, clothing, and matters of this kind, having food and clothing, he is content with them; touching the earth, he hastens toward higher things (1 Tim. VI).

The one who runs and hastens toward higher things possesses your word. We also read in the prophet that the holy stones roll upon the earth (Ezek. I). See what he said: “The holy stones roll upon the earth.” Because they are wheels, they roll upon the earth and hasten toward higher things.

Do you wish to know about several wheels? We read also of “a wheel within a wheel.” We read in Ezekiel as well: “The wheels cling to one another.” The two wheels are the New and the Old Testament. This wheel clings to that one, and that one to this one.

Yet see what is also said in Ezekiel: “Wherever the spirit led them,” he says, “the wheels followed.” This is also said in Ecclesiastes: “At the consummation of the world the wheel will roll upon the cistern” (Ecclus. XII).

There is much that could be said about the wheels, but our discourse hastens toward what remains.

Your flashes illumined the world: the apostolic preaching. The earth was shaken and trembled. Unless our earth had been shaken and troubled, we would not be Christians. The earth was shaken and trembled. For the Spirit of the Lord rests upon no one except the humble, the peaceful, and the one who trembles at his words (Isa. LXVI).

[Col. 1043B] Your way is in the sea. Where there are waves, where the water is bitter, where the dragon dwells, where tiny fish cling. Your way is in the sea. You who were in heaven descended to earth.

According to the letter, we may say: at the time when Moses led Israel out, it was you who led them out (Exod. XIV). Your way is in the sea. We may then also speak according to the historical sense in another way: the seas became a road for you.

But he did this only once. Every day, however, he says to the sea: “Be silent; be still.” The Lord calms you so that we may pass through this age by means of it.

Your way is in the sea. He came as the fountain of life to sweeten the sea—the bitter sea, the dead sea. Therefore, according to Ezekiel, a fountain of living water goes out from the temple of the Lord and flows toward the Dead Sea, which had nothing living in it (Ezek. XLVII). No little fish could exist in the Dead Sea; nothing lived in the Dead Sea.

From the temple of the Lord—that is, from his bosom—the Savior went forth, sweetened the Dead Sea, and sweetened the bitter waters.

Your way is in the sea, and your paths are in many waters. Therefore your way is in the sea, so that you might make a road and your apostles might follow you.

And your paths are in many waters, and your footprints will not be known. You led your people like sheep. The good shepherd led his people like sheep, by the hand of Moses and Aaron.

This he did according to the letter. But every day he does it in us: “by the hand of Moses,” that is, by the Law. We know, however, that the Law is spiritual. By your spiritual Law and Aaron—that is, by your priesthood—you led your people (Rom. VII).

[Col. 1043D] Let us understand this according to the letter of Moses and Aaron. Moses and Aaron were indeed brought out, but they were not brought into the land of promise. Jesus succeeded them.

See what is written: Moses died in the wilderness; Aaron died; Miriam died. This is what is written in the prophet: “I will strike the three shepherds in one month.” They died, for they could not enter the land of promise (Zech. I). They saw the land of promise only from opposite it, but they could not enter.

The Jews saw the land of promise, but they could not enter it. For they died in the wilderness, and their corpses are in the desert—the corpses of those who died in the wilderness.

We, the sons, came under Jesus our leader to the Jordan and entered the land of promise. We came to Gilgal and were circumcised a second time with spiritual circumcision, and the reproach of Egypt was removed from us.

Now Jesus himself, our leader, holds the sword; he always goes before us, fights for us, and conquers our adversaries. For seven days we circle Jericho—that is, this world. We sing with priestly trumpets and circle Jericho—that is, this world. Its walls fall, and we enter and emerge victorious.

Then we conquer the city of Ai; afterward we come to Jebus; we come to Hazor; we come to the other cities. We conquer the adversaries whom we could not conquer under Moses.

Let us therefore give thanks to our leader Jesus. With him as leader and combatant, we conquer. He commanded the sun to stand still, and it stood still. In this figure he was great: he commanded, but the Lord brought it about.

He emerged victorious; he—the one whom I have often mentioned—killed five kings in the cave; he brought us into the land of promise. Let us give thanks to him.

He is the son of Nun, whom we read as Nave; he is the one who was called Hosea, whom we read as Ause.

[Note: Rather, the true Jerome strongly criticized this reading. See *Against Jovinian*, book I, chapter 12, and the beginning of the *Commentary on Hosea*.]

For according to the Hebrew truth he is not called Ause, but Hosea, that is, “savior.” Truly he is the Savior: for he saves us, brings us out of the wilderness, and leads us into the land of promise. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

PSALM LXXVII

[Col. 1044C] Divine Scripture instructs us that, when we have been invited to a rich person’s dinner, we should approach the dishes with understanding. Accordingly, a rich banquet of the Scriptures has also been set before us.

We have come into a meadow where the grasses are flowering: here a rose glows red, there lilies gleam white, and there are flowers of many kinds. Our soul is drawn here and there, seeking to gather the more beautiful flowers.

If we gather the rose, we leave the lily; if we take the lily, violets remain for us. So also in the seventy-seventh psalm, which is mystical and wrapped in many mysteries: whatever letter you look upon, there are flowers. The flowers are various, and we cannot gather them all. Let us choose whatever we can; from a few, one can also contemplate the beauty of the remaining flowers.

“An understanding of Asaph.” This is announced in the title. The title itself urges us toward understanding. Asaph was one of the directors of the chorus, as were the sons of Korah, Jeduthun, and the others. Thus, among the other directors of the chorus, this man too is a prophet.

Because, then, the understanding is simple and a history is narrated in the psalm, we are compelled by necessity to understand everything that is written according to its meaning. It is written: “In the land of Egypt, in the field of Tanis; he divided the sea and led them out in the cloud by day and throughout the night in the illumination of fire,” and so forth.

We see that a simple history is being narrated. If, therefore, we understand it exactly as it is written, the title “An understanding of Asaph” has been prefixed without reason. But if we understand it as the title indicates, we are necessarily compelled to have one thing in the letter and to discover another in the spirit.

Attend, my people, to my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth. I will open my mouth in parables [Col. 1045A], and I will speak propositions from the beginning.

You see that what was written above was written well: “The understanding of Asaph.” Indeed, the prophecy itself begins in this way: “Attend, my people, to my law”—not the law of Moses, but my law. “Incline your ear to the words of my mouth.” This is what he says in the Gospel: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke VIII).

“I will open my mouth in parables.” I will open to you what has been closed to the Jews. “I will open my mouth in parables.” And, he says, “he did not speak to them without parables; but to his disciples he explained the parables privately” (Mark IV). “I will open my mouth in parables.” What I speak to them outwardly in parables, I will open to you inwardly.

“And I will speak propositions from the beginning.” In place of “propositions,” the Hebrew has “in an enigma.” Therefore everything that is said is an enigma [Col. 1045B]. An enigma is not what is said, but something else is signified.

Let someone say to me: “You are doing violence to Scripture. Since the title reads, ‘The understanding of Asaph,’ you interpret this saying for me as spoken in the person of Christ.”

Let us interpret this saying as spoken in the person of Christ, if we are Christians. We are Christians, having received Christ’s baptism, and we not only confess but also profess that we are Christians. Therefore we must believe the Evangelists.

It is written in the Gospel according to Matthew: “When,” he says, “our Lord and Savior had spoken in parables, and they did not understand” (Matt. III), and the rest that is written in the Gospel. And afterward what did the Evangelist add? “All these things,” he says, “took place so that what was written might be fulfilled: ‘I will open my mouth in parables [Col. 1045C], and I will speak propositions from the beginning.’”

You see, therefore, that the Evangelist Matthew understood this as spoken in the person of Christ. For when he had introduced the Lord speaking in parables, and they did not understand, he said: “This took place so that what was written might be fulfilled: ‘I will open my mouth in parables, and I will speak propositions from the beginning.’”

It seems to us that no question remains, but listen carefully (John V). My concern is not to declaim in the rhetorical manner, but to open up the meanings of the Scriptures.

Indeed, what did our Lord and Savior say? “Search the Scriptures, and there you will find how it is written about me.” And elsewhere he said to the Jews: “You are mistaken, because you do not know the Scriptures or the power of God.” See what he says: “You are mistaken.” Why? “Because you do not know the Scriptures” (Mark XII) [Col. 1045D]. Since you do not know the Scriptures, therefore you do not know Christ, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God.

Thus it is said in Matthew: “These things,” he says, “took place so that what was written in the prophet Asaph might be fulfilled.” This is how it is found in all the ancient manuscripts, but ignorant people removed it. Indeed, many Gospels still have the following wording: “So that what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: ‘I will open my mouth in parables, and I will speak propositions from the beginning.’” Isaiah did not say this, but Asaph.

That impious man Porphyry, moreover, brings this very charge against us [Col. 1046A], saying: “Your Evangelist Matthew was so unlearned that he said, ‘What was spoken through the prophet Isaiah: “I will open my mouth in parables, and I will speak propositions from the beginning.”’”

Let us therefore speak simply: just as that is written in the Gospel, so it is written in Matthew and John that our Lord was crucified at the sixth hour. Again, it is written in Mark that he was crucified at the third hour. This appears to be different, but it is not different. It was a scribal error: in Mark “the sixth hour” was written; but many mistook the Greek episēmon ϛ for γ, just as there was a scribal error there when they wrote Isaiah instead of Asaph.

For we know that the first Church was gathered from unlearned Gentiles. Therefore, when they read in the Gospel, “So that what was written in the prophet Asaph might be fulfilled” [Col. 1046B], the one who first wrote the Gospel began to say: “Who is this prophet Asaph? He was not known among the people.” In trying to correct the error, he created an error.

Let us give a similar example from another passage in the Gospel according to Matthew: when Judas returned the thirty pieces of silver, and the priests would not accept them or put them into the treasury, since it was the price of blood, they bought with them the potter’s field as a burial place for foreigners (Matt. XXVII). The price of Christ is our burial, and that field is called Acheldemach, which means “field of blood.” The field of blood is not the field of the Jews, but our burial place. For we were foreigners and sojourners, and had nowhere to rest. He was crucified and died, and we were buried with him.

“So that what was written in the prophet Jeremiah might be fulfilled,” he says: “He returned the thirty pieces of silver, the price at which he was valued,” and so forth. “As it is written,” he says, “in the prophet Jeremiah”—this is what is written in Matthew. We searched for it in the prophet Jeremiah and could not find it anywhere, but we found it in Zechariah. You see, therefore, that here too there was an error, as there was there (Zech. XI).

“How many things we have heard and known.” These verses, from “Attend, my people, to my law” up to this verse, “I will speak propositions from the beginning,” are spoken in the person of Christ, and the Savior himself is speaking.

From this point onward, however, we must understand the remaining verses, to the end of the psalm, as spoken in the person of the apostles. When the Lord says, “Incline your ear to the words of my mouth,” he means: “O apostles, what you have heard in secret, proclaim upon the housetops” (Matt. X) [Col. 1046D].

What do the apostles say? “How many things we have heard and known”; the patriarchs and prophets spoke to us. “And our fathers told us.” These things were not hidden from their children, and so forth. They spoke for this reason, so that we, their children, might know.

“And he established a law in Jacob, and appointed a law in Israel”—all that he commanded our fathers. They spoke to them carnally, but we understand these things spiritually, “so that they might make them known to their children” [Col. 1047A]—that is, to us. He spoke to them for this reason, so that they might benefit us.

“To the children who will be born and rise up, and tell them to their children.” “In place of your fathers,” he says, “sons have been born to you” (Ps. XLIV). We are their children. They told us, and we have told our children; we are their children.

“So that they might place their hope in God.” So that they might no longer believe in idols, but believe in God. “So that they might not forget the works of God.” So that they might observe the order of creation and understand the Creator from creation. “And seek his commandments.” Let them not despise them like the Jews, but seek them like Christians (1 Cor. X).

“And not become like their fathers.” Let them not murmur as certain people murmured in the desert and perished [Col. 1047B]. “A crooked and provoking generation.” I am not saying this: your prophet is saying this about you. “A crooked and provoking generation.” An adulterous and wicked generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given it except the sign of Jonah (Matt. XVI).

Why did he say “crooked”? Because they became like a twisted bow. A bow is never stretched toward the person who shoots it, but against adversaries. This generation, however, although created upright by God and held in God’s hand like a bow so that he might shoot arrows through it, was turned into a twisted bow, blaspheming its Creator.

“A generation that did not direct its heart.” To this day Israel is crooked. “And its spirit was not faithful to God.” Because it did not receive the Son, it did not receive the Holy Spirit. Indeed, when the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove, he did not descend upon the crowds of Jews, but upon the one Jesus. Therefore, if you wish, Jew, to receive the Spirit, believe in Jesus, because the Holy Spirit rests in Jesus.

“The sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow.” O how many mysteries! O how many flowers! Not merely one day, but even a whole month would not suffice for understanding this psalm. There are meanings in each individual word. We also have a treasure in these earthen vessels.

Many interpret this of the body and the Holy Spirit: “We have a treasure in earthen vessels.” That interpretation too is valid, but this one is much better, because we have a most precious treasure in earthen vessels—that is, in the rustic words [Col. 1047D] of the Scriptures.

“The sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow, turned back on the day of battle,” and so forth. We read in the Books of Kings that under Rehoboam, son of Solomon, Jeroboam son of Nebat separated the people from the rest of the people and led ten tribes to Samaria (1 Kings XII). The tribes of Judah and Benjamin remained under Rehoboam’s rule, and many from the tribe of Levi—priests and Levites who lived in Jerusalem—as it is written in Chronicles, returned to the temple of God, that is, to Jerusalem (2 Chron. XI).

Thus there were three tribes: Judah—that is, Judah itself, the royal tribe—Benjamin, and the Levites, who afterward came there from various tribes to the temple. Those who were in Samaria had a king from the tribe of Ephraim [Col. 1048A]. For just as those who ruled in Judea had a king from the tribe of Judah and the family of David, so those who ruled in Samaria had a king from the tribe of Ephraim, and their kings were called Ephraim.

Let us read the prophet Hosea, and we will find his entire prophecy directed against Ephraim (Hos. VII). It says there: “Ephraim,” he says, “has become like a senseless dove.” See what he says. A senseless dove leaves the temple and lives in the woods. A dove always lives in houses. But Ephraim, my dove, left the temple, left the house, and lives in the woods and in the deserts.

For the present, this is according to the literal sense, since we must also set forth the history. Now, however, after the literal sense, we must ascend, as though by certain steps, to greater things.

Let us say, then, that all heretics are the sons of Ephraim. They too departed from the house of God; they too abandoned David and lived in the deserts. They are called doves because they read the Scriptures, but they understand them foolishly.

There are many who are called “the sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow.” Look at all the heretics who abandoned Jerusalem, who abandoned the temple of God, who live in Samaria. Where did they make golden calves? In Bethel and in Dan.

And see what he says: They made golden calves in Bethel, in the house of God; they became idolaters. And they made one in Dan—that is, for their own judgment and condemnation. They abandoned the house of the Lord and think of nothing except gold.

Someone may say: “Why did they make golden calves?” Our treasure is stored in earthen vessels [Col. 1048C]. Ecclesiastical people are rustic and simple, whereas all heretics are Aristotelians and Platonists.

Finally, so that you may know that all secular eloquence is called gold—that is, because their speech is said to be like gold on account of its brilliance—“Babylon is a golden cup in the hand of the Lord.” See what he says: “Babylon of confusion.” Therefore this world is a golden cup. From this golden cup all the nations are given to drink (Jer. LI).

“The sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow.” Whatever writing of the heretics you look at, they all contain superstitions. “They turned back on the day of battle.” They do not know the one who said: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (John XIV), but they are prepared for words. They have words, but they will hear what is written: “Scatter the nations that desire wars” (Ps. LXVII).

Someone may say that this is our interpretation. Let us examine what follows:

“They did not keep the covenant of God, and they refused to walk in his law, and they forgot his benefits.” They rose up against the one who regenerated them in baptism. “And his wonders that he showed them.” Observe the meaning of the Scriptures: how, from the sons of Ephraim, he moves to past histories, so that what is written—“I will open my mouth in parables; I will speak propositions from the beginning”—may be shown to have been spoken parabolically.

“In the presence of their fathers he performed wonders in the land of Egypt, in the field of Tanis: he divided the sea and led them through; he set the waters as though in a wineskin, and led them by a cloud during the day.”

Someone may say: “You are doing violence to Scripture. It is simply speaking about the people of Israel when they were led out of the land of Egypt, and therefore it is spoken according to the historical sense” [Col. 1049A]. We read that the ten tribes abandoned God, became idolaters, and followed, as it were, golden calves.

Let us see at what time the prophet Asaph lived. Clearly, he lived at the time when David reigned for forty years. Solomon then reigned for another forty years. After eighty years, under Rehoboam, the ten tribes were divided. You see, therefore, that what is said is not said about the ten tribes, but is a prophecy about heretics.

“In the presence of their fathers he performed wonders.” Heretics, therefore, have forgotten their father, who performed wonders in the land of Egypt, in the darkness of this age, and liberated them. They were reborn in the Church, and afterward, once born there, they became displeased with the Church [Col. 1049B].

“In the land of Egypt, in the field of Tanis”: where there was idolatry, where there was the king of Egypt, where there was the cavalry of Egypt, where Jannes and Jambres, the adversaries of Moses, were, where there was idolatry. We were all in Egypt, and we were liberated by the Lord.

“He divided the sea and led them out.” The Lord walked upon the sea, calmed the waves of the sea, and led us through. “He divided the sea and led them out.” To this day, faithful monk, whenever you are led out of Egypt, the sea is divided, and thus you are led out.

“He set the waters as though in a wineskin.” In Hebrew it does not have “wineskin,” but “like a heap.” “And he led them by a cloud during the day.” Behold, the Lord comes into Egypt in a light cloud. We must understand the light cloud either properly as the Savior’s body, which was light and was not weighed down by any sin; or certainly as holy Mary, the light cloud, not weighed down by any human seed [Col. 1049C].

Behold, the Lord comes into Egypt, this world, upon a light cloud, the Virgin. “And he led them by a cloud during the day.” Beautifully he said “during the day”: that cloud was not in darkness, but always in light. “And throughout the night by the illumination of fire.” “Darknesses are not hidden from you. As is the light to you, so is the night to you” (Deut. IV).

“And throughout the night by the illumination of fire.” Our Lord is a consuming fire. “A consuming fire”—he did not say what it consumes, leaving the meaning to us. To those who built upon the foundation of Christ with wood, hay, and straw (1 Cor. III), the Lord is a consuming fire. Fire has a twofold nature: it gives light and it burns. If we are sinners, it sets us ablaze; if we are righteous, it gives us light.

“He divided the rock in the desert.” The rock was divided for us in the wilderness [Col. 1049D]. The rock was struck, and waters flowed—the rock that says, “Let the one who thirsts come and drink,” from whose belly rivers flowed (John VII). “And he watered them as though from a great abyss …” In the desert, where there was no water, an abundance of waters was made available to us.

“And he brought water from the rock, and brought forth waters like rivers, and they continued still to sin against him,” and so forth. O perversity of a crooked heart! It speaks wickedly against God, and the one who ought to have hungered for righteousness demands meat and vegetables.

For just as Moses struck the rock in the wilderness and brought forth waters for the people (Num. XX), so the Lord, whom Paul says was struck because of our sins, brought forth for us immeasurable springs (Rom. IV): namely, the apostles, whom the rock revealed and through whom torrents flowed [Col. 1050A].

We understand the torrents as teachers, through whom the subsequent teachers of the churches were filled. From their preaching we quench our thirst for the word of God. The same rock also showed us the fountain of baptism and martyrdom. For when he was struck, blood and water came forth from his side, signifying baptism and martyrdom (John XIX).

They are called torrents because, before they believed, they had been filled by the rains and whirlpools of this age. Now, washed by baptism, they have overflowed from the fountain of eternal life.

Then Jewish murmuring adds:

“Can he also give bread, or prepare a table for his people?” They consider the power of God difficult, as though the one who brought water from the rock could not give manna from heaven.

[Col. 1050B] Therefore the Lord heard and delayed. Certainly he held himself back from them so that they would not enter the promised land. “And fire was kindled in Jacob, and anger rose against Israel.”

Jacob is not always understood as “one who supplants vices,” nor is Israel in every instance taken as “one who sees God.” The Apostle, however, teaches that there is an Israel according to the flesh (1 Cor. X), of whom it is said: “And Israel committed fornication” (Judg. VIII). For if he had seen God with his mind, he would certainly not have committed fornication.

Likewise, in the case of Jacob, when Esau, polluted by idols, worshiped him and said, “I see your face as the face of an angel of God” (Gen. XXIII), or when, having grown fat, he kicked, he was not one who supplanted vices. Therefore this passage too must be understood in this way: an earthly fire of desire was kindled in Jacob, and thus, in divine vengeance, it rose against carnal Israel.

[Col. 1050C] “Because they did not believe in God, nor hope in his salvation.” They did not believe either in the Father or in the Son, who is the salvation of the world.

“And he commanded the clouds from above, and opened the doors of heaven. And he rained manna upon them to eat.” These things were provided to the Hebrews; but even now, in the Church, the prophets and apostles are commanded to announce to us the word of preaching by which the soul is spiritually nourished.

“He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels.” He himself provided food for humanity, who said: “I am the bread of life, who came down from heaven; whoever eats of it will live forever” (John VI). From this bread of heaven the saints and angels are refreshed. “He sent them food in abundance,” so that they might no longer be satisfied with the barley of the letter, but with the spiritual teaching of wheat.
