[Col. 1050D] “And he transferred the South wind from heaven, and brought in the Southwest wind by his power, and rained flesh upon them like dust,” and so forth. In the winds he indicates the breath of the Holy Spirit. The comparison with a multitude like dust or the sand of the sea, however, reveals that their understanding was earthly and hard.

“And they fell in the midst of their camp, around their tents, and they ate and were filled exceedingly.” By “camp” he means synagogues. By “tents,” their hearts, into which these things flowed. That he indicates that they were filled exceedingly rebukes their carnal gluttony: those who ought to have been refreshed by God’s commandments consider themselves satisfied with dusty flesh.

“And he brought their desire upon them; they were not deprived of their desire.” Immense is the Lord’s compassion: while he feeds those who hunger for earthly food, so also he fills with the heavenly bread mentioned above whoever desires him. Let us see, then, what those who desired only flesh and not God brought upon themselves afterward.

“While the food was still in their mouths, the anger of God rose against them, and he killed their stout ones.” This concerns those who abandoned God after receiving manna. Even now in the Church, if someone is nourished by the flesh and blood of Christ and turns toward vices, let him know that God’s judgment threatens him, as the Apostle Paul says: “Whoever receives the body and blood of Christ unworthily receives and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. XI).

“And he impeded the chosen of Israel.” Even now the chosen of the Church are impeded, lest even the priests themselves receive these sacraments innocently.

[Col. 1051B] “In all these things they still sinned, and they did not believe in his wonders. And they failed,” and so forth. The wicked sin daily until they fail, and they fail in haste—those who disdain to obey God’s priests, just as that people murmured against God’s servant Moses.

“When he killed them, they sought him, and returned, and came to him at dawn.” Beaten because of their sins, they returned; and, having shaken off the sleep of unbelief, they hastened to hear the word of God.

“And they remembered that God was their helper, and that God Most High was their redeemer.” They understood that no one could provide help except the one who had liberated them from the slavery of Egypt.

“And they loved him with their mouth.” When they said: “Whatever Moses commands, we will do” (Exod. II) [Col. 1051C]. “And they lied to him with their tongue,” saying to Moses: “Whatever the Lord has said, we will do.”

“But their heart was not right with him, nor were they regarded as faithful in his covenant.” For the Lord too, using the testimony of the prophet Isaiah, said: “This people honors me with its lips, but its heart is far from me” (Isa. XXIX).

“But he is merciful, and he will be propitiated for their sins,” and so forth. The abundance of his mercies restrains him, so that while he awaits repentance, he does not punish the offender, because he does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live (Ezek. XVIII).

“And he remembered that they were flesh.” For he knows that flesh always resists the law of God. “A spirit that goes and does not return.” For he knows that when a human being loses the spirit, he returns to dust. The Holy Spirit also, when he departs from sinners, does not return to them as long as they remain in the whirlpools of sin.

“How often they provoked him in the desert; they angered him in the waterless place.” Certainly, in the unbelief and dryness of their hearts.

“And they turned back and tested God, and provoked the Holy One of Israel.” At that time Moses was the Holy One of Israel, who saw God both with his mind and with his eyes; they often provoked him [Col. 1052A]. Even now they provoke him when they hear that Christ the Lord is announced as destined to be born in the flesh.

“They did not remember his hand, the day when he redeemed them from the hand of the oppressor.” That is, from Pharaoh, who is figuratively called the devil.

“As he placed his signs in Egypt and his wonders in the field of Tanis.” Just as Moses then liberated the people from Egypt through ten signs, that is, plagues, so the Apostle Paul suppressed the darkness of the present world through ten Epistles.

“He turned their rivers into blood, and their rains, so that they might not drink.” The empty words of the philosophers, which in Platonic doctrines were killing the little ones of the Church, were turned against them by divine vengeance and into gore, so that those who shed blood—that is, who slaughtered souls by leading them astray—might thereafter drink blood [Col. 1052B].

“He sent among them the dog-fly, and it devoured them.” By the dog-fly he indicated the sect of the Cynics, which proclaims lust and luxury to be the highest good. “And the frog, and it destroyed them.” In the voices of frogs, and [Note: [Col. 1051D] Origen, Homily 4 on Exodus: “I think that the songs of poets are indicated individually by frogs, who in a certain empty and inflated melody, like the sounds and songs of frogs, have introduced fables into this world,” and so forth. The commentator transferred this into his own work.] in the songs of poets, he designates those who, through inflated verbosity, introduced destructive fables.

“And he gave their fruits to the rust.” In rust, or mildew, a figure of fornication is displayed. For just as this creeps along with slow and stealthy effort and most cruelly attacks the fruits of trees, so this, enticing human beings gently, devours them most savagely with wicked and hidden bites. “And their labors to the locust.” In the locust, the discord of the human race is rebuked. Although it leads an organized army without a king, the human race nevertheless is always divided and discordant.

“He killed their vines with hail, and their mulberry trees with frost. And he gave their beasts to hail, and their possessions to fire.” In hail divine chastisement is shown, by which vines and trees are scourged—those, namely, that instead of good fruits produced thorns. By this hail even the beasts are killed, so that the folly of those who gave the divine name to beasts may be exposed.

Fire too is sent to consume vices and illuminate the hearts of believers, as the Lord says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” (Luke XII).

“He sent against them the anger of his indignation: indignation, anger, and tribulation; a sending through evil angels” [Col. 1052D]. Thus those who were not corrected by divine plagues might be battered by diabolical snares. The Lord himself explained in the Gospel who these angels are: “Go,” he says, “into the fire that my Father prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV).

“He made a path for the way of his anger, and did not spare their souls from death, and enclosed their beasts in death.” Divine anger has a path when someone, handed over in punishment for sin, does not free his soul from the torment of Gehenna. Or when folly, which is like that of beasts, is enclosed in eternal death.

[Col. 1053A] “And he struck every firstborn in their land, the first fruits of all their labor in the tents of Ham.” Just as these events are reported as having taken place in Egypt, so the Lord, at his holy and sacred coming, destroyed and triumphed over the rulers and powers—whether of demons or of vices—in this world, on the wood of his cross. He drove them from the hearts of those who had been devoted to diabolical cunning, because “Ham” is interpreted as “cunning.”

[Note: [Col. 1053D] “Cunning,” with a double *l*, is quite unsuitable here and has an entirely different meaning. The commentator explains the name Ham as “hot” or “heat,” which the true Jerome interprets in that way. The Origenian Lexicon likewise has Χᾶμ, θέρμη—“Ham, heat.” [Col. 1054D]]

“And he took away his people like sheep, and led them like a flock in the desert.” Having scourged Egypt with these plagues, the Lord led his people out of the slavery described above—the people whom he had redeemed with his blood—and placed them in the Church, which had previously been barren and deserted. Of it he said: “The children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of the woman who has a husband” (Isa. LIV).

[Col. 1053B] “And he led them in hope, and they did not fear, and the sea covered their enemies.” Having established them in the hope of eternity, he covered their enemies with the sea: namely, so that while they were washed in baptism, the devil with his armies might be drowned.

“And he brought them to the mountain of his sanctification, to the mountain that his right hand acquired.” That is, to the very Church which he acquired by the power of his glorious resurrection.

“And he cast out the nations from before them, and divided the land among them by lot, by the measuring-cord of distribution, and made the tribes of Israel dwell in their tents.” When the nations of sins had been cast out from human hearts, they were given possession of the land of the living. It came about that where once a fortune-teller and diviner had lived, one who sees God with the mind now dwells [Col. 1053C].

“And they tested and provoked God Most High, and did not keep his testimonies. And they turned away and did not keep the covenant, like their fathers.” The discourse now turns to the Jews, whom neither divine power nor benefits softened. Just as their fathers killed the prophets, so they too persecute the Lord himself.

“They turned into a crooked bow.” A crooked bow is one that, while it is thought to shoot an arrow against enemies, wounds the person holding it. So too the Jews, who shoot wicked arrows of words against God their liberator.

“They provoked him to anger on their hills, and with their carved images they aroused him to jealousy.” For, abandoning him, they served idols and images, worshiping them even on the mountains [Col. 1053D].

“The Lord heard and rejected them, and utterly reduced Israel to nothing”—the one who was Israel in name only, and not in vision.

“And he rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh, his tabernacle, in which he dwelt among human beings.” Either the tabernacles of Shiloh under Eli, or Jerusalem under Solomon. But after rejecting these, he chose instead the temple of the king born of the incorrupt Virgin, or the holy Church called forth from the Gentiles.

“He handed their strength into captivity, and their beauty into the hand of the enemy; and he enclosed his people in the sword, and rejected his inheritance. Their young men,” and so forth.

Here he plainly foretold that destruction which took place in Jerusalem under Titus and Vespasian. Since he foretold future events as though they had already occurred, let the reader know that with God future things are already accomplished.

But would that the same might take place in us also, with the Lord cooperating: that desire might fall, while the power of virtues is raised up; that the form of wicked love might collapse, while the beauty of the Church is raised up; that the people of vices might be destroyed, while the multitude of virtues is brought to life; that earthly inheritance might be rejected, while the kingdom of God is acquired.

Let the young man—that is, sin in its beginning—be burned up by the power of the Holy Spirit, and let the virgin soul rejoice. Let the instigators of vices be slaughtered by the sword, that is, by the word of God [Col. 1054B], so that minds, widowed from them, may rejoice with Christ.

“And the Lord awoke as one sleeping, like a powerful man overcome by wine, and he struck his enemies from behind; he gave them everlasting disgrace.” The Lord is regarded as sleeping and, as it were, drunk in the hearts of the wicked. But when they begin to repent, he is awakened. After vices have been struck down to the end of time and handed over to everlasting disgrace, he keeps watch within them.

“And he rejected the tabernacle of Joseph, and did not choose the tribe of Ephraim; but he chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion, which he loved.” He did not reject the tribe of Joseph or Ephraim in order to despise it forever. But he did not wish to receive flesh from it, choosing the tribe of Judah, from which blessed [Col. 1054C] Mary would proceed and from which he himself would be born, so that he might raise up the mountain of his love—that is, the Church.

“And he built his sanctuary like a unicorn on the earth, which he established forever.” He firmly established his Church with singular power, so that it might remain immovable throughout the everlasting ages.

“He chose David, his servant, and took him from the sheepfolds, and from following the nursing ewes he took him. To shepherd,” and so forth. All these things must be referred to Christ the Lord, who was chosen from the flock of mortals, from the Father’s counsel, for our redemption. Taking on flesh, he feeds the Christian people—whether the people who supplant vices or those who see God with the mind.

May he now deign to feed his Church, which clings to his desires, in the goodness of his heart, and place it in the heavenly Jerusalem. To him be glory with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM LXXVIII

### A Psalm of Asaph

This psalm contains the voice of the prophet lamenting the captivity of earthly Jerusalem. That captivity must be referred not so much to that city as to the soul, which is often called a city in Scripture.

“God, the nations have entered into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple.” The Apostle says: “You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you” [Col. 1055A] (1 Cor. III). “If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him.”

Therefore, if the Christian soul succumbs as vices increase, then the inheritance that ought to belong to God is subjected to the adversary; and then the temple dedicated to the Holy Spirit, defiled by the crimes of the nations, is destroyed.

“They have made Jerusalem a place for guarding apples.” For just as apples, when they begin to ripen, are guarded by their owners, and when ripe are more easily devoured, so our adversary, when vices break in, guards the soul that consents to him until, bringing it to complete agreement with his will, he is able to devour it. For as long as a spark of faith shines in it, it is unripe to the enemy’s teeth.

“They have given the corpses of your servants as food to the birds of heaven, the flesh of your holy ones to the beasts of the earth” [Col. 1055B]. “They poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them.”

These things indeed took place in Jerusalem before the Savior’s coming, but they prefigured the slaughter of the infants, when their flesh was exposed to beasts and birds—that is, to persecutors—and so great a multitude of blood was poured out that scarcely could the little bodies of all be buried.

The circuit around Jerusalem is understood as the mourning of the weeping Church, in accordance with the saying: “Rachel weeping for her children, and she refused to be comforted, because they are not” (Jer. XXXI; Matt. II).

“We have become a reproach to our neighbors,” and so forth. The saints become a reproach to those who had previously been brothers but who, after separating themselves from the Church, persecute those who fear God. This refers to heretics:

“How long, Lord, will you be angry forever? Will your jealousy burn like fire? Pour out your anger upon the nations that have not known you, and upon the kingdoms that have not known your name,” and so forth. Do not be angry with us, we ask, Lord, who know you; instead, turn your fury against those who do not know your Christ.

“Because they have devoured Jacob and laid waste his dwelling.” That carnal Jacob, who was deceived by the cunning of the enemy.

“Do not remember our ancient iniquities. Let your mercies, Lord, quickly precede us, because we have become exceedingly poor.” May your mercy, we ask, Lord, precede us—your only-begotten Son—so that, coming, he may pardon our iniquities and rescue us from sins. For we became poor in the world on his account.

[Col. 1055D] “Help us, God our Savior; for the glory of your name, Lord, deliver us, and be propitious toward our sins,” and so forth. You then either help us or show us mercy, if the radiance of your name, which is blessed among the nations, rescues us from death by his death.

“Lest the nations say, ‘Where is their God?’ And let it become known among the nations before our eyes.” The nations, or peoples, are the hostile powers that prevail against us, saying: “Where is your true God?”—just as pagans often said this to the martyrs.

The vengeance for the blood of your servants that has been shed. Here he invokes judgment, so that the blood of the martyrs may be demanded by the Lord, who says in the Apocalypse: “Rest a little while, until the number of your fellow servants [Col. 1056A] is fulfilled” (Rev. VI). Let the groaning of the prisoners enter into your presence. They seek you through prolonged tears and desire to be set free and to be with you.

According to the greatness of your arm, possess the sons of those who were put to death. That is, those who, running by the examples of the martyrs, have crucified themselves to vices and desires.

Repay our neighbors sevenfold into their bosom. Thus they may not be condemned by the punishment of judgment, but may, through repentance, discharge a sevenfold recompense in this age. “Bosom” often means the breast of a human being, in which the soul rests. The reproach with which they reproached you, Lord. For they reproach you because they afflict with insults your martyrs, in whom you dwell.

But we are your people and the sheep of your pasture. Because of the [Col. 1056B] innocence they possess, they are called sheep, or because they have Christ as their shepherd. We shall give thanks to you forever, from generation to generation. That is, from the prophets to the Gospels. We shall proclaim your praise, because with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit you possess honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM LXXIX

For the end, for those who will be changed; a testimony of Asaph. This psalm contains the voice of the prophet pleading and recounting the mighty works of God.

You who shepherd Israel, attend. He is shepherded by God who sees God with his mind. Therefore the prophet asks him to attend to himself. You who lead Joseph like sheep. Not that Joseph whose type he rejected in another psalm, but the one [Col. 1056C] who, sold by a disciple for thirty pieces of silver, was led forth from hell by the Father’s power together with the flock of the righteous.

You who sit upon the cherubim. Upon the fullness of all knowledge. Appear. Show yourself to this world to be seen. Before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh. He mentions Ephraim and Manasseh, whom elsewhere he calls the strength of his head—that is, the Church or the apostles. By placing Benjamin in the middle, he signifies the apostle Paul, who descended from the tribe of Benjamin and was to be joined to the other apostles (Phil. III).

Stir up your power, which you displayed to the Egyptians and to the children of Israel. And come, that you may save us. Just as you brought them out of Egypt, so save us from the power of demons.

God, turn us back—to the knowledge of you. And show [Col. 1056D] your face, and we shall be saved. Show your Son, that we may be saved.

Lord God of hosts, how long will you be angry at the prayer of your servant? For he is not angry if we ask for justice; but, because of the consciousness of guilt, one thinks that he is angry even at the prayer.

You will feed us with the bread of tears, and give us drink in tears by measure. Often, because of our longing for God or our remembrance of sin, tears become our bread and drink. But when he says “by measure,” he indicates that in this prayer—in which we desire to be absolved from sins or long to see God—a meager nourishment should be received, if the prayer is offered in prayer rather than in excessive words.

[Col. 1057A] You have made us a reproach to our neighbors, etc. To the Jews and heretics who clamor around the Church and attack us.

Lord God of hosts, turn us back to yourself, and show your face, etc. The one who said: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John XIV).

You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it. You were its guide on the journey, etc. Although these things prefigured the synagogue, they must be referred to the Church, which, with faith assisting, has been transferred from the darkness of this age to heavenly dignity, the nations of vices having been driven out. To it also a way—that is, commandments by which it might walk—was given, with teachers planted in it through whom the sound of the Gospels would be proclaimed throughout the whole earth. It is itself also guarded, directed, and nourished by the Lord seated upon the cherubim.

[Col. 1057B] Its shadow covered the mountains, and its branches the cedars of God. Together with the patriarchs and apostles of his glory.

It extended its branches. We are the vines who have sprouted from that vine. As far as the sea. That is, we have advanced as far as baptism, though previously we were tossed about in the vanity of this world. In the Apocalypse, the sea signifies baptism. And its shoots as far as the river. So that those who were reborn in it might be washed in baptism. From here he returns to the synagogue.

Why have you torn down its wall? The synagogue’s defense was removed when blindness came upon it, until the fullness of the nations should enter. And all who pass along the way pluck its grapes. It is stripped by those who pass through the way of this world toward God, while by preaching they cause the [Col. 1057C] Jews to be converted.

The boar from the forest ravaged it, and the solitary wild beast devoured it. In the boar and the solitary wild beast the savagery of the devil is understood; by him it was ravaged because of unbelief.

Lord God of hosts, turn us back. The synagogue to the Church.

Look down from heaven, see, and visit this vine. Of which I spoke above. And perfect it, which your right hand planted. Which your power—that is, your Son—established by his resurrection. And upon the son of man. The son of the virgin. Whom you confirmed for yourself. Whom, after conquering death, you placed at your right hand.

Burned with fire and dug up, they will perish at the rebuke of your face. The synagogue, certainly, together with the unbelieving Jews.

[Col. 1057D] Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand. Upon the people whom your right hand—that is, your Christ—will save. And upon the son of man whom you confirmed for yourself. That same Mediator and Savior of ours.

We shall not depart from you; you will give us life. If we cling to you in faith, then we are refreshed by that bread of life which you sent from heaven. And we shall invoke your name. The one to whom you gave a name above every name.

Lord God of hosts, turn us back, and show your face, and we shall be saved. Him who is your image; him who is your face; him who is the illumination of your countenance, in whom you dwell and who dwells in you. May he graciously enter our purified minds, show himself to us as the [Col. 1058A] Savior of the world, and save us by his holy vision. To him be glory and dominion with you and with the Holy Spirit, now and forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM LXXX

For the end, for the winepresses; a psalm of Asaph himself. In the Law it is written that there are three solemnities: Passover, Pentecost, and Tabernacles. Before Tabernacles, there was a fast for ten days, and the fast lasted until evening. At that time they sounded trumpets—that is, they fasted, and during the fast they sounded trumpets—and after ten days came Tabernacles.

Pay close attention: three solemnities are recorded in the Law. First Passover, then Pentecost, then Tabernacles. Before Tabernacles, a fast; during the fast they sounded trumpets. Observe what Scripture signifies. Remove the veil placed before the eyes of Moses, and see that [Col. 1058B] we cannot become tabernacles unless we first fast. But unless that fast bears the sign of victory, which frightens our adversaries, Amalek is not conquered.

Since, therefore, there are three solemnities—Passover, Pentecost, and Tabernacles—there are also three psalms with the title “for the winepresses”: Psalm Eight, Psalm Eighty, and Psalm Eighty-Three. You see, then, how three psalms are written in the Psalter and prefaced “for the winepresses.” See what Psalm Eight, Psalm Eighty, and Psalm Eighty-Three say; and before we discuss the number, let us say what the winepresses signify.

For the winepresses. Winepresses exist nowhere except where there are vineyards and an abundant vintage. For the winepresses. Therefore the Lord and Savior says: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there was no man with me” (Isa. LXIII). Therefore he brought the vine out of Egypt and planted it. And he says in Jeremiah: “I planted you as a wholly [Col. 1058C] true, choice vine; how have you been changed for me into the bitterness of a foreign vine?” (Jer. II).

And Noah drank wine and became drunk. It is said also by Solomon, and it is said in the mystery: “Drink, friends, and become drunk” (Song V). We read also elsewhere that Joseph, that holy man who went before as a type of the Savior, was sold by his brothers and reigned in Egypt (Gen. XLIII). So our Lord and Savior was sold by the Jews and reigned in the Egypt of this age.

That Joseph, then, the holy and preeminent man who overcame cruelty by devotion—who was sold into Egypt for the purpose of feeding Egypt and his brothers who had sold him—that Joseph invited his brothers. But observe: he is said to have become drunk at midday. This cannot stand according to the literal sense, that a holy man became drunk. Noah also became drunk, but he truly had been intoxicated. Joseph became drunk like Noah, and he became drunk in his own house.

Observe the mystery. Let us [Col. 1058D] first see what it signifies in the mystery, and afterward discuss what it signifies in the literal sense. After the flood of this world, Noah drank and became drunk in his house, and his thighs were uncovered and his shame appeared; his elder brother came and mocked him, while the younger brother covered him (Gen. IX).

All this is said concerning the Savior, because during the suffering of the cross he said: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. XXVI). He drank and became drunk; his thighs were uncovered, and the disgrace of the cross appeared. The elder brother, the Jewish people, came and mocked; the younger, the people from the nations, covered the disgrace. Therefore Canaan was cursed and would be the servant of his brother. Behold, that curse endures to this day. We, the younger people, rule over the elder Jewish people.

Just as the Lord became drunk in his Passion, so the saints too are daily made drunk in the ardor of faith by the Holy Spirit. You who [Col. 1059A] yesterday were gathering gold and today are throwing it away—do you not appear mad among strangers? Finally, when the apostles were filled after the Holy Spirit had descended upon them and they spoke in various tongues, they were therefore said to be full of new wine (Acts II).

There is much that can be said about the mystery of wine and drunkenness. For the end, for the winepresses; of Asaph. Psalm Eight, Psalm Eighty, and Psalm Eighty-Three. No other psalms could bear the numbers of the winepresses except Psalm Eight, Psalm Eighty, and Psalm Eighty-Three.

The eighth day is the day of resurrection, in the singular number. Again, in eight decades, the eightieth is another, greater number. You see, therefore, that these winepresses are assigned only to the day of resurrection: the eighth and the eightieth. Someone may ask: Why are winepresses later mentioned in Psalm Eighty-Three? These winepresses pertain to the mystery of the Trinity. Therefore there are also three choir-leaders: in Psalm Eight, David; in Psalm Eighty, Asaph; in Psalm Eighty-Three, the sons of Korah.

David is associated with the eighth; his name is interpreted as [Col. 1059B] “strong of hand.” For our first victory involves combat and struggle. Therefore David is called “strong of hand.” The second is in Psalm Eighty, Asaph. Asaph is interpreted as “Synagogue.” Thus in the eighth we conquer, and in the eightieth we are gathered together with the Lord.

In Psalm Eighty-Three, it is the sons of Korah. Korah is interpreted as “Calvary.” “Ascend, Baldhead; ascend, Baldhead” (2 Kings II). The children said this to Elisha because he had suffered at the place of Calvary. Much can be said about how Elisha was mocked at Bethel by forty-two boys. These are the winepresses of which the Savior also says: “Make friends for yourselves from unrighteous mammon, so that they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke XVI).

Rejoice in God, our helper, who delivered us from the darkness of Egypt. Shout for joy to the God of Jacob, the overthrower of enemies.

[Col. 1059C] Take up the psalm and give the tambourine, the pleasant psaltery with the lyre. A hymn from a pure heart or mind, and from the lessening of worldly sins.

Sound the trumpet at the new moon, on the notable day of our solemnity. They sounded the trumpet at Passover, Pentecost, and Tabernacles. We, however, in the Church ought to sing to God at all times; but especially at the resurrection, in remission, and in the renewal of the dwelling—that is, when we rise again in Christ, when we receive remission, and when the dwelling of our breast has been renewed after its ruin.

For it is a commandment in Israel, and a judgment for the God of Jacob. His commandment and judgment are that we should be saved by grace, and not from ourselves.

A testimony in Joseph. In Christ, who was sold [Col. 1059D] for us. He appointed it when he went out from the land of Egypt—whether in the bush, or in the fire, or in other mysteries. He heard a language that he did not know. That people of the nations received in the Church the commandments that previously it did not know.

He turned his back away from burdens. When we were in Egypt, we built Pharaoh’s cities, carried mud and bricks, and our whole soul sought straw. We had no grain; we did not have the heavenly bread that came from heaven. We had not yet received manna from heaven; the serpent had not yet been hung up for us in the wilderness; the rock had not yet sent us water; we had not yet stretched out our hands, and Amalek had not yet fallen. We sat in mud and performed the works of Egypt; we built Pharaoh’s cities.

[Col. 1060A] He turned his back away from burdens. How great the burdens we previously bore! Therefore our Moses says: “Come to me, all you who are burdened with sins, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI).

His hands served in the basket. Whose? Israel’s. There are Egyptian baskets, and there are Jesus’ baskets. Jesus also has his baskets, and our Savior filled twelve baskets with fragments (Luke IX). O wondrous thing, signifying immense mysteries!

Five thousand people were fed in the wilderness, apart from children and women. In a deserted place only five loaves are found, for the place was deserted. I ask you who follow only the literal sense: in a deserted place only five loaves are found, and how are twelve baskets found? If the place was deserted, surely it could not have twelve [Col. 1060B] baskets. But all this signifies that the Lord led his people out of Egypt into the wilderness of this world; he fed them with his loaves, and whatever remained he stored in twelve baskets—that is, in the twelve apostles—so that what had perished among the twelve tribes might be saved in the twelve apostles.

In tribulation you called upon me, and I delivered you. The prophets and the psalms are obscure for this reason: suddenly, when you do not realize it, the speaker changes. Until this point the prophet has been speaking; now the person of God speaking to the people is suddenly introduced.

In tribulation you called upon me, and I delivered you. Whoever is in tribulation, be confident: call upon me, and you will be heard. I answered you in the hiding-place of the storm. That storm, when it pressed upon you and dragged you here and there as though [Col. 1060C] by waves—I was in the midst of the storm.

I tested you at the water of contradiction. Literally, this is said of Moses and Aaron: they offended God at the water of contradiction (Exod. XVII; Num. XX). For that reason they did not enter the promised land. But God says to us: “I tested you at the water of contradiction.” Simon was tested at the water of contradiction because he received baptism in hypocrisy (Acts VIII). Therefore whoever receives baptism in hypocrisy is tested at the water of contradiction.

Hear, my people, and I will testify to you. God is speaking to us. Whatever he said to the people, he also says to us. Israel, if you will hear me. What are you asking them to hear? Let us see what he commands.

There shall be no [Col. 1060D] new god among you. For one whose god is his belly, his belly is a new god. As many vices and sins as we have, so many new gods do we have. I became angry: anger is my god. I saw a woman and desired her: lust is my god. For whatever each person desires and venerates is his god. The miser has gold as his god. Nor shall you worship a foreign god. Our God is virtue; the gods of others are vices.

I am the Lord your God who brought you out of the land of Egypt. We are those who were brought out of the land of Egypt—provided that we have actually departed, that we are in the wilderness, and that we desire to see the promised land. If we have left Sodom, let us not look back toward Sodom. We have been saved on the mountain; let us not desire the Egyptian [Col. 1061A] meats.

Let us not say: “How well we were in Egypt, when we ate meat in pots, and garlic, and cucumbers!” (Num. XI). Do you wish to receive the Lord’s food? Do you wish to eat the Lord your God and Savior himself? Hear what he says: “Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it.” Open your mouths wide: he himself is the Lord, and the bread. He urges us to eat, and he himself is our food. However widely you open your mouth, so much will you receive. It is therefore not in my power, but in yours. If you wish, you will receive all of me; if you do not wish, receive at least a part.

And my people did not hear my voice. I stand at the door and knock. I want you to open and let me enter, but you do not want to open (Rev. VIII).

And Israel did not attend to me; so I let them go according to the [Col. 1061B] desires of their heart, etc. Unfortunate is the person whom God does not correct. If someone sins and is not struck, that person is miserable. Therefore he says: “I let them go according to the desires of their heart.” I let them go for this reason: because I often struck them, and they did not accept discipline. I pleaded, and they did not listen; I struck them, and they did not feel the pain. I let them go in their own desires, so that, satiated with their vices, they might at least then repent.

If my people had listened to me. O most merciful Father, O compassionate God! He pleaded and was not heard; as though angry, he lets his dissolute son go. Again he sees him perishing and grieves because he is perishing. And what does he say? “If Israel had walked in my ways, for nothing,” etc.

Was it a great thing for me to deliver you from tribulation? Could I not send my majesty and [Col. 1061C] rescue you from danger? But because I left you to free choice, set the arena before you, and no one is crowned except the one who has fought, I therefore leave the victory to your choice (2 Tim. II).

The enemies of the Lord lied to him. In Hebrew it is better: “The enemies of the Lord will deny him”—that is, the Jews; for his enemies denied him. But will these enemies who will deny him therefore perish? Will there therefore be no remnant? And how did you swear to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob that their offspring would be like the stars of heaven and like the sand of the sea? Why did you promise this to the fathers and not fulfill it for their sons?

“The enemies of the Lord will deny him.” But what does he say? “And their time will be forever.” When the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel will be saved (Rom. XI). In the future they will believe; for now they have not [Col. 1061D] believed.

Now I shall speak to the Jews. They are accustomed to applaud themselves and say: “And their time will be forever.” Let us say: It is true; for some of the Jews will believe. Finally, we read in the Apocalypse of John that twelve thousand from each tribe—that is, one hundred and forty-four thousand—will believe, and this number is said to consist of virgins. But if there will be so great a number of virgins, how great will the number of non-virgins be? Therefore let us also say to the Jews: Your time will not be forever—that is, in the age to come.

But what does this have to do with you, who do not believe today? “And their time will be forever.” What sort of time will belong to the enemies of God?

And he fed them from the fat of grain. He brought them into the promised land. He fed them not with manna as in the wilderness, [Col. 1062A] but with grain that fell and rose again. And he fed them from the fat of grain.

Observe the mystery of the Scriptures: “From the fat of grain.” Does grain have fat? Did it have intestines as well? But he wished to show the abundance and richness of spiritual grace, and therefore he called it “fat.”

And he satisfied them with honey from the rock. He himself is the grain; he himself is the rock, who satisfied the people of Israel with water in the wilderness. Spiritually he satisfied them with honey, not with water, so that all who believed and received food might taste honey in their mouths. “How sweet are your utterances to my throat, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!” (Ps. CXVIII).

Finally, our Lord also ate a honeycomb after his resurrection for this reason, and he was satisfied with honey from the rock (Luke XXIV). Therefore I say something new: The [Col. 1062B] rock itself ate honey in order to give us honey and sweetness, so that those who had drunk myrrh—that is, bitterness—in the Law might afterward eat the honey of the Gospel. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM LXXXI

A psalm of Asaph. This psalm urges us that, if we wish the Lord to dwell with us, we should always do the things that please him.

God stood in the assembly of gods. There are many figures of speech. We frequently sit; sometimes we stand; sometimes we lie down; sometimes we run; sometimes we walk. In the same way God is described according to the variety of human beings, and different postures are attributed to him.

If we are holy and are like Moses, it is said to us: “But you, stand here with me” (Exod. XVII). For [Col. 1062C] God said this to Moses. Moses was standing upon the rock, and therefore the Lord also stood with him.

But if we were holy at first and afterward became sinners, God no longer stands for us but walks—that is, he moves from his place, where he had previously stood for us. After we have moved, he too moves together with us.

Finally, as long as Adam was in paradise and kept the commandment, God stood for him. But after he transgressed, he heard the voice of God walking in paradise. Do you wish to know that God was walking for him? What did he say to him? “Adam, where are you?” He who had not fled from God standing afterward fled from him walking (Gen. V).

We have spoken of the one who stands and of the one who walks; let us speak of the one who sits. Whenever God is presented as sitting, he is presented in two ways: either as a king or as a judge.

If as a king, he appears as [Col. 1062D] Isaiah saw him: “I saw the Lord seated upon a high and exalted throne” (Isa. VI). There he is presented as a reigning king. But when he is presented as a judge, thrones are set up and books are opened, as it is written in Daniel: “Thrones were set up, and books were opened” (Dan. VII). That is, the Lord is about to sit as judge and review the works of all.

The books that are now closed will then be opened. For everything we do, everything we say, and everything we think, we shall render an account, even for an idle word. It is written in the books of God.

Someone may think that there are books in heaven in which our sins are written. I think the books are our consciences, which will then be opened, and each person will see what he has done. [Col. 1063A] Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed. Therefore thrones are set up and books are opened.

How much is written in my book, which I do not dare confess even to my brother or my friend! The angels know what I have done; the Thrones know; the Seraphim know; the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit know.

We have spoken of God standing for some, walking for others, and sitting for others—either as king or as judge. For still others he sleeps. Whenever he abandons us to temptations, although we may be holy, we are left to temptations so that we may be tested. At that time the Lord sleeps for us.

Finally, what does the Psalmist say? “Awake; why do you sleep, Lord?” (Ps. XLIII). And when the apostles were in the boat and the boat was battered by the waves, the Lord was sleeping for them. For that reason the boat was battered by the waves. Finally they roused him, [Col. 1063B] he awoke, and immediately the storm became calm (Mark IV).

We have spoken of the four figures of God: for some he stands, for others he walks, for others he sits, and for others he is as though asleep; for still others he awakens and rises.

God stood in the assembly of gods. Because they were gods, God stood for them. In our assembly God has various figures: for some he stands, for others he sits, for others he walks, and for others he sleeps. Though he himself is unchanging, he changes according to our variety.

See the dignity of the human being: “God stood in the assembly of gods.” He grants us the name so that he may also grant the merit. And in the midst of the gods he judges. As a commander judges in the midst of an army, so God judges gods. A fearful matter, full of terror. If he judges gods, what does he do with a sinner?

The prophet spoke these two verses; but what follows is this:

How long will you judge unjustly? God himself speaks to the judges—that is, to the rulers of the people. Specifically, the verses that follow are spoken to judges.

If they are judges of the world, this is clear. But if they are judges of the Church, let us understand them as bishops and presbyters.

How long will you judge unjustly? Whoever judges unjustly is a judge of injustice. That man was a judge of injustice of whom it is said in the Gospel that he did not fear the Lord and did not respect human beings.

How long will you judge unjustly? I gave you authority over my flock and over the people of God. You ought to be judges, not wolves.

And you assume the faces of sinners. Judge the needy and the orphan; justify the humble and the poor. Rescue the poor and the needy, etc.

When a case comes before you, you do not consider the cause; you do not consider the [Col. 1063D] judgment, but the persons of those who have cases. It is as though he said: If a poor man comes with a just case, and a rich man comes with an unjust case, you look at the person, not at the case. This is according to one interpretation.

There is, however, another, more sacred interpretation. In theaters, one person is often assigned different roles: now he enters as a woman, now as a man, now as a king; and the one who came forward as a king later appears as a servant.

I have given this example so that we may pass from the physical to the spiritual. We too assume different roles. When I am angry, I assume the role of a lion. When I seize what belongs to others, I assume the role of a wolf. When I am cruel and kill, I assume the role of a cruel person.

But just as [Col. 1064A] sinners have different roles in their sins, so conversely the saints also have different roles, but in goodness. When I give alms, I have the role of one who shows mercy. When I judge well, I have the role of a good judge. When I suffer injury and am humble, I have the role of a humble person.

Unfortunate is the person who has many roles in evil. Blessed is the person who has different roles in goodness.

They did not know, nor did they understand; they walk in darkness. Who? The wicked judges. Those whom I was calling gods have, because of their vice, been called wicked.

They did not know me, nor did they understand my judgment; they walk in darkness. Because they abandoned the light, they walk in darkness. I said: “You are the light of the world,” but you turned away from the light and became darkness.

Since they have [Col. 1064B] done this, let us see what follows. All the foundations of the earth will be shaken. Observe what retribution wicked rulers receive. Because of wicked judges, the foundations of the earth are shaken.

For the moment we have said this first according to the literal sense: the shaking of the whole world comes because of wicked rulers. But let us speak in another way: “All the foundations of the earth will be shaken.” I will overthrow the wicked judges who laid foundations on earth and not in heaven; they ought to have Christ as their foundation, the one whom the architect Paul laid, but they were unwilling and laid their foundations on earth.

I said, “You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High.” Let Eunomius hear; let Arius hear—those who say that the Son of God is a son in the same way that we are.

That we are gods is not a matter of nature but of grace. “As many as received him, [Col. 1064C] he gave them power to become children of God” (John I). Therefore I made the human being so that gods might come from human beings.

I said, “You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High.” See how great the dignity is: we are called both gods and sons. I made you gods, just as I made Moses the god of Pharaoh (Exod. VII), so that after you have become gods you might be made worthy to be my sons.

Consider the divine Scripture: “There is no partiality with God.” He did not say: “I said, You are gods”—kings and rulers—but “all,” to whom I gave equally a body, a soul, and a spirit; equally I bestowed divinity and adoption. We are all born equal, emperors and poor alike, and we also die equally. For our condition is equal.

But you will die like human beings. You see, then, that the one who is human dies. God does not die. Adam too, as long as he kept the commandment and was also a god, [Col. 1064D] did not die. But after he tasted from the forbidden tree, he immediately died. Finally God says to him: “On whatever day you taste of it, you will die by death” (Gen. II).

In Hebrew it is better: “But you will die like Adam.” Just as he was expelled from paradise, so we too have been expelled.

And like one of the princes you will fall. Since he had said, “All are sons of the Most High,” a son of the Most High cannot be [a son] unless he himself is also exalted. I said this so that you might all be exalted, as I am exalted. But you will fall like one of the princes.

Because we were exalted, we are said to have fallen. Where are those who say that the devil was made a devil? Where are those who say that an evil nature [Col. 1065A] was created by God?

According to the Hebrew, two things are said here: “But you will die like Adam.” Just as your father did not wish to hear the Lord’s commandment and fell, so you too will die. Therefore that statement was made about Adam.

But what follows—“And like one of the princes you will fall”—who is this one of the princes who fell? If you wish to say Adam, it has already been said in the preceding verses: “But you will die like Adam.”

At the same time, observe the force of the word: “But you will die like Adam.” Because Adam died, we too die. But the devil, who was a prince and fell, did not die. For angelic dignity cannot receive death, but only ruin. Therefore he said: “Like one of the princes you will fall.”

As Lucifer fell, who rose in the [Col. 1065B] morning—“and behold, here too he fell, and there he fell.” He fell because he had always dwelt in heavenly places. He is the one to whom it is said in Ezekiel: “You are the seal of likeness” (Ezek. XXVIII).

Observe what he says: “The seal of likeness.” He did not say, “You are the likeness of the seal,” but “the seal of likeness.” God had sealed you and made you like himself. But afterward you unsealed yourself with respect to the likeness and image of God, and you were created.

Finally, it is said in that same prophecy: “You were nourished in the midst of the cherubim; you were among stones of jasper and carbuncle in the paradise of God, and you fell,” he says, “and from the mountain of God you were wounded.”

This is the prince of Tyre from the time when he fell. For Tyre in the Hebrew language is called *Sor*—that is, “tribulation.” Therefore this prince, who was at first [Col. 1065C] in heaven, has now become the prince of Tyre, that is, of the tribulation of this age.

Like one of the princes you will fall. When he says “like one,” he shows that there are others as well. Read the Apocalypse of John: when the dragon fell from heaven, he dragged with him a third of the stars (Rev. XII).

Up to this point God has spoken to human beings, and again he speaks through the prophet.

Rise, O God, judge the earth. Rise, because our ship is being battered by the waves. Rise: O God, judge the earth, because wicked judges do not judge but overturn your law and tear apart your flocks. Rise, you who are the true judge. Since wicked judges have died like Adam and have fallen like one of the princes, therefore rise, judge, and save your creation.

“For when the hired man sees the wolf, he flees” (John 10) and abandons the sheep; he cannot grieve for another’s loss as he grieves for his father and mother. Let us say it another way: Rise, you who suffered for us and died for us; rise and save us. Let us say it another way: You who came humble and despised, come as judge and avenge us.

Rise, O God, judge the earth. Observe the significance and exact propriety of the words. He did not say, “Judge heaven,” but “the earth.” Therefore the earth is judged, not heaven. If, then, the earth is judged and not heaven, sins are not committed in heaven; for if sins were committed in heaven, he would have said, “Rise, O God, judge the earth and heaven.”

And observe the mercy of the prophecy. He did not say, “Destroy the earth,” but “Judge,” and save. He did not say, “Judge through angels; judge through your ministers.” For if they judge, they cannot show mercy, since they are executors of your sentence. But if you judge, you yourself can show mercy. Rise, O God, judge the earth. An emperor can change his own sentence; a prefect cannot. Therefore we implore you as judge—not despising you, but entreating you. For human beings and angels are cruel in comparison with you. You alone are the most merciful judge.

Do you wish to know that God is a merciful judge and every human being is cruel? While the master of the house slept, an enemy sowed weeds over the crop. The servants want to pull them up, but the master of the house says: “Let them grow together, lest while you pull up the weeds from the wheat you uproot the wheat also” (Matt. 13).

“For you will inherit among all the nations.” Therefore we implore you as judge, because you have had mercy on all nations. Why did he not say, “You will possess all the nations,” but “You will inherit”? Wherever inheritance is mentioned, death has first preceded it. Therefore we are called heirs and co-heirs. He called us heirs of Christ because he died for us; co-heirs because he will reign with us.

“You will inherit.” For you sent your servants. Let us return to the apostles: one to the circumcision, another to the Gentiles. As long as you had sent Moses, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the other prophets, God was known in Judea, and his name was great in Israel. Knowledge of God was proclaimed within a small territory.

You sent Peter, a fisherman who had left his net and whose hand had become calloused through labor. You did not send an orator; you did not send a philosopher. You sent a countryman, a fisherman. This fisherman, this countryman, went from Jerusalem to Rome, and the countryman captured Rome, which eloquent men could not capture.

Again the apostle Paul went forth and preached from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum. He preached where the Gospel had not been preached, so that he would not build upon another’s foundation (Rom. 15). Then he says that he would go from the city of Rome to Spain. Observe Paul the persecutor, who had been a persecutor in Judea, preaching to the Gentiles.

Where are those who praise Alexander the Great, emperor of the Macedonians, because he conquered so many nations in a short time? He had an army; he had immense crowds; yet he could not accomplish anything of this kind, but only something small. But this Paul, once a persecutor, who said, “And if I am unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge” (2 Cor. 11), who commits solecisms when he speaks, carries the cross of Christ and, like a triumphant conqueror, captures everyone. He subdued the whole world, from the Ocean to the Red Sea.

Someone may say: “They did all this for profit.” This is what Porphyry says: “Uneducated and poor men, since they possessed nothing, performed certain signs by magical arts.” But performing signs is not a great thing. The magicians in Egypt also performed signs against Moses (Exod. 7). Apollonius did so, and Apuleius did so. Countless people have performed signs.

I grant you, Porphyry, that they performed signs by magical arts in order to receive riches from wealthy little women whom they had led astray—for that is what you say. Why did they die? Why were they crucified? Others also performed signs by magical arts, but they did not die for a dead man, nor were they crucified for one who had been crucified. These men know that the man was dead, and do they die without cause? Blessed, then, is our victory, which was consecrated in the blood of the apostles. Our faith is confirmed only through their blood.

Let us therefore bless God, to whom belongs glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM 82

A song, a psalm of Asaph. This psalm contains the voice of the prophet praising God together with others. He says:

“God, who will be like you?” For no one is like you; we seek no other author besides you. “Do not be silent, nor be restrained, O God.” We are silent; speak on our behalf. It is the voice of the righteous man who says, “Do not be restrained, O God.” He is confident in his own righteousness.

[Col. 1067B] “For behold, your enemies have made a noise.” We can interpret this tropologically of the Church and the heresies. We can also interpret it according to the literal sense of the Jewish people and the other nations that attack Judea from all sides.

“For behold, your enemies have made a noise.” He wished to call the voice and slander of the adversaries a “noise.” Observe what he says: “They have made a noise,” that is, like a clanging cymbal, so they have sounded in my ears. Properly speaking, a noise is what is heard when only a sound is perceived and the voice is not understood. Therefore what he says is this: They were speaking and, as it were, wished to accuse me; but I heard not a voice, as it were, but merely a noise.

“And those who hate you have lifted up their head.” Observe what he says: whoever raises his head hates God. For “the Lord resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4; 1 Pet. 5).

“And those who hate you have lifted up their head.” If you have a grievance against someone, if your brother slanders you, and you are humble for Christ’s sake while he is proud because of the devil, you imitate the one who says, “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. 11). But the man who exalts himself imitates the one who says, “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will set my throne; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14).

“And those who hate you have lifted up their head.”

“Against your people they have plotted wickedly.” It is enough for someone if he is the people of God. “They have taken counsel against your saints.” This requires no interpretation. To have read it is to have understood it.

“They said, ‘Come, let us destroy them as a nation.’” And let there be no nation, because it is the people of God. “And let the name of Israel no longer be remembered.” Let no one who sees God in understanding be remembered here.

“For they have conspired with one accord.” Wretched are we! The people of God cannot have as much concord in what is good as the wicked have in what is evil.

“Against you they made a covenant: the tents of the Edomites and the Ishmaelites; Moab and the Hagrites; Gebal, Ammon, and Amalek; foreigners together with the inhabitants of Tyre. Indeed, Assyria also came with them; they became an assistance to the sons of Lot.”

There are eleven who fight against the holy one. Since they fought against the saints, they could not reach the perfect number, that is, twelve.

[Col. 1068A] “The tents of the Edomites.” They do not have houses with foundations, but tents that quickly pass away. Edom is interpreted in two ways: either “bloody” or “earthly.” Observe, then, who are fighting against the saints.

“The tents of the Edomites”: the earthly. “And the Ishmaelites” are interpreted as “obedient to themselves,” that is, whatever the heart and evil thought may desire, they immediately do. Therefore it is said in Ezekiel: “Son of man, speak against the prophets who follow their own heart, and whatever their thought impels them to do, they do” (Ezek. 13).

We, however, ought not to follow our own thought, nor be called Ishmaelites—that is, “obedient to themselves”—but Ishmael, that is, “obedient to God.”

“Moab”: from the father, that is, those who depart from God the Father.

“Hagrites”: proselytes. Although they ought to have been inhabitants of God, they became proselytes.

“Gebal” is interpreted as “a vain valley.” *Ge* means “valley,” while *bal* is interpreted as “vain.” Therefore those who are against the people of God are not from the mountain, but from a vain valley.

“Ammon” is interpreted as “a turbulent people”: those who trust in multitude and not in simplicity.

“Amalek” is interpreted as “licking the earth.” For all who fight against the people of God do not eat heavenly bread, but lick the earth like the serpent.

“Foreigners.” Where “foreigners” occurs, the Hebrew has *Philistiim*. *Philistiim* is interpreted as “falling through drinking,” that is, those who became drunk from the devil’s cup and fell while intoxicated.

“Together with the inhabitants of Tyre.” In the Hebrew language Tyre is called *Sor*, which is interpreted as “tribulation” and “distress.” Those who ought to have been pilgrims in this world have become inhabitants. Therefore those who attack the people of God dwell in *Sor*, that is, in the distress and tribulation of their own soul.

These are such great nations fighting against the holy one. Let us see who they have as their prince: the Savior or the devil. What follows?

“Indeed, Assyria came with them.” Assyria is Nebuchadnezzar, the adversary of God, who led the people of God into captivity. Although they appear to have many nations fighting on their side, they have Assyria as their prince—that is, the devil.

“They became an assistance to the sons of Lot.” Lot is interpreted as “the one who turns aside.” The demons were formerly angels, but afterward fell with the devil and became his attendants, as it is written in the Apocalypse of John: “The dragon fell and dragged down with him a third of the stars” (Rev. 12).

What, then, does he say? These who came with so many nations and attacked your people, and Assyria came with them, and they have the devil as their prince, became an assistance to the sons of Lot—that is, to the demons. Those who have turned aside from you do what the demons also do.

You see that these are extremely difficult passages; you see that they are obscure, and that great mysteries lie in each word. Necessity compels us to linger longer over the Hebrew words, which are filled with mysteries. For we are not now displaying a rhetorical exercise, but attempting to interpret what was spoken by the Holy Spirit.

Unless it is interpreted in the way we have stated, what benefit is there for the churches of Christ in reading “the tents of the Edomites and the Ishmaelites” and the other names? Since they have come against your people, let us see what the psalmist invokes upon them.

“Treat them like Midian and Sisera, like Jabin.” You have read in the Book of Judges: this is the Midian whom Gideon defeated (Judg. 7–8). Jabin and Sisera are those whom Deborah and Barak defeated (Judg. 4). “They perished at the torrent of Kishon, at Endor.” Deborah and Barak killed Sisera, the commander of the army.

Observe, then, what this means: “Lord, how great is their pride! They come with so large an army; they have Nebuchadnezzar, prince of the Assyrians; they have become an assistance to the sons of Lot; they do what the demons do; their pride has been lifted up even to you. Therefore I entreat you that, to their shame, they may be defeated not by a man but by a woman.”

“They became like dung of the earth.” Who? Midian, Sisera, and Jabin. These three became like dung of the earth.

“Midian” is interpreted as “abandoning judgment.” Whoever fights against my people does not consider that judgment will come.

“Sisera” is interpreted as “vision of a horse.” Those who fight against your people are not from your flock or your herds, but from the horses that rage after females. Therefore these horses are always prepared for battle.

“Like Jabin.” Jabin is interpreted as “understanding.” These are those who trust in their own wisdom and not in the glory of God.

“They became like dung of the earth.” Those who gloried in their army, who had Assyria as their prince, and who said, “I will ascend into heaven,” have not merely fallen to earth; they have become dung upon the earth.

[Col. 1069C] “Set their princes.” Whose princes? Those who fight against your people. “Like Oreb and Zeeb, and Zebah and Zalmunna”—all their princes.

I think you have read the history in the Book of Judges: Gideon, who is called by another name Jerubbaal, fought for the people of God and defeated and killed these four kings (Judg. 6–7).

Observe what sort of princes the Midianites had, who abandoned the judgment of God: Oreb, Zeeb, Zebah, and Zalmunna. Who would think that mysteries concerning the Savior are contained in these words? Philosophers read them and mock. Orators read them and think they are ravings. Not only orators, but also the Jews do not possess the key of knowledge, because a veil has been placed before their eyes.

“Oreb” is interpreted as “a hole,” into which the serpent enters.

“Zeeb” is interpreted as “wolf.” Observe the names of the princes who are adversaries of Christ.

“Zebah”: sacrifice, that is, those whom the wolf has strangled.

“And Zalmunna”: perfected in wickedness.

Observe, then, the mysteries of the names.

“Those who said, ‘Let us take possession of the sanctuary of God as an inheritance.’” They said this, but did not accomplish it, because the Lord fought for his people.

“My God, make them like a wheel.” Observe the prophet’s mercy: he does not pray against them, but for them. Observe what he says: “My God”—the God of all, but specifically my God—“make them like a wheel.” Let those who seem to have a foundation in wickedness have no foundation, but let them waver and not stand in wickedness.

“Like stubble before the face of the wind, like fire that burns the forest.” He says “like stubble,” not like grain. What he means is this: if there is anyone among them who is stubble and chaff, let him perish.

“Like fire that burns the forest.” He did not say fruitful trees, but “the forest,” which bears no fruit. Therefore, if anyone is stubble and has no grain, if anyone is a forest and bears no fruit, let him perish.

“Like a flame burning the mountains.” Let pride perish in them.

“So you will pursue them in your tempest, and in your wrath.” What does that mean? Will you kill them? No, but “you will trouble them”—so that they may be saved.

“Fill their faces with disgrace,” so that they may be confounded. Why this? “So that they may seek your name, O Lord.” You see, then, that he prays not against them but for their salvation. Finally, observe what he says in what follows:

“Let them be ashamed and troubled forever and ever; let them be confounded and perish.” Let them perish according to what is evil in them, and let what is good be saved. Observe, then, that “perdition” here does not signify annihilation, but salvation.

What follows?

“And let them know that you alone are called Lord, the Most High over all the earth.” Let whoever wishes raise himself up. Let us say: “You alone are the Most High over all the earth.” However much anyone may exalt himself, let us possess God, whose name is higher than all, to whom belongs glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM 83

At the end, for the winepresses, for the sons of Korah, a psalm. Three psalms are assigned “for the winepresses”: the eighth, the eightieth, and the eighty-third. The eighth is assigned to David; the eightieth is assigned to Asaph; and the eighty-third is assigned to the sons of Korah.

I give you a rule, so that you may know what you ought to observe in the Scriptures. Whenever a psalm is assigned to the sons of Korah, it contains nothing sad but always signifies joyful things. Since Korah, Dathan, and Abiram acted against Moses and were punished by the Lord, the sons of Korah, who did not follow their father, were blessed with eternal joy.

Moreover, since Korah is interpreted as “Calvary,” and it is clear that Calvary signifies the place of resurrection, whoever is a son of Korah is a son of resurrection; and whoever is a son of resurrection can have nothing that is sad.

“How beloved are your tents, O Lord of hosts! My soul longs and languishes for the courts of the Lord.” Then it says: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house.” Observe that there are three things: tents, courts, and finally a house.

“How beloved are your tents, O Lord of hosts!” What are these tents? Let us see whether the Gospel offers us any indication. The Lord says: “Make friends for yourselves from the unrighteous mammon, so that when you fail, they may receive you into the eternal tents” (Luke 16).

You see, then, that unrighteous mammon fails in this world. Yet consider that this unrighteous thing prepares righteousness. In the Hebrew language *mammon* means “riches,” not gold, as some think.

“From the unrighteous mammon.” There is also a true statement among philosophers: “Every rich person is either unrighteous or the heir of an unrighteous person.” Therefore the Lord and Savior says that the rich enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty (Matt. 19).

Someone may say: “How did Zacchaeus enter the kingdom of heaven, since he was rich?” But he gave away his riches, and immediately exchanged riches for the kingdom of heaven. He did not say, “Whoever is rich will not enter the kingdoms of heaven”; rather, he said that the rich will enter the kingdoms of heaven with difficulty.

“How beloved are your tents, O Lord of hosts!” Some desire possessions; others the riches of this world; others to preside in the churches of this world and to have some glory among human beings. My only desire is to see the eternal tents. Those tents are beloved to me where there is an assembly of virtues, not of vices.

“My soul longs and languishes for the courts of the Lord.” This alone is my desire, this alone my love: to see your courts.

Observe the order. First he desires the tents: tents that have no foundation, tents that are quickly changed. For a tent is always moved and transferred from one place to another. The courts, however, are not houses, but they do have certain foundations, and from the court we enter the house.

Therefore this man first desires the tents; afterward he languishes and wastes away with love in order to see the courts; and when he has been in the court, then he says: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house.”

“My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God.” It is difficult for anyone’s heart and flesh to agree together. For if, according to the Apostle, the spirit fights against the flesh and the flesh against the spirit (Gal. 5), how can he say here, “My heart and my flesh have rejoiced”?

Only the one who is fixed with his whole mind in the love of God can say this. “My heart and my flesh”: this is what he also says elsewhere: “My soul thirsted for you; how greatly my flesh [thirsts] for you” (Ps. 62). This is the flesh that desires the Lord, of which it is said elsewhere: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Isa. 40).

But the flesh of which it is said, “All flesh is grass” (Ecclus. 14), does not desire the Lord.

“My heart and my flesh.” Show me an ascetic who regards the death of his flesh as gain for his soul. These are the works of the flesh: fasts and injuries. Finally, what does the Apostle also say? “He handed him over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit might be saved” (1 Cor. 5). Unless the flesh has died, the spirit cannot be made alive.

Therefore the Apostle also says: “When I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Cor. 12). Let each person consider himself when he is wearied and weakened by fasting: how the soul becomes vigorous; how the mind considers nothing else except God; how it always says, “How beloved are your tents, O Lord of hosts!”

“For the sparrow has found a house for itself, and the turtledove a nest for itself where it may place its young. Your altars, O Lord of hosts, my king and my God.”

For the moment let us interpret simply. Observe what he says: “I desire, O Lord, your eternal tents; my soul longs and languishes for the courts of the Lord.” I desire to have some seat and little nest for my soul and my body. Birds that wander freely here and there nevertheless, after they have flown, have a place and little nests where they may rest. How much more ought my soul and my flesh to prepare a place for themselves where they can rest!

Now let us ascend to something deeper. “I trust in the Lord. How then can you say to my soul, ‘Migrate to the mountains like a sparrow’?” Observe, then, that no one flees to the mountains except one who is a sparrow.

“And the turtledove a nest for itself.” This is the turtledove of which it is said in the Song of Songs: “The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land” (Song 2).

“The turtledove a nest for itself.” The turtledove is an animal of chastity. The turtledove does not dwell in low places, but always makes its nests in lofty trees. Therefore, just as the sparrow and the turtledove, very chaste birds, make their nests in higher places, so the tents, courts, and house are not in this lowly earth, but on high—that is, in the kingdoms of heaven.

Finally, observe what he says.

“Blessed are those who dwell in your house.” We do not dwell in a tent, but are pilgrims there. And while we are in the court, we do not dwell there either, but are pilgrims. For from the courts we pass into the house. But when we have entered the house, what is said?

“Blessed are those who dwell in your house”—the house that has a foundation. For we may not go out of the house, whereas we may leave the courts.

“Blessed is the man whose help is from you.” We desire your tents, courts, and house, but to be able to receive this itself is not a matter of our virtue but of your help.

“He has arranged ascents in his heart.” Who has arranged ascents in his heart? The blessed man whose help is from the Lord: he has arranged ascents in his heart. Whoever is holy stretches forward daily toward what lies ahead and forgets what is behind.

Therefore there are also fifteen psalms of ascent in the Psalter. The first says: “When I was in distress I cried to the Lord.” The second: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from where my help will come.” The third: “I rejoiced in the things that were said to me.” And he always advances, progresses, and ascends toward higher things.

What he means is this: “He has arranged ascents in his heart.” Blessed is the person who makes progress daily, who does not consider what he did yesterday but what he does today in order to advance. The holy person places ascents in his heart; the sinner places descents. Just as the holy person progresses daily, so the sinner diminishes daily.

Blessed is the person who arranges ascents in his heart. Observe the sequence of the Scriptures:

“In the valley of tears, in the place that he has established.” Wherever “valley” is mentioned, we must necessarily understand, by contrast, a mountain. Therefore whoever arranges ascents in his heart—where is he placed? “In the valley of tears.”

Let us consider that we are in a valley; we are not on the mountain, nor are we in paradise—not in the height of paradise, but in the lowliness of the earth, the accursed earth, the earth cursed to produce thorns and thistles for us, which is the food of the serpent, of which it is said to Adam: “You are earth, and to earth you shall return.”

As long, then, as we are in the valley of tears, we ought not to laugh but to weep. Therefore the Lord also says: “Blessed are those who weep, for they shall laugh” (Matt. 5). For the present, while we are in the valley of tears, this world is a world of tears, not of joy. We ought not to laugh, because this world and this time are of tears; that world is of joy.

“In the valley of tears, in the place that he has established.” What does “in the place that he has established” mean? “In the place,” that is, in the valley of tears. “In the place that he has established”: God has placed us here for combat, so that we may always struggle in this place. Therefore this place, that is, the valley of tears, is not a place of peace or security, but of combat and battles.

“For the lawgiver will give blessings.” Someone may say: “In the valley of tears, in the place that he has established, for the contest—that is, for combat—why did he place us in combat? Why did he wish us to fight?”

The psalmist answered himself and says: “For this reason he wished us to fight in this place, so that he might be able to give crowns. For the lawgiver will give blessings.” This Lawgiver, that is, our contest-master, wished us to fight for this reason: so that he might bless us.

Observe the sequence. What are the blessings of this contest-master?

“They will go from strength to strength.” Here they conquer, so that there they may be crowned. If a man proves strong here, he becomes stronger there: “They will go from strength to strength.” Therefore, unless we possess strength here, we cannot possess greater strength there.

For he did not say, “They will go from weakness to strength,” but “They will go from strength to strength.” Do you wish to be strong there? Be strong here first. Do you wish to be crowned there? Fight here.

“They will go from strength to strength.” We can also say it another way: Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1). Whoever possesses this power here will possess the same power there.

“They will go from strength to strength.” What profit will they have when they go from strength to strength? What reward will they have? “The God of gods will be seen in Zion.”

“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5). It is enough for the victors; it is enough for those who have fought, to see the face of Christ. To see God is an infinite crown.

“The God of gods will be seen in Zion.” What joy, what happiness it is to go from strength to strength and to have this very reward: that we may be worthy to see Christ!

“Our protector, look, O God, and look upon the face of your anointed.” Observe what he says: “And look upon the face of your anointed.” A human being entreats that the Father look upon the face of the Son. But observe what he says.

Since the Apostle said, “Do you seek proof of the Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. 13), and the Savior himself again said, “Whoever receives you receives me” (Matt. 10), this is what he means: Look upon us. For in us you look upon your Son, who dwells in us.

“For one day in your courts is better.” Observe what he says: “One day.” Someone may think that it should be understood this way: It is better for me to have a short time in the kingdom of heaven than to have everything here, that is, in this world.

This interpretation is not bad. But let us say: If it could happen that someone were in the kingdom of heaven for one day and afterward were cast down, he would rightly say, “One day in your courts is better.” But now, when he says “one day,” this is what he means by the kingdom of heaven. That one day has neither night nor darkness, but is always light. Therefore whoever is in the kingdom of heaven for one day is there forever.

“I chose to be rejected in the house of my God rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners.” This is also what the Savior says about John: “Amen, amen, I say to you, among those born of women there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptist” (Matt. 11). Then he said that John himself was an angel. And afterward he said: “But the one who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.”

The meaning there is this: John is greater than all human beings. And if you wish to know, he himself is the angel. But this man who is an angel on earth is the least in the kingdom of heaven—that is, he is less than the angels. But the one who is least in the kingdom of heaven, that is, the angel, is greater than this man who is greatest of all on earth.

This, then, is what the prophet now says: “I chose to be rejected in the house of my God”—that is, I wished to be lesser in the kingdom of heaven—“rather than to be first in this world.”

“I chose to be rejected in the house of my God rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners.” Tents have no foundation; they pass away. Yet the sinner never merely inhabits the earth, but dwells in it and possesses it.

“For God loves mercy and truth.” God loves two things: mercy and truth. If he were only merciful, he would provoke all of us to sins. If he loved only truth, no one would have hope of repentance. Therefore he seeks both, so that one may temper the other.

If you are a sinner, hear the merciful God and do not despair, but do penance. If, however, you are righteous, do not become negligent because God is merciful; for God is also just and loves truth.

“The Lord will give grace and glory.” He did not say, “He will give glory and grace,” but “The Lord will give grace and glory.” First he forgives sins, and afterward he crowns.

“He will not deprive those who walk in innocence of good things.” The Hebrew has a better reading: “in perfection.” Innocence is not perfect virtue; for the innocent person, unless he possesses prudence, does not possess perfect and complete virtue.
