Therefore the Gospel also says: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. 10).

“O Lord of hosts.” Observe what he says: “O Lord of hosts.” Therefore when we have sins within us, God, who is Lord of hosts, is not our Lord, because he is not Lord of sinners but of the righteous.

“Blessed is the man who hopes in you.” The one who hopes in the Lord is the person who has no awareness of sins, who raises free eyes toward heaven. He hopes who knows that he has not offended his Lord, to whom belongs glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM 84

For the sons of Korah, at the end. The psalm is prefaced by this title. I have often said that wherever the title “of the sons of Korah” occurs, there is nothing sad but always something joyful. For the father’s sorrow is consoled by the joy of his sons.

Finally, read through the psalms carefully, and wherever you find the title “of the sons of Korah,” you will find nothing sad. I have often said that Korah is interpreted as “the place of Calvary”; necessarily, therefore, it signifies something joyful.

Finally, who is this Korah? The one who was going up from Jericho to Bethel. Bethel means “house of God.” Pay close attention. Whoever is in Jericho and wishes to go to the house of God must ascend.

Therefore our Korah from Jericho—that is, Elisha—went up to the house of God in Bethel. And from Bethel, that is, from the house of God, namely, from the synagogue where formerly the house of God had been, forty-two boys came out and mocked Elisha, our Korah, saying: “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead.”

He came to his house and was mocked by the little boys of Bethel. But that very patient Elisha, who had come to Bethel for the purpose of saving, looked back at himself. He looked back and commanded two bears to come out of the woods, and they killed forty-two boys (2 Kings 2).

So also our Lord, that is, our Korah, when he came to Bethel and wished to ascend, was mocked by the little boys. He ordered two bears to come out—that is, Vespasian and Titus—and they killed forty-two boys.

Who are these forty-two boys? From Christ’s ascension until the overthrow of Jerusalem there are forty-two years. Observe carefully, and you will find it so. Therefore he gave them forty-two years as an opportunity for repentance after his resurrection, when he ascended to Bethel. But because they mocked him, saying, “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead,” the two bears came out and killed them.

“You blessed your land, O Lord.” This is said concerning the coming of the Savior. This is the proper historical interpretation. But according to the tropological interpretation, after we have spoken of the history, we shall speak later.

“You blessed your land, O Lord.” We have said this concerning the coming of the Savior. The land that had offended you and had been defiled by idolatries was saved when you came.

“You blessed your land, O Lord.” The sinner speaks after receiving forgiveness. “You blessed your land, O Lord.” Although it brought forth thorns and thistles, it is nevertheless your creation, and therefore it was saved.

“You turned away the captivity of Jacob.” This concerns those who believed in Christ. “You turned away the captivity of Jacob.” Whoever is in sins is held captive.

“You forgave the iniquity of your people.” You saved your people not because of their works, but because of your mercy. “And you covered all their sins.” The psalm concerns the coming of the Savior throughout, just as he said, “mercy and truth.”

“Yet salvation is near those who fear him, so that glory may dwell in our land.” Truly the glory of God dwelt in our land, and afterward righteousness looked forth from heaven.

“For the Lord will give goodness.” What goodness? “Our land has given its fruit.” Mary, our land, our flesh, has given its fruit.

“Righteousness walked before him.” The virgin earth gave righteous fruit.

For the present we have said this according to the historical sense. Now let us speak according to the tropological sense:

“You forgave the iniquity of your people.” No one forgives except what is owed.

“You covered all their sins.” You covered them with virtues, and therefore the sins do not appear. It is as though he said: You covered iniquity with righteousness; you covered impurity with chastity; you covered blackness with whiteness.

“You softened all your wrath; you turned away from the anger of your indignation. Turn us, O God of our salvations,” and so forth.

Observe what he says: You, for your part, turned away from wrath because of your mercy. “Turn us, O God.” You, turning away from wrath, turned us away from sins.

“Turn us, O God of our salvations.” Why did he not say, “of our salvation,” but “of our salvations”? If we sinned only once, we would need one salvation. We have sinned many times; therefore we need many salvations.

“O God, when you turn, you will make us alive.” As long, then, as the Lord does not turn toward us, we are dead.

“Show us, O Lord, your mercy, and grant us your salvation.” That the Savior descended is the mercy of God. The physician would not have come unless many were sick. Because many were sick, the physician came. Because we needed mercy, the Savior came.

I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me. Many think that when Moses speaks and says, “Thus says the Lord,” or Isaiah and the others do so, and when it is said, “The word of the Lord came to Isaiah,” or to the prophet Ezekiel, the speech comes from outside, and that the prophet hears through these ears what is spoken by the Lord. It is not so. Indeed, what does our Lord say to the Pharisees and the Jews? “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8). And Isaiah says: “The Lord added an ear to me” (Isaiah 5). See what he says: “The Lord added an ear to me.” I did not possess that ear which is in the heart; he added it to me so that I might be able to hear the words of God. And so now, whatever the prophet hears, he hears in his heart. [Col. 1076B] For when we cry out in our hearts, “Abba, Father,” and that cry is one of silence, and the silence is heard by the Lord, so also the Lord speaks to our heart, which cries, “Abba, Father.” Therefore the prophet now says: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me.” The prophet Habakkuk says something similar: “I will stand at my watch and see what he will answer me, and what I shall answer him” (Habakkuk 2). “And I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me.” Therefore, when he says, “I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me,” the Lord speaks in the heart; he speaks in the understanding. Do you wish to know what the cry of the heart is like? Do you wish to know that the cry before God is not one of the voice but of tears? It is said in the Lamentations of Jeremiah: “The pupil of my eye did not keep silent” (Lamentations 2). [Col. 1076C]

For he will speak peace to his people. This is properly said of the Jewish people, who are going to believe in Christ. It concerns the coming of Christ. It is also said concerning the faith of the Jewish people—that is, concerning the apostles and all who believed the apostles. “For he will speak peace to his people.” Peace is not spoken of unless there is no war.

And upon his holy ones, and upon those who turn to the heart. That is, those who first followed the flesh and afterward turn to the heart. So that you may know that this verse is spoken concerning the Jews, that is, concerning those who believed in the Savior, see the examples we have given. Let a Jew read Leviticus to me, together with all those rites that are written there: how the leper enters the synagogue, how the hen is taken and its neck twisted. Then it is said [Col. 1076D] how the blood is sprinkled; it speaks of water; it speaks of hyssop; it also says how his garments are torn, and thus the one who had been a leper enters the synagogue. If we read according to the letter, what benefit is there for us in what we read? But if we have turned to the heart, if we have understood spiritually, we shall see that the leper cannot enter the people of God unless his garments are torn, unless whatever has been closed is revealed. Indeed, see that this leper does not enter the synagogue except through blood and water and hyssop.

Therefore you, who until today have been a leper, did not display your leprosy before you came to the priest. But when you came to the priest, the priest tore open [Col. 1077A] your garments and showed what had appeared covered and sound to be leprous. He placed all your sins and your leprosy before your eyes, and therefore he leads you back into the synagogue of God through blood and water: through blood, through the passion of Christ; and through water, through baptism. Therefore, after leprosy, you cannot be healed except through the passion and through baptism. And when you have done this, that saying also applies: “You will sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you will wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow” (Psalm 50).

Until today you are in Egypt. As long as you have not come to the blood and to the water, you cannot be saved. Do you wish the destroyer who killed Egypt not to kill you? Take hyssop, dip it in the blood, and sprinkle your doorposts. When the destroyer sees the blood on your forehead, [Col. 1077B] he will not be able to approach. Why have I said all this? Because it is written: “And upon those who turn to the heart.” Therefore God cannot speak peace to his people except to those who turn to the heart.

Nevertheless, his salvation is near to those who fear him. I show the way of salvation; I give mercy. Although you have not yet turned to the heart, nevertheless I wait and give you room for repentance. And what is the whole point of this? So that glory may dwell in our land. Therefore he calls you to repentance, so that you, who were a leper, may have Christ as your guest.

Mercy and truth have met one another; righteousness and peace have kissed. O how splendid a friendship! “Mercy and truth have met one another.” You are a sinner: hear what mercy says. You are holy: hear what truth says. If you are a sinner, do not despair; if you are righteous, do not grow proud.

Let us put it another way. There are two believing peoples: one from the people of the nations, and the other from the Jews. To the Jews it was promised that the Savior would come; but to us, who were strangers to the law of God, it was not promised. Mercy, therefore, is in the people of the nations, and truth in the Jewish people, because what was promised has come—that is, what was promised to the fathers is fulfilled in their children.

“Righteousness and peace have kissed.” See what he says: “Righteousness and peace have kissed.” This is the same as what he said above: “Mercy and truth.” Mercy is the same as peace, while truth is the same as righteousness. For whatever pertains to peace also pertains to mercy, and whatever pertains to truth also pertains to righteousness. See, therefore, what he says: “Righteousness and peace have kissed one another”—that is, mercy and truth have made a friendship; that is, both the people of the nations and the Jewish people are under one shepherd, Christ.

Truth has sprung up from the earth. “I am the way, and the life, and the truth” (John 14). He who says, “I am the truth,” has sprung up from the earth. What is this truth that has sprung up from the earth? “A branch shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isaiah 11). And in another place: “For God has worked salvation in the midst of the earth” (Psalm 73).

What do you say, Manichaean, who deny that the Savior had flesh? Behold, the truth—that is, the Savior—has sprung from the earth, that is, from Mary. And righteousness has looked down from heaven. For it was right that the Savior should have mercy on his people. See what he says: “O righteous judgments of God, and how unsearchable are his ways!” Truth has sprung [Col. 1078A] from the earth—that is, the Savior. And again: “And righteousness has looked down from heaven.” Righteousness is the Savior himself.

How has he sprung from the earth? How has he looked down from heaven? He sprang from the earth because he was born a human being; he looked down from heaven because, as God, he is always in heaven. That is, he was indeed born from the earth, but he who was born from the earth is always in heaven. In this way he appeared on earth without abandoning heaven. For God looked down everywhere; but while we were sinning, he turned his eyes away from us.

What he says means this: It is right that the potter should have mercy on his work, and that the shepherd should have mercy on his flock. We are his people; we are his creation. Therefore he has sprung from the earth and looked down from heaven, to fulfill his righteousness and have mercy on his work. Indeed, so that you may know that righteousness does not signify cruelty but mercy, see what he says:

For the Lord will give goodness. Therefore he looked down from heaven, to have mercy on his works. And our earth will give its fruit. “Truth has indeed sprung from the earth”—this concerns the past. Now the future is spoken of: “And our earth will give its fruit.” Do not despair: what was once born from Mary is born daily in us as well. “And our earth will give its fruit.” We too can give birth to Christ, if we wish. “And our earth will give its fruit,” from which the heavenly bread may be made, concerning which it is said: “I am the bread that came down from heaven” (John 6).

We have said all this concerning the mercy of the Lord, because he came for the very purpose of saving the human race. Nevertheless, we must know that he himself will judge the living and the dead; he himself will come to judgment.

Righteousness will walk before him, and will set his footsteps on the way. Do not be negligent. “Righteousness will walk before him, and will set his footsteps on the way.” See what he says: “his footsteps”—where there are no stones, where there are no thorns and thistles, where the way is level, where he can walk without stumbling. Let us therefore make a way for the Lord in our heart—the way for which John also labored and cried out in the wilderness, so that we might make a way for the Lord (Matthew 3).

Therefore it is now also said: “And he will set his footsteps on the way.” Where he finds a way, he walks. Although previously we had thorns and thistles, and stones as well, it is said to us in Isaiah: “Cast the stones out of the way” (Isaiah 57). He says this so that, when he wishes to walk on our way, he may not strike his foot. The stones that are on the way and are commanded to be cast out are our sins. Christ does not walk in our heart if there is any sin; immediately he stumbles against the stones.

“And he will set his footsteps on the way.” Let us make a way, and Jesus will set his footsteps on the way. To him be glory and honor forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM 85

A prayer of David. This psalm contains the voice of our Mediator as he comes to his passion. At its conclusion, however, the prophet himself takes up the prayer.

Incline your ear, O Lord, and hear me, for I am holy. In accordance with the frailty of the body he assumed, he pours out prayer to the Father. According to his divinity, however, he calls himself holy, just as he once said to Moses: “Be holy, because I am holy” (Leviticus 19 and 20).

Save your servant, my God, who hopes in you. Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I have cried to you all day long. He assumed the form of a servant, and in it he prays to be saved throughout the whole time of the present life. For he knows that, although the spirit is willing, the flesh is weak.

Gladden the soul of your servant. The soul made sorrowful by present tribulations. For I have lifted up my soul to you, O Lord, believing that it would be raised again to you.

For you, O Lord, are sweet and gentle, and rich in mercy to all who call upon you. To those who call upon you with a pure heart, you show yourself gentle, and you grant them abundant mercy.

Give ear, O Lord, to my prayer, etc. For I ask what is right.

[Col. 1079B] In the day of my tribulation. That is, in the day of my passion. I cried to you. From the cross. For you heard me. So that you might restore to you my spirit, which I had commended to you.

There is none like you among the gods, O Lord, and there is nothing according to your works. Among the images of the nations there is no one who can act as you do.

All the nations that you have made will come and worship before you, O Lord, etc. For through my passion they will recognize the greatness of your power. At this point the prophet speaks.

Lead me, O Lord, in your way, and I shall walk in your truth. For if you lead me to your Christ, who is the way, no deception will hold me back. Let my heart rejoice, so that it may fear your name. When I have been rescued from the sorrow of my crimes, then I shall rejoice in you with spiritual joy.

[Col. 1079C] I will confess to you, O Lord my God, with all my heart, and I will glorify your name forever, etc. Why he confesses to the Lord’s name or honors him, the following verse explains, saying:

You have rescued my soul from the lowest hell. He did not mean that there are two hells, but called sin the upper hell and the lower hell the true hell, where sinners are condemned. He therefore praises the Lord’s mercy because he has been rescued from the punishment of the lower hell.

O God, the unrighteous have risen up against me, and the assembly of the powerful have sought my soul. This concerns vices, or demons. The prophet does not speak these words in the person of Christ; rather, they are understood concerning the Jews. They did not set God before their eyes. Their wickedness had blinded them. [Col. 1079D]

But you, Lord God, are compassionate and merciful, patient and rich in mercy and truthful. You are merciful when you forgive; patient when you await the sinner so that he may repent; truthful when you restore what you have promised.

Look upon me and have mercy on me; give your power to your servant. So that he may resist the opposing powers. And save the son of your handmaid. Of the Church, in which I have been reborn.

Work a sign of favor for me, so that those who hate me may see and be put to shame, because you, O Lord, have helped me and comforted me. May I be fortified by the sign of your cross, so that when the opposing powers see it, they may flee in confusion and depart from me. The prophet asks this for our people. But we too beseech you, Lord, that, protected by the sign of your cross and guarded by its defense, we may deserve to be freed from all the snares of the devil; for to you belong honor and glory with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM 86

A psalm, a song, for the sons of Korah. I have often explained the difference between a psalm and a song: a psalm is spoken from the Psalter, while a song is uttered by the voice. A psalm pertains to the hands—that is, to works; a song pertains to contemplation.

Its foundations are in the holy mountains. He did not say whose they were, but said: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains.” The one who speaks is the prophet. They are the sons of Korah. I have often explained what Korah means: “skull,” that is, the sons of the resurrection.

“Its foundations”—whether of God or, certainly, of the Church. What are the foundations except the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit? These foundations, therefore, are not in valleys but in mountains, and not in just any mountains but in holy mountains. Paul says: “As a wise architect I laid the foundation” (1 Corinthians 3)—that is, the faith of the Trinity. Again, in another place, he says: “For they were awaiting a city having foundations, whose architect and builder is God” (Hebrews 11): “Its foundations are in the holy mountains.”

He said “in the holy mountains” because there are also other mountains that are not holy. Indeed, it is said in Isaiah: “Raise a signal upon the dark mountain” (Isaiah 13). And in another place it is said: “Who are you, corrupted mountain?” (Zechariah 4). It is also said in Jeremiah: “Give glory to the Lord your God, before your feet stumble against the dark mountains” (Jeremiah 13). You see, therefore, that there are also dark mountains, and Jeremiah tells us to give glory to God before our feet stumble against the dark mountains. For if our feet stumble against those mountains, we cannot give glory to the Lord.

“Its foundations are in the holy mountains.” Whom can we call its foundations? The apostles. In them were the foundations; there the faith of the Church was first established, and there the foundations were laid. And because each person builds upon the foundation—one gold, another silver, another precious stones—the Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tents of Jacob.

He loves these gates, which we see have fallen. He loves these gates, and he loves this Zion, which has been plowed like a field. And see what he says: “The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tents of Jacob.” See what he says: above all the cities of Jacob, that is, of the Jews; he loves this one city alone. And how do we see the others standing in part, while this one has fallen utterly?

Let us read the Apocalypse of John (chapter 21), and let us read Isaiah (chapter 62), where the city of Jerusalem is built, and its twelve gates are said to be constructed of precious stones; the city itself descends from heaven; its walls are said to be of gold; its streets are said to be paved with emerald; and each gate is said to be made from a single precious stone (Ezekiel 28). These are all the Lord’s riches. Does the Lord love this as human beings do? He forbids us to be greedy, yet he himself builds a city from riches. Therefore, “the Lord loves the gates of Zion.”

Those twelve gates of Zion were clearly written concerning the apostles. “Above all the tents of Jacob”—above all the ancient saints. We have said this for the moment according to one interpretation. Let us also speak in another way: “The Lord loves the gates of Zion.” It seems to me that the gates of Zion are the virtues. For just as the gates of death are vices and sins, so the gates of Zion seem to me to be the virtues. Indeed, he says in another place: “You who lift me up from the gates of death” (Psalm 9). If the gates of death are sins, then the gates of Jerusalem are virtues.

“Above all the tents of Jacob.” See how Jacob, that is, the ancient people, has no foundation, no house established upon foundations, but tents that quickly pass away.

Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God. Therefore, what was said—“Its foundations are in the holy mountains”—we can also say concerning God. We can also say this: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God.” What is this city in which glorious things have been spoken? It was spoken of in all the prophets.

Isaiah says: “Arise, arise, Jerusalem; put on the strength of your arm” (Isaiah 52). Again Isaiah himself says: “I am a fortified city, a city that cannot be attacked.” David also says: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” (Psalm 45). And in another place: “Lord, in your city you will destroy their images” (Psalm 72). The Savior also spoke glorious things concerning this city: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matthew 5).

I will remember Rahab and Babylon, those who know me. Since he said, “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God,” and yet we understand that city, the Church, as gathered from the nations, therefore now the calling of the nations is spoken of: “I will remember Rahab and Babylon, those who know me.”

Let every sinner be confident. The Lord remembered Rahab. I said, “Be confident,” if he returns to the Lord. Otherwise, confidence without tears has no remedy.

“I will remember Rahab”—that prostitute who received the spies of Jesus, who was in Jericho, where Jesus had come, and sent two spies to Jericho (Joshua 2). This world, which is overturned in seven days, wants to kill the spies. And while it desires to kill the spies, Rahab alone, the prostitute, received them. She received them not in a lower place but in an upper room.

Let us first speak according to what is commonly said; for we ought not to omit that interpretation either. She received them not in a lower place but in an upper room, on the roof—that is, in the height of her faith—and hid them in flax, that is, in flax-straw.

For the moment we have spoken according to history, and you see how from that history we gradually ascend to mystical mysteries.

Jesus the leader, who had led the people out of Egypt; Jesus the leader, whose name means “Savior”—with Moses dead and buried in the land of Moab, in the land of Arabia, that is, with the Law dead—wishes to lead his people into the Gospel. He sends two spies to Jericho: two spies, one for circumcision and the other for the nations, Peter and Paul.

Jericho seeks to kill them; the prostitute receives them, the Church gathered from the nations. She believes in Jesus, and those whom Jericho wished to kill she herself saves in her upper room. She places them in her upper room, in the height of her faith, and hides them in flax-straw.

Although she is a prostitute, she nevertheless places them in flax. Flax comes to whiteness only through much labor and diligence. You know that flax grows from the earth, and when it has grown in the earth it is black; it has no appearance and no use. First it is lifted from the earth and broken; then it is twisted; afterward it is washed; then it is beaten; then it is woven; and with much care and labor it scarcely reaches whiteness.

Therefore this is what is said: this prostitute received the spies in her flax, so that those spies might turn her flax into whiteness.

What then? She gives them advice and says: “Wait these three days.” It was not one day, nor two, but three days. See what he says: “Wait three days.” He does not name three nights but three days, because her heart was illuminated.

Then he says, after three days—and what does he say? “Do not go by the level ground, but climb into the mountains.” For the faith of the Church is not established in valleys but in mountains.

Jericho, therefore, is afterward overthrown by Jesus, and this prostitute alone is preserved unharmed. Therefore this is what is said: “I will remember Rahab”—that is, the woman who received my spies—and I will remember her on the day of judgment.

“I will remember Rahab.” What does Rahab mean? We have spoken according to history; let us also speak according to the interpretation of the name. According to the anagogical interpretation, Rahab has two meanings. It means either “breadth” or, certainly, “pride.”

Therefore see what he says. She who once walked on the broad and spacious way that leads to death (Matthew 7), she who was proud and was rushing toward ruin, afterward was changed into humility.

“I will remember Rahab and Babylon.” Babylon means “confusion.” See what he says: “I will remember not only Rahab but also Babylon”—every soul that has been confused by vices and sins.

“And Babylon, those who know me.” See what he says: although someone was Rahab, although someone was Babylon, nevertheless I will remember whoever has known me.

Therefore, if we have been Rahab and Babylon, we too should be confident and say: God has said, “I will remember Rahab and Babylon.” But see what follows: “Those who know me.” There were Rahab and Babylon, but afterward they were converted to me. “I will remember Rahab and Babylon, those who know me.” She who once existed in the breadth of sins afterward rose into the memory of God.

Up to this point he has spoken, as it were, by way of an enigma; now he speaks more openly concerning the calling of the nations. See what he says:

Behold, the foreigners, and Tyre, and the people of the Ethiopians—these were there. He calls them foreigners to distinguish them from Israel. For we are the foreigners, and Tyre. Tyre means “tribulation,” that is, *sor*; and the people of the Ethiopians are black and wrapped in the filth of sins. [Col. 1083A]

“And the people of the Ethiopians.” This is what is said: “Ethiopia will hasten to stretch out her hands to God” (Psalm 67).

“Behold, the foreigners, and Tyre, and the people of the Ethiopians.” What is said means this: those who were formerly strangers, those who were in tribulation, who were placed in the heart of the sea. For it is said concerning Tyre: “Tyre is placed in the heart of the sea.” Those, therefore, who were previously in the sea and were battered by the waves were afterward found in the Church.

“And the people of the Ethiopians.” We were once Ethiopians—Ethiopians through vices and sins—because our sins had made us black. But afterward we heard: “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isaiah 1). And we said: “You will wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow” (Psalm 50). We Ethiopians, therefore, have been changed into whiteness.

“Behold, the foreigners, and Tyre, and the people of the Ethiopians—these were there.” Where were they? Where glorious things were spoken of you, city of God.

Will Zion say, “A man,” and “a man was born in her”? The Seventy translators rendered it in this way: “Will Zion say, ‘A man’?” Many therefore rejected the passage and did not understand what *mēti Siōn* (μήτι Σιών) means; they added the letter rho and read *mētēr Siōn erei anthrōpos* (μήτηρ Σιών ἐρεῖ ἄνθρωπος), “Mother Zion will say, ‘A man.’”

They say this because what follows is: “And a man was born in her.” They also thought it should be said in this way: “Mother Zion will say, ‘A man,’” because a son is said to have been born; hence they go astray through the word “mother.”

Let us first speak according to what is commonly said; for we ought not to omit that interpretation either. Let us say: “Mother Zion will say, ‘A man,’ and a man was born in her.” Those who were born in the Church—the foreigners, Tyre, and the people of the Ethiopians—are those who are born in the Church. They believe in the Church and are born in the Church. For unless they have been baptized, they will not be children of the Church. Those who have been baptized in the Church call the Church their mother.

Let us also speak according to the Hebrew Truth: “Will Zion say, ‘A man,’ and a man was born in her?” What he says means this: Who among human beings will be able to announce to Zion that a man will be born in her and that he himself will save her? That is, no human being can announce to her that Zion will be saved by the man who is born in her.

“And a man was born in her.” Who is this man? “And the Most High himself founded her.” Let the Arians answer, since they say that the Father alone is the Most High: here it is said concerning the Son, “And the Most High himself founded her.” He did not say, “The Son of God, who was in the beginning with the Father.” But what did he say? “A man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her.” If he is called the Most High, how much more is he the Word of God!

The Lord will recount in the writing of the peoples and of these princes who were in her. He did not say, “who are in her,” but “who were in her.” “The Lord will recount”—and how will he recount? Not by speech but by writing. In whose writing? In that of the peoples. It is not enough to say “in that of the peoples”; he also says “of the princes.” And which princes? “Who are in her.” He did not say this, but “who were in her.”

See, therefore, how Sacred Scripture is full of mysteries. We read the apostle Paul; we read Peter; and we read the one who says: “Are you seeking proof of Christ speaking in me?” (2 Corinthians 13). What Paul speaks, Christ speaks. For “whoever receives you receives me” (Matthew 10).

Therefore our Lord and Savior recounts and speaks to us in the writings of his princes. “The Lord will recount in the writing of the peoples”—in the holy Scriptures. The Scripture is read to all peoples, so that all may understand.

What he says means this: Just as the apostles wrote, so the Lord himself also spoke through his Gospels—not so that a few might understand, but so that all might. Plato wrote in a book, but he did not write for the peoples; he wrote for a few. Scarcely three men understand him. But these men—that is, the princes of the Church and the princes of Christ—did not write for a few but for the entire people.

“And of the princes”—that is, of the apostles and evangelists—“who were in her.” See what he says: “who were,” not “who are,” so that, apart from the apostles, whatever may be said afterward is cut off and has no authority afterward. Even if someone is holy after the apostles, even if he is eloquent, he has no authority. For “the Lord recounts in the writing of the peoples and of these princes who were in her.”

Like the dwelling of all who rejoice, [my] dwelling is in you. The prophet speaks to the Church and says to her: “Like the dwelling of all who rejoice, [my] dwelling is in you.” Why did he not say, “The dwelling of all who rejoice is in you,” but said, “as of all who rejoice”?

It is said in another psalm: “When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion, we became as those who are comforted” (Psalm 130), and it did not say, “we were comforted.” So in this place also he says: “Like the dwelling of all who rejoice, [my] dwelling is in you.”

Why did he say all this? Because in the present age, although someone may be holy, although he may renounce the world, he does not possess perfect victory. Indeed, it is said in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew 5). If it had been said, “Blessed are those who weep, for they shall laugh,” it is clear that in the present age there is no certain joy. Therefore our joy is only as joy.

“Her dwelling is in you.” See what he says, so that no one may ever depart from the Church.

We must know that what we have interpreted concerning the Church can also be understood concerning our soul. For if Zion is interpreted as “watchtower,” while our soul does nothing else except continually contemplate higher things, the true Church, the true temple of Christ, is none other than the human soul. The Church of Christ is none other than the soul of those who believe in Christ. “You,” he says, “are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you” (1 Corinthians 3).

“Its foundations are in the holy mountains”—that is, the foundations of God are nowhere except in holy mountains, in the doctrines of the believing soul.

“The Lord loves the gates of Zion.” Our Zion has very many gates; if we open them, the bridegroom enters us and sleeps with us. Indeed, he himself says: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone opens to me, I will enter and dine with him” (Revelation 3).

“Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God.” A city is not one building but consists of many buildings. So too our Zion will not be the city of God unless it possesses many virtues.

“I will remember Rahab and Babylon, those who know me.” She who once existed in the breadth of sins afterward rose into the memory of God.

“Will Zion say, ‘A man,’ and a man was born in her?” I am telling you something astonishing, but true. Our Zion, in which at times there are foreigners, Tyre, and Ethiopians—that watchtower, that prostitute, that Rahab, that Babylon, that woman who spread her legs to every passerby, according to Ezekiel (chapter 16)—if that prostitute wishes, she suddenly becomes a virgin. She becomes a virgin, conceives the Son of God, and gives birth.

“Because of your fear, O Lord, we conceived and gave birth; we brought forth the spirit of your salvation upon the earth.” See, therefore, that that prostitute conceived from God and gave birth to the Savior: “We brought forth the spirit of your salvation upon the earth.”

Therefore our soul—that Rahab, that prostitute—can conceive and give birth to the Savior.

“And a man was born in her.” [Col. 1085B] If we wish, Christ is born daily. Christ is born through each virtue. For if Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God, whoever performs virtue generates virtue.

“And the Most High himself founded her.” He who is born in you himself gives a foundation to your Zion.

“The Lord will recount in the writing of the peoples.” It is clear that what the Lord speaks in Scripture he speaks to no one in the same way as he speaks to Zion.

And yet, when all these things have taken place, when Christ has been born in her, victory is not certain or secure; we are always in danger.

“As of all who rejoice, her dwelling is in you.” The one who is joyful is secure because of his very gladness. But the one who is secure is quickly deceived. The one who fears ambushes, however, can quickly escape, by the favor of the Lord, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM 87

A song of a psalm, for the sons of Korah; to the end, concerning Mahalath, for responsive singing; an instruction of Heman the Israelite. This psalm contains the mysteries of the Lord’s passion, setting them forth to their consummation: the things that the same Lord, suffering for the salvation of the world, spoke to the Father.

Lord God of my salvation, by day I cried out. Dwelling with you in that glory which I have always possessed, I preached repentance to the peoples. And by night before you. Among the darkness of the Jews.

Let my prayer enter into your presence; incline your ear to my supplication, which [I utter] while set in this deep body.

[Col. 1085D] For my soul has been filled with evils. With the sins of the perishing people. And my way has drawn near to hell. When I am handed over for those who are perishing.

I have been counted among those descending into the pit. They thought that, like the other sinners, they were bringing me down into death; they did not believe that I would rise again. I have become like a man without help. Since there is no companion of my freedom in hell, nor any helper to deliver me. Free among the dead. No one bound me in hell; rather, by my own power I loosened the chain of those who were bound.

Like the wounded who sleep in the tombs, whom you remember no longer. Just as those who are sated with the riches of the world and buried in fornications and obscenities are not remembered by you, so I too was snatched from the heart of the Jews. [Col. 1086A] And they were driven back from your hand, separated from your power.

They placed me in the lowest pit. With thieves and sinners deserving punishment. In darkness and in the shadow of death. Into the constrictions of hell, in which death alone will rule.

Your wrath has been made strong against me, and you have brought all your waves upon me. You have brought upon me the anger and storm of the slaughter of your fury, which you were going to pour out upon the nations, because I took their sins upon myself, as he says elsewhere: “Because of the sins of my people I struck him” (Isaiah 53).

You have put my acquaintances far from me. Angels or apostles, so that no one might offer assistance. For I too could have asked you, Father, to present more than twelve legions of angels to me (Matthew 26), but I was silent so that the Scriptures might be fulfilled.

They made me an abomination to themselves. Not the acquaintances, but the Jews.

I have been handed over to death, and I was not coming forth. I was not separated from the Father’s divinity; yet I did not come out of the tomb immediately, so that the delay in the resurrection might demonstrate the reality of death.

My eyes have grown weak because of poverty. In the weakness, so to speak, of understanding, when the apostles, having left him, either fled or denied him, because they did not know that he would rise again, as that beloved disciple says: “For he did not yet know the Scriptures, that he must rise from the dead.”

I cried to you, O Lord, saying: “Eli, Eli, lema azavtani” (“My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”) (Matthew 27). All day long I stretched out my hands to you, extended upon the cross.

[Col. 1086C] Will you work wonders for the dead? Not for those who, while alive, are dead, but for me, who live in you. Or will physicians raise them up, and will they confess to you? Not the physicians’ spices, but you, Father, raise me up. Nor will they confess to you, but I will confess to you among the peoples.

Will anyone recount your mercy in the tomb, or your truth in destruction? One buried in the riches of the world will not praise you, nor will one who dwells in the destruction of sin.

Will your wonders be known in darkness, and your righteousness in the land of forgetfulness? For everyone who commits sin hates the light, and when the body is oppressed by earthly vices, your righteousness is concealed.

But I cried out to you, O Lord, in the secrecy of prayer. And in the morning my prayer will go before you. For in the morning of the resurrection you will glorify me.

Why, O Lord, do you reject my prayer? Do you turn your face away from me? So that this cup may not pass.

I am poor, and in troubles from my youth—from the time when I assumed flesh. But I was exalted—in the cross. I was humbled—in the tomb. And I was troubled—in death.

Your wrath passed over me. It passed over me and did not remain. And your terrors disturbed me—the very terrors which above I declared that I would pour out upon the nations.

They surrounded me like water all day long—the Jews in the waves of persecution. They surrounded me together—the Pharisees with the priests, Pilate with the rulers and the peoples.

[Col. 1087A] You have put far from me friend and neighbor. A neighbor is one who shows mercy, yet no such one was found with me; and you have put my acquaintances far from me because of misery. Because of the confusion of the Passion, even the apostles were separated from me. From there, now descending into hell, and carrying away spoils from the hand of the bound strong man, his work at dawn anticipated the Father, when he rose in the morning and appeared to many. We humbly beseech him to deign to free the people, through his Passion, from the snare of hell, to strengthen them by his might, and to release them from the bonds of the second death, so that, set free and liberated, we may deserve to be joined to his kingdom. To him be glory and dominion, with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM LXXXVIII

**The understanding of Ethan the Israelite.** This psalm is contained in many voices. For it has the voice of the Father addressing the Son, of the Son addressing the Father, of the Church, and of the prophet himself or of the apostles. Thus, beginning with a prophetic voice, he addresses the Father:

I will sing the mercies of the Lord forever—the mercies by which you deigned to visit, through the Son, humanity dead in sin.

From generation to generation—from the Old Testament into the New—I will proclaim your truth—your Christ—in my mouth, in which confession is made unto salvation.

For you said: Mercy shall be built up forever. For your compassion is always exalted and is never destroyed. Your truth shall be prepared in the heavens. It is predestined in the apostles. Here begins the voice of the Father:

I have made a covenant with my chosen ones—with the teachers of the Churches, so that they may teach and instruct the peoples acquired by grace. I have sworn to David my servant. For God’s oath is the confirmation of his promise. “David my servant,” that is, Christ the Lord, who assumed flesh from the race of David. I will prepare your offspring forever—in the believers of the Church.

And I will establish your throne from generation to generation. The Church itself, in which you will sit as king forever. Again the prophet says:

The heavens shall confess your wonders, O Lord, and indeed your truth in the Church of the saints. For the apostles will preach Jesus Christ and the things you accomplish through him in the assembly of the saints.

For who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord? Among the prophets, certainly. Or who shall be like the Lord among the sons of God? There are many sons of God by adoption, but no one can be made like the only-begotten Son, true God.

God, who is glorified in the council of the saints—that is, the Paraclete, who was to be adored in the apostolic assembly and is proclaimed to be equal to the Father and the Son. For the Lord Jesus Christ, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, subsists in one omnipotence. Great and terrible above all who are around him—those who have deserved to draw near to him through an innocent life.

Lord God of hosts, who is like you—in power and might? You are mighty, O Lord, and your truth is all around you. These are the ones of whom you who are truth yourself say: “Father, I will that where I am, they also may be with me” (John XVII).

You rule the power of the sea—the powers of this age. [Col. 1088A] But you still the movement of its waves—the temptations that they stir up against your servants.

You humbled the proud one as though wounded—the devil, who, wounded by the nails of your cross, was humbled among the spoils. By the strength of your arm you scattered your enemies—his attendants.

The heavens are yours, and the earth is yours—the apostles and the other saints, who, placed on earth, lead a heavenly life. You founded the world and its fullness. There is no doubt that the fullness of this world was created by you. But you also prepared for your chosen ones that land of the living in which, when you introduce it, the fullness of holiness will dwell. You created the north and the sea. “The north” is understood as the Antichrist, concerning whom God says to Jeremiah: “From the north evil shall be opened against all the inhabitants of the earth” (Jeremiah I).

Thabor and Hermon shall rejoice in your name. Hermon, I say, is interpreted as “anathema,” as we explained in the forty-first psalm. Thabor, however, means “coming light,” or “let light come.” Therefore, this one who is proclaimed either optatively or prophetically as coming—the light—is understood as the Old Testament. But the one who brings anathema, that is, destruction, points to the New Testament, in which sins are commanded to be anathematized, as the Lord says: “Unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.” Let both therefore rejoice in the name of the Lord: the one when it prophesies that the light of the world will come, and the other when it demonstrates by signs and mighty works that he already shines in the world itself. Your arm is with power. Your strength, with the effectiveness you will, shall prevail.

Let your hand be strengthened—the works that you perform in the world. And let your right hand be exalted—your majesty, or the Church acquired among the nations. Justice and judgment are the preparation of your throne. Unless someone first practices justice and judgment, he cannot become your throne.

Mercy and truth go before your face. For wherever mercy and truth accompany one another, there too the gaze of your face is turned. Blessed is the people who know jubilation—spiritual jubilation, by which the wickednesses of the world are overthrown, just as once Jericho fell at the jubilation of Jesus and the priests, serving as a figure of the world (Joshua).

Lord, they shall walk in the light of your face—in the illumination of the Holy Spirit. And they shall rejoice all day in your name—in that new name which is blessed on earth, namely, “Christian.” And in your justice they shall be exalted—following and keeping it.

For you are the glory of their strength. For they glory in you and in no other. And by your good pleasure our horn shall be exalted. For just as your commandments were pleasing to them, so it was pleasing to you that their strength should be exalted in you.

For the Lord’s is our assumption—of flesh, certainly—and the Holy One of Israel is our king: the Lord Jesus Christ himself, who reigns in the Church. Here again the prophet speaks to the Father:

Then you spoke in a vision to your saints—to the prophets and the other chosen ones—and you said: I have placed help in one who is mighty—for the people, certainly—in one who is powerful, that is, against the devil, to suppress his pride. And I exalted the chosen one from my people—Christ the Lord. He is called “chosen from the people” because he assumed flesh from a human being.

I found David my servant. He found him—he chose him, certainly, so that he might assume flesh from his race. But when he says “servant,” the Apostle explains it: “He did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but took the form of a servant” (Philippians II). With my holy oil I anointed him—not with sorrowful and corrupt oil, but with oil full of joy and holiness.

For my hand shall help him, and my arm shall strengthen him—in the body he assumed.

The enemy shall profit nothing against him—the devil, certainly. And the son of iniquity shall not add to harming him—Judas the betrayer, who is rightly called the son of iniquity, that is, of the devil, because the devil entered his heart so that he might betray Christ.

And I shall cut off his enemies from before him—the Jews, certainly, who, often confounded by the Lord and as though cut apart by swords, withdrew from his sight. And I shall put to flight those who hate him. He speaks of the wicked demons, who often fled before him, crying: “Why have you come to torment us before the time? We know that you are the Son of God” (Matthew VIII).

And my truth and my mercy are with him. Truth, because he speaks the things he has heard from me. Mercy, because he heals the sick, both in mind and in body. And in my name his horn shall be exalted—the strength of the Church redeemed by his blood.

[Col. 1089C] And I shall place his hand upon the sea—I shall display his works to the world—and his right hand upon the rivers—over the principalities and powers of the world.

He shall call upon me: You are my Father, my God, and the protector of my salvation. We read in the Gospels that he called God the Father many times, as in: “Father, glorify me with yourself” (John XVII). And again: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke XXIII). “My God.” He also calls him God when he says: “God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” and many other such things.

And I shall make him my firstborn, exalted above the kings of the earth. For the Lord Jesus is the firstborn from the dead (Colossians I), as the Apostle says: “Having been exalted, he ascended into heaven, subjecting all the kingdoms of the world.”

Forever I will keep my mercy for him, and my faithful covenant with him. In the Church, which he redeemed through mercy and the covenant of his commandments, these things are perpetually preserved.

And I shall establish his offspring forever and ever, and his throne like the days of heaven. For the congregation of the saints that is in the Church, in which God sits as upon a throne, shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of the Father.

But if his sons forsake my law, and so forth. The fact that those who abandon the law, forget judgments, profane ordinances, and transgress commandments are corrected with the rod—that is, with God’s discipline—and that divine mercy is not taken away, demonstrates that no one is to be excluded from the Church without hope of restoration. For just as divine severity terrifies, with justice administering rebuke, so piety restores, with clemency moderating it.

Once I have sworn by my holiness—in that Lordly man. If I lie to David. For God is circumscribed by no lie, as the Evangelist says: “Not one iota or one stroke shall pass from the law until all things are accomplished” (Matthew V). His offspring shall remain forever—the acquired people. And his throne shall be like the sun before me. He again and again promises that the Church itself will remain in the glory of future blessedness. And like the full moon forever—entirely luminous, entirely perfect, containing no darkness within itself. And a faithful witness in heaven—Christ the Lord himself, who gave faithful testimony concerning the Father’s work in the world and is to be raised into the heavens. Here begins the apostolic voice to the Father:

But you have rejected and despised. For we are separated from our king while he suffers. You have delayed your Christ—by handing him over to his enemies.

You have overturned the covenant of your servant—the covenant by which he had promised that we would reign with him. You have profaned his sanctuary on earth. For you had promised that you would not allow your holy one to see corruption, and now he is covered in the tomb.

You have torn down all his hedges—the words of the Law and the prophets by which he was held in. You have made his stronghold fear—us, who listened to him when he taught the crowds.

All those who pass along the way have plundered him. For they pass by him who said: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John XIV), when they either divide his garments or pierce his body with nails and a sword. He became a reproach to his neighbors—to the Jews and the chief priests, who said: “Ah! You who destroyed the temple of God and rebuilt it in three days, come down from the cross” (Matthew XXVII).

You exalted the right hand of those who oppressed him—when you humbled him unto death. You gladdened all his enemies—Pilate with the Gentiles and the Jews.

You turned away the help of his sword—when the word of his preaching profited the Jews nothing. And you did not assist him in battle—in the conflict, certainly, of the Passion.

You destroyed him from purification. For if his purity had been bound to him, his garments would certainly not have been stained by our crimes, as he himself says: “Their blood was sprinkled upon my garments, and I stained all my clothing” (Isaiah LIII). For he was also counted among the wicked and crucified with thieves. And you struck his throne to the ground—the souls of the saints upon whom he rested, who were troubled at his death.

You shortened the days of his time. His days were shortened so that he might return more quickly to the Father. You drenched him with confusion—with the confusion of death, certainly. The apostles said these things, ignorant that he had to rise from the dead. That they did not know this, the Evangelist records. For concerning the beloved disciple he says: “For he did not yet know the Scriptures, that he had to rise from the dead” (John XX). And Peter regarded the words of this resurrection as though they were delirious ravings. Thomas, however, said: “Unless I see, I will not believe” (ibid.). Therefore the apostles spoke such things as though reproaching the Father, because they were ignorant that he would return from the underworld. Following these words, the Church says:

How long, O God, will you be angry to the end? Will your wrath burn like fire? How long will you be angry, so that you do not bring him back from death?

Remember, Lord, what my substance is. I have no substance of life except in him whom I await, returning from Tartarus. For did you establish all the children of human beings in vain? If you established them not in vain but truly in the hope of resurrection, how much more ought you to raise your Son!

[Col. 1091B] Who is the human being who shall live and not see death? Or who shall rescue his soul from the hand of hell? I know that no human being of flesh escapes death, nor can he preserve his soul from the underworld. But I know that God lay hidden, concealed beneath the veil of flesh, whom death and hell ought not to retain.

Where are your ancient mercies, Lord, as you swore to David in your truth?—if he is not raised here?

Remember, Lord, the reproach of your servants—who await him—the reproach which I have held in my bosom from many nations, whom I gathered as though into one bosom, in one house of belief.

The reproach with which your enemies reproached, Lord—the Jews, Pharisees, and Sadducees. The reproach with which they reproached him. What did they reproach him for? The exchange of your Christ. For, exchanging himself from them to the nations, he said: “Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate” (Luke XIII).

Blessed be the Lord forever; let it be, let it be. Behold, blessed; behold, glorified, when he returns from the underworld, when he presents himself to the disciples, when he restores the Church’s vows and pious desires, saying to the saints: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew, final chapter). May he deign to change us from evil works to good ones, and, having made us worthy through his mercy and filled with the Holy Spirit, establish us in his kingdom according to his customary compassion. For to him belong glory and dominion, with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, unto ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM LXXXIX

**A prayer of Moses, the man of God.**

[Note: [Col. 1091D] Yet the author does not conclude from this title—although the point was readily available—that the psalm should be attributed to Moses. Jerome had taught this elsewhere, including from Origen’s view in Book I Against Rufinus: “Origen thinks that the eighty-ninth psalm also, which is entitled ‘A Prayer of Moses, the man of God,’ and the remaining eleven that have no titles, belong, according to Huilli’s exposition, to the same Moses; nor does he disdain, when interpreting the Hebrew Scripture, to insert at each passage what seems to the Hebrews to be the case.” [Col. 1092D]]

There are four psalms prefaced with the word “prayer”: the sixteenth, the eighty-fifth, the eighty-ninth, and the hundred and first. In the hundred and first it says: “The prayer of the poor man when he is anxious and pours out his prayer before God.” This one is entitled: “A prayer of Moses, the man of God.” We read the song of Moses which, in Exodus, at the time when the people crossed the Red Sea and Pharaoh and all his army had been drowned, Miriam and Moses sang (Exodus XV). Then we also read in Deuteronomy that he had written that song in Deuteronomy (chapter XXXII). If, therefore, these psalms and these songs belong to Moses, why are they not found in their proper books? We have explained, then, how the hundred and first psalm is entitled “A prayer of the poor man,” and that another person wrote about him, and that the poor man who intercedes for us is the Lord, who, although he was rich, became poor for our sake, and so forth (II Corinthians VIII). Thus also here: since Moses himself wrote the history of the human race from its beginning—for he himself wrote how heaven and earth were made, how the human being was made, and about the creation of humanity—this psalm speaks about the creation of humanity: what the human being is and why he was born. Therefore the one who wrote in Genesis about the creation of human beings is now also introduced by the Holy Spirit to discuss what the human being is.

Lord, you have become our refuge from generation to generation. Whoever seeks refuge seeks it either from excessive heat and burning, or because a wild beast is pursuing him, or because enemies pursue him in order to kill him. We too are in the heat of this age, and a beast pursues us, concerning which we say: “Do not hand over to beasts the soul that confesses you” (Psalm LXXIII). Enemies also pursue us; therefore we flee beneath your wings for refuge. “From generation to generation”: in the past, the present, and the future. Alternatively: “From generation to generation”: in the former Jewish people and in the new Christian people.

Before the mountains were made, and the earth and the world were formed.

[Note: [Col. 1092D] See the letter in our recension, number 140, to Cyprian, section 6, and the notes that we add to that passage. From this you may also conclude that, if Jerome had composed this work, he plainly could not have remained silent about it, given the strikingly similar recurring formulation.]

Heresy intrudes at this point. If he became our refuge before the mountains were made and the world was formed, then souls existed before the world existed. [Col. 1092C] For what does Scripture say? “Lord, you have become our refuge,” it says, “from generation to generation”—from the beginning of the world, before the beginning of the world. That is what they say. And lest you think, he says, that I am saying “before the mountains were made, and the earth and the world were formed,” you yourself, he says, became our refuge. But if our refuge existed before the world came to be, then souls existed before the world came to be. You make a bad distinction, heresy. Why do you slander the Holy Spirit? Speak as the Holy Spirit spoke.

Thus it must be read: “Lord, you have become our refuge from generation to generation”—up to this point there is a division. Again, another beginning: “Before the mountains were made, and the earth and the world were formed, from age to age you are God.” You are God before the mountains were made; you are God before the earth and the world were formed. From age to age you are God. You always are; you are eternal.

Do not turn the human being toward humiliation, and you said: “Turn back, children of human beings.” O Lord, we dare to ask this and to say: “Do not turn the human being toward humiliation.” You gave us confidence by saying: “Return to me, children; return, and I will heal your breaches” (Ezekiel XVIII; Hosea XIV). And you said: “Turn back, children of human beings.”

For a thousand years in your sight are like one day that has passed, and like a watch in the night, they are counted as nothing; so shall their years be. According to the historical sense, we must know that the night is divided into four watches. Thus it is also said in the Gospel: “But in the fourth watch” (Matthew XIV and Mark IV). One watch, therefore, is three hours. The night is divided into four watches. Hence soldiers have four stations when they keep watch, remain on guard, and serve.

See, then, what he says: O how brief is our eternity! Adam, our ancestor, who lived nine hundred and thirty years—even Methuselah, who lived nine hundred and sixty-five years (Genesis V)—suppose that he lived a thousand years: in comparison with your eternity, whatever was great is brief. For what can be great that has an end? Our thousand years, before we offended, were one day with you. Why do I say one day? One watch. See what he says: You deigned to descend for our salvation; you poured out your blood for us; do not allow us to perish and die in humiliation. You yourself said: “When I have been lifted up, I will draw all things to myself” (John XII). You were lifted up and lifted us up; do not abandon us, so that we may be brought low.

In the morning, let it pass like grass; in the morning let it bloom and pass away; in the evening let it fall, grow hard, and wither. O mysteries of Scripture! “In the morning, let it pass like grass.” Our Lord and Savior speaks in the Gospel about hay which grows in one day and withers in one day (Matthew VI). How grass, which is green and flowering, appears in the morning to be like a flower and green, but when the sun comes and covers it, toward evening it withers and falls away—so also our whole life appears like a flower while it is green and withers. You saw a young man ten years ago. Nothing was more beautiful than he; he ran here and there. If you look at him now, he appears in old age almost dead. Though he may live in old age, youth has nevertheless perished. “In the morning, let it pass like grass”—that is, our youth. For youth itself is the morning. “Like grass, let it pass; in the morning let it bloom, and let it pass.” We bloom in youth; we wither in old age. In the evening let it fall, grow hard, and wither.

For we have failed because of your anger, and in your wrath we have been troubled. Formerly we lived nine hundred and thirty years and had nearly reached a thousand. Behold, our life has been contracted into a brief span.

You have placed our iniquities before your sight. Nothing is hidden from you—that is, our sins; neither night hides them, nor darkness envelops them. Everything shines before you. Our age is in the illumination of your face. The Hebrew has it better: “Our life is in the illumination of your face.” Whatever we do, whatever we think we do in secret, lies open before your eyes.

For all our days have failed. Time has run its course, and while we are unaware, we perish grievously. Even this very thing that we are saying is about death, and we do not understand it.

[Col. 1094A] Our years shall be meditated as a spider’s web. See what he says. Just as a spider sends out threads, runs here and there, and weaves all day long, and the labor is indeed great but the result is nothing, so human life also runs here and there. We seek possessions, desire riches, beget children, labor, are raised up into kingdoms, and do everything, yet we do not understand that we are weaving a spider’s web.

The days of our years are seventy years. Where are the thousand years? We have been contracted into seventy years. But if much, eighty. If we live longer, it is no longer life but death.

And if they are in strength, eighty years. For whom will you find who is eighty years old and healthy? The Greek saying also says: old age itself is a disease. And their surplus is labor and sorrow. Whatever exceeds this is not life but sorrow.

Thus far we have spoken according to the historical sense. Let us otherwise speak according to the anagogical sense. Every psalm indeed admits a tropological interpretation, and I could now run through each verse and explain the spiritual meaning in each, but the hour is excluding us. Nevertheless, I give you, in one verse as it were, a taste of spiritual understanding, so that whatever I leave unsaid here you may consider to have been said here.

“The days of our years are seventy years.” Seventy years are seven decades, and eighty years are eight decades. Observe, then, how the seventh and the eighth numbers are proclaimed. And just as we said, “You have become our refuge from generation to generation,” in the Old and New Testaments, so now he places the seventh and eighth numbers. He says this in Ecclesiastes: “Give a portion to seven, and also give a portion to eight” (Ecclesiastes XI). Therefore there are also fifteen psalms of degrees—that is, seven and eight. Together the fifteen lead us to the kingdoms of heaven.

Indeed, after the seventh psalm of degrees has been completed, what is said in the inscription of that psalm? “A psalm of Solomon,” it says, “who built the former house.” And what does it say? “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Psalm CXXVI). What, then, does Solomon himself say, whose name is written in the title? “I built the temple, but unless the eighth number builds it, the house has been built in vain.”

We also read in the Gospel according to Matthew: “Blessed are the poor; blessed are the meek; blessed are those who hunger and thirst,” and so forth—and there are eight Beatitudes (Matthew V). Therefore our Lord concluded the Gospel with the number eight. Indeed, nowhere do we find eight Beatitudes together except in the Gospel. The number eight is the day of resurrection.

“The days of our years are seventy years.” Do you wish me to show you, for the moment, that the seventh and eighth numbers contain many mysteries? Let us read Ezekiel. At one gate it says: “Let him enter,” it says, “through the eastern gate into the temple that is being built.” In Ezekiel, toward the end, it says: “The priest shall ascend first by seven and eight steps.” It could happen that at that gate there were seven steps and eight. But observe what he says: the eastern gate, from which the light comes, is our Lord and Savior. It is indeed one gate, and no one enters it except the great priest. And what is said there? “This gate shall always remain closed. It shall not be opened except to the priest” (Ezekiel XLIV).

Thus both the New and the Old Testament were always closed; they were opened only to the Savior. For he is the one who has the key, who opens and no one shuts, who shuts and no one opens. One gate, therefore, has seven and eight steps. In the Old Testament there are Gospel mysteries, and in the New Testament there are mysteries of the Law.

Hear greater mysteries. At the time when Solomon—that is, our “peaceful one,” who says, “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John XIV), for he is our peace, and the peace that surpasses all understanding—built the temple for God, observe what Scripture says there. “There were,” it says, “seventy thousand stonecutters, and eighty thousand carriers” (III Kings V). Observe the number.

The stonecutters, who cut stones, who prepare what is like the foundations of buildings, who lift stones from the earth for the building of God’s temple, are placed under the seventh number—in the prophets and patriarchs. For they, as it were, cast the human race out of the earth and prepared it for the Lord’s temple. The others, namely the eighty thousand, signify apostolic and evangelical preaching: those who, together with God the Savior and with Solomon himself, carried the heavy sins of the nations.

Up to this point the mystery seems complete. Hear greater mysteries. “Those who presided,” it says, “over these works and the temple numbered three thousand.” They cannot be greater. And who presides over the works except those who preach the Trinity?

“The days of our years are seventy years.” There are many things that could be said, but the hour is excluding us.

Make your right hand known in this way, and those who are fettered in heart in wisdom. In some manuscripts it says “the instructed”; in others it says “the fettered.” “Instructed” signifies one thing, and “fettered” another. What, then, does he say? “Make your right hand known.” Why do you contract your right hand for so long? In another psalm it says: “God, why do you turn your hand back into your bosom?” What does this mean? We are placed in sickness; we lie in sins. Send your right hand and raise us. Why do you keep your right hand so long in your bosom? Let your heart pour forth a good word; send your right hand and free us.

Make known to us the mystery that was hidden from generations. “Make your right hand known.” Why do you creep in, Arius? He did not say, “Make a right hand for yourself.” For God was never without his right hand. But what did he say? “Make known your right hand,” which always existed and was in your bosom. Since we cannot know him as he remains in his divinity, let him assume a human being, and thus let us understand him.

“Make your right hand known in this way, and those who are fettered in heart in wisdom”—those who have the fetters of wisdom, that is, who are bound in heart by your wisdom. Let it not trouble you that the passage is obscure. The prophets possessed wisdom, but wisdom itself fettered them; they could not fly without Christ. See, then, who says: “Send your right hand,” that is, your Son. Make him known to us, so that the prophets too, who prophesied as though in shadow, may begin to preach the Lord more clearly.

Turn, Lord—how long? We have sinned greatly; you turn your face away. Our sins are not worthy to be seen by your eyes. Therefore we beseech you: “Turn, Lord—how long?” Behold, so many ages have already passed. The prophets have always proclaimed to the nations that you would come, and you have still not come.

And direct the children of human beings. Since we are crooked, let us be directed by you. And direct the children of human beings. Direct them for this reason: because they are children of human beings. For if they were your children, they would be upright. You said: “I have said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Psalm LXXXI). “But you shall die like human beings, and fall like one of the princes.” And elsewhere: “My spirit shall not remain in these human beings, because they are flesh” (Genesis VI). Because they are human beings, therefore they are flesh. Since, then, they are children of human beings, have lost their status as children of God, and have become crooked, therefore direct us, so that we may again become your children.

And let the splendor of the Lord our God be upon us. The Apostle also says to the Hebrews: “The Lord and Savior is the splendor of the Father’s glory” (Hebrews I). And let the splendor of the Lord our God be upon us. This is also what is said elsewhere: “The light of your face has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Psalm IV). The sign of the cross is our standard.

Thus far we have spoken about the psalm, and, as I think, we have lingered longer than we ought. We understand that we have said much more than we ought to say, but we cannot keep silent about the words of our Lord; we cannot abandon the psalm we have begun. Whatever benefits the soul is not too much; nothing good is sufficient if it is truly good.

Let us therefore ask our Lord and Savior that his splendor may shine in our hearts, drive away from us the assaults of darkness and filthy thoughts, and repel all sins from our hearts; that he may illuminate our darkness, so that the darknesses may flee and the splendor of light may dwell in our hearts. May the temple of the Lord, the tabernacle, and the Holy of Holies always have a burning lamp; may the lamp always shine above in the house of the Lord. For if the lamp is extinguished, the Lord does not dwell in darkness.

Let us also say: “Your word is a lamp to my feet, O Lord” (Psalm CXVIII). To him be glory unto ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM XC

This psalm has no title, because it is sung concerning the head or the members: the head is in heaven, the members on earth. It is properly understood as concerning the fast and that temptation in the wilderness. The prophet foresaw that Christ would come in the flesh to be tempted by the devil (Matthew IV).

He who dwells in the help of the Most High. “Help” is interpreted as *Ezras*. Hence the prophet Ezra is called **βοηθός** (*boēthos*, “helper”), Ezra. He is the one who brought the people back from the captivity of Babylon and led them into the promised land. Therefore, whoever dwells in Ezra dwells in Jesus.

For the moment, according to the tropological sense: he who built a house without hands, according to the Apostle—the house which the Lord had built even for the midwives in Egypt (Exodus I)—shall abide in the protection of the God of heaven. He shall say to the Lord: You are my protector and my refuge, my God. Many enemies pursue me; therefore you are my refuge, my God.

I will hope in the Lord, for he will free me from the snare of the hunters. He did not say, “I hope,” but “I will hope.” For as long as we sin, we do not hope. If we cease to sin, we hope.

For he will free me from the snare of the hunters. There are many hunters in this world who try to hunt our soul. Thus that giant Nimrod was a great hunter before God (Genesis X), and Esau was a hunter (Genesis XXVII):

[Note: [Col. 1097D] Jerome, truly, in his Commentary on Micah, chapter V: “As far as I can recall from my memory, I have never read of a hunter in a favorable sense. Ishmael and Esau were hunters, and they went before as a type of the Jewish people.” [Col. 1098D] Ambrose agrees with this in Psalm CXVIII: “In the whole sequence of the divine writings we find no righteous person among the hunters.”]

—for he was a sinner; and in the holy Scriptures we find no holy hunter at all. We do find holy fishermen.

For he will free me from the snare of the hunters. Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters. The snare has been broken, and we have been freed (Psalm CXXIII). What is this snare that has been broken? “May the Lord,” he says, “crush Satan beneath our feet swiftly”; and the Apostle says: “So that you may be freed from the snare of the devil” (Romans XVI).

You see, then, that this is the hunter who desires to hunt our souls for destruction. The devil has many snares, and he has different snares. Greed is the devil’s snare; so are anger, slander, and so forth. And he will free me from a harsh word. As long as we are in holiness, our soul is tranquil. But when our soul begins to think about sins, it is disturbed and shaken as though by certain waves.

He will shelter you beneath his shoulders. But this is according to that passage in Deuteronomy: “The Lord, like an eagle protecting its young, protects us with his wings” (Deut. XXXII). For it is said there that he protects his young like an eagle. Therefore we may say that God protects us like a father, and like a hen protects her chicks, lest they be snatched by a hawk (Matt. XXIII). Yet we may also say something else: “He will shelter you beneath his shoulders.” He will be exalted upon the cross, stretch out his hands, and protect us. “And under his wings you will hope.” Looking, he says, upon his hands crucified—and if the serpent bites you, you will be healed (Num. XXI). Although you may walk in the desert of this age, if a scorpion strikes you, or a basilisk, or an asp, or any other poisonous creature, be confident [Col. 1097D] of your healing: the serpent has been hung up in the wilderness.

“His truth will surround you with a shield.” Our shield is round—that is, it encloses us on every side. It is not merely a shield, but also a wall. “Lord, with the shield of your good will you have crowned us.” He crowns some people with a shield. See what he says: “Lord, with the shield of your good will you have crowned us” (Ps. V). What does he mean? “You will protect us; you will make us victorious, and after the victory you will crown us.”

“His truth will surround you with a shield.” Since he had spoken of “the harsh word,” we may understand the harsh word as that of heretics, philosophers, and Jews. Such a harsh word is not true but false. It is turbid because it is false; it is turbid because, through its lie, it troubles our souls. The Lord, then, who is truth and says, “I am the truth” (John XIV), surrounds us with his truth as with a shield, so that we may not be struck by the devil’s burning arrows. Therefore Christ, who is truth, holds up his shield, so that with the shield of truth he may overcome falsehood.

“You will not fear the terror of the night.” For the devil is always in darkness, so that he may strike, as it says, “in secret” the innocent (Ps. IX and LXIII). You see, therefore, that the one who is simple is innocent, and is always struck in secret. “You will not fear the terror of the night.” What this means is: even if you have been in error—which is night—you will not fear, because you have the shield of truth.

“From the arrow flying by day.” The devil’s flying arrow seems to me to be the speech of heretics and philosophers. They too promise the light of knowledge and say that they possess day; and they can deceive only if they have promised light. But the light they promise is made of burning arrows. Therefore it says: “From the arrow flying by day, from the business that walks about in darkness.”

The arrow indeed flies as if by day, but the business is something that walks about in darkness. “From assault and from the noonday demon.” It is better to say in Greek, ἀπὸ συμπτώματος. *Symptōma* means an event—that is, when we are not expecting it and something new occurs. Or *symptōma* is used when many fall together.

See, then, what he says: although many have been unlearned, you who are holy must not be led astray. I shall give an example, so that simpler people may understand what is being said.
