If you go alone as a monk into a city and begin to walk about, and hear a shout in the circus, and someone says to you, “Come and watch; it is the circus,” and you begin to tell him, “It is not permitted; I cannot go”; if he shows you countless thousands of people and says to you, “Two hundred thousand people are there,” are all those people therefore going to perish, while you alone will be saved? You must understand that this is the devil’s *symptōma*—that is, you must know that many fall.

“And from the noonday demon.” Many people say that there are demons who are active at noon, and this is commonly said. But I speak simply: the demon has power over us at the time when we sin. Whether we sin in the morning, in the evening, or at night, whenever we sin, the demon enters us. You see, therefore, that what is commonly said is frivolous.

What, then, does “from the noonday demon” mean? Abraham received angels at noon, and Joseph invited his brothers to lunch at noon (Gen. XVIII and XLIII). Both Abraham and Joseph were holy, and therefore their banquet was in clear light, with the sun at its full strength. For this reason they feed at noon. And I too, if I possess complete knowledge of the Scriptures, even if it is the third hour, nevertheless feed you at noon.

Indeed, the bride also says in the Song of Songs: “Where do you feed?” she says; “where do you lie down? At noon” (Song I). You see that the bridegroom neither feeds nor reclines at the third hour, but at noon. “Where do you feed, where do you lie down, where do I find you, where do you enjoy delights, where can I find you, my bridegroom?” Do you wish to find me? At noon—in perfect knowledge, in good works, in clear light.

Since, then, we have our noon, the devil too is transformed into an angel of light (II Cor. XI), and he himself pretends to possess light and noon. When heretics promise what seem to be mysteries, when they promise the kingdoms of heaven, continence, fasting, holiness, and renunciation of the world, they promise noon. But because it is not Christ’s light, it is not noon, but the noonday demon.

“A thousand will fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand.” Each word of Scripture is a sacrament; these words, which worldly people think rustic, are full of sacraments. For “we have this treasure in earthen vessels” (II Cor. IV). We have the treasure—the divine meaning—in words of the humblest kind.

“A thousand will fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand.” At whose side? At the side of the one to whom it had been said: “His truth will surround you with a shield; you will not fear the terror of the night.” Who is this? The one of whom it was said above: “The one who dwells in the help of the Most High will abide under the protection of the God of heaven.” From him, then, who dwells in the Lord’s help, a thousand will fall at his side, and ten thousand at his right hand.

The saint is said to have a right side; a left is not mentioned, but rather a side. See what is said: “And ten thousand at your right hand.” How could you have said, “A thousand will fall at your side”? Whenever the right hand is mentioned and the left is not named, the side is named in place of the left. It would not have been right for a righteous man to have a left side. “If anyone strikes you,” he says, “on your right cheek, offer him the other also.” He did not say “the left”; for what is offered is not a left, but another right. Therefore I say simply: the righteous man has two right hands.

Indeed, that Ehud who is mentioned in the Book of Judges is said for this reason to have had two right hands: because he was righteous [Col. 1099D] and killed that exceedingly fat king. “A thousand will fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand.” There are more who lie in wait for our right hand; there are not as many who lie in wait for our left. Therefore a thousand will fall at the side and ten thousand at the right hand. Where the battle is greater, the victory is greater. Few lie in wait at the side; more lie in wait at the right hand.

“For he has commanded his angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways,” and so forth. The devil interpreted this passage concerning the Lord at the time when he tempted him: “If you are the Son of God,” he said, “throw yourself down” (Matt. IV). “For it is written concerning you: ‘He has commanded his angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways. In their hands they will carry you, lest you perhaps strike your foot against a stone.’”

The devil said nothing more than this: “He has commanded his angels concerning you, to carry you in their hands, lest you perhaps strike your foot against a stone.” He omitted the middle part. For here it says: “He has commanded his angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways.” He did not say “to guard you,” for he knew that this was against him. The Lord could have answered him: “If the Lord guards me in all my ways, then I am also guarded from you.” He therefore kept silent about what he knew was against him and included what favored his own case.

Truly, the devil, as a devil, interprets concerning the Savior something that does not concern the Savior. For if the whole psalm concerns the Savior, as you interpret it, O devil, then the following too concerns him:

“I will protect him, because he has known my name.” This means: “I, the Father, will protect my Son.” If you interpret it in this way, devil, let us see how you understand it; let us see whether the meaning stands: “I will protect him, because he has known my name”—that is, “I, the Father, will protect my Son.”

“He cried out to me, and I will hear him.” This refers to the day of the cross.

“I am with him in tribulation; I will rescue him and glorify him.” This means: “I will make him rise again.”

“With length of days I will fill him.” This means: “He will live forever.” Let us understand this also of the Son of God: “With length of days I will fill him.”

But how does what follows stand with reference to the Savior? “And I will show him my salvation.” The salvation of God is the Son of God. If this is said of the Son, how can the statement stand, since the salvation of God is the Son of God? You see, then, that you have interpreted it badly, O devil.

But let us grant that it should be interpreted as you say. You said: “He has commanded his angels concerning you, to carry you in their hands, lest you perhaps strike your foot against a stone.” Say what follows. Why are you silent? “He will walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and he will trample the lion and the dragon”—Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM XCI

*A psalm of a song for the day of the Sabbath.*

This psalm is marked in advance by this title. No one can keep the day of the Sabbath unless he has passed through the six days. We labor for six days; on the seventh day we rest. Therefore we cannot sing to the Lord except on the day of the Sabbath. As long as we perform the works of this world—that is, during the six days—we cannot sing to the Lord.

Accordingly, it is said in Leviticus: “You shall do no servile work on the day of the Sabbath” (Lev. XXIII). Whoever is in the Sabbath and in the Lord’s rest ought not to perform servile work—that is, work belonging to this world—but ought to perform the work belonging to the Sabbath.

Do you wish to know that priests work in the temple of the Lord on the Sabbath? No one is permitted to cut wood on the Sabbath (Num. V). Indeed, one man who was found in the wilderness was stoned and killed. It is not permitted to kindle a fire; it is not permitted to perform any kind of work.

Yet you see that everything which no one is permitted to do in the world is permitted to the priests alone on the Sabbath. They cut wood, place fuel under the fire, perform other services, and sacrifice victims. Why have I said all this? To show that the law commands us to cease even on the day of the Sabbath from the works of the world and to do those things that pertain to God.

The psalm, therefore, is a song for the day of the Sabbath: when we do not work for the world but work for God. Let us see what we ought to sing on the Sabbath, when we cease from the works of the world.

[Col. 1101A] “It is good to confess to the Lord and to sing praises to your name, O Most High.” He did not say, “It is good to sing praises, and afterward to confess,” but observe the order: “It is good to confess, and it is good to sing praises.” First do penance, erase your sins with tears, and afterward sing to the Lord: “It is good to confess to the Lord”—not to human beings, but to God; confess your sins to the one who can heal.

“And to sing praises to your name, O Most High.”

“To proclaim your mercy in the morning and your truth through the night.” Understand carefully what is said: “To proclaim your mercy in the morning and your truth through the night.” Each verse refers to a separate verse. “It is good to confess to the Lord” refers to “to proclaim your mercy in the morning.” If you confess to the Lord, proclaiming the Lord’s mercies in the morning.

“And to sing praises to your name, O Most High.” This verse refers to the one that follows: “and your truth through the night.” For when we confess to the Lord, we hope for mercy; but when we sing praises, we practice virtues.

“To proclaim your mercy in the morning.” Where are those who understand the Scriptures according to the letter? Can we not proclaim God’s mercy at midday? Certainly it is characteristic of Christians and monks, especially during the nights, to confess their sins. How, then, does he now say, “To proclaim your mercy in the morning”?

What he means is this: we cannot confess to the Lord and obtain his mercy unless a clear light begins to shine in our heart. Unless darkness has preceded and morning has come, we cannot obtain the Lord’s mercy. You proclaim the Lord’s mercy in the morning when the sun of righteousness has risen in your heart.

“And your truth through the night.” The Lord’s truth is not proclaimed except in the night; it cannot be proclaimed in the day. The weak cannot bear what is great, nor can they endure what is precious. Therefore it is said elsewhere of God: “He made darkness his hiding place” (Ps. XVII)—that is, the Lord made darkness his hiding place.

The Lord’s truth, therefore, is proclaimed in the night; it is wrapped, as it were, in a kind of darkness of words. It is spoken in a riddle and in parables, “so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand” (Mark IV).

We read in Hosea, and it is said to the prophet: “Go and take for yourself a wife, a wife of prostitution” (Hos. I). Jews and Gentiles laugh. Why do they laugh? Because the truth has been placed in the night, not in the day.

Do you wish to know that God’s truth is in the night, as it were in darkness, and placed in parables? Moses ascended Mount Sinai and, it says, entered into the whirlwind, the gloom, and the darkness, and there spoke with the Lord (Exod. XXIV). For the people of Israel could not see the mysteries of God, because they had not entered into God’s gloom.

“On a ten-stringed psaltery, with song and lyre.” I say simply: whenever we raise our hands without distracting thoughts and disputes, we sing to the Lord on a ten-stringed psaltery.

“On a ten-stringed psaltery, with song on the lyre.” In our lyre, body, soul, and spirit are arranged with all their strings.

“For you have delighted me, Lord, by your creation, and in the works of your hands I will exult.” Whatever a Christian sees always builds him up. Nothing will destroy a monk except sin. Whatever you look upon is your building. You see the heavens, the sun, the stars, and the moon: this builds you up.

You ought to think and say: “If the sun, the moon, the heavens, and the stars serve God, why do I not serve him?” You see the earth, the animals, and everything that is on the earth; compare this with your mind, and it builds you up. Say to your mind: “Everything moves in its proper season.”

Indeed, spring and summer, autumn and winter—these seasons never change, but according to the Lord’s ordering everything serves him. Heaven serves, earth serves, and I, wretched man, do not serve.

Let us come to the small animals. I shall now set aside elephants; I shall set aside lions; I shall set aside the various animals; I shall come to the small animals. Look at the bee; look at the ant. Observe the body and inquire into wisdom (Prov. VI and XXX). The wisdom is greater than the size of the body.

Bees and ants consider that winter is coming, while a monk and a Christian do not consider that judgment is coming. They consider that they may suffer from hunger if they do not labor in summer to provide what they will live on in winter; we do not consider that we shall be tormented in Gehenna without works.

Why have I said all this? Because it is now written: “For you have delighted me, Lord, in your creation.” Whatever I look upon delights me. For I understand the Creator and bless God.

“And in the works of your hands I will exult.” I see a tree and consider how the bark of the tree is like a tunic with which it is clothed, and how its shoot becomes green. Then I see how the flower is formed, how the flower falls, and how the flower itself is transformed into fruit.

Day by day, in each season, I see nature working for me and growing into my food. I see how God labors for me in everything, so that I lack nothing. Therefore I exult in you, Lord.

“How greatly magnified are your works, Lord!” At this point Marcion and Mani­chaeus break out. For what do they say? “If God made everything and made it for the benefit of human beings, why was it necessary to make a bedbug and a flea?”

I answer you briefly: so that your frailty might be shown, O man. You who place your thoughts in heaven, look: you are bitten by a bedbug and tremble. Why do you raise yourself toward heaven, and why does your thought transcend into heaven? Behold, you are wounded by a flea.

“How greatly magnified are your works, Lord!” The bodies are small, but the design is great. Each has its own usefulness. I marvel at the Lord in elephants just as in ants; I praise him in the camel just as in the gnat.

Observe the gnat: it is like a mere point of some tiny body. Yet look at that point of a body and see that all its limbs are divided within it. It has six feet, two eyes, a mouth, a belly, a tube for its voice, and wings. If you consider its limbs, you find no body, and yet God is magnified, because all the limbs exist without a body.

“Your thoughts have become exceedingly deep.” Whatever I may think, I cannot discover it. “Your judgments are an abyss.” “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!”

I too shall say with Ecclesiastes: “I said, ‘I will become wise,’ and it itself became far from me—much farther than it was. And who can discover the deep things?” (Eccles. VII).

What Ecclesiastes means is this: before I put my thought into practice, I did not see the magnificence of God. “I said, ‘I will become wise’”—that is, “I said, ‘I ought to seek the reasons for each individual cause’”—and “it itself became far from me, much farther than it was.” That is, the wisdom which I had previously ignored and did not seek, I afterward began to seek, but could not discover.

“The foolish man does not know, and the stupid does not understand these things.” Whoever is not a Christian and does not understand the Creator in his works is foolish.

“When sinners have sprung up like grass.” You have seen emperors; you have seen prefects; you have seen armies, victories, and triumphs. Yesterday he existed, and today he does not.

“And all who work iniquity have appeared, so that they may perish for ever and ever.” Yesterday he appeared like a flower; today the flower itself is nowhere to be seen. Yesterday the grass was green; today it is withered. Where is that beauty?

Nothing is good except what is eternal. Nothing is good except what is everlasting. Whatever has an end ought not even to be counted among good things. What does it profit me if I was prefect yesterday and today am dying of hunger? What does it profit me if I was king the day before yesterday and today am dying in prison?

Everything that has passed and has an end is nothing. Each of us came from the world into this life. One left a mother, another children, another a wife, another parents. Let us remember our infancy; let us remember our adolescence; let us remember that at some time we possessed wealth, and each of us possessed what he could according to his ability.

Behold, we have passed into this life. Where are all those things? The things remembered cause pain more than pleasure. Therefore nothing is good except what is everlasting.

“But you, O Most High, are for ever, Lord; for behold, your enemies, Lord—for behold, your enemies will perish, and all who work iniquity will be scattered.”

If they will perish, how will they be scattered? For one who has perished once cannot be scattered. He ought to have said: “Behold, they will be scattered and will perish.”

What he means, then, is this: “Your enemies, Lord, will perish when everything has been subjected to you.” Everyone who has been your enemy will afterward become your friend. The human being will not perish; the enemy will perish. The one who was an enemy will be a friend, and thus the enemy will perish.

“For behold, your enemies will perish, and all who work iniquity will be scattered.” Just as it is pleasing when the saints are together, so, if sinners are together, it is like the worst possible assembly (Gen. XVIII). For the more of them there are together, the worse they are.

Indeed, at the time when the tower was being built against God, they were scattered for their own benefit. Their agreement was evil, but the scattering benefited even those who were scattered.

“My horn will be exalted like that of a unicorn.” The horn always signifies kingship. “In you we will gore our enemies with the horn” (Ps. XLIII).

Indeed, no animal is sacrificed to the Lord in the temple unless it has a horn. Three animals were sacrificed to the Lord in the temple: a bull, a ram, and a goat. Three were sacrificed, and all were horned. Unless someone has a horn with which to gore his enemies, he is not worthy to be sacrificed to God.

Therefore the Lord is also called a horn for those who believe in him: “With the horns of his cross he gored his enemies.” There he put the devil and all his army to shame. Christ was crucified there in the body, but in truth he was crucifying the demons there.

It was not a cross, but a triumph; it was a standard. Therefore he mounted the cross, so that he might lift us from the earth on high. And I think that the Savior’s cross is the ladder Jacob saw. On that ladder angels descended and ascended (Gen. XXVIII).

On this ladder—that is, the cross—Jews descend and Gentiles ascend. “My horn will be exalted like that of a unicorn.” Let others have many horns; I have only one horn. “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI).

“And my old age in abundant mercy.” Our old age needs the oil of God. Just as our bodies, when they labor—I speak more simply for the sake of the simpler brothers who cannot understand more elevated matters—just as our bodies, when they labor, are not restored except by anointing with oil; just as the light in a lamp goes out unless you add oil; so the light of my old age needs the oil and mercy of God [Col. 1104C] in order to increase.

Indeed, the apostles also ascend the Mount of Olives so that, since they were weary and their lamps needed the Lord’s oil, they might be illuminated by the Lord’s oil. Hence the righteous man also says: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord” (Ps. LI). And elsewhere it says: “Your children are like young olive trees around your table” (Ps. CXXVII).

Was there no other mountain from which the Lord could ascend into the kingdoms of heaven except the Mount of Olives? Was there not a higher mountain in Galilee, Tabor? Why was it necessary for the Lord to ascend from the Mount of Olives into the kingdom of heaven?

But see what Scripture teaches you: unless you put oil into yourself and your lamps, you will not be able to ascend into the kingdoms of heaven. You must be on the Mount of Olives, and not in the valley of olives, but on the Mount of Olives.

Someone may say: What is this valley of olives? The devil has his olives; he has philosophers; he has heretics; they too have oil. They too promise the light of knowledge, but those olive groves lead to destruction: “May the oil of the sinner not make my head fat” (Ps. CXL).

Let us therefore ask the Lord that our old age, all our labor, and all our darknesses may be illuminated by the Lord’s oil.

I pay close attention in the Scriptures to where I first read of old age. Adam lived nine hundred and thirty years, yet he is not called old. Methuselah lived nine hundred and sixty-nine years, yet he is not called old. I come down to the Flood and, after the Flood, through nearly three thousand years, and I find no one who is called old.

Abraham is the first to be called old—and certainly he was much younger than Methuselah. But he is called old because his old age was anointed with abundant oil. Indeed, it is written there: “And Abraham died, nourished in a good old age, full of days” (Gen. XXV).

He was therefore in a good old age because he was full of days. All the time of his life consisted of days and not of night. The same thing that is said of Abraham is said of Isaac and Jacob. Those who served the Lord together are rightly called the Lord’s old men together.

“He will multiply like the cedar of Lebanon”—a fragrant wood, wood with which the roofs of the temple were covered. “He will multiply like the cedar of Lebanon”—an imperishable wood.

[Col. 1105B] “Planted in the house of the Lord, they will flourish in the courts of our God.” Elsewhere we are planted; in the kingdom of heaven we will flourish.

“I planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the growth” (I Cor. III). Planted in the house of the Lord—that is, in the Church—not in its walls, but in its doctrines. “For the kingdom of God,” he says, “is within you” (Luke XVII).

Whoever is planted in the house of the Lord, if he sends down roots here, bears flowers there. “Planted in the house of the Lord, they will flourish in the courts of our God.” These are the eternal dwelling places.

What are these courts? The various dwellings in heaven. Consider together what he says: “Planted in the house of the Lord, they will flourish in the courts of our God.” Here there is a house; there there is a court. He ought, in proper order, to have said “court” first and then “house.” But see what he says.

Here, although we may seem to be in a house, when we have migrated to the kingdoms of heaven, in comparison with angels and the other powers we are not in a house but in a court; we are at the beginning, not in perfection. For we will not be angels, but like angels (Matt. XXII). Do not think it a small thing for you to be a human being if you become like an angel.

“They will still multiply in abundant old age.” Blessed is the one who grows every day, who grows old in age and grows old in virtues.

For the present we have said these things from the Psalter; we have also spoken a little from the Gospel, and we have spoken likewise from the Apostle. Let us pray to the Lord that we may complete in deeds everything we have said and everything you have heard, and turn words into works, so that we who have been planted here in the house of the Lord may flourish in the court of Christ; to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM XCII

[Col. 1105D]

*A song of praise to David on the day before the Sabbath, when the earth was founded.*

This psalm contains the voice of the prophet, singing of the Lord’s power and magnificence.

“The Lord has reigned; he has put on beauty.” When, rising from the dead, he joined the choir of the saints to himself, “the Lord put on strength,” because he crushed the devil. “And he girded himself with power,” when, surrounded by the angelic multitude, he returned to the Father.

“For he established the world, which will not be shaken.” It would still be unstable and movable unless it had been made firm by his resurrection.

“Your throne is prepared.” In holy souls. For you chose them beforehand, before the foundation of the world, to be an elect race. “And you are from eternity.” And before the resurrection of the world.

“The rivers have lifted up, Lord; the rivers have lifted up their voice.” The apostles, whose streams of preaching watered the dryness of the Gentiles.

“At the sound of many waters.” Of peoples who revile.

“Wonderful are the surges of the sea.” Amid the waves of this age.

“Wonderful is the Lord on high.” Glorious as he sits at the right hand of the Father.

“Your testimonies, Lord, have become exceedingly trustworthy.” Through your apostles.

“Holiness befits your house, Lord, for length of days.” Your Church, which you presented to yourself without spot or wrinkle, in which you deign to keep us pure and radiant [Col. 1106B] (Eph. V), and not to defile the grace of baptism, through which we have been reborn in you for life; because to you, with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, belong honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM XCIII

*A psalm of David, for the fourth day of the week.*

We are always discussing the title, so that the psalm may also be understood from the title. “A psalm of David, for the fourth day of the week.” The fourth day of the week is in the middle of the week, as if in the heart of the Sabbath—that is, in the middle of the week.

It is the fourth day, and the fourth day has equal numbers of days on either side. On one side it has the first, second, and third days; on the other side it has the fifth, sixth, and seventh days. You see, therefore, that the fourth day—that is, the fourth day of the week—is made firm on either side by a double group of three.

At the same time we must consider that the number four is, by its power, the number ten. How so? If you add in sequence—one, two, three, four—the number ten results. You have therefore seen that the number four produces ten, and from this consider that the four Gospels are counted in the Decalogue, so that whatever was spoken in the Decalogue may be fulfilled in the four Gospels, and the old law may not disagree with the dignity of the Gospel.

For the present we have said this about the title; now let us come to the psalm.

“God of vengeance, Lord, God of vengeance has acted openly.” He who for so long lay hidden and did not appear among the people afterward acted openly. Previously he was unknown; afterward he triumphed on the cross.

“God of vengeance, Lord.” If the Lord is the God of vengeance, and the Lord says, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay,” why do you wish to avenge yourself, O man? You have God as your avenger.

The Apostle says this too: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him. If he is thirsty, give him drink. For by doing this you will heap burning coals upon his head” (Deut. XXXII; Rom. XII).

This does not seem to be piety but cruelty. For if I do good to him so that God may do evil to him, this does not arise from piety but from a cruel mind. What the Apostle says—“If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink”—appears to be mercy up to this point. But when he adds, “For by doing this you will heap burning coals upon his head,” you see that he tells us to give him bread and water to drink so that he may be tormented throughout the ages.

Does the Apostle say this, and does the preacher of mercy teach cruelty? It must not be understood in this way, but in another sense. If your enemy strikes you, offer him the other cheek as well (Matt. V). If he does evil to you, do good to him. For if you do this, you will heap burning coals upon his head.

What he means is that you will cleanse him from sin. His cruelty is overcome by your patience. If you shoot an arrow at a stone and the stone is hard, the arrow is not only not fixed in it but rebounds. So if your enemy strikes and is not struck back, overcome by your patience he is converted to better things.

“How long, Lord, how long will sinners exult?” Human impatience does not wish God to have patience. Wretched are we, who want God to be patient with us and impatient with our enemies. When we sin, we want God to be patient; when someone has sinned against us, we do not want God to be patient with him.

“How long will sinners exult?” It is not enough for them to sin; they also exult in their sins. The first misfortune is to sin; the second misfortune—or rather, the final one—is not to do penance. These sinners, therefore, not only do not bow their necks, but openly exult after their sin.

“They will utter and speak iniquity.” This speaks especially of heretics. “All who work iniquity will speak.” Observe the indication: the one who speaks must necessarily do evil. “For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Luke VI). Wherever the conscience is wounded, sin is easily committed with the mouth.

“Your people, Lord, they have humbled.” The people of God are always humbled; the people of God are oppressed. “Your people, Lord, they have humbled.” The people of God are always humbled and imitate God, who was humble and gentle of heart.

“They have killed the widow and the sojourner, and they have murdered the orphans; and they said, ‘The Lord will not see.’” Although this is clear according to the historical sense—for whoever needs protection is always easily oppressed, and the more humble someone is, the more the oppressor offends God—let us also interpret it according to the tropological sense.

For I had said that this refers to heretics. “They have killed the widow.” That widow who has ceased to have God as her husband is the soul of the sinner. The sojourner is one who is not an inhabitant—that is, one who does not dwell. The one who had only recently believed is suddenly scandalized and perishes.

“And they have murdered the orphans, and they said, ‘The Lord will not see.’” We may wonder: if the orphans are mentioned, where is the widow? For just as the widow is the soul of the sinner, so he calls those orphans who have lost the Father—God.

“And they said.” What did they say? “‘The Lord will not see, nor will the God of Jacob understand.’” Every oppressor of the saints says this. While they say this, see what the Holy Spirit replies.

Understand, you who are foolish among the people; and you fools, become wise at last! He who planted the ear—will he not hear? [Col. 1108A] Or he who formed the eye—will he not consider? He who is the potter—does he not know his vessel? He who makes another hear—will he himself therefore not hear? He who gave me eyes—does he himself therefore not see? He who is the author of my understanding—does he himself not understand?

*[Note: [Col. 1107D] Saint Augustine cites this entire section, from the words “This passage” to the end, in his Commonitory to Fortunatianus, or Letter 148, and asserts that it was written by Jerome when he was expounding this psalm. For he says: “Lest I cause greater delays by recalling many things, I insert this one passage from Saint Jerome, so that this brother may know, etc. . . . . .” When, therefore, that man most learned in the Scriptures was expounding the psalm where it says, “Understand, then, you who are foolish among the people, and you fools, become wise at last; he who planted the ear, will he not hear, or he who formed the eye, will he not consider?” among other things he says: “This passage is directed especially against them,” etc. See what we have said on this matter in the admonition prefixed to this work.]*

This passage is directed especially against those who are Anthropomorphites, who say that God has the bodily members that we also have. For example, they say that God has eyes: “The eyes of the Lord look upon all things”; the hand of God does everything. And, it says, “Adam heard the sound of the feet of the Lord walking in paradise” (Gen. III). They hear these things in a simple-minded way and transfer human weaknesses to God’s majesty. I, however, say that God is entirely eye, entirely hand, entirely foot. He is entirely eye because he sees everything. He is entirely hand because he accomplishes everything. He is entirely foot because he is everywhere. Therefore, see what it says: “He who planted the ear, will he not hear?” It did not say, “He who planted the ear, therefore does he himself not have an ear?” It did not say, “Therefore does he himself not have eyes?” But what did it say? “He who planted the ear, will he not hear? And he who formed the eyes, will he not consider?” Has he taken on bodily members and assigned them their functions?

He who rebukes the nations—will he not punish? He who teaches others—does he himself therefore not know? “He who teaches man knowledge”: the implied meaning is, “does he himself therefore not possess knowledge?”

The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, for they are futile. We read in a secular poet:

> “O cares of human beings! O how much emptiness there is in things!”

Both the Gentiles and the philosophers raise this verse to the heavens. And what do they say? “Nothing wiser could have been said. Behold, our rustic Hebrew spoke this before so many ages.” And what did he say? “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, for they are futile.”

Do you wish to know that human thoughts are futile? A father and mother raise a son; they promise themselves happiness from him; they send him to his studies and educate him. He reaches adolescence, and they arrange for him also to serve as a soldier. After they have planned everything for thirty years, a slight fever comes and destroys all their thoughts.

I have an enemy, and the day of judgment is thirty days away. Day and night I think of nothing else except how I shall answer him. I am in my little bed, and my thought answers the absent enemy. You do not have an enemy, yet your words answer an enemy. Day and night I am absorbed in thought. But when the day of judgment arrives, all those things I had imagined perish, and whatever God says—that is what I speak.

Therefore the Lord also says in the Gospel: “When you stand before judges, do not consider beforehand what you will answer, for the Lord will give you in that hour what you should answer” (Luke XII). The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, for they are futile. There is one happy thought: to think about the Lord.

[Col. 1109A] Blessed is the person whom you instruct, Lord. Happy is the one who uses God as his teacher. “And whom you teach from your law, so that you may give him relief from the days of trouble.” See what it says: “Blessed is the person whom you instruct, Lord, and whom you teach from your law”—that is, from your Scriptures. But what benefit is it for him to be taught from your law? “So that you may give him relief from the days of trouble.”

Do you therefore see that knowledge, discipline, and works drawn from the Scriptures alleviate our days of trouble? “Until a pit is dug for the sinner.” When you are instructed from the Lord’s law, one thing is divided into two for you. For it gives you relief from evil days, and it digs a pit for the sinner.

Who will rise up for me against the wicked? Or who will stand with me against those who practice iniquity? The psalms are obscure, and they continually change speakers; therefore they are obscure, and it is exceedingly difficult to know who is speaking in each verse.

“Who will rise up for me against the wicked? Or who will stand with me against those who practice iniquity?” The Savior speaks these verses: “I am holy; I have been lifted up on the cross; I died, I rose again, and I ascended victoriously to heaven. Who, do you think, among the saints will rise again with me?” Therefore what he says means this: “I rose again for this reason, so that others might also rise again with me.”

“Who will rise for me?” When he says “Who,” he challenges the others to rise. For how do we read in Isaiah: “Whom shall I send to this people, and who will go for us?” (Isa. VI), and so forth? Just as Isaiah himself offers himself, so the Lord also challenges us, saying: “Who will rise for me against the wicked?” Whoever rises will rise for me; he belongs to my army. “Against the wicked”—against the devil and his army.

“Or who will stand with me?” Observe the order: he did not first say, “Who will stand, and who will rise?” but “Who will rise, and who will stand?” First we rise, and then we stand. “Or who will stand with me against those who practice iniquity?” It is as though a commander were standing and saying, “Who will come into my army?”

If the Lord had not helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in hell. Therefore, Lord, I rise again because you went to the lower world and rose again. My soul would have been held in the lower world if your soul had not risen from the lower world.

If I said, “My foot has slipped,”—considering my frailty and human weakness, I did not suppose that my foot stood firmly and securely. Wherever I placed my foot, I feared a fall. But then I thought again of your name, and I stood firm on my foot.

According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul. The Apostle says the same thing: that in proportion to the labors and miseries we suffer in this world, we have a reward with God in heaven (I Cor. III). The greatness of tribulations is the greatness of rewards. As many wounds as we suffer, so many crowns do we deserve.

This is what he says: “As often as I performed penance, so often you consoled me. I shed one tear; I deserved one consolation. I shed ten tears; I deserved ten consolations. However great the weight of penance was, so great also was the number of consolations.”

He who fashions labor in the commandment. No one is crowned while sleeping; no one securely possesses the kingdom of heaven; no one with a filled belly can speak worthily about fasting. You therefore see what it says: “He who fashions labor in the commandment.” All the Lord’s commandments involve labor. Without labor we cannot possess the kingdom of heaven.

Do you wish to know that this is so? “If you wish,” he says, “to be perfect, go, sell everything you possess, give it to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matt. XIX). Whoever wishes, he says, to attain the kingdom of heaven must pray day and night, keep vigil, fast, and lie in sackcloth, not on feathers or silk. Penance does not love luxuries. “For I ate ashes,” he says, “like bread, and I mixed my drink with weeping” (Ps. CI).

“He who fashions labor in the commandment: they will lie in wait for the soul of the righteous.” See how it does not seem to agree. What connection is there between “He who fashions labor in the commandment” and “they will lie in wait for the soul of the righteous”? But what the carnal ear does not understand, the spiritual ear will understand.

What, then, does it say? “He who fashions labor in the commandment.” For this reason, he says, we labor in the Lord’s commandments day and night; we keep vigil, pray, and fast, because we have many adversaries who lie in wait for the soul of the righteous.

Observe what it says: they lie in wait for the soul of the righteous, not of the unrighteous. They do not wish to deceive those who have already been deceived, but the righteous. Hence it is said in Habakkuk: “His chosen foods” (Hab. I).

And they will condemn innocent blood. Some people are accustomed to say: “The one who was killed would not have been killed unless he had been a fornicator or had committed some sin. Ruin would not have overtaken him unless he had been a sinner. Shipwreck would not have overwhelmed him unless he had been a sinner.”

See, therefore, what Holy Scripture says: “And they will condemn innocent blood.” As long as we are in this world, we suffer everything in common. The righteous and the sinner suffer shipwreck equally; they have the same flesh and the same conditions of the flesh. The righteous and the sinner perish equally. They have a similar end, but the righteous and the sinner have different rewards. One is led to Gehenna; another is led to the kingdom of heaven.

“And they will condemn innocent blood.” Your conscience is enough for you, righteous one. Even if you are condemned, let your blood be innocent, and it will cry out to the Lord.

And the Lord became my refuge. This passage is directed against the Arians. Since they contradict the Lord Savior on the ground that he is said to have “become” something, behold, we say: “The Lord became my refuge.” There is no doubt that we should understand this as referring to the Father. But if it is said of the Father, “The Lord became my refuge,” it must be understood in this sense: the Lord who always existed became my refuge. So also the Savior, who always existed, became my Savior.

## PSALM XCIV

A song of praise, belonging to David. This psalm contains the voice of the prophet, exhorting people to turn to God with their whole heart.

Come, let us exult in the Lord; let us rejoice aloud in God our Savior. Let us understand that he is the Lord, and that by his death he brought us salvation.

Let us anticipate his presence with confession. Before he grows angry with us, turning his face away, let us confess our sins. And let us rejoice aloud to him in psalms, singing in our hearts and giving thanks to God.

For the Lord is a great God. No one is equal to his greatness—that is, to his power. And a great king above all gods, for he rules all things.

For the Lord will not reject his people, whom he redeemed with his own blood.

For in his hand are all the ends of the earth. For in his fist—that is, in his power—he encloses the whole breadth of the earth. And the heights of the mountains belong to him: the apostolic proclamations that he himself inspires.

For the sea is his, and he made it. These words are to be understood both of the world and of this actual sea, against those who say that the waters were not created by God. Solomon too, speaking in the person of Wisdom, who is Christ, says: “Before he produced the springs of the waters, I existed” (Prov. III). And his hands formed the dry land, whether fields or human bodies.

Come, let us worship and fall down and weep before the Lord who made us, for he is the Lord our God. Again and again the prophet exhorts us to prostrate ourselves before him and confess our sins to him with weeping and tears; they know him to be the God of all ages. And we are the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand, by whose blood we are either redeemed or nourished.

“Today, if you hear his voice,” and so forth. The Apostle explains this most clearly in the Letter to the Hebrews, and we do not presume to insert another interpretation. He says this:

“Some provoked him to anger, but not all those who went out of Egypt through Moses” (Heb. III). With whom was he offended for forty years? Surely with those who sinned, whose bodies were also struck down in the desert. To whom did he swear that they would not enter into his rest, if not to those who were unbelieving? And we have seen that they could not enter because of unbelief.

Let us therefore fear, lest perhaps, after receiving the promise of entering his kingdom, someone among us should be judged to be lacking. For the good news was announced to us just as it was to them. Let us therefore present ourselves as holy, so that we may deserve to enter, through cruelty, into that rest which we hope to receive. Through Christ our Lord, to whom, with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, belong honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM XCV

When the house was being built after the captivity, a song of David. This psalm is marked beforehand by this title. The whole mystery is contained in the title. The sacrament and salvation of our entire life are contained in the title.

“When the house was being built after the captivity, a song of David.” The Jews understand this passage in the following way. When, after the Babylonian captivity, under Ezra and Zerubbabel [Col. 1112A] and Jesus son of Josedech, the temple was rebuilt, David knew in the Spirit five hundred years beforehand that the temple would be rebuilt. This is what they say.

If this is so, O Jew, according to your interpretation, what does the following mean: “Sing to the Lord a new song,” and then, “Declare his glory among the nations”? What is this new song? Who are these nations? You therefore see that, according to the murderous literal sense, the passage cannot stand at all.

It must therefore be interpreted mystically: “When the house was being built after the captivity.” Many of us have been taken captive; many have been led away to Babylon; many have carried the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar on their necks; many have been thrown into the furnace of fire and burned; many have lost the temple, and in them the house of God has been overthrown.

Unhappy Judas, when he was an apostle, was the house of God. The devil came, took the morsel of bread, and immediately Satan entered into him (John XIII); his house was overthrown and was not restored, because he did not perform penance.

But if anyone performs penance after sin, that person’s house is rebuilt after the captivity. Let us therefore also pray to the Lord, first of all that our house may not be overthrown, lest the Chaldean and the Assyrian come and overthrow Christ’s temple in us.

But if it has been overthrown as in a shipwreck, we can be saved a second time by means of a plank. “When the house was being built after the captivity.” Every day this house of Christ is constructed in those who perform penance.

Finally, he did not say, “When the house was built,” lest it appear to have happened only in the past, but “was being built,” to show that this happens every day.

This is what we have said for the moment concerning our soul. For the rest, we can also say: “When Christ’s Church was being built after its ruin.” Let us therefore see what follows this title.

Sing to the Lord a new song. Blessed is penance: even if you have fallen, nevertheless, if you perform penance, you are called a new house of God. Sing to the Lord a new song. A new house deserves a new song.

Sing to the Lord a new song. To whom should you sing? “Sing to the Lord, all the earth.” If this is said of the temple of Jerusalem, O Jew, why is the whole earth summoned to praise? “Sing to the Lord, all the earth.” This passage overcomes both the Jew and the Novatianist. “Sing to the Lord, all the earth”—not Jerusalem, but the whole world. Here the Jew is slain.

“Sing to the Lord, all the earth.” Here the Novatianist is slain. How so? For the Novatianist says: “There are certain sins for which we ought to perform penance.” As if he were to say: “For lying, perjury, or theft. But whoever has committed fornication or homicide cannot perform penance.”

Hear what it says: “Sing to the Lord, all the earth.” The whole earth is both adulterous and murderous, and all sins are earthly. If, then, all sins are earthly, whatever sins you may have, perform penance and you will be saved.

Sing to the Lord and bless his name. The name of the Lord is Savior, from the fact that he became this for us. Sing to the Lord. Declare his salvation from day to day.

What does “Declare his salvation from day to day” mean? A simple person understands it this way: Praise the Lord on every day—that is, let one day follow another; you praised him today, praise him tomorrow as well.

The meaning certainly seems simple, but it seems to me that a mystery lies hidden here. “Declare his salvation from day to day.” The Savior cannot be praised except in the day. For if it referred to this ordinary day, it ought to have said, “Praise the Lord by day and by night.” For we ought to say this if we understand it according to the letter.

If, then, we praise the Lord in the day, can we not praise him again at night? See, therefore, what it says: Whenever you praise the Lord, praise him always in the light—not in the darkness of sins, but in the light of virtues. May the sun of Christ always rise in your soul, so that a new light may always be born in you.

“Declare his salvation from day to day.” Let us say it in another way: There are two days, not three, not four, not five. There are two days: the Old Testament and the New. Christ shines in the one, and Christ shines in the other.

Do not praise him only in the Old Testament, lest you become Jews; do not praise him only in the New Testament, lest you become Manichaeans. Praise him from day to day—that is, in the Old and in the New Testament; these two days make one light.

Therefore it is also written in Leviticus: “Every animal that divides the hoof and chews the cud is clean” (Lev. XI). That is, if it has two hoofs and chews the cud, it is clean. If it has one hoof, it is not clean.

The Jew has one hoof and is therefore unclean. The Manichaean has one hoof and is therefore unclean. And because he has one hoof, he does not chew his food: he does not bring back to his throat what he has once put into his stomach, chew it again, and make it fine, so that what was coarse may once more be sent fine into the stomach. This indeed pertains to speaking of the divine mysteries.

Every animal that divides the hoof and chews the cud is clean. The Jew has one hoof: for he believes in only one Testament, and he does not chew the cud. He reads only the letter and considers nothing; he seeks nothing inwardly.

But the ecclesiastical person divides the hoof and chews the cud: that is, he believes in both Testaments and frequently searches both Testaments. Whatever lies hidden in the letter, he brings forth in the spirit.

Why have I said all this? Because it is written: “Declare his salvation from day to day.” Therefore also the apostles are sent in pairs; therefore we do not have one eye but two; therefore we have two ears, two nostrils, two lips, two hands, and two feet. We have nothing in our body that is single except what is shameful. And the members of our body bear witness to the mysteries of the two Testaments.

Bring to the Lord, families of the nations; bring to the Lord glory and honor. If this is said of the temple of Jerusalem, what does “Bring to the Lord, nations of the Gentiles; bring to the Lord glory and honor” now mean? It means the multitude of the nations, the calling of the nations, and the gathering of the Church.

Bring to the Lord glory and honor. When we honor the Lord in our body, the Lord is glorified in us. Bring to the Lord glory to his name. The glory of the servant is the glory of the Lord. “Whoever receives you receives me” (Matt. X). Blessed is the servant on account of whom the Lord is glorified.

Take up sacrifices and enter his courts. “A holy, living sacrifice, pleasing to God” (Rom. XII; Phil. IV). Take up sacrifices. You yourselves bring sacrifices. What sacrifices? Be yourselves the sacrifices.

Virginity is Christ’s burnt offering. All chastity—whether in virginity, widowhood, or continence—is Christ’s sacrifice. I speak of a new thing: the sacrifice of chastity carries itself.

Take up sacrifices and enter his courts. Worship the Lord in his holy court. I see several courts; I see one court. “Take up sacrifices and enter his courts”—behold, several courts. Again: “Worship the Lord in his holy court”—behold, one court.

See, therefore, that one cannot come from one court to several courts; rather, from several courts one comes to one court.

Do you wish to know this same mystery? Behold, elsewhere that merchant who had many pearls sold many in order to buy one (Matt. XIII). And in Micah it is said: “Stand,” he says, “in the ways of the Lord, and seek,” he says, “the way of the Lord” (Mic. IV). Unless we stand in many ways, we cannot find one way.

What are these many pearls? What are these many ways? What are these many courts, so that we may find one pearl, one way, and one court?

Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; Moses; Joshua son of Nun; Isaiah; Jeremiah; Ezekiel; the twelve prophets; David; and Solomon were courts—that is, they are our courts. First we enter into them, and from those courts afterward we come to the court of the Gospel, where Christ is found.

Let all the earth be moved before his face. See what it says: Heaven is not moved before the face of God; but whoever is earthly—that person looks upon the Lord, and is moved and trembles.

Say among the nations, “The Lord has reigned.” Unless the earth is moved and withdraws from its earthly works, the Lord will not reign among the nations.

For he corrected the world, which will not be moved. Nothing is ever corrected unless it was previously straight and afterward became crooked.

Thus we too, and the whole human race, naturally understand God. For there are no nations that do not naturally understand their Creator. Although they worship stones and wood, nevertheless they understand that something greater exists than they themselves, and in their error they show that they possess wisdom. That is, there is no nation that does not naturally understand God.

Indeed, the Gentiles worship idols—that is, they venerate stones and wood. And if perhaps they quarrel, and if some oath arises among them, they do not say, “These stones see; these pieces of wood see,” but “God sees, and God hears.”

See, therefore, what it says: “For he corrected the world, which will not be moved.” For this reason Christ came and corrected the human race, which had previously been made crooked, so that it would not be moved forever.

For his cross is the pillar of the human race. On that pillar his house was built. I speak of the cross, not of the wood, but of the Passion. In any case, this cross is in Britain, in India, and throughout the whole world.

Finally, what does the Lord also say in the Gospel? “Unless you take up my cross and follow me daily” (Luke IX). See what it says: Unless your soul has been prepared for the cross just as mine was for you, you cannot be my disciples.

Blessed is the one who carries the cross, the resurrection, the place of Christ’s birth, and the place of his ascension in his breast. Blessed is the one who has Bethlehem in his heart, in whose heart Christ is born every day.

Finally, what does Bethlehem mean? “House of bread.” Let us also be the house of him who descended from heaven. Every day Christ is crucified for us; we are crucified to the world; and Christ is crucified in us.

Blessed is the one in whose heart Christ rises again every day, if every day he performs penance for his sins, even his lesser sins. Blessed is the one who ascends from the Mount of Olives to the kingdom of heaven, where the Lord’s fruitful olive trees are, where Christ’s light is born, where the Lord’s olive groves are.

“For I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord.” Let us therefore also light our lamp from this olive tree, and immediately we shall go with Christ to the kingdom of heaven.

For he corrected the world, which will not be moved, although previously it was twisted because of sins. He will judge the peoples in equity. He spoke of the future judgment, at which he will come again to judge the living and the dead.

Let the heavens rejoice—the apostles or the other saints. Let the earth exult—that is, the bodies of the heavenly ones. Let the sea and its fullness be moved—the world and all who dwell in it. The age, certainly, so that it may be changed for the better.

The fields will rejoice, and all that is in them—the holy souls, and especially virgins, who flourish with the varied sweetness of flowers.

Then all the trees of the forests will exult before the face of the Lord, because they are not subject to burning.

For he has come: at his first coming, to redeem. For he has come to judge the earth: at his second coming, to judge.

He will judge the world in equity and the peoples in his truth, so that he may subject sinners to punishments and bestow eternal rewards upon the righteous.

May he, who grants us fear of his name, deign to ensure that at that dreadful time of judgment we are not placed among those on the left, we who confess that we have been redeemed by his blood. To him, with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, be glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM XCVI

A psalm belonging to David, when his land was restored to him. We read in the books of Kings and Chronicles that David was a warlike man, that he subjected all the surrounding nations, and reduced them to his power.

For the present, let us understand this according to the letter in the following way: “A psalm of David, which he sang to the Lord when, after defeating his adversaries, he restored peace to his land”—that is, to Judaea. This is according to the historical sense.

But if David is interpreted as “strong of hand,” no one is strong of hand except the one who conquered all the nations—our David, to whom the demons cried out: “Why have you come to torment us before the time, Son of David?” (Matt. VIII).

This psalm was composed by him when the land was restored. And someone said very aptly that this land which is restored is our bodies. For we truly ought to sing to the Lord at the time when our land has been set in order.

Let us also speak in another way. It does no harm if we understand the same matter in two or three ways. For it is written in Solomon: “You shall take them upon the tablet of your heart threefold” (Prov. III and VII).

It does no harm to say something different when it is spoken by one Spirit: “When his land was established.” Before our David conquered all the nations, this land had no peace; everywhere there was discord. One nation worshiped Jupiter, another Mercury, another Juno, and all the nations had different idols. The banner of the cross was raised, and the whole earth was established.

The Lord has reigned; let the earth exult. Let the whole earth and the entire world, which had previously been subjected to demons and idols, rejoice while our God reigns.

“The Lord has reigned.” The Lord, the Creator who made us, has himself reigned. O you who were previously subjected to the dominion of the devil, now you are subjected to the Lord the Creator.

Let the many islands rejoice. He spoke well concerning our souls, which are battered by various thoughts as though by various waves from every side. Let us also say that the islands are the Churches.

Finally, it is said elsewhere: “Many islands will be turned to me.” Do you wish to know that the Churches are called islands? The prophet says in the person of the Lord: “Speak,” he says, “to the inhabitants of this island.”

Let the many islands rejoice. Just as islands are situated in the midst of the sea, so the Churches are situated as though in the midst of the sea of this world, and are battered by persecutions as though by various waves. These islands are battered every day, but they are not overthrown. They are indeed in the sea, but they have Christ as their foundation, and he cannot be moved.

Cloud and darkness surround him. I think this is the cloud of which it is said in the Gospel: “And a bright cloud overshadowed them” (Matt. VII). At the time when the Lord was transfigured and the apostles fell down, a bright cloud overshadowed them.

I think these are the clouds to which the Lord commanded that they should not rain rain upon Israel (Isa. V). I think these are the clouds of which it is said elsewhere: “Your truth reaches to the clouds” (Ps. XXXV).

The truth of the Lord is that which says in the Gospel: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). The truth of God is Christ. “The truth of the Lord reaches to the clouds.” The clouds are the apostles and prophets; they were commanded not to rain rain upon Israel.

For ever since, according to the historical account, that fleece mentioned in the Book of Judges was dried (Judg. VI), rain runs throughout the whole world. What is said means this: Israel has been dried up, and rain runs over the whole world.

“Cloud and darkness surround him.” We have spoken about the cloud; let us speak about the darkness. The Lord is in darkness. The Lord is either in light or in darkness. He is in light for beginners. For he speaks simply to beginners; to those who are perfect he speaks mystically.

Finally, he did not speak to the apostles as he did to the crowds, but spoke inwardly to them. And what does he say? “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.”

What, then, does this mean: “And darkness surrounds him”? It means, “and mysteries surround him.” Therefore it is also said in Exodus: “All the people stood below, but Moses alone entered the mountain of Sinai into the darkness” (Exod. XIX). For the whole people of God could not know the mysteries that Moses alone was able to know.

It is said of God: “He made darkness his hiding place” (Ps. XVII).

Righteousness and judgment are the correction of his throne. What does “the correction of his throne” mean? It ought to have said, “the stability of his throne.” When it says, “the correction of his throne,” it shows that whatever is corrected was crooked before it was corrected.

Therefore God’s judgment, before he comes to judge, appears as though it were crooked. Now God’s judgment appears to be unjust and crooked. For when unrighteous people grow rich and the saints are poor, does not God’s judgment seem to be crooked?

But when he comes to judge, so that he may repay each according to his works, at that time his throne will, as it were, be corrected.

Finally, do you wish to know that this refers to the day of judgment?

Fire will go before him. Let the person who is holy fear this fire; let the sinner fear it. This fire purifies the holy and consumes sinners.

“Fire will go before him.” He who makes his angels spirits and his ministers a burning fire (Ps. CIII). I think these are the fires—that is, his angels. These angels, therefore, who are his fire, will go before him.

Whom does this fire consume? Whoever is wood, hay, or straw. But whoever is gold, silver, or precious stones is indeed thrown into the fire, but is found purer.

His lightning flashes have illuminated the world; the earth saw and was moved. Philosophers say that lightning is generated by the collision of clouds. For unless a sound has first been heard, lightning is not seen.

The same is said of the fire-producing stone: unless it is struck, the fire within does not emerge. We speak according to the historical sense, and, being still little children, we speak of the nature of things.

Let us therefore discuss the nature of things, so that from the nature of things we may draw forth something spiritual. The stone commonly called firestone cannot emit fire if it is alone; but if it is struck against another stone, the fire is struck out from between them.

Imagine Jeremiah, Isaiah, and Elijah to be one cloud; and Paul, Peter, and the other apostles to be another cloud. When these clouds are struck together, they emit the fire between them, and it shines upon the world.

“His lightning flashes have illuminated the world; the earth saw and was moved.” The apostles’ lightning flashed throughout the whole world. It was moved. They spoke, and the whole world heard the thunder of their voice. Together they possessed both a great voice and shining lightning.

These lightning flashes illuminated believers; they burned unbelievers.

The mountains melted like wax before the face of the Lord. It seems to me that these mountains are the powers of demons, or certainly all proud people. This fire does not consume the humble, but whoever is mountainous. Finally, when lightning is sent forth, it strikes those who are in the valley only with difficulty; it always strikes those who are on the mountain.

The heavens have proclaimed his righteousness. These are the heavens of which it is also said in the eighteenth psalm: “The heavens declare the glory of God.” The heavens proclaim his righteousness; the earth does not proclaim it.

Whoever is heaven does not fear the just God. Whoever is of heaven does not fear proclaiming his righteousness. Whoever is holy and is heaven does not fear the just God. But the sinner seeks a merciful God.

The heavens have proclaimed his righteousness—that is, the evangelists. And all the peoples have seen his glory, because even those to whom he had not been proclaimed understood that God had come in the flesh.

Let all who worship carved images be confounded, those who glory in their idols. So that, while they are confounded in their vain hope, they may be able to reach the true one.

Worship him, all his angels—the proclaimers of his kingdom.

Zion heard and rejoiced—the Church that contemplated his glory.

And the daughters of Judah exulted—the souls of confessors—because of your judgments, Lord, for they have kept them.

For you, Lord, are Most High over all the earth; you are greatly exalted above all gods, and not only above gods but also above the heavens of heavens.

You who love the Lord, who alone is good, hate evil—the devil.

The Lord guards the souls of his saints; he will deliver them from the hand of the sinner, so that nothing may harm them.

Light has arisen for the righteous. Christ shines in his heart. And for the upright of heart, there is joy, because they have been deemed worthy to behold the one whom they awaited.

Rejoice, you righteous, in the Lord, and give thanks at the remembrance of his holiness. You who contemplate him in the light of an upright heart, praise him continually—whether for his holiness, because he remembered you in order to sanctify you, or for his kindness, by which he admitted you into his kingdom. May he deign to grant us that, when his light rises in our hearts, we may be worthy to be delivered by him from present things—from him by whose baptism we have been freed from harmful original sins. To him be glory, with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM XCVII

[Col. 1118D]

A Psalm of David. This psalm, containing the prophet’s voice, recounts the power of the Lord’s name and might.

Sing to the Lord a new song. The new song is the crucified Son of God, something never before heard. A new thing has a new song. Sing to the Lord a new song. It is indeed a human being who suffered, but you must sing to the Lord. He suffered as a human being, but he saved as God. Sing to the Lord a new song. May the new song be worthy of the new name. Therefore it is also said elsewhere: “And it shall be called,” he says, “a new name” (Isa. LXII). A new name deserves a new song. And in the Apocalypse it is said: “Whoever conquers,” he says, “I will give him a stone, and I will write a new name upon him” (Apoc. III). The new name is that of Christians. Sing to the Lord. Why? What has he done? Why should he deserve a new song? Because he has done marvelous things. He performed signs among the Jews: he healed paralytics, cleansed lepers, raised the dead. Other prophets did this as well. He turned a few loaves into many and fed an immense multitude. Elisha did this too. What new thing, then, did he do to deserve a new song? Do you wish to know what new thing God did? He died as a human being so that human beings might live. The Son of God was crucified so that he might raise us to heaven. For he has done marvelous things. Do you wish to know that he has done marvelous things? The widow’s son lay in the upper room; Elisha came and contracted himself, and placed mouth to mouth, hand to hand, [Col. 1119B] and feet to feet (2 Kings IV). For if he had stretched himself out, the widow’s son would not have returned to life. Therefore he contracted himself in order to give life. Since he existed in the form of God, for this reason he took the form of a human being (Phil. II); for this reason he contracted himself, so that he might make us higher.

His right hand saved for himself. What he says is this: He saved human beings—not someone else’s work, but his own; that is, what he had made for himself, he himself saved for himself. He had made the human being for salvation, but the human being had perished through his own fault. This one died so that by his right hand he might save the human being for himself. “Right hand” here signifies power, and “arm” signifies strength. And his holy arm. Although Christ is also called both “arm” and “right hand”—“The right hand of the Lord has done mighty deeds,” and “to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Ps. CXVII)—here too it is spoken of Christ.

[Col. 1119C]

The Lord has made his salvation known. He did not say “he showed,” but “he made known.” What he says is this: They once knew God, but through their own fault they forgot him. Therefore, when God came, by his grace he made manifest to them what they had lost. Thus he says this: The one whom Adam knew, whom Seth knew (Gen. IV), whom Enoch knew—he who called upon the Lord and hoped in him—and whom Noah knew; and afterward the human race had forgotten him: he came again into the world so that human beings, who had later forgotten him, might know him again. The Lord has made his salvation known. In Hebrew it reads: “The Lord has made known his Jesus.” For wherever “Savior” is said, *Jesus* is found in Hebrew. He has revealed his righteousness in the sight of the nations. It was entirely fitting that the Savior should save his creature. He revealed his righteousness, which had been obscured by human unbelief.

He remembered his mercy. He shut all things under sin so that he might have mercy on all (Rom. XI). And his truth to the house of Israel. He remembers mercy; he fulfills truth. He remembered his mercy—that is, among the people of the nations—and his truth to the house of Israel, fulfilling through this work what he had promised to the patriarchs.

All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God. It was not Israel and Judah alone who saw it, but all the ends of the earth—and likewise, according to the mystical understanding, the ends of the earth. As long as we are in the midst of the earth, we cannot see God. [Col. 1120A] When, therefore, we seem to leave the earth and stand at its summit, then we are deemed worthy to see God. Do you wish to know how the ends of the earth see God? We read in Ezekiel: “And those wheels,” he says, “which were turning, were called Gelgel,” which means “revolution” (Ezek. I). For *gel* means “rolling”; *gelgel*, “revolution.” Those wheels, therefore, are called “revolution.” For a wheel touches the earth over only a small area, and hastens wholly toward heaven. Therefore it is also said elsewhere: “Holy stones roll upon the earth” (Zech. IX). And what is said in Ezekiel? “Wherever,” he says, “the spirit went, there the wheels followed also.” Let us too follow the Holy Spirit, so that we may be called wheels. And what is said there? “They did not,” he says, “go backward, but always went forward.” At the same time, consider what he says: “They did not,” he says, “turn back, but always went forward.” For they forgot what lay behind and stretched themselves toward what lay ahead (Phil. III). And they were full of eyes, he says. For all those wheels were full of the light of God. This is not the time to discuss Ezekiel’s wheels, Cherubim, and living creatures.

Shout joyfully to God, all the earth. Not Judea alone, but all the earth, shout joyfully to the Lord. Send forth the cries of a victorious army. Sing, rejoice, and play psalms. Sing with your thought; play psalms with your word—that is, with all your limbs. Let the hand play a psalm through almsgiving; let the foot play a psalm by walking in a good work.

Play psalms to the Lord on the lyre. Let all your strings be sounding. There can be no lyre if one string is missing. What does it profit you to be chaste and generous [Col. 1120C] in almsgiving, while you are envious? What does it profit you to have six strings intact and one broken? If one string is missing, the lyre’s perfect sound cannot exist. With trumpets of beaten metal, and with the voice of a horn-trumpet. We read in the Book of Numbers that there are two kinds of trumpets: one kind made of beaten silver, and another kind of horn-trumpets (Num. X). Thus both are mentioned here: “With trumpets of beaten metal, and with the voice of a horn-trumpet.” What does this mean? The trumpet of beaten silver is the word of God, and the Lord’s utterances are pure utterances—silver tested by fire, purified sevenfold (Ps. XI and XIV). Again, in “the voice of a horn-trumpet,” the man of God who reigns is introduced. In Scripture, “horn” properly signifies kingship and power, as it is written there: “He has raised up a horn of salvation for us” [Col. 1120D] (Luke I). And elsewhere it is written: “Through you we shall gore our enemies with the horn” (Ps. XLIII). Therefore see what he says here: Have two trumpets, one silver and one horn. The silver one, so that you may have the word; the horn one, so that you may have power. Do you wish to know that “horn” is always used in a good sense? We read in Leviticus: “No animal is to be offered unless it is horned.” Three kinds of animals are offered: the ox, which has a horn; the ram, which has a horn; and the goat, which has a horn. Do you think it is said without reason that no animal is to be offered unless it is horned? Therefore, as long as we have a horn, we are worthy to be God’s victim. But if our horn has been struck off, we are like the weak and cannot come among God’s priests. [Col. 1121A]

Let the sea and its fullness be moved. Let the sea be moved, and let the bitter waters be changed into sweet ones. Indeed, even Marah was changed and made sweet in taste (Exod. XV). Nothing else made that bitter water sweet except the wood of the cross that was cast into it. It seems to me that the bitter sea is the law of Moses. This is what is called *mara*, that is, “bitter.” This bitter water of the old law received the wood of the cross and became sweet.

Let the rivers clap their hands together. Let us question the Jews who understand according to the letter: rivers have a belly; rivers have voices; rivers have feet; rivers have hands. Someone may say: It is not written that they have a belly or feet. But I tell you: from one limb we understand the others as well. [Col. 1121B] For we cannot understand hands without feet, without a belly, without the other limbs. Let the rivers clap their hands together. The rivers that drank from the fountain of Jesus. “They have forsaken me,” he says, “the fountain of living water” (Jer. II). Those rivers themselves flow from the fountain of Christ. He is the fountain; we are the rivers—provided that we deserve to be rivers. Christ is the fountain; the saints are rivers. Those who are lower are streams. Others are torrents. Who are the torrents? Those who have water for a time and, when temptation comes, dry up. Let the rivers clap their hands together. There is not one river; there are many rivers. As many as there are saints, so many are the rivers. But these rivers have no disagreement among themselves. Since they are Christ’s rivers, they therefore have harmony among themselves. Let the rivers clap their hands together. [Col. 1121C] They clap because the works of the saints are the praise of God. Christ is not praised by voice but by deed. He does not hear a voice, but works. Let the rivers clap their hands together. Therefore he himself says in the Gospel: “Let the one who thirsts come and drink, and rivers,” he says, “will flow from his belly” (John VII).

The mountains will rejoice in the presence of the Lord. What do rivers and mountains have in common? But since he is speaking of perfect saints, he did not say, “Let the streams clap their hands together,” but “Let the rivers clap their hands together.” Observe the order: Let the sea and the whole world be moved. Let the rivers clap their hands together. Likewise, the mountains, which have attained the highest righteousness. I shall express it another way: Let the sea, which previously had been unmoved, be moved at Christ’s coming. “Let the sea be moved,” as we have already said, means the law of Moses. “Let the rivers clap their hands together,” that is, the prophets. [Col. 1121D] “The mountains will rejoice before the Lord,” that is, the apostles. For he has come to judge the earth. He has not come merely in lowliness in the flesh, but has come glorious in his majesty. For he has come to judge the earth. He did not say “to destroy,” but “to judge.” He came to judge, so that he might separate the weeds from the grain (Matt. XV). He came to separate the bad little fish from the good.

He will judge the world in righteousness and the peoples in equity. Both righteousness and equity are mentioned. First righteousness is mentioned, and afterward equity—*εὐθύτης* is properly that which makes what is crooked straight. Therefore he comes to judge in his righteousness, so that what is crooked may be made straight in him. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM XCVIII

[Col. 1122A]

A Psalm of David. This psalm contains the voice of the prophet, the priest of the Lord, exhorting people to render thanks to the grace of almighty God.

The Lord reigns; let the peoples rage. Three psalms have this same opening: the ninety-second, the ninety-sixth, and the ninety-eighth. Although they have the same opening in the verse, they differ at the end. For when the ninety-second says, “The Lord reigns; he is clothed in beauty”; the ninety-sixth, “The Lord reigns; let the earth rejoice”; and the ninety-eighth, “The Lord reigns; let the peoples rage,” the order seems almost contradictory to itself. It ought first to have said, “The Lord reigns; let the peoples rage”; afterward, “The Lord reigns; let the earth rejoice”; and finally, “The Lord reigns; he is clothed in beauty.” Yet this different order gives us some intimation of the meaning. “The Lord reigns; he is clothed in beauty.” The Lord reigns, and he has clothed himself with the patriarchs, the prophets, and the believing people. He is clothed in beauty because the patriarchs and prophets were, as it were, Christ’s garment. This is the loincloth mentioned in Jeremiah; this is the loincloth that Jeremiah wore around his loins. Do you wish to know that the saints are, as it were, God’s loincloth and garment (Jer. XIII, 11)? Therefore God himself speaks to Jeremiah: “Just as you,” he says, “placed this loincloth around your loins, so I too have attached my people to myself.” As a garment is around a human being, so the people are around God. [Col. 1122C] But because this loincloth—because this beauty with which the Lord had been clothed—was taken beyond the Euphrates, placed in a hole in the rock, and there rotted, and was carried away by the Assyrians into captivity, what does the Lord do? He is not naked; he cannot be without a loincloth, and he cannot be without a garment. Once the former people have been lost, he makes a garment for himself from the people of the nations. And what is said? “The Lord reigns; let the earth rejoice.” Let the whole earth rejoice—that is, the people of believers. Finally, do you wish to know that the second loincloth is spoken of as coming from the people of the nations? “The Lord,” he says, “reigns; let the earth rejoice; let the many islands rejoice.” Not one island, Judea, but many islands—that is, the whole world. Someone may say to me: Give me an example from the Scriptures where Judea alone is called an island.
