Everything we say must be confirmed from the holy Scriptures: “For every word shall stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deut. XVII, 6). The speaker’s assertion does not have as much authority as the Lord’s command. We read in the prophet Ezekiel: “And you,” he says, “son of man, speak to the inhabitants of this island” (Ezek. XXVII)—that is, Judea. Since, therefore, one island has been abandoned, it now says: “Let the many islands rejoice.” Thus the loincloth is spoken of in the former people: “The Lord reigns; he is clothed in beauty.” In the second people, gathered from the nations: “The Lord reigns; let the earth rejoice; let the many islands rejoice.” Now, in the third, it says: “The Lord reigns; let the peoples rage.” Whether they are from the nations or from the Jews, let all who do not believe rage. [Col. 1123A] “Why did the nations rage, and the peoples meditate on vain things?” (Ps. II). “The Lord reigns; let the peoples rage.” The Lord suffered; the Lord was crucified; the Lord died; the Lord rose again; the Lord ascended victoriously to heaven. “The Lord reigns; let the peoples rage.” Who are these peoples? Let us give an example from the Gospel: “A certain nobleman went away to receive a kingdom for himself from a distant land” (Luke XIX). What is more distant than heaven from earth? He left the earth and went to heaven to receive a kingdom for himself. “But his citizens,” he says, “who hated him, sent a delegation, saying: ‘We do not want this man to reign over us.’” Yet he received the kingdom and came to the wicked citizens. He came to those who did not want him as king. And now the Holy Spirit says to the evil citizens: Whether you wish it or not, “the Lord reigns; let the peoples rage.” [Col. 1123B] O the mercy of the Holy Spirit! He did not say, “Let them perish,” but “Let them rage.” He wished to signify a vice, not punishments. They rage, and the Lord pleads with them. And what does he say? “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened” (Matt. XI). I received the kingdom from the Father—or rather: in the human being whom I assumed, I give as God and receive as a human being.

The one who sits upon the Cherubim: let the earth be moved. As long as the earth is unmoved, it cannot be healed. He is not speaking about the earthquake by which we see lands shaken and the entire human race afraid, but about our earth. As long as it remains unmoved, it cannot be healed. But when it has been moved and trembled, then it will receive healing. “Upon whom,” he says, “shall I rest, except upon the humble and quiet person who trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI). Because the trembling earth has been moved, therefore the one who sits upon the Cherubim begins to sit upon the trembling earth. Blessed is the one who is God’s throne. Blessed is the one in whom God always sits. There are different postures. For we either sit, stand, walk, or lie down. Unhappy is the one with whom God lies down; for he lies down with the one who lies down. Just as he mourns with the one who mourns and laughs with the one who laughs, so he lies down with the one who lies down. Just as he thirsts with the thirsty, hungers with the hungry, and is naked with the naked, so he lies down with the one who lies down. Therefore the one who has been wounded and lies down is, in a certain sense, said to make God lie down with him. But the one who walks has God walk with him. The one who walks seems indeed to be better than the one who lies down, yet has not reached the blessedness of the one who stands. Finally, when Adam hid himself from God’s presence, God was walking with him in the afternoon (Gen. III). Someone may say: If Adam had offended and had been expelled from paradise, then anyone for whom God walks must possess an imperfect blessedness. And I say: If Adam had been completely killed, and no place for repentance had been given to him, God would have lain down for him. But because a place for repentance is given to him, God therefore walks for him.

The Lord is great in Zion and exalted above all peoples. Ascending to heaven, he was made higher than all; from there he observes us and our deeds each day.

Let them give thanks to your great name, for it is terrible and holy. Let the saints prepare themselves to give thanks to your name, which is holy, since you said: “Be holy, for I am holy” (Lev. XIX and XX). And the honor of the king loves judgment. A person must first judge himself, condemn his own evils by his own judgment, and thus honor the eternal King, God.

You established acts of love among the peoples. But through their own fault they were corrupted. You enacted judgment and righteousness in Jacob. Not only among the patriarchs, but also among the Christian people, who were deemed worthy to receive the firstborn status of the elder.

Exalt the Lord our God. Let him be exalted in your hearts. And worship the footstool of his feet, for it is holy. There are many opinions concerning the footstool, but here the prophet calls it the Lord’s body, in which the majesty of divinity stands as upon a footstool. We have often taught that it is called holy. That it ought to be worshiped, the apostles showed when, after worshiping him, they returned to Jerusalem at his ascension [Col. 1124B] (Acts I). But these words should also be referred to the Lord’s cross and to the holy soul.

Moses and Aaron among his priests. Although one holds the rule of the law and the other that of the priesthood, both nevertheless announced the Lord’s coming with priestly proclamation—whether through the lawful trumpets or through the bells. And Samuel among those who call upon his name. Samuel holds the rule of the Levitical order, as that linen and shining ephod prefigured (2 Sam. VI), showing that one can become radiant who, by calling upon the Lord through repentance, has washed away the blackness of sin with tears.

They called upon the Lord. The apostles. And he himself answered them; he spoke to them in the pillar of cloud. The Lord spoke from the cloud to the children of Israel (Exod. XVI and XIX), but afterward he also addressed the apostles from behind the veil of the assumed flesh, in which the divinity lay hidden beneath a shadow.

They kept his covenant and the commandment that he gave them. They rendered none of these things void.

Lord our God, you answered them; God, you were gracious to them, while taking vengeance on all their inventions. For you brought to perfection everything they endeavored to do, because it was pleasing to you.

Exalt the Lord our God, and worship on his holy mountain, for the Lord our God is holy. Present yourselves as holy in his Church, just as he presented it as holy, without spot or wrinkle (Eph. V). May he deign to grant us that, while holding to the manner of the priestly order with perfect holiness, he himself may deign to bring to completion the good things we strive to do.

## PSALM XCIX

A Psalm for thanksgiving. This psalm contains the voice of the prophet, who urges the faithful to exercise themselves unceasingly in the Lord’s praises.

Shout joyfully to God, all the earth; serve the Lord with gladness. You rejoice because the yoke of the law has been shaken from your necks—not in the sorrow of the former servitude, but in the freedom of the new human being.

Enter his presence with rejoicing. Do not dissolve yourselves in shameful amusements, but do everything you do for the glory of God.

Know that the Lord himself is God: he made us, and not we ourselves. For we were made by him not only bodily, but also recreated as a new human being. And this was not by our merit, but by his gift.

We are his people and the sheep of his pasture. He is the good shepherd who laid down his life for his sheep (John X). We, however, are the sheep who follow him and have heard his voice. Enter his gates with thanksgiving. For just as he himself is the Father’s gate when he says, “Whoever enters through me will be saved” (ibid.), so the apostles are his gates, through whom one approaches him; no one can enter them unless he has cleansed himself by confessing his sins. Give thanks to him in his courts with hymns. Bring to him minds made spacious through spiritual hymns and songs.

Praise his name, for the Lord is sweet. [Col. 1125B] He has nothing bitter. His mercy is forever, because he redeemed us and continually saves us. And his truth remains from generation to generation, by which he will judge the peoples. May he deign to grant us that, having been made by him and redeemed by him, we may be worthy also to sing, with thanksgiving, the jubilant song of rejoicing in everlasting gladness. To him be glory, with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM C

A Psalm of David himself. This psalm contains the voice of the prophet recounting God’s mercies.

I will sing mercy and judgment to you, Lord. Let sinners hear “mercy”—those who despair of their salvation and are engaged in repentance. Let the contemptuous hear “judgment”—those who say, “The Lord is merciful; let us sin, and he will forgive us.” I will sing psalms and understand in the blameless way. This is so that a person may understand what he sings and contemplate the meaning of the psalm, so that his mind may not wander outward and, although he seems to sing with his body, his mind may be without fruit. In the blameless way: so that, walking in this world, I may act justly and have no stain.

When will you come to me? When I have received understanding and acted justly, then I say to the Lord with confidence: When will you come to me? “You will come” is to be understood of his second coming.

I walked in the innocence of my heart, in the midst of my house. Nothing pleases God so much as simplicity and innocence. Indeed, the Holy Spirit was pleased among the other birds with the dove because of its simplicity, and among four-footed animals with the sheep because of its gentleness.

I did not set an unjust thing before my eyes. I did not place anything before the Lord, nor did I consent to iniquity; I was wholly directed toward God.

I hated those who commit transgression. Whether it was my father, mother, brother, sister, or friend, if that person had turned aside from fear of the Lord, I hated him and did not approach him at all. I did not place kinship or friendship before devotion to the Lord.

A crooked heart did not cling to me. There was nothing difficult or perverse in me, but equity [Col. 1126A] and righteousness. I did not acknowledge the wicked man who turned away from me. That is, if he was my friend or relative, whether a bishop, presbyter, or someone established in any position of dignity, if he was perverting his ways, I avoided him so completely that I did not even preserve his memory.

The one who slandered his neighbor, him I pursued. We ought not to consent to the slanderer to such an extent that, insofar as it lies within us, we even pursue such a person, looking to the usefulness of both: so that we neither willingly listen nor permit him to sin. For there is such a difference between the fornicator and the slanderer that the one who fornicates kills only himself, whereas the one who slanders destroys both himself and the one who listens.

The one with a proud eye and an insatiable heart—I did not eat with him. If someone was proud or greedy, I did not eat with him at all.

My eyes were upon the faithful of the earth, so that they might sit with me. He did not say “the rich,” “emperors,” “bishops,” “presbyters,” or “deacons,” but “the faithful”; I sat with these. A holy bishop may say this as well, since I did not ordain as presbyter the one who served me or my relative, but the one whom I knew to be faithful. He can say the same again: I regarded all my clergy and faithful laypeople as faithful. This verse can also be spoken in the person of the Lord: “The one walking in the blameless way served me.” For I did not ordain those who were related to me, but the just and faithful.

The one who speaks wickedness did not set himself right before my eyes. For I so turned away from the one who slandered his neighbor that I neither believed nor listened to him.

In the morning I killed all the sinners of the earth. He rightly said “sinners of the earth,” for sinners are earthly. This means that I cast from my heart the assaults of the devil that he suggested to me and did not receive them. For when evil thoughts are expelled, demons are killed. The Jews, hearing this verse and following the killing letter, desiring to shed blood, kill anyone who has transgressed the law. Indeed, they were not satisfied with killing the prophets, but also crucified the Lord himself. So that I might destroy from the city of the Lord all who practice iniquity. Would that we too might destroy from the city of the Lord those who practice iniquity. The city of the Lord is the Church of the saints, the assembly of the righteous. “I shall destroy” means: I shall convict and rebuke the one who sins, so that he may repent and destroy iniquity from his heart. For he did not say “so that he may be cast out,” but “so that he may be saved.”

## PSALM CI

A prayer of the poor man when he was anxious and poured out his prayer in the presence of the Lord. This psalm initially contains the voice of the prophet in the person of the sinner; afterward it contains praise of the Lord’s name.

Lord, hear my prayer, etc. Because it is uttered from the whole heart.

Do not turn your face away from me. If someone prays with a pure heart and is not reproved by his conscience, he can say this. For a sinner does not dare to say, “Do not turn your face away from me,” but rather says, “Turn your face away from my sins.” On whatever day I am afflicted, incline your ear to me; on whatever day I call upon you, hear me quickly. He prays concerning present distresses, so that through divine contemplation he may be rescued from them.

For my days have faded like smoke. It is as though he says: I was a little child, and without knowing it I reached youth, and again full maturity, and without knowing it I grew old. And my days have faded like smoke. Some, however, think they are everlasting and persist in their sin. And my bones have dried like kindling. By “bones” he means strength itself. If, therefore, what is strong in me has dried up and become weak, how much more the flesh, which by nature is weak?

I was struck like grass, and my heart dried up. As it is also written elsewhere: “A human being is like grass; his days are as grass.” For human life grows green in this way and quickly dries up. Because I forgot to eat my bread. He did not say, “I did not desire to eat,” or “I despised eating.” The memory of my sins came upon me so strongly, and I practiced such repentance, that I even forgot to eat, having desire for God and contemplating him alone.

At the voice of my groaning, my bones clung to my flesh. Let those who practice repentance learn how they ought to practice repentance. For I dried myself out so completely that I was without flesh, and my skin clung to my bones [Col. 1127C]. He said “flesh” for “skin.”

I became like a pelican of the wilderness. There are said to be two kinds of these birds. One lives in the waters, and its food is fish; the other lives in the wilderness, and its food is poisonous animals—that is, snakes, crocodiles, and lizards. These birds are called *onocrotali* in Latin. I therefore became like the one that lives in the wilderness, which eats poisonous animals; that is, my food was like poison to me. I became like a night-raven in a dwelling. We know that a raven is black and has nothing white in it. He wished to speak hyperbolically, saying: I became like a night-raven. If it is black in the daytime, how much more at night? Thus I became because of my sins, considering myself.

[Col. 1127D]

For I ate ashes like bread. I dipped my bread in ashes, and so I ate it. If the prophet says this, what shall we do? And I mixed my drink with weeping. Nothing was sweet to me, neither bread nor drink; I desired only the heavenly bread, that is, Christ.

Because of the face of your anger and indignation. I did all these things while contemplating your coming and the future judgment. For, having lifted me up, you dashed me down. Let those who were once saints and have fallen say this. For, having been exalted in virtues, they afterward fell. Indeed, the saints say: “Because you lifted me up, you held me.”

My days have declined like a shadow. If this is true of the days, how much more of the nights? That is, if of the light, how much more of the darkness? [Col. 1128A] And I have dried up like grass. For as grass passes away, so the human being passes away and dries up.

You will arise and have mercy on Zion. From this verse it is clear that this psalm was spoken in the person of Zion, not in the person of the prophet. Zion is the one set upon a watchtower, looking out from afar at the things that are coming. This Zion, therefore, which had been placed on high, fell from the heights. Therefore, “let the one who stands take care lest he fall” (1 Cor. X). For it is the time for having mercy on her; the time has come. Either the time for mercy is present because of repentance, or it signifies the Savior’s coming. Therefore let the one who repents have confidence, because the time of salvation has come. For the Lord is merciful (Ps. LXXVII and Eccles. II).

For her stones have been pleasing to your servants. The stones are the saints. But the earth—that is, sinners—needs the Lord’s mercy. And they will have mercy on her earth, so that it may produce the fruit of holiness.

The nations will fear the name of the Lord, and all the kings of the earth your glory. Those who formerly feared idols and invoked the names of demons will now honor and fear your name.

For the Lord will build Zion, his Church, upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets; and he will appear in his glory, when he has glorified his whole body according to the likeness of his glory.

And he regarded the prayer of the humble and did not despise their petitions. Rather, by his coming he visited the world—he who had long been desired.

Let these things be written for a future generation, in the New Testament. [Col. 1128C] And the people that will be created will praise the Lord—the Christian, certainly, who, having previously been dead in sins, has been recreated in him.

For he looked down from his holy height; the Lord looked from heaven upon the earth, to hear the groaning of the prisoners, to release the sons of those who had been killed. He looked in order to have mercy. He descended in order to loosen the bonds by which we had been bound.

So that they may proclaim the name of the Lord in Zion and his praise in Jerusalem. A good message always presents new joys, as with the angel to Mary: “The Holy Spirit,” he says, “will come upon you” (Luke I). And again to the shepherds: “Behold, I announce to you today great joy, for a Savior has been born to you” (ibid., II). So now it is proclaimed in Zion or in Jerusalem: [Col. 1128D] the one who would bring life to the world, dead in sins, has been born on earth.

When peoples gather together as one, and kings, to serve the Lord. They will gather in one faith so that they may serve the Redeemer.

He answered him in the way of his strength: make known to me the small number of my days. The Lord answered Jerusalem on the day of his strength—that is, when he was approaching his passion—and announced the small number of his days, saying: “The days will come when you will be surrounded by enemies and uprooted” (Luke XIX), and so forth.

And do not call me back in the middle of my days; your years endure through generation and generation. The wicked do not reach even half their days (Ps. LIV). But this one prays that he not be taken away in the middle of his days, that is, that, having come to maturity, he may enjoy perpetual ages with the Lord.

In the beginning, you, Lord, founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. For just as you created these things in the beginning, so now you either restore the earth of our body into a new human being, or fashion our minds according to the dignity of heaven. But concerning the former heavens he says:

They will perish, but you remain. In accordance with this: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matt. XXIII and Mark XIII). And all of them will grow old like a garment. And like a covering you will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same, and your years will not fail. This means: You who were in heaven show yourself to be the same on earth. The same in the virgin’s womb; the same descending into hell. The same rising from the dead; the same returning to heaven.

The children of your servants will dwell there, because through the apostles they have been reborn for you. And their offspring will be established forever. Either their preaching or their virtue is spread throughout every nation. Let us, however, entreat the Lord to hear the prayers of those who plead, to implant his light in our minds, so that, recounting his magnificence, we may be deemed worthy to become companions of his saints in the heavenly kingdoms. To him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM CII

A Psalm of David. This psalm dwells especially upon the kindness and mercy of God, for it says:

[Col. 1129C] Bless the Lord, my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name. It is also said elsewhere: “And know that the Lord himself is God” (Ps. XCIX). And now it says: “And all that is within me, bless his holy name.” If we say, “Bless the Lord, my soul,” and “The Lord is Lord,” what name does the Lord seek here? If he is called “Lord, Lord,” what does “And all that is within me, bless his holy name” mean? The coming of the Son is the name of the Father. Before Christ’s coming, God was known; the Father was unknown. Indeed, he himself says in the Gospel: “Father, I have revealed your name to human beings” (John XVII). We cannot linger over every single verse, since the psalm is long; rather, we ought to attach brief interpretations to each verse, explaining the meaning more than weaving together the words.

Bless the Lord, my soul, and do not forget all his recompenses. The Lord has granted us many recompenses; he has bestowed great benefits upon us, since he made heaven, earth, and all the elements for our sake.

He who is merciful toward all your iniquities. So that he may erase them as though they were a cloud. He who heals all your infirmities. The sins by which you are weakened. Our soul has many infirmities. As many sins as there are, so many infirmities. Indeed, there was also that woman in the Gospel who had had a spirit of infirmity for eighteen years and could not lift her head upward (Luke XIII). See what he says: when someone has a spirit of infirmity, he is bent over, looks downward, gazes at the earth, and cannot see heaven.

He who redeems your life from destruction. “You were bought at a price,” he says; “do not become slaves of human beings” (I Cor. VI and VII). What price is greater than the Creator shedding his blood for his creature? He who crowns you with mercy and compassion. By means of preceding mercy he grants victory and bestows the palm.

He who satisfies your desire with good things. Joining you to the saints in the heavenly Jerusalem.

Your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s. So that you may be changed from the old person into the new.

He performs the mercies of the Lord and judgment for all who suffer injustice. So that, when the wicked are overthrown, he may raise up his poor [Col. 1130B].

He made his ways known to Moses, and his purposes to the children of Israel. To the one who understands the law spiritually, or to the one who contemplates him with the eyes of the mind.

The Lord is merciful and compassionate, patient and greatly merciful. Because he is quickly moved to mercy.

He will not be angry forever, nor will he threaten for eternity, and so forth. For he has spared us things better than we deserved.

For according to the height of heaven above the earth, he has strengthened his mercy over those who fear him. Heaven is very far removed from earth; yet divine mercy continually protects and strengthens its own.

As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our iniquities from us [Col. 1130C]. Where God draws near, sins are driven far away, so that, according to the Apostle, “where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. V).

As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has had compassion on those who fear him. A father has compassion on his son when he beats him in order to correct him. So also the Lord sometimes chastises us in order to save us; yet he does not abandon us forever so as to destroy us.

For he himself knew our formation. The prophet knows that the human race is like a potter’s vessel formed from clay and adopted for the honor of being a child. Therefore, considering that the judgment of death for sins was approaching it, he says, imploring mercy:

He remembered that we are dust; a human being’s days are like grass [Col. 1130D]. It is as though he were saying: You are not angry in order to crush us; rather, you remember that we are potter’s vessels, which, once broken, cannot be repaired, but immediately fall apart and wither. “Like a flower of the field, so he will blossom.” For a time.

For the spirit has passed through him, and he does not remain; and he no longer knows his place. When the spirit has passed away, all the delight of his greenness is handed over to oblivion.

But the mercy of the Lord is from eternity and unto eternity upon those who fear him. For when he rebukes sinners, he grants mercy to the righteous.

And his righteousness is upon children’s children, for those who keep his covenant and remember his commandments [Col. 1131A], to do them. That is, in good works, by which God’s commandments are continually remembered so that they may be kept by those who remember them.

The Lord prepared his throne in heaven, and his kingdom will rule over all. He foretells the Lord’s Ascension, which took place after the restoration of humanity; through it Christ the Lord subjected all the ends of the world to his dominion.

Bless the Lord, his angels. Messengers of truth. Mighty in strength, doing his word. Immediately fulfilling whatever he has spoken. To hear the voice of his words. That is, to understand what he has commanded.

Bless the Lord, all his powers, his ministers who do his will. You who, strengthened by his power, minister his word to the churches.

[Col. 1131B] Bless the Lord, all his works. You, certainly, who live in him. For every work that has been made in him is life (John I). In every place of his dominion. Nothing is found where he does not rule. He contains all things and spreads himself everywhere. Bless the Lord, my soul. The prophet is speaking these words not only about his own soul but also to our souls, so that they may continually bless him who bestows good things, who is merciful toward sins, who redeems from destruction, and who fulfills every desire with good things. May he now deign to have mercy on us as a father has mercy on his children, remitting here the burdens of our sins. To him, with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM CIII

[Col. 1131C] A psalm of David. This psalm contains the voice of creation itself praising and blessing God. But we must perceive this very subject spiritually.

Bless the Lord, my soul. So that, while you bless him, you may be blessed by him. The prophet stirs himself to bless God. To bless the Lord—that is, whoever praises the Lord blesses himself.

O Lord my God. You are indeed both God and Lord of all; but you are especially mine, because I am not a servant of sin.

You have been greatly magnified. Either in me or in your other saints. Although you are God of all, you are especially my God because I am not a servant of sin and have deserved to be called your servant. You have been greatly magnified.

You have put on confession and beauty. You put on confession when you said: “I will confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth” (Matt. XI). You put on beauty when the one speaking from the bright cloud answered: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matt. XVII).

“Confession” is understood in two ways: either in repentance or in the glory of God. That is: you put on glory, just as the Savior himself says in the Gospel: “I will confess to you, Father”—that is, “I glorify you”—or because we confess our sins to the Lord. For in confessing our sins to God, we glorify him.

And you put on beauty. Observe the order: first someone confesses, and thus receives beauty and splendor, and afterward light. For this follows: “Clothed with light as with a garment.” This verse seems contrary [Col. 1132A] to the one that says: “He made darkness his hiding place,” or to the one that says: “Cloud and darkness are around him.” But we should know that these statements concern hidden mysteries; for from the fullness of this light the whole earth shines.

Stretching out heaven like a skin. For heaven, in the manner of a book or a scroll, is either stretched out or folded up when the majesty of God wills it, as the faith of the Gospel attests.

You who cover its upper parts with waters. According to Genesis, the upper parts of heaven are covered by waters (Gen. I), because it says that waters were placed above the firmament. We understand these waters as the multitude of angels, according to the words: “The waters that are above the heavens, let them praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXLVIII).

You who make the cloud your ascent. For the Lord Jesus, after blessing the disciples, was lifted up, and a cloud received him, and they watched him going into heaven (Acts I).

You who walk upon the wings of the winds. The Lord moves upon all the swiftness of the winds. But he also walks upon and rests in the souls of the saints who strive toward heavenly things.

You who make your angels spirits. So that they may inspire human beings to do his will, because the carnal person does not grasp the things that belong to God.

And your ministers a burning fire. So that in some they may pour in the light of truth, and in others consume sins.

You who founded the earth upon its stability, and so forth. These words seem to disagree with the passage that says: “Heaven and earth will pass away.” But this visible earth passes away; the earth of the body, however, which produces the fruit of holiness, is surrounded by the mantle [Col. 1132C] of heavenly mysteries.

The waters will stand upon the mountains. Foolish peoples dwell upon lofty pride.

At your rebuke they will flee; at the voice of your thunder they will fear. For your voice is heard when you say: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matt. III). It is like thunder, so that they may fear, when you threaten and say: “Unless you repent, you will all perish together” (Luke XIII).

They all ascend. The saints advance toward spiritual understanding.

And the plains descend. The peoples subjected to their teachings, so that they may be filled with the flowers of virtue.

Into the place that you founded for them. Into the ecclesial assembly.

You set a boundary that they will not cross. That is, the Catholic faith, which they preserve to the end of the present life.

Nor will they return to cover the earth. With the crimes in which they previously lived.

You who send forth springs in the valleys. Among the nations’ deserts he grants the grace of baptism.

In the midst of the mountains. That is, of the churches.

The waters will pass through. The waters of that washing—or of the teacher—irrigating the people with heavenly gifts.

And all the beasts of the field will drink; the wild asses will await it in their thirst. So that this grace may be administered equally to all, as Paul says: “I am a debtor both to the wise and to the foolish” (Rom. I).

Upon them the birds of heaven will dwell. Those who have merited a loftier understanding.

From the midst of the rocks [Col. 1133A]. That is, of the churches.

They will give their voice. To praise God together.

Watering the mountains. That is, the apostles.

From his upper chambers. From heavenly things, pouring the Holy Spirit over them.

The earth will be satisfied with the fruit of your works. With the benefits of your generosity.

Producing grass for cattle and plants for human service. Giving to each according to his particular need.

So that you may bring bread from the earth, and wine may gladden the human heart. From the field of the earthly body that he assumed from us, he brings forth the mystery of heavenly bread and the saving cup, by which the Church may be refreshed.

So that he may brighten his face with oil. For the faces of the righteous are brightened before God by the oil of mercy.

And bread strengthens the human heart [Col. 1133B]. That bread itself strengthens our hearts—the bread that, descending from heaven, gives life to the world.

The trees of the field will be satisfied. Whether rational or irrational human beings, as we explained above concerning the beasts and wild asses.

And the cedars of Lebanon. The saints who are loftier by merit.

Which he planted. In the unity of ecclesial faith.

There the sparrows will build nests. The wise build.

The heron’s house is their leader. The heron is greater than all birds; it overcomes and eats the eagle. Therefore, let such a person, who dwells in the house of God, provide leadership for overcoming the devil, since the eagle is often understood as the devil.

The high mountains are for the deer. This animal kills and eats serpents. Therefore, he rightly [Col. 1133C] dwells in the mountains who kills the intelligible serpent—the one who was wiser than all the beasts in paradise and deceived Eve (Gen. III).

The rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs. Whoever is timid has the rock as a refuge; the rock, however, is Christ.

He made the moon for the appointed times. They say that when the moon grows, all fruits grow, and when it wanes, the fruits likewise diminish. Therefore he rightly said: “He made the moon for the appointed times.”

Or let us understand the moon otherwise as the Church. As the Church advances, we advance with it; when it suffers persecution and is diminished, we too are diminished with it and suffer persecution.

The sun knew its setting. If the sun sets, do we imagine that we ourselves are eternal? Yet this is astonishing: how such great light and such brilliance, which covers the whole world with its radiance, sets in an instant. Let us pray, however, that the sun of righteousness may not set for us.

You appointed darkness, and it became night; in it all the beasts of the forest will pass through. According to the literal sense, the order is appropriate: night came into being so that human beings might rest from their works and the beasts might go out to feed.

According to the tropological sense, however, when the sun of righteousness has set for us, everything is dark to us, and then the beasts pass over us—the roaring lion, wishing to seize and devour us.

The young lions roar, so that they may seize and seek their food from God. He rightly said “from God,” since the devil desires to deceive the saints—as though he were saying: Judas, David, Solomon, Peter. As it is written: “His food is chosen” (Hab. I).

The sun arose, and they were gathered together. Let the one who has fallen not grieve, but let him repent. The sun of righteousness rises for him, and all the beasts and sins flee from him; he becomes as he was before. For the sun of righteousness has risen again.

A human being will go out to his work and to his labor until evening. After the sun of righteousness has risen, we again go out to our work until evening—that is, until the consummation. Therefore we ought at all times to practice righteousness.

How greatly your works are magnified, O Lord. The prophet entered into an ecstasy of mind [Col. 1134B]. Finding no way to praise the Lord, he said: “How greatly your works are magnified, O Lord.” Your works surpass human understanding.

You made all things in wisdom. In our Lord Jesus Christ. For he is the wisdom of God, according to the Apostle, who says that all things were created in him (Rom. XI).

The earth is filled with your possession. And truly, all the works of the Lord are full of wisdom. When we see an ant knowing when winter comes, storing food for itself, and then a gnat so tiny possessing eyes, a belly, and all its limbs just as we do, and likewise a flea and other creatures; when we see an elephant, such a huge beast, possessing eyes, nostrils, feet, and a belly just as we do in those same places; and likewise a bee, how it makes honey and wax—are these not things worthy of wonder and full of wisdom?

This sea is great and spacious in extent; there are reptiles there without number. Small animals together with great ones. Is it not a marvel of wisdom that in the sea there are reptiles without number, and fish both larger and smaller; that they live in the depths and draw life from there, where a human being would die if he fell, while they die if they come onto land?

There ships will pass through. Who among us is a strong ship that can escape this world and not be submerged or strike against a rock and yet possess understanding to guide it, so that it may be saved?

This dragon, which you formed to play with it. The Jews say that God made a great dragon called Leviathan, which is in the sea; and, they say, when Ocean withdraws, the dragon turns over. We, however, should say: this is the dragon that was expelled from paradise, who deceived Eve and was given over to this world to mock us. How many monks and clerics he has cast down!

All things await you, that you may give them their food in due season, and so forth. For all things live by God’s command.

You will take away their spirit, and they will fail, and they will return to their dust. This signifies the consummation of the world, when all things are destroyed at God’s command, as it is written: “You are earth, and to earth you will go” (Gen. III).

Send forth your spirit, and they will be created. On the day of consummation [Col. 1135A]. If the Spirit creates, then he is God. For he creates in the same way as the Father does.

May the glory of the Lord endure forever. Therefore, we too, who glorify him, will be eternal.

The Lord will rejoice in his works. For the Lord’s joy is present when we, his creatures, bless him on the day of resurrection.

He looks upon the earth, and makes it tremble. For our earth will tremble on the day of judgment. He signifies earthly sinners.

He touches the mountains, and they smoke. If the mountains smoke, how much more the earth? The saints smoke, because we will all be saved through fire. They would not have smoke unless there were fire.

I will sing to the Lord in my life; I will sing psalms to my God as long as I am. As he says elsewhere: “Let me recover before I depart, and I shall be no more” (Ps. XXXVIII). Let me have a little time, so that I may repent of my sins, since in hell there is no one who can confess his sins.

May my speech be pleasing to him. May it be pleasing to him that someone is able, as he deserves, to praise and bless God. He spoke in the optative mood, not the imperative.

But I will delight in the Lord. Blessed are those who say this after the judgment.

May sinners vanish from the earth. He did not say that sinners should perish, but that sin itself should disappear, so that it may not appear. When sin no longer appears, there are plainly no longer any sinners; all will be found righteous.

And may the wicked be no more. That is, may there be no wicked, but righteous people.

## PSALM CIV

[Col. 1135C] Alleluia. This psalm chiefly repeats the history of the patriarchs, but it must be understood spiritually. For all the things that happened in ancient times happened in figure, so that we might be instructed (II Cor. X).

Confess to the Lord, and call upon his name. Confess and say: “We are sinners. But you are merciful and have mercy on us.”

And call upon his name. So that we do not fashion idols in our hearts, but call upon our Lord; and he will be our redemption.

Declare his works among the nations. Let the Jews be ashamed, who say that his wonders and works were done only in Israel.

Sing to him and sing psalms to him. Whoever understands the holy Scriptures, continually meditates on the law of the Lord, and contemplates heavenly things with his mind—this person sings to God.

But whoever possesses all the virtues, that is, whoever is a worker of good works, composes a kind of lyre of virtues and sings psalms to the Lord [Col. 1135D].

Tell of all his wonders. In the hundred-and-sixth psalm it says: “Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing their work upon great waters: they have seen the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep.” If we pass unharmed through the sea in our bodily ship, and no storm overwhelms us, and we do not strike a rock and break our ship, we can tell of the wonders of God. And truly, it is a great wonder to pass through this world without stain.

Glory in his holy name. For he prophesies concerning the people of the Gentiles. That is, so that we may be and be called Christians, from the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Col. 1136A] Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice. Let the monks rejoice, because the hearts of those who seek the Lord rejoice. If the hearts of those who seek him rejoice, how much more the hearts of those who find him? For those who find him are immovable.

Seek the Lord and be strengthened. Before we sought the Lord, we were weak. But now, seeking him, we are firm and strong. And if we should also find him, how much more perfect shall we be?

Seek his face always. Among the Hebrews it is written that they should appear before the Lord three times a year (Exod. XIII). And what sort of righteousness was that? What great thing did they do by appearing in God’s presence three times a year? There he was speaking to children; here the prophet tells those who believe in God to seek him always, just as it is written in the Gospel: “Pray without ceasing” (I Thess. V) [Col. 1136B].

Remember his wonders, which he performed. In Egypt, at the Red Sea, and in the wilderness.

The seed of Abraham, his servant; the children of Jacob, his chosen one. If someone is seed but not already a son, according to what is written in the Gospel: “If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of your father” (John VIII). Therefore, they boast that they are his seed, but they are not sons. They are servants placed under fear, not possessing the perfect love that casts out fear (I John IV). We are sons of Jacob, the one who supplanted his brother and took his birthright. “Many are called, but few are chosen.”

And they passed from nation to nation. Many think that he is speaking about the captivity of the Jews. It is not so. He is speaking about Abraham [Col. 1136C]. He went out from the land of the Chaldeans and came to Mesopotamia, and from Mesopotamia to the promised land, and then again into Egypt. And from one kingdom to another people. We pass through many kingdoms in order to reach the promised land.

He permitted no one to harm them. He did not permit Pharaoh to harm Abraham concerning Sarah, nor Abimelech to harm Isaac concerning Rebekah (Gen. XII and X).

And he rebuked kings for their sake. He is saying the same thing about Pharaoh and Abimelech.

Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not act wickedly against my prophets. He is speaking of the patriarchs themselves. Let the Jews, then, be ashamed, who say that unless someone is anointed with royal oil, he cannot be called Christ. They say this because our Lord is not Christ, since he was not anointed with royal oil. Behold, before the law the patriarchs, who were not anointed with royal oil, are called Christs. Those who are anointed with the Holy Spirit are Christs. Therefore our Lord is rightly called Christ. They deny this while going against the Scriptures.

And he called a famine upon the land. It has often happened that things thought to be contrary are brought about by God’s providence for the sake of benefit. For if Joseph’s brothers had not been jealous of him, if they had not sold him, how would he have gone down into Egypt? If there had been no famine, how would the patriarchs have gone down into Egypt and been recognized by their brother? How would Pharaoh have been struck with the ten plagues? How would they have gone out from Egypt? How would waters have flowed from the rock in the wilderness? How would we have understood spiritually the mysteries that occurred figuratively in the wilderness [Col. 1137A]? If Judas had not betrayed the Lord, how would we have been saved? If the Jews had not crucified him and had not been unbelieving, how would we have believed? Joseph therefore went into Egypt to prepare lodging and provisions for his brothers.

He sent a man before them. He is speaking of Joseph himself.

Joseph was sold into slavery. A well-born and holy man is sold.

They humbled his feet with fetters. Because he refused to consent to the Egyptian woman. They humbled his feet with fetters, but they could not humble his righteousness. For he was sixteen years old when the woman desired him, and he was at an age more devoted to pleasure; yet he refused to consent to iniquity and instead feared the danger to his soul.

Iron passed through his soul [Col. 1137B]. He calls sin itself iron, because it kills the soul.

Alternatively: because he was in danger, accused by the woman of such a crime. For the woman burned with desire for him, as it is written: “All adulterers’ hearts are like an oven” (Hos. VII).

Until his word came. He means the word of the Lord, who set him free.

The utterance of the Lord inflamed him. For unless he had been inflamed by the Holy Spirit, he could not have overcome lust. The Spirit of the Lord inflamed him and extinguished the fire of lust.

The king sent and released him. According to the literal sense, Pharaoh sent and released him. Alternatively: if someone is tempted by lust, unless the Lord appears and releases him, he cannot escape sin.

The king sent and released him, the ruler of peoples, and dismissed him. “King” and “ruler” are understood as the Father, as in: “A great king over all the earth,” and: “The Lord is our ruler; the Lord is our judge” (Ps. XLVI).

He himself therefore sent his angel, who rolled away the stone from the entrance of the tomb and dissolved the burial cloths of his corpse (Mark XV). By paternal power, having conquered death, he too was sent back from hell. Nothing here should be understood or supposed carelessly, as though he had been raised by angels. For he was made a little lower than the angels when, as a human being, he accepted death (Ps. VIII). But in the resurrection, as the true God, he made use of angelic ministry.

This kingdom does not belong to the principalities, nor to Pharaoh, who is the destroyer, nor to the one who is merely the ruler of the Egyptians.

[Col. 1137D] He appointed him lord of his house. Of the Church acquired by his blood.

And ruler of all his possession. Which he drew away from the devil’s power.

To instruct his princes as himself and teach his elders wisdom. The apostles were princes and elders of the peoples; they were called his own by possession, not by political rule. He instructed them with sacred utterances. Indeed, while repeatedly teaching the priestly princes and elders of the peoples, he educated them in the temple when he opened the divine Scriptures to them.

And Israel entered Egypt, and Jacob was a resident in the land of Ham [Col. 1138A]. Everyone who begins to see God with the mind, or to supplant vices, descends into tribulation and dwells among hostile nations.

And he greatly increased his people and strengthened them over their enemies. For they went down into Egypt with seventy-five souls, and six hundred thousand came out of Egypt (Deut. X). Observe the mystery. Those who once were few in number are now said to have been increased and strengthened. The righteous are increased and strengthened by the Lord, so that hostile powers may not prevail over them.

He turned their heart so that they hated his people and dealt deceitfully with his servants. That is, so that they might observe their iniquities.

He sent Moses, his servant, and Aaron, whom he had chosen [Col. 1138B]. That is, the law and the priesthood.

He placed in them the words of his signs and wonders in the land of Ham. Pay attention, O Jew, who understand the words according to the letter: Did Moses and Aaron receive the command concerning signs in the land of Ham, and not rather in the land of Midian? Or did they perform wonders in the land of Ham, and not in Egypt? But so that you may understand that these things are carried out even today among unbelieving nations through the law and the priesthood, the prophet therefore named the land of Ham.

He sent darkness and darkened them. They began to explain to him the hidden things of God’s mysteries, and the brilliance of worldly wisdom was darkened. Thus it says elsewhere: “I will seize the wise in their craftiness” (II Cor. I).

And he embittered his words. Because they were hard for them, like those whom the Gospel reports as saying: “This is a hard saying; who can hear it?” (John VI).

He turned their waters into blood. So that those who had shed the blood of little children by leading them astray might thereafter drink blood instead of water. But this verse especially concerns heretics.

And he killed their fish. Those who thought that the kingdom consisted in the fluctuating prosperity of this world.

And their land brought forth frogs in the inner chambers of their kings. In the frogs, the songs of poets are signified—those who disagree with the Catholic rule and fill the hearts of earthly kings with the fables of deceptions.

[Note: [Col. 1137D] Recall what we noted somewhat earlier in Psalm LXXVII concerning the corresponding passage. Concerning the cynomyia that follows, and the fact that this author, contrary to the opinion of the true Jerome, translates it as a “dog-fly,” see what we briefly discussed in the prefatory warning.]

He spoke, and the cynomyia came. In the cynomyia—that is, the dog-fly, which wallows in mud and dung—luxury is indicated, which often breeds when it is suppressed. As the Apostle Peter says: “The dog has returned to its vomit, and the sow, after being washed, to wallowing in the mire” (II Pet. II).

And gnats throughout all their borders. In the gnat, the sting of dialectical art is understood. Although it may seem to have a small barb of deception, it nevertheless wounds human minds most severely.

He made their rains hail. So that they might be reproved by divine scourges.

Fire burning in their land. Not illuminating but burning, because holy fire illuminates the righteous and consumes sinners.

And he struck their vines and their fig trees, and shattered every tree within their borders [Col. 1139A]. In the vines, fig trees, and other trees, he displays the whole human race struck by heavenly blows for the purpose of correction.

He spoke, and the locust and the young locust came, whose number was without end. And it devoured all the grass in their land, and it devoured all the fruit of their land. In the grass and the remaining fruit of the land, he teaches about the chastisement of humanity. For power is given to the opposing side to harm those who refuse to repent, as the Apocalypse teaches (Rev. IX).

And he struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, the first fruits of all their labor. The principal vices, which human beings loved as though they were firstborn children.

And he led them out with silver and gold, and there was no weak person among their tribes [Col. 1139B]. With these blows he scourges Egypt—that is, either this world or human flesh. But souls are led out with the bright silver of confession and the shining gold of purity, every weakness of sin having been removed.

Egypt rejoiced at their departure, because fear of them had fallen upon them. For while light dwelt among them, they could not practice the works of darkness, because “everyone who does evil hates the light” (John III).

He spread out a cloud for their protection, and fire to give them light by night. By the cloud and fire he means the Holy Spirit, who both defends us from the heat of day and illuminates us in the darkness of night.

They asked for meat, and quail came. Israel was satisfied with this quail and became nauseated. Therefore we must beware lest someone who feels himself free from Egypt and illuminated by the Holy Spirit should again desire the pots of Egypt—that is, the desires of the flesh, which produce lethargy or vices in him. For “no one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke IX).

He satisfied them with the bread of heaven. Just as they were refreshed by manna flowing from heaven, so today in the Church we are refreshed when we receive the body of the Lamb.

He split the rock, and waters flowed, and rivers went forth through the dry land. For that precious cornerstone was struck, and it brought forth immense springs for us, which wash away our errors and irrigate our arid places.

For he remembered his holy word, which he had spoken to Abraham his servant. He fulfilled his promise not concerning seeds, but concerning his seed—that is, concerning Christ [Col. 1139D]. For God was born from a Virgin; by his death he conquered death, through which the Church has now received in reality what had been promised to Abraham in hope.

And he led out his people with rejoicing and his chosen ones with gladness. For, always victorious and free, they celebrate a song in gladness and rejoicing, as did Moses, Miriam, and Deborah.

And he gave them the regions of the nations, and they took possession of the labor of peoples. Holy souls and bodies in which sin had previously reigned.

So that they might keep his ordinances and seek his law. So that they might live with righteousness and carefully understand the mysteries of the law.

And let us entreat the Lord that, after the harmful nations have been destroyed before our face, he himself may become the guide of our journey [Col. 1140A], so that, continually rejoicing in him, we may deserve to be led into the promised land and, admitted into his kingdom, be able to rejoice with his saints in everlasting joy. For to him, with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, belong honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM CV

Alleluia, alleluia. This psalm strengthens penitents, reproves the negligent, and promises mercy. We should hold to this rule wherever two Alleluias are prescribed in a psalm: one is to be understood as belonging to the end of the preceding psalm, and the other to the psalm that follows.

Confess to the Lord, for he is good. O you who are weighed down by serious sins, who despair of your salvation, and who think that, because of the greatness of your sins, you cannot obtain forgiveness [Col. 1140B]: I command you—or rather, I prophesy to you: “Confess to the Lord, for he is good.” Your sins are great, but the Lord who has mercy on you is great. Therefore confess to the Lord. Repent; do not despair of your salvation; the Lord is kind.

Confess to the Lord, you who have great sins. Do not trust in your own strength, but in the mercy of the Lord.

For his mercy is forever. Observe what he says: “forever.” But in hell, who will confess to the Lord (Ps. VI)? No one can repent in hell. While you are in this world, I urge you to repent. Therefore confess to the Lord, because he is merciful only in this world. Here he can have mercy on the penitent; there he is judge, not merciful [Col. 1140C]. Here he is merciful; there he is judge. Here he extends his hand to the one who falls; there he sits as judge. I have said all this concerning those who say that there is repentance in hell.

Who can speak of the powers of the Lord? No one is worthy to proclaim the powers of the Father except the Son. No one can speak of the Father’s power except one who is himself powerful. The one who is powerful can himself proclaim and speak of the powers of the Powerful.

He will make all his praises heard. Before our Lord preached in the Gospel, the praises of the Father had not been heard in the world. Everything written in the Old Law, if it is understood spiritually, can be understood as referring to the Father.

Blessed are those who keep judgment and practice justice at all times. David could rightly say this, for he himself had practiced judgment and justice [Col. 1140D]; but because he did not do so at all times, he sang this psalm. For what does it say? “Blessed are those who keep judgment and practice justice at all times.” What good does it do someone to remain continent for twenty years and then fall? As it is written in the prophet: “The righteousness of the righteous man will not benefit him in whatever way he goes astray; it will not deliver or save him” (Ezek. 33). And the sin of the sinner will not harm him on whatever day he turns and does penance. The righteous person should not be secure, nor should the sinner despair of his salvation. For in both of them there are both fear and hope.

“Who practices justice.” Our Lord is Justice. For our Lord is called the Justice of the Lord and Savior [Col. 1141A]. Blessed, therefore, is the one who practices justice—that is, who makes Christ. How, then, do we make Christ, that is, Justice? If we act justly, justice is conceived in us and justice is born from us, and we become the mother of justice. Happy and blessed is the one who at all times is both father and mother of justice.

Remember us, Lord, in the favor shown to your people. What blessed David says is this: “I know, Lord, the ancient Law. Perfect blessedness is not in the old Law but in the Gospel. I know that the former people offended you, and that a new people is being created to serve you. I know that your Son will come and save the whole human race, and that those who are chosen will believe in him. Therefore I ask, since I was born first under the old Law, that you credit me with a reward together with the new people [Col. 1141B].” This appears to be our interpretation. Let us read the verses themselves, and we shall find that they have the meaning we have stated.

“Visit us with your salvation.” That is, with your Son, when he comes.

“To see the goodness of your chosen ones.” That is, grant us a share with the apostles. For we preceded them in time, but they will precede us in spiritual matters—that is, grant that we may see your goodness, which you will accomplish with your chosen ones.

“To rejoice in the joy of your nation.” We are the Lord’s nation, provided, however, that we are his nation. “For the people that will be born,” he says, “whom the Lord has made.” “That we may be praised together with your inheritance.” That is, that we too may have a share with the Gospel, we who came to be under the old Law (John 8). For Abraham our father saw your day [Col. 1141C] and rejoiced. Let us, then, also see it and rejoice with your inheritance.

We have sinned with our fathers. We sons have followed our fathers. We have done what our fathers also did. For he shut everyone up under sin, so that he might have mercy on everyone (Gal. 3).

We have acted unjustly; we have committed iniquity. Pay close attention to what he says: “We have sinned with our fathers, we have acted unjustly, we have committed iniquity.” Did he say, “We have acted impiously”? It is one thing to be a sinner and unjust, another to be impious. The sinner is often overcome by bodily weakness, whereas the impious person denies God. Therefore, because I am not impious but a sinner, I dare to pray for my sins.

Our fathers in Egypt did not understand your wonders [Col. 1141D]. They saw, and did not see. They saw with bodily eyes, but did not see with spiritual eyes. He did not say, “They did not see,” but “They did not understand.” They saw the wonders but did not understand them, for they did not contemplate them with spiritual insight.

“And they did not remember the multitude of your mercies”—how you rescued them from the hands of their enemies. But even today, Lord, you perform wonders when you deign to enlighten us after rescuing us from the darkness of the world.

“And they provoked him as they went up to the Red Sea; and he saved them,” and so forth. These things happened in Israel. But it must be understood that what was a shadow there has been fulfilled as reality in the Church. Thus baptism or the cross of Christ is foolishness to those who are perishing [Col. 1142A]. God is provoked by them when they do not understand. The instructed, however, will then recognize the power of God. The sea has two meanings: baptism, that is, and the world.

“He rebuked the Red Sea, and it dried up.” The stormy world comes to a halt before the people of God when it recognizes the source of life. “And he led them through the abysses as through a desert” (Exod. 14). Just as though they were walking through a dry desert, so they were not overwhelmed by any waves.

“And he saved them from the hand of those who hated them, and redeemed them from the hand of the enemy.” Humanity’s liberation and redemption were accomplished through the passion of Christ.

“And the water covered those who troubled them; not one of them remained” (ibid.). So it also happens now in our baptism. A person is washed with water, and the devil perishes together with his minions [Col. 1142B].

“And they believed his words and praised his praise,” because they were victorious.

“They acted quickly; they forgot his works.” For many in the Church, by living badly and thinking wrongly about God, lose the grace of baptism. “They did not endure his counsel,” so that they might preserve the life they had previously chosen.

“And they desired desires in the desert,” in the solitude of this world. “And they tested God in the waterless place.” For they were in dryness because they did not know the irrigation of the Holy Spirit in the pillar of cloud that went before them.

“And he gave them their requests, and sent fullness into their souls,” so that they might be refreshed with spiritual food and drink.

“And they provoked Moses in the camp, and Aaron, the holy one of God” [Col. 1142C]. Fools provoke the Law and the priesthood when they do not heed the commandments of God announced through them.

“The earth opened and swallowed Dathan, and covered over the congregation of Abiron; and fire burned in their synagogue, and flame consumed sinners.” These things happened according to the literal sense. But even now the earth devours and fire burns those who think earthly thoughts and depart from God’s commandments—those whom the grace of the Holy Spirit does not enlighten, but whom the flame of sin sets ablaze.

“And they made a calf in Horeb, and worshiped a carved image, and exchanged their glory for the likeness of a calf that eats grass.” Their glory ought to have been in God. But when they abandoned him and gave glory to a mute and deaf image [Col. 1142D], they said: “These are your gods, Israel” (Exod. 32). So even now, if someone abandons the Church and consults lots and python-spirits, his glory is changed and he becomes like a beast, as once happened to Nebuchadnezzar (Dan. 4).

“They forgot God, who saved them, who had done great things in Egypt,” so that he might liberate the people after striking that land with plagues. “And wonders in the land of Ham,” when, after abandoning the nations, he planted them in their land. “And awesome deeds at the Red Sea,” so that, after Pharaoh had been destroyed, he might provide the people with a dry passage (Exod. 14).

“He said that he would destroy them, had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him,” and so forth. Pay attention to this, O priest: the people would have perished unless Moses had broken the anger of almighty God. And when you see the people of God sinning, sound the trumpet: announce their sins to them, and stand in the breach before God, so that his fury may be turned away from them [Col. 1143A].

“And they thought nothing of the desirable land,” because they loved this transitory one. “And they did not believe his words,” by which he promised the kingdoms of heaven.

“And they murmured in their tents.” Concerning murmuring, the Apostle teaches, saying: “Do not murmur, as some of them murmured and perished by serpents” (1 Cor. 10). Let us therefore not murmur, lest demons wound and devour us with their poisonous bites.

“He lifted up his hand against them, to overthrow them in the desert, and to cast down their seed among the nations and scatter them throughout the regions” [Col. 1143B]. The Jews were scattered throughout various lands. But the one who is carried about by every wind of teaching and does not stand firmly established in God is also scattered in various directions.

“And they were initiated into Beelphegor, and ate the sacrifices of the dead.” Those who ought to have consecrated themselves to God were consecrated to an idol. Those who ought to have hungered for living bread ate sacrifices of the dead.

“And they provoked him by their inventions,” because they were perverse. “And ruin multiplied among them.” Ruin occurs when the walls of houses collapse; it multiplies when they have been overturned from their foundations. Thus these people were destroyed together with their foundation—that is, with the very letter of the Law on which they thought they stood—because they were not established upon the rock.

Phinehas stood, made propitiation, and the plague ceased. “And it was credited to him as righteousness,” and so forth [Col. 1143C]. Earlier he said that Moses had stood in the breach; here he says that Phinehas made atonement (Num. 25). Listen carefully to this, O priest, to whom souls have been entrusted: draw the sword; kill the fornicators—that is, bring forth the word; insist upon it in season and out of season; rebuke, reprimand, exhort with complete patience and instruction (2 Tim. 4)—so that it may be credited to you as righteousness. For the Lord God says: “The one who brings forth the precious from the worthless shall be like my mouth.”

“And they provoked him at the waters of contradiction, and Moses was afflicted because of them, because they embittered his spirit.” The waters of contradiction are understood as the waters of baptism, at which the devil and his works are opposed. If someone defiles himself with vices after these waters, the priest is afflicted because that person has embittered the Spirit of God through whom the priest preaches, just as Paul said: “Who is made to burn, and I do not burn?” (1 Cor. 9). He also testified concerning this Spirit when he said: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (Eph. 4).

“And he distinguished with his lips,” so that he might continually plead for them.

“They did not destroy the nations of which the Lord had spoken to them”: that is, idolatry and various crimes.

“And they mingled with the nations and learned their works; they served their carved images, and it became a stumbling block to them.” Just as it is credited as righteousness to the priest who pleads for the people, so it became a stumbling block to those who turned themselves toward fanatical desires.

“And they sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons” [Col. 1144A]: their understanding and their souls.

“And they poured out innocent blood, the blood of their sons and daughters whom they sacrificed to the carved images of Canaan.” The blood of the soul is poured out when a person devoted to idols withdraws from the worship of God.

“The land was slain with bloodshed, and it was defiled by their works, and they prostituted themselves in their inventions.” It is infected by the decay of iniquity when the human body is polluted by various fornications. Therefore the wrath of God also rages against the impious; hence what follows:

“And the Lord was angry with his people in fury, and abhorred his inheritance,” because he abandoned it. The people that had once been God’s became a troop of the devil.

“And he handed them over to the hands of the nations, and those who hated them ruled over them. Their enemies afflicted them, and they were humbled under their hands” [Col. 1144B].

But you will say, O human being: “The way of the Lord is not right, since he allows us to be brought low amid such evils.” But please consider carefully: sinners are brought low because of their own crimes, while God is endowed with such great compassion that he always deigns to grant protection, as he says: “Often he delivered them.” He always delivers, and you are not corrected? The blow already inflicted stands at the doors, and you are not reformed?

“But they provoked him by their counsel,” by which they decided to abandon him and follow idols. “And they were humbled by their iniquities.” Now they are humbled not by God but by their own sins. Yet customary mercy comes first, as the prophet says:

“And he saw when they were afflicted, and he heard their prayer” [Col. 1144C]. He teaches you also that, if you turn back and groan, the prayers of your humility immediately draw near to his exalted ears.

“He remembered his covenant,” which he established with Abraham, the beginning of our faith. “And he repented according to the abundance of his mercies, and he granted them mercies before all those who had taken them captive.” On behalf of those who repent, God repents of the evil he had said he would do and did not do, establishing you in the bosom of Abraham your father, whose faith you followed. Therefore the prophet, rejoicing, says:

Save us, Lord our God. Let vices not rule over us. “And gather us from the nations,” because the Hebrew nation is scattered throughout the regions.

“That we may confess your holy name and glory in your praise” [Col. 1144D]—in the Son, certainly, because the name of the Son is your praise.

Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, from age to age, and so forth. Rightly is he blessed forever, through whom the ages were made—and not only were they made, but they were also redeemed. May he now deign to restore us in salvation, that is, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom, with him and the Holy Spirit, belong honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM 106

### Alleluia

This psalm is recognized as narrating the whole condition of the human race, which it either assumed by sinning or undertook through repentance, as well as the multitude of God’s mercies—for in the present passage it says [Col. 1145A]: “Who is wise and will keep these things? Then he will understand the mercies of the Lord” [Col. 1145A]. It also most clearly reveals the rejection of the Jews and the calling of the nations.

Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever. Therefore confess your sins to him, because he is good and forgives sins. If he were not good, he would not say to you, “Confess,” and, “Confess to him, for his mercy is forever.” Here there is mercy; in the passage above there is justice. “For his mercy is forever.” As long as you are in this world, confess.

Let those redeemed by the Lord say so, whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy. He is speaking specifically about the calling of the nations. This psalm contains their mystery, those who were redeemed in the Lord’s passion [Col. 1145B]. “Let those who were redeemed say so.” For he is Savior, Redeemer, and price. “Let those who were redeemed say so.” He redeemed them; he gives the price, his blood.

Why did he give his blood as the price? To redeem us from the hand of the enemy. We were held captive in the hand of the devil. Therefore he came and redeemed us, so that he might free us from the devil’s hand. He redeemed them from the hand of the enemy in order to destroy the enemy and defender. “An enemy sowed weeds over it” (Matt. 13). The enemy is the devil. He himself is both enemy and possessor. Therefore he holds us by his hand—not because he loves us, but because he hates us.

“Whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy.” Great is the majesty and great the power of the Lord’s blood, which releases the devil’s hand. For just as there are certain animals that hold something enclosed within them—as physicians and natural philosophers say—so that, unless the thing is broken, it cannot be separated from them, nor do they release what they hold shut inside; but if oil is introduced, it is immediately dissolved, and what had been tightly held is scattered and divided into parts, so the blood of Christ releases the devil’s exceedingly hard hand [Col. 1145C]. The devil did not want to release us. The Lord poured out his blood like the oil of mercy, and through it he set us free.

“He gathered them from the regions.” See how great the devil’s hand is: “whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy.” Those whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy were held by the enemy’s hand in every region. “He gathered them from the regions.” Throughout the whole world the devil’s hand possessed us.

From the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and from the sea [Col. 1145D]. It seems that he has named four regions: east, west, south, and north. These are the four regions of the world. But the psalm does not actually contain it in this way. It says: “From the rising and setting of the sun”—there are two regions. “From the north,” that is, from the north wind—there are three. “And from the sea.” The sea is in the west. Thus see that he has named the west, but not even once the south.

Why, then, did he name three regions and refuse to name one? We read in Habakkuk: “God will come from the south” (Hab. 3). It is said of the Savior: “God was born in the south.” For Bethlehem is situated south of Jerusalem. Therefore it is said: “God will come from the south” [Col. 1146A].

But if God will come from the south, how is it now said, “From the rising and setting of the sun, and from the north”? The south and the south wind have been kept silent. “From the rising and setting of the sun.” “Amen, amen, I say to you, many will come from the east and the west, and will recline in the bosom of Abraham; but the sons of this generation will be far away” (Matt. 8). “From the rising and setting of the sun”: namely, the foreigners.

“And from the north.” The north wind is exceedingly harsh, but by name it is called the right hand. “From the north,” he says, “evils will be kindled upon the earth” (Jer. 1). The sea is mentioned in Numbers, in Exodus, and throughout all of Holy Scripture; wherever you hear “sea,” according to the regions it always signifies the west. For, in relation to Jerusalem, this great sea that is called the sea lies in the west.

Observe, then, the mystery of the Scriptures. In this passage the west is named twice, and the south not once [Col. 1146B]. Why is this said? Because the Jewish people are not written as being called in this psalm, but only the nations. Finally, what does it say?

They wandered in the wilderness, in a waterless place; they did not find the way to a city of habitation, hungry and thirsty. And so that you may know that this is written specifically about the calling of the nations and the expulsion of the Jews, the psalm itself says later: “He made rivers in the desert,” evidently referring to the Jews.

“They wandered in the wilderness, in a waterless place.” We have said what the waters were; we have said what the rivers were. “They did not find the way to a city of habitation, hungry and thirsty.” Let us explain how the people of the nations were in the desert, where there were no waters—that is, in a waterless place—and how they did not find the way to a city of habitation, hungry and thirsty.

Of those of whom it says “they did not find,” it is clear that they sought the way to a city of habitation but did not find it. They therefore sought the way by which they might come to the city; they sought it hungry and thirsty [Col. 1146C]. Their soul failed within them. “Those who search with searching have failed” (Ps. 63). They failed, they sought, and they did not find; and in their hunger and thirst they did not find the way to a city of habitation.

“Hungry and thirsty.” There were many who promised this way that would lead to the city. Socrates promised it, Plato promised it, Aristotle promised it. The woman with the flow of blood (Luke 8) sought many physicians and could not be healed by any of them. “They did not find the way to a city of habitation.” Their teaching produced hunger for truth more than satiety [Col. 1146D].

The woman with the flow of blood spent her entire substance on physicians. “Hungry and thirsty, their soul failed within them.” But because she had lost all her substance—that is, the Church gathered from the nations—and because her soul had failed within her, she cried out to the Lord when she was afflicted. Touching the Lord’s fringe was the cry of one who believed.

“And they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their necessities.” “To the Lord,” he says, “when I was afflicted I cried, and he heard me” (Ps. 11). We are heard by the Lord when not a simple voice but affliction cries out to the Lord.

“And he led them by a straight way, so that they might go to a city of habitation.” Because they had not found the way to a city of habitation, he led them by a straight way [Col. 1147A]. Thus he shows that previously they did indeed find ways, but crooked and not straight ones.

“And he led them by a straight way.” The way led them to the Way. The Lord and Savior himself led them by a straight way: he made them walk in himself; he is both guide and way. “And he led them by a straight way,” so that by this way—that is, through the Lord and Savior—they might go to the city of habitation, to his Church, which had been founded upon him as rock, way, and guide.

It must also be considered that in this psalm the following is said three times:

Let them confess to the Lord his mercies and his wonders to the sons of men. For he satisfied the empty soul, and he filled the hungry soul with good things. Those who were empty of his grace and suffered hunger for the word, he satisfied with heavenly goods [Col. 1147B].

Those who sat in darkness and the shadow of death, bound in poverty and iron. The human race was bound by chains of crimes and consigned to the prison of the devil. And why did this happen? See what follows:

Because they embittered the word of the Lord, not keeping what he had commanded. And they provoked the counsel of the Most High, which he had given so that they might choose life.

Their heart was humbled by labors, because they were not exalted in the works of God. They grew weak, and there was no one to help, because they were not firm in God and did not seek him who is the true physician.

“And they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their necessities.” After original sin, the human race failed; then, a second time, it failed to observe the Law handed down through Moses. But he also rescued it from this necessity.

“And he led them out of darkness,” and so forth. And for this reason:
