Let them confess to the Lord his mercies and his wonders to the sons of men. What follows teaches why his mercies must be confessed and his wonders proclaimed.

“For he shattered bronze doors and broke iron bars.” For “the Dawn from on high visited us” (Luke 1), and illuminated the darkness of our errors. He broke the chains of the Law so that we might serve with free will.

He received them from their way of iniquity. The devil had therefore shut bronze doors with the strongest bars of his dwellings, so that the human race might not be able to leave his authority. The Lord shattered all these things, as we have said, by his visitation, receiving humanity into himself [Col. 1147D]. They were humbled because of their injustices, so that they might be exalted in him.

Their soul abhorred every kind of food, and they drew near to the gates of death. And they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their necessities. But see how he delivered them: they had abhorred every word of life that the prophets foretold, and they had drawn near to death.

“Then he sent his word and healed them.” The Son himself, who in the beginning was the Word, who in the Gospel heals every sickness and every infirmity among the people. “And he rescued them from their destructions,” into which they themselves had plunged.

Let them confess to the Lord his mercies [Col. 1148A]—for whom the Exalted One humbled himself, for whom God became human, for whom the immortal submitted to death for the life of mortals—and his wonders to the sons of men. For he shattered the bronze doors and bars of hell; he returned victorious to those above; he went back to heaven.

And let them sacrifice a sacrifice of praise. Let goats and calves cease, because God seeks a sacrifice from a pure heart. And let them proclaim his works with rejoicing. With joy let them proclaim to all the choirs how he saved them by his visitation.

Those who go down to the sea—that is, the world—in ships, in the Churches that carry Christ and are battered by the waves of this world, doing their work upon many waters—that is, among the peoples. But these words must also be referred to the apostles [Col. 1148B]. They saw the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep. For in the profound darkness, through their preaching, the light of truth shone forth, and, as the Lord worked, they saw the light of the most true Trinity shining in the thickest darkness.

“He spoke, and the spirit of the storm stood still.” The world’s temptation ceased. So also, when the Lord was sleeping in the boat and was awakened by his disciples, he commanded the wind, and the sea grew quiet (Matt. 8).

“And its waves were lifted up.” They were suspended so that they would not harm—that is, the movements of this diabolical temptation, which the wicked stir up against the righteous.

“They rise up to the heavens.” They are lifted up in their pride, to the injury of the saints. “And they descend to the abysses.” They are humbled in confession. And so that you may understand that this is figuratively spoken of wicked people, it follows:

“Their soul melted away in evils.” For waves of water do not have a soul. But the soul melts when, struck by heavenly blows, it recognizes that it has sinned and inflicted injury upon the saints.

“They were troubled and staggered like a drunken man.” Their understanding possessed nothing joyful, stable, or sober. “And all their wisdom was swallowed up”—away from the wisdom of the true God, just as once Moses’ dragon swallowed the dragons of the Egyptians (Exod. 7).

“And they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their necessities,” so that, abandoning luxurious drunkenness, they might follow the wisdom of God.

“He made their storm into a breeze,” so that it might now come not with fire and hail, but with the gentle breath of the Holy Spirit [Col. 1148D]. “And its waves grew quiet.” By doing penance, they were converted to tranquility.

“They rejoiced because they grew quiet.” While those people rested, these others rejoiced. “And he led them to the harbor of their desire.” With the waves now quiet, they devoted their whole will to being led to him who, calming the waves, is the true harbor. “And he delivered them from their necessities,” so that they would not be battered by these tempests.

Let them confess to the Lord his mercies, by which he protects the human race, and his wonders to the sons of men, because he wondrously restrained these waves.

Let them exalt him in the assembly of the people, in the congregation of the faithful. “In the seat of the elders let them praise him”—not in that seat in which the scribes and Pharisees sat [Col. 1149A], who, reading the Law, did not understand that the Lord was announced in it, but in that seat in which the prophets or patriarchs, contemplating him with spiritual sight, recognized him in miracles or proclaimed him in oracles.

For he made rivers in the desert and springs of water in thirst; fertile land into saltiness, because of the wickedness of those who dwelt in it. Rightly is he to be exalted, rightly praised, for in the Church—which had previously been deserted and hated—he placed the apostles, who both consoled it by their address and fertilized it by their nourishing flood. He also gave to thirsty souls the springs of his word, the outlets of preaching, and filled with eternal fruits the soil of the body, which had previously produced thorns of bitterness.

He made the desert into pools of water, providing baptism in the Church [Col. 1149B], and dry land into springs of water, establishing preachers in the aridity of the nations.

And he settled the hungry there, so that they might be refreshed with heavenly goods. And they established a city of habitation, presenting their souls as protected from the incentives of vices, in which the fruit of the Spirit might dwell.

“And they sowed fields, and planted vineyards, and produced the fruit of their growth.” These words refer to the apostles, who cast seed into the hearts of believers, from whom they might receive the fruit of eternity—that is, the hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold (Matt. 13).

“And he blessed them, and they multiplied exceedingly,” because they did what pleased him. So also God blessed everything in the hand of Joseph, because he guarded himself from wicked thoughts and desires (Gen. 41 and following). “And he did not diminish their cattle.” The irrational people among them were not reduced to something lower, but restored to something better.

Thus, having explained the calling and redemption of the nations, he returns to the expulsion of the Jews, saying:

They became few, because the works of God had not multiplied among them. “And they were afflicted by the tribulation of evils and by sorrow,” because the wicked persecuted the innocent.

“Contention was poured out upon their princes,” so that those who had despised the Lord might themselves be despised. “And their empty images deceived them,” namely, the images they worshiped. “And he led them into a trackless place, and not into the way.” Deceiving them away from the way of the Lord, they led them into the trackless place of Satan [Col. 1149D].

Finally, after these people had been led into the trackless place, let us see what God did for his people.

“And he helped the poor man out of poverty.” He satisfied the Christian people with eternal banquets. “And he established families like sheep,” so that, hearing the voice of the true shepherd, they might follow him in faith.

“The upright will see and rejoice,” those through whose preaching they were converted. “And every iniquity will shut its mouth”: the devil, or the Jews, or the heretics who had presumed to speak iniquity arrogantly.

Who is wise and will keep these things, and then understand the mercies of the Lord? For if you consider wisely and understand spiritually [Col. 1150A], you will see in this fourth psalm mercies that were sought and graciously granted—mercies that may he deign, in his overflowing kindness, to grant when sought, open when knocked upon, and not deny when requested. To him be glory, with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM 107

### A Song of a Psalm, David himself

A song always refers to contemplation; a psalm, however, refers to bodily matters. To put it more clearly, a song refers to theory [Note: See what we observe at the beginning of Epistle 30 to Paula in our recension, note e, col. 444.], whereas a psalm refers to practice—that is, to works. Therefore, since the title says “A song of the psalm,” he rightly and consistently says in the second verse: “I will sing and psalm in my glory.”

My heart is ready, O God; my heart is ready. I am ready not only in action but also in heart and understanding [Col. 1150B]. “My heart is ready”: in understanding; “my heart is ready”: in action—that is, in practice. For I am ready not only in heart and understanding but also in action. Therefore I say a second time: “I will sing and psalm in my glory.” “I will sing,” that is, in my heart, “and I will psalm.”

Just as a psalter is composed of many strings, and if one string is broken the psalter is ruined, so also in our actions, if we transgress one commandment, our psalter is broken. Therefore he said: “I will sing and psalm in my glory.” In other books it is read, “in your glory.” But it is better to read according to the Hebrew, “in my glory.” What he says means this: “I will sing and psalm in my glory.” Lord, in what I psalm to you and sing to you, I do not confer a favor upon you but upon myself [Col. 1150C]. In another psalm he says: “You have no need of my goods” (Ps. 15). Therefore what I do, I do for myself. Thus my service to you is my glory.

We fast: do we give anything to God? We do this for our sins. We lie in sackcloth: what do we offer the Lord by this? We offer him only this much—that we save our souls. For he himself desires this, like a good and merciful physician. If he has healed someone, both he and the one who has been healed rejoice; so it is also with our Lord.

Rise up, psalter and lyre. O psalter, O lyre, you were made and created so that you might psalm to God. Rise up and play; why are you lying down? O monk, who stand bodily, why does your soul lie down and not psalm to the Lord? “Cursed is the one who does the work of God negligently” (Jer. 48) [Col. 1150D]. If you are a psalter, if you are a lyre, why are you deaf and do not glorify God?

I will rise at dawn. God cannot be blessed and praised in darkness, but he is blessed in the light. I say something remarkable: even if we rise at night, we bless God in the light. It is never night for a Christian; for a Christian the sun of justice always rises.

These things we say according to the Jews. But according to the higher meaning, it is the Lord who sings: “My heart is ready, O God; my heart is ready.” I am ready here; I am ready in the future. I save both on earth and in heaven—that is, I save both angels and human beings.

Rise up, psalter and lyre. The Lord speaks to his own body: “Psalter and lyre, you who descended into hell and lay there, rise up and praise the Lord.” And see what he says: it is not the one who moves the lyre and the psalter who praises, but the lyre and the psalter themselves bless the Father. For he is God, and he is blessed and praised by others. His body, however, and the human being whom he assumed, praises the Lord [Col. 1151A].

And so that you may know that the prophet speaks in the person of the Lord, and that I am not saying this from myself, see what follows:

I will confess to you among the peoples, Lord. Understand “peoples” to mean the Jews. And I will psalm to you among the nations. He is speaking about us. By “Jews” he means those who first believed from among the Jews. And observe the order: first he praises God among the peoples, and afterward he praises the Lord among the nations. For they first believed from among the Jews, and afterward they believed from among the nations.

For great is your mercy above the heavens. There is no creature that does not need the mercy of God. We all need God’s mercy. Gabriel, Michael, Seraphim, Cherubim, Powers, Dominions—these are indeed holy, but they need the mercy of their Creator. I do not disparage the angels; I proclaim the Creator, since the angels themselves gladly hear their Creator proclaimed.

We can also say: “For your mercy raises from earth to the heavens.” And your truth reaches to the clouds. Where are the Jews, where are those like the Jews, who understand only according to the letter? How does the truth of God reach to the clouds [Col. 1151C]? The Son of God says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14), and he came down to earth and lived among human beings (Baruch 3). How, then, does your truth reach to the clouds?

The meaning is clear: he is speaking about the apostles and the saints, so that they may not pour down their rain upon the Jews but upon the nations, as it is written: “I will command my clouds not to pour rain upon Israel” (Isa. 5). Thus the truth of God is in these clouds.

But if the truth of God is in these clouds, how can Montanus and the Cataphrygians say that what was not revealed to the apostles has been revealed to them?

Be exalted above the heavens, O God. God is not exalted except above the heavens; he is not exalted above the earth. When we are earthly, we do not exalt God. But if we have been made heavenly from earthly beings, then we exalt God. And our Lord, when he was on earth, did not exalt us. Someone may say: “You are speaking rashly.” Indeed, he himself says in the Gospel: “When I have been exalted, I will draw all things to myself” (John 12). Consider what he says: “When I have been exalted in heaven, then I will draw all things to myself.” This is indeed the first sense, but I understand something else: “When I have been exalted, when I have been crucified, then I will draw everyone to myself.”

“That your beloved may be delivered.” O wondrous understanding! The Lord is crucified and exalted for this reason: that his beloved may be delivered. “That your beloved,” he says, “may be delivered.” Be exalted above the heavens, O God. What we asked has happened. He has been exalted, and we have been delivered.

[Col. 1152A] God has spoken in his holy place. Whether in the temple, or in each of the saints, or in the prophet. He is heard in Moses, he is heard in the apostle; and I speak more truly: “He has spoken in his Son.” What, then, has God spoken? The words that follow.

“I will be exalted and divide Shechem.” “For this reason,” he says, “I am crucified, that I may divide Shechem.” *Shechem* is interpreted in our language as “shoulders.” The shoulders, however, signify works. The sense, therefore, is this: “For this reason I am crucified, that I may divide my works among my saints.” “For this reason I am crucified, that I may place my easy yoke and my light burden upon the necks of human beings.” You have done, Lord, what you promised. You have been exalted and have divided Shechem.

“And I will measure out the Valley of Tents.” Truly our Lord and Savior entered this [Col. 1152B] valley of tears, this place of our lowliness—that is, this world—in which, however holy anyone may be, he does not yet know as he ought to know. “For we know in part, and we prophesy in part” (1 Cor. 13).

“Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine.” Our Lord and Savior rejoices, possessing greater riches. *Gilead* is interpreted as “migration.” He rejoices, therefore, when a people from the nations migrates and comes to him. *Manasseh* is interpreted as “from forgetfulness.” See, therefore, what he says: “That son who received his inheritance, consumed it, and had forgotten me is now mindful of me” (Luke 15). And he is called Manasseh, that is, “from forgetfulness,” because he did not remain forgetful but returned to his father.

“And Ephraim is the receiving of my head.” [Col. 1152C] *Ephraim* is interpreted as “fruitful.” “Ephraim,” he says, “is the receiving of my head.” Here he has used “receiving” for “crown.” For whatever is placed on the head is a crown, and in Scripture it is called by various names. Elsewhere it says: “His truth will encircle you like a shield” (Ps. 90). And in another psalm: “Who crowns you with mercy and compassion” (Ps. 102). Just as there he used “shield” for “crown,” so here he has used “receiving” for “crown.”

See, therefore, what he says: “You have become Gilead; you have become Manasseh”—that is, “You have migrated to the Lord, and after forgetfulness you have returned to your father. Be Ephraim; be fruitful. Have good works, and afterward you will be the Lord’s crown.”

“Judah is my king.” See in what great glory is the one who practices repentance. *Judah* is interpreted as “confession.”

“Moab is the cauldron of my hope.” A great mystery is recognized in a few words. I ask you to pay close attention, since it benefits both me who speak and you who listen. *Moab* is interpreted as “from a father.” *Ab* means “father”; *mo* means “from.” Who is this “from a father”? The one who lost his father, who abandoned his father, who did not return to his own father and is not worthy to be called Manasseh.

Who is this Moab? The enemy of the Lord, from whose lineage, even to the fourth and tenth generation, and forever, no one will enter the Church of the Lord. Who is this Moab? The one born from an unclean union in a dark cave. For from Lot and his daughters were born two sons, Moab and Ammon, and Moab was the elder son (Gen. 19).

See, therefore, how a mystery is hidden in the letter: in darkness, in a cave—not in the sun, not in the light. Moab, then, is interpreted as the devil, who forgot his father. Finally, Absalom too, who persecuted his father, is interpreted as the devil.

How, then, is this Moab the cauldron of the Lord’s hope? *Cauldron* is interpreted as “pot.” How is he the pot of the Lord’s hope? Is it credible that Moab, who is interpreted as “the devil,” should be the cauldron of the Lord’s hope? How is he the Lord’s hope?

Let the Apostle speak: “Those whom I handed over to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Tim. 1). The devil is, as it were, the Lord’s torturer. Those who do not walk rightly toward God are handed over to the devil. Why? So that they may perish forever. And where is God’s clemency? Where is the merciful father? Where is the one who makes his sun rise over the just and sinners, and sends rain upon sinners and the just (Matt. 5)?

What he says is this: “I handed sinners over to the devil so that, tormented by him, they might be converted to me.” It is also said in Jeremiah: “What do you see, Jeremiah?” “A boiling pot,” he says (Jer. 1). See, therefore, that flesh is placed in this pot. This is written in Ezekiel: “Put flesh into the pot,” he says, “so that it may become tender” (Ezek. 24)—so that hard things may be converted to God, so that a heart of stone may become a heart of flesh, and what previously could not be written because of its hardness may afterward be written because of its softness.

“I will set this pot boiling,” he says, “and I will cook the flesh and the bones until they lose all moisture and filth.” And afterward see what is said: “And let them learn,” he says, “that I am the Lord.” Great is the mercy, and great is the mystery. Flesh is put into the pot so that it may be cooked and learn that he is the Lord. There are many things that could be said about Moab and the pot, but for now it would take too long.

“Into Idumea I will extend my sandal.” *Idumea* is interpreted as “earthly” and “bloodstained.” The merciful God wishes to possess not only heavenly things but also earthly ones. Foreigners have become my friends. He speaks of us, who have believed from the nations.

“Who will lead me into a fortified city?” No one, Lord. For you are the one who says: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and no man from the nations was with me” (Isa. 63). “For all have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. 13).

Who, then, will lead me into a fortified city? No one, Lord. Even Peter, who had promised to die for you, afterward denied you. What is this fortified city? Hell, where the impious are confined, from which it is not permitted to leave. Truly, from this city no one else emerged victorious except you, Lord. And truly this is a fortified city. Moses could not leave this city. Jacob likewise entered this city and did not return. Finally, he says to his sons: “Mourning, I will descend to the underworld” (Gen. 37).

He descended to the underworld because paradise had not yet been opened by the thief. This city is fortified for departing, but open for entering. “Who will lead me as far as Idumea?”—where there is a place of punishments [Col. 1154A] and blood. For Idumea is interpreted as “bloodstained,” the place of the slaughter of souls, where many souls are killed. No one descended into hell victorious except you alone, Lord.

“O God, who have rejected us.” He did not say, “who are rejecting us,” but “who once rejected us.”

“And will you not go forth, O God, with our forces?” These words must be read interrogatively: “And will you not go forth, O God, with our forces?” You who suffered for us, why do you not help us, but permit us to be trampled by the most savage devil?

“And will you not go forth, O God, with our forces?” See what he says. He did not say, “You did not go forth,” but, “You will not go forth, O God, with our forces.” He means this: When we labor, then God helps us. “It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9).

See what he says. He did not say, “It is not of the one who lies down or of the one who sleeps, but of God who shows mercy.” Rather, see what he says: “It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy.” If, therefore, we are unwilling and do not run, God will profit us nothing. Our part is to will and to run, and afterward God has mercy. For an athlete who sleeps loses the victory.

“Give us help in tribulation.” He did not say, “Give us help in pleasures,” but “in tribulation.” “To the Lord I cried when I was in distress, and he heard me” (Ps. 119). He did not say, “I cried when I was in pleasures,” or “I cried while sleeping.” Do you wish to be heard by the Lord? Be in tribulation; cry out, and you will be heard. If someone is not in tribulation, he cannot invoke the Lord’s help.

“For vain is the salvation of man.” “Cursed is the man who places his hope in man” (Jer. 17). There is no need to interpret this. The statement is clear to everyone. Someone placed his hope in an emperor, in a prince, in a father or mother; in some sudden matter the breath of the one in whom he had hoped was taken away, and his salvation vanished. He did not say, “The salvation of man is vain,” but “the salvation of the one who hopes in man.”

“In God we will act valiantly.” Let us place our hope in no one except the Lord. Let us not say: “If this or that happens to me, how will I live?” I give you an answer that is greater. If persecution comes, how will you live? For the Christian there is always persecution; nakedness is always set before him.

Therefore no one should despair of this life. No one should be afraid. No one should say: “If I grow old, how will I live? If I become ill, how will I survive?” You have Christ, and you are afraid? If he feeds the birds of heaven, do you doubt that he can feed you? The devil feeds his own people, and will Christ not feed his servants? The devil makes the judges of this world rich, and can Christ not ensure that you do not beg? The devil gives gold and gems, and can Christ not give bread?

Let us cast all anxiety from our hearts and say: “In God we will act valiantly.” He will be our strength; he will be our bread; he will be our ruler. And he will bring our enemies to nothing. He crowns us; he fights with us; rather, he himself will conquer in us.

For what do we say? “In God we will act valiantly.” When we have become strong, he will bring our enemies to nothing. He did not say, “He will fight,” or “He will kill,” but “He will bring them to nothing.” He will bring them to nothing so that, if they wish, he may make them strong and glorify them. Let us therefore bless God, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM 108

**For the end, a psalm of David.** What it says, “for the end,” let us understand as referring not to the present but to the future. If it refers to the future, it is a prophecy about Christ.

“O God, do not be silent about my praise.” This means: Judas betrayed me; the Jews persecuted and crucified me, and thought that they would destroy me completely. But you, O God, do not be silent about my praise. The whole Church praises the Lord each day, and the prayer of the Lord who says, “O God, do not be silent about my praise,” has been fulfilled.

See what dignity priests possess. Priests speak, and in the priests God does not keep silent about the praise of his Son.

“For the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of deceit have been opened against me.” Let us see how the mouth of Judas the betrayer was opened against the Lord. He came to the Lord in order to hand him over and said, “Rabbi”—that is, “Teacher” (Mark 14). Behold the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of deceit. I wish to save him by my clemency; I offer him a kiss; I wish to overcome his wickedness; but he persists in doing evil so that he may betray me.

This is understood specifically of Judas, but generally of the Jews at the time when they were saying, “Crucify, crucify” (John 19). Such was the mouth of the sinner opened against the Lord. But so that you may see that he spoke about all the Jews, you will recognize it from what follows. For what does he say?

[Col. 1155C] “They have spoken against me with a deceitful tongue.” I was being crucified for them, and they mocked me. My wounds were their medicine, and I appeared ridiculous to them.

“And they surrounded me with words of hatred.” Not so that they might believe, but so that they might attack.

“And they attacked me without cause.” This is understood in two ways: “without cause,” that is, for no reason. For I had not sinned, nor did I deserve for them to wage war against me. What worthy cause did they have for attacking me? Because I had healed their sick, raised their dead, and performed other signs. See, therefore, that they attacked him without cause.

It can also be understood another way. They wished to extinguish and erase my name, yet they could not. When someone persecutes another and accomplishes nothing, and does not fulfill his desire, he persecutes in vain.

“In place of loving me, they slandered me; but I was praying.” In return for the benefits I had bestowed upon them, they heaped insults upon me. But what was I doing? I was praying. These are the Lord’s weapons; let these also be our weapons: prayer.

Therefore, whenever someone persecutes and hates us, let us say: “In place of loving me, they slandered me. But what was I doing? I was praying.” Was it in order to conquer them? Far from it. The Lord did not pray in order to conquer. What, then, did he say? “But I was praying.” What was I saying? “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23).

“And they repaid me evil for good.” Nailed to the cross, I was asking on behalf of those crucifying me, and they were saying: “Ha! You who destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, save yourself” (Mark 15). “If the Father loves you, let him come now and deliver you” (Matt. 28). I rose from the dead for them, and they say: “His disciples came by night and stole him” (Luke 23).

“And hatred in place of my love.” Consider, O Christian; consider, O monk: if the Lord received his persecutor and betrayer with a kiss, and prayed for those crucifying him, what ought we to do for our brothers?

“Appoint a sinner over him.” Because I prayed for them on the cross and they saw my wounds, I gave them an opportunity for repentance. But they do not repent, and they refuse to have me as king. Let them have the devil as king. They refuse to have Jesus as king; let them have Barabbas as king, whose name is interpreted as “son of the father”—that is, of the devil.

Who was this Barabbas? A rebel and a robber. And truly they have Barabbas as king: even to this day, a rebel and a robber who kills the Jews themselves. Barabbas the robber, who delighted in blood, was imprisoned before the Lord was crucified, before the Jews crucified him. They denied the Lord, and Barabbas was released (John 18).

From that time Barabbas began to have power over them. And that demon which had been expelled from the man and from that generation, which wandered in the desert and could not find a place, brought with it seven other demons worse than itself (Luke 11), entered the synagogue, and the last condition of that man became worse than the first.

Finally, the synagogue of the Jews, before it crucified the Lord, was indeed sinful, but had only one demon. It crucified the Lord, and eight demons entered it at once. Therefore what he said was fulfilled: “Appoint a sinner over him, and let the devil stand at his right hand.”

Because he stood at his right hand, the synagogue had its right hand withered, as it is written in the Gospel. But let us pray that the Lord may stand at our right hand and the devil at our left (Luke 6).

It is written in Zechariah: “And the Lord showed me Jesus the high priest standing before the angel of the Lord, and Satan was standing at his right hand to oppose him” (Zech. 3). If, then, the devil stands at the right hand, how does he now say concerning Judas, “And let the devil stand at his right hand”? But consider what he says: “The devil was standing at the right hand of Jesus in order to oppose him”—that is, he wished to oppose his right hand. Here, however, he does not say that he wishes to fight, but that he had already conquered Judas. There the devil desires to fight against the right hand; here he has become master of Judas’s right hand.

But this too must be considered. At that time he stood at the Lord’s right hand in order to oppose him, when Jesus was wearing filthy garments. For it is also written there: “And Jesus was wearing filthy garments.” As long as the Lord Jesus wears filthy garments, the devil stands at his right hand—as long as he bears our sins, the devil opposes him through our sins.

But when it is said in Zechariah, “Take away his filthy garments and clothe him in festal garments,” Jesus immediately says to the devil: “May the Lord rebuke you, Satan; may the Lord who chose Jerusalem rebuke you.”

We have said all this because it is written: “And let the devil stand at his right hand.”

“When he is judged, let him go out condemned.” Let him not come into judgment but into condemnation. For where there is judgment, there is condemnation; where there is condemnation, the sentence is already manifest.

“And let his prayer become sin.” Judas’s repentance became a worse sin. How did Judas’s repentance become a worse sin? He went away and perished by hanging. The one who became the Lord’s betrayer also became his own executioner. I say this because of the Lord’s clemency: he offended the Lord more by hanging himself than by betraying the Lord.

His prayer ought to have become repentance, but it was turned into sin. You see a heretic praying; you see a Jew; you see a Manichaean. Even if they fast, even if they pray, their prayer is nevertheless turned into sin.

“Let his days be few.” His days became few, but his nights increased. He was taken away in the middle of his days. The sun withdrew from him, and behold, darkness was multiplied for him.

“And let another receive his episcopate.” This has been interpreted more clearly in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 1). But it was not spoken only about that time concerning Judas; it is said even to this day, and even until the day of judgment.

If Judas himself lost the apostolate, let priests and bishops guard themselves, lest they too lose their priesthood. If an apostle fell, a monk can fall more easily. Virtue does not perish, even if a human being falls and perishes. Yet the Lord lends out his denarii at interest. If a person does not double them, his money is taken and given to the one who has. The Lord’s money cannot lie idle.

“Let his sons become orphans, and his wife a widow.” See that the things being said are mysteries. Whom do you think Judas’s sons are? The Jews. And the Jews are called Jews not from that holy Judah but from this betrayer.

From that holy Judah we are spiritual Jews; from this betrayer they are fleshly Jews. Finally, there are two apostles who bear the name Judah. The eleventh apostle is called Judas of James. The twelfth, and last, is called Judas Iscariot.

From Judas of James, therefore, we are called spiritual Jews; from this Iscariot, they are called fleshly Jews. That Judah of James is called our father—“of James,” that is, “Judah, son of the supplanter.” For we supplanted the Jewish people and received their firstfruits.

They, however, are called from Iscariot—a matter of uncertainty, whether it signifies “father” or “his village.” In any case, however you interpret it, it signifies “payment” and “price.” Therefore Judas, who was about to betray the Lord and receive a price, took his name from the price.

Although he returned the price to the Jewish priests, they nevertheless condemn him, since they refuse to accept the price of blood. [Col. 1158A] See the disagreement of the Pharisees and the wretchedness of Judas. If you bought Jesus’ blood rightly, why did you not accept your money? But if you refuse to accept it because it is the price of blood, you show that you yourselves shed the blood unjustly and wickedly.

But see what they do. They do not put the money, he says, into the treasury; rather, they buy a field with it and call it *Acheldemach*, which is interpreted as “the price of blood” (Matt. 27). Why do they buy it? For the burial of foreigners.

Blessed are we, for whom a field is bought with the price of the Lord’s blood.

“And his wife a widow.” The synagogue, which was first made God’s wife, concerning which he said: “And he gave her a certificate of divorce” (Deut. 24). And again: “I received her, and I said to her, ‘Return to me’” (Jer. 3).

That synagogue, therefore, received a divorce from the Savior and became the wife of Judas the betrayer. Finally, what did she do? She did not receive a dowry; rather, she gave a dowry to her husband.

Again, that most wretched Judas who betrayed the Lord did not wish to accept an evil dowry, but returned to his prostitute-wife the evil dowry that he had received from her. And what does he say? “You displeased your former husband; he repudiated you, cast you out, and gave you a certificate of divorce. I do not wish to have you as my wife. You gave me a price and deceived me. You who killed the Lord your God will also kill me.” For I cannot find in Scripture that Judas had either a wife or children.

[Note: [Col. 1157] It will be useful to recall what Euthymius transmits concerning this passage.]

“Let his sons be continually shaken and wander about, and let them beg.” Consider carefully, for what follows is difficult. From the time when the Lord was crucified, the Jews have continually been shaken and are always wandering; they do not remain in their own place.

It is also said concerning Cain: “And Cain went out from the presence of God and dwelt in the land of Nod” (Gen. 4). *Nod*, however, is interpreted as “shaking.” Because Cain had gone out from the presence of God, he rightly did not stand firm but dwelt in the land of Nod—that is, in shaking.

So these people too, because they crucified their God and Lord, will be carried away in agitation. They are not in their own places, but are scattered throughout the whole world. Here “begging” refers to a poverty of spiritual riches. For they do not have prophets, they do not have the Law, they do not have priesthood, they do not have sacrifice; they have truly become beggars.

“Let the creditor search out all his substance.” You gave him money, Lord; you gave it to him as you did to others. But what did he do? He did not bind it in a cloth or bury it in the ground; he was negligent. When he had the Lord’s talent and money, he accepted a price from the Lord’s enemies and sold his Lord (Luke 19).

Therefore I say to you, Lord: demand from him the interest on your money. “And let strangers plunder his labors.” The Lord lends at interest and openly demands repayment. And what happened? Strangers will plunder his labors.

This may be understood generally of all the Jews, because they were devastated by the Romans. Or it may be understood specifically, because Judas—and the people themselves—were plundered by demons.

“Let him have no helper, and let there be no one who pities his orphans.” At that time the Jewish people had no helper. Answer me, O Jews. You were in Babylon; you had prophets there, Daniel and Ezekiel, and indeed you were idolaters. You were in captivity for seventy years, and afterward you returned to your own land.

Behold, now it has been four hundred years. Why has no prophet been sent to you? At that time you worshiped idols, and God had mercy on you. But now you do not worship idols; why has the Lord abandoned you? Behold, it has been four hundred years.

But then you abandoned the Lord and worshiped idols; now you have crucified and killed the Lord, and therefore you will have no helper.

[Note: [Col. 1159D] Learned men consider this work later than Jerome’s time and attribute it to a writer using a false name. Nevertheless, this passage also appears in the Aquicinctine manuscript apud Martene, *Anecdota*, vol. IX, where the work is attributed to Hilary of Poitiers, the elder Father. See what we observe in the Prefatory Notice.]

“In one generation let his name be blotted out.” O prophecy, O mystery of prophecy! “In one generation let his name be blotted out.” After the Lord’s passion, forty-two years passed, and that people was blotted out. For the completed age arrives at the fortieth year. After the Lord’s passion, therefore, Jerusalem was destroyed in the forty-second year.

See, therefore, that his name was blotted out in one generation. But even in this there is the Lord’s clemency. They crucified him, and he gave them forty-two years for repentance. I speak simply: he destroyed them after forty-two years because none of those who crucified the Lord remained alive. Judas is cursed so that the Jews may be cursed in Judas.

“Let the iniquity of his fathers return to the memory of the Lord.” They sinned in the desert, and you forgave them. Now he reckons against them what they sinned then, because they crucified the Lord.

Or let us interpret it another way: he reckons against them the cruelty of their murders and forgives them nothing.

“And let the sin of his mother not be blotted out.” Who is Judas’s mother? Jerusalem, which rejoices in blood, which killed the prophets and its own Lord.

“Because he did not remember to show mercy.” You see how great is the Lord’s clemency. He sees him coming with attendants; he sees him coming with clubs, and he offers him a kiss. He comes to betray, and the Lord gives him a kiss, so that the one who did not fear his teacher might at least be overcome by clemency.

“And he pursued the poor and needy man.” Although he was rich, he became poor for our sake (1 Cor. 8). The Lord calls himself poor and needy; who, then, will glory in his own riches? You have consolation, O poor, and the Lord is poor with you.

“And to kill the brokenhearted.” What does he mean by “to kill the brokenhearted”? It is what he said in the Gospel: “My soul is sorrowful even to death.” And again, when he said: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26).

Alternatively: “This caused me grief, and I was sorrowful for those persecuting me, because they did not wish to repent. I was hanging on the cross and washing away their filth with my blood, but they did not wish to repent.” These were the tears; this was the contrition: I could not save those who were persecuting me.

“Deliver me, because I am needy and poor.” The Lord called himself poor in order to console the poor. He became poor among human beings so that at least no one might despise a poor person.

“And my heart was troubled within me.” See what he says: “And my heart was troubled within me.” It is the same as what he says elsewhere: “I was troubled, and I did not speak.” To be troubled is human; to overcome trouble and anger is a matter of great virtue.

Therefore the prophet also says: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. 4). To become angry is human; not to remain in anger is Christian.

“I have been shaken off like a locust.” I had come to protect my people, and I said: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to you, how often I wished to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings” (Matt. 23).

I had come like a hen to protect them, but they received me with the most hostile intent. I had come as a mother, and they killed me as though I were their murderer.

“I have been shaken off.” What does this mean? They persecuted me; they cast me out. They persecuted me from Nazareth. I came to Capernaum; they persecuted me. From Capernaum I went to Bethsaida, and from there they persecuted me. I came to Jerusalem; I did not wish to withdraw from my people, and from there they persecuted me, and so they treated me like a locust.

And what did I do? Did I become angry, defend myself, curse them, and abandon them? I did none of these things. What, then, did I do? I prayed for them.

“My knees have grown weak from fasting.” Take consolation, O monk, by fasting, since the Lord also did this. I say that when a monk fasts, he becomes stronger through fasting. And when his knees grow weak through fasting, then he is strengthened most of all.

“And my flesh was changed because of the oil.” I seem to be about to say something difficult, and I interpret it according to the letter in order to edify those listening. For the letter edifies me. It is good to fast; it is good to flee pleasures.

Before I come to the spiritual understanding, I am astonished at the literal wording, which says that he ate oil. It is far removed from other desires. I have said all this because it says: “And my flesh was changed because of the oil.”

I have interpreted this in another way. What it means is this: Oil is an image of glory; oil is, as it were, food for light. Thus the Jews received oil from me; they received life; they received light.

Let no one suppose that “oil” signifies mercy. In Hebrew it signifies “intelligible oil.” He was changed not into joy but into sorrow, not so that he might appear more beautiful but so that he might appear more disfigured. Therefore he says: “We saw him, and he had no beauty” (Isa. 53). Why? Because his flesh was changed because of the oil.

He did not have bodily pleasures, but the Spirit of God. Therefore, when we fast, when our faces are pale, and when we appear unattractive, let us recognize that then we appear more beautiful to Christ. Christ loves such soldiers, those who devote themselves to fasts. Our provision and our food is fasting. Why? Because in fasting there is victory, and in victory there is triumph.

Finally, the Apostle also says: “He does not glory in abundance but in weakness” (1 Cor. 4). “For when I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Cor. 12).

“And I became a reproach to them.” For they called me a Samaritan and said: “He casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons” (John 8). “Is this not the son of Joseph the carpenter? Are not all his brothers and sisters here with us?” (Luke 11). And again: “You who destroy the temple and build it in three days” (Mark 15). And again: “Let us see whether Elijah comes to save him.”

He was calling out, “Eli, Eli,” which means “My God, my God” (Matt. 27), and they thought he was calling Elijah. See the uneducated Jews. Was the Son of God asking Elijah for help?

“They saw me and shook their heads.” Why did they shake their heads? Because they had already moved their feet as well.

“Save me because of your mercy.” He also says in the Gospel: “I have authority to lay down my soul, and I have authority to take it up again” (John 10). And again: “No one takes it from me.” How, then, does he ask for mercy? He himself asks for mercy, and he himself grants it. As a human being he asks; as God he grants.

“And let them know that this is your hand, and that you, Lord, have made it.” What does he mean: “Let them know that this is your hand, and that you, Lord, have made it”?

Let the Jews understand that they did not prevail over me; rather, my will and your will were fulfilled, that I should suffer, and I wished to suffer. Therefore I say, according to what I am as a human being: “My God, I wished to do your will.” It was your will and mine that I should suffer, not theirs.

Therefore it was not their plot and strength that accomplished this; you and I wished that I should suffer. For you struck your shepherd, and the sheep were scattered. This is written in Zechariah: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered” (Zech. 13). That I should suffer was my will and yours. What you willed, I also willed.

“Scandal must come, but woe to the one through whom it comes” (Matt. 18).

“Let them curse, and you will bless.” This happens even to this day: They curse in the synagogue, and the Lord blesses in the Church.

“Let those who rise up against me be confounded, but your servant will rejoice.” They rise up against me, but I, your servant, will rejoice. Why “your servant”? Because although he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2).

“Let those who slander me be clothed with shame.” It greatly benefits us to understand what we are saying. God’s clemency appears in the word “let them be clothed.” He does not say, “Let them perish”; he does not say, “Let them be erased forever.” What, then, does he say? “Let them be confounded”—that is, let them understand their error, be ashamed, and fail in repentance.

The one who is clothed with shame is near salvation. For if someone is truly ashamed, he begins to repent.

Consider, O monks: if you ever have anything against your brother, you must always pray to the Lord for him. The Lord is crucified and prays for those crucifying him. If you hear an evil word, do not hold on to anger. “Do not let the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. 4).

“And let them be covered, like a double cloak, with their shame.” *Diplois* is a kind of cloak. Indeed, in Hebrew it is also called *MAIL* (). It is called *diplois* because the cloak is double.

Therefore I say to you, Lord: My enemies are the Jews; they persecuted me, crucified me, did every evil to me, and blasphemed me. Forgive them, for I, who suffered, pray for them.

And what do I pray? Let them blush and be confounded, and so be saved. They stripped me of my tunic and lost their own. Give them confusion; give them disgrace; let them have a double cloak—that is, let them not have simple confusion but double confusion, so that they may repent more deeply.

He does not speak against the Jews but for them. For he is the Creator both of them and of us; he has not utterly uprooted them. Do you wish to know? Peter was one of them, and all the apostles were from them. We have been grafted into their root. We are the branches; they are the root. We ought not to curse the roots but to pray for our roots.

We who have been grafted into the root should beseech the Lord that, just as these branches have been saved, so the root may also be saved. Perhaps someone will say: “You pray for blaspheming Jews?” I pray to the Lord for them. For if he has mercy on his persecutors, how much more will he have mercy on me?

“I will give great thanks to the Lord with my mouth.” This is said after the resurrection and sung concerning the future Church.

“And in the midst of many I will praise him.” Not in Judea alone, but throughout the whole world, in the Church, I will praise you.

Because he stood at the right hand of the poor man. The devil stood at the right hand of Judas. But the Lord stood at my right hand, to save my soul from those who persecuted me (Matt. 26). “He will save the soul,” he says. And elsewhere he says: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death.” Whoever is sorrowful possesses sensation. For an insensible soul has no sensation. An insensible soul has neither sensation nor pain. For wherever there is pain and sadness, there is sensation. If, therefore, he experienced sadness and pain, then he also experienced the sensation of pain.

If they should wish to say to us, “For this reason we do not say that he possessed sensation, so that he may not appear to have sin,” let us answer them: Did he have a body like ours, or did he not? If they say, “He did,” let us answer them [Col. 1162D]: “Then he also had the sufferings of our body.” Let each person understand what I am saying. But if they deny that he had the sufferings of the body, then we say to them that he did not have a body either.

And let us say to them: Just as he had a true body, like ours, and yet did not have the sin of the body, so also he had a true soul, and did not have the sins of the soul. Let us therefore confess that he had a true body and a true soul. For if the Lord did not assume everything that belongs to a human being, he did not save the human being. But if he assumed the body and did not assume the soul, then he saved the body but did not save the soul. Yet we desire our soul to be saved more than our body.

Jesus therefore assumed both body and soul [Col. 1163A], so that he might save both, so that he might save the complete human being, just as he had created him. If, then, they say that the Lord did not take on sensation for this reason—that he might not sin—and if they think that whoever possesses human sensation cannot overcome, let them tell us: Did John the Baptist have sensation, or did he not? When he was in the desert, did he sin? Certainly they say that he did not sin. Indeed, our Lord also says: “Amen, I say to you, among those born of women there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptist” (Matt. 11).

Did Peter have sensation, or did he not, and did the other holy apostles? If, then, the apostles overcame human sensation, was the Lord afraid to take on sensation lest he be overcome by it? And while they wish to glorify the Lord, they disparage him. How do they disparage him? By making it appear that the Lord was afraid of what the apostles were not afraid of [Col. 1163B].

Let us therefore give thanks to almighty God and say: “In your sensation you had no sin. And the prince of this world came and found nothing in you” (John 14). So may you grant us this: just as in your sensation you overcame the devil, so may you overcome the devil in our sensation, so that, just as you created us perfect, you may also save us perfect. For you are the Creator, you are the Teacher, you are the Lord, and you are also the one who suffered for us; you who live and reign forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM 109

[Note: [Col. 1163] Compare the genuine Jerome at the beginning of Book IV, p. 181, *Commentary on Matthew*.]

A psalm of David himself. This psalm contains the voice of a prophet speaking about Christ. Thus the prophet says: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand.”

It is David who speaks—the prophet, the holy man, the king. What, then, does the king say? What does the king and prophet say? [Col. 1163C] “The Lord said to my Lord.” The Savior explained this passage in the Gospel, saying: “If Christ is,” he says, “the son of David, how does he call him Lord in the Spirit?” (Matt. 22).

You see, therefore, what he is saying: If he is David’s son, how do you say, “How does he call him Lord in the Spirit?” Someone may say: “Then he is not David’s son?” He was saying this about the Pharisees, who confessed Christ merely as the son of David.

I say this same thing to the Jew and to Photinus: If he is David’s son, how does he call his own son Lord? But to the one who confesses him as Lord God and Son of God—for example, the Manichaean, who denies that he is David’s son—I prove that he is David’s son. For us, therefore, the one who is the Son of God is himself also the son of David. There is not one Son of God and another son of David [Col. 1163D]. I do not make two persons in God and man; rather, the one who is the Son of God is himself also the son of David.

“The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand.” In Hebrew the first name, “Lord” (), is written with these letters, which are written only of God. The second name, “Lord” (), is written with the letters by which human beings customarily call someone “lord,” just as a servant calls his master “lord,” and kings are called “lords.”

See, therefore, what he says: “The Lord said to my Lord.” Godhead does not sit; the assumed body sits. It is to this Lord, to whom it is commanded that he sit, that this applies. It is to the one who is human, who has been assumed [Col. 1164A], that it is commanded that he sit.

We say this against the Arians and against those who say: “The Father who commands him to sit is greater than the one who is commanded.” All the Gospels resound concerning the human person, and now proof is unnecessary, because everything that appears lowly is referred to the human being, referred to the flesh.

Now let us speak from the Psalm:

“The Lord will send forth from Zion the rod of your power.” In Hebrew, “rod” is not so much *rod* as *scepter*, that is, the emblem of royal power. “The Lord will send forth from Zion the rod of your power.” For from Zion the law goes forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem (Isa. 23). “Rule in the midst of your enemies.” He did not say, “Destroy your enemies,” but what did he say? “Rule in the midst of your enemies.” Cause those who were strangers to become yours. “Rule in the midst of your enemies” [Col. 1164B]—your enemies, of whom it is written in Psalm 67: “The tongue of your dogs from the enemies, from him.” These are the enemies who were under another’s power. Now, therefore, the Psalmist prays for this: Rule over your enemies; deign to be Lord of your enemies.

“With you is the beginning on the day of your power, in the splendors of the holy ones.” This verse is obscure. Let us examine the day of the Lord’s power, so that, once we know the day, we may then know what “the beginning” is, and how this beginning is and has been with him; how this very beginning is in the day of his power, in the splendors of the holy ones.

This beginning, therefore, which is with the Lord in the day of his power, is with the Lord so that the holy ones may shine. “With you is the beginning on the day of your power.” “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1). “This was in the beginning with God” [Col. 1164C].

The Father is the beginning, but the Son also is the beginning. For the beginning has no beginning. If it had another beginning, it would already cease to be the beginning. Whatever, therefore, we attribute to the Father, we attribute also to the Son. For if the Father is in the Son, and the Son in the Father, and everything that belongs to the Father belongs to the Son, and everything that belongs to the Son belongs to the Father, then the Father’s beginning is the Son’s beginning.

Therefore, what he says is this: At the time when you were suffering and saying, “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23), you were speaking as though from human feeling, not pleading as though you were weak. For the beginning was with you; divinity was with you. But for this reason you were asking for help: so that, having received help, you might give it to your holy ones, and they might shine [Col. 1164D].

Let no one be scandalized by what is said—“having received, you might give”—for he is speaking according to the human being. If he assumed a human body, it is necessary that he also assume human words. Christ is human, and truly human; we say this according to the assumption of the flesh. If, then, he is human according to the body, you see the body and are not scandalized. Why are you astonished if he speaks with human words?

But if the lowliness of the body scandalizes you—the cross, the insults, the blows, the scourges, and every outrage of the cross—if this scandalizes you, return to the beginning, and you will not be scandalized. For the Father says to the Son: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.” Are you astonished [Col. 1165A] that our Lord and Savior, who truly assumed a human being, speaks according to the human being, when God the Father himself, who did not assume a human being, speaks as a human being: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you”?

“I have no womb; but I cannot otherwise reveal myself as Father unless I speak in human words. From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.” From the womb—that is, from my substance. From the womb. Listen, Eunomius; listen, Arius. If the Lord is a creature, if he is a made thing, does an artisan beget his work? Does an artisan call his work his son? A carpenter makes a bench: did he beget it from his womb? Does he say to it, “From my womb I begot you, O bench”? Certainly he does not say this. What, then, does he say? “I made you with my hand.”

But when “womb” is mentioned, a son is signified—and a son who is not adopted. Adopted sons are also called sons: “But to all who received him he gave power to become children of God” (John 1). There he gave them power. Here, however, he begot him from the womb—from his own nature, from his own inward being, from his own substance [Col. 1165B]. “From the womb,” that is, from the very marrow of his divinity. Everything that the Father is in divinity, he gave to the Son whom he begot.

“From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.” “Before the morning star.” This figure of speech is called in Greek *συνεκδοχή* (*synekdochē*), which grammarians call “the whole from a part.” Therefore, when “before the morning star” is said, one creature is named but all creatures are indicated. When he says “before the morning star,” let us understand it as though he had said: before the moon, before the sun, before every creature.

“From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.” Before the morning star—before this morning star that is seen in the world, true light was begotten [Col. 1165C]. Hence the Psalm says elsewhere: “In your light we shall see light” (Ps. 35). This is speech addressed to the Father: O Father, in the light of the Son we shall see the light, the Holy Spirit. “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.”

“The Lord has sworn and will not repent.” “The Lord has sworn.” What he says—“has sworn”—is not sworn to the one who was begotten before the morning star, but to the one who was born afterward from a virgin.

“You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” It is superfluous for us to wish to interpret this verse, since the holy Apostle has discussed it fully in the Letter to the Hebrews. For he says: “This is Melchizedek, without father, without mother, without genealogy” (Heb. 7). There he explains most carefully why he is said to be without father, without mother, and without genealogy [Col. 1165D]. All the ecclesiastical writers have said that “without father” is spoken according to the flesh, and “without mother” according to God.

Let us interpret only this: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” Let us say only why he said “according to the order.” “According to the order”: you will by no means be a priest according to the Jewish sacrifices, but you will be a priest according to the order of Melchizedek (Gen. 14). For just as Melchizedek, king of Salem, offered bread and wine, so you will offer your body and blood—true bread and true wine. This Melchizedek gave us these mysteries that we possess. He is the one who said: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood” (John 6). According to the order of Melchizedek, he handed over his sacrament to us [Col. 1166A].

“The Lord is at your right hand.” I see something new. At the beginning it says: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand”; and now it says to him: “The Lord is at your right hand.” If he sits at the right hand of the Father, how does the Father in turn sit at the right hand of the Son?

When it says, “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand,” it most clearly says that the Son sits at the Father’s right hand. But when it says, “The Lord is at your right hand,” it says that the Father sits at the Son’s right hand. All this is said so that the Son may be equal to the Father.

There is much that could be said. But the devil stands at the right hand of the sinner. Every sinner has the devil standing at his right hand. Someone may ask: How, then, is it also said in Zechariah that the devil stood at the right hand of Jesus son of Jehozadak, and that the devil stood at the Savior’s right hand (Zech. 3)? You see that there is a question here [Col. 1166B].

But at the time when the devil stood at the Savior’s right hand, “Jesus,” it says, “was wearing filthy garments.” He was carrying our sins, wrapped in our vices; therefore the devil stood at his right hand.

“He will crush kings on the day of his wrath.” “All these things have been handed over to me. In an instant,” he says, “he showed him all the kingdoms of the earth.” The devil shows the kingdoms of the world. And what does he say? “All these things have been handed over to me. If you fall down and worship before me, all will be yours” (Matt. 4). On the day of battle, therefore, on the day of combat, he will crush the kings in his wrath.

“He will judge among the nations.” Observe the distinctions: the kings are crushed; he will judge the nations. “He will fill the ruins” [Col. 1166C]. Our Lord ascended the cross, and many ruins were made. He was appointed for the fall and resurrection of many, and as a sign that would be opposed (Luke 2).

“He will fill the ruins”—of those who do not believe, who did not believe the apostolic scouts (Num. 21–22). Moses also sent scouts into the world; and because the people did not believe the scouts, they fell in the desert. To this day the bodies of unbelievers fall in the desert of this age.

“He will crush the heads in the land of many.” He will fill the ruins of unbelievers; he will crush the heads of those who are doubtful, of those who do not have perfect faith. “He will crush the heads in the land of many,” not of all. For if he had said “of all,” none of us would have any hope. “Of many” is said so that others may be left.

“He drinks from the torrent on the way.” Who drinks from the torrent on the way? The one to whom it was said: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand”; the one who heard: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek”; the one who “crushed kings on the day of his wrath,” who “filled the ruins,” who “crushed the heads in the land of many” [Col. 1166D].

What else does this one do? “He drinks from the torrent on the way.” Let us first examine the way, so that afterward we may examine the torrent on the way. “The way” is called this present age, through which he walked. Thus it is written in the Gospel: “Be reconciled with your adversary while you are on the way” (Matt. 6)—that is, while you walk in this age and go by the way toward the one who is the true way. Hence it is also said in Psalm 118: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way.”

Blessed are those who are undefiled on this way of the age, and in this world. Therefore, the priest according to the order of Melchizedek, because he came on the way of the age and walked on our way, also drank from the torrent that was in the age [Col. 1167A].

A torrent does not have natural waters, nor waters that flow continuously; rather, it has waters from storms, rains, whirlwinds, and squalls. A torrent is never in the mountains, but always in valleys and precipitous places. It gathers foreign waters, gives them birth, and moves along swollen.

“He drinks from the torrent on the way.” A torrent never has clean water, but always muddy water. This is what is meant: the waters of this age are always turbid, always full of storm. Do you wish to know how he drank from the muddy torrent? He himself says: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26). And it is said in the Gospel: “He began,” it says, “to be sorrowful and troubled” (ibid.) [Col. 1167B].

Our Lord, therefore, also drank from the torrent of this age—turbid waters, sorrowful waters, waters that have no joy. He took the cup and filled it from the torrent of the world; and because the waters were turbid, he said: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” He drank, therefore, from the torrent of this world, but he did not drink as though in his own house; he was hastening on the way toward other things. “He drinks from the torrent on the way.” For this reason he drank from the torrent: because he was on the way.

He drank from the torrent. If the Lord drank from the torrent of this world, how much more the saints? Do you wish to know that the saints drink from the torrent? He says elsewhere: “Our soul has passed through the torrent” (Ps. 123). “He drinks from the torrent on the way.”

We have spoken about the torrent; let us also cite a testimony: “Our soul has passed through the torrent.” Do you wish to know another torrent? When the holy prophet Elijah was being pursued by Jezebel, after he had received food and had gone through the wilderness for forty days, he was, it says, in the desert and drank from the torrent of Chobar (1 Kings 19) [Col. 1167C].

But when you hear of the torrents of this age, do not despair. This torrent frequently fails. It appears to swell; it appears to have many waters; but it quickly fails if you endure. Elijah did indeed drink water in the desert at the time when he was in sadness and distress (ibid.). He had left Judea and gone to Mount Sinai, for Jezebel was pursuing him; and therefore he drank from the torrent of Chobar.

But because he persevered to the end, the water of the torrent consequently failed. And because the water of the torrent had failed, the Lord said to him: “Go to the widow at Zarephath of the Sidonians,” and so forth. Behold, Elijah also drank from the torrent [Col. 1167D].

But the Lord and Savior himself drank—and drank the cup—from the torrent of Cedron. For Scripture relates this when they came and seized him: “They came,” it says, “and seized him in the torrent,” and so forth (John 18). You see how low and rugged the place of the torrent is. *Cedron* is interpreted in the Hebrew language as “darkness.” You see, therefore, that the torrents of this age are in darkness.

When the Lord was handed over, then, he was not handed over again on the Mount of Olives, nor was he handed over in the Temple; he was handed over at the torrent, at the torrent of darkness—namely, Cedron [Col. 1168A]. For all who hate the light love darkness.

“He drinks from the torrent on the way.” Since, therefore, the Lord drank from the torrent and tasted death, the Father therefore exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name.

Then it is now said: “He drinks from the torrent on the way.” And because he drank from the torrent on the way, “therefore he exalted the head.” And what does he say? “When I am lifted up, I will draw all things to myself” (John 12). He was exalted, and he exalted us.

His head was exalted; but as for the dragon, he crushed its heads, and they were broken in the sea. “Therefore he exalted the head.” He did not say, “Therefore his head was exalted,” that is, exalted by another; rather, the one who had humbled himself exalted it himself. For he himself says in the Gospel: “I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10) [Col. 1168B].

“Therefore he exalted the head.” He exalted himself, who is the head of all. Or certainly, when he says “he exalted the head,” he did not exalt himself. “Therefore he exalted the head.” For he was always high. But when he says, “He exalted the head,” he exalted our head—we who, being bent down, could not look toward heaven but toward the earth.

Do you wish to know that he himself exalted the head? He himself freed that woman whom the devil had bound (Luke 13). He exalted the head of the woman who had always been bent over, and she worshiped him.

To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM 110

Alleluia. This psalm is written first according to the order of the letters, although many also think that the twenty-fourth and the thirty-sixth psalms are written in Hebrew according to the order of the letters [Col. 1168C]. But in those psalms some letters are either missing or added, and sometimes one verse is short while another is much longer without limit. From this I think that the arrangement arose more from the practice of readers than from the writer’s design. Indeed, the translators of the Septuagint, because some difficulty arose among them, did not wish to place the Hebrew letters in the translation.

“I will confess to you, Lord, with all my heart.” If David had not been guileless and had possessed deceit, he would not have said: “I will confess to you, Lord, with all my heart.” Not with the lips alone, but with the whole heart. “In the council of the righteous and in the congregation: the works of the Lord are great.” He calls them “upright”—those who were formerly sinners but are now righteous. For this is no cause for astonishment. You see an elephant and a camel [Col. 1168D], and likewise a fly and a gnat, possessing the same movement, breath, and limbs.

“He gave food to those who fear him.” In famine he fed Elijah; in the desert he rained manna upon the Jewish people (Exod. 16), and what is said was fulfilled: “He gave food to those who fear him.” This is according to the literal sense.

But he gave food—the bread that came down from heaven (John 6)—by which, if we are worthy, we are nourished. For how many martyrs were wasted by hunger and are now with the Lord?

“Holy and terrible is his name.” Holy to the holy; terrible to sinners. “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” Those who do not fear the Lord have no wisdom. Or those who do not possess wisdom do not possess fear.

[Col. 1169A] His praise remains forever and ever. Since “Alleluia” was written beforehand in the title, the psalm rightly ends with praise. For *Alleluia* is interpreted: “Praise the Lord.”

## PSALM 111

Alleluia. This psalm urges us to be established in the dwelling of the eternal house through the fear of God.

“Blessed is the man who fears the Lord.” I have often said that everything interpreted as referring to the person of the righteous is referred to Christ. For if the saints are types and figures of the Savior—if someone is truly holy, for example Isaac is a type of the Lord and Savior, and Joseph, Solomon, David, and the other saints—then this blessed man who is now described also refers to the righteous man [Col. 1169B].

Indeed, it is truly said of a righteous man; but this righteous man is a type of the righteous man. “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord.” For the moment we have set aside the psalm; now let us speak about the righteous man: “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord.”

Psalm 111 is alphabetic. Psalm 110 also follows the alphabet. The first verse is written from *aleph*: “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord.” The second from *beth*: “He will greatly desire his commandments.” The third from *gimel*: “His offspring will be mighty in the earth,” and so on up to the twenty-second letter, *tau*. Let us therefore discuss each verse through your prayers.

“Blessed is the man who fears the Lord”: this is the beginning of the psalm. It does not yet say, “Blessed is the man who loves the Lord.” Fear belongs to those who are beginning, but love to those who are perfect (1 John 4). For perfect love casts out fear [Col. 1169C]. Thus it speaks of the beginning, that is, of the holy man who is beginning.

Let us therefore examine the order of the psalm: “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord.” What does the one who fears the Lord do? Does he hear God’s words and become learned in the law? It does not say this. What does it say? “He will greatly desire his commandments.” The one who fears the Lord, the one who is blessed, gladly performs his commandments.

“He will greatly desire his commandments.” Observe what it says. It does not say, “He performs his commandments.” Many perform them out of fear and receive no reward. For whoever fears Gehenna and therefore does not commit fornication does not have as great a reward as the one who acts out of love of God.

“He will greatly desire his commandments”—that is, he wishes very much to perform them; he longs to carry out his commandments. Just as someone thirsts when he is in intense heat, so he desires the commandments of the Lord. He does not perform his commandments anxiously, but he wills them; and he wills them not superficially, but greatly [Col. 1169D].

The third verse is:

“His offspring will be mighty in the earth.” I who have performed God’s commandments willingly am worthy to become the father of saints. We speak briefly, so that the discourse may not be prolonged.

“The generation of the upright will be blessed.” May the Lord grant that you too, who hear me, may be a generation of the upright.

“Glory and riches will be in his house.” Glory and riches—do we suppose that the glory and riches of this age are meant? Does someone perform God’s will and his commandments in order to obtain the riches of this world? And certainly no one performs God’s commandments unless he has despised the riches of this world (Ps. 111).

“Glory and riches will be in his house.” The glory of believers is meant, as the Apostle says: “Are you not my glory and my riches?” The riches of which the same Apostle says: that you may become rich in all knowledge and righteousness. And his righteousness remains forever and ever [Col. 1170A].

“Light has risen in the darkness for the upright in heart.” Formerly we were wandering in darkness; we were sitting in darkness and the shadow of death. But light has risen for us, according to Isaiah (ch. 58).

“Merciful and compassionate and righteous.” Merciful and righteous. If you are a sinner, do not despair of forgiveness: he is merciful. But if you are proud and rely upon God’s clemency, do not be negligent, for he is also righteous.

“Merciful and compassionate and righteous.” Observe what the Psalmist’s wisdom has done: righteousness is singular, but mercy is expressed twice—“merciful and compassionate and righteous.” Since the Lord is merciful and compassionate, let the righteous man imitate his Lord and be merciful himself [Col. 1170B].

“A good man is merciful and lends.” Does someone suppose that he is speaking about gold and silver and money? The righteous possessed so little that they could lend to others that they themselves received food from others.

If, then, I do not have anything to give, am I no longer righteous? If I do not give alms, will I not be counted among the righteous? How many saints gave alms but fell away from holiness. The perfect did not give alms because they had nothing with which to give them. Not to give alms is a crime for one who possesses something. But one who has nothing with which to give alms is free. However much he wishes to give, that much he has given, because he has given through his intention.

Yet the saints also have something with which to give alms. Peter says: “I have neither silver nor gold; but what I have, this I give you” (Acts 3) [Col. 1170C]: “In the name of the Lord Jesus, rise and walk.” What is greater: to give money, or to make a disabled person well?

“A good man is merciful and lends.” What are these alms? What is it that the righteous man lends? The following verse shows this: “He arranges his words in judgment.” He did not say, “He arranges his gold, his silver, and his money in judgment,” but “He arranges his words in judgment.”

This is mercy: if a holy man teaches others who are not holy. “He arranges his words in judgment.” We have understood, therefore, what the money is that is lent. But what he says—“He arranges his words in judgment”—is what is said in the Gospel: that we should not cast our pearls before swine (Matt. 7). That is, each person should know to whom he gives, what the other can receive, and what he cannot [Col. 1170D].

Hence the holy man says: “In my heart I have hidden your words, so that I may not sin against you” (Ps. 118). I did not give them to whomever I pleased. I did not give what is holy to dogs, nor did I give pearls to swine. Great, therefore, is the danger for a teacher who pours out the Lord’s words upon swine.

There is much that could be said about the psalm. But since the hour excludes us, let us bless almighty God; and let the one who possesses such riches give to those who do not possess them. Let the one who does not possess them receive gladly.

May the Lord also grant me to have these riches, so that I may give to those who do not possess them and increase the riches of those who possess them, so that I may possess this blessedness both by speaking and by hearing. For blessed is the one who speaks into the ears of one who hears [Col. 1171A].

What benefit is it for me to speak if another does not receive my words? What benefit is there in sending wine if what is sent is immediately poured out? You see that in the Gospel water is poured into the water jars, changed into wine, and preserved so that it does not perish (John 2).

“He is merciful”—that is, in his heart—and he believes in action. It is good to give earthly possessions, but it is better to proclaim mercy: that is, to consign to oblivion the one who has done you harm; in other words, to forgive the one who has sinned against you.

“He arranged his words in judgment”—that is, he is his own judge. He says within himself. The Lord said: “If you forgive, you will be forgiven; if you give, it will be given to you” (Matt. 6). For the one who judges himself in this way in the present, God crowns in the future.

“For he will never be shaken.” Such a person will not be shaken [Col. 1171B], because he has been founded upon a rock.

“The righteous man will be in eternal memory.” That righteous man is always in God’s memory.

“He will not fear evil report.” He will not fear that word: “Depart from me, you accursed” (Matt. 25).

“His heart is ready to hope in the Lord.” That is, his hope is always ready in God. His heart has been strengthened; his soul is in faith. He will not be shaken from that faith into unbelief, because he has been founded upon a rock—that is, upon Christ.

“Until he looks down upon his enemies.” That is, he looks down upon vices and sins, all heresies, or the power of his enemies.

“He scattered; he gave to the poor; his righteousness remains forever and ever.” “He scattered”—that is, he divided. He did not say, “Give everything to one man,” but he says: “Go, sell everything that you have, and give to the poor” (Mark 10 and Luke 18).
