Because he divided or scattered it among many, for the prayer of many is more powerful than that of one person [Col. 1171C].

“His righteousness remains forever and ever”—that is, his works themselves remain. “His horn will be exalted in glory.” That is, his kingdom will be exalted in glory; that is, he will be with God.

“The sinner will see.” How will he see, since the Prophet says: “Let the impious be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of God”? Yet what follows says: “They will see and be confounded” (Zech. 12). And elsewhere: “They will look upon the one whom they pierced”—that is, they will see that form of servant and human being which he deigned to assume from our humanity.

But the glory that the saints will have, they will neither possess nor see; and whatever they see, they will see to their punishment. “And he will be angry”—that is, against themselves, because they did not do good things [Col. 1171D]. Their repentance will come too late. They will say: “These are the ones whom we held in contempt; behold, they are counted among the servants of God. The abundance of our riches did us no good. The sun did not rise for us.”

“He will gnash with his teeth and waste away.” By the gnashing of teeth, cold is understood, as in: “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 5 and Luke 13). For both cold and heat will be there, and no rest.

“The desire of sinners will perish”—that is, all the good things they possessed here in the present. Let us therefore listen carefully to the words of God, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM 112

Alleluia. This psalm teaches us that, having laid aside our old wickedness, we should glory in the praises of God like newborn infants. For it says:

“Praise the Lord, children; praise the name of the Lord.” Here children are summoned to praise; concerning them the Savior says through Isaiah: “Behold, I and the children whom the Lord gave me” (Isa. 8). For from the mouth of infants and nursing children full praise is perfected for God.

“May the name of the Lord be blessed.” Every creature blesses him. Perhaps it was not previously blessed? It was always blessed, but previously only one nation, the Jewish people, blessed and believed in him; now he is believed in and blessed among all nations.

“From this time forth and forever.” From this time forth—that is, from the time when human beings began both to believe and to praise; and now—that is, in the present; and forever—that is, without end [Col. 1172B]. For it was always blessed beforehand as well.

“From the rising of the sun to its setting.” That is, from the beginning of our birth until death. “The name of the Lord is worthy of praise,” as I said above.

“The Lord is exalted above all nations.” Was he not exalted previously? He was exalted in Judea; now he is exalted above all nations. He says through the prophet that he wished to reject the Jews and choose the nations. “And his glory is above the heavens.” That is, his glory is above the saints.

“Who is like the Lord our God?” As though he said: No one is like him. As in: “Who is like him among the sons of God?” And elsewhere he says: “There is none like you among the gods, O Lord” (Ps. 85).

“Who dwells on high and regards the lowly in heaven and on earth.” “On high”—that is, among the holy ones. Does he not also dwell among the lowly? He does, because he regards the lowly, as in: “Upon whom shall I look, except upon the humble and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66) [Col. 1172C].

When are the saints on high? When they contemplate heavenly things. And then they are lowly on earth: when they humble themselves in the active life, they are raised up in the contemplative life. Those who are lowly here on earth are high with God.

Why did he not say, “He dwells among the lowly,” but “He regards the lowly”? Because where he regards, there he dwells; and where he dwells, there he regards.

“Raising the needy from the earth.” This is understood both of the head and of the members. “Raising”—that is, God the Father raised up Christ, who became needy and poor for us. And we, the needy—that is, without a father, the devil, and without a mother, paganism—are raised up by Christ [Col. 1172D].

“And lifting the poor from the dung heap.” What he called “earth,” he also called “dung heap”; and what he called “needy,” he also called “poor.” For he raised us from the earth and the corruption of our sins, as in: “Why are you proud, dust and earth?” (Sir. 10).

He may set him with princes, with the princes of his people. God the Father has placed his Son in the heavenly places, at his right hand. And he will rule over the princes—that is, over the nine orders of angels—according to the saying: “I am the prince of the army,” or “the prince of the powers.” Moreover, he has placed the saints, his members, with those nine orders of angels.

He makes the barren woman dwell in a house, a joyful mother of children [Col. 1173A]. The barren woman is the holy Church. Hence the prophet says: “Rejoice, barren woman,” and so forth (Isa. LIV). At first the holy Church was barren, because she did not beget children except a few. The Synagogue had God as her husband, yet she begot only a few (Acts II and following). Later the Church, which had previously been barren, brought forth great offspring in one or two days, when she begot eight thousand. And the prophet says: “Who are these, or who has begotten them for me?” (Isa. XLIX). “Make room for me, and cities where I may dwell.” And the Lord said: “I will do so” (Ps. XVIII). “Their sound has gone out into all the earth,” that is, throughout the whole world.

He makes the barren woman dwell in a house, that is, in the Church. She herself is barren, and she herself is a mother; they themselves are children, and she dwells within herself. This means the unity of the Church: it is one reality and many [Col. 1173B] members. Many are one body, as Paul says, and there she will rejoice within herself—that is, in unity (Rom. XII).

## PSALM CXIII

**Alleluia.** This psalm contains the voice of the prophet, showing that the things narrated in it historically are to be understood as spoken spiritually.

**When Israel went out of Egypt, the house of Jacob from a barbarous people.** Historically, this psalm recalls the time when the children of Israel went out of Egypt (Exod. XIII). But it pertains even more to the spiritual meaning, namely, when we were freed from Egypt—that is, from the darkness of ignorance of our sins—through baptism.

**The house of Jacob from a barbarous people.** Those Israelites were freed from a barbarous people, that is, from those nations [Col. 1173C] that dwelt in Egypt. In the spiritual sense, however, the house of Jacob means those who supplant vices. They were freed, and we, the spiritual house of Jacob, have been freed from those unbelievers who remained in unbelief (Gen. XXXII).

**The house of Jacob.** At first he was called Jacob; afterward, Israel. Hence he said: “I saw the Lord face to face, and my soul was saved.” And the Lord said to him: “You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name.” We too must first be Jacob—that is, supplanters of vices—so that afterward we may be Israel, that is, souls who see God and contemplate God with the eyes of the heart, according to the saying: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V).

**Judah became his sanctuary.** At first God’s sanctification was in Judah [Col. 1173D]. But “Judah” is interpreted as “confession,” that is, among those who confess faith in the Trinity and come to baptism, where God’s sanctification is found.

**Israel was his power.** And God’s power is that we may be found worthy to be Israel, that is, that we may be called souls who see God.

**Israel reigned in it.**

**The sea saw and fled.** The sea saw and fled when Moses came with his people (Exod. XIV). And how did it see? It understood the will of the Creator and gave way to that people.

Alternatively, according to the spiritual meaning: the sea, that is, the Gentile world, saw the holy preachers, the supplanters of vices, and the souls who see God fled—that is, they were unable to resist the apostles, because God was in them.

**The Jordan turned back.** The Jordan’s turning back is not read in the historical account (Josh. III), except when they entered it with the ark: as though that water had moved backward, it stood like a wall, while the other water flowed into the sea. What, then, is understood by this? “Jordan” is interpreted as “their descent.” These are understood to be those who come to baptism. When they saw the martyrs suffering many persecutions, they turned back toward the sea—that is, in the Gentile world they denied the faith. Later the Lord called them through his preachers: “Turn to me, and I will return to you” (Zech. I). And afterward many were converted to God.

“That other water flowed into the sea”: these are the unbelievers who flowed into the sea, that is, into the sea of perdition.

**The mountains leaped like rams, and the hills like lambs of the sheep [Col. 1174B].** The holy preachers leaped for joy when they saw those who had previously been blasphemers converted. They leaped like rams, that is, leaders of the flocks who beget children—the holy apostles. Hence one of them said: “Through the Gospel I begot you” (I Cor. IV).

Alternatively, preachers of higher merit are understood, who now beget children through their preaching. Hence Paul said: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. IV).

**What is the matter with you, sea, that you fled; and you, Jordan, why did you turn back?** The prophet asks through himself and answers himself, as though he were saying: What happened to you, Gentile world, that you fled? And you, Jordan—that is, you Christians—what happened that you turned back? Why? Did you see the holy preachers, that is, the mountains? Did you see the rams, that is, the supplanters of vices and the souls who see God the Father? Therefore did you flee?

**Mountains, you leaped like rams, and hills like lambs of the sheep.** This is a repetition.

**The earth was moved at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of Jacob.** The prophet explained this elsewhere when he said: “He saw, and the earth was shaken” (Ps. LXIX). And shortly afterward he says: “At the presence of the Lord,” and so forth. The earth was moved—that is, by God’s presence, because God was in his preachers. The Gentile world was moved; “at the presence of the God of Jacob,” that is, at the presence of the one whom Jacob worshiped.

**Who turns the rock into pools of water.** The rock is Christ; and historically, streams came forth from the rock (Exod. XVII). Before Christ came in the flesh, such great waters—that is, such great teaching—had not yet burst forth. Later four rivers came forth from Christ, the four Gospels, and watered the whole world.

**And the cliff into springs of water.** This is a repetition. Cliffs are the same as rocks. “Rock” is also called a cliff. “And the cliff into springs of water”: abundant teaching concerning Christ.

**The Red Sea**, which is so called because that sea-water was like blood and prefigured baptism.

**Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory.** Those good Jews say: It was not our merit that freed us, but your power, so that your name might be glorified among all the nations.

Alternatively, the preachers of the New Testament say the same. When they perform mighty works, God performs them through them, so that his name may be glorified and praised through him.

**Because of your mercy and your truth.** Your mercy and your truth accomplish this.

**Lest the nations should ever say, “Where is their God?”** For this reason God performs these wonders, so that the nations may not say that God was unable to save them. Or, in the New Testament, he does the same thing now among his saints.

**But our God is in heaven; he has done whatever he desired.** God is above, in heaven. The saints say to those unbelievers who worship idols: You touch your gods with your hands and see them with bodily eyes, but our God is above, in heaven.

**In heaven and on earth, he has done whatever he desired.** In those who lead a heavenly life while still enclosed in earthly flesh, he has fulfilled [Col. 1175B] his will.

**The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands.** It is called an “idol” because it has been made in the likeness of some dead human being.

“Silver and gold.” Why did he not say “of stone,” or “of bronze,” or “of clay,” or “of wood,” but “of silver and gold”? The Holy Spirit foresaw what answer they would give when they were reproved. He therefore mentioned gold and silver, because they would say: “I do not worship a god of wood, stone, or bronze, but a god of gold and silver.” You say to him: “If you worshiped gold and silver, such an error would not exist.” And they say: “We do not worship gold or silver.” He replies: “I worship not gold and silver, but my god.” What is this image, and what is the power that is in it? You say to him: “The devil is there.” He says: “Far be it from me. I do not wish to worship the devil.” How do you not worship the devil, since we read in another psalm: “All the gods of the nations are demons” (Ps. XCV)? He says: “I do not worship that either.” What, then, do you worship? “I worship the sun, the moon, and the stars. These are my gods; they save me.”

You say to him: “If the sun is your god, why does it not always shine for you?” You say to another, who worships the moon—or to the one who worships the sun: “The sun is complete. You worship the moon; why does your god wax and wane, and shine at night? Why does it not always shine for you? And when you are submerged in the sea, why do your moon and stars not rescue you and give you light from above?”

Why does he add: “the work of human hands, silver and gold”? Human beings dig it from the earth, work it, and color it, and thus it becomes beautiful. Therefore, with your own hands you make the god whom you worship. These things were said to refute the wicked.

**They have eyes, but will not see; they have ears, but will not hear; they have nostrils, but will not smell. They have hands, but will not touch; they have feet, but will not walk; they will not cry out through their throat. For there is no spirit in their mouth.** You say to him: Even if you had worshiped an animal, although that would also have been evil, it would at least have eyes or feet. But this thing that you worship neither sees nor hears.

Why does he add: “They will not cry out through their throat”? Because animals cry out with a voice, but their cry is confused. You cannot understand or grasp it through letters or syllables, as you understand a human voice.

**Let those who make them, and all who trust in them, become like them.** “Become like them” means this: if someone does not correct his eyes because he has seen that gold and that image, he also becomes like it in his soul, since he does not correct himself. He neither sees, understands, nor discerns, because he places greater trust in error. Therefore he is said to be like them.

“And all who trust in them”: not only those who make them, but also those who trust in them.

**The house of Israel hoped in the Lord.** The house of Israel means the twelve tribes of Israel. Did Aaron, of the tribe of Levi, not hope? He did not hope in such dead gods, but in the Lord.

The house of Israel—that is, the house of souls who see God—hopes in the Lord. And Aaron, “the mountain of strength,” that is, those who are strong and lofty in merit, hope in the Lord [Col. 1176B].

**He is their helper and protector.** Those gods are of no benefit, according to Jeremiah’s statement: they do not rescue a person from war or establish a king. But this God defends and protects them, according to Daniel’s statement (Dan. II and III). Truly he is their God; he changes times, removes kings, and establishes them.

**The house of Aaron hoped in the Lord; he is their helper and protector.** Those who fear the Lord have hoped in the Lord. Apart from these—the house of Israel and Aaron—he protects and defends all who fear and love him.

**The Lord remembered us and blessed us.** He remembered us because he freed the children of Israel. He remembered us because he fulfilled in deed what he had promised. He sent his Son, who assumed flesh, and he freed us. This is what I mean by saying that God remembered us.

“And he blessed us”: that is, with every spiritual blessing.

**He blessed the house of Israel; he blessed the house of Aaron.** He blessed all who fear the Lord, the small together with the great—that is, those higher in merit and those lower.

**May the Lord add to you.** Other preachers. At first there were few; afterward preachers became numerous throughout the world.

**You are blessed by the Lord, who made heaven and earth.** “Blessed”: that is, you holy people are blessed by the Lord.

**The heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord, but he gave the earth to the children of men.** “The heaven of heavens,” as the psalm-song says, and the song of the psalm. This heaven is subject to the higher heaven, where the firmament is, and from there it receives its light. The earth, in turn, is subject to that aerial heaven; from it she receives rain and everything necessary [Col. 1176D].

According to the spiritual meaning, the higher heaven is the holy apostles, who heard preaching from Christ himself and received the illumination of the Holy Spirit, and were thereby instructed. The other heaven is the apostles’ successors, to whom they preached, and the Lord illuminated them in their souls.

“But he gave the earth to the children of men.” These are the simpler people who believe only in the Incarnation, who eat milk and are nourished through preaching. Those who were earthly become heavenly.

**The dead will not praise you, O Lord.** This means sinners. For when the sinner comes into the depth of evils, he despises correction (Prov. XIII).

**Nor all those who descend into hell.** This means the inhabitants of hell.

**But we who live will bless the Lord.** We faithful who live—that is, who possess faith and works—praise God.

**From this time now and forever.** “From this time”: from the moment when we begin to understand. “Now”: at the present time. “Forever”: without end.

## PSALM CXIV

**Alleluia.** This psalm contains the voice of the faithful soul who is a pilgrim away from God and who, after long labors, is received by him.

**I have loved, because the Lord will hear the voice of my prayer.** He did not say, “I will love,” but “I have loved.” He does not promise that he will do it, but testifies that he has done it.

“I have loved.” Why have I loved? “Because the Lord will hear the voice of my prayer.” “I have loved” belongs to past time, whereas “he will hear” belongs to the future. For he did not say: “Because I loved that the Lord heard me,” but: “I have loved because the Lord will hear me.”

**Because he inclined his ear to me.** Since we are small and humble and cannot stretch ourselves out or exalt ourselves, the Lord therefore inclined his ear and deigned to hear us. Indeed, because we are human beings and cannot become gods, God became human and humbled himself, according to what is written: “He bowed the heavens and came down” (II Kings XXII).

**And in my days I will call upon you.** Here the question is how he calls upon him in the days and not in the nights. How does he say elsewhere: “At midnight I rose to give thanks to you,” when the saints generally pray more at night (Ps. CXIII)? And elsewhere it is said: “In the nights lift up your hands in the holy places, and bless the Lord” (Ps. CXXXIII).

How, then, does he say, “In my days I will call upon you”? He did not say, “I called upon you,” but “I will call upon you,” in the future. While we are in this world, we call upon him in the night. In the future we call upon the Lord in the day; therefore he said, “In my days.” For it is night for sinners, but for me it is day.

**The pains of death surrounded me.** It seems to me that the pains of death are foul thoughts, when the soul thinks and desires to sin, because it is in labor with sins and is near death.

**And the dangers of hell found me.** O unhappy, miserable, and pitiable us, because sin is always seeking us! But if sins are always seeking us, let us hasten so that they may not find us.

The distinction between the pains of death and the dangers of hell is this: the pains of death are evil thoughts; the dangers of hell are evil deeds. To put it another way: one belongs to theory, the other to practice. There is pain and labor there; here there is danger close to death.

**I found tribulation and sorrow.** He says something new. He does not say, “I found rest”; he does not say, “I found satisfaction.” If he had said, “Tribulation found me; sorrow found me,” there would have been no question. But what does he now say? “I found tribulation and sorrow,” as though he found them by seeking them. For nothing is found unless it is sought.

The saint does not seek rest, but tribulation. For he knows that “tribulation produces endurance; endurance, proven character; and proven character, hope; and hope does not disappoint” (Rom. V). Something similar is also said in Jeremiah (Jer. VI and XIV): “I called upon tribulation and misery.” “Because of your bitter word,” he says, “I will laugh”—that is, in this age, what else do I desire except tribulation, so that in the future I may have rest and happiness? And therefore, he says, I now endure bitterness so that afterward I may deserve sweeter things.

The people of the Lord, departing from Egypt, came to Marah, which is interpreted as “bitterness,” and from Marah to Sinai, which is interpreted as “temptation” (Exod. XV). And again Jeremiah says: “I sat alone, because I was filled with bitterness” (Jer. XV).

**O Lord, deliver my soul.** The Greek and Latin languages cannot express the particularity of the Hebrew language. For “O,” Hebrew has **ANNA**. *Anna* is interpreted as “I ask” and “I beseech.” What he says, therefore, is: “I beseech you, Lord; deliver my soul.” For this is not the attitude of one calling out, but of one beseeching. He is placed in great danger.

**The Lord is merciful and just, and our God will have mercy.** Raise your ears, sinner. The Lord is merciful, but do not be negligent, for what follows is “and just.” If you are a great sinner, hear that the Lord is merciful; if you are negligent, hear that he is just.

But it appears that “the Lord is merciful and just” gives equal weight to the two qualities. For example, he is ten parts merciful and ten parts just—and I speak this way for the sake of the simpler people. Someone may say: If my sins are weighed, can I not have as many good deeds as I have evil ones? Yet now it is said that he is merciful and just. He is merciful toward sinners and just toward the good.

My sins begin to weigh me down, and in his mercy he prevails. Therefore he mentioned “just” once and “merciful” a second time. He could also have spoken of the past. “And our God,” he says, “has mercy,” so that he may always show him to be merciful.

**The Lord preserves the little ones.** If someone is great, exalts himself, and is proud, the Lord does not preserve him. If someone considers himself great, the Lord does not have mercy on him. But if someone humbles himself, the Lord has mercy on him and preserves him.

For he says: “Behold, I and the children whom the Lord has given me.” And again: “I was humbled, and he saved me.” We understand this in two ways: “I was humbled, and he saved me.” Either I sinned and he saved me, or, when I was proud, he humbled me and saved me.

**Return, my soul, to your rest.** When it is said, “Return to your rest,” it follows that he had a rest before he lost it. For no one returns except one who proceeds to the place where he previously was.

God created us good, left us to our own will, and placed us all with Adam in paradise. But because by our own will we fell from that blessedness and came into the valley of tears, the righteous therefore urges his soul to return to the place from which it descended.

“Return, my soul, to your rest.” For this place is a place of tribulation, a land of combatants. This is a place of tears, where one may not walk securely. Wherever anyone may be, there is danger. In the desert there are scorpions; in the cities, the eye of a prostitute is a man’s destruction; at sea, there are robbers and pirates. I speak of all these things mystically. For now there is no danger to a holy man from being killed by robbers, since the martyrs conquered by their blood.

“Return, my soul, to your rest, because the Lord has dealt beneficially with you.” Where, he says, will you return, O soul? To paradise. Not because you are worthy, but because it is the Lord’s mercy. Your departure from paradise happened through your fault; your return, however, is due to the Lord’s mercy.

Let us also say to our soul: “Return to your rest.” Our rest is Christ, our God. Whenever we are in distress and thought begins to take us captive into sin, let us say: “Return, my soul, to your rest.”

[Col. 1179B] **Because he has rescued my soul from death.** He has not yet returned to paradise, and already he says that he has returned to safety. He said, “Return, my soul, to your rest,” and, as though secure, he says: “Because he has rescued my soul from death.”

How has he rescued my soul from death? My God suffered for me; my God was crucified for me. And I say: “Where is your victory, O death? Where is your sting, O hell?” (Hos. XIII; I Cor. XV).

**My eyes from tears.** I wept so that I might laugh; I mourned so that I might rejoice forever. Whoever does not weep in the present will weep in the future. “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V). Conversely it is said: “Woe to you who laugh, for you shall mourn.”

**My feet from falling.** Because my feet did not stand upon the rock, therefore my feet were almost moved, and my steps nearly slipped away. My feet have been delivered from falling. Why? Because my soul has returned to its rest.

**I will please the Lord in the land of the living.** I appear, he says, just to human beings; why do I not have good works? I appear holy to human beings; why do I not have good words? David says these things; the saints say them; the apostles speak them. A sinner does not speak in this way.

What does the righteous person say? I do not have good words or good works, yet I appear holy and am praised by human beings. But I know my conscience. I know by what thoughts my heart is tossed; I know how many lusts come upon me; and I see another law resisting the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin (Rom. VII). Therefore I say: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?” (ibid.). And therefore I say: “Cleanse me from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those belonging to others” (Ps. XVIII).

“From those belonging to others.” What I bring forth is not mine. I do not wish to think evil, yet I think it. I do not wish to think evil, yet, as though unwilling and captive, I am dragged into an evil thought. But since it is not in my power either to think or not to think the evil things, I therefore say that the sins that come into my heart are foreign.

But since a kind of necessity is imposed upon me, I therefore say: “Cleanse me from my hidden faults.” The sins are indeed foreign, but because I receive them, I say: “In the sins of others, spare your servant.”

Why did I say this? Because the prophet said: “I will please the Lord.” He did not say, “I please,” but “I will please.” For by what I do now I cannot be a perfectly righteous person. Therefore the Apostle also says: “We know in part and we prophesy in part, and now we see through a mirror in an enigma” (I Cor. XIII).

This is why we have used such a long discussion: in the present age no one can be perfectly righteous—not David, not the apostles, nor any of the saints. For no one is free from sin, even if his life should last a single day (Job XV).

Indeed, the apostles and saints did not dare to say, “We are holy”; nor did they dare to say, “I please,” but “I will please.” The one who is concerned for the future confesses what he has not accomplished in the past.

“I will please the Lord.” Where will I please him? “In the land of the living.” This land is the land of the dead; another is the land of the living. David too was in this land, and truly in the land of promise, when he said: “I will please the Lord in the land of the living.” He confesses that this land is not the land of the living, but of the dead.

Do you want to know what that land of the living is? The Lord says in the Gospel: “The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob”—and they were dead (Luke XXIII). And what follows? “He is not God of the dead,” he says, “but of the living.” Therefore what does the righteous person also say? “I will please the Lord in the land of the living”—in the land of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Luke XVI). That is, when I am truly in Abraham’s bosom, then I will please the Lord.

## PSALM CXV

[Col. 1180C] **Alleluia.** The fifth and sixth editions join this psalm to the preceding ones; Symmachus and the Seventy Translators, however, divide them.

**I believed, and therefore I spoke.** In the Hebrew, the one hundred fourteenth and one hundred fifteenth psalms are a single psalm. Therefore he said: “I believed, and therefore I spoke.” What did you believe? What did you speak?

The preceding psalm ended in this way: “I will please the Lord in the land of the living.” The prophet therefore says: “I believed, and therefore I spoke.” What did I believe? That I will please the Lord in the land of the living. This I believed, and this I spoke.

But what did I say? **I was greatly humbled.** O great understanding of the divine word! “I believed,” he says, “that I will please the Lord, that I will be an angel, that I will be in heaven”; and I was not proud. I was not lifted up, but “I was greatly humbled.” That I will be in the land of the living is due to the Lord’s mercy. But I know myself, that I am earth and ashes. Therefore I say: “I was greatly humbled.” What, then, does “earth and ashes” mean?

**But I said in my ecstasy: Every human being is a liar.** In Hebrew it reads differently: “I said in my ecstasy: Every human being is falsehood,” which is expressed by **ZECAM**.

[Note: [Col. 1179D] Martianus noted that this is the reading of the manuscript codices in place of *chazab*, which the printed editions preferred. From this he also accuses this commentator of incompetence, because he confused the final syllable of the noun *chazab* with the first syllable [Col. 1180D] of the following word *ma*, that is, “what”; and from this he produced the word *zecam*, or *zecham*, reading *Caph* for *Beth*. See our note.]

“I will please the Lord in the land of the living”; but I know myself, according to the condition of the body, to be nothing. For there is no truth in our substance, but it is a shadow and, as it were, falsehood. I speak of bodily substance, not of the soul.

What he says, then, is this: “I will please the Lord in the land of the living.” But when I consider human life and contemplate its various errors, I find no truth in this world. For “we know in part and we prophesy in part” (II Cor. XI). Therefore I say: Everything we see, everything we understand, is falsehood.

How, then, is it falsehood? Here he called it falsehood in the sense of a shadow, in the sense of an image, just as it is said elsewhere: “Nevertheless, a person passes by as an image” (Ps. XXXVIII). The same understanding is intended here: “Every human being is a liar,” that is, every human being is a shadow.

We say this according to the Hebrew truth. Let us also speak according to the Seventy Translators. Someone may say: What does it matter to me what is found in Hebrew? I follow the Church.

**I said in my ecstasy: Every human being is a liar.** Is David speaking truth or lying? If it is true that every human being is a liar, then this statement, “Every human being is a liar,” is true. Therefore he too is lying, since he too is a human being. But if he too is lying, then what he said, “Every human being is a liar,” is not true. Whichever way you turn, the statement contradicts itself.

And since he is a human being, he therefore lies—that every human being is a liar. Therefore he lies in another sense. You see, then, that these are syllogisms of the philosophers.

Indeed, according to this opinion Aristotle’s syllogism is constructed. You say: “Speak to another: If you are lying, and you speak truthfully when you say that you are lying, then you are lying.” See how the statement turns back upon itself. What does it say? “You who are speaking with me: if you are lying, and you speak the truth in saying precisely that you are lying, then you are lying.” In the same statement he comes to speak both truth and falsehood.

Therefore it is written in the Apostle: “See that no one deceive you through philosophy and empty deceit according to the elements of the world” (Col. II). For the philosophers devised their deceptions through their own art, showing how, in the same statement, someone may speak truth and lie.

Let us say, however, that David spoke the truth when he said that every human being is a liar. As long as we are human beings, we lie; but when we become gods, we cease to lie. “Where there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not human beings, and do you not walk according to human standards?” (I Cor. III). “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High.’ But you shall die like human beings, and fall like one of the princes” (Ps. LXXXI).

If someone is holy, then he becomes God; and when he has become God, he ceases to be human and no longer lies. For what does the Apostle also say? “Every human being is a liar, but God is truthful” (Rom. III).

Let us interpret it another way: **I believed, and therefore I spoke.** When a teacher instructs a student, unless he himself first believes what he teaches, he cannot teach another. He therefore says that he first believed and thus taught another.

**But I was greatly humbled.** When I obtained the grace of God, I was not lifted up in pride; knowledge did not inflate me. What did I do? I was greatly humbled. Nevertheless, what I taught by speech I was also able to teach by humility.

**I said in my ecstasy: Every human being is a liar.** I was teaching my student, he says, and, considering heavenly contemplation and thinking about divine realities, I understood that everything human beings know is falsehood. For what truth can there be in this world, since our life on earth is a shadow?

If the one who teaches the student confesses that every human being is a liar, how much less should the student exalt himself and think himself to be anything?

**What shall I repay the Lord for all that he has repaid me?** Since he said, “I will please the Lord in the land of the living,” and I believed this very thing, for which reason I spoke, and was greatly humbled, and said, “Every human being is falsehood; every human being is a shadow; every human being is an image”—for such great benefits, by which I will please the Lord in the land of the living, what worthy thing do I have to repay him?

I am earth; I am ashes. He promised me that I would please him in the land of the living; he made me a teacher. “I believed, and therefore I spoke.” What worthy thing do I have to repay him for such great benefits?

Whatever I give him belongs to him, and I return it to him rather than give it. I have nothing else to repay him except to pour out my blood for him, except to become a martyr for him. This is the only worthy repayment: to repay blood with blood, so that, having been freed by the Savior, we may gladly pour out our blood for the Savior.

[Col. 1182C] **I will take the cup of salvation, and I will call upon the name of the Lord.** In Hebrew it reads: “I will take the cup of Jesus.” The angel also interprets this very thing: “You shall call his name Jesus” (Luke I), for he himself will save his people.

I will therefore take the cup of Jesus. What is this cup of Jesus? “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Luke XXII). And he says: “Can you drink my cup?” Immediately it follows: “You shall indeed drink my cup” (Matt. XX).

Why did I say this? So that we may understand the cup of passion to be martyrdom. Martyrdom is a great thing. How is it great? Because it repays the Lord what it received from the Lord. Christ suffered for him, and he suffers for Christ’s name.

Since we have said that the martyr has nothing else with which to repay the Lord, the Lord reckons it to him according to its value, because he sees that his servant has nothing else with which to repay him. For what comparison is there? God suffered for human beings; the Lord for a servant; the righteous one for a sinner. What equality is there?

But since the servant has nothing else with which to repay the Lord, God, as a merciful one, accepts martyrdom as though it were equal. It is as if a rich person had fed a poor person, but then the same rich person happened to come with his household and by chance entered the poor man’s house, while the poor man had nothing to set before him or his household. The poor man would merely say to him, “Enter the house of your client,” and would show his willingness, since he had nothing else to give. Thus the poor man would do more, like that widow who contributed two small coins (Luke XXI).

**I will take the cup of salvation, or of Jesus.** This martyrdom too, he says, is not a matter of my own virtue, but of God’s grace. Therefore I cannot drink it unless I call upon the name of the Lord. Jesus conquers; in his martyrdom he is crowned.

**Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.** Let the Jews now answer, since they say in the Law that every human body is unclean. Indeed, if someone dies among the Jews—whether a prophet or any other holy person—and someone touches him, even a priest, that person is unclean until evening (Lev. XIX and XXI). This is written according to the literal sense in the Law.

Let us say to them: If a dead body is unclean, how is it now said, “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints”? If the body of a dying saint is precious, how is it unclean? Therefore this is spoken of an evangelist and proclaimed of a martyr.

**O Lord, for I am your servant: I am your servant, and the son of your maidservant.** I already said in the one hundred fourteenth psalm, where it reads, “O Lord, deliver my soul,” that in Hebrew it has **ANNA**, which is interpreted as “I ask” or “I beseech.” Here too it reads in Hebrew: “I beseech you, Lord, for I am your servant; I am your servant.”

What is said appears to express humility. Yet it is a great dignity and merit to be the servant of the Lord and not the servant of sin. “I have no human master,” he says; “I have no sin as my master” (Rom. VI). For sin does not rule in my mortal body; therefore I am your servant.

This is a great merit. Indeed, it is said of Moses: “But not as my servant Moses.” Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are also called servants of the Lord. Therefore the Apostle likewise begins: “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ.”

You have broken my bonds: to you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise. Truly, it is a mark of great blessedness to go to the Lord without a defiled conscience. Whoever, though holy, dies his own death—even if he has performed acts of mercy, worked signs, and cast out demons—does not go securely to the Lord: his conscience shudders when it sees the Lord. But if a martyr has sinned even after baptism, nevertheless, cleansed by the second baptism of martyrdom, he goes securely to the Lord. You have broken my bonds. Each person is bound by the chains of his own sins; but in my martyrdom you have broken the bonds of my sins and, from those bonds, woven for me a crown of victory. For where sin abounded, grace also abounded exceedingly (Rom. V). To you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise. Where does he sacrifice after martyrdom? In the land of the living. “I will sacrifice,” he says, “a sacrifice to you.” What sort of sacrifice? A goat or a calf? Those were Jewish sacrifices, and they have passed away. “To you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise.” This is the praise of martyrs. For just as the martyrs praise the Lord purely in the land of the living, so monks who chant to the Lord day and night ought to possess the same purity as the martyrs, since they themselves are martyrs. For what angels do in heaven, monks do on earth.

I will pay my vows to the Lord in the presence of all his people [Col. 1184A]. What are the prayers of martyrs? What are the prayers of the saints? “I will hold fast,” he says, “and I will not let you go.” “I will worship,” he says, “the Lord whom, when reading the Gospel, I found crucified; in heaven I see him reigning with the angels.” In the presence of all his people. Before the entire assembly of the saints. In your midst, Jerusalem: in the midst of that heavenly city which is our mother, whose citizens and household members we have already become. Through our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who is our peace. May he deign to grant us that, once carnal warfare has been restrained and the peace of his charity bestowed upon us, and having become sons in the heavenly Jerusalem, we may, according to our merits, deserve to be joined to his saints. To him be glory with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM CXVI

[Col. 1184B]

Alleluia. This psalm is small in the number of its verses, but great in the mystery of its spiritual meaning. Nevertheless, it possesses an apostolic voice, since according to the evangelical pattern it is contained in four verses.

Praise the Lord, all nations. You who, having abandoned idols, have approached him through faith. That all nations would praise and worship the Lord was begun by the Magi who came from the East, offering gifts to the man born as king and Lord, as the evangelist Matthew says. And praise him together, all peoples (Matt. II). Those who were converted from the Jews were foretold by that title which Pilate placed above the Lord’s cross, written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin: “King of the Jews,” as the evangelist John testifies (John XIX).

For his mercy has been confirmed over us. We have often testified that, with God, future things have already become present realities (Acts II). Thus the Lord’s mercy was confirmed when he poured out the Holy Spirit upon believers, according to the promise which the evangelist Luke records, saying: “Behold, I send the promise of my Father upon you; but you remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke XXIV). And the truth of the Lord endures for ever. The truth of the Lord remains when the righteous are built in the heavenly Jerusalem like living stones; or when the wicked are handed over to eternal fire and to worms that never die. As the evangelist Mark says: “Their fire will not be extinguished, and their worm will not die” [Col. 1184D] (Mark IX). Let us, however, suppliantly entreat the Lord to grant us the power to praise him and to confirm his mercy over us, sending into us the Holy Spirit, who, burning away what is harmful, may illuminate what is beneficial. To him be glory with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages for ever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM CXVII

Alleluia. This psalm sometimes contains the voice of the Church founded by Christ’s calling, or of a people slain for Christ’s name and magnifying God.

Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures for ever. This confession does not pertain to the remission of sins, but to the praise of the Godhead.

[Col. 1185A]

Let the house of Israel now say: for he is good, for his mercy endures for ever. That house which was formerly blinded by sins now contemplates the glory of God with a serene mind.

Let the house of Aaron now say: for he is good, for his mercy endures for ever. The house which had previously sacrificed to idols now, attracted by the goodness of the Most High, exercises the priesthood of its own soul.

Let those who fear the Lord now say: for he is good, for his mercy endures for ever. You who formerly feared mute and deaf idols, now sing the mercy of the almighty Lord with reverent fear.

In tribulation I called upon the Lord, and the Lord heard me in an open place. In the narrow confines of tribulation [Col. 1185B] he heard me in the expansiveness of joy.

The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me. The devil, certainly, is often presented in Scripture as both man and male.

The Lord is my helper, and I will despise my enemies. Whether heretics or Jews.

It is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in man. We ought to hope in God alone, and not in man, whose salvation is vain (Ps. LIX). For another prophet says: “Cursed is the man who places his hope in man” (Jer. XVII).

It is good to trust in the Lord, who bestows eternal life, rather than to trust in princes, whose power passes away with this world.

All nations surrounded me, and in the name of the Lord I took vengeance upon them [Col. 1185C]. The nations of tribulations, certainly, surrounded me like a wall, but in the name of the Lord I resisted them.

They surrounded me, yes, they surrounded me, and in the name of the Lord I took vengeance upon them. I was protected by the banner of the one to whom I belonged.

They surrounded me like bees. Like bees around a honeycomb, so that they might carry away the sweetness which Christ had infused into me. And they blazed up like fire among thorns. They blazed up in their envy when they were unable to burn me. And in the name of the Lord I took vengeance upon them, when the things they had inflicted upon me were turned back upon them.

I was pushed and overthrown so that I might fall, but the Lord received me. Trusting in him, I sought him alone as my helper.

[Col. 1185D]

My strength and my praise is the Lord, and he has become my salvation. I will sing to him; I will call him my strength. All my praise rests in him, who in this death of tribulation became my salvation.

The voice of exultation and salvation is in the tents of the righteous. In the hearts, certainly, of the martyrs and the other saints, who have become God’s dwelling place through the Holy Spirit dwelling in them.

The right hand of the Lord has done mighty deeds. So that he might grant me victory in suffering. The right hand of the Lord has exalted me. By his power I have been lifted up from the humility of various sufferings.

I shall not die, but live, and recount the works of the Lord [Col. 1186A]. The people of the martyrs speak these words, whose victories are sung in all the Churches.

The Lord chastising has chastised me, but he has not handed me over to death. The Lord chastises us for correction with many blows, so that he may test us and preserve us from everlasting death.

Open to me the gates of righteousness, and entering through them I will give thanks to the Lord. Blessed is that people of the Church or of the martyrs for whom the gates of righteousness are opened—that is, the gates of eternal life—in which it may continually confess and praise God.

This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it. The Lord Jesus Christ is the Father’s gate, through which one enters to him, as the Lord himself says: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved.” And again: [Col. 1186B] “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John X). Through this gate, therefore, one comes to the Father, but no one enters it except the righteous.

I will give thanks to you, for you have heard me, and you have become my salvation. In this salvation you either healed the wounds of sin or became salvation for me against the wicked enemy.

The stone which the builders rejected. Our Lord Jesus Christ, the true stone found in the letter of the Law, was rejected by the Jewish builders—that is, by those clinging to the letter. This one has become the cornerstone, joining together two walls: one from circumcision, the other from uncircumcision, in one new man, that is, in himself.

From the Lord, the Father. He has become our mediator and the Father’s. And he is wondrous in our eyes—not in the eyes of those [Col. 1186C] who rejected him, but in ours, who received him by believing.

This is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it. This cornerstone itself is the day of salvation, in which we have either risen from death or, having laid aside the sorrow of sin, rejoice in newness of life.

O Lord, save me. As I come to you. O Lord, grant prosperity. Make prosperous that journey by which, after many labors, I may return to you. Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. Christ the Lord comes in the name of the Father, as he himself says: “I have come in the name of my Father” (John V), and so forth.

We bless you from the house of the Lord. The saints of the heavenly Jerusalem bless the little ones of the Church. God is the Lord, and he has shone upon us. For by his resurrection he illuminated [Col. 1186D] our darkness.

Establish the solemn day. Present yourselves as temples and altars to God, in which you may also celebrate sacred solemnities. In dense places: in abundant powers, in which either the Lord himself or his angels frequently appear. Up to the horn of the altar: up to the Lord himself, who is the strength of the soul which you have made his altar.

You are my God, and I will give thanks to you. Having received remission through confession of sins, I will now confess your praises: you are my God, and I will exalt you, because by you I have been raised up from humility.

I will give thanks to you, for you have heard me, and you have become my salvation. So that you might join me with your saints in the heavenly Jerusalem.

Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures for ever [Col. 1187A]. With these words the psalm reaches its conclusion, from which it took its beginning: namely, that from the beginning of our faith until the end, trusting in our God, we should persistently confess his praises, according to the Lord’s saying: “He who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X and XXIV). May he deign to grant us confidence in hoping in him. To him be glory with the eternal Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM CXVIII

Alleluia. This psalm contains a great mystery within itself. We have said something about it in the prologue; but since it contains the Law, commandments, ordinances, testimonies, judgments, and ways, it is necessary to distinguish how these differ from one another. The Law, therefore, which was given through Moses, must be understood spiritually in Christ [Col. 1187B], because although the Apostle calls it holy, he nevertheless describes it as a shadow of future things (Heb. X). Commandments are those in which the observance of the Lord’s precepts is enjoined, according to the words: “You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery,” and the rest. Ordinances are those by which God commands, through love of himself and of one’s neighbor, that the weeds of hatred be torn from the human heart. Testimonies are those in whose presence the order of holy observances is entrusted to us, as Moses calls heaven and earth as witnesses (Deut. IV). And Paul says to Timothy: “I testify to you before the living God and before his chosen angels,” and the rest (II Tim. IV). Judgments are those by which he either honors the righteous with glorious rewards or condemns transgressors to eternal punishments. Ways are the apostles and prophets, through whom one comes to the true way, which is Christ. Thus the psalm begins: “Blessed are the undefiled.” Because of the length of what is said, we have resolved, with the Lord’s consent, to explain it in three homilies [Col. 1187C]. This entire psalm is written according to the order of the letters, so that eight verses begin with one letter, and then another eight are completed from the next letter. The same pattern is woven through to the end. Josephus, however, reports in the books of ἀρχαιολογίας (*archaiologias*, “Antiquities”) that this psalm and the song of Deuteronomy are composed in the same meter, and he thinks that an elegiac meter can be detected in both: namely, that the first verse consists of six feet, while the second ends in a pentameter one foot shorter.

### ALEPH

Blessed are the undefiled in the way. This is, certainly, in the way of the world through which we walk. Blessed are the undefiled. Misery is set against blessedness. In our language, “blessed” means immortal, or praiseworthy or glorious. Those are blessed who deserve to enter eternal life; and those are miserable who descend into hell. How does he say “undefiled,” since a human being cannot exist without minor sins, as Saint John said: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John I). And the prophet says: “He who walks without blemish and practices righteousness” (Ps. XIV). “Without blemish,” that is, without mortal crimes. Nevertheless, he distinguishes between blemish and blemish: although we cannot be without minor sins, we must not fall into greater ones. In the way: those who walk in the Law of the Lord. In the way, in Christ, as he himself says: “I am the way and the truth” (John XIV). Those who walk in the Law of the Lord—that is, in his commandments. “Who walk,” that is, persevere. Those who [Col. 1188A] walk in the Law of the Lord: those who, having subdued the desires of the flesh, also trample underfoot the earthly honor of glory.

Blessed are those who search out his testimonies. So that, when they sin, they may understand that they have transgressed in the presence of witnesses. With their whole heart they seek him, and not superficially or sluggishly.

For those who practice iniquity have not walked in his ways. The ways are the apostles and prophets, through whom one comes to that way which said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life,” as we have already said. For the wicked do not walk in this way, because they follow the way of Satan.

You have commanded that your commandments, O Lord, be kept exceedingly. He teaches us to keep his commandments not with a lukewarm heart or a careless mind, but firmly and attentively.

Would that my ways might be directed toward keeping your ordinances [Col. 1188B]. Unless our ways are directed by the Lord himself, we will be too weak to keep his ordinances, because of the frailty of the flesh.

Then I shall not be put to shame when I have looked into all your commandments. It is not fitting to neglect some and observe others; rather, all must be kept equally, lest we be put to shame at the future judgment.

I will give thanks to you, O Lord, in the uprightness of my heart. For it is not perverse, as in the faction of the heretics. In learning the judgments of your righteousness, so that I might praise you with an upright heart.

I will keep your ordinances; do not utterly abandon me. Even if we are abandoned for a time, let us not be abandoned completely, so that we perish.

### BETH

[Col. 1188C]

How does a young man correct his way? By keeping your words. Here the prophet teaches not only advanced age to be corrected, but also instructs youth to be educated and to keep the divine words in such a way that, even if an old fault has been mourned, no thought should now consent to sin.

With my whole heart I have sought you; do not cast me away from your commandments. He confesses that he sought God not in part but with his whole heart, so that he might not be cast away from his commandments, because he who came to save sinners casts no one away.

In my heart I have hidden your sayings, so that I may not sin against you. In the hidden place of his heart he stores the mysteries of God: when he avoids a heretic after two admonitions (Titus III), when he does not expose what is holy to dogs, or when he does not throw his pearls before swine (Matt. VII). He acts negligently in nothing that belongs to God, because he knows that the one who performs the work of the Lord negligently is accursed (Jer. XLVIII).

Blessed are you, O Lord; teach me your ordinances. For I know that the ordinances of vain glory which the Pharisee displayed in the temple did not proceed from you (Luke XVIII).

With my lips I have proclaimed all the judgments of your mouth. The Apostle calls the judgments of God incomprehensible (Rom. XI). Therefore this man announced with his lips only what he heard and learned from the prophets, and he announced it to believers, not to the unworthy.

[Col. 1189A]

I have rejoiced in the way of your testimonies, as in all riches. For just as an earthly person delights in fields and vineyards, so this man rejoices in God’s testimonies with a pure conscience, having despised the world and been enriched by God.

I will exercise myself in your commandments and consider your ways. Exercise is the continual practice of works. If this man had not been trained in God’s commandments, he could not have considered his ways—that is, the apostolic and prophetic teachings.

I will meditate on your ordinances; I will not forget your words. I meditate on them and exercise myself in them so that, not consigning them to forgetfulness, I may fulfill them wholly and perfectly.

### GIMEL

[Col. 1189B]

Repay your servant; give me life, and I will keep your words. He persistently begs to be repaid for the fact that he serves God. And because he knows that he is not a servant of sin, he desires to live in the one who is life, and to keep his words while the present life passes away.

Unveil my eyes, and I will consider the wonders of your Law. Wipe away from the eyes of my heart the veil of the letter, and make me contemplate the wonders of your Law with spiritual understanding. For in your light we shall see light (Ps. XXXV).

I am a sojourner on the earth; do not hide your commandments from me. So the Apostle also says: “While we are in the body, we are away from the Lord” (II Cor. V). The prophet says that, while placed in the body, he is a stranger to the heavenly assembly, because he knows that these commandments are contained among thrones and dominions; he begs that they not be hidden from him.

My soul has longed to desire your ordinances at all times. So that, whether I eat or drink or do anything else, I may always desire, meditate upon, and grasp them.

You have rebuked the proud. So that you might bring them back to the holy humility which you taught. You have rebuked the proud. Thus he acted toward the devil and Adam, who raised themselves up in pride. Or now, through your teachers, you rebuke the opposing powers, the members of the devil—heretics or wicked people—who act against God’s commandments. You rebuked them through your saints. Cursed are those who turn away from your commandments. Those who turn away from God’s commandments are accursed; but the wicked—that is, heretics and the rest—will then receive the curse in full, because he will say: “Go, you cursed, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV).

Take away from me reproach: the reproach of sin and judgment. And contempt: the judgment of mortal death. For I have searched out your testimonies—not idly or sleepily, but vigorously and watchfully.

For princes sat and spoke against me, but your servant was exercising himself in your ordinances. What the prophet says here about himself, he sees as something that will occur among the apostles and the other martyrs, who suffered many things before kings and governors, as the Lord himself foretold (Matt. X; Mark XIII; Luke XXI). Although they were afflicted with various punishments, [Col. 1190A] even to the cutting off of their necks, they continually exercised themselves in God’s ordinances.

For your testimonies are also my meditation. Certainly, in these pressures. And your ordinances are my counsel, because they promise eternal life.

### DALETH

My soul has clung to the pavement; give me life according to your word. I understand the soul to be joined to a mortal body. Therefore, lest sin grow strong, I ask you to give me life, knowing that the desire of the flesh produces death.

I have declared my ways to you. How can he say, “I have declared them to you,” when elsewhere he says, “Declare them to me”? Does God not know or understand something, since he is present everywhere, foresees all things, and is within them? But when he says, “I have declared my ways to you,” it is as though he were saying: “You must first declare your iniquities” (Isa. XLIII)—that is, your deeds, what you have done against God’s commandment. Declare them through confession or repentance, so that you may be justified in God’s words.

I declared my ways, and you heard me; teach me your ordinances. I confessed the ways of my sin, and you forgave me. Now grant me instruction, because I will be taught in your ordinances.

Teach me the way of your ordinances. May I receive spiritually the ordinances which the letter of the Law brought forth. And I will exercise myself in your wonders, in the apostles and the other ecclesiastical teachings which were represented in it.

My soul slumbered, in the station of this mortal dwelling. From weariness—from bodily weakness. Strengthen me in your words [Col. 1190C], so that, once the sleep of sin has been removed, I may keep watch over them attentively.

Remove from me the way of iniquity: that desire by which one comes to sin. And have mercy on me in your Law, for the Law was established by you so that you might always have mercy.

I have chosen the way of truth: Christ, the Son of God, whom, foreseeing his coming into the world, I hear saying: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). I have not forgotten your judgments: those judgments which he set forth in the Gospels when he said: “This is the judgment: that everyone who believes in the Son of Man may have eternal life” (John III).

I have clung to your testimonies, O Lord; do not put me to shame. Because, by clinging to them, I have deserved forgiveness for my former crimes, I ask that you not allow me to be put to shame by repeating sin.

I have run in the way of your commandments. When I endured many things for the word, in hope of future blessedness. When you enlarged my heart, when you disclosed to me, in the breadth of the Holy Scriptures, the mystery of the blessed Trinity. Or, “when you enlarged my heart”: that is, in the breadth of charity, in hope, and in faith.

### HE

Establish for me, O Lord, the Law, the way of your ordinances. The prophet, speaking in the person of the Church, says: “Establish the Law for me,” that is, yourself, because Christ is the Law. It is as though he were saying: “Establish yourself for me,” that is, give yourself. And I will seek it continually: that Law itself, that is, the commandments, or yourself.

[Col. 1191A]

Give me understanding, and I will search out your Law—that is, your commandments. Give me understanding, so that I may not be like a horse and a mule, which have no understanding (Ps. XXXI). The Church asks to understand the distinction between good and evil, between life and death, and between the letter and the meaning: so that I may understand, preach, and fulfill it in my works. And I will keep it with my whole heart—that is, with complete love.

Lead me in the path of your commandments. A path is smaller than a way; that is, it is the narrow and constricted way, the higher commandments which lead to life, because broad and spacious is the way which leads to death (Matt. VII). Because I have desired it. The voice of the Church. It is as though the Church were saying: “I have desired nothing else, nor delighted in anything except your commandments. Therefore I ask that you lead me in your commandments,” that is, make me understand them.

Incline my heart toward your testimonies. The voice of the Church. The proud do not incline their hearts toward God’s testimonies, because they think themselves higher and that they understand God’s precepts better than the Church does. And not toward avarice—that is, vanity. For those proud people do not incline their hearts toward God’s testimonies, but toward vanity or avarice. “Incline my heart,” says the Church, that is, in humility, according to the words: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. XI).

Turn my eyes away, so that they may not see vanity. “Turn my eyes away,” that is, my senses, so that they may not see vanity, that is, ruin. It is as though he were saying: “Let me not fix my eyes—that is, my senses—upon this vanity which is ruin.” But what then? “Give me life in your way” [Col. 1191C]—that is, in yourself. Or, “Give me life in your commandments,” in my soul.

Establish your word for your servant: for the Christian people. Your saying: your commandments. In your fear: that is, holy fear.

Cut away the reproach which I suspected. The Church says: remove, cut off, sever the reproach I suspected from others. That reproach which the Gentiles used to utter: “You are a worshiper of the crucified one; you adore one who died an evil death; you venerate one who was killed.” And they said: “Behold our god, whom you say is made by human hands. Where is your God? Let him come.” “Which I suspected.” What did they suspect? That the Church was maintaining a deception because it worshiped Christ. For your judgments are delightful—that is, clear: joyful and clear to those who love and desire them, that is, to those who willingly seek them, not to those unwilling.

Behold, I have desired your commandments; give me life in your righteousness. It is one gift of your mercy, O Lord: that, keeping the holy words, we may be given life in your righteousness—that is, when we confess you to be equal to the Father and the Holy Spirit.

### VAV

Let your mercy come upon me, O Lord, so that you may forgive sins. And your salvation according to your word. This is the salvation—the word which, through another prophet, you promised, saying: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. XXXIII). This means that you should come to redeem us, according to what you promised to Abraham, as it is said: “In your seed all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII).

And I will answer those who reproach me with a word. The Church speaks. It is as though she were saying: “If you come to redeem us, I will answer those who reproach me because of my faith—because of how I believe—and say: ‘Where is your God? Behold our god,’ or their idols which they worship.” For I have hoped in your words. I will answer firmly those who call my hope in you vain, because their hope is empty.

And do not utterly take the word of truth from my mouth. I will not consent to sinners, lest I hear: “Why do you declare my righteousness?” (Ps. IX). For I have hoped exceedingly in your judgments. Hoping in these, I have always proclaimed them in the churches of the peoples.

[Col. 1192B]

And I will keep your Law continually, for ever and ever. “Continually” indicates the entire period of the present life. “For ever and ever” points to the future age.

And I walked in spaciousness. For I was enlarged through keeping your Law. Because I searched out your commandments, examining them carefully. I searched them out for this purpose: so that I might believe and understand.

And I spoke of your testimonies before kings, and I was not put to shame. Knowing that whoever confesses you in this age, you will confess him before your Father and his angels (Matt. X). If we stand before kings and governors for the Lord’s sake, as the martyrs did, whether we announce the word of truth or contend for righteousness (Matt. X; Mark XIII), we too must be steadfast, not ashamed.

And I meditated on your commandments, which I loved, so that the work of meditation might bring to completion the fruit of love.

And I lifted up my hands—that is, I raised them—toward your commandments, which I loved: cleansed from sin and separated from the shedding of innocent blood. And I exercised myself in your ordinances, so that I might be able to perceive spiritually what was indicated in them by the letter.

### ZAIN

Remember your word to your servant, O Lord, in which you gave me hope. Deign to make me such that I may be considered worthy, remembering your word, amid the pressures of this world, to deserve consolation through hope in eternal goods, as follows:

[Col. 1192D]

This has consoled me in my humility: for your word will give me life. When he is placed in distress, it supplies the nourishment of eternal life.

The proud were acting wickedly without limit. Having abandoned the humility of the divine commandment, they exalted themselves in the vanities of this world. But I did not turn aside from your Law, because, as they approached condemnation, I was raised up in it.

I remembered your judgments. I did nothing unworthy in this life, fearing that I might be condemned by them. From the beginning, O Lord—from the beginning of this life. And I was consoled, knowing myself secure from the judgment of death. “I was consoled,” the Church herself says, because God came to redeem his members. It is as though she were saying: “From the beginning I knew and understood [Col. 1193A] through the Holy Spirit that you were going to come in the flesh.”

Despondency seized me because of the sinners who abandon your Law. The voice of the Church. She displays the feeling of compassion, so that she may grieve over the transgressions of the wicked, according to the Apostle’s words: “When one member suffers, all the members suffer with it” (I Cor. XII). Therefore she does not want anyone to sin, but desires all to recognize the way of truth (I Tim. II).

Your ordinances were songs for me in the place of my pilgrimage. The prophet teaches us, during our pilgrimage in this world, to sing spiritual songs continually once they have been received by the ear, because, while we are in the body, we are away from the Lord (II Cor. V).

I remembered your name by night, O Lord, and kept your Law [Col. 1193B]. Human frailty ought, especially though always, to remember the Lord’s name at night (I Cor. V), whether it is weighed down by the recollection of riches or tormented by the fire of desire; and above all it ought to pray that, if it has begun to keep God’s Law, it may not be torn away from it in any respect.

This happened to me because I searched out your ordinances. This Law became consolation for me, not a stumbling block, so that I might be able to examine your ordinances more diligently. We too suppliantly beseech the Lord to disclose his ordinances to us, to open his ways, and to reveal his wonders; and, if the Law conceals anything beneath its shadow, to reveal it when the Paraclete illuminates it, so that, if we do not attain the palm of blessedness, we may at least obtain forgiveness for our sins [Col. 1193C]. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who, with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, possesses honor, power, and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

We have already described the distinction among ordinances, commandments, laws, and ways in the preceding homily (Homily II). Now let us return to the section of the eighth letter.

### HETH

The Lord is my portion, I said, to keep your Law. Whoever abandons the pride of the world, the heights of honors, and the boastfulness of riches, and places his treasures in heaven, has God as his portion, as Peter says to the paralytic: “Silver and gold I do not have; but what I have, this I give you: in the name of Jesus Christ, rise and walk” [Col. 1193D] (Acts III). O great treasure, O splendid accumulation of blessed riches, that one who keeps God’s Law, and whose portion is God, should cure diseased infirmities!

I have entreated your face with my whole heart. The prophet rightly entreats God’s face with his whole heart, knowing that he has a pure heart. For “blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V). Have mercy on me according to your word, by which you promised that you would not overwhelm the sinner in death, but would console him with mercy.

I considered my ways, that they were straight. And I turned my feet toward your testimonies: my senses toward your commandments, so that I might observe them and fulfill them in my works.

[Col. 1194A]

I am ready and have not been troubled. I am ready to preach; I have not been troubled about enduring tribulation for Christ. So that I may keep your commandments. The unjust arrows of those who reproached me did not disturb me.

The cords of sinners have entangled me, but I have not forgotten your Law. The prophet says that he was enclosed by the reproaches of sinners, yet he does not claim to have forgotten the divine Law, knowing that we must enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations (Acts XIV).

At midnight I rose to give thanks to you for the judgments of your righteousness. For he knows that at midnight he may either suffer dangers or attain rewards: just as at midnight the angel struck Egypt (Exod. XI), so at midnight the wise virgins are brought [Col. 1194B] to the bridegroom (Matt. XXV). There are many other testimonies concerning midnight. Therefore he rises at that time with judgment and righteousness, so that he may obtain what he asks.

I am a participant with all those who fear you and keep your commandments. David was a participant in the kingdom with all those who endured tribulation; and now the Church is a participant with those who fear God with holy fear and fulfill his commandments. She is a participant with them in faith, hope, and charity.

The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord. When he makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the unjust (Matt. V). Teach me your ordinances. So that I may not become like those who possess the key of knowledge but neither enter themselves nor allow others to enter [Col. 1194C] (Luke XI). He showed mercy when he came to redeem us. Hence the earth is full—that is, the holy Church. Teach me your ordinances: that is, your commandments, so that I may understand, preach, and fulfill them in my works.

### TETH
You have dealt kindly with your servant, Lord. The prophet’s voice in the person of the Church. You dealt kindly when you came in the flesh and redeemed us; when you fulfilled what you had promised to Abraham and the other fathers, namely, that “in your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XX). “With your servant”: with the Christian people. “According to your word.” The Son is the Father’s Word. “According to your word”: so that, when I sinned, you would not punish me in anger, but console me with mercy. “Teach me goodness [Col. 1194D] and discipline and knowledge.” The Church’s voice. He ought first to have said “knowledge,” and afterward “discipline,” because a person cannot be good unless he possesses knowledge. What sort of goodness does he say that God practices? That he sends rain upon the earth, makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust. And “discipline”: that is, first he must measure it within himself and practice discipline, and afterward in others. And “knowledge”: that is, that he may possess discernment and know how to distinguish between good and evil, between life and death, between body and soul. “Teach me,” so that I may understand how to fulfill your commandments in practice. “Because I have believed your commandments.” Therefore teach me, because I have believed in your precepts; that is, I have fulfilled them in practice.

[Col. 1195A] Before I was humbled, I sinned; therefore I kept your utterance. We are humbled after sin has preceded us, and through this we are instructed, so that we may keep the divine utterances.

You are good, Lord. For no one is good except you alone. And in your goodness teach me your ordinances, because they are good, just as you are good.

The iniquity of the proud has been multiplied against me; but I shall search out your commandments with all my heart. When the divine scourges reproved me and the proud of the world attacked me, saying, “Where is your help? Where is your hope? Where is the goodness of your God?” I searched your commandments all the more earnestly, seeking consolation in them.

Their heart has thickened like milk. Although milk is naturally [Col. 1195B] sweet, when corrupted it coagulates and turns sour. So too the proud—that is, heretics—at first had a heart sweet toward the holy Scriptures; but by perverting them in the intoxication of their own understanding, they became coagulated and exceedingly bitter. But I meditated on your law. Through it you humble the proud; through it you grant grace to the humble.

It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I may learn your ordinances. The Church’s voice says: It was good for me that you humbled me, because through this I learned to fulfill your commandments in action. It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I may learn your ordinances, because they are learned not in pride but in humility.

The law of your mouth is good for me, more than thousands of pieces of gold and silver. The law of God’s mouth is Christ, who did not come to abolish the law [Col. 1195C] but to fulfill it (Matt. V). Foreseeing him, the prophet desires him above all treasures, because he commands not only that friends be loved but also that enemies be forgiven.

IOD.

Your hands made me and fashioned me; give me understanding, so that I may learn your commandments. For it is a great thing for a person to understand that he was made and fashioned by God’s hand and formed according to his image. Once he has recognized this, he ought to ask for knowledge, so that he may understand and keep God’s commandments; lest, departing from them, he who was the image of God should begin to be the image of the devil.

Those who fear you will see me and rejoice. The Church’s voice: that is, that those who fear God may see their own understanding and possess joy, because when the Church sees others observing God’s commandments, she has great joy. Thereafter they will rejoice with one another, both here and in the future. Because I have hoped beyond hope in your word—that is, I have hope in Christ.

I have known, Lord, that your judgments are just and are in accordance with your truth. Your justice is that you rebuke sinners for their offenses; your truth is that you humble the proud from their prosperity. Therefore, because you humbled me in order to correct me:

Let your mercy now come, so that it may console me. The prophet’s voice in the person of the Church. Through the Holy Spirit the prophet foresaw that Christ would come in the flesh, who was mercy, so that he might redeem us according to [Col. 1196A] what he had promised and console me. He fulfilled what he promised, for elsewhere he says: “There are many mercies with God, and our sins are many” (Ps. CXLIII). Hence he says: “Your mercies are many.” “According to your utterance to your servant”: according to what you promised, come to redeem your servant, the Christian people, who serve you in a special way.
