Let your mercy now come, so that it may console me, according to your utterance to your servant. For you promised that after the humility of affliction you would grant the protection of consolation.

Let your mercies come to me, and I shall live, because your law is my meditation. I now meditate on your law, but I cannot enter eternal life unless I am changed there by you.

[Col. 1196B] Let the proud be put to shame, because they acted wickedly against me unjustly. Let them be put to shame in their sins and recognize that they have acted unjustly against the righteous. But I shall exercise myself in your commandments, showing them what ought to be done. “But I”: the Church’s voice. “I shall exercise myself in your commandments.” While the people mentioned above acted in this way, I exercise myself in your precepts.

Those who fear you and those who know your testimonies will turn to me. That is, by my teaching, they will come to know them and be converted to you.

Let my heart be made blameless in your ordinances, so that I may not be put to shame. Since an abundance of vices proceeds from the heart, as the Lord says in the Gospel, the prophet therefore asks to be made blameless in God’s ordinances, so that the sentence of condemnation at the judgment may not [Col. 1196C] put him to shame (Ps. CXVIII). So we too must restrain various thoughts, lest they prepare shame for us when we desire to carry them out. “Let my heart be made blameless.” Here “heart” stands for the soul. It is as though he says: Let my soul be without mortal sin. “In your ordinances, so that I may not be put to shame”: that is, so that I may not suffer eternal shame.

CAPH.

My soul has failed for your salvation. For Jesus, because he came to save his people from their sins. And I have hoped beyond hope in your word, which in the beginning was God with God, so that it might come for the redemption of humanity.

My eyes have failed for your utterance, saying, [Col. 1196D] “When will you console me?” Pay attention: in the failure of my spiritual eyes I accept this consolation—that you will come from heaven.

For I have become like a wineskin in frost; I have not forgotten your ordinances. The Lord said in the Gospel: “No one puts new wine into old wineskins” (Mark II), signifying that a human breast filled with long-standing vices cannot contain God’s commandments. Therefore, if we grow hot with our natural ardor so as to sin, when we receive God’s commandments this heat is suddenly extinguished, and we become like a wineskin in frost, the heat of sin within us having been cooled.

How many are the days of your servant? When will you execute judgment upon those who persecute me? The days of this life are few. [Col. 1197A] Lord, crush Satan and his minions beneath our feet swiftly in your judgment, for they persecute us.

The wicked have told me tales, but not according to your law. I have heard many things from heretics and pagans that do not agree with God’s commandments. Therefore he adds:

All his commandments are truth. For they contain no falsehood. The wicked have persecuted me; help me. I endure severe battles against principalities and powers, and therefore I do not ask that this contest be removed, but that I be helped, knowing that no one can be crowned except one who has competed lawfully.

They almost finished me upon the earth; but I did not abandon your commandments. Bodily vices would have greatly humbled me upon the earth [Col. 1197B] had I not kept the divine commandments.

According to your mercy give me life, unto eternal life, because I no longer live for myself; but Christ lives in me. So that I may keep the testimonies of your mouth: either the things you commanded in the Law, or those you proclaimed in the Gospels.

LAMED.

Forever, Lord, your word remains in heaven. In that heavenly man who, having abandoned the earthly image, became heaven.

Your truth is from generation to generation. One generation is that of the Law and the prophets; another is that of the Gospels. In these generations God’s truth remains, because they proclaimed nothing false. You founded the earth, and it remains—not that earth which passes away with heaven, but [Col. 1197C] that in which God’s word is multiplied.

By your ordinance the day endures, because all things serve you. Whoever, having abandoned the darkness of the world, lives in God’s light, remains in God, who is the true day. And whatever he accomplishes by God’s ordinance he attributes to service of him.

If your law had not been my meditation, I might perhaps have perished in my humiliation. He gives an example, so that even if we are humbled by various persecutions, we may meditate on the law and not perish.

I shall never forget your ordinances, because through them you have given me life, transferring me after many struggles into eternal life.

I am yours; save me, Lord, because I have sought your ordinances. I am your servant, and you are [Col. 1197D] my God. I ask to be saved by you, because my belly is not my god, nor am I devoted to empty glory, but to your ordinances.

Sinners waited for me in order to destroy me; I understood your testimonies. Hostile powers attack me in a long struggle, but, understanding your testimonies, I received consolation from them.

I have seen the end of every consummation: Christ, certainly, who is the end of the Law and the consummation of the prophets. In the Spirit the prophet foresaw that he would complete all that had been written about him in the Law, the prophets, and the psalms. Indeed, during his Passion he himself said: “It is finished” (John XIX). Your commandment is exceedingly broad. For he foresaw that the time extending from when he declared through the Law and the prophets that he would come [Col. 1198A] until his coming forth through the Gospel would be spacious.

MEM.

How I have loved your law, Lord! All day long it is my meditation. It is apparent that he loves God’s Law because he is known to meditate on it throughout the whole time of his life. He said “day” because it shines forth from the splendor of the divine light.

You have made me wiser than my enemies through your commandment, for it is mine forever. The prophet’s enemies are the Jews, who do not understand spiritually. The prophet says that he is wiser than they are because, in the commandments that he has kept forever, he foresaw the Lord’s coming.

I have understood more than all who teach me, because your testimonies [Col. 1198B] are my meditation. At that time the scribes and Pharisees taught, possessing the key of knowledge; but this man understands more than they, for in the Gospels he saw that the mystery of the anointings, festivals, and burnt offerings was to be fulfilled.

I have understood more than the elders, because I sought your commandments. I seek all the commandments of the law beyond the priests and rulers, because in the New Testament I await the performance of what I see prefigured in the Old.

I restrained my feet from every evil way, so that I might keep your words. I have always held myself back from the precipice of filthy wrongdoing, so that I might more easily be able to keep the word of your commandments.

I did not turn aside from your judgments, because you established the law for me. I received the law of commandments from you; if I turned aside from these [Col. 1198C] judgments, I would be condemned in the eternal judgment.

How sweet your utterances are to my throat, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth! Once honey, or any other food, has passed over the palate, it has no further taste; but your utterances, Lord, whether in the mouth, the throat, or the secret recess of the hidden breast, are always sweet to those who meditate on them. For just as visible honey wards off bitterness from our throats, so the Lord’s utterances mitigate the bitterness of our crimes.

From your commandments I have understood; therefore I hated every way of iniquity. Having drunk in the sweetness of the commandments mentioned above, I hated the way of iniquitous bitterness.

NUN.

Your word is a lamp for my feet, Lord. If the light of God’s word shines within us during the nights of this age, our feet do not fall into the snares of ropes or the precipices of pits that the hand of diabolical skill prepares as stumbling blocks for us. And a light for my paths: with this light going before us, as we walk the paths of this life, may we be led to the one that is the true way.

I swore and resolved to keep the judgments of your justice. First he swore, so that he would not withdraw from this observance. Then he resolved, so that he might confirm what he had sworn, knowing that nothing is proclaimed in God’s judgments except through justice.

I have been humbled exceedingly, Lord; give me life according to your word. He learned the humility that Christ taught, for Christ is meek and humble of heart. [Col. 1199A] Therefore he now begs that, just as Christ was exalted into the glory of God the Father after the humility of the servant’s form, so he too may be transferred from this bodily humility into eternal life.

Make the free offerings of my mouth acceptable, Lord. The Church’s voice. It is as though he says: May the vows that I offer you be pleasing to you—that is, acceptable and delightful. And teach me your judgments: that is, your commandments, so that I may understand and fulfill them.

My soul is in your hands. That is, in your understanding, because I am ready to act. Elsewhere he says: “My soul is in my hands.” How does he say “in my hands”? Because I am ready to endure martyrdom for Christ.

Sinners have set traps for me. Observe that a snare is placed beside the road, and if you depart from the road, you fall into the snare. What are these snares except the devil’s traps or the demon’s suggestions? Vices and sins may also be understood. Yet I have not erred from your commandments. The Church’s voice: I have not erred from your commandments, but have kept them in practice.

I have acquired your testimonies as an inheritance. Your testimonies and your precepts are my inheritance forever, both here and in the future. For they are the rejoicing of my heart. Your testimonies are rejoicing, because the Church delights and exults in God’s commandments.

I have inclined my heart. I was not proud but humble, and therefore I inclined my heart so that I might understand you, because the proud do not incline their hearts toward humility. To what did I incline my heart? the Church says. To practice [Col. 1199C] your ordinances—that is, your commandments. Forever, because of the recompense of eternal life, so that I may deserve to receive it.

SAMECH.

I hated the iniquitous and loved your law. The prophet’s voice in the person of the Church. How does he say, “I hated the iniquitous,” when the Lord says: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Luke VI)? And elsewhere: “Pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matt. V). How, then, does he say, “I hated”? He can defend himself according to the law of the Old Testament, as it is said: “You shall love your friend and hate your enemy” (Lev. XIX). But now it must be understood in this way: “I hated”—vices and sins. “And I loved”—that is, the nature itself, because it is not permitted to hate God’s creature, but sin. As he says elsewhere: “With perfect hatred I hated them” (Ps. CXVIII). Yet the hatred is not perfect. Why? Because “whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John XIII). And “I loved your law”: that is, I loved the law that you commanded and fulfilled it in practice.

You are my helper and protector. A helper in the present; a protector in the future. And I hope in your word: that is, in Christ, because the Son is the Father’s Word.

Depart from me, evildoers, and I shall search out the commandments of my God. The prophet’s voice in the person of the Church: he speaks by way of desire: “Depart from me, evildoers.” If you wish to practice perfect repentance, you must separate yourself from the company of sinners and of all evil people and flee [Col. 1200A] to another place, so that you may be able to perform it perfectly. “Depart from me, evildoers”: these are demons, vices, and sins, or hostile powers. While they prepare snares and evil suggestions for you, you cannot search out God’s commandments so as to understand them well. But if you wish to practice repentance, you must separate yourself from their company.

Receive me according to your utterance. David says: Receive me from the flesh, according to what you promised, so that you might take flesh from my flesh and redeem me. And I shall live: that is, in my soul, if you redeem me, both here and in the future. And do not put me to shame in my expectation: because of the salvation I have awaited, may I not be put to shame when you come, so that I may have no shame either here or in the future.

[Col. 1200B] Help me. He asks for help. And I shall be saved: in my soul, if you come to help me. And I shall meditate on your ordinances: that is, on your commandments. Always, without end.

You have despised all who depart. That is, you have scorned them. From your ordinances. Why? Because their thought is unjust. Therefore you have despised them: because they depart from your commandments and their thought is unjust—whether they are heretics, Jews, or any evil people, and whether they are against Christ or against the Church.

I have regarded all the sinners of the earth as transgressors. The prophet speaks by way of desire in the person of the Church: before Christ’s coming they were transgressors, held under a debt because of the transgression of the first man, Adam, and all descended into hell. [Col. 1200C] Even infants descended into hell, because on account of that debt they were regarded as transgressors unless they had been cleansed through baptism. And now those who are not baptized descend into hell. “I have regarded them as transgressors,” because not all sinners are transgressors, but all transgressors are sinners. Therefore I loved your testimonies, so that I might not appear a transgressor among them.

Nail my flesh with your fear, for I have feared your judgments. I fear the future judgment; therefore, nailing all the desires of the flesh to your cross, I am ready to live with you, die with you, and be buried with you, so that in the future I may deserve to rise with you. But we too, Lord, beseech you that, nailed fast in your fear, with the lamp of sacred light going before us, freed from the ropes of sin and made your portion, we may be able to walk along that way which, having freed us from the punishments of the wicked, makes us fellow heirs with the angels. Through the same Lord Jesus Christ, to whom, with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, belong honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

With saving counsel and sacred utterance the blessed prophet continually exhorts us to carry out faithfully and retain indissolubly the justice that he himself kept in practice. And so that he might more easily rouse sluggish and inactive minds to keep these things, he teaches what reward we shall attain through the justice of this observance, saying:

AIN.

I practiced judgment and justice; do not hand me over to those who slander me. A host of vices continually persecutes us in this mortal body, but if the measure of God’s judgments and ordinances remains within us, so that by prudent counsel we do what accords with them, we shall not be handed over to the hands of these persecutors.

Receive your servant for good. For I no longer know how to serve sin. So that the proud may not slander me: the devil and his ministers.

My eyes have failed for your salvation, for Jesus, who is called “Savior” in Hebrew. And for the utterance of your justice: for that Word which was in the beginning with God, who did not come to abolish the ordinances of the law but to fulfill them.

Deal with your servant according to your mercy. So that you yourself may bring my vows to completion. And teach me your ordinances, so that I may be able to perceive them, as I have often desired.

I am your servant; give me understanding, so that I may know [Col. 1201B] your testimonies. I shall learn them from you, not from heretics or Jews, because no time is free for me from the practice of your service.

It is time to act, Lord; the wicked have destroyed your law. The Jews, certainly, who did not understand it spiritually. But a time will come when the Lord will cause its hidden meanings to be opened through the preaching of the Gospel.

Therefore I loved your commandments more than gold and topaz. For just as gold surpasses all metals in value, so topaz, containing within itself the beauty of all precious stones, surpasses the honors of them all. Therefore the prophet loves all God’s commandments above these things, because he understands that in them the coming of the Lord, who is to redeem the world, has been announced.

Therefore I was directed toward all your commandments; I hated every iniquitous way. Nothing from the ways of iniquity approached me; but just as I walked with integrity, so I hated everything that dwelt in the ways of iniquity.

PHE.

Your testimonies are wonderful, Lord; therefore my soul has searched them out. I saw that one thing was enacted in them and another prefigured. Therefore, because it is wondrous to me, I investigate it more diligently and, with you revealing it, learn everything, as follows.

The unfolding of your words gives light and grants understanding to little ones. God’s words are the writings of the prophets and of the Law, which are explained in the Gospels, while the Word made flesh dwells among us and displays God through many mighty works. But understanding of these things is granted to our littleness, since we have been reborn in innocence, as the Lord says: “I confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven [Col. 1201D] and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to the simple” (Matt. X).

I opened my mouth and drew in breath, because I desired your commandments. I opened the recesses of a pure heart and made myself worthy of desiring your commandments, so that the Holy Spirit might be poured into me.

Look upon me and have mercy on me, according to the judgment of those who love your name. Grant me the judgment by which you reward the others who love your name.

Direct my steps according to your utterance, and let no iniquity rule over me. For I have been given over to your service.

Redeem me from the slanders of men, so that I may keep [Col. 1202A] your commandments. Slanders occur when the charge of impiety is brought against righteous people. He asks God to redeem him from them, so that he may keep God’s commandments.

Make your face shine upon your servant. Confirm me through the likeness of your glorious image. And teach me your ordinances, so that what I now see in a mirror I may behold through certain contemplation.

Streams of waters ran down from my eyes, because they did not keep your law. This holy man continually practices true repentance and does not cease to wash away ancient offenses with streams of tears, so that you may understand that, unless you practice true repentance, what you have done will not easily be forgiven you. True repentance consists in continually washing away sins through tears and not repeating what has been cleansed away.

SADE.

[Col. 1202B] You are righteous, Lord, and your judgment is right; you commanded that your testimonies be justice, and your truth exceedingly great. Everything we suffer at your command is just, right, and true, because it either comes upon us for our sins or occurs so that we may be shown to have been tested.

Zeal for your house has made me waste away. When God’s house is made a den of thieves by evil inhabitants, or when I see bodies dedicated to God polluted by the haunts of crimes. Because my enemies have forgotten your words. For by forgetting the precepts of the Law they made your house a den of thieves.

Your utterance is exceedingly refined by fire, and your servant loved it. For just as it consumes sin, so it also illuminates the sinner if he turns back.

I am younger and despised; I have not forgotten your ordinances. Although David says this in reference to himself—he was younger than his other brothers and, as though despised, was sent to pasture sheep, and afterward was chosen for the kingdom—nevertheless it must be referred to the Christian people, who, previously despised and expelled from their father’s house, remembered God’s ordinances and, having received the firstborn status of the former people, became first.

Your justice is justice forever. The former people did not recognize that it would always endure. And your law is truth. For them it was a shadow; now it is truth for the people of the Church. But the prophet, enduring many things for this truth, says:

Tribulation and distress found me; your commandments are my meditation. However much he may be afflicted by punishments or confined in chains, his voice, always free, meditates continually on God’s commandments.

The equity of your testimonies is forever; give me understanding, and I shall live. So that, through understanding them, I may be able to receive eternal life.

COPH.

I cried out with my whole heart; hear me, Lord; I shall seek your ordinances. I cried out to you: save me, so that I may keep your commandments. We have often pointed out that this cry is not of bodily voice but of spiritual mind, through which the righteous are heard by God—or by which he graciously opens his ear to their prayers.

I anticipated the dawn and cried out, because I hoped in your word. He anticipated ancient vices through youthful chastity; through the maturity of a vigorous spirit he never removed his hope from God’s words.

My eyes anticipated you at dawn, so that I might meditate on your utterances. The light did not find him asleep, but vigorously watchful and meditating on the divine utterances with the attention of his spiritual eyes.

Hear my voice, Lord, according to your mercy, etc. He continually sends forth a groan of spiritual voice, so that he may be transferred from this mortality into eternal life.

My persecutors have drawn near in iniquity; but they have gone far from your law. For everyone who approaches the holy iniquitously in order to harm him is distanced from God’s law.

You are near, Lord, and all your commandments are equity. You are not confined by places, but through the truth of your commandments you pour yourself into the hearts [Col. 1203B] of the holy.

From the beginning I have known from your testimonies. From Adam, through all the patriarchs and prophets. Because you founded them forever: in the Gospels, in which we too have been founded upon the foundation mentioned above, as we often remember the apostle Paul saying.

RES.

See my humiliation and rescue me, because I have not forgotten your law. I humble myself before you; I beg you to rescue me, so that I may be exalted, because I remember your law, in which you said: “Whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke XIV).

Judge my judgment and redeem me; give me life because of your utterance. I judged that I know nothing except Jesus Christ, who was promised to come for the redemption of the world. In accordance with this judgment, therefore, may I [Col. 1203C] be given life by you through your utterances.

Salvation is far from sinners, because they have not sought your ordinances. Our salvation is Christ, who is far from negligent Jews, because they do not understand him as prefigured in the ordinances of the law.

Your mercies are many, Lord, because they rescue us from many dangers. According to your judgment give me life, so that nothing may be found in me that the judgment of death might consume.

Many persecute and afflict me; I have not turned aside from your testimonies. Let them rage with hatred; let them attack with insults; I am raised up by your testimonies, not bent down.

I saw those who did not keep the covenant, and I wasted away, because they did not keep your utterances. There was a covenant between Israel and God, which he said to Moses: “Everything that the Lord has said, we shall do” (Exod. XXIV). But now we too enter into a covenant at baptism, promising to renounce the devil and his works. Therefore the prophet wastes away on account of those who violate this covenant. So too Paul, who said: “Who is made to stumble, and I am not made to burn?” (2 Cor. XI).

See that I have loved your commandments, Lord; in your mercy give me life. He loved them not through fear but through the affection of good will. Therefore he asks to be given life in them.

The beginning of your words is truth. So that the new person, reborn in Christ, may live. And all the judgments of your justice are forever, so that thereafter, recognizing that he was created in the image and likeness of God, he may do nothing unworthy of God’s judgments and ordinances.

SIN.

[Col. 1204A]

Princes persecuted me without cause, and my heart feared your words. I feared that word which says: “Whoever denies me before men, I too shall deny before my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. X). Therefore he remained strong in his Passion.

I shall rejoice over your utterances like one who finds much spoil. After the strong man has been bound and his goods plundered (Luke XI), I rejoice in that Gospel utterance which says: “When they persecute you and curse you and speak every evil against you because of justice, rejoice and exult, because your reward is great in heaven” (Matt. V).

I hated and abhorred iniquity, but I loved your law. While he hates iniquity and loves God’s justice [Col. 1204B], he extends himself to a greater duty, saying:

Seven times a day I gave you praise for the judgments of your justice. He praises God seven times a day because his mind, enduring in complete radiance, hastens toward that seventh day—that is, the Sabbath of Sabbaths—which is eternal rest.

There is much peace for those who love your law, Lord, and there is no scandal for them. Whoever loves God must have peace with his brothers. For the one who is scandalized by his brother loves God with false love.

I awaited your salvation, Lord, and I did your commandments. Awaiting Jesus, the salvation of all, I did what had been commanded in the Law and the prophets.

My soul kept your testimonies and loved them exceedingly. Along with the vigor of its observance, it applied a strong love.

I kept your precepts and your testimonies, because all my ways are before you, Lord. Whoever walks in God’s ways keeps his precepts and testimonies; he does nothing in action, word, or thought that would be considered unworthy of the divine gaze.

TAU.

Let my prayer draw near before you, Lord; according to your utterance give me understanding. I beg that my prayer may be made near to you, Lord, so that, receiving understanding from you, I may ask for nothing except what I ought.

Let my petition enter before you, Lord; according to your utterance rescue me. Receiving it graciously through its fragrance in the night of this life, may you rescue it from this [Col. 1204D] corruption of carnal desire.

My lips shall pour forth a hymn when you teach me your ordinances. If my lips are opened by you through a pure conscience, then I shall utter a hymn worthy of praise, which I am taught after being imbued with your ordinances.

My tongue shall proclaim your utterances, because all your commandments are equity. There is nothing else in your utterances, Lord, but peace, equity, and life. This I shall believe in my heart, this I shall speak with my lips, and this I shall proclaim with my tongue.

Let your hand come to save me, because I have chosen your commandments. When he says, “Let your hand come,” he designates the Lord Savior, who was made for him from David’s seed according to the flesh, through whom all things were made and [Col. 1205A] are governed. Here we must understand “hand” as the right hand. He asks the Savior to come, through whom he knew that he would be saved. By saying, “I have chosen the commandments,” he testifies that he has set every danger aside for love of the Lord.

I longed for your salvation, Lord, and your law is my meditation. I longed to see the very one whom, even in those times, I believed would come from a virgin’s womb. And to show that this knowledge had come to him from the divine Scriptures, he continues: “And your law is my meditation.” For in the prophets he had longed for Christ the Lord to be born; the Law and the prophets spoke of him.

My soul shall live and praise you, and your judgments shall help me. With the weakness of earthly corruption swallowed up, he confesses that he lives for God through the help of his judgments.

I have gone astray like a sheep that was lost; seek your servant, because I have not forgotten your commandments. He says that he was a wandering sheep but is no longer one; he begs to be carried back on the shepherd’s shoulders, so that now joy may be given to the angels over his discovery. The Lord, however, was sent only to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel (Matt. XV). We humbly beseech him that, having become doers of his judgments, keepers of his commandments, and searchers of his testimonies, when the lost sheep has been found (Luke XV), restored through the diligence of the good shepherd to the ecclesiastical fold and carried back upon his sacred shoulders, we may deserve to rejoice in the fellowship of the holy angels—to him be glory with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages [Col. 1205C] of ages. Amen.

PSALM CXIX.

A Song of Ascents. The fifteen psalms of the steps lead us, through successive advances, to the summit, so that in the courts of the Lord we may be able to say: “Behold now, bless the Lord, all servants of the Lord, in the courts of the house of his God” (Ps. CXXXIII). And since most people have discussed these matters at very great length, it is foolish to wish to say little in place of great things.

To the Lord, when I was in tribulation, I cried out, and he heard me. Three things are quickly explained in one verse: distress, prayer, and being heard, because no one is afflicted except one who desires to live piously in Christ. Therefore, if we desire to be heard, we ought to cry out to the Lord not with the loudness of our voices but with humility of heart.

[Col. 1205D] Lord, free my soul from lying lips: from the Jews, who not only do not believe in Christ the Lord but also do not fear to blaspheme him with unclean lips. And from a deceitful tongue: from the teaching of the heretics, who strive to drive us from the straight line of the faith.

What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, for a deceitful tongue? In a spirit of merciful affection, the Lord deigned to ask the soul that was faithfully crying out to him what should be given or added to it against a deceitful tongue. Many say that in this passage the preposition has been changed and wish it to read: “What shall be given to you against a deceitful tongue?” They intend that, as though from God’s teaching, that soul may hear the answer.

[Col. 1206A] The sharp arrows of the mighty one, with desolating coals. In place of “desolating coals,” the Hebrew has ἀρκευθίνοις (*arkeythinois*), “juniper coals.” I think that the coal brought to Isaiah’s lips is also a destroyer (Isa. VI), so that it may cleanse the faults he had contracted either by speaking or by keeping silent about what was good. Here too, therefore, he asks for a similar coal, so that a coal from God’s altar may be given to him, one that, placed upon his lips, may make the solitude of sins—that is, may render him free from vices.

Alas for me, for my sojourn has been prolonged. He whose citizenship is in heaven is a pilgrim in this body, and this pilgrimage seems long to him, because he does not contemplate in visible form what he has received through hope. Therefore, groaning like wheat among the chaff, he says: “I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Cedar.” Cedar is interpreted as “darkness.” [Col. 1206B] This man, then, dwells with those who inhabit darkness, but he is not darkened by the darkness, just as “the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1). “My soul has been a long sojourner.” For I desired to depart and be with Christ.

“With those who hated peace, I was peaceable.” Fulfilling the Apostle’s command: “If possible, so far as it depends on you, living at peace with all people” (Philippians 1; Romans 12). Thus he is among those who hate peace, yet is peaceable, so that he might preach peace to them more freely. “And when I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause.” He announced peace; but the enemies of peace not only refused to receive it, but also attacked the very preacher of peace with their wickedness.

## PSALM 120

[Col. 1206C] **A Song of Ascents.** This psalm contains the second ascent, and its title is “A Song of Ascents.” For there are several of them, signifying—as you have already heard in the first of them—our ascent, which takes place in the heart toward God, from the valley of weeping, that is, from the humility of contrition.

“I lifted up my eyes to the mountains.” I raised my spiritual eyes to the heights of the books, namely, of the Prophets and the Law. “From where will my help come?” From where, I suppose, will the Lord, the helper of all, come?

“My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth.” From him I await help, through whom the Father established heaven and earth. At this point, in accordance with his faith, this man received from the Holy Spirit an answer of consolation. For he says:

“May he not give your foot over to agitation.” He does not allow the stability by which you have been established in him to be removed. “Nor may he slumber who guards you.” For God protects and watches over the one who remains in him with vigilant guardianship.

“Behold, he will neither slumber nor sleep, who guards Israel.” He is guarded by God without any interruption—the one who has perceived him through the focused attention of spiritual eyes.

“The Lord guards you.” He himself who made heaven and earth, because the gods who did not make it perish from it.

“The Lord is your protection, over your right hand.” He protects you, lest the hostile side obstruct your right-hand work, that is, your good work.

“By day the sun will not burn you, nor the moon by night.” The righteous person cannot be exalted in prosperity, nor cast down in sorrow. What is signified by day and night is likewise signified by the sun and the moon.

[Col. 1207A] “The Lord guards you from every evil.” From all the ambushes of the enemy. “May the Lord guard your soul.” May he not allow the opposing power to dominate it.

“May the Lord guard your entrance.” Through which you entered into the knowledge of the Father. “And your departure, from this time forth and forever.” So that, when you have departed from the body, you may be protected by his guardianship—not cast into that chaos where the rich man is seen burning, but enjoy everlasting rest with Lazarus in the bosom of Abraham (Luke 16).

## PSALM 121

“A Song of Ascents.” This psalm is the third step of ascent, containing the voice of a man whose citizenship [Col. 1207B] is in heaven.

“I rejoiced in the things that were said to me.” They had been said to me through the Law, the Prophets, and the Apostles. But I too say the things that I had contemplated in a mirror, and now see face to face (1 Corinthians 13). “And what things,” you ask? “We shall go into the house of the Lord.” That is, into the heavenly Jerusalem, so that we may become fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household.

“Our feet were standing in your courts, Jerusalem.” Firm within its expanse. But lest you think this refers to the earthly city, listen to what follows:

“Jerusalem, which is built as a city.” “It is not yet,” he says, “that the construction of this city has been completed; rather, it is built daily from living stones upon the foundation [Col. 1207C] of the Apostles and Prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the chief cornerstone” (Ephesians 4), as the Apostle says. “Whose fellowship is in unity.” In the one body of the Church, through Christ.

“For there the tribes went up, the tribes of the Lord.” Not tribes subject to sin, but “the tribes of the Lord,” which, recognizing the Lord, did not delay in following him—a statement that must be referred to the Gentiles. “A testimony to Israel.” So that it may condemn him, because Israel did not recognize him, although he had been demonstrated through many miracles. But the tribes of the Gentiles immediately received him once he was recognized. Thus also the queen of the South, or the Ninevites, will rise in the judgment of this testimony and will condemn him (Luke 11). “To confess to your name, O Lord.” For they confess that “at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth” (Philippians [Col. 1207D] 2), and that you, Lord Jesus Christ, are in the glory of God the Father.

“For there thrones have sat in judgment.” The thrones of God are the Apostles, upon whom the Lord rests. These thrones will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel, as he himself says in the Gospel (Matthew 19). “Thrones over the house of David.” Governing and admonishing the Church of Christ by their precepts.

“Ask for the things that belong to the peace of Jerusalem.” Inquire into the things that pertain to the peace of this city, and pursue them, so that through love of peace you may obtain the fruit of eternal blessedness. “And abundance for those who love you.” Whoever, having abandoned transitory things, loves God above all else—he enjoys an abundance of heavenly goods.

“Let there be peace in your strength.” The Lord Christ is our peace, who binds us together in one bond of charity; if his strength grows strong within us, he too enters into our hearts. “And abundance in your towers.” The prophet asks that an abundance of heavenly goods be produced in those who, surpassing others in merit like very strong towers, both fortify this city by their strength and adorn it by their height.

“For the sake of my brothers and my neighbors I spoke peace concerning you.” So that they too might present themselves perfected for the completion of this building.

“For the sake of the house of the Lord our God, I sought good things for you.” By preaching peace to the neighboring brothers who make them the city of the eternal King, for whom he sought these good things, so that from the whole city he might pass into its one dwelling, saying: “Father, I ask that where I am, they also may be with me. I in them, and you in me, so that they may see my glory, because you loved me before the foundation of the world” (John 17).

## PSALM 122

“A Song of Ascents.” This psalm unfolds the fourth Song of Ascents. In it, that faithful man who previously lifted his eyes toward the mountains, now making progress in his ascent, raises them to the very inhabitant of heaven, saying:

“To you I lifted up my eyes, who dwell in heaven.” It should be noted that through the individual psalms there are certain stages of progress. In the first he had said, “To the Lord I cried when I was in distress,” and in the second he had reported that he had raised his eyes to the mountains. He had also rejoiced because entry into the house of God had been promised to him. Now he has advanced further, so that he lifts his eyes to God himself. “Who dwell in heaven.” As he ascended, where would he have wished to lift his eyes, unless he desired to ascend to the place toward which he was striving?

“Behold, as the eyes of servants are upon the hands of their masters, and as the eyes of a maidservant are upon the hands of her mistress, so are our eyes upon the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us.” We are servants, and we are maidservants; he is Lord and mistress. Let your charity pay attention. It is not surprising that we are servants and he is Lord; but it is surprising that we are maidservants and he is mistress. Yet this too is not surprising, because we are maidservants—we are the Church—nor is the other surprising, because he too is mistress: for he is the power and wisdom of God. Hear, therefore, the Apostle saying: “But we preach Christ crucified, to the Jews a stumbling block, and to the Gentiles foolishness, but to those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1). When we are subjected to many kinds of persecution, we must always keep the attention of our eyes fixed without any defect upon God’s help, until he grants us mercy.

“Have mercy on us, O Lord, have mercy on us, because we have been filled exceedingly with contempt.” That is, with despair, because the saints are despised by wicked people.

“Our soul has also been filled exceedingly: with reproach for the prosperous, and with contempt for the proud.” He does not speak only of those who abound in riches, but of those who abound in wickedness; they despise the poor of Christ. The rich despise the poor, the proud despise the humble, and they themselves utter many reproaches against the holy Church.

## PSALM 123

“A Song of Ascents.” This psalm is the fifth step of ascent, teaching that faithful man to advance who, by raising his spiritual eyes and overcoming all the snares of demonic assault, thus begins, saying:

“Unless the Lord had been among us—let Israel now say—unless the Lord had been among us, when people rose against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive.” The Lord dwells well among us if we contemplate him with a holy mind. The wicked did not try to devour our flesh, but to swallow our souls through the instigation of crimes; yet we were rescued from them by him who was among us. For this we must give thanks to him, because we have been saved by his grace.

“When their anger raged against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us like water.” The upheavals of wicked minds, which seek to swallow God’s saints, are compared to waters; but when the Lord dwells in the saints, they flow and run downward.

“Our soul passed through the torrent.” The Hebrew has it better: “The torrent passed over our soul.” That is, many whirlwinds of temptations passed over his soul, but they could not kill it, since the righteous man says: “Unless the Lord had been among us—let Israel now say—perhaps the water would have passed over our soul, the unbearable water.” The word ἀνυπόστατον (*anypóstaton*) in Greek is ambiguous: it can mean “that which subsists” and “that which is unbearable,” that is, which no one can endure. For this, Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, and all the interpreters agree with one voice, translating ἀνυπόστατον as “proud and arrogant waters.”

“Blessed is the Lord, who did not give us as prey to their teeth.” The teeth of these torrents are the multitude of vices; so that we may not be captured by them, we are rescued by God’s grace.

“Our soul, like a sparrow, has been rescued from the snare of the hunters.” Snares are laid for us in desires and in the various deceits of diabolical cunning; but, with Satan crushed beneath our feet, we fly out from them like a sparrow escaping its captor. For it follows:

“The snare was broken, and we were freed.” For if the Lord dwells among us, he himself—as we have said—will break these snares, so that they do not hinder us.

“Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.” This is the name that is above every name. By the help of this name, the snares of death are overcome, if we remain fixed in him.

## PSALM 124

“A Song of Ascents.” This psalm is reckoned the sixth among the Songs of Ascents. From the prophet’s voice it exhorts us to abandon worldly affairs and place all our confidence in God alone, saying:

“Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion; they will not be shaken forever.” Zion is the Church; but the mountain, according to Daniel, is Christ the Lord (Daniel 2). Therefore those who place all their hope in him are not shaken forever, because they are made conformable to the body of his glory. “Who dwells in Jerusalem.” In that mother of ours, the Jerusalem above, which is free (Galatians 4).

“Mountains surround it.” The protections of the saints, angels, Prophets, and Apostles, which, rising like the height of mountains, tower above all in holiness. “And the Lord surrounds his people, from this time forth and forever.” Just as he graciously promised, saying: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matthew, last chapter).

“For the Lord will not leave the rod of sinners over the lot of the righteous.” In place of “rod,” the Hebrew has “scepter.” This, then, is what we ask: “Do not lead us into temptation” that we cannot endure. “So that the righteous may not stretch out their hands toward iniquity.” So that they do not think: “What benefit is there for me in being righteous, if the wicked are always persecuting me?” “May they not stretch out” means that they should endure the wicked and not do evil.

“Do good, O Lord, to those who are good and upright in heart.” Those who are either good in their conduct or considered upright in faith.

“But those who turn aside to entanglements the Lord will lead away.” In place of “entanglements,” Aquila translated διαπλοκάς (*diaplokas*), Symmachus, σκολιότητας (*skoliotētas*), and the Fifth Edition, διεστραμμένα (*diestrammena*). [Note: [Col. 1209] At this point the older editions were unable to restore the Greek translators’ words, which are found somewhat corrupted in our manuscript codices. MART.] “With those who work iniquity.” Those who turn aside from God’s commandments are led away with those who do not know God, so that they may be struck by the same judgment. “Peace be upon Israel.” Christ the Lord is our peace (Ephesians 2). Removing the dividing wall of hostility between Jews and Gentiles, he made the two one, though they had previously been divided.

## PSALM 125

“A Song of Ascents.” This is the seventh psalm of the Songs of Ascents. It brings forth a song, or ascent, in which the faithful soul rejoices in the Lord against the captivity of sins and says:

“When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion.” The ancient captivity of vices had spread throughout the whole world; but when the sun of righteousness dawned for us, it was driven away. Thus the Church too, which is specially called Zion, appeared. “We became like those who are comforted.” In place of “those who are comforted,” all editions alike have translated “those who dream.” And rightly “those who dream,” for joy is not yet complete, since some remain in captivity.

“Then our mouth was filled with joy, and our tongue with exultation.” With spiritual and boundless joy. Either our mouth or our tongue is filled, because it is not enough to express such great praises for the grace by which we are saved.

“Then they will say among the nations, ‘The Lord has done great things with them.’” For if, having abandoned transitory things, we place our hope in eternal things, then it is said that the Lord has made us great, captivity having been driven away. Just as once the nations, terrified by fear, spoke about the Israelite people, saying: “God dried up the waters of the sea and of the Jordan for the entry of the children of Israel” (Joshua 2). In this joy, therefore, we give thanks.

“The Lord has done great things with us; we became rejoicing.” Previously we served Pharaoh, that is, the destroyer, in harsh labor; but now we serve the heavenly King, whose yoke is easy and whose burden is light (Matthew 11).

“Turn back our captivity, O Lord.” The prophet confesses that he shares a common captivity with the rest of the people, because one member suffers with the other members. “Like a torrent in the south.” For just as ice melts when the south wind blows, and when the torrents are filled every terror flows down with its force, so, when the Holy Spirit blows, our sins are dissolved, so that, having received forgiveness, what is written may come to pass for us: “As ice in fair weather, your sins will be dissolved” (Sirach 3).

“Those who sow in tears will reap in joy; going, they went and wept, carrying their seeds.” The saints of God therefore sowed the word of God among the nations in tears of confession and through various sufferings, going and weeping over the hardness of their hearts. In the future they will carry it with the fruits of their sheaves, when the Lord says to them: “Amen, I say to you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice; and your sorrow will be turned into joy” (John 16). Therefore let us too, crying out in tribulation, raise the eyes of our minds to God our helper, so that he may rescue us from the savage teeth of the envious; remove from us the scepter of unjust domination; and, granting his customary mercy, release us from the captivity of vices, so that we may be joined together like living stones in the building of the heavenly Jerusalem.

## PSALM 126

“A Song of Ascents of Solomon.” This psalm is marked with Solomon’s title so that the builder of the temple himself might teach that he could not complete its construction without the Lord’s help.

“Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain.” According to the Apostle, we are God’s temple; unless we are built by the Lord our Jesus Christ upon the foundations of the Apostles and Prophets (2 Corinthians 6), the building of the philosophers and of the other teachers of worldly things will be empty.

“Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it have labored in vain.” The faithful soul is understood as the city of the eternal King, frequented by good citizens, that is, by upright conduct. No guardianship can protect it except that of the one who, without sleeping, protects Israel.

“It is vain for you to rise before dawn.” Whoever rises before dawn gropes through the darkness of night. Likewise, whoever, abandoning the light of the Gospel, has turned to the doctrine mentioned above remains in darkness and cannot enjoy the brightness of the Lord’s resurrection. “Rise after you have sat, you who eat the bread of sorrow.” You who rest in humiliation, rise up—you who remember that you were born or live in sins and desire to pass over to God. Or, “you who eat the bread of sorrow.” In place of “sorrow,” Theodotion and the Fifth Edition translated “idols,” while the Sixth translated “error.” Thus, according to the straightforward sense, the meaning is this: You run to the temple at dawn for no reason and think that you are worshiping God, while you also worship idols and consume unclean bread.

“When he gives sleep to his beloved”—as though someone had asked when this would happen, the answer is given: “When he gives sleep to his beloved.” The beloved are the saints, who, after the sleep of the present life, seem to slumber here so that they may deserve to attain eternal life in the resurrection. “Behold, the inheritance of the Lord is sons, the reward, the fruit of the womb.” When the saints depart from this age after receiving the sleep of rest, then they will become the Lord’s inheritance, because they are no longer subject to temptations. But the Lord himself, born of a Virgin, also became the fruit of the womb. His assumed humanity received this reward: that the called Gentiles, in their sonship, should be his inheritance. “He gave them,” he says, “power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name” (John 1).

“Like arrows in the hand of the mighty, so are the sons of the unencumbered.” He calls the “unencumbered” those who are prepared, equipped, and girded for battle; the Septuagint translators rendered the same word in the books of Ezra.

“Blessed is the man who has fulfilled his desire from them.” In place of “desire,” the Hebrew has “quiver.” Since he had compared the saints to arrows, he appropriately introduces a quiver to be filled with arrows. “He will not be put to shame when he speaks with his enemies in the gate.” The gate, the entrance or doorway, is the one who said: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John 10). Therefore, whoever among the sons of the expelled is fixed in Christ will not be put to shame on the day of judgment, when he reproaches the enemies of the Law of God for their disobedience and perversity—or for all their wickedness.

## PSALM 127

“A Song of Ascents.” This psalm, the ninth step or song of ascent, conveys the fear and love of the Lord, saying:

“Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways.” Those who join themselves to the love of God with fear and exercise themselves in the things preached by the Prophets, Apostles, and Evangelists.

“You will eat the labors of your fruits; blessed are you, and it will be well with you.” The labors of fruits are produced when a person exercises himself in the world so that he may be able to attain the fruit of eternity. For one proceeds laboriously along these ways of God, as he himself says: “Narrow and arduous is the way that leads to life” (Matthew 7). But this labor is filled with eternal fruits when a person is enriched with that heavenly bread. It was with this desire that the one who said, “Blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of God” (Luke 14), was also moved.

“Your wife is like a flourishing vine, on the sides of your house.” According to Solomon (Proverbs 7), the wife is understood as wisdom. Brought into the house of the purified soul like a beautiful vine, she spreads along the sides of our works.

“Your children are like young olive trees around your table.” The works of good people stand around the heavenly teaching, with the richness of peace and the shade of virtue.

“Behold, thus shall the man who fears the Lord be blessed.” He is enriched with these riches.

“May the Lord bless you from Zion.” He who reigns in the Church. “And may you see the good things of Jerusalem all the days of your life.” In that heavenly mother about whom we have spoken in other psalms, in which the saints will see the good things of everlasting life.

“And may you see the children of your children.” Those who await the recompense of good works. “Peace be upon Israel.” May our peace, Jesus Christ, continually look upon the mind that beholds him.

## PSALM 128

“A Song of Ascents.” This psalm brings us the tenth song or ascent. Beginning with the prophetic voice, it teaches us to resist incessantly the wickednesses that attack us, lest they overcome us.

“Often they attacked me from my youth.” This man says that he has been attacked from the beginning of his life, but he is silent about who attacks him, so that it may be understood that the battle is sent by the devil. You can more easily recognize this either from the testing of Job or from the betrayal of Christ by Judas.

“Let Israel now say: ‘Often they attacked me from my youth, yet they could not prevail against me.’” Therefore the one who is Israel can say this, because he is attacked throughout all the days of his life. But this battle does not prevail against him, because the Lord fights for him.

“Sinners built upon my back; they prolonged iniquity for themselves.” For one who continually runs toward God and strives toward greater things, machines of wickedness are constructed behind his back, because they cannot be displayed openly. But when they do not reach their intended result, they prolong them for themselves: by acting out of envy, they provoke sin and divine vengeance against themselves. For it follows:

“The righteous Lord will cut off the necks of sinners.” In place of “necks,” the Hebrew has “bonds” or “chains,” so that the meaning is: Those who had surrounded me on every side with their snares also held me bound; but, with the Lord’s help, all the bonds have been loosened.

“Let all who hate Zion be put to shame and turned backward.” Zion is the Church, which is the body of Christ, of which we are members.

“May they become like the grass of roofs, which withers before it is plucked up.” This is not said of buildings founded upon rock, but of those placed upon sand, as though they were soon to collapse. It refers to works of the flesh, in which not only is no grain of goodness found, but they also dry up before they reach any growth.

“Of which the reaper did not fill his hand.” He did not receive a reward worthy of his work as recompense. “Nor his bosom, who gathers sheaves.” He who, through purity of conscience, brought good will, even if he had less to offer. Therefore, as though he had given much, he brings sheaves back from God, like the widow from her two small coins (Mark 12).

“And those who passed by did not say, ‘The blessing of the Lord be upon you.’” The saints of God did not bless them; for, regarding this world as nothing, they passed over to heavenly and eternal things. “We have blessed you in the name of the Lord.” So that, abandoning fruitless and dry works, you may sow those that fill both the reaper’s hand and the bosom of those who gather sheaves.

## PSALM 129

“A Song of Ascents.” This psalm unfolds for us the eleventh step and song of ascent. Expressing the faithful soul’s effort as it strives toward higher things, while complaining that it is immersed as though in the deep, it urges us to understand heavenly things, saying:

[Col. 1214B] “From the depths I cried to you, O Lord; Lord, hear my prayer.” He cries from the depths who knows the height of the riches of God’s wisdom, who suffers persecutions, who implores him with a merciful sigh.

“Let your ears be attentive to the prayer of your servant.” The prophet does not ask here for a bodily ear, knowing that God is incorporeal; rather, he asks for the power by which God graciously hears his own.

“If you observe iniquities, O Lord, Lord, who will endure?” For if the frailty of the human race, transgressing your laws, is immediately struck by your vengeance, who will be able to escape?

“For with you there is propitiation.” For you will reconcile us to the Father through the cross. “And because of your law I have endured you, O Lord.” The law is spiritual and contains words of life; we must endure it, lest, by sinning against it, we be judged through the law (Romans 7).

“My soul has endured the Lord,” and so forth. “From the morning watch until night.” From that morning hour when he was placed in the Lord’s vineyard, he fixed his hope upon the hour at which he would receive the denarius of his reward. “From the morning watch.” Let Israel hope in the Lord. From the time when the light of truth shone upon him, let him contemplate heavenly things without failing.

“For with the Lord there is mercy.” When he graciously consented to become human for us. “And abundant redemption is with God.” When he redeemed us not with gold or silver, but with precious blood.

“And he himself will redeem Israel from all their iniquities.” For the Son himself, when the fullness of the Gentiles enters, will save the remnant of Israel, with their iniquity forgiven.

## PSALM 130

“A Song of Ascents.” This psalm is reckoned the twelfth in this ascent, whether of song or of step. From the prophet’s person, it teaches us the humility that Christ was to bear in the flesh, saying:

“Lord, my heart was not exalted.” Rather, in his contrition and humiliation I offered you an acceptable sacrifice. “Nor were my eyes lifted up.” So that they might desire transitory and perishable things.

“Nor did I walk in great things, nor in marvelous things beyond me.” I did not walk amid those things that seemed great and marvelous to human beings, lest they overwhelm me.

[Col. 1215A] “If I did not think humbly, but exalted my soul.” He is humble in heart, but exalted in understanding. I thought humbly in the world, but I exalted my soul in heaven.

“As one who has been weaned from his mother, so will you repay my soul.” He perceives nothing childish in himself, because, having moved beyond the nourishment of milk, he has reached mature manhood; he implores to be nourished now by that bread which came from heaven.

“Let Israel hope in the Lord, from this time forth and forever.” He teaches that our hope should not be enclosed by any limit of time, so that through hope we may grasp the good things of the age to come during the present life.

## PSALM 131

“A Song of Ascents.” This psalm is reckoned the thirteenth among the Songs of Ascents. Through the ascent of progress, it teaches us from the prophetic voice about the coming of the Son of God, saying:

“Remember, O Lord, David.” The Son of almighty God, intending to assume flesh for the redemption of the people, wished to be called David—called by the name of the one from whose lineage he was also to assume his body. “And all his gentleness.” He did not contend or cry out, but was led like a gentle lamb to the sacrifice (Isaiah 53).

“As he swore to the Lord, he vowed a vow to the God of Jacob.” He used an oath and a vow for the firmness of the statement, so that we would not hesitate to follow him. But what he wished in the meantime is worth considering. “Remember, O Lord, David, and all his gentleness, as he swore to the Lord.” In place of “as,” the Hebrew has “who,” so that the sense is: “Remember, O Lord, David and all his gentleness, who swore to the Lord and made a vow to the God of Jacob.”

“If I enter the tabernacle of my house; if I climb upon the bed of my couch; if I give sleep to my eyes or slumber to my eyelids, and rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob.” The tabernacle of the house indicates the heavenly dwelling; in the bed of the couch, the sleep of the eyes, the slumber of the eyelids, and the rest of the temples, he signified eternal rest, which is never interrupted. He promises that he will not return to these things until he has first built, through his resurrection, a place worthy of God the Father in humanity, or a congregation of the Church.

[Col. 1215D] “Behold, we heard of it in Ephrata.” The region of Bethlehem is called Ephrata to this day. Other Scriptures also bear witness to this. Ephrata itself is Bethlehem, where the Church was first heard of, that is, where Christ the Lord assumed flesh. In that place Rachel, beloved of Israel, also rests (Genesis 35), and she bore the type of the Church. “We found it in the fields of the forest.” Among the Gentiles, which were formerly the lairs of the devil, but are now fields made fruitful by worshiping the Lord.

“We shall enter into the tabernacle of God.” We who are gathered by the Lord into the one house of the Church. “We shall worship in the place where his feet stood.” In the place where apostolic teachings are heard, which, like feet, support the whole body of the Church.

“Arise, O Lord, into your rest.” You have now fulfilled your oath, repaid your vow; you have now found a place for God; you have now brought forth the Church from your side. Arise now from the dead, return to the tabernacle, departing into rest, concerning which you spoke above. And not only you, but “you and the ark of your sanctification.” That is, the assumed body, by which divinity was veiled. From it the words of life, the heavenly bread, and the way, the truth, and the life were shown to us.

“Let your priests be clothed with righteousness.” So that, clothed in the breastplate of righteousness, they may not be wounded by the enemy’s arrows. “And let your saints exult.” In heavenly goods.

“For the sake of David your servant, do not turn away the face of your Christ.” For the sake of the one who, from David’s seed, assumed the form of a servant: may the brightness of your image not be turned away from the saints, in whom Christ himself dwells, but may it illuminate them.

“The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not frustrate him.” The Father swears truth to the God-man, and does not annul it but fulfills it, saying: “From the fruit of your womb I will place upon your throne.” We are the fruit of his womb, whom he spiritually generated as though from a womb. If we keep what follows, we shall sit upon his throne—not only we, but also our children. For he says:

“If your children keep my covenant and these testimonies of mine that I shall teach them, their children also forever and ever shall sit upon my throne.” If we keep his covenant, he will make us sit in the heavenly places, as the Apostle says (Ephesians 1): “They shall sit upon his throne.” But those too will sit upon his throne to whom it was said: “You shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19). Our children too shall sit there—that is, they will remember before him the good works that we performed out of love for him.

“For the Lord chose Zion; he preferred her as his dwelling.” The ecclesial host that is in harmony with him, or souls sanctified by heavenly sacraments for you.

“This is my rest forever and ever; here I will dwell, because I have chosen her.” The soul which, through the glory of resurrection and the cleansing of sin, has become his house and rest.

“I will surely bless her widow; I will satisfy her poor with bread.” In place of “widow,” that is, χήρα (*chēra*), both the Hebrew volumes and the Septuagint themselves have θήρα (*thēra*). But because of the unfamiliarity of the word and the alteration of a single letter, it gradually became established that χήρα should be read in place of θήρα, especially because “the poor” followed in the next verse. [Col. 1217A] Symmachus and Aquila translated θήρα as “provisions.”

[Note: [Col. 1215D] The true Jerome, *Questions on Genesis*, chapter 45: “Although in many codices, instead of ‘widow,’ that is, instead of χήρα, some read θήραν, the Hebrew has *Seda*, that is, ‘provisions.’ Some Alexandrian copies also have χήραν, and Saint Hilary, in this passage, praises the same reading on the authority of the translation. See *Questions on Genesis*, at the passage cited, and what we have observed there.]

“I will clothe her priests with salvation, and her saints will exult with exultation.” For he himself clothes us either with righteousness or with salvation, when he makes us conformable to his body, which is our righteousness and salvation, preparing eternal dwellings for us.

“There I will bring forth the horn of David.” The kingdom of Christ, which is displayed in those to whom it was said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5). “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ.” John the Baptist, or the precursor of our Lord and Savior, is called a lamp prepared by God the Father, for he announced that Christ would come into the darkness of this world. Thus the Lord himself also calls him, saying: “He was the burning lamp” (John 5), and so forth.

“I will clothe his enemies with shame.” This refers to the unbelieving Jews when they see the Lord in his majesty. “But upon him my sanctification will flourish.” In place of “sanctification,” the Hebrew has *NESER*, which Aquila translates as “consecrated.” It signifies a plate of gold that was fastened to the forehead of the high priest, bearing the name of the Lord engraved upon it.

## PSALM 132

“A Song of Ascents.”

Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one. He says two things: “good” and “pleasant.” Martyrdom is good, but it is not pleasant: it has torments and punishments, and there is always pain amid the tortures; and surely there is no pleasure in pain. “Behold how good and how pleasant.” Again, pleasure is pleasant. It is as though he were saying: Eating sweet food seems pleasant, but it incites lust. Thus he has placed two things here, and joined in one expression what seemed contrary to each other—namely, “good” and “pleasant.” “Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one.” Brothers in mind, not in body. Esau and Jacob were brothers, and because they dwelt together, this became a cause of discord for them. Therefore, when he says here “brothers,” he does not mean brothers in the body, but spiritual brothers—brothers of whom the Savior also spoke when he said to the women: “Go, announce to my brothers” (Matt. 28).

“Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one.” This psalm properly applies to coenobia and monasteries. It may also be understood of churches, but there, because of the diversity of their purposes, such concord does not seem to exist. For what brotherhood is there? One hastens to go home; another to the circus; another, while in church, thinks about usury. In monasteries, however, just as there is one purpose, so there is one mind. “Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one.” Truly good, truly pleasant. We have left behind one brother, and behold how many we have found. My secular brother [Note: See the admonition prefixed to this book.]—and in speaking of my own case, I speak of each person—does not love me so much as he loves my property. But spiritual brothers neglect what belongs to them and seek nothing else. Thus we also read in the Acts of the Apostles, that “the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4). And, he says, “everything was held in common among them.” Rightly was everything held in common among them, since they possessed one Christ. We have said much, but let us hurry on to what remains.

“Like ointment on the head, which descended upon the beard, the beard of Aaron.” If only there were time for us to discuss each point; a single day would not suffice us. We read in Exodus how priestly ointment is prepared (Exod. 25, 30). Then we read how one ointment with which kings were anointed was one thing, and another ointment with which prophets were anointed was another. Why say more? All ointments had their distinctions and their mysteries. Are we surprised at the holy ones? After the leper has been cleansed, after he has been sprinkled with hyssop and with the blood of a hen, and after one hen has been released into the wilderness, he too has his own ointment. Nothing is sanctified except through ointment. Therefore the young women also say in the Song of Songs: “Your name is poured-out ointment. We will run after you in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1).

“Like ointment on the head, which descended upon the beard, the beard of Aaron.” Beautifully he says “on the head,” which descended upon Aaron’s beard. The beard is an indication of manhood. For nature distinguishes woman and man by this sign; therefore the beard is an indication of manhood. The head, then, signifies divinity, that is, deity. The beard, however, indicates the man. “Until we attain,” he says, “to the perfect man, who is Christ” (Col. 1). See, then, what he says: “Like ointment,” like the blessing of ointment, descended from the head—that is, from the discourse of divinity—upon the beard; it descended upon the perfect man, who is Christ; afterward that same ointment descended upon the hem of his garment.

Thus the blessing, and the dew of Mount Hermon, descended upon Mount Zion. Here “ointment” is used for blessing. “You loved righteousness,” he says, “and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions” (Ps. 44). See what he says: “You loved righteousness,” he says, “and hated iniquity.” It is not enough to love righteousness; one must, conversely, hate iniquity. See what he says: “And hated iniquity.” What did he receive in return for these virtues? “Therefore God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions.”

This is said of Christ: you were therefore anointed so that you might anoint others. You were anointed with the oil of gladness beyond your companions—that is, more than your apostles. For you possessed the fountain of ointment; they possessed only drops. “Like ointment on the head.” May the Lord grant us also this ointment of divinity, which came upon the beard—that is, upon the perfect man Aaron, upon Aaron the priest. Aaron, moreover, is interpreted as “mountainous” or “of the mountain.” You see that this priest is not from the valleys but from the mountains.

“Upon the beard,” he says, “of Aaron.” The ointment on the head came upon the beard; from the Word who is God it came to the man whom he deigned to assume. And what benefit does this anointed beard and this perfect man bring us? Let us see what benefit it has.

“It descended upon the hem of his garment.” If we are Christ’s garment, by our faith we clothe his nakedness. Behold, he hung naked on the cross—“a stumbling-block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles” (1 Cor. 1)—and yet by our faith, speech, and confession he is clothed. Noah lay naked in his house, and his shame was exposed: the elder son mocked him, and the younger covered him (Gen. 9). Why do I say all this? To show that we are Christ’s garment. I tell you something new—or rather, not new, but from the Scriptures. We are Christ’s garment, and when we have clothed him with our confession, we in turn put on Christ himself. For the Apostle also says that Christ is our garment (Gal. 3). When we are baptized, we put on Christ and are clothed with him.

Do you wish to know how we clothe the Lord? We read in Jeremiah: “Take for yourself,” he says, “a loincloth, and go,” he says, “to the Euphrates, and place it in the cleft of the rock.” And I did, he says, what the Lord had commanded me. After some days I returned to the Euphrates, and behold, he says, the loincloth had rotted and was useful for nothing. And the Lord spoke to me, he says: Pay close attention. “Just as you had the loincloth around your loins, so I had this people around me,” says the Lord (Jer. 13). Why did I say all this? To show that believers are Christ’s garment.

“It descended upon the hem of his garment; it descended upon the beard, the beard of Aaron.” It is not appropriate at this time to speak about the priestly garments. The high priest has eight kinds of garments. It would take too long now to speak of the ephod and the tunic. It would take too long to speak of the breastpiece, the manifestations, the chains, the girdle, the undergarments, the fringes, the cord, and the bells; or to explain by what virtues the priest ought to enter the temple of the Lord and the Holy of Holies.

Therefore, if we too wish to belong to the priestly garment, we are either the shoulder-piece, which is interpreted as the ephod, so that we may have good works and carry Christ’s commandments upon our shoulders; or certainly we ought to be the inner tunic. This tunic is tight and clings to the body; it is not loose or spread apart, but adheres wholly to the body. You see, then, that whoever is inward—and is an inner tunic—is joined more closely to the body.

But if someone is the breastpiece, which is called λογεῖον (*logeion*), he is placed only upon the breast. Observe the order of Scripture: whoever is the breastpiece, the *logeion*, possesses reason and is placed upon the breast. Yet it is possible for someone to have prudence, to have λόγος (*logos*), to have speech. Whoever, then, is truly a priest ought to have δηλώσεις (*dēlōseis*), that is, manifestations—so that whatever he has conceived in his mind, he may bring forth and teach everything.

And all these things are useless unless chastity has been increased and adorned. Therefore there is a girdle: it encircles the loins, tightens them, and mortifies them. Then it is said that he must have undergarments, so that whatever in us is shameful and filthy may, as it were, be cleansed and mortified by this belt. Then it is said that we must have a robe, which adorns our feet, as it were. In this robe there are various flowers: there are pomegranates, and there are also fringes. I think that the woman suffering from an issue of blood touched this fringe and was healed (Matt. 9).

Consider this also: at the very ends of the feet, among the pomegranates, there were bells, and the high priest did not enter the Holy of Holies unless those bells rang out. The bells and those pomegranates are the diverse virtues, each of which has its own voice; and the priest’s departure from the Holy of Holies is itself vocal. For whether we eat or drink, we do everything in the name of the Lord (1 Cor. 10). We promised lesser things, and we have said greater ones.

“Like the dew of Hermon, which descended upon Mount Zion.” The dew of Hermon. We read in a certain book [Note: This is clearly the Book of the *Egregoroi*—the Watchers.]—an apocryphal book—that at the time when the sons of God descended to the daughters of men, they descended upon Mount Hermon and there made an agreement about how they would go to the daughters of men and take them as their companions. The book is very well known and is counted among the apocrypha, and the ancient interpreters spoke about it. We ourselves have said some things about it, not as an authority, but by way of recollection.

“Like the dew of Hermon, which descended upon Mount Zion.” I read [Note: That is, Origen, *Commentary on Job*.] in the book of someone who was using this apocryphal book to confirm his own heresy. What does he say? “The sons of God,” he says, “who were descending from heaven, came to Hermon and desired the daughters of men.” They are angels, he says, descending from heavenly places, and souls that desired bodies. For the daughters of men are bodies. Do you see how the doctrine of the Manichaeans arises? Just as the Manichaeans say that souls desired human bodies and were joined to the pleasure of bodies, so also those who say that angels desired bodies—that is, the daughters of men—do they not seem to be saying the very same thing as the Manichaeans? It would take too long now to argue against them; I wished only to judge which book they use, by this opportunity, to confirm their doctrine.

Hermon in our language is interpreted as ἀνάθεμα (*anathema*), that is, condemnation. The dew of the Lord, then, was formerly upon the Jewish people, who were later anathematized; and that blessing which formerly descended upon the accursed people afterward descended upon Mount Zion—that is, upon the Church.

We, if indeed we belong to the Church—for by “Church” I mean the truth of the doctrines and confession of Christ—we are in the building. How many holy people are in the wilderness, and how many of us are not in the Church; and those who are not of the Church move about within Christ’s Church. If, then, we are in the Church, if we possess the faith of the Church, the faith of the apostles, the faith of Christ, and the truths of the doctrines, we are the mountains of Zion.

We do not wish to be the valleys of Zion, but the mountains of Zion. For Zion has its valleys, and it also has its plain. Whoever is a sinner is a valley of Zion; he is not Mount Zion. Someone may say: “You are speaking from your own opinion.” Let us call Isaiah as a witness. At the time when Zion had sinned, after many visions—where it says, “A vision against Idumaea”; “a vision against Moab”; “a vision against Edom and the children of Ammon” (Isa. 13 ff.)—at the end there is placed: “A vision of the valley of Zion” (ibid. 22). Since it had descended from the height of faith, it therefore fell from the mountain into the valley.

Let us, then, first flee the valley of Zion. Let us come to the plain; from the plain let us come to the hills; from the hills let us come to the mountains. Let us follow Christ upon the mountains. For our kinsman, like a doe and a fawn of the deer, leaps over the hills and bounds across the mountains (Song 2).
