Hence also, in accordance with the truth of the ascents, after the resurrection he did not ascend into heaven from a valley, but from a mountain. Unless we become mountains in virtues, we cannot ascend to heaven. For there—in the mountains of Zion, in virtues, in faith, in confession, in the truth of the doctrines—is the blessing.

“And life forevermore.” Our life is Christ. Whoever confesses Christ will receive life forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM CXXXIII

“Behold, now bless the Lord, all servants of the Lord.” This is the final psalm of the Song of Ascents. The first psalm of the ascents had been: “To the Lord, when I was in distress, I cried, and he heard me.” In the second he had ascended: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains.” In the third: “I rejoiced in the things that were said to me.” In the fourth: “To you I lifted up my eyes, who dwell in heaven.”

See how he gradually ascends by steps and reaches higher things. It would take too long, if we wished to state the beginnings of each of these psalms of the ascents. He comes to the thirteenth psalm—or rather, he comes to the twelfth—and after every virtue he places humility. For we possess virtues in vain if those virtues themselves are not crowned by the Lord’s humility.

What did he say? “Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up.” Since, then, he had shown himself to be humble, he seeks the coming of Christ. And what does he say? “Remember, Lord, David and all his meekness.” And again, in another place: “For the sake of David your servant, do not turn away the face of your anointed” (Ps. 131). Since he has received Christ, after the faith of Christ he gathers the Church. And what does he say? “Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one.” The Church of the Lord has been gathered.

What does the final psalm say? “Behold, now bless the Lord, all servants of the Lord.” Since it is good and pleasant to dwell together as one, and you have been gathered together, “behold, now bless the Lord.” Bless the Lord now, after the coming of Christ, because you have been gathered in him. Bless him now, in the final psalm of the ascents, because you have been gathered at the summit of virtues. Before you reached the fifteenth ascent—that is, the height—you could not bless the Lord. Therefore I now say to you: “Behold, now bless the Lord.”

When “behold” is said, the matter is somehow pointed out with a finger. “Behold, now bless the Lord.” Who are to bless the Lord? “All servants of the Lord”—you who are not servants of sin but servants of the Lord.

Do we think it is a small thing that is said: “Therefore I am a servant of the Lord”? It is the highest virtue to be worthy of this. How so? It is as though someone claims a dignity when he says: “I am therefore the emperor’s servant,” and no one dares approach the emperor’s servant. Thus it is an immeasurable dignity to say that one is the servant of the Lord. Hence the Apostle also glories in the Lord’s service, and at the beginning of his Epistles he writes: “Paul, servant of Christ.” And Moses is described in these words: “Not as with Moses my servant, to whom I spoke face to face” (Exod. 33). See what he says: “With the others I spoke in a vision and in a riddle, but not as with Moses my servant, to whom I spoke face to face” (Heb. 3).

Let us give an example. Suppose there is some exceedingly wealthy lord. He has a household, and he also has servants who minister to him. Do the servants who are in the fields have as much confidence as those who minister daily? Great is the dignity of those who see their lord’s face and minister to him. Indeed, the other servants, who do not see their lord’s face, if they wish to obtain anything, ask their fellow servants. Why have I said all this? Our Lord Jesus also has a large household. He has some who minister, as it were, in his presence; he has others in the fields. I think that monks and virgins are those who minister to their lord in his presence, while secular people, who are as though in the field, belong to his household.

Indeed, those who are in the fields ask these others to intercede with the lord if they have some need. How great is the dignity of those who see their lord’s face daily; so great is the punishment of those who neglect their lord’s service. Wicked servants, when they are in the fields, are accustomed to fear their lord more, because they do not see him. But if they begin to see him daily, they despise him, and familiarity produces pride. Therefore we too must not despise the goodness of our God because of familiarity.

Bless the Lord, then, all servants of the Lord, because you are not servants of sin but servants of the Lord. All servants of the Lord, who have the Lord alone as your God. All servants of the Lord, over whom anger does not rule, in whom lust does not reign, in whom other sins do not reign; those whom vices do not dominate are ruled by the Lord.

“All servants of the Lord.” It seems that he has stopped here. But observe the increase. It is not enough merely to be servants of the Lord unless those servants themselves also stand. Some stand; others fall; others sit; others lie down. Therefore those who fall, sit, or lie down cannot praise the Lord. You who stand, praise him.

But someone may say: “Others also stand.” There are many churches; there are many congregations. Who, then, are standing? Are the Arians standing? The Eunomians and the other heretics name Christ; are they therefore standing? So that he might not seem to give them permission to praise the Lord, see what he says:

“You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God.” This is in accordance with what the Apostle said: “Until I come, so that you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of God, which is the Church” (1 Tim. 3). The Church does not consist in walls, but in the truth of the doctrines. The Church is there where the true faith is.

But fifteen or twenty years ago, the heretics possessed all the walls of the churches here. For twenty years ago, the heretics possessed all these churches. The true Church, however, was there where the true faith was. Therefore you bless the Lord, who are servants of the Lord. “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Eccl. 15). Therefore praise him, you who are servants of the Lord, and who are servants and stand.

Who are standing? “He established my feet upon the rock” (Ps. 39). And to Moses: “But you, stand here with me” (Exod. 34). “God stood in the assembly of the gods.” And you who stand, stand not just anywhere, but “in the house of God, in the courts of the house of our God.”

This is not found in the Hebrew volumes, but it belongs to the following psalm. How does it follow in that psalm? “Praise the name of the Lord; praise the Lord, servants. You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God” (Ps. 81). Since this psalm has “You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God,” someone therefore thought that in the preceding psalm also, after “You who stand in the house of the Lord,” one ought to add “in the courts of the house of our God.” What “in the courts of the house of our God” signifies, and what the difference is between the house and the courts, will be discussed when the following psalm is read.

“In the nights lift up your hands in the holy places.” “The world is placed in the power of the evil one” (1 John 5), and “our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers of this darkness” (Eph. 6). Hence the Apostle also says: “The night has advanced; the day has drawn near” (Rom. 13). Therefore this age is night, while the age to come is day. Hence the Apostle also says: “Let us walk honorably as in the day” (ibid.). How will we live in the day—that is, in the age to come—if we do not live now?

“In the nights lift up your hands in the holy places.” Whether we wish it or not, we are in the nights. As long as we are in this age, we are in the nights. Night has darkness. The nights of these darknesses are the sins of human beings. See, therefore, what he says: “In the nights lift up your hands in the holy places.” While you are in this age and in these nights, he says, lift up your hands. Do not lower them, but lift them up. Lift them up with Moses (Exod. 17). If you lift up your hands, Amalek is defeated; but if you lower them, Jesus is overcome.

At the same time, consider the mystery. If we lift up our hands, Jesus conquers. If we lift up our hands in good works, Christ overcomes the devil through our good works. Hands are interpreted as works. Hence it is written: “The word of the Lord came through the hand of Haggai”; “the word came through the hand of Jeremiah the prophet.” Surely God’s word does not come through a hand, but through the mouth. Yet observe the mysteries of Scripture: God’s word does not come without a good work.

Even a murderer confesses Christ, but the Lord does not come to him, because his hands do not deserve the Lord’s coming. Hence it is written elsewhere: “In the hand of the tongue are death and life” (Prov. 18). Does the tongue, then, have a hand? Tell me, why is it said: “In the hand of the tongue are death and life”? See what he says: God does not hear the tongue or the words, but the works, so that whoever says something may also do it.

Therefore we are commanded in the final psalm of the ascents: “In the nights lift up your hands in the holy places.” Lift up your hands, he says, because Jesus lifted them up on the cross. “In the nights lift up your hands in the holy places.” Why did he wish to add and say “in the holy places”? Heretics also seem to lift up their hands; pagans also seem to lift up their hands; Jews also seem to lift up their hands. For they too give alms: if they see a poor person, they extend their hand. When a Jew gives alms, does it not seem to you that he is lifting up his hand? He does lift up his hand, but he does not lift it up in the holy places, because he does not confess Christ.

But you who are in the house of the Lord, who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God, who are servants of the Lord, to whom he had said, “Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one” (Ps. 132), lift up your hands in such a way that you lift them up in the holy place—that is, so that you confess Christ and do whatever you do for Christ.

Virtues differ according to the character of the one who performs them. It is as though he were saying: A Christian gives alms; a pagan also gives alms; a Jew also gives alms; another Christian, a holy man, also gives alms. You will find some Christians who give alms so that they may be praised by the people. Whenever a poor person asks for a morsel of bread, they look around in every direction, and unless they see a witness, they do not give the money. If he is alone, they draw back their hand; they do not give willingly.

O Christian, a poor man asks you to give him money. Why do you not give it secretly, but give it publicly? If you seek God as your witness, why do you seek human eyes? Your almsgiving appears to be almsgiving to the ignorant; but before God it is an insult. For you insult your brother. You wish to display the beggar to others who are watching.

Therefore, when we give, let us not give as though it were from our own resources, but from Christ’s gift. We must not give as to a beggar, but as to a brother. We give material things; he gives spiritual things. The poor person gives more than he receives. We give bread, which is consumed that same day; he will repay us with the kingdoms of heaven.

Therefore I say this so that what we do, we may do in the holy place; or so that whatever we do, we may do for Christ’s sake. Many pagans, moreover, who give alms, if they see someone with a severed hand, or if they see someone with a foot afflicted by cancer and rotting, are immediately moved in spirit. The human soul is overcome by natural compassion. And what does it say? “If I were such a person, what would I, wretched man, do? And it could happen that I might become such a person; who would give to me? Therefore I too ought to give to this person, so that someone may give to me if I should become such.”

This man gives bread to the poor person, but in the poor person he pities himself, not the other. This is compassion, but not the compassion of Christ; it is compassion for himself. Therefore let us do everything for Christ’s sake; let us do it in the holy place. Whether we eat or drink, let us do everything in the name of Christ (1 Cor. 10).

We read the Scriptures. We memorize the psalms. We study the Gospels. We explain the prophets. We must not do this so that we may boast before our brothers, but so that we may please Christ, so that his word may resound in our mouths. Men, monks, and little women often engage in this contest among themselves: that more of them may memorize the Scriptures; and they think themselves better if they have memorized more.

He has memorized more who does more. But if I do what you memorize, my works hold the Scriptures more firmly than your speech, which rings out vainly. “In the nights lift up your hands in the holy places.” Lift up your hands toward the cross; raise the standard. “In the nights lift up your hands in the holy places.” And when you have lifted them up in the holy places and have done what is holy, let Christ be, as it were, the medicine of your good works. And bless the Lord.

Hence the Apostle also says: “Lifting up holy hands in every place” (1 Tim. 2); and bless the Lord. Whatever you do, refer it to the Lord. Let the hands be lifted up; let the mouth resound with Christ.

And in the nights lift up your hands. Give alms to the poor and bless the Lord. Give thanks to the Lord because he has given you something with which to give to your brother. You should give thanks to Christ more when you have given than the brother who has received from you should give thanks to you. The poor confer a great benefit upon us. Almsgiving extinguishes sins that we can no longer wash away by any other means.

What is written? “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sins” (Ecclus. 3). Almsgiving does what baptism also does. Just as baptism forgives our sins, so almsgiving also forgives our sins. As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sins. For the fires of Gehenna have been prepared for sins. Almsgiving extinguishes these.

“May the Lord bless you from Zion, who made heaven and earth.” You bless the Lord, and the Lord blesses you. From Zion—from the watchtower, from the Church, from true doctrines, from devout faith. “May the Lord bless you from Zion.” The Holy Spirit speaks this verse, or certainly the prophet speaks in the Spirit. And what does he say?

O you who have ascended through fifteen steps to the final one, who have done these things and those things, who bless the Lord, who lift up your hands in the nights and bless the Lord: receive your reward as well. “May the Lord bless you from Zion.” Receive what you gave. You gave alms; you performed virtues; from God you will obtain a reward and a blessing.

“May the Lord bless you from Zion.” Zion is the heavenly Jerusalem, the mother of the firstborn, where future joys are, where the archangels are, where the other powers are, where the apostles are, where the prophets are, where the holy martyrs are, where the multitudes of angels and saints follow the Lamb wherever he goes (Rev. 21).

Finally, John also saw the holy city descend from heaven, built with jewels and having twelve gates. It was entirely golden; it had golden walls, and it also had streets made of different gems. In this city Christ reigns. Those who inhabit it are themselves both inhabitants and gates; they themselves are both the houses and the inhabitants. Do you wish to know that they are houses? Christ dwells in them; Christ walks about in them. “I will dwell in them,” he says, “and I will walk among them” (Lev. 26; 2 Cor. 6).

See how great a holy soul is: it contains Christ, whom heaven cannot contain. See what he says: “I will dwell,” he says. Yet it could happen that someone dwells in a cramped space. “I will dwell and walk among them.” Wherever he walks about, the house is surely spacious.

Where does he walk? “You are,” he says, “the temple of God, and the Holy Spirit dwells in you.” Let us prepare our temple so that Christ may come and dwell in us; so that our soul may be Zion, may be a watchtower, may be established upon the heights; so that it may be above, not below.

We read in the prophet Zechariah: “And the angel,” he says, “who spoke in me said to me” (Zech. 1). If an angel spoke in the prophet, how much more does he dwell in us! He himself has us both as houses and as companions in conversation.

“May the Lord bless you from Zion, who made heaven and earth.” If you are holy, hear what he says: “who made heaven.” If you are a sinner, hear: “who made earth.” He made both heaven and earth.

For now, let us speak according to the literal sense. He says this to distinguish the idols: “The gods,” he says, “who did not make heaven and earth, let them perish from the earth. But the Lord made the heavens.” This is said to distinguish the idols. For now, this is according to the literal sense.

But according to the spiritual understanding, just as it is said to the sinner, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go,” so also it is said to the holy person, “You are heaven, and to heaven you shall go.” Why have I said all this? To prove that the holy ones are heavens. “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands” (Ps. 18). And “let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. 148). “The heavens of heavens belong to the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Ps. 113).

Although we are earthly, although we walk upon the earth, our citizenship is in heaven. There we have our civic communities. “Who made heaven and earth.” Although you are a sinner, do not despair: the Lord can do all things. Many who were earth become heaven, and many who were heaven become earth. Wretched Judas was heaven and became earth. The Apostle Paul, at the time when he was persecuting the Church (Acts 7), was earth. He confessed, and became heaven.

Nor should the one who is heaven be secure; nor should the one who is earth despair of life. At the time when Jacob was fleeing from his brother to Mesopotamia, he came to Luz, and there, he says, he placed a stone at his head (Gen. 35). Beneath his head was a stone, which was Christ. He never placed a stone at his head except at the time when he was fleeing from a persecutor. As long as he was in his father’s house and had the comforts of the flesh, he had no stone at his head. He left his house naked; he left with only a staff, and immediately that night he found a stone and placed it at his head.

He who had such a pillow on which to rest, consider his vision. He saw, he says, a ladder extending from earth to heaven, and he saw angels descending and ascending. He saw angels coming from heaven to earth, and others ascending from earth to heaven.

Do you wish to know that the stone which was at Jacob’s head was Christ, the cornerstone? “The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner” (Ps. 117). That stone which is written of in the Book of Kings, *Abenezer* (2 Sam. 7), is Christ. *Abenezer* is interpreted as “stone of help.” “Jacob rose in the morning,” he says. And what did he say? “This,” he said, “is the house of God.” And what did he do? “He took oil,” he says, “and anointed the stone.” Unless we understand the mysteries of the Scriptures, what reason was there for him to anoint a stone with oil?

“May the Lord bless you from Zion, who made heaven and earth.” Bringing the fifteen Songs of Ascents to a conclusion in blessing, he admonishes us with the prophetic voice, saying:

## PSALM CXXXIV

“Praise the name of the Lord.” The name which you have recognized through faith to be above every name.

“Praise the Lord, servants.” You who have ceased to be servants of sin.

“You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God.” You who have been planted immovably in him.

“Praise the Lord, for the Lord is gracious.” For he quickly grants forgiveness to those who repent, and also fulfills our hope through his own graciousness.

“Sing praises to his name, for it is sweet.” For no harsh perversity of heretics has proceeded from him; rather, through that very sweetness we have been rescued from the squalor of paganism.

“For the Lord chose Jacob for himself.” Namely, the one who, after supplanting the people, seized its blessing.

“Israel as his possession.” The one who, after many struggles, was worthy to see God with the mind.

“For I have known that the Lord is great.” With the Son revealing him, we know the Father, as he himself says: “No one knows the Father except the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Luke 10). “And our God is above all gods.” Above all the holy angels who are worthy to be called gods.

“Everything that the Lord wished, he did in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses.” In accordance with the will of his goodness, it pleased God to perform wonders in exalted souls, in arid minds, amid the waves of the age, and in the depth of wickedness, as follows.

“Bringing up clouds from the end of the earth.” Raising apostles and prophets from earthly lowliness.

“He made lightning for the rain.” So that first they might pour out the light of the knowledge of God, and then the rain of teachings.

“He brings forth winds from his treasuries.” Sending the holy angels from the heavenly mysteries, so that through these clouds and rains they might bring strength and growth.

“He struck the firstborn of Egypt, from man to beast.” The ruling vices and crimes of the world.

“And he sent signs and wonders in your midst, Egypt.” Terrifying the world through the Passion, through darkness, or through the shaking of the earth.

“Against Pharaoh and all his servants.” Affixing the devil, or his principalities, to his cross.

“He struck great kings and killed mighty kings.” The countless vices that had oppressed the world.

“Sihon, king of the Amorites.” The despisers of God have with them a barren tree; when struck down together, they are cast into the eternal fire.

“And Og, king of Bashan.” The wall of confusion that stood in our way so that we might not recognize God.

“And all the kingdoms of Canaan.” He killed the kingdoms of agitation that disturbed us away from God and ruled over us.

“And he gave their land as an inheritance, as an inheritance to Israel his people.” God destroyed and overturned all these things, and through his knowledge admitted us as an inheritance, granting us dominion over those who had not oppressed us.

“O Lord, your name is forever.” Since it endures perpetually, let this be our everlasting inheritance.

“O Lord, your memorial is from age to age.” So that what the shadow of the old Law prefigured may be recognized in the other age—that is, in the Gospels.

“For the Lord judged his people.” The unbelieving Jews, who have now been judged because they did not believe.

“And in his servants he will be comforted.” In believers, certainly.

Images of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands [Col. 1228B]; they have mouths but will not speak, etc. He mockingly recalls the abominable objects of the Gentiles: although they possess no movement of any bodily member, they wished to ennoble them with gold and silver metal. Therefore he added:

“Let those who make them, and all who trust in them, become like them.” Let those who believe in them be confounded by them; but let us, who worship the one in whose image we were made, be consoled.

House of Israel, bless the Lord. The assemblies of the saints, who contemplate God with the eyes of the mind. House of Aaron, bless the Lord. The perfect order of ministers.

You who fear the Lord, bless the Lord: so that, just as you fear his majesty, you may praise him with love.

[Col. 1228C] Blessed is the Lord God from Zion, who dwells in Jerusalem. He himself is our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom, with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, belong honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

PSALM CXXXV

Alleluia. This psalm discloses the Lord’s mercies bestowed upon the human race in various necessities, saying:

Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever. Confess your sins, and praise him who, through mercy, forgives those who remain in him.

Give thanks to the God of gods. To him who has given those who believe in him the power to become children of God.

Give thanks to the Lord of lords. This refers to the Son, while “God of gods” refers to the Father. Therefore we give thanks to the Father and the Son. For the Father is in the Son, and the Son in the Father.

Who alone does great wonders. First he said, “Give thanks to the God of gods,” and again, “to the Lord of lords”; and because he has spoken of two persons, he now says, “Who alone does great wonders,” so that he may not speak of two gods. For it is written: “There is one God, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus, through whom are all things, and we through him” (1 Cor. VIII).

Who made the heavens with understanding. These are the heavens that declare the glory of God, which have been clothed with the heavenly image; and they are heavens that have not been clothed with an earthly image, in understanding and wisdom. For Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. As Wisdom herself also says in Proverbs: “When he made the heavens, I was with him” (Prov. VIII), and so forth.

Who established the earth upon the waters. Although it is said that the earth hangs upon the waters, that is, by an empty weight, nevertheless he founded and established our earth in baptism. He did not say “he lifts up,” or “he exalts,” or “he made it ascend into the heavens.” For baptism forgives sins and, as if from prison, sets one free; but it cannot grant the kingdom of heaven. For unless someone enters through works and faith, he cannot be secure.

Who made the great lights. Literally, he speaks of the stars: although we see them as small, they are nevertheless great. For just as, if we climb a high mountain and see a person in the valley below, he appears to us as something tiny, so the stars are great, but from our height they appear small to us. He says this to those to whom he said: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. V).

The moon and stars for the dominion of night. He placed the Church, or its teachers, under the night of the old Law, so that they might spiritually fulfill and observe what that Law announced in the letter.

Who struck Egypt together with its firstborn, and brought Israel out from its midst, with a strong hand and an outstretched arm. Having struck the world by the power of his might, he brought us out from its works.

Who divided the Red Sea into divisions, and led Israel through its midst. For one ascends through many stages amid the waves of this age, so that one may approach him whom one beholds with the mind.

And he shook off Pharaoh and his army in the Red Sea. If we are Israel, God fights for us while we keep silent, and he casts down the devil with his followers, so that they cannot harm us.

Who led his people through the desert. The people of God are always led through the deserts of this world until they are brought into the promised land. Who brought water out of the rock, the crag. From Christ the Lord, who is the steadfast rock, either baptism proceeded or the cup of eternal life flowed.

Who struck many nations and killed mighty kings. He killed Sihon, king of the Amorites, and Og, king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan. He says that all the kingdoms of sin were struck by Christ: “Who struck great kings.” First he struck Pharaoh, who is understood as the devil, and then his army, as we explained in the preceding psalm.

And he gave their land as an inheritance, as an inheritance to Israel his people. To the Christian, of course.

For the Lord remembered us in our lowliness, for his mercy endures forever. So that he might visit us by his coming.

And he redeemed us from the hand of our enemies. Pouring out his blood as the price of our redemption.

[Col. 1230A] Who gives food to all flesh. Offering himself as living bread and as the giver of life to this world.

Give thanks to the God of heaven. Render him the praise that is due, for he changes you from earthly beings into eternal ones.

Give thanks to the Lord of lords. To him who has appointed you either judges or lords of the world. He himself is our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom, with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, belong honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

PSALM CXXXVI

A psalm of David concerning Jeremiah. This psalm, uttered by the prophetic voice, teaches that human minds are taken captive by sins, using as an example that earthly Jerusalem which, carried away by the nations into captivity, mourned. Therefore let the souls that, after many errors, turn back to the Lord say:

[Col. 1230B] By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered Zion. If someone is not ill, he does not know the value of health. Again, the lame person does not know the value of being sound in his feet, and likewise the blind person does not know the value of sight. Why has all this been said? Because the psalm says: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered Zion.” Babylon is interpreted as “confusion.” Therefore Babylon here is this world. The sinner, then, who fell from paradise came into the valley of tears, that is, into Babylon, into this world. More precisely, the prophet speaks in the person of the one who fell: “By the rivers of Babylon.” The river of Babylon is this: when you see someone beautiful for a time, and illness causes him to lose his beauty and his flower to wither, he passes like a river; its successive waters come and go and perish, and again others arise and themselves perish. So in this world, for a moment or for some period, we are rich, or strong, or beautiful, and shortly afterward it passes like water and perishes. There, then, we sat and wept, when we remembered Zion. Although we fell from paradise through our own fault, we nevertheless remember our former happiness and do not forget it. And the one who descended from Jerusalem into Jericho—which is interpreted as “moon,” that is, as something that is always changing, and which signifies the present world—fell among robbers; the Samaritan took him and healed him with oil and wine, mixing severity with mercy (Luke X).

Upon the willows in its midst we hung our instruments. [Col. 1230D] The willow has this nature: it is a fruitless tree, and it is said [Note: [Col. 1229D] The ancient writers reported this not of the willow but of another plant called the chaste tree. Nevertheless, in this interpretation the true Jerome agreed, in book II, chapter XIV, of his Commentary on Zechariah.] that if anyone takes a potion made from it or eats it, he does not produce children. Therefore there we hung our instruments. The instrument of a human being is the body. For just as an instrument is composed of many pipes yet sends forth a melody in a single modulation, so we too possess an instrument: through touch—that is, through works—we offer melody, song, and hymn to God. Likewise through hearing, smell, taste, sight, and through all these faculties, as if from one instrument, we offer hymn and song to the Lord. It is also said [Col. 1231A] that the willow has no root. But if a branch is cut off and [Note: [Col. 1231D] He seems to have borrowed this from St. Hilary, where he says: “The nature of willow wood is such that, even when dried, if it is merely washed by water it becomes vigorous again; then, when cut and fixed in moist soil, it sends itself down into roots.” Under the nature of this tree, prophetic authority signifies holy and faithful men.] planted beside water, it immediately becomes vigorous. So also the sinner, even if he has sinned and fallen, nevertheless, if he is beside the waters—that is, if he reads the holy Scriptures and hears the word of God from a holy man—his soul becomes green again and is converted to repentance.

For there those who took us captive asked us for words of songs, etc. The demons who deceived us and led us captive now, as if mocking and boasting over us, say: “Give us a word from your faith; just as, when you were in Jerusalem, you used to sing a hymn to God.” Those who sinned and were deceived answer and say:

How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land? [Col. 1231B] Established in sins, having fallen from Jerusalem into Babylon? Therefore no one can praise the Lord unless he is holy. For the sinner ought not to sing to the Lord, but to mourn his sins.

If I forget you, Jerusalem, let my right hand be forgotten. Since he sinned and fell, he remembers his former way of life and Jerusalem, and proposes to himself: “Unless I always remember you and always keep you in mind, let my right hand”—that is, my works—“be forgotten.” He did not say “my left,” but “my right.” For the left is always in forgetfulness. Do you wish, then, always to be in the Lord’s memory? Perform the works of the right hand.

Let my tongue cleave to my throat, if I do not remember you. That is, let me have neither works nor speech if your memory does not continually remain in my heart.

Remember, Lord, the sons of Edom on the day of Jerusalem. Edom is interpreted as “earthly” and “bloody.” Who, then, is he except the devil? See, therefore, what he says. This is spoken in the person of Adam: “Lord, remember how he deceived me, and how the serpent—the devil, understood as Nebuchadnezzar—dragged me away and cast me out of paradise. Remember him and repay him, and let him suffer the punishment that by his wickedness he brought upon me. Dragging me away, he brought me into Babylon and into Assyria.”

Daughter of miserable Babylon. The daughter of Babylon is the soul, which is always in motion and confusion, possessing no stability, but existing in vices and sins; she is truly miserable. Blessed is he who repays you with the repayment that you repaid us. Blessed is he who repays her for what she herself did. For example: she cast me out of paradise; through abstinence I bring her back there. She deceived me through fornication; through chastity I restore her to Jerusalem, and from vices to virtue. Therefore I do not act as an enemy, but as a friend.

Blessed is he who will seize and dash your little ones against the rock. “Little ones” means thoughts. As if he were saying: “I saw a woman and desired her. If I do not immediately cut off that desire, and, as if seizing its foot, dash it against the rock while the desire is small, it cannot afterward be cut off when it has grown.” [Col. 1232A] Blessed, therefore, is he who immediately cuts it off and dashes it against the rock. The rock is Christ.

PSALM CXXXVII

I will give thanks to you, Lord, with all my heart. As the wounds are, so must the plaster be. Just as the body has different passions and wounds, so the soul has its passions and wounds, and different wounds require us to perform corresponding repentance against sin. If someone confesses all his sins, he confesses to the Lord with his whole heart. It is as if he had said: Someone has committed fornication and confesses for fornication. But since he may also be greedy, or angry, or a slanderer, or a blasphemer, and may have many vices, he does not confess with his whole heart. But if someone repents for all the vices and passions of his soul, he can say: “I will give thanks to you, Lord, with all my heart.” For you have heard all the words of my mouth. This verse is not found in the Hebrew. Nevertheless, what he says means this: “Therefore I will give thanks to you with all my heart,” that is, for all my vices and sins, because I did not confess one single vice to you and you heard me.

In the presence of the angels I will sing to you. Observe the progress of the penitent: after confession and repentance, he is deemed worthy to sing with the angels. But whoever sings is no longer doing penance; he gives thanks and blesses. I will worship toward your holy temple. If this is the temple now seen as deserted, in which one ought to worship, then the Jews ought not to worship, since the temple has been overthrown. By the temple he means [Col. 1232C] the holy and heavenly Jerusalem.

Because of your mercy and your truth. Let the sinner hear of mercy, but let the righteous and proud hear of truth.

You will multiply strength in my soul: that is, strength in a soul subject to many anxieties.

Let all the kings of the earth give thanks to you, Lord. The kings of the earth are those who reign over sin. Therefore let those who reign over sin give thanks. For it is not written of the kings of this world: “The heart of the king is in the hand of God” (Prov. XXI). Do you suppose that the heart of the most impious Julian was in the hand of God? Certainly not; nor that of Nero, or Maximian, or Decius, the persecutors. Rather, he says this of those who reign over sin: the hearts of those who conquer vices and the passions of the soul, and reign over sin, are in the hand of God. For they have heard all the words of your mouth, because they have kept your commandments.

And let them sing in the ways of the Lord. The philosophers of this age did not sing in the ways of the Lord; but we sing in the ways of the Lord, that is, in Moses, Isaiah, and Jeremiah, and from these ways we come to that way which says: “I am the way.”

PSALM CXXXVIII

Lord, you have tested me, etc. Your knowledge has become wondrous through me. Symmachus translated this more clearly: “Your knowledge surpasses me,” that is, I cannot know your secrets, and my mind cannot enter into the depth of your wisdom.

Where shall I go from your spirit? Or where shall I flee from your face? How can I comprehend your knowledge, since everything is in you, nothing escapes you, and your spirit is everywhere? From this we understand that God is wholly present everywhere.

If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present, etc. No height is higher than you; no depth is deeper than you; east and west are contained in your hand.

And I said: Surely darkness will trample me, and night will be my light in my pleasures. In the Hebrew the sense is this: “And I said: Perhaps darkness will trample me”; but, on the contrary, “the night itself was light in your presence,” because nothing can be hidden from you. Symmachus translated it better, saying: “And night sits as light around me.” The following verses also signify the same thing.

For darkness will not be darkened by you, and night will be illuminated like day; its darkness is like its light. That is, everything that is thought hidden from you is so clear that it is more evident than light.

You received me from my mother’s womb. The Fifth Edition translated it thus: “You fashioned me from my mother’s womb.”

Your eyes saw my unfinished state. Here he used “unfinished” for “unformed,” meaning that God knows even the elements of a human being before they are formed in the womb. And in your book they will all be written. He also means that no one is born without God’s will, lest anyone escape his knowledge.

[Col. 1233C] Days will be formed, and there will be none among them. Symmachus translated this passage thus: “The days on which they were formed—not one of them is missing.” The sense is: the whole period of life, whose courses have been assigned from the beginning of this life, runs its appointed course to a fixed end; no day is either more or less than you, the Creator, willed it to be. According to the Septuagint translators, however, and according to a deeper understanding, the sense is: “You form everyone for the day; you will all to be children of God. Yet there is no one among human beings who does not become subject to sin, and thereby begin to be a child of night; nor does any of them accomplish, throughout the whole period of his life, what is worthy of the light of that day.” Therefore the Apostle also speaks to those who had ceased to be children of night: “But we, brothers, are not children of night, but children of God” (1 Thess. V).

PSALM CXXXIX

[Col. 1233D] Rescue me, Lord, from the evil man, etc. The devil cannot deceive us so much except through the instrument of a human being; the prophet asks to be freed from him.

Those who devised iniquities in their hearts. He speaks of heretics.

The venom of asps is under their lips. For they appear to have words of friendship, but they are full of deadly poison.

Beside the path they placed a stumbling block for me. That is, producing testimonies from the Scriptures which seemed, as it were, to have some rational basis, they will try to deceive me.

[Col. 1234A] I said to the Lord: You are my God. If you are not holy, you cannot say this verse. The one over whom sin does not reign says this: “The Lord is my portion” (Ps. XV).

Do not hand me over, Lord, to the sinner because of my desire. Scripture says: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V). Therefore the prophet says: “Do not hand me over to the devil because of my desire; but it is better for me to be judged for a deed and not for a thought.”

The head of their circuit; the labor of their lips will cover them. Just as, when a serpent sees someone coming to strike it, it forms a circle with its entire body and hides its head in the middle, where it knows its life to be, so these heretics, through the discourse of philosophers, Aristotle, and the others, seem to hide and, as it were, protect and defend themselves. But the ecclesiastical man, as with a rod—that is, with the cross—breaks the circle, finds the hidden head, and strikes it there, that is, produces a testimony from the Scriptures.

The upright will dwell with your face. What is the face of God except Christ, “who did not consider equality with God something to be seized” (Phil. II)?

PSALM CXL

Lord, I cried out to you; hear me. Moses stood with the people, and Pharaoh pursued behind him, while distress surrounded him on every side. At that time he wept before God. Immediately God said to him: “Why are you crying out to me?” While he prayed in silence, he was heard. Scripture does not mention that he spoke, but only that he wept. The blood of martyrs also continually cries out to the Lord and is heard. And the Lord said to Cain: “The blood of your brother cries out to me” (Gen. IV). In the Apocalypse of John, the souls of the righteous beneath the altar said to the Lord: “How long, Lord, will you not defend us?” (Rev. VI). Let us also consider that the souls of the righteous are the Lord’s altars. Attend to my voice when I cry to you. That is: See and consider, Lord, what I ask, because I am not asking from bodily desire for gold or anything of that kind, but to obtain your mercy. Therefore he says “attend,” that is, hear carefully, because I am asking for nothing alien.

Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight. That is, let my prayer come straight to you, [Col. 1234D] containing no defilements, vices, or diabolical thoughts. Incense is the prayers of the saints. We learn this from the Apocalypse, when the twenty-four elders held censers and said (Rev. VIII): “These are the prayers of the saints.” The lifting of my hands is an evening sacrifice. “The lifting of my hands” signifies the Lord. In the lifting of the hands we behold the Creator. Observe, however, that he did not say “the extension of my hands.” Extension is not elevation. Someone may extend his hands behind him or to the side, that is, toward vices, as the Lord says: “When you stretch out your hands toward me, I will not hear you” (Jer. XV). As an evening sacrifice, at the eleventh hour—that is, in the Gospel—I lift my hands. Again the Apostle says: “Lift up your hands in prayer” (1 Tim. II). And when Moses lifted his hands, Jesus prevailed; when he lowered them, he was defeated (Exod. XVII). If I understand the Scriptures according to history and the letter, Moses has his hands downward. But if I understand them spiritually, he lifts his hands on high.

Place, Lord, a guard over my mouth. Death and life are in the hands of the tongue. And again: “Amen I say to you, for every idle word that you speak, you will give an account on the day of judgment” (Matt. XII). The prophet therefore asks that everything he says be not idle, but holy and worthy of God. And place a door of enclosure around my lips. By a door of enclosure he asks for something like a wall around the whole house, so that he may not be overcome in any respect. For Jeremiah says: “Death entered through your windows” (Jer. IX). We have five windows: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. If, then, I look at a woman in order to desire her, I have already committed adultery with her in my heart (Matt. V), and death has entered through my window—that is, through sight. If a flute, an instrument, or a reed pipe seems to dissolve me, death has entered through my hearing. If I touch something soft and am undone by the softness of the body, death has entered through my touch, and so likewise in the other cases. Therefore the prophet asks for a door of enclosure, that is, that his whole house be fortified, so that the adversary may find no way to enter and rule human beings. For it is said in the Epistle of Saint Peter: “Our adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Pet. V). The devil does not immediately fight against someone through great vices, but through small ones, so that he may enter by some means, rule the person, and afterward drive him toward greater vices. He enters not through fornication or greed, but through lesser vices.

Do not incline my heart toward words of wickedness, to make excuses for sins. O most wretched human race, which excuses its sins by saying: “I was overcome by nature,” although it is in our power both to sin and, with the Lord’s help, not to sin. We always excuse ourselves and say: “I did not want to sin; the flesh overcame me. That woman came to me; she sent for me; she touched me; she said that to me; she called me.” Thus, when we ought to repent and say, “Lord, I have sinned,” we excuse ourselves and add sins to sins. We all have the same body, but different labors. God is not a respecter of persons. Do you wish to know that we and the saints have the same body? The Apostle Paul says: “I see another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin” (Rom. VII). And again afterward: “Therefore I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be found disqualified” (1 Cor. IX). And again: “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death?” (Rom. VII). We therefore have different labors, and each person will receive a reward in proportion to his labor.

And with people who practice iniquity. The implied sense is: “Do not incline my heart with people who practice iniquity.” And I will not associate with their chosen ones. Just as the Lord has his chosen holy ones, so the devil has his chosen ones. Understand this of the leaders of heretics, and you will not doubt who their chosen ones are. For if he had said simply “chosen ones,” without the qualifying “their,” he would have included God’s chosen ones. “I will associate” has two possible meanings: either “I will consent,” or “I will become second,” that is, unclean. For you know that Scripture speaks of two things as unclean. The Apostle says: “That he might make the two into one” (Eph. II), that is, two people into one new person: two—the inner and the outer—so that I may make the unclean holy. Again, Noah brought seven of the clean animals into the ark with him, but of the unclean, two and two (Gen. VII).

Let the righteous person correct me in mercy and rebuke me. “The Lord disciplines the one whom he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives” (Heb. XII). Blessed is the one who is corrected; the Lord will not repay him twice for the same thing. Great is God’s anger when he does not become angry with us (Nah. I). For he reserves us like a calf for slaughter. He says to Jerusalem: “Your sins are many, and your iniquities are numerous; therefore I am not angry with you” (Jer. III). That is: when you were merely adulterous, I was jealous for you as one who loved you; but when you had many lovers, I despised you and am not angry with you (Ezek. XVI). Just as a husband is jealous of his wife when he loves her, but if he is not jealous he hates her, and he does not fulfill the statement: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod” (Ps. LXXXVIII). And again: “I will not visit their daughters when they commit fornication” (Hos. IV). Let the righteous person correct me in mercy and rebuke me. Place here some teacher, or father, or physician. If a physician sees rotten flesh on the body and says, “What does it matter to me?” know that he is cruel. But if he cuts it away and applies a cautery, he is merciful, because he heals the person. Likewise, if a teacher lets a child go and does not demand discipline from him, he hates him. But if he demands it, and the physician treats him, what appears to be harshness is clemency. Ahab is reproved by the Lord concerning Naboth (1 Kings XXI): he killed him, took his vineyard, and shed innocent blood. The prophet Elijah was sent to him and said: “You have killed and taken possession.” Immediately struck in conscience, he lowered his neck and eyes—even though he was an impious king clothed in purple. Scripture later says that, upon hearing this, he put on sackcloth beneath the purple. And God, seeing this, said: “Because Ahab has reverenced me, I will not bring evil upon him.” See, then, how much the sackcloth accomplished, how much fasting accomplished, and how much blood a small tear washed away. Thus one ought to wear sackcloth and fast so that no one sees it. “Correct” has two meanings: either “rebuke” or “teach.” Let the oil of the sinner not make my head fat. “My people, those who pronounce you blessed, lead you astray” (Isa. III). The praise of heretics and their oil, with which they anoint people’s heads and promise them signs from heaven, makes their heads fat. Scripture reproves everything fat, as it says: “Jacob grew fat, and grew thick, and kicked; the beloved grew fat, grew thick, and became broad” (Deut. XXIII; Jer. V). But the manna of the angels is thin (Exod. XVI).

For still my prayer is among their good pleasures. He says this: “They indeed seemed wise, but I was praying for them, that they might be converted.” Their judges have been swallowed up, joined to the rock. As he says elsewhere: “Blessed is he who will seize and dash his little ones against the rock” (Ps. CXXXVI). The rock was Christ (1 Cor. XV). The little ones are the smaller, immature thoughts, before they grow. And now these heretics, although through Aristotle [Col. 1237B] and Plato they seem to despise the simplicity of the Church, nevertheless, when they come to the Scriptures, they will immediately be swallowed up by the rock—that is, by Christ—and will be converted to him. “Swallowing” is used for victory, as the Apostle says: “Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where is your death, your victory? Where, O hell, is your sting?” (1 Cor. XV). He calls the swallowing itself victory, the victory that he had in swallowing up.

They will hear my words, for they have prevailed. The Lord himself says: “Because they came to me, they were conquered, delighted in my words, turned to me, and are in my Church.” Like the thickness of the earth. Everything thick is close to the earth. The soul that sins clings to the earth. For from the beginning the Lord made everything thin. Each person therefore grows thick through his own fault and is brought down to the earth. Let us give an example: a wound on the body, swollen and full of thick matter, is treated by the physician, who cuts it and heals it, making it thin; then it is restored to its own nature, in the form in which it was created. Therefore he says: “As the thickness of the earth has been poured out upon the earth, so it is saved.”

Our bones have been scattered beside hell. In the twenty-first psalm he says: “All my bones have been scattered.” If we understand this according to the letter, it does not hold, since only he was crucified. When you see Arius and Eunomius outside the Church, understand that the Lord’s bones have been scattered beside hell. The bone, being hard, signifies those greater men who seem to be something; through their excessive speech, philosophy, and contentiousness, they are introduced by heretics.

Guard me from the snare that they have set for me. Heretics or demons are always setting snares for us. Vices are close to virtues. They set a snare for me in almsgiving if I stretch out my hand so that people may see me; as if doing something good, I fall into vice and sin. If I give a tunic to a brother so that another may see, they have set a snare for me. Nets and snares are always set for deer where the hunter detects their tracks. The deer is understood in a holy sense, because it is lofty, has large horns, and kills serpents. Therefore he says elsewhere: “He made my feet like those of deer” (Ps. XVII). It is said to possess such virtue that, by the breath of its nostrils, it can draw serpents from their caves and then eat them. These serpents therefore place stumbling blocks in our paths—that is, demons set them in the very tracks along which we walk: in virtues, in almsgiving, so that we may do it before people for the sake of empty glory; in fasting, prayer, and wearing sackcloth, so that we may display them to people. Whoever wears sackcloth ought to mourn his sins, not boast and display himself to people. And from the stumbling blocks of those who practice iniquity. That is, so that I may not offend.

Sinners will fall into his net. Above he said, “Guard me from the snare that they have set for me,” speaking of many; now he speaks of one: “Sinners will fall into his net.” Just as the Lord casts a net, gathers a multitude of fish, and has the apostles as fishermen who collect them and bring them to him—those who believe through them—so the devil has demons subject to him, who deceive people and bring them to him. I am alone until I pass over. Jeremiah says: “I sat alone, for I was filled with bitterness” (Jer. XV). That is: in repentance, I alone guard against these deceits. Moses also says: “I will pass over and see this great vision” (Exod. III). Unless he passes over—that is, all vices—he cannot see the great vision. The great vision is that the bush was burning and was not consumed: the thorns were burning, that is, sins. Isaiah too is cleansed by this fire; this is the coal that touched his lips, which was from the altar (Isa. VI). The prophet David also recalls this coal: “The sharp arrows of the mighty one, with desolating coals” (Ps. CXIII). This coal is desolating: it creates solitude and purifies the sinner.

PSALM CXLI

A contemplation of David when he was in the cave: a prayer. According to the historical sense, this title is prescribed for the time when David was fleeing from Saul, hidden in a cave in the desert of Engaddi (1 Sam. XXIV). Saul entered without knowing that David was there, as though for his own purpose. But because the title says “A contemplation of David,” we ought to understand the psalm spiritually. The true David is understood in the Lord, and Saul is understood as the devil. The cave is this world, and the devil does not send anything good into this world, but filth and whatever is rotten. This world is understood as a cave because it does not possess perfect light in comparison with the future; nevertheless, as though some light had shone, the Lord came into this world. Therefore the Apostle says: “He is the brightness of his glory” (Heb. I). Thus, just as David entered the cave, hiding himself from Saul, so the Lord entered this world and suffered persecution.

With my voice I cried out to the Lord; with my voice I entreated the Lord. I pour out my prayer before him. He speaks all these things in bodily humility, to show that he is truly human, as we have often said. I declare my affliction before him, when my spirit fails within me. Neither present tribulation nor the failing of the spirit prevents him; rather, he does not cease continually to cry out in prayer with a spiritual voice. And you know my paths: the teachings that I teach.

On this way in which I walked, the proud hid snares for me. We have explained elsewhere, in other psalms, the snares of temptation that the Jews repeatedly hid for him along the path of the present life.

I looked to the right. So that they might be brought from the left to the right. And I saw that there was no one who knew me: God concealed by flesh.

My escape has failed. His escape failed when, after being handed over by the Jews, he repeatedly offered himself voluntarily again and was not recognized by them. And there is no one who seeks my soul. They take the body to crucify it, but they do not seek the soul; that is, they do not touch it.

I cried out to you, Lord—from the cross. I said: You are my hope. “Into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke XXIII). My portion is in the land of the living, among the saints who are transferred into it, just as he also said to the thief: “Amen I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.”

[Col. 1239B] Give heed to my prayer, for I have been humbled exceedingly. Deliver me from those who persecute me, for they have grown stronger than I, and so forth. He asks the Father to lead him out from the prison of hell, so that his resurrection may be an honor to the Father’s name. He shows by whom that confession must be made, saying: The righteous wait for me. The apostles, or the other saints, whose expectation I satisfy when I have risen. Until you reward me. With that glory which I had with you before the world existed (John XVII). And we too humbly beseech and ask that, having received the voice of our cry, you may command us, brought out from the prison of hell, to be transferred from death to that place where you prepared a bright dwelling and rest for the thief hanging beside you: for honor and glory are yours with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM 142

[Col. 1239C]

A psalm of David, when his son Absalom was persecuting him. This psalm contains the voice of the one who emptied himself for the redemption of humankind, taking the form of a servant in order to rescue us from slavery (Philippians II).

Lord, hear my prayer. Humble words, full of humility and mercy. Hear with your ears my supplication in your truth. These are the words of one who trusts. In your truth—that is, in your Christ. “I am the way, the life, and the truth” (John XIV). And hear me in your righteousness. And in your Christ. That is, I do not trust in myself, but I seek your truth and righteousness, so that they themselves may have mercy on me.

And do not enter into judgment with your servant. Behold, he has shown most clearly that he awaits God’s mercy, saying: And do not enter into judgment with your servant. Here it is as though someone were judging between God and the prophet, just as it is also written in the fiftieth psalm: “So that you may be justified in your words, and prevail when you are judged.” And for this reason God enters into judgment, so that he may punish justly. Cyrus, king of the Persians and Medes, did something similar to the king of the Armenians when he violated his friendship. He defeated him and took him captive; and he made the man’s own relatives, wife, and children judge between them, so that he might either show mercy or punish justly. For no living person will be justified in your sight. God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob: God of the living, and not of the dead (Luke XX). Therefore even the patriarchs will not be justified in God’s sight. For the stars are not pure in his sight (Job XXV).

For the enemy has pursued my soul. This requires no interpretation. There is no doubt that the enemy is the devil. He humbled my life to the ground. This is what he says: “Previously I had wings, and I flew; but now the enemy pursued my soul, seized me, and bound my feet and hands, just as a bird is captured by a human being, so that it seems almost to be dead, because it has no freedom to fly with its wings. So also,” he says, “the enemy has bound me by the consciousness of my sins.”

He placed me in dark places, like the dead of the age. If he says “like the dead of the age,” then he is not yet dead, because he remains in repentance. But if a sinner does not practice repentance, he is dead to the age—not merely like the dead, but completely dead. The enemy therefore thought that I was not doing penance for the sins which he himself had suggested that I commit. And my spirit was anguished within me. “First declare your sins, and you will be saved” (Isaiah XLIII). And again: “If you merely sigh over your sins, you will be saved” (Ezekiel XVIII). My heart was troubled within me. Because of my conscience, since I sinned.

I remembered the days of old. I remembered my former days, when I had confidence; but now it is night for me.

I stretched out my hands toward you. Bound by the enemy, I can do nothing else except practice repentance and raise my hands toward you. My soul is like thirsty land to you. Just as land without water thirsts and seeks rain, so my soul desires and thirsts for you, its God.

Hear me quickly, Lord; my spirit has failed. My soul has failed, and my flesh has failed; only my spirit remained in me, and it too failed. But hear me quickly, Lord, and have mercy on me.

Make known to me the way in which I should walk. Make your Christ known to me, who said: “I am the way” (John XIV).

Your good Spirit will lead me into a straight land. Here the most impious Arians put forward their argument and say: “Good Teacher, what good must I do in order to be saved?” He says: “Why do you call me good? No one is good except one—God” (Luke XVIII). Therefore, if the Son is not good, but the Father is, the Father is greater than the Son. So, according to your reasoning, most impious Arian, which is greater: the Son or the Holy Spirit? You certainly say, “The Son.” Here, then, he says: “Your good Spirit will lead me into a straight land.” Therefore, if the Spirit is good, although he is the lesser one, as you say, then much more is the Son good, whom you call greater.

In the Gospel, however, it reads as follows: “One of the scribes came up, testing him, and said, ‘Good Teacher,’ and he said, ‘Why do you call me good, yet do not confess [me as such]?’” (Matthew XIX). It is as if someone, testing his bishop whom he despises, were to say to him, “Bishop,” and the bishop replied, “I am not your bishop; go away from me.” But elsewhere, have you not read: “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (John X)? And what is better than the Son, who put on flesh for our sake, suffered, and, descending from his majesty, remained for nine months in the Virgin’s womb in blood; who was in a cradle, suffered the gradual process of growth, was scourged, struck with blows, and crucified? What is better than this?

## PSALM 143

For the sake of those who do not know the Latin language, although we have said much from the Gospel, we must also say something from the Psalter, so that, while some are satisfied, others may not return hungry. Since the psalm is long, and if we linger over every little verse the day will pass, we ought to repeat briefly for each passage the sense rather than the words.

Blessed is the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle and my fingers for war. The one who interprets briefly achieves this: he himself receives no praise, yet those who have heard retain whatever belongs to the interpretation. Blessed is the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle and my fingers for war. Let us raise our hands in holiness, without thoughts of contention and dispute; let us raise them in every place. When we have raised our hands, our prayers are weapons against the devil. Who teaches my hands for battle and my fingers for war. This is our lyre; this is our harp. With it we sing to the Lord.

My mercy, my refuge, my supporter and my deliverer. My protector, and in him I have hoped. God is called by so many names. As many benefits, so many names. Who subjects my people beneath me. This can be said from the person of Christ—that is, from the human being he assumed. It can also be said from the person of the apostles, because it says: Who subjects my people beneath me. The holy father in the monastery also says this, and, giving thanks to God, says: “Blessed is the Lord my God, who subjects my people beneath me.” For the people are not subjected to me, but to you. Therefore they serve me so that they may serve you.

Lord, what is a human being, that you have made yourself known to him, or a son of man, that you regard him? This same thing is also said in the eighth psalm: “What is man, that you remember him, or the son of man, that you visit him?” Lord, what is a human being, that you have made yourself known to him? Is he speaking of the frailty of the body and the human condition? And what does he say? If you look at the flesh, what is a human being? If you look at the Spirit, a human being is something great. Let us not despise the flesh, but let us despise the works of the flesh. Let us not despise the flesh, which reigns with Christ in heaven. “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians XV). Not flesh and blood, but the works of the flesh. “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God”—and how then do they reign in Christ, and how do we sit with Christ in the heavenly places?

Lord, what is a human being, that you have made yourself known to him, or a son of man, that you regard him? He gives thanks to God, and what he says is this: As far as the human condition is concerned, a human being is nothing. “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity,” says Ecclesiastes. If all is vanity, then heaven also, and therefore the angels. If heaven and the angels are vanity, how great a vanity is a human being! And if the angel is vanity, if heaven is vanity, why then did God make vanity? Vanity in comparison with God; otherwise, in itself it is not vanity (Ecclesiastes I).

Lord, what is a human being, that you have made yourself known to him? Great is the happiness of a human being who knows his creator. In this we differ from beasts: we understand our Creator, whereas they do not. Yet even the posture of the body seeks its maker. Other animals look toward the earth; where the belly is, there also are the eyes. Our eyes, however, are raised toward heaven; and even if the mind has been blinded, nevertheless with unvanquished eyes we behold heaven.

A human being has become like vanity; his days pass like a shadow. Truly, our days are like a shadow. I was a little child; I was a boy; I was an adolescent; I was a young man; I was a man—that is, I reached mature age, and then middle age. Before I know it, I am old. Death creeps up upon old age. I change daily, and I do not fail to perceive that I am nothing. We do not remain in our condition even for a single moment of an hour; we are always either growing or diminishing. Therefore a human being changes moment by moment, and, while he is unaware, perishes.

I, an old man, remember what I was as a little child, what I did, how I played, how I ran here and there. Now I see myself weighed down by excessive burden. His days pass like a shadow. Our life seems to be a shadow and has no substance. Whatever has no substance quickly perishes. Since, then, a human being is so wretched and so weak, what do we ask from this? What do we seek? What does the prophet say here? What does he pray for?

[Col. 1242C] Lord, incline your heavens and descend. You will not be able to save this lowliness of the human being unless you yourself put it on. Lord, incline your heavens and descend. Your wandering sheep cannot be healed unless it is carried back upon your shoulders (Luke XV). Touch the mountains, and they will smoke. “Amen, amen, I say to you: if you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will be able to say to this mountain, ‘Move from here,’ and it will be moved” (Matthew XVII). There he was speaking about the lunatic—that is, about the mountain which they could not move.

It is written in Jeremiah: “Give glory to the Lord our God, before your feet stumble against the dark mountains” (Jeremiah XIII). Why have we said all this? Because what follows now is: Touch the mountains, and they will smoke. Mountains that rule; mountains raised up through pride; mountains that say: “My rivers are mine, and I made them.” Touch the mountains, and they will smoke. He did not say, “They will be set on fire,” but “They will smoke.” Let the mountains have the sign of punishment, not of brightness or splendor.

You will flash forth lightning, and disperse them. Observe what he says. He did not say, “You will destroy them,” but “You will disperse them.” We read in Genesis that, at the time when they were building the tower, God said: “Come, let us go down and confuse their languages, so that they may never again have agreement among themselves, but may be scattered” (Genesis XI). This benefits them.

Send out your hand from on high. “Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isaiah LIII). Send out your hand from on high. Lord, incline your heavens and descend. This is said to the Son: Incline your heavens and descend.

And how did he say, Send out your hand from on high? If he descended, how does he send his hand from on high? Yet although he is on earth, he sends his hand from heaven; for he does not depart from heaven.

Rescue me and deliver me from many waters. Since you descended, since you inclined the heavens, sent your hand from on high, and deigned to assume human flesh, many believed in you. Instead of one water, many waters began to exist. You see various heresies scattered throughout the whole world. Rescue me and deliver me from many waters, and grant me a living spring. For there is one God, one faith, one baptism (Ephesians IV). Deliver me from many waters. Those many waters do not produce your children, but the children of strangers. Hence what follows: Deliver me from many waters, and from the hand of the children of strangers. Those who are born in the many waters are not your children; they are children of strangers.

Whose mouth has spoken vanity. They promise themselves knowledge and raise their mouth against their Creator. They have set their mouth in heaven. Whose mouth has spoken vanity. Their knowledge is knowledge of vanity. And their right hand is a right hand of iniquity. Both are condemned—the mouth and the hands, knowledge and works. Whose mouth has spoken vanity—that is, knowledge. And their right hand is a right hand of iniquity. The right hand refers to conduct. They say that they have a right hand, but they are entirely left-handed. It is a right hand of iniquity, not of righteousness. Therefore it is said to such a left hand: “May the devil stand at his right hand.” Whoever has such a right hand—a right hand of iniquity—has the devil standing at his right hand (Psalm CVIII).

God, I will sing a new song to you. A new human being, a new song. God, I will sing a new song to you. “Sing to the Lord a new song” (Psalm XCV). How beautifully he did not say, “I sing,” but “I will sing.” He promised it for the future; in the present he knows that there is a struggle, not a song. An army never sings except when it has won. Therefore, since I am fighting in the present, I have no leisure to sing. When I have conquered, then I will sing: On a ten-stringed psaltery I will sing to you. Then I shall stretch out both hands and sing to you with living strings. My prayer is your psaltery.

Who gives salvation to kings, and so forth. Which kings? “The heart of a king is in the hand of God” (Proverbs XXI): those who reign over their own body, subject their body, and bring it into servitude, lest, after preaching to others, they themselves be found rejected (1 Corinthians IX). These are the kings of whom Wisdom says in Proverbs: “He gives kingship to kings” (Proverbs VIII).

Rescue me and deliver me from the hand of the children of strangers. The verses mentioned above are repeated: Whose mouth has spoken vanity, and their right hand is a right hand of iniquity. Whose children are like newly planted shoots in their youth. From the hand of the children of strangers. Let us see what the children of heretics are like. Whose children are like newly planted shoots in their youth. From the hand of the children of strangers. Pay close attention to what is said about heretics.

Their daughters are adorned, ornamented like the likeness of a temple, and so forth. They called the people blessed for whom such things exist. They said this. What do I say? Blessed is the people whose Lord is its God.

We shall briefly explain each point in your prayers. Whose children are like newly planted shoots in their youth. Their planting is not old but new. It is not from the ancient law; it is not from the prophets; it is not from the apostles; it is from new teachers. Their daughters are like newly planted shoots in their youth. In their youth: they are always young. Although many heresies are old, they change daily, and new ones are discovered daily. The heresies themselves are new, even if they are old; nevertheless, because they renew their teachings every day, they are new. For they are not content with the error of ancient teachers, but continually discover new things for themselves: whose children are like newly planted shoots in their youth.

What is said of the Church, of those who fear the Lord? “Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways.” What is said of them? “Your children are like newly planted olive trees around your table.” Those children are around Christ’s table; they are not far from Christ’s table. There they are not called daughters, but only sons.

Heretics, on the other hand, have daughters as well; they have the weaker sex, pleasures, and luxuries. Their daughters are adorned. Their speech is polished, but their meaning is sordid. In the Holy Scriptures, thoughts are always called “sons”; words, “daughters.” See, therefore, what he says: Their thoughts—that is, their new children—are new. But their words, that is, the words of the heretics, which they derive from secular wisdom, are polished; they have elaborate and admired speech.

Their daughters are adorned. They appear to be adorned, but because they are daughters and not sons, they have no strength. Ornamented like the likeness of a temple. He beautifully said, “the likeness of a temple.” They do not possess the true Church, but only the likeness of the Church.

Their storerooms are full, belching forth from one thing into another. They are prepared for argument. If you hold them to one testimony, they move on to another. If you hold them to the Scriptures, they flee to Aristotle. If you hold them to Aristotle, they move on to Plato. Their storerooms are full, belching forth from one thing into another.

A storeroom is properly so called because it contains arranged riches. Heretics have storerooms. They have prepared words with which to argue. Church people, on the other hand, are simple; they have nothing prepared. They open their mouth, and it is filled by the Lord, according to what is said: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Psalm LXXX). And: “Do not consider what you should answer them; for your Father will give you in that hour what you should say” (Matthew X).

You see that we do not have prepared storerooms; rather, our riches are placed beneath us. Someone may say: “Give testimony that the saints do not have storerooms.” “Look,” he says, “at the birds of heaven, for they have neither storerooms nor barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them” (Matthew VI). These birds are specifically monks. They have no storerooms, no shops; but they have the Lord of shops and storerooms, Christ himself. They have no barns, but they have the Lord of barns. They do not have the riches of the devil, but the poverty of Christ.

What does the devil say? “All these things are mine; if you fall down and worship me, I will give them to you” (Matthew III). What does Christ say to his own? “Whoever does not sell all that he has and give it to the poor cannot be my disciple” (Matthew XIII and Luke XII). The one promises kingdoms and riches in order to kill; the other promises poverty in order to save.

We do nothing great if we abandon what is ours. Christ abandoned the Father—and the kingdoms of heaven—for our sake. Let no one think that I am blaspheming because I said, “He abandoned the Father.” I am speaking according to the dispensation, according to the fact that he is sent, as it is said: “The Father who sent me is greater than I” (John X and XIV). God is not sent; God is not subjected to slavery; it is the dispensation that is sent. If God is everywhere and all things are in God, how is God sent to something, since God is all things? Christ, therefore, became poor for our sake (2 Corinthians VIII).

Why have we said all this? Because it has now been read: Their storerooms are full, belching forth from one thing into another. He beautifully said “belching forth,” because of excessive fullness. They belch from fullness and perish; we do so from fasting, that we may be saved.

Their sheep are prolific. They have many children. For the number of heretics is great. Their sheep are prolific. Hence it is also said in the prophet Hosea: “Lord, give them”—what will you give them?—“a barren womb and dry breasts.” Of whom is this said? Of the teachers of heretics, who applaud themselves over the number of their disciples.

Their sheep are prolific, abundant in their departures. He did not say “in their entrances,” but “in their departures.” For they do not enter the Church; they depart from the Church—that is, “They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us.” Abundant in their departures. Every day they depart from the Church; abundant in their departures.

What is said of the Church? “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Psalm XLIV). Their oxen are fat. Pharaoh also saw fat oxen in a dream (Genesis XLI): the Israelite people are lean, the Egyptians fat. For you see that the teachers of heretics do nothing but devote themselves to riches. They devote themselves to riches and despise poor Christ. Their oxen are fat. He says beautifully, “fat oxen”: those “whose god is the belly, and whose glory is in their shame” (Philippians III).

There is no breach in the wall, nor a passage. Does it not seem obscure to you what is said: There is no breach in the wall, nor a passage, nor a cry in their streets? You will find it difficult to find heretics who are uneducated. For all their teachers are equipped with secular learning.

There is no breach in the wall, nor a passage.
