Whenever they are engaged in disputes, when they begin to argue with you, their words are so brief and so enclosed by artful speech that it is difficult to escape from them. When they have bound you with their syllogisms, shut you in, and, as it were, woven and built a syllogistic wall around you, you cannot turn aside; you cannot pass through; you are held enclosed.

There is no breach in the wall, nor a passage. And when they have held you there, enclosed in a kind of circle, you will not then be on the narrow way that leads to life, but on the broad way that leads to death (Matthew VII).

Nor is there a cry in their streets. The cry of Jesus calls one back to himself and says: “Let the one who thirsts come and drink” (John VII). The cry of Jesus is on the narrow way; it is not in the streets of the heretics.

They called the people blessed for whom such things exist. Many who do not know better consider such people blessed. For us, however, there is Christian simplicity. We do not want Platonic eloquence, but apostolic simplicity. This fisherman holds a net, has muddy feet, and calloused hands from his work.

Blessed is the people whose Lord is its God. Blessed is the people that possesses Christ in place of all riches. They have sons and daughters, storerooms, prolific sheep, and fat, sleek, beautiful oxen. We, on the other hand, do not have great numbers, but we know what was said in the Gospel: “Wherever two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in their midst” (Matthew XVIII).

Do not be afraid, little flock, because it has pleased God to dwell in you. Let the monks not say: “Behold, there are such great multitudes; the cities are full, the whole world is full. Therefore no one is saved except those who are in monasteries.” Behold, there are such great multitudes: are we therefore alone saved?

When you have considered these things, listen: Do not be afraid, little flock. It was said in the Gospel that one soul is saved, while two thousand swine perish (Mark V). Why do I say all this? Because the soul of one saint is more precious than infinite multitudes of sinners.

From the whole world he chose twelve apostles; from the twelve, one departed, and eleven remained. The cross came; ten fled; one Peter remained—one with one. And that one himself fled; would that he had fled and not denied! Therefore let us say that the whole human race perished. Since it had perished, the Lord was crucified and said: “I alone have trodden the winepress, and of the nations there was no man with me” (Isaiah LXIII). At that time the psalm was fulfilled: “Save me, Lord, for the holy one has failed” (Psalm XI). “There is no one who does good, not even one.”

The man who had promised, saying, “If I must die or go to prison, I will not deny you,” denied him (Mark XIV). Why do I say all this? Because a monk ought not to look toward the multitude of sinners, but toward the conduct and small number of the saints.

All Judea was being led into captivity. Nebuchadnezzar had come, and so many thousands of people were being led captive into Babylon. Jeremiah alone was confessing God, and he himself was being thrown into a pit of mud; nevertheless, the soul of that one man was more precious than the whole people (Jeremiah XV).

Do you wish to know what one man can do? Jesus son of Nave, when the whole earth was inhabited, was alone. Certainly there were infinite multitudes, and he was alone. Alone he commands the sun and the moon, and they stand still; a human being commands, and heaven obeys (Joshua X). Heaven obeys him because he himself obeyed the Lord.

Jeremiah was in captivity, and there were also many multitudes. And what does he say? “I sat alone, because I was filled with bitterness” (Jeremiah XV). How were you alone in the city? But he was alone for this reason: he had the companion of his purpose.

## PSALM 144

Praise of David himself. This psalm contains, in the prophetic voice, the praise of God, as he himself addresses him, saying:

I will exalt you, my God and king, and I will bless your name forever and ever. He exalts God because he knows him to be equal to the Father; he calls him king because he knows him to be the judge of the world.

Every day I will bless you, and I will praise your name forever and ever. He praises him especially for this reason: because he hopes to be made conformed to his name—that is, to Christ the Lord—in the age to come.

The Lord is great and exceedingly worthy of praise, and there is no end to his greatness. For he is great without end and worthy of praise without end.

Generation. The generation brought forth by faith. And progeny. The progeny brought about by Christ’s passion. They will praise your works and proclaim your power, whether the works were made by you or protected by you.

They will speak of the magnificence of your majesty and your holiness. You wish us to be holy, saying: “Be holy, for I am holy” (Leviticus XIX, XX). We also speak this to others. And they will recount your wonders, which you perform daily in the Church.

They will speak of the power of your awesome deeds, and they will proclaim your greatness. His power is awesome when he avenges himself upon the impious, as upon Pharaoh. His greatness is shown when the righteous are raised up, as Israel was.

They will pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness, because you deign to cherish them. And they will rejoice in your righteousness, because you avenge yourself upon the impious.

[Col. 1247C] The Lord is merciful and compassionate, patient and greatly merciful. And holy in all his works, because whatever has been made in him is life.

The Lord is sweet to all, and his mercies are over all his works. For by his mercy he makes and protects every work.

Let all your works confess to you, Lord, and let your saints bless you, so that through the saints who continually bless you, you may be understood to be the creator and maker of all.

They will speak of the glory of your kingdom, so that it may be desired by all. And they will proclaim your power, so that it may be feared by all.

So that they may make your power known to the children of men, and the glory of the magnificence of your kingdom, so that no excuse based on ignorance may be offered.

Your kingdom, Lord, is the kingdom of all ages. For all ages turn under the dominion of your kingdom. And your dominion extends through every generation and progeny, as the ecclesiastical generation is expanded through the progeny of the age to come.

The Lord is faithful in all his words, since he has fulfilled everything he spoke through the prophets. And holy in all his works, so that just as he is holy, we too, who are his works, may be made holy in him.

The Lord raises up all who fall, lest they be plunged into eternal ruin. And he lifts up all who have been cast down, those whom the goad of bodily pleasure has thrown down, if they practice repentance.

[Col. 1248A] The eyes of all hope in you, Lord, and you give them food at the proper time. The inward gaze of the saints is directed toward that future time when recompense is received.

You open your hand and fill every living creature with blessing. This refers to the one who endured curses and reproaches from the world for your name.

The Lord is righteous in all his ways and holy in all his works, as has already been said above.

The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth. What does he himself say? “I am God who is near, and not God who is far away” (Jeremiah XXIII).

He will do the will of those who fear him, hear their prayers, and save them, as he rescues them either from the devil’s instigation or from the heat of sin.

[Col. 1248B] The Lord guards those who love him, and he will destroy all sinners. He loves those who have preferred his love to worldly loves. But he destroys those who have placed the love of the age before love for him.

My mouth will speak the praise of the Lord, now and in the future time of recompense. And let all flesh bless his holy name forever and ever. When he says “all flesh,” this is not to be referred to insensible things, but to the whole body of the Church, which we are—the people who ought to praise, bless, exalt, and proclaim God, through whom we live, through whom we are nourished, and through whom we exist. To him, with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, belong honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM 145

Alleluia. Of Haggai and Zechariah. This psalm, inscribed with the names of the two prophets, speaks in the voice of one of them, saying:

Praise the Lord, my soul. This psalm bears the title “Of Haggai and Zechariah.” But we must first know that this title is not found in the Hebrew, but in the Septuagint translators. Let us also speak of the Vulgate edition, “Of Haggai and Zechariah.” Since the restoration of Jerusalem is mentioned here—“The Lord your God will reign forever, O Zion, throughout generation and generation”—they think that it is speaking of the restoration of Jerusalem which took place under Haggai and Zechariah.

Praise the Lord, my soul. He did not say, “Praise, body,” but “Praise, soul”—not because he condemned the body, but because he condemned the works of the flesh.

Praise the Lord, my soul. The soul itself exhorts itself. Just as if David were to say, “Praise the Lord, David,” so the soul itself says to itself: Praise the Lord, my soul. I will praise the Lord in my life. Observe what he says: It exhorts itself, and it itself responds. What does it say? It says to me: Praise the Lord, my soul. I myself reply: I will praise the Lord in my life.

At present I cannot praise; I am weighed down by sins. Whenever I open my lips in praise of God, the conscience of my sins glues them shut. I will praise the Lord in my life. He beautifully said, “I will praise,” not “I praise.” When I am with my Lord, then I will praise the Lord in my life. Now I am in death; I cannot praise. I will praise the Lord in my life. Our life is Christ. Let us praise the Lord in life.

I will sing to my God as long as I exist. Observe what he says: When we do something just, we exist; but when we sin, we cease to exist. Much could be said, but the prayer is hastening toward its end.

Do not put your trust in princes, nor in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation. He says this generally to everyone: Do not put your trust in princes. Not in the emperor, not in prefects, not in the judges of the world.

Do not put your trust in princes. Who are the princes? The sons of men. Who are the sons of men? Those in whom there is no salvation.

His spirit will go forth, and he will return to his own earth. But when he has returned to his own earth, what will happen? On that day all their thoughts will perish. All the confidence of princes will perish, and all their thoughts will perish.

Do not put your trust in princes. Today he existed; tomorrow he does not. Today an army precedes him, and by evening he lies in a tomb. After such greatness and such splendor, no interval intervenes; the operation of Christ occurs in the same moment.

In the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation. Who are the princes? The sons of men. If the men themselves are nothing, what are their sons?

His spirit will go forth. Whose spirit? The human being’s. His spirit will go forth. Here he uses “spirit” for “soul.” “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke XXIII).

His spirit will go forth, and he will return to his own earth. It is not the spirit that will return to its own earth—for the spirit is not from the earth—but the spirit goes forth, and the human being will return to his own earth.

On that day all their thoughts will perish. We ourselves, who are not [variant: “now are not”] princes, think and say so many things every day: “Tomorrow I will do this; I will tear down my barns, and tomorrow I will build them again.” It is said to me: “Fool, this night your soul will be taken from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke XII). He says this about those who trust in princes.

But what is said of the saint?

Blessed is the one whose helper is the God of Jacob. “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we will call upon the name of the Lord” (Psalm XIX). They have many helpers, but they are princes, they are human beings, and they fall. We have one who is able to save.

His hope is in the Lord his God. Let us see what the three boys say in the Babylonian furnace, when King Nebuchadnezzar calls them: “We have no need to answer you concerning this matter. Our God is indeed able to deliver us from the burning furnace. But even if he does not deliver us, know, O king, that we will not worship the image which you have set up” (Daniel III).

Observe their faith. “We believe,” they say, “that he is able to deliver us. But if our sins should perhaps prevent it, nevertheless we believe in him who does not wish to deliver us. For we do not believe in this life, but in the future one. We do not believe in him for the sake of avoiding burning here, but so that through these fires we may not pass into others. Burn, then; prepare the furnace. This heat, this burning, is our purification.”

Blessed is the one whose helper is the God of Jacob. Observe the force of the words: His helper—and he could do no mighty work there because of their unbelief (Matthew XIII). God is our helper. He delivers those who are willing and laboring, and he labors together with them; he does not deliver those who sleep, remain silent, and are unwilling.

His hope is in the Lord his God. He spoke excellently when he said “hope.” Even if he does not deliver in the present, hope nevertheless belongs to the future.

He who made heaven and earth. This is the God who made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them. In comparison with heaven, earth, and the sea, we human beings, according to the condition of the flesh, are like ants and fleas. Therefore, if he made heaven and earth, can he not deliver the human being whom he made?

[Col. 1250B] He who guards truth forever. If falsehood oppresses us, let us not be distressed. The Lord guards truth forever. I do not know who has lied against us, and the liar is believed more than we who speak the truth. We must not despair. The Lord guards truth forever. He beautifully said, “guards.” He guards it and keeps it in his treasury; he will return to us what he has preserved. He who guards truth forever. Christ is the truth. Let us speak the truth, and the truth preserves the truth for us.

“He executes judgment for those who suffer injustice.” Even if he delays, do not despair. He will come; coming, he will come, and he will save. “He executes judgment for those who suffer injustice.” Let this alone be in our conscience: that we suffer justly. Let us hold this in our conscience: that we suffer on account of our sins [Col. 1250C] and do not do what we are accused of doing.

“He gives food to the hungry.” Even according to the literal sense this edifies; and if it is understood simply, it edifies the hearer. Consider the birds of the sky: “for they neither sow nor reap, and your heavenly Father feeds them.” He gives food to the hungry. He gives to the hungry, not to those belching with fullness. Therefore, if a monk has nothing, let him receive confidently. Whoever has something and is belching with fullness should not receive. You know that you are hungry; you know that you have nothing. If you are hungry and have nothing, you confer a greater benefit by accepting what is given to you. But if you have something and are not hungry, you ought not to take away the food of the hungry and accept it while full. Take what you can put into your stomach, not what you can put into a bag; accept a tunic to cover your body, not one to fill your chests.

“He gives food to the hungry.” [Col. 1250D] This is according to the literal sense. Let us speak in another way: let us hunger for Christ, and he himself gives us heavenly bread. “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matthew 6). Those who say this are hungry. Those who desire bread are hungry. Whoever says, “Give us this day our daily bread,” is certainly speaking as one who is hungry.

“He gives food to the hungry.” Someone may think that he is speaking of heavenly bread from the mysteries. And [Note: [Col. 1249D] This is a notable passage for establishing the truth of Christ’s body in the mystery of the Eucharist, from a very ancient ecclesiastical author. Although the editions of Erasmus and Marianus plainly demonstrate it, where we read, “because it is the true flesh of Christ,” nevertheless let us say, [Col. 1250D] etc., the reading of the manuscript Codex Corbeiensis no. 134 is fuller and more explicit. This manuscript contains an exposition of fifty-eight psalms, most of which that spurious Jerome, a compiler of the ancients, transcribed into his own commentaries, [Col. 1251D] as I shall soon say in the warning immediately following the present Explanation, or Breviary attributed to St. Jerome. Thus, in the aforesaid Codex Corbeiensis we read: “And this indeed we receive, BECAUSE IT IS TRULY THE FLESH OF CHRIST AND TRULY THE BLOOD OF CHRIST. But let us speak in another way,” etc. These words most decisively demonstrate that Christians of the fourth century were thoroughly convinced that the true body and true blood of Christ were contained in the mystery of the Eucharist, given to us as food and drink and received under the symbols of bread and wine. MART.---The older editions omit the second clause, “and truly the blood of Christ,” through the customary scribal error caused by the recurrence of the same word. Martianaeus, who restored the passage from the Codex Corbeiensis, also directs attention to this outstanding testimony for establishing the truth of Christ’s body in the Eucharist.]

this indeed we receive, because it is truly the flesh of Christ, and [Col. 1251A] truly the blood of Christ. But let us speak in another way. The bread of Christ and his flesh are the divine Word and heavenly teaching. Whoever receives this bread and is filled, what will happen? What?

“The Lord releases those in chains.” If this bread has restored our soul—that is, the divine Word and heavenly teaching—then at once our feet, which had been bound, are released. “The Lord releases those in chains.” Lazarus too was bound, and he said, “Release him” (John 11). “The Lord releases those in chains.” Abraham’s daughter had been bent over and bound for eighteen years; she is released and looks up toward heaven. See what is said there in the Gospel: “Behold,” he says, “there was a woman who had a spirit of infirmity for eighteen years and could not,” he says, “raise her neck” (Luke 13). [Col. 1251B] Because she had a spirit of infirmity, she could not lift her neck upward.

“The Lord releases those in chains.” These chains are also works, since the same sins that bend our necks also bind our feet. Whoever is fettered cannot run. Whoever is fettered cannot run in Christ’s stadium. His feet are weighed down by fetters, pressed into the earth, and fixed in the earth.

“The Lord releases those in chains.” Observe the order. He gives food to the hungry. First we hunger; then we receive food. Once we have been filled, our feet, which had been fettered, are released. Once they have begun to walk freely, what follows? “The Lord gives sight to the blind.” See what he says. If he were speaking about those physically blind, he ought to have said, “The Lord gives sight to the blind.” But he did not say this. According to the Hebrew and Greek truth, what did he say? “The Lord makes the wise blind.” If he were speaking about these physical eyes, he ought to have said, “The Lord gives sight to the blind.” But now it is said, “The Lord makes the wise blind.” “If you were blind,” he says, “you would have no sin.” Our heart has been blinded by the darkness of sins. Folly and stupidity are darkness—not of the eyes, but of conduct. Once, therefore, we have been nourished in our hunger and our feet have been freed, then the eyes of our heart begin to see the light that they once lost and to possess wisdom. If he has become wise, what follows?

“The Lord raises up those who have been cast down.” Even if you were lying prostrate, be confident: the Lord extends his hand.

“The Lord loves the righteous.” I see two things: he loves and he guards. Whoever loves, loves him as his own. Whoever guards, guards him who is placed in danger. “The Lord loves the righteous.” Whoever is righteous and perfect is loved by him. Whoever is a stranger and comes into the service of the Lord is preserved.

[Col. 1252A] “The Lord guards the newcomers; he will receive the orphan and the widow.” Even according to the literal sense this is beneficial: he will receive the orphan and the widow. O martyr, who are being held so that you may pour out your blood for me, do not be anxious about your children; do not be anxious about your wife: they have me in your place.

Let us speak according to the spirit: “He will receive the orphan and the widow.” He will receive the orphan who, through sins, had lost God the Father. And he will receive the widow—that is, the soul that had lost Christ, her husband. But see what he says: “the orphan and the widow.” He did not say “he will guard”; he did not say “he will save”; but “he will receive”—if she returns to the Father, if she returns to her husband.

“And he will destroy the way of sinners.” He did not say, “He will destroy sinners,” but, according to the first psalm, “the way of the ungodly will perish.” If Christ is the way of the righteous, the devil is the way of sinners. And [Col. 1252B] “he will destroy the way of sinners.” Therefore the devil is the way of all sinners; he destroys him. But he will save us, who used to walk in that way and have ceased to walk in it.

“The Lord will reign forever.” Because the way of sinners has perished, then the Lord will reign forever. He did not say, “forever” in the singular, but “forever” in the plural. As long as the way has not perished, Christ does not reign in us. As long as the way of sinners has not perished, Christ does not reign in us. As long as our feet walk in the devil’s way, Christ does not reign in us.

“I am angry with my brother without cause”: I walk in the devil’s way; Christ does not reign in me. “I slander my brother”: I walk in the devil’s way; Christ does not reign in me. In whatever sin I walk, I walk in the devil’s way; [Col. 1252C] Christ does not reign in me.

“My mind is vain and is distracted in different directions.” I am in one place, and my mind wanders throughout the whole world. The world contains angels; it contains kings; it contains armies; it cannot contain one monk. Why do I say all this? Because of those who wander throughout the whole world and cannot sit in one place.

“Your God, O Zion, from generation to generation.” “Your God, O Zion.” We have often said that Zion is interpreted as a watchtower, or as the Church, or as the soul contemplating God. “Your God, O Zion, from generation to generation.” In the first generation, that of the Jews; in the second, that from the Gentiles. Throughout all the Scriptures and all the psalms, “generation and generation” is said to signify two peoples.

But we can also speak in another way: “The Lord your God reigned forever, O Zion”—in this generation and in the generation to come. Let Christ reign in us; let sin not reign in our body. “The heart of the king is in the hand of God” (Proverbs 21). Let us be kings: let us rule our body and subject it, and let our heart be in the hand of God.

To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM 146

[Col. 1253A]

**Alleluia.** This psalm admonishes us, saying that we should praise the builder of the heavenly city:

“Praise the Lord, for the psalm is good.” This psalm is prefaced by the title **ALLELUIA**. Those who do not know the Hebrew language, when they see that *Alleluia* has been placed at the beginning of a psalm’s title, customarily ask what it means. This psalm therefore has *Alleluia* not only in its title but also at its beginning. Where it says, “Praise the Lord,” the Hebrew says **ALLELUIA**. For among the Hebrews God has ten names: he is called **Sabaoth**; he is called **Shaddai**; he is called **Elohim**; he is called **El**; he is also called [Note: [Col. 1253D] The name **IAO** is confused in older editions with the following name of God, **IA**. Erasmus and Marianus Victorius did not know that the tetragrammaton was read among the ancients as **IAO**. See above the copies of Origen’s lexicon of Hebrew names, where *Iao* is interpreted as **Κύριος, ἢ Θεὸς, ἢ Ἀόρατος**—“Lord,” or “God,” or “invisible.” MART.---Refer here to the letter on the ten names of God to Marcella in our recension 25. For *Iao*, the older editions give *Ia*.] **Iao**; he is called **Eser Jaja**. Among the other names there is one name called **Ia**. *Ia* is interpreted as “invisible.”

[Col. 1253B] Where, therefore, it says “praise,” in Hebrew it says *Allelu*. Thus this says *Alleluia*, as if it said *Allelu Sabaoth*, *Allelu Shaddai*, or *Allelu Elohim*; so now also it says *Allelu Ia*. Finally, Theodotion, who was one of the translators, wishing to make the truth of the interpretation known, said: **αἰνεῖτε τὸν Ἰά**—“praise Ia.” Why have we said all this? So that we may know that *Alleluia* is prefixed to this psalm: “Praise the Lord.” This is the interpretation.

Once we have gone out, it will be considered in our hearts. Otherwise the expression will be expanded: “Praise the Lord, for the psalm is good.” He did not say, “the good psalm,” but absolutely, “good is the psalm”—that is, singing psalms is a good thing. But one should sing not with the voice, but with the heart. How many have a good voice and, because they are sinners, sing badly! He sings well who sings in his heart, who sings to Christ in his conscience.

“Let praise of our God be pleasing.” Let praise be pleasing not in the voice but in the conscience. Finally, Noah too offered sacrifices, and the Lord smelled the fragrance of sweetness (Genesis 8). There is much that could be said, but we must briefly touch upon the chief points, so that we may indicate the meaning rather than expand the words.

“The Lord builds Jerusalem; he will gather the dispersed of Israel.” How Jerusalem is built and how it is gathered has already been said. Since, therefore, these two verses have been discussed, and we ought not to build upon another’s foundation, let us proceed to what remains. Let us see, then, how Jerusalem is built. In what follows, the prophetic word has described it.

[Col. 1253D] “He heals the brokenhearted.” “God does not despise a broken and humbled heart” (Psalm 50). “And he binds up their wounds.” Break your heart, and the Lord gathers up your wounds. That Samaritan who was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, when he saw the wounded man lying on the road, bound up his wounds (Luke 10). This is the one of whom it is now also said: “And binding up their wounds.” This is said of those who practice repentance. But of those who do not practice repentance it is said: “There is no ointment to apply, nor oil, nor bandages” (Isaiah 1).

“He numbers the multitude of the stars.” What connection is there, according to the literal sense, between “he binds up their wounds” and “he numbers the multitude of the stars”? But when he heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds, he transforms those who had previously been broken and afterward healed into stars.

“He numbers the multitude of the stars.” There had been many who sinned; there are many who have been healed. He numbers the multitude of the stars. He does not number the wounded, but those who have already been turned into stars. God numbers no one except those who are worthy of being numbered by him.

“And he calls them all by name.” This may be understood of Lucifer and of Orion, whom we see in the sky. And this indeed can be understood: God is wondrous, who made heaven and earth and all that is in them. But let us understand it in such a way that what happens daily may benefit us.

“And he calls them all by name.” Do you wish to know how the brokenhearted become stars? It is written in Genesis that God led Abraham out, showed him the stars, and said to him, “So shall your seed be” (Genesis 15). “And he calls them all by name.” From Abram he calls him Abraham. He was called Abram in Chaldea, but in heaven he is called Abraham. At the time when he became a star, he was called Abraham (Genesis 17). He who was previously Saul afterward was called Paul in heaven (Acts 9). John and James were “sons of thunder” (Mark 3). Thunder is certainly in heaven. Thus the stars are numbered: the countless saints are numbered, but Christ alone cannot be numbered.

[Col. 1254C] “Great is our Lord, and great is his power, and there is no number of his wisdom.” Great is the power: Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1). “And there is no number of his wisdom.” Christ is wisdom. And the one wisdom cannot be numbered.

“The Lord receives the meek.” What are these stars? “The Lord receives the meek.” The meek are turned into stars. “The righteous will shine like the stars of heaven” (Daniel 12): Daniel speaks.

“But he humbles sinners to the ground.” Observe the difference between these things. Angels fall to the earth; human beings go to the heavens. “The Lord receives the meek.” Meekness calls to heaven; pride drags down to earth. “But he humbles sinners to the ground.”

“Sing beforehand to the Lord with confession.” David fulfilled this. He had given us an example of righteousness, and he also gave us an example of repentance. He taught us how we ought to practice repentance by practicing it himself. See the holy prophet: not only did his righteousness benefit us, but so did his sin.

“Sing praises to our God on the lyre.” Let no string of the virtues be broken. Let the entire string of the virtues sing together. “Sing praises to our God on the lyre.” A lyre has many strings; if one is broken, it cannot produce a sound. [Col. 1255A] So too a holy man, however holy he may be, if one virtue is lacking, cannot produce a harmonious sound.

“He covers the heavens with clouds.” This heaven that we see cannot be covered with clouds. But there is another heaven, and there are other clouds. “And your truth reaches to the clouds” (Psalm 35). Does the truth of God, then, reach to these clouds which, when the wind blows, are quickly dissolved? The truth of God is Christ: “I am the way, and the life, and the truth” (John 14). Therefore the truth of Christ is in these clouds that do not possess the reality of substance within them. Can it therefore be that truth is there where the wind has the power to scatter it?

“I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon them” (Isaiah 5)—that is, upon the people of the Jews. The clouds are the prophets. The Lord commanded them not to rain upon Israel. [Col. 1255B] The prophetic word has been turned toward us.

If these clouds are struck together there, they make thunder and lightning. “He covers the heavens with clouds.” If the clouds are the prophets and the apostles, how are the heavens covered by the apostles and prophets? The heavens are the divine mysteries. Since, therefore, whatever is divine in the mysteries is called heaven, whoever is worthy is protected by these clouds. If anyone is unworthy to receive the sacraments, he cannot be covered by the clouds.

“He prepares rain for the earth.” Our earth needs rain, and unless it receives rain—that is, the fountain of teachings—it will not produce fruit. Once the earth has been moistened by such a fountain of teachings, what follows?

“He makes grass grow on the mountains,” and so forth. If he were speaking only of grass, grass would certainly grow more in the valleys than in mountainous places. Wherever there has been more abundant rain, there grass grows more abundantly. Waters flow down from the mountains into the valleys, and more vegetation grows there.

“And he gives their food to the beasts.” This Scripture that we read, expound, and hold in our hands calls the holy prophets “mountains” (Psalm 35). Abraham is called a mountain; Isaac is called a mountain; Jeremiah is a mountain: the holy prophets are mountains. These mountains have both grain and grass. If you are a human being, you receive grain from them; if you are cattle, you receive grass. “You will save human beings and beasts, Lord.” You are saved according to your faith.

“He makes grass grow on the mountains and gives their food to the beasts.” If you are a human being, you receive spiritual understanding from the Holy Scriptures; [Col. 1255D] if you are a beast, you receive the literal sense in the Jewish manner.

I see a great thing. God, who has been praised with such great proclamations, is brought down to lesser things, and it is said: “And to the young ravens that call upon him.” If he were speaking of the birds of heaven, he would have named eagles or vultures rather. “And to the young ravens that call upon him.” No other bird is named here, but the young of ravens—and not the ravens themselves, but the young of ravens. The raven is not saved, but the young born from it.

We are young ravens. For we are born from idolatrous parents. We read in Solomon: “The eye that mocks its father and scorns its mother’s speech, may the ravens of the valleys pluck it out” (Proverbs 30). He did not say “the young of ravens,” but the ravens themselves. Whoever is a raven cannot be saved.

The raven was sent out from the ark and did not return (Genesis 8). During the flood it was with the others; after the flood it was cast into misery—that is, when tranquility comes, it cannot remain in the ark of God. When there is a flood, its body is in the midst of it. Tranquility returns, and the raven flees.

Who are these ravens? Who are the young of ravens? I think that the ravens, black in color, who always pursue the corpses of the dead and always provoke quarrels with their very hoarse voice, are demons; and whoever has served demons receives, like ravens, the color of ravens. Therefore our parents, as we have already said, who served idols and demons, were ravens. For ravens are found only where there is filth, uncleanness, and corpses of the dead.

But we, who were born from ravens, do not wait for corpses but for dew. For the young of ravens are said to live on dew. Thus the philosophers say that the young of ravens live on dew.

Do you wish to know another mystery concerning ravens? Elijah is interpreted as “God the Lord.” Elijah—that is, our Lord and Savior—suffers persecution from the Jews and is fed by ravens, that is, by the people of the Gentiles.

“And to the young ravens that call upon him.” If you call upon him, you are a young raven; if you are silent, you are a raven. “And to the young ravens that call upon him.” We read in the prophet: “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved” (Joel 2). If we understand this simply of ravens, then will ravens also be saved? Answer, Jew; answer, you who follow only the Jewish literal text: do you say that these are truly ravens? You do not interpret spiritually but carnally, for you say that it is written about ravens. If, then, it is written about the young of ravens, and here too it is said, “to the young ravens that call upon him,” and it is written, “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved,” then the young of ravens too will be saved in the resurrection.

We, therefore, the young of ravens, call upon him and are saved. Finally, the apostle Paul also wrote to the Church of the saints; he wrote to those who call upon the name of the Lord (1 Corinthians 1).

“He will not delight in the strength of the horse.” We promised brevity, but necessity compelled us to argue at greater length. We lied, but it is a most useful lie. Would that Herod had lied and sworn falsely (Matthew 14)! We too promised less and gave you more as you prayed. The hour compels me to be silent; the greatness of the mysteries compels me to speak.

“He will not delight in the strength of the horse.” I hear a horse neighing, and we cannot pass it by. It is written in the Psalter: “The horse is deceitful for salvation” (Psalm 32). And elsewhere: “He cast horse and rider into the sea” (Exodus 15). Israel is also commanded not to maintain horses. Finally, Solomon, because he brought chariots from Egypt, was overcome by pleasure (Deuteronomy 17; 1 Kings 10).

“He will not delight in the strength of the horse.” “He cast horse and rider into the sea.” “I have become to them like horses in heat; each one neighed after his neighbor’s wife” (Jeremiah 5): Jeremiah speaks. Therefore God does not delight in such horses.

We have spoken about the horse: “He cast horse and rider into the sea.” We have said who the horses are; let us say who the riders are. I think that the horses are sinful human beings, and the riders are demons who ride in them. Therefore, whenever we see a brother persecuting someone and being hostile, let us know that he is a horse. But the rider is the devil, who strikes us with his lance. The one runs, and the other strikes. Yet the horse itself is driven by spurs, stabbed, and made to rage unwillingly.

“Nor will he be pleased with the legs of a man.” Observe what he says. He did not say “with the head of a man”; he did not say “with the hands of a man”; but “with the legs,” which are below. “Nor will he be pleased with the legs of a man.” Here “legs,” like “thighs,” are always understood in connection with lust. Thus in Ezekiel God is seen from the loins upward as electrum, and from the loins downward as fire (Ezekiel 1). If someone is above, he is golden; if someone is below, Gehenna has been prepared for him.

“Nor will he be pleased with the legs of a man.” Let us speak according to the literal sense. Since he had said, “He will not delight in the strength of the horse,” and had described a man as a warrior, it seems to me that where he says “not in the legs,” he is not calling them *tibiae* but **περικνημίδες**—leg coverings or greaves. [Note: [Col. 1257D] Rather, the legs themselves, namely **κνήμαι**, not greaves or **περικνημίδες**, must be understood from the Greek text and the interpretation of the Fathers. Ambrose, in his exposition of the Psalter, has *in tibialibus*—“in greaves.”]

We see, therefore, that whatever covers the legs does not please God, but what is above does. Strength does not please God; the legs of a man do not please him; but the fear of God does. Strength does not please; fear pleases. It overthrows the warrior, raises up the one who prays, exalts the humble, and casts down the proud.

“The Lord is pleased with those who fear him.” One fear casts out many fears. It is better to fear one, so that you may not fear many, than to fear many, so that you may not fear one. “And with those who hope in his mercy.” They hope not in their own works, but in the mercy of judgment.

“Praise the Lord, for the psalm is good”: those who hope in his mercy are healed by salvation alone.

To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM 147

“Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion.”

We have just heard the holy prophet proclaiming that, because of the transgression of the Law, the Jewish people had been abandoned. How, then, is it now said: “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion”? What follows?

“For he has strengthened the bars of your gates.” Therefore he is speaking of that Jerusalem, of that Zion: “Praise your God, Zion.” Why? “For he has strengthened the bars of your gates.” There are no gates—how, then, are the bars safe? “He has blessed your children within you.” How has he blessed them, when he said, “Your house will be left to you desolate” (Luke 13)?

“He has established peace as your boundaries.” Where has peace been established, when it was overthrown by war? “And he satisfies you with the fat of grain.” Does grain have fat? Answer, Jew. Does grain have fat? If, then, grain does not have fat, and necessity compels you to understand this spiritually, then the other verses must also be understood according to the same verse.

“Praise the Lord, Jerusalem.” Jerusalem means “vision of peace.” “Praise your God, Zion.” Zion is interpreted as “watchtower.” You see, then, what he says: “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem.” Wherever there is a vision of peace, wherever there is contemplation of God, there praise of God is made.

The Church therefore praises the Lord when she begins to believe in him and to have peace, and begins to see peace—that is, Jerusalem, the vision of peace. You who were previously a servant of idols have become a servant of God. Therefore praise your God. When you have begun to possess knowledge and to be a watchtower—that is, Zion—praise the Lord. That is: you, praise Jerusalem; you, praise Zion—you ecclesiastical soul, you Church.

Let the heretics not praise; let the synagogues not praise; but you praise. Why? “For he has strengthened the bars of your gates.” “The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the dwellings of Jacob” (Psalm 86). We have said that the gates of Zion signify the prophets. Since, then, we know that the gates of Zion are called the prophets, let us see what the bars of the gates are.

The true gates of the Church are the prophets. Without the prophets we cannot enter the Church. Mani wanted to enter without gates, and he did not enter. Marcion does not accept the Old Testament, and without the gates of the Old Testament he could not enter the Gospel. We, therefore, accept the prophets as gates and enter through the gates.

But let us see what the bars of the gates are. Many robbers, many thieves want to enter through the gates. “All who came before me were thieves and robbers” (John 10).

If only the Lord would grant me to be a bar of the gates of Zion! If one of the heretics wanted to enter through them into the order of the Gospel, I would stand at the gates and prevent him.

“For he has strengthened the bars of your gates.” Give me some ecclesiastical man learned in the heavenly Scriptures. If he sees Eunomius or Arius coming and wanting to take something from the prophets against us, does he not stand like a bar? Does he not prevail like a bar?

“For he has strengthened the bars of your gates.” He beautifully said “strengthened,” so that when you see an ecclesiastical man disputing, you should not think that he is the one who is disputing, but the one who strengthens the ecclesiastical order.

“And he satisfies you with the fat of grain.” “Unless,” he says, “a grain of wheat falls into the earth, it remains alone” (John 12). But if it falls, it saves many. Our Lord, the grain of wheat, fell into the earth and multiplied us. But this grain is exceedingly rich; it has marrow; it has fat.

“And he satisfies you with the fat of grain.” Blessed is the one who understands the fat in this grain. We read the Holy Scriptures. [Note: [Col. 1257D] Refer here to the interpolator of the Ignatian Epistle to the Philadelphians, where he says that he has recourse to the Gospel as to the flesh of Jesus Christ. See also Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus*, book I, chapter 6; Origen, *Homilies on Leviticus*, homily 7, chapter 10; and Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical Theology* III against Marcellus of Ancyra. Some books read “the body of Christ” in place of “Jesus.”] I think that the body of Jesus is the Gospel; I think that the Holy Scriptures are his teaching. And when he says, “Whoever does not eat my flesh and drink my blood” (John 6), although it can also be understood in the mystery, nevertheless more truly the body of Christ and his blood are the word of the Scriptures and divine teaching.

Whenever we go to the mystery, the faithful person understands; if he falls into defilement, he is in danger. Whenever we hear the word of God—and the word of God, and the flesh of Christ, and his blood are poured into our ears—and we think about something else, into what danger do we fall?

“And he satisfies you with the fat of grain.” The divine word is exceedingly rich. It contains every delight. Whatever you wish is born from the divine word, as the Jews relate: when they ate manna, it tasted in each person’s mouth according to that person’s desire (Wisdom 16). It is as though he had said: Whoever ate manna—if he desired an apple, a pear, a grape, bread, or meat—the taste in the manna was accordingly, in keeping with the quality and desire of the one eating.

So too with the flesh of Christ, which is the word of teaching—that is, the interpretation of the Holy Scriptures. As we wish, so we receive the food. If you are holy, you find refreshment. If you are a sinner, you find torment.

“And he satisfies you with the fat of grain.” He leaves no remnants. “He has blessed your children within you.” “But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God” (John 1).

“He has established peace as your boundaries.” In another psalm we read: “And his place was made in peace” (Psalm 75). “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace, not as the world gives peace” (John 14), since the peace of the world is our war.

“I give you my peace.” Have war with the world, and you will have my peace. “He has established peace as your boundaries.” Therefore whoever is not at peace with his brother is not within the boundaries of Jerusalem.

Someone may say: “What shall I do? My brother does not wish to be reconciled with me. Am I therefore outside the boundaries of Jerusalem?” “As far as it depends on you,” he says, “live at peace with all people” (Romans 12). “With those who hated peace I was peaceful” (Psalm 119). You should have peace, even if another is angry. He has war, and through his war peace is born for you.

Do you wish to know how war too can be peace? Unhappy Judas was coming to betray him, and the Lord offered him the kiss of peace (Luke 22); he created war through the kiss.

“He sends his word to the earth.” Answer, Jew: if he was speaking of grain, and “he satisfies you with the fat of grain,” how does he now say, “He sends his word to the earth”? “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1). This Word is sent in the flesh. “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid.).

“He sends his word to the earth.” This was fulfilled at the time when “the earth gave its fruit” (Psalm 66). “He sends his word to the earth.” He is speaking of the preaching of the Gospel and of the teaching of the apostles.

Finally, it follows: “His word runs swiftly.” For his word was heard throughout all the earth, and apostolic teaching throughout the world. One poor man, already old, preached from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum, and his word ran swiftly.

Since, therefore, he had come from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum and his word had run swiftly, the same word that had spoken beforehand of Jerusalem as far as Illyricum then follows and says: “But I desire to go also to Spain.” The apostle Paul speaks this (Romans 15). See the speed of the word! He is not content to run toward the East; he desires to run toward the West.

[Col. 1260A] “He gives snow like wool; he scatters mist like ashes,” and so forth. You see how difficult it is, how obscure are the things being said. “Who can withstand the presence of his cold?” Whose? Nothing is said. Then it says:

“He sends his word, and he will melt them.” This concerns the one of whom he had said, “He sends his word to the earth.” He sends his word. Who sends it? God the Father. “And the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” We have spoken of the Father; we have spoken of the Son; we cannot believe in a dual number unless the Trinity is completed.

His spirit blew, and the waters will flow. You see that wherever the Father and the Word of God are, immediately the Holy Spirit is also present. Let us therefore examine from the beginning what is said: “He satisfies you with the fat of wheat; he sends forth his utterance upon the earth; his word runs swiftly.” What follows immediately? “He gives snow like wool.” The Lord’s word, which runs swiftly, is given like snow, and that snow itself is like wool.

See the Lord’s mercy. The Lord’s food is changed for us into clothing. John had said of the Lord and Savior: “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world” (John I). And Isaiah says elsewhere: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter” (Isaiah LIII). Of this lamb, then, and of this sheep, this wool is like snow. Isaiah says: “Though your sins be like scarlet, I will whiten them like snow” (Isaiah I). “You will sprinkle me, Lord, with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you will wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow” (Psalm L). “He gives snow like wool.” Take away, Lord, my filth; take away whatever there is of vice. Grant your snow and your purity to Christian minds. Unless you give us the snow of your cleansing, we cannot have your clothing. Christ is our clothing. If we wish to have Christ’s clothing, let us be pure like snow.

“He scatters mist like ashes.” The Latin translator has rendered *mist* incorrectly. What is called ὁμίχλη (*homíchlē*, “mist”) in Greek has *hoarfrost* in Hebrew [Hebrew term not supplied]. Hence the passage continues: “He scatters hoarfrost like ashes.” He teaches us and makes clothing for us like snow; and when he has clothed us in his garment, [Col. 1260D] then he grants us nourishment. “He scatters hoarfrost like ashes.” Observe what he says: “like ashes.” Do you wish to be pure? Do penance. “I have eaten my bread like ashes, and I mingled my drink with weeping” (Psalm CI). Do you not see how he scatters his hoarfrost like ashes? A great transformation of things: snow is made from ashes; through repentance, a person is made pure.

“He sends his ice like morsels.” Just as loaves are broken and become morsels, so ice is broken and turned into morsels. Ice has this nature, like water when it freezes—the substance we call ice. The difference between ice and water is the same as that between water [Col. 1261A] and ice: water spreads out very widely, whereas ice is, as it were, compacted within itself and reduced to a single form. When water freezes, it produces ice. Since, then, we cannot receive the flesh of the Word in its entirety, it is broken so that we may receive it in portions. The matters are obscure, and the difficulty of interpretation does not allow us to speak at greater length.

“Before his cold, who can stand?” Whose cold? Some say it is the cold of the ice; others, that of the Lord. I think, however, that it is said of God. “Before his cold, who can stand?” What torments are said in the holy Scriptures to have been prepared for the sinner? Nothing is hotter than Gehenna, and yet it is itself cold. Gehenna consists of fire. But if someone grows cold away from charity, he is cast into the fire of Gehenna. It is written: “In the last days the charity of many will grow cold” (Matthew XXIV). Whoever, then, has grown cold in this way is cast into the fire. May the Lord grant that cold never enter our hearts; we do not sin unless charity has first grown cold.

Accordingly, what does the Apostle say? “Fervent in spirit” (Romans XII). And our God is fire (Deuteronomy IV). If, then, our God is fire, he is fire for this reason: that he may drive out the devil’s cold. The north wind is exceedingly cold, though it is called by the name “right.” Beautifully he said, “it is called.” For it has taken this name for itself, although it is left. If, then, someone’s soul grows cold, it is like the north wind, which is exceedingly cold. But when does the warmth of charity grow cold in our heart? When it has sinned, when it has grown cold, when it has died.

Pay close attention to what I say: “when it has grown cold, when it has died.” Growing cold belongs to the dead; being warm belongs to the living. If, then, someone has grown cold and died, God will send his word and melt him. May the Lord grant that our cold too may melt, that this ice may dissolve and become soft.

“He will send his word, and melt them.” Show me a sinner whom the Lord does not regard: one who has no warmth, but is entirely cold and dead. If he is pierced by the word of God, begins to do penance, and his exceedingly hard heart is softened, then this is fulfilled: “He will send his word, and melt them.” The Father sends; the Word is sent; the Holy Spirit anoints. “His spirit blew”: “fervent in spirit.” Cold is not driven out except by the warmth of the Holy Spirit.

Where are the Eunomians, where the Arians, where the Macedonians, who say [Col. 1261D] that the Holy Spirit is not numbered with the Father and the Son? God the Father sends; the Word is sent; and yet there is no complete healing unless the Holy Spirit has breathed. “His spirit blew, and the waters will flow.” The waters that were previously hard will become soft. The person who previously could neither hear nor impart righteousness is now a disciple.

Since we have said much, and what follows is clear, let us pray to the Lord that our hardness may grow soft and our sins be cleansed; that we may become like fire, so that whatever cold of the devil there is in our hearts may be driven out, and we may grow warm through the Holy Spirit. For there is also an evil warmth: “All the adulterers: their hearts are like an oven” (Hosea VII). [Col. 1262A] But that warmth is driven out by the warmth of the Holy Spirit. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM 148

“Alleluia of Haggai and Zechariah.” This psalm has two alleluias in its title, and many think that both alleluias have been placed in the title of the psalm. We must understand, however, that one alleluia belongs to the end of the preceding psalm, while the other alleluia is the beginning of the following psalm. We must accept and understand this rule: all the psalms that have “Alleluia” at the beginning also have it at the end. Many think that the second belongs to the beginning of another psalm. It is not so; the psalm that has “Alleluia” at the beginning also has it at the end. Why have I said all this? So that you may know why two alleluias have been placed before this psalm.

“Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights.” Human nature alone is not sufficient for the praise of God; let the heavens join it. “Praise the Lord from the heavens.” He did not say, “Heavens, praise”; rather, “You who are in the heavens, praise”—that is, you who dwell in the heavens: thrones, dominions, powers, seraphim, cherubim, and every name that is named, not only in the present age but also in the future. “Praise the Lord from the heavens; you who are in the heavens, you who are in the heights, praise him in the heights.” You who are exalted, praise the Exalted One. He did not say to the humble and those placed below, “Praise”; rather, to you who are on high.

“Praise him, all his angels.” Do you see in what rank the angels stand? First, thrones are mentioned. Thrones—seats. Let us not suppose that these are chairs on which God sits, but rather certain powers in the heavenly places in which God always sits, as upon his chariot. “Praise him, all his angels.” Whoever is an angel praises; whoever is a demon cannot praise.

“Praise him, all his powers.” Since we have summoned the angels to the praises of God, and no human being can know the names of all the powers, I speak generally: “Praise him, all his powers.” Thus far he has spoken of invisible things: you who are invisible, praise him. The human eye cannot behold invisible things. Now he comes to the creatures that we see with our eyes.

“Praise him, sun and moon.” See, Gentiles; see, Manichaeans. The sun praises; it is not praised. “Praise him, sun and moon.” You call the sun God. See how many stand before it in praise: “Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights. Praise him, all his angels. Praise him, all his powers.” Your god is placed in the fifth rank of those praising. “Praise him, sun and moon.”

He did not say “moon and sun,” but “sun and moon.” That which is greater in light praises first. Observe the order of visible things: “Praise him, sun”; after the sun, the moon; after the moon, all the stars. Not only the morning star, not only the greater stars, but the lesser ones also should praise the Lord.

Someone may say: How do the sun, moon, and stars praise God? They praise him in that they do not depart from their appointed function and service. Their service is the praise of God. Great is the honor you possess, human soul. The sun, moon, and stars run for you and serve for you. The angels, thrones, and dominions do not need the sun, moon, or stars. They are above the sun and moon [Col. 1263A] in the heavenly places. The sun, moon, and stars exist because of us; they serve us. The Apostle also says that creation itself groans together and labors in childbirth for the liberation of the servants of God (Romans VIII). But when the sons of God have been taken up, creation itself will be liberated from this service.

Someone may say: How does the sun serve and become free? How does the moon? How are the stars set free? The sun is set free from seeing Jews, Gentiles, and those who blaspheme its Lord. It sees parricides; it sees murderers; and yet it serves the command of the one who ordered it. For he makes his sun rise upon the just and the unjust (Matthew V).

“Praise him, all stars and light.” Someone may say: What is light apart from the sun, the stars, and the moon? We can say that between night and day, or between day and night, there is something that shines without the sun, although many think it is the sun’s own radiance. Thus he says: “Praise him, all stars and light.” Just as he had said of invisible things, “Praise him, all his powers,” so also of visible things he says, “Praise him, everything that shines.”

“Praise him, heavens of heavens.” We speak of several heavens. The Apostle says that he was caught up to the third heaven (II Corinthians XII). See, then, how great the splendor is, that there is a heaven of heaven. And the remaining words that follow he spoke concerning visible things.

“For he spoke, and they came to be.” God’s having commanded is his having made; his command is creation. “For he spoke, and they came to be,” in accordance with what is written in Genesis: “And God said,” and God made (Genesis I). That is: God the Father spoke; the Son made.

Someone may say: Then the one who commands is greater, and the one who is commanded is lesser. The Arians say this; the Eunomians say this; the Macedonians say this. I answer you according to your own reasoning, heretic: you say that the Father who commands is greater, and that the Son is lesser because he is commanded by him. If you understand this according to human reasoning, answer me: which is greater, to command or to make? I say, “Let a house be made,” and another makes the house. To speak is nothing great; to make is difficult. Therefore the one who makes is greater than the one who commands.

But even this is impious. For the Son is not greater than the Father. Just as it is impious to believe this concerning the Son against the Father, so it is impious to believe that concerning the Father against the Son. “For he spoke, and they came to be; he commanded, and they were created.” One nature both commands and makes. God commands, and God makes. The painter commands the painter to paint, and the painter paints what he had been ordered to paint.

“He established them forever and for the age of the age; he issued a command, and it shall not pass away.” Great is the honor of humanity, and great its unhappiness. The sun runs for you; the elements serve you; and you do not know your Creator? “He issued a command, and it shall not pass away.” He issued a command to the sun. Behold, for so many years God’s command has never passed away. It has not passed away to such an extent that its course has been grasped through human observation.

“He issued a command, and it shall not pass away.” He issued a command to the moon, that it should wax and wane over thirty days. Does it ever alter its courses? In heaven God’s command is observed, but on earth it is not observed. [Col. 1264A] He issued a command to the sea, that it should not pass beyond its shores. The ocean comes, swelling with waves, then returns into itself and remembers God’s command. The whole world serves God and remembers his command, while humanity alone does not remember.

Therefore we also say in the Lord’s Prayer: “Your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth” (Matthew VI). As the angels serve you in heaven and creation serves you, so let humanity also serve you. O unhappy human race! God descends to you because you do not wish to ascend to heaven. Is it not enough that you do not receive him? Do you also kill, crucify, blaspheme, and scourge him? Is it not enough that you kill him, but you do not even do penance for having killed him?

He has spoken of invisible things; he has spoken also of visible things, but of visible heavenly things. Now he speaks of the earth as well. Observe the order of the praise: first the invisible things praise, then the visible. The visible things themselves are divided into two groups: heavenly and earthly. He has spoken of the heavenly; now he speaks of the earthly.

“Praise the Lord from the earth.” Since the angels have praised and heaven has praised, let earth also praise. Let us see which things from the earth praise first: “Dragons and all the abysses, fire, hail, snow, ice, storm winds, which perform his word; mountains and all hills, fruitful trees and all cedars; beasts and all cattle, creeping things and winged birds.”

What is said after all these? After dragons, serpents, fire, hail, beasts, and all cattle: O human being, who seem great to yourself, it is said of you—not of an ordinary human being, but of those human beings who are great among human beings:

[Col. 1264C] “Kings of the earth and all peoples; princes and all judges of the earth.” Then what follows?

“Young men and maidens, old men with the young, let them praise the name of the Lord, for his name alone has been exalted,” and the rest that follows.

O how many mysteries are contained in these words! The heavenly things have praised; the invisible things have praised. Now he descends to earthly things, and for the praise of God the dragons and the abysses are first stirred up. “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Romans V). You who were once a dragon, who had the venom of a serpent; you who were once an abyss, over which darkness was borne (Genesis I)—see what he says: Where are the dragons? Where are the venoms? Where is the abyss? Where is the darkness? Do not despair, then. You who were a dragon, who were dark and did not dare to praise God: [Col. 1264D] do penance, and you will immediately be converted.

Although the Hebrew does not have *dragons*, but *thaninim*, which is translated “sea monsters” (*cete*). Sea monsters are said to be of immeasurable size. Indeed, this sea monster is said to be in the abysses.

Let us therefore speak first according to the literal sense. See what he says: Praise the things that are in the sea, and praise the things that are outside the sea. “Dragons and all the abysses”: the whole is expressed synecdochically by a part.

Then follows: “Fire.” Observe the harmonious discord between water and fire: they praise God together. “Dragons and all the abysses.” All things that are born from water are born from fire—that is, from moisture and heat. Neither fire alone can generate without moisture, nor moisture without fire. Nothing is so contrary [Col. 1265A] as moisture to heat and heat to moisture. Yet by God’s will these things, different from one another, agree in our birth.

“Hail, snow, ice, and storm winds, which perform his word.” There is much that could be said, and I cannot dwell on each item. “Hail, snow, ice, and storm winds.” Everything that we see in the world serves us. Serpents, abysses, fire, hail, snow, and storm winds seem to exist without reason, but they serve us. Yesterday there was a storm; it seemed contrary to us. There was cold; there was moisture; there were rains. What seems contrary to us for an hour is for us, for it produces fruit. See what he says: those things and those things “which perform his word.” Be ashamed, human being. Serpents, abysses, snow, rain, and storm perform God’s word, and you do not.

“Mountains and all hills.” Mountains are not changed into hills, nor valleys into mountains; they preserve their nature. “Fruitful trees and all cedars.” You see a tree, as if dry, having lost its leaves; when summer comes, it sends you a shoot and brings forth fruit for you. The tree bears fruit for you, and you bear no fruit for God. “And all cedars.” Imitate the cedar. Cedars strive toward the heights; they seem to hasten toward heaven. And you, imitate the irrational trees.

“Beasts and all cattle.” They do not change their nature. Everything remains in its order, except humanity alone, to which everything has been subjected. “Creeping things and winged birds.” Those things that are in heaven do not come down to earth; there they serve God.

Someone may say: You are speaking according to history; you are not speaking allegorically. If you speak according to history, why do the abysses, snow, and hail first praise God, then fruitful trees and the other irrational things, and humanity last? Let us read Genesis, and according to the order of birth and of creation we shall see all things praising. For it is written there that first the living creatures in the water were made; then those that are on the earth; then the winged creatures; and afterward he made one human being. Therefore, just as each thing was first made, so it praises the Lord.

But there is another sense: O human being, for whose sake were all these things I have mentioned made? Beasts, serpents, fruitful trees, winged birds—all these praise God in this respect: that they do not change their nature.

“Kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all judges of the earth. Young men and maidens, old men with the young, let them praise the name of the Lord, for his name alone has been exalted.” Let every age, every sex, and every power praise him, to whom the Father, after stripping the powers, gave an exalted name. Let no one reclaim for himself the name he uses, but let him ascribe it to the one of whom the passage also continues:

“His praise is above heaven and earth.” For, according to the Apostle, all things confess him—not only heavenly and earthly things, but also those beneath the earth (Philippians II). “And he has exalted the horn of his people”: namely, the ecclesiastical people.

“A hymn for all his saints, for the sons of Israel, the people drawing near to him.” The heavenly hymn is assigned to those who have been made holy in him; who behold him with the mind; who draw near to his faith; whom wicked perversity does not separate from him. May he deign to deliver us in the kingdom to God the Father and to make us conformable to the glory of his body, so that we may sing to him no longer with a local and transitory song, but with the perpetual and immovable hymn of the heavenly assembly, in unceasing melody. For honor and glory belong to him with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM 149

This psalm has been read, and at its beginning it has:

“Sing to the Lord a new song.” For Psalms 95 and 97 also have the same beginnings. Psalm 95 is prefaced by this title: “A psalm of David, when the house was being built after the captivity”—that is, after repentance, the house of Christ is built. Since, then, he first said, “Sing to the Lord a new song,” and the new people sing a new song and he blessed them, let us hasten on to the remaining words.

“Let Israel rejoice in him who made him.” Let the one rejoice who sees God with understanding. For here Israel is interpreted as “seeing God with understanding.” “And let the sons of Zion rejoice in their king.” Let the sons of the Church, the sons of the new people, rejoice in their king, in Christ, who reigns in them. You see how lightly we touch upon the principal points.

“Let them praise his name in the assembly.” Wherever there is an assembly, different voices are gathered into one song. For when different voices—that is, when they have been gathered together—are united, they form the Lord’s assembly.

“Let them praise his name in the assembly.” Where there is disagreement, where there is envy, there is no assembly.

[Col. 1266C] “Let them praise his name in the assembly; let them sing to him with tambourine and psaltery.” This assembly has a song; it also has a tambourine and a psaltery. Let us crucify our bodies for Christ, and with such a tambourine let us sing to God.

“With tambourine and psaltery let them sing to him.” A tambourine has no flesh, but a skin. And as long as we are fleshly, we are not a tambourine. It is a tambourine only when it has no flesh, when it is stretched. A tambourine cannot be contracted but must be extended. Let our sins not contract us; let righteousness enlarge us.

Let us hasten on to the remainder: “With tambourine and psaltery let them sing to him.” What we say in the assembly, let us say also on the psaltery. The psaltery is properly a type of musical instrument, something like a lyre. It resembles a lyre, but it is not a lyre. The difference between a psaltery and a lyre is this: a lyre is struck downward; a psaltery, on the other hand, is struck upward, which in ordinary speech is called a *polyphthongum* (“many-sounding instrument”). This, then, is the psaltery. We are therefore commanded to sing to God in a new song—not downward on the lyre, but upward, that is, on the psaltery.

“For the Lord has been well pleased with his people, and has exalted the meek unto salvation.” “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matthew V). If it is said there, “Blessed are the meek”—that is, the gentle—“for they shall possess the earth,” and here it is said, “He has exalted the meek unto salvation,” then these meek will possess the earth by inheritance. Therefore this earth is not below, but above. For what does he say? “He has exalted the meek unto salvation.” [Col. 1267A] If the meek were to possess this earth, which is below, he would not say, “He has exalted.”

“The saints shall rejoice in glory.” In what glory? “Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery and lyre; I will rise at dawn.” In what glory? For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified (John VII)—that is, he had not yet been crucified. “The saints shall rejoice in glory.” This, then, is what I say: the saints shall rejoice in the cross. “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians VI). Behold, through the Apostle’s voice the prophecy has been fulfilled.

“They shall rejoice in their beds.” “Every night I shall wash my bed; I shall water my couch with my tears.” That belongs to the sinner; that belongs to the penitent. But what is said here—“They shall rejoice in their beds”—belongs to the saints, belongs to the righteous.

Who among us rejoices in his bed? Who does not struggle with his flesh? When I wake from my little bed, I do not rejoice but struggle; I do not sigh for the kingdom of heaven but struggle with my flesh. I water the fire of the flesh with tears and extinguish it. Therefore it is said: “Every night I shall wash my bed; I shall water my couch with my tears” (Psalm VI). My little bed, which burns with lust, is extinguished by tears. Blessed are those of whom it is said: “They shall rejoice in their beds.”

“The praises of God are in their throat.” Certainly one who cries out does not cry out in the throat but with the lips. How, then, does it say, “The praises of God are in their throat”? We cry out in our hearts, “Abba, Father” (Romans VIII). The voice that cries to God is not of the lips but of the heart. Accordingly, the Lord says to Moses: “Why do you cry out to me?” (Exodus XIV). Yet Moses had said nothing.

“And two-edged swords are in their hands.” This passage, which says that those who rejoice in their beds are saints and perfect men, asks what else they possess: “And two-edged swords in their hands.” The swords of the saints are two-edged. We read in the Apocalypse of John, which is read and accepted in the churches—for it is not counted among the apocryphal Scriptures but among the ecclesiastical writings—that it says there concerning the Lord and Savior: “And a sword,” he says, “sharp on both sides, was coming forth from his mouth” (Revelation I).

You see, then, that these saints received from the Lord’s mouth the two-edged swords that they hold in their hands. The Lord therefore gives swords from his mouth to his saints: a two-edged sword, that is, the word of his teaching. A two-edged sword, both according to history and according to allegory, both according to the letter and according to the spirit. This two-edged sword has two points; it speaks both of the present age and of the future. Here it kills adversaries, and in heaven it opens the kingdoms of heaven. Why do the saints possess these swords?

“To execute vengeance,” he says, “upon the nations.” If only I could possess this two-edged sword, so that I could execute vengeance upon the nations; I could kill the Gentiles; I could kill Arius; I could kill Eunomius; I could kill the Manichaean; I could kill all the heresies!

But observe what he says: “To execute vengeance upon the nations.” Is this so that they may be killed and perish? He does not say this. “Reproofs among the peoples.” He reproves so that the peoples may be saved. [Col. 1268A] Let those who have been led astray by evil teachers be saved. But the peoples cannot be set free unless the teachers have been bound. Hence it follows:

“To bind their kings with fetters.” Do you wish to free the people? Bind the teachers. “To bind their kings.” He did not call them teachers but kings, for they reign in their sins and miseries. “To bind their kings with fetters.” He rightly said “with fetters,” so that the teachers would not run about excessively or deceive many, but would be bound together and stand still.

“And their nobles with iron manacles.” Among the heretics you may hear their nobles saying: “This man is learned; that one performs signs; this one casts out demons.” The saints of the Lord, because they possess two-edged swords—that is, swords with two edges, from both the Old and the New Testament—bind those teachers and impede [Col. 1268B] their feet, so that they cannot run.

“And their nobles with iron manacles.” They bind; they do not kill. They do not slay, but bind. They tie their hands and lead them captive to the Church in iron bonds. These chains are made only from the testimonies of Scripture, as I join testimony to testimony. If you want these chains not to break, let them not be single but woven from both sides: “A threefold cord is not broken.”

Why is all this done?

“To execute upon them the judgment that has been written.” What is the judgment that has been written? It is so that those who had first denied God may afterward return to repentance. It is a written judgment so that they may release their captives; so that those whom they had bound and whom they had led away from the Church may afterward be loosed within the Church.

“To execute upon them the judgment that has been written.” [Col. 1268C] I speak in simpler words: so that they may judge them in the manner laid out in the holy Scriptures.

“This glory belongs to all his saints.” Truly, glory does not consist in gold, silver, gems, or silk clothing. Whoever possesses these swords, what else does he need? See what he says: “This glory belongs to all his saints.” Let us ask God that we may possess this glory, so that the sword proceeding from the mouth of our Savior may arm our hands. Whoever possesses this sword does not fear the sword of the age.

I tell you something new: often the sword of this age has cut down that sword; often it happens that the sword of this age gives us that sword. For if we fear this one, we shall not receive the other. Let us therefore give thanks to him who possesses this sword, and [Col. 1268D] bless him forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM 150

“Alleluia.” This psalm contains the mystery of the third group of fifty, namely: the first restores us through baptism and repentance to the good of innocence; the second attains the fruit of innocence after judgment; the third, once the building of the divine city has been completed and the hope of all the saints has been brought to its fulfillment, exhorts us to eternal rejoicing and praise. For it says:

“Praise the Lord in his saints.” He will place them, after the judgment has been celebrated, in the glory of eternity. “Praise him in the firmament of his power,” because, after every weakness has been removed, he will bring them into the firmament of eternal strength.

[Col. 1269A] “Praise him in his powers,” because, having powerfully consumed death through immortality, he will grant them the glory of unchangeable life, “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (I Corinthians II). “Praise him according to the multitude of his greatness,” because he assigns dwellings distinguished by manifold honor among the heavenly bodies, as the Lord says: “In my Father’s house are many dwellings” (John XIV).

“Praise him with the sound of the trumpet,” in which battle those who were killed conquered, while the Lord crushed Satan beneath their feet. “Praise him with psaltery and lyre,” because he has granted them either to fulfill the song of the Law from heaven, or, after the flesh has been put to death (Romans XVI), which is understood as the lyre, to bring it to life in himself.

[Col. 1269B] “Praise him with tambourine and assembly”: with the tambourine, because the deadened body has been given immortality; with the assembly, because it has been joined to the angelic choirs. “Praise him with strings and organ,” because, through abstinence from food, with their inward parts drawn tight and their carnal desires conquered, they have been found worthy of the kingdom of God, to sing divine praises in harmony.

“Praise him with well-sounding cymbals; praise him with loudly ringing cymbals.” This praise is fulfilled in well-sounding and exultant cymbals, because, once the corruption of flesh and blood has been driven away, they have been conformed to the image of the Creator and, filled with the fullness of hope, shine like the sun in the kingdom of God the almighty Father.

“Let every spirit praise the Lord.” In this kingdom, then, there is no flesh, blood, or corruption; rather, the human being, having become wholly spiritual, does not cease to praise God—who is spirit—in spirit. May he deign to grant us that, having become doers of the Law in this age, tested in the contest of this life, found faithful, and enriched with spiritual fruits, we may deserve to be joined to those who sing these praises. To him be glory and dominion with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages forever and ever. Amen.

## SECOND EXPOSITION ON PSALM 119

[Col. 1269]

[Col. 1269B] Let us come to the psalm that was read after Psalm 118. Psalm 118—as we have often said—is an alphabetic psalm, that is, an *alphabetites*: it begins with ALEPH and continues to the final Hebrew letter, which in Hebrew is called TAU. Each verse begins with one of the individual letters. There are twenty-two Hebrew letters, and eight verses begin with each letter. For example, eight verses begin with the letter called ALEPH.
