When these have again been completed, another eight verses begin with the second letter, called BETH. When those have been completed in turn, another eight verses begin with the next letter, called GIMEL. Thus Psalm 118 is an alphabetic psalm.

If we wish to read a letter, we cannot read it unless we first know the letters. So too we cannot know the Scriptures unless we first know the alphabet. Psalm 118, then, is an alphabetic moral psalm, and it instructs our life. Since this is not now the time to speak about the whole psalm, let us speak now about the first psalm of the Songs of Ascents, which begins as follows:

To the Lord, when I was in distress, I cried out, and he heard me.

These psalms are called “Songs of Ascents,” as we have often said, because by certain steps we ascend to greater things. Now is not the time to discuss all the Songs of Ascents and explain how, through each individual psalm, steps are formed so that we may reach the highest things. For the present, let us speak about the first step, leaving aside the mystery of why it is called the fifteenth step; for to say the same thing repeatedly is wearisome to those who listen. Hence the Apostle also testifies that he spent fifteen days with Peter in Jerusalem, in order to compare the two Testaments, the sevenfold and the eightfold [Gal. II].

There are many things that could be said. “To the Lord, when I was in distress, I cried out, and he heard me.” Whoever is still on the lowest step looks toward the highest, the fifteenth step. Whoever is on the fifteenth is already near the temple; and this temple, whose ruins we now see, offended its Lord. And what did the Lord say? “Rise, let us go away from here” [John XIV]. And what does he say elsewhere? “Your house will be left to you desolate” [Luke XIII]. The Lord went out, and the temple collapsed.

This temple, then, has fifteen steps around it. We see certain indications: count them, and you will see that it is as we say. The Levites and priests therefore stood on the steps, each according to his rank. For example, the one who was high priest stood on the first step—that is, on the fifteenth step from below upward. On the second step stood the priests, and among the priests there were distinctions. On the third, in turn, stood those of lesser rank. On the fourth stood the Levites. Among the Levites too there were many distinctions: whoever was lowest stood on the last step.

Consider that this earthly temple is a figure of the heavenly temple: “Star differs from star in glory; so also is the resurrection of the dead” [II Cor. XV]. Blessed is the one who has deserved to be on the fifteenth step, in the heavenly Jerusalem and in the temple. Yet because that place is great—and I think it belongs to the apostles and holy martyrs—let us pray that at least we may deserve to be on the lowest step of the Lord’s temple. They stand on different steps, but they sing one psalm in praise of the Lord. The places are different, but the praise of the Lord is one.

What we have said about the heavenly Jerusalem, I think is now being practiced every day while we remain in this age. One of us is on the first step: let him not despair of the second. Whoever is on the second should not despair of the third. Blessed are the martyrs, many of whom have deserved to ascend from the lowest step to the first. Whoever lives in this age cannot immediately climb from the first step to the highest. We must not, therefore, be content with the first step; we must always strive toward greater things. Nor should the one who is on the lowest despair of the first; nor should the one who is on the first be secure, for he can fall to the lowest.

I think this is also what Jacob’s ladder signifies, when Jacob was fleeing from his brother Esau. “And he came,” it says, “to Bethel, and slept there, and placed a stone under his head” [Gen. XXVIII]. Observe our ascetic—*askētēn* (ἀσκητήν): he was fleeing a most cruel man, fleeing his brother, and he found help in a stone. That stone is Christ; this stone is a help to those who suffer persecution. But to unbelieving Jews it is “a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense” [I Pet. II].

“And Jacob saw there,” it says, “a ladder set up from earth to heaven, and in heaven,” it says, “the Lord. And he saw,” it says, “angels ascending and descending.” Observe what he says: he saw angels ascending—he saw Paul ascending. He saw angels descending—the betrayer Judas was falling. He saw angels ascending—holy people proceeding from earth to heaven. He saw angels descending—the devil and his demons hurled down from heaven with their army.

Great is the difficulty of ascending from earthly things to heavenly ones. We fall more easily than we ascend; we fall easily, whereas in ascending there is great labor and great sweat. If I am on the first step, how much remains for me before heaven! If I am on the second, the third, the fourth, or the tenth, what benefit is it to me unless I reach the highest? Suppose this ladder has fifteen steps: I have come as far as the fourteenth; unless I hold the fifteenth, what benefit is it that I reached the fourteenth? And if I reach the fifteenth and then fall, the higher the ascent, the greater the fall.

At the same time, consider the mystery: because the labor and sweat involved in ascending from earth to heaven are great. Do you want to know what these steps are? What is the first step? I think the first step is fasting, for it is still close to the earth. We withdraw from the earth and ascend, yet we still think about earthly and bodily things.

Someone may say: “What benefit is fasting to me?” I ask that my soul may be pure before the Lord. How many do not fast and yet are holy! I am not saying this. If the Apostle Paul disciplined his body and brought it into subjection, lest, after preaching to others, he himself should be found disqualified [I Cor. IX]; if he says, “I see another law resisting the law of my mind and leading me captive”; and afterward says, “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?”—if he fears the snares of the body, are we secure? If he says, “When I am weak, then I am stronger”: the weakness of the body is the health of the soul.

Why do I say all this? Because abstinence is the first step, and we must not immediately think that if we fast, we ascend to the kingdoms of heaven. Fasts do not lead us to the kingdoms of heaven; but without fasts we do not ascend to the kingdoms of heaven. Fasts alone do not profit; they profit together with other things. Why have I said all this? Because it is, as it were, the foundation for those ascending to greater things.

The second step, however, is to renounce the world, to seek nothing from the world, and to despise earthly things. Someone may say, “Is doing this also the second step?” I say that it is the second. It is nothing great to abandon earthly possessions; it is great to abandon the vices of the soul. For if I fast—that is, if I am on the first step—and if I abandon my possessions—that is, if I am on the second step—what benefit is it to me if I am quarrelsome, angry, slanderous, or envious? It is nothing great to abandon earthly things; the vices that must be abandoned are greater.

But someone may say, “It is difficult; it is a great thing; it is hard.” And that is why it is great: because it is difficult. “An athlete is not crowned unless he has competed according to the rules.” Let no one be driven to despair: the ascent is steep and difficult, and despair arises. Do not despair, O human being: the Lord is above, on the fifteenth step; he looks upon you and gives help.

If you are on the first step, and the distance between the first and the fifteenth seems great to you, do not look at the step; look at heaven. And see what he says. He did not say, “I saw the Lord standing on the fifteenth step,” for we could not reach the Lord standing upright and erect. But see what he says: “I saw the Lord leaning upon the ladder” [Gen. XXXVIII]. See what he says about the one who was standing: “He bent himself and humbled himself,” so that we might be able to ascend. The Lord is bent down for your sake; he humbled himself. Ascend without fear.

This one, then, who is now on the first step, is no longer in distress; for he has already withdrawn from distress and has placed his foot on the first step. He does not say, “I am now in distress; I now cry out”; rather, because he is on the first step, he reports what he suffered. And what does he say? “To the Lord, when I was in distress, I cried out, and he heard me.” Before I placed my foot on the first step, I was in distress because I could not abandon earthly things. “To the Lord, when I was in distress, I cried out, and he heard me.”

This little verse seems to contain nothing inwardly. The verse is short, but it has three meanings joined together in it. What does it say? “When I was in distress”—there is one; “I cried out”—and after the cry, what? “He heard me.” In one verse there are distress first, then crying out, then being heard. It does not say, “When I was secure, when I was joyful, I cried out,” but “when I was in distress, I cried out.” “You ask,” it says, “and you are not heard, because you ask carelessly” [James IV].

“To the Lord, when I was in distress, I cried out, and he heard me.” What did he do by hearing me? Did he make me stand on the first step? Yet in comparison with the fifteenth step, what does it mean to be on the first? I have abandoned earthly things, but I have not yet ascended to the heights. Therefore I must not be secure; on the remaining steps I must ask for God’s help.

Lord, deliver my soul from wicked lips and from a deceitful tongue.

He says this about all heresies. He says it about the Jews, about the Arians, about the Manichaeans, and about the other heresies. When an Arian says, “The Father is greater, the Son lesser,” what shall we say? “Lord, deliver my soul from wicked lips and from a deceitful tongue.”

When a Manichaean, or someone like the Manichaeans, says, “The Lord did not rise in the reality of the body; and so that you may know that it was not a real body, he entered when the doors were closed” [John XX], what shall we say? “Lord, deliver my soul from wicked lips and from a deceitful tongue.”

The wounds inflicted by the tongue are greater than those inflicted by swords. A sword kills the body; it does not kill the soul. An evil tongue is an evil thing, a great evil: a small member, but it causes great ulceration. Read the Epistle of Saint James to learn how many evils the tongue contains [chapter III]. The tongue has nothing intermediate: it is either a great evil or a great good. It is a great good if it confesses Christ as God; it is a great evil if it denies Christ as God.

Therefore let no one think or say for the moment, “I have not sinned in deed.” If I have sinned, I have sinned with my tongue. What sin is greater than blasphemy against God? And yet the tongue sins.

Why did the devil fall from heaven? Was it because he committed theft? Because he committed murder? Because he committed adultery? These too are evils, but the devil did not fall on account of them; he fell on account of his tongue. For he said, “I will ascend into heaven; I will set my throne above the stars of heaven, and I will be like the Most High” [Isa. XIV].

Therefore monks should not think themselves secure and say for the moment, “We do not commit great crimes in the monastery: I do not commit adultery, I do not steal, I do not murder, I do not commit parricide,” and the other things that are great vices. It is a great crime when I slander my brother; with my tongue I kill my brother. “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” [John III].

See what Solomon says: “In the hand of the tongue are death and life” [Prov. XVIII]. See what he says: “In the hand of the tongue.” You see how great an evil the tongue is: it has a hand. For what does he say? “In the hand of the tongue.”

It is a great vice to slander one’s brothers, to be unable to keep silent, to go around the cells slandering others. “I am a sinner; that man is a sinner—what is that to you? Consider yourself, lest you fall. Why do you rejoice at another’s ruin? If I fall, will you stand?”

Even if it is my ruin, the ruin of a brother should be your fear, not your rejoicing. He has fallen: are you happy or sad? Answer me: a brother has fallen; are you happy or sad? If you are happy, why are you happy at another’s ruin? But if you are sad, why do you go around? Why do you tell others? Let God see your sadness, and let that brother himself perceive it; let the ears of the brothers not hear it.

“Lord, deliver my soul from wicked lips and from a deceitful tongue.”

What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, for a deceitful tongue?

The Holy Spirit responds to the prophet who says, “Lord, deliver my soul from wicked lips and from a deceitful tongue”: “What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, for a deceitful tongue?” He answers him and says: You who say, “Lord, deliver my soul from wicked lips and from a deceitful tongue,” what do you wish to be given to you? And once it has been given to you, what do you again wish to be added to you for a deceitful tongue?

See what he says. He did not say “against a deceitful tongue,” but “for a deceitful tongue.” If he had said “against a deceitful tongue,” he would seem to be speaking about an adversary. Observe what the mystery is—of the prophet, or rather of the holy man established on the first step.

I shall put it more simply, for the sake of the simpler people. What does he say? “Lord, deliver my soul from wicked lips and from a deceitful tongue.” For example, from the lips of my adversary who slanders me. But the Lord gives another answer. And what does he say? He does not say, “What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, against a deceitful tongue?” That is, he does not say, “What do you wish to be done to your adversary?” Rather, what does he say? “What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, for a deceitful tongue?” He does not say “against the tongue,” but “for the tongue.”

Observe what he says: “for a deceitful tongue”—for your tongue, not your adversary’s. If your adversary slanders you, it does you no harm; you kill yourself if you slander someone else.

For example, if a brother slanders me, what harm has he done me? If he calls me a murderer, an adulterer, a criminal, or a liar, what harm has he done me? There are only two possibilities: either he speaks the truth or he lies. If he speaks the truth, it is not what he said that harms me, but the fact that I truly did it. If he lies, his lie does not harm me, but it kills the soul of the one who speaks.

We are unhappy; we are miserable. When we have an enemy, while we think that what we do is against him, we are doing it against ourselves. We slander him, go around here and there, and tell everyone about him. Do we think we are harming him? We do not harm him; rather, we kill our own souls by lying. “The mouth that lies kills the soul” [Wis. I].

“What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, for a deceitful tongue?” It is as with a good physician who says, “For this illness, for this wound, what do you wish to have placed upon you? What plaster do you wish to have applied to you?” It is as if someone were to say to a wounded person, “What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, for the wound from which you suffer?”

The Lord asks—not because he is ignorant, but so that the one who was asking may know how he ought to ask.

Sharp arrows of the mighty one, together with desolating coals.

“Sharp arrows of the mighty one.” Now he answers the Lord concerning what he is asking. Since the Lord had said, “What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you?” this man now says what he is asking: “Lord, this is what I ask: sharp arrows of the mighty one, together with desolating coals.”

Observe what he says. Nothing can drive out the poison of my tongue and my slander unless your arrows, which make my tongue desolate, do so. My tongue swells and contains poison within; unless it is pierced and struck by your arrows, the poison does not come out.

We should give an example. If there is a wound on the body, and within that wound there are already putrid tissues, cancer, and pus inside, the pus does not come out unless the wound is opened. And if the pus has come out, unless the wound is cauterized, pus grows again.

Observe, then, what he says: Because my tongue swells, contains pus, and contains poison, first wound it with arrows so that the pus may come out; then place your coals and fire upon it, so that whatever evil there is may be boiled away and made desolate.

Observe, then, what he says: “Sharp arrows of the mighty one, together with desolating coals.”

Would that this desolating coal were given to us! Would that we too might say, “Was not our heart burning within us on the way, when he opened the Scriptures to us?” [Luke XXIV].

Isaiah also says to Babylon: “You have coals of fire; you shall sit upon them; they shall be your help” [Isa. XLVII]. And before they received the Holy Spirit, the Apostles still had certain human swellings on their tongues. Therefore the Holy Spirit descended upon their tongues in the form of fire [Acts II], so that the Holy Spirit might boil away whatever pus they had.

Let us give another example. When Isaiah saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne, what does he say? “Woe is me, miserable that I am, for I am pierced through, because I have unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people that has unclean lips” [Isa. VI].

See what he says: “Woe is me, miserable that I am, because I have unclean lips.” And afterward what does he say? Because he had unclean lips, therefore one of the seraphim is sent. He takes a coal of fire from the altar, touches his lips and his tongue, and cleanses them. And what does he say? “Behold, I have touched your lips, and I have cleansed your tongue.”

And immediately what does he say? “Whom shall I send to this people, and who will be there?” O mysteries of the Scriptures! As long as he had a deceitful tongue and unclean lips, he was not told, “Whom shall I send, and who will go?” His lips are cleansed, and immediately he is sent to speak.

Therefore whoever has unclean lips cannot prophesy and cannot be sent into the service of God.

“Together with desolating coals.” Would that this desolation too might be granted to us, so that whatever evil there is may be taken away from our tongue: so that where there are thorns, briars, and nettles, the Lord’s fire may be sent, burn everything up, and become Christ’s wilderness.

Woe is me, because my sojourn has been prolonged!

The holy man says this, the one who does not desire the body, who does not seek the earth, who longs for heaven. “Woe is me, because my sojourn has been prolonged.”

When we are sick, when we are feverish, when we suspect that we are dying, when we toss our arms about, when we are afraid, when we ask for leave—then we cannot say this verse. This man was healthy; he was not sick. And what did he say? “Woe is me, because my sojourn has been prolonged.”

For as long as we are in this bodily tent, we are away from the Lord [II Cor. V]. “Woe is me, because my sojourn has been prolonged.” He says “my sojourn”; he did not say “my dwelling.” In the present age we do not have a dwelling, but a pilgrimage. Hence the Apostle also says: “As strangers and pilgrims. I am a stranger and a pilgrim” [I Pet. II].

“Woe is me, because my sojourn has been prolonged.” What does he mean? “Wretched am I, as long as I am in this body.” Who among us can say this? If we are eighty years old, we fear death; and if we are a hundred years old and are sick, we still ask for leave and additional time.

Why do we do all this? Because the consciousness of our sins gnaws at us. We know that if we depart from the body, we do not go to Christ but to Gehenna. What does the Apostle say? “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” [Phil. I]. Give me assurance that after death I will be with Christ, and even now I desire to die. Therefore, because he is holy, this man says: “Woe is me, because my sojourn has been prolonged.”

I dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar.

“Kedar” is interpreted in our language as “darkness.” Observe, then, what he says: In what place are we? In what kind of world are we? “I dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar.” For a long time I was in darkness; for a long time I lived in darkness; for a long time I was in this body of death. My soul was a sojourner for a long time.

Observe what the holy man says: “Even if I lived ten years, my soul was a sojourner for a long time.” For what blessedness is it, in comparison with heavenly things, to be in earthly things? There are many things that could be said, but the discourse is now hastening toward its conclusion.

With those who hated peace I was peaceful; when I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause.

We are wretched: we cannot restrain our tongue from slandering. If someone has offended us, we display, as it were, a peaceful face, but inwardly the heart contains poison. We are called monks, and although we are not what we ought to be, we are nevertheless called monks.

At the third hour we pray; at the sixth hour we pray; at the ninth hour we hold the lighting service; at midnight we rise; then we pray at cockcrow. Observe at what hours we are continually roused for the service of God. Consider what he says: the third hour, the sixth, the ninth, the lighting service, the middle of the night, cockcrow, early morning.

We do all this and do not consider that if our soul is hostile toward a brother, we pray without purpose. For what is said in the Gospel? “If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you” [Matt. V].

Observe what he says. He did not say, “If you have something against your brother,” but “if your brother has something against you.” It seems to impose something unjust upon us. For if he had said, “If you have something against your brother,” it was within our power to control what we had. But now what does he say? “If you remember that your brother has something against you.”

I answer him: “Lord, it is not within my power if my brother has something against me. I have nothing against him. If he has something against me, what does it concern me?” And why do you refuse to accept my gift, and say, “If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift and go first to be reconciled with your brother, and then offer your gift”? Look, I have nothing against him. If he has something against me, what does it concern me?

The Lord answers you. And what does he say? “Wicked servant, I understand your mind. You have nothing against your brother? Nothing? Do you love him? Why, then, do you not want him to be saved? If you love him, go and ask him not to have anything against you, so that he may be saved.”

But you show that you do not love him, because you do not want him to be saved. Go, ask him; throw yourself at his feet; entreat him day and night. Say: “I left my gift at the altar because of you; I cannot offer sacrifices.”

He is moved, and what does he say? “If this man who is asking me does not offer his gift, what will I, who have been asked and do not forgive, do?”

Therefore the Apostle also says that we should give our enemies food and drink [Rom. XII]. And what does he say? “For by doing this,” he says, “you will heap burning coals upon his head.”

Someone may say that enemies do this—that is, they do good to their adversary in order to heap burning coals upon his head. But something else is meant: if he does evil to you and you do good to him, you heap burning coals upon his head—that is, you cleanse his vices and boil away his wickedness, so that he may turn to repentance.

Observe, then, what the holy prophet says: “With those who hated peace I was peaceful.” He did not say, “with those who wanted peace,” but “with those who hated peace.” They hated peace, and I loved those who hated peace. Therefore the Apostle also says: “As far as it depends on you, living at peace with all people” [Rom. XII].

Let us ask our brother. If he is our enemy, let us ask him once, twice, three times, and seven times. Yet if my brother sins, how often shall I forgive him—seven times? I say to you, not seven times, but seventy times seven, that is, four hundred and ninety times [Matt. XVIII].

If we were to count from morning until evening, we could not commit as many as four hundred and ninety sins. Yet what does the Lord say? “If he sins seventy times seven in a day, and turns and asks you, forgive him.”

But you say, “He is not turning with his whole heart; he is lying.” Let us leave judgment to God. He asks me and entreats me; whether he says this sincerely, God knows. I hear the voice; Christ understands the heart. I accept what I hear; may Christ accept what he knows.

Then observe your reward: he lies, but you accept the truth. His is destruction; yours is salvation.

Why have I said all this? Because these vices are accustomed to exist in monasteries, and especially in coenobia. We are not ashamed; we do not grieve. We have left mothers, we have left fathers, we have left brothers, we have left sisters, we have left wives, we have left children, we have left our native lands, we have left our homes, we have left our little rooms, we have left the cells in which we were born and raised, and we have left the servants with whom we were brought up. We came to the monastery, and did we leave all these things for this reason—that we might quarrel with our brothers in the monastery over some trivial matter?

We abandoned our possessions, we abandoned our homeland, we abandoned the world, and do we quarrel in the monastery over a pen? If I hear a bitter word, I cannot bear it. It seethes in my heart; it is written in my marrow for ten or fifteen days; it cannot be removed from my heart. I speak to my brother who had insulted me, promise peace with my lips, and hold poison in my heart.

Often the eyes and face are signs of the mind. When our heart has been wounded against someone, we cannot look at him with straightforward eyes. The face and eyes themselves are, as it were, a mirror of our soul. What does Scripture say? “They could not speak a peaceful word to him” [Gen. XXXVII]. The tongue could not lie about what the heart did not contain within.

This, then, I say to you and to myself, for I do not preach this in order to make myself seem secure. The occasion of this verse compelled us to speak in this way. Great is the evil of the tongue.

“Lord, deliver my soul from wicked lips and from a deceitful tongue.” Not from another’s tongue, but from my own tongue deliver me. Another’s tongue does me no harm; my own tongue is my enemy.

“Lord, deliver my soul.” Deliver me from my tongue. My tongue is a sword; it kills my soul. I think that I am harming my enemy, and I do not know that I am killing myself.

My adversaries fight when I speak to them, while I speak peacefully. Let them have a hostile mind, but let us have a peaceful mind, since it is also written in Chronicles: “And the children of Israel went out,” it says, “to fight with a peaceful mind.”

Someone goes into battle and has a peaceful mind. But the weapons of Christians are peace: the peace of Christ, which surpasses all understanding [Phil. IV].

“Blessed are the peacemakers”—not only those who make peace between quarrelling people, but those who make peace within themselves. “Blessed are the peacemakers.” If others quarrel, and I intervene between them and make peace between them, but I myself do not have peace in my mind, what benefit is it to me that they have made peace?

“Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” [Matt. V]. Blessed are the peacemakers who speak peaceful words to those who hate peace. Blessed are the peacemakers.

Christ is peace. For if “Solomon” is interpreted as “Christ,” and Solomon is interpreted as “peaceful,” then Christ our God is peace. When he went to heaven, he left us a standard, saying: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” [John XIV].

Let us preserve what Christ gave. Let us have peace. Let us preserve peace, and it will preserve us in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1277]

# BOOK ON THE EXPOSITION OF THE PSALMS (C, G, S)*

## PROEM

[Col. 1277D] The Psalter is like a great house, which has one exterior key at the door, but within its various chambers has its own proper keys.

[Note: [Col. 1277D] This comparison is taken from Origen, who presents it in the preface to his Commentary on the Psalms as having been handed down by a certain Hebrew, although he applies it to Scripture as a whole. “For he said,” Origen writes, “that the whole divinely inspired Scripture, because of the obscurity within it, was like a number of dwellings enclosed within one building; each dwelling had a key assigned to it, but not the key appropriate to it, and thus the keys were scattered among the dwellings, with each one failing to correspond to the dwelling to which it had been assigned,” and so forth. This Jewish exposition is also approved by Saint Hilary in the prologue to his commentary on the Psalms.]

Although the Holy Spirit is the one more capacious key of the great door, each chamber nevertheless has its own little keys. If someone takes a key at random from the house and wishes to open a chamber, he cannot do so unless he finds the key. Thus the individual psalms are like individual cells, each possessing its own keys. The great door of this house, therefore, is the first psalm, which begins as follows:

## PSALM ONE

Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly.

Some think that the key of this psalm should be referred to the person of Christ our Lord, so that this blessed man, according to his humanity, is Christ. The intention is good, but the interpretation is uninformed. For if the blessed man is Christ, and Christ gave the law, how can it now be said of Christ, “His delight is in the law of the Lord”? Moreover, how can he be compared with another tree and be told: “And he shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water”?

For if he is compared with a tree, and everything that is compared is lesser than the thing to which it is compared, then the tree with which the Lord is compared is greater than the Lord. You see, therefore, that the psalm cannot be interpreted as referring to the person of the Lord.

Rather, it is said generally of any just man, although many think that it was spoken specifically of Joseph of Arimathea, who did not go in the counsel of the Jews, did not stand in the way of sinners, and did not sit in the seat of the Pharisees. Nevertheless, what others interpret specifically of him, we interpret generally of the just man.

[Note: [Col. 1279D] The genuine Jerome, in his Commentary on Matthew [last chapter], says: “In another Evangelist this Joseph is called *Bouleutēs* (βουλευτής), that is, ‘councillor’; and some think that the first Psalm was composed about him: ‘Blessed is the man who…,’ and so forth. Likewise, the Commentary on the Psalms under the name of Athanasius, in the Justinian Library at Venice and in the Ambrosian Library at Milan, is entirely different from the published work; its beginning is: ‘Indeed, the prophecy is fulfilled in Joseph of Arimathea’ (*hē men prophēteia plērouται eis ton Iōsēph ton Arimathaion*; ἡ μὲν προφητεία πληροῦται εἰς τὸν Ἰωσὴφ τὸν Ἀρημαθαῖον).]

Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly.

We read in Genesis that Adam was cursed when it was said, “Cursed is the earth in your works” [Gen. III, 17]. The curse of the first man is therefore now dissolved by blessing. It is as though one beatitude were set forth in the Old Law; but in the Gospel eight beatitudes are named together [Matt. V].

Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly. “Blessed is the man,” not merely a human being, but a man—a man who has reached the perfect man, Christ, who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly.

He described three general sins of human beings: either we think, or we do, or we teach. First we think; then, once we have thought, we turn the thought into action; and when we have done something, it also happens that we teach others what we ourselves have done.

“Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly,” who has not thought evil; “and has not stood in the way of sinners, and has not sat in the seat of pestilence.” That is, he has neither taught others nor stood in the way of sinners.

It is difficult for anyone not to sin. Hence John the Evangelist also says: “Whoever denies that he has committed sin lies and is a liar” [I John I, 8]. If, then, we all sin, but no one is blessed except the one who does not sin, then, because we all sin, no one is blessed.

But observe what he says: “and has not stood in the way of sinners.” He did not say, “Blessed is the man who has not sinned,” but “Blessed is the man who has not persevered in sin and has not stood in the way of sinners.”

I sinned yesterday; I am not blessed. If I do not remain in sin, if I withdraw myself from it, then I am already blessed.

“And has not sat in the seat of pestilence.” Just as there he said “stood,” so here he says “sat.” Just as there the one who did not persevere in sin is blessed, so here the one who did not persevere and sit in evil teaching is blessed.

What, then? You see how blessedness is granted in three ways: if we do not think evil, if we do not persevere in sin, and if we do not teach what is evil.

This is what the prophet says: “For three transgressions and for four I will not turn her away,” says the Lord [Amos I, 9]. Amos says this eight times. That is: you thought—I forgave; you acted—I forgave. Surely you should not also teach evil?

This is what is meant by: “For three transgressions and for four, let him not be angry with you,” says the Lord.

And he shall meditate on his law day and night.

He has stated three things that one ought not to do: not to go in the counsel of the ungodly, not to stand in the way of sinners, and not to sit in the seat of pestilence. He has stated three things that we ought not to do; he now states two things that we ought to do. For it is not enough for us to flee evil unless we also pursue good.

But his delight is in the law of the Lord.

He did not say “his fear,” but “his delight.” Many act out of fear, but the one who acts out of fear receives no reward. “But his delight is in the law of the Lord”: he wishes to do what the Lord has commanded.

And he shall meditate on his law day and night.

Speech cannot express how much the mind conceives. “But his delight is in the law of the Lord.” Someone says: “Look, I want to do the law of God; therefore I am blessed because I want to.” But see what follows: it is not enough to want to do the law of God; “he shall meditate on his law day and night.”

“He shall meditate day and night.” Someone may say: “Human nature cannot endure this, for one must walk, drink, eat, sleep, and acquire the things necessary for life. How can he meditate on the law of God day and night?”—especially since the Apostle says, “Pray without ceasing” [I Thess. V, 17].

Can I pray while I am sleeping? The meditation of the law is therefore not found in reading, but in doing. Hence it is said elsewhere: “Whether you eat or drink or do anything else, do everything in the name of the Lord” [I Cor. X, 31].

If I give alms, my feet meditate on the law of God; if I visit someone who is sick, my feet meditate on the law of God; if I do what has been commanded, I meditate with my body on what others meditate with their mouths. The Jews therefore meditate with their mouths; our meditation is action.

He has stated three things that we ought not to do, and two that we ought to do. What reward will the one who does this deserve?

And he shall be like a tree planted beside [Col. 1281A] channels of waters, which will yield its fruit in its season. And its leaf shall not fall.

Those who interpret this simply say that, just as a tree, if it has been planted beside waters, must flourish and not dry up, because its roots have moisture from which they live, so whoever meditates on the law of God is made both flourishing and alive by that very meditation on the law. This is how they interpret it simply. We, however, comparing spiritual things with spiritual, read that the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil were planted in paradise, and that the tree of life was planted in paradise, and that from paradise there went forth a spring divided into four sources (Gen. II).

We also read in Solomon—if anyone is willing to accept the book—for there he speaks of wisdom: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (I Cor. I, [Col. 1281B] 24). Therefore, where Solomon says, “She is a tree of life to all who grasp her” (Prov. III, 18), he is speaking of Wisdom. But if wisdom is the tree of life, and Wisdom itself is Christ, you see, then, that the blessed and holy man is compared to this tree, that is, to wisdom.

You see, therefore, that this blessed and righteous man, who did not walk in the counsel of the impious, who did not do those things but did these things, shall be like a tree planted beside channels of waters. That is, he shall be like Christ, since he has made us sit with him in the heavenly places and reign with him (Ephes. II, 6). You see, then, that we shall reign with Christ in heaven. You see that this tree was planted in paradise, and that we have all been planted together with him.

“And he shall be like a tree planted beside [Col. 1281C] channels of waters.” For from that spring all the rivers proceed. “Which shall yield its fruit in its season.” This tree does not yield fruit at every time, but “in its season.” This tree does not yield fruit in the present age, but in the future, that is, on the day of judgment. This tree now has flowers; this tree now puts forth shoots and promises future crops.

This tree has two things: it has both fruit and leaves. Its fruit is the meaning in the Scriptures; its leaves are the simple words. The fruit lies in the meaning, while the leaves are in the words. Whoever, therefore, reads the holy Scriptures, if he reads them according to the Jews, understands only the leaves; but if he understands them spiritually, he gathers the fruit.

“And its leaf shall not fall.” Nevertheless, even the leaves of this tree are useful. Indeed, if someone understands even according to the historical sense [Col. 1281D], he gains benefit for his soul.

We read in the Apocalypse of John—a book that is not accepted in these provinces; nevertheless, we should know that throughout the West, and in the other provinces of Phoenicia and in Egypt, the book is accepted and is ecclesiastical, for ancient ecclesiastical men also, among whom are Irenaeus, Polycarp, and Dionysius, as well as other Roman interpreters, among whom is the holy Cyprian, accept and interpret the book—we read there:

“And behold,” he says, “I saw one throne set in place, and one Lamb; and,” he says, “a tree beside the river, and on both sides of the bank the same tree” (Apoc. XXII). That is, it was on this side and on that side. “And the tree,” he says, “had fruits, and each year, in each month, it bore fruit twelve times” [Col. 1282A]. “And it had,” he says, “leaves, and its leaves were for the healing of the nations.”

“I saw,” he says, “one throne set in place.” For although we believe in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and although there is a Trinity, there is nevertheless one kingdom. “I saw,” he says, “one throne set in place, and I saw,” he says, “one Lamb standing in the sight of the throne.” This is said of the assumption of the Savior’s body: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.”

“And,” he says, “a spring went forth from beneath the middle of the throne.” You see, therefore, that from the middle of the throne there proceeds a spring of graces. Yet that spring does not proceed from the throne unless the Lamb stands opposite it. For unless we believe in Christ’s incorporation, we do not receive these graces.

“And,” he says, “one lofty tree had been set there.” He did not say “trees,” but “one tree.” If it is one tree, how is it on this side of the bank and on that side of the bank? If he had said, “I saw trees,” it could have happened that some were on one side and others on the other. But now one tree is said to be on both sides [Col. 1282B]; one river proceeds from the throne of God, that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit. And this grace of the Holy Spirit is in the holy Scriptures, that is, in this river of the Scriptures. Yet this river has two banks: the Old and the New Testament. And the tree planted on both sides is Christ.

This tree bore fruit twelve times in the year, that is, in each month. For we cannot receive fruit from this tree except through the apostles. Whoever, therefore, comes to the tree through the apostles must receive fruit; he must gather fruit from the holy Scriptures, that is, the divine meaning dwelling within the letter [Col. 1282C].

Whoever, then, comes to this tree through the apostles gathers its fruit. But whoever cannot do so is still weaker; he is not yet a disciple, but belongs to the crowd, is outside, is a gentile. Whoever cannot gather the fruit should gather the words, that is, the leaves for the healing of the nations. For it is written: “And its leaves were for the healing of the nations.” If someone still belongs to the nations, if he is not a disciple and still belongs to the crowd, let him receive its leaves, that is, let him receive the simple words as medicine.

Thus it is written: “Its leaves were for the healing of the nations,” that is, for medicine. Why have we said all this and gone on to the Apocalypse? Because it is written that it “shall yield its fruit in its season, and its leaf shall not fall, and everything that it does shall always prosper” [Col. 1282D].

We have spoken of the blessedness of the righteous man; we have spoken of his reward. For the one who has not done the three things and has done the two is compared with the tree of paradise, that is, with Christ’s wisdom. We have therefore spoken of the holy man. Now let us look at the opposite man. What is said about the sinner and the impious?

“Not so the impious.” All those kinds of rewards that we said belonged to the righteous, the impious will not receive. “Not so the impious.” He did not say, “Not so sinners”; for if he had spoken of sinners, we would all have been excluded. “Not so the impious.”

There is this difference between the impious person and the sinner: the impious person denies God; the sinner confesses God and sins. “Not so the impious.” In some copies this second phrase is read: “Not so.” “Not so the impious, not so.” But we should know [Col. 1283A] that in Hebrew it is written only once.

We have spoken of the holy man and of his comparison. “And he shall be like a tree planted beside channels of waters.” Now, by contrast, the impious person is described. Just as the righteous man is compared with a tree, so the impious person is compared with dust that the wind drives from the face of the earth.

Although dust comes from the earth, nevertheless it ceases to be earth. But he is like dust that the wind drives from the face of the earth. Consider what is said: the impious person will be so wretched that he will not even be earthly dust. He seems not to have substance, yet he has his own substance. He has nothing solid; but whatever he has, he has for punishment. He is scattered here and there. He is never in one place. Wherever the wind drags him, there its force directs him.

So too the impious person who has once denied God: wherever the devil’s breeze drags him, there he is led by error [Col. 1283B]. Since we have said what the righteous person is and with what he is compared, what the impious person is and with what he is compared, and since we have spoken of the present age, we must now learn about the future and eternal age.

“Therefore the impious do not rise in the judgment, nor sinners in the council of the righteous.”

We read in the Gospel according to John: “Whoever believes in me will not be judged; whoever does not believe in me has already been judged” (John III, 18). Who, then, is to be judged, if the one who believes will not be judged, and the one who does not believe has already been judged? Who will be judged on the day of judgment?

Let us therefore seek the middle position between the believer and the unbeliever: who is to be judged? The one who believes will not be judged. Whoever believes does not sin; whoever truly believes does not sin; whoever has true faith does not sin. Indeed, when we sin, our mind wavers in faith. At the time when we sin, when we grow angry, when we slander, when we commit murders, when we commit fornication [Col. 1283C]—where is faith?

Therefore, when he says, “Whoever believes in me will not be judged,” the one who is already blessed has no need to be judged. “Whoever does not believe in me has already been judged”: he has already been predestined for punishment. Who, then, is judged? The one who indeed believes but is overcome by sins; the one who has good things and also has evil things; the one who does good when he believes and does evil when he does not believe.

Let us see, then, what is now said: “Therefore the impious do not rise in the judgment.” They do not rise in order to be judged, because they have already been judged. For “whoever does not believe in me has already been judged.”

“Nor sinners in the council of the righteous.” He did not say, “Sinners do not rise,” but “they do not rise in the council of the righteous” [Col. 1283D]. They do not deserve to rise with those who are not to be judged. If they believed in me, they would rise with those who are not to be judged.

“For the Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the path of the impious will perish.”

“For the Lord knows the way of the righteous.” And what is so great if the Lord knows the way of the righteous, if the Lord is said to know those whom he deigns to know? Thus it is said of sinners: “Depart from me, workers of iniquity; the Lord does not know you” (Luke XIII, 27). The Apostle says: “If anyone knows, he will be known” [Note: [Col. 1283D] In the sacred text the sense is the opposite: εἰ δέ τις ἀγνοεῖ, ἀγνοεῖται, “if anyone is ignorant, he will be ignored.” Martianaeus thinks that the author either read without the privative prefix or certainly took it as equivalent to γνοεῖ, “knows.” Yet this may have been the reading of the ancient Latin translation.]

“For the Lord knows the way of the righteous” [Col. 1284A] (I Cor. XIV, 38).

The sinner is not known by God; the righteous person is known by God.

We read in Genesis that, at the time when Adam transgressed—when he listened to the serpent more than to God, when he hid himself from the face of God—the Lord came into the garden after the meal and walked there (Gen. III). Consider what is said: God seeks Adam not at midday but toward evening. For Adam had already lost the sun; he did not have midday. He came at evening, that is, δειλινόν, and he walked, for God does not stand still for the sinner, but walks.

He knew that Adam was in the garden and was not ignorant of what had happened; but because Adam had sinned, God does not know him. And God said: “Adam, where are you?” We have spoken of how the sinner is unknown to God.

By contrast, we must learn [Col. 1284B] how the righteous person is known by God. God says to Abraham: “Go out from your land and from your kindred” (Gen. XII, 1). He came to Palestine; he stayed in Hebron and in Gerar for a long time. When a son, Isaac, had been born to him and he had received the promise, “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed,” he took Isaac and offered him to God. A voice was heard from heaven: “Spare your son.” And immediately it is written that, at the time when he had offered his son, God said to Abraham: “Now I know that you fear the Lord your God.”

You had spoken for so long, and only now did you know Abraham? But because his faith was great in offering his son, God then first began to know him.

Why have I said all this? Because it is written: “For the Lord knows the way of the righteous.”

Let us state it another way [Col. 1284C]: the way, the life, and the truth are Christ. Let us therefore walk in Christ, and God the Father will know our way.

“But the path of the impious will perish.” He did not say, “The impious will perish.” For if they do penance, they too will be saved. At the time when the apostle Paul persecuted Christ and the churches, he was impious. If, therefore, the impious will perish, there is no place for repentance. But he did not say, “The impious will perish,” but “the path of the impious will perish.” That is, impiety will perish—not the impious person, but impiety itself. The human being who was impious will not perish; rather, when the human being performs penance, impiety will perish.

May God therefore grant us not to do the three things and to do the two; may we be compared with the tree of life; may we not be impious, being compared with dust; may we not be sinners, since sinners do not rise in the council of the righteous; and may the evil way [Col. 1284D] perish. And may we bless God, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM V

The fifth psalm is introduced by this title: “For the end, for her who receives the inheritance: a psalm of David.”

Many think that the titles do not belong to the psalms. They do not know for what reason they hold this opinion. If the titles were not found in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin volumes, they would be right to think so. But now, since they are found in Hebrew books—and especially this title, which is prefixed to the fifth psalm—I am astonished that they wish to say that something in Scripture exists without purpose [Col. 1285A]. If not one iota or one stroke will pass away from the Law, how much more will such words or syllables not pass away!

“For the end, for her who receives the inheritance: a psalm of David.” The inheritance is not promised at the beginning, but at the end of the world. The Jews thought they would obtain it at the beginning; we shall receive it at the end. Hence the apostle John also says: “Little children, it is the last hour” (I John II, 18). Therefore the end is in the last hour. “For the end”: the inheritance is at the end; “for her who receives the inheritance.”

Who is this woman who receives the inheritance? It seems to me that she is the Church, for she is the one who receives the inheritance. The psalm of David sings at the beginning what the Church receives at the end. Therefore the fifth psalm is spoken in the person of the Church.

Others interpret many things. Many say, according to the historical sense, that it concerns the people of Israel wishing to return from Babylon to Judaea [Col. 1285B]. That is how they interpret it, but they have not interpreted “for the end, for her who receives the inheritance.” We, therefore, comparing spiritual things with spiritual, attempt, with your prayers, to expound this psalm in the person of the Church.

## PSALM VII

Names are assigned to individual things so that things may be recognized from their names. So too the psalms have been prefixed with titles, so that the psalms may be understood from their titles.

The fifth psalm is also prefixed with this title: “For the end, for her who receives the inheritance.” The sixth psalm is prefixed with this title: “For the end, in hymns, for the eighth: a psalm of David.” In the fifth it says, “for her who receives the inheritance”; in the sixth it says, “for [Col. 1285C] the eighth.”

But in the seventh, since it too is to be sung with alleluia, and since the sixth psalm was read on that other Sunday and we were unable to interpret it because of illness, the seventh psalm has now been read. It has this sort of title: “A psalm of David, which he sang to the Lord because of the words of Cush the son of Jemini.”

Consider the mysteries. Were these things written without purpose? In the fifth it says, “for her who receives the inheritance”; in the sixth, “for the eighth”; in the seventh, “because of the words of Cush the son of Jemini.” You see, therefore, how many mysteries are woven together: “for her who receives the inheritance.” For in the fifth psalm we argued, interpreting it in the person of the Church, that the psalm was sung by the Church, which has obtained Christ’s inheritance.

The sixth psalm properly concerns Christ’s resurrection, which is the eighth day. For we have both the first day and the eighth day. On the eighth day we received the kingdoms of heaven. The eighth day is after the Sabbath; the first is at the beginning.

It would take too long if we now wished to speak about the number eight: the eight beatitudes in Matthew; the fact that in the one-hundred-eighteenth psalm each letter has eight verses; the fifteen psalms of the Steps; how there are seven and eight; how Ecclesiastes says, “Give a portion to seven, and also give a portion to eight” (Eccles. XI, 2); how the eastern gate in Ezekiel has seven and eight steps; and how David, the eighth of the sons of Jesse, received the kingdom [Col. 1285D].

This is what is now meant [Col. 1286A] by “for the eighth”: on the eighth day we received the kingdom of heaven. Hence he says: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your wrath.”

But since we cannot interpret two psalms at the same time, it is enough for us to have discussed the title of the sixth psalm. Now let us come to the beginning of the seventh psalm, which begins as follows: “A psalm of David, which he sang to the Lord because of the words of Cush the son of Jemini.”

I know that many, and indeed very learned men, have interpreted this title in the following way: At the time, they say, when Absalom rose up against his father David—I ask you to listen patiently, for we wish to interpret the Scriptures, not to declaim—at the time, then, when Absalom rose up against David, one of David’s friends, named Cush, wished to go with David. But David sent him back to Absalom so that he might destroy Ahithophel’s counsels.

At the time when Ahithophel gave counsel that Absalom should immediately pursue David while he was unprepared and kill him, Cush gave counsel and overthrew Ahithophel’s plan. Cush himself sent a messenger to David, saying, “Absalom is preparing this and this” [Col. 1286B]. David began to flee and to make preparations. At the time when Cush reported these words to David, David sang this psalm to the Lord because Ahithophel’s counsels had been overthrown.

That is what they say, and they have indeed explained it reasonably. But let us read the Scriptures carefully. There it is written that this Cush was the son of an Arachite. Hence that Cush is written with another letter in the Book of Kings: there Cush is written with SAMECH; here, however, Cush is written with the letter SIN.

Moreover, that Cush was the son of Arachi. Hence many Greeks, not knowing this, read “Cush, David’s friend.” You see, therefore, that the Greeks are also mistaken in their reading [Col. 1286C].

It is perfectly clear, then, according to the rule of the Scriptures, that the former Cush was the son of Arachi, whereas this Cush is called the son of Jemini.

Since we have said that the former Cush was the son of Arachi, who is this Jemini? We must compare spiritual things with spiritual and discover the rule governing this name. Where do we find “Jemini” in the Scriptures? There is no doubt that it is one of the twelve tribes, called Benjamin.

Benjamin is interpreted as “son of the right hand.” At the time when Rachel died at Ephrath—for we have seen the tomb with our own eyes and do not need to seek examples [Col. 1286D]—at the time when Rachel was dying, she gave birth, it says, to a child, and the women, or the woman herself who was dying, called his name Benoni, that is, “son of my sorrow.”

But Jacob the father turned his mother’s sorrow into glory. He did not call him Benoni, that is, “son of my sorrow,” but Benjamin, that is, “son of the right hand,” that is, “son of my strength.” Benjamin, therefore, is a name composed of two parts: “son” and “right hand.” Ben means “son”; Jamin means “right hand.”

We should therefore know that the tribe of Benjamin is always called Jemini. We read in the Book of Kings that, at the time when Saul is mentioned, it says: “And behold, a man from the tribe of Benjamin, named Saul, son,” it says, “of Kish, son of Abiel, son of Jetta, son of Jether, son of Jera, son of Jemini.” And immediately there it says, “a Jeminite man,” that is, from the Jeminite tribe, that is, from the tribe of Benjamin.

Let us give another testimony, so that we may have no doubt. Concerning that Shimei who, on the Mount of Olives, at the time when David was fleeing from his son Absalom, the Scripture says: “And behold, Shimei, from the family of Saul, from the tribe of Benjamin.” And he was throwing stones at David and saying, “Go away, go away, you man of blood.”

At the time when one of David’s commanders, named Abishai, said, “I will go and kill him,” what did David say to him? “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? And behold, he who came forth from my loins is fighting against me. And do you marvel if the son of Jemini”—that is, one from the tribe of Benjamin, from the tribe of Saul, who was an enemy—is doing so? [Col. 1287A]

Why have I said all this? To show that Jemini is the tribe of Benjamin. We have said what Benjamin is; we have identified the father’s name. Let us see what “Cush the son of Jemini” means.

“Cush” in the Hebrew language is interpreted [Col. 1287B] as “Ethiopian,” that is, “black” and “dark.” What kind of soul he has, and what kind of body, Jeremiah indicates: “If the Ethiopian will change his skin and the leopard his spots” (Jer. XIII, 23).

Therefore this Cush signifies the black Ethiopian, his enemy Saul. And he says this: Just as an Ethiopian cannot change his skin, so this man cannot change his character. He came into my hands; I could have killed him, I could have shed his blood. I wished to overcome him by showing him kindness, but his wickedness cannot be conquered. For just as an Ethiopian cannot change his skin, so his wickedness cannot be changed.

Finally, what does he say? “Lord my God, if I have done this,” that is, if I have done him some evil; “if there is iniquity in my hands; if I have repaid those who repaid me with evil” [Col. 1287C]. Consider what he says: I returned good for evil; he returned evil for good. It is therefore clear that the psalm is directed against Saul.

## PSALM IX

Jesus the son of Nun fought in the wilderness, and while Moses prayed, he prevailed: one fought, another conquered in prayer. So too I, according to what is written, “Open your mouth, and I will fill it”: I seem to be speaking, but I speak to others while they pray.

The ninth psalm, which you sang to the Lord, is great in its verses and great in its mysteries. Since we cannot discuss everything, let us meanwhile say something about the title. We cannot enter the house, for it is the great palace of the king, nor can we know all the king’s mysteries. For the moment, then, let us show, as though at the title of the house, in its very vestibule, whose house it is.

“For the end, concerning the hidden things of the Son: a psalm of David” [Col. 1287D].

“For the end,” as it is said, does not pertain to the Jews, but to us, who have believed in the end. They were the first son; we are the last. We, therefore, who belong to the end, ought to hear this psalm, because it pertains to those who are at the end.

“Concerning the hidden things of the Son.” What are these hidden things of the Son? The mystery that had been hidden throughout all former ages has been revealed to us at the end.

“Concerning the hidden things of the Son.” In Hebrew it is different. In Hebrew it has ALMOTH, which is interpreted as “for death”: al means “for,” and moth means “death.” Thus “for death” is written in Hebrew, “for the death of the Son.”

Consider, therefore, the Seventy Interpreters, who were translating for Ptolemy, a gentile king. It was difficult to say “the death of the Son,” for they knew that this referred to the Son of God. They saw that it was written, yet they feared to say that the Son of God would die [Col. 1288A].

Let this suffice for the discussion of the title. The whole psalm concerns the death of the Savior.

It is said concerning the Jews: “In the snare that they set, their foot was caught.” Then concerning the calling of the nations: “All the nations that forget God.” And finally against the devil: “God is not before his eyes; he sits in ambush with the rich.”

Wretched are the rich with whom the devil sits. Consider, finally, what is said about the devil: “He sits in ambush with the rich.” For whoever is rich cannot be rich unless he has stripped the poor; therefore it says, “He sits in ambush with the rich.” Whenever the rich persecute [Col. 1288B] Christians, let us say: “The devil sits in ambush with the rich.”

“He lies in wait to seize the poor,” seizing the poor man while he draws him in. “In his snare he will humble him.” This is the impious person; this is the devil. He humbles the poor man not only in wealth but also in spirit, for “blessed are the poor in spirit.”

“In his snare he will humble”—whom? “The poor man” is understood. Consider what is said: “He will humble,” not “he will kill.” But when he has humbled the poor man, the poor man’s humiliation is the devil’s downfall.

For what follows? “He will bend down and fall when he has gained power over the poor.” Does it not seem to you that the devil, in the persecution when he was killing Christians and putting martyrs to death, was himself killed precisely in killing them? “He will bend down and fall when he has gained power over the poor.” The martyr, once killed [Col. 1288C], goes to heaven; the one who kills him is humbled and falls.

This, for the moment, has been briefly discussed from the psalm “concerning the hidden things of the Son.” And this was said in the Old Testament: in the Old Testament the Son is spoken of secretly. Now let us read in the Gospel openly, concerning the revealed things of the Son.

## PSALM LXXVIII

“For we have become poor.” Because you became poor for us, therefore we too have become poor. “A prayer of the poor man when he is anxious and pours out his prayer before the Lord.”

Because you became poor, although you were rich, we too have become poor: “Help us, O God our Savior.” In Hebrew it has: “Help us, Jesus our Savior.” For wherever “Savior” occurs in Hebrew, it has “Jesus.”

Thus [Col. 1288D], when Gabriel came to Mary, he said: “And you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people.” “Help us, Jesus our Savior.”

Consider what he says: “Help.” The one who says “help” is himself also striving to be delivered. For he does not help those who sleep, but those who labor.

“For the glory of your name, O Lord, deliver us,” because your new name has been called upon us, the name that is blessed among the nations. “And be propitious toward our sins for the sake of your name.” You are Savior as Christ, and we are Christians; have mercy on us for the sake of your name.

“Let the groaning of those in chains enter into your sight.” Those who follow Origen’s doctrines are accustomed to say that this means the groaning of those in chains, namely, angels who, they say, have been bound in bodies. For just as fetters placed on the feet weigh down the body and do not allow it to run, so our bodies enclose souls—that is, angels—and weigh them down upon the earth [Col. 1289A].

With what words do they support this? “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. VII, 24). And also what is said: “I desire to be dissolved and be with Christ. To return and be with Christ” (Phil. I, 23).

Consider, he says, what the Apostle says. Whoever says, “I desire to return,” certainly speaks of going to the place where he had previously been.

But I will answer you simply, with rustic simplicity and ecclesiastical simplicity. For this is how the apostles answered and spoke, not with rhetorical and devilish words: “For it is better to return and be with Christ” [Col. 1289B]. For in Greek it has not “to be dissolved,” but “to return”: “to return and be with Christ.”

Where my father Adam was, there I too desire to be. From where he was expelled, I desire to return. In Adam we were all expelled from paradise: “Let the groaning of those in chains enter into your sight.”

Why should I not understand this simply as spoken of the martyrs who are confined in prisons? How many have also been sent into the mines? I say, therefore, that God truly hears the voice of those who are in chains.

“According to the greatness of your arm, possess the sons of the slain.” We are all, if indeed we are worthy, sons of the martyrs. The Apostle, when he was in prison, was in chains; all the apostles, when they were in prisons, were in chains; all the martyrs who were killed had been bound in prisons [Col. 1289C]. Therefore it now says: “Possess the sons of the slain.”

“Repay our neighbors sevenfold into their bosom.” It seems to me that he is not praying against them but for them, that is, “Give them your Sabbath.” Sabbath is interpreted as rest. What he says is this: Make them rest in their wickedness—or, alternatively, repay them here, and do not repay them in the future.

“But we, your people and the sheep of your pasture.” Where he says “sheep,” he signifies innocence. Sheep have no one but a shepherd.

“We shall confess you forever.” “We shall confess” may mean that we do penance, or, what is better, that we glorify you. “From generation to generation”: in the first people and in the second people.

Although according to the historical sense it is said differently in Ezekiel [Col. 1289D], nevertheless, according to the spiritual understanding, we say that these two peoples—that is, the two rods—are joined in Ezekiel and become one kingdom.

“From generation to generation we shall announce your praise.” This is the voice of the apostles: Peter among the people of the circumcision; Paul and Barnabas among the nations.

## PSALM CXXVII

“Blessed are all who fear the Lord.” What reward, what crown do those who fear the Lord possess? Let us see what praise and what reward they have. “You are blessed, and it shall be well with you.”

I have already spoken about blessedness; I am asking what the blessedness is. What blessedness does the one who fears the Lord have? “Your wife shall be like a fruitful vine on the sides of your house. Your sons shall be like shoots of olive trees around your table” [Col. 1290A].

I think that, with Christ’s favor, we all fear God. Do we therefore not possess this blessedness? For it is written: “The one who fears the Lord has this blessedness: your wife shall be like a fruitful vine on the sides of your house; your sons shall be like shoots of olive trees around your table.”

Then is the one who has one son or two not blessed? For what does it say? “Your sons shall be like shoots of olive trees around your table.” Unless we have so many sons that they encircle our table, shall we not possess the blessedness of the one who fears the Lord?

Isaac did not possess this blessedness, for he had two sons, one of them the most wicked Esau, and it would have been much better if he had not been born. He also had one son, Jacob. Did he therefore not possess blessedness, because one could not encircle the table?

Then virgins do not fear God. For what does it mean that the one who fears the Lord is said to possess blessedness? “Your wife shall be like a fruitful vine on the sides of your house; your sons shall be like shoots of olive trees around your table.”

John did not possess this blessedness—John, both the Evangelist and the Baptist, for each was a virgin. Paul did not possess this blessedness [Col. 1290B], he who says: “But I wish that all were as I myself am” (I Cor. VII, 7).

You see, therefore, that the wife and the sons must be understood spiritually. Otherwise, unless we understand them spiritually, the angels do not possess this blessedness, since they have us as sons. Let us therefore return to the order of the reading.

“Blessed are all who fear the Lord.” Just as no one can say, “The Lord is my portion,” unless he has no other [Col. 1290C] portion in the world, so the one who fears something else apart from the Lord does not fear God.

Finally, the Savior himself says: “Do not fear those who can kill the body, but fear him who can destroy both body and soul in Gehenna” (Matt. X, 28). You see, therefore, that the one who does not fear God fears something else apart from God.

What signs does the one who fears the Lord possess? “The one who walks in his ways.” There are many ways, and many ways lead to one way. Thus it is also said in Jeremiah: “Stand in the ways of the Lord, and ask about his eternal paths, and you will find the way, and walk in it” [Col. 1290D] (Jer. VI, 16).

Consider what he says: “Stand in the ways, and ask about the eternal ways of the Lord, and you will find one way, and walk in it.” See how through many ways we come to one way.

This is also said in the Gospel, in other words and under another meaning in the parable about that merchant who had many pearls, sold them, and bought one exceedingly precious pearl. What it says is this: “Have many pearls, and stand in the ways.” That is, “Stand in the ways, and ask about the eternal paths of the Lord.”

Beautifully he says “eternal,” lest we think that, with the coming of Christ, the Law and the prophets have come to an end. But consider what he says: “Stand in the ways”—in the Law and the prophets—and “stand in the ways.”

Do not believe in one way in such a manner that you abandon the many ways. Rather, stand in the ways and ask about the eternal paths of the Lord. Ask about the paths of the Lord: what Jeremiah said, what Isaiah said, what Ezekiel said, and what the other prophets said.

“Ask about the paths.” It is better expressed in Greek as τρίβους, *tribous* [Col. 1291A]. A path is so called because it has been worn down by the feet of those walking upon it. And what is said is this: ask about the paths, that is, the τρίβοι, because the Lord’s foot has worn them down. For the Lord himself also walked in them.

When you have asked about the eternal paths of the Lord, through those paths you will find one way that says, “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” Walk in it.

Consider the mysteries of the Scriptures; consider how many sacraments are contained in the simple words of the Scriptures—in the ways, in the paths, in the Law and the prophets.

He did not say, “Walk,” but “stand.” Stand, so that you do not abandon the Law or the prophets. Nevertheless, when you have found those ways, walk through those ways, in that one way.

You shall eat the labors of your hands. Many, not understanding, have interpreted this passage otherwise: “You shall eat the labors of your fruits.” Indeed, the Latin copies read in this way: “You shall eat the labors of your fruits.” But we read it written thus in the Hebrew: “You shall eat the labors of your hands.” For who eats the labors of fruits? Surely the meaning must be understood in the opposite way, since someone eats the fruit of his labors, not the labors of fruits. Since, therefore, it is written thus in the Hebrew, “You shall eat the labors of your hands.”

[Note: The passage in the manuscript copies has been corrupted by scribes through ignorance of the Greek language. I do not know whether the first author wrote this, for καρπός is some part of the hand; indeed, καρπός is said in Greek to derive from ἀπὸ πάω. The Corbie manuscript, with several words erased, reads as follows: “But *kaaph* is interpreted as some part of the hand; indeed, καρπός is said in Greek to be ΑΡΟΡΑ.” Perhaps ἄρουρα, “arable land, field.” But it would be more suitable to read ἄρθρον, that is, “joint” or “articulation,” of the hand. MART. — The genuine Jerome, *Epistle* 35 in our recension, to Marcella, no. 5: “In this passage,” he says, “it was not the Seventy Translators, but the Latins, deceived by the ambiguity of the Greek word, who interpreted καρπούς, ‘fruits,’ rather than ‘hands,’ although καρποί can also mean hands, which is what is written in Hebrew, *Chaphach*. See also Saint Hilary, *Treatise on this Psalm*, nos. 4 and 5. Here Martianaeus doubts whether the author wrote: “For καρπός is some part of the hand; indeed, καρπός is said in Greek to derive from ἀπὸ πάω.”]

I think that the Greek Septuagint translators also translated this passage correctly: for “hand” is called *JAD* in the Hebrew language; but in this passage they do not have *JAD*, but *CHAAPH*. Now *Chaaph* is interpreted as καρπός—not καρπός in the sense of “fruit,” but as some part of the hand; indeed, καρπός is said in Greek to be ΑΡΕΡΑ. Thus far we have spoken about the interpretation.

“You shall eat the labors of your hands.” [Col. 1291C] Everyone shall reap what he has sown. Behold the human being, and his works. Therefore we too shall eat the labors of our hands. “Hands” signifies works. “You shall eat the labors of your hands.”

Someone may say: “Then shall we eat after the resurrection?” For this is said of the blessed man: “You shall eat the labors of your hands.” I state the matter simply. Since the human being is composed of two substances—that is, of soul and body—the soul is immortal, while the body is mortal. What is mortal, namely the body, also has mortal foods. But what is immortal, namely the immortal soul, also has immortal foods.

Do you wish to know that the soul too has its foods? When the Lord and Savior was hungry, what does he say? “My food is to do the will of him [Col. 1291D] who sent me” (John 4:34). Do you wish to know what foods the soul has? The prophet also tells us: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33:9). For just as the body dies unless it receives its foods, so also the soul dies unless it receives spiritual foods.

Why do I say all this? Because some are accustomed to [Col. 1292A] say: “I have no need of sacred Scripture; it is enough for me simply to fear God.” For this reason we have said that, just as there are foods for the body, so also our souls have foods: the sacred Scriptures.

Your wife is like a fruitful vine within the sides of your house. Solomon says that he wished to take Wisdom as his bride (Wis. 8:2). And elsewhere he says of Wisdom: “Love her, and she will embrace you. Surround her, and she will guard you” (Prov. 4:6). Let us therefore also take this wife and hold her in our embraces. Let us never release her from our bosom. Let her never flee from our hands. If this wife is always in our embrace, we shall beget children by her—not daughters, but sons.

Indeed, here too it is said: “Your children are like olive shoots around your table.” [Col. 1292B] Could he not have said, “Your daughters”? Or could he not have said τὰ τέκνα σου (“your children”), so that both males and females could be understood? But see what he says: “Your sons.” Whoever has Wisdom as his wife does not make daughters of her, but sons. His mind has nothing soft, nothing delicate, nothing tender, nothing effeminate.

Do you suppose that the saints are recorded as having had no daughters but sons for no reason? Let us read Genesis, for there the order of generations is preserved. The holy Abraham had Sarah as his wife; he had Hagar as a concubine; afterward he had Keturah. From the two wives he produces sons. He does not make daughters.

Let us come to Isaac. Isaac too produces two sons and has no daughters. For he was holy and had nothing soft, tender, or effeminate in himself, but everything manly and firm.

Blessed Jacob has twelve patriarchs as sons. And he has one daughter named Dinah, which is interpreted as “a cause of quarrels,” or “a dispute.” Thus he had one daughter and twelve sons. And because of that one daughter so many wars arose at Shechem. Jacob never said, “I am afraid; you have made me hateful.” He says to Levi and Simeon, “Let my soul not enter their council” (Gen. 49:6). Why? Because they wished to undertake the cause of a woman.

Why have I said all this? Because the saints do not have daughters, but have sons only. I tell you something new—new to those who do not know it. For those who read the Scriptures, and read them carefully, it is not new, but something they know.

Jacob had twelve sons who were patriarchs: Reuben, Simeon, Judah, Levi, Issachar, Asher, and the others down to the twelfth. Read in the book of Genesis, and you will never find that any one of those twelve patriarchs produced a daughter, but only sons.

I will tell you one thing, lest you perhaps forget it. Asher had a daughter, Sarah. Jacob had twelve sons and one daughter. Thus, among the twelve patriarchs, one patriarch alone had one daughter. Why have I said all this? [Col. 1293A] So that we ought to understand sons and daughters spiritually in the Scriptures.

Your wife is like a fruitful vine within the sides of your house. Just as a fruitful vine bears many clusters, so also our wife—that is, Wisdom, our wife, who is the bride—bears many clusters. Indeed, elsewhere it is written: “Come, my sister, my bride” (Song 5:1). Lest, when he had said “bride,” you understand something shameful, “sister” is added, so that every shameful love may be excluded. “Come, my sister”: let the love be holy. For this reason I call you both my sister and my bride. I call you my bride so that I may have a wife and beget many sons by you, many sons like clusters from a vine.

Consider how a vine bears various clusters. There is one root. But it spreads its branches far and wide in every direction, and those branches bear their fruits; within those fruits are clusters. One cluster is larger, another smaller; some grapes are larger, others smaller. So also from Wisdom, who is our wife: provided we never release her, many clusters are born, that is, very many virtues, holy thoughts, and excellent works.

“Your children are like olive shoots around your table.” We read elsewhere: “And wine gladdens the heart of man” (Ps. 103:15). We also read in the Song of Songs: “Come, brothers, drink and be drunk.” And wine gladdens the heart of man. This wine does not gladden the heart of man, but overwhelms it and makes it insane. Indeed, it is written that those who are powerful should not drink wine (Prov. 31:4). The Apostle too writes that we ought not to drink wine and eat meat (Rom. 14).

Again it is said to us: “And wine gladdens the heart of man.” But “wine” is understood spiritually: whoever drinks it is immediately made drunk. You all, in order to abandon your possessions, your parents, your children, and your relatives, drank wine and, made drunk for Christ, began to be insane. Does this not seem to you drunkenness? Does it not seem to you a spiritual madness to despise delights, seek filth, flee cities, pursue deserts, know nothing of natural affection, disregard kinship according to the flesh, and know Christ alone?
