Indeed, the apostles were drunk with this wine, and therefore it is said to them: “They are full of new wine” (Acts 2:13). For they had not been made drunk with the Old Law, but with the Gospel. I think, therefore, that Noah was drunk with this wine.

“Your children are like olive shoots.” Our children are compared to nothing else but olive shoots. He did not say “old olive trees,” but “olive shoots.” Just as in the passage concerning the apostles’ drunkenness it does not speak of old wine but of new wine, so here too it says “olive shoots,” which are wholly green in the youth of the Gospel.

Olive shoots are full of light. Oil has this nature: it seasons foods, supplies fuel for light, and restores the body of one exhausted by a long journey, as though returning it to its former labor and health. Indeed, whoever is weary and is anointed seems to recover his former vigor.

Do you suppose that wine and oil are mentioned here without reason? He could not have mentioned honey, other spices, or another tree, but only the vine and the olive: wine and oil. In wine there is severity; in oil, mercy.

Indeed, when the man who was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho had been wounded, the Samaritan—that is, the guardian—poured nothing into him except wine and oil. Wine signifies the severity of the commandments, wine in the symbolic sense, so that whatever evil humor there is may be boiled out and consumed.

But because human weakness cannot bear the truth—for “if you mark iniquities, O Lord, Lord, who shall endure?” (Ps. 129:3)—if the Lord were only just, we could not live. Therefore oil, that is, the oil of mercy, has been joined to his justice, symbolized by wine.

Behold, thus shall the man who fears the Lord be blessed. We have already said much; let us hasten to the end.

May the Lord bless you from Zion. Concerning this Zion, another prophet says: “Zion shall be plowed like a field” (Jer. 26:18). The Lord also says: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to you” [Col. 1294B] (Matt. 23:37). Indeed, when the Lord had drawn near to Jerusalem and saw it, he wept. Why did he weep over it? Certainly he wept because it was about to fall, as though it were about to perish. Indeed, what does he say? “Rise, let us go from here.” And elsewhere he says: “Your house shall be left to you desolate.”

Therefore, when it says, “May the Lord bless you from Zion,” it does not mean that Zion which we see lying desolate. Its very gates, its very field, and its very ruins signify the Lord’s anger. Even if we do not understand, the eyes themselves cry out the Lord’s anger.

“May the Lord bless you from Zion.” Zion is interpreted as “watchtower.” Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace.” If our soul has a watchtower, if it is raised on high, if it does not think about earthly things but about heavenly things; if our soul has a vision of peace—that is, if Christ, who is true peace, dwells in it—he himself blesses us.

If Christ dwells in us, then we too shall be Zion. We too shall be Jerusalem. “And may you see the children of your children.” I am speaking to you. If I instruct others through my discourse, I have seen my children; if you instruct others, I have seen the children of my children.

Let us therefore pray to the Lord that we may have children, that we may have grandchildren, and that we may always have a numerous offspring. Let us hasten to make such children. This is a holy union. I tell you something new: without the embrace of a wife, many such children are born.

Peace be upon Israel. Israel is interpreted as “a mind seeing God.” See, therefore, what is said: “Peace be upon Israel”—upon those who have a mind that sees God. If my mind has a vision of God, if I always see Christ, I shall see no one else. Whoever has Christ within himself has peace within himself: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27).

Although there are many persecutions, although there are many who persecute, nevertheless the one in whom Christ dwells always possesses Christ. To him be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM 128

“They have often fought against me from my youth; let Israel now say. They have often fought against me from my youth.”

Two things are said: “They have often fought against me,” and “They have fought against me from my youth.” Therefore, if I began to serve the Lord in middle age—for example, at forty years old—I cannot say, “They have fought against me from my youth.” But what shall I say? “They killed me from my youth”; “They wounded me from my youth”; “They trampled me from my youth.”

But he who begins to serve the Lord from childhood is often attacked by the devil and his angels, and yet is not conquered. What should he say? “They have often fought against me from my youth; yet they could not prevail against me.”

An athlete is not crowned unless he has competed according to the rules: unless he has received a blow, unless his face has been bruised, unless blood has flowed from his face. Bruising earns the crown; pain earns joy.

“They have often fought against me from my youth.” Let the virgin of the Lord say this verse. Let the monk who began to serve the Lord at an early age say it. But I, who began to serve the Lord at forty or fifty years old, how can I say, “They have often fought against me from my youth”? Let the virgin say this.

[Col. 1295B] Let the monk who is whole in body and spirit say it. And what should he say? “They have often fought against me from my youth.”

Someone may say: “O monk, how did demons and the devil fight against you?” It was indeed human beings who seemed to be attacking me, but in the human beings I understood the devil. Therefore, when people persecute them, let us not be angry with those who persecute, but let us suffer with them and mourn for them, because there is another who persecutes through the persecutors.

If a demoniac—one who has a demon—comes and strikes me with his fist and kicks me, surely I do not become angry with him? He strikes with his fist, while I weep and mourn for the one striking. For I see that he is struck more grievously by the one working within him than I am by his hand.

Therefore, whenever we suffer something and endure various temptations, let us understand that it is he, and those who generate temptations for us, who are present in human beings.

Someone may say: “Establish this very point from the Scriptures, for we ought not to say anything unless it has been adorned and approved by the Scriptures.”

Judas was a betrayer, but Satan entered into him, and he himself betrayed through the betrayer. The wife of Potiphar, at the time when she seized Joseph, her slave—a mistress her slave, a very rich woman a poor man, a citizen a foreigner—she was the one who seized Joseph, but the holy man understood that the devil was present in the hands of the woman and was holding him.

Why have I said all this? So that when we suffer anything at the hands of human beings, we may not be angry with human beings, but may mourn for them. Let us see that instigator lying in ambush, who works within them.

“They have often fought against me from my youth; yet they could not prevail against me.” They fought against me through shameful thoughts; they fought against me through anger. I consented to the thoughts; but [Perhaps “I did not” should be added] I consented to the temptations. Yet I did something to which the thought was compelling me. If anger overcame me and I wronged my brother, I cannot say, “Yet they could not prevail against me.” For they did prevail against me.

## PSALM 129

“Sinners have built upon my back.”

Pay close attention to what Scripture says. The holy man is an athlete, and no one is crowned unless he has competed according to the rules. You know that there are many kinds of athletes. There are some athletes; others, however, are *Pammacharii* [Note: *Pammacharii* is corrupt. Since this word denotes the very fortunate rather than fighters, I think it should be read thus. I would prefer it to be emended to *Pancratiarii*, which is the same name as *Pancratiastae*.]

; others compete for days; still others are runners, that is, those who run in the stadium. Indeed, the Apostle says that he runs in order to reach the crown (1 Cor. 9:26). And elsewhere he says: “Forgetting what lies behind, I stretch forward to what lies ahead” (Phil. 3:13).

See, therefore, what Scripture says: “Sinners were building upon my back.” I always ran in this way, and I ran so much that my adversary never went before me, but was always found behind me. He never came before my eyes; for he could not endure the light of my eyes. Rather, he always pursued that part which is blind, which has no eyes.

“Sinners were building upon my back.” Whenever someone slanders his brothers, that person is building behind his back. “Sinners were building upon my back,” but I did not see their ambushes. They were building behind my back, while I was gazing with my eyes upon paradise. They were plotting ambushes for me, while I desired to see the crown.

“They prolonged their iniquity.” What does “they prolonged their iniquity” mean? If I sin and afterward do penance for my sin, my iniquity is short and not long. But if I sin, then on whatever day I sin, the cord of my sins becomes longer.

Hence it is also said elsewhere: “The cords of sinners have surrounded me” (Ps. 118:61). See what it says: “The cords of sinners have surrounded me.” And elsewhere it is written: “Everyone shall be bound by the cords of his sins” (Prov. 5:22). See what it says: “Everyone shall be bound by the cords of his sins.”

A cord of sins cannot be woven unless I have several sins. If I commit one sin, it is not yet so much a cord as a single thread. But if it is a single thread, it is quickly broken and cannot hold or bind. If there are several sins and they prolong the iniquities, a cord is made from the several sins as from several threads; it binds and is not quickly broken.

Why have I said all this? Because we read in this verse: “They prolonged their iniquity.”

“The just Lord shall cut the necks of sinners.” See what it says: it did not say, “He shall cut down sinners.” If it had said this, no one could be saved, since we are all sinners. But what does it say? “The just Lord shall cut the necks of sinners”—those who are both sinners and proud, because “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble.” Therefore he shall cut the necks of sinners.

## PSALM 131

“Remember, Lord, David and all his meekness.”

Many think that, because it is written in the Gospel, “Have mercy on us, Son of David”—these are the words of the blind men who were sitting at Jericho—this David, who is interpreted as “strong of hand,” refers to the Lord the Savior.

But if in this psalm we wish to refer it to him, as they think, it greatly harms our understanding. For if the words “Remember, Lord, David and all his meekness” refer to Christ, how [Col. 1297A] does he speak as though of someone else: “Until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob”? “Behold, we heard of it in Ephrata; we found it in the fields of the wood.” And how is it said: “For the sake of David your servant, do not turn away the face of your Christ”?

If, as they think, Christ is David, how does it say, “For the sake of David your servant, do not turn away the face of your Christ”? The order does not stand. For if David is called Christ, we begin to understand it thus: “For the sake of Christ your servant, do not turn away the face of your Christ.”

I say this concerning those who interpret David as Christ in this passage—not that we deny that David can be interpreted as Christ according to the circumstances of particular passages, but in this passage the sense does not permit it.

And I shall tell you why they err. It is written: “Remember, Lord, David and all his meekness.” And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble in heart.” This is indeed a proper meaning; but they err in interpreting David here as Christ and referring his meekness to Christ.

Let us therefore interpret this psalm with reference to David, so that the one who will be born from David may truly be understood as Christ. Indeed, observe the order. Since the psalm is long and we have already said much, we ought briefly to touch upon its meanings and not argue at length, so that the intelligent listener may understand for himself, from what we have said, even those things we do not say.

“As he swore to the Lord, he vowed a vow to the God of Jacob.” In the Hebrew it does not have ὼ, that is, “as,” nor is this the sense; rather, it has ὸς, that is, “who.” The sense is therefore: “Remember, Lord, David and all his meekness, who swore to the Lord and vowed a vow to the God of Jacob.” And I think this arose not so much through a fault of the Septuagint translators as through an error of the scribes.

“If I enter into the tent of my house.” David says this: “I seek no other rest than Christ, who is to be born from my seed”—that is, the one whom you promised, because he is to be born from my loins.

“If I give sleep to my eyes and slumber to my eyelids, and rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob.” Many think that this is said of the Church, but it seems to me to be said not so much of the Church as of holy Mary. Indeed, it says:

“Behold, we heard of it in Ephrata; we found it in the fields of the wood.”

Let us read the holy Scriptures and, by day and by night, examine each syllable and letter. Someone may say that by “Ephrata” he means Bethlehem. For we read in Genesis: “He came to Bethlehem,” that is, Ephrata. This is said of Jacob when his wife Rachel died. This is Ephrata.

But let us see why Ephrata received its name. For it is written in Chronicles that Maria, the sister of Moses and Aaron, had a husband [Note: This is the opinion of the Hebrews. MART. — Jerome is mistaken in his *Hebrew Questions on the Book of Chronicles*: “Caleb took another wife named Ephrata, from whom he begot Hur, the husband of Maria, the sister of Moses, and father of Huri,” and so forth.]

—or rather, not Ur but Or (1 Chr. 11). The order is then described, and it is said: “Maria, the sister of Moses and Aaron; this is Ephrata.” This is written in the books of Chronicles. Search, and you will find it. Indeed, this Ephrata too received its name. It may perhaps seem to someone that this is not true because it is unusual; but I refer him to the authority of the book.

“Behold, we heard of it in Ephrata.” In the Hebrew it does not have “it” in the feminine, but “him,” that is, the one who is to be born from the seed. “We heard of it in Ephrata”—which is the sense when it refers to Mary. But we can also understand it simply, since Ephrata is called Bethlehem, and Christ was born in Bethlehem.

Blessed, therefore, is the place that was sung so long beforehand by the voice of the prophets. All holy places are indeed venerable: where he was born, where he was crucified, where he rose again, and where he ascended victoriously into heaven. But this place is especially more venerable.

See how great was God’s mercy: here a little infant was born. He is placed in a manger, [Col. 1298B] for “there was no room for them in the inn.”

O monk, the Lord is born on earth, and he has no private cell: “there was no room for them in the inn.” The entire human race has a place; Christ found no place among human beings. He found no place in Plato, no place in Aristotle, but in a manger—among beasts, brute animals, and the simple and innocent.

Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Foxes have dens, and the birds of heaven have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.”

## PSALM 141

“An understanding of David, when he was in the cave.” A prayer is prescribed.

According to the historical sense, this title refers to the time when David was fleeing from Saul in the desert of Engaddi, hidden in a cave. Saul entered without knowing it, as though by his own intention. But because the title says, “An understanding of David,” we ought to understand the psalm spiritually.

This psalm is also received as referring to the true David, the Lord, and Saul is understood as the devil; the cave, however, is this world. The devil sends nothing good into this world, but filth and whatever is rotten.

The cave is understood as this world because it does not possess perfect light in comparison with the future; nevertheless, the Lord’s coming into this world caused a kind of light to shine. Therefore the Apostle says: “Who is the radiance of his glory” (Heb. 1:3). Thus, just as David entered the cave, hiding himself from Saul, so also the Lord entered this world and suffered persecution.

[Col. 1298D] “I pour out my prayer in his sight.” He spoke more significantly: “I pour out my whole heart in the sight of the Lord,” just as someone confesses his wound to a physician and tells him all the maladies he has, so that the physician may apply appropriate treatment.

“I declare my tribulation before him”—that is, the tribulation which the Apostle counts, and which, when counted together with the others, produces hope; and hope does not disappoint.

“When my spirit was failing within me.” Unless the evil spirit that was suffocating Saul departs from us, the Lord cannot know our paths. What are the paths of the righteous? Justice, good works, the straight way, chastity, self-restraint, and other things like these.

“On this way in which I walked they hid a snare for me.” Vices are close to virtues. On whatever way someone wishes to walk, they set snares on it—whether in fasting, almsgiving, or the other virtues.

“I looked to the right and saw, and there was no one who knew me.” If we understand the psalm as spoken by God, the Lord himself is speaking: “All my disciples abandoned me and fled.” One remained, Peter, who promised, saying: “If I must die for you, I will not abandon you”; yet he too denied him.

Therefore he said, “I looked to him on the right,” and did not say, “on the left,” because Peter did penance.

[Col. 1299B] “Flight has perished from me.” This was when he was seized by the Jews. “And there is no one who seeks my soul.” For they were all crying out: “Crucify, crucify” (Luke 23).

“Attend to my supplication, because I have been humbled exceedingly.” Unless someone has been humbled, he is not heard by the Lord. For what does it profit someone to pray in words while holding his neck erect? But if we understand this as referring to the Lord: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble in heart.”

“Deliver me from those who persecute me, because they have grown stronger than I.” Those who fight against us are stronger than we are—that is, the rulers of this world.

“Bring my soul out of prison, that I may confess your name.” That is, out of this body. “To confess,” that is, to glorify. As he says: “I confess to you, Father.”

“The righteous await me until you repay me.” The Lord says: “The apostles await me until I rise from the dead.”

## J. MARTIANAEUS’ NOTICE TO THE FOLLOWING PREFACE TO THE BOOK OF PSALMS

In three manuscript copies of the Canon of Hebrew Truth, which I recently published in volume 1 of this new edition of the works of Saint Jerome, I consistently found the following Preface to the Book of Psalms, translated from Hebrew into Latin by the same Jerome who had prefaced his version with another, very different preface.

The distinguished man Ludovicus Ferrandus published this prologue at the end of the volume of his *Paraphrase on David’s Psalter*. But the learned writer was mistaken when he thought that it had been written by that false Jerome, the compiler of the *Commentary on the Psalms*. Hence Jean-Baptiste Cotelier, in his notes to volume 3 of the *Ecclesiastical Greek Monuments*, openly declared that the aforementioned preface belonged to neither Jerome.

“It seems,” he says, “to belong neither to Jerome nor to that Jerome-like compiler.” Although I am not entirely certain whose it was, I scarcely doubt that this prologue ought to be attributed to Eusebius of Caesarea. For a considerable portion of it seems to have been derived from his *Hypotheses* on the Psalter, and appears to announce this to us.

But whoever rendered the preface into Latin had scarcely been imbued with the rudiments of learning, since he translated it into Latin without writing it in Latin. For the rest, see my brief annotations.

[Col. 1299]

[Note: In the Memmian manuscript and in our Sangerman manuscript this preface is attributed to Jerome: “Here begins the preface of Jerome the presbyter to the Book of Psalms.” The Carcassonne manuscript is better, since it does not retain Jerome’s name. MART. — We said in the notice prefixed to this appendix that this preface should be compared with the *Hypotheses* of Eusebius, which the author transferred here for the most part, though with little success. Martianaeus praises two manuscript copies, one Memmian and the other Sangerman, which attribute this writing to Jerome. We compared it with one marked in the Ambrosian Library by the letter I and the number 6, which has no author’s name attached and is often of better quality.]

## PREFACE ON THE BOOK OF PSALMS  
*(C, G, S)*

[Col. 1299C] In the Hebrew Book of Psalms, all the psalms are written without the addition of numbers, and indeed in different ways: some are joined together, while others are divided. Accordingly, the first and second are joined together according to the Hebrew text, while the seventy-seventh is joined together among us; in Hebrew, however, they are divided into two.

The Hebrews divide the Book of Psalms into five books [or: “books”]. The first extends from “Blessed is the man” to the end of the fortieth psalm. The second extends from “As the deer longs for the fountains [or: “fountain”] of waters” to the end of the seventy-first. The third is “How good is the God of Israel,” extending to the eighty-eighth. The fourth is “Lord, you have been made our refuge,” extending to the hundred and fifth. The fifth is “Give thanks to the Lord,” extending to the last psalm.

It should be observed that the order of the psalms was not composed according to their history or chronology. Rather, much was threatened over a long period of time [Perhaps: “by many threats over a long period of time”], as the Book of Kings makes clear.

For the Jewish people, largely given over to the worship of idols, had been infected with forgetfulness of their ancestral Scriptures, so that they neither obeyed the book of the Mosaic Law nor retained among themselves the memory of their fathers’ piety. Thus they also killed the prophets who rebuked their impiety, and on account of this they were first handed over to Assyrian captivity.

Therefore, under such circumstances, it is not surprising that the things committed to the Book of Psalms fell away and were handed over to oblivion through the passage of many years.

After this, either Ezra or some prophetic man, together with the others of their assembly, hastened to collect the Book of Psalms, not finding them all at once but over different periods. They first arranged those that were found earlier; consequently, not even all of David’s psalms lie in order [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads: “in order, as though they were lying,” and so forth.]

Then, finding in the book, intermingled, the psalms of the sons of Korah, Asaph, Solomon, Moses, Ethan, Heman, Jeduthun, and David himself, they arranged them not according to the times when they were spoken but according to the times when they were found.

This also caused those who belonged to later periods but were found first to be received first, while those who belonged to earlier periods but were found later were arranged in second place. You will find the same thing done among the prophets.

[Note: From this passage and others that follow, it can be demonstrated clearly that Eusebius of Caesarea was the author of the words of this prologue. For his *Hypotheses* on the Psalter exist in Greek in volume 6 of the London Polyglot, p. 137, and in Latin in Thomas Car’s prefaces to the Psalter. But the person who transmitted Eusebius in this prologue in fragments and sections [Col. 1302D] to Latin strove to overturn the order of the *Hypotheses*, lest we recognize the theft. MART.]

This is their division of the Book of Psalms, as it is contained in the certain and most carefully written copies of the ancients and in the Hebrew text itself.

The persons to whom the psalms belong are: without inscription, 17; with superscriptions, 133. Of the superscribed psalms, David has 72; the sons of Korah, 11; Asaph, 12; Ethan, 1; Heman, 1; Moses, 1; Solomon, 2; without a name, 17; Hallelujah psalms, 17; “for the winepresses,” 3; “Songs of Ascents,” 15. There are also 17 without a name—that is, psalms that have superscriptions but do not indicate whose they are—making 150 altogether.

Let no one therefore assume that all the psalms are David’s, but recognize that they also belong to other prophets who prophesied in song. For this reason, the whole Scripture which among the Hebrews is superscribed with the name “Psalter,” not “David’s,” is indiscriminately called the Book of Psalms.

[Note: The scholiast on Psalm 118, volume 6 of the Polyglot, makes the same statement. Eusebius also expressly said this in *Preparation for the Gospel*, book 11, chapter 5. MART.]

As someone said, among the Hebrews the Song of Deuteronomy is written in hexameter; but the psalms are written in trimeter and tetrameter verse. Therefore, the psalms that are found among the Hebrews differ from those found among us.

To David himself: the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, tenth, eleventh, twelfth, thirteenth, fourteenth, fifteenth, sixteenth, [Note: [Col. 1302D] The same manuscript adds “and the seventeenth.”] seventeenth, eighteenth, nineteenth, twentieth, twenty-first, twenty-second, twenty-third, twenty-fourth, twenty-fifth, twenty-sixth, twenty-seventh, twenty-eighth, twenty-ninth; thirtieth, [Col. 1301D] thirty-first, thirty-second, thirty-third, thirty-fourth, thirty-[Col. 1302A]fifth, thirty-sixth, thirty-seventh, thirty-eighth, thirty-ninth; fortieth; fiftieth, fifty-first, fifty-second, fifty-third, fifty-fourth, fifty-fifth, fifty-sixth, fifty-seventh, fifty-eighth, fifty-ninth; sixtieth, sixty-first, sixty-second, sixty-third, sixty-fourth, [Note: [Col. 1302D] Again the manuscript adds “the sixty-fifth and the sixty-sixth.”] sixty-seventh, sixty-eighth, sixty-ninth; one hundredth, one hundred second, one hundred seventh, one hundred eighth, one hundred ninth; one hundred twenty-first, one hundred twenty-third; one hundred thirtieth, one hundred thirty-second, one hundred [Note: [Col. 1302D] Conversely, here this manuscript omits the one hundred thirty-third, thirty-fourth, thirty-fifth, and thirty-sixth.] thirty-[Col. 1302B]third, one hundred thirty-fourth, one hundred thirty-fifth, one hundred thirty-sixth, one hundred thirty-seventh, one hundred thirty-eighth; one hundred thirty-ninth; one hundred fortieth, one hundred forty-first, one hundred forty-second, one hundred forty-third, one hundred forty-fourth—seventy-two in all.

Those not inscribed above are: the first, second, thirty-second, forty-second, seventieth, ninety-first, ninety-second, ninety-third, ninety-fourth, ninety-fifth, ninety-sixth, ninety-seventh, ninety-eighth; one hundred third, one hundred fifteenth, one hundred thirty-sixth, one hundred forty-[Col. 1302C]seventh—seventeen in all.

To the sons of Korah: the forty-first, forty-third, forty-fourth, forty-fifth, forty-sixth, forty-seventh, forty-eighth; the eighty-third, eighty-fourth, eighty-sixth, and eighty-eighth—eleven in all.

Anonymous psalms, which have superscriptions but do not indicate whose they are: the sixty-fifth, sixty-sixth, ninety-first, ninety-eighth, ninety-ninth; one hundred first, one hundred nineteenth, one hundred twentieth, one hundred twenty-second, one hundred twenty-third, one hundred twenty-fourth, one hundred twenty-fifth, one hundred twenty-seventh, one hundred twenty-eighth, one hundred [Col. 1302D] twenty-ninth; one hundred thirtieth, [Note: [Col. 1302D] The Ambrosian manuscript reads “one hundred thirty-first.”] one hundred thirty-third—seventeen in all.

Songs of Alleluia: [Col. 1303A] the one hundred fourth, one hundred fifth, one hundred sixth, one hundred tenth, one hundred eleventh, one hundred twelfth, one hundred thirteenth, one hundred fourteenth, one hundred fifteenth, one hundred sixteenth, one hundred seventeenth, one hundred eighteenth; one hundred thirty-fourth, one hundred thirty-fifth; one hundred forty-fifth, one hundred forty-sixth, one hundred forty-eighth, one hundred [Note: [Col. 1303C] This one hundred forty-ninth is missing from the Ambrosian manuscript.] forty-ninth, and one hundred fiftieth—seventeen in all.

Ethan: LXXXVIII; Solomon’s: LXXI, CXXVI.

Asaph: the forty-ninth, [Note: [Col. 1303C] Here too the seventy-ninth is absent from the Ambrosian manuscript.] seventy-ninth, seventy-second, seventy-third, seventy-fourth, seventy-fifth, seventy-sixth, seventy-[Col. 1303B]seventh, seventy-eighth, seventy-ninth; eightieth, eighty-first, and eighty-second—twelve in all.

Of Moses: the eighty-ninth.

All the psalms together number one hundred fifty. “For the winepresses,” three, and “Songs of Ascents,” fifteen, are placed according to their titles. There are no others beyond the one hundred fifty.

[Note: [Col. 1303C] This too that ignorant Latin translator borrowed from Eusebius. MART.] In those psalms whose superscriptions contain an obelus [Note: [Col. 1303C] Understand “obelus,” which cuts out what is superfluous.]—these additions occur only in the Septuagint. They are not found among the other translators. [Note: [Col. 1303C] These two words—“asterisk, obelus”—had slipped from the margin into the text; the learned J.-B. Cotelerius, mentioned above, had already observed this before us. [Col. 1304C] MART.—The Ambrosian manuscript adds here “asterisk and obelus.”]

Whatever material is present in the Hebrew and among the other translators but is not found in the Septuagint and Theodotion, we have added with asterisks. Whatever, however, we found in the aforementioned Septuagint or in Theodotion, but neither in the Hebrew nor among the others, we have placed under an obelus.

As for the superscriptions mentioned above, because the Septuagint translated them according to a certain dispensation, they rendered *For the hidden things of the son* as *For the death of the son*. Just as the earth first brought forth four-footed creatures and the things generated from it, and just as at first we feed a child with milk, so, before the Savior’s coming, the interpretation of the Scriptures was arranged for Ptolemy. For they were translated under [Note: [Col. 1304C] He says most incompetently that the Septuagint translators translated the Scriptures into Greek under the apostles, although the Septuagint translation was completed approximately three hundred years before Christ. MART.] the apostles, since, because of unbelief, it was impossible that the Scriptures should prophesy about Christ.

**Ninth Psalm.** “I will confess to you with my whole heart,” instead of “I give thanks.” “I will recount all your wonders.” Moses was not able to recount everything, but only some of the wonders that occurred in Egypt; Christ, however, also recounts those above the heavens.

“By turning my enemy backward.” The devil was the enemy who held the human race.

“You rebuked the nations; the impious perished.” The devil.

“How shall I proclaim your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion?” The city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, is the daughter of Zion.

**Eighty-ninth Psalm.** “Lord, you have become our refuge from generation to generation.” According to the generations, Enoch was a refuge; thereafter, Abraham, and the rest.

“The earth,” having mountains hidden within it, at last—as the water revealed them—laid the earth bare according to the seasons, and the mountains were shown.

“And you said, ‘Return, children of men.’” Concerning the calling of the nations.

“Because a thousand years.” What he did for Moses.

“Like the morning watch, let it pass away like grass.” The things according to [Note: [Col. 1304C] From the same manuscript we again insert the name “David.”] David and Solomon: “In the evening let it fall.”

Concerning the completion of the desolations of Jerusalem—this Moses [Col. 1304B] prophesied by the Spirit [Note: [Col. 1304C] The same manuscript reads: “prophesied by the Spirit concerning Israel.”] of the God of Israel.

**The beginnings of David’s psalms according to the historical account contained in the Book of Kings:**

Psalm 143: against Goliath, when he stood forth;

Psalm 58: when Saul sent men and guarded his house in order to kill him;

Psalm 56: when he fled from Saul’s presence into the cave;

Psalm 33: when he came to Abimelech the priest, changed his appearance before Abimelech the king, and he dismissed him, so that he departed;

Psalm 141: when he fled from Gath and came to the cave of Modollam;

Psalm 51: when Doeg the Idumean came and reported to Saul, saying to him, “David has come to the house of Ahimelech”;

Psalm 72: when he was in the wilderness of Judea;

Psalm 53: when the Ziphites came and said to Saul, “Look, is not David hidden among us?”;

Psalm 55: when the foreigners seized him in Gath;

Psalm 26: after Saul’s death, before he was anointed king;

Psalm 95: when the house was built after the captivity and the Lord’s ark was brought back;

Psalm 28: at the completion of the Tabernacle in which the ark was placed;

Psalm 29: at the dedication of David’s house;

Psalm 59: when Joab had struck Mesopotamia of Syria, Syria of Zobah, and the Valley of Salt—twelve thousand men;

Psalm 50: when the prophet Nathan came to him and he went in to Bathsheba;

Psalm 3: when he fled from the presence of his son Absalom;

Psalm 7: concerning the words of Cush, son of Gemini;

Psalm 142: when his son Absalom pursued him;

Psalm 17: on the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul.

In what sense is he alone truthful and every human being a liar? 690. What does God’s sitting signify? 565. Who is God said to know? 455. He does not know those who perish, 41. With regard to what does he become especially angry? 644. What are anger and fury in God? 636. He swears in order to make us more secure, 690. By the hand of the Mediator, his power and might must be understood, 442. How God is to be imitated, 639. Many seek him and do not find him, 733. Whenever we do anything well, we confess God, 712. Whoever believes in God also believes in his saints, 752. What does it mean to deny God? 712. God’s will must be consulted in every work, 650. He is far from the impious and near to the saints, 580. Which bishop should be chosen? What is required in a bishop? 696 and following. He should be learned and holy in life, 703. His words should be a rule of truth, ibid. What kind of innocence and chastity are required of him? 696, 702. How far does a bishop’s justice differ from that of a layman? 703. He should not be proud but a good steward, 699. He should live from the altar but not become rich, 701. His house should be open to all, ibid. The people are not the bishop’s servants but fellow servants, 699. Presbyters and bishops were appointed by the apostles throughout the provinces, 207. From where and why were they established in the Church? 694. Bishops are greater than presbyters by ecclesiastical custom alone, not, etc., ibid. and 696. They offer unblemished victims daily, 702. In conduct and speech they should surpass all the people, 728. Bishops and presbyters are servants of their servants, 653. Let bishops who have authority to appoint presbyters listen, 694. Bishops and presbyters assume something of the Pharisees’ arrogance, 125. It is their task to pass judgment on the variety of sins, ibid. The arrogance of bishops, 458. Let them learn humility from the Apostle, ibid. Their pride is brought low, 598. Laymen as judges of bishops, 702. Their envy of holy laymen, ibid. Some received bishops back into their rank after blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, 81. Why are fathers prevented from the episcopate because of their children’s vices? 698. Bishops and presbyters who educate their sons in secular literature should read this, 666. See Prelate, Presbyter, Priest.

Paul’s Epistle to the Romans: to whom and why was it written? 478. It contains nothing contrary to the Epistle to the Galatians, ibid. and 479. The Epistle to the Galatians was subscribed by Paul’s hand but written by another, 529. The Epistles to the Galatians and Romans have the same subject matter, 369. Punishments differ among sinners, 60. The punishments of the guilty, 674. — How can the deaf receive the Gospel? 420. — What is syllepsis? 211, 235. — An inevitable syllogism, 81. The solution and consequence of syllogisms, 416. — Christ spoke synecdochically, 83. — Syria is called “lofty” and “sublime,” 397.

T

[Col. 1325]

The founders of the city of Tartessus, 427. It is now called Cartela, ibid. — Tatian, patriarch of the Encratites, 685. He rejects certain Epistles of Paul, ibid. Tatian’s errors and arguments, 526. They are refuted, ibid. His syllogism deceives the hearer by a sophism, ibid. — What the angels who preside over the temple are said to have cried aloud, 401. — What does “buying time” mean? 649. Some do not think that the present is time, but either the past or the future, 691. — The temple of God, the Church: from what it was constructed, 292. — Why are the outer darknesses so called? 45. — It is impossible for the human soul not to be tempted, 220. — What is the great temptation of human beings? 597. — Who is the tempter when he asks questions? 180. — Why John did not describe Christ’s temptation, 254. — No one possesses this earth through meekness, but through pride, 23. — Tertullian, 537. He is praised, 383. He wrote a heretical book on Monogamy, 697.

The God of the New and Old Testament is the same, 594. There is one providence for both, 446. In true visions of the Old and New Testaments, fear is first driven away, 407. The New Scripture preserves the custom of the Old Testament, 377. The history of the Old Testament, 752. Prophets of the New Testament, 615. Those who bark against the Old Testament are refuted, 494, 663. Some reject it, 54. Heretics tearing apart the Old Testament, 686. Which Scriptures of the New Testament do these same people reject? ibid. — What is a false witness? 223. — What history relates about Thaddaeus, 57. He had three names, ibid. — Tarsus, a city of Cilicia, 762. — The city of Thebes: what it was formerly called and by whom it was built, 427. — Theodore, 3. His commentary, 369. — What does Theophilus mean? 249. Theophilus’s commentaries, 3. — Tiberius, Augustus’s stepson, 177. He succeeded to his place, ibid. Christ suffered under him, ibid. The same is noted at 530, 688.

The fear of the perfect, 662. Servile fear does not make people perfect, ibid. The fear of a wife and a slave, 667. Two meanings in the word “fear,” 662. — Titus remained a virgin, 720. Titus receives great praise because Paul had all salute him, 740. — Titus, Vespasian’s son, 528. How great was his goodness? ibid. He is proposed to us as an example, ibid. The greatness of torments is shown, 175. — Apostolic tradition, 203. — One translated by God is secure. Who are called “translated”? 379. — The prudent money-changer, 646. Who is the best? 753.

The mystery of the Holy Trinity, 451, 732. Its eternity, 691. In the Holy Trinity there is one divinity, 130, 244, 563. A distinguished exposition of the Holy Trinity, 611. Eternity is coequal in the Father and the Son, and the nature of both is the same, 551. Equality in both, 609. The operation is the same, 639. The Father and the Son have one nature, 751. The salvation of believers is the mystery of the Trinity, 732. — Tullius, 537. His twofold speech, 416, 417. A saying, 517. See **Cicero**. — The crowd is always changeable, 172. — What is disgrace? 642. — The *Tusculan Disputations* and monstrosities of words, 387. — A question is proposed concerning Tyre, Sidon, and Sodom, 73.

U

Wives are often found to be much better than their husbands, 662.

V

Valentinus, 120, 737, 743. His error and doctrine, 88, 593, 602. What are the ravings of Valentinus? 378. He argues that there are two baptisms, 610. He is refuted, 493. How Valentinus reads the Scriptures, 340. — Marcus Varro is praised, 425. [Col. 1326] He wrote much about the Galatians, ibid. — How and by whom the veil of the Law was removed, 270.

Why the word of God is not perfected in the disciple, 466. What is an idle word? 82. Empty and full words, 644. What words are criminal? 82. How Jerome interpreted a Greek word, 398. The translation of certain words is not approved, 481. — Truth is not found without the grace of the Holy Spirit, 501. Truth was in no one except Jesus alone, 624. Two kinds of truth, or knowledge, are assigned: one according to godliness, the other, etc., 690. Those who speak the truth are not enemies, although, etc., 506. Those who persecute people speaking the truth become enemies of truth, ibid. Obsequiousness wins friends; truth produces hatred, 462. — Vesta has virgin priestesses, 528. — What the tearing of garments by the high priest signifies, 224.

What is fitting for old women, 716 and following. Their conduct should be holy, ibid. In what matters some of them are reproved, ibid. They ought to correct young women privately, not accuse them publicly, ibid. — Victorinus, 3. Victorinus the martyr’s commentaries on Matthew, 249. — What does it mean to see the word of God? 241. — The example of widows: the prophetess Anna, 307.

Jerome taught that wine should be avoided by young women, 651. Its effects, 508, 509. In what sense Jerome condemns it, ibid. It is consecrated into the blood of Christ, ibid. The slavery of wine-drinking, 717. What does one possess who is filled with wine? 650, 651. — What is great violence? 70. — Virbius, 619. — What is related about Virgil? 485. Virgil’s verses, 611. — The reward of virginity, 145. Why it has greater rewards, 761. — The purity of a virgin soul is one thing, and that of a soul subjected to lust another, 524. A virgin who was prostituted against her will remains a virgin, 75.

Love is fitting for a man, fear for a wife, 661. The union of a man with his wife is close and severe, 146. Christ is the power of God, and in what things this is so, 261. The connection of the virtues, 645. The way of the virtues is praised, 461. They are denied through vices, 712. Virtues are understood in two ways, 376. What is the greatest virtue? 653. It is a mark of virtue not to have begun but to have completed, 60. There is implanted in those being born a certain seed of justice and of the other virtues, 391. Each person is named from the virtue that he possesses most strongly, 425. Things intermediate between virtues and vices are neither to be done nor desired, 481. It is not the virtue but the motive for virtue that receives a reward from God, 32. It is one thing to compose books about vices and virtues, another to enter into the meaning of the prophets and apostles, 539. — What are the “inward parts”? 756. — Perpetual vices have no fear of collapse, 210. The Lord accepts the good life of philosophers and Gentiles, 208. — A vice is not shown except by comparison with virtue, 52. Whenever we are overcome by vices, so often we deny God, 712. It is of no benefit to have withdrawn from vices unless the best things are grasped, 461. Vices end and perish in themselves; virtues overflow with fruits, 505. A purse is despised more easily than pleasure, 149. — Freedom of the will to do good is in us, 311. — Although many fat people endure continual vomiting, etc., 114. — The living voice has great power, 467. — Who is difficult to wound? 679.

One kind is near to envy, ibid. — What Zeno, with the Stoics, conjectures concerning God and created things, 611.

**Homily I.** On the prologue of Luke, up to the place where he says: “To write to you, most excellent Theophilus.” Ibid.

**Homily II.** On what is written: “Now both were righteous in the sight of God.” Chapter I, 223.

**Homily III.** On what is written: “An angel of the Lord appeared to him at the right side of the altar of incense.” Chapter I, 225.

**Homily IV.** On what is written: “Do not be afraid, Zechariah,” up to the place where he speaks of John: “He will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah.” Chapter I, 227.

**Homily V.** On why Zechariah became mute, 228.

**Homily VI.** On what is written: “When Elizabeth had conceived, she had hidden herself,” up to the place where he says: “He will be great.” Chapter I, 230.

**Homily VII.** On what is written: “Mary arose and went with haste into the hill country,” up to the place where he says: “Their completion will be,” etc. Chapter I, 232.

**Homily VIII.** On what is written: “My soul magnifies the Lord,” up to: “Those who fear,” etc. Chapter I, 235.

**Homily IX.** On what is written: “She remained with her for three months,” up to the place where he says: “And he spoke, blessing the Lord.” Chapter I, 237.

**Homily X.** On what is written: “Full of the Holy Spirit, he prophesied,” up to the place where he says: “For he will go before the Lord to prepare his ways.” Chapter I, 238.

**Homily XI.** On what is written: “The child grew and was strengthened in spirit,” up to: “This is the enrollment,” etc. Chapters I and II, 240.

**Homily XII.** On how the angel announced the Lord’s birth to the shepherds. Chapter II, 212.

**Homily XIII.** On what is written: “And there was made a multitude of the heavenly host,” up to the place where he says: “They found Mary and Jesus lying in the manger.” Chapter II, 244.

**Homily XIV.** On what is written: “When the days of his circumcision had been fulfilled,” up to the place where he says: “A pair of turtledoves and two young pigeons.” 246.

**Homily XV.** On Simeon, who came in the Spirit to the temple, up to the place where he says: “Now dismiss your servant, Lord, in peace.” Chapter II, 251.

**Homily XVI.** On what is written: “His father and mother were marveling,” etc., up to: “Behold, this one is appointed,” etc. 253.

**Homily XVII.** On what is written: “His father and mother were wondering,” etc., up to the place where Anna is mentioned. Chapter II, 256.

**Homily XVIII.** On what is written: “The child grew,” etc., up to the place where he says: “Did you not know,” etc. Chapter II, 260.

**Homily XIX.** On what is written: “The child grew,” etc., up to the place where he says: “He questions the elders in the temple.” Chapter II, 262.

**Homily XX.** On what is written: “What is the reason that you were seeking me?” up to the words: “Mary kept all these words in her heart.” Chapter II, 264.

**Homily XXI.** On what is written: “In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar,” up to: “Make his paths straight.” Chapter III, 266.

**Homily XXII.** On what is written: “Every valley shall be filled,” up to the words: “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham.” Chapter III, 268.

**Homily XXIII.** On what is written: “Behold, the axe is laid at the root of the trees,” up to: “Tax collectors also came to be baptized by him.” Chapter III, 271.

**Homily XXIV.** On what is written: “I indeed baptize you with water,” up to: “He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire.” Chapter III, 274.

**Homily XXV.** On the suspicion the people had concerning John, whether perhaps he himself was the Christ, 275.

**Homily XXVI.** On what is written: “His winnowing fan is in his hand,” up to: “And he will gather the wheat into the granary.” Chapter III, 278.

**Homily XXVII.** On what is written: “And exhorting many other things he announced,” up to: “The Holy Spirit descended upon him.” Chapter III, 279.

**Homily XXVIII.** On the genealogy of the Savior. The difference between Matthew and Luke. Chapter III, 281.

**Homily XXIX.** On what is written: “Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned”; and on his first temptation. Chapter IV, 283.

**Homily XXX.** The second temptation. Chapter IV, 285.

**Homily XXXI.** On the third temptation, 286.

**Homily XXXII.** On what is written: “Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit,” up to: “And the eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed upon him.” Chapter IV, 288.

**Homily XXXIII.** On what is written: “Surely you will say to me this proverb,” etc., up to: “But none of them was cleansed.” 290.

**Homily XXXIV.** On what is written: “Master, what good thing must I do to possess eternal life?” up to: “Go, and do likewise.” 291.

**Homily XXXV.** On what is written: “When you go with your adversary,” up to: “And you will pay the last penny.” 294.

**Homily XXXVI.** On what is written: “Whoever wishes to lose his soul will lose it,” up to: “The kingdom of God is within you.” 299.

**Homily XXXVII.** On how the colt of a donkey was untied by the disciples, 300.

**Homily XXXVIII.** On what is written: “When he drew near, he saw the city and wept over it,” up to: “He cast out all those selling doves.” 302.

**Homily XXXIX.** On the question the Sadducees proposed to the Lord concerning the woman who had seven husbands; and on the denarius that the Savior ordered to be shown to him, 303.
